Initially created: 2025-12-17T09:26:44.187+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Běnjì No. 1: Wǔdì I
Gāozǔ Wǔhuángdì, personal name Yù,
courtesy name Déyú,
nickname Jìnu,
was a native of Suíyú Lǐ, Péngchéng Xiàn.
He was a descendant of Liú Jiāo, Prince Yuán of Chǔ, younger brother of Hàn Gāodì.
Jiāo begot Hóngyì Hóu Fù.
Fù begot Zōngzhèng Bìqiáng.
Bìqiáng begot Yángchéng Miù Hóu Dé.
Dé begot Yángchéng Jié Hóu Ānmín.
Ānmín begot Yángchéng Xī Hóu Qìngjì.
Qìngjì begot Yángchéng Sù Hóu Cén.
Cén begot Zōngzhèng Píng.
Píng begot the Prefect of Dōngwǔchéng (whose name is unknown).
He begot the Grand Administrator of Dōnglái, Jǐng.
Jǐng begot Míngjīng Qià.
Qià begot Bóshì Hóng.
Hóng begot Lángxié Dūwèi Kuī.
Kuī begot the Grand Administrator of Wèi Dìngxiāng (whose name is unknown).
He begot the Prefect of Xiéchéng, Liàng.
Liàng begot the Grand Administrator of Jìn Běipíng, Yīng.
Yīng begot Xiàngguó Yuàn Xī.
Xī begot the Prefect of Kāifēng, Xùsūn.
Xùsūn begot Hùn,
who was the first to cross the Jiāng [River],
settling in Jīngkǒu Lǐ, Dāntú Xiàn, Jìnlíng Jùn,
and serving as Prefect of Wǔyuán.
Hùn begot the Grand Administrator of Dōng'ān, Jìng.
Jìng begot the Commandery Merit Officer Qiáo,
who was the Imperial Father.
Gāozǔ was born on the night of Rén Yín in the third month of the Xīngníng first year, Guǐ Hài, of Jìn Āidì's reign.
When he grew up,
he was seven *chǐ* and six *cùn* tall,
with extraordinary bearing.
His family was poor,
but he had great ambitions
and did not bother with trivial matters of integrity.
He was known for his filial piety and reverence toward his stepmother.
Initially, he served as Sīmǎ for Guànjūn Sūn Wúzhōng.
In the eleventh month of the third year of Lóng'ān under Āndì,
the rogue Sūn Ēn started a rebellion in Kuàijī.
The Jìn court's Wèi Jiāngjūn Xiè Yǎn and Qián Jiāngjūn Liú Láozhī campaigned in the east.
Láozhī invited Gāozǔ to participate in the army's affairs.
In the twelfth month,
Láozhī arrived in Wú,
but the rebels had formed encampments along the road.
Láozhī ordered Gāozǔ and several tens of men to scout the distance of the rebels.
They encountered the arriving rebels,
numbering several thousand men.
Gāozǔ immediately advanced and engaged them in battle.
Many of his men died,
but his fighting spirit grew fiercer.
Wielding a long saber,
he killed and wounded a great many.
Láozhī's son Jìngxúan, suspecting Gāozǔ had been delayed for too long,
feared he was trapped by the rebels,
and so rode lightly to find him.
Soon after, all the cavalry arrived,
and the rebels fled in retreat.
Over a thousand were slain and captured.
They pushed forward,
pacified Shānyīn,
and Ēn retreated back into the sea.
In the fifth month of the fourth year,
Ēn re-entered Kuàijī
and killed Wèi Jiāngjūn Xiè Yǎn.
In the eleventh month,
Liú Láozhī again led his forces on an eastern campaign,
and Ēn retreated.
Láozhī garrisoned in Shàngyú
and ordered Gāozǔ to defend Jùzhāng Chéng.
Jùzhāng Chéng was low and small,
with fewer than several hundred combatants.
Gāozǔ constantly wore heavy armor and wielded sharp weapons,
leading his soldiers.
In every battle, he broke through the enemy's vanguard and lines,
causing the rebels to retreat to Xiá Kǒu.
At that time, the various commanders in the eastern campaign
exercised no discipline over their armies;
their soldiers plundered violently,
causing great suffering to the common people.
Only Gāozǔ's laws and orders were clear and orderly,
and wherever he went, he was trusted and relied upon.
In the spring of the fifth year,
Sūn Ēn repeatedly attacked Jùzhāng.
Gāozǔ repeatedly defeated him,
and Ēn again fled into the sea.
In the third month,
Ēn went north to Hǎiyán.
Gāozǔ pursued and flanked him,
building a city at the old site of Hǎiyán.
The rebels attacked the city daily,
and the city's military strength was very weak.
Gāozǔ selected several hundred "death-defying" soldiers,
all of whom removed their armor,
wielded short weapons,
and charged out with drums and shouts.
The rebels were shaken with fear and lost morale.
Taking advantage of their fear, they charged them,
and the rebels abandoned their armor and scattered.
Their great commander Yáo Shèng was slain.
Although they won consecutive battles,
the disparity in numbers was too great,
and Gāozǔ alone worried deeply about it.
One night,
he lowered their flags and hid the troops,
appearing as if they had fled.
The next morning, he opened the city gates
and had a few weak and sick people ascend the wall.
The rebels asked from afar where Liú Yù was.
They replied:
"He fled last night."
The rebels believed this
and led their forces in a great assault.
Gāozǔ seized their complacency
and struck furiously,
dealing them a great defeat.
Ēn knew the city could not be taken,
so he advanced toward Hùdú.
Gāozǔ again abandoned the city and pursued him.
Bào Lòu, the Prefect of Hǎiyán, sent his son Sìzhī with a thousand Wú soldiers
and asked to serve as the vanguard.
Gāozǔ said:
"The rebel forces are very strong,
and the Wú people are not accustomed to battle.
If the vanguard suffers a loss,
it will surely defeat our army.
You can stay behind to provide support."
He did not comply.
That night,
Gāozǔ set up many ambushes
and also placed flags and drums,
though no more than a few men were at each location.
The next day,
the rebels led over ten thousand troops to meet them in battle.
As soon as the vanguard engaged,
all the ambushes emerged,
raising flags and beating drums.
The rebels thought there were armies on all sides
and retreated.
Sìzhī pursued the fleeing enemy
and was overwhelmed by the rebels.
Gāozǔ fought and retreated,
but the rebels were strong,
and most of his men were killed or wounded.
Gāozǔ, fearing he would not escape,
reached the location of the ambush and stopped.
He ordered his左右 (attendants) to strip clothes from the dead.
The rebels, thinking he would flee but instead stopped,
suspected there was still an ambush.
Gāozǔ then called out to fight again,
his expression fierce.
The rebels believed him
and withdrew their forces.
Gāozǔ slowly returned,
and then his scattered soldiers gradually reassembled.
In the fifth month,
Sūn Ēn defeated Hùdú
and killed the Internal Administrator of Wú Jùn, Yuán Shānsōng.
Four thousand people died.
That month,
Gāozǔ again defeated the rebels in Lóu Xiàn.
In the sixth month,
Sūn Én, capitalizing on his victory, sailed across the sea
and suddenly arrived at Dāntú.
He had over ten myriad warriors.
Liú Láozhī was still garrisoned at Shānyīn,
and the capital was shaken.
Gāozǔ traveled day and night, at double speed,
arriving at the same time as the rebels.
At this time, the available forces were few,
and furthermore, they were fatigued from the long march,
while the Dāntú garrison had no will to fight.
Sūn Én led several myriad troops,
beating drums and shouting as they ascended Suànshān.
The residents all stood with burdens on their shoulders.
Gāozǔ led his subordinates to charge and attack,
thoroughly defeating them.
Many plunged off cliffs and into the water, dying.
Sūn Én used a "péngpái" (a raft) to carry himself,
barely managing to return to his ship.
Although he had been crushed and broken,
he still relied on his numerous forces
and headed straight for the capital.
His tower ships were tall and large,
and due to the wind, they could not advance.
It took ten days to reach Báishí.
Soon after, he learned that Liú Láozhī had already returned
and the imperial court was prepared,
so he fled towards Yùzhōu.
In the eighth month,
Gāozǔ was appointed as Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn and Xiàpī Tàishǒu,
leading the navy to pursue and attack Sūn Én at Yùzhōu,
where he again thoroughly defeated Sūn Én.
Sūn Én fled south.
In the eleventh month,
Gāozǔ pursued Sūn Én to Hùdú,
and at Hǎiyán,
again defeated him.
In these three battles, he achieved great victories,
capturing and beheading tens of thousands.
From then on, Sūn Én suffered from famine and disease,
with more than half of his forces dying.
He fled from Jiákuǒ to Línghǎi.
In the first month of Yuánxīng first year,
Piàojì Jiāngjūn Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn marched west to attack Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Huán Xuán.
Huán Xuán also led the great armies of Jīngchǔ
to march down and attack Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn.
Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn dispatched Zhènbei Jiāngjūn Liú Láozhī to resist him,
and Gāozǔ participated in his military affairs.
They arrived at Lìzhōu.
When Huán Xuán arrived,
Gāozǔ requested to attack him,
but was refused.
Liú Láozhī intended to send his son Jìngxúan to Huán Xuán to seek peace.
Gāozǔ and Hè Wúji, Liú Láozhī's nephew from Dōnghǎi, both strongly advised against it,
but Liú Láozhī did not listen.
So Jìngxúan was sent to Huán Xuán.
Huán Xuán conquered the capital,
killed Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn,
and appointed Liú Láozhī as Kuàijī Nèishǐ.
Frightened, Liú Láozhī told Gāozǔ,
"If he seizes my troops,
disaster will surely befall me.
Now I must go north to join Gāo Yǎ at Guǎnglíng to raise an army.
Can you come with me?"
Gāozǔ replied,
"General, with several myriad elite soldiers,
you submitted at the mere mention of his name.
He has just gained his ambition
and his prestige shakes the world.
The sentiment of the entire army
has already deserted you.
How can you possibly reach Guǎnglíng?
Yù will return to Jīngkǒu instead."
Liú Láozhī rebelled and fled, then hanged himself.
Hè Wúji said to Gāozǔ,
"Where shall I go?"
Gāozǔ said,
"Zhènbei's flight will surely not escape punishment.
You can follow me back to Jīngkǒu.
If Huán Xuán can truly maintain his integrity and acknowledge the north (the imperial court),
I will serve him with you;
otherwise,
I will plan with you.
Now is precisely the time for Huán Xuán to feign sincerity and calculate his moves,
he will surely employ people like us."
Huán Xuán's cousin, Xiū, was stationed at Dāntú as Fǔjūn,
and appointed Gāozǔ as Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
his military and civil posts remaining as before.
After Sūn Én's defeat and flight,
his followers gradually dispersed.
Fearing capture alive,
he drowned himself in the sea at Línghǎi.
The remaining forces elected Lú Xún, Sūn Én's brother-in-law, as their leader.
Huán Xuán wished to temporarily pacify the eastern regions,
and appointed Lú Xún as Yǒngjiā Tàishǒu.
Although Lú Xún accepted the appointment,
his banditry did not cease.
In the fifth month,
Huán Xuán again dispatched Gāozǔ to campaign in the east.
At that time, Lú Xún entered Dōngyáng from Línghǎi.
In the first month of the second year,
Huán Xuán again dispatched Gāozǔ to defeat Lú Xún in Dōngyáng.
Lú Xún fled to Yǒngjiā, where Gāozǔ again pursued and defeated him,
beheading his chief commander Zhāng Shìdào,
and pursuing him to Jìn'ān.
Lú Xún then sailed south.
In the sixth month,
Gāozǔ was given the additional title of Péngchéng Nèishǐ.
Huán Xuán was made King of Chǔ,
and planned to usurp the throne.
Huán Xuán's cousin, Wèijiāngjūn Qiān, dismissed his attendants and asked Gāozǔ,
"The King of Chǔ's achievements and virtues are immense,
and the four seas gravitate towards him.
The sentiment of the imperial court
is that he should yield (the throne).
What do you think?"
Gāozǔ, already determined to overthrow Huán Xuán,
humbly replied,
"The King of Chǔ
is the son of Xuānwǔ.
His achievements and virtues surpass the age.
The Jìn dynasty is weak,
and the people's hopes have long shifted.
To seize the opportunity and transfer the mandate (of heaven)
– what is there that is not permissible?"
Huán Qiān joyfully said,
"If you say it is permissible,
then it must truly be permissible."
In the twelfth month,
Huán Xuán usurped the imperial throne,
and moved the emperor to Xúnyáng.
Huán Xiū returned to the capital,
and Gāozǔ accompanied him to Jīngyì.
When Huán Xuán saw Gāozǔ,
he said to Sītú Wáng Mì,
"Yesterday I saw Liú Yù.
His demeanor is extraordinary,
truly a hero."
Whenever there were gatherings,
he would always greet him warmly and hospitably,
and bestow generous gifts.
Gāozǔ disliked him even more.
Someone advised Huán Xuán,
"Liú Yù has the bearing of a dragon and the stride of a tiger,
his gaze is extraordinary.
He will probably not remain subordinate to others.
You should deal with him early."
Huán Xuán said,
"I am about to pacify the Central Plains.
No one but Liú Yù can be entrusted with such a great task.
Once Guān and Lǒng are pacified,
then we will discuss it separately."
Huán Xuán then issued an imperial edict stating,
"Liú Yù, with few forces against many,
has repeatedly crushed the demonic vanguard.
Pursuing them across the sea,
he annihilated eight out of ten of them.
Many generals fought valiantly
and sustained severe injuries.
From the marshal down to the officers and soldiers,
all should be rewarded
for their meritorious service."
Earlier, when Gāozǔ campaigned against Lú Xún in the east,
Hè Wúji accompanied him to Shānyīn,
and urged him to raise an army in Kuàijī.
Gāozǔ believed that Huán Xuán had not yet fully seized power,
and Kuàijī was remote,
making success difficult.
He preferred to wait until Huán Xuán's usurpation became undeniable,
then gradually plan his uprising in Jīngkǒu,
certain of success.
By this time, Huán Xiū returned to the capital.
Gāozǔ feigned that an old wound had flared up,
making him unable to follow on foot,
and so returned together with Hè Wúji by boat,
planning the restoration of the dynasty.

At this point, he and his brother Dàoguī, Pèijùn Liú Yì, Píngchāng Mèng Chǎng, Rènchéng Wèi Yǒngzhī, Gāopíng Tán Píngzhī, Lángyá Zhūgě Chángmín, Tàiyuán Wáng Yuándé, Lǒngxī Xīn Hùxīng, and Dōngguǎn Tóng Hòuzhī,
all joined the righteous plot.
At that time, Huán Xiū's brother Hóng was Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
garrisoned at Guǎnglíng.
Dàoguī was Hóng's Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
and Mèng Chǎng was the provincial secretary (zhǔbù).
So Liú Yì was secretly sent to join Mèng Chǎng,
gather followers north of the river,
and plan to raise an army and kill Hóng.
Zhūgě Chángmín, who was Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Diāo Kuí's Zuǒjūn Fǔ Cānjūn,
planned to occupy Lìyáng in response.
Wáng Yuándé and Tóng Hòuzhī planned to gather forces in the capital to attack Huán Xuán,
and they all set a date for a simultaneous uprising.
In the second month of the third year, on the day Jǐchǒu at the new moon,
on Yǐmǎo,
Gāozǔ pretended to go hunting
and, with Hé Wújì and others, gathered righteous volunteers.
All those who were part of the conspiracy were Hé Wújì, Wèi Yǒngzhī, Yǒngzhī's younger brothers Xīnzhī and Shùnzhī, Tán Píngzhī, Píngzhī's cousin Sháo, Sháo's younger brothers Zhī and Lóng, Dàojì,

Dàojì's older cousin Fànzhī, Gāozǔ's younger brother Dàolián, Liú Yì, Yì's cousin Fān, Mèng Chǎng, Chǎng's clan cousin Huáiyù, Xiàng Mí from Hénèi, Guǎn Yìzhī, Zhōu Ānmù from Chénliú, Liú Wèi from Línhuái, his cousin Guīzhī, Zāng Xī from Dōngguǎn,
his cousin Bǎofú, his nephew Mùshēng, Tóng Màozōng, Zhōu Dàomín from Chénjùn, Tián Yǎn from Yúyáng, Fàn Qīng from Qiáoguó, and twenty-seven others.
Over a hundred people wished to follow.
On Bǐngchén,
at dawn,
the city gates opened.
Hé Wújì wore the imperial messenger's attire,
claiming to be delivering an imperial edict, and went in front.
The righteous army charged in,
shouting in unison.
The officials and soldiers were startled and scattered,
none daring to move.
Immediately, Xiū was beheaded and his head displayed to the public.
Gāozǔ wept very bitterly
and gave him a lavish funeral.
Mèng Chǎng advised Hóng to go hunting on that day.
Before dawn, the gates were opened
to let the hunting party out.
Chǎng, Dàoguī, Yì and others led fifty to sixty brave men and entered directly through the open gates.
Hóng was eating porridge
when he was immediately beheaded.
They then gathered the troops and crossed the river.
When the righteous army first captured the capital city,
Xiū's Sīmǎ, Diāo Hóng, led civil and military aides and officials to come.
Gāozǔ ascended the city wall and addressed them, saying:
"Guō Jiāngzhōu has already welcomed the emperor back to Jiānyáng,
and we have all received secret imperial edicts
to eliminate the rebellious faction.
We gather today.
The head of the rebel Xuán
must already be hanging from the great beam.
Are you gentlemen not subjects of Great Jìn?
What do you wish to do by coming now?"
Hóng and the others believed him
and withdrew with their troops.
Once Yì arrived,
Gāozǔ ordered Hóng to be executed.
Yì's elder brother, Mài, was already in the capital.
A few days before the incident,
Gāozǔ sent his fellow conspirator Zhōu Ānmù to inform him
to be an internal confederate.
Though Mài outwardly agreed,
he was inwardly very much terrified.
Ānmù, seeing his panic and fear,
feared the matter would surely be leaked,
and so he galloped back.
At that time, Xuán had appointed Mài as the Administrator of Jìnglín.
Mài, not knowing what to do,
boarded a boat, intending to go to his commandery.
That night,
Xuán wrote to Mài, saying:
"What is the sentiment of the Běifǔ people like?
What did Liú Yù say when you recently saw him?"
Mài thought Xuán already knew of his plot,
so he arose in the morning and reported it to him.
Xuán was surprised and fearful,
and enfeoffed Mài as Marquis of Chóng'ān.
But later, he resented Mài for not apprehending Ānmù,
allowing him to escape,
and so he killed him.
Yuándé, Hù Xìng, Hòuzhī, and others were executed.
Huán Qiān, Biàn Fànzhī, and others were summoned to plan resistance against Gāozǔ.
Qiān and others said:
"Quickly send troops to attack them."
Xuán said:
"No.
Their troops are swift and sharp,
their plans born of facing certain death.
If we send a naval force,
it will not be enough to resist them.
If there is any slip-up,
then their morale will be established, and our cause will be lost.
It is better to mass our troops at Fùzhōushān to await them.
They will have traveled two hundred *lǐ* for nothing,
with nowhere to make a move,
their sharp morale already blunted.
When they arrive,
suddenly seeing a large army,
they will surely be startled and dismayed.
We will hold our troops in a strong formation,
and not engage them in battle.
Unable to seek battle, they will naturally scatter and flee.
This is the best plan."
Qiān and others insisted,
so Wú Fǔzhī, Administrator of Dùnqiu, and Huángfǔ Fū, General of the Right Guard, were sent north to resist the righteous army.
When Xuán first heard that the army had risen,
he was anxious and fearful and could no longer form a plan.
Someone said:
"Liú Yù and the others have very weak forces.
How can they accomplish anything?
Why is Your Majesty so worried?"
Xuán said:
"Liú Yù is indeed a hero of his age;
Liú Yì has no stored grain at home,
yet he gambles a million at a single throw of *chūpú*;
Hé Wújì,
Liú Láozhī's nephew,
closely resembles his uncle.
How can a great undertaking they embark on together fail?"
The crowd nominated Gāozǔ as the alliance leader.
A proclamation was sent to the capital,
saying: "Order and chaos follow each other,
governance is not always stable.
Those who are cunning and unleash tyranny
may happen upon a sagely and enlightened ruler.
Since our Great Jìn,
calamities have repeatedly arisen.
Since Lóng'ān,
troubles have
afflicted the imperial house.
Loyal ministers have been torn apart by tigers,
and upright and good people have been ruined by jackals.
The rebel minister Huán Xuán
oppressed men and spirits,
used his forces in Jīng-Yǐng,
and unleashed violence in the capital.
Heaven
did not destroy the calamity,
and his malevolent power flourished.
Within a year,
he toppled the imperial throne.
The Emperor was exiled,
wandering to an improper place.
The sacred regalia sank into ruin,
and the Seven Ancestral Temples were destroyed and collapsed.
The
calamity suffered by the Xià empress at the hands of Zhuó and Yì,
or that of the Hàn through Wáng Mǎng and Dǒng Zhuó,
compared to Xuán,
is not enough to serve as an analogy.
Since Xuán usurped power,
many years have passed.
Drought has prevailed for a long time,
and the people have no vitality.
Moreover, the gentry and commoners are exhausted by transport,
and civil and military officials are troubled by construction.
Fathers and sons are separated,
families are dispersed.
How can it be only that the Great East suffers
the sorrow of the loom
and the falling plums merely lament a tipped basket?
Looking up at the heavens,
and observing human affairs,
if this can last long,
then what can be destroyed?
All those with a heart
would wring their wrists.
This is why Yù and others beat their chests and wept blood,
having no time to rest.
Therefore,
we have arisen at night and slept at dawn,
supported and encouraged the loyal and valiant,
secretly constructing a difficult path,
more perilous
than treading on a tiger.

Liú Yì, General Who Assists the State, Hé Wújì, General Who Expands Military Might, Mèng Chǎng, Registrar of the Northern General, Wèi Yǒngzhī, Registrar of Yǎnzhōu, Liú Dàoguī, General Who Pacifies the Distant,
Liú Fān, General Who Soars Like a Dragon, Tán Píngzhī, General Who Manifests Awe, and others,
whose loyalty and valor cut through metal,
whose spirit penetrates the bright sun,
bearing spears and rolling up their sleeves,
are determined to give
their lives.
Máo Qú, Inspector of Yìzhōu,
has united with us from a thousand *lǐ* away,
to sweep and pacify Jīng-Chǔ.
Guō Chǎngzhī, Inspector of Jiāngzhōu,
has welcomed the emperor,
establishing the palace at Xúnyáng.
Wáng Yuándé,
Staff Officer to the Northern General, and others
have all led their troops
to hold Shítóu.
Zhūgě Chángmín, General Who Manifests Martial Might,
has gathered righteous gentlemen
and already occupies Lìyáng.
Yǔ Zézhī,
Staff Officer to the General Who Conquers Rebels, and others
have secretly linked up
to act as internal confederates.
With united strength and coordinated plans,
they have risen like bees everywhere.
On that very day, the false Administrator of Xúzhōu, Prince Ānchéng Xiū,
and Hóng, Administrator of Qīngzhōu, were beheaded.
Once the righteous army was gathered,
civil and military officials vied for precedence.
All believed that without a unified command,
the undertaking could not be accomplished.
Yù, unable to refuse,
thus took overall command."
The military's crucial objective.
We rely on the spirits of our ancestors above,
and exhaust the strength of righteous men below,
to cut down the rebellious fugitives,
and cleanse the capital region.
My Lords, the Dukes and Marquises,
some of whom have for generations upheld loyalty and integrity,
and some of whom personally bear titles and favors,
yet all bow their heads to crafty scoundrels,
unable to exert themselves.
Looking around at the state of affairs,
how can we not lament
it!
Today's undertaking
is truly the opportune moment.
Yù, with his humble virtues,
whose talents are not those of the ancients,
finds himself in a position that connects with an already established opportunity,
and accepts a mission in a time of already declining fortunes.
My sincere heart has not yet been declared,
I am filled with emotion and zeal,
gazing at the heavens with lasting thoughts,
and looking at mountains and rivers to increase my resolve.
On the day the declaration was issued,
my spirit sped to the rebels' court.
Mèng Chǎng was made Chief Clerk,
overseeing all logistical matters;
Tán Píngzhī was made Grand Administrator.
Over a thousand common people wished to follow.
On the *wùwǔ* day of the third month,
he encountered Wú Fǔzhī at Jiāngchéng.
Fǔzhī
was Xuán's fierce general,
and his troops were very sharp.
Gāozǔ personally wielded a long saber,
and charged at them with a great shout;
the multitude all crumbled,
and Fǔzhī was immediately slain.
Advancing to Luóluòqiáo,
Huángfǔ Fū led several thousand men to meet them in battle.
The General Pacifying Distances, Tán Píngzhī, and Gāozǔ each commanded a squad;
Píngzhī was defeated in battle and killed,
and his troops dispersed.
Gāozǔ advanced in battle with even greater ferocity,
striking fiercely from front to rear,
shattering them on the spot,
and immediately cut off Fū's head.
Originally, when Gāozǔ and Hé Wújì and others collectively planned their great strategy,
a skilled physiognomist had examined Gāozǔ and Wújì and others, saying they would all become greatly honored,
and that this would happen very soon,
but only said that Píngzhī had no such physiognomy.
Gāozǔ and Wújì secretly said to each other:
"Since we are all in the same boat,
there is no reason for any partial difference.
If all of us become rich and honored,
then Tán should not be uniquely different."
They deeply did not understand the physiognomist's words.
By this point, Píngzhī had died in battle,
and Gāozǔ knew that their enterprise was sure to succeed.
Xuán, hearing that Fū and others had all perished,
became even more afraid.
He sent Huán Qiān to garrison Dōnglíngkǒu,
and Biàn Fànzhī to garrison the west of Fùzhōushān,
their forces totaling twenty thousand.
At dawn on the *jǐwèi* day,
the righteous army finished eating,
abandoned their remaining provisions,
and advanced to the east of Fùzhōushān.
They sent beggars to display banners on the mountain,
to serve as a deceptive force.
Xuán also dispatched the General of Agile Cavalry, Yǔ Yīzhī,
equipped with elite soldiers and sharp weapons,
to assist Qiān and the others.
Gāozǔ personally led the soldiers to charge them;
the generals and soldiers all fought to the death,
everyone matching a hundred,
their shouts shaking heaven and earth.
At that time, the northeast wind was strong,
so he commanded to set fires,
smoke and flames spread across the sky,
and the sound of drums and shouts shook Jīngyì.
Qiān's and the other armies
collapsed instantly.
Although Xuán had initially sent troops to set up formations,
his intention to flee was already decided;
he separately ordered the General Overseeing the Army, Yīn Zhòngwén, to prepare boats at Shítóu,
and then took his sons and nephews to flee south of the river.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
Gāozǔ garrisoned Shítóuchéng,
established temporary government offices,
burned Huán Wēn's spirit tablet outside Xuānyángmén,
made a new spirit tablet for the Jìn dynasty,
and placed it in the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
He sent his generals and commanders to pursue Xuán,
and the Minister of Personnel, Wáng Gǔ, led the officials to welcome the emperor's carriage.
[一０] The Grand Minister, Wáng Mì, and the assembly discussed promoting Gāozǔ to oversee Yángzhōu,
but he firmly declined.
So, Mì was appointed Supervising Minister of Personnel,
and Governor of Yángzhōu.

Thereupon, Gāozǔ was promoted to Commissioner with Staff, Grand Director of Military Affairs of Yáng, Xú, Yǎn, Yù, Qīng, Jì, Yōu, and Bìng eight provinces, General Overseeing the Army, and Governor of Xúzhōu.
[一一]
Previously, the imperial court had suffered from the chaotic governance of the Jìn clan,
and all officials were lax and undisciplined.
Although Huán Xuán wished to rectify and regulate,
the populace did not follow him.
Gāozǔ set an example by his own conduct,
first establishing authority and prohibitions internally and externally;
all officials respectfully performed their duties,
and within two or three days,
customs were completely reformed.
Moreover, although Huán Xuán was respected for his heroic and powerful nature,
he attained the highest position in a single morning.
The Jìn clan's regional governors and ministers in court
served him wholeheartedly,
and the division between lord and subject was settled.
Gāozǔ's position in court was minor,
and he had not a single troop.
He raised his arms from the midst of the common people,
advocating a great cause to restore the imperial throne.
Because of this, Wáng Mì and the others, who had at times lost popular support,
[一二] all felt ashamed and apprehensive.
Zhūgě Chángmín missed his timing and could not set out;
Diāo Kuí arrested and sent him,
but before he arrived, Xuán was defeated.
Xuán passed through Xúnyáng,
and the Governor of Jiāngzhōu, Guō Chǎngzhī, provided him with imperial carriages and ritual objects.
Xuán gathered about two thousand men,
and fled with the Son of Heaven to Jiānglíng.
The General of Agile Cavalry, Liú Yì; General Assisting the State, Hé Wújì; and General Manifesting Martial Might, Liú Dàoguī, led their armies to pursue and attack.
The Senior Minister and Left Assistant Director, Wáng Yú, and his son, the Governor of Jīngzhōu, Suí, and others,
were the leading aristocratic families of the eastern part of the Yangtze River.
Suí had a great reputation in his youth,
but because Gāozǔ rose from commoner status,
he greatly disdained him.
Suí,
being Huán's nephew,
also harbored self-doubt.
Gāozǔ had them all executed.
In the fourth month,
Prince Wǔlíng, Zūn, was appointed Grand General,
acting according to imperial authority.
A general amnesty was declared throughout the empire,
except for Huán Xuán's immediate family.
Initially, Gāozǔ was poor,
and once owed Diāo Kuí thirty thousand *qián* in community funds,
and for a long time could not repay it.
Kuí's arrest and detention was very strict.
Wáng Mì went to see Kuí,
and secretly paid the debt on his behalf,
thus he was released.
Gāozǔ's reputation was minor and his position low;
all the prominent figures did not associate with him,
only Mì did.
When Huán Xuán was about to usurp the throne,
Mì personally removed Emperor Ān's imperial seal and ribbons,
serving as a meritorious official assisting Xuán in his usurpation.
When the righteous banner was raised,
everyone thought Mì should be executed,
but only Gāozǔ protected him.
Liú Yì once, during a court assembly,
asked Mì about the whereabouts of the imperial seal and ribbons,
which made Mì even more afraid.
When Wáng Yú and his son were executed,
Mì's cousin, Chén, said to Mì:
"Wáng Jū was innocent,
yet the righteous army executed him.
This is to eliminate those superior to oneself,
and to cut off popular support.
Since you were a partisan of the Huán clan,
and your status and position are as such,
how can you hope to escape?"
Jū
was Yú's childhood name.
Mì was afraid,
and fled to Qǔ'ā.
Gāozǔ submitted a memorial to the Grand General,
strongly protecting and vouching for Mì,
and had him welcomed back to his position.
The Minister of Imperial Clan Affairs, Biàn Chéngzhī; [一三] the Left General of the Palace Guard, Chǔ Càn; and the General of Roaming Cavalry, Sīmǎ Xiù, employed officials for personal service.
This was investigated and exposed by the Censor-in-Chief, Wáng Zhēnzhī.
Chéngzhī sent a memorial expressing resentment and indignation.
Chéngzhī went to the Director of Personnel to hide.
Gāozǔ submitted a memorial to the Grand General,
stating
"Càn and others hold ministerial positions,
and must have their full thoughts expressed.
If the enforcement of the law is not agreeable,
they should naturally present their case based on reason,
instead of arbitrarily harboring resentment and indignation,
and blaming the relevant authorities.
They should be duly disciplined,
to purify moral conduct."
All were dismissed from office.
Huán Xīn,
〔一四〕the son of Huán Xuán’s brother, gathered a multitude and headed towards Lìyáng.
Gāozǔ ordered Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Zhūgě Chángmín to attack and repulse him.
Wú Jì and Dào Guī defeated Huán Xuán’s grand general Guō Quán and others at Sāngluò Zhōu.
〔一五〕The combined armies advanced and occupied Xúnyáng.
Gāozǔ was additionally appointed Dūdū Jiāngzhōu Zhū Jūnshì.
After Huán Xuán returned to Jīngyǐng,
he greatly gathered troops,
summoned his navy to build楼船 (lóuchuán, “tower ships”) and weapons,
and led a force of twenty thousand.
He coerced the Son of Heaven and departed from Jiānglíng,
sailing down the Jiāng River.
He encountered Guànjūn Jiāngjūn Liú Yì and others at Zhēngróng Zhōu.
The combined armies attacked,
and greatly defeated him.
〔一六〕Huán Xuán abandoned his forces,
and again coerced the Son of Heaven back to Jiānglíng.
Huán Xuán’s partisan, Yīn Zhòngwén, escorted the two empresses of Jìn back to the capital.
Huán Xuán reached Jiānglíng,
and then fled west.
Nánjùn Tàishǒu Wáng Téngzhī and Jīngzhōu Biéjià Wáng Kāngchǎn escorted the Son of Heaven into the Nánjùn mansion.
Previously, Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Máo Qú
had sent his grand-nephew Yòuzhī and Cānjūn Fèi Tián to escort his younger brother’s coffin downriver,
with a force of two hundred.
Máo Qú’s nephew, Xiūzhī, was at the time Huán Xuán’s Túqí Xiàowèi.
〔一七〕He lured Huán Xuán to enter Shǔ.
Upon reaching Méihuí Zhōu,
Fèi Tián and Yòuzhī ambushed and shot him.
Yìzhōu Dūhù Féng Qiān decapitated Huán Xuán,
and sent his head to the capital.
Huán Xuán’s son, Shēng, was also beheaded in the Jiānglíng marketplace.
When Huán Xuán was first defeated at Zhēngróng Zhōu,
the righteous army believed the great task was accomplished,
and their pursuit was not swift.
Huán Xuán had been dead for nearly ten days,
yet the combined armies still had not arrived.
Huán Zhèn, Huán Xuán’s grand-nephew, fled to Yǒng Zhōng in Huáróng,
〔一八〕and gathered several thousand rebels.
They launched a dawn raid on Jiānglíng city,
and the residents rushed out to join them.
Wáng Téngzhī and Wáng Kāngchǎn were both killed.
Huán Qiān, who had previously hidden in Jǔ Chuān,
also gathered forces to respond.
Huán Zhèn mourned for Huán Xuán,
and set up a mourning hall.
Huán Qiān led his officials to present the imperial seals and ribbons to Ān Dì.
When Wú Jì and Dào Guī arrived at Jiānglíng,
they battled Huán Zhèn at Língxī.
Huán Xuán’s partisan, Féng Gāi, also set up an ambush at Yánglín,
and the righteous army was routed,
retreating back to Xúnyáng.
Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Xīn Yú harbored disloyalty.
At this time, Běiqīngzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Gāi rebelled.
Xīn Yú requested to campaign against Liú Gāi,
and upon reaching Huáiīn,
he too rebelled.
Xīn Yú’s Chángshǐ, Yáng Mùzhī, beheaded Xīn Yú,
and sent his head to the capital.
In the tenth month,
Gāozǔ assumed the title of Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
One hundred armored guards entered the palace hall.
Liú Yì’s armies again advanced to Xiàkǒu.
Liú Yì attacked Lǔchéng,
and Dào Guī attacked Yǎnyuè Lěi;
both were captured.
In the twelfth month,
the combined armies advanced and pacified Bālíng.
In the first month of Yìxī first year,
Liú Yì and others reached Jiāngjīn,
defeated Huán Qiān and Huán Zhèn,
Jiānglíng was pacified,
and the Son of Heaven returned to his rightful place.
In the third month,
the Son of Heaven arrived from Jiānglíng.
An imperial edict stated: “Of old, it is said that the greatest are Heaven and Earth,
followed by ruler and minister.
Thus, they are arrayed like the Three Luminaries,
with divine and human succession in order.
The principle truly originates from the primordial chaos,
and its cycle spans ten thousand
generations.
Hence, waxing and waning occur seasonally,
the Four Spirits convey their changes,
and when the kingly way is obscured,
loyal and virtuous individuals rescue it from peril.
This is why Heaven’s mandate is eternally secure,
and why human hearts are peaceful.
Though the Xià and Zhōu dynasties faltered in their middle period,
they relied on the achievements of Mǐ and Shēn.
Though Wáng Mǎng and Dǒng Lún usurped in succession,
it was indeed these two generations that upheld [the dynasty].
Some rode on their resources and titles,
while others established their legacy in a different era.
Yet, the Odes
and Documents praised them,
and historical records made them fine tales.
But there has never been one who, relying on his heart and soothing the people,
whose sincerity brought forth a fitting response,
and who retrieved the divine artifacts from their utter ruin
like the glorious one of today.
I, being ignorant,
suffered misfortune in my family,
and since encountering distress,
have faced extreme hardship.
The rebellious minister, Huán Xuán,
exploited the situation and unleashed his wickedness,
committing heinous crimes and tyranny,
his wickedness reaching to the heavens
and disrupting China.
He then deceived gods and men,
and unleashed his usurpation and rebellion.
The foundation of our ancestors was buried,
the sacrifices to the seven ancestral temples were all extinguished.
To fall into an abyss
would not be sufficient to compare with this.
The imperial rule of Jìn,
by Heaven’s grace, produced an outstanding and brilliant man,
the Holder of the Imperial Seal, Grand Military Governor of the armies of Yáng, Xú, Yǎn, Yù, Qīng, Jì, Yōu, Bìng, and Jiāng nine provinces, Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn,
and Governor of Xú and Qīng two provinces.
His loyalty shines like Heaven,
his divine might destined for his age.
Thus, he was able to uphold virtue and forge a covenant,
and righteous men responded in unison.
Therefore, with one shout of righteousness,
the two oceans rolled
back their waves,
and with his heroic wind sweeping the path,
the imperial residence was cleansed of shadows.
Along with Guànjūn Jiāngjūn Yì, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Wú Jì, and Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn Dào Guī,
their ships and banners swiftly advanced,
and
the head of the arch-villain was delivered.
Turning their spears and repeatedly striking,
Jīng and Hàn were cleared of mist.
This allowed the destiny of Xuān and Yuán
to be eternally secured at Sōng and Dài,
the overturned foundation rebuilt,
and gathered again upon
My person.
The ancestral temples received the blessings of seven hundred years,
and the imperial foundation embraced a new mandate.
Considering these merits and virtues,
I will forever engrave them in My heart.
Truly, his Way surpasses the beginning of creation,
unparalleled
throughout all ages.
Since the invention of writing,
it has never been heard of before.
Although his achievements are so high that none can surpass them,
and the principle is too profound to articulate,
yet honoring virtue and bestowing titles
is what wise kings prioritize,
in order to propagate the Way and govern,
deeply concerning rise and fall.
Therefore, Yī and Wàng received extraordinary mandates,
and Huán and Wén enjoyed the full rites of honor.
How much more so for one whose grand achievements are unparalleled in his age,
and who looks down
upon a hundred generations!
He should be granted the highest honors and titles,
to glorify the greatness of the state.
However, Zhèn Jūn is modest and humble within himself,
and his sincere requests have been repeatedly expressed.
My reluctance to oppose My paternal uncle,
is precisely
how His virtue is further glorified.
Let Zhèn Jūn be promoted to Shìzhōng, Chēqí Jiāngjūn, Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūnshì,
with the titles of Shǐchíjié and Governor of Xú and Qīng two provinces
as before.
May he establish a grand state and open up new territories.”
Gāozǔ firmly declined.
He was then additionally appointed Lù Shàngshūshì,
but he again refused to accept,
repeatedly requesting to return to his fief.
The Son of Heaven did not permit it,
and sent all the officials to earnestly persuade him,
and even personally visited his residence.
Gāozǔ, fearful, went to the imperial court to state his plea,
and the Son of Heaven could not force him.
In that month,
he returned to garrison Dāntú.
The Son of Heaven again sent a grand envoy to earnestly persuade him,
but he still refused to accept.
Thereupon, he was re-appointed Dūdū of Jīng, Sī, Liáng, Yì, Níng, Yōng, and Liáng seven provinces,
in addition to the previous sixteen provinces,
with his original office unchanged.
Thereupon, he accepted the order to relinquish Qīngzhōu,
and was additionally appointed Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
Lú Xún sailed by sea and conquered Guǎngzhōu,
capturing Cìshǐ Wú Yǐnzhī.
Immediately, Lú Xún was appointed Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and his associate Xú Dàofù was appointed Shǐxīng Xiāng.
In the third month of the second year [of Yìxī (義熙)],
he was appointed Supervisor of Jiāo and Guǎng prefectures.
In the tenth month,
Gāozǔ memorialized, saying:
"Formerly, Heaven brought misfortune upon the imperial house,
and the great villain usurped the throne.
Your subjects, adhering to our former allegiance,
having previously received the nation's grace,
look up to the symbol of loyalty and obedience,
and humble ourselves with the indignation of subjects.
Although it was the spiritual power of the altars of soil and grain,
it was also through the combined efforts of many that the matter was accomplished.
Those loyal and diligent assistants who lent their support,
and the civil and military officials who exerted their full strength,
expressed their humility by claiming that the achievements were their own,
thus diminishing the grandeur of the state.
I took it upon myself to lead the various armies first,
〔一九〕and conspired together to raise the standard of righteousness,
first pacifying the two cities of Jīngkǒu and Guǎnglíng.
I, your subject, and Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn Yì (撫軍將軍毅) and 272 others,
together with 1,566 others who later joined the righteous cause, departing from the capital and fighting great battles along the way,
and also Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Zhǎngmín (輔國將軍長民) and the late Gěishìzhōng Wáng Yuándé (給事中王元德) and ten others,
totaling 1,848 people,
beg to be justly enfeoffed and rewarded.
As for the armies in the western campaign,
their contributions will be discussed and memorialized later."
Thereupon, the Shàngshū (尚書) memorialized to enfeoff and reward the chief strategist who initiated the righteous cause, Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn Yù (鎮軍將軍裕), as the Duke of Yùzhāng Commandery,
with a stipend of ten thousand households,
and bestowed upon him 30,000 bolts of silk.
The rest of the enfeoffments and rewards varied according to rank.
The officials and clerks of the Zhèn Jūn Fǔ (鎮軍府)
were ranked one grade lower than those of the late Tàifù Xiè Ān Fǔ (太傅謝安府).
In the eleventh month,
the Son of Heaven reiterated the previous decree,
adding Shìzhōng (侍中) to Gāozǔ's titles,
and promoting him to Chēqí Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
He firmly declined.
An imperial edict ordered all officials to earnestly persuade him.
In the second month of the third year,
Gāozǔ returned to the capital,
intending to go to the Tíngwèi (廷尉).
The Son of Heaven had already decreed that the prison officials should not receive him.
He went to the palace gate to present his refusal,
and it was then accepted.
He then returned to Dāntú.
In the intercalary month,
the prefectural general Luò Bīng (駱冰) conspired to cause a rebellion.
As he was about to be apprehended,
he fled alone on horseback,
but was pursued and beheaded.
Bīng's father, the Grand Administrator of Yǒngjiā, Qiú (球), was executed.
Qiú was originally a clerk in Dōngyáng Commandery.
During the rebellion of Sūn Ēn (孫恩),
he raised a righteous army in Chángshān,
which is why he was promoted and employed.
When Huán Xuán (桓玄) was first defeated,
because Huán Chōng (桓衝) was loyal and upright,
his grandson Yìn (胤) was appointed.
At this time, Bīng conspired to make Yìn his leader,
and secretly colluded with Yīn Zhòngwén (殷仲文), the Grand Administrator of Dōngyáng.
Thereupon, Zhòngwén and his two younger brothers were executed.
All remaining partisans of Huán Xuán
were exterminated at this point.
The Son of Heaven sent Kēm Tàicháng Gě Jí (兼太常葛籍) to confer a decree upon the Duke, saying:
"Yǒuhù (有扈) brought disaster,
and Yí Yì (夷羿) took advantage of the opportunity.
They disrupted order and violated principles,
truly shaking the imperial foundation.
The rebel minister Huán Xuán,
presuming on favor, acted rebelliously,
dismantling the splendor of Huá and Huò (華、霍),
uprooting Sōng and Dài (嵩、岱).
With the five sacred mountains leveled,
the six regions changed their places.
The Duke, a peerless hero of his age,
concealed his talent, awaiting the opportune moment.
Inspired by his innate reverence,
he swore to avenge the national disgrace,
indignant at the decline,
his sincerity manifesting in sleepless nights.
After years passed,
the divine artifacts of state had been long absent.
His loyalty and filial piety, though hidden,
truly pierced the three realms.
Then, seizing the opportune moment,
he announced his pledge and initiated his plan,
appealing to the azure heaven for justice,
and deploying his righteous army in a single charge.
With a few hundred vanguard troops,
their might was as fierce as flashing lightning.
Millions could not withstand their advance;
they directly established control over the roads and cities.
〔二０〕Thus, they caused the charging whales to scatter,
and their violent scales to be thrown into the Jiāng and Hàn (江、漢) rivers.
The victory extended far and wide,
the heavy miasma was cleared away,
the two luminaries were purified,
and the three lights shone again.
The enterprise will endure for eternity,
his achievements surpass the creation of the world,
and his subtle principles and reputation
have moved Our heart.
If one who achieves righteousness for himself
is still bound by his rank,
how much more so one whose sincerity and virtue are profound,
and whose merits surpass those of heaven and man?
Therefore, We establish this state,
to eternally sustain the mountains and rivers.
Recalling these matters, We feel
that words are insufficient to repay him.
Go forth and be reverent!
Assist Us, the One Man,
to long support the imperial Jìn (晉) dynasty,
that your lasting influence and legacy may be
resplendent and boundless.
Receive this auspicious decree,
and respond to Our command."
In the twelfth month,
Sītú (司徒), Lù Shàngshū (錄尚書), and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (揚州刺史) Wáng Mì (王謐) died.
In the first month of the fourth year,
the Duke was summoned to assist in governance.
He was appointed Shìzhōng (侍中), Chēqí Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (揚州刺史), and Lù Shàngshū (錄尚書),
while retaining his positions as Xú and Yǎn prefectures' Cìshǐ (刺史).
He memorialized to resign from Yǎn prefecture.
Previously, Guānjūn (冠軍) Liú Jìngxūan (劉敬宣) had been sent to attack the Shǔ (蜀) rebel Qiáo Zòng (譙縱),
but returned without success.
In the ninth month,
because Jìngxūan had suffered a defeat and retreated,
he offered to resign his position,
but it was not permitted.
Instead, he was demoted to Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn (中軍將軍),
but retained his Kāifǔ (開府) status.
Initially, the false Yàn (燕) King, the Xiānbēi Mùróng Dé (慕容德), usurped the title in Qīngzhōu.
When Dé died,
his nephew Chāo (超) succeeded him.
They frequently caused border troubles.
In the second month of the fifth year,
they plundered extensively north of the Huái River,
capturing the Grand Administrator of Yángpíng (陽平), Liú Qiānzài (劉千載), and the Grand Administrator of Jǐnán (濟南), Zhào Yuán (趙元),
and driving away over a thousand households.
In the third month,
the Duke sent a memorial to campaign north,
appointing Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹) Mèng Chǎng (孟昶) to supervise the affairs of the Zhōngjūn Liúfǔ (中軍留府).
In the fourth month,
the naval forces departed from the capital,
sailing up the Huái River into the Sì River.
In the fifth month,
they reached Xiàpī,
where they left their ships, vessels, and heavy baggage,
and the infantry advanced to Lángyá.
They built cities and left garrisons everywhere they passed.
The Xiānbēi garrisons at Liángfù (梁父) and Jǔchéng (莒城) both fled.
Mùróng Chāo (慕容超) heard that the imperial army was approaching.
His great general Gōngsūn Wǔlóu (公孫五樓) advised Chāo:
"It would be wise to secure Dàxiàn (大峴),
cut down the grain sprouts,
and strengthen fortifications and clear the countryside to await them.
Their foreign army will lack provisions,
and will be unable to engage in battle.
Within a month,
we can beat them with mere sticks."
Chāo disagreed,
saying:
"They have traveled far and are weary;
their strength cannot last long.
We should simply let them pass Dàxiàn,
and then I will crush them with my iron cavalry.
There is no worry that we won't defeat them.
Why should we preemptively cut down our crops
and weaken ourselves?"
When the Duke was about to set out,
some argued that when the enemy heard that the large army was marching far out,
they would certainly not dare to fight.
If they did not block Dàxiàn,
they would surely hold Guǎnggù (廣固) firmly,
cut down crops and clear the countryside,
to cut off supplies for the three armies.
Not only would it be difficult to achieve success,
but they might not even be able to return.
The Duke said:
"I understand them well.
The Xiānbēi are greedy
〔二一〕and do not plan far ahead.
They prioritize immediate gains from plunder
and regret losing their grain sprouts.
They believe that my isolated army, having marched far,
cannot last long,
and will do no more than advance to occupy Línqú (臨朐)
and retreat to defend Guǎnggù (廣固).
Once I enter Dàxiàn,
no one will have thoughts of retreat.
Driving a force determined to die
against a foe with divided loyalties,
why would we worry about not winning?
They will not be able to clear the countryside and hold firm;
I guarantee this to you all."
Once the Duke entered Dàxiàn,
he raised his hand to the sky and said:
"My mission is accomplished!"
In the sixth month,
Mùróng Chāo sent Wǔlóu and Guǎngníng Wáng Hèlài Lú to first seize Línqú City.
Upon hearing that the main army had arrived,
he left the weak and old to guard Guǎnggù,
and then led out all his forces.
In Qú there was the Jùmiè River,
forty *lǐ* from the city.
Chāo told Wǔlóu:
“Hurry and secure it.
If the Jìn army gets the water,
it will be difficult to attack them.”
Wǔlóu galloped forward.
Dragoon General Mèng Lóngfú led the cavalry at the front,
rushing to contend for it,
and Wǔlóu retreated.
The main army advanced on foot,
with four thousand chariots.
They divided the chariots into two wings,
advancing slowly abreast,
all chariots unfurling their awnings,
the drivers holding spears.
Light cavalry were also used as a mobile force.
The military discipline was strict,
and the ranks were orderly.
Before reaching Línqú by several *lǐ*,
the enemy’s iron cavalry, over ten thousand strong,
arrived from front and rear.

The Duke ordered Yǎnzhōu Inspector Liú Fān, his younger brother Bìngzhōu Inspector Dào Lín, Adviser-cum-Army-Supervisor Liú Jìngxuān, Táo Yánshòu, Army Supervisors Liú Huáiyù, Shèn Zhòngdào, Suǒ Miǎo and others
to attack them with combined effort.
As the sun was setting,
the Duke sent Adviser-cum-Army-Supervisor Tán Sháo directly towards Línqú.
Zhào led General of Establishing Might Xiàng Mí and Army Supervisor Hú Fān to rush there,
and that same day they captured the city,
cut down its *yáqí*,
and seized all of Chāo’s baggage train.
When Chāo heard that Línqú had been taken,
he led his troops and fled.
The Duke personally beat the drums,
and the enemy routed completely.
Chāo escaped back to Guǎnggù.
They captured Chāo’s horses, imitation imperial carriage, jade seal, leopard-tail standard, and so on,
and sent them to the capital.
They executed his grand general Duàn Huī and over ten others,
while thousands of others were killed or captured.
The next day,
the main army advanced on Guǎnggù,
immediately breaching the outer city.
Chāo retreated to defend the inner city.
Thereupon, a long siege was set up,
the rampart being three *zhàng* high,
with three layers of trenches dug outside.
The transport of supplies from the Jiāng and Huái rivers was halted,
and grain was provisioned from the Qí region.
He placated and embraced those who surrendered,
and both Chinese and non-Chinese rejoiced.
Talented individuals were promoted and granted titles,
and then appointed to positions.
In the seventh month,
an imperial edict added the Duke to the posts of Inspectors of Běiqīng and Jì prefectures.
Chāo’s grand general Yuán Zūn and his younger brother Miáo both led their troops to surrender.
As the Duke was preparing siege equipment,
people on the city wall said:
“If you don't get Zhāng Gāng,
what can you do?”
Gāng was
Chāo’s imitation Minister-Secretary,
a man of ingenious skill.
It happened that Chāo had sent Gāng to proclaim himself a vassal to Yáo Xīng,
begging for troops and requesting aid.
Xīng falsely agreed,
but in reality feared the Duke
and dared not send aid.
When Gāng returned from Cháng'ān,
Taìshān Prefect Shēn Xuān seized and delivered him.
When Gāng was brought up to a siege tower
all in the city turned pale.
Thereupon, Gāng was made to greatly improve the siege equipment.
Chāo failed to obtain rescue,
and Gāng was captured instead,
making him increasingly worried and fearful.
He then requested to proclaim himself a vassal,
asking to cede Dàxiàn as a border
and offering a thousand horses.
This was not accepted,
and the siege became more urgent.
Residents from north of the Yellow River, carrying spears and provisions, arriving daily,
numbered in the thousands.
The Record-keeping Army Supervisor Liú Mùzhī
possessed strategic talent and ability.
The Duke considered him his chief strategist,
consulting him on every action and decision.
At this time, Yáo Xīng sent an envoy to inform the Duke, saying:
“Mùróng Jiàn has a good relationship with us,
and moreover, has urgently appealed to us in his distress.
Now we will dispatch one hundred thousand iron cavalry
to directly occupy Luòyáng.
If the Jìn army does not retreat,
we will then dispatch our iron cavalry to advance unhindered.”
The Duke called Xīng’s envoy and replied:
“Tell your Yáo Xīng,
after I pacify Yān,
I will rest my arms for three years,
then I will pacify Guān and Luò.
If he can deliver himself now,
he can come quickly.”
Mùzhī, hearing of the Qiāng envoy,
rushed in,
but the Duke had already dispatched him.
He then fully related Xīng’s words and his own reply
to Mùzhī.
Mùzhī reprimanded the Duke, saying:
“Normally, no matter how small or large the matter,
you always grant me consultation.
This matter should have been carefully considered,
why did you answer so abruptly?
Your reply to Xīng’s words
cannot intimidate the enemy;
it will only provoke them.
If Yān cannot be taken,
and the Qiāng rescue suddenly arrives,
how will you contend with them?”
The Duke smiled and said:
“This is a military secret,
not something you understand,
which is why I didn’t tell you.
Speed is paramount in war.
If they could truly send aid,
they would surely fear me knowing,
how could they first send a messenger?
This is them seeing me attack Yān,
and having fear within,
these are just words to exaggerate themselves.”
In the ninth month,
the Duke was promoted to Grand Commandant and Director of the Central Secretariat,
but he firmly declined.
The imitation Xúzhōu Inspector Duàn Hóng had previously defected to the barbarians of the north.
In the tenth month,
he returned from north of the Yellow River to surrender.
Zhāng Gāng completed the siege equipment,
designing various ingenious devices,
such as flying towers and wooden mantlets,
all were fully prepared.
Fire stones, arrows, and bows on the city walls
were rendered useless.
In the second month, *dìnghài* day, of the sixth year
Guǎnggù was breached.
Chāo fled by scaling the wall.
The General who Subdues Barbarians, Captain Qí Zhāo Xū, captured him.
He killed his princes and dukes and below,
and two thousand horses.
Chāo was sent to the capital,
and executed in Jiànkāng market.
When the Duke marched north,
Xú Dàofù still harbored ambitions of encroaching,
and urged Lú Xún to exploit the emptiness and emerge.
Xún did not comply.
Dàofù then went to Pānyú and persuaded Xún, saying:
“Our original residence south of the mountains,
was it because we reached an impasse there?
It was precisely because Duke Liú was difficult to contend with.
Now he is stalled with his troops before a strong city,
With this thought, if we send brave soldiers
to ambush people like Hé and Liú,
it would be as easy as turning over one's hand.
If we do not seize this opportunity and only ensure a day's peace,
after he pacifies Qí,
he will rest his arms and gather his forces for no more than one or two years,
and then he will surely send an imperial edict to summon you.
If Duke Liú personally leads his troops to Yùzhāng,
and sends his elite forces over the mountains,
even if you, General, are divinely mighty,
I fear you will certainly
be unable to resist him.
Today's opportunity
must not be missed at any cost.
Once we conquer the capital,
overturning its foundation,
even if Duke Liú returns,
he will be powerless.”
Xún followed his advice,
and then led his troops over the mountains.
That month,
he attacked Nánkāng, Lúlíng, and Yùzhāng.
All the prefects of these commanderies abandoned their posts and fled.
At that time, news of the pacification of Qí had not yet arrived,
so a messenger was swiftly dispatched to summon the Duke.
When the Duke first conquered Qí,
he intended to station his forces in Xiàpī
and clear the Héf and Luò regions,
but then the summoning messenger arrived,
and he immediately ordered the army to return.
Zhènnán Jiāngjūn Hé Wújì 何無忌 fought against Xú Dàofù 徐道覆 in Yùzhāng 豫章,
suffered a defeat,
and Wújì 無忌 was killed.
There was shock both inside and outside the court.
The imperial court wished to escort the emperor north to join Gōng 公 (Liu Yu),
but soon learned that the rebels had not yet arrived,
and people's spirits somewhat calmed.
When Gōng 公 reached Xiàpī 下邳,
he transported heavy equipment by boat,
and personally led his elite troops on foot.
Upon reaching Shānyáng 山陽,
he heard that Wújì 無忌 had been killed,
and feared that the capital might fall.
So, he rolled up his armor and marched day and night,
arriving at the Huái 淮 River with several dozen men,
where he questioned travelers about the court's news.
People said:
"The rebels have not yet arrived.
If Liú Gōng 劉公 returns,
there will be nothing to worry about."
Gōng 公 was greatly pleased,
crossed the river in a single boat,
and went straight to Jīngkǒu 京口.
The people then felt greatly relieved.
On the guǐwèi 癸未 day of the fourth month,
Gōng 公 arrived at the capital,
lifted the state of emergency, and rested his troops.
Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn Liú Yì 劉毅 submitted a memorial requesting to campaign south.
Gōng 公 wrote a letter to Yì 劉毅 saying:
"I am accustomed to fighting the demonic rebels
and understand their changing tactics.
Having just gained an illicit advantage,
their sharp edge should not be taken lightly.
It is advisable to wait until preparations are complete,
and then we can launch the campaign together, my brother."
He also sent Yì's 劉毅's cousin Fān 藩 to stop him.
Yì 劉毅 did not comply,
and with a fleet of twenty thousand soldiers,
he departed from Gūshú 姑孰.
When Xún 循 (Lu Xun) first descended south,
he sent Dàofù 道覆 (Xu Daofu) towards Xúnyáng 尋陽,
while he himself attacked the various commanderies in Xiāngzhōng 湘中.
Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Dàoguī 荊州刺史道規 sent troops to Chángshā 長沙,
but they were defeated by Xún 循.
Xún 循 then went straight to Bālíng 巴陵,
intending to advance towards Jiānglíng 江陵.
When Dàofù 道覆 heard that Yì 劉毅 was coming up,
he sent a swift messenger to report to Xún 循, saying:
"Yì's 劉毅's army is very strong.
Success or failure depends on this.
We should combine our forces to crush them.
If we achieve victory here,
there will be no more trouble in the world.
Once the foundation is secure,
we need not worry about the top not being peaceful."
Xún 循 immediately departed Bālíng 巴陵 that day,
and joined forces with Dàofù 道覆 to advance downriver.
They also had eight large ships, nine in number,
with four decks,
twelve zhàng 丈 (around 36 meters) high.
Gōng 公, seeing that the southern provinces were overrun,
memorialized to return his official seal and ribbon,
but an imperial edict did not permit it.
In the fifth month,
Liú Yì 劉毅 suffered a defeat at Sāngluòzhōu 桑落洲,
abandoned his ships, and fled on foot.
The remaining troops who could not escape
were all captured by the rebels.
Initially, when Xún 循 arrived in Xúnyáng 尋陽,
he heard that Gōng 公 had already returned,
but did not believe it.
After defeating Yì 劉毅,
he verified the news of Gōng 公's victorious return,
and they (Lu Xun and Xu Daofu) all looked at each other, turning pale.
Xún 循 wanted to retreat to Xúnyáng 尋陽,
then advance to take Jiānglíng 江陵,
and hold the two prefectures against the imperial court.
Dàofù 道覆 argued strongly that they should take advantage of their victory and advance directly.
He firmly debated this.
After many days of deliberation,
Dàofù's 道覆's view was adopted.
When the news of Yì's 劉毅's defeat arrived,
there was turmoil both inside and outside the court.
At that time, the northern army had just returned,
many suffering from wounds and illness.
The soldiers in the capital
did not number even a few thousand.
The rebels, having already defeated the two garrisons of Jiāng 江 and Yù 豫,
had over a hundred thousand soldiers,
and their boats and chariots stretched for a hundred *lǐ* 里 without interruption.
Those who fled back from the defeat
all spoke of their formidable strength.
Mèng Chǎng 孟昶 and Zhūgě Chángmín 諸葛長民 feared that the rebels were gradually approaching,
and wanted to take the emperor across the river.
Gōng 公 did not permit it,
but Chǎng 昶 insisted without ceasing.
Gōng 公 said:
"Now that the important garrisons outside have fallen,
and strong rebels are pressing inwards,
people's spirits are anxious and fearful,
and no one has a firm resolve.
If we move suddenly,
we will spontaneously disintegrate and collapse,
and how could we even reach north of the Jiāng 江 river?
Even if we could reach there,
it would only prolong things for a few days.
Although our soldiers are few now,
they are sufficient for one battle.
If we succeed,
then sovereign and subject will share in peace;
if indeed a dire fate is inevitable,
I shall die protecting the state,
my corpse lying across the temple gate,
fulfilling my long-held ambition to dedicate myself to the nation.
I cannot flee far into the wilderness seeking to survive.
My plan is decided;
you need say no more!"
Chǎng 昶 feared that it would not succeed,
so he wrote a memorial saying:
"When your servant Yù 裕 campaigned north,
everyone disagreed,
only your servant supported Yù's 裕 plan of action,
which has led to strong rebels taking advantage of the situation,
and the state being in grave danger.
This is your servant's crime.
I now respectfully take my leave to apologize to the world."
After sealing the memorial,
he took poison and died.
Thereupon, great rewards and recruitment were offered,
and those who committed themselves to the cause
were all given the same status as those who served in the capital.
Residents were mobilized to fortify Shítouchéng 石頭城,
and the general's standard was erected, declaring martial law.
At the time, some argued that troops should be divided to guard various important crossings.
Gōng 公 believed:
"The rebels are numerous, and we are few.
If we divide our forces into garrisons,
people will discern our strengths and weaknesses.
Moreover, a defeat in one place
would discourage the morale of the entire army.
Now, by gathering our forces at Shítou 石頭,
we can respond as needed.
This prevents the rebels from gauging our numbers,
and also keeps our collective strength undivided.
If more troops gather,
we can then discuss it further."
He moved his camp to Shítou 石頭,
and then barricaded the Huái 淮 River and cut off Chápǔ 查浦.
Soon after, the massed rebels arrived.
Gōng 公 assessed them, saying:
"If the rebels advance directly at Xīntíng 新亭,
their vanguard will be unstoppable,
and we should temporarily avoid them.
The outcome of victory or defeat
cannot yet be measured.
If they turn to anchor on the west bank,
they will be caught."
Xú Dàofù (徐道覆) wanted to burn his boats at Xīntíng (新亭) and Báishí (白石) and advance upstream.
Lú Xún (盧循) was often doubtful and rarely decisive.
He always sought to act with absolute safety in mind,
and said to Dàofù (道覆):
"The main army has not yet arrived.
Mèng Chǎng (孟昶) will undoubtedly collapse at the mere sight of our forces.
Broadly speaking,
they will naturally disintegrate within days.
To decide the outcome in a single morning now
is not a certain path to victory,
and moreover, it will cause casualties among our soldiers.
It is better to hold our troops and wait."
The Duke (Gōng) at that time ascended Shítouchéng (石頭城) to observe Xún's (循) army.
At first, when he saw them being led towards Xīntíng (新亭),
the Duke (Gōng) looked around with a pale face.
Soon after, they turned and anchored at Càizhōu (蔡洲).
Dàofù (道覆) still wanted to advance,
but Xún (循) forbade him.
From then on, all the armies gathered,
repaired and fortified Yuèchéng (越城),
and built three strongholds: Chápǔ (查浦), Yàoyuán (藥園), and Tíngwèi (廷尉),
all of which were garrisoned with substantial forces.
Champion General Liú Jìngxuān (劉敬宣) was stationed in the northern suburbs.
Auxiliary General Mèng Huáiyù (孟懷玉) was stationed west of Dānyáng Jùn (丹陽郡).
Jianwu General Wáng Zhòngdé (王仲德) was stationed at Yuèchéng (越城).
Guangwu General Liú Huáimò (劉懷默) was stationed outside Jiànyángmén (建陽門).
〔二六〕 He sent Ningguo General Suǒ Miǎo (索邈) to lead over a thousand Xianbei (鮮卑) heavily armored "Tiger-striped" cavalry,
all clad in multicolored mail,
from north of the Huái (淮) River to Xīntíng (新亭).
The bandits all gathered to watch,
and were all awed and fearful of them.
However, they still hoped that there would be a response from the capital (Jīngyì 京邑) and Sānwú (三吳).
They sent over ten ships to attack Shítouzhà (石頭柵).
The Duke (Gōng) ordered his divine crossbows to shoot at them;
each shot caused devastation,
so Xún (循) stopped and did not attack the palisade again.
They set up an ambush on the south bank,
and sent the weak and old to board boats and ships towards Báishí (白石).
The Duke (Gōng) worried they would march upstream from Báishí (白石),
so he led Liú Yì (劉毅) and Zhūgě Chángmín (諸葛長民) to go north to resist them,
leaving Military Advisor Xú Chìtè (徐赤特) to guard the south bank,
ordering him to hold fast and not move.
As soon as the Duke (Gōng) left,
the bandits burned Chápǔ (查浦) and marched upstream.
Chìtè's (赤特) army was defeated,
and over a hundred men died or were missing.
Chìtè (赤特) abandoned his remaining troops
and crossed the Huái (淮) in a single skiff.
The bandits then led tens of thousands to camp in Dānyáng Jùn (丹陽郡).
The Duke (Gōng) led all his armies back in haste.
The multitude worried about the bandits crossing,
and all thought the Duke (Gōng) should return directly to engage them.
The Duke (Gōng) first divided his army and sent them back to Shítou (石頭),
which the multitude did not understand.
He had them remove their armor and rest,
bathe and eat,
and then arrayed them in battle formation at Nántáng (南塘).
Because Chìtè (赤特) had disobeyed orders,
he was executed.
He ordered Military Advisors Chǔ Shúdù (褚叔度) and Zhū Língshí (朱齡石) to lead over a thousand elite warriors across the Huái (淮).
〔二七〕 Several thousand bandits,
all with long sabers, spears, and lances, their gleaming armor shining in the sun,
leaped forward in fierce competition.
Língshí (齡石)'s contingent was mostly Xianbei (鮮卑),
skilled in foot-combat with long spears,
and they formed ranks to await them.
The bandits' short weapons could not withstand them;
several hundred were killed or wounded,
and they retreated.
When night fell,
the troops also returned.
After Liú Yì (劉毅)'s defeat,
Yùzhōu (豫州) Chief Clerk Yuán Xīngguó (袁興國) rebelled,
occupying Lìyáng (歷陽) to support the bandits.
Lángyá (琅邪) Internal Administrator Wèi Shùnzhī (魏順之) sent his general Xiè Bǎo (謝寶) to attack and execute him.
Xīngguó (興國)'s Army Advisor attacked Bǎo (寶),
but Shùnzhī (順之) did not rescue him and retreated.
The Duke (Gōng) angrily executed him.
Shùnzhī (順之)
was the younger brother of Yǒngzhī (詠之).
Thereupon, the meritorious officials were terrified,
and none dared to disobey orders.
In the sixth month,
the Duke (Gōng) was further appointed Grand尉 (Tàiwèi) and Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshūjiān 中書監),
and granted the yellow axe (Huángyuè 黃鉞).
He accepted the yellow axe,
but declined the rest.
He appointed Army Advisor Yǔ Yuè (庾悅) as Jianwei General (Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn 建威將軍) and Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (江州 Cìshǐ 刺史),
to set out from Dōngyáng (東陽) to Yùzhāng (豫章).
On the Gēngshēn day of the seventh month,
the bandits fled south from Càizhōu (蔡洲),
and returned to camp at Xúnyáng (尋陽).
He sent Auxiliary General Wáng Zhòngdé (王仲德), Grand Administrator of Guǎngchuān (廣川) Liú Zhōng (劉鍾), and Grand Administrator of Héjiān (河間) Kuǎi Ēn (蒯恩) to pursue them.
The Duke (Gōng) returned to Dōngfǔ (東府),
and greatly prepared the navy,
all with large ships and multi-storied towers,
some over ten *zhàng* (丈) tall.
Lú Xún (盧循) sent his grand general Xún Lín (荀林) to raid Jiānglíng (江陵).
〔二八〕 Huán Qiān (桓謙) had previously fled from Jiānglíng (江陵) to the Qiāng (羌) people,
and then entered Shǔ (蜀) from the Qiāng (羌),
where the false ruler Qiáo Zòng (譙縱) appointed him Inspector of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
Qiān (謙) and Qiáo Dàofú (譙道福) led an army of twenty thousand
to raid Jiānglíng (江陵),
just meeting Lín (林),
about a hundred *lǐ* (里) apart.
Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史) Dàoguī (道規) executed Qiān (謙) at Zhījiāng (枝江),
defeated Lín (林) at Jiāngjīn (江津),
and pursued him to Zhúyìng (竹町) where he executed him.
When Xún (循) first fled,
the Duke (Gōng) knew he would certainly raid Jiānglíng (江陵),
so he immediately sent Huáilíng (淮陵) Internal Administrator Suǒ Miǎo (索邈) to lead cavalry to march on foot to reinforce Jīngzhōu (荊州).
He also sent Jianwei General Sūn Jìgāo (孫季高) to lead three thousand men
to attack Pānyú (番禺) by sea.
Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (江州刺史) Yǔ Yuè (庾悅) reached Wǔmǔqiáo (五畝嶠).
The bandits sent over a thousand men to occupy and block the mountain pass.
Yuè (悅)'s vanguard, Póyáng (鄱陽) Grand Administrator Yúqiū Jìn (虞丘進), attacked and broke through them.
The Duke (Gōng) prepared his troops extensively.
In the tenth month,
he led Yǎnzhōu (兗州) Cìshǐ (刺史) Liú Fān (劉藩), Ningguo General Tán Sháo (檀韶) and others with a naval force to campaign south.
He appointed Posterior General Liú Yì (劉毅) to supervise the Grand尉 (Tàiwèi) Resident Office,
entrusting all subsequent matters to him.
In this month,
Xú Dàofù (徐道覆) led thirty thousand men to raid Jiānglíng (江陵).
Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史) Dàoguī (道規) again greatly defeated him,
beheading over ten thousand,
and Dàofù (道覆) fled back to Péngkǒu (盆口).
When the Duke (Gōng) first sent Suǒ Miǎo (索邈),
Miǎo (邈) was intercepted by bandits on the way,
and only arrived after Dàofù (道覆) was defeated.
Since Xún (循) moved east,
communications between Jiānglíng (江陵) and the capital (Jīngyì 京邑) were cut off,
and all reports said it had fallen.
Only when Miǎo (邈) arrived
was it known that Xún (循) had fled.
Xún (循) had initially fled south from Càizhōu (蔡洲),
leaving five thousand of his close associates, Fàn Chóngmín (范崇民),
and over a hundred tall ships,
to garrison Nánlíng (南陵).
Wáng Zhòngdé (王仲德) and others, hearing that the main army was approaching,
then advanced to attack them.
In the eleventh month,
they greatly defeated Chóngmín's (崇民) army,
burned their boats and ships,
and gathered their scattered soldiers.
Xún (循)'s garrison at Guǎngzhōu (廣州)
did not defend the sea route.
In this month,
Jianwei General Sūn Jìgāo (孫季高) arrived unexpectedly by sea,
and although the city walls were steep and intact,
there were still several thousand soldiers.
Jìgāo (季高) burned the bandit ships,
exerted all his strength,
attacked it from four sides,
and sacked the city that same day.
Xún (循)'s father fled in a light boat to Shǐxīng (始興).
Jìgāo (季高) pacified the old residents,
executed Xún (循)'s close associates,
and disciplined his troops to guard diligently.
When the Duke (Gōng) first sent Jìgāo (季高),
everyone believed the sea route was difficult and distant,
and it would certainly be arduous;
moreover, splitting off current forces
was not essential.
The Duke (Gōng) did not agree.
He instructed Jìgāo (季高), saying:
"The main army will surely defeat the wicked bandits
around the twelfth month.
You should arrive at Guǎngzhōu (廣州) around this time,
overthrow their lair,
so that when the bandits flee,
they will have nowhere to return."
Jìgāo (季高) received the order and departed,
achieving victory as scheduled.
Xún 方治兵旅舟艦,
設諸攻備.
Gōng 欲御以長算,
乃屯軍雷池.
賊揚聲不攻雷池,
當乘流逕下.
Gōng 知其欲戰,
且慮賊戰敗,
或於京江入海,
遣 Wáng Zhòngdé 以水艦二百於吉陽下斷之.
十二月,
Xún, Dàofù 率眾數萬,
方艦而下,
前後相抗,
莫見舳艫之際.
Gōng 悉出輕利鬬艦,
躬提幡鼓,
命眾軍齊力擊之.
又上步騎於西岸.
右軍參軍 Yǔ Yuèsheng 乘艦不進,
斬而徇之.
於是眾軍並踊騰爭先.
軍中多萬鈞神弩,
所至莫不摧陷.
Gōng 中流蹙之,
因風水之勢,
賊艦悉泊西岸.
岸上軍先備火具,
乃投火焚之,
煙爓張天,
賊眾大敗,
追奔至夜乃歸.
Xún 等還 Xúnyáng.
初分遣步軍,
莫不疑怪,
及燒賊艦,
眾乃悅服.
召 Wáng Zhòngdé,
請還為前驅.
留輔國將軍 Mèng Huáiyù 守 Léichí.
Xún 聞大軍上,
欲走向 Yùzhāng,
乃悉力柵斷 Zuǒlǐ.
大軍至 Zuǒlǐ,
將戰,
Gōng 所執麾竿折,
折幡沈水,
眾並怪懼.
Gōng 歡笑曰:
「往年覆舟之戰,
幡竿亦折,
今者復然,
賊必破矣.」
即攻柵而進.
遁兵雖殊死戰,
弗能禁.
諸軍乘勝奔之,
Xún 單舸走.
所殺及投水死,
凡萬餘人.
納其降附,
宥其逼略.
遣 Liú Fān, Mèng Huáiyù 輕軍追之.
Xún 收散卒,
尚有數千人,
逕還 Guǎngzhōu.
Dàofù 還保 Shǐxīng.
Gōng 旋自 Zuǒlǐ.
天子遣侍中、黃門勞師于行所.
校勘記
本紀第二武帝中
七年正月己未,
振旅于京師.
改授大將軍、揚州牧,
給班劍二十人,
本官悉如故,
固辭.
凡南北征伐戰亡者,
並列上賻贈.
尸喪未反,
遣主帥迎接,
致還本土.
二月,
Lú Xún 至 Pānyú,
為 Sūn Jìgāo 所破,
收餘眾南走.
Liú Fān, Mèng Huáiyù 斬 Xú Dàofù 于 Shǐxīng.
Jìn 自中興以來,
治綱大弛,
權門并兼,
強弱相凌,
百姓流離,
不得保其產業.
Huán Xuán 頗欲釐改,
竟不能行.
Gōng 既作輔,
大示軌則,
豪強肅然,
遠近知禁.
至是 Kuàijī Yúyáo Yú Liàng 復藏匿亡命千餘人.
Gōng 誅 Liàng,
免 Kuàijī 内史 Sīmǎ Xiūzhī.
天子又申前命,
Gōng 固辭.
於是改授太尉、中書監,
乃受命.
奉送黃鉞,
解 Jìzhōu.
Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ Dù Huìdù 斬 Lú Xún,
傳首京師.
先是諸州郡所遣秀才、孝廉,
多非其人,
Gōng 表天子,
申明舊制,
依舊策試.
征西將軍、荊州刺史 Dào Guī 疾患求歸,
八年四月,
改授 Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
以後將軍、Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Yì 代之.
Yì 與 Gōng 俱舉大義,
興復 Jìn 室,
自謂京城、Guǎnglíng,
功業足以相抗.
雖權事推 Gōng,
而心不服也.
Yì 既有雄才大志,
厚自矜許,
朝士素望者多歸之.
與尚書僕射 Xiè Hùn, Dānyáng Yǐn Xī Sēngshī 並深相結.
及西鎮 Jiānglíng,
Yùzhōu 舊府,
多割以自隨,
請 Sēngshī 為南蠻校尉.
既知 Yì 不能居下,
終為異端,
密圖之.
Yì 至西,
稱疾篤,
表求從弟 Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Fān 以為副貳,
偽許焉.
九月,
Fān 入朝,
Gōng 命收 Fān 及 Xiè Hùn,
並於獄賜死.
自表討 Yì.
又假黃鉞,
率諸軍西征.
以前鎮軍將軍 Sīmǎ Xiūzhī 為平西將軍、Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Dào Lián 鎮 Dāntú,
Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Zhūgě Chángmín 監太尉留府事,
加太尉司馬、Dānyáng Yǐn Liú Mùzhī 建威將軍,
配以實力.
Rénwǔ,
發自京師.
遣參軍 Wáng Zhèn'è, 龍驤將軍 KuǎI ēn 前襲 Jiānglíng.
十月,
Zhèn'è 剋 Jiānglíng,
Yì 及黨與皆伏誅.
十一月己卯,
Gōng 至 Jiānglíng,
下書曰: 夫去弊拯民,
必存簡恕,
捨網修綱,
雖煩易理.
Jiāng, Jīng 彫殘,
刑政多闕,
頃年事故,
綏撫未週.
遂令百姓疲匱,
歲月滋甚,
財傷役困,
慮不幸生.
凋殘之餘,
而不減舊,
刻
剝徵求,
不循政道.
宰莅之司,
或非良榦,
未能菲躬儉,
苟求盈給,
積習生常,
漸不
知改.
近因戎役,
來涉二州,
踐境親民,
愈見其瘼,
思欲振其所急,
卹其所苦.
凡租稅調
役,
悉宜以見戶為正.
州郡縣屯田池塞,
諸非軍國所資,
利入守宰者,
今一切除之.
州
The officials of the commanderies and counties
all followed the regulations of the Shàngshū to establish households according to the actual population.
The court's levies of guǐmǎo梓材 (zīcái)
and gēngzǐ皮毛 (pímáo)
may all be suspended and abolished,
and a separate assessment made of what is produced.
Bālíng
was equally assessed to pay for military expenses,
and continued with the old system of military transport.
All who were pardoned for crimes of five years' imprisonment or less,
and all remaining members of families of bandits who had been seized and registered,
were also fully pardoned and released.
The ten commanderies of Jīngzhōu were made into Xiāngzhōu,
and Gōng was then promoted to governor-general.
Zhū Língshí, the Administrator of Xīyáng, was made Governor of Yìzhōu,
and led an army to attack Shǔ.
Gōng was promoted to Grand Tutor and Shepherd of Yángzhōu,
with the addition of feathered parasols and drums and pipes,
and twenty swordsmen in attendance.
On the *yǐchǒu* day of the second month of the ninth year (413 CE),
Gōng arrived back from Jiānglíng.
Initially, Zhūgě Chángmín was greedy, licentious, arrogant, and oppressive,
and was a source of suffering for the gentry and common people.
Gōng, because he shared the same great cause,
tolerated him.
After Liú Yì was executed,
Chángmín said to his intimates,
"In former years, Péng Yuè was pickled,
and this year Hán Xìn was executed.
Calamity will surely come."
He planned to rebel.
Gōng set a date to arrive in the capital,
but repeatedly delayed his advance.
The grandees and ministers waited for days at Xīntíng,
and Chángmín also frequently went out.
Soon after, Gōng arrived secretly by light boat,
and had already returned to the Eastern Residence.
Chángmín arrived at the gate.
He was led in,
and after sending others away, they conversed intimately.
Gōng spoke with him about all matters
that he had previously kept from Chángmín.
Chángmín was very pleased.
Meanwhile, Gōng secretly ordered his strong attendants Dīng Wǔ and others to come out from behind a curtain,
and they seized him where he sat.
Chángmín fell from the bed,
and they beat him on the ground.
He died by the side of the bed.
His corpse was carried and handed over to the Grand Judge.
His younger brother, Límín, was also executed.
Wǔ was brave and strong,
and people at the time made a saying about him:
"Don't be overbearing,
or you'll be handed over to Dīng Wǔ."
Previously, mountains, lakes, rivers, and marshes
were all monopolized by powerful families.
The common people who gathered firewood, hunted, fished, and trapped
were all charged taxes.
At this time, this was forbidden.
At that time, the residences of the people were not unified,
and Gōng submitted a memorial saying: "I have heard that the sage kings of old, in establishing governance,
ordered the nine regions,
divided territories and marked boundaries,
so that each could live in peace in their place.
In those prosperous ages of the past,
people did not change their occupations.
Thus, the system of the well-field (jǐngtián)
flourished
from the Three Dynasties onwards.
Qín reformed this policy,
and Hàn subsequently did not change it,
leading to the evils of the rich and powerful merging and annexing.
However, the nine regions were not disturbed,
and what was relied upon became tradition.
In
the Western Hàn capital,
the clans of Tián and Jǐng were greatly relocated
to populate Guānzhōng.
They then made the three *fǔ* their native villages,
no longer tying them to Qí or Chǔ.
Since the scattering
and
crossing of the Yǒngjiā era,
we have relied upon the Huái and the Sea.
The court has calculations for restoration,
and the people harbor thoughts of returning to their origins.
Plans for strategy
do not allow for a moment's rest.
Therefore, there has been no leisure
to pacify the people and establish stable governance.
When it came to Grand Marshal Huán Wēn,
he considered that the people having no fixed homes
was a deep harm to governance.
In the *gēngxū* year (370 CE), he implemented the 'land survey' (tǔduàn)
to unify their occupations.
At that time, wealth
and national abundance
truly stemmed from this.
From then until now,
many years have passed,
and the unified system
has gradually become dilapidated.
Mixed residents and sojourners,
with neighborhoods and communities not properly maintained.
This is why royal
transformation is not yet pure,
and the people's suffering still exists.
I, your servant, bear a heavy responsibility,
and my shame and blame are deep.
Unless changes are made and restrictions eased,
there will be no way to improve governance.
Now, human nature is attached to the familiar,
and it is difficult to plan new beginnings with them.
The so-called land
of one's parents, considered as one's native place (sāngzǐ),
is truly because one is born and dies there,
and it is the object of respect and love.
Now, where they have lived for generations,
with graves forming rows,
how can their sincerity of respect and reverence
not arise with the circumstances?
I request that the regulations of the *gēngxū* 'land survey' be adopted,
so that the foundations of the people may be extended,
and gradually established with the circumstances.
Then, by guiding them with benevolence and righteousness,
and inspiring
them with military might,
crossing the Great River and straddling the Yellow River,
pacifying the nine provinces and restoring the old lands,
then the will to return to one's roots
will be swiftly realized in that very year.
Though initially temporarily
arduous,
it will enable an easy completion.
I humbly beseech Your Majesty,
to have compassion for the myriad people,
pity them for what they have lost,
ever bear in mind the poem of the wild geese (hóngyàn zhī shī),
