On the *xīnhài* day of the eighth month,
an edict stated:
"Rectifying customs by dividing regions
was established in the records of Yú,
and the different systems in rivers and valleys
were brilliantly displayed in the姬 (Jī) canons.
Thus, there were distinctions in wells and fields,
and no mixture in communities and groups,
which enabled the seven teachings to be proclaimed,
and the eight policies to be ordered.
Although successive dynasties have had different paths,
and evolutions have had different systems,
sometimes the people desired to change customs,
or states valued encouraging migration.
Hànyáng gathered the prominent families of Yān and Dài,
and Guānxī flourished with the clans of Qí and Chǔ,
all registered in new cities
and settled as old inhabitants.
By the time the Jin (Jīn) dynasty lost power,
and rites and music moved south,
the common people of the central plains
carried their infants and migrated to Yáng and Yuè.
The sagely martial (Shèngwǔ) founded the dynasty,
unifying the vast region,
establishing rules for long generations,
and implementing the system of 'land demarcation' (tǔduàn).
However, danger and safety followed each other,
and prosperity and decline alternated.
Years of famine caused displacement,
and military service led to idleness and dispersion,
causing people to leave their homes and reside in foreign territories,
gradually accumulating to a great extent.
It is fitting to follow the grand path
as an eternal law,
so that customs may flourish and people prosper,
reversing trends and ensuring stable lives.
It will level the dangers of Xūxúshān,
clear the waves of the vast sea,
encompass the river charts within the nine domains,
and wield the jade rein in the five capitals."
Wáng Jiǎn, Secretary of the Imperial Library (Mìshūchéng), presented his compiled "Qīzhì" (Seven Treatises) in thirty scrolls.
The capital suffered a drought.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
an edict stated:
"Recently, the soaring heat has been prolonged,
the lingering warmth burning the daylight hours,
damaging the autumn crops,
and bringing suffering to the people.
I, in my small and ailing state,
have not yet broadly promoted the way of governance.
Prisons are still crowded,
and cases of injustice and stagnation still accumulate.
I grieve morning and night,
and always feel sorrow in my heart.
The Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng) may, together with those below the law enforcement officials,
investigate all prisons,
so that wrongful accusations may be cleared,
and the distressed and destitute may be revived.
This order shall be distributed to all prefectures and commanderies,
ensuring that none obstruct it."
On the *guǐhài* day,
Jiànníng Wáng Jǐngsù, General of the Guard and Inspector of Nánxú Prefecture, was promoted to General who Guards the North (Zhènběi Jiāngjūn).
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
Cáo Xiǎn, King of Chénliú, passed away.
In the ninth month, on the day Rénwǔ,
an edict stated:
"The national levy and commoners' taxes
have generally been categorized.
Previously, during the military crisis,
military provisions were prioritized,
and the appropriateness of collections and levies
sometimes deviated from old standards.
In the two prefectures of Xiāngzhōu and Jiāngzhōu,
grain transport was overly concentrated,
and the frequent conscription and labor duties
increasingly burdened the common people.
Due to procrastination in temporary governance,
some things may not have been reformed,
leaving the populace exhausted and depleted,
growing worse with each passing year.
I constantly sigh with pity,
my concern extends to sleepless nights.
An envoy should be dispatched to those localities
to conduct a thorough investigation.
Any levies that violate old decrees,
and labor duties that exceed public limits,
shall all be immediately abolished and reformed,
with a detailed report submitted for my information."
On the day Dīnghài,
Bóyù, son of Héngyáng Wáng Yì, was enfeoffed as Nánpíng Wáng.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day Rénzǐ,
Wáng Xuánzài, Fǔjūn Sīmǎ, was appointed Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu and Nánqínzhōu.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
Zhōnglí from Nányánzhōu and Mǎtóu from Yùzhōu were ceded;
Xīnchāngjùn was also established by dividing Qínjùn, Liángjùn, and Lìyáng;
Xúzhōu was established.
In the eleventh month, on the day Bǐngzǐ,
Yuán Hóng, Sànqí Chángshì, was appointed Cìshǐ of Xúzhōu.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Yuán Càn, Shàngshū Lìng, left his post due to his mother's mourning.
In the twelfth month, on the day Guǐmǎo (the first day of the month),
there was a solar eclipse.
On the day Yǐsì,
Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn, Sīkōng and Cìshǐ of Jiāngzhōu, was promoted to Tàiwèi;
Yuán Càn, Shàngshū Lìng, was reinstated to his original post,
and granted the title Wèijiāngjūn.
On the day Guǐhài,
Bóróng, the crown prince of the former Jiàn'ān Wáng, was enfeoffed as Shǐ'ān Xiàn Wáng.
On the day Bǐngyín,
the King of Hénán sent envoys to present local products.
In the second year, spring, the first month, on the day Gēngzǐ,
Zhāng Yǒng, Yòuguānglù Dàfū, was appointed Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn and Cìshǐ of Nányánzhōu.
In the second month, on the day Jǐsì,
Chǔ Yuān, Hùjūn Jiāngjūn, was promoted to Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the third month, on the day Guǐyǒu,
Wáng Kuān, Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn, was appointed Cìshǐ of Nányùzhōu.
Summer, the fourth month, on the day Guǐhài,
an edict stated:
"Recently, titles and merits have been granted,
and honors conferred as rewards for righteousness.
The categories and procedures have accumulated extensively,
and yet each has been left pending.
Years pass, but matters remain unresolved,
leading to inevitable arrears and congestion,
with discrepancies in various places,
often violating regulations.
Rewards have not been equitably distributed,
causing me constant distress.
Let all be carried out in accordance with the old standards,
and all be assigned to their proper offices."
In the fifth month, on the day Rénwǔ,
Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn, Tàiwèi and Cìshǐ of Jiāngzhōu, raised an army in rebellion.
On the day Gēngyín,
military alerts were issued both inside and outside the capital.
Liú Miǎn, Zhōnglǐngjūn, was promoted to Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn;
Qí Wáng, Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn, was promoted to Píngnán Jiāngjūn,
serving as vanguard for the southern expedition,
and stationed at Xīntíng.
Zhāng Yǒng, Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn, was stationed at Báixià;
Shěn Huáimíng, former Cìshǐ of Nányánzhōu, guarded Shítóu;
Yuán Càn, Wèijiāngjūn, and Chǔ Yuān, Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn, entered the palace to guard the inner court.
On the day Rénchén,
the rebels suddenly arrived,
attacking the Xīntíng fortress.
Qí Wáng resisted and counterattacked,
greatly defeating them.
Zhāng Jìng'ér, Yuèqí Xiàowèi, beheaded Xiūfàn.
The rebel factions under Dù Hēilí and Dīng Wénháo divided their forces and advanced towards Zhūquè Háng;
Liú Miǎn resisted the rebels but was defeated,
fighting bravely until his death.
Wáng Dàolóng, Yòujūn Jiāngjūn, fled and was killed.
Zhāng Yǒng collapsed at Báixià,
and Shěn Huáimíng dispersed from Shítóu.
On the day Jiǎwǔ,
Máo Tián, Fǔjūn Diǎnqiān, opened the eastern government gate and let in the rebels;
the rebels entered and encamped in the central hall.
Chén Xiǎndá, Yǔlín Jiān, attacked and greatly defeated them.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
Zhāng Jìng'ér and others defeated the rebels at Xuānyángmén, Zhuāngyánsì, and Xiǎoshì,
then advanced to pacify the eastern government city,
capturing and executing the rebel leaders.
Rewards and enfeoffments varied accordingly.
On the day Dīngyǒu,
an edict ordered the two counties of the capital to bury the slain rebels,
and the war dead,
and restored them to the capital's administration.
On this day, the alert was lifted,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire,
and all civil and military officials were granted a promotion of one rank.
On the day Wùxū,
arrears and debts in Jiāngzhōu were forgiven and abolished;
any levies that were extraordinary and duties that were burdensome to the people
were all to be abolished and stopped.
An edict stated:
"Recently, the national revenue has been greatly reduced,
and public reserves have been scarce.
Although the recent military action was minor,
military expenses have already been significant,
leaving granaries and treasuries empty,
making it difficult to manage distant affairs.
It is appropriate to rectify excessive indulgence
and strive for frugality.
All provisions for imperial service and attire
shall be reduced and curtailed;
ornate and extravagant decorations
shall be abolished and not repaired.
All miscellaneous expenses
shall be strictly prohibited,
and detailed regulations shall be drawn up for external affairs."

Shěn Yōuzhī, Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu; Jiànpíng Wáng Jǐngsù, Cìshǐ of Nánxúzhōu; Jìnxī Wáng Xiè, Cìshǐ of Yǐngzhōu; Wáng Sēngqián, Cìshǐ of Xiāngzhōu; and Zhāng Xīngshì, Cìshǐ of Yōngzhōu, all raised righteous armies and marched to the capital.
On the day Jǐhài,
the seventh imperial brother Yǒu was appointed Cìshǐ of Jiāngzhōu.
The state of Ruìruì sent envoys to present local products.
In the sixth month, on the day Gēngzǐ,
Qí Wáng, Píngnán Jiāngjūn, was appointed Zhōnglǐngjūn, Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn, and Cìshǐ of Nányánzhōu.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
Jìnxī Wáng Xiè dispatched troops to capture Xúnyáng,
and Jiāngzhōu was pacified.
On the day Wùshēn,
Rèn Nóngfū, Huáinán Tàishǒu, was appointed Cìshǐ of Yùzhōu;
Wáng Kuān, Yòujiāngjūn and Cìshǐ of Nányùzhōu, was promoted to Píngxī Jiāngjūn.
On the day Rénxū,
Fǔshī Jiāngjūn was changed back to Fǔguó.
Autumn, the seventh month, on the day Gēngchén,
the seventh imperial brother Yǒu was enfeoffed as Shàolíng Wáng.
On the day Xīnsì,
Mèng Cìyáng, Fǔjūn Sīmǎ, was appointed Cìshǐ of Yǎnzhōu.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
Shěn Yōuzhī, Zhènxī Jiāngjūn and Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu, was promoted to Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn;
Jiànpíng Wáng Jǐngsù, Zhènběi Jiāngjūn and Cìshǐ of Nánxúzhōu, was promoted to Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn,
both with the right to establish an administration and enjoy the privileges of Sānsī.
Jìnxī Wáng Xiè, Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Cìshǐ of Yǐngzhōu, was promoted to Ānxī Jiāngjūn;
Wáng Sēngqián, Qián Jiāngjūn and Cìshǐ of Xiāngzhōu, was promoted to Píngnán Jiāngjūn.
In the eighth month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
Liú Yánzǔ, Zhēnglǔ Xíngcānjūn, was appointed Cìshǐ of Níngzhōu.
In the ninth month, on the day Rénchén,
Lǚ Ānguó, Yóujī Jiāngjūn, was appointed Cìshǐ of Yǎnzhōu.
On the day Dīngyǒu,
Yuán Càn, Shàngshū Lìng and newly appointed Wèijiāngjūn, was appointed Zhōngshū Jiān,
with his current title and the right to establish an administration and enjoy the privileges of Sānsī,
and concurrently serving as Sītú;
Chǔ Yuān, Hùjūn Jiāngjūn, was promoted to Shàngshū Lìng;
Ānchéng Wáng, Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn and Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu, was promoted to Chējì Jiāngjūn.
Winter, the tenth month, on the day Gēngshēn,
Wáng Yùn, newly appointed Shìzhōng, was appointed Cìshǐ of Xiāngzhōu.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Chén Xiǎndá, Yóujī Jiāngjūn, was appointed Cìshǐ of Guǎngzhōu.
In the eleventh month, on the day Bǐngxū,
the Emperor came of age (underwent the capping ceremony),
and a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
Civilian men were granted one rank of nobility;
those who succeeded their fathers, and the Sanlao (elders), filial and fraternal individuals, and diligent farmers were granted two ranks of nobility;
the widowed, solitary, orphaned, and those with severe illnesses who could not support themselves
were granted five hú of grain per person;
those eighty years and older
were additionally granted one bolt of silk.
There was a grand banquet for five days;
kings and dukes and those below them were granted gifts varying according to their rank.
In the twelfth month, on the day Guǐhài,
the eighth imperial brother Jī was enfeoffed as Jiāngxià Wáng,
and the ninth imperial brother Zàn as Wǔlíng Wáng.
In the third year, spring, the first month, on the day Xīnsì,
the imperial carriage personally offered sacrifices at the southern suburb and the Míngtáng.
In the third month, on the day Bǐngyín,
the King of Hénán sent envoys to present local products.
On the day Jǐsì,
Zhāng Jìng'ér, Chējì Jiāngjūn, was appointed Cìshǐ of Yōngzhōu.
On that day,
there was a great flood in the capital,
and Shàngshū Láng and other officials were dispatched to inspect and distribute relief.
On the *wùxū* day of the intercalary month,
an imperial edict stated:
“Lately, popular customs have become extremely decadent,
the state treasury is not yet abundant,
harvests have frequently been poor,
and registered households lack sufficiency.
Moreover, border anxieties remain acute,
and corvée taxes are increasingly numerous.
I reflect on this constantly,
and my distress grows whether I am resting or active.
I desire to expand the system of thrift and conservation,
to cultivate a spirit of frugality and simplicity,
hoping thereby to store provisions to relieve the people,
and thus stabilize the path of governance.
The rare delicacies of the Imperial Kitchen,
the splendid garments of the Imperial Wardrobe,
and all other provisions and supplies
are to be entirely reduced and eliminated.
Detailed regulations for this should be formulated,
aiming for utmost simplicity.”
In the fourth month of summer,
a Shàngshū Láng was dispatched to all the *zhōu* to investigate and register households.
For the extremely poor among the old and infirm,
their taxes and levies were exempted.
For able-bodied individuals who still had a livelihood,
leniency and extension were granted as appropriate.
For those whose assets were sufficient to meet their obligations,
they were urged to complete payment.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
the imperial carriage proceeded to the Central Hall to hear lawsuits.
On the *guǐwèi* day of the sixth month,
an envoy from the Northern Kingdom arrived.
Jiān Sītú Yuán Càn and Shàngshū Lìng Chǔ Yuān both firmly declined their appointments.
On the *gēngxū* day of the seventh month of autumn,
Càn was appointed Shàngshū Lìng.
On the *rénxū* day,
Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng Liú Huáizhēn was appointed Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the *gēngzǐ* day of the eighth month,
Hùjūn Jiāngjūn Chǔ Yuān was additionally appointed Zhōngshū Jiān.
On the *bǐngchén* day of the ninth month,
Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn Hénán Wáng Tǔyǔhún Shíyín was promoted to Chējì Dàjiāngjūn.
On the *bǐngxū* day of the tenth month of winter,
the kingdom of Gāolí sent an envoy to present local products.
On the *yǐchǒu* day of the twelfth month,
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn Yáo Dàohé was appointed Sīzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the first month of spring of the fourth year, on the *jǐhài* day,
the imperial carriage personally ploughed the sacrificial field,
and a general amnesty was granted throughout the empire.
Farmers who exerted themselves were granted one rank of nobility;
grain and seeds were lent to the poor.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
Liáng, Nánqín Èrzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Xuánzài was appointed Yìzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the *rénxū* day of the second month,
Bùbīng Xiàowèi Fàn Báinián was appointed Liáng, Nánqín Èrzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū Wáng Kūn was additionally appointed Tèjìn.
In the fifth month of summer,
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Wǔdū Wáng Yáng Wéndù was appointed Běiqínzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
Shàngshū Yòuchéng Yú Wánzhī submitted a memorial discussing current affairs, stating: "The imperial treasury is empty and scattered,
for nearly thirty years.
The *zhōu* of Jiāng and Jīng,
whose taxes and levies were originally small,
have since then
frequently lacked recruits for the army.
The income from grain and silk
is directly used to supply military and civil officials.
Yù, Yǎn, Sī, and Xú
are like mouths waiting to be fed,
and the generals in the northwest
are naked and seeking clothes.
What is remitted to the capital
is meager.
The
imperial treasury's resources
rely solely on Huái and Hǎi.
The people are impoverished and resources are scarce,
not like in former days.
Yet the state's expenses are vast,
〔一０〕four times that of Yuánjiā.
The manpower of the two imperial guards and palace offices
is
less than one-fifth of what it should be;
the carpenters of the Waterways Bureau are decayed and scattered,
fewer than two-tenths remain.
The reserve storerooms of the capital
are entirely depleted of timber and bamboo;
the two eastern and western imperial walls
lack both bricks and tiles.
Imperial orders for provisions and grants
are entirely reliant on market purchases.
The offices of the Department of State Affairs
are daily falling into disrepair,
and residences and government offices
are mostly ruined and damaged.
Seeing this, there is no time to save it;
knowing this, there is no time
to attend to it.
Reviewing the established income and levies,
they are insufficient for expenditures.
Since there are no reserves,
it is naturally coming to complete emptiness.
Accumulated弊 and repeated consumption
have culminated today.
Last year, by imperial decree,
I was tasked with collecting outstanding taxes from the populace of Yáng and Xú.
A total of 600,000 *hú* of rice and grain,
over 50 million cash,
50,000 bolts of cloth and silk,
and various other items were collected.
We relied on these to sustain ourselves,
thus we managed to carry on.
Currently, the outstanding arrears are even greater,
and expenditures are gradually increasing.
I deeply fear that imperial provisions will suddenly cease,
military equipment production will halt,
soldiers will be hungry and resentful,
and all officials will suffer reduced stipends.
Government offices will lack beautiful decorations,
and construction will cease to have elegant appearances.
Imperial relatives will have nothing to sustain them,
and meritorious officials will have nothing to be granted.
As this foolish official foresees,
it will not be a matter of months but
of years.
Long-term strategies for governing the state
are what this humble servant dares not speak of;
working diligently morning and night,
my heart is committed to never being lax.
Arising and prostrating with trepidation,
this matter compels me to report.
I humbly pray Your Majesty
will grant a moment's consideration,
establish plans for generations to come,
issue an unprecedented edict,
and implement enforceable decrees.
Then the common people will rejoice together,
〔一一〕and high and low will share in peace."
The Emperor responded with a gracious edict.
On the *gēngxū* day,
Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Cáo Xīnzhī was appointed Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the *yǐhài* day of the sixth month,
Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn Qí Wáng was additionally appointed Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè.
On the *wùzǐ* day of the seventh month of autumn,
Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn, Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ Jiànpíng Wáng Jǐngsù rebelled, occupying the capital city.
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
internal and external preparations for defense were made.
Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Rèn Nóngfū and Guānjūn Jiāngjūn Huáng Huí were dispatched to suppress the rebellion in the north.
Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn Qí Wáng commanded all the armies.
A limited amnesty was granted to Nánxúzhōu.
Shǐ'ān Wáng Bóróng and Dūxiāng Hóu Bóyóu were granted death.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Duàn Fórong commanded the vanguard cavalry and infantry.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Jūnjǔ, Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn Zhāng Bǎo was defeated in battle and killed.
Huáng Huí and others reached the capital city,
fought with Jǐngsù's armies,
and repeatedly defeated them.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
the capital city was taken.
Jǐngsù was beheaded,
and all those who joined the rebellion were executed.
On that day, the state of emergency was lifted.
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
a general amnesty was granted to the empire,
and rewards were given according to rank.
Outstanding taxes in the two counties of Jīngyì from before the first year were waived.
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
Wǔlíng Wáng Zàn was appointed Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the *dīngmǎo* day of the eighth month,
the tenth imperial brother Huì was enfeoffed as Nányáng Wáng,
the eleventh imperial brother Sōng as Xīnxīng Wáng,
and the twelfth imperial brother Xǐ as Shǐjiàn Wáng.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng Ruǎn Diànfū was appointed Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Xíng Qīng, Jì Èrzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Shànmíng was appointed Qīng, Jì Èrzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the *dīnghài* day of the ninth month,
Suí Jùn of Yǐngzhōu was detached and attached to Sīzhōu.
On the *wùzǐ* day,
Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Gāo Dàoqìng was found guilty
and granted death.
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
Chējì Jiāngjūn, Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Ānchéng Wáng was promoted to Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and Ānxī Jiāngjūn, Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ Jìnxī Wáng Xiè was promoted to Zhènxī Jiāngjūn.
On the *xīnyǒu* day of the tenth month of winter,
Lìbù Shàngshū Wáng Sēngqián was appointed Shàngshū Yòupúshè.
Dàngchāng Wáng Liáng Míjiā was appointed Ānxī Jiāngjūn, Hé, Liáng Èrzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
Zhōngshū Jiān, Hùjūn Jiāngjūn Chǔ Yuān resigned due to mourning for his mother.
On the *gēngxū* day of the eleventh month,
an imperial edict ordered him to temporarily resume his original post.
In the second month of spring of the fifth year, on the *rénshēn* day,
Jiànníng Tàishǒu Liǔ Hé was appointed Níngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the fourth month, on the *Jiǎxū* day,
Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Ruǎn Diànfū, Bùbīng Xiàowèi Shēn Bózōng, and Zhū Yòumóu attempted to depose and enthrone.
Diànfū and Yòumóu were imprisoned and died,
Bózōng was executed.
In the fifth month, on the *Jǐhài* day,
Shěn Jǐngdé, General of the Left Army, was appointed Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ,
and Quán Jǐngwén, General of the Swift Cavalry, was appointed Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ.
Sūn Tánguàn, Colonel of the Mounted Cavalry, was appointed Yuèzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the sixth month, on the *Jiǎxū* day,
Shěn Bó, Left Chief Clerk of the Minister of Works, Dù Yǒuwén, Attendant-in-ordinary, Sūn Chāozhī, General of the Roaming Cavalry, and Dù Shúwén, Colonel of the Long Water Army, were executed.
On the *Bǐngwǔ* day,
In the seventh month, on the night of the *Wùzǐ* day,
the Emperor perished in the Rénshòu Diàn,
aged fifteen.
On the *Jǐchǒu* day,
the Empress Dowager issued an edict: "To the General of the Guards, Commander of the Imperial Guard, Director of the Central Secretariat, and the Eight Dignitaries: Yù, as the eldest legitimate son,
succeeded to the imperial lineage.
It was hoped that his understanding and discernment would daily grow,
and that the altars of soil and grain would have someone to rely on.
How
could it be that he reached such extreme wickedness and perversity,
from childhood to adulthood,
violating every small good,
and inevitably committing every great evil?
His upbringing and guidance, offered repeatedly,
were always met with concealment,
his treacherous and perverse nature was difficult to
change,
and worsened day by day.
He abandoned his crown and destroyed his ceremonial robes,
constantly wearing military attire.
He consorted with dogs and horses,
and delighted in hawks and falcons.
Filthy things traversed within the palace and halls,
and leashes and bonds were by the imperial
throne.
He even rode alone to distant suburbs,
sleeping solitary in deep wilderness.
He wielded spears and short lances with his own hands,
personally engaged in disemboweling and slaughtering.
White blades were his playthings,
killing and harming were his pursuits.
He abandoned the guard of the crossed
halberds,
and neglected the ceremony of the celestial canopy.
He roamed through markets,
singing drunkenly in taverns.
He roamed at night, forgetting to return,
and slept in army camps.
He seized people's sons and daughters,
and plundered people's wealth and possessions.
Such acts are not recorded in history books,
and unheard of since ancient times.
Shěn Bó was a scholar,
Sūn Chāo a meritorious official,
the Yòuwén brothers
were all involved in meritorious service.
These four innocent people,
in one morning,
were all slaughtered.
Flying arrows and clashing swords left
no children unscathed.
He ripped apart livers and intestines
for amusement,
and threw corpses into rivers
for joy.
Furthermore, his extravagance was limitless,
emptying the imperial treasury.
He imposed arbitrary taxes on the region between the passes and rivers,
to exclusively fill his private hoard.
The common people were wailing,
with nowhere to find a livelihood.
I, together with his mother, always admonished him with righteous principles,
yet he planned
to poison us,
intending to unleash his fierce anger.
Our deep sorrow made us fear for every passing day,
that we might not survive the morning.
From the ancient times of Xīn and Guǐ,
and extending to Yōu and Lì,
compared to this,
they cannot even be likened to one ten-thousandth.
The people's resentment is already deep,
and the gods' anger has accumulated.
The Seven Ancestral Temples are in perilous danger,
and the Four Seas are filled with dread.
Deposing the corrupt and enthroning the enlightened is a praiseworthy example from previous generations.
How much more so when he has extinguished righteousness and defied the Dao,
abandoned by Heaven and humanity?
His transgressions are deeper than Mùyě,
and his reason cut off like Tónggōng.
Therefore, I secretly ordered Xiāo
Lǐngjūn to subtly deploy his brilliant strategies,
with both visible and hidden forces working in concert,
so that peace might prevail throughout the world.
The Grand General of Agile Cavalry, the Prince of Ānchéng, is of the lineage of Tàizōng,
naturally endowed with profound wisdom.
His demeanor is calm
and far-reaching,
his virtue shines through the fields.
His noble birth and close relation
make him the rightful heir to the imperial mandate.
The myriad people fix their hearts on him,
and all living beings look to him with hope.
He should honor the ancestors
and rule over all nations.
Let the old traditions be followed
and implemented in due course.
I, the survivor, recall the past with sorrow,
and am forever moved with emotion."
The Empress Dowager further ordered:
"Yù, in his extreme wickedness and brutality,
brought about his own destruction.
Although his crimes provoked this,
how can I not feel sorrow?
To abandon him as a commoner
is something I cannot bear.
He may be posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Cāngwú Commandery."
He was buried west of the suburban altar in Mòlíng County, Dānyáng.
Initially, Yù was in the Eastern Palace.
When he was five or six years old,
he began to study books,
but he was lazy in his studies and loved to play,
and his chief tutor could not restrain him.
He loved to climb along lacquered tent poles,
more than a *zhàng* (about ten feet) above the ground,
and would remain there for half an eating period
before coming down.
As he gradually grew older,
his moods became erratic,
and if those around him displeased him,
he would immediately strike them with his hands.
Walking barefoot and squatting became
his usual practice.
His chief tutor reported this to Tàizōng,
and the emperor would repeatedly order Yù's birth mother
to discipline him strictly with beatings.
When he succeeded to the throne,
he was inwardly fearful of the empress dowager
and outwardly apprehensive of the various high ministers,
so he could not yet act as he pleased.
After he came of age (underwent the capping ceremony),
his erratic behavior intensified,
and those inside and outside the palace were gradually unable to control him.
In the autumn and winter of the third year (of Yuánhuī),
he began to love going out and traveling.
The empress dowager (Tài Fēi) often rode in a green bamboo-woven carriage
to follow and supervise him.
Yù gradually became unrestrained,
and the empress dowager could no longer restrain him.
He would take only his personal attendants,
abandoning his retinue,
traveling ten or twenty *lǐ*,
or entering markets and residential areas,
or going to military camps and offices,
returning only at dusk.
In the spring and summer of the fourth year,
these excursions became even more frequent.
After the capital city was pacified,
his will became even more arrogant,
and so there was no day he did not go out.
He would race with his attendants Xiè Sēngzhì and Zhāng Wǔ'ér,
going out at night,
opening the Chéngmíng Gate,
leaving in the evening and returning in the morning,
or leaving in the morning and returning at dusk.
His followers all carried spears and lances,
and any pedestrians, men or women,
as well as dogs, horses, cattle, or donkeys,
who happened to be in their path, none escaped harm.
The common people were disturbed and afraid,
daring not to open their doors during the day,
and travelers on the roads almost disappeared.
He often wore short trousers and jackets,
never donning official robes and caps.
If anyone displeased him,
he would immediately inflict cruel punishments.
He had dozens of white wooden staves,
each with a name,
and torturers with needles, mallets, chisels, and saws
were never far from his side.
He once used an iron mallet to smash a man's genitals,
causing his attendants to knit their brows in distress.
Yù became furious,
ordered this person to bare his shoulder and stand upright,
and then stabbed his shoulder with a spear, piercing it through.
He kept dozens of donkeys in the Yàolíng Palace,
and his own riding horses
were kept beside the imperial bed.
Previously, there were rumors among the people
that Tàizōng was impotent,
and that Chén Tài Fēi was originally Lǐ Dào'ér's concubine.
Roadside talk
even claimed that Yù was Dào'ér's son.
Whenever Yù went in or out,
he often referred to himself as Liú Tǒng,
or adopted the title General Lǐ.
He had an illicit affair with a woman from the Right Guard Wing Litter Camp,
and whenever he went out with her,
he would carry several thousand coins
to cover the cost of wine and meat.
Ruǎn Diànfū's trusted confidant Zhāng Yáng was greatly relied upon by Diànfū.
When Diànfū was defeated and
fled, he was later captured.
Yù himself crushed him to death with a carriage at the Chéngmíng Gate.
Dù Yánzài, Shěn Bó, Dù Yǒuwén, and Sūn Chāo
all personally wielded spears and lances,
and carved flesh with their own hands.
He seized Yǒuwén's elder brother Shúwén north of Xuánwǔ Lake,
and Yù rode his horse, wielding a *shuò* (long spear),
personally going to stab him.
He had an open carriage made,
with a canopy on top,
which he rode in and out.
His followers numbered no more than several tens of people.
The imperial guard could not keep up with him;
and they all feared disaster,
also not daring to pursue him,
they merely maintained their ranks
and watched from a separate location.
As for all sorts of vulgar crafts,
he could master them at a glance,
such as forging gold and silver,
and tailoring clothes and making hats;
none of them were not exquisitely done.
He had never played the *chí* (flute),
yet when he held the instrument, it immediately produced a melody.
His nature was to love killing,
finding joy in it.
If there was nothing to do for a day,
he would feel sad and unhappy.
Within and outside the palace, among all officials,
no one felt safe,
and the palace departments were filled with anxiety and fear,
from evening till morning.
Qí Wáng, aligning with the will of heaven and men,
secretly plotted to depose and replace him.
He discussed this with the Commander of the Imperial Bodyguards, Wáng Jìngzé.
On the seventh day of the seventh month,
Yù rode in his open carriage,
followed by about two hundred people,
without any imperial procession or guard of honor.
He went to Qīngyuán Buddhist Nunnery,
and in the evening, he arrived at Xīn'ān Temple to drink wine with the Daoist monk Tándù.
Drunk,
he was helped back in the evening
to sleep in a felt tent east of Rénshòu Hall.
At this time, Yù would come and go without restraint,
and the various gates within the palace
were not closed at night.
Moreover, his subordinates feared encountering him,
and none dared to go out.
The palace guards all fled and hid,
and there was no internal or external restraint.

Wáng Jìngzé had already allied with Yù's attendants Yáng Yùfū, Yáng Wànnián, Lǚ Xīnzhī, Tāng Chéngzhī, Chén Fèngbó, Zhāng Shíliú, Luó Sēngzhì, Zhōng Qiānzài, Yán Dàofú, Léi Dàocì, Dài Zhāozǔ, Xǔ Qǐ, Qī Yuánbǎo, Shèng Dàotài, Zhōng Qiānqiū, Wáng Tiānbǎo, Gōngshàng Yánsūn, Yú Chéng, Qián Dàobǎo, Mǎ Jìngzhī, Chén Bǎozhí, Wú Qúzhī, Liú Yìnlǔ, Táng Tiānbǎo, Yú Sūn, and twenty-five others,
planning to seize Yù.
That evening,
Jìngzé went out.
Yùfū saw Yù deeply drunk and unaware of anything,
so he and Wànnián entered the felt tent
and used Yù's self-defense knife to kill him.
Fèngbó carried Yù's head,
and following the usual procedure,
claimed an imperial edict to open the Chéngmíng Gate and exited.
He gave the head to Jìngzé,
who galloped to the Commandery-General's office
and presented the head to Qí Wáng.
The King then donned his military attire,
led several tens of his attendants,
announced his return,
opened the Chéngmíng Gate, and entered.
Whenever Yù had opened the gate on other nights,
the gatekeepers were intimidated and dared not look,
so they did not suspect anything this time.
After Qí Wáng entered,
at dawn,
he then issued an order from the empress dowager to welcome Ánchéng Wáng.
The historian says: The rulers who lost their states and ruined their families,
though their ultimate paths were the same,
their initial departures might have been different.
The former deposed emperor indulged in low pleasures and illicit visits,
always using imperial carriages and regalia,
with warning calls clearing the way;
while the King of Cāngwú hid his imperial seal and carried his sash,
disguised himself as a commoner and forgot to return,
wearing a precarious hat and short clothes,
traveling alone on a single horse.
Yet regarding their downfall and the destruction of their reigns,
the principle was the same.
The flourishing of Jī and Xià dynasties,
though their substance and refinement differed,
the path to losing a state,
was it not also so?
Collation Notes
Annals Chapter 10: Shùn Dì
Emperor Shùn, personal name Zhǔn,
courtesy name Zhòngmóu,
nickname Zhìguān,
was the third son of Emperor Míng.
He was born on the *Guǐchǒu* day of the seventh month in the fifth year of Tàishǐ.
In the seventh year,
he was enfeoffed as Ánchéng Wáng,
with a stipend of three thousand households.
He was concurrently appointed General Who Guards the Army,
and assigned assistant officials.
When the deposed emperor ascended the throne,
he became the Inspector of Yángzhōu.
In the second year of Yuánhuī,
he was promoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs for Yáng and Nányù Provinces,
and granted a drum and pipe band,
while retaining his position as Inspector.
In the fourth year,
he was again promoted to Grand General of Agile Cavalry, given the privilege of establishing a *kāifǔ* (administrative office) with status equal to the Three Excellencies,
granted thirty attendants with swords,
and retained his positions as Grand Administrator and Inspector.
On the *wùzǐ* night of the seventh month of the fifth year of Yuánhuī,
the deposed emperor perished.
They welcomed the prince and moved him into the imperial hall.
On *rénchén*,
he ascended the imperial throne.
In the first year of Shēngmíng,
the era name was changed,
a great amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire,
and civil and military officials were granted two ranks.
On *jiǎwǔ*,
Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the Army), the Prince of Qí, went out to garrison Dōngchéng,
assisting in government and acting as prime minister.
On *bǐngshēn*,
an edict stated:
“The cessation of construction on the Terrace Pavilion glorified the Han virtue;
the burning of pheasant robes was a grand affair in the Jin way.
Thus, luxury was curbed and customs transformed,
and thrift was promoted to govern the populace.
Recently, the imperial domains have not been peaceful,
and military campaigns have continued for years.
Reserves have frequently been depleted,
and exhaustion cannot be quelled.
Yet, the adornments of vermilion and fresco
are costly beyond measure,
and the expenses of treasures and bribes
are immeasurable in terms of levies.
Now, the regulations for chariots and attire
should indeed be reduced,
so that insignia have order
and do not become extravagant.
The two offices of the Imperial Treasury can be abolished.
All elaborate carvings and engravings,
which damage customs and undermine governance,
are to be entirely prohibited.
This is to perpetually illustrate constitutional principles
and promote this new administration.”

Zhēng Xī Dà Jiāngjūn (General-in-Chief Who Conquers the West) and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Jīngzhōu), Shěn Yōuzhī, was promoted to Chējì Dà Jiāngjūn (General-in-Chief of Chariots and Cavalry) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (Establishing a Government Office with the Same Privileges as the Three Excellencies).

Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs), Zhōng Lǐngjūn (Director of the Central Army), Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the Army), and Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Nányǎnzhōu), the Prince of Qí, was made Sīkōng (Minister of Works), Lù Shàngshū Shì (Manager of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs), and Piàojì Dà Jiāngjūn (General-in-Chief of Agile Cavalry).
His governorship remained as before.

Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Central Secretariat), Wèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Guards), and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (Establishing a Government Office with the Same Privileges as the Three Excellencies),
Fǔ Jūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Protects the Army), Liú Bǐng, was made Shàngshū Lìng (Director of the Department of State Affairs),
and additionally Zhōng Jūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Central Army).

Ān Xī Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the West) and Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yǐngzhōu), Prince Xiè of Jìnxī, was made Fǔ Jūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Protects the Army) and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yángzhōu).
Prince Huì of Nányáng was made Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yǐngzhōu).
On *xīnchǒu*,
Shàngshū Yòu Púyè (Right Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs), Wáng Sēngqián, was made Shàngshū Púyè (Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs).
Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn (Right General of the Guards), Liú Yùn, was made Zhōng Lǐngjūn (Director of the Central Army).
Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Gold and Purple Seal) Wáng Kūn was made Yòu Guānglù Dàfū (Right Grand Master of Glorious Happiness).
Sīkōng (Minister of Works), the Prince of Qí, was granted five million coins
and five thousand bolts of cloth.
On *guǐmǎo*,
the imperial carriage visited the Grand Ancestral Temple.
On *bǐngwǔ*,
Ān Xī Cānjūn (Adjutant to the General Who Pacifies the West) Míng Qìngfú was made Cìshǐ (Governor) of Qīngzhōu and Jìzhōu.
Prince Zàn of Wǔlíng was made Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yǐngzhōu).
The newly appointed Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yǐngzhōu), Prince Huì of Nányáng, was made Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Xiāngzhōu).
Sīkōng (Minister of Works) and Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Nányǎnzhōu), the Prince of Qí, was given additional charge of Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Nánxúzhōu).
Zhēng Lǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the Barbarians), Lǐ Ānmín, was made Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Nányǎnzhōu).
Yōngzhōu suffered a great flood.
On *rénzǐ* of the eighth month,
an envoy was dispatched to provide relief,
and taxes and levies were exempted.
Piàojì Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk to the General of Agile Cavalry) Liú Chéngzhī was made Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Nányùzhōu).
Shānyáng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Shānyáng) Yú Tiānbǎo and Xīnwú Xiànzǐ (Viscount of Xīnwú) Qín Lì were found guilty
and died in prison.
On *wǔwǔ*,
the Píngzhǔn Shǔ (Office of Standardizing Measures) was reformed.
On *xīnyǒu*,
Xuānchéng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Xuānchéng) Lǐ Língqiān was made Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yǎnzhōu).
On *guǐhài*,
Sītú (Minister of the Masses) Yuán Càn garrisoned Shítou.
On *dīngmǎo*,
back taxes from before the first year were pardoned;
fief lands for commanderies and counties were restored.
On *wùchén*,
the Emperor’s birth mother, Chén Zhāohuá, was revered and appointed Huáng Tàifēi (Imperial Grand Consort Dowager).
On *gēngwǔ*,

Sīkōng Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works) Xiè Fēi, Wèi Jūn Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk to the General of the Guards) Jiāng Xiáo, Zhōngshū Shìláng (Gentleman of the Central Secretariat) Chǔ Xuàn, and Wǔlíng Wáng Wénxué (Literary Scholar to the Prince of Wǔlíng) Liú Hòu entered the palace to take up their posts,
participating in literary and moral discussions.
The Prince of Qí firmly declined the post of Sīkōng (Minister of Works).
On *gēngchén*,
he was made Piàojì Dà Jiāngjūn (General-in-Chief of Agile Cavalry) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (Establishing a Government Office with the Same Privileges as the Three Excellencies).
On *jǐchǒu* of the ninth month,
an edict stated:
“After the sagely kings passed away,
the pure customs declined,
the turtle books were forever lost,
and the dragon diagrams long hidden.
Hence, in the late Three Dynasties,
virtue and punishment were intertwined,
the world fell into competition,
and the Way was distorted by human flattery.
Yet, righteous scholars arrived in succession,
and extraordinary talents followed one after another.
I have received the mandate of the golden pivot,
inheriting the spiritual jade extreme.
Governing from behind the screen,
I forget fatigue even late in the day,
pondering rise and fall,
and reflecting on antiquity fills my thoughts.
The records of Jī and Xià
are still preserved in silk scrolls;
the remaining writings of Hàn and Wèi
are found in square tablets.
Thus, Yuánfēng established the system of *màocái* (flourishing talents),
and Dìjié initiated the ranking of *dúxíng* (solitary conduct).
To revitalize the foundation,
the priority is to find worthy individuals.
Now, it is permissible to issue proclamations to the provinces and commanderies,
to search out the obscure and hidden,
and to select from townships and villages,
recommending them by name.
I will personally review them
to discern their flourishing uniqueness.
May there be no forgotten talents in the wilds,
to eternally inspire distant excellence.”
On *jǐyǒu*,
Prince Gǎo of Lúlíng passed away.
On *jǐyǒu* of the eleventh month of winter,
the king of Wōguó sent envoys to offer local products.
On *bǐngwǔ*,
Yuánwài Sànjí Shìláng (Supernumerary Palace Attendant Censor) Hú Xiànshēng acted as Yuèzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yuèzhōu).
Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Jiāozhōu) Shěn Jǐngdé was made Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Guǎngzhōu).
On *dīngsì* of the twelfth month,
Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (General of Swift Cavalry) Wáng Guǎngzhī was made Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Xúzhōu).
Chējì Dà Jiāngjūn (General-in-Chief of Chariots and Cavalry) and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Jīngzhōu) Shěn Yōuzhī raised an army in rebellion.
On *dīngmǎo*,
Lù Gōng (Manager of Public Affairs), the Prince of Qí, entered to guard the imperial hall.
Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) Xiāo Yí garrisoned the eastern mansion.
On *wùchén*,
internal and external defenses were tightened.
On *jǐsì*,
Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yǐngzhōu), Prince Zàn of Wǔlíng, was made Ān Xī Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the West) and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Jīngzhōu).
Zhēng Lǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the Barbarians) and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yōngzhōu) Zhāng Jìng'ér was promoted to Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the Army).
Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn (Right General of the Guards) Huáng Huí was made Píng Xī Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the West) and Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yǐngzhōu),
and commanded the vanguard of various armies in the southern campaign.
Zhēng Lǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the Barbarians) Lǚ Ānguó was made Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Xiāngzhōu).
Dūguān Shàngshū (Minister of the Bureau of Supply) Wáng Kuān was additionally made Píng Xī Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the West).
On *gēngwǔ*,

the newly appointed Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn (Left General of the Guards), the heir of the Prince of Qí, accompanied the newly appointed Fǔ Jūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Protects the Army) and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yángzhōu), Prince Xiè of Jìnxī, to garrison Pénchéng in Xúnyáng.

Shàngshū Lìng (Director of the Department of State Affairs) Liú Bǐng, Huángmén Shìláng (Palace Attendant) Liú Shù, and Guānjūn Wáng (Prince of Champion) Yùn led their forces to join him.

Huáng Huí, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General Who Assists the State) Sūn Tán'guàn, Tú Qí Xiàowèi (Colonel of Cavalry) Wáng Yíxīng, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General Who Assists the State) Rèn Hòubó, and Zuǒ Jūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Left Army) Péng Wénzhī secretly allied with them.

The rest were not investigated.
Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yùzhōu) Liú Huáizhēn, Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yōngzhōu) Zhāng Jìng'ér, and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Guǎngzhōu) Chén Xiǎndá all raised righteous armies.
Sīzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Sīzhōu) Yáo Dàohé, Liángzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Liángzhōu) Fàn Bǎinián, and Xiāngzhōu Xíngshì (Acting Governor of Xiāngzhōu) Yǔ Pèiyù gathered forces with wavering loyalty.

Shàngshū Púyè (Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs) Wáng Sēngqián was made Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs).

Wú Jùn Tàishǒu (Administrator of Wú Commandery) Liú Xiá rebelled, seizing his commandery.

Shěn Yōuzhī attacked and besieged Yǐngchéng.

Wúxīng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Wúxīng) Shěn Wénjì attacked and beheaded him.
On *jǐhài*,
internal and external defenses were tightened,

The historian comments: A sagely king receives the mandate,
not because they succeed to chaos or take over in decline,
but because the heavenly mandate arrives.
Since the time of the Sān Wǔ [Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors],
no ruler who received the mandate
has failed to rise at the very peak of collapse and ruin,
and then attain the destiny of universal acclamation.
The Water Virtue declined and departed
a long time ago;
how could it be limited to the mere abdication in Rǔyīn?
Collated Notes
Treatise One, Preface to Treatises, Treatises on Pitch-pipes and Calendar, Part One
The left historian records words,
the right historian records events.
Events are what the Chūnqiū [Spring and Autumn Annals] is about,
words are what the Shàngshū [Book of Documents] is about.
As for the chapters in Chǔ Shū [Book of Chǔ], Zhèng Zhì [Records of Zhèng], Jìn Chéng [Annals of Jìn], and Chǔ Wù [Chronicles of Chǔ],
all of these were for the purpose of clarifying and expounding upon previous histories,
so that they would not be forgotten by later generations.
Sīmǎ Qiān compiled his own work,
and first distinguished names and topics.
However, regarding rites, ceremonies, punishments, and government,
there were things he did not exhaust.
Thus, beyond the Annals and Biographies,
he originally established eight treatises (shū),
recording every fragment of text and every single event,
from the grand to the minute.
Bān Shì followed this,
not deviating from the former model,
encompassing an entire generation,
and the ramifications consequently broadened.
The names of Lǜlì [Pitch-pipes and Calendar] and Lǐyuè [Rites and Music]
remained unchanged.
He changed Tiānguān [Heavenly Offices] to Tiānwén [Astronomy],
changed Fēngshàn [Sacrifices to Heaven and Earth] to Jiāosì [Suburban Sacrifices],
altered the terms Huòzhí [Money-making] and Píngzhǔn [Stabilization],
and reformed the names Héqu [River Canals] and Gōuxù [Irrigation Ditches].
He appended the words of Sūn Qīng [Xúnzǐ]
to narrate Xíngfǎ [Punishments and Law],
and excerpted from the book of Mèng Kē [Mencius]
to preface Shíhuò [Food and Commodities].
Liú Xiàng's Hóngfàn [Grand Norm]
began with the Chūnqiū.
Liú Xīn's Qīlüè [Seven Summaries]
separated the Ruists and Mohists into different sections.
Zhū Gàn broadly collected folk songs,
which was especially detailed and thorough.
These were all adopted and continued,
to form the three Treatises.
However, the Lǐyuè [Rites and Music] treatise was brief and simple,
with many omissions;
of the codes, statutes, and affairs,
it recorded not even one in a hundred.
Although Tiānwén [Astronomy] was comprehensive,
it did not discuss the form of heaven,
which led to the divergent theories of the Three Heavens
being impossible to distinguish clearly.
This is why Cài Yǒng presented a memorial from Shuòfāng,
saying that these should be recorded.
When the Hàn arose,
it followed the Qín's burying of scholars.
The classic texts were incomplete,
and the elderly scholars
were constantly worried about their loss.
Liú Xīn's Qīlüè [Seven Summaries],
which was indeed the Yìwén Zhì [Treatise on Literature],
was created for this reason.
The Yellow River flows eastward from Lóngmén,
spanning across Zhōngguó [China].
Whenever it overflowed and burst its banks,
the damage was severe and burdensome.
The effort of building dikes
taxed the whole country.
Furthermore, Guān [Guānzhōng] and Luò [Luòyáng] are high and dry,
with few rivers and springs.
Thus, Hào, Fēng, Láo, and Jué [names of rivers/canals]
were all included in the rites.
The richness of Zhāng, Fǔ, Zhèng, and Bái [names of rivers/canals],
and the benefits of irrigation from ditches,
were all foundational to the people's lives;
the state regarded them as heaven.
Establishing a treatise on Gōuxù [Irrigation Ditches]
was therefore appropriate.
Times change and affairs alter;
today, it can be abbreviated.
I humbly submit that Bān Shì's Lǜlì [Pitch-pipes and Calendar]
has already detailed previous matters.
Since Yáng Wěi's revision and creation of the Jǐngchū calendar,
the Wèi Shū [History of Wèi] lacks a treatise.
And since Yuánjiā's major revision to create a new method,
and Dàmíng's extensive discussions and changes,
from Wèi to Sòng,
these should be included in the present book.
Bān Gù's Lǐyuè [Rites and Music] and Jiāosì [Suburban Sacrifices],
Mǎ Biāo's Jìsì [Sacrifices] and Lǐyí [Ceremonies],
Cài Yǒng's Cháohuì [Court Assemblies],
and Dǒng Bā's Yúfú [Carriages and Attire]
each established treatises.
However, the scope of rites
is not limited to one function.
Suburban sacrifices, court banquets,
are not separate matters.
Banners, insignia, clothing, and objects—
what are they if not rites?
Now I will combine and edit them,
calling them all the Lǐ Zhì [Treatise on Rites].
As for Xíngfǎ [Punishments and Law] and Shíhuò [Food and Commodities],
previous explanations are already comprehensive.
Following their respective branches,
they are appended to the Annals and Biographies.
The Lè Jīng [Classic of Music] has been incomplete
for a long time.
What Bān Shì described
was merely an excerpt from the Lè Jì [Record of Music].
Mǎ Biāo's Hòu Shū [Later History]
also did not completely continue it.
As for the eight sounds and various instruments,
they are not recorded in books.
Although some appear in the Shìběn [Genealogical Records],
many are still missing.
Even the refined and vulgar
sections of odes and folk songs
have all been omitted,
without even a general mention.
The music for suburban temples
changed with each era.
There are still surviving texts of ancient and refined music.
Furthermore, examining the current drum and wind music
and the nǎogē [military songs],
though they have chapters and tunes,
musicians learn and pass them down
orally from their masters and ancestors.
Their focus is on the sound,
not on first instructing in its meaning.
Comparing the current Yuèfǔ nǎogē [Music Bureau military songs]
with the old tunes of Hàn and Wèi,
the tune names are sometimes the same,
but the lyrics are perpetually different.
Searching for meaning in the text,
not a single one is comprehensible.
I do not know what era's tunes
the current nǎozhāng [military songs] belong to.
In this treatise, from the suburban temples downwards,
all musical pieces,
that are not licentious songs,
are recorded in detail.
As for Tiānwén [Astronomy] and Wǔxíng [Five Phases],
after Mǎ Biāo,
there are no further records.
Hé Shū's began from the start of Huángchū,
and Xú Zhì's initiated at the beginning of Yìxī.
Now, connecting Wèi to Hàn,
we shall follow Hé Shì's approach.
Thus, from the first winter of the fifth year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn
to the first summer of the second year of Shèng Míng under Emperor Shùn of Sòng,
the two luminaries and six atmospheric disturbances
have no discrepancies in their jiǎzǐ cycles.
Sagely emperors and wise kings
all have records of auspicious mandates,
which serve to sacralize the precious throne
and secretly assist the auspicious portents,
hoping to quell ambitions for the throne
and prevent covetousness from arising.
The writings like those concerning holding the river and encompassing the earth,
with green patterns and red characters,
speak of this in detail.
Furthermore, when the Way reaches heaven, sweet dew descends;
when virtue penetrates the earth, sweet springs emerge.
The auspicious signs of golden ganoderma and black millet,
and the auspicious portents of crimson grass and white crows,
these indeed cannot be falsely reported.
However, if in a declining age, virtue wanes,
and yet auspicious responses do not cease,
this indeed means that the Way of Heaven is obscure,
and difficult to predict by calculation.
It is also like a brilliant ruler being in power,
and yet earthquake and eclipse disasters are not stopped;
all spirits are compliant,
and yet the celestial phenomena alone deviate.
Now, I establish the Fúruì Zhì [Treatise on Auspicious Omens] to supplement the omissions of previous histories.
Geographical divisions were complex,
and it was difficult to comprehensively clarify matters.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
there have been hundreds of shifts and migrations.
One commandery was divided into four or five,
and one county was split into two or three.
Perhaps yesterday it belonged to Jīng or Yù,
but today it is subordinate to Sī or Yǎn.
In the morning one might be a scholar from Líng or Guì,
and in the evening a commoner from Lú or Jiǔ.
The comings and goings were tumultuous,
without a moment's rest.
Registers and maps were thereby confused,
and the Ministry of Works was unable to record them.
Since the Róng Dí invaded internally,
and the Jìn dynasty moved eastward,
the remnants of the Central Plains
scattered and migrated beyond the Jiāng River.
The territories of Yōu, Bìng, Jì, Yōng, Yǎn, Yù, Qīng, and Xú
were all engulfed by the rebels.
From those who were forced to bundle up their feet and offer their heads,
to those who escaped to Jīng or Yuè,
hundreds of commanderies and thousands of cities
were filled with transient residents.
People yearned for the song of the wild geese,
and scholars harbored thoughts of returning to their origins.
None failed to establish their own states and districts,
hoping to restore their old homelands.
However, with sparse populations and few households,
they could not build independently.
Thus, there were Hán settlements in Wèi territory,
and Zhào people in Qí counties.
Moreover, changes in administrative divisions were frequent,
shifting daily and monthly.
Temporary residents moved about,
and there was no permanent settlement.
Therefore, state names and district designations
were difficult to record in detail.
When the great Sòng received the mandate,
it reopened border defenses.
The five prefectures north of the Huái River
were cut off and became rebel territory.
Those who fled or were scattered
re-established commanderies and counties.
This refers to the Yuánjiā and Tàishǐ eras,
where names were the same but realities different.
Now, taking the two treatises of Bān Gù and Mǎ Biāo,
and the court records of Jìn and Sòng,
along with all other notes and records,
I have thoroughly examined them.
I have analyzed each entry,
making sure everything is comprehensive and detailed.
For the establishment of various offices,
there are already previous accounts.
Tracing the source and following the stream
makes the task easier.
In the Yuánjiā era,
Hé Chéngtiān of Dōnghǎi received an imperial decree to compile the Sòngshū.
His fifteen treatises
were intended to continue Mǎ Biāo's Hànshū treatise.
Where his evidence and citations were comprehensive and extensive,
I have followed them.
This is also like Bān Gù and Mǎ Qiān both belonging to the same school.
As for omissions and deficiencies,
and events after Hé's time,
I have thoroughly gathered information
and supplemented and mended them as appropriate.
The source flows widely and diffusely,
not something my solitary learning can fully grasp;
my feet are lame and the path is long,
how can a short plan succeed?
Although I have weighed the previous histories
and seen both their beauty and their flaws,
yet affections and preferences differ,
and choices vary.
Whenever I held the brush and grasped the bamboo slips,
I forgot to eat while working.
Ultimately, I am not fit to run alongside Bān and Zuǒ,
or ride in tandem with Dǒng and Nán.
I merely hope to be a whetstone for the gentlemen of later generations.
The Huángdì commanded Líng Lún to go west of Dàxià,
to the north of Ruǎn Yú,
and take bamboo growing in the Xiègǔ valley,
whose internodes were thick and even.
He was to cut a section between two nodes and blow into it,
to make the *huángzhōng* pitch.
He then fashioned twelve pipes,
to listen to the phoenix's call,
and to establish the *lǜlǚ* (musical scale).
Sounds have clear and turbid qualities,
thus they are harmonized with *gōngshāng*;
shapes have long and short dimensions,
thus they are measured with *zhàngchǐ*;
vessels have large and small capacities,
thus they are fixed with *húdǒu*;
substances have light and heavy weights,
thus they are balanced with *jūnshí*.
Therefore, the Yúshū says:
"Then he unified the *lǜ*, measures, capacities, and weights."
Thus, *lǜlǚ*
is the origin of *gōngshāng*.
Music has instruments and movements,
it has emotion and function.
Bells, drums, shields, and axes
are the instruments of music;
bending, stretching, quickness, and slowness
are the movements of music;
"Orderly relations without calamity
are the emotion of music;
joy, delight, and love
are the function of music."
"Therefore, the *jūnzǐ* turns inward to harmonize his will,
and expands music to achieve education.
Thus he can have deep emotions and clear literary expression,
abundant energy and divine transformation.
Harmony and compliance accumulate within,
and brilliance manifests outwardly."
Therefore it is said:
"Music
is the movement of the heart;
sound
is the manifestation of music."
The Zhōulǐ says:
"Then perform the *huángzhōng*,
sing the *dàlǚ*,
and dance the *yúnmén*,
to worship the celestial deities.
Then perform the *tàicù*,
sing the *yìngzhōng*,
and dance the *xiánchí*,
to sacrifice to the terrestrial deities."
For the four cardinal directions, mountains, rivers, and ancestors,
each had its own music.
It also says:
"The *yuánzhōng* is the *gōng*,
the *huángzhōng* is the *jiǎo*,
the *tàicù* is the *zhǐ*,
the *gūxǐ* is the *yǔ*;
the thunder drum and thunder rattle-drum,
the pipes of Gūzhú,
the *qín* and *sè* of Yúnhé,
the dance of Yúnmén,
on the winter solstice,
are performed on the circular mound on the ground.
If the music transforms six times,
then all celestial deities descend,
and can be accorded proper rites."
For terrestrial deities and human ghosts,
the rites are also similar.
Its ability to move beings and inspire transformation is indeed profound like this.
"The Way begins with one;
one gives birth to two;
two gives birth to three;
three times three is nine.
Therefore, the number of the Huángzhōng is six,
divided into twelve *cí* and *xióng* bells.
A bell is formed by three,
thus placing one and multiplying it by three,
the total integral is 177,147,
which is the actual quantity of the Huángzhōng.
Therefore, the Huángzhōng is positioned at *Zǐ*,
governs the eleventh month,
and gives birth downwards to the Línzhōng.
The number of the Línzhōng is fifty-four,
governs the sixth month,
and gives birth upwards to the Tàicù.
The number of the Tàicù is seventy-two,
governs the first month,
and gives birth downwards to the Nánlǚ.
The number of the Nánlǚ is forty-eight,
governs the eighth month,
and gives birth upwards to the Gūxǐ.
The number of the Gūxǐ is sixty-four,
governs the third month,
and gives birth downwards to the Yìngzhōng.
The number of the Yìngzhōng is forty-three,
governs the tenth month,
and gives birth upwards to the Ruíbīn.
The number of the Ruíbīn is fifty-seven,
governs the fifth month,
and gives birth upwards to the Dàlǚ.
The number of the Dàlǚ is seventy-six,
governs the twelfth month,
and gives birth downwards to the Yízé.
The number of the Yízé is fifty-one,
governs the seventh month,
and gives birth upwards to the Jiázhōng.
The number of the Jiázhōng is sixty-seven,
governs the second month,
and gives birth downwards to the Wúshè.
The number of the Wúshè is forty-five,
governs the ninth month,
and gives birth upwards to the Zhōnglǚ.
The number of the Zhōnglǚ is sixty,
governs the fourth month,
and does not give birth further.
(It does not give birth further,
meaning the bells and pitches can no longer generate each other again.)
Gōng gives birth to Zhǐ,
Zhǐ gives birth to Shāng,
Shāng gives birth to Yǔ,
Yǔ gives birth to Jué,
Jué gives birth to Gūxǐ,
Gūxǐ gives birth to Yìngzhōng,
which corresponds to the main tone,
therefore it is in harmony.
(Gūxǐ is in the third month,
Yìngzhōng in the tenth month,
matching the main tone,
hence it is in harmony.
Harmony [Hé],
means following the sound.)
Yìngzhōng gives birth to Ruíbīn,
Ruíbīn does not correspond to the main tone,
therefore it is a discord.
(Discord [Miù],
means the sounds clash.
The Zhōu dynasty pitches therefore had discords and harmonies,
which were the seven tones used by King Wǔ [Wǔ Wáng] to conquer Zhòu [Zhòu Wáng].)
On the winter solstice,
the sound corresponding to the Línzhōng gradually becomes murky;
on the summer solstice,
the sound corresponding to the Huángzhōng gradually becomes clear.
The twelve-month pitches correspond to the twenty-four solar terms.
*Jiǎzǐ* is the Zhǐ of Zhōnglǚ;
*Bǐngzǐ* is the Yǔ of Jiázhōng;
*Wùzǐ* is the Gōng of Huángzhōng;
*Gēngzǐ* is the Shāng of Wúshè;
*Rénzǐ* is the Jué of Yízé."
"Ancient people's measurements of length, capacity, and weight
all originated from the Way of Heaven.
The pitch pipe of Huángzhōng is nine *cùn* long.
Things are generated by three;
three times three is nine;
three times nine is twenty-seven.
Therefore, a bolt of cloth is two *chǐ* and seven *cùn* wide,
which was the ancient system.
Sounds are generated by eight mutually;
therefore, a person is eight *chǐ* tall.
A *xún* is double this;
therefore, eight *chǐ* makes a *xún*.
Where there is form, there is sound.
The number of sounds is five.
Multiplying five by eight,
forty *chǐ* makes a *pǐ*.
A *pǐ*
is the measure for an average person;
one *pǐ* was the standard.
At the autumn equinox, the awns of the grain are settled.
(The awn [Mèng]
is the spikelet of the grain.)
When the awns are settled, the grain ripens.
The number of pitches is twelve.
Therefore, twelve awns correspond to one grain of millet;
twelve grains of millet correspond to one *cùn*.
The pitches correspond to the earthly branches;
the sounds correspond to the heavenly stems.
The number of heavenly stems is ten.
Therefore, ten *cùn* make one *chǐ*;
ten *chǐ* make one *zhàng*.
As for weight,
twelve grains of millet correspond to one *fēn*;
twelve *fēn* correspond to one *zhū*;
twelve *zhū* correspond to half a *liǎng*.
A balance has left and right sides,
thus it is doubled.
Therefore, twenty-four *zhū* correspond to one *liǎng*.
Heaven has four seasons,
completing one year,
thus it is quadrupled.
Four times four is sixteen.
Therefore, sixteen *liǎng* make one *jīn*.
Three months make one season;
thirty days make one month.
Therefore, thirty *jīn* make one *jūn*.
Four seasons make one year.
Therefore, four *jūn* make one *dàn*."
"As for sounds,
one pitch generates five tones;
twelve pitches make sixty tones.
Multiplying by six,
six times six is thirty-six.
Therefore, three hundred and sixty tones correspond to the days of one year.
Thus, the numbers of the pitches and the calendar
are the Way of Heaven and Earth.
Those generated downwards are doubled,
then divided by three;
those generated upwards are quadrupled,
then divided by three."
Yáng Zǐyún said:
"Sounds are generated by the heavenly stems,
(meaning *Jiǎ* and *Jǐ* are Jué;
*Yǐ* and *Gēng* are Shāng;
*Bǐng* and *Xīn* are Zhǐ;
*Dīng* and *Rén* are Yǔ;
*Wù* and *Guǐ* are Gōng.)
Pitches are generated by the earthly branches,
(meaning *Zǐ* is Huángzhōng and its likes.)
Sounds are based on their nature,
(Nature [Zhì]
means correctness.
Each takes its original nature as correct.)
Pitches harmonize the sounds.
(One should use pitch pipes and bells to equalize [Jūn]
their clear and murky sounds.)
When sounds and pitches harmonize and accord,
then the eight musical instruments [Bāyīn] are produced.
(Accord [Xié]
means harmony.)
Gōng, Shāng, Jué, Zhǐ, Yǔ
are called the five tones [Wǔshēng].
Metal, stone, gourd, hide, silk, bamboo, earth, and wood
are called the eight musical instruments [Bāyīn].
When sounds are harmonious and instruments are in accord,
this is called the five musical forms [Wǔyuè]."
When yin and yang are in harmony, the shadows arrive;
when the lǜ-qì responds, the ashes scatter.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven regularly presides over the front hall at the winter and summer solstices,
assembling scholars of the eight abilities,
arranging the eight sounds,
listening to the uniformity of music,
measuring the length of shadows,
observing the pitch-pipes (zhōng-lǜ),
weighing earth and charcoal,
and verifying yin and yang.
At the winter solstice, when the yang energy responds,
the musical harmony is clear,
the shadow is at its longest,
the Huángzhōng pipe resonates,
and the earth and charcoal become lighter, causing the balance to tilt up.
At the summer solstice, when the yin energy responds,
the musical harmony is turbid,
the shadow is at its shortest,
the Ruíbīn pipe resonates,
and the earth and charcoal become heavier, causing the balance to tilt down.
Within five days before and after these solstices,
each of the eight able scholars reports their observations.
The Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐ Lìng) seals and submits these reports.
If the verification is successful, it indicates harmony;
otherwise, it foretells an omen.
The method for observing the qì involves
constructing a chamber with three layers,
its doors closed,
and its cracks sealed tightly with plaster,
then hanging gauze curtains.
Inside the chamber, wooden tables are arranged,
one for each lǜ-pipe,
lower on the inside and higher on the outside,
following their respective directions.
The lǜ-pipes are placed upon them.
Reeds and cattail ashes are spread inside their ends,
and observations are made according to the calendar.
When the qì arrives, the ashes move.
When the ashes are moved by the qì, they scatter;
when moved by people or wind,
they gather.
For observations within the palace,
twelve jade lǜ-pipes are used.
Only at the two solstices are observations made at the Spirit Terrace (Língtái),
using sixty bamboo lǜ-pipes.
Bamboo from Jīnménshān in Yíyáng Xiàn, Hóngnóng Commandery, is used for the pipes,
and reeds from Hénèi Commandery for the ashes.
As the Three Dynasties declined,
musical pitch and the calendar fell into disorder.
With the rise of the Hàn dynasty,
Běipíng Hóu Zhāng Cāng first established the lǜ-lì (pitch-pipes and calendar).
During the reign of Xiàowǔ,
an office for harmonizing lǜ-pipes (Xiélǜ) was established.
In the time of Yuándì,
the Langzhong Jīng Fáng understood the numbers of the five tones and sixty lǜ-pipes,
having studied under Xiǎohuáng Lìng Jiāo Yánshòu.
His "lower generation" (xiàshēng) and "upper generation" (shàngshēng)
finally reached Zhōnglǚ,
and the twelve lǜ-pipes were complete.
From Zhōnglǚ, the "upper generation" started "zhíshǐ" (執始),
from "zhíshǐ," the "lower generation" proceeded to "qùmìe" (去滅),
ending at "nánshì" (南事),
and the sixty lǜ-pipes were complete.
The transformation of the twelve lǜ-pipes into sixty
is like the transformation of the eight trigrams into sixty-four.
Fúxī created the Yì,
recording the beginning of yang energy,
and used this as the lǜ-law.
He established the sound for the winter solstice as the beginning,
taking Huángzhōng as the gōng tone,
Tàicù as the shāng tone,
Gūxǐ as the jué tone,
Línzhōng as the zhǐ tone,
Nánlǚ as the yǔ tone,
Yìngzhōng as the biàngōng,
and Ruíbīn as the biànzhǐ.
These are the origin of sounds and qì,
the correct form of the five tones.
Thus, each governs one day.
The others circulate in sequence,
with the tone corresponding to the day serving as its own gōng,
and shāng, jué, zhǐ, and yǔ following it by analogy.
The Lǐyùn chapter says:
"The five sounds, six lǜ, and twelve pipes cycle and become each other's gōng."
This is what is meant.
With the sixty lǜ-pipes dividing the days of one cycle,
Huángzhōng begins at the winter solstice,
and returns at the winter solstice,
from which prognostications of yin and yang, cold and warmth, wind and rain arise.
Jīng Fáng also said:
"The sound of bamboo cannot be used to determine tuning,
so I made a zhǔn (pitch-standard) to fix the numbers.
The zhǔn resembles a sè (zither),
one zhàng long with thirteen strings,
with the main interval nine chǐ,
corresponding to the nine cūn of the Huángzhōng lǜ-pipe;
a central string,
below which are markings in cūn,
to determine the clear and turbid pitches of the sixty lǜ-pipes."
Jīng Fáng's discourse on the lǜ-pipes is more detailed than that submitted by Liú Xīn,
[一一] his method was implemented by the imperial historians (shǐguān)
and used by the observation department.
The Xù Hàn Zhì (Continuation of the Hàn History) fully records his lǜ-zhǔn dimensions.
In the first year of Yuánhé (84 CE) of Hàn Zhāngdì,
Yīn Róng, an official awaiting orders to observe the zhōng-lǜ, submitted a memorial stating:
"The government has no one who understands the sixty lǜ-pipes to calibrate the musical tones with the zhǔn.
Therefore, I, Yán Sōng, an official awaiting orders, have fully taught the zhǔn method to my son, Xuān,
and I request that Xuān be summoned and appointed to the academy,
to be in charge of tuning musical instruments."
An imperial edict stated:
"If Sōng's son truly understands the lǜ-pipes,
can distinguish their families,
and harmonize their sounds,
let him be rigorously tested.
He must not rely on his father's learning,
pretending to hear when deaf.
Sounds are subtle,
if only one is wrong, no one knows;
if only one is right, no one understands.
By playing the lǜ-pipes incorrectly,
if he can identify the twelve lǜ-pipes without a single error,
then he will be deemed capable of transmitting Sōng's learning."
Xuān was tested on the twelve lǜ-pipes;
he got two right,
four wrong,
and for six he did not know which lǜ they were.
Xuān was consequently dismissed.
From then on, no lǜ-pipe expert could create a zhǔn.
In the sixth year of Xīpíng (177 CE) of Língdì,
the Dōngguān (Eastern Hall) summoned Zhāng Guāng and others, palace attendants in charge of lǜ-pipes, to ask about the meaning of the zhǔn.
Zhāng Guāng and the others did not know.
They returned to examine old collections
and found the instrument,
whose form and construction matched Jīng Fáng's writings,
yet they still could not determine the tension of its strings.
Sound cannot be written to enlighten people;
[一二] those who knew wished to teach but had no means,
those who instinctively understood had physical knowledge but no teacher.
Thus, the imperial historians capable of distinguishing clear and turbid pitches were lost.
That which could be transmitted
was only the observation of qì.

Discussion: The lǜ and lǚ pipes are generated by "dividing by three and increasing or decreasing."
Previous scholars derived the twelve lǜ-pipes,
from zǐ to hài.
Each is multiplied by three,
totaling 177,147,
and then reduced by three.
This is the "upper generation."
Therefore, the Hàn Zhì states: "Subtracting one-third generates Línzhōng (lower generation),
adding one-third generates Tàicù (upper generation)."
Since Wúshè generates Zhōnglǚ (upper generation),
then Zhōnglǚ should again generate Huángzhōng (upper generation).
Only then can the five sounds, six lǜ, and twelve pipes cycle and become each other's gōng.
However, the current "upper generation" falls short of Huángzhōng by 2,384.
Divided by nine, this is actually 1,968 for one fēn.
This means the nine-cūn lǜ-pipe is incomplete by more than one fēn.
How then can they cycle and become each other's gōng?
Generally, adding one-third is for "upper generation,"
and subtracting one-third is for "lower generation."
This is the broad outline,
like the four quarters of the celestial circle.
Jīng Fáng did not consider this meaning;
he made a slight increase to the twelve lǜ-pipes
and then extended them,
from Zhōnglǚ generating zhíshǐ (upper generation),
and zhíshǐ generating qùmìe (lower generation),
to nánshì,
resulting in sixty lǜ-pipes.
Ultimately, they still did not match,
further increasing the discrepancy.
Bān Gù's records
fail to fully grasp the fundamental origin of the lǜ and lǚ.
He merely explains jué as 'touch' (chù),
zhǐ as 'blessing' (zhǐ),
and the yang qì seeding itself in Huángzhōng,
and similar matters,
needlessly complicating his text
and indulging in verbosity.
Furthermore, he derived the numbers nine and six,
desiring them to conform to Liú Xīn's "Three Systems" numbers,
falsely associating dissimilar things
to embellish his theories.
These are all the errors of Mèngjiān (Bān Gù).
Cài Yōng (蔡邕) submitted a memorial from Shuòfāng (朔方),
stating that the former Hàn (漢) treatise only recorded the twelve lǜ (律),
〔二五〕not the sixty.
The dimensions and creation of the six lǜ (律) were all recorded by Sīmǎ Biāo (司馬彪).
At the end of the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
the yǎyuè (雅樂) was lost.
During the Huángchū (黃初) reign,
the caster Chái Yù (柴玉) was skillful and imaginative,
making many innovations
in the forms of instruments.
The Colonel of Harmonizing Music, Dù Kuí (杜夔), ordered Yù (玉) to cast bells,
but their pitches, whether clear or turbid,
often did not conform to the standards.
After numerous destructions and reconstructions,
Yù (玉) became very annoyed,
telling Kuí (夔) that the pitches were arbitrary.
They then complained to the King of Wèi (魏王) about each other.
The King of Wèi (魏王) took the bells cast by Yù (玉),
mixed and tested them again,
and only then realized Kuí (夔) was skilled.
Thereupon, Yù (玉) and his sons were punished,
all made stablemen.
〔二六〕
In the tenth year of Tàishǐ (泰始) of the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
the Palace Secretary Xún Xù (荀勗) and the Director of the Palace Secretariat Zhāng Huà (張華)
brought out twenty-five sets of bronze and bamboo lǜ (律) from the imperial treasury.
They ordered the Grand Music Director Liú Xiù (劉秀) and others to test them.
Three sets were consistent with the lǜfǎ (律法) of Dù Kuí (杜夔) and Zuǒ Yánnián (左延年).
As for the other twenty-two sets,
examining their inscriptions and dimensions,
they were dìlǜ (笛律) (flute pitches).
They questioned the Colonel of Harmonizing Music, Liè Hé (列和),
who replied:
“In the time of Emperor Míng of Wèi (魏明帝),
Hé (和) was ordered to receive flute sounds
to make these lǜ (律),
intending for scholars to reside in a separate quarter,
singing, studying, and practicing,
tuning according to these lǜ (律).
When it came to harmonizing all music,
by merely recognizing the names of their dimensions,
then stringed instruments, wind instruments, and singing
could all achieve harmony.
For those with turbid singing voices,
long flutes and long lǜ (律) were used;
for those with clear singing voices,
short flutes and short lǜ (律) were used.
Generally, the system of tuning stringed instruments and singing for clear and turbid pitches
cannot be understood unless named according to the dimensions of the flute.”
Xù (勗) and others memorialized:
“In ancient times, when the former kings created music,
it was to invigorate customs,
to appease gods and bless the worthy.
〔二七〕It had to conform to the harmony of lǜlǚ (律呂),
to regulate the pitches of the eight sounds.
〔二八〕Therefore, for suburban sacrifices, court assemblies, and banquets,
its use had regulations,
with distinctions in singing and playing,
and appropriate clear and turbid pitches.
Hence it is said, ‘The five sounds and twelve lǜ (律)
revolve to become the gōng (宮) scale.’
This is known from the classics, commentaries, and records.
As Hé (和) replied,
the lengths of flutes
had no imitative standard,
but were made according to whim,
without following any established measure.
When examined against proper lǜ (律),
they all did not correspond,
and when their sounds were played,
they were often disharmonious.
He also stated: ‘My former teacher transmitted flutes,
distinguishing their clear and turbid pitches
simply by their lengths,
crafted by artisans,
not traditionally according to lǜ (律).’
This means that the making of flutes had no method.
Yet Hé (和) transcribed flutes to create lǜ (律),
〔二九〕and furthermore made qín (琴), sè (瑟), and singing
follow them as correct,
which is not the way to examine ancient sages
and establish laws for posterity.
We respectfully list all the lǜ (律) and question Hé’s (和) intentions as stated below.
And according to the canonical system,
we made twelve flute models based on the twelve lǜ (律),
with harmonious sounds
and convenient instruments.
When practicing and performing,
they must conform to lǜlǚ (律呂),
how much more so when used for banquets of all nations
and performed in the ancestral temple!
Although Líng (伶) and Kuí (夔) are distant figures,
and ultimate music is difficult to master,
it is still appropriate to emulate the ancients
〔三０〕to seek the core truth,
conforming to ritual,
making the system detailed.
If it can be implemented,
please reassign flute artisans,
select bamboo for crafting,
and send it to the Grand Music Office and Music Bureau for implementation.
〔三一〕Our humble opinion is that all the lǜ (律) of Dù Kuí (杜夔) and Zuǒ Yánnián (左延年) should be kept.
As for the imperial treasury’s flutes for zhèngshēng (正聲) and xiàzhǐ (下徵), each one set,
all should be inscribed with the names of their makers.
The rest, having no use,
should be returned to the imperial treasury to be destroyed.”
The memorial was approved.
Xù (勗) then asked Hé (和):
“Is it possible to make twelve flutes according to the twelve lǜ (律),
such that each hole corresponds to one lǜ (律),
and only then consider it music?”
Hé (和) replied:

for a turbid sound, the flute should be longer,

Furthermore, as for the various holes of the flute,
though not yet tested,
I believe it is impossible for one hole to correspond to one lǜ (律).”
It was examined that

should correspond to Ruíbīn (蕤賓).
By the method of the twelve lǜ (律) revolving to become the gōng (宮) scale,

The Dàlǚ (大呂) flute is two chi six cun and a fraction long,

They ordered the Grand Music Directors Liú Xiù (劉秀) and Dèng Hào (鄧昊) and others to make a Dàlǚ (大呂) flute according to the lǜ (律) to show Hé (和).
Then, they blew seven lǜ (律),

After that, they ordered Hǎo Shēng (郝生) to play the zither

Hé (和) then said:

which is truly beyond my reach.”
Hǎo Shēng (郝生), Lǔ Jī (魯基), Zhǒng Zhěng (种整),
