They further asked Hé (和):
“A flute has six holes,
and including its internal cavity, there are seven sounds.
Can Hé (和) name all its gōng (宮), shāng (商), jué (角), zhǐ (徵)?
How can one determine if a hole is in tune or out of tune?”
Hé (和) replied:
“My former teachers passed down that
when playing the flute, one only communicates by means of compositions,
saying ‘for a certain piece, lift a certain finger,’
〔三二〕and never knew what sounds the seven holes fully corresponded to.
If one were to make a flute,
one would rely on the artisans of the Imperial Manufactory,
who, after inspecting old models,
would simply blow to get a sound,
never checking whether the various holes were in tune or out of tune.”
It was examined that
the Rites of Zhōu (周禮) states that when tuning metal and stone instruments,
there are fixed sounds.
Therefore, makers of bells and chimes
first tune them according to lǜ (律)
before mounting them on stands.
When music is performed,
all sounds receive their tuning from the bells and chimes,
meaning they all conform to the lǜ (律).
As for banquets in palace halls,
without mounted bells and chimes,
since the flute has a fixed tuning,
all stringed instruments and singing follow the flute as correct.
Thus, the flute is like bells and chimes,
and should necessarily conform to lǜlǚ (律呂).
As Hé (和) replied,
he made them purely by intuition,
recklessly shortening by one cun (寸),
and did not know what lǜ (律) the sounds of the seven holes corresponded to.
Whether in tune or out of tune,
there was no way to verify.
He merely took bamboo that produced a sound,
which shows a lack of method.
We immediately ordered Bureau Director Liú Xiù (劉秀), Dèng Hào (鄧昊), Wáng Yàn (王豔), Wèi Shào (魏邵) and others to collaborate with flute artisans in making flutes,

Then the instruments would have a system,

He further asked Hé:

Hé replied:

depending on the clear or turbid voice of the singer,
flutes of varying lengths are used.
For example, if the voice is turbid, a three-chi two-cun flute is used,
and so it is named 'this three-chi two-cun tune.'
If the voice is clear, a two-chi nine-cun flute is used,
and so it is named 'this two-chi nine-cun tune.'
This tradition was passed down through the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
and all practices were like this."

are manifested as the Five Talents;
the spirits of the Five Talents
are the Five Planets.
The calendar therefore imitates the movements of Heaven to regulate the Seven Luminaries,
and records the affairs of all nations, granting humanity its seasons.
**Huángdì** sent **Dà'nào** to create the **Liùjiǎ** (sexagenary cycle),
**Róngchéng** devised calendrical phenomena,
**Xīhé** observed the sun,
and **Chángyí** observed the moon.
**Shǎohào Shì** had the auspicious sign of the phoenix,
and named officials after birds;
the **Fèngniǎo Shì** (Phoenix Officer) was in charge of the calendar.
In the time of **Zhuānxū**,
**Nánzhèng Chóng** was in charge of Heaven,
and **Běizhèng Lí** was in charge of Earth.
**Yáo** later fostered the descendants of **Chóng Lí**,
making them manage their ancestral duties,
and specially appointed **Xī** and **Hé**,
to reverently conform to **Hàotiān** (August Heaven).
Therefore, the **Yúshū** states:
"A year consists of three hundred and sixty-six days,
with an intercalary month to fix the four seasons and complete the year."
After that, it was passed to **Shùn**,
who said:
"The calendrical calculations of Heaven reside in your person."
**Shùn** also passed this mandate to **Yǔ**.
Subsequently, in the two dynasties of **Yīn** and **Zhōu**,
both established new foundations and reformed institutions,
and their clothing colors followed suit.
By conforming to the seasonal *qì*,
and responding to the Way of Heaven,
all myriad beings
received its benefits and blessings.
When the Three Kings had passed,
the historical offices were abolished.
Therefore, **Kǒngzǐ** rectified the **Chūnqiū** (Spring and Autumn Annals) to clarify the errors of the **Sīlì** (calendar officials).
When **Qín** unified the realm,
it considered itself to possess the virtue of **Shuǐdé** (Water Element),
took the tenth month as the beginning of the year,
and favored black for clothing.
When **Hàn** arose,
it adopted the **Qín** calendar and new year.
**Běipíng Hóu** **Zhāng Cāng** was the first to speak about matters of pitch-pipes and the calendar,
comparing the **Zhuānxū Lì** (Zhuānxū Calendar) to the **Liùlì** (Six Calendars),
and found its discrepancies to be slight.
It was used until the seventh year of the **Yuánfēng** era of Emperor **Wǔdì**.
Then **Tàizhōng Dàfū** **Gōngsūn Qīng**, **Hú Suì**, **Tàishǐ Lìng** **Sīmǎ Qiān**, and others,
stated that the calendar records were dilapidated,
and that it was proper to reform the calendar and the new year,
and change the clothing colors,
to clarify that this mandate was received from Heaven.
Thereupon, an imperial edict commanded **Suì** and others to create the **Hànlì** (Hàn Calendar).
They selected **Dèng Píng**, **Chánglè Sīmǎ** **Kě**, and more than twenty other calendar experts among the populace.
The *fangshi* (master of esoterica) **Táng Dū** divided the celestial regions,
and **Luòxià Hóng** calculated and adjusted the calendar.
Their method accumulated eighty-one *cun* (units of length),
which represented a division of a day.
**Hóng** and **Dèng Píng**'s methods were identical.
Thereupon, they all observed the celestial degrees
and the movements of the sun and moon.
They further calculated using arithmetic,
and according to **Hóng** and **Píng**'s methods,
a month consisted of twenty-nine and forty-three eighty-firsts of a day.
An edict commanded **Qiān** to use the eighty-one-part pitch-pipe and calendar system created by **Dèng Píng**,
and appointed **Píng** as **Tàishǐ Chéng** (Assistant Grand Astrologer).
By the third year of the **Yuánfèng** era,
**Tàishǐ Lìng** **Zhāng Shòuwáng** submitted a memorial,
believing that the first year had used the **Huángdì Tiáolì** (Yellow Emperor's Adjusted Calendar),
and stated, "Now *yīn* and *yáng* are out of harmony;
this is the fault of the calendar reform."

An imperial edict ordered **Zhǔlì Shǐzhě** **Xiānyú Wàngrén**, **Dàsīnóng Zhōngchéng** **Má Guāng**, and more than twenty other calendar experts to collectively observe the dark moon, new moon, first quarter, and full moon, as well as the **Èrshísì Qì** (Twenty-four Solar Terms).

Furthermore, an edict commanded one official each from the **Chéngxiàng** (Chancellor), **Yùshǐ** (Imperial Censor), **Dàjiāngjūn** (General-in-Chief), and **Yòujiāngjūn** (General of the Right) to collectively observe from the **Shànglín Qīngtái** (Clear Terrace of the Upper Forest Park),
to evaluate the various discrepancies.
There were eleven schools in total.
This spanned from the third to the fifth year.
**Shòuwáng**'s calculations were distant (i.e., less accurate).
Moreover, the first year of the **Hàn** dynasty did not use the **Huángdì Tiáolì** (Yellow Emperor's Adjusted Calendar).
Therefore, **Shòuwáng** was impeached for opposing Heaven and Earth,
a great disrespect.
An edict ordered not to impeach him.
Observations were resumed,
until the sixth year,
and the **Tàichū Lì** (Tàichū Calendar) was ranked first.
**Shòuwáng**'s calendar was in fact the **Yīnlì** (Yīn Calendar) used by the Grand Astrologer's office.
**Shòuwáng** was impeached again but remained defiant,
and was eventually handed over to officials.
During the time of Emperor **Xiàochéng**,
**Liú Xiàng** compiled the **Liùlì** (Six Calendars),
listed their pros and cons,
and wrote the **Wǔjì Lùn** (Discourse on the Five Records).
**Xiàng**'s son, **Xīn**, created the **Sāntǒng Lì** (Sāntǒng Calendar) to explain the **Chūnqiū** (Spring and Autumn Annals);
though his rhetoric and historical comparisons
were extremely refined and ingenious,
they were not truly accurate.
**Bān Gù** called it the "Secret Essential,"
and thus it is recounted in the **Hànlì Zhì** (Treatise on Calendars of the Hàn Dynasty).
Comparing it with the calendars of the six schools, including **Hé Chéngtiān**,
although their "six *yuán*" (initial epochs) differed,
and their divisions and sections were sometimes distinct,
the discrepancies up to the present day
were sometimes three days,
or two days and several hours.
Examining their origins,
they were generally all created by people from the **Liù Guó** (Six States) and **Qín** periods.
Their methods had too many discrepancies,
upwardly they could not be verified against the **Chūnqiū** (Spring and Autumn Annals),
downwardly they were not confirmed by **Hàn** and **Wèi** dynasties.
Even if they falsely claimed imperial authority,
they merely served to delude the people of their time.
In the eighth year of the **Jiànwǔ** era of Emperor **Guāngwǔ**,
**Tàipú** **Zhū Fú** submitted a memorial stating that the calendar records were incorrect,
and ought to be reformed.
At that time, the discrepancies were still minor,
so there was no time to thoroughly verify and correct them.
In the middle of the **Yǒngpíng** era of Emperor **Míngdì**,
**Dàizhào** **Yáng Cén**, **Zhāng Shèng**, **Jǐng Fáng**, and others were in charge of calendrical calculations.
They only altered the added hours for the first and last quarters of the moon,
but were unable to comprehensively verify the calendar's epoch.
By the second year of the **Yuánhé** era,
the **Tàichū** Calendar's divergence from Heaven had grown further,
and the perceived differences in asterism degrees had gradually increased.
All observers knew that the sun's position in the asterisms was off by five degrees,
the winter solstice sun was at twenty-one degrees of the **Dǒu** constellation,
and the dark moon, new moon, first quarter, and full moon,
were one day ahead of the celestial phenomena.
Emperor **Zhāngdì** summoned calendar experts like **Biān Xīn** and **Lǐ Fàn** to comprehensively verify the situation.
Thereupon, he issued an imperial edict stating:
"The **Chūnqiū Bǎoqiántú** states: 'Every three hundred years, the **Dǒulì** (Dipper Calendar) should reform its system.'
The historical officials used the method of **Dèng Píng** from the **Tàichū** Calendar,
which had a remainder of one unit,
within the three-hundred-year cycle.
Its degree of motion became increasingly erroneous,
gradually accumulating errors and mistakes,
so that the armillary sphere was inaccurate,
and astronomical phenomena could not be verified.
On the day of the winter solstice,
the sun was at twenty-one degrees of the **Dǒu** constellation,
one day before **Lìchūn** (Start of Spring),
which corresponds to the **Lìchūn** day of the **Sìfēn** (Four Quarters) system.
If this is used to judge cases and pass major sentences,
it is already contrary to the *qì*;
if used for observing and bringing peace and harmony,
it is also far off.
Now, we shall change to implement the **Sìfēn** (Four Quarters) Calendar,
to follow **Yáo** and conform to **Kǒng** (Confucius),
and uphold the principles of Heaven.
With united hearts, we shall reverently transmit it,
hoping thereby to achieve universal prosperity."
Thereupon, the **Sìfēn** Calendar was put into effect.
All calendars since **Huángdì** that placed the winter solstice at the beginning of **Qiānniú** (Altair) were abolished.
In the fourteenth year of the **Yǒngyuán** era of Emperor **Hédì**,
**Dàizhào Tàishǐ** **Huò Róng** submitted a memorial stating:
"The official clepsydra's rate of adding or subtracting one *ke* (unit of time) every nine days
does not correspond with Heaven,
sometimes diverging by as much as two and a half *ke*;
it is not as precise as the **Xiàlì** (Xià Calendar)."
In the eleventh month, on the *jiǎyín* day of that year,
an edict stated:
"The clepsydra is used to regulate time divisions
and determine dawn and dusk.
The length of dawn and dusk
arises from the sun's distance from the celestial pole;
the sun's path is circular,
and cannot be divided by fixed ratios.
The official clepsydra's rate of adding or subtracting one *ke* every nine days
deviates from the truth.
Using the sundial's shadow for timing
is precise and verifiable.
Therefore, we now issue the sundial and clepsydra method with forty-eight *jian* (arrows)."
The positions of the sun on the **Èrshísì Qì** (Twenty-four Solar Terms),
as well as the ecliptic's distance from the pole, sundial shadows, clepsydra readings, and central stars at dawn and dusk,
are all listed in the **Xù Hàn Lǜlì Zhì** (Treatise on Pitch-pipes and Calendars in the Continuation of the Hàn History).
In the third year of Yánguāng of Emperor Ān,
the palace attendant Zhǎn Sòng submitted a memorial stating that the Jiǎyín era should be used.
Liáng Fēng from Hénán said that the Tàichū era should be reinstated.
Shàngshū Láng Zhāng Héng and Zhōu Xìng, both skilled in calendrical calculations,
frequently challenged Sòng and Fēng.
Sometimes they could not respond,
or they admitted errors.
Héng and others consulted and examined the ceremonial regulations,
compared the past with the present,
and concluded that the Jiǔdào method was the most precise.
An imperial edict was issued for the high officials to deliberate.
Tàiwèi Kǎi and others deliberated, saying:
"The Tàichū calendar is one degree ahead of the heavens,
and the moon appears in the west on its last day.
The Yuánhé calendar changed to follow the Sìfēn method.
Although Sìfēn is more precise than Tàichū,
it is still incorrect.
Neither can be used.
The Jiǎyín era corresponds with the heavens,
and aligns with the prognostic charts and apocrypha.
It can be implemented."
The deliberators were not in agreement.
Shàngshū Lìng Zhōng submitted a memorial, stating:
"The calendrical calculations of Heaven
should not be based on doubt or emptiness,
replacing what is right with what is wrong."
Zhǎn and others were then silenced.
In the fourth year of Xīpíng of Emperor Líng,
Wǔguān Lángzhōng Féng Guāng and Pèixiàng Shàngjì Yuàn Chén Huàng and others said:
"The calendrical era is incorrect,
which is why bandits cause harm.
The calendar should use Jiǎyín as its era,
not Gēngshēn.
We request the original Gēngshēn era's calendrical principles and clear documentation."
An imperial edict was issued to the three ducal ministries,
and to those among the literati who were clear in the Way and techniques, for detailed deliberation.
The officials gathered in the Sītú Fǔ for discussion.
Yìláng Cài Yōng said:
"Calendrical calculations are intricate and subtle,
and no single method is always correct.
When the Hàn dynasty arose, it inherited from Qín,
using the Zhuānxù calendar,
with the era beginning in Yǐmǎo.
After 102 years,
Emperor Xiàowǔ first changed to Tàichū,
with the era beginning in Dīngchǒu.
After 189 years of its operation,
Emperor Xiàozhāng changed to Sìfēn,
with the era beginning in Gēngshēn.
Now Guāng and others consider Gēngshēn incorrect,
and Jiǎyín correct.
According to calendrical laws,
Huángdì, Zhuānxù, Xià, Yīn, Zhōu, and Lǔ
each had their own era.
What Guāng and Huàng advocate
is the Yīn calendar's era.
In the past, after the initial use of Tàichū Dīngchǒu,
the six schools became confused and conflicting,
disputing right and wrong.
Zhāng Shòuwáng held the Jiǎyín era to be correct and challenged the Hàn calendar,
mixing observations from the Qīngtái,
but his calculations were inferior.
The Tàichū calendar proved effective,
without any omissions.
Thus, although it was not the era of the prognostic charts and apocrypha,
it was effective in the past.
And since the use of Sìfēn,
when examined against celestial movements,
it is more precise than Tàichū;
this is a new era that is effective in the present.
Therefore, during the Yánguāng era,
Zhǎn Sòng also criticized Sìfēn,
saying the Jiǎyín era should be used.
The high officials deliberated,
but ultimately did not implement it.
Furthermore, the movements of the three luminaries
—their varying speeds, advancements, and retreats—
are not necessarily constant.
Hence there are ancient and modern methods.
The current methods cannot reach back to ancient times,
just as ancient methods cannot extend to the present.
Moreover, Guāng and Huàng base their arguments on the Kǎolíng Yào,
but the degrees of the Twenty-Eight Mansions at the sun's position
are inconsistent and cannot be compared.
The Yuánhé calendar has been in use for 92 years to date,
yet Guāng and Huàng say that the imbalance of Yin and Yang,
and the presence of corrupt officials and bandits,
are all faults of the era.
The imperial edict for Yuánhé
is thoroughly worded and clearly principled,
and cannot be altered by the deliberations of officials."
The Three Dukes agreed with Yōng's proposal,
and considered Guāng and Huàng disrespectful, deserving of the Guǐxīn punishment.
An imperial edict stated not to punish them.
Hé Chéngtiān said: "If one's mind does not grasp the art of calendrical calculations,
even if one is a knowledgeable person with foresight,
it will not save one from error.
Therefore, after many years,
no definitive solution has been reached.
The Sìfēn calendar, when applied to the heavens,
exceeds by one day over 300 years.
Successive generations failed to realize this,
merely saying that the foundation of establishing a calendar
must first be to set an era,
falsely invoking prognostic charts and apocrypha,
and thus connecting it to order and disorder.
This kind of delusion
is indeed extreme.
Liú Xīn's Sāntǒng Fǎ was even more imprecise;
compared to Sìfēn,
it added another day over 6,000 years.
Yáng Xióng was confused by this theory,
and adopted it for his Tàixuán.
Bān Gù called it the most precise,
and recorded it in the Hàn Zhì;
Sī Biāo then said,
'Since the first year of Tàichū, the Sāntǒng Lì was used,
and implemented for over a hundred years.'
He did not even remember that Liú Xīn's birth
did not precede Tàichū.
When these two or three gentlemen speak of calendars,
do they not speak presumptuously out of ignorance?
During the Guānghé era, Liú Hóng, a gate guard at Gǔchéng, first realized the imprecision of Sìfēn when applied to the heavens.
He instead used 589 as the 'jìfǎ' (cycle divisor),
and 145 as the 'dòufēn' (degree fraction),
creating the Qiánxiàng Fǎ.
He also devised a calendar for the moon's varying speeds to calculate its motion.
Compared to Tàichū and Sìfēn,
it became even more precise.
During the Huángchū era of Emperor Wén of Wèi, Tàishǐ Chéng Hán Yì believed that the Qiánxiàng subtracted too much from the dòufēn,
and would eventually anticipate the heavens.
He created the Huángchū Lì,
using 4883 as the jìfǎ,
and 1205 as the dòufēn.
Thereafter, Shàngshū Lìng Chén Qún memorialized,
stating:
'Calendrical calculations are difficult to understand,
and many learned scholars of previous generations have disagreed over them.
The Huángchū era,
considering the Sìfēn calendar to be long-standing and imprecise,
and as the Great Wèi received the Mandate of Heaven,
it is fitting to correct the calendar and clarify the seasons.
Hán Yì first proposed Huángchū,
but fearing it might not be accurate,
he used Qiánxiàng for mutual cross-referencing.
After three years,
they continued to contradict each other,
abandoning the fundamental for the trivial,
disputing lengths and doubting measures,
never reaching a conclusion.
Upon reviewing the deliberations of the Three Dukes,
they all thoroughly analyzed the intricate principles,
reaching the same conclusion through different paths,
desiring to test them against the armillary sphere,
each employing their method,
so that within a year,
the gains and losses could be determined,
in line with practical needs.'
The memorial was approved.
During the reign of Emperor Míng, Shàngshū Láng Yáng Wěi created the Jǐngchū Lì,
which remained in use until the Jìn and Sòng dynasties.
Among the ancient calendar makers,
Dèng Píng was able to revise old systems and create new ones.
Liú Hóng first reduced the Sìfēn,
and also fixed the varying speeds of the moon's motion.
Yáng Wěi weighed both sides,
to establish a moderate balance of surplus and deficit,
and based on the calculated new moons, set differences
to predict conjunctions and lunar eclipses.
These three individuals
were the skilled calendar makers of Hàn and Wèi.
However, Hóng's varying speeds
cannot be verified against the Spring and Autumn Annals,
and Wěi's five planets
greatly diverge from later generations.
This indicates that Hóng's approach was still imprecise,
and Wěi was constrained by the common origin of Shàngyuán Rénchén.
In the first year of Jǐngchū of Emperor Míng of Wèi, the calendar was revised and fixed,
taking the month of Jiànchǒu as the first month.
The third month of that year was changed to the fourth month, Mèngxià.
Although its first, middle, and last months
differed from the standard year,
for suburban sacrifices, welcoming the qi,
ancestral rites, autumnal sacrifices,
imperial tours, hunting expeditions,
solstices and equinoxes, openings and closures,
and promulgating seasonal decrees,
all continued to use Jiànyín as the first month.
In the first month of the third year,
the emperor died,
and the Xià calendar was reinstated.
Yáng Wěi submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has perused the records,
and critically examined the calendrical calculations.
Time is used to mark agricultural seasons,
and months are used to record events.
The origin of this [system]
is ancient and long-standing.
Starting from Shàohào,
Xuánniǎo supervised the solstices and equinoxes.
During the reigns of Zhuānxù and Dì Kù,
Chóng and Lí supervised the heavens.
During the reigns of Emperor Táng (Yáo) and Emperor Yú Shùn, Xī and Hé managed the sun.
The Three Dynasties continued this tradition,
so there were sun officials in every generation.
When sun officials managed the calendar,
it was distributed to the feudal lords.
When the feudal lords received it,
they distributed it within their territories.
During the Xià Hòu dynasty,
Xī and Hé indulged in drunkenness and debauchery,
neglecting the seasons and disordering the days,
which is recorded in the 'Yìn Zhēng'.
From this, we can see
that prioritizing agricultural seasons and human affairs
has been the case throughout the dynasties.
Reaching the time when the Zhōu dynasty had declined
and the Warring States contended fiercely,
the lamb for announcing the new moon
was abandoned and not continued.
The ritual of ascending the platform
was extinguished and not observed.
The intercalary divisions became irregular and unrecognized,
and the beginning of the first month (Mèngzōu) was lost and not understood.
The star Dàhuǒ would still be in the west,
yet people wondered why hibernating insects did not hide.
At this time,
the Son of Heaven did not harmonize with the seasons,
the calendar officials did not record the days,
the feudal lords did not receive their duties,
and the sun observers did not distinguish the new moons.
Human affairs were not cared for,
and agricultural seasons were neglected.
When Zhòngní (Confucius) brought order out of chaos in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
he used praise and blame to correct.
If the calendar officials erred in intercalations,
he criticized and recorded it.
If they ascended the platform to distribute the new moon calendar,
he called it 'having ritual'.
From this time onwards,
down to Qín and Hàn,
they again took the first month of winter (Mèngdōng) as the beginning of the year,
and the intercalation as the 'ninth month after'.
The middle solar terms were erroneous and misplaced,
and the seasonal months were askew.
The added time lagged behind the heavens,
and eclipses did not occur at the new moon.
This accumulated over many years,
and was not reformed for a long time.
It was not until the seventh year of Yuánfēng of Emperor Wǔ,
that the error was finally recognized.
Thereupon, the beginning of the year (Zhèngshuò) was corrected,
and the calendrical calculations were reformed.
Great talents and accomplished individuals were commissioned
to create the Tàichū Lì (Grand Inception Calendar).
They calibrated the discrepancies in the middle and new moons,
to correct the intercalary divisions,
and assessed the degrees of the middle stars,
to examine their density and sparsity.
They took the month of Jiànyín as the Zhèngshuò,
and the month of Huángzhōng as the beginning of the calendar.
Its lunar degree division (Dǒufēn) was too large,
and later became sparse.
By the second year of Yuánhé,
the Sìfēn Lì (Four-Part Calendar) was again adopted,
and put into practice.
As of today,
observations of solar eclipses
consistently show them occurring at the last day of the month (huì).
This indicates that the Dǒufēn is too large,
so it is initially dense then sparse, and thus unusable.
Therefore, your servant previously used the remaining days from the prescribed canon,
deduced the celestial paths,
verified them against previous canons,
and tested them with observed new moon eclipses.
Having scrutinized and refined them,
I have established a more precise calendar,
which is neither too early nor too late,
aligning with the celestial mid-point for both ancient and modern times.
It is like in the past, during the time of Emperor Táng,
when he harmonized the sun and corrected the seasons,
justly ordering all officials,
so all achievements flourished.
I wish to make the current national ceremonies,
and all institutions,
completely conform to ancient times,
grand and fully adequate.
Therefore, the Zhèngshuò should be corrected,
and the calendrical calculations reformed,
taking the month of Dàlǚ as the beginning of the year,
and the month of Jiànzǐ as the beginning of the calendar.
Your servant believes that in the past, during the imperial eras,
the calendar was called Zhuānxù,
and from the time of Xuānyuán,
the calendar was called Huángdì.
When it came to Emperor Xiàowǔ of Hàn,
he reformed the Zhèngshuò,
and changed the calendrical calculations.
He changed the era name to Tàichū,
and thus named it the Tàichū Lì.
Now the era name has been changed to Jǐngchū,
so it should be called the Jǐngchū Lì.
The Jǐngchū Lì established by your servant
has a concise method,
and its application is precise.
Its governance saves effort,
and its study is easy to understand.
Even if one were to employ the mental calculations of Yánsāng,
the strategic planning of Líshǒu,
the gnomon supervision of Chóng and Lí,
and the shadow observation of Xī and Hé,
to investigate the celestial paths,
and measure and verify the sun and moon,
delving into the utmost intricacies,
to the extreme of mathematical arts,
none would be as ingenious as your servant's method.
This is why the calendrical calculations of successive generations
have all been coarse and imprecise,
and since Huángdì,
reforms have never ceased.
From the first year of Rénchén,
to the first year of Jǐngchū (Dīngsì),
the accumulated years are four thousand and forty-six.
Calculated upwards.
This epoch takes the month of Jiànzǐ (Huángzhōng) as the beginning of the calendar, following the celestial Zhèng.
In the first year of the epoch, at midnight on Jiǎzǐ, the new moon occurred at the winter solstice.

The conjunction *jì* difference is
one hundred three thousand six hundred ten.
To find the origin of this number:
Place the accumulated months of one *jì* and multiply it by the common divisor.
Subtract the full conjunction cycle from it.
The remainder after subtraction
is the *jì* difference number.
Add this progressively to the previous *jì*
to obtain the subsequent *jì*.
If the addition does not reach the full conjunction cycle,
then at the start of the *jì*'s year, in the first month (zhēngyuè) conjunction,
the Moon is within the Sun's path.
If it reaches the full cycle and is subtracted,
then the Moon is outside the Sun's path.
If adding the outer position reaches the full cycle, it is within the path;
if adding the inner position reaches the full cycle, it is outside the path.
The speed *jì* difference is
thirty thousand one hundred eighty.
To find the origin of this number:
Place the accumulated months of one *jì*,
multiply it by the common divisor,
subtract the full cycle.
The remainder is then subtracted from the full cycle.
The remainder after this subtraction
is the *jì* difference number.
Subtract this progressively from the previous *jì*
to obtain the subsequent *jì*.
If it is insufficient for subtraction,
add the full cycle.
To find the *yuán* difference rate:
progressively subtract the previous *yuán*'s Jiǎyín *jì* difference rate.
The remainder is then the *yuán*'s Jiǎzǐ *jì* difference rate.
To find the subsequent *jì*,
follow the method above.
The method for calculating accumulated months of the new moon: Place the years from the Rénchén *yuán*
up to the year you are seeking.
Exclude the current year you are seeking,
divide by the *jì* method.
The quotient, excluding the current calculation,
is the *jì* number entered,
the remainder is the number of years within the *jì*.
Multiply the years by the *zhāng* months.
For each *zhāng* year, one unit represents the accumulated months,
the remainder is the leap month remainder.
If the leap month remainder is twelve or more,
that year has a leap month.
A leap month is defined by having no *zhōngqì*.
The method for calculating the new moon: Multiply the accumulated months by the common divisor
to get the new moon integral.
For each unit of the day method, it is one accumulated day,
the remainder is the small remainder.
Subtract sixty from the accumulated days,
the remainder is the large remainder.
The large remainder, designated by the *jì* calculation,
excluding the current calculation,
is the day of the new moon in the eleventh month (Shíyīyuè) of the first month (zhēngyuè) of the year you are seeking.
To find the next month:
Add to the large remainder twenty-nine,
and to the small remainder two thousand four hundred nineteen.
When the small remainder reaches a full day according to the day method, carry it over to the large remainder.
Designate as before,
this is the new moon day of the next month.
If the small remainder is two thousand one hundred forty or more,
that month is a long month.
To calculate the first quarter and full moon:
Add to the new moon's large remainder seven,
and to the small remainder one thousand seven hundred forty-four,
and to the small fraction one.
When the small fraction reaches two, carry it over to the small remainder.
When the small remainder reaches a full day according to the day method, carry it over to the large remainder.
When the large remainder reaches sixty, subtract it.
The remainder, designated by the *jì* calculation,
excluding the current calculation,
is the day of the first quarter moon.
Further additions yield the full moon, the last quarter moon, and the new moon of the following month.
For months with a lunar eclipse at full moon,
determine the small remainder,
according to the limit of the interval closest to the middle *jié* (節).
If it is below the limit number,
the count indicates the day.
If the full moon is within four days before or after the middle *jié*,
refer to the limit number;
if the full moon is five days or more before or after the middle *jié*,
refer to the interval limit.
The method for calculating the twenty-four *qì*: Place the number of years in the current *jì*,
excluding the current year you are seeking.
Multiply it by the remainder number.
When it reaches the full *jì* method, it becomes the large remainder;
the remainder is the small remainder.
When the large remainder reaches sixty, subtract it.
The remainder, designated by the *jì* calculation,
excluding the current calculation,
is the day of the Winter Solstice in the eleventh month (Shíyīyuè) of the first month (zhēngyuè) of the year.
To find the next *qì*:
Add to the large remainder fifteen,
to the small remainder four hundred two,
and to the small fraction eleven.
When the small fraction reaches the full *qì* method, carry it over to the small remainder.
When the small remainder reaches the full *jì* method, carry it over to the large remainder.
Designate as before,
this is the day of the next *qì*.
The method for calculating intercalary months is as follows: Subtract the intercalary remainder from the chapter year.
Multiply the remainder by the number of days in the year.
When this reaches the chapter intercalary number, one month is obtained.
If the remainder is half or more of the divisor, one month is also obtained.
The count starts from the eleventh month of the first month of the calendar (Tiānzhèng).
The calculation outside [this period]

Intercalary months can advance or retreat,
controlled by the absence of a *zhōngqì* (middle solar term).

The method for calculating *mòmiè* (disappearance and reappearance):
If the accumulated days from Dōngzhì have a small remainder,
add one to the accumulated value,
multiply by the *mòfēn* (disappearance fraction),
and divide by the *mòfǎ* (disappearance modulus).
The result is the large remainder,
and what is left over is the small remainder.
If the large remainder reaches sixty, subtract sixty.
The remaining value is designated by *jì* (cycle),
and the calculation outside [this period]
is the day of disappearance after Dōngzhì of the previous year.
To find the next disappearance,
add sixty-nine to the large remainder
and 592 to the small remainder.
If the small remainder reaches the *mòfǎ*, it obtains one,
which is added to the large remainder.
Designate as before.
When the small remainder is exhausted,
it is *miè* (reappearance).
The method for calculating the days when the Five Phases are in charge: Lìchūn, Lìxià, Lìqiū, and Lìdōng
are the days when Wood, Fire, Metal, and Water respectively begin to be in charge.
Subtract eighteen from their respective large remainders,
483 from their small remainders,
and six from their small fractions.
The remaining values are designated by *jì*,
and the calculation outside [this period]
is the day when Earth is in charge before each of the Four Beginnings.
If the large remainder is insufficient for subtraction,
add sixty.
If the small remainder is insufficient for subtraction,
subtract one from the large remainder
and add the *jìfǎ* (cycle modulus).
If the small fraction is insufficient for subtraction,
subtract one from the small remainder
and add the *qìfǎ* (solar term modulus).
The method for calculating the days when the *guà* are in charge: Based on the Dōngzhì large remainder,
multiply the small remainder by six.
This is the day when the Kǎn *guà* is in charge.
Add 10,091 to the small remainder.
If it reaches the *yuánfǎ* (prime modulus), add to the large remainder.
This is the day when the Zhōngfú *guà* is in charge.
To find the next *guà*,
add six to the large remainder
and 967 to the small remainder.
For each of the Four Cardinal *guà*, take its middle day
and multiply its small remainder by six.
The method for calculating the daily degree: Multiply the accumulated days from the new moon by the *jìfǎ*.
Subtract any full celestial circuits.
Divide the remainder by the *jìfǎ*.
The result is the degree,
and what is left over is the fraction.
The degrees are designated starting from five units before Niú.
Divide by the number of mansions.
If it does not reach a full mansion,
then this is the degree and fraction of the sun's position at midnight on the new moon of the eleventh month of Tiānzhèng.
To find the next day,
add one degree to the degree.
The fraction is not added.
If it passes Dǒu, subtract the Dǒu fraction.
If the fraction is small, subtract one degree.
The method for calculating the monthly degree: Multiply the accumulated days from the new moon by the month's circumference.
Subtract any full celestial circuits.
Divide the remainder by the *jìfǎ*.
The result is the degree,
and what is left over is the fraction.
Designate as per the above method,
then this is the degree and fraction of the moon's position at midnight on the new moon of the eleventh month of Tiānzhèng.
To find the next month:
For a small month, add twenty-two degrees
and 806 fractions.
For a large month, additionally add one day,
thirteen degrees,
and 679 fractions.
If the fraction reaches the *jìfǎ*, it obtains one degree.
This is then the degree and fraction of the moon's position at midnight on the new moon of the next month.
In the last ten days of winter,
the moon is within Zhāng, Xīn, and Shǔ.
〔一九〕 The method for calculating the degree of conjunction (hèshuò): Multiply the new moon's small remainder by the chapter year.
If it reaches the *tōngfǎ* (general modulus), it becomes the large fraction,
and what is left over is the small fraction.
Add the large fraction to the degree and fraction of the sun at midnight on the new moon.
If the fraction reaches the *jìfǎ*, it is added to the degree.
〔二０〕 Designate as before,
then this is the common degree of conjunction of the sun and moon at the new moon of the eleventh month of Tiānzhèng.
To find the next month:
Add twenty-nine degrees,
977 large fractions,
and forty-two small fractions.
If the small fraction reaches the *tōngfǎ*, it is added to the large fraction.
If the large fraction reaches the *jìfǎ*, it is added to the degree.
If it passes Dǒu, subtract its fraction.
This is then the common degree of conjunction of the sun and moon at the new moon of the next month.
To calculate the degree of the sun's position at the syzygy: Add the degree of the conjunction, seven,
seven hundred and five *dàfēn*,
ten *xiǎofēn*,
one *wēifēn*.
When *wēifēn* reaches two, it makes one *xiǎofēn*.
When *xiǎofēn* reaches the full regular amount, it makes one *dàfēn*.
When *dàfēn* reaches the full regular amount, it makes one degree.
Proceed as before.
This gives the degree of the sun's position at the first quarter.
Adding further yields the full moon, the last quarter, and the following month's conjunction.
To calculate the degree of the moon's position at the syzygy: Add the degree of the conjunction, ninety-eight,
one thousand two hundred seventy-nine *dàfēn*,
thirty-four *xiǎofēn*.
When the numbers are full, proceed as before.
This gives the degree of the moon's position at the first quarter.
Adding further yields the full moon, the last quarter, and the following month's conjunction.
The method for calculating the degrees of brightness and darkness of the sun and moon is as follows: For the sun, use the *jìfǎ* (epoch method);
for the moon, use the *yuèzhōu* (lunar circumference).
Multiply by the night clepsydra of the nearest *jiéqì* (solar term).
Divide by two hundred to get one [part].
This is the *míngfēn* (brightness portion).
For the sun, subtract from the *jìfǎ*;
for the moon, subtract from the *yuèzhōu*.
The remainder is the *hūnfēn* (darkness portion).
Add each to midnight,
and according to the method, convert to degrees.
The method for calculating the syzygy, nodes, and lunar eclipse is as follows: Set down the accumulated *shuò* (conjunction) integral of the current epoch.
Add the number of the *jiāohuì chālǜ* (node difference rate) of the current epoch.
Subtract the *huìtōng* (full cycle of nodes) from it.
The remainder is the *qùjiāodùfēn* (degree and fractional part away from the node) of the *héshuò* (conjunction) in the eleventh month of the *Tiānzhēng* year to be found.
Add the *tōngshù* (common number).
Subtract the *huìtōng* when full.
The remainder is the *qùjiāodùfēn* of the *héshuò* of the next month.
Add the *shuòwàng héshù* (sum of new and full moon differences) to each month's *héshuò qùjiāodùfēn*.
Subtract the *huìtōng* when full.
The remainder is each month's *wàng qùjiāodùfēn* (full moon degree and fractional part away from the node).
If the *shuòwàng qùjiāofēn* (new and full moon degree and fractional part away from the node) is less than the *shuòwàng héshù*,
then for the *shuò*, there is a conjunction,
and for the *wàng*, there is a lunar eclipse.
The method for calculating the syzygy, nodes, and lunar eclipse when the moon is above or below the ecliptic is as follows: Set down the accumulated *shuò* integral of the current epoch.
Add the number of the *xiàjiāohuì chālǜ* (lower node difference rate) of the current epoch.
Subtract the *bèihuìtōng* (double full cycle of nodes) from it.
If the remainder is less than *huìtōng*,
at the beginning of the epoch, it is *biǎo* (above the ecliptic),
and the *héshuò* in *Tiānzhēng* (Heavenly Equinox) month has the moon above the ecliptic.
At the beginning of the epoch, it is *yǐn* (below the ecliptic),
and the *héshuò* in *Tiānzhēng* month has the moon below the ecliptic.
If it is full, subtract *huìtōng*.
If it was *biǎo*, it becomes *yǐn*.
If it was *yǐn*, it becomes *biǎo*.
To find the next month,
add the *tōngshù*.
Subtract the *huìtōng* when full.
If it was *yǐn*, when full, it becomes *biǎo*.
If it was *biǎo*, when full, it becomes *yǐn*.
If the node occurs first and then the lunar eclipse,
if the *shuò* is *biǎo*, then the *wàng* is *biǎo*.
If the *shuò* is *yǐn*, then the *wàng* is *yǐn*.
If the lunar eclipse occurs first and then the node,
looking at the *shuò* of the eclipse month, if it is *yǐn*, then the *wàng* is *biǎo*.
If the *shuò* is *biǎo*, then the *wàng* is *yǐn*.
For a syzygy, node, or lunar eclipse, if it is less than or equal to the *shuòwàng héshù*,
If it is greater than or equal to the *rùjiāoxiànshù*,
then the syzygy occurs before the node.
If the node occurring before the syzygy is close to the *xiànshù* (limit number),
then investigate the previous month in advance.
If the syzygy occurring before the node is close to the *xiànshù*,
then investigate the following month later.
The method for calculating the *qùjiāodù* (degree away from the node) is as follows: For cases where the node occurs before the syzygy,
divide the current *qùjiāodùfēn* by the *rìfǎ* (day method) to get one [part].
subtract the *qùjiāodùfēn* from the *huìtōng*.
The remainder, divided by the *rìfǎ* to get one [part],
is the *qiánqùjiāodù* (degree away from the node going forward).
The rest are all degree fractions.
If the *qùjiāodù* is fifteen or more,
although there is a node, there is no eclipse.
Ten or less is an eclipse.
Above ten, the eclipse is very small,
merely touching the disk of light.
The amount of the eclipse is determined by taking fifteen as the standard.
The method for calculating the starting angle of a solar eclipse is as follows: If the moon is on the outer path,
and the node occurs before the syzygy, the eclipse begins from the southwest corner.
If the syzygy occurs before the node, the eclipse begins from the southeast corner.
If the moon is on the inner path,
and the node occurs before the syzygy, the eclipse begins from the northwest corner.
If the syzygy occurs before the node, the eclipse begins from the northeast corner.
The amount of the eclipse,
as above, takes fifteen as the standard.
If it occurs at the middle of the node,
it is a total eclipse.
For a lunar eclipse, it is opposite the sun.
The eclipse angle is reversed from the above.

The method for calculating the entry into the *chídílì* (slow and fast calendar) for the syzygy, nodes, and lunar eclipse is as follows: Set down the accumulated *shuò* integral of the current epoch.
Add the number of the *chídí chālǜ* (slow and fast difference rate) of the current epoch.
Subtract the *tōngzhōu* (full cycle of speed) from it.
If the remainder is full to a *rìfǎ*, one day is obtained.
The incomplete part is the day remainder.
Cast it out of the day calculation.
This is the calendar day for the *héshuò* in the eleventh month of the *Tiānzhēng* year to be found.
To find the next month,
add one day.
The day remainder is 4,450.
To find the *wàng* (full moon),
add fourteen days.
The day remainder is 3,489.
When the day remainder is full to a *rìfǎ*, it forms a day.
When the days are full to twenty-seven, subtract it.
Also, divide the remainder as the *zhōurì yú* (circumference day remainder).
If the *zhōurì yú* is insufficient for division,
subtract one day,
and add the *zhōuxū* (circumference deficit).
To determine the major and minor remainders for the syzygy, nodes, and lunar eclipse: Use the day remainder of the entry into the calendar.
Take the *sǔnyì yíngsuō jīfēn* (increase/decrease expansion/contraction integral) as the *dìng jīfēn* (fixed integral).
Subtract the *suǒrùlì yuèxíngfēn* (lunar motion fraction for the entered calendar) from the *zhāngsuì* (chapter year).
Divide the remainder by it.
The result, if *yíng* (expansion), subtract from *suō* (contraction); if *suō*, add to *yíng* to the original *xiǎoyú* (minor remainder).
If adding makes it full to the *rìfǎ*,
the *jiāohuì jiāshí* (additional time for the node) is on the following day.
If subtracting,
and it is insufficient,
the *jiāohuì jiāshí* is on the preceding day.
For a lunar eclipse,
the *rì jiāshí* (additional time of day) follows the fixed major and minor remainders.
If the entry into the calendar is on a *zhōurì*,
multiply the *zhōurì rìyú* (circumference day remainder) by the *suō jīfēn* (contraction integral).
This is the *dìng jīfēn*.
Multiply the *sǔnlǜ* (decrease rate) by the *rùlì rìyú* (calendar entry day remainder).
Also multiply by the *zhōurì rìyú*.
Add the *zhōurì rìdù xiǎofēn* (circumference day degree minor fraction).
Subtract the *sǔn dìng jīfēn* (decrease fixed integral).
The remainder is the *hòu dìng jīfēn* (later fixed integral).
Subtract the *zhōurì yuèxíngfēn* (circumference day lunar motion fraction) from the *zhāngsuì*.
Multiply the remainder by the *zhōurì rìyú*.
Add the *zhōurì dù xiǎofēn* (circumference day degree minor fraction).
Divide the *hòu dìng jīfēn* by this.
Add the result to the original *xiǎoyú*,
according to the method above.
To calculate the *jiāshí* (additional time): Multiply the fixed *xiǎoyú* by twelve.
When it reaches the *rìfǎ*, one *chén* (double hour) is obtained.
The count starts from *zǐ*.
Cast it out of the calculation.
This is the *chén* where the *shuò* and *wàng jiāshí* (additional time) are located.
If there is an incomplete remainder, multiply it by four.
If it is one according to the *rìfǎ*, it is *shǎo* (small).
If it is two, it is *bàn* (half).
If it is three, it is *tài* (great).
If there is a further remainder, multiply it by three.
If it is one according to the *rìfǎ*, it is *qiáng* (strong).
Above half the *fǎ*, it is rounded up.
Below half the *fǎ*, it is discarded.
Combine *qiáng* with *shǎo* to get *shǎoqiáng*.
Combine with *bàn* to get *bànqiáng*.
Combine with *tài* to get *tàiqiáng*.
Getting two *qiáng* is *shǎoruò* (small weak).
Combine this with *shǎo* to get *bànruò* (half weak).
Combine this with *bàn* to get *tàiruò* (great weak).
Combine this with *tài* to get *yīchén ruò* (one *chén* weak).
The Five Planets are:
Wood is called Suìxīng,
Fire is called Yínghuò,
Earth is called Chénxīng,
Metal is called Tàibái,
Water is called Chénxīng.
As for the movements of the Five Planets,
some are slow, some are fast,
some stop, some retrograde.
From ancient times, since the creation,
when the pure and the turbid first separated,
the sun, moon, and Five Planets gathered in Xīngjì.
Starting from Xīngjì,
they moved together through the heavens,
slow, fast, stopping, and retrograding,
mutually catching up with each other.
When a planet meets the sun,
occupying the same lodging and sharing the same degree,
it is called a conjunction (hé).
The number of days from one conjunction to the next
is called a cycle (zhōng).
By taking the number of days in one cycle for each planet and the number of days in one year,
simplify them by common division,
and then express them as ratios:
the number of years for the planet is called the cycle-conjunction-year number (hézhōng suìshù),
and the number of cycles for the year is called the cycle-conjunction-conjunction number (hézhōng hésù).
the fundamental numbers are derived.
Multiply the chapter-year (zhāngsuì) by the conjunction number (hésù) to get the conjunction-month modulus (hémoyue fǎ),
multiply the record modulus (jǐfǎ) by the conjunction number to get the day-degree modulus (rìdù fǎ),
multiply the chapter-month (zhāngyuè) by the year number (suìshù) to get the conjunction-month fraction (hémoyue fēn),
then divide by the conjunction-month modulus (hémoyue fǎ) to get the conjunction-month number (hémoyue shù),
the remainder of the conjunction-month is the month remainder (yuèyú).
Multiply the general number (tōngshù) by the conjunction-month number,
divide by the day modulus (rìfǎ) to get the great remainder (dàyú),
remove multiples of sixty from the great remainder,
the remainder is the planet's conjunction-new moon great remainder (xīnghé shuò dàyú).
The remainder of the great remainder is the new moon small remainder (shuò xiǎoyú).
multiply the conjunction-month modulus by the new moon small remainder,
add them together,
then divide by the day modulus multiplied by the conjunction-month modulus,
the result is the number of days the planet enters the moon (xīnghé rùyuè rìshù).
Divide the remainder by the general modulus (tōngfǎ),
Once these two ratios are determined,
Multiply the general number by the month remainder,
to get the remainder of days entered into the moon (rùyuè rìyú).
Subtract the day modulus from the new moon small remainder,
to get the planet-degree-dou fraction (xīngdù dǒufēn).
For Mù, Huǒ, and Tǔ, subtract the year number from the conjunction number,
multiply the remainder by the circumference of the heavens (zhōutiān),
divide by the day-degree modulus (rìdù fǎ),
the result is the planetary degree number (xíngxīng dùshù),
the remainder is the degree remainder (dùyú).
For Jīn and Shuǐ, multiply the circumference of the heavens by the year number,
divide by the day-degree modulus,
the result is the planetary degree number,
the remainder is the degree remainder.

The method for calculating the Five Planets states: Take the total number of years since the *Rénchén* (壬辰) epoch until the year being sought.
Multiply this by the total number of conjunctions.
When the sum reaches the total number of years per conjunction, it yields one.
This is called the accumulated conjunctions (*jīhé* 积合).
Any remainder is called the conjunction remainder (*héyú* 合餘).
Subtract the conjunction remainder from the total number of conjunctions.
If the result is one, the planetary conjunction occurred in the previous year.
If the result is two, the conjunction occurred two years ago.
If there is no remainder,
the conjunction occurs in the current year.
The remainder is used to subtract from the total number of conjunctions,
giving the degrees and minutes.
For Jīn (金) and Shuǐ (水), in accumulated conjunctions,
an even number indicates a morning appearance,
an odd number indicates an evening appearance.
To calculate the conjunction month of the Five Planets: Multiply the accumulated conjunctions by the number of months and the remainder of months respectively.
When the remainder reaches the *héyuè fǎ* (合月法) for months, it becomes one month,
forming the accumulated months (*jīyuè* 积月).
Any remainder is the month remainder.
Divide the accumulated months by the *jìyuè* (紀月).
The quotient, exclusive of the calculation,
is the number of *jì* (紀) entered.
The remainder is the entered *jì* month.
Next, multiply it by the *zhāngrùn* (章閏).
[五一] When it reaches the *zhāngyuè* (章月), one is a *rùn* (閏) month.
Subtract this from the entered *jì* month.
The remainder is then removed from the *suìzhōng* (歲中).
The remainder is the entered year month.
Starting from *tiānzhèng* (天正),
the quotient, exclusive of the calculation,
is the planetary conjunction month.
When it falls within the *rùn* (閏) intercalation,
use the *shuò* (朔) to manage it.
To calculate the conjunction month *shuò*: Multiply the entered *jì* month by the general number.
When it reaches the *rìfǎ* (日法), it yields one accumulated day (*jīrì* 积日).
Any remainder is the small remainder (*xiǎoyú* 小餘).
Subtract sixty from the accumulated days.
The remainder is the large remainder (*dàyú* 大餘).
Based on the entered *jì*,
the quotient, exclusive of the calculation,
is the *shuò* day of the planetary conjunction.
To calculate the day of entry into the month: Multiply the month remainder by the general number.
Multiply the small remainder of the *shuò* by the *héyuè fǎ* (合月法).
Combine them.
Divide by the general *fǎ* (法).
When the result reaches the *rìdùfǎ* (日度法), it yields one,
which is the day the planet enters the month of conjunction.
Anything less is the day remainder.
Starting from the *shuò* day,
the quotient, exclusive of the calculation,
is the day of entry into the month.
To calculate the conjunction degree of the planet: Multiply the degrees and minutes by the *zhōutiān* (周天).
When it reaches the *rìdùfǎ* (日度法), it yields one degree.
Any remainder is the residual.
Starting from five degrees before Niú (牛),
the quotient, exclusive of the calculation,
is the degree of the planetary conjunction.
To find the next conjunction month: Add the number of months to the entered year month.
Add the remainder to the month remainder.
When the remainder reaches the *héyuè fǎ* (合月法), it yields one month.
If the month is not full in the *suìzhōng* (歲中),
it is in that year.
If it is full, remove it.
If there is an intercalary month, account for it.
The remainder is for the next year.
If it is full twice,
it is in the year after the next.
For Jīn (金) and Shuǐ (水), adding a morning appearance yields an evening appearance;
adding an evening appearance yields a morning appearance.
To find the next conjunction *shuò*: Add the *shuò* large and small remainders to the conjunction *shuò* month large and small remainders.
If the month remainder becomes a full month,
then add twenty-nine to the large remainder
and two thousand four hundred nineteen to the small remainder.
[五二] If the small remainder reaches the *rìfǎ* (日法), it follows the large remainder.
The calculation method is as before.
To find the next day of entry into the month:
[五三] Add the day of entry into the month and the day remainder to the current day of entry into the month and its remainder.
[五四] When the remainder reaches the *rìdùfǎ* (日度法), it yields one.
If the small remainder of the previous conjunction *shuò* is full within its deficient fraction,
remove one day.
If the subsequent small remainder is two thousand four hundred nineteen or more,
remove twenty-nine days.
If it is less,
remove thirty days.
The remainder is then the day of entry into the month for the next conjunction.
Base it on the *shuò*.
To find the next conjunction degree:
Use the number of degrees and minutes.
Determine the *xiù* (宿) sequence as in the previous conjunction.

Method for calculating the steps of the Five Planets: Using the number of degrees remaining from the planet's invisibility period,
add the number of degrees remaining from the day of planetary conjunction.
If the sum reaches a full degree according to the solar degree calculation, one integral unit is obtained.
Designate it as before,
and one obtains the planet's appearance day and the remaining degrees.
Multiply the fractional part of the observed degrees by the denominator of the planet's movement fraction.
If the result reaches one according to the solar degree calculation,
and the fraction is not exhausted,
if it is half of the denominator or more,
one integral unit is also obtained,
and the sun's movement fraction is added.
If the fraction reaches its denominator, one degree is obtained.
The denominators for retrograde and direct motion are different.
Multiply the original fraction by the denominator of the current motion.
Divide by the original denominator,
to get the current motion fraction.
The stationary period carries over from the previous state.
If retrograde, subtract.
Invisibility periods do not record degrees.
Subtract the *dǒu* (segment) fractions,
[五五] taking the motion denominator as the rate.
Fractions have gains and losses;
those before and after balance each other.
Generally, for the Five Planets moving across the sky,
their slowness, swiftness, stationarity, and retrogression,
although their general rates are constant,
it is difficult to calculate their transgressions, guarding, retrogression, and direct motion with this method.
Even the moon's movement across the sky
still has variations in speed,
let alone the Five Planets.
Only the sun's movement across the sky is constant,
with fixed rates of advance and retreat,
neither slow nor fast,
neither outward nor inward.
This is the virtue of a sovereign.
Method for finding the total number of years for Mù (Jupiter) conjunctions:
Multiply the total days of one cycle of Mù (Jupiter) by the solar degree calculation for Mù (Jupiter).
Insert the fractional part.
Divide by the degrees in a full circle,
and the result is obtained.
Method for finding the total number of conjunctions for Mù (Jupiter) conjunctions:
Multiply the degrees in a full circle by the solar degree calculation for Mù (Jupiter).
If it reaches the *jì* (cycle) calculation,
then divide the result again by the degrees in a full circle,
and the result is obtained.
All Five Planets follow this.
"In the eleventh month, which was small, of the first year of Huángchū of Wèi (220 CE),
*Jǐmǎo* was the beginning of the *bù* (period),
in the *Jǐhài* year,
the new moon on *Jǐmǎo* in the eleventh month was the Winter Solstice.
Submitted by your minister, Wěi."
The Liú (royal house) in Shǔ (Shu Han)
did not see the calendar change,
so it is probable they still used the Hàn Sìfēn calendar.
Kàn Zé, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat in Wú (Eastern Wu), received Liú Hóng's Qiánxiàng method from Xú Yuè, courtesy name Gōnghé, of Dōnglái.
Therefore, the Sūn (royal house) used the Qiánxiàng calendar
until the fall of Wú.
In the first year of Tàishǐ of Jìn Wǔdì (265 CE),
the relevant officials memorialized:
"The king derives his *qì* from the ancestral origin and respects its end.
The Jìn, in the order of the Five Phases, should honor Metal.
Metal is born in *jǐ*,
serves in *yǒu*,
and ends in *chǒu*.
It is fitting to take *yǒu* day as the ancestral day,
and *chǒu* day as the Lày (Winter Sacrifice) day.
The Jǐngchū calendar should be changed to the Tàishǐ calendar."
The memorial was approved.
The official historian comments: According to Zōu Yǎn’s (鄒衍) theory of the Five Virtues (Wǔdé),
the Zhōu (周) dynasty operated under the element of Fire.
Zōu Yǎn (鄒衍) lived during the Zhōu (周) period,
so it is impossible that he did not know the elemental progression of the Zhōu (周) house.
Moreover, the Zhōu (周) lasted for eight hundred years,
and the Qín (秦) dynasty was established after the Zhōu (周).
The matter of the Zhōu’s (周) Fire and Wood [elements]
is easily explained.
Furthermore, regarding the succession of the Five Virtues (Wǔdé),
there are only two schools of thought.
Zōu Yǎn (鄒衍) established his theory based on mutual conquest (xiāngshèng),
while Liú Xiàng (劉向) defined his by mutual generation (xiāngshēng).
Based on these,
one cannot depart from these two schools.
If we adopt Liú Xiàng’s (劉向) theory,
the Zhōu (周) was Wood.
When the Qín (秦) succeeded the Zhōu (周),
it changed its elemental progression.
If it was not by mutual conquest,
then the element that conquers Wood is Metal;
if by mutual generation, then Wood actually generates Fire.
The Qín (秦) then claimed the virtue of Water,
which is not illogical.
In this case, what Liú Shì (劉氏) attested to would be worthless.
Your subject believes that although Zhāng Cāng (張蒼) was a minister of the Hàn (漢),
he lived concurrently with the Zhōu (周),
served under the Qín (秦) as a pillar official,
and fully observed its records and documents.
Moreover, though the Qín (秦) suppressed learning,
it did not abolish divination and numerology.
Thus, although the surviving Zhōu (周) texts were not complete,
the Hàn (漢) claiming the element of Water
was not a baseless fabrication.
Jiǎ Yì (賈誼) stated about the Qín (秦):
“The Hàn (漢) is the virtue of Earth.”
This was likely based on the Hàn (漢) succeeding the Qín (秦).
Examining the two theories in detail,
each has its own meaning.
Zhāng Cāng (張蒼) held that Hàn (漢) Water conquered Zhōu (周) Fire,
and excluded the Qín (秦) from the Five Virtues (Wǔdé) progression.
Jiǎ Yì (賈誼) held that Hàn (漢) Earth conquered Qín (秦) Water,
treating the Qín (秦) as a legitimate dynasty.
Though their views on Qín (秦) and Hàn (漢) differed,
they both agreed that the Zhōu (周) was Fire.
Thus, the principle of mutual conquest (xiāngshèng)
is superior in this matter.
If we follow Zhāng Cāng (張蒼) in rejecting the Qín (秦),
then Hàn (漢) is Water, Wèi (魏) is Earth, Jìn (晉) is Wood, and Sòng (宋) is Metal.
If we follow Jiǎ Yì (賈誼) in accepting the Qín (秦),
then Hàn (漢) is Earth, Wèi (魏) is Wood, Jìn (晉) is Metal, and Sòng (宋) is Fire.
Skeptics say:
“When Emperor Gāo of Hàn (漢高) cut the serpent, its divine mother wept at night,
saying that the son of the Red Emperor had killed the son of the White Emperor.
Therefore, if Hàn (漢) is not Fire, what is it?”
This is again incorrect.
If Hàn (漢) were Fire,
it should be referred to as the Red Emperor,
not the son of the Red Emperor.
And what is the meaning of the son of the White Emperor?
It is because Hàn (漢) is the virtue of Earth,
and Earth generates Fire.
Qín (秦) is the virtue of Water,
and Water generates Metal.
Thus, Hàn (漢) represents Earth as the son of the Red Emperor,
and Qín (秦) represents Water as the son of the White Emperor.
Skeptics further ask:
“You said earlier that the Five Virtues (Wǔdé) succeed by mutual conquest (xiāngshèng),
but now you say Earth is the son of the Red Emperor.
Why?”
The answer is:
“The Five Elements (Wǔxíng) inherently have the principle of mutual conquest (xiāngshèng)
and inherently have the principle of mutual generation (xiāngshēng).
One cannot dismiss mutual generation (xiāngshēng) because of mutual conquest (xiāngshèng),
nor mutual conquest (xiāngshèng) because of mutual generation (xiāngshēng).
Mutual conquest (xiāngshèng) means
Earth conquers Water;
mutual generation (xiāngshēng) means
Earth is the child of Fire.
How can these principles be related?”
Cuī Shí’s (崔寔) Sì Mín Yuè Lìng (四民月令) says: Zǔ (祖) refers to
the spirit of the road.
The Yellow Emperor’s (Huángdì) son was named Léi Zǔ (累祖).
He loved to travel far
and died on the road,
so he was sacrificed to as the spirit of the road.
Jī Hán’s (嵇含) Zǔ Dào Fù Xù (祖道賦序) says:
the Wèi (魏) used dīngwèi (丁未),
and the Jìn (晉) used the you (酉) day of the first month.
It is said that no one knows the origin of Zǔ (祖).
Commentators say that to pray to the spirit of the road
is called Zǔ (祖). When gentlemen embark on a journey,
they arrange offerings in the middle of the road.
When the deceased are about to be moved,
their names are invoked in the courtyard.
Alternatively, it is said that
the names and posthumous titles of distant ancestors from a hundred generations
have been obliterated,
and their tombs no longer bear inscriptions.
Their wandering souls have nowhere to rely in ancestral temples.
Therefore, on a propitious day at the beginning of the year,
a canopy is erected,
and colorful banners are flown,
to summon their spirits,
so that all ancestors may come and take repose.
〔五七〕
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn (晉武帝),
Liú Zhì (劉智) of Píngyuán (平原), a chamberlain,
〔五八〕revised the calendar based on three hundred years of the Dǒu Lì (斗曆),
believing that the Sì Fēn Fǎ (四分法) subtracted one day every three hundred years.
He set one hundred and fifty as the degree measure [of the moon’s motion],
and thirty-seven as the Dǒu (斗) division.
He embellished it with fanciful theories
to support his reasoning.
Wáng Shuòzhī (王朔之) of Lángyá (琅邪), the Chief Commandant of the Capital Guards in Jiāngzuǒ (江左), because his Uppersource year was jiǎzǐ (甲子),
admired his method
and wished to use the jiǎzǐ (甲子) of ninety-seven thousand years as the beginning of creation.
Hé Chéngtiān (何承天) said
“he lamented the intention.”
The sun dial shadow at noon in Jǐngchū (景初)
used the Hàn (漢) Sì Fēn Fǎ (四分法),
which led to gradual discrepancies.
Its calculation of the five planets
was extremely inaccurate.
Since the Jìn (晉) in Jiāngzuǒ (江左),
the Qián Xiàng Wǔ Xīng Fǎ (乾象五星法) was adopted to replace it,
but it still had advancements and retrogradations.
Emperor Tàizǔ of Sòng (宋太祖) was quite fond of calendrical calculations.
Hé Chéngtiān (何承天), the Grand Astrologer to the Crown Prince, privately compiled a new method.
In the twentieth year of Yuánjiā (元嘉)
he submitted a memorial stating: Your subject is naturally dull and lazy,
and has little understanding.
Since my youth,
I have been quite fond of calendrical calculations,
devoting my attention and passion to them
until my hair turned white.
My deceased maternal uncle, the former Secretarial
Archivist Xú Guǎng (徐廣),
was skilled in this matter,
and had a record of past seven luminaries’ calendars,
noting their accuracy and errors.
From Tàihé (太和) to the end of Tàiyuán (太元),
about forty years.
Your subject
then consecutively reviewed and verified them,
and it has now been another forty years.
Therefore, their tightness and looseness, differences and agreements
are all knowable.
Indeed, the celestial sphere is constantly moving,
the seven luminaries operate,
their conjunctions, separations, departures, and arrivals,
though having fixed patterns,
with the interference of new and old,
naturally have minute discrepancies.
Day after day
and year after year,
tiny differences accumulate into significant ones.
Therefore, the Yú Shū (虞書) recorded the canon of respectful observation,
and the Zhōu Yì (周易) clearly taught the principles of calendrical calculation,
stating that one should conform to Heaven to seek agreement,
not to use agreement to
verify Heaven.
During the Hàn (漢) dynasty, various observations were made from the Qīngtái (清臺),
using the central star at dusk and dawn
to ascertain the sun’s position.
Although the sun itself cannot be seen,
when the moon is full, it eclipses
precisely at opposition.
By calculating the sun
from the moon,
its orbital position can be known.
To abandon what is easy and not do it,
but to toil one’s mind over difficult matters,
this is what your subject does not understand.
The Yáo Diǎn (堯典) says:
“The day is longest when the Fire star is central,
thereby correcting mid-summer.”
Now, in late summer, the Fire star is central.
Also,
“At mid-night, the Xū (虛) star is central,
thereby correcting mid-autumn.”
Now, in late autumn,
the Xū (虛) star is central.
Since then, over two thousand seven hundred years have passed.
Examining it by the central star,
the difference is twenty-seven or twenty-eight degrees.
Thus, in Yáo’s (堯) command, the winter solstice
was when the sun was around ten
degrees in Xūnǚ (須女).
The Tàichū Lì (太初曆) of Hàn (漢) placed the winter solstice at the beginning of Qiānniú (牽牛).
The later Hàn (漢) Sì Fēn (四分) and Wèi (魏) Jǐngchū Fǎ (景初法)
both placed it at Dǒu (斗) twenty-one.
Your subject,
When a lunar eclipse is observed,
it is found that in the Jǐngchū era, the current winter solstice
should fall in Dǒu (Sagittarius) at 17 degrees.
Moreover, the imperial astronomers received an edict
to measure the shadow with a gnomon (tǔguī)
and verify the two solstices.
There was a discrepancy of three
days and more.
The accumulated years since then, and the reports submitted by Jiāozhōu,
when checked for their increases and decreases,
also matched and were verified.
Therefore, the current two solstices
are not the true (celestial) two solstices.
The true (celestial) southern solstice
〔五九〕falls on Dǒu (Sagittarius) at 13 or 14 degrees.
This means that the nineteen-year, seven-intercalation cycle
has a slightly larger error.
If we again change the method and revise the system,
then the calculations will become excessively
numerous.
It is appropriate to adapt and reform with the times
to achieve accuracy.
According to the "Treatise on Astronomy" in the *Hòu Hàn Shū*,
the spring equinox day is longer,
and the autumn equinox day is shorter,
differing by more than half a *kè*.
Upon reflection, the two equinoxes fall
between the two solstices,
yet they have different lengths.
This indicates that the spring equinox is closer to the summer solstice,
hence it is longer;
the autumn equinox is closer to the winter solstice,
hence it is shorter.
Yáng Wěi did not realize this
and applied
it,
submitting a calendrical memorial stating:
"From ancient times to the present,
all calendrical calculations
have not been able to match its marvel."
If he does not understand this,
what else can he claim?
Therefore, I, your minister,
have newly established the Yuánjiā Calendar,
with six hundred and eight days as one *jì*,
half of which is the degree measure,
seventy-five as the *shì* division,
taking the month of *jiànyín* as the start of the year,
and *yǔshuǐ*
as the beginning of the *qì*.
The year in which the remainder of all methods for intercalations is one is the start of the *zhāng*.
The winter solstice is shifted by three days and five *shí* from the previous calculation.
The sun's position
is shifted by four degrees from the old calculation.
Furthermore, if the moon
has varying speeds,
then conjunctions (héshuò) and lunar eclipses
do not fall on the new moon (shuò) or full moon (wàng),
which is also not the intent of the calendar.
Therefore, the Yuánjiā calendar determines the *xiǎoyú* (fractional remainders) based on the waxing and waning,
to correct the days of the new moon and full moon.
I humbly submit that Your Majesty, in accordance with the sagely and wise,
acts in harmony with Heaven,
diligently manages all affairs of state,
and reverently promotes the grand enterprise,
delving into profound thoughts from past records,
and exploring subtle principles from what has not
been heard,
exhausting divine knowledge and comprehending transformations,
with nothing beyond your comprehensive view.
Thus, this foolish minister rejoices in encountering this glorious era
to offer his humble contribution.
I humbly request that Your Majesty refer the Yuánjiā method I have submitted to the imperial astronomers
to examine its precision.
If there are errors that can be adopted,
it may perhaps correct existing flaws and errors,
to be prepared for all eventualities.
An edict stated:
"What Hé Chéngtiān has presented
has indeed strong reasons.
It can be handed over to the relevant department for detailed examination."

The Grand Astrologer Qián Lèzhī and Acting Assistant Yán Càn memorialized: The Heir Apparent's Master of the Left and concurrently Academician of the National University, Hé Chéngtiān, has memorialized to change and reform the Yuánjiā calendrical method,
stating that an examination of lunar eclipses shows the current winter solstice falls in Dǒu (Sagittarius) at 17 degrees.
By
measuring the shadow with a gnomon (tǔguī),
it is known that the winter solstice has already shifted by three days.
An edict commanded that it be handed over to the relevant department for examination and verification.
In the eleventh year of Yuánjiā, an imperial order was received
to examine lunar eclipses
and measure the
shadow with a gnomon (tǔguī).
An examination revealed that according to the Wěi Jǐngchū method previously in use,
on the day of the winter solstice,
the sun was in Dǒu (Sagittarius) at 21 degrees, a little less.
An examination of the full moon eclipse on the sixteenth day of the seventh month of the eleventh year,
the eclipse
started at the *jiāshí* (additional hour) of Mǎo,
and by the fourth watch and second beat of the fifteenth day, at the beginning of Chǒu, the eclipse began,
reaching totality by the fourth beat.
It was in Yíngshì (Pegasus) at 15 degrees at the end.
In Jǐngchū, the sun on that day
was in Zhěn (Crater) at 3 degrees.
Comparing this with the opposition point of the lunar eclipse,
the sun on that day should have been in Yì (Corvus) at 15.5 degrees.
〔六０〕Again, for the full moon eclipse on the sixteenth day of the twelfth month of the thirteenth year,
the *jiāshí* was at Yǒu,
the eclipse began at Hài,
and reached totality at the first watch and third beat.
It was in Guǐ (Cancer) at 4 degrees.
In Jǐngchū, the sun on that day was in Nǚ (Virgo) at 3 degrees.
Comparing with the opposition,
the sun on that day should have been in Niú (Capricorn) at 6.5 degrees.
Again, for the full moon eclipse on the sixteenth day of the twelfth month of the fourteenth year,
〔六一〕the *jiāshí* was at half
of Xū,
the eclipse began at the end of Hài at the second watch and fourth beat,
and reached totality at the third watch and first beat.
It was in Jǐng (Gemini) at 38 degrees.
〔六二〕In Jǐngchū, the sun on that day was in Dǒu (Sagittarius) at 25
degrees.
Comparing with the opposition,
the sun on that day should have been in Dǒu (Sagittarius) at 22.5 degrees.
〔六三〕For the full moon eclipse on the fifteenth day of the fifth month of the fifteenth year,
the *jiāshí* was at
Xū,
the moon had just risen,
and one-quarter of the eclipse light had already occurred,
in Dǒu (Sagittarius) around 16 degrees.
In Jǐngchū, the sun on that day was in Jǐng (Gemini) at 24 degrees.
Comparing with its opposition,
the sun on that day should have been in Jǐng (Gemini) at 20 degrees.
Again, for the full moon eclipse on the sixteenth day of the ninth month of the seventeenth year,
the *jiāshí* was a little before Zǐ,
the eclipse began on the fifteenth
day at the second watch and first beat,
and by the third beat, twelve-fifteenths of the eclipse had occurred,
in Mǎo (Pleiades) at 1.5 degrees.
In Jǐngchū, the sun on that day was in Fáng (Scorpii) at 2 degrees.
Comparing
with the opposition,
the sun on that day should have been in Dī (Libra) at 13.5 degrees.
In all these five eclipses,
comparing the moon's opposition at 182.5 degrees,
on the day of the winter solstice,
the sun was not in Dǒu (Sagittarius) at 21 degrees and a little less,
but rather in Dǒu (Sagittarius) at around 17.5 degrees,
all as reported by Chéngtiān.
Furthermore, starting from the eleventh year,
the shadow was measured with a gnomon (tǔguī).
In that year, according to the Jǐngchū method, the winter solstice was on the seventh day of the eleventh month,
but before and after, it was cloudy, and no shadow was seen.
By the
winter solstice on the eighteenth day of the eleventh month of the twelfth year,
the shadow was longest on the fifteenth day.
By the winter solstice on the twenty-ninth day of the eleventh month of the thirteenth year,
the shadow was longest on the twenty-sixth
day.
By the winter solstice on the eleventh day of the eleventh month of the fourteenth year,
it was cloudy before and after, and no shadow was seen.
〔六四〕By the winter solstice on the twenty-first
day of the eleventh month of the fifteenth year,
the shadow was longest on the eighteenth day.
By the winter solstice on the second day of the eleventh month of the sixteenth year,
the shadow was longest on the twenty-ninth day of the tenth month.
By the
winter solstice on the thirteenth day of the eleventh month of the seventeenth year,
the shadow was longest on the tenth day.
By the winter solstice on the twenty-fifth day of the eleventh month of the eighteenth year,
the shadow was longest on the twenty-first
day.
〔六五〕By the winter solstice on the sixth day of the eleventh month of the nineteenth year,
the shadow was longest on the third day.
By the winter solstice on the sixteenth day of the eleventh month of the twentieth year,
it was cloudy before
and after, and no shadow was seen.
Upon reviewing and comparing the events,
taking the day of the longest shadow as the winter solstice,
there is a consistent discrepancy of three days.
Examining the sun's position by lunar eclipses,
it has already shifted by four degrees.
Measuring the
shadow with a gnomon (tǔguī),
the winter solstice has again shifted by three days.
The current winter solstice
is now around Dǒu (Sagittarius) at 14 degrees,
again as reported by Chéngtiān.
Furthermore, according to Chéngtiān's method,
the *shuò*, *wàng*, and *xián* (first and last quarter moons) of each month
are all determined by precise *xiǎoyú* (fractional remainders).
Although the calculation of conjunction and opposition times is precise,
all employing waxing and waning principles,
the moon consequently has frequently
three large and two small lunar months in sequence,
which is quite different from the old method.
In the old method, solar eclipses were not only on the *shuò* (new moon),
but also occurred on the *huì* (last day of the month) and the second day.
The *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* refers to this as
"sometimes missing
before,
or after missing."
I humbly believe that this article should remain as is.
Yuánwài Sànqí Láng Pí Yánzōng (員外散騎郎 皮延宗) further challenged Chéngtiān (承天):
"If the New Moon and Full Moon determine the length of the month (dàxiǎoyú 大小餘),
and the beginning of the ji (紀) falls on a 'full' month,
then we should subtract one day.
Therefore, the last day of the old year
should be the first day of the new ji."
Chéngtiān (承天) then revised the new method to conform to the old technique,
no longer determining the length of the month (dàxiǎoyú 大小餘) monthly,
as Pí Yánzōng (皮延宗) had challenged,
and as the Grand Astrologer had submitted.
The officials reported:
"Reforming the calendar and changing the system
is a grand undertaking for governing the state.
From the Hàn (漢) to the Wèi (魏) dynasties,
there have been frequent changes.
This is because methods are not perpetually correct;
they are adopted to suit the present time.
Now that the imperial virtue shines brightly,
and its light covers the old territories,
it is indeed appropriate to comprehensively examine the gnomon and degrees
to broadcast renewal.
Chéngtiān's (承天) calendar method
is suitable for implementation.
In the twenty-second year of Sòng (宋),
the Yuánjiā (元嘉) calendar was universally adopted."
The emperor approved the诏.
