Method for entering the ji (紀): Place the years from the end of Shàngyuán Gēngchén (上元庚辰) to the year sought.
Divide by yuánfǎ (元法).
If less than yuánfǎ (元法),
divide by jìfǎ (紀法).
The remainder, if less than jìfǎ (紀法), is the number of years entered in the ji (紀).
If it reaches the modulus, remove it to obtain the next ji (紀).
(From the year Rénchén (壬辰) entering the Jiǎwǔ Jì (甲午紀),
up to the current twentieth year of Yuánjiā (元嘉),
which is Guǐwèi (癸未),
two hundred and thirty-one years,
beyond calculation.)
Method for accumulating months: Place the number of years entered in the ji (紀) beyond calculation.
Multiply by zhāngyuè (章月).
The result, if equal to zhāngsuì (章歲), is the accumulated months;
the remainder is the surplus for intercalation.
If the intercalary surplus is twelve or more,
that year is an intercalary year.
Method for calculating the New Moon: Multiply the accumulated months by tōngshù (通數),
to get the accumulated score for the New Moon.
If it reaches rìfǎ (日法), it is the accumulated days;
the remainder is the small surplus (xiǎoyú 小餘).
Subtract sixty from the accumulated days.
The remainder is the large surplus (dàyú 大餘),
named by ji (紀),
beyond calculation.
This is the day of the New Moon in the first month of the sought year.
To find the next month,
add twenty-nine to the large surplus (dàyú 大餘)
and three hundred and ninety-nine to the small surplus (xiǎoyú 小餘).
If the small surplus (xiǎoyú 小餘) reaches rìfǎ (日法), it adds to the large surplus (dàyú 大餘).
This is the New Moon of the next month.
If the small surplus (xiǎoyú 小餘) is three hundred and fifty-three or more,
that month is a long month.
Method for calculating the first and last quarters: Add seven to the New Moon's large surplus (dàyú 大餘),
two hundred and eighty-seven to the small surplus (xiǎoyú 小餘),
and three to the small fraction (xiǎofēn 小分).
If the small fraction (xiǎofēn 小分) reaches four, it adds to the small surplus (xiǎoyú 小餘);
if the small surplus (xiǎoyú 小餘) reaches rìfǎ (日法), it adds to the large surplus (dàyú 大餘).
Name as before.
This is the day of the first quarter.
Adding again yields the Full Moon.
Adding again yields the last quarter.
Method for calculating the twenty-four solar terms: Place the years entered in the ji (紀) beyond calculation.
Multiply by yúshù (餘數).
If it reaches dùfǎ (度法) of three hundred and four, it is the accumulated mò (積沒);
the remainder is the small surplus (xiǎoyú 小餘).
Subtract sixty from the accumulated mò (積沒).
The remainder is the large surplus (dàyú 大餘),
named by ji (紀),
beyond calculation.
This is the day of Rǔshuǐ (雨水) in the sought year.
To find the next solar term,
add fifteen to the large surplus (dàyú 大餘),
sixty-six to the small surplus (xiǎoyú 小餘),
and eleven to the small fraction (xiǎofēn 小分).
If the small fraction (xiǎofēn 小分) reaches qìfǎ (氣法), it adds to the small surplus (xiǎoyú 小餘);
if the small surplus (xiǎoyú 小餘) reaches dùfǎ (度法), it adds to the large surplus (dàyú 大餘).
This is the day of the next solar term.
(If Rǔshuǐ (雨水) falls after the sixteenth day,
subtract according to the method to get Lìchūn (立春).)
Method for calculating the intercalary month: Subtract zhāngsuì (章歲) from the intercalary surplus.
Multiply the remainder by suìzhōng (歲中).
If it reaches zhāngrùn (章閏), it gets one.
Count from the first month.
This is where the intercalary month is.
Intercalary months have advances and retreats;
they are governed by not having a mid-solar term.

Báilù (白露) is the eighth month's jiéqì (節氣) (limit 157, interval 162). Qiūfēn (秋分) is the eighth month's zhōngqì (中氣) (limit 167, interval 172).
Hánlù (寒露) is the ninth month's jiéqì (節氣) (limit 177, interval 182). Shuāngjiàng (霜降) is the ninth month's zhōngqì (中氣) (limit 186, interval 190).
Lìdōng (立冬) is the tenth month's jiéqì (節氣) (limit 194, interval 197). Xiǎoxuě (小雪) is the tenth month's zhōngqì (中氣) (limit 200, interval 203).
Dàxuě (大雪) is the eleventh month's jiéqì (節氣) (limit 205, interval 206). Dōngzhì (冬至) is the eleventh month's zhōngqì (中氣) (limit 207, interval 206).
Xiǎohán (小寒) is the twelfth month's jiéqì (節氣) (limit 205, interval 203). Dàhán (大寒) is the twelfth month's zhōngqì (中氣) (limit 200, interval 197).
Method for calculating eclipses: Based on the accumulated Rǔshuǐ (雨水),
multiply by mòyú (沒餘).
If it reaches mòfǎ (沒法), it becomes the large surplus (dàyú 大餘);
the remainder is the small surplus (xiǎoyú 小餘).
As before,
this is the day of the eclipse before Rǔshuǐ (雨水) in the sought year.
To find the next eclipse,
add sixty-nine to the large surplus (dàyú 大餘)
and one hundred and ninety-six to the small surplus (xiǎoyú 小餘).
If it reaches mòfǎ (沒法), it adds to the large surplus (dàyú 大餘).
Name as before.
This is the day of the eclipse after Rǔshuǐ (雨水).
(Eclipses before Rǔshuǐ (雨水) often occur in the previous year.
There are usually five eclipses.
Officials correct this with eclipses.
There are usually five or six eclipses in a year.
When the small surplus (xiǎoyú 小餘) is exhausted, it is the day of the eclipse.)
If the small surplus (xiǎoyú 小餘) of Rǔshuǐ (雨水) is thirty-nine or less,
it only occurs after sixty days from Rǔshuǐ (雨水).
Method for calculating the earth's position: Set the numbers for *lìchūn* (start of spring) for the greater remainder (*dàyú*), lesser remainder (*xiǎoyú*), and lesser fraction (*xiǎofēn*).
Subtract eighteen from the *dàyú*.
Subtract seventy-nine from the *xiǎoyú*.
Subtract eighteen from the *xiǎofēn*.
Designate this as the *jì*.
Beyond the calculation,
this is the day when the earth's position occurs before *lìchūn*.
If the *dàyú* is insufficient, add sixty.
If the *xiǎoyú* is insufficient to subtract,
subtract one from the *dàyú*,
add the *dùfǎ* (degree method) and then subtract.
Calculating the earth's position for *lìxià* (start of summer) and *lìdōng* (start of winter) all follow the above method.
Method for calculating the sun's position: Multiply the *dùfǎ* by the accumulated days from the new moon (*shuò*).
Subtract the total degrees of the celestial sphere (*zhōutiān*).
The remainder, if it equals the *dùfǎ*, is the accumulated degrees (*jīdù*).
[一０]The unexhausted part is the fraction.
Designate the degrees starting from *Shì* two,
then subtract the next lunar lodge (*xiù*).
Beyond the calculation,
this is the sun's degree and fraction at midnight on the first new moon of the first month.
To find the next day,
add one degree daily,
and remove degrees and fractions passing through the lunar lodge.
Method for calculating the moon's position: Multiply the moon's synodic period (*yuèzhōu*) by the accumulated days from the new moon.
Subtract the *zhōutiān*.
The remainder, if it equals the *dùfǎ*, is the *jīdù*.
The unexhausted part is the fraction.
Designate the degrees as before.
This is the moon's degree and fraction at midnight on the first new moon of the first month.
To find the next month,
for a small month, add twenty-two degrees
and one hundred thirty-three fractions.
For a large month, add thirty-five degrees
and two hundred forty-five fractions.
If the fractions equal the *dùfǎ*, it forms one degree.
Designate as before.
This is the moon's degree and fraction on the new moon of the next month.
Method for previous month in the calendar: Divide the moon's fractional movement by sixteen to get the greater fraction.
Add or subtract according to its fastness or slowness.
Remove degrees and fractions passing through the lunar lodge.
Method for calculating the conjunction (new moon) and lunar eclipse: Set the accumulated months of the year to be calculated.
Multiply by the conjunction number (one hundred sixty).
Add the difference in the conjunction cycle (*jiāohuìjìchā*) (twenty-two).
If it reaches the *huìyuè* (conjunction month), subtract it.
The remainder is the difference from the node fraction (*jiāofēn*) for the new moon of the first month of that year.
To find the next month,
add the conjunction number.
If it reaches the *huìyuè*, subtract it.
To find the full moon (*wàng*),
add the conjunction number.
If the new moon or full moon's *jiāofēn* is below the conjunction number
and above the node limit number (*jiāoxiànshù*),
a new moon indicates a conjunction,
and a full moon indicates a lunar eclipse.
Method for calculating the calendar's fastness and slowness: Set the accumulated fraction of the new moon for the year to be calculated.
Add the fast/slow difference (fifteen thousand two hundred forty-five).
If it reaches the total cycle (*tōngzhōu*), subtract it.
The remainder, if it reaches the day method (*rìfǎ*), yields one day.
[一一]The unexhausted part is the remaining day fraction (*rìyú*).
Designate the days beyond calculation.
This is when the first new moon of the year to be calculated enters the calendar.
To find the next month,
add one day
and seven hundred thirty-four *rìyú*.
To find the full moon,
add fourteen days
and five hundred seventy-five and a half *rìyú*.
If the remainder reaches the *rìfǎ*, it becomes one day.
If the days reach twenty-seven, subtract it.
Divide the *rìyú* by the *zhōurìrìyú* (remaining day fraction of the week day).
If insufficient, subtract.
Subtract one day
and add the *zhōuxū* (week void).
(If the days reach twenty-seven and the *rìyú* does not reach the *zhōurìrìyú*,
it is a deficit.
If the *zhōurì* is reached, subtract it.
This is one day entering the calendar.)
Method for determining the greater and lesser remainders for conjunction and lunar eclipse: Multiply the *rìyú* entering the calendar by the gain/loss rate below entering the calendar.
(One day enters, twenty-five is gained.
This is it.)
Use the accumulated gain/loss and contraction/expansion (*sǔnyìyíngsuōjīfēn*).
(If it's a loss, subtract it;
if it's a gain, add it.)
This is the fixed accumulated fraction (*dìngjīfēn*).
Multiply the *rìyú* entering the calendar by the listed difference (*lièchā*).
If it reaches the *rìfǎ*, subtract for expansion (*yíngjiǎn*), and add for contraction (*suōjiā*), obtaining the difference method (*chāfǎ*).
Divide the *dìngjīfēn*.
Subtract or add the result to the original lesser remainder of the new or full moon.
(If it's expansion, subtract;
if it's contraction, add.)
This is the fixed lesser remainder (*dìngxiǎoyú*).
If adding it reaches the *rìfǎ*, the new moon or lunar eclipse advances by one day.
If subtracting it is insufficient,
add the *rìfǎ* and then subtract,
then it retreats by one day.
For *zhōurì* (week day) values,
use the fixed number for *zhōurì*.
Method for calculating the added hour (*jiāshí*): Multiply the *dìngxiǎoyú* by twelve.
If it reaches the *rìfǎ*, it yields one *chén* (two-hour period).
Counting starts from *Zǐ*.
Beyond the calculation,
this is the *chén* where the new or full moon's *jiāshí* falls.
If there is a remainder, multiply it by four.
If it reaches the *rìfǎ*, one is *shǎo* (small),
two is *bàn* (half),
three is *tài* (great).
[一二]If there is still a remainder, multiply it by three.
If it reaches the *rìfǎ*, one is *qiáng* (strong).
If it's above half the *fǎ* (method/standard), it is rounded up to one.
If it's below half the *fǎ*, it is discarded.
Combining *qiáng* with *shǎo* gives *shǎoqiáng*.
Combining with *bàn* gives *bànqiáng*.
Combining with *tài* gives *tàiqiáng*.
If it gets two, it is *shǎoruò* (small weak).
[一三]Combining it with *shǎo* gives *bànruò* (half weak).
Combining it with *bàn* gives *tàiruò* (great weak).
Combining it with *tài* gives *yīchénruò* (one *chén* weak).
Name it according to the *chén* it falls into.
Method for calculating the exact *kè* for the *jiāshí* of conjunction and lunar eclipse:
[一四]Multiply the *dìngxiǎoyú* by one hundred *kè* each.
Divide by the *rìfǎ* to get one.
If unexhausted, multiply by ten
to find the fraction. First subtract half of the night clepsydra.
This is the added *shíkè* and fraction for the day clepsydra.
When the day clepsydra ends,
the night clepsydra begins again.
For those within four days before and after the *zhōngjié* (mid-term),
observe the limit number.
For those five days or more before and after the *zhōngjié*,
observe the interval limit number.
If the *dìngxiǎoyú* for the *jiāshí* of a lunar eclipse does not reach the limit number or interval number,
all are considered days in the calculation.

Method for calculating the degrees of conjunction (new moon): Multiply the *zhāngsuì* (cycle year) by the new moon's lesser remainder.
If it reaches the *tōngfǎ* (general method), it becomes the greater fraction.
The unexhausted part is the lesser fraction.
Add the greater fraction to the sun's daily fraction at midnight of the new moon.
If it reaches a degree, designate as before.
This is the total conjunction degree of the sun and moon at the new moon of the first month.
To find the next month,
add twenty-nine degrees,
one hundred sixty-one greater fractions,
and fourteen lesser fractions.
If the lesser fractions reach the *tōngfǎ*, add to the greater fractions.
If the greater fractions reach the *dùfǎ*, add to the degrees.
Remove degrees and fractions passing through the lunar lodge.
To find the full moon,
add fourteen degrees,
two hundred thirty-two greater fractions,
and thirty and a half lesser fractions.
(To find the moon's position at full moon,
add one hundred eighty-two sun degrees,
one hundred eighty-nine fractions,
and twenty-three and a half lesser fractions.)

To calculate the Five Planets: Set each of their origins (yuán) up to the requested year's calculation.
Multiply this by the total number (héshù).
When it reaches a full total year (hésuì), it becomes the accumulated total (jíhé).
The remainder is called the total remainder (héyú).
If there is more, divide it by the total number.
If you get one,
the planet total is for the previous year (wǎngnián).
If you get two,
the total is for the year before the previous year (qiánwǎngnián).
If it is less than the total number,
it is for the current year (qínián).
(For Mù, Tǔ, and Jīn, there are previous year totals (wǎngnián hé).
For Huǒ, there are previous year totals (qiánwǎngnián hé).
For Shuǐ, there are three or four totals in one year.)
Subtract the total remainder (héyú) from the total number (héshù) to get degrees and minutes (dùfēn).
(For Shuǐ, if the degrees and minutes reach a full total year, they are removed.)
Multiply the degrees and minutes (dùfēn) by the circumference of the heavens (zhōutiān) (111,035).
When it reaches a full daily degree method (rìdùfǎ), it becomes accumulated degrees (jídù).
The remainder is called the degree remainder (dùyú).
The designated degrees (mìngdù) are for the second position (shì'èr) in the mansion (shì).
Exclude outside calculations (suànwài).
This is the degree where the planet total (xīnghé) is located.
Multiply the current year (qínián) by the total number (héshù).
Add the small remainder of rain and water (yǔshuǐ xiǎoyú) to it.
Combine this with the degree remainder (dùyú) to get the day remainder (rìyú).
When it reaches a full daily degree method (rìdùfǎ), it forms an accumulated day (jíré).
Designate this as rain and water (yǔshuǐ).
Exclude outside calculations (suànwài).
This is the planet total day (xīnghé rì).
To find the day a planet is seen:
Add the hidden days (fú rì) and remainder according to the method (fǎfú rì jíyú) (for Mù, it is 16 days and remainder).
[二三] to the planet total day (xīnghé rì) and remainder.
When it reaches a full daily degree method (rìdùfǎ), it becomes one day.
Designate it as before.
This is the day the planet is seen (xīngjiàn rì).
To find the degree a planet is seen:
Add the hidden degrees (fú dù) and remainder according to the method (fǎfú dù jíyú) (for Mù, it is 2 degrees and remainder).
to the planet total degree (xīnghé dù) and remainder.
When it reaches a full daily degree method (rìdùfǎ), it becomes one degree.
Designate it as before.
This is the degree where it is seen (suǒjiàn dù).
Multiply the seen degree remainder (jiàndù yú) by the planet's movement denominator (xíngfēnmǔ) (for Mù, it is seen as 23).
[二四]
When it reaches a full daily degree method (rìdùfǎ), it gets one.
The fraction (fēn) then adds the daily movement fraction (rìjiā suǒxíng fēn).
(Mù moves forward by 4/23 daily.)
When the fraction (fēn) reaches its denominator, it becomes one degree.
The direct and retrograde denominators are different.
(Mù's retrograde denominator is 7.)
Each should multiply the degree remainder.
The retained part follows the preceding.
If retrograde, subtract it.
Do not record degrees during hiding (fú).
[二五] Remove fractions when passing through a mansion (jīngshì).
If there is not enough to subtract,
break a whole degree.
(The five planets' mansion fractions (shìfēn) are all different.
If in a moving fraction,
remove them according to their respective mansion fractions.)

In the 20th year of Yuánjiā,
Chéngtiān memorialized the Shàngshū:
"Now that the Yuánjiā Calendar has been adopted,
the clepsydra is different from before,
it should be reformed.
According to the Jǐngchū Calendar, the vernal equinox day is long,
the autumnal equinox day is short.
The clepsydra used for generations
has a longer daytime rate after the winter solstice than before the winter solstice.
Moreover, the increase and decrease in length
and the advances and retreats are without gradual progression.
Not only is the old method imprecise,
but there are also errors in various transcriptions.
Now, the two solstices and two equinoxes
are each based on their correct positions.
Thus, before and after the solstices,
there will be no more discrepancies.
We have further augmented and reduced the old markings,
comparing them with gnomon shadows,
and revised them into a standard,
changing to use twenty-five 'arrows' (units of time).
We request that the Court instruct the Lòulángjiàng to test and implement this."
It was approved.
Scholars of previous generations, following diagrams and apocrypha, said that
the Moon has nine paths.
Therefore, they drew nine circles,
intersecting each other,
to examine its movement sequence.
The speeds (slow and fast) changed,
not following a regular degree.
Liú Xiàng discussed the nine paths, saying:
"Two Qīngdào (Azure Paths) emerge east of the Huángdào (Ecliptic),
two Báidào (White Paths) emerge west of the Huángdào,
two Hēidào (Black Paths) emerge in the north,
and two Chìdào (Red Paths) emerge in the south."
It also says:
"At Lìchūn (Start of Spring) and Chūnfēn (Spring Equinox),
it follows the Qīngdào in the east;
at Lìxià (Start of Summer) and Xiàzhì (Summer Solstice),
it follows the Chìdào in the south.
In autumn, it follows the White; in winter, the Black;
each following its respective direction."
According to this, the Sun travels along the Huángdào,
which is the Yang path.
The Moon is the essence of Yin,
and does not follow the Yang path.
Therefore, it sometimes appears outside it,
sometimes enters inside it.
Its deviation from the Huángdào, whether entering or exiting, does not exceed six degrees.
It enters for thirteen and a fraction days, then exits;
it exits for thirteen and a fraction days, then enters.
In total, twenty-seven days for one entry and one exit.
When it crosses the Huángdào,
and is obscured by the Sun,
an eclipse occurs.
During the Hàn era, Liú Hóng deduced and examined lunar motion,
and created the Yīnyáng Calendar method.
In the 20th year of Yuánjiā,
Tàizǔ commanded the Zhùzuò Lìshǐ, Wú Guǐ, to follow Hóng's method,
and formulate a new system,
ordering the Tàishǐ to implement it.

In the sixth year of Dàmíng,
Zǔ Chōngzhī, the Secretary of the Inspectorate of Nánxúzhōu, submitted a memorial, saying: "The ancient calendars are flawed and erroneous,
and quite imprecise.
Various schools are in disarray,
unable to grasp the essentials.
〔四六〕What Hé Chéngtiān proposed,
while aiming for reform,
had a simplified
and brief method,
which is now far off.
In my examination,
I have thrice observed its errors: the positions of the sun and moon
are off by about three degrees;
the gnomon's shadow at the two solstices
is off by almost a day;
the five planets'
visibility and invisibility
are off by as much as forty days,
and their retrograde, direct, and stationary motions
may shift by two xiù (lunar mansions).
If the equinoxes and solstices are incorrect,
then the jié and rùn (solar terms and intercalary months) are not proper.
If the positions of the xiù deviate from the heavens,
then observations
lack accuracy.
I was born in a sagacious era,
and live in a flourishing age.
I dare, despite my foolishness and blindness,
to innovate a new calendar.
I respectfully present two intentions for modification
and three reasons for establishing the method.
Regarding the modifications:
Firstly,
〔四七〕the old method's one zhāng (nineteen years) had seven intercalary months.
The number of intercalary months was too many,
and after two hundred years,
it would consistently be off by one day.
Since the jié
and rùn shifted,
the method should be reformed.
The frequent changes in calendrical records
are indeed due to this clause.
Now, the zhāng method is changed to
three hundred ninety-one years having one hundred forty-four intercalary months.
This will now align with the Zhōu and Hàn dynasties,
and will be permanently used in the future,
without further discrepancies.
Secondly,
the Yáo Diǎn states:
‘When the day is shortest and the star is Mǎo,
this marks mid-winter.’
Based on this
calculation,
the winter solstice during the Táng dynasty
was about fifty degrees to the left of the present xiù.
At the beginning of the Hàn dynasty,
the Qín calendar was used,
and the winter solstice was at six degrees in Qiānniú.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn reformed and established the Tàichū calendar,
and the winter solstice was at the beginning of Niú.
The Four-Part calendar of the Later Hàn
had the winter solstice at twenty-one degrees in Dǒu.
〔四八〕During the Jìn dynasty, Jiāng Jí examined the sun using
lunar eclipses,
and knew the winter solstice was at seventeen degrees in Dǒu.
Now, by referencing the central stars
and verifying with eclipses and full moons,
the winter solstice
is at eleven degrees in Dǒu.
Calculating broadly,
less than a hundred years,
there is a difference of two degrees.
The old methods all fixed the position of the winter solstice,
but since the heavenly count is off,
the xiù positions of the seven luminaries gradually deviate from the calendar.
Once the discrepancies
and errors become evident,
a reform should be enacted.
Merely fitting it for a moment
cannot last long,
and endless reforms
are also due to this clause.
Now, the position of the winter solstice
will subtly
shift each year.
Re-examining the Hàn annotations,
they are all precise.
This will be used for a long time in the future,
without the trouble of frequent revisions.
Regarding the establishment of the method:
Firstly,
with Zǐ as the head of the chén (earthly branches),
located at due north,
corresponding to chūjiǔ in the yáo,
the beginning of Dǒu's qi,
Xū as the northern region,
in the middle of the
arrayed xiù,
where the primordial qi first begins,
it is appropriate for this position.
The former scholar Yú Xǐ
has thoroughly discussed its meaning.
Now, the calendar's yuánrì dù (degree of the prime day)
starts from Xū yī.
Secondly,
with
the designation of the day's chén,
Jiǎzǐ is first.
When establishing the calendar's yuán,
it should be in this year.
However, since the time of Huángdì,
the eleven calendars used by successive generations
did not have
their yuán year
correspond to this name.
Now, the calendar's yuán is
in the year Jiǎzǐ.
Thirdly,
in the yuán year,
all items in the calendar
should begin from this point.
However, the Jǐngchū calendar's conjunctions and conjunctions with slow and fast motions
〔(its) beginning had discrepancies.
Also, in Hé Chéngtiān's method,
the sun, moon, and five planets
each had their own yuán,
and their conjunctions with slow and fast motions,
〕were also all set.
errors,
〔四九〕merely harmonized the qi of the new moon.
The rules were chaotic and intertwined,
failing to capture the ancient spirit.
Now, with the methods I have devised,
the Sun, Moon, and Five Planets',
conjunction and opposition, their slowness and swiftness,
are all calculated from the beginning of the
epoch.
Then the celestial splendor of the "union of jades" (planets in conjunction with the moon),
will be verifiable and true,
and the brilliance of the "strung pearls" (planets in a line),
will reside therein.
All streams sharing a common source,
this truly refines the ancient methods.
As for using observation to determine form,
and basing calculations on actual effects,
with the celestial phenomena clearly manifest,
the verification by gnomon can be deduced.
Even the subtle movements of qi,
can be precisely observed with a small tube.
What your servant has established now
is easy to trust.
It deeply refines the beginning and end,
maintaining great integrity and precision,
innovating and reforming the old,
with both simplicity and complexity.
The simple rules
are not
inherently flawed,
and the intention behind the complex ones
is certainly not mistaken.
Why?
Because the recording of intercalary months varies,
and each number has its own division.
The essence of these divisions
requires meticulous detail.
Your servant
therefore deeply cherishes every hair's breadth,
to fully achieve the standard of seeking perfection,
and does not shy away from accumulation,
to establish an everlasting system.
This is not because I sought but could not comprehend,
or knew but did not change
it.
I secretly fear that praise may be uncertain,
always valuing the distant and neglecting the near;
and that discussions may have right and wrong,
sometimes valuing hearsay and ignoring direct observation.
Therefore, I have exhausted my limited understanding,
humbly setting aside the suspicion of common
differences,
and opened my heart to the sun and moon,
looking up, hoping for the illumination of a sunflower.
If what your servant has submitted
can by any chance be adopted,
I humbly wish for it to be proclaimed to all officials,
and for careful consideration to be granted,
so that
I may present my humble contribution,
and slightly augment the grand ceremony.

Method for calculating the entry into the *Yīnyánglì*: Place the *tōngshí* and remove the *huìzhōu* from it.
If it does not reach half of the *jiāoshù* (358,888), it is recorded as the *shuò* entering the *yánglì fēn*.
If it reaches or exceeds it, remove it,
and it becomes the *shuò* entering the *yīnlì fēn*.
Each time it reaches the *tōngfǎ*, it becomes one day;
the remainder is *rìyú*.
This is calculated outside the daily calculation,
as the *rìlì* for midnight of the *shuò* in the eleventh month of *Tiānzhèng*.
To find the next month,
for a long month, add two days;
for a short month, add one day.
The *rìyú* for all is twenty thousand seven hundred seventy-nine.
When the calendar reaches thirteen days,
and the *rìyú* is fifteen thousand nine hundred eighty-seven and a half, then remove it.
When *yáng* ends, *yīn* begins;
when *yīn* ends, *yáng* begins.
To find the next day,
add one day.
To find the *shuòwàng chā* (difference between new and full moon),
multiply the *shuò xiǎoyú* by two thousand twenty-nine.
When it reaches three hundred three, it becomes *rìyú*;
the remainder is doubled to become *xiǎofēn*.
This is the *shuò chāshù*.
Add fourteen days,
twenty thousand one hundred eighty-six *rìyú*,
and one hundred twenty-five *xiǎofēn*.
When the *xiǎofēn* reaches six hundred six, it is transferred to the *rìyú*;
when the *rìyú* reaches the *tōngfǎ*, it becomes a day.
This is the *wàng chāshù*.
Add this again,
and it is the *shuò* of the following month.
To find the *héshuò* (conjunction) and lunar eclipse: Place the *shuòwàng* (new and full moon) calendar day and its remainder at midnight in the *yīnyánglì*.
Remove any halves.
Place three hundred three *xiǎofēn*.
Add the *chāshù* to it.
When the *xiǎofēn* reaches six hundred six, it is transferred to the *rìyú*;
when the *rìyú* reaches the *tōngfǎ*, it is transferred to a day.
When the day reaches one calendar cycle, remove it.
This is calculated outside the daily calculation,
and gives the calendar entry for the *shuòwàng jiāshí* (additional time for new/full moon).
When the *shuòwàng jiāshí* enters the calendar as one day,
and the *rìyú* is four thousand one hundred ninety-eight,
and the *xiǎofēn* is four hundred twenty-eight or less,
or twelve days,
and the *rìyú* is eleven thousand seven hundred eighty-eight,
and the *xiǎofēn* is four hundred eighty-one or more,
then for *shuò* it is a conjunction,
and for *wàng* it is a lunar eclipse.
To find the *dìng xiǎoyú* (corrected small remainder) for *héshuò* and lunar eclipse: Let the *rìyú* of the *chāshù* be added to the remainder of the *chízílì* entry at midnight.
When the *rìyú* reaches the *tōngfǎ*, it is transferred to a day.
This is the calendar entry for the *shuòwàng jiāshí*.
Multiply the remainder of the calendar entry by the *sǔnyìlǜ*.
Using the gain/loss accumulated excess/deficiency,
divide it by the *chāfǎ*.
Subtract for excess or add for deficiency from the original *shuòwàng xiǎoyú*.
This is the *dìng xiǎoyú*.
If adding makes it exceed the *fǎ*,
or subtracting makes it insufficient,
advance or retreat the day by the *rìfǎ*.
To find the *shuòwàng jiāshí*: Multiply the *dìng xiǎoyú* by twelve.
When it reaches the *rìfǎ*, it becomes one *chén*.
Label it as *zǐ*.
This is calculated outside the calculation,
and gives the *chén* (double hour) for the *jiāshí*.
If there is a remainder, multiply it by four.
When it reaches the *rìfǎ*, one is *shǎo* (a little),
two is *bàn* (half),
three is *tài* (a lot).
If there is still a remainder, multiply it by three.
When it reaches the *rìfǎ*, one is *qiáng* (strong).
Combine *qiáng* with *shǎo* to get *shǎoqiáng*;
combine with *bàn* to get *bànqiáng*;
combine with *tài* to get *tàiqiáng*.
If it gets two, it is *shǎoruò* (a little weak).
Combine with *tài* to get *yīchénruò* (one *chén* weak).
To find the Moon's distance from the ecliptic in *dù*: Place the remainder of the *yīnyánglì* entry and multiply by the *sǔnyìlǜ*.
Divide by the *tōngfǎ*.
Using the gain/loss *jiānshù*, this becomes the *dìngshù*.
Divide the *dìngshù* by twelve to get *dù*.
The remainder, divided by three, becomes *shǎo*, *bàn*, *tài*.
If there is still a remainder, one is *qiáng*, two is *shǎoruò*.
This is the Moon's distance from the ecliptic.
The *yánglì* is on the *biǎo* (outer surface);
the *yīnlì* is on the *lín* (inner surface).

the year was *jiǎzǐ*.

I humbly offer my humble opinion,

Zǔ Chōngzhī's newly proposed calendrical method states,
'The location of the winter solstice today

Your servant Fǎxīng (法興) argues: The two solstices mark the extremes of contraction and expansion,
the northern and southern limits.

Precisely because the moon governs the four seasonal midpoints,

This is why Xī (羲) and Hé (和) rectified the seasons,

Monograph Four: Rites One
For those who possess a state or a family,
the use of rites and ceremonies has been long-standing.
However, through successive dynasties, there have been gains and losses,
often resulting in differences.
This was not due to an intentional desire for mutual alteration,
but rather because of adaptation to the circumstances of the time.
Emperor Wén of Hàn, considering the human condition to be increasingly frivolous,
reduced the mourning period for national losses from three years;
Emperor Guāngwǔ, ushering in a restoration emphasizing frugality,
instituted the system of a common hall for the Seven Ancestral Temples;
Wèi Zǔ, believing extravagance and delusion required correction,
ultimately abolished the practice of adopting repeated imperial titles;
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, noting no difference between mound sacrifices and suburban sacrifices,
combined the northern and southern sacrifices for the two solstices.
They borrowed from and built upon each other,
up to the present day.
Could it be that the institutions of the Three Dynasties did not exist?
Rather, they adopted what suited the changes of their times.
Moreover, Mǐn Zǐ criticized ancient rites
and then withdrew from public service;
Shūsūn Tōng established the Hàn system
and his reforms influenced later generations.
From this, it can be said:
relying on oneself without following the ancients,
the Qín clan brought about its demise;
following the ancients but not adapting to current needs,
was the reason for Wáng Mǎng's destruction.
Thus, from Hàn and Wèi onwards,
each weighed the balance between ancient and modern
to establish the rites of their own era.
Sīmǎ Biāo compiled the numerous annotations from the Later Hàn
into a 'Treatise on Rites and Ceremonies,'
and comparing its practices,
they already differed considerably from the Former Hàn.
How much more so with the Three Kingdoms standing in rivalry,
through Jìn to Sòng,
as times changed
and each established its own according to circumstances.
After the turmoil and breakdown at the end of Hàn,
the old regulations were in disarray.
In the early Wèi, Wáng Càn and Wèi Jì compiled and settled numerous rites;
in the Shǔ dynasty, Mèng Guāng and Xǔ Cí created and managed institutions;
at the beginning of Jìn, Xún Yǐ and Zhèng Chōng deliberated and settled the Jìn rites;
in the Jiangzuǒ (Eastern Jìn), Xún Sōng and Diāo Xié organized the chaotic and disordered practices.
Among these, famous Confucians and learned scholars,
in their various discussions,
often produced new ideas,
which cannot all be recorded.
Now, I have excerpted the significant state documents from the Wèi period onwards
to complete this treatise.

emulating the sprouting of things;
its color favored white.
Zhōu (周) took the eleventh month as the first month,
emulating the budding of things;
its color favored red.
One who can observe these categories
and rectify their fundamentals
will cause mountains and rivers to yield clouds and rain,
the four seasons to be harmonious,
the five grains to ripen,
and麒麟 (qílín) and Fenghuang (fènghuáng) to soar and gather.’
The Chūnqiū (春秋) states: ‘In the seventeenth year, in the summer, on the first day (jiǎzǐ) of the sixth month,
there was a solar eclipse.’
The Zhuàn (傳) says: ‘This was in the fourth month of Xià (夏),
which is called early summer.’
The Chūnqiū Yuán Mìng Bāo (春秋元命苞) says: ‘When a king receives the mandate,
it is clearly manifested in the principles of Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, he must change his residence,
change his title,
reform the calendar,
and change the color of his attire,
to make manifest the heavenly mandate and the treasure of the sage.
Substance and refinement change twice and then change again;
when one reaches its limit, it is succeeded;
when one cycle is complete, it begins anew.
When the calendar is reformed, the Mandate of Heaven is made manifest.’
All records in the classics
are not limited to these,
but these brief examples
are sufficient to illustrate.”

Tàiwèi Sīmǎ Yì (太尉司馬懿), Shàngshū Púyè Wèi Zhēn (尚書僕射衞臻), Shàngshū Xuē Tì (尚書薛悌), Zhōngshū Jiān Liú Fàng (中書監劉放), Zhōngshū Shìláng Diāo Gàn (中書侍郎刁幹), Bóshì Qín Jìng (博士秦靜), Zhào Yí (趙怡), and Zhōng Hòu Zhōng Zhào Jì Qí (中候中詔季岐) believed that it should be changed.
Shìzhōng Miù Xí (侍中繆襲), Sànqí Chángshì Wáng Sù (散騎常侍王肅), Shàngshū Láng Wèi Héng (尚書郎魏衡), and Tàizǐ Shèrén Huáng Shǐsì (太子舍人黃史嗣) believed that it should not be changed.
In the fifth year of Qīnglóng (青龍),
Shānchí (山茌) county reported seeing a yellow dragon.
The Emperor then issued an edict to the Sān Gōng (三公), saying: “In ancient times, Bàoxī (庖犧) [Fúxī],
who reigned by succeeding Heaven,
first based himself on the virtue of wood [mùdé],
and was the first among all generations.
From then onwards,
those who established new dynasties and proclaimed their legitimacy,
who initiated new eras and established their lines of succession,
having
received the destined period of the Heavenly Mandate and the cosmic numbers,
and holding the imperial spiritual power for changes and rise,
followed Heaven in changing things
and ordered their principles.
Although Yán (炎) and Huáng (黃), Shàohào (少昊),
Zhuānxū (顓頊) and Gāoxīn (高辛),
Táng (唐), Yú (虞), and Xià Hòu (夏后),
their lineages were inherited one after another,
and they shared the same vital energy and common ancestors,
they still sought to clearly display the mandate they had received,
and to manifest the signs of Heaven and man departing and succeeding.
There was none who did not reform
the institutions,
change and establish rites and music,
summon all the princes,
and distribute tokens of trust,
so that they would be resplendent and noteworthy for later generations.
As for the matter of the calendar reform,
it should be clearly indicated as a change,
to distinguish different eras.
How can there be doubt that it should be so?
When Emperor Wén (文皇帝) first ascended the throne,
affairs were just being initiated,
and so he adopted the Hàn (漢) calendar,
not reforming its system.
When I was in the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng) [Crown Prince],
and now that I have assumed the throne,
I have often consulted the multitude of
records
and summarized the discussions of the high officials and ministers.
Those who speak of the three cosmic systems (sāntǒng) alternating
have clear texts;
those who say Yú (虞) and Xià (夏) followed each other
do not have such words.
The Lì Zhì (曆志) says:
‘The celestial system (tiāntǒng) has its first month in zǐ (子) [eleventh month], and things sprout red;
the terrestrial system (dìtǒng) has its first month in chǒu (丑) [twelfth month], and things transform white;
the human system (réntǒng) has its first month in yín (寅) [first month], and things complete black.’
But
it contains
vital energy,
and from subtle it becomes manifest.
Thus, the Great Ultimate (tàijí) moves the three luminaries and five planets above,
and the primal qi (yuánqì) rotates the three systems and five elements below.
Ascending, descending, revolving,
when finished, it
begins again,
indicating how Heaven, Earth, and man are interconnected.
Zhòngní (仲尼) [Confucius], with his great sagely talent,
emulated Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜),
followed the exemplary rules of Wén (文) and Wǔ (武),
authored the Chūnqiū (春秋),
and thoroughly discussed
human affairs,
thereby貫 (guàn) [unifying] the principles of all kings.
Therefore, in the months of the three subtle beginnings (sānwēi),
each month is called ‘king,’
to clarify that the three first months (sānzhèng) alternate as the beginning.
If he emulated Yáo (堯)
and Shùn (舜)
to discuss the three first months,
then its clear meaning
could not be limited to the near past of Yīn (殷) and Zhōu (周) only.
I, with my humble person,
have inherited this grand lineage,
and since I cannot restore the
legacy of the previous sages,
or glorify the excellent virtues of the former emperors,
and have also allowed the slackened royal teachings to remain unrevived,
and the omissions in imperial ordinances to remain uncompensated,
if the diligent virtue is not made manifest,
how
can it be acceptable?
Now, calculating the sequence of the three cosmic systems,
Wèi (魏) obtains the terrestrial system (dìtǒng),
and thus should take the month of jiànchǒu (建丑) [twelfth month] as the first month.
Examining it against all the classics,
its meaning is manifest.
In Qīnglóng (青龍) five
In the spring, third month of that year, it was the first year of Jǐngchū. In the early summer, fourth month,
the preferred color for clothing was yellow,
the sacrificial animals used were white,
for military affairs, black-headed white horses were ridden,
large scarlet
flags were raised,
and for court assemblies, large white flags were raised.
For the first, middle, and last months of spring, summer, autumn, and winter,
although they differed from the regular year,
when it came to suburban sacrifices to welcome the qi,
the yuè, sì,
zhēng, cháng sacrifices,
imperial tours, hunting expeditions,
the solstices and equinoxes, and the opening and closing of passes,
the promulgation of seasonal decrees,
the early or late arrival of mid-qi,
and the respectful assignment of agricultural tasks to the people,
all such matters
were determined by the dǒu jiàn (handle of the Big Dipper's pointing direction) of the regular year
as the divisions.
This ordering of calendrical calculations
is in accord and in covenant with the ancient sages,
repeating their rules and regulations.
Now, by following this principle,
we can perhaps make manifest the great foundation laid by our ancestors
and fathers,
and elevate the mandate of Wèi’s renovation.
Alas!
Princes, dukes, and all high officials,
the numerous civil and military officers,
should maintain peace and perform their duties,
and follow the intent without slackening,
to perpetuate Heaven’s favor.
The Grand Minister of Works (Sītú) shall issue a public bulletin,
making it known
to all,
in accordance with Our will.
According to this, the preferred color for clothing is yellow,
based on the element Earth.
The sacrificial animals and flags,
all followed the Rites of Yīn,
because the era of Yīn was being followed.
In the Rites of Zhōu, the officer in charge of carriages (Jīnchē Zhí)
said, “‘Raise large scarlet flags for court audiences,’
and ‘large white flags for military campaigns.’”
This means Zhōu used flags of the 正色 (primary color) for court,
and flags of previous dynasties for military campaigns.
Wèi adopted the Rites of Yīn,
changing the system of Zhōu;
therefore, they raised large white flags for court,
and large scarlet flags for military campaigns.
Emperor Míngdì further decreed:
“For those who take the month of jiàn yín as the first month,
their sacrificial animals should be black;
for those who take the month of jiàn chǒu as the first month,
their sacrificial animals should be white;
for those who take the month of jiàn zǐ as the first month,
their sacrificial animals should be russet.
This means the color of sacrificial animals follows their respective primary element,
not the yīn and yáng of the sacrifice itself.
If sacrificing to Heaven does not object to the use of black,
then sacrificing to Earth should not exclusively doubt the use of white.
For Heaven and Earth, when using sacrificial animals,
is it not inappropriate for them to be different?
Discuss further.”
Thereupon, the debaters each presented their arguments,
but none could be followed.
Another decree stated:
“The bases for all arguments are conflicting.
If yáng sacrifices use russet,
and yīn sacrifices use dark-colored,
then it is also said that Heaven sacrifices use black,
and Earth sacrifices use yellow.
If this is the case,
the principle of using sacrificial animals
is not yet consistent.
Heaven and Earth are of supreme reverence;
the sacrificial animals should uniformly use the preferred color,
and not be solely distinguished by yīn and yáng.

Now, for sacrifices to the August Imperial Heaven (Huánghuáng Dì Tiān), the August Imperial Earth (Huánghuáng Hòutú), the suburban Heaven and Earth (Tiāndì Jiāo), the Míngtáng, and the ancestral temples (Zōngmiào),
all should use white.
For separate sacrifices to the Five Suburbs (Wǔ Jiāo),
each should follow its directional color;
for sacrifices to the sun, moon, stars, and similar entities, use russet;
for sacrifices to the altars of grain and soil (Shèjì), mountains, and rivers, use black.
This way, the distinctions of reverence, directional colors,
and the various meanings of yīn and yáng are all made clear.”
In the first month of the third year,
the Emperor passed away, and King Qí ascended the throne.
In the twelfth month of that year,
the Minister of Personnel (Shàngshū), Lú Yù, memorialized:
“The Illustrious Ancestor, Emperor Míngdì, departed the myriad nations on the first day of this year.
According to the Rites,
one does not engage in joyous activities on a忌日 (jìrì) or day of mourning,
referring to ordinary days of misfortune.
The Illustrious Ancestor, Emperor Míngdì, departed the world in the month of jiàn chǒu.
The feelings of your subjects,
on this particular first day,
are more intense than on an ordinary day of misfortune.
If we were to conduct a court audience for the four quarters on the first day of jiàn chǒu,
assemble the officials,
and set up grand music,
it would not be in accordance with the Rites.”
The Erudite (Bóshì), Yuè Xiáng, deliberated:
“On the first day, receive court tributes in the morning,
with officials presenting their offerings;
five days later,
then hold a grand banquet with music.”
Zhū Dàn, an attendant to the Grand Marshal (Tàiwèi), deliberated:
“Now, at this time of suitable change,
it would be opportune to revert to the old regulations,
with jiàn yín as the first month,
which is convenient for the system.”
Liú Zhào, an attendant to the General-in-Chief (Dàjiàngjūn), deliberated:
“It is fitting to hold the court audience and grand assembly one day after the first day,
to make it clear to all under Heaven
that no court is held on the day of the Emperor’s passing.”
The decree stated:
“Having reviewed the memorial,
Our heart is utterly broken.
How sorrowful!
The Illustrious Ancestor, Emperor Míngdì, departed the world on the first day of the month.
Each time We and the Empress Dowager contemplate the arrival of this day,
Our hearts feel torn apart.
It is not permissible to hold court with the multitude of officials on this day,
or to receive congratulations.
To convene on the second day of the month
is also not customary.
Therefore, We permit the reversion to the Xià first month.
Although this goes against the late Emperor’s principle of connecting the Three Dynastic traditions,
this is also a manifestation of Our sorrow and eternal remembrance as a descendant.
Moreover, the Xià first month corresponds to Heaven’s numbers,
so let the month of jiàn yín be the beginning of the year.”
In the ninth month of the second year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
the various dukes memorialized:
“Táng Yáo, Shùn, and Yǔ did not change their system when they changed their reigns;
as for Tāng and Wǔ,
each promoted their respective calendrical computations.
When Xuánní (Confucius) answered the question about governing a state,
he said, ‘Follow the time system of Xià,’
and the system of carriages and caps,
which was a general statement for a hundred generations.
This was probably aimed at managing government and achieving good governance,
and was not tied to the cyclical movement of the elements.
Now, Dà Jìn follows the footsteps of the Three August Ones,
and treads the path of Shùn and Yǔ.
Responding to Heaven and obeying the people,
it received the abdication from Wèi.
It is appropriate to uniformly adopt the calendrical system,
clothing colors, and all other customs of the preceding dynasty,
just as Yǒuyú (Shùn) followed the precedents of Táng (Yáo).
This would be a grand principle.”
The memorial was approved.
Sūn Shèng said:
“Retaining the old system
was wrong.
Furthermore, Jìn was of the Metal element,
and should have preferred red for clothing;
examining this by the Way of Heaven,
the deviation was great.”
When Sòng received the abdication,
they also followed the precedents of Wèi and Jìn.
In the early reign of Emperor Míngdì of Wèi,
the Minister of Works (Sīkōng), Wáng Lǎng, deliberated:
“In ancient times, there were years,
but no reign titles,
and this was still the case in early Hàn.
Sometimes, they changed within a reign,
with zhòngyuán and hòuyuán.
When reign titles changed too frequently,
the titles zhòng and hòu were insufficient,
so they borrowed auspicious names instead,
which was not ancient practice.
When recounting events from the Spring and Autumn period (Chūnqiū),
saying ‘the first year of Duke Yǐn,’
is simple and easy to understand.
When recording events from the Hàn era,
saying ‘the first year of Jiànyuán,’
then later generations would not understand.
It would be better to simply refer to the ‘first year’ as in ancient times.”
Emperor Míngdì did not follow this.
He then decreed:
“The first year of the late Emperor’s ascension
had the reign title Yánkāng,
and at the beginning of receiving the abdication,
it was called Huángchū.
It is permissible to name the years now.”
Thereupon, the Minister of Personnel (Shàngshū) memorialized:
“The Yì Jīng says: ‘The Way of Qián transforms,
each rectifying its nature and destiny.
It preserves and unites the great harmony,
thus it is propitious and firm.
It gives birth to all things,
and the myriad states are all peaceful.’
It is fitting to name it Tàihé Yuánnián.”
The decree (incomplete)
Among the Five Rites of the Zhōu dynasty,
the fifth was Jiā.
Jiā. The [text is missing] Zuǒshìzhuàn of Spring and Autumn states:
“The Marquis of Jìn asked Duke Xiāng his age.
Jì Wǔzi replied, ‘Our humble ruler was born in the year of the meeting at Shāsuí.’
The Marquis of Jìn said, ‘Twelve years have passed;
this is called one cycle.
One stellar cycle.
A ruler of a state begets a son at fifteen.
To be capped and then beget a son
is in accordance with the rites.
Your lord may now be capped.
Why do the Dàifū not prepare for the capping ceremony?’
Wǔzi replied, ‘For our lord’s capping, it must be performed with the rite of pouring libations,
regulated by the music of metal bells and stone chimes,
and take place in the ancestral temple of the former ruler.
Currently, our lord is on a journey;
it is not possible to prepare fully.
Please allow us to borrow preparations from a fraternal state.’
The Marquis of Jìn assented.
Returning to Wèi,
the capping ceremony was performed in the temple of Duke Chéng,
borrowing bells and chimes for the occasion.
This was in accordance with the rites.”
Jiǎ and Fú both held the view that a ruler is capped at the age of twelve.
According to the Gǔ Shàngshū,
King Wǔ of Zhōu died when King Chéng was thirteen.
Inferring that King Wǔ died in the Gēngchén year,
Duke Zhōu departed to live in the East in the Rénwǔ year,
and returned in the Guǐwèi year.
Duke Zhōu capped King Chéng
and commanded the historians to recite an address.
An address
is a pronouncement.
This was a capping ceremony after mourning was concluded.
Before Duke Zhōu had returned from living in the East,
King Chéng put on his cap and a ceremonial cap (biàn) to open the Golden Casket (Jīn téng) text;
he was then sixteen years old.
This means King Chéng's mourning period ended at fifteen,
and Duke Zhōu capped him before his departure.
According to the texts of the Lǐ and Zhuàn,
the Son of Heaven and feudal lords were capped at around twelve,
or at the latest, fifteen.
The Zhōu Lǐ, though it mentions the number of ceremonial caps and crowns,
does not contain a text for the capping of the Son of Heaven.
The Yí Lǐ states:
“The capping rites for dukes and marquises
originated at the end of the Xià dynasty.”
Wáng and Zhèng both believed that during the late Xià,
there was chaos between superiors and inferiors,
and usurpations and assassinations arose;
hence the capping rites for dukes and marquises were created.
This clearly indicates the absence of reliable capping rites for the Son of Heaven.
Furthermore, Dàifū did not have capping rites.
In ancient times, one was only granted a noble rank after fifty;
how could Dàifū have capping rites?
Among the people of Zhōu, if a person of fifty possessed talent and virtue,
they would be tested with the duties of a Dàifū,
which was still performed with the rites of an ordinary scholar (shì).
Thus, divining the day and the guest,
being capped in the eastern chamber (zuò) to signify succession,
toasting in the guest's position,
and the three additions (sān jiā) making it more venerable
were all just scholar's rites.
However, since the Hàn dynasty,
the Son of Heaven and feudal lords
have largely adopted these practices.
The Zhì says,
“The ceremony followed the capping rites,”
which is correct.
When Emperor Shùn of Hàn was capped,
the new rites of Cáo Bāo were also adopted.
Cáo Bāo's new rites are not extant today.
The Lǐyí Zhì also states:
“For the imperial carriage, the first addition was the zībù jìnxíán (black cloth cap for promotion of worthies),
followed by the juébìan (magistrate's cap) and wǔbiàn (military cap),
then the tōngtiān (heaven-connecting crown).
All were performed at the Gāomiào (High Temple).
For kings, dukes, and below,
only the jìnxíán was added first.”
According to this text,
the initial capping with a zībù was in accordance with ancient custom,
and being capped in the ancestral temple was correct.
The Emperor of Wèi had only one addition (yī jiā) for his capping.
The explanation for this was that
the scholar's rite had three additions,
each addition signifying an accomplishment.
As for the Son of Heaven and feudal lords,
there was no text specifying the number of additions,
because in ascending the throne and governing the people,
their venerable and complete virtue
could not be equated with that of a scholar.
This statement is incorrect.
Even with the talent of a sage,
one still "establishes oneself" at thirty (sānshí ér lì).
How much more so for one at twelve,
who has not yet reached the age of studying with a purpose (zhìxué)?
To then claim their virtue is complete
and there is no need for further encouragement
is neither logical nor factual.
The Crown Prince of the Wèi dynasty had two additions (zài jiā),
while imperial princes and royal princely heirs had three additions (sān jiā).
Sūn Yù believed that one addition or two additions were both incorrect.
The libation address in the rites states,
“On an auspicious day of a propitious month,”
and also,
“In the correct month of the year,
in the propitious month.”
Duke Xiāng of Lǔ was capped in winter,
and Emperor Huì of Hàn was capped in the third month,
indicating there was no fixed month.
Since the Later Hàn dynasty,
when emperors underwent the first capping (yuánfú),
it was always in the first month.
In the second year of Xiánníng of Jìn (autumn, intercalary ninth month),
an envoy was sent to cap Rǔnán Wáng Jiǎn.
This shows that in Jìn rites, it was also not necessarily at the beginning of the year.
The rites specified capping in the temple,
but since Wèi, this was no longer strictly followed.
However, when Emperor Wǔ and Emperor Huì of Jìn capped the Crown Prince,
they both visited the temple,
which was an emulation of the temple ceremony.
When Emperor Mù and Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn were about to be capped,
they first announced it to the temple with silk offerings,
and after the ceremony, they also visited the temple.
When Emperor Huì of Jìn, as Crown Prince, was about to be capped,
Emperor Wǔ presided from the veranda,
and ordered the acting Sītú, Gāoyáng Wáng Guī, to add the cap,
and the acting Guānglùxūn and Túnqí Xiàowèi, Huá Yì, to assist in the capping.
When emperors of the Eastern Jìn (Jiāngzuǒ) were about to be capped,
metal bells and stone chimes were set up overnight,
and all officials attended.
A large couch was also prepared in advance in the hall.
The director of the imperial treasury offered the miǎn (ceremonial crown), cè (headdress), zān (hairpin), dǎo (hair-fastener), and gǔnfú (dragon robe),
handing them to the Shìzhōng and Chángshì.
The Tàiwèi added the cè,
and the Tàibǎo added the miǎn.
Before adding the miǎn,
the Tàiwèi knelt and read the prayer text:
“On this propitious day of this auspicious month,
the first ceremonial cap is added.
The Emperor, solemn and dignified,
intends to uphold the duties of his dragon robe.
He reverently follows the vast heavens,
setting an example for the universe.
He diligently adheres to his ancestors,
everlastingly without end.
Longevity is his wish,
bestowing this great fortune.”
After the miǎn was added,
the Shìzhōng tied the xuándǎn (black tassel).
The Shìzhōng removed the jiàngshāfú (crimson gauze robe)
and added the gǔnfú.
When the capping ceremony was complete,
the Tàibǎo led all officials to offer a cup and wish for longevity.
Kings, dukes, and below cried out “Wànsuì!” (long live!) three times,
then retired.
According to the ceremonial records,
only one addition of the cè and miǎn was made.
When the Sòng dynasty capped the Crown Prince and vassal kings,
it was also one addition.
The officials had their records for this.
In the tenth year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
Nángōng Wáng Chéng, aged fifteen,
was to be capped according to old customs.
The officials deliberated and reported:
“The rites state that a boy becomes an adult (chéngtóng) at fifteen.
A ruler of a state begets a son at fifteen,
which illustrates the appropriateness of being capped.
Furthermore, the Hàn and Wèi dynasties sending envoys to cap various kings
is not an ancient custom.”
Thereupon, it was decreed that kings should be capped at fifteen,
without further imperial command.
In the eleventh year of Yuánjiā,
Yíngdào Hóu was about to be capped.
An imperial edict stated:
“Yíngdào Hóu Yìqí may be capped on an appointed day.
Let the old practices be followed.”
Hé Zhēng’s capping ritual and Wáng Kān’s privately compiled capping ritual
were also acceptable for use by ordinary families.
In the fourth year of Zhèngshǐ, during the reign of Qí Wáng of Wèi,
Empress Zhēnshì was established;
her ceremony is not extant.
In the second year of Xiánníng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
he presided from the veranda
and sent the Tàiwèi, Jiǎ Chōng, to formally install Empress Yángshì,
who was to be the Dàohòu.
Consequently, a general amnesty was granted,
and gifts were bestowed upon kings, dukes, and others, with differing amounts.
All officials offered congratulations.
In the eighth year of Tàikāng,
the responsible officials submitted a memorial:
“For wedding rituals and the presentation of betrothal gifts,
for a grand marriage, black and crimson silks are used,
a bundle of silk with an added guī,
and two quadrigae of horses.
For kings and marquises, black and crimson silks,
a bundle of silk with an added bì,
and a team of horses.
For grandees, black and crimson silks,
a bundle of silk with an added sheep.
In ancient times, hides and horses were used as courtyard offerings.
The Son of Heaven added a gǔguī,
and feudal lords added a dàzhāng.
It is permissible to follow the Rites of Zhōu and change the bì to a zhāng.
The sheep, geese, wine, rice, black and crimson silks remain as before.
For the wedding rituals of feudal lords, the nàcǎi, gàoqī, and qīnyíng each receive five rolls of silk,
and for the nàzhēng, four horses.
All these are to be prepared by the groom’s family,
only the zhāng will be provided by the officials.”
〔一０〕Shàngshū Zhū Zhěng deliberated:
“According to the precedents of the Wèi dynasty,
for the marriage of a king to a consort, and the marriage of a princess,
the Son of Heaven and feudal lords used hides and horses as courtyard offerings.
The Son of Heaven added a gǔguī,
and feudal lords added a dàzhāng.
Empress Gāo of Hàn decreed that
for the empress’s betrothal, two hundred catties of gold
and twelve horses were used;
for a fūrén, fifty catties of gold
and four horses.
For Wèi’s betrothal of an empress, the marriage of a king to a consort, and the marriage of a princess,
one hundred ninety rolls of silk were used.
When Jìn arose,
the precedent was to use three hundred rolls of silk.”
An imperial edict stated:
“The marriage of a princess is for the groom’s family to arrange.
It is not suitable for everything to be prepared [by the state].
Grant money to make it sufficient, that is all.
Only the zhāng is to be provided;
the rest follows precedent.”
In the second year of Xiánkāng of Emperor Chéng,
he held court at the imperial pavilion,

On the same day, she entered the palace.

and all the officials offered congratulations,

For the wedding rites of a ruler,
the rites did not have such a regulation.
The Spring and Autumn Annals records that Duke Jì received the queen from Jì.
The explanations of Gǔliáng and Zuǒshì also differ from Gōngyáng.
And there are many omissions and deficiencies in the surviving records of Hàn and Wèi.
When Emperor Wǔ and Emperor Huì of Jìn received their empresses,

This means that the command of the Son of Heaven
can naturally be conveyed downwards,
and the reply of a subject
can directly be communicated upwards.
Early Confucians believed that Qiū Míng recorded this matter in detail,
〔一一〕probably as the wedding ritual for a ruler.
Therefore, Emperor Chéng held court at the imperial pavilion and dispatched envoys to enthrone the empress, declaring it by imperial command.
However, the ceremonial notes

In the first year of Jiànyuán of Emperor Kāng,

If the old system is to be used,

〔一二〕An imperial edict stated:
“The reason for donning the proper ceremonial robes and ascending to the Tàijí [Diàn]
is to revere the beginning of the reign,

How can we now omit what is important and remove the ritual objects?
Moreover, when the spirit tablet of Empress Gōng entered the ancestral temple,
the previous emperor decreed that the empress’s ritual should be reduced,
and it was not appropriate to set up the Wǔniú Qí.
Why is it still being set up now?
Since the Wǔniú Qí are not to be set up,
then the máotóu and bìhǎn implements are easy to prepare.”
Another imperial edict stated:
“Since the old system is difficult to follow precisely,
and it is not suitable to fully prepare everything now.
The stores in the government treasury
should only be used to cover military and state expenses.
The ceremonial robes and decorations should be roughly maintained;
the rest of the subsidiary and miscellaneous objects,
should be suspended.”
When it came to the first year of the Shēngpíng reign of Emperor Mù,
when Empress Hé was to be taken into the palace,
Tàicháng Wáng Biāozhī for the first time extensively cited classics, commentaries, and various historical events
to rectify the rites.
He strongly disagreed with the Gōngyáng school's view that the wedding ceremony should not mention the host.
He also said:
"Among the Four Seas, the Son of Heaven
has no one who is not his subject or maidservant.
Even if they are beloved relatives like father and elder brother,
or virtuous mentors and friends,
they are all pure subjects.
Indeed, to establish the three cardinal guides from the beginning,
to settle the decorum of Heaven and Earth,
how can there be the veneration of the Heavenly Father,
yet use the designation of a subordinate's command
to take a spouse?
How can there be the lowliness of a subordinate,
yet use the title of the Heavenly Father
to perform a grand rite?
Searching ancient rites far back,
there is no such system for a monarch;
seeking in recent historical records,
there is no such precedent for a monarch.
It is unsettling emotionally,
and illogical ethically.
Consider that in the second year of Xiánníng,
when Empress Dào was taken into the palace,
Empress Dàihòu Hóngxùn presided over the world as a mother,
yet there was no text instructing a relative or subject to act as the father or elder brother for Emperor Wǔ's marriage.
Furthermore, examining the events already carried out in the Great Jìn,
the precedent of Xiánníng
did not mention fathers, elder brothers, teachers, or friends.
Therefore, the proposal submitted by Huá Suǒ in Xiánkāng was in line with the old ways.
〔一三〕Your humble servant believes that the current rites for taking an empress
should entirely follow the precedents of Xiánkāng."
Thereupon, it was followed.
The six rites established by Huá Suǒ
stated that they should follow the old Hàn customs and the established rites of the Great Jìn.
This shows that he was aware of previous events,
which is why Wáng Biāozhī mostly followed Xiánkāng,
and this is the reason.
Only regarding the custom that the family receiving the bride

The rituals for reporting to the ancestral temple, the texts for the six rites, and other ceremonies

Upon detailed examination, they are based on established regulations.
The text of the Nàcǎi (presenting betrothal gifts) tablet and the imperial letter said:
"The Emperor decrees to the former Tàiwèi Cānjūn Hé Qí:
The primordial chaos gave birth to all things,

we solemnly observe the regulations.
Your humble servant, Hé Qí, former Tàiwèi Cānjūn and Dūxiāng Hóu, prostrates himself twice and receives the imperial decree."
Next, the text for the Wènmíng (asking the name) tablet said:

The host replied:
