In the eleventh month of the fifth year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Míng,
the officials reported:
"According to the practices of the Jìn dynasty since its move to the south of the Jiāng River,
when the Crown Prince marries,
for the formal betrothal gifts,
the ritual uses one piece of jade
and two tiger skins.
It is not clear what these were based on.
Perhaps the tiger symbolizes ferocity and splendor,
and the jade symbolizes virtue and a warm, lustrous quality.
However, *guīzhāng* are among the finest jades,
〔一八〕leopard skins also embody splendor and vibrancy,
and bear and grizzly bear skins are also auspicious omens for marriage rites.
Taking symbols by analogy,
these should also be used together.
It is not clear why they were omitted from the text.
During the Jìn dynasty south of the Jiāng River,
many ritual items were lacking,
and later generations followed this custom,
without time to thoroughly study and correct it.
Now, as the laws and regulations are about to be fully established,
and the ceremonial system is being greatly prepared,
it is fitting to take the classics as a model
and consult the old statutes.
For the current marriage of the Crown Prince,
for the formal betrothal gifts,
should *guīzhāng*, leopard skins, and bear and grizzly bear skins be used or not?
Let the ritual officials thoroughly revise this based on the classics and records.
If they should be used,
should one of each be used,
or two of each?"
The erudite Péi Zhāomíng deliberated:
"According to the *Zhōu Lǐ*,
for the formal betrothal gifts,
black and red silk and a pair of skins were used.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states: 'A bundle of silk [consists of ten pieces.
A pair
means two.
Two skins are used as offerings,
and these are deer skins.'
The ritual notes for the Jìn Crown Prince's betrothal to a consort
state: 'two tiger skins are used.'
〔一九〕In the Tàiyuán era,
for a princess's formal betrothal gifts,
one tiger skin and one leopard skin were used.
Could it be that the marriage rites did not distinguish the ranks of kings and dukes,
and therefore tiger and leopard skins were chosen to dignify and alter the matter?
Although tiger and leopard skins are ornate,
they are not used in the formal betrothal ritual.
Bear and grizzly bear skins are auspicious,
but they are not mentioned in the marriage canon.
Although *guīzhāng* are beautiful,
their uses may differ.
Now, the imperial way is grand and illustrious,
and the virtuous principles are widely propagated.
For the Crown Prince's betrothal,
it is appropriate to follow the canons and proclamations.
All deviations and errors
should be thoroughly considered and corrected.
Although the rites differ across dynasties,
and the form and substance may vary,
since Zhèng Xuán is a Confucian master,
and has given a clear explanation,
those who adhere to the text with shallow understanding
may have doubts.
Moreover, Sūn Shēn, Assistant Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, also deliberated, believing: '
The regulation of betrothal gifts, whether to increase or decrease, depends on propriety.
Throughout history, practices
have been adapted from the marriage rites of scholars.
If the use of *guīzhāng*
is indeed equivalent to *bì* jades,
and the display of leopard skins
is equal in significance to tiger patterns,
and bear and grizzly bear skins symbolize auspiciousness
and are associated with abundant progeny,
then for the betrothal of the esteemed Crown Prince,
with rites that prioritize distant teachings,
the beauty of skins and jades
should be fully displayed.
The rites mention "a bundle of silk and a pair of skins,"
which implies that *guīzhāng* should be of the same number as *bì* jades,
and bear, grizzly bear, and leopard skins
should each be used in pairs.'
Yú Hé, concurrently an erudite of the Imperial Academy, deliberated: 'According to the *Yí Lǐ* on formal betrothal gifts,
it simply states "black and red silk and various skins."
The *Lǐ Jì - Jiāo Tè Shēng* mentions tiger and leopard skins with jade *bì*,
which is not made up.
Thus, it is clear that two tiger and leopard skins are used,
and *guī* and *bì* should remain one of each as before.'
Comparing the deliberations of Shēn and Hé, they are not different.
Now, let one *guī* and one *zhāng* be added,
and two leopard skins and two bear and grizzly bear skins,
taking Hé's deliberation as acceptable."
The Emperor issued an edict approving it.
In the tenth year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
when he was about to formally invite and appoint the Three Ladies (*sānfūrén*) and Nine Concubines (*jiǔpín*),
the officials reported:
"According to the rites,
the Empress is betrothed with a *gǔguī*,
but there is no regulation for the ritual gifts of concubines and maids."
The Emperor decreed:
"The appointments may follow the precedents of the Wèi dynasty."
Thereupon, the Emperor, facing the courtyard, sent envoys bearing credentials and concurrently acting as Grand Master of Ceremonies to appoint the Ladies,
and concurrently acting as Imperial Censorate Chief to appoint the Nine Concubines.
In the rites of the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
princesses resided in their own residences,
and those marrying princesses would come to the residence to marry.
Sīkōng Wáng Lǎng considered this inappropriate,
and it was later reformed.
Whenever a grand envoy was dispatched to appoint an Empress or the Three Grand Ministers,
or to crown the Crown Prince,
or to appoint a princely vassal,
the Emperor always faced the courtyard.
The ceremony was as follows:
The Director of Grand Music would prepare musical instruments (bells and chimes) on four sides in front of the palace hall overnight.
Two *kè* after the clepsydra began,
the Palace Attendants, Retainers, Aide-de-camps, Central Envoys, Cavalry Attendants, and Tiger-Strength Guards,
with banners and pennants, would arrange themselves in formation,
and all five ox banners would enter.
The Colonel of Tiger-Strength Guards and the Supervisor of Feathered Forest Guards would descend the steps to divide the area inside the Duānmén.
One Imperial Censor and one Envoy would each supervise the Duānmén.
The Supervisor of the Court of Judicial Review and the Arbitrator would descend the steps to divide the area to the east and west of the Zhōnghuámén.
Three *kè* after the clepsydra began,
the Palace Imperial Censor would announce the opening of the palace hall's main gate, the Southern Carriage Stop Gate, and the Xuānyáng City Gate.
Military officers, Palace Attendants, Palace Regular Mounted Attendants, Yellow Gate Attendants, and Mounted Attendants would ascend the hall and stand flanking the imperial seat.
The Director of the Department of State Affairs and those of lower rank who were to stand on the steps would enter in order.
The Official of Rites would lead the Grand Herald in,
who would arrange the nine guests.
Four *kè* after the clepsydra began,
a Palace Attendant would report:
"Ready outside."
The Emperor, wearing his ceremonial *gǔnmiǎn* robes,
would ascend the Tàijí Hall,
face south from the courtyard.
An Envoy would advance, bow once facing north,
and kneel to report:
"Your servant, the Grand Herald, so-and-so, respectfully states that
all officials are in position.
All is prepared."
A Palace Attendant would announce the imperial command, saying:
"Approved."
The Envoy would call for bows,
and all present would bow twice.
The Grand Herald, identifying himself as a servant, would bow once,
and looking up, report:
"Request to proceed with the ceremony."
A Palace Attendant would announce the imperial command, saying:
"Approved."
The Grand Herald would raise his hand and say:
"Proceed with the ceremony."
An Envoy would lead the escorts of the designated envoys and appointees to their positions.
Music from the four sides would begin.
When about to bow,
the music would stop.
After the ceremony, they would exit.
There are notes for this in the official records.
In earlier times, on New Year's Day,
reeds, mugwort, peach branches,
and slaughtered chickens were often placed at the palace and the gates of all temples,
〔二０〕to ward off evil influences.
According to Hàn rituals,
these were placed in the middle month of summer,
with peach talismans,
but no slaughtered chickens.
Considering that Emperor Míng greatly revised the exorcism rituals,
〔二一〕Hé Yàn's deliberation on exorcism sacrifices refers to the use of chicken sacrifices for warding off evil and purification,
so the practice of slaughtering chickens likely began in Wèi.
Peach talismans were originally a Hàn practice,
and metal talismans were likely abolished in Wèi,
but it is not yet clear when the change from mid-summer to New Year's Day originated.
All these practices were abolished in Sòng,
but in various commanderies and counties, this ritual often still persisted.
The rites of diplomatic visits and tribute in previous eras,
though somewhat seen in the classics and commentaries,
are nevertheless incomplete from beginning to end.
The biography of Shūsūn Tōng records the Hàn Yuánhuì Yí (Rites for the Hàn Grand Assembly) that he established;
its general framework is roughly presented,
but when applied today,
it is still not fully comprehensive.
When Wèiguó was first established,
many matters were lacking,
thus in the third year of Huángchū,
they first presented jade discs for the court congratulatory ceremony.
Hé Chéngtiān said,
"The Wèi Yuánhuì Yí (Rites for the Wèi Grand Assembly) no longer exist."
According to Hé Zhēn's Xǔdū Fù (Rhapsody on Xǔdū), it says:〔二二〕
"On Yuánzhèng (New Year's Day), the grand banquet
was held on an altar in the southwest.
Banners and curtains soared high,
and the eaves and halls were vast and deep."
Wáng Shěn's Zhènghuì Fù (Rhapsody on the Grand Assembly) also says:
"Splendid tents reflected the flying clouds,
crimson curtains were spread in the front courtyard.
Green canopies were strung between the two stairs,
resembling the majesty of the Purple Forbidden Enclosure.
All officials were invited to the Hémén (Gate of Harmony),
where high and low alike offered jade tablets."
This implies that the grand banquet was entirely outside the city,
not inside the palace.
Your servant has examined Wèi Sīkōng Wáng Lǎng's memorial, which states:
"According to established practice,
on the first day of the first month,
congratulations were offered.
Below the palace hall, two hundred splendid lanterns were set up,
positioned between the two staircases.
At the Duānmén (Upright Gate), courtyard torches were set up;
outside the Duānmén, five-foot and three-foot lanterns were placed.
With the moon shining and stars bright,
even at night it was like day."
If this is the case,
then it was not outside the city.
The two rhapsodies by Hé and Wáng
were originally not about Luòjīng.
Hé's is called Xǔdū Fù (Rhapsody on Xǔdū),
indicating it was at Xǔchāng at the time.
Wáng's rhapsody also says,
"Four states offered tribute during the eastern tour,"
also describing the grand assembly at Xǔchāng.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
the regulations for the Yuánhuì (New Year's court assembly) were revised.
The extant Xiánníng regulations are an example of this.
Fù Xuán's "Yuánhuì Fù" (Rhapsody on the New Year's Assembly) states:
"Examining the bequeathed teachings of the Xià dynasty rulers,
synthesizing the ceremonial arts of the Yīn and Zhōu,
adopting the old rituals of Qín and Hàn,
to establish the grand assembly of the first month."
This indicates that it drew upon various dynasties.
According to the Xiánníng regulations,
first, on the first day of the first month,
〔二三〕the palace guards would set up temporary seats for dukes, princes, ministers, and commanders outside the Duānmén Gate.
Grand music and drum-and-pipe bands would also set up music and ox-and-horse canopies in four wings in front of the palace.
When less than ten "kè" (a unit of time) of the night's clepsydra remained,
all officials would gather,
and courtyard torches would be lit.
The Emperor would offer congratulations and report,
and then offer congratulations to the Empress.
Returning from the Yúnlóng East Huázhōngmén Gate, he would enter to pay respects,
and proceed to a temporary seat beneath the East Gate.
When less than seven "kè" of the clepsydra remained,
all bureaus' officials, riding in carriages, along with the hundred officials and the gift-receiving attendants, down to the accountancy clerks,
〔二四〕would all enter
and stand in ranks before the steps.
The guards on the steps
would follow the protocol for a court audience.
When less than five "kè" of the clepsydra remained,
the Attendant Secretary and the Grand Minister of the Court of State Ceremonials would each report:
"All officials are in position."
When the clepsydra ran out,
the Grand Preceptor would report:
"Outside preparations are complete."
The Emperor would emerge.
Bells and drums would sound,
and all officials would prostrate themselves.
The Grand Master of Ceremonies would guide the Emperor to ascend the throne.
Bells and drums would cease.
All officials would rise.
The Grand Minister of the Court of State Ceremonials would kneel and report:
"Requesting the court assembly."
The Ritual Assistant would proclaim:
"The Emperor invites the kings to ascend."
The Grand Minister of the Court of State Ceremonials would kneel and proclaim:
"Your vassal kings, such-and-such, respectfully present one white jade disc each,
and bow twice in congratulations."
The Grand Master of Ceremonies would respond:
"All kings ascend."
The Attendant would lead them up the hall,
facing the Emperor's seat.
The Emperor would rise,
and the kings would bow twice.
The Emperor would be seated,
and they would bow twice again,
kneel and place the jade discs before the Emperor's seat,
and bow twice again.
When the ceremony was complete,
the Attendant would lead them down the hall,
returning to their original positions.

The Ritual Assistant would lead the dukes, special appointees, the sons of the Southern Chányú of the Xiongnú, and the Golden-Purple Generals to the west of the Grand Minister of the Court of State Ceremonials.
Officials of the two-thousand-dàn rank (Intermediate), two-thousand-dàn rank, thousand-dàn rank, and six-hundred-dàn rank would stand to the west of the Grand Minister of State Ceremonials,
all facing north and prostrating.
The Grand Minister of the Court of State Ceremonials would kneel and proclaim:
"The Grand Commandant, officials of the two-thousand-dàn rank (Intermediate), etc., respectfully present jade discs, skins, silks, lambs, geese, and pheasants,
and bow twice in congratulations."
The Grand Master of Ceremonies would proclaim:
"The Emperor invites the lords to ascend."
The Ritual Assistant would lead the dukes up to the Golden-Purple Generals onto the hall,
〔二五〕facing the Emperor's seat.
The Emperor would rise,
and they would all bow twice.
The Emperor would be seated,
and they would bow twice again.
They would kneel and place the jade discs, skins, and silks before the Emperor's seat,
and bow twice again.
When the ceremony was complete,
the proclaimer would lead them down the hall,
returning to their original positions.
When the kings and dukes completed the ceremony of presenting jade discs,
the Grand Minister of State Ceremonials would proclaim simultaneously,
with officials of the two-thousand-dàn rank (Intermediate) and below in the hall following suit.
When the ceremony was complete,
the gifts would be handed to the gift-receiving attendants,
〔二六〕who would pass the jade discs and silks to the Attendant,
and the lambs, geese, and pheasants to the Grand Steward.
The Grand Music Director would kneel and request the performance of elegant music.
〔二七〕Music would be performed in order.
The Director of Imperial Carriages would then bring out the carriages.
The Emperor would retire,
and all officials would be seated.
When six "kè" of water had entered the day clepsydra,
the various barbarians and foreign guests would enter in order,
〔二八〕all bowing twice before
being seated.
Three "kè" after the Emperor entered,
he would emerge again.
Bells and drums would sound.
The Attendant Secretary would kneel and report:
"Requesting all officials to ascend."
The Attendant would lead the kings and dukes up to officials of the two-thousand-dàn rank onto the hall,
〔二九〕while officials of the thousand-dàn rank and six-hundred-dàn rank would remain in their original positions.
The Attendant would lead the kings to the wine vessel to pour longevity wine,
〔三０〕and kneel to hand it to the Grand Preceptor.
The Grand Preceptor would kneel and place it before the Emperor's seat.
The kings would return to pour for themselves,
and place it before their seats.
The Attendant would kneel and report:
"Your vassal kings, such-and-such, respectfully present a cup and bow twice,
offering ten thousand years of longevity."
The Grand Preceptor would say:
"The cup has been presented."
All officials would prostrate themselves and shout "Long live!"
Music from the four wings would begin.
All officials would bow twice.
After drinking,
they would bow twice again.
The Attendant would lead the various kings, etc., back to their original positions.
The ushers would announce "take your seats,"
and all officials would kneel and respond "yes."
The Grand Preceptor, the Director of the Central Secretariat, and the Director of the Department of State Affairs would each offer longevity wine in the hall,
and the ceremonial song music would ascend.
The Grand Steward would also serve imperial wine.
When the imperial wine reached the steps,
the Grand Steward would kneel and hand it to the Imperial Attendant,
who would kneel and present it before the Emperor's seat.
Then, wine would be served to all officials.
The Grand Music Director would kneel and report:
"Perform the ceremonial song."
Thrice.
When it ended,
it would descend.
The Grand Steward would kneel and request the imperial meal to arrive at the steps,
and all officials would rise.
The Grand Steward would hold the soup and kneel to hand it to the Minister of Works;
hold the rice and kneel to hand it to the Grand Minister of Agriculture;
the Imperial Food Steward would hold the tray and hand it to the Imperial Attendant,
who would kneel and present it before the Emperor's seat.
〔三一〕All officials would take their seats.
The Grand Music Director would kneel and report:
"Eat.
Raise the music."
The Grand Steward would distribute meal trays to all officials.
When the meal was finished,
the Grand Music Director would kneel and report:
"Please proceed."
Music would be performed in order.
The Director of the Drum-and-Pipe Band would then advance and kneel to report:
"Please proceed with various performances in order."
Then, the accountancy clerks from various commanderies would be summoned forward
to receive imperial edicts and instructions below the steps.
When the banquet and entertainment were finished,
one Attendant would kneel and report:
"Please dismiss."
Bells and drums would sound,
and all officials, facing north, would bow twice and depart.
In the East Jìn, positions were established according to circumstances,
but the general pattern remained unchanged.
When the Sòng dynasty came to power,
it largely followed the old rituals,
and the additions and deletions are discernible.
According to the East Jìn regulations,
if the Crown Prince attended the assembly,
he would be positioned below the Three Revered Vassals and above the kings and dukes.
In the eleventh year of Yuánjiā during the reign of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
he was elevated to a position above the Three Revered Vassals.
According to Wèi regulations,
vassal kings were not allowed to attend court audiences.
During the reign of Emperor Míng, those who did attend
did so only by special imperial favor,
and this was not to be a regular practice.
During the Tàishǐ era of Jìn,
officials memorialized:
"For the feudal states, among their kings and dukes and lower officials who enter court,
the four directions shall each be divided into two groups,
rotating every three years,
and restarting after a full cycle.
If there is a temporary reason
〔三二〕to defer, it will be in the next year.
After attending court,
they must wait three full years before attending again,
and not follow the original count.
The court ceremony for presenting jade discs shall follow the old court system.
〔三三〕In years when they do not attend court,
they shall each send a minister to present tribute."
The memorial was approved.
In the East Jìn, kings and marquises did not reside in their feudal states.
If they were assigned to duties and resided outside,
they followed the same etiquette as regional governors, inspectors, and officials of the two-thousand-dàn rank,
and there was no system of court audiences or tribute presentation,
thus this ritual was abolished.
On the first day of the first month, during the grand court assembly,
a Báihǔ Zūn was placed in the palace courtyard.
On the lid of the zūn was a white tiger.
If anyone was able to offer frank advice,
then this zūn would be opened for drinking.
According to the Lǐjì,
when Zhī Dàozǐ died
and had not yet been buried,
Píng Gōng was drinking wine.
Shī Kuàng and Lǐ Diào attended him,
playing the bells.
Dù Kuì came from outside.
Hearing the sound of the bells, he asked,
"Where is he?"
Someone replied,
"In the sleeping chamber."
Dù Kuì entered the sleeping chamber,
ascended the steps,
and poured a drink, saying,
"Kuàng, drink this."
He poured another, saying,
"Diào, drink this."
He poured yet another,
sat facing north in the hall, drank it,
descended,
and hurried out.
Píng Gōng called him back and brought him forward, saying,
"Kuì,
just now your words opened my mind somewhat,
which is why I did not speak to you.
You gave Kuàng a drink,
why?"
He replied,
"On the days of Zǐ and Mǎo, one should not make music.
Zhī Dàozǐ is in the hall;
this is a great 'Zǐ-Mǎo' occasion.
Kuàng
is the Grand Music Master.
He did not warn you,
therefore I gave him a drink."
"You gave Diào a drink,
why?"
He replied,
"Diào
is Your Lordship's intimate minister.
For the sake of a drink and a meal,
he forgot Your Lordship's affliction,
therefore I gave him a drink."
"You drank,
why?"
He replied,
"Kuì is a chief cook.
I only provide knives and spoons,
yet I dared to participate in guarding against impropriety,
therefore I drank."
Píng Gōng said,
"I too have erred.
Pour a drink for me."
Dù Kuì washed his hands and raised the zhì cup.
The Duke said to his attendants,
"If I die,
this cup must never be abolished."
Until today,
after all offerings are completed,
this zhì cup is raised,
and it is called
"Dù Jǔ."
The Báihǔ Zūn
is likely a surviving model of Dù Jǔ.
The depiction of a tiger
was probably added by later generations,
wishing to make speakers fierce as a tiger,
without any fear or hesitation.
The Hàn dynasty, from Gāo Dì's tenth month when Qín was pacified, considered that the beginning of the year.
Although Emperor Wǔ changed to the Xià calendar,
the first day of the month was still often celebrated with assemblies,
like the ceremony of Yuánzhèng.
The Wèi and Jìn dynasties received congratulations from all states and officials on the winter solstice,
followed by a small gathering.
Its ceremony was secondary to that of New Year's Day,
and the Jìn has a commentary on it.
In the eighth month of Yǒngchū first year of the Sòng dynasty,
an imperial edict stated:
"Whether to send winter envoys or not,
the service duties should be reduced.
〔三四〕Now all of them can be suspended.
Only the great celebration of Yuánzhèng
must not be abolished.
The sending of winter envoys from commanderies and counties to the prefectural and capital supervisory offices
should also be suspended."
Sūn Quán, when he first established his capital at Wǔchāng and then Jiànyè,
did not establish altars for suburban sacrifices.
It was not until the eleventh month of Tàiyuán first year in his later years
that he sacrificed at the Southern Altar.
Its location is now about ten li south of Mòlíng County, within the suburban area.
When the Jìn clan moved south,
they established the Southern Altar in a sì (巳) position,
which was not in accordance with the meaning of the "yang position" as prescribed by ritual.
In the ninth month of Dàmíng third year of Sòng Xiàowǔ,
〔三五〕Xú Yuán, Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, proposed:
"The position for suburban sacrifices
was rarely heard of in ancient times.
The Lǐjì says, 'Burning firewood on the Tàitán
is to sacrifice to Heaven.'
'Establishing a mound in the Southern Altar
is to approach the yang position.'
In early Hàn, the altars at Gānquán and Hédōng for yīn and mái sacrifices were moved,
and eventually relocated to the north and south of Cháng'ān.
Guāngwǔ inherited the throne,
and set up the two altars north and south of Luòyáng.
When the Jìn clan crossed the river,
they were all in the north.
When the altars and mounds were discussed,
opinions were divergent.
Moreover, the southern road was narrow
and its widening had not been discussed,
so a mound altar was built in the southeastern sì position.
When the August Sòng received the Mandate,
it did not change it.
Furthermore, it was within the residential area,
not outside the city.
Now, with the sacred plan for reconstruction,
old regulations are being renewed,
the southern post road is opened,
and the yang road is long and wide.
It is fitting to move the altar to the true south (wǔ position)
to establish the position for Heaven."
Dr. Sīmǎ Xīngzhī, Fù Yù, and Grand Master of Ceremonies Assistant Lù Chéng all agreed with Xú Yuán's proposal.
Thus, the suburban altars were moved to the west of Niútóu Mountain in Mòlíng,
exactly in the wǔ position relative to the palace.
After Shìzǔ died,
the former deposed emperor ascended the throne.
Considering the old site of the altar auspicious,
he moved it back to its original place.
The Northern Altar
was first established during the reign of Jìn Chéng Dì,
originally south of Fùzhōu Mountain.
Sòng Tàizǔ used that land for the Lèyóu Garden,
and moved the altar to the northwest of the mountain.
Later, that land was made into the Northern Lake,
and the altar was moved to the northwest of Hútáng.
That area was low-lying and damp,
so it was again moved to the east of Báishí Village.
That land was also made into a lake,
so it was moved to the west of the road on the northern slope of Zhōngshān,
〔三六〕facing the Southern Altar.
Later, Báishí East Lake was abolished,
and the Northern Altar returned to its old place.
At the Southern Suburban Altar (Nánjiāo),
the Emperor (Huángdì) observes a period of *sànzhāi* for seven days,
and *zhìzhāi* for three days.
Officials in charge of purification also do the same.
On the morning of the *zhìzhāi* observance,
the Emperor sits under an awning in the Tàijí Hall (Tàijí Diàn).
He wears a crimson gauze robe,
a black cap (*jièzé*),
and a tōngtiān gold *bóshān* crown.
On the day before the suburban sacrifice, five *kè* before dusk,
the animals for the evening sacrifice are inspected.
The Three Dukes (Gōng), Nine Ministers (Qīng), the Prefect of Jīngzhào (Jīngzhào Yǐn), and all officials take their places to the east of the altar.
The Grand Supplicator (Tàizhù Shǐ) leads the sacrificial animals in.
Upon reaching the placard,
he reports to the sacrificial superintendent (xīlìng), kneels, and says:
"Please inspect the sacrificial animals."
The superintendent raises his hand and says:
"Fat."
The Grand Supplicator (Tàizhù Lìng) walks around the animals,
raises his hand, and says:
"Sufficient."
The Grand Supplicator (Tàizhù Lìng) leads the animals to the kitchen.
Two earthenware vessels (*táodòu*) are used to present the hair and blood.
One is placed before the divine seat of August Heaven (Huángtiān),
and the other before the divine seat of the Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ).
On the day of the suburban sacrifice, eight *kè* before dawn,
the Grand Supplicator (Tàizhù Lìng) presents the offerings,
and the court gentlemen (*láng*) arrange them.
For the sacrificial animals, two *xǐlì* are used,
and for the various gods, one ox is used.
For the sweet wine (*lǐ*), *jùchàng* is used,
and for the matting (*jiè*), white *máo* grass is used.
One vessel of black wine (*xuánjiǔ*) is used.
The vessels are made of gourds and earthenware (*páotáo*).
Wine is held in a pottery *zūn*,
and poured with a pottery *xū*.
For the ceremonial jade disk (*bì*), dark jade is used.
Two *kuǎixí* mats each are used,
and no cushions (*yīnrú*) are provided.
In ancient times, mats (*xí*) were used;
during the Jìn (Jìn) dynasty in the area south of the Yangtze River (Jiāngzuǒ), *kuǎi* grass was used.
When the imperial carriage departs,
all officials who are observing the fast or accompanying the carriage, and those who have taken their positions early filling the streets,
each follow according to their delegated duties.
At one *kè* after sunrise,
the Emperor dons the dragon robe (*lónggǔn*),
and the Píngtiān Crown (Píngtiān Guān),
ascends the gold-rooted carriage (*jīngēnchē*),
and arrives outside the east gate of the altar.
The erudite scholars (Bóshì) and the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng) lead him to the black screen (*hēizǎn*).
The Grand Supplicator (Tàizhù Lìng) kneels, holding a gourd and earthenware vessel (*páotáo*),
and pours wine onto the ground.
The Emperor bows twice (zàibài) and
rises.
All ministers bow twice and prostrate themselves.
The Master of Ceremonies (Zhìlǐ) says:
"Rise."
The erudite scholars (Bóshì) and the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng) lead the Emperor to the south steps.
He removes his shoes (*xì*) and ascends the altar,
proceeds to the wine vessel (*léi*) to wash his hands.
The Imperial Household Grandee (Huángmén Shìláng) washes the cup (*jué*),
kneels, and hands it to the Emperor.
The cup-bearing court gentleman (Zhízūn Láng) hands over the cup,
pours *jùchàng* wine, and hands it to the Emperor.
He kneels and places it before the divine seat of August Heaven (Huángtiān),
bows twice, and
rises.
Next, he proceeds to the divine seat of the Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) who is co-worshiped with Heaven,
holds the cup, kneels and places it,
following the ritual for August Heaven.
Facing south, bowing north,
he bows once and prostrates himself.
The Grand Supplicator (Tàizhù Lìng) pours the blessed wine into separate cups,
then combines them into one cup,
kneels and presents it to the Emperor,
who bows twice and prostrates himself.
After drinking the blessed wine,
the erudite scholars (Bóshì) and the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng) lead the Emperor down the east steps,
and return to the south steps.
The usher (Yèzhě) leads the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng) up the altar
for the second libation (*yàxiàn*).
The usher (Yèzhě) then leads the Minister of the Imperial Clan (Guānglù) up the altar
for the final libation (*zhōngxiàn*).
This concludes the ceremony.
Each descends the steps and returns to their original position.
The Grand Supplicator (Tàizhù) sees off the spirits,
kneels, holding a gourd and earthenware vessel (*páotáo*),
and pours wine onto the ground.
He rises.
Walking directly south out of the altar gate,
the Master of Ceremonies (Zhìlǐ) raises his hand and announces,
and all ministers bow twice and prostrate themselves.
The Emperor turns around.
The Master of Ceremonies (Zhìlǐ) says:
"Rise."
The erudite scholar (Bóshì) kneels and says:
"The sacrificial rites are completed.
Proceed to the burning (*liáo*)."
The erudite scholars (Bóshì) and the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng) lead the Emperor to the burning site (*liáowèi*),
adjacent to the east steps of the altar.
The Emperor stands facing south.
The Grand Supplicator (Tàizhù Lìng) presents on a tray the jade disks, sacrificial animal bodies, cups of wine, millet rice, and other offerings,
ascends the firewood altar (*chái tán*), and arranges them.
The Master of Ceremonies (Zhìlǐ) raises his hand and says:
"The burning may commence."
Three men carrying torches ascend.
The fire ignites.
The Grand Supplicator (Tàizhù Lìng) and others descend from the altar.
Twenty people each on the east and west sides of the altar
throw their torches onto the altar,
and the half-burnt firewood collapses.
The erudite scholar (Bóshì) looks up and announces:
"The ceremony is completed."
The Emperor leaves and takes his seat.
The restrictions are lifted.
If the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) has a reason not to attend,
then the Three Dukes (Sāngōng) perform the rites.
The Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) performs the first libation (*chūxiàn*),
while the second and final libations (*yàxiàn, zhōngxiàn*)
are still performed by the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng) and the Minister of the Imperial Clan (Guānglùxūn), respectively.
For the Northern Suburban Sacrifice (Běijiāo Zāi), the evening sacrifice, the presentation of cooked offerings,
and the arrival of the imperial carriage and all officials at the altar for the three libations,
all follow the rites of the Southern Suburban Sacrifice (Nánjiāo Zhī Lǐ);
however, after the ceremony is concluded,
the Grand Supplicator (Tàizhù Lìng) brings the sacrificial animals, jade, and offerings to the pit (*kǎn*), places the animals on top of them, and completes this.
Then, another animal is placed over them.
The Master of Ceremonies (Zhìlǐ) raises his hand and says:
"It may be buried."
Twenty people simultaneously shovel earth down.
When the pit is about half-filled,
the erudite scholar (Bóshì) looks up and announces:
"The ceremony is completed."
The Emperor departs.
Since the Wèi (Wèi) dynasty,
the Three Dukes (Sāngōng) were often made to perform the rites,
and the imperial carriage rarely went out.
In the early Wèi (Wèi) and Jìn (Jìn) dynasties,
although the ceremonial protocols (*yízhù*) are not fully preserved,
the modifications made to the Hàn (Hàn) system are discernible.
After the Jìn (Jìn) dynasty's relocation to the east of the Yangtze River (Jiāngzuǒ),
officials had records of these protocols.
Emperor Wén of Wèi (Wèi Wéndì) issued an edict saying:
"The Hàn (Hàn) dynasty did not worship the sun at the eastern suburban altar,
but instead, morning and evening, consistently bowed to the sun from the east side of the palace hall.
This is cumbersome and disrespectful, akin to a family affair,
and not the way to serve Heaven and the suburban gods."
On the *yǐhài* day of the first month of Huángchū second year (Huángchū Èr Nián),
the sun was worshipped outside the east gate.
According to the rites,
the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) should worship the sun in the east during the spring equinox,
and the moon in the west during the autumn equinox.
Now, it is the first month,
which is not the correct time.
In the Hàn (Hàn) Dynastic History's Treatise on Sacrifices to Heaven and Earth (Hàn Jiāosì Zhì),
At dawn, he exited the bamboo palace (*zhúgōng*) and bowed to the sun facing east;
that evening, he bowed to the moon facing west.
This indicates that the suburban sacrifice day itself was used,
without waiting for the two equinoxes.
On the *dīnghài* day, the first day of the second month of Tàihé first year (Tàihé Yuán Nián) of Emperor Míng (Míngdì),
In the eighth month, on the *jǐchǒu* day,
the moon was worshipped at the western suburban altar.
This is the ancient rite.
The Comprehensive Discussion in the White Tiger Hall (Báihǔ Tōng) states:
"The King (Wángzhě) takes Heaven as father, Earth as mother,
the Sun as elder brother, and the Moon as elder sister."
This is its meaning.
In the Greater Tradition of the Book of Documents (Shàngshū Dàzhuàn),
the words for welcoming the sun say:
"In a certain year, certain month, on the auspicious day.
Brilliant light above and below,
diligently bestowing upon the four quarters,
spreading its gentle radiance,
for I, the One Man.
So-and-so respectfully bows and welcomes the sun at the suburban altar."
During the Wú (Wú) period, the court gentleman Chén Róng (Chén Róng) presented a eulogy for the eastern suburban altar,
indicating that this rite was also practiced during the Wú (Wú) period.
In Tàikāng second year (Tàikāng Èr Nián) of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn (Jìn Wǔdì),
the relevant officials petitioned:
"According to tradition for the spring equinox, we request the imperial carriage to sacrifice to the morning sun.
it may be permissible not to go in person."
An edict said:
"Rituals and ceremonies should be constant.
What is proposed
and again creates a lack of fixed regulations.
Recently, difficulties have not been settled,
so we have always followed what was proposed.
Now that military matters have ceased,
only this is of great importance."
This edict implies that
the Emperor personally performed the morning sun worship again.
Afterwards, this practice was abolished.
For the Dì Ancestral Sacrifice,
the Huángdì fasted for seven days (sǎnzhāi),
and purified himself for three days (zhìzhāi).
Pure officials likewise observed these.
[四一]On the day of purification,
the Huángdì would sit veiled in the Tàijí Diàn,
wearing a crimson gauze robe,
a black jièzé cap,
and a Tōngtiān Jīnbóshān crown.
On the day of the sacrifice,
the imperial carriage would depart.
Officials who were observing purification, accompanying the imperial carriage, remaining to guard, filling the streets, or positioned in advance,
would each act according to the announcements and their duties.
At the first quarter of the shàngshuǐ (morning water-clock),
the Huángdì would wear the píngmiǎn lónggǔn attire,
ascend the Jīngēn Chē,
and arrive at the temple’s north gate.
Zhìlǐ and Yèzhě officials would each lead Tàiyuè, Tàicháng, Guānglùxūn, and the Sāngōng, etc., to enter and take their places.
The Huángdì would descend from the carriage and enter the temple,
remove his slippers,
wash his hands and rinse the wine cups.
After this,
he would ascend the hall.
For the first offering,
wine cups were presented,
and music played.
The Tàizhù Lìng would kneel and read the prayer text.
After this,
it was advanced and placed before the spirit tablet,
and the Huángdì returned to his original position.
The Bóshì would lead the Tàiwèi for the second offering.
After this,
the Yèzhě would again lead the Guānglùxūn for the final offering.
For all Dì and Xiá grand sacrifices,
the spirit tablets would all be brought out to the temple hall,
arranged by zhāomù for their seats,
and no longer kept in the private chambers.
The Jìn clan also had four premature deaths in the Yīn Shì (private chamber).
The Zhìlǐ official would lead them from the Yīn Shì to present wine cups in sequence before the offerings.
For meritorious officials who were accorded supplementary offerings,
seats were set up in the courtyard,
and the Yèzhě would present wine cups before their offerings.
If the Huángdì did not personally perform the sacrifice,
then the Sāngōng would conduct the ceremony,
with the Tàiwèi making the first offering,
the Tàicháng the second offering,
and the Guānglùxūn the final offering.
For the seasonal sacrifices,
it was also customary to prepare the sacrificial animals the evening before the sacrifice,
with the ceremony similar to the suburban sacrifice.
In the seventh year of Tàishǐ (271 CE) in the fourth month, during the reign of Jìn Wǔdì,
the emperor was about to personally perform the sacrifice.
The imperial carriage performed the evening preparation of animals,
but the ritual protocol did not include bowing.
An imperial edict questioned the reason.
The Bóshì submitted:
"This has been passed down through generations."
The emperor said:
"This is not a ritual for showing reverence to the ancestral temple."
Thereupon, actual bowing was performed before returning,
and this was then established as a system.
During the Tàikāng period,
officials proposed that
on the first day of the eleventh month, when the new moon (héshuò), winter zheng sacrifice, and evening preparation of animals coincided,
officials could conduct the ceremony.
The edict stated:
"For the evening preparation of animals to be conducted by officials
is incorrect.
Another day in the first ten days of the month should be chosen."
This indicates that Jìn Wǔdì personally attended and bowed during the evening preparation of animals,
but this practice ceased again from the time of the Eastern Jìn.
On the xīnmǎo day in the third month of the first year of Jiànwǔ (317 CE), Jìn Yuándì
assumed the title of King of Jìn,
[四二]and performed the ceremonial Dì sacrifice of the Son of Heaven,
which was an extraordinary event.
In the ninth month of the eleventh year of Tàiyuán (386 CE), during the reign of Xiàowǔ,
an imperial princess died, which coincided with an impending zheng sacrifice.
Zhōngshū Shìláng Fàn Níng submitted a memorial:
"According to the Sāngfú Zhuàn,
if someone dies within the palace,
no sacrifices are to be performed for three months,
regardless of age, or noble or humble status.
Although the imperial princess was an infant,
your servant secretly believes this to be a matter of doubt."
Thereupon, the Shàngshū proposed that the Sāngōng should perform the ceremony.
In the past, during the reign of Hàn Língdì,
on Lìchūn (Beginning of Spring), fasting and welcoming the qi in the eastern suburbs were still observed.
Shàngshū Zuǒchéng ōushā Mòshǐ (name) in the Nánshū temple,
whereupon an imperial edict stated:
"Yìláng Cài Yōng and Bóshì Rèn Mǐn,
are asked whether it is permissible to fast and sacrifice?
Is there anything inappropriate?"
Yōng and others replied:
"According to the sacrifice to Shàngdì,
it cannot be abandoned for any reason.
The palace is vast,
the Mòshǐ is of low status,
and the day is still far off.
Fasting is permissible without doubt."
Fàn Níng was not unaware of this discussion,
but he did not follow it.
In Wèi and early Jìn,
although the sacrificial rites were not fully preserved,
they were complete in the Eastern Jìn.
The official procedures had their annotations.
For the sacrifices to Tàishè, Dìshè, and Tàijì,
they were always performed on the second shè day of the second and eighth months of the year.
The Tàizhù Lìng prepared the sacrificial animals the evening before and presented the cooked offerings,
following the rites for suburban and ancestral temple sacrifices.
The Sīkōng, Tàicháng, and Dàsīnóng made the three offerings.
The official procedures had their annotations.
In the Rites of Zhōu, the king personally performed the sacrifice;
since the Hàn dynasty,
officials have performed the ceremony.
In the sixth year of Yuánchū (119 CE), during the reign of Hàn Āndì,
six Zōng ancestral temples were established in the xu-hai direction northwest of the capital.
[四三]The sacrificial rites were comparable to those of Tàishè.
When the sun and moon were about to conjoin,
the Tàishǐ reported the new moon.
Three days before the event, the Shàngshū
would announce and manage internal and external affairs,
and issue a warning of strict vigilance.
Zhì Yú, in his resolution of doubts, stated:
"Those who rescue from an eclipse
all wear red caps
to aid the yang.
When the sun is about to be eclipsed,
the Son of Heaven wears plain clothes and avoids the main hall.
Internal and external areas are strictly vigilant.
The Tàishǐ ascends the Língtái
to observe the changes in the sun.
Drums are beaten at the gates.
Upon hearing the drum sounds,
attendant officials all wear red caps
and enter with swords to serve.
From the Língshǐ of the Sāntái and above,
they each hold swords and stand before their doors.
The Wèiwèi Qīng races around the palace,
observing and guarding,
circulating repeatedly.
When the sun returns to normal,
they all dismiss."
In the seventeenth year of Lǔ Zhāogōng,
on the first day of the sixth month,
there was a solar eclipse.
The Zhùshǐ requested the silks to be used.
[四四]Shūsūn Zhāozǐ said:
"When there is a solar eclipse,
the Son of Heaven does not play music,
[四五]but beats drums at the Shè (altar of soil);
feudal lords use silks at the Shè,
and beat drums at court,
this is the proper ritual."
Also, red silk ropes were tied to the Shè,
and the Zhùshǐ presented words of reproach.
The Shè,
the spirit of Gōulóng,
is the Huángdì's prime minister,
thus he is reprimanded.
For the new moon,
official procedures had their annotations.
In the past, during the Jiàn'ān period of Hàn,
a grand court assembly was planned,
but the Tàishǐ reported that there would be a solar eclipse on New Year's Day.
Court officials doubted whether the assembly should proceed.
They all went to consult Shàngshū Lìng Xún Wénruò.
At that time, Liú Shào, a jílì official from Guǎngpíng, was present
and said:
"Zǐshèn and Píbào,
ancient excellent historians,
still made errors in predicting water and fire,
and miscalculated heavenly phenomena.
The ritual states that there are four cases where feudal lords, when paying homage to the Son of Heaven, should not complete the ceremony upon entering the gate,
and a solar eclipse is one of them.
However, the sages established regulations
not to preemptively abandon court ceremonies due to anomalies or unusual occurrences,
as either the disaster might dissipate or the anomaly might recede,
or the calculations might be erroneous."
Wénruò and the others were all pleased and followed his advice,
and the court assembly proceeded as usual,
and the sun also did not undergo an eclipse.
Shào thereby gained prominence,
and the Wèi History praised and recorded it.
In the second year of Zhèngyuán of Wèi Gāoguì Xiānggōng, on the first day of the third month,
the Grand Astrologer reported a solar eclipse, but it did not occur.
At that time, Jìn Wénwáng was the Grand General.
He greatly faulted the astrological officials for their inaccuracy.
The astrological officials replied:
“At the time of conjunction,
sometimes the sun obscures the moon,
and sometimes the moon obscures the sun.
When the moon obscures the sun,
it blocks the body of the sun,
causing its light to diminish,
hence it is called a solar eclipse.
When the sun obscures the moon,
the sun passes above the moon.
This is called 'Yīn does not invade Yáng',
and although they intersect, there is no change.
The principle that the sun and moon must eclipse when they obscure each other,
〔四六〕cannot be known by any technique.
Thus, in the past, when performing the dì and jiāo shè sacrifices,
if a solar eclipse occurred, the sacrifice was suspended and resumed.
This also shows that previous generations of astrological officials could not accurately predict eclipses.
According to Hàn precedents,
it was believed that a solar eclipse must occur at the time of conjunction.
Whenever that time arrived,
officials were alerted
to prepare for the celestial anomaly.
Therefore, the jiǎyín edict established regulations for preparing for eclipses,
but no law for penalizing inaccuracy.
The six calendars from ancient times — Huángdì, Zhuānxù, Xià, Yīn, Zhōu, and Lǔ —
all had no method for predicting solar eclipses,
only for evaluating the density or sparseness of celestial events.
The provision for punishment
stems from the lack of a technique to be evaluated in the first place,
it is not the fault of the officials in charge.”
So, the matter was dropped.
In the third and fourth years of Xiánníng of Jìn Wǔdì,
on both occasions, the imperial assembly was cancelled due to the conjunction occurring on New Year's Day.
This was a change from Wèi precedents.
In the first year of Tàixīng of Jìn Yuándì, in the fourth month, a conjunction occurred.
Zhōngshū Shìláng Kǒng Yú memorialized, saying:
“The Chūnqiū states that 'when the sun is eclipsed,'
the Son of Heaven beats drums at the shè altar,
to attack the Yīn forces.
The feudal lords beat drums in their courts,
to attack themselves (their own faults).
However, the Shàngshū Fú states
that if there is an anomaly in the sun,
drums should be beaten at all gates,
which violates the old canons.”
An imperial edict stated:
“What you have presented has righteous meaning.
I will immediately command the outer court to change it.”
By the first year of Jiànchuán of Kāngdì,
the Grand Astrologer reported a conjunction on Yuánrì.
Court officials again debated whether the assembly should be cancelled or not.
Yǔ Bīng, who was assisting in governance,
copied Liú Shào’s discussion and showed it to the Eight Councillors.
At that time, some believed Shào had misunderstood the intent of the rites,
and Xún Wénruò followed them,
which was one of his failures as a superior person.
Therefore, Cài Mó then wrote an essay refuting him, saying:
“Shào discusses the disappearance and concealment of disasters and anomalies,
and also states that Shèn and Zào still made mistakes,
and that the Grand Astrologer's report is not necessarily accurate.
His reasoning is indeed sound.
But to say that the sages established regulations,
and would not, because of anomalies, prematurely abolish court ceremonies,
this is a mistake.
The occurrence of auspicious and inauspicious signs
is meant to admonish the ruler,
and is greatly heeded by kings.
Therefore, one wears plain clothes, abolishes music,
retreats to the main chamber,
all officials offer goods,
uses ceremonial silks and beats drums,
personally intervening to remedy it.
Regarding matters of reverence and admonition,
rather than doubting and neglecting them,
it is better to be cautious and carry them out.
Thus, Kǒngzǐ and Lǎodān assisted at a funeral in Xiàngdǎng.
They proceeded because it was a funeral and the stars were not visible.
Therefore, when there was a solar eclipse, they halted the coffin,
saying, 'How do we know the stars are not visible?'
Now, the astrological official says there will be an eclipse,
how do we know it will not occur?
The Master and Lǎodān took precautions against the stars being visible,
but Shào disregards this,
which is to abandon the established rules of the sages and worthies.
When Lǔ Huánggōng suffered a disaster on a réngshēn day,
and held the cháng sacrifice on a yǐhài day,
the Chūnqiū criticized him.
Even after the disaster had passed,
〔四七〕he was still worried and fearful,
thus abolishing the ancestral temple sacrifice.
How much more so, upon hearing that a heavenly calamity is approaching,
to hold a celebratory assembly?
This is contrary to the rites.
What the Lǐjì says about 'feudal lords entering the gate and not being able to complete the rites'
refers to when the celestial official did not predict it in advance,
and the feudal lords, having already entered, only realized it upon seeing the eclipse;
it does not mean hearing in advance that there will be an eclipse
and still not abolishing the court assembly.
Shào's citation of this
〔四八〕can be said to have missed its true meaning.
What Liú Shào relied on was the Lǐjì;
the incident of the Master and Lǎodān in Xiàngdǎng
is also mentioned in the Lǐjì.
Yet he violated and contradicted it,
having no basis for his advance or retreat.
What Xún Lìng approved,
and what the Hàn court followed,
has caused this statement to be praised even now,
without its error being recognized.
Later gentlemen
will likely take it as a model,
therefore I am correcting it.”
Thereupon Yǔ Bīng followed the public opinion
and cancelled the assembly.
By the Yǒnghé era,
Yīn Hào, assisting in governance,
again wished to follow Liú Shào's proposal and not cancel the assembly.
Wáng Biāozhī cited the precedents of Xiánníng and Jiànchuán,
and also said:
“The rites state,
'Feudal lords meeting the Son of Heaven are unable to complete the rites and thus abandon them in four situations.'
This refers to sudden and unexpected occurrences,
not to pre-existing knowledge of the event and then hoping for the astrological official's prediction to be wrong,
〔四九〕and therefore not prematurely abolishing the court assembly.”
Thus, Yīn Hào again followed Biāozhī,
and this precedent has been followed until today.
The rite of plowing the imperial field is ancient;
Hàn Wéndì revived it.
When Zhāodì ascended to the throne in his youth,
he plowed at the Gōudùn's experimental field.
In the fifteenth year of Yǒngpíng of Míngdì, in the second month,
he made an eastern tour
and plowed at Xiàpī.
In the third year of Yuánhé of Zhāngdì, in the first month, he made a northern tour
and plowed at Huáixiàn.
The three ancestors of Wèi all personally plowed the imperial field.
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ of Jìn Wǔdì,
the relevant officials memorialized that for the initial plowing and sacrifice to the First Farmer,
the officials could carry out the ceremony.
〔五０〕An imperial edict stated:
“The great matters of the people
are in sacrifice and agriculture.
Therefore, the sage kings of antiquity
personally plowed the imperial fields
to provide grains for the jiāo and miào sacrifices,
and also to instruct and transform the world.
In recent times,
the plowing of the imperial field has been limited to a few steps,
merely having the empty name of emulating antiquity,
but lacking the substance of providing for sacrifices and instructing farmers,
while incurring the expenses of officials' carriages and retinues.
Now, by restoring the system of a thousand mù,
I, along with the dukes, ministers, and gentlemen,
will personally experience the difficulties of farming,
to lead the world.
〔五一〕The responsible officials should detail the regulations,
and also instruct Hénán to designate land in the south of the eastern suburb,
north of the Luòshuǐ River,
that is level, fertile, and well-watered.
If there is no government land,
they should exchange land as appropriate,
without encroaching on the people's property.”
After this,
the matter was abandoned.
Historical annotations often have omissions.
The two emperors Yuán and Āi of the Eastern Jìn,
〔五二〕were about to revive the plowing of the imperial field.
The annotations submitted by Hè Xún and others,
and the ceremonies set by Péi Xiàn in Húzhōng,
were also not sufficiently detailed or appropriate.
In the twentieth year of Yuánjiā,
Tàizǔ was about to personally plough,
but as it had long been neglected,
he ordered Hé Chéngtiān to compile and fix the rituals.
Shān Qiānzhī, a student of history, had already privately gathered records,
and then presented them.
An imperial edict was then issued, stating:
"The state takes the people as its foundation,
and the people take food as their heaven.
If one man ceases to plough,
the hungry will surely be affected.
When food is truly abundant,
rituals and ceremonies flourish.
Recently, wherever one looks, there is poverty and depletion;
families have no stored provisions.
When yin and yang are temporarily out of balance,
〔五三〕people are filled with worry and distress;
if the year is not abundant,
then illness and destitution are widespread.
This is truly due to a lack of moral governance,
leading to these弊 (malpractices/ills),
and also because cultivation and sericulture are not widespread,
and much of the land's bounty is neglected.
The local officials lack methods of transformation and guidance,
and the common people forget the duty of diligent effort.
Reflecting on the need for widespread relief,
I have pondered it day and night.
Although decrees are frequently issued,
they ultimately fail to punish or encourage,
so how can we expect prosperity
by merely sitting and wishing for it?
Let the relevant authorities proclaim the old regulations,
and diligently enforce the assigned tasks.
Let all those who live by wandering
be attached to an occupation.
Examine diligence and laziness,
and administer rewards and punishments;
observe ability and deficiency,
and strictly implement promotions and demotions.
In ancient times, land was divided according to the seasons
to instruct farmers in their work.
The emperor personally ploughed the imperial fields
to respectfully provide grains for offerings.
Looking up to former kings,
I wish to follow their excellent precedents.
Therefore, an area of a thousand mǔ can be measured out,
and an auspicious day calculated.
I will personally lead all the officials
to perform the rites in the suburban fields.
Hopefully, with sincerity,
this will encourage and benefit the people."
Thereupon, various regulations were deliberated upon,
and the ritual diagrams and notes were compiled.
Nine days before the Beginning of Spring,
the Shàngshū was to manage internal and external affairs,
ordering everyone to act according to their respective offices.
The Sīkōng, Dànóng, Jīngyǐn, Líng, and Wèi
were to measure out a place eight lǐ from the palace
to organize a thousand mǔ,
and open up the crisscrossing paths.
The Altar to the First Farmer was to be set up south of the western path in the middle path,
and the Imperial Ploughing Altar north of the eastern path in the middle path.
Before ploughing,
a blue tent was to be set up overnight above the ploughing altar.
The Empress, leading the women of the six palaces, was to bring out the seeds of early and late ripening grains,
and hand them over to the Jítián Líng (Director of the Imperial Fields).
On the day of ploughing,
the Tàizhù was to offer one grand sacrifice (tàiláo) to the First Farmer,
all according to the ritual for sacrificing to the Emperor's She (Altar of Soil).
In the first month of spring,
an auspicious dìnghài day after the first xīn day was chosen.
The emperor would ride in a three-tiered covered carriage for ploughing,
drawn by four grey horses,
with a blue banner.
He would wear a tōngtiānguān,
a blue headscarf,
a blue embroidered court robe,
and a belt with blue jade ornaments.
From the vassal kings down to officials of six hundred shí (dan), all were to wear blue.
Only the Sāntái (Three Ducal Ministers) and the Wǔwèi (Military Guards) did not plough,
and did not change their attire.
When the imperial carriage set out,
all other matters were handled according to the suburban temple rituals.
When the imperial carriage arrived at the imperial fields,
the Shìzhōng (Attendant Counselor) would kneel and report:
"Your Majesty, please alight from the carriage."
Upon reaching the altar,
the Dàsīnóng (Minister of Agriculture) would kneel and report:
"The First Farmer has been honored with sacrifice;
please, Emperor, personally plough."
The Tàishǐlíng (Grand Astrologer) would announce:
"The Emperor personally ploughs."
He would push the plough three times forward and three times back.
Then the officials would plough in sequence.
The kings, dukes, and nobles of the five ranks who established states would push five times forward and five times back.
The gū (dukes), qīng (ministers), and dàfū (grandees) would push seven times forward and seven times back.
The shì (scholars) would push nine times forward and nine times back.
The Jítián Líng, leading his subordinates, would plough
to complete the mǔ,
sow the seeds,
and immediately harrow the soil.
The ceremony would then conclude.
Although the Wèi dynasty had the Son of Heaven plough the imperial fields,
its vassal rulers and nobles
lacked the hundred-mǔ ritual.
Towards the end of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn's reign,
the relevant authorities memorialized:
"In ancient times, feudal lords ploughed a hundred mǔ of imperial fields,
personally holding the plough and spade,
to serve the altars of soil and grain and the ancestral temple,
and to encourage agricultural work.
Now, as the various kings govern their states,
they should observe the ritual of ploughing the imperial fields."
However, it was not implemented.
After Sòng Tàizǔ's eastern ploughing,
it was then decreed for all zhōu, jūn, and xiàn
to fully observe the ritual.
According to the Zhōulǐ (Rites of Zhōu),
the Queen led the inner and outer noblewomen
in sericulture at the northern suburb.
The Hàn dynasty did it in the eastern suburb,
which was not ancient practice.
The Wèi dynasty did it in the northern suburb,
following the Zhōulǐ.
The Jìn dynasty did it in the western suburb,
presumably to correspond with the imperial fields in orientation.
In the first month of the seventh year of Huángchū of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
the empress was ordered to conduct sericulture in the northern suburb.
According to Wéi Dàn's eulogy for the empress's sericulture,
the Hàn dynasty's annotations had already been lost at that time,
and its rituals were subsequently re-examined and compiled.
By the time of the Jìn dynasty,
the 'first silkworm' ritual largely adopted Wèi dynasty methods.
In the sixth year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
Sànqí Chángshì Huá Jiào memorialized:
"The system of the former kings was that
the Son of Heaven and feudal lords personally ploughed a thousand mǔ,
and the empress and noblewomen personally engaged in sericulture at the palace.
〔五四〕Now, Your Majesty, with your sagely wisdom and utmost benevolence,
continues the legacy of the former kings.
The Empress embodies the virtue of nurturing life,
and aligns with the principle of complementing Heaven.
Yet, the teaching and guidance have not been initiated,
and the sericulture ritual is still lacking.
I believe it is appropriate to follow ancient models
and prepare for this grand ceremony."
An edict stated:
"In ancient times, the Son of Heaven personally ploughed the imperial fields to provide grains for offerings,
and the empress and noblewomen personally engaged in sericulture to prepare sacrificial attire.
This was to diligently follow filial piety and reverence,
and to clearly demonstrate teaching and instruction.
Currently, the imperial field system is established,
but the sericulture ritual is not observed.
Due to many pressing matters in between,
there has been no leisure to fully prepare for it.
Now the world is at peace,
and it is fitting to perform the ritual to show the four seas.
Let it be meticulously based on ancient classics and recent precedents,
combined with present appropriateness.
It shall be implemented next year."
Thereupon, Shìzhōng Chéng Càn was ordered to draft the ritual.
〔五五〕The Empress's mulberry-picking altar was west of the silkworm chamber,
outside the middle gate of the curtained palace.
The mulberry grove was to its east,
and the First Silkworm Altar was outside the palace's outer gate, to the southeast.
Six common women were chosen as 'silkworm mothers'.
When the silkworms were about to hatch,
an auspicious day was chosen.
The Empress wore a twelve-pin hara-kiri,
and according to Hàn and Wèi dynasty precedents,
wore a blue robe,
rode in an oil-covered, mica-decorated comfortable carriage,
drawn by six horses.
The female Shàngshū wore mink cicada ornaments,
carried the imperial seal,
accompanied her in the carriage,
carrying baskets and hooks.
Princesses, the Sān Fūrén, Jiǔ Pín, Shìfù, all the Tàifēi, Gōng Tàifūrén, Gōng Fūrén,
as well as Xiànxiāng Jūn, Jùngōng Hóu Tèjìn Fūrén, Wài Shìfù, and Mingfù,
all wore bùyáo (hair ornaments that sway) and blue robes,
each carrying baskets and hooks, followed.
The day before the sericulture and mulberry picking,
silkworms were placed on thin boards in the silkworm palace.
〔五六〕On the day of personally picking mulberry leaves,
〔五七〕the Tàizhù Líng was to offer one grand sacrifice (tàiláo) to the First Silkworm.
The Empress arrived at the western suburb,
ascended the altar,
and the princesses and those below them lined up on the east side of the altar.
The Empress faced east and personally picked three branches of mulberry leaves;
the various imperial concubines and princesses each picked five branches;
the Xiànxiāng Jūn and those below them each picked nine branches.
All the mulberry leaves were given to the silkworm mothers.
They then returned to the silkworm chamber.
After the event,
the Empress returned to her seat,
and the princesses and those below them took their places in sequence.
A banquet was held, and silk was bestowed, with different amounts for each.
In the fourth year of Dàmíng of Sòng Xiàowǔ,
this ritual was again reformed.
In the 22nd year of Jiàn'ān during the reign of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn,
the State of Wèi constructed a Pàngōng in the south of Yèchéng.
In the 5th year of Huángchū during the reign of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
the Imperial Academy was established in Luòyáng.
In the Zhèngshǐ era during the reign of Qí Wáng,
Liú Fù submitted a memorial, saying:
"Since Huángchū,
the Imperial Academy has been grandly established,
but after more than twenty years,
those who have succeeded are truly few.
This is because the selection of Erudites is lax,
students avoid service,
and sons of prominent families
are ashamed to associate with those not of their class,
hence there are no scholars.
〔五八〕Although it has the name,
it lacks the substance;
although its teachings are set up,
they bear no fruit.
It is fitting to select Erudites of high caliber,
who serve as models for others in their conduct,
and whose knowledge of the classics qualifies them as masters,
to instruct the sons of the state.
Following ancient laws,
the descendants of officials of the two-thousand-dàn rank and above,
from the age of fifteen,
should all enter the Imperial Academy.
Clear regulations for promotion and demotion should be established,
and the paths to honor and disgrace should be laid out."
This was not adopted.
In the 8th year of Tàishǐ during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
the relevant authorities memorialized:
"There are over seven thousand students in the Imperial Academy.
Those whose talents are suitable for the fourth rank
should be permitted to remain."
An imperial edict stated:
"Those who have already been tested in the classics may remain;
the rest shall be sent back to their commanderies and kingdoms.
Sons of high officials who are capable of receiving instruction
shall be ordered to enter the academy."
In the 2nd year of Xiánníng,
the Guózǐ School was founded.
This generally refers to the "sons of the state"—the noble youths of the state mentioned in the *Zhōu Lǐ*—
who received instruction from the masters.
In the 5th year of Tàikāng,
the Míngtáng, Pìyōng, and Língtái were repaired and constructed.
In the 1st year of Yǒng'ān during the reign of Sūn Xiū,
an edict stated:
"In ancient times, when a state was founded,
education was prioritized.
This was to guide the world, cultivate nature,
and nurture talent for the times.
Since Jiànxīng,
events have been turbulent,
and officials and common people have tended to pursue immediate goals,
abandoning fundamentals for superficialities,
not following the ancient way.
If what is valued is not pure,
it damages culture and corrupts customs.
Therefore, establish education officials according to the old system,
set up Erudites for the Five Classics,
rigorously select those qualified,
and grant them generous emoluments.
Command those existing officials and the sons of generals and officials who are aspiring and virtuous
〔五九〕to each take up their studies.
Once a year, test and evaluate them,
rank them,
and bestow upon them positions and rewards.
May those who see it delight in its honor,
and those who hear of it envy its renown,
to purify the royal transforming influence
and elevate social customs."
Thereupon, schools were established.
When Emperor Yuán was Prince of Jìn,
in early Jiànwǔ,
General of Agile Cavalry Wáng Dǎo submitted a memorial: "The foundation of governance and transformation
lies in rectifying human relations.
The rectification of human relations
depends on establishing schools.
When schools are established and the five teachings are made clear,
then moral transformation will be harmonious
and pervasive,
the constant norms will be ordered,
and people will have a sense of shame and be upright.
When the order of father and son, elder and younger siblings, husband and wife, and old and young is harmonious,
then the righteousness between ruler and minister will be firm.
This is what the *Yìjīng* refers to as 'rectifying
the family, and the world will be settled.'
Therefore, the sage kings nurtured rectitude from infancy,
and educated them from youth,
making the transformation permeate their flesh and bones,
forming their character through habit,
as if by nature,
daily
progressing towards good and moving away from evil,
without even realizing it.
When conduct is perfected and virtue established,
then they are assigned positions.
Even the legitimate sons of the king
were ranked alongside the sons of the state,
so that they would understand the Way
before becoming noble.
In selecting and employing talent,
all were first based on learning.
Thus, in the *Zhōu Lǐ*,
the xiāng dàfū
'presented the books of the worthy and capable to the king,
and the king bowed and received them.'
This was to honor the Way and value scholars.
People knew that the value of scholars
