was sometimes abolished, sometimes revived.
This led to the process of cultivation lacking its daily
efficacy,
and the people's nature gaining no benefit of plain silk.
The profound threads of thought, ever diligently pursued,
became obscured and none were extracted.
This is why I have long pondered and deeply reflected,
sighing endlessly, whether awake or asleep.
Now, imperial might reverberates afar,
and military chariots are becoming still.
We are about to spread the profound influence throughout the four regions,
and guide these people to utmost virtue.
How can we not widely disseminate rites and music,
making them
brilliant and admirable?
I request the revival of the Guóxué,
to educate the aristocratic youth;
and to issue orders to the various prefectures and commanderies,
to universally repair village schools.
By carving and polishing these precious materials,
true treasures will certainly emerge.
Greatly enlighten the masses
of the ignorant,
and flourish this development of virtue.
If we are not remiss in these matters,
and necessarily proceed through them to achieve understanding,
then people will vie in their pursuits,
and the Way will flourish, and learning will be complete."
Emperor Liè Zōng accepted his words.
In that year,
sons of grandees, high officials, and those with emoluments of two thousand piculs were selected as students,
and one hundred fifty-five additional temple buildings were constructed.
However, the grading and curriculum lacked clear regulations,
and upright gentlemen were ashamed to be among them.
Guózǐ Jìjiǔ Yīn Mào stated: "I have heard that to spread transformation and correct customs,
depends on ritual education.
To assist nature and perfect virtue,
necessarily relies on learning.
The former kings thus molded and refined the world,
serving as a bridge for all things,
guarding against evil and leading to good,
subtly influencing daily life.
Therefore, they could elucidate profound principles,
comprehensively grasp the subtle and obscure,
unify antiquity and modernity,
and govern and transform perfectly.
Moreover, the Master
praised Huí,
for taking love of learning as his foundation.
At seventy, he still yearned and looked up,
leading by good example back to the fundamental principles.
The sounds of the Yǎ and Sòng,
have flowed and been sung for a thousand years.
The profound models of sages and worthies,
are what wise kings
emulate.
Since the restoration of the Great Jìn,
when its foundation was established in Jiāngzuǒ,
schools were highly esteemed and enlightened,
and xiángxù were constructed.
Sons of grandees and high officials,
all entered the Guóxué.
Soon after, encountering many troubles,
the teachings
their studies.
Your Majesty, with sagely virtue and profound unity,
desires to revive past glories,
to follow and spread throughout the land,
to guide and bring out the nature of things,
to revive Confucian academies,
and to gather with the younger generation.
Since
the establishment of schools many years ago,
no achievements worth mentioning have been made.
Those who dread their studies and shirk their duties
and actually remain are few.
Some feign illness of their relatives,
making it hard to distinguish true from false.
Reputation and reality are confused,
and
nothing is worse than this.
I have heard that by old regulations,
students of the Guózǐ (National University) were all from prominent clans and illustrious families,
ranking alongside the imperial heirs.
But now, the middle ranks are a mix of orchids and wormwood,
causing people to feel ashamed of them.
Zǐgòng wanted to abolish the sacrificial lamb of the first day of the month,
but Zhòngní still cherished the ritual.
How much more so when both reputation and reality are lost,
and an entire generation faces a wall?
If the current urgent problems
do not allow for this
ritual,
and it is temporarily suspended,
that is another matter.
If that is not the case,
then the old standards should be followed.
I humbly suggest that all officials, both within and outside the court,
and the sons and nephews of upright officials,
should all enter
schools
and be governed by fixed curricula.
As for the current students,
some are at an unyielding age,
with different dispositions;
they should be allowed to stay or leave
as they feel comfortable.
If my humble suggestions are somewhat appropriate,
I request that they be referred to external deliberation.
Lièzōng issued an imperial edict praising and accepting it,
but it was not put into practice.
Those in the court and among the common people who were devoted to learning
all expressed indignation and sighed.
Lǐ Liáo from Qīnghé again submitted a memorial, saying:
“I have heard that education
is the foundation of governance and transformation,
the beginning of human relations,
whereby all regions are guided and enlightened,
virtue is advanced and benevolence is promoted,
like earth and stone
being molded into vessels.
Even though a hundred kings had different rituals,
and their substance and refinement varied,
this principle
remained unfailing in its application.
Since Zhōnghuá fell into ruin,
Quèlǐ became desolate and damaged,
the benevolence of the former kings ceased,
and the customs of the sages and worthies vanished.
From then until now,
nearly a hundred years have passed.
Creation has its spirit;
hardship ends in prosperity.
The Hé and Jǐ Rivers have shifted,
the Hǎi and Dài Mountains are clear and accessible.
The common people have revived,
and culture is flourishing.
Yet canonical teachings are not widely spread,
and the Yǎ and Sòng odes are silent and forgotten.
The long-decayed customs,
the great evils, remain unchanged.
If we do not propagate and spread this culture,
and illuminate these grand strategies,
how can we assist and glorify the present era,
and greatly expand the flourishing transformation?
Some matters seem distant but are urgent,
and this is precisely what is meant.
My late father, former minister Huí,
pacified and gathered the territories,
and offered sincere allegiance to the present court.
In the tenth year of Tàiyuán,
he sent me to present a memorial.
On my way through Quèlǐ,
I passed by and visited the Kǒng Temple.
The courtyards were dilapidated,
and the structures were crumbling.
The master of ten thousand generations
had suddenly fallen into ruin and neglect.
Looking up and sighing down,
I could not help but shed tears.
Upon reaching the capital,
I presented a memorial requesting the revival of the sage's sacrifices
and the establishment of schools.
On the seventeenth day of the eleventh month of the fourteenth year,
an imperial edict was received,
adopting my humble suggestion,
and an order was sent to Yǎnzhōu and Lǔjùn
to restore it according to the old design.
The former Shàngshū Lìng, Xiè Shí, instructed me to list the necessary items,
and also donated household cloth
to modestly assist in the construction.
The former Zhèn Běi Jiāngjūn, King Qíao Tián, appointed me as Acting Prefect of Běilǔ County,
and granted permission for supplies and provisions.
When these two ministers passed away,
the plans were not completed.
Your Majesty embodies the beauty of Táng Yáo’s cultured thoughts,
and seeks the diligence of Xuānnǐ’s good guidance.
You pity the desolation and ignorance of the neglected,
and lament that the teachings have not yet permeated.
I humbly suggest that the Governor of Yǎnzhōu be again instructed
to complete the old temple,
and to exempt several households from taxes
to provide for its cleaning.
Additionally, grant the Six Classics,
establish schools,
invite seasoned scholars,
and widely gather the younger generation,
so that they may naturally enter the Way
and achieve the merit of carving and polishing.
By applying benevolence and righteousness in campaigns,
and spreading morality to bring distant lands into submission,
what will not be attracted and cherished,
and what will not be softened and followed?
What is done is small,
but what is promoted is immense.
Since I arrived in the capital,
eight years have passed.
My separation from my parents has increasingly accumulated,
and I have been restless day and night.
Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn Hé Dàizhī is now guarding Sān Qí,
and I should return with him.
Lingering in the imperial city,
I feel boundless longing and attachment.
I request that my memorial be referred to external deliberation.”
But again, it was not taken into consideration.
When Sòng Gāozǔ received the mandate,
he ordered the authorities to establish schools,
but he died before it was completed.
In the twentieth year of Yuánjiā of Tàizǔ,
the Guózǐxué (National University) was re-established,
but it was abolished in the twenty-seventh year.
In the third year of Gānlù of Wèi Gāoguì Xiānggōng,
〔七０〕the emperor personally led all officials to perform the ritual of honoring the elderly at the Tàixué (Imperial Academy).
Thereupon, Wáng Xiáng became the Sānlǎo (Three Elders),
and Zhèng Xiǎotóng became the Wǔgēng (Five Overseers).
Its commentary is now lost,
but the Hàn rituals are fully preserved.
In the twelfth month of the sixth year of Tàishǐ of Jìn Wǔdì,
the emperor personally attended the Bìyōng (Circular Moat),
and performed the ritual of xiāngyǐnjiǔ (village drinking ceremony).
An edict stated:
“The rituals have long been neglected,
but now the old ceremonies are again being lectured and practiced.
One hundred bolts of silk are bestowed upon the Tàicháng (Grand Master of Ceremonies),
and oxen and wine upon the chéng (assistants), bóshì (academicians), and students.”
In the third year of Xiánníng,
and the ninth year of Yuánkāng of Huìdì,
the ritual was performed again.
During the Zhèngshǐ reign of Emperor Qí of Wèi,
whenever Emperor Qí lectured on the classics,
he would invariably instruct the Grand Minister of Ceremonies to perform the Rìshì ceremony for the former sages and former teachers at the Pìyōng,
When Emperor Huì of Jìn and Emperor Míng were crown princes,
and when Crown Prince Mǐnhuái finished lecturing on the classics,
they all personally performed the Rìshì ceremony at the Imperial Academy.
The crown prince offered a toast to the former teachers,
and the zhongshùzǐ offered a toast to Yán Yuān.
Emperor Yuán issued an edict saying:
"I remember this matter concerning the crown prince.
After the sacrifice, he would invite the princes and dukes and those below them,
and in Lúo,
they often attended the pure assembly."
Emperors Chéng, Mù, and Xiàowǔ
also all personally performed the Rìshì ceremony.
During the time of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
as the Imperial Academy was far away on the south side of the river,
the relevant authorities deliberated on following the precedent of the first year of Shēngpíng,
and temporarily established a temporary Imperial Academy in the central hall.
At that time, there were no Imperial College students anymore,
so the relevant authorities memorialized:
"One hundred and twenty students are needed.
Sixty Imperial Academy students should be selected from existing personnel,
and sixty Imperial College students should be temporarily chosen from the children and grandchildren of high officials.
They will be dismissed after the event."
The memorial was approved.
After the Rìshì ceremony,
officials of the sixth rank and above were assembled.
In the twenty-second year of Yuánjiā,
when the crown prince performed the Rìshì ceremony,
he adopted the precedents of Jìn,
and the officials had records of it.
After the sacrifice,
Emperor Tàizǔ personally attended the academy banquet,
and the crown prince and those below him all participated.
Military affairs
are preparations for defending the state.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"To lead uninstructed people to war
is to abandon them."
Military matters
are inauspicious and
should not be set up without reason;
they should be practiced during hunts.
Whenever troops are dispatched, it is called "drilling the troops" (zhìbīng);
when they return, it is called "reforming the ranks" (zhènlǚ).
These are all matters of battle formations,
distinguishing the use of drums, bells, clappers, and gongs,
to teach the rhythm of sitting, standing, advancing, retreating, speed, slowness, looseness, and density.
Then they proceed with the spring hunt (sōu tián).
The captured animals are offered in sacrifice to the god of the soil (shè).
In midsummer, they practice setting up camps (báshè),
like the formations of reforming the ranks,
then proceed with the summer hunt (miáo tián),
following the method of the spring hunt.
The captured animals are offered in sacrifice to the yāo (yào).
In mid-autumn, they practice drilling the troops (zhìbīng),
like the formations of reforming the ranks,
then proceed with the autumn hunt (mǐn tián),
following the method of the spring hunt.
The captured animals are offered in sacrifice to the gods of the four directions (fāng).
In midwinter, they practice grand reviews (dàyuè),
then proceed with the winter hunt (shòu tián).
The captured animals are offered in sacrifice to the zhēng.
Sōu refers to
searching for and taking animals that are not pregnant.
Miáo refers to
removing harm for the crops.
Mǐn refers to
but did not personally attend.
It is because many are killed by the autumn air.
Shòu refers to
when all things in winter are fully grown;
whatever is caught is taken,
without selection.
According to Hàn rituals,
on the day of Lìqiū,
after the suburban sacrifice,
military might was first displayed.
Animals were slaughtered in the suburbs,
to be offered to the imperial tombs and ancestral temples,
named Chūliú.
The ritual involved
the imperial carriage riding in a war chariot (róng lù),
with white horses having red manes.
The emperor personally held a crossbow and shot the animals.
The Grand Minister of Justice ordered the captured animals to be sent to the imperial tombs and ancestral temples by carriage.
Thereupon, the imperial carriage returned to the palace,
and envoys were sent to bestow bundles of silk on military officials.
They practiced the military strategies and battle formations of Sūn and Wú,
making it a regular practice.
By the twenty-first year of Jiàn'ān, during the reign of Emperor Xiàn,
the relevant authorities of the state of Wèi memorialized:
"Anciently, military drills were conducted four times a year,
all during agricultural slack seasons.
The Western Hàn dynasty followed the Qín system,
not drilling in three seasons,
only holding a grand review in the tenth month.
Now that military conflict has not ceased,
and soldiers and common people are already accustomed to it,
Instead, on Lìqiū, a propitious day should be chosen for a grand assembly of chariots and cavalry,
called 'drilling the troops' (zhìbīng).
This aligns with the ancient ritual names
and follows the Hàn system."
The memorial was approved.
That winter,
they drilled the troops.
The King of Wèi personally sounded the gongs and drums to command advance and retreat.
In the first year of Yánkāng,
when Emperor Wén of Wèi was the King of Wèi,
Lìqiū fell in the sixth month of that year.
They drilled the troops in the eastern suburbs,
with the dukes and ministers observing the ceremony.
The king rode in a huágài,
personally commanding the rhythms of gongs and drums.
In the tenth month of the first year of Tàihé, during the reign of Emperor Míng,
they drilled the troops in the eastern suburbs.
In the fourth and ninth years of Tàishǐ, the first year of Xiánníng, and the fourth and sixth years of Tàikāng, during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
all personally oversaw the grand review of the armies from Xuānwǔ Guān.
However, they did not personally command advance and retreat.
After Emperor Huì,
this ritual was subsequently abolished.
In the fourth year of Tàixīng, during the reign of Emperor Yuán,
an edict ordered the Left and Right Guards and various camps to practice drills,
performing the "Wild Goose Feather Formation" (Yànyǔ Zhàng) according to the grand review ritual.
During the Xiánhé period of Emperor Chéng,
an edict ordered internal and external armies to perform mock battles in the southern suburban field,
hence that place was consequently named Dòuchǎng.
Thereafter, various regional governors (fāngbó) like Huán and Yǔ
often reviewed and practiced,
but the imperial court had no involvement in such matters.
When Tàizǔ was on the throne,
he would, following precedent, drill the various armies,
and simultaneously employ the rites of Hàn and Wèi.
Thereafter, at appropriate times, he would hold military exercises in Xuānwǔtáng.
In the intercalary second month of Yuánjiā twenty-fifth year,
a grand hunt was held at Xuānwǔchǎng.
The officials in charge, by imperial decree, submitted a memorial detailing the arrangements.
〔七三〕On the appointed day, the imperial hunt took place,
with all officials making preparations.
Temporary imperial palaces and comfortable seats in military tents were set up on the southern slope of Mùfúshān.
Comfortable seats and screened awnings for princes, dukes, and all officials were set up as per usual ceremony.
Four lines of banner gates were arranged: north, south, left, and right.
A "harvest banner" (huòqí) was erected to mark the "harvest carts" (huòchē).
One Diànzhōngláng was in charge of the harvest carts.
Two principal officers collected the game.
Twenty-four clerks were assigned to the harvest carts.
Twelve harvest carts were prepared.
Officials participating in the imperial hunt wore kùzhé (trousers and tunic).
Some wore military caps with straps.
Those who took off their caps would tie up their hair with a ribbon.
Officials of the second rank and above carried swords,
and were equipped with spears and signal banners.
Officials of the third rank and below carried daggers.
All rode horses.
The generals and their subordinate troops would hunt one day in advance,
and were sent to set up the encirclement.
One Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn supervised the right flank of the encirclement (zhēn);
one Hùjūn supervised the left flank of the encirclement;
one Dàsīmǎ remained in the center,
supervising and rectifying all armies,
all of whom were subject to his command.
The Diànzhōngláng led the harvest carts and their subordinate troops,
following behind the Dàsīmǎ.
The Shàngshū Púyè, Dūguān Shàngshū, Wǔbīng Shàngshū, Zuǒ Yòuchéng, Dūguān Zhūcáoláng, Dūlìngshǐ, Dūguān Zhūcáolìngshǐgàn, Lántái Zhìshūshìyùshǐlìngshǐ, and Zhūcáolìngshǐgàn,
supervised and inspected,
to ensure there were no improprieties during the imperial hunt.
On the appointed day,
they assembled at Xuānwǔchǎng,
forming a double encirclement.
Positions for the Liúshǒu Tiánjiē were set up outside the Yúnlóngmén, on the north side of the inner official road,
and on the south side of the outer official road,
with west being the place of honor.
Positions for the Cóngguān were set up inside the Yúnlóngmén, on the north side of the large official steps,
and on the south side of the small official steps,
with west being the place of honor.
Positions for the Xiānzhìguān were set up outside the Xíngzhǐchēmén, on the west side of the inner official road,
and on the east side of the outer official road,
with north being the place of honor.
Positions for the returning Xiānzhìguān were set up outside the Guǎngmòmén, on the east and west sides of the road,
with south being the place of honor.
At dawn on the day of the imperial hunt,
the Zhèngzhí Shìzhōng announced the "rigorous" (yán) call to attention.
After one kè (quarter) of the first watch,
he announced:
"Beat the drum once!"
This was the first "rigorous" call.
After two kè of the first watch,
he announced:
"Beat the drum twice!"
This was the second "rigorous" call.
The Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ announced the opening of the Dōngzhōnghuá Yúnlóngmén,
and the imperial procession (xiǎojià lǔbù) was led out.
All officials not participating in the imperial hunt,
wearing crimson robes,
assembled outside the Guǎngmòmén.
Those who were to return to their departments did so.
The rear division of the Cóngguān, the Liúshǒu Tiánjiē, took their positions;
the front division of the Cóngguān followed the imperial procession;
the Xiānzhìguān went first.
After three kè of the first watch,
he announced:
"Beat the drum thrice!"
This was the third "rigorous" call.
After four kè of the first watch,
he announced:
"Preparations outside are complete!"
The Zhèngcìzhí Shìzhōng, Sànqí Chángshì, Jìshì Huángménshìláng, and Jūnxiào, bearing swords, advanced to stand beside the emperor's inner chamber.
The Zhèngzhí Shìláng carried the imperial seal on his back.
The Tōngshì Lìngshǐ carried the tortoise-shaped seal and the seal of the Zhōngshū.
After five kè of the first watch,
the Emperor emerged.
He wore a black jièzé (headscarf) and a single garment,
and rode in a palanquin.
The Zhèngzhí Shìzhōng, carrying the imperial seal on his back, accompanied him in the palanquin,
but did not carry a sword.
The Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ supervised all within the "yellow banner" (huánghuī).
The Cìzhí Shìzhōng and Cìzhí Huángménshìláng protected the imperial carriage in front.
Another Cìzhí Shìzhōng carried the xìnxǐ and xíngxǐ (two types of seals),
and followed with the Zhèngzhí Huángménshìláng, protecting the imperial carriage from the rear.
No drums or horns were sounded;
there was to be no clamor.
They proceeded out in order,
with standard imperial warnings (jǐngbì) as per usual ceremony.
As the imperial carriage departed,
the outriders cheered,
and those on the steps bowed twice.
The Huáng Tàizǐ entered to stand guard.
As the imperial carriage approached,
the master of ceremonies (wēiyí) announced:
"Lead the front division of the Xiānzhì Cóngguān to their positions!"
They bowed twice.
When the imperial carriage reached the temporary palace, the palanquin turned around.
The Zhèngzhí Shìzhōng knelt and announced:
"Descend from the palanquin!"
The Cìzhí Shìzhōng pronounced the imperial command, saying:
"Permitted."
The Zhèngzhí Shìzhōng prostrated himself and then rose.
The Emperor descended from the palanquin and ascended to the imperial seat,
and the attending officials ascended the hall.
The Zhíwèi (guards) with sheathed halberds, Hǔbēn (imperial guards),
Maótóu Wényī (guards with feathered headdresses and embroidered robes),
and Hèwěi (guards with pheasant tail feathers),
lined up in order on the steps.
The Zhèngzhí Shìzhōng announced:
"Relax the rigor!"
The Xiānzhì Cóngjià Bǎiguān returned to their comfortable seats in the screened awnings.
If the Emperor personally wished to shoot game,
he would change into military attire.
The inner and outer Cóngguān, as well as the Hǔbēn, would all change their attire,
according to the imperial hunt ceremony.
The halberds would be unsheathed,
in preparation for military guard duties.
Officials within the "yellow banner",
would follow into the hunting enclosure (wéiè).
Troops were arrayed,
the encirclement (zhēn) was widely spread,
flags and drums were visible to each other,
and they advanced in silence (xiánméi).
When the encirclement was complete,
the Dūzhēn Lìngshǐ rode swiftly and announced the regulations, saying:
"In spring, birds are pregnant,
so encircle them but do not shoot;
meat of birds and beasts that will not be placed on the sacrificial vessels,
do not shoot;
leather, teeth, bones, horns, fur, and feathers that will not be placed in implements,
do not shoot."
The encirclement was complete.
The Dàsīmǎ beat the drum to tighten the encirclement.
The various armies shouted and blew horns to alarm the game,
until they stopped at Xuānwǔchǎng.
The Dàsīmǎ garrisoned the north banner gate;
the two Zhēnshuài (commanders of the encirclement flanks) garrisoned the left and right banner gates;
the Diànzhōng Zhōngláng led the harvest carts and their subordinate troops to take up position to the right inside the north banner gate.
The Emperor entered from the south banner gate to shoot game.
The Yèzhě (ushers) collected and loaded the game onto the harvest carts,
and returned to display them north of the harvest banner.
Princes, dukes, and all below them, shot game in turn,
each sending their catches beneath the harvest banner,
to be handed over to the principal officers collecting game.
When the event was concluded,
the Dàsīmǎ beat the drum to disband the encirclement and return to their garrisons.
The Diànzhōngláng led his subordinates to collect the game,
filling the harvest carts,
and providing for the kitchens.
They reported to the Tǒngcáozhèng (official in charge of statistics),
who placed honored wine and meat on sacrificial vessels at the crossroads,
to reward and entertain the armies participating in the imperial hunt.
At dusk,
the Zhèngzhí Shìzhōng assessed the situation and announced the "rigorous" call to attention.
The Cóngguān returned to wearing crimson robes,
and their halberds were resheathed.
At the second "rigorous" call, the Xiānzhìguān returned first.
Two kè after the third "rigorous" call,
the Zhèngzhí Shìzhōng announced:
"Preparations outside are complete."
The Emperor wore a black jièzé (headscarf) and a single garment.
The Zhèngcìzhí Shìzhōng, Sànqí Chángshì, Jìshì Huángménshìláng, and Jūnxiào advanced to stand beside the imperial seat.
The Zhèngzhí Shìzhōng knelt and announced:
"Return to the palace!"
The Cìzhí Shìzhōng pronounced the imperial command, saying:
"Permitted."
The Zhèngzhí Shìzhōng prostrated himself and then rose.
The Emperor ascended the palanquin to return,
with his retinue as per usual ceremony.
The Dàsīmǎ beat the drum to disperse the garrisons,
who then returned to their quarters in order.
As the imperial carriage approached,
the master of ceremonies announced:
"Lead the Liúshǒu Tiánjiē and the front division of the Xiānzhì Cóngguān to their positions!"
They bowed twice.
When the imperial carriage reached the palace hall, the palanquin turned around.
The Zhèngzhí Shìzhōng knelt and announced:
"Descend from the palanquin!"
The Cìzhí Shìzhōng pronounced the imperial command, saying:
"Permitted."
The Zhèngzhí Shìzhōng prostrated himself and then rose.
The Emperor descended and entered.
The Zhèngzhí Cìzhí Shìzhōng, Sànqí Chángshì, Jìshì Huángménshìláng, Sànqí Shìláng, and Jūnxiào followed him to the inner chamber,
also as per usual ceremony.
The Zhèngzhí Shìzhōng announced:
"Relax the rigor!"
All inner and outer officials bowed and inquired about his well-being as per usual ceremony,
and then,
when finished,
they dispersed.
Collation Notes
Zhì Volume 5, Lǐ 2
In ancient times, the ritual of the Son of Heaven's inspection tour [xúnshòu],
was recorded in official documents [fāngcè].
When it came to the inspection tours [xúnxìng] of Qín and Hàn,
some were for suppressing inauspicious portents [wàngqì],
others for seeking responses from immortals [shénxiān].
The burdensome and disruptive duties [fánrǎo zhī yì],
were mostly not in accordance with old precedents [jiùdiǎn].
Only the emperors of the Later Hàn [Hòu Hàn]
somewhat adhered to ancient rites.
Wèi Wéndì [Wèi Wéndì], at a time when the Three Kingdoms [Cānfēn] had just been established,
and there were many affairs in various regions [fāngyú],
the imperial carriage [huángyú] moved frequently,
with hardly a peaceful year.
This was due to the exigencies of the time [yìngshí zhī wù],
and also not in accordance with old regulations [jiùzhāng].
Míngdì [Míngdì] made three eastern tours [dōngxún] in total.
Wherever he went, he visited and inquired after the elderly [gāonián],
sympathized with the people's sufferings [jíkǔ],
and sometimes bestowed grain and silk [gǔbó].
This had the style of ancient inspection tours [xúnxìng].
During Qí Wáng's [Qí Wáng] first year of Zhèngshǐ [Zhèngshǐ],

Thus, even the secluded and humble [yōuxiá cèwēi]

The people's sentiments could reach the top [rénqíng shàngtōng],

Even the lonely and widowed [jùguǎ]
all found their proper place.
By this, their legacy [yíliè] was passed down,

I have been on the throne for several years [lěizài],
as if standing on the edge of a deep abyss [línshenquán],
rising early and staying vigilant until night [sùxīng xīxī],
awake and sleepless at dawn [míngfā bùmèi],
sitting until daybreak [zuò ér dàidàn].
I ponder the droughts and floods [shuǐhàn zāishěng] in the four directions [sìfāng],
and for them I am deeply distressed [dántán].
I exert myself and restrain myself [qíngōng yuējǐ],

I often fear that the many officials [zhònglì] act on personal feelings [yòngqíng],
and their sincerity [chéngxīn] is not yet manifest.
With myriad affairs [wànjī] concurrently numerous and complicated [jiānwěi],

Due to the instability of the year [suì zhī bùyì],

On the Dīng Wèi day of the sixth month in the fifth year of Xiánhé (330 CE) of Emperor Chéng of Jìn,
〔一一〕the responsible officials memorialized to read the Autumn Edict.
Jiān Shìzhōng Sànqí Shìláng Xún Yì and Jiān Huángmén Shìláng Sànqí Shìláng Cáo Yǔ rebutted, saying:
"The Shàngshū Sāngōng Cáo memorialized to read the Autumn Edict according to the ritual notes.
Since the recent desolation,
old traditions have not been fully prepared.
We have deliberated;
Guānglù Dàfū Chén Huá deliberated,
saying that Emperor Wǔ, due to the intense heat of summer and autumn,
often omitted reading the edict,
but did not abandon it in spring and winter.
The reason the former kings read edicts according to the seasons
〔一二〕was to comply with the celestial timing by following it.
The correct attire
is a matter of great solemnity and reverence,
but now many items of attire are missing.
Given the recent intense heat,
we believe it is advisable to follow the proposal,
and omit reading it according to established practice."
The imperial rescript approved.
In the third month of the sixth year (331 CE),
the responsible officials memorialized:
"Lìxià falls on the sixteenth day of this month.
According to the rebuttal from Ménxià on the thirtieth day of the sixth month of the fifth year,
the reading of the edict was omitted in summer by Emperor Wǔ's precedent.
Now, with proper attire gradually being prepared,
reading edicts in the four seasons
is a way to reverently narrate the majestic path of celestial harmony.
Therefore, we believe it is appropriate to read the Summer Edict today."
The memorial was approved.
In the sixth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén of Sòng, in the sixth month, on the Xīnyǒu day, the first day of the month,
Fùmǎ Dūwèi Fèng Cháoqǐng Xú Dàoyú submitted a memorial, saying:
"I respectfully note that in the discourse of the Jìn scholar Cáo Hóng,
when the order for the Beginning of Autumn is read,
the emperor should wear a xiāng cè (yellowish-brown turban).
However, it was then changed to plain white,
and this has been followed until today.
I, with my shallow learning and limited insight,
secretly have doubts.
Upon reviewing the 'Yuèlìng' chapter of the Lǐjì,
it states that the king's attire for the four seasons should be 'riding a blue dragon,
carrying a red banner,
wearing white clothes,
and adorned with black jade.'
For the end of summer, it is yellow.
The text stops here,
without mentioning a white cap or particular shoes.
Moreover, the cè (turban) is not an ancient garment;
it originated in later generations.
It is attached to the crown
but not part of the clothes.
If the crown should not be changed,
how can the cè be of a different color?
I humbly believe it should be the same color as the crown
and not change its color with the seasons.
Since the 'Earth' order is approaching,
I respectfully submit this for your consideration.
If it can be adopted,
I request that it be sent out for further deliberation."
Tàixué Bóshì Xún Wànqiū deliberated, saying:
"Upon reflection, the cè (turban) is not an ancient garment for crowns or ceremonial hats,
and there is no mention of it in the rites.
According to Cài Yōng's Dúdùan, it says: 'The cè was worn by lowly and humble people who served and did not wear crowns.'
Dǒng Zhòngshū's Zhǐyǔ Shū also says: 'All those performing duties wore red cè.'
This shows it was a garment for those without crowns.
It was adopted in the Yuánshǐ era of Hàn,
and all officials followed suit.
Therefore, Sīmǎ Biāo's Yúfú Zhì states: 'The Shàngshū's cè was called Nàyán.
For welcoming the Qi at the five suburban altars,
each wore a color corresponding to it,
following the ceremonial robes.'
From then on, it has been passed down
until the Jìn Dynasty.
When the great Sòng received the Mandate,
the ceremonial system followed the previous customs.
Since this has become the standard over successive dynasties,
I believe it should remain as it is."
The responsible officials reported:
"We respectfully note Xú Dàoyú's memorial,
stating that since the 'Earth' order is approaching,
the cè should not change.
Although Xún Wànqiū says the cè should remain as it is,
he does not clearly state that there is no text for reading the 'Earth' order.
Now, we record the old matters below.
The Wèi Tái Záfǎng states: 'Previously, only the orders for the four seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—were read.
However, during the time for wearing yellow,
it was uniquely omitted and not read.
We do not understand the reason for this now.'
On the twenty-first day of the twelfth month of the first year of Jǐngchū of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
Sànqí Chángshì and concurrently Tàishǐ Lìng Gāotáng Lóng submitted a report, saying: 'Yellow, among the Five Phases,
is the central Earth.
The king rules for eighteen days in each of the four seasons.
Earth is born from Fire, so at the end of Fire's influence, yellow is worn,
but not in the other three seasons.
The orders follow the four seasons,
not divided by the Five Phases.
Therefore, there is no order for wearing yellow.'
After this, Emperor Tàizǔ often referred to the 'Earth' order.
Whenever the Sāngōng Láng read the seasonal orders,
and the emperor presided from the veranda,
the hundred officials in their positions
were often terrified and lost their usual composure.
In the Sòng Dynasty, only Liú Xié in Emperor Shìzǔ's time and Xiè Wěi in Emperor Tàizōng's time served as Sāngōng Láng,
and they were skilled in this task,
earning the admiration and praise of the emperor and high officials.
Xié's biography can be found in the 'Zōngshì Zhuàn'.
Wěi
was Xiè Zōng's younger brother.
According to old accounts, in the Later Hàn Dynasty, there was a man named Guō Yú,
who had three daughters.
Two daughters were born on the third month's Shàngchén day,
and one on the Shàngsì day.
Within these two days,
all three daughters died.
The common people considered this a great taboo.
Therefore, on this month and this day,
they dared not stay at home,
but all performed prayers and purifications by the eastern flowing water,
cleansing themselves,
which was called Xìcí.
They shared wine and floated cups,
eventually forming the Qúshuǐ custom.
The imperial historians note that the Zhōulǐ states: 'Female shamans were in charge of seasonal purifications and bathing with fragrant herbs,'
which is like the present custom of going to the water on the Shàngsì day of the third month.
Xìyù refers to bathing with fragrant herbs.
The Hán Shī says:
"According to the custom of the state of Zhèng,
on the Shàngsì day of the third month,
they would go to the banks of the Zhēn and Wěi rivers
to invoke souls and restore spirits.
They held orchid grass
to ward off misfortune."
[一四]This custom has a long history,
not originating from the lingering influence of Guō Yú or the present-day crossing of water.
The 'Yuèlìng' states:
In late spring,
the Son of Heaven first embarks on a boat.
Cài Yōng's Zhāngjù says:
"When the yang qi is warm and harmonious,
and sturgeon arrive,
they are taken to be offered in the ancestral temple.
Therefore, by this occasion, one embarks on a boat for xì (purification) in famous rivers.
The Lúnyǔ states:
In late spring, bathe in the Yí River.
From the top down,
this ritual existed in ancient times.
The present custom of
purification by the water's edge on the Shàngsì day of the third month
probably originates from this."
Cài Yōng's words are correct.
Zhāng Héng's Nándū Fù mentions purification by the sunny riverside, which is also this.
Sometimes it was done in autumn;
the Hàn Shū mentions purification at Bàshàng in the eighth month.
Liú Zhēn's Lǔdū Fù says:
"On the fourteenth day of the clear autumn,
the Milky Way points to the corner,
people perform purifications,
and the state's sons enjoy water sports."
This is using the fourteenth day of the seventh month.
Since the Wèi Dynasty, only the third day was used,
not specifically the SÌ day.
At the south of Emperor Míng of Wèi's Tiānyuān Pool,
a winding stone channel for floating cups was set up,
where he feasted his officials.
In the Jìn Dynasty, behind Zhōngshān Mountain in Hǎixī, there was a winding channel for floating cups,
where officials were entertained;
these were all related to this custom.
Officials have followed it to this day.
Emperor Hàn Wén Dì first reformed the three-year mourning system.
On his deathbed, he issued an imperial edict saying:
"All officials and common people in the empire shall mourn for three days,
then all shall remove their mourning attire.
There shall be no prohibitions against taking a wife, giving a daughter in marriage, offering sacrifices, drinking wine, or eating meat.
Those who are required to attend to funeral matters
shall not go barefoot.
The hempen fillets and sashes shall not exceed three cùn.
Those who are to attend the mourning
shall raise their voices in lamentation fifteen times each morning and evening.
They shall wear deep red mourning for fifteen days,
light red for fourteen days,
and fine white for seven days, then remove their mourning attire."
Emperor Wén Dì died on the Jǐhài day,
and was buried on the Yǐsì day,
a total of seven days in between.
From then on,
the empire complied with this order,
and the three-year ritual was no longer observed.
According to Shī Zǐ,
Yǔ, when controlling the floods,
established mourning laws,
saying that when one mourns to the point of emaciation, one must lean on a staff,
and mourning must last three years.
This implies that the floods could not be remedied.
Therefore, those who died in the hills were buried in the hills,
and those who died in the marshes were buried in the marshes.
A paulownia coffin three cùn thick,
and mourning limited to three days.
This shows that the sages, in times of urgent crisis,
would necessarily make expedient regulations.
However, during Emperor Hàn Wén's reign, which achieved peace and prosperity,
with all four seas tranquil,
to abolish rites and promote frugality was
incorrect.
In the fourth year of the Dìjié era of Emperor Xuān Dì,
an edict stated:
"Currently, some common people encounter mourning or misfortune,
but are prevented from burying their dead by official duties, which pains the hearts of filial children.
From now on, all those who have lost grandparents or parents
shall be exempt from official duties,
so that they may collect and inter the deceased,
fulfilling their filial duty."
By the time of Emperor Chéng Dì,
Chancellor Zhái Fāngjìn was known for his filial piety and reverence towards his parents.
When his mother died,
after the burial,
he removed his mourning attire and returned to official duties
thirty-six days later.
He considered himself to be a Hàn Chancellor,
and dared not overstep the national regulations.
Nevertheless, Yuán Shè observed a three-year mourning period for his father,
and gained renown throughout the empire.
The Prince Huì of Héjiān observed a three-year mourning period for his mother,
and an imperial edict praised him,
considering him a model for the imperial clan.
Xuē Xiū observed a three-year mourning period for his mother,
but his elder brother Xuān said:
"Few people can carry this out when they are young."
Thus, the brothers disagreed,
and Xuān was consequently criticized by the world for this.
This shows that the value of mourning rites has always been recognized.
When Emperor Hàn Píng Dì died,
Wáng Mǎng, wishing to deceive the world and demonstrate loyalty and filial piety,
ordered all officials above 600 dàn to observe a three-year mourning period.
When Wáng Mǎng's own mother died,
he only observed the mourning ritual of an Emperor lamenting a feudal lord,
attending one condolence visit and two gatherings only.
However, he ordered his son, Xīndū Hóu Yǔ, to observe a three-year mourning period.
When Empress Yuán died,
Wáng Mǎng himself then observed the three-year ritual.
All these actions were treacherous and deceitful,
and the world detested them.
At the beginning of Emperor Hàn Ān Dì's reign,
many senior officials avoided duties and abandoned their posts.
It was then ordered that, except for mourning one's parents,
one was not permitted to leave office.
After this, officials remained in their posts
and did not observe the three-year mourning attire.
Later, leave of absence for senior officials and below was again permitted.
Some who submitted memorials suggested that Inspectors (cǐshǐ) and officials with salaries of two thousand dàn should also follow this regulation,
and the Emperor agreed.
In the first year of Jiànguāng,
and abolish leave of absence for Inspectors (cǐshǐ) and officials with salaries of two thousand dàn, as well as for parental mourning,
and this was also adopted.
By the second year of Yǒngxīng during Emperor Huán Dì's reign,
Inspectors (cǐshǐ) and officials with salaries of two thousand dàn were again ordered to observe three-year mourning.
In the second year of Yǒngshòu,
eunuchs holding the rank of Zhōngchángshì and below were also ordered to observe three-year mourning.
By the first year of Yánxī,
all these regulations were again abolished.
In the Latter Hàn period,
when various Emperors were unwell,

they all sent messages to the Grand Administrators of Tài Shān, Hóngnóng, Lújiāng, Chángshān, Yǐngchuān, Nányáng, Hédōng, Dōngjùn, and Guǎnglíng to offer prayers and sacrifices to the Five Peaks and Four Rivers,
and dispatched the Minister of Works (Sītú) to visit the suburban altars, ancestral temples, and altars of soil and grain.
Wèi Wǔ Dì, on his deathbed, left a will stating:
"The empire is not yet stable,
and ancient customs cannot yet be followed.
Officials present in the palace
shall raise their voices in lamentation fifteen times.
After the burial, mourning attire shall be removed immediately.
Those commanding troops or stationed in garrisons
shall not leave their posts."
The Emperor died on the Gēngzǐ day of the first month,
and was provisionally interred on the Xīnchǒu day.
He was buried on the Dīngmǎo day of the same month.
Upon completion of the burial, auspicious rituals were performed,
meaning it did not exceed one month.
Zhūgě Liàng received Liú Bèi's dying wishes.
When Liú Bèi died,
the assembled officials observed mourning.
After three full days, they removed their mourning attire,
and for the burial, they reverted to the proper rituals.
The Grand Administrators, Chancellors, Commandants, and Magistrates of various commanderies and states removed their mourning attire after three days.
This shows that the mourning systems of Wèi and Shǔ
were also different from that of Hàn.
Sūn Quán ordered that all officials in charge who encountered a three-year mourning period
must wait for a replacement before leaving,
but many violated this.
In the sixth year of Jiāhé,
he ordered his officials to deliberate on establishing regulations.
Hú Zōng believed that a capital punishment clause should be established.
He also stipulated that if a replacement had not yet arrived,
one could not take leave,
and those who took leave would be punished with a crime.
Gù Yōng and others agreed with Hú Zōng's proposal.
This was adopted.
Later, Méng Rén, a Magistrate in Wú, left his post upon hearing of a death.
Lù Xùn presented his good conduct,
and he was allowed a reduction of one degree from the death penalty.
From then on, such incidents ceased.
When Emperor Xuān of Jìn died,
Wén and Jǐng both followed an expedient system.
When Emperor Wén died,
mourning was observed throughout the country for three days.
Emperor Wǔ also followed the precedents of Hàn and Wèi.
After the burial, mourning was set aside,
but he still wore simple robes and a plain cap,
sat on a lower mat, and reduced his meals.

Grand Chancellor Sīmǎ Fú, Grand Tutor Zhèng Chōng, Grand Guardian Wáng Xiáng, Grand Commandant Hé Céng, Minister of Works concurrently Central Leader of the Imperial Army Sīmǎ Wàng, Minister of Education Xún Yǐ, General of Chariots and Cavalry Jiǎ Chōng, President of the Department of State Affairs Péi Xiù, Vice President of the Department of State Affairs Wǔ Gāi, Grand General Protector Guō Jiàn, Palace Attendant Guō Suí, Director of the Central Secretariat Xún Xù, General of the Central Army Yáng Hù, and others memorialized, saying:
“Your servants have heard that the rites and their standards,
their lavishness or simplicity, adapt to the times.
The Yú, Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu dynasties
did not all inherit each other’s practices,
and there was a reason for this.
The Great Jìn inherits from Hàn and Wèi,
with both reforms and continuations,
aiming only to be sufficient to promote transformation and achieve good governance.
Therefore, it has not yet been possible to fully return to the ultimate simplicity,
〔一七〕or to conform to the rules of high antiquity.
Your Majesty has already humbly followed the Hàn and Wèi precedent of reducing mourning rites,
to meet the needs of the time;
yet you personally practice great filial piety,
with feelings exceeding mere grief,
wearing a plain cap and simple robes,
sitting on a lower mat, and reducing your meals.
Even though Wǔ Dīng practiced this in the Yīn era,
and Zēng and Mǐn practiced it as commoners,
this is insufficient to describe Your Majesty’s conduct.
Currently, the southern barbarians are not yet pacified,
and many government affairs are not yet in order.
The myriad affairs of state are pressing,
constantly taxing Your Majesty’s mind.
How can there be leisure to fully carry out Your Sacred will,
and follow your deepest feelings?
Furthermore, the seasons change,
and the appointed time passes quickly.
The imperial tomb is increasingly distant,
and our longing forever severed.
Your servants believe that Your Majesty should redirect your thoughts and cut off your feelings,
to bring peace to the times and aid in governance.
We have therefore ordered the Imperial Household Department to change Your Majesty’s clothes,
the inner palace to change your seating,
and the Imperial Kitchen to restore your meals.
All other implementations
shall revert to the old system.”
The Emperor issued an edict, saying:
“Every time I contemplate the departed in the underworld,
and cannot end my mourning wearing coarse hemp and sitting on straw and earth,
to preserve this pain,
how can I eat fine rice and wear splendid robes?
This truly stirs and pierces my heart,
and is not a way to console myself.
I originally come from a family of scholars,
who have long transmitted the rites.
How can I suddenly change this feeling for my revered father?
Much has already been complied with.
You may try to consult Confucius’s reply to Zǎi Wǒ’s question;
there is no need for further debate.”
His words reached a point of heartbreaking grief,
“Alas, alas!”
Fú and others memorialized again:
“We humbly read Your Majesty’s clear edict,
and are moved with sorrow.
We then considered why Zhòng Ní suppressed Zǎi Wǒ’s question,
and why the Sage’s thoughts could not cease—
they are indeed very profound and very earnest.
However, at present, weapons have not been sheathed,
and military affairs have not ceased.
The myriad affairs are of utmost importance,
and the world is vast.
Your Majesty, with the dignity of ten thousand chariots,
practices the rites of a commoner,
wears coarse clothes and sleeps on straw,
drinks water and eats simple food.
Profound sorrow fills your heart,
and your emaciated appearance is evident externally.
Yet you personally toil over myriad affairs,
sitting until dawn,
humbly receiving subordinates,
so preoccupied that you have no time to eat.
The strain on Your Majesty’s strength is thus exceedingly great.
Therefore, your servants are anxious and restless,
truly fearing that Your Majesty’s health will be impaired,
which would harm great affairs.
We have therefore ordered the relevant officials to change your seating and restore it to normal,
following the old precedents.
We only hope that Your Majesty will examine and accept our humble sincerity,
to comfort the heart of the Empress Dowager.”
Another edict said:
“I have re-read your memorial and discussion,
and it has only increased my heartbreaking grief,
I cannot control myself,
alas, alas!
The three-year mourning period
is a rite understood since ancient times.
Indeed, the sages established this mourning period to match human feelings,
acting with clear understanding and empathy.
The divine spirit is becoming more distant day by day,
and there is no one to whom I can express my feelings.
Even if I were callous in my feelings,
to eat delicious food and wear beautiful clothes,
I cannot bear it.
It is inappropriate to repeatedly contradict me,
and deeply wound my heart again.
My words are broken off,
alas, alas!”
The Emperor thus maintained this rite for the entire three years.
Later, during the Empress Dowager’s mourning,
he also did the same.
In the eighth month of the second year of Tàishǐ
, an imperial edict stated:
"The first ten days of this month
mark the day Our late emperor departed this world.
It is now a full year.
How
can I ever express the feelings of a son again?
My grief is unbearable and consumes me.
I wish to visit the mausoleum to attend
and fully express my sorrow and indignation.
Let the relevant officials prepare for the journey."
[一八]Grand Tutor Sīmǎ Fú, Minister of Personnel Péi Xiù, Assistant Minister of Personnel Wǔ Gāi, and others memorialized:
"Your Majesty's filial piety is profound and evident,
your grief boundless.
Although the mourning clothes have been removed,
your emaciation and pallor exceed the proper rites.
Simple food and rough clothes
are detrimental to your health.
Although it is now autumn,
the lingering heat remains.
Visiting the mountain mausoleum
will surely cause sorrow and anguish,
a matter that secretly causes all your subjects to tremble with apprehension.
Our collective counsel is that Your Majesty should consider your long-term health
and restrain your sacred feelings
to comfort all the myriad states."
The edict stated:
"I am alone and desolate;
a year has passed in a flash.
My painful longing and sorrow are overwhelming,
and I can never reach him again.
I wish to pay my respects at the mountain mausoleum
to express my grief and indignation.
My physical condition is good,
and it has indeed cooled down.
I shall depart at once,
contrary to your memorial.
Let the relevant officials immediately prepare for the journey."
Another edict stated:
"In the past, my grief lasted only thirty days
before I was abandoned by the coffin
and separated from my mourning clothes.
How can the pain be fully expressed?
Considering that Emperor Hàn Wén did not allow the whole world to express full grief,
and it was also the late emperor's utmost modesty,
I have thus curtailed my own [mourning],
not to comply with you gentlemen.
There is three years of love,
yet the ritual for my person is wide open.
When I see the mountain mausoleum,
how can I have no mourning clothes?
Let me wear the mourning clothes for the journey."
Fú and others memorialized again:
"We have heard that in remote antiquity, there was no set duration for mourning;
it was only in later generations that years and months were gradually fixed.
Emperor Hàn Wén, following the expediency of his time,
established a short period of mourning
which has been passed down since.
Your Majesty, considering the importance of the altars of soil and grain and the imperial ancestral temple,
and for the sake of the myriad regions and countless people,
has already followed the expedient system
and discarded the coarse hemp mourning clothes.
All ministers and officials now wear auspicious clothes.
Now, when visiting the mausoleum
to express grief and longing,
if mourning clothes were added,
and close ministers wore their one-year mourning clothes,
they would again have to follow a new regulation.
This would be inconsistent and inappropriate,
and we dare not obey the edict."
The edict stated:
"I also know that it is not about this hemp cloth.
However, the feelings of a son
desire to have objects of mourning on their person;
this is indeed a natural sentiment.
The ministers should naturally follow the old system.
The principle of one-year mourning clothes
was not the late emperor's intention."
Fú and others memorialized again:
"We have heard that the Sages, in their institutions,
always followed the exigencies of the time.
Thus, the Five Thearchs had different music,
and the Three Kings had different rites.
This is why ancient and modern times differ,
and why simplicity and refinement were used alternately.
Your Majesty, following the expediency of the time,
has already humbled your heart and restrained yourself,
condescending to the expedient system,
and having removed the coarse hemp mourning clothes,
you perform the rite of mourning in your heart.
Now, to resume wearing mourning attire
would have no basis in principle.
If the sovereign wears mourning clothes while the subjects do not,
even with the late emperor's abundant benevolence,
we would not dare to feel at ease.
After careful deliberation and collective counsel,
it is appropriate to adhere to our previous memorial.
Your subjects dare to firmly request this."
The edict stated:
"My concern is that my feelings cannot reach him,
what do clothes matter?
The utmost diligence of you gentlemen,
how can I casually go against it?"
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ,
the Empress Dowager passed away.
The relevant officials memorialized:
"According to precedents from previous dynasties,
in the mourning hut, a white silk canopy and mat are installed,
with a plain bed,
and straw pillows wrapped in cloth towels.
All carts, plank litters, and small calf carts are adorned with silk ornaments."
The edict did not permit this,
ordering only the use of cloth-covered carriages.
The rest of the mourning regulations
were to be strictly according to the rites.
The officials also memorialized:
"The late Empress Dowager is to be interred on the twenty-fifth day of the fourth month.
According to precedent,
one wears mourning clothes for the ‘Yú' ceremony,
and removes them after the ‘Yú' ceremony.
All officials, both inside and outside the court,
should attend the morning and evening lamentations.
After Your Majesty removes your mourning clothes,
each [official] shall return to their respective stations and remove their mourning clothes."
The edict stated:
"Indeed, three years of mourning
is a universal rite under Heaven.
Having received a lifetime of love
without years of repayment,
how can one immediately return to auspiciousness after the burial?
My feelings cannot bear it."
The officials memorialized again:
"The world has its difficulties and ease,
and the Dao has its rises and falls.
The circumstances encountered at different times differ,
and there are indeed reasons for this,
not a disregard for the rites.
Currently, the military is not yet disbanded,
and state affairs are extremely busy.
Decisions are still needed
to promote various achievements.
In antiquity, King Zhōu Kāng, upon ascending the throne in the 'Dayroom,'
still wore his ceremonial cap to preside over court.
Descending to Hàn and Wèi,
the mourning clothes were removed after burial,
and the rite of 'lǐang'àn' (mourning silence)
has been abolished since ancient times.
May Your Majesty set aside the system of Gāozōng
and follow the expediency of the present time.
We firmly request this."
The edict stated:
"Reviewing the memorial
only increases my sorrow and distress.
Indeed, three years of mourning
is for fully expressing emotion and observing rites.
To remove them immediately after burial
is something I cannot bear.
My heart is filled with such grief
that my words fail.
How can this be! How can this be!"
The officials again firmly requested.
The edict stated:
"I cannot be truly filial,
do not worry about my emaciation and pallor.
I indeed know that clothes are a minor matter.
However, now, when I think of him under the earth,
and then I am constantly forced to abandon mourning for auspicious things,
[一九] this only deeply wounds my sincere heart,
it is not showing concern for me.
The ritual codes of each generation, whether simple or ornate, were all different.
Why should my person be limited by recent regulations,
causing this universal mourning to be incomplete?"
The ministers again firmly requested,
and the Emperor, after weeping for a long time, finally consented.
Emperor Wén's Chóngyáng Mausoleum was opened one day in advance,
and court attendants were dispatched to attend the coffin.
Additionally, one general, one commandant, one acting commander, and one internal supervisor were dispatched,
leading generals of the palace and below, as well as the attendants and servants who had served the late emperor, to the mausoleum to guard it overnight.
When Empress Wénmíng and Empress Wǔyuán Yáng passed away,
the officials and common people of the empire expressed grief for three days and then stopped.
In the first year of Tàishǐ,
an edict permitted generals, officials, and those with salaries of two thousand stones and below who experienced a three-year mourning period
to return home for the entire mourning period,
and commoners were exempted from corvée labor.
In the seventh year of Tàikāng,
the Grand Minister of Ceremonies Zhèng Mò's mother passed away.
After the burial,
he was supposed to temporarily resume his duties according to old custom,
but he firmly refused to rise [from mourning].
It was then that a system was first established allowing high ministers to observe the full three-year mourning period.
However, during the Yuánkāng era,
individuals like Chén Zhǔn and Fù Xián
were still compelled by expediency
and could not complete the full rites.
From that time until now,
this has often become an established precedent.
When Emperor Wén of Jìn died,
Yáng Hù said to Fù Xuán:
"The three-year mourning period
extends to the Son of Heaven.
Emperor Wén of Hàn abolished it,
thereby damaging ritual and injuring righteousness.
Now the Emperor possesses the nature of Zēng Shēn and Mǐn Zǐ Qiān,
and truly practices the mourning rites.
If the mourning rites are truly practiced,
why should the mourning attire be removed?
If we were to uphold the laws of the ancient kings because of this,
would that not be excellent?"
Xuán replied:
"Emperor Wén of Hàn, seeing the shallowness and weakness of later generations,
believed they could not uphold the mourning rites for a ruler of the state,
and therefore abolished them.
To revert to ancient practices after several centuries,
I fear it would be difficult to implement."
Hù said:
"What if the Emperor were allowed to observe the full mourning period;
would that still be good?"
Xuán replied:
"If the Emperor does not remove it while his ministers and subordinates do,
this would mean there are only fathers and sons,
but no longer rulers and ministers,
and the Way of the Three Bonds would be deficient."
Xí Zuòchǐ said:
"Fù Xuán knew the harm to teaching caused by a lack of ruler-minister relationship,
but did not know that the simultaneous lack of father-son relationship was more severe;
how could he not be deluded?
Moreover, Hàn abolished the mourning for ruler and ministers,
but did not reduce the mourning attire for father and son;
thus, the common people throughout the realm
all fully expressed their feelings towards their parents.
Regarding the Way of the Three Bonds,
the two periods of mourning were observed in private households,
but the sovereign alone completely abolished them;
how could this be the way to govern the realm with filial piety?
The *Shī Jīng* says, 'Their plans were not far-reaching,'
this refers to Fù Xuán."
In the tenth year of Tàishǐ,
Empress Wǔyuán Yáng died.
Doctor Zhāng Jìng deliberated:
"The Crown Prince should follow Emperor Wén of Hàn's provisional system,
and cut short his grief by removing his mourning attire."
Doctor Chén Kuí deliberated:
"The Crown Prince should be ordered to observe full mourning."
Minister Lú Qīn, Minister Wèi Shū, and Dù Yù memorialized:
"The system of *liàng'àn* (mourning for a ruler)
has its origins in antiquity,
which is why Gāo Zōng had no text regarding mourning attire,
only mentioning that he did not speak.
Emperor Wén of Hàn limited it to thirty-six days,
and the Wèi dynasty made the *Jìyú* sacrifice the endpoint.
The Crown Prince forms one body with the state,
and it is appropriate to remove the mourning attire."
Doctor Duàn Chàng adopted Dù Yù's opinion,
citing rituals and commentaries to support his argument.
After the *Cùkū* ceremony,
the Crown Prince and the Three Fūrén and below all removed their mourning attire following the Emperor.
Since Emperor Wén of Hàn adopted the provisional rite,
there were no longer prohibitions,
and successive dynasties followed this practice.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn died,
Grand Tutor and Director of the Department of State Affairs, Prince Huìjī Dàozi, deliberated:
"After the imperial burial, marriages may proceed,
but music is not allowed,
with a limit of one year."
When Emperor Gāozǔ of Sòng died,
after the burial,
officials and common people, even within the palace,
were all allowed to play music,
only within the main halls was it prohibited.
In the first year of Yǒngchū of Emperor Wǔ of Sòng,
Palace Attendant Wáng Zhǔnzhī deliberated:
"Zhèng Xuán's mourning system of twenty-seven months concluding
is often said by scholars to be in accordance with ritual.
The early Jìn dynasty used Wáng Sù's deliberation,
combining the *Xiáng* and *Tǎn* sacrifices in the same month,
and thus made it a system.
Since the relocation to the south,
only the Jìn court applied it;
however, gentry scholars
still largely followed Zhèng Xuán's deliberation.
It is proper to make the court and the populace uniform."
An imperial edict approved it.
In the first year of Yǒngkāng of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
Crown Prince Mǐnhuái died.
The Emperor, in accordance with ritual, observed three years of mourning for his eldest son,
while the officials observed *qīcuī jī* (one-year mourning).
In the twenty-first year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn,
Emperor Xiàowǔ died,
and Empress Dowager Lǐ decreed the three-year mourning system.
In the third year of Yǒngchū of Emperor Wǔ of Sòng,
Emperor Wǔ died,
and Empress Dowager Xiāo decreed the three-year mourning attire.
In the third month of the first year of Tàian of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
Grandson Shàng died.
The officials concerned memorialized:
"The Emperor should wear *qīcuī jī*."
An imperial edict called for a general discussion.
Cavalry Regular Attendant Xiè Héng believed that for a prince's heir apparent,
whether designated or not designated,
their status differed in honor;
the mourning rites stated
that for a deceased legitimate eldest son who died young (*chángshāng*),
it referred to one not yet designated.
If already designated, then it was not *shāng*.
Director of the Central Secretariat Biàn Cuì said:
"As soon as the Crown Prince is born,
he is already respected,
not waiting for designation.
If Xiè Héng's deliberation is that if already designated, it is not *shāng*,
then a son who has reached adulthood
should wear *zhǎncūi* for three years;
if not designated and died young,
then even if nineteen,
he should wear *dàgōng* for nine months.
The difference between designated and not designated
is slight in terms of promotion or demotion;
the difference between *zhǎncūi* and *dàgōng*
is great in terms of severity.
Yet the current commentary says
that princes do not reduce mourning for a deceased legitimate son (*díshāng*),
emphasizing the objection to having no mourning,
〔二一〕and considers *dàgōng* as the mourning for a legitimate son.
If *dàgōng* is the mourning for a legitimate son,
then even if designated,
there is clearly no reason for three years of mourning.
A male who can serve and protect the state,
and a female who can uphold the feminine virtues,
each at the age when they can achieve these things,
and have achieved them,
therefore are not considered *shāng*;
this does not refer to an infant.
Regarding those who are considered *shāng* later,
even if honored as a father,
nothing is added,
and only *shāng* mourning is observed.
How much more so for the Son of Heaven,
to observe *shāng* mourning with no attire,
and practice the system for adults?
All *shāng* for whom mourning should be heavy,
officials and gentry do not add attire,
but to make the most honorable one alone bear such heavy mourning,
I have never heard of this before."
Doctor Cài Kè agreed with Biàn Cuì.
Secretary of the Imperial Library Zhì Yú deliberated:
"When the Crown Prince is first born,
he is treated with the rites of an adult,
thus the concept of *shāng* is eliminated.
The Grandson also embodies the succession of the ruler and the weighty transmission,
〔二二〕due to his established position, the mourning is complete,
not by age.
The Son of Heaven has no ceremony for *shāng* mourning,
because it is cut short after one year."
Thereupon, all officials from the Censorate upwards wore *qīcuī*.
On the last day of the first month of the first year of Jiànjuán of Emperor Kāng of Jìn,
the first anniversary of Empress Chénggōng Dù's death occurred.
The officials concerned memorialized:
"The Emperor should change his mourning attire after one year."
The Emperor issued an edict saying:
"Ruler and parents
are the most important in the teachings of names and duties.
Provisional systems emerged only in recent times."
Thereupon, he continued to wear plain clothes as before.
This was not the tradition of Hàn or Wèi.
In the ninth year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn,
〔二三〕Empress Dowager Chóngdé Chǔ died.
〔二四〕The Empress was the Emperor's cousin-in-law,
and there was doubt regarding his mourning attire.
Imperial Academy Doctor Xú Zǎo deliberated:
〔二五〕"Serving one's father and serving one's ruler are of equal reverence.
Moreover, the ritual commentaries state,
that if the husband belongs to the Way of the Father,
then the wife is also of the Way of the Mother.
Thus, if the husband belongs to the Way of the Ruler,
the wife is also of the Way of the Empress.
Mourning for the Empress should be based on the principle of providing for the Mother.
Lǔ criticized perverse sacrifices
to illustrate the veneration of the venerable.
Now the Emperor personally observes the sacrifices for Emperors Kāng, Mù, and Āi, as well as Empress Jìng,
showing the same reverence as to Heaven.
How can he show reverence according to the Way of the Ruler,
yet abandon mourning for his original kin?
Therefore, it is appropriate to observe *qīcuī jī*."
Thereupon, the Emperor decreed one year of mourning.
In the fourth year of the Lóng'ān reign of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
Grand Empress Dowager Lǐ passed away.
Xú Guǎng, Director of the Department of Rites in the Ministry of Personnel Affairs, deliberated:
“The Grand Empress Dowager's status and position were perfectly correct,
her person was in accord with the imperial standard.
The rules and regulations should be fully observed,
and the feelings and rites should be fully expressed.
According to the meaning of the Chūnqiū,

If one is posthumously granted the title of Wáng,
how can one not be a Wáng?
Thus, whether one is ennobled during life
or granted a rank after death,
both receive imperial decrees
and are not subject to different rites based on their fortune or misfortune;
since they share the same regalia and culture,
how can their status differ whether alive or dead?
Now, the imperial seal and edict are complete,
which are rites for an adult;
the various rulers expressing their condolences
are not regulations for one who died young.
If the funeral employs adult rites,
but relatives wear mourning for one who died young,
junior scholars will be confused
and unable to discern it.
I dare to request a detailed and balanced decision as stated.”
Shēn Yáng Xī, Assistant of the Left, participated in the deliberation:
“Upon reviewing Lù Chéng’s deliberation,
since there is no clear prior precedent,
it should not be adopted.
According to the Rites,
a son does not mourn for his father as one who died young,
nor does a subject mourn for his ruler as one who died young.
The ruler and father are of utmost尊,
and the subject and son bear great grace,
thus their status cannot be lowered due to youth.
It also states,
‘If the status is the same, one wears the mourning attire for a close relative.’
Extending this principle,
collateral relatives should naturally wear mourning for one who died young,
and those for whom one does not mourn as such are only subjects and sons.”
The edict approved this.
In the sixth month of the first year of Xiàojiàn,
the Prince of Xiāngdōng submitted a report stating,
“The State Grand Consort passed away on the twenty-eighth day of the intercalary sixth month thirty years ago.
It is unclear whether the anniversary of her death should be in the sixth month
or the seventh month?
I request ritual officials to deliberate and decide.”
Qiū Màizhī, a Doctor, deliberated:
“According to the deliberation of Wú Shāng,
for those who die in an intercalary month,
the anniversary of death should be taken as the original regular month.
Although there are different views on the regular and intercalary months,
Wú Shāng’s deliberation is reasonable.
It is appropriate to observe the anniversary in the current sixth month.”
Jiànpíng Wáng Hóng, Grand Palace Grandee of the Left, said:
“Màizhī’s deliberation cannot be adopted.
According to the Jìn dynasty and subsequent imperial eras,
for those who die in an intercalary month,
the anniversary of mourning is observed in the month following the intercalary month.
It is appropriate to observe the anniversary in the coming seventh month.”
Then, in the second month of the first year of Dàmíng,
the relevant authorities again reported:
“Tàicháng Póyáng Āi Wáng passed away on the eighteenth day of the intercalary third month last year.
In which month this year should the mourning period conclude?”
This was referred to ritual officials for deliberation.
Fù Xiū, a Doctor, deliberated:
“Upon reviewing the three Rites,
when mourning encounters an intercalary month,
if it is counted by months, the intercalary month is counted;
if it is counted by years, the intercalary month is ignored,
because the intercalary month falls within the year of mourning.
Póyáng Āi Wáng passed away in the intercalary third month last year.
According to the sequence of months and seasons,
this definitively falls within the fourth month,
so the mourning should conclude at the end of the fourth month this year.
Emperors Yuán and Míng of Jìn
both died in the intercalary second month,
and their mourning concluded in the month after the intercalary month.
This has become a standard precedent from previous generations,
and this case is similar.”
Yǔ Wèizhī, Assistant of the Grand Historian, deliberated:
“In the Rites,
one commemorates a deceased parent in the first month,
hence the sentiment of observing the anniversary.
As the four seasons have changed,
human emotions also wane,
hence there are two degrees of mourning in the anniversaries.
This implies that both the mourning anniversary and conclusion are determined by the same month,
but for those who die in an intercalary month,
the next year will certainly not have that month.
One cannot fail to observe the anniversary because the month is absent,
therefore, it is imperative to use the month to which the intercalary month is attached.
The intercalary month is attached to the regular month,
as clearly argued by Gōngyáng.
Hence, Bān Gù referred to the intercalary ninth month as the ‘later ninth month.’
Since the month name is not different,
the celestial time is also not distinct.
If one uses the month after the intercalary month,
then spring and summer would be permanently altered,
and the seasons would also be misaligned.
Suppose someone died in an intercalary twelfth month;
if the mourning anniversary were observed in the month after the intercalary month,
then the anniversary would fall in the first month of the year after next.
Mourning extending over three years would
lose the meaning of a full cycle;
〔三五〕dying in winter and commemorating in spring
also deviates from the original purpose of expressing grief.
For example, if someone died on the thirtieth day of the end of this year,
and the end of next year has a short month,
if one were to consider that the relative was still alive on the twenty-ninth day of last year,
then the anniversary should be observed on the New Year’s Day of the year after next.
This is certainly not the case.
Thus, the case of dying in an intercalary month is clear.”
The various officials agreed with Yǔ Wèizhī’s deliberation,
that mourning should conclude at the end of the third month.
In the seventh month of the fifth year of Dàmíng,
the relevant authorities reported:
“The former founding Marquis of Yǒngyáng Commandery, Liú Shúzǐ, died prematurely
at the age of four.
There are doubts regarding the mourning regulations for collateral relatives.”
Yú Hé, a Doctor of the Imperial Academy, Zhōu Jǐngyuǎn, Chief Clerk of the Army, Zhū Yīngzhī, Sīmǎ, and former Assistant of the Grand Historian, Yǔ Wèizhī, and others deliberated,
all stating
“It is appropriate to adopt the mourning attire for an adult.
Dōngpíng Chōng Wáng’s mourning as one who died young
was solely due to his posthumous grant,
which differs from having already received a fief.”
Sīmǎ Xīngzhī, a Doctor, deliberated:
“It should be the same as Dōngpíng’s mourning for one who died young.”
Xún Wànqiū, Assistant of the Left, and others participated in the deliberation:
“One who rules a state facing south,
succeeds to the family line,
even if wearing the hairpin of childhood,
is not lacking in adult virtue.
The ruler and father’s status is proper,
and subjects and sons are not permitted to mourn them as one who died young.
〔三六〕Therefore it is said, ‘A subject does not mourn his ruler as one who died young,
nor does a son mourn his father as one who died young.’
Extending this,
we know that collateral relatives should still follow the regulations for one who died young.
The case of Dōngpíng Chōng Wáng has already been deliberated.
If one rises to the ranks of officialdom,
then they are considered fully adult,
which is why Póyáng Āi Wáng was posthumously granted the title of Grand Historian,
and his relatives did not lower their mourning.
I believe that from the status of dying young upwards,
if one holds an enfeoffed noble rank,
it is appropriate to treat them as an adult.
For those who die young without a prescribed mourning period,
their attainment of official position serves as the determinant.
Now, the subjects of Yǒngyáng State
should naturally wear full mourning,
but as for collateral relatives,
they should follow the rites for one who died young.”
The edict stated,
“Jǐngyuǎn’s deliberation is reasonable.”
Later, in the seventh month of the second year of Yuánhuī of the Deposed Emperor,
the relevant authorities reported:
“The seventh imperial brother is mourning for his foster mother, Zhèng Xiūróng.
The mourning regulations are unclear,
so it is referred to ritual officials for a decision.”
Zhōu Shānwén, a Doctor of the Imperial Academy, deliberated:
“According to the Rites, for a concubine who shows kindness like a mother,
the mourning period is five months of minor mourning.
Zhèng Xuán said: ‘If one is raised by such a person but not formally designated as mother and son,
〔三七〕one also wears the mourning attire for a concubine who shows kindness like a mother.’
I believe that the seventh imperial brother should follow the five-month minor mourning regulations.”
The participating officials all agreed.
During the Hàn and Wèi dynasties, the deposed emperors observed a three-year mourning period for their parents,
and in the Wèi era, some also mourned for their former rulers for three years.
By the fourth year of Tàishǐ of Jìn,
Shàngshū Hé Zhēn reported: 〔三八〕
“Former officials of the Guiding Principles (gāngjì) appointed through recommendations,
regardless of whether they have changed their allegiance,
all return to wear the three-month mourning of Qīcuī for their former rulers.”
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued approving his report,
stating that regardless of the status of their new allegiance,
all should uniformly follow the ancient rites.
Wèi Wǔ (曹操) died in the first month.
Wèi Wén (曹丕) in the seventh month of that year established musical performances and all kinds of acrobatics.
This shows that Wèi (曹魏) did not cease entertainment due to mourning.
Since Jìn Wǔdì (司馬炎)'s time,
when the state had a major funeral that had not yet concluded,
the New Year's assembly also ceased entertainment.
In the first year of Tàiaān (太安),
the Crown Prince's funeral had not yet concluded,
and the New Year's assembly also ceased entertainment.
In the Yǒnghé (永和) reign of Mùdì (司馬聃),
because the imperial tombs in the Central Plains had not been restored,
for several consecutive years during the assemblies,
entertainment was always ceased.
At this time, the Empress Dowager (褚蒜子) was regent,
and her father Chǔ Póu (褚裒) passed away,
so the New Year's assembly again ceased entertainment.
In the sixth year of Tàiyuán (太元) of Jìn Xiàowǔ (司馬曜),
because of the funeral of Empress Wáng Shì (王法慧),
entertainment was also ceased.
Sòng (劉宋) also ceased entertainment during major funerals.
At the end of Jiàn'ān (建安) of Hàn Xiàndì (劉協),
Wèi Wǔdì (曹操) issued a will stating:
"Those buried in ancient times
were always in barren land.
I plan to establish a longevity tomb (壽陵) on the western ridge.
Using the high ground as the base,
there should be no mound and no trees.
The 'Rites of Zhōu' (周禮) state that
the tomb master is in charge of the land for public graves.
All feudal lords are buried to the left and right in front,
while ministers and high officials are buried behind.
The Hàn (漢) system also called this 'accompanying mausoleum.'
Those dukes, ministers, high officials, and meritorious generals
should be allowed to accompany the longevity tomb.
The burial ground should be made extensive
to accommodate them sufficiently."
Wèi Wǔ (曹操), for the funeral arrangements, prepared four chests of clothes,
labeled them,
and specified clothes for spring, autumn, winter, and summer, to be used for interment according to the season.
and placed near the south side of the courtyard,
Gold earrings, pearls, jade, copper, and iron objects
were not allowed to be interred.
Wén Dì (曹丕) respected and followed this,
without any additions.
When he received the abdication,
he had a gold seal carved
and added an honorific title.
He did not dare to open the tomb passage;
instead, he made a stone chamber
to store the seal at the entrance of the tomb passage,
to show that there were no gold, silver, or other valuables inside the tomb.
The Hàn (漢) rites included many funerary objects;
from then on, they were all reduced.
In the third year of Huángchū (黃初) of Wén Dì (曹丕),
he again made his own will:
"According to the Rites,
when a ruler ascends the throne,
a coffin-plank is made
to remember death while alive.
The longevity tomb should use the mountain as its form,
without a mound or trees,
without establishing a sleeping hall,
constructing a garden city,
or connecting a spirit path.
Indeed, burial (葬)
means to hide (藏).
It is desired that people cannot see it.
The Rites do not permit tomb sacrifices,
desiring that the living and the dead are not defiled.
Empresses and noble consorts below,
who do not follow the king to his state,
when they eventually die,
should all be buried west of the ravine,
and their location has already been marked previously."
This edict was stored in the ancestral temple,
and copies were in the three offices of Shàngshū (尚書) and Mìshū (祕書).
