Míng Dì (曹叡) also followed it.
Although Míng Dì (曹叡)'s nature was extravagant,
he did not immediately begin constructing his mausoleum.
Jìn Xuāndì (司馬懿) personally built an earthen tomb for himself on Shǒuyáng Shān (首陽山),
without a mound or trees,
and wrote a will for his last instructions.
He was interred in seasonal clothes,
and no funerary objects were placed.
Wén (司馬昭) and Jǐng (司馬師) (Dì) all diligently obeyed the established command,
without adding anything.
When Jǐng Dì (司馬師) died,
the funeral regulations
also followed the precedent of Xuāndì (司馬懿).
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ (泰始) of Wǔdì (司馬炎),
Empress Wáng Shì (王元姬), the Wenming (文明) Empress, passed away.
When she was to be interred with her husband, the Chóngyáng Líng (崇陽陵) was opened.
Tàiwèi (太尉) Sīmǎ Wàng (司馬望) was ordered to offer sacrifices,
presenting the emperor's honey seal and cord at the spirit seat in the side chamber.
The gold seal of the Wèi (曹魏) clan – this was already frugal.
In the second year of Tàishǐ (泰始),
an edict stated:
"Formerly, when Shùn (舜) was buried at Cāngwú (蒼梧),
farmers did not change their fields;
when Yǔ (禹) was buried at Kuàijī (會稽),
markets did not change their shops.
Considering the simple and frugal intent of our ancestors,
and desiring to move residents within ten li of the imperial tombs,
all such plans are to be stopped."
In the eastern Jìn (晉) dynasty, Yuán (司馬睿) and Míng (司馬紹) (Dì) advocated frugality,
and furthermore, as everything was just beginning,
the arrangements for imperial tombs and funerals
were already sufficiently simplified.
In the seventh year of Xiánkāng (咸康) of Chéng Dì (司馬衍),
Empress Dù (杜陵) passed away.
An edict ordered external officials to visit the mourning hall once every five days,
and internal officials once in the morning only.
This practice was to cease after the funeral and Yu (虞) sacrifices.
The officials reported:
"For the imperial tomb of the late Empress, a funeral gate and cypress path (凶門栢歷) are to be constructed,
with the gate named Xiǎnyáng Duānmén (顯陽端門)."
The edict stated:
"The gate may be placed as proposed,
involve great trouble and expense,
so they are to be stopped."
According to Cài Mó (蔡謨)'s explanation,
two earthenware vessels containing offerings for the deceased
were tied to a wooden stake,
wrapped in a reed mat,
called zhòng (重).
The present-day funeral gate (凶門)
is its remnant.
after the Yu (虞) sacrifice, the spirit tablet (主) is made.
Since the burial has not yet taken place,
there is no spirit tablet yet,
so the zhòng (重) serves this purpose.
The Rites refer to this as the 'path of the spirit tablet' (主道),
which is its meaning.
Fàn Jiān (范堅) also said:
"The funeral gate is not ancient.
Anciently there was the suspended zhòng (重),
similar in form to the funeral gate.
Later generations placed it outside the gate to mark the mourning,
and this custom then became widespread.
The thin curtain (薄帳)
is akin to the ancient mourning curtain."
At this time, another edict stated:
"Beneath the heavy earth,
how can useless adornments be exalted?
The tomb should only be kept clean and swept."
The officials again proposed selecting sixty young men from families of dukes, ministers, and below the sixth rank to serve as pallbearers (挽郎), following old custom.
The edict again stopped this.
In the ninth month of the fourth year of Tàiyuán (太元) of Xiàowǔdì (司馬曜),
Empress Wáng Shì (王法慧) passed away.
An edict stated:
"Funeral matters should only follow frugality and speed."
Another edict said:
"No mountain tomb envoys are to be sent from near or far."
The officials proposed selecting twenty-four pallbearers.
The edict stopped this.
In the seventeenth year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) of Sòng Wéndì (劉義隆),
Empress Yuán (袁齊媖) passed away,
and an edict also stopped the selection of pallbearers.
The Hàn (漢) rites involved ascending the mausoleum after the five offerings were completed,
making it a yearly custom.
However, Wèi (曹魏) had no fixed rites.
Qí Wáng (曹芳) reigned for nine years,
and only visited Gāopíng Líng (高平陵) once,
after which Cáo Shuǎng (曹爽) was executed.
Thereafter, this practice was abolished,
and remained so throughout the Wèi (曹魏) dynasty.
Jìn Xuāndì's (晉宣帝) dying edict stated:
"My sons, nephews, and all officials
are not permitted to visit my tomb."
Thereupon, Jǐngdì (景帝) and Wéndì (文帝) followed this command.
When Wǔdì (武帝) ascended, he still visited Chóngyáng Líng (崇陽陵) twice,
and Jùnpíng Líng (峻平陵) once.
However, he then dared not visit Gāoyuán Líng (高原陵).
When Huìdì (惠帝) ascended, this practice was again stopped.
Upon the early Jìangzuǒ (江左) period,
after Yuándì's (元帝) death,
various dukes first began to have matters of visiting tombs and taking leave of tombs.
This was likely due to their bond with peers and colleagues,
acting on emotion,
not an old custom from Luòjīng (洛京).
During Chéngdì's (成帝) time,
the Empress also annually paid respects at the tomb.
Debaters considered this contrary to ritual,
so it was stopped,
and established as a permanent regulation.
When Mùdì (穆帝) ascended,
Chǔ Tàihòu (褚太后) presided over the court,
and again paid respects at the tomb,
because the Emperor was young.
When Xiàowǔdì (孝武帝) died,
Pìaoqí Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍) Sīmǎ Dàozǐ (司馬道子) ordered:
"Although we now temporarily set aside mourning clothes,
for the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month and other festivals,
one should express feelings at the tomb,
with one year as the limit."
Thus, upon arriving at the tomb, they changed into plain clothes,
which was cumbersome and unregulated,
and not in line with ritual intentions.
When Āndì (安帝) ascended, in Yuánxīng (元興) first year,
Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè (尚書左僕射) Huán Qiān (桓謙) memorialized:
"Officials visiting tombs
began during the restoration,
not an old Jìn (晉) custom.
Accumulated habits became common practice,
thus becoming a recent law.
Reviewing Emperor Wǔ's (武皇帝) edict,
it did not permit the ruler or various kings to visit tombs,
let alone officials.
We should follow this."
This was then implemented.
In the early Yìxī (義熙) era,
it reverted to the old Jìangzuǒ (江左) custom.
Sòng Míngdì (宋明帝) again prohibited officials from initial tomb visits,
but the leave-taking remained as before.
Since the Yuánjiā (元嘉) era,
every year in the first month,
the imperial carriage would certainly visit Chūníng Líng (初寧陵),
restoring the Hàn (漢) ritual.
Shìzǔ (世祖) and Tàizōng (太宗) also annually paid respects at Chūníng (初寧) and Chángníng Líng (長寧陵).
After the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
the world indulged in extravagant funerals,
often making stone chambers, stone beasts, steles, inscriptions, and other such items.
In Jiàn'ān (建安) tenth year,
Wèi Wǔdì (魏武帝), seeing the world was impoverished and damaged,
issued an order prohibiting elaborate burials,
and also forbade erecting steles.
In Gāoguìxīang Gōng (高貴鄉公) of Wèi's (魏) Gānlù (甘露) second year,
Dàjiāngjūn Cānjūn (大將軍參軍) from Tàiyuán (太原), Wáng Lún (王倫), died.
Lún's (倫) elder brother, Jùn (俊), composed the "Biǎodé Lùn (表德論)"
to narrate Lún's (倫) posthumous virtues,
saying
"out of reverence for royal regulations,
I could not create an inscription,
so I compiled and recorded his deeds,
and had them carved on the back of his tomb."
This shows that the prohibition on steles was still strict.
After this, it again relaxed.
In Jìn Wǔdì's (晉武帝) Xiánníng (咸寧) fourth year,
an edict again stated:
"These stone beasts and steles,
being private commendations,
foster falsehood,
waste wealth, and harm people;
nothing is worse than this.
They are all to be prohibited and stopped.
Those who violate this, even if covered by an amnesty,
shall have their works destroyed."
When Yuándì (元帝) ascended, in Tàixīng (太興) first year,
the responsible officials memorialized:
"The former Pìaoqí Fǔ Zhǔbù (驃騎府主簿), Gù Ēn (故恩), burying his old lord Gù Róng (顧榮),
requests to erect a stele."
An edict specially permitted it.
From then on,
the prohibition gradually weakened again.
High officials and chief administrators,
everyone privately erected them.
In the Yìxī (義熙) era,
Shàngshū Cíbù Lángzhōng (尚書祠部郎中) Péi Sōngzhī (裴松之) again proposed a prohibition,
which lasted until now.
In Shùndì's (順帝) Shēngmíng (昇明) third year, fourth month, on the day Rénchén (壬辰),
the Emperor ascended the imperial carriage,
sent an envoy to offer the imperial seal and ribbon, abdicating the throne to the King of Qí (齊王),
but was suspended and unhappy.
In Sòng Míngdì's (宋明帝) Tàishǐ (泰始) second year, ninth month,
the responsible officials memorialized:
"The birth mother of the Crown Prince, Chén Guìfēi (陳貴妃), has a ritual rank equivalent to the Crown Prince's palace;
it is unclear whether palace officials and court officials should show respect, and to what extent?
Also, when concubines meet inside,
what etiquette should be followed?"
Bóshì (博士) Wáng Qìngxù (王慶緒) debated:
"All officials, both inside and outside, should respectfully greet Guìfēi (貴妃),
and this should be the same as for the Crown Prince.
As for the Eastern Palace officials and subordinates,
they naturally fall under the duties of subjects."
Tàicháng Chéng (太常丞) Yú Yuàn (虞愿) and others agreed with Qìngxù (慶緒).
Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) Jiàn'ān Wáng (建安王) Xiūrén (休仁) argued:
"The Rites state,
'A concubine cannot embody the ruler's status,
and her rank is ordered by her child.'
'A mother becomes noble through her son'
is clearly written in the classics.
Respect from inside and outside to Guìfēi (貴妃) is indeed as Qìngxù (慶緒) suggested.
However,
the Emperor's concubines
are not allowed to communicate with the outside.
Although it is right to show reverence,
there should be no memorials or reports."
After deliberation, Xiūrén's (休仁) argument was considered appropriate.
The edict approved it.
In Tàiyù (泰豫) first year,
the later deposed Emperor ascended the throne and
honored his birth mother Chén Guìfēi (陳貴妃) as Huáng Tàifēi (皇太妃).
The responsible officials memorialized:
"Huáng Tàifēi's (皇太妃) position is second only to the highest尊極;
it is unclear whether royal relatives should express grief in the same manner as for the Huáng Tàihòu (皇太后)?
Or is there a difference in grade?
Also, for her immediate relatives within the year-long mourning period,
should they still wear mourning clothes or not?"
Qiáncáo Láng (前曹郎) Wáng Xièzhī (王燮之) argued:
"According to the 'Sāngfú Zhuàn (喪服傳)',
'A concubine mourns for her lord's relatives,
and may be equated with the mistress.'
If so,
Huáng Tàifēi's (皇太妃) mourning for the clan is no different from the Empress Dowager's.
However, since the Empress Dowager, due to her supreme status, wears no mourning,
the Tàifēi's (太妃) ritual should not be different.
Therefore, no mourning clothes are worn at all.
Considering expressions of grief based on true feelings,
the ritual is no different.
Also, the Rites state,
'A feudal lord's mourning is for one year.'
Although Huáng Tàifēi (皇太妃) does not hold the highest position,
she cannot be considered lesser than a feudal lord.
Therefore, her immediate relatives within the year-long mourning period
should not wear any mourning clothes.
If there is genuine sorrow, expressing grief is appropriate.
The two rituals for close and distant relatives
should be aligned with those for the Empress Dowager."
Jiān Tàicháng Chéng (兼太常丞) Sīmǎ Xiè (司馬燮) argued:
"The Rites state,
'A concubine mourns for her lord's concubine's sons and for her mistress's relatives.'
This refers to officials and scholars.
Although the term 'concubine' is general,
there are noble and lowly ranks.
The Sān Fūrén (三夫人) and Jiǔ Pín (九嬪) are ranked as dukes and ministers.
Even high officials have noble concubines,
let alone the Son of Heaven.
A feudal lord's concubine does not mourn for the son of another concubine.
If she does not mourn for the son of another concubine,
how could she mourn for the lord's or mistress's other relatives?
Moreover, the Empress Dowager and Empress's noble status is second only to the highest;
their rituals surpass those of other queens.
Their glorious ceremonies
exceed those of the Crown Prince.
Even they do not wear one-year mourning,
so how could the Tàifēi (太妃) be different?
If her immediate relatives have sorrow,
the ritual for expressing grief
should follow that of the Empress Dowager."
After deliberation, Xiè's (燮) argument was considered appropriate.
The Tàifēi (太妃) wore no mourning for royal relatives.
Therefore, it was deemed appropriate that, moved by emotion, the various kings and princesses, for their supreme kin who would observe year-long mourning,
and the Tàifēi (太妃), royal consorts, Sān Fūrén (三夫人), and Jiǔ Pín (九嬪) should each express grief.
In the eighth month, on the day Wùzǐ, of the third year of Xiàojiàn of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng,
the responsible officials reported:
"The State of Yúndù has requested that Wáng, the birth mother of the Guózǐ Tán Hézhī,
be granted the title of Tàifūrén.
Upon investigation, there is no precedent for a guózǐ's mother being granted the title of Tàifūrén,
nor is there any law stipulating it.
The matter should be referred to the ritual officials for deliberation and decision."
Sūn Huòzhī, a doctor of the Imperial Academy, deliberated, saying:
"The Chūnqiū says,
'The mother is honored through her son.'
Although Wáng was a concubine,
she is the one whom Hézhī bore.
According to the precedent of the five ranks,
the Bó of Zhèng and the Nán of Xǔ both held the title of Fūrén.
Regarding the status of a guózǐ,
Wáng should be treated the same as one born in a state."
Yú Wèizhī, a Tàicháng丞, deliberated, saying:
"'The mother is honored through her son,'
though a clear principle from the Chūnqiū,
ancient and modern institutions differ,
and changes and reforms are not the same.
Since recent generations,
only the mothers of various princes
have received honor through their sons.
As she is a concubine of a king,
it is appropriate for her to be respected in a vassal state.
If one's achievements are great and merits weighty,
and one is ranked among gōng or hóu,
there is also the ritual of being appointed Tàifūrén.
All these are special favors bestowed by the court,
not something requested by a state.
There is no prior precedent for the concubine mother of a zǐ or nán."
Zhū Yīngzhī, a Cíbù Lángzhōng, deliberated, believing that:
"A son cannot bestow a noble title upon his parents,
yet the Chūnqiū states 'the mother is honored through her son.'
This refers to the mother of a sovereign who inherits the throne,
who was originally a concubine or attendant of a former gōng,
whose status had a reason and basis.
The case of one newly enfeoffed
cannot be the same.
If there are extraordinary achievements and weighty merits,
and special grace is bestowed,
it may happen sometimes,
but it is not determined by the responsible officials."
Of the submitted deliberations,
Wèizhī's was deemed acceptable.
An edict approved it.
In the sixth month of Dàmíng second year,
the responsible officials reported:
"When the heir apparent of any hóu, bó, zǐ, or nán dies
without issue,
a request is made to promote the next son to be the heir apparent.
Upon investigation, there is no such precedent.
The matter should be referred to the ritual officials for deliberation and decision."
Doctor Sūn Wǔ deliberated, saying:
"According to the case of Xún Xù, the Jìběi Hóu of Jìn, whose eldest son Lián died,
his second son Jí was appointed heir apparent.
This is an established precedent from an earlier generation,
and should serve as a current example."
Doctor Fù Yù deliberated, saying:
"The Lǐjì states,
'Wēizǐ established Yǎn,
thus the Shang rites were followed.'
'Zhòngzǐ set aside his grandson,'
this was criticized in the Jī canon.
Successive generations have followed this,
never deviating from the old ways.
Now, the lord of the enfeoffed territory is alive, and the heir apparent has died.
His successor has not yet been raised,
so this is not a case of setting aside a grandson.
[四三]I believe that if the second son has a son,
he should naturally succeed as the heir-grandson.
If he does not,
there is no need to search far for a distant relative,
to maintain the lineage and continue the body.
The succession has its reasons.
For a father to establish a son while he is alive
is truly in accordance with reason and the canon."
Cáo Láng Zhūgě Yǎzhī deliberated, saying:
"According to the Zuǒzhuàn, it states,
'If the heir apparent dies,
and there is a uterine brother, he shall be established.
[四四]If not, the eldest shall be established.
If their ages are similar, the more virtuous shall be chosen.
If their virtues are similar, divination shall be used.'
This is an ancient institution.
Now, the eldest son died young,
without issue.
To promote and establish the next son as the heir apparent
is taken from Master Zuǒ,
and there is no deviation in principle or righteousness.
Furthermore, the case cited by Sūn Wǔ, where the eldest son of Xún Xù, the Jìběi Hóu of Jìn, died
and the next son was established,
is also an established precedent from recent times.
Following the text and comparing the cases,
I humbly deem it acceptable and appropriate.
I suggest it should be permitted
and established as a permanent regulation."
The deliberations were deemed acceptable.
An edict approved it.
In the eleventh month of Dàmíng twelfth year,
[四五]the responsible officials reported:
"The State of Xīngpíng has requested that Wáng Shì, the mother of the Guózǐ Yuán Mǐnsūn,
be granted the title of Tàifūrén.
Upon investigation, there is no precedent for a guózǐ's mother being granted the title of Tàifūrén.
The matter should be referred to the ritual officials for deliberation and decision."
Sīmǎ Xīngzhī, a doctor of the Imperial Academy, deliberated, saying:
"According to the Rites,
the wives of qīng and dàfū of lesser states
were all appointed by the Son of Heaven.
From this, it can be inferred that
the mothers of zǐ and nán
should not be uniquely different."
Doctor Chéng Yàn deliberated, believing that:
"Although the five ranks differ,
the matter of continuing the family line is the same.
The mothers of gōng and hóu,
whose exalted titles are followed,
the mothers of zǐ and nán, in relation to their kin,
should also have their honorable rank made manifest.
Therefore, the principle of the Chūnqiū states,
'The mother is honored through her son.'
Thus, it is known that the honor derived from the son is equal to that of the state.
Yàn, having participated in the deliberations,
deems Xīngzhī's deliberation acceptable.
Wáng Shì should be granted the title of Xīngpíng Xiàn Kāiguó Zǐ Tàifūrén."
An edict approved it.
In the ninth month of Dàmíng fourth year,
the responsible officials reported:
"In the State of Chénliú, Wáng Cáo Qiánxiù's elder brother Qiánsì died young.
[四六]After Xiù succeeded to the enfeoffment,
he bore a son Xiǎn to succeed Qiánsì.
Now, according to precedent, he should be appointed heir apparent.
It is unclear whether Xiǎn should be the heir apparent
or if the second son Kǎi should be established?"
Wáng Wēnzhī and Jiāng Cháng, doctors of the Imperial Academy, deliberated,
both believing that Xiǎn should be the rightful heir.
Tàicháng Lù Chéng deliberated for the establishment of Kǎi.
Yòuchéng Xú Yuán deliberated, stating:
"The rites honor the senior lineage
because its sacrifices must not be interrupted.
The hereditary succession of feudal lords
is an established principle in the Chūnqiū.
Qiánsì inherited the family and transmitted the title,
serving as the King of the state.
Although he died without a son,
he is still ranked in the ancestral temple.
On the day a successor is established,
he should immediately assume the state's lineage.
At that time, there was no successor,
so Qiánxiù succeeded in turn. [四七]
Since Qiánsì is arrayed in the temple offerings,
he naturally moves with the generational count.
How can the regular offerings be maintained without interruption
by arbitrarily taking another son as heir?
As a descendant,
one should also respectfully offer sacrifices to one's own father.
According to the ritual texts,
a gōngzǐ cannot venerate a feudal lord as his father.
Qiánsì has no reason to descend to the temple and move into the sleeping chamber.
Xiǎn is the original eldest son;
he should return to being Qiánxiù's heir apparent."
An edict was issued in accordance with Yuán's deliberation.
In the seventh month of Yuánjiā thirteenth year of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
the responsible officials reported:
"Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Liú Shìzhī deliberated,
'Whenever I go out,
I am unsure with which officials I should share the road,
and there should be an old regulation.
The law only states that the zhōngchéng has an exclusive path,
to transmit edicts and carry messages.
When an edict summons officials,
those summoned shall proceed.
There is no text stating a distinction for other officials in regulating orders.
As there is no clear and defined rule, [四八]
there are doubts about how to proceed.
I believe that Huáng Tàizǐ is the legitimate heir to the Eastern Palace,
and should not be treated the same as other officials.
The zhōngchéng should share the road with him.
The Císhǐ of Yángzhōu, the Dānyáng Yǐn, and the Jiànkāng Lìng
are all masters of the capital's territory.
They either investigate wrongdoing
or respond to floods and fires.
Their duties require divine speed
and should not be delayed,
so they should also share the road.
Furthermore, looking at the area inside the Six Gates,
it is within the barriers.
Any transgressions by guards are handled by the two guards and the Lǐngjūn.
It is unclear whether the 京尹 and Jiànkāng Lìng's subordinates within the gates and their public duties
are also permitted to share the road with the zhōngchéng or not.
Based on the old ceremonies,
inform and deliberate on who should share the road.'
The court approved what the Tái had submitted.
Regarding the area inside the Six Gates,
since it is not part of the prefectural, commandery, or county boundaries,
it should not follow the rules for outside the gates.
The Shàngshū Lìng and the two Púshè, with whom the zhōngchéng should share the road,
shall also all be treated the same as the zhōngchéng."
In the fifth month of the sixth year of Dàmíng of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
an edict was issued to establish an ice chamber for storing ice.
The relevant officials reported,
“In the last month of winter,
when the ice is thick,
the director of the ice chamber shall lead the mountain guards and porters to retrieve ice from deep mountains, remote valleys, and places of dried-up yin and extreme cold,
and store it in the ice cellar.
It must be done thoroughly and carefully,
without allowing its coldness to leak.
First, sacrifice to Sīhán with a black ox and black millet north of the ice chamber.
〔四九〕In the second month of spring,
on the day of the vernal equinox,
sacrifice to Sīhán with a black lamb and black millet.
Open the ice chamber,
and first offer it to the ancestral temples.
For the summer sacrifices at the two temples, use basins filled with ice,
one basin per chamber,
to ward off warmth, flies, and gnats.
For the three imperial halls and the imperial kitchen’s delicacies,
ice is also supplied in basins.
From the vernal equinox until Lìqiū,
〔五０〕if there is a death among imperial servants or concubines,
an edict grants them secret burial objects.
From Lìxià until Lìqiū,
there is no limit to the quantity provided to assist with funeral matters.
‘Yípán’ are constructed
and lent out with the ice.
〔五一〕The ice chamber is located within the Lèyóu Yuàn,
with one director
and two entrusted clerks.
Regarding the ‘Huánggé’ of the Sāngōng,
there is no explanation in previous histories.
The court historian notes,
“The Lǐjì states,
‘A scholar is the same as the Son of Heaven;
dukes, marquises, and high officials are different.’
Zhèng Xuán’s commentary says,
‘A scholar is lowly,
and being the same as the ruler is not presumptuous.’”
Now, the ‘Zhūmén’ opening wide
is the proper color for the position facing south.
The Sāngōng and the Son of Heaven
have similar ceremonial ranks,
hence their gates are yellow (Huánggé),
to show humility and not dare to assert parity with the Son of Heaven.
This is probably a custom from the Hàn dynasty.
Zhāng Chāo’s letter to Chén Gōng states,
“When one is appointed to the Huánggé, there will be days and months,”
which confirms this.
The court historian notes: Nowadays, when court officials visit the Sāngōng,
or when a Shàngshū丞 (Céng) or Láng visits a Lì, Púyè, or Shàngshū,
they all dismount from their carriage outside the gate,
put on their shoes,
and only after crossing the threshold do they put on their clogs.
During the Hàn era, court officials, upon seeing the Sāngōng,
all bowed.
Céng and Láng, upon seeing the eight ministers (Bāzuò),
all held their tablets and bowed.
These matters are recorded in the Hàng Yí and Hàng Jiù Yí,
indicating that respect was shown.
When Chén Fān was Guānglùxūn,
and Fàn Pāng was Zhǔshì,
Pāng visited Fān according to public etiquette,
entered the gate holding his tablet,
and upon reaching the seat,
Fān did not take Pāng’s tablet.
Pāng threw down his tablet, shook his robes, and left.
Guō Tài reproached Fān, saying:
“In terms of rank,
Pāng ought to show respect;
but considering the general custom,
once inside the gate, such formality should be dispensed with.”
Therefore, the practice of stopping respect at the gate
has a long history.
Collation Note
Volume Six, Rites Three
“The great affairs of the state
lie in sacrifices and warfare.”
From the written records and classics,
this principle has always been highly esteemed,
and among the virtues of the sages,
none is greater than revering one’s ancestors.
Thus, Sīmǎ Qiān wrote the Fēngshàn Shū,
Bān Gù fully compiled the Jiāosì Zhì,
which documented the proper sacrifices of emperors and kings above,
and recorded the hundred deities of various commanderies and states below.
Sīmǎ Biāo also wrote the Jìsì Zhì to continue the account for the end of the Hàn dynasty.
After the restoration,
the old regulations were grandly manifested,
brilliantly and comprehensively.
From that point onward,
there have been further variations.
Therefore, this compilation is again made.
In the eleventh month, on the day Jǐchǒu, of the first year of Yánkāng of Emperor Xiàndì of Hàn,
an edict commanded the Gōngqīng to perform a sacrificial announcement at the Gāomiào.
He dispatched Jiān Yùshǐ Dàfū Zhāng Yīn to respectfully present the imperial seals and ribbons and the edict,
ceding the imperial throne to Wèi.
At this time, Emperor Wén of Wèi had succeeded to the royal throne,
and was on a southern tour in Yǐngyīn.
Officials then erected an altar in the former city of Fányáng in Yǐngyīn.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
he ascended the altar.
Wèi Xiàngguó Huà Xīn knelt to receive the imperial seals and ribbons and presented them to the king.
After receiving them,
he descended the altar to observe the burning sacrifice,
completed the ritual, and returned.
There was no act of ancestral pairing yet.
In the first month of the second year of Huángchū of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
sacrifices were made to Heaven and Earth at the Míngtáng.
At this time, Wèi’s capital was Luòjīng,
and the sites for the gods, altars, Míngtáng, and Língtái
were all based on previous Hàn practices.
In the seventh month of the fourth year,
the emperor was preparing for an eastern tour,
and since a large army was to be dispatched,
he ordered the Tàicháng to offer a single bull in sacrifice at the Southern Suburb,
which became a regular practice thereafter.
When Emperor Wén passed away,
Tàiwèi Zhōng Yáo announced the posthumous title at the Southern Suburb,
all these were affairs related to the suburb.
In the first month, on the day Dīngwèi, of the first year of Tàihé of Emperor Míng,
a suburban sacrifice was made to Emperor Wǔ to match with Heaven,
and an ancestral sacrifice was made to Emperor Wén at the Míngtáng to match with the Supreme Lord.
At this time, the systems of suburban sacrifices and offerings of the two Hàn dynasties were still complete,
so what Wèi added or removed can be known.
In the eighth month of the fourth year,
the emperor went on an eastern tour,
passing Fánchāng.
He ordered Zhí Jīn Wú Zāng Bà to act as Tàiyèi,
and sacrifice a single bull at the altar where the abdication took place.
The Hòu Hàn Jì records that
Emperor Zhāng ordered sacrifices at the enthronement altar in Gāoyì.
Although this was a practice from previous dynasties,
an altar is built to sacrifice to Heaven,
and the altar itself is not a deity.
Now, there is no affair with the Supreme Lord,
yet a sacrifice is offered at an empty altar,
the basis for which is not clear.
In the tenth month, on the day Yǐmǎo, of the first year of Jǐngchū,
the construction of the round mound (Yuánqiū) on Mount Wěisù in the south of Luòyáng began.
An edict stated:
“Indeed, when emperors and kings receive the Mandate,
none fail to respectfully serve Heaven and Earth
to manifest their divine brilliance;
and to honor and sacrifice to their dynastic lineage
to illuminate their merits and virtues.
Thus, when the ancient canons are established,
the regulations for Dì and Jiāo sacrifices and ancestral veneration are complete.
In the early period of the Hàn dynasty,
following the Qin’s destruction of scholarship,
they collected fragmented remnants
to complete the suburban sacrifices.
However, the sites of the deities at Gānquán, Hòutǔ, Yōnggōng, and the five Zhì
were often not historically verifiable,
and due to constant changes in their establishment and abolition,
shifting from one to another,
for over four hundred years,
the Dì sacrifice was abolished.
What was newly established in ancient times
thus had gaps.
The lineage of the Cáo clan
originates from the Yǒuyú clan.
Now, in the sacrifice at the Yuánqiū,
the ancestor Emperor Shùn is matched,
and the Yuánqiū is called the August Imperial Heaven (Huáng Huángdì Tiān).
The sacrifice at the Fāngqiū is called the August Imperial Earth (Huáng Huánghòu Dì),
matched with Shùn’s consort, Lady Yī.
The sacrifice at the Heavenly Suburb (Tiān Jiāo) is called the Spirits of August Heaven (Huáng Tiān zhī Shén),
matched with Grand Ancestor Emperor Wǔ.
The sacrifice at the Earthly Suburb (Dì Jiāo) is called the Deities of August Earth (Huáng Dì zhī Qí),
matched with Empress Wǔxuān.
The ancestral sacrifice to the August Departed Father, High Ancestor Emperor Wén, is performed at the Míngtáng,
matched with the Supreme Lord.”
In the twelfth month, on the day Rénzǐ, at the winter solstice,
the sacrifice to the August Imperial Heaven (Huáng Huángdì Tiān) at the Yuánqiū began,
matched with the founding ancestor, Emperor Shùn of Yǒuyú.
From Zhèngshǐ onward,
until the end of the Wèi dynasty,
suburban sacrifices were no longer performed.
Sūn Quán first assumed the imperial title in Wǔchāng,
offered sacrifices at the southern suburban altar, and announced to Heaven.
The text read:
"Your servant, the Emperor Sūn Quán,
dares to use a dark bull,
to solemnly announce to the August Sovereign and Supreme Emperor.
The Hàn enjoyed the nation for twenty-four generations,
lasting four hundred and thirty-four years.
Their reign's vital energy and destiny have ended,
their blessings and fortune are exhausted.
All under Heaven is in disarray and broken,
the entire land is fragmented and collapsing.
The traitorous minister Cáo Pī,
thus usurped the divine instruments of power.
Pī's son Rùi succeeded him in wickedness,
stealing the name and disrupting the system.
Quán was born in the southeast,
met with the destined era,
upholding Heaven's mandate and wielding military power.
His ambition is to save the world,
to execute punishment according to the charge,
and to act for the people.
All the ministers, generals, chancellors, provincial and commandery officials, and those in charge of the hundred cities,
all believe that Heaven's will has departed from the Hàn,
that the Hàn clan has ended according to Heaven's decree,
that the imperial throne is vacant,
that the suburban sacrifices have no master.
Auspicious omens and propitious signs
have appeared one after another.
The mandate of Heaven rests upon my person,
and I cannot but accept it.
Quán fears the mandate of Heaven,
how dare I not respectfully obey?
I respectfully choose an auspicious day,
ascend the altar, burn firewood, and offer sacrifices,
and assume the imperial throne.
May you, spirits, accept these offerings!
May Wú endure,
and forever peacefully hold the supreme celestial position."
Afterwards, he considered that his residence was not in the central plains,
and no longer performed these ceremonies.
In his middle years,
his ministers submitted a memorial,
suggesting that suburban sacrifices should be performed.
Quán said:
"Suburban sacrifices should be performed in the central plains,
this is not the right place now."
They memorialized again, saying:
"Under all of Heaven,
there is no land that is not the king's land.
A king considers all under Heaven his home.
In the past, King Wén and King Wǔ of Zhōu performed suburban sacrifices in Fēng and Hào,
which were not necessarily in the central plains."
Quán said:
"King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
and assumed the throne in Hào Jīng;
thus, he performed suburban sacrifices there.
King Wén was not yet the Son of Heaven,
establishing suburban sacrifices in Fēng.
In what classic is this found?"
They memorialized again, saying:
"We humbly found in the 'Treatise on Suburban Sacrifices' of the Hàn Shū,
that Kuāng Héng memorialized to move the Gānquán and Hédōng suburban sacrifices to Cháng'ān,
and stated that King Wén performed suburban sacrifices in Fēng."
Quán said:
"King Wén was humble and yielding in character,
holding the position of a feudal lord.
It is clear he did not perform suburban sacrifices.
There is no clear text in the classics and commentaries,
this is merely Kuāng Héng's interpretation as a common scholar,
not the correct meaning of the classics,
and cannot be used."
Yú Xǐ's Zhìlín states:
"The Lord of Wú corrected and refuted the suburban sacrifices,
and posthumously criticized Kuāng Héng.
All who witnessed it
universally sighed in approval."
Hé Chéngtiān said:
"I observe that Quán established his reign, succeeding Heaven,
yet his suburban sacrifices were incomplete.
This was certainly wrong.
In his later years, although he performed one southern suburban sacrifice,
he never performed the northern suburban ritual.
Huán Shì's Wú Jì states: 'Quán thought of honoring his esteemed father and associating him with Heaven,
and posthumously granted his father, Jiān, the exalted title of Wú Shǐzǔ.'
If this account is true,
then the sacrifice Quán performed in his later years
was Jiān's association with Heaven.
After Quán's death,
the three succeeding rulers never performed suburban sacrifices throughout the Wú dynasty.
This means Quán did not enjoy the ritual of being associated with the Emperor."
In the first year of Zhāngwǔ, Liú Bèi
assumed the imperial throne,
and established an altar.
"On the bǐngwǔ day of the fourth month of summer in the twenty-sixth year of Jiàn'ān,
Your servant, the Emperor Bèi,
dares to use a dark bull,
to solemnly announce to the August Heaven and Supreme Emperor, and to the Sovereign Earth and all its spirits.
The Hàn possessed all under Heaven,
and its mandate was boundless.
In the past, Wáng Mǎng usurped and stole power.
Emperor Guāngwǔ, in his furious wrath, executed him,
and the altars of soil and grain were restored.
Now Cáo Cāo, relying on military might and acting with cruel indifference,
and his son Pī continued his evil rebellion,
usurped the divine instruments of power.
The ministers and generals believed that the altars of soil and grain were falling into ruin,
and that Bèi should restore them,
succeeding the two ancestors,
and reverently carry out Heaven's punishment.
Bèi, with his meager virtue,
fears to disgrace the imperial throne.
He consulted with the common people,
and externally with the chieftains of the barbarians.
All said that the mandate of Heaven cannot be left unanswered,
the ancestral legacy cannot be long abandoned,
the four seas cannot be without a master,
and the entire land looks with hope
to Bèi alone.
Bèi fears Heaven's majesty,
and also fears that the Hàn state will be swallowed by the earth.
I respectfully choose an auspicious day,
and with all my officials, ascend the altar,
and receive the imperial seal and sash.
I perform the burning and burying sacrifices,
announcing to the great spirits.
May the great spirits accept these offerings!
May blessings be bestowed upon the Hàn house,
and may the four seas be forever at peace."
In the tenth month of the second year of Zhāngwǔ,
an imperial edict commanded Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng to construct northern and southern suburban altars in Chéngdū.
On the jiǎzǐ day of the twelfth month of the second year of Xiánxī of Emperor Yuán of Wèi,

the acting Imperial Envoy, Palace Attendant, and Grand Guardian Zhèng Chōng, concurrently Grand Commandant and Colonel Director of Retainers Lǐ Xǐ, presented the imperial seal, sash, and official document,
abdicating the imperial throne to the Jìn.
On the bǐngyín day,
the Jìn established an altar in the southern suburbs,
performing the burning and burying sacrifices to announce the succession,
but without an ancestral associate.
The text read:
"Your servant, the Emperor Yán,
dares to use a dark bull,
to clearly announce to the August Sovereign and Supreme Emperor.
The Emperor of Wèi, conforming to the imperial mandate,
and continuing Heaven's clear command,
commanded Yán, saying: 'In ancient times, Táng Yáo abdicated the throne to Yú Shùn,
and Yú Shùn in turn abdicated to Yǔ.
Their surpassing virtues became an enduring teaching,
lasting for many years.
When the Hàn's virtue declined,
Grand Ancestor Emperor Wǔ brought order out of chaos and saved the people,
assisting the Liú clan.
Then he received the abdication from the Hàn.
As for the Wèi house,
it has faced many challenges over generations,
nearly falling into ruin.
It truly relied on the Jìn's virtue of rescue and assistance,
thus preserving its ancestral sacrifices,
and greatly helping it through difficulties.
This shows that the Jìn has rendered great service to the Wèi.
All the people of the four directions,
without exception, reverently submit.
Establishing states and enfeoffing nobles,
proclaiming rites and clarifying punishments,
pacifying Liáng and Mín,
embracing Yáng and Yuè,
extending benevolence throughout China,
the eight cardinal points follow the same track,
near and far hasten to righteousness.
Auspicious signs and portents repeatedly arrive,
Heaven and man respond in unison,
none fail to submit.
Therefore, I follow the example of the three ancient sovereigns,
and gather the great mandate here.'
Yán, with his insufficient virtue,
declined but could not refuse the command.
Thereupon, all the dukes, ministers, and gentlemen,
numerous feudal lords and various officials,
common people and retainers,
as well as the chieftains of the hundred barbarian tribes,
all said: 'August Heaven looks down,
seeking the distress of the people.
Since there is an established mandate,
it cannot be resisted or refused through self-effacement.'
The celestial order cannot be without a sovereign,
and the human and divine spirits cannot be without a master.
Yán reverently accepts the imperial mandate,
fearing Heaven's majesty.
How dare I not respectfully receive the auspicious command,
reverently choose an auspicious day,
ascend the altar and receive the abdication,
and announce the succession to the Supreme Emperor,
to forever answer the people's hopes,
and spread blessings to all nations.
May only the illustrious virtue be accepted as an offering."
In the first month of the second year of Tàishǐ,
an edict stated:
"The relevant officials previously memorialized that the suburban sacrifices temporarily used Wèi rites.
I did not foresee the difficulty of changing and reforming these practices,
and now they have become a permanent system.
The diverse opinions have been conflicting,
and thus no decision has been reached in a timely manner.
Unable to offer timely sacrifices to the spirits,
and to associate them with the ancestral spirits,
I have sighed and longed day and night,
neglecting food and forgetting comfort.
Let the suburban sacrifices be performed immediately."
At that time, the ministers again deliberated:
"The Five Dì
are in fact Heaven itself.
The five qi vary with the seasons,
hence their differing appellations.
Although there are five names,
they are in fact one deity.
In the Míngtáng and the southern suburbs,
the altars for the Five Dì should be removed.
The Five Suburbs should change the names of the Five Jīng
and all be uniformly called Hàotiān Shàngdì,
each having only one altar.
The northern suburbs should also remove the associated sacrifices to the empresses."
The emperor followed all of their suggestions.
On the Dīngchǒu day of the second month,
the Xuānhuángdì was sacrificed to in the suburbs as a counterpart to Heaven,
and the Wénhuángdì was sacrificed to in the Míngtáng,
as a counterpart to Shàngdì.
In the eleventh month of this year,
the relevant officials again deliberated and memorialized:
"In ancient times, the qiū and jiāo sacrifices were not separate.
It is fitting to combine the Yuánqiū and Fāngzé at the northern and southern suburbs,
and to reconstruct the altars.
The sacrifices of the two solstices
should be combined at the two suburbs."
The emperor again followed this.
This was entirely in accordance with the deliberations of Wáng Sù that Xuāndì had adopted.
On the Gēngyín day of this month, which was the winter solstice,
the emperor personally sacrificed at the Yuánqiū in the southern suburbs.
From then on,
the Yuánqiū and Fāngzé were not established separately, and this has continued to the present.
In the tenth month of the tenth year of Tàikāng,
a new edict was issued, stating:
"The Xiàojīng says: 'Sacrifice to Hòujì in the suburbs as a counterpart to Heaven,
and sacrifice to Wénwáng in the Míngtáng
as a counterpart to Shàngdì.'
And the Zhōuguān says: 'Sacrifice to Heaven and to the numerous Shàngdì.'
It also says: 'Sacrifice to Earth and to the numerous Four Wàng.'
Since the Four Wàng are not Earth,
it is clear that Shàngdì cannot be Heaven.
The previous public deliberation to remove the altars of the Five Dì in the Míngtáng,
when examined against the ritual texts and orthodox classics, is not acceptable.
Moreover, the Shīxù says: 'The achievements of Wén and Wǔ
began with Hòujì.'
Therefore, he was extended to be a counterpart to Heaven.
Xuāndì, having founded the dynasty with divine martial power,
was already a counterpart to Heaven.
To again make the former emperor a counterpart to Heaven
is also not appropriate in principle.
Restore the altars of the Five Dì in the Míngtáng and the southern suburbs."
In the first month of the third year of Tàikāng of Jìn Wǔdì,
the emperor personally performed the suburban sacrifices.
The crown prince, imperial brothers, and imperial sons all attended the sacrifice,
which was not in accordance with previous precedents.
Mǐndì resided in Cháng'ān,
but perished before he could establish suburban altars and ancestral temples.
Yuándì revived the dynasty south of the Jiāngnán,
and in the first year of Tàixīng,
he first established new suburban altars.
Their system and regulations were all based on the old Hàn and Jìn precedents by Tàicháng Hè Xún.
On the Xīnmǎo day of the third month,
the emperor personally performed the suburban sacrifices,
and the rites of offering and association followed exactly the precedent of Wǔdì's initial suburban sacrifice.
Initially, Shàngshūlìng Diāo Xié and Guózǐ Jìjiǔ Dù Yí
argued that it should wait until the capital was moved back to Luòyì before being carried out.
Sītú Xún Zǔ argued that Hàn Xiàndì, when residing in Xǔ,
immediately established suburban altars,
so it was appropriate to perform the rites here.
Piàojì Wáng Dǎo, Púshè Xún Sōng, Tàicháng Huá, and Zhōngshū Shìláng Yú Liàng all agreed with Xún Zǔ's suggestion.
The matter was thus implemented.
According to records, when Yuándì continued the mandate and revived the dynasty,
following the precedents of the Hàn dynasty,
it was appropriate to perform the rites of the Míngtáng ancestral sacrifices.
As the Míngtáng was not established south of the river,
it was thus omitted.
In the seventh month of the third year of Tàiníng of Míngdì,
an edict was first issued to establish the northern suburbs.
Before it could be built, the emperor passed away.
Thus, in the first month of the eighth year of Xiánhé of Chéngdì,
recalling the former edict,
it was established south of Fùzhōushān.
On the Xīnwèi day of this month,
the northern suburban sacrifice was performed,
and for the first time, Xuānmù Zhāng Huánghòu was associated with Earth.
This was a precedent from the Wèi dynasty,
not an old Jìn practice.
In the first month of the first year of Jiàn yuán of Kāngdì,
when about to perform the northern suburban sacrifice,
there was doubt and discussion.
Tàicháng Gù Hé memorialized, saying:
"In the Tàishǐ period,
the sacrifices of the two solstices were combined at the two suburbs.
The month for the northern suburban sacrifice
has no clear ancient text.
Some take it as the summer solstice,
others use the same month as the return of Yang.
Hàn Guāngwǔ first established the northern suburban sacrifice on the Xīnwèi day of the first month.
This would be the same month as the southern suburban sacrifice.
And during the initial founding of the restoration,
all practices followed simplicity,
combining the northern suburban sacrifice at one altar.
The constitutional regulations were not yet complete,
and the temporary use of this rite
was probably appropriate for the time.
By the Xiánhé period,
it was deliberated to establish a separate northern suburban sacrifice,
using the same first month.
Wèi followed the Later Hàn,
sacrificing to Heaven in the first month,
with Earth as a counterpart,
and citing the Zhōulǐ,
the suburban sacrifices of the Three Kings
all used the Xià calendar's first month."
Thereupon, Gù Hé's suggestion was followed.
On the Xīnwèi day of this month,
the southern suburban sacrifice was performed.
On the Xīnsì day,
the northern suburban sacrifice was performed.
The emperor personally performed both.
In the third month of the third year of Yuánxīng of Āndì,
Sòng Gāozǔ pursued Huán Xuán, who fled.
On the Jǐmǎo day,
he announced his righteous achievements at the southern suburbs.
In this year,
the emperor was in exile in Jiānglíng and had not yet returned.
The following year the suburban sacrifice was due.
The court deliberated that it should follow the Zhōulǐ,
where the Zōngbó assumes the duties,
and the Sāngōng perform the rites.
Shàngshū Zuǒchéng Wáng Nèzhī alone said:
Since the suburban sacrifice is performed during a period of mourning,
it is the Son of Heaven who should preside.
With a ruler present,
acting upon his command,
what is there to debate?
Whether one fasts or not,
how can it be compared to the present situation?
Some debaters also say that it is appropriate to perform the suburban sacrifice now,
and thus by authorization, instruct the Sāngōng to perform the rites.
Moreover, the suburban sacrifice to Heaven is of the utmost reverence,
and only one can perform it.
Therefore, it is not performed by anyone other than the Son of Heaven.
From commoners upwards,
all perform ancestral sacrifices,
but if the legitimate son is away,
a concubine's son performs the duties.
The ritual texts are clear.
There has never been anyone who did not personally receive the mandate and could sacrifice to Heaven.
Furthermore, when Wǔhuáng received the abdication,
he performed the suburban sacrifice in the second month.
When Yuándì revived the dynasty,
he performed the suburban sacrifice in the third month.
The time for the suburban sacrifice has not yet passed,
and we await the emperor's return daily.
There is no need to be hasty and without basis,
which would cause the imperial carriage to return and still be unable to personally perform the rites."
Thereupon, Wáng Nèzhī's suggestion was followed.
In the fifth month of the second year of Yuánxī (元熙) of Emperor Gōng (恭) of Jìn (晉),
an envoy was sent to present the document
abdicating the imperial throne to Sòng (宋).
On the *dīngmǎo* (丁卯) day of the sixth month of the first year of Yǒngchū (永初),
an altar was set up in the southern suburbs,
the emperor's seal and sash were received,
and a burnt sacrifice was offered to announce the event.
The document stated:
"Your servant, Emperor Yù (裕),
dares to use a dark bull
to solemnly announce to the August Empress and August Emperor.
The Jìn (晉) emperor, seeing that the line of his destiny had concluded
and the celestial mandate had shifted,
reverently followed the auspicious cosmic turn,
thereby entrusting the mandate to Yù (裕).
Indeed, the establishment of a ruler to govern the people
is for the benefit of all under Heaven.
When virtue fills an emperor or king,
joyful support naturally gathers around him.
From the earliest times of Táng (唐) and Yú (虞),
down to the Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏) dynasties,
there has been none who did not ascend to the ancestral temple with supreme wisdom
and whose great merits did not elevate them to the imperial throne,
thus enabling them to greatly rescue the common people
and leave behind boundless teachings.
Since Jìn (晉) moved east,
the four cardinal principles have not been established.
Where have the chief ministers relied?
This has been the case for a long time.
The difficulties of Lóng'ān (隆安)
and the disaster that culminated in Yuánxīng (元興)
led to the displacement of emperors and kings
and the extinction of ancestral sacrifices.
Although Yù (裕)'s territory is not comparable to Qí (齊) or Jìn (晉),
and his forces are not even a single brigade,
he looks up, indignant at the difficulties of the time,
and looks down, grieving over the widespread chaos.
Donning his robes and waving his banner,
he restored the imperial throne.
He was able to hold on in times of danger,
and support what had fallen.
Traitors and villains were completely annihilated,
and usurpers and imposters were certainly destroyed.
Truly, decline must end in prosperity,
and rise and fall have their appointed times.
As for restoring order, saving the people,
and greatly building up the Jìn (晉) house,
he relied on the opportune moment
to assume this arduous task.
Moreover, foreign peoples admired righteousness,
and interpreters came to pledge allegiance.
Wherever the calendar reached,
all submitted to the transforming influence of his virtue.
Furthermore, the Three Spirits showed auspicious signs,
mountains and rivers announced propitious omens,
and men and gods were in harmony,
manifesting clearly over the years.
Therefore, the numerous dukes, ministers,
and billions of common people
all said: 'The imperial spirits look down with great favor from above,
and the Jìn (晉) court sincerely offers its allegiance from below.
The mandate of Heaven cannot be long delayed,
and the imperial throne cannot be left vacant even for a moment.'
Thus, pressured by the unanimous counsel,
I reverently undertake this great ceremony.
Unworthily, with meager virtue,
I am entrusted to rule over the myriad people.
Although I look up in awe of the majesty of Heaven,
and may overlook minor details,
I deeply ponder the matter and
am fearful as if facing a plague.
I respectfully chose an auspicious day
to ascend the altar and receive the abdication,
announcing it to the Supreme Emperor,
thereby fulfilling the earnest hopes of all nations.
May Heaven's protection be greatly enhanced,
and may the Sòng (宋) dynasty enjoy eternal prosperity.
May the bright spirits accept this offering."
In the first year of Yǒngchū (永初),
the Crown Prince performed sacrifices at the northern and southern suburbs.
On the *shàngxīn* (上辛) day of the first month of the second year of Yǒngchū (永初),
the Emperor himself performed the suburban sacrifice.
In the third year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) of Emperor Wén (文),
when the imperial carriage embarked on the western campaign against Xiè Hùì (謝晦),
cloths were offered as announcement to the two suburbs.
On the *guǐsì* (癸巳) day of the sixth month of the first year of Xiàojiàn (孝建) of Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武),
the Eight Seats presented a memorial:
"Liú Yìxuān (劉義宣) and Zāng Zhì (臧質),
acting contrary to the times and rebellious,
committed monstrous evils,
linking up with Huái (淮) and Dài (岱)
to endanger the imperial ancestral altars.
At the beginning of Zhì (質)'s rebellion,
on the day of martial law,
announcements had already been made to the two suburban altars, the ancestral temple, and the altars of earth and grain.
However, no joint announcement was made regarding Yìxuān (義宣)'s rebellion.
Before the imperial carriage was to depart,
the rebels had already melted away;
Zhì (質) was already executed and displayed,
and Yìxuān (義宣) was captured.
With both enemies annihilated,
it is appropriate to make a joint announcement.
Upon examining the precedents, in the third year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) at the beginning of the campaign against Xiè Hùì (謝晦),
a general announcement was made to the two suburbs and the Grand Ancestral Temple.
After the rebels were pacified,
announcements were made only to the Grand Ancestral Temple and the Grand Altar of Earth,
but not to the two suburbs."
The ritual officials widely deliberated.
Xú Hóng (徐宏), Sūn Bó (孫勃), and Lù Chéng (陸澄), Doctors of the Imperial Academy, argued:
"There is no ritual act that does not have a corresponding report.
Since a general announcement was made at the beginning,
and now the rebels have been captured,
it should not be treated differently."
Sū Wěishēng (蘇瑋生), an Assistant Instructor of the Directorate of Education, argued:
"According to the 'Wáng Zhì' (王制) chapter,
when the Son of Heaven makes a tour of inspection,
'upon returning,
he reports to his ancestors.'
Also, in 'Zēng Zǐ Wèn' (曾子問): 'When a feudal lord goes to the Son of Heaven,
he announces it to his ancestors,
makes an offering to his deceased father,
and orders the祝史 (zhùshǐ) to announce it to the altars of earth and grain, the ancestral temples, mountains, and rivers.
The announcement uses sacrificial animals and silks,
and upon returning, it is likewise.
When feudal lords meet each other,
upon returning, they must announce it to their ancestors,
and then order the zhùshǐ (祝史) to announce it to those to whom they had previously made announcements.'
It also says: 'When the Son of Heaven or feudal lords are about to depart,
they must use silks, hides, and jade tablets
to announce it to their ancestors.
Upon returning, they must announce their arrival.'
Although the affairs of the Son of Heaven and feudal lords may differ in magnitude,
their rituals are generally similar;
the principle of announcing departure and announcing return
should not be different.
Zhèng (鄭) said: 'The rituals for going out and coming in are the same.'
Its meaning is very clear.
When the Son of Heaven goes on a campaign,
he makes a classified sacrifice to the Supreme Emperor.
Extending the principle that those previously announced to must be reported to upon return,
then the suburban altars should be reported to;
there is no room for doubt.
In the third year of Yuánjiā (元嘉), only the ancestral temple and the altar of earth were reported to,
the reasoning for which is unclear.
Perhaps it was based on the 'Lǐ Jì' (禮記) only stating 'upon returning, he reports to his ancestors,'
without mention of reporting to the suburban altars.
If this interpretation is adopted,
it is even less understandable.
The 'Lǐ Jì' (禮記) is an incomplete book,
originally lacking a comprehensive structure;
with damaged slips and missing characters,
much has been omitted.
One should indeed infer the meaning by analogy,
and not insist on explicit textual evidence for every action.
There is also no explicit record for the Son of Heaven announcing his return to the altar of earth;
why should reporting to the suburban altars
alone be subject to objection?
However, reporting both upon departure and upon return
is an expression of filial piety and reverence.
Since reporting return is considered a matter of righteousness,
it is not originally a ceremony for presenting trophies.
Now, if the imperial carriage did not actually leave the palace,
there is no need for a text announcing arrival.
If the ritual of announcing a non-departure is to be presented,
then there is no prior precedent.
I believe that the zhùshǐ (祝史) delivers the message
to demonstrate sincerity and faithfulness.
If its meaning conflicts with ritual,
it can certainly be omitted in practice.
Your servants have deliberated,
and believe that an announcement should be made,
and it is appropriate to use sacrificial animals to announce to both the northern and southern suburban altars, the Grand Ancestral Temple, and the Grand Altar of Earth,
following the old practice of the dukes and ministers."
An edict approved this.
In the first month, on the *gēngyín* day, of the second year of Xiàojiàn [455 CE],
the officials concerned reported:
"The Southern Suburban Sacrifice is scheduled for the fifteenth day of this month.
Recalling the old rituals,
for the ancestral temple sacrifices, the emperor performs the main offering himself,
with the Grand Marshal (Tàiwèi) making the secondary offering.
For the Southern Suburban Sacrifice, the emperor performs the main offering himself,
with the Grand Master of Rites (Tàicháng) making the secondary offering.
Furthermore, at the beginning of the ancestral temple sacrifice,
wine is poured on the ground.
When sending off the spirits, it is not poured.
However, for the suburban sacrifice, it is poured at the beginning,
similar to the temple sacrifice,
and also poured when sending off the spirits.
The ceremonial procedures differ,
creating doubts in practice.
We have accordingly submitted this to the Ritual Officials for detailed rectification."
Wáng Sìzhī, an erudite of the Imperial Academy (Tàixué Bóshì), deliberated:
"According to the *Rites of Zhōu*,
the Grand Master of the Ancestral Temple (Dàzōngbó) 'assists the king in protecting the state,
serving ghosts and spirits with auspicious rites,
and sacrificing with purity to Hào Tiān (August Heaven).'
This corresponds to the current Grand Master of Rites (Tàicháng).
Therefore, for the suburban sacrifice to Heaven,
the Grand Master of Rites (Tàicháng) should make the secondary offering.
Moreover, the 'Outer Clan' chapter of the *Rites of Zhōu* states: 'If the Queen (Wánghòu) does not participate,
then [the Grand Master of the Ancestral Temple] assists the Grand Master of the Ancestral Temple (Zōngbó).'
Zhèng Xuán commented: 'If the Queen does not participate in the sacrifice,
the Grand Master of the Ancestral Temple (Zōngbó) performs her duties.'
It is also said: 'The lord holds the jade goblet (guīzàn) to perform the libation (guàn) to the impersonator of the deceased (shī);
the Grand Master of the Ancestral Temple (Dàzōngbó) holds the jade tablet (zhāngzàn) to make the secondary offering.'
Since the Middle Ages,
the Queen has not participated in temple sacrifices.
Thus, according to the rites, the Grand Master of the Ancestral Temple (Dàzōngbó) should perform the secondary offering.
However, currently, the Grand Marshal (Tàiwèi) makes the secondary offering.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the *Book of Rites*'s 'Monthly Ordinances' states: 'The Three Kings had Ministers of War (Sīmǎ),
but no Grand Marshals (Tàiwèi).
Grand Marshal (Tàiwèi)
is a Qín dynasty office.'
It is probably because as generations passed,
and the ancestral temple was held in increasing reverence,
the responsibility of assisting the Queen (hòu) became significant.
Therefore, a senior ducal minister (shànggōng) makes the secondary offering."
He further deliberated:
"When contemplating the passage of time,
emotions are as profound as frost and dew;
when sensing the spirits in the house and door,
one feels a presence of form and sound.
Not knowing where the spirits reside,
one does not seek them in a single place.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the 'Officials' chapter of the *Book of Rites* states that
the Son of Heaven and feudal lords sacrifice at the *bāng* (front gate of the ancestral temple) and then perform the *yì* (repetition of the sacrifice).
*Yì* is also a sacrifice.
If the current temple sacrifice omits the libation for sending off the spirits,
it may be that the sacrifice is moved to the *bāng yì*,
implying that the spirits are to remain,
not to be dispatched.
The rites for suburban and temple sacrifices differ,
hence the difference in libation at sending off."
Zhū Yīngzhī, an Assistant Minister of Rites (Tàicháng Céng), deliberated:
"According to the *Rites of Zhōu*,
the Grand Master of the Ancestral Temple (Dàzōngbó) commands the Master of Rituals (Zhǎngdiǎnlǐ)
to prioritize serving the spirits,
overseeing all sacrifices,
with Hào Tiān (August Heaven) being supreme.
The current Grand Master of Rites (Tàicháng) is precisely the Grand Master of the Ancestral Temple (Zōngbó).
Furthermore, Yuan Shānsōng's *Records of Han Official Ranks* states: '
For suburban sacrifices, the Grand Marshal (Tàiwèi) performs the secondary offering,
and the Minister of the Imperial Household (Guānglù) performs the third offering.
The Grand Master of Rites (Tàicháng) always first presents the ritual procedures
and the actual conduct of affairs
for every sacrifice, and is in charge of assisting the Son of Heaven.'
He is not in charge of making offerings.
According to the *Records of Rites*,
the secondary offering in the Hàn dynasty
was exclusively performed by a senior official (shàngsī),
not by a high-ranking ritual official (zhìzōng guìguān).
Currently, for ancestral temple sacrifices, the Grand Marshal (Tàiwèi) makes the secondary offering,
and the Minister of the Imperial Household (Guānglù) makes the third offering,
which is the Hàn ritual.
Moreover, Hè Xún prescribed that the Grand Marshal (Tàiwèi) ascends the altar via the southeast path,
indicating that this official must participate in the suburban sacrifice.
Although ancient rites designated the Grand Master of the Ancestral Temple (Zōngbó),
generations have seen changes and reforms,
and a senior official (shàngsī) making the secondary offering
is the practice followed in the Hàn ritual.
Your humble servant believes that the suburban sacrifice is a weighty rite,
and should align with the ancestral temple.
Furthermore, since the Grand Master of Rites (Tàicháng) is already responsible for assisting the Son of Heaven,
he cannot undertake both duties.
As for the libation (*guàn*) matter,
the *Book of Rites* says: 'Sacrifices seek the meaning of yin and yang.
The people of Yīn first sought the yang.'
'After three rounds of music, the sacrificial animal is welcomed.'
This means the Yīn people performed the libation later.
'The people of Zhōu first sought the yin,'
'used fragrant black millet wine (chàng) for libation.
It reaches the deep springs.
After the libation,
the sacrificial animal is welcomed.'
This means the Zhōu people performed the libation first.
This refers to temple sacrifices,
not suburban sacrifices.
According to the 'Heavenly Officials' chapter of the *Rites of Zhōu*: 'For all sacrifices, assist the king in matters of libation (*guàn*) and presentation.'
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states: 'Libation (*guàn*) is pouring.
Only the human realm's ancestral temple has libation; Heaven and Earth and the great, supreme deities do not have libation.'
And the suburban sacrifice has never had libation from the beginning.
This is not clearly explained in the rites.
The annotations of profound scholars [on this matter] are clear and evident.
If the current libation [in the suburban sacrifice] is considered a longstanding error,
then there should be no libation."
The Assistant Directors (chéngláng) and erudites (bóshì) of the Eight Divisions of the Secretariat (Bāzuò)
all concurred with Zhū Yīngzhī's deliberation.
The Grand Minister of the Secretariat (Shàngshūlìng), King Jiànpíng, Liú Hóng,
reviewed the deliberations and deemed Zhū Yīngzhī's opinion acceptable.
An imperial edict approved it.
In the second year of Dà Míng, on the *bǐng-wǔ* day of the first month, which was the first day of the month,
the officials concerned reported:
"On the sixth day of this month, the Southern Suburb sacrifice is to be performed,
with His Majesty personally presiding.
It might rain at that time.
In the Wèi dynasty, when it rained,
Gāo Tánglóng suggested that a later *xīn* day should be used instead.
In the Jìn dynasty, when the procession had already departed and encountered rain,
Gù Hé also said it would be appropriate to announce a change again.
Xú Chán said: 'In the time of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
sometimes *bǐng* days were used,
sometimes *jǐ* days,
and sometimes *gēng* days.'
Let the ritual officials deliberate and determine this, and examine it in detail.
If the day can be moved,
should the ancestral temple be notified again or not?"
The deliberation of Academian Wáng Xiè zhī stated:
"Moving the suburb sacrifice due to rain
is a matter on which previous generations have reached a consensus.
The *Lǐ Zhuàn* records that
the *xīn* day has significance.
The *Jiāo Tè Shēng* says: 'As for the use of the *xīn* day for the suburb sacrifice,
the Zhōu dynasty's initial suburb sacrifice was on this day.'
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states: 'The suburb sacrifices of the Three Kings
all followed the Xià calendar.
The use of the *xīn* day
is to emphasize purification and renewal.'
Furthermore, the *Yuè Lìng* says: 'Then choose an auspicious day
to pray for grain to the Lord on High.'
The commentary states: 'Auspicious day
refers to the first *xīn* day.
The suburb sacrifice is to Heaven.'
Moreover, the *Chūn Qiū* records two suburb sacrifices:
in the 17th year of Chéng, in the ninth month, on the *xīn-chǒu* day,
the suburb sacrifice was performed.
The *Gōng Yáng* commentary asks: 'Why was the suburb sacrifice performed?'
It was performed on the first *xīn* day of the first month.
In the first year of Āi, in the fourth month, on the *xīn-sì* day,
the suburb sacrifice was performed.
The *Gǔ Liáng* commentary says: 'From the first month to the third month,
is the time for the suburb sacrifice.
The first *xīn* day of the first month is divined on the last *xīn* day of the twelfth month.
If it is not suitable,
the first *xīn* day of the second month is divined on the last *xīn* day of the first month.
If it is not suitable,
the first *xīn* day of the third month is divined on the last *xīn* day of the second month.'
From this, it is clear
that for the rite of the suburb sacrifice,
there has never been a case where a *xīn* day was not used.
The Jìn dynasty's use of *bǐng*, *jǐ*, or *gēng* days
all involved separate discussions.
Emperor Wǔ performed the Southern Suburb sacrifice on the *bǐng-yín* day of the twelfth month when accepting the abdication,
which means a *xīn* day could not be used then.
Also, in the second year of Tài Shǐ, on the *jǐ-mǎo* day of the eleventh month,
the sacrifices to the round mound and square pool, performed at the solstices, were combined with the two suburb sacrifices for the first time.
In the third year, on the *gēng-yín* day of the eleventh month, the Winter Solstice sacrifice was offered to Heaven,
a suburb sacrifice at the round mound.
This still followed the rites of the round mound,
not specifically the sacrifice for praying for grain,
hence again a *xīn* day could not be used.
Our current suburb banquet,
as it follows the Xià calendar,
even if it is to be postponed,
I believe it should still necessarily use a *xīn* day.
Xú Chán's basis
may be inappropriate.
Furthermore, the *Jiāo Tè Shēng* says: 'Receiving the mandate at the ancestral temple,
and divining with tortoise shells at the paternal shrine.'
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says: 'Receiving the mandate means reporting the postponement and divining.'
Thus, the announcement is inherent in the suburb sacrifice,
not specifically for the date.
Even if today there is a postponement,
the suburb sacrifice itself does not change;
I humbly believe there is no need to make an announcement again."
The deliberation of Bureau Director Zhū Yīng stated:
"According to the discussions of previous scholars on the suburb sacrifice,
their opinions are not uniform.
The *Zhōu Lǐ* mentions the sacrifice at the round mound on the Winter Solstice.
The *Yuè Lìng* mentions praying for grain to the Lord on High in the first month of spring.
Mr. Zhèng's explanation is that
the round mound sacrifice is to Hào Tiān Shàng Dì,
with Dì Kù as co-sacrificed,
which is called *dì*.
The prayer for grain sacrifice is to the Emperors of the Five Essences,
with Hòu Jì as co-sacrificed,
which is called *jiāo*.
The two sacrifices are at different times,
and their deities are not the same.
Various scholars say that
the round mound sacrifice
has Hòu Jì as co-sacrificed.
Taking its location,
it is named *jiāo*.
In terms of its physical form,
it is called the round mound.
Though the names are two,
it is in fact one sacrifice.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn abandoned Zhèng's view and followed the various scholars,
which is why the suburb sacrifice was performed on the Winter Solstice.
Since it was on the solstice day,
there is no logical reason for it to always be a *xīn* day.
Therefore, during the Jìn dynasty in the Central Plains, the suburb sacrifice was not performed on a *xīn* day,
as Xú Chán argued.
Since the period of the Eastern Jìn (Jiāng Zuǒ),
all have used the first month,
presumably because the tradition states that the suburb sacrifices of the Three Kings
each followed their own calendar.
Jìn did not correct the calendar,
but followed the Xià calendar's timing,
hence it was based on the beginning of the year,
not on the winter day,
and all used the first *xīn* day.
This has become the established practice in recent times.
As for the ritual of sacrifice,
'if the time is passed, it is not performed.'
Currently, it is in the first month of spring,
the time for the suburb sacrifice has not passed.
Encountering rain and postponing the day
is not contrary to ritual.
Since the day has already been announced,
but due to circumstances it cannot be followed,
and *yīn* sacrifices require utmost reverence,
I believe it is appropriate to announce it again.
Gāo Tánglóng said:
'The Southern Suburb sacrifice on the ninth,
the Northern Suburb sacrifice on the tenth.'
This suggests that the Northern Suburb sacrifice may not need to be on a *xīn* day."
Minister Hè Yǎn deliberated:
"Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the *Lǐ Jì*
cites the *Yì* to say that the suburb sacrifices of the Three Kings
all followed the Xià calendar.
The *Zhōu Lǐ* states that
for all major national affairs,
the first month of the year is mostly used.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* also states that the suburb sacrifice is performed at the stirring of insects.
Thus, Zhèng's statement
is indeed well-founded.
The differing opinions of various schools,
some saying that the Three Kings each used their own calendar's first month for the suburb sacrifice to Heaven,
this is likely a sophistry of narrow learning,
and has no basis in ritual.
Therefore, to know that the *Gǔ Liáng* says all three spring months can be months for the suburb sacrifice
is truly what is called superficial.
However, the argument for using the *xīn* day
is almost universally agreed upon.
The Jìn dynasty's use of *gēng* and *jǐ* for the suburb sacrifice
is inconsistent and lacks prior precedent.
I humbly believe it is appropriate to follow the Jìn precedent of postponing the suburb sacrifice and using a *xīn* day according to ritual.
Xiè zhī's understanding that receiving the mandate and divining with tortoise shells
implies that the announcement is not about the day,
is an intricate aspect of his scholarship."
Vice Director Xú Yuán deliberated, believing that:
"The use of a *xīn* day for the suburb sacrifice,
if it hinders postponing the day,
the ritual officials and the Bureau of Sacrifices
have thoroughly examined it.
Hè Yǎn's argument, based on ritual,
that there should be no repeated announcement,
is what I personally agree with.
As for finding the right time for the suburb sacrifice,
it should be changed now,
and only the matter needs to be announced.
The next *xīn* day is ten days away,
which would indeed extend the period of fasting.
The sacrificial animals are being purified,
so it cannot extend to three months.
I believe that after the animals have been announced as pure and their blood offered,
even if there are unforeseen circumstances,
the officials concerned should proceed with the rite,
and the suburb sacrifice should not be postponed."
The opinions of the assembly differed.
The joint deliberation concluded:
"It is appropriate to follow the classics:
if rain is encountered, postpone it to the next *xīn* day,
and do not make a repeated announcement.
If it rains after the animals have been slaughtered and their blood offered,
then the officials concerned should proceed with the rite."
The imperial edict approved it.
In the second year of Tàishǐ (466 CE), in the eleventh month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
〔一０〕Emperor Míng issued an edict saying:
"I have recently received the mandate to rule,
yet have endured many difficulties.
My war chariots swiftly moved,
and my strategies were intensely focused.
Although the sacrifices were prepared,
I was unable to personally perform the rites.
Now that the nine regions are settled,
and all the hundred sacrifices are in order,
it is fitting to follow the ancient precedents
and offer sacrifices to the High Emperor in the suburbs."
The officials concerned reported that upon inspection,
there was no prior standard for this.
Huángmén Shìláng Xú Ái (徐爰) deliberated:
"Yú (虞) spoke of 'extensive categories,'
Yīn (殷) described 'clear announcements.'
This is because when a world is founded and achievements are made,
and virtue is flourishing and the enterprise far-reaching,
when the rule is established and the foundation laid,
it is imperative to offer sacrifices to the High Emperor.
Since the Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏) dynasties,
this tradition has been followed.
Gāozǔ Wǔhuángdì (高祖武皇帝), having conquered the false Chǔ (楚),
and with Emperor Ān of Jìn (晉安帝) still in Jiānglíng (江陵),
immediately in the capital, announced his righteous achievements in the suburban altars.
I respectfully consider that Tàishǐ (泰始), in accordance with the divine mandate,
with his divine military prowess and heroic decisiveness,
went forth on a royal punitive expedition,
and the military preparations took a long time.
Although the prescribed rituals were not neglected by the officiants,
the personal appearance was still lacking.
I recall that Emperor Wǔ of Jìn (晉武) performed the suburban sacrifice in the second month,
and Emperor Yuán of Jìn (晉元) performed the burnt offering in the third month.
When there is an extraordinary joyous occasion,
there must be an extraordinary ceremony,
which should not be constrained by ordinary sacrifices
or limited to the first Xīn (辛) day of the first month.
I humbly suggest that the historians be instructed
to choose an auspicious day in the eleventh month,
for the emperor to personally go to the suburbs
and offer reverence to Hào Tiān Shàngdì (昊天上帝),
with Gāozǔ Wǔhuángdì (高祖武皇帝) enshrined as a co-sacrificer.
The other ancestral spirits sharing the meal
are not relevant to the current sacrifice."
Shàngshū Lìng Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén (尚書令建安王休仁) and others agreed with Ái’s deliberation.
The joint deliberation was deemed appropriate.
The emperor approved it.
In the sixth year of Tàishǐ (470 CE), in the first month, on the day Yǐhài,
〔一一〕an edict stated:
"According to ancient rites, kings performed suburban sacrifices every year,
extending to the Míngtáng (明堂).
Since the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
suburban sacrifices have been performed every other year,
with the Míngtáng (明堂) on the same day.
The substance and refinement, detail and brevity, had their distinctions.
From now on, suburban sacrifices may be performed every two years,
and the Míngtáng (明堂) every other year.
The details can be discussed further."
The officials concerned reported:
"Former jiān cáo láng Yú Yuàn (兼曹郎虞愿) deliberated:
'Suburban sacrifices and ancestral worship
both primarily address celestial deities,
and performing them on the same day for a grand offering
is considered disrespectful by etiquette.
The clear edict mandates that the Yuánqiū (圓丘) should report achievements,
with a sacrifice every three years.
The Míngtáng (明堂) should honor the emperor's ancestors,
with a clear offering every other year.
A detailed consideration of the timing to find a middle ground
is indeed a splendid and fitting arrangement.'
Consultations with all the participants in the deliberation confirmed agreement.
Cáo láng Wáng Yánxiù (曹郎王延秀) further deliberated:
'The appropriateness of the reform
is indeed as the imperial edict states.
The previous deliberation by Yú Yuàn (虞愿)
merely expressed agreement with the directive,
without clarifying subsequent examples.
Upon careful review, if the first suburban sacrifice is every two years,
and the Míngtáng (明堂) every one year,
then the second suburban sacrifice and the third Míngtáng (明堂)
would again fall in the same year.
Yuàn (愿) believes that after the initial suburban sacrifice and Míngtáng (明堂),
they should each be spaced two years apart.
By extending this, they would always be in different years.'
This was communicated to the Eight Grandees,
who agreed with Yánxiù's (延秀) deliberation."
Later, in the second year of Yuánhuī (元徽) (474 CE) of the deposed emperor, in the tenth month, on the day Dīngsì,
the officials concerned reported that suburban sacrifices and the Míngtáng (明堂)
should revert to being performed on the same day,
every other year.
Emperor Wén of Hàn (漢文帝) first sacrificed to the Earth God in Wèiyáng (渭陽),
with Emperor Gāo (高帝) as co-sacrificer.
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) established the Hòutǔ (后土) shrine in Fényīn (汾陰),
also with Emperor Gāo (高帝) as co-sacrificer.
The Hàn (漢) imperial house made its founder co-sacrificer with Heaven and Earth,
but did not yet have an empress co-sacrificer with Earth.
When Wáng Mǎng (王莽) became chancellor,
he cited the Rites of Zhōu (周禮) to sacrifice to the deceased mother as co-sacrificer in the northern suburb.
On the summer solstice, he sacrificed to Hòutǔ (后土)
with Empress Gāo (高后) as co-sacrificer;
this practice began from him.
During the Jiànwǔ (建武) era of Emperor Guāngwǔ (光武),
no northern suburb was established,
so the Earth Goddesses
were always offered sacrifices in co-worship at the Altar of Heaven.
Mountains, rivers, and all other objects of worship were within the imperial encampment,
totaling one thousand five hundred and fourteen deities.
In the first year of Zhōngyuán (中元),
the northern suburb was established,
and Sīkōng Féng Fáng (司空馮魴) was sent to announce to the Gāomiào (高廟) that Empress Báo (薄后) replaced Empress Lǚ (呂后) as co-sacrificer with Earth.
In the early period south of the Yangtze,
no northern altar was yet established,
so the Earth God and all other deities
were worshipped together at the Altar of Heaven.
Emperor Chéng of Jìn (晉成帝) established two suburban altars:
the Heavenly Altar included sixty-two deities:

the assistants of the Five Emperors, the sun, moon, five planets, twenty-eight lunar mansions, Wénchāng (文昌), Běidǒu (北斗), Sāntái (三台), Sīmìng (司命), Xuānyuán (軒轅), Hòutǔ (后土), Tàiyī (太一), Tiānyī (天一), Tàiwēi (太微), Gōuchén (鈎陳), Běijí (北極), Yǔshī (雨師), Léi (雷), Diàn (電), Sīkōng (司空), Fēngbó (風伯), Lǎorén (老人) – sixty-two deities in total.
The Earthly Altar included forty-four deities:

the Five Sacred Mountains, the Four Wàng (望) mountains, the Four Seas, the Four Great Rivers, the Five Lakes, the assistants of the Five Emperors, Mount Yí (沂山), Mount Yuè (嶽山), Mount Bái (白山), Mount Huò (霍山), Mount Yīwúlǘ (毉無閭山), Mount Jiǎng (蔣山), Sōngjiāng (松江), Mount Kuàijī (會稽山), Qiántángjiāng (錢唐江), and Xiānnóng (先農) – forty-four in total.
The various small mountains south of the Yangtze
were established as objects of worship in the Jiangzuǒ (江左),
