just like the small rivers in the Guānzhōng (關中) area of the Western Hàn (漢) capital,
all of which had their sacrificial ranks.
The ranks of the two suburban altars
were officially recorded.
In the ninth month of the third year of Yǒngchū (永初) (422 CE) of Emperor Wǔ of Sòng (宋武帝),
Sīkōng Xiànzhī (司空羨之) and Shàngshū Lìng Liàng (尚書令亮) and others reported:
"We have heard that exalting virtue and clarifying sacrifices
is a constant practice of all kings;
emulating Heaven and humans
has been a shared principle throughout history.
Although reforms and changes have varied with different times,
and substance and refinement have differed across eras,
the fundamental sentiment of earnest teaching
remains consistent.
We respectfully submit that Gāozǔ Wǔhuángdì (高祖武皇帝) truly harmonized with the divine spirits,
having received the mandate from Heaven,
diligently brought peace to the world,
and established the ultimate standard for the common people.
The emperor moved his bright virtue,
gloriously dwelling in all eight directions,
and his great harmony spread,
his profound transformation extending far and wide.
Your Majesty, with your sagely wisdom, inherited this splendor,
and your Way has permeated all nations.
The sacrificial rites have long been neglected,
and you now contemplate glorifying these grand achievements,
offering sacrifices to the Emperor and honoring your ancestors.
This is indeed appropriate now.
Gāozǔ Wǔhuángdì (高祖武皇帝) should be enshrined as co-sacrificer at the Heavenly Altar;
as for the co-sacrificer for the Earth God,
although there is no clear textual evidence in the rites,
the old statutes of previous dynasties
have always been followed.
The old precedents of Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉)
are sufficient as a model.
We suggest that Empress Wǔjìng (武敬皇后) should be enshrined as co-sacrificer at the Northern Altar.
This would be to express remembrance in filial piety,
elevating holy reverence to eternity,
corresponding with the two cosmic forces (Heaven and Earth),
truly harmonizing the visible and the invisible.
In the first month of next spring,
when there are affairs at the two suburban altars,
we request that orders be issued throughout the inner and outer courts
to meticulously follow the old statutes."
The emperor approved it.
In the winter of the second year of Tàikāng (太康) (281 CE) of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn (晉武帝),
the officials concerned reported:
"In the first month of the third year, the spring begins with the Lí Chūn (立春) sacrifice.
As the weather is still cold,
it can be performed by the responsible officials."
The emperor issued an edict:
"Suburban sacrifices are highly regarded in the rites.
In the interim, due to numerous military and state affairs,
there have been temporary impediments and postponements,
hence each time the request has been approved.
From now on, with fewer external affairs,
this alone is of great importance,
and personally performing the burnt offerings
is indeed a constant practice."
When Emperor Chéng (成帝) sacrificed at the southern suburb,
it rained.
Shìzhōng Gù Hé (侍中顧和) petitioned:
"It is advisable to return.
Another date should be set."
The emperor approved it.
Emperor Míng of Hàn (漢明帝), based on the Yùelìng (月令) which prescribes the attire and colors for the five suburban sacrifices to welcome the qi (氣) of the seasons,
adopted the precedents from the Yuánshǐ (元始) era,
establishing five suburban altars in Luòyáng (洛陽)
to sacrifice to their respective emperors and deities,
with chariots and attire following the colors of the respective directions.
Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) followed this.
Since the Jiāngzuǒ (江左) era,
there has been no time to construct these.
In the fifth year of Dà Míng, in the fourth month, on the day Gēngzǐ, of Sòng Xiàowǔ's reign,
an edict stated:
"In ancient times, Wéndé was in Zhōu,
and the Míngtáng was grandly offered sacrifices;
Gāoliè was solely in Hàn,
and Wènyì was honored.
This is why sacrificial duties were never neglected,
and the vital energies were thus rectified.
Illustrious names were at the forefront,
and their reputation spread throughout the world.
My August Forefather, Tàizǔ Wénhuángdì, his achievements shone profoundly,
his sacred spirit enlightened the populace,
he brought harmony to the four gates within,
his benevolence aided all beings,
he reached the eight directions without,
his might awed foreign lands.
He subdued the powerful Yuè in the south,
and the formidable Róng in the west.
He established rites to foster the roots of agriculture,
and arranged music to accord with the cycles of the four seasons.
He adorned the tombs and ancestral temples,
extending beyond those without titles;
he honored and promoted worthy officials,
fully embodying the example of supreme virtue.
His teachings profoundly encouraged agriculture,
his governance was so high that punishments were laid aside.
All myriad things freely flourished,
and a hundred spirits offered blessings.
His actions accorded with the celestial measure,
and descended along with the terrestrial virtue.
Thus, his essence intertwined with the spirits above,
and gave rise to auspicious omens below.
Feudal lords followed the right path,
the Hé and the seas were pacified.
I rely on his magnificent achievements,
and have ruled the myriad people for
the August Heaven's blessings,
approaching one full cycle (of twelve years).
I contemplate upholding and proclaiming his excellent virtue,
to spread it endlessly.
Therefore, an in-depth study should be conducted of the Jī records,
to initiate the construction of the Míngtáng,
to offer ancestral sacrifices to the former spirits,
and formally present them to Shàngdì.
With sincere reverence duly shown,
the visible and invisible will all be in order.
My thoughts dwell on eternity,
and my heart breaks with longing."
The officials in charge reported:
"We have extensively searched for information on the Míngtáng and Bìyōng,
but there is no fixed text on their system;
the records are inconsistent,
and the traditions diverge.
Renowned scholars and enlightened thinkers
each maintain their own views,
some believing that the names differ but the reality is the same,
others that both names and reality differ.
From Hàn to Jìn,
no one has been able to distinguish them.
The Zhōu Shū states that
the Qīngmiào, Míngtáng, and Lùqǐn were of the same design.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the rites
gives rise to this interpretation.
Other scholars also say that the Míngtáng is in the south of the capital,
in the Bǐngsì region,
within three lǐ.
As for the structure of the rooms, halls, and individual chambers,
and the orientation of doors and windows,
generations have passed,
making it difficult to obtain detailed information.
Péi Wěi, a Shìzhōng of Jìn,
a great scholar of the Western Capital,
examined previous records in detail,
but was unable to determine a fixed system.
He believed that honoring ancestors and matching them with Heaven
was a clear and evident principle,
but the system of ancestral temples
lacked a clear basis.
It would be acceptable to simply build a grand hall
to solemnize the sacrifices.
All other trivial details
should be removed.
Comparing this with Zhèng Xuán's commentary,
it has some basis;
Péi Wěi's proposal,
we secretly believe, is acceptable.
To the south of the Guóxué,
the land is indeed Bǐngsì,
spacious, bright, and level,
sufficient for construction.
Its building plan
should imitate the Tàimiào,
but with twelve bays,
to correspond to the number of months in a year.
According to the Hàn Wènshàng Tǔyí,
five Dì positions should be established,
with Tàizǔ Wénhuángdì enjoying the sacrifice in opposition.
Although sacrificing to Huángtiān Shàngdì
is a different rank,
regarding the respectful sacrifice every three years,
the principle does not allow for difference.
From the suburb to the temple,
it should also be on the same day.
The Lǐjì states that suburban sacrifices use a single animal,
while the Shī mentions sheep and oxen for the Míngtáng.
Although the auspiciousness and purity are the same,
the substance and refinement are distinct rituals.
Moreover, suburban sacrifices involve burning firewood,
while the hall does not have smoke offerings.
Therefore, the tripods, chopping boards, ceremonial vessels, and food containers
should all follow the temple rites.
Order all departments,
to search for materials and select skilled workers,
temporarily appoint a Qǐbù Shàngshū and a Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng,
to estimate materials and plan the schedule,
and ensure its completion by this autumn."
Accordingly, Pei Wěi's suggestion was followed;
only a grand main hall with carved and painted roofs was built,
without the ancient system of thirty-six doors and seventy-two windows.
In the first month of the sixth year,
upon returning from the southern suburb,
Shìzǔ personally attended the Míngtáng,
offering sacrifices to the Dì of the five seasons,
with Wénhuángdì as the co-sacrificed deity.
This followed Zhèng Xuán's proposal.
The officials had his commentary.
In the ninth month, on the day Jiǎzǐ, of the fifth year of Dà Míng,
the officials reported:
"The southern suburban sacrifice uses three oxen.
The four seasonal sacrifices in the temple's six chambers use two oxen.
The Míngtáng is newly built,
for sacrificing to the five Dì,
with Tàizǔ Wénhuángdì as co-sacrificed deity.
We are unsure how many oxen should be used for the sacrifice."
Sīmǎ Xīngzhī, a Bóshì of Tàixué, proposed:
"According to Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the Lǐjì Dàzhuàn, it states: 'The Xiàojīng's suburban sacrifice to Hòujì is to match him with Heaven,
matching him with Língwēiyǎng.
The ancestral sacrifice to Wénwáng in the Míngtáng is to match him with Shàngdì,
matching him with the five Dì.'
Now, the five Dì preside over the directions,
their positions differ but their merit is one.
The use of sacrificial animals,
by principle, should not differ in rank.
Tàizǔ Wénhuángdì personally accomplished Heaven and Earth,
thus his way encompassed covering and containing;
he nurtured all living beings,
thus his transformation permeated the four vital energies.
The titles of Zǔ and Zōng
are insufficient to manifest his infinite beauty;
the sounds of metal and stone
cannot broadcast the grandeur of his achievements.
Therefore, the Míngtáng was diligently built,
which is how the sacred heart illuminates the profound ultimate;
its general association with the ancestral temple
is how former scholars grasped the essence of ritual.
In my humble opinion,
I believe six oxen should be used."
Bóshì Yú Hé proposed:
"Although there are five names for the sacrifice to the Dì,
the reality of their origin is always one.
The Dì of the five virtues
alternately possess excellent sovereignty,
each having their own purview,
hence there are five chambers.
The main object of ancestral sacrifice
must follow the ruling Dì to receive the sacrifice.
One main and one co-sacrificed,
together require two oxen."
Cíbù Láng Yán Huàn proposed:
"The meaning of sacrifice,
when referring to the five Dì together,
even though there are five Dì,
the use of sacrificial animals,
I believe, should not exceed the suburban sacrifice or temple sacrifices.
Two oxen should be used."
In the tenth month, on the day Gēngzǐ, of the seventh year of Tàishǐ under Míngdì's reign,
the officials reported:
"Next year, on the eighteenth day of the first month,
sacrifices will be offered in the Míngtáng.
We recall that in the past, the southern suburban sacrifice and the Míngtáng sacrifice occurred on the same day,
and both were announced to the Tàimiào.
We are unsure whether the current Míngtáng sacrifice
should also be announced or not."
Cíbù Láng Wáng Yánxiù proposed:
"According to Zhèng Xuán, it states: 'Jiāo is the name for sacrificing to Heaven,
Shàngdì is
another name for Heaven.
The deities have no two masters,
thus the Míngtáng is in a different location
to avoid Hòujì.'
Carefully considering the two sacrifices, Jiāo and Zōng,
since their names differ but their reality is the same,
as for the announcement,
there should be no difference."
Shǒu Shàngshūlìng Yuán Càn and others all agreed with Wáng Yánxiù's proposal.
During the reign of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
Zhōnghùjūn Jiǎng Jì memorialized, saying:
"Of the great rites of an emperor,
imperial tours are foremost;
to glorify ancestors and exalt forbears,
the Fēngshàn sacrifices are supreme.
Thus, from ancient times, those who revolutionized and received the mandate
never failed to tread Líangfù,
ascend Tài Shān,
engrave their boundless names,
and record the connection between Heaven and man.
Therefore, Sīmǎ Xiāngrú said that among the seventy-two rulers since the invention of writing,
some followed the precedents of their predecessors,
and diligently preserved their traces for posterity.
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said: 'If a sovereign is sagacious and enlightened but this is not proclaimed,
it is the fault of the officials.'
Therefore, without engraving the stones of
Mounts Shān and Líang for
great achievements and splendid virtues,
it is impossible to manifest the emperor's merits and spread an immortal spectacle to the people.
A saying goes,
when serving one's own lord and praising the beauty of Yáo and Shùn,
it is like a child facing their own parents
and praising another's father.
Now, Great Wèi has rectified the abuses and chaos of a hundred kings,
rescued those adrift from hardship and peril,
taken up the fading thread of a thousand years,
and continued the neglected governance of a hundred generations.
From Emperor Wǔ and Emperor Wén down to Your Sacred Person,
the way of Heaven and Earth has been brought to fruition,
and the transformation of men and spirits has been guided.
Heaven has responded,
with auspicious portents and manifest omens,
which, when compared to antiquity,
are so exceedingly abundant and magnificent
that there is nothing comparable.
Yet through successive reigns until now,
the great rite has not been performed.
Although Your Majesty's intention is to utterly sweep away the remaining brigands,
and cleanse the lingering impurities,
there has been no leisure for this matter.
If that were the case,
had Sānmiáo been obstinate in the Jiāng and Hàn regions,
Great Shùn should have abandoned his eastern inspection ceremony;
had the Xúyí tribe leaped about in the Huái and Sì regions,
King Chéng of Zhōu should have halted the rites at Dài Yuè.
Moreover, last year the Wú barbarians were defeated at the Jiāng and Hàn,
and this year the Shǔ rebels were slaughtered in Lǒngyòu.
Their internal collapse and tremor
are such that they will not recover.
Even if we must seek them out in their lairs,
it would not impede the matter of the Fēngshàn sacrifices.
This ceremony has long been abandoned;
it cannot be determined in haste.
It is proper to instruct the gōngqīng [dukes and ministers]
to extensively compile its rites,
divine the year and examine the time,
and report it to the Supreme Emperor,
to fulfill the expectations of all under Heaven.
Your servant, burdened with military duties,
cannot suppress this great wish,
and risks death to make this known."
The imperial edict said:
"Hearing Ji's words
makes my sweat flow to my feet.
Since the beginning of the world,
only seventy-odd rulers have performed the Fēngshàn sacrifices.
Hence, Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said: 'Even among those who received the mandate,
some did not fully realize their accomplishments,
which is why there were vast gaps in between,
some over a thousand years,
others several hundred years.
The rituals are so incomplete that they cannot be recorded.'
What virtue have I cultivated
that I dare aspire to this?
Does Ji perhaps think that there is no Guǎn Zhòng in this age,
and that I have the ambition of Duke Huán to ascend Tài Shān?
I dare not deceive Heaven.
What Ji has said,
though splendid, is not helpful to me.
The gōngqīng, Shìzhōng, Shàngshū, and Chángshì should simply examine this
and nothing more.
There is no need for further discussion,
nor is there a need to reply to the edict."
Although the emperor rejected Ji's proposal,
he did in fact have Gāotáng Lóng draft the Fēngshàn rituals.
However, because the realm was not yet unified,
he did not wish to perform the great rite immediately.
When Lóng passed away,
it was therefore not carried out.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn pacified Wú,
unifying the realm.
In the ninth month, on the Gēngyín day of the first year of Tàikāng,
Wèi Guàn (尚書令 Shàngshū Lìng), Shān Tāo (尚書左僕射 Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè), Wèi Shū (右僕射 Yòu Púyè), [一五]and Shàngshū Liú Shí and Zhāng Huà, among others, memorialized, saying:
"Your sagely virtue is profoundly magnificent,
its brilliance extends to the four quarters,
all of Zhūxià is tranquil,
and even the remote and wild submit.
With divine strategy and brilliant calculation,
you swept across Wú and Yuè.
Sūn Hào prostrated himself,
and the whole world became one family.
These towering achievements
reach to Heaven and Earth.
It is fitting to follow ancient precedents,
to inscribe a封 (fēng) ceremony on Dōngyuè,
and to instruct the Sānfǔ and Tàicháng to prepare the ritual."
Wèi Guàn and others further memorialized:
"Your ministers have heard that ever since the birth of mankind,
there have been rulers.
The number of reigns and sacrifices
is beyond reckoning.
Seventy-four houses, through establishing virtue and benefiting the world,
and spreading benevolent influence,
have ascended Mount Tài for the fēng ceremony.
Among them, those whose posthumous titles are known
are fourteen.
Those who have sunk into oblivion and silence,
without a single trace remaining,
are innumerable.
Before Huángdì,
ancient traditions are obscure and brief.
From Táng and Yú onwards,
the canons and counsels are brilliantly clear.
The Sān Wáng rose in succession,
their institutions and achievements inherited.
When the Zhōu Way declined,
the Qín clan took over,
and up to Hàn and Wèi,
the balance between plainness and refinement had not been restored.
The virtue of Dàjìn
began with Chóng and Lí,
who truly assisted Zhuānxū.
Through Xià and Shāng,
they served Heaven and Earth in succession.
As for the Zhōu,
they did not lose their lineage.
As the virtue of metal was about to ascend,
wise sages succeeded one another,
pacifying Shǔhàn externally,
and winning the hearts of all within the seas.
The flourishing military achievements
truly stemmed from civil virtue.
As for Your Majesty, upon receiving the mandate and ascending the throne,
you grandly established a great enterprise.
All living beings look up to your influence.
Only the regions beyond the Jiāng, Hú, Yuán, and Xiāng
were occupied by fierce and rebellious elements,
who had not submitted through successive generations.
With divine foresight and decisive judgment,
you commanded generals to launch punitive expeditions.
Military might was applied for a brief period,
and within a few tens of days, they were swept away and pacified.
You captured their monstrous leaders
and pardoned their rebellious crimes.
Like clouds covering and rain showering,
the eight directions came together in submission.
The sound of your teachings reached
the four furthest points.
Even the expeditions of Huángxuān,
the far-reaching strategies of Dà Yǔ,
and the glorious generations of Zhōu,
how could they surpass the present?
As for the dark stones and plain inscriptions,
recording titles from former times,
symbolized by surnames,
and announced by events,
the auspicious omens of the Hétú and Luòshū,
do not exceed this.
Furthermore, auspicious animals like the Zōuyú and Línzhǐ,
and numerous other auspicious signs have all arrived.
In the past, Xià and Yīn considered great flourishing as auspicious,
and King Wǔ of Zhōu regarded the black fish as beautiful.
All proclaimed them excellent.
However, the abundance of auspicious omens,
and the grandeur of complete offerings,
have never been as rich as they are now.
It is fitting to proclaim the grand ceremony,
to perform rituals at the Zhōngyuè,
to perform the fēng ceremony on Mount Tài,
to perform the shàn ceremony at Liángfù,
to declare your virtuous title,
to make known your supreme reverence,
to enjoy the blessings of Heaven,
to deepen the welfare of the common people,
to engrave a record for a thousand years,
and to spread your renown to future generations,
so that descendants for a hundred ages
will all be inspired.
This is the grand undertaking of emperors and kings,
and the ultimate hope of both Heaven and humanity."
The imperial edict stated:
"Although the lingering rebels have been eliminated,
externally there are alarms at the frontiers,
and internally the common people are not yet at ease.
This matter of great virtue
is not yet to be discussed."
Wèi Guàn and others further memorialized:
"Now, from the east to the sea,
to the west reaching the shifting sands,
north of the vast desert,
and south to the doors of the sun,
all are connected.
The boundless traces of Yǔ
are now truly surpassed.
Thus, the Way of Heaven and humanity is complete,
and your towering achievements are manifest.
It is fitting to perform the ritual at Liángfù,
to conduct the rites for the Earth spirits,
to ascend Mount Tài for the fēng ceremony,
and to offer sincerity to the Supreme Emperor,
in order to respond to the aspirations of humanity and the spirits.
We humbly request that the previous memorial be enacted."
The imperial edict stated:
"Now the Yīn and Yáng are not yet in harmony,
governance and punishments are not yet appropriate,
and the hundred surnames have not yet found their proper place.
How can achievements be inscribed and proclaimed complete?"
Wèi Guàn again memorialized:
"Your ministers have heard that those who occupy the position of emperor or king
must have a destined period of fate,
and a response from Heaven's mandate.
Those who achieve great merit in benefiting the people
must possess the countenance of great virtue,
and a ceremony to proclaim their completion.
There is nothing that can be falsely claimed,
and something that cannot be declined.
This has been the Way since ancient times.
Yet, the clear imperial edict is modest and humble,
repeatedly declining this ritual.
Though great virtue resides within you,
you push it away and do not accept it.
The Sān Gōng are charged with governing Heaven and Earth,
and truly control the people and affairs.
Matters of national importance
are deliberated upon here.
The Hàn dynasty's fēng and shàn ceremonies
were not overseen by these officials,
nor were they within their purview.
Your ministers' previous memorial
was to set forth the merits of your ancestors,
and the corresponding response from Heaven's mandate.
Your Majesty's virtue
has united the four seas.
Reviewing the ancients and examining the present,
it is fitting to perform this ritual.
[一六]As for deciding the specific year and month,
it requires deliberation by the Wǔfǔ,
and then a memorial to be presented.
We request that the edict and memorial be copied,
and submitted for discussion as before."
The imperial edict stated:
"Although the region south of the Jiāng has been cleared,
it was all due to the efforts of those involved in the task.
How can this be sufficient to proclaim completion?
I look forward to the collective efforts of the high officials,
to grandly advance the great transformation,
to pacify the realm,
so that the hundred surnames may benefit
and enjoy peace and rest.
This is what I hope for day and night.
There is no need to send this down to the various offices again.
Do not trouble yourselves further."
Wèi Guàn and others again memorialized:
"Your ministers have heard that the rulers of the Táng and Yú eras,
who performed great deeds benefiting the world,
all looked up to respond to Heaven's will,
and bowed down to accord with the people's aspirations.
They ascended Jièqiū,
and trod on Liángfù.
None ever declined it,
for indeed it cannot be declined.
Now, Your Majesty's accomplishments surpass those of a hundred kings,
and your virtue is unparalleled.
Your magnificent achievements and grand designs,
your towering enterprise,
are truly beyond what your ministers can fully articulate.
Yet, your sagely will is humble and modest,
repeatedly restraining itself.
When the time arrives, you do not respond,
pushing away glory and not accepting it,
thus omitting the supreme ceremony of the imperial age,
and obstructing the earnest hopes of the spirits.
This would make the canons and counsels of Dàjìn
different from the customs of the Sān and Wǔ.
Your ministers truly dare not obey the edict.
We request that the previous memorial be put into practice."
The imperial edict stated:
"It is time to jointly promote the way of governance
to bring prosperity to all undertakings."
Wait until other years,
and there will be no more disputes.”
In the winter of the first year of Tàikāng,
the princes, dukes, and officials again memorialized:
“Since ancient times, sagacious and enlightened rulers,
whose radiant virtue embraced the four seas,
have performed the fēng and shàn sacrifices on famous mountains,
as recorded in historical annals;
there have been seventy-four such sovereigns.
When Shùn and Yǔ possessed All-under-Heaven,
they made inspection tours to the four sacred mountains,
personally embodying their Way.
The Yì records ‘observing the people and inspecting the regions,’
the Lǐ has ‘ascending to the center for Heaven,’
and the Shī praises ‘ascending its high mountains’—
all are recorded in books and documents.
King Wén served as the Xībó,
submitting to the Yīn dynasty.
The Duke of Zhōu, as the ruler of Lǔ,
was ranked among the feudal lords.
Some offered sacrifices at Qíshān,
〔一七〕while others performed ceremonies at Tàishān.
Merely with sagely virtue,
they were still able to perform these rites.
Since then,
those whose merits were meager but who usurped these ceremonies
〔一八〕are too numerous to recount,
yet their posthumous titles and appellations have not vanished,
up to the present day.
How much more so for Gāozǔ Xuānhuángdì, who first established the imperial enterprise,
unifying all within the four seas;
〔一九〕Shìzōng Jǐnghuángdì, who completed it with great achievements,
pacifying and harmonizing the central states;
Tàizǔ Wénhuángdì, who received the mandate to establish the Jìn dynasty,
conquering and stabilizing Shǔ and Hàn;
and Your Majesty, who rose to power in accordance with the destined time,
unifying the six directions,
extending benevolence to all living beings,
and whose might shakes all beyond the realm.
In the past, when the Hàn dynasty lost its rule,
Wú and Shǔ stood like the legs of a tripod,
and since the start of warfare,
nearly a hundred years have passed.
The terrain was treacherous and customs diverse,
the people’s hopes were cut off by impassable barriers,
considering these areas as outside the realm,
and it had been so for a long time.
The flourishing of this great enterprise,
its brilliance shining through four generations,
subdued unrestrained rebels,
pacifying them in two reigns.
Were it not for Your Majesty’s wisdom, divine martial prowess,
and compliance with the heavens,
who could achieve such a magnificent success as this?
We, your ministers, are fortunate to have encountered this epochal gathering
in a thousand years,
personally serving under this great transformation,
witnessing the era of great peace with our own eyes.
Who would contend against the beauty of this utmost impartiality?
It is fitting to follow the precedents of previous dynasties,
to emulate the ancients,
to engrave merits on Dàiyuè,
to perform the fēng sacrifice and announce its completion,
to expand the system of rites and music,
to rectify the ceremonies of the Sānyōng,
to spread Your Majesty’s name for ten thousand generations,
and thereby to glorify the ancestors.
Therefore, overcome by this great desire,
we dare to risk death to present this.
We request the Grand Minister of Ceremonies to prepare the rituals.”
The Emperor again issued an edict saying:
“The matter you discuss is indeed a glorious undertaking of previous eras.
However, it is not yet appropriate at this time.
Let this be immediately reported and dismissed.”
Sòng Tàizǔ was on the throne for a long time
and had the intention of performing the fēng and shàn sacrifices.
He sent envoys to survey the old path on Tàishān,
and ordered the scholar Shān Qiānzhī to draft the fēng and shàn rituals.
Later, when the northern barbarians invaded the south,
and six prefectures were devastated,
his intention then ceased.
In the first year of Dà Míng of Shì Zǔ, on the day Wù Shēn of the eleventh month,
Tài Zǎi, the Prince of Jiāngxià, Yìgōng, submitted a memorial, stating:
“Only August Heaven highly extols the Great Way,
and first practiced abdication.
Down to the Jìn dynasty,
although they continued the former traditions,
their traces have been lost and their words discarded,
and what is not recorded in historical documents
cannot be singularly written about.
Those who continued the heavenly mandate,
established glorious titles,
spread their influence,
and had their deeds sung in music,
from Wúhuái onwards,
whose deeds can be transmitted and are imperishable,
are seventy-four rulers.
Without benevolence and generosity, the Way perishes;
rarely are the unrighteous prosperous and their virtue proclaimed.
Before the age of musical instruments,
long ages were severed,
difficult to know and hear.
Those clearly recorded by Qiū and Suǒ
still have lingering brilliance.
Therefore, the Yì says, ‘Before Heaven, one does not go against;
after Heaven, one follows the times.’
Indeed, the rulers of Táotáng, Yáo, Sì, Shāng, and Jī,
none did not follow this Way.
Thus, their moral influence was widely spread,
shining brightly for later generations.
The two emperors of the burning Hàn
also followed the ancient precedents,
responding to the hearts of the common people
and listening to the praises of the populace.
They rode dragon carriages, wore imperial robes,
carved jade at Liángfǔ,
declared their achievements with illustrious words,
announcing their success to the spirits above.
How much more so with the great Sòng, which manifests auspicious signs like Táng and Yú,
receiving the mandate with its pristine virtue.
Mountain dragons reveal omens,
gold and jade display auspiciousness,
unusual colors rise in Zhěnxū,
purple mist shrouds the capital region.
Granting of crowns portends the nine-five omen,
and the patterned leopard arrives at the meeting of the heavenly calendar.
These are truly the hidden blessings of the two ancestors,
and the unseen prosperity of the sacred empress.
Their Way surpasses Xuān and Yáo,
their benevolence is deeper than Tíng and Dú;
yet they still adhere to humility and restraint,
not speaking of the Fēngshàn ceremony,
which the four seas secretly find shameful.
I have heard that only the August One matches the cosmos,
and only the Emperor sacrifices to Heaven,
thus able to investigate the heavenly model above,
shining upon the black-haired people,
harmonizing with the vast sky,
and receiving these abundant blessings.
Gāo Zǔ Wǔ Huángdì’s brilliance matched the sun and moon,
his light shook the eight regions.
He rescued the submerged Jìn,
saved the world from turmoil,
rectified chaos, settled the people,
responded to Heaven, and received the mandate.
His vast achievements reached beyond the seas,
his awe-inspiring power shook beyond the sands.
Tài Zǔ Wén Huángdì embodied sageliness and practiced benevolence,
continued the work and promoted rites.
He corrected music and odes,
created astronomical calendars.
His wisdom reached the gods and spirits,
his profound benevolence covered both heaven and earth.
Rén Xiào Mìngshì,
[二０]睿武英挺,
encountered an age of difficulty and decline,
when the three powers (heaven, earth, man) were obscured.
He then rose like a dragon in the five continents,
soared like a phoenix over the nine rivers.
His person preceded the eight hundred-year cycle,
his decisions surpassed those of men and spirits.
Auspicious smoke responded to the establishment of the tall banner,
and brilliant winds corresponded to the time of his rise.
He personally eliminated the wicked and rebellious,
personally cleansed the chaos and dust.
Heaven and earth were renewed,
and husband and wife were recreated.
How can he be compared
to those who merely inherited an enterprise and continued a lineage,
who merely extended Yǔ’s traces,
whose chariots followed one gauge,
and whose writings had no different characters?
Now, the dragon-kylin has arrived,
the phoenix has displayed its auspicious form,
the linked plum has borne fruit,
the numinous mao grass has flourished.
Auspicious vapor descends as mist upon the palace terraces,
precious dew presents its flavor in the imperial gardens,
auspicious grain piles its ears upon the palace roofs,
and trees with connected branches intertwine in the imperial park.
All shine their essence in the detached palaces,
and root in the orchid gardens.
As for the white hairs with dark patterns,
the white feathers with vermilion plumes,
the auspicious signs of springs, rivers, mountains, and peaks,
and the portents of plants, trees, metals, and stones,
the petitions from distant lands and frontier regions,
and the memorials from post-stations interrupting ancestral rites—
they are all brilliant and numerous,
truly too many to recount.
The omens of great peace
are abundant here.
It is fitting to follow the sincerity of heaven and men,
and abide by the precedents of the former kings:
prepare the imperial carriage,
arrange the ceremonial retinue,
perform the Fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài,
and bury the jade at the foot of Dài.
Invite Qiáo and Sōng to the eastern chamber,
and summon Hán and Qí to the western hall.
Wave to the gatekeeper of Heaven
to open the gate,
visit the Purple Palace,
and pay homage to Tài Yī.
Play the music of Jūn Tiān,
sing the songs of Yún Mén,
praise the profound and recondite,
and surpass the fame of ancient times.
Would this not be magnificent!
I humbly pray that at this time, the Zōng Bó
be ordered to prepare these ceremonies and standards.”
An imperial edict stated:
“The Tài Zǎi’s memorial is thus.
Ancient sage kings
forever preserved their grand names,
always being hailed as foremost,
by following this Way.
I encountered many difficulties in my family,
and succeeded to a broken legacy.
My virtue is meager, and my achievements shallow;
I feel ashamed in my dreams and waking hours.
Recently, the kylin and phoenix displayed auspicious signs,
and mao grass and grain also showed omens.
Although the auspicious signs are manifest,
my shame is still deep.
I hope to follow the aspirations of my predecessors,
to pacify and purify the central realm.
When the rites for worshipping gods are performed,
I shall attempt it.”
In the fourth year, in the fourth month, on the day Xīn Hài,
the officials memorialized, saying: “I have heard that in establishing a supreme title and a governing standard,
one must observe customs to establish teachings;
in holding a proper position and embodying it,
one must examine the age to establish words.
Therefore, the successive sages of many generations
all followed that
Way.
Profound merits and supreme deeds,
like fused brilliance not yet separated,
or shining light at the end of a thread,
vanished and were not hidden.
As for those whose glorious posthumous titles soared,
their fame and splendor are recorded,
their achievements slightly heard
and listened to.
Down to Jī and Hàn,
the customs still existed,
their lingering fragrance and remaining glory
extended through records and annals.
Although years have severed the ancestral sacrifices,
and eras have transformed the essence,
it is still possible to raise the golden
splendor,
present the jade luster,
carve their traces to enlighten the present,
and engrave their virtues to beautify the distant future.
Yet the rites of offering to the four directions have been buried,
and the solemnity of performing the Fēng sacrifice on Rìguān has been relaxed.
Is this not because the work of the divine
and bright is difficult to achieve,
and the traces of foundational achievements are easily erased?
From this point onwards,
down to the very end of the era,
none did not wish to glorify their magnificent position
and firmly secure their grand reputation.
How could they merely
profoundly cultivate culture,
and deeply and obscurely govern the world?
It is understood that the silken scrolls are not presented in vain,
nor are the books buried groundlessly.
If one beats the rain and spares the gods,
and the pure shade grows back,
how can one get the purple altar?
Sùzhī,
the bamboo palace stands tall;
scattered fires cast upon the fields,
shooting stars rush to their seats.
The precious cosmic thread establishes the first foundation,
taming spirits and ordaining the calendar.
Virtue restores the sagging order,
merit aids the submerged phenomena.
Profound
immersion flows profusely,
glorious essence subtly moistens.
The norm of eternal governance is preserved,
thoughts are detailed in establishing the distant.
Emperor Tàizǔ Wén, having initiated the grand destiny,
his bright hopes shone forth.
He collected music to harmonize customs,
assembled rites to promulgate standards.
Ancestors and descendants mutually reflected,
their traces re-illumined.
The sagacious sovereign stores the registry by the Fánhé,
soars and hovers by the Hénghàn.
The golden waves obscure the illumination,
the glorious radiance halts its brightness.
Movement arrives with the opportune moment,
leaping and flying, lifted by the wind.
Clearing the miasma from the Hǎi and Dài,
opening up the bright
central region.
Resting the spirits and restoring their power,
rejuvenating heaven and re-illuminating.
The legitimate heir firmly positioned in universal brightness,
the mighty peaks flourish in the celestial ranks.
Thus, auspicious signs reflect the prosperous foundation,
connected to the origins of the
scripted texts.
Furthermore, arranging court ceremonies,
adorning decrees with detailed rituals.
Compiling what was lost and neglected,
seeking out what was scattered and abandoned.
Presenting jade in the suburban palace,
offering gui-jade at the Xuanzhi.
Auspiciousness gathers at the Heavenly
Temple,
the earth veins bless agriculture.
At the arrival of the season, in the morning sun,
rivers and hills perform ancient rites.
The majestic authority patrols the
central plains,
historians transmit their odes,
the people admire their style.
Thereupon
concealed tracks reveal the shadows,
vibrating sounds echo with might.
The leaders of successive dynasties,
submerged within their aspirations.
The chiefs of peace and marquises,
wise kings attending the court.
Unusual beings and strange auras,
presenting customs and returning to their homes.
Winged creatures and plant forms,
their sounds cherished, their forms transformed.
Border silks cease correspondence,
authority's light dims its flame.
The Heavenly Dài emits spiritual energy,
the Zōnghé opens its treasures.
Lofty hills submerge their tripods,
radiance flashes in the Sì
Yuan.
Cloudy emperors and kingly peaks,
spreading their literary grace across the
Hàn. Paired horns sound together,
perching and soaring in the forbidden areas.
Scaly armor with frosty beaks,
fluttering and dancing in the river market.
Glorious springs flow like mirrors,
later illuminating the river
source.
Thus, waves boil beyond the outer passes,
clouds steam within the inner marshes.
Such as snow-footed green feathers,
dark patterns and crimson colors,
sun and moon in the suburban fields,
choosing trees to make sounds.
Moreover,
glorious dew rises to the carriage,
sparse clouds cover the pavilions.
Hàogǎo and Yǐngchuan yield shoots,
transferring their splendor to the deep forbidden areas.
Mountain chariots stand poised,
cloud-jias stretch their wings.
Sea-dies swim and flow,
river-maos sprout shade.
The ranks of collators,
look up and adorn their words with their brushes.
The vassals of Jì and Dài,
offer their towns to await the rites.
Is this not the vitality of the spirit flourishing,
the auspiciousness of things illuminated by clouds?
Púxuān and guī
zhěn,
clear springs with pure fragrance.
Grand Tutor Jiāngxiàwáng, your subject Yìgōng, savors the Way and follows the virtuous,
extracting the wondrous and beautifying the ancient.
Comprehensively enriching records and histories,
applying details to hidden records.
Indicating that his merits surpass those of the past,
his virtue
shines upon Yán and Hào.
His literary accomplishments ascend to the central peak,
his name recorded in the Heavenly Pass.
His glory crowns illustrious fame,
spreading and asserting his renown.
Yet he humbly claims to be foremost,
respectfully yielding with modesty.
He will ensure that the profound earth spirit's
view is not lacking,
and that mysterious auspiciousness arrives on schedule.
Liángfǔ will not lack the appearance of great virtue,
Jièqiū will not miss the sound of ascending fame.
Furthermore, the wilderness of Qióngquán
presents the steeds of eight generations.
The land of jiāo
wood,
offers the precious golden kū-wood.
Reverently manifesting spiritual power,
precious talismans bestow blessings.
I humbly reflect, Your Majesty's plans are detailed and profound,
extending into excellent chapters.
Relying on omens of divine spirits,
polishing
the luster of reputation and deeds.
Consulting auspicious times and examining ancient practices,
solemnly arranging the alert ranks.
Scholarly officials display their talents,
ritual officers coordinate the ceremonies.
Suspended chimes move with sound,
great bells ring out the rhythm.
The sun-drenched path is properly guarded,
the main
road is clear and restricted.
Thereupon, adjusting the jade pendants,
straightening the jade tassels.
Chirping phoenixes stand poised to the rhythm,
soaring carriages stream with patterns.
Variegated colors resemble auspicious forms,
brightly illustrating the garments for counting ages.
Brilliant banners shine in the heavenly array,
adorned figures move divinely.
Emerald canopies embrace the shade,
feathered splendor arrays its light.
Then, an edict was issued for combined efforts to manage the sacrifices,
guests to assist in the rituals.
Golden stands are hung for the night,
bronze bells and stone chimes
resonate.
Commanding the five spirits to arrange in order,
opening the nine gates to gather the spirits.
Alerting the guards to open the clouds,
sending the rain deities to sprinkle the road first.
Haze congeals to form palace gates,
smoke rises
to form palaces.
Terraces crowned with crimson light,
altars float in white mist.
Then, approaching the central altar,
preparing the grand rituals.
Heaven bestows auspicious gifts,
solidifying the imperial foundation.
Valleys echo with divine sounds,
mountains
transmit responding echoes.
Thereafter, discerning the age and inquiring of the elders,
presenting poems to observe customs.
Returning offerings to inform the spirits,
presenting relics to the clear temple.
The greatness of its splendor
shines for ten thousand ages;
the intensity of its profound auspiciousness
overflows to infinity.

“Tàicháng wishes to restore the two lords to complete the seven generations,

Sūn Shèng's Jìn Chūnqiū states:
“The Yángqiū Zhuàn says,
‘A subject and a son are alike.’
Even if one succeeds to the ruler's position,
one should not, on account of later reverence,
demote or abandon former respect.
Formerly, Duke Xī of Lǔ succeeded Duke Zhuāng,
and was deemed rebellious for treating him as an elder brother and ascending to his position.
This was deemed rebellious.
According to ancient principles,
the clear edict is correct.”
In the seventh month of the second year of Yǒnghé, Emperor Mù,
the relevant officials memorialized:
“During the grand sacrifice (yīnjì) in the tenth month,
the Lord of Jīngzhào should be moved to the tiāo chamber.
Formerly, the spirit tablets of the three lords — Zhēngxī, Yùzhāng, and Yǐngchuān — were destroyed.
At the beginning of the restoration,
they were temporarily placed in the imperial treasury,
to the west of the temple gate.
During the Xiánkāng era,
Tàicháng Féng Huái memorialized to have them returned and placed in the western side chamber,
calling it a tiāo.
This is also questionable in terms of ritual.
Now that Jīngzhào is moving in,
he becomes the fourth-generation distant ancestor,
long positioned above Tàizǔ.
In ancient times, in the Zhōu dynasty, Tàizǔ's generation was distant,
so there was a place for his spirit tablet to be moved to.
Now, in the Jìn temple, Emperor Xuān is the principal spirit,
but four ancestors reside there,
which means lowering the ancestors to accommodate the grandson.
The grand sacrifice (yīnji) being above [the principal spirit]
means replacing Tàizǔ.”
The acting Sītú Cài Mó discussed:
“The four lords should have separate chambers built for them,
if that is not yet feasible,
they should enter and occupy the chambers of the Grand Ancestral Temple.
No one dares to humble their ancestors;
Wén and Wǔ did not precede Bùqú.
On the day of the grand sacrifice,
Zhēngxī should face east,
positioned above Emperor Xuān.
Thereafter, the spirit tablets moved from the temple
should be stored in Zhēngxī's tiāo,
and offerings should continue without interruption.”
Hùjūn Jiāngjūn Féng Huái memorialized:
“The rites state,
‘For those without a temple,
an altar is erected for sacrifice.’
A separate chamber can be built to store them,
and during the grand decennial sacrifice (yīndì),
they would be sacrificed to at the altar.”
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Qiáo Wáng Sīmǎ Wúqí and others discussed:
“Various scholars believe that the spirit tablets of Tàiwáng and Wángjì were moved and stored in the tiāo of Wén and Wǔ.
If so,
the spirit tablets of the lords, when moved,
should be within Emperor Xuān's temple.
However, there are no sleeping chambers (qǐnshì) now,
so it is appropriate to adapt and build anew.
Also, during the grand pentennial sacrifice (yīnxia) in the Grand Ancestral Temple,
Zhēngxī should face east.”
Shàngshū Láng Sūn Chuò agreed with Wúqí's discussion.
He said:
“Although Tàizǔ's position initially reached the highest rank,
his Dao was expansive,
he transcended the honor of human rank,
〔三０〕and upheld the Dao of natural human relationships,
thereby establishing the fundamental teachings and glorifying a hundred generations.”
Shàngshū Láng Xú Chán discussed:
“The rites state,
‘When a tiāo is removed, it becomes an altar (tán);
when an altar is removed, it becomes a levelled area (shàn);
during the annual grand sacrifice (suìxia), they are sacrificed to.’
Now the spirit tablets of the four ancestors, when moved,
can be stored in a stone chamber.
When there is a prayer, they can be sacrificed to at the altar or levelled area.”
Then Chán was sent to Kuàijī to consult the recluse Yú Xǐ.
Xǐ replied:
“In the Hàn dynasty, Wéi Xuánchéng and others buried the destroyed spirit tablets in the imperial park.
In the Wèi dynasty, deliberators said they should be buried between the two steps.
Moreover, the spirit tablets were originally in the Grand Ancestral Temple;
if they are now sacrificed to in a separate chamber,
it is better to store them permanently.
Furthermore, the four lords received no posthumous titles,
which further clarifies that they should be destroyed and not sacrificed to.”
Thereupon, Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn Kuàijī Wáng Sīmǎ Yù, Shàngshū Liú Shào, and others memorialized:
“The four ancestors reside together in the western tiāo,
their spirit tablets stored in a stone chamber,
and are sacrificed to during the grand decennial and pentennial sacrifices (dìxia),
following the old custom of the former court.”
At that time, Fàn Xuān of Chénliú's nephew asked about this rite.
Xuān replied:
“Those sacrificed to in Shùn's temple
were all commoners.
Later, when their generations were distant, their spirit tablets were destroyed.
They were not placed above Shùn,
nor were they ordered by zhāo and mù.
Now the titles of the four lords still follow their original ones,
not because of their merit or virtue to warrant the rite.
If following the burial of Yú's spirit tablets,
they are still stored in the place of descendants;
if following the burial of Xià's spirit tablets,
it is again not between the steps of the original temple.
One should consider a change,
and build a separate chamber.
If the kin relationship is not yet exhausted, they should be sacrificed to during the dìxia,
positioned above Emperor Xuān;
if the kin relationship is exhausted, there is no reason for them to be positioned among the descendants.”
Thereafter, Tàicháng Liú Xiá and others agreed with Cài Mó's discussion.
Bóshì Zhāng Píng discussed:
“Some may wonder if those displayed with Tàizǔ
are all spirit tablets that were later destroyed.
〔三一〕I, Píng, examine ancient principles and find no text that distinguishes between before and after.
Yǔ did not precede Gǔn,
so placing the moved spirit tablets above Tàizǔ
should also be unquestionable.”
In the fourth month of the ninth year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān,
there was to be an Yīn sacrifice.
An edict was issued for extensive discussion on the rites of relocation and destruction (of ancestral tablets).
Sīmǎ Déwén (司馬德文), King of Lángxié and Grand Marshal, deliberated:
“At the beginning of Tàishǐ,
the position of Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) was left vacant,
and out of sentiment, going back far,
up to the General who Pacifies the West (Zhēngxī),
it was deemed appropriate to destroy the tablets when their generations ended.
However, Emperor Xuān (Xuān Huángdì) occupies the position of Grand Ancestor.
Furthermore, Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn (Hàn Guāngwǔdì) moved the ancestral tablets of eleven emperors to Luòyì,
meaning the tablets were destroyed and not re-established.
The principle can thus be inferred.
It is advisable to follow Fàn Xuān’s (范宣) suggestion
to build a separate chamber to house the tablets of the four noble lords (fǔjūn),
to be permanently stored and not worshipped.”
Xú Guǎng (徐廣), Grand Minister of Agriculture, deliberated:
“The four noble lords once occupied the foremost position in the ancestral temple,
receiving sacrifices from across the land.
If they are to be buried in the netherworld,
it may not fully align with sentiment and reason.
I propose that they be relocated and stored in the western repository,
to serve as distant ancestral spirits (yuǎntiāo),
and that the dì and xiǎng sacrifices be permanently discontinued.”
Yuán Bào (袁豹), Attendant Aide to the Grand Commandant, deliberated:
“Remain as before, without change.
The Yīn sacrifice still extending to the four noble lords
is reasonable and fitting.”
Zāng Táo (臧燾), Director of the Bureau of Sacrifices, deliberated:
“As for the tablets of the four noble lords,
if the rites of sacrifice are abolished,
then the spirits will not depend on them either.
It is advisable to inter them like the tablet of Yú (Yú Zhǔ).”
At that time, Gāozǔ (高祖) assisted the Jìn (Jìn),
and his view aligned with that of the Grand Marshal.
The reform awaited implementation after the Yīn sacrifice.
In the fifth month, on the day of Rénxū, of the twelfth year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn (Jìn Xiàowǔdì),
an edict stated:
“When the Grand Ancestral Temple was established in the past,
every matter followed frugality and restraint,
with the thought of the whole land
striving to prepare the rites.
Moreover, the position of Grand Ancestor was left vacant,
and the Bright Hall (Míngtáng) has not yet been built.
The suburban sacrifice (jiāosì)
is a great affair of the state,
yet the ancient regulations are incomplete.
This should be thoroughly discussed.”
Xú Miǎo (徐邈), Director of the Bureau of Sacrifices, deliberated:
“Regarding the suburban sacrifice at the Circular Mound (Yuánqiū),
there is no ambiguity in the classics;
Emperor Xuān (Xuān Huángdì) once clarified this matter.
Having examined it against the sacred classics,
and further, since the restoration (zhōngxīng),
it has been thoroughly studied
to establish the two northern and southern suburbs (of the altar).
It is truly not something that can be lightly altered by heterodox scholars.
I propose remaining as before for stability.
When Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ Huángdì) established the temple,
it followed the 'six generations, three zhāo and three mù' rule.
Emperor Xuān (Xuān Huángdì), who laid the foundation,
is truly the Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ).
He is the royal grandfather by kinship.
With four temples above him,
and not yet having passed through the prescribed generations for relocation,
the east-facing position was temporarily left vacant.
Succession between brothers
does not count as two generations.
Therefore, in the present temple worship,
the number of generations is not yet sufficient.
If one desires to establish the Grand Ancestor in his rightful position now,
it would violate the principle of 'serving seven generations'.
Moreover, the rites say, 'A son of a concubine who becomes king also offers the dì sacrifice to his ancestor and establishes a temple.'
This implies that if a branch lineage is granted the throne,
then their close relatives must be reinstated.
The noble lord of Jīngzhào (Jīngzhào fǔjūn) is now six generations away.
It is fitting to re-establish this chamber,
meaning Emperor Xuān (Xuān Huángdì) is not yet above the sixth generation.
Only after the earlier generations have been relocated
can the Grand Ancestor's position be finalized.
When the Jīngzhào tablet is relocated and destroyed,
it should be stored in a stone chamber.
Even then, it would not yet qualify for the dì and xiá sacrifices.
Why?
The tradition states that a destroyed tablet ascends and is united with the Grand Ancestor.
‘Ascending’ is a term from a lower position;
it does not mean that a revered one can descend to a lowly position.
The four tablets of the crown prince and the imperial grand-son in the hidden chamber (yīnshì),
given their importance as heirs,
should ascend and be enshrined in the temple where the imperial ancestor (huángzǔ) is worshipped.
〔三二〕When their generations are distant, they should be relocated,
and then the grandson who partakes in the sacrifices,
will be destroyed along with them.
As for the circular and square form of the Bright Hall (Míngtáng),
its general principles have been laid out,
and the sacrifice to the co-emperor should not be omitted.
Furthermore, a king takes the whole world as his home,
not necessarily just one region.
Thus, there was no abandonment of the two capitals by King Píng of Zhōu (Zhōu Píng) or Emperor Guāngwǔ.
The Duke of Zhōu (Zhōu Gōng) sacrificed to King Wén as his ancestor,
and Emperor Míng of Hàn (Hàn Míng) paired him with the Ancestor of the World (Shìzǔ).
Other than a newly founding ancestor (wéixīn zhī kǎo),
who else could be paired with the Supreme Emperor (Shàngdì)?”
Miǎo (邈) further said:
“The deity to be paired in the Bright Hall (Míngtáng)
has long been a subject of unresolved doubt.
According to the Yì (Yì),
‘Yīn offers sacrifice to the Supreme Emperor (Shàngdì),
pairing him with ancestors (zǔkǎo).’
If ancestors (zǔkǎo) are paired with him,
then the Supreme Emperor (Shàngdì) is also Heaven,
and the meaning of ‘stern father’ becomes evident.
The Zhōulǐ (Zhōulǐ) states that when there is a reason to offer the lǚ sacrifice to the Supreme Emperor (Shàngdì),
announcing to Heaven and the regular suburban sacrifice use four jade tablets equally,
hence they are mentioned together.
If the Supreme Emperor (Shàngdì) refers to the Five Emperors (Wǔ Dì),
〔三三〕why does the classic not say ‘sacrifice to Heaven and lǚ to the Five Emperors,’
or ‘sacrifice to Earth and lǚ to the Four Directions (Sì Wàng)’?
The human emperor (rén dì) and the heavenly emperor (tiān dì),
though both are general terms for heaven and man,
the five directions cannot be called Supreme Emperor (Shàngdì),
nor can feudal lords be called Great Rulers (Dà Jūn).
There is no complete proof in the Shū (Shū),
and the meaning allows for both interpretations,
hence during the periods of Tàishǐ and Tàikāng,
different practices of establishment and abolition were used alternately.”
Chē Yìn (車胤), Attendant Minister, concurred.
〔三四〕He further said:
“The regulations for the Bright Hall (Míngtáng)
are indeed difficult to detail.
Furthermore, music focuses on harmony,
and rites focus on reverence.
Thus, the simple and refined styles differ,
and musical instruments are also distinct.
Since thatched huts and grand mansions
do not have a single standard,
why must one adhere to its specific form
and not know how to promote the fundamental principle of according with the people?
Only when the nine regions are all peaceful
and the region north of the Yellow River (Héshuò) is free of dust,
then the Bright Hall (Míngtáng) and the Imperial Academy (Bìyōng)
can be exalted and repaired.”
Wáng Mín (王珉), Director of the Central Secretariat, shared Yìn’s (胤) opinion.
Kǒng Wāng (孔汪), Grand Master of Ceremonies, deliberated: 〔三五〕
“The reason for sacrificing to the four noble lords (fǔjūn) at the beginning of Tàishǐ
was truly because their generations were still close,
and they could receive sacrifices.
This is not like the ancient generations of Yīn and Zhōu,
from whom the royal lineage originated.
If the noble lord of Jīngzhào (Jīngzhào) had been beyond the seventh generation at that time,
these four kings would naturally not have been sacrificed to.
Inferring from this, after their tablets are destroyed,
the Yīn dì sacrifice will be discontinued.”
Wáng Chén (王忱), Director of the Bureau of Civil Office, deliberated:
“The Bright Hall (Míngtáng) embodies the heavens and symbolizes the earth.
It is a great and magnificent structure,
which should await the restoration of the imperial residence to its former state,
and only then be repaired.”
Sīmǎ Dàozǐ (司馬道子), King of Kuàijī and General of Agile Cavalry, and Xiè Shí (謝石), Minister of the Secretariat, shared Chén’s (忱) opinion.
Consequently, everything was carried out without any changes.
In the sixth month of the second year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
Kǒng Ān-guó (white-clad official, acting Grand Master of Ceremonies, Right Minister of the Secretariat) submitted:
"In the summer of the third year of Yuánxīng,
the Yīn sacrifice was due.
In the third month of the previous year,
the imperial carriage returned.
In the fourth month of that year,
the Yīn sacrifice was due,
but Xú Gān and other Erudites of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices argued: 'It should be performed in the first month of autumn.'
The Secretariat's investigation found that from the fourth year of Tàihé onwards, it had consistently been performed in winter or summer.
Since Gān and others had already conceded that it should be performed in the first month of winter,
they later asserted that the first month of autumn was not a mistake.
Fàn Tài, the Censor-in-Chief, argued: 'Although now, after the enthronement of the new emperor in the ancestral temple,
it is permissible to perform the zhēng and cháng sacrifices,
there is no comparison to the Yīn offering.
The Yīn sacrifice was due in the tenth month of the twenty-first year of Tàiyuán,
but Emperor Lièzōng passed away in the ninth month of that year.
It was not until the third year of Lóng'ān,
when the state was auspicious,
that the Yīn ritual was performed.
Moreover, the Rites state that during mourning, auspicious sacrifices are suspended,
and the new lord is sacrificed to in the sleeping quarters.
Now, since no separate sleeping quarters are set up,
once enthroned,
sacrifices are performed in the temple.
Therefore, the four-season zhēng and cháng sacrifices
are for expressing thoughts of remembrance,
and the three-year dì sacrifice
is for maintaining the order of zhāo and mù;
their meanings are fundamentally different.
When the three years of mourning are complete,
one joins in the ancestral meals with the Grand Ancestor.
When the time comes, the Yīn sacrifice is performed,
with no need to limit it to thirty months.
This is likely because the inner bureau has consistently applied the month limit in the past.'
Even if what he says is true,
the Yīn sacrifice can be performed during mourning.
In the early Lóng'ān period,
it was indeed suspended due to mourning.
The number of months, whether too few or too many,
again leads to a deviation from the proper timing.
As for performing it when it should be in the sleeping quarters,
the reasoning is not yet clear."
Ān-guó further submitted:
"Fàn Tài said: 'Now that he is enthroned,
sacrifices are performed in the temple,
hence the four-season zhēng and cháng sacrifices.'
According to Tài's statement,
the Yīn and zhēng/cháng sacrifices
are fundamentally different.
After enthronement, one may personally perform the zhēng and cháng sacrifices but not the Yīn sacrifice.
Liú Jǐn of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices said: 'Empress Zhāng's mourning period has not yet completed a full year,
so sacrifices should not be performed.'
I have investigated: in the fifth month of the fifth year of Shēngpíng,
Emperor Mù passed away;
in the seventh month of that year,
he was interred in the imperial tomb;
in the tenth month,
the Yīn sacrifice was performed.
In the second month of the third year of Xīngníng,
Emperor Āi passed away.
In the fifth month of the first year of Tàihé,
Lady Yǔ of Hǎixī (then empress) passed away;
in the seventh month,
she was buried;
in the tenth month,
the Yīn sacrifice was performed.
These instances occurred within two full years of Emperor Āi's passing, and after Lady Yǔ's burial.
The texts of the two Yīn proclamations are still in the temple.
Furthermore, Empress Dowager Wén passed away in the seventh month of the fourth year of Lóng'ān.
His Majesty, following previous instructions,
personally observed the severe mourning rites.
In the tenth month of the fifth year,
the Yīn sacrifice was performed.
Within two full years,
it was not suspended.
Now, because of the mourning for the junior consort,
Tài instead says that the great ritual cannot be performed.
I have investigated that from the tenth year of Yǒnghé until now, for over fifty years,
the Yīn sacrifice has consistently been performed every thirty months,
all recorded in annotations,
which is in accordance with the rites:
two Yīn sacrifices in five years.
What Tài said
is not a genuine challenge to me,
but rather implies that the timing of the sacred dynasty's practices
is either too early or too late.
As the Censor-in-Chief, Tài
should naturally discern right from wrong.
If my submission is not approved,
Yet he has procrastinated and delayed,
thus neglecting his former duties.
I request that Tài and Jǐn be dismissed from office."
On the day Dīngsì,
an imperial edict commanded that all should hold their positions as white-clad officials.
Thereupon, the Erudite Xú Gān and all others were dismissed from office.
Initially, in the fourth month of the third year of Yuánxīng,
the Yīn sacrifice was not performed; it was moved to the tenth month.
If calculated by the usual limit,
If a new starting point is established,
then it should be performed in the fourth month of next year.
Wáng Mì, acting Grand Minister of Works, and Mèng Chǎng, Administrator of Dānyáng, argued:
"When there is an extraordinary joyous event,
there must be extraordinary rites.
The former standard for the Yīn sacrifice is not incorrect;
it is generally applied to regular circumstances.
As for the joyous event of Yìxī,
it is unprecedented in ancient times;
although called a 'return of the imperial carriage,'
its principle is akin to receiving the Mandate of Heaven.
We believe that the renewal of governance
begins at this point.
It should be performed in the fourth month."
Xiè Hùn, Central Leader of the Army, and Liú Jǐn, Grand Master of Ceremonies, argued:
"The Yīn sacrifice has no fixed date;
respect is shown by considering the timing,
and the spirit of the rites values simplicity.
The sacrifice performed in the tenth month of last year,
though deviating in date,
was complete in spirit and ritual,
and should properly be maintained as the standard."
Xú Gān, Erudite of the Imperial University, argued:
"The xiá sacrifice once every three years,
and the dì sacrifice once every five years,
are recorded in the classics and commentaries,
but there is no mention of making up for the Yīn sacrifice."
Xú Guǎng, Gentleman-in-Waiting to the Emperor (supernumerary, acting Literary Editor), argued:
"Considering previous events:
In the tenth month of the sixth year of Tàihé,
Duke Hǎixī performed the Yīn sacrifice.
In the tenth month of the second year of Níngkāng,
Emperor Xiàowǔ performed the Yīn sacrifice.
If we follow the usual thirty months from the previous one,
then it should have been performed in the fourth month.
At that time, there must have been some reason
for it to be moved to winter,
but the specific reason is unclear.
The Yīn sacrifice in the tenth month of the first year of Tàiyuán,
according to the usual thirty months,
should have been performed in the fourth month of the second year.
This implies that the Yīn sacrifice in the tenth month of the Xīnwèi year
was performed a second time before sixty months had passed.
'The xiá sacrifice follows the former rulers,
with accumulated numbers as the limit.'
'From the eighth year of Xī to the second year of Wén,
it is known as the xiá sacrifice.'
Thus,
to establish the beginning,
to trace the source and form the flow,
the principles of understanding and assembly
are distantly rooted in the ancestral origin.
In past years, there were reasons for postponement,
which were not regular.
The previous events of Níngkāng and Tàiyuán can be followed.
Although there are differences in the closeness or remoteness of the years,
the principle of retrospective calculation is the same.
We believe that following the return to the regular sequence
is the way to restore correctness."
Liú Rùn-zhī, Left Administrator, and others argued:
"The Yīn sacrifice was due in the fourth month of the first year of Tàiyuán,
but the ritual officials neglected their duty
and set it for the tenth month.
This was not the correct period,
and it should not be taken as the starting point simply because of the error.
It should revert to the initial fourth month as the starting point.
It should be performed in the tenth month of the third year."
The Ministry of Personnel submitted a memorial adopting Wáng Mì's argument,
taking the tenth month of the first year as the starting point.
On the *wùzǐ* day of the twelfth month of the first year of Xiàojiàn of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng,
the relevant officials reported:
"According to the old rules, the tenth month of this first year is the month for *Yīncí*.
Fàn Tài, the *lǐng Cáo láng* and a participant in the discussion,
the *yīnjì* should be performed after the second anniversary.
Considering that the second anniversary of the mourning falls in the third month,
if the *yīn* sacrifice were to be held in the fourth month,
it would still be within the period of *dǎn*."
The matter was submitted to the officials of rites for deliberation and rectification.
Sū Wěishēng, the *guózǐ zhùjiào*, debated:
"According to the rites,
after the three-year mourning period is completed,
then the *xiá* sacrifice is performed at the Grand Ancestor's temple.
It also says, 'For three years, no sacrifices are offered,
except to Heaven, Earth, and the altars of grain and soil;
the *fú* [armband of mourning] is removed and affairs are conducted.'
Moreover, not observing *dǎn* and immediately sacrificing [to the ancestors]
was criticized in the *Chūnqiū*.
Seeking guidance from ancient rites,
before the mourning attire is set aside,
there is certainly no meaning to libations and offerings.
Since Emperor Wén of Hàn,
a provisional system has been adopted,
where all matters concerning ancestral temples and court audiences
are considered auspicious.
Although the *xiáng* and *dǎn* rites nominally exist,
there is no change in *jīnggǎo* [white silk mourning clothes],
are no different from ordinary days.
Since the rites for *Yīncí* are not different,
how can personal sorrow be the sole impediment?"
Xú Hóng, the *tàixué bóshì*, debated:
"Although the three-year mourning period
follows a provisional system,
at the *xiáng* ceremony of the second anniversary,
one still wears white mourning attire,
which is not yet fully auspicious.
proposed that, following the precedent of the third year of Yǒngchū,
It is suggested that the coming fourth month
is not suitable for *Yīn*.
The tenth month would be appropriate."
Zhū Yīngzhī, the *tàicháng chéng*, debated:
"The *Yú Lǐ* says: 'If *dǎn* is performed in the middle month,
then in that month auspicious sacrifices are made,
but the spouse is not yet paired.'
This means that after the *dǎn* sacrifice in the twenty-seventh month,
on the day of the four seasonal sacrifices,
the deceased's consort is not yet paired,
as grief has not yet been forgotten.
Inferring from this,
one may not sacrifice before *dǎn*.
Also, in the second year of Duke Mǐn of *Chūnqiū*,
an auspicious *dì* sacrifice was performed for Duke Zhuāng.
Zhèng Xuán commented: 'Duke Mǐn was fearful of disaster
and sought to elevate and strengthen himself to avert misfortune.
He removed mourning after a total of twenty-two months,
and did not observe *dǎn*.'
The phrase 'did not observe *dǎn*'
makes it clear that *dì* sacrifices are not allowed during the *dǎn* period.
It is noted that Wáng Sù and others stated in the Wèi court
that it is expedient now to preserve ancient rites,
waiting until the three years are completed.
The old saying is that after the three-year mourning is complete,
if it meets *dì*, then *dì*; if it meets *xiá*, then *xiá*.
Zhèng Xuán said: '*Dì* is in early summer,
*xiá* is in early autumn.'
Now, the tenth month is customarily used.
Regarding the text of *Gōngyáng* cited by Hóng,
if there is doubt,
it also refers to Duke Mǐn of Lǔ establishing the mourning attire,
thus speaking of the regulations for mourning.
Why must it fully endorse auspicious *dì* sacrifices while wearing plain caps?
Even if *Gōngyáng* has a different view,
officials take the rites as correct,
and should also seek to measure appropriateness."
Zhōu Jǐngyuǎn, the *lángzhōng* and a participant in the discussion, debated:
"On the tenth day of the ninth month of the third year of Yǒngchū, Fù Liàng's memorial stated: 'A provisional system is auspicious;
it is fitting for governing the world.
For major rites of the ancestral temple,
it is appropriate to follow ancient classics.'
This became the established standard for the founding of Imperial Sòng.
Therefore, the proposals of *bóshì* Xú Hóng and *tàicháng chéng* Zhū Yīngzhī to perform *Yīncí* in the tenth month of the coming year are appropriate."
The edict approved.
All *Yīnjì* in the Sòng dynasty were performed only after being deemed auspicious.
On the *xīnhài* day of the second month of the seventh year of Dàmíng,
the relevant officials reported:
"The *Yīncí* is due in the fourth month.
If it cannot be performed then,
may it be performed in early autumn or not?"
Zhōu Jǐngyuǎn, the *lǐngjūn chángshǐ*, debated:
"According to the *Lǐjì*, it says: 'The Son of Heaven performs *xiá*, *dì*, *xiá*, *cháng*, *xiá*, *zhēng*.'
According to the ritual text,
then all three seasons—summer, autumn, and winter—are for *Yīn*,
not just winter and summer.
In early Yìxī of Jìn,
Kǒng Ānguó, the *púyè*, memorialized,
stating that since the fourth year of Tàihé, *Yīnjì* were always performed in winter and summer.
Ānguó also memorialized that from the tenth year of Yǒnghé until now, for over fifty years,
*Yīncí* has been performed every thirty months.
*Bóshì* Xú Qián challenged Ānguó based on the rites.
Qián also cited the *Yīncí* in the seventh month of the sixth year of Xiánkāng of Jìn,
showing it was not exclusively in winter and summer.
Although the Jìn court at that time did not follow Qián's proposal,
Qián's arguments based on rites and Xiánkāng precedents
left Ānguó with no way to refute them.
If the coming fourth month is not suitable for *Yīncí*,
moving it to early autumn
would not violate the rites."
The participants in the discussion, based on ritual evidence,
deemed it appropriate to use early autumn.
The edict approved.
On the *jǐyǒu* day of the eleventh month of the fifth year of Xiánníng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
Empress Dowager Yáng, the *hóngxùn*, passed away.
The ancestral temples ceased sacrifices for a season,
and music was removed from Heaven and the Bright Hall,
and *zuò* [sacrificial meat] was not offered.
On the *jǐmǎo* day of the tenth month of the fifth year of Shēngpíng,
during the *Yīncí*,
music was not performed due to the passing of Emperor Mù.
Earlier, during Yǒngjiā,
Jiāng Tǒng, the *sànqí chángshì*, debated:
"The meaning of *Yángqiū* is
to remove music and complete the affair."
This shows that even for auspicious sacrifices, music was sometimes omitted.
Therefore, it was practiced at the end of Shēngpíng.
Subsequently, Jiāng Yōu, the *tàicháng*, memorialized:
"After the burial of Emperor Mù, for the *Yīnjì* in the tenth month,
following the advice of *tàicháng* Qiū Yí and others,
music was withdrawn.
Yōu extensively reviewed the current Hàn system,
which has no distinction for special sacrifices.
Since it is an auspicious *dì* sacrifice entering the temple,
why should there be doubt about music?"
The historian commented: Hearing music is not joyful,
thus emotions are expressed by stopping it.
As for *liàng'àn* [strict mourning] and removing mourning attire,
it is out of concern for the neglect of governance.
Therefore, discretion is exercised to implement changes,
weighing the severity and making concessions.
As for playing music versus silencing sounds,
it does not affect government affairs.
Even if there is lingering doubt between the two,
it is certainly appropriate to follow grief out of affection.
In the Sòng era, when there was a national misfortune,
temple sacrifices were suspended without music.
Collation Notes
Treatise 7, Rites 4
On the *gēngwǔ* day of the fifth month of the third year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
because Xú Xiànzhī and others had been executed,
and the shame and hatred avenged,
silk was offered to the Grand Ancestral Temple.
On the *jiǎyín* day of the twelfth month of the third year of Yuánjiā,
when campaigning west against Xiè Huì,
offerings were made to the Grand Ancestral Temple and the Grand Altar of Soil.
After Huì was pacified,
the imperial carriage returned,
and offerings were made again.
In the seventh month of the sixth year of Yuánjiā [429 CE],
Xú Dàoyú, a Doctoral Scholar of the Imperial Academy, submitted a memorial stating:
"I humbly observe that in the ceremonial procedures for the zhēngcháng sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
after the Emperor has completed the rites,
he proceeds to the convenient seat.
The Three Dukes and officials above them present offerings.
The Grand Invoker escorts the spirits to the gate.
Then His Majesty returns and bows,
the hundred officials perform the praise-bow,
and only then do they withdraw.
I carefully reflect on the way of the Clear Temple,
which is to solemnly pacify the spirits.
The Lǐ [Book of Rites] says,
'A temple is a semblance.'
It is where the spirits rely and reside.
One serves the departed as if they were present,
as if they are always there.
Therefore, there should not be any text about 'escorting the spirits.'
From the arrangement of the ritual vessels (dòu and zǔ)
to the arrival and departure of the imperial carriage,
no welcoming is performed.
If one does not welcome but then escorts,
and escorts before taking leave,
this humble understanding [of mine]
truly finds it uncomprehending.
According to private sacrifices of people today,
they indeed both welcome and escort,
because they have no temple,
hoping to induce the spirits to descend and attend.
This arises from personal sentiment [rather than established rites],
and is not the ritual of a king.
Although the Yílǐ [Book of Etiquette and Ceremonial] states that the Grand Invoker welcomes the 'shī' (representative of the dead) at the gate,
this is a ceremony for inviting the 'shī,'
how could it be a canon for revering the spirits?
I fear there is a doubt regarding the ritual.
I respectfully submit this deliberation."
The relevant authorities then presented a memorial to the ritual officials for detailed deliberation and judgment.
Jiāng Suì, a Doctoral Scholar, deliberated:
"Not welcoming at the start
makes it clear they are already in the temple.
Escorting at the completion of the ritual
regulates filial devotion.
If one does not escort but takes leave,
it is like abandoning one's parents.
If one takes leave before escorting,
it is like dismissing the spirits.
Therefore, a filial son cannot bear to abandon his parents,
nor can he bear to dismiss the spirits.
Hence, the Invoker and Scribe escort the spirits to complete the meaning of the zhēngcháng sacrifice."
Hè Dàoqī, a Doctoral Scholar, deliberated:
"Music is used to welcome the arrival,
and sorrow to bid farewell.
The Jìtǒng [Treatise on Ritual Practice] states: 'One welcomes the sacrificial animal but does not welcome the 'shī'.'
The Shī [Book of Odes] says: 'Bells and drums escort the 'shī'.'
Zhèng [Xuán]'s commentary says: 'The 'shī'
is an image of the spirit.'
This aligns with the current ritual procedure of not welcoming but then escorting,
as if matching a tally."
Xún Wànqiū, a Doctoral Scholar, deliberated:
"The ancient practice of serving the 'shī'
and the present practice of serving the spirits
have the same meaning.
In the Zhōu Lǐ [Rites of Zhou],
when the 'shī' departs, he is escorted to the temple gate.
One bows,
and the 'shī' does not look back.
The Shī [Book of Odes] says: 'Bells and drums escort the 'shī'.'
Thus, the meaning of escorting the spirits
has a long history.
The Jì [Book of Rites] says: 'One welcomes the sacrificial animal but does not welcome the 'shī',
to distinguish between what is suspect [or avoid impropriety].
If the 'shī' is outside the gate,
he is mistaken for a minister;
if he enters the temple,
he is complete as a lord.
If the lord is outside the gate,
he is mistaken for a lord [being welcomed],
if he enters the temple,
he is complete as a minister.
Therefore, not going out [to welcome]
clarifies the meaning of the lord and minister.'"
Suì and the other two [scholars] considered the old ritual correct,
while only Chén Mín, a Doctoral Scholar, agreed with Xú Dàoyú's deliberation.
After detailed deliberation,
it was concluded that
"although the deliberations of Suì and others are not exhaustive,
they are all based on the classical rites.
The arguments of Dàoyú and Mín are difficult to follow.
Since the opinions of the assembly are not uniform,
it is appropriate to adhere to the old system."
An imperial edict approved this.
In the ninth month of the sixth year of Yuánjiā,
Xú Dàoyú, a Doctoral Scholar of the Imperial Academy, submitted a memorial stating:
"The Ministry of Rites has set the Yīn sacrifice for the third day of the tenth month,
and the Zhēng sacrifice for the twelfth day.
I humbly note that the rites of Dì and Xiá
are performed once every three years,
and twice every five years.
The Gōngyáng [Commentary] refers to 'twice-repeated Yīn sacrifices every five years.'
These occur at different times during the four seasons,
which the Zhōu Lǐ refers to as 'seasonal sacrifices.'
Indeed, the specific years and months are not fixed,
and for the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords, the timing is not identical.
The Lǐ [Book of Rites] states: 'The Son of Heaven performs the Xiá and Cháng sacrifices,
the feudal lords perform the Zhēng and Xiá sacrifices.
If there are fields, they sacrifice;
if there are no fields, they present offerings.'
Zhèng [Xuán]'s commentary notes: 'The Son of Heaven first performs Xiá and then the seasonal sacrifices;
the feudal lords first perform seasonal sacrifices and then Xiá.
Those with fields perform both sacrifices and present new offerings.
Sacrifices are made in the first month of the season,
offerings in the middle month.'
Thus, the four great sacrifices
each occur in different months.
The Son of Heaven performs Yīn in the first month and Zhēng in the middle month;
