the feudal lords perform Cháng in the first month and Xiá in the middle month.
In the seventh month of autumn in the eighth year of Duke Xī of Chūnqiū [Spring and Autumn Annals],
the Dì sacrifice was held.
In the eighth month of the second year of Duke Wén,
a great ritual was performed at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
The Gǔliáng Zhuàn [Commentary] says: 'This refers to the Xiá and Cháng sacrifices.'
In the second month of the fifteenth year of Duke Zhāo,
'a ritual was performed at Wǔgōng.'
The Zuǒ Zhuàn [Commentary] says: 'This was in accordance with the rites.'
Also, the Zhōu Lǐ states: 'In mid-winter, the Zhēng sacrifice is offered.'
The Yuè Lìng [Monthly Ordinances] states: 'In late autumn, new grain is offered.'
The state of Jìn performed the spring Zhēng sacrifice at Qǔwò,
and Qí performed the Cháng sacrifice for Tàigōng in the tenth month.
These are all clear texts demonstrating the distinction between the first and middle months, and that they are not shared.
All sacrifices must first be divined.
If the day Dīngsì is not suitable,
further divination for a later day is performed.
If the divination is not auspicious,
how can two such events [be held so close]?
Postponing the date is even more obviously the correct principle.
Considering that the Yīn and Zhēng sacrifices are significant,
while general offerings are less important.
If the lesser rites still observe different months,
how can the greater rites be the same?
Furthermore, 'sacrifices should not be frequent;
frequency leads to irreverence.'
Now, to offer sacrifices so frequently, with only a ten-day interval,
I fear it would be troublesome according to the rites.
From the classics (jīngwěi) and ancient proclamations (fén gào),
there is no instance of two offerings in one month.
Earlier scholars and old teachings
all speak of different months.
The practice passed down since the Jìn dynasty –
I do not understand its origin.
Of the weighty affairs of the state,
none is greater than sacrifice.
My foolish and shallow understanding
leads me to secretly harbor doubts.
I request a detailed discussion on this matter."
The matter was shelved and not responded to.
On the yǐchǒu day of the fourth month of the seventh year of Yuánjiā,
the relevant authorities presented a memorial stating:
"The Lǐ Sāngfú Zhuàn [Commentary on Mourning Rites in the Book of Rites] says: 'If someone dies in the palace,
then for three months, no sacrifices are offered.'
Now, the Yuè sacrifice has already been announced,
but there has been an incident in the Yètíng (Imperial Harem).
We have referred this to the Grand Minister of Ceremonies to examine and correct according to the rites.
Jiāng Suì, Yuán Lǎng, Xú Dàoyú, Chén Mín, and other Doctoral Scholars of the Imperial Academy
have presented differing opinions.
Xiè Yuán, the Palace Secretariat Administrator and concurrently head of the Ministry of Rites, deliberated: '
To follow the Lǐ Zhuàn [Commentaries on the Rites]
and instruct the relevant authorities to perform the rites
would be proper in terms of righteousness.'
We have again deliberated in detail.
The ancestral temple is held in great reverence,
and offerings must be made with utmost clarity and purity.
Although the Emperor's emotions are boundless,
he must personally attend.
However, if there is indeed doubt,
then sentiment must yield to ritual.
Having no other arguments,
the current proposal has a basis in righteousness.
We request approval for Yuán's submission."
An imperial edict approved this.
In the twelfth month, on the day *Guǐyǒu*, of the tenth year of Yuánjiā [433 CE],
the Grand Sacrificer, Xú Rùn, submitted a memorial:
“In the ancestral temples, altars to the land and grain, and other sacrificial rites, five types of animals are offered:
oxen, sheep, pigs, and chickens are all to be male.
However, when one of these is purchased from the market,
it has always been the practice to send a female.
I have heard that during the time of King Jǐng of Zhōu,
Bīn Qǐ saw a male chicken voluntarily sever its own tail,
and said: ‘
A chicken fearing sacrifice is inauspicious.’
Why, then, do we now use females?
I request that the ritual officials below thoroughly review and correct this.”
An imperial edict instructed the Imperial Academy to review the matter thoroughly based on ritual texts.
The academicians, Xú Dàoyú and others, deliberated, stating:
“According to the Rites, in the first month of spring,
‘in this month,
no female sacrificial animals are to be used.’
If this is the case,
it only means that females are not to be used in the spring month,
and there is no prohibition in autumn or winter.
The male chicken severing its tail
could well have occurred in the spring month.”
The Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Sīmǎ Cāo, deliberated:
“Upon examining the ‘Monthly Ordinances,’ it states for the first month of spring: ‘command to sacrifice to mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes,
no female sacrificial animals are to be used.’
If the academy’s deliberation were correct,
then for spring sacrifices, three sacrificial animals and below
should all be changed at once
to comply with the ‘Monthly Ordinances.’
Why would this only apply to one chicken?”
Another imperial edict instructed the Imperial Academy to deliberate and reply.
The academicians, Xú Dàoyú and others, again deliberated, stating:
“For all ancestral sacrifices, the use of male and female animals is not uniform.
Regarding the previous point that the ‘Monthly Ordinances’ do not allow females,
it is likely to clarify that in spring, males are mandatory,
while in autumn and winter, females are permissible.
This does not mean that mountains and forests are treated the same as ancestral temples.
That the other four sacrificial animals are not changed, but the chicken is distinct,
has been the custom for a long time,
and there might be a reason for this,
though it is certainly beyond the detailed investigation of junior scholars like us.
We request a thorough deliberation and report,
as per the stated instruction.”
After thorough consideration, it was deemed that Xú Rùn’s statement had considerable evidence,
and it was appropriate to follow his proposal.
From now on, male chickens are to be used.
In the fifth month, on the day *Dīngsì*, of the third year of Xiàojiàn [456 CE] of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
an imperial edict decreed that the fourth imperial prince be adopted as the successor to Lǐ Ruì, the heir apparent of the Prince of Jiāngxià.
The relevant officials memorialized:
“Regarding an imperial prince being adopted as a successor,
we find no precedent for announcing this to the ancestral temple beforehand.
We have therefore instructed the ritual officials of the two academies to deliberate and decide
whether an announcement should be made or not.
If an announcement is to be made,
how many chambers should be informed?”
The Imperial Academy academician, Fù Xiū, deliberated:
“The Rites contain no clear text regarding an imperial prince being adopted as a successor and announcing it to the ancestral temple.
In the fourth year of Tàikāng of the Jìn dynasty [283 CE],
Shí, Prince of Běihǎi, was enfeoffed to succeed the Prince Shāng of Guǎnghàn,
and an announcement was made to the Grand Temple.
In the early Hàn dynasty, each emperor had a different temple,
so announcements did not necessarily have to be the same.
From Emperor Míng of Hàn onwards,
they shared a main hall but had separate chambers,
and Wèi and Jìn followed this.
Now that they share a main hall,
if only one chamber is announced,
and others are omitted,
it would not be emotionally proper.”
The Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Yǔ Liàngzhī, deliberated:
“According to the Rites, ‘for important matters, announcements are made to the ancestors and deceased father;
for minor matters, only to the deceased father.’
Now that an imperial prince is adopted as successor,
an announcement should be made to the temple of the deceased father.”
The Director of the Board of Rites, Zhū Yīngzhī, deliberated, believing:
“Making announcements to the ancestral temple for important events
is a regular national institution.
Now that an imperial prince is adopted as successor,
this matter is not an ordinary one.
I humbly believe an announcement should be made.
Hé Xún said that
in ancient rites, with separate temples,
only visiting one chamber was correct.
Since all now share a temple,
omitting other emperors
would not be emotionally proper.
I believe Hé Xún’s words are correct,
and all should be announced.”
The concurrently holding Right Assistant and Palace Gentleman, Xú Yuán, deliberated, believing:
“For major national affairs,
announcements must be made to the ancestors and deceased father.
An imperial prince being adopted as successor cannot be considered a minor matter.
In the past, when the fifth imperial prince succeeded to the princely title of Lúlíng,
all seven temples were announced.”
The deliberations concluded that Xú Yuán’s opinion was correct.
An imperial edict approved it.
On the first day of the sixth month, *Jǐmǎo*, of the first year of Dàmíng [457 CE],
an imperial edict decreed that Xīn, son of the former Crown Prince’s Infantry Commander Zhī, succeed Láng, Prince of Nánfēng.
The relevant officials memorialized:
“Láng previously succeeded to the princely title of Yíngyáng,
and an announcement was made to the ancestral temple at the imperial audience.
Upon examination, succession by inheritance
does not involve an announcement to the ancestral temple at the imperial audience.”
The ritual officials were instructed to deliberate and decide.
The Imperial Academy academician, Wáng Xièzhī, deliberated:
“Nánfēng originally had a separate territory established for him
to succeed Yíngyáng,
the principle was the same as a newly enfeoffed prince,
hence there was the rite of announcing to the ancestral temple at the imperial audience.
Now that Xīn is acting on an imperial edict to succeed,
it constitutes an inheritance,
the former peerage still exists,
and the matter is one of transmission by succession;
it should not involve an announcement to the ancestral temple at the imperial audience.”
The Director of the Board of Rites, Zhū Yīngzhī, deliberated:
“The princely title of Nánfēng had been extinguished.
The sacred benevolence was extended,
and a special edict commanded the succession to the fief,
reaffirming the principle as being the same as a newly enfeoffed prince,
and thus an announcement to the ancestral temple at the imperial audience was made.”
The Palace Gentleman, Xú Yuán, deliberated:
“Yíngyáng succeeded to the imperial lineage,
and upon his death, the enfeoffment was extinguished.
A benevolent edict posthumously enfeoffed him,
granting him a city.
Since it was a new establishment of a fief,
it was appropriate to announce to the ancestral temple at the imperial audience.
Now Xīn succeeds Nánfēng;
both are classified as princely states.
Chángshā and Nánfēng
should naturally each announce to their own ancestors,
and it does not concern the Grand Temple.
Since this matter is not a new enfeoffment,
it does not fit the rite of announcing at the imperial audience.
I agree with the academician Wáng Xièzhī’s deliberation.”
After thorough consideration,
Xú Yuán’s deliberation was deemed correct.
An imperial edict approved it.
In the sixth month, on the day *Yǐchǒu*, of the third year of Dàmíng [459 CE],
the relevant officials memorialized:
“On the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
there will be a seasonal sacrifice at the Grand Temple and the Temple of Empress Dowager Zhāng,
and the imperial carriage will personally attend.
However, since the emperor will personally command the army after leaving the temple,
should the Crown Prince participate in the sacrifice personally or not?
Furthermore, on the twenty-fourth day of this month,
the eighth imperial princess died prematurely.
According to the Rites, ‘if there is an incident in the palace,
sacrifices are not held for three months.’
As the Crown Prince resides in the inner palace,
there are doubts about this matter.”
The ritual officials were instructed to deliberate and decide.
The Imperial Academy academician, Sīmǎ Xīngzhī, deliberated:
“I humbly believe that ‘the great affairs of the state
are sacrifice and warfare.’
The Crown Prince has the way of commanding the army,
but not the authority to personally lead it.
Since warfare is like this,
sacrifices should also be so.
According to the ‘Treatise on Sacrifices,’
‘the way of sacrifice is that
the grandson acts as the representative of the paternal grandfather.’
It also says,
‘sacrifices have a sequence of generations (zhāomù),
which distinguishes father and son.’
Although the Crown Prince supervises the state,
he does not act as regent.
As for the ancestral temple,
the sequence of generations (zhāomù) truly exists,
meaning affairs cannot be disordered.
It also says,
‘if there is an incident, a proxy is sent.’
According to these two or three points,
the Crown Prince has no path to personally offer sacrifices.
Furthermore, with the premature death of an imperial princess,
it truly constitutes a shared sorrow within the palace;
there is no reason to differentiate.
Even if sacrifices were permissible,
there would still be no justification for him to personally offer them.”
The academician Yù deliberated:
“According to the *Chūnqiū*,
the Crown Prince serves the grain offerings to the altars of the land and grain.
The eldest son presides over the sacrificial vessels.
If he leaves the capital, he can guard the ancestral temple
and act as the sacrificer,
which is clearly stated in the *Yì Tuàn*.
The grave responsibility of supervising the state
naturally entails personally participating in sacrifices.
As for the premature death of the imperial princess,
since they were in the same palace at that time,
suspending sacrifices for three months
is appropriate according to the rites.”
The two deliberations differed.
The Department of State Affairs considered the matter
and deemed Yù’s deliberation correct.
An imperial edict approved it.
In the third year of Dàmíng, on the *yǐchǒu* day of the eleventh month, the first day of the month,
the officials in charge reported:
"For the four seasonal ancestral temple sacrifices,
auspicious days have been set.
When rain is encountered or mourning is undertaken,
it was formerly the custom to suspend personal attendance
and have the officials in charge perform the rites.
We previously instructed the ritual officials to discuss broadly
whether it is appropriate according to ritual to postpone the day or not."
The Erudite, Jiāng Cháng, deliberated:
"The Lǐjì, 'Jìtǒng' states: 'When the ruler offers sacrifice,
if there is a reason, he sends someone,
and the ruler does not lose his propriety.'
Zhèng Xuán said: 'Even if the ruler does not attend in person,
the sacrificial rites are not deficient,
and the ruler's virtue is not diminished.'
I believe that 'if there is a reason, he must send someone'
clearly indicates that there is no text allowing postponement.
If the officials in charge fulfill the duties,
I suggest it is not appropriate to change the day."
The Assistant Grand Minister of Ceremonies, Lù Chéng, deliberated:
"According to the Zhōulǐ, 'Zōngbó zhī zhí' (Duties of the Minister of Rites): 'If the King does not participate in the sacrifice, then he appoints a substitute.'
Lord Zhèng said: 'If the King has a reason,
he proceeds with the sacrificial affairs.'
I believe this refers to a situation where the period of purification (zhìzhāi) has been entered,
all sacrificial preparations are complete,
the deities must not be profaned,
purification cannot be prolonged,
and the King has another reason;
then he sends the officials in charge to act as a substitute.
In the seventh year of Tàishǐ of Jìn, in the fourth month,
Emperor Shìzǔ was about to personally offer sacrifice at the Grand Ancestral Temple.
On the *gēngxū* day,
the imperial carriage performed the evening sacrifice of the animal.
On the *xīnhài* day,
it rained.
The officials in charge performed the rites.
Although this was not a human reason,
it was also an obstruction from heaven.
Seeking this in ancient rituals,
it does not deviate from the Zhōu system.
According to the Lǐjì,
'Kǒngzǐ answered Zēngzǐ,
if on the day of sacrifice there is a solar eclipse or a fire in the Grand Ancestral Temple,
and the sacrificial animal has arrived but not yet been slain,
then it should be abandoned.'
Thus, sacrifices are not without a way to be abandoned.
It is merely a matter of weighing the gravity of the circumstances.
A solar eclipse or a temple fire
are extremely severe changes,
and thus even if the animal has arrived, it can still be abandoned.
Inferring from this,
lesser circumstances can be understood by analogy.
Now, within the period of preliminary purification (sǎnzhāi),
before reaching the full purification (zhìzhāi),
if there is minor mourning or heavy rain,
postponing the event
can extend reverence.
It does not deviate from the principles of propriety,
nor does it harm the orthodox code.
To select another auspicious day,
what is there to doubt?
I suggest that if there is mourning or rain during the period of preliminary purification (sǎnzhāi),
the day can be changed.
Only upon entering the full purification (zhìzhāi) or when the day is too close to the end of the month
should the officials in charge perform the rites."
Moreover, in a memorial by the former Minister of Works, Gù Hé,
it was proposed that if the imperial carriage had already departed for the southern suburban sacrifice (Nánjiāo) and encountered rain,
the day should be postponed and the sacrifice performed again,
a practice which was subsequently adopted.
The reverence for the suburban sacrifice and the temple sacrifice
is comparable.
If the former can be postponed even on the day itself,
how much more so during the preliminary purification (sǎnzhāi)?
The Palace Attendant, Yīn Dàn, deliberated:
"Zēngzǐ asked, 'If there is a solar eclipse or a fire in the Grand Ancestral Temple,
and the sacrificial animal has not yet been slain, then it should be abandoned.'
However, if there is a reason, one sends someone.
The ancestral temple (Qīngmiào) is held in great reverence,
and the suburban sacrifice (Jiāoyīn) is a grand ritual.
Thus, if the temple burns or there is a solar eclipse,
postponement is permitted.
But for minor mourning or a slight reason,
the event should not be changed.
This is why changing the divination for a mouse eating an ox
is contrary to ritual.
As for Emperor Shìzǔ of Jìn having officials in charge perform the rites,
and Minister Gù postponing the suburban sacrifice,
since the appropriateness of those times is not evident,
these are not sufficient as standards.
I believe that only for a solar eclipse or a temple fire,
which are divine reproaches,
can the day be postponed.
As for minor reasons like undertaking mourning,
the day should not be changed."
The opinions of the assembly differed.
After discussion,
since there were rational bases,
and moreover, the Jìn dynasty postponed the suburban sacrifice,
and the early Sòng dynasty postponed temple sacrifices,
both serving as established precedents,
it was decided that in the middle of the preliminary purification (sǎnzhāi) of the first month of the season (mèngyuè),
if rain or minor mourning is encountered,
an auspicious day should be chosen for postponement,
with no fixed limit to the number of times.
Only when entering the full purification (zhìzhāi) or when it encroaches upon the *zhòngyuè* period
should the officials in charge perform the rites.
An imperial edict approved this.
In the fifth year of Dàmíng, on the *jiǎyín* day of the tenth month,
the officials in charge reported:
"On the eighth day of this month, the *zhēng* sacrifice will be offered at the two ancestral temples,
with the dukes and ministers performing the rites.
The Crown Prince is observing mourning for his consort."
The former Assistant Grand Minister of Ceremonies, Yǔ Wèizhī, deliberated:
"The reason why rituals prescribe suspension of sacrifices for mourning
is because sacrifices must include music.
The Crown Prince, due to his paramount status as the legitimate heir,
is subject to the ruler's mourning rites for his consort,
not diminishing due to his subordinate position.
Since he is in the full *dàgōng* mourning attire,
I believe he should not sacrifice.
In cases of unavoidable circumstances,
the Three Ducal Ministers perform the rites,
but that is for an auspicious day of sacrifice,
not comparable to the present situation.
Even for the death of a minister, the *yì* (final ceremony) is not performed,
how much more so for the Crown Prince's consort?"
The Erudite, Sīmǎ Xīngzhī, deliberated:
"That one does not sacrifice during *sīmā* mourning
is a major principle of ritual.
That the *yì* (final ceremony) is not performed for the death of a minister
is clearly defined in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Furthermore, examining the Wei dynasty, when Princess Píngyuán died,
Gāo Tánglóng argued that the three-month suspension of sacrifices was inappropriate,
yet still said that during the period of encoffinment and burial,
the event could be temporarily suspended and an auspicious day changed,
so that the fragrant offerings could be presented.
Considering the meaning of these words,
it does not mean sending officials in charge.
For a mourning period without formal attire,
it was still considered suspended until burial.
How much more so for the Crown Prince's consort who is in *dàgōng* mourning and not yet interred?
Looking up to the ritual texts
and down to previous generations,
the *zhēng* sacrifice should not be performed."
The Chief Clerk of the Imperial Guards, Zhōu Jǐngyuǎn, deliberated:
"According to ritual, 'one does not sacrifice during *sīmā* mourning.'
That *dàgōng* mourning causes suspension of sacrifices
is a principle that needs no further explanation.
Now, since the Crown Prince's deceased consort has not yet been interred in the mountain tomb,
this cannot be considered a temporary expedient.
Therefore, according to ritual, the *zhēng* and *cháng* sacrifices should be suspended.
The emperor, being in *dàgōng* mourning attire,
is ritually unable to attend in person.
This is not a case of 'unavoidable circumstances,'
nor should dukes and ministers perform the rites."
The Right Vice Minister, Xú Yuán, deliberated:
"The ritual, 'one does not sacrifice during *sīmā* mourning,'
is generally a common consensus.
Even for a high official, due to his esteemed status,
when he observes mourning,
it should not be treated differently.
The 'Jìtǒng' states 'if the ruler has a reason, sending someone is permissible'
which refers to cases where ritual demands sacrifice,
but the ruler cannot maintain purification,
and the sacrifice cannot be omitted,
thus ministers are sent to act as substitutes.
It does not mean that if the ruler should not sacrifice,
the officials in charge perform the rites.
In the fourth year of Xiánníng of Jìn,
when Empress Jǐngxiàn (Emperor Wǔ of Jìn's paternal aunt) died,
the ancestral temple suspended one seasonal sacrifice.
Although her title was highly esteemed,
this can roughly serve as a precedent.
Now, the Crown Prince is observing full *dàgōng* mourning for his consort,
which is not comparable to an 'unavoidable circumstance.'
Since she has not yet been interred in the mountain tomb,
I suggest that the *zhēng* sacrifice should be suspended.
Examining the deliberations of Wèizhī and others,
their conclusions are not dissimilar;
omitting the *zhēng* sacrifice is appropriate.
After the *zúkū* ceremony (end of initial mourning) and her enshrinement in the temple,
all should follow the regular rites."
An imperial edict approved this.
In the second month, on the day *bǐngchén*, of Dàmíng's seventh year,
the officials reported:
"When the imperial chariot makes its inspection and hunt east of the Jiāng River,
practicing military skills and hunting,
the meat obtained should first be offered to the Tàimiào and the Zhāng Tàihòu Temple.
Minced meat and wine should also be prepared,
with the *gōngqīng* performing the rites,
and in the inner chamber of the deceased concubines,
the chamber head performing the rites."
Yú Hé, the Erudite of the Imperial Academy, deliberated:
"Upon examining the *Zhōu Lǐ*,
the offering of sacrificial animals during military exercises in the four seasons
each has its specific application.
When troops are reviewed for the spring hunt (*chūn sōu*),
it is for offering sacrifices to the *Shè*;
when encamping for the summer hunt (*xià miáo*),
it is for offering sacrifices to the *Yào*;
when marshaling troops for the autumn hunt (*qiū xiǎn*),
it is for offering sacrifices to the *Bìng*;
and when holding a grand review for the winter hunt (*dōng shòu*),
it is for offering sacrifices to the *Zhēng*.
According to the *Hàn Jìsì Zhì*: 'Only on the day of Lìqiū,
after the suburban sacrifice to Bái is completed,
is military might first displayed,
which is named
"chūliú."
The imperial carriage enters the preserve,
the emperor personally holds a crossbow and shoots,
and the sacrificial animal is a fawn.
The Tàizǎi orders one attendant each
to send the hunted game by carriage to the imperial tombs and temples.'
Therefore, offering the spring hunt to the temples
has no prior precedent."
Yǔ Wèizhī, concurrently Assistant of the Tàicháng, deliberated:
"What Hé said about not missing the timing of the seasonal hunts
is a rite that has long been abandoned.
Now, Hé's memorial is late in the season,
and while practicing military skills teaches people,
it also reverently provides dried meat and grains,
first offered to the two temples.
Both the rite and the sentiment are appropriate.
The *shè* represents the god of earth,
and the Sīkōng is the official in charge of earth matters;
therefore, the Sīkōng performs the rites for the sacrifice to the *Shè*.
The Tàimiào should be presided over by the Shanggōng.
Regarding the deliberations on the rites of hunting,
the four seasons have different interpretations;
rites are subject to modification and alteration,
and eras differ.
Now that the sacrifices to the four directions
and the ceremonies of three killings no longer exist,
having been abandoned for a long time,
animals obtained from the hunt
that are injured or have their fur cut
are not to be offered if they are not intact.
The Tàizǎi orders the attendants to select the best kill and send it,
first offering it to the ancestral temple and the two *Shè* temples,
with the Tàiwèi performing the rites as before."
The emperor approved the edict.
In the seventh month, on the day *gēngshēn*, of Míngdì's Tàiyù first year,
the officials reported:
"For the seasonal sacrifice in the seventh month,
should His Supreme Majesty, being in a state of profound mourning (*liàng'àn*),
personally perform the offering or not?
Let the officials of rites discuss this.
Upon reflection on the three-year mourning system,
it extends from the Son of Heaven downwards.
Hàn Wén, in pity of the abuses of the Qín dynasty,
then established a provisional code.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
after the *cùkū* ceremony and enshrinement, it is considered auspicious.
According to the *Wáng Zhì* chapter of the *Lǐ Jì*,
'During the three years, no sacrifices are made,
except for sacrifices to Heaven, Earth, and the *Shèjì*,
for which one crosses the mourning ropes to perform the rites.'
Zhèng Xuán stated: 'It is only that one dares not use the humble to negate the revered.'
Fàn Xuān debated Dù Yù and Duàn Chàng,
saying that the reason for omitting sacrifices to the ancestral temples
is entirely due to human reason,
and the sorrowful feelings
are the same as for the living.
Qiáo Zhōu's *Jì Zhì* states: 'According to the rites,
when one is in mourning,
no auspicious sacrifices are made.
For the mourning of *sīmá*, if one has mourning attire for an ancestor,
then no sacrifices are made either,
because the spirits will not partake.'
Upon reflection, if there is a death in the palace,
even if one is not in mourning attire,
sacrifices are still suspended for three months;
one does not sacrifice when in mourning.
If it is not the case that during the three-year period one must personally perform the offerings,
then one should follow the sequence of *dì* and the *zhāomù*.
However, one must now be out of mourning
before *dì* and *xiá* sacrifices can be performed.
Therefore, the meaning of not sacrificing
is worth considering.
The *Qǐjū Zhù* records that
Jìn Wǔdì had two mourning periods,
and within those two full years,
he did not personally offer sacrifices.
This is also a recent precedent.
We humbly believe that His Supreme Majesty's filial piety surpasses that of Jī Wén,
his feelings are profoundly manifest,
and although the public mourning attire has been removed,
pure sorrow still lingers within.
Consulting the established precedents and regulations,
it appears that he should not personally perform the offerings.
The responsible officials should reverently respond,
so that the sacrifice is not omitted.
Reflecting on this respectful course,
we humbly deem it appropriate.
Our joint deliberation
has clear evidence,
and it is fitting to proceed as presented."
The emperor approved the edict.
Later, in the tenth month, on the day *bǐngyín*, of Fèidì's Yuánhuī second year,
the officials reported:
"On the day when His Supreme Majesty personally offers sacrifices at the Tàimiào to Wén Huángdì and the Tàihòu,
should Xiàowǔ Huángdì and Zhāo Huángtàihòu,
although not of the main lineage in terms of kinship,
but having once held the imperial position,
be offered libations by His Supreme Majesty personally or not?
This is unclear."
It was submitted to the officials of rites for deliberation.
Zhōu Shānwén, Erudite of the Imperial Academy, deliberated:
"According to the rites,
the revered are revered in the ascending lineage,
and the humble are revered in the descending lineage.
Although Xiàowǔ Huángdì, in relation to His Supreme Majesty,
was not of the main lineage in terms of kinship,
his imperial title
is listed among the seven ancestral temples.
I believe that on the day of personal offerings,
libations should be personally poured.
As Zhāo Huángtàihòu is not of the main lineage according to ritual propriety,
the Sāngōng should perform the rites."
Doctors Yán Xiè and four others concurred with Shānwén.
Hán Bēn, concurrently Assistant of the Tàicháng, deliberated:
"Jìn Jǐngdì in relation to Shìzǔ,
and Sùzǔ in relation to Xiàowǔ,
were both collateral revered figures,
and personally poured libations.
Now, Xiàowǔ Huángdì, in relation to His Supreme Majesty,
was personally his paternal uncle,
and his achievements are listed among the ancestors.
On the day of offering sacrifices,
I believe it is appropriate for His Majesty to personally perform it.
Regarding Zhāo Huángtàihòu, in relation to the current emperor,
her kinship has no official rank;
the sentiment is distant.
If a stepmother is alive,
the nephew sacrifices to the grandson only,
let alone the stepmother of a paternal uncle.
I believe that the libations for Empress Zhāo
can be assigned to the responsible officials."
Sūn Miǎn, former Assistant of the Zuǒ Chéng, deliberated:
"Jìn Shìzǔ's ancestral sacrifices to Xiǎnzōng, Lièzōng, and Sùzǔ
were all to paternal uncles of the Jìn Emperor.
Now, the current dynasty has a clear precedent,
and there was originally no rite for officials to perform these.
I believe that the current emperor personally pouring libations for Xiàowǔ Huángdì
would be in line with respectful sentiment.
Zhāo Huángtàihòu, with the noble status of a ruler's mother,
was revered for a time.
However, for her to partake in the sacrifices alongside the Zhāng and Xuān temples in the sacred palace,
not only should the emperor not personally offer libations,
but it should even be deliberated whether her inclusion should be abolished.
I request that for now, the Sāngōng perform the rites as before."
The emperor decreed that Miǎn's deliberation was appropriate.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn of Sòng Xiàowǔdì, in the tenth month, on the day Wùchén,
the officials memorialized on the rites of demolishing and placing the temple of Empress Dowager Zhānghuáng.
Six hundred and sixty-three officials of the second rank participated in the discussion.
Tàifù, the Prince of Jiāngxià, Yìgōng, believed:
"The classics and records are incomplete and falsified,
and the teachings and traditions come from different schools.
It is truly the case that those who speak are not uniform,
and therefore those who seek rarely reach a conclusion.
This is why the debates on the Six Zōng
contradict those of some Rú scholars,
and the arguments for successive demolition
confuse various schools of thought.
Empress Dowager Zhānghuáng was born of a divine spirit and inaugurated a sage,
her rites were complete for the restoration,
her blessings flowed through her descendants,
and her virtue shone far and wide.
It is fitting that her fragrant memory be honored for generations,
and her example be passed down through successive ages.
How can she be lowered to the level of common folk,
and made to follow ordinary practices?
Indeed, those who debate create doubt,
actually relying on chronicles and traditions,
knowing one aspect but missing another,
and failing to grasp the true meaning of the texts.
According to the Lǐjì, 'do not replace the sacrifice,'
and this extends to the compassionate mother,
placing the words so they have an application.
Gǔliáng states that at the grandson, the sacrifice stops,
and a separate lord is established for sacrifice.
Thus, personally holding the devout sacrifice
is a matter different from previous records.
This is perhaps due to the appropriateness for a great sovereign,
whose responsibilities are exceedingly heavy,
and the nobility of the human ultimate,
whose number is uniquely central.
Moreover, during the great era of the Hàn dynasty,
they were indeed elevated to be associated and enshrined;
during the enlightened rule of the Jìn clan,
they consistently retained sacrificial offerings.
Examining ancient historical records,
and relying on recent observations,
it should not be demolished;
this is superior in terms of righteousness.
The Gōngyáng on which this is based
is only sufficient to firmly uphold this.
How can one equate her nobility with that of emperors and kings,
but make her sacrifices follow those of commoners?
To seek regulations based on emotion
would be an even greater subversion.
I believe she should be treated like the Seven Miào,
and only be demolished after six generations."
Six hundred and thirty-six people agreed with Yìgōng not to demolish.
Sànqí Shìláng Wáng Fǎshī and twenty-seven others argued that it should be demolished.
Lǐng Cáo Lángzhōng Zhōu Jǐngyuǎn re-examined the discussion,
and deemed Yìgōng's and others' argument against demolition to be correct.
An edict approved it.
In the second month of the second year of Dà Míng, on the day Gēng Yín,
the officials reported:
“In the grand sacrifices of the imperial dynasty,
there have been no observances at Empress Zhāng’s temple.
Gāo Táng-Lóng discussed that Empress Wén-Sī of Wèi should follow the precedent of Jiāng Yuán’s temple in Zhōu for the dì and xiá sacrifices,
and Xú Miǎo answered regarding the old matter of Empress Xuān-Tài of Jìn’s yīn-jiàn sacrifices.
Let the ritual officials deliberate and correct this.”
Dr. Sūn Wǔ deliberated:
“According to the Lǐ Jì’s Jì Fǎ,
‘When a capital is established and a city founded,
temples, tiāo, altars, and platforms are set up to offer sacrifices,
and the number of close and distant relatives is determined accordingly.
Therefore, the king establishes seven temples,
with the distant temples serving as tiāo.’
Zhèng Xuán says: ‘The tablets of the ruler from a moved temple,
arranged according to zhāo and mù, are jointly interred within the two tiāo,
and then the xiá sacrifice is offered.’
The Wáng Zhì says: ‘Xiá and dì.’
Zhèng Xuán says: ‘Xiá
means joining.
To join the tablets of former rulers in the ancestral temple and sacrifice to them
is called xiá.
Dì in the summer every three years,
and xiá in the autumn every five years,
is called two yīn sacrifices in five years.’
Also, ‘Dì
is a great sacrifice.’
In the second year of Duke Wén of the Chūn Qiū,
‘a great affair was held at the great temple.’
The commentary says: ‘The tablets of destroyed temples
are arranged before the great ancestor;
the tablets of temples not yet destroyed
are all brought up to partake in the meal with the great ancestor.’
The commentary says: ‘The clan gathers to eat,
arranged according to zhāo and mù.’
The Jì Tǒng says: ‘When there is an affair at the great temple,
all zhāo and all mù are present,
not losing their proper order.’
Currently, the yīn sacrifice involves joint eating with the great ancestor,
arranged by zhāo and mù.
Empress Zhāng has already been demoted from the highest position,
not listed among the principal temples.
If her tablet were brought into the great temple,
it would neither dare to be arranged in the principal order,
nor have we heard of a separate position being established outside of the zhāo and mù order.
If, according to Xú Miǎo’s discussion,
the current yīn sacrifice were offered at a separate temple,
it would deviate from the meaning of dì and xiá as great sacrifices involving joint eating and arrangement by zhāo and mù.
Miǎo said: ‘The four shāng in the inner chamber
are not included in the xiá sacrifice but are sacrificed to at their own place.’
This is also his meaning.
The Sāng Fú Xiǎo Jì states:
‘Shāng and those without descendants
partake in the meal, attached to their ancestor.’
The Jì Fǎ states:
‘The king sacrifices to shāng below.’
Zhèng Xuán says: ‘To sacrifice to the principal shāng in the innermost part of the temple
is called yīn yàn.’
Since they partake in the meal with their ancestor in the innermost part of the temple,
this means shāng have a position in the innermost part,
not that they are sacrificed to in a separate palace.
Currently, Empress Zhāng’s temple
receives offerings in all four seasons.
Even if it does not cease with the grandson,
if the great temple has dì and xiá,
and she alone is sacrificed to in a separate palace,
it would be no different from the four seasonal zhēng and cháng offerings.
This would not be the meaning of the great dì sacrifice,
nor would it take from the text of xiá and joint eating.
I believe it is not proper to include her in the yīn sacrifice ritual of the great temple.”
Dr. Wáng Xiè-Zhī deliberated:
“Gāo Táng-Lóng’s answer that Empress Wén-Sī of Wèi should follow the precedent of Jiāng Yuán’s temple for the dì and xiá sacrifices
also does not clarify the meaning of xiá,
but changes xiá to a great offering,
which likely had a reason.
My limited learning in adhering to the texts makes me fear deviating from the core of the Rites.”
Dr. Wáng Xiè-Zhī deliberated:
“Although the dì sacrifice is smaller and the xiá sacrifice is greater,
there is no definitive text in the rites.
Seeking based on practical examples,
there seems to be a standard that can be applied.
Examining the name ‘xiá,’
although it refers to joint eating,
the solemnity of the sacrificial ceremony
is greatest at this time.
Indeed, to show filial piety to one’s relatives,
respect and love are boundless.
Since a grand offering is made to the great ancestor,
a splendid sacrifice should also be rendered at a minor temple.
This is like an affair concerning a superior that can also extend to a subordinate.
Therefore, Gāo Táng-Lóng said that it is solely for the sake of the xiá sacrifice that she is sacrificed to.
Thus, Empress Wén-Sī of Wèi
and Empress Xuān-Hòu of Jìn,
though not included in the order of the great temple,
still received the dì sacrifice equally with Jiāng Yuán,
and this is the intent.
Furthermore, Xú Miǎo’s citation that the four shāng are not included in the xiá sacrifice,
but are sacrificed to at their own place,
serves as an example of separate offerings,
which is proof of this.
I humbly believe that Empress Zhāng-Huáng-Tài-Hòu’s temple
should also receive grand offerings.”
Tài-Cháng-Chéng Sūn Miǎn deliberated, believing:
“The name of the xiá sacrifice
means joint eating.
Adhering to the classics and ancient precedents,
Sūn Wǔ is more thorough.
I humbly find that the ritual for minor temples
began in the recent Wèi period,
and the practices of Jìn
can serve as a precedent.
Gāo Táng-Lóng offered sacrifices with the xiá,
attaching to sentiment and reverence.
Xú Miǎo cited the separate sacrifice to the four shāng
to prove separate offerings.
Sūn Wǔ relied on shāng being attached to their ancestor,
meaning there is a shāng position in the temple.
While the matter of the temple is the same,
the sacrifice is not joint eating.
Moreover, seven temples in the same palace
began in the Later Hàn.
The ritual for sacrificing to shāng
is for each to be attached to their ancestor.
Since they are included in the xiá,
they must be sacrificed to in a different temple.
I humbly believe that the grand offering at Empress Zhāng’s temple
can be understood from this reasoning.”
Sī-Bù Zhū Yīng deliberated:
“Regarding the sacrifices at the Bì Gōng,
Gāo Táng-Lóng and Zhào Yí both said that the people of Zhōu performed xiá,
and annually conducted xiá sacrifices.
The Wèi and Jìn dynasties
adopted this as a model for offerings.
Renowned scholars who understood the rites
did not criticize or fault each other;
without error or omission,
they followed the old regulations.
My humble opinion agrees with the deliberations of Wáng Xiè-Zhī and Sūn Miǎn.”
The imperial edict stated:
“Empress Zhāng-Huáng-Tài-Hòu was posthumously honored with the highest title,
and her rites are equivalent to the seven temples.
How can she alone be deprived of the grand offerings,
and this splendid sacrifice be neglected?
The remote xiá at Bì Gōng
was already practiced in Zhōu;
Wèi and Jìn followed this offering,
and the model remained unbroken.
It is appropriate to follow the former precedents
to express sentiment and reverence.”
In the first month of the second year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Míng,
Empress Zhāo, the mother of Emperor Xiàowǔ, passed away.
In the fifth month, on the day of Jiǎyín,
the officials reported:
“During the Tàiyuán era of the Jìn dynasty,
the honorable title of empress dowager was first standardized.
Xú Mó discussed the ancestral temple system,
and from then on,
it was established as a universal code.
Now, Empress Zhāo, the empress dowager, had no blood relation to the supreme ruler,
and the emperor specially prescribed mourning attire for her.
The ritual of enshrining her in the ancestral temple
should be submitted to the ritual officials for detailed discussion.”
Doctor Wáng Lüè and Grand Master of Ceremonies’ Assistant Yú Yuàn deliberated, saying:
“Rectifying names and preserving righteousness
is a glorious code for a state;
uniformity for ministers and sons
is clearly stated in historical records.
Now, Empress Zhāo, the empress dowager, rightly held the position of mother of the realm,
and her honorable title is truly established.
The ritual of enshrining her in the ancestral temple
should follow the established norms.
‘The mother is honored through her son’
is a fact illuminated by sacred texts.
Since the sacrifices to Emperor Xiàowǔ
will not cease for a hundred generations,
then the enshrinement of Empress Zhāo
should not be incomplete.
I believe her spirit tablet should be placed in the temple of Empress Zhāng.
Furthermore, it should follow the precedent of Emperor Yuán of Jìn with respect to Emperor Mǐn,
and Emperor Ān with respect to Empress Yǒng'ān.
On the day of sacrifice,
the emperor should not personally offer wine,
but should let the relevant officials perform the rite.”
At that time, Empress Xuān, the empress dowager of Tàizōng, had already been enshrined in Empress Zhāng’s temple.
The acting Administrator of the Bureau of Rites, Yú Hé, deliberated, believing:
“According to the meaning of the Chunqiu,
even if a secondary mother shares a high title,
she is fundamentally different from the principal wife.
Therefore, she is still buried in a separate palace,
and the duke’s son presides over her sacrifices.
Now, since Empress Zhāo, the empress dowager, was not the birth mother,
there is even less reason for personal offerings.
The Zhōu Lǐ, in the section on the office of the Zōngbó, states: ‘If the king does not participate in the sacrifice,
then he appoints a substitute.’
Therefore, it is appropriate to have the relevant officials perform the rites.
Furthermore, women do not have fixed ranks;
their status is determined by their husband's clan,
and if the husband dies, by their son.
Empress Zhāo, the empress dowager, was formally established in her position earlier,
while Empress Xuān was posthumously honored later.
Considering the sequence,
it is appropriate to place the new spirit tablet higher.”
After detailed deliberation,
Hé’s proposal was deemed correct.
An imperial edict approved it.
In the sixth month of the second year of Tàishǐ, on the day of Dīngchǒu,
the officials reported:
“In the seventh month, the annual sacrifices to the two temples will be performed.
As before, the emperor will personally preside.
In the chamber of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
the supreme ruler will personally offer wine and prostrate himself.
Also, obeisance should be made in the chamber of Empress Zhāo, the empress dowager,
and the emperor’s personal name should be used in the prayer text.
Furthermore, the empress will reverently visit the ancestral temple on the twenty-fifth day of this month,
to pay respects to Emperor Xiàowǔ and Empress Zhāo, the empress dowager.
Since there is no clear text on this,
it should be submitted to the ritual officials for discussion and rectification.”
Doctor of the Imperial Academy Liú Gǔn deliberated, saying:
“I recall that Emperor Yuán of Jìn, facing north, declared himself a subject to Emperor Mǐn,
and for the seasonal sacrifices and offerings,
he also had the relevant officials perform the rites.
Moreover, ‘brothers do not succeed each other as heirs’
is clearly recorded in the Lǔ History.
Inferring from this,
in the chamber of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
it is inappropriate for the supreme ruler to personally offer wine and prostrate himself.
On that day, he will personally offer sacrifices at the temple of Empress Zhāng, the empress dowager.
When passing by the chamber of Empress Zhāo, the empress dowager,
since the previous discussion decided to have officials perform the rites,
I believe he should not make an offering.
Empress Zhāo, the empress dowager’s formal title has long been established,
and she is listed among the ancestral temple sacrifices.
Upon careful examination of the prayer text,
it is appropriate to use the emperor’s personal name.
According to the Rites,
there is no rule for a wife to visit her husband’s older brother.
Empress Zhāo held a position of collateral honor,
and the ritual of reverent visitation
logically cannot be fully prepared.
In the two chambers of Emperor Xiàowǔ and Empress Zhāo,
the animal offerings should be omitted.”
Grand Master of Ceremonies’ Assistant Yú Yuàn deliberated, saying:
“The ritual of seasonal sacrifices
is about continuing the lineage.
Therefore, even if collateral relatives are close,
nephews do not sacrifice to uncles.
Even if the ruler’s position is high,
ministers have no sacrificial rites.
According to the case of Emperor Jǐng of Jìn with respect to Emperor Wǔ,
he was an elder paternal uncle.
On the day of Emperor Wǔ’s sacrifice,
he still offered wine.
Now, since the emperor has inherited the ancestral rites of Emperor Wén,
in the chamber of Emperor Xiàowǔ, I believe it is appropriate to merely bow,
and have officials perform the offering of wine.
According to the Rites, ‘one bows when passing a tomb,
and dismounts when passing a sacrifice.’
For all deities,
one still shows respect;
how much more so for Empress Zhāo, the empress dowager, who ruled the four seas,
and to whom the supreme ruler once bowed as a subject.
There is respect due to an elder brother's wife,
so I believe it is appropriate to bow,
and the prayer text should use the emperor’s personal name.
Regarding the empress’s temple visit ritual,
it is fundamentally about showing reverence.
Now, concerning Emperor Xiàowǔ,
if we discuss the relationship of sister-in-law and brother-in-law,
there is no rule for interaction.
If we speak of status,
there is also no meaning of meeting.
Furthermore, when the empress first ascended the throne,
Empress Zhāo still held her proper position in the palace,
and the custom of respectful visitation
had long been completed previously.
I believe that for the two chambers of Emperor Xiàowǔ and Empress Zhāo, the empress dowager,
no further offerings or announcements should be made.”
After deliberation, Yuàn’s proposal was deemed correct.
An imperial edict approved it.
In the tenth month, on the day Rén-yín, in the second year of Yuánhuī, during the reign of Hòu Fèi-dì,
the relevant authorities memorialized for the dismantling and relocation of the temple of Zhāo Tàihòu.
The matter was sent to the ritual officials for detailed deliberation.
Hán Bēn, a minister of the Tàicháng, deliberated:
"According to the reverence due to a sovereign's mother,
an principle established in the Chūnqiū,
there should be no interruption in the offerings and sacrifices made by later generations.
However, even the seven temples of the Zhōu dynasty, which carried the legitimate succession,
were dismantled when the family relationship became too distant.
How much more so for one born of a paternal aunt
for whom there are no mourning rites or substitute sacrifices?
Examining previous eras,
no precedent for this can be found."
Yīn Fěi-zǐ, a secretary in the Dudulingshi, deliberated:
"As Zhāo Huángtàihòu is not directly linked to the ancestors,
it is appropriate to dismantle her temple.
The debaters say,
'A concubine is interred with her paternal aunt by marriage.'
Since interment necessarily involves announcement,
dismantling should not be different.
An announcement should be made to the chamber of Zhāng Huángtàihòu.
However, the record states: 'A concubine is interred with her paternal aunt by marriage;
if there is no paternal aunt by marriage,
then one may change the sacrificial animal and inter her with the principal wife.'
Originally, regarding Zhāng Tàihòu and Zhāo Tàihòu,
in terms of the zhāomù order,
Zhāo Tàihòu was neither a paternal aunt by marriage
nor a principal wife;
this is improper according to ritual principles.
Upon reflection, Zhāo Tàihòu's name and position were of the utmost importance.
When she was first interred,
she was interred with Zhào Hòu by imperial command,
and then settled in the western temple.
All chambers were informed with offerings.
In ancient times, important matters required announcement,
and it was also said that every matter required announcement.
In ritual,
sacrificial animals and offerings were used together.
Upon examining the practices since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
there have been variations.
In the sixteenth year of Yuánjiā,
the ritual officials were ordered to clarify the matter.
Yīn Língzuò, a博士 (bóshì) of the Tàixué, deliberated, stating:
'Auspicious events use sacrificial animals, inauspicious events use offerings.'
From then on,
distinguishing between auspicious and inauspicious became the standard,
already forming a established practice of the era.
Although the current matter is not entirely inauspicious,
it is also not entirely auspicious,
therefore it is appropriate to follow the old practice
and inform the two temples with offerings.
Furthermore, regarding the dismantling of Zhāo Tàihòu's spirit tablet,
there is no justification for displaying it at the temple of Tàizǔ.
The 博士 (bóshì) wished to bury it between the two steps of the temple, in accordance with the burial of the Yúzhǔ.
However, the space between the steps was originally meant for burying announced offerings and the Yúzhǔ.
Formerly, Yú Xǐ said
that, based on the deliberations of the Five Classics,
to inter the dismantled tablet with the Yúzhǔ
and bury it along the north wall of the temple
is the most reliable approach.
After Zhāo Tàihòu's spirit tablet is dismantled and buried,
the upper chamber must not remain empty.
The Tàihòu should then be moved up.
When she is moved up,
dried meat and minced offerings should be set out to appease the spirit.
The current deliberations by the ritual officials
are erroneous, cursory, and incomplete.
The matter of relocation and dismantling is grave;
I request a broader and more detailed investigation."
Liú Bǐng, the Zuǒ Púyè, and six others agreed with Fěi-zǐ.
Wáng Chén, the Zuǒ Chéng, further participated in the deliberation,
stating:
"To inform the two temples with offerings,
and to bury the dismantled spirit tablet along the north wall.
To move Xuān Tàihòu to the upper chamber,
and to set out dried meat and minced offerings to appease the spirit—
Fěi-zǐ's deliberation is sound."
An imperial edict approved it.
In the third year of Tàihé, during the reign of Wèi Míng-dì,
an edict stated:
"According to ritual,
if a queen has no heir,
a son from a side branch is chosen to succeed the main lineage.
He should then uphold the legitimate succession and serve the public good;
how can he consider his private kinship?
Hàn Xuān-dì succeeded Zhāo-dì,
and later bestowed an imperial title upon his lamented father;
Aí-dì, being supported by an external lineage,
allowed Dǒng Hóng and others to cite the defunct Qín dynasty,
thereby misleading the court deliberations,
and consequently honored Gōng Huáng,
establishing a temple in the capital.
He further favored a concubine from a vassal state,
making her comparable to Chángxìn,
a transgression and irreverence
that neither men nor gods would bless.
It was not the fault of Shī Dān's loyal and upright remonstrance
that led to the calamity of the burning of Dīng and Fù.
From then on,
this practice was followed successively.
Therefore, let the ducal ministers and relevant authorities
take the previous eras as a deep warning.
If, by any chance, a later heir should come from a vassal lord to uphold the great succession,
he must clearly understand the principle of being an adopted heir.
Should anyone dare to be cunning and perverse,
flatter the sovereign,
and presumptuously establish an illegitimate title,
calling a father 'emperor'
or a mother 'empress,'
then the highest ministers
shall execute them without mercy.
Let this be inscribed on golden tablets,
〔一０〕stored in the ancestral temple,
and recorded in the legal code."
After this, when Gāo Guì and Cháng Dào were supported to ascend,
none externally honored their birth parents.
In the fourth year of Jiànxīng, during the reign of Jìn Mǐn-dì,
Sītú Liáng Fēn deliberated on the rites of posthumous honoring.
The Emperor did not follow,
and Zuǒ Púyè Suǒ Qín and others also cited the Wèi system,
deeming it impermissible.
Therefore, Wú Wáng was merely posthumously granted the title of Tàibǎo.
In the second year of Tàixīng, during the reign of Yuán-dì,
the relevant authorities stated that Lángyá Gōng Wáng should be called Huángkǎo.
Hè Xún deliberated, saying:
"According to the principles of ritual codes,
a son may not use his own noble title to augment his father's designation."
The Emperor again followed this.
This practice of the two Hàn dynasties was abandoned.
Wèi Míng-dì had a beloved daughter named Shúshè,
who died at three months old.
The Emperor grieved deeply,
posthumously enfeoffing and bestowing upon her the谥 (shì) title of Píngyuán Yì Gōngzhǔ,
burying her in Nánlíng,
and establishing a temple in the capital.
There was no prior precedent,
and it was contrary to ritual.
In the seventh month, on the day Xīn-yǒu, in the first year of Xiàojiàn, during the reign of Sòng Xiàowǔ-dì,
the relevant authorities memorialized:
"Dōngpíng Chōng Wáng was young and without heir,
and only observed five months of mourning for a child who died young.
Although a subject does not observe mourning for a child-monarch,
〔一一〕there should be someone to preside over the sacrifices,
but as the state posthumously granted him a title,
he also has no subjects.
It is unclear whether to dismantle the spirit tablet and establish a temple,
or whether he should be interred elsewhere.
We have sent it to the ritual officials for detailed deliberation."
Xú Hóng, a minister and 博士 (bóshì) of the Tàixué, deliberated:
"Since the King had no heir,
and posthumous grants imply no subjects,
and the mourning period for a child-who-died-young is complete,
the spirit tablet should be dismantled.
The record states: 'For those who die young and those without heirs,
they partake of sacrifices from their paternal ancestors.'
It also states: 'A shidàfū may not be interred with a feudal lord,
but with his paternal ancestor who was a shidàfū.'
According to this, a feudal lord may not be interred with the Son of Heaven.
Chōng Wáng should therefore be interred in the temple of an ancestor who was a king;
he should be interred in the temple of Chángshā Jǐng Wáng."
An imperial edict approved it.
In Dà Míng 4, Dīngsì [460 CE],
“Although the State of Ānlù is established,
the place for libations
has not yet been constructed.
Therefore, for the four seasonal sacrifices,
she is inducted into the temple of Jiāngxià.
Should the lady who gave birth to Xuān Wáng
be sacrificed to or not?”
Fù Yù, Doctor of the Imperial University, deliberated:
“The sacrifice should be abolished.”
the officials reported:
“According to the Rites,
‘a kind mother or a concubine mother is not sacrificed to for generations.’
the tradition says that a son sacrifices, but a grandson stops.’
It also says: ‘For one who succeeds a kind mother,
it is permissible for a paternal concubine.’
The commentary states: ‘Based on the principle of succeeding a kind mother,
if a father's concubine has no son,
one may also appoint one's own concubine-born son to succeed her.’
Upon examining this principle,
the sacrifice to a mother's concubine
is not necessarily limited to the son.
The Crown Prince of Jiāngxià Xuān Wáng,
being a grand minister by birth,
a descendant of a prominent relative,
unfortunately met troubled times.
The Emperor, out of compassion and sorrow,
extended imperial love,
succeeded the illustrious lineage,
and splendidly founded a great state,
with the subordinate state as his ancestor.
The first king's lady, having nurtured him with clarity and excellence,
is thus the principal wife of one state.
There is nothing above that should be displeased,
and her sorrow and respect can be expressed.
Since she has not been granted induction into Jiāngxià,
nor is she included in the sacrifices of Ānlù,
seeking the appropriate sentiment in this matter,
I believe it is proper to follow the principle of a grandmother having a successor,
meaning she should be formally enshrined and sacrificed to in the temple.”
The two deliberations differed,
and a joint deliberation found Yuán's opinion to be acceptable.
An imperial edict approved it.
In Dà Míng 6, the tenth month, Bǐngyín,
the officials reported:
“The deceased Jìnlíng Xiào Wáng, Zǐyún, has no successor.
Three days after the establishment of the temple,
the state officials, acting under temporary regulations, were relieved of their duties.
For the new moon, full moon, and annual anniversaries,
should they return to mourn or not?
On the day of the sacrifice,
who should preside?”
Yú Wèizhī, Assistant Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, deliberated:
“Three days after the burial,
the state officials were relieved of their duties under temporary regulations.
However, the spirit couch still remains.
the officials should return to mourn and weep,
change into rough mourning clothes,
and have the Senior Minister preside over the sacrifice.
Since the King has no successor,
and there are no three-year mourners,
after the mourning period for close relatives is over,
it is appropriate to establish a temple
as the founding ancestor of the state.
On the day the mourning period ends,
the spirit tablet should temporarily be inducted into the ancestral temple for food.
Lords may not take the Son of Heaven as their ancestor.
They should be inducted into the temple of their ancestral state,
and return to reside in the new temple's chamber.
Before a successor is established,
the Senior Minister should always preside over the four seasonal sacrifices.”
Xú Yuán, Assistant Director of the Left, participated in the deliberation,
and found Wèizhī's opinion to be acceptable.
An imperial edict approved it.
In Dà Míng 7, the first month, Gēngzǐ,
the officials reported:
“The deceased Xuān Guìfēi has been granted special rites,
but it is unclear whether a temple should be established for her.”
Yú Hé, Doctor of the Imperial University, deliberated:
“The ‘Qū Lǐ’ says: ‘The Son of Heaven has a Queen [Hòu] and has Ladies [Fūrén].’
The ‘Tán Gōng’ says: ‘Shùn was buried at Cāngwú,
and his three consorts did not follow him.’
The ‘Hūn Yì’ says: ‘The Queen establishes the Six Palaces,
and there are three Fūrén.’
Thus, the three consorts are the three Fūrén.
The Queen having three consorts
is like the Son of Heaven having three Gōng.
According to the ‘Zhōu Lǐ’,
the three Gōng receive eight mandates,
while the feudal lords receive seven mandates.
Since the three Gōng are more esteemed than the feudal lords of various states,
the three consorts are also nobler than the ladies of ordinary states.
According to the ‘Chūnqiū Zhuàn’,
even though Zhòngzǐ was not the legitimate heir of Lǔ Huì Yuán,
she was still allowed to have her own separate palace.
Now, Guìfēi holds this rank,
a high position granted by Heaven.
It is right that this new temple should be established.”
Xú Yuán, Assistant Director of the Left, deliberated:
“Since Xuān Guìfēi has been granted a special mandate,
her rites transcend the five palaces.
Examining the classical records,
there is clear precedent.
A temple may be constructed,
and an appropriate Master of Works should be selected.”
A joint deliberation found Hé's and Yuán's opinions to be acceptable.
An imperial edict approved it.
In Dà Míng 7, the third month, Wùxū,
the officials reported:
“Xīn’ān Wáng observes one-year mourning (qīcuī qī) for Xuān Guìfēi,
changing to plain white clothes in the eleventh month,
to light plain silk in the thirteenth month,
and performing the xiáng sacrifice in the fifteenth month,
with three years of heart mourning.
It is unclear when Xuān Guìfēi should be inducted into the temple.
On the day she enters the temple,
should there first be an induction ceremony,
or merely an entry into the new temple?
will she immediately receive sacrifices for the four seasons?
may he personally offer sacrifices?”
Yú Hé, Doctor of the Imperial University, deliberated:
“The ‘Chūnqiū Zhuàn’ says: ‘After induction, a spirit tablet is made,
and seasonal and quinquennial sacrifices are offered in the temple.’
‘Cháng’ refers to the name of an auspicious sacrifice.
During dàxiáng and tǎn,
one may not yet enter the temple.
It should be after the tǎn period is over.
Within Xīn’ān Wáng's period of heart mourning,
if a seasonal occasion arises,
he should perform auspicious sacrifices in the temple.
His personal offering would also be without impropriety.
The term ‘fù’ [induction]
refers to inducting a later deceased person into an earlier temple.
The ‘Xiǎo Jì’ says: ‘Feudal lords may not be inducted into the temple of the Son of Heaven.’
Now, Guìfēi's rank is equivalent to that of a feudal lord,
so she obviously cannot be inducted into the temple of earlier Queens.
Moreover, a separate new palace has been established,
so there is no appropriate place for induction.
Furthermore, after the ‘cùkū’ ceremony,
there is even less reason for induction.”
Xú Yuán, Assistant Director of the Left, deliberated:
“Rites have additions and subtractions,
and ancient and modern ceremonies differ.
Although it is said that after the ‘cùkū’ one is inducted,
and after induction a spirit tablet is made,
the feudal lords of the time
all entered the temple after the tǎn.
Moreover, rough mourning clothes with crimson trim
were changed during Yuánjiā,
and mourning mats and headbands were altered and abolished
to express sentiment in the August Sòng.
Furthermore, Xuān Guìfēi gave birth to an enlightened sovereign,
and her burial was accorded special rites.
The spirit couch and mourning hut positions
were all presided over by the wise king.
The establishment of her palace and sacrifices
should not be subject to the court.
I believe that after the tǎn period,
he should personally perform the rites of libation.
If there is an impediment,
the three Senior Ministers shall conduct the affairs.
Guìfēi is superior to an imperial aunt,
and separated from the various states;
there is no place where she should be inducted.”
In a joint deliberation,
Hé's opinion largely did not differ from Yuán's.
It was decided that Yuán's opinion should be adopted.
An imperial edict approved it.
In the eleventh month, on the day *guǐwèi* of the seventh year of Dàmíng,
the responsible authorities reported:
"As for the Chìxiào Temple of Jìnlíng Guó: following the precedent of Lúlíng and other states,
〔一八〕there should be five sacrifices per year.
Due to the fact that the king [wáng] [has mourning attire for Héngyáng Wáng,
there will be no sacrifices this year.
Considering that the state does not yet have an heir,
〕should the three ministers [qīng] preside over the sacrifices?
〔一九〕Should this follow the precedent of those in mourning attire?"
The Erudite Yán Sēngdào debated:
"The *Lǐjì* says: 'If the one to whom a sacrifice is offered has no mourners, then sacrifice.'
〔二０〕Now, Jìnlíng Wáng observes minor mourning for Héngyáng,
so it is appropriate to follow the example of the two states and suspend the sacrifices."
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies Assistant Yǔ Wèizhī debated:
"The rule of not sacrificing during *sīmā* mourning
is based on the principal mourner.
Although Jìnlíng does not yet have an heir,
it should observe mourning as if there were an heir,
and be limited to suspended sacrifices.
As Héngyáng is a paternal cousin and the mourning is *sīmā*,
sacrifices should resume after three months."
〔二一〕Assistant to the Left Xu Ái also debated:
"If an heir is not yet established,
it is unknown whether the future inheritor will be distant or close.
How can one merely calculate mourning relationships
and thus diminish the respect of sacrifices?"
The deliberators considered Ái's debate to be reasonable.
An imperial edict approved it.
In the first month, on the day *rénchén* of the eighth year of Dàmíng,
the responsible authorities reported:
"Regarding the establishment of an heir for the deceased Qí Jìng Wáng Zǐ Yǔ,
is it appropriate to immediately establish a main spirit tablet and temple?
Or should we wait until an heir is present?
For those who have not yet established a temple,
where should the sacrifices be performed?"
The Mobile General Xu Ái debated, considering:
"If a state has no heir,
it is abolished according to regulations.
However, for the first-enfeoffed lord,
the continuation of heirs should be preserved.
〔二二〕When an imperial prince is posthumously granted a title,
he becomes the founding ancestor.
A subject does not mourn for his lord as if he were a junior relative (shāng), this principle is evident from previous precedents.
How can one allow the seasonal sacrifices to be empty and wanting,
while waiting for an heir?
It is appropriate to establish a temple and a main spirit tablet,
with the three ministers [qīng] presiding over the sacrifices as before."
The general debate considered Ái's debate to be reasonable.
It was ordered to immediately establish a temple.
Once the temple is completed and the main spirit tablet made,
following the recent precedent of Jìnlíng Wáng,
it should first temporarily be enshrined in the temple of Lúlíng Xiàoxiàn Wáng.
After the sacrifices are completed,
the spirit tablet should immediately return to the new temple.
Before an heir is established,
the highest minister [shàngqīng] of the state should always preside over the sacrifices.
The Lǐ said:
“When Gònggōng Shì held sway over the Nine Provinces,
his son Jùlóng was called Hòutǔ.
He was able to level the nine lands,
and so he was sacrificed to as the Shè.”
The Zhōu offered sacrifices to him on a jiǎ-day,
using the beginning of the day.
“The Shè is the Way of divining the earth.
The earth carries all things,
and heaven displays its phenomena.
We take wealth from the earth,
and take laws from heaven.
Therefore, heaven is revered and earth is cherished.
Thus, the people are taught to give beautiful returns.
[二三] The head of a family attends to the zhōngliù (central hearth), and the ruler of a state attends to the shè;
this shows the origin.”
Therefore, it is said to return to the origin and to the source.
When Lièshān Shì possessed the world,
his son was called Nóng,
who was able to propagate all grains.
His descendant was called Zhù,
who assisted Zhuānxū as the Jì officer,
in charge of agricultural affairs.
Zhōu Qì was connected to him.
He bestowed laws upon the people,
and so he was sacrificed to as the Jì.
The Lǐ states:
“The king establishing a shè for all the surnames is called the Tàishè.
The king establishing a shè for himself is called the Wángshè.”
Therefore, a state has two shè,
and the jì also has two.
During the Hàn and Wèi, there was the Guānshè (official shè),
but no jì,
so it was always two shè and one jì.
In the early Jìn, the Wèi system was maintained,
with no additions or subtractions.
In the ninth year of Tàikāng (288 CE),
the ancestral temple was rebuilt,
and the altars of shè and jì were moved along with the temple.
An imperial edict then proclaimed:
“The shè is truly one deity,
so the sacrifices of the two shè should be combined.”
[二四] Thereupon, the Chēqí Sīmǎ Fù Xián submitted a memorial saying:
“In the Jìfǎ, the two shè each have their own meaning.
The Son of Heaven respectfully serves the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
and therefore wears a crown and personally plows.
The reason for personally plowing
[二五] is to emphasize the importance of the grains used for filial offerings,
and to present abundant sacrifices to the Supreme Lord.
The Gǔliáng Zhuàn says: ‘The Son of Heaven personally plows to provide the grains for offerings.’
‘Personally plowing’
refers to making an offering for oneself.
Establishing a shè for oneself
is for the purpose of the tilled fields and making offerings.
A state takes its people as its foundation,
and people take grain as their life.
Therefore, a shè is also established for the common people to pray and make offerings.
The matters are different and the returns are distinct;
this is why there are two shè.
Wáng Jǐnghóu's discussion of the Wángshè
also stated that it was to pray for the tilled fields in spring
and make offerings in autumn.
In his discussion of the Tàishè,
he said, ‘The king establishes it for the common people
throughout the realm,
and it is called the Tàishè.
He does not establish it for himself in the capital.’
Jǐnghóu's argument here
is based on the Jìfǎ, which says: ‘From the Grand Master downwards,
groups establish shè,
called Zhìshè.’
Jǐnghóu explains: ‘These are the current lǐshè (village shè).’
Jǐnghóu's explanation of the Jìfǎ
thus takes the Zhìshè as the shè of the common people.
But in another discussion, he again takes the Tàishè as the shè of the common people,
which is unclear in its meaning.
The Tàishè
is where the Son of Heaven sacrifices for the people,
[二六] hence it is called the Son of Heaven's shè.
The Jiāotèshēng says: ‘The Son of Heaven's Tàishè
must receive frost, dew, wind, and rain.’
Indeed, because of the multitude of surnames,
the king generally establishes a shè for them,
hence it is called the Tàishè.
As for the Zhìshè,
their number is not fixed.
They are probably named after the villages.
The Zuǒshì Zhuàn's ‘swearing an oath at the shè of Qīngqiū’ is an example.
The shè of the common people
is already not called ‘tà’ (great).
If it is not established in the capital,
where should it be established?
The Jìfǎ also says: ‘The king establishes seven sacrifices for all the surnames.
He establishes seven sacrifices for himself.’
‘For himself’ means
sacrificing for himself.
‘For all the surnames’ means
sacrificing for all the surnames.
The Tàishè and the seven sacrifices
are exactly equivalent in their text.
Commentators, at a loss here,
then say that the ancient texts only mention five sacrifices, not seven sacrifices.
In my opinion, the five sacrifices are the great sacrifices of the state,
and the seven are minor sacrifices.
What is referred to in the Zhōulǐ as ‘all minor sacrifices’
is of the type that wears a black cap.
Jǐnghóu's explanation of ‘dàlì’ (great pestilence) says: ‘Like Dù Bó of Zhōu,
when the ghost has a place to return to,
it will not become a pestilence.’
Now, those who say there are no two shè
claim that Jǐnghóu's Jìfǎ does not say there are no two,
or they say that oral tradition does not have such a text.
Indeed, with Jǐnghóu's clarity,
he would deliberate before providing an explanation.
To attempt to abolish a clear text with an oral argument—
if this were the case,
not only the two shè,
but even the subsequent explanations of Jǐnghóu
would not be easy to abolish.
Previously, an imperial decree stated,
regarding Shàngshū Zhàogào: ‘The shè in the new city
has only one tàiláo (grand offering),’
indicating the clear meaning of not having two shè.
[二七] In my opinion, the Jiāotèshēng says: ‘Shèjì, tàiláo.’
If one must cite the text of ‘one tàiláo’
to demonstrate that there are no two shè,
then the jì would have no sacrificial animal.
Commentators then say
that mentioning shè is to imply jì.
If shè can imply jì,
[二八] why can't ‘one’ imply ‘two’?
‘The great affairs of a state
are sacrifice and war.’
If there is an error and it is removed,
it is better to tolerate the error than remove it.
Moreover, there is meaning in retaining it,
and no basis for removing it.
The Zhōulǐ Fēngrén (boundary officer) ‘is in charge of setting up the shè and its enclosure.’
There is no mention of ‘jì’.
The absence of jì in the current Dìshè (imperial shè)
probably comes from this.
However, the ruler of the state oversees both shè and jì,
which is why the classics and commentaries often refer to ‘shèjì’.
In the Zhōulǐ,
when the king sacrifices to jì, he wears a fine linen crown.
This is a text indicating that the Wángshè includes jì.
The absence of the character ‘jì’ in the Fēngrén's setting up of the enclosure
is considered by commentators to be an abbreviation,
which is understandable.
It is appropriate to retain the old system of establishing two shè,
and furthermore, to establish the jì for the Dìshè.”
At that time, Chéng Càn argued:
“Jǐnghóu's argument that the Tàishè is not established in the capital
seeks to refute Zhèng Shì's scholarship.”
Xián submitted another memorial, stating:
“According to Càn's argument,
Jǐnghóu's explanation of the text would be undermined by this.
The Dàyǎ says: ‘Then he established the zhǒngtǔ (mound earth).’
Máo Gōng explains: ‘The zhǒngtǔ
is the Tàishè.’
Jǐnghóu, when explaining the Shī,
used this very explanation.
The Yǔgòng says: ‘The earth has five colors.’
Jǐnghóu explains: ‘The king takes earth of five colors to make the Tàishè,
and enfeoffs the feudal lords of the four directions.
Each cuts a piece of earth of its corresponding direction's color to cover the four directions.’
[二九] If this is the case,
the Tàishè is again established in the capital.
I do not know where this argument comes from,
as it contradicts the clear texts of the classics and records,
and undermines Jǐnghóu's explanation.
Although I am dull and ignorant,
having studied since youth,
I cannot remain silent;
I respectfully submit this continuation.”
Liú Shí's opinion agreed with Xián.
[三０] An imperial edict stated:
“The shè is truly one deity,
yet traditionally two positions have been maintained.
Since public opinion differs,
why must there be a change?
It is expedient to keep the old system,
[三一] entirely according to the Wèi regulations.”
When Yuán Dì
established the Jiànwǔ reign in his first year, he again set up two Earth Altars and one Grain Altar in Luòjīng.
The prayer for the Grand Altar of Earth (Tàishè) read:
“The Earth’s virtue universally bestows,
its benevolence is boundless.
Therefore, the Grand Altar of Earth is established,
to protect and bless all nations.
Throughout the vast four seas,
all rely on its auspicious blessings.”
The prayer for the Imperial Altar of Earth (Dìshè) read:
“The Earth’s virtue carries richly,
protecting the royal domain.
Therefore, the Imperial Altar of Earth is established,
to deify the Way of Earth.
May brilliant sacrifices be timely,
〔三二〕and great blessings arrive.”
According to ritual,
the ancestral temple is on the left,
and the altars of earth and grain are on the right.
This was followed by successive dynasties,
hence the altars of earth and grain in Luòjīng were to the right of the temple,
and it was the same in Jiāngzuǒ.
During the Wú period, the Yúmén gate was to the east of the palace.
It is presumed that Wú’s altars of earth were also to the east of the palace,
in the same location as its temple.
Sòng maintained the old system,
making no changes.
The three ancestors of the Wèi clan all personally ploughed the ceremonial field.
This means that the Xīannóng (First Farmer) never lacked offerings.
Since there are no different accounts of the rituals,
they should follow the Hàn practices.
The officiants announced the sacrifice with a tàiláo (grand offering).
Jìn Yuán Dì and Āi Dì both wished to plough the ceremonial field but did not succeed.
〔三三〕The ritual records are also incomplete.
In the spring of the twenty-first year of Yuánjiā of Sòng Wén Dì,
he personally ploughed,
and then established the Xīannóng Altar in the ceremonial field, west of the middle path and south of the western path.
It was four chǐ high
and two zhàng square,
with four access ramps.
Each ramp was five chǐ wide,
with an outer enclosure.
It was twenty zhàng away from the paths.
Before the imperial carriage arrived,
the Sīkōng and Dàsīnóng, leading the Tàizhùlìng and all officiants, early in the morning, announced the sacrifice with one tàiláo.
The sacrificial vessels used were those for the altars of earth and grain.
After the sacrifice,
the remaining sacrificial meat was distributed to those who participated in the sacrifice.
According to old rites, Xīannóng was also usually included in the suburban sacrifices.
According to Hàn practices,
the empress personally gathered mulberry leaves in the eastern suburban park.
The silkworm room worshipped the Silkworm God, saying:
“Yuànyǔ Fùrén,
Yùshì Gōngzhǔ.”
The sacrifice used a shàoláo (lesser offering).
In the ninth year of Tàikāng of Jìn Wǔ Dì,
Empress Yáng personally gathered mulberry leaves in the western suburb
and sacrificed to the Xīancán (First Silkworm).
The altar was one zhàng high
and two zhàng square,
with four access ramps,
each ramp five chǐ wide.
It was southeast of the mulberry-gathering altar, outside the temporary palace,
ten zhàng away from the temporary palace.
Before the empress arrived,
the Tàizhùlìng, early in the morning, announced the sacrifice with one tàiláo.
One Yèzhě supervised the sacrifice.
After it was completed,
the offerings were removed,
and the remaining sacrificial meat was distributed to those who gathered mulberry leaves and participated in the sacrifice.
In the sixth month, Gēngzǐ day, of the second year of Huángchū of Wèi Wén Dì,
the Five Sacred Mountains and Four Great Rivers were first ritually honored,
and all gods were offered sacrifices in their proper order,
burying and submerging jade tablets.
In the seventh month of the sixth year,
the emperor entered the Huái River with a naval force.
In the ninth month, Rénxū day,
