envoys were sent to submerge jade discs in the Huái River;
this was a ritual.
In the eighth month of the fourth year of Tàihé of Wèi Míng Dì,
the emperor made an eastern tour,
and sent envoys to sacrifice a special ox to Zhōngyuè (Mount Sōng);
this was a ritual.
In the first year of Xiánxī of Wèi Yuán Dì,
the emperor traveled to Cháng’ān,
and sent envoys with jade and silk to honor Huáshān (Mount Huà);
this was a ritual.
During the Shēngpíng era of Jìn Mù Dì,
Hé Qí discussed revising the sacrifices to the Five Sacred Mountains, saying:
“In the system of Táng and Yú,
the Son of Heaven made a grand tour every five years,
inspecting the regions in season,
burning sacrifices to the Five Sacred Mountains,
making offerings to mountains and rivers,
and extending them to all spirits.
Thus it is said, ‘Ascending to Heaven via famous mountains.’
This was to make announcements to the gods,
and to offer thanks and report on merits.
Therefore, calamities did not arise,
and wind, rain, cold, and heat occurred in due season.
Down to the Three Dynasties,
though the number of years differed,
the rituals did not change.
The Five Sacred Mountains were treated like the Sāngōng (Three Dukes),
and the Four Great Rivers like the Zhūhóu (feudal lords);
this is recorded in the classics,
meaning that when it was established,
no one dared to abolish it.
When Qín and Hàn established their capital in Xīpíng,
the Jīng and Wèi rivers, though not in the sacrificial canon,
because of their proximity to Xiányáng,
were accorded the same sacrifices as great rivers.
And how could the established sacrifices
〔三四〕be omitted?
Since the chaos of Yǒngjiā,
the divine land was overturned,
and these matters were neglected.
Only Tiānzhù in Qián,
within the royal domain,
had a hundred clerks and soldiers formerly selected by the court
to perform its duties.
At the time of the restoration,
there were no official custodians,
so Lújiāng Jùn often sent a senior official to act temporarily,
praying and offering sacrifices in the four seasons,
releasing the cold in spring and requesting ice in winter.
From Xiánhé until now,
this has again fallen into neglect.
Currently, the unofficial sacrifices
can be said to be numerous.
Examining their true nature,
they are wanton and corrupt spirits;
considering their extravagance,
they are a bane to the common people.
〔三五〕Yet the great gods of mountains and rivers
are even more neglected and lacking,
rituals and customs are in disarray,
humans and spirits are mixed up,
and public and private matters are rushed,
〔三六〕gradually becoming more chaotic.
This is truly because the state has recently faced many difficulties,
leaving no time to attend to everything,
and the hastily established and abandoned matters
have not yet been addressed.
Now that the principal rebels have been annihilated,
the old rites should be restored.
In the regions of the mountains and rivers,
where moral teachings have spread,
the people who have returned to peace
have all received benevolent favor,
yet the sacrifices to the gods have not been properly distinguished,
and the grand tours and burning sacrifices
have long been abolished.
To restore the brilliant old ceremonies
will await the emperor’s return to the north,
to examine ancient precedents
and greatly reform the system.
As for the places where the Five Sacred Mountains and Four Great Rivers should be honored and repaired,
although the sacrificial vessels,
livestock,
and the prayers and blessings
are not recorded in the old chapters,
the ritual officials can be ordered to create a form,
returning to sincerity and simplicity,
to convey bright virtue and fragrant offerings;
this is all.
As for the various evil spirits,
they can be broadly dealt with according to the law,
〔三七〕first removing the most egregious ones,
so that the proper and the邪 (evil) are not profaned.”
It was not approved.
In the seventh year of the Dà-Míng reign of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng, on the bǐng-chén day of the sixth month,
the relevant authorities memorialized:
“An imperial edict has been issued to perform a sacrifice at Huòshān,
but it is not yet clear which official should be appointed to lead the mission?
What animals and provisions should be used?
And on the day of the sacrifice,
what vessels should be used?”
Qiū Jǐngxiān, a court gentleman of the Hall, deliberated:
“Performing sacrifices to mountains and rivers
has illuminated successive dynasties;
the graded ranks of jades and insignia
have been clearly manifested in official records.
However, the tradition has been neglected in the middle periods,
and the rituals are missing from the classics.
Tracing back, the Jī (Duke of Zhōu)’s affairs were continued by the Zōngbó;
the Hàn records show officials bearing credentials attending sacrifices;
blood sacrifices and burial in the ground
established clear precedents in the classics,
with detailed examples for wine, dried meat, and sacrificial animals
all available.
Furthermore, famous mountains have different jade and silk offerings,
and major tombs have additional grain offerings.
The Shānhǎi Cí (Mountains and Seas Sacrifices) to Huòshān
uses a grand animal sacrifice to announce to the jade;
these can be understood by referring to records and biographies,
which are available for discussion.
Now, the imperial virtue extends far and wide,
and the glorious sacrifices reach all mountains.
I humbly suggest that the Grand Master of Rites (Tài-cháng) should be sent with credentials,
the sacrifice should use the full set for a grand animal offering,
the provisions should include wine, dried meat, and seasonal grains,
and the ceremonial items should be a red zhāng-jade and dark red silk.
Moreover, according to the duty of the chāng-rén (perfumed wine officer),
‘all sacrifices to mountains, rivers, and the four directions use shèn (clam shells),’
so the wine should be served in lí-cups (clam-shell cups).
Regarding other vessels,
there is no basis to draw upon.
According to the suburban sacrifices to mountains and rivers,
sincerity is expressed through plainness,
vessels favor pottery and gourds,
and mats are made of straw.
This can be approximated as a standard.
For mountains and rivers, a sacrificial mound (zhào) is appropriate,
so a platform and enclosure should be made.”
The other deliberators agreed with Jǐngxiān’s proposal as reasonable.
It was ordered that an official兼Tài-cháng (acting Grand Master of Rites) with credentials be sent to perform the mission,
the sacrifice should use a grand animal offering,
augmented with jade and silk,
the vessels should be pottery and gourds,
and since shèn (clam shells) are no longer used for the season,
it should follow the suburban sacrifices,
offering with jué (wine cups).
All types of dishes and provisions should follow the community sacrifices (shè-jì) as appropriate.
The edict was approved.
In the second year of Xiánníng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, in the spring,
there was a long drought.
On the dīng-sì day of the fourth month,
“Extensive prayers should be offered in all drought-stricken areas.”
On the gēng-wǔ day of the fifth month,
prayers for rain were first offered to the deities of the land and grain (shè-jì) and to the mountains and rivers.
On the wù-zǐ day of the sixth month,
a heavy rain was received.
This was an old tradition of rain sacrifices and expiatory rites.
In the fourth month of the third year of Tàikāng and the second month of the tenth year,
the same occurred.
This practice has been followed ever since.
In the first month of the second year of Huángchū of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
an imperial edict stated:
“In ancient times, Zhòngní (Confucius), endowed with the talent of a great sage
and possessing the capacity of an emperor or king,
lived at the end of the declining Zhōu dynasty,
and did not receive the mandate of heaven.
He then retired to study the rites of the five ancient dynasties,
and performed the deeds of a ‘Plain King’ (sù-wáng).
He based his Chunqiū on the history of Lǔ,
and rectified the Yǎ and Sòng with the Grand Master of Music.
As a result, even a thousand years later,
none fail to revere his writings in their compositions
or look up to his sagehood to form their plans.
He can truly be called a great sage born for his time,
a model for a hundred million years.
Because of the great chaos in the world,
all sacrifices were ruined and abandoned.
The temple at his old residence
was destroyed and not repaired,
and the lineage of the Bāochéng Marquis
was broken and not continued.
The sounds of lectures and odes were not heard in Quēlǐ,
and positions for seasonal sacrifices were not seen.
How can this be called honoring transformation and repaying merit,
a glorious virtue that must be sacrificed to for a hundred generations?
with an estate of a hundred households,
to maintain the sacrifices to Kǒngzǐ.
The Lǔ commandery is ordered to repair the old temple,
and to establish one hundred households of officials and soldiers
to guard it.”
In the eleventh month of the third year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
the Zōngshèng Hóu Kǒng Zhèn was re-enfeoffed as Fèngshèng Tínghóu (Marquis of the Pavilion of Honoring the Sage).
It was also decreed that the Imperial Academy (Tài-xué) and the state of Lǔ should prepare three sacrificial animals for Kǒngzǐ at all four seasons.
In the third year of Tàiníng of Emperor Míng,
an edict ordered the Palace Attendant Fèngshèng Tínghóu Kǒng Tíng to perform seasonal sacrifices to Kǒngzǐ,
and the rituals should follow the precedent of Tàishǐ.
Tíng’s descendant five generations later, Jìzhī, indulged in gambling without restraint,
often selling the sacrificial income to advance himself,
and negligently failed to perform sacrifices.
In the eighth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
the relevant authorities memorialized to strip him of his title.
In the nineteenth year,
Kǒng Yǐnzhī was again granted the title.
His nephew Xīxiān conspired in rebellion,
and again lost the title.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Kǒng Huìyún was made Fèngshèng Hóu.
Later, he suffered a serious illness,
and lost the title.
In the second year of Dà-Míng of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
Kǒng Mài was again made Fèngshèng Hóu.
Mài died,
and his son Fú succeeded.
and lost the title.
In the third month of the second year of Zhèngshǐ of King Qí of Wèi,
the Emperor thoroughly lectured on the Lúnyǔ.
In the fifth month of the fifth year,
he thoroughly lectured on the Shàngshū.
In the twelfth month of the seventh year,
he thoroughly lectured on the Lǐjì.
sacrificing to Kǒngzǐ with a grand animal offering at the Bìyōng,
with Yán Yuān as co-sacrificed.
In the seventh year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
the Crown Prince thoroughly lectured on the Xiàojīng.
In the third year of Xiánníng,
he thoroughly lectured on the Shī.
In the third year of Tàikāng,
[the Crown Prince] thoroughly lectured on the Lǐjì.
In the third year of Yuánkāng of Emperor Huì,
the Crown Prince
thoroughly lectured on the Lúnyǔ.
the Crown Prince thoroughly lectured on the Lúnyǔ.
In all these instances, the Crown Prince personally performed the shīdiàn,
sacrificing to Kǒngzǐ with a grand animal offering,
with Yán Yuān as co-sacrificed.
In the first year of Xiánkāng of Emperor Chéng,
the Emperor thoroughly lectured on the Shī.
In the third month of the first year of Shēngpíng of Emperor Mù,
the Emperor thoroughly lectured on the Xiàojīng.
In the seventh month of the third year of Níngkāng of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
the Emperor thoroughly lectured on the Xiàojīng.
All performed shīdiàn according to precedent.
Emperor Mù and Emperor Xiàowǔ both temporarily used the central hall as the Imperial Academy.
In the fourth month of the twenty-second year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
the Crown Prince thoroughly lectured on the Xiàojīng,
and performed shīdiàn at the Guózǐ-xué (National University),
following the Jìn precedent.
When King Gōng of Dōnghǎi of Hàn died,
Emperor Míng went out to the Jīnmén Tíng to express his sorrow.
During the Wèi period, when attending funerals or sending envoys to offer condolences and sacrifices,
following the advice of Scholar Dù Xī,
all removed their black caps,
and added cloth turbans.
When Wèi Wǔ-dì was young,
Grand Commandant Qiáo Xuán of Hàn alone treated him with special courtesy.
Therefore, during the Jiàn'ān reign,
an envoy was sent to sacrifice to him with a grand animal offering.
In the twelfth month of the sixth year of Huángchū of Emperor Wén,
he passed through Liáng-jùn,
and again sacrificed to him with a grand animal offering.
In the first month of the second year of Huángchū,
the Emperor was hunting and reached Yuánlíng,
and sent an envoy to sacrifice to Emperor Shìzǔ of Hàn with a grand animal offering.
On the bǐng-chén day of the fourth month of the twenty-fifth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
the imperial carriage traveled to Jiāngníng,
and passing the tomb of Minister of Works (Sītú) Liú Mùzhī,
an envoy was sent to offer sacrifices there.
On the wù-shēn day of the second month of the third year of Dà-Míng of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
he went to the Jítián (field for ceremonial plowing),
and passing the tomb of the Grand Master of Splendid Happiness of the Left (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū) Yuán Zhàn,
an envoy was sent to offer sacrifices.
On the gēng-wǔ day of the ninth month of the fifth year of Dà-Míng,
and passing the tomb of Minister of Works (Sīkōng) Yīn Jǐngrén,
an envoy was sent to offer sacrifices.
In the eleventh month of the seventh year of Dà-Míng,
he made a southern tour.
On the yǐ-yǒu day,
envoys were sent to sacrifice at the tombs of Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ) Huán Wēn of Jìn and General Who Conquers the West (Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn) Mao Qú.
In the sixth year of Jǐngyào of Liú Chán,
an imperial edict was issued to erect a temple for Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng in Miǎnyáng.
Previously, those who resided in the area had each requested to erect a temple,
but this was not permitted.
Consequently, the common people privately offered sacrifices to him.
Some who spoke on the matter suggested that a temple could be erected in the capital,
but their intentions were followed,
and all were rejected.
The Commandant of Infantry Xí Lóng and the Palace Assistant Secretary Xiàng Chōng and others said to Chán: (45)
"In ancient times, the people of Zhōu cherished the goodness of Shào Bó,
and for him, the sweet pear tree was not cut down.
The King of Yuè, recalling the achievements of Fàn Lǐ,
cast gold to preserve his image.
Since the rise of the Hàn dynasty,
there have been many who, for minor good deeds and small virtues,
had their images painted and temples erected;
how much more so for Liàng, whose virtue and example extended far and wide,
whose achievements overshadowed his era,
and who ensured the survival of the imperial house.
Truly, this man was relied upon.
Yet, the offerings are confined to private homes,
and a temple image is lacking and not erected.
The common people sacrifice in alleys,
and the barbarians offer sacrifices in the wilds.
This is not the way to preserve his virtue and remember his achievements,
or to recall and pursue the past.
If we were to follow everyone's wishes now,
it would be profane and without principle.
If we were to build it in the capital,
it would also encroach upon the ancestral temple.
This is why Your Sacred Majesty has been hesitant.
We humbly believe it would be appropriate to build it near his tomb,
in Miǎnyáng,
and appoint an official to make periodic offerings.
As for all his former subordinates who wish to offer sacrifices,
they should all be restricted to the temple.
Stop their private sacrifices
to uphold proper rites."
Thereupon, this was followed.
Hé Chéngtiān said:
"The Rites of Zhōu state: 'All those with meritorious achievements are sacrificed to in the great autumn offering.'
Therefore, later generations followed this,
to have great heroes partake in the offerings.
Chōng and others did not take this as their model, (46)
and Chán also followed them,
which was both improper according to ritual."
In the Hàn dynasty, the people of Chéngyáng Commandery erected a shrine for Liú Zhāng because of his contributions to Hàn.
Various commanderies in Qīngzhōu
followed suit,
with Jìnán being especially fervent.
When Wèi Wǔdì served as the Chancellor of Jìnán,
he destroyed and abolished them all.
Later, when he held supreme political power,
he universally suppressed and eliminated them,
and the corrupt sacrifices of the era were thus brought to an end.
In the eleventh month of the fifth year of Huángchū of Wén Dì,
an imperial edict stated:
"The rites established by the former kings
were to manifest filial piety and serve the ancestors;
the great ones were the suburban sacrifices,
the next were the ancestral temples,
the Three Luminaries and Five Phases,
and famous mountains, rivers, and lakes.
Things not of this category
are not included in the sacrificial canon.
In later chaotic ages,
(47) people devoutly believed in shamans and scribes,
to the extent that within palaces
and between doors and windows,
there was nothing without libations,
so great was their delusion.
From now on, whoever dares to set up unauthorized sacrifices
or perform the words of shamans and diviners
shall all be judged as practicing unorthodox ways
and this shall be enshrined in law."
In the first year of Qīnglóng of Míng Dì,
another edict stated:
"Mountains and rivers in commanderies and states
not included in the sacrificial canon
shall not be sacrificed to."
In the twelfth month of the first year of Tàishǐ of Jìn Wǔdì,
an edict stated:
"In ancient times, the sagely emperors and enlightened kings
maintained the Five Sacred Mountains and Four Great Rivers,
and famous mountains, rivers, and lakes,
each with established regulations.
This was to repay the merits of yin and yang
and to align with the ways of the visible and invisible.
However, when one governs the world with the Dao,
its spirits do not become uncanny,
and its deities do it no harm.
Thus, the ritual officials offer sacrifices without words of shame, (48)
which is why its people are respectful and cautious of the unseen,
and perverse sacrifices do not arise.
In later ages, faith in the Dao was not profound;
they trespassed against ritual, profaned spirits,
indulged in desires and prayers,
never showing reverence and keeping distance,
but rather furtively seeking fortune.
Witchcraft and delusion fanned each other,
abandoning the righteous for the wicked.
Therefore, the Wèi court detested this.
Let the old rites be followed,
and regulations be thoroughly established,
so that those whose achievements benefit humanity
will surely receive their due recompense,
and perverse and licentious spirits
will not disrupt the order."
In the first month of the second year,
the relevant officials reported:
"During the vernal equinox, sacrifices are offered to avert calamities and to ward off evil."
The imperial edict stated:
"Not included in the sacrificial canon,
abolish them."
In the second year of Yǒngchū of Sòng Wǔdì,
all illicit sacrifices were universally prohibited.
Thereupon, from the shrine of Jiǎng Zǐwén downwards,
all were destroyed and abolished.
At the beginning of Xiàojiàn of Xiàowǔ,
the Jiǎngshān shrine was rebuilt,
and various mountain and river shrines in different locations
were gradually restored.
Míng Dì erected the Jiǔzhōu Temple on Jīlóngshān,
gathering a great multitude of deities.
During the Sòng dynasty, Marquis Jiǎng's rank was gradually elevated,
reaching the position of Chancellor, Grand Commander, and Commander of all military affairs at home and abroad,
with special rites,
and he was enfeoffed as King of Zhōngshān.
Marquis Sū was made General of Agile Cavalry.
All deities from the four directions
were likewise granted titles and ranks.
In the fourth year of Yuánchū of Hàn Ān Dì,
an imperial edict stated:
"The Monthly Ordinances state,
'In mid-autumn,
care for the old and frail,
bestow walking sticks,
and offer gruel and congee.'
Currently, in the eighth month, during the time of population registration,
many commanderies and counties do not follow these instructions.
Although gruel and congee are provided,
chaff, husks, and mud are mixed in half and half,
making them unfit for consumption."
According to this edict,
the Hàn dynasty still governed by the Monthly Ordinances.
Collation Notes
Monograph Eight: Rites Five
Qín abolished ritual studies,
and many practices deviated from antiquity.
At the beginning of Hàn, simplicity was valued,
and no reforms were made;
the ceremonies of chariots and clothing
largely followed the old Qín customs.
It was not until Míng Dì that the former canons were restored,
as detailed in Sīmǎ Biāo's Monograph on Carriages and Attire.
During the Wèi dynasty, only the south-pointing chariot was made;
although other minor changes were made,
they were not significant enough to be transformative.
The Jìn established regulations for attire,
clarifying various ceremonies,
and Xú Guǎng's Commentary on Carriages and Attire
briefly explains the items,
which are still in use today.
Therefore, they are listed again
to illustrate the ceremonial practices of several dynasties.
In high antiquity, a sage, observing a tumbleweed,
first made a wheel.
As a wheel could be ridden,
it was then made into a carriage.
It could carry heavy loads and travel far,
its movement ceaseless.
Later sages, observing the handle of the Dipper constellation (Běidǒu Kuí Fāng Sháo Qū Xié Lóngjiǎo),
made the Emperor's carriage,
curving its shafts to facilitate harnessing.
The Xìběn states:
"Xīzhòng (奚仲) first made carriages."
However, Fúxī (伏羲) delineated the eight trigrams and created the great carriage,
harnessing oxen and riding horses,
to benefit the world.
Xīzhòng was merely the director of carriages during the Xià (夏) dynasty.
How could he have been the first to create them?
The statement in the Xìběn is incorrect.
"Carriages and robes are used for official service,"
is recorded in the Táng (唐) ordinances.
The Xià established banners and flags
to distinguish rank.
The Zhōu (周) had six professions,
with artisans comprising one of them.
Many artisans contributed their skill to a single object,
with carriages being the most common example.
The Míngtáng Wèi says:
"The luánchē (鸞車) was the carriage of the Yǒuyú (有虞) clan.
The dàlù (大路) was the carriage of the Yīn (殷).
The chénglù (乘路) was the carriage of the Zhōu."
The Yīn had the auspicious omen of the shānchē (山車),
meaning a carriage made of mulberry roots.
The Yīn people then fashioned it into the dàlù.
The Lǐwěi says:
"The shānchē has a hanging hook."
Jù (句)
means curved.
It means it was naturally curved without being bent or treated.
The Zhōu's five carriages
were those adorned with jade, gold, ivory, leather, and wood.
The decorations for these five
are fully detailed in the Kǎogōng Jì.
The carriage body (yú) is square, symbolizing the earth;
the canopy (gài) is round, symbolizing heaven;
the spokes (fú) symbolize the sun and moon;
the twenty-eight bows (gōng) symbolize the constellations (lièsù).
Jade, gold, and ivory
were decorations for the ends of the carriage,
which gave them their names.
The "leather" (gé) one was lacquered leather,
and the "wood" (mù) one was lacquered wood.
The yùlù (玉路) [jade carriage] bore the dàcháng (大常) banner for sacrifices;
the jīnlù (金路) [gold carriage] bore the dàqí (大旂) banner for receiving guests;
the xiànglù (象路) [ivory carriage] bore the dàchì (大赤) banner for court audiences;
the gélù (革路) [leather carriage] bore the dàbái (大白) banner for military affairs;
the mùlù (木路) [wood carriage] bore the dàhuī (大麾) banner for hunting.
Black was the color
favored by the Xià dynasty.
Qín (秦) examined the carriages of the Three Dynasties
and adopted only the Yīn system.
What was anciently called the mulberry root carriage
was called the gold root carriage by Qín.
The Hàn (漢) dynasty followed the old Qín system,
also making it the emperor's carriage (chéngyú),
which was what was meant by "riding the Yīn's carriage."
The Lǐlùn Yújiàyì says:
"In the Zhōu, the yùlù (玉輅) was the most revered.
The Hàn's jīngēn (金根) [gold root carriage]
was also the Zhōu's yùlù."
According to Hàn regulations,
the emperor's jīngēnchē (金根車) [gold root carriage]
had wheels that were all vermilion-spotted,
double hubs (chónggū) and two axles (liǎngxiá),
and flying streamers (fēilíng).
Outside the hub was another hub,
with an axle pin (xiá) fitted;
outside that, another axle pin was set,
with a bronze rod inserted through it.
The Dōngjīng Fù says:
"Double wheels and two axle pins,
hollow hubs and flying streamers."
The fēilíng were made of red oil paint,
eight inches wide,
three feet long, touching the ground,
attached to the two axle heads.
This was called fēilíng.
They used gold leaf to entwine dragons
to form the carriage's side rails (yǐjiào).
The jiào were above the box.
The patterns and paintings were numerous (fán).
Fán
means box.
Patterned tigers lay on the footrest (shì),
dragon heads bit the yoke (è),
phoenixes and sparrows stood on the crossbar (héng),
the shafts were patterned and painted,
and kingfisher feathers covered the yellow awning (huángshū),
which was called the huángwū (黃屋) [yellow canopy].
Golden flowers were applied to the ends of the rafters (lǎo),
and the dàcháng (大常) banner with twelve streamers was erected,
painted with the sun, moon, and rising dragons.
It was drawn by six black horses,
with twelve luán (鸞 bells) attached,
and gold forked plumes (chāmáo)
were inserted with pheasant tails.
Additionally, yak tails were added,
as large as dippers,
placed on the yoke of the left outrider horse (zuǒfēimǎ),
which was called the zuǒdúyú (左纛輿) [left yak-tail carriage].
The carriage (lù) was like the Zhōu's yùlù system.
According to Yìng Shào's (應劭) Hàn Guān Lǔbù Tú (漢官鹵簿圖),
for the grand imperial procession (chéngyú dàjià),
the emperor rode the Fènghuáng Chē (鳳皇車),
with the jīngēn (金根) as a secondary carriage.
There were also five carriages each of the five-colored ānnchē (安車) and five-colored lìchē (立車).
They bore dragon banners,
were drawn by four horses,
and had eight luán bells.
The rest was according to the jīngēn system,
similar to the Zhōu's jīnlù.
Each of these carriages was of its respective directional color,
known as the "five seasonal auxiliary carriages" (wǔshí fùchē),
commonly called
"Five Emperors' Carriages" (wǔdìchē).
These were absent south of the Jiāng (長江).
The white horses
had vermilion manes.
The ānnchē (安車) was a seated carriage.
There was also a magnificent canopy (huágài) with nine layers.
The Gānquán Lǔbù included
five ceremonial carriages (dàochē) and
nine pleasure carriages (yóuchē),
positioned in front of the emperor's carriage.
There were also xiàngchē (象車) [elephant carriages],
at the very front,
to test the bridge paths.
During the Jìn (晉) dynasty, these still existed south of the Jiāng.
All women's carriages were seated carriages,
which is why in the Zhōu Lǐ, the queen had an ānnchē (安車) but the king did not.
In the Hàn system, the emperor also had one.
The emperor's personal carriage (tiānzǐ suǒyù) was drawn by six horses;
all other auxiliary carriages were drawn by four.
The Shū (書) mentions "rotten ropes controlling six horses."
The Yì Lǐ Wángdù Jì says:
"The Son of Heaven drives six horses,
a feudal lord five,
a minister four,
a grandee three,
a scholar two,
and commoners one."
King Píng (平王) of Chǔ (楚) rode white horses.
King Huì (惠王) of Liáng (梁) sent Chúnyú Kūn (淳于髠) in an ānnchē (安車) drawn by three horses,
the standard for a grandee.
In the Zhōu Lǐ,
four horses constituted a team (chéng).
The Máoshī states,
"From the Son of Heaven to grandees, all drive four horses;
scholars drive two."
Yuán Àng (袁盎) admonished Emperor Wén (文) of Hàn for racing with six swift horses.
During the Wèi (魏) dynasty, the Son of Heaven also drove six horses.
In the Jìn dynasty's first silkworm ceremony (xiāncán yí),
the empress's ānnchē (安車) was drawn by six horses,
with a two-shafted ānnchē (安車) drawn by five horses as an auxiliary.
Since the Jiāngzǔo (江左) period,
this tradition has been maintained without six horses,
only four.
In the third year of Dàmíng during the reign of Sòng Xiàowǔ,
the Emperor ordered the Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs, Xún Wànqiū, to construct five types of carriages.
The Lǐtú (Ritual Diagrams)
mentions the Yùlù (Jade Carriage).
It was equipped with a red banner,
had no canopy,
and was rebuilt to resemble the Jīngēn (Golden Root Carriage),
but it was painted with red lacquer,
and its ends were adorned with jade.
It was equipped with a blue banner,
with twelve streamers,
drawn by four dark-colored horses,
and had a feather-adorned canopy,
for sacrificial rites.
The Jīngēn was then used as the Jīnlù (Golden Carriage),
equipped with a large blue banner,
with twelve streamers,
drawn by four dark-colored horses,
and a feather-adorned canopy,
for receiving guests.
The Xiànglù (Elephant Carriage), Gélù (Leather Carriage), and Mùlù (Wooden Carriage) –
the Zhōuguān (Rites of Zhou), Yúfúzhì (Treatise on Carriages and Attire), and Lǐtú do not record their specific forms.
All were constructed to resemble the Yùlù,
lacquered and painted,
with feather-adorned canopies,
their ends adorned with elephant ivory.
They were equipped with red banners,
with twelve streamers,
for holding morning court.
The Gélù
was equipped with a red banner,
with twelve streamers,
for military expeditions.
The Mùlù
was equipped with a red command banner,
for hunting.
The Xiànglù and Gélù were drawn by dark-colored horses,
while the Mùlù was drawn by red horses,
four horses each.
In earlier times, for major events,
the Fǎjià (Imperial Carriage) would be dispatched,
and each of the five carriages had its specific purpose,
they did not all go out together.
In the Dàmíng era,
it was first decreed that all five carriages should be dispatched together.
When the Emperor personally ploughed the sacrificial field,
he rode a three-canopy carriage,
one name for which was the Zhīchē (Auspicious Carriage),
and another the Gēnggēnchē (Ploughing Root Carriage),
with a ploughshare placed on the armrest.
The Róngchē (Military Carriage) was designed for standing,
in the Xià dynasty it was called Gōuchē,
in the Yīn dynasty Yínchē,
and in the Zhōu dynasty Yuánróng.
It was equipped with a tooth banner and a command banner,
pointing obliquely,
carrying golden drums and feather banners,
with armor and crossbows placed on the armrest.
The Lièchē (Hunting Carriage)
had a canopy and side-curtains,
its wheels painted with coiling dragons.
One name for it was Tàzhūchē (Pig-Trampling Carriage).
Wèi Wéndì renamed it Tàhǔchē (Tiger-Trampling Carriage).
The Zhǐnánchē (South-Pointing Carriage)
was originally created by Zhōugōng,
to send off envoys to distant, desolate lands.
When the terrain was flat and vast,
and they lost their way regarding east and west,
this carriage was built
to ensure they always knew north and south.
Guǐgǔzǐ said:
"When the people of Zhèng collect jade,
they must carry a Sīnán (South-Pointer),
so that they do not get confused."
By the time of Qín and Hàn,
its design was no longer known.
In the Later Hàn, Zhāng Héng first recreated it.
At the end of the Hàn, due to chaos and warfare,
the device no longer existed.
In the Wèi dynasty, Gāotáng Lóng and Qín Lǎng,
both learned men,
debated in court,
claiming there was no Zhǐnánchē,
and that records were mere fabrications.
In the Qīnglóng era of Míngdì,
he ordered the scholar Mǎ Jūn to recreate it, and the carriage was completed.
During the chaos of the Jìn dynasty, it was lost again.
Shí Hǔ ordered Xiè Fēi,
and Yáo Xīng ordered Línghú Shēng to create it again.
In the thirteenth year of Yìxī during the reign of Āndì,
Sòng Wǔdì pacified Cháng'ān,
and first obtained this carriage.
Its design was like a drum carriage,
with a wooden figure on top of the carriage,
raising its hand to point south.
Although the carriage turned,
what it pointed to did not shift.
In the grand imperial procession (Lǔbù),
it was the first to set off.
This carriage was made by the Róng and Dí (barbarians),
and its mechanism was not precise.
Although it claimed to point south,
it was often inaccurate.
When turning and maneuvering,
it still required human intervention to correct it.
Zǔ Chōngzhī from Fànyáng,
who possessed ingenious skills,
often said it should be reconstructed.
At the end of Shēngmíng during the reign of Sòng Shùndì,
Qí Wáng was prime minister,
and ordered its construction.
When the carriage was completed,
he ordered the General of the Household and Administrator of Dānyáng, Wáng Sēngqián, and the Censor-in-Chief, Liú Xiū, to test it.
Its mechanism was extremely precise,
turning a hundred times and winding a thousand times,
it never deviated.
During the Jìn dynasty, there was also a Zhǐnánzhōu (South-Pointing Boat).
The Suǒlǔ leader Tuòbá Tào ordered the artisan Guō Shànmíng to build a Zhǐnánchē,
but it took an entire year and was not completed.
Mǎ Yuè from Fúfēng also constructed one,
and as it was nearing completion,
Guō Shànmíng poisoned and killed him.
The Jìlǐchē (Odometer Carriage),
its origin is not clearly known,
but it was also obtained by Gāozǔ when he pacified the Three Qín.
Its design was like the Zhǐnánchē,
with a drum on top,
and when the carriage traveled one lǐ,
the wooden figure would strike one beat.
In the grand imperial procession (Lǔbù),
it followed the Zhǐnánchē.
The Niǎnchē (Sedan Carriage)
was the lowest-ranked of the five carriages of the empress in the Zhōulǐ (Rites of Zhou).
It was ridden casually by empresses and concubines within the palace,
not an imperial carriage.
Under the Hàn system, the imperial carriage was driven by the emperor,
or sometimes pulled by people,
or drawn by a Guǒxiàmǎ (under-tree horse).
Hàn Chéngdì desired to share a Niǎn with Bān Jiéyú, which is an example of this.
In the Later Hàn, Yīn Jiù, a proud and noble maternal relative,
also used a Niǎn.
Jǐng Dān criticized him, saying:
"Did Jié of old ride a human-drawn carriage?
Was it this?"
Thus, the Niǎn was created in the late era of the Xià Hóu clan.
Jǐng Dān criticized Yīn Jiù for riding a human-drawn carriage,
but did not mention that it was an act of usurpation (jiànshàng).
Could it be that high-ranking officials were also permitted to ride it?
It is unknown in which dynasty its wheels were removed.
Fù Xuánzǐ said:
"In the Xià dynasty it was called Yúchē,
in the Yīn dynasty Húnú,
and in the Zhōu dynasty Zīchē."
Zīchē
is the same as Niǎn.
In Wèi and Jìn, when the emperor made minor excursions,
he often rode a horse,
and also frequently rode a Yúchē.
Yúchē
is today's small palanquin.
The Dúchē (Calf Carriage)
was a type of Píngchē (screened carriage).
In the Hàn dynasty, only poor nobles rode it,
but later it became increasingly valued.
Sūn Quán said
"eight oxen in the carriage,"
which refers to the Dúchē.
When the emperor traveled in the Jiāngzuǒ (Southern Dynasties),
it also carried provisions and supplies.
In the Hàn dynasty, the Yáochē (light carriage) was lowly regarded, and Zīpíng (covered carriages) were valued.
In Wèi and Jìn, Zīpíng were lowly regarded, and Yáochē were valued.
There was also the Zhuīfēngchē (Wind-Chasing Carriage),
which had its small flat canopy removed,
and a continuous curtain added,
like a Yáochē,
but drawn by horses.
Also, the Dúchē was adorned with mica,
and called Yúnmǔchē (Mica Carriage);
subordinates were not allowed to ride it,
but it was sometimes bestowed upon kings and dukes.
The Jìn dynasty also had the Sìwàngchē (Four-Gazing Carriage),
which is still in use today.
Moreover, under the Hàn system,
only merchants were not allowed to ride horse-drawn carriages;
all others rode them.
Except for officials with red-canopied sedan chairs, the rest had blue-canopied sedan chairs.
According to the Rítuals of Zhōu, the queen also had five types of carriages:
the chóngzhái, yànzhái, ānchē, zháichē, and niǎnchē;
a total of five.
Under the Hàn system,
the tài huángtàihòu, huángtàihòu, and huánghòu, when using their ceremonial carriage, rode in a chóngzhái with feather canopy, a golden-rooted carriage,
pulled by a team with blue interwoven harness,
with blue curtains and valances,
a pole painted with clouds,
and five gold-coated tips.
The canopy's claws were adorned with golden flowers.
It was pulled by three horses,
with a left and right outside horse.
When not using the ceremonial carriage, they rode in a zǐjì píngchē.
According to the Zìlín,
a píngchē has a covering,
but no rear shaft.
One with a rear shaft is called a zī.
Yìng Shào's Hàndian reports that
in the seventh year of Yǒngpíng of Míngdì,
when Guāngliè Yīn Huánghòu was buried,
her soul carriage
was a luánlù with a green feather canopy,
pulled by four horses,
with a dragon banner with nine streamers,
and a fāngxiàng in front.
In the phoenix carriage,
the wife of the dàjiāngjūn rode as an attendant,
and the wives of the tàipú and the imperial women rode flanking the hubs.
This was an old system from the Former Hàn.
The Jìn's Xiāncán Yízhù states that
the empress rode in an ānchē painted with oil and mica,
pulled by six guīmǎ.
Guī
means light black.
An ānchē painted with oil with two shafts,
pulled by five guīmǎ, served as a secondary carriage.
A princess's ānchē, painted with oil,
was pulled by three.
The Sān Fūrén's ānchē, with blue interwoven harness,
was pulled by three.
All of them had a zǐjiàngjì píngchē,
pulled by three, as a secondary carriage.
The Jiǔpín and Shìfù used píngchē,
pulled by two.
Palace women used zīchē,
pulled by one.
Royal consorts, wives of gōng and hóu holding the rank of tèjìn, and fèngjūn used ānchē with black interwoven harness,
pulled by three.
Under the Hàn system,
guìrén, princesses, royal consorts, and fèngjūn all used oil-covered píngchē pulled by two,
with only the right outside horse.
Under the Hàn system,
the Crown Prince and imperial princes all used ānchē,
with vermilion spotted wheels,
a tiger-patterned leaning-bar,
a deer-patterned crossbar,
black patterned side-boards,
a green canopy,
golden flowers adorning the ends of the spokes,
a pole painted with black patterns,
and five gold-coated tips.
[一０] When an imperial prince was enfeoffed as a king,
he was bestowed with this carriage,
hence it was called the king's green-canopy carriage.
All were pulled by a team with left and right outside horses,
with five banners,
each banner with nine streamers,
painted with descending dragons.
Imperial grandsons rode in green-canopy carriages,
[一一] also pulled by three.
Under the Wèi and Jìn systems,
the Crown Prince and all princes were pulled by four.
In the third year of Tàixīng of Jìn Yuándì,
when the Crown Prince performed the Shìdiǎn ritual,
an imperial edict stated:
"As there is no gāochē available,
an ānchē may be used."
A gāochē
is a standing carriage.
The gōng and lièhóu used ānchē with vermilion spotted wheels, a deer-patterned leaning-bar, a bear-patterned crossbar, and black side-boards, which were called xuān,
with a black silk canopy,
pulled by two,
with the right outside horse.
Kings and gōng had banners with eight streamers,
hóu with seven streamers,
and qīng with five streamers,
all with descending dragons.
When gōng, qīng, zhòng'èrqiānshí, and èrqiānshí used their ceremonial carriages for outings to the suburbs and imperial tombs,
they all rode in dàchē (standing carriages),
pulled by four.
The accompanying dàchē were
pulled by two,
with the right outside horse.
For other outings, they rode in ānchē.
Those who resigned from their positions and retired
were all bestowed with an ānchē and four horses.
Zhòng'èrqiānshí all had black canopies,
vermilion side-boards,
copper tips,
pulled by two,
with the right outside horse.
The Jìn statutes stipulated that
the designated heir of a king or gōng who governed a state
[一二] used an ānchē,
pulled by three,
with a banner of seven streamers.
The designated heir of a hóu
had five streamers.
Fù Chàng's Guòshì states that
the Sān Gōng used ānchē,
pulled by three.
Tèjìn were pulled by two.
Qīng by one.
Under the Hàn system,
the wives of gōng, lièhóu, zhòng'èrqiānshí, and èrqiānshí, when attending ancestral temples and the silkworm ritual,
each rode in her husband's ānchē,
with the right outside horse,
adorned with a black interwoven harness,
and all curtains and valances were black.
[一三] For non-official gatherings,
they rode in a lacquered cloth zīpíng,
with copper tips.
In the fourth year of Tàikāng of Jìn Wǔdì,
an imperial edict mandated following the Hàn precedent,
granting each of the Jiǔ Qīng one court carriage and one ānchē.
Fù Chàng's Guòshì states that
the Shàngshūlìng's imperial carriage
had black "ears" and a rear door.
The Púyè only had a rear door but no "ears."
The Zhōngshūjiān and Zhōngshūlìng were like the Púyè.
According to the Hàn system,
the imperial carriage used the grand procession (dàjià).
The gōngqīng (dukes and ministers) served as guides.
The Tàipú (Grand Coachman) drove.
〔一四〕The Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General) rode as參乘 (cānchéng, the right-hand attendant).
It comprised a thousand chariots and ten thousand cavalry.
There were eighty-one attached carriages (shǔchē).
In ancient times, feudal lords had nine auxiliary carriages.
When Qín destroyed the nine states,
it incorporated their carriages and attire.
Thus, there were eighty-one carriages.
Hàn followed this without change.
When Hàn had its capital at Cháng'ān,
this procession was used for sacrifices to Heaven at Gānquán.
When the capital was at Luòyáng,
it was used for ascending the Yuánlíng mausoleum,
and also for grand funerals.
For the regular procession (fǎjià), the Hénán Yǐn (Administrator of Hénán) and the Luòyáng Lìng (Magistrate of Luòyáng) served as guides.
The Fèngchēláng (Gentleman of the Chariot) drove.
The Shìzhōng (Attendant at Court) rode as cānchéng.
There were thirty-six shǔchē.
All shǔchē had black canopies and red axles.
The Later Hàn used the fǎjià for sacrifices to Heaven at the suburban altars,
and the small procession (xiǎojià) for sacrifices at the imperial ancestral temples.
The xiǎojià
was a reduced version of the auxiliary carriages.
The vanguard had nine streamers (jiǔliú), cloud-net banners (yúnhǎn),
〔一五〕leather-covered carriages (píxuān), and luan-bird banners (luánqí).
All carriages were driven by dàfū (grand masters).
Luánqí means
feathers and yak tails woven together and attached in rows to the sides of the banners.
There were golden gongs (jīnzhēng) and yellow bronze bells ([jīnwù]),
and the Huángmén (Palace Gate) drum carriages.
Behind the imperial carriage were the shǔchē,
carrying Shàngshū (Secretaries) and Yùshǐ (Imperial Censors).
The last carriage had a leopard tail hung from it.
Before the leopard tail,
it was similar to within the palace (shěngzhōng).
Whenever the procession went out, an alert (jǐng) and a clearing of the way (bì) were announced.
Five banners were erected.
The Tàipú presented the procession roster (lǔbù).
Shàngshūláng (Secretaries of the Secretariat), Shìyùshǐ (Attending Censors), and lìshǐ (clerks) all held notes to supervise and organize the chariots and cavalry.
This was called "guarding the procession" (hùjià).
For ascending mausoleums in spring and autumn,
it was even more simplified than the xiǎojià.
Only one Zhíshì Shàngshū (Duty Secretary) followed.
The rest, from lìshǐ downwards, all preceded the procession.
This was called "advance placement" (xiānzhì).
Xuē Zōng's commentary to the Dōngjīng Fù states that yúnhǎn and jiǔliú are alternative names for banners and flags,
but he does not distinguish their forms.
Upon examination, when Wèi ordered the King of Jìn to establish the Son of Heaven's banners and flags,
it included máotóu (yak-tail banners) and yúnhǎn.
From this, we know that yúnhǎn are not banners and flags.
Xú Guǎng's commentary on carriages and attire considers jiǔliú to be
nine carriages with streamers.
Yúnhǎn is suspected to be hǎn.
The Shī says:
"The Marquis of Qí hunted and shot birds;
the common people suffered from it."
Hǎn was originally used for hunting expeditions;
did it then become an ornament for processions?
Pān Yuè's Jítián Fù first mentions "five roads and nine flags,"
then speaks of "qióngsà and yúnhǎn."
If hǎn were a flag,
then Yuè should not have mentioned it so soon after "nine flags."
Furthermore, since this object is paired with sà,
it should clearly be today's hunting net (wǎng).
This explanation is accurate.
Píxuān means
the carriage is covered with tiger skin.
Xú also cites the Huáinánzǐ:
"The military officer holds a leopard skin to regulate his troops."
The Lǐjì says:
"If there is a Shìshī (judicial officer) in front,
then a tiger skin is carried."
The leopard tail on the imperial carriage
might also belong to the same category of meaning.
The five banners (wǔqí) are
one banner of each of the five colors,
supported underneath by wooden oxen.
Xú also said:
"Wooden oxen are probably used because they are heavy-bearing and stable."
The five banners with their poles wrapped
are like the Lǐjì's "virtuous carriages with tied flags, not fully adorned,"
which are only unfurled for military affairs.
Also, "military carriages with draped flags"
means they are lowered and spread out.
The historian notes: Today, tied flags and draped flags are the same,
but they are not erected on virtuous carriages or military carriages.
Moreover, the meaning of wooden oxen
is not yet clearly understandable.
Furthermore, upon examining the Zhōulǐ's distinctions of objects for carriages,
nothing is not thoroughly investigated,
yet there is no mention of wind-catchers (xiāngfēng), nets (wǎng), or yak-tail banners (máotóu).
This clearly shows they were not ancient systems.
Hé Chéngtiān believed that during the Warring States period, as states constantly contended and armies frequently set out,
the placement of suspended ravens (xuánwū)
was to observe portents in the wind.
This should belong to Qín.
Jìn Wǔ once asked his courtiers:
"What is the meaning of máotóu?"
Péng Tuī replied:
"Qín had strange creatures
that crashed through mountains and broke through water,
destroying everything.
They only feared máotóu.
Thus, the 'tiger warriors' wore them.
So, it is a Qín system."
Zhāng Huá said:
"This statement exists, but the event is not attested in classics.
I believe it takes its meaning from
the rage of a strong man,
whose hair rises and pushes up his cap."
Zhì Yú, in his "Resolving Doubts," did not confirm or deny it.
Xú Yuán said:
"Péng and Zhāng's explanations
each state their own meanings
without any supporting evidence.
Upon examination of astronomy, the space between Bì and Mǎo is called the Celestial Street.
Thus, the imperial carriage is led by bì and hǎn in front,
because Bì is square and Mǎo is round,
adopting their imagery.
The Xingjīng (Star Classics) states that
Mǎo is also named Máotóu.
Therefore, those who carry them wear caps made of fur and hair."
Light carriages (qīngchē)
were ancient war chariots.
Their wheels and axle boxes were red,
without covers or canopies.
They had erected spears, banners, and pennants,
and crossbows placed on the dashboard.
They were drawn by two horses.
The Shèshēng Xiàowèi (Commander of the Sound-Shooting Division) and his sīmǎ (officers) and lìshì (clerks) rode in them,
following the attached carriages in order.
The Hàn Yí states:
"When going out, 'jǐng' is called;
when entering, 'bì' is called."
Commentators say
that when the imperial carriage goes out, 'jǐng' should be called,
and when it enters, 'bì' should be called.
But now, both are shouted together.
The historian believes that jǐng means
to alert and warn.
Bì means
to stop movement.
Today, those who follow the imperial carriage when it exits
are all alerted to prepare for the unexpected.
Those who come from outside and interfere with the imperial carriage when it enters
are stopped by bì.
Dǒng Bā and Sīmǎ Biāo said:
"Feudal kings, when obstructing passage for entry and exit,
call 'jǐng' and establish 'bì'."
Wǔgāngchē (heavy armored carriages)
had covers and canopies.
They served as vanguard in front,
and also as rearguard behind the qīngchē.
They were drawn by one horse.
The Shǐjì records that
Wèi Qīng campaigned against the Xiōngnú
using wǔgāngchē as camps.
According to the Hàn system,
the grand procession (dàxíng) carried a wēnlángchē (sleeping carriage),
which had four wheels.
Its decorations were like those of a jīngēn (gold-rooted carriage),
with additional woven ribbons and joined jade bi discs,
interlaced.
At the four corners, golden dragon heads held bi discs in their mouths,
from which hung five-colored
feathers and flowing tassels.
In front and behind were painted curtains with cloud patterns,
and intricately painted curved screens (qūfān)
as long as the carriage itself.
The Tàipú drove
six white dappled horses,
whose bodies were marked with black medicine to resemble tiger stripes.
These were called bùshīmǎ (painted horses).
Once dismounted,
the horses were sold off,
and the carriage was stored in the secret palace north of the city.
Now, the horses are not marked with tiger stripes
and are not sold off;
the carriage is destroyed.
Since Hàn Huò Guāng, Jìn Ānpíng, Qíwáng, Jiǎ Chōng, Wáng Dǎo, Xiè Ān, and Sòng Jiāngxià Wáng, those buried with special rites
all used a dàlù (grand chariot) with a huángwū (yellow canopy)
and carried a wēnlángchē.
Jìn regulations state:
"When traveling on official missions by relay carriage (chuán),
if one encounters a funeral above a certain rank,
one should immediately report it in a memorial,
and is permitted to wear white clothing and ride a luóche (mule carriage)
until the deputy takes over the duties."
Xú Guǎng's commentary on carriages and attire says:
"The luóche that is rumored
has the body of a calf carriage but the shafts of a horse carriage."
A carriage without a canopy is called a kēchē.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
the Protector-General Yáng Xiù rode in a sheep-drawn carriage.
The Commandant of the Capital, Liú Yì, submitted a memorial impeaching him.
An imperial edict declared:
“Although there is no regulation against a sheep-drawn carriage,
it is still not something worn by commoners.”
In the region south of the Jiāng, there had been no such prohibition.
In ancient times, there was a system of "filling the court,"
where, during grand assemblies facing the imperial presence,
the emperor’s carriages, palanquins, banners, and drums were displayed in the palace courtyard.
Zhāng Héng’s Dōngjīng Fù says:
“Dragon carriages filled the court,
phoenix banners brushed the clouds.”
This practice was abolished in the Jìn dynasty south of the Jiāng.
During the Dàmíng era of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng, it was restored.
In high antiquity, people slept in furs and skins,
and there was no established system.
Later, sages observed the feathers and patterns of birds and beasts, and the vibrant colors of plants and flowers,
and consequently dyed silk and colors to make clothing,
creating black and yellow garments
to emulate the upper and lower forms of heaven and earth.
They observed the shapes of birds’ and beasts’ crests and wattles
to devise the decorations of crowns, caps, and pendants.
The Yú clan created embroidered patterns,
with colorful designs making up the elaborate patterns.
Although the Xiàhòu esteemed simplicity,
they still valued the beautiful ceremonial robes and crowns.
When Gāoyáo presented his counsel,
he spoke of the five types of robes and five types of patterns.
These were all things that later kings could not alter.
The Zhōu dynasty observed the two previous dynasties,
and its ritual system was detailed and meticulous.
Therefore, the Biànshī managed the six types of ceremonial caps,
and the Sīfú managed the six types of robes,
establishing differentiations and grades,
each with its proper order.
The Lǐjì, in the Guānyì chapter, says:
“The capping ceremony is the beginning of rites,
and the most important of auspicious affairs.”
when performing sacrificial rites, they were dyed black.
In the Xià dynasty, they were called Wúzhuī;
in the Yīn dynasty, Zhāngfǔ;
in the Zhōu dynasty, Wěimào.
These were all commonly [worn in] the three dynasties. The sacrificial caps of Zhōu
were adorned with elaborate embroidery and ornaments,
which is why the Master said,
“I would wear the caps of Zhōu,”
using it as a term of highest praise.
When Qín came to the imperial throne from the Warring States period,
it abolished the ancient systems.
The garments for suburban sacrifices
were all black.
It was not until Emperor Míng of Hàn that, drawing from the theories of various scholars in the Zhōuguān, Lǐjì, and Shàngshū,
the ceremonial robes and crowns were fully restored.
Emperor Míng of Wèi, considering that the embroidered patterns on the robes of the dukes and ministers resembled those of the supreme ruler,
again curtailed and simplified them.
Since the Jìn dynasty, there has been no further alteration.
When the Son of Heaven performs rites at the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
he wears a black jièzī cap,
and a level miǎn crown,
what is now called the Píngtiān Guān.
seven cùn wide
and one chǐ two cùn long,
with twelve dangling beaded tassels.
A red ribbon is used for the chin strap.
with three panels in front
and four panels in back.
The upper garment is painted, and the lower garment is embroidered,
with images of the sun, moon, stars, mountains, dragons, pheasants, insects, aquatic plants, fire, grains of rice, axes, and fǔ symbols—
in all, twelve embroidered patterns.
A plain belt, four cùn wide,
is red-lined,
and edged with red trim on its sides.
A red leather knee-cover is worn.
The knee-cover
is the ancient fú.
Crimson trousers are worn,
crimson socks,
and red slippers.
Those who have not yet undergone the capping ceremony
When offering sacrifices to the Former Sages,
they wear a black gauze skirt,
a crimson-edged inner garment,
and black slippers.
When presiding over court, they also wear the ceremonial robe and crown.
For court attire,
a Tōngtiān Guān is worn,
nine cùn high,
with a golden Bóshān ornament on the front,
a black jièzī cap,
a crimson gauze skirt,
and a black-edged inner garment.
When paying respects at imperial tombs,
a black jièzī cap
and a plain unlined robe are worn.
For other various garments,
there are blue, red, yellow, white, brown, and black jièzī caps,
five-colored gauze skirts,
the five-ridged Jìnxián Guān,
the Yuǎnyóu Guān,
the Píngshàng Zé,
and the Wǔguān.
For mourning attire,
a white unlined robe is worn.
According to Hàn rituals,
on the day of Lìqiū, hunting attire included a brown cap.
At the beginning of Emperor Āi of Jìn’s reign,
the academician Cáo Hóngzhī and others proposed:
“On Lìqiū, when the emperor reads the decrees,
a brown cap should not be worn.
We request it be changed to plain white.”
The imperial edict approved this.
In the sixth year of Yuánjiā during Emperor Wén of Sòng’s reign,
Xú Dàoyú, who was in charge of imperial receptions, memorialized:
“A plain white cap should not be worn.”
The emperor ordered the Gate-Keepers to deliberate,
and the emperor insisted it should remain as before.
Thus, it was not changed.
The Jìnxián Guān
is seven cùn high in front
and three cùn high in back,
eight cùn long.
The number of ridges varies according to rank.
It is the ancient black cloth cap.
It is worn by literary scholars.
Senior dukes and ministers assisting at suburban and ancestral temple sacrifices
Kings and dukes have eight tassels,
ministers seven tassels,
with ribbons for chin straps,
the color matching their sashes.
Kings and dukes wear robes with patterns from mountains and dragons downward,
totaling nine patterns.
Ministers wear robes with patterns from pheasants and insects downward,
totaling seven patterns.
When performing the Xiāngshè ceremony,
dukes and ministers wear the Wěimào Guān,
made of black silk,
shaped like an inverted cup,
and of the same style as the Píbàn.
It is seven cùn long
and four cùn high.
The upper garment is black and the lower garment is plain white.
The inner garment has black-edged collar and cuffs.
Those attending to duties wear the Píbàn,
made of deerskin.
The Wǔguān
was formerly the Huìwén Guān,
originally a Zhào garment,
also called Dàguān.
All attending officials wore it with mink and cicada ornaments.
Yì Shào’s Hànguān says:
“Commentators believe that gold symbolizes strength and hardness,
unworn by a hundred refinements;
the cicada lives in high places and eats cleanly, with its mouth under its armpit;
These are meanings derived from the objects themselves,
not their true origin.
In reality, King Wǔlíng of Zhào adopted Hu attire,
and when Qín destroyed Zhào,
it bestowed the Zhào ruler’s crown upon its attending officials.
Therefore, from Qín and Hàn onward,
attending officials had mink and cicada ornaments.
Xú Guǎng’s Chēfú Zhù states its meaning thus:
“The northern lands are cold,
and it was originally used to cover the forehead with mink fur,
attached to the cap.
Did it then transform into a head ornament?”
A侍zhōng wore a left mink ornament;
a chángshì, a right mink ornament.
The Fǎguān
was originally a Chǔ garment,
also called Zhùhòu,
and also Xièzhì.
Commentators say:
“The xièzhì beast knows right from wrong,
and uses its horn to gore the unrighteous.”
When Qín destroyed Chǔ,
it bestowed the Chǔ ruler’s crown upon legal officials.
The Yèzhě’s Gāoshān Guān
was originally a Qí garment,
also called Cèzhù Guān.
When Qín destroyed Qí,
it bestowed the Qí ruler’s crown upon the yèzhě.
Emperor Míng of Wèi, seeing its shape resembled the Tōngtiān and Yuǎnyóu crowns,
then destroyed and altered it.
Fán Kuài’s guān,
nine cùn wide,
was styled like a píngmiǎn,
worn by the guards at the palace gates.
The Hàn general Fán Kuài often carried an iron shield.
At the Hóngmén banquet,
Xiàng Yǔ intended to harm the Hàn King,
so [Fán Kuài] tore his robe to wrap his shield,
and bearing it, went in to see Yǔ.
The Hàn dynasty inherited the Qín system;
there were thirteen types of guān.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
not all of them have been in use.
Here, we record those that are in use.
The zé
was the attire of commoners in ancient times who did not wear guān.
Hàn Yuándì had thick hair on his forehead,
and first started to pull his hair into a zé and wear it.
Wáng Mǎng was bald on top,
so he added a 'roof' to it.
A Hàn commentary says:
"For a guān of the 'jìnxián' type, the 'ears' should be long,
this is now the jièzé.
For a guān of the 'huìwén' type, the 'ears' should be short,
this is now the píngshàngzé.
〔二四〕[We] know that at different times, each followed what was suitable,
and later this became a distinction based on the guān."
The jièzé was worn by civil officials,
and the píngshàngzé by military officers.
A child's zé had no 'roof',
to indicate they were not yet adults.
There was also the nàwánzé,
which was gathered at the back,
with another layer,
three cùn square.
There was also the chìzé,
worn by cavalry officers, military officers, and those in the imperial drum and wind band.
When saving the sun from an eclipse,
civil and military officials all removed their guān,
wore a chìzé,
and faced the court in court attire,
to display might and majesty.
The Sòng imperial drum and wind band wore black zé and military guān.
According to Hàn regulations,
for sacrifices to the Five Suburbs,
the Emperor and those performing duties each wore attire according to the directional color;
for officials not performing duties,
they wore their regular attire to attend.
Regular attire
was a jiàngyī.
Qín Jìng, the Wèi Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat, said:
"The Hàn clan inherited from Qín,
and changed the system of the six miǎn,
wearing only xuánguān and jiàngyī."
The Jìn dynasty called it the Wǔshí cháofú;
there was the Sìshí cháofú,
and also the cháofú.
All military matters
are generally referred to as róng.
The Shàngshū says:
"One donning of armor and the world was settled."
The Zhōulǐ says:
"To use a leather chariot to go to war."
It also says:
"For military matters, wear a wéibiànfú."
A biàn was made of leather,
and also used for clothing.
The Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn says:
"To conduct affairs in military attire."
It also says:
"Jìn Xì Zhì wore leather fū."
The commentary,
ancient Confucians said:
"Fū
is jiàngsè."
Today, it is the clothing of the wǔbó.
Commentators say that
during the wars of the Five Hegemons,
there were still shòu fú, guān yīng, and màn hú,
so róngfú was not of the kùzhě system,
its origin is not yet clear.
In recent times, the attire for the imperial carriage personally going to war or for internal and external martial law,
had no fixed color,
wearing a black hat,
with a purple biāo attached.
The biāo was made of silk,
four cùn long
and one cùn wide.
At the waist was a luòdài,
to replace the pán gé.
Central officials wore purple biāo,
outer officials wore jiàng biāo.
There was also the zuǎnyán róngfú,
without the biāo attached.
When traveling or staying, civil and military officials were all the same.
For hunting and imperial tours,
only the attendant officials wore róngfú,
with a pán gé;
civil officials did not lower their yīng,
military officials removed their guān.
During the Yuánjiā reign of Sòng Wéndì,
imperial tours and hunts were all like this;
to save palace temples from water and fire,
it was also like this.
According to Hàn regulations,
when empress dowagers entered temples to offer sacrifices to the gods, they wore
gànshàng zàoxià;
for personally tending silkworms,
qīngshàng piáoxià,
all were shēnyī.
The shēnyī
is the dàn yī.
The head ornament was a jiǎn máo guó.
According to Hàn regulations,
when empresses visited temples, they wore
gànshàng zàoxià.
For personally tending silkworms,
qīngshàng piáoxià.
The head ornaments were
false hair buns,
bùyáo,
eight sparrows,
nine flowers,
and adorned with emeralds.
According to Jìn regulations for the first silkworm ceremony,
the Empress wore twelve tǎ,
bùyáo,
a large hand-shaped bun,
a pure green robe,
and a shòu pèi.
Today, when the Empress visits a temple, she wears a guī [⿰王老] dàyī,
called the huīyī.
Princesses and the Three Fūrén wore large hand-shaped buns,
seven tǎ,
and bìjì.
The Nine Pín and the Dàfūrén of Dukes wore five tǎ.
Shìfù wore three tǎ.
When princesses met,
they wore large hand-shaped buns.
The eldest princesses were allowed to have bùyáo.
Princesses and those above the rank of Fēngjūn all wore shòu,
with a colored silk cord as a gǔndài,
〔二五〕each according to the color of their shòu.
Fūrén of Dukes, Special Entourage Grand Masters, and Marquises, Qīng, Xiào, and Shìfù, and senior mìngfù of two thousand shí rank,
wore gànzēng guó.
When assisting in sacrifices, they wore black silk for both upper and lower garments.
When assisting in silkworm cultivation, they wore green silk for both upper and lower garments.
From the Empress down to the mìngfù of two thousand shí rank,
all used silkworm attire as court attire.
Liú Xiàng said:
"In ancient times, from the Son of Heaven to the shǐ,
and from the Queen to the mìngfù,
they all wore jade pendants,
with specific regulations for different ranks."
The Lǐjì says:
"The Son of Heaven wore white jade with xuánzǔshòu,
Dukes and Marquises wore shānxuányù with zhūzǔshòu,
Qīng and Dàfū wore shuǐcāngyù with zīzǔshòu,
and shǐ wore ruǎnmín with yùnzǔshòu."
Yùn
is reddish-yellow.
The shòu
is what is threaded through the pèi to support it.
The fú was worn above and below like a bìxī,
and also varied according to rank.
After the Five Hegemons,
warfare was incessant,
pèi were not weapons,
and fú were not instruments of war,
so pèi and fú were removed,
leaving only their attached ties.
〔二六〕The Qín then used colored silk cords to connect to the ties,
which were passed around and tied,
called shòu.
The Hàn adopted this.
It was not until Míngdì that the pèi system was reinstituted,
but it was again lost by the end of the Hàn dynasty.
Wèi Shìzhōng Wáng Càn recognized its form,
and thus re-created it.
Today's pèi
is what Càn created.
The pèi worn by empresses down to mìngfù,
their ancient system no longer exists,
today it is the same as that for external officials,
and the Qín zǔshòu
is still applied.
According to the Hàn system,
from the Son of Heaven down to all officials,
none did not wear a saber.
Sīmǎ Biāo's
When Hàn Gāozǔ was the Magistrate of Sìshuǐ Pavilion,
he drew his sword and slew a white snake.
Jùn Bùyí said:
"A sword
is a gentleman's martial preparation."
Zhāng Héng's *Dōngjīng Fù* [Eastern Capital Rhapsody] says,
"[He] wore a yellow cord,
and a Gānjiàng at his waist."
Thus, from the ruler to the scholar,
they also wore swords.
From the Jìn dynasty onwards,
wooden swords began to replace bladed swords.
The Six Seals of the Emperor's carriage
were a Qín institution.
The *Hàn Jiùyí* [Old Rites of Hàn] says:
"The Emperor's Traversing Seal,
the Emperor's Seal,
the Emperor's Credential Seal,
the Son of Heaven's Traversing Seal,
the Son of Heaven's Seal,
the Son of Heaven's Credential Seal."
This shows that Hàn followed Qín.
Initially, when Gāozǔ entered the Pass,
he obtained the Lántián jade seal of Qín Shǐhuáng,
with a *chīhǔ* knob,
and the inscription read
"Received the Mandate of Heaven,
the Emperor's Longevity and Prosperity."
Gāozǔ wore it,
and later generations called it the Seal of State Succession.
It, along with the sword that slew the white snake, was treasured by the imperial carriage.
The Seal of State Succession
has not been abolished from Wèi and Jìn to the present;
the sword that slew the white snake
was burned in a fire in Jìn Huìdì's arsenal,
and is now lost.
When Jìn Huáidì was captured by the Hú,
the Seal of State Succession fell into the hands of Liú Cōng,
and later belonged to Shí Lè.
And when Shí Lè's younger brother Shí Hǔ died,
and chaos ensued among the Hú,
in the reign of Jìn Mùdì,
it was returned to the imperial treasury.
Yú Xǐ's *Zhìlín* [Forest of Records] says:
"The Seal of State Succession
is separate from the six seals;
the Son of Heaven has a total of seven seals."
The *Hàn Zhù* [Commentary on Hàn] says:
"A *xǐ*
is an *yìn* [seal].
Before Qín,
ministers all used gold or jade for their seals,
with dragon or tiger knobs,
according to their preference.
From Qín onwards,
it was referred to as *xǐ*,
and exclusively used jade,
which ministers were forbidden to use."
According to the Hàn system,
the Emperor wore a yellow and crimson ribbon,
of four colors:
yellow, crimson, light blue, and dark blue.
The Empress had a gold seal,
and her ribbon was also like this.
According to rites,
the color of a scholar's ribbon was like this;
later generations changed the ancient custom.
Wú had no jade carving artisans,
so they made seals of gold.
Sūn Hào's creation of six gold seals is an example of this.
There were also seals with *lín*, phoenix, tortoise, dragon,
horse, duck heads, and miscellaneous seals;
these are now lacking in the present age.
The Imperial Crown Prince
had a gold seal,
a tortoise knob,
a vermilion-red ribbon,
four colors:
crimson, yellow, light blue, and dark blue.
He was granted five seasonal court robes,
a far-ranging travel cap,
and also a three-beamed *jìnxián* cap.
He wore a *yú* jade pendant.
All Princes
had a gold seal,
a tortoise knob,
a vermilion-red ribbon,
four colors:
crimson, yellow, light blue, and dark blue.
They were granted five seasonal court robes,
a far-ranging travel cap,
and also a three-beamed *jìnxián* cap.
They wore a *shānxuán* jade pendant.
Commandery Dukes
had a gold insignia,
a dark red ribbon.
They were granted five seasonal court robes,
a three-beamed *jìnxián* cap,
and wore a *shānxuán* jade pendant.
The Grand Tutor, Grand Preceptor, Grand Guardian, Chancellor, Minister of Education, Minister of Works
had a gold insignia,
a purple ribbon.
They were granted five seasonal court robes,
a three-beamed *jìnxián* cap.
They wore a *shānxuán* jade pendant.
The Chancellor of State had a green *lì* ribbon,
three colors:
green, purple, dark blue.
*Lì*
is the name of a grass,
its color is green.
The Grand Marshal, Grand General, Grand Commandant, and all Generals of ducal rank
had a gold insignia,
a purple ribbon.
They were granted five seasonal court robes,
a martial cap.
They wore a *shānxuán* jade pendant.
Commandery Marquises
had a gold insignia,
a blue-red ribbon.
They were granted five seasonal court robes,
a three-beamed *jìnxián* cap.
They wore an aquamarine jade pendant.
The General of Agile Cavalry, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and all Generals with augmented titles,
such as Generals Who Punish, Who Guard, Who Pacify, Who Tranquilize, Central Army, Garrison Army, Pacification Army, Front, Left, Right, Rear Generals,
Generals Who Punish Barbarians, Who Are Champions, Who Aid the State, Who Soar Like Dragons,
had a gold insignia,
a purple ribbon.
They were granted five seasonal court robes,
a martial cap.
They wore an aquamarine jade pendant.
Noble Consorts, Furen, Guiren
had a gold insignia,
inscribed "Insignia of Noble Consort, Furen, Guiren."
A purple ribbon.
They wore Khotan jade.
Shūfēi, Shūyuán, Shūyí, Xiūhuá, Xiūróng, Xiūyí, Jiéyú, Rónghuá, Chōnghuá
had a silver seal,
inscribed "Seal of Shūfēi, Shūyuán, Shūyí, Xiūhuá, Xiūróng, Xiūyí, Jiéyú, Rónghuá, Chōnghuá."
A blue ribbon.
They wore five-colored *qióng* jade.
The Imperial Crown Prince's Consort
had a gold seal,
a tortoise knob,
a vermilion-red ribbon.
She wore a *yú* jade pendant.
All Princes' Grand Consorts, Consorts, all Senior Princesses, Princesses, and Enfeoffed Ladies
a purple ribbon.
They wore a *shānxuán* jade pendant.
All Princes' Heirs
a purple ribbon.
They were granted five seasonal court robes,
a two-beamed *jìnxián* cap.
They wore a *shānxuán* jade pendant.

In the fourth year of Yuánhuī, during the reign of Emperor Hòufèi of Sòng,
Wáng Jiǎn, the Yòu Chángshǐ of the Sītú, proposed that the gōngfǔ Chángshǐ should wear court attire.
He said:
“The 'Chūnqiū Guóyǔ' states: '
Appearance is the flower of emotion; clothing is the pattern of the heart.'
In the grand ceremonies of the imperial court,
clothing and caps are paramount.
Therefore, military and civil functions have different appearances,
and internal and external orders are distinct.
However, in recent times, this practice has been adopted,
but often with deviations.
The duties of the fǔ involve managing people
and providing a model for the four directions.
As your subject, residing as an assistant,
my aspiration is to perform my official duties.
Reflecting on previous codes,
I constantly feel vigilant.
According to the Jìn statutes,
the gōngfǔ Chángshǐ,
holding the sixth official rank,
used a bronze seal
and a black sash.
They wore court attire
and a Jìnxián two-beam cap.
The Yuàn and Shǔ,
holding the seventh official rank,
wore court attire
and a Jìnxián one-beam cap.
The commentary in the 'Jìn Guānbǐa'
also states the same as the statutes.
However, now the Chángshǐ, Yuàn, and Shǔ
only wear red robes.
This is a public violation of clear regulations,
and accumulated habits have become an error.
I suggest that according to the old system,
the Chángshǐ wear a two-beam cap,
and the Yuàn and Shǔ a one-beam cap,
and both should be equipped with court attire.
The zhōngdān and wéixī
should all follow the old regulations.
If this proposal is approved,
I also request that it be extended to the two fǔ of Sītú and various Yítóng Sānfǔ,
to become a permanent standard.
Furthermore, examining old practices,
the officials of the Sītú Gōngfǔ who commanded infantry were all treated the same as those who did not command troops during court attendance.
The Zhǔbù and Jìjiǔ
were fully equipped with zhōngdān and wéixī.
From Lìshǐ downwards,
only dark clothes were worn.
Now that the fǔ is open to the public,
we should strictly adhere to this system.
However, for those who hold positions in the tái,
wearing dark clothes is questionable.
According to the statutes, it is stated that all who hold concurrent offices
should follow the rules of their higher office.
Considering that an internal office is higher,
those who hold positions in the tái
should all wear the attire of their tái position,
and not be subject to the rule of dark clothes.
If one holds positions in various qīng temples concurrently with fǔ duties,
even if it is a third-rank position,
since the qīng temple is lower,
they should follow the gōngfǔ's system of dark clothes.
Matters of attire are important,
and rites and ceremonies come first.
I request the tái to review this in detail.”
Shěn Yǔzhī, the Yícáo Lángzhōng, deliberated and said:〔三四〕
“The making of guī symbolizes virtue,
its reduction or replacement depends on the times;
the tailoring of clothes symbolizes achievement,
its application changes with the era.
Carriages and banners changed in Shāng and Zhōu,
caps and pendants were reformed in Qín and Hàn.
How can it be necessary for different eras to inherit the same appearance
or for changed preferences to follow old things?
The biāndiāo was granted for the lucky attendance of attendants,
the humble cè was worn on the faces of the most revered.
Once it suited the times,
it became a venerable later system.
Moreover, attending court in red skirts
has lasted for a hundred years,
and the absence of wéixī
has remained unchanged.
Clothing is a fixed regulation,
and matters become eternal rules.
Wáng Jiǎn's adherence
is certainly not an ancient teaching.
The green and plain have followed each other,
with additions and subtractions over the generations.
Why abandon the thriving laws of the flourishing Sòng
to pursue the declining customs of the former Jìn?
Changes are needlessly bothersome,
I suggest no reform.”
Wáng Jiǎn again submitted a proposal, saying:
“In recent times, much of the attire has been deficient,
deviating from previous standards.
A recent proposal to follow the statutory text
was met with a response that reform was inappropriate.
It also cited Liú, the Zuǒchéng's, argument,
'According to the statutory text,
all are supposed to have court attire,
but many are now lacking.
Thus, while the text remains, the attire is deficient.
This is not only true for the Yuán and Zuǒ.
Since this has been adopted and discarded for a long time,
it has become an old regulation.'
This was stated in an imperial decree.
I humbly observe that when the imperial Sòng received the Mandate,
it always followed the old Jìn system.
The laws and regulations,
aligned with past norms.
If there is something that ought to be done,
it must be corrected or changed.
Then it should be referred upwards to an imperial edict
and discussed by the court assembly below,
setting specific dates
to establish a model for future generations.
How can one, due to the errors of external fǔ,
consider it a thriving custom of the flourishing Sòng,
using the laws and regulations of the Jìn dynasty
and calling their ceremonies declining practices?
To follow what is contrary and accept what is wrong
is not what I expect from high deliberations.
To reaffirm old codes,
what reform can be discussed?
Furthermore, the Zuǒchéng cites the deficient attire of the Lìshǐ
as a clear comparison for the Yuán and Zuǒ.
However, positions and ranks differ,
and rituals vary.
The Lìshǐ's simplicity
might be due to expediency;
for high-ranking officials to be unadorned
is a much more serious transgression.
Moreover, the Zhǔbù and Jìjiǔ
are fully clothed in court,
while the Chángshǐ, Yuàn, and Shǔ
line up in red robes.
This comparison
creates a contradiction.
If this can be endured,
what cannot be tolerated?
To cite the statutes to follow the old,
while the tái takes the error as an example –
a detailed examination of the imperial intention
is indeed something I do not comprehend.
To act according to one's official duty,
what is there to force?
The regulations are clear,
and should be adhered to without deviation.”
Shěn Yǔzhī again argued:
“Clouds and fire follow things,
changing their forms as they diminish;
imperial music varies in five ways,
royal rites change three times.
Why must the great Sòng, in establishing its mandate,
necessarily adhere to all the old Jìn customs?
If there are questionable texts concerning the imperial ancestral altars,
or deficient rites in the ancestral temples,
perhaps an imperial edict is issued from above,
and the court assembly below concurs.
Why then, for the robes and sashes of the Yuánfǔ's assistants,
change the edicts of Báihǔ
and cease the consultations of Xuānshì?
Also, you permit the Lìshǐ's simplicity,
but fault the high-ranking officials' unadorned state.
If laws are to be followed,
there is no distinction between noble and humble;
if rules must be equal,
what does it matter about expediency?
To adopt one and discard another
only increases the confusion.
Moreover, the assistant's role is not of wéixī,
but the official's is indeed of court attire.
All who are in the ranks
are no different from each other.
This is because the former statute was violated and then changed,
while the current system is approved and used for a long time.
Ranks differ and attire varies;
how can this constitute a contradiction?
When discussing questionable systems,
where does one find a distinction of strong or weak?
The fǔ holds to the remnants of a past reform,
while the tái relies on an established code that has been in effect for a long time.
There is indeed hope for unwavering adherence,
not for losing one's way.”
The deliberation concluded, and all agreed with Wáng Jiǎn.
The proposal was then shelved.

The Bìxià Jiǎ Púshè Zhǔshì Lìjiāng Qí, Tíngshàng Wǔniú Qí Jiǎshǐ Hǔbēn,
when attending the imperial court and forming part of the imperial procession,
shall wear brocade patterned robes,
martial caps,
and quail-tail plumes.
Bìzhǎng,
shall be granted bronze seals,
black ribbons,
and yak-tail plumes.
The Yǔlín, when attending the imperial court and forming part of the imperial procession,
shall wear crimson lined single robes,
and a leather-painted waist jacket over it.
They shall be granted yak-tail plumes.
Jǔniǎnjìqín Qiánqūyóujī Qiángnǔ Sīmǎ, Shǒulíng Hǔbēn,
those who wear seals of Wǔměng Dūwèi and above,
shall be granted green ribbons.
Biébù Sīmǎ and below,
shall be granted black ribbons.
Shǒulíng Hǔbēn
shall be supplied with crimson lined single robes
and martial caps.
Diànzhōng Nǔcóng Hǔbēn, Diànzhōng Hǔbēn, and Shǒulíngzhě Chíshá Nǔcóng Hǔbēn,
those who wear seals of Wǔměng Dūwèi and below,
shall be granted green ribbons.
Biébù Sīmǎ and below,
shall be granted black ribbons.
Crimson lined single robes,
〔三九〕and martial caps.
Chíchuífǔ Wǔqí Hǔbēn, Wǔqí Chuánzhào Hǔbēn, Diànzhōng Yǔlín, and Shǒulíngzhě Tàiguān Shàngshí Hǔbēn, Chēngfàn Zǎirén, Zhūgōng Shàngshí Hǔbēn,
those who wear seals of Wǔměng Dūwèi and above,
shall be granted green ribbons.
Biébù Sīmǎ and below,
shall be granted black ribbons.
They shall be supplied with crimson jackets
and martial caps.
When attending the imperial court and forming part of the imperial procession,
the Wǔqí Hǔbēn
shall wear brocade patterned robes
and quail-tail plumes.
The Zǎirén shall wear lízhī robes.

Huángmén Gǔchuī, and Dīngguān Púshè, Huángmén Gǔchuīshǐ Zhǔshì, Zhūguān Gǔchuī, Shàngshū Lángxià Dūzuòménxià Shǒugé, Diànzhōng Wēiyí Zōu, Hǔbēn Chángzhídàndiàn Huángyúnlóngménzhě, Ménxià Zuǒyòubù Hǔbēn Yǔlín Zōu, Gěichuánshìzhě Zhūdǎozōu, Ménxià Zhōngshū Shǒugé,
shall be supplied with crimson jackets
and martial caps.
Nánshū Ménxià Hǔbēn Yǔlín Zōu, Lántái Wǔcáo Jiézàng Shèlángxià Shǒugé, Wēiyí, Fāfú Zōu, Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě Huángshā Lángxià Shǒugé, Yèzhě, Lùshì, Wēiyí Zōu, Hédī Yèzhězōu, Zhūguān Yèzhězōu,
shall have crimson jackets
and martial caps.
Their clothing shall be supplied
as per old regulations.
Dàshuíshì shall have black lined single robes
and Fánkùi caps.
Wèishì shall have black cloth jackets
and Quèdí caps.
Among all these aforementioned various offices,
many were not fully established south of the Yangtze,
and many lacked court robes.
Those who should be supplied with court robes and jade pendants,
but are not in the capital, shall be supplied with court robes.
Except for Hù Wūhuán Qiāng Yí Róngmán Zhū Xiàowèi and above, Cìshǐ, and Xīyù Wùjǐ Xiàowèi,
all others shall not be supplied with jade pendants.
When they come to the imperial court,
these shall be temporarily lent to them,
