and returned after the assembly.
All those who should wear court robes,
but whose offices do not provide them,
are permitted to procure them themselves.
Those who are granted seals and ribbons but whose offices do not provide sash-purses,
may procure and make them themselves.
Those who are granted seals but not ribbons,
may not wear ribbons.
The sash-purse (pán),
was an ancient system.
During the Hàn dynasty, those who wore sash-purses
had them at their waist.
Some called them side-purses (bàngnáng),
some called them ribbon-purses (shòunáng).
Thus, these purses were used to hold ribbons.
Perhaps they were sometimes kept inside and sometimes loosely worn,
each having its proper time.
One set of court robes,
one crown and one headband each,
one crimson-red robe, one black-edged undergarment with one collar and two sleeves,
one leather belt and one lined trousers each,
one pair of slippers and one pair of socks each,
hairpins and hair guides shall be provided as accessories.
For those who wear court robes for the four seasons,
one crimson silk, yellow-crimson, blue-crimson, and black-crimson single robe each shall be added;
for those who wear court robes for the five seasons,
one white silk single robe shall be added.
For all who receive court robes,
the single robe requires seven zhang and two chi of fabric;
the lined single robe and jacket require five zhang and two chi;
the undergarment requires five zhang of silk;
the black trim requires one zhang and eight chi;
the collar and sleeves require one bolt and one chi of refined silk,
and seven chi and five cun of ordinary silk.
The trousers require one zhang and four chi of refined silk,
and two zhang of fine silk.
Socks require three chi of cloth.
The single robe and jacket's lined belts
each require one piece of fine silk,
seven chi long.
South of the Yangtze, only silk was supplied, with varying quantities.
At the end of Yuánjiā era of Sòng,
the supply was cut off,
and remains so to this day.

Mountain deer, nà deer, zhùnà, white nà deer, shīmáo fox white collars, yellow leopard, mottled white mink, qúsōu furs, bùyáo (hair ornaments), bātǎ (eight-tiered hats), bìjié (hair ornaments), duōfúchán (cicada-shaped ornaments), míngzhōng (ornaments), qúbái (white quills),
and all woven garments and hats, brocade tents, pure gold and silver vessels, mica objects measuring one cun or more in width,
are all prohibited items.
All officials of the second rank and above in the official ranking system,
may wear
any items that are not prohibited.
Those of the third rank and below

are additionally prohibited from wearing three-tiered (sāntǎ) hats and above, bìjié, juéchā (bird-fork hairpins), imitation pearls and kingfisher feathers for decorative tassels and pendants, variegated clothing, cup-patterned damask, Qí embroidered ceremonial robes, bǎoyí (embroidered robes), and guīpáo (sleeved robes).
Those of the sixth rank and below

are additionally prohibited from wearing golden hairpins (jīntǎ), damask, brocade, embroidered brocade, seven-edged damask,貂豽 furs, golden hairpins, rings, and earrings, and using gold to decorate vessels, and pitching crimson tents.
Those of the eighth rank and below
are additionally prohibited from wearing gauze, thin silk, damask, crepe,
and variegated genuine patterns.
Knights, soldiers, hundreds of artisans,

are additionally prohibited from wearing large crimson-purple hems, imitation knots, pearl earrings, rhinoceros horn, tortoiseshell, Yuèdá (a type of fabric), decorating objects with silver, pitching tents, and riding ox carts.
The color of their footwear must not exceed green, blue, or white.
Slaves, maidservants, and retainers
are additionally prohibited from wearing white headbands, dark red, crimson, golden-yellow or silver hairpins, rings, bells, embroidered robes, and earrings.
The color of their footwear must not exceed pure blue.
For those who leave office, or die and whose families do not receive official stipends,
the clothes worn by their family members
may follow the regulations of their former official rank.
All princes are prohibited from privately making prohibited items,
and wool felt saddles,
and pearls, jade, gold, and silver inlaid, carved, and sculpted useless objects.
The Son of Heaven sits on a lacquered bed
and resides in a red house.
The court historian remarks that in the Zuǒzhuàn,
it mentions painting the pillars of the Huángōng palace red.
Hé Xiū's commentary on the Gōngyáng
also states that there were red houses for residence.
This custom has a long history.
The lacquered bed also ought to be an old Hàn dynasty custom,
but it is not recorded in the Hàn rituals.
Upon examining why it must be red and lacquered,
there is a logical explanation.
Rare and beautiful timbers,
of which there are many types,
all grow rooted in deep, rugged places,
making them difficult to obtain.
If one relies on vast land resources
and the strength of many people,
then the labor will be arduous and the cost high,
leading to greater harm.
Therefore, in high antiquity, the sagely kings
had rafters that were not polished.
If they were, there would be fear of carving rafters and decorating pillars,
with no end in sight.
Wise men, with far-reaching foresight,
nip troubles in the bud and prevent problems from emerging,
knowing that unpolished rafters would not satisfy the hearts of later generations,
and would not be useful for the future.
Therefore, they added red and applied lacquer
to pass it down to posterity.
Common wood and ordinary materials
could all be put to use.
Could the profound intention be found here?
The construction of palace halls with round ponds and square wells, and the planting of lotuses,
was to suppress fire omens.
In ancient times, both the noble and the humble carried hù.
When they had business, they would tuck it into their waistbands.
What were called "jìn shēn zhī shì"
were those who tucked their hù and let their sýn belt hang down.
The sýn hung three chǐ.
Those with a hù would write on it when they had business,
so they always wore a pen in their hair.
The white pens of today
are its lingering image.
Officials of the second rank in the Sān Tái and Wǔ Shěng would wear them.
Princes, dukes, marquises, counts, viscounts, barons, qīng, yĭn, and military officials did not wear them.
Those who were promoted to the position of court attendant
would then wear them.
The shǒu bǎn
is the ancient hù.
The Shàng Shū Lìng, Pú Shè, and Shàng Shū also had white pens at the top of their shǒu bǎn,
wrapped in purple leather,
called hù.
On the shoulder of the court attire was a purple lined bag
attached to the outside of the court attire,
commonly called "zǐ hé."
Some say that during the Hàn dynasty, it was used to hold memorials and
carried while walking,
but this is not fully ascertained.
In the third year of Huáng Chū (222 CE), Wèi Wén Dì
issued an edict granting Hàn Tàishòu Yáng Biāo a small table and a staff,
treating him with guest etiquette.
On the day he was invited,
he was allowed to bring his staff into court.
He was also ordered to wear a deerskin crown.
Yáng Biāo declined,
but was not allowed.
So he was made to wear a plain cloth unlined garment and a pí biàn when he appeared.
Fù Xuán wrote:
"In the late Hàn dynasty, many princes and renowned scholars
abandoned royal attire,
considering the fú jīn elegant.
This is why people like Yuán Shào and Cuī Jūn,
though they were generals and commanders,
all wore yī jīn."
Because the world was in turmoil and desolate,
and resources were scarce, Wèi Wǔ
modeled a pí biàn after ancient styles,
cutting silk to make a lú,
in line with the principle of simplicity and adapting to the times.
Its color differentiated noble and humble.
It was originally used as military decoration,
not for national ceremonial use.
Xú Yuán said:
"Popular belief holds that the lú originally had no split.
Xún Wénruò wore it,
and it caught on a tree branch, creating a split.
This was deemed good,
and so it was not changed."
It was generally used for festive and mourning attire.
The jīn was made of kudzu fiber,
shaped like a lú,
but worn horizontally.
Both the noble and the humble wore it in ancient times.
Therefore, the demonic rebels at the end of the Hàn dynasty wore yellow jīn,
and were then called
"Huáng Jīn Zéi."
Today, students of the Guó Zǐ Tàixué wear it,
wearing a plain unlined garment as court attire,
holding a scroll of scriptures in place of a shǒu bǎn.
Reclusive scholars and commoners
all wear jīn.
Xú Yuán said:
"The name 'mào' is like 'guān.'
Its meaning is derived from covering the head.
Its origin is the shǐ.
In ancient times, there were guān but no cé,
and below the guān was the shǐ,
made of silk.
Later generations applied the cé to the guān,
and thus cut the shǐ to make the mào.
From the emperor's informal wear
down to commoners without rank,
all wore it."
The historian states that in the ninth year of Xián Hé (334 CE) of Jìn Chéng Dì, an edict stipulated
that the Bā Zuò Chéng Láng of the Shàng Shū and the Sān Shěng Shì Láng of the Mén Xià were permitted to enter and exit the Yè Mén in carriages, wearing white quē and low cé.
Furthermore, officials on duty in the two palaces wore black gauze lú.
Thus, scholars in informal settings
all wore quē.
And during the time of Jiāng Zuǒ, commoners already wore mào,
and scholars also often did so,
but their tops were round.
Later, their crowns were raised, it is said.
In ancient times, the monarch had court attire,
sacrificial attire,
informal attire,
and mourning attire.
Mourning attire was the pí biàn, resembling a suāi.
Nowadays, a plain unlined garment and black cé are used as informal attire,
and also for paying respects at tombs.
A plain unlined garment and white quē are used as mourning attire,
and are also worn to show respect to those of senior rank.
The plain unlined garment
is the ancient shēn yī.
Today's plain unlined garment is cut and made the same as the shēn yī,
only the silk belt is different.
The shēn yī and silk mào are worn during mourning.
The plain unlined garment and plain quē are worn for auspicious occasions.
In the third year of Tài Shǐ (267 CE) of Jìn Wǔ Dì,
an edict ordered Tàizǎi, Ān Píng Wáng Fú, to wear the attire of a Shì Zhōng,
and granted Dà Sī Mǎ, Yì Yáng Wáng Wàng, the attire of gǔn miǎn.
In the fourth year,
an edict again ordered Zhào, Lè Ān, and Yàn Wáng to wear the attire of a Sàn Qí Cháng Shì.
In the tenth year,
Péng Chéng Wáng was granted the attire of gǔn miǎn.
When the usurper Huán Xuán of the伪 Chǔ was about to usurp the throne,
he also conferred gǔn miǎn attire upon Ān Dì's maternal younger brother, Tàizǎi Láng Yá Wáng.
Since the rise of Sòng,
princes and high-ranking officials who were additionally appointed Shì Zhōng or Sàn Qí Cháng Shì
were then permitted to wear diāo dāng.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn of Sòng Xiàowǔ,
Prime Minister Nánjùn Wáng Yìxuān,
and in the second year,
Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Wǔchāng Wáng Hún,
harbored rebellious intentions.
Shìzǔ was concerned about the increasing power of the marquises and princes,
and wished to curtail it.
In the tenth month, day Jǐwèi, of that year,
Grand Marshal Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng and General of Agile Cavalry Jìnglín Wáng Dàn memorialized to reform the system of carriages and attire for the princes,
a total of nine articles,
which are found in Yìgōng's biography.
The Emperor then prompted the relevant authorities to further expand the articles.
The memorial stated:
"Carriages and attire are used to distinguish status,
a splendid institution from the Yú Book;
it is important to be cautious in bestowing titles and ceremonial objects,
a clear warning from the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Therefore, what was decreed by the Bureau of Imperial Manufactories
was strictly enforced by Han laws,
and if feudal lords secretly wore forbidden attire,
even if they were relatives, they would surely be punished.
Since recent times,
the transgression by subordinates has become increasingly prevalent.
Ceremonial objects, attire, and decorations,
music and dance,
are common among princes and dukes,
and even accessible to the common people.
There is no distinction between high and low,
and the people's aspirations are not unified.
[四０] The proposals in this memorial
are truly in accordance with propriety and regulations.
The nine articles,
however, are still incomplete,
so we respectfully add to them,
making a total of twenty-four articles.
One is not permitted to sit facing south in the audience hall,
nor to use screens or curtains made of fine bamboo.
Officials of feudal states are not permitted to enter the state palace barefoot in midwinter,
nor to stand alongside and assist the State Grand Tutor or Imperial Tutor in issuing commands or dispensing oil.
Princesses and princely consorts issuing commands
are not permitted to wear red attire.
Palanquins are not permitted to have double poles.
Ceremonial fans are not permitted to have pheasant feathers.
Swords are not permitted to be shaped like a deer's antler.
Spear pennants are not permitted to be made of peacock or white pheasant feathers.
The entourage flanking the carriage is not permitted to wear crimson jackets.
The horses for the accompanying carriage (píngchéng) must not exceed two.
Foreign performers are not permitted to wear colorful clothes.
Dancers performing in midwinter wearing guīyī [a kind of skirt-like garment]
are not permitted to put on heavy makeup or cover their faces with flowers.
Bell dances and cup-and-tray dances are not permitted at midwinter gatherings.
Stilt-walking acts, shénshū (possibly a type of acrobatics), sword-swallowing, Bóshān acts, pole-climbing acts, and five-table acts
are not permitted to be performed unless at a midwinter gathering or for musical performances.
[This line is a continuation of the previous one, indicating these acts are forbidden unless for specific occasions.]
Princesses and imperial consorts are not permitted to wear gǔndài [imperial sashes].
For signal banners,
all officials not belonging to the Central Secretariat or Imperial Chancellery must use crimson.
Regarding the commandants (nèi shǐ) of commanderies and counties and other officials within a prince's fief,
for their feudal lord,
since they are not among the three highest officials,
upon dismissal from office, they are no longer required to pay respect,
nor are they permitted to refer to themselves as subjects.
It is merely appropriate for them to show respect as between superior and subordinate officials.
For the regular travels of various garrisons,
the carriages must not be preceded or followed by more than six ranks,
with the exception of the white-clad guards flanking the carriage.
[This line clarifies the exception.]
Knives are not permitted to have silver or bronze ornamentation.
[四一] For the daughters of princes enfeoffed as xiànzhǔ, the consorts of princes who have inherited their titles, and the wives of those enfeoffed as marquises when they travel,
[四二] none are permitted to have a full imperial escort (lúbù).
For princes who have inherited their titles,
for their marriages, funerals, auspicious and inauspicious events,
[四三] all must follow the rites of dukes and marquises of various states,
and not be the same as those of imperial brothers and imperial sons.
Carriages are not permitted to have oil-painted awnings,
though light carts (yáochē) are not subject to this restriction.
Flat-bottomed boats (píngchéng fǎng) must all have flat, open ends,
and are not permitted to be designed to resemble dragon boats,
and are all forbidden from being painted with red oil.
Screens are not permitted to be made with five-flower patterns or vertical bamboo shoot shapes.
If there are existing objects of these types,
they must all be sent to the imperial storehouse.
Twenty days after the arrival of this document,
if anyone is found secretly using forbidden items or violating the prohibitions,
or if the supervisory officials fail to investigate and report,
then punishment will be deliberated at the time. "
The Emperor approved.
"Five hundred men for the front of the carriage" refers to
ministers traveling with a retinue,
with five hundred men forming one 'lǚ' (rank).
The Han dynasty unified the realm,
hence the 'men' were removed,
but the 'name' (lǚ) was retained.
In the eleventh month, day Yǐsì, of the second year of Xiàojiàn of Sòng Xiàowǔ,
the relevant authorities memorialized:
"Attendant-in-ordinary and Libationer Hé Yǎn proposed: 'From now on, when approaching the imperial presence,
the Emperor, wearing ceremonial robes
and covered by the huágài parasol,
should ascend the hall escorted as if for a temple purification ritual,
with the Attendant-in-ordinary and Regular Attendants assisting him up the steps.
And when it is appropriate for princes and dukes to rise,
they should also be assisted.
Once finished,
they return to their original positions.'
We seek a detailed discussion."
Bureau Chief Xú Yuán participated in the discussion, stating:
"It should be as stated by the Ministry,
to serve as a permanent standard."
The Emperor approved.
In the fifth month, day Rénxū, of the third year of Xiàojiàn,
the relevant authorities memorialized:
"According to Hú Guǎng and Cài Yōng of the Han dynasty, both stated that in ancient times feudal lords had nine auxiliary carriages.
When Qín destroyed the six states, it appropriated their carriages and attire,
thus the emperor's grand imperial carriage was accompanied by eighty-one auxiliary carriages.
The Minister of Personnel (Shàngshū) and the Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ) rode in them.
The last carriage
had a leopard tail hung from it.
The imperial escort (fǎjià) had thirty-six carriages.
Examining the situation since the Eastern Jìn dynasty to the present,
when the emperor travels,
five auxiliary carriages follow one another."
Minister of Personnel and Prince of Jiànpíng, Hóng, participated in the discussion, stating:
"Eighty-one carriages
implies the nine states,
but thirty-six carriages has no basis,
and neither is found in the classics.
Moreover, the accounts of Yōng and Guǎng
refer to carriages ridden by attending officials,
not the precise number of the emperor's auxiliary carriages.
The five carriages in the Eastern Jìn
are too frugal and not in accordance with propriety.
According to the Zhōu Guān, it states:
'A duke of the highest rank (shànggōng) has nine commissions (mìng),
and nine auxiliary carriages.
A marquis or count (hóubó) has seven commissions,
and seven carriages.
A viscount or baron (zǐnán) has five commissions,
and five carriages.'
Therefore, an emperor should have twelve carriages."
The Emperor approved.
On the first day of the ninth month, day Dīngwèi, of the first year of Dàmíng,
the relevant authorities memorialized:
"There is no set number of auxiliary carriages for the Empress Dowager's travels.
We submit this to the officials of rites for discussion and correction."
Dr. Wáng Xièzhī proposed:
"In the Rites of Zhōu,
the Empress's six garments and five types of carriages
are all the same as the King's,
so the system of auxiliary carriages
should not be uniquely different.

Furthermore, records state: 'In ancient times, the Empress established six palaces, three empresses' assistants (fūrén), nine consorts (pín), twenty-seven junior concubines (shìfù), and eighty-one imperial concubines (yùqī),
to oversee the internal governance of the realm.'
'The Son of Heaven established six officials, three dukes, nine ministers, twenty-seven grand masters, and eighty-one primary scholars,
to oversee the external governance of the realm.'
Zhèng Zhù noted: 'The Empress, resembling the King, established six palaces and resided in them,
also having one main chamber and five private chambers.'

[This sentence is slightly different, usually Zheng Xuan's note says the queen has six palaces (六宮) to reside in, one main, five subsidiary. The passage means she has six palaces to reside in, one is the main chamber, and five are private chambers.]
From this, we infer that what is established for her is always the same as for the King,
and it is clear that there should be no reduction in her rites.
Since the Empress Dowager's rites are already of the highest order,
it is even more inappropriate for them to be different.
We believe she should also have twelve carriages."
This proposal was deemed acceptable.
The Emperor approved.
In the first month, day Wùchén, of the fourth year of Dàmíng,
Shàngshū Zuǒchéng Xún Wànqiū memorialized:
"The 'Ceremonial Rites for Plowing the Imperial Fields' states:
'The Emperor wears the Tōngtiān Crown,
a red chin strap (zhūhóng),
a dark cap (qīng jièzé),
and a green gauze robe.
The Attendant-in-ordinary accompanies him in the carriage,
and the Director of Carriages holds the reins.'
However, the 'Treatise on Carriages and Attire of Han' states: 'The Tōngtiān Crown
is the Emperor's everyday attire.'
If so, how can everyday attire be used for the ceremony of the thousand acres?
The Lǐ Jì states: 'In ancient times, the Son of Heaven plowed the thousand acres,
wearing a ceremonial cap (miǎn) with a red chin strap,
personally holding the plow.'
Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the 'Director of Clothing' (Sīfú) in the Zhōu Guān says: 'The six types of attire all share the same miǎn,'
because of their reverence.
Although the attire for the time changes, the miǎn system does not.
Furthermore, Pān Yuè's 'Rhapsody on Plowing the Imperial Fields' states: 'The Permanent Imperial Attendant (Chángbó) accompanies him in the carriage,
and the Grand Coachman (Tàipú) holds the reins.'
Based on this,
when the imperial carriage goes to plow the imperial fields,
the Emperor should wear a miǎn,
with twelve pendants (zǎoshí’èrliú),
a red chin strap,
a black cap,
and a green gauze robe.
The Permanent Imperial Attendant should accompany him in the carriage,
and the Grand Coachman should hold the reins.
The ceremonial notes should be amended,
to fully conform to these two rites as the definitive ceremony."
The Emperor approved.
On the *jǐmǎo* day of the first month of the fourth year of Dàmíng,
the responsible officials reported:
"For the personal conduct of rituals at the Southern Altar,
the Emperor first wears the Píngtiān Crown
and robes adorned with fire dragons and *fǔfú* patterns.
Upon returning,
he changes to the Tōngtiān Crown
and crimson gauze robes.
For personal conduct at ancestral temples,
according to the old rites,
the Emperor's initial attire was no different from that for the suburban sacrifices,
but upon returning, he would change into a black *jiécè* [headband]
and a single garment for the event,
which was inconsistent with proper form.
It is fitting that, like returning from the suburban sacrifices,
he also changes into the Tōngtiān Crown
and crimson gauze robes.
Furthermore, the old rites prescribed riding in a Jīngēn Chē.
Now that the Wǔlù are complete,
and in accordance with the rites, the Yùlù is used for sacrifices,
it is also fitting to change the Jīngēn Chē to the Yùlù."
An imperial edict approved it.
On the *rénxū* day of the eighth month of the sixth year of Dàmíng,
the responsible officials reported:
"The Hàn ceremonial records state
the Gōng and Qīng lead,
the Dàjiāngjūn is an outrider,
and the Tàipú Qīng drives.
For the Fǎjià,
the Shìzhōng is an outrider,
and the Fèngchē Láng drives.'
When the Jìn clan moved south of the Yangtze,
the Dàjià was not established,
hence the Fǎjià was used for suburban sacrifices,
and the Xiǎojià for ancestral temples.
As for ceremonial attire,
the two carriages were not different.
For visiting imperial tombs,
the imperial attire was a single garment and a *cè*,
while the hundred officials accompanying wore
crimson robes only,
also called Xiǎojià,
which was a mismatch of name and reality.
that 'for the Dàjià Lǔbù,
the Dàjià was used for visiting imperial tombs
and the Northern Altar.
The *Zhōu Lǐ* states that ancestral temples receive a lesser status than Hàotiān,
so it is appropriate to use the Dàjià for suburban sacrifices,
the Fǎjià for temple sacrifices,
and the Xiǎojià for visiting imperial tombs,
as a proper hierarchy.
Now we propose to change the temple sacrifices to use the Fǎjià Lǔbù,
and the number of military banners
will be assigned as needed.
His Majesty will ride in the Yùlù,
with the Jīnlù, Xiànglù, Gélù, Mùlù, Xiǎoniǎn, Lúnyù, Yáo, Yīshū, and other carriages as supplementary.
All other arrangements will follow the usual rites."
An imperial edict approved it.
On the *jiǎyín* day of the second month of the seventh year of Dàmíng,
the imperial carriage toured the two prefectures of Nányù and Yǎn.
Wearing the *miǎn* robes,
the Emperor rode in the Yùlù
to bid farewell at the two imperial temples.
He then changed into the Tōngtiān Crown,
rode in the Mùlù,
raised a large banner,
and prepared for the spring hunt ceremony.
On the *jiǎxū* day of the fifth month of the fourth year of Tàishǐ of Míngdì,
Shàngshū Lìng, the Prince of Jiàn'ān, Xiūrén, participated in a discussion:
"The sons of the Son of Heaven,
like common scholars, observe age-based deference
when reaching the Bìyōng;
none are born noble.
Once bestowed with rank and honor,
their rites are equivalent to those of a Shànggōng.
The Zhōu system of five ranks,
with carriages and attire overlapping,
had the Gōng rank one level
below that of the King.
Kings bestowed Jīnlù upon princes of the same clan,
and Xiàng, Gélù, and Mùlù
upon marquises and counts of other clans;
courtiers in attendance
also followed these rites.
According to this system,
the Crown Prince should ride in a Jīnlù.
Since Emperor Wǔ of Jìn crossed the Yangtze,
rites and ceremonies became disordered,
and the carriages and attire of princes and dukes downward
were humble and mixed;
only the Crown Prince
had elevated and distinct ritual status,
ranking just below the imperial family
and above marquises and kings.
However, the Crown Prince riding in a Shíshān Ānchē
has no basis in the classics
and no precedent.
What the rites refer to as Jīnlù and Yùlù
is merely a matter of decorating the carriages with gold and jade.
The left, right, front, and rear
are uniformly painted with lacquer.
Qín changed the Zhōu carriage,
creating the Jīngēn,
which was entirely covered with gold foil
on all four sides.
Hàn, Wèi, and the two Jìn dynasties
followed this custom without change.
It was not until Dàmíng
that the Wǔlù were fully established.
The Jīn and Yù systems
both resemble the Jīngēn,
and upon casual inspection,
there is hardly any difference.
If bestowed upon the Crown Prince,
it would be considered too weighty according to the rites,
not serving to emphasize the imperial rank
and display the hierarchy.
Moreover, according to the principles of the *Chūnqiū*,
inferior ranks are distinguished by a reduction of 'two',
and the principle for subjects and sons
should be one of humility and restraint.
It is fitting that the Crown Prince's carriage and attire
be two grades below that of the Son of Heaven,
pulled by four horses,
riding in an Xiànglù,
with a sky-blue banner adorned with nine dragon leaves.
This would neither diminish the superior
nor encroach upon the inferior,
thus adapting ancient wisdom to contemporary circumstances,
and would be appropriate according to the rites."
An imperial edict approved it.
On the *jiǎyín* day of the eighth month of the fourth year of Tàishǐ,
"The ornamentation of carriages and attire
must follow symbolic numbers.
Therefore, eminent emperors have left models,
and successive sages have established regulations.
Recently, I revised and fixed the Wǔlù,
drawing from antiquity and adjusting for the present,
and completed the Liùfú,
adapting rites to the times.
The matters implemented
each have their stipulations.
They can now be promulgated
and recorded in the statutes.
I wear the Dàmiǎn with pure jade tassels,
black upper garment and yellow lower garment,
and ride in the Yùlù
for suburban sacrifices to Heaven
and ancestral sacrifices in the Míngtáng.
Also, I wear the Fǎmiǎn with five-colored tassels,
black upper garment and crimson lower garment,
and ride in the Jīnlù
for sacrifices at the Tàimiào
and grand assemblies of princes on New Year's Day.
Also, I wear the Shìguānmiǎn with four-colored tassels,
purple upper garment and red lower garment,
and ride in the Xiànglù
for small assemblies and banquets,
seeing off princes,
and meeting with kings and dukes from the imperial platform.
Also, I wear the Xiùmiǎn with three-colored tassels,
crimson upper and lower garments,
and ride in the Gélù
for punitive expeditions against the disobedient
and military exercises and hunts.
Also, I wear the Huángmiǎn with two-colored tassels,
and ride in the Mùlù
for plowing ceremonies
and entertaining the Guózǐ.
Also, the Tōngtiān Crown
and crimson gauze robes
are for attending to government affairs."
In the first month, on the day Wùchén, in the sixth year of Tàishǐ,
the officials reported:
"We have been instructed that the Crown Prince, during the New Year's Day audience,
〔四七〕should he wear the gǔnmiǎn (ceremonial cap with twelve strings of beads) and the jiǔzhāngyī (robe with nine emblems)?"
Qīu Zhòngqǐ, a secretary in the Office of Rites, deliberated, saying:
"According to the Rites of Zhōu,
from the Duke downwards, all wore the gǔnmiǎn.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states: 'The gǔnmiǎn, down to the xuánmiǎn of the high ministers and grand masters,
were all their ceremonial attire when having an audience with or being summoned by the Son of Heaven.'
Considering the ancient highest-ranking dukes,
they were still permitted to wear the gǔnmiǎn for an audience.
The Crown Prince, with the尊 (honor) of being the heir apparent,
is looked up to by the entire realm.
I believe it is fitting to follow the glorious ancient customs
and wear the gǔnmiǎn with nine strings of beads for the New Year's Day audience."
Lù Chéng, concurrently Assistant Left Grandee Secretary, deliberated, saying:
"Wearing the miǎn (ceremonial cap) for an audience
is indeed established in the classics.
The Qín Dynasty abolished the system of the six miǎn,
and it was not until Emperor Míng of Hàn that it was restored with the scholars to complete the ancient regulations.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
except for performing rites in the ancestral temples,
it was not desired for officials to wear the gǔnmiǎn.
Therefore, those in the rank of Duke
were always given additional court titles.
Now the Crown Prince, as the heir apparent and assistant,
his ritual status surpasses that of all other princes.
It is appropriate to follow the glorious ancient customs of the sage kings
and reform the crude systems of recent times.
We, your ministers, have discussed this together,
and according to the rites,
the Crown Prince, for the New Year's Day audience,
should wear the gǔnmiǎn and jiǔzhāngyī.
We deem Qīu Zhòngqǐ's deliberation to be correct.
It shall be recorded in the ritual procedures."
An edict approved it.
Later, when the deposed emperor ascended the throne,
he honored his birth mother, Concubine Chén, as Empress Dowager Tàifēi.
Her carriages and attire were all in accordance with the precedent of Emperor Xiàowǔ's Tàifēi of Jìn.
Only the five-ox banner and the red banner were omitted.
Collation Notes
Treatise 9, Music 1
The Yì Jīng says:
"The former kings created music to exalt virtue,
offering it to the Supreme Emperor,
and thereby aligning with their ancestors."
From the Huáng Dì to the Three Dynasties,
the names differed.
When Zhōu declined, music became fragmented,
and was further corrupted by the music of Zhèng and Wèi.
Although Marquis Wén of Wèi was fond of antiquity,
he was still confused about ancient music.
Thus, licentious sounds flourished and refined music declined.
When Qín burned the classics,
the Music Classic was lost.
When Hàn arose,
the music masters had the Zhì clan,
who could only remember its clang and dance,
but could not explain its meaning.
Zhōu preserved the music of six generations;
by Qín, only Sháo and Wǔ remained.
Shǐhuángdi changed the Zhōu dance to Wǔxíng.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn changed the Sháo dance to Wénshǐ,
to show that they did not inherit each other.
He also created the Wǔdé dance,
in which the dancers all held shields and battle-axes,
to symbolize that the world was pleased with his military campaigns to eliminate chaos.
Therefore, in Emperor Gāozǔ's ancestral temple, the Wǔdé, Wénshǐ, and Wǔxíng dances were performed.
Zhōu also had the music of Fángzhōng.
Qín changed its name to Shòurén.
Its sound
was Chu sound.
Emperor Gāozǔ liked it,
and Emperor Xiàohuì changed its name to Ānshì.
Emperor Gāozǔ also created the Zhāoróng music and Lǐróng music.
Zhāoróng originated from Wǔdé,
and Lǐróng originated from Wénshǐ and Wǔxíng.
In the early Hàn, there was also Jiāzhì music,
which Shūsūn Tōng adapted from Qín musicians to create music for welcoming the spirits in the ancestral temples.
Emperor Wén also personally created the Sìshí dance,
to manifest the peace and harmony of the world.
Indeed, those who performed the music of the former kings
made clear that there was a standard;
those who performed music they created themselves
made clear that there was a system.
Emperor Xiàojǐng adopted the Wǔdé dance to create the Zhāodé dance,
offering it in the temple of Tàizōng.
Emperor Xiàoxuān adopted the Zhāodé dance to create the Shèngdé dance,
offering it in the temple of Shìzōng.
The Hàn emperors performed the Wénshǐ, Sìshí, and Wǔxíng dances.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ,
King Xiàn of Héjiān, along with Máo Shēng and others, collected texts on music from the Zhōu Guān and various philosophers,
and compiled the Yuè Jì (Record of Music).
They presented the Bāyì dance,
which did not differ significantly from that of the Zhì clan.
The Palace Clerk, Wáng Dìng, transmitted it,
and passed it on to Wáng Yǔ of Chángshān.
Yǔ,
during Emperor Chéng's reign, was an usher.
He repeatedly spoke of its meaning
and presented twenty-four scrolls of the record.
Liú Xiàng collated the books
and obtained twenty-three chapters,
but ultimately, it was not adopted.
At the beginning of Emperor Míng's reign,
King Xiàn of Dōngpíng, Cāng, summarized and finalized the deliberations of the high ministers and grandees,
saying:
"Ancestral temples should each perform their own music,
and should not inherit each other's,
this is to clarify their merits and virtues.
Wénshǐ, Wǔxíng, and Wǔdé should be combined into the Dàwǔ dance."
He also created one chapter of dance songs
to be offered in the temple of Guāngwǔ.
At the end of Hàn, there was great chaos,
and much of the music was lost and fragmented.
When Wèi Wǔ (Emperor Wǔ of Wèi) pacified Jīngzhōu,
he obtained Dù Kuí,
who was skilled in the eight sounds (types of musical instruments).
He had once been a Hàn Yǎyuèláng (Gentleman of Court Music)
and was particularly knowledgeable about musical matters.
Thus, he was made Jūnmóu Jìjiǔ (Libationer for Military Strategy)
and tasked with establishing court music.
At that time, there were also Dèng Jìng and Yǐn Shāng,
who were good at teaching court music. Yǐn Hú, a song master, could sing the songs for ancestral temples and suburban sacrifices.
Féng Sù and Fú Yǎng, dance masters, understood the various dances of previous generations.
Kuí oversaw all of them.
By extensively consulting classics and records,
and recently adopting historical practices,
the restoration of ancient music in Wèi
began with Kuí.
However, Zǔo Yánnián and others
were exceptionally skilled in Zhèng music,
while Kuí alone preferred antiquity and maintained correctness.
In the second year of Huángchū during Emperor Wén's reign,
the Hàn Bāyú dance was changed to Zhāowǔ dance,
the ancestral temple's Ānshì music was changed to Zhèngshì music,
Jiāzhì music to Yínglíng music,
Wǔdé music to Wǔsòng music,
Zhāoróng music to Zhāoyè music,
Yúnqiáo dance to Fèngxiáng dance,
Yùmìng dance to Língyìng dance,
Wǔdé dance to Wǔsòng dance,
Wénshǐ dance to Dàsháo dance,
and Wǔxíng dance to Dàwǔ dance.
Many of its numerous songs and poems
were simply old ones from previous generations;
only when the Wèi state was first established,
Wáng Càn was ordered to revise and compose the Dēng songs and the Ānshì and Bāyú poems.
In the beginning of Tàihé during Emperor Míng's reign,
an edict stated:
"The creation of rites and music
is for classifying things, demonstrating merit, and not forgetting their origins.
All music primarily involves dance.
From Huáng Dì's Yúnmén onwards,
down to Zhōu's Dàwǔ,
all were names of dances in the imperial ancestral temple.
Therefore, the officials in charge
were all called Tàiyuè (Grand Music),
to comprehensively manage all things,
and not to be named after a single thing.
The music for Emperor Wǔ's temple is not yet appropriate.
Deliberate and decide on the temple music and dance,
the items held by the dancers,
the arrangement of the formations,
and the verses of the songs,
ensuring they are detailed and complete.
The music officials shall remain as before, as Tàiyuè."
Tàiyuè
was the old name of Hàn.
The Later Hàn changed Tàiyǔ Yuèguān (Grand Entertainer Music Official) according to a prophecy,
and now it was restored to the old name.
Thereupon, the gōng-qīng奏曰:
“Your subjects have heard that when virtue is abundant and transformation profound,
then music and dance are sufficient to portray its form,
and sounds are sufficient to express its songs and chants.
Therefore, when offered in the suburbs and ancestral temples,
ghosts and spirits enjoy its harmony;
when used in the court,
monarch and ministers delight in its order.
To enable all within the four seas
to fully know the abundance of supreme virtue,
and for its glory to renew daily,
this is what is meant by rites and music.
Hence, the former kings grandly offered sacrifices to Shàngdì,
to match with their ancestors,
for it was appropriate to their time that these were instituted.
In the late era of Zhōu,
nearly two thousand years after Táng and Yú,
the music of Sháo, Xiāo, Nán, Yuè, Wǔ, and Xiàng,
their melodies and enduring influence,
can all be discussed.
From this, it can be said
that the matters of rites and music
cannot be dispensed with.
Now, the music of Tài-zǔ Wǔ Huángdì
should be called the Music of Wǔshǐ.
Wǔ
means divine martial prowess.
Wǔ
also means a king's footsteps.
It speaks of the beginning of divine martial prowess,
and also where the king's footsteps arose.
The music of Gāo-zǔ Wén Huángdì
should be called the Dance of Xiánxī.
Xián
means all.
Xī
means to flourish.
It speaks of responding to the destiny of receiving the mandate,
whereby all under heaven flourished through it.
As for the ministers elaborating on virtue and discussing merits,
establishing the designation of Liè-zǔ,
but not yet instituting music and dance,
this is not how virtue is illuminated and merits recorded.
For songs chant virtue,
and dances symbolize events.
Regarding literature,
civic and martial elements are equally brilliant,
possessing both civic and martial qualities,
which is how sacred virtue is made manifest.
Your subjects respectfully propose naming the music and dance ‘Zhāngbīn zhī Wǔ’.
In ancient times, the nine performances of Xiāo-Sháo
were personally played in the court of Yú Dì;
the Wǔ, Xiàng, and Dà-Wǔ
also resounded on the steps of Wén and Wǔ.
This was specifically to highlight their virtuous teachings,
and to manifest their achievements,
so that all under heaven would embrace their glory,
and learn to chant their melodies.
From Hàn Gāo-zǔ and Wén Dì, each in their time,
they created the Dances of Wǔdé and Sìshí.
Considering the appropriateness of previous generations' creations,
and the beauty of present achievements,
the propagation of great deeds
is none more glorious than Zhāngbīn.
The 'Music Treatise' says: 'Bells, chimes, shields, and axes
are used to sacrifice at the temples of former kings,
and also for presenting and returning toasts and libations.
Within the ancestral temple,
monarch and ministers all show reverence;
among the clan elders,
old and young all follow in harmony.'
Therefore, Zhòng-ní, in response to Bīn-Mó-Jiǎ's question, said: 'The Way of Zhōu extends in all four directions,
and rites and music are interconnected.'
The commentary states: 'Lǔ had dì music,
which was used for guest sacrifices.'
These all clearly show that for major sacrificial rites,
magnificent music was generally used.
Now, when performing affairs for heaven, earth, and the ancestral temple,
these three dances should all be used for offerings and sacrifices;
and when holding grand banquets in court,
they should also be danced.
Only then will it conform to the ancient system of serving the spirits and instructing the people,
extending to ten thousand generations,
and its meaning will become even clearer.
Furthermore, your subjects have considered
that the three dances should have a collective name;
they can be named the Music of Dà-jūn.
Jūn
means equilibrium.
It speaks of the three generations of Dà Wèi having shared merits,
leading to great peace and prosperity.
In name, it is beautiful;
in meaning, it is appropriate.”
The Shàngshū reported:
“It should be as presented.”
The emperor initially refused to permit the institution of the Music of Zhāngbīn.
After three requests,
he then granted permission.
Thereupon, the Shàngshū further reported:
“For sacrifices at the Yuánqiū and below,
those performing the Wǔshǐ Dance wear
a flat miǎn cap,
a black jiè-zé,
black upper and lower garments,
white collar and cuffs,
a crimson-collared and cuffed inner garment,
crimson full-width trousers,
crimson [⿰糸末] leggings,
and black wéi-dī shoes.
Those performing the Xiánxī Dance wear
a wěimáo cap,
with the rest of their attire as before.
Those performing the Zhāngbīn Dance
wear the same attire as the Wǔshǐ and Xiánxī dancers.
When performed in the court,
those performing the Wǔshǐ Dance wear
a wǔ-guān,
a red jiè-zé,
an unlined crimson robe,
a crimson collar and cuffs,
a black-collared and cuffed inner garment,
tiger-striped full-width trousers,
white cloth *bù-bì*,
and black wéi-dī shoes.
Those performing the Xiánxī Dance wear
a jìnxián-guān,
a black jiè-zé,
an unlined yellow robe,
white full-width trousers,
with the rest of their attire as before.”
The report was approved.
The historiographer notes:
The Wǔshǐ and Xiánxī dances
have different cap regulations,
yet it states that Zhāngbīn dancers wear the same attire as Wǔshǐ and Xiánxī dancers.
It is unclear which cap they wear.
Shìzhōng Miào Xí further reported:
“The Ānshì-gē was originally a song name from the Hàn dynasty.
Now the poetic lyrics are not the same as the texts of that time,
so they should be changed.
According to the commentary on the Zhōu Lǐ, it says: ‘Ānshì music
is like the 'bedroom' music of Zhōu.’
Therefore, earlier commentators
considered the 'bedroom' songs to describe the virtues of queens and concubines,
thereby influencing the world
and rectifying husband and wife relationships.
It was fitting to change the name of Ānshì to Zhèngshǐ zhī Yuè.
Since the initial establishment of the Wèi State,
the ‘Ānshì-shī’ composed by the former Shìzhōng Wáng Càn
specifically focused on praising divine spirits and explaining the idea of spirits observing and enjoying offerings.
Subsequently, Xí also, by reviewing the Hàn Ānshì songs and chants,
also spoke of: ‘Greatly display the four-tiered bells,
spirits come to feast and enjoy,
with auspicious offerings and proper demeanor,
eternally receiving their blessings.’
There is no mention of the 'Two Nán' or the transformative influence of queens and concubines upon the world.
Now, I reflect that those who previously referred to 'bedroom' music as songs for queens and concubines
might have misunderstood its meaning.
When performing sacrifices to entertain the spirits,
one chants the merits and virtues of ancestors in the hall,
and chants about banquets and enjoyment below the hall.
There is no need to chant about the transformative influence of queens and concubines.
It is appropriate to name the music and songs according to their purpose;
the Ānshì-gē should be changed to Xiǎngshén-gē.”
The report was approved.
The historiographer notes:
Wén Dì had already changed Ānshì to Zhèngshǐ,
yet Xí now again changed Ānshì to Xiǎngshén.
The meaning is unclear. The Ānshì-shī composed by Wáng Càn
is now lost.
Xí further reported:
“For the temple of Wénzhāo Huánghòu,
where the music of four-tiered bells is installed,
its order of playing should be clearly inscribed,
and named, following the precedent of Tài-zǔ’s temple,
the ‘Zhāomiào zhī Jùyuè’.”
The Shàngshū reported:
“According to the Rites,
when a woman inherits her husband’s rank
and shares the same sacrificial feast,
the music should not differ in form.
Although Zhāozhēn Huánghòu now has a separate temple,
regarding the bell-chime music and its melodic system,
it should be as Xí suggests.”
The report was approved.
Sànjì Chángshì Wáng Sù (散騎常侍王肅) deliberated, saying:
"Kings govern heaven and earth, each according to their own ritual system.
Now, some interpreters rely on the isolated texts of the *Zhōu Guān* (周官) as the grand blueprint for governing the state,
fearing that they are narrow and do not understand broadness.
When Hàn Wǔdì (漢武帝) returned from his eastern tour and Fēngshàn (封禪) sacrifices,
he offered sacrifices to Tàiyī (太一) at Gānquán (甘泉),
and sacrificed to Hòutǔ (后土) at Fényīn (汾陰).
All these rites fully employed their music.
The phrase 'fully employed'
means fully employing the music of *gōngxiàn* (宮縣).
That the nature of Heaven and Earth values simplicity
probably refers to the unadorned nature of their vessels,
not that common things should be reduced.
According to ritual,
the Son of Heaven uses *gōngxiàn* (宮縣),
and dances the *bāyì* (八佾).
Now, in sacrificing at Yuánqiū (圓丘) and Fāngzé (方澤),
it is fitting to follow the Son of Heaven's system,
arranging *gōngxiàn* (宮縣) music
and the *bāyì* (八佾) dance."
Wèi Zhēn (衞臻), Miáo Xí (繆襲), Zuǒ Yánnián (左延年) and others all agreed with Sù's (肅) deliberation.
The memorial was approved.
Sù (肅) further deliberated, saying:
"Some interpreters believe that when the Zhōu (周) house sacrificed to Heaven,
they only danced the *Yúnmén* (雲門);
when sacrificing to Earth,
they only danced the *Xiánchí* (咸池);
and in the ancestral temple,
they only danced the *Dàwǔ* (大武).
This seems to lose its true meaning.
The *Zhōu Lǐ* (周禮) states that guests were all presented with complete music.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* (左傳) says: 'Wángzǐ Tuí (王子頹) hosted five high officials,
and the music included all the dances.'
These were the music of the six generations.
If so, on the day of a single gathering,
all six generations of music were performed.
Heaven, Earth, and the ancestral temple are the greatest matters,
while entertaining guests and feasts are minor in comparison.
The *Wáng Zhì* (王制) says:
'Various delicacies should not exceed sacrificial animals;
informal attire should not exceed sacrificial robes.'
How can the music for banquets exceed the music for Heaven, Earth, and the ancestral temple?
The *Zhōu Guān* (周官) says: 'With the six *lǜ* (律), six *lǚ* (呂), five notes, eight sounds, and six dances, a grand musical performance is brought together,
to invoke spirits,
to harmonize the nation,
to bring accord to all the people,
to bring peace to guests,
and to please distant people.'
Now, the six *lǜ* (律), six *lǚ* (呂), five notes, and eight sounds
are all performed at the same time.
But if the six dances are uniquely divided and used,
it will not satisfy people's hearts.
Furthermore, the *Zhōu Guān* (周官) says: 'The *Mò Shī* (韎師) is in charge of teaching music;
for sacrifices, he leads his subordinates to perform the dance;
for grand banquets, it is also so.'
*Mò* (韎)
is the music of the Eastern Yí (夷).
It also says: 'The *Dīliú Shì* (鞮鞻氏) is in charge of the music of the Four Yí (夷) and their songs;
for sacrifices, they play and sing;
for banquets, it is also so.'
The music of the Four Yí (夷) then enters the ancestral temple;
the classics of previous generations
alone should not be used?
That grand banquets and feasts are 'also so'
clarifies that ancient and modern, Yí (夷) and Xià (夏) music
are all principally used in the ancestral temple,
and then extended to other occasions.
Indeed, those who compose the music of the former kings
value being able to encompass and use it.
Admitting the music of the Four Yí (夷)
beautifies the reach of virtue.
The temples of Gāo Huángdì (高皇帝), Tài Huángdì (太皇帝), Tàizǔ (太祖), Gāozǔ (高祖), and Wénzhāo (文昭)
should all concurrently use the dances of previous generations, as well as *Wǔshǐ* (武始) and *Dàjūn* (大鈞)."
The officials memorialized:
"It should be as Sù (肅) deliberated."
The memorial was approved.
Sù (肅) privately composed twelve poems and eulogies for the ancestral temple,
but they were not set to music.
In the second year of Tàishǐ (泰始) of Jìn Wǔdì (晉武帝)
(266 CE), the sacrificial temple songs were reformed,
but their music and dances remained as before.
When Hàn Guāngwǔ (漢光武) pacified Lǒng (隴) and Shǔ (蜀),
he expanded the suburban sacrifices,
with Gāo Huángdì (高皇帝) as co-sacrificed.
The music performed was *Qīngyáng* (青陽), *Zhūmíng* (朱明), *Xīhào* (西皓), *Xuánmíng* (玄冥),
and the dances *Yúnqiáo* (雲翹) and *Yùmìng* (育命).
For the northern suburban sacrifice and the sacrifice at Míngtáng (明堂),
music was performed as at the southern suburban sacrifice.
To welcome the seasonal *qì* (氣) at the Five Suburban altars: in spring, *Qīngyáng* (青陽) was sung;
in summer, *Zhūmíng* (朱明) was sung;
both accompanied by the *Yúnqiáo* (雲翹) dance.
In autumn, *Xīhào* (西皓) was sung;
in winter, *Xuánmíng* (玄冥) was sung;
both accompanied by the *Yùmìng* (育命) dance.
In late summer, *Zhūmíng* (朱明) was sung,
accompanied by both dances.
In the second year of Yuánhé (元和) of Zhāngdì (章帝)
(85 CE), for ancestral temple music,
according to custom,
the *shíjǔ* (食舉) had two pieces: *Lùmíng* (鹿鳴) and *Chéngyuánqì* (承元氣).
In the third year (86 CE),
he personally composed four poems:
the first called *Sīqí Huáng Yáo* (思齊皇姚),
the second *Liù Qílín* (六騏驎),
the third *Jiésùyōng* (竭肅雍),
and the fourth *Zhìchìgēn* (陟叱根).
Combined with the previous six pieces,
these formed the *shíjǔ* (食舉) for the ancestral temple.
Two pieces, *Chónglái* (重來) and *Shànglíng* (上陵), were added to the ancestral temple *shíjǔ* (食舉),
making eight pieces for the *shànglíng shíjǔ* (上陵食舉).
One piece, *Chéngyuánqì* (承元氣), was removed from the ancestral temple *shíjǔ* (食舉),
and two pieces, *Wéitiānzhīmìng* (惟天之命) and *Tiānzhīlìshù* (天之曆數), were added,
making seven pieces for the *Diànzhōng Yùshífànjǔ* (殿中御食飯舉).
There were also thirteen pieces for the Hàn (漢) Tàilè (太樂) *shíjǔ* (食舉): the first was *Lùmíng* (鹿鳴),
the second *Chónglái* (重來),
the third *Chūzào* (初造),
the fourth *Xiá'ān* (俠安),
the fifth *Guīlái* (歸來),
the sixth *Yuǎnqī* (遠期),
the seventh *Yǒusuǒsī* (有所思),
the eighth *Míngxīng* (明星),
the ninth *Qīngliáng* (清涼),
the tenth *Shèdàhǎi* (涉大海),
the eleventh *Dàzhìjiǔ* (大置酒),
the twelfth *Chéngyuánqì* (承元氣),
and the thirteenth *Hǎidàndàn* (海淡淡).
The Wèi (魏) dynasty and Jìn (晉) period scholars Xún Xù (荀勗) and Fù Xuán (傅玄) all composed lyrics for these.
During the Wèi (魏) period, the three pieces *Yuǎnqī* (遠期), *Chéngyuánqì* (承元氣), and *Hǎidàndàn* (海淡淡) were often difficult to perform smoothly,
so they were omitted.
The four pieces of Wèi (魏) elegant music were: the first, *Lùmíng* (鹿鳴),
later renamed *Yúhè* (於赫),
praising Wǔdì (武帝).
The second, *Zōuyú* (騶虞),
later renamed *Wēiwēi* (巍巍),
praising Wéndì (文帝).
The third, *Fátán* (伐檀),
later abolished.
The fourth, *Wénwáng* (文王),
later renamed *Yángyáng* (洋洋),
praising Míngdì (明帝).
*Zōuyú* (騶虞), *Fátán* (伐檀), and *Wénwáng* (文王) were all re-tuned by Zuǒ Yánnián (左延年).
At the grand assembly on New Year's Day,
the Tàiwèi (太尉) presented a jade tablet,
and the various lords performed their rites.
The performers of the elegant music in the eastern annex were the ones who created this.
Now called the 'Rites Performing Tune,'
it was performed in the *Gūxǐ Xiāng* (姑洗箱).
Based on the fact that *Lùmíng* (鹿鳴) was originally for banquets,
it was inappropriate for court offerings and sacrifices,
a mistake of previous times.
In the fifth year of Tàishǐ (泰始) of Jìn Wǔdì (晉武帝)

(269 CE), the Shàngshū (尚書) memorialized to have Tàipú (太僕) Fù Xuán (傅玄), Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監) Xún Xù (荀勗), and Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎) Zhāng Huà (張華) each compose lyrics for the New Year's Day rites and the wine *shíjǔ* (食舉) music for the dukes and nobles wishing longevity.
The emperor also ordered Zhōngshū Láng (中書郎) Chéng Gōngsuí (成公綏) to compose as well.
Zhāng Huà (張華) presented a memorial saying:
"According to the Wèi (魏) dynasty's longevity *shíjǔ* (食舉) poems and those used by the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
their verses varied in length,
and not all conformed to ancient standards.
This is probably because they followed the melody of stringed instruments,
which had established traditions,
and those who understood music and tones
were sufficient to create sounds.
The methods for measuring and composing music
were generally not something ordinary people could change.
Two dynasties and three capitals
inherited them without alteration.
Although the poems and lyrics differed,
and their rise and fall followed the times,
their rhymes and melodic twists
were all tied to the old forms,
for which there was a reason.
Therefore, I have followed them completely
and dared not make any changes."
Xún Xù (荀勗), however, said:
"The Wèi (魏) dynasty's songs and poems,
some with two characters,
some with three,
some with four,
some with five,
do not resemble ancient poetry."
He asked Sīlǜ Zhōngláng Jiàng (司律中郎將) Chén Qí (陳頎),
and Qí (頎) said:
"When set to metal bells and stone chimes,
they may not all be appropriate."
Therefore, Xù (勗) composed Jìn (晉) songs,
all in four-character verse,
except for one poem for the dukes and nobles wishing longevity, which was in three- and five-character verse.
This shows the distinct views of Huà (華) and Xù (勗).
In the ninth year (273 CE),
Xún Xù (荀勗) eventually took charge of music affairs.
He ordered Guō Qióng (郭瓊) and Sòng Shí (宋識) to create the dances *Zhèngdé* (正德) and *Dàyù* (大豫).
Xù (勗), Fù Xuán (傅玄), and Zhāng Huà (張華) also each composed lyrics for these dances.
Xù (勗) created twelve new pitch pipes (flutes).
Sànjì Chángshì Ruǎn Xián (散騎常侍阮咸) criticized the new pitch pipes for being high-pitched.
Their high pitch approached melancholy
and did not conform to moderation and harmony.
Xù (勗), because Xián (咸) differed from him,
exiled Xián (咸) to be Shǐpíng Xiàng (始平相).
The Jìn also changed the Wèi Zhāowǔ Dance to Xuānwǔ Dance,
and the Yǔyuè Dance to Xuānwén Dance.
In the first year of Xiánníng,
an edict was issued to determine the titles of ancestors,
and the temple music uniformly used the Zhèngdé and Dàyù dances.
When the ancestral temple was first established on the left bank of the Jiāng River,
the Shàngshū submitted to the Tàicháng the names of the musical pieces used for sacrifices.
Tàicháng Hè Xún replied, saying:
"The Wèi dynasty augmented and reduced Hàn music,
establishing it as the ritual music for an entire era.
It is unclear why the Jìn dynasty's music names are different.
Having suffered from chaos and loss,
old institutions no longer exist.
However, these musical pieces
are harmonized with bells and pitch-pipes,
embellished with the five notes,
chanted in lyrics,
and presented in dance formations.
The suspended chime stands are below,
the qín and sè zithers are in the hall,
the eight sounds are played in turn,
and the Yǎyuè is performed concurrently.
The ascending chants and descending wind instruments
each have their established lyrics,
which is an old custom of the Zhōu people.
Since the Hàn dynasty,
this ritual has been followed,
with only new poems created.
The old capital is desolate and ruined,
and now scattered and lost.
The musical rhythms and variations
are also unknown to anyone.
Thus, it is difficult to express it with words today."
At that time, because there were no Yǎyuè instruments or musicians,
the Tàiyuè and Gǔchuī commands were abolished.
Thereafter, some ascending chants were obtained,
but the music for sacrificial banquets
was still incomplete.
At the end of Emperor Míng's Tàiníng reign,
an edict was again issued to Ruǎn Fú and others to augment it.
In the middle of Emperor Chéng's Xiánhé reign,
the office of Tàiyuè was re-established,
gathering surviving talents,
but still lacking metal and stone instruments.
Originally,
Xún Xù, having created two dances with the new pitches,
also set about revising the bells and chime-stones.
The work was not yet complete when Xù passed away.
In the third year of Emperor Huì's Yuánkāng reign,
his son, Huángmén Shìláng Fān, was ordered to complete the revision of the metal and stone instruments,
for use in suburban and ancestral temples.
Soon after, due to chaos and strife,
the surviving sounds and old systems
were no longer remembered by anyone.
Yǔ Liàng, while serving as Jīngzhōu,
collaborated with Xiè Shàng to revise the Yǎyuè for the court.
Liàng soon passed away.
Yǔ Yì and Huán Wēn were solely occupied with military affairs,
and the musical instruments in the arsenal
eventually decayed and broke.
During the Jìn dynasty's disturbances,
all musicians were captured by the "Róng lǔ" (barbarians).
When the Hú dynasty fell,
some musicians from Yèxià
came to the Jìn.
Xiè Shàng, then Shàngshū Púyè,
used them to procure bells and chime-stones.
In the Tàiyuán reign,
Fú Jiān was defeated,
and musicians like Yáng Shǔ were captured,
who were skilled in the old music.
Thus, the four sets of metal and stone instruments were finally complete.
In the ninth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén of the Sòng,
Tàiyuè Lìng Zhōng Zōngzhī re-tuned the metal and stone instruments.
In the fourteenth year,
Zhìshū Lìshǐ Xī Zòng again revised them.
The details are in the Lǜlì Zhì.
During the Jìn era, Cáo Pí, Wáng Xún and others also augmented and created temple chants and poems.
However, music was not performed for suburban sacrifices.
Hé Chéngtiān said:
"It is commonly believed that the Wú dynasty had no Yǎyuè.
Examining Sūn Hào's reception of his father's funeral procession at Mínglíng,
it only mentions performers and entertainers ceaselessly active day and night.
Thus, it is clear there were no metal and stone instruments or ascending chants."
Chéngtiān also said:
"Some say that the 'Shénxián' of today
was used by the Sūn family for temple ascending chants."
The court historian notes that Lù Jī's elegy for Sūn Quán states:
"Sìxià in the temple,
Yúnqiáo succeeding..."
Lù Jī would not have made this statement groundlessly.
Furthermore, Wéi Zhāo's memorial on Sūn Xiū's "Shàng Gǔchuī Náogē Shíèr Qǔ" says:
"It should be handed to the music officials who are skilled in singing to practice the songs."
If so, the Wú dynasty was not without music officials,
and skilled singers were able to set lyrics to strings and wind instruments.
How could they have used only "Shénxián" for temple music?
In the seventh month of the first year of Yǒngchū of Emperor Wǔ of the Sòng,
the relevant authorities reported:
"With the establishment of the imperial dynasty,
Yǎyuè should be performed for temple sacrifices.
Tàicháng Zhèng Xiānzhī and eighty-eight others have each composed new songs.
The seven lyrics composed by Huángmén Shìláng Wáng Sháozhī
are suitable for use."
The emperor approved the edict.
In the twelfth month,
the relevant authorities again reported:
"According to old custom, music is to be performed on the first day of the New Year.
After consulting the three departments, the Tàiyuè songs and dance poems have been revised.
Huángmén Shìláng Wáng Sháozhī has established thirty-two chapters,
suitable for teaching and testing.
As the day is approaching,
it is advisable to recite and practice them in advance.
We shall provisionally enforce their implementation."
The emperor approved the edict.
The Zhèngdé Dance was also renamed Qián Dance,
and the Dàyù Dance was renamed Hòu Dance.
In the ninth month of the eighteenth year of Yuánjiā,
the relevant authorities reported:
"Ascending chants should be performed at the two suburban altars."
They also deliberated on temple dance matters.
Lù Shàngshū Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng and twelve others presented a unanimous proposal,
but before it could be formally submitted,
military affairs arose and the matter was suspended.
In the twenty-second year,
at the Southern Suburban sacrifice,
ascending chants were first performed.
An edict ordered Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Yán Yánzhī to compose song-poems,
but temple dances were still missing.
On the Jiǎwǔ day of the ninth month of the second year of Xiàojiàn,
the relevant authorities reported:
"Former Diànzhōng Cáo Láng Xún Wànqiū's proposal: According to rites,
when music is performed for sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
it is for the descent of deities.
Therefore, the Yì Jīng says: 'Thunder bursts from the earth, inspiring exuberance (yù).
The former kings used this to create music to exalt virtue,
offering it grandly to the Heavenly Emperor,
and matching it with their ancestors.'
The Zhōu Guān says: 'When music is performed atop the Round Mound,
all celestial deities descend.
When music is performed within the Square Marsh,
all terrestrial deities emerge.'
It also says: 'Then perform the Huángzhōng,
sing the Dàlǚ,
and dance the Yúnmén,
to sacrifice to the celestial deities.
Then perform the Dàcù,
sing the Yìngzhōng,
and dance the Xiánchí,
to sacrifice to the terrestrial deities.'
From this, it can be seen
that using music for sacrifices to Heaven and Earth
has a long history.
Now, music is lacking in suburban sacrifices,
which I secretly consider questionable.
The Jì Tǒng says: 'There are three important aspects to sacrifice:
among offerings, none is more important than guàn (libation);
among sounds, none is more important than shēnggē (ascending chants);
among dances, none is more important than Wǔsùyè.
This is the way of Zhōu.'
As for Qín performing the Wǔxíng,
and Wèi dancing Xiánxī,
both were used for enjoyment.
Reaching the Jìn dynasty,
in the early years of Tàishǐ,
Fù Xuán composed thirty-two pieces of Jìn suburban and temple song-poems.
In the Yuánkāng reign,
Xún Fān received an edict to complete his father Xù's work,
and the four suspended sets of metal and stone instruments
were used for suburban and temple sacrifices.
This is proof that suburban and temple sacrifices have continuously included music.
Although ascending chants are now performed for temple sacrifices,
the ceremonial dances are not yet displayed,
which I fear leaves the full ritual incomplete.
Holy kings, in governing the world,
have maintained similar customs across different eras.
Although augmentations and reductions may vary,
and degrees of ritual evolve,
they never fail to grasp the ancient to guide the present,
conforming to the same patterns and rules.
At this bright and auspicious time,
with cultural artifacts greatly complete,
no ritual or custom is left unfulfilled.
How much more so when inviting terrestrial deities and celestial spirits,
should music not be omitted from suburban sacrifices,
and when proclaiming virtue and displaying merit,
should dances not be lacking in temple offerings?
I suggest that suburban and temple sacrifices
should be equipped with music."
於是使內外博議．
驃騎大將軍竟陵王誕等五十一人並同萬秋議．
尚書左僕射建平王宏議以為：
「聖王之德雖同，
創制之禮或異，
樂不相沿，
禮無因襲．
自寶命開基，
皇符在運，
業富前王，
風通振古，
朝儀國章，
並循先代．
自後晉東遷，
日不暇給，
雖大典略備，
遺闕尚多．
至於樂號廟禮，
未該往正．
今帝德再昌，
大孝御宇，
宜討定禮本，
以昭來葉．
尋舜樂稱韶，
漢改文始，
周樂大武，
秦革五行．
眷夫祖有功而宗有德，
故漢高祖廟樂稱武德，
太宗廟樂曰昭德．
魏制武始舞武廟，
制咸熙舞文廟．
則祖宗之廟，
別有樂名．
晉氏之樂，
正德、大豫，
及宋不更名，
直為前後二舞，
依據昔代，
義舛事乖．
今宜釐改權稱，
以凱容為韶舞，
宣烈為武 舞．
祖宗廟樂，
總以德為名．
若廟非不毀，
則樂無別稱，
猶漢高、文、武，
咸有嘉號，
惠、景二主，
樂無餘名．
章皇太后廟，
依諸儒議，
唯奏文樂．
何休、杜預、范甯注『初獻六羽』 ，
並不言佾者，
佾則干在其中，
明婦人無武事也．
郊祀之樂，
無復別名，
仍同宗廟而已．
尋諸漢志，
永至等樂，
各有義況，
宜仍舊不改．
爰及東晉，
太祝唯送神而不迎神．
近議者或云廟以居神，
如在也，
不應有迎送之事，
意以為並乖其衷．
立廟居靈，
四時致享，
以申孝思之情．
夫神升降無常，
何必安所處？
故祭義云： 『樂以迎來，
哀以送往． 』
鄭注云： 『迎來而樂，
樂親之來，
送往而哀，
哀其享否不可知也． 』
尚書〔曰『祖考來格』 ．
漢書安世房中歌曰： 『神來宴娛． 』
詩云： 『三后在〕天． 』
又詩云： 『神保遹歸． 』
注曰： 『歸於天地也． 』
此並言神有去來，
則有送迎明矣．
即周肆夏之名，
備迎送之樂．
古以尸象神，
故儀禮祝有迎尸送尸，
近代雖無尸，
豈可闕迎送之禮？
又傅玄有迎神送神哥辭，
明江左不迎，
非舊典也． 」
散騎常侍、丹陽尹建城縣開國侯顏竣議以為：
「德業殊稱，
則干羽異容，
時無沿制，
故物有損益．
至於禮失道諐，
稱習忘反，
中興釐運，
視聽所革，
先代繆章，
宜見刊正．
郊之有樂，
蓋生周易、周官，
歷代著議，
莫不援准．
夫『掃地而祭，
器用陶匏』 ，
唯質與誠，
以章天德，
文物之備，
理固不然．
周官曰： 『國有故，
則旅上帝及四望． 』
又曰： 『四圭有邸，
以祀天旅上帝．
兩圭有邸，
以祀地旅四望． 』
四望非地，
則知上帝非天．
孝經云： 『郊祀后稷以配天，
宗 祀文王於明堂，
以配上帝． 』
則豫之作樂，
非郊天也．
大司樂職，
『奏黃鍾，
哥大呂，
舞雲門，
以祀天神』 ．
鄭注： 『天神，
五帝及日月星辰也． 』
王者以夏正月祀其所受命之帝於南郊，
則二至之祀，
又非天地．
考之眾經，
郊祀有樂，
未見明證．
宗廟之禮，
事炳載籍．
爰自漢元，
迄乎有晉，
雖時或更制，
大抵相因，
為不襲名號而已．
今樂曲淪滅，
知音世希，
改作之事，
臣聞其語．
正德、大豫，
禮容具存，
宜殊其徽號，
飾而用之．
以正德為宣化之舞，
大豫為興和之舞，
庶足以光表世烈，
悅被後昆．
前漢祖宗，
廟處各異，
主名既革，
舞號亦殊．
今七廟合食，
庭殿共所，
舞蹈之容，
不得廟有別制．
後漢東平王蒼已議之矣．
又王肅、韓祗以王者德廣無外，
六代四夷之舞，
金石絲竹之樂，
宜備奏宗廟．
愚謂蒼、肅、祗議，
合於典禮，
適於當今． 」
Zuǒ Púshè Jiànpíng Wáng Hóng (建平王宏) further deliberated:
“Jùn (竣) based his argument on the *Zhōu Lǐ* and *Xiàojīng*:
‘Heaven’ (天) and ‘Shàngdì’ (上帝)
appear together repeatedly in the texts.
Therefore, if one claims that Shàngdì is not Heaven,
then the *Yì*’s creation of music
was not for sacrificing to Heaven.
According to the *Yì*, it is said: ‘The Former Kings, by making music, extolled virtue,
solemnly offered sacrifices to Shàngdì,
and thus honored their ancestors.’
The *Shàngshū* says: ‘Then they performed the class sacrifice to Shàngdì.’
The *Chūnqiū Zhuàn* says: ‘They announced it to Hàotiān Shàngdì (昊天上帝).’
All mentions of Shàngdì
refer to nothing other than Heaven.
Heaven is so revered that it cannot be referred to by a single name;
thus, it is sometimes called Hàotiān (昊天),
sometimes Shàngdì,
and sometimes Hàotiān Shàngdì.
One should not, because Heaven has several names,
then assert that Shàngdì is not Heaven.
Xú Mò (徐邈) cited the *Zhōu Lǐ*’s phrase, ‘If the state has a serious matter,
then a ritual offering is made to Shàngdì,’
to show that ritual offerings to Heaven
and ritual offerings to Shàngdì
are both sacrifices to Heaven.
The phrase ‘ritual offerings to Heaven’
refers to regular sacrifices;
‘ritual offerings to Shàngdì’
refers to sacrifices made on special occasions.
The *Xiàojīng* states: ‘No reverence for one’s father is greater than honoring him by associating him with Heaven,’
and thus it says: ‘The suburban sacrifice to Hòujì (后稷) to associate him with Heaven,
and the ancestral sacrifice to Wén Wáng (文王) in the Míngtáng (明堂),
to associate him with Shàngdì.’
Since Heaven is for deliberation,
then Shàngdì being Heaven becomes even clearer.
Not wishing for the two names for Heaven to be identical in text,
they therefore varied it to Shàngdì.
The *Zhōu Lǐ* mentions sacrifices to Heaven twice;
thus Zhèng’s (鄭) commentary interpreted the former Heaven-gods as the Five Dì (五帝),
and the latter sacrifice during the winter solstice as being to Hàotiān.
Jùn further said, ‘The sacrifices at the two solstices
are also not to Heaven and Earth.’
We do not know when Heaven and Earth are eventually supposed to receive offerings.
The *Jì* says: ‘Sweeping the ground and sacrificing,
using earthenware and gourds.’
The meaning is clear that the implements used are simple,
which does not hinder the descent of spirits with music.
Wàn Qiū (萬秋) believed that suburban sacrifices should have music,
and this has canonical basis.
Jùn (竣) also said, ‘Dōngpíng Wáng Cāng (東平王蒼) believed that since the former Hàn (漢) had separate temples for various ancestors,
the ancestral temples could each have their own dance music.
As for the joint sacrifice in the temple of the progenitor,
only the progenitor’s dance was used.
Therefore, he argued that since the later Hàn (漢) ancestors
shared a temple and a courtyard,
even though there were various ancestors,
it was not appropriate to introduce separate dances.’
This is indeed one school of thought,
but it fails to encompass the changes appropriate to the times.
The Later Hàn followed frugality,
hence various ancestors shared a temple,
yet the rites of separate temples were preserved by having different chambers.
[一０]Since the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
the ‘Dēng Gē’ (登哥) has been sung in praise,
and various chambers continued to perform.
As for ancestral dance music,
why should it not be performed in turns?
If the subjects being sung about are different,
even if they share a courtyard,
there is no objection.
The three ancestors of Wèi (魏) each had their own dance music,
surely they were not in separate temples then?”
The general consensus agreed with Hóng (宏):
“For welcoming the spirits at the Southern Suburban Sacrifice,
the ‘Sì Xià’ (肆夏) is played.
When the Emperor first ascends the altar,
the ‘Dēng Gē’ is played.
For the initial offering,
the dances ‘Kǎi Róng’ (凱容) and ‘Xuān Liè’ (宣烈) are performed.
For sending off the spirits,
the ‘Sì Xià’ is played.
For welcoming the spirits at the ancestral temple sacrifice,
the ‘Sì Xià’ is played.
When the Emperor enters the temple gate,
the ‘Yǒng Zhì’ (永至) is played.
When the Emperor proceeds to the east wall,
the ‘Dēng Gē’ is played.
For the initial offering,
the dances ‘Kǎi Róng’ and ‘Xuān Liè’ are performed.
For the final offering,
the ‘Yǒng Ān’ (永安) is played.
For sending off the spirits, the ‘Sì Xià’ is played.”
An edict approved this.
In the tenth month, Xīnwèi (辛未) day, of the second year of Xiàojiàn (孝建),
the officials again memorialized:
“For the dance music at the suburban and ancestral temple sacrifices,
when the Emperor personally officiates,
upon first ascending the altar and entering the temple to proceed to the east wall,
the ‘Dēng Gē’ is to be played,
and not when the Three Gōng (三公) perform the rites.”
Zuǒ Púshè Jiànpíng Wáng Hóng (建平王宏) again participated in the discussion:
“When the Gōng (公) and Qīng (卿) perform the rites,
the ‘Dēng Gē’ should also be played.”
The officials again memorialized:
“For the Yuán Huì (元會) assembly and the fast-sacrifices at the two temples,
the ‘Dēng Gē’ will as before be performed in the palace courtyard.
Recalling the temple sacrifices,
according to the new ritual regulations,
the ‘Dēng Gē’ performers ascended the hall,
while string and wind instruments remained below;
now for the Yuán Huì,
the ‘Dēng Gē’ performers will also ascend the hall,
and string and wind instruments will remain below.”
An edict approved all of these.
Emperor Wén’s (文帝) Zhāng Tàihoù (章太后) temple did not yet have musical pieces.
During the Dàmíng (大明) era of Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武), the Shangshu Zuǒchéng (尚書左丞) Yīn Dàn (殷淡) was ordered to compose new gē (哥).
Emperor Míng (明帝) also personally composed gē shī (哥詩) for Zhāo Tàihoù (昭太后) and Xuān Tàihoù (宣太后).
On the first day of the first month of the Later Hàn (後漢),
the Son of Heaven presided at the Déyáng Diàn (德陽殿) to receive court felicitations.
A shèlì (舍利) came from the west,
playing in front of the hall,
stirring water to transform into paired fish (bǐmùyú),
leaping and spouting water,
creating mist that obscured the sun;
when finished,
it transformed again into a yellow dragon,
eight or nine *zhàng* (丈) long,
emerging from the water to play,
dazzling the sunlight.
Two large silk ropes were tied to the tops of two pillars,
several *zhàng* apart,
and two female performers danced opposite each other,
walking on the ropes,
meeting shoulder to shoulder without tipping.
From Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) up to the time of the Jìn (晉) in Jiāngzuǒ (江左),

there were still entertainments such as Xià Yù (夏育) lifting tripods, a giant elephant walking on milk, a divine turtle dancing with flapping flippers, carrying a spiritual mountain on its back, laurel trees and white snow, and drawing on the ground to form rivers.
In the seventh year of Xiánkāng of Emperor Chéng of the Jìn dynasty,
Gu Zēn, a Sànqí Shìláng, presented a memorial, stating:
“I have heard that the sage kings instituted music
to extol the ways of governance,
to nurture with benevolence and righteousness,
to guard against depravity and excess,
to be offered to the ancestral temples above,
and to instruct the common people below.
It embodies the correct sounds of the Five Phases
and harmonizes with the Eight Winds to cultivate the spirit.
With the gōng sound, it rectifies the cardinal directions and fosters righteousness;
with the jué sound, it establishes steadfastness and guides conduct;
the playing of strings, singing, bells, drums, and metal and stone instruments are all complete.
Thus, through communication with the divine and ultimate transformation,
there is the inspiration for people to dance in unison;
it changes customs and transforms traditions,
achieving the utmost harmony and joy.
The performances of later generations,
however, present spectacles outside of ritual norms.
They involve acts like inverted walking and continuous tumbling,
where heads and feet enter baskets,
causing the skin to be peeled away externally,
and the liver and heart to be crushed internally.
Even regarding the 'Luxuriant Reed' [of the *Shījīng*],
it is said, 'do not tread upon it';
how much more so for living beings,
should one not feel sorrow and compassion?
Moreover, when the peoples from the Four Seas come to court,
they observe the imperial court,
hear the sounds of refined music and odes,
and witness the order of solemn ceremonies.
But acts like treading on the heavens [with the feet]
and placing the head on the earth
reverse the proper order of the two cosmic forces (Yīn and Yáng)
and greatly harm the cardinal human relationships.
Currently, barbarian tribes face us across the river,
and external defense is urgent.
Soldiers subsist on seven shéng of grain,
forgetting themselves as they rush to face danger,
while these extravagant performances
are allotted five dǒu of grain daily.
While we are still sweeping clean the Divine Land [China]
and planning to govern the central regions,
such matters [as these performances]
should not be displayed to distant peoples.
It is fitting to instruct the Tàicháng [Court of Imperial Sacrifices]
to compile and prepare refined music.
The shāo and xiāo music, performed nine times,
will be renewed in this glorious era;
songs of merit and virtue
will be eternally recorded for future generations.
This is what the *Shījīng* refers to when it says, ‘
It brings peace to the August Heaven,
and greatly prospers their descendants.’
Miscellaneous performances that harm people
should all be abolished.
Let the virtue of frugality and simplicity be propagated,
surpassing the praises of 'Kāngzāi' [Peace and prosperity].
Once pure customs prevail,
the people will respond like grass bending in the wind.
This is what is meant.
My humble sincerity,
I hope you will deign to consider and examine.”
Thereupon, high-rope walking, purple deer performance, stilt-walking, tortoise-eating, the performance of Qí Wáng Juǎnyī, and acrobatics were abolished.
[一一]Their rations were also reduced.
Later, high-rope walking and purple deer performance were reinstated.
In the thirteenth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
Sītú Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng held a grand assembly at the Eastern Palace,
and performers were provided as before.
Féng Dà, a Zǒngzhāng Gōng, listed:
“Traditionally, fourteen types of performers are provided to the various kings,
with thirty-six dancers.”
Fù Lóng, the Tàicháng, believed:
“It is unclear where this number of people originated.
Only Dù Yù’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuàn* regarding the *yìwǔ* states that feudal lords performed with six rows of six, totaling thirty-six people,
which has always been considered incorrect.
Now, dancers are meant to regulate the eight sounds,
and only when the eight sounds are harmonious
can music be achieved.
Therefore, they must be arranged in rows of eight people.
[一二]From the Son of Heaven down to the *shì* (scholarly officials),
the reduction should be by two rows.
‘Two rows’ means
reducing the number of rows by two.
If Dù [Yù] believed that one row was also reduced by two people,
then the *shì* would be left with only four people,
which could hardly constitute music.
According to Fú Qián’s commentary on the *Zuǒzhuàn*, it says: ‘The Son of Heaven has eight rows of eight,
feudal lords have six rows of eight,
high officials have four rows of eight,
and *shì* have two rows of eight.’
This interpretation is very appropriate.
Currently, the various kings no longer perform the *yìwǔ*;
the Zǒngzhāng dancers [refer to]
the female musicians of ancient times.
Just as the imperial court has eight rows of eight,
the kings should have six rows of eight,
which is a clear and consistent principle.
Moreover, in the *Chūnqiū*,
Zhèng Bó presented Jìn Dào Gōng with two rows of eight female musicians,
and Jìn in turn bestowed one row of eight upon Wèi Jiàng.
This is proof that music was arranged in rows of eight people.
If it were as the debaters suggest,
that only the Son of Heaven had eight [rows of eight],
then Zhèng should have presented Jìn with two rows of six,
and Jìn should have bestowed one row of six upon Jiàng.
From the Son of Heaven down to the *shì*,
the cultural artifacts and institutional regulations,
with their distinctions of rank,
were all based on 'two' (i.e., multiples of two or reductions by two).
It is unprecedented for feudal lords, having already been reduced by two rows,
to then have each row further reduced by two people.
[一三]This is almost a reduction by more than half.
Not only would the eight sounds not be complete,
but it would also contradict the meaning of 'two'.
Dù [Yù]'s error is thus evident.
This is a major national affair,
and it should be thoroughly investigated and corrected.”
The matter was not implemented.
Of the birth of humankind,
no one knows its beginning.
Possessing spirit and embracing wisdom,
they are born between Heaven and Earth.
The emotions of joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness,
the nature of liking gain and disliking loss,
are learned without instruction,
and occur without knowing why they are so.
When angry, they fight;
when joyful, they sing.
Singing, indeed,
is the origin of music.
When singing is insufficient,
they then wave their hands and dance with their feet.
Thus, dancing is secondary to singing.
Singing and dancing
are how one expresses joy.
But joy without restraint
leads to excessive indulgence from which there is no return.
Therefore, the sages harmonized human nature with the five sounds
and regulated its excesses with the eight sounds,
calling it music.
Thus, it can change customs and transform traditions,
calming the mind and rectifying the body.
In ancient times, the Yǒusōng clan had two daughters
who lived on a nine-layered terrace.
The Heavenly Emperor sent a swallow at night.
The two daughters covered it with a jade basket.
Afterward, they uncovered and looked at it,
and the swallow left two eggs,
of five colors,
which flew north and did not return.
The two daughters composed a song,
which became the origin of northern music.
When Yǔ inspected the southern lands,
the daughter of Mount Tú instructed her maid to await Yǔ on the sunny side of Mount Tú.
The daughter then composed a song,
which became the origin of southern music.
Xià Hòu Kǒngjiǎ was hunting in the eastern region of Bèishān.
A great wind brought darkness.
He lost his way and entered a commoner's house.
The mistress was then breastfeeding.
Someone said,
“The King’s coming is an auspicious day,
it will surely bring great fortune.”
Another said,
“A child that cannot be surpassed [by others]
will surely bring disaster.”
The King then took the child home,
saying,
“I will consider him my son;
who would dare bring disaster upon him?”
Later, when he split kindling,
the axe broke and severed the child’s foot.
Kǒngjiǎ said,
“Alas!
There is fate.”
He then composed the song of the broken axe,
which became the origin of eastern music.
When King Zhāo of Zhōu campaigned in the south,
he perished in Hànzhōng.
The King’s right-hand man, Xīn Yúmí, was tall and strong.
He rescued the King [his body] across the northern river.
The Duke of Zhōu then enfeoffed him in Xīdí,
and he moved his residence to Xīhé.
Remembering the former place, he composed a song,
which became the origin of western music.
These are presumably the songs of the Four Directions.
In the eras of Huángdì and Dì Yáo,
the royal transforming influence spread downwards,
and the people were content and without troubles.
