Therefore, due to the joy of 'beating the earth' (jīrǎng)
and the auspiciousness of 'celebratory clouds' (qìngyún),
the people then composed songs.
Thereafter, the customs declined, the classical style was lost,
and songs of seduction and extravagance arose.
When the Zhōu dynasty declined,
there was Qín Qīng,
who was skilled in singing.
Xuē Tán learned singing from Qín Qīng,
but before he had mastered Qīng's skill, he took leave to return home.
Qīng saw him off in the suburbs,
then tapped the rhythm and sang a mournful song.
His voice shook the trees,
and its echoes stopped the moving clouds.
Xuē Tán then stayed and did not leave,
completing his studies.
There was also Hán É,
who traveled east to Qí.
Upon reaching Yōngmén,
she ran out of provisions.
She then sold her singing for food.
After she left,
her lingering echoes wrapped around the rafters,
not ceasing for three days.
Those nearby thought she had not yet left.
Passing by an inn,
the innkeeper insulted her.
Hán É then cried mournfully in a lingering voice.
The old and young of the entire village
sadly wept, facing each other,
and did not eat for three days.
They urgently pursued her,
and Hán É returned.
She again sang a long song in a lingering voice,
and the old and young of the entire village
rejoiced, clapped, and danced,
unable to restrain themselves,
forgetting their previous sorrow.
They then lavishly bribed her and sent her away.
Thus, the people of Yōngmén were skilled in singing and crying,
imitating Hán É's lingering sounds.
Wáng Bào of Wèi lived in Qíchuān
and was skilled in singing.
The people west of the Yellow River were all influenced by him.
Mián Jū of Qí resided in Gāotáng
and was skilled in singing.
The western region of Qí
also passed on his art.
In the Former Hàn dynasty, there was Yú Gōng,
who was skilled in singing,
able to make dust rise from the rafters.
Things of this kind
were all unaccompanied songs.
The Éryǎ states:
"Unaccompanied songs are called yáo (ballads)."
Among ancient musical compositions and lyrics,
those that survive today
are all street ballads and songs from the Hàn era,
such as "Jiāngnán Kě Cǎilián," "Wū Shēng," "Shíwǔ," and "Báitóu Yín."
〔一四〕 Wú songs and various tunes
all originated in Jiāngdōng.
Since the Jìn and Sòng dynasties,
they have gradually increased and expanded.
As for "Zǐyè Gē,"
there was a woman named Zǐyè
who created this tune.
During the Tàiyuán reign of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn,
there was a ghost singing "Zǐyè" in the household of Wáng Kē of Lángyá.
When Yīn Yǔn was in Yùzhāng,
there was also a ghost singing "Zǐyè" in the household of Gǒng Sēngdù, an émigré in Yùzhāng.
〔一五〕 Yīn Yǔn's time in Yùzhāng
was also during the Tàiyuán reign.
Therefore, Zǐyè must have been a person from before this time.
As for "Fèng Jiāng Chú Gē,"
it is an old tune.
Yīng Qú's "Bǎiyī Shī" states:
"Composing 'Mòshàng Sāng'
but instead speaking of 'Fèng Jiāng Chú.'"
If so, then "Fèng Jiāng Chú" has a long history.
Could it be that it has degenerated and changed to reach this form?
"Qián Xī Gē"
was composed by Shěn Chōng, Commander of Cavalry of Jìn.
〔一六〕
As for "Āzǐ Jí Huān Wén Gē,"
in the early Shēngpíng reign of Emperor Mù of Jìn,
after singing, one would always call out,
"Āzǐ!
Did you hear?"
This is recorded in the "Wǔxíng Zhì."
〔一七〕 Later generations adapted its sound
to create two pieces.
As for "Tuánshàn Gē,"
Wáng Mín, Minister of the Central Secretariat of Jìn, had feelings for his sister-in-law's maid,
and loved her deeply.
His sister-in-law beat the maid too severely.
The maid was skilled in singing,
and Wáng Mín liked to hold a white round fan.
Therefore, this song was composed.
As for "Dūhù Gē,"
Xú Kuízhī, Administrator of Péngchéng, was killed by Lǔ Guǐ.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Sòng ordered Dīng Wǔ, Administrator of the Palace Guard, to collect and bury him.
Xú Kuízhī's wife,
who was Emperor Gāozǔ's eldest daughter,
called Dīng Wǔ to her chamber.
She personally inquired about the collection and burial matters.
Each time she asked,
she sighed and said,
"Dīng Dūhù!"
Her voice was mournful and poignant.
Later generations, based on her voice,
expanded the tune.
As for "Ào Gē,"
in the early Lóng'ān reign of Jìn,
it was a popular ballad among the people.
It is recorded in the "Wǔxíng Zhì."
Emperor Shǎodì of Sòng composed a new song,
which Emperor Tàizǔ often referred to as "Zhōngcháo Qǔ."
The "Liùbiàn" and other tunes
were all composed based on specific events.
"Chángshǐ Biàn"
was composed by Wáng Yìxūn, Left Chief Clerk of the Minister over the Masses, on the verge of his defeat.
"Dúqǔ Gē"
was composed by the common people for Wáng Yìkāng of Péngchéng.
Its lyrics say:
"Death to Liú Lǐngjūn,
who mistakenly killed Liú the Fourth."
This is it.
All these tunes
were initially unaccompanied songs,
but were later set to strings and winds.
There were also instances where songs were created to be set to strings, winds, bronze, and stone instruments,
such as the "Sāndiào Gēcí" of the Wèi era.
In ancient times, when the Son of Heaven governed,
he ordered the dukes, ministers, and grand masters to present poems,
which were then refined by the elders,
and only then did the king deliberate upon them.
The Qín and Hàn dynasties lacked officials for collecting poems.
Songs and odes mostly borrowed from previous eras,
which were not in harmony with contemporary events,
and thus could not be passed down to later generations.
Although Emperor Wǔ of Hàn did compose some new songs,
he did not prioritize glorifying his ancestors or advocating proper virtue,
but mostly sang about sacrifices, current events, and their auspicious omens.
The poetic forms of the Shāng and Zhōu "Yǎ" and "Sòng" were missing.
The "Pí Wǔ" (shield dance)
its origin is not clearly known, but
it was already performed at banquets in the Hàn dynasty.
The rhapsodies of Fù Yì and Zhāng Héng
all relate to this.
Cáo Zhí's preface to the "Pí Wǔ Gē" states:
"In the old custom of Emperor Líng of Hàn's Xīyuán,
〔一八〕 there was Lǐ Jiān,
who was skilled in the pí wǔ.
Due to the chaos,
he followed Duàn Wēi west.
The late Emperor heard of his old skill
and summoned him.
Lǐ Jiān had already fallen into disuse,
and many ancient tunes had errors.
Texts from different eras
may not necessarily be passed down.
Therefore, I have adapted the old tunes to compose five new songs,
not daring to offer them to the Imperial Secretariat,
but merely to complete the humble music of a lesser state."
The Jìn "Pí Wǔ Gē" also had five pieces,
plus one "Duó Wǔ Gē" (bell dance song),
one "Fān Wǔ Gē" (banner dance song),
and six "Gǔ Wǔ Jì" (drum dance pieces),
all presented at the New Year's grand assembly.
Today, the lyrics for "Fān" and "Gǔ" songs still exist,
but the dances are all missing.
The pí wǔ
is today's píshàn wǔ (shield-fan dance).
It is also said that in early Jìn, there were "Bēipán Wǔ" (cup-tray dance) and "Gōngmò Wǔ" (do-not-be-too-modest dance).
The historian observes: Bēipán
is today's Jìn Shìníng.
〔一九〕 Zhāng Héng's "Wǔ Fù" states:
"Stepping across seven trays."
Wáng Càn's "Qī Shì" states:
"Seven trays arranged in the wide courtyard."
The contemporary scholar Yán Yánzhī said:
"Alternately crossing between trays and fans."
Bào Zhāo said:
"Seven trays rise with long sleeves."
All consider the "seven trays" to be a dance.
The "Sōushén Jì" states:
"In the Tàikāng reign of Jìn,
the world performed the Jìn Shìníng dance,
using their hands to grasp and turn over cups and trays."
This indicates that in the Hàn era, there was only the "pán wǔ" (tray dance), but Jìn added cups to it and turned them over.
Gōngmò Wǔ (公莫舞),
is the khăn-dance of today.
Tradition says that when Xiàng Zhuāng (項莊) was performing a sword dance,
Xiàng Bó (項伯) used his sleeve to block him,
preventing him from harming Hàn Gāozǔ (漢高祖).
And he said to Zhuāng (莊),
"Gōng Mò (公莫)."
Ancient people called each other
"Gōng" (公),
meaning "Do not harm the King of Hàn (漢)."
The use of a khăn today
is probably an imitation of Xiàng Bó's (項伯) sleeve.
According to the Qín Cāo (琴操), there is a song "Gōng Mò Dù Hé Qǔ (公莫渡河曲),"
so its origin must be ancient.
The popular saying that it refers to Xiàng Bó (項伯)
is incorrect.
In the early period of the Jiāngzuǒ (江左),
there was also the Fú Wǔ (拂舞).
It was formerly called Fú Wǔ (拂舞),
or Wú Wǔ (吳舞).
Examining its songs,
they are not Wú (吳) lyrics.
All were performed in the palace courtyard.
Yáng Hóng (揚泓) in his "Fú Wǔ Xù" (拂舞序) said:
"Since arriving in Jiāngnán (江南),
I have seen the Báifú Wǔ (白符舞),
or some say Báijiū Wǔ (白鳩舞),
which is said to have existed for several decades.
Upon examining its words and meaning,
it is indeed about the people of Wú (吳) suffering from Sūn Hào's (孫晧) tyrannical rule,
and longing to belong to Jìn (晉)."
There was also the Báizhù Wǔ (白紵舞).
According to the dance lyrics, there is mention of khăn-robes;
since zhù (紵) (ramie) originally came from the Wú (吳) region,
it should be a Wú Wǔ (吳舞).
The Jìn Páigē (晉俳歌) also says:
"Gleaming white xu (緒) (thread),
each knot a pair."
The Wú (吳) pronunciation for xù (緒) is zhù (紵),
so it is suspected that Báizhù (白紵) is Báixù (白緒).
The Běi Wǔ (鞞舞) traditionally had two eights (sixteen performers).
When Huán Xuán (桓玄) was about to assume the imperial throne,
the Tàilè (太樂) dispatched all its performers.
Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng (尚書殿中郎) Yuán Míngzǐ (袁明子) petitioned to increase it to a full bāyì (八佾) (sixty-four performers),
and this was subsequently maintained without change.
Sòng Míngdì (宋明帝) personally revised the dance music and lyrics,
and also ordered his close minister Yú Hé (虞龢) to compose some.
There were also various dances from Xī (西), Cāng (傖), Qiāng (羌), and Hú (胡).
Suí Wáng Dàn (隨王誕) created the Xiāngyáng Yuè (襄陽樂) while in Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Nánpíng Mùwáng (南平穆王) created the Shòuyáng Yuè (壽陽樂) while serving as Yùzhōu (豫州).
Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史) Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) also created the Xīwū Fēigē Qǔ (西烏飛哥曲).
All were included in the music bureau.
Many of the song lyrics were licentious, coarse, and not proper.
In former generations, at joyful drinking parties,
when drunk,
people would surely get up and dance by themselves.
The poem says,
"repeatedly dancing xiānxiān (僊僊),"
which
is this.
It is customary to dance at banquets,
but it is not appropriate to do so too often.
The criticism is for dancing too often,
not for dancing itself.
When Hàn Wǔdì (漢武帝) was enjoying wine,
Chángshā Dìngwáng (長沙定王) danced, which is also an example of this.
Since Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) times,
it has been especially common to offer a dance to others,
whereupon the one to whom it is offered would then rise and dance,
much like offering wine cups to each other.
Xiè Ān (謝安) dancing to offer to Huán Sì (桓嗣) is an example of this.
In recent times,
this custom has ceased.
During the Dàmíng reign of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
the bì, fú, and various dances were combined with zhong and shi [bells and lithophones],
and performed in the palace courtyard.
In the second year of Shēngmíng of Emperor Shùn,
Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Sēngqián submitted a memorial discussing this,
and also discoursed on the three modes of gē, saying:
“Your servant has heard that the creation of fēng and yǎ [odes]
dates back a long time.
The greater ones are linked to rise and fall;
the lesser ones are manifest in ritual dances.
Residing in the heart, wood and stone are moved;
when the harmonious sounds play, national customs change.
Thus, when the Prime Minister of Zhèng went out into the suburbs,
he discerned sorrow from the sounds;
when Yánlíng entered to offer tribute,
he understood the customs from the music.
This shows that sounds are not idly initiated,
and melodies are not merely played.
Once gē and chàng are established,
joy and sorrow are already manifested;
when clear and turbid are balanced,
the mountain zither naturally responds.
This is the spiritual harmony of heaven and earth,
the clear rhythm of ascent and descent.
Now, the imperial dao extends in all four directions,
and ritual and music are interconnected;
this is truly not something that an ignorant and narrow-minded person dares to adjust.
I humbly reflect that in the three ancient eras, information was lacking;
for six generations, echoes lay dormant;
dance and song vanished with the sun and moon,
and their essence perished with wind and clouds.
To reflect on the remaining melodies with long-held emotions,
and sigh over the lost instruments—
this is indeed so.
The suspended bells and chimes [zhōng xuán zhī qì]
use yǎ as their function;
the system of kǎi róng [processional music]
takes the eight-row dance as its form.
Therefore, the yǔ and yuè [flutes and feathered staffs] strike and clap
to achieve harmony.
The blame incurred by Jì Shì
would lie in this.
Now, the former eight-row dances of Zǒngzhāng, of the two-eight type,
have different robes [guī fú]
and different melodies [qū lǜ].
Comparing the present with the past,
it is clearly discernible.
Furthermore, gē zhōng yī sì [a set of gē zhōng bells]
harmonizes with female musicians [nǚ yuè].
Being called gē,
it is not an yǎ instrument.
During the Dàmíng reign,
court bells [gōng xuán] were combined with bì and fú.
Although the number of beats [jié shù] coincided,
it was feared that it violated the yǎ form.
Future connoisseurs [zhī yīn]
might criticize the sagely era.
If it is said that the bell dances are already harmonious
and should not be abolished,
then a separate set of gē zhōng should be established
to accompany the yǔ yǐ [feathered dances],
limited to separate banquets [bié yàn],
not related to court ceremonies [cháo xiǎng].
The music played by the four sets of bells [sì xuán]
should strictly follow the yǎ rules.
In this way, the old music and former precedents
will not fall to the ground.
Your servant previously made gē qìng [chimes],
which are still with the music officials.
If they are fully used as supplementary bells [fù zhōng],
to form a complete set,
then the meaning follows the principle,
and it might be acceptable.
Moreover, the Qīngshāng music of today
actually originated from Tóngquè.
[二○]The three ancestors of the Wèi dynasty
had admirable style.
Jīng and Luò competed in their appreciation,
and it was even more highly valued in Jiāngzuǒ.
It is truly a pity that the use of jin xuán and gān qì [bells and shields/axes]
has ceased in this regard.
However, with changes in sentiment and listening habits,
it gradually declined,
and within a dozen years,
nearly half of it was lost.
Recently, families compete in new wa [songs],
and people favor popular tunes [yáo sú],
focusing on shrill and dangerous sounds,
disregarding rules and regulations.
They drift without limits,
not knowing where it will end,
rejecting classical uprightness,
and promoting chaotic and excessive styles.
Officials have ranks,
and without reason, rituals cannot be abandoned;
music has its order,
and old and young cannot share listening.
Therefore, vulgar and ugly creations
are increasingly prevalent in the markets,
while the charm of refined taste
is found only among the elite.
When rivers quake and altars fall,
it is a warning of similar disasters;
[二一]when sorrow spreads unchecked,
different generations rejoice equally.
The ominous signs are not different,
yet joy and fear are used simultaneously.
This is what I have not yet understood.
Currently, the dust has settled in the capital region,
and waves are calm overseas.
Yǎ and sòng have found their place,
truly at this moment.
Your servant believes that the officials in charge should be instructed
to diligently teach and practice,
to restore the old sounds,
and enlighten each other.
All that has been lost
should be fully recovered.
Those who fully complete a melody should be generously rewarded,
and those skilled in art should be given superior positions.
If motivated by profit,
people will encourage themselves;
if influenced by custom,
they can be reformed without instruction.
Returning to the origin,
we may then hope to reach it.”
The imperial edict said:
“Sēngqián’s memorial is thus.
When bells and drums are displayed,
yǎ and sòng are distinguished.
This is how people and spirits are delighted and moved,
and flying and swimming creatures are influenced.
Recently, since the sounds of the jin yuè [metal flutes] have slackened,
and the yǔ yǐ [feathered dances] have not solidified,
correcting customs and changing trends
truly lies in this day.
In the past, Ruǎn Xián had pure discernment,
and Wáng Dù displayed extraordinary talent.
The musical tradition was reformed and improved,
achieving the same merit across different eras.
This may be handed over to external officials for thorough deliberation.”
There are generally eight musical instruments: called jīn [metal],
shí [stone],
tǔ [earth],
gé [leather],
sī [silk],
mù [wood],
páo [gourd],
zhú [bamboo].
Among the eight sounds, the first is jīn.
Jīn refers to
zhōng [bells], bó [large bells],
chún [bronze drum], zhuó [small bells/gongs],
náo [cymbals], duó [large bells with clappers].
Zhong refers to
bells.
The Shìběn says:
“It was created by the artisan Chuí for the Yellow Emperor.”
The Erya says that a large bell is called yǒng.
The Shū [Classic of History] says
“shēng and yǒng in alternation,”
which is this.
Medium-sized ones are called piāo.
Piāo is pronounced like piáo.
Small ones are called zhàn.
Zhàn is pronounced like zhǎn,
and this refers to the zhàn zhōng first acquired by Jìn Jiāngzuǒ.
The stands for suspending bells and chimes are called sǔnjù.
The horizontal beam is sǔn,
and the vertical post is jù.
Cài Yōng said:
“Sculpting the shapes of birds and beasts,
those with loud and powerful sounds are made into zhōngjù [bell stands],
and those with clear and weak sounds are made into qìngjù [chime stands].
When striking what is suspended from them,
it is known that the sound comes from their jù.”
Bó are like zhōng but larger.
The Historian notes:
Previous dynasties had large bells,
such as the Wúshè of Zhōu,
and more than one.
All were called zhōng;
the term bó
has not been heard in recent times.
Chún refers to
chúnyú.
It is circular like a pestle head,
larger at the top and smaller at the bottom.
Even today, this instrument is still occasionally found among the common people.
The Zhōu Lǐ says,
“to harmonize drums with a jīn chún.”
Zhuó refers to
zhēng.
Its shape is like a small bell.
It is sounded during military marches
to mark the drum beats.
The Zhōu Lǐ says,
“to regulate drums with a jīn zhuó.”
The náo
is like a bell but without a clapper.
It has a handle.
One holds it and strikes it to make sound.
The Zhōu Lǐ states,
“Use a metal náo to stop the drum.”
Hàn drum and wind music refers to it as náo gē.
The duó
is a large bell.
The Zhōu Lǐ states,
“Use a metal duó to announce the drum.”
The second of the eight sounds is stone.
Stone
refers to the qìng.
The Shì Běn says Shú (叔) created it,
but it is unknown which era Shú (叔) belonged to.
The Ér Yǎ states:
“Its shape resembles a plow handle,
and it is made of jade.”
The large one is called huāng.
Huāng (毊) is pronounced xiāo.
The third of the eight sounds is earth.
Earth
refers to the xūn.
The Shì Běn states
that Bào Xīn Gōng (暴新公) created it,
[二二] but it is also unknown which era he belonged to.
There was a state of Bào within the royal domain of Zhōu.
Could he have been a person from that time?
It is made of fired earth,
as large as a goose egg,
pointed at the top and flat at the bottom,
shaped like a steelyard weight,
with six holes.
The Ér Yǎ says,
“The larger one is called yáo,
[⿰土郎] etc.”
“The smaller one is like a chicken egg.”
The fourth of the eight sounds is leather.
Leather
refers to the gǔ,
the táo,
and the jié.
The large one is called gǔ,
the small one is called chèn.
It is also called yìng.
Yìng Shào’s (應劭) Fēng Sú Tōng states:
“It is unknown who created it.”
When struck with a drumstick, it is called a gǔ;
when shaken by hand, it is called a táo.
Gǔ and táo with eight faces are called léi gǔ and léi táo.
Those with six faces are called líng gǔ and líng táo.
Those with four faces are called lù gǔ and lù táo.
The Zhōu Lǐ states:
“Use the léi gǔ to worship the heavenly spirits,
[二三] use the líng gǔ to beat for the she (社) sacrifice,
and use the lù gǔ to beat for offerings to ghosts.”
A gǔ eight chi long is a fén gǔ,
used to beat for military affairs.
One twelve chi long is called a gāo gǔ,
which is beaten for all defense and labor tasks.
In the present age, it is called xià gāo.
Gāo (鼜),
in the Zhōu Lǐ, is pronounced qī,
but in the present age, it is pronounced as the sound of “qiè chǐ fǎn.”
One six chi six cùn long is called a jìn gǔ,
which is beaten when playing metal instruments.
The yìng gǔ is placed beside the large gǔ.
The Shī Jīng says,
“The yìng chèn hangs with the gǔ,”
which refers to this.
[二四] A small gǔ with a handle is called a táo.
A large táo is called a pí.
The Yuè Lìng says,
“In midsummer, repair the táo and pí,”
which refers to this.
Thus, the táo and pí are types of táo.
There is also the tuó gǔ.
The jié,
it is unknown who created it.
Fù Xuán’s (傅玄) Jié Fù states:
“The huáng zhōng sings,
the Jiǔ Sháo (九韶) excites the dance.
The mouth does not sing without the jié,
the hand does not clap without the jié.”
From this, its origin is also distant.
The fifth of the eight sounds is silk.
Silk
refers to the qín and sè,
the zhú,
the zhēng,
and the pí pá and kōng hóu.
Qín,
Mǎ Róng’s (馬融) Dí Fù states:
“Fú Xī (宓羲) created the qín.”
The Shì Běn states:
“Shén Nóng (神農) created it.”
The Ér Yǎ says,
“A large qín is called a lí,”
with twenty strings.
This instrument no longer exists.
Qí Huán (齊桓) had the Hào Zhōng (號鍾),
Chǔ Zhuāng (楚莊) had the Rào Liáng (繞梁),
Xiāng Rú (相如) had the Jiāo Wěi (燋尾),
Bó Jiē (伯喈) had the Lǜ Qǐ (綠綺).
These stories are from Fù Xuán’s (傅玄) Qín Fù.
The world says the Jiāo Wěi (燋尾) was Bó Jiē’s (伯喈) qín,
and Bó Jiē’s (伯喈) biography also says so.
According to Fù (傅) family’s words,
then it was not Bó Jiē’s (伯喈).
Sè,
Mǎ Róng’s (馬融) Dí Fù states:
“Shén Nóng (神農) created the sè.”
The Shì Běn,
“Fú Xī (宓羲) created it.”
The Ér Yǎ says:
“A sè with twenty-seven strings is called a sǎ.”
This instrument no longer exists.
Zhú,
it is unknown who created it.
Historical records only say Gāo Jiàn Lí (高漸離) was skilled at playing the zhú.
Zhēng,
the sound of Qín.
Fù Xuán’s (傅玄) Zhēng Fù Xù states:
“The world believes Méng Tián (蒙恬) created it.
But looking at its form today, it conforms to proper standards,
and its divisions thoroughly express joy and sorrow.
It is truly an instrument of benevolence and wisdom.
How could it be something conceived by a minister of a doomed state?”
The Fēng Sú Tōng, however, says:
“A zhú body with sè strings.”
It is unknown who modified it.
Pí pá,
Fù Xuán’s (傅玄) Pí Pá Fù states:
“The Hàn sent the Wū Sūn (烏孫) princess to marry the Kūnmí (昆彌).
Thinking of her longing during the journey,
they had artisans cut a zhēng and zhú
to create music for horseback.
Wishing to follow the local custom,
they named it pí pá,
to make it easy to spread abroad.”
The Fēng Sú Tōng says:
“One plays it with the hand, ‘pí pá,’
hence the name.”
Dù Zhì (杜摯) says:
“During the construction of the Great Wall,
they strung a táo and beat it.”
It is not clear which account is true.
This instrument is not among the four sections.
Kōng Hóu,
originally named Kǎn Hóu.
When Hàn Wǔ Dì (漢武帝) suppressed and extinguished Nán Yuè (南越),
he used music for sacrifices to Tài Yī (太一) and Hòu Tǔ (后土).
He ordered musician Hóu Huī (侯暉) to create the Kǎn Hóu (坎侯) based on the qín,
meaning its “kǎn kǎn” sound responded to the rhythm.
The “Hóu” (侯) part
was due to the artisan’s surname.
Later, it was called “kōng” (空),
a phonetic error.
In ancient times, it was used for courtly music in suburban temples;
in recent times, it has been exclusively used for Chǔ (楚) music.
In the Dà Míng (大明) era of Sòng Xiào Wǔ Dì (宋孝武帝),
Shěn Huái Yuǎn (沈懷遠) of Wú Xīng (吳興) was exiled to Guǎng Zhōu (廣州).
He created the Rào Liáng (繞梁),
an instrument similar to the kōng hóu.
After Huái Yuǎn (懷遠) died,
the instrument also disappeared.
The sixth of the eight sounds is wood.
Wood
refers to the zhù
and the yù.
It is unknown who created either.
The Yuè Jì says:
“The sages made the qiāng, jié, xūn, and chí.”
Their origins are also ancient.
The zhù is like a lacquered tube,
two chi four cùn square,
and one chi eight cùn deep.
Inside is a pestle handle,
which is pushed down to the bottom.
Nowadays, it is struck from side to side.
The yù
resembles a crouching tiger,
[二五] with twenty-seven jagged teeth on its back.
A bamboo stick one chi long, called a zhēn,
[二六] is drawn across it horizontally
to mark the end of the music.
The seventh of the eight sounds is gourd.
Gourd
refers to the shēng
and the yú.
The Shēng (笙):
Its inventor,
and the era in which they lived, are unknown.
Tubes are arranged inside a gourd,
with reeds attached to the end of the tubes.
The gōng tube is in the center.
An instrument with thirty-six reeds is called a Yú (竽),
with the gōng tube on the left side.
An instrument with nineteen to thirteen reeds is called a Shēng (笙).
Other aspects are all similar.
The Yú (竽) is now lost.
"A large Shēng (笙) is called Cháo (巢),
a small one is called Hé (和)."
The reeds within the Shēng (笙)
were invented by Nǚwā (女媧).
The Commentary on the Odes says:
"When the Shēng (笙) is blown, the reeds vibrate."
This refers to the reeds within the Shēng (笙).
The Éryǎ (爾雅) says:
"A Shēng (笙) with nineteen reeds is called Cháo (巢)."
During the reign of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn (漢章帝),
Xī Jǐng (奚景), a scholar from Línglíng (零陵), obtained a Shēng (笙) at Shùn's (舜) temple.
It had white jade tubes.
Did later generations replace them with bamboo?
Among the Eight Sounds, the eighth is bamboo.
Bamboo refers to the
Lǜ (律),
Lǚ (呂),
Xiāo (簫),
Guǎn (管),
Chí (篪),
Yuè (籥),
and Dí (笛).
The Lǜ (律) and Lǚ (呂) are discussed in the Lǜlì Zhì (律曆志).
〔二七〕
The Xiāo (簫),
according to the Shìběn (世本),
"was invented by Shùn (舜)."
The Éryǎ (爾雅) says:
"Twenty-three tubes arranged,
one chi and four cun long, are called Bá (跋);
〔二八〕sixteen tubes arranged, one chi and two cun long, are called Jiǎo (筊)."
Jiǎo (筊) is pronounced like Yáo (爻).
Any Xiāo (簫) is also called Lài (籟).
In earlier generations, there was the Dòngxiāo (洞簫);
this instrument is now lost.
Cài Yōng (蔡邕) said:
"The Xiāo (簫) is made of plaited bamboo and has a bottom."
Therefore, during Yōng's (邕) time, the Dòngxiāo (洞簫) no longer existed.
The Guǎn (管),
the Éryǎ (爾雅) says:
"One chi long,
one cun in circumference,
lacquered throughout,
and has a bottom."
A large one is called Qiáo (簥).
Qiáo (簥) is pronounced like Jiāo (驕).
A medium one is called Fēng (篞).
A small one is called Miào (篎).
Miào (篎) is pronounced like Miào (妙).
In ancient times, jade was used for Guǎn (管);
this refers to when Xīwángmǔ (西王母) presented a white jade Guǎn (管) during Shùn's (舜) time.
The Yuèlìng (月令) states:
"Harmonize the qín, sè, Guǎn (管), and Xiāo (簫)."
Cài Yōng's (蔡邕) Zhāngjù (章句) says:
"The Guǎn (管)
is one chi long,
one cun in circumference,
has holes, but no bottom."
This instrument is now lost.
The Chí (篪),
the Shìběn (世本) says:
"was invented by Bào Xīngōng (暴新公)."
〔二九〕The Old Records say
it is also called Guǎn (管).
The court historian commented: This is incorrect.
Although the era of Bào Xīngōng (暴新公) is unknown,
it is clear he was not a predecessor of Shùn (舜).
During Shùn's (舜) time, Xīwángmǔ (西王母) presented a Guǎn (管),
meaning the instrument already existed.
How could Xīngōng (新公) then invent the Chí (篪)?
The Éryǎ (爾雅) says:
"A large Chí (篪)
is one chi and four cun long,
three cun in circumference,
and is called Yí (沂)."
Yí (沂) is pronounced like Yín (銀).
It is also called Qiáo (翹).
"A small one is one chi and two cun long."
Currently, there is the Húchí (胡篪),
which originates from Hu music,
and is not a refined instrument.
The Yuè (籥),
its inventor is unknown.
The Zhōulǐ (周禮) mentions a Yuèshī (籥師),
who was in charge of teaching the sons of nobles to play the Yuè (籥) in autumn and winter.
This is the feathered Yuè (籥) held in today's Kǎiróng (凱容) and Xuānliè (宣烈) dances.
This is what the Odes refer to as:
"In the left hand, they hold the Yuè (籥);
in the right hand, they grasp a pheasant feather."
The Éryǎ (爾雅) says:
"The Yuè (籥) is like a Dí (笛),
with three holes and short."
The Guǎngyǎ (廣雅) says
it has seven holes.
A large one is called Chǎn (產).
A medium one is called Zhòng (仲).
A small one is called Wò (箹).
Wò (箹) is pronounced like Wò (握).
The Dí (笛),
according to Mǎ Róng's (馬融) Fù on the Chángdí (長笛賦),
originated in recent times,
coming from the Qiāng (羌) region.
Jīng Fáng (京房) perfected its five notes.
It also states that Qiū Zhòng (丘仲) was skilled in its making,
but does not say Zhòng (仲) invented it.
However, the Fēngsú Tōng (風俗通) says:
"Qiū Zhòng (丘仲) invented the Dí (笛).
He lived during the reign of Emperor Wǔ (武帝)."
Later, there was also the Qiāngdí (羌笛).
These three accounts differ,
and it is unclear which is true.
The Gē (鞨),
Dù Zhì's (杜摯) Fù on the Jiā (笳賦) says:
"was invented by Lǐ Bóyáng (李伯陽) when he entered the Western Róng (西戎) territory."
The Old Hàn (漢) Commentary says:
"The Gū (箛)
is called 'blowing whip'."
The Jìn (晉) Commentary on the Ritual of First Silkworm Cultivation states:
a small Gū (箛) is blown;
when it departs,
a large Gū (箛) is blown."
The Gū (箛) is identical to the Gē (鞨).
There is also the Hújiā (胡笳).
The Old Hàn (漢) Record of Zither and Flute Music contains its melodies,
but does not record its origins.
The Gǔchuī,
is perhaps the Duǎnxiāo Náogē.
Cài Yōng said:
"It is military music,
composed by the Huángdì and Qíbó,
to extol virtue and build martial might,
encouraging soldiers and intimidating enemies."
The Zhōu Guān states:
"When the army achieves merit, there is victory music (kǎiyuè)."
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says that when Jìn Wéngōng defeated Chǔ,
"the army was arrayed,
and entered victoriously."
The Sīmǎ Fǎ states:
"When triumphant, there is victorious music (kǎiyuè) and victorious songs (kǎigē)."
Yōngmén Zhōu, in persuading Mèngcháng Jūn, said,
"Gǔchuī in an unfathomable abyss."
Commentators say that
the drum (gǔ) is one instrument,
while the wind (chuī) comes from instruments like the yú and lài,
not a joint performance of xiāo and drum;
it is a separate name for a type of music.
Therefore, the Duǎnxiāo Náogē
was not yet called Gǔchuī at this time.
Yìng Shào's Hàn Lǔbù Tú
only depicts cavalry holding gū.
The gū is the jiā,
and it does not mention Gǔchuī.
Yet in the Hàn era, there was the Huángmén Gǔchuī.
The thirteen pieces of court music (Xiǎngyàn Shíjǔ Yuè) for Hàn banquets
were the same as the Wèi era Gǔchuī Chángxiāo.
For Chángxiāo and Duǎnxiāo,
the records of performers all state that
strings and winds perform together,
and those holding clappers sing.
The Jiànchū Lù also states that
Wùchéng, Huángjué, Xuányún, and Yuǎnqī
were all cavalry wind music (qíchuī qǔ),
not Gǔchuī music (gǔchuī qǔ).
This means that what was performed in the palace hall was Gǔchuī,
while today's marching Gǔchuī is Qíchuī;
the two types of music are different.
Also, when Sūn Quán observed the Wèi Wǔ army,
they performed Gǔchuī upon their return;
this should also be today's Gǔchuī.
In the Wèi and Jìn eras,
various generals and commanders were also granted Yámén Qǔgài Gǔchuī;
this indicates that at that time, it was called Gǔchuī.
In the Wèi and Jìn eras, the granting of Gǔchuī was very lenient;
Yámén Dūjiāng and Wǔxiào
all had Gǔchuī.
At the beginning of the Eastern Jìn (Jìn Jiāngzuǒ),
the Administrator of Línchuān, Xiè Chī, whenever he slept,
would dream of hearing Gǔchuī.
Someone interpreted the dream for him, saying:
"You will not obtain Gǔchuī in life,
but you will certainly obtain Gǔchuī in death."
Chī was killed in battle while attacking Dù Tāo,
and was posthumously granted the title of Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi,
and his funeral was provided with Gǔchuī.
When Xiè Shàng was the Administrator of Jiāngxià,
he went to see General of the Pacified West (Ānxī Jiāngjūn) Yǔ Yì in Wǔchāng to discuss matters.
Yì shot arrows with Shàng,
and said:
"If you hit the bullseye,
I shall reward you with Gǔchuī."
Shàng hit the bullseye,
and Yì immediately gave him his secondary Gǔchuī ensemble.
Nowadays, however, it is held in high regard.
The jué
is not recorded in documents.
Some say it originated from the Qiāng Hú
to startle Chinese (Zhōngguó) horses.
Others say it came from Wú Yuè.
Old records say:
"Ancient music included the lài and fǒu."
Now, neither exists.
The court historian notes: The Ěryǎ states,
lài is simply another name for the xiāo.
The Shī says:
"Its fǒu is struck with a 'kǎn, kǎn'."
Máo Zhuàn comments:
"An earthenware jar (àng) is called a fǒu."
The custom of ramming earth for city walls with accompanying pestles
originated with Liáng Xiàowáng.
When the King built Suīyáng city,
which was twelve lǐ square,
he created accompanying songs.
He used a small drum to mark the rhythm,
and the builders lowered their pestles in harmony with it.
Later generations called this music the Suīyáng Qǔ,
and it is still passed down today.
In the Wèi and Jìn eras,
there was a Mr. Sūn (Sūn Shì) skilled in extending old melodies,
Sòng Shí skilled in beating rhythm and leading harmonies,
Chén Zuǒ skilled in clear singing,
Liè Hé skilled in playing the flute,
Hǎo Suǒ skilled in playing the zheng,
and Zhū Shēng skilled in the pípá,
especially in inventing new sounds.
Fù Xuán wrote in his book:
If people admire what they hear but ignore what they see,
is this not perplexing!
If these six individuals had been born in antiquity,
they would have surpassed all from past to present without peer;
how could Kuí and Yá alone be their equals!"
According to this statement,
then from this time onwards,
all were following the precedents left by Sūn, Zhū, and others.

How grand were the august ancestors,
who brought peace to our grandchildren.
Their grace extended to future generations,
bestowing abundant blessings.
Right: The ascending song for the祠征西將軍 (Cí Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn).
Joyful music filled the courtyard,
as sacrifices were offered in the hall.
How splendid was the ancestral temple,
where our ancestors and former emperors resided.
Many princes and dukes,
assisted us in the seasonal sacrifices.
The offerings were faultless,
and blessings descended in abundance.
Right: The ascending song for the祠豫章府君 (Cí Yùzhāng Fǔjūn).
Oh, the distant former rulers,
truly served in Heaven.
Illustrious were the august ancestors,
whose imperial blessings first arrived.
Main and branch lines could prosper,
initiating a new era.
They bestowed boundless favor upon us,
enjoying a reign of eternal years.
Right: The ascending song for the祠潁川府君 (Cí Yǐngchuān Fǔjūn).
Oh, our great-august ancestors,
whose excellent virtues were so manifest.
Lofty and bright, pure and clear,
not competing, but gentle and capable.
Preserving their mandate and blessing us,
their founding mandate was a model.
They gave birth to a sagely ancestor,
who brilliantly brought peace to the four states.
Right: The ascending song for the祠京兆府君 (Cí Jīngzhào Fǔjūn).
Oh, how glorious were the august ancestors,
whose sacred virtues were revered and brilliant.
Diligently spreading influence in the four directions,
respectfully resting day and night.
They widely spread civilizing education,
and proclaimed martial prowess.
They brought peace and stability to the altars of soil and grain (the state),
and carried out Heaven's punishment.
They founded a great enterprise,
and established the imperial foundation.
They feared Heaven's mandate,
and thus preserved it.
Right: The ascending song for the祠宣皇帝 (Cí Xuānhuángdì).
Mighty were the august Jǐng Huángdì,
who were discerning and wise.
They appeared dignified and respectful on all sides,
being ever reverent and awe-inspiring.
They inherited the legacy of Xuān,
and established their merits with wisdom.
They elevated the worthy,
and suppressed the many villains.
They were diligent in their positions,
the emperor was indeed assiduous.
Heaven's mandate,
was continuously excellent.
Right: The ascending song for the祠景皇帝 (Cí Jǐnghuángdì).
Oh, how august was this Jìn Dynasty,
truly cultivated was the Wén Huángdì.
Intelligent and sagacious,
sacred, reverent, and martial.
When all affairs of state were in disarray,
the emperor brought order to them.
When tigers and rhinos (rebels) acted wantonly,
the emperor pacified them.
He could soothe the distant and bring peace to the near,
appointing outstanding and virtuous individuals.
He founded the enterprise and established the lineage,
his achievements reached august Heaven.
Right: The ascending song for the祠文皇帝 (Cí Wénhuángdì).
It is said that the Jìn is eternal,
its sacrifices are timely and orderly.
Respect is paid in the ancestral temple,
rites and music are fully performed.
When the offerings come,
from all under Heaven.
Sacrificial vessels are already set,
pure wine is already served.
There is also harmonious broth,
delicious offerings are all prepared.
Deep and eternal longing,
stirred by the times, evoking thoughts.
Ascending songs and dances are performed,
the divine music is harmonious.
Ancestors arrive,
blessing our state and family.
Under all Heaven,
none are not excellent and auspicious.
Solemnly in their positions,
numerous ministers and officials.
The four seas come to visit,
rites and ceremonies are conducted with dignity.
Bells and drums resound,
strings and pipes are in tune.
Dances celebrate the founding,
songs celebrate the eternal beginning.
The spirits are all joyful!
Solemnly in their positions,
ministers and officials in abundance.
Great and small all reverent,
upper and lower with proper禮 (lǐ).
Strings and pipes are tuned,
drums and bells are beaten.
Dances symbolize virtue,
songs praise achievements.
The spirits are all joyful!
Solemnly in their positions,
those who come are harmonious.
Dignified is the Son of Heaven,
assisted by the princes and dukes.
Rites have their proper forms,
music has its rules.
Dances symbolize achievements,
songs praise virtue.
The spirits are all joyful!
Right: Two pieces of divine songs for the ancestral temple offerings.
Thirteen pieces of ancestral temple songs of Jìn on the Left of the River; eleven pieces composed by Cáo Pí, two pieces composed by Wáng Xún. Song for Gāozǔ Xuānhuángdì, composed by Cáo Pí.
Oh, how glorious was Gāozǔ,
whose virtue accorded with divine omens.
Responding to the era, he quelled chaos,
and rectified the celestial path.
His achievements reached the universe,
his influence moved the eight regions.
He brought order with laws and punishments,
and nurtured with profound wisdom.
Divine stones revealed auspicious omens,
and spiritual ganoderma spread by itself.
He laid the foundation for the Mandate of Heaven,
his Dao was equal to that of Táng and Yú.
Song for Shìzōng Jǐnghuángdì.
Jǐnghuángdì inherited the mandate,
and developed the great legacy.
The imperial foundation was re-established,
the heavenly radiance shone again.
How foolish were the two rebels,
disturbing our Yáng and Chǔ.
He then mobilized the grand army,
to anoint the battle-axes.
How diligent was his divine strategy,
how majestic was the royal army.
Once the whales and rhinos (rebels) were pacified,
his achievements crowned the imperial domain.
Song for Tàizǔ Wénhuángdì.
Tàizǔ was sagely and discerning,
his royal principles expanded greatly.
Benevolent teachings filled the four quarters,
the heavenly foundation was repeatedly elevated.
When the imperial house faced many difficulties,
he strictly purified the Forbidden Palace.
His might was like autumn frost,
his benevolence exceeded spring breeze.
He pacified Shǔ and subdued Chǔ,
with both civil and military means.
He encompassed Cān Xū,
his fame flowed endlessly.
Song for Shìzǔ Wǔhuángdì.
Oh, how dignified was Wǔhuáng,
truly reverent and brilliant.
Responding to the opportune moment, he ascended the throne,
like a dragon soaring into the Purple Court.
All government affairs were in order,
decisions were made with empathy.
Distant lands were brought to submission,
and the false Wú was also pacified.
Sweet dew flowed in the morning,
bright stars shone at night.
In the fields, there were songs of contentment,
on the roads, songs of praise were heard.
Song for Zhōngzōng Yuánhuángdì.
The mandate suffered a major calamity,
the celestial net was broken.
Yuánhuángdì rose valiantly,
his net encompassed the Jiāng and Hàn.
He looked up to align the seven luminaries,
and looked down to pacify disasters and chaos.
His transformation was like the swift wind,
his benevolence like scattered rain.
The faded light shone anew,
the golden brilliance was restored.
His virtue crowned a thousand years,
with enduring splendor.
Song for Sùzǔ Mínghuángdì.
Brilliant was Sùzǔ,
who expanded the imperial legacy.
His heroic spirit emerged early,
his pure radiance filled the roads.
When traitors and rebels acted wrongly,
disregarding imperial laws.
He personally waved the crimson banner,
and thus cleared the heavenly path.
His grand strategies were profound and secure,
his lofty net spread like clouds.
All things found peace,
the great foundation was forever solid.
Song for Xiǎnzōng Chénghuángdì.
Oh, illustrious Xiǎnzōng!
Your virtuous influence spread profoundly.
You proclaimed your virtuous edicts,
Bringing harmony and joy to all things.
You pursued virtue and trod the path of benevolence,
Never transgressing the rites.
You spread pure customs,
And cleansed with clear waves.
Intertwined trees reflected on the hills,
Singing phoenixes nested on branches.
You followed the example of Fàngxūn,
Your righteousness surpassed mountains and rivers.
Song for Kāng Huángdì
Kāng Huáng was solemn and grand,
Inheriting a vast virtue.
He acted but did not dominate,
His elegant music filled the four directions.
He suppressed evil with sincerity,
And calmed the world with silence.
His majesty pacified the realm,
His Dao was proclaimed in all states.
Song for Xiàozōng Mù Huángdì
Xiàozōng was wise from an early age,
His excellent reputation truly good.
Like the morning star,
Its light shone on Fúsāng.
He imparted teachings in splendid tents,
His beneficence flowed to the eight directions.
He subtly aided the profound and mysterious,
Thus encompassing all canons and statutes.
He pacified the usurping Shǔ in the west,
And quieted the old territories in the north.
His lofty plans spread far and wide,
Leaving a lasting fragrance in the court.
Song for Āi Huángdì
Oh, solemn Āi Huáng!
His sacred heart was vast and distant.
He cherished the profound antiquity,
And trod the path of Dàtíng.
His Dao valued non-action,
His governance preserved simplicity and ease.
His transformation was like the wind passing,
The people like grass bending.
Though he ascended to heaven,
His excellent reputation spread ever wider.
The harmonious Cloud Music,
Was utterly beautiful and utterly good.
Song for Tàizōng Jiǎnwén Huángdì, composed by Wáng Xún
Glorious Jiǎnwén,
Shining brightly as the heavens.
Spiritually brilliant like a deity,
Profound and vast like a deep abyss.
His humble responses came forth,
Truly moving with the times.
His gentle heart transformed,
Daily acting without words.
Easy yet親,
Simple yet transmissible.
Observing the flow, it goes ever further,
Seeking the root, it becomes ever more profound.
Song for Lièzōng Xiàowǔ Huángdì, composed by Wáng Xún
Heaven watched over Jìn,
Revered indeed was Lièzōng.
He followed the example of Wénkǎo,
Profoundly silent and truly diligent.
Majestic but not fierce,
Restrained yet capable of understanding.
When the divine chime resonated,
The nine regions came together.
His Dao accumulated in Huáihǎi,
Elegant odes spontaneously arose from the east.
His spirit refined the pure dew,
His transformation harmonized with the times of peace.
Songs for the Four Seasons' Sacrifices, composed by Cáo Pí
Solemn and pure is the ancestral temple,
Lofty and grand are the holy achievements.
All nations come as guests,
With graceful rituals and ceremonies.
Bells and drums reverberate,
Metal and stone instruments resound with joy.
They proclaim the auspicious founding,
And the martial establishment of the base.
The spirits are pleased!
The pipes and strings are arranged,
All who come are in harmony.
We speak of accomplishments and virtues,
And utter clear songs.
The spirits are pleased!
Vast and profound is the divine transformation,
Its beneficence covers the nine lands.
There is no one who is not joyful,
No place where the Dao does not reach.
The rites have their ceremonies,
The music has its forms.
We sing of the nine achievements,
Forever without end.
The spirits are pleased!
Eight Temple Ascent Songs of Sòng, composed by Wáng Sháozhī
Continuous and long is the lineage,
Shining brightly and burgeoning.
The virtue of Hàn is not far off,
Yáo's lingering customs remain.
Oh, solemn imperial ancestors!
May you forever prosper.
The main branch is blessed,
Its inheritance is inexhaustible.
Right: Ascent Song for the Sacrifice to the Lord of Běipíng Prefecture.
A pure temple was established,
The pure temple is solemn.
The ritual attire was prepared,
The ritual attire is grand.
Illustrious and sincere imperial ancestors,
You made this succession manifest.
Grant these abundant blessings,
And possess many fortunes.
Right: Ascent Song for the Sacrifice to the Lord of Xiàngguóyuàn Prefecture.
The four-county ritual is in order,
The flutes and pipes are played.
Six jade vessels offered in the hall,
Eight feathered dances in the courtyard.
The former kings had their rites,
To purify and sacrifice to the imperial ancestors.
Greatly manifest their grand achievements,
Forever bestow excellent blessings.
Right: Ascent Song for the Sacrifice to the Lord of Kāifēng Prefecture.
Bells and drums resound loudly,
Majestic and grand are the ceremonies.
Gentle and respectful with rites and music,
Reverently we offer to the great emperor.
Pursuing virtue and bestowing benevolence,
Continuing the path and shining brightly again.
Heaven bestows pure and great blessings,
Benefiting us without end.
Right: Ascent Song for the Sacrifice to the Lord of Wǔyuán Prefecture.
Splendid are the imperial ancestors,
The Emperor measured their hearts.
Forever they corresponded to Heaven's mandate,
Spreading this excellent reputation.
We reflect on our splendid plans,
Like jade and like gold.
Swiftly we hasten to the steps,
To be observed and accepted.
Right: Ascent Song for the Sacrifice to the Lord of Dōng'ān Prefecture.
Grand indeed is Xiào Huáng,
Perfectly sagely, vast and profound.
He initiated auspicious blessings and great joy,
His grand fortune came from Heaven.
His virtue spread to metal and stone,
His Dao covered pipes and strings.
His mandate is now assembled,
His excellent customs will be proclaimed forever.
Right: Ascent Song for the Sacrifice to Xiào Huángdì.
Heaven has its mandate,
And sought a supreme sage.
Glorious and mighty was Shèngwǔ,
Who managed the shifting destiny.
His achievements equaled the spreading of land,
His Dao was as widespread as Rǔfén.
To stop the spear is called military,
To organize the world is called culture.
Bird and Dragon lost their order,
Cloud and Fire took their names.
He received the final mandate, changed the world,
And established our Sòng capital.
The ultimate Dao is kingship,
The great enterprise is splendid.
He bestowed virtue upon the myriad people,
And ascended to sing in the pure temple.
Right: Ascent Song for the Sacrifice to Gāozǔ Wǔ Huángdì.
Spacious and grand are the sleeping temples,
Jade scepters offered in the courtyard.
Sheng and yue flutes arranged,
Sacrificial vessels in the shape of oxen and elephants filled.
Millet and grain are not fragrant,
Only sincerity makes the bright sacrifice fragrant.
Music complete, rites fulfilled,
Pure offerings presented with sincerity.
May the spirits arrive,
And bestow excellent omens.
Many are the gathered lords,
Forever observing its perfection.
Right: Ascent Song for the Sacrifice to the Spirits of the Seven Temples.
(Also including the song for the Empress Dowager.)
Song for Shìzǔ Xiàowǔ Huángdì, composed by Xiè Zhuāng
The emperor bestowed upon the two ancestors,
a long reign with abundant blessings.
Oh, how reverent was the sagacious deceased emperor,
who inherited the sagely path and followed the rules.
When the profound ultimate principle lost its reins,
and the heavenly order’s thread was broken,
he opened up our imperial foundation,
and established our Sòng realm.
He rectified and pacified the four seas,
and first built the divine capital.
He restored rites and compiled music,
released warhorses and dismantled city walls.
His beneficence filled the nine regions,
his transformation spread over the eight seas.
Auspicious clouds supported and protected,
sweet dew flew over the rooftops.
Solemn, solemn, the pure temple,
magnificent, magnificent, the secluded palace.
Dances symbolized virtue,
sheng and qìng displayed customs.
Millet offerings are not abundant,
but bright virtue is truly esteemed.
May the spirits savor this,
and bestow endless blessings.
Yuánxuān Huáng Tàihòu Miào Gē
Receiving auspicious radiance from the moon,
nurturing virtue with the glow of Xuān.
Inheriting the glory of Guīruì,
seeking to please Zhōu Jiāng.
A mother overlooking all under heaven,
her instructions filled the purple chambers.
With zither and jade flute,
let us offer these fragrant jewels.
Jìn Sì Xiāng Yuè Gē Sān Shǒu by Fù Xuán
Heaven observed Jìn,
and bestowed the imperial throne upon its sagely emperor.
He aligned the seven regulators of time,
and held court over all regions.
(First) Bells and drums thunder forth,
the nine ranks of guests observe the rites.
His righteous position is in the court,
solemn and orderly.
(Second) Resplendent are the three luminaries,
truly beautiful in the sky.
The ruler and empress emulate them,
with utmost solemnity and reverence.
(Third) Following the rites without error,
none failed to advance in virtue.
Emulating the sagely emperor,
all nations take him as their model.
(Fourth) Above, Tiān Jiàn, four stanzas,
each of four lines.
Zhèngdàn Dàhuì Xínglǐ Gē
Oh, how glorious and brilliant,
the sagely virtue of the dragon rising.
For three mornings wine is offered,
may myriad long lives be received.
He spreads blessings to the four directions,
like the rising sun.
From heaven comes bestowed fortune,
great auspiciousness has its signs.
Above, Yū Hè, one stanza,
eight lines.
Shàng Shòu Jiǔ Gē
Heaven commanded great Jìn,
to nurture all beings.
Oh, how majestic its supreme virtue,
transforming and completing with the seasons.
(First) From the ancestors, who matched Heaven's mandate,
the empress and imperial consort.
Following Heaven to found the enterprise,
the accomplishments of Xuān Wén.
(Second) Grand and manifest was Xuān Wén,
who first understood farming.
He was reverent and frugal,
sufficient in teaching and providing food.
(Third) Having taught and fed them,
he broadly saved them from hardship.
The High Lord blessed him,
and the common people found peace.
(Fourth) Heaven blessed the sagely emperor,
and myriad nations came to congratulate.
Though at peace, he did not rest,
diligently and without leisure.
(Fifth) He then rectified the hills and suburbs,
and established the altars of the earth gods.
Reverently he became the ancestral lord,
gloriously dwelling in the world.
(Sixth) With reverence for morning sacrifices,
he presented the food offerings.
Performing rites fully to serve the emperor,
with beautiful music in order.
(Seventh) Feathers were set up, musical frames arranged,
sheng and yōng chimed intermittently.
Qín and sè were arranged in rows,
and there were also chí and xūn.
(Eighth) Booming were the drums and bells,
clanging were the qìng and flutes.
The eight sounds harmonized,
both soothing and simple.
(Ninth) Both soothing and simple,
its greatness could not be resisted.
Transformative influence arose subtly,
like clouds and rain.
(Tenth) Like the covering of clouds,
like the moistening of rain.
Wherever his voice and teachings reached,
none failed to submit.
(Eleventh) He taught to transform them,
and used music to harmonize them.
Harmonizing and nurturing them,
it was truly peaceful and prosperous.
(Twelfth) Rites carefully ordered their forms,
music regulated their sounds.
Oh, how glorious the imperial teachings,
both harmonious and peaceful.
(Thirteenth) Above, Tiān Mìng, thirteen stanzas,
each of four lines.
Shíjǔ Dōngxī Xiāng Gē.
Jìn Zhèngdé Dàyù Èr Wǔ Gē Èr Piān by Fù Xuán
Heaven mandated Jìn,
to gloriously bring prosperity to myriad nations.
Solemn, solemn, the sagely emperor,
a model in both civil and military.
He is righteous in heaven,
and achieves virtue on earth.
He concealed severe punishments,
and upheld ritual teachings.
I spread profound transformation,
reaching the middle way.
Above, Zhèngdé Wǔ Gē.
Oh, how splendid the imperial Jìn,
matching Heaven in receiving the mandate.
Brightening the light of the emperor,
his inherited virtue is sagely.
Auspicious music, great joy,
protecting and blessing the myriad people.
Deep and inexhaustible,
humble yet used.
Not deviating from Heaven's preordained path,
reverently observing heavenly times.
Above, Dàyù Wǔ Gē.
Jìn Sì Xiāng Yuè Gē Shíqī Piān by Xún Xù. Zhèngdàn Dàhuì Xínglǐ Gē Sì Piān
Oh, splendid primal sovereign,
from whom all beings derive their origin.
At the beginning of the year, a great feast,
reverently performing numerous blessings.
Attended by all the lords,
and also the ministers.
Respectfully compliant, he is the primal one,
truly the Son of Heaven.
Above, Yū Huáng, one stanza,
eight lines.
(Corresponds to Yū Hè.)
Bright, bright, the Son of Heaven,
impressive in his rule over the world.
The four borders turn their hearts to him,
his benevolence reaches the wild tribes.
He pacifies the distant and draws near the close,
most excellent and unopposed.
They come reverently, in orderly procession,
and the nation-states are thus brought to submission.
Above, Míng Míng, one stanza,
eight lines.
(Corresponds to Wēiwēi.)
Resplendent, resplendent, the nation-state,
Heaven bestows its blessings.
Greatly manifest is the wise mandate,
he looks upon the three ancestors with kindness.
Inherited virtue seeks fulfillment,
and he possesses the nine lands.
Reflecting on our imperial system,
the constant norms are well-ordered.
Above, Bāng Guó, one stanza,
eight lines.
(Corresponds to Yáng Yáng.)
Only the ancestors,
lofty and radiant, continuously glorious.
Responding to and revering Heaven,
they bring great blessings here.
Seeking their fulfillment,
our emperor venerates them.
Thus solidifying his plans,
he diligently governs.
Above, Zǔ Zōng, one stanza,
eight lines.
(Corresponds to Lù Míng.)
Zhèngdàn Dàhuì Wánggōng Shàng Shòu Jiǔ Gē Yī Piān
Treading the primal auspiciousness,
extending profound harmony.
Presenting feathered cups,
praying for a good end.
Our Emperor is long-lived and great,
Our Emperor is prosperous and eminent.
The main branch flourishes for a hundred generations,
excellent blessings converge upon the sacred person.
"Treading the Primal Auspiciousness" is one stanza,
eight lines.
(To be sung with "Yǔshāng".)
Music for the Imperial Feast — Songs of the East and West Boxes, twelve pieces.
Blazing are the seven luminaries,
their double brightness flows freely.
We have esteemed guests,
they respond and bring gifts.
State affairs are already planned,
followed by a great banquet.
Those who are fond of us,
follow the path of virtue and humility.
"Blazing" is one stanza,
eight lines.
(To be sung with "Lùmíng".)
At the beginning of the guests' banquet,
numerous and orderly.
Having had the morning audience, they now feast,
to complete all the rites.
Distributed by rank,
some in the courtyard, some on the steps.
Those ascending the host's platform are old,
and also have their brothers.
Aides accompany officials,
establishing these standards and models.
Observing nourishment and upholding righteousness,
blessings descend in abundance.
"At the Beginning of the Guests' Banquet" is one stanza,
twelve lines.
(To be sung with "Wū Mù".)
Of old, our Three Sovereigns (Sān Hòu),
maintained the great enterprise.
Now our Sacred Emperor (Shèng Huáng),
brightly shines upon the former glory.
In successive generations, he renews the rules,
brilliantly illuminating the nine regions (jiǔ jī).
He contemplates unity and uses light,
at no time is there deviation.
Ascending the tracks of Yǔ,
none do not come in awe.
Heaven bestows manifest blessings,
good fortune and prosperity are secured.
"Three Sovereigns" is one stanza,
twelve lines.
(To be sung with "Zhāozhāo".)
Mighty is the Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ),
able to expand bright virtue.
He opened up the universe,
rectified the world and established rules.
His transformations were boundless,
the people were without fault or evil.
He founded the enterprise and established the lineage,
initiating our Jìn State (Jìn Guó).
"Mighty" is one stanza,
eight lines.
(To be sung with "Huáhuá".)
Illustrious and martial is the Elder Grandfather (Bó Kǎo),
indeed Emperor Jǐng (Dì Jǐng).
He pacified dangers and calmed chaos,
awe-inspiring but not fierce.
He governed the balance without error,
the imperial road shone brightly.
The Seven Virtues (Qī Dé) were all proclaimed,
his peace will be eternal.
"Illustrious and Martial" is one stanza,
eight lines.
(To be sung with "Cháoyàn".)
How splendid, how magnificent,
the Sacred Virtue (Shèng Wén) of the Former Emperor (Xiān Huáng).
Following Heaven, he engendered trust,
truly a great ruler.
He carefully upheld the Five Canons (Wǔ Diǎn),
diligently working for the imperial task.
Civil and martial virtues flourished,
greatly establishing glorious achievements.
Cultivating himself to assist in governance,
the people thus lived in peace and prosperity.
Cherishing the distant and illuminating the obscure,
his profound teachings spread widely.
He benefited the world without boasting,
service participated in three parts.
His virtue was vast, his transformation profound,
his Dao encompassed the boundless.
"How Splendid" is one stanza,
sixteen lines.
(To be sung with "Shèngdé".)
His profound transformation flows abundantly,
the imperial mandate spreads widely.
Ascending our Jìn Dao (Jìn Dào),
he is indeed the Sacred Emperor (Shèng Huáng).
He soared like a dragon, renewing the era,
presiding over and illuminating the eight directions (bā huāng).
Sagacious, wise, revered, and enlightened,
his footsteps matched those of Yú (Yú) and Táng (Táng).
He established his blessings,
greatly bringing forth auspiciousness.
Three imperial courts practiced auspiciousness,
finally, all was truly good.
What is its goodness?
It gathers all ten thousand regions.
Grand marquises and feudal lords,
the Four Peaks (Sì Yuè) and vassal kings.
They appeared at the seasonal offerings,
consistently following this.
Guests bowed in the courtyard,
esteemed guests were in the hall.
Sòng (Sòng) and Wèi (Wèi) have arrived,
Chénliú (Chénliú) and Shānyáng (Shānyáng).
We have envoys and guests,
observing the glory of the state.
Presenting the worthy and offering counsel,
offering jade discs and jade tablets.
May Heaven protect and command him,
repeatedly bestowing boundless blessings.
"Profound Transformation" is one stanza,
twenty-eight lines.
(To be sung with "Suí Wàn Bāng".)
Egret flying,
wild goose gradually spreading its wings.
The capital city (jīngyì) is tranquil and solemn,
serving as a model for the four directions.
No one competes,
the royal order (wáng gāng) is truly disciplined.
Gentlemen come to court,
to observe its ultimate goal.
"Egret Flying" is one stanza,
eight lines.
(To be sung with "Zhāozhāo".)
Reverent is the great ruler,
the one whom the people look up to.
He faithfully manages Heaven's work,
his benevolent compassion is inexhaustible.
He will remove the unkind,
instructing them with purity and sincerity.
There is order in the visible and invisible,
the excellent are in their positions.
The nine kindred are harmonious,
all states submit and align.
He established the foundation and promulgated the laws,
the four seas gather like scales.
He aligned with the times and rectified the orthodoxy,
different paths lead to the same goal.
With thick virtue, he sustains all things,
his spiritual heart is noble and esteemed.
He presents frank words,
accepting them without concealment.
He establishes models and standards,
instructing them in righteousness.
The instruction from above is like wind,
the response from below is like plants.
When one person is blessed,
all living beings prosper.
Our ruler rejoices at the banquet,
his good name will not fall.
"Reverent" is one stanza,
