grass and trees wither and fall, dew becomes frost.
(Stanza 1) Flocks of swallows depart, returning south, geese fly southward,
I think of my lord, a guest traveling far, with a heart full of yearning.
(Stanza 2) Deeply I yearn to return home, missing my native village,
why do you linger and stay in another land?
(Stanza 3) Your humble concubine, lonely and desolate, guards an empty room,
sorrow comes, I think of you and dare not forget.
(Stanza 4) Unconsciously tears fall, wetting my clothes,
I pluck the zither, sounding the clear Qīngshāng tune.
(Stanza 5) A short song, softly hummed, cannot be long,
the bright moon shines clearly on my bed.
(Stanza 6) The River of Stars flows westward, the night is not yet over,
the Cowherd and Weaver Maid gaze at each other from afar,
what sin did you alone commit to be separated by the Bridge of the River (Milky Way)?
(Stanza 7)
Looking Up – Duǎngē Xíng – Emperor Wén's Lyrics (Six Stanzas)
looking down at the tables and mats.
The objects are as before,
the person is no longer here.
(Stanza 1) The spirit suddenly vanished,
leaving me, migrating far away.
Nowhere to look, nowhere to rely on,
my tears flow incessantly.
(Stanza 2) Yelp, yelp, the wandering deer,
holds grass in its mouth and calls its fawn.
Flutter, flutter, the flying birds,
carry their young to nest and roost.
(Stanza 3) I alone am solitary and forlorn,
bearing these myriad separations.
My heart is deeply pained,
no one can know me.
(Stanza 4) People also say,
sorrow makes one old.
Alas, my white hair,
why did it appear so early?
(Stanza 5) Long sighs and eternal laments,
I recall my sagely deceased father.
It is said that the benevolent live long,
why was this not preserved?
(Stanza 6)
Parting is so easy, meeting is hard;
Mountains and rivers are vast and the road is long.
(First stanza) Deeply I yearn for you, but dare not speak,
Sending a letter on floating clouds, it goes and does not return.
(Second stanza) Tears stream down my face, disfiguring my appearance,
Who can bear sorrow and not sigh alone?
(Third stanza) Restless, I lie on my pillow, unable to sleep,
Donning my clothes, I step out of the door and wander east and west.
(Fourth stanza) I open a poem and sing clearly, trying to comfort myself,
Joy departs, sorrow arrives, crushing my heart and liver.
A mournful wind howls sharply, the autumn air is cold,
The silk curtains gently stir, passing through Qín xuān.
(Fifth stanza) I look up at the stars and moon, gazing at the clouds,
Birds chirp in the morning,
Their sounds and spirits are piteous,
Lingering, my thoughts wander, I cannot control myself.
(Sixth stanza) Facing wine – Short Song – Wǔdì cí (six stanzas)
Facing wine, one should sing,
How long is life?
Like the morning dew,
The days gone are truly many.
(First stanza) Filled with noble fervor,
Sorrowful thoughts are hard to forget.
With what can I dispel my grief?
Only
Dùkāng.
(Second stanza) Green, green are your lapels,
Long, long is my heart's yearning.
It is all for your sake,
That I have pondered silently until now.
(Third stanza) Bright, bright as the moon,
When can it be plucked?
Sorrow comes from within,
And cannot be severed.
(Fourth stanza) "Yōu yōu" goes the deer's call,
Eating the wild Artemisia.
I have noble guests,
Playing the sè and blowing the shēng.
(Fifth stanza) Mountains do not disdain height,
Nor do waters disdain depth.
When Zhōu Gōng spit out his food,
The whole world turned its heart to him.
(Sixth stanza) Clear Melody for Morning Ascent – Qiū Hú xíng – Wǔdì cí
In the morning, ascending Sànguān Shān,
How difficult this path must be!
In the morning, ascending Sànguān Shān,
How difficult this path must be!
The ox refuses to move,
The carriage tumbles into the valley.
Sitting on a round rock,
Playing a five-stringed qín,
Composing a clear jiǎo melody,
Expressing the vexation in my heart.
Singing to express my resolve,
In the morning, ascending Sànguān Shān.
(First stanza) Who is that venerable old man,
Suddenly coming to my side?
Who is that venerable old man,
Suddenly coming to my side?
His round face covered by a fur coat,
Seeming not human.
He asks, "What troubles you,
Suffering and lamenting to yourself,
What is it you anxiously desire,
Having come to this place?"
Singing to express my resolve,
Who is that venerable old man?
(Second stanza) I dwell on Kūnlún Shān,
Where are the true immortals.
I dwell on Kūnlún Shān,
Where are the true immortals.
The Dao is profound and can be attained.
I traverse famous mountains,
Roaming the eight cardinal points.
Pillowing on rocks, rinsing my mouth in streams, drinking from springs.
Pondering, irresolute,
Then ascending to heaven.
Singing to express my resolve,
I dwell on Kūnlún Shān.
(Third stanza) Gone, gone, not to be pursued,
Long regret ties and binds me.
Gone, gone, not to be pursued,
Long regret ties and binds me.
How can I sleep night after night,
Melancholy, pitying myself.
Upright and not deceitful,
My rhymed prose follows tradition.
Passing through classics and commentaries,
Transmitted from the west.
Singing to express my resolve,
Gone, gone, not to be pursued.
(Fourth stanza.
Another version: In the morning, ascending Sànguān Shān,
How difficult this path must be!
Who is that venerable old man,
Suddenly coming to my side?
I dwell on Kūnlún Shān,
Where are the true immortals,
Gone, not to be pursued,
Long regret ties and binds me.)
Ascending North – Kǔ Hán xíng – Wǔdì cí (six stanzas)
Ascending north on Tàiháng Shān,
How arduous and lofty!
The Sheep's Intestines Slope is winding and steep,
For which carriage wheels are crushed.
(First stanza) How desolate are the trees,
The north wind's sound is truly sorrowful.
Bears and grizzlies squat facing me,
Tigers and leopards cry by the roadside.
(Second stanza) Few people in the valleys and streams,
Snow falls so densely.
I crane my neck and sigh long,
A long journey brings many thoughts.
(Third stanza) How vexed is my heart,
I wish to return east.
The water is deep, the bridges are broken,
I hesitate in the middle of the road.
(Fourth stanza) Lost and mistaken the path,
At dusk, nowhere to stay.
Walking on, day by day, further away,
Both men and horses are hungry.
(Fifth stanza) Carrying a bag, I gather firewood,
Chopping ice, I make gruel.
I grieve for that poem on Dōng Shān,
Its length makes me sorrowful.
(Sixth stanza) Wishing to Ascend – Qiū Hú xíng – Wǔdì cí (five stanzas)
Wishing to ascend Tài Huà Shān,
To wander far with divine beings.
Passing through Kūnlún Shān,
Arriving at Pénglái.
Drifting among the eight cardinal points,
Together with divine beings.
Longing to obtain the divine medicine,
To live for ten thousand years.
Singing to express my resolve,
Wishing to ascend Tài Huà Shān.
(First stanza) How long are heaven and earth,
Human life within them is short.
The world speaks of Bóyáng,
Yet does not know the old man (Lǎozi),
Chìsōng and Wáng Qiáo,
Also said to have attained the Dao.
Whether they attained it, I have not heard,
Perhaps it is to live long.
Singing to express my resolve,
How long are heaven and earth!
(Second stanza) Bright, bright is the light of the sun and moon,
What is not illuminated?
The two forces (heaven and earth) merge into sacred transformation,
Only humans are noble.
All nations, all lands,
Are nothing but subjects of the king.
Benevolence and righteousness as names,
Rites and music as glory.
Singing to express my resolve,
Bright, bright is the light of the sun and moon.
(Third stanza) The four seasons pass by in turn,
Day and night make a year.
The Great Man anticipates heaven,
And heaven does not oppose him.
Not grieved by passing years,
The world's sorrows cannot be remedied.
Life and death are fated,
To worry about them is foolish.
Singing to express my resolve,
The four seasons pass by in turn.
(Fourth stanza) What sad thoughts should I dwell on,
To what do laughter and joy lead?
Youthful strength and wisdom,
Truly will not come again.
Cherish time and strive forward,
To whom will this benefit?
Floating aimlessly and being unrestrained,
What purpose does that serve?
Singing to express my resolve,
What sad thoughts should I dwell on?
(Fifth stanza) Ascending to present – Dǒng Táo xíng – Ancient lyric (five stanzas)
I wish to ascend to meet the gods from the lofty mountains,
the mountaintops are perilous and exceedingly difficult.
Looking afar at the peaks of the Wǔyuè,
their gates are made of gold,
resplendent and variegated.
One only sees the zhī grass,
its leaves falling in profusion.
(Verse 1) A hundred birds gather,
arriving like smoke.
Mountain beasts teem,
qílín and bìxié at its front.
Kūnjī cry and sing,
one only sees mountain beasts assisting and playing, entangled.
(Verse 2) A little further one proceeds to the jade hall,
yet the mind harbors no thought of returning.
The messenger comes out of the gate,
asking, "What do the people outside the gate seek?"
They say, "We wish to follow the holy path,
to gain an extended life."
(Verse 3) The divine edict commanded the officials to receive the word,
"Gather the divine medicine from the top of the Ruòmù tree."
The white rabbit kneels long, pounding the toad elixir,
offering it up to His Majesty on a jade plate,
saying, "Taking this medicine will grant immediate immortality."
(Verse 4) Having taken this divine medicine,
there was none who was not joyful.
May Your Majesty live long and be blessed with old age,
all around solemnly bow their heads,
heavenly spirits guard on the left and right,
may Your Majesty forever be preserved with Heaven.
(Verse 5) Púshēng tángshàngxíng Wǔdì Cí
(Verse 5)
The rush grows in my pond,
how luxuriant are its leaves.
It can move gracefully by the side,
yet none can discern its inner workings.
Many mouths melt gold,
causing you, my lord, to be separated from me.
(Verse 1) Remembering when you left me,
alone, I always suffered in sorrow.
Imagining your countenance,
my heart and spleen are pained and knotted.
Now, night after night, I sorrow and cannot sleep.
(Verse 2) Do not, for the sake of the mighty and virtuous,
abandon that which you originally cherished;
Do not, for the sake of expensive fish and meat,
abandon onions and shallots;
Do not, for the sake of cheap hemp and ramie,
abandon cogon grass and sedge.
(Verse 3) Those who betray kindness suffer like the bitter gourd,
capsizing boats always lead to drowning.
I advise you to rest quietly and steadily,
be careful not to act impulsively.
Thinking of our shared separation,
when shall we ever sit together and face each other again?
(Verse 4) Going out, I am again sorrowful,
coming in, I am again sorrowful.
The frontier lands have many mournful winds,
how desolate are the trees.
Today, let us enjoy ourselves,
extending our lives for a thousand autumns.
(Verse 5) Yōuyōu kǔhánxíng Míngdì Cí (Verse 5)
Vast and distant, I depart Luòdū,
leading my eastern expedition.
The journey spans more than two decades,
stationed and camping at Lóngpí Chéng.
(Verse 1) Looking back at the site of the old fortress,
that which my imperial ancestor constructed.
The houses are as they were in the past,
the beams and pillars without a crooked tilt.
(Verse 2) Alas, my imperial ancestor,
his hidden virtue obscured his sagely form.
Though deceased, he is not forgotten,
his precious writings preserve his auspicious name.
(Verse 3) How glorious is my imperial ancestor,
his radiance shining with equal splendor.
His transforming influence spread throughout the four seas,
the eight directions were pacified.
(Verse 4) Although there are the bandits of Wú and Shǔ,
spring and autumn are sufficient to display military might.
I only grieve for my imperial ancestor,
who did not enjoy a hundred years of life.
I compose this poem to express my feelings,
leaning on the armrest, tears moisten my cap-strings.
(Verse 5) Sèdiào Cháozhì Shànzāixíng Wéndì Cí (Verse 5)
In the morning sun, we delight and enjoy each other's company,
drinking heartily, unaware of intoxication.
The sorrowful strings stir new melodies,
the long flute emits a clear sound.
(Verse 1) String music moves one's heart,
all seated are joyful and pleased.
In the vast, high hall,
a cool breeze enters my chamber.
(Verse 2) Holding a full cup as if it's not full,
only the virtuous can finish.
A noble person has many worries,
their sorrows are not merely one.
(Verse 3) With earnestness, I reside in a humble dwelling,
spitting out a mouthful of food or holding hair to receive a guest must not be missed.
All guests return fully satisfied,
but the host suffers from not having enough.
(Verse 4) Paired wings soar in the Milky Way,
where can the fowler bind them?
Tranquility achieves naturalness,
what is glory and splendor worth?
(Verse 5) Shàngshān Shànzāixíng Wéndì Cí (Verse 6)
Ascending the mountain to pick vetch,
by dusk, I suffer from hunger.
The valleys are windy,
frost and dew wet my clothes.
(Verse 1) Wild pheasants flock and crow,
monkeys chase each other.
Looking back at my homeland,
how melancholic and desolate it appears.
(Verse 2) High mountains have cliffs,
forest trees have branches.
Sorrows arise without a source,
no one knows them.
(Verse 3) Life is like a temporary lodging,
what is the purpose of so many worries?
If I am not happy now,
the years and months will rush by.
(Verse 4) The river flows mightily,
with boats traveling in it.
Drifting with the waves,
it is like a traveler's journey.
(Verse 5) I spur my good horse,
and put on my light fur coat.
Galloping and driving,
I seek to forget my worries.
(Verse 6) Zhāoyóu Shànzāixíng Wéndì Cí (Verse 5)
In the morning, I stroll upon the high terrace,
in the evening, I feast in the shade of the ornate pond.
The chief distiller offers sweet wine,
the hunter presents fine fowl.
(Verse 1) Qí singers perform the eastern dance,
Qín zithers play western tunes.
A guest comes from the south,
playing a clear qín for me.
(Verse 2) The five notes converge in a profusion,
the players stir a subtle hum.
Lascivious fish ride the waves to listen,
leaping and submerging themselves.
(Verse 3) Flying birds flutter and dance,
crying mournfully, gathering in the northern woods.
When joy reaches its extreme, sadness comes,
piercingly, it crushes the liver and heart.
(Verse 4) How could the pure jiǎo not be exquisite?
But those of scant virtue cannot bear it.
How profound are Zǐyě's words,
put down the strings and restrain yourself.
(Verse 5) Gǔgōng Shànzāixíng Wǔdì Cí (Verse 7)
Gǔgōng Dǎnfǔ,
accumulated virtue and extended benevolence.
He desired to promote a single Way,
a sagely king in Bīn.
(Verse 1) Tàibó and Zhòngyōng,
possessed the benevolence of a king.
Their deeds spread for a hundred generations,
cutting hair and tattooing bodies.
(Verse 2) Bóyí and Shúqí,
ancient forgotten worthies.
They declined the throne,
starving to death on Shǒushān.
(Verse 3) How wise was Shānfǔ,
assisting King Xuān.
Why was Dùbó used,
to implicate our sages?
(Verse 4) The hegemony of Qí Huán,
depended on Zhòngfù.
Later, he employed Shùdiāo,
and worms flowed out of the household.
(Verse 5) Yànzǐ Píngzhòng,
accumulated virtue and benevolence.
He concealed his virtue from the world,
not necessarily seeking fame.
(Verse 6) In the era of Zhòngní,
the state was ruled by a king.
He drank wine according to the custom,
and served as an official in Yángbō.
(Verse 7) Zìxī Shànzāixíng Wǔdì Cí (Verse 6)
I regret my shallow fortune,
Having been humble from youth, suffering loneliness and hardship.
Neither did I have the instruction of a mother moving thrice,
Nor did I hear the words from the courtyard.
(Verse 1)My poverty is like being torn apart,
I think of whom I can rely on.
Though I harbor a resolute will,
How could I achieve it at this time?
(Verse 2)One who clings to poverty remains poor and humble,
Sighing and shedding tears like rain.
Weeping in sorrow for him,
How can one hope to live?
(Verse 3)I wish for heaven's endlessness,
That Lángyá tilts to the left.
Though I desire to exhaust my loyalty,
I am pleased that the lord returns to his Chǔ.
(Verse 4)Happy people sigh,
Holding feelings that cannot be expressed.
Heaven teaches people to act righteously,
Who knows that all things follow in succession?
(Verse 5)When will my wish come true?
This sigh is also hard to bear.
Now what glory shall I illuminate?
Releasing the bridle is not like rain.
(Verse 6)I departed... Shànzāixíng, Emperor Míng's Lyrics (Verse 8)
I departed, I marched,
To attack those Mán barbarians.
Seasoned generals and picked soldiers,
Thereby arrayed their troops.
(Verse 1)Light boats raced across the river,
Wild geese first rested by the bank.
Mighty and resolute,
Like bears and tigers.
(Verse 2)Cannons roared like thunder,
Exhaling breath formed rain.
Banners pointed, commanders directed,
Advance and retreat according to the rules.
(Verse 3)A hundred horses abreast,
Driven as by Zàofǔ.
Peaceful and harmonious are the six armies,
All sharing in this might.
(Verse 4)Covering roads, marching like stars,
Indeed, this journey is arduous.
Marching on, days grow distant,
Turning west from Jīng Xǔ.
(Verse 5)Traveling not a full ten days,
We reached Yángtǔ.
Fleeing rebels trembled with fear,
None dared to resist.
(Verse 6)Tiger ministers and arrayed generals,
Filled with indignation and rage.
The Huái and Sì rivers are pacified,
Exerting their slight power.
(Verse 7)Wielding virtue and displaying might,
Both suppressing and pacifying.
Turning the banners, we speak of returning,
Reporting our entry to the imperial ancestors.
(Verse 8)Majestic... Shànzāixíng, Emperor Míng's Lyrics (Verse 4)
Majestic is the great Wèi,
Its royal army on an expedition.
Braving the summer heat to suppress rebellion,
Displaying brilliant and awe-inspiring power.
(Verse 1)Boating on the Yellow River,
Following the murmuring waves.
Canals twisting and turning,
The journey stretching endlessly.
(Verse 2)Colorful banners obscured the sun,
Streamers overshadowed the sky.
Excessive fish splashed about,
Playing in the deep abyss.
Following like a stream.
Not for a single person,
Holding Yángchǔ.
My heart is wistful,
Singing "Cǎiwēi".
My heart is long,
At Huáiféi.
May my lord quickly achieve victory and return soon.
(Verse 4)Tomorrow... Shànzāixíng, Ancient Lyrics (Verse 6)
Tomorrow is a great hardship,
Mouth dry and lips parched.
Today we enjoy ourselves,
All should be joyful.
(Verse 1)Passing through famous mountains,
Reishi mushrooms flourished.
The immortal Wáng Qiáo,
Offered a pill of medicine.
(Verse 2)Regretting my short sleeves,
Putting my hand in, I knew the cold.
Ashamed of not having a Líng Zhé,
To repay Zhào Xuān.
(Verse 3)The moon has set, Shēn is horizontal,
The Big Dipper is scattered.
Close friends are at the gate,
Hunger prevents me from eating.
(Verse 4)Days of joy are still few,
Days of sorrow are indeed many.
How to forget sorrow?
Plucking the zither and singing of wine.
(Verse 5)The Eight Dukes of Huáinán,
Reached the Way without difficulty.
Harnessing six dragons,
Playing on the cloud tops.
(Verse 6)Great Melody of the East Gate... Dōngménxíng, Ancient Lyrics (Verse 4)
Exiting the east gate,
Not looking back to return;
Entering the gate,
Sorrowful and about to weep.
No measure of grain in the jar,
Looking back, no clothes hanging on the rack.
(Verse 1)Drawing my sword, I leave the house,
My children tugging at my clothes and crying.
Other families only wish for wealth and nobility,
But your humble wife will share gruel with you.
(Verse 2)Sharing gruel,
Above for the sake of the vast heavens,
Below for the sake of our young children.
Today is an era of integrity,
It is hard to violate the teachings;
My lord, love yourself and do not commit evil.
(Verse 3)Today is an era of integrity,
It is hard to violate the teachings;
My lord, love yourself and do not commit evil.
Go!
I will be late if I delay,
Walk carefully and safely,
And await my return.
(Verse 4)West Mountain... Zhéyángliǔxíng, Emperor Wén's Lyrics (Verse 4)
How high is the West Mountain,
High, high, without end.
Above are two immortal youths,
Neither drinking nor eating.
They gave me a pill,
Its radiance had five colors.
(Verse 1)After taking the pill for four or five days,
My body grew wings.
Lightly I flew on floating clouds,
Swiftly traveling millions of miles.
Gazing across the four seas,
Vast and unrecognizable.
(Verse 2)Péngzǔ is said to have lived seven hundred years,
How could such a long time be traced?
Lǎo Dān went to the Western Róng,
And has not returned to this day.
Wáng Qiáo used empty words,
Chì Sōng uttered hollow promises.
(Verse 3)The discerning person knows truth from falsehood,
Foolish people love to spread baseless rumors.
Recalling ancient matters,
They are confused and number in thousands.
The hundred schools have much that is strange and remote,
The path of the sages is what I observe.
(Verse 4)Luófū... Yàngēluófūxíng, Ancient Lyrics (Verse 3)
The sun rises in the southeast corner,
shining upon my Qín clan's tower.
The Qín clan has a beautiful daughter,
whose name is Luófū.
Luófū loves raising silkworms,
picking mulberries at the corner south of the city.
Green silk makes the basket's cords,
cassia branches make the basket's hook.
On her head, a twisted bun (wōduòjì);
in her ears, bright moon pearls (míngyuèzhū).
Yellow-patterned silk (xiāngqǐ) is her skirt,
purple-patterned silk (zǐqǐ) is her jacket.
Passersby see Luófū,
they set down their carrying poles and stroke their beards.
Young men see Luófū,
they take off their caps and adjust their headscarves (qiàotóu).
Farmers forget their plows,
hoe-weavers forget their hoes.
When they return, they blame each other angrily,
all because they gazed at Luófū.
(Verse 1) An envoy (shǐjūn) comes from the south,
his five horses stand hesitant.
The envoy sends an officer forth,
asking, "Whose fair lady is this?"
"The Qín clan has a beautiful daughter,
whose name is Luófū."
"How old is Luófū?"
"Not yet twenty,
but quite a bit over fifteen."
The envoy (shǐjūn) makes an offer to Luófū,
"Would you care to ride with me?"
Luófū speaks out,
"Envoy (shǐjūn), how foolish you are!
The envoy (shǐjūn) already has a wife,
Luófū already has a husband."
(Verse 2) From the east, over a thousand horsemen,
my husband (fūxù) is at the very front.
How do you recognize my husband (fūxù)?
His white horse follows a black colt (líqú).
Green silk ties its tail,
gold adorns its head.
At his waist, a lùlú sword,
worth over ten million.
At fifteen, he was an assistant clerk (xiǎoshǐ) in the prefecture;
at twenty, a grand master (dàfū) at court;
at thirty, a chamberlain (shìzhōngláng);
at forty, he governed a city.
He is a man pure and fair,
with a neatly trimmed beard (liánlián).
Gracefully he steps into the public office,
slowly he proceeds within the yamen.
Among the several thousand people present,
all say my husband (fūxù) is extraordinary.
(Verse 3.
Before this is the seductive melody,
after is the quick beat.
) Xīmén (West Gate) — Xīmén Xíng (West Gate Ballad) — Ancient Lyrics (6 stanzas)
I go out the west gate,
and walk contemplating.
If not making merry today,
when shall I wait?
(Verse 1) Indeed, for merriment,
merriment should be timely.
Why sit in sorrow and dejection,
and again wait for next year?
(Verse 2) Drink rich wine,
roast fatty beef.
Please call those whom my heart delights,
they can dispel my sorrow and worry.
(Verse 3) Human life is less than a hundred years,
yet one often harbors a thousand years of worries.
Days are short and nights are long,
why not hold a torch and wander?
(Verse 4) I am not an immortal like Wáng Zǐqiáo,
whose lifespan can be measured and anticipated.
(Verse 5) Human life is not like metal or stone,
how can one's years be certain?
Greedy for wealth, sparing expenses,
one is merely scorned by later generations.
(Verse 6.
One version
after "zhúyóu" (秉燭游)
has:
"Go forth,
like clouds dispersing,
broken carriages and lean horses are pushed by oneself,"
and
lacks
the forty-eight characters from "Zì fēi" (自非) onwards.
) Mòmò (Silently) — Zhé Yángliǔ Xíng (Breaking Willow Branches Ballad) — Ancient Lyrics (4 stanzas)
Silently wrongs are committed,
and their punishments follow.
Mòxǐ killed Lóngfēng,
Jié was exiled to Míngtiáo.
(Verse 1) Zǔ Yī’s words were not heeded,
Zhòu's head was displayed on a white banner.
Pointing at a deer and calling it a horse,
Húhài thus lost his body.
(Verse 2) Fūchā, at the point of death,
only then said he had wronged Zǐxū.
The Róng King took in female musicians,
and by this lost his Yóuyú.
Jade and horses brought disaster to Guó,
both states became ruins.
(Verse 3) Three men make a tiger in the market (sān fū chéng shì hǔ),
a loving mother throws her shuttle and flees (cí mǔ tóu zhù qū).
Biàn Hé had his feet cut off,
Jiē Yú returned to his thatched hut.
(Verse 4) Yuántáo (Garden Peach) — Huánghuáng Jīng Luò Xíng (Grand Capital Luò Ballad) — Emperor Wén’s Lyrics (5 stanzas)

Shí Yuè of Winter (second interpretation)

The span of life,

below is _qū_.) Luòyáng Xíng Yànmén Tàishǒu Xíng Ancient Poem (8 Sections)
When Xiàohé Dì was alive,
the Magistrate of Luòyáng, Lord Wáng,
originally a native of Guǎnghàn in Yìzhōu,
served in office young,
and mastered the five classics and their commentaries.
(Section 1) He clearly understood the laws and ordinances,
and his family had held official positions for generations.
From Wēn, he was appointed Magistrate of Luòyáng,
his governance led to worthiness,
protecting the common people,
nurturing the myriad citizens as his children.
(Section 2) Outwardly, he carried out strict policies,
inwardly, he harbored compassion and benevolence.
Equipped with both civil and martial skills,
he surveyed the people's wealth and poverty,
moved the names of evil children,
and inscribed five chapters at the head of the village.
(Section 3) For murder,
neighbors in the same unit were held jointly guilty and faced the door.
He forbade the possession of eight-foot spears,
arrested frivolous youths,
administered corporal punishment for their crimes,
and brought them to the horse market for judgment.
(Section 4) He did not levy arbitrary taxes,
his mind was set on rectifying grievances,
he commanded officials to judge cases fairly,
and not to be harsh or bothersome.
He used thirty coins of his own money
to buy ropes and ceremonial poles.
(Section 5) How worthy, how worthy!
Lord Wáng, our county magistrate.
His subordinate officials,
served the Emperor.
The Registrar and Chief Clerk
were all capable individuals.
(Section 6) When overseeing his department and holding his office,
he dared not dispense favors.
He kept his person pure and his body toiled,
laboring diligently day and night.
His governance earned a reputation for ability,
heard far and wide.
(Section 7) His heavenly years were not fulfilled,
he prematurely met his demise.
A shrine was built for him as a lord,
west of the Ānyáng pavilion.
Wishing that future generations
would all praise and transmit his name.
(Section 8) Báitóu Yín Same Tune as Song of the Oars Ancient Poem (5 Sections)
Your brightness is like the clouds on the mountain,

I heard you had two intentions,

(Section 1) All my life in the city together,

Today we meet for a cup of wine,

Treading lightly by the imperial ditch,
the ditch water flows east and west.
(Section 2) East of the outer wall there are woodcutters,

The two woodcutters push and yield to each other,

(Section 3) So desolate, again so desolate,
getting married, yet not weeping;
I wish for a person with one heart,

(Section 4)
The bamboo pole, how slender and graceful,

If a man desires to know me,

It is like five horses eating fodder,

Today we face each other in joy,
a promise of extending life for ten thousand years.
(Section 5)

The bright moon shines on the high tower,
its flowing light lingers.
Above, there is a sorrowful wife,
sighing with lingering grief.
(Section 1) May I ask who is sighing?
She says she is a traveler's wife.
My husband has been away for over ten years,
this humble concubine always dwells alone.
(Section 2) My longing for you surpasses thirst,
my yearning for you is more severe than hunger.
You are the cypress on the high mountain,
I am the turbid mud in the stream.
(Section 3) The north wind blows mournfully,
fiercely entering my ears.
In my heart, I think of my old friend,
tears fall unceasingly.
(Section 4) We drift and float on different paths,
how can we ever reunite?
I wish for the northeast wind
to blow me into your embrace.
(Section 5) Your embrace is always closed,
on whom can this humble concubine rely?
Our affection is cut off midway,
I flow and stop, left to east or west.
(Section 6) I wish to finish this melody,
this melody is sad and long.
Today we are happy together,
after parting, do not forget each other!

The sagely emperor accords with the Mandate of Heaven,
and the Dao of Zhèngkāng Dì is excellent.
The nine provinces are all submissive,
his might and virtue penetrate the eight hidden realms.
The Sāngōng report that the various princes
must not stay long.
Their princely positions bear heavy responsibility,
and old statutes must all be followed.
The attending ministers review the memorials,
stating that Your Majesty embodies benevolence and compassion.
Hesitating with love and attachment,
he cannot bear to agree to it.
Forced by official codes and laws,
he cannot regard personal favors.
The various kings must proceed to their fiefs;
how sorrowful are the seals and sashes!
They were then lodged in the outer palace halls,
where the palace courts were silent and empty.
The sovereign feels increasing care,
and the Empress Mother harbors bitter pain.
What can be given as gifts?
The treasury is emptied, and all precious treasures are exhausted.
Billions of copper coins,
colorful silks like smoke and clouds.
Imperial carriages and personal accoutrements,
brocade, gauze, gold, and silver.
Dragon banners with nine streamers,
feathered canopies with speckled wheels.
The various kings reflect to themselves,
that they have no merit to bear such profound kindness.
They wish to exert their strength,
to sacrifice their bodies to repay the country.
Hónglú Temple officials escort with banners,
while副shǐ accompany their management.
Noble relatives all come out to send them off,
their carriages and palanquins filling the road.
Carriages and robes are arranged uniformly,
resplendent and shining with heavenly brilliance.
Armed cavalry guard before and behind,
with sounds of drums, flutes, and pipes.
They offer sacrifices for a safe journey at Wèi Dōngmén,
tears falling and moistening their cap strings.
Pulling back their canopies, they look back inside,
bowing and looking up, longing for their kin.
They travel on and on as the day darkens,
when will they return to the imperial court?
The carriage wheels turn reluctantly,
the four horses hesitate and neigh.
Even passersby feel a pang in their noses,
how much more so the feelings of flesh and blood!
Spirit Ganoderma Chapter: When a cassia tree grew before the hall.
Spirit ganoderma grows on jade ground,
vermilion grass covers the banks of the Luò River.
Their splendor illuminates each other,
their brilliant colors shine like spirits.
In ancient times, there was Yú Shùn,
whose parents were stubborn and foolish.
He was filial in the fields,
always adhering to benevolence.
Bóyú, at seventy,
wore colorful clothes to amuse his parents.
When his kind mother whipped him and it didn't hurt,
he sighed and wept, wetting his scarf.
Dīng Lán lost his mother young,
grieving his early orphanhood.
He carved wood to represent his strict parent,
and offered three sacrificial animals morning and evening.
When his violent son showed contempt and insult,
he committed a crime and fled.
The wooden figure wept blood for him,
absolving him of his offense and preserving his name.
Dǒng Yǒng encountered family poverty,
his elderly father leaving him nothing.
He borrowed money for his father's support,
and worked as a laborer to provide sweet and rich food.
Creditors filled his door,
he knew not where to return.
Heavenly spirits were moved by his ultimate virtue,
and a divine maiden wove for him.
Years and months pass unsettlingly,
alas, my deceased father!
You gave birth to me so late,
why did you abandon me so early?
Who composed the Lùé poem?
Thinking of it makes one grow old.
I retire to recite the "Nánfēng" poem,
tears drenching my bosom.
Refrain: The sagely emperor rules the four seas,
his virtues and teachings are proclaimed morning and evening.
All nations are courteous and yielding,
the hundred surnames are solemn and devout in their homes.
In schools, etiquette is not lost,
filial piety and brotherly love are practiced in the fields.
Every household has Zēngshēn and Mǐn Zǐ-like sons,
neighboring houses are all benevolent and worthy.
Children have no untimely deaths,
the elderly live out their years.
May Your Majesty live thirty thousand years,
and the kind mother likewise!
The Great Wèi Chapter: When Jíchāng of Hàn.
The Great Wèi accords with the spiritual talismans,
heavenly blessings have just begun.
Sagely virtue achieves great harmony,
and spirits are commanded.
The left and right should be supplied,
the central hall should house the imperial princes.
May Your Majesty have a long life,
all ministers bow and joyfully congratulate!
Accumulated good deeds bring abundant blessings,
glory and fortune are indeed heaven's constant.
All good things fill the door,
your ministers and sons receive blessings and auspiciousness.
No harm nor misfortune,
they assist and protect our sagely emperor.
All auspiciousness gathers,
while evil, treachery, and wickedness are all extinguished.
Yellow swans swim before the palace,
divine tripods encircle the four corners.
Jade horses fill the imperial carriages,
a ganoderma canopy with nine blossoms is raised.
White tigers play in the western courtyard,
relics follow the辟xié.
Qílín dance on their feet,
phoenixes sing, flapping their wings.
In a year of abundance, a grand feast is held,
jade goblets are arranged in the spacious courtyard.
Joyfully drinking beyond three cups,
ruddy faces reveal themselves.
The banquet does not deviate from ritual,
sovereign and ministers sing "Lùmíng."
Musicians dance with hand drums,
all officials clap thunderously and praise in amazement.
Accumulated rituals are like rivers and seas,
accumulated good deeds are like towering mountains.
The imperial progeny are numerous and flourishing,
grandsons and great-great-grandsons are arrayed.
All ministers exclaim "Long live!",
May Your Majesty enjoy eternal joy and longevity!
The imperial wine is paused, not yet drunk,
noble relatives kneel in the east wing.
Attendants observe his countenance,
presenting golden and jade goblets.
This wine is indeed true wine,
bringing fortune and prosperity to the sagely emperor.
Your Majesty smiles from the balcony,
and all around are joyful and peaceful.
Why does the cup come so slowly?
The officials proceed in order.
Rewards amount to thousands of millions,
all officials are rich and prosperous.
Subtle Chapter: When there was a worthy woman in Guāndōng.
Extreme subtlety can penetrate metal and stone,
Utmost sincerity can move the gods.
A widow wept for her deceased husband,
And Mount Liángshān tilted for her.
When Jǐng Kē went west as a hostage to Qín,
Crows turned white and horses grew horns.
When Zōu Yǎn was imprisoned in the market of Yān,
Heavy frost fell in summer.
In Guāndōng, there was a virtuous woman,
Whose self-given name was Sū Láiqīng.
In her prime, she avenged her father,
And though she died, her meritorious name lives on.
Nǚ Xiū met with a pardon,
When the white blade was nearly at her neck.
Both ascended to the register of immortals,
Escaping death and achieving life.
The Prefect of Tàicāng had committed a crime,
And was summoned from afar to be apprehended.
He lamented that he had no sons,
And that when disaster struck, there was no one to accompany him.
Tíyíng was pained by her father's words,
And shouldered a petition to the west.
She lingered beneath the northern gate of the palace,
Her tears flowing like a stream.
She pleaded to be allowed to join her siblings,
And to use her entire life to redeem her father's body.
Emperor Hàn Wén was moved by her righteousness,
And the law of corporal punishment was abolished.
Her father was thus spared,
Her righteousness recorded in the illustrated biographies.
What need is there for many sons?
One daughter is enough to establish a household.
Jiǎnzǐ crossed the Hé (Yellow River) southwards,
But the ferryman abandoned his boats.
The enforcer of the law was about to inflict punishment,
When the woman Juān stood before him, holding an oar.
"My father, hearing of your coming,
Was about to cross the unfathomable abyss.
Fearing that winds and waves might rise,
He prayed and offered sacrifices to the famous river.
He prepared rituals to feast the spirits,
Seeking blessings for you first.
Unable to withstand the sincerity of his libations and offerings,
It led to this difficult violation of the law.
If you must inflict punishment,
I beg that you let him know his offense and fault.
I wish to take his place,"
Her utmost sincerity moved the azure heaven.
The lord of the state honored her righteousness,
And her father was pardoned and released.
The river surged in the middle of its flow,
And Jiǎnzǐ knew of her virtue.
He returned and betrothed her to be his wife,
Her honor and favor surpassing all predecessors.
A quick-witted woman saved her father's life,
How much more so a vigorous youth?
In Huángchū, harmonious qi emerged,
And in the Míngtáng, virtuous teachings were disseminated.
The way of governance achieved great peace,
And rites and music transformed customs.
Punishments were set aside, and the people suffered no wrongs,
What more could resentful women do?
The Sage Emperor enjoys a long life,
And auspicious blessings constantly arrive.
Poem on the First Month of Winter: Hunting the Cunning Rabbit
In the first month of winter,
The yin qi is severe and clear.
Military officials admonish about the hunt,
Gathering troops and commanding armies.
The mystic tortoise portends good fortune,
The mystic light shines brightly.
Chīyóu clears the path,
Wind subsides and rain ceases.
The imperial carriage sets forth,
Luan birds cry with a deep, grinding sound.
Tiger guards and colorful riders,
With flying elephants and horn-mounted egret plumes.
Bells and drums clang sonorously,
Flutes and pipes play boisterously.
Ten thousand riders keep pace,
A thousand chariots share the same canopy.
Mountains are leveled, valleys filled,
Forests cleared, and thickets swept away.
Nets are spread for ten thousand li,
Catching all that flies and runs.
The agile cunning rabbits,
Flash white and leap high.
Hunted by black-legged falcons,
And surrounded by long poles.
Hánlú and Sòngquè,
Display their talent and speed.
They bite without fully securing the leash,
Pulling down elk and bringing down deer.
Wèi Shì sets the trap,
Yǎng Jī pulls the bowstring.
Dōulú climbs high,
Searching for monkeys and apes.
Qìjì and Mèngbēn,
Leap over valleys and vault over peaks.
Their eyes wide with rage,
Their fury piercing their caps.
They beat bears and throttle tigers,
Kick leopards and fight wildcats.
With surplus strength,
They carry elephants and run.
When the hunt carriages are full,
And the sun is setting, the music ends.
The laborers are dismissed, the multitude disbanded,
A grand feast is held at the detached palace.
A postlude says: The Sage Emperor oversees from his high pavilion,
Assessing the merits of the hunting party.
Dead birds pile up like a capital city,
Blood flows forming ditches.
A clear imperial edict bestows great rewards,
The Imperial Kitchen provides all that is needed.
Horses ride carrying wine,
Carriages drive distributing meat and fish.
Drums beat as goblets are raised,
Bells strike, leaving no one out of place.
Nets are cut to release young qílín,
Traps are loosened to let out phoenix chicks.
Merit is collected by the feathered banners,
Majestic power shakes the realm of ghosts.
May Your Majesty enjoy everlasting joy,
Forever in accord with Heaven's mandate.
Five Pieces of Jìn Píwǔgē, Hóngyè Piān: Píwǔgē,
A Wèi melody, "The Brilliant Wèi Emperor."
An ancient melody, "In Guāndōng, there was a virtuous woman."
Xuān Wén established a grand enterprise,
His abundant virtue was in the Tàishǐ era.
The Sage Emperor responded to auspicious omens,
Received the mandate to rule the four seas.
What joy do the myriad states have?
Above them is a brilliant Son of Heaven.
Táng Yáo ceded the imperial throne,
Yú Shùn merely composed himself.
Composing himself, he faced south,
His transforming influence moved with the times.
A grand amnesty purged budding evils,
Civilizing influence reached Huángzhī.
Emulating Heaven and patterning himself on Earth,
Embodying non-action.
His wisdom matches the sun and moon,
His divinity rivals the two cosmic forces.
Though there were three kinds of fierce evildoers,
In his serene words, they found no place to act.
Emulating Heaven and patterning himself on Earth,
Embodying non-action.
Jì and Xiè both aided his mandate,
Yī and Lǚ rose to become royal ministers.
Orchids and angelica adorned the court,
Below, no people were without lodging.
A sound is made, an echo naturally responds,
A gnomon stands, a shadow naturally attaches.
Fierce tigers follow his reins,
Hidden dragons ascend to the path of heaven.
All things are prepared and become useful tools,
Transformation reaches its utmost extent.
A hundred affairs are handled according to the season,
Ten thousand state affairs have a constant order.
He instructs them with self-restraint,
And receives them with loyalty and compassion.
The multitude below gazes up at his pure conduct,
Lands beyond the seas share their joy and admiration.
Emulating Heaven and patterning himself on Earth,
His transforming influence spreads like clouds.
In former days, elaborate decoration was valued,
Now, frugality and simplicity are cherished.
In former days, there were many minor disputes,
Now, sentiment and old grievances are abandoned.
Emulating Heaven and patterning himself on Earth,
His transforming influence spreads like clouds.
The numerous great court officials,
From dawn to dusk, manage ten thousand state affairs.
Ten thousand state affairs are not left neglected,
Brilliantly, they descend to consult.
Ministers are like the light of arrayed stars,
The ruler is like the radiance of the morning sun.
Their undertakings are equally successful,
Their meritorious achievements are so grand.
The Five Emperors succeeded the Three Sovereigns,
The Three Kings were those to whom the world returned.
His sacred virtue accords with the opportune moment,
Heaven and Earth cannot resist.
The more one looks up, the higher it becomes,
Like heaven, it cannot be ascended.
He will again command the dragon-riders,
And phoenixes will nest in his court.
Poem on Heaven's Mandate: Píwǔgē,
A Wèi melody, "The Sage Emperor of Tàihé."
An ancient melody, "In the second year of Zhānghé."
The Sagely Ancestor received the Mandate of Heaven,
responding to the opportune moment to assist Emperor Wèi.
At court, he managed myriad affairs;
abroad, he campaigned in all directions.
The imperial court was without unadministered matters,
and the regions were peaceful and prosperous.
His Way was as exalted as Shùn assisting Yáo;
his accumulated virtue surpassed Tàiwáng.
Méng Dù blocked off a rugged and dangerous region,
creating rebellion in a corner of the realm.
Divine troops appeared unexpectedly,
bearing a command to execute Heaven's punishment.
The good were pardoned, the guilty executed,
the prime villain and his clan were made null.
His powerful aura shook the strong Shǔ,
his martial achievements overawed the mighty Wú.
Zhūgě Bùzhīmìng,
presumptuously rebelled against the constant order of Heaven.
He gathered over a hundred thousand followers,
repeatedly invading the borders.
Our Emperor displayed divine martial prowess,
wielding the battle-axe to guard Yōng and Liáng.
Liàng then feared Heaven's might,
and collapsed before battle.
Waxing and waning naturally circulate,
times of change are inherently fraught with difficulty.
The eastern campaign reached beyond the seas,
a thousand li away, the bandit Yuān was beheaded.
Having received the testament, he regulated the seven governmental affairs,
but Cáo Shuǎng then became overbearing.
The various villains were punished and exterminated,
all blessings arrived.
Huáng Huá marked the beginning of good fortune,
Wáng Líng was the precursor of disaster.
Emperor Jǐng's "Pí Wǔ Gē,"
To the tune of "Wèi Qǔ Wèi Lì Cháng,"
Ancient tune: "Yuè Jiǔ Cháng."
Emperor Jǐng,
Intelligent and born to his age,
His great virtue matched Heaven and Earth.
The Way of an Emperor,
Establishing a foundation is already difficult,
Continuing it through generations is also not easy.
Externally, Xiàhóu Xuán,
Internally, Zhāng and Lǐ,
Three villains claimed rebellion,
Disrupting the Imperial Annals.
From Heaven, punishment was enacted,
Their treachery fully exposed.
He suppressed and prevented their gradual rise,
Secret plots could not emerge.
The guilty were all brought to justice,
His prestige shook ten thousand li.
He balanced and managed myriad affairs,
And none were left unadministered.
Zhàolíng Huán was not a true lord,
Inside and out, how chaotic it was,
Small men formed factions.
Ignorant and self-indulgent,
They distinguished not between order and chaos.
The Sagely and Wise alone made decisions,
Always combining military might with civil virtue.
From Heaven, he deposed and enthroned,
Sweeping away rainbows and parting floating clouds.
Once clouds and rainbows were cleared,
Peace and harmony lasted but a short while.
Urgent dispatches arrived one after another,
Trouble arose in the southeastern regions.
Jiǎn Qīn became a long serpent,
Externally, Féng Wú Mán.
The myriad states were in turmoil and disturbance,
Everyone in the world was fearful and uneasy.
The divine martial prowess commanded the six armies,
Our Emperor wielded the battle-axe for the campaign.
Jiǎn Qīn rose in Shòuchūn,
His vanguard occupied Xiàngchéng.
Appearing unexpectedly,
And simultaneously deploying surprise troops.
Surprise troops are indeed difficult to counter,
Victory in the temple strategies is truly hard to sustain.
The two armies met unexpectedly,
The enemy retreated, their plans rendered useless.
The tiger cavalry advanced with martial spirit,
Engaging in a great battle at Shāyáng Pō.
Qīn then fled in terror,
The routed captives scattered like clouds.
Heaven's grace pardoned the guilty,
The eastern lands released the whales.
The "Dà Jìn Piān" "Pí Wǔ Gē,"
To the tune of "Wèi Qǔ Tiān Shēng Zhēng Mín,"
Ancient tune: "Sì Fāng Huáng."
Splendid, great Jìn,
Solemnly, Emperor Wén.
Expansive and majestic,
His Way surpasses Táo Táng.
The world speaks of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
Now their glory is redoubled.
The nine virtues are clearly manifest,
Civil affairs are brilliant,
Military might is also illustrious.
His benevolence extends to the six directions,
Benefiting all regions.
Internally, Yuán Kǎi was promoted,
The court was governed with principle.
Externally, valiant ministers were selected,
At that time, they were like soaring eagles.
None did not submit,
Those who defied the mandate perished.
His benevolence matched the spring sun,
His might surpassed autumn frost.
Many distinguished gentlemen,
Shared this fragrant purity.
The perfect governance of Táng and Yú,
The four villains were overbearing.
When Jiǎn Qīn was punished,
All were solemn and reverent.
His influence moved beyond the seas,
Overseas guests arrived.
Offering their songs and music,
And all calling themselves humble subjects.
The Western Shǔ tricked Xià,
Usurping titles in their domain.
Generals were ordered to attack,
The state submitted and knelt in surrender.
The people of Wú acted recklessly,
Blocking access by sea and river.
Flying letters announced his decrees,
They responded and joined.
The former kings established myriad states,
The nine domains served as defenses.
The fallen Qín destroyed the feudal lords,
The enfeoffment order lasted not two generations.
Successive dynasties could not restore it,
Suddenly over five hundred years passed.
Our Emperor displayed sagely virtue,
Responding to the opportune moment to create institutions.
Dividing the land into five ranks,
The feudal states' boundaries were properly established.
Many civil and military assistants,
Met this auspicious assembly for a thousand autumns.
His grand enterprise overflowed within the realm,
Benevolent winds soared overseas.
"Míng Jūn Piān" "Pí Wǔ Gē,"
To the tune of "Wèi Qǔ Wèi Jūn Jì Bù Yì,"
Ancient tune: "Diàn Qián Shēng Guì Shù."
A wise ruler governs the four seas,
Listening and discerning all affairs.
When he looks upon others, there are punishments and rewards,
Those who exhaust their loyalty will surely be honored.
Orchids and angelica emerge from the wilderness,
Ascending a myriad li to the imperial court.
Thorns and weeds infest the palace steps,
They are swept away and not allowed to grow.
Competent and incompetent must not be obscured,
All officials must be rightly named.
Be diligent and cautious in action,
Then nothing attempted will fail.
An ignorant ruler does not trust himself,
His subordinates hold various deviant views.
The upright suffer slander and calumny,
Treacherous ministers seize their power.
Even if they wish to be utterly loyal,
They are silenced and dare not speak.
Why fear being silenced?
Utmost loyalty brings harm to oneself.
How could a clear stream not be pure?
Flying dust muddies its source.
Forked paths lead one astray,
It is better not to return than to go too far.
Loyal ministers stand in the sovereign's court,
With righteous countenance, disregarding their own lives.
Evil and upright cannot coexist,
Like Hú and Qín.
When Hú and Qín can merge,
Evil and upright will each have their own path.
When loyal ministers meet a wise ruler,
They are diligent and ever-renewing.
All eyes are on the main rope,
All stars revolve around the North Star.
Should they encounter an ignorant lord,
They are dismissed and become common folk.
Though humble in utility,
White cogongrass is still precious.
Ice and frost form day and night,
Orchids and osmanthus are broken for firewood.
Treacherous ministers are full of tricks and changes,
How crooked their intentions.
They are obsequious and follow every whim,
Acting according to the ruler's desires.
They seek temporary ease and immediate pleasure,
Caring not about purity or impurity.
They accumulate falsehoods to deceive the ruler of the time,
Cultivating connections to maintain their emolument.
Their words and actions contradict each other,
They are insatiable like valleys.
They risk death for reckless gain,
If exposed, their clan is exterminated.
The above are five chapters of "Pí Wǔ Gē Xíng."
"Duò Wǔ Gē Shī" two chapters, "Shèngrén Zhì Lǐ Yuè Piān."

In the past, the august Wénwǔ was misguided, but he abandoned evil for goodness. Who at my time, or my time, follows the imperial Way? He held the path of governance, ten thousand evils. The path of governance, ten thousand evils. Resplendent is the Yellow Emperor's Way within me. The path of governance, ten thousand evils. The good Way is bright and golden. The good Way, bright and golden, is imperial. Close to Dì Wǔwǔ. The Eight Tones of the Sagely Emperor. They come in unison, revered. The Eight Tones of the Sagely Emperor. They come in righteousness, in harmony. Oh, they come in righteousness. Good herbs supply our nation. Oh, listen to the myriad of sounds! Close to Dì Wǔ. Close to Dì Wǔwǔ. In rhythm and accordance, Wǔ is revered. In rhythm and accordance, the wine feast is in righteousness, in harmony. The wine feast is in righteousness. Good herbs supply our nation. Oh, listen to the myriad of sounds! Close to Dì Wǔ. Close to Dì Wǔwǔ. The lower notes are like wood, the upper notes are for the drum's righteousness. Responding to the multitude's righteousness. Is the music extended? It is righteous, oh, it is auspicious in ritual. Oh, listen to the myriad of sounds! The plain maidens are peerless in their holiness. Oh, Wǔ Yúnmén Piān. Duó Wǔ Gēxíng.
During the Tàihé reign of Wèi.
Huáng Yúnmén.
Táng Xiánchí.
Yú Sháowǔ.
Xià Xià Yīn Hù.
Five generations have existed in succession.
Shaking bells and striking metal.
Approaching Dà Wǔ.
Clear songs rise forth.
Form is primary.
Sounds harmonize the eight tones.
Accord with the lǜ and lǚ.
The body moves not in vain.
The hands are not idly raised.
In rhythm and accordance with the measure.
Throughout its entirety.
At times, play gōng and shāng.
Mixed with zhǐ and yǔ.
Below, satisfy the eyes of the multitude.
Above, accompany bells and drums.
Music to transform customs.
Assisted by virtue and ritual.
How could it be out of place?
Above are two pieces of Duó Wǔ Gēxíng.
Fú Wǔ Gē Shī five pieces, Bái Jiū Piān.
Fluttering white doves.
Flying and calling again and again.
Cherishing my lord's virtue.
Coming to gather in my lord's court.
White sparrows present good omens.
Plain feathers bright and fresh.
Soaring in the court, dancing with wings.
To respond to benevolent qián.
Chirping, cooing doves.
Some red, some yellow.
Rejoicing in my lord's grace.
Flapping wings, they come soaring.
The lingering light of the eastern wall.
Fish in the rivers and lakes.
Benevolent but not wasteful.
Respect my humble self.
Whip my good steeds.
Practice my driving.
To associate with my lord.
Rejoice in the Way, without hunger.
My heart is empty and still.
My will is soaked and moist.
Playing the qín and beating the sè.
Merely to entertain myself.
Ascending the clouds, climbing the terrace.
Drifting in the Great Purity.
Clinging to dragons, attaching to phoenixes.
Daily hoping my body becomes light.
Jìjì Piān.
Freely flying, freely dancing.
Qi flows with fragrance.
Recalling the great, splendid yellow of Sānwǔ.
There are losses.
The time is right to act.
Coming and going at the same time, this Wèiyāng.
Time passes quickly.
Approaching sāngyú.
One should only drink wine for pleasure.
Old age departs.
What is there to expect?
Many worries keep the mind troubled.
The deep pond is vast.
Fish are scarce there.
I wish to obtain Huángpǔ, where all can rely.
Grace moves people.
Unequaled in the world.
Sad songs and complete dances are endless.
Dúlù Piān.
Dúlù, Dúlù.
The water is deep, the mud is turbid.
Turbid mud is still tolerable.
Deep water kills me.
Harmonious pair of geese.
Playing by the field.
I wish to shoot the geese.
But I think of them scattered and alone.
Fluttering duckweed.
Carried lightly by the wind from afar.
How my heart accords.
With them, joining together.
An empty bed, lowered curtains.
Who knows there is no one?
Wearing splendid clothes at night.
Who can distinguish false from true?
A sword rings in its sheath.
Leaning against the bed, nothing to do.
Father's grievance unavenged.
What is the point of living?
Striped fierce tiger.
Playing in the mountains.
The tiger wishes to devour people.
It spares neither the powerful nor the worthy.
Jiéshí Piān.
To the east, I ascend Jiéshí.
To behold the vast sea.
The water so grand and surging.
Mountains and islands stand towering.
Trees grow densely.
A hundred grasses flourish abundantly.
The autumn wind soughs.
Great waves surge forth.
The journey of the sun and moon.
Seems to issue from within it.
The brilliant Milky Way.
Seems to issue from within its midst.
How fortunate and splendid!
I sing to express my aspirations.
Guān Cānghǎi.
In the first month of winter, the tenth month.
The north wind lingers.
The weather is clear and crisp.
Dense frost falls lightly.
Kūn Jī crow in the morning.
Geese fly past, heading south.
Birds of prey hide themselves.
Bears and grizzlies dwell in their lairs.
Money and hoes are put aside.
Harvests are piled in the fields.
Inns are prepared and set up.
To facilitate merchants.
How fortunate and splendid!
I sing to express my aspirations.
Dōng Shíyuè.
The local customs are different.
North of the Yellow River, it is bitterly cold.
Floating ice drifts.
Boats struggle to pass.
An awl cannot pierce the ground.
The wind's music is deep and profound.
Water dries up and doesn't flow.
The ice is firm enough to walk on.
Recluses are poor.
Brave knights take wrongs lightly.
Hearts often sigh with resentment.
Disturbed by much sorrow.
How fortunate and splendid!
I sing to express my aspirations.
Tǔ Bùtóng.
Though the divine tortoise lives long.
It still has an end.
Though the soaring serpent rides the fog.
Eventually, it turns to dust and ash.
An old steed in the stable.
Its aspiration is a thousand lǐ.
A valiant man in his twilight years.
His grand heart never ceases.
The duration of waxing and waning.
Is not solely determined by Heaven.
The blessing of nurturing peace and joy.
Can attain long life.
How fortunate and splendid!
I sing to express my aspirations.
Guī Suī Shòu. Huáinán Wáng Piān.
The King of Huáinán.
Claims to be revered.
His hundred-foot-high tower reaches to the sky.
In his rear garden, a well is dug, with a silver bed.
A golden vase and a plain rope draw cold spring water.
Drawing cold spring water.
To drink, young man.
How can a graceful young man be virtuous?
Raising his voice, he sings a tragic song, its sound reaching the heavens.
I wish to cross the river, but there is no bridge.
I wish to transform into a pair of yellow swans.
And return to my homeland.
Returning to my homeland.
Entering my old village.
Lingering in my homeland.
Working my body endlessly.
〔一０〕Numerous dances convey sounds, all without discontent.
Lingering in my hometown, wandering beyond the heavens.
Above are five pieces of Fú Wǔ Xíng.
〔一一〕Bēi Pán Wǔ Gē Shī one piece.
The [Jìn] Shì is tranquil,
the Four Seas are peaceful,
all under heaven enjoys peace and great tranquility forever.
The Four Seas are calm,
the world rejoices,
flourishing under good governance, dancing with cups and platters.
Dancing with cups and platters,
how gracefully they twirl,
turning the entire assembly upside down, wishing ten thousand years of longevity.
Heaven and sun,
beginning and end are one,
turning left and right without losing each other.
[Zhēng] and flute mourn,
wine and dance tire,
a brave man's heart is filled with emotion.
The wine in the [zūn] is sweet,
the strings and winds are clear,
may all you gentlemen get drunk and then sober up.
Drunk and then sober up,
when the times align,
the whole assembly rejoices, all saying "excellent."
The sound of strings and winds,
how can one not listen?
Also dance this platter lightly left and right.
It matches perfectly,
the whole assembly rejoices, people's lives are long.
People's lives are long,
they should make friends,
for a thousand autumns and ten thousand years, all will be old and long-lived.
End of the "Right Cup and Platter Dance Song."
"Turban Dance Song Poem," one piece.

I did not see [Gōngmò] when I was a child. What did I embrace when [Gōng] came to embrace mother? My suckling sounds, why were they flourishing? When I was a child, I should have thought of my bright moon rising above. What did I embrace when the earth came to embrace and turn? My suckling sounds, why did the earth turn south? When I was a child, I should have left. The sheep on the city wall came down to eat grass. What did I embrace when I came down to eat grass? My suckling sounds, why did your three years of sewing shrink? When I was a child, I too grew old. My tears fell profusely at the flat gate. What did I embrace? How did my tears fall? My suckling sounds, formerly I made friends with a horse-guest. When I was a child, I should have gone. I traveled through the Four Prefectures, crossed the Four Seas. What did I embrace in the seas? How did the seas come? How did the seas come, the Four Seas? My suckling sounds, the fragrant horse-head in the hot west. When I was a child, I entered the road. I managed to draw water for five [zhàng]. Alas, my suckling, who should seek the child's mother? What meaning, the fleeting money, a brisk walk, suckling, who should I seek for the child's mother? What is my suckling sound? Three needles, one hair, when they return at the junction, what meaning, the crossbow's heart is fleeting? The crossbow's heart comes from afar, child, the crossbow's heart, suckling sounds, again facing the headscarf, what meaning, what is this suckling? The headscarf, I came, child, the headscarf, mother, what, what? I again pushed, what meaning, fleeting? Suckling, pushed, I came, child, pushed, not mother, what? I again, the wheel, what meaning, fleeting? Child, why, suckling, the turning wheel, I came, child, turning, mother, what? My lord leaves, what meaning, fleeting? Child, why, my lord leaves, when he came, child, leaving, mother, what? I miss my lord leaving, what meaning, fleeting? Child, why, I miss my lord leaving, when I came, child, leaving, mother, what, what? End of "Right [Gōngmò] Turban Dance Song."
"White Silk Dance Song Poems," three pieces.
Raising both hands high, like a white swan soaring.
Light body slowly rises, how graceful and expansive.
Pausing, gazing well, with radiant countenance and bearing.
Like a dragon turning, rising and falling.
Changing with the world, truly without fixed form.
Like pushing, like pulling, pausing and moving.
The [Sòng] era is flourishing, joy is endless.
Dancing to fully express the spirit, how can it be forgotten?
Love it, who shall I give it to? To a beautiful woman.
Its quality like light clouds, its color like silver.
The robe illuminates the body, the scarf brushes away dust.
Made into a robe, the remainder made into a scarf.
The whole assembly rejoices, how can it be expressed?
Clear singing and slow dancing bring down gods.
End of piece one.
Both sleeves raised together, phoenixes soaring.
Silk skirts fluttering, like [Zhāoyí]'s radiance.
Steps create beauty, exuding fragrance.
String music and clear singing reach the three yang.
Life in the world is like a flash of lightning.
Joyful times are always few, days of suffering many.
Fortunate to reach a good season, spring flowers glow.
[Qí] dancers perform, [Zhào] women sing.
[Xīhé] drives the sun's chariot, ceaselessly moving on.
Spring dew not yet dried, severe frost falls.
All grasses wither, flowers shed their petals.
Crickets chirp by the window, cold cicadas sing.
A hundred years of life suddenly collapses.
Knowing its swiftness early, one should walk with a torch.
East to [Fúsāng], wandering in the purple court.
West to [Kūnlún], playing in the layered cities.
End of piece one.
In the bright days of spring, wind carries the fragrance of flowers.
Steps like shining jade, dancing with jade pendants.
Sounds like metal and stone, charming like [shēng] and [huáng].
Silk robes slowly turn, red sleeves flutter.
Clear singing resonates, circling the phoenix beam.
As if proud, as if thinking, pausing and soaring.
Turning eyes, shedding essence, brilliant and glowing.
About to flow, about to draw, a pair of geese soar.
Joy comes how late, emotions how long.
A wise ruler governs the world, forever singing and leading.
End of piece one.
"Old and New White Silk" combined, three pieces.
"Songs and Dances of [Sòng] [Tàishǐ] Era, Imperial Achievement Eulogies (songs from [Yáo] to King [Yuán] of [Chǔ], and Emperor [Gāozǔ],
generation after generation carried sacred virtue.)" Composed by Emperor [Míng].
The imperial enterprise was founded on virtue,
the imperial destiny aided by meritorious integration.
The descendants of [Táng] inherited a glorious path,
the offspring of [Chǔ] carried a beautiful tradition.
Emperor [Yáo] manifested deep auspiciousness,
King [Yuán] extended the distant blessings.
Accumulated good deeds passed down a supreme legacy,
blessings inaugurated a sagely line.
The declining numbers followed the golden emolument,
ascending the calendar, the water destiny flourished.
Sòng Shìníng,
in Tàishǐ.
Drunken and joyful,
full of virtue and happiness.
Ten thousand nations pay tribute,
offering longevity wine.
The Emperor is one with Heaven,
May he live forever.
Zhìbīng Dàyǎ (On Governing the Army) Composed by Emperor Míng
The King commands the army,
There is punishment but no war.
Wiping clean with a kerchief,
The ugly change their faces.
The King's retinue returns triumphant,
Sheathing weapons at the right time.
A kerchief wipes clean the center,
The four corners are quieted of dust.
Báizhùpiān Dàyǎ (White Silk Robe Poem) Composed by Emperor Míng
What is in the heart is called zhì, expressed in speech as poetry,
Sounds form into words, accompanied by pipes and strings.
Hands dance and feet stomp, a time of joy and peace,
Changing customs and transforming traditions, the foundation of the King's influence.
The qín's corner waves with rhythm, white clouds unfurl,
The xiāo and sháo harmonize, divine phoenixes arrive.
Clapping and striking to the beat, the chant begins,
When the chapter and melody end, feelings still linger.
Culture follows the same path, morals and virtues prevail,
The nation is tranquil, the people harmonious, rites and music are perfected.
The four districts' courtyards resound with praise for noble deeds,
Eight ranks on the steps sing of the voices of the noble.
The dance adornments are beautiful, the music graceful and skillful,
Gauze skirts gleam in the sun, sleeves follow the wind.
Gold and jade shimmer in rows, the fragrance of huì and shè is rich,
Their elegant posture naturally suits the Emperor's heart.
Hàn Drum and Fife Raoge, Eighteen Pieces: Zhūlù Qǔ (Red Heron Song)
Red heron,
fish and black path, zǐ yé.
What does the heron eat?
It eats under the eggplant.
It doesn't eat it,
nor does it spit it out,
It will ask the censor (one version says: remonstrator).
Sībēi Wēng Qǔ (Old Man of Sad Thoughts Song)
Old man of sad thoughts,
Táng Sī,
snatched away my beauty and defiled her,
it is the old man of sadness,
but I think of her.
Shaggy-headed (one version says: small) dog,
chasing a cunning rabbit,
eating the Lord of Jiāo,
five owl chicks.
Six owl mothers,
flying high in disarray, cannot find a peaceful roost.
Àirú Zhāng Qǔ (Ai Ru Zhang Song)
Ài and Zhāng set a net,
where is Yí?
Affairs will be accomplished,
the four seasons harmonious.
From the mountains come yellow sparrows, also with nets,
The sparrow flies high, what can be done about the sparrow?
For this desire,
who is willing to polish the room.
Shàngzhīhuí Qǔ (Ascending the Bend Song)
