His transforming influence was like heaven and earth;
who would dare to withhold themselves?
The Great Jìn Inherits the Fated Era An ancient song: My Love
The Great Jìn Inherits the Fated Era,
refers to the Sacred Emperor responding to the charts and receiving the diagram,
his transformation resembling that of the divine.
The Great Jìn Inherits the Fated Era,
with the profound virtue of the Sacred Emperor.
The times are peaceful and tranquil,
the white sun casts its light.
Responding to the charts and diagrams,
he ascended the imperial throne,
succeeding Heaven to govern the Jade Regulator,
his transforming influence resembling the divine.
How supreme, his Way as profound as Yú and Táng.
The monarch spreads his vast influence,
all officials, his arms and legs, are loyal and good,
the people are in great peace.
Majestic and illustrious,
his blessings and prosperity boundless.
The Auspicious Metal Era An ancient song: My Yellow Horse
Auspicious Era,
refers to the Sacred Emperor ascending the throne,
showing reverence in the ancestral temples,
and filial piety extending throughout the world.
The Auspicious Metal Era,
Heaven's signs are revealed.
Sacred omens appear,
rivalling the sun and moon.
As for our Emperor,
he embodies the divine and sacred.
He received the abdication from Wèi,
responding to Heaven's mandate.
The Emperor's rise,
was auspicious and evident.
He ascended the great mountain,
commanding myriad chariots.
The Emperor's aides,
are like roaring tigers.
Claws and teeth brandished,
none can resist them.
The Emperor's assistants,
aid in his pure transformation.
All affairs are well-ordered,
myriad nations congratulate him.
Gods and spirits respond,
auspicious omens manifest.
Reverently offering sacrifices,
presenting to the former emperors.
Music of the time is played,
chime stones and flutes resound.
Drums boom deeply,
bells clang grandly.
Libation vessels are placed,
filled with jade goblets.
The spirits feast and enjoy,
all are pleased and at peace.
He banquets his descendants,
blessings without limit.
Great filial piety flourishes,
moral teachings spread to myriad lands.
Oh, Majestic Our Emperor An ancient song: The Pheasant
Oh, Majestic,
refers to the Sacred Emperor receiving the mandate,
his virtue aligning with the divine.
Oh, Majestic Our Emperor,
his magnificent virtue is sacred and brilliant.
He received the abdication and ruled the world,
shining brightly and benefiting all beings.
Throughout all under heaven,
none failed to come to court.
Solemnly within the six directions,
they looked up to the supreme purity with admiration.
The myriad nations were harmonious,
raising songs of praise.
His great transformation spread universally,
earth was flat and heaven complete.
The seven regulators were aligned,
the Jade Regulator was perfectly balanced.
Lofty aides to his mandate,
numerous heroes gathered.
Diligent day and night,
they managed myriad affairs.
Though governance flourished,
they were not idle or complacent.
The Way of humility shines,
modesty never overflows.
Heaven and Earth combine their virtue,
Sun and Moon share their glory.
Illustrious and resplendent,
shining even into the deep darkness.
The three luminaries obey,
and lo, Heaven reveals an auspicious star.
Dragons and phoenixes arrive,
sweet dew falls at night.
Revering the gods and spirits,
honoring the supreme divine.
All beings rejoice and uphold him,
Heaven itself manifests its perfection.
In Mid-Spring, the Army Mobilizes An ancient song: The Sage's Journey
Mid-Spring,
refers to the Great Jìn proclaiming the teachings of civil and martial arts,
and hunting in season.
In Mid-Spring, the army mobilizes,
bringing together the people,
martial training renewed daily.
Commanders hold their standards,
artisans hold their drums,
sitting and standing in order,
with rhythm and sequence,
truly grand, both civil and martial.
The hunting ground is marked with a sacrifice to the god of roads,
laws and oaths are declared,
then the hunting ground is enclosed,
and sacrifices offered to the god of the soil,
truly the state's regulations are clear at the right time.
Civil and martial arts are used together,
this is the principle of ritual,
the ranks are like an army ready for battle,
the great teaching is clear,
who in ancient and modern times can abandon warfare?
The Great Jìn succeeds Heaven,
benefiting all beings.
Summer Hunting An ancient song: Ascending the High Terrace
Summer Hunting,
refers to the Great Jìn hunting in accordance with the season,
to eliminate harm to crops.
In the summer, hunting in the fields,
the army is about to depart.
The military and the state assume different appearances,
the civil and the martial are distinct.
So orders were issued to the multitude of officials,
to select chariots and foot soldiers,
to distinguish their names and designations,
and to record them in documents.
The King's army opens its eight gates,
its movement is like the dwelling of Shàngdì.
At this time, large banners were erected along the road,
cloud banners obscured the purple void.
The hundred officials imitated their duties,
hastening when it was time to hasten,
slowing when it was time to slow.
Turning the compass and rotating the pivot,
discarding the old chariots that had served their purpose.
Presenting game for the ancestral sacrifices,
in abundance, matching Yǒuyú.
Ah, the great Jìn,
whose virtue equals the two primordial powers,
and whose transforming influence spreads like clouds.
Mid-Autumn Hunt in the Fields
Mid-autumn.
It means that although the great Jìn possesses civil virtues,
it does not neglect military affairs,
acting in accordance with the season for killing and punishing.
In the mid-autumn hunt,
the Metal element is consistently rigid.
Cool winds are clear and sharp,
congealed dew forms frost.
The White Tiger presides over the hour,
and the green falcon soars like an eagle at the right time.
The soaring eagle is like Zhōu Shàngfù,
killing and punishing in accordance with Heaven.
In the Spring and Autumn period,
thunder and lightning displayed their awe-inspiring power,
advancing and retreating by gongs and drums.
Game was presented for sacrifice at the ancestral temple,
and the feathers and fur were sufficient for the army's treasury.
Splendid is the virtue of the great Jìn,
its fragrance and brilliance surpass the Sān Wǔ,
spreading civilization through culture,
but not neglecting military might even in peace.
Its glorious dwelling extends across the four seas,
forever enjoying the blessings of Heaven.
Following the Way of Heaven
Following the Way of Heaven.
It speaks of the great review in mid-winter,
using military power to cultivate culture,
and the virtue of the great Jìn matching Heaven.
Following the Way of Heaven,
grasping the divine tally.
In the three seasons, military affairs are also practiced,
with a great review in winter.
Ringing bells and beating drums,
banners and flags resemble rainbows.
Civil governance is within it,
military action is not inexhaustible,
mobilizing the army and swearing in the multitude,
rituals are completed and righteous deeds are carried out.
Three drives to uphold benevolence,
advancing and stopping without losing order.
Soldiers are trained,
generals are like tigers.
Ah, the fierce tigers,
their spirit mounts the blue clouds.
They lift the siege on three sides,
but do not exterminate the multitude in their killing.
Lowering banners and flags,
they array the six armies.
Offering sacrifices in abundance,
cultivating rites and culture.
Excellent is the great Jìn,
whose virtue matches Heaven.
Rewards are given for merit,
ranks await the worthy.
Feasting and merrymaking,
receiving these hundred blessings,
for a myriad years.
Táng Yáo
Táng Yáo.
It speaks of the Sage Emperor ascending the imperial throne,
his virtuous transformation illuminating the four quarters.
Táng Yáo consulted Wùchéng,
humble and modest, whence virtue arises.
Gradual accumulation eventually leads to great brilliance,
stepping on frost leads to solid ice.
Divine wisdom follows nature,
rivers and seas can still be congealed.
Shùn and Yǔ governed the hundred affairs,
Yuánkǎi and others rose in succession.
Abdication responded to Heaven's calendar,
wise sages succeeded each other through the generations.
Our Emperor ascended the imperial throne,
balancing and rectifying the standard.
His virtuous transformation reaches the four quarters,
[二四]propitious qi manifests as its sign.
The rising king awaits the dawn seated,
the fallen ruler is complacent and self-satisfied.
Reaching far begins near,
a basketful of soil builds mountains and hills.
Consulting maps and ancient records,
there is evidence of its spiritual essence.
[二五]Dark Clouds
Dark Clouds.
It speaks of the Sage Emperor employing people,
each exhausting their talents.
Dark clouds rise from mountains and peaks,
propitious qi gathers from ten thousand *lǐ*.
How gracefully the dragon soars,
how majestically the phoenix flies.
In the ancient court of Táng and Yú,
it was seen at the edge of the blue clouds.
Now it personally travels through the states,
[二六]its light overflowing beyond the heavens.
Cranes cry in the back garden,
their clear notes travel with the wind.
Chéng Tāng elevated his glorious mandate,
Yī Zhì came like a swift flight.
Zhōu Wén hunted by the Wèi River,
and then brought Lǚ Wàng back.
Matching perfectly like shadow and echo,
anticipating Heaven without defiance.
Stopping farming to compile the land's order,
unbuttoning coarse clothes to embrace Heaven's principles.
His great merits match the two lords,
his fragrance and reputation are rare in the world.
Our Emperor's multitude of talents,
how grand and magnificent their great achievements.
Valiant, they conquer the four quarters,
numerous, they manage myriad affairs.
Divine transformation inspires boundlessly,
talented individuals fill the imperial domain.
Greatly manifest even at dawn,
daily renewed, much consulted.
How abundant is the sagely enlightened virtue,
its brilliance equals the sun and moon.
Bó Yì
Bó Yì.
It speaks of the red crow carrying a scroll,
by which Zhōu arose;
now the Sage Emperor receives the mandate,
and the divine sparrow comes.
Bó Yì assisted Shùn and Yǔ,
his office presiding over mountains and rivers.
His virtue equaled the sixteen ministers,
his discerning mind penetrated all without impediment.
His wisdom governed myriad things,
he even understood the speech of birds.
Yellow sparrows respond to the clear transformation,
how gracefully they fly and gather.
Singing in harmony, they perch on garden trees,
lingering between clouds and sun.
Xià Jié was without the Way,
he spread dense nets in the mountain valleys.
The cruel priest shook the fine nets,
what could the yellow sparrows do?
Yīn Tāng revered Heaven's virtue,
removing the net on three sides.
They flew freely,
and their calls became harmonious again.
The Vermilion Bird forms the southern constellation,
the Phoenix presides over the feathered multitude.
A red bird arrived carrying a scroll,
Heaven's mandate blessed Zhōu Wén.
Divine sparrows now come to roam,
for our Heaven-mandated sovereign.
Auspicious signs bring harmony from Heaven,
rich dew descends from the blue clouds.
Orchid winds release their fragrance,
the entire world shares its scent.
Fishing Rod
[This is not included in the twenty-two *Ráogē* of Hàn.]
Fishing Rod.
It speaks of the Sage Emperor whose virtue matches Yáo and Shùn,
and who also has the assistance of Lǚ Wàng to achieve great accomplishments and bring about great peace.
The fishing rod, how long and pliant,
The sweet bait, fragrant and fresh.
Beside the stream, my mind ponders deeply,
The fine line sinks into the nine abysses.
Tài Gōng cherished this art,
It is found in the chapter of spiritual mysteries.
Contingencies change with circumstances,
Its subtlety pervades the unforeseen.
Swimming fish are startled, caught by the hook,
A latent dragon soars to the heavens.
To the heavens it soars, where does it arrive?
Flapping its wings, it flies in the Great Purity.
How different is the Great Purity?
The Two Principles emerge, perfectly formed.
The Jade Scepter rectifies the three luminaries,
Creation bestows forms upon all beings.
Retreating, I wish to assist a sagely ruler,
Uniting with the spirits in their numinous power.
My lord possesses far-reaching strategies,
Heaven and man cannot compare.
When heaven and man first united,
Dim and boundless it was.
The sun and moon had omens,
And their patterns gave rise to the Two Sovereigns.
Chí Yóu caused chaos among the people,
Huáng Dì used military force to conquer all lands.
Reaching Xià Yǔ, virtue declined,
The Three Dynasties did not equal Yú and Táng.
Our Emperor's sagely virtue matches Yáo and Shùn,
Receiving the abdication, he ascended the throne and enjoyed heavenly auspiciousness.
All within the four seas received his blessings,
None were not reverent,
All affairs were prosperous.
All affairs were prosperous,
Majestic and radiant.
Bearing a hundred blessings,
Preserving infinity,
Eternal peace.
The Twelve Pieces of Wú Drum and Wind Music, composed by Wéi Zhāo. The text "Yán Jīng Quē" [Deficiency of the Fiery Essence]
states that the Hàn dynasty was in decline.
Emperor Wǔliè roused his fierce ambition,
His thoughts were on rescuing and rectifying,
And thus the kingly enterprise began with him.
There is a Hàn song "Zhū Lù" [Red Egret],
And this piece corresponds to it.
First.
The fiery essence deficient,
The Hàn Way weak.
The imperial纲 relaxed,
Political virtue violated.
Many villains raged,
The people had no one to rely on.
Mighty Wǔliè,
Soared like a dragon.
Ascending the celestial path,
Manifesting divine might.
Beating thunderous drums,
Raising electric banners.
Gripping the celestial balance,
Securing the earthly mechanism.
Sharpening tiger troops,
Driving bears and brown bears.
Uttering divine pronouncements,
Speaking forth wondrous talents.
Zhāng Jiǎo defeated,
Biān Hán fettered.
Wǎn and Yǐng pacified,
The southern lands tranquil.
Divine martial prowess manifest,
Bountiful favor bestowed.
Golden sounds reverberated,
Benevolent winds sped forth.
Exalting a noble house,
Founding an imperial base.
Unifying the boundless,
Enduring for the future.
The above "Yán Jīng Quē" song has thirty lines in total,
Each line has three characters.
"Hàn Zhī Jì" [The End of Hàn]
speaks of Emperor Wǔliè lamenting the decline of Hàn,
And grieving the chaos of Zhuó,
Raising an army and fighting valiantly,
His achievements covering the whole land.
There is a Hàn song "Sī Bēi Wēng" [Old Man Grieving],
And this piece corresponds to it.
Second.
At the end of Hàn,
Dǒng Zhuó caused chaos.
Mighty Wǔliè,
Met the era's destiny.
Righteous armies rose,
Cloud banners erected.
Six armies disciplined,
Eight formations arrayed.
Whistling arrows flew,
White blades clashed.
Light cavalry deployed,
Armored warriors fought.
Ugly foes trembled,
Causing their multitude to scatter.
He abducted the Hàn lord,
Moved him to the western lodge.
Brave heroes raged,
The chief villain overthrown.
Illustrious Imperial Ancestor,
His achievements and fame known.
The above "Hàn Zhī Jì" song has twenty lines in total,
Eighteen lines have three characters each,
Two lines have four characters each.
"Shū Wǔ Shī" [Expanding the Martial Army]
speaks of the Great Emperor continuing the work of Wǔliè and embarking on expeditions.
There is a Hàn song "Ài Rú Zhāng",
And this piece corresponds to it.
Third.
Expanding the martial army,
He slew Huáng Zǔ.
Swiftly pacifying the fierce tribes,
Reforming and stabilizing the Western Xià.
Its burning great might,
Shook the world.
The above "Shū Wǔ Shī" song has six lines in total,
Three lines have three characters each,
Three lines have four characters each.
"Wū Lín" [Wū Lín]
speaks of Cáo Cāo, after conquering Jīngzhōu,
Sailing eastward downstream,
Desiring to contend for supremacy.
The Great Emperor ordered General Zhōu Yú to meet and defeat him at Wū Lín.
There is a Hàn song "Shàng Zhī Huí",
And this piece corresponds to it.
Fourth.
Cáo Cāo campaigned north,
Taking Liǔchéng.
Riding the victory, sweeping all before him,
He then marched south.
The Liú clan was disunited,
Eight commanderies were shaken and alarmed.
The multitude having surrendered,
Cāo massacred Jīngzhōu.
One hundred thousand ships and chariots,
Spread his reputation.
Those who debated were hesitant,
Fearing no success.
Relying on our Great Emperor,
Who manifested sagely wisdom.
Tiger-like ministers, valiant and fierce,
Zhōu and Chéng.
Defeating Cāo at Wū Lín,
Displaying their achievements and fame.
The above "Fá Wū Lín" [Conquering Wū Lín] song has eighteen lines in total,
Ten lines have four characters each,
Eight lines have three characters each.
"Qiū Fēng" [Autumn Wind]
speaks of the Great Emperor persuading the people to serve,
And the people forgetting their fear of death.
There is a Hàn song "Yǒng Lí",
And this piece corresponds to it.
Fifth.
Autumn winds raise dust,
Cold dew dampens clothes.
The horn bow's string is taut,
Doves transform into eagles.
Feathered dispatches fly from the border,
Invaders encroach upon the frontier.
Astride horses, clad in armor,
Magnanimous yet with sorrow in their hearts.
Bidding farewell to kin on the long road,
How can one know if they will live or die?
Success and failure have their divisions,
A person of ambition thinks of achieving merit.
Enticing them to the battlefield,
If the body escapes, a high reward is gained;
If the body perishes, a posthumous title is left.
The above "Qiū Fēng" song has fifteen lines in total,
Fourteen lines have five characters each,
One line has four characters.
"Kè Wǎn Chéng" [Conquering Wǎnchéng]
speaks of Cáo Cāo's ambition to unite all,
And his appointment of Zhū Guāng as the Administrator of Lújiāng.
The Emperor personally led a campaign against Guāng,
And defeated him at Wǎnchéng.
There is a Hàn song "Zhàn Chéng Nán" [Battle South of the City],
And this piece corresponds to it.
Sixth.
We overcame and destroyed Wǎnchéng,
checking the bandit invaders.
We detested these wicked evils,
obstructing the treacherous villains.
The royal army grandly marched,
overthrowing the multitude.
We eliminated the foul and removed the violent,
sheathing the weapons of war.
The people could return to farming,
and the borders were at peace.
We executed the ruler and consoled the ministers,
manifesting utmost virtue.
The above "Overcoming Wǎnchéng" song has a total of twelve lines,
of which six lines have three characters each,
and six lines have four characters each.
"Guān Bèidé" refers to
the Sǔn general Guān Yǔ abandoning the virtue of Wú,
harboring rebellious intentions.
The Great Emperor led his army across the river and captured him.
The Hàn song "Wūshān Gāo"
is analogous to this piece.
The seventh.
Guān Bèidé,
acted arrogantly.
He seized our cities,
plotting ill omens.
Raising troops for a northern expedition,
he besieged Fán and Xiāngyáng.
Alas, his arm was mightier than his thigh;
he would suffer the consequences.
How majestic is the sagely lord of Wú!
His brilliant virtue communicates with the cosmos.
Communicating with the cosmos,
he personally entrusted Lǚ Méng.
Sailing boats on the vast Hóngfàn Pond,
he ascended and traversed the long Jiāng.
How valiant and mighty is his divine prowess!
His glorious reputation soars with the wind.
He successively pacified Jiāng'ān City,
[二八] and firmly occupied Yǐng Bāng.
Yǔ was captured and beheaded,
and all the bár (various tribes) came to submit,
truly incomparable in its grandeur.
The above "Guān Bèidé" song has a total of twenty-one lines,
of which eight lines have four characters each,
two lines have six characters each,
seven lines have five characters each,
and four lines have three characters each.
"Tōng Jīngmén" refers to
the Great Emperor making good relations and forming an alliance with Shǔ.
In the midst, Guān Yǔ committed a fault of his own making,
the barbaric tribes delighted in chaos,
creating conflict and trouble.
Shǔ suspected it was a delusion,
Wú detested its deceit.
So, Wú greatly prepared its army,
and eventually restored the initial good relations.
The Hàn song "Shàng Líng"
is analogous to this piece.
The eighth.
Jīngmén borders Wūshān,
high and steep, connected to the clouds.
The barbarians relied on its dangers,
throughout generations harboring disloyalty.
The Hàn King occupied Shǔjùn,
greatly fostering good relations and kinship.
Discord arose, and suspicion grew within,
slanderous men sowed chaos among them.
The Great Emperor was greatly enraged,
and his tiger-like ministers trembled with courage.
Sweeping away the hidden lairs,
punishing the disrespectful.
Displaying his troops and radiating a fiery glow,
sharpening his might and regulating the frontiers.
Regulating the frontiers,
proclaiming his majestic martial appearance.
His achievements are grand and spectacular,
his great fame shines brightly.
Far-reaching like the Imperial era,
the sagely Wú shares that spirit.
Remote regions gaze upon the enlightened transformation,
the transformation is vast and grand.
Glorious and splendid is Great Wú,
its reign is extended, never-ending.
The above "Tōng Jīngmén" song has a total of twenty-four lines,
of which seventeen lines have five characters each,
four lines have three characters each,
and three lines have four characters each.
"Zhāng Hóngdé" refers to
the Great Emperor manifesting his great virtue,
and distant regions coming to submit.
The Hàn song "Jiāng Jìnjiǔ"
is analogous to this piece.
The ninth.
Manifesting great virtue,
surpassing divine might.
Affecting distant customs,
embracing far-off neighbors.
Pacifying the southern territories,
unifying the seacoasts.
Yuèshāng offers tribute,
Fúnán submits.
Precious goods fill the court,
what is seen is new every day.
The above "Zhāng Hóngdé" song has a total of ten lines,
of which eight lines have three characters each,
and two lines have four characters each.
"Cóng Lìshù" refers to
the Great Emperor following the auspicious signs of the charts and tallies,
and thus establishing his great reign.
The Hàn song "Yǒu Suǒ Sī"
is analogous to this piece.
The tenth.
Following the calendar's decrees,
how profound and reverent is our Emperor!
Sagely and wise, he received it from Heaven,
divine and brilliant, manifesting extraordinary signs.
He established his title and founded the imperial foundation,
his wisdom conforming to divine thoughts.
His benevolent favor permeated even insects,
vast and surpassing previous generations.
The three luminaries displayed brilliant radiance,
yin and yang proclaimed supreme governance.
Beasts with fleshy horns roamed the fields,
phoenixes nested in sacred gardens.
Divine turtles swam in ponds,
omens and prophecies were inscribed.
Yellow dragons revealed their scales,
auspicious signs recorded by the sun and moon.
Observing the past to understand the present,
our Emperor has many joyful accomplishments.
Above, he reveres the celestial phenomena,
below, he fulfills the wishes of the myriad people.
His light extends across all living beings,
every household receives his benevolence.
His civilizing influence is solemn and peaceful,
songs of praise proclaim joy and celebration.
Great Wú rises in prosperity,
with ample abundance.
The above "Cóng Lìshù" song has a total of twenty-six lines,
of which one line has three characters,
three lines have four characters each,
twenty-two lines have five characters each,
and one line has six characters.
"Chéng Tiānmìng" refers to
the ruler ascending the throne with sagely virtue,
and his moral influence reaching its peak.
[二九] The Hàn song "Fāngshù"
is analogous to this piece.
The eleventh.
Receiving the mandate of Heaven,
how glorious is his sagely virtue!
The three essences let fall their omens,
auspicious spirits manifest virtue.
Giant stones stand,
nine-grained crops grow.
Dragons have golden scales,
crows have red color.
Cart-bearers sing,
myriad men sigh in admiration.
Surpassing dragons, he ascends,
inheriting the emperor's robes.
His person is pure and excellent,
embodying profound tranquility.
Rising early to attend court,
working diligently until sunset.
Simple and easy, he values benevolence,
banishing slander and treachery.
Promoting worthy talents,
befriending the virtuous.
Equalizing fields,
flourishing crops.
Examining laws and regulations,
establishing standards.
Assessing merits and abilities,
clarifying promotions and demotions.
People strive to do their best,
with heart and strength.
The family and state are governed,
the kingly way is righteous.
We think of our Emperor,
wishing him ten thousand myriad years of life.
May he long preserve Heaven's favor,
his reign boundless.
The above "Chéng Tiānmìng" song has a total of thirty-four lines,
of which nineteen lines have three characters each,
two lines have five characters each,
and thirteen lines have four characters each.
"Xuán Huà" refers to
the ruler cultivating civility and training in martial arts,
acting in accordance with Heaven,
his benevolence flowing widely,
and the world rejoicing.
The Hàn song "Shàng Yé"
is analogous to this piece.
The twelfth.
Profound transformation models itself on Heaven,
Your Majesty is truly sagely.
Expanding the imperial principles,
You lead with the Way to pacify the people.
Beneficence spreads and flows, diffusing like clouds,
Superiors and inferiors live in harmony.
Ruler and ministers feast merrily,
Inspiring string music and song to praise the marvelous and new.
Cultivating culture, planning strategies for the state,
The time will come to prepare the carriage and tour the Luòjīn.
How peaceful and great!
The whole world rejoices,
Even the Yuè people become neighbors with all peoples.

Song of Àirúzhāng.
The vermilion carriage raises its harmonious bells,
The jade-green canopy gleams with golden ornaments.
Dark horses are adorned with ornamental straps,
Flowing banners brush against the flying rosy clouds.
Mighty halberds clear the wide road,
Ranks of swordsmen flank the grand carriage.
Let the army not clamor,
Listen to me perform the cymbal song.
The clear drum resonates with the short flute,
The bright drum keeps time with the sounding reed pipe.
People's hearts are only joyful and harmonious,
This music is clear and harmonious.
A light breeze stirs the red dust,
Still waters give rise to tiny waves.
Transcendent melodies soar towards the heavenly path,
Lingering echoes gather at the city corners.
Benevolent influence spreads throughout the world,
Its prestige shakes the nine distant regions.
Oh, armored warriors,
Strive earnestly, and remember the imperial house!
Chapter of Remembering Lord Bēi
Remembering Lord Bēi,
Cherishing the imperial robe.
How sad for the Eastern State,
The lord returns west.
The lord returns west,
Banish the two uncles.
The young ruler has awakened,
Peace and bounty restored.
Peace and bounty restored,
The sagely will is declared.
A new capital city is built,
For the people.
For the people,
Virtue is clear.
Rites are established and music composed,
Raising songs of praise.
Raising songs of praise,
Bringing about auspicious omens.
Singing phoenixes gather here,
And myriad states are prosperous.
Myriad states are prosperous,
Yet it does not cease.
Grasping hair and spitting out food,
He humbles himself before all scholars.
Only our ruler,
Succeeds Yī Yǐn and the Duke of Zhōu.
Personally witnessing a prosperous era,
What more could one seek?
Chapter of Yōng's Separation
The people of Yōng are often disloyal,
The people of Jīng harbor resentment.
Two villains do not measure virtue,
Stirring up trouble and raising their troops.
The royal army bears the imperial command,
With righteous words to correct the unruly.
The prime minister declares the widespread punitive expedition,
Raising long banners across vast distances.
Tower ships cover the riverbanks,
Armored chariots fly swiftly with heavy might.
Submit to virtue, warning those who come later,
But they still boast bravery, seeking to be first to attack.
The rebellious followers have already failed,
The foolish and wise alike turn against each other.
The frosty blades have not yet been stained,
But Yān and Yǐng are suddenly already cleared.
In the western rivers, there are no hidden rebels,
On the northern islets, there are fleeing leviathans.
Overwhelming might reaches the fertile lands,
One battle levels three cities.
The Jiāng and Hàn region is pacified,
The world sings of great peace.
Only our people of Dōngjùn,
Have always deeply offered sincerity.
Chapter of Fighting South of the City
Fighting south of the city,
Yellow dust fills the air.
Red banners flash like lightning,
Drums shake like thunder.
The powerful enemy is fierce,
Warhorses are teeming.
Spreading out across the fields,
Like massed clouds.
Relying on the great following,
Moved by righteousness,
Warriors forget their lives.
Long swords strike,
Decorated bows twang.
Flying arrows glitter dazzlingly,
Like scattered shooting stars.
Fierce cavalry charges,
Feathered plumes whirl.
Vermilion fires spread and rise,
Soaring up as flying smoke.
Valiant heroes are cut down,
High banners are captured.
Long horns sound loudly,
Echoing across the clear sky.
Wiping out hordes of bandits,
Slaughtering rebellious followers.
The remaining common people receive benefits,
Singing of revival.
Performing triumphal music,
Returning to the imperial capital.
Bestowing titles and presenting captives,
The nation is delighted.
Chapter of High Wū Mountain
Wūshān is high,
The Sānxiá are precipitous.
Green cliffs a thousand fathoms high,
Deep valleys ten thousand ren deep.
Lofty peaks crown the spirits,
Forests are dark and deep.
Mountain birds cry at night,
Morning apes call to each other.
Vast waves are swift and turbulent,
Sometimes moving on, sometimes stopping.
Sorrowful merchant travelers,
Harbor bitter feelings.
In the past, during the Yángjiǔ disaster,
The imperial order was weak.
The Lǐ clan usurped the mandate,
Xuānwǔ displayed divine power.
Those foolish rebellious groups,
Again trampled the mechanism of chaos.
The royal army launched a punitive expedition,
Sending the heads (of enemies) to the capital.
In ancient times, in governing a state,
Only virtue was valued.
Fighting strenuously and exhausting the people,
Moreover, to be rebellious and perverse,
How could one succeed?
Ah, you Bāzi,
Do not be presumptuous.
Chapter of Those Who Ascend the Mounds
Those ascending the mounds
chase and climb each other.
Their clothing is fine and beautiful,
their silk gauze rustles.
They lead their children,
ascending the high peaks.
Looking south at the city gates and watchtowers,
it is densely winding.
Princely mansions
stand at the end of the main thoroughfares.
High roofs and splendid houses
display vermilion eaves.
Overlooking deep valleys,
they pluck autumn orchids.
Gentlemen and ladies roam expansively,
reflected in the wetlands and plains.
Pointing to Yíngqiū,
they are moved by Niúshān.
When Shuǎngjiū had perished,
Jǐngjūn sighed.
Alas, the years pass quickly,
and youth does not return.
〔三四〕Spirit and ambition decline and droop,
black hair turns grey.
Wild grasses sleep,
grave mounds are dry.
Looking at these numerous graves,
my heart is filled with sorrow.
The living must die,
what is there to resent?
Take pleasure today,
express joy and delight.
Jiāng Jìn Jiǔ Piān (Bring Forth the Wine)
Bring forth the wine,
celebrating three mornings.
Prepare elaborate rituals,
offer choice delicacies.
Prosperity and decay interchange,
frost and fog intermingle.
Loosen the spring sash,
summon friends and colleagues.
Carriages are like banners,
horses trot abreast.
Embrace warmth and gentleness,
enjoy the forest and moat.
When a scholar loses his ambition,
anger and toil weigh upon his heart.
He longs for good wine,
to indulge in wandering and pleasure.
People of corrupt morals
indulge in strong wine.
They revel through long nights,
or give in to lewdness and depravity.
They repeatedly rise to dance,
uttering shrill, mournful cries.
Their forms sway tipsily,
their voices clamor noisily.
Their heads are already wet,
their will also becomes wild.
Lives are cut short,
the state perishes.
Alas, later generations,
control your drinking.
It is not the wine's fault,
who then is the calamity?
Jūn Mǎ Piān (The Lord's Horse)
The lord's horse is beautiful and calm,
its bit flying, its posture spirited.
Its swift feet tread on fleeting light,
its high steps chase the lightly flying.
Gently soft are its six reins,
brightly gleaming is its golden splendor.
Light clouds wing the feathered canopy,
a long wind waves the fine banner.
May it be willing to drive for the Fàn Shì,
gracefully treading the central capital.
How could it imitate the perverse opportunist,
galloping towards danger?
In Qiānlíng, harnessing good steeds,
Zàofù grieved for them.
Do not resent the steepness of Wú Bǎn,
but only regret the rarity of Bólè.
Forgive those bandits of Qíshān,
they truly aided the army at Hányuán.
Why do the Han and Wei lords
indulge their desires, pursuing their private interests?
The weary common people subsist on coarse food,
while horses are plagued by excessive fat.
Humans and animals trade their sustenance,
where will the common people go?
Fāng Shù Piān (The Fragrant Tree)
The fragrant tree grows in the northern courtyard,
Fēnglóng just lingers there.
Its green tips bloom through winter,
its red blossoms open to greet spring.
A beautiful woman idles in her secluded chamber,
her kind heart gentle and harmonious.
The orchid room covers its embroidered screen,
green grass covers the long steps.
At dusk, she roams by the clouds,
returning birds call to share their roost.
The bright moon fills the clear scene,
a cool breeze brushes the inner chamber.
Sorrowful strings are played in the empty hall,
exquisitely clear and mournful.
She whistles and sings with intense emotion,
grieving the feelings of this great woman.
Dust gathers on the vermilion curtains,
a faint breeze lifts her silken skirt.
How could she resent the lateness of the good times,
she only laments that her good wishes are unfulfilled.
Yǒu Suǒ Sī Piān (What I Think Of)
What I think of,
I think of people of the past.
The two disciples, Zēng and Mǐn,
were good at caring for their parents.
They kept their countenances mild,
serving them morning and evening.
Their utmost sincerity steadily
communicated with the bright spirits.
Zōu Mèngkē (Mencius of Zōu),
became a minister of Qí.
He accepted emoluments according to his worth,
not coveting glory.
When his Way was not used,
he leaned alone against a pillar.
After his three departures were admonished,
ritual and righteousness became clear.
Birds gathered,
fierce beasts attached themselves.
When merit was achieved and affairs completed,
only then did he remarry.
Alas for my life,
I encountered a cruel fate.
In youth, I suffered great misery,
enduring all hardships.
My benevolent mother's face is gone,
there is no way to see her.
Longing and eternal thoughts,
entrusted to the grave mound.
Zhì Zǐ Yóu Yuán Zé Piān (The Pheasant Roams the Plains and Marshes)
The pheasant roams the plains and marshes,
from youth, harboring an unyielding heart.
Though drinking and pecking are diligent and hard,
it does not wish to roost in gardens or forests.
In ancient times, there were reclusive scholars,
who held their aspirations high in the clear, lofty mountains.
Magnanimously they stayed at divination stalls,
paddling their oars to the shady side of streams.
Wandering free from the dust of the world,
with disheveled hair, they played the zither.
Ministers and prime ministers were not looked upon,
much less a thousand pieces of gold.
Fame and achievement are not unbeautiful,
but favor and disgrace also follow.
Ice and fire form in the six viscera,
worries and anxieties entwine the heart.
In this age, one must be magnanimous,
measuring oneself as incapable of bearing the burden.
Repeatedly pondering the warning of the flowing spring,
I am deeply alarmed.
Shàng Xié Piān (Oh Heaven!)
If the top is not straight, the bottom is hard to correct,
many wrongs cannot be rectified.
When sound is harmonious, the echo must be clear,
a straight shadow follows a straight gnomon.
Though the great transformation spreads benevolent winds,
people of Qí still bend like grass.
Since the sage kings have already departed,
who can promote the ultimate Way?
In early spring, the soft dew soaks,
at the end of the year, stern frost settles.
During peace, Kǒng and Mèng are valued,
when government is corrupt, Shēn and Shāng are honored.
Xiàogōng made rewards and punishments clear,
and for six generations, success still flourished.
Lǐ Sī indulged in excessive punishments,
which is why the Qín dynasty perished.
Hàn Xuān presided over a grand revival,
Wèi Zǔ pacified the three regions.
Likening them to a needle and a stone probe,
their effectiveness in treating illness is acclaimed.
The dense reeds are not unthick,
but how can their endlessness be known?
If the qín and sè are out of tune,
〔三五〕one must change the strings and retune.
How much more so in governing the world,
how can this essential be forgotten?
Lín Gāo Tái Piān (Ascending the High Terrace)
Ascend the high terrace,
Gaze upon the celestial path.
Lightly and airily soaring,
Rising above the Grand Void.
Bringing along Liè Zǐ,
Transcending the abode of the Di.
With cloud robes and rain sashes,
Soaring on the wind.
Commanding the dragon chariot,
Meeting at Yáo Tái.
Clear radiance floats upon the scenery,
Overflowing Péng Lái.
Crossing the western sea,
Washing in Wěi Pán.
Standing still on the cloud-capped peaks,
Plucking fragrant orchids.
Racing on swift winds,
Roaming the fiery continent.
Wishing to speak of my homeland,
Recalling old friends.
Tilting the canopy of the sky,
Waving the banner of lightning.
Descending that heavenly path,
Plunging into the deep darkness.
Bidding farewell to the immortal clan,
Returning to the human multitude.
Harboring loyalty and embracing righteousness,
Serving the enlightened monarch.
Accepting poverty or prosperity,
Following whatever befalls.
Why have far-reaching thoughts,
Allowing the heart to toil?
Yuǎn Qī Piān
A guest from a thousand *lǐ* is awaited,
His carriage hastened for the auspicious hour.
Soon, city friends are summoned,
To gather, for you are beloved kin.
High gates open their double leaves,
Long tables arrayed with esteemed guests.
In the central hall, the Liù Yì dance,
Three side chambers filled with musicians.
Flutes and pipes play mournful tunes,
Feathers wave in splendid patterns.
Metal and stone resound through the high halls,
Strings and songs stir the dust on the beams.
Elegant spears are artfully quick and agile,
Pellets and swords are truly divine.
Moving towards goodness comes from refined harmony,
Transformation is achieved through pure melody.
The host extends great blessings,
The scholars joyfully lose themselves.
May our sagely and enlightened monarch,
Soon preserve ten thousand springs.
Shí Liú Piān
Water flowing over stones,
Its waves rippling.
Originating in a secluded valley,
Forever returning to the long river.
Beholding those who pass away,
Years and months accompanying them.
As Zǐ stood by the river,
Only adding to his thoughts.
Alas, my deep sorrow,
Causing toil in waking and sleep.
Encountering these myriad troubles,
My aspirations unfulfilled.
Years pass swiftly,
Long diligence is what afflicts.
Forever speaking of being forgotten after death,
Mourning this lack of achievement.
Fortunately encountering an era of prosperity,
Bathing in good fortune.
Loosening the belt and resting peacefully,
What more is there to resent?
The benevolent ones of antiquity,
Sought it from themselves.
Empty sentiments and distant yearnings,
Ultimately end in vain.

Jīn Wǔ Gē Yī Piān,

the character for [three-six] is corrupt,
and the sounds and words are mixed.
The Sòng *Gǔ Chuī Ná Gē*
has four pieces.
The old histories say
the commentaries are incomprehensible.
The Hàn *Gǔ Chuī Ná Gē* has eighteen pieces.
According to the *Gǔ Jīn Yuè Lù*,
all are mixed with sounds, words, and charms,
and can no longer
be distinguished.)
Jiào Kān Jì
Zhì, Chapter Thirteen, Tiān Wén I
There are three schools of thought concerning the heavens:
one is Xuān Yè,
two is Gài Tiān,
and three is Hùn Tiān.
But the true form of the heavens,
the classics had no prior explanation.
Mǎ Shū's writings and Bān Zhì's records
also lacked such texts.
Cài Yōng, a Yìláng during the reign of Emperor Líng of Hàn, submitted a memorial from Shuò Fāng, saying:
"There are three schools that discuss the celestial bodies;
the teachings of Xuān Yè
are utterly without masters or methods.
The mathematical techniques of Zhōu Bì are all extant,
but when examining the celestial phenomena,
they contain many discrepancies.
Only Hùn Tiān somewhat captures its essence.
The bronze instrument on the observation platform currently used by the imperial historians
is based on its method.
It establishes an eight-foot spherical body,
fully representing the form of heaven and earth,
to correct the yellow path,
observe and detect occurrences,
to track the sun and moon,
and to calculate the five planets.
It is a profound and subtle method,
a principle that will not change for a hundred generations.
The officials have the instrument but not the original book,
and previous records also lack discussion of it.
Originally, I wished to present a memorial,
contemplate its subtle meaning,
and based on calculations,
compose a chapter.
But with my crimes and disgrace,
I am cast to the far north,
destroyed and cut off,
with no way to proceed.
It is fitting to inquire of the ministers,
and even those in secluded places,
those who understand the principles of Hùn Tiān,
to elaborate on its meaning."
At that time, eunuchs were in power,
and Cài Yōng's proposal was not adopted.
Towards the end of the Hàn dynasty, Lù Jī of Wú, who excelled in astronomy,
first expounded on the meaning of Hùn Tiān.
Wáng Fān,
a native of Lú Jiāng,
served as Zhōng Cháng Shì during the Wú period.
He was skilled in numerology
and transmitted Liú Hóng's *Qián Xiàng Lì*.
Based on the *Qián Xiàng* method, he constructed a Hùn Yí,
and established his theory and calculations, saying: "Previous scholars' old theories stated
that the body of heaven and earth
is shaped like a bird's egg.
Heaven encloses earth,
like a shell wraps around the yolk.
It revolves endlessly,
its form is perfectly round
and continuous,
hence it is called Hùn Tiān.
The circumference of heaven is 365 degrees and 589/145 parts of a degree.
Half of it is exposed above the ground,
and half is beneath
the ground.
Its two ends are called the South Pole and the North Pole.
The North Pole is elevated 36 degrees above the ground,
and the South Pole is also 36 degrees below the ground.
The two poles are separated by 182 and a half degrees,
plus a little more.
The region around the North Pole, with a diameter of 72 degrees,
is always visible and never hidden;
this is called the upper boundary.
The region around the South Pole, 72 degrees,
is always hidden and not
visible;
this is called the lower boundary.
The celestial equator girdles the heavens,
each pole being a little more than 91 degrees away.
The ecliptic is the path followed by the sun.
Half of it is outside the equator,
and half is inside the equator.
It intersects the equator in the east at a little less than 5 degrees of Jiǎo,
and in the west at a little more than 14
degrees of Kuí.
The furthest it extends outside the equator
is 24 degrees from the equator,
which is 21 degrees of Dǒu.
The furthest it extends inside the equator
is also 24 degrees,
which is 25 degrees of Jǐng.
The winter solstice is at 21 degrees of Dǒu,
which is a little more than 115 degrees from the pole.
When the sun is furthest south,
it is furthest from the pole,
hence the shadow is longest.
The ecliptic at 21 degrees of Dǒu
rises at Chén and sets at Shēn,
thus the sun also rises at Chén and sets at Shēn.
The sun travels 146 degrees over the ground during the day,
plus a little more,
hence the day is short;
the night
It travels 219 and a little less degrees below the earth,
hence the night is long.
After the winter solstice (Nánzhì),
the sun gradually approaches the pole,
hence the shadow gradually shortens.
The sun's daytime journey above the earth
covers slightly more degrees,
hence the day is slightly longer;
its nighttime journey below the earth covers slightly fewer degrees,
hence the night is slightly shorter.
The sun's position is slightly further north,
hence the sun rises and sets slightly further north,
until
the summer solstice (Xiàzhì).
At the summer solstice, the sun is at 25 degrees in Jǐng,
67 and a little more degrees from the pole.
On this day, the sun is furthest north,
closest to the pole,
and the shadow is shortest.
The ecliptic at 25 degrees in Jǐng
exits at Yín and enters at Xū,
hence the sun also exits at Yín and enters at Xū.
The sun's daytime journey above the earth covers 219 and a little less degrees,
hence the day is long;
its nighttime journey below the earth
covers 146 and a little more degrees,
hence the night is short.
After the summer solstice (Xiàzhì),
the sun gradually moves further from the pole,
hence the shadow gradually lengthens.
The sun's daytime journey above the earth covers slightly fewer degrees,
hence the day is slightly shorter;
its nighttime journey below the earth covers slightly more degrees,
hence the night is slightly longer.
The sun's position is slightly further south,
hence the sun rises and sets slightly further south,
until the winter solstice (Nánzhì),
when it returns to its initial state.
Dǒu is 21 degrees,
Jǐng is 25 degrees,
the difference in north-south position is 48 degrees.
On the vernal equinox,
the sun is at 14 and a little more degrees in Kuí.
On the autumnal equinox,
the sun is at 5 and a little less degrees in Jiǎo.
This is the midpoint where the two paths, the ecliptic (Huángdào) and the celestial equator (Chìdào), intersect.
They are both 91 and a little more degrees from the pole.
Their north-south position is between 21 degrees in Dǒu and 25 degrees in Jǐng,
hence the shadow length is in the middle of the longest and shortest at the solstices.
Kuí at 14 degrees
and Jiǎo at 5 degrees
exit at Mǎo
and enter at Yǒu,
hence the sun also exits at Mǎo and enters at Yǒu.
The sun's daytime journey above the earth
and its nighttime journey below the earth
both cover 182 and a half and a little more degrees.
Therefore, the visible portion of the clepsydra is
50 kè,
and the invisible portion of the clepsydra is 50 kè,
which is called "equal day and night".
The day and night of the heavens
are divided by the sun's rising and setting,
while the day and night of humans
are delimited by
dusk and dawn.
It becomes bright two and a half kè before the sun rises,
and it becomes dark two and a half kè after the sun sets.
Thus, five kè are deducted from the night to add to the day,
which is why at the vernal and autumnal equinoxes, the
day is 55 kè according to the clepsydra.
The movements of the three luminaries
are not necessarily constant.
Astrologers calculate them,
and there are similarities and differences,
hence the calendrical methods of various schools are disparate.
The Luòshū Zhēnyào Dù (洛書甄燿度) and the Chūnqiū Kǎoyì Yóu (春秋考異郵) both state that the circumference of the heavens is 1,071,000 lǐ.
One degree is 2,932 lǐ, 71 bù, 2 chǐ, 7 cùn, and 362/487 of a cùn.
Lù Jì (陸績) said: "The diameter of the heavens from east to west and north to south is 357,000 lǐ."
This means that
the circumference is three times the diameter.
Upon examination, the diameter is more than one-third of the circumference.
At a ratio of 142 for the circumference and 45 for the diameter,
then the diameter of the heavens is 339,401 lǐ, 122 bù, 3 chǐ, 2 cùn, and 9/71 of a cùn.
The Zhōulǐ (周禮) states:
"The shadow at the summer solstice (Rìzhì)
is one chǐ and five cùn,
which is called the 'center of the earth' (Dìzhōng)."
Zhèng Zhòng (鄭衆) explained:
"The length of the earth-groma (Tǔguī)
is one chǐ and five cùn.
On the day of the summer solstice (Xiàzhì),
an eight-chǐ gnomon is erected.
When its shadow is equal to the earth-groma,
it is called the 'center of the earth' (Dìzhōng),
which is now Yǐngchuān Yángchéng (潁川陽城) land."
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) said:
"Generally, the sun's shadow on the ground changes by one cùn per thousand
lǐ.
If the shadow is one chǐ and five cùn,
it means it is 15,000 lǐ south of the point directly beneath the sun."
Based on this,
the sun should be 80,000 lǐ from the earth below it.
If the sun shines obliquely on Yángchéng,
then this is half the diameter of the heavens.
The celestial body is round like a pellet,
the earth is in the middle of the heavens,
and Yángchéng is the center.
Then the sun, in spring, autumn,
winter, and summer,
at dusk and dawn, day and night,
would be equidistant from Yángchéng,
with no change in distance.
Therefore, we know that the oblique ray from the sun to Yángchéng is half the diameter of the heavens.
In terms of the Gougu (句股) method (Pythagorean theorem),
15,000 lǐ is the gōu (勾, shorter leg),
80,000 lǐ is the gǔ (股, longer leg),
and the oblique ray from the sun to Yángchéng
is the xián (弦, hypotenuse).
Applying the method of finding the hypotenuse from the two legs,
we get 81,394 lǐ, 30 bù, 5 chǐ, 3 cùn, 6 fēn.
This is half the diameter of the heavens
and the distance from the earth to the heavens.
Doubling this
gives 162,788 lǐ, 61 bù, 4 chǐ, 7 cùn, 2 fēn,
which is the diameter of the heavens.
Multiplying this
by the ratio of circumference to diameter,
and dividing by the diameter ratio,
we get 513,687 lǐ, 68 bù, 1 chǐ, 8 cùn, 2 fēn,
which is the circumference of the heavens.
This is 557,312 and a fraction lǐ less than the Zhēnyào Dù and Kǎoyì Yóu figures.
One degree is 1,406 lǐ, 124 bù, 6 cùn, and 19,039/107,565 of a cùn,
which is 1,525 lǐ, 256 bù, 3 chǐ, 3 cùn, and 160,730/215,130 of a cùn less than the old degree.
The two paths, the ecliptic (Huángdào) and the celestial equator (Chìdào),
intersect with each other,
with a separation of 24 degrees between them.
By using the liǎngyí (兩儀) method,
both paths are 365 and a fraction degrees.
From this, we know that the celestial body is round like a pellet.
However, Lù Jì (陸績) constructed an armillary sphere (Húnyàng)
whose shape was like a bird's egg.
If so, the ecliptic (Huángdào) should be longer than the celestial equator (Chìdào).
Lù Jì (績) said
the diameter of the heavens from east to west and north to south is 357,000 lǐ.
If so, Lù Jì (績) also considered the heavens to be perfectly round.
But if the armillary sphere (Húnyàng) is like a bird's egg,
then it contradicts
itself.
The
ancient old armillary spheres (Húnyàng) used two fēn as one degree,
making a total circumference of seven chǐ, three cùn, and a half fēn.
Zhāng Héng (張衡) later modified it,
using four fēn as one degree,
making a total circumference of one zhàng, four chǐ, six cùn.
Fān (蕃) considered the ancient system too small,
with stars too dense;
Zhāng Héng's (衡) instrument too large,
difficult to move.
He then redesigned the armillary sphere (Húnyàng),
using three fēn as one degree,
making the total circumference of the heavens one zhàng, nine cùn, five fēn, and three-quarters of a fēn.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Hé Chéngtiān debated the form of the armillary sphere, saying:
"Upon careful consideration of previous theories,
and observing the armillary sphere,
studying its meaning,
I have come to realize that the shape of heaven is perfectly round,
and water encircles it below.
As for the 'four quarters,'
the East is called Yánggǔ,
where the sun rises;
the West extends to Méngsì,
where the sun sets.
Zhuāngzǐ also said: 'The fish of the Northern Míng
transformed into a bird
and will migrate to the Southern Míng.'
This is also an ancient record,
serving as proof that all four quarters are water.
The four quarters all being water
is what is meant by the 'Four Seas.'
In the cycle of the Five Phases,
water is generated by metal;
therefore, all rivers originate
from mountains,
flowing from high to low,
converging into the sea.
The sun, being the essence of Yang,
shines with scorching heat.
When it enters the water overnight,
the areas it passes through are parched.
The convergence of all rivers
is sufficient to replenish it,
so drought does not diminish it,
nor does flooding increase it.
Wáng Fān's calculations regarding the diameter of the heavens
are close to the truth."
Tàizhōng Dàfū Xú Yuán said:
"The construction of the armillary sphere
is not clearly known as to its origin.
Wáng Fān said: 'The Yú Shū states:
"It resided in the xuánjī and yùhéng,
with which the Seven Regulators were aligned."
This refers to the sun, moon, and five planets of the present-day armillary sphere.
Zhèng Xuán explained:
"The moving mechanism is jī,
that which holds steady is héng;
both are made of jade.
Observing their movements
determines whether the abdication was right or wrong."
The armillary sphere
was an old instrument of the Xīhé clan,
passed down through generations,
called jīhéng.
Its origins
are well-established.
However, this instrument was set up on the observation terrace,
and the records of the historians were kept secret,
so scholars rarely heard of or saw it.
Those who indulged in forced interpretations,
not understanding the meaning of jīhéng,
upon seeing the mention of the Seven Regulators,
mistakenly took them for the seven stars of the Northern Dipper,
fabricating empty theories
and attributing them to apocryphal texts and prognostications.
Sǐ Qiān and Bān Gù
were still deluded by this.
Zhèng Xuán possessed profound and elegant talent,
with tranquil and refined thought,
seeing beyond others,
correcting this theory.
Even if a sage were to reappear,
he would not change these words.'
Wáng Fān's statement is thus.
Indeed, to accurately observe the seven luminaries,
one must take their movements as the basis.
If an instrument is set up to imitate this,
how can one determine their waxing and waning?
Inferring from this,
it is not a comprehensive theory.
Even if, in the era of Táng and Yú,
there was already an armillary sphere,
and it passed through the Three Dynasties
as a fixed standard,
and later generations diligently followed it,
who would dare to challenge or change it?
Yet the instruments of the three theories
were confusing and indistinguishable,
until Yáng Xióng finally questioned the theories of Gài and Hún.
Zhāng Héng, serving as Tàishǐlìng,
then cast bronze to create a model.
Héng's biography states: 'His creation of the armillary sphere
for calculating Yin and Yang
was most detailed and precise.'
Therefore, we know that before Héng,
this instrument did not exist.
Wáng Fān also said: 'The Hún Tiān suffered during the chaos of Qín,
and its masters and followers were lost,
and its texts were missing;
only the Hún Tiān instrument remained on the observation terrace.'
However, it was neither the xuán jade of Shùn,
nor is the creation of the present instrument recorded.
To consider apocryphal texts as forced interpretations
and Zhèng Xuán as truly learned,
but to selectively believe without evidence
is not acceptable.
Xuányù is a noble and beautiful name,
and jīhéng is a detailed designation,
which is why earlier scholars took them to be the seven stars of the Northern Dipper,
the celestial mechanism's rotation.
Sages looked up and looked down
to discern changes in the times.
Sages looked up and looked down
to discern changes in the times."
The historian comments: Setting up an instrument to symbolize
and fix its degrees,
if it matches, it is auspicious;
if it misses, it is inauspicious.
Using it for divination and observation,
what is there to object to?
The Hún texts were lost,
hence the debates of Xuān and Gài.
Their methods were both deficient,
hence later generations did not elaborate on them.
Yáng Xióng's Fǎyán says:
"Someone asked Yáng Xióng about the Hún Tiān.
Yáng Xióng replied: 'Luòxià Hóng designed it,
Xiānyú Wàngrén calculated it,
and Gěng Zhōngchéng modeled it.
It was almost without error.' "
If the question was about the fixed shape of heaven,
or the precision of the armillary sphere,
then Yáng Xióng should have answered with the principles of Hún.
But by mentioning these three individuals,
we know that these three individuals manufactured the armillary sphere
to chart the sun's path and the celestial longitudes.
The questioner was probably asking about the precision of the armillary sphere,
not its underlying principles.
From this, we can deduce
that such an instrument already existed in Cháng'ān during the Western Hàn dynasty.
Was it lost due to war and chaos,
which is why Zhāng Héng re-cast it?
Wáng Fān also recorded the dimensions of ancient armillary spheres and Zhāng Héng's revised designs,
which clearly shows that this instrument was not first created by Zhāng Héng.
The armillary sphere created by Zhāng Héng
was passed down to the Wèi and Jìn dynasties.
When Zhōnghuá was defeated,
it was submerged by the Rónglǔ.
The old instruments of Jī and Fān
also no longer existed.
In the fourteenth year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān of Jìn (418 CE),
Gāozǔ pacified Cháng'ān
and obtained Zhāng Héng's old instrument.
Although its form was complete,
it did not have the fixed stars or seven luminaries attached.
In the thirteenth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén (436 CE),
an imperial edict ordered Tàishǐlìng Qián Lèzhī to cast a new armillary sphere.
Its diameter was six feet eight fen less,
its circumference one zhang eight chi two cun six fen less.
The earth was inside the heaven,
and the yellow and red paths (ecliptic and equator) were established,
as well as the north and south polar circles for the twenty-eight mansions,
the North Dipper, and the polar star.
Each degree was five fen.
The sun, moon, and five planets were placed on the ecliptic.
A clepsydra was set up,
and water was used to rotate the instrument,
so that the central stars at dusk and dawn
corresponded with the heavens.
In the seventeenth year (440 CE),
a smaller armillary sphere was also made,
with a diameter of two feet two cun
and a circumference of six feet six cun.
Each fen was one degree.
The inner and outer palaces of the twenty-eight mansions were installed,
with white, black, and yellow beads representing the stars of the three schools.
The sun, moon, and five planets
were all situated on the ecliptic.
The theory of the Gài Tiān (Canopy Heaven) model,
is said to have originated when Zhōu Gōng Dàn inquired about it from the Yīn-Shāng dynasty,
but this is a fabricated claim.
Its book is titled Zhōu Bì.
Bì means a gnomon.
It describes the numbers of the celestial sphere.
Its theory states:
"Heaven is like an inverted cover,
and Earth is like an inverted basin.
The middle of the Earth is high and slopes down on all four sides.
The sun and moon revolve with the heavens,
hiding behind the high parts of the Earth,
which creates day and night.
Heaven and Earth are separated by a total of eighty thousand *lǐ*.
The middle part of Heaven
is sixty thousand *lǐ* higher than its outer rim,
and the high part of the Earth
is twenty thousand *lǐ* higher than Heaven's outer rim."
Someone once asked Yáng Xióng about Gài Tiān.
Yáng Xióng said:
"It's a canopy!
It's a canopy!"
He raised eight objections to it.
Zhèng Xuán further raised two objections to it.
Those who studied the Gài Tiān theory
could not resolve these issues.
Liú Xiàng's Wǔ Jì Shuō (Discourse on the Five Records) states that,
according to the Xià calendar, all the constellations, the sun, and the moon move westward.
The constellations are fast, followed by the sun,
and the moon is the slowest.
Therefore, the sun and the constellations set together in the west in the evening;
after ninety-one days,
this constellation is in the north;
after another ninety-one days,
this constellation is in the east;
and after ninety-one days,
it is in the south.
This indicates that the sun moves slower than the constellations.
Three days after the new moon,
the sun sets and the moon appears in the west;
by the fifteenth day,
the sun sets and the moon appears in the east;
just before the end of the month,
the sun has not yet risen,
but the moon appears in the east.
This demonstrates that the moon moves slower than the sun,
and they both move westward.
Liú Xiàng challenged this with the Hóng Fàn Zhuàn (Commentary on the Great Plan) which says:
"When the moon appears in the west on the last day of the month,
it is called *tiǎo*.
Tiǎo means
speed.
When the moon appears in the east on the new moon,
it is called *cè nì*.
Cè nì means
slow and hesitant to advance.
When stars move westward,
the official historians call it retrograde motion."
All three of these statements
contradict the Xià calendar.
Tracing their intent,
they seem to be creations of those who favored novel ideas.
During the Xiánkāng reign of Emperor Chéng of the Jìn dynasty,
Yú Xǐ of Kuàijī composed the Ān Tiān Lùn (Treatise on the Fixed Heaven),
believing that
"Heaven is infinitely high,
and Earth is immeasurably deep.
Earth has a static body,
and Heaven has a constantly stable form.
Considering their general form,
they should cover each other.
If one is square, both are square;
if one is round, both are round.
There is no reason for them to be different in shape."
Yú Xǐ's paternal grand-ancestor, the Administrator of Héjiān, Sǒng, also established the Qióng Tiān Lùn (Treatise on the Dome Heaven), saying:
"The shape of Heaven is vaulted,
like an eggshell,
its edges reaching the four seas,
floating above the primal *qì*."
And Yáo Xìn, the Grand Minister of the Court of Wú, composed the Xīn Tiān Lùn (Treatise on the Bright Heaven), saying:
"I once read in the Hàn Shū that: during the winter solstice, the sun is in Qiāniú,
far from the celestial pole;
during the summer solstice, the sun is in Dōngjǐng,
near the celestial pole.
To use this to determine the length of the day,
I believe that the Great Ultimate (celestial pole) is in the center of the twenty-eight lunar mansions.
Although there are differences in distance,
they cannot be multiples of each other."
Now, the Xīn Tiān theory
believes that
"during the winter solstice, the celestial pole is low,
and the heavenly motion is closer to the south,
so the sun is far from people,
and the Big Dipper is close to people.
Northern *qì* arrives,
hence it is icy cold.
During the summer solstice, the celestial pole rises,
and the heavenly motion is closer to the north,
so the Big Dipper is far from people,
the sun is close to people,
Southern *qì* arrives,
hence it is scorching hot.
When the celestial pole is high,
the sun travels shallowly within the Earth,
thus the night is short,
and Heaven is high above the Earth,
thus the day is long.
When the celestial pole is low,
the sun travels deeply within the Earth,
thus the night is long,
and Heaven is shallow beneath the Earth,
thus the day is short.
Therefore, the heavenly motion in winter conforms to the Hùn Tiān (Armillary Sphere) model,
and in summer to the Gài Tiān model."
Based on this explanation, the character
"軒昂" (xuānáng - lofty) should have used
the character
"軒" (xuān),
but it used
"昕" (xīn).
This is unclear.
All three theories are discussions that favor novel ideas,
and are far off the mark.
Regarding astronomical fixed stars,
the constant constellations of the inner and outer palaces,
previous histories have already detailed them.
Now we only record star changes since the Huángchū era of Emperor Wén of Wèi as the Astronomical Treatise,
to continue Sīmǎ Biāo's work.

which was the fulfillment of the splitting and flowing north and south.
When Zhōng Huì rebelled,
the three armies were enraged,
with a rumbling sound,
a sign of the anger of the soldiers and generals.
In the tenth month of the fourth year of Jǐngyuán,
Suìxīng guarded Fáng.
The prognostication said:
"Generals and prime ministers will have worries."
Another interpretation said:
"There will be a great amnesty."
In the first month of the following year,
Grand Commandant Dèng Ài and Minister of Education Zhōng Huì were both executed,
and a special amnesty was granted for Yìtǔ.
In the autumn of the second year of Xiánxī,
another great amnesty was granted.
In the fifth month of the second year of Xiánxī of Chénliú Wáng,
a comet appeared in Wángliáng,
over ten feet long,
white in color,
pointing southeast,
and disappearing after twelve days.
The prognostication said:
"Wángliáng
is the Son of Heaven's imperial four-horse chariot.
A comet sweeping it away
is a sign of abdication and dynastic change,
an omen of removing the old and establishing the new.
White color signifies mourning.
Wángliáng is in the Dōngbì constellation,
and also corresponds to Bìngzhōu."
In the eighth month,
Jìn Wén Wáng passed away.
In the twelfth month,
the emperor abdicated in favor of Jìn.
In the first month, on the day Bǐngxū, of the fourth year of Tàishǐ of Jìn Wǔdì,
a comet appeared in Zhěn,
bluish-white in color,
moving northwest,
then turning eastward.
〔二二〕The prognostication said:
"It signifies war and loss.
Zhěn also corresponds to Chǔ."
In the third month,
Empress Dowager Wáng passed away.
In the tenth month,
Wú general Shī Jì raided Jiāngxià,
Wàn Yù raided Xiāngyáng,
and Posterior General Tián Zhāng and Jīngzhōu Inspector Hú Liè and others defeated and repelled them.
In the seventh month of the fourth year of Tàishǐ,
stars fell like rain,
all flowing westward.
The prognostication said:
"Falling stars signify rebellion of the people,
flowing westward is an omen of the people of Wú returning to Jìn."
Two years later,
Sūn Xiù, the commander of Xiàkǒu in Wú, led over two thousand troops and surrendered.
In the ninth month of the fifth year of Tàishǐ,
a broom star appeared in Zǐgōng,
the prognostication being as above.
Zǐgōng
is the inner palace of the Son of Heaven.
Ten years later,
Empress Wǔyuán Yáng passed away.
In the twelfth month of the tenth year of Tàishǐ
, a comet appeared in Zhěn.
The prognostication said:
"Troops will rise throughout the world.
Zhěn is also the division of Chǔ."
In the sixth month of the second year of Xiánníng
, a comet appeared in Dī.
The prognostication said:
"The Son of Heaven will lose his virtue and change his administration.
Dī is also the division of Yǎnzhōu."
In the seventh month
, a comet appeared in Dàjiǎo.
Dàjiǎo represents the imperial seat.
In the eighth month
, a comet appeared in Tàiwēi
, extending to Yì, Běidǒu, and Sāntái.
The prognostication said:
"Tàiwēi is the court of the Son of Heaven
, and great men dislike it."
Another interpretation said:
"There will be a relocation of the king.
Yì is also the division of Chǔ."
"Běidǒu governs killing and punishment
, and Sāntái are the Sāngōng."
In the third year
, a comet appeared in Wèi.
Wèi
is the division of Xúzhōu.
In the fourth month
, a comet appeared in Nǚyù.
Nǚyù represents the imperial harem.
In the fifth month
, it appeared again in the East.
In the seventh month
, a comet appeared in Zǐgōng.
The prognostication said:
"The world will change its master."
In the third month of the fifth year
, a comet appeared in Liǔ.
The prognostication said:
"External officials will insult the ruler.
Liǔ is also the division of Sānhé.
Dàjiǎo, Tàiwēi, Zǐgōng, and Nǚyù
, all represent the ruler."
The following year Wú perished
, which was its fulfillment.
Comets signify military disasters and funerals.
In the campaign against Wú
, troops from Sānhé, Xú, and Yǎn all marched out
and engaged in battle in the lands of Wú and Chǔ.
Below the Chancellor and Grand Commandant of Wú
, dozens were executed by beheading and displaying their heads
; among the lesser generals and soldiers
, tens of thousands were beheaded.
These were all its omens.
In the Spring and Autumn period, when a comet appeared in the North
, the rulers of Qí, Lǔ, Jìn, Zhèng, Chén, Sòng, and Jǔ
all suffered the calamity of killing and turmoil.
When a comet appeared in the East
, Chǔ annihilated Chén,
and the Sānjiā and the Tián clan divided and usurped Qí and Jìn.
At the end of the Hàn Wéndì reign
, a comet appeared in the West
, and later the Seven States of Wú and Chǔ were exterminated.
Upon examination, from the end of Tàishǐ to the beginning of Tàikāng
, numerous calamities and anomalies appeared
, yet the Jìn clan flourished
and Wú was indeed destroyed.
It is clear that the celestial changes were related to Wú.
In ancient times, in the third year of Hàn
, a comet appeared in Dàjiǎo
, and Xiàng Jí perished because of it
, while the Hàn clan had no trouble.
This was because it concerned Xiàng's destiny.
In the time of Wú and Jìn
, the world was split horizontally.
When Dàjiǎo was affected by a comet, Wú perished
, which is the same as Xiàng's affair.
Later scholars all attributed the Xiánníng calamity to the Jìn dynasty
, which is incorrect.
In the fourth month of the fourth year of Xiánníng of Jìn Wǔdì
, the Chīyóuqí appeared.
According to star treatises
, the Chīyóuqí resembles a comet
, but its tail is curved like a flag.
It was seen during the time of Hàn Wǔdì
, and stretched across the sky.
It was seen again during the time of Xiàndì
, stretching over ten *zhang*
, all of which were long stars.
During the time of Wèi Gāoguìdì, it appeared as a white gas.
Upon reviewing various records
, there were no long stars that year
, so it must have been another strange gas.
Two years later
, three forces were mobilized to attack Wú
, which was its fulfillment.
Upon the death of Wǔdì
, troops rose again throughout the world
, leading to the downfall of all Zhūxià.
In the ninth month of the fourth year of Xiánníng
, Tàibái should have been visible but was not.
The prognostication said:
"This is called 'losing its mansion'.
If there is no broken army
, there will surely be a deceased king's tomb.
Also, there will be a fallen state."
At this time, Yáng Hù presented a memorial requesting to attack Wú
, and the Emperor permitted it.
In the eleventh month of the fifth year
, the army set out
, and Tàibái first appeared in the evening in the West.
In the third month of the first year of Tàikāng
, the Wú army was utterly defeated
, Sūn Hào surrendered with his hands bound and begged for death
, and the state of Wú was thus destroyed.
In the eighth month of the second year of Tàikāng of Jìn Wǔdì
, a comet appeared in Zhāng.
The prognostication said:
"It signifies military disaster and funerals."
As a division of Zhōu
, the calamity would be in Luòyì.
In the eleventh month
, a comet appeared in Xuānyuán.
The prognostication said:
"The imperial harem will be affected by this."
On the *wùshēn* day of the third month of the fourth year
, a comet appeared in the Southwest.
On the *guǐchǒu* day of the third month of the fourth year
, Qí Wáng Yōu died.
On the *wùyín* day of the fourth month
, Rèchéng Wáng Líng died.
On the *jǐhài* day of the fifth month
, Lángxié Wáng Zhòu died.
On the *wùmǎo* day of the eleventh month
, Xīndū Wáng Gāi died.
In the third month of the eighth year of Tàikāng
, Yínghuò guarded Xīn.
The prognostication said:
"The king dislikes this."
On the *jǐyǒu* day of the fourth month of the first year of Tàixī
, Wǔdì died.
In the ninth month of the eighth year of Tàikāng
, a comet appeared in Nándǒu
, tens of *zhang* long
, and vanished after more than ten days.
The prognostication said:
"Dǒu governs rank and emoluments
; the state will have great sorrow."
Another interpretation said:
"A comet in Dǒu
means the king is ill
, a minister will execute his father
, the world will change its government
, and great chaos and war will arise."
In the fourth month of the first year of Tàixī
, a guest star appeared in Zǐgōng.
The prognostication said:
"It signifies military disaster and funerals."
At the end of Tàikāng
, Wǔdì indulged in banquets and excursions
and was frequently ill.
On the *jǐyǒu* day of this month
, the Emperor died.
In the first year of Yǒngpíng
, Empress Jiǎ executed Yáng Jùn and his partisans
, exterminating their three clans.
Empress Yáng Tàihòu was also killed.
In this year
, Rǔnán Wáng Liàng, Tàibǎo Wèi Guàn, and Chǔ Wáng Wěi were also executed
, which was the fulfillment of the royal house's military disasters and funerals.
Collation Notes
Treatise 14, Astronomy 2
In the second month of the second year of Yuánkāng of Jìn Huìdì
, there was a great裂 in the northwest of the sky.
According to Liú Xiàng's explanation:
"When the sky cracks
, *yáng* is insufficient;
when the earth quakes
, *yīn* is excessive."
At this time, the ruler remained silent
, and the empress monopolized power.
In the fourth month of Yuánkāng 3rd year (293 CE),
Huǒxīng (Mars) guarded Tàiwēi for sixty days.
The prognostication said:
"The feudal lords and Three Ducal Ministers will conspire against their superior,
and there will certainly be an execution of a minister."
Another interpretation said:
"The Son of Heaven's state will perish."
In this spring,
Tàibái (Venus) guarded Bì,
lasting over a hundred days until this point.
The prognostication said:
"There will be the sorrow of urgent decrees."
Another interpretation said:
"The prime minister will perish.
It also indicates unrest on the borders."
In this year,
Zhèn (Saturn), Suì (Jupiter), and Tàibái (Venus) gathered in Bì and Mǎo.
The prognostication said:
"This signifies warfare and death.
Bì and Mǎo
are the territory of Zhào."
Later, Empress Jiǎ (Jiǎ Hòu) trapped and killed the Crown Prince.
Prince Lún of Zhào (Zhào Wáng Lún) then deposed the Empress
and killed her,
and executed Zhāng Huà and Péi Wěi.
He then usurped the throne,
and deposed the Emperor as the Grand Emperor Emeritus (Tàishàng Huáng).
From this point, chaos and calamity spread throughout the empire.
In the fourth month of Yuánkāng 5th year (295 CE),
a comet appeared in Kuí,
and moved to Xuānyuán and Tàiwēi,
passing through Sāntái and Dàlíng.
The prognostication said:
"Kuí is Lǔ,
and also represents weapons in the armory.
Xuānyuán represents the imperial harem.
Tàiwēi is the Emperor's court.
Sāntái represents the Three Ducal Ministers (Sān Sī).
Dàlíng signifies events of accumulated corpses and death."
The following year,
the imperial armory caught fire,
and the Western Qiāng revolted.
Five years later,
Sīkōng Zhāng Huà met with disaster.
Empress Jiǎ was deposed and died,
and Duke Mì of Lǔ (Lǔ Gōng Jiǎ Mì) was executed.
The year after that,
Prince Lún of Zhào usurped the throne.
Thereupon, the Three Princes (Sān Wáng) raised armies to punish Lún,
and over a hundred thousand soldiers and common people died in battle.
On the night of Bingwǔ in the sixth month of Yuánkāng 6th year (296 CE),
a crooked arrow (comet) traveled southeast from Dǒukuí.
According to the prognostication, it said:
"Chaos will be used to suppress chaos.
The Northern Dipper (Běidǒu) governs executions.
If it emerges from Dǒukuí,
it indicates that the one in power carrying out executions is not upright."
In the tenth month,
Tàibái (Venus) was visible during the day.
Later, Prince Lún of Zhào killed Zhāng and Péi,
and deposed Empress Jiǎ,
claiming to avenge the Crown Prince's injustice.
He then usurped the throne himself,
which led to his downfall and extermination.
Using chaos to suppress chaos
was the manifestation of warfare, death, and powerful ministers.
In the second month of Yuánkāng 9th year (299 CE),
Huǒxīng (Mars) guarded Xīn.
The prognostication said:
"This is ill-omened for the ruler."
In the eighth month,
Huǒxīng entered Yǔlín.
The prognostication said:
"The imperial guards will rise en masse."
Two years later,
Emperor Huì (Huì Dì) was deposed as the Grand Emperor Emeritus.
Soon after, the Three Princes raised armies to punish Lún.
Lún dispatched all the central army troops,
and they fought for several months.
In the third month of Yǒngkāng 1st year of Emperor Huì of Jìn (Jìn Huì Dì Yǒngkāng 1st year) (300 CE),
an ominous star appeared in the south.
The central star of the Sāntái split,
and Tàibái (Venus) was visible during the day.
The prognostication said:
"When an ominous star appears,
great wars will break out in the empire.
When the Tái stars are abnormal,
the Three Ducal Ministers will be in distress.
Tàibái being visible during the day signifies insubordination."
In this month,
Empress Jiǎ killed the Crown Prince.
Prince Lún of Zhào then deposed and killed the Empress and Sīkōng Zhāng Huà,
and also deposed the Emperor and enthroned himself.
Thereupon, the Three Princes rose simultaneously,
each seizing great power in turn.
In the fifth month of Yǒngkāng 1st year (300 CE),
Huǒxīng (Mars) entered Nándǒu.
The prognostication said:
"The prime minister will die,
and great wars will break out.
Dǒu also corresponds to the territory of Wú."
At this time, Prince Lún of Zhào served as prime minister.
The following year, he usurped the throne,
and the Three Princes raised armies to execute him.
In Tàiyán 2nd year (303 CE),
Shí Bīng conquered Yángzhōu.
In the eighth month of Yǒngkāng 1st year (300 CE),
Huǒxīng (Mars) entered Jī.
The prognostication said:
"The ruler will lose his position,
and wars will break out."
In the twelfth month,
a comet appeared west of Qiānniú,
pointing towards Tiānshì.
The prognostication said:
"Niú is the beginning of the Seven Regulators (Qī Zhèng).
A comet appearing there
is a sign of changing the era name and title."
Tiānshì is also called Tiānfǔ,
and also Tiānzǐ Méi,
and the Imperial Seat (Dìzuò) is within it.
The following year,
Prince Lún of Zhào usurped the throne
and changed the era name,
but was soon destroyed by a great army.
In the second month of Yǒngkāng 2nd year (301 CE),
Tàibái (Venus) appeared in the west,
retrograde, entering Dōngjǐng.
The prognostication said:
"The state loses its governance,
and ministers cause chaos."
In the fourth month,
a comet appeared in the region of Qí.
The prognostication said:
"Qí will experience warfare and death."
At this time, Prince Jiǒng of Qí (Qí Wáng Jiǒng) raised an army to punish Prince Lún of Zhào.
After Lún's destruction,
Jiǒng kept his troops and did not attend court,
monopolizing power and indulging in extravagance.
He was executed the following year.
In Yǒngníng 1st year of Emperor Huì of Jìn (Jìn Huì Dì Yǒngníng 1st year) (301 CE),
from the first month until the intercalary month,
the five planets passed through the sky.
The treatise on stars said:
"The sun is Yang,
the way of the ruler.
Stars are Yin,
the way of the ministers.
When the sun rises, the stars disappear,
meaning ministers cannot act independently.
If stars are visible in the sky at noon, it is called passing through the sky (jīngtiān).
Its prognostication signifies insubordination
and a change of rulers.
Now all five planets have passed through the sky;
this is an unprecedented celestial anomaly."
Shí Shì's commentary said:
"If Chénxīng (Mercury) is visible during the day,
if the state does not perish,
then there will be great chaos."
After this, the high officials (tái dǐng) and regional governors (fāng bó)
alternately held great power.
The Two Emperors (Èr Dì) fled and perished,
eventually leading to the rise of the Six Barbarian Tribes (Liù Yí),
who successively occupied Huáxià.
This, too, was unprecedented in historical records.
In the fifth month of the first year of Yǒngníng,
Táibái (Venus) was seen in daylight.
The prognostication is the same as the previous entry.
In the seventh month,
Suìxīng (Jupiter) guarded Xūwēi.

"If Mù (Jupiter) guards Xūwēi,
there will be military worries."
Another account said:

Chénxīng (Mercury) entered Tàiwēi.

"This means warfare,
chaos,
and banditry."
In the eighth month, on the day Wùwǔ,

"Shàngxiàng will be worried."

The prognostication said:
"Zhào and Wèi will suffer disaster."
Chénxīng (Mercury) guarded Yúguǐ.
The prognostication said:
"Qín will suffer disaster."
In the ninth month, on the day Dīngwèi,
the moon trespassed against the Left Jiǎo.
The prognostication said:

In the fourth month, on the day Guǐyǒu, of the second year,

In the tenth month,

In the twelfth month,

a warning of the downfall of a ruler."
Another account said:

Initially, Qíwáng Jǐng pacified the capital,
