and the commanderies and states reported over eighty categories of auspicious omens.
The Emperor modestly declined to publicize them.
Textual Criticism Notes
Chapter 25, Line 1
In ancient times, when the Eight Trigrams were manifested, the principles of Heaven and man became clear;
when the Nine Divisions were ordered, the responses of emperors and kings became evident.
Although one can thereby know that those who follow virtue receive aid from Heaven,
and those who violate the Way incur the punishment of divine retribution,
yet the specific signs and effects have not been exhaustively listed,
nor the dark and bright realms fully examined.
Though sometimes anomalies like tripods, pheasants, courtyards, and valleys are listed,
there are still many things that have not been thoroughly investigated.
As for providing insights to later kings,
much is still lacking.
Therefore, Zhòngní composed the *Chūnqiū*,
fully recording both auspicious and inauspicious events,
to verify actions.
This means the Nine Divisions laid out their principles beforehand,
and the *Chūnqiū* listed their effects afterwards.
Later, when Fú Shēng first established the *Dàzhuàn* (Great Commentary),
the substance of the Five Phases began to be detailed;
when Liú Xiàng broadly expanded upon the *Hóngfàn* (Great Plan),
the texts of auspicious and inauspicious signs became more complete.
Therefore, Bān Gù deliberated upon the classics and commentaries,
meticulously recording the categories and flows,
truly because the records of a single reign
could not be uniquely deficient.
Although the Way of Heaven has neither sound nor smell,
yet its responses are like shadow and echo;
the verifications between Heaven and man,
their principles cannot be falsified.
Sīmǎ Biāo compiled events from Emperor Guāngwǔ onwards,
to thoroughly investigate the Hàn affairs;
the chapters of Wáng Shěn's *Wèi Shū* (History of Wèi) were incomplete,
and all its disasters and anomalies
were merely compiled into the imperial annals.
From Huángchū onwards,
for over two hundred years,
examining its calamities and portents,
and comparing them with events,
they constantly reoccurred as if superimposed,
not deviating from earlier predictions.
Moreover, Gāo Tánglóng, Guō Jǐngchún, and others,
based their words on the classics,
and all their predictions eventually came true.
To omit and not narrate them
would diminish the historical style.
Now, from Sīmǎ Biāo onwards,
all have been compiled and ordered in discussions and prefaces.
This also follows Bān Gù's precedent of broadly drawing from the *Chūnqiū*,
to illuminate the near by citing the distant.
Furthermore, regarding non-compliance with words,
there are misfortunes from shelled insects,
which Liú Xīn considered hairy insects;
regarding unclear vision,
there are misfortunes from naked insects,
which Liú Xīn considered feathered insects.
According to the *Yuèlìng*,
summer insects are feathered,
autumn insects are hairy;
it should be as Xīn said,
and therefore the old histories followed it.
The essence of the Five Phases is subtle,
not something that later scholars can fully investigate.
All matters that have been previously discussed
are explained using their existing words;
for those without old explanations,
we deduce based on principles and facts,
awaiting future sages.
The *Wǔxíng Zhuàn* says:
"If hunting is not stopped,
if food is not offered,
if comings and goings are not regulated,
if the people's farming time is seized,
or if there are treacherous schemes,
then wood will not be straight or curved,
meaning wood loses its nature and becomes a disaster."
It also says:
"Disrespectful appearance
is called irreverence.
Its fault is madness,
its punishment is rain,
its extreme is evil.
At such times there are 'clothing-portents' (fúyāo),
at such times there are 'turtle-misfortunes' (guīniè),
at such times there are 'chicken-calamities' (jīhuò),
at such times there are diseases where lower body parts grow on the upper body,
at such times there are 'green-maladies' (qīngshěng) and 'green-auspices' (qīngxiáng).
Only metal afflicts wood."
Bān Gù says:
"It is probably that many artisans making wheels and arrows suffer damage and destruction,
and wood undergoes strange transformations."
All these are cases of wood not being straight or curved.
Wood not being straight or curved.
In the first month of the sixth year of Huángchū of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
it rained,
and wood iced over.
According to Liú Xīn's explanation,
this is wood not being straight or curved.
Liú Xiàng said:
"Ice is the extreme of *yīn*,
wood is lesser *yáng*,
symbolizing high officials.
If these people are about to suffer harm,
then *yīn* energy threatens wood,
wood becomes cold first,
hence it rains and ice forms."
In the sixth month of that year,
in Lìchéng Commandery, soldiers like Cài Fāng killed the administrator Xú Zhì,
occupied the commandery, and rebelled,
coercing and plundering many,
and gathering fugitives.
Two commandants were sent to suppress them together with the Inspector of Qīngzhōu.
The administrator,
like the feudal lords of old,
was an omen of harm to high officials.
Another theory considers wood icing over as a symbol of military conflict.
In that year,
after Cài Fāng was suppressed,
in the eighth month,
the Son of Heaven personally led a naval force to conquer Wú,
with over ten myriad soldiers,
their banners stretching for hundreds of *lǐ*,
reviewing the troops by the river.
In the second month, *xīnwèi* (辛未), of the third year of Tàixīng of Emperor Yuán of Jìn,
it rained,
and wood iced over.
Two years later,
Zhōu Yǐ, Dài Yuān, Diāo Xié, and Liú Wěi were all killed.
This event coincided with the *Chūnqiū* records,
thus it was its fulfillment.
Another says that
after this, Wáng Dūn attacked the capital,
which was also its symbol.
In the first month, *yǐsì* (乙巳), of the eighth year of Yǒnghé of Emperor Mù of Jìn,
it rained,
and wood iced over.
In that year,
Yīn Hào launched a northern expedition;
the next year,
his army was defeated,
and in the tenth year,
he was deposed.
It also says this was a symbol of
Xún Xiàn and Yīn Hào's northern expeditions,
and Huán Wēn's entry into the Pass.
In the twelfth month, *yǐsì* (乙巳), of the fourteenth year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn,
it rained,
and wood iced over.
In the second month of the next year,
Wáng Gōng became Northern Protector;
in the eighth month,
Yǔ Kǎi became Western Protector;
in the ninth month,
Wáng Guóbǎo became Director of the Central Secretariat,
soon thereafter concurrently appointed General of the Army;
in the seventeenth year, Yīn Zhòngkān became Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
Although the wicked and the righteous pursued different paths,
they ultimately met the same destruction.
This was its fulfillment.
Another says that
although Fú Jiān was defeated,
the Guān and Hé regions were not unified.
The Dīnglíng Xiānbēi invaded the Sī and Yǎn regions,
Dòu Yángshèng fanned strife and pressed upon Liáng and Yōng,
and military campaigns did not cease.
This was also its symbol.
In the second year of Jiànxīng of Sūn Liàng of Wú,
Zhūgě Kè led an expedition to Huáinán.
After his departure,
the central beam of the main hall where he sat to hear cases broke.
Kè arbitrarily raised troops for an expedition,
deprived the people of their farming season,
engaged in wicked schemes,
and harmed the nation's financial and material resources.
Thus, the wood lost its natural properties,
leading to its breaking and collapse.
When he returned from the expedition, he was executed and exterminated,
which in the Zhōu Yì is the omen of a "bent beam."
In the fifth month of the fifth year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
the ground of Emperor Xuān's temple collapsed, and its beams broke.
In the first month of the eighth year,
the grand ancestral temple's hall also collapsed.
A new temple was built,
with its foundation laid down to the spring water.
In the ninth month of that year,
a new temple was constructed,
with famous timber brought from afar,
and supplemented with bronze pillars.
Chén Xié was the master craftsman,
and 60,000 people worked on it.
In the fourth month of the tenth year,
it was completed.
In the eleventh month, on the Gēngyín day,
the beams broke again.
According to observations, the collapse of the ground
is a sign of separation,
and the breaking of the beams
means the wood is not straight or bent.
Sūn Shèng said: "At that time, there was an unnatural fire in the imperial concubines' palace,
and the temple beams broke without cause.
Before this, the emperor had been frequently unwell,
and this made things even worse."
The following year,
the emperor died,
and the royal house experienced frequent turmoil,
eventually leading to the loss of the empire.
In the second year of Tàipíng of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
Wáng Yǐng of Chéngdū ordered Lù Jī to lead troops towards the capital,
to attack Wáng Yì of Chángshā.
As soon as the army set out, the banner pole broke.
Soon after, they were defeated in battle,
and Jī was executed.
Yǐng subsequently fled in defeat,
and was eventually granted death.
Initially,
Wáng Yǒng of Héjiān plotted to first execute Chángshā,
depose the crown prince,
and enthrone Yǐng.
Chángshā learned of this,
and executed his partisans, such as Biàn Cuì.
Thus, Yǐng came to attack.
Jī also believed that Yǐng had won the hearts of both near and far,
and would become a substitute king for the Hàn dynasty,
so he pledged his allegiance to Yǐng,
and became a general who defied the imperial court.
These were all punishments for wicked schemes,
indicating that the wood was not straight or bent.
When Wáng Dūn was in Wǔchāng,
the ceremonial staffs beneath his bell grew flowers resembling lotuses.
They withered and fell after five or six days.
This was the wood losing its natural properties and transforming.
Gān Bǎo said:
"The 'bell gate'
is the etiquette of the noble;
'beneath the bell'
refers to the official in charge of decorum.
Now, wild flowers grow on dead wood,
and also within the 'bell gate.'
This means that the richness of decorum
and the flourishing of glory
are all like the blooming of wild flowers,
not lasting long."
Afterward, he indeed rebelled against the mandate,
and was even punished after his death,
which was its fulfillment.
Another theory is that these flowers were an unnatural growth,
which in the Zhōu Yì is "a withered poplar producing flowers."
When Huán Xuán first usurped power,
the pole of his dragon banner broke.
Xuán would go hunting at all hours, day and night,
was excessively extravagant in eating and drinking,
and his construction projects hindered agriculture.
Moreover, he had many wicked schemes,
thus the wood lost its natural properties.
Now, banners are used to represent the three luminaries,
and to display brightness.
The breaking of the banner pole
means that the high and bright have departed.
He was defeated after eighty days in power.
In the fifth month, on the Bǐngwǔ day, of the second year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Míng of Sòng,
a pillar in the hall of the Daoist Shèng Dàodù on Huángchéng Shān in Línyí, Nán Lángyá, naturally
glowed at night, illuminating the room.
This was the wood losing its natural properties.
Some say it was rotten wood that glowed by itself.
In the first year of Shēngmíng of the Deposed Emperor,
a Hécén tree in a pavilion shed in Yúháng, Wúxīng, bore plum fruit.
A Hécén tree
is what the common people call a Hútuí tree.
Disrespectful Bearing
At the beginning of his period of mourning, Emperor Wén of Wèi
frequently went out hunting and wandering,
his bearing was not dignified,
and his conduct was unrestrained and informal.
Thus, Dài Líng was punished for his direct remonstrance,
and Bào Xūn was given the death penalty for defying the imperial will.
The world was influenced by him,
and all scorned upholding integrity.
This was his disrespectful bearing.
Therefore, his reign was not long,
and his imperial lineage was short-lived.
In the Spring and Autumn period, a ruler of Lǔ was not sorrowful during mourning,
and showed a joyful countenance while in distress.
Mùshū called it improper,
and he eventually fled the state.
This is the same type of event.
Dèng Yáng, a Minister of Wèi,
walked loosely,
his muscles not supporting his body,
and when sitting or standing, he would lean,
as if without hands and feet.
This was his disrespectful bearing.
Guǎn Lù called it "demonic restlessness."
"Demonic restlessness"
is an omen of a tragic end.
He was later executed.
In the Yuánkāng era of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
noble youths would drink with their hair unbound and bodies unclothed,
playing with their maids and concubines in public.
Those who opposed them were seen as harming friendships,
and those who criticized them incurred censure.
Those who desired to live in their generation
were ashamed not to participate.
This was perhaps the genesis of the Hú and Dí invasions of the central plains.
How could it be merely the people of Yīchuān
who offered sacrifices with unbound hair?
In the Yuánkāng era of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
Jiǎ Mì was influential and powerful,
frequently entering the two palaces,
and playing games with the crown prince,
showing no humility.
He once even argued over the path while playing Go,
and Wáng Yǐng of Chéngdū sternly said:
"The Imperial Crown Prince
is the heir to the nation.
How dare Jiǎ Mì be so disrespectful!"
Mì did not repent,
and thus met with disaster.
After Wáng Jiǒng of Qí executed Zhào Lún,
he remained to assist in governing,
receiving officials while seated,
issuing decrees to the ministries,
and indulging in excessive arrogance,
not attending court for a single day.
This was a demeanor of wild indulgence and lack of solemnity.
Everyone in the world highly praised his achievements,
yet worried about his downfall.
Jiǒng ultimately did not change,
and eventually met with extermination.
In the Tàiyuán era,
people no longer wore headscarves (qiàotóu).
The head
is the sovereign,
and the qiào
prevents hair from hanging down,
assisting the sovereign in maintaining decorum.
Now, suddenly abandoning it
is like a ruler standing alone without assistance,
leading to danger and downfall.
Afterward, Huán Xuán usurped the throne.
In the past, when clogs were made,
the teeth always reached the top of the side plank,
and were called "exposed tenons" (lùmǎo).
In the Tàiyuán era,
they suddenly did not penetrate through,
and were called "hidden tenons" (yīnmǎo).
Afterward, there were many hidden plots,
eventually leading to great chaos.
In the seventh year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
the Jìn court conferred the title of heir apparent upon Liú Yì.
Yì, considering the importance of the royal decree,
should have held a banquet in person,
and invited officials to supervise.
However, on that day,
the court officials did not report it with due solemnity,
and merely offered their respects in private.
When the royal envoy was about to report back,
Yì only then learned of it,
and was greatly aggrieved,
dismissing Liú Jìngshū, the Lángzhōnglìng, from office.
The discerning were puzzled by this.
This was the neglect of a solemn ceremony,
an omen of disrespect.
Xiè Língyùn (謝靈yùn) of Chénjùn (陳郡) had exceptional talent.
Every time he went out or came in,
there were always several people supporting and assisting him.
A folk rhyme said:
"Four people lift his skirt and robe,
three people hold his mat."
This is it.
This was probably due to his lack of solemnity,
and he was later executed.
In the Tàishǐ (泰始) reign of Emperor Míng (明) of Sòng (宋),
the favored minister Ruǎn Diànfū (阮佃夫) wielded immense power at court.
His residences were grand and luxurious,
his carriages and attire were brilliant.
When riding in a carriage, he always leaned to one side,
deviating from the proper posture of standing upright and holding the rein.
Many people at the time emulated this.
This was also a fault of disrespectful demeanor.
At that time, the trend of leaning to the left prevailed,
and the righteous path was abandoned.
The later deposed emperor (廢帝) often rode alone, roaming about,
entering and exiting markets, residential areas, and temples,
never using the imperial carriage.
He eventually met his demise.
Rain
In the autumn of the first year of Tàihé (太和) of Emperor Míng (明) of Wèi (魏),
there were several heavy rains,
with many violent thunder and lightning storms,
which were unusual,
even killing birds.
According to Yáng Fù's (楊阜) memorial,
this was a punishment by rain.
At that time, the emperor was in mourning but showed no grief,
going out for hunting without restraint,
luxury and extravagance flourished,
depriving the people of their farming season.
Thus, wood lost its nature and rain became a disaster.
In the eighth month of the fourth year of Tàihé (太和),
heavy incessant rain fell for over thirty days.
The Yī (伊), Luò (洛), Hé (河), and Hàn (漢) rivers all overflowed,
resulting in a year of famine.
On the Jiǎyín (甲寅) day of the second month of the second year of Tàipíng (太平) of Sūn Liàng (孫亮),
there was heavy rain with thunder and lightning;
on the Yǐmǎo (乙卯) day,
snow fell,
and it was extremely cold.
According to Liú Xīn's (劉歆) explanation,
at this time, it should rain but not heavily.
Heavy rain
is a punishment by rain.
On the day after the initial thunder and lightning, snow fell and it was extremely cold,
which is also a punishment by cold.
Liú Xiàng (劉向) believed that since there had already been thunder and lightning,
snow should not fall again;
both are anomalies of untimely events.
The warning from Heaven seems to say:
"If the ruler acts out of season,
rebellious ministers will rise."
Thunder and lightning first, then snow, indicates that
the yin (陰) element sees a gap,
rises and overcomes the yang (陽).
The disaster of rebellion and killing is imminent.
Liàng (亮) did not realize this,
and was soon deposed.
This is similar to Lǔ Yǐn (魯隱) in the Spring and Autumn period.
In the sixth month of the sixth year of Tàishǐ (泰始) of Emperor Wǔ (武) of Jìn (晉),
there was heavy incessant rain.
On the Jiǎchén (甲辰) day,
the Hé (河), Luò (洛), and Qìn (沁) rivers all overflowed simultaneously,
sweeping away over four thousand nine hundred households,
killing over two hundred people,
and submerging over one thousand three hundred and sixty qīng (頃) of autumn crops.
In the seventh month of the fifth year of Tàikāng (太康) of Jìn Wǔ (晉武),
Rènchéng (任城) and Liángguó (梁國) experienced torrential rain,
harming beans and wheat.
In the ninth month of the fifth year of Tàikāng (太康),
Nán'ān (南安) had incessant rain and sudden heavy snow,
breaking trees and harming autumn crops;
Wèijùn (魏郡), Huáinán (淮南), and Píngyuán (平原) had rain and floods,
damaging autumn crops.
In this autumn,
Wèijùn (魏郡) and nine counties of Xīpíngjùn (西平郡) had incessant rain and flash floods,
and frost damaged autumn crops.
In the tenth month of the first year of Yǒngníng (永寧) of Emperor Huì (惠) of Jìn (晉),
Yìyáng (義陽), Nányáng (南陽), and Dōnghǎi (東海) had incessant rain,
flooding and harming autumn wheat.
On the Yǐchǒu (乙丑) day of the eighth month of the first year of Xiánkāng (咸康) of Emperor Chéng (成) of Jìn (晉),
in the three counties of Chángshā (長沙) (Yōu (攸), Lǐlíng (醴陵)) and Wǔlíng (武陵) (Lóngyáng (龍陽)) of Jīngzhōu (荊州),
floodwaters floated away houses,
killed people,
and damaged autumn crops.
In the sixth month of the twenty-first year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) of Emperor Wén (文) of Sòng (宋),
the capital (Jīngyì (京邑)) had continuous rain for over a hundred days,
causing a great flood.
In the first month of the first year of Dàmíng (大明) of Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武),
the capital (Jīngyì (京邑)) had rain and floods.
In the seventh month of the fifth year of Dàmíng (大明),
the capital (Jīngyì (京邑)) had rain and floods.
In the eighth month of the eighth year of Dàmíng (大明),
the capital (Jīngyì (京邑)) had rain and floods.
In the sixth month of the second year of Tàishǐ (泰始) of Emperor Míng (明),
the capital (Jīngyì (京邑)) had rain and floods.
On the Yǐhài (乙亥) day of the fourth month of the third year of Shēngmíng (昇明) of Emperor Shùn (順),
Tónglú (桐廬) County in Wújùn (吳郡) experienced a violent storm with thunder and lightning,
blowing sand and breaking trees.
The water level reached two zhàng (丈) on flat ground,
carrying away residents.
Clothing Omen
Because the world was in chaos and famine,
and resources were scarce,
Emperor Wǔ (武) of Wèi (魏) initially imitated the ancient leather cap (píbàn 裨弁),
cutting silk to make white headscarves (báicā 白帢),
to replace old attire.
Fù Xuán (傅玄) said:
"White is for military attire,
not for national attire."
Gān Bǎo (干寶) believed that plain white (gǎosù 縞素) symbolized mourning,
and "cā (帢)"
implied disgrace and humiliation.
This was probably an omen of
violence and killing
after a change of dynasty.
Initially, the white cā (帢)
had a horizontal seam in the front to distinguish it from the back,
and it was called
"yán (顏)" (face).
It was popularly worn.
By the Yǒngjiā (永嘉) period of Jìn (晉),
the seam was gradually removed,
and it was called
"wúyáncā (無顏帢)" (faceless headscarf).
Also, women's hair buns
became increasingly loose,
the bun (jì 紒) could not stand firm by itself,
hair covered the forehead,
with only the eyes visible.
"Wúyán (無顏)"
means shame;
"fù'é (覆額)" (covering the forehead)
is an expression of embarrassment;
"its looseness increasing"
means that the world had forgotten propriety and righteousness,
indulging in their passions,
and ultimately,
leading to great disgrace.
After Yǒngjiā (永嘉),
the two emperors did not return,
and the world was ashamed.
Emperor Míng (明) of Wèi (魏) wore an embroidered cap
and a light blue silk half-sleeve.
He once showed himself in this attire to the upright minister Yáng Fù (楊阜).
Fù (阜) admonished him, saying:
"What kind of ceremonial attire is this according to propriety?"
The emperor remained silent.
This was a recent clothing omen.
Light blue (piǎo 縹)
is an improper color,
and informal clothing should not be repeated.
Now, the ruler
personally wears unlawful symbols.
This is what is called "one brings disaster upon oneself, which cannot be averted."
The emperor
did not enjoy a long life,
his body perished, and his emoluments left the royal house,
his successors did not endure,
and thus the empire was lost.
In the first year of Jǐngchū (景初) of Emperor Míng (明) of Wèi (魏),
copper was cast to make two giant figures,
named
"Wēngzhòng (翁仲)."
They were placed outside the Sīmǎmén (司馬門) gate.
According to ancient records, when a tall person appeared,
it foreboded the downfall of a state;
when the tall Dí (狄) people appeared in Líntáo (臨洮),
it foreboded the calamity of Qín's (秦) demise.
Shǐhuáng (始皇) did not realize this,
but instead considered it an auspicious sign,
and cast bronze figures to imitate them.
Wèi (魏) used an instrument of national demise,
and in terms of meaning, there was no benefit in it.
This was a clothing omen.
Hé Yàn, Minister of Personnel for [Wèi],
liked to wear women's clothing.
Fù Xuán said:
"This is a clothing omen."
The regulations regarding clothing
are for establishing distinctions between superior and inferior,
and differentiating between inner and outer.
The Dàyǎ says:
"Black robes and red slippers,
hooked breast-bands and carved forehead-plates."
It sings of their formality.
The Xiǎoyǎ says:
"Solemn and dignified,
they wear military attire."
It hymns their martial spirit.
If inner and outer are not distinguished,
the royal regulations are lost.
Once clothing omens arise,
one's person follows to ruin.
Mòxī wore a man's cap,
and Jié lost the empire.
Hé Yàn wore women's clothing,
and likewise lost his family.
Their faults were the same.
Among the women of Wú who practiced self-beautification,
they tightly bound their hair,
and trimmed the edges beyond their ears.
Perhaps this custom arose from overly strict self-restraint,
where 'angles' were lost in moderation.
Thus, the customs of Wú
drove people to be overly strict.
In their speech and criticism,
they esteemed each other for being harsh and critical.
Those observing the three-year mourning period
often damaged their health and died.
Zhūgě Liàng was concerned about this,
and wrote the Zhèngjiāo Lùn.
Although it could not use classic teachings to rectify the chaos,
it was also an effort to save the times.
After Sūn Xiū's reign,
the style of clothing
was long on top and short on the bottom,
and piled five or six collars while the skirt accounted for only one or two parts.
Gān Bǎo said:
"The top is extravagant,
the bottom is constrained and cramped;
this is an omen of surplus above and insufficiency below."
When it came to Sūn Hào,
he was indeed extravagant, violent, and indulged his desires at the top,
while the common people were emaciated and distressed below.
Ultimately, the state perished.
This was its fulfillment.
After the rise of Jìn,
clothing was simple on top and voluminous on the bottom.
Those wearing clothes all valued old, patched cover-skirts.
The ruler was weak and declining,
the ministers were unrestrained;
this was an image of the lower concealing the upper.
Declining further until the end of Yuánkāng,
women wore two-piece bodices
above their shins.
This was the inner appearing outside.
Those who made carriages
merely valued lightness and fineness,
and frequently changed their shapes.
All used white bamboo strips for decoration,
a remnant image of ancient mourning carriages.
Carriages
are the vessels of a jūnzi.
Perhaps the jūnzi's mind was empty,
and affairs did not value substance.
Gān Bǎo said:
"And as for the calamities of Jìn,
the Son of Heaven lost his authority,
power and control resided with favored ministers.
This was the fulfillment of the lower concealing the upper.
At the end of Yǒngjiā,
the palace women and talented ladies
were scattered to the Róng and Dí.
This was the fulfillment of the inner appearing outside.
And when the empire was in chaos,
the prime ministers and regional governors
often failed in their responsibilities,
and were frequently replaced.
This was the fulfillment of not valuing substance."
After Jìn Wǔdì's Tàishǐ reign,
people in the Central Plains vied to use Hú and Mò dishes,
and to make Qiāng and Mò roasted meat.
Nobles and wealthy families
would certainly acquire these utensils;
at festive gatherings and auspicious banquets,
these were always given priority.
During Tàikāng,
the empire also used felt for headscarves, girdles, and collar-bands.
The common people joked among themselves, saying,
"The Central Plains will surely be destroyed by the Hú."
Felt originates from the Hú,
and the empire uses it for headscarves, girdles, and collar-bands.
The Hú have already taken triple control of them.
Can they not be defeated?
Gān Bǎo said:
"During Yuánkāng,
the Dí and Qiāng rebelled.
By Yǒngjiā,
Liú Yuān and Shí Lè then possessed the central capital.
Thereafter, the Four Barbarians successively occupied the Chinese land.
This was its fulfillment."
After Jìn Wǔdì's Tàikāng reign,
those who had private residences in the empire
moved their women to the east,
emptying the northern court
to make gardens.
Gān Bǎo said:
"The imperial court faces south,
which is the positive principle;
the empress resides in the northern palace,
which is the position of great yin;
the crown prince resides in the eastern palace,
which is the position of lesser yang.
Now, residing the inner women in the east
means they face south along with the outer men.
Overpowering yang harms yin,
an omen of women losing their proper place and encroaching upon lesser yang.
Empress Jiǎ slandered and murdered Mǐnhuái,
and soon thereafter disaster and ruin also befell her."
In ancient times, when shoes were first made,
women's shoes had rounded toes,
and men's had square toes.
The round shape
signified obedience,
thus distinguishing male and female.
At the beginning of Jìn Tàikāng,
women all wore square-toed shoes.
This was to abandon their round obedience,
making no distinction from men.
During Tàikāng,
people in the empire performed the "Jìn Shì Níng" dance,
holding cups and plates in their hands and turning them over.
They sang:
"The Jìn era is peaceful,
dance with cups and plates."
Music arises from people's hearts,
thus observed to understand affairs.
Therefore, the record says:
"Holding shields and standing like mountains,
this was the affair of King Wǔ;
leaping and stomping with vigor,
this was the ambition of Tàigōng;
when the military dances are all seated,
this was the governance of Zhōu and Shào."
It also says:
"For those whose people are toiled,
the dance rows are far apart;
for those whose people are at ease,
the dance rows are close together.
Now, holding cups and plates in hand and turning them over
is extremely precarious.
Cups and plates
are vessels for wine and food.
Naming it 'Jìn Shì Níng'
means that the gentlemen of the Jìn era
were content with temporary pleasure in wine and food,
and their foresight did not extend far.
The 'peace' of the Jìn era
was like cups and plates in hand."
During Jìn Huìdì's Yuánkāng reign,
women's ornaments included "five weapons pendants."
They also used gold, silver, and tortoiseshell
to make axes, battle-axes, spears, and halberds, for hairpins and hair ornaments.
Gān Bǎo said:
"The distinction between male and female
is a great principle of the state.
Therefore, clothing and objects differ in rank,
and ceremonial gifts are not the same.
Now, for women to use weapons as ornaments
is also a great omen.
Subsequently, the affair of Empress Jiǎ occurred,
and ultimately the empire perished by military force."
During Yuánkāng,
when women tied their hair,
once it was done,
they tightly bound its loop with silk,
calling it a "jié zǐ jì."
It originated from the Central Palace,
and the whole empire was influenced by it.
Later, Empress Jiǎ indeed harmed the crown prince.
During the Yuánkāng
era, people throughout the realm began to imitate the practice of using a *chēngzhàng* (crutch),
supporting their rear with it.
Gradually, its tip was applied,
and when stopping, it was planted upright.
Wood,
representing the element of the East,
is a subordinate to metal.
The support,
the instrument that constitutes the staff's body,
with its head propped,
is particularly convenient to use.
That it must be propped and supported from the side
is an omen of side-support.
The royal house was plagued by many troubles,
and yet Emperor Yuán, as a vassal, established virtue in the East,
maintaining the realm;
this was the fulfillment of the staff's support.
When the altars of soil and grain were without a master,
and all within the seas turned to him,
he then received the Mandate of Heaven
and established his capital outside the Jiāng region,
which was the fulfillment of the upright planting.
From the end of the Yuánkāng era to the Tài'ān period,
in the region of Jiāng and Huái,
there were broken sandals that gathered by themselves on the road,
many reaching forty or fifty *liàng* (quantities).
Gān Bǎo once sent people to scatter and remove them,
some throwing them into forests and grass,
others into pits and valleys.
The next day, when they looked,
they were all back as they were.
Some people said they saw civets carrying and gathering them,
but this was not verified.
Bǎo remarked:
"Sandals are
the humble attire of people,
worn lowest,
and subject to labor and humiliation.
They are a symbol of the common people.
Brokenness
is a symbol of exhaustion and collapse.
The road
represents the four directions of the land,
the means by which royal decrees are communicated and travel.
Therefore, broken sandals gathering on the road
symbolize the common people becoming weary and sick,
who will gather together to create disorder,
cutting off the four directions and obstructing royal decrees.
Those in power did not realize this.
During the Tài'ān era,
the *rénwǔ* forces were conscripted,
and the common people lamented.
Zhāng Chāng, a man from Jiāngxià, then initiated rebellion in Jīngchǔ,
and those who followed him were like a flowing stream.
Consequently, warfare erupted year after year,
the realm was affected,
and suffered great destruction.
This was a recent instance of clothing portents."
Since Emperor Xiào-Huái's Yǒngjiā era of the Jìn dynasty,
scholars and officials competed in wearing plain gauze single garments.
Those with far-sightedness were surprised by this,
and secretly pointed out:
"This is the coarse cloth of ancient mourning attire,
which feudal lords and high officials wore for the Son of Heaven.
Now, without cause, everyone wears it;
is there perhaps a corresponding omen?"
Afterward, Emperors Mǐn and Huái died untimely deaths,
and did not obtain their proper resting places.
Since Emperor Yuán's Tàixīng era of the Jìn dynasty,
soldiers bound their hair knots with crimson pouches.
The hair knot is on the head,
nothing is above it.
In the *Zhōu Yì*, *qián* (heaven) represents the head,
and *kūn* (earth) represents the pouch.
*Kūn*
is the way of the subordinate.
The Jìn dynasty corresponded to the element of metal,
while crimson is the color of fire,
the destroyer of metal.
Binding hair knots with crimson pouches
was a symbol of subordinates encroaching upon superiors.
By the first year of Yǒngchāng,
the Grand General Wáng Dūn raised an army and attacked the interior,
and the six armies scattered and collapsed.
Previously, feather fans were made
with handles carved from wood,
resembling bone shapes,
using ten feathers,
taking the complete number.
At the beginning of the Jìn restoration,
Wáng Dūn led a southern expedition,
and began to change them to have long handles extending downwards,
which could be grasped,
and reduced the number of feathers to eight.
Those who understood criticized this, saying:
"A feather fan
is called 'wings'.
Creating a long handle means to grasp the handle and control the wings.
Changing ten to eight
means that the incomplete will seize from the complete."
At that time, the clothes worn
were also short on top,
with the belt reaching the armpit;
those wearing caps
bound their necks with a cord.
The lower pressed upon the upper,
and the upper had no ground.
As for lower trousers,
they were made with straight panels, with no narrowing at the opening,
the bottom being excessively wide and ill-cut.
Soon there were military disturbances,
and the capital was attacked twice within three years.
When Emperor Hǎixī of Jìn first ascended the throne,
he forgot to set up the leopard tail during the welcoming ceremony for officials.
Those who understood considered this an omen of not finishing his reign,
a recent clothing portent.
Sīmǎ Dàozǐ of Jìn set up a wine stove and stalls in his northern garden,
and had concubines sell wine and delicacies,
like petty vendors.
He frequently wandered among them,
personally buying and selling,
and then, while drunk, would sleep there,
sometimes for days and nights.
Emperor Líng of Hàn once did likewise.
Gān Bǎo believed:
"This is an omen that the ruler will lose his position
and be reduced to the status of a menial servant."
Dàozǐ was eventually deposed and exiled,
ending his life as a commoner.
When Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
he installed crimson silk brocade curtains in the palace hall,
with golden carvings for the face,
and golden dragons at the four corners,
holding five-colored feathered canopies and streamers in their mouths.
His subordinates secretly said to each other:
"It somewhat resembles a funeral carriage."
This was a clothing portent.
In the late Jìn, everyone wore small caps,
while their robes and skirts were wide and large,
a fashionable imitation,
becoming common even among porters.
Those who understood said:
"This is a symbol of abdication and dynastic change."
After Yǒngchū,
caps again became large.
In the sixth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
among common women, those who tied their hair
divided their hair into three parts,
pulling their hair knots straight upwards,
calling it
"Flying Heavenly Hair Knot."
It originated from the Eastern Palace,
and spread among the common people.
At that time, Sīkōng Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng resided in the Eastern Palace,
and later was indeed deposed and exiled for disrespecting his superior.
During Emperor Xiào-Wǔ's reign,
Liú Déyuàn, the Governor of Yùzhōu, was skilled at driving carriages.
Emperor Shìzǔ once had him drive a painted carriage,
and visited the residence of Grand Tutor Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng.
Déyuàn, holding a cattle prod, urged Emperor Shìzǔ, saying:
"It's getting late, you should return!"
He also asked for an increase in the carriage rental fee.
Emperor Shìzǔ was very pleased.
This incident is similar to Emperor Líng of Hàn accumulating private funds in the Western Garden.
During Emperor Xiào-Wǔ's reign,
the favored minister Dài Fǎxīng's power rivaled that of the sovereign.
He created round-toed shoes,
and everyone in the world imitated them.
At that time, the custom of advancing roundness greatly prevailed,
and the trend of square patterns ceased entirely.
At the beginning of Emperor Míng's reign,
Sīkōng Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén commanded troops at Zhèqí.
He devised a black gauze cap,
with the cap's brim turned upwards,
which the common people called
"Sīkōng style."
The capital enthusiastically adopted it.
Xiūrén later indeed brought disaster upon himself due to suspicion and pressure.
Turtle Portents
At the beginning of Yǒngxī of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
Wèi Guàn's family cooked rice,
which, when it fell to the ground,
all turned into snails,
extending their feet and beginning to walk.
Snails
are a type of turtle,
a near-turtle portent.
Gān Bǎo said:
"Snails wear armor,
a symbol of warfare.
In the *Zhōu Yì*, it is *lí* (clinging),
and *lí* represents spears and weapons."
The next year,
Guàn was executed.
Chicken Calamity
In the second year of Jǐngchū [景初] of Emperor Míng of Wèi [魏明帝],
in the Tíngwèi Fǔ [廷尉府] (Court of the Imperial Grandee) there was a hen that transformed into a rooster,
but it neither crowed nor paired.
Gān Bǎo [干寶] said:
“In this year,
Emperor Xuān of Jìn [晉宣帝] pacified Liáodōng [遼東],
and the common people began to have discussions about who was capable of taking power.
This was its omen.”
However, the three empresses of Jìn [晉] all ended their lives as subjects,
neither crowing nor pairing,
which was also Heaven’s will.
In the sixth year of Yuánkāng [元康] of Emperor Huì of Jìn [晉惠帝],
in Chénguó [陳國], a hen gave birth to a male chick without wings.
Once grown,
it fell into a pit and died.
Wáng Yǐn [王隱] said:
“The male [chick]
is an omen for the imperial heir,
the pit and ground are omens for the mother.
Empress Jiǎ [賈后] falsely accused and killed Mǐnhuái [愍懷],
which was probably its fulfillment.”
During the Tàiaān [太安] era of Emperor Huì of Jìn [晉惠帝],
in Zhōu Qǐ’s [周玘] household, a hen escaped into the eave gutter.
After six or seven days it came down,
flapped its wings, crowed, and paired,
but its feathers alone did not change.
Afterward, there was the affair of Chén Mǐn [陳敏].
Although Mǐn [敏] controlled the region south of the Yangtze,
he ultimately lacked discipline and cultural refinement,
which was probably its omen.
He was eventually destroyed by Qǐ [玘].
The chicken calamity appearing in Qǐ’s [玘] household
was also Heaven’s will.
During the Tàixīng [太興] era of Emperor Yuán of Jìn [晉元帝],
Wáng Dūn [王敦] was stationed in Wǔchāng [武昌],
and a hen transformed into a rooster.
Heaven’s warning seemed to say:
“A hen turning into a rooster
means a subject will usurp the superior.”
Later, Wáng Dūn [王敦] twice attacked the capital.
In the fourth month of the thirteenth year of Tàiyuán [太元] of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn [晉孝武],
in Guǎnglíng [廣陵], the rooster belonging to Yán Sōng [閻嵩] of Gāopíng [高平]
was born without a right wing;
the chicken belonging to Dào Xiàng [到象] of Péngchéng [彭城]
was without a right leg.
The Jīng Fáng Yì Zhuàn [京房易傳] says:
“If the ruler follows the words of women,
then chickens will produce anomalies.”
In the eighth month of the first year of Lóng’ān [隆安] of Emperor Ān of Jìn [晉安帝],
a blue hen in the household of Lángyá [琅邪] Prince Wáng Dàozǐ [王道子] transformed into a red rooster,
but it neither crowed nor paired.
Afterward, there was the affair of Huán Xuán [桓玄],
which perfectly matched this omen.
In the fourth year of Lóng’ān [隆ān],
in Jīngzhōu [荊州], a chicken grew a horn,
which soon fell off.
At this time, Huán Xuán [桓玄] had just begun to dominate Xīxià [西夏],
acting madly and disrespectfully,
hence this chicken calamity.
The horn
was an omen of military action;
its quick falling off
was an omen of a temporary uprising that would not last.
In the second year of Yuánxīng [元興] of Emperor Ān of Jìn [晉安帝],
in Héngyáng [衡陽], a hen transformed into a rooster,
and after eighty days its comb withered.
Héngyáng [衡陽]
was within the feudal domain of Huán Xuán’s [桓玄] state of Chǔ [楚].
Later, he usurped the throne and was defeated eighty days later.
Xú Guǎng [徐廣] considered this to be an omen of Huán Xuán [玄].
In the twelfth year of Yuánjiā [元嘉] of Emperor Wén of Sòng [宋文帝],
a hen in the Huálín Yuán [華林園] gradually transformed into a rooster.
Later, after Emperor Xiàowǔ [孝武] ascended the throne,
the Empress Dowager's [皇太后] orders were carried out externally,
just like in the time of Emperor Xuān of Hàn [漢宣帝],
when a hen became a rooster,
and in the time of Emperor Āi [哀帝],
when Empress Yuán [元后] shared in governing.
During the Tàishǐ [泰始] era of Emperor Míng [明帝],
a chicken in the household of Shěn Fǎfú [沈法符] of Dōngqiān [東遷], Wúxīng [吳興], had four spurs.
Green Omen, Green Auspice
In the eighth month, on the Dīngyǒu [丁酉] day, of the first year of Xiánníng [咸寧] of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn [晉武帝],
a great wind broke the tree of the Grand Altar of Soil and Grain,
and a green qi [氣] emerged from it.
This was a green auspice.
The divination said:
“There will be an emperor in Dōngguǎn [東莞].”
The next year,
Emperor Yuán [元帝] was born.
At that time, the emperor’s paternal grandfather, King Wǔ [武王], was enfeoffed in Dōngguǎn [東莞],
and from there he moved his enfeoffment to Lángyá [琅邪].
Sūn Shèng [孫盛] considered this a sign of the restoration.
During the chaos of the Jìn [晉] dynasty,
none of Emperor Wǔ’s [武帝] descendants were left,
which corresponded to the breaking of the altar tree,
and was also the punishment of the wind.
During the Yuánkāng [元康] era of Emperor Huì of Jìn [晉惠帝],
on the southern mountain of Luòyáng [洛陽] there was a voice that said:
“Hán Shīshī [韓屍屍].”
Those who recognized it said:
“The Hán [韓] clan is about to die.
The repetition of ‘shīshī’ [屍屍]
means they will all die.”
Afterward, Hán Mì [韓謐] was executed and the Hán [韓] clan was annihilated.
This was a green auspice.
Metal Overcoming Wood
In the first month of the seventh year of Huángchū [黃初] of Emperor Wén of Wèi [魏文帝],
he traveled to Xǔchāng [許昌].
The south gate of Xǔchāng [許昌] city spontaneously collapsed,
the emperor was displeased in his heart,
and consequently did not enter,
returning to Luòyáng [洛陽].
This was metal overcoming wood,
wood moving.
In the fifth month,
the imperial carriage departed (the emperor died).
The Jīng Fáng Yì Zhuàn [京房易傳] says:
“When superiors and inferiors are all perverse,
the omen is that the city gate collapses.”
In the sixth month of the second year of Tàixīng [太興] of Emperor Yuán of Jìn [晉元帝],
the granary in Wújùn [吳郡] spontaneously collapsed.
This year there was a great famine,
and thousands died.
In the first year of Tàiníng [太寧] of Emperor Míng of Jìn [晉明帝],
Zhōu Yán [周筵] pledged allegiance to Wáng Dūn [王敦].
After he had established his residence,
the five bays and six rafters that he had erected
suddenly jumped out and fell to the ground,
while the remaining purlins still spanned the pillar tops.
This was metal overcoming wood.
In the fifth month of the next year,
Qián Fèng [錢鳳] plotted rebellion,
and consequently annihilated Yán’s [筵] clan,
and Húshú [湖熟] soon became ruins.
In the first month, on the Bǐngzǐ [丙子] day, of the first year of Yuánxīng [元興] of Emperor Ān of Jìn [晉安帝],
Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn [司馬元顯] was about to march west to attack Huán Xuán [桓玄].
He erected a commander’s banner at the south gate of Yángzhōu [揚州],
but the eastern one was difficult to set up,
and only after a long time was it straightened.
This was an omen of proximity being overcome.
He was soon captured by Huán Xuán [桓玄].
In the fifth month of the third year of Yuánxīng [元興],
the Lèxián Táng [樂賢堂] (Hall of Delighting in the Worthy) collapsed.
Heaven’s will seemed to say that
Emperor Ān [安帝] was foolish and dim-witted,
and lacked the heart to delight in the worthy,
therefore this hall was afflicted.
In the fifth month, on the Yǐyǒu [乙酉] day, of the ninth year of Yìxī [義熙] of Emperor Ān of Jìn [晉安帝],
the Guózǐ Shèngtáng [國子聖堂] (Imperial Academy’s Hall of Sages) collapsed.
In the seventeenth year of Yuánjiā [元嘉] of Emperor Wén of Sòng [宋文帝],
Liú Bīn [劉斌] was governor of Wújùn [吳郡].
The owl-tail ornament at the west end of the county hall roof spontaneously fell,
and before it was repaired,
the owl-tail ornament at the east end fell again.
Shortly thereafter,
Bīn [斌] was executed.
Collation Notes
Zhì [志] Chapter 21, Line 2 of 5
The Wǔ Xíng Zhuàn [五行傳] says:
“If one is fond of war and aggression,
disregards the common people,
adorns city walls,
and invades border regions,
then metal will not follow change.
This means metal loses its nature and becomes a disaster.”
It also says:
“If words are not followed,
this is called disorder.
Its fault is usurpation,
its punishment is drought,
its extreme is sorrow.
Then there are poetic anomalies,
then there are plagues of shelled insects,
then there are dog calamities,
then there are afflictions of speech,
then there are white omens and white auspicious signs.
Only wood overcomes metal.”
Jièchóng [介蟲] (shelled insects),
Liú Xīn [劉歆]’s biography considers them to be máochóng [毛蟲] (hairy insects).
Metal Not Following Change
The stone auspicious sign from Zhāngyè [張掖] during the Wèi [魏] era,
though it was a symbol of the Jìn [晉] clan’s mandate,
was an anomaly for Wèi [魏].
Fondness for attacking and waging war,
disregarding the common people,
adorning city walls,
and invading border regions—
all three ancestors of the Wèi [魏] clan had such deeds.
Liú Xīn [劉歆] believed that metal and stone are of the same kind,
and the stone diagram revealing extraordinary text
was a manifestation of metal not following change.
The Jìn [晉] dynasty established its great enterprise,
largely by harming the Cáo [曹] clan,
and the stone auspicious text
“Greatly Punish Cáo”
was its fulfillment.
During the Qīnglóng reign of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
palaces were extensively repaired and constructed.
Golden statues of Dī from Cháng'ān were brought west.
The dew-collecting plates broke,
and the sound was heard for dozens of *lǐ*.
The golden Dī wept.
Consequently, they were left in Bàchéng.
This was the gold losing its nature and causing an anomaly.
During the Wú period,
in Lìyáng County, there was a rock hollowed out like a seal.
Everyone said,
"When the stone seal is opened,
all under heaven will be at peace."
In the first year of Tiānxǐ of Sūn Hào, the seal was opened.
Also, in Yángxiàn Mountain, there was a stone cave
over ten *zhàng* long.
Hào initially repaired the Wǔchāng Palace,
with the intention of relocating the capital.
At that time, Wǔchāng was a detached palace.
Bān Gù said:
"Detached palaces are subject to the same divination as city walls."
This refers to decorating the city walls.
In the third year of Bǎodǐng,
Hào went out through Dōngguān,
sending Dīng Fèng to Héféi.
In the third year of Jiànhéng,
Hào again launched a large expedition from Huálǐ.
This refers to invading the border regions.
Thus, the gold lost its nature,
and ultimately Wú perished, with its people bound in front.
In the first year of Yǒngxīng of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
Chéngdū attacked Chángshā.
Every night, the tips of the spears and halberds had firelight like hanging candles.
This was due to disregarding human lives
and being fond of warfare,
where the gold lost its nature and caused a change.
Heaven's warning seemed to say,
"Weapons are like fire;
if not restrained, they will burn themselves."
Chéngdū did not realize this,
and ultimately met with defeat and destruction.
In the first year of Yǒngjiā of Emperor Huái of Jìn,
in Xiàng County, there was a stone tablet of Jiǎ Kuí, the Inspector of Yùzhōu for Wèi,
from which gold grew and could be harvested.
This was the gold changing without being melted down.
In the fifth month,
Jí Sāng rebelled,
and bandits rose like a whirlwind.
When Tán, Prince Qīnghé of Jìn, was the heir apparent,
the golden bell he wore suddenly grew protuberances like millet grains.
Kāng Wáng's mother suspected it was inauspicious
and had it destroyed and discarded.
Later, when he became the Crown Prince for Emperor Huì,
he did not remain in that position to the end
and was ultimately killed by Sīmǎ Yuè.
In the first year of Yǒngchāng of Emperor Yuán of Jìn,
Gān Zhuó was about to attack Wáng Dūn,
but then stopped.
When he returned home,
many strange things happened;
looking in a mirror, he could not see his head.
This was the gold losing its nature and causing a malevolent omen.
Soon after, he was attacked by Dūn
and utterly destroyed.
During the time of Shí Hǔ,
two golden phoenixes on the Fèngyáng Gate of Yèchéng
flew into the Zhāng River.
During the Tàihé period of Emperor Hǎixī of Jìn,
a granary was built in Shānyīn County of Kuàijī.
Digging the ground, two large boats were found,
full of coins.
The coins all had wheel patterns and were large in shape.
It was late in the day at that time,
and the diggers rushed to report it to the authorities.
The authorities sent a strict guard that night.
By the next morning,
the coins were gone,
only the boats remained.
Looking at their condition,
there were traces everywhere where the coins had been.
In the early Yìxī period of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
Yīn Zhòngwén, the Administrator of Dōngyáng, looked in a mirror and could not see his head.
Soon after, he was also executed,
the omen being the same as Gān's.
In the fourth year of Yuánhuī of Emperor Hòufèi of Sòng,
in the two commanderies of Yìxī and Jìnlíng,
a *pīlìchē* (catapult-like vehicle) fell to the ground,
like a bluestone,
and grass and trees were scorched dead.
This refers to not following advice.
In the early Jiāpíng period of Qí Wáng of Wèi,
in Dōngjùn, there was a rumor that
a demonic horse came out of the Báimǎ River.
At night, it passed by the government pastures and whinnied,
and all the horses responded.
The next day, its tracks were seen,
as large as a *hú*,
traveling for several *lǐ*,
then returning into the river.
Liú Biāo, Prince Chǔ, was originally enfeoffed as Báimǎ.
Lìnghú Yú, the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, considered Biāo intelligent and brave.
Upon hearing this rumor,
he plotted with Wáng Líng to enthrone him.
He sent someone to say to him:
"The affairs of the world are uncertain;
may the prince take good care of himself."
Biāo replied:
"I understand your kind intention."
The plot was exposed,
Líng and Yú were executed,
and Biāo was granted death.
This was the punishment for not following advice.
The *Shī Jīng* says:
"The people's deceptive words,
who dares not punish them?"
When Liú Chán succeeded to the throne,
Qiáo Zhōu cited the events of Jìn Mùhóu and Emperor Líng of Hàn regarding their sons' names to criticize him, saying:
"The late emperor's given name was Bèi,
which means 'to be prepared' or 'to have everything.'
The current emperor's given name is Chán,
which means 'to bestow' or 'to surrender.'
If it means 'Liú has everything ready,
it should be bestowed upon others,'
it is far more ominous than the omens of Mùhóu and Emperor Líng."
Shǔ indeed perished;
this was the advice not being followed.
When Liú Bèi died,
Liú Chán ascended the throne.
Before the burial,
and not even a month had passed,
he changed the reign title to Jiànxīng.
This was the advice not being followed.
Xí Zuòchǐ said:
"According to ritual,
a ruler of a state changes the reign title after more than a year in office,
because of the sentiment of ministers and sons,
who cannot bear to have two rulers in one year.
Now, this can be called hasty and ignorant of ritual.
Thus, a gentleman knows that Shǔ would not be able to move its capital eastward."
Later, it surrendered to Jìn.
Sūn Liàng of Wú, Emperor Huì of Jìn, and Yuánxiōng of Sòng were similar.
Liàng did not finish his term in office,
Emperor Huì's decrees were not his own,
and Yuánxiōng was soon executed.
Advice was not followed.
During the Tàihé period of Wèi,
Jiāng Wéi returned to Shǔ,

The Wèi people had his mother write a letter calling for Wéi to return,

Wéi replied in a letter:

is not worth one *mǔ*.
I only see 'far-reaching ambition' (*yuǎnzhì*),

Wéi ultimately did not escape.
In the first year of Jǐngchū of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
officials proposed that the Emperor be designated Lièzǔ,

This was followed.
According to the system of ancestral temples,
the titles of 'Zǔ' and 'Zōng'
are conferred after death and when one's name is established,
only then are their rituals formalized.
Therefore, even if one's achievements shake heaven and earth,
and one's virtue surpasses former kings,
there has never been a precedent for pre-determination.
This is indeed a case of not following advice,
a serious transgression.
Two years later, the imperial carriage departed (the emperor died),
and thereafter, the rule weakened and administration became lax.
In the time of Sūn Xiū of Wú,
a person from Wūchéng suffered from a severe illness.
After recovering,
he could speak with an echoing voice,
speaking here and being heard there.
From where he listened himself,
he did not perceive the loudness of his voice;
from a distance,
it was like someone speaking face to face,
and one did not perceive the voice coming from afar.
The direction of the sound
followed his intention,
the furthest not exceeding ten-odd *lǐ*.
A neighbor of his had lent money at interest to someone abroad,
who had not returned it for years.
So, he borrowed the man to make reproaches and demands,
frightening the debtor with threats of misfortune and promises of blessings.
The debtor, thinking it was a ghost or spirit,
immediately poured out and gave him the goods.
The man himself did not know why this was so.
This was the fault of not following advice.
During the Wèi dynasty, the Ānshì Palace was built.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn later resided there.
Ānshì
was Emperor Wǔ's courtesy name.
When Jìn Wǔdì often hosted his officials,

This shows that his words were not followed.
Hé Zēng said to his son Zūn:

it only cares for the present.

This was the concern of his descendants.
After Yǒngxī,
the imperial house gradually fell into chaos.
During Yǒngjiā,
the world was greatly ruined.

everything was as Zēng had said.
Zhào Wáng Lún deposed Huìdì at Jīnyǒngchéng,

In the first year of Yǒngxīng of Jìn Huìdì,

Grand Commander,
leading the Chancellor,
receiving the nine bestowals,

According to the Rites of Zhōu,
the transmission of the state is by lineage, not by merit;
thus, even with the sageliness of Gōng Dàn,
the succession of Chéng Wáng was not altered.
This was to decisively cut off covetous ambitions
and eternally unite the ancestral sacrifices.
Later generations followed this,
and changing it led to chaos.
Now, the imitation does not match the reality;
the usurpation and deviation are already too extreme.
Moreover, since he was already the deputy of the state,
he should not have again been enfeoffed with territory

This shows that these words were not followed,
and his advance and retreat were contradictory and disastrous.
Therefore, after the Emperor was driven from his capital,
Yǐng also did not have a good end;

Later, they still did not learn,
and again established Huáidì as the Imperial Younger Brother.
Huái eventually suffered exile and assassination,
not enjoying his reign for long;
this was its consequence.
The saying goes:
“To change the old and alter the constant,
if not chaos, then destruction.”
Is this what it refers to?
During the Tàiyān era of Jìn Huìdì,
Zhōu Qǐ built a residence in Yángxiàn.
As it was completed,
there were sounds from the adjoining household like someone sighing and wailing.
After Qǐ’s death,
his family was executed and annihilated.
This is an instance of immediate words not being heeded.
In the fourth year of Tàixīng of Jìn Yuándì,
the people of Wújùn rumored that there was a large worm in ramie and on Ailanthus trees,

The people of Jìnlíng also said

Thereupon, the common people were mutually terrified and agitated,
saying that dozens had already died.
As far west as the capital,
families that had Ailanthus or ramie trees
cut them down.
Soon after, it stopped on its own.
In the first year of Yǒngchāng of Jìn Yuándì,
Níngzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Xùn sent his son Chéng to enter as a hostage,

Soon, they again said that the perpetrators who ate people had been apprehended,

Scholars of the court who asked each other

Wáng Chéng was greatly alarmed,
not allowing them to go out.
There was absolutely no evidence of such an event,
nor had any family ever lost a child.
Only then did they realize it was a rumor.
These two incidents,
Gān Bǎo said,
“I have not been able to discuss them.”
In the second year of Yǒngchāng,
Grand General Wáng Dūn descended to take up position at Gūshú.
The common people rumored a marching worm disease,
which ate a large hole in people,
entering the abdomen in a few days,
and death followed upon entering the abdomen.
There was a method to cure it:
one must obtain the gall of a white dog as medicine.
From Huái and Sì, it spread to the capital.
Within a few days,
the common people were agitated and alarmed,
everyone claiming to have contracted the worm disease.
They also said
that when it was still outside,
one should burn iron to brand it.
Thereupon, seventeen or eighteen out of ten were branded.
And white dogs suddenly became expensive,
to the point of being fought over,

earning fifty or sixty thousand per day,

After four or five days, it gradually quieted down.
The explanation states:
Naked creatures are humankind,
and humans are their masters.
Now it says worms eat people,
meaning creatures of the same kind destroy each other.
From bottom to top,
this is its perversity.
That it must enter the abdomen
means the harm comes from within, not from outside.
Dogs have a nature to guard and defend;
white is the color of metal (gold),
and the gall is for a martial leader.
The fortune of emperors and kings,
the five hegemonies meet at Xū,
and Xū governs the use of military force.
Metal is the element of the Jìn dynasty;
burning iron with fire to treat the illness
means one must remove one's own kind,
and fire and metal combine virtues
to jointly cure the worm plague.
Consider that during the revival,
the Grand General was initially entrusted with the vital responsibilities of Yī and Lǚ;
but in the last years of Yuándì,
he then attacked the capital,
and during Míngdì’s mourning period,

This is why the lower rebelled against the upper,
the inner core rotted away.
And when Qián Fèng, Shěn Chōng, and other rebellious forces converged from four directions,
they were thwarted by the imperial army,
and could not succeed for over a month.
Northern Colonel Liú Xiá and Huáilíng Administrator Sū Jùn led the forces from Huái and Sì to rescue the court,
hence the rumor first started in Huái and Sì.
The court ultimately controlled the strong with the weak,
and the culprits were decapitated.
This is the effectiveness of using white dog gall for salvation.
During the Hǎixī era of Jìn,
Yǔ Xī, for four or five years,
loved to compose dirges,
shaking a large bell himself to lead the singing,

its sound mournful and poignant.
People at the time found it strange,
and later he indeed failed.
Since the Tàihé era of Jìn Hǎixī Gōng,
women of aristocratic families
wore loose hair and slanted buns

Because much hair was used,
they didn't wear it on their heads directly.
Instead, they first made false buns,
placed them on wood,
and called them

If someone wanted to borrow one,

“borrowed head” (jiè tóu).

Since then,
many literati suffered separation from their loved ones,
or lost their heads,
or had them made of grass and wood.
The saying of "false heads" (jiǎ tóu),
this was its omen.
During the Tàiyuán era of Emperor Xiàowǔ of
Jìn, an inner hall was erected and named Qīngshǔ.

People at the time said,
“Qīngshǔ”
was
a reverse pronunciation of chǔ聲.

During the Tàiyuán era,
children used two iron pieces to hit each other in the dirt,

Later, Wáng Guóbǎo and Wáng Xiàobó, within the same clan,

Pánlóng
was Yì’s childhood name.
Huán Xuán initially changed the era name to Dàhēng.
People far and near joyfully said:

When Xuán usurped the throne,
