he again changed it to Yǒngshǐ.
Yǒngshǐ,
however, was also the year Wáng Mǎng received his investiture.
First, Sīmǎ Dàozǐ was relocated to Ānchéng.
The Jìn ruler abdicated,
left the Yǒng’ān Palace,
and was enfeoffed as Pínggù Wáng.
Lángyá Wáng Déwén was enfeoffed as Shíyáng Gōng.
Both were made to reside in Xúnyáng City.
Those who understood all considered this an omen of words not being heeded.
The fault was usurpation.
When Jìn rose,
Hé Céng disdained the imperial meals from the Grand Provisioner,
and took private food for himself.
His son Shào exceeded him,
and Wáng Kǎi then exceeded Shào.
Wáng Kǎi, Yáng Xiù and their ilk
lavishly indulged in music and women,
exhausting rare treasures and extreme beauty.
By the Yuánkāng era,
extravagance had become a custom,
each striving to outdo the other.
Shí Chóng’s extravagance
then surpassed Wáng and Hé, and rivaled that of the sovereign.
After Chóng was executed,
the empire soon also fell.
This was the fault of transgression and usurpation.
Yáng
In the fifth month of Tàihé second year of Wèi Míngdì,
there was a great drought.
Since the first year,
this was the consequence of expanding palaces and official residences.
Also, in this spring,
Jìn Xuāndì captured Mèng Dá in the south,
and established two commanderies;
Zhāng Hé broke Zhūgě Liàng in the west,
and killed Mǎ Sù.
The excessive yang (fire) of arrogance
was also its consequence.
Jīng Fáng’s Yì Zhuàn says:
“When virtue is desired but not employed,
this is called zhāng.
Its calamity is desolation.
Its drought is yin clouds without rain,
turning into red smoke everywhere.
When the masses go forth out of season,
this is called guǎng.
Its drought causes nothing to grow.
When both upper and lower are obscured,
this is called gé.
Its drought makes the sky red for three months,
sometimes with hail killing flying birds.
When the superior seeks concubines by climbing,
this is called jiàn.
Its drought lasts three months with great warmth and no clouds.
When the ruler builds high platforms and residences,
this is called fàn.
Yin invades yang.
Its drought kills the roots of all things,
and often has fire disasters.
When common officials exceed their proper measure,
this is called jiàn.
Its drought makes marsh plants wither,
and they are harmed by fire.”
In the third month of Tàihé fifth year,
from the tenth month of last winter until this month, there was no rain.
On the day of Xīnsì,
there was a grand rain-making ceremony.
In this spring,
Zhūgě Liàng invaded Tiānshuǐ.
Jìn Xuānwáng resisted and repelled him,
mobilizing the masses with excessive yang.
Also at this time, three corners were separately occupied,
and the masses were frequently mobilized out of season.
The Chūnqiū Shuō says:
“Damage to two grains
is called no rain.”
In the second month of Zhèngshǐ first year of Wèi Qíwáng,
from the twelfth month of last winter until this month, there was no rain.
In the first month of the previous year,
Míngdì passed away.
In the second month,
Cáo Shuǎng reported to the successor ruler,
transferring Jìn Xuānwáng to Tàifù.
Outwardly showing respect,
inwardly he actually wanted to make sure all matters first went through himself.
At this time, Xuānwáng’s achievements surpassed the Wèi court,
which was the consequence of virtue being desired but not employed.
In the first month of Gānlù third year of Wèi Gāoguìxiāng Gōng,
from last autumn until this month, there was a drought.
At that time, Jìn Wénwáng besieged Zhūgě Dàn,
which was the consequence of the masses going forth out of season.
Initially,
Shòu County always had heavy rain in spring and summer,
and the city was often flooded.
But this drought lasted over a year,
and only when the city fell did heavy rain come.
Everyone believed it was Heaven’s destruction.
In the Wǔfèng second year of Wú Sūn Liàng,
there was a great drought,
and the people starved.
In this intercalary month of the year,
Wèi general Wén Qīn defected with tens of thousands of people from Huáinán;
Sūn Jùn also defeated Wèi general Cáo Zhēn at Gāotíng.
In the third month,
Zhū Yì raided Ānfēng,
but did not succeed.
In the seventh month,
Gguǎnglín and Dōnghǎi two commanderies were fortified.
In the twelfth month,
Féng Cháo was appointed supervisor of military affairs,
commanding all troops in Xúzhōu.
The soldiers resented and rebelled.
This was the punishment for excessive yang and arrogance,
and for troubling the people and losing their support.
The campaign lasted for a year,
so the drought also lasted the entire year.
In the spring and summer of Bǎodǐng first year of Wú Sūn Hào, there was a drought.
At this time, Hào moved the capital to Wǔchāng,
which was the consequence of troubling the people and mobilizing the masses.
In the intercalary fifth month of Tàishǐ seventh year of Jìn Wǔdì,
there was a drought,
and a grand rain-making ceremony.
In this spring,
Sūn Hào came out of Huálǐ,
and Grand Marshal Wàng led the troops to Huáiběi.
In the fourth month,
northern Hú invaders attacked Jīnchéng and Xīpíng.
Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Qiān Hóng went out to battle,
was defeated and died.
In the fifth month of Tàishǐ eighth year,
there was a drought.
At this time, the emperor listened to Xún Xù’s perverse advice,
keeping Jiǎ Chōng from returning to garrison the west.
Instead, Rèn Kǎi was gradually estranged,
which was the consequence of both upper and lower being obscured.
Also, Lǐ Xǐ, Lǔ Zhī, Lǐ Yìn and others were all in nominal positions,
which was close to the saying “virtue is desired but not employed.”
In Tàishǐ ninth year,
from the first month there was a drought,
until the sixth month.
Prayers were offered to the ancestral temples, altars of soil and grain, and mountains and rivers.
On the day of Guǐwèi, it rained.
In the ninth month of the previous year,
Bù Chǎn, the supervisor of Xīlíng in Wú, occupied the city and surrendered.
Yáng Hù was sent to lead Yáng Zhào and others with eighty thousand troops to rescue and welcome Chǎn.
In the twelfth month,
Lù Kàng heavily defeated Zhào’s army,
attacked and annihilated Chǎn.
In the fourth month of Tàishǐ tenth year,
there was a drought.
Last autumn and winter,
daughters of ministers and officials such as Zhūgě Chōng were selected.
In this spring, over fifty people entered the palace for selection.
Also, dozens of daughters of minor generals and officials were taken,
and their mothers and daughters cried aloud in the palace,
their voices heard outside,
making passers-by feel sad.
This was probably the consequence of accumulated yin giving rise to yang.
In the fifth month of the second year of Xiánníng of
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, there was a drought.
A grand prayer for rain was held,
and offerings were made to the deities of grain and soil, mountains, and rivers.
It was not until the sixth month
that heavy rain fell.
In the second year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
there had been a drought since last winter.
By this spring, Wú had been pacified.
This was a response to the great display of power in moving the masses during the extreme heat.
In the fourth month of the third year of Tàikāng,
there was a drought.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
an imperial edict commanded Sīkōng Qí Wáng Yōu (Sīkōng, Prince Yōu of Qí) to collaborate with the Shàngshū, Tíngwèi, and Hénán Yǐn to investigate and interrogate prisoners,
and their cases were to be treated with clemency and pardon.
In the sixth month of the fifth year of Tàikāng,
there was a drought.
In the first month of this year,
the sky was overcast,
then cleared and became overcast again.
Liú Yì submitted a memorial stating:
“There must be officials who form factions
and serve the ruler with treachery;
they ought to be executed without pardon.”
The Emperor did not respond.
At this time, Xún Xù and Féng Dǎn usurped power,
and brought great disorder to the court.
In the third month of the sixth year of Tàikāng,
there was a drought in the commanderies and states of Qīng, Liáng, Yōu, and Jì.
In the sixth month of the sixth year of Tàikāng,
there was a drought in Jìyīn and Wǔlíng,
damaging the wheat.
In the summer of the seventh year of Tàikāng,
thirteen commanderies and states suffered from drought.
In the fourth month of the eighth year of Tàikāng,
Jìzhōu suffered from drought.
In the summer of the ninth year of Tàikāng,
thirty-three commanderies and states suffered from drought.
In the sixth month of the ninth year of Tàikāng,
Fúfēng, Shǐpíng, Jīngzhào, and Āndìng suffered from drought,
damaging the wheat.
In the second month of the tenth year of Tàikāng,
there was a drought.
In the second month of the first year of Tàixī of
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, there was a drought.
After the Tàikāng era,
even though upright individuals filled the court,
they were not trusted or relied upon;
instead, Jiǎ Chōng, Xún Xù, Yáng Jùn, and Féng Dǎn,
alternately held crucial positions.
The reason why there was no year without drought
was that virtuous talent was not utilized,
and both high and low officials concealed the truth.
This was the punishment for officials exceeding their proper status.
In the seventh month of the first year of Yuánkāng of
Emperor Huì of Jìn, there was a severe drought in Yōngzhōu,
followed by frost and epidemics.
There was famine in Guānzhōng,
and a *hú* of rice cost ten thousand cash.
In the seventh month of the seventh year of Yuánkāng,
there was a severe drought in the two provinces of Qín and Yōng.
Consequently, in that year, the Dǐ and Qiāng rebelled,
and Xiè Xì, the Inspector of Yōngzhōu, was defeated.
In the first month of this year,
Zhōu Chǔ, Lú Bō, and others were again defeated,
and Guānxī was plunged into chaos.
Fighting continued for a full year.
By this time, famine and epidemics were prevalent,
both the barbarians and the Jìn were in distress,
and the imperial court was unable to provide relief.
An edict permitted people to sell themselves.
In the ninth month of the seventh year of Yuánkāng,
five commanderies and states suffered from drought.
In the first year of Yǒngníng of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
from summer to autumn,
the four provinces of Qīng, Xú, Yōu, and Bìng suffered from drought.
In the spring of this year,
the Three Princes campaigned against Zhào Wáng Lún (Prince Lún of Zhào).
Within sixty days,
there were dozens of battles, both large and small,
and over a hundred thousand people died.
In the twelfth month,
twelve commanderies and states again suffered from drought.
In the fifth month of the third year of Yǒngjiā of
Emperor Huái of Jìn, there was a severe drought.
The Tányuān Pool in the Liángshuǐ river in Xiāngpíng County dried up,
and the Hé, Luò, Jiāng, and Hàn rivers were all fordable.
In the third month of this year,
Sīmǎ Yuè returned to the capital,
sent troops into the palace,
arrested Miù Bō, the Central Secretariat Director, and eight others, and killed them.
This was the punishment for usurpation and transgression.
Furthermore, many regional lords in the four directions
harbored intentions of disloyalty to the ruler.
Liú Yuān, Shí Lè, Wáng Mí, Lǐ Xióng, and their like
harmed the lives of the people,
shedding blood until it became mud,
which was also a manifestation of this.
In the fifth year of Yǒngjiā,
there was a drought from last winter until this spring.
In the twelfth month of the previous year,
Sīmǎ Yuè abandoned the capital,
moved south with a large army,
taking many princes, dukes, and court officials with him,
and also brought the travelling imperial court.
He dismissed the palace guards
and replaced them with his own men.
The palace became desolate,
and the proper etiquette between ruler and minister no longer existed.
The *Jìn Yángqiū* states:
“When Emperor Mǐn was in the western capital,
drought and famine were frequent.”
The year and month are not noted.
In the sixth month of the first year of Jiànwǔ of
Emperor Mǐn of Jìn, Yángzhōu suffered from drought.
In the twelfth month of the previous year,
Chúnyú Bó was unjustly killed,
and that year immediately saw a drought.
Then, in the sixth month of the first year of Tàixīng, there was another drought.
Gān Bǎo said,
“After Bó was killed, there was a drought for three years,”
which is correct.
Examining the Former Hàn, when a filial wife was executed, there was a drought.
In the Later Hàn, if there was an unjustly imprisoned person, there was also a drought.
When their grievances were redressed and justice was served,
rain fell.
This is of the same category.
Bān Gù said:
“When punishments are unjustly applied,
the yin forces do not adhere,
then the yang energy prevails,
hence the punishment is drought.”
In the fourth month of the first year of Jiànwǔ,
Qū Yǔn and others gathered all their forces to resist the invaders.
In the fifth month,
Zǔ Tì attacked Qiáo.
In that winter,
Zhōu Fǎng campaigned against Dù Zēng.
This was also a response to the movement of the masses.
In the fifth month of the fourth year of Tàixīng of
Emperor Yuán of Jìn, there was a drought.
At this time, Wáng Dūn's aspirations for usurpation and transgression were gradually becoming apparent.
Also, in the previous year, Cài Bào, Zǔ Tì, and others
were all engaged in military expeditions.
In the first year of Yǒngchāng of Emperor Yuán of Jìn,
there was a severe drought.
In the third month of this year,
Wáng Dūn staged the Shítóu Incident;
the two palaces were desecrated,
and high officials were executed.
His usurpation and disrespect for authority were boundless,
hence the drought was particularly severe.
In the intercalary eleventh month of the first year of Yǒngchāng,
the capital experienced a severe drought,
and all rivers and valleys dried up.
In the third year of Tàiníng of Emperor Míng of Jìn,
there was no rain from spring
until June.
In the autumn of the previous year,
Wáng Dūn was eliminated.
This was a response to the great display of power in moving the masses during the extreme heat.
In the autumn of the first year of Xiánhé of
Emperor Chéng of Jìn, there was a drought.
At this time, Empress Dowager Yǔ presided over the court and issued edicts.
Officials addressed her as
“Her Imperial Majesty, the Empress Dowager.”
This was a punishment for a woman monopolizing state affairs,
her words not being followed, and her usurpation and transgression.
It was similar to Empress Dowager Dèng of Hàn.
In the summer of the second year of Xiánhé,
there was a drought.
In the fifth month of the fifth year of Xiánhé,
there was a drought.
In the previous year, Sū Jùn's faction was annihilated,
and this spring Guō Mò was again attacked and eliminated.
This was a response to the movement of the masses during the extreme heat.
In the fourth month of the sixth year of Xiánhé,
there was a drought.
In the eighth month of the previous year,
Shí Lè sent Guō Jìng to invade Xiāngyáng,
and Zhōu Fǔ, the Southern Central Commander, fled to Wǔchāng.
In the tenth month,
Lǐ Xióng sent Lǐ Shòu to invade Jiànpíng,
and Yáng Qiān, the Administrator of Jiànpíng, fled to Yídū.
In the first month of this year,
Liú Zhēng plundered Lóu County,
and consequently troops were raised for defense.
In the seventh month of the eighth year of Xiánhé,
there was a drought.
In the ninth year of Xiánhé,
there was no rain from the fourth month
until the eighth month.
In the sixth month of the first year of Xiánkāng of
Emperor Chéng of
Jìn,
there was a drought.
At this time, Emperor Chéng was young and weak,
not personally managing the myriad affairs of state.
Internal and external policies
were entrusted to the generals and chancellors.
This was the punishment for usurpation and overstepping,
hence the successive years of drought.
By the fourth year,
Wáng Dǎo firmly declined the position of Grand Tutor (Tàifù),
restoring his son Míngpì.
After this, there was no drought,
which was probably the response.
At the time, there was a widespread drought across the land.
Kuàijī and Yúyáo were particularly severe.
A dou of rice cost five hundred [cash],
and people sold their children to each other.
In the third month of the second year of Xiánkāng,
there was a drought.
In the sixth month of the third year of Xiánkāng,
there was a drought.
In the fifth month of the first year of Jiànyuán of
Emperor Kāng of
Jìn,
there was a drought.
At this time, the chancellors wielded exclusive power,
and the regional governors (fāngbó) monopolized heavy troops.
This was also the same situation as in the early Xiánkāng period.
In the fifth month of the first year of Yǒnghé of
Emperor Mù of
Jìn,
there was a drought.
Officials proposed following Dǒng Zhòngshū's method:
moving the markets, opening water gates,
and sending imperial envoys (yèzhě) to sacrifice to the Grand Altar of the Soil (Tàishè).
At this time, the emperor was in swaddling clothes,
and Empress Dowager Chǔ oversaw the court, following the precedent of Empress Dowager Míngmù.
In the seventh month of the fifth year of Yǒnghé,
there was no rain,
until the tenth month.
In the second month of this year,
General Zhengbei Chǔ Póu dispatched troops to attack Pèi,
bringing its people back.
In the sixth month,
he again dispatched Western Commandant Chén Kuí to advance and occupy Shòuyáng.
He himself, with a navy of twenty thousand, reached Xiàpī,
lost his vanguard, and returned.
Chén Kuí also retreated.
In the intercalary month of the sixth year of Yǒnghé,
there was a drought.
In this spring,
Huán Wēn, with a large army, departed from Xiàkǒu,
submitting a memorial intending to launch a northern expedition with naval forces.
The imperial court was alarmed by this.
Xiāo Jìngwén stole Fú,
and the Western Man Commander Cǎi Shòu was defeated.
In the twelfth month of the third year of Shēngpíng of
Emperor Mù of
Jìn,
there was a great drought.
In the tenth month of this winter,
Northern Commandant Xī Tán led over ten thousand men out of Gāopíng,
campaigning in Hé and Yǎn.
He also dispatched General Zhūgě Yōu with a naval force to enter the Yellow River,
where they were defeated.
Western Commandant Xiè Wàn encamped at Xiàcài,
but his troops scattered and returned.
In the twelfth month of the fourth year of Shēngpíng,
there was a great drought.
In the summer of the first year of Lónghé of
Emperor Āi of
Jìn,
there was a drought.
At this time, Huán Wēn was powerful and arbitrary,
controlling the imperial court.
This was the punishment for usurpation and overstepping.
Also, last year Mùróng Kè besieged Lǚ Hù, the Inspector of Jìzhōu.
Huán Wēn encamped at Wǎnlíng.
Fàn Wāng and Yuán Zhēn both launched northern expeditions.
The number of troops dispatched was excessive for the time.
In the second month of the first year of Níngkāng of
Emperor Xiàowǔ of
Jìn,
there was a drought.
At this time, Huán Wēn entered the court and made obeisance at Gāopínglíng.
The entire court bowed to him.
This was the consequence of his overstepping and usurpation.
In the winter of the third year of Níngkāng,
there was a drought.
Before this,
the Dī bandits had broken through Liángzhōu and Yìzhōu.
Inspectors Yáng Liàng and Zhōu Zhòngsūn fled.
The next year,
General Wēiyuǎn Huán Shíqián attacked Yáo Cháng at Diànjiāng,
defeated him,
and retreated to Wǔchéng.
Inspector of Yìzhōu Zhú Yáo led his troops to garrison Bādōng.
In the sixth month of the fourth year of Tàiyuán of
Emperor Xiàowǔ of
Jìn,
there was a great drought.
Last year,
the Dī bandits besieged Southern Commandant Zhū Xù at Xiāngyáng,
and also besieged General Yángwēi Dài Dùn at Péngchéng.
Huán Sì, with the forces from Jiāngzhōu, encamped at Ruò to assist Zhū Xù.
The Northern Command (Běifǔ) dispatched people from three prefectures to reinforce Hé Qiān to rescue Dài Dùn.
In this spring,
Xiāngyáng, Shùnyáng, and Wèixīng cities all fell.
The bandits then plundered Huáinán,
advancing towards Guǎnglíng.
General Zhenglǔ Xiè Shí led his naval forces and encamped at Túzài.
Inspector of Yǎnzhōu Xiè Xuán supervised the various generals and defeated them.
In the sixth month of the eighth year of Tàiyuán,
there was a drought.
In early summer,
Huán Chōng campaigned in Xiāngyáng,
sending General Guànjūn Huán Shíqián to advance and occupy Fánchéng.
The imperial court also sent Administrator of Xuānchéng Hú Bīn to encamp at Xiáshí to bolster Huán Chōng's influence.
In the seventh month of the tenth year of Tàiyuán,
there was drought and famine.
Initially, in the eighth year,
Fú Jiān was defeated.
In the ninth year,
various generals reclaimed territory,
campaigning in Xú and Yù.
Yáng Liàng and Zhào Tǒng attacked Bā and Miǎn.
In the first month of this year,
Xiè Ān again moved to garrison Guǎnglíng,
sending his son Xiè Yǎn to advance and encamp at Péngchéng.
In the sixth month of the thirteenth year of Tàiyuán,
there was a drought.
Last year,
the Northern Command dispatched troops to garrison Hú Lù,
and Jīngzhōu campaigned in Hénán.
This year,
Guō Quán established a garrison at Yěwáng,
and also dispatched troops to defeat Huáng Huái.
In the seventh month of the fifteenth year of Tàiyuán,
there was a drought.
In this spring,
the Dīnglíng plundered Yǎn and Yù,
and the Xiānbēi raided the banks of the Yellow River.
Zhū Xù, Huán Bùcái, and others campaigned north to Tàiháng,
and east to Huátái,
attacking for over a season,
and also garrisoning Shímén.
In the autumn of the seventeenth year of Tàiyuán,
there was a drought,
lasting until winter.
At this time, Rú Qiānqiū, serving as Counselor to the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Cányì),
secretly wielded the emperor's and chancellor's authority;
also, Qiū Ní's wet nurse's relatives, and the sons of his maids and servants,
rose through their close proximity to power,
leading the people and commanding troops.
Moreover, in many places, all spring convicts were wrongly imprisoned,
without proper cause.
The prison officials in Jiànkāng were particularly oppressive and brutal.
This was the punishment for usurpation, disobedience,
and wrongful oppression.
In the fifth month of the fourth year of Lóng'ān of
Emperor Ān of
Jìn,
there was a drought.
Last winter, Huán Xuán compelled Yīn Zhòngkān to his death,
and the imperial court immediately granted him the post of Jīngzhōu.
Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn also influenced all officials to revere him.
These were all punishments for arrogance and usurpation.
In the summer and autumn of the fifth year of Lóng'ān,
there was a great drought,
with no rain in December.
In the summer of the previous year,
Sūn Ēn entered Kuàijī,
killing Administrator Xiè Yǎn.
In the summer of this year,
he plundered Wú,
and also killed Administrator Yuán Shānsōng.
Military expeditions were launched to the east,
and the number of troops dispatched was excessive for the time.
In the seventh month of the first year of Yuánxīng of
Emperor Ān of
Jìn,
there was a great famine,
with no rain in September and October.
In the first month of this year,
Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn, with a large army, campaigned against Huán Xuán.
Soon after, Huán Xuán arrived
and killed Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn.
In the fifth month,
he again dispatched troops to the east to suppress Sūn Ēn's remnants.
In the tenth month,
he campaigned north against Liú Guǐ.
In the sixth month of the second year of Yuánxīng,
there was no rain.
In winter,
In the eighth year of Yìxī (義熙), in the tenth month,
there was no rain.
That autumn,
the royal army marched west to suppress Liú Yì (劉毅);
a detachment was sent to conquer Shǔ (蜀).
In the tenth year of Yìxī (義熙), in the ninth month,
there was a drought,
and in the twelfth month,
there was another drought.
Many wells and drains dried up.
In the second year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) under Sòng Wéndì (宋文帝), in summer,
there was a drought.
In the fourth year of Yuánjiā (元嘉), in autumn,
the capital suffered a drought.
In the eighth year of Yuánjiā (元嘉), in the fifth month,
various commanderies in Yángzhōu (揚州) suffered a drought.
In the nineteenth and twentieth years of Yuánjiā (元嘉),
Nányǎn (南兗) and Yùzhōu (豫州) suffered droughts.
In the twenty-seventh year of Yuánjiā (元嘉), in the eighth month,
there was no rain,
until the third month of the twenty-eighth year.
At that time, the Suǒ (索) barbarians were invading the south.
In the seventh and eighth years of Dàmíng (大明) under Xiàowǔdì (孝武帝),
the eastern commanderies suffered a severe drought,
and sixteen or seventeen out of ten people died of starvation.
Before this, since the Jiāngzuǒ (江左) period,
many institutions were incomplete.
Xiàowǔdì (孝武帝) established the Míngtáng (明堂)
and built five chariots (wǔlù).
At this time, he conscripted large numbers of commoners,
made a southern tour to hunt,
and greatly boasted of his own grandeur,
thus leading to the drought disaster.
In the first year of Yuánhuī (元徽) under Hòufèidì (後廢帝), in the eighth month,
the capital suffered a drought.
Poetic Portents
In the Tàihé (太和) period under Wèi Míngdì (魏明帝),
the capital sang the "Dōulíng Cáozǐ" (兜鈴曹子) song.
Its refrain was:
"What can be done about you, Cáozǐ (曹子)?"
This was a poetic portent.
Afterwards, Cáo Shuǎng (曹爽) was executed,
and the Cáo (曹) clan was subsequently deposed.
In the Jǐngchū (景初) period under Wèi Míngdì (魏明帝),
a children's rhyme said:
"Father, Father, driving a carriage,
unexpectedly Father crosses the river eastward.
If Father returns eastward, what will happen?!"
When Xuānwáng (宣王) pacified Liáodōng (遼東)
and returned to Báiwū (白屋),
he was supposed to return to garrison Cháng'ān (長安).
It happened that the Emperor was seriously ill
and urgently summoned him.
So he rode a zhuīfēng (追鋒) carriage and crossed the river eastward,
eventually destroying the Wèi (魏) house,
just as the children's rhyme had said.
In the Jiāpíng (嘉平) period under Wèi Qíwáng (魏齊王),
there was a rhyme that said:
"A white horse with a plain bridle gallops southwest,
who rides it? Zhūhǔ (朱虎) rides it."
Zhūhǔ (朱虎)
was the given name (xiǎozì) of Chǔwáng Biāo (楚王彪).
Wáng Líng (王淩) and Línghú Yú (令狐愚) heard this rhyme
and plotted to enthrone Biāo (彪).
The plot was discovered,
Líng (淩) and others were executed,
and Biāo (彪) was granted death.
In the early reign of Wú Sūn Liàng (吳孫亮),
a children's rhyme said:
"Alas, Rǔ Kè (汝恪),
why such?
Reed single garment, bamboo-strip woven net,
where shall I seek you, Chéngzǐgē (成子閣)?"
Chéngzǐgē (成子閣)
is a reversed pronunciation of Shízǐgāng (石子堈).
Gōuluò (鈎落)
refers to a fishing net/belt.
When Zhūgě Kè (諸葛恪) died,
he was indeed wrapped in reed mats,
his waist bound with bamboo strips,
and thrown into Shízǐgāng (石子堈).
Later, Kè's (恪) former subordinates were allowed to collect his remains,
and they sought them in this mound.
In the early reign of Sūn Liàng (孫亮),
a white alligator cried out in Gōng'ān (公安).
A children's rhyme said:
"White alligator cries,
turtle's back flat,
in Nánjùn (南郡) city one can live long,
to guard until death without leaving achieves nothing."
"In Nánjùn (南郡) city one can live long" means
in times of emergency,
it is easy to escape.
The next year,
Zhūgě Kè (諸葛恪) was defeated,
his younger brother Róng (融) was garrisoned at Gōng'ān (公安),
and was also attacked.
Róng (融) scraped the golden seal turtle,
wore it, and died.
Alligators have scales and armor,
symbolizing weapons and soldiers.
Moreover, white signifies white soldiers (unlucky soldiers).
In the second year of Yǒng'ān (永安) under Sūn Xiū (孫休),
some barbarian hostages were gathered, playing happily,
when a strange small boy suddenly appeared
and said:
"The Three Dukes are hoed,
Sīmǎ (司馬) is like."
He also said:
"I am not human,
I am the planet Yínghuò (熒惑)."
After speaking, he ascended,
looking up like a piece of white silk being pulled up,
and disappeared shortly after.
Gān Bǎo (干寶) said,
four years later Shǔ (蜀) fell,
six years later Wèi (魏) was deposed,
and twenty-one years later Wú (吳) was pacified,
thus the nine provinces returned to Jìn (晉).
Wèi (魏), Wú (吳), and Shǔ (蜀)
were all warring states,
which is what "The Three Dukes are hoed,
Sīmǎ (司馬) is like"
refers to.
In the early reign of Sūn Hào (孫晧),
a children's rhyme said:
"Rather drink Jiànyè (建業) water,
than eat Wǔchāng (武昌) fish;
rather return to Jiànyè (建業) to die,
than stop living in Wǔchāng (武昌)."
Hào (晧) soon moved the capital to Wǔchāng (武昌),
and the people, having to supply provisions against the current,
all resented him bitterly.
Sūn Hào (孫晧) sent envoys to sacrifice at the demonic shrine below Shíyìnshān (石印山).
The envoy then wrote in red on the cliff:
"Chǔ (楚) is the nine-province islet,
Wú (吳) is the nine-province capital.
A scholar from Yángzhōu (揚州)
will become Son of Heaven.
After four generations of rule,
there will be great peace."
Hào (晧) heard this,
his ambition grew,
and he said:
"From Grand Emperor (Dà Huángdì) to Me is four generations.
A ruler of great peace,
who else but Me?"
His tyranny became even more excessive,
and he soon fell and perished.
This was a recent poetic portent.
In the Tiānjì (天紀) period under Sūn Hào (孫晧),
a children's rhyme said:
"Ā Tóng (阿童) again Ā Tóng (阿童),
carrying a knife, roaming and crossing the river.
Not fearing the tiger on the bank,
only fearing the dragon in the water."
Jìn Wǔdì (晉武帝) heard this
and bestowed Wáng Jùn (王濬) the title of Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍).
When Wú (吳) was conquered,
no army west of the river could pass,
but Wáng Jùn (王濬) first secured Mòlíng (秣陵).
After the Tàikāng (太康) period under Jìn Wǔdì (晉武帝),
a children's rhyme in Jiāngnán (江南) said:
"Shrunken flesh,
many sideways glances,
the Central Plains will lose, Wú (吳) will revive."
It also said:
"Palace gate pillars,
do not rot yet,
Wú (吳) will revive,
in thirty years."
It also said:
"If the rooster crows without flapping its wings,
Wú (吳) will revive without effort."
At that time, all the Wú (吳) people believed it referred to the descendants of the Sūn (孫) clan,
so those who secretly instigated rebellion followed one after another.
According to "sideways glances" (héngmù, 橫目)
is the character "sì" (四),
(meaning four).
From the fall of Wú (吳) to the rise of Jìn Yuándì (晉元帝),
it was almost forty years,
all as the children's rhyme had said.
Yuándì (元帝) was timid and indecisive,
"shrunken flesh" (júsuōròu, 局縮肉) directly refers to him.
Gān Bǎo (干寶) said
"I don't know who it refers to",
concealing it.
At the end of Tàikāng (太康),
the capitals, Jīng (京) and Luò (洛), began to have
the song "Zhélíuyáng" (折楊柳).
Its melody initially contained words of hardship from war,
and concluded with events of capture and beheading.
At this time, the three Yáng (楊) families were powerful and prosperous but were exterminated,
and the Empress Dowager was deposed and died in confinement.
During the Yǒngxī
reign of Emperor Huì of Jìn, there was a man in Wēn Xiàn,
Hénèi, who seemed mad.
He created a text which said:
“Brilliant, brilliant Wéncháng,
a great *jǐ* (halberd) forms a wall.
Though poison proceeds,
the *jǐ* will wound itself.” He also said:
“Two fires fall to earth,
alas, Qiūlán.
Her form returns to Jiēyóu,
passersby sigh.”
When Yáng Jùn resided in the inner palace,
he used *jǐ* as guards.
When he died,
he was also harmed by *jǐ*.
Empress Dowager Yáng was deposed,
and Empress Jiǎ cut off her provisions.
She died after eight days,
and was buried north of Jiēyóu Tíng.
The common people mourned her.
“Two fires”
refers to the given name of Emperor Wǔ;
“Lán”
was the courtesy name of Empress Yáng.
During the Yǒngxī
reign, a children's rhyme said:
“At the end of the second month,
beginning of the third month,
Jīng-brushes and Yáng-boards issue imperial decrees,
the great horses in the palace almost become donkeys.”
When Yáng Jùn first monopolized power,
Chǔ Wáng Sīmǎ Xún was in charge of affairs.
Thus it said
“Jīng-brushes and Yáng-boards.”
If these two men were not executed,
then the etiquette between ruler and minister would be perverted.
Thus it said
“almost become donkeys.”
During the Yuánkāng reign of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
a children's rhyme in Jīng and Luò said:
“The south wind rises,
blowing white sand.
Looking afar at Rǔguó, how lofty it is,
a thousand-year-old skull grows teeth.”
It also said:
“Little horses east of the city, do not make a fuss,
by the third month, your manes will be bound.”
“South wind”
was the courtesy name of Empress Jiǎ.
“White”
referred to the prevailing element of Jìn.
“Shāmén”
was the crown prince’s nickname.
“Sāi”
was the state of Jiǎ Mì.
It meant that Empress Jiǎ would conspire with Mì,
to endanger the crown prince;
and Zhào Wáng would seize the opportunity to chew up the powerful and worthy,
in order to achieve usurpation.
At this time, Mǐnhuái had considerably lost popular support,
and was eventually deposed,
not dying a natural death.
During the Yuánkāng reign,
throughout the realm, merchants and farmers generally wore large sun-shades.
A children's rhyme said:
“Túsū sun-shades cover both ears,
soon a blind child will become emperor.”
When Zhào Wáng usurped the throne,
his eye was indeed blind.
After Zhào Wáng Lún usurped,
a children's rhyme in Luò said:
“A tiger comes from the north, its nose sweating,
a dragon comes from the south, climbs the wall to watch,
water comes from the west, how turbulent.”
A few months later, Qí Wáng, Chéngdū, and Héjiān gathered their righteous armies to execute Lún.
According to records, Chéngdū was a western vassal and was in Yè,
so it said
“a tiger comes from the north”;
Qí was an eastern vassal and was in Xǔ,
so it said
“a dragon comes from the south”;
Héjiān was in a watery region and was in Guānzhōng,
so it said
“water comes from the west.”
Qí remained to assist in governance,
residing west of the palace,
harboring rebellious intentions.
Thus it said
“climbs the wall to watch.”
During the Tài'ān reign of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
a children's rhyme said:
“Five horses roam and cross the river,
one horse transforms into a dragon.”
Later, the Central Plains fell into great chaos,
and many imperial clans were cut off.
Only Lángxié, Rǔnán, Xīyáng, Nándùn, and Péngchéng all reached the south of the Yangtze River,
and Emperor Yuán then inherited the Jìn.
When Sīmǎ Yuè returned to Luò,
a children's rhyme said:
“A big rat in Luò is a foot and two inches long,
if it doesn't leave early, a big dog will arrive.”
When Gǒu Xī was about to defeat Jí Sāng,
another rhyme said:
“The Yuánchāo brothers are very dissolute,
climbing mulberries to pick fruit for Gǒu.”
From this, Yuè became angry with Xī,
took his Yǎnzhōu,
and a rift of difficulty thus formed.
During the Jiànxīng reign of Emperor Mǐn of Jìn,
a folk song in Jiāngnán said:
“Boom like a white *kēng* breaking,
gathered together and made into *wǔ*.
Yángzhōu is broken and ruined,
Wúxīng is overturned and shattered like *bùyǔ*.”
According to this, “white” refers to the Jìn dynasty's element,
a *kēng* is a vessel with an opening,
related to an *wèng* (urn),
made of strong pottery,
also similar to metal.
“Boom like a white *kēng* breaking”
means
that the two capitals were overthrown,
and the royal house was greatly damaged.
“Gathered together and made into *wǔ*”
means
that Emperor Yuán gathered the remnants,
to govern the state,
unable to retake the Central Plains,
ruling only in Jiāngnán,
thus the metaphor is small.
As for the affair of Shítóu,
the six armies were greatly defeated,
soldiers plundered the capital,
even reaching the two palaces.
Three years later,
Qián Fèng again attacked the capital,
defending by relying on water,
a standoff for over a month,
burning the city,
wells were filled and trees felled.
Fèng and others were defeated and retreated.
Shěn Chōng led his partisans back to Wúxīng,
and the government army pursued them,
trampling through commanderies and counties.
Chōng and his son were executed,
and those among their partisans who were put to death numbered in the hundreds.
This is what was called
“Yángzhōu is broken and ruined,
Wúxīng is overturned and shattered like *bùyǔ*.”
*Bùyǔ*
are pottery vessels,
also smaller than *wǔ*.
In the early Tàiníng reign of Emperor Míng of Jìn,
a children's rhyme sang:
“Cè lì cè lì,
let the horses graze on the mountain side.
The great horse dies,
the small horse starves,
the high mountain collapses,
stones break by themselves.”
When Emperor Míng died,
Emperor Chéng was young,
forced by Sū Jùn,
moved to Shítóu,
and imperial meals were insufficient.
“The high mountain collapses”
meant that Jùn would soon die;
“stones”
referred to Jùn's younger brother Sū Shí.
After Jùn died,
Shí occupied Shítóu,
and was soon defeated by the various dukes.
Towards the end of Emperor Chéng of Jìn's reign,
a folk rhyme said:
“How rumbling,
chariots enter the royal mausoleum.”
A few days later, the imperial carriage departed (the emperor died).
In the twelfth month of the second year of Xiánkāng of Emperor Chéng of Jìn,
a folk rhyme in Héběi said:
“Wheat enters the soil,
kill Shí Hǔ.”
Later, it happened as the rhyme said.
Yǔ Liàng 初出鎮武昌,
出石頭,
百姓於岸上歌曰:
"Yǔ Gōng 上武昌,
翩翩如飛鳥.
Yǔ Gōng 還揚州,
白馬牽旒旐."
又曰:
"Yǔ Gōng 初上時,
翩翩如飛烏.
Yǔ Gōng 還揚州,
白馬牽流蘇."
後連徵不入,
及薨,
還都葬.
Yǔ Xī 在吳郡,
吳中童謠曰:
"寧食下湖荇,
不食上湖蓴.
Yǔ Wú 沒命喪,
復殺Wáng Lǐngjūn."
無幾而Yǔ Xī, Wáng Qià 相繼亡.
晉穆帝 Shēngpíng 中,
童子輩忽歌於道曰
"Ā Zǐ 聞",
曲終輒云
"Ā Zǐ 汝聞不?"
無幾而穆帝崩,
太后哭曰:
"Ā Zǐ 汝聞不?"
Shēngpíng 末,
民間忽作廉歌.
有Hù Qiān 者聞之,
曰:
"廉者臨也.
歌云'白門廉,
宮廷廉',
內外悉臨,
國家其大諱乎?"
少時而穆帝晏駕.
晉哀帝 Lónghé 初,
童兒歌曰:
"Shēngpíng 不滿斗,
Lónghé 那得久!
Huán Gōng 入石頭,
陛下徒跣走."
帝聞而惡之,
復改年曰 Xīngníng.
民復歌曰:
"雖復改 Xīngníng,
亦復無聊生."
哀帝尋崩,
Shēngpíng 五年,
穆帝崩.
不滿斗,
不至十年也.
晉海西公 Tàihé 中,
民歌曰:
"青青御路楊,
白馬紫游韁.
汝非皇太子,
那得甘露漿."
白者金行;
馬者國族;
紫為奪正之色,
明以紫間朱也.
海西公尋廢,
三子非海西子,
並死,
縊以馬韁死之.
明日,
南方獻甘露.
Tàihé 末,
童謠云:
"犁牛耕御路,
白門種小麥."
及海西被廢,
處吳,
民犁耕其門前,
以種小麥,
如謠言.
晉海西公生皇子,
百姓歌云:
"鳳皇生一雛,
天下莫不喜.
本言是馬駒,
今定成龍子."
其歌甚美,
其旨甚微.
海西公不男,
使左右Xiàng Lóng 與內侍接,
生子以為己子.
Huán Shímín 為荊州,
鎮上明,
民忽歌曰
"Huáng Tánzǐ".
曲終又曰:
"Huáng Tán Yīng,
揚州大佛來上明."
頃 之而Shímín 死,
Wáng Chén 為荊州.
"Huáng Tánzǐ"
乃是Wáng Chén 之字也.
Chén 小字 Fódà,
是
"大佛來上明"
也.
Tàiyuán 末,
京口謠曰:
"黃雌雞,
莫作雄父啼.
一旦去毛衣,
衣被拉颯拪."
尋Wáng Gōng 起兵誅Wáng Guóbǎo,
旋為Liú Láozhī 所敗也.
Sīmǎ Dàozǐ 於東府造土山,
名曰 Língxiùshān.
無幾而Sūn Ēn 作亂,
再踐會稽.
會稽,
Dàozǐ 所封.
靈秀,
Ēn 之字也.
Yǔ Kǎi 鎮歷陽,
民歌曰:
"重羅犁,
重羅犁,
使君南上無還時."
後Kǎi 南奔Huán Xuán,
為Xuán 所誅.
Yīn Zhòngkān 在荊州,
童謠曰:
"芒籠目,
繩縛腹.
Yīn 當敗,
Huán 當復."
無幾而Zhòngkān 敗,
Huán Xuán 有荊州.
Wáng Gōng 鎮京口,
舉兵誅Wáng Guóbǎo,
百姓謠云:
"昔年食白飯,
今年食麥屑.
天公誅讁汝,
教汝捻嚨喉.
嚨喉喝復喝,
京口敗復敗."
"昔年食白飯",
言得志也.
"今年食麥屑",
屑,
粗穢,
其精已去,
明將敗也,
天公將加譴讁而誅之也.
"捻嚨喉",
氣不通,
死之祥也.
"敗復敗",
丁寧之辭也.
Gōng 尋死,
京都大行咳疾,
而喉並喝焉.
Wáng Gōng 在京口,
民間忽云:
"黃頭小人欲作賊,
阿公在城下,
指縛得."
又云:
"黃頭小人欲作亂,
賴得金刀作蕃扞."
字上,
字頭也.
"小人",
字下也.
尋如謠者言焉.
晉安帝 Lóng'ān 中,
民忽作懊惱歌,
其曲中有
"草生可擥結,
女兒可擥抱"
之言.
Huán Xuán 既篡 居天位,
義旗以三月二日掃定京都,
Xuán 之宮女及逆黨之家子女伎妾,
悉為軍賞.
東及Ōu, Yuè,
北流Huái, Sì,
皆人有所獲焉.
時則草可結,
事則女可抱,
信矣.
As Huán Xuán 篡 usurped the throne,
a children's rhyme said:
"Grass grows up to the horse's belly,
Crows peck Huán Xuán's eyes."
When Huán Xuán was defeated and fled to Jiānglíng,
he was executed in the fifth month,
just as the prophecy stated.
During Huán Xuán's time,
a folk rhyme said:
"When the 'zhēng zhōng' lands, Huán will flee."
Zhēng zhōng
refers to a most defiled garment,
and 'Huán'
is a term for the lower body.
Huán Xuán rose from low status to high,
just as 'zhēng zhōng' entered the song,
and the lower body was sung by the people's mouths.
And the phrase
"lands"
signified a downfall,
and the words "will flee"
were clearly validated.
During Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn's time,
a folk poem said:
"There will be eleven mouths,
They will be harmed by soldiers.
Mù Gèng will cross north,
And enter the vast wilderness."
It also said:
"The golden knife has already carved,
Wěi wěi within the golden city."
This poem was said to be composed by Zhú Tánlín, a Daoist from Xiāngyáng,
who spoke of many things
that circulated in the world.
Mèng Yǐ interpreted it, saying:
"Eleven mouths"
is
an image of the character 'Xuán' (玄).
"Mù Gèng" (木亘)
is 'Huán' (桓).
The Huán clan would all flee to Guānzhōng and Luòyáng,
hence it says
"vast wilderness" (hào hào xiāng)
(浩浩鄉).
"Golden knife" (jīn dāo)
is 'Liú' (劉).
Many of the righteous leaders
were surnamed Liú.
"Wěi wěi" (娓娓)
describes beauty and prosperity.
When Huán Xuán achieved his ambition,
a children's rhyme said:
"Chánggān Alley,
Alley of Chánggān.
This year kills the young lord,
Next year beheads all Huáns."
When Huán Xuán fled, all the Huáns were indeed executed.
The "young lord"
was Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn.
At the beginning of Emperor Ān of Jìn's Yìxī reign,
a children's rhyme said:
"The official family raises reeds that turn into rushes,
Reeds grow endlessly and pile up on their own."
At that time, the court raised Lú Lóng,
favored him with gold and purple robes,
and granted him important prefectures.
Though he was nurtured to the extreme,
he could not harbor goodwill,
but instead raised an army to invade internally,
thus becoming an enemy.
"Reeds grow endlessly and pile up on their own"—
when Lú Lóng rebelled,
people at the time recalled the children's rhyme,
disliking its mention of "piling up."
Those who understood said:
"If they are mowed down and stored,
and then burned,
that is the end of the grass.
If they are cut down and piled up,
and then used as firewood,
that is also the end of reeds and rushes.
When their flourishing reaches its peak,
they will also be mowed down and piled up."
Lú Lóng, having exhausted his military power
and amassed his ships,
eventually perished,
his corpses piling up like a mound.
When Lú Lóng occupied Guǎngzhōu,
a folk rhyme said:
"Reeds grow boundless, half reaching the sky."
Later he possessed several upstream prefectures,
pressing inward on the capital,
fulfilling
the words
"half reaching the sky."
In the third year of Yìxī,
children meeting on the road
would invariably raise both hands and say
"Lú jiàn jiàn" (盧健健),
then say
"Dòu tàn,
dòu tàn" (鬬嘆，鬬嘆),
and finally say
"Wēng nián lǎo,
wēng nián lǎo" (翁年老，翁年老).
At the time, no one knew what it meant.
Later, Lú Lóng pressed inward,
his ships covering the river,
which was the meaning of
"jiàn jiàn."
When he reached Chápǔ,
he repeatedly set dates to fight the government forces,
which was the fulfillment of
"dòu tàn."
"Wēng nián lǎo"
meant that the elder statesmen would enjoy a long and peaceful life,
knowing that the rebellious faction
would naturally disappear and perish.
At that time, there was also a rumor that said:
"Lú chéng chéng (盧橙橙),
flows with the water,
If the east wind suddenly rises,
How can he enter Shítou?"
Lú Lóng was indeed defeated,
and could not enter Shítou.
In the past, Wēn Jiào asked Guō Jǐngchún to divine the fortune of himself and Yǔ Liàng.
Jǐngchún said
"Yuánjí" (元吉, supremely auspicious).
Wēn Jiào said to Yǔ Liàng:
"Jǐngchún, with every divination,
probably dares not speak fully.
Since we share the country's safety and danger, and he said 'supremely auspicious,'
it means the affair will succeed."
Thereupon, they collaborated to suppress and eliminate Wáng Dūn.
During Fú Jiān's reign,
a children's rhyme said:
"Ā Jiān has been continuously leading for thirty years,
If later he wishes to be defeated,
It will be by the rivers and lakes."
Later, Fú Jiān was defeated at Féishǔi,
having been in his usurped position for exactly thirty years.
During Fú Jiān's reign,
a rumor said:
"The river waters clear again and again,
Fú Zhào dies in Xīnchéng."
Fú Jiān was killed by Yáo Cháng,
dying in Xīnchéng.
During Fú Jiān's reign,
a song said:
"Yú Yáng Tián Dǒu will destroy Qín."
"Yú Yáng" (魚羊)
is 'Xiān' (鮮).
"Tián Dǒu" (田斗)
is 'Bēi' (卑).
Fú Jiān called himself Qín,
meaning that those who would destroy him were the Xiānbēi.
His officials advised Fú Jiān
to execute all Xiānbēi.
Fú Jiān did not comply.

What is this anomaly for?"
It meant there was no disorder.

Nányáng

Six
is the number of water,

fourteen years from this point.
Two times seven is fourteen,

From the time the emperor received the mandate

In the ninth year of Tàikāng,

In the first month, day dīngsì, of the sixth year of Xiánhé of Jìn Chéng Dì,
outstanding talents and filial individuals from the various commanderies and prefectures gathered at the Lèxiántáng.
A appeared before them

Dog Omens
In Gōngsūn Yuān's household, a dog wearing a cap and scarlet robe went onto the roof.
This was a dog omen.
The rooftop is a place of excessive yang and high peril.
Heaven's warning seemed to say that
Yuān was excessively yang and had no superior,
illicitly elevating himself,
like a dog wearing a cap.
When he later proclaimed himself Wáng of Yān,

Wèi Attendant-in-ordinary Yīng Qú was in his duty lodge

He asked the others, but no one else saw it.

This was a recent dog omen.
Zhūgě Kè returned from his campaign in Huáinán,

Kè said:

He returned to his seat.
After a moment, he rose again,

He merely chased the dog away and changed the mat.
In the second year of Yǒngchū of Sòng Wǔ Dì,
a dog spoke in Jīngyì.
In the twenty-ninth year of Yuánjiā of Wén Dì,
in Dōngqiān, Wúxīng, Mèng Huìdù's maid Mán had relations with a dog like husband and wife for a full year.
In the early Xiàojiàn period of Xiàowǔ,
Yán Jùn was the Left Guard.
In the provincial office, he heard the sound of a puppy underground.
He dug and found a black puppy.
He raised it for a long time,

In the early Míng Dì period,
Zǐxūn, the Prince of Jìn'ān, claimed a false title in Xúnyáng.
In Cáisāng, a dog mated with a woman,

During the Tàishǐ period of Míng Dì,
in Mòlíng, Zhāng Sēnghù's family dog gave birth to a piglet.
White Portents and White Auspices
In the tenth year of Tàikāng of Jìn Wǔ Dì,

The following year,
the imperial carriage died (the emperor died young),

hair grew on the ground.

In the sixth month of the third year of Xiánkāng,
hair grew on the ground.

In the fourth month of the fourteenth year of Tàiyuán,
hair grew on the ground in the capital.

In the fourth month of the seventeenth year of Tàiyuán,
hair grew on the ground.

hair grew on the ground,

In the third month of the third year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
white hair grew from the ground.
In the third month of the tenth year of Yìxī,
white hair grew from the ground.
The following year,
the royal army marched west to suppress Sīmǎ Xiūzhī.

the northern regions of Guān and Luò were swept.

During the time of Qín Shǐhuáng, there was a meteorite fall.

On the Dīngsì day of the fifth month of the fifth year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,

In the first month of the sixth year of Tàikāng,

In the first month of the ninth year of Xiánhé,

Gān Bǎo believed it was the response to Sūn Hào succeeding to the throne from an abolished family.

Some said it was an omen of Sūn Xiū being enthroned.
In the twelfth month of the fifth year of Yuánkāng of Emperor Huì of Jìn,

In the fifth month of the eighth year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,

Jīng Fáng's Yì Zhuàn says:

All three predictions were fulfilled.
In the first year of Yǒngníng of Emperor Huì of Jìn,

this was a white omen.

of decline and fall.

During the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Wén of Sòng,

This was a white omen.
In the first year of Jǐnghé of the Former Deposed Emperor,

Wood harms Metal
At the end of Zhèngshǐ of King Qí of Wèi,
Lǐ Shèng, the Administrator of Hénán, was managing his official duties.
A small piece of wood was dislodged and fell,
striking and severing the neck of Shí Hǔ, an officer receiving a tally.
〔一０〕This was wood harming metal.
Shèng was defeated a few days later.
In the third month of the eighth year of Yuánkāng of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
the stone in the Jiāoméi Altar split in two without cause.

The Jiāoméi Altar

Its spontaneous destruction without cause
was an omen that the Crown Prince would be endangered.
The following year,
Mǐnhuái was deposed and died.

As he first set out from Shítóu,

This was an anomaly of wood harming metal.
Heaven's will seemed to say
that Ān merely made a show of strategic plans,
but would ultimately have no substance;
it was a symbol of cymbals and drums not being used.
In the eighth month,
he returned due to illness,
and died that month.

Zhì, Chapter 22, Line 5, Paragraph 3
The Wǔxíng Zhuàn says:
"If one abandons laws,
banishes meritorious officials,
kills the Crown Prince,
and takes a concubine as wife,

This means that fire loses its nature and becomes a disaster.
It also says:
"If one does not see clearly,

its punishment is distress,

At such times there are plant anomalies,
at such times there are calamities of unscaled creatures,
at such times there are sheep misfortunes,
at such times there are eye diseases,
at such times there are red disasters and red omens.
Only water harms fire."
Liú Xīn's Zhuàn considers unscaled creatures
to be feathered creatures.
Fire does not rise upwards
In the fifth month of the fifth year of Tàihé of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
Qīngshāng Diàn suffered a disaster.
Initially,
when the Emperor was the Prince of Píngyuán,
he took Lady Yú of Hénán as his consort.
When he ascended the throne,
he did not make her Empress,
but instead established the daughter of the musician Máo Jiā, a worker of chariot parts,
who became Empress Dào.
The Empress was originally of humble status
and not suitable for such elevation.
This was the punishment for taking a concubine as wife.
In the sixth month of the first year of Qīnglóng of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
the Jú Shì of Luòyáng Palace suffered a disaster.
In the fourth month of the second year,
Chónghuá Diàn (崇華殿) caught fire,
extending to the south pavilion.
It was repaired.
By the seventh month of the third year,
this palace caught fire again.
The Emperor asked Gāotáng Lóng (高堂隆):
"What is the meaning of this misfortune?
Does ritual allow for prayers or exorcisms?"
He replied:
"Calamities and abnormal phenomena occur
all to provide instruction and warnings.
Only by adhering to ritual and cultivating virtue
can one overcome them.
The Yìzhuàn (易傳) says: 'If the superiors are not frugal,
and the inferiors are not restrained,
calamitous fire will burn their dwellings.'
It also says: 'When the ruler elevates their terraces,
heavenly fire becomes a disaster.'
This means that if a ruler merely adorns their palaces,
unaware of the people's destitution,
Heaven responds with drought,
and fire originates from the high palaces.
According to ancient divination,
the occurrence of calamitous fires
all serves as a warning concerning terraces, pavilions, and palaces.
Now, it is advisable to dismiss the civilian laborers,
focus on frugality,
and clear the burnt areas,
daring not to construct anything there.
Shàpú (萐莆) and auspicious grains
will surely grow in this place,
to reward Your Majesty's reverent virtue."
The Emperor did not comply.
Consequently, Chónghuá Diàn (崇華殿) was restored,
and renamed Jiǔlóng (九龍).
As there were nine reports of dragons appearing from commanderies and kingdoms,
it was thus given this name.
This was the consequence of frequently abandoning laws and regulations,
exhausting the people to satisfy desires,
and treating concubines as wives.
In the twelfth month of the first year of Jiànxīng (建興) under Sūn Liàng (孫亮) of Wú (吳),
the Duānmén (端門) gate in Wǔchāng (武昌) caught fire.
After rebuilding the Duānmén (端門) gate,
the inner palace caught fire again.
According to the Chūnqiū (春秋), the Zhìmén (雉門) and the two watchtowers of Lǔ (魯) caught fire.

the Gāomiào (高廟) in Liáodōng (遼東) caught fire,

The current incident is quite similar to these two events.
Moreover, the gate
is where imperial decrees are issued,

At that time, Zhūgě Kè (諸葛恪) held political power,

On the first day of the second month of the first year of Tàipíng (太平) under Sūn Liàng (孫亮) of Wú (吳),

In the second month of the fifth year of Yǒng'ān (永安) under Sūn Xiū (孫休) of Wú (吳),

In the third month of the second year of Jiànhéng (建衡) under Sūn Hào (孫晧) of Wú (吳),

On the yǐchǒu (乙丑) day of the third month of the eighth year of Tàikāng (太康) under Jìn Wǔdì (晉武帝),

The lightning striking his residence,
