the military arsenal caught fire.
Zhāng Huà (張華) suspected there was chaos,
first fortified the defenses,
and then responded to the disaster.
As a result, accumulated treasures from successive generations,
Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) head,
Kǒngzǐ's (孔子) shoes,
Hàn Gāo's (漢高) sword that severed the white snake, and weapons for two million people
were all destroyed at once.
After this, Mǐnhuái (愍懷) was killed;
this was the punishment for killing the Crown Prince.
Heaven's warning seemed to say:
Setting up defenses and beating watchman's clappers
is to secure the state;
stockpiling military equipment
is to guard against unforeseen events.
Now, the heir apparent is about to fall,
and the altars of soil and grain are about to perish.
Where will the imperial guard find use,
and who will the imperial army protect?
The Emperor and Empress did not comprehend,
ultimately losing the empire.
This was its fulfillment.
Zhāng Huà (張華) and Yán Zuǎn (閻纂) both said,
"The military arsenal caught fire, and the Dī (氐) and Qiāng (羌) rebelled;
the Crown Prince was deposed,
then the fate of the empire is clear."
In the eleventh month of the eighth year of Yuánkāng (元康),
Gāoyuán Líng (高原陵) caught fire.
At this time, Empress Jiǎ (賈后) was cruel and arbitrary,
and Jiǎ Mì (賈謐) monopolized the court.
Their accumulated evil and ripened crimes
deserved to be punished and eradicated.
Heaven's warning seemed to say:
Unacceptable officials and concubines,
even if their closeness and nobility are unmatched,
should still be resolutely executed,
just as I burned Gāoyuán Líng (高原陵).
The Emperor was already dim-witted and weak,
and Zhāng Huà (張華) also did not accept the advice of Péi Wěi (裴頠) and Liú Biàn (劉卞).
Therefore, the Empress and Mì (謐) conspired to falsely accuse and kill the Crown Prince.
Gān Bǎo (干寶) said:
"Gāoyuán Líng (高原陵) caught fire,
and the Crown Prince was deposed;
that was its fulfillment.
In the era of Hàn Wǔdì (漢武帝),
the Gāoyuán Biàndiàn (高園便殿) caught fire,
and Dǒng Zhòngshū's (董仲shu) explanation for that omen was the same as this."
In the first year of Yǒngkāng of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
the emperor married Empress Yáng.
When the empress was about to enter the palace,
fire suddenly appeared in her clothing,
which everyone found strange.
In the second year of Tàian,
Yáng Xuánzhī, the empress's father, died of grief
due to the coercion by Chéngdū.
In the first year of Yǒngxīng,
Chéngdū then deposed the empress,
confining her to the Jīnyǒng Fortress,
and killed her uncle, Tóng.
After this, she was reinstated,
and then deposed four more times.
An imperial edict was also issued to grant her death,
but Xún Fān petitioned for her preservation.
Although she eventually remained in her position,
the distress, coercion, and humiliation she suffered
were unprecedented throughout history.
This was the omen of the disastrous fire.
On the jiǎwǔ day of the seventh month of the second year of Yǒngxīng of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
the various bureaus of the Shàngshū caught fire,
extending to the Chónglǐ Tà and the gallery.
Now, the various bureaus are the foundation of the king's governance,
and this was an omen that the king had abandoned laws.
Qīnghé Wáng Tán entered to become the heir of Jìn,
but did not remain in his position to the end.
This was also a punishment for killing the Crown Prince.
In the eleventh month of the fourth year of Yǒngjiā of Emperor Huái of Jìn,
Xiāngyáng caught fire,
and over three thousand people died.
At this time, Wáng Rú proclaimed himself Grand General and Governor of Yōng and Sī provinces,
with a force of forty or fifty thousand men,
raiding and occupying commanderies and counties,
making them his own territories.
The commander's forces were depleted,
and he held the city by staying within its walls.
The bandits then attacked and pressed Xiāngyáng.
This was a case of inferiors transgressing against superiors,
the yang losing its proper measure,
leading to a fire disaster.
In the Tàixīng reign of Emperor Yuán of Jìn,
Wáng Dūn was stationed in Wǔchāng.
A fire broke out in Wǔchāng,
and he mobilized his troops to extinguish it.
While they were extinguishing it in one place, it ignited elsewhere,
with dozens of places to the east, west, north, and south all igniting simultaneously,
and it did not cease for several days.
This is what Bān Gù meant by "wanton fires spontaneously arising,
which even raising an army cannot extinguish."
Gān Bǎo said:
"This is a disaster where a minister acts as a ruler,
and the亢yáng loses its proper measure."
On the guǐsì day of the first month of the second year of Yǒngchāng of Emperor Yuán of Jìn,
the capital suffered a great fire.
In the third month,
Ráoān, Dōngguāng, and Ānlíng counties caught fire,
burning over seven thousand homes,
and fifteen thousand people died.
In the first month of the first year of Tàiníng of Emperor Míng of Jìn,
the capital caught fire.
At this time, Wáng Dūn was contemptuous of the imperial court,
and committed many acts of impropriety.
Officials both inside and outside the court
harbored resentment and malice.
When extreme yin gives rise to yang,
there are fire disasters.
This is similar to the fire in Chén described by Dǒng Zhòngshū in his commentary on the Chūnqiū.
In the sixth month of the fifth year of Yǒnghé of Emperor Mù of Jìn,
a lightning strike caused a disaster at Shí Hǔ's Tàiwǔ Hall, its two wings, and the Duānmén Gate.
The brilliant light illuminated the sky,
metal and stone were all consumed,
and the fire did not extinguish for over a month.
In the fourth month of that year,
Shí Hǔ had died.
Afterward, the Hú state was destroyed.
In the Tàihé reign of Emperor Hǎixī of Jìn,
Xī Yīn was the Administrator of Kuàijī.
In the sixth month,
there was a great drought disaster,
and fire burned thousands of homes,
extending to several million hú of rice in the Shānyīn granary.
The flames and smoke covered the sky,
and could not be put out.
In the third month of the first year of Níngkāng of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn,
the capital experienced a wind,
and a great fire broke out.
At this time, Huán Wēn had entered the court,
with ambitions to transgress against his superiors.
The young emperor had ascended the throne,
and people harbored worry and fear.
This is similar to the Tàiníng fire.
In the first month of the tenth year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn,
the Guózǐxué (Imperial Academy) was established.
Many students were stubborn and unruly,
and due to the wind, they set fires,
burning over a hundred rooms.
After this, evaluations were not strict,
rewards and punishments were without order.
There was a name for nurturing talent,
but no actual recruitment of worthy individuals.
The Shū Jīng says:
"He who knows men is wise."
This was a harbinger of the punishment for being unwise.
On the yǐwèi day of the twelfth month of the thirteenth year of Tàiyuán,
the Yánxiántáng (Hall of Extending Worthies) suffered a disaster.
On the bǐngshēn day,
the Zhōngsī and Zébǎi Halls, as well as the guest houses and the general of cavalry's arsenal, all suffered disasters.
At that time, the court had many malpractices,
and signs of decline grew daily.
The punishments for being unwise
all had symbolic similarities.
The ruler and prime minister did not comprehend this,
eventually leading to chaos and ruin.
In the third month of the second year of Lóng'ān of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
two dragon boats suffered a disaster.
This was water harming fire.
On the gēngzǐ day of the eighth month of the first year of Yuánxīng of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
the Shàngshū's Xìashècáo caught fire.
In the third year of Yuánxīng,
Lú Xún raided and occupied Guǎngzhōu,
and the provincial governor Wú Yǐnzhī closed the city and defended it resolutely.
On the rénxū night of the tenth month of that year,
a great fire broke out.
At that time, the people, avoiding the bandits,
filled the city.
Yǐnzhī feared an attack by the bandits,
and only focused on strict military discipline,
not prioritizing extinguishing the fire.
Consequently, the government offices were completely burned,
over ten thousand people died,
and the population then dispersed and scattered,
all captured by the bandits.
This omen was almost the same as the Xiāngyáng fire.
On the dīngyǒu day of the seventh month of the fourth year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
the Shàngshū's Diànzhōnglìbùcáo caught fire.
In the eleventh year of Yìxī,
the capital experienced widespread fire disasters,
especially severe in the Wú region.
Fire prevention measures were very strict,
yet it did not cease.
Wáng Hóng, who was then Administrator of Wú Commandery,
saw a red object descend from the sky in broad daylight while in the audience hall.
It was shaped like a messenger's banner,
and directly landed on a house south of the road,
whereupon the fire immediately flared up again.
Hóng knew it was a disaster caused by Heaven,
and did not blame the person responsible for the fire.
On the wùzǐ day of the first month of the fifth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
the capital experienced a great fire.
On the yǐhài day of the twelfth month of the seventh year of Yuánjiā,
the capital caught fire,
extending to burn the north wall of the Tàishè (Grand Altar).
On the rénwǔ day of the third month of the twenty-ninth year of Yuánjiā,
the capital experienced a great fire,
with very strong winds and thunder.
On the jǐsì day of the first month of the third year of Yuánhuī of the Later Deposed Emperor,
the capital experienced a great fire.
On the wùchén day of the second month of the third year of Yuánhuī,
the capital experienced a great fire,
burning thousands of homes on both banks.
Concerning warmth:
the omen of warmth is,
according to Liú Xiàng and Bān Gù, when there is no ice in winter or frost does not kill grass.
Jīng Fáng's Yìzhuàn also says:
"In summer, heat kills people;
in winter, plants blossom and bear fruit."
In the ninth month of the first year of Jiànxīng of Sūn Liàng of Wú,
peaches and plums blossomed.
During Sūn Quán's reign,
governance was burdensome and taxes heavy,
and the people were exhausted by labor.
At this time, Zhūgě Kè began to assist in governance,
stopping the recruitment of school officials,
forgiving outstanding debts,
abolishing customs barriers,
and promoting leniency.
This was an omen of relaxation and easing.
Another interpretation is that peach and plum blossoms in cold weather are a plant prodigy,
or belong to the category of 'blossoming calamities'.
In the tenth month of the third year of Jǐngyuán of Emperor Yuán of Wèi,
peaches and plums blossomed.
After Gāo Guì was assassinated,
Jìn Wén Wáng deeply cultivated kindness and virtue,
and affairs were conducted with great leniency and ease.
This was its omen.
In the twelfth month of the ninth year of Yǒnghé of Emperor Mù of Jìn,
peaches and plums blossomed.
At this time, Jiǎnwén assisted in governance,
and many affairs were lax and neglected.
This was an omen of relaxation and easing.
In the tenth month of the first year of Shēngmíng of Emperor Shùn of Sòng,
peaches, plums, and apples in Yúqián bore fruit.
Plant prodigy.
In the spring, the first month of the 25th year of Jiàn'ān, during the reign of Hàn Xiàndì,
Wèi Wǔdì was in Luòyáng.
He was about to begin construction of the Jiànshǐ Palace
when he cut down a tree at the Zhuólóng Temple, and blood flowed out.
He also dug up and transplanted a pear tree,
and its roots were injured and bled too.
The Emperor was disturbed by this,
and subsequently fell ill,
dying that month.
This was an omen of plant anomalies,
and also an auspicious red omen.
That year
was the first year of Huángchū, during the reign of Wèi Wéndì.
In the sixth month of the first year of Wǔfèng, during the reign of Wú Sūn Liàng,
weeds in Jiāozhǐ transformed into rice.
Formerly, when Sānmáo was about to perish,
the five grains mutated.
This was a plant anomaly.
Thereafter, Liàng was deposed.
In the fifth year of Jǐngyào, during the reign of Shǔ Liú Chán,
a large tree in the palace courtyard inexplicably broke off by itself.
Qiáo Zhōu was worried about this
but had no one to speak to,
so he wrote on a pillar:
"Numerous and great,
they will gather;
prepared and bestowed,
how can it be restored?"
He meant that the Cáo clan was numerous;
Wèi was great;
when the numerous and great
gather, the empire will indeed converge;
prepared and bestowed,
how can there be any more who can establish themselves?
Shǔ indeed perished,
as Zhōu had said.
This was a plant anomaly.
In the first year of Tiānxǐ, during the reign of Wú Sūn Hào,
Línpíng Lake in Wújùn, which had been choked with weeds since the end of the Hàn dynasty,
suddenly opened up in one night, becoming clear of weeds.
Elders passed down that
when this lake was choked,
the world was in chaos;
when this lake opened,
the world would be at peace.
Wú soon perished,
and the nine provinces became one.
In the eighth month of the third year of Tiānjì, during the reign of Wú Sūn Hào,
in Jiànyè, a "ghost-eye vegetable" grew in the home of Artisan Huánggǒu,
twining around a jujube tree,
more than a *zhàng* in length,
its stem four *cùn* wide
and three *fēn* thick.
There was also a "stone vegetable" that grew in the home of Artisan Wú Píng,
four *chǐ* tall,
shaped like a loquat,
the upper part a *chǐ* and eight *cùn* in diameter,
the lower stem five *cùn* wide,
with green-edged leaves on both sides.
The Dōngguān consulted diagrams
and named the "ghost-eye vegetable" as *zhīcǎo*,
and the "stone vegetable" as *pínglǜ*.
Consequently, Huánggǒu was appointed as Shìzhīláng,
and Píng as Pínglǜláng,
both with silver seals and green ribbons.
Gān Bǎo said:
"The following year, Jìn pacified Wú,
and Wáng Jùn stopped his boats
precisely at Píngzhǔ.
The names are strikingly clear,
a verification of the omens.
As for Huánggǒu (Yellow Dog),
Wú succeeded Hàn with the earth element,
hence initially there was the auspicious omen of the Yellow Dragon;
by its final years,
there was the anomaly of the ghost-eye vegetable,
taking lodging in the home of Huánggǒu;
the yellow appellation remained unchanged,
but the status of noble and humble differed greatly.
This was a subtle and precise response from the Dao of Heaven."
In the spring of the second year of Yuánkāng, during the reign of Jìn Huìdì,
bamboo in the territory of Bāxī Commandery bloomed,
purple in color,
bearing fruit like wheat,
with a green outer skin,
red and white inside,
and a sweet taste.
On the *gēngzǐ* day of the sixth month of the ninth year of Yuánkāng,
a mulberry tree grew in the west wing of the Eastern Palace,
growing more than a *chǐ* each day;
on the *jiǎchén* day,
it withered and died.
This was the same anomaly as that of Yīn Tàiwù.
The Crown Prince was unable to comprehend it,
hence he was eventually deposed and executed.
Bān Gù stated:
"When wild trees grow in the court and grow rapidly,
petty individuals will suddenly occupy the positions of high ministers,
endangering and destroying the state,
symbolizing that the court will become ruins."
Thereafter, Sūn Xiù and Zhāng Lín soon came into power,
leading to great chaos.
On the *dīngsì* day of the fourth month of the first year of Yǒngkāng, during the reign of Jìn Huìdì,
Imperial Grandson Zāng was established as Imperial Great-grandson.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day of the fifth month,
he took up residence in the Eastern Palace.
A mulberry tree again grew in the west wing.
The following year,
Zhào Lún usurped the throne
and poisoned Zāng to death.
This was the same anomaly as that of Mǐnhuái.
In the fourth month of the first year of Yǒngkāng,
in Zhuàngwǔ State, a mulberry tree transformed into a cypress.
That month,
Zhāng Huá was killed.
In the winter of the third year of Yǒngjiā, during the reign of Jìn Xiàohuáidì,
in Xiàng County, a mulberry tree made a sound like breaking wood.
The people called it "the mulberry grove weeping."
According to Liú Xiàng's explanation,
mulberry (*sāng*) implies mourning (*sāng*),
and it also made a weeping sound,
which was extremely inauspicious.
At that time, the capital was weakened,
and barbarian invaders pressed from all sides.
Sīmǎ Yuè had no intention of defending the imperial capital.
In the winter of the fourth year,
he abandoned it and moved south.
By the spring of the fifth year,
he died in that city.
Shí Lè ambushed his forces,
surrounded and shot at them.
From princes and dukes down to commoners,
over one hundred thousand people died.
He also opened Yuè's coffin and burned his corpse.
With this defeat,
the Central Plains had no one to turn to for protection,
and Luòjīng soon fell.
This was the fulfillment of the weeping mulberry.
In the fifth month of the sixth year of Yǒngjiā,
in Wúxī County, there were four dogwood trees
that intertwined and grew,
resembling Siamese twins.
Earlier,
Guō Jǐngchún had divined about the "sleeping rat of Yánlíng,"
encountering the hexagrams Lín and Yì.
He said:
"Later, there will again be an anomalous tree growing,
which seems auspicious but is not;
it is a bitter, pungent wood.
If this occurs,
within several hundred *lǐ* to the southeast, there will surely be a rebel."
Thereafter, Xú Fù started a rebellion.
This was a plant anomaly,
which Guō believed indicated that "wood does not bend or straighten."
In the seventh month of the sixth year of Yǒngjiā,
in Yùzhāng Commandery, a camphor tree that had been withered for a long time
suddenly revived and flourished that month.
This was the same omen as the withered earth altar of Chāngyì reviving.
Huáidì did not complete his reign,
and Yuándì rose from a collateral branch, fulfilling this omen.
In the ninth month of the first year of Tàiníng, during the reign of Jìn Míngdì,
a tree in Shàn County, Kuàijī, grew a face like a human's.
Thereafter, Wáng Dūn raised troops and rebelled,
but his calamity and defeat were unsuccessful.
During the reigns of Hàn Āi and Líng,
both had this anomaly,
but with fully formed human features,
hence their calamities were also great.
Now this was merely a human face,
hence its change was also slight.
On the *guǐhài* day of the fifth month of the sixth year of Xiánhé, during the reign of Jìn Chéngdì,
in Qǔ'ā, a willow tree that had been fallen for six years
suddenly rose again and grew that month.
On the *jiǎxū* day of the fifth month of the ninth year of Xiánhé,
in the home of Wú Xióng, a dead elm tree
rose and grew that day due to wind and rain.
This was the same omen as the broken willow in Shànglín during the Hàn dynasty rising again.
Initially,
Kāngdì was King of Wú.
Although he was later enfeoffed as Lángyá,
he still received the territory of Wújùn as his fief.
This was an omen of the Emperor exceeding the proper lineage and inheriting the state.
Qǔ'ā was also formerly part of Wú territory,
and the omen appeared in the Wú settlement of Wú Xióng's house,
which was also the will of Heaven.
On the *guǐmǎo* day of the fifth month of the third year of Xīngníng, during the reign of Jìn Āidì,
in the home of Xiūmíng in Xīchāng County, Lúlíng, a dead chestnut tree
suddenly rose and grew that day.
At that time, Xiàowǔ was four years old,
and Jiǎnwén was a regional prince,
with the hearts of the four seas.
When he attained the throne and established the lineage,
Xiàowǔ's reign became prosperous.
Knowledgeable people secretly said it was the auspicious omen of Xīchāng Xiūmíng,
and the Emperor's taboo name indeed corresponded to it.
This was quite similar to the omen of Hàn Xuāndì.
In the first year of Tàihé of Hǎixī, Jìn dynasty,
pine trees grew on poplars in Liángzhōu.
Heaven's warning seemed to say:
Pines do not change their branches or leaves;
poplars are soft and brittle trees.
This eternal enterprise
will converge in a place of danger and destruction.
After this, Zhāng Tiānxī surrendered to the Dī.
In the sixth month of the fourteenth year of Tàiyuán of Jìn Xiàowǔ,
a withered tree in Tónglè County, Jiànníng, broke and fell,
then suddenly stood up and reattached itself.
Jīng Fáng's *Yì Zhuàn* says:
"Abandoning righteousness for licentiousness,
the omen is a tree breaking and reattaching itself.
If the empress or consort has undue power,
a fallen tree will stand upright again."
At that time, the governance was deviating from the path,
largely losing its correctness.
Afterward, Lady Zhāng monopolized favor,
and when the emperor died,
the common people blamed the Zhāng clan.
In the third year of Yuánxīng of Jìn Āndì,
bamboo in the Jīng and Jiāng regions bore fruit like wheat.
In the ninth month of the second year of Yìxī of Jìn Āndì,
at the home of Chén Gài, a soldier in the camp of the General of Yángwǔ in Yángzhōu, there grew a bitter herb (kǔpòcài),
four feet six inches tall,
and three feet two inches wide.
This is probably the same omen as the end of Wú.
During Yìxī,
caltrops grew on both sides of the imperial road above the palace wall.
This is a plant omen.
Caltroops have thorns,
making it impossible to tread upon them.
Their growth on the palace wall and imperial road
is Heaven's warning, seeming to say:
The ruler is silent and unable to hear state affairs;
though dwelling in the imperial palace,
it is like an empty palace.
Though there is an imperial road,
it is never ridden upon,
and caltrops grow everywhere, as if it is empty and abandoned.
In the eighth year of Yìxī,
a *xūn* tree grew beside the altar of the Grand Altar of the State (Tàishè).
In writings, *xūn* refers to black,
which is an auspicious sign for the Sòng's water-virtue to become king.
Calamities of Feathered Creatures
In the fifth month of the fourth year of Huángchū of Wèi Wéndì,
pelicans gathered at the Língzhī Pond.
According to Liú Xiàng's explanation,
this is a calamity of feathered creatures,
and also a blue auspicious sign.
An edict said:
"These are what the poets refer to as defiled marshes.
The poems of Cáo criticized Gōnggōng for distancing himself from gentlemen
and associating with petty men.
Are there now wise and sagacious men
in low positions?
Otherwise, why would these birds come?
Let all outstanding and virtuous talents in the empire,
and upright gentlemen, be widely recommended,
to respond to the criticism of the Cáo people."
Thereupon, Yáng Biāo, Guǎn Níng, and their like
were all recommended.
This is called "seeing an omen and knowing fear."
However, they were unable to be magnanimous towards the brilliant and upright,
and instead were mostly swayed by favoritism.
Jīng Fáng's *Yì Zhuàn* says:
"If the virtuous are dismissed,
the omen is water birds gathering in the country's wells."
At the end of Huángchū,
a swallow in the palace gave birth to a hawk,
with red mouth and claws.
This is the same omen as Shāng Zhòu and Sòng Yǐn.
In the first year of Jǐngchū,
a swallow again gave birth to a giant chick at the home of Lǐ Gài in Juāntáo Lǐ, Wèiguó.
Its shape was like a hawk,
its beak like a swallow's.
According to Liú Xiàng's explanation,
this is a calamity of feathered creatures,
and also a red omen.
Gāo Tánglóng said:
"This is a great anomaly for the Wèi house;
one should guard against 'hawk-like' ministers within the inner walls."
Later, King Xuān of Jìn rose,
and thus took over the Wèi house.
In the twenty-third year of Jiàn'ān of Hàn Xiàndì,
a bald stork gathered at the pond behind the Wénchāng Hall of the Yè Palace.
The next year,
King Wǔ of Wèi died.
In the third year of Huángchū of Wèi Wéndì,
it gathered again at the Fānglín Park pond in Luòyáng.
In the seventh year,
it gathered again.
That summer,
Wéndì died.
At the end of Jǐngchū,
it gathered again at the Fānglín Park pond.
As it had appeared twice before,
each time followed by a great funeral,
the emperor detested it.
That year,
Míngdì died.
In the tenth month of the ninth year of Jiànxīng of Shǔ Liú Shàn,
from Jiāngyáng to Jiāngzhōu, birds flew from south of the Jiāng River to north of the Jiāng River,
but could not reach their destination,
and thousands fell into the water and died.
At that time, Zhūgě Liàng continuously mobilized troops for years,
determined to annex the Central Plains,
but eventually died south of the Wèi River,
and his plans were not achieved.
Also, various generals contended,
losing many soldiers.
Birds flying north unable to reach their destination,
falling into the water and dying,
all bear this omen.
Liàng ultimately could not cross the Wèi River;
was this not its fulfillment?
This is somewhat similar to the birds of Hàn and Chǔ fighting and falling into the Sì River.
In the third year of Qīnglóng of Wèi Míngdì,
a hoopoe nested at the home of Zhāng Jiàn of Jùlù.
Jiàn was learned and of high integrity,
not responding to the summons of Yuán Shào or Gāo Gàn.
Wèi Tàizǔ also did not reach him.
He lived a leisurely, reclusive life,
with hundreds of disciples.
Grand Administrator Wáng Sù respectfully regarded him.
At that time, he was over one hundred years old,
and said to his disciples:
"The hoopoe is a yang bird,
but it nests in the shade of the gate.
This is an ominous sign."
He then took up his zither and sang,
composing a poem,
and died within ten days.
According to divination,
it was a calamity of feathered creatures.
In the first year of Jǐngchū of Wèi Míngdì,
when the Língxiāo Pavilion was first built,
magpies nested on it.
Magpies are black and white in color.
This is a calamity of feathered creatures,
and also a black and white auspicious sign.
The emperor asked Gāo Tánglóng about it,
who replied:
"The *Shī* says: 'Though the magpie has a nest,
the cuckoo dwells in it.'
Now, having started to build a palace,
magpies come to nest.
This is an omen that the palace will not be completed,
and the self will not be able to dwell in it.
Heaven's will seems to say:
Before the palace is complete,
another surname will control it;
this must be deeply considered."
Thereupon, the emperor changed his expression and countenance.
In the fourth month of the twelfth year of Chìwū of Wú Sūn Quán,
two crows held a magpie and dropped it in the Eastern Hall.
Quán ordered Chancellor Zhū Jù to burn the magpie as a sacrifice.
According to Liú Xīn's explanation,
this is a calamity of feathered creatures,
and also a black auspicious sign.
It is the punishment for not seeing clearly
and not hearing acutely.
At that time, Quán's ambition overflowed and his virtue declined;
he believed slanders and was fond of killing.
His two sons were in danger,
and both chancellors and generals were imperiled.
He saw the omen but did not understand,
and even added burning to it;
this was extreme blindness to the Dao.
The next year,
Crown Prince Hé was deposed,
King Bà of Lǔ was granted death,
Zhū Jù was demoted,
and Lù Yì died of worry;
this was its fulfillment.
The Eastern Hall,
the seat of education;
the magpie falling into the Eastern Hall,
was this also Heaven's will?
In the first month of the second year of Tàiyuán of Wú Sūn Quán,
the former Crown Prince Hé was enfeoffed as King of Nányáng,
and sent to Chángshā.
A magpie nested on his ship's mast.
Hé's former palace officials heard of it,
and were all distressed,
believing that the mast's tip was precarious,
not a sign of long-term peace.
After this, he indeed did not die a natural death.
In the eleventh month of the second year of Jiànxīng of Sūn Liàng of Wú,
five large birds were seen in Chūnshēn.
The people of Wú considered them to be Fènghuáng (phoenixes).
The following year,
the era name was changed to Wǔfèng.
During the reign of Hàn Huán Dì,
there were large five-colored birds.
Sīmǎ Biāo said:
“When governance is in decline and deficient,
it is impossible to attract a phoenix.
These are merely calamities brought by feathered creatures.”
Sūn Liàng had not yet implemented virtuous governance,
and Sūn Jùn was still immensely arrogant and tyrannical.
This situation was similar to that of Huán Dì.
According to the Ruìyìngtú (Illustrations of Auspicious Omens),
there was more than one instance of large birds resembling phoenixes that were actually omens of disaster.
It is suspected that these were all such cases.
In the third year of Jiànhéng of Sūn Hào of Wú,
it was reported from the Western Garden that phoenixes had gathered,
and because of this, the era name was changed.
The meaning was the same as during Liàng’s reign.
In the eighth month of the fourth year of Tàishǐ of Jìn Wǔ Dì,
a long-tailed pheasant flew up to the Chānghémén gate.
When Zhào Lún usurped the throne,
a strange bird was found in Luòyáng,
which no one could name.
Lún sent someone to carry it out
and circulate it through the city and towns to ask people about it.
After several days,
a young boy in the western part of the palace saw it
and spontaneously said:
“It is a Fúliú bird-yì.”
The bearer immediately returned and reported to Lún.
Lún sent someone to fetch the boy again.
When he arrived,
he saw it again.
He was brought into the palace,
the bird was secretly caged,
and the boy was confined in a room.
The next day, when they looked,
both were gone.
This was a calamity of feathered creatures,
and a particularly ominous one.
When Zhào Lún usurped the throne,
a quail entered the Tàijídiàn palace,
and pheasants gathered in the Eastern Hall.
According to the Tàijí and Eastern Hall,
both were places for court audiences and hearing political matters.
That quails and pheasants gathered there on the same day,
Heaven’s will seemed to say,
that he should not occupy this position.
The Shī (Classic of Poetry) says:
“The magpies fly in multitudes,
the quails dart about.
When a man is without goodness,
I take him as my lord.”
Is this not what it refers to?
In ancient times, when the sovereign of Yīn was moved by the crowing of pheasants,
he feared and cultivated virtue.
Lún saw these two creatures,
but never knew to take warning,
hence he met his demise.
In the second month of the first year of Yǒngjiā of Jìn Xiàohuái Dì,
the ground collapsed in Bùguǎnglǐ, northeast of Luòyáng,
and geese emerged.
The dark-colored ones flew up to the sky,
while the white ones remained.
This was a calamity of feathered creatures,
and also an omen of black and white.
Dǒng Yǎng said:
“Bùguǎng was
Díquán of Zhōu,
a place of alliances and gatherings.
The white ones are like gold,
the dark ones symbolize the Hú (barbarians),
how can it all be explained?”
After this, Liú Yuān and Shí Lè successively usurped power in Huá,
and the two emperors Huái and Mǐn perished in unsuitable places.
During the reign of Jìn Xiàohuái Dì,
there was a goose in a cage in Zhōu Qǐ’s home,
but its head was severed outside the cage.
After Qǐ died, his family was executed.
On the day Gēngxū in the eighth month of the third year of Tàiníng of Jìn Míng Dì,
there were two birds,
dark-colored and black,
with wings spanning fourteen feet.
One gathered at the Sītúfǔ (Ministry of Works),
was shot and killed;
the other gathered at a family's house north of the market,
and was also captured.
This was a calamity of feathered creatures,
and also a black omen.
On the day Wùzǐ of the intercalary month,
the emperor passed away.
Later, there were the rebellions of Sū Jùn and Zǔ Yuē.
In the first month of the second year of Xiánhé of Jìn Chéng Dì,
five seagulls gathered in the palace courtyard.
This was another white omen.
At this time, Yǔ Liàng arbitrarily disregarded the public's counsel
and was about to summon Sū Jùn,
which led to the fault of not heeding advice,
hence the white omen appeared first.
In the second month of the third year,
Jùn indeed rebelled,
the palace buildings were burned down,
turning into ruins and overgrown land,
which was its manifestation.
In the seventh month of the eighth year of Xiánkāng of Jìn Chéng Dì,
white egrets gathered on the palace roof.
At this time, Kāng Dì had just ascended the throne,
this was an omen of not reigning long.
Later, after two years, the emperor passed away.
Liú Xiàng said:
“When wild birds enter a dwelling,
the palace will soon be empty.”
Zhāng Guàn, while in his correct court in Liángzhōu,
released sparrows and various birds.
Those he released died immediately;
those released by his attendants all flew away.
In the first month of the sixteenth year of Tàiyuán of Jìn Xiàowǔ Dì,
magpies nested on the owl-tail at the eastern end of the Tàijí palace,
and also nested at the western end of the Guózǐxuétáng (National Academy).
In the eighteenth year,
the Eastern Palace was completed.
In the first month of the nineteenth year,
magpies again nested at its western gate.
This is likely the same omen as during Wèi Jǐngchū.
The Academy
is where customs and teachings gather;
the western gate
is an omen of the element Metal.
In the third year of Yìxī of Jìn Ān Dì,
Zhū Yī, the Longxiáng General, was garrisoned at Shòuyáng.
A maid was cooking rice,
when suddenly a flock of crows gathered at the stove,
competing to peck and eat.
The maid drove them away, but they would not leave.
A hunting dog bit and killed a magpie.
The remaining crows then together pecked the dog until it died,
and also ate its flesh,
leaving only bones.
In the sixth month of the fifth year,
Yī died.
In the third year of Yǒngchū of Sòng Wǔ Dì,
when Xú Xiànzhī was appointed Sīkōng (Minister of Works) from the imperial dais,
and all officials attended the ceremony,
two wild storks gathered on the Tàijí owl-tail and cried out.
In the spring of the second year of Jǐngpíng of Shào Dì,
storks nested on the western owl-tail of the Tàimiào (Ancestral Temple);
they were driven away but returned.
In the spring of the second year of Yuánjiā of Wén Dì,
hundreds of江ōu (river gulls) gathered inside the small steps in front of the Tàijídiàn palace.
The following year,
Xú Xiànzhī and others were executed.
Calamity of Sheep
In the fifth month of the second year of Xiánhé of Jìn Chéng Dì,
Sītú Wáng Dǎo
had a lamb born without hind legs.
This was a calamity of sheep.
The Jīng Fáng Yì Zhuàn (Commentary on the Yi by Jing Fang) says:
“One with fewer legs
means that the subordinates are not competent.”
The following year,
Sū Jùn entered the capital,
and Dǎo and Chéng Dì were both imprisoned at Shítóu,
barely escaping with their lives.
This was its manifestation.
In the seventh year of Dàmíng of Sòng Xiàowǔ Dì,
Yǒngpíng Commandery presented a three-horned sheep.
This was a calamity of sheep.
Red Omen of Disaster and Red Omen of Auspiciousness
During Gōngsūn Yuān’s time,
raw flesh grew in the northern market of Xiāngpíng,
several feet long and wide,
with a head, eyes, mouth, and beak,
but no hands or feet,
yet it moved.
This was a red omen of disaster.
The divination says:
“Having form but not forming,
having body but no sound,
that country will perish.”
Yuān was soon executed by Wèi.
Dèng Jiā, a garrison commander in Wú, killed a pig to sacrifice to the gods.
After preparing it, he hung it up,
and suddenly saw a human head come to eat the meat.
Jiā drew his bow and shot it,
it made a "zhā zhā" sound,
and circled the house for three days.
This was a near-red omen of auspiciousness.
Later, someone reported that Jiā was plotting to defect to the north,
and his entire family was executed.
The Jīng Fáng Yì Yāo (Jing Fang's Yi Anomalies) says:
“Mountains show bào (covered with lush vegetation),
rivers flow into cities,
cities have soldiers,
shaped like a human head, red in color.”
When Zhūgě Kè of Wú was about to be executed,
the water he washed in smelled of blood;
when his attendant gave him clothes,
the clothes also smelled.
This was a proximate red omen.
In the eleventh month of the seventh year of Tàikāng during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
there was red snow covering two qǐng in Héyīn.
This was a red omen.
Four years later, the emperor passed away,
and the royal court subsequently fell into chaos.
In the third month of the fifth year of Yuánkāng during the reign of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
blood flowed in Lǚ Xiàn,
covering over a hundred paces east to west.
This was a red omen.
At the end of Yuánkāng,
there was extreme wickedness and chaos,
corresponding to the corpses lying and blood flowing.
Gān Bǎo believed that eight years later, Fēng Yún caused chaos in Xúzhōu,
killing and injuring tens of thousands of people,
which was its manifestation.
In the third month of the first year of Yǒngkāng during the reign of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
it rained blood in Wèishì.
Indeed, when government and punishments are lenient,
there are omens of constant warmth and red portents.
In the first month of this year,
Mǐnhuái Tàizǐ was sent to be imprisoned in Xǔ Gōng.
Heaven's warning seemed to say,
"You should not be lenient and indulge villains,
lest the Crown Prince die unjustly."
Emperor Huì, being foolish and unaware,
the Crown Prince Mǐnhuái died that very month.
Thereupon, the royal house's misfortune was complete,
and disaster spread throughout the realm.
On the day Nàochǐ killed Qí Mǐnwáng,
it rained blood which stained his clothes;
Heaven announced this,
is this what it refers to?
Jīng Fáng's Yì Zhuàn says:
"If prisoners are not released from jail,
this is called chasing wrongs.
The calamity for this is that Heaven rains blood.
This is called 'not亲' (not 친),
the people have resentment.
Before three years pass,
their clan will be gone."
It also says:
"If sycophants are rewarded,
and meritorious officials are executed,
Heaven rains blood."
On the bingyín day of the twelfth month of the fourth year of Jiànxīng during the reign of Emperor Mǐn of Jìn,
the Chancellor's office executed Chúnyú Bó, the order history for supervising transport.
His blood flowed upwards two zhàng and three chǐ on the pillar.
This was a red omen.
At that time, General of the Rear Chǔ Póu was garrisoned in Guǎnglíng.
The Chancellor announced a northern expedition.
Bó was executed according to military law for delaying transport and for corruptly employing people,
on the basis of the laws for conscripted armies.
His son appealed, stating:
"Bó completed the transport duties,
without any delays or deficiencies.
Although he received bribes and employed people,
his crime does not warrant death.
The situation for military campaigns
is one of initial declaration followed by actual deployment;
in reality, it was a garrison deployment,
not a conscripted army.
Since the fourth year,
transport by water has been delayed,
but none have been judged by the laws for military expeditions."
None of the officials dealt with this matter.
When this unusual event occurred,
the Investigating Censor impeached many officials,
but Emperor Yuán also did not inquire into it.
Thereupon, there were frequent droughts for three years.
Gān Bǎo believed this was the manifestation of unjust qi.
Guō Jǐngchún said:
"Blood is a type of water,
both belonging to Kǎn.
Kǎn represents the Legalists.
Water naturally flows downwards,
it should not flow upwards.
This is a sign that the government has faults and errors."
Textual criticism notes
Zhì, twenty-third chapter, fifth line, fourth character.
The Wǔxíng Zhuàn says:
"If ancestral temples are neglected,
sacrifices are not offered,
ritual ceremonies are abolished,
and natural seasons are defied,
then water will not flow downwards smoothly."
This means water loses its natural properties and becomes a disaster.
It also says:
"If one does not listen intelligently,
this is called not consulting.
Its calamity is urgency,
its punishment is cold,
its extreme is poverty.
At such times there are drum omens,
at such times there are fish anomalies,
at such times there are pig misfortunes,
at such times there are ear ailments,
at such times there are black calamities and black omens.
Only fire pollutes water."
Fish anomalies,
Liú Xīn's Zhuàn believed to be anomalies of shelled insects,
referring to locusts and such.
Water not flowing downwards smoothly.
In the sixth month of the fourth year of Huángchū during the reign of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
there was heavy continuous rain.
The Yī and Luò rivers overflowed to the city gate of Jīnyáng,
sweeping away several thousand homes
and drowning people.
Originally,
when the emperor ascended the throne,
he moved the capital from Yè to Luò,
constructing palaces,
but did not build ancestral temples.
The spirit tablets of Tàizǔ were still in Yè.
He once held a feast and sacrifice in Jiànshǐ Diàn according to family rites,
and throughout Huángchū, he never returned to Yè.
The altars for Yuánqiū, Fāngzé, the northern and southern suburbs, Shè, and Jì,
had no fixed locations.
This was the punishment for neglecting ancestral temples
and abolishing sacrifices.
Jīng Fáng's Yì Zhuàn says:
"If specialists have knowledge,
but punishments are unjustly carried out,
its calamity is water.
As for this water,
rain kills people after frost has fallen,
a great wind makes the sky yellow.
If there is famine but no loss,
this is called 'tà' (excessive).
Its calamity is water killing people.
If the virtuous are avoided and restrained,
this is called madness.
Its calamity is water,
water flowing and killing people;
after the water, the earth breeds insects.
If prisoners are not released from jail,
this is called chasing wrongs.
Its water kills people with cold.
If the pursuit of punishment is not resolved,
this is called 'not lý' (unreasonable).
Its water causes the five grains not to be harvested.
If a great defeat is not resolved,
this is called 'all yīn' (excessive yin).
Its water flows into cities and towns,
and falling frost kills grains."
In the summer of the eighth year of Chìwū during the reign of Sūn Quán of Wú,
great floods overflowed in Chálíng Xiàn,
sweeping away over two hundred homes.
In the autumn of the thirteenth year,
great floods again overflowed in Dānyáng's Gùzhāng and other counties.
It is noted that although Quán claimed emperorship for thirty years,
he ultimately did not establish seven ancestral temples in Jiànyè;
there was only one temple for his father, Jiān,
far away in Chángshā,
and the suburban sacrifices were deficient.
At the beginning of Jiāhé,
officials proposed that suburban sacrifices should be performed,
but he again refused.
In his later years, although he performed one southern suburban sacrifice,
there was no record of a northern suburban sacrifice.
Furthermore, the Three Rivers, Five Lakes, Héng, Huò, and Kuàijī
were all prominent places in Wú and Chǔ,
but they were not seen to be properly honored.
Instead, he performed rites to the demonic deities of Luóyáng,
seeking blessings and assistance.
Heaven's will seemed to say,
"Quán neglected ancestral temples,
did not offer sacrifices,
and abolished ritual ceremonies.
This punishment is shown
to make him realize his error."
In the first year of Tàiyuán,
there were also strange phenomena of great winds and surging waters.
That winter,
Quán performed the southern suburban sacrifice.
Perhaps this was in response to the ominous signs.
Upon returning, he fell ill.
In the fourth month of the following year,
he passed away.
Alternatively, it is said that
Quán at that time believed and accepted slanders,
so even though Lù Yì had great merit,
and Zǐhé was the heir apparent,
they did not meet their proper ends.
This is similar to Emperor Ān of Hàn listening to slanders, dismissing Yáng Zhèn, and deposing the Crown Prince.
Moreover, throughout the Chìwū period, there was no year without military campaigns,
causing the common people to be distressed and resentful.
In the autumn of the eighth year,
General Mǎ Mào and others again planned a rebellion.
In the ninth month of the first year of Jǐngchū of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
excessive rain fell continuously.
Ji, Yǎn, Xú, and Yù four prefectures suffered floods,
drowning and killing people,
and washing away property.
Since the emperor first ascended the throne,
he indulged in extreme extravagance and desire,
seizing many young girls,
or taking away the wives of officials.
He extensively adorned palaces and chambers,
hindering agriculture and warfare.
He gave free rein to his desires.
By this time, it was even worse.
His decrees went against the seasons,
and he did not reduce labor even during famine.
This was the manifestation of water not moistening downwards.
In the summer of the first year of Wǔfèng of Sūn Liàng of Wú,
there was a great flood.
Four years after Liàng ascended the throne,
he established a temple for Quán.
Moreover, throughout the Wú dynasty,
he did not confer ancestral titles
nor perform the rites of honoring his strict father,
leaving a deficiency in the number of generations (zhāomù).
Liàng, Xiū, and Hào also abolished the two suburban sacrifices
and did not properly rank the various deities.
This was the punishment for neglecting ancestral temples
and failing to offer sacrifices.
Also at this time,
Sūn Jùn held exclusive power,
was this the manifestation of the flourishing of Yīn over Yáng?
In the fifth month of the fourth year of Yǒng'ān of Sūn Xiū of Wú,
there was heavy rain,
and springs overflowed.
In previous years, the Pǔlǐ Embankment was constructed,
at countless expense,
yet the fields could not be cultivated,
and soldiers died or rebelled,
or killed each other.
The common people were distressed and resentful,
the Yīn energy was strong.
Xiū also solely entrusted Zhāng Bù,
and dismissed Shèng Chōng and others.
This was the manifestation of the Wú people rebelling against him.
On the rénwǔ day of the eighth month of the fifth year of Yǒng'ān of Sūn Xiū of Wú,
there was heavy rain with thunder and lightning,
and springs overflowed.
In the ninth month of the fourth year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
Qīng, Xú, Yǎn, and Yù four prefectures suffered great floods.
In the sixth month of the seventh year,
there was continuous heavy rain.
The Hé, Luò, Yī, and Qìn rivers all overflowed,
killing over two hundred people.
The emperor, having ascended to the revered position,
did not confer ancestral titles upon the three empresses (hòus) and ancestors.
In the second year of Tàishǐ,
he also abolished the thrones of the Five Emperors in the southern suburbs of the Míngtáng,
calling them all Hàotiān Shàngdì,
as only one deity.
He also omitted the ritual of pairing the empress with the earth.
This was the punishment for neglecting ancestral temples
and abolishing sacrifices,
the same as Emperor Chéng of Hàn.
One account states,
in the previous year and this year, Yàolán Ní and Báihǔ Wén Qínliáng killed the Inspector Hú Liè and Qiān Hóng.
Tián Zhāng was dispatched to suppress Ní.
Moreover, Sīmǎ Wàng with a large army was stationed north of the Huái River to resist Sūn Hào.
With internal and external military campaigns,
and famine and unrest in the western prefectures,
the common people were distressed and resentful,
the Yīn energy was strong.
At the beginning of Xiánníng,
ancestral titles were finally conferred.
At the beginning of Tàixī,
the thrones of the Five Emperors were restored.
In the ninth month of the first year of Xiánníng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
Xú Prefecture suffered floods.
On the guǐhài day of the seventh month of the second year,
Hénán Wèijùn suffered sudden floods,
killing over a hundred people.
In the eighth month,
five commanderies and kingdoms in Jīng Prefecture suffered great floods.
In the previous year, good family daughters were selected,
appearing unveiled in the palace,
personally reviewed by the emperor,
with emphasis on their appearance and beauty,
not inquiring about their virtue or conduct.
Those who concealed them
were charged with disrespect.
Officials were distressed and resentful,
and the whole empire condemned it.
This was the manifestation of flourishing Yīn.
In the sixth month of the third year of Xiánníng,
eight commanderies and kingdoms in Yì and Liáng two prefectures suffered sudden floods,
killing over three hundred people.
In the seventh month,
Jīng Prefecture suffered great floods.
In the ninth month,
Shǐpíng Commandery suffered great floods.
In the tenth month,
Qīng, Xú, Yǎn, Yù, Jīng, Yì, and Liáng seven prefectures again suffered floods.
At this time, Jiǎ Chōng and others' influence grew daily,
while upright individuals were often alienated.
In the seventh month of the fourth year of Xiánníng,
Sī, Jì, Yǎn, Yù, Jīng, and Yáng twenty commanderies and kingdoms suffered great floods.
In the sixth month of the second year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
Tàishān and Jiāngxià suffered great floods.
In Tàishān, three hundred households were swept away,
killing over six thousand people.
Jiāngxià also had fatalities.
At this time, after the conquest of Wú,
Wáng Jùn, who rendered great service,
was slandered and falsely accused.
Xún and Jiǎ, who lacked strategy,
both received heavy rewards.
Five thousand Wú concubines were taken,
and placed in the imperial harem.
This was its manifestation.
In the seventh month of the fourth year of Tàikāng,
Sī, Yù, Xú, Yǎn, Jīng, and Yáng twenty commanderies and kingdoms suffered great floods,
damaging autumn crops,
destroying houses,
and causing deaths.
In the third month of the sixth year of Tàikāng,
Qīng, Liáng, Yōu, and Jì fifteen commanderies and kingdoms suffered great floods.
In the ninth month of the seventh year of Tàikāng,
eight commanderies and kingdoms in the western region, such as Āndìng, suffered great floods.
In the sixth month of the eighth year of Tàikāng,
eight commanderies and kingdoms suffered great floods.
In the second year of Yuánkāng of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
there was a flood disaster.
In the fifth month of the fifth year of Yuánkāng,
Yǐngchuān and Huáinán suffered great floods.
In the sixth month,
Chéngyáng and Dōngguǎn suffered great floods, killing people.
Jīng, Yáng, Xú, Yǎn, and Yù five prefectures again suffered great floods.
At this time, the emperor had been on the throne for five years,
yet had not performed the suburban sacrifices,
and often did not personally attend the zēngcháng sacrifices.
This was the punishment for neglecting ancestral temples
and abolishing sacrifices.
Bān Gù said:
"When a king ascends the throne,
he must perform suburban sacrifices to heaven and earth,
and rank sacrifices to mountains and rivers.
If he does not respect ghosts and spirits,
and his decrees are perverse and disobedient,
then mist and water will suddenly arrive,
all rivers will overflow contrary to nature,
destroying villages and towns,
and drowning people.
This is water not moistening downwards."
In the fifth month of the sixth year of Yuánkāng,
Jīng and Yáng two prefectures suffered great floods.
According to Dǒng Zhòngshū's explanation,
water signifies the flourishing of Yīn energy.
At this time, Empress Jiǎ disrupted the court,
and favored and promoted the Jiǎ and Guō clans.
This was the manifestation of a female ruler monopolizing power.
In the fifth month of the eighth year of Yuánkāng,
the well water in Jīnyǒng City overflowed.
Such an omen occurred during the time of Emperor Chéng of Hàn,
which Bān Gù considered to be an omen of Wáng Mǎng.
When Zhào Lún usurped the throne,
this was its manifestation.
Lún deposed the emperor in this city,
where the well overflowed;
was this also heaven's will?
In the ninth month of the eighth year of Yuánkāng,
Jīng, Yáng, Xú, Yǎn, and Jì five prefectures suffered great floods.
At this time, Empress Jiǎ's tyranny grew increasingly severe,

are all punishments for persistent cold."
The *Jīng Fáng Yì Zhuàn* says:
"When a virtuous person encounters danger,
this is called defying destiny.
Its anomaly is cold.
When punishments are excessively severe,
and it is cold when it should be warm,

it also results in hail.
When a righteous person is not punished for harm caused,
this is called nurturing a villain.
Cold lasts for seventy-two days,
killing flying birds.
When righteous people begin to leave,
this is called injury.
In this case, things die from cold without frost,
and gushing water appears.
When one goes to war without gauging the enemy,
this is called disgracing a mandate.
In this case, even with rain, things do not flourish due to the cold."

Bān Gù's account mentions the second day of the ninth month,

Lǚ Yī was later executed.
The *Jīng Fáng Yì Zhuàn* says:
"To raise an army and execute wantonly,
this is called lawlessness.
Its calamity is frost,
killing five grains in summer,

To punish without considering the circumstances,
this is called inhumanity.
In this case, frost in summer is preceded by great thunder and wind,

then frost falls,
with sharp edges.
When the wise and sagely suffer harm,
the frost adheres to trees and does not reach the ground.
When flatterers rely on legalism,
this is called private thievery.
In this case, the frost is in the grass roots and soil crevices.
To punish without instruction,

In this case, the frost is beneath the grass."

In the sixth month,
a yellow vapor appeared in Zǐguī,
over ten li long,
and several dozen zhàng wide.
More than ten days later,
Bèi was defeated by Lù Yì.
This was an omen of a yellow auspice.
During the Zhèngshǐ era of King Qí of Wèi,
Wáng Zhōunán, the Prince of Zhōngshān, was the Prefect of Xiāngyì.
A rat came out of a hole,
and said:
“Wáng Zhōunán,
you will die on a certain day.”
Nán did not respond.
The rat returned to its hole.
Later, on the appointed day,
it came out again, wearing a cap and black clothes,
and said:
“Zhōunán,
you will die at midday.”
Again, he did not respond.
The rat went back in,
and a moment later came out again,
speaking as before.
Just as it was about to be midday,
the rat went in and came out again,
came out and went in again,
repeating its words several times as before.
Exactly at midday,
the rat said:
“Zhōunán,
you did not respond to me,
what more is there to say?”
Its words ceased,
it staggered and died,
instantly losing its clothes and cap.
Upon inspection,
it was just an ordinary rat.
According to Bān Gù’s explanation,
this was a yellow auspice.
At that time, Cáo Shuǎng held power,
and factions competed,
hence the rat caused this anomaly.
In the spring of the seventh year of Dàmíng, during the reign of Emperor Xiàowǔ of the Sòng,
there were suddenly many rats by the Tàihú lake.
That summer,
the waters rose,
and all transformed into carp.
The people caught
thirty to fifty húk of them in one day.
The next year,
there was a great famine.
In the eighth month of the fourth year of Tàixīng, during the reign of Emperor Yuán of the Jìn,
yellow fog filled all four directions,
and dusty air obscured the sky.
According to Yáng Xuān’s reply,
this was a sign related to the earth’s energy,
an omen of chaos.
On the Guǐsì day of the first month of the second year of Yǒngchāng, during the reign of Emperor Yuán of the Jìn,
yellow fog filled all four directions.
In the third month of the seventh year of Yǒnghé, during the reign of Emperor Mù of the Jìn,

At that time, Zhāng Chónghuá listened to slanders,
and dismissed Xiè Ài to be the Administrator of Jiǔquán,
and the person he appointed was not suitable.
By the ninth year, he died,
and his heir was assassinated.
This was its fulfillment.
The Jīng Fáng Yì Zhuàn says:
“To hear good and not grant it,
this is called not knowing.
Its anomaly is yellow,
its fault is deafness,
its disaster is no successor.
Yellow
refers to yellow, turbid air filling the world in all directions,
obscuring the worthy and severing the Way,

an auspicious sign of great peace (tàipíng zhī xiáng),
and submitted a memorial to celebrate.
Earthquakes
In the fourth year of Huángwǔ of Sūn Quán of Wú,
the Jiāngdōng region experienced continuous earthquakes.
At this time, Quán had accepted the peerage and mandate from Wèi,
serving as Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn) and King of Wú (Wú Wáng),
had changed the reign title and exercised autocratic rule,
not maintaining the conduct of a subject.
Jīng Fáng's Yìzhuàn says:
"Even if a subject's affairs are proper,
autocracy will inevitably lead to earthquakes."
Dǒng Zhòngshū and Liú Xiàng both said
that "when subjects are powerful and prosperous,
they are about to cause movement and harm,"
and this was the manifestation of that.
〔一八〕
In the second year of Qīnglóng of Emperor Míng of Wèi, in the eleventh month,

〔一九〕with a faint rumbling sound,

and the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, Hú Zhì, repelled him.
Also, Gōngsūn Yuān declared himself King of Yān,
changed the reign title,
and appointed numerous officials.

Jiāngdōng experienced an earthquake.
In the first month of the second year of Chìwū,
the earth shook twice again.
At this time, Lǚ Yī was in power,
and Bù Zhì submitted a memorial, saying:
"I have heard that the investigators (xiàoshì),
splitting hairs to find fault (chuīmáo qiúxiá),
eager to entrap people
to establish their prestige and power (wēifú),
the innocent and blameless
are arbitrarily subjected to severe punishment,
and even important ministers
are not trusted.
Given this,
how can Heaven and Earth not manifest changes?
Therefore, the continuous earthquakes in the sixth year of Jiāhé and the second year of Chìwū
are the manifestations of subjects monopolizing power.
It is hoped that this will alert and awaken the ruler;
how can one not deeply ponder its meaning?"
Yī later failed and perished.

Mountain Collapses and Ground Subsidence and Cracks
In the eighth month of the thirteenth year of Chìwū of Sūn Quán of Wú [250 CE],
mountains in Dānyáng, Jùróng, Gùzhāng, and Níngguó collapsed,
and great floods overflowed.
According to Liú Xiàng's interpretation,
"Mountains
are *yáng*,
representing the sovereign;
water
is *yīn*,
representing the people.
Heaven's warning is as if to say,
'If the way of the sovereign collapses and is ruined,
the common people will lose their proper place.'"
This is similar to the collapse of Liángshān in the *Chūnqiū*,
and the floods from the multitude of mountains in Qí and Chǔ during the Hàn dynasty.
"For the three dynasties, sacrifices were commanded,
and offerings did not exceed the designated mountains.
Auspiciousness, inauspiciousness, calamity, and blessings,
did not go beyond this."
Although Wú claimed emperorship,
it was in reality a federated state.
The disaster occurring in Dānyáng,
was Heaven's intention.
The sovereign governs the mountains and rivers;
when mountains collapse and rivers dry up,
it is an omen of destruction.
Two years later, Quán died,
and twenty-six years after his death, Wú perished.

Until the emperor passed away,

Huái and Mǐn were exiled to the north,
and Emperor Yuán restored the dynasty in the south;
this was its fulfillment.
Jīng Fáng's *Yì Zhuàn* says:
"That which descends from above is called a collapse.
Its manifestation is the rocks of Tàishān toppling downwards,
a sage king receives the Mandate,
and the ruler is captured."
