and one hundred thirty *zhàng* long,
and water emerged, killing people.
In the third month of the first year of Yǒngjiā of Emperor Xiàohuái of Jìn [307 CE],
the ground in Bùguǎnglǐ, northeast of Luòyáng, subsided.
On the *yǐhài* day of the eighth month in the second year of Yǒngjiā [308 CE],
Sīmǎ Yuè disliked this omen,
and relocated to Púyáng.
This was an anomaly of malevolent influence.
Yuè died on the imperial tomb,
and ultimately suffered calamity.
On the *wùchén* day of the seventh month in the third year of Yǒngjiā [309 CE],
the ground in Dāngyáng cracked in three places,
each crack three *zhàng* wide,
and over two hundred paces long.
Jīng Fáng's *Yì Zhuàn* says:
"When the earth cracks and splits,
it signifies that ministers and subordinates will separate,
unwilling to follow each other."
Thereafter, Sīmǎ Yuè and Gǒu Xī fell out,
and the regional governors everywhere became scattered,
and the royal house consequently perished.
In the tenth month of the third year of Yǒngjiā [309 CE],
a mountain in Yídū Yídào collapsed.
In the fourth month of the fourth year of Yǒngjiā [310 CE],
Hēishíshān in Xiāngdōng Líng collapsed.
In the eighth month of the fourth year of Tàixīng of Emperor Yuán of Jìn [321 CE],
Chángshān collapsed,
water emerged,
the Hūtuó River overflowed,
and large trees were uprooted.
In the tenth month of the fourth year of Xiánhé of Emperor Chéng of Jìn [329 CE],
the northwest cliff of Lúshān in Cháishāng collapsed.
In the twelfth month,
Liú Yìn was killed by Guō Mò.
On a night in the sixth month of the ninth year of Yuánkāng of Emperor Huì of Jìn [299 CE],
there was a sudden thunderstorm.
The pillars of Jiǎ Mì's study sank into the ground,
crushing Mì's bed curtains.
This was wood afflicting earth,
and earth losing its nature,
unable to support.
The following year,
Mì was executed.
In the fifth month of the first year of Guāngxī of Emperor Huì of Jìn [306 CE],
the ground in Fányáng burned,
and could be used for cooking.
This was fire afflicting earth.
At this time, rituals, music, military expeditions, and punishments originated from the feudal lords.
On the *rén yín* day of the third month in the eighth year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān of Jìn [412 CE],
in Shānyīn, there was a sound like thunder,
and the ground subsided four *chǐ* deep and four *chǐ* wide.
On the *wùyín* day of the fifth month in the tenth year of Yìxī [414 CE],
the ground at Xīmíngmén was pierced,
and gushing water emerged,
destroying the gate leaves and threshold.
The *Wǔxíng Zhuàn* says:
"If the sovereign does not reach the utmost,
this is called not being established.
Its fault is dimness,
its punishment is darkness,
its extreme is weakness.
At such times there are 'shooting omens' (*shèyāo*),
at such times there are calamities of dragons and snakes,
at such times there are misfortunes related to horses,
at such times there are diseases of subordinates attacking superiors,
at such times the sun and moon move erratically,
and the stars move in reverse."
Constant Gloom
In the third year of Tàipíng of Sūn Liàng of Wú [258 CE],
from the eighth month, there was constant gloom without rain,
for over forty days.
At this time, Sūn Chén was to be executed,
but the plot was leaked.
On the *wùwǔ* day of the ninth month,
Chén surrounded the palace with troops,
and deposed Liàng as King of Huìjī.
This was the punishment of constant gloom.
In the twelfth month of the first year of Bǎodǐng of Sūn Hào of Wú,
the Grand Astrologer reported that it had been long cloudy and without rain,
and that there would be a conspiracy.
Hào was greatly alarmed and fearful.
At that time, Lù Kǎi and others planned to depose him while he was visiting the temple.
When Hào came out,
Liú Píng led the troops as his vanguard.
Kǎi spoke to Píng,
but Píng did not agree,
and thus the plan did not materialize.
As Hào indulged in tyranny,
many of his subordinates harbored different ambitions,
eventually leading to his surrender and downfall.
In the fourth month of the third year of Yuánhuī of Emperor Hòufèi of Sòng,
it was continuously cloudy without rain.
In the eighth month of the third year of Yuánhuī,
it was mostly cloudy.
Two years later,
the deposed emperor perished.
Shooting Omens
Dèng Zhī, the General of Cavalry and Chariots of Shǔ, was on a campaign in Fúlíng.
He saw a black ape climbing a mountain,
and shot it with an arrow.
The ape pulled out the arrow
and used rolled-up leaves to plug its wound.
Zhī said:
"Alas!
I have violated the nature of a creature,
and I shall soon die."
Soon after, he died.
This was a shooting omen.
One account says the ape mother was holding her child,
and Zhī shot her.
The child pulled out the arrow
and took leaves to plug the wound.
Zhī sighed,
threw his bow into the water,
and knew he was about to die.
When Emperor Gōng of Jìn was the Prince of Lángyá,
he was fond of strange games.
He once enclosed a horse inside a gate
and ordered people to shoot it,
wanting to see how many arrows it would take for it to die.
One of his attendants advised him,
saying:
"The horse
is the imperial surname.
To shoot it now
is extremely inauspicious."
Thereupon he stopped,
but the horse had already been hit by about ten arrows.
This was likely a shooting omen.
Soon after, Huán Xuán usurped the throne.
Calamities of Dragons and Snakes
On the Jiǎshēn day of the first month of the first year of Qīnglóng of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
a green dragon appeared in the well of Mópo in Jiā.
Whenever auspicious signs appear out of season,
they become calamities;
how much more so when confined in a well,
it is not a propitious omen.
Wèi changed the year name for this,
which was wrong.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn did not offer congratulations,
which was correct.
Gān Bǎo said:
"From Emperor Míng to the end of the Wèi dynasty,
the appearances of green dragons and yellow dragons
were all omens for the rise and fall of their rulers.
Wèi had the earth element;
green
is the color of wood,
which is not stronger than metal.
Yellow gaining position
and green losing position is the omen.
Frequent appearances of green dragons
indicate an internal struggle between the virtue of the ruler and the fate of the dynasty.
Therefore, Gāoguìxiānggōng ultimately perished by military force.
According to Liú Xiàng's explanation: 'Dragons are noble symbols,
but being confined in a well means
the feudal lords will suffer the disaster of imprisonment.'
During the Wèi dynasty, no dragon was seen outside of a well,
which was an omen of those in higher positions oppressing and restraining.
Gāoguìxiānggōng's poem 'Latent Dragon'
refers to this meaning."
On the Wùxū day of the tenth month of winter in the first year of Zhèngyuán of Gāoguìxiānggōng of Wèi,
On the Xīnchǒu day of the first month of the first year of Gānlù of Gāoguìxiānggōng of Wèi,
a green dragon appeared in a well in Zhǐ county;
on the Yǐchǒu day of the sixth month,
a green dragon appeared in a well within Yuánchéng county.
In the second month of the second year of Gānlù,
a green dragon appeared in a well in Wēn county.
In the third year of Gānlù,
yellow dragons and green dragons continued to appear in wells within Dùnqīu, Guānjūn, and Yángxià counties.
In the second month of the third year of Jǐngyuán,
During the Tiāncè era of Sūn Hào of Wú,
a dragon nursed in a civilian's house in Chángshā,
eating chicks.
Jīng Fáng's 'Changes and Omens' says:
"When a dragon nurses in a common household,
the king will become a commoner."
Afterward, Hào surrendered.
On the Bǐngshēn day of the sixth month of the second year of Xiánníng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
two white dragons appeared in a well in Jiǔyuán.
On the Guǐmǎo day of the first month of the fifth year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
two dragons appeared in a well in the Imperial Armory.
When the Emperor saw the dragons,
he showed signs of joy,
and all the officials were about to offer congratulations.
Liú Yì alone submitted a memorial, saying:
"In the past, dragon saliva in Xià's court
led to disaster for the Zhōu dynasty;
when a dragon appeared at Zhèng's gate,
Zǐchǎn did not offer congratulations."
The Emperor replied:
"My virtuous governance is not yet perfected,
and I am not worthy to receive such an auspicious sign."
So, no congratulations were offered.
Sūn Shèng said:
"A dragon
is a creature of water.
What does it have to do with humans?
What Zǐchǎn said was correct.
However, if it is not in its proper place,
it is truly an ominous disaster.
A dragon is considered beautiful when it flies and appears prominently;
therefore, to be latent and confined in a dark place
is not a propitious omen.
In the second year of Emperor Huì of Hàn,
two dragons appeared in a well in Lánlíng.
The original records considered this an omen of the later Prince Zhào dying in confinement.
The Imperial Armory
is where the emperor's instruments of power and control are treasured and stored.
Its chambers are deep and secure,
not a place for dragons.
Seven years later,
the feudal princes harmed each other,
and twenty-eight years later,
there were indeed two 'Hú' (barbarians) who usurped the divine instruments of power.
The two rebels, Lè and Hǔ, both had 'Dragon' (Lóng) in their courtesy names,
and this unusual manifestation
is thus confirmed."
The court historian remarks: Dragons are auspicious omens,
but when they are confined in a well,
previous histories have already discussed it in detail.
However, the portents are subtle and obscure,
not to be conjectured,
thus both Wǔxíng (Five Elements) and Fúruì (Auspicious Signs) are retained.
In the eleventh month of the second year of Jiànxīng of Emperor Mǐn of Jìn,
a Qiāng female entertainer in Fúhǎn gave birth to a dragon child.
Its color resembled brocade patterns,
and it used to nurse from its mother.
When a divine light was seen from afar,
it became difficult to approach and observe.
During the Xiánníng era of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
there were two large snakes in the residence of the Minister of Works,
each about ten *zhàng* long.
They lived on the flat rafters of the reception hall,
for several years without anyone knowing,
but people merely wondered why the household frequently lost young children, pigs, and dogs.
Later, one snake came out at night,
was injured by a blade,
and could not leave,
only then was it discovered.
People were mobilized to attack it,
and it died after some time.
The residence of the Minister of Works is the office of the Five Teachings.
This indicates that the supreme principle was not established,
hence the snake calamity appeared.
During the time of Emperor Líng of Hàn,
a snake appeared on the imperial throne.
Yáng Cì believed this was an omen for the emperor being addicted to lust.
The court women of Wèi were excessively numerous,
and Jìn surpassed them.
They indulged in banquets and pleasure,
this was their calamity.
The *Shī* (Classic of Poetry) says:
"Be they vipers, be they snakes,
they are omens for women."
On the Guǐsì day of the third month of the fifth year of Yuánkāng of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
a large snake, more than ten *zhàng* long, in Línzī
carrying two small snakes,
entered the north gate of the city
and went straight through the market into the shrine of King Chéngyáng Jǐng of Hàn, then disappeared.
Heaven's warning seemed to say that
Qí would achieve the merit of Lú Zhāng in restoring order,
but if he did not adhere strictly to integrity and loyalty,
he would again tread the path of Zhāng losing his position and having his achievements taken away.
Prince Jìng of Qí did not realize this.
Although he accomplished the restoration,
he incurred disaster due to his arrogance and oppression.
The large snake carrying two small snakes appearing in the court market,
all had symbolic meanings.
In the early years of the Tàiníng
era of Emperor Míng of Jìn,
there was a large snake in Wǔchāng,
which often lived in the hollow of a tree in an old temple. Each time it emerged, it would extend its head to receive food from people.
Jīng Fáng’s Yì Yāo (Changes and Portents) states:
“When a snake is seen in a city,
within three years,
there will be great warfare.
The state will face great sorrow.”
Afterward, Wáng Dūn and his confederates were suppressed and annihilated.
Misfortunes involving Horses
In the first year of the Tàixī
era of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, a horse in Liáodōng grew horns,
located below both ears,
three inches long.
According to Liú Xiàng’s explanation,
this is a sign of warfare.
After the emperor passed away,
the imperial house was afflicted by military disasters,
which was the fulfillment of this omen.
Jīng Fáng’s Yì Zhuàn (Commentary on the Changes) states:
“When ministers usurp the emperor,
and governance is not smooth,
〔三０〕the omen for this is a horse growing horns.”
It also states:
“When the Son of Heaven personally campaigns,
horses grow horns.”
The Lǚ Shì Chūnqiū (Master Lǚ’s Spring and Autumn Annals) states:
“When a ruler loses the Way,
horses grow horns.”
In the twelfth month of the first year of the Yuánkāng
era of Emperor Huì of Jìn, when the Crown Prince was about to perform the ritual offering,
Grand Tutor Zhào Wáng Lún was riding in the secondary carriage position.
Upon reaching the southern city gate,
the horse stopped,
and strongmen could not move it by pushing.
Lún entered a small carriage,
and then it proceeded.
This was a misfortune involving a horse.
It was as if Heaven warned that
Lún did not know the path of righteousness,
and would eventually commit rebellion and treason,
unfit to be the one to guide the ritual.
Lún did not comprehend,
and thus perished.
In the eleventh month, day wùyín, of the ninth year of the Yuánkāng
era, a dappled mare bolted in fright to the Grand Judge’s interrogation hall
and died with a sorrowful neigh.
This was likely an omen of Mǐnhuái’s unjust death.
That it appeared in the Grand Judge’s interrogation hall,
was that also Heaven’s will?
In the second month of the sixth year of the Yǒngjiā
era of Emperor Xiàohuái of Jìn, a divine horse neighed at the southern city gate.
In the second year of the Tàixīng
era of Emperor Yuán of Jìn, a horse belonging to Púyáng Yáng Yǎn, an official of Dānyáng Commandery, gave birth to a foal
with two heads separating from the front of its neck;
it died at birth.
According to Sīmǎ Biāo’s explanation,
this is an omen of governance being in the hands of private households,
the image of two heads.
After this, Wáng Dūn overstepped the emperor.
On the jiǎxū day of the fifth month of the eighth year of the Xiánkāng
era of Emperor Chéng of Jìn, there was a horse as red as blood,
which ran directly from Xuānyáng Gate into the front of the palace hall,
circled, and then ran out,
and was pursued but its whereabouts remained unknown.
On the jǐmǎo day,
the emperor became ill,
and died in the sixth month.
This was a horse misfortune,
and also a red omen.
When Zhāng Chónghuá was in Liángzhōu,
he was about to execute his Xīhé Chancellor Zhāng Zuò.
Dozens of Zuò’s horses
simultaneously had their tails completely severed.
In the tenth month of the fourth year of the Lóng’ān
era of Emperor Ān of Jìn, a horse in Liángzhōu grew a horn.
The Inspector Guō Quán sent it to Commander-in-Chief Huán Xuán.
According to Liú Xiàng’s explanation,
a horse should not grow a horn,
just as Huán Xuán should not have raised an army against the emperor.
He saw the calamity but did not comprehend it,
and thus met his destruction.
Human Anomalies
In the early years of the Huángchū
era of Emperor Wén of Wèi, the mother of Sòng Shìzōng of Qīnghé transformed into a turtle
and entered the water.
In the third year of the Tàihé
era of Emperor Míng of Wèi, the daughter of Xī Nóng, a soldier in Cáo Xiū’s contingent, died and was revived.
At that time, someone opened Zhōu Shì’s tomb
and found a girl buried as a sacrifice,
who regained breath after several days,
and could speak after several months.
Empress Dowager Guō loved and raised her.
Also, commoners in Tàiyuán opened a tomb and broke open a coffin,
and inside the coffin was a living woman.
When asked about her past,
she did not know.
Looking at the wood of the tomb,
it appeared to be about thirty years old.
According to Jīng Fáng’s Yì Zhuàn,
“the ultimate yin becomes yang,
the lower people become the upper,”
which was an omen of Jìn Xuānwáng’s rise.
Emperor Píng of Hàn and Emperor Xiàn of Hàn both experienced such anomalies,
which were interpreted as omens of Wáng Mǎng and Cáo Cāo.
When Gōngsūn Yuān was cooking,
a small child was steamed to death in the steamer;
afterward, Gōngsūn Yuān was annihilated.
In the second year of the Jiànxīng
era of Sūn Liàng of Wú, when Zhūgě Kè was about to campaign against Huáinán,
a filial son wearing mourning clothes entered his private chamber.
When questioned,
he replied:
“I did not realize I had entered.”
At that time, the guards inside and outside
had also not seen him.
Everyone found this strange.
When Kè returned,
he was indeed killed.
After Kè had been killed,
his wife was in her room,
and told a maid to pour water for washing.
She smelled the maid's blood.
Also, the maid’s eyes had an unusual gaze.
When the wife asked the reason,
the maid suddenly leaped up,
her head reaching the ridgepole,
and with bared arms and gnashing teeth said:
“Lord Zhūgě was killed by Jùn!”
In the fourth year of the Yǒng’ān
era of Sūn Xiū of Wú, Chén Jiāo, a commoner of Ānwú, died for seven days
and then emerged from his grave.
Gān Bǎo said:
“This is similar to what happened during Emperor Xuān of Hàn’s time.
It is an auspicious sign for Háo, Marquis of Wūchéng, to gain the throne,
inheriting from a ruined former family.”
In the first year of the Bǎodǐng
era of Sūn Hào of Wú, Xuān Qiān’s mother from Dānyáng,
aged eighty,
transformed into a soft-shelled turtle while bathing.
Her brothers closed the doors to guard her,
dug a large pit in the hall,
and filled it with water.
The soft-shelled turtle played in the pit for a day or two,
then stretched its neck to look outside,
and when the door was slightly ajar,
it tumbled and leaped out,
entering a distant deep pool,
never to return.
This was similar to the case of Madam Huáng during Emperor Líng of Hàn’s time.
It was an omen of Wú’s downfall.
In the eighth month of the second year of the Xiánxī
era of Emperor Yuán of Wèi, Xiāngwǔ County reported seeing a giant,
over thirty feet tall,
whose footprints were three feet two inches long,
with white hair,
wearing a yellow turban and a yellow unlined garment,
leaning on a staff,
who called out to the commoner Wáng Shǐ and said:
“There will now be great peace.”
Soon after, Jìn replaced Wèi.
In the fifth year of the Tàishǐ
era of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, a seventy-year-old man from Yuánchéng
grew horns.
According to the Hàn Zhì (History of the Han Dynasty),
this was likely an omen of Zhào Wáng Lún’s usurpation and rebellion.
In the second month of the second year of the Xiánníng
era of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, Yán Jī from Lángyá died of illness.
His coffin had been sealed for a long time,
when all his family members dreamed that Jī told them:
“I shall live again,
you must quickly open the coffin.”
So they took him out.
He gradually became able to eat, bend and stretch, and see,
but could not walk or speak.
He died again two years later.
After this, Liú Yuān and Shí Lè destroyed the Jìn dynasty.
During the Yuánkāng
era of Emperor Huì of Jìn, there was a girl named Zhōu Shìníng in Ānfēng,
aged eight,
who gradually transformed into a boy.
By seventeen or eighteen,
her temperament had become masculine.
This was an omen of Liú Yuān and Shí Lè overthrowing the Jìn dynasty.
Emperor Āi of Hàn and Emperor Xiàn of Hàn both had similar anomalies,
all of which were signs of dynastic change.
Jīng Fáng’s Zhuàn states:
“When a girl transforms into a man,
this is called yin flourishing,
and a person of low status becomes king.
When a man transforms into a woman,
this is called yin overpowering yang,
〔三一〕and the calamity is destruction.”
In the early years of
Yǒngníng
during the reign of Emperor Huì
of Jìn,
Qí Wáng Jǐong
raised a righteous army,
exterminated the rebels and traitors,
and restored the imperial carriage to its rightful place.
Suddenly, a woman came to the gate of the Grand Marshal’s residence,
seeking to deposit her property.
The gatekeepers questioned her,
and the woman said:
“I will cut Qí and then leave.”
At this time, Qí Wáng Jǐong
was restoring the royal house,
and the whole world attributed his success to him.
Those who understood the implications considered this an ill omen for him.
Afterward, he was indeed executed.
In the twelfth month, on the jiǎzǐ day, of the first year of Yǒngníng,
a white-haired old man entered
Qí Wáng Jǐong’s
Grand Marshal’s residence,
shouting loudly that a great army would rise,
not beyond a jiǎzǐ period.
Jǐong
killed him.
In the twelfth month, on the wùchén day, of the following year,
Jǐong
was defeated,
which was indeed within the jiǎzǐ period.
In the fourth month, on the guǐyǒu day, of the first year of Tàiyán
during the reign of Emperor Huì
of Jìn,
a person entered the front of the palace from the Lóngmén Gate,
bowed twice facing north, and said:
“I am to be the Director of the Central Secretariat.”
He was immediately arrested and executed.
Gān Bǎo
said:
“The Forbidden Court
is a place of reverence and secrecy.
Now a base person directly enters,
and the gate guards do not notice;
this is an omen that the palace will become empty,
and common people will transgress it.”
After this, the emperor moved north to Yè,
then west to Cháng'ān;
thieves and bandits trampled the palace,
and consequently, the empire was lost.
During the reign of Emperor Huì
of Jìn,
a woman from Liángguó
was betrothed,
and the engagement gifts had already been received.
Soon after, her husband was garrisoned in Cháng'ān,
and did not return for a year.
The woman’s family betrothed her to another man.
The woman was not happy to go,
but her parents forced her,
and she had no choice but to depart.
Soon after, she fell ill and died.
Later, her former husband returned,
and asked where the woman was.
Her family told him everything.
Her husband went directly to the woman’s tomb,
overcome with sorrow,
he then opened the tomb and coffin,
and the woman came back to life.
Consequently, he returned home with her.
The later husband heard of this,
and went to the authorities to dispute it.
The local officials could not decide.
Mìshū Láng
Wáng Dǎo
deliberated, saying:
“This is an extraordinary matter,
and cannot be judged by ordinary principles.
It should be returned to the former husband.”
The court followed his deliberation.
During the reign of Emperor Huì
of Jìn,
Dù Xī’s
family held a funeral,
and a maid was mistakenly left inside, unable to get out.
More than ten years later,
when the tomb was opened for additional burial,
the maid was still alive.
At first, she seemed to be in a trance,
but after a while, she gradually awoke.
When questioned,
she said she thought it had only been a night or two.
When the maid was initially buried,
she was fifteen or sixteen years old,
and when the tomb was opened and she revived,
she was still fifteen or sixteen.
She was married and had children.
In the first year of Guāngxī
during the reign of Emperor Huì
of Jìn,
Xiè Zhēn
of Kuàijī
gave birth to a child
with a large head and sideburns,
both soles of its feet faced upward,
and it had both male and female organs.
At birth, it made a man’s voice,
and died after a day.
During the reigns of Emperors Huì
and Huái
of Jìn,
in Jīng
and Luò,
there were people with both male and female organs,
who could also engage in both forms of human intercourse,
and their nature was especially lustful.
This is evidence that such anomalies are born of chaotic qi.
Since the time after Xiánníng
and Tàikāng,
male favoritism greatly flourished,
even more than female beauty;
no scholar-official did not value it,
and everyone in the world imitated it,
some even leading to the dissolution of marriages,
and resentment, loneliness, and jealousy.
Therefore, the qi
of male and female became disordered,
and monstrous forms appeared.
In the early years of Tàixīng
during the reign of Emperor Yuán,
there was another woman
whose vulva was on her abdomen,
in Yángzhōu.
Her nature was also very lustful.
Jīng Fáng’s
Yì Yāo
says:
“If a person gives birth to a child
with the vulva on its head,
there will be great chaos under heaven;
on the abdomen,
there will be trouble under heaven;
on the back,
there will be no successor under heaven.”
In the first year of Yǒngjiā
during the reign of Emperor Xiàohuái
of Jìn,
a maid of Wàn Xiáng
from Wúxiàn
in Wúqùn
gave birth to a child
with a bird’s head,
two horse hooves for feet,
one hand without hair,
yellow in color,
and as large as a pillow.
In the fourth year of Jiànxīng
during the reign of Emperor Mǐn
of Jìn,
Hú,
the twenty-five-year-old wife of Rèn Qiáo,
an official of Xīncài Xiàn,
gave birth to two daughters.
They faced each other,
their abdomens and hearts joined,
but from the chest upward
and from the navel downward,
they were separate.
This was probably an omen that the world was not yet unified.
At that time, Nèishǐ
Lǚ Huì
reported:
“According to the Ruìyìngtú,
different roots with a common body are called ‘liánlǐ’ (intertwined branches),
and different stalks with common ears are called ‘jiāhé’ (auspicious grain).
Even anomalies in plants are considered auspicious signs;
now two people are of one heart.
The Yì
says: ‘Two people of one heart,
their sharpness can cut through metal.’
An auspicious omen is clearly visible,
born in the land east of Shǎn.
This is surely an omen of unity of heart throughout the four seas.
I cannot but rejoice and leap,
and respectfully present a drawing.”
At that time, those with understanding ridiculed him.
In the fifth year of Xiánkāng, fourth month,
Wáng Hé, a commoner from Xiàpī, was a sojourner in Jìyáng.
His daughter, Kě,
aged twenty,
declared:
"I have returned from Heaven,
having received an auspicious seal and ribbon,
and I am to be the mother of the world."
The Grand Administrator of Jìnlíng considered this witchcraft,
and had her arrested and imprisoned.
By the eleventh month,
a person carrying a cudgel of mulberry wood,
dressed in crimson,
arrived at the gate of Zhǐchē Ménkǒu,
claiming to be an envoy of a sage,
seeking an audience with the Son of Heaven.
The gate guard took down his statement,
listing his surname as Lǚ and given name as Xī.
He said that Wáng Hé's daughter Kě
had seven stars on the sole of her right foot,
all with hair,
seven cùn long,
and that Heaven had now appointed Kě as the mother of the world.
When this was reported,
he was immediately executed.
Orders were also sent to Jìnlíng to execute Kě.
In the second year of Jiànyuán of Emperor Kāng of Jìn, tenth month,

She had a marking on her foot,

"Mother of the World."
When it was cauterized, it became even clearer.
The capital was abuzz.
The authorities arrested and imprisoned her and reported the matter.
Shortly thereafter, she escaped from Jiànkāng county prison.

In the seventeenth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
Liú Bīn was the Administrator of Wújùn.
In Lóu county, there was a girl

and indistinctly arrived inside the county city.
She felt that she had been away from home for just the time it takes to cook a meal,
and her clothes were not wet.
At dawn, she stood at the gate seeking entry,

"I am an envoy of Heaven."
Bīn ordered her to come forward,

"Your Excellency should rise and welcome me;
you will become greatly wealthy and noble.
If not,
there will surely be misfortune."
Bīn asked why she had come,
but she did not know herself.
He considered her mad,
imprisoned her,
and issued a warrant for her family to collect her.
After several days, she was allowed to leave.
About twenty days later,
Bīn was executed.

In the early years of the Tàihé reign of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
the Grand Astrologer, Xǔ Zhī, reported a solar eclipse,
and together with the Grand Commandant, prayed and performed rituals at the Língtái Terrace.
The Emperor issued an edict saying:
"I have heard that when the ruler's governance is improper,
Heaven frightens him with calamities and anomalies,
thereby admonishing him to cultivate himself.
Thus, when the sun and moon are eclipsed,
it clearly indicates that the way of governance has improprieties.
Since I ascended the throne,
I have been unable to illuminate the sagely virtues of the former emperors,
and my policies and transformations have not been in harmony with the august spirits;
hence, High Heaven has awakened me.
It is fitting that I exert myself in governance and cultivate myself,
to repay the gods and spirits.
Heaven's relation to man
is like a father's relation to his son.
There has never been a father who wishes to reprimand his son,
and yet can be appeased by sumptuous feasts.
Now, it is desired externally to send a Grand Minister and the Grand Astrologer to perform all the propitiatory sacrifices;
this is something unheard of in terms of righteousness.
All you dukes, ministers, and gentry,
each strive to cultivate your respective duties.
Anyone who can compensate for my shortcomings,
each of you should present your suggestions."

and everything it illuminated was red.
Something like a flying lamp was seen in the sun.
On the *gēngzǐ* day in the first month of the first year of Jiànwǔ of Emperor Mǐn of the Jìn dynasty,
a white rainbow filled the sky,
three suns shone simultaneously,
the sun had a double halo,
and two ears on its left and right.
The prognostication said:
"A white rainbow
is the qi of war.
If three, four, five, or six suns appear simultaneously and contend,
war will break out in the world,
and the number of kings established will correspond to that number."
It also states:
"If three suns appear simultaneously,
within three *xún* (a period of ten days),
feudal lords will contend to be emperor.
there will be a king established in the world.
If it has a halo and ears,
there will be marquises established in the world."
Therefore, Chén Zhuó said:
"There will be great celebrations,
and the world will perhaps be divided into three."
Three months later, Jiāngdōng changed its era name,
the Hú also changed their era name,
straddling the territories of Cáo and Liú.
Thereupon, wars continued for generations.
On the *guǐhài* day in the third month of the fourth year of Tàixīng of Emperor Yuán of the Jìn dynasty,
there was a black spot on the sun.
On the *xīnhài* day in the fourth month,
On the *xīnmǎo* day in the tenth month of the first year of Yǒngchāng of Emperor Yuán of the Jìn dynasty,
On the *jǐchǒu* day in the first month of the first year of Tàiníng of Emperor Míng of the Jìn dynasty,
on the *guǐsì* day,
a yellow fog filled all four directions.
The prognostication said:
"The ruler's Way has lost its clarity,
and ministers have a conspiracy."
At this time, Wáng Dūn was oppressing the superior,
and eventually suffered his punishment.
In the seventh month of the first year of Xiánkāng of Emperor Chéng of Jìn,
a white rainbow pierced the sun.
〔四八〕
In the first month, Rénshēn day, of the eighth year of Xiánkāng,
there was a black spot in the sun.
On Bǐngzǐ day,
it disappeared.
In the fourth month, Wùchén day, of the fourth year of Tàihé of Duke Hǎixī of Jìn,
the sun's halo was thick and dense,
and a white rainbow pierced the center of the sun.
In the third month, Xīnwèi day, of the sixth year of Tàihé,
a white rainbow pierced the sun,
and there were five layers of sun halo.
In the eleventh month,
Huán Wēn deposed the emperor.
When Zhāng Chónghuá was in Liángzhōu,
the sun was intensely red like fire,
and there was a three-legged crow within it,
its form clearly visible,
and it ceased after several mornings.
In the second month, Jiǎzǐ day, of the first year of Yuánxīng of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
there was a sun halo,
and a white rainbow pierced the sun.
The following year,
Huán Xuán usurped the throne.
In the fifth month, Gēngwǔ day, of the first year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
the sun had a colored ear-like halo.
In the eleventh year of Yìxī,
the sun was in Dōngjǐng,
and there was a white rainbow more than ten zhàng long,
covering the sun from the south.
According to Sīmǎ Biāo's explanation,
then the disaster was in the corresponding astrological division,
a sign of the collapse of the Qiāng.
In the first month, Rénchén day, of the second year of Yuánxī of Emperor Gōng of Jìn,
there was a sun halo,
with straight ear-like halos, each one zhàng long, to the east and west,
and white energy pierced through them, encircling them.
On the night of Bǐngshēn day in the third month of the fifth year of Yǒngjiā of Emperor Xiàohuái of Jìn,
there was a total lunar eclipse;
on the night of Dīngyǒu day,
there was another total eclipse.
〔四九〕The prognostication said:
"A total lunar eclipse
brings sorrow to the empress."
It also said:
"A nobleman of that country will die."
On the first day, Xīnmǎo, of the twelfth month of the ninth year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān,
the moon was still visible in the east at dawn.
〔五０〕According to the prognostication, this is called
"hidden to the side."
On the first day, Jǐmǎo, of the eleventh month of the twenty-ninth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
〔五一〕when the sun first rose,
its color was red like blood,
with projections like teeth on its exterior,
uneven and not round.
In the second month of the following year,
the imperial carriage departed (the emperor died).
In the eleventh month of the seventh year of Dàmíng of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
when the sun first rose four or five zhàng high,
its color was red like blood,
and when it was four or five zhàng from setting,
it was also like this,
until the spring of the eighth year,
this occurred three times in total,
which was called the death of the sun.
In the intercalary fifth month,
the emperor passed away.
In the third month, Yǐhài day, of the third year of Yuánhuī of the Later Deposed Emperor,
when the sun was a few zhàng from setting,
its color was purplish red and without luster.
In the third month, Gēngyín day, of the fifth year of Yuánhuī,
there were five layers of sun halo,
and two additional straight halos were born,
one embracing and one on its back.
During the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Wén,
two white rainbows appeared outside Xuānyángmén.
On the night of Rénzǐ day in the eighth month of the second year of Yuánhuī of the Later Deposed Emperor,
a white rainbow appeared.
On Jǐyǒu day in the first month of the fourth year of Yuánhuī,
a white rainbow pierced the sun.
On the night of Yǐwèi day in the ninth month of the first year of Shēngmíng of Emperor Hòu,
a white rainbow appeared in the east.

Treatise Twenty-five: Commanderies and Prefectures, Part One: Yángzhōu, Nánxúzhōu, Xúzhōu, Nányǎnzhōu, Yǎnzhōu.
In the era of Táng Yáo,
twelve Mù were established.
When Yǔ pacified the waters and lands,
he further established the Nine Provinces.
Jìzhōu was the capital of Yáo,
its territory vast and extensive.
The Jì and Yellow Rivers formed Yǎnzhōu.
The Sea and Mount Dài formed Qīngzhōu.
The Sea, Mount Dài, and Huái formed Xúzhōu.
The Huái and Sea formed Yángzhōu.
Jīng and Héngyáng formed Jīngzhōu.
Jīng and the Yellow River formed Yùzhōu.
Huáyáng and Hēishuǐ formed Liángzhōu.
Hēishuǐ and Xīhé formed Yōngzhōu.
From Yú to Yīn, there were no changes.
When the Zhōu clan possessed the empire,
they merged Xú with Qīng,
merged Liáng with Yōng,
and divided the land of Jìzhōu to form Yōu and Bìng.
In the early Hàn dynasty, Xú and Liáng two provinces were re-established.
Emperor Wǔ repelled the Hú and Yuè,
expanded territory and borders,
established Jiāozhǐ in the south,
established Shuòfāng in the north,
changed Yōng to Liáng,
changed Liáng to Yì,
making a total of thirteen provinces,
and the Sīlìbù governed the three fǔ and three hé commanderies.
In Dōngjīng (Eastern Hàn), Shuòfāng no longer existed,
Jiāozhǐ was changed to Jiāozhōu,
making a total of twelve provinces;
the commanderies governed by Sīlì remained as before.
When the Three Kingdoms contended,
Wú obtained Yáng, Jīng, and Jiāo three provinces;
Shǔ obtained Yìzhōu;
and the Wèi clan still obtained nine.
Wú further divided Jiāo into Guǎng.
At the end of Wèi, after pacifying Shǔ,
Yì was further divided into Liáng.
In the first year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
the empire was unified,
with a total of sixteen provinces.
Later, Liáng and Yōng were divided to form Qín,
Jīng and Yáng were divided to form Jiāng,
Yì was divided to form Níng,
and Yōu was divided to form Píng,
making a total of twenty.
Since the barbarian tribes disturbed Huá,
the provinces of Sī, Jì, Yōng, Liáng, Qīng, Bìng, Yǎn, Yù, Yōu, and Píng were all lost at once.
The surviving populace migrated south,
and Mù and Sī offices were temporarily established,
not in their original territories.
In Jiāngzuǒ (Eastern Jìn), Jīng was further divided into Xiāng,
sometimes separated and sometimes combined,
with a total of Yáng, Jīng, Xiāng, Jiāng, Liáng, Yì, Jiāo, Guǎng.
As for Xúzhōu, it occupied more than half,
and Yùzhōu only obtained Qiáochéng.
By the Sòng era,
Yángzhōu was divided into Nánxú,
Xúzhōu into Nányǎn,
all of Yángzhōu west of the Jiāng River belonged to Yùzhōu,
Jīng was divided into Yōng,
Jīng and Xiāng were divided into Yǐng,
Jīng was divided into Sī,
Guǎng was divided into Yuè,
Qīng was divided into Jì,
and Liáng was divided into Northern and Southern Qín.
In the early days of Tàizōng,
the Suǒlǔ invaded from the south,
and Qīng, Jì, Xú, Yǎn, and Huáixī of Yùzhōu
were all undefended.
North of the Huái River,
it was transformed into barbarian territory.
Therefore, Xúzhōu was established in Zhōnglí,
Běiyǎn in Huáiyīn,
and the two provinces of Qīng and Jì were governed from Gànyú county.
This treatise generally takes the eighth year of Dàmíng as the standard,
and subsequent divisions and branches are recorded as they occurred.
As for the Nèishǐ, Hóu, and Xiàng,
they are fixed at the end of Shēngmíng.
The geographical variations
are difficult to detail,
owing to the frequent changes in names
and repeated divisions of territories.
Sometimes, one commandery or one county
was split into four or five,
and within these four or five,
there were immediate separations and mergers.
With a thousand transformations and a hundred revisions,
even skilled chroniclers cannot fully account for them.
To seek out and examine them thoroughly
is not easy to do with precision.

Now, we have cross-referenced and verified the information using Bān Gù's and Mǎ Biāo's two Treatises on Geography, the household registrations from Tàikāng and Yuánkāng eras, Wáng Yǐn's Treatise on Topography, the Jin Dynasty's Daily Records of the Imperial Court, the Yongchū Registry of Commanderies and States, Hé Xúzhōu's Commanderies and Prefectures, and various other geographical texts.
Furthermore, as there is no Treatise on Geography for the Three Kingdoms period,
matters appear in the Imperial Annals.
Although the establishment of commanderies is sometimes mentioned,
the establishment of counties is not recorded.
Therefore, we now only use the Geography of Commanderies and States in the *Xù Hàn Shū* to cross-reference the Tàikāng Geographical Treatise,
comparing similarities and differences
to verify each other.
For commanderies and counties that remained unchanged from Hàn to Sòng,
we note
"Hàn jiù" (old Hàn system).
For those that were moved or altered,
we discriminate based on their origin.
If it only states
"Mǒu wú" (such-and-such did not exist),
it implies that all previous ones did exist.
If the establishment is not noted,
it means the history is deficient.

The former Hàn Cìshǐ did not have a fixed administrative seat.
(The same applies to other prefectures.)
The latter Hàn administered Lìyáng.
Wèi and Jìn administered Shòuchūn.
After Jìn pacified Wú, it administered Jiànyè.
In the fourth year of Xiánkāng of Emperor Chéng,
Wèi Jùn was provisionally established,

Guǎngchuān Jùn was also provisionally established,
(See separate entry.)
administering Guǎngchuān county.
In the early Sòng, it was abolished and became a county,
subordinate to Wèi Jùn.
East of the Jiāng, Gāoyáng

Later, Tángyì was abolished and merged with Gāoyáng,

all becoming subordinate to Yángzhōu,
with its provisional seat in the capital.
In the eleventh year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén, it was abolished,
and its population was merged with Jiànkāng.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn,
Huìjī, Dōngyáng, Xīn'ān, Yǒngjiā, and Línhǎi five commanderies of Yángzhōu were separated to form Dōngyángzhōu.
In the third year of Dàmíng, the prefecture was abolished,
its territory becoming the royal domain,
and the various commanderies were inspected by the Nántái Shìyùshǐ,
like an attendant inspecting and reporting.
Dōngyángzhōu was simply called Yángzhōu.
In the eighth year,
the royal domain was abolished,
Yángzhōu was re-established,
and Yángzhōu reverted to Dōngyángzhōu.
In the first year of Yǒngguāng of the Former Deposed Emperor,
Dōngyángzhōu was abolished and merged with Yángzhōu.
In the third year of Shēngmíng of Emperor Shùn,
the Yángzhōu Cìshǐ was renamed Mù.
It administered ten commanderies
and eighty counties.
There were 143,296 households
and 1,455,685 individuals.
Dānyáng Yǐn:
Originally Qín Zhāng Jùn,
administered from the old Zhāng Xiàn in modern Wúxīng.
In early Hàn, it belonged to the State of Wú.
After Wú Wáng Bì's rebellion and defeat, it belonged to the State of Jiāngdū.
In the second year of Yuánfēng of Emperor Wǔ,
it became Dānyáng Jùn,
administered from the modern Wǎnlíng Xiàn in Xuānchéng.
In the second year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
Dānyáng was divided to form Xuānchéng Jùn,
administered from Wǎnlíng,
while Dānyáng moved its administration to Jiànyè.
In the first year of Tàixīng of Emperor Yuán,
it was changed to Yǐn.
It administered eight counties.
There were 41,010 households
and 237,341 individuals.
Jiànkāng Lìng:
Originally Mòlíng Xiàn.
In the sixteenth year of Jiàn'ān of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn, the county was established.
Sūn Quán changed Mòlíng to Jiànyè.
After Emperor Wǔ of Jìn pacified Wú,
it reverted to Mòlíng.
In the third year of Tàikāng,
the area north of the river in Mòlíng was separated to form Jiànyè.
Upon Emperor Mǐn's accession,
to avoid using the emperor's tabooed name,
it was changed to Jiànkāng.
Mòlíng Lìng:
Its land was originally named Jīnlíng,
changed by Qín Shǐhuáng.
It was originally administered sixty *lǐ* from the capital,
which is the site of the old Zhìcūn today.
In the ninth year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
its administration moved to the capital,
at Dòuchǎng.
In the first year of Yuánxī of Emperor Gōng,
the Yángzhōu Fǔ Jìnfáng Cānjūn was abolished,
and the county's administration moved to its place.
Dānyáng Lìng:
An old Hàn county.
Jiāngníng Lìng:
In the first year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,

In the second year,
its name was changed.

Wú divided Lìyáng to form Yǒngpíng Xiàn.

it was transferred to Yìxīng,
but soon reverted to its original status.
Yìxīng also had Pínglíng Xiàn.
Dǒng Lǎn's *Wú Dì Zhì* states:

The Tàikāng and Yǒngníng geographical treatises do not mention it,

it was merged with Yǒngshì and Lìyáng two counties.
Lìyáng Lìng:
An old Hàn county.

In the first year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, it was re-established.
Húshú Lìng:

The Grand Administrator of Huáinán:
Qín established it as Jiǔjiāng Commandery,

with its seat in Shòuchūn County.
Later Hàn moved its seat to Yīnlíng County.
Wèi restored the name Huáinán,
and moved its seat to Shòuchūn.
In the first year of Tàikāng, Emperor Wǔ of Jìn
re-established Lìyáng, (See elsewhere.
) Dāngtú, and Qūndào counties.
In the second year,

) these being old counties from both Hàn dynasties.
During the Three Kingdoms period,
the Jiāng-Huái region was a battleground,
and for several hundred lǐ in between, there were no inhabitants.
These counties, all located north of the Jiāng and south of the Huái,
lay deserted,
with no households remaining.
After Wú was pacified,
the people returned to their homelands,
hence they were re-established.
Later, when the Central Plains fell into chaos,
and Hú bandits frequently invaded the south,
many people from Huáinán crossed south.
In the early years of Emperor Chéng,
Sū Jùn and Zǔ Yuē caused disturbances in the Jiāng-Huái region.
Hú bandits again arrived in great numbers,
and even more people crossed the Jiāng to the south.
Therefore, Huáinán Commandery and its various counties were established as a refugee administration south of the Jiāng.
At the end of Jìn, Yúhú County of Dānyáng was eventually partitioned to form the territory of Huáinán.
In the sixth year of Dàmíng, under Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng,
Huáinán Commandery was merged with Xuānchéng,
and Xuānchéng Commandery moved its seat to Yúhú.
In the eighth year,
Huáinán Commandery was re-established,
belonging to Nányùzhōu.
In the third year of Tàishǐ, under Emperor Míng,
it was returned to Yángzhōu.
It administered six counties.
There were 5,362 households,
with 25,840 individuals.
It was 170 lǐ by water
and 140 lǐ by land from the capital.
Yúhú County Magistrate:
In the second year of Tàikāng, under Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
it was established by partitioning Dānyáng County.
It was originally the seat of Wú's Dū nóng xiàowèi.
Dāngtú County Magistrate:
During Emperor Chéng of Jìn's reign,
it was established as a refugee county along with Qūndào.
At the end of Jìn, it was formed by partitioning Yúhú.
Fánchāng County Magistrate:
An old Hàn name,
originally belonging to Yǐngchuān.
Wèi partitioned Yǐngchuān to form Xiāngchéng,
and it then belonged to that.
During the Jìn chaos,
Xiāngchéng Commandery was abolished,
and this county belonged to Huáinán,
formed by partitioning Yúhú.
Xiāngyuán County Magistrate:
This place was originally Wúhú,
Wúhú County,
an old Hàn county.
Towards the end of Jìn,
Xiāngyuán County was established,
belonging to Shàngdǎng.
People from Shàngdǎng crossed south of the Jiāng
and established refugee commanderies and counties,
provisionally based in Wúhú.
Later, Shàngdǎng Commandery was abolished and became a county,
belonging to Huáinán.
In the ninth year of Yuánjiā, under Emperor Wén,
Shàngdǎng County was abolished and merged with Xiāngyuán.
Dìnglíng County Magistrate:
An old Hàn name,
originally belonging to Xiāngchéng,
later formed by partitioning Wúhú.
Qūndào County Magistrate:
Hàn wrote it as Qūnjú,
Jìn wrote it as Qūndào,
and later formed by partitioning Wúhú.
Xuānchéng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Xuānchéng).
In the first year of Tàikāng (280 CE) of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
it was separated from Dānyáng Commandery.
It governed ten counties.
There were 10,120 households
and 47,992 individuals.
It was 580 *lǐ* by water
and 500 *lǐ* by land from the capital.
Wǎnlíng Magistrate (Wǎnlíng Lìng).
An old county from the Hàn dynasty.
Guǎngdé Magistrate (Guǎngdé Lìng).
Hé Zhì states:
“An old county from the Hàn dynasty.”
Neither of the two Hàn Records mentions it,
so it is probably one established by Wú.
Huái'ān Magistrate (Huái'ān Lìng).
Established by Wú.
Níngguó Magistrate (Níngguó Lìng).
Established by Wú.
Xuānchéng Magistrate (Xuānchéng Lìng).
An old county from the Hàn dynasty.
Ānwú Magistrate (Ānwú Lìng).
Established by Wú.
Jīng Magistrate (Jīng Lìng).
An old county from the Hàn dynasty.
Línchéng Magistrate (Línchéng Lìng).
Established by Wú.
Guǎngyáng Magistrate (Guǎngyáng Lìng).
During the Hàn dynasty, it was called Língyáng.
Zǐmíng attained immortality in the mountains of this county,
thus it was named after him.
Due to the taboo name "Líng" (陵) of Empress Dù of Emperor Chéng of Jìn,
it was renamed in the fourth year of Xiánkāng (338 CE).
Shíchéng Magistrate (Shíchéng Lìng).
An old county from the Hàn dynasty.
Dōngyáng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Dōngyáng).
Originally the Western Commandant of Kuàijī.
It was established in the first year of Bǎodǐng (266 CE) by Sūn Hào of Wú.
It governed nine counties.
There were 16,022 households
and 107,965 individuals.
〔一一〕It was 1,700 *lǐ* by water
and the same by land from the capital.
Chángshān Magistrate (Chángshān Lìng).
In the second year of Chūpíng (191 CE) of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn,
it was separated from Wūshāng.
Tàimò Magistrate (Tàimò Lìng).
An old county from the Hàn dynasty.
Wūshāng Magistrate (Wūshāng Lìng).
〔一二〕Yǒngkāng Magistrate (Yǒngkāng Lìng).
In the eighth year of Chìwū (245 CE), it was separated from Shàngpǔ, Wūshāng.
Xìn'ān Magistrate (Xìn'ān Lìng).
In the third year of Chūpíng (192 CE) of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn,
it was separated from Tàimò and named Xīn'ān.
It was renamed in the first year of Tàikāng (280 CE) of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
Wúníng Magistrate (Wúníng Lìng).
In the second year of Xīngpíng (195 CE) of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn,
the Sūn clan separated it from Zhūjì.
Fēng'ān Magistrate (Fēng'ān Lìng).
In the second year of Xīngpíng (195 CE) of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn,
the Sūn clan separated it from Zhūjì.
〔一三〕Dìngyáng Magistrate (Dìngyáng Lìng).
In the twenty-third year of Jiàn'ān (218 CE) of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn,
the Sūn clan separated it from Xìn'ān.
Suíchāng Magistrate (Suíchāng Lìng).
In the second year of Chìwū (239 CE) of Sūn Quán,
it was separated from Tàimò and named Píngchāng.
It was renamed in the first year of Tàikāng (280 CE) of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
Línhǎi Tàishǒu (Administrator of Línhǎi).
Originally the Eastern Commandant of Kuàijī.
During the Former Hàn, the Commandant governed Yín.
After the Later Hàn separated Kuàijī to form Wú Jùn,
it is likely that the Commandant moved its seat to Zhāng'ān.
It was established in the second year of Tàipíng (257 CE) by Sūn Liàng.
It governed five counties.
There were 3,961 households
and 24,226 individuals.
It was 2,019 *lǐ* by water
and the same by land from the capital.
Zhāng'ān Magistrate (Zhāng'ān Lìng).
The *Xù Hàn Zhì* states:
“Formerly Yě,
Minhzhong territory,
〔一四〕Emperor Guāngwǔ renamed it.”
The *Jìn Tàikāng Jì* states:
“Originally the Huípǔ Township south of Yín County,
established in the Zhānghé period of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn.”
It is unclear which is correct.
Línhǎi Magistrate (Línhǎi Lìng).
Wú separated it from Zhāng'ān.
Shǐfēng Magistrate (Shǐfēng Lìng).
Wú established it as Shǐpíng.
It was renamed in the first year of Tàikāng (280 CE) of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
Nínghǎi Magistrate (Nínghǎi Lìng).
Hé Zhì states it was
an old county from the Hàn dynasty.
However, it is not found in the two Hàn Records or the *Jìn Tàikāng Dìzhì*.
〔一五〕Lè'ān Magistrate (Lè'ān Lìng).
Emperor Kāng of Jìn separated it from Shǐfēng.
Yǒngjiā Tàishǒu (Administrator of Yǒngjiā).
In the first year of Tàiníng (323 CE) of Emperor Míng of Jìn,
it was separated from Línhǎi.
It governed five counties.
There were 6,250 households
and 36,680 individuals.
It was 2,800 *lǐ* by water
and 2,640 *lǐ* by land from the capital.
Yǒngníng Magistrate (Yǒngníng Lìng).
In the fourth year of Yǒngjiàn (129 CE) of Emperor Shùn of Hàn,
it was separated from the Dōng'ōu Township of Zhāng'ān.
Some say it was established in the third year of Yǒnghé (138 CE) of Emperor Shùn.
Āngù Magistrate (Āngù Lìng).
Wú established it as Luóyáng.
Sūn Hào renamed it Ānyáng.
It was renamed in the first year of Tàikāng (280 CE) of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
Sōngyáng Magistrate (Sōngyáng Lìng).
Established by Wú.
Lèchéng Magistrate (Lèchéng Lìng).
In the third year of Níngkāng (375 CE) of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn,
it was separated from Yǒngníng.
Héngyáng Magistrate (Héngyáng Lìng).
In the fourth year of Tàikāng (283 CE) of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
because of the Héngxǔ boat garrison, it was made Shǐyáng,
and then renamed again.
Xīn'ān Tàishǒu (Administrator of Xīn'ān).
In the thirteenth year of Jiàn'ān (208 CE) of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn,
Sūn Quán separated it from Dānyáng and named it Xīndū.
It was renamed in the first year of Tàikāng (280 CE) of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
It governed five counties.
There were 12,058 households
and 36,651 individuals.
It was 1,860 *lǐ* by water
and 1,800 *lǐ* by land from the capital.
Shǐxīn Magistrate (Shǐxīn Lìng).
Sūn Quán separated it from Shè.
Suí'ān Magistrate (Suí'ān Lìng).
Sūn Quán separated Xīndìng County from Shè.
It was renamed in the first year of Tàikāng (280 CE) of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
Shè Magistrate (Shè Lìng).
An old county from the Hàn dynasty.
Hǎiníng Magistrate (Hǎiníng Lìng).
Sūn Quán separated Xiūyáng County from Shè.
It was renamed in the first year of Tàikāng (280 CE) of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
This was the beginning of separating various counties from Shè.
Liángyáng County was also separated.
In the eighth year of Dàmíng (464 CE),
it was abolished and merged with Hǎiníng.
Yī Magistrate (Yī Lìng).
An old county from the Hàn dynasty.
Nán Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (Provincial Governor of Southern Xúzhōu).
During the great chaos of Yǒngjiā of Jìn,
refugees from Yōu, Jì, Qīng, Bìng, Yǎnzhōu, and the area north of the Huái River in Xúzhōu,
led by one another, crossed the Huái River,
and some also crossed the Yangtze River, residing within the bounds of Jìnlíng Commandery.
In the fourth year of Xiánhé (329 CE) of Emperor Chéng of Jìn,
Sīkōng Xī Jiàn relocated the refugees who were south of the Huái River to the various counties of Jìnlíng.
Those who had moved south of the Yangtze River and those who remained north of the Yangtze,
all had temporary commanderies and counties established to govern them.
Xú and Yǎnzhōu sometimes governed from north of the Yangtze.
North of the Yangtze, temporary Yōu, Jì, Qīng, and Bìng four *zhōu* were also established.
In the seventh year of Yìxī (411 CE) of Emperor Ān,
the area north of the Huái River was first separated and designated Běi Xú (Northern Xú),
while the area south of the Huái remained Xúzhōu.
Later, Yōu and Jì were combined with Xú,
and Qīng and Bìng were combined with Yǎn.
In the second year of Yǒngchū (421 CE) of Emperor Wǔ,
Xúzhōu was augmented to be Nán Xú (Southern Xú),
while the area north of the Huái was simply called Xú.
In the eighth year of Yuánjiā (431 CE) of Emperor Wén,
the area north of the Yangtze was again designated Nán Yǎnzhōu (Southern Yǎnzhōu),
and the area south of the Yangtze was Nán Xúzhōu (Southern Xúzhōu).
Its seat was at Jīngkǒu.
Jìnlíng from Yángzhōu and the nine temporary commanderies of Yǎnzhōu located south of the Yangtze were attached to it.
Thus, Nán Xúzhōu was fully equipped with the commanderies and counties of Xú, Yǎn, Yōu, Jì, Qīng, Bìng, and Yáng seven *zhōu*.
The *Jùn Guó Zhì* of Yǒngchū second year also lists eight commanderies: Nánpèi, Nán Xiàpī, Guǎngpíng, Guǎnglíng, Xūyí, Zhōnglí, Hǎilíng, and Shānyáng.
〔一六〕Nánpèi, Guǎnglíng, Hǎilíng, Shānyáng, Xūyí, and Zhōnglí were assigned to Nán Yǎn.
Nán Xiàpī was merged with Nán Péngchéng.
Guǎngpíng was merged with Nán Tàishān.
It currently governs seventeen commanderies
and sixty-three counties.
There are 72,472 households
and 420,640 individuals.
It is 240 *lǐ* by water
and 200 *lǐ* by land from the capital.
Grand Protector of Nán Dōnghǎi,
(Dōnghǎi Commandery is described elsewhere.
)In the early years of Emperor Yuán of Jìn,
the northern border of Hǎiyú County in Wú Commandery was carved out to form Dōnghǎi Commandery.
Tán, Qú, and Lìchéng three counties were established.
Zhùqí, Xiāngbēn, and other counties were temporarily administered in Qǔ'ā.
In the Yǒnghé era of Emperor Mù,
the commandery moved out to Jīngkǒu.
The three counties of Tán, etc., were also temporarily administered in Jīng.
In the eighth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén, Nán Xú Commandery was established,
with Dōnghǎi as a subordinate commandery,
and Dāntú was assigned to it.
Tán and Lìchéng both became actual territories.
The Yǒngchū Record of Commanderies and States lists Xiāngbēn, (described elsewhere.
)Zhùqí, Hòuqīu, (both old names from the Hàn dynasty.
) and Xīxí (established by Hé Jiāngzuǒ.
) four counties.
In the twelfth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén,
Hòuqīu was abolished and merged into Xiāngbēn.
Hé and Xú do not have Hòuqīu,
the rest is consistent with the Yǒngchū Record of Commanderies and States.
Xiāngbēn, Zhùqí, and Xīxí
were abolished after Xú Zhì.
It governed six counties.
There were 5,342 households,
and 33,658 people.
Magistrate of Tán,
an old name from the Hàn dynasty.
In the eighth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén,
the area west of Xiàn in Dāntú was separated to form its territory.
Magistrate of Dāntú,
originally belonged to Jìnlíng.
Its ancient name was Zhūfāng,
later named Gǔyáng.
Qín changed it to Dāntú.
In the third year of Jiāhé of Sūn Quán,
it was changed to Wǔjìn.
In the third year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
it reverted to Dāntú.
Magistrate of Wǔjìn,
in the second year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
it was established by dividing Dāntú and Qǔ'ā.
Magistrate of Pílíng,
〔一七〕at the end of Dàmíng of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng,
it was transferred to this commandery.
Magistrate of Qú,
an old name from the Hàn dynasty.
It was provisionally established by Jìn in Jiāngzuǒ.
During the reign of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng,
the western border of Tán was separated to form its territory.
Magistrate of Lìchéng,
an old name from the Hàn dynasty.
It was provisionally established by Jìn in Jiāngzuǒ.
During the reign of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
it became an actual territory along with the commandery.
Grand Protector of Nán Lángyá,
(Lángyá Commandery is described elsewhere.
)During the Jìn disturbances,
over a thousand households from Lángyá State followed Emperor Yuán across the river.
In the third year of Tàixīng,
Huáidé County was established.
Although Dānyáng had a Chancellor of Lángyá, it had no territory.
〔一八〕In the first year of Xiánkāng of Emperor Chéng,
Huán Wēn was appointed Grand Protector,
stationed on Jīnchéng on Púzhōu of Jiāngchéng.
He requested to carve out the territory of Jiāngchéng County from Dānyáng to establish a commandery.
He also divided Jiāngchéng's land to establish Línyí County.
The Yǒngchū Record of Commanderies and States lists Yángdū, (in the Former Hàn, it belonged to Chéngyáng;
in the Later Hàn and the Jìn Tàikāng Gazetteer, it belonged to Lángyá.
)Fèi, and Jíqiū (all described elsewhere.
)three counties,
all carved from Línyí and Jiànkāng to form their territories.
Fèi County's seat was north of the palace city.
In the eighth year of Yuánjiā,
Jíqiū was abolished and merged into Yángdū.
In the fifteenth year,
Fèi was abolished and merged into Jiànkāng and Línyí.
In the fifth year of Dàmíng of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
Yángdū was abolished and merged into Línyí.
Now it governs two counties.
There were 2,789 households,
and 18,697 people.
It is 200 *lǐ* by water and
100 *lǐ* by land from the province.
It is 160 *lǐ* by water from the capital.
Magistrate of Línyí,
an old name from the Hàn dynasty.
In the Former Hàn, it belonged to Dōnghǎi;
in the Later Hàn and Jìn, it belonged to Lángyá.
Magistrate of Jiāngchéng,
an old county from the Hàn dynasty.
Originally belonged to Dānyáng.
Wú abolished it and made it a Supervisor of Agricultural Production (*Diannong Duwei*).
In the first year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, it was re-established.
Grand Protector of Jìnlíng,
during the Wú period, the area west of Wúxī in Wú Commandery was separated to become the Agricultural Production Commandant (*Diannong Xiaowei*) of Pílíng.
In the second year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
the commandant was abolished,
and it was established as Pílíng Commandery,
governed from Dāntú.
Later it returned to Pílíng.
The heir apparent of Wáng Yuè of Dōnghǎi was named Pí,
and Dōnghǎi State had previously held Pílíng as its fief.
In the fifth year of Yǒngjiā,
Emperor Yuán changed it to Jìnlíng.
〔一九〕It first moved its seat from Pílíng to Dāntú.
In the early Tàixīng era,
the commandery and Dāntú County were both administered in Jīngkǒu.
Xī Jiàn moved it back to Dāntú.
In the ninth year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān,
it returned to Jìnlíng.
Originally belonged to Yángzhōu.
In the eighth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén,
it was transferred to Nán Xú.
It governed six counties.
There were 15,382 households,
and 80,113 people.
It is 175 *lǐ* by water and
the same by land from the province.
It is 400 *lǐ* by water and
the same by land from the capital.
Magistrate of Jìnlíng,
originally named Yánlíng.
Hàn changed it to Pílíng.
Later it was changed along with the commandery.
Magistrate of Yánlíng,
in the second year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
it was established by dividing Yánlíng Township from Qǔ'ā.
Magistrate of Wúxī,
an old county from the Hàn dynasty.
Wú abolished it.
In the first year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, it was re-established.
Magistrate of Nánshā,
originally the office of the Salt Supervisor (*Siyán Duwei*) in Wú County.
During the Wú period, it was called Shāzhōng.
After the pacification of Wú,
Jìyáng County was established and assigned to it.
In the seventh year of Xiánkāng of Emperor Chéng of Jìn,
the salt office was abolished,
and it was established as Nánshā County.
Magistrate of Qǔ'ā,
originally named Yúnyáng.
Qín Shǐhuáng changed it to Qǔ'ā.
In the third year of Jiāhé of Wú,
it reverted to Yúnyáng.
In the second year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
it reverted to Qǔ'ā.
Magistrate of Jìyáng,
in the second year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
it was established by dividing Wúxī and Pílíng.
Grand Protector of Yìxīng,
in the first year of Yǒngxīng of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
it was established by dividing Yángxiàn from Wúxīng and Yǒngshì from Dānyáng.
Yǒngshì soon returned to Dānyáng.
Originally Yángzhōu.
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Míng,
it was transferred to Nán Xú.
It governed five counties.
There were 13,496 households,
and 89,525 people.
It is 400 *lǐ* by water and
the same by land from the province.
It is 490 *lǐ* by water and
the same by land from the capital.
Magistrate of Yángxiàn,
an old county from the Hàn dynasty.
Magistrate of Línjīn,
formerly belonged to Yángxiàn.
It was established upon the establishment of the commandery.
Magistrate of Yìxiāng,
formerly belonged to Chángchéng and Yángxiàn.
It was established upon the establishment of the commandery.
Magistrate of Guóshān,
formerly belonged to Yángxiàn.
It was established upon the establishment of the commandery.
Magistrate of Suī'ān,
in the third year of Yǒngchū of Emperor Wǔ,

)It governed two counties.

Magistrate of Lánlíng.

Tàishǒu.
(Dōngguǎn Jùn is seen elsewhere.
) In Yǒngchū Jùnguó, there was also Gài Xiàn.

) It administered three counties.

Jǔ Lìng.

) In the twelfth year of Yuánjiā during Emperor Wén's reign

Gūmù Lìng,
an old name from the Hàn dynasty.
Línhuái Tàishǒu.

Emperor Guāngwǔ merged it with Dōnghǎi.
In the fifteenth year of Yǒngpíng during Emperor Míng's reign,

Hǎixī Lìng.
In the Former Hàn, it belonged to Dōnghǎi;
in the Later Hàn and Jìn, it belonged to Guǎnglíng.
Shèyáng Lìng.
In the Former Hàn, it belonged to Línhuái;
in the Later Hàn, it belonged to Guǎnglíng.
It was abolished during the Three Kingdoms period.
In the first year of Tàikāng during Emperor Wǔ of Jìn's reign, it was re-established.
Líng Lìng.
In the Former Hàn, it belonged to Sìshuǐ;

Huáiyīn Lìng.

Dōngyáng Lìng.

two counties.

Sīwú Lìng.

to establish Xīnchāng Commandery,
and Xúzhōu was established,
reverting its seat of government to Zhōnglí.

Nán Yānzhōu Cìshǐ:
When the Central Plains fell into disorder,
many refugees from the northern provinces migrated south.
Jìn Chéngdì established Nán Yānzhōu,
with its temporary seat in Jīngkǒu.
At that time, Nánqīngzhōu and Bìngzhōu were also established.
In the first year of Wǔdì Yǒngchū,
Bìngzhōu was abolished and merged into Nán Yānzhōu.
〔三二〕In the eighth year of Wéndì Yuánjiā,
its territory was first demarcated in the region between the Yangtze and Huái rivers,
with its seat in Guǎnglíng.
The Yǒngchū Jùnguó administered fourteen commanderies.
Nán Gāopíng, Nán Píngchāng, Nán Jìyīn, Nán Púyáng, Nán Tàishān, Jìyáng, and Nán Lǔ – seven commanderies –
〔三三〕now all belong to Xúzhōu.
There was also Dōngyān Commandery,
which was established south of the Yangtze River by dividing Púyáng.
It administered Yān County (in the Former Hàn, it was called Nányān;
in the Later Hàn, it was called Yān,
both belonged to Dōngjùn;
in the Tàikāng geographical gazetteer, it belonged to Púyáng),
Báimǎ, Píngchāng, and Kǎochéng, a total of four counties.
In the eighteenth year of Wéndì Yuánjiā,
Kǎochéng was abolished and merged into Yān.
In the nineteenth year,
Dōngyān Commandery was abolished and became Dōngyān County,
belonging to Nán Púyáng,

Nán Qí Commandery administered Xī'ān and Línzī, a total of two counties.

a total of three counties.

Collation Notes
Volume 26, Commanderies and Provinces 2: Nányùzhōu, Yùzhōu, Jiāngzhōu, Qīngzhōu, Jìzhōu, Sīzhōu.
Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ.
During the Jìn dynasty, the Hú bandits south of the Jiāng River were strong and numerous.
The Yù department was wiped out.
In the first year of Yuándì’s Yǒngchāng reign (311 CE),
Cìshǐ Zǔ Yuē first retreated from Qiáochéng to Shòuchūn.
In the fourth year of Chéngdì’s Xiánhé reign (329 CE),
Yùzhōu was provisionally established,
with Yǔ Liàng as Cìshǐ,
governing Wúhú.
In the fourth year of Xiánkāng (338 CE),
Máo Bǎo became Cìshǐ,
governing Zhūchéng.
In the sixth year (340 CE),
Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Yǔ Yì garrisoned Wǔchāng
and concurrently held Yùzhōu.
In the eighth year (342 CE),
Yǔ Yì became Cìshǐ,
again garrisoning Wúhú.
In the first year of Mùdì’s Yǒnghé reign (345 CE),
Cìshǐ Zhào Yìn garrisoned Niúzhǔ.
In the second year (346 CE),
Cìshǐ Xiè Shàng garrisoned Wúhú;
in the fourth year (348 CE),
he advanced to Shòuchūn;
in the ninth year (353 CE),
Shàng again garrisoned Lìyáng;
in the eleventh year (355 CE),
he advanced to Mǎtóu.
In the first year of Shēngpíng (357 CE),
Cìshǐ Xiè Yì was stationed at Qiáo.
In the first year of Āidì’s Lónghé reign (362 CE),
Cìshǐ Yuán Zhēn retreated from Qiáo to defend Shòuchūn.
In the first year of Jiǎnwén’s Xián’ān reign (362 CE),
Cì[shǐ Huán Xī was stationed at Lìyáng.
In the first year of Xiàowǔ’s Níngkāng reign (363 CE),
Cì]shǐ Huán Chōng was stationed at Gūshú.
In the tenth year of Tàiyuán (385 CE),
Cìshǐ Zhū Xù was stationed at Mǎtóu.
In the twelfth year (387 CE),
Cìshǐ Huán Shíqián was stationed at Lìyáng.
In the second year of Āndì’s Yìxī reign (406 CE),
Cìshǐ Liú Yì was stationed at Gūshú.
Sòng Wǔdì wanted to expand into Hénán
and pacify the lands of Yù.
In the ninth year (413 CE),
he ceded the lands west of the Great River and north of Dàléi in Yángzhōu,
all of which were attached to Yùzhōu.
Thus, the foundation of Yù was established.
In the thirteenth year (417 CE),
Cìshǐ Liú Yìqìng garrisoned Shòuyáng.
In the third year of Yǒngchū (422 CE),
Huáinán was divided into Nányùzhōu,
governing Lìyáng;
and Huáixī became Yùzhōu.
In the seventh year of Wéndì’s Yuánjiā reign (430 CE) [the two Yùzhōu were merged into one;
in the sixteenth year (439 CE) they were divided again;
in the twenty-second year (445 CE) they were merged again;
in the third year of Xiàowǔ’s Dàmíng reign (459 CE)] they were divided again.
In the fifth year (461 CE),
Huáinán and Xuānchéng of Yángzhōu were again attached to it.
The seat of government was moved to Gūshú.
In the second year of Míngdì’s Tàishǐ reign (466 CE) they were merged again,
and Huáinán and Xuānchéng were returned to Yángzhōu.
In the ninth month, they were divided again,
and the government returned to Lìyáng.
In the fifth month of the third year (467 CE),
they were merged again.
In the fourth year (468 CE),
Huáinán and Xuānchéng of Yángzhōu were made Nányùzhōu,
governing Xuānchéng.
In the fifth year (469 CE), it was abolished.
At that time, all lands west of the Huái River
had been lost to the bandits.
In the seventh year (471 CE), Lìyáng, Huáiyīn, Nánqiáo, and the area bordering the river in Nányànzhōu were again separated to establish Nányùzhōu.
In the first year of Tàiyù (472 CE),
Nánruyīn Dù was assigned to Yùzhōu,
and Lújiāng Dù of Yùzhōu was assigned to Nányùzhōu.
According to records, from Yǒngchū to Dàmíng, Huáinán
was Nányù.
Although there were occasional mergers and divisions,
divisions predominated.
From Tàishǐ, upon losing Huáixī,
two Yùzhōu were re-established in Huáidōng.
Currently, Nányù uses Huáidōng as its boundary.
We will not list the two prefectures separately here.
Readers should note that Huáidōng serves as the boundary,
and by further inquiry, they will understand the division of the two Yùzhōu in Tàishǐ.

Jiàn'ān (建安) Grand Administrator.
Originally Mǐnyuè (閩越).
Qín (秦) established it as Mǐnzhōng Jùn (閩中郡).
In the era of Emperor Wǔ (武) of Hàn (漢),
Mǐnyuè (閩越) rebelled,
and was annihilated.
Its people were resettled between the Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮) rivers,
leaving the land empty.
Later, some who had fled into the mountains and valleys emerged,
and Yě Xiàn (冶縣) was established for them,
belonging to Kuàijī (會稽).
Sīmǎ Biāo (司馬彪) says
Zhāng'ān (章安) is the old Yě (冶).
If so, then Línhǎi (臨海) was also Yě (冶) territory.
Zhāng Bó's (張勃) Wúlù (吳錄) says:
"The Mǐnyuè (閩越) King's casting ground,
hence called Ānmǐn Wáng Yě (安閩王冶).
This should not be named exclusively after him.
Perhaps it was Gōujiàn's (句踐) casting place,
hence called Yě (冶)?"
"There is a mountain in Mǐnzhōng (閩中) named Zhàn (湛).
It is suspected that the furnace on Zhàn Shān (湛山) for casting swords was the Zhàn Lú (湛爐)."
Later, the Yě (冶) territory was divided into the eastern and southern parts of the Kuàijī Dūwèi (會稽都尉).
The eastern part was
Línhǎi (臨海);
the southern part was
Jiàn'ān (建安).
In the third year of Yǒng'ān (永安), during the reign of Sūn Xiū (孫休) of Wú (吳),
Jiàn'ān Jùn (建安郡) was established by dividing the southern part.
It administered seven counties.

Collation Notes
Monograph Twenty-seven: Commanderies and Prefectures Three: Jīngzhōu, Yǐngzhōu, Xiāngzhōu, Yōngzhōu, Liángzhōu, Qínzhōu.
The Governor of Jīngzhōu:
during the Hàn dynasty, its seat was in Hànshòu, Wǔlíng;
during Wèi and Jìn, it was in Jiānglíng;
Wáng Dūn governed from Wǔchāng;
Táo Kǎn initially governed from Miǎnyáng,
later from Wǔchāng;
Wáng Yì governed from Jiānglíng;
Yǔ Liàng governed from Wǔchāng;
Yǔ Yì advanced to Xiāngyáng,
then returned to Xiàkǒu;
Huán Wēn governed from Jiānglíng;
Huán Chōng governed from Shàngmíng;
Wáng Chén returned to Jiānglíng;
thereafter, its seat remained in Jiānglíng.
At the beginning of the Sòng dynasty, it administered thirty-one commanderies.
Later, Nányáng, Shùnyáng, Xiāngyáng, Xīnyě, and Jìnglíng were separated to form Yōngzhōu;
the ten commanderies of Xiāngchuān became Xiāngzhōu;
Jiāngxià and Wǔlíng belonged to Yǐngzhōu;
Suíjùn and Yìyáng belonged to Sīzhōu;
Běiyìyáng was abolished.
In total, eleven commanderies remained.
During the reign of Emperor Wén,
Sòng'ān Zuǒjùn was also established,
administering seven counties: Tuòbiān, Suímù, Lèníng, Mùhuà, Yǎngzé, Géyīn, and Guīdé.
Later, it was abolished and reorganized.
Wènyáng Commandery was also transferred.
Currently, it administers twelve commanderies
and forty-eight counties.
It has sixty-five thousand six hundred and four households.
It is three thousand three hundred and eighty *lǐ* by water from the capital.
The Grand Administrator of Nánjùn:
established by Qín.
In the first year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
it was made Línjiāng Guó.
In the middle second year of Emperor Jǐng, it was restored to its former status.
In the first year of Tàikāng during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, it was renamed Xīnjùn,
but soon restored to its former name.
At the beginning of Sòng, it administered nine counties.
Later, Zhōulíng and Jiānlì were transferred to Bālíng;
Jīngyáng was abolished and merged into Zhījiāng in the eighteenth year of Yuánjiā during Emperor Wén's reign.
Jīngyáng did not exist during the Two Hàn dynasties,
but is mentioned in the Jìn Tàikāng Gazetteer,
suggesting it was probably established by Wú.
In total, six counties remained.
It has fourteen thousand five hundred and forty-four households
and seventy-five thousand eighty-seven mouths.

an old county from Hàn.
Huáróng Gōngxiàng:
an old county from Hàn.

and later re-established.
Dāngyáng Nánxiàng:
an old county from Hàn.

an old county from Hàn.

but it was later transferred.
Biānxiàn Nánxiàng:
an old county from Hàn.
Zhījiāng Hóuxiàng:
an old county from Hàn.

Wú's Nánjùn governed the area south of the river,
administering counties like Jiānglíng and Huáróng.
In the first year of Tàikāng during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
the area south of the river in Nánjùn was separated to form Nánpíng Commandery,
with its seat in Zuòtáng,
later in Jiāng'ān.

The Grand Administrator of Tiānmén:
in the sixth year of Yǒng'ān during the reign of Sūn Xiū of Wú,

Chōngxiàn has Sōngliángshān.
On the mountain there is a rock,
where it splits open for dozens of *zhàng*,
so high that an arrow shot upwards with effort cannot reach its top.
Its top is named
"Tiānmén" (Heaven's Gate),
and thus the commandery was named after it.
Chōngxiàn was later abolished.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn during Emperor Xiàowǔ's reign,
it was transferred to Yǐngzhōu.
In the third year of Tàishǐ during Emperor Míng's reign, it was restored to its former status.
It administers four counties.
