and six hundred *lǐ* by land.
It is three thousand five hundred *lǐ* by water from the capital.
Lǐyáng Lìng:
established in the fourth year of Tàikāng during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
Límlǐ Lìng:
established in the fourth year of Tàikāng during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
Língyáng Lìng:
an old county from Hàn,
belonging to Wǔlíng.
Lóuzhōng Lìng:
not present in the Two Hàn dynasties.
The Jìn Tàikāng Gazetteer mentions it,
suggesting it was probably established by Wú.
The Grand Administrator of Yídū:
The Tàikāng Gazetteer, Wáng Yǐn's Dàodì, and Hé Zhì all state that Wú established it by separating it from Nánjùn;
Zhāng Bó's Wúlù states that Liú Bèi established it.
According to Wúzhì,
Lǚ Méng pacified Nánjùn
and occupied Jiānglíng,
while Lù Xùn separately took Yídū,
capturing Zǐguī, Zhījiāng, and Yídào counties.
Initially, Quán and Liú Bèi divided Jīngzhōu,
and Nánjùn belonged to Bèi.
Therefore, it was Bèi who established Yídū by separating it from Nánjùn,
not Wú.
Xí Záochǐ stated that
when Wèi Wǔ pacified Jīngzhōu,
he separated the area west of Zhījiāng in Nánjùn to form Línjiāng Commandery.
In the fifteenth year of Jiàn'ān,
Liú Bèi renamed it Yídū.
It administers four counties.
It has one thousand eight hundred and forty-three households
and thirty-four thousand two hundred and twenty mouths.
It is three hundred and fifty *lǐ* by water from the prefecture,
with no land route.
It is three thousand seven hundred and thirty *lǐ* by water from the capital.
Yídào Lìng:
an old county from Hàn.
Hénshān Nánxiàng:
in Former Hàn, it belonged to Wǔlíng.
In Later Hàn, it belonged to Nánjùn.
In the first year of Tàikāng during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, it was renamed Xīngshān,
and later restored to its former name.
Yíchāng Lìng:
Hé Zhì states that Emperor Wǔ of Jìn established it.
However, the Tàikāng and Yǒngníng Gazetteers do not mention it,
suggesting it was probably established after that time.
Yílíng Lìng:
an old county from Hàn.
Wú renamed it Xīlíng.
In the first year of Tàikāng during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, it was restored to its former name.
Bādōng Gōngxiàng (Commander of Bādōng Commandery),
Qiáo Zhōu’s Bājì states:
In the first year of Chūpíng (190 CE),
Zhào Wěi (趙韙), the Sīmǎ (司馬) in the staff of Jīngzhōu (荊州), proposed to divide the various counties of Bājùn (巴郡) from Ānhàn (安漢) downwards to form the Yǒngníng (永寧) Commandery.
In the sixth year of Jiàn'ān (201 CE),
Liú Zhāng (劉璋) changed Yǒngníng (永寧) to Bādōng (巴東) Commandery.
From Fúlíng (涪陵) County, Dānxīng (丹興) and Hànjiā (漢葭) counties were established separately.
A Bādōng Shǔguó Dūwèi (巴東屬國都尉) was established,
which later became Fúlíng (涪陵) Commandery.
According to the Jìn Tàikāng Dìzhì (晉太康地志),
Bādōng (巴東) belonged to Liángzhōu (梁州).
In the second year of Tàiyán (303 CE) of Emperor Huì (惠), it was transferred to Yìzhōu (益州).
In the early Yǒnghé (永和) period of Emperor Mù (穆), when Shu (蜀) was pacified,
it was transferred to Jīngzhōu (荊州).
The Yǒngchū Jùnguózhì (永初郡國志) does not include Bāqú (巴渠) and Mǐnyáng (黽陽) counties.
It administered seven counties.
There were 13,795 households
and 45,237 mouths.
It was 1,300 lǐ (里) by water from the provincial capital.
It was 4,680 lǐ (里) by water from the imperial capital.
Yúfù Hóuxiàng (Marquis-Chancellor of Yúfù),
an old county of the Hàn (漢),
belonged to Bājùn (巴郡).
In the second year of Zhāngwǔ (222 CE) of Liú Bèi (劉備),
it was renamed Yǒng'ān (永安).
In the first year of Tàikāng (280 CE) of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn (晉武帝), it reverted to its old name.
Qú Lìng (令 of Qú),
an old county of the Hàn (漢),
belonged to Bājùn (巴郡).
Xīnpǔ Lìng (令 of Xīnpǔ),
newly established according to Hézì (何志).
Nánpǔ Lìng (令 of Nánpǔ),
in the tenth month of the eighth year of Jiànxīng (230 CE) of Liú Chán (劉禪),
Yìzhōu Mù (益州牧) Yán Yǔ (閻宇) submitted a memorial to change Yángqú (羊渠) to establish it.
The location of Yángqú (羊渠) is unknown.
Established by Wú (吳) according to Hézì (何志).
Hànfēng Lìng (令 of Hànfēng),
Hézì (何志) does not note its establishment.
The Tàikāng Dìzhì (太康地志) states that Bādōng (巴東) had Hànchāng (漢昌) County,
which is likely it.
Bāqú Lìng (令 of Bāqú),
Hézì (何志) does not note its establishment.
Mǐnyáng Lìng (令 of Mǐnyáng),
Hézì (何志) does not note its establishment.
At the end of the Jìn (晉) when Wú (吳) was pacified,
Wǔlíng (武陵) Commandery was established in the Gorges,
which included Mǐnyáng (黽陽) and Qiányáng (黔陽) counties.
In the first year of Xiánníng (275 CE), they were both abolished.
Wènyáng Tàishǒu (太守 of Wènyáng),
newly established according to Hézì (何志).
It first belonged to Liángzhōu (梁州).
In the eleventh year of Yuánjiā (434 CE) of Emperor Wén (文), it was transferred.
In the early Sòng (宋), it had four counties.
Later Wènyáng (汶陽) County was abolished.
Now it administers three counties.
There were 958 households
and 4,914 mouths.
It was 700 lǐ (里) by water and 400 lǐ (里) by land from the provincial capital.
It was 4,100 lǐ (里) from the imperial capital.
Tóngyáng Lìng (令 of Tóngyáng),
newly established according to Hézì (何志).
Jǔyáng Lìng (令 of Jǔyáng),
newly established according to Hézì (何志).
Gāo'ān Lìng (令 of Gāo'ān),
newly established according to Hézì (何志).
Nányìyáng Tàishǒu (太守 of Nányìyáng),
(Yìyáng (義陽) Commandery is seen separately.)
established by the Jìn (晉) at the end of its rule for displaced people from Yìyáng (義陽).
In the early Sòng (宋), it had four counties.
In the second year of Xiàojiàn (455 CE) of Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武), Píngyáng (平陽) County was merged into Juéxī (厥西).
Píngyáng (平陽) was originally a commandery,
established by displaced people south of the Yangtze.
In the Wèi (魏) period, Hédōng (河東) was divided to form Píngyáng (平陽) Commandery.
At the end of the Jìn (晉), it was abolished and became a county.
〔一０〕Now it administers two counties.
There were 1,607 households
and 9,741 mouths.
Juéxī Lìng (令 of Juéxī),
did not exist in the two Hàn (漢) dynasties.
The Jìn Tàikāng Dìzhì (晉太康地志) states it belonged to Yìyáng (義陽).
Píngshì Lìng (令 of Píngshì),
an old Hàn (漢) name,
belonged to Nányáng (南陽).
Xīnxīng Tàishǒu (太守 of Xīnxīng),
Wèizhì (魏志) states that in the twentieth year of Jiàn'ān (215 CE),
the four commanderies of Yúnzhōng (雲中), Dìngxiāng (定襄), Wǔyuán (五原), and Shuòfāng (朔方) were abolished.
One county was established in each commandery,
and they were combined into this commandery,
belonging to Bìngzhōu (并州).
Established by displaced people south of the Yangtze in the Jìn (晉).
In the early Sòng (宋), it had six counties.
Later Yúnzhōng (雲中) was abolished.
(An old Hàn (漢) name,
belonged to Yúnzhōng (雲中).)
In the second year of Xiàojiàn (455 CE) of Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武),
Jiǔyuán (九原) County was also abolished (An old Hàn (漢) name,
belonged to Wǔyuán (五原).)
and merged with Dìngxiāng (定襄).
Dàngqú (宕渠) (established for displaced people)
was merged with Guǎngmù (廣牧).
In total, it now administers three counties.
There were 2,301 households
and 9,584 mouths.
Dìngxiāng Lìng (令 of Dìngxiāng),
an old Hàn (漢) name.
Guǎngmù Nánxiàng (廣牧男相),
an old Hàn (漢) name,
belonged to Shuòfāng (朔方).
Xīnfēng Lìng (令 of Xīnfēng),
an old Hàn (漢) name,
belonged to Jīngzhào (京兆).
Established for displaced people.
Nánhédōng Tàishǒu (太守 of Nánhédōng),
Hédōng (河東) Commandery,
established by Qín (秦).
In the third year of Xiánkāng (337 CE) of Emperor Chéng of Jìn (晉成帝),
Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (征西將軍) Yǔ Liàng (庾亮) established it for displaced households from Sīzhōu (司州).
In the early Sòng (宋), it had eight counties.
In the second year of Xiàojiàn (455 CE) of Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武),
Guǎngqī (廣戚) (in the Former Hàn (漢) it belonged to Pèi (沛),
in the Later Hàn (漢) and Jìn Tàikāng Dìzhì (晉太康地志) it belonged to Péngchéng (彭城).
Established for displaced people south of the Yangtze.)
was merged with Wénxǐ (聞喜).
Hóngnóng (弘農) (a refugee commandery established south of the Yangtze,
later abolished and became a county)
and Línfén (臨汾) were merged with Sōngzī (松滋).
Ānyì (安邑) was merged with Yǒng'ān (永安).
(Línfén (臨汾) and Ānyì (安邑) were old Hàn (漢) names.
Línfén (臨汾) later belonged to Píngyáng (平陽).)
〔一一〕Now it administers four counties.
There were 2,423 households
and 10,487 mouths.
It was 120 lǐ (里) by water from the provincial capital.
It was 3,500 lǐ (里) by water from the imperial capital.
Wénxǐ Lìng (令 of Wénxǐ),
formerly Qǔwò (曲沃).
Qín (秦) changed its name to Zuǒyì (左邑).
In the sixth year of Yuándǐng (111 BCE) of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn (漢武帝),
when he was touring here,
he heard of the defeat of Nányuè (南越),
and changed its name to Wénxǐ (聞喜) (meaning 'heard good news').
Yǒng'ān Lìng (令 of Yǒng'ān),
in the Former Hàn (漢) it was Zhì (彘) County.
In the second year of Yángjiā (133 CE) of Emperor Shùn (順), its name was changed.
Later it belonged to Píngyáng (平陽).
Sōngzī Lìng (令 of Sōngzī),
in the Former Hàn (漢) it belonged to Lújiāng (廬江).
It did not exist in the Later Hàn (漢).
In the Jìn (晉), it belonged to Ānfēng (安豐).
It is suspected that displaced people settled in the Jīng (荊) region,
and thus it was established.
Qiáo Xiànlìng (令 of Qiáo County),
(seen separately.)
established for displaced people from Qiáo (譙).
Jiànpíng Tàishǒu.
During the third year of Yǒng'ān under Sūn Xiū of Wú,
it was established by partitioning Yídū Commandery.
It administered the four counties of Xìnlíng, Xìngshān, Zǐguī, and Shāqú.
Later, the Jìn dynasty also had a Jiànpíng Dūwèi,
which administered the four counties of Wū, Běijǐng, Tàichāng, and Jiànshǐ.
In the first year of Xiánníng under Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
the Dūwèi was changed to a Jùn (commandery).
Thus, both Wú and Jìn had Jiànpíng Jùn.
In the first year of Tàikāng, Wú was pacified,
and they were merged.
In the fifth year,
Jiànshǐ County was abolished,
but later re-established.
The Yǒngchū Jùnguó lists seven counties: Nánlíng, Jiànshǐ, Xìnlíng, Xìngshān, Yǒngxīn, Yǒngníng, and Pínglè.
Today, none of these exist.
According to the Tàikāng Dìzhì, the five counties of Nánlíng, Yǒngxīn, Yǒngníng, Pínglè, and Xīnxiāng are not mentioned.
It is suspected that these were established east of the Jiāng.
Xìnlíng, Xìngshān, and Shāqú
are suspected to have been established by Wú.
Jiànshǐ
was established in the early Jìn dynasty.
It administered seven counties.
It had 1,329 households,
and a population of 20,814.
It was 1,000 *lǐ* by land and water from the prefecture (zhōu).
It was 4,380 *lǐ* by water from the capital (jīngdū).
Wū Lìng:
an old county from the Hàn dynasty.
Zǐguī Hóuxiàng:
an old county from the Hàn dynasty, Guīxiāng Gōngxiàng.
Hé Zhì states
it originally belonged to Zǐguī,
and was partitioned by Wú.
According to the Tàikāng Dìzhì,
Zǐguī included Guīxiāng,
which was the former state of Kuízi,
destroyed by Chǔ.
However, there is no Guīxiāng County,
so what Hé Zhì said is incorrect.
〔一二〕Běijǐng Lìng:
listed in the Jìn Tàikāng Dìzhì.
It originally belonged to Bādōng,
but in the fifth year of Tàishǐ under Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, it was transferred to Jiànpíng.
Tàichāng Lìng:
listed in the Jìn Tàikāng Dìzhì.
Shāqú Lìng:
In the Jìn Qǐjūzhù,
it was established in the first year of Tàikāng.
However, Shāqú was administered by Wú's Jiànpíng Jùn,
so it should not have been established immediately after Wú's pacification.
This is unclear.
Xīnxiāng Lìng.
Yǒngníng Tàishǒu:
During Emperor Ān of Jìn, it was provisionally established as Chángníng Jùn.
Emperor Míng of Sòng changed its name to Yǒngníng,
because its name was the same as Emperor Wén's mausoleum.
In the early Sòng dynasty, it had five counties,
but Suí'ān was later abolished.
〔一三〕(Established by Emperor Ān of Jìn.)
After the second year of Xiàojiàn under Emperor Xiàowǔ,
Tóngyáng (established by Emperor Ān of Jìn)
was merged into Chángníng,
and Suíníng (established by Emperor Ān of Jìn)
was merged into Shànghuáng.
It now administers two counties.
It has 1,157 households,
and a population of 4,274.
It is 60 *lǐ* by land from the prefecture (zhōu).
It is 3,430 *lǐ* from the capital (jīngdū).
Chángníng Hóuxiàng:
established by Emperor Ān of Jìn.
Shànghuáng Nánxiàng:
In the early Sòng dynasty, it belonged to Xiāngyáng,
but was later transferred.
Neither of the Hàn dynasties nor the Jìn dynasty had this county.
Wǔníng Tàishǒu:
In the fifth year of Lóng'ān under Emperor Ān of Jìn, Huán Xuán established it for the Mán people who surrendered from Jū and Zhāng.
It administers two counties.
It has 958 households,
and a population of 4,914.
Lèxiāng Lìng:
established by Emperor Ān of Jìn.
Chánglín Nánxiàng:
established by Emperor Ān of Jìn.
Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ:
In the third year of Huángchū under Emperor Wén of Wèi,
the northern Jiāng commanderies of Jīngzhōu were made Yǐngzhōu.
It was abolished and merged with Jīngzhōu in the same year,
so it is not the current area.
Wú also established Yǐngzhōu.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn under Emperor Xiàowǔ,
Jiāngxià, Jìnglíng, Suí, Wǔlíng, and Tiānmén from Jīngzhōu,
Bālíng from Xiāngzhōu,
Wǔchāng from Jiāngzhōu,
and Xīyáng from Yùzhōu were partitioned.
Additionally, Zhōulíng and Jiānlì counties from Nánjùn were transferred to Bālíng,
and Yǐngzhōu was established.
Tiānmén later returned to Jīngzhōu.
It administers six commanderies
and thirty-nine counties.
It has 29,469 households,
and a population of 158,587.
It is 2,100 *lǐ* by water from the capital (jīngdū).
Jiāngxià Tàishǒu:
established by Emperor Gāoa of Hàn. It originally belonged to Jīngzhōu.
Yǒngchū Jùnguó and Hé Zhì both state it was governed in Ānlù.
After this, it was governed in Xiàkǒu.
There were also Ānlù and Qǔlíng.
Qǔ later became a separate commandery.
〔一四〕It administers seven counties.
It has 5,072 households,
and a population of 23,810.
Rǔnán Hóuxiàng:
originally the land of Shāxiàn.
At the end of the Jìn dynasty, people from Rǔnán Jùn migrated to Xiàkǒu,
and it was consequently established as Rǔnán County.
Shāxiàn Lìng:
an old county from the Hàn dynasty, abolished by Wú.
It was re-established in the first year of Tàikāng under Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
governed in Xiàkǒu.
In the third year of Tàiyuán under Emperor Xiàowǔ,
it was abolished and merged with Shāyáng.
Later, its land became the actual territory of Rǔnán.
Dùnyáng Zǐxiàng:
established east of the Jiāng.
Xiàochāng Hóuxiàng:
not listed in Yǒngchū Jùnguó or Hé Zhì.
Xú Zhì has it,
so it is suspected to have been established during the reign of Emperor Xiàowǔ.
Huìhuái Zǐxiàng:
established east of the Jiāng.
Shāyáng Nánxiàng:
an old county from the Two Hàn dynasties,
originally named Shāxiàn,
belonging to Wǔchāng.
In the first year of Tàikāng under Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, it was renamed,
and Shāxiàn was also established,
while Shāyáng moved to its current seat.
In the sixteenth year of Yuánjiā under Emperor Wén, it was transferred to Bālíng.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn under Emperor Xiàowǔ, it was transferred to Jiāngxià.
Xiànyáng Zǐxiàng:
During the reign of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
Zhū Sì, a native of Ānlù and a general under Táo Kǎn,
requested to partition the eastern border of Ānlù for this county.
〔一五〕Púqí Nánxiàng:
established in the first year of Tàikāng under Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
It originally belonged to Chángshā.
In the sixteenth year of Yuánjiā under Emperor Wén, it was transferred to Bālíng.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn under Emperor Xiàowǔ, it was transferred to Jiāngxià.
Jìnglíng Tàishǒu:
In the ninth year of Yuánkāng under Emperor Huì of Jìn, it was established by partitioning the western border of Jiāngxià.
Hé Zhì also lists Sòng County,
but Xú does not.
It administers six counties.
It has 8,591 households,
and a population of 44,375.
It is 1,400 *lǐ* by water from the prefecture (zhōu).
It is 3,400 *lǐ* by water from the capital (jīngdū).
Chángshòu Lìng:
established in the sixth year of Tàishǐ under Emperor Míng.
Jìnglíng Hóuxiàng:
an old county from the Hàn dynasty, belonging to Jiāngxià.
Xīnshì Zǐxiàng:
an old county from the Hàn dynasty,
belonging to Jiāngxià.
Xiāochéng Hóuxiàng:
〔一六〕listed in Yǒngchū Jùnguó.
Hé and Xú do not note its establishment.
Xīnyáng Nánxiàng:
listed in Yǒngchū Jùnguó.
Hé and Xú do not note its establishment.
Yúndù Hóuxiàng:
an old county from the Hàn dynasty,
belonging to Jiāngxià.
Wǔlíng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Wǔlíng).
According to the Former Hàn's Dìlǐ Zhì (Treatise on Geography),
Emperor Gāodì established it.
The Xù Hàn Jùnguó Zhì (Treatise on Commanderies and Kingdoms in the Later Hàn) says
Qín Zhāowáng established it,
naming it Qiánzhōng Jùn.
In the fifth year of Gāodì, its name was changed.
It originally belonged to Jīngzhōu.
It administered ten counties.
There were 5,090 households
and 37,555 people.
It was 1,000 *lǐ* by water from the *zhōu* (province) capital.
It was 3,000 *lǐ* by water from the imperial capital.
Línyuán Nán Xiàng (Administrator of Línyuán County),
an old Hàn county.
Lóngyáng Hóu Xiàng (Administrator of Lóngyáng County),
the Jìn Tàikāng Dìlǐ Zhì and Hé Zhì state it was established by Wú.
Hànshòu Bó Xiàng (Administrator of Hànshòu County),
established in the Former Hàn,
〔一七〕in the third year of Yángjiā of Emperor Shùn of the Later Hàn, its name was changed.
Wú called it Wúshòu,
and Emperor Wǔ of Jìn restored the old name.
Yuánnán Lìng (Magistrate of Yuánnán County),
established in the twenty-sixth year of Jiànwǔ by Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn.
Qiānlíng Hóu Xiàng (Administrator of Qiānlíng County),
an old Hàn county.
Chényáng Nán Xiàng (Administrator of Chényáng County),
an old Hàn county.
Wǔyáng Lìng (Magistrate of Wǔyáng County),
the Former Hàn wrote it as Wúyáng,
the Later Hàn had none,
but the Jìn Tàikāng Dì Zhì has it.
Yǒuyáng Zhǎng (Chief of Yǒuyáng County),
an old Hàn county.
Qiányáng Zhǎng (Chief of Qiányáng County),
the Two Hàn had none,
but the Jìn Tàikāng Dì Zhì has it.
Yuánlíng Lìng (Magistrate of Yuánlíng County),
an old Hàn county.
Bālíng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Bālíng).
In the sixteenth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén,
the four counties of Bālíng, Púqí, Xiàjùn from Chángshā,
and Shāyáng from Jiāngxià were separated and established,
belonging to Xiāngzhōu.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
Jiānlì and Zhōulíng from Nánjùn were transferred across the Jiāngxià,
〔一八〕belonging to Yǐngzhōu.
In the second year,
Suí'ān from Chángníng was again transferred to Bālíng.
Hé Zhì concludes in the twentieth year of Yuánjiā.
Bālíng Jùn was established in the sixteenth year,
so it should be in Hé Zhì but is missing.
It administered four counties.
There were 5,187 households
and 25,316 people.
It was 500 *lǐ* by water from the *zhōu* capital.
It was 2,500 *lǐ* by water from the imperial capital.
Bālíng Nán Xiàng (Administrator of Bālíng County),
established in the first year of Tàikāng by Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
belonging to Chángshā.

in the first year of Tàikāng,

When the Hú perished and the Dī rebelled,
many refugees from Yōng and Qín moved south, passing Fán and Miǎn.
Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn first established a provisional Yōngzhōu in Xiāngyáng,
and also established provisional commanderies and counties.
In the twenty-sixth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
Xiāngyáng, Nányáng, Xīnyě, Shùnyáng, and Suí five commanderies of Jīngzhōu were detached to form Yōngzhōu.
However, the provisional commanderies and counties were still temporarily located within the borders of various commanderies.
In the Dàmíng period of Xiàowǔ,
actual commanderies and counties were again divided to serve as territories for the provisional commanderies and counties.
Xú Zhì's Yōngzhōu included Běishàngluò, Běijīngzhào, and Yìyáng three commanderies.
Běishàngluò,
established by Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn,
administered Shàngluò, Běishāng, Fēngyáng, Yángtíng, and Běijùyáng five counties.
Běijīngzhào administered Běilántián, Bàchéng, and Shānběi three counties.
It is stated that they were all established during Jǐngpíng.
Yìyáng,
it is stated, was established by Emperor Ān of Jìn,
and administered Píngshì and Xiāngxiāng two counties.
Fēngyáng, Yángtíng, and Běijùyáng,
it is stated, were all established by Emperor Ān.
The establishment dates of the other counties are not noted.
Currently, these three commanderies no longer exist.
Currently, it administers seventeen commanderies
and sixty counties.
There are 38,975 households
and 167,467 people.

Níngzhōu Cìshǐ (Inspector of Níngzhōu).
In the seventh year of Tàishǐ (271 CE) of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, it was established by partitioning the four commanderies of Jiànníng, Xīnggǔ, Yúnnán, and Yǒngchāng from Nánzhōng of Yìzhōu.
In the third year of Tàikāng (282 CE), it was abolished,
and the Nányí Xiàowèi was established.
In the second year of Tàian (303 CE) of Emperor Huì, it was re-established,
with the addition of three commanderies: Āi, Yuèxī, and Zhūtí.
In the fourth year of Xiánkāng (338 CE) of Emperor Chéng, the four commanderies of Āi, Yèláng, Zhūtí, and Yuèxī were partitioned to form Ānzhōu,
but it was soon abolished and merged into Níngzhōu.
Yuèxī later returned to Yìzhōu.
Currently, it administers fifteen commanderies,
and eighty-one counties.

Textual Notes
Treatise Twenty-Nine, Bureaucracy I
Grand Tutor (Tài zǎi),
one person.
In the time of King Wǔ of Zhōu,
Zhōu Gōngdàn first held this position,
managing the governance of the state,
and was the head of the Six Ministers.
Qín, Hàn, and Wèi did not always establish it.
In the early Jìn dynasty, following the Rites of Zhōu,
the Three Dukes were fully established.
Among the duties of the Three Dukes,
the Grand Master (Tài shī) held the primary position.
Emperor Jǐng's personal name was Shī,
therefore, the Grand Tutor (Tài zǎi) was established to replace it.
The Grand Tutor (Tài zǎi),
was probably the ancient Grand Master (Tài shī).
In the time of Zhòu of Yīn,
Jīzǐ was Grand Master (Tài shī).
In the time of King Wǔ of Zhōu,
Tàigōng was Grand Master (Tài shī).
In the time of King Chéng of Zhōu,
Zhōu Gōng was Grand Master (Tài shī).
When Zhōu Gōng died,
Bì Gōng replaced him.
In the early Western Hàn, it was not established.
Emperor Píng first re-established the office of Grand Master (Tài shī),
and Kǒng Guāng held it.
In the Eastern Hàn, it was again abolished.
In the early reign of Emperor Xiàn,
Dǒng Zhuó was Grand Master (Tài shī).
When Zhuó was executed, it was again abolished.
During the Wèi dynasty, it was not established.
Since Jìn established the Grand Tutor (Tài zǎi) based on the Grand Master (Tài shī),
Ānpíng Wáng Fú held the position.
Grand Mentor (Tài fù),
one person.
In the time of King Chéng of Zhōu,
Bì Gōng was Grand Mentor (Tài fù).
In the first year of Empress Gāo of Hàn,
Wáng Líng was first appointed.
Grand Guardian (Tài bǎo),
one person.
In the time of Tàijiǎ of Yīn,
Yī Yǐn was Grand Guardian (Tài bǎo).
In the time of King Wǔ of Zhōu,
Shào Gōng was Grand Guardian (Tài bǎo).
In the first year of Yuánshǐ of Emperor Píng of Hàn,
Wáng Shùn was first appointed.
From the Later Hàn to Wèi, it was not established.
In the early Jìn, it was re-established.
From Grand Master (Tài shī) to Grand Guardian (Tài bǎo),
these were the Three Dukes.
They discussed the Way and managed the state,
regulating Yin and Yang.
If there was no such person, the position was left vacant.
They instructed and protected the sovereign,
guiding them with virtue and righteousness.
Chancellor (Xiàngguó),
one person.
It was first established in the eleventh year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
with Xiāo Hé holding the position,
and the Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng) position was abolished.
When Hé died,
Cáo Cān replaced him.
When Cān died,
it was abolished.
King Qí of Wèi appointed Jìn Jǐngdì as Chancellor (Xiàngguó).
In the time of Emperor Huì of Jìn, Zhào Wáng Lún;
in the time of Emperor Mǐn, Nányáng Wáng Bǎo;
in the time of Emperor Ān, Sòng Gāozǔ;
in the time of Emperor Shùn, King Qí;
all served as Chancellor (Xiàngguó).
Since Wèi and Jìn,
it was no longer a position for a subject.
Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng),
one person.
Yīn Tāng appointed Yī Yǐn as Right Minister (Yòu xiàng)
and Zhòng Huǐ as Left Minister (Zuǒ xiàng).
In the second year of King Dàowǔ of Qín,
the office of Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng) was first established.
Chéng means
to offer.
Xiàng means
to assist.
King Zhāoxiāng, son of King Dàowǔ, first appointed Chūlǐ Jí as Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng).
Later, Left and Right Prime Ministers (Zuǒyòu Chéngxiàng) were also established.
In the early reign of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
one Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng) was established.
In the eleventh year,
it was renamed Chancellor (Xiàngguó).
Emperor Xiàohuì and Empress Gāo established Left and Right Prime Ministers (Zuǒyòu Chéngxiàng).
In the second year of Emperor Wén,
one Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng) was again established.
In the second year of Yuánshòu of Emperor Āi,
it was renamed Grand Minister of Education (Dà Sītú).
In the Eastern Hàn, it was not re-established.
Until the thirteenth year of Jiàn'ān of Emperor Xiàn,
the Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng) was re-established.
During the Wèi dynasty and early Jìn, it was again abolished.
In the reign of Emperor Huì,
when Zhào Wáng Lún usurped the throne,
he appointed Liáng Wáng Róng as Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng).
In the first year of Yǒngxīng,
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng was appointed Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng).
In the first year of Jiànxīng of Emperor Mǐn,
Lángyá Wáng Ruì was appointed Left Prime Minister (Zuǒ Chéngxiàng),
and Nányáng Wáng Bǎo was appointed Right Prime Minister (Yòu Chéngxiàng).
In the third year,
Bǎo was appointed Chancellor (Xiàngguó),
and Ruì was appointed Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng).
In the first year of Yǒngchāng of Emperor Yuán,
Wáng Dūn was appointed Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng),
and the Minister of Education (Sītú) Xún Zǔ was transferred to Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
The staff of the Minister of Education (Sītú) and the Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng) were combined to form a resident office (liúfǔ),
but Dūn did not accept it.
In the time of Emperor Chéng,
Wáng Dǎo was appointed Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng),
the Minister of Education (Sītú) office was abolished and made the Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng) office.
When Dǎo died,
the Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng) position was abolished,
and it reverted to the Minister of Education (Sītú) office.
In the early reign of Emperor Shìzǔ of Sòng,
Nánjùn Wáng Yìxuān was appointed Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng),
and the Minister of Education (Sītú) office remained as before.
Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
one person.
Wèi means to calm those below from above.
They managed military affairs.
During suburban sacrifices, they managed the second offering.
During grand mourning, they announced the posthumous title at the southern suburb.
In the time of Yáo, Shùn served as the official of Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
Hàn followed this.
In the second year of Jiànyuán of Emperor Wǔ, it was abolished.
In the twenty-seventh year of Jiànwǔ of Emperor Guāngwǔ,
the Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ) was abolished,
and the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) was established to replace it.
At the end of Emperor Líng's reign,
Liú Yú was appointed Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ),
and the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) remained as before.
Minister of Education (Sītú),
one person.
They managed civil affairs.
During suburban sacrifices, they managed inspecting the sacrificial animals and watching the ablutions.
During grand mourning, they secured the coffin.
Shàohào Shì named officials after birds,
and Zhùjiū Shì was Minister of Education (Sītú).
In the time of Yáo, Shùn was Minister of Education (Sītú).
When Shùn assumed the imperial throne,
he appointed Qì as Minister of Education (Sītú).
Qì's great-great-grandson Míng,
also served as Minister of Education (Sītú) of Xià.
In the time of Zhōu, the Minister of Education (Sītú) was the Earth Official (Dìguān),
managing state education.
In the early Western Hàn, it was not established.
In the second year of Yuánshòu of Emperor Āi,
the Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng) was abolished,
and the Grand Minister of Education (Dà Sītú) was abolished.
In the twenty-seventh year of Jiànwǔ of Emperor Guāngwǔ,
the "Grand" (Dà) was removed.
Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
one person.
They managed water and land affairs.
During suburban sacrifices, they managed sweeping and arranging musical instruments.
During grand mourning, they managed supervising the burial of the earth.
When Shùn assumed the imperial throne,
he appointed Yǔ as Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Míng, the son of Qì's great-great-grandson,
also served as Minister of Works (Sīkōng) of Xià.
Yīn Tāng appointed Jiùdān as Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
In the time of Zhōu, the Minister of Works (Sīkōng) was the Winter Official (Dōngguān),
managing state affairs.
In the early Western Hàn, it was not established.
In the first year of Suīhé of Emperor Chéng,
the Grandee Secretary (Yùshǐ Dàfū) was renamed Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sīkōng).
In the second year of Jiànpíng of Emperor Āi,
it reverted to Grandee Secretary (Yùshǐ Dàfū).
In the second year of Yuánshòu,
it reverted to Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sīkōng).
In the twenty-seventh year of Jiànwǔ of Emperor Guāngwǔ, the character "Grand" (Dà) was removed.
In the thirteenth year of Jiàn'ān of Emperor Xiàn,
the Minister of Works (Sīkōng) was again abolished,
and a Grandee Secretary (Yùshǐ Dàfū) was established.
When the Grandee Secretary (Yùshǐ Dàfū) Xī Lǜ was dismissed,
the position was not refilled.
In the early Wèi, the Minister of Works (Sīkōng) was again established.
The Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ),
one person.
In charge of military affairs.
Sī
means to preside over.
Mǎ
means military.
During Yáo’s (Yáo) time, Qì (Qì) was made Houji (Hòují),
and also concurrently held the position of Sīmǎ.
During the Zhōu (Zhōu) dynasty, Sīmǎ was a summer official (xiàguān),
in charge of state administration.
Xiàng Jí (Xiàng Jí) made Cáo Wújiù (Cáo Wújiù) and Zhōu Yīn (Zhōu Yīn) both Grand Marshals.
The Hàn (Hàn) dynasty initially did not establish this position.
In the fourth year of Yuánshòu (Yuánshòu) during Emperor Wǔ’s (Wǔdì) reign,
the Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ) was first established.
Initially, it was simply called Sīmǎ.
Debaters argued that since the Hàn had the position of Jūnhóu Qiān rén Sīmǎ (jūnhóu qiān rén sīmǎ),
they therefore added 'Dà' (great).
When Sīkōng (Sīkōng) was established,
it was again argued that county and road officials had the position of Yù Sīkōng (yù sīkōng),
so 'Dà' was added again.
When Wáng Mǎng (Wáng Mǎng) acted as regent,
because the Hàn had no Minor Minister of Education (Xiǎosītú),
he decided to add 'Dà' to the titles of Sīmǎ, Sītú (Sītú), and Sīkōng.
In the twenty-seventh year of Jiànwǔ (Jiànwǔ) during Emperor Guāngwǔ’s (Guāngwǔdì) reign,
the Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ) was abolished,
and the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) took its place.
In the second year of Huángchū (Huángchū) during Emperor Wén (Wéndì) of Wèi’s (Wèi) reign,
the Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ) was re-established,
with Cáo Rén (Cáo Rén) holding the position,
while the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) remained as before.
The Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn),
one person.
All generals were in charge of expeditions.
According to the Zhōu (Zhōu) system,
the king established six armies.
Duke Xiàn (Xiàngōng) of Jìn (Jìn) created two armies,
with the Duke leading the upper army.
The name Jiāngjūn (General)
originated from this.
King Huái (Huáiwáng) of Chǔ (Chǔ) sent three generals into the pass,
with Sòng Yì (Sòng Yì) as the Senior General (Shàngjiāng).
Emperor Gāodì (Gāodì) of Hàn (Hàn) made Hán Xìn (Hán Xìn) the Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn).
In the Western Capital of Hàn (Hàn Xījīng), the Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ) was placed above him.
In the Eastern Capital of Hàn (Hàn Dōngjīng), the Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn) was an independent official,
ranking above the Three Ducal Ministers (Sānsī).
In the third year of Qīnglóng (Qīnglóng) during Emperor Míng (Míngdì) of Wèi’s (Wèi) reign,
Emperor Xuān (Xuāndì) of Jìn (Jìn) was promoted from Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn) to Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
Thus, the Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn) was below the Three Ducal Ministers.
Afterwards, he was again placed above the Three Ducal Ministers.
When Emperor Jǐng (Jǐngdì) of Jìn (Jìn) was Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn),
and Emperor Jǐng’s (Jǐngdì) uncle Fú (Fú) was Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
he memorialized to change the Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn) to be below the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
Later, it was restored to its old position.
When Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì) of Jìn (Jìn) ascended the throne,
Prince Ānpíng (Ānpíngwáng) Fú (Fú) was Grand Preceptor (Tàizǎi),
Zhèng Chōng (Zhèng Chōng) was Grand Mentor (Tàifù),
Wáng Xiáng (Wáng Xiáng) was Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo),
Prince Yìyáng (Yìyángwáng) Wàng (Wàng) was Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
Hé Zēng (Hé Zēng) was Minister of Education (Sītú),
Xún Yǐ (Xún Yǐ) was Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
Shí Bāo (Shí Bāo) was Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ),
Chén Qiān (Chén Qiān) was Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn).
All eight Ducal Ministers were established concurrently at that time,
with only no Chancellor (Chéngxiàng).
There was a servant named Yílù (Yílù).
By the Hàn (Hàn) dynasty,
whenever the Chancellor's (Chéngxiàng) office had something to report,
upon arrival at the palace gate, they would always call out
"Yílù!"
This became a regular practice.
The Chancellor (Chéngxiàng) established three Chief Clerks (Zhǎngshǐ).
If the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng) was ill,
the Grandee Secretary (Yùshǐ Dàfū) would lead all officials to inquire about his health for three mornings,
and when he recovered,
an imperial edict would be issued, sending the Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng) or a Grand Master of Light Chariots (Guānglù Dàfū) to bestow a fattened ox
and fine wine.
When the Three Ducal Ministers (Sāngōng) were ill during Emperor Jǐng’s (Jǐngdì) reign of Hàn (Hàn),
he sent Palace Eunuchs (Zhōnghuángmén) to inquire about their illness.
During Wèi (Wèi) and Jìn (Jìn), it was a Palace Attendant (Huángménláng),
and for particularly important cases, perhaps an Attendant at Court (Shìzhōng).
Since Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ) of Wèi (Wèi) became Chancellor (Chéngxiàng),
he only established two Chief Clerks (Zhǎngshǐ), a Left and a Right.
The Grand Mentor's (Tàifù) office in the Eastern Capital of Hàn (Hàn Dōngjīng) established ten Supervisors (Yuàn) and Subordinates (Shǔ),
one Imperial Attendant (Yùshǔ),
and twelve Clerks (Lìshǐ).
It is unknown what their respective departments were.

From the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) to the Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn), General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn), General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Jiāngjūn), and General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn),
all had one Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ).
Generals also each established one Army Supervisor (Sīmǎ).
The Grand Mentor (Tàifù) did not establish a Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ).
The Grand Commandant's (Tàiwèi) office established twenty-four Supervisors (Yuàn) and Subordinates (Shǔ).
The Western Bureau (Xīcáo) managed the appointment and duties of palace officials.
The Eastern Bureau (Dōngcáo) managed the promotion and transfer of chief officials receiving two thousand dàn of grain.
The Household Bureau (Hùcáo) managed household registration, ancestral sacrifices, and agriculture and sericulture.
The Memorials Bureau (Zòucáo) managed memorials and proposals.
The Litigation Bureau (Cícáo) managed lawsuits.
The Penal Bureau (Fǎcáo) managed postal stations and regulations.
The Military Service Bureau (Wèicáo) managed soldiers and transport.
The Bandit Bureau (Zéicáo) managed banditry.
The Judgment Bureau (Juécáo) managed legal judgments.
The Military Bureau (Bīngcáo) managed military affairs.
The Finance Bureau (Jīncáo) managed currency, salt, and iron.
The Granary Bureau (Cāngcáo) managed grain.
The Chief Clerk of the Yellow Pavilion (Huánggé Zhǔbù) oversaw and recorded all matters.
One Imperial Attendant (Yùshǔ),
and twenty-two Clerks (Lìshǐ).
The Imperial Attendant (Yùshǔ) was primarily responsible for driving the Duke's chariot.
Among the Clerks (Lìshǐ) were those of the Pavilion (Géphú), Record Office (Jìshì), and Gate (Ménxià Lìshǐ).
The remaining clerks are not recorded.
There were twenty-four Supervisors (Yuàn) and Subordinates (Shǔ),
and from the Eastern and Western Bureaus, there were a total of twelve bureaus.
Therefore, each bureau had one Supervisor (Yuàn) and one Subordinate (Shǔ),
totaling twenty-four people.
The Minister of Education (Sītú) established thirty-one Supervisors (Yuàn) and Subordinates (Shǔ),
one Imperial Attendant (Yùshǔ),
and thirty-five Clerks (Lìshǐ).
The Minister of Works (Sīkōng) established twenty-nine Supervisors (Yuàn),
one Imperial Attendant (Yùshǔ),
and thirty-one Clerks (Lìshǐ).
The Minister of Works (Sīkōng) also had a separate Supervisor for Roads and Bridges (Dàojiáo Yuàn).
The remaining names for additions and reductions
are missing from historical records and cannot be known.
In the Eastern Capital of Hàn (Hàn Dōngjīng), the Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn) and General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn) had two Palace Attendants for Military Affairs (Cóngshì Zhōngláng),
twenty-nine Supervisors (Yuàn) and Subordinates (Shǔ),
one Imperial Attendant (Yùshǔ),
and thirty Clerks (Lìshǐ).
The General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Jiāngjūn) and General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn) had two Palace Attendants for Military Affairs (Cóngshì Zhōngláng),
twenty Supervisors (Yuàn) and Subordinates (Shǔ),
one Imperial Attendant (Yùshǔ),
and twenty-four Clerks (Lìshǐ).
The Military Bureau Supervisor and Clerk (Bīngcáo Yuànshǐ) were in charge of military affairs.
The Ration and Leave Supervisor and Clerk (Bǐngjiǎ Yuànshǐ) were in charge of rations and leave.
Additionally, an External Inspector (Wàicìjiān) was established to manage legal judgments.
When leading troops for external campaigns,
the camp had five divisions,
each division had one Colonel (Xiàowèi),
and one Army Supervisor (Jūnsīmǎ);
below a division was a company (qū),
each company had one Army Commander (Jūnhóu);
below a company was a platoon (tún),
each platoon had one Platoon Leader (Túnzhǎng).
If no Colonel (Xiàowèi) was appointed,
then the division would only have one Army Supervisor (Jūnsīmǎ).
There were also Acting Army Supervisors (Jūnjiǎ Sīmǎ) and Acting Army Commanders (Jūnjiǎ Hóu).
Those with separate camps were Separate Division Supervisors (Biébù Sīmǎ).
Other generals appointed for campaigns
had no fixed official positions in their headquarters,
but also had Division and Company Supervisors (Bùqū Sīmǎ) and Army Commanders (Jūnhóu) to lead troops.
The Supervisors (Yuàn) and Subordinates (Shǔ) for the Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn) and below, as well as the additions and reductions for the Three Ducal Ministers' (Sānfǔ) offices,
are missing from historical records and cannot be known.
Those who established Clerks (Lìshǐ) and Imperial Attendants (Yùshǔ)
were the same as the Three Ducal Ministers' (Sānfǔ) offices.
Where it mentions "Supervisors and Clerks" (Yuànshǐ),
it means there were Supervisors (Yuàn) but no Subordinates (Shǔ),
nor Clerks (Lìshǐ) or Imperial Attendants (Yùshǔ),
which was different from the Three Ducal Ministers' (Sānfǔ) offices.
In the early Wèi (Wèi) dynasty, the historical records for the officials in the Ducal Ministers' (Gōngfǔ) offices were incomplete.
When Emperor Jǐng (Jǐngdì) of Jìn (Jìn) was Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn),
he established ten Supervisors (Yuàn),

one each for the Western Bureau (Xīcáo), Eastern Bureau (Dōngcáo), Household Bureau (Hùcáo), Granary Bureau (Cāngcáo), Bandit Bureau (Zéicáo), Finance Bureau (Jīncáo), Water Bureau (Shuǐcáo), Military Bureau (Bīngcáo), and Cavalry Bureau (Qíbīng).
This means there were no Subordinates (Shǔ).
In the Xiánxī (Xiánxī) era of Emperor Yuán (Yuándì) of Wèi (Wèi),
Emperor Wén (Wéndì) of Jìn (Jìn) became Chancellor of State (Xiàngguó).

The Chancellor of State's (Xiàngguó) office established a General of the Central Guards (Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn), a General of Valiant Cavalry (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn), Left and Right Chief Clerks (Zhǎngshǐ), a Supervisor (Sīmǎ), four Palace Attendants for Military Affairs (Cóngshì Zhōngláng),
four Chief Clerks (Zhǔbù),
nineteen Gentlemen-in-Waiting (Shèrén),
twenty-two Consultative Officers (Cānjūn),
eleven Military Advisers (Cānzhàn),
and thirty-three Supervisors (Yuàn) and Subordinates (Shǔ).
One Supervisor (Yuàn) and one Subordinate (Shǔ) for the Eastern Bureau (Dōngcáo),
one Subordinate (Shǔ) for the Western Bureau (Xīcáo),
one Supervisor (Yuàn) for the Household Bureau (Hùcáo),
two Subordinates (Shǔ),
one Supervisor (Yuàn) for the Bandit Bureau (Zéicáo),
two Subordinates (Shǔ),
one Supervisor (Yuàn) and one Subordinate (Shǔ) for the Finance Bureau (Jīncáo),
one Supervisor (Yuàn) and one Subordinate (Shǔ) for the Military Bureau (Bīngcáo),
two Supervisors (Yuàn) for the Cavalry Bureau (Qíbīng),
one Subordinate (Shǔ),
one Supervisor (Yuàn) and one Subordinate (Shǔ) for the Chariot Bureau (Chēcáo),
one Supervisor (Yuàn) and one Subordinate (Shǔ) for the Armor Bureau (Kǎicáo),
one Supervisor (Yuàn) and one Subordinate (Shǔ) for the Water Bureau (Shuǐcáo),
one Supervisor (Yuàn) and one Subordinate (Shǔ) for the Collection Bureau (Jícáo),
one Supervisor (Yuàn) and one Subordinate (Shǔ) for the Law Bureau (Fǎcáo),
one Supervisor (Yuàn) and one Subordinate (Shǔ) for the Memorials Bureau (Zòucáo),
two Subordinates (Shǔ) for the Granary Bureau (Cāngcáo),
one Subordinate (Shǔ) for the Military Supplies Bureau (Róngcáo),
one Subordinate (Shǔ) for the Horse Bureau (Mǎcáo),
and one Subordinate (Shǔ) for the Matchmaking Bureau (Méicáo),
totaling thirty-three people.
Nine miscellaneous Subordinates (Sǎnshǔ),
making a total of forty-two people.
In the early Jìn dynasty, all officials from Gōng (Duke) and above
had one Zhǎngshǐ, one Xīgé Jìjiǔ, one Dōnggé Jìjiǔ, one Xīcáo Yuàn, one Dōngcáo Yuàn, one Hùcáo Shǔ, one Cāngcáo Shǔ, and one Zéicáo Shǔ.
Those who commanded troops also had one Sīmǎ, one Cóngshì Zhōngláng, one Zhǔbù, and one Jìshì Dū.
There were four Shèrén.
Those who held the Jié and were Dūdū
had six Cānjūn.
Ānpíng Xiànwáng Fú, when he was Tàizǎi,
increased the Yuàn and Shǔ to ten.
The five sections of Bīng, Kǎi, Shì, Yíngjūn, and Cìjiān all had Shǔ,
making a total of ten including the previous ones.
Yáng Jùn, when he was Tàifù,
increased the Jìjiǔ to four,
and the Yuàn and Shǔ to twenty.
The Bīngcáo was divided into ten sections: Zuǒ, Yòu, Fǎ, Jīn, Tián, Jí, Shuǐ, Róng, Chē, and Mǎ.
All of them had Shǔ,
totaling twenty.
Zhào Wáng Lún, when he was Xiàngguó,
appointed one Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ, one Yòu Zhǎngshǐ, one Sīmǎ, and four Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
There were twenty Cānjūn,
four Zhǔbù, four Jìshì Dū, and four Jìjiǔ each.
There were forty Yuàn and Shǔ.
The Dōngcáo and Xīcáo also had Shǔ.
The remaining eighteen Cáo all had Yuàn,
thus making forty in total.
All Cáo generally had Yùshǔ, Lìshǐ, and Xuégàn.
The Yùshǔ's duty was to record affairs.
Since the time of the Jiāngzuǒ (Eastern Jìn),
the various Gōng (Dukes) appointed one Zhǎngshǐ, one Cāngcáo Yuàn, one Hùcáo Shǔ, and one Dōngxī Gégé Jìjiǔ each.
There were two Zhǔbù and two Shèrén.
There were two Yùshǔ.
The number of Lìshǐ was not fixed.
Those commanding troops had one Sīmǎ,
and two Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
The number of Cānjūn was not fixed.
Those with higher honors appointed one Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ, one Yòu Zhǎngshǐ, one Sīmǎ, and four Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
There were four Yuàn and Shǔ.
In this case, the Cāngcáo had an additional Shǔ,
and the Hùcáo had a Yuàn.
This was the highest honor
reached in the Jiāngzuǒ.
Zhǎngshǐ, Sīmǎ, and Shèrén
were Qín dynasty officials.
Cóngshì Zhōngláng, Yuàn, Shǔ, Zhǔbù, and Lìshǐ
were officials from the Former Hàn dynasty.
Chén Tāng serving as Dà Jiāngjūn Wáng Fèng's Cóngshì Zhōngláng is an example.
Yùshǔ and Cānjūn
were officials from the Later Hàn dynasty.
Sūn Jiān serving as Chēqí Cānjūnshì is an example.
Originally, there was no deference shown to the head of the府 (fǔ).
During the Jìn dynasty, Sūn Chǔ of Tàiyuán, when he was Dà Sīmǎ Shí Bāo's Cānjūn,
treated Bāo disrespectfully.
This was the beginning of regulations requiring deference.
Jìjiǔ
was a Jìn dynasty official title.
In the Hàn dynasty, Wú Wáng Bì was Liú Shì's Jìjiǔ.
Since wine is fundamental to sacrifices,
and the eldest presides over them,
the term Jìjiǔ was used.
In the Hàn dynasty, the Shìzhōng, and in the Wèi dynasty, the Sànqí Chángshì who achieved high merit,
were all appointed as Jìjiǔ.
The Gōngfǔ Jìjiǔ
merely adopted this name.
The Zhǎngshǐ and Cóngshì Zhōngláng managed administrative affairs.
The Sīmǎ managed military commanders.
The Zhǔbù, Jìjiǔ, and Shèrén managed internal household affairs.
The Cānjūn, Yuàn, Shǔ, and Lìshǐ managed affairs of the various Cáo.
If a Sītú did not hold the rank of Gōng (Duke),
only the Shèrén would be omitted.
Their office was always retained.
Their official duties differed from other Fǔ.
There were Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ and Yòu Zhǎngshǐ, and one Zuǒ Xīcáo Yuàn and one Shǔ each.
The rest were the same.
Other Fǔ appointed them if there was a Gōng,
and omitted them if not.
When Jìn Yuándì served as Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn and Céngxiàng,
he appointed Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
There was no fixed number.
They were divided to manage the various Cáo.
There were Lùshì Zhōngláng, Dùzhī Zhōngláng, and Sānbīng Zhōngláng.
As for Cānjūn, there were two Zīyì Cānjūn,
whose main duty was to advise on matters.
They were first appointed in the early Jiāngzuǒ Jìn dynasty,
derived from the Jūnzi Jìjiǔ.
When Sòng Gāozǔ was Xiàng,
he only appointed Zīyì Cānjūn,
with no fixed number.

Currently, the various Cáo include Lùshì, Jìshì, Hùcáo, Cāngcáo, Zhōngzhíbīng, Wàibīng, Qíbīng, Chángliú Zéicáo, Xíngyù Zéicáo, Chéngjú Zéicáo, Fǎcáo, Tiáncáo, Shuǐcáo, Kǎicáo, Chēcáo, Shìcáo, Jí, Yòuhù, and Mòcáo.
These are all eighteen Cáo Cānjūn.
Cānjūn not assigned to a Cáo
had no fixed number.
In the early Jiāngzuǒ,

Jìn Yuándì's Zhèndōng Céngxiàng Fǔ had Lùshì, Jìshì, Dōngcáo, Xīcáo, Dùzhī, Hùcáo, Fǎcáo, Jīncáo, Cāngcáo, Lǐcáo, Zhōngbīng, Wàibīng, Qíbīng, Diǎnbīng, Bīngcáo, Zéicáo, Yùncáo, Jìnfáng, Diǎnbīn, Kǎicáo, Tiáncáo, Shìcáo, Qíshì, and Chēcáo Cānjūn.
The Dōngcáo, Xīcáo, Dùzhī, Jīncáo, Lǐcáo, Diǎnbīng, Bīngcáo, Zéicáo, Yùncáo, Jìnfáng, Diǎnbīn, Qíshì, and Chēcáo, totaling thirteen Cáo,
are now missing from the remaining twelve Cáo.
Later, there were also the seven Cáo of Zhíbīng, Chángliú, Xíngyù, Chéngjú, Shuǐcáo, Yòuhù, and Mòcáo.
When Gāozǔ was Xiàng,
Zhōngbīng and Zhíbīng were combined into one Cānjūn,
though the Cáo remained two.
Currently, smaller Fǔ that do not appoint Chángliú Cānjūn
appoint Jìnfáng Cānjūn.
Shǔ Céngxiàng Zhūgě Liàng's Fǔ had Xíng Cānjūn.
Jìn Tàifù Sīmǎ Yuè's Fǔ also had Xíng Cānjūn and Jiān Xíng Cānjūn.
Later, the characters 'Zhǎng Jiān' were gradually added.
Appointment was as Cānjūnshì,
while the Fǔ's official document listed them as Xíng Cānjūn.
Since the late Jìn dynasty,
Cānjūnshì and Xíng Cānjūn each had separate appointments and official documents.
Below the official document for Xíng Cānjūn was that for Zhǎng Jiān Xíng Cānjūn.
Cānjūn Dūhù
was established in Jiāngzuǒ.
Originally, they all commanded battalions
and had retainers.
Now, they do not.
The Zhǎngshǐ and Sīmǎ of a Gōngfǔ
had a salary of one thousand Dàn (Shí).
The Cóngshì Zhōngláng
had six hundred Dàn.
The Dōngxī Cáo Yuàn
had four hundred Dàn.
Other Yuàn had three hundred Dàn.
The Shǔ had two hundred Dàn.
Tèjìn
was established during the Former Hàn dynasty.
Both the Former and Later Hàn, Wèi, and Jìn dynasties considered it an honorary title.
They followed the carriage and attire of their principal office
and had no subordinate officials or soldiers.
During the Yuánkāng reign of Jìn Huìdì, its rank was set below all Gōng (Dukes)
but above Piàojí Jiāngjūn.
Piàojí Jiāngjūn,
one person.
In the second year of Yuánshòu (119 BCE) of Hàn Wǔdì,
Huò Qùbìng was first appointed Piàojí Jiāngjūn.
The system in Hàn Xījīng (Western Capital) stipulated that
the Dàjiāngjūn and Piàojí Jiāngjūn ranked next to the Céngxiàng.
Chēqí Jiāngjūn,
one person.
In the first year of Hàn Wéndì (179 BCE),
Bó Zhāo was first appointed Chēqí Jiāngjūn.
Yú Huàn said:
"In the Wèi dynasty, the Chēqí served as Dūdū,
and their ceremonial status was equal to the Four Zhēng (Generals)."
"If not serving as Dūdū,
even if holding the Jié and subordinate to the Four Zhēng,
they were equivalent to the various generals with miscellaneous titles like Qiánhòu Zuǒyòu."
"If they were dismissed and returned to the rank of civil officials,
then their rank was next to the Sānsī."
In the Jìn and Sòng dynasties, the Chēqí and Wèi were no longer supervised by the Four Zhēng.
Wèi Jiāngjūn,
one person.
In the first year of Hàn Wéndì (179 BCE),
Sòng Chāng was first appointed Wèi Jiāngjūn.
These three titles (Chēqí, Wèi, Piàojí) ranked subordinate to the Sānsī.
In the third year of Jiànchū (78 CE) of Hàn Zhāngdì,
Chēqí Jiāngjūn Mǎ Fáng was first ordered to rank equally with the Sānsī.
Ranking equally with the Sānsī began from this point.
In the late Hàn dynasty, Fènwēi Jiāngjūn,
and in the Jìn Jiāngyòu (Eastern Jìn), Fúbō and Fǔguó Jiāngjūn
were all promoted and had ceremonial status equal to the Sānsī.
Since the Jiāngzuǒ (Eastern Jìn) period,
generals of Zhōng, Zhèn, Fǔ, and the Four Zhèn and above were sometimes promoted,
and other officials from Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū and Yòu Guānglù Dàfū and above were all granted ceremonial status equal to the Sānsī.
Those below this rank were not permitted.
Chíjié Dūdū (Controller with Imperial Credentials)
had no fixed number of appointees.
The Former Hàn dynasty dispatched envoys,
and it was then that the office of Chíjié first appeared.
In the early Jiànwǔ era of Guāngwǔ,
during campaigns to conquer the four directions,
the office of Dūjūn Yùshǐ (Supervising Military Censor) was temporarily established as a matter of expediency,
but it was abolished after the campaigns concluded.
In the Jiàn'ān era,
when Wèi Wǔ Dì served as Chancellor,
Dàjiàngjūn (General-in-Chief) was first dispatched to supervise the armies.
In the 21st year (216 CE),
upon returning from a campaign against Sūn Quán,
Xiàhóu Dūn supervising twenty-six armies is an example of this.
In the second year of Huángchū (221 CE) during Wèi Wén Dì's reign,
the office of Dūdū Zhū Zhōu Jūnshì (Supervisor of Military Affairs of Various Provinces) was first established,
sometimes concurrently holding the post of Cìshǐ (Provincial Governor).
In the third year (222 CE),
Shàngjūn Dàjiàngjūn Cáo Zhēn was appointed Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūnshì (Supervisor of All Military Affairs, Internal and External),
and granted a Jiǎhuángyuè (axe of authority),
thus taking overall command of all armies, both internal and external.
In the fourth year of Tàihé (230 CE) during Míng Dì's reign,
when Jìn Xuān Dì campaigned against Shǔ,
he was granted the additional title of Dà Dūdū (Grand Supervisor).
In the second year of Zhèngyuán (255 CE) during Gāoguìgōng's reign,
Jìn Wén Dì was appointed Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūn (Supervisor of All Armies, Internal and External),
and soon after was promoted to Dà Dūdū.
During the Jìn dynasty, Dūdū Zhū Jūn (Supervisor of All Armies) was considered the highest rank,
Jiān Zhū Jūn (Inspector of All Armies) was next,
and Dū Zhū Jūn (Supervisor of Armies) was the lowest.
Shǐ Chíjié (Envoy with Imperial Credentials) was the highest,
Chíjié (Bearer of Imperial Credentials) was next,
and Jiǎjié (Temporary Bearer of Imperial Credentials) was the lowest.
Shǐ Chíjié had the authority to execute officials of 2,000 shí salary or below;
Chíjié could execute people without official rank,
or if it was a military matter, they held the same authority as Shǐ Chíjié;
Jiǎjié could only execute those who violated military orders in military matters.
Since the Jìn moved to the left bank of the Jiāng (Yangtze River),
Dūdū Zhōngwài (Supervisor of Internal and External Affairs) became particularly important,
and only Wáng Dǎo held this position.
No subject of the Sòng dynasty held it.
Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng was granted a Jiǎhuángyuè.
A Jiǎhuángyuè
conferred the exclusive power to execute generals bearing credentials,
which was not an ordinary instrument for a subject.
Zhēngdōng Jiàngjūn (General Who Conquers the East),
one person.
In the third year of Chūpíng (192 CE) during Hàn Xiàn Dì's reign,
Mǎ Téng held this position.
Zhēngnán Jiàngjūn (General Who Conquers the South),
one person.
In the Jiànwǔ era of Hàn Guāngwǔ,
Cén Péng held this position.
Zhēngxī Jiàngjūn (General Who Conquers the West),
one person.
In the Jiànwǔ era of Hàn Guāngwǔ,
Féng Yì held this position.
Zhēngběi Jiàngjūn (General Who Conquers the North),
one person.
Yú Huàn said:
"The Four Zhēng Generals
were established by Wèi Wǔ Dì,
with a salary rank of 2,000 shí.
[一０]In the Huángchū era,
their rank was next to the Sān Gōng (Three Excellencies).
In the old Hàn system, the various Zhēng Generals were grouped with Piānpí and other miscellaneous titles."
Zhèndōng Jiàngjūn (General Who Guards the East),
one person.
In the late Latter Hàn dynasty,
Wèi Wǔ Dì held this position.
Zhènnán Jiàngjūn (General Who Guards the South),
one person.
In the late Latter Hàn dynasty,
Liú Biǎo held this position.
Zhènxī Jiàngjūn (General Who Guards the West),
one person.
In the third year of Chūpíng (192 CE) in the early Latter Hàn,
Hán Suì held this position.
Zhènběi Jiàngjūn (General Who Guards the North),
one person.
Zhōngjūn Jiàngjūn (General of the Central Army),
one person.
Hàn Wǔ Dì appointed Gōngsūn Áo to this position,
which was then a miscellaneous title.
Zhènjūn Jiàngjūn (General Who Suppresses the Army),
one person.
Wèi appointed Chén Qún to this position.
Fǔjūn Jiàngjūn (General Who Pacifies the Army),
one person.
Wèi appointed Sīmǎ Xuānwáng to this position.
The three titles of Zhōng, Zhèn, and Fǔ were comparable to the Four Zhèn Generals.
Āndōng Jiàngjūn (General Who Pacifies the East),
one person.
In the late Latter Hàn dynasty,
Táo Qiān held this position.
Ānnán Jiàngjūn (General Who Pacifies the South),
one person.
Ānxī Jiàngjūn (General Who Pacifies the West),
one person.
In the late Latter Hàn dynasty,
Duàn Wēi held this position.
Ānběi Jiàngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North),
one person.
Yú Huàn said:
"Zhènběi and the Four Ān Generals
were established in the Huángchū and Tàihé eras of Wèi."
Píngdōng Jiàngjūn (General Who Brings Peace to the East),
one person.
Píngnán Jiàngjūn (General Who Brings Peace to the South),
one person.
Píngxī Jiàngjūn (General Who Brings Peace to the West),
one person.
Píngběi Jiàngjūn (General Who Brings Peace to the North),
one person.
The Four Píng Generals
were established during the Wèi dynasty.
Zuǒ Jiàngjūn (General of the Left).
Yòu Jiàngjūn (General of the Right).
Qián Jiàngjūn (General of the Vanguard).
Hòu Jiàngjūn (General of the Rear).
The Zuǒ Jiàngjūn and below
were offices from the late Zhōu dynasty,
which Qín and Hàn both inherited.
They were abolished in the seventh year of Jiànwǔ (31 CE) by Guāngwǔ,
and re-established from the Wèi dynasty onwards.
Zhēnglǔ Jiàngjūn (General Who Conquers Barbarians),
in the Jiànwǔ era of Hàn Guāngwǔ,
Jì Zūn was first appointed to this position.
Guànjūn Jiàngjūn (General of Champion),
Chǔ Huái Wáng appointed Sòng Yì as Qīngzǐ Guànjūn.
The name Guànjūn
began from this.
In the Zhèngshǐ era of Wèi,
Wén Qīn was appointed Guànjūn Jiàngjūn and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ.
Fǔguó Jiàngjūn (General Who Protects the State),
Hàn Xiàn Dì appointed Fú Wán to this position.
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ (468 CE) during Sòng Tàizōng's reign,
it was changed to Fǔshī,
and later reverted to its original name in the second year of Yuánhuī (474 CE) during Fèi Dì's reign.
Lóngxiáng Jiàngjūn (General Soaring Dragon),
Jìn Wǔ Dì first appointed Wáng Jùn to this position.
[一ㄧ]
Dōng Zhōnglángjiàng (Central Commander of the East),
Hàn Líng Dì appointed Dǒng Zhuó to this position.
Nán Zhōnglángjiàng (Central Commander of the South),
in the Jiàn'ān era of Hàn Xiàn Dì,
Línzī Hóu Cáo Zhí held this position.
Xī Zhōnglángjiàng (Central Commander of the West).
Běi Zhōnglángjiàng (Central Commander of the North),
in the Jiàn'ān era of Hàn,
Líng Hóu Cáo Zhāng held this position.
Regarding all Four Zhōnglángjiàng,
Hé Chéngtiān said
they were all established by the Latter Hàn.
Jiànwēi Jiàngjūn (General Who Establishes Might),
in the Jiànwǔ era of Hàn Guāngwǔ,
Gěng Yǎn was appointed Jiànwēi Dàjiàngjūn (General-in-Chief Who Establishes Might).
[一二]Zhènwēi Jiàngjūn (General Who Manifests Might),
in the early Latter Hàn,
Sòng Dēng held this position.
Fènwēi Jiàngjūn (General Who Rouses Might),
in the Former Hàn dynasty,
Rèn Qiānqiū held this position.
Yángwēi Jiàngjūn (General Who Displays Might),
established by Wèi.
Guǎngwēi Jiàngjūn (General Who Extends Might),
established by Wèi.
Jiànwǔ Jiàngjūn (General Who Establishes Martial Prowess),
established by Wèi.
Zhènwǔ Jiàngjūn (General Who Manifests Martial Prowess),
in the late Former Hàn dynasty,
Wáng Kuàng held this position.
Fènwǔ Jiàngjūn (General Who Rouses Martial Prowess),
in the late Latter Hàn dynasty,
Lǚ Bù held this position.
Yángwǔ Jiàngjūn (General Who Displays Martial Prowess),
in the Jiànwǔ era of Guāngwǔ,
Mǎ Chéng held this position.
Guǎngwǔ Jiàngjūn (General Who Extends Martial Prowess),
established on the left bank of the Jiāng (Yangtze River) by Jìn.
Yīngyáng Jiāngjūn,
during the Jiàn'ān reign of the Hàn dynasty,
Wèi Wǔ appointed Cáo Hóng to this post.
Zhéchōng Jiāngjūn,
during the Jiàn'ān reign of the Hàn dynasty,
Wèi Wǔ appointed Yuè Jìn to this post.
Qīngchē Jiāngjūn,
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn appointed Gōngsūn Hè to this.
Yángliè Jiāngjūn,
during the Jiàn'ān reign,
was falsely granted to Gōngsūn Yuān.
Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn,
established by the Jìn dynasty south of the Yangtze River.
Cáiguān Jiāngjūn,
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn appointed Lǐ Xī to this.
Fúbō Jiāngjūn,
when Emperor Wǔ of Hàn campaigned against Nányuè,
this title was first established,
and Lù Bódé was appointed to it.
Língjiāng Jiāngjūn,
established by the Wèi dynasty.
From Língjiāng downward,

there were Xuānwēi, Míngwēi, Xiāngwēi, Lìwēi, Wēilì, Wēikòu, Wēilǔ, Wēiróng, Wǔwēi, Wǔliè, Wǔyì, Wǔfèn, Suíyuǎn, Suíbiān, Suíróng, Tǎokòu, Tǎolǔ, Tǎonán, Tǎoyí, Dàngkòu, Dànglǔ, Dàngnán, Dàngnì, Tiánkòu, Tiánlǔ, Tiánnán, Sǎoyí, Sǎokòu, Sǎolǔ, Sǎonán, Sǎonì, Lìwǔ, Lìfēng, Hǔwēi, Hǔyá, Guǎngyě, Héngyě, Piān Jiāngjūn, and Bí Jiāngjūn,
forty titles in total.
As for Wēilǔ,
Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn appointed Féng Jùn to this post.
〔一三〕Hǔyá,
Gài Yán was appointed to it,
as Hǔyá Dàjiāngjūn.
Héngyě,
Gěng Chún was appointed to it.
Dàngkòu,
during the Jiàn'ān reign of the Hàn dynasty,
Mǎn Chǒng held this post.
Hǔwēi,
Yú Jìn held this post.
The rest were either established by the Later Hàn or Wèi dynasties,
and currently, some are established and some are not.
From the Zuǒ Yòu Qián Hòu Jiāngjūn down to these forty titles,
only the four Zhōnglángjiāng each had one person,
the rest had no fixed number of personnel.
From Chējì downwards, for those who served as Cìshǐ or Dūdū and Yítóng Sānsī,
officials were appointed as if leading troops,
but for those only referred to as Dūdū and not Yítóng Sānsī,
no Cóngshì Zhōngláng was appointed;
one Gōngcáo was appointed,
who managed the clerks,
ranking above the Zhǔbù;
this was an official of the late Hàn dynasty.
In the Eastern Capital of Hàn, the Sīlì had a Gōngcáo Cóngshìshǐ,
similar to the Zhìzhōng of various prefectures,
named after them.
One Gōngcáo Cānjūn,
who assisted □ □ and ranked below Jìshì,
and above Hùcáo.
From Jiān downwards, no Zīyì or Jìshì were appointed,
the rest was the same.
Since Sòng Tàizōng,
even if imperial princes and imperial brothers were not Dūdū,
a Jìshì Cānjūn was still appointed.
For lesser general titles, when assigned to a grand prefecture's border defense to appoint subordinate officials,
a Zhǎngshǐ was also appointed,
the rest was the same.
Tàicháng,
one person.
When Shùn assumed the imperial throne,
he ordered Bó Yí to be Zòngzōng,
in charge of the three rites;
this was that office.
During the Zhōu dynasty, it was called Zōngbó,
which was the Spring Official,
in charge of the state's rites.
Qín changed it to Fèngcháng,
and Hàn followed.
In the sixth year of the middle period of Emperor Jǐng's reign,
it was renamed Tàicháng.
Yìng Shào said:
"Wishing the state to be grand and to exist perpetually,
hence the name Tàicháng."
The Former Hàn often appointed loyal, filial, respectful, and cautious marquises to this post;
the Later Hàn did not necessarily appoint marquises.
Bóshì,
Bān Gù said,
was a Qín official.
Historians investigate and note that
during the Six States period, there were often Bóshì,
who were in charge of communicating ancient and modern knowledge.
In the fifth year of Jiànyuán during Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's reign,
the Five Classics Bóshì were first established.
During the reigns of Xuān and Chéng,
the Five Classics schools gradually increased,
and one Bóshì was established for each classic.
By the Eastern Capital period, there were fourteen people in total.
For the Yì,
Shī, Mèng, Liángqiū, and Jīng schools;
for Shàngshū,
Ōuyáng and the greater and lesser Xiàhóu schools;
for Shī,
Qí, Lǔ, and Hán schools;
for Lǐ,
the greater and lesser Dài schools;
for Chūnqiū,
Yán and Yán schools: each had one Bóshì.
And one intelligent and authoritative person served as Jìjiǔ.
Wèi and the Western Jìn dynasty established nineteen people;
when the Jìn moved east of the river, they were initially reduced to nine people,
none of whom were known to specialize in any particular classic.
At the end of Emperor Yuán's reign,
one Bóshì each for the Yílǐ and Chūnqiū Gōngyáng were added,
making a total of eleven people.
Later, they were increased to sixteen people,
no longer divided by the Five Classics,
and were called Tàixué Bóshì.
Their rank was six hundred dàn of grain.
One Guózǐ Jìjiǔ,
two Guózǐ Bóshì,
ten Guózǐ Zhùjiào.
Zhōuyì, Shàngshū, Máoshī, Lǐjì, Zhōuguān, Yílǐ, Chūnqiū Zuǒshìzhuàn, Gōngyáng, and Gǔliáng each constituted one classic;
Lúnyǔ and Xiàojīng constituted one classic;
making a total of ten classics.
The Zhùjiào were assigned to manage these.
Guózǐ,
an old name from the Zhōu dynasty;
the Zhōu dynasty had the office of Shīshì,
which is the current Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
The Jìn dynasty initially re-established the Guózǐxué
to educate students,
and it was subordinate to the Tàixué.
Initially, the Jìn dynasty had fifteen Zhùjiào;
since the Jìn moved east of the river,
their number was reduced.
From the Sòng dynasty onwards, if no school was established,
only one Zhùjiào was appointed,
while the Jìjiǔ and Bóshì were always appointed.
Tàimiàolìng,
one person.
One Chéng.
Both established by the Former Hàn.
In the Western Capital, it was called Zhǎng;
in the Eastern Capital, it was called Lìng.
It commanded twenty-four Zhāiláng.
Míngtánglìng,
one person.
One Chéng.
The Chéng
was first established in the Eastern Capital of Hàn;
the Lìng
was established during Dàmíng of Sòng Shìzǔ's reign.
Tàizhùlìng,
one person.
One Chéng.
In charge of sacrificial rituals, reading invocations, and welcoming and sending off spirits.
Tàizhù,
an old Zhōu official.
The Western Capital of Hàn established Tàizhùlìng and Chéng;
in the first year of Tàichū during Emperor Wǔ's reign,
it was renamed Miàosì.
The Eastern Capital of Hàn changed it back to Tàizhù.
Tàishǐlìng,
one person.
One Chéng.
In charge of the three luminaries, auspicious and calamitous signs of times and days,
and presenting the new calendar at the end of the year.
Tàishǐ,
an old official from the Three Dynasties;
during the Zhōu dynasty, in charge of establishing the six regulations of the state,
correcting the year,
to order affairs and distribute the calendar to the states.
There was also the Féngxiàngshì,
in charge of astronomical orders;
Bǎozhāngshì,
in charge of astronomy.
The current Tàishǐ
combines the three Zhōu offices of Tàishǐ, Féngxiàng, and Bǎozhāng.
The Western Capital of Hàn called it Tàishǐlìng.
The Eastern Capital of Hàn had two Chéng,
one of whom was in the Língtái.
Tàiyuèlìng,
one person.
One Chéng.
In charge of all musical affairs.
During the Zhōu dynasty, it was Dàsīyuè.
The Western Capital of Hàn called it Tàiyuèlìng.
The Eastern Capital of Hàn called it Dàyǔyuèlìng.
Wèi reverted to Tàiyuèlìng.
Línglìng,
one person for each mausoleum.
An old Hàn official.
Chénghuánglìng,
one person.
In charge of the imperial carriages and sedan chairs, and all horses.
Established during the Wèi dynasty.
From Bóshì to Chénghuánglìng,
all were subordinate to the Tàicháng.
The Grand Master of Splendid Felicity (Guānglùxūn)
has one incumbent.
An Assistant (Chéng) has one incumbent.
*Guāng*
means "bright."
*Lù*
means "rank."
*Xūn*
means "merit."
During the Qín dynasty, it was called the Administrator of Palace Gentlemen (Lángzhōnglìng).
The Hàn dynasty followed this.
In the first year of Tàichū (太初), in the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
its name was changed to Grand Master of Splendid Felicity (Guānglùxūn).
It was in charge of the gentlemen (láng) of the Three Bureaus (Sānshǔ).
The gentlemen (láng) stood guard with halberds at the palace gates.
The Grand Master of Splendid Felicity (Guānglùxūn) resided within the Forbidden Palace, like the Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ).
If there was a prison case outside the palace gate,
it was called the External Department of Splendid Felicity (Guānglù Wàibù).
The Grand Master of Splendid Felicity (Guānglùxūn) presided over the three libations at suburban sacrifices.
From the Wèi and Jìn dynasties onwards,
the Grand Master of Splendid Felicity (Guānglùxūn) no longer resided within the Forbidden Palace,
nor were there any gentlemen (láng) of the Three Bureaus (Sānshǔ).
Only for imperial audiences at the outer palace
would they attend by name.
a tally would be issued to the Grand Master of Splendid Felicity (Guānglù) to impose a ban.
Lifting the ban was done in the same manner.
The ban (jìnzhǐ)
meant that one could not enter the palace or ministries,
because the Grand Master of Splendid Felicity (Guānglù) was in charge of the palace gates.
The palace gates
are still under their jurisdiction to this day.
In the second year of Xīngníng (興寧), in the reign of Emperor Āi of Jìn,
the office of Grand Master of Splendid Felicity (Guānglùxūn) was abolished
and merged with that of the Minister of Works (Sītú).
In the first year of Níngkāng (寧康), in the reign of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
it was reinstated.
In the Eastern Hàn capital, among the gentlemen (láng) of the Three Bureaus (Sānshǔ), those who distinguished themselves in the four categories of conduct
would annually recommend two outstanding talents (màocái)
and two of the "four conducts" (sìxíng).
Even after the Three Bureaus (Sānshǔ) and their gentlemen (láng) were abolished,
the Grand Master of Splendid Felicity (Guānglùxūn) still continued to recommend the "four conducts" (sìxíng) as before,
filled by sons of aristocratic families.
The Three Bureaus (Sānshǔ) were
the Bureau of Five Officers (Wǔguān Shǔ), the Left Bureau (Zuǒshǔ), and the Right Bureau (Yòushǔ).
Each had a Commander of Palace Gentlemen (Zhōnglángjiàng) to oversee it.
Filial and Incorrupt (Xiàolián) candidates were recommended from the commanderies to fill positions as gentlemen (láng) of the Three Bureaus (Sānshǔ).
Those fifty years of age or older
belonged to the Bureau of Five Officers (Wǔguān),
while the others were divided between the Left and Right Bureaus.
In total, there were four ranks: Commander of Palace Gentlemen (Zhōngláng), Consultative Gentleman (Yìláng), Attendant Gentleman (Shìláng), and Gentleman of the Interior (Lángzhōng).
There was no fixed number of incumbents,
sometimes reaching as many as ten thousand.
Grand Master of Splendid Felicity of the Left (Zuǒguānglù Dàfū),
Grand Master of Splendid Felicity of the Right (Yòuguānglù Dàfū).
These two Grand Masters (Dàfū)
were established in the early Jìn dynasty.
The Grand Master of Splendid Felicity (Guānglù Dàfū)
was called Grand Master of the Center (Zhōng Dàfū) during the Qín dynasty.
In the first year of Tàichū (太初), in the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
its name was changed to Grand Master of Splendid Felicity (Guānglù Dàfū).
In the early Jìn dynasty, Left and Right Grand Masters of Splendid Felicity (Zuǒyòu Guānglù Dàfū) were added,
while the Grand Master of Splendid Felicity (Guānglù Dàfū) remained as before.
The Grand Master of Splendid Felicity (Guānglù Dàfū) had a silver seal and a blue ribbon.
Those of greater importance were given a gold seal and a purple ribbon,
and were then called Golden Purple Grand Master of Splendid Felicity (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū).
Traditionally, their salary rank was comparable to two thousand *dàn* of grain.
The Grand Master for Scattered Gentlemen (Zhōngsàn Dàfū)
was established by Wáng Mǎng,
and the Later Hàn dynasty followed this.
In the Former Hàn, all Grand Masters (Dàfū) had no fixed number of incumbents
and were in charge of discussions and deliberations.
In the Later Hàn, there were three Grand Masters of Splendid Felicity (Guānglù Dàfū),
twenty Grand Masters of the Center (Zhōng Dàfū),
and thirty Grand Masters for Scattered Gentlemen (Zhōngsàn Dàfū).
From the Wèi dynasty onwards, there was again no fixed number of incumbents.
From the Left Grand Master of Splendid Felicity (Zuǒguānglù Dàfū) downwards,
they were for supporting the aged and sick,
without specific duties.
The Grand Master for Scattered Gentlemen (Zhōngsàn)
had a salary rank of six hundred *dàn* of grain.
The Commandant of the Guards (Wèiwèi)
has one incumbent.
Two Assistants (Chéng).
They were in charge of the palace gates and garrisoned troops,
a Qín dynasty office.
In the early Jǐngchū (景初) reign of Hàn,
it was changed to Commander of Palace Gentlemen (Zhōng Dàfū Lìng).
In the *hòu* first year,
it was restored to Commandant of the Guards (Wèiwèi).
During the Jìn dynasty south of the Yangtze (Jiāng Yòu), they were in charge of metallurgy and casting,
overseeing thirty-nine Metallurgical Prefects (Yělìng),
with 5,350 households.
All foundries were north of the Yangtze,
and south of the Yangtze, there were only the Méigēn and Yětáng foundries,
both belonging to Yángzhōu (揚州),
and not to the Commandant of the Guards (Wèiwèi).
The Commandant of the Guards (Wèiwèi) was not established during the Eastern Jìn (Jiāng Zuǒ).
It was reinstated in the first year of Xiàojiàn (孝建), in the reign of Emperor Shìzǔ of Sòng.
Traditionally there was one Assistant (Chéng).
Emperor Shìzǔ added another Assistant.
The Minister of Justice (Tíngwèi)
has one incumbent.
An Assistant (Chéng) has one incumbent.
They were in charge of criminal law and punishment.
All prison cases had to be presented to the court,
with the meaning of sharing them with the multitude.
Military and prison affairs were under the same system,
hence it was called Minister of Justice (Tíngwèi).
When Shùn assumed the imperial throne,
Gāoyáo (咎繇) served as the Minister of Justice (Shì),
which was this same responsibility.
During the Zhōu dynasty, the Grand Minister of Justice (Dà Sīkòu) was the Autumn Officer (Qiūguān),
in charge of national penalties.
In Qín, it was the Minister of Justice (Tíngwèi).
In the sixth year of Zhōng (中), in the reign of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
its name was changed to Grand Judge (Dàlǐ).
In the fourth year of Jiànyuán (建元), in the reign of Emperor Wǔ,
it was restored to Minister of Justice (Tíngwèi).
In the second year of Yuánshòu (元壽), in the reign of Emperor Āi,
it was again changed to Grand Judge (Dàlǐ).
In the early Eastern Hàn capital,
it was again restored to Minister of Justice (Tíngwèi).
The Chief Justice (Tíngwèi Zhèng)
has one incumbent.
The Minister of Justice's Supervisor (Tíngwèi Jiān)
has one incumbent.
The Chief Justice (Zhèng) and Supervisor (Jiān) were both Qín dynasty offices.
Originally there were Left and Right Supervisors.
Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn abolished the Right,
still referring to the Left Supervisor.
From the Wèi and Jìn dynasties onwards,
they simply referred to the Supervisor (Jiān).
The Minister of Justice's Reviewer (Tíngwèi Píng)
has one incumbent.
In the third year of Dìjié (地節), in the reign of Emperor Xuān of Hàn,
Left and Right Reviewers were first established.
Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn abolished the Right,
still referring to the Left Reviewer.
From the Wèi and Jìn dynasties onwards,
they simply referred to the Reviewer (Píng).
The Chief Justice (Zhèng), Supervisor (Jiān), and Reviewer (Píng) all treated the Minister of Justice (Tíngwèi Qīng) with the courtesy due to a superior.
The Chief Justice (Zhèng) and Supervisor (Jiān) had a salary rank of one thousand *dàn* of grain,
the Reviewer (Píng) six hundred *dàn* of grain.
The Minister of Justice's Law Scholar (Tíngwèi Lǜ Bóshì)
has one incumbent.
This was established by Emperor Wǔ of Wèi when he first founded the state of Wèi.
The Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dà Sīnóng)
has one incumbent.
An Assistant (Chéng) has one incumbent.
They were in charge of supplying grains and six types of livestock for meals.
When Shùn assumed the imperial throne,
he ordered Qì (棄) to be Master of Agriculture (Hòujì),
which was this same responsibility.
In Zhōu, it was the Grand Steward (Tàifǔ).
In Qín, it was the Administrator of Grain (Zhìsù Nèishǐ).
In the *hòu* first year of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn,
its name was changed to Grand Administrator of Agriculture (Dànónglìng).
In the first year of Tàichū (太初), in the reign of Emperor Wǔ,
its name was changed to Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dà Sīnóng).
Towards the end of Emperor Āi of Jìn's reign,
it was abolished and merged with the Chief Hydraulic Engineer (Dūshuǐ).
It was reinstated during Emperor Xiàowǔ's reign.
In the Hàn dynasty, there were two Assistants (Chéng).
From Wèi onwards, there was one.
The Prefect of the Grand Granary (Tàicāng Lìng)
has one incumbent.
An Assistant (Chéng) has one incumbent.
This was a Qín dynasty office.
From the Jìn dynasty south of the Yangtze (Jiāng Zuǒ) onwards,
there were also one Assistant (Chéng) each for the Eastern Granary (Dōngcāng) and the Shítou Granary.
The Prefect for Processed Grains (Guānlìng)
has one incumbent.
An Assistant (Chéng) has one incumbent.
They were in charge of pounding and selecting imperial rice.
This was established in the Eastern Hàn capital.
*Guān* (官)
means "to select."
It means to select rice to make it refined.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's (司馬相如) *Book of Feng and Shan* says,
"A single stalk with six ears of grain in the kitchen."
The Prefect for the Imperial Fields (Jìtián Lìng)
has one incumbent.
An Assistant (Chéng) has one incumbent.
They were in charge of cultivating the fields for the ancestral temples, altars of soil, and grain,
which in Zhōu was the Field Master (Diànshī).
Emperor Wén of Hàn first established the imperial fields
and appointed one Prefect (Lìng) and one Assistant (Chéng).
The Eastern Hàn capital and Wèi did not establish this.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn reinstated it in the tenth year of Tàishǐ (泰始).
It was abolished in the Eastern Jìn (Jiāng Zuǒ).
Emperor Tàizǔ of Sòng reinstated it during the Yuánjiā (元嘉) era.
From the Prefect of the Grand Granary (Tàicāng) to the Prefect for the Imperial Fields (Jìtián Lìng),
all belonged to the Grand Minister of Agriculture (Sīnóng).
Shǎofǔ,
one person.
Chéng, one person.
They manage the imperial clothing and personal effects.
This was a Qín official,
which Hàn continued.
They managed the restricted funds to supply private expenses,
hence the name Shǎofǔ.
At the end of Emperor Āi of Jìn's reign,
it was abolished and merged with the Dānyáng Yǐn.
It was re-established during Emperor Xiàowǔ's era.
Zuǒ Shàngfāng Lìng and Chéng, one each.
Yòu Shàngfāng Lìng and Chéng, one each.
They both managed the manufacture of military weapons.
This was a Qín official,
which Hàn continued.
In Zhōu, it was known as the Yùfǔ.
In Jìn, to the east of the river (Jiāngzuǒ), there were the Zhōng Shàngfāng, Zuǒ Shàngfāng, and Yòu Shàngfāng.
Since the time of the Eastern Jìn (Jiāngzuǒ),
there was only one Shàngfāng.
When Sòng Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he assigned the production department of the prime minister's office (xiàngfǔ) to the court (tái),
〔一五〕calling it the Zuǒ Shàngfāng,
while the original department was called the Yòu Shàngfāng.
He also assigned the fine crafts department of the prime minister's office to the court,
and named an official to head it, appointing one Lìng,
two Chéng,
subordinate to the Ménxià.
During Emperor Shìzǔ's Dàmíng period,
it was renamed Yùfǔ,
with one Lìng,
and one Chéng.
The Yùfǔ
in the Hàn dynasties was the official in charge of palace maids making intimate clothing and mending and washing them.
Wèi and Jìn still retained this position,
but it was abolished in the Eastern Jìn.
In the early reign of the later deposed emperor,
the Yùfǔ was abolished,
and the Zhōngshǔ was established,
subordinate to the Yòu Shàngfāng.
In Eastern Hàn, among the subordinate officials of the Tàipú, there was a Kǎogōng Lìng,
who was in charge of weapons such as bows, crossbows, swords, and armor.
Once completed, they were transferred by the Zhí Jīnwú to the Wǔkù,
and also managed the weaving of sashes and other miscellaneous crafts.
〔一六〕The Shàngfāng Lìng was only in charge of making imperial swords, sashes, and various recreational and valuable objects.
Thus, the Kǎogōng Lìng is like today's Shàngfāng,
and the Shàngfāng Lìng is like today's Zhōngshǔ.
Dōngyě Lìng,
one person.
Chéng, one person.
Nányě Lìng,
one person.
Chéng, one person.
Hàn had iron officials.
Jìn established a Lìng,
who managed the workers and the smelting,
subordinate to the Wèiwèi.
Since the Eastern Jìn,
the Wèiwèi was abolished,
and it was transferred to the Shǎofǔ.
Although the Sòng dynasty established the Wèiwèi,
the Yě was still subordinate to the Shǎofǔ.
In the southern regions, some commanderies and counties with iron mines either established a Yě Lìng
or a Chéng;
most of these were established by Wú.
Píngzhǔn Lìng,
one person.
Chéng, one person.
Managed dyeing.
This was a Qín official,
which Hàn continued.
Hàn was subordinate to the Sīnóng;
it is unknown in which era it became subordinate to the Shǎofǔ.
When Sòng Shùndì ascended the throne,
to avoid using the imperial name,
it was renamed Rǎnshǔ.
Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng,
one person.
Chéng, one person.
Managed earth and wood construction projects.
During the Qín dynasty, the Jiàngzuò Shǎofǔ was established,
which Hàn continued.
In the sixth year of Emperor Jǐng's middle reign,
it was renamed Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng.
In the second year of Emperor Guāngwǔ's Jiànwǔ Zhōngyuán period, it was abolished,
〔一七〕and the Yèzhě took charge of it.
In the first year of Emperor Zhāng's Jiànchū period, it was re-established.
Since the Jìn dynasty,
it was established when there were projects,
and abolished when there were none.
Dàhónglú,
managed introducing and officiating the conferment of titles to various kings.
During the Qín dynasty, it was the Diǎnkè.
In the sixth year of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn's middle reign,
it was renamed Dàxíng Lìng.
In the first year of Emperor Wǔ's Tàichū period,
it was renamed Dàhónglú.
Hóng
means "great".
Lú
means "to arrange" or "to display".
It was initially abolished in the Eastern Jìn (Jiāngzuǒ).
It was temporarily established when there were matters,
and abolished once the matters were concluded.
Tàipú,
managed carriages and horses.
Established by King Mù of Zhōu,
Qín continued it.
In Zhōu officialdom, the Xiàorén managed horses,
the Jīnchē managed carriages,
and the Tàipú was established
to combine their responsibilities.
In the Eastern Jìn, it was sometimes established and sometimes abolished.
Since the Sòng dynasty, it has not been established.
During suburban sacrifices, the Tàipú was temporarily appointed to hold the reins,
and abolished once the ritual was concluded.
Tàihòu Sān Qīng,
one person each.
Yīng Shì's record of Hàn officials states:
"The Wèiwèi and Shǎofǔ
were Qín officials;
the Tàipú was established by Emperor Chéng of Hàn.
All were named according to the empress dowager's palace,
and ranked above the regular Qīng.
They were vacant when there was no empress dowager."
Wèi changed the Hàn system,
ranking them below the Jiǔ Qīng.
Jìn restored the old system,
ranking them above the similarly titled Qīng.
Dàchángqiū,
the empress's minister.
Established when there was an empress,
and abolished when there was none.
During Qín, it was the Jiàngxíng.
In the sixth year of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn's middle reign,
it was renamed Dàchángqiū.
Wéi Yào said:
"Chángqiū,
because the empress is a 'yin' official,
