and autumn is the beginning of 'yin',
taking its enduring end,
wishes for its longevity."
From Tàicháng to Chángqiū,
all established Gōngcáo, Zhǔbù, and Wǔguān.
In the Eastern Hàn, various commanderies had Wǔguān Yuàn,
and this name was adopted.
Under the Hàn system, all Qīng and Yǐn ranked at Zhōng Èrqiān Shí,
and Chéng at Yīqiān Shí.
Shàngshū
was an ancient official.
When Shùn (舜) assumed the imperial throne,
he appointed Lóng (龍) as Nàyán (納言),
which was effectively this role.
The Zhōu (周) official Sīhuì (司會),
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) said,
was like the Shàngshū (尚書) of today.
In the Qín (秦) era, the Shǎofǔ (少府) dispatched four officials to preside over the issuance of documents in the palace,
hence they were called Shàngshū (尚書).
Shàng (尚) here means to preside.
In the early Hàn (漢) dynasty, there were Shàngguān (尚冠), Shàngyī (尚衣), Shàngshí (尚食), Shàngyù (尚浴), Shàngxí (尚席), and Shàngshū (尚書),
known as the Liùshàng (六尚) (Six Stewards).
During the Warring States period, there were already officials like Shàngguān (尚冠) and Shàngyī (尚衣).
In the Qín (秦) dynasty, there were Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令), Shàngshū Púshè (尚書僕射), and Shàngshū Céng (尚書丞).
By the early Hàn (漢), they were all subordinate to the Shǎofǔ (少府).
In the Eastern Hàn (漢東京), they were still considered civil subordinates.
Ancient people valued military officials,
and those skilled in archery were put in charge of affairs,
hence the title Púshè (僕射).
Púshè (僕射) means
one who serves in archery matters.
In the Qín (秦) era, there were Zuǒ Cáo Zhū Lì (左右曹諸吏) (Left and Right Departments of Various Officials),
whose positions had no specific duties.
Generals, grandees, and all below them could be appointed to this office.
In the reign of Hàn Wǔdì (漢武帝),
the Zuǒ Cáo Zhū Lì (左右曹諸吏) were tasked with jointly adjudicating matters submitted to the Shàngshū (尚書).
〔一八〕When Zhāodì (昭帝) ascended the throne,
Huò Guāng (霍光) held the affairs of the Shàngshū (尚書);
in the early reign of Chéngdì (成帝),
Wáng Fèng (王鳳) recorded the affairs of the Shàngshū (尚書).
In the Eastern Hàn (漢東京), whenever an emperor ascended the throne,
a Tàifù (太傅) was appointed
to record the affairs of the Shàngshū (尚書),
and this office was abolished upon his death.
In the reign of Jìn Kāngdì (晉康帝),
Hé Chōng (何充) declined the recording appointment, stating in his memorial:
"In the Xiánkāng (咸康) period,
three recording positions were established separately.
Wáng Dǎo (王導) recorded one of them,
while Xún Sōng (荀崧) and Lù Yè (陸曄) each recorded six items."
If so, it seems there were twenty-four items,
or if there were only twelve items,
then Xún (荀) and Lù (陸) each recorded six items,
but what then did Dǎo (導) oversee?
If Dǎo (導) had overall recording authority,
and Xún (荀) and Lù (陸) managed parts,
then it could not be said that Dǎo (導) recorded one of them.
Thereafter, whenever two recording positions were established,
it was said that each managed six items,
which again suggests there were only twelve items.
As for the twelve items,
it is unknown what they all were.
In the Jiāng Yòu (江右) of Jìn (晉), there were four recording positions,
meaning four people participated in recording.
Zhāng Huá (張華) in Jiāng Yòu (江右) and Yǔ Liàng (庾亮) in Jiāng Zuǒ (江左) were both involved in seven items of the Shàngshū (尚書),
but it is also unknown what these matters were.
Later, Hé Chōng (何充) resigned from recording
and again participated in the Shàngshū (尚書).
The office of Lù Shàngshū (錄尚書) held comprehensive authority.
Wáng Sù (王肅), in his commentary on the Shàngshū (尚書),
on "Nà yú Dà Lù" (納于大麓),
said:
"Yáo (堯) appointed Shùn (舜) to a position of high honor,
making him broadly manage the myriad affairs of government."
〔一九〕All generals with exalted titles and provincial governors
were allowed to appoint officials to the various departments,
but were not allowed to dismiss them or grant them imperial credentials (jié 節).
During the Xiàojiàn (孝建) period of Sòng Shìzǔ (宋世祖),
desiring to prevent external usurpation of power,
the recording office was abolished.
It was re-established at the end of Dàmíng (大明).
Thereafter, it was sometimes established and sometimes abolished.
In the fourth year of Jiàn'ān (建安) of Hàn Xiàndì (漢獻帝),
Zhí Jīn Wú Róng Hé (執金吾榮郃) was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè (尚書左僕射),
and Wèi Zhēn (衞臻) was appointed Yòu Púshè (右僕射).
The separate establishment of the two Púshè (僕射)
began from this time.
In the fourth year of Jiànshǐ (建shǐ) of Hàn Chéngdì (漢成帝),
the Shàngshū (尚書) were first established,
with four members,
and the Cchéng (丞) (assistants) were also increased to four.
Among the departments (cáo 曹) of the Shàngshū (尚書), one was called Chángshì Cáo (常侍曹),
which managed affairs of the dukes and ministers;
the second was Èrqiānshí Cáo (二千石曹),
which managed affairs of the two-thousand-pic officials in commanderies and states;
the third was Mín Cáo (民曹),
which managed memorials from officials and common people;
the fourth was Kè Cáo (客曹),
which managed affairs of foreign countries and barbarians.
Guāngwǔ (光武) divided the Èrqiānshí Cáo (二千石曹) into two,
and also divided the Kè Cáo (客曹) into Nán Zhǔkè Cáo (南主客曹) and Běi Zhǔkè Cáo (北主客曹),
and renamed Chángshì Cáo (常侍曹) to Lì Cáo (吏曹),
making a total of six Shàngshū (尚書) departments.
Two Céng (丞) (assistants) were reduced,
leaving only the Zuǒ (左) and Yòu (右) Céng (丞).
Yīng Shào (應劭)'s Hàn Guān (漢官) states:
"The Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) and Zuǒ Céng (左丞)
held overall command and discipline,
overseeing everything.
The Púshè (僕射) and Yòu Céng (右丞)
were in charge of granting money and grain.
The two Sāngōng Shàngshū (三公尚書)
managed the annual collection of taxes nationwide;
the Lì Cáo (吏曹) managed selections and sacrificial rites;
the Èrqiānshí Cáo (二千石曹) managed water, fire, bandits, lawsuits, and criminal laws;
the Kè Cáo (客曹) managed meetings with Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡) peoples,
the emperor's ceremonial procession,
and guarding the emperor;
the Mín Cáo (民曹) managed repairs, public works, salt ponds, and imperial parks.
The Lì Cáo (吏曹) was a crucial office,
and many gained rapid promotion from it."
Thus, the department names and duties in the late Hàn (漢) differed from those in Guāngwǔ (光武)'s time.
In the Wèi (魏) dynasty, there were five departments of Shàngshū (尚書): Lìbù (吏部), Zuǒmín (左民), Kè Cáo (客曹), Wǔbīng (五兵), and Dùzhī (度支).
In the early Jìn (晉) dynasty, there were six departments of Shàngshū (尚書): Lìbù (吏部), Sāngōng (三公), Kè Cáo (客曹), Jiàbù (駕部), Túntián (屯田), and Dùzhī (度支).
In the second year of Xiánníng (咸寧) of Wǔdì (武帝),
the Jiàbù Shàngshū (駕部尚書) was abolished;
in the fourth year, it was re-established.
During the Tàikāng (太康) period,
there were six Shàngshū (尚書) departments: Lìbù (吏部), Diànzhōng (殿中), Wǔbīng (五兵), Tián Cáo (田曹), Dùzhī (度支), and Zuǒmín (左民).
In the reign of Huìdì (惠帝),
there was also a Yòumín Shàngshū (右民尚書).
The Shàngshū (尚書) offices were limited to six departments,
so it is unknown which department was abolished at this time.
In Jiāng Zuǒ (江左), there were Cíbù (祠部), Lìbù (吏部), Zuǒmín (左民), Dùzhī (度支), and Wǔbīng (五兵),
totaling five departments of Shàngshū (尚書).
In the early reign of Sòng Gāozǔ (宋高祖),
Dūguān Shàngshū (都官尚書) was added.
If there was a Yòu Púshè (右僕射),
then no Cíbù Shàngshū (祠部尚書) was established.
In the second year of Dàmíng (大明) of Shìzǔ (世祖),
two Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) were established,
and the Wǔbīng Shàngshū (五兵尚書) was abolished.
〔二０〕Later, one Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) was re-established.
In the first year of Shēngmíng (昇明) of Shùndì (順帝),
the Wǔbīng Shàngshū (五兵尚書) was again established.
The Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令)
was responsible for the overall balance of government;
the Púshè (僕射) and Shàngshū (尚書)
individually managed the various departments.
The Zuǒ Púshè (左僕射) oversaw the Diànzhōng (殿中) and Zhǔkè (主客) departments;
the Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) oversaw the Lìbù (吏部), Shāndìng (刪定), Sāngōng (三公), and Bǐbù (比部) departments;
the Cíbù Shàngshū (祠部尚書) oversaw the Cíbù (祠部) and Yícáo (儀曹) departments;
the Dùzhī Shàngshū (度支尚書) oversaw the Dùzhī (度支), Jīnbù (金部), Cāngbù (倉部), and Qǐbù (起部) departments;
the Zuǒmín Shàngshū (左民尚書) oversaw the Zuǒmín (左民) and Jiàbù (駕部) departments;
the Dūguān Shàngshū (都官尚書) oversaw the Dūguān (都官), Shuǐbù (水部), Kùbù (庫部), and Gōnglùn (功論) departments;
〔二一〕the Wǔbīng Shàngshū (五兵尚書) oversaw the Zhōngbīng (中兵) and Wàibīng (外兵) departments.
In the past, there were Qíbīng (騎兵), Biébīng (別兵), and Dūbīng (都兵),
hence they were called Wǔbīng (五兵) (Five Militias).
The five Shàngshū (尚書), two Púshè (僕射), and one Lìng (令)
were known as the Bāzuò (八坐) (Eight Sits).
If ancestral temples or palaces were to be constructed,
a Qǐbù Shàngshū (起部尚書) was established,
and abolished once the work was completed.
When Emperor Chéng of Hàn established the four Shàngshū,
there was no text mentioning the establishment of Láng.
According to Hàn protocols,
there were four Shàngshū Láng.
One was in charge of the Xiongnú Chányú camp department;
one was in charge of the Qiāng and Yí officials and people;
one was in charge of households and cultivated land;
one was in charge of wealth, silk, and tribute.
The Xiongnú Chányú,
during the reign of Emperor Xuān,
secured the borders and submitted internally.
By Emperor Chéng's reign,
the Chányú had returned to the Northern Court.
One Láng was in charge of the Xiongnú Chányú camp department.
〔二二〕Therefore, the establishment of Láng was likely during the time of Emperor Guāngwǔ,
and the Xiongnú they were in charge of
were the Southern Chányú.
Hàn official records state
that thirty-six Láng were appointed,
but it is unknown which emperor increased the number of staff.
Thus, one Shàngshū would oversee six Láng.
They were responsible for drafting documents
and initiating drafts of affairs.
Initially, they served as Lángzhōng,
and after a full year, they became Shìláng.
The Shàngshū office was located inside the Jiànlǐ Mén.
When Shàngshū Láng were on duty,
the office provided them with quilts of green silk and white damask,
or sometimes of cotton floss.
They were supplied with curtains, felt mats, and a pillow with a central opening.
The Tàiguān provided food,
and the Tāngguān provided cakes, pastries, and various cooked fruits.
Each Shàngshū was given one Bóshǐ
and two female attendants,
all selected for their uprightness and beauty.
They held incense burners,
guarded clothing,
and presented matters in the Míngguāng Diàn.
The palace walls were painted with white lead,
depicting ancient sages and martyrs.
The ground was colored with cinnabar,
called the Dānchí.
Shàngshū Láng held "chicken tongue" incense in their mouths,
so that when they presented matters and responded,
their breath would be fragrant.
When presenting matters, they would bow in salute to the Huángmén Shìláng.
The Huángmén Shìláng would acknowledge with "I have heard,"
and then they would depart.
The five seasonal robes worn by the Son of Heaven were bestowed upon the Shàngshū Lìng and Pú.
As for the Chéng and Láng, they were monthly granted a pair of red-handled large brushes
and one cake of Yúmí ink.

During the Wèi dynasty, there were the Diànzhōng, Lìbù, Jiàbù, Jīnbù, Yúcáo, Bǐbù, Nánzhǔkè, Cíbù, Dùzhī, Kùbù, Nóngbù, Shuǐbù, Yícáo, Sāngōng, Cāngbù, Míncáo, Èrqiānshí, Zhōngbīng, Wàibīng, Biébīng, Dūbīng, Kǎogōng, Dìngkē,
a total of twenty-three Láng.
In the second year of Qīnglóng, due to military affairs,
Shàngshū Lìng Chén Jiǎo proposed the establishment of Dūguān and Qíbīng two Cáo Láng,
making a total of twenty-five Cáo.

During the Western Jìn dynasty, there were the Zhíshì, Diànzhōng, Cíbù, Yícáo, Lìbù, Sāngōng, Bǐbù, Jīnbù, Cāngbù, Dùzhī, Dūguān, Èrqiānshí, Zuǒmín, Yòumín, Yúcáo, Túntián, Qǐbù, Shuǐbù, Zuǒzhǔkè, Yòuzhǔkè, Jiàbù, Chēbù, Kùbù, Zuǒzhōngbīng, Yòuzhōngbīng, Zuǒwàibīng, Yòuwàibīng, Biébīng, Dūbīng, Qíbīng, Zuǒshì, Yòushì, Běizhǔkè, Nánzhǔkè, making thirty-four Cáo Láng.
Later, Yùncáo was also established,
making a total of thirty-five Cáo.
In the early Eastern Jìn,
there were no Zhíshì, Yòumín, Túntián, Chēbù, Biébīng, Dūbīng, Qíbīng, Zuǒshì, Yòushì, Yùncáo, ten Cáo Láng,
and each of Zhǔkè and Zhōngwàibīng only had one Láng,
leaving seventeen Cáo.
〔二三〕Since Kāng and Mù,
there were also no Yúcáo and Èrqiānshí two Láng,
still having the Diànzhōng, Cíbù, Lìbù, Yícáo, Sāngōng, Bǐbù, Jīnbù, Cāngbù, Dùzhī, Dūguān, Zuǒmín, Qǐbù, Shuǐbù, Zhǔkè, Jiàbù, Kùbù, Zhōngbīng, Wàibīng, eighteen Cáo Láng.
Later, Zhǔkè, Qǐbù, and Shuǐbù were abolished,
leaving fifteen Cáo.
In the early Southern Sòng dynasty under Emperor Gāozǔ,
four Cáo Láng were added: Qíbīng, Zhǔkè, Qǐbù, Shuǐbù,
making a total of nineteen Cáo.
In the tenth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Tàizǔ,
four Cáo Láng were again abolished: Yícáo, Zhǔkè, Bǐbù, Qíbù.
In the eleventh year,
they were all re-established.
In the eighteenth year,
Sāndìng Cáo Láng was added and deleted,
ranking above Zuǒmín Cáo.
This was likely the Dìngkē Láng of the Wèi dynasty.
In the thirtieth year,
Gōnglùn Láng was again established,
ranking below Dūguān
and above Sāndìng.
During Emperor Tàizōng's reign,
Qíbīng was abolished.
Currently, there are a total of twenty Cáo Láng.
Sāngōng and Bǐbù are in charge of laws and regulations.
Dùzhī is in charge of calculations.
Zhī means
branching out.
Dù means
measurement.
Dūguān is in charge of military and judicial affairs.
The responsibilities of the other Cáo
are as their names suggest.
According to Hàn regulations,
from the Gōng, Qīng, Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng downwards,
upon encountering a Shàngshū Lìng, Pú, Chéng, or Láng,
all had to move their carriages aside and avoid them.
Only after the Tái officials passed
were they allowed to leave.
Today, when Shàngshū officials attend court or depart,
pedestrians are forbidden,
which is still in accordance with that system.
Hàn also stipulated that
Chéng and Láng, when seeing a Shàngshū,
should address him as "Míngshí."
Láng, when seeing the two Chéng,
should address them as "Zuǒjūn" and "Yòujūn."
Below Láng were the Dūlìngshǐ, Lìngshǐ, Shūlìngshǐ, and Shūlìgàn.
In the Eastern Hàn, there were eighteen Shàngshū Lìngshǐ.
In the early Jìn, there were one hundred and twenty Zhènglìngshǐ
and one hundred and thirty Shūlìngshǐ.
From Jìn to the present,
the numbers have either decreased or increased,
making a precise statement difficult.
Hàn protocols included Céngxiàng Lìngshǐ.
Lìngshǐ were likely officials of the Former Hàn.
The Western Jìn had a Shàngshū Dūlìngshǐ named Zhū Dàn,
indicating that the Dūlìngshǐ have a long history.
Their departmental responsibilities were similar to those of the Shàngshū.
During the Western Jìn, the Bāzuò Chéng Láng
would attend court at the Dūzuò in the morning and evening.
In the Eastern Jìn, they only attended in the morning.
When the Bāzuò Chéng Láng were first appointed,
they would all gather at the Dūzuò
to exchange greetings.
When transferred,
they would again dissolve the exchange.
This was an old Hàn system.
Now, only the Bāzuò dissolve the exchange;
the Chéng and Láng no longer dissolve the exchange.
The Shàngshū Lìng received one thousand *dàn* of grain (as salary),
the Púyè Shàngshū six hundred *dàn*,
and the Chéng and Láng four hundred *dàn*.
Wǔkù Lìng,
one person.
In charge of military equipment.
A Qín official.
By the two Hàn dynasties,
it belonged to the Zhíjīnwǔ.
In the early Jìn, the Zhíjīnwǔ was abolished,
and since then, it has been subordinate to the Shàngshū Kùbù.
Chēfǔ Lìng,
one person.
Chéng, one person.
A Qín official.
During the two Hàn, Wèi, and Jìn, both were subordinate to the Tàipú.
After the Tàipú was abolished,
it was subordinate to the Shàngshū Jiàbù.
Shànglín Lìng,
one person.
Chéng, one person.
In the Western Hàn Shànglín, there were eight Chéng, twelve Wèi, and ten Chíjiān.
The Chéng and Wèi were subordinate to the Shuǐhéng Dūwèi.
〔二四〕The Chíjiān were subordinate to the Shǎofǔ.
In the Eastern Hàn, it was called Shànglínyuàn Lìng and Chéng, one each,
subordinate to the Shǎofǔ.
In the Eastern Jìn, it was absent.
In the third year of Dàmíng of Emperor Shìzǔ of Sòng, it was re-established,
subordinate to the Shàngshū Diànzhōng Cáo and Shǎofǔ.
Cáiguān Jiāngjūn,
one person.
Sīmǎ, one person.
In charge of artisan and construction affairs.
The Hàn Zuǒyòuxiào Lìng
had similar responsibilities.
The Wèi Yòuxiào also established a Cáiguān Xiàowèi,
in charge of all timber affairs in the empire.
In the Eastern Jìn, the Cáiguān Xiàowèi was renamed Cáiguān Jiāngjūn,
and the Zuǒxiào Lìng was abolished.
Currently, Cáiguān is subordinate to the Shàngshū Qǐbù and Lǐngjūn.
Shìzhōng [Grand Regular Attendant],
four persons.
They were in charge of presenting memorials,
attending directly on the Emperor’s left and right,
and offering counsel and suggestions.
When the imperial carriage [fǎjià] went out,
one Shìzhōng would carry the imperial seal on foot and accompany the carriage.
They managed all matters within the palace gates.
The "Chángbó" [常伯] mentioned in the chapter where Zhōugōng [周公] admonished King Chéng [成王] on establishing governance
was precisely this position.
The Shìzhōng were originally secretaries [shǐ] to the Qin [秦] prime minister.
Five persons were sent to go back and forth in the East Wing of the palace to present memorials,
hence they were called Shìzhōng.
During the Western Hàn [漢] dynasty, there was no fixed number for this position;
it sometimes reached several dozens of people.
They attended in the Forbidden Palace,
dividing the duties of managing the Emperor's clothing and personal items,
down to intimate utensils like chamber pots [hǔzǐ].
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ [武帝],
Kǒng Ānguó [孔安國] served as Shìzhōng.
Because he was a scholar,
he was specially permitted to manage the Emperor's spittoon,
which was considered an honor by the court.
Those who served for a long time and rose through the ranks became Púshè [僕射].
During the Eastern Hàn [漢] dynasty, they were subordinate to the Shàofǔ [少府],
and still had no fixed number.
They were in charge of attending on the left and right of the Emperor,
assisting in various matters,
and answering queries.
When the imperial carriage went out,
one knowledgeable person would carry the Imperial Seal of the State [chuánguóxǐ]
and hold the "Sword for Slashing the White Serpent" [zhǎnbáishéjiàn],
accompanying the carriage;
the rest would ride on horseback,
following behind the Emperor's carriage.
During the reign of Emperor Guāngwǔ [光武],
the Púshè was changed to Jìjiǔ [祭酒].
During the Hàn dynasty,
they resided in the Forbidden Palace together with the eunuchs [zhōngguān].
In the time of Emperor Wǔ,
the Shìzhōng Mǎng Hélúo [莽何羅] attempted a rebellion with a weapon.
Because of this, Shìzhōng were thereafter moved outside the Forbidden Palace,
only entering when there was business,
and departing once their duties were finished.
When Wáng Mǎng [王莽] seized power,
Shìzhōng were again permitted to reside
together with the eunuchs.
In the Yuánhé [元和] era of Emperor Zhāng [章帝],
the Shìzhōng Guō Jǔ [郭舉] had an affair with a concubine in the imperial harem [hòugōng],
and startled the Emperor by drawing his ceremonial dagger.
Guō Jǔ was executed,
and Shìzhōng were again moved outside as a result.
Since the Wèi [魏] and Jìn [晉] dynasties,
four persons were appointed,
but these were additional appointments and not part of the main establishment.
Their rank was equivalent to a Two-Thousand-Picul official [èrqiānshí].
Textual Notes
Gazetteer 30, Officials Down
Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng [給事黃門侍郎] [Attendant at the Yellow Gates],
four persons.
Together with the Shìzhōng, they managed all matters within the palace gates.
When the Emperor conducted suburban sacrifices or held court from the imperial dais,
one of them would hold the banner [huī].
The "Table of Hundred Officials" [Bǎiguānbiǎo] of Hàn states that Qín [秦] had Jǐshì Huángmén [給事黃門],
with no fixed number,
who were in charge of attending on the Emperor's left and right.
Hàn followed this system.
During the Eastern Hàn dynasty, they were called Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng,
also with no fixed number,
in charge of attending on the Emperor's left and right,
and communicating between the inner and outer courts.
When various kings [zhūwáng] had an audience,
they would escort the kings to their seats.
Yìng Shào [應劭] said:
“Every evening they bowed towards the Qīngsuǒmén [青瑣門],
hence they were called Xīláng [夕郎] [Evening Attendants].”
The Historian comments that Liú Xiàng [劉向] wrote in a letter to his son Xīn [歆]:
“The Huángménláng [黃門郎] is a prominent position.”
Thus, during the Former Hàn [漢] dynasty, they were already called Huángmén Shìláng.
Dǒng Bā's [董巴] "Hànshū" [漢書] states:
“The Forbidden Gate is called Huángtà [黃闥],
and inner palace officials [zhōngrén] managed it,
hence the title Huángmén Lìng [黃門令].”
Therefore, the Huángménláng served within the Huángtà,
which is why they were called Huángménláng.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties, there were four persons,
with a rank of Six Hundred Picul [liùbǎishí].
Gōngchē Lìng [公車令] [Director of the Public Carriage Office],
one person.
In charge of receiving memorials.
Qín had the Gōngchē Sīmǎ Lìng [公車司馬令],
subordinate to the Wèiwèi [衛尉],
and Hàn followed this.
They managed the Southern Gate Tower [quēmén] of the palace.
All memorials from officials and common people,
tributes from the four directions,
and those summoned to the public carriage [gōngchē],
were under their charge.
Since the Jìn [晉] moved east of the Yangtze River [Jiāngzuǒ],
they were simply called Gōngchē Lìng.
Tàiyī Lìng [太醫令] [Director of the Imperial Medical Office],
one person.
Chéng [丞] [Assistant Director], one person.
During the Zhōu [周] dynasty, they were Physicians [yīshī];
Qín called them Tàiyī Lìng;
during the two Hàn dynasties, they were subordinate to the Shàofǔ.
Tàiguān Lìng [太官令] [Director of the Imperial Provisioning Office],
one person.
Chéng [丞] [Assistant Director], one person.
During the Zhōu dynasty, they were Chefs [shànfū];
Qín called them Tàiguān Lìng;
during the Hàn dynasty, they were subordinate to the Shàofǔ.
Huá liú Chéng [驊騮丞] [Assistant Director of the Imperial Stables],
one person.
During the Western Hàn dynasty, they were Lóngmǎ Zhǎng [龍馬長] [Chief of Dragon Horses];
during the Eastern Hàn dynasty, they were Wèiyāng Lìng [未央令] [Director of the Weiyang Palace];
Wèi called them Huá liú Lìng [驊騮令] [Director of the Imperial Stables].
From Gōngchē Lìng to this point,
they were all subordinate to the Shìzhōng.
Sǎnjì Chángshì [散騎常侍] [Palace Regular Attendant],
four persons.
In charge of attending on the left and right of the Emperor.
Qín established Sǎnjì [散騎], and also established Zhōng Chángshì Sǎnjì [中常侍散騎],
both riding behind the Emperor's carriage.
The Zhōng Chángshì were permitted to enter the Forbidden Palace.
None had a fixed number,
and both were additional appointments.
In the early Eastern Hàn dynasty, Sǎnjì were abolished,
and Zhōng Chángshì were then exclusively filled by eunuchs.
In the early Huángchū [黃初] era of Emperor Wén [文帝] of Wèi,
Sǎnjì were re-established
and combined with Zhōng Chángshì,
called Sǎnjì Chángshì.
Mèng Dá [孟達] was the first to be appointed to this position.
Those who served for a long time and rose through the ranks became Jìjiǔ Sǎnjì Chángshì [祭酒散騎常侍],
with a rank equivalent to a Two-Thousand-Picul official.
Tōngzhí Sǎnjì Chángshì [通直散騎常侍] [Directly Communicating Palace Regular Attendant],
four persons.
At the end of the Wèi dynasty, there were also Sǎnjì Chángshì who were outside the regular establishment.
Emperor Wǔ [武帝] of Jìn appointed two persons to communicate directly with the Sǎnjì Chángshì,
hence they were called Tōngzhí Sǎnjì Chángshì.
After the Jìn moved east of the Yangtze River, five persons were appointed.
Yuánwài Sǎnjì Chángshì [員外散騎常侍] [Supernumerary Palace Regular Attendant],
established at the end of the Wèi dynasty,
with no fixed number.
Sǎnjì Shìláng [散騎侍郎] [Palace Attendant],
four persons.
Established at the beginning of Wèi together with Sǎnjì Chángshì.
During Wèi and Jìn, Sǎnjì Chángshì and Shìláng
jointly reviewed memorials to the Shàngshū [尚書].
This practice was abolished after the Jìn moved east of the Yangtze River.
Tōngzhí Sǎnjì Shìláng [通直散騎侍郎] [Directly Communicating Palace Attendant],
four persons.
Initially, Emperor Wǔ of Jìn established four Yuánwài Sǎnjì Shìláng.
Emperor Yuán [元帝] appointed two persons to communicate directly with the Sǎnjì Shìláng,
hence they were called Tōngzhí Sǎnjì Shìláng.
Later, the number was increased to four.
Yuánwài Sǎnjì Shìláng [員外散騎侍郎] [Supernumerary Palace Attendant],
established by Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
with no fixed number.
Jǐshìzhōng [給事中] [Attendant-in-ordinary],
no fixed number.
Established during the Western Hàn dynasty.
In charge of responding to imperial queries,
their position was second only to the Zhōng Chángshì.
Abolished during the Eastern Hàn dynasty,
re-established during the Wèi dynasty.
Fèng Cháoqǐng [奉朝請] [Officials Summoned for Court Audience],
no fixed number,
and not considered an official position.
During the Eastern Hàn dynasty, when the Sāngōng [三公], imperial relatives by marriage [wàiqī], imperial clan members [zōngshì], and feudal lords [zhūhóu] were dismissed from their posts,
many were given the Fèng Cháoqǐng status.
Fèng Cháoqǐng simply meant
being summoned to imperial court audiences.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn also appointed imperial clan members and imperial relatives by marriage as Fèngchē Dūwèi [奉車都尉], Fùmǎ Dūwèi [駙馬都尉], and Qí Dūwèi [騎都尉],
and also as Fèng Cháoqǐng.
When Emperor Yuán was King of Jìn,
he made his Cānjūn [參軍] into Fèngchē Dūwèi,
his Yuàn [掾] and Shǔ [屬] into Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
and his Xíng Cānjūn [行參軍] and Shèrén [舍人] into Qí Dūwèi,
all with Fèng Cháoqǐng status.
Later, Fèngchē Dūwèi and Qí Dūwèi were abolished,
only Fùmǎ Dūwèi and Fèng Cháoqǐng remained.
Since the Yǒngchū [永初] era,
because the selection for Fèng Cháoqǐng was varied,
only those who married princesses were appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
The three Dūwèi were all established by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
In the early Xiàojiàn [孝建] era,
Fèng Cháoqǐng was abolished.
The Fùmǎ Dūwèi and the three Dūwèi had a rank equivalent to a Two-Thousand-Picul official.
The Grand Chancellor of the Secretariat,
one person.
The Superintendent of the Secretariat,
one person.
The Gentlemen of the Secretariat,
four persons.
The Palace Attendants of the Secretariat for Communication,
four persons.
When Emperor Wǔ of Hàn feasted in the rear palace,
he first made eunuchs preside over the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat,
calling them the Palace Attendants of the Secretariat,
and established a Grand Chancellor and a Palace Prefect.
During Emperor Yuán’s time,
the Grand Chancellor Hóng Gōng
and the Palace Prefect Shí Xiǎn
wielded power and managed affairs,
their influence overshadowing both the court and the provinces.
Emperor Chéng changed the title of Palace Attendant of the Secretariat to Palace Attendant Chief,
and abolished the Palace Prefect.
The Palace Attendant Chief was abolished in the Eastern Hàn capital.
However, there was still a Palace Attendant Chief for the palace eunuchs,
which was not their proper function.
When Emperor Wǔ of Wèi was King,
he established a Secretariat Director,
who presided over the memorials to the throne,
which was also his responsibility.
At the beginning of the Huángchū era of Emperor Wén,
this was changed to Grand Chancellor of the Secretariat,
and a Superintendent was also established,
along with the Gentlemen for Communication,
who were next to the Gentlemen of the Yellow Gate.
After the Gentlemen of the Yellow Gate had already signed off on the documents,
the Gentlemen for Communication would then present them
to the Emperor for review, reading, and approval.
The Jìn dynasty changed this title to Gentlemen of the Secretariat,
with a quota of four persons.
At the beginning of the Eastern Jìn,
the Gentlemen of the Secretariat were changed to Gentlemen for Communication,
but soon reverted to Gentlemen of the Secretariat.
At the beginning of the Jìn, one Palace Attendant [shèrén]
and one Communicator [tōngshì] were established.
At the beginning of the Eastern Jìn,
the Palace Attendant and Communicator were combined and called Palace Attendant for Communication,
in charge of presenting memorials and documents.
Later, the Communicator was abolished,
and the Secretariat assigned one Gentleman of the Secretariat to serve in the Western Palace,
also in charge of imperial edicts.
At the beginning of the Sòng dynasty, Palace Attendants for Communication were again established,
and the responsibilities of the Gentlemen of the Secretariat became lighter.
The Palace Attendants served inside the palace chambers,
subordinate to the Secretariat.
Below them were the Principal Clerks,
originally using military officials,
but the Sòng dynasty changed to using civil officials.
The Superintendent of the Imperial Library,
one person.
The Assistant of the Imperial Library,
one person.
The Gentlemen of the Imperial Library,
four persons.
In the second year of Yánxī, during the reign of Emperor Huán of Hàn,
the Superintendent of the Imperial Library was established.
This is confirmed by Huángfǔ Guī’s letter to Zhāng Huàn, which says:
"What is the news from my cousin, the Secretary [mìshū]?"
Thus it is.
Yìng Shào’s Hàn Guān says:
"One Superintendent of the Imperial Library,
with a salary of six hundred shí."
Later abolished.
When Emperor Wǔ of Wèi was King of Wèi,
he established a Director of the Imperial Library and an Assistant of the Imperial Library.
The Imperial Library presided over the memorials to the throne.
At the beginning of the Huángchū era of Emperor Wén,
the Grand Chancellor of the Secretariat was established,
presiding over the memorials to the throne,
and the Director of the Imperial Library was changed to Superintendent.
Later, when Hè Zhēn was to be made Assistant of the Imperial Library,
the Imperial Library already had an Assistant,
so Zhēn was made Assistant of the Imperial Library of the Right.
Later abolished.
In charge of literary works, maps, and records.
The duties of the Outer Scribe in the Zhōu dynasty, who was in charge of the records of the four directions and the books of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
were exactly this.
The collections of maps and records in the Western Hàn capital
were stored in the Tiānlù, Shíqú, Lántái, Shíshì, Yángé, and Guǎngnèi repositories.
In the Eastern Hàn, the books were in the Dōngguān.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn combined the Imperial Library with the Secretariat,
abolished the Superintendent,
and called the Assistant the Assistant of the Secretariat and Imperial Library.
Emperor Huì later re-established one Compiler [zhùzuò láng]
and eight Assistant Compilers,
in charge of national history.
In the Zhōu dynasty, the Left Scribe recorded events and
the Right Scribe recorded speeches;
this was their function.
In the Eastern Hàn, the maps and records were in the Dōngguān,
so famous scholars and great academics
were made Compilers in the Dōngguān
to compile national history.
The title of Compiler [zhùzuò]
began from this point.
In the Wèi dynasty, they were subordinate to the Secretariat.
During Emperor Wǔ of Jìn’s reign,
Móu Zhēng was a Compiler of the Secretariat.
In the Yuánkāng era,
they were reassigned to the Imperial Library,
and later became a separate department,
but still subordinate to the Imperial Library.
The Compiler was called the Grand Compiler,
exclusively in charge of historical duties.
Under the Jìn system,
when an Assistant Compiler first took office,
he had to compile a biography of one famous minister.
At the beginning of the Sòng clan’s reign,
when the imperial court was first established,
there were no joint compilers,
so this system was abolished.
The General Who Leads the Army,
one person.
In charge of the inner army.
The Hàn dynasty had Northern and Southern Armies,
guarding the capital.
Emperor Wǔ established the Colonel of the Central Encampment,
in charge of the Northern Army camps.
Guāngwǔ abolished the Colonel of the Central Encampment
and established the Central Inspector of the Northern Army,
supervising the camps of the Five Colonels.
When Emperor Wǔ of Wèi was Prime Minister,
the Prime Minister’s office established its own General Who Leads the Army,
which was not a Hàn official position.
When Emperor Wén ascended to the throne of King of Wèi,
Wèi first established the General Who Leads the Army,
in charge of the Five Colonels, Central Encampment, and Wǔwèi—three camps.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn initially abolished it,
and made the Central Army General Yáng Hù command the two guards, the Front, Rear, Left, and Right Elite Cavalry—seven army camps,
which were the duties of the General Who Leads the Army.
After Hù was promoted and dismissed,
the Central Inspector of the Northern Army was re-established.
The Central Inspector of the Northern Army had one Assistant.
In the Yǒngjiā era of Emperor Huái,
the title was changed to Central General Who Leads the Army.
In the first year of Yǒngchāng of Emperor Yuán,
it was again changed to Central Inspector of the Northern Army.
Soon after, it reverted to General Who Leads the Army.
In Emperor Chéng’s reign,
it was again made a Central Inspector,
and Táo Huí held this position.
Soon after, it reverted to General Who Leads the Army.
The General Who Leads the Army still has the Superintendent of the Southern Army.
The General Who Protects the Army,
one person.
In charge of the outer army.
During the Qín dynasty, there was the Commandant Who Protects the Army,
and the Hàn dynasty followed this.
Chén Píng was the Central Commandant Who Protects the Army,
protecting all the generals.
However, it was then changed from Commandant to Central Commandant.
In the fourth year of Yuánshòu of Emperor Wǔ,
the Commandant Who Protects the Army was made subordinate to the Grand Marshal,
and at that time, it was again a Commandant.
In the "Biography of Lǐ Guǎng" in the Hàn Shū,
Lǐ Guǎng was the General of Elite Cavalry,
subordinate to the General Who Protects the Army.
Presumably, the General Who Protects the Army protected all generals.
In the first year of Yuánshòu of Emperor Āi,
the Commandant Who Protects the Army was renamed Grand Judge.
In the first year of Yuánshǐ of Emperor Píng,
it was renamed Commandant Who Protects the Army.
It was abolished in the Eastern Hàn.
Bān Gù was the Grand General’s Protector of the Army,
subordinate to the General’s headquarters,
not a formal Hàn court position.
When Emperor Wǔ of Wèi was Prime Minister,
he appointed Hán Hào as Protector of the Army
and Shǐ Huàn as General Who Leads the Army,
which were not Hàn official positions.
In the twelfth year of Jiàn'ān,
the Protector of the Army was changed to Central Protector of the Army,
and the General Who Leads the Army to Central General Who Leads the Army,
and a Chief Clerk and Marshal were established.
At the beginning of the Wèi dynasty, the Protector of the Army was retained,
in charge of selecting military officials,
and was subordinate to the General Who Leads the Army,
but in the Jìn dynasty, it was not.
In the first year of Yǒngchāng of Emperor Yuán of Jìn,
the Protector of the Army was abolished and combined with the General Who Leads the Army.
In the second year of Tàiníng of Emperor Míng,
it was re-established.
In Wèi and the Eastern Jìn, the General Who Leads the Army and the General Who Protects the Army each commanded their own camp soldiers;
since the Eastern Jìn,
the General Who Leads the Army no longer had separate camps,
but generally commanded the two guards, the elite cavalry, and all other camps;
the General Who Protects the Army still had its own camps.
Those of higher rank among the General Who Leads the Army and General Who Protects the Army were called General Who Leads the Army and General Who Protects the Army,
while those of lower rank were called Central General Who Leads the Army and Central Protector of the Army.
Their subordinates included a Chief Clerk, a Marshal, a Merit Officer, a Chief Recorder, and five officers.
When ordered to lead an expedition,
military advisors were appointed.
Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Left Guard),
one person.
Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Right Guard),
one person.
The two Weì Jiāngjūn were in charge of the palace guards and camp soldiers.
The Two Hàn and Weì dynasties did not establish these positions.
When Emperor Wén of Jìn was Xiàngguó,
the Xiàngguó's office established a Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn.
At the beginning of Emperor Wǔ's reign,
the Zhōngwèi was divided to establish Zuǒyòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
Yáng Xiù was made Zuǒwèi,
and Zhào Xù was made Yòuwèi.
The two Weì on the south bank of the Yangtze River had Chángshǐ, Sīmǎ, Gōngcáo, and Zhǔbù;
those on the north bank did not have Chángshǐ.
Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (General of Agile Cavalry).
In the sixth year of Yuánguāng reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Lǐ Guǎng was Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
In the Weì dynasty, it was established as Nèijūn (Inner Army),
with camp soldiers,
and those with high merit presided over them.
Initially, there were Sīmǎ, Gōngcáo, and Zhǔbù,
but these were later abolished.
Yóují Jiāngjūn (General of Roaming Cavalry).
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Hán Shuō was Yóují.
These were the six armies.
Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Left Army).
Yòujūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Right Army).
Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Front Army).
Hòujūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Rear Army).
During the reign of Emperor Míng of Weì,
there was a Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn;
thus, Zuǒjūn was a Weì official position.
At the beginning of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn's reign,
Qiánjūn and Yòujūn were established.
In the eighth year of Tàishǐ,
Hòujūn was also established.
These were the four armies.
Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng (Left Central Cavalier Commander).
Yòu Zhōnglángjiàng (Right Central Cavalier Commander).
These were Qín official positions,
which Hàn adopted.
Together with Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng, they commanded the Sānshǔ Láng.
The Weì dynasty had no Sānshǔ Láng,
but still established these positions.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn abolished them.
Emperor Shìzǔ of Sòng re-established them during the Dàmíng period.
Túnqí Xiàowèi (Colonel of Garrison Cavalry).
Bùbīng Xiàowèi (Colonel of Infantry).
Yuèqí Xiàowèi (Colonel of Vietnamese Cavalry).
Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi (Colonel of Chángshuǐ).
Shèshēng Xiàowèi (Colonel of Shooting by Sound).
The five colonels were all established by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
Túnqí and Bùbīng were in charge of garrisoning soldiers at the gates of the Shànglínyuàn;
Yuèqí was in charge of the Yue people who came to surrender,
thus making them cavalry;
another explanation is that it referred to their superior talent and strength.
Chángshuǐ was in charge of the Hú cavalry of Chángshuǐ and Xuānqǔ.
Chángshuǐ
was the name of a Hú tribe.
The Hú cavalry were garrisoned below the Xuānqǔ observatory.
Weí Yào said:
"Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi
commanded Hú cavalry,
close to Chángshuǐ,
hence the name.
Chángshuǐ
is probably the name of a small river in Guānzhōng."
Shèshēng was in charge of "shooting by sound" soldiers,
who shot upon hearing a sound,
hence the name.
At the beginning of Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn's reign, Túnqí was changed to Xiāoqí,
and Yuèqí to Qīngjīn.
In the fifteenth year of Jiànwǔ,
they reverted to their old names.
The five colonels in the Eastern Hàn capital
were in charge of palace guards.
From Yóujī to the five colonels,
during the Weì, Jìn, and up to the Jìn on the south bank of the Yangtze River,
they initially still commanded camp soldiers,
and Sīmǎ, Gōngcáo, and Zhǔbù were all established;
later they were abolished.
The two Zhōnglángjiàng originally did not command camps.
The Wǔyíng Xiàowèi (Colonels of the Five Camps)
had a rank of two thousand dàn.
Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng (Central Cavalier Commander of the Tiger Guards).
The Zhōu official system had Hǔbēnshì.
In the third year of Jiànruán of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
he first began to travel in disguise,
selecting strong and capable men to carry weapons and escort him,
meeting them at various gates,
hence the name Qímén (Gate of Rendezvous).
There was no fixed number,
sometimes up to a thousand people.
In the first year of Yuánshǐ of Emperor Píng,
they were renamed Hǔbēn Láng,
and a Zhōnglángjiàng was established to command them.
Hǔbēn was formerly written as Hǔbēn (跑),
meaning running like a tiger.
When Wáng Mǎng assisted in government,
because there was an ancient valiant warrior Mèng Bēn,
he changed bēn (跑) to bēn (賁).
Their rank was comparable to two thousand dàn.
Róngcóng Púyè (Attendant Officer of Supernumerary Retainers).
In the Eastern Hàn capital, there was a Zhōnghuángmén Róngcóng Púyè,
which was not their proper function.
The Weì dynasty adopted the name and established Róngcóng Púyè.
Yǔlín Jiān (Supervisor of Feathered Forest Guards).
In the first year of Tàichū of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Jiànzhāng Yíngqí were first established,
also in charge of escorting and following Qímén;
later they were renamed Yǔlínqí,
and a Lìng and a Céng were established.
Emperor Xuān ordered a Zhōnglángjiàng and a Qí Dūwèi to supervise the Yǔlín,
called Yǔlín Zhōnglángjiàng.
The Eastern Hàn also established Yǔlín Zuǒjiān and Yǔlín Yòujiān,
which remained unchanged until the Weì dynasty.
Jìn abolished Yǔlín Zhōnglángjiàng,
and also abolished one Jiān,
leaving only one Jiān.
From Hǔbēn to Yǔlín,
these were the three generals.
Emperor Āi abolished them.
At the beginning of Yǒngchū of Emperor Gāozǔ of Sòng,
they were re-established.
Those on the south bank of the Yangtze River commanded camp soldiers,
those on the north bank no longer had camp soldiers.
Yǔlín Jiān had a rank of six hundred dàn.
Jīshè Jiāngjūn (General of Massed Archers).
Qiángnǔ Jiāngjūn (General of Strong Crossbows).
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn appointed Lù Bódé as Qiángnǔ Xiàowèi,
and Lǐ Jǔ as Qiángnǔ Jiāngjūn.
Emperor Xuān appointed Xǔ Yánshòu as Qiángnǔ Jiāngjūn.
Qiángnǔ Jiāngjūn became a miscellaneous title in the Eastern Hàn.
There was no Jīshè from the Former Hàn to the Weì.
In the tenth year of Tàikāng of Jìn,
the Shè Yíng (Archery Camp) and Nǔ Yíng (Crossbow Camp) were established,
and Jīshè and Qiángnǔ Jiāngjūn were appointed to oversee them.
From Xiāoqí to Qiángnǔ Jiāngjūn,
initially one person was appointed to each position;
since Tàishǐ of Emperor Tàizōng of Sòng,
many obtained these positions through military merit,
and now there is no longer a fixed number.
Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn (General of the Palace Interior).
Diànzhōng Sīmǎ Dū (Supervisor of Palace Interior Cavalry Commanders).
During Emperor Wǔ of Jìn's reign,
the palace guards
were called Sānbù Sīmǎ (Cavalry Commanders of the Three Divisions).
These two officials were established,
subordinated to the Zuǒ and Yòu Weì.
Initially, on the south bank of the Yangtze River,
there were ten people.
During court audiences and banquets,
the generals wore military attire,
standing directly on the left and right;
at night, when opening the city gates,
they held the Báihǔ Fān (White Tiger Banner) to supervise.
During the Tàiyuán period of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn,
a re-selection was made,
and people from prominent clans were appointed.
At the beginning of Yǒngchū of Emperor Gāozǔ of Sòng,
the number was increased to twenty people.
Those who exceeded the quota
were called Diànzhōng Yuánwài Jiāngjūn and Yuánwài Sīmǎ Dū.
Later, there was no longer a fixed number.
Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn (General of Martial Guards),
no fixed number.
Initially, King Weì first established Wǔwèi Zhōnglángjiàng.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
it was changed to Wèijiāngjūn,
in charge of the forbidden army,
like the current two Weì,
which was not its original duty.
The Jìn clan did not always establish it.
During the Dàmíng period of Emperor Shìzǔ of Sòng,
it was re-established,
taking over the duties of Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn,
comparable to Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng.
Wǔqí Chángshì (Mounted Attendant-in-ordinary),
no fixed number.
An official position in the Western Hàn capital.
When the emperor went hunting,
they often accompanied him to shoot fierce beasts.
The Later Hàn, Weì, and Jìn did not establish it.
During the Dàmíng period of Emperor Shìzǔ of Sòng,
it was re-established.
Comparable to Fèng Cháoqǐng.
The Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
one person.
〔一０〕They were in charge of impeaching those who violated the law.
During the Qín dynasty, the Yùshǐ Dàfū had two Cénɡ.
〔一一〕One was called the Yùshǐ Cénɡ,
the other was called the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
The documents and records of the palace's Lántái Bìmìshū were kept there,
and the Zhōngchéng resided in it.
Externally, they supervised the Bù Cìshǐ;
internally, they led the Shìyùshǐ.
They received memorials from Gōngqīng,
and impeached officials by investigating cases according to regulations.
At that time, the Zhōngchéng also received memorials,
so it seems they had their own specific duties.
In the first year of Suīhé of Emperor Chéng,
the Yùshǐ Dàfū was renamed the Dàsīkōng,
and a Zhǎngshǐ was appointed,
but the official duties of the Zhōngchéng remained unchanged.
In the second year of Jiànpíng of Emperor Āi,
it was restored to Yùshǐ Dàfū.
In the second year of Yuánshòu,
it was restored to Dàsīkōng.
However, the Zhōngchéng went out to be the head of the Yùshǐ Tái,
and was named the Yùshǐ Zhǎngshǐ.
Guāngwǔ reverted to calling it Zhōngchéng,
and it was again subordinate to the Shǎofǔ.
During the time of Emperor Xiàn,
the Yùshǐ Dàfū was re-established,
and one Zhǎngshǐ was appointed independently,
no longer leading the Zhōngchéng.
In the Eastern Hàn dynasty, when the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng met a Shàngshū Cénɡ Láng,
the Zhōngchéng would stop their carriage, hold their tablet, and bow,
while the Cénɡ Láng would remain seated in their carriage and merely raise a hand in greeting.
It is unknown when this system was abolished.
On the 25th of each month, the Zhōngchéng
would patrol the white walls of the palace.
Historians note that the Hàn Zhì states the Zhí Jīnwú patrolled the palace city three times each month,
suspecting that the Zhí Jīnwú was abolished,
and this duty was merged with the Zhōngchéng.
The Zhōngchéng held a rank of one thousand dàn.
The Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ
was in charge of impeaching officials of rank six and above.
Emperor Xuān of Hàn made decisions from his private residence,
ordering two Yùshǐ to manage documents,
hence they were called Zhìshū Yùshǐ.
In the Eastern Hàn dynasty, those skilled in law served in this position.
When doubtful cases from across the empire were deliberated,
they would apply the law to determine right and wrong.
From Wèi and Jìn onwards,
they divided responsibilities among the various departments previously managed by the Shìyùshǐ,
similar to the two Cénɡ of the Shàngshū.
The Shìyùshǐ,
in Zhōu, were the Zhùxià Shǐ.
The Zhōu Guān had Yùshǐ,
who were in charge of administering orders,
which was also their duty.
Qín established Shìyùshǐ,
and Hàn continued the practice.
Both Hàn dynasties had fifteen members.
They were in charge of investigating and reporting illegal activities,
receiving memorials from Gōngqīng,
and impeaching those who made errors or transgressions.
There were five departments in total:
the first was the Lìng Cáo,
in charge of laws and ordinances;
the second was the Yìn Cáo,
in charge of carving seals;
the third was the Gōng Cáo,
in charge of fasts and sacrifices;
the fourth was the Wèi Mǎ Cáo,
in charge of official horses;
the fifth was the Chéng Cáo,
in charge of guarding the imperial carriage.
Wèi appointed eight Yùshǐ,
and had a Zhìshū Cáo,
in charge of expenditure and transport,
and a Kèdì Cáo,
in charge of performance evaluation;
the other departments are unknown.
The Western Jìn dynasty had the Lì Cáo, Kèdì Cáo, Zhíshì Cáo, Yìn Cáo, Zhōng Dūdū Cáo, Wài Dūdū Cáo, Méi Cáo, Fújié Cáo, Shuǐ Cáo, Zhōnglěi Cáo, Yíngjūn Cáo, Suàn Cáo, and Fǎ Cáo,
a total of thirteen departments,
〔一二〕and appointed nine Yùshǐ.
In the early Eastern Jìn,
the Kèdì Cáo was abolished,
and a Kù Cáo was established,
in charge of pasturing cattle and horses and collecting market taxes.
Later, the Kù Cáo was divided again,
establishing Wài Zuǒkù and Nèi Zuǒkù, two departments.
During Yuánjiā of Sòng Tàizǔ,
Wài Zuǒkù was abolished,
and Nèi Zuǒkù was simply called Zuǒkù.
During Dàmíng of Shìzǔ,
it was re-established.
In the first year of Jǐnghé of Fèi Dì, it was again abolished.
〔一三〕In the early period of Emperor Shùn,
Yíngjūn was merged with Shuǐ Cáo,
Suàn Cáo was merged with Fǎ Cáo,
and no Yùshǐ was appointed to Lì Cáo,
resulting in a total of ten Yùshǐ.
Wèi also had two Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ,
who were probably two Yùshǐ dispatched from Lántái to observe illegal activities within the palace.
The Western Jìn had four,
and the Eastern Jìn had two.
Qín and Hàn had a Fújié Lìng,
subordinate to the Shǎofǔ,
leading the Fúxǐ Láng and Fújié Lìngshǐ.
This was probably the responsibility of the Diǎn Ruì and Zhǎng Jié in the Zhōu Lǐ.
From Hàn to Wèi, it was separated into an independent office,
ranking below the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
in charge of bestowing credentials, bronze tiger tallies, and bamboo messenger tallies.
In the ninth year of Tàishǐ of Jìn Wǔdì,
it was abolished and merged with Lántái,
and a Fújié Yùshǐ was appointed to manage its affairs.
〔一四〕
The Yèzhě Púyè,
one person.
They were in charge of major enfeoffments and appointments, and the ranking of all officials.
They led ten Yèzhě.
The Yèzhě were in charge of minor enfeoffments and appointments, and reporting official documents.
This was a Qín official position.
Yè (謁)
means to request.
Yīng Shì's Hàn Guān says,
Yáo tested Shùn
by making him guest to the four gates,
which was his duty.
The Qín dynasty had seventy Yèzhě,
and Hàn continued this practice.
The Hòu Hàn Bǎiguān Zhì states
that the Yèzhě Púyè was in charge of ushering.
During the reign of Emperor Hé,
Hé Xī of Chénjùn served as Yèzhě Púyè,
〔一五〕leading bows and salutations in the palace,
his voice resonating around.
Therefore, he was also in charge of calling out praises.
〔一六〕There were five Chángshì Yèzhě,
and thirty-five Yèzhě were appointed,
half the number of the Western Capital.
Both Hàn dynasties were subordinate to the Guānglù Xūn.
The Wèi dynasty appointed ten Yèzhě.
Jìn Wǔdì abolished the Púyè,
and made the Yèzhě subordinate to Lántái.
The Eastern Jìn re-established the Púyè,
but later abolished it again.
During Dàmíng of Sòng Shìzǔ,
it was re-established.
Its rank was equivalent to one thousand dàn.
The Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě,
one person.
They were in charge of boats and transportation.
Qín and Hàn had Dūshuǐ Zhǎng and Cénɡ,
who managed reservoirs and irrigation,
and maintained rivers and canals,
subordinate to the Tàicháng.
The Eastern Hàn abolished Dūshuǐ
and established Hédī Yèzhě,
which Wèi continued.
During the Hàn dynasty, the Shuǐhéng Dūwèi managed the imperial hunting park;
during the Wèi dynasty, they managed all naval vessels and equipment in the empire.
Jìn Wǔdì abolished Shuǐhéng
and established Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě,
and Hédī became a subordinate official of Dūshuǐ.
There were two Cānjūn,
one Yèzhě,
and Lìngshǐ were appointed without fixed numbers.
The Western Jìn had Cānjūn but no Yèzhě;
the Yèzhě was appointed in the Eastern Jìn.
In the sixth year of Yǒngjiā of Emperor Huái,
when the Hú entered Luòyáng,
Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě Yuán Jùn was the first to leave and supervise transport, thus escaping.
Therefore, the position established by Emperor Wǔ
was already in charge of transport.
The Eastern Jìn abolished Hédī.
The Tàizǐ Tàifù,
one person.
One Cénɡ.
The Tàizǐ Shàofù,
one person.
One Cénɡ.
Fù (傅)
is an ancient official title.
The Wén Wáng Shìzǐ states:
“When the three kings taught their crown princes,
the Tàifù was in front,
the Shàofù was behind,
both serving as assistants and guides.”
In the ninth year of Hàn Gāodì,
Shúsūn Tōng was appointed Tàizǐ Tàifù,
ranking below the Tàicháng.
Neither Hàn dynasty had a Cénɡ.
The Wèi dynasty had no Eastern Palace (crown prince's establishment),
so it must have been the Jìn family who appointed the Cénɡ.
In the fifth year of Tàishǐ of Jìn Wǔdì,
an edict commanded the crown prince to bow to the Tàifù and Shàofù
with the rites of a student serving a teacher;
the two Fù were not allowed to submit memorials to show special reverence.
Both Fù had Gōngcáo, Zhǔbù, and Wǔguān.
The Tàifù ranked at two thousand dàn (or above),
the Shàofù at two thousand dàn.
Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
one person.
Chéng, one person.
Its duties are comparable to those of a tái shàngshūlìng or lǐngjūnjiāngjūn.
Zhān
means "inspection" (shěng).
In the Western Hàn capital, the Tàizǐ Mén Dàfū, Shùzǐ, Xǐmǎ, and Shèrén belonged to the two Fù;
the Shuàigēnglìng, Jiālìng, Pú, and Wèishuài belonged to the Zhānshì.
All were Qín officials.
The Later Hàn abolished the Zhānshì.
All officials of the Crown Prince's establishment then belonged to the Shǎofù,
and the Tàifù no longer commanded any officials.
In the early Jìn, all officials of the Crown Prince's establishment were collectively attached to the two Fù.
In the first year of Xiánníng
the Zhānshì was re-established,
and the two Fù no longer commanded officials.
The Zhānshì had a salary of two thousand dàn of grain.
〔一七〕
Jiālìng,
one person.
Chéng, one person.
Established during the Jìn era.
In the Hàn era, the Crown Prince received ten counties as a soup-and-bath fief,
and the Jiālìng managed it.
They also managed criminal justice and provisions,
with duties comparable to those of a Tíngwèi, Sīnóng, or Shǎofù.
In the Eastern Hàn, the Shígūanlìng was in charge of provisions.
The Shígūanlìng
became an independent office in the Jìn era,
no longer subordinate to the Jiālìng.
Shuàigēnglìng,
one person.
Managed palace gates and the awarding of punishments,
with duties like those of a Guānglùxūn or Wèiwèi.
In the Eastern Hàn, they oversaw the Shùzǐ and Shèrén,
but not so in the Jìn era.
From Hàn to Jìn,
the Jiālìng was below the Shuàigēnglìng;
in Sòng, it was above.
Pú,
one person.
In the Hàn era, the Crown Prince paid court every five days.
On days when he did not attend court,
the Pú and Zhōngyǔn were sent in the morning to inquire about his well-being.
They managed carriages, horses, and close relatives,
with duties like those of a Tàipú or Zōngzhèng.
From Jiālìng to Pú,
these were the three ministers (sān qīng) of the Crown Prince.
The three ministers had a salary of one thousand dàn of grain.
Mén Dàfū,
two people.
Established in the Eastern Hàn,
with duties like those of a Zhōnglángjiàng,
managing memorials (biǎojiān) from near and far.
Salary of six hundred dàn of grain.
Zhōngshùzǐ,
four people.
Duties like those of a Shìzhōng.
In the Eastern Hàn, there were five;
Jìn reduced them to four.
Salary of six hundred dàn of grain.
Zhōngshèrén,
four people.
In the Eastern Hàn, among the Crown Prince's officials, there was the office of Zhōngyǔn,
below the Zhōngshùzǐ
and above the Xǐmǎ.
It is likely similar to today's Zhōngshū Shèrén.
The Zhōngshèrén,
established in the early Jìn,
had duties like those of a Huángmén Shìláng.
Shígūanlìng,
one person.
Duties like those of a Tàigūanlìng.
An Eastern Hàn official.
Now subordinate to the Zhōngshùzǐ.
Shùzǐ, four people.
Duties comparable to those of a Sànqí Chángshì or Zhōngshū Jiān-Lìng.
This was a Jìn system.
In the Western Hàn, there were five;
in the Eastern Hàn, there was no fixed number,
with duties like those of the three yámen’s Zhōngláng.
In ancient times, feudal lords received hereditary salaries.
The sons of qīng and dàfū would become deputies,
called Guózǐ.
The Son of Heaven and feudal lords had the office of shùzǐ
〔to manage their instruction〕〔一八〕Qín adopted this name.
Salary of four hundred dàn of grain.
Shèrén,
sixteen people.
Duties like those of a Sànqí or Zhōngshū Shìláng.
This was a Jìn system.
In the two Hàn dynasties, there was no fixed number;
they managed palace guard duties like the three yámen’s Zhōngláng.
Xǐmǎ,
eight people.
Duties like those of an Yèzhě or Mìshūláng.
In the two Hàn dynasties, there were sixteen.
When the Crown Prince traveled out,
those on duty would precede him to guide and maintain decorum.
Salary comparable to six hundred dàn of grain.
Tàizǐ Zuǒ Wèishuài,
seven people.
Tàizǐ Yòu Wèishuài,
two people.
The duties of the two Shuài were like those of the two Wèi generals.
In Qín times, they were simply called Wèishuài.
Hàn continued this,
managing gate guards.
In early Jìn, they were called Zhōngwèishuài.
In the Tàishǐ era, they were divided into Left and Right,
each commanding one army.
During Emperor Huì's reign,
when Crown Prince Mǐnhuái was in the Eastern Palace,
Front and Rear Shuài were added.
When the King of Chéngdū, Sīmǎ Yǐng, became the Imperial Younger Brother,
a Zhōngwèi was also established,
making a total of five Shuài.
At the beginning of the Eastern Jìn (Jiāngzuǒ),
the Front and Rear Shuài were abolished.
They were re-established during Emperor Xiàowǔ's Tàiyuán reign.
All had a Chéng,
first established in early Jìn.
In the Sòng era, only the Left and Right Shuài were kept.
Their old salary was four hundred dàn of grain.
Tàizǐ Túqí Xiàowèi.
Tàizǐ Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
Tàizǐ Yìjūn Xiàowèi.
The three Xiàowèi each had seven people,
all established in early Sòng.
Túqí and Bùbīng
were based on the Tái Xiàowèi;
Yìjūn
was first established by Emperor Wǔ of Jìn in the early Tàikāng era,
initially as a Tái Xiàowèi,
with Táng Bīn holding the position.
It was abolished in the Eastern Jìn (Jiāngzuǒ).
Tàizǐ Rǒngcóng Púshè,
seven people.
Established in early Sòng.
Tàizǐ Lǚbēn Zhōnglángjiàng,
ten people.
Duties like those of a Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng.
Established in early Sòng.
The Zhōu Rites had Lǚbēnshì.
In the Hàn system,
the Son of Heaven had Hǔbēn,
and kings and marquises had Lǚbēn.
Lǚ
means "multitude."
Tàizǐ Zuǒ Jīnú Jiāngjūn,
ten people.
Tàizǐ Yòu Jīnú Jiāngjūn,
two people.
In the Eastern Hàn, Jīnú Jiāngjūn
was a miscellaneous title,
without Left or Right Jīnú.
From the Wèi era to the Eastern Jìn (Jiāngzuǒ),
Left and Right Jīnú were Tái offices,
commanding garrison troops.
In the Sòng era, when they were transferred to the Eastern Palace,
there were no more garrisons.
Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn,
ten people.
Diànzhōng Yuánwài Jiāngjūn,
twenty people.
Established in early Sòng.
Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiàng,
established by Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
governed Guǎngzhōu,
primarily to protect Nányuè.
〔十九〕
Nánmán Xiàowèi,
established by Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
governed Xiāngyáng.
Abolished at the beginning of the Eastern Jìn (Jiāngzuǒ).
Soon after, it was re-established,
governing Jiānglíng.
Abolished during Emperor Shìzǔ Xiàojiàn's reign in Sòng.
Xīróng Xiàowèi,
established in early Jìn,
governed Cháng'ān.
Re-established during Emperor Ān's Yìxī reign,
governed Hànzhōng.
Níngmán Xiàowèi,
established by Emperor Ān of Jìn,
〔二０〕governed Xiāngyáng,
and was conferred upon Lǔ Zōngzhī.
Nányí Xiàowèi,
established by Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
governed Níngzhōu.
In the Eastern Jìn (Jiāngzuǒ), it was renamed Zhènmán Xiàowèi.
The Four Barbarian (Sìyí) Zhōngláng Xiàowèi
all had a Chángshǐ, Sīmǎ, and Cānjūn.
Wèi and Jìn had various miscellaneous title Hùjūn,
like generals;
today there are still Zhènmán and Ānyuǎn Hùjūn.
Zhènmán was conferred upon the Administrators of Lújiāng, Jìn xī, and Xīyáng.
Ānyuǎn was conferred upon the Intendant of Wǔlíng.
The Cìshǐ
had one person in each zhōu.
The Huángdì established four jiān to govern all the states.
In the times of Táng and Yú, there were twelve mù;
this was their function.
The Zhōu changed the name to diǎn.
The Qín called them Jiān Yùshǐ,
and additionally dispatched Cóngxiàngshǐ to divide and investigate the various zhōu,
calling them Cìshǐ.
The meaning of cì is akin to cānzhān (inspect and spy).
Copying books was also called cì.
The Hàn system forbade cì in matters of the Shàngshū; this is an example.
The Cìshǐ carried out six articles of imperial edicts.
One article said:
powerful clans and influential individuals,
whose fields and residences exceed regulations,
use their strength to oppress the weak,
and their numbers to bully the few.
The second article said:
officials of two-thousand-dàn rank do not follow imperial edicts,
or adhere to established regulations,
turning their backs on public duty and favoring private interests,
seeking personal gain through corrupt means,
exploiting the common people,
and accumulating wealth through illicit practices.
The third article said:
officials of two-thousand-dàn rank do not investigate ambiguous cases,
kill people through intimidation,
impose penalties when angry,
or grant rewards when pleased,
causing vexation, harshness, and cruelty,
harming and slaughtering the common people,
being resented by the populace,
causing mountains to collapse and rocks to crack,
and strange omens and distorted rumors to appear.
The fourth article said:
officials of two-thousand-dàn rank are unfair in their selection and appointment of personnel,
only favoring those they love,
obscuring the worthy and promoting the dull.
The fifth article said:
children and younger brothers of two-thousand-dàn officials rely on their glorious power,
and make requests of those under their supervision.
The sixth article said:
officials of two-thousand-dàn rank violate public duty and collude with inferiors,
curry favor with powerful families,
allow bribery to pass through,
and undermine correct decrees.
At the end of the year, they would travel by post-carriage to the capital to report on their affairs.
In the first year of Suíhé of Emperor Chéng (18 BCE),
they were changed to Mù.
In the second year of Jiànpíng of Emperor Āi (5 BCE),
they were restored as Cìshǐ.
In the Former Hàn period,
Cìshǐ traveled around the commanderies and states by post-carriage,
with no fixed place of administration.
In the Later Hàn period,
their place of administration began to have a fixed location,
and they only traveled their circuit for eight months,
no longer reporting to the capital.
In the Jìn Jiāngzuǒ, the commandery and county edicts were still in effect,
[二一] as Zǎo Jù's poem "Zhuīyuǎn" states:
"My late father was the Tàishǒu of Jùlù,
until now three jǐ have passed.
I humbly served as the Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu,
issuing edicts next to the commandery records,"
this is it.
In Emperor Líng's time,
the world gradually became chaotic,
and heroes and powerful individuals each occupied zhōu and commanderies.
Liú Yān and Liú Yú both, having served as Jiǔqīng, became the Mù of Yìzhōu and Yōuzhōu,
their responsibilities gradually becoming heavier.
Subordinate officials included one Biéjià Cóngshìshǐ,
who traveled the circuit with the Cìshǐ;
one Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ,
who was in charge of financial and grain records;
one Bīngcáo Cóngshìshǐ,
who was in charge of military affairs;
one Bù Cóngshìshǐ for each commandery,
who was in charge of investigating illegal activities;
one Zhǔbù,
who recorded all matters below the main gate and reviewed documents;
one Mén Tíngzhǎng,
who was in charge of the main gate of the zhōu;
one Gōngcáo Shūzuǒ,
who was in charge of selection and appointment;
one Xiàojīng Shī,
who was in charge of examining the classics;
one Yuèlìng Shī,
who was in charge of seasonal festivals and sacrifices;
one Lǜlìng Shī,
who was in charge of legal judgments;
one Bùcáo Shūzuǒ,
who was in charge of records;
and one Diǎnjùn Shūzuǒ for each commandery,
who was in charge of the documents of one commandery:
this was the Hàn system.
Now there are Biéjià Cóngshìshǐ, Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ, Zhǔbù, Xīcáo Shūzuǒ, Jìjiǔ Cóngshìshǐ, Yìcáo Cóngshìshǐ, and Bùjùn Cóngshìshǐ.
From the Zhǔbù downwards,
the number of personnel appointed
varied with each zhōu,
there was no fixed system historically.
In the middle of the Xiánkāng reign of Emperor Chéng of Jìn,
Jiāngzhōu also had a Biéjià Jìjiǔ,
who held a position above other officials,
while the Biéjià Cóngshìshǐ remained as before,
but this no longer exists today.
The Biéjià and Xīcáo were in charge of personnel and election matters,
while the Zhìzhōng was in charge of documents of all offices.
The Xīcáo
was the Gōngcáo Shūzuǒ of the Hàn.
The Jìjiǔ was in charge of various offices for military, banditry, granaries, households, water, and armor, among others.
Yángzhōu had no Jìjiǔ,
and the Zhǔbù managed these affairs.
Jīngzhōu had a Cóngshìshǐ,
who was subordinate to the Yìcáo Cóngshìshǐ;
it is generally believed that this was established since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties.
Now Guǎngzhōu and Xúzhōu have Yuèlìng Cóngshì,
which, like the Cáoshǐ of other zhōu,
is an old Hàn name.
In the fourth year of Yuánfēng of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn (107 BCE),
it was ordered that each zhōu should annually recommend one Xiùcái.
In the Later Hàn, to avoid the taboo of Guāngwǔ's name,
it was changed to Màocái.
The Wèi restored it to Xiùcái.
In the Jìn Jiāngzuǒ, Yángzhōu recommended two annually,
other zhōu recommended one,
or one every three years,
depending on the size of the zhōu,
and all involved policy questions.
When Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè of Jìn became the Mù of Yùzhōu,
the Mù appointed a Chángshǐ and a Cānjūn.
Yǔ Gāi served as Chángshǐ,
[二二] Xiè Kūn as Cānjūn.
This meant that those serving as Mù had no such appointments.
Mù were officials of two-thousand-dàn rank,
Cìshǐ were of six-hundred-dàn rank.
The Jùnshǒu
was a Qín official.
After Qín conquered the various feudal states,
it forthwith converted their territories into commanderies (jùn),
appointing one Shǒu, one Céng, and one Wèi to each.
The Shǒu governed the people,
and the Céng assisted him.
In commanderies situated along border garrisons,
the Céng acted as the Zhǎngshǐ.
To the east of the Jiāng River (Jiāngzuǒ), the Jìn dynasty generally referred to them as Céng.
The Wèi commanded the troops
and guarded against bandits.
In the second year of the middle period of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn's reign (148 BCE),
the Shǒu was renamed Tàishǒu,
and the Wèi became the Dūwèi.
Emperor Guāngwǔ abolished the Dūwèi,
but later, Dōngbù Dūwèi and Xībù Dūwèi were often re-established.
Where there were Mányí (barbarian tribes),
there were also Shǔguó Dūwèi.
In the late Hàn dynasty and the Three Kingdoms period,
many Dūwèi of various departments were made into commanderies.
In the seventh year of Xiánkāng of Emperor Chéng of Jìn (331 CE),
all Jùncéng were again abolished.
In the fourth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Tàizǔ of Sòng (427 CE),
they were re-established.
The staff of a commandery generally resembled that of a Gōngfǔ,
without Dōngcáo or Xīcáo,
but with a Gōngcáoshǐ
responsible for selections (elections),
a Wǔguān Yuán
responsible for the affairs of all bureaus.
In the constituent counties, there were Dūyóu and Méntíngzhǎng,
and also a Zhǔjìshǐ
who urged and supervised deadlines and meetings.
This was a Hàn system,
and it is largely similar today.
Each commandery had its own traditional customs,
and the names of its various bureaus
often differed.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn adopted Dǒng Zhòngshū's advice,
and in the first year of Yuánguāng (134 BCE),
he first ordered commanderies and kingdoms to recommend Xiàolián.
The regulation stipulated that commanderies with a population of 200,000 or more
should recommend one person annually;
400,000 or more,
two persons;
three persons;
four persons;
five persons;
six persons.
If under 200,000,
one person every two years;
if under 100,000,
one person every three years.
They were limited to four categories:
the first was "of lofty and excellent virtue,
pure and upright in spirit and integrity";
the second was "versed in learning and refined in conduct,
a Ph.D. within the Classics" (Jīngzhōng Bóshì);
the third was "familiar with laws and regulations,
sufficient to resolve doubts,
able to investigate statutes and review interrogations,
a Yùshǐ in writing" (Wénzhōng Yùshǐ);
the fourth was "resolute and resourceful,
unconfused by events,
clear-sighted enough to make decisions,
talented to serve as a county magistrate in the Sānfǔ."
In the early Wèi dynasty,
the system was changed: for populations of 100,000 or more,
one person per year,
with outstanding individuals
not restricted by household registration.
To the east of the Jiāng River (Jiāngzuǒ), Dānyáng, Wú, Kuàijī, and Wúxìng were all considered large commanderies,
each recommending two people annually.
The Hàn system stipulated sending one Shàngjì Yuán and one Shǐ annually,
to list all matters within the commandery.
This was called the Jiēbù,
and it is still practiced today.
The Tàishǒu received two thousand dàn of grain,
the Céng six hundred dàn.
The Xiànlìng and Zhǎng
were Qín officials.
Larger counties had a Lìng,
smaller ones a Zhǎng,
and marquisates had a Xiàng.
The Hàn system
appointed one Céng,
and for Wèi, two in large counties,
one in small counties.
Five households formed a Wǔ,
led by a Wǔzhǎng;
two Wǔ formed a Shí,
led by a Shízhǎng;
ten Shí formed a Lǐ,
led by a Lǐkuí;
ten Lǐ formed a Tíng,
led by a Tíngzhǎng;
ten Tíng formed a Xiāng,
with one Xiāngzuǒ, one Sānlǎo, one Yǒuzhì, one Sèfū, and one Yóujiào.
The Xiāngzuǒ and Yǒuzhì were in charge of taxes,
the Sānlǎo of education,
the Sèfū of disputes,
and the Yóujiào of criminal matters.
The other various bureaus
were generally similar to commandery positions.
The Wǔguān became Tíngyuán,
but later there was no longer a Céng,
except for a Yùcéng in Jiànkāng.
As for other various posts,
some counties had them while others did not,
each following its own old customs,
without a fixed system.
To the west of the Jiāng River (Jiāngyòu), the Jìn dynasty's Luòyáng county established six Dūwèi departments,
other large counties had two Dūwèi,
and secondary and small counties each had one.
In the fifteenth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Tàizǔ of Sòng (438 CE),
these were again abolished in smaller counties.
All official offices up to the commandery level
each had 500 retainers.
Old sayings suggest that ancient rulers traveled with an army (shīcóng),
and ministers with a retinue (lǚcóng).
A lǚ
consisted of 500 people.
Today, officials from county magistrate (xiànlìng) upwards
are like the ancient feudal lords,
hence they establish 400 or 500 retainers to symbolize the shīcóng and lǚcóng,
following ancient meaning.
Wéi Yào said,
the character "Wǔbǎi" (five hundred) was originally "Wǔbó".
Wǔ means
proper (Dāng).
Bó means
path (Dào).
It means to guide and direct people in the proper path to clear it.
The Zhōu system considered 500 as a lǚ,
and their commanders were all Dàfū,
so it should not be taken as lowly as this explanation suggests.
Moreover, the Zhōu Lǐ (Rites of Zhōu) Autumn Officials had the Tiáolángshì,
who were in charge of holding whips to clear the way.
When the King traveled, eight people flanked the road;
for a Gōng, six people;
for a Hóubó, four people;
for a Zǐnán, two people.
This is close,
only the names are different.
Also, among Hàn officials, there was the Bóshǐ,
whose main duty was to drive away and clear roads for various officials in the middle of the road,
hence the name Bóshǐ.
This is an analogy.
A Xiànlìng received 1,000 to 600 dàn of grain,
a Zhǎng 500 dàn.
At the beginning of the Hàn dynasty, kingdoms established a Tàifù,
responsible for assistance and guidance;
an Nèishǐ presided over governing the people;
a Chéngxiàng commanded all officials;
and a Zhōngwèi was in charge of military posts.
The division of officials and establishment of posts
was roughly similar to the capital (Jīngshī).
When Emperor Jǐng, punishing the Rebellion of the Seven States,
reformed the system such that kings were not allowed to govern their states,
the Hàn court appointed officials for them,
renaming the Chéngxiàng as Xiàng,
and abolished the Yùshǐ Dàfū, Tíngwèi, Shǎofǔ, Zōngzhèng, and Bóshì posts.
Their Dàfū, Yèzhě, and various chiefs and aides
all had their staff numbers reduced.
Later, the Hàn Nèishǐ was changed to Jīngzhàoyǐn,
the Zhōngwèi to Zhí Jīnwú,
and the Lángzhōnglìng to Guānglùxūn.
But the kingdom system remained as before.
The Tàipú was also renamed Pú,
and the Sīnóng became Dànóng.
Emperor Chéng later ordered the Xiàng to govern the people like a Jùn Tàishǒu,
and abolished the Nèishǐ.
Their Zhōngwèi was like a Jùn Wèi,
and the Tàifù was simply called Fù.
The Hàn Dōngjīng also established one Fù,
whom the king honored as a teacher;
one Xiàng,
who presided over governing the people;
one Zhōngwèi,
who handled bandits and thieves;
one Lángzhōnglìng,
who managed the Lángzhōng guards;
one Pú;
one Zhìshū (this Zhìshū
was originally called Shàngshū,
then later renamed Zhìshū);
unranked Zhōngdàfū,
who were in charge of diplomatic missions to the capital and various states;
one Yèzhě, and one chief each for ceremonial music, palace guards, medical artisans, the Yong Lane, and sacrificial rites.
[二三]Unranked Lángzhōng.
The officials subordinate to the Yèzhě in the Wèi clan,
the historical records are missing and their sequence is unknown.
In the early reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, one Shī, one Yǒu, and one Wénxué were initially established for each.
The Shī was the Fù.
Emperor Jǐng, out of naming taboo for Shī,
changed it to Fù.
During the Sòng period, it was changed back to Shī.
As for Wénxué,
it had already been established in the Former Hàn.
The Yǒu was named after the Four Friends of King Wén and Zhòngní.
The Tàishǒu was changed to Nèishǐ,
and the Xiàng and Pú were abolished.
There were Lángzhōnglìng, Zhōngwèi, and Dànóng as the three ministers (Sānqīng).
Large states appointed three Zǔoyòuchángshì each,
abolished the Lángzhōng,
and appointed two Shìláng.
Large states also appointed three generals: Shàngjūn, Zhōngjūn, and Xiàjūn.
Medium states had one Shàngjūn Jiāngjūn and one Xiàjūn Jiāngjūn each.
Small states only had Shàngjūn.
One Diǎnshū, Diǎncí, Diǎnwèi, Xuéguānlìng, and Diǎnshūlìngcéng each.
Four Zhìshū.
One Zhōngwèi, Sīmǎ, Shìzǐ Shùzǐ Língmiào, and Mùzhǎng each.
Four Yèzhě.
Six Zhōngdàfū.
Ten Shèrén.
One Diǎnyīcéng and one Diǎnfǔcéng each.
Since the Sòng clan,
the Jìn system was uniformly adopted.
Even small and large states
all had three armies (Sānjūn).
In the Jìn system,
the Diǎnshūlìng was below the Chángshì
and above the Shìláng.
In Jiāngzuǒ, the Shìláng came after the Chángshì,
and the Diǎnshūlìng was below the Sānjūn.
Since Jiāngzuǒ,
dukedoms had no Zhōngwèi, Chángshì, or Sānjūn.
Marquisates further had no Dànóng or Shìláng.
For earldoms, viscounties, and baronies, only officials from Diǎnshū downwards remained,
and they also had no Xuéguānlìng.
Official posts were all reduced in sequence.
In Jìn Jiāngyòu, the officials subordinate to dukes and marquises were
determined by the size of the state,
without a fixed system.
All states in Jìn Jiāngzuǒ
originally received one-third of the revenue.
In the first year of Tàixīng of Emperor Yuán,
it was first stipulated to receive one-ninth.

[二四]Collation Notes
Biographies, First, Empresses and Consorts
The emperor's paternal grandmother was titled Tàihuáng Tàihòu (太皇太后),
his mother Huáng Tàihòu (皇太后),
and his consort Huánghòu (皇后).
This was the old system of the Hàn (漢).
Jìn Wǔdì (晉武帝) adopted the systems of the Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏),
establishing Guìpín (貴嬪), Fūrén (夫人), and Guìrén (貴人).
These were the Sān Fūrén (三夫人),
whose ranks were equivalent to the Sān Gōng (三公).
Shúfēi (淑妃), Shúyuàn (淑媛), Shúyí (淑儀), Xiūhuá (修華), Xiūróng (修容), Xiūyí (修儀), Jiéyú (婕妤), Rónghuá (容華), and Chōnghuá (充華)
constituted the Jiǔpín (九嬪),
whose ranks were equivalent to the Jiǔ Qīng (九卿).
The rest included Měirén (美人), Cáirén (才人), and Zhōngcáirén (中才人),
whose titles were equivalent to officials of a thousand shí (石) or less.
Gāozǔ (高祖) received the mandate
and abolished the two ranks of Cáirén (才人),
while retaining the rest of the Jìn (晉) system.
Guìpín (貴嬪)
was established by Wèi Wéndì (魏文帝).
Fūrén (夫人)
was established by Wèi Wǔdì (魏武帝) when he first founded the state of Wèi (魏).
Guìrén (貴人)
was established by Hàn Guāngwǔ (漢光武).
Shúfēi (淑妃)
was established by Wèi Míngdì (魏明帝).
Shúyuàn (淑媛)
was established by Wèi Wéndì (魏文帝).
Shúyí (淑儀) and Xiūhuá (修華)
were established by Jìn Wǔdì (晉武帝).
Xiūróng (修容)
was established by Wèi Wéndì (魏文帝).
Xiūyí (修儀)
was established by Wèi Míngdì (魏明帝).
Jiéyú (婕妤) and Rónghuá (容華)
were old titles from the Former Hàn (前漢).
Chōnghuá (充華)
was established by Jìn Wǔdì (晉武帝).
Měirén (美人)
was established by Hàn Guāngwǔ (漢光武).
In the third year of Xiàojiàn (孝建), during Shìzǔ's (世祖) reign,
Fūrén (夫人), Xiūhuá (修華), and Xiūróng (修容) were abolished,
and Guìfēi (貴妃) was established,
her rank equivalent to Xiàngguó (相國).
Guìpín (貴嬪) was promoted,
her rank equivalent to Chéngxiàng (丞相).
Guìrén (貴人) had a rank equivalent to the Sān Sī (三司),
these constituting the Sān Fūrén (三夫人).
Also, Zhāoyí (昭儀), Zhāoróng (昭容), and Zhāohuá (昭華) were established
to replace Xiūhuá (修華), Xiūyí (修儀), and Xiūróng (修容).
Additionally, Zhōngcáirén (中才人) and Chōngyī (充衣) were established
as minor positions.
Zhāoyí (昭儀)
was established by Hàn Yuándì (漢元帝).
Zhāoróng (昭容)
was established by Shìzǔ (世祖).
Zhāohuá (昭華)
was established by Wèi Míngdì (魏明帝).
Zhōngcáirén (中才人)
was established by Jìn Wǔdì (晉武帝).
Chōngyī (充衣)
was an old system from the Former Hàn (前漢).
In the first year of Tàishǐ (泰始), during Tàizōng's (太宗) reign,
Shúfēi (淑妃), Zhāohuá (昭華), Zhōngcáirén (中才人), and Chōngyī (充衣) were abolished.
Xiūhuá (修華), Xiūyí (修儀), Xiūróng (修容), Cáirén (才人), and Liángrén (良人) were reinstated.
In the third year,
Guìrén (貴人) was again abolished,
and Guìjī (貴姬) was established
to complete the number of the Sān Fūrén (三夫人).
Zhāohuá (昭華) was also established,
and Shúróng (淑容), Chénghuī (承徽), and Lièróng (列榮) were added.
Shúyuàn (淑媛), Shúyí (淑儀), Shúróng (淑容), Zhāohuá (昭華), Zhāoyí (昭儀), Zhāoróng (昭容), Xiūhuá (修華), Xiūyí (修儀), and Xiūróng (修容) were designated as the Jiǔpín (九嬪).
Jiéyú (婕妤), Rónghuá (容華), Chōnghuá (充華), Chénghuī (承徽), and Lièróng (列榮), a total of five positions,
ranked second to the Jiǔpín (九嬪).
Měirén (美人), Zhōngcáirén (中才人), and Cáirén (才人), three positions, were classified as miscellaneous duties.
Thereafter, Tàizōng (太宗) devoted his attention to the imperial harem,
intending to staff the inner offices
in imitation of the outer civil officials.

Relative families:
Empress Xiàomù Zhào (孝穆趙皇后), personal name Ānzōng (安宗),
was a native of Tóng (僮), Xiàpī (下邳).
Her grandfather, Biāo (彪), courtesy name Shìfàn (世範),
was a Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ (治書侍御史).
Her father, Yì (裔), courtesy name Yànzhòu (彥冑),
was the Píngyuán Tàishǒu (平原太守).
The Empress became a consort to Emperor Xiào (孝皇) in the fourth year of Shēngpíng (升平) of Emperor Mù of Jìn (晉穆帝).
She gave birth to Gāozǔ (高祖) on the second day of the fourth month in the first year of Xīngníng (興寧) of Emperor Āi of Jìn (晉哀帝).
On that day,
the Empress died of puerperal fever in the official residence at Dāntú (丹徒),
at the age of twenty-one.
She was buried on Yúshān (雩山) in Liànbì Lǐ (練璧里), Dōngxiāng (東鄉), Dāntú Xiàn (丹徒縣), Jìnlíng (晉陵).
In the early Sòng (宋) dynasty, posthumous titles and an epithet were bestowed upon her,
and her mausoleum was named Xīngníng (興寧).
In the second year of Yǒngchū (永初),
the officials reported:
"The virtue of great filial piety
thrives in honoring one's parents.
When one person is blessed,
their glory extends to all nations.
This is why Líng Wén (靈文) was favored in the Western Capital,
and Shòu Zhāng (壽張) was honored in the glorious Hàn (漢).
Therefore, the former Píngyuán Tàishǒu (平原太守) Zhào Yì (趙裔) and the former Táoyáng Lìng (洮陽令) Xiāo Zhuó (蕭卓),
who are both respected relatives by marriage,
have not yet received due honor.
We, your ministers, respectfully convey the Emperor's thoughts,
and after examining old statutes,
propose that both be posthumously granted the title of Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫),
and presented with a gold seal and purple ribbon.
Yì's (裔) wife, Sūn (孫) by maiden name, may be granted the title of Yùzhāng Jùn (豫章郡) Jiànchāng Xiànjūn (建昌縣君),
and Zhuó's (卓) wife, Zhào (趙) by maiden name, may be granted the title of Wújùn (吳郡) Shòuchāng Xiànjūn (壽昌縣君)."
Lady Sūn (孫氏)
was from Dōngguǎn (東莞).
In the same year,
an imperial edict was also issued, stating:
"The rite of extending grace
is in accordance with natural sentiment.
Thus, establishing royal princes internally
and honoring the empresses' families externally,
from the Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏) dynasties onwards,
this practice has always been followed.
Our maternal grandfathers, Guānglù Zhào (光祿趙) and Guānglù Xiāo (光祿蕭),
though their official ranks are high,
have not yet been enfeoffed with land.
Both should be posthumously enfeoffed as Kāiguó Xiànhóu (開國縣侯),
with a stipend of five hundred households."
