Thus, Yì (裔) was posthumously enfeoffed as Línhè Xiànhóu (臨賀縣侯).
Yì's (裔) eldest son, Xuānzhī (宣之),
served as Jiāngchéng Lìng (江乘令).
He died early
without sons,
so his younger brother, Xízhī (襲之), inherited Xuānzhī's (宣之) title as his successor.
When Xízhī (襲之) died,
his son Zǔlián (祖憐) succeeded him.
When Qí (齊) received the abdication,
the marquisate was abolished.
Xuānzhī's (宣之) younger brother, Lúnzhī (倫之),
has his own biography.
Empress Xiàoyì Xiāo (孝懿蕭皇后), personal name Wénshòu (文壽),
was from Lánlíng (蘭陵), Lánlíng (蘭陵).
Her grandfather, Liàng (亮), courtesy name Bǎozuò (保祚),
was a Shìyùshǐ (侍御史).
Her father, Zhuó (卓), courtesy name Zǐlüè (子略),
was the Táoyáng Lìng (洮陽令).
After Empress Xiàomù (孝穆后) died,
Emperor Xiào (孝皇帝) took the Empress as his second wife,
and she gave birth to Chángshā Jǐngwáng Dàolián (長沙景王道憐) and Línchuān Lièwǔwáng Dàoguī (臨川烈武王道規).
In the seventh year of Yìxī (義熙),
she was appointed Yùzhāng Gōng Tàifūrén (豫章公太夫人).
When Gāozǔ (高祖) became the King of Sòng (宋王),
she was also granted the title of Tàifēi (太妃).
In the twelfth year, Gāozǔ (高祖) went on a northern expedition,
and remained in Péngchéng (彭城) and Shòuyáng (壽陽).
He returned to the capital in the second year of Yuánxī (元熙),
and subsequently received the abdication from Jìn (晉),
having been away for five years in total.
The Empress (蕭皇后) always remained in the eastern residence.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) ascended the throne,
the officials reported:
"We, your ministers, have heard that those with abundant virtue receive lasting blessings,
and those with widespread virtue are honored with complete rites.
Thus, reverence is shown to the highly esteemed,
and auspicious titles are proclaimed in grand ceremonies.
We humbly believe that Her Highness the Tàifēi's (太妃) virtue as a mother
has transformed without words, and her guidance in protecting and assisting
has illuminated the grand enterprise.
Although the spiritual and mortal realms rejoice together,
her appellation is not yet complete.
Examining previous generations,
there are precedents in rites,
and it is fitting to follow the old statutes
to fulfill the aspirations of the multitude.
We, your ministers, request that the title of Sòngwáng Tàihòu (宋王太后) be elevated to Huáng Tàihòu (皇太后)."
Therefore, the officials' report still referred to her as Tàifēi (太妃).
The Emperor (Gāozǔ), known for his respectful filial piety,
had always been diligently attentive to the Tàihòu (太后).
When he ascended to the great position,
being already advanced in age,
he would visit the Tàihòu (太后) every morning at court,
never once missing the appointed time.
When Shàodì (少帝) ascended the throne,
her title was further elevated to Tàihuáng Tàihòu (太皇太后).
In the first year of Jǐngpíng (景平),
she died in the Xiǎnyáng Diàn (顯陽殿)
at the age of eighty-one.
Her last will stated:
"Emperor Xiào (孝皇) passed away over fifty years ago,
and ancient custom does not permit joint burial.
Moreover, in the Hàn (漢) dynasty, the mausoleums of emperors and empresses were all in different places.
Now, a separate burial pit should be made within the burial grounds.
The burial mound of Emperor Xiào (孝皇) originally followed the rites of a commoner's family,
and differed from the lavishness of a king's system.
For a woman, there are specific rites to follow,
so the past practice should be adhered to."
Thus, a separate burial pit was opened,
and it was combined with the Xīngníng Líng (興寧陵).
Initially,
when Gāozǔ (高祖) was in obscurity,
he was extremely poor.
When Emperor Xiào (孝皇) died,
many funeral rites were lacking.
Gāozǔ (高祖) had left instructions that after the Tàihòu (太后) passed away, there was no need for a joint burial.
Therefore, the Empress's (蕭皇后) last will was followed in its execution.
Zhuó (卓) was initially posthumously granted the title of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (金紫光祿大夫) along with Zhào Yì (趙裔),
and was also posthumously enfeoffed as Fēngyáng Xiànhóu (封陽縣侯).
His wife, Lady Zhào (趙氏) of Xiàpī (下邳), was enfeoffed as Wújùn Shòuchāng Xiànjūn (吳郡壽昌縣君).
Zhuó's (卓) son Yuánzhī (源之) inherited the title.
Yuánzhī (源之) can be found in the biography of his son Sīhuà (思話).
Empress Wǔjìng Zāng (武敬臧皇后), personal name Àiqīn (愛親),
was from Dōngguǎn (東莞).
Her grandfather, Wāng (汪), courtesy name Shānfǔ (山甫),
was a Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎).
Her father, Jùn (儁), courtesy name Xuānyì (宣乂),
was the Jùn Gōngcáo (郡功曹).
The Empress married Gāozǔ (高祖),
and gave birth to Huìjī Xuāncháng Gōngzhǔ (會稽宣長公主) Xīngdì (興弟).
Gāozǔ (高祖) led his subordinates with frugality and rectitude,
and the Empress was respectful and compliant.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) restored the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
and held the important position of prime minister,
the Empress's attire and utensils were still plain and simple,
and she did not make requests for her relatives.
On the jiǎwǔ (甲午) day of the first month in the fourth year of Yìxī (義熙),
she died in the Eastern City
at the age of forty-eight.
She was posthumously granted the title of Yùzhāng Gōng Fūrén (豫章公夫人)
and reburied in Dāntú (丹徒).
When Gāozǔ (高祖) was on his deathbed,
he left an edict that she should be buried in the capital.
Thus, a full imperial funeral procession was prepared,
and her coffin was welcomed for joint burial at Chūníng Líng (初寧陵).
In the early Sòng (宋) dynasty, Jùn (儁) was posthumously granted the title of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (金紫光祿大夫),
and his wife, Lady Shūsūn (叔孫氏) of Gāomì (高密), was enfeoffed as Qiānlíng Yǒngpíng Xiāngjūn (遷陵永平鄉君).
Jùn's (儁) son Táo (燾),
Táo's (燾) younger brother Xī (熹),
and Xī's (熹) son Zhì (質)
all have their own biographies.
Lady Zhāng (張夫人) of Emperor Wǔ (武帝), personal name Quē (闕),
her native county is unknown.
In the early Yìxī (義熙) period,
she gained favor with Gāozǔ (高祖),
and gave birth to Shàodì (少帝)
and also to Yìxīng Gōngcháng Gōngzhǔ (義興恭長公主) Huìyuán (惠媛).
In the first year of Yǒngchū (永初),
she was appointed Fūrén (夫人).
When Shàodì (少帝) ascended the throne,
the officials reported:
"We, your ministers, have heard that honoring one's parents is the foundation,
and the way of profound filial piety
emanates from within and extends outward.
We humbly believe that Her Highness the Fūrén's (夫人) virtue matches that of the Earth,
and her auspicious reputation is glorious and excellent.
She brought forth auspicious signs and blessings,
and gave birth to the sagely and enlightened one.
It is fitting to elevate her noble title to the highest,
to truly complete the grand regulations.
Following the principle of 'mother honored by son' from the Spring and Autumn Annals,
and adhering to the precedent of extending love from the Hàn (漢) and Jìn (晉) dynasties,
we respectfully propose the honorable title of Huáng Tàihòu (皇太后)
and name her palace Yǒnglè (永樂)."
After Shàodì (少帝) was deposed,
the Tàihòu (太后) returned her imperial seals and ribbons,
and resided in Wú Xiàn (吳縣).
In the first year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) of Tàizǔ (太祖),
she was appointed Yíngyángwáng Tàifēi (營陽王太妃).
In the third year,
she died.
Empress Sīmǎ Maòyīng of Emperor Shào
was from Wēn, Hénèi.
She was the daughter of Emperor Gōng of Jìn.
Initially, she was enfeoffed as Princess Hǎiyán.
Emperor Shào, as a princely son, married her.
At the beginning of Sòng,
she was appointed Crown Princess.
When Emperor Shào ascended the throne,
she was established as empress.
In the first year of Yuánjiā,
she was demoted to Princess Yíngyáng,
and later became Grand Consort of the Prince of Nánfēng.
She passed away in the sixteenth year,
at the age of forty-seven.
Lady Hú Dáòān, a concubine of Emperor Wǔ,
was from Huáinán.
In the early years of Yìxī,
she was taken by Emperor Gāozǔ
and gave birth to Emperor Wén.
In the fifth year,
she was reprimanded and given death,
at the age of forty-two.
She was buried in Dāntú.
When Emperor Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
she was posthumously granted the title of Jiéyú.
When Emperor Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
the officials reported:
"We hear that those of profound virtue are honored with high rites,
and those of deep blessings attain the highest positions.
Therefore, when the splendid temple is built,
songs are sung for the revered ancestors;
when the imperial tombs are grandly guarded,
this is an act of filial piety.
We humbly consider that the late Jiéyú was gentle, intelligent, and profound,
her radiance complete among the six ranks of consorts,
her virtue illuminating the female model,
her teachings permeating the maternal demeanor.
Thus, she was able to initiate the mandate for a sagely and enlightened ruler,
who swiftly governs the four seas.
Her esteemed parent could not be reached,
and heavenly blessings were forever lost.
We, your subjects, referencing the Spring and Autumn Annals from afar,
and consulting the Hàn and Jìn dynasties nearby,
respectfully propose the esteemed title of Zhāng Huáng Tàihòu,
and her mausoleum be named Xīníng."
A temple was erected for her in the capital.
Her nephew, Yuánqìng,
attained the position of Fèng Cháoqǐng.
Empress Yuán Qíjī of Emperor Wén
was from Yángxià, Chénjùn.
She was the illegitimate daughter of Yuán Zhànzhī, Duke Jìng, who held the title of Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū.
Her mother was of humble birth,
and when the empress was five or six years old,
she was finally acknowledged.
Later, she married Emperor Tàizǔ,
and was initially appointed Princess Yídū.
She gave birth to Shào and Princess Dōngyáng Xiàn, Yīng'é.
The emperor treated the empress with extremely deep affection and courtesy.
The Yuán clan was poor,
and the empress often asked the emperor for money and silk to provide for them.
The emperor's nature was frugal,
so what she received was no more than thirty to fifty thousand coins or thirty to fifty bolts of silk.
Later, Consort Pān became favored,
her affection dominating the empress's palace.
Everyone said that whatever she asked for, she would obtain.
The empress heard this
and wanted to know if it was true.
So, she asked Pān to request three hundred thousand coins for her family,
to observe the emperor's intention.
She received it overnight.
Because of this, her resentment and hatred became very deep.
She feigned illness and no longer saw the emperor.
Whenever the emperor entered,
she would avoid him by going to another place.
The emperor often tried to ambush her,
but could not succeed.
When the illegitimate sons of Jùn, Prince Shǐxīng, came to inquire,
the empress never looked at them.
The empress eventually became ill from anger and resentment.
In the seventeenth year of Yuánjiā,
her illness became critical.
The emperor held her hand, shedding tears, and asked what she wished to say.
The empress looked at the emperor for a long time,
then pulled the quilt over her face.
She passed away in Xiǎnyáng Palace,
at the age of thirty-six.
The emperor mourned her deeply.
He decreed that Yán Yánzhī, former Administrator of Yǒngjiā, compose an elegy,
the text of which was extremely beautiful.
Its words were: The dragon coffin with silken cords,
the phoenix banner with charioted steeds.
The imperial path brightly arranged,
the divine road deep and solemn.
The Emperor personally attends the departure sacrifice,
himself watching the night-laden bier.
Adorning the final rites
with embroidered tassels,
imagining her departing sounds from jade pendants.
Grieving the relocation of the embroidered mat,
pained by the double eclipse of the phoenix robe.
Descending from the carriage to the guest seat,
removing the offerings from the bierside steps.
Then he commanded
the historian,
to eulogize her virtue and express his feelings.
Its words were: As relationships illuminate, couples ascend;
there is existence, there is reliance.
When the round essence first sparkled,
the square earth first congealed.
How splendid the noble clan,
auspiciousness arising, blessings received.
Mysterious rites, illustrious lineage,
their brilliance
illuminates the Jade Constellation.
Prosperous radiance in the feminine realm,
gentle clarity about to advance.
Following rites, treading harmony,
matching poetry, accepting obedience.
From the time of waiting for marriage,
her pure reputation shone early.
Once she had
conduct,
her plain brilliance further enhanced.
Donning the ceremonial robes,
her words and actions served as a model.
Allowing our royal customs
to be founded on the virtue of the empress.
Her fragrant wisdom flowed like a river,
her virtuous counsel deep and profound.
Like the Jiāng flowing into the Hàn,
the
songs of the southern state renewed.
Alas, in former times, when there was misfortune,
the great transformation was in decline.
Thus, the precious mandate was gathered,
and she ascended to the celestial mechanism.
Leaving her position in the ducal palace,
ascending to shine in the imperial inner quarters.
Respectfully obeying the imperial
aunt,
truly following previous merits.
Filial piety reaching parents,
reverence practiced in ancestral worship.
Advancing in thought with talent and grace,
comprehensively studying history.
Her voice expressed in song,
her movements forming records.
The
administration of the inner palace solemnly declared,
the harmony of the chambers brightly ordered.
The feminine principle smoothly accomplished,
the starry canopy adorned.
Where virtue reaches,
what is deepest is surely fathomed.
The lower segment rumbled and rose,
the upper clear quarter moon
inclined.
All who came were harmonious,
no thought was unfulfilled.
It is said that the Dao assists benevolence,
and its transformations are indistinct.
When things symbolize arrival,
ominous portents herald disorder.
When great harmony fused,
she gathered her brilliance and left the world.
The orchid hall forever shadowed,
the pepper-scented path relaxed its guard.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Coolness cautioned at the preparation,
late autumn immediately bringing burial.
Frosty night flowing with song,
morning moon ascending its phase.
Eight spirits alertly leading,
five chariots moving their tracks.
Wailing
heirs,
mourning princes.
Tears falling on the jade steps,
rain of sorrow in the cinnabar wings.
Comforting the living, mourning the dead,
feeling the present, remembering the past.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Southward from the capital gate,
northward facing the mountain garden.
Attendants holding standards,
outriders looking back at the chariot.
Distantly saddened by the purple canopy,
faintly weeping at the plain carriage.
Extinguishing colors in the clear capital,
leveling
Tǐ Shòu Yuán.
The towns and wildernesses were engulfed in sorrow,
the Róng and Xià wept mournfully.
The coming fragrance could be recounted,
but the departing carriage could not be retrieved.
Alas, how lamentable!
After the memorial was presented,
the Emperor himself added
"comfort the living and mourn the dead,
be moved by the present and recall the past,"
eight characters
to express his sentiment.
The officials proposed the posthumous title Xuān Huánghòu,
but the Emperor issued a special edict saying
"Yuán."
Initially,
when the Empress gave birth to Shào,
she personally examined him thoroughly
and rushed to inform Tàizǔ:
"This child's appearance is extraordinary;
he will surely ruin the state and destroy the family.
He cannot be raised."
She immediately wished to kill him.
Tàizǔ frantically arrived outside the Empress's palace door,
parted the curtain with his hand to forbid it,
and thus she stopped.
After the Empress died,
there were often small spiritual manifestations.
Shěn Měirén,
whom Tàizǔ favored,
〔一０〕was once accused of a crime
and sentenced to death.
She passed by the Huīyīn Diàn, where the Empress used to live.
This palace had five chambers,
and had been kept closed since the Empress's demise.
When the beauty reached the palace entrance,
she wept and cried out loudly:
"Today I am to die innocent;
if the late Empress has a spirit,
she must know!"
All the windows and doors of the palace opened wide in response to her voice.
The officials in charge immediately reported to Tàizǔ,
who, startled, went to see it,
and the beauty was then released.
In Dàmíng fifth year,
Shìzǔ issued an edict saying:
"In the past, when the Hàn dynasty was in decline,
Bó Píng's glory ceased;
when the Wèi state was at peace,
Jiā Xiàn initiated plans—
all were due to the mind's expansion,
drawing from rituals and following edicts.
My deceased maternal grandmother, the wife of a Prince, possessed gentle virtue and a refined demeanor,
illuminating and supporting the feminine realm.
When the inner court lacked a proper mistress,
she managed the affairs of the women's quarters,
her demeanor graced the fragrant chambers,
her reputation spread throughout the imperial relatives' neighborhoods.
Thinking of her with enduring gratitude,
I wish to honor her with a distinguished rank.
It is fitting to follow the grand precedents
and respectfully elevate her in the ancestral order."
Thereupon, she was posthumously granted the title Pínglè Xiāngjūn of Xīngàn County, Yùzhāng Commandery.
She was the mother of the Empress.
Another edict said:
"The tombs of Zhào, Xiāo, Zāng Guānglù, Yuán Jìnggōng, and Pínglè Xiāngjūn
〔一一〕have not yet been provided with tomb-guard households.
Moreover, many generations have passed,
and their descendants are in decline.
It is not fitting for the graves of respected imperial maternal relatives to become overgrown.
Each may be provided with three Mán households
to supply sweeping and cleaning services."
The Empress's father, Zhàn,
has his own biography.
〔一二〕
Empress Wén's (Wén Dì) concubine, Lù Shūyuàn, whose personal name was Huìnán,
was from Jiànkāng in Dānyáng.
She was selected into the imperial harem for her beauty,
gave birth to Emperor Xiàowǔ,
and was granted the title Shūyuàn.
As she grew older,
she lost favor
and often accompanied Shìzǔ when he left the capital for a fief.
When Shìzǔ entered to suppress Yuánxiōng,
Shūyuàn remained in Xúnyáng.
Upon the Emperor's accession,
he dispatched Jiànpíng Wáng Hóng to escort her.
The officials presented a memorial saying:
"Your servant has heard that when the mandate gathered in the Zhōu state,
its glorious influence continued;
〔一三〕when the vital essence purified the Hàn state,
blessings emerged from Shālù.
In ancient times,
when enterprises flourished and destinies were long-lasting,
there was never a time when the feminine teachings were not spread to expand the grand foundation,
and auspicious blessings were not received to bear sagacious and wise individuals.
We humbly believe that Shūyuàn's gentle brilliance shone internally,
her admirable conduct served as an external model.
When her spiritual harmony first began to lead,
the many concubines looked up to her radiance;
when she guided and taught within the ducal household,
the family and state were imbued with virtue.
The people responded with harmony,
and the spirits belonged to her blessings.
Therefore, she was able to give birth to the sagacious person
and gather the great mandate,
solidifying the spiritual roots that were nearly extinguished,
and restoring the grand achievements in a middle restoration.
Her deep virtue and profound transformation,
her reputation and praise were truly harmonious.
It is fitting to follow the ancient rites
and respectfully enjoy the highest title.
We respectfully propose the honorable title Huáng Tàihòu,
〔一四〕and her palace to be Chóngxiàn."
The Empress Dowager resided in Xiǎnyáng Diàn.
Within the private chambers,
the Emperor's respect was very scant.
When he had concubines,
he would sometimes stay in the Empress Dowager's room.
Therefore, rumors spread among the people,
all of them ugly.
Palace matters were secret,
and no one could discern the truth.
In Xiàojiàn second year,
the Empress Dowager's father, Xīngzhī, was posthumously granted the title Sànqí Chángshì;
Xīngzhī's wife, Lady Xú, was posthumously granted the title Guǎngchāng Xiāngjūn of Yúháng County.
In Dàmíng fourth year,
the Empress Dowager's nephew, Fǔjūn Cānjūn Qióngzhī, submitted a memorial saying:
"My late uncle, the former Prefect of Huái'ān, Dàoqìng, had an unfortunate fate,
and departed from this enlightened age.
I dare to avail myself of the precedent of requesting titles for those who guarded the borders,
and specifically beg for 'clouds and rain,'
a slight bestowal of grace."
The edict was submitted to the Ménxià.
The officials, acting on the imperial will, proposed granting him the posthumous title Gěishì Zhōng.
Qióngzhī and his younger brothers Xiūzhī and Màozhī were all promoted to prominent positions.
The Empress Dowager often participated in political affairs
and bestowed wealth and goods upon Qióngzhī and others.
Their families accumulated thousands of gold pieces,
their residences, clothing, and utensils
were comparable to those of imperial sons.
Qióngzhī's residence shared a gate with Tàicháng Wáng Sēngdá.
He once ostentatiously visited Sēngdá with a grand retinue of carriages and servants,
but Sēngdá did not show him proper courtesy.
Qióngzhī complained about this to the Empress Dowager,
who became greatly enraged
and told the Emperor:
"I am still alive,
yet people are all bullying my family.
After I die, they will be begging for food!"
She wished to punish Sēngdá.
The Emperor said:
"Qióngzhī is young,
and should not have visited so lightly.
Wáng Sēngdá is a noble son;
how can he be punished for this matter?"
In Dàmíng fifth year,
the Empress Dowager accompanied the Emperor on a tour to Nányùzhōu,
with concubines and princesses also attending.
Upon the accession of the Deposed Emperor,
she was given the title Tàihuáng Tàihòu.
Tàizōng (太宗) ascended the throne,
and designated [his stepmother] as Chóngxiàn Tàihòu (崇憲太后).
Initially, Tàizōng (太宗) had lost his birth mother young,
and was raised and nurtured by the Tàihòu (太后).
Tàizōng (太宗) served her with utmost devotion,
〔一五〕and the Tàihòu (太后) loved and cared for him deeply.
When the emperor ascended the throne,
the rituals and provisions [for her]
did not differ from former days.
An official submitted a memorial, saying:
“Indeed, when virtue spreads internally,
ordinances and regulations are surely far-reaching;
when transformation extends externally,
auspicious titles should be proclaimed.
We humbly consider that Her Imperial Majesty the Empress Dowager is sagely and virtuous by nature,
and her maternal example is truly manifest.
Her righteousness illuminates the eight directions,
and her Way transforms the nine regions.
Now that the sagely and enlightened one has ascended the throne,
the auspicious blessings have changed;
it is proper for Her Imperial Majesty the Empress Dowager to succeed to her former title,
and reside in an outer palace.”
An imperial edict stated:
“I suffered the calamity of an early loss,
and became an orphan young.
I particularly received the sacred teachings and upbringing of Chóngxiàn Tàihòu (崇憲太后).
In the past, when I was at the frontier,
I always presented medicinal food,
but later, forced by cruel circumstances,
my filial aspirations could not be fulfilled.
Now that the prosperous era has just begun,
my filial sentiments and duties can be expressed.
I wish to personally serve her morning and evening,
and bring joy within the palace.
It is not to be as proposed.”
Soon after, she passed away,
at the age of fifty-five.
Her coffin was moved to the eastern palace,
and the gate was named Chóngxiàn Gōng (崇憲宮).
The emperor again issued an edict, saying:
“As a child, I endured bitter hardship,
and early on relied on her virtuous teachings.
To suppress rebels and establish the imperial domain,
I truly drew upon her benevolent example.
Her kindness was manifest in times of difficulty and ease,
exceeding ordinary affection.
Indeed, rites are extended by sentiment,
and righteousness is established in accordance with circumstances.
It is permissible for me to specifically wear mourning attire for three months,
to express my reverence and remembrance.”
She was posthumously granted the title Zhāo Huángtàihòu (昭皇太后),
and buried southeast of Shìzǔ (世祖)’s mausoleum,
named Xiūníng Líng (修寧陵).
Before this, when Jìn’ān Wáng Zǐxūn (晉安王子勛) was not yet pacified,
a shaman suggested opening Zhāo Tàihòu (昭太后)’s tomb for a protective charm.
The repairs were done in haste,
and not in accordance with ritual.
The emperor was by nature apprehensive [of ill omens],
fearing future disaster.
In the summer of Tàishǐ (泰始) fourth year (468 CE),
an edict was issued to the officials, saying:
“The site of Chóngxiàn Zhāo Tàihòu (崇憲昭太后)’s Xiūníng Líng (修寧陵)
was long surveyed and divined during the Dàmíng (大明) era.
The previous year, due to the difficulties with various barbarian tribes,
the rites were handled expediently.
The construction was rushed,
and there was no time for changes.
Moreover, the location of the tomb tunnel
is on low and inferior terrain.
In recent years, it has fallen into disrepair,
worsening day by day.
Repairs are costly,
and it will never be permanently secure.
Furthermore, a detailed examination of the topography
reveals it deviates significantly from auspicious geomantic principles.
I received her maternal care early,
with affection and ritual exceeding the usual.
I wish to make the meaning of beginning and end [of life]
manifest in both the visible and invisible worlds.
Let the court historians select a new auspicious site
around Yánshān (巖山).
They must carefully consult tortoiseshell and milfoil,
select an auspicious day,
follow the old ordinances,
and establish the system with proper rites.
Although the central realm is now peaceful,
the border barbarians have not yet ceased,
so the construction work
must prioritize simplicity.
Every word uttered brings sorrow,
my heart feels torn.”
Officials memorialized:
“The northern frontier is not yet settled,
and military affairs are a priority.
The detail or brevity of rites
should each follow the needs of the time.
We, your ministers, have discussed and propose that
the dark palace of Xiūníng Líng (修寧陵) be repaired where it is damaged,
a temporary oil-lamp hall be erected,
the imperial coffin temporarily moved out,
and then re-interred once the work is complete.
This would be appropriate for the situation.”
An edict approved this.
Qióng (瓊) was the Internal Administrator of Héngyáng (衡陽).
His mother died before him.
During the Jǐnghé (景和) era of the Deposed Emperor,
Xiūzhī (休之) was made a Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎),
and Màozhī (茂之) a Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn (左軍將jūn),
both enfeoffed as Kāiguó Xiànhóu (開國縣侯),
with an income of one thousand households.
Furthermore, Xìngzhī (興之) was posthumously granted Sàngzhōng (侍中) and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (金紫光祿大夫),
with the posthumous title Xiàohóu (孝侯);
Dàoqìng (道慶) was granted Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍), Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫), and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司),
with the posthumous title Jìnghóu (敬侯).
Dàoqìng (道慶)’s daughter was established as Empress,
and Xiūzhī (休之) was made Sàngzhōng (侍中),
Màozhī (茂之) Huángmén Láng (黃門郎).
Tàizōng (太宗) deposed the young emperor,
and wishing to appease the Empress Dowager,
issued an edict stating:
“Her Grand Imperial Majesty the Empress Dowager bestowed her affection early,
and in her sentiments and actions,
is like a blood relative.
Former Chējì Zīyì Cānjūn (車騎諮議參軍) Lù Xiūzhī (路休之) and former Dānyáng Céng (丹陽丞) Lù Màozhī (路茂之)
are close relatives of Chóngxiàn (崇憲),
and have long enjoyed renown.
Both have rendered service,
and should receive special honors.
Xiūzhī (休之) is appointed Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎),
concurrently leading Bùbīng Xiàowèi (步兵校尉);
Màozhī (茂之) is appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎).”
Tàizōng (太宗) had not yet ascended the throne,
hence it was called a “command letter” (lìngshū).
Màozhī (茂之) was later promoted to Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng (司徒從事中郎),
and Xiūzhī (休之) became Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn (桂陽王休範)’s Zhènběi Zīyì Cānjūn (鎮北諮議參軍).
Tàizōng (太宗) killed all of Shìzǔ (世祖)’s sons,
and consequently implicated Xiūzhī (休zhī) and others,
but pardoned their sons.
Xiàowǔ Wénmù Wáng Huánghòu (孝武文穆王皇后), given name Xiànjié (憲嫄),
was from Línyí (臨沂), Lángxié (琅邪).
In Yuánjiā (元嘉) twentieth year (443 CE),
she was appointed Wǔlíng Wáng Fēi (武陵王妃).

She gave birth to the Deposed Emperor, Yùzhāng Wáng Zǐshàng (豫章王子尚), Shānyīn Gōngzhǔ Chǔyù (山陰公主楚玉), Línhuái Kāng'āi Gōngzhǔ Chǔpèi (臨淮康哀公主楚佩), Princess Chǔxiù (楚琇), and Kānglè Gōngzhǔ Xiūmíng (康樂公主脩明).
When Shìzǔ (世祖) was at the frontier,
the Empress was much favored.
When the emperor went to suppress the rebels,
the Empress remained in Xúnyáng (尋陽),
and returned to the capital with the Empress Dowager,
where she was established as Empress.
In Dàmíng (大明) fourth year (460 CE),
the Empress led the six palaces in personally picking mulberry leaves in the western suburbs,
while the Empress Dowager observed the rites.
An imperial edict stated:
“I divined auspiciousness at dawn,
and measured the auspicious time by the feathers,
then ordered the six palaces
to personally cultivate silkworms in the silkworm house.
Her Imperial Majesty the Empress Dowager descended from her carriage and followed the imperial retinue,
pausing to observe the rites.
With the green silkworm baskets ready,
and the black drums now beating,
may the auspicious ceremony bring forth fragrant blessings,
and the inner transformative influence move the central realm.
Princesses and all below them
may be granted additional emoluments as appropriate.”
When the Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
she was honored as Huángtàihòu (皇太后),
and her palace was named Yǒngxùn (永訓).
In that same year,
she passed away in the Hánzhāng Diàn (含章殿),
at the age of thirty-eight.
She was interred with Shìzǔ (世祖) at Jǐngníng Líng (景寧陵).
Hòufù Yǎn
—style name Zǐyóu—
was the great-great-grandson of Jìn Chancellor Dǎo,
and the son of Shàngshū Gǔ.
[一六]His mother was Pōyáng Gōngzhǔ, daughter of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn.
[一七]When the Sòng dynasty received the abdication,
she was enfeoffed as Yǒngchéng Jūn.
Yǎn married Gāozǔ's second daughter, Wúxīng Zhǎnggōngzhǔ, whose taboo name was Róngnán.
In his youth, he held prominent official positions:
Huángmén Shìláng,
Mìshūjiān,
and Shìzhōng.
At the end of the Yuánjiā reign,
he served as Sànqí Chángshì and Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
as the Hòufù,
he was granted the title of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
appointed as tutor to Yìyáng Wáng,
and retained his position as Chángshì.
He was promoted to Yòuguānglù Dàfū,
and his positions as Chángshì and Wángshī remained unchanged.
Yǎn was humble and cautious,
and did not concern himself with worldly affairs.
He died in the second year of Xiàojiàn,
aged fifty-four.
He was posthumously granted Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
his former official position remained,
and he was posthumously enfeoffed with the epithet Gōnggōng.
His eldest son, Zǎo,
rose to the position of Dōngyáng Tàishǒu.
He married Tàizǔ's sixth daughter, Línchuān Zhǎnggōngzhǔ, whose taboo name was Yīngyuán.
The Princess was jealous,
and Zǎo had a separate affection for a servant, Wú Chóngzǔ.
During the Jǐnghé reign of the former deposed emperor,
the Princess slandered him to the deposed emperor,
and Zǎo was imprisoned and died.
The Princess divorced the Wáng clan.
At the beginning of Tàishǐ,
the Princess was married to Yùzhāng Tàishǒu Yǔ Chōngyuǎn,
but Chōngyuǎn died before the ceremony could be completed.
Among the princesses of the Sòng dynasty,
there was none who was not strictly jealous,
and Tàizōng often resented this.
The wife of Húshú Lìng Yuán Tāo was given death for her jealousy,
and the emperor ordered his close minister Yú Tōngzhī to compile "Jì Dùfù Jì" (Records of Jealous Wives).
When Jiāng Zhàn's grandson, Jiào, the Zǔoguānglù Dàfū, was about to marry Shìzǔ's daughter,
the emperor had someone write a memorial for Jiào to decline the marriage,
which stated: "I humbly acknowledge the imperial edict,
that Línrǔ Gōngzhǔ is to be given in marriage.
[一八]This honor surpasses my expectations,
and this grace is beyond the usual custom.
Considering my meager and humble status,
I am filled with trepidation.
My family is of humble origin, a declining clan;
I am an ordinary and simple person.
Among the common folk, there are matches;
but originally, I am separated from imperial marriage.
For someone of my common background,
whose household is poor and occupation meager,
who is nearing the age of capping,
most already have
wives.
With a thorn hairpin and plain skirt,
a marriage can be accomplished.
I have never understood why
I have remained single until now.
No matchmakers were sought,
[一九]nor were noble families inquired about.
I only considered my family's fortune,
that it should be blessed with a princess.
The imperial grace has extended
even to such an insignificant one as myself.
I am filled with worry and apprehension,
fearing that I cannot escape it.
Since it is an imperial command,
I am indeed destined for this undertaking.
Although it brings honor to my family
and glory to my ancestors,
it is not fortunate for me.
I rely on Your Majesty's pardon
to humbly present my true feelings.
Since the Jìn dynasty,
those who married imperial princesses,
though they might have been from noble families for generations
and often possessed remarkable talents,
yet Wáng Dūn was intimidated,
Huán Wēn restrained his authority,
Zhēncháng
feigned foolishness to seek exemption,
and Zǐjìng burned his foot to defy the edict.
Wáng Yǎn lacked the qualities of Zhòngdū,
and yet was stripped naked on the northern steps.
Hé Yǔ lacked the demeanor of Lónggōng,
and
threw himself into a deep well.
Xiè Zhuāng almost equated himself with a blind old man,
[二０]and Yīn Chōng nearly could not escape being forcibly tilled.
These several men,
[二一]were not without talent or intelligence,
yet
their power was subservient to their noble wives,
and their affairs were hidden from public view.
They swallowed their sorrow and suppressed their anger,
having nowhere to flee or complain.
Their restraint was stricter than that of servants,
and their restrictions exceeded those for maids and concubines.
Coming and going,
entering and exiting,
are normal human activities.
Hosting guests
is a matter of friendship.
Yet they were made to sweep their tracks and halt their carriages,
with no hope of peering at their gates;
to dismantle their banquets and withdraw their mats,
cutting off the possibility of meeting
and interacting.
Not only were their friends alienated,
but even their brothers became distant.
They were allowed to receive gifts of wine and meat,
but their movements were controlled;
the husbands were burdened with private expenses in money and silk,
and their speech and laughter were restricted.
The wet nurses competed to flatter,
encouraging strictness;
the maids and old women vied to come forward,
flattering with urgency.
They were all ordinary, mediocre talents,
and the husbands were all foolish commoners
from Jiāmáng.
When discussing conduct, they were unskilled in distinguishing right from wrong;
when listening to speech, they were mistaken about truth and falsehood.
The wet nurses dared to rely on their seniority,
only advocating jealousy.
The maids and old women proclaimed themselves to be knowledgeable,
and
made it their business to guard speech.
Among them, there were also those who answered questions and inquired about matters,
such as diviners and wet nurses.
Even with leftover food and drink,
they would question with whom it was shared.
If clothes and bedding were old and worn,
they would certainly
demand an accounting from the head.
Moreover, the propriety of going out and coming in
was difficult to reconcile between frequent and sparse.
Sometimes, one wished to advance but could not;
sometimes, one entered but was not allowed to leave.
If one did not enter, one was suspected of wishing to be distant;
if one sought to leave, one was
suspected of having other intentions.
When summoned, the deadline was always three o'clock in the afternoon;
when dismissed, the limit was always sunrise.
In the evening, one did not see the late moon;
in the morning, one did not know the dawn star.
As for walking in the moonlight
and playing the zither at night,
or bowing one's sleeves and perusing scrolls by day,
throughout one's life,
one was constantly estranged from these pleasures.
Moreover, if a sound or shadow was barely heard,
the young maids would rush out;
if one's skirt or sleeve approached a mat,
the
old and ugly women would flock together.
If one tidied oneself up,
one was suspected of seeking favor and thus resented;
if guests were not yet capped,
they were dismissed for their youthful appearance.
In ritual, there are concubines arranged in order;
in symbolism, there are fish
strung together.
Originally, there was no suspicion of disrespecting the principal wife,
so how could there be a reproach of disparaging the wife?
Moreover, now that private affairs are cut off by righteousness,
and one sincerely reveres the proper spouse,
yet in every matter, it is said that there is no proper conduct;
when
words are spoken, it is always said, 'You treat me lightly.'
Furthermore, I secretly heard that when the princesses gather,
they only discuss their husbands' families.
The lenient are not sufficient as models for the strict,
but the strict can be teachers for the lenient.
They
incite and tempt each other,
and their original intention
is not to lend or borrow,
but it is truly a constant refrain.
Some say, 'He failed and left,'
or 'People laugh at me.'
Although family matters are said to be private,
they are more
severe than the royal laws.
What is spoken
is equivalent to legal codes.
Although Wáng Zǎo was stubborn
and quite learned,
a matter of jest
led him to become a wronged spirit.
Chǔ Ài worried."
憤，
用致夭絕．
傷理害義，
難以具聞．
夫螽斯之德，
實致克昌；
專妒之行，
有妨繁衍．
是以尚主之門，
往往絕嗣；
駙馬之
身，
通離釁咎．
以臣凡弱，
何以克堪．
必將毀族淪門，
豈伊身眚．
前後嬰此，
其人雖
衆，
然皆患彰遐邇，
事隔天朝，
故吞言咽理，
無敢論訴．
臣幸屬聖明，
矜照由道，
弘物以
典，
處親以公，
臣之鄙懷，
可得自盡．
如臣門分，
世荷殊榮，
足守前基，
便預提拂，
清
官顯宦，
或由才升，
一叨婚戚，
咸成恩假．
〔二二〕是以仰冒非宜，
披露丹實．
非唯止陳
一己，
規全身願；
實乃廣申諸門憂患之切．
伏願天慈照察，
特賜蠲停，
使燕雀微羣，
得保叢蔚，
蠢物含生，
自己彌篤．
若恩詔難降，
披請不申，
便當刊膚剪髮，
投山竄
海．
太宗以此表徧示諸主．
於是臨川長公主上表曰：
「妾遭隨奇薄，
絕於王氏，
私庭囂戾，
致此分異．
今孤疾煢然，
假息朝夕，
情寄所鍾，
唯在一子．
契闊荼炭，
持兼憐愍，
否泰枯榮，
繫以為命．
實願申其門釁，
還為母子．
推遷僶俛，
未及自聞．
先朝慈愛，
鑑妾丹衷．
若賜使息徹歸第定省，
仰揆天旨，
或有可尋．
今事迫誠切，
不顧典憲，
敢緣恩燾，
觸冒披聞．
特乞還身王族，
守養弱嗣．
雖死之日，
實甘於生． 」
許之．
藻弟懋，
昇明末貴達．
懋弟攸，
太宰從事中郎．
蚤卒，
追贈黃門侍郎．
弟臻，
昇明末 顯宦．
前廢帝何皇后諱令婉，
廬江灊人也．
孝建三年，
納為皇太子妃，
大明五年，
薨于東宮徽光殿，
時年十七．
諡曰獻妃．
上更為太子置內職二等，
曰保林，
曰良娣．
納南中郎長史太山羊瞻女為良娣，
宜都太守袁僧惠女為保林．
廢帝即位，
追崇獻妃曰獻皇后．
太宗踐阼，
遷后與廢帝合葬龍山北．
后父瑀，
字稚玉，
晉尚書左僕射澄曾孫也．
祖融，
大司農．
瑀尚高祖少女豫章康長公主諱欣男．
公主先適徐喬，
美容色，
聰敏有智數，
太祖世，
禮待特隆．
瑀豪競於時，
與平昌孟靈休、東海何勗等，
並以輿馬驕奢相尚．
公主與瑀情愛隆密，
何氏外姻疏戚，
莫不沾被恩紀．
瑀歷位清顯，
至衞將軍．
〔二三〕大明八年，
公主薨，
瑀墓開，
世祖追贈金紫光祿大夫，
加散騎常侍．
子邁，
尚太祖第十女新蔡公主諱英媚．
邁少以貴戚居顯宦，
好犬馬馳逐，
多聚才力之士．
有墅在江乘縣界，
去京師三十里．
邁每游履，
輒結駟連騎，
武士成羣．
大明末，
為豫章王子尚撫軍諮議參軍，
加寧朔將軍、南濟陰太守．
廢帝納公主於後宮，
偽言薨殞，
殺一婢送 出邁第殯葬行喪禮．
常疑邁有異圖，
邁亦招聚同志，
欲因行幸廢立．
事覺，
廢帝自出討邁誅之．
太宗即位，
追封建寧縣侯，
食邑五百戶．
子曼倩嗣，
齊受禪，
國除．
Yǔ's elder brother's son, Liàng,
in the early Xiàojiàn era,
was appointed as the Administrator of Guìyáng.
When Chancellor Nánjùn Wáng Yìxuān rebelled,
he dispatched his staff officer Wáng Shīshòu to block the Guìyáng road,
to prevent the Governor of Guǎngzhōu, Zōng [Píng],
from advancing. Liàng arrested and executed him.
〔二四〕He rose to the position of Intendant of Xīn'ān.
Liàng's younger brother, Huī,
in the early Yuánhuī era of the Deposed Emperor,
was appointed Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
Before he reached his post,
he was implicated for not arriving during the prescribed period of mourning for the nation,
and was dismissed from office.
He was later reinstated as Minister of the Court of Judicial Review,
but died
before his official investiture.
Huī's younger brother, Dàn,
was the Right Chief Clerk of the Minister of Works.
Dàn's younger brother, Yǎn,
was the most well-known.
His nature was restless and volatile.
In the early Tàizōng era,
he served as the Assistant Administrator to the Minister of Works for Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén,
and was subsequently appointed as Yellow Gate Attendant.
Before he was fully invested,
he sought a transfer to the Aide-de-camp of the Minister of Works.
After obtaining the Aide-de-camp position,
he again sought the Right Commander of the Crown Prince's Guard.
After serving as Right Commander for one or two days,
he again sought the position of Palace Attendant.
Within a mere ten days,
he ceaselessly sought advancement.
Failing to obtain the Palace Attendant position,
he was granted death by his own hand due to his resentful curses.
Emperor Wén's Concubine Shěn, whose given name was Róngjī,
〔二五〕her origins are unknown.
She was brought into the imperial harem
as a court lady of beauty (měirén).
She gave birth to Emperor Míng,
and was elevated to the rank of Concubine (jiéyú).
She died in the thirtieth year of Yuánjiā,
at the age of forty.
She was buried on Mòfǔshān in Jiànkāng.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
she was posthumously granted the title of Grand Consort of Xiāngdōng Commandery.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
the relevant officials memorialized, saying:
"In ancient Bīndū, they honored the distant ancestors;
in Zhèngyì, they were steeped in sorrow.
With profound admiration for their virtue and righteousness,
they respectfully maintained the imperial tombs.
The late Grand Consort's virtuous conduct was resplendent and elegant,
her bright qualities were illustrious and majestic.
Her influence graced the imperial palace,
her teachings flowed through the national court.
Having nurtured the sage and given birth to the divine,
she prematurely relinquished her great fortune.
We, your servants, emulate the Han records from afar,
and follow the Jin precedents nearby,
and respectfully present the esteemed title of Empress Dowager."
The ritual officials were instructed to deliberate on a posthumous name.
She was posthumously named Xuān Tàihòu,
and her mausoleum was named Chóngníng.
The Empress Dowager's younger brother, Dàoqìng, was appointed Gěishìzhōng.
He died in the third year of Tàishǐ,
and was posthumously granted the title of Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì,
and bestowed the peerage of County Marquis.
The Empress Dowager's father was also posthumously granted the title of Sànqí Chángshì,
and her mother, Lady Wáng, was ennobled as Chénglè Xiāngjūn.
Empress Mínggōng Wáng, whose given name was Zhēngfēng,
was from Línyí, Lángyá.
In the twenty-fifth year of Yuánjiā,
she was appointed Princess of Huáiyáng.
When Tàizōng changed his enfeoffment,
she became Princess of Xiāngdōng.
〔二六〕She gave birth to Princess Jìnlíng Bó Sī and Princess Jiàn'ān Bó Yuán.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
she was established as Empress.
Once, the Emperor held a grand assembly within the palace,
and the women watched,
taking pleasure and laughter in it.
The Empress, however, covered her face with a fan,
and said nothing.
The Emperor angrily said:
"Your family outside are poor beggars.
Now everyone is enjoying themselves,
why are you the only one not looking?"
The Empress replied:
"There are many ways
to enjoy oneself.
How can a gathering of aunts and sisters
be a display of women's bodies
to be enjoyed?
The enjoyment of my family outside
is truly not like this."
The Emperor was greatly angered,
and ordered the Empress to leave.
The Empress's elder brother, Governor of Yángzhōu Jǐngwén, recounted this incident to his maternal cousin, Xiè Wěi of Chénjùn, saying:
"At home, the Empress was a timid woman,
I did not know that she could be so upright now."
When the Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
she was honored as Empress Dowager,
and her palace was named Hóngxùn.
The Deposed Emperor indulged in misconduct,
and the Empress Dowager frequently admonished him.
Initially, he still complied,
but later, his wild and perverse behavior worsened,
and he gradually became displeased.
On the fifth day of the fifth month of the fifth year of Yuánhuī,
the Empress Dowager gifted the Emperor a jade-handled fur fan.
The Emperor disliked its unadorned fur handle,
and because of this, wished to poison her.
He had already ordered the imperial physician to prepare the medicine,
but his attendants dissuaded him, saying:
"If Your Majesty carries out this deed,
you will then have to act as a filial son.
How could you possibly continue to go in and out mischievously?"
The Emperor said:
"What you say is very reasonable."
And so he stopped.
When Emperor Shùn ascended the throne,
Qí Wáng held power,
and members of the imperial clan like Líu Huàng, Líu Chuò, and Bǔ Bóxīng harbored rebellious intentions.
The Empress Dowager was somewhat involved.
When Emperor Shùn abdicated the throne,
the Empress Dowager and the Emperor moved to the Eastern Residence,
and subsequently relocated to Dānyáng Palace,
where she was appointed Grand Consort of Rǔyīn.
After Emperor Shùn died in Dānyáng,
she established another residence in the capital.
In the first year of Jiànyuán,
she died in her residence
at the age of forty-four.
She was posthumously honored with a title and posthumous name,
and buried with the rites of a Song Empress.
Her father, Sēnglǎng,
is mentioned separately in Jǐngwén's biography.
Emperor Míng's Noble Consort Chén, whose given name was Miàodēng,
was from Jiànkāng, Dānyáng,
the daughter of a butcher.
Shìzǔ often ordered his county officials to search among the common people for beautiful daughters.
The Grand Consort's family lived in Jiànkāng County,
and was poor,
with only two or three thatched huts.
When the Emperor was out traveling,
he asked the official:
"How can there be such thatched huts by the imperial road?
This must be due to poverty."
He bestowed thirty thousand cash,
ordering them to build tiled houses.
The official personally delivered the money to them.
All the family members were out,
only the Grand Consort was at home,
then twelve or thirteen years old.
The official saw her exceptionally beautiful appearance,
and immediately reported it to Shìzǔ.
Thereupon, she was welcomed into the palace.
She stayed in the Empress Dowager's chambers for
two or three years,
and was called upon twice,
but did not gain imperial favor.
The Empress Dowager then spoke to the Emperor,
and she was bestowed upon Tàizōng.
She initially gained favor,
but after about a year, her favor declined,
and she was given to Lǐ Dào'ér.
Soon after, she was brought back
and gave birth to the Deposed Emperor.
Hence, among the common people, the Deposed Emperor was called Lǐ Shì Zǐ (Son of the Lǐ clan).
The Deposed Emperor later often referred to himself as General Lǐ,
or sometimes as Lǐ Tǒng.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
he appointed Guì Fēi
with a ritual rank equivalent to that of the crown prince’s consort.
When Fèi Dì ascended the throne,
the appropriate officials memorialized, saying:
“Your servants have heard that the river dragon initiated sagely governance,
its order pervasive among men and spirits;
the suburban lightning established imperial rule,
its auspiciousness shining through heaven and earth.
Therefore, the way of reverence
has been purely inscribed in ancient customs;
the principle of honoring the noble
has been eternally established as a norm.
We humbly observe that Guì Fēi embodies harmony like the sun’s shadow,
manifests virtue like the celestial pivot.
Her illustrious reputation is lofty and ancient,
her gentle brilliance illuminates the world.
Her fame and splendor fill the imperial palace,
her conduct is exquisite among the heavenly concubines.
Her glory radiates imperial brilliance,
and her fortune brings prosperity to the sagely mandate.
Yet the statutes for her full endowment
have not yet been clearly established in the permanent regulations.
Drawing remotely from former kings,
we should indeed elevate her to the grand canon.
Your servants have deliberated
and respectfully propose the venerable title ‘Huáng Tàifēi’.
Her carriages and attire shall be entirely in accordance with the precedent of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn’s empress dowager.
A household manager (jiālìng) shall be appointed for her.
All other princely consorts (guó tàifēi) shall be retitled ‘Tàifēi’.
(Fēi is pronounced yī.)
〔二七〕Her palace shall be named Hónghuà.”
Posthumously, Tàifēi’s father, Jīnbǎo, was granted the title Sànqí Chángshì,
and Jīnbǎo’s wife, Lady Wáng, was granted the title Yǒngshì Xiàn Chènglè Xiāngjūn.
In the beginning of Shēngmíng,
she was demoted to Cāngwú Wáng Tàifēi.
Her paternal uncle, Zhàozōng,
was a Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén.
Her paternal uncle, Fóniàn,
was a Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
Her elder brother, Jìngyuán,
was a Tōngzhí Láng
and Administrator of Nánlǔ Jùn.
Fóniàn indulged in extensive bribery
and disrupted court politics.
In the beginning of Shēngmíng,
he was given death.
The later Fèi Dì’s Empress Jiāng, whose taboo name was Jiǎn Guī,
was a native of Kǎochéng in Jìyáng,
and the granddaughter of Zhìyuān, the Běi Zhōngláng Chángshǐ.
In the fifth year of Tàishǐ,
Tàizōng sought a consort for the Crown Prince.
Being overly reliant on minor numerology,
many daughters from prominent families were deemed unsuitable.
The Empress was young and small,
with no powerful patronage,
but as divination showed her to be most auspicious,
she was consequently chosen as the Crown Prince’s consort.
He implicitly ordered court officials and prefectural governors to present gifts,
the most valuable of which would be worth a hundred gold coins.
Sūn Fèngbó, the Administrator of Shǐxīng, merely presented a qín and books,
with no other items.
The Emperor was greatly angered,
sent poisoned medicine, ordering his death,
but later pardoned him.
When the Crown Prince ascended the throne,
she was established as Empress.
After the Emperor was deposed,
she was demoted to Cāngwú Wáng Fēi.
A separate biography exists for Zhìyuān.
Míng Dì’s Chén Zhāohuá, whose taboo name was Fǎróng,
was a native of Jiànkāng in Dānyáng.
In Tàizōng’s later years,
he suffered from a wasting illness and was unable to engage in intimate relations.
Whenever a concubine of his brothers became pregnant,
he would take her into the palace.
When a son was born,
he would kill the mother
and give the child to one of the beloved women in the six palaces to raise.
Shùn Dì was
the son of Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn,
and took Zhāohuá as his mother.
When Míng Dì died,
Zhāohuá was appointed Ānchéng Wáng Tàifēi.
When Shùn Dì ascended the throne,
she was promoted to Huáng Tàifēi.
When Shùn Dì abdicated,
the title of Huáng Tàifēi was removed.
Shùn Dì’s Empress Xiè, whose taboo name was Fànjìng,
was a native of Yángxià in Chénjùn,
and the granddaughter of Zhuāng, the Yòu Guānglù Dàfū.
In the second year of Shēngmíng,
she was established as Empress.
When Shùn Dì abdicated,
she was demoted to Rǔyīn Wáng Fēi.
A separate biography exists for Zhuāng.
The court historian says: Food and drink, men and women,
are where man’s great desires lie.
〔二八〕Therefore, the sages followed human nature and established norms for them.
The royal palace had six ranks,
and the scholar's dwelling had two grades,
all with specific officials and defenses,
and detailed literary regulations.
As for those whose righteousness was firm in the private quarters
and whose transforming influence shaped the nation,
ancient wise kings achieved good governance through them.
Indeed, when empresses and consorts solely presided over the nights,
they were chosen for their virtue;
when concubines and maids were equally favored,
their advancement was not due to physical allure.
The aim was to ensure that affection was broadly distributed,
and love was not partial,
that loyalty was upheld internally,
and corrupting influences ceased externally.
As for betrothal and marriage, there were established rules,
matching them to the heavenly consort,
they must be descendants of the Four Peaks.
Although they held the rightful position in the inner chambers,
and their ritual honor was supreme,
yet decline and disillusionment were easily portended,
and grace and favor were difficult to retain.
Once dismissed, like the dust of a passing carriage,
they were forever separated from the green rush mats.
This is why the principal consorts were cautious about their end,
and there was good reason for it.
Since Yuánjiā,
the inner offices gradually proliferated.
The pepper palace’s ornate structures had thousands of gates and tens of thousands of households,
and the lavish and grotesque decorations
were endlessly varied and dazzling.
Even the splendor of the Zhāoyáng Palace of the Hàn dynasty
or the brilliance of the Jiǔhuá Palace of the Wèi dynasty
could not rival even a fraction of their magnificence.
It was merely that those selected were confined to the military headquarters,
and recruitment extended to the servants and attendants,
not like the Jìn dynasty, which indiscriminately selected from among the gentry.
〔二九〕Moreover, affection was confined to the inner chambers,
and power was not granted externally.
Relatives received provisions and gifts
that at most amounted to a few dishes and drinks annually.
This was considered excellent.
However, when Tàizǔ was infatuated with Pān Yù,
he consulted a woman on matters of state;
and Dàmíng was deeply immersed with Yīn Jī,
elevating her to the status of Empress and principal consort.
This led to many difficulties arising from personal indulgence,
and lives being taken among immediate family members.
How much more so for those who went further than this!
From this perspective,
the ruin of the Three Dynasties and the Two Hàns due to licentiousness and favoritism
was no accident.
Collator's Notes
Biographies, Chapter Two: Liú Mùzhī, Wáng Hóng
Liú Mùzhī,
courtesy name Dàohé,
childhood name Dàomín,
was a native of Jǔ in Dōngguǎn,
and a descendant of Féi, King Dàohuì of Qí during the Hàn dynasty.
His family had resided in Jīngkǒu for generations.
In his youth, he loved books and biographies,
read widely and was extensively knowledgeable.
He was recognized by Jiāng Yǎn of Jìyáng.
Yǎn was the Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn and Lángyé Nèishǐ,
and appointed him as his Fǔ Zhǔbù.
Initially,
Mùzhī once dreamt he was on a boat journey with Gāozǔ across the sea,
when suddenly a great wind struck,
filling him with terror.
Looking down beneath the boat,
he saw two white dragons flanking the vessel.
Soon after, they arrived at a mountain,
with peaks and ridges soaring elegantly,
and dense forests of trees,
which pleased him greatly.
When Gāozǔ conquered Jīngchéng,
he asked Hé Wújì,
"I urgently need a principal clerk for the commandery,
how can I find one?"
Wújì replied,
"None is better than Liú Dàomín."
Gāozǔ said,
"I know him too."
He immediately dispatched a messenger to summon him.
At that time, Mùzhī heard the sounds of shouting and clamor in Jīngchéng,
and rising in the morning, went out to the roadside,
where he happened to meet the messenger.
Mùzhī stared straight ahead, speechless for a long time.
Afterward, he returned to his room,
cut up a cloth gown to make trousers,
and went to see Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ said to him,
"I have just raised the banner of righteousness,
and am embarking on a difficult enterprise.
I urgently need a military officer;
who do you think is suitable for this selection?"
Mùzhī replied,
"As your esteemed commandery is newly established,
a military officer truly needs talent.
In this urgent situation,
there is probably no one who surpasses me."
Gāozǔ laughed and said,
"If you are willing to humble yourself,
my affairs will be accomplished."
He was immediately appointed on the spot.
From the pacification of Jīngyì,
when Gāozǔ first arrived,
all major arrangements
were swiftly decided,
and all were proposed by Mùzhī.
Consequently, he was entrusted with vital responsibilities,
and consulted on every move.
Mùzhī also exerted himself to the utmost, with complete sincerity,
concealing nothing.
At that time, the Jìn dynasty's governance was lax,
its authority unenforced.
Powerful clans and wealthy magnates,
relying on their influence, acted wantonly,
while common people were impoverished and desperate,
with no means to establish themselves.
Compounding this, Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn's decrees were inconsistent and contradictory,
and Huán Xuán's regulations were numerous and strict.
Mùzhī carefully considered what was appropriate for the times,
correcting matters as circumstances required.
In less than ten days,
customs were completely reformed.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Cíbù Láng,
then again served as Fǔ Zhǔbù,
Jìshì Lùshì Cānjūn,
and concurrently held the post of Tángyì Tàishǒu.
For his achievements in pacifying Huán Xuán,
he was enfeoffed as a fifth-rank viscount of Xīhuá Xiàn.
In the third year of Yìxī,
Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Mì died.
It was Gāozǔ's turn to enter the administration as a regent,
but Liú Yì and others did not wish for Gāozǔ to enter,
proposing that Zhōnglǐngjūn Xiè Hùn be made Yángzhōu.
Some also wished for Gāozǔ to govern the province from Dāntú,
entrusting internal affairs to Shàngshū Púyè Mèng Chǎng.
Shàngshū Yòuchéng Pí Shěn was sent to consult Gāozǔ on these two proposals.
Shěn first met Mùzhī,
and fully explained the court's discussions.
Mùzhī feigned going to the latrine,
then secretly penned a memorial to Gāozǔ, saying,
"Pí Shěn has just arrived;
his words should not be followed."
When Gāozǔ met Shěn,
he first dismissed him outside,
then called Mùzhī and asked,
"You said Shěn's words should not be followed;
what do you mean?"
Mùzhī replied,
"In the past, the Jìn court's misrule
was not a matter of a single day.
Moreover, with Huán Xuán's usurpation,
the Mandate of Heaven had already shifted.
You have revived the imperial lineage,
achieving everlasting merit.
Having great merit,
you should then hold a great position.
A great position and high merit
cannot be maintained indefinitely.
Given your current situation,
how can you be humble and weaken yourself,
becoming merely a border-defending general?
Liú, Mèng, and other gentlemen
rose from common origins with you,
and together established this great righteous cause,
originally intending to assist the ruler and achieve merit,
thereby gaining wealth and honor.
Affairs have their progression;
thus, for a time, they deferred credit,
not truly submitting wholeheartedly
or having long established the distinction between minister and sovereign.
With equal strength and power,
they will eventually devour each other.
Yángzhōu is fundamentally important,
and cannot be entrusted to others.
Previously, it was given to Wáng Mì,
which was a temporary expedient,
not necessarily a long-term grand strategy.
If it is now given to someone else again,
you will become subject to others.
Once you lose power,
you will have no way to regain it.
And with your high achievements and heavy merit,
you cannot simply remain in your current position.
Doubts and fears will intertwine,
and various factions will arise,
bringing future dangers
that must be carefully considered.
Since the court's discussion is thus,
you should respond appropriately.
If you insist it must be you,
it will be difficult to frame the words.
You should only say, 'The governance of the Divine Land is fundamental,
and the prime minister is of crucial importance.
The rise and fall hinge upon this,
so careful selection is necessary.
As this matter is great,
it cannot be decided in advance.
I will temporarily enter the court,
and we can thoroughly discuss our differing views.'
When you arrive in the capital,
they will certainly not dare to pass over you and appoint someone else; that is clear."
Gāozǔ followed his advice,
and thus entered the administration as a regent.
He participated in the campaign against Guǎnggù,
then returned to resist Lú Xún.
He often stayed in the command tent, devising strategies
and making decisions on all matters.
Liú Yì and others resented Mùzhī's favor
and often subtly spoke of his excessive power.
However, Gāozǔ trusted and relied on him even more.
Everything Mùzhī heard or saw externally,
no matter how big or small, he reported.
Even trivial gossip from neighborhoods
and minor incidents on the roads
were all reported one by one.
Gāozǔ often gained insights by receiving secret information from the populace,
all thanks to Mùzhī.
He also enjoyed entertaining guests,
his hall always full of visitors.
He spread his network of ears and eyes to gather intelligence.
Thus, Mùzhī knew all the agreements and disagreements in the court and among the populace.
Even the virtues and flaws of his close associates
were reported without concealment.
Some criticized him,
to which Mùzhī replied:
"With the Duke's perceptiveness,
these matters will eventually come to light on their own.
I have received the Duke's kindness,
and it would be against my duty to hide anything.
This is like Zhāng Liáo informing Guān Yǔ of his intention to defect."
Mùzhī laid down the regulations for all of Gāozǔ's actions and conduct.
Gāozǔ's handwriting was naturally clumsy.
Mùzhī said:
"Although this is a small matter,
it is to be proclaimed to the four distant regions;
I hope the Duke will pay a little more attention."
Since Gāozǔ could not focus on it
and his innate ability was what it was,
Mùzhī then said:
"Just write freely with large characters,
each character a foot wide,
there will be no objection.
Large characters can encompass enough,
and their appearance is also beautiful."
Gāozǔ followed this advice,
and a single sheet would be full with no more than six or seven characters.
Whenever he recommended someone for promotion,
he would not stop until they advanced.
He often said:
"Though I cannot match Xún Lìngjūn in promoting the good,
I do not fail to promote the not-bad."
Mùzhī and Zhū Língshí were both skilled in writing letters.
Once, in Gāozǔ's presence, they exchanged letters with Língshí.
From dawn until midday,
Mùzhī received a hundred letters,
and Língshí received eighty.
Yet, Mùzhī's replies were made without any delay.
He was transferred to Zhōngjūn Tàiwèi Sīmǎ.
In the eighth year,
he was appointed Dānyáng Yǐn.
When Gāozǔ campaigned west against Liú Yì,
he appointed Zhūgě Chángmín to supervise the acting government (liúfǔ),
managing all affairs in the rear.
Gāozǔ suspected Chángmín might be difficult to trust alone,
so he left Mùzhī to assist him.
He was granted the title of Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn,
provided with staff officers,
and allocated actual resources.
Chángmín indeed harbored treacherous designs,
but he hesitated and could not act.
He then dismissed his attendants and said to Mùzhī:
"The common rumors
all say that the Grand Marshal (Tàiwèi) and I are not on good terms.
Why is this so?"
Mùzhī replied:
"The Duke is campaigning far upstream,
and has entrusted his aged mother and young children to your Excellency.
If there were the slightest shortcoming,
how could this be allowed?"
Chángmín's mind was then somewhat eased.
When Gāozǔ returned,
Chángmín was executed.
In the tenth year,
Mùzhī was promoted to Qián Jiāngjūn,
and his Qiánjūn fǔ was granted ten thousand bolts of cloth
and three million coins annually.
In the eleventh year,
Gāozǔ campaigned west against Sīmǎ Xiūzhī.
Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn Dàolián was in charge of the acting government,
but all matters, big or small,
were decided by Mùzhī.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Yòupúshè,
in charge of selections (lǐngxuǎn);
his titles of general and Yǐn remained as before.
In the twelfth year,
Gāozǔ campaigned north.
He left the crown prince as Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn,
supervising the Tàiwèi liúfǔ.
Mùzhī was transferred to Zuǒpúshè,
and concurrently served as Jīanjūn and Mùsī for the two fu's of Zhōngjūn;
his titles of general, Yǐn, and lǐngxuǎn remained as before.
Fifty armored guards
were allowed into the palace.
He resided in the eastern city.
Mùzhī internally managed court affairs,
and externally supplied the military.
He made decisions swiftly like flowing water,
and nothing was delayed.
Guests flocked to him,
presenting a hundred kinds of requests and appeals.
Consultations from inside and outside
filled the steps and rooms.
He reviewed petitions with his eyes,
replied to letters with his hands,
listened with his ears,
and responded with his mouth,
without any interference among these tasks,
handling all completely and capably.
He also frequently entertained intimate guests,
engaging in conversation, appreciation, and laughter,
stretching from morning to late afternoon,
never showing weariness.
When he had a moment of leisure,
he would personally copy books,
peruse essays and chapters,
and proofread ancient texts.
He was extravagant by nature.
His meals always covered a square table,
and in the morning he would prepare dishes for ten people.
Since Mùzhī enjoyed entertaining guests
and never dined alone,
whenever it was mealtime,
if there were ten or fewer guests,
food would be served to them as usual in the tent.
This was his custom.
He once reported to Gāozǔ:
"Mùzhī's family was originally poor and humble,
and often lacked provisions for sustenance.
Since I have been honored with this position,
although I always try to be frugal,
what is needed day and night
is slightly more than abundant.
Beyond this,
I have not taken a single thread from the Duke."
In the thirteenth year,
he fell gravely ill.
An imperial edict dispatched an upright Huángmén Láng to inquire about his health.
He died in the eleventh month,
at the age of fifty-eight.
Gāozǔ was in Cháng'ān.
Upon hearing the news, he was shocked and grieved,
mourning for several days.
He had originally intended to stay in Guānzhōng
to plan campaigns against Zhào and Wèi.
But with Mùzhī's death,
the key posts in the capital were vacant.
So he hurried back to Péngchéng,
appointing Sīmǎ Xú Xiànzhī to take over the acting government.
All major court affairs, which Mùzhī used to decide,
were now all referred north for consultation.
From Mùzhī's Qiánjūn fǔ, twenty thousand civil and military personnel,
three thousand were assigned to Xiànzhī's Jiànwēi fǔ,
and the rest were all assigned to the crown prince's Zhōngjūn fǔ.
Mùzhī was posthumously honored as Sànqí Chángshì, Wèi Jiāngjūn, and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Gāozǔ further submitted a memorial to the Son of Heaven, saying:
“Your servant has heard that honoring the worthy and commending the good
are what royal instruction prioritizes;
reflecting on merits and acknowledging toil
embodies the profound meaning of remembering the past.
Therefore, the Minister of Merits, holding the records,
always inscribes diligence;
the brilliance of virtue,
after death, becomes even more manifest.
The former Minister of the Left of the Department of State Affairs, and former General, your servant Mùzhī,
from the time he was a commoner,
assisted at the beginning of the righteous cause,
inwardly offering counsel,
outwardly diligently attending to all governmental affairs,
assiduously working for the military and the state,
exhausting his heart and strength.
When he ascended to the court,
he governed the capital region,
assisting the new royal transformations,
and widely promoting and supporting all policies.
Recently, when the war chariots went on a distant expedition,
he remained in the capital acting as a bulwark,
his achievement in handling the entrusted matters
truly satisfied both court and commoners.
He was just about to proclaim and support your grand plans,
and establish and glorify this sagely era,
but his ambitions and achievements were not yet fully realized,
causing sorrow in the hearts of both near and far.
Your imperial grace praised and honored him,
ranking him equal to the Three Excellencies,
with both glory and mourning,
his posthumous favor was already generous.
Your servant humbly reflects that
since the initial establishment of Yìxī,
difficulties and misfortunes were unceasing;
external threats were numerous,
and internal troubles were increasingly intertwined,
the times were turbulent and full of vicissitudes,
never enjoying a moment of peace.
How could your servant, with his meager abilities,
bear the heavy burden of the state,
were it not for Mùzhī’s beneficial assistance?
Not only were his honest words and excellent strategies
heard by the people;
but his loyal counsel and far-reaching plans,
his deep thoughts and secret schemes,
his close-at-hand, subtle advice,
whose extent could not be seen.
His merits, hidden from sight and hearing,
and matters concealed from the imperial court,
are innumerable.
It is for these reasons that, after a full twelve years of effort,
success was achieved;
campaigning abroad and assisting at home,
I fortunately did not disgrace my commission.
Without his support,
no one could have brought things to peace and completion.
He maintained humility and modesty,
holding firm to them even more strongly;
whenever discussions arose about enfeoffments and rewards,
he always deeply restrained and declined them.
Therefore, though his achievements were high in his time,
he did not receive the grant of land and altars.
Reflecting on this matter, I am perpetually saddened;
how can this be overlooked?
I propose that he be posthumously promoted to a principal ministry,
and his territory retrospectively granted,
so that the great bounty may reach him,
and the good person be eternally ranked,
and the deeds of the loyal and upright
not vanish after his death.
Your servant shared adversity and prosperity with him,
witnessing his beginning and end;
our bond was like gold and orchids,
our friendship profound and intimate.
Therefore, I present my heartfelt sentiments,
to be heard by the court.”
Thereupon, he was posthumously granted the titles of Attendant Official and Grand Chancellor,
enfeoffed as the Marquis of Nánchāng County,
with a taxable estate of one thousand five hundred households.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
he remembered his founding meritorious officials,
and issued an edict saying:
“The late Attendant Official and Grand Chancellor, Marquis of Nánchāng, Liú Mùzhī,
with his deep foresight and far-reaching plans,
initiated the royal enterprise,
his merits establishing the great undertaking,
sincerely and selflessly.
Now that the administration is renewed,
and the frontier defenses are established,
reflecting on these matters and remembering this person,
I feel profound sorrow.
He is to be advanced to Duke of Nánkāng Commandery,
with an estate of three thousand households.
The late General of the Left and Inspector of Qīngzhōu, Wáng Zhèn’è,
with his victories in Jīng and Yǐng,
defeated the rebels,
his merits in the northern expedition
rivaled those of Fāngshú.
Recalling his diligence and reflecting on his achievements,
his heart shall not be forgotten.
He is to be advanced to Marquis of Lóngyáng County,
with an increase in his estate by one thousand five hundred households.”
Mùzhī was given the posthumous title Wénxuān Gōng.
In the ninth year of Yuánjiā of Tàizǔ,
he was granted the honor of sharing sacrifices in Gāozǔ's ancestral temple.
In the fourth month of the twenty-fifth year,
the imperial carriage traveled to Jiāngníng,
passing by Mùzhī’s tomb,
and an edict was issued, saying:
“The late Attendant Official, Grand Chancellor, and Duke Wénxuān of Nánkāng, Mùzhī,
upholding virtue and assisting in the founding of the dynasty,
supported and illuminated the grand enterprise,
his strategies far-sighted,
his foundational merits greatly flourishing,
his achievements inscribed on tripods and ritual vessels,
his righteousness manifest in historical records.
He has already succeeded the glory of previous sages,
and proclaimed his influence to future generations.
Recently, during my travels,
I gazed upon his tomb,
and the thought of the Nine Springs
filled me with deep sorrow and lamentation.
Let sacrifices be offered at his tomb,
to express my everlasting remembrance.”
Mùzhī had three sons.
The eldest, Lǜzhī, succeeded him,
serving as a Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary before his death.
His son Yōng succeeded.
Previously, for commanderies and counties designated as enfeoffed states,
the Grand Administrator and Prime Minister would both address the lord of the state as ‘your servant,’
and this ceased upon leaving office.
It was not until the Xiàojiàn era of Shìzǔ
that this system was first changed,
where lower officials merely showed respect.
Wáng Xīīnzhī, the Prince of Hédōng, once served as the Prime Minister of Nánkāng,
and had always held Yōng in slight regard.
Later, Xīnzhī and Yōng both attended a grand assembly,
and sat together.
Yōng was fond of wine,
and said to Xīnzhī:
“You once addressed me as ‘your servant’;
can you not offer me a cup of wine now?”
Xīnzhī then imitated Sūn Hào’s song in reply:
“Once I was your servant,
now I stand shoulder-to-shoulder with you.
I will neither offer you wine,
nor wish you longevity.”
Wherever Yōng went, he enjoyed eating scabs,
believing their taste resembled abalone.
Once, he visited Mèng Língxiū,
who had recently suffered from moxibustion sores,
and the scabs had fallen onto the bed.
Yōng picked them up and ate them.
Língxiū was greatly astonished.
Yōng replied:
“It’s what I am fond of by nature.”
Língxiū then stripped off all the scabs that had not yet fallen
and gave them to Yōng to eat.
After Yōng left,
Língxiū wrote a letter to Hé Xù, saying:
“Liú Yōng just visited and ate from me,
causing my whole body to bleed.”
The approximately two hundred officials of Nánkāng Commandery,
regardless of guilt or innocence,
would take turns whipping each other,
and the scabbed wounds were regularly used to provide Yōng with food.
Upon his death,
his son Róng succeeded.
In the fourth year of Dàmíng,
he was stripped of his title and territory
for striking his wife with a knife;
his younger brother Biāo was enfeoffed in his place.
When Qí received the abdication,
his title was reduced to Marquis of Nánkāng County,
with a taxable estate of one thousand households.
Mùzhī's middle son, Shìzhī (式之), whose courtesy name was Yánshū (延叔),
was well-versed in the *Yìjīng* and fond of scholars.
He successively rose to the positions of Prime Minister's Staff Officer (相國中兵參軍),
Palace Gentleman of the Crown Prince (太子中舍人),
Palace Attendant (黃門侍郎),
General of Tranquilizing the North (寧朔將軍), and Administrator (太守) of Xuānchéng (宣城) and Huáinán (淮南) Commanderies.
While in office, he was notoriously corrupt with illicit gains.
Wáng Hóng (王弘), the Governor (刺史) of Yángzhōu (揚州), dispatched a subordinate to investigate.
The subordinate summoned the officials and common people,
intending to cross-examine them.
Shìzhī summoned the subordinate and said:
"When you return to the provincial capital, report to your lord:
Liú Shìzhī (劉式之) has rendered minor services to the state.
What is it to steal a few million coins,
let alone not steal?
The officials, common people, and documents are not available."
The subordinate returned and reported everything to Hóng.
Hóng said:
"Liú Shìzhī's argument is as forceful as a galloping horse!"
Because of this, the matter was suspended.
He later became Right Leader of the Crown Prince's Household (太子右率),
Left General of the Guards (左衞將軍),
and Administrator of Wú County (吳郡).
When he died,
he was posthumously granted the title of General Who Conquers Barbarians (征虜將軍).
For his meritorious service in campaigns against Guān (關) and Luò (洛),
he was enfeoffed as a Fifth-Class Marquis of Déyáng County (德陽縣).
His posthumous name was Gōng Hóu (恭侯).
His eldest son was Āi (敳).
At the beginning of Shìzǔ's (世祖) reign,
he was a Palace Attendant (黃門侍郎).
Āi's younger brother was Yǎn (衍).
At the end of Dàmíng (大明) era,
he was appointed Palace Attendant (黃門郎),
and then served as Internal Administrator (內史) of Yùzhāng (豫章).
When Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn (晉安王子勛) claimed a false title,
he appointed Yǎn as Central Protector of the Army (中護軍).
When the plot failed, he was apprehended and executed.
Yǎn's younger brother was Yǔ (瑀), whose courtesy name was Màolín (茂琳).
In his youth, he showed talent and spirit,
and was recognized by Tàizǔ (太祖).
When Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn (始興王濬) was the Governor of Nánxúzhōu (南徐州),
he appointed Yǔ as his Aide-de-camp (別駕從事史),
and Yǔ was highly favored by Jùn.
Yǔ was by nature arrogant and protective of his position,
disliking anyone to be above him.
At that time, Gù Mài (顧邁) from Wú County (吳郡), a Staff Officer (行參軍) under Jùn (who was General Who Conquers the North), was frivolous but talented.
Jùn treated him exceptionally well,
discussing profound and secret matters,
and involving him in everything.
Yǔ then humbled himself and served Mài,
expressing deep sincerity and friendship.
Even private family matters involving women,
things that would normally be unspoken,
he disclosed fully and completely.
Mài, believing Yǔ was entirely sincere with him,
felt deeply moved and trusted him.
The secret matters Jùn had discussed,
Mài revealed everything to Yǔ.
One day, Yǔ and Mài were together in the archery hall.
Yǔ suddenly looked around for a single garment and a headcloth.
Mài asked him why.
Yǔ said:
"The Duke treats you like a family member,
speaking to you without concealment,
but you reveal it externally,
causing everyone to know.
I am an official of the Duke,
how can I not report this?"
He then reported it to Jùn.
Jùn was furious
and memorialized Tàizǔ to exile Mài to Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
While Mài was in Guǎngzhōu,
he encountered Xiāo Jiǎn's (蕭簡) rebellion.
He exerted himself fully for Jiǎn
and died with him.
Yǔ was promoted to Central Supervising Secretary (從事中郎),
also serving as Administrator of Huáinán (淮南).
In the 29th year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) (452 CE),
he was appointed General Who Pacifies the Distant (寧遠將軍) and Governor of Yìzhōu (益州).
When the prime culprit usurped the throne and established himself,
Yǔ was appointed Governor of Qīngzhōu (青州).
Upon hearing the news, Yǔ
immediately raised an army and dispatched troops,
also sending resources to Jīngzhōu (荊州).
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he summoned Yǔ to be Imperial Censor (御史中丞).
When he returned to Jiānglíng (江陵),
he encountered Nánjùn Wáng Yìxuān (南郡王義宣) in rebellion.
Yǔ argued strongly against it,
his words extremely earnest and direct.
Yìxuān appointed him Left Chief Clerk to the Prime Minister (丞相左司馬),
and they both went to Liángshān (梁山).
Yǔ still used his boats and rafts from Shǔ (蜀),
and Yìxuān's former troops secretly deserted to the imperial army off the islet of Liángshān.
He was appointed Left Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works (司徒左長史).
The following year,
he was promoted to Imperial Censor (御史中丞).
Yǔ was proud and looked down on others;
as the censorate, he was very much in his element.
He impeached Wáng Sēngdá (王僧達), stating:
"His connections are grand,
but his character is insignificant."
No official in court failed to fear his pen.
Soon after, he was transferred to Left General of the Guards (右衞將軍).
Yǔ wished to be an Attendant at the Imperial Gate (侍中),
but did not get it.
He said to his intimates:
"One who is an official either goes out (to provincial posts) or comes in (to court posts).
If one does not come in, one should go out.
How can one remain long on the threshold?"
He then requested Yìzhōu.
Shìzǔ understood his intention
and granted it.
In the third year of Xiàojiàn (孝建) (456 CE),
he was appointed General Who Guards the State (輔國將軍) and Governor of Yìzhōu (益州).
After departing,
he was very discontent.
Upon reaching Jiānglíng (江陵),
he wrote to Yán Jùn (顏竣), saying:
"Zhū Xiūzhī (朱脩之), whose family has been rebellious for three generations,
now resides in Jīngzhōu,
under the blue oilcloth tent,
acting like Xiè Xuānmíng (謝宣明) in my presence,
and making a vegetarian master use a long sword to force me from my seat.
What can I do about it?
I am only afraid that the Xiongnú will belittle the Hàn!"
In that year,
he was dismissed from office for seizing another man's wife as his concubine.
He was dismissed from office.
In the first year of Dàmíng (大明) (457 CE),
he was reinstated as Administrator of Dōngyáng (東陽).
The following year,
he was transferred to Administrator of Wúxīng (吳興).
Shìzhōng Hé Yǎn (何偃) once commented:
"He is a mixed bag among the prominent figures of his time."
Yǔ was furious and said:
"What is this 'mixed bag' that I am among the prominent figures of my time?"
He then broke off relations with Yǎn.
When he became Minister of Personnel (吏部尚書),
his indignation grew even stronger.
His cousin Xiùzhī (秀之) became the Administrator of Dānyáng (丹陽).
Yǔ again wrote to his relatives and old friends, saying:
"My family's 'Black-faced Ā Xiù (阿秀)' has actually taken Liú Ānzhòng's (劉安衆) place.
The court does not have many capable men."
That year, he developed a carbuncle on his back.
Hé Yǎn also developed a carbuncle on his back.
