Yǔ's illness was already severe.
When he heard of Yǎn's death,
he rejoiced and shouted.
Then he too died.
His posthumous name was Gāngzǐ (剛子).
His son was Juàn (卷),
Aide-de-camp of Nánxúzhōu (南徐州).
Juàn's younger brother was Zàng (藏),
Assistant Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs (尚書左丞).
Mùzhī's youngest son was Zhēnzhī (貞之),
Palace Attendant in the Central Secretariat (中書黃門侍郎), Right Leader of the Crown Prince's Household (太子右衞率), General of Tranquilizing the North (寧朔將軍), and Internal Administrator of Jiāngxià (江夏).
He died in office.
His son was Póu (裒),
Chancellor (相) of Shǐxīng (始興).
He was imprisoned in Dōngyě (東冶) for corruption.
Mùzhī's daughter married Cài Yòu (蔡祐) of Jìyáng (濟陽).
He was old and poor.
Shìzǔ appointed Yòu's son Píngnán Cānjūn Sūn (平南參軍孫) as Administrator of Shǐ'ān (始安).
Wáng Hóng (王弘), courtesy name Xiūyuán (休元),
was a native of Línyí (臨沂), Lángyé (琅邪).
His great-grandfather was Dǎo (導), Prime Minister of Jìn (晉).
His grandfather was Qià (洽), Central Commander of the Guards (中領軍).
His father was Xún (珣), Minister of Works (司徒).
Hóng was fond of learning from a young age,
and was known for his purity and tranquility.
He was good friends with the Shàngshū Púyè, Xiè Hùn.
When he came of age,
he served as the Piàojí Cānjūn Zhǔbù for Sīmǎ Dàozǐ, the King of Kuàijī.
At that time, agricultural work was stalled,
and minor corvée duties were proliferating.
Hóng believed it was appropriate to establish military agricultural colonies (túntián),
and he presented his case thus:
"The matter of establishing túntián, which I recently consulted with you about,
has already been fully presented to your sagely mind.
The work in the southern fields is commencing,
and the opportune moment must not be missed.
It is advisable to quickly oversee the agricultural officials,
to secure the year's harvest.
However, the prefectural resources for corvée are meager,
[一０]and there is no means of obtaining labor.
Even if we invigorate them with heavy rewards,
and discipline them with strict authority,
it will merely lead to prisons overflowing,
without actually remedying the situation.
I humbly observe that the various foundries in the Southern Bureau
recruit several hundred clerks.
Although they are provided with stipends,
their output is very low.
I believe that if they were repurposed for agriculture,
the benefits would be a hundredfold.
However, military equipment is essential
and cannot be entirely abolished.
I propose to retain one large copper foundry (tóngguān dàyě) and one small urban foundry (dūyì xiǎoyě) each,
increase their production quotas,
and align them with Yángzhōu's standards.
The province's demands
would then not be lacking.
The rest should be disbanded,
to fill the urgent need for spring farming.
Furthermore, I suggest that the agricultural offices of both bureaus
each establish military officials (diǎnjūn) to recruit clerks,
following the proportion of foundry recruitment.
They should also be allowed to recruit people from the mountains and lakes.
These measures would not harm private interests
but would greatly benefit the public.
Within this, there should also be consideration
for assigning shifts and holidays,
and determining the amount of stipends to be provided.
These matters can be entirely entrusted to the relevant offices.
The departments directly under your control
must be thoroughly familiar with these matters.
Moreover, the Cānjūn Nà Zhī of the Eastern Bureau's Water Office has recently been appointed to this task.
He is quite capable
and sufficient to manage this affair.
In recent years,
these duties have been neglected,
resulting in overgrown fields and empty granaries.
This is truly due to these reasons.
I, Hóng, have been undeservedly promoted,
and my ambition is to contribute my humble efforts.
How can I remain silent
and not express what is on my mind!
As for whether this is appropriate or not,
Your Excellency will naturally decide with foresight.
If what I have proposed is deemed correct,
I humbly request that it be implemented in due time.
Then, the year will see diligence in farming,
and the granaries will be full.
The flourishing of rituals and etiquette
can then be awaited with folded hands."
Dàozǐ wanted to appoint him Huángmén Shìláng,
but Xún firmly declined due to his youth.
Xún was quite fond of accumulating wealth,
and his assets were spread among the common people.
When Xún died,
Hóng burned all the bonds and documents,
not collecting any debts.
The rest of his former property he entrusted to his younger brothers.
Before his mourning period was over,
Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn, the Hòujiāngjūn, appointed him Cānyì Cānjūn,
added the title Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn,
and put him in charge of secretarial affairs (jìshì shì).
He firmly declined the appointment.
Dàozǐ again appointed him Cānyì Cānjūn,
added the title Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn,
and put him in charge of the central army (zhōngbīng).
He again firmly declined.
At that time, there were many internal and external troubles,
and those in mourning generally did not complete their period of grief.
Only Hóng firmly insisted and was exempted.
When Huán Xuán conquered the capital (Jīngyì),
he arrested Dàozǐ and handed him over to the Supreme Court (Tíngwèi).
The officials were fearful
and dared not look or send him off.
Hóng was still in mourning,
but he alone bowed by the roadside,
clung to the carriage, and wept,
which commentators praised.
Gāozǔ, as Zhènjūn,
summoned him and appointed him Cānyì Cānjūn.
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as a fifth-rank Marquis of Huáróng Xiàn.
He was promoted to Dàsīmǎ Cóngshì Zhōngláng for the King of Lángxié.
He was sent out as Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Lángxié Nèishǐ,
then Shàngshū Lìbù Lángzhōng,
and Yùzhāng Xiàng.
When Lú Xún invaded the various commanderies of Nánkāng,
Hóng fled to Xúnyáng.
Gāozǔ again appointed him Zhōngjūn Cānyì Cānjūn,
promoted him to Dàsīmǎ Yòuzhǎngshǐ,
and then to Wúguó Nèishǐ.
In the eleventh year of Yìxī,
he was summoned to be Tàiwèi Zhǎngshǐ,
and then promoted to Zuǒzhǎngshǐ.
He followed on the northern expedition.
The vanguard had already pacified Luòyáng,
but the "Nine Bestowals" (jiǔxí) had not yet been dispatched.
Hóng took on the mission to return to the capital (Jīngshī),
to subtly convey the message to the imperial court.
At that time, Liú Mùzhī was in charge of remaining in the capital,
but the imperial directive came from the north.
Mùzhī was ashamed and fearful,
fell ill, and subsequently died.
When Gāozǔ returned to Péngchéng,
Hóng was appointed Péngchéng Tàishǒu.
Upon the initial establishment of the State of Sòng,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Púyè Língxuan,
while retaining his position as Tàishǒu.
He submitted an impeachment memorial against Xiè Língyùn, stating:
"Your servant has heard that 'keeping one's family in order'
is a teaching passed down in the Dàyì,
and 'exercising arbitrary power to kill'
is a warning given in the Zhōushū.
If these norms are violated,
punishment is unforgivable.
The Heir Apparent's Zuǒwèishuài and Duke of Kānglè Xiàn, Xiè Língyùn,
forcefully took his favored concubine from her husband, Guì Xīng.
He killed Xīng by the riverbank
and cast his body into the torrent.
The incident occurred in the imperial domain (Jīngjī)
and spread far and wide.
He ought to be severely impeached,
to rectify the court's conduct.
I observe that the Heir Apparent's Zuǒwèishuài and Duke of Kānglè Xiàn, Xiè Língyùn, has received excessive imperial favor
and frequently held honorable appointments.
He has known propriety and prohibitions for a long time.
Yet, he was unable to control his household,
leading to such scandal.
Disregarding regulations,
he acted out of anger and killed freely.
If this is not punished,
the laws will be undermined.
I request that Língyùn be dismissed from his current office for this offense,
that the imperial court strip him of his title and fief,
and that he be handed over to the Dàlǐ to be judged and punished.
The Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng and Dūtínghóu, Wáng Zhǔnzhī,
[一一]holds a prominent and important position,
as the chief law enforcement officer of the state.
With rumors spreading widely,
he did not impeach him even once.
If he knew but did not correct it,
then his sentiment interfered with the law.
If he did not know,
then his ignorance is extreme.
How can he continue to participate in the ranks of high officials
and serve as a model for the national law?
I request that he be dismissed from his current office
and that his marquisate be reverted to that of a commoner.
The old system of the inner court
did not allow impeachment based on rumors.
However, this matter is manifest
and exposed to the court and the public.
If the enforcers of the law remain silent,
and all officials follow old customs,
the national laws will crumble,
and the loss will be great.
I, Hóng, though undeserving,
hold a position at the head of the court.
If I were to merely adhere to conventional procedures,
I would never be able to correct this.
Therefore, I dare not remain silent
and conform to custom.
As for the transgression of violating old customs,
I humbly await your judgment."
Gāozǔ decreed:
"Língyùn is to be dismissed from office,
and nothing more.
The rectifying of conduct by the Dūan Yòu
truly meets expectations.
Why should it be bound by common formalities?
This shall be a permanent regulation from now on."
In his fourteenth year,
he was transferred to be the Grand Administrator of military affairs of Jiāngzhōu, Yùzhōu's Xīyáng and Xīncài commanderies, Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn, and Cìshǐ of Jiāngzhōu.
Upon arrival at the province,
he reduced taxes and simplified corvée labor,
and the common people found peace.
In the first year of Yǒngchū,
he was given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
For his meritorious service in supporting the founding of the dynasty,
he was enfeoffed as Húaróng Xiàn Gōng,
with a stipend of two thousand households.
In the third year,
he entered the court,
and was promoted to Wèi Jiāngjūn, with the privilege of establishing a fu (administrative office) and yítóng sānsī (equal in status to the Three Ducal Ministers).
Gāozǔ, during a banquet gathering,
said to the various dukes:
"I, a commoner,
initially did not expect to reach this position."
Fù Liàng and others all drafted speeches, intending to lavishly praise his accomplishments and virtues.
Hóng casually replied:
"This is what is called the Mandate of Heaven;
it cannot be gained by seeking,
nor can it be cast off by pushing away."
People at the time praised his succinctness and precision.
In the second year of Jǐngpíng of Shàodì,
Xú Xiànzhī and others plotted to depose and enthrone,
and summoned Hóng to court.
Upon Tàizǔ's enthronement,
for his role in settling the grand strategy and securing the state,
he was promoted to Sīkōng,
and enfeoffed as Jiàn'ān Jùn Gōng,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
He submitted a memorial firmly declining, saying:
"Your servant has heard that Zhào Wǔ praised Suí Huì as a master whose household affairs were well-managed,
and whose words to the state of Jìn had no hidden meanings.
Your servant, by a fortunate chance in a thousand years,
has wrongly received glorious treatment.
Although my intelligence and virtue are shallow and weak,
and my political achievements are negligible,
that my words have no hidden meanings,
I secretly aspire to.
If Heaven had enlightened my mind
and pre-ordained the great strategy,
and my name were recorded in the records of merit,
but my achievements were not evident in the chronicles,
I would certainly request the punishment for not deserving rewards,
and display the writings of the dragon and snake (a metaphor for meritorious service),
how could I then hesitate to defy the established decree,
and merely cultivate minor virtues?
But I have no meritorious service,
which is known throughout the four seas.
On the one hand, I lack the schemes that a gentleman would labor his heart over;
on the other, I fall short of the efforts that a humble man would exert.
Yet the sagely court excessively rewards me above,
and your foolish servant unworthily accepts below.
This would be a grave deception of the present age,
and would forever invite criticism.
The reproach of 'secretly stealing wealth'
is lighter than this;
only by defiling your great design
is the blemish greater.
My humble self, what I cherish,
will also perish one day.
Not only would I be tarnishing the national records,
but I would also be fearing the judgment of friends.
My worried heart is greatly afflicted,
where can my face find refuge?
Moreover, even in ordinary human interactions,
one still expresses oneself to a confidant;
how much more so before an enlightened ruler,
where one can appeal with reason.
Therefore, I dare to persist in my foolish obstinacy,
and will uphold this even unto death."
He was then permitted.
He was given the additional titles of Shǐchíjié and Shìzhōng,
his supervisory role was changed to Dūdū,
and he was promoted to Chējì Dàjiāngjūn,
his kǎifǔ and Cìshǐ positions remaining as before.
As Xú Xiànzhī and others were about to be executed for the crime of deposing and assassinating,
Hóng, not being a primary conspirator,
and his younger brother Tánshǒu being entrusted and favored by the emperor,
before the event broke,
secretly sent a message to inform Hóng.
After Xú Xiànzhī and others were executed,
Hóng was summoned to be Shìzhōng, Sītú, and Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu,
and Lù Shàngshū.
He was granted thirty guards with ceremonial swords.
When the emperor campaigned westward against Xiè Huì,
Hóng, along with the Pàoxī Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng, remained to guard the capital,
moving into the Zhōngshū Xiàshěng,
entering and exiting with an honor guard.
The Sītú's mansion temporarily established a Cānjūn.
In the spring of the fifth year,
there was a severe drought.
Hóng took the blame and resigned his position,
saying:
"Your servant has heard that although the three cosmic powers (Heaven, Earth, Man) are distinct,
their outcome is one.
Therefore, when the world is peaceful and enlightened,
the five blessings respond;
when governance has lost its virtue,
omens of calamity inevitably appear.
Your servant has also heard that
the duty of the grand ministers (tái fǔ) is to discuss the Way and assist in its alignment,
to assist the sovereign above,
and to regulate yin and yang.
If the position is granted based on virtue,
then the harmonious qi will be pure and serene;
if it is occupied by usurpation or unworthily,
then punishment will be seen from Heaven.
This is why Chén Píng had his excuses,
not overstepping the bounds of the chief minister;
Bǐng Jí stopped his carriage,
greatly fearing the cause of the ox's panting.
This is indeed common to all states,
and a profound principle between Heaven and man.
Your Majesty, with sagely wisdom, governs the world,
bringing glorious revival,
〔一二〕and should be blessed with auspicious omens,
with sweet springs bubbling forth.
However, recently yin and yang have been discordant,
severe drought has become a disaster,
there has been no harsh frost in autumn,
no accumulated snow in winter,
and the qi of pestilence
has persisted through all four seasons.
Is this not because the appointment has missed the right person,
the fault of overturning the tripod (a metaphor for failing to govern)?
Your servant, being mediocre and short-sighted,
among common folk,
mistakenly encountered good fortune,
and received grace in the past.
Your Majesty overlooked my unworthiness,
and further burdened me with the present responsibility.
Occupying the position of grand minister (huái dǐng),
governing the divine land,
wearing marten tails and imperial robes (symbols of high office),
presiding over the court,
crucial internal and external responsibilities,
all gathered upon my humble self,
reaching the extreme of favor and honor,
unequaled by any subject.
If a person of excellent virtue held this,
it might still be difficult to fulfill;
how much more so for one as ignorant and dim-witted as I,
how can I possibly be competent?
This is easily understood,
and does not require keen insight.
However, at the beginning of my appointment,
it was a time of difficulty,
with the six armies (enemies) personally threatening,
and anxiety reaching the state,
it was truly a time for subjects to exert themselves and forget their bodies,
how could I have any thought
to bother your sagely hearing?
Therefore, I reluctantly engaged in affairs,
striving to the best of my ability,
my ambition being to exert my strength,
not considering distant consequences.
Now that the leviathans are defeated,
and the Western regions are pacified,
it is opportune to express my original intention,
to yield to the virtuous and confess my incompetence.
However, common people covet comfort,
growing more accustomed day by day,
and I indeed relied on your imperial favor,
unable to stop myself.
Time passed,
and three years suddenly went by.
This allowed the flaw of occupying a position without merit
to be manifest in both the seen and unseen realms;
and the disaster of hidden transgressions
to afflict the common people.
Above, it detracts from the beauty of the imperial court's flourishing prosperity;
below, it increases the disaster of public censure and downfall.
I humbly reflect with fear and shame,
my five senses scatter,
though I am said to be thick-skinned,
how can I find peace?
'Not far, returning' is what
the great Yì (I Ching) refers to;
'small correction, great warning' is the blessing of humble people.
The beauty of prompt return
is not what I dare to expect,
but the good fortune of being warned and corrected
I secretly hope for.
Now, at the beginning of the year,
after the court celebrations are complete,
I shall immediately return to my private dwelling,
to reflect on my faults in the household,
hoping to slightly avert Heaven's rebuke,
and somewhat mitigate criticism.
I humbly beg Your Majesty to observe my resolve
and immediately grant my request.
As I close this memorial, I am filled with shame and unable to express myself fully."
Formerly, Péngchéngwáng Yìkāng was the Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
stationed at Jiānglíng.
Pínglù Order Hénán Chéng Càn wrote to Hóng, saying:
"I have heard that in establishing regulations and giving instructions,
one must adapt to the times;
the waxing and waning of generations
also follows this principle of ebb and flow.
Now, where power resides,
it should not be held by those who are not kin.
Thus, in the Zhou dynasty's ancestral alliances,
those of different surnames were relegated to lesser positions.
The crucial pivot of power
was entrusted to the two Nán,
this was a clear strategy of previous generations,
and a distinct precedent for the present.
Your Excellency's position reaches the highest echelons of government,
all within the four seas look to you,
toiling day and night,
your righteousness is like that of Tǔwò.
Yet you oversee all governmental affairs,
and also govern the imperial domain,
your achievements and merits are vast,
none can compare.
The Dao of Heaven blesses humility,
it is fitting to practice modesty and self-restraint.
The General of Cavalry, Péngchéngwáng, is abundant in virtue and integrity,
the Emperor's esteemed younger brother,
the root of the imperial clan,
whom one should defer to as superior,
[he should enter to preside over court affairs,
assisting and supporting the imperial plans.
Jìnglíng and Héngyáng are already advanced in years,
they] should be sent out to command the various feudal states,
shining as brightly as Lǔ and Wèi.
[一三]Your Excellency, relaxing and discussing the Dao,
harmonizing Yin and Yang,
then the world will be peaceful,
disasters will not arise,
blessings and prosperity will ascend with the great Sòng dynasty,
your lifespan will be as long as Sōng and Qiáo,
your name will endure for ten thousand generations,
would this not be splendid!"
Hóng originally had intentions to retire,
and took Càn's words,
thereby he steadfastly presented his request,
and was consequently demoted to General of the Guards, Administrator with the rank of the Three Ducal Ministers.
Six years later,
Hóng again submitted a memorial, saying:
"I have heard that assigning those of different surnames to lesser positions
was the clear principle of the Zhou dynasty;
that close kin should not be outside
is what a state values first.
Therefore, the Ruler of Lǔ, Zhǎng Téngjūn,
is praised in the Spring and Autumn Annals;
Chǔ's banishment of Qìjí
serves as a warning in previous histories.
How much more so when esteemed kin, with bright virtues,
whose Dao shines throughout their time,
are performing duties in the feudal domains,
and are not reached by court governance,
while mediocre and superficial officials of common lineage
exceed ancient precedents,
and are placed in central positions to assist and cooperate?
How can this serve to uphold ancient styles
and illuminate the path of governance?
General of Cavalry, your minister Yìkāng,
has profound and distant meritorious achievements,
his bright virtue is increasingly esteemed,
he has administered governance in Jiāng and Hàn,
and his civilizing influence has spread throughout Jīngnán.
The gentry and officials express their feelings,
wishing for him to take on the present duties.
The trust placed in Zhōu Dàn
is unanimously desired;
though dividing the administrative responsibilities is weighty,
compared to this, it is light.
I am truly ignorant and dark,
my rank and favor exceed my worth,
I accumulate provisions without merit,
and shame the grand transformation from above.
Both public and private considerations are conflicting,
none of them are appropriate.
In the past, before Sūn Shū was promoted,
Yōu Mèng made a spectacle;
when Zhǎn Jì was in a lower position,
Zāng Wén incurred ridicule.
How much more so when the Dao is exalted and the position is intimate,
and the principle combines with ancient rites.
I, compared to ancient figures,
am unable to be of service;
riding on an empty cart and usurping a position,
what would all things say?
Even if I were thick-skinned,
how could I bear to remain in this position?
The fear of ruin
truly pains my heart.
I beg to resign my position as Inspector,
to fulfill the hopes of the people.
I humbly wish Your Majesty to consider the utmost impartiality from afar,
and examine my sincere devotion from nearby,
to comply with the court and the common people,
and reassign the position to virtuous kin.
Not only would I, your humble minister,
be spared from great transgression,
but all common subjects
would not but rejoice.
If Heaven's favor is unending,
and you should still hesitate,
please release my memorial,
to be heard by those within and without;
perhaps among the court discussions and public opinions,
there might be something to choose."
The imperial edict stated:
"Having read your memorial,
you distantly imitate the system of state governance of the flourishing Zhou dynasty,
and closely describe the humble and self-effacing aspirations of the great Yìjīng.
Having repeatedly pondered your sincere intentions,
I am truly moved.
You embody the Dao, profound and humble,
your insight is clear and far-reaching,
you have assisted in difficult times,
your achievements and merits are brilliant and grand,
enabling Us to reside in the palace and govern with folded hands,
and entrust the administration to be successfully completed.
How can you nobly withdraw from overseeing all affairs,
and steadfastly decline the imperial province,
thereby causing the accomplishment of affairs to be deficient,
and increasing Our unworthiness?
You must deeply consider the welfare of the state,
We hope you will assist diligently.
As for the trust in the virtuous kin, the General of Cavalry,
his position is equal to Dàn and Shì,
he shall return to assist within the court,
and participate in deliberating state affairs;
We respectfully comply with your insistence."
Yìkāng consequently replaced Hóng as Sītú,
and they divided the responsibilities.
Hóng又表曰：
“Recently, I presumptuously submitted a memorial,
laying out my humble and limited views,
sincerely hoping that the Heavenly Sovereign would discern,
and appreciate my utmost sincerity.
However, I received a returned imperial edict,
and my suggestions were not considered.
I have merely troubled Your Sacred Gaze,
and look up, awaiting Your gracious decree.
Reflecting on myself, I am ashamed and fearful,
not knowing how to rectify my position.
I have unworthily held an important office,
for four years now.
I have both violated the admonition of former historians to assess one's own capabilities,
and lacked the virtue of ancient sages in promoting the worthy.
Occupying a position without merit and clinging to favor,
day by day, official criticism accumulates.
Looking back on my conduct,
my shame is already profound.
Moreover, when there are truly worthy people,
whose virtue is recognized by both court and commoners,
if I were to only now consider withdrawing myself,
how could I say that I am compensating for my failings?
I would only be tarnishing the great principles,
and causing much loss.
I did not expect the depth of Your Heavenly Favor,
again bestowing grace and commendation.
My official position remains unchanged,
and I am favored as before.
I, in my foolishness and confusion, consider myself,
〔一四〕and find myself adrift, as if without limit.
Since Chén Yìkāng already oversees all governmental affairs,
assisting in the flourishing transformation,
I unworthily occupy a subordinate position,
and can consult and rely on him.
For the minor duties within the imperial court,
I can perhaps avoid complete failure.
But for the heavy responsibility of Shénzhōu,
one must possess both reputation and substance.
Who am I, that I,
a mere usurper, continue to cling to this position?
If I remain in this capacity,
failure and ruin will soon follow.
Even if there are no human errors on my part,
there will surely be calamities from the Yin and Yang.
I reflect and worry about this,
it afflicts me like a severe headache.
I do not know by what reason
I can feel at ease.
However, the imperial decree has already been made,
and an imperial utterance is difficult to reverse.
Moreover, I am cowardly and incompetent,
and have never had such ambition.
When advancing, I cannot speak out and present my case,
to secure my position with death.
When retreating, I cannot suffer hardships like repeatedly forming calluses or lying on ice,
nor can I starve myself to emaciation by eating sparingly.
I merely fear the imperial majesty,
and so I submit myself.
As for overseeing my department,
and managing the documents,
the clerks and staff of the various offices
do not require many.
The remaining civil and military personnel
are all redundant officials.
The Prime Minister's office has just been established,
and there may be some deficiencies.
I request to retain only the necessary colleagues to work together,
and everything else beyond this,
including all resources and assets,
should be sent to the Sītú.
I have received profound imperial grace,
and share in its joys and sorrows.
It is my duty not to be pretentious,
or to merely belittle myself.
I humbly pray for Your Sacred Discernment,
to especially grant my request,
and not to let my sincere plea
be seen as suppressed or denied.”
〔一五〕The Emperor again issued an edict, saying:
“The Wèijūn’s memorial is thus.
The Sītú indeed needs manpower.
His refined wishes may be granted,
and two thousand men be assigned to his office.
There is no need to trouble him with sending resources.”
Hóng was well-versed in governance,
and paid close attention to all matters.
He weighed the circumstances of the time,
always striving for fairness and appropriateness.
He wrote to the eight chief secretaries and assistant secretaries, saying:
“When a member of the same Wǔ violates the law,
there is no provision for a scholar not to be punished.
However, whenever investigations and reprimands occur,
there are always requests and pleas.
If grace and leniency are granted,
then the law becomes defunct and cannot be enforced.
If accountability is pursued strictly according to the facts,
then people resent it as hardship.
It is appropriate to formulate a new regulation for this,
so that they may express their feelings of hardship.”
〔一六〕He also said: “Currently, a guard stealing five bolts of cloth,
and an ordinary thief stealing forty bolts,
both incur the death penalty.
Discussants all consider this too severe.
It is appropriate to propose that a guard stealing ten bolts, and an ordinary thief stealing fifty bolts, be put to death,
while forty bolts should lead to reduction to soldier status.
This would both slightly extend the lives of the people,
and still be sufficient as a deterrent.
I imagine each of you has your own thoughts.”
Zuǒchéng Jiāng Ào deliberated:
“For a scholar who commits theft, if the stolen goods do not warrant public execution,
after the punishment is carried out,
he will be categorized as one stained by theft and lewdness.
His reputation will be tarnished for life,
and he will not be pardoned even by imperial amnesty.
For those who experience this, it is sufficient to atone for their transgressions,
and for those who hear of it, it is sufficient as a warning.
If they are to be indiscriminately grouped with commoners,
and punished with military service,
I believe it would be a hardship.
Although Fúwǔ are grouped together as neighbors,
the distinction between scholars and commoners
is truly as vast as heaven.
The crime of harboring
should not relate to them.
If slaves and retainers interact with Fúwǔ,
and harbor something,
it can be discovered,
and thus the punishment extends to slaves and retainers.
This means the retainer himself commits the offense,
not that he suffers punishment on behalf of his master.
If there are no slaves,
then one should not be implicated.”
Yòuchéng Kǒng Mòzhī deliberated:
“Gentlemen and commoners
are indeed mixed together in Fúwǔ,
and thus cannot but be responsible for monitoring each other.
Although scholars and commoners differ,
there is a principle of being aware and observing.
For example, just as all officials are above,
it is not necessary for the subordinates to personally act before they are jointly implicated.
Therefore, on the day of transgression,
the responsibility naturally extends to all involved.
〔一七〕Now, punishing their adopted sons and stewards
is perhaps based on the principle of executing servants.
If this is the case,
how can households without slaves
rest in peace?
However, since it is said that scholars should be reinstated,
it is appropriate to allow them to pay a ransom.
For ordinary theft of forty bolts, and a guard stealing five bolts,
reducing the death penalty to soldier status
would indeed greatly demonstrate leniency and kindness,
to spare the lives of the people.
However, if officials up to two thousand Dàn, and disgraced gentry,
occasionally commit such offenses,
their crimes are indeed punishable by death,
and I fear they cannot be reduced to soldier status.
I believe this regulation should be applied to commoners,
while scholars should still follow the old laws.”
Shàngshū Wáng Zhǔnzhī
deliberated: "Formerly, when I was the magistrate of Shānyīn,
shīrén were grouped
and called 'yāfú'.
If someone in the same group committed an offense,
they would not be implicated.
If a shīrén committed a crime,
the fúwǔ would report it.
This was not a distinct system for shī and commoners,
but truly to ensure that punishments matched crimes.
Gentlemen of refined upbringing
are separated from commoners.
If there is no means of prevention and inspection,
it is appropriate for these unruly individuals
to be connected to the masses of commoners.
Since they are in the same fúwǔ,
they are thus made to report offenses.
At that time, this was practiced
in more than one place.
The Zǒuchéng's deliberation that slaves and retainers are related to their neighbors and groups,
and can be inspected,
and if there is an offender among the fú,
they are made to bear the punishment,
seeking this based on the facts,
deviates from practical principles.
Those who have slaves and retainers
mostly employ them for service,
scattered east and west,
with few living at home.
Among those who do reside there,
they are driven to and fro,
what is needed for their movements and stops
rarely takes them outside the gate.
Those who manage accounts are at home in less than one out of ten cases.
If slaves and retainers are punished as part of the group,
excessive punishments will surely be numerous,
which I fear is not the original intent of legislating appropriate punishments.
The Yòuchéng deliberated that if shīrén commit theft
and do not incur capital punishment,
they should be pardoned and made to serve in the army.
Although one desires to show leniency to shīrén,
I fear there will be no means to deter evil.
Following principle makes one a jūnzi,
violating it makes one a xiǎorén.
Even when regulations are strict,
people still presume to offend.
With such a lenient provision,
offenders may become numerous.
Making them fear the law and reform their hearts
[一八] is truly the way to grant great pardon.
Moreover, the differing systems for shī and commoners
indicate different intentions."
Diànzhōngláng Xiè Yuán
deliberated: "Matters must first have their foundation set right,
[一九] and then their consequences can be managed.
The original reason for appointing shīdàfū to fúwǔ
was to inspect commoners, was it?
[二０] Or to make them subject to inspection by commoners?
[二一] According to the Zǒuchéng's claim that shī and commoners are separated by heaven,
[二二] then there is no reason for shī to supervise commoners.
To appoint them to the group without their knowing [the commoners]
would be to subject them to inspection by commoners.
If so, when commoners commit crimes,
shīrén have nothing to do with it,
what crime have servants committed
that they should be made to bear the punishment?
If it is based on actual interrelation,
and they are held responsible for hearing and observing,
[二三] then there is an aspect that is not well-founded.
Why?
Names and realities are distinct,
public and private mandates differ.
Slaves are not appointed to fú,
which means they have no official designation.
The common people lack wealth and property,
which means they are privately humble.
To entrust persons who are privately humble and without official designation
with public responsibilities that are substantial,
mixes public and private,
and makes names and realities incongruous.
From this perspective,
I say they should not be held responsible.
To return to their masters' responsibility
would be appropriate.
Shīrén without slaves
are not included in this example.
If shīrén were originally meant to inspect commoners,
then if commoners commit offenses,
the shīrén themselves should be punished.
And their slaves, then, would justly be subject to punishment for their servitude.
If so, shīrén without slaves
are not yet able to live in peace.
Making them pay a ransom
is not erroneous.
The two categories attached
are merely the foundation of the system.
This is to distinguish between the two foundations,
wishing each to follow its proper division.
As for what I can observe,
it is appropriate to adhere to the former category,
distinguishing shī from commoners,
which is beautiful in principle.
Regarding the regulation on theft,
according to the Zǒuchéng's deliberation,
since shīrén ultimately do not become soldiers,
it is fortunate that they can share in the benefit of leniency.
There is no need to follow the old law.
This is generally agreeable."
Lìbù Láng Hé Shàngzhī
deliberated: "According to Kǒng Yòuchéng's deliberation,
if shīrén are punished for offenses in the fúwǔ,
if they have slaves, the slaves are punished;
if they have no slaves, they pay a ransom.
Since it is granted that shī and commoners are vastly separated,
then hearing and observing is naturally difficult.
It is not appropriate to determine a law of certain knowledge
based on something difficult to know.
Indeed, having slaves does not make one virtuous,
and not having slaves does not necessarily make one not virtuous.
Now, those with many servants are arrogant towards royal decrees,
while those without servants are constrained by the nets of the times.
This means that the benefit of grace
falls upon Chéng and Zhuó,
and the law, once established,
must be applied to Yán and Yuán.
Seeking this from my humble perspective,
I am secretly displeased.
Xiè Diànzhōng's argument that slaves not following their masters
is unclear in terms of their status
is indeed reasonable.
However, slaves and servants are actually related to their neighborhoods.
If they are not questioned at all now,
I fear something will be lost.
My opinion is similar to the Zǒuchéng's deliberation."
Hóng Yì
said, "Upon examination, the penal codes do not differentiate between scholar-officials (shì) and commoners (shù).
Moreover, there is no place where scholar-officials have not been implicated and punished for offenses committed by their co-residents.
Many of these cases
were pardoned by imperial grace at the time,
and thus they were not fully subjected to the punishment themselves.
In Wú and Yìxīng, there were cases of people like Xǔ and Lù,
who were given stipends due to fulfilling the same conditions.
Officials of the two-thousand-dàn rank would memorialize to have their names inscribed in the red books.
Around the Jǐwèi year,
scholar-officials in Kuàijī said that ten years prior,
there were also four prominent families who were implicated and punished for this reason,
but were granted a reprieve due to imperial grace.
Yet Shàngshū Wáng said that it was historically unheard of for people to be punished for their co-residents' offenses,
which I do not understand.
Perhaps when he held office,
he simply did not encounter such incidents.
With a sagely and enlightened ruler governing the world,
scholar-officials genuinely do not have to worry about extreme suffering.
However, it is essential to discuss and resolve matters as they arise.
To repeatedly bother the Emperor with petitions is disruptive;
it would be better to establish clear regulations
to ensure that severity and leniency are balanced.
Furthermore, upon examining the regulations concerning military tallies (jiǎfú),
it states that scholar-officials are exempted from transmitting tallies.
Clerical officials (lìshǐ) who are re-appointed
also enjoy the same exemption.
Yet, when collectively managing and leading,
if there is a violation or an accusation,
there is absolutely no differentiation in severity.
This does not allow scholar-officials to be outside of their communities.
The various discussions claim that scholar-officials and commoners are vastly separated
and do not intermingle or know each other.
If this were the case, when scholar-officials break the law,
commoners would not need to know.
But if commoners are not allowed to be ignorant,
why should scholar-officials be allowed to be ignorant?
Unless the common people are truly transcendent and reclusive,
forever cut off from the dust and grime of the world,
living side-by-side and sharing roofs,
even if it's a small matter of concern,
they will ultimately come to know it;
they do not need to interact day and night.
The words of the Right Vice-Director (Yòuchéng) and the various departments
roughly reflect this situation.
For scholar-officials of declining status,
who genuinely interact with their neighborhoods and alleys,
is actually comparable to that of common people with official attire.
Now, if they are called scholar-officials,
they are exempted from the commoners' punishments;
if they are designated as common people,
they immediately receive the scholar-officials' punishments.
From the perspective of emotion and law,
is this not quite inconsistent?
Moreover, if the general regulations do not apply to the scholar-official class,
making the scholar-official class less burdened,
then if commoners are made to bear the punishment in advance,
they will immediately accuse each other when incidents occur,
and the defense system of the communities and fives (lǘwǔ)
will also be inconsistent.
It is argued that scholar-officials can be exempted from punishment for their co-residents' offenses,
but punishing their slaves and retainers (núkè),
how would that cause harm?
If they have no slaves or retainers,
they can be ordered to pay a ransom.
And if there are no slaves or servants who are well-known to the public,
the imperial officials (guānzhǎng) and officials of the two-thousand-dàn rank
should personally attend to the matter and issue a judgment according to the facts.
Regarding the principal thief of five bolts of silk,
and the habitual thief of forty bolts,
are indeed ignorant minor officials,
who are easily blinded by wealth,
or commit severe offenses due to negligence.
When one considers their inner feelings,
there is often something pitiable about them.
Therefore, we wish to slightly increase the number of bolts
to spare their lives.
As for officials and above,
who are bestowed with salary and honor,
and entrusted with official duties,
they ought to rectify themselves, uphold the laws,
and restrain their subordinates from wrongdoing.
If they themselves violate the laws and regulations,
disrupting the law and seeking illicit gains,
five bolts of silk are already a great deal.
There is no reason for a scholar-official to privately steal forty bolts of silk.
Even if it reaches this point,
to punish them severely
is certainly appropriate.
How can there be any room for further compassion?
Moreover, it is said that this type of scholar-official
can be killed but not punished,
as some discussions suggest.
However, the original intent
is not truly about this.
I recently heard on the road
that people wished to discuss this,
but it is surprisingly difficult to refine without calling for a proper debate.
Since there is much confusion in the public discussion,
it might be better to let it be.
If, however, it is determined that it should not be suspended,
I suggest that a conference be convened to memorialize the Emperor
and let the imperial decree decide."
Tàizǔ
decreed, "The proposal of the Guard General (Wèijūn) is acceptable."
Hóng then further memorialized,
"According to the old system,
commoners aged thirteen performed half service,
and sixteen performed full service.
It was presumed that those aged thirteen and above
were capable of managing both private and public affairs,
and thus were conscripted.
However, examining current situations,
this is perhaps not entirely accurate.
Physical constitutions vary in strength and weakness,
and not all are commensurate with age.
While at home and living with family,
the labor one can endure
is not excessively harsh.
When transferred to public service,
there are often fixed regulations.
If officials are diligent and compassionate,
there might be no problems.
But if mediocre administrators simply follow the usual practices,
the labor is already strenuous,
and if it happens to be during a harsh administration,
it is beyond description.
There are even those who focus on abundant conscription,
lowering the age,
which causes particular hardship for the isolated, distant, poor, and weak.
This leads to them having nowhere to rely,
and no one to report to in life or death.
In their dire personal circumstances,
they flee and seek to escape.
Their families are sought after over long distances,
pregnant women are unable to carry to term,
and clever evasion of the law
is truly a consequence of this.
Now, with the imperial transformation being renewed,
and peace across the four directions,
the appropriateness of conscription
Those aged fifteen to sixteen
should be half-adults (bàndīng),
and seventeen should be full-adults (quándīng)."
After this, Hóng
suffered from a prolonged illness. Hóng
repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to retire, but the emperor always issued gracious edicts refusing.
In the ninth year [of the Yuánjiā era],
he was promoted to Tài bǎo,
and concurrently held the position of Zhōngshū Jiān.
All other posts remained as before.
That
year, he passed away.
He was fifty-four years old at the time.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Tài bǎo and Zhōngshū Jiān,
given a jié (credentials),
awarded the yú bǎo (feathered canopy) and gǔ chuī (military music),
and the number of guards with drawn swords was increased to sixty.
His positions as Shìzhōng, Lù Shàngshū, and Cìshǐ remained unchanged.
His posthumous title was Wénzhāo Gōng.
He was enshrined in the ancestral temple of Gāozǔ.
In that same year,
an edict stated:
"In recent times, the three rebels incited turmoil,
and indeed had numerous followers.
From the beginning of nurturing and pacifying [the realm],
until the clear application of punishments,
external worries and internal anxieties
were truly difficult.
The late Tài bǎo, Huáróng Xiàn Gōng Hóng; the late Wèi Jiāngjūn, Huá; and the late Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū, Tánshǒu,
embraced righteousness and harbored loyalty,
their sentiments were profoundly sincere.
They strategized in the imperial court,
exhausted their wisdom and strength,
and managed affairs through both calm and perilous times.
[二八]This was personally selected by Our heart.
Now that the national disgrace has been avenged,
they truly deserve enfeoffment.
Yet, they all maintained humility and modesty,
and their ambitions did not exceed their mandates.
Therefore, We paused the court procedures,
intending to issue a later decree.
Their great achievements were not fully realized,
and they successively perished,
causing Us to forever lament and sigh,
with endless grief and regret.
Hóng shall have his enfeoffment increased by a thousand households.
Huá and Tánshǒu shall be enfeoffed as Kāiguó Xiàn Hóu,
each with an additional thousand households in their taxable land.
Hùjūn Jiāngjūn, Jiànchāng Gōng Yànzhī,
with his deep sincerity and secret strategies,
was comparable to Qí Wàng.
His former taxable land shall be restored,
to reward his loyal service."
Another edict stated:
"We hear that Wáng Tài bǎo's family is already impoverished.
The beauty of their purity and frugality
is comparable to that of the ancients.
Thinking of his entire life,
Our sorrow and sighs only increase.
He shall be granted a million coins
and a thousand húl of rice."
In the fifth year of Dàmíng of Shìzǔ,
the imperial carriage traveled
past Hóng's tomb.
An edict was issued saying:
"The late Shìzhōng, Zhōngshū Jiān, Tài bǎo, Lù Shàngshū Shì, Yángzhōu Cìshǐ, Huáróng Wénzhāo Gōng Hóng,
possessed glorious and outstanding virtue and conduct,
with brilliant and far-reaching discernment.
The late Sànqí Chángshì, Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū, Tàizǐ Zhānshì, Yùníng Wénhóu Tánshǒu,
[二九]had long valued tranquility and simplicity,
and his mind was upright and firm.
Both were intricately bound to Our former favor,
sharing both prosperity and adversity.
Internally, they enlightened the imperial way;
externally, they spread admirable reputations.
With their meritorious service to the state,
the people yearned for their great benevolence.
As We briefly toured outside the capital,
We beheld their tombs,
and deeply pondered with emotion,
feeling profound thoughts in Our heart.
Therefore, an envoy shall be dispatched to offer sacrifices at their tombs."
Hóng was intelligent, sharp, and thoughtful.
Moreover, as he was highly esteemed by the people,
he always adhered to propriety and law in his every action.
All his movements and actions,
as well as the style of his letters,
were imitated by later generations,
who called it the Wáng Tài bǎo Jiāfǎ (Wáng Tài bǎo's family style).
Although he held various important positions as a provincial official,
[三０]he did not accumulate wealth.
After his death,
his family had no surplus assets.
However, he was somewhat impulsive and lacked solemnity,
and his temperament was also narrow-minded.
If anyone crossed him,
he would immediately rebuke and humiliate them face-to-face.
When he was young, he once played dice at Gōng Chéngzǐyě's rustic home.
Later, when he held power,
someone came to Hóng to request a county magistracy,
pleading quite earnestly.
This person had once offended him during a dice game.
Hóng questioned him, saying:
"You won money from gambling,
why do you need an official salary?"
The man replied:
"I wonder where Gōng Chéngzǐyě is now?"
Hóng fell silent.
His son Xī succeeded him.
While young, as the son of a chancellor,
he began his career as Yuánwài Sànqí,
and successively held clean official posts:
Zhōngshū Láng,
Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài,
and Jiāngxià Nèishǐ.
He held himself in high regard.
When Tàiwèi, Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng, presided over court,
Xī sat cross-legged on a large chair,
showing almost no deference.
He died in office.
His son Sēngliàng succeeded him.
When Qí received the abdication,
his noble rank was reduced to Hóu,
with a taxable land of five hundred households.
Hóng's younger son, Sēngdá,
has a separate biography.
Hóng's younger brother, Yú,
was Tíngwèi Qīng.
Yú's son, Shēn,
had a good reputation,
and his highest official position was Xīn'ān Tàishǒu.
Yú's younger brother, Yì,
was Guānglù Dàfū.
Yì's younger brother, Rú,
was Shìzhōng.
Rú's younger brother, Tánshǒu,
has a separate biography.
Hóng's paternal cousin, Liàn,
was the son of Mín, who was Jìn Zhōngshū Lìng.
During the Yuánjiā era,
he successively held prominent official positions:
Shìzhōng,
and Dùzhī Shàngshū.
Liàn's son, Zhāo,
during the Dàmíng era of Shìzǔ,
also held clean official posts:
Huángmén Láng,
Línhǎi Wáng Zǐxù Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn Zhēnglǔ and Qiánjūn Zhǎngshǐ,
and Zuǒmín Shàngshū.
In the early reign of Tàizōng,
he served as Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ.
He accompanied Sītú Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén to Chèqí.
At that time, he was mourning his mother, and was additionally granted the title of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
However, he offended Xiūrén,
and was sent out as Shǐxīng Xiāng.
Xiūrén's resentment did not cease,
so Tàizōng had him arrested and handed over to the Tíngwèi,
and he was granted death.
The historian states: The order of Jìn was lax and chaotic,
and its decline had a gradual cause.
Xiàowǔ merely preserved the existing norms from above,
and his influence did not extend downwards.
Dàozǐ, with his muddled virtue, was at the head of the imperial clan,
and the institutions collapsed.
Moreover, Guóbǎo initiated chaos,
and Yuánxiǎn succeeded in tyranny.
Consequently, the ancestral decrees
and the old regulations of the high officials
all scattered like leaves and melted like ice,
swept away completely.
The sovereign's authority was not established,
and the minister's way prevailed exclusively.
State laws differed for individuals,
and court order varied by family.
The lives of the common people
were exhausted by powerful families,
and the wealth of the royal treasury
was converted into private possessions.
Thus, disaster originated from the eastern rebellion,
and turmoil engulfed the world.
The imperial way, vast and boundless, seemed to be preserved only by a thread.
Gāozǔ, in a single court, founded righteousness.
When affairs were in disarray,
he reformed the chaotic institutions,
established the path of peace,
and the principle of respecting the sovereign and humbling the ministers
was settled amidst the use of the horse whip.
Once his authority was exercised,
both inside and outside followed the prohibitions,
thereby transforming the customs of Tàiyuán and Lóng'ān
with the spirit of Jiànwǔ and Yǒngpíng.
This was truly the doing of Wénxuān Gōng.
To be a paramount minister of an era,
and to be enshrined in the pure ancestral temple,
how could it be without reason!
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 3: Xú Xiànzhī, Fù Liàng, Tán Dàojì
Xú Xiànzhī, courtesy name Zōngwén,
was a native of Tán, Dōnghǎi.
His grandfather, Níng,
was Shàngshū Lìbù Láng,
and Jíangzhōu Cìshǐ,
but died before taking office.
His father, Zuòzhī,
was Shàngyú Lìng.
Xiànzhī, while young, served as Wáng Yǎ's Tàizǐ Shǎofù Zhǔbù,
Liú Láozhī's Zhènběi Gōngcáo,
Shàngshū Cíbù Láng (not taken),
and
Huán Xiū's Fǔjūn Zhōngbīngcáo Cānjūn.
He was in the same office as Gāozǔ,
and they became very close.
When the righteous banner was raised,
Gāozǔ appointed him Zhènjūn Cānjūn,
Shàngshū Kùbù Láng,
and Lǐngjūn Sīmǎ.
He worked with Xiè Hùn,
who knew him well.
He was appointed Lángyá Wáng Dàsīmǎ Cānjūn,
Sītú Zuǒxīshǔ,
Xúzhōu Biéjià Cóngshìshǐ,
and Tàiwèi Zīyì Cānjūn.
In the eleventh year of Yìxī,
he was made Yīngyáng Jiāngjūn and Lángyá Nèishǐ,
while still serving as Dàsīmǎ Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
with his general title unchanged.
When Gāozǔ campaigned in the north,
he was transferred to Tàiwèi Zuǒsīmǎ,
in charge of the remaining affairs,
as an assistant to Liú Mùzhī.
Initially,
when Gāozǔ discussed a northern campaign,
many court officials advised against it,
but Xiànzhī remained silent.
Someone asked why he alone did not speak,
and Xiànzhī replied:
"My position has reached the second rank,
my office is that of a two-thousand-dàn official,
and my aspirations have long been fulfilled.
Now, the two regions are pacified,
and territory has been expanded for ten thousand *lǐ*;
only a small part remains unsettled,
yet Your Grace never forgets it, whether sleeping or eating.
Our intentions are so different,
how can I lightly involve myself?"
When Liú Mùzhī died,
Gāozǔ ordered Xiànzhī to be Lìbù Shàngshū, Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn, and Dānyáng Yǐn,
to oversee all remaining affairs,
with twenty armored guards for his entry and exit.
He was then transferred to Shàngshū Púyè,
with his general and *yǐn* titles unchanged.
In the fourteenth year,
Zhōu, the wife of Zhū Xīng, a soldier of the Dàsīmǎ府, was charged because her son Dàofú, three years old,
had previously suffered from epilepsy.
Zhōu, during one of his seizures,
dug a hole and buried him alive.
This was reported by Dàofú's maternal aunt's daughter,
and Zhōu was sentenced to execution in the marketplace.
Xiànzhī deliberated, saying:
"Even tigers and wolves show kindness in their natural affection.
Zhōu's ferocity and cruelty
should indeed be severely punished.
However, I believe that beyond the law,
we should still uphold the principle of things.
If the mother is executed,
the law is made clear through the son;
for the way of a son,
how can there be a place for self-forgiveness?
Although the one who violates the law must be punished,
those who are spared find no tolerance.
I humbly suggest that she be specially exiled to a distant frontier."
This was adopted.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn,
and given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
When the Emperor first ascended the throne,
remembering the contributions of those who assisted in his establishment,
he issued an edict saying:
"Sànqí Chángshì, Shàngshū Púyè, Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn, Dānyáng Yǐn Xú Xiànzhī;
Jiān Jíangzhōu Yùzhōu Zhī Xīyáng Xīncài Zhūjūnshì, Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn, Jíangzhōu Cìshǐ, Huáróng Hóu Wáng Hóng;
Sànqí Chángshì, Hùjūn Jiāngjūn, Zuòtáng Nán Tán Dàojì;
Zhōngshū Lìng, Lǐng Tàizǐ Zhānshì Fù Liàng;
Shìzhōng, Zhōnglǐngjūn Xiè Huì;
Qián Zuǒ Jiāngjūn, Jíangzhōu Cìshǐ, Yíyáng Hóu Tán Sháo;
Shǐchíjié, Yōngliáng Nánběiqín Sìzhōu Jīngzhōu Zhī Hébĕi Zhūjūnshì, Hòujiāngjūn, Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ, Guānzhōng Hóu Zhào Lúnzhī;
Shǐchíjié, Dū Běixú Yǎnqīng Sānzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Běixúzhōu Cìshǐ, Nánchéng Nán Liú Huáishèn;
Sànqí Chángshì, Lǐng Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ, Xīngàn Hóu Wáng Zhòngdé;
Qián Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, Běiqīngzhōu Cìshǐ, Ānnán Nán Xiàng Mí;
Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn, Shèyáng Nán Liú Cuì;
Shǐchíjié, Nánmán Xiàowèi, Héngshān Zǐ Dào Yànzhī;
Xīzhōngláng Sīmǎ, Nánjùn Xiāng, Yíyáng Hóu Zhāng Shào;
Cān Xīzhōngláng Jiāngjūnshì, Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn, Hédōng Tàishǒu, Zīzhōng Hóu Shěn Línzǐ,
and others,
some for their loyal counsel and far-reaching plans,
assisting and praising the grand enterprise;
others for their diligent efforts and achievements,
greatly helping through difficulties.
From beginning to end,
their merits and achievements were outstanding,
and they should all share the prosperity of the nation,
and enjoy this great bounty.
Xiànzhī is to be enfeoffed as Nánchāng Xiàn Gōng;
Hóng as Huáróng Xiàn Gōng;
Dàojì's title is to be changed to Yǒngxiū Xiàn Gōng;
Liàng as Jiànchéng Xiàn Gōng;
Huì as Wǔchāng Xiàn Gōng;
each with a fief of two thousand households.
Sháo's fief is to be increased by two thousand five hundred households;
Zhòngdé's fief by two thousand two hundred households.
Huáishèn and Yànzhī are each promoted to the rank of Hóu,
Cuì's title is changed to Jiàn'ān Xiàn Hóu,
and their fiefs are all increased to one thousand households.
Lúnzhī is to be enfeoffed as Xiāochéng Xiàn Hóu,
with a fief of one thousand households.
Shào is to be enfeoffed as Línjǔ Xiàn Bó;
Línzǐ as Hànshòu Xiàn Bó,
each with a fief of six hundred households.
The system of founding the state
largely follows old regulations."
Xiànzhī was promoted to Shàngshū Lìng and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
and given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
He was advanced to the position of Sīkōng and Lù Shàngshū Shì,
with his *chángshì* and *cìshǐ* titles unchanged.
Xiànzhī rose from commoner status,
and was without scholarly learning,
but solely by his determination, strength, and sagacity,
he suddenly held a position in the imperial court,
winning the respect of both court and commoners,
all believing him to have the potential of a chief minister.
He was reserved and spoke little,
showing no joy or sorrow on his face.
He was quite skilled at *yì* (Go),
but when watching a game, he often appeared as if he did not understand,
which made the people of his time respect him even more.
Fù Liàng and Cài Kuò often said:
"Minister Xú understands everything,
and reconciles differences."
When Gāozǔ became ill,
he was granted thirty additional guards with swords.
When the imperial carriage departed (the emperor died),
he, along with Zhōngshū Lìng Fù Liàng, Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Xiè Huì, and Zhènběi Jiāngjūn Tán Dàojì, received the Emperor's dying instructions.
Shàodì issued an edict saying:
"Fairly adjudicating lawsuits
is the priority of governance.
I am deeply saddened by mourning,
and not yet able to personally review them.
Sīkōng and Shàngshū Lìng may lead the officials to decide cases once a month."
Later, the Emperor lost his virtue,
and Xiànzhī and others planned to depose and enthrone.
However, Lúlíng Wáng Yìzhēn was impetuous and made many mistakes,
unsuitable to govern the realm.
So they first deposed Yìzhēn,
and then the Emperor.
At that time, Xiè Huì was Lǐngjūn,
and because the inner buildings of his mansion were in disrepair and needed renovation,
he moved his entire family out of the residence
and gathered his generals and soldiers inside the mansion.
Zhènběi Jiāngjūn and Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Tán Dàojì, an old general from the previous court,
commanded respect in the palace,
and also had troops.
He was summoned to the court,
and informed of the plot.
When the event was about to occur,
Dàojì stayed overnight at the Lǐngjūn mansion.
Zhōngshū Shèrén Xíng Āntài and Pān Shèng acted as inside collaborators,
guarding the gates on that day.
Dàojì led the troops in front,
and Xiànzhī and others followed him,
entering through the Dōngyèmén, Yúnlóngmén.
The guards had already received instructions,
and none moved.
Earlier, the Emperor had set up stalls in Huálín Yuán,
personally selling goods.
He also dug a ditch and piled up earth
to imitate Pògāng,
and led his attendants in shouting and pulling boats for fun.
That evening,
he slept on a dragon boat
in the Tiānyuān Chí.
The soldiers advanced and killed two people,
and also injured the Emperor's finger.
They helped the Emperor out of the Dōnggé,
and seized his imperial seals.
The officials bowed in farewell,
and escorted him to the former Crown Prince's palace,
then relocated him to Wújùn.
Shìzhōng Chéng Dàohuì urged the enthronement of the fifth imperial brother, Yìgōng,
but Xiànzhī did not permit it.
Envoys were sent to kill Yìzhēn in Xīn'ān,
and to kill the Emperor in Wúxiàn.
At that time, the Emperor's palace was still under construction,
and he temporarily resided in the Jīnchāng Tíng.
The Emperor burst out of the Chāngmén,
but the pursuers struck him down with a gate bar,
and then killed him.
When Emperor Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
Xiànzhī was promoted to Sītú,
the rest remaining as before.
He was re-enfeoffed as the Duke of Nánpíng Commandery,
with an income of four thousand households.
He firmly declined the additional enfeoffment.
The officials memorialized that the imperial carriage should, as before, attend to lawsuits in Huálín Park.
An imperial edict stated:
"Many matters of governance and punishment are not yet fully understood.
Let them be investigated as before by the two former high officials."
In the second year of Yuánjiā (425 CE),
Xiànzhī, together with Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū Fù Liàng, submitted a memorial to return governance to the emperor,
saying:
"Your subjects have heard that the sovereign takes charge of the mandate,
and the turning pivot accomplishes affairs;
the path of the subject reaches its end,
their duties fulfilled as wings assisting.
The way of wearing the imperial crown,
which totally ceased with the Ancient Sovereigns;
and the matter of folding one's hands in idleness,
did not prevail in the Middle Antiquity.
Therefore, Gāozōng did not speak,
making the three years a limit;
the prime minister governed,
making two full years a period.
Since the Hundred Kings,
none have been otherwise.
Your Majesty, with your sagely virtue, has revived and
taken on the great enterprise.
The myriad commoners eagerly look up,
desiring to be transformed by your flourishing reign.
However, Your Majesty's sagely will is humble and modest,
entrusting accomplishment to all the officials.
Since the completion of the great rites,
three changes of the fire drill have passed [i.e., three years],
and the great sun awaits to shine,
near and far leaning and belonging [to you].
Although we, your subjects, have repeatedly expressed our sincerity,
we have not been able to move you from above.
We dare to rely on the sentiments of all things,
and respectfully act on the will of the common people.
We humbly wish Your Majesty to recall the distant path of King Wén of Zhōu, who worked until sundown,
and to consider close at hand the difficulty of the imperial house's foundation,
to at times oversee all affairs,
and personally attend to court administration.
Broaden the four ears (listen widely),
and extensively inquire into all matters;
then peace and prosperity can be achieved,
and all living beings will be exceedingly fortunate."
The Emperor did not grant it.
Xiànzhī and others memorialized again, saying:
"Recently we expressed our humble sentiments,
our words emptying our hearts.
We received a returning edict,
stating that your approval had not changed.
It is not only we, your foolish subjects,
who hold this conviction in our hearts;
when we inquired in the court and throughout the land,
no one had a different opinion.
Why is this?
The spread of influence in all directions
is truly tied to the king's virtue;
the affairs of the nation
originate from one person.
Although generations differ,
and times and customs vary,
regarding the sovereign presiding and the subjects assisting,
it is consistent throughout ancient and modern times.
There has never been a case where one completely entrusted all responsibilities,
yet hoped for brilliance and prosperity;
this impropriety
is known far and wide.
We, your subjects, have been favored for two generations,
sharing both joy and sorrow equally.
Our feelings are utmost for the nation,
how can we remain silently compliant?
We once again reveal our loyal hearts,
presumptuously to request."
The Emperor still declined.
Xiànzhī and others again firmly argued, saying:
"Our previous memorial laid out our case,
our words and sincerity fully expressed.
The imperial edict was profound and distant,
not yet granting our hearing and acceptance.
We repeatedly ponder with trepidation,
and our worry and sighs increase.
We have heard that to successfully establish the former foundation
is the great enterprise of repairing the errors of the ancestors;
to become greatly manifest at dawn
is the lofty principle of emperors and kings.
Since the Sòng dynasty began its operations,
the sagacious and wise have created,
but severe worries have not ceased,
and difficulties and troubles have continued.
Relying on Heaven's decree,
the sagacious and enlightened succeeded to the enterprise,
but the difficult times and national losses
still weigh on the people's hearts.
The stability of Tài Shān
cannot easily be assured;
obscurity and enlightenment, rise and fall,
depend on Your Sacred Person.
This is truly the time of the Zhōu poem 'rising early,'
the day the Yīn king awaited dawn;
how can one remain idle and inactive,
returning to the style of remote antiquity,
hesitantly yielding and being modest,
following the example of an ordinary man?
We humbly wish Your Majesty to consider the ancestral temples as paramount,
and the common people as your heart.
Extend the great enterprise to succeed the former path,
and magnify the sagely way to increase past achievements.
What these ignorant and blind subjects have presented,
our sincerity ends here."
The Emperor then granted their request.
Xiànzhī thereupon resigned his position and returned to his private residence.
His nephew Pèizhī, along with Shìzhōng Chéng Dàohuì, Wúxīng Tàishǒu Wáng Sháozhī, and others, all deemed it inappropriate
and urged him with great earnestness,
so he again received an imperial edict to temporarily assume his duties.
In the first month of the third year,
an edict stated:
"The people are born in three (generations),
and serve as one.
Love and reverence share the same extreme,
how can this merely be about moral teachings?
Moreover, if actions are comparable to those of the Creator,
then the principle dictates that they should be honored and magnified.
Xú Xiànzhī, Fù Liàng, and Xiè Huì
rose through their talents and connections,
having received favor in the past.
They were elevated from obscurity
to high and crucial positions.
To say they were nurtured and raised like chicks under wings
is still insufficient to describe it.
In the late *Yǒngchū* period,
heavenly calamity spread everywhere,
the great brightness dimmed its radiance,
and the four seas were shrouded in silence.
They truly received the solemn entrustment,
bearing a responsibility akin to carrying the state's mandate.
Yet, they failed to exert their utmost effort,
to dedicate their hearts and strength.
In sending off the departed, they lacked the integrity of remonstrance,
and in serving the incumbent, they fell short in loyalty and fidelity.
They indulged in compliance without keeping records,
and their efforts to rectify and save were unheard of.
They harbored a desire for favor and sought to curry approval,
leading to the loss of virtue through their acquiescence.
Although in the end they acted out of fear of disaster
to establish a great strategy,
they unleashed their perverse hearts,
unfearing of injustice.
At the beginning of the removal,
they plotted insidious poison.
Not long after their arrival,
they openly committed acts of resentful murder,
reaching the extreme of cruelty and oppression.
Suffering and torment were fully inflicted,
causing him to fall into the hands of base servants,
and his life ended in a temporary lodging house.
The capital and the countryside were filled with grief and shock,
and passersby shed tears.
Therefore, the former Lúlíng Wáng (Prince of Lúlíng), being brilliant and far-sighted,
his admirable reputation had spread early.
The entrustment of Lǔ and Wèi
was anticipated by both court and commoners.
Xiànzhī and others, being cruel and contemptuous, seeking exclusive power,
were jealous of the virtuous and feared being pressured.
They fabricated slanders
to bring about this baseless calamity.
They deceived the sovereign and misled the emperor,
arbitrarily imposing exile and banishment.
They falsely invoked imperial decrees
to cause this disaster.
They were entrusted with the fate of the nation,
yet they cut it down as if it were an enemy.
Within a mere month,
they twice unleashed insidious poison.
The pain moved the three spiritual realms,
and resentment formed between humans and ghosts.
Since the invention of writing,
abandoning norms and embracing cruelty,
and overturning the clear decrees of Heaven,
there has been none as extreme as this.
In the past, Zǐjiā participated in regicide,
and the people of Zhèng launched an attack.
Sòng Féi was innocent,
yet was slain in Dàngzé.
How much more so now, as this rebellion far exceeds past transgressions,
and the pain is deeper for the state and the family.
If this can be tolerated,
what cannot be endured?
They ought to be executed immediately,
to make amends to both the living and the dead.
However, at that time, the great matter had just begun,
and dissenting opinions were numerous.
The merits of stabilizing the state were truly outstanding,
while the greatest crimes had not yet been fully exposed.
Therefore, after careful consideration of the people's sentiments
and listening to public opinion,
though I desired to suppress the rebellion,
I feared it would be difficult to accomplish.
Thus, I bore my sorrow and grief,
harboring shame for years.
Every time I thought of how difficult life truly is,
and how my feelings and affairs had not been resolved,
how could I not look at my reflection with a broken heart,
and weep blood on my pillow?
Now, the transgressions of these rebellious officials
are manifest and notorious far and wide.
Noble persons grieve,
and righteous individuals long to act.
Family vengeance and national shame
can now be avenged.
Therefore, I command the Minister of Justice
to swiftly enforce the laws.
As Xiè Huì occupies the upper reaches of the river,
he might not be immediately punished.
I shall personally lead the six armies
to defend against him.
Let the Central Leader of the Army, Dào Yànzhī, be dispatched immediately,
and General Who Conquers the North, Tán Dàojì, follow him continuously.
The guards, army headquarters, and prefectures are to apprehend and eliminate them in due time.
I have already ordered General Who Conquers Barbarians, Liú Cuì, to cut off their escape and hiding places.
The crime extends only to the principal culprits;
the rest are not to be questioned.
Considering the eternal past,
my heart and feelings are shattered.
Now that the haze and mist have been cleared,
I hope for good governance."
On that day, an edict summoned Xú Xiànzhī.
When he reached outside Xīmíng Mén (West Bright Gate),
Xiè Huì's younger brother, Xiè Hù, who was a Yellow Gate Regular Attendant
and upright,
informed Fù Liàng, saying:
"There is an unusual order in the palace."
Liàng galloped to inform Xú Xiànzhī.
Xú Xiànzhī returned to Xīzhōu (West Prefecture),
left the city in a carriage used by palace women for greetings,
walked to Xīnlín,
and committed suicide by cutting his throat in a pottery kiln,
at the age of sixty-three.
Initially, Xú Xiànzhī did not answer the summons.
The emperor sent the Central Leader of the Army, Dào Yànzhī, and the Right Guard General, Wáng Huá, to pursue and arrest him.
When Xú Xiànzhī died,
a villager reported it,
and his body was transported to the Court of Judicial Review.
His son, Xú Qiáozhī,
was married to Gāozǔ's sixth daughter, Princess Fùyáng,
and held the official title of Literary Scholar to the Prince of Jìnglíng.
Xú Qiáozhī and his younger brother Xú Qǐnú were executed.
In the beginning,
when Xú Xiànzhī was young,
a man once came
and said to him:
"I am your ancestor."
Xú Xiànzhī then rose and bowed to him.
This man said:
"You have noble features,
but you will face a great calamity.
You can bury twenty-eight coins in the four corners of your dwelling
to avoid disaster.
After this, you can reach the highest position among officials."
Later, Xú Xiànzhī accompanied his relatives to a county
and resided in the county seat.
He once went out for a short while,
and bandits subsequently sacked the county.
None of the people in the county were spared;
even chickens and dogs were all killed.
Only Xú Xiànzhī, who was outside, survived.
He followed his cousin, Xú Lǚzhī, who was the magistrate of Línhǎi and Lè'ān counties.
He once traveled through the mountains
and saw a black dragon over a *zhàng* (about 3.3 meters) long.
It had horns on its head,
both front legs were complete,
but it had no hind legs,
and it dragged its tail as it moved.
When he was appointed Sīkōng (Minister of Works),
the official guarding the pass reported that
a comet was seen in the morning, appearing in the south.
Also, at the time of his appointment,
a pair of storks gathered on the eastern *chīwěi* (owl-tail roof ornament) of the Tàijí (Grand Ultimate) Hall and cried out.
His elder brother's son, Pèi Zhī (佩之),
was frivolous and fond of profit.
Gāo Zǔ (高祖), considering him a relative by marriage,
repeatedly granted him favor and trust,
making him Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹)
and Wú Jùn Tàishǒu (吳郡太守).
In the early Jiǐngpíng (景平) reign,
because Xuān Zhī (羨之) held power,
Pèi Zhī (佩之) frequently interfered in state affairs.
He formed a faction with Wáng Sháo Zhī (王韶之), Chéng Dào Huì (程道惠), and the Zhongshū Shèrén (中書舍人) Xíng Ān Tài (邢安泰) and Pān Shèng (潘盛).
At that time, Xiè Huì (謝晦) had been ill for a long time,
having continuous moxibustion,
and was unable to receive guests.
Pèi Zhī (佩之) and others suspected he was feigning illness with ulterior motives.
They rode with Sháo Zhī (韶之) and Dào Huì (道惠) to Fù Liàng (傅亮),
claiming it was Xuān Zhī's (羨之) intention,
and wished Liàng (亮) to issue an edict to execute him.
Liàng (亮) replied,
“We three,
who all received the dying charge,
how can we slaughter each other?
If you gentlemen indeed carry out this matter,
I shall simply don my turban and walk out of the Yèmén (掖門).”
Pèi Zhī (佩之) and the others then stopped.
After Xuān Zhī (羨之) was executed,
Tài Zǔ (太祖) specially pardoned Pèi Zhī (佩之),
only dismissing him from office.
In the winter of that year,
Pèi Zhī (佩之) again conspired to rebel with Diànzhōng Jiān (殿中監) Máo Hēng (茅亨),
and also informed the former Níngzhōu Cìshǐ (寧州刺史) Yīng Xí (應襲),
proposing Hēng (亨) for Yǎnzhōu (兗州) and
Xí (襲) for Yùzhōu (豫州).
Hēng (亨) secretly reported this,
and Xí (襲) also informed Sītú (司徒) Wáng Hóng (王弘).
Pèi Zhī (佩之) gathered over a hundred partisans,
slaughtered oxen as rewards,
and drafted documents assigning
positions to the people of the time,
planning to revolt in the palace during the New Year's assembly
the following year.
Before a few days passed,
he was arrested and beheaded.
Fù Liàng (傅亮), courtesy name Jì Yǒu (季友),
was a native of Língzhōu (靈州), Běidì (北地).
His great-grandfather, Xián (咸),
was Sīlì Xiàowèi (司隸校尉).
His father, Yuàn (瑗),
was known for his scholarship
and rose to the position of Ānchéng Tàishǒu (安成太守).
Yuàn (瑗) was good friends with Xī Chāo (郗超).
Chāo (超) once visited Yuàn (瑗),
and Yuàn (瑗) introduced his two sons, Dí (迪) and Liàng (亮).
Liàng (亮) was four or five years old.
Chāo (超) had someone remove Liàng's (亮) clothes
and had attendants take them away.
Liàng (亮) showed no sign of distress.
Chāo (超) said to Yuàn (瑗),
“Your younger son's talent and official position
will greatly surpass his elder brother's.
However, preserving the family and transmitting its legacy
will ultimately rest with the elder.”
Dí (迪), courtesy name Cháng Yóu (長猷),
was also a Confucian scholar.
He rose to the position of Wǔbīng Shàngshū (五兵尚書).
He died in the second year of Yǒngchū (永初)
and was posthumously granted the title of Tàicháng (太常).
Liàng (亮) was widely read in classics and history,
and was especially skilled in literary composition.
He first served as Jiànwēi Cānjūn (建威參軍),
then Huán Qiān (桓謙)'s Zhōngjūn Xíngcānjūn (中軍行參軍).
When Huán Xuán (桓玄) usurped the throne,
he heard of Liàng's (亮) extensive learning and literary talent,
and selected him as Mìshū Láng (祕書郎),
intending him to put the Secret Archives in order.
He had not yet been appointed when Xuán (玄) was defeated.
At the beginning of the Righteous Uprising,
Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹) Mèng Chǎng (孟昶) made him Jiànwēi Cānjūn (建威參軍).
In the first year of Yìxī (義熙),
he was appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng (員外散騎侍郎),
directly serving in the Xīshěng (西省)
and overseeing imperial edicts.
He was transferred to Lǐngjūn Chángshǐ (領軍長史),
with Zhōngshū Láng (中書郎) Téng Yǎn (滕演) replacing him.
Liàng (亮) had not yet taken up the post
when he suffered the sorrow of his mother's death.
After the mourning period,
he became Liú Yì (劉毅)'s Fǔjūn Jìshì Cānjūn (撫軍記室參軍),
and was later appointed Lǐngjūn Sīmǎ (領軍司馬).
In the seventh year,
he was promoted to Sànqí Shìláng (散騎侍郎),
again replacing Yǎn (演) in directly serving in the Xīshěng (西省).
He was subsequently transferred to Zhōngshū Huángmén Shìláng (中書黃門侍郎),
continuing to serve directly in the Xīshěng (西省) as before.
Gāo Zǔ (高祖), seeing his prolonged diligent service,
wished to appoint him to Dōngyáng Jùn (東陽郡),
and first mentioned it to Dí (迪).
Dí (迪) was overjoyed and told Liàng (亮).
Liàng (亮) did not reply,
but immediately hastened to see Gāo Zǔ (高祖) and said,
“I humbly heard of your gracious command,
proposing me for Dōngyáng (東陽).
As my family is poor and I am undeservedly honored with salary,
I privately consider it fortunate.
However, the desire to rely on your shelter
is truly embedded in my original heart.
I beg to remain under your heavenly aegis
and do not wish to be sent out.”
Gāo Zǔ (高祖) laughed and said,
“I thought you needed the salary.
If you can be like this,
it greatly accords with my expectations.”
It happened that there was a campaign against Sīmǎ Xiū Zhī (司馬休之) in the west,
so he was appointed Tàiwèi Cóngshì Zhōngláng (太尉從事中郎),
in charge of the Secretariat.
Yáng Huī (羊徽), Tàiwèi Cānjūn (太尉參軍), was appointed Zhōngshū Láng (中書郎)
to replace him in serving directly in the Xīshěng (西省).
Liàng (亮) accompanied the expedition to Guān (關) and Luò (洛),
returning to Péngchéng (彭城).
When the State of Sòng (宋) was first established,
an imperial decree appointed him Shìzhōng (侍中),
concurrently Lǐng Shìzǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (領世子中庶子).
He was transferred to Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令),
still concurrently Lǐng Zhōngshùzǐ (領中庶子).
He followed the return to Shòuyáng (壽陽).
Gāo Zǔ (高祖) had the intention of receiving the abdication,
but found it difficult to speak of.
So he gathered his ministers for a banquet,
and casually remarked,
“Huán Xuán (桓玄) violently usurped power,
and the mandate of the tripod had already shifted.
I was the first to advocate for righteousness,
restoring the imperial house.
Campaigning in the south and conquering in the north,
I pacified the four seas.
My achievements are complete and my deeds are manifest,
and thus I have been granted the Nine Bestowments.
Now my years are nearing old age,
and my eminence is such.
Things at their peak warn against excess,
and cannot long remain secure.
Today I wish to return my titles and ranks,
and retire in the capital.”
The assembled ministers only profusely praised his merits and virtues,
none comprehending his true intent.
As the day grew late and the gathering dispersed,
Liàng (亮) returned outside,
then realized the meaning.
But the palace gates were already closed.
Liàng (亮) then knocked on the gate, requesting an audience,
and Gāo Zǔ (高祖) immediately opened the gate to see him.
Liàng (亮) entered and said,
“Your servant ought to return to the capital for a short while.”
Gāo Zǔ (高祖) fully understood this intention,
and said nothing further,
only asking,
“How many men do you need to escort you?”
Liàng (亮) replied,
“A few dozen men will suffice.”
Thereupon, he immediately took his leave.
As Liàng (亮) left,
it was already night,
and he saw a long star spanning the sky.
Liàng (亮) patted his thigh and said,
“I have always disbelieved in astronomy,
but now it is proven true!”
Upon reaching the capital,
he immediately summoned Gāo Zǔ (高祖) to assist.
In the first year of Yǒngchū (永初),
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhānshì (太子詹事),
