remaining Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令) as before.
For his meritorious assistance in establishing the new dynasty,
he was enfeoffed as Jiànchéng Xiàn Gōng (建城縣公),
with an income of two thousand households.
He entered to serve directly in the Zhōngshūshěng (中書省),
exclusively managing imperial edicts.
Because Liàng (亮) was in charge of state power,
he was permitted to receive guests in the province.
Outside the Shénhǔ Mén (神虎門),
there were often hundreds of carriages every morning.
At the beginning of Gāo Zǔ's (高祖) ascension,
all official writings were by Jìshì Cānjūn (記室參軍) Téng Yǎn (滕演);
during the northern campaign against Guǎnggù (廣固),
everything was entrusted to Chángshǐ (長史) Wáng Dàn (王誕);
from then until the reception of the mandate,
all memorials, strategies, and imperial pronouncements
were Liàng's (亮) compositions.
Yǎn (演), courtesy name Yàn Jiāng (彥將),
was a native of Xī'è (西鄂), Nányáng (南陽).
He rose to the position of Huángmén Láng (黃門郎)
and Mìshū Jiān (祕書監).
He died in the eighth year of Yìxī (義熙).
In the second year,
Liàng (亮) was transferred to Shàngshū Púyè (尚書僕射),
remaining Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令) and Zhānshì (詹事) as before.
The following year,
Gāo Zǔ (高祖) fell ill,
and along with Xú Xuān Zhī (徐羨之) and Xiè Huì (謝晦), received the dying charge,
and was granted twenty guards with ceremonial swords.
When the young emperor ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監),
then Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令).
In the second year of Jǐngpíng (景平) [424 CE],
he took up the post of Hùjūn Jiāngjūn (護軍將軍).
When the young emperor was deposed,
Liàng (亮) led the acting government (xíngtái 行臺) to Jiānglíng (江陵) to welcome the Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ 太祖).
Upon arrival,
he erected a temporary gate (xíngmén 行門) south of Jiānglíng (江陵) city,
inscribing it
“Dàsīmǎ Mén” (大司馬門, Gate of the Grand Marshal).
He led the officials of the acting government to the gate to bow and present their memorials,
the ceremony and demeanor were most grand.
When the Grand Ancestor was about to descend,
he summoned Liàng (亮) for an audience.
Liàng (亮) wept profusely,
his sorrow moving those around him.
Then, when asked about the full story of Yìzhēn’s (義真) and the young emperor's deaths and depositions,
he wailed and choked with sobs,
and those attending could not look up.
Liàng (亮) was soaked with sweat on his back,
unable to reply.
Thereupon, he confided in Dào Yànzhī (到彥之) and Wáng Huá (王華),
forming deep connections.
When the Grand Ancestor ascended the throne,
he was additionally granted the titles Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍), Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū (左光祿大夫), and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司),
with all his original offices remaining as before.
The civil and military officials of the Sīkōng Fǔ (司空府) then became those of the Zuǒ Guānglù Fǔ (左光祿府).
He was further advanced in peerage to Shǐxīng Jùn Gōng (始興郡公),
with an income of four thousand households,
but he firmly declined the advancement.
In the third year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) [426 CE],
the Grand Ancestor wished to execute Liàng (亮).
He first summoned him for an audience.
Someone secretly reported this from within the palace,
and Liàng (亮) excused himself, saying his sister-in-law was gravely ill,
and requested to return home temporarily.
He sent a messenger to inform Xú Xiànzhī (徐羨之),
then rode in a carriage out of the city gate,
and galloped on horseback to his brother Dí’s (迪) tomb.
Guō Hóng (郭泓), the Túnqí Xiàowèi (屯騎校尉), arrested him and handed him over to the Tíngwèi (廷尉),
where he was executed.
He was fifty-three years old at the time.
When he first arrived at Guǎngmò Mén (廣莫門),
the emperor sent a Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人) to show Liàng (亮) the imperial edict,
and also said:
“Given your sincerity at Jiānglíng (江陵),
your sons shall be unharmed.”
Earlier,
Liàng (亮), seeing the perilous state of the world,
wrote an essay titled Yǎn Shèn (演慎),
which said: The Great Way states,
“Be as careful at the end as at the beginning,
and there will be no failure.”
The *Yì* (易) says:
“Keep it in the bag; no blame.”
Caution causes no harm.
It also says:
“If you use
white grass for a mat,
what blame can there be?”
This is the utmost caution.
King Wén (文王) was cautious,
and the *Dàyǎ* (大雅) sings of his many blessings;
Zhòng Yóu (仲由) loved courage,
and crossing a river without a guide brought him bitter admonishment.
The *Yú Shū* (虞書)
records praise for self-caution,
and inscriptions adorned the steps of the Zhōu (周) ancestral temple.
From this, we can say that what can best
preserve one's body and maintain one's virtue,
is none other than caution.
The four ways (sìdào 四道) favor humility,
the three talents (sāncái 三材) dread fullness;
auspiciousness gathers in an empty room,
ghosts peep at a tall house;
a richly furnished house harbors the disaster of a collapsed roof (bùjiā zhī zāi 蔀家之災),
and a lavish feast (dǐngshí 鼎食) does not guarantee a hundred years of
nobility.
Yet those who pursue desires and cling to life,
neglect and are not warned;
those who know how to advance but forget how to retreat,
never learn their lesson.
The chariot in front has already crashed,
but the carriage behind does not stop;
they ride through danger
hoping for safety,
and traverse perils relying on luck.
Thus come the disasters of falling and perishing,
the misfortunes of a truncated life and untimely death.
Why is this so?
They are adrift and forget to turn back,
and
treat their own lives lightly compared to external things.
Thus, the noble men of old
regarded fame and rank as fragrant bait,
so peril did not reach them;
they contemplated troubles and guarded against them in advance,
then acupuncture and moxibustion (zhēnshí 針石) were unnecessary.
A great flood is blocked by
trickles,
a trunk of clasped arms is broken by a fine sapling (xiānchén 纖𠬞);
thus, one takes heed,
and takes action at the slightest sign.
One learns from the high-flying bird that swiftly departs,
and throws away the sash upon seeing sweet wine.
How could it be that only after reaching a desperate situation
is a plan devised,
and only after trouble has arisen is recovery considered?
Thus, the *Shī* (詩) says:
“Be cautious in your lordly conduct,
so as to guard against unforeseen events.”
This speaks of preventing things in their nascent stage.
Being too simple leads to internal loss and external display,
being too expansive leads to external order but internal imbalance.
Qí (齊) and Qín (秦) suffered failures by adhering to one extreme,
and relying solely on one side yields no benefit of comprehensive governance.
Ice and charcoal are purged from
the heart,
and a strong wall (yánqiáng 巖牆) cuts off the four limbs.
If one does this,
then body and spirit are both complete,
inside and outside are at peace,
the soul is inwardly clear,
and the hundreds of bones are outwardly firm.
Evil influences cannot
assault,
and worries cannot reach.
Then one can speak of the utmost truth and ultimate words.
Take Jīzǐ (嵇子), whose lofty heart aspired to antiquity,
breaking free from restraints and living independently.
The roots of the five difficulties (wǔnán 五難) were already pulled out,
and the path to living was unburdened,
human troubles were almost entirely absent.
Yet merely by neglecting caution with Zhōng (鍾) and Lǚ (呂),
and speaking freely of Yǔ (禹) and Tāng (湯),
the seeds of disaster sprouted from a hair's breadth,
and his soaring wings were clipped just as he was about to take flight.
Looking at his letter to his good friend,
he compares
rich flavors to sweet poison (gāndàn 甘酖),
.........his fear of trouble,
is like riding a runaway horse without reins;
his caution against disaster,
is like walking on ice or approaching a precipice.
Some shake off their coarse clothes and dwell high,
raising their fishing rods and going off alone;
some keep to frugality and shun extravagance,
content with a humble position.
Thus, the man of Qīyuán (漆園) (Zhuāngzǐ 莊子) shunned Chǔ (楚),
fearing the fate of the tortoise for sacrifice (guīxī 龜犧);
those who fled to Shāngluò (商洛),
feared the four horses (sìmǎ 駟馬).
Píngzhòng (平仲) (Yàn Yīng 晏嬰) declined a fief,
taking Cén (崔) and Qìng (慶) as a warning (yīnjiàn 殷鑒);
Zhāng Lín (張臨) (Zhāng Hàn 張翰) withdrew from abundance,
mindful of Sāng (桑) and Huò (霍).
If a noble man examines these two paths,
then the distinction between the worthy
and the ignoble will be clear,
and the reality of preservation and ruin will also be evident.
It is not difficult to know,
but only difficult to be cautious.
Caution,
is the pivot and key to words and actions.
Indeed, facing a diagram to wield a blade,
even a fool would not do it;
standing on the edge of an abyss or climbing a steep cliff,
no one is not trembling.
Why?
Because danger is imminent, so caution is profound;
trouble is pressing, so fear is deep.
Thus, the *Shī* (詩) says:
“Dare not attack a tiger,
dare not cross a river without a guide.”
This speaks of caution in the minute.
Thus, when Páozi (庖子) (Dīng 丁) navigated the bones of the ox (shèzú 涉族),
he was startled and took warning;
a difference of a hair's breadth,
and the outcome is still
like this.
How much more so when one courts danger and violates taboos,
throwing oneself into a death trap?
The tools of fortune and misfortune,
are filled within and stretched without.
Crossing the nine bends of Qióngbó (卭僰),
or navigating the surging waves of Lǚliáng (呂梁),
a tilt can happen in an instant,
and life is tragically lost beyond saving.
Alas!
Alas!
Thus, there is a saying:
“If one can truly be cautious,
it is the root of blessings.”
“If one says, 'What harm is there?',
it is the gate of disaster.”
It simply speaks of caution.
Liàng was a scholar in plain clothes,
luckily encountering an opportune moment.
Once he occupied the position of prime minister,
and concurrently held great power,
the young emperor (shǎo dì) became immoral,
causing him inner worry and fear.
He composed the "Gǎnwù Fù" (感物賦, Rhapsody on Being Moved by Things) to express his feelings.
Its words are: "In the month of late autumn,
I performed my duties in the inner palace.
The night was clear and my tasks were few,
so I let my gaze wander through the art garden.
At that time, frost began to warn,
but dormant creatures were still numerous.
Moths
with fluttering wings,
fluttered abundantly throughout the chamber,
rushing towards the windows and curtains,
gathering on the bright candles.
They were bound to meet their end by burning.
Though they were tiny creatures,
this brought me deep compassion for a long time.
I retreated, reflecting on
Zhuāng Shēng's (莊生) story of the exotic magpie,
and how they, like me, were lost and forgot the path of self-reflection.
This is why the former master (xiān shī) disdained cleverness,
and why the guest from Qí (齊客) found the 'Sun Discourse' (Rì Lùn) difficult.
Saddened,
with thoughts in my heart,
moved by things and inspired to ponder,
I then composed this rhapsody.
In the late dusk of the western setting sun,
I respectfully received the imperial command in the palace.
I heard crickets by the front veranda,
and saw the bright moon through the window latticework.
The wind rustled, assaulting the curtains,
and thick frost covered the walls.
I pitied the cicadas singing in response to the season,
and regretted the fading light that cherished the east.
Alas, the gathered emotions of a toiling man,
how long the night, and how full of worries!
I gazed at
the past and present with distant thoughts,
like an endless cycle.
I recited Yǐ Xiāng's (倚相) preserved rules,
and hoped for Dǒng Shēng's (董生) harmonious way.
I drilled by lamplight and spread out scrolls,
warming myself with the
remaining traces of the sages and philosophers.
The ancient texts (fén sù) are distant and hard to reach,
the Nine Schools (Jiǔ Liú) are diverse in their boundaries.
I comprehend the three hundred odes without evil thoughts,
and penetrate the five thousand (words of the Dào Dé Jīng) with a common origin.
I examined old accounts in the former
histories,
and sought my inner motives in rise and fall.
Is it that obstacles and smooth paths are determined by fate,
or that complete ruin comes from oneself?
I wandered through the brilliant forest of literature (hàn lín),
praising the beautiful works of skilled craftsmen.
Their words are elegant and free from impurity,
their meaning is refined and clear.
Although the sources are deep and vast,
they can still be summarized and enlighten the ignorant.
Fluttering gnats,
lightly flying flies,
creeping along the curtains, seeking gaps,
gazing at the flame, yearning to ascend.
They consume the fragrant oil without regret,
and rush towards the bright candle undeterred.
Seeing the former
path already destroyed,
they forget to change course for the next ride.
It is not that these tiny creatures are worthy of lament,
but I am saddened by deep thoughts and beat my breast.
That the way of humanity (rén dào) is precious,
equaling the two cosmic forces (èr yí) and
matching the spirits.
Receiving pure tranquility to be endowed with vital energy,
cultivating the 'due mean' (yuán dū) as a principle.
Illuminating safety and danger in the mind's art,
mirroring subtle omens before they take shape.
Some pursue trifles and abandon
fundamentals,
others indulge in desires and forget life.
They shatter the Pearl of Suí Hóu (Suí Hóu) for a petty rank,
discarding what is valued for what is trivial.
How much more so for insects who are ignorant,
yet even wise men are entangled by this.
I understood Diāo Líng (雕陵) in Zhuāng Shì's (莊氏) tale,
almost discerning the turbid and mistaking it for clear.
I looked up to the noble path of former cultivators,
knowing my own footsteps do not match.
Though the external divination of Sòng Yuán (宋元) exists,
how can
I achieve such clarity?
How can I not understand the need for turning back?
Alas, I lay down my brush and my feelings increase."
Initially,
when welcoming the imperial carriage,
he composed three poems on the road.
One of them contained words of regret and fear,
saying:
"Early in the morning, my oar departs the imperial city,
someone bids farewell to my boat.
The farewell is not given with gifts,
but with words more precious than jade spheres.
To know when to stop is a valuable way,
to covet emolument is a fault in righteousness.
My four horses are weary of the long road,
your reins, my lord, can be pulled back.
Zhāng Bǐng (張邴) tied his morning carriage,
Shū Dǒng (疎董) rested his evening axle.
The eastern corner has indeed faded,
the western light departs and does not stay.
How can life and destiny be planned?
I hold this as a former lesson.
I spread my lapel, engraving the earnest teaching,
and tied my belt, carrying the good counsel.
To be deluded by favor is not my ambition,
my deep virtue is indeed unrewarded.
I touch my body, ashamed of its fatigue and decay,
thrice reflecting, I am embarrassed by my floating rank.
The bright sun illuminates the weeds,
all things follow this principle.
Loyal remonstrance needs no special knowing,
the 'Shi Wēi' (式微) ode utters plain songs."
Liàng knew his downfall was imminent,
but found no way to retire.
He also wrote praises for Xīn Yǒu (辛有), Mù Shēng (穆生), and Dǒng Zhòngdào (董仲道),
commending their beauty of discerning the subtle.
His eldest son, Yǎn (演),
a secretary in the imperial library (mì shū láng),
died before Liàng.
Yǎn's (演) brothers, Kuī (悝) and Zhàn (湛), fled.
Zhàn's (湛) brother, Dū (都),
was relocated to Jiàn'ān (建安) Commandery;
during the reign of Shì Zǔ Xiào Jiàn (世祖孝建),
they all returned to the capital.
Tán Dàojì (檀道濟),
a native of Jīnxiāng (金鄉), Gāopíng (高平),
was the younger brother of General of the Left, Sháo (韶).
He was orphaned young,
and observed mourning rituals meticulously.
He served his elder sister and brother,
earning praise for his harmony and prudence.
When Gāo Zǔ (高祖) initiated his righteous cause,
Dàojì (道濟) followed him into the capital city,
participating in Gāo Zǔ's (高祖) military affairs for the Jiànwǔ (建武) army,
and was transferred to be General Who Conquers the West (Zhēng Xī Jiāngjūn).
He subjugated Lǔ Shān (魯山),
captured Huán Zhèn (桓振),
and was appointed Fǔguó Cānjūn (輔國參軍) and Administrator of Nányáng (Nányáng Tàishǒu).
For his achievements in establishing the righteous cause (jiàn yì),
he was enfeoffed as a fifth-rank Marquis of Wúxīng (吳興) County.
When Lú Xún (盧循) rebelled,
and various bandits rose in succession,
Guō Jìshēng (郭寄生) and others gathered to form Táng (唐).
Dàojì (道濟) was appointed General Who Manifests Martial Might (Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Tiānmén (Tiānmén Tàishǒu) to suppress them, which he achieved.
He also followed Liú Dàoguī (劉道規) to suppress Huán Qiān (桓謙) and Xún Lín (荀林) and others.
He inspired the civil and military officials,
leading his soldiers from the front,
and wherever he went, he crushed and destroyed.
When Xú Dàofù (徐道覆) came to press,
Dàoguī (道規) personally went out to resist in battle,
and Dàojì (道濟) contributed greatly to the war effort.
He was promoted to An'yuǎn Hùjūn (安遠護軍) and Wǔlíng Nèishǐ (武陵內史).
He again served as Cānjūn (參軍) for the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
and was appointed Attendant Secretary of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng),
then transferred to General Who Brings Peace to the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn),
participating in the Grand Commandant's military affairs.
For his combined achievements, he was enfeoffed as a Baron (nán) of Zuòtáng (作唐) County,
with an income of four hundred households.
He was appointed Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù) and Advisory Counselor (Zīyì Cānjūn) to the Grand Commandant.
When the Heir Apparent of Prince Yùzhāng (Yùzhāng Gōng Shìzǐ) was General Who Conquers the Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn) garrisoned at Jīngkǒu (京口),
Dàojì (道濟) served as Marshal (Sīmǎ) and Administrator of Línhuái (Línhuái Tàishǒu).
He also served as Marshal (Sīmǎ) to the Heir Apparent's Central Commander of the West (Xī Zhōngláng Sīmǎ) and Administrator of Liáng (Liángguó Nèishǐ).
He again served as Marshal (Sīmǎ) to the Heir Apparent's General Who Conquers the Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn),
and was additionally appointed General Who Establishes Might (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn).
In the twelfth year of Yìxī,
Gāozǔ led a northern expedition.
He appointed Dàoqì as the vanguard, sending him out to Huái and Féì.
At every city and outpost he reached, they surrendered at the mere sight of his army.
He advanced and captured Xǔchāng,
taking captive the pretender Níngshuò General and Yǐngchuān Administrator, Yáo Tǎn,
and the Great General Yáng Yè.
Upon reaching Chénggāo,
the pretender Yǎnzhōu Provincial Governor Wéi Huá surrendered.
He proceeded directly to Luòyáng,
where the pretender Píngnán General and Chénliú Duke, Yáo Guāng, submitted.
In all, he took cities and broke strongholds,
capturing over four thousand people.
Some deliberated that they should all be massacred to form a jīngguān (pyramid of heads).
Dàoqì said:
"Punishing the guilty and bringing comfort to the people
is precisely for today."
He released them all.
Thereupon, the various barbarian tribes were moved and delighted,
and a great many came to submit to him.
He advanced to take Tóngguān,
and, with the various armies, jointly defeated Yáo Shào.
After Cháng'ān was pacified,
he was appointed Zhēnglǔ General and Lángyá Chief Administrator.
When the heir apparent was to be garrisoned at Jiānglíng,
Dàoqì was again appointed Xīzhōngláng Sīmǎ, Chíjié, and Nánmán Commandant.
He was also given the additional title of Zhēnglǔ General.
He was transferred to Sòngguó Attendant,
concurrently serving as the heir apparent's Zhōngshùzǐ,
and Yǎnzhōu Dàzhōngzhèng.
When Gāozǔ received the mandate,
he was transferred to Hùjūn,
with the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì,
and was put in charge of the Shítóu garrison.
He was permitted to enter the palace chambers directly.
For his meritorious service in assisting the foundation of the dynasty,
he was re-enfeoffed as Yǒngxiū County Duke,
with an estate of two thousand households.
He was transferred to Dānyáng Mayor,
retaining his Hùjūn title.
When Gāozǔ became ill,
he was granted twenty "class swords" (ceremonial guard).
He was sent out to supervise military affairs of the various commanderies north of the Jiāng River and south of the Huái River in Nánxú and Yǎn, as Zhènběi General and Nányǎnzhōu Provincial Governor.
In the first year of Jǐngpíng,
the barbarians besieged Qīngzhōu Provincial Governor Zhú Kuí at Dōngyáng City.
Kuí sent an urgent appeal.
Dàoqì was given the additional titles of Shǐ Chíjié and Supervisor of all punitive expeditionary forces,
and, with Wáng Zhòngdé, went to relieve Dōngyáng.
Before they could arrive,
the barbarians burned their camps,
set their siege equipment ablaze, and fled.
They intended to pursue,
but there was no food within the city.
So they opened cellars to retrieve long-stored grain.
The cellars were several *zhàng* deep.
It took two nights
to extract the grain and process it into rice.
By then, the barbarians had gone far,
and could no longer be pursued.
So they stopped.
He returned to garrison Guǎnglíng.
Xú Xiànzhī was about to depose Lúlíng King Yìzhēn,
and informed Dàoqì.
Dàoqì disagreed,
repeatedly stating it was not permissible,
but was not heeded.
Xiànzhī and others, planning the deposition and enthronement,
hinted to Dàoqì to attend court.
Upon his arrival,
they informed him of their plan.
On the night of the planned deposition,
Dàoqì entered the Lǐngjūn mansion and stayed overnight with Xiè Huì.
Huì was agitated that night and could not sleep,
but Dàoqì fell asleep soundly as soon as he lay down.
Huì was impressed by him because of this.
Before Tàizǔ arrived,
Dàoqì entered to guard the court hall.
When the emperor ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Zhēngběi General,
given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì,
and granted a drum and pipe band.
He was further enfeoffed as Wǔlíng Commandery Duke,
with an estate of four thousand households.
He firmly declined the additional enfeoffment.
He was also given additional supervision over the military affairs of the five commanderies of Huáiyáng, Xiàpí, Lángyá, and Dōngguǎn in Qīngzhōu and Xúzhōu.
When Xiè Huì was to be suppressed,
Dàoqì led his army to follow Dào Yànzhī.
Yànzhī was defeated in battle
and retreated to defend Yǐnqí.
Just then, Dàoqì arrived.
Huì had initially believed that Dàoqì would be punished along with Xiànzhī and the others,
but suddenly heard he was coming to support the emperor.
The morale of his men plummeted in fear,
and they disintegrated without a fight.
After the matter was settled,

he was promoted to Grand Administrator of military affairs of Jiāngzhōu, Jiāngxià in Jīngzhōu, Xīyáng, Xīncài, and Jìnxī in Yùzhōu; Zhēngnán Grand General; Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī; and Jiāngzhōu Provincial Governor.
[一０]Chíjié and Chángshì remained as before.
He was given an additional enfeoffment of a thousand households.
In the eighth year of Yuánjiā,
Dào Yànzhī attacked the Suǒ barbarians.
He had already pacified Hénán,
but soon lost it again.
Jīnyǒng and Hǔláo both fell,
and the barbarians pressed on Huátái.
Dàoqì was given the additional title of Grand Administrator of all punitive expeditionary forces,
and led his troops on a northern campaign.
His army reached Dōngpíng Shòuzhāng County,
where they encountered the barbarian Ānpíng Duke Yǐzhān Juàn.
Dàoqì led Níngshuò General Wáng Zhòngdé and Xiāoqí General Duàn Hóng in a fierce attack,
and utterly defeated them.
Fighting their way to Gāoliángtíng,
the barbarian Níngnán General and Jìzhōu Provincial Governor Shòuchāng Duke Xījiákù Jié engaged them in a pincer attack.
Dàoqì dispatched Duàn Hóng and the commander of the imperial guard, Shěn Qiánzhī, with crack troops to attack them,
and immediately cut down Xījiákù Jié.
Dàoqì advanced to Jìshàng,
fighting continuously for over twenty days,
with dozens of engagements.
The barbarian forces were strong,
and consequently, Huátái fell.
Dàoqì returned to Lìchéng with his army intact.
He was promoted to Sīkōng.
Chíjié, Chángshì, Grand Administrator, and Provincial Governor remained as before.
He returned to garrison Xúnyáng.
Tán Dàojì 檀道濟 had established merits in the previous dynasty,
and his formidable reputation was very great.
His close confidants
had all experienced a hundred battles,
and his sons also possessed talent and spirit.
The imperial court regarded him with suspicion and awe.
Emperor Tàizǔ 太祖 had been ill for several years,
repeatedly facing mortal danger.
Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng 彭城王義康 worried that if the emperor were to die,
Tán Dàojì 檀道濟 would be beyond control.
In the twelfth year [of Yuánjiā 元嘉],
the emperor's illness became critical.
At that time, the Suǒlǔ 索虜 (Tuoba) became border invaders,
so Tán Dàojì 檀道濟 was summoned to court.
After his arrival,
the emperor's condition improved.
In the spring of the thirteenth year,
Tán Dàojì 檀道濟 was to be sent back to his garrison.
He had already boarded the boat,
but then the emperor's illness recurred.
He was summoned to court for a farewell audience,
then arrested and handed over to the Tíngwèi 廷尉 (Minister of Justice).
An imperial edict stated:
"Tán Dàojì 檀道濟, having attained his rank through timely good fortune,
received favor in the past.
His honors and emoluments were exceedingly generous,
beyond comparison.
Yet, he was ungrateful for such exceptional treatment,
failing to consider how to repay it in the slightest.
Instead, he secretly harbored doubts and disloyalty,
treading on thin ice for a long time.
Since Yuánjiā 元嘉,
his suspicions and animosity have intensified,
displaying disloyalty and lack of affection,
engaging in acts of currying favor with subordinates and defying superiors.
These have already become public knowledge,
manifest far and wide.
Xiè Língyùn 謝靈運, with his vicious ambition and ugly words,
clearly showed insubordination.
Tán Dàojì 檀道濟 accepted his邪說 xiéshuō (heterodox views),
often covering up for him.
Moreover, he secretly distributed gold and goods,
luring ruthless and cunning individuals,
ensuring that fugitives would come to him,
their numbers steadily increasing.
Day and night, he watched for opportunities,
hoping for what was beyond his rightful aspirations.
The Zhènchūn Jiāngjūn 鎮軍將軍 (General who Guards the Army) Zhòngdé 仲德, when he came to court last year,
repeatedly reported these activities.
I, considering that he held a position among the highest officials,
part of the esteemed ranks,
tried to mend and tolerate,
hoping he might reform.
But he persisted in his wickedness,
and his treachery eventually materialized.
Taking advantage of my illness,
he planned to unleash his malevolent intentions.
The former Nánmán Xíngcānjūn 南蠻行參軍 (Acting Military Adviser for the Southern Barbarians) Páng Yánzǔ 龐延祖 fully understood his treachery,
and secretly reported it.
A subject who plots against his ruler and kin,
such a crime is unforgivable.
How much more so when the sins are so deep and grave,
to such an extent!
He should immediately be arrested and handed over to the Tíngwèi 廷wèi (Minister of Justice),
to enforce the law strictly.
The matter concerns only the principal culprit;
no others are to be questioned."

Thereupon, Tán Dàojì 檀道濟 and his eight sons—the Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng 給事黃門侍郎 (Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate) Zhí 植, Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng 司徒從事中郎 (Middle Official for the Minister of Works) Càn 粲, Tàizǐ Shèrén 太子舍人 (Attendant of the Crown Prince) Xí 隰, Zhēngběi Zhǔbù 征北主簿 (Chief Clerk of the General who Conquers the North) Chéngbó 承伯, and Mìshū Láng 祕書郎 (Secretary of the Palace Library) Zūn 遵—
were all executed at the Tíngwèi 廷尉.
Also arrested was the Sīkōng Cānjūn 司空參軍 (Military Adviser for the Minister of Works) Xuē Tóng 薛彤,
who was sent to Jiànkāng 建康 for execution.

Furthermore, the Shàngshū Kùbù Láng 尚書庫部郎 (Director of the Bureau of Treasury Accounts) Gù Zhòngwén 顧仲文 and the Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn 建武將軍 (General who Establishes Martial Power) Máo Hēng 茅亨 were dispatched to Xúnyáng 尋陽,
to arrest and execute Tán Dàojì's 檀道濟 sons Yí 夷, Yōng 邕, and Yǎn 演, as well as the Sīkōng Cānjūn 司空參軍 Gāo Jìnzhī 高進之.
Xuē Tóng 薛彤 and Gāo Jìnzhī 高進之 were both Tán Dàojì's 檀道濟 confidants,
possessing great courage and strength,
and were at the time compared to Zhāng Fēi 張飛 and Guān Yǔ 關羽.
Initially,
when Tán Dàojì 檀道濟 was arrested,
he removed his scarf and threw it to the ground, saying:
"You are destroying your Great Wall of ten thousand *lǐ*!"
Yōng's 邕 son, Rú Nǎi 孺乃, was pardoned.
During the reign of Shìzǔ 世祖,
he served as Fèngcháoqǐng 奉朝請 (Attendant at Court).
The historian says: When one dons the official's cap and emerges from the village,
tying the official's sash and ascending to court,
their aspirations may be fulfilled on the smooth path,
or their fortune may be difficult on a perilous track.
This is why the ancients hesitated at their career choices,
and were conflicted at the crossroads.
If one's responsibilities weigh heavily upon their person,
and their loyalties are bound to their master,
then even if they hold the tripod (power) and bear the sword (authority),
When the two dukes received their instructions in the Western Hall,
kneeling to accept the imperial entrustment,
if they could die and be reborn,
they would surely have rushed to their duty as their ultimate aim.
they are serene and do not dwell on their survival or demise.
in a position that could shake the ruler,
they merely sought to suppress future troubles
and ward off personal calamities,
causing the Tónggōng 桐宮 (Palace of Tong) to suffer an urgent calamity,
and the Huáinán Wáng 淮南王 (King of Huainan) to fall victim to an unexpected illness.
If the state's survival or demise were the paramount concern,
then their righteousness would be different from this.
However, Péngchéng 彭城 (referring to Liú Yìkāng 劉義康) had no offense like Yàn Lài 燕剌 (referring to Jí Zhì 姬職, Marquis Lài of Yan) committed,
yet suffered the execution of Chǔ Yīng 楚英 (referring to Chǔ Yǐng 楚郢, King Yǐng of Chu).
If one of the imperial kinsmen had extended the dynasty,
the ultimate outcome would still be unknown.
Xiè Huì 謝晦 said that one should not leave a villain to their lord and father.
How could this merely be a saying?
Biographies, Volume Four: Xiè Huì 謝晦
Xiè Huì 謝晦, courtesy name Xuānmíng 宣明,
was a native of Yángxià 陽夏, Chénjùn 陳郡.
His grandfather, Lǎng 朗, was the Grand Administrator of Dōngyáng 東陽.
His father, Zhòng 重, was the Pìqí Chángshǐ 驃騎長史 (Chief Clerk of the Cavalry General) for Kuàijī Wáng Dàozǐ 會稽王道子.
His elder brother, Xuàn 絢, was the Zhènchūn Chángshǐ 鎮軍長史 (Chief Clerk of the General who Guards the Army) for Gāozǔ 高祖 (Emperor Wǔ of Song), and died young.
Xiè Huì 謝晦 initially served as the Jiànwēi Fǔ Zhōngbīng Cānjūn 建威府中兵參軍 (Central Military Adviser in the General who Establishes Martial Might's Headquarters) for Mèng Chǎng 孟昶.
After Mèng Chǎng's 孟昶 death,
Gāozǔ 高祖 asked Liú Mùzhī 劉穆之:
"Among Mèng Chǎng's 孟昶 subordinates, who is suitable to join my headquarters?"
Liú Mùzhī 劉穆之 recommended Xiè Huì 謝晦,
who was immediately appointed Tàiwèi Cānjūn 太尉參軍 (Military Adviser for the Grand Commandant).
Gāozǔ 高祖 once interrogated prisoners.
That morning, the Xíngyù Cānjūn 刑獄參軍 (Military Adviser for Judicial Affairs) was ill,
so Gāozǔ 高祖 ordered Xiè Huì 謝晦 to take his place.
In the carriage, he quickly reviewed the interrogation documents
and promptly proceeded with the questioning.
As the Prime Minister's office had many affairs,
prisoners accumulated.
Xiè Huì 謝晦 responded to each question with eloquence and clarity,
without any mistakes.
Gāozǔ 高zǔ was amazed by him,
and immediately appointed him Xíngyù Zéicáo 刑獄賊曹 (Section Chief of Judicial Affairs),
then transferred him to Yùzhōu Zhìzhōng Cóngshì 豫州治中從事 (Middle Official for Governance in Yuzhou).
In the eighth year of Yìxī 義熙,
when land was assigned based on household registration for the displaced residents in commanderies and counties,
Xiè Huì 謝晦 was tasked with equitably managing the households in Yáng and Yù prefectures,
and was praised for his fairness.
He was then appointed Tàiwèi Zhǔbù 太尉主簿 (Chief Clerk of the Grand Commandant).
He accompanied the expedition against Sīmǎ Xiūzhī 司馬休之.
At that time, Xú Kuízhī 徐逵之 was defeated and killed.
Gāozǔ 高zǔ was enraged and
intended to don armor himself and land ashore.
His generals remonstrated,
but he did not listen,
growing even more furious.
Xiè Huì 謝晦 stepped forward and embraced Gāozǔ 高zǔ to restrain him.
Gāozǔ 高zǔ said:
"I will execute you!"
Xiè Huì 謝晦 replied:
"The world can do without me, Xiè Huì 謝晦,
but it cannot do without you, Your Grace.
What does my death matter!"
Just then, Hú Fān 胡藩 had successfully landed,
and the enemy retreated,
so Gāozǔ 高zǔ stopped.
Xiè Huì 謝晦 had a handsome demeanor,
was good-humored and witty,
with clear eyes and brows,
and hair as black as lacquer.
He was well-read in literature,
articulate, learned, and well-versed in many subjects.
Gāozǔ 高zǔ greatly admired and appreciated him,
surpassing all other officials.
He accompanied the expeditions to Guān and Luò,
and all important internal and external affairs were entrusted to him.
When Liú Mùzhī 劉穆之 sent envoys to report matters,
Xiè Huì 謝晦 often offered differing opinions,
which angered Liú Mùzhī 劉穆之, who said:
"Will His Grace ever return?"
Gāozǔ 高zǔ wanted to appoint him Cóngshì Zhōngláng 從事中郎 (Middle Official for Affairs),
and consulted Liú Mùzhī 劉穆之,
who firmly opposed it.
He was not promoted throughout Liú Mùzhī's 劉穆之 lifetime.
When news of Liú Mùzhī's 劉穆之 death arrived,
Gāozǔ 高zǔ wept bitterly.
Xiè Huì 謝晦, who was at that time upright,
was very pleased,
and personally went into the inner chambers to verify the news of Liú Mùzhī's 劉穆之 death.
On that very day, an imperial decree was issued,
promoting Xiè Huì 謝晦 to Cóngshì Zhōngláng 從事中郎.
When the Sòng dynasty was first established,
he was appointed Right General of the Guards.
Soon after, he was made Palace Attendant.
When Gāozǔ received the Mandate of Heaven,
he ascended the altar at Shítou,
and entered the palace with imperial equipage.
Huì led the mobile army for security,
and was promoted to Central Leader of the Army,
with his position as Palace Attendant remaining unchanged.
For his contributions in supporting the new dynasty,
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Wǔchāng County,
with a stipend of two thousand households.
In the second year,
he was punished for mistakenly enfeoffing the Grand Administrator of Běihǎi, Qiú,
while he was supposed to enfeoff Wáng Huá, the Sīmǎ of Zhènxī and Grand Administrator of Nánjùn, who was tasked with handling the imperial seal.
Huì was stripped of his position as Palace Attendant.
Soon after, he was transferred to Leader of the Army General and Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary,
and, following the precedent of Yáng Hù of Jìn as Central Leader of the Army,
he entered and resided in the Imperial Palace Department,
and commanded the imperial guards.
In the third month,
Gāozǔ became unwell,
and Huì was granted twenty guards with ceremonial swords,
and, along with Xú Xiànzhī, Fù Liàng, and Tán Dàojì, attended to the emperor's medicine.
When Shàodì ascended the throne,
Huì was additionally appointed Leader of the Central Secretariat,
and, with Xiànzhī
and Liàng, jointly assisted in governing the court.
After Shàodì was deposed,
Sīkōng Xú Xiànzhī issued an imperial edict,

appointing Huì as Acting Grand Inspector of Military Affairs of Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, Yì, Níng, Southern and Northern Qín seven provinces, General of the Garrison Army, concurrently Commander of the Southern Man Barbarians, and Governor of Jīng Province.
The intention was for him to be stationed outside as support,
as it was feared that if Tàizǔ arrived, he might appoint someone else,
hence this urgent appointment.
Elite soldiers and veteran generals
were all assigned to him,
and his arsenal and military supplies were abundant.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was additionally granted the authority of Imperial Commissioner,
and appointed to his original position.
Huì worried that he would not be allowed to leave,
and was extremely anxious.
When he departed Xīntíng,
he looked back at Shítou City,
and joyfully exclaimed:
"Now I am free!"
Soon after, he was promoted to General of the Guards,
additionally appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary,
and advanced in enfeoffment to Duke of Jiànpíng Commandery,
with a stipend of four thousand households.
He firmly declined the advanced enfeoffment.
He was also granted one set of imperial music.
When he first became Governor of Jīng Province,
he was very self-satisfied.
Before departing for his post,
he visited his paternal uncle, Grand Master of Guanglu, Dàn, to bid farewell.
Dàn asked Huì's age.
Huì replied:
"Thirty-five."
Dàn laughed and said:
"In the past, Xun Zhōngláng was appointed Grand Inspector of the Northern Garrisons at twenty-seven.
Compared to him,
you are already old."
Huì showed a look of shame.
Upon arriving in Jiānglíng,
he formed a deep bond with Palace Attendant Wáng Huá,
hoping to avoid disaster.
His two daughters were to be married to Pénchéngwáng Yìkāng and Xīnyěhóu Yìbīn.
In the second year of Yuánjiā,
he sent his wife Cáo and eldest son Shìxiū to escort his daughters back to the capital.
Before this, during the Jǐngpíng era,
the Suǒ captives became bandits,
and overran Hénán.
At this time, the emperor wished to execute Xiànzhī and others,
and also to punish Huì.
He publicly announced a northern expedition,
and also said he would pay respects at the imperial mausoleum,
preparing equipment and boats.
Fù Liàng wrote to Huì, saying:
"The minor punitive expedition to Hèshuò
is not yet over,
and many in the court and throughout the country
are worried and fearful."
He also said:
"Many court officials are advising a northern campaign,
and the emperor will send the external supervisor Wàn Yòuzōng to consult you."
At that time, the court's arrangements were unusual,
and their plot was somewhat leaked.
In the first month of the third year,
Huì's younger brother, Imperial Secretary of the Yellow Gate Shí Hú, sent a swift messenger to inform Huì.
Huì still thought it was not true,
and called upon the Consultative Adjutant Hé Chéngtiān,
showing him Liàng's letter,
saying:
"I estimate Yòuzōng will arrive in a day or two.
Duke Fù fears I will cause trouble,
so he sent this letter first."
Chéngtiān said:
"What is heard outside
is that the western campaign has already been decided.
How could Yòuzōng come to the upper reaches?"
Huì still thought it was false,
and had Chéngtiān prepare a draft of a memorial in reply to the edict,
saying that the expedition against the captives should wait until next year.
Chéng Dàohuì, the Administrator of Jiāngxià, received a letter from a person in Xúnyáng,
saying
"the court will undertake a major disposition,
and the matter is already certain."
He had his Aide-de-camp and Military Adjutant Lè Jiǒng seal and show it to Huì.
Huì again said to Chéngtiān:
"Yòuzōng has not yet arrived.
If there is no news for another two or three days,
does that mean he is not coming?"
Chéngtiān replied:
"There is no reason for an imperial envoy to come.
As Chéng said,
the matter has already been decided.
How can you still doubt?"
Huì wished to burn the military registers of the Southern Man barbarians,
and lead his current forces to decisive battle.
Many gentlemen advised him to raise troops.
So he erected a banner and declared a state of emergency,
saying to Sīmǎ Yǔ Dēngzhī:
"I will now go down myself.
I wish to trouble you to guard the city with three thousand men,
and defend against Liú Cuì."
Dēngzhī replied:
"My elderly parents are in the capital,
and I have no soldiers.
Considering these two or three things,
I dare not accept this order."
Huì then asked his subordinates:
"Are three thousand soldiers
enough to guard the city?"
Zhōu Chāo, Sīmǎ of the Southern Man, replied:
"Not only for guarding the city,
but if there is an external enemy,
we can achieve merit."
Dēngzhī then said:
"Chāo will certainly be able to manage it.
I request to resign as Sīmǎ and Grand Administrator of Nánjùn to offer it to him."
Immediately, he appointed Chāo on the spot as Sīmǎ, General of Building Power, and Grand Administrator of Southern Yìyáng,
and transferred Dēngzhī to Chief Clerk,
with his position in Nánjùn remaining unchanged.
Tàizǔ executed Xiànzhī and others, as well as Huì's son, the newly appointed Secretary of the Imperial Library, Shìxiū,
and arrested Shí Hú, Shí Hú's son Shìpíng, and his nephew, Aide-to-the-Compiler, Shào, and others.
Lè Jiǒng again sent a messenger to inform Huì:
"Duke Xú and Duke Fù, and Shí Hú and others, have all been executed."
Huì first mourned for Xiànzhī and Liàng,
and then received the ominous news about his sons and nephews.
Afterward, he personally went out to the archery hall,
and distributed uniforms to the army.
He had frequently followed Gāozǔ on campaigns,
and had witnessed all his strategies.
At this point, his commands and dispositions
were all perfectly appropriate.
Within two or three days,
people from all directions gathered,
and he obtained thirty thousand elite soldiers.
Then he presented a memorial, saying: "Your subject, by fortunate circumstance,
received the extraordinary favor of Emperor Wǔ,
hearing about state affairs externally,
and planning in the imperial tent internally.
I managed affairs through both danger and safety,
assisted the royal enterprise,
participated in the merit of establishing the dynasty,
and received the rewards of the rivers and mountains.
When the late emperor was unwell,
and conveyed his final instructions,
your subject, along with the former Sītú, your servant Xiànzhī, the Left Grand Master of Guanglu, your servant Liàng,
and the General Who Conquers the North, your servant Dàojì, and others,
all ascended the imperial bed,
knelt to receive the imperial will,
and were entrusted with the aftermath of affairs.
Although your subject is ordinary and shallow,
I am grateful for the grace and strive to excel,
serving the past and attending to the present with sincerity that pierces the unseen and seen.
When Yíngyáng lost virtue
and cut himself off from the ancestral temple,
the court and the people were in peril,
worried about disaster and calamity.
Loyal counsel and shared agreements,
sacrificing oneself for the state,
elevated the sagely dynasty,
and renewed the imperial foundation.
Your Majesty, speeding by carriage and following the current,
did not hesitate,
and diligently attended court,
further elevating my enfeoffment and titles.
This shows that your subjects'
sincere hearts have been illuminated by the heavens' mirror,
and all distant nations have understood the imperial will.
If your subjects wished to monopolize power
and disregard state laws,
we would then assist the young
My
Lord, how could I, a solitary figure, turn my back on the heavens and the sun,
and still idly wait for seventy days in my empty residence,
gazing upwards for the imperial standard?
Thus, Lúlíng Wáng (廬陵王), during the Yíngyáng (營陽) era,
was repeatedly suspected and reviled.
His accumulated grievances
led him to offend his superiors,
thereby bringing about his own untimely demise.
Heaven bestows its favor on virtuous rulers,
and when the era of prosperity arrives,
if something is not abolished,
how can anything flourish?
To help others achieve their good,
is the high principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
To enthrone an emperor in a serene hall,
is the duty of a minister.
Gěng Yǎn (耿弇) did not leave rebels for his sovereign and father;
how could I, your minister, ever betray the Sòng (宋) dynasty?
Moreover, the strife has escalated within the court,
and calamity has come
from forced oppression.
The eyes and ears of the world
cannot be deceived.
I, your unworthy minister, held a feudal post,
and was truly diligent and never remiss.
In all matters of governance, great or small,
I invariably reported them first.
I purged and cleansed the various barbarian tribes,
bringing peace to the borders.
My younger brothers and nephews were sent to remain
and
attend at the palace.
Your Majesty earnestly followed the aspirations of the late emperor,
and further strengthened ties with marriage.
Even a mere child
was graciously summoned for an audience,
and when my daughter was promoted and my son was moved,
the entire household saw them off.
The way
of serving a ruler,
my duty has been completely fulfilled.
I admired Xú Xiànzhī (徐羡之) for overseeing all state affairs,
and assisting three generations of emperors.
Advanced in years, he requested retirement,
repeatedly submitting memorials and petitions,
but the gracious imperial decree, while cordial,
had not yet
granted his request.
I, your minister Liàng (亮), managed the imperial secretariat,
diligently and reverently day and night,
with utmost respect and sincerity,
ready to die for the good path.
These were all foundational ministers of the Imperial Sòng (宋),
and bulwarks of the state.
Yet, slanderers brought about their downfall,
maliciously creating discord within the nation.
Imperial wrath shook the land,
and extreme punishments were inflicted,
even extending to my household,
all subjected to being enslaved and executed.
Although I do not know how Dào Jì (道濟) is faring,
inferring from the current situation,
it is impossible for him to remain untouched.
The late emperor entrusted his chief ministers to assist the heir,
but they were exterminated by treacherous and evil hands.
Loyal and selfless辅弼
could not escape
the punishment of annihilation.
Your Majesty is in the prime of your youth,
and have just begun to oversee myriad affairs;
the true nature of the people
you may not yet fully discern.
Wáng Hóng (王弘) and his brothers
are frivolous and rash in their advancement.
Wáng
Huá (華) is suspicious, jealous, and cruel in causing harm,
scheming to manipulate power,
first removing the current administrators
to satisfy his desires.
Among the people of the world,
who, whether they know or not,
does not feel pain and indignation
because of this?
We, your ministers, served the late emperor
for nearly twenty years,
with caution and prudence,
without a single fault.
Having served so long,
we now face such a crime.
If
this is not due to the late emperor's mistaken judgment of people,
then it is because Your Majesty has not perceived our humble sincerity.
When I, your minister, returned from my mission at the end of last year,
I received letters from court officials and generals from the palace guard,
all saying that a rift
had already formed,
and that today's events were inevitable.
I, your minister, with sincere devotion, looked up with no
ulterior motives,
not anticipating that cunning deceit would secretly conspire,
that justice would be hard to rely upon,
that loyal and virtuous men would fall at court,
and that I, a foolish minister, would be attacked.
Dào Yànzhī (到彥之) and Xiāo Xīn (蕭欣) are on the nearby road.
In ancient times, when Bái Gōng (白公) caused chaos,
Zhū Liáng (諸梁) donned his armor.
When evil men were in court,
Zhào Yǎng (趙鞅) led an invasion.
I, your minister,
share in their joys and sorrows,
and hold a post governing a border region.
How can I see it fall and not uphold it,
thus failing the late emperor's dying wish?
I shall immediately lead my officers and soldiers,
repair our ships and armor,
and await their self-inflicted demise,
ready to draw my sleeve and strike them down.
If Heaven blesses the Great Sòng (宋),
and its destined reign is long,
and the righteous army triumphs,
clearing the central plains,
then I shall immediately sail eastward,
slaughter these three villains,
redress
our grievances and shame,
and beg forgiveness at the imperial court.
Even if I face the chopping block and the boiling cauldron,
I will have no regrets in my heart.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty will recall the trust bestowed during the Yǒngchū (永初) reign,
and uphold the sincerity of allegiance during the Yuánjiā (元嘉) era,
then the profound loyalty
of your humble minister may still be discerned.
As I face this memorial, I choke with emotion,
and
cannot express myself fully.
At the time of Tàizǔ (太祖), martial law had already been declared,
and various armies were advancing one after another.
The Shàngshū (尚書) issued a communiqué to Jīngzhōu (荊州) saying: "Calamity and fortune have no fixed gate;
rebellion and submission have their destined numbers.
The Way of Heaven is subtle, like a shadow's echo,
and human affairs are reflected in past precedents.
Never has one followed righteousness without fortune extending,
nor followed evil without
calamity befalling.
Therefore, astute strategists
recognize defeat to achieve merit,
and upright ministers
face hardship to preserve their integrity.
Xú Xiànzhī (徐羡之), Fù Liàng (傅亮), and Xiè Huì (謝晦)
ruthlessly
poisoned and murdered,
thereby offending Heaven.
This is an extreme transgression against moral teachings,
and a target of state punishment.
It has already been widely proclaimed throughout the four seas,
and announced in an imperial edict.
Xiànzhī's (羡之) father and son, Liàng (亮), and Huì's (晦)
sons
were immediately brought to justice at the outset of the swift judgment.
To avenge the royal house,
and to assuage the indignation of righteous men,
the national laws are clear and bright,
and both men and gods rejoice.
The three families shared the same guilt;
two of them have already been captured.
Huì's (晦) family members
are shackled in prison cells.
If both the visible and invisible worlds resent them,
their isolated roots are easily pulled out.
By attacking rebels with righteousness,
even a strong force will collapse.
However, their desperate resistance
is difficult to predict,
for a cornered beast will bite.
Therefore, we have prepared our forces,
to act as a precautionary measure.
The troops from the capital
have gathered from all corners of the empire.
The soldiers are well-trained, the weapons are sharp,
and a mighty roar echoes.

The commander holding the imperial credentials, General of the Central Guard, Kaiming Hou (開國侯) of Hènshān (佷山) County, Dào Yànzhī (到彥之), leads twenty thousand elite and valiant Feathered Forest guards.
Their cloud-like banners lead the way,
and armored
troops illuminate the
rivers.

The commander holding the imperial credentials, Regular Mounted Attendant, Supervisor of Military Affairs for Nán Xú (南徐), Yǎn (兗) and the northern bank of Jiāng (江), Huáinán (淮南) of Qīngzhōu (青州), Xúzhōu (徐州), Huáiyáng (淮陽), Xiàpī (下邳), Lángyá (琅邪), Dōngguǎn (東莞), seven prefectures,
General
of the Expedition to the North, Governor of Nán Yǎnzhōu (南兗州), Kaiguo Duke (開國公) of Yǒngxiū (永脩) County, Tán Dàojì (檀道濟), commands thirty thousand elite and valiant warriors.
Their warships cover the river,
and their star-like
reports follow one after another.
A thousand sails rise together,
and ten thousand oars swiftly advance.
Regular Mounted Attendant, General of Elite Cavalry, Duàn Hóng (段宏), with two thousand iron cavalry,
sweeps like the wind and strikes like lightning,
marching from Jìng
Líng,
directly to Yānyǐng.
He also ordered the General Who Conquers Barbarians and Governor of Yōngzhōu, Liú Cuì, to command the troops at Héyīn,
to strike their lair.
The Governor of Xiāngzhōu, Zhāng Shào,
gathered the multitude from Xiāngchuān,
and directly seized critical points.
Bā and Shǔ blocked the strategic passes of Jīngmén,
Qín and Liáng cut off the path to Dānqí.
The net of clouds closed in from all four sides,
leaving no escape route for those who fled or hid.
Then the imperial carriage set off,
the six armies soared like roc,
imperial guards preceded the emperor,
and the "Five Oxen" banner was arrayed.
Even with the valor of Yīng Bù,
or the resources of Péng Chǒng,
climbing the ramparts would gain no renown,
and who could resist when arms were deployed?
Furthermore, the people of the western lands
all received imperial benevolence,
and the officers and soldiers of Dōngwú
yearned for their homeland.
They would surely not implicate themselves in the party of criminals,
nor wantonly participate
in a campaign of rebellion and ruin.
If they deployed their army, it would scatter like fish;
if they defended a city, they would disperse like birds.
Such was the inevitable situation.
The Sage Emperor earnestly pitied and grieved,
that the guilt lay with Huì,
and what sin had the officers and common people
committed?
Therefore, a division of the vanguard was sent forth,
to declare the imperial decree.
Upon arrival of the tally,
immediately seize and capture Huì himself,
and escort him quickly by light boat.
If he has already run amok,
and acted to resist
and defend,
you should readily turn your back on the rebellion,
and lead each other to return to the court.
Recently, severe punishments were meted out,
but vast imperial grace was extended;
Fù Liàng’s three sons
were especially granted full pardon,
and Huì’s blood relatives
and below,
as well as Xuàn’s nephews,
were all untainted.
Moreover, the civil and military officials of those prefectures and provinces
are all appointed royal officers,
bearing the nation’s honorable trust.
Though their bodies are afar,
their hearts are with the pole star.
Indeed, it is crucial to turn misfortune quickly,
for delay will lead to disaster.
Should the imperial army reach the suburbs,
thunder and lightning would all descend.
The regret of biting one's navel
would then be too late.
At this time, the Governor of Yìzhōu, Xiāo Mózhī, and the Grand Administrator of Bāxī, Liú Dàochǎn, were recalled.
Upon first arriving in Jiānglíng,
Huì imprisoned them both,
confiscated their wealth,
to provision his army.
The Internal Administrator of Jìnglíng, Yīn Dàoluán, had not yet arrived at his commandery,
so he appointed him as Advisor to the Military.
He appointed his younger brother, Dùn, as General Who Campaigns Like a Champion and Internal Administrator of Jìnglíng,
overseeing the stationed forces.
His elder brother’s son, Shìyóu, was made General Who Builds Awe and Grand Administrator of Nánpíng.
If Liú Cuì were to arrive,
whoever among Zhōu Chāo’s forces could defeat him,
would immediately be made General Who Soars Like a Dragon and Governor of Yōngzhōu.
Huì led an army of twenty thousand,
departing from Jiānglíng.
The ships stretched from Jiāngjīn to Pòzhǒng,
their banners and flags reflecting each other,
obscuring the sunlight.
Huì then sighed, saying:
"I regret not being able to use this as an army to assist the Emperor!"
He himself assumed the title of Governor of Xiāngzhōu,
and made Zhāng Shào Auxiliary General of the State,
but Shào refused the appointment.
Huì issued a manifesto to the capital, saying: The royal house faces many troubles,
and calamities repeatedly arrive.
Yíngyáng lost virtue,
and estranged himself from the ancestral temple.
The Prince of Lúlíng had a fundamental quarrel,
and was repeatedly suspected and disliked.
Furthermore, during mourning, he lost
propriety,
which was known to all far and near.
Accumulating resentment, he offended his superiors,
thus bringing upon himself an unrighteous path.
The various marquises vacated their positions,
and ascended to the enlightened sage.
While the chaos is not yet settled,
responsibilities are tied to certain individuals.
We find the General of Chariots and Cavalry, Wáng Hóng, and the Palace Attendant, Wáng Tánshǒu,
mistakenly receiving private favors of the time,
presumptuously usurping vital power.
Hóng, at the beginning of Yǒngchū,
indeed received extraordinary grace,
yet during the concessions of Yuán
Jiā,
he claimed his appointment and treatment were superficial,
slandering the late Emperor's trust when he advanced,
and fostering discord and differences when he withdrew.
Tánshǒu, on a previous mission,
inquired about
the current Emperor's daily life,
but failed to glorify his excellent virtue,
or make it known to the court.
His words were mostly deceitful,
so they will not be detailed.
Wáng Huá, after the death of the traitor,
during the period of rewards and promotions,
the late Emperor frequently inquired about him,
hoping there might be one admirable quality,
but Huá's nature was fierce and suspicious,
inflicting much harm.
Previously, he allowed people into the city,
feigning illness to resign from duties.
The gentry and commoners
of this capital
all heard and knew of this.
Based on his memorials and the Emperor's replies shown to his uncle Zōng Xùn,
and also announced to Xu and Fù, the two Dukes.
And when Zhōu Jiū’s envoy arrived,
he was again consulted,
saying:
"I wish to take charge of government affairs myself,
and request to leave my post and return to the capital."
He also ordered Tánshǒu to fully elaborate this intention.
Furthermore, the monk Huì Guān said
that outsiders reported
Huá and Dào Yànzhī were plotting rebellion,
which is not to say it is untrue.
Within the city, the eastern generals,
for several days,
held spears, awaiting action.
Huá said he was repeatedly slandered by Qiū Dāng,
and was always uneasy.
In all these matters,
how could there be such deep and loyal sincerity?
He considered that his father died by the roadside,
a circumstance different from others;
externally he abstained from alcohol,
but indulged in it at night.
His shameless face was [text missing] All the gentry and commoners,
who did not cast sidelong glances?
He also often lamented that there were suddenly several prime ministers,
why such indignation,
aiming to control all authority,
disregarding national statutes?
Those who protected the royal house
faced execution and slaughter,
those who diligently served the altars of soil and grain
suffered extermination and calamity.
Among the officials,
who was not indignant?
So he forged an imperial edict,
sending Dào Yànzhī and Xiāo Xīnzhī with light boats to launch an attack.
On that very day, the Left Commandant of Jiānlì revealed the manifesto that the assembled troops
had already reached Yángzǐ.
Though I am not mighty,
I have humbly borne a regional command.
With the nation in difficulty,
sorrow and indignation gather.
If petty men are allowed to succeed,
the path of the gentlemen will decline.
All will suffer the grief of destruction
and exhaustion,
and the common people will deeply fear widespread turmoil.
I shall then gather and lead righteous volunteers,
repair boats and armor.
Prow to stern, they will stretch across the river;
armored chariots will cover the plains.
The warriors are fierce and brave,
each
a hundredfold in sincerity.

Now I dispatch the Southern Man Commander, General Who Pacifies the Distant, Yú Dēngzhī, to command the Attendants to Military Affairs, General Who Builds Awe, Grand Administrator of Jiànpíng Ān Tài, General Who Declares Awe Zhāo Hóngzōng, Attendants to Military Affairs, General Who Declares Awe Wáng Shàozhī, and others,
with ten thousand elite troops,
as the vanguard to strike.
The Southern Man Attendant to Military Affairs, General Who Arouses Martial Might, Wèi Xiàng, commands
the Attendant to Military Affairs, General Who Declares Awe, Chén Zhēn, with two thousand tiger warriors;
the Attendant to Military Affairs, General Who Builds Awe, Grand Administrator of Xīnxīng, Hè Yīn, with three thousand armored soldiers,
following one another
on the road.
The Southern Man Attendant to Military Affairs, General Who Inspires Awe, Guō Zhuó, with two thousand iron cavalry,
moving by both water and land.
The main army of thirty thousand,
will advance continuously and swiftly like lightning.
Acting General Who Campaigns Like a Champion will
The army of Jìnglíng Nèishǐ and Hédōng Tàishǒu, Xiè Dùn (謝遯), and Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Nánpíng Tàishǒu, Xiè Shìyóu (謝世猷), a force of ten thousand valiant men,
remained to guard Jiānglíng.
Orders were separately given to Cānjūn
and Chángníng Tàishǒu, Dòu Yìngqī (竇應期), with five thousand cavalry and infantry,
to march directly to Yìyáng.
Sīmǎ, Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn, and acting Nányìyáng Tàishǒu, Zhōu Chāozhī (周超之), leading the army of
Sīmǎ and Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn, Hú Chóngzhī (胡崇之), a formidable ten thousand,
while Chángjiān Xíng Cānjūn and Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn, Zhū Dànzhī (朱澹之), with five thousand
marched north to Gāoyáng,
marched west to Yànsài,
to jointly attack Liú Cuì (劉粹),
all converging on Xiāngyáng.
The surprise forces moved with speed,
advancing simultaneously toward their objectives.
All these worthy men shared in the nation's grace,
their feelings imbued with valor and righteousness.
This is truly the day for devoted men to forget themselves,
and for righteous heroes to achieve great deeds.
They should act when the opportunity arises,
and move with the wind without needing further exhortation.
When Huì (晦) reached the mouth of the river,
Dào Yànzhī (到彥之) had already arrived at Péngchéng Zhōu.
Yǔ Dēngzhī (庾登之) held Bālíng,
but was timid and dared not advance.
It happened that the continuous heavy rain lasted for several days.
Cānjūn, Liú Hézhī (劉和之), said:
"Both sides have rain;
Tán Zhēngběi (檀征北) will arrive soon,
and the eastern army is growing stronger.
It is only fitting to fight quickly."
Dēngzhī (登之), being fearful,
ordered his junior general, Chén Yòu (陳祐), to make large sacks
and fill them with several thousand hú of thatch,
hanging them from the sails and masts,
claiming they could be used to burn enemy ships.
He said that using fire would require clear weather,
thus delaying the battle.
Huì (晦) agreed,
and so halted the army for fifteen days.
Then they attacked Xiāo Xīn (蕭欣) at Péngchéng Zhōu.
Zhōngbīng Cānjūn, Kǒng Yánxiù (孔延秀), led three thousand men in a fierce attack,
fighting with great might.
Xīn (欣) shielded himself behind his formation,
then abandoned his army and returned to his ship,
suffering a great defeat.
Yánxiù (延秀) then attacked and captured the palisade at the mouth of the island,
and Yànzhī (彥之) retreated to defend Yǐnqí.
Huì (晦) again submitted a memorial, saying: "I have heard that wicked and treacherous individuals ruin the country,
becoming a menace to previous generations;
slanderous sycophants disrupt the court,
causing disaster in different eras.
Thus, Zhào Gāo (趙高) usurped power by coercion,
and the Qín (秦) dynasty consequently collapsed;
Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) initiated
chaos,
and the Hàn (漢) imperial line was thereby overturned.
Even when sagely kings govern the world,
with great wisdom shining upon it,
they cannot prevent these evils from gradually arising,
nor this harm from being done.
Treacherous officials Wáng Hóng (王弘) and others illicitly seized
authority and power,
instigating disaster and rebellion.
They then, with his younger brother Huá (華), colluded internally and externally,
achieving their evil goals together,
harming and envying loyal and virtuous officials,
scheming for illicit aspirations.
Therefore, the former Sītú, your servant Xiànzhī (羨之),
and Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū, your servant Liàng (亮), were cruelly persecuted,
and this also extended to my own family.
Although I do not know if Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn, your servant Dàojì (道濟), is alive or dead,
it is impossible for him to be the only one to escape.
They then sent
Xiāo Xīn (蕭欣), Dào Yànzhī (到彥之), and others with light boats to attack us.
Their treachery and deceit
has reached such an extent.
Xiànzhī (羨之) and Liàng (亮),
one a veteran of virtue and a senior minister,
related to the imperial family by marriage,
the other
holding overall responsibility for civil and military affairs,
his position equal to the Three Ministers;
Dàojì (道濟) served as a supreme general,
responsible for defending cities;
all received kind treatment from the previous court,
and were pillars of their generation.
In the past, I, by timely fortune,
excessively received the former emperor's favor,
heard about political affairs internally,
and managed military campaigns externally.
I, along with Xiànzhī (羨之), Liàng (亮), and others, were all regarded with favor.
Having established the royal foundation
and assisted in the great enterprise,
from the very
beginning,
up to the abdication,
though my accumulated sincerity was meager,
it was still recorded,
and I received the oath written in cinnabar,
and the rewards of mountains and rivers,
intending that I should rise and fall with the Sòng (宋),
and that this inheritance should be passed on endlessly.
When the Sacred Body (the former emperor) fell ill,
and the divine divination yielded no auspicious sign,
he summoned us four ministers,
to ascend the imperial bed together,
entrusting us with his dying commands and
the care of his family and state.
I respectfully
followed the imperial will,
exerting myself with all my might,
vowing to fulfill my loyalty even unto death.
However, Yíngyáng (營陽) (referring to the deposed emperor) violated moral principles,
alienated himself from Heaven,
and the peril of the state
lay in the trust
placed in him.
If he were not deposed,
how could the state prosper?
Therefore, after consulting the precedents of Yīn (殷) and Hàn (漢),
we elevated Your Majesty to virtue.
Your Majesty followed the current and rode in the imperial carriage,
not listening to Zhāng Wǔ's (張武) doubts;
you entered
the residence and ascended to the throne like a dragon,
not waiting for Sòng Chāng's (宋昌) counsel.
This demonstrates the mutual trust between sovereign and minister,
and the convergence of Heaven's will and human agreement.
The Nine-Five (the emperor) resides in the position of the sun,
transforming the four seas.
Xiànzhī (羨之) and Liàng (亮)
internally
assisted the imperial plan;
I and Dàojì (道濟)
shared the responsibilities externally.
Throughout the whole world,
who would say
it was improper?
Thus, I received your gracious appointment,
to govern this region,
and left my younger brother and nephews
to serve in the imperial court.
Since taking office,
for three full years,
although I was physically far away,
my heart was bound to the imperial court.
In matters large or small,
I consulted and sought instructions in every action,
and in the governance of the eight provinces,
I never acted
on my own authority.
My reverence for my superiors is profound enough to pierce both the seen and unseen realms.
Your Majesty further upheld the former emperor's decree,
strengthening it with marriage alliances,
greatly benefiting the peace of the world,
and again summoning me.
This is why last year I sent my daughter and son,
with my whole family, down (to the capital).
My sincere loyalty is such;
I know not what I should be ashamed of.
Yet, the wicked and cunning, without cause,
created this calamity.
Xiànzhī (羨之) was executed
internally,
and I am attacked externally.
Reflecting upon my heart,
I know not what crime I have committed.
Heaven's hearing is distant,
and there is no way to present my plea.
Hóng (弘) and others, having received your favor and trust,
and being permitted to serve by your side,
consider themselves to have usurped power like foxes and rats,
their principles far removed from the norm.
Furthermore, they believe that Your Majesty, being young in years,
has only recently begun to manage state affairs,
and they wish to presume upon your grace and favor,
eyeing the state's power,
establishing
their kinsmen in secure positions,
to cultivate their own influence.
Without removing us,
they cannot monopolize power.
That is why they colluded with treacherous evildoers
to create this path to rebellion.
They also calculated that their scheme against Hóng (弘) and others
would involve using Yíngyáng (營陽) as a pretext
and Lúlíng (廬陵) as a crime.
They also knew that our positions were high and our merits similar,
and that we were firmly united internally and externally.
Your Majesty trusted their superficial appearance,
forgetting their sinister ways.
When one is thrice brought down to the lower machine,
how can one not be momentarily perplexed?
I humbly reflect upon myself:
setting aside the obscure and establishing the clear,
my actions were not for myself.
As for the matter of Lúlíng [Wáng],
it did not come from outsiders,
but accumulated internal discord within the screens [of the palace];
outwardly, it was like the punishment
of Shūdùan.
Since his dismissal had a master,
how could I, your subject, have been involved?
However, Lúlíng's nature was fickle and treacherous,
lacking in brotherly loyalty and filial piety.
When Wǔhuáng was on his deathbed,
he also issued an oral decree.
Although it [his removal]
came from Yíngyáng,
it was truly not a national disaster.
As for Xiànzhī, Liàng and others,
we associated as one body,
being close as heart and stomach, inside and out.
We truly wished to exert ourselves for the imperial house,
and dedicate our loyalty to our
lord.
If we, your subjects, truly desired to wield power,
and not solely for the nation,
when Yíngyáng was first deposed,
Your Majesty was far away.
Among Wǔhuáng's sons,
there were still children.
Had we embraced one of them and issued
commands,
who would have dared to oppose it?
Yet we went upstream for three thousand *lǐ*,
kept the palace empty for three months,
and reverently welcomed the imperial carriage,
to comply with the successor's rule.
Such heartfelt devotion
is easily verifiable.
Furthermore,
we, your subjects, served the former court
for seventeen years,
all occupying prominent positions,
and were widely praised for our deference and prudence.
We never expected to incur such discord and punishment in a single day.
Even Zhōugōng, a great worthy,
still
suffered the slander of rumors;
Bóqí, though perfectly filial,
could not escape the calamity of calumny.
A loving father is not without affection for a benevolent son,
nor does an enlightened ruler harbor ill will towards a loyal minister.
When
treachery spreads,
it can sway mountains and valleys.
How much more so for those whose sincerity is slight and shallow,
can they hope to be trusted?
Does the *Shī* [Jīng] not say:
"Slanderers are endless,
bringing disorder to the four states.
O amiable gentleman,
do not believe slanderous words!"
May Your Majesty personally examine the documents,
and carefully scrutinize right and wrong.
The root of this discord,
should be thoroughly investigated.
I secretly fear that the royal house
will suffer the calamity of Huángfǔ,
or even greater, the disaster of Yánlè.
Morning and night, I am deeply anxious,
as if headless.
When the Way of Zhōu was in decline,
Huán and Wén undertook punitive expeditions.
When those near the ruler brought chaos to
the state,
Zhào Yǎng entered to punish them.
How much more so now, when disaster is overwhelming,
the celestial pole is in peril,
and the high officials are slaughtered,
and the regional governors are overthrown.
My talent is not that of Jiànghóu,
yet to secure Hàn
is my duty;
I am ashamed to be less than Bólù,
yet I follow the last will.
The national calamity is deep,
and family grief is also keen.
I have immediately marshaled the troops and armored them,
and the army is now stationed at Bālíng.
Xiāo Xīn was distressed and terrified,
and fled
at the mere whisper of our approach.
Though I am truly inadequate,
I have forgotten myself for the state.
Relying on the spiritual power of the altars of soil and grain,
and rousing the spirit of righteous valor,
I will sweep forward like lightning,
directly entering Shítou,
beheading the chief culprit,
and executing the primary offenders,
to avenge the wronged souls of the two dukes,
and relieve the suffering of my private house.
Thereafter, I will submit myself to the Grand Judge,
and willingly face the cauldron of boiling.
Even the day of
my death
would be like a year of life.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty, whose virtue matches the origin of Heaven,
and whose Way equals the profound ultimate,
will discern the baselessness of this calamity,
and perceive the foundation of loyalty and integrity.
Turn back the light of the sun and moon,
unleash the might of frost
and lightning,
execute the four culprits in the ancestral temple,
and hang the three overseers at the Crimson Gate-tower.
Declare the innocence of the two high officials,
and make clear the blamelessness of the two border commanders.
Above, to account to the ancestors;
below, to inform
the people.
Send an envoy in a single carriage,
bearing a brief letter,
and I, your subject, will immediately order the troops to turn their banners,
and return to my appointed post.
I shall await orders on the nearby road,
and promptly submit further reports.
Initially,
Huì, Xu Xiànzhī, and Fù Liàng conspired for a self-preservation plan.
Huì held the upper reaches of the river,
while Tán Dàojì garrisoned Guǎnglíng,
each having strong forces,
to control the court;
Xiànzhī and Liàng held power in the center,
thus they could maintain their position for a long time.
When Tàizǔ was about to carry out the execution,
Wáng Huá and others all said:
"Dàojì cannot be trusted."
Tàizǔ said:
"Dàojì was merely coerced,
he did not originally serve them.
Moreover, he was not involved in the murders.
I will summon him and question him,
he will surely be different."
Thereupon, Dàojì was summoned to court,
entrusted with an army,
and charged with conquering the west.
When Huì heard that Xiànzhī and the others were dead,
he believed Dàojì would not be spared either.
But when he heard that Dàojì was leading his troops upstream,
he was terrified and at a loss.
When Dàojì arrived,
his army joined Yànzhī's army,
pulling their ships along the bank.
〔一一〕Huì initially saw that the number of ships was not many,
and underestimated them,
not immediately going out to battle.
By evening,
driven by the wind, the sails came up,
front and rear ships lined up throat to throat,
the westerners became separated and isolated,
losing the will to fight.
The imperial army reached the end of Jìzhì Islet,
and arrayed their ships across the river.
Huì's large army immediately scattered.
Huì fled by night,
to Bālíng,
obtained a small boat, and returned to Jiānglíng.
Initially,
Liú Cuì, the Inspector of Yōngzhōu, sent his younger brother, the Administrator of Jìnglíng, Dàojì, and the imperial army commander Shěn Chǎngzhī, to raid Jiānglíng.
Upon reaching Shāqiáo,
Zhōu Chāo led over ten thousand men to fight them,
and utterly defeated them.
Soon after, news of Huì's defeat arrived.
When Huì reached Jiānglíng,
he had no other plan of action,
only feeling ashamed and apologizing to Zhōu Chāo.
That night, Chāo abandoned his army and went alone by boat to Dào Yànzhī to surrender.
Most of Huì's forces had scattered,
so he took his younger brother Dùn, and his nephew Shìjī, among seven horsemen, and fled north.
Dùn was stout and could not ride a horse,
so Huì had to wait for him repeatedly,
and could not travel fast.
Upon reaching Yántóu in Ānlù,
he was captured by the garrison commander Guāng Shùnzhī.
Shùnzhī was
a former subordinate of Huì.
He was sent in a cage to the capital,
and on the way he composed "Melancholy on the Human Path,"
the words of which were: "Melancholy on the human path,
melancholy how truly difficult the human path is!
Alas for the many dangers of the human path,
grieved by the scarcity of peace on the human path!
How splendid is the noble lineage of high-born,
truly pure
flow far from its source.
Establishing cultured virtue in homes,
and upright learning at the humble gate.
Responding to the accumulated good deeds with extra blessings,
they ought to be extended by the path of fortune.
How could this young man's
ferocity and wantonness
truly invite disaster and commit offenses?
Having met the great fortune of a radical transformation,
I received a single glance from the Sagely Emperor.
Participating in the planning for creation,
I assisted in the imperial system of the grand scheme.
Going out to manage the army in the imperial guards,
and entering to speak on affairs in the private chamber.
Dividing the mountains and rivers with scepters and insignia,
succeeding the tortoise-shell insignia of civil and military officials.
Receiving the dying injunction in the western palace,
I accepted the final entrustment by the imperial bed.
Alas, my incompetence
and inferiority had no integrity,
but I truly cherished this and did not forget it.
Having received such great favor from the former ruler,
I wished to repay it to the later king.
I worried that the entrustment would be ineffective,
and feared being shamed by talk of
life and death.
I believed that the successor would continue the enterprise,
and be able to add luster to the former glory.
But not long after the period of national mourning,
he transgressed ritual and became dissolute and depraved.
If all under heaven
perishes,
the altars of soil and grain will surely be lost.
Moreover, we, who embody the state,
truly have no leisure to rest.
By relying on the singular will of the countless people,
darkness is indeed overcome and brightness shines forth.
Verily, the lord is revered and the people are at peace,
and indeed the destiny of the dynasty is boundless.
The state, once endangered, is rebuilt,
the family, once decayed, flourishes again.
Having been able to support the fallen and avert misfortune,
we hoped that the ways of the
world would recover.
In court, merits were praised and titles conferred,
and the mandate to serve in the western border regions was respectfully given.
The pipes and flutes played a cacophony,
and the crimson yaks' tails shone brilliantly.
〔一二〕Facing the eight directions as a
governor,
echoing the valor of civil and military might.
Exerting myself for the weak in governance,
I truly forgot to eat until late in the day.
How could I dare to emulate Shēn Bǔ (申甫),
but merely serve as a protective screen for Sòng (宋).
Scarcely three years had passed,
and indeed not yet a second cycle.
How could there be worries within... that it would be curtailed.
I grieve for the two prime ministers who assisted,
both executed
without mercy.
I pity my frail children who suffered disaster,
my sorrow erupts from my chest and my heart is sick.
Alas, the excellent gentlemen of Jīng-Hàn (荊漢),
and the common people, civil and military.
Seeing loyalty and integrity unheeded,
and witnessing injustice that cannot be redressed.
All were stirred by righteous indignation,
and all took up arms and eagerly converged.
The boats and ships were numerous,
the chariots and cavalry arrayed.
Observing the harmony of the people and the order of the army,
we said, "Who can withstand this army?"
May the souls of the departed
have their grievances redressed,
and restore the Jīng (涇) and Wèi (渭) rivers to their proper order.
Gathering light boats in the river bend,
all sharp enemies were annihilated.
Stationing foot soldiers at Bái Shuǐ (白水),
the enemy fled without a
single wheel remaining.
Our morale, having gained victory, grew stronger,
our prestige, already awe-inspiring, was further shaken.
Alas, the times were not with us,
we encountered wind and rain for over ten days.
We planned battles but did not
succeed,
while they pursued us, treading in our dust.
Lacking extraordinary wisdom and courage,
we suddenly followed the example of Mèng Míng (孟明).
If success and failure are predestined,
how can one blame Heaven or fault others?
I regret that our arrows and stones were not exhausted,
yet our army was crushed and our formation overthrown.
Truly, such are the fortunes of gain and loss,
and one should accept it without regret.
I grieve for my beloved young son,
who tragically
suffered this calamity.
My wisdom was not exhausted, yet the affair collapsed;
my strength was not depleted, yet I could not recover.
I swore to die together in battle,
but I was timid and weak, and broke my promise.
I pity my younger brothers and nephews,
who were innocent,
but were truly entangled in my faults.
Thinking that the Nine Yi (九夷) lands could be a refuge,
I sought to escape to preserve my life.
Alas, life's aspirations are hard to fulfill,
and I am now held captive at the frontier post.
How did I offend Heaven and Earth,
to experience such severe dangers?
I heard in ancient admonitions,
that the higher the achievement, the more restricted the person.
Huò (霍) narrowly escaped assassination,
but eventually his clan was overthrown and exterminated.
Zhōu (周) was lamented as noble even by jailers,
but ultimately he was sent to the frontier and never investigated.
Even great worthies of illustrious virtue,
could not escape cruel slaughter.
Holding fear now, they bear with others,
forgetting past kindness and not reciprocating.
