Achievements go
unrewarded and alarm the ruler,
〔一三〕how then can one govern oneself?
If not for the illuminating mirror of the rock,
who can avert misfortune and gain blessings?
The lesson of Yin (殷) is evident from antiquity,
why lament only
Jì Shū (季叔)?
To be able to comfort one's parents and glorify one's name,
is truly praised by the former sages.
To preserve one's integrity and fulfill filial piety to the end,
is lamentably lacking in me.
I have disgraced the integrity of my ancestors
through the generations,
and suddenly, in fullness, it is overthrown and extinguished.
Only the ancestral sacrifices and daily upkeep,
alas, are forever severed in one morning.
Who caused this?
Truly, it is the treacherous evil of an isolated man.
My sins are greater than mountains,
even a hundred deaths cannot wash them away.
Tied up like an ox with upturned horns by the village gate,
my relatives and friends were righteous in their dealings.
Though our ways of life were not
uniform,
our good relations were strong, our affections devoted.
All of us, disliking farming, sought official salaries,
seeing the world's ways as difficult and crooked.
Planning for fame and achievement,
we often said it was easy.
Now that my posthumous title is determined and my coffin closed,
I am ashamed of my intelligence and past discussions.
Though awaiting
death is shameful,
alas, my thick skin has no place.
I bow deeply to you, my friends,
and thank you for your wisdom.
A hundred years is fleeting and short,
in the end, one
is judged and measured.
I lie down as if chopped by axes,
my fate is the same as theirs.
The world values that one and not this one,
how can it understand distinctions and discern illusions?
I accept Zhuāng Shēng's (莊生) profound words,
and ask to follow his example.
After Zhōu Chāo (周超) surrendered,
Dào Yànzhī (到彥之) was sent to participate in government affairs.
Liú Cuì (劉粹) sent his staff officer Shěn Chǎngzhī (沈敞之) to inform Yànzhī of the defeat at Shā Qiáo (沙橋),
which was caused by Zhōu Chāo.
Yànzhī then apprehended him.
He first imprisoned Hú (胡) and others,
but had not yet executed them.

Then, he, along with Huì (晦), Dùn (遯), his nephew Shìjī (世基), Shìyóu (世猷), and their associates Kǒng Yánxiù (孔延秀), Zhōu Chāo (周超), Fèi Yīn (費愔), Dòu Yìngqī (竇應期), Jiǎng Qián (蔣虔), Yán Qiānsī (嚴千斯) and others, were all executed.
〔一四〕Shìjī (世基)
was the son of Xuàn (絢),
and possessed talent and spirit.
Before his death, he composed a linked verse poem:
"Grand indeed is the scale crossing the sea,
magnificent are the wings reaching the sky.
Once the wind and water are lost,
they become food for ants."
Huì (晦) continued it, saying:
"Achievements equal those of ancients,
but there is no wisdom or strength to retreat.
Having already traversed the perilous Tàiháng (太行) mountains,
this path is truly difficult to ascend."
When Huì (晦) died,
he was thirty-seven years old.
Yǔ Dēngzhī (庾登之), Yīn Dàoluán (殷道鸞), Hé Chéngtiān (何承天) were all pardoned and exempted.
Initially,
Shāng Xuánshí from Hédōng served as Huì’s army supervisor.
When Huì rebelled,
Xuánshí secretly wanted to enthrone Yǔ Tiánfū and Dào Yànzhī’s younger cousin, both from the west,
but Tiánfū and the others dared not agree.
Xuánshí knew that his lone plan would not succeed,
〔一五〕so he became Huì’s standard bearer.
After the affair was settled,
he regretted that his original intention was not fulfilled,
and drowned himself in water.
Tàizǔ praised him,
and appointed his son, Huáifú, as the Right Army Staff Officer and Inspector for Yìjì, Prince of Héngyáng.
When Huì fled,
all his attendants abandoned him,
except for Gài from Yánlíng, who followed him closely.
Tàizǔ praised him,
and later appointed Gài as the Army’s Merits Officer and Inspector for Yìxīn, Prince of Chángshā.
The historian says: Xiè Huì was punished for the error in the imperial seal,
and thus lost his position as Attendant Minister.
This shows Gāozǔ’s understanding of governance
and the competence of his ministers.
Indeed, when capital punishment is applied,
it involves severe offenses.
Demotion is sometimes used
for minor transgressions.
Minor transgressions
are lightly regarded by the populace,
while severe offenses
are gravely regarded by people.
Therefore, the axe and battle-axe are rarely used in society,
while light punishments are daily used at court.
Even for minor faults of high-ranking officials,
the law is not relaxed due to their importance,
leading to the lower ranks being respectful and the superiors revered.
This is the way it works.
Since Tàizǔ took office,
this principle has gradually been violated.
The law is loosely enforced,
and justice is suspended for favor,
which hinders virtue and harms goodness.
This is the cause.
By the time of Dàmíng,
the partiality became even more extreme.
Unless it involved deep personal revelations or theft,
or violation of strict taboos,
the penalty of demotion
was not applied to powerful relatives.
If someone offended the emperor’s will,
even if the offense was not a state crime,
as soon as the dismissal decree arrived,
mourners would already be waiting at their gate.
Thus, the laws became uncodified,
and the superiors often acted loosely.
The mainstays of the legal system were not upheld,
and the details of the law followed suit.
This is why virtuous people guard against conspicuous faults in their subtlety,
and are cautious in great matters by starting with small ones.
This is what is meant.
Collated Notes
Biographies Volume 5: Wáng Zhèn’è, Tán Sháo, Xiàng Jìng, Liú Huáishèn, Liú Cuì
Wáng Zhèn’è was
a native of Jù, Běihǎi.
His grandfather Měng,
courtesy name Jǐnglüè,
was a minister when Fú Jiān usurped the title in Guānzhōng.
Měng served as a general and prime minister,
possessing both literary and martial talents.
The people of the north held him in high regard.
His father Xiū was
the illegitimate Prefect of Hédōng.
Zhèn’è was born on the fifth day of the fifth month.
His family, due to popular taboo,
wanted to have him adopted into a distant branch of the clan.
Měng, seeing his extraordinary qualities,
said:
“This is an extraordinary child.
In the past, Lord Méngcháng was born in the 'evil month' but became Prime Minister of Qí.
This child will also bring prosperity to our family.”
Hence, he was named Zhèn’è.
At the age of thirteen, the Fú clan was defeated and perished,
Guānzhōng fell into chaos,
and he drifted between Xiáo and Mǐn.
He once stayed at the home of Lǐ Fāng, a man from Mǐnchí, who provided him with food.
Fāng treated him well.
Zhèn’è said to Fāng:
“If I encounter a heroic lord,
and obtain the title of a marquis of ten thousand households,
I will repay you generously.”
Fāng replied:
“You are the grandson of the Prime Minister, and your talent is such,
why worry about not achieving wealth and high status?
When that time comes, I only wish to be appointed as the magistrate of my home county.”
Later, he followed his uncle Yào to Jìn,
and resided as a guest in Jīngzhōu.
He read extensively on various philosophers and military texts,
and discussed military and national affairs.
Riding was not his strength,
and his archery was also very weak,
but his strategic vision was broad and far-reaching,
and he was decisive and capable of making judgments.
During the campaign of Guǎnggù,
someone recommended Zhèn’è to Gāozǔ.
At that time, Zhèn’è was the Magistrate of Tiānmén-Línlǐ,
so Gāozǔ immediately sent for him.
Upon his arrival, Gāozǔ spoke with him
and found him to be very extraordinary.
He then kept him overnight.
The next morning, he said to his assistants:
“Zhèn’è is
the grandson of Wáng Měng;
as the saying goes, a general’s family produces generals.”
He immediately appointed him as Administrator-in-Chief of Qīngzhōu,
acting as Staff Officer for the Grand Commandant of the Central Army,
and assigned him as Chief Bandit Investigator for the Vanguard.
He repelled Lú Xún at Zhāpǔ,
and achieved merits in numerous battles,
being ennobled as a fifth-rank baron of Bólù County.
When Gāozǔ planned to attack Liú Yì,
Zhèn’è said:
“If Your Grace has business in Xīchǔ,
please grant me a hundred boats to serve as the vanguard.”
In the eighth year of Yìxī (412 CE),
Liú Yì fell ill
and requested his younger cousin, Liú Fān, the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, to serve as his deputy.
Gāozǔ feigned agreement.
In the ninth month,
the main army marched west.
Zhèn’è was transferred to Staff Officer,
and given the additional title of General of Martial Might.
When Gāozǔ arrived at Gūshú,
he dispatched Zhèn’è to lead General Lóngxiáng Kuǎi Ēn with a hundred boats to set off first.
This was on the twenty-ninth day of that month.
He admonished them:
“If the enemy knows of our approach,
even when our army arrives, it will take a few days.
They will surely deploy troops on the bank,
and not be able to immediately descend into their boats.
When you arrive there,
plan carefully.
If it is possible to attack,
then burn their ships,
and keep your boats floating by the water’s edge
to await my arrival.
Comfort the common people,
and proclaim the imperial edict and amnesty,
as well as my letters to the civil and military officials of the Wèijūn Mansion.
The crime applies to one person only;
the rest are entirely blameless.
If the enemy has no news at all,
and has not prepared defenses,
then you may launch a surprise attack.
Now,
just say that Inspector Liú of Yǎnzhōu is coming upriver.”
Zhèn’è received the order,
and traveled day and night,
being held back by winds for four days at Quèzhōu, Xúnyáng, Hékǒu, and Bālíng.
On the twenty-second day of the tenth month,
he reached Yùzhāngkǒu,
twenty *lǐ* from Jiānglíng city.
Throughout Zhèn’è’s advance,
he spread the word that Inspector Liú of Yǎnzhōu was coming upriver,
and Yì believed it to be true,
unaware that he was about to be attacked.
Zhèn’è abandoned his boats at Yùzhāngkǒu and proceeded on foot.
Kuǎi Ēn’s troops were in front,
and Zhèn’è followed.
One or two men were left with the boats,
and six or seven flags were erected on the bank opposite the boats,
with a drum placed beneath each.
He instructed the men left behind:
“Estimate when I will reach the city,
then beat a prolonged alarm,
making it seem as if a large army is approaching from the rear.”
He also divided a detachment to follow behind,
ordering them to burn the enemy’s ships at Jiāngjīn.
Zhèn’è advanced directly to attack the city,
telling the vanguard:
“If anyone asks,
just say that Inspector Liú of Yǎnzhōu has arrived.”
The garrison guards and common people all said that Liú Fān had indeed arrived,
and were at ease and unsuspicious.
When he was five or six *lǐ* from the city,
he met Yì who was about to lead Zhū Xiǎnd zhī,
with some ten horsemen
and dozens of foot attendants,
intending to go out to Jiāngjīn.
He asked who they were,
and they replied:
"Liú Yānzhōu has arrived."
Xiǎnd zhī rode forward to ask where Pán was,
and they replied:
"He is behind."
When Xiǎnd zhī saw the army but not Pán,
and saw soldiers carrying *péng pái* battle equipment,
and observed that the ships at Jiāngjīn had been burned,
with smoke and flames reaching to the sky,
and the sound of drums for battle was very loud,
he knew it was not Pán.
He immediately spurred his horse and galloped back to inform Yì:
"There is a large army outside,
seemingly coming from downstream,
almost at the city.
All the ships at Jiāngjīn have been set on fire!"
He ordered the city gates to be closed.
Zhèn'è also galloped in.
The soldiers scaled the city walls and entered.
The gates had not yet been fully lowered and locked,
so they managed to open the East Gate of the Outer City.
Inside the Outer City,
Yì had eight divisions in total,
with over a thousand armored soldiers,
who had already been put on high alert.
Kuǎi Ēn entered the East Gate,
then turned north to attack Shè Táng,
and advanced to attack the East Gate of the Inner City.
Zhèn'è entered the East Gate,
then directly attacked the West Gate of the Inner City.
The army split to attack the South Gate of the Inner City.
Inside Yì's Inner City, his former generals from the east
still had six divisions, over a thousand men.
His western generals and competent subordinates and quick-handed officials
had another two thousand or more men.
The fighting began at mealtime
and continued until mid-afternoon.
The western forces then retreated, scattered, and mostly surrendered.
Zhèn'è entered the city,
and immediately used the wind to set fires,
burning the South Gate and East Gate of the Outer City.
He also sent people with an imperial edict, an amnesty proclamation, and three personal letters from Gāozǔ to show Yì,
but Yì burned them all without looking.
Those inside the Inner City also did not believe that Gāozǔ himself had come.
There was a Wáng Huán,
whose home was in Jiānglíng.
He had personally beheaded Huán Qiān in the past,
and was thus appreciated and promoted by Gāozǔ,
and often remained by his side.
He requested to return west to bring his family,
and now led over ten men to assist Zhèn'è in battle.
In the late afternoon,
thirty *bù* north of the East Gate of the Inner City, they dug a hole in the wall.
Huán then entered the hole first, ahead of everyone.
Zhèn'è followed him from behind,
and as more followers joined,
they engaged in close-quarters combat.
Among Zhèn'è's soldiers and Yì's generals and soldiers from the east,
some were fathers, brothers, sons, nephews, or close relatives.
Zhèn'è ordered them to fight and talk simultaneously.
Everyone then knew that Gāozǔ himself had come,
and morale began to waver.
After about one *gēng*,
the front lines in the hearing hall collapsed and scattered,
and Yì's brave general, Zhào Cài, was slain.
Yì's personal guards still blocked the east and west side chambers and resisted.
Zhèn'è feared that they might accidentally injure each other in the dark of night,
so he withdrew his troops,
circled the Inner City,
and left its south side open,
as a route for retreat.
Yì feared there might be an ambush to the south.
Around the third *gēng*,
he led about three hundred of his personal guards to open the North Gate and burst out.
Initially,
the horse Yì usually rode was outside the city and could not get in.
In the haste, he had no horse.
Yì then asked Sù Mín, his son, for his horse,
but Sù Mín would not give it.
Zhū Xiǎnd zhī said to him:
"Others are capturing your father,
yet you begrudge a horse and won't give it?
Now you're running away yourself,
where do you intend to go?"
He seized the horse and gave it to Yì.
As Yì first exited,
he ran straight into Zhèn'è's army and could not get away by charging through them.
He turned and charged into Kuǎi Ēn's army.
The soldiers had been fighting for a day
and were fatigued.
Yì managed to escape through the East Gate of the Outer City and fled to Niú Mù Fó Sì,
where he hanged himself.
Zhèn'è himself was hit by five arrows.
An arrow shot the spear Zhèn'è was holding in his hand,
and it broke in his grasp.
Twenty days after Jiānglíng was pacified,
the main army arrived.
He was appointed Zhōng Bīng,
and sent out as Ānyuǎn Hùjūn and Wǔlíng Nèishǐ.
For his meritorious service in suppressing Liú Yì,
he was enfeoffed as the Viscount of Hànshòu County,
with a fief of five hundred households.
The barbarian chieftain Xiàng Bódǐ, based in Ruǎntóu,
repeatedly caused disturbances.
Zhèn'è suppressed and pacified him.
Initially, when he set out,
he informed the Inspector Sīmǎ Xiūzhī,
requesting troops as a show of force.
Xiūzhī sent his general Zhū Xiāng to lead his men to assist Zhèn'è.
Coincidentally, Gāozǔ campaigned west against Xiūzhī.
Zhèn'è then told his generals:
"The common people all know that the official army has already advanced.
Zhū Xiāng and others are another group of bandits,
and we will be attacked from both sides.
My plan has failed."
So he led his army downstream by night.
The river current was swift,
and they traveled several hundred *lǐ* in a flash,
directly occupying Dūwèi Zhì.
Upon arrival,
he used bamboo cages filled with stones
to block and fill the waterway.
When Xiāng's army came downstream,
they were attacked from both banks.
Xiāng's head was cut off,
and over a thousand men were killed.
Zhèn'è was by nature greedy.
After defeating Xiāng,
he consequently halted his army to plunder the various barbarian tribes
and did not return in time.
When he eventually arrived at Jiānglíng,
Xiūzhī had already been pacified.
Gāozǔ was angry
and refused to see him for some time.
Zhèn'è smiled and said:
"Just let me see His Grace once,
and I'll have no worries."
Soon after, Gāozǔ ascended the city wall and called Zhèn'è.
Zhèn'è was a strong debater,
quick-witted,
and responded appropriately to every situation.
Gāozǔ then released his anger.
Xiūzhī and Lǔ Zōngzhī fled to Xiāngyáng.
Zhèn'è commanded Kuǎi Ēn's various armies to pursue them by water.
Xiūzhī and others fled to the Qiāng.
Zhèn'è pursued them to the very border and then returned.
He was appointed Yóujī Jiāngjūn.
In the twelfth year,
Gāozǔ was about to launch a northern expedition.
Zhèn'è was transferred to Cányì Cānjūn,
and acted as Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn,
leading the vanguard.
Before setting out,
the Former General Liú Mùzhī met Zhèn'è at Jī Nǔ Táng
and said to him:
"Your Grace pities these remnants of the people
and is determined to eradicate the rebels.
In the past, Jìn Wénwáng entrusted the conquest of Shǔ to Dèng Ài.
Today, I likewise entrust Guānzhōng to you.
I hope you will strive to achieve great merit
and not fail this assignment."
Zhèn'è said:
"If I do not conquer Xiányáng,
I swear I will never cross the Jiāng back!"
Zhèn'è entered the enemy territory,
and was victorious in every battle.
Shàolíng and Xǔchāng
scattered upon hearing of his arrival.
He broke through Hǔláo and Bǎigǔ Wù,
slaying the bandit chief Zhào Xuán.
The army advanced to Luòyáng,
and the pretender Prince of Chénliú, Yáo Guāng, surrendered.
He then advanced to Miǎnchí,
visited the home of his old acquaintance Lǐ Fāng,
ascended the hall to see Fāng’s mother,
and generously rewarded her.
He immediately appointed Fāng as the Magistrate of Miǎnchí.
He dispatched Sīmǎ Máo Dézǔ to attack the pretender Administrator of Hóngnóng, Yǐn Yǎ, at Líchéng,
taking him alive.
He then acted as the Administrator of Hóngnóng.
Advancing swiftly,
he marched directly to Tóngguān.
The pretender Grand General Yáo Shào led a large force to defend the strategic pass,
digging deep moats and building high ramparts to secure himself.
Zhèn'è, with his army far from base,
suffered from inadequate supplies.
After a prolonged standoff with the enemy,
his officers and soldiers were short of food.
He personally went to Hóngnóng to oversee the collection of civilian grain taxes.
The common people eagerly delivered voluntary grain,
and the army's provisions were restored.
Originally,
Gāozǔ had an agreement with Zhèn'è and others:
if Luòyáng were conquered,
they should wait for the main army to arrive
and not advance recklessly.
However, Zhèn'è and the others marched directly to Tóngguān,
were blocked by Shào and could not advance,
and the army was again short of food.
They urgently reported this to Gāozǔ,
requesting the dispatch of provisions and reinforcements.
At that time, Gāozǔ was moving along the river,
but the suǒ-lǔ (barbarians) were entrenched along the riverbanks,
preventing the army from advancing.
Gāozǔ called the messenger he had sent, opened the northern door of his boat,
pointed at the barbarians on the riverbank, and said to him:
"I told you not to advance,
but you recklessly went deep into enemy territory.
With the situation on the bank like this,
how can I send an army?"
After Zhèn'è obtained the voluntary grain,
Shào also died of illness.
The pretender Fǔjūn Yáo Zàn replaced Shào in defending the pass,
and his forces were still strong.
When Gāozǔ arrived at Húchéng,
Zàn retreated.
The main army reached Tóngguān,
and a plan for further advance was deliberated.
Zhèn'è requested to lead a naval force from the Yellow River into the Wei River.
The pretender Zhènběi Jiāngjūn Yáo Qiáng had troops stationed on the Jīng River.
Zhèn'è dispatched Máo Dézǔ to attack and defeat him,
advancing directly to Wèiqiáo.
All the vessels Zhèn'è used were small méngchōng (assault boats).
All the boat operators were inside the vessels.
When the Qiāng saw the vessels advancing upstream on the Wei River,
no one was visible operating the boats from the outside.
The northern lands had always lacked boats and oars,
so everyone was astonished and amazed,
all believing it to be divine intervention.
Upon Zhèn'è's arrival,
he ordered his officers and soldiers to eat,
then abandoned the boats and landed.
The Wei River flowed swiftly,
and in a flash,
all the vessels were swept away downstream.
At that time, Yáo Hóng's army was stationed beneath Cháng'ān city,
still numbering tens of thousands.
Zhèn'è comforted his soldiers, saying:
"All of you have your homes south of the Yangtze River.
This is outside the north gate of Cháng'ān city,
ten thousand lǐ from home.
And your boats, clothing, and provisions
have all been swept away downstream.
How can there be any plan for survival now?
You should only fight to the death;
this way, you can achieve great merit.
Otherwise,
not a single one of us will remain."
He then personally led the charge, and
the multitude, knowing there was no retreat,
all leapt forward, vying to be first.
Hóng's forces instantly collapsed,
and Cháng'ān city was captured.
Hóng barely escaped with his life,
but the next day,
he led his wife and children to surrender.
Within the city were over sixty thousand households of Yí and Jìn people.
Zhèn'è proclaimed the imperial benevolence,
comforted the newly surrendered,
and enforced strict discipline in his commands,
allowing the common people to settle in peace.
When Gāozǔ was about to arrive,
Zhèn'è welcomed him at Bàshàng.
Gāozǔ commended him, saying:
"It is truly you who have accomplished my hegemonic enterprise."
Zhèn'è bowed twice in thanks, saying:
"This is due to Your Grace's prestige
and the efforts of the generals;
what merit do I, Zhèn'è, have?"
Gāozǔ laughed and said:
"You wish to emulate Féng Yì."
At this time, Guānzhōng was prosperous and complete,
with abundant granaries and treasuries.
Zhèn'è collected all sorts of valuables without restraint,
including women, children, jade, and silk,
which were countless.
Gāozǔ, considering his immense contributions,
did not question him.
He was promoted to the title of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
At that time, someone reported to Gāozǔ that Zhèn'è, having conquered Cháng'ān,
was hiding Yáo Hóng's imperial carriage,
suggesting he harbored ulterior motives.
Gāozǔ secretly sent someone to investigate the location of the carriage.
Hóng's carriage was adorned with gold and silver.
Zhèn'è had stripped all the embellishments,
and discarded the carriage by a wall.
When Gāozǔ heard this,
he was reassured.
Gāozǔ left his second son, Guìyáng Gōng Yìzhēn, as Ānxī Jiāngjūn and Inspector of Yōng and Qín Provinces,
to garrison Cháng'ān.
Zhèn'è, with his original title, served as Ānxī Sīmǎ and Administrator of Féngyì,
entrusted with the duty of defense.
At that time, the western barbarian Fúfú was powerful,
and during the reign of Yáo Xīng, he frequently harassed the northern border,
destroying armies and killing generals on numerous occasions.
When Gāozǔ arrived at Cháng'ān,
Fúfú was intimidated and dared not move.
But when the main army returned east,
he immediately threatened Běidì.
Yìzhēn dispatched the Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Shěn Tiánzǐ to resist him.
The barbarians were very strong.
Tiánzǐ stationed his troops at Liúhuíbǎo
and sent a messenger back to report to Zhèn'è.
Zhèn'è, facing Tiánzǐ's messenger,
said to Chángshǐ Wáng Xiū:
"His Grace has entrusted us with a ten-year-old child;
we should all think of exerting our utmost effort.
If we hold back our troops and do not advance,
how can the barbarian invaders be pacified?"
The messenger returned
and recounted Zhèn'è's words in detail.
Tiánzǐ had always been at odds with Zhèn'è,
and this made him even angrier.
The two constantly harbored intentions to harm each other,
and were always wary and suspicious of each other.
Zhèn'è led his army out to Běidì
and was killed by Tiánzǐ.
The details are in the biography's preface.
He was forty-six years old at the time.
Tiánzǐ also, within Zhèn'è's camp,
killed Zhèn'è's elder brother Jī, younger brothers Hóng, Zūn, Yuān, and cousins Zhāo, Lǎng, Hóng,
a total of seven people.
This was in the fourteenth year,
on the fifteenth day of the first month.
Gāozǔ's memorial stated:
“The former Anxī Sīmǎ and Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Wáng Zhèn'è,
possessed a bright and upright character and integrity,
and his strategies were clear and outstanding.
Since he first entered the service of the provincial government,
he repeatedly achieved sincere accomplishments.
When disaster struck Jīngnán,
and the situation held the upper reaches of the river,
trouble arose from strong feudal lords,
and internal betrayal also caused worry.
Zhèn'è advanced first with light boats,
his divine troops arriving like lightning,
the anxieties of eating late
dispersed like mist in a single morning.
When the imperial army campaigned westward,
and there were affairs in the Central Plains,
he marched directly to Luòyáng,
clearing Hú and Shǎn.
In the victory of entering the Wèi River,
his command was unparalleled,
and he consequently pacified Xiányáng,
capturing the false empress.
His effectiveness in achieving victory
was unmatched;
he was truly the one entrusted with defending the city,
the state's Fāng Shào.
Recently, the northern barbarians, like wandering spirits,
raided north of the Wèi River.
He commanded all the armies,
displaying his might in suppression.
When the bandits had already fled back,
he returned to his station on the Jīng River.
The former Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn, Shěn Tiánzǐ, suddenly went mad,
and unexpectedly inflicted a fatal wound.
His loyal achievements were not yet complete,
and he suffered an unforeseen calamity.
Both sorrow and pity arrived,
and there was endless regret and lamentation.
I respectfully believe that the imperial heart
was wounded by this.
Tiánzǐ's madness and perversity
have already been duly judged.
Zhèn'è's sincerity was evident in difficult times,
his merits comparable to previous heroes.
His extraordinary achievements remain unrewarded,
and he ought to receive posthumous honors.
I request an imperial edict to the relevant authorities
to deliberate on his posthumous commendation and bestowals.”
Thereupon, he was posthumously granted the titles of Zuǒ Jiāngjūn and Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Gāozǔ received the Mandate of Heaven,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as the Marquis of Lóngyáng County,
with a fief of one thousand five hundred households,
and given the posthumous title of Zhuàng Hóu.
He was granted the privilege of being enshrined alongside Gāozǔ in the imperial ancestral temple.
His son, Língfú, succeeded him, and his
position reached Nánpíng Wáng Shuò Yòujūn Zīyì Cānjūn.
When Língfú died,
his son, Shùzǔ, succeeded him.
When Shùzǔ died,
his son, Ruì, succeeded him.
When Qí received the abdication,
the peerage was abolished.
Zhèn'è's younger brother, Kāng,
remained in Guānzhōng.
When Gāozǔ campaigned northward,
Zhèn'è was the vanguard,
and Kāng hid in a rural dwelling.
When Zhèn'è was stationed at Tóngguān,
Kāng brought his family to join him.
Gāozǔ appointed him as Péngchéng Gōng Qián Jiāngjūn Xíng Cānjūn.
When Zhèn'è was murdered,
Kāng escaped by hiding.
He took his family out of Luòyáng,
arrived at Péngchéng,
and returned to Gāozǔ.
Kāng was then made Xiàngguó Xíng Cānjūn.
He requested to return to Luòyáng to see his mother.
Soon after, when Guān and Shǎn could not be defended,
Kāng, along with migrating citizens Zhāng Gànchǒu and Liú Yún from Cháng'ān, rallied volunteers,
gathering about a hundred people.
They led seven hundred odd households of expatriates from the city and suburbs,
together defending Jīnyǒngchéng,
preparing for defense and battle.
At that time, a man named Shào Píng
led his subordinates and over a thousand households of "Qǐhuó" from Bìngzhōu, encamping south of the city,
and welcomed the fugitive Sīmǎ Wénróng as their leader.
There was also the fugitive Sīmǎ Dàogōng, who led three thousand men from Dōngyuán and encamped west of the city.
The fugitive Sīmǎ Shùnmíng had five thousand men encamped at Língyúntái.
Shùnmíng sent someone to assassinate Wénróng,
and Píng then again promoted Shùnmíng as the leader.
There was also Sīmǎ Chǔzhī encamped at Bóyǔ Wù,
and the Yěbǎn garrison commander of the Suǒ barbarians, Hēiqiāo Gōng, with his cavalry, was on Máng Shàng.
Their attacks and pressures came simultaneously.
Kāng held firmly for sixty days.
When Sòng Tái was established,
Kāng was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Hédōng Tàishǒu.
Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Jiāng Qú was sent to lead troops to rescue him,
and all the fugitives dispersed.
Gāozǔ praised Kāng's integrity,
enfeoffed him as Baron of Xīpíng County,
with a fief of three hundred households,
and advanced his title to Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn.
Kāng's family was welcomed back to the capital.
He encouraged agriculture and sericulture,
and the common people greatly relied on him.
In the first year of Yǒngchū, he died at Jīnyǒng,
aged forty-nine.
He was buried west of Yǎnshī City.
He was posthumously granted the title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
He had no son,
so his elder brother, Héxī Tàishǒu Jī's son Tiānyòu, succeeded him.
In the twenty-seventh year of Tàizǔ Yuánjiā,
he followed Liú Kāngzǔ in the campaign against the Suǒ barbarians and was defeated and killed.
His son, Huáizǔ, succeeded him.
Tán Sháo, courtesy name Lìngsūn,
was a native of Gāopíng Jīnxiāng.
His family had resided in Jīngkǒu for generations.
Initially, he was appointed as the province's Cóngshì,
Xīcáo Zhǔbù,
and Fǔguó Sīmǎ.
When Gāozǔ raised his righteous army,
Sháo and his younger brothers Zhī and Dàojì participated in pacifying Jīngchéng,
and acted as Cānjūn for Gāozǔ's Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn.
After the capital was pacified,
he became Zhèn Jūn Cānjūn,
was granted Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu,
and his title was advanced to Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn.
He was promoted to Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn, Qínjùn Tàishǒu,
and Běi Chénliú Nèishǐ.
For his merit in pacifying Huán Xuán,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Bāqiū County,
with a fief of five hundred households.
He again served as Cānjūn for Chēqí Jiāngjūn,
was granted Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn,
promoted to Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn,
Zhōngjūn Zīyì Cānjūn,
and granted Níngshuò Jiāngjūn.
He participated in the campaign against Guǎnggù,
leading Xiàng Mí, Hú Pān, and fifty others to attack Línqú City,
and captured it.
When Guǎnggù was besieged,
Mùróng Chāo burned the watchtowers at night in Sháo's siege sector,
and Sháo was demoted in title to Héngyě Jiāngjūn.
On the day the city fell,
Sháo led his subordinates in the first ascent,
and was made Běi Lángxié Tàishǒu,
with his title advanced to Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Lángxié Nèishǐ.
He followed in the campaign against Lú Xún at Zuǒlǐ,
and again achieved military success.
Considering his merits at Guǎnggù,
he was further enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yíyáng County,
with a fief of seven hundred households,
and his previous enfeoffment was demoted one rank to Earl,
with half the households reduced, two hundred and fifty households,
given to Zhī's son Zhēn.
He was punished for riding in the imperial carriage inside the Six Gates,
serving his office in plain clothes.
In the seventh year of Yìxī,
he was given the title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
In the eighth year,
he observed mourning for his mother,
but was recalled to serve as Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
The following year,
he again became Lángxié Nèishǐ,
Huáinán Tàishǒu,
and his general title remained as before.
He was stationed at Gūshú.
Soon after, his title was advanced to Zuǒ Jiāngjūn,
and he was concurrently the Dà Zhōngzhèng of his native province.
In the twelfth year,
he was promoted to Dū Jiāngzhōu Yùzhōu Zhī Xīyáng Xīncài Èr Jùn Zhū Jūnmì, Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his general title remaining as before.
For an offense,
he was dismissed from office.
When Gāozǔ received the Mandate of Heaven,
for his merit in assisting the founding of the dynasty,
his fief was increased by eight hundred households,
making a total of one thousand five hundred households.
Sháo was fond of alcohol and greedy,
and his administration had no achievements.
The emperor praised his entire family for joining the righteous cause,
and his younger brother Dàojì also had great merits,
so he received special favor and appointments.
In the second year of Yǒngchū, he died in the capital,
aged fifty-six.
He was posthumously granted the title of Ānnán Jiāngjūn,
and additionally Sànqí Chángshì.
His son Xù succeeded him.
When Xù died,
he had no son,
and the peerage was abolished.
Zhī's son was Zhēn.
When Zhēn died,
his son Xiá succeeded him.
When Qí received the abdication,
the peerage was abolished.
Zhī and his younger brother Dàojì
each have separate biographies.
Xiàng Jìng, courtesy name Fèng-rén,
had the informal name Mí.
He was from Shān-yáng, Hé-nèi.
As his given name was the same as the taboo name of Gāo-zǔ’s ancestor,
he changed to be known by his informal name.
His family had lived in Jīng-kǒu for generations,
and he had been acquainted with Gāo-zǔ since childhood.
He followed in quelling the capital city,
and participated in military affairs for the Jiàn-wǔ army.
After advancing to pacify Jīng-yì,
he was appointed to participate in military affairs for the Zhèn-jūn army,
and was given the additional title of Níng-yuǎn Jiāng-jūn.
Although Jīng-yì was pacified,
numerous bandits arose.
Mí, along with Liú Fān and Mèng Lóng-fú, campaigned and defeated Huán Xīn, Huán Shí-kāng, and Shí Suī at Bái-máo,
then attacked Shòu-yáng and captured it.
In the third year of Yì-xī (407 CE),
he was promoted to Jiàn-wǔ Jiāng-jūn and Qín-jùn Tài-shǒu,
and Běi Chén-liú Nèi-shǐ,
and garrisoned Táng-yì.
For his achievements in pacifying the capital city,
he was enfeoffed as a fifth-rank Marquis of Shān-yáng County.
He followed in campaigning against the Xiān-bēi,
and a great battle took place at Lín-qú,
which remained undecided for several months.
Mí, along with Tán Sháo and others, divided their forces and attacked Lín-qú city by a hidden path.
Mí donned armor and was the first to scale the walls,
and it immediately collapsed.
They captured their standard,
and the bandits then fled.
When Guǎng-gù was attacked and captured,
Mí was again the first to scale the walls.
Lú Xún garrisoned Cài-zhōu,
and appointed his relative Ruǎn Cì as Yù-zhōu Cì-shǐ,
who then attacked and pressed Gū-shú.
Mí led Zhào Huī, the Nèi-shǐ of Qiáo-guó, to suppress him.
At that time, Fǔ-guó Jiāng-jūn Máo Xiū-zhī was garrisoning Gū-shú,
and urgent pleas for help arrived continuously.
Mí marched quickly to suppress them,
defeating Cì
and seizing his baggage.
He was appointed Zhōng-jūn Zī-yì Cān-jūn,
with his general title remaining as before.
When Lú Xún retreated,
Gāo-zǔ campaigned south,
and Mí was the vanguard.
In three battles at Nán-líng, Léi-chí, and Zuǒ-lǐ,
they were all greatly victorious.
Upon the army's return,
he was appointed Tài-wèi Zī-yì Cān-jūn and Xià-pī Tài-shǒu,
with his general title remaining as before.
In the eighth year (412 CE),
he was transferred to Yóu-jí Jiāng-jūn.

Soon after, he was appointed Supervisor of Military Affairs for various prefectures west of Huái River from Mǎ-tóu, Lóng-xiáng Jiāng-jūn, Zhèn-mán Hù-jūn, Tài-shǒu of Ān-fēng and Rú-yīn, and Nèi-shǐ of Liáng-guó,
and garrisoned Shòu-yáng.
For his achievements in pacifying Guǎng-gù and Lú Xún,
he was enfeoffed as a Baron of Ān-nán County,
with a stipend of five hundred households.
In the tenth year (414 CE),
he was promoted to Guān-jūn Jiāng-jūn and Gāo-yáng Nèi-shǐ,
and Lín-huái Tài-shǒu,
and was in charge of the Shí-tóu garrison.
When Gāo-zǔ campaigned west against Sī-mǎ Xiū-zhī,
Mí was made Wú-xīng Tài-shǒu,
with his general title remaining as before.
The next year,
Gāo-zǔ campaigned north,
and Mí accompanied him with his current rank.
He was left to garrison Què-áo,
and advanced to station at Shí-mén and Bǎi-gǔ.
He was promoted to Supervisor of Military Affairs for various prefectures in Běi Qīng-zhōu and Běi Qīng-zhōu Cì-shǐ,
with his general title remaining as before.
When Gāo-zǔ received the Mandate,
for his assisting achievements,
he was enfeoffed as a Marquis of Qǔ-jiāng County,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
He was promoted to Tài-zǐ Zuǒ-wèi-shuài,
and was given the additional title of Sàn-qí Cháng-shì.
In the second year (421 CE),
he died in office,
at the age of fifty-nine.
He was posthumously granted the title of Qián Jiāng-jūn.
Mí lived a frugal life,
did not engage in building houses,
and had no business in gardens, fields, or commerce.
People of his time praised him for this.
His son, Zhí, succeeded him,
but committed many transgressions
and did not heed his mother's instructions,
so his title was revoked.
Then, Zhí’s younger brother, Zhēn, was granted the enfeoffment to succeed,
but he was also found guilty of murder,
and the marquisate was abolished.
Zhí’s younger brother, Liǔ,
courtesy name Xuán-jì,
possessed learning, righteousness, and talent.
He conducted himself with dignity and elegance,
never seeking to advance himself,
and was accepted by all prominent figures.
Tài-wèi Yuán Shú, Sī-kōng Xú Zhàn-zhī, and Dōng Yáng-zhōu Cì-shǐ Yán Jùn were all close friends with him.
He successively served as Zhēng-běi Zhōng-bīng Cān-jūn for Shǐ-xīng Wáng Jùn,
Shǐ-xīng Nèi-shǐ,
and Nán-kāng Xiàng.
When Zāng Zhì rebelled,
he summoned Liǔ to Xún-yáng,
and went downriver with him.
Zhì was defeated and surrendered,
was imprisoned and died.
Mí’s younger brother, Shào,
during the Yǒng-chū reign,
served as Xuān-chéng Tài-shǒu.
Shào’s nephew, Liàng,
out of personal resentment, killed Mí’s wife, Lady Shī,
claiming that a servant or guest had killed her.
Shào then immediately killed Liàng, Mí’s concubine, and seven or eight servants and maids at the grave site,
concealing it and not reporting it to the authorities.
He was impeached by the judicial officials,
but an imperial edict cleared him of any charges.
In the early Yuán-jiā period,
he died while serving as Yì-xīng Tài-shǒu.
Liú Huái-shèn
was a native of Péng-chéng
and the younger brother of Zuǒ Jiāng-jūn Huái-sù.
From a young age, he was cautious, upright, and honest.
He first participated in military affairs for Gāo-zǔ’s Zhèn-jūn Jiāng-jūn,
then was Zhèn-wēi Jiāng-jūn and Péng-chéng Nèi-shǐ.
He followed in campaigning against the Xiān-bēi,
and in every battle, he personally led the soldiers.
When Guǎng-gù was captured,
Huái-shèn led his subordinates to be the first to scale the walls.
He followed Gāo-zǔ in resisting Lú Xún at Shí-tóu,
winning repeated victories in battles,
and was given the additional title of Fǔ-guó Jiāng-jūn.
In the eighth year of Yì-xī (412 CE),
with his current rank, he was appointed Supervisor of Military Affairs for various prefectures in Běi Xú-zhōu,
and garrisoned Péng-chéng.
Soon after, he was given the additional title of Xú-zhōu Cì-shǐ.
His governance was strict and fierce,
and the region was awed.
In the ninth year (413 CE),
when the fugitive Wáng Líng-xiù became a bandit,
Huái-shèn suppressed and pacified him.
In the eleventh year (415 CE),
he was promoted to Běi Zhōng-láng-jiāng.
For his achievements in pacifying Guǎng-gù and Lú Xún,
he was enfeoffed as a Baron of Nán-chéng County,
with a stipend of five hundred households.
In the thirteenth year (417 CE),
Gāo-zǔ campaigned north,
and appointed him Zhōng-lǐng-jūn and Zhēng-lǔ Jiāng-jūn,
to guard the imperial carriage.
He was dismissed from office
due to a murder within his residence.
Although his status and position became increasingly prominent,
he became even more respectful and humble.
Whenever he visited someone whose rank was not superior to his own,
he would tie his belt, dismount outside the gate,
displaying such caution and humility.
When the Sòng court was established,
he was summoned to be Wǔ-bīng Shàng-shū,
and continued to supervise the military affairs of various armies north of the Jiāng River and south of the Huái River, as Qián Jiāng-jūn and Nán Qīng-zhōu Cì-shǐ.
He was again summoned to be Dù-zhī Shàng-shū,
and was given the additional title of Sàn-qí Cháng-shì.
When Gāo-zǔ moved the capital to Shòu-chūn,
Huái-shèn was left to supervise the military affairs of various armies in Běi Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, and north of the Huái River, as Zhōng-jūn Jiāng-jūn and Xú-zhōu Cì-shǐ.
Because fugitives entered Guǎng-líng city,
his rank was demoted to Zhēng-lǔ Jiāng-jūn.
In the first year of Yǒng-chū (420 CE),
for his assisting achievements,
his noble rank was advanced to Marquis,
and his stipend was increased by one thousand households.
His title was advanced to Píng-běi Jiāng-jūn.
He was summoned to be Wǔ-bīng Shàng-shū,
and was given the additional titles of Sàn-qí Cháng-shì
and Guāng-lù Dà-fū.
In the first year of Jǐng-píng (423 CE),
he was promoted to Hù-jūn Jiāng-jūn,
with his Cháng-shì title remaining as before.
His salary and stipends were distributed among his relatives,
and his family had no surplus wealth.
In the second year (424 CE), he died,
at the age of sixty-one.
He was posthumously granted the title of Fǔ-jūn,
and given the posthumous name Sù-hóu.
Zǐdé Yuàn 嗣.
Shìzǔ's Dàmíng reign period, early on,
he served as a yóují jiāngjūn (游擊將軍, Roaming General),
supervising affairs at Shítóu garrison.
He was imprisoned for accepting goods from a merchant, Hán Fózhì,
and sent to jail.
His title and fief were confiscated.
Later, he was reinstated as the Prefect of Qínjùn.
Déyuàn was coarse and blunt by nature,
and was often treated with familiarity and contempt by Shìzǔ.
When the Emperor's favored concubine, Yīn Guìfēi, died,
and after her burial,
the Emperor frequently visited Yīn's tomb with his officials.
He said to Déyuàn:
"If you cry for Guìfēi as if truly grieved,
you will be generously rewarded."
Déyuàn immediately responded with loud wails and laments,
beating his chest and leaping about,
his tears and snot streaming down.
The Emperor was very pleased
and appointed him Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (豫州刺史, Governor of Yùzhōu).
He also ordered the physician Yáng Zhì to cry for the Yīn clan.
Zhì also sobbed.
Another day, someone asked Zhì:
"How did you manage such ready tears?"
Zhì, who had recently lost his beloved concubine,
replied:
"I was crying for my own deceased concubine that day."
〔一三〕Zhì was witty and good at humor,
and the Emperor also loved and treated him with familiarity.
Déyuàn was skilled at driving chariots.
He once set up two pillars
with just enough space between them for a chariot axle to pass through.
Then, from over a hundred paces away, he shook the reins and drove at full speed,
and when he was still a few feet away,
he made the oxen bolt directly through the space between the pillars.
Such was his precision.
Shìzǔ heard of his skill
〔一四〕and, riding in a painted wheeled chariot,
visited the residence of the Grand Tutor, Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng.
Déyuàn, wearing a tall-crowned hat and
a short vermilion robe,
held the reins and guided the chariot,
presenting a very dignified appearance.
During the Yǒngguāng reign,
he served as Tíngwèi (廷尉, Minister of Justice)
and was very close to Liǔ Yuánjǐng.
When Yuánjǐng was defeated,
he was imprisoned and executed.
Huáishèn's eldest illegitimate son, Róngzǔ,
was fond of archery and horsemanship in his youth
and was known to Gāozǔ.
〔一五〕When Lú Xún attacked and pressed,
the bandits at that time came in small vessels,
entering the Huái River and tearing down barriers.
Gāozǔ issued an order to the three armies
not to shoot the bandits arbitrarily.
Róngzǔ could not contain his anger
and, defying the prohibition, shot at them.
Those hit fell instantly upon the arrow's twang.
The Emperor admired him even more for this.
For his military achievements, he was appointed to the staff of the Grand Commandant.
He accompanied the expedition against Sīmǎ Xiūzhī.
When the Prefect of Péngchéng, Xú Kuízhī, was defeated and perished,
and the morale of the other generals was low,
Róngzǔ urged battle with greater fervor.
Gāozǔ then took off his own armor and gave it to him.
Róngzǔ led his subordinates to assault the enemy lines,
suffering several wounds himself,
and happened to break and drive off the bandits.
He was promoted to Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn (振威將軍, General Who Manifests Awe).
Soon after, he joined the Crown Prince's staff as Zhēnglǔ Jūnjūn (征虜軍軍, General Who Conquers the Barbarians)
and served as Magistrate of Suìchéng.
〔一六〕When Gāozǔ launched his northern expedition,
he was transferred to Zhèn Xī Zhōng Bīng Cānjūn (鎮西中兵參軍, Central Army Advisor to the General Who Guards the West)
and Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (寧遠將軍, General Who Pacifies the Distant).
The navy entered the river
and, with Zhū Chāoshí, utterly defeated the Suǒ虜 (Tuoba-Xianbei) at Bànchéng.
They also attacked Liú Dù's encampment and captured it.
Gāozǔ hosted a grand feast for his warriors
and said to Róngzǔ:
"You, with few, overcome many,
and assault no strong city.
Even ancient famous generals,
how could they surpass this?"
He was transferred to Tàiwèi Zhōng Bīng Cānjūn (太尉中兵參軍, Central Army Advisor to the Grand Commandant)
and granted the title Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (建威將軍, General Who Establishes Awe).
After Cháng'ān was broken,
Yáo Hóng's son-in-law, Xú Zhòng, led his remaining forces to rebel and flee, setting up continuous camps.
Róngzǔ, with Tán Dàojì and others, attacked and broke their camps,
beheading and capturing countless numbers.
It was beyond calculation.
In the fourteenth year [of Yǒngchū],
he was appointed Prefect of Péngchéng
and also made Xiàngguó Cānjūn (相國參軍, Advisor to the Prime Minister).
That same year,
Róngzǔ was sent back to the capital
and served as the Crown Prince's Zhōng Bīng Cānjūn.
In the first year of Yǒngchū,
he was appointed Yuèqí Xiàowèi (越騎校尉, Colonel of the Elite Cavalry)
and soon after transferred to Yòujūn Jiāngjūn (右軍將軍, General of the Right Army).
When the Suǒ虜 raided the south,
and Sīzhōu Cìshǐ (司州刺史, Governor of Sīzhōu) Máo Dézǔ was defeated and captured,
Róngzǔ, who was then in mourning for his father,
was raised from mourning to be Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍, General Who Assists the State).
In recognition of his achievement at Bànchéng,
he was granted the title Dūxiāng Hóu (都鄉侯, Marquis of Dūxiāng).
Róngzǔ was a man who slighted wealth and valued righteousness,
and was good at treating his officers and soldiers well.
However, his nature was biased, treacherous, and narrow-minded,
which somewhat alienated the hearts of gentlemen.
The Commander of the Army, Xiè Huì, treated him with deep respect.
During the time of deposition and establishment [of the Emperor],
Xiè Huì urged Róngzǔ,
who firmly declined and escaped involvement.
When Huì went out to garrison Jīngchǔ,
he wanted to invite Róngzǔ to be Nánmán Xiàowèi (南蠻校尉, Colonel of the Southern Barbarians),
but Róngzǔ again firmly refused.
He died in the winter of that year.
Déyuàn's younger brother, Xīngzǔ,
was Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ (青州刺史, Governor of Qīngzhōu).
Huáishèn's younger brother, Huáimò,
was Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍, General Who Conquers the Armies), Jiāngxià Nèishǐ (江夏內史, Prefect of Jiāngxià),
and Tàizhōng Dàfū (太中大夫, Grand Master of the Court).
Huáimò's son, Dàloángqiú,
was Prefect of Bādōng and Jiànpíng commanderies.
Dàloángqiú's younger brother, Sūndēng,
was Wǔlíng Nèishǐ (武陵內史, Prefect of Wǔlíng).
Sūndēng's son, Liàng,
during Shìzǔ's Dàmíng reign,
served as Magistrate of Wǔkāng.
At that time, there were many counterfeit coin makers in the region.
Liàng's raids caught all of them,
and those killed numbered in the thousands.
In the early Tàishǐ reign of Tàizōng,
he served as the Zhèn Dōng Zhōng Bīng Cānjūn (鎮東中兵參軍, Central Army Advisor to the General Who Guards the East) for Bālíng Wáng Xiūrùo.
In northern and southern expeditions,
his achievements surpassed all other generals.
He was enfeoffed as Shùnyáng Xiàn Hóu (順陽縣侯, Marquis of Shùnyáng County),
with a stipend of six hundred households.
He successively held the positions of Huángmén Láng (黃門郎, Gentleman of the Yellow Gate)
and Cìshǐ of Liáng and Yì provinces.
In office, he was incorruptible and frugal,
not seeking wealth.
All his remaining official salary
was returned to the government.
Tàizōng praised him
and issued an edict of commendation.
While Liàng was in Liángzhōu,
he suddenly began to practice Taoist self-cultivation by ingesting elixirs,
hoping to achieve immortality.
He invited the Taoist priest Sūn Dàoyìn from Wǔdāng Mountain
to concoct immortal medicine.
When he reached Yìzhōu,
the elixir was finally completed in the first year of Tàiyù,
but had not yet been purged of its fiery toxins.
Sūn did not allow Liàng to take it,
but Liàng desperately wanted to take it.
At dawn, he opened the city gate, drew fresh well water, and took the elixir.
After the meal drum sounded,
his heart throbbed as if pricked,
and then he died.
Later, people encountered him,
riding a white horse,
leading dozens of men,
leaving the pass and heading west,
speaking clearly.
This is what Taoists call "corpse liberation."
He was posthumously granted the title Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍)
and given the posthumous name Gāng Hóu (剛侯).
Sūndēng's younger brother, Dàolóng,
in the twenty-second year of Yuánjiā,
was Prefect of Lújiāng.
When Shìzǔ raised his righteous army,
he abandoned his commandery and came to join him.
He was appointed Nán Zhōngláng Cānjūn Shì (南中郎參軍事, Advisor to the Central Gentlemen of the South)
and granted the title Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍, General Who Soars Like a Dragon).
At that time, Shìzǔ divided his subordinates into three banners.
Dàolóng, along with Zhōng Bīng Cānjūn Wáng Qiānzhī and Mǎ Wéngōng, each led one.
During the Dàmíng reign,
he successively held the positions of Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎, Palace Attendant),
and Cìshǐ of Xú, Qīng, and Jì provinces.
During the Jǐnghé reign of the Former Deposed Emperor,
he was made Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (右衞將軍, General of the Right Guard)
and Yǒngchāng Xiàn Hóu (永昌縣侯, Marquis of Yǒngchāng County),
with a stipend of five hundred households,
and entrusted with important responsibilities.
In the early Tàishǐ reign,
he exerted himself for Tàizōng,
and was promoted to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (左衞將jūn, General of the Left Guard)
〔一七〕and Zhōnghù Jūnjūn (中護軍, Central Protector of the Army).
Soon after, he was granted death.
His deeds are recorded in the biography of Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén.
Wáng Qiānzhī, courtesy name Xiūguāng,
was a man from Línyí, Lángyé.
He was the great-grandson of Hú Zhī, Inspector of Sīzhōu in the Jìn dynasty.
In the early reign of Shìzǔ,
he successively held the posts of General of Valiant Cavalry,
Imperial Censor,
and Administrator of Wúxīng.
For his achievements in the southern campaign,
he was enfeoffed as a Viscount of Shíyáng County,
with a taxable income of five hundred households.
He died in the third year of Dàmíng,
and was posthumously granted the title of Former General,
with the posthumous name Sù.
His son Yìngzhī inherited his title.
At the end of Dàmíng,
he served as Internal Historian of Héngyáng.
When Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxún rebelled,
Yìngzhī rose in righteousness to resist Hé Huìwén, who was acting Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
He was killed by Huìwén.
The details are in the biography of Dèng Wǎn.
He was posthumously granted the title of Attendant Censor.
Yìngzhī's younger brother, Yúnzhī,
achieved prominence during Shùndì's Shēngmíng era.
Mǎ Wéngōng
was a man from Fúfēng.
He was also enfeoffed as a Viscount of Quánlíng County for his achievements,
with a taxable income of five hundred households.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he became General of Mobile Warfare.
He died shortly thereafter.
Liú Cuì, courtesy name Dàochōng,
was a man from Xiāo, Pèijùn.
His grandfather, Huī,
held a staff of authority, supervised military affairs in Hézhōng,
and was a General Who Conquers Barbarians.
Cuì's family resided in Jīngkǒu.
From a young age, he possessed ambition and capability.
Initially, he served as a provincial aide.
When Gāozǔ conquered the capital city,
he participated in military affairs of the Jiànwǔ.
Following the pacification of Jīngyì,
he was transferred to participate in military affairs of the Zhèn.
Soon after, he was appointed General of Jiànwǔ and Administrator of Pèijùn,
and also took charge of the Administrator of Xiàpī.
He then became an aide in the central army of the Chējì.
He followed in the campaign against Guǎnggù,
where he distinguished himself in battle.
For his foundational achievements,
〔一八〕he was enfeoffed as a Fifth-Rank Marquis of Xī'ān County.
After the army returned,
he was transferred to be a consultative aide in the central army.
When Lú Xún threatened Jīngyì,
Jīngkǒu was strategically important.
Tàizǔ was four years old at the time.
Gāozǔ sent Cuì to serve Tàizǔ and guard Jīngchéng.
He was transferred to General of Mobile Warfare.
He was promoted to General of Jiànwēi and Chancellor of Jiāngxià.
General of the Guard Yì
was Cuì's clan cousin.
Cuì devoted himself wholeheartedly to Gāozǔ,
and did not align with Yì.
When Gāozǔ intended to plot against Yì,
everyone suspected Cuì, who was in Xiàkǒu.
Gāozǔ trusted him even more.
When the main army arrived,
Cuì exerted his utmost loyalty and effort.
After the matter was settled,
he was enfeoffed as a Baron of Shèyáng County,
〔一九〕with a taxable income of five hundred households.
He left his post due to his mother's mourning.
Soon after, Gāozǔ campaigned against Sīmǎ Xiūzhī,
and appointed Cuì as General Who Pacifies the North and Administrator of Jìnglíng,
leading naval forces into the river.
The following year,
he was promoted to General Who Protects the State,
and transferred to Prime Minister's Right Sīmǎ, Attendant Censor, Central Army Sīmǎ, and General Who Conquers an Army.
He was then transferred to General of the Left Guard.
In the first year of Yǒngchū,
for his contributions in aiding the founding of the dynasty,
he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiàn'ān County,
with a taxable income of one thousand households.
In the second year,
he was dismissed from office
for misusing supervising officials.
Soon after, he was appointed Supervisor of all counties north of the Jiāng and south of the Huái, General Who Conquers Barbarians, and Administrator of Guǎnglíng.
In the third year,

with his original title, he was appointed Supervisor of military affairs for the four prefectures of Yù, Sī, Yōng, and Bìng, as well as the three commanderies of Liángjùn, Yìyáng, and Mǎtóu in Southern Yùzhōu, and Inspector of Yùzhōu,
also administering the Administrator of Liángjùn.
He was stationed in Shòuyáng,
where his governance showed good results.
In the second year of Jǐngpíng, during the reign of Shàodì,
more than sixty families of refugees from Qiáojùn rebelled and fled to the barbarians.
Six families, including Zhào Jiǒng and Qín Gāng, repented and returned, seeking refuge in Xiāngyì County, Chénliú,
and settled in villages such as Dùnmóu.
Cuì dispatched his general Yuàn Zòngfū to pursue the rebellious households, but failed to catch them.
Consequently, he executed thirty families, including Móu,
one hundred thirty-seven men,
and one hundred sixty-two women and children,
and handed them over to the labor department.
Cuì was demoted to General Who Pacifies the North for this.
At that time, the barbarians from the north raided south.
Cuì sent General Lǐ Yuándé to attack Xǔchāng,
killing Yú Lóng, the pseudo-Administrator of Yǐngchuān.
Thereupon, Dǒng Miǎo of Chénliú declared himself the leader of Xiǎohuáng Alliance,
beheaded Sīmǎ Shìxián, the pseudo-General Who Conquers Barbarians and Inspector of Guǎngzhōu,
and sent his head to the capital.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,

Cuì was promoted to Bearer of a Staff of Authority, Supervisor of military affairs for the four prefectures of Yōng, Liáng, North Qín, and South Qín, as well as the six commanderies of Nányáng, Jìnglíng, Shùnyáng, Xiāngyáng, Xīnyě, and Suí in Jīngzhōu, General Who Conquers Barbarians, concurrently holding the title of Colonel Who Pacifies the Man, Inspector of Yōngzhōu, and Administrator of Xiāngyáng and Xīnyě.
During his tenure, he simplified corvée labor and loved the people.
He dismissed over two thousand Buddhist monks,
using them to fill positions as government clerks.
In the third year of Yuánjiā, when campaigning against Xiè Huì,
he sent Cuì's younger brother Dàojì, who was a Chariot and Cavalry Aide, and General of Dragon Might Shěn Chǎngzhī to join Cuì,
traveling by land towards Jiānglíng.
Cuì made Dàojì acting Internal Historian of Jìnglíng.
Together with Chǎngzhī and Shěn Dàoxīng, the Administrator of Nányáng, they reached Shāqiáo with their infantry and cavalry,
where they were defeated by Xiè Huì's Sīmǎ Zhōu Chāo.
More than half of their troops were wounded or killed.
His title was demoted to General Who Pacifies the North.
Initially,
Xiè Huì and Cuì were very close friends.
Xiè Huì had made Cuì's son Kuàngzhī his aide.
When Cuì received orders to campaign south,
he showed no hesitation.
Tàizǔ praised him for this.
Xiè Huì sent Kuàngzhī back to Cuì,
and did not harm him.
The following year,
Cuì died
at the age of fifty-three.
He was posthumously granted the title of General Who Pacifies the North,
with the staff of authority and his original posts retained.
Kuàngzhī inherited his title,
and served as Administrator of Jìnxī.
After Kuàngzhī died,
his son Chēn inherited the title.
After Chēn died,
he had no son,
so the peerage was abolished.
Chēn's younger brother, Liàng,
was a Secretariat Bureau Director of the Censorate
at the end of Shùndì's Shēngmíng era.
Cuì's eldest concubine son, Huáizhī,
served as Internal Historian of Línchuān.
He joined Zāng Zhì in rebellion
and was executed.
Cuì's younger brother Dàojì,
was a Secretariat Bureau Director of the Ministry of Works,
Chariot and Cavalry Aide to Wáng Hóng,
Mobilized Army Sīmǎ to Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng,
Administrator of Hédōng,
and then promoted to General Who Manifests Martial Power and Inspector of Yìzhōu.
His Chief Clerk Fèi Qiān, Supervisor of Household Zhang Xī, and Aide Yáng Dénián, among others,
all engaged in extortion and profited,
while Dàojì entrusted them.
This harmed governance and oppressed the people,
and the people all resented him.
When Tàizǔ heard of this,
he sent an imperial edict to Dàojì,
admonishing him:
"I hear that during your tenure,
you have not been entirely clean and frugal,
and have accumulated some wealth.
If there is any truth to this,
you must certainly change.
Recently, it has been reported that the sentiments of the people are not harmonious.
〔二０〕You should govern your subordinates according to the law,
reflect deeply and be vigilant,
and comply with this expectation."
Although Dàojì received this decree,
his governance remained as before.
There was a Sīmǎ Fēilóng,
who claimed to be a member of the imperial clan of the Jìn,
and fled to Qiúchí at the end of the Jìn dynasty.
In the ninth year of Yuánjiā (432 CE),
hearing that Dàojì’s pacification and appeasement efforts were failing,
he then entered Miánzhú from Qiúchí.
He stirred up the common folk,
gathered over a thousand men,
and attacked Bāxīng County,
killing its magistrate, Wáng Zhēnzhī.
They advanced to attack Yīnpíng,
and the Administrator of Yīnpíng, Shěn Fǎxīng, burned the city and fled.
Dàojì sent troops to attack Fēilóng and beheaded him.
Initially,
Dàojì appointed Bái Dīnú and Liáng Xiǎn, both from Wǔchéng, as staff officers (cānjūn dūhù),
but Fèi Qiān firmly objected and would not allow it.
Many distant merchants came to the land of Shǔ with goods and capital,
some of which were worth several million.
Qiān and others set a limit that no more than fifty catties each of cloth, silk, and cotton could be bought,
and for horses, regardless of quality,
the limit was twenty thousand Shǔ coins.
The prefecture also established its own ironworks,
completely prohibiting private casting by the people,
〔二一〕but sold iron implements at high prices.
Merchants sighed in frustration,
and the common people all desired rebellion.
Dīnú, already harboring resentment and anger,
then gathered a gang to become bandits.
In the seventh month of that year,
Dàojì dispatched Luó Xí as the magistrate of Wǔchéng.
Dīnú and others plotted, saying:
“Magistrate Luó is His Excellency’s confidant,
and yet you continue to act as bandits without stopping.
If it is exposed one day,
the calamity will be immeasurable.
It is advisable to make a solemn pact
to mutually restrain and inspect each other.”
Thereupon, they slaughtered an ox and swore an oath.
Soon after, Dīnú and Zhào Guǎng chanted, saying:
“The officials prohibit the slaughter of oxen,
yet in our village, we openly violate the prohibition.
If Magistrate Luó reports this to His Excellency,
suspecting that we are still trying to commit robbery,
then there will be no escape.”
Thereupon, they falsely claimed that “His Highness Sīmǎ is still in Yángquán Mountain.
If we can jointly achieve a great undertaking,
then fame and success can be established;
otherwise,
we will be annihilated soon.”
Since the crowd was eager for chaos,
they then followed him en masse,
gathering several thousand people,
and again headed towards Guǎnghàn.
Dàojì sent his Staff Officer Chéng Zhǎnhuì and Chief Secretary Lǐ Kàngzhī with five hundred men to attack them,
but they were all killed.
The bandits then proceeded directly to Fúchéng.
Táng Pín from Bāxī gathered a crowd to respond to them.
Wáng Huáiyè, General Níngyuǎn and Administrator of the two commanderies of Bāxī and Zītóng, repeatedly sent troops to resist them,
but they were defeated and suffered losses.
Huáiyè, along with his Sīmǎ and Administrator of Nánhànzhōng, Wéi Chǔbó, both abandoned the city and fled.
Upon hearing that Fúchéng was undefended, Ruǎn Huì, Administrator of Fúlíng, Dù Xuánqǐ, Administrator of Jiāngyáng, and Féng Qiān, Administrator of Suìníng,
all abandoned their commanderies and fled.
Both the immigrant and native populations of Shǔ
unanimously rebelled.
Dàojì was alarmed and frightened.
He then discharged thirty-six Wú military camps, making them civilians,
and established two new commanderies, Sòngxīng and Sòngníng.
He also recruited merchants and released civilian and monastic slaves and servants.
He gathered about four thousand fighting men from east and west.
Tens of thousands of bandits encamped west and north of the city,
and Dàojì fortified the city and held it himself.
Zhào Guǎng had originally gathered his troops through trickery,
but with his troops stalled outside the city
and Fēilóng nowhere to be seen,
they each wanted to disperse.
Guǎng, fearing this,
then took three thousand men and imperial regalia,
and falsely told his followers that he was going to welcome Fēilóng.
Upon arriving at Yángquán Temple,
he said to the Daoist monk Chéng Dàoyǎng:
“Just say you are Fēilóng,
and you will enjoy wealth and honor without effort;
if you do not comply,
your head will be chopped off today.”
Dàoyǎng, terrified, agreed.
Dàoyǎng was
a native of Páohǎn.
Guǎng changed his name to Lóngxīng,
proclaimed himself King of Shǔ, Grand General of Cavalry, and Governor of the two provinces of Yì and Liáng.
He established the reign title Tàishǐ First Year,
and appointed a full complement of officials.
He made Dàoyǎng’s younger brother Dàozhù the General of Agile Cavalry and King of Chángshā,
to guard Fúchéng.
Guǎng proclaimed himself General of the Garrison,
Bái Dīnú General who Punishes Rebels,
Liáng Xiǎn General who Guards the North,
the bandit leader Zhāng Níng Inspector of Qín Province,
and Yán Xiá General of the Vanguard.
They escorted Dàoyǎng back to Chéngdū.
With a host of over one hundred thousand,
they surrounded the city on all sides.
They demanded Fèi Qiān and Zhāng Xī from Dàojì,
saying:
“Just send these men,
and we will no longer be bandits.”
Dàojì dispatched Middle Army Staff Officers Péi Fāngmíng and Rèn Làngzhī, each leading over a thousand men, to fight out of the west gate,
but they both suffered losses.
In the eleventh month,
Fāngmíng and others again sallied forth to battle,
destroying the bandit camp
and burning their accumulated supplies.
A bandit leader, Yáng Mèngzǐ from Jiāngyáng, led over a thousand men and encamped south of the city.
Dàojì’s Staff Officer Liáng Jùnzhī, who commanded the south tower,
frequently conversed with Mèngzǐ,
and then threw a letter explaining the consequences (of his actions) and promising good fortune,
asking him to enter the city.
Mèngzǐ agreed,
entered to see Dàojì,
and Dàojì was greatly pleased.
He immediately appointed him as a scribe (zhǔbù),
and sent his son to assume office,
setting a date to suppress the bandits.
Zhào Guǎng learned of his plan,
and Mèngzǐ, afraid,
fled with his followers to Jìnyuán.
The Administrator of Jìnyuán, Wén Zhòngxīng, gathered over two thousand men,
and joined forces with Mèngzǐ to defend themselves.
Guǎng sent his associate Yuán Xuánzǐ to attack Jìnyuán,
but he was killed by Zhòngxīng.
Guǎng again sent Bái Dīnú to attack them.
After continuous battles,
Zhòngxīng’s army was defeated,
and he and Mèngzǐ both died.
Fāngmíng again sallied forth from the east gate,
destroying three bandit camps
and beheading several hundred.
Although the bandits were defeated,
they regrouped again.
Fāngmíng again feigned an exit from the north gate,
then turned his army to attack the large camp east of the city,
killing over a thousand men
and beheading the false Minister (púshè) Cài Tāo.
At this time, there was a heavy fog.
Fāngmíng and others again loudly proclaimed they were exiting the east gate,
but secretly exited the north gate to attack the various camps north and west of the city.
The bandit forces suffered a major rout,
and then scattered.
Dàoyǎng regrouped seven thousand men and returned to Guǎnghàn,
while Zhào Guǎng, with his separate force of over five thousand men, returned to Fúchéng.
Initially,
the Vice-Prefect, Zhāng Xī, persuaded Dào Jǐ to sell grain from the grand granary.
The bandits besieged the city at the end of the ninth month.
By the end of the twelfth month,
their provisions were exhausted.
Fāng Míng led two thousand men out of the city to forage for food,
but was defeated by the bandits,
returning alone on horseback.
The bandits then pursued them,
and their numbers greatly increased again.
Fāng Míng was lowered into the city from the west wall at night,
and Dào Jǐ prepared food for him,
but he was too grief-stricken to eat,
only weeping.
Dào Jǐ was at that time gravely ill,
but forced himself to comfort and encourage him, saying:
“You are not a true man if
you are so distressed by a minor defeat.
The bandits’ strength is already waning,
and the imperial troops will soon arrive.
Just let you return,
and what is there to worry about with the bandits?”
He immediately reduced his personal guard by several tens of men to assign to Fāng Míng.
Outside the city, the bandits announced:
“Fāng Míng is dead;
you may come and collect his corpse.”
Great fear spread within the city.
Dào Jǐ lit a line of torches at night,
and Fāng Míng appeared,
which reassured the people.
Dào Jǐ brought out all his wealth to the Northern Archery Hall
and ordered Fāng Míng to recruit men.
At that time, rumors circulated in the city that Dào Jǐ had died,
so no one came forward.
Liáng Jùnzhī said to Dào Jǐ:
“General, your breath is faint,
and outside opinions vary.
Now the army has been repeatedly defeated,
and the demonic bandits are not yet eliminated.
If an unexpected disaster strikes,
danger and calamity will immediately follow.
It would be advisable to claim a minor ailment
and allow your attendants to temporarily leave;
otherwise, we will be defeated.”
Dào Jǐ followed this advice,
and immediately summoned over thirty of his attendants, telling them:
“I have been ill for a long time,
and you all are tired from attending to me.
Now that I have a minor improvement,
you may each return home to rest.
I will call you back later.”
When the attendants left,
their fathers and elder brothers all asked:
“How many days has the Prefect been dead?”
Their sons and younger brothers all said:
“The Prefect is gradually recovering;
who said he was dead!”
This news was spread by word of mouth,
and the city became calm.
Because of this, over a thousand people enlisted in a single day.
In the first month of the tenth year,
a large bandit force arrived
and attacked Chéngdū.
Dào Jǐ died.
Liáng Jùnzhī and Fāng Míng,
along with several of his old acquaintances and disciples,
secretly buried his body in the back study.
They had someone whose handwriting resembled Dào Jǐ’s write official orders,
responding to documents and memorials,
just as on normal days,
so even his mother and wife
did not know.
In the second month,
Dào Yǎng ascended the altar at Huǐjīnqiáo to sacrifice to Heaven,
and just as he was about to light the pyre,
Fāng Míng led three thousand men to attack him.
The bandits formed a battle array in front of their camp and fought desperately,
and were finally routed in the evening.
On the battlefield, they beheaded over eight hundred individuals, including the false General Who Conquers the Barbarians, Zhào Shízhī.
Dào Yǎng and his group retreated to defend Guǎnghàn.
In this month,
the Prince of Línchuān, Yìqìng, General Who Pacifies the West,

appointed Zhōu Jízhī, General Who Manifests Martial Might and Administrator of Bādōng, to his original title and position as Supervising Military Affairs of Bāxī, Zītóng, Dàngqú, Suìníng, and Bājùn Commander, and Administrator of Bāxī and Zītóng Commanderies,
and ordered him to lead Fèi Dàn, an aide-de-camp to the General Who Pacifies the West, and Luó Měng, General Who Springs Like a Dragon, with two thousand men to reinforce Chéngdū.
Guǎng and others encamped at Guǎnghàn,
divided their forces to guard Píchuān,
and formed hundreds of continuous camps,
stationing troops everywhere.
Jízhī, Fāng Míng, and Fèi Dàn attacked Pí
and conquered it.
Guǎng and others retreated to the commandery city,
fortifying themselves among the bamboos.
Luó Měng led squad leader Wáng Xū and others to pursue them with full force.
Zhāng Xún led twenty thousand men from Fúchéng to assist Guǎng and his group.
Fāng Míng and Dàn cut down bamboos to open a path and intercepted them,
but were defeated in battle and
retreated to Píxiàn.
Guǎng and others again moved their camp to Jiàngānqiáo.
Fāng Míng and his group broke six of their camps,
and pressed on in victory,
reaching Guǎnghàn directly.
Guǎng and others fled back to Fú and Wǔchéng.
On the tenth day of the fourth month,
Dào Jǐ’s funeral was held.
In the fifth month,
Fāng Míng advanced his army towards Fúchéng.
[二二]Zhāng Xún and Táng Pín crossed the water to resist,
but Fāng Míng defeated them,
capturing alive and beheading the false General of Agile Cavalry and Inspector of Yōng and Qín Provinces, Sīmǎ Lóngshēn.
Lóngshēn was
Dào Zhù.
Yán Dàodù, an official of the province, beheaded Yán Xiá.
Guǎng and others all scattered,
and Fú and Shǔ were pacified.
Soon after, Zhāng Xún attacked and captured Yīnpíng,
rejoining Dào Yǎng.
Bó Dīnǔ attacked Guǎnghàn.
Fèi Dàn commanded General Zhǒng Sōng and others to fight him,
beheading over a hundred individuals, including Dù Chéng, the Inspector of Liáng Province.
In the ninth month,
Zhēn Fǎchóng, Inspector of Yì Province, arrived in Chéngdū,
executed Fèi Qiānzhī,
[二三]and Dào Jǐ’s funeral cortege and Fāng Míng and others all returned east.
Dào Yǎng and others led over two thousand households to flee to Qīshān.
The remaining bandit groups
also each gathered their households and hid,
emerging to commit robberies without cease.
In the sixth month of the thirteenth year,
Grand Ancestor sent Xiāo Wāngzhī, General Who Pacifies the North, to lead an army to suppress them.
When the army reached Qīkǒu,
Bó Dīnǔ beheaded the false General of the Guards, Sīmǎ Fēiyàn, and surrendered.
Wāngzhī defeated Dào Yǎng,
who retreated back into Qīshān.
In the fourth month of the fourteenth year,
Zhào Guǎng, Zhāng Xún, and Liáng Xiǎn each led their forces to surrender.
Wáng Dào'ēn, the false General Who Assists the State, beheaded Dào Yǎng
and sent his head,
thus pacifying the remaining factions.
Zhào Guǎng and Zhāng Xún were relocated to the capital.
In the sixteenth year,
Guǎng and Xún again conspired to rebel with Sīmǎ Jìnglín, the Prefect of Guóshān,
and were executed.
Prior to this,
Rèn Huìzhī, Dào Jǐ’s Sīmǎ of Manifesting Martial Might and Administrator of Shǔ Commandery, although not involved in military affairs,
was appointed
Regular Member of the Lang Corps after the pacification.
Péi Fāngmíng became Colonel of the Tigers,
and remained Yìqìng’s Mid-Army Aide of the General Who Pacifies the West, General Who Springs Like a Dragon, and Administrator of Hédōng.
Fèi Dàn became
Colonel of Agile Cavalry for the Heir Apparent.
Zhōu Jízhī later became Inspector of Yì Province.
Cuì’s younger cousin, Sǔn,
courtesy name Zǐqiān,
was the cousin of Wèi Yì, General of the Guards.
His father, Zhènzhī, courtesy name Zhòngdé,
because of Yì’s prominence, held various high positions,
but preferred to live in retirement in Jīngkǒu,
never responding to summons.
He often told Yì:
“You will surely bring ruin to my family.”
Yì greatly feared him,
and whenever he returned to the capital,
[二四]he never dared to enter Zhènzhī’s gate with his official entourage.
He was offered the position of Grand Master of Glorious Happiness of the Left,
but did not accept it.
In the second year of Yuánjiā,
at over ninety years old,
he died at home.
Sǔn served
as Administrator of Yìxīng during the Yuánjiā era.
When the eastern regions suffered famine,
Grand Ancestor sent Shěn Yǎnzhī, Judicial Administrator of Yáng Province, to the east to provide relief.
Sǔn was praised as an excellent administrator
for his effective pacification and appeasement.
He rose to the position of Administrator of Wú Commandery
and was posthumously granted the title of Grand Master of Ceremonies.
The Grand Astrologer said: Emperors receive the Mandate
not merely by quelling chaos through merit,
or benefiting the people through virtue;
otherwise, their path would be inaccessible.
Since the Three Dynasties,
the pure customs gradually weakened.
Achieving success and managing affairs,
honor arose from expedient power.
Even if they sat facing south on the imperial screen
and were compared in title to Xuān and Xī,
none failed to humble themselves before the imperial way,
but rather followed the path of hegemonic virtue.
Gāozǔ rose from commoner status,
not relying on popular acclaim.
He lacked the heroic renown of Cáo Gōng
and also the foundation of the Jìn clan in assisting Wèi.
Yet, in a single day, he mustered a disorganized crowd
and, in less than a morning, controlled the nation's destiny.
Though his merit was ample,
his virtue was insufficient.
Therefore, Wáng Mì inwardly feared fleeing,
and Wáng Suī outwardly risked provoking enmity.
Had he not established extraordinary achievements in difficult circumstances,
and displayed great might throughout the Four Seas,
he could not have inherited the heaven-matched enterprise
and unified diverse hearts.
After Yìxī,
great merits were continuously established.
Wherever Huán Wēn's banners and pennants arrived,
none failed to offer treasures and accept his edicts.
When Jīnyǒng requested officials,
and the founding minister was about to be elevated,
the rites of the Nine Bestowments were already performed,
and the omen for the end of the dynasty had arrived.
He then reviewed his troops at Hán and Wèi,
employing his army in perilous terrain.
Such an unassisted victory
is rarely spoken of in antiquity.
If he had closed his gates, returned power,
and dispersed his troops,
his later failures would have been blamed on his previous accomplishments,
and a single flaw would have diminished his grand enterprise.
How could he then, with the yellow carriage and vermillion doors,
have been a loyal minister to the declining Jìn?
And when his awe-inspiring might reached
where even heavily guarded passes could not be held,
it became known that his profound calculations
always ensured victory before battle.
Wáng Zhèn'è spearheaded the attack directly,
encountering no strong formations ahead.
He was like Sòng Fāngshū;
truly magnificent!
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 6
Zhào Lúnzhī, Dào Yànzhī (missing), Wáng Yì, Zhāng Shào
Zhào Lúnzhī, courtesy name Yòuchéng,
was a native of Tóng, Xiàpī.
He was the younger brother of Empress Xiàomù.
As a child, he was orphaned and poor,
and was known for his filial piety towards his mother.
When Wǔdì raised an army,
he was enfeoffed as a Fifth Rank Marquis of Làngzhōng County for his military merits,
and was successively promoted to Inspector of Yōngzhōu.
When Wǔdì campaigned in the north,
Lúnzhī dispatched the Administrator of Shùnyáng, Fù Hóngzhī, and the Administrator of Fúfēng, Shěn Tiánzǐ, to emerge from Yáoliǔ,
severely defeating Yáo Hóng at Lántián.
When Wǔdì received the Mandate,
for his meritorious assistance,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiāochéng County,
General of Pacifying the North,
and stationed at Xiāngyáng.
When Shǎodì ascended the throne,
he was summoned and appointed Protector of the Army.
In the third year of Yuánjiā,
he was appointed General of Suppressing the Army,
and soon after promoted to Grand Master of Glorious Happiness of the Left,
and concurrently General of the Army.
Although Lúnzhī, as an imperial relative, was distinguished and prosperous,
he lived frugally and simply.
His nature was rough and unsophisticated;
he often misunderstood human nature and worldly affairs.
Having served as a regional governor for a long time,
he felt quite wealthy and prosperous.
Upon entering service as Protector of the Army,
his financial resources did not match his position,
and he considered it a demotion.
The Grand Master of Glorious Happiness Fàn Tài, who enjoyed jesting, said to him:
"If the Grand Minister of Works position becomes vacant,
they will surely use you, old fellow.
I'm not saying you're suitable for the position,
but rather that it's merely the progression of high ranks for imperial relatives."
Lúnzhī was greatly pleased
and thereafter often brought wine and food to Tái.
In the fifth year,
he died.
His son Bófú succeeded him.
Bófú, courtesy name Rùnyuǎn.
In his youth, he was fond of archery and horsemanship.
When Lúnzhī was in Xiāngyáng,
Bófú served as Administrator of Jìnglín.
At that time, the Jìnglín Man frequently raided,
and Bófú campaigned against them,
defeating them all,
thus earning the reputation of a commander.
Later, he became General of Pacifying the Distant,
commanding loyal volunteers.
As he resided north of the palace city,
whenever there was a fire or a robbery,
he would personally don armor,
assisting the commandery and county in pursuing the perpetrators.
Wǔdì greatly praised him.
When Wéndì ascended the throne,
he was successively promoted to Inspector of Xú and Yǎn two Prefectures.
His governance was harsh and violent;
officials and common people feared him like jackals and tigers.
Nevertheless, bandits fled far away,
none daring to violate the border.
In the eighteenth year of Yuánjiā,
he was summoned to be General of the Army.
Previously,
external supervisors were not subordinate to the General of the Army;
if they were to be brought under unified command,
there would be a separate imperial edict.
From this point, they were brought under unified command.
In the twenty-first year,
he was transferred to be Inspector of Yùzhōu.
The following year,
he became General of the Protector of the Army,
and then again Administrator of Dānyáng.
In the commandery, he was severe and cruel;
officials and common people suffered from it,
some even abandoning their posts or committing suicide by drowning when captured.
An official responsible for pens, if he did not provide satisfactory pens,
would receive fifty lashes.
His son Qiàn
married Wéndì's fourth daughter, Princess Hǎiyán.
Initially,
Shǐxīngwáng Jùn, favored by Consort Pān,
was able to enter and exit the inner palace,
