and consequently had a secret affair with the princess.
When she married Qiàn,
Qiàn entered the palace and, in anger,
verbally abused and physically assaulted her,
even pulling off her curtain sash.
The matter was reported to the emperor,
who issued an edict for divorce,
and had Concubine Jiǎng, the princess's birth mother, executed.
Bófú, ashamed and fearful, fell ill and died.
His posthumous title was Sù.
The lineage passed down to his grandson Xù.
When Qí received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
Wáng Yì, courtesy name Zhòngdé,
was a native of Qí, Tàiyuán.
He claimed to be the seventh-generation descendant of Mào, Inspector of Yōuzhōu, who was the brother of Sìtú Yǔn of Hàn.
His grandfather Hóng
served Shí Jìlóng.
His father Miáo
served Fú Jiān.
Both held positions of two thousand piculs.
Zhòngdé (仲德) was quiet and thoughtful in his youth,
possessing strategic acumen.
He understood Yin-Yang,
and was skilled in prosody.
When the Fú (苻) clan was defeated,
Zhòngdé (仲德) was seventeen.
He and his elder brother Ruì (叡) raised an army of righteousness together.
They fought against Mùróng Chuí (慕容垂),
and were defeated.
Zhòngdé (仲德) was severely wounded and fled,
separated from his family.
He passed through a great marsh,
unable to proceed,
and lay exhausted in the forest.
Suddenly, a boy in green clothes rode an ox by.
He saw Zhòngdé (仲德)
and asked,
"Have you eaten?"
Zhòngdé (仲德) told him he was hungry.
The boy left,
and after a short while returned,
bringing food for him.
When Zhòngdé (仲德) finished eating and wished to leave,
a flash flood suddenly arrived,
and he knew not where to go.
A white wolf came before him,
howled at the sky,
and after howling, held Zhòngdé's (仲德) clothing in its mouth.
It then crossed the water,
and Zhòngdé (仲德) followed it,
successfully getting across.
He was reunited with Ruì (叡).
They crossed the river to Huátái (滑臺),
but were again detained by Zhái Liáo (翟遼),
who made them generals.
After several years,
Zhòngdé (仲德) wished to return south,
so he fled to Tài Shān (泰山).
Liáo (遼) sent cavalry in close pursuit.
As he traveled by night,
suddenly a torch-light guided him forward.
Zhòngdé (仲德) followed it,
traveling for about a hundred *lǐ*,
and thus escaped.
At the end of Jìn (晉) Tài Yuán (太元) era,
he relocated to Péngchéng (彭城).
His and his brother's names violated the personal names of two Jìn (晉) emperors, Xuān (宣) and Yuán (元),
so they were both referred to by their courtesy names.
Ruì's (叡) courtesy name was Yuándé (元德).
In the northern lands, people valued those of the same clan,
calling them "flesh and blood."
If someone came from afar to seek refuge,
everyone would do their utmost to provide for them.
If one failed to do so,
it was considered unrighteous,
and they would not be tolerated by their community.
Zhòngdé (仲德) heard that Wáng Yú (王愉) was in Jiāngnán (江南)
and was from Tàiyuán (太原),
so he went to rely on him.
Yú (愉) treated him very meagerly,
so he went to Gūshú (姑孰) to seek Húán Xuán (桓玄).
He happened to be there when Xuán (玄) usurped the throne.
He met the辅国将军 (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn) Zhāng Chàng (張暢),
and spoke of current affairs.
Zhòngdé (仲德) said,
"Since ancient times, revolutions
have indeed not been limited to one clan,
but those who rise up now,
I fear, are insufficient to accomplish great deeds."
Yuándé (元德) was brave and resourceful.
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) knew him well
and informed him of the righteous uprising,
sending him to attack Xuán (玄) in the capital.
Zhòngdé (仲德) heard of the plan
and said to Yuándé (元德),
"Affairs of the world
must not be less than secret.
Act swiftly when the opportunity arises,
rather than cleverly but slowly.
Xuán (玄) goes in and out almost every night.
If we plot against him now,
it only requires the strength of one man."
The matter was leaked,
and Yuándé (元德) was executed by Xuán (玄).
Zhòngdé (仲德) fled and hid.
When the righteous army conquered Jiànyè (建業),
Zhòngdé (仲德) carried Yuándé's (元德) son Fānghuí (方回) out to greet Emperor Wǔ (武帝).
The emperor, while on horseback, embraced Fānghuí (方回) and wept with Zhòngdé (仲德).
Yuándé (元德) was posthumously granted the position of 給事中 (Jǐshìzhōng)
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Ānfù (安復) County.
Zhòngdé (仲德) was made 中兵參軍 (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn).
When Emperor Wǔ (武帝) attacked Guǎnggù (廣固),
Zhòngdé (仲德) served as the vanguard,
fighting more than twenty battles, large and small,
and winning every single one.
When Lú Xún (盧循) threatened the capital,
defeating Líu Yì (劉毅) at Sāngluò (桑落),
the Emperor had just returned from the northern expedition.
The soldiers were wounded,
and only a few thousand were fit for battle.
The enemy numbered one hundred thousand,
with ships stretching for a hundred *lǐ*.
Those who fled in defeat
all spoke of their might.
The general consensus was to move the capital.
Zhòngdé (仲德) said with a stern expression,
"Today, the Son of Heaven rules from the center,
and Your Excellency serves as an assistant for this age,
having achieved great merits,
with prestige shaking the six directions.
The demonic bandits, like wild boars,
took advantage of our distant campaign.
Now that they hear of our triumphant return,
they will scatter on their own.
If we throw ourselves into the wilderness now,
we become like commoners.
How can a commoner's commands
inspire awe?
Righteous scholars and heroes
will seek their own masters.
If this plan proceeds,
please allow me to resign from this point."
The Emperor was pleased,
and sent Zhòngdé (仲德) to garrison Yuèchéng (越城).
When the bandits fled south from Càizhōu (蔡洲),
Zhòngdé (仲德) was dispatched to pursue them.
The bandits left their close associate Fàn Chóngmín (范崇民) with five thousand men
and over a hundred tall ships,
fortifying the southern hill of the city.
Zhòngdé (仲德) attacked them,
severely defeating Chóngmín (崇民),
burning his ships,
and gathering his scattered troops.
His achievements surpassed all other generals,
and he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xīngàn (新淦) County.
In the twelfth year of Yìxī (義熙), during the northern expedition,
Zhòngdé (仲德) was promoted to 征虜將軍 (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn),
additionally appointed Jìzhōu Cìshǐ (冀州刺史),
and made the commander of the vanguard forces.
Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍) Tán Dàojì (檀道濟) and Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) Wáng Zhèn'è (王鎮惡) advanced towards Luòyáng (洛陽).
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) Líu Zūnkǎo (劉遵考) and Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn (建武將軍) Shěn Línzǐ (沈林子) exited through Shímén (石門).
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) Zhū Chāoshí (朱超石) and Hú Fān (胡藩) marched towards Bànchéng (半城).
All were under Zhòngdé's (仲德) command.
Zhòngdé (仲德) led Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) Zhū Mù (朱牧), Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (寧遠將軍) Zhú Língxiù (竺靈秀), Yán Gāng (嚴綱) and others to open up Jùyě (鉅野) and enter the river.
He then took overall command of the armies
and advanced to occupy Tóngguān (潼關).
Cháng'ān (長安) was pacified,
and Zhòngdé (仲德) was appointed Tàiwèi Zīyì Cānjūn (太尉諮議參軍).
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) wished to move the capital to Luòyáng (洛陽),
and the general consensus was that it was appropriate.
Zhòngdé (仲德) said,
"Extraordinary matters
are startling to ordinary people.
Now, the army has been deployed for a long time,
and the soldiers wish to return home.
It is proper to establish Jiànyè (建業) as the royal base,
and only when the culture and customs are largely unified
should we then discuss this."
The Emperor deeply accepted his advice,
and had him escort Yáo Hóng (姚泓) back to Péngchéng (彭城) first.
When Emperor Wǔ (武帝) received the Mandate of Heaven,
Zhòngdé (仲德) was successively promoted to Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (徐州刺史),
and given the additional title of Dūdū (都督).
In the third year of Yuánjiā (426 CE),
he was promoted to General Ānběi.
He joined Dào Yànzhī on the northern expedition,
where they heavily defeated the barbarian army.
All the armies advanced and encamped at Língchāngjīn.
After Sī and Yǎn prefectures were pacified,
all three armies rejoiced,
but Zhòngdé alone showed a worried expression,
saying:
"Although the Hú barbarians lack benevolence and righteousness,
they are more than cunning and fierce.
Now they have put away their spears and returned north,
concentrating their forces and gathering.
If the river freezes in winter,
how can it not be a cause for concern for our three armies?"
In the tenth month,
the barbarians crossed the river at Wěisùjīn,
advancing to besiege Jīnyǒng.
The armies at Hǔláo and Luòyáng
successively fled.
Yànzhī, hearing that the two cities could not be held,
wished to burn their boats and proceed on foot.
Zhòngdé said:
"Since Luòyáng has fallen,
Hǔláo cannot remain intact alone;
circumstances dictate it.
Now the bandits are a thousand *lǐ* away from us,
and Huátái still has a strong army.
If we immediately abandon our boats and flee,
the soldiers will surely scatter.
For now, we should enter the Jì River and proceed to Mǎ'ěrgǔkǒu,
and then deliberate further on what is appropriate."
So they turned the army around, went along the Jì River, marched north past Lìchéng on foot,
burned their boats, abandoned their armor,
and returned to Péngchéng.
Zhòngdé and Yànzhī were both dismissed from office.
Soon after, he joined Tán Dàojì in relieving Huátái,
but they returned when their provisions ran out.
In the ninth year (432 CE),
he was again appointed General Zhènběi and Inspector of Xúzhōu.
The following year,
he was additionally appointed Inspector of Yǎnzhōu.
Zhòngdé oversaw Xúzhōu three times,
and his prestige and virtue were well-known in Péngchéng.
He built a Buddhist temple and placed statues of a white wolf and a boy in the pagoda,
commemorating his encounter in Hébĕi.
In the thirteenth year (436 CE),
he was promoted to Grand General Zhènběi.
In the fifteenth year (438 CE),
he died.
His posthumous title was Huán Hóu.
A white wolf and boy altar was also set up in his ancestral temple,
and they were worshipped at every sacrifice.
His son, Zhèngxiū, succeeded him,
but was killed by a household slave.
Zhāng Shào, courtesy name Mòuzōng,
was the younger brother of Yù, the Administrator of Kuàijī.
He first served as Records Keeper in the Longxiáng Prefectural Office of Wáng Dàn, the Jin Administrator of Lángyé.
When Huán Xuán exiled Dàn to Guǎngzhōu,
all his relatives and old friends abandoned him,
but only Shào remained exceptionally diligent and devoted,
tearfully seeing him off.
At that time, there were upheavals and famine,
yet he still sent provisions to Dàn's wife and children.
When Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
Shào's father, Chǎng, had previously been a Shàngshū,
but due to a minor error in his official report,
he was demoted to Court Steward.
When Emperor Wǔ attacked Xuán,
Shào advised Chǎng to submit a memorial expressing his loyalty.
The Emperor was greatly pleased
and ordered a sign to be placed on their gate saying:
"Anyone who offends Court Steward Zhāng
shall be judged by military law."
Later, Chǎng was made Administrator of Wújùn.
When Wáng Mì was Governor of Yángzhōu,
he summoned Shào to be his Chief Clerk.
Liú Yì, serving as Second Prime Minister,
admired talent and favored scholars,
so everyone at the time flocked to him,
but Shào alone did not go.
Someone asked him about it,
and Shào replied:
"Our lord is a peerless hero;
why bother asking too many questions?"
When Liú Mùzhī heard this and reported it,
the Emperor became even closer to him,
transferring him to Taìwèi Cānjūn,
and appointing him Chief of Bandit Affairs for the Long River.
When Lú Xún's rebellion approached the capital,
Shào was ordered to defend Nánchéng.
At that time, the common people watched the bandits from the waterfront.
The Emperor found this strange and asked Shào,
to which Shào replied:
"If our imperial ensigns had not yet returned,
they would be too busy fleeing and scattering,
how could they possibly be observing?
Now they must no longer be afraid."
Soon after, he was appointed Provincial Chief Clerk.
Shào dedicated himself wholeheartedly to government affairs,
with extraordinary energy.
When Liú Fān was to be executed,
Shào was in the western office at the time.
That very night, he instructed all the clerks:
"The great army is about to undertake a major campaign.
You must each repair boats, ships, and warehouses,
and have them ready by dawn."
The next morning,
when the Emperor requested various registers and official documents,
they arrived immediately.
He was surprised and asked about their speed,
and the clerks replied:
"Last night, we received instructions from Chief Clerk Zhāng."
The Emperor said:
"Zhāng Shào can truly be said to share my worries."
In the ninth year (413 CE),
when the Crown Prince first established his Conquering General's office,
Shào was appointed Recorder and Staff Officer.
He was then transferred to the Central Army
and promoted to Consultative Staff Officer,
also serving as Chief Scribe.
In the twelfth year (416 CE),
when Emperor Wǔ launched his northern expedition,
Shào requested an audience,
saying:
"Life is fragile and transient,
one must always think far ahead.
If Mùzhī were to unfortunately meet with an accident,
who could replace him?
Your esteemed enterprise is such that,
should anything untoward happen,
what would become of affairs?"
The Emperor replied:
"This is entrusted to Mùzhī and you, of course."
Tán Zhī, Inspector of Qīngzhōu, was garrisoned at Guǎnglíng.
At that time, a group of fugitives gathered in Chú.
Zhī led his troops to ambush them.
Liú Mùzhī feared this would cause a rebellion
and was about to dispatch troops.
Shào said:
"Tán Sháo holds the middle stream,
and Dàojì is the head of the army.
If suspicions are openly expressed,
I fear a major upheaval will arise.
It is advisable to first send an envoy to offer comfort and encouragement,
to observe his intentions."
After this, Zhī indeed did not make a move.
When Mùzhī died,
the imperial court was terrified
and immediately wanted to issue an edict appointing Sīmǎ Xú Xiànzhī to replace him.
Shào countered:
"Although this is indeed an urgent matter,
the responsibility will ultimately fall to Xú.
However, the Crown Prince does not have the authority to issue decrees independently.
We should wait to consult with the north."
When the messenger returned,
only then did he have the Crown Prince issue an order saying:
"All matters concerning the imperial court and the grand administration
shall be consulted with Sīmǎ Xú.
Other requests are to be returned."
Emperor Wǔ valued his steadfastness in the face of crisis
and his bearing as a great minister.
In the fourteenth year (418 CE),
when the Crown Prince was to be garrisoned in Jīngzhōu,
Shào remonstrated:
"The importance of the Heir Apparent
is connected to the entire realm.
He should not be stationed outside the capital.
I humbly request this even if it means death."
The Emperor complied.
When Emperor Wén served as Central Affairs General and Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
Shào was made his Sīmǎ
and concurrently Administrator of Nánjùn.
All matters were decided by Shào.
When Emperor Wǔ received the Mandate of Heaven,
for his meritorious service in supporting the dynastic change,
he was enfeoffed as Count of Línjǔ.
Jīngzhōu was divided to establish Xiāngzhōu,
and Shào was made its Inspector.
When about to establish the prefectural office,
Shào believed that Chángshā was an inland region,
not a place for military deployment,
and setting up an office would hinder people
and go against the essentials of governance.
The Emperor agreed with him.
When Xiè Huì rebelled,
he sent a letter to summon Shào.
Shào did not open the letter
but immediately dispatched a messenger to present it to the Emperor.
In the fifth year of Yuánjiā,
he was transferred to be General Zheng Lǔ,
concurrently Commandant Níngmán and Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
with the added title of Dūdū.
Initially,
Zhāng Huá and Zhāng Shào had a feud.
When Huá participated in important affairs,
Shào's old acquaintances worried for him.
Shào said:
"Zǐlíng will certainly uphold the greatest impartiality,
and will not harm justice with a private enmity."
For this appointment,
it was indeed Huá who recommended him.
Upon arriving in Xiāngyáng,
he built long embankments,
repaired and erected dikes,
and opened up several thousand qǐng of farmland.
The people of the commandery relied on this for their prosperity.
The Mán tribes of the Dān and Xī rivers repeatedly committed banditry.
Shào enticed their chieftain,
and then executed him at a grand assembly,
capturing all his followers.
Having lost the trust of the Mán tribes,
they rose up everywhere,
cutting off routes by water and land.
His son, Zhāng Fū, came to Xiāngyáng to pay his respects and visit his parents.
When he was about to return to the capital,
the Mán tribes lay in wait, intending to capture him.
It happened that an envoy from the Rúrú kingdom arrived to pay tribute.
The bandits mistook him for Fū,
and consequently seized him.
Shào was demoted to General Yángliè for this.
Liú Yìgōng, the Prince of Jiāngxià, was garrisoned in Jiānglíng.
He appointed Shào as Fǔjūn Chángshǐ,
with a jié, and Commandant of the Southern Mán.
He was impeached for embezzling and hoarding private wealth in Yōngzhōu,
with illicit gains totaling 2,450,000 cash.
He was sent to the Tíngwèi,
dismissed from office,
and stripped of his noble title and fief.
Later, he became Administrator of Wúxīng.
When he died,
his noble title and fief were posthumously restored,
and he was granted the posthumous title of Jiǎnbó.
On his deathbed, Shào
bequeathed instructions that his offerings should consist of vegetables and fruits,
his carriage be a reed mat,
and his sons follow it.
His sons Zhāng Fū, Zhāng Yǎn, and Zhāng Jìng
were famous in their time.
Zhāng Fū's courtesy name was Jǐngyìn.
His mother died when he was born.
When he was a few years old,
he inquired and learned of this.
Although he was a child,
he immediately showed signs of sorrow and longing.
Around the age of ten,
he sought out his mother's relics.
However, everything had already been distributed,
and he only found one fan,
which he then sealed away.
Whenever he felt nostalgic,
he would open the chest and weep.
Upon seeing his maternal aunt,
he would be overcome with grief and sob.
He was naturally meticulous and dignified,
with an elegant bearing.
He enjoyed Xuánxué discourse
and was skilled in writing.
Initially,
his father Shào sent him to discuss xiàngshù with Zōng Shǎowén of Nányáng.
They went back and forth several times,
and each time Shǎowén almost yielded,
he would grasp his fly-whisk and sigh, saying:
"My Way has moved eastward!"
Thereupon, his reputation grew daily.
Emperor Wǔ of Sòng heard of his excellence,
summoned him, and was impressed,
saying:
"Truly a colt that can travel a thousand lǐ!"
He was appointed Aide to the Crown Prince's Central Army,
and was frequently received and guided.
He was successively promoted to Fǔjūn Jìshì Cānjūn for Liú Yìgōng, Prince of Jiāngxià.
Yìgōng asked Emperor Wén for a monk learned in doctrine.
It happened that Fū was going to Jiānglíng for a leave.
When he went to bid farewell,
Emperor Wén ordered the monk to be carried in the rear carriage,
saying to Fū:
"You can converse on the way."
Fū did not obey the edict,
and the emperor was very displeased.
He was promoted to Zhèngyuán Zhōngshū Láng.
Fū's childhood name was Chá (medlar),
and his father Shào's childhood name was Lí (pear).
Emperor Wén playfully asked him:
"How does chá compare to lí?"
Fū replied:
"The pear is the patriarch of all fruits;
how can the medlar compare?"
Zhōngshū Shèrén Qiū Dāng and Zhōu Jiū both managed important affairs.
[一０]Knowing that Fū was from a prominent family in the same ministry,
they wanted to visit him.
Jiū said:
"He might not be amenable to receiving us;
it's better not to go."
Dāng said:
"We are both Yuánwài Lángs;
why worry about not being able to sit together?"
Fū had already set up two couches,
three or four chǐ from the wall.
When the two guests took their seats,
Fū called to his attendants, saying:
"Move my distant guests!"
Jiū and the others lost color and left.
Such was his self-regard.
He was good at maintaining his demeanor,
fully achieving an unhurried grace.
When bidding farewell to people,
he would hold their hand and say:
"Remember to keep in touch."
His lingering voice would not cease for a long time.
Later generations of the Zhāng clan all emulated him;
its origin stemmed from Fū.
He was promoted to Huángmén Shìláng and then Hòujiāngjūn Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ for Liú Jùn, Prince of Shǐxīng.
Before he was formally appointed,
his father died in Wúxīng.
He wore mourning clothes for over ten days,
only then consuming water and gruel.
After the burial,
he refused to eat salt or vegetables,
and consequently became emaciated and fell ill.
His paternal uncle, Zhāng Màodù, repeatedly tried to persuade him to stop,
but Fū became even more agitated and grieved,
fainting and then reviving.
Màodù said:
"I try to stop you,
but you only get worse."
After this, he stopped visiting.
He died within a year.
[一一]When Emperor Xiàowǔ ascended the throne,
he honored his filial piety,
posthumously granted him the title of Shìzhōng,
and renamed the area where he lived to Xiàozhāng Lǐ.
Fū's younger brother, Zhāng Jiǎn,
inherited his father's fief,
and held the position of Tōngzhí Láng.
Jiǎn was courageous and strong,
able to fight fierce beasts barehanded.
The Arch-rebel (Liú Shào) appointed him Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ reached Xīntíng,
Jiǎn fled,
fell into the Huái River, and died.
His son Zhāng Shì succeeded him.
Zhāng Chàng, courtesy name Shǎowēi,
was the son of Shào's elder brother, Zhāng Wěi.
Wěi was principled in his youth
and served as Lángzhōnglìng for the Principality of Lángyá in the Jìn dynasty.
He followed the Prince to Luòyáng,
and when he returned to the capital,
Emperor Wǔ sealed a jar of medicated wine and gave it to Wěi,
ordering him to secretly add zhèn poison.
He received the order and drank it himself on the road, dying.
Chàng was renowned in his youth, alongside his cousins Fū, Yǎn, and Jìng,
as an outstanding talent of the younger generation.
He began his career as Zhǔbù for Administrator Xú Pèizhī.
When Pèizhī was executed,
Chàng rushed to attend his funeral,
wearing mourning clothes and expressing his deepest sorrow.
Contemporaries praised him for this.
His younger brother Zhāng Méi was once bitten by a rabid dog.
The doctor said eating shrimp could cure it,
but Méi found it difficult.
Chàng, with a smile, tasted it first,
and Méi then ate it,
and thus recovered.
He was successively promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
When Xiàowǔ 孝武 garrisoned Péngchéng 彭城,
Chàng 暢 was appointed Anběi Zhǎngshǐ 安北長史 and Pèijùn Tàishǒu 沛郡太守.
In the 27th year of Yuánjiā 元嘉 (450 CE),
the Wèi 魏 ruler Tuòbá Tàodào 托跋燾 marched south.
Tàiwèi 太尉, the Prince of Jiāngxià 江夏, Yìgōng 義恭, commanded all the armies and went to garrison Péngchéng 彭城.
The barbarian forces were dozens of *lǐ* 里 from the city.
Although Péngchéng's 彭城's forces were numerous,
military provisions were insufficient.
Yìgōng 義恭 wished to abandon Péngchéng 彭城 and return south,
but deliberations continued for a full day without a decision.
At that time, Lìchéng 歷城 had few troops but ample provisions.
Anběi Zhōngbīng Cānjūn 安北中兵參軍 Shěn Qìngzhī 沈慶之 proposed forming a wagon camp into a box-like array,
with elite troops forming outer wings,
to escort the two princes and their consorts directly to Lìchéng 歷城.
The city troops would be divided and assigned to Hùjūn Jiàngjūn 護軍將軍 Xiāo Sīhuà 蕭思話 to remain and guard the city.
Tàiwèi Zhǎngshǐ 太尉長史 Hé Xù 何勗 disagreed,
wishing to sweep everything up and flee to Yùzhōu 鬱洲,
and return to the capital by sea.
With the two proposals undecided,
a meeting of all officials was convened again to discuss them.
Chàng 暢 said:
"If Lìchéng 歷城 and Yùzhōu 鬱洲 were reachable,
your humble servant would not dare not praise them highly.
Now, with provisions scarce inside the city,
people have no firm resolve.
It is only because the gates are strict and secure
that they cannot flee.
If there is any disturbance,
they will scatter in disorder,
and even if they wished to reach their destination,
how could it be achieved?
Though provisions are currently few,
we are not yet in dire straits day to day.
How can we abandon a perfectly safe method
and immediately pursue a path of danger and destruction?
If this plan must be implemented,
your humble servant requests to stain your horse's tracks with my neck's blood!"
Xiàowǔ 孝武 heard Chàng's 暢's counsel
and said to Yìgōng 義恭:
"Zhāng Zhǎngshǐ's 張長史's words
cannot be ignored."
Yìgōng 義恭 then stopped.
When the Wèi 魏 ruler arrived,
he ascended the tomb of Yàfù 亞父 south of the city,
and erected a felt tent on the Xìmǎtái 戲馬臺.
Earlier,
Duìzhǔ 隊主 Kuǎi Yìng 蒯應 had been captured.
That afternoon,
he was sent to Xiǎoshìmén 小市門 to convey a message requesting sugarcane and wine.
Xiàowǔ 孝武 sent two vessels of wine
and one hundred stalks of sugarcane.
He also requested camels.
The next day,
the Wèi 魏 ruler again personally ascended Xìmǎtái 戲馬臺,
and again sent an envoy to Xiǎoshìmén 小市門,
requesting to meet Xiàowǔ 孝武.
He sent camels,
along with various other items,
instructing that they be received at the South Gate.
Chàng 暢 conversed with Wèi Shàngshū 魏尚書 Lǐ Xiàobó 李孝伯 from atop the city wall.
Xiàobó 孝伯 asked:
"What is your surname?"
He replied:
"My surname is Zhāng 張."
Xiàobó 孝伯 said:
"Is it Zhāng Zhǎngshǐ 張長史?"
Chàng 暢 said:
"How do you know me?"
Xiàobó 孝伯 said:
"Your reputation is widely known,
enough for me to know."
There was a man named Jù Sī 具思 in the city,
who had once been in Wèi 魏.
Yìgōng 義恭 sent him to observe,
and he identified him as Xiàobó 孝伯.
So they opened the gate and presented gifts.
The Wèi 魏 ruler again requested wine and sweet tangerines.
Xiàowǔ 孝武 again sent shell cups and various other items,
treasures of the southern land.
The Wèi 魏 ruler again had Xiàobó 孝伯 convey a message saying:
"The Wèi 魏 ruler has issued an imperial edict to borrow gaming boards."
Chàng 暢 said:
"The gaming boards will be sent,
but the words 'imperial edict'
can only be applied in your country,
how can they be applied here?"
Xiàobó 孝伯 said:
"It is as a minister of a neighboring country."
Xiàobó 孝伯 also said:
"Tàiwèi 太尉 and Zhènjūn 鎮軍
have long lacked communication from the south,
and must be quite worried.
If you send a messenger,
we will escort him."
Chàng 暢 said:
"There are many roads in between here,
and there is no need to trouble Wèi 魏."
Xiàobó 孝伯 said:
"I also know there is a waterway,
which seems to be cut off by the White Bandits."
Chàng 暢 said:
"You wear white clothing,
hence you are called White Bandits."
Xiàobó 孝伯 smiled and said:
"Today's White Bandits
are no different from the Yellow Turbans or Red Eyebrows,
only they are not in Jiāngnán 江南."
He again requested gaming boards,
which were sent shortly after.
The Wèi 魏 ruler again sent felt and nine types of salt, along with foreign fermented beans,
saying:
"These salts
each have their specific uses.
White salt is eaten by the Wèi 魏 ruler.
〔一二〕The black one cures abdominal bloating and gas,
scrape off six *zhū* 銖 and take it with wine.
Foreign salt cures eye pain.
Soft salt is not for eating,
it cures sores on horses' backs.
Red salt, mottled salt, smelly salt, and horse-tooth salt, these four types,
are not suitable for eating.
Foreign fermented beans are also good to eat."
He also requested yellow tangerines,
and said:
"The Wèi 魏 ruler sends his regards to Tàiwèi 太尉 and Anběi 安北,
why do you not send someone to inquire,
observe my appearance,
and discern my character?"
Chàng 暢 again conveyed a reply saying:
"The Wèi 魏 ruler's physique and abilities
have long been seen by those coming and going.
As Li Shàngshū 李尚書 personally conveys the message,
there is no concern that either side will be incomplete,
〔一三〕hence no further envoy is sent."
He also said:
"The Wèi 魏 ruler regrets that the horses sent earlier were not quite satisfactory.
If Anběi 安北 needs large horses,
I shall send them.
If by chance you need Shu 蜀 horses,
there are also good ones."
Chàng 暢 said:
"Anběi 安北 is not short of fine steeds.
Sending them is your intention,
this is not what is requested here."
Yìgōng 義恭 again sent ten bundles of torches and candles,
and Xiàowǔ 孝武 also sent one bolt of brocade.
He also said:
"I know you need more yellow tangerines.
If they are for your army,
then there will not be enough;
if they are for the Wèi 魏 ruler,
they will not be insufficient,
therefore I will not send them again."
Xiàobó 孝伯 again said:
"You, a fine gentleman from the southern land,
why are you wearing straw sandals?
If you are like this,
what about the generals and soldiers?"
Chàng 暢 said:
"Your words about 'fine gentleman'
indeed make me feel ashamed.
It is only because I am not a military man
that I received orders to command the army.
In the midst of military arrays,
casual attire is not permissible."
The Wèi 魏 ruler again sent to borrow *kōnghóu* 箜篌, *pípá* 琵琶, and other instruments and their players from the two princes.
Xiàobó 孝伯 was articulate and eloquent,
also a talent from the northern land.
Chàng 暢 responded appropriately,
very quick-witted.
His pronunciation was refined and elegant,
and the Wèi 魏 people admired it.
At that time, the Wèi 魏 rumor was that they would march out towards Xiāngyáng 襄陽,
so Chàng 暢 was appointed Nánqiāo Wáng Yìxuān Sīkōng Zhǎngshǐ 南譙王義宣司空長史 and Nánjùn Tàishǒu 南郡太守.
When the prime culprit committed regicide,
Yìxuān 義宣 raised an army
on the very day he expressed his grief.
Chàng 暢 was his prime assistant.
After expressing grief,
he changed his clothes to a yellow *kùzhé* 袴褶,
went out to the archery hall to select men.
His voice, demeanor, and deportment
all attracted people's attention,
and all who saw him were willing to die for him.
After the matter was settled,
he was summoned to be Lìbù Shàngshū 吏部尚書,
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yídào Xiàn 夷道縣.
When Yìxuān 義宣 had other ambitions,
Cài Chāo 蔡超 and others, seeing that Chàng 暢 commanded popular support,
persuaded Yìxuān 義宣 to keep him.
So, he relinquished the position of Nánmán Xiàowèi 南蠻校尉 and bestowed it upon Chàng 暢,
adding the title of Guànjūn Jiāngjūn 冠軍將軍,
and appointing him as Chéngxiàng Zhǎngshǐ 丞相長史.
Chàng 暢 dispatched his disciple Xún Sēngbǎo 荀僧寶 to the capital,
〔一四〕who then, through Yán Jùn 顏竣, presented Yìxuān's 義宣's transgressions.
Sēngbǎo 僧寶 had private goods,
and stopped at Bālíng 巴陵, not arriving in time.
At that time, Yìxuān 義宣 raised an army,
the ferry routes were cut off,
so he could not proceed.
When Yìxuān 義宣 was about to rebel,
he sent his favorite, Zhái Língbǎo 翟靈寶, to inform Chàng 暢.
Chàng 暢 stated that such a thing was absolutely impossible,
and requested to guarantee it with his life.
Língbǎo 靈寶 returned and reported to Yìxuān 義宣,
saying that Chàng 暢 could not be won over,
and requested to kill him to set an example for the masses.
Fortunately, Chéngxiàng Sīmǎ 丞相司馬 Zhú Chāomín 竺超民 saved him from this fate.
He was promoted to Fǔjūn 撫軍,
and a separate military department was established
to garner popular support.
Although Chàng 暢 signed official documents and proclamations,
he was often drunk,
and did not attend to affairs.
When Yìxuān 義宣 was defeated at Liángshān 梁山,
Chàng 暢 was plundered by soldiers,
losing all his clothes.
He met Yòujiāngjūn 右將軍 Wáng Xuánmó 王玄謨 riding out of the camp in his carriage.
Chàng 暢 had already acquired some tattered clothes,
and immediately pushed Xuánmó 玄謨 to get into the carriage,
which displeased Xuánmó 玄謨 greatly.
The various generals requested to kill him,
but Duìzhǎng 隊長 Zhāng Shì 張世 saved him.
〔一五〕He was arrested and sent to the capital,
handed over to the Tíngwèi 廷尉,
and was pardoned.
He was reinstated as Dūguān Shàngshū 都官尚書,
then transferred to Shìzhōng 侍中.
Xiàowǔ 孝武 hosted a banquet for the court officials,
and Chàng 暢 was also present.
Hé Yǎn 何偃, being drunk, said:
“Zhāng Chàng 張暢 is indeed a remarkable talent.
He conspired with Yìxuān 義宣 as a rebel,
yet ultimately suffered no harm.
If not for such remarkable talent,
how could he have achieved this!”
Chàng 暢 replied:
“In the Tàichū 太初 era,
who painted his chamber yellow?”
The emperor said:
“Why trouble each other?”
Initially,
Shàngzhī 尚之, as the Yuánxiōng Sīkōng 元凶司空,
when the loyal army reached Xīnlín Mén 新林門,
everyone fled,
but Shàngzhī 尚之 and his son together painted the yellow chamber.
Therefore, Chàng 暢 used this to mock him.
In the second year of Xiàojiàn 孝建,
he was sent out as Huìjī Tàishǒu 會稽太守,
and died.
His posthumous name was Xuān 宣.
Chàng 暢 loved his disciple Jí 輯,
〔一六〕and in his dying testament, he instructed to be buried in the same tomb as Jí 輯.
Public opinion at the time disapproved of this.
His younger brother Yuè 悅 also had a good reputation,
serving successively as Shìzhōng 侍中, Línhǎi Wáng Zǐxù Qiánjiāngjūn Zhǎngshǐ 臨海王子頊前將軍長史, and Nánjùn Tàishǒu 南郡太守.
When Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn 晉安王子勛 established his pseudo-regime,
he was summoned and appointed as Lìbù Shàngshū 吏部尚書,
and together with Dèng Wǎn 鄧琬, they assisted the false government.
When the plot failed,
Yuè 悅 killed Wǎn 琬 and surrendered,
and was reinstated as Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ 太子中庶子.
Later, he was appointed Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ 雍州刺史.
In the sixth year of Tàishǐ 泰始,
Míngdì 明帝 established the Sānbā Xiàowèi 三巴校尉 in Bājùn 巴郡,
and appointed Yuè 悅 to this position,
adding the titles of Chíjié 持節 and Fǔshī Jiāngjūn 輔師將軍,
and concurrently Bājùn Tàishǒu 巴郡太守.
He died
before taking office.
Chàng's 暢 son Hào 浩,
reached the office of Yìyáng Wáng Chǎng Zhēngběi Zīyì Cānjūn 義陽王昶征北諮議參軍.
Hào's 浩 younger brother Yān 淹,
was Huángmén Láng 黃門郎,
ennobled as Guǎngjìn Xiànzǐ 廣晉縣子,
Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ 太子左衞率,
and Dōngyáng Tàishǒu 東陽太守.
He forced county officials to burn their arms to illuminate Buddhas,
and when common people committed crimes,
he made them worship Buddhas to atone for their punishments,
often requiring thousands of prostrations.
He was dismissed from office and banned from public service.
He was reinstated as Guānglùxūn 光祿勳,
and rebelled together with Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn 晉安王子勛.
When the army was defeated,
he was killed.
(Your ministers Mù 穆 and others note that in Gāo Shì Xiǎoshǐ 高氏小史,
there is a biography of Dào Yànzhī 到彥之 after the biography of Zhào Lúnzhī 趙倫之,
but this book is uniquely missing it.
According to the historical methods of Yuēzhī 約之,
emperors are referred to by their temple names,
and Wèi 魏 is called "the barbarians."
Now, emperors are referred to by their reign names,
and Wèi 魏 is called Wèizhǔ 魏主,
which is consistent with the style of Nánshǐ 南史.
However, there is no historical minister's comment at the end of the biography,
which makes us suspect it is not a book by Yuēzhī 約之.
Nevertheless, its wording differs slightly from Nánshǐ 南史,
so we have specially preserved it.)
Collated Notes
Biography VII: Liú Huáisù 劉懷肅, Mèng Huáiyù 孟懷玉 (younger brother Lóngfú 龍符), Liú Jìngxúān 劉敬宣, Tán Zhī 檀祗.
Liú Huáisù 劉懷肅,
a native of Péngchéng 彭城,
was the maternal cousin of Gāozǔ 高祖.
His family was impoverished for generations,
but he personally tilled the land and loved learning.
Initially, he served as Níngshuò Fǔ Sīmǎ 寧朔府司馬 under Liú Jìngxúān 劉敬宣.
During the eastern campaign against Sūn Ēn 孫恩,
he achieved military merit,
and later became Lóngxiáng Sīmǎ 龍驤司馬 and Fèi Lìng 費令.
Hearing of Gāozǔ's 高祖 uprising,
he abandoned his county and came to join.
After the capital was pacified,
Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn 振武將軍 Dàoguī 道規 pursued Huán Xuán 桓玄,
appointing Huáisù 懷肅 as Sīmǎ 司馬.
Xuán 桓 left Hé Dànzhī 何澹之, Guō Quán 郭銓 and others to guard Sāngluòzhōu 桑落洲.
They advanced and defeated them.
Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu 潁川太守 Liú Tǒngpíng 劉統平,
was appointed Gāopíng Tàishǒu 高平太守.
After Xuán 桓 died,
his nephew Zhèn 振 severely defeated the righteous army at Yánglín 楊林,
and the righteous army retreated to Xúnyáng 尋陽.
Huáisù 懷肅 and Jiāngxià Xiāng 江夏相 Zhāng Chàngzhī 張暢之 attacked Dànzhī 何澹之 at Xīsài 西塞,
and defeated him.
The pseudo-Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn 鎮東將軍 Féng Gāi 馮該 garrisoned the east bank of Xiàkǒu 夏口,
Mèng Shāntú 孟山圖 occupied Lǔshān Chéng 魯山城,
and Huán Xiānkè 桓仙客 guarded Yǎnyuè Lěi 偃月壘;
all were connected walls facing each other.
Huáisù 懷肅 and Dàoguī 道規 attacked them.
He personally donned his armor and helmet,
and stormed two cities.
Féng Gāi 馮該 fled to Shíchéng 石城,
and Xiānkè 仙客 was captured alive.
In the first month of the first year of Yìxī 義熙,
Zhèn 振 was defeated and fled.
Dàoguī 道規 sent Huáisù 懷肅 to pacify Shíchéng 石城,
and he beheaded Féng Gāi 馮該 and his son Shānjìng 山靖.
In the third month,
Huán Zhèn 桓振 again attacked Jiānglíng 江陵,
and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ 荊州刺史 Sīmǎ Xiūzhī 司馬休之 fled.
Huáisù 懷肅 hurried from Yúndù 雲杜,
traveling day and night,
arriving in seven days.
Zhèn 振 commanded thirty thousand troops,
their banners covering the fields,
and he personally charged into the array, spurring his horse and wielding his spear across.
A stray arrow wounded Huáisù's 懷肅 forehead.
The troops were fearful and wanted to flee,
but Huáisù 懷肅 glared and fought fiercely,
which boosted the morale of the soldiers.
Thus, the soldiers vied to be first,
and Zhèn's 振 head was cut off in battle.
After Jiānglíng 江陵 was pacified,
Xiūzhī 司馬休之 returned to his post,
and holding Huáisù's 懷肅 hand, said:
“Without your strength,
I would have nowhere to return.”
The pseudo-Fǔguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍 Fú Sì 符嗣, Mǎ Sūn 馬孫, and pseudo-Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn 龍驤將軍 Jīn Fúqīng 金符青, Lè Zhì 樂志 and others gathered in Jiāngxià 江夏.
Huáisù 懷肅 again campaigned against them,
and beheaded Lè Zhì 樂志 and others.
Dàoguī 道規 added the title of Dū Jiāngxià Jiǔjùn 督江夏九郡 to Huáisù 懷肅,
and he temporarily governed Xiàkǒu 夏口.
He was appointed Tōngzhí Láng 通直郎,
and continued to serve as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍 and Huáinán Lìyáng Èrjùn Tàishǒu 淮南歷陽二郡太守.
In the second year,
he also concurrently served as Liú Yì Fǔjūn Sīmǎ 劉毅撫軍司馬,
his military and administrative posts remaining unchanged.
For his meritorious service, he was enfeoffed as Dōngxīng Xiànhóu 東興縣侯,
with a stipend of a thousand households.
In that winter,
Huán Shísuí 桓石綏, Sīmǎ Guóyù 司馬國璠, and Chén Xí 陳襲 gathered a mob at Hútáo Shān 胡桃山 to become bandits.
Huáisù 懷肅 led infantry and cavalry to suppress and defeat them.
When various barbarian tribes between Jiāng 江 and Huái 淮 rivers and remnants of the Huán 桓 clan caused disturbances,
he volunteered to lead an expedition.
However, once he set out, he deviated from orders.
Yì 毅 submitted a memorial requesting Huáisù's 懷肅 dismissal.
In the third year,
he died,
at the age of forty-one.
He was posthumously granted Zuǒ Jiāngjūn 左將軍.
Having no sons,
his younger brother Huáishèn 懷慎's son Wèizǔ 蔚祖 succeeded to the title,
and reached the office of Jiāngxià Nèishǐ 江夏內史.
Wèi Zǔ 蔚祖 died.
His son, Dào Cún 道存, succeeded him.
At the end of Tàizǔ's 太祖 Yuánjiā 元嘉 reign,
he served as Cān Jūn 參軍 (Counselor) to the Tàiwèi 太尉 (Grand Commandant) Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng 江夏王義恭.
When Shìzǔ 世祖 attacked the arch-villain (Yuán Xiōng 元凶),
the righteous army reached Xīntíng 新亭.
Dào Cún 道存 fled,
and Yuán Xiōng 元凶 killed his mother to display her head.
During the Jǐnghé 景和 reign of the former deposed emperor (Qián Fèidì 前廢帝),
he served as Cóngshì Zhōngláng 從事中郎 (Acting Central Clerk) to Yìgōng 義恭, who was Tàizǎi 太宰 (Grand Tutor).
When Yìgōng 義恭 was defeated,
he was imprisoned and died for being a partisan.
Huáisù's 懷肅 next younger brother was Huáijìng 懷敬,
who was slow, dull, and untalented.
Initially,
when Gāozǔ 高祖 was born, his imperial mother (Huáng Bǐ 皇妣) passed away.
The filial emperor (Xiào Huángdì 孝皇帝) was poor,
with no means of acquiring a wet nurse,
and considered not raising Gāozǔ 高祖.
Gāozǔ's 高祖 maternal aunt gave birth to Huáijìng 懷敬.
Before a full year had passed,
she stopped breastfeeding Huáijìng 懷敬
and personally nursed Gāozǔ 高祖.
Because of this old favor, Gāozǔ 高祖
repeatedly bestowed favors and appointments upon Huáijìng 懷敬,
who rose to be Huìjī Tàishǒu 會稽太守 (Administrator of Huìjī Commandery),
Shàngshū 尚書 (Minister of the Imperial Secretariat),
and Jīn Zǐ Guānglù Dàfū 金紫光祿大夫 (Grand Master of the Golden and Purple Light).
Huáijìng's 懷敬 son, Zhēndào 真道,
was Qiantang Lìng 錢唐令 (Magistrate of Qiantang County).
In the thirteenth year of Yuánjiā 元嘉 (436 CE),
the eastern land suffered from famine.
The emperor sent Yángzhōu Zhìzhōng Cóngshì Shǐ Shěn Yǎnzhī 揚州治中從事史沈演之 (Administrator of Yang Province and Censor) to inspect the affected areas.
Yǎnzhī 演之 submitted a memorial stating:
"When administering a county,
one must rely on simplicity and benevolence to achieve competence.
When taking office and promoting governance,
one must strive to benefit the people and achieve results.
Thus, Wáng Huàn 王奐 was recorded in the past,
and Shū Qīng 叔卿 is praised in later times.
I humbly observe that Liú Zhēndào 劉真道, the Magistrate of Qiantang, and Liú Dàoxī 劉道錫, the Magistrate of Yúháng,
both uphold public duty and show compassion for the people,
working diligently without slackness.
The common people praise them,
and lawsuits are few and simple.
They also suppressed villains and wrongdoers,
repeatedly capturing them.
At the beginning of the flood disaster,
the high dike in Yúháng collapsed,
and the torrent was swift and fierce,
its force immeasurable.
Dàoxī 道錫 personally led officials and commoners,
and personally supervised the building of defenses.
Once the dike was re-established,
the county and city were saved.
Having visited various counties
and investigated their reputation and reality,
these two are the foremost in the two regions,
excellent administrators of the people."
The emperor commended this
and bestowed a thousand *hú* 斛 of grain upon each.
Zhēndào 真道 was appointed Bùbīng Xiàowèi 步兵校尉 (Colonel of Infantry).
In the fourteenth year (437 CE),
he was appointed Cìshǐ 刺史 (Governor) of Liáng and Nán Qín 梁南秦 two provinces.
In the eighteenth year (441 CE),
the Dī 氐 bandit Yáng Nándāng 楊難當 invaded Hànzhōng 漢中.
Zhēndào 真道 led his army and defeated him.
However, Nándāng's 難當 banditry did not cease.
Tàizǔ 太祖 dispatched Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Péi Fāngmíng 龍驤將軍裴方明 with five thousand imperial guards,
to be commanded by Zhēndào 真道.
In the nineteenth year (442 CE),
Fāngmíng 方明 arrived at Wǔxìng 武興.

He led Tàizǐ Jīnǔ Jiāngjūn Liú Kāngzǔ 太子積弩將軍劉康祖, Hòujūn Cānjūn Liáng Tǎn 後軍參軍梁坦, Chén Mí 陳彌, Péi Sùzhī 裴肅之, Ānxī Cānjūn Duàn Shúwén 安西參軍段叔文, Lǔ Shàngqī 魯尚期, Shǐxīng Wángguó Chángshì Liú Sēngxiù 始興王國常侍劉僧秀, Suīyuǎn Jiāngjūn Mǎ Xǐ 綏遠將軍馬洗, Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn Wáng Huànzhī 振武將軍王奐之, and others,
and advanced to Tángǔ 潭谷,
a few *lǐ* 里 from Lán'gāo 蘭臯.
Nándāng 難當 sent his Jiànjié Jiāngjūn Fú Hóngzǔ 建節將軍苻弘祖 and Dàn Yuán 啖元 to hold Lán'gāo 蘭臯,
while Zhènběi Jiāngjūn Fú Déyì 鎮北將軍苻德義 acted as a mobile force outside,
and Nándāng's 難當 son, Fǔjūn Dàjiāngjūn Hé 撫軍大將軍和, with heavy troops, followed behind.
Fāngmíng 方明 attacked,
greatly defeating them at Zhuóshuǐ 濁水,
beheading Hóngzǔ 弘祖 and over three thousand others.
He sent Kāngzǔ 康祖 to pursue them,
over two thousand *lǐ* 里 past Lán'gāo 蘭臯.
Hé 和 again sent Déyì 德義 to assist in the battle.
Kāngzǔ 康zǔ again greatly defeated them,
and Hé 和 retreated to guard Xiūchéng 脩城.
Nándāng 難當 sent Jiànzhōng Jiāngjūn Yáng Lín 建忠將軍楊林 and Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn Yáo Xiàn 振威將軍姚憲 with two thousand cavalry to join Hé 和.
Fāngmíng 方明 again led his generals to attack them.
Hé 和 was defeated and fled.
They were pursued to Chìtíng 赤亭,
and Nándāng 難當 packed up and rebelled, fleeing.
Fāngmíng 方明 sent Kāngzǔ 康祖 directly to Bǎiqǐng 百頃.
The self-proclaimed Chancellor, Yáng Wànshòu 楊萬壽, and others immediately surrendered.
Nándāng's 難當 third son Hǔxiān 虎先 garrisoned Yīnpíng 陰平.
After Nándāng 難當 fled,
Hǔxiān 虎先 went into hiding among the people.
He was captured alive
and sent to the capital (Jīngdū 京都),
where he was executed in Jiànkāng 建康 market.
Qínzhōu Cìshǐ Hú Chóngzhī 秦州刺史胡崇之 was stationed in the west at Bǎiqǐng 百頃.
When he reached Zhuóshuǐ 濁水,
he was ambushed by the Suǒ Lǔ 索虜 (Tuoba barbarians)
and was defeated and killed.
Zhēndào 真道 was appointed Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn 建威將軍 (General Establishing Awe) and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ 雍州刺史 (Governor of Yong Province).
Fāngmíng 方明 was appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍 (General Assisting the State) and Cìshǐ 刺史 (Governor) of Liáng and Nán Qín 梁南秦 two provinces.
Fāngmíng 方明 declined the appointment.
An imperial edict stated:
"Last year, the Dī 氐 rogue Yáng Nándāng 楊難當 instigated rebellion,
and many bowed their heads (in submission).
His Chángshǐ 長史 (Chief Clerk) Yáng Wànshòu 楊萬壽 and Jiànjié Jiāngjūn Yáo Xiàn 建節將軍姚憲
did not defy the proper order of things and
repeatedly offered candid advice.
When the villainous horde fled by night,
the entire region collapsed in chaos.
Jiànzhōng Jiāngjūn Lǚ Xùn 建忠將軍呂訓 guarded the granaries awaiting the royal army.
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Jiāng Tán 寧朔將軍姜檀 was brave, resolute, and sincere,
devoted to exerting his strength.
In the victory at Zhuóshuǐ 濁水,
his merit was evident.
Recently, he assisted with righteous fervor,
and his loyalty has not faltered.
Fú Zhāo 苻昭 of Luèyáng 略陽
was truly loyal to the imperial court
and likewise participated in this endeavor,
capturing the pseudo-general
and singly overcoming Wǔxìng 武興,
displaying his prowess and achieving results,
even losing his life to the enemy.
Their deeds are recorded in times of difficulty and danger,
moving my heart.
They should be honored
and their living and deceased relieved.
Wànshòu 萬壽 is hereby posthumously granted Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn 龍驤將軍 (Dragon Gallop General)
and Zhāowǔ Dū Tàishǒu 昭武都太守 (Grand Administrator of Zhaowu Commandery).
Xiàn 憲 is appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng 員外散騎侍郎 (Supernumerary Palace Attendant).
Xùn 訓 is appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi 駙馬都尉 (Equerry) and Fèng Cháoqǐng 奉朝請 (Attendant at Court).
Tán 檀 is appointed Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn Sīmǎ 征西大將軍司馬 (Military Advisor to the Generalissimo Who Conquers the West) and Qiúchí Tàishǒu 仇池太守 (Grand Administrator of Qiúchí).
All should be resettled within the interior.
Yōng 雍 and Liáng 梁 two provinces are commanded
to provide generous support and relief."
Lǚ Xùn 呂訓 was
Lǚ Xiānzǐ's 呂先子, a Dī 氐 man from Luèyáng 略陽.
Another imperial edict stated:
"The late Jìnshòu Tàishǒu Jiāng Dàoshèng 晉壽太守姜道盛,
when he previously attacked Qiúchí 仇池,
devoted his sincerity and strength.
In military service, he showed effectiveness,
and when faced with wealth, he remained incorruptible.
Recently, he was among the first to attack at Zhuóshuǐ 濁水,
losing his life to weapons.
His sincerity and integrity both shone brightly,
and I feel pity and sorrow in my heart.
He is hereby posthumously granted Jǐshìzhōng 給事中 (Gentleman-in-Waiting)
and bestowed a hundred thousand *qián* 錢 (cash)."
Dàoshèng 道盛 annotated the ancient text of the *Shàngshū* 尚書,
which circulated in his time.
Zhēndào 真道 and Fāngmíng 方明 were both imprisoned for plundering Qiúchí 仇池,
dividing gold, silver, and various other treasures,
and also hiding Nándāng's 難當 good horses,
and died in prison.
Liú Kāngzǔ 劉康祖 and others were given varying degrees of leniency.
Fāngmíng 方明
was from Hédōng 河東.
He served as Liú Dàojì's 劉道濟 Zhènwǔ Zhōngbīng Cānjūn 振武中兵參軍 (Military Advisor of the Central Army under the General Establishing Might).
He achieved merit in Shǔtǔ 蜀土
and successively served as Yǐngchuān Nán Píngchāng Tàishǒu 潁川南平昌太守 (Administrator of Yingchuan and Nan Pingchang Commanderies).
All were dismissed from office due to corruption.
Mèng Huáiyù 孟懷玉
was from Ānqīu 安丘, Píngchāng 平昌.
His great-grandfather, Héng 珩,
was Jìn Hénán Yǐn 晉河南尹 (Administrator of Henan under the Jin Dynasty).
His grandfather, Yuān 淵,
was Yòu Guānglù Dàfū 右光祿大夫 (Right Grand Master of the Palace).
His father, Chuò 綽,
after the Righteous Banner (Yì Qí 義旗), served as Jǐshìzhōng 給事中 (Gentleman-in-Waiting)
and Guānglù Xūn 光祿勳 (Superintendent of the Imperial Household),
and was posthumously granted Jīn Zǐ Guānglù Dàfū 金紫光祿大夫 (Grand Master of the Golden and Purple Light).
His family resided in Jīngkǒu 京口 for generations.
When Gāozǔ 高祖 marched east against Sūn Ēn 孫恩,
he appointed Huáiyù 懷玉 as Jiànwǔ Sīmǎ 建武司馬 (Military Advisor to the General Establishing Might).
He participated in the Righteous Banner (Yì Qí 義旗)
and followed in the pacification of Jīngchéng 京城,
then advanced to pacify Jīngyì 京邑.
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as Pányáng Xiàn Hóu 鄱陽縣侯 (Marquis of Panyang County),
with an estate of a thousand households.
When Gāozǔ 高祖 was stationed at Jīngkǒu 京口,
he appointed Huáiyù 懷玉 as Zhèn Jūn Cānjūn 鎮軍參軍 (Military Advisor to the General Guarding the Army) and Xiàpéi Tàishǒu 下邳太守 (Administrator of Xiapi Commandery).
In the third year of Yìxī 義熙 (407 CE),
he was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn 寧朔將軍 (General Who Pacifies the North), Xīyáng Tàishǒu 西陽太守 (Administrator of Xiyang Commandery), and Xīncài Nèishǐ 新蔡內史 (Internal Historian of Xincai).
He was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng 中書侍郎 (Gentleman of the Central Secretariat),
then transferred to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍 (General Assisting the State),
commanding the Dānyáng Fǔ Bīng 丹陽府兵 (Danyang Provincial Army),
and garrisoning Shítou 石頭.
Méng Huáiyù (孟懷玉) pressed the capital,
and Huáiyù (懷玉) repeatedly fought with merit along the bank of Shítóu (石頭),
becoming the Zhōngjūn Cányì Cānjūn (中軍諮議參軍).
The rebel leader Xú Dàofù (徐道覆) frequently wished to land his elite troops,
but feared Huáiyù (懷玉) and dared not go ashore.
When Lú Xún (盧循) fled south,
Huáiyù (懷玉) and the various armies pursued him,
reaching as far as Lǐngbiǎo (嶺表).
Xú Dàofù (徐道覆) encamped at Shǐxīng (始興),
and Huáiyù (懷玉) besieged him.
He personally faced arrows and stones,
and it took ten days to a month to breach the defenses.
He then continued south to pursue Lú Xún (盧循).
After Lú Xún (盧循) was pacified,
he was again enfeoffed as Yángfēng Xiàn Nán (陽豐縣男),
with a stipend of two hundred and fifty households.
He again served as Tàiwèi Cányì Cānjūn (太尉諮議參軍),
and Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (征虜將軍).
In the eighth year,
he was transferred to Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (江州刺史),

and soon after supervised the military affairs of Xīyáng (西陽), Xīncài (新蔡), Rǔnán (汝南), Yǐngchuān (潁川) in Jiāngzhōu (江州) and Yùzhōu (豫州), and Nóng (農) in Sīzhōu (司州), and Sōngzī (松滋) in Yángzhōu (揚州), a total of six commanderies, and was appointed Nánzhōnglángjiāng (南中郎將),
with his position as Cìshǐ (刺史) remaining unchanged.
At that time, Sīmǎ Xiūzhī (司馬休之), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Jīngzhōu (荊州), was in the upper reaches of the river,
and harbored rebellious intentions,
so Huáiyù (懷玉) was given this post to guard against him.
In the eleventh year,
he was granted Jié (節).
Upon the death of his father,
Huáiyù (懷玉) had a filial nature,
and consequently suffered from a serious illness.
He submitted a memorial requesting to resign,
but it was not granted.
He again stated that his younger brother Xiānkè (仙客) had been adopted into another family,
and that he alone was the chief mourner.
Only then was he permitted to resign.
Before he could leave his post,
he died in office that year.
He was thirty-one years old at the time.
He was posthumously granted Píngnán Jiāngjūn (平南將軍).
His son Yuán (元) died
without a son,
and the peerage was abolished.
Huáiyù (懷玉) was separately enfeoffed as Yángfēng Nán (陽豐男).
His son Huìxī (慧熙) succeeded,
but was punished for neglecting ancestral sacrifices and had his peerage stripped.
Huìxī's (慧熙) son Zōng (宗) succeeded,
becoming Jìnglíng Tàishǒu (竟陵太守)
and Zhōng Dàfū (中大夫).
Méng Lóngfú (孟龍符)
was Huáiyù's (懷玉) younger brother.
He was brave and decisive, possessing great courage
and exceptional strength.
In his youth, he enjoyed chivalry
and gathered followers in his village.
He was known to Gāozǔ (高祖) early on.
After conquering the capital,
Lóngfú (龍符) was appointed Jiànwǔ Cānjūn (建武參軍).
In the three battles of Jiāngchéng (江乘), Luóluò (羅落), and Fùzhōu (覆舟),
he all had merits.
He participated in military affairs as Zhèn Jūn (鎮軍軍事),
was enfeoffed as a fifth-rank Zǐ (子) of Píngchāng Xiàn (平昌縣),
and was promoted to Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (寧遠將軍) and Huáilíng Tàishǒu (淮陵太守).
He and Liú Fān (劉藩) and Xiàng Mí (向彌) campaigned against Huán Xīn (桓歆) and Huán Shíkāng (桓石康),
defeating and beheading them.
He was appointed Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (建威將軍) and Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu (東海太守).
When the barbarian robbers Húlán (斛蘭) and Suǒ Duózhēn (索度真) invaded the border,
causing disturbances in Péng (彭) and Pèi (沛),
Gāozǔ (高祖) dispatched Lóngfú (龍符) and Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (建威將軍) Dàolián (道憐) to campaign north,
and they defeated them in one battle.
They pursued Húlán (斛蘭) to the edge of Guāngshuǐgōu (光水溝),
where he was wounded and fled.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) attacked Guǎnggù (廣固),
he appointed Lóngfú (龍符) as Chējì Cānjūn (車騎參軍),
promoted him to Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) and Guǎngchuān Tàishǒu (廣川太守),
to command infantry and cavalry as the vanguard.
The army reached Línqú (臨朐),
and competed with the enemy for water.
Lóngfú (龍符) charged alone on horseback,
breaking their ranks instantly.
He immediately secured the water source,
and the enemy then retreated.
Lóngfú (龍符) pursued them, taking advantage of the victory,
but his cavalry could not keep up.
Several thousand enemy cavalry surrounded and attacked him.
Lóngfú (龍符) fought fiercely with his spear,
killing several men in each encounter.
Outnumbered,
he was ultimately killed.
He was thirty-three years old at the time.
〔一０〕Gāozǔ (高祖) deeply grieved his loss,
and posthumously granted him Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ (青州刺史).
He also memorialized, saying:
"The late Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) and Guǎngchuān Tàishǒu (廣川太守) Méng Lóngfú (孟龍符),
loyal, brave, resolute,
and sacrificed his life for the state,
should fittingly receive commendation
to manifest his integrity.
His Majesty's compassionate grief
has graciously bestowed a provincial governorship.
Lóngfú (龍符) joined the righteous cause at its beginning,
serving as the vanguard,
pushing forward to victory three times,
always leading the troops.
When he cut down Huán Xīn (桓歆) in the west,
and annihilated the barbarian robbers in the north,
the court's deliberations on titles and rewards
had not yet been implemented.
Now, during this Northern Expedition,
he again led the vanguard.
In the battle of Línqú (臨朐),
his spirit surpassed all three armies.
At that time, the rebels were truly numerous,
with archers covering the marshes.
Lóngfú (龍符), on a single horse, galloped like lightning,
crushing all in his path.
He wielded his spear and plunged deep,
knowing death but not regretting it.
The robbers fled in panic,
gathering in the dangerous terrain like birds.
Our grand army, taking advantage of the situation,
advanced rapidly.
Considering his contributions and achievements,
he participated in the decisive actions.
I humbly believe he should be granted a noble title and land,
to honor his great merits."
He was then posthumously enfeoffed as Lín Yuán Xiàn Nán (臨沅縣男),
with a stipend of five hundred households.
He had no son,
so his younger brother Xiānkè (仙客)'s son Wēishēng (微生) succeeded to the peerage.
During the Yuánjiā (元嘉) reign of Tàizǔ (太祖),
Wēishēng (微生) was stripped of his peerage for an offense
and exiled to Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
Wēishēng's (微生) younger brother Yànzǔ's (彥祖) son Fóhù (佛護) then inherited the peerage.
When Qí (齊) received the abdication,
the peerage was abolished.
In the early Dàmíng (大明) reign of Xiàowǔ (孝武),
all exiles were permitted to return to their hometowns.
Wēishēng (微生) had already died,
and his son Xìzǔ (係祖) returned to the capital.
He possessed extraordinary strength and power,
capable of carrying several people.
He joined the Yǔlín (羽林) imperial guard,
becoming Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn (殿中將軍).
In the second year,
when the barbarian robbers attacked Qīng (青) and Jì (冀) provinces,
Shìzǔ (世祖) dispatched troops to aid them,
and Xìzǔ (係祖) volunteered to go.
During the battle at Dùliáng (杜梁),
he bravely charged into the enemy formation,
killing many,
and was subsequently killed.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him Yǐngchuān Jùn Tàishǒu (潁川郡太守).
Liú Jìngxuān (劉敬宣), courtesy name Wànshòu (萬壽),
was from Péngchéng (彭城),
a descendant of Jiāo (交), King Yuán (元) of Chǔ (楚) of the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
His grandfather Jiàn (建) was Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (征虜將軍).
His father Láozhī (牢之) was Zhènběi Jiāngjūn (鎮北將軍).
Jìngxuān (敬宣) lost his mother at the age of eight,
and wept day and night,
which astonished his maternal and paternal relatives.
Huán Xù (桓序), the Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍), was stationed in Wúhú (蕪湖),
and Láozhī (牢之) served as his military aide.
On the eighth day of the fourth month,
Jìngxuān (敬宣) saw everyone bathing the Buddha,
so he took off the golden mirror from his head to bathe it for his mother,
and was overcome with sorrow.
Huán Xù (桓序) sighed
and said to Láozhī (牢之):
"This son of yours, being a filial son to his family,
will surely be a loyal minister to the state."
He began his career as Wáng Gōng (王恭)'s Qiánjūn Cānjūn (前軍參軍),
and also served in military affairs for Huìjī (會稽) Crown Prince Yuánxiǎn (元顯)'s Zhēnglǔ Jūn (征虜軍).
In the second year of Lóng'ān [398 CE],
Wáng Gōng (王恭) raised an army at Jīngkǒu,
under the pretext of executing Sīmǎ Shàngzhī's (司馬尚之) brothers.
Láo Zhī (牢之) was then Gōng's (恭) Front Army Sīmǎ, General Fǔguó, and Administrator of Jìnlíng,
appointing his own officers and leading troops.
However, Gōng (恭), considering himself a prominent imperial relative,
treated Láo Zhī (牢之) with great condescension and contempt,
which Láo Zhī's (牢之) heart could not accept.
When Gōng (恭) made this move,
he made Láo Zhī (牢之) his vanguard.
The Grand Tutor, King Kuàijī Dàozǐ (會稽王道子), wrote a letter to Láo Zhī (牢之),
fully explaining the fortunes and misfortunes,
urging him to turn his army against Gōng (恭).
Láo Zhī (牢之) called Jìngxuān (敬宣) and said:
"Wáng Gōng (王恭) received extraordinary grace from the late emperor in the past,
and now holds the important position of an imperial uncle.
His righteous heart is not yet manifest;
he merely gives free rein to his military power.
I cannot be sure that when Gōng's (恭) enterprise succeeds,
he will certainly uphold the Son of Heaven
and bring peace and order to the prime minister or not.
Now I wish to uphold the nation's majesty,
to clarify what is rebellious and what is loyal.
What do you think of this?"
Jìngxuān (敬宣) replied:
"Although the court does not have the prosperity of Chéng and Kāng,
it has not yet suffered the chaos of Huán and Líng.
However, Gōng (恭) relies on chaos and obstructs the army,
aiming to dominate the capital.
You and Gōng (恭) are not related by blood,
nor are you in a lord-vassal relationship.
Although you have served together for a short time,
your intentions are not aligned.
To attack him today,
what emotional ties would be broken?"
Láo Zhī (牢之) arrived at Zhúlǐ,
where he beheaded Gōng's (恭) grand general Yán Yán (顏延).
He sent Jìngxuān (敬宣) to lead Gāo Yǎzhī (高雅之) and others back to the capital to attack Gōng (恭).
Gōng (恭) was just outside the city displaying his troops;
they charged and struck him horizontally,
and his forces scattered and collapsed instantly.
Yuánxiǎn (元顯) was promoted to the title of General Hòujiāngjūn.
Jìngxuān (敬宣) was appointed Cīyì Cānjūn,
and granted the title of General Níngshuò.
In the third year [399 CE],
Sūn Ēn (孫恩) incited a rebellion,
disturbing the eastern regions.
Láo Zhī (牢之) personally submitted a memorial requesting to lead an eastern expedition.
His army encamped at Hǔtǐ.
The bandits fought to the death.
Jìngxuān (敬宣) requested to lead cavalry along the southern mountain to approach their rear.
The Wú (吳) bandits feared horses
and also dreaded being attacked from both front and rear,
and thus suffered a great defeat.
They then pacified Kuàijī.
Soon after, he was granted the additional title of Administrator of Línhuái,
and promoted to Fromagistrate (Cóngshì Zhōngláng) of the Rear Army.
In the fifth year [401 CE],
Sūn Ēn (孫恩) again entered Jiákoǔ.
Gāozǔ (高祖) garrisoned Gōuzhāng.
The bandits frequently attacked but could not overcome it.
Jìngxuān (敬宣) requested to go and provide aid.
Bandit Ēn (恩) thereupon retreated far away into the sea.
At this time, disturbances arose from all directions,
and the court was weak.
Jìngxuān (敬宣) always worried that the difficulties would not end.
Since Gāozǔ (高祖) had repeatedly defeated the demonic bandits,
his merits and fame grew daily.
Thus, Jìngxuān (敬宣) deeply relied on him and allied with him,
and their friendship was very strong.
Yuánxiǎn (元顯) was promoted to the title of General Piàojì.
Jìngxuān (敬宣) accordingly transferred with his office,
his military and administrative positions remaining as before.
Yuánxiǎn (元顯) was arrogant, decadent, and unrestrained,
and his subordinates were influenced by him.
Jìngxuān (敬宣), whenever he attended banquets,
never drank alcohol.
When jesting and teasing came his way,
he offered no response.
Yuánxiǎn (元顯) was very displeased.
Soon after, he was promoted to the title of General Fǔguó,
the rest remaining as before.
In the first year of Yuánxīng [402 CE],
Láo Zhī (牢之) marched south to attack Huán Xuán (桓玄).
Yuánxiǎn (元顯) was the Grand Commander of the Expedition.
He was drunk day and night.
Láo Zhī (牢之) frequently went to his gate
but could not see him.
The emperor went out to see them off
and only then did they meet in a public sitting.
When Huán Xuán (桓玄) reached Lìzhōu,
he sent a messenger to persuade Láo Zhī (牢之).
Láo Zhī (牢之), considering Dàozǐ (道子) to be muddled and dim,
and Yuánxiǎn (元顯) to be depraved and wicked,
feared that on the day Xuán (玄) was pacified,
political chaos would just begin.
He intended to use Xuán (玄)
to eliminate the powerful officials,
and then seize the opportunity created by Xuán (玄)
to achieve his ambition for the world.
He was about to agree to surrender to Xuán (玄).
Jìngxuān (敬宣) remonstrated, saying:
"Currently, the state is in turmoil,
and the whole world is in chaos.
The fate of the world
rests with you and Xuán (玄).
Xuán (玄) relies on his late father's foundation
and holds the strategic position of Jīngnán.
Although he lacks the virtue of Jī Wén (姬文),
he truly represents a power-sharing situation.
If you let him go for once,
allowing him to dominate the court,
once his prestige is established,
it will be difficult to contend with him.
The calamity of Dǒng Zhuó (董卓)
will arise today."
Láo Zhī (牢之) angrily said:
"How could I not know that defeating Xuán (玄) today is as easy as turning over my hand?
But after pacifying Xuán (玄),
what should I do with that General Piàojì?"
He sent Jìngxuān (敬宣) to
〔一一〕be Xuán's (玄) Staff Officer (Cīyì Cānjūn) in his administration.
After Xuán (玄) achieved his ambition,
he harmed Yuánxiǎn (元顯)
and deposed Dàozǐ (道子).
He made Láo Zhī (牢之) General Zhēngdōng and Administrator of Kuàijī.
Láo Zhī (牢之) conspired with Jìngxuān (敬宣) to jointly attack Xuán (玄),
setting the next morning as the date.
It happened to be a day of heavy fog.
The government gate opened late.
As the day wore on,
Jìngxuān (敬xuān) did not arrive.
Láo Zhī (牢之) thought his plan had been leaked.
He led his personal troops towards Báizhōu,
intending to flee to Guǎnglíng.
But Jìngxuān (敬宣) had returned to Jīngkǒu to fetch his family.
Láo Zhī (牢之) searched for him but could not find him,
believing he had already been captured by Xuán (玄).
Thereupon he hanged himself.
Jìngxuān (敬宣) rushed to the funeral.
After weeping,
he immediately crossed the river to join Sīmǎ Xiūzhī (司馬休之) and Gāo Yǎzhī (高雅之) and others.
They all fled to Luòyáng,
and traveled back and forth to Cháng'ān,
each offering their sons and younger brothers as hostages,
seeking aid from Yáo Xīng (姚興).
Xīng (興) gave them credentials,
ordering them to recruit soldiers east of the pass.
They gathered several thousand men
and returned to the area of Péngchéng,
collecting their loyal former associates.
Xuán (玄) sent Sūn Wúzhōng (孫無終) to attack the Inspector of Jìzhōu, Liú Guǐ (劉軌).
Guǐ (軌) invited Jìngxuān (敬宣), Yǎzhī (雅之), and others to jointly hold Shānyáng and defeat him,
but they did not succeed.
They then advanced to Chāngpíng Jiàn,
where the battle went unfavorably,
and their forces scattered.
They all then fled to the Xianbei Mùróng Dé (慕容德).
Jìngxuān (敬宣) had always understood astronomy
and knew that someone would surely revive the Jìn dynasty.
He then dreamed of swallowing a clay ball.
Upon waking,
he rejoiced, saying:
"A ball (wán) is Huán (桓).
Since Huán (桓) has been swallowed,
will I return to my homeland?"
Thereupon he allied with the prominent families of Qīngzhōu, the Cuī (崔) and Fēng (封) clans,
〔一二〕and also enlisted the great Xianbei leader Miǎn Kuí (免逵),
plotting to overthrow Dé (德).
They nominated Xiūzhī (休之) as their leader
and set a date for their departure.
At that time, Liú Guǐ (劉軌) was Dé's (德) Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
and greatly trusted.
Yǎzhī (雅之) also wanted to enlist Guǐ (軌).
Jìngxuān (敬宣) said:
"This gentleman is old.
I observe that he has the ambition to secure Qí,
and will surely not move;
he should not be told."
Yǎzhī (雅之) thought otherwise
and consequently told Guǐ (軌).
Guǐ (軌) indeed did not comply.
The plot was largely leaked,
so they killed Guǐ (軌) and left.
Upon reaching the area between the Huái (淮) and Sì (泗) rivers,
they met Gāozǔ (高祖) who had pacified Jīngkǒu.
He personally wrote a letter summoning Jìngxuān (敬宣).
Those around him suspected a trick.
Jìngxuān (敬宣) said:
"I certainly know it to be so.
Xìapí (下邳) will not tempt me."
He then galloped back.
Upon arriving at the capital,
Jìngxuān (敬宣) was appointed General Fǔguó and Administrator of Jìnlíng,
and inherited the title of Male (Nán) of Wǔgāng County.
This year [404 CE]
was the third year of Ān Dì's (安帝) Yuánxīng (元興) era.
Huán Xīn 率 (shuài) the Di (Dí) bandits Yáng Qiū (Yáng Qiū) invaded Lìyáng (Lìyáng).
Jìngxuan (Jìngxuan) and the Jianwei General Zhūgě Chángmín (Zhūgě Chángmín) thoroughly defeated them.
Xīn (Xīn) fled alone on horseback across the Huái (Huái) River.
Yáng Qiū (Yáng Qiū) was beheaded at Liàngù (Liàngù), and then they returned.
He was promoted to Jianwei General and Governor of Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu).
Jìngxuan (Jìngxuan) firmly declined,
saying to Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ):
"The shame of our revenge has been avenged,
the four seas are cleared and pacified.
My wish is to return to the humble life
to live out my remaining years.
If your grace does not forget me,
〔一三〕and I am compelled to accept,
what I hold now
〔一四〕is already exceptionally generous.
Moreover, Pánlóng (Pánlóng) and Wújì (Wújì) have not yet received favor,
and my two virtuous younger brothers' positions are still humble.
To be promoted ahead of them in one morning
will surely invite criticism from both court and commoners."
Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) did not permit it.

He sent a messenger to present Chángmín's letter to Gāozǔ,

In the first month of the eleventh year,
he was promoted to Yòujiāngjūn.
Sīmǎ Dàocì,

When Gāozǔ went on a western expedition against Sīmǎ Xiūzhī,

The civil and military aides immediately hunted down Dàocì, Měngzǐ and others,
and executed them all.
Before this, while Jìngxuān was still alive,

A single straw sandal fell from the air into the gathering,
〔一九〕landing on Jìngxuān's food tray.
It was three feet five inches long,

with its toe and heel parts nearly worn out.
Soon after, he was defeated.
When the coffin arrived,
Gāozǔ wept over it with great sorrow.
His son was Zǔsì.
〔二０〕When Sòng received the abdication,
his state was abolished.
Tán Zhī, courtesy name Gōngshū,
was a native of Jīnxiāng, Gāopíng, and the second younger brother of Zuǒjiāngjūn Sháo.
〔二一〕In his youth, he served as Sūn Wúzhōng's Fǔguó Cānjūn,
following Wúzhōng on the eastern expedition against Sūn Ēn,

He then served as Wáng Dàn's Lóngxiáng Cānjūn.

After Jiānglíng was pacified,

He defeated Huán Liàng in Chángshā,
and Fú Hóng in Xiāngdōng.
Wǔlíng Nèishǐ Yǔ Yuè fell ill,
so Dàoguī replaced Yuè with Zhī,
adding the title Níngshuò Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffing him as Xīchāng Xiànhóu,

Five years later,
he entered court as Zhōngshū Shìláng.
When Lú Xún threatened the capital,
he was given the additional title Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
and commanded troops stationed outside Xīmíng Mén.
When Xún retreated,
Zhī led his command
to march and reinforce Jiānglíng,
but before he could depart,
he fell ill and stopped.
Eight years later,
he was promoted to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
and then appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, Xuānchéng Nèishǐ,
and immediately, with his original title, Dū Jiāngběi Huáinán Jūnjùnshì, Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Guǎnglíng Xiàng.
He was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn,
and given the *jié* (credentials).
Ten years [416 CE],
the renegade Sīmǎ Guófán brothers gathered several hundred men from the northern Xúzhōu region.
They secretly managed to cross the Huái River.
As it was a dark and overcast night,
they led about a hundred men who scaled the walls of Guǎnglíng City and entered.
They shouted and went straight up to the administrative office.
Zhǐ was startled awake,
came out of the door to give orders,
but the bandits shot him,
wounding his thigh,
so he went back in.
Zhǐ told his attendants:
"The bandits took advantage of the darkness to enter,
intending to catch me unprepared.
But if we beat the fifth watch drum,
fearing dawn,
they will surely flee."
When the bandits heard the drum,
they thought it was dawn,
so they scattered in flight.
More than a hundred of them were pursued, attacked, and killed.
Zhǐ was demoted to the rank of Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn.
In the eleventh year [417 CE],
he was promoted to Yòujiāngjūn.
Gāozǔ campaigned in the north,
and the renegade Sīmǎ □ raided on the road.
Liú Jī, the Administrator of Qínjùn, requested aid.
A portion of the army was dispatched to ambush and attack them,
and immediately defeated and beheaded them.
In the fourteenth year [420 CE],
when the Sòng state was first established,
the Son of Heaven issued an edict saying:
"The Sòng state has just been founded,
with everything inside and out in its initial stages.
The imperial guards and crucial positions
all require talented individuals to manage them.
Yòujiāngjūn Zhǐ may be appointed Sòng Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
and additionally Sànqí Chángshì."
Zhǐ was arrogant and uninhibited by nature,
enjoying freedom and indulgence outside,
and was unwilling to be transferred to the capital.
He was very discontent.
He fell ill and did not recover,
and died that year in Guǎnglíng,
at the age of fifty-one.
He was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì and Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn,
and given the posthumous title Wēihóu.
His son Xiàn succeeded him.
He died during the Yuánxī period [420-421 CE],
without a son,
so Zhǐ's second son Lǎng inherited the enfeoffment.
When Lǎng died,
his son Xuānmíng succeeded him.
When Xuānmíng died,
his son Yì succeeded him.
When Qí received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
The court historian says: "Liú Jìngxuān and Gāozǔ had forged a bond of kindness during their humble beginnings.
Their righteous connection was formed early.
Although at the start of the restoration,
circumstances separated their meetings,
their deep aspirations and long-standing commitments
were never broken.
The duty of great responsibility
ceased when the person was gone,
and the rites of posthumous honors
were not heard of after his death.
Is there a reason
for the disparity in favor and courtesy?"

Biographies, Chapter 8: Zhū Língshí (younger brother Chāoshí), Máo Xiūzhī, Fù Hóngzhī.
Zhū Língshí, courtesy name Bó'ér,
was a native of Pèijùn, Pèi.
His family had been generals and commanders for generations.
His grandfather, Téng, was Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Wúguó Nèishǐ.
His paternal uncles Xiàn and Bīn
were both assistants to Yuán Zhēn, the Xī Zhōngláng,
Xiàn serving as Liángguó Nèishǐ,
and Bīn as Rǔnán Nèishǐ.
When Dàsīmǎ Huán Wēn attacked Zhēn at Shòuyáng,
Zhēn, believing that the Xiàn brothers were secretly in contact with Wēn,
killed them both.
Língshí's father Chuò fled to Wēn,
and always fought at the forefront,
not shunning arrows or stones.
When Shòuyáng was pacified,
and Zhēn was already dead,
Chuò immediately opened his coffin and mutilated his corpse.
Wēn was enraged
and was about to execute him,
but Wēn's younger brother Chōng earnestly pleaded for his life, and he was spared.
Chuò was loyal and brave by nature,
and, having received the grace of a second life from Chōng,
served Chōng as if he were his father.
He participated in Chōng's cavalry military affairs and was Xīyáng Guǎngpíng Tàishǒu.
When Chōng died,
Chuò vomited blood and died.
Chōng's sons treated Língshí like a brother.
Língshí was fond of military matters in his youth,
but was quite frivolous and did not cultivate strict conduct.
His maternal uncle, from the Jiǎng clan of Huáinán,
was a person of weak talent.
Língshí made his uncle lie down at one end of the administrative office,
cut paper into one-inch squares,
and pasted them onto his uncle's pillow.
He then took a small knife and threw it,
from a distance of eight or nine chi,
hitting the target every time.
Although his uncle was terrified and trembling,
he feared Língshí
and ultimately dared not move.
His uncle had a large tumor on his head.
Língshí waited until his uncle was asleep,
secretly went and cut it off,
and his uncle died immediately.
He first served as Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn,
often following the Huán Xiū brothers.
He became Huán Xiū's Fǔjūn Cānjūn,
stationed in Jīngkǒu.
When Gāozǔ captured the capital,
he appointed him Jiànwǔ Cānjūn.
He followed Gāozǔ to Jiāngchéng.
Before the battle,
Língshí said to Gāozǔ:
"My family has received great kindness from the Huán clan for generations;
it is not permissible for me to confront them with weapons.
I beg to remain behind the army."
Gāozǔ, deeming it righteous, agreed.
After the situation settled,
he was appointed Zhènjūn Cānjūn,
then promoted to Wǔkāng Magistrate,
and additionally Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn.
After the chaos,
Yáo Xìzǔ of Wǔkāng gathered renegades,
specializing in banditry.
His dwelling was in a perilous, inaccessible place,
and the commanderies and counties feared him and could not suppress him.
Upon arriving in the county,
Língshí feigned intimacy with Xìzǔ,
and summoned him to be a Cānjūn.
Xìzǔ, relying on the strength of his brothers and followers,
believed Língshí would certainly not dare to plot against him,
and thus came to respond to the summons.
Língshí secretly gathered his trusted confidants,
learned of Xìzǔ's dwelling and path,
and then invited Xìzǔ to a banquet,
where he shouted to his attendants to behead him.
He then led his officials and people to rush to Xìzǔ's home,
catching them unprepared.
No one could even raise a hand.
All of Xìzǔ's brothers were beheaded,
and dozens of people were killed.
From then on, the entire commandery became clear of bandits.
Gāozǔ again summoned him to be a Cānjūn,
appointed him Xúzhōu Zhǔbù,
then promoted him to Shàngshū Dūguānláng,
and soon after he again became Cānjūn.
He followed in a campaign against the Xiānbēi,

When Guǎnggù was pacified,
he again became Cānjūn.
When Lú Xún reached Shítou,
he commanded the Central Army.
Lú Xún selected several thousand brave and desperate soldiers to land on the south bank.
Gāozǔ sent Língshí to lead the Xiānbēi infantry armed with spears,
to cross the Huái and attack them.
He inspired his officers and soldiers,
who all fought desperately,
killing several hundred people,
whereupon the bandits retreated.
Língshí was both militarily capable
and skilled in administrative duties,
so Gāozǔ greatly trusted and relied on him.
When Lú Xún was pacified,
he was appointed Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn, Níngmán Hùjūn, and Xīyáng Tàishǒu.
In the eighth year of Yìxī [412 CE],
Gāozǔ marched west to attack Liú Yì,
and Língshí followed him to Jiānglíng.
In the ninth year,
the various armies were dispatched to attack Shǔ,
and Lìngshí was made Marshal,
appointed as Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Yìzhōu Cìshǐ.
He led Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Zāng Xī, Héjiān Tàishǒu Kuǎi Ēn, Xiàpī Tàishǒu Liú Zhōng, Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Zhū Lín, and others,

Soon after, he was granted command over all military affairs in Yìzhōu (Jié Yìzhōu Zhū Jūnshì).
Initially,
Gāozǔ and Lìngshí secretly planned the advance,
saying:
"Liú Jìngxún went out through Huánghǔ last year,

If we head towards Huánghǔ,

Now, with a large force, we will take Chéngdū via the outer waterway,

However, fearing that this plan might leak out prematurely

with the inscription on the envelope:

Upon reaching Báidì,
