"All armies shall proceed via the outer waterway to take Chéngdū.
Zāng Xī and Zhū Lín shall take Guǎnghàn via the middle waterway.
A small, weak force, on more than ten tall warships,
shall proceed via the inner waterway towards Huánghǔ."
The armies then marched double time.
Qiáo Zòng indeed prepared for the inner waterway,
stationing his great general Qiáo Dàofú with heavy troops at Fúchéng.
He dispatched his former general, Qínzhōu Cìshǐ Hóu Huī, and Shàngshū Púyè, Shǔjùn Tàishǒu Qiáo Shēn, among others, leading over ten thousand men to encamp at Péngmó,
building a city on both sides of the river.
In the sixth month of the tenth year,
Lìngshí arrived at Péngmó.
The generals believed that the rebel city north of the river was heavily fortified and had numerous obstructions,
and all wished to attack the southern city first.
Lìngshí said:
"No, that is not right.
Although the enemy is in the north,
even if we now slaughter the southern city,
it will not be enough to break the northern one.
If we commit all our strength to capturing the northern stronghold,
the southern city will disperse without even being signaled to surrender."
In the seventh month,
Lìngshí led Liú Zhōng, Kuǎi Ēn, and others to attack the city.
They fought from dawn
until dusk,
burning down its watchtowers,
and ascending from all four sides.
They beheaded Hóu Huī and Qiáo Shēn.
Then, they turned their army and signaled,
and the southern city immediately scattered and collapsed.
They beheaded a total of fifteen great generals.
The various camps and garrisons then crumbled in succession.
The armies then abandoned their boats and advanced on foot.
Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Zāng Xī reached Guǎnghàn
and died of illness.
Zhū Lín reached Guǎnghàn
and again defeated Qiáo Dàofú.
A separate detachment on boats captured Niúpíchéng,
beheading its great general Qiáo Fǔ.
Qiáo Zòng heard that all his positions had been defeated
and fled to Fúchéng.
Wáng Zhì, a man from Bāxī, captured and delivered him, beheaded.
The fake Shàngshū Lìng Mǎ Dān sealed the armory and treasury, awaiting the royal army.
Dàofú heard that Péngmó could not be held,
and led five thousand elite soldiers on a forced march to reinforce it.
When he heard that Zòng had already fled,
Dàofú's troops also scattered.
He then fled into the lands of the Liáo people.
Dù Yáo, a commoner from Bāxī, captured and delivered him bound.
He was beheaded at the army gate.
Huán Qiān's younger brother Tián had followed Qiān into Shǔ
and served as Níngshǔ Tàishǒu.
At this point, he was also beheaded.
When Gāozǔ launched the campaign against Shǔ,
he considered appointing a Marshal but found it difficult to choose.
Then he put forward Lìngshí.
Everyone believed that historically, all who pacified Shǔ
were heroic, outstanding, and important generals.
Lìngshí's standing and reputation were still light,
and they feared he would not succeed.
Many advised against it,
but Gāozǔ did not listen.
He then divided half of the grand army,
along with fierce generals and strong soldiers,
and assigned them all to him.
Zāng Xī
was the younger brother of the Jìng Empress.
His rank and position were above Lìngshí's,
but he was also ordered to follow Lìngshí's command.
This campaign did not take long,
and was victorious in one battle.
Everyone was
convinced of Gāozǔ's discernment of character and praised Lìngshí's skill in his duties.
Lìngshí sent Sīmǎ Shěn Shúyùn to guard Fú.
A Shǔ local, Hóu Chǎndé, rebelled
and attacked Fúchéng.
Shúyùn defeated him,
beheading Chǎndé.
Initially,
when Lìngshí pacified Shǔ,
those executed were only descendants of Zòng's ancestor.
When Chǎndé's affair arose,
many were implicated,
and so a thorough purge was carried out,
with many dying.
He was promoted to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.

Soon after, he was further promoted to oversee military affairs of the six commanderies: Bāxī, Zǐtóng, Dàngqú, and Nánhànzhōng in Liángzhōu, and Āngù and Huáiníng in Qínzhōu (Jiān Liángzhōu zhī Bāxī Zǐtóng Dàngqú Nánhànzhōng, Qínzhōu zhī Āngù Huáiníng Liùjùn Zhū Jūnshì).
For his meritorious service in pacifying Shǔ,
he was enfeoffed as Fēngchéng Xiànhóu,
with an income of one thousand households.
In the eleventh year,
he was summoned to serve as Tàiwèi Zīyì Cānjūn
and granted the title of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the twelfth year, during the northern expedition,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Jiāngjūn,
retaining his original title.
He was entrusted with military forces
to guard the palace.
Liú Mùzhī greatly trusted and relied on him.
He was consulted on all matters, both internal and external.
Gāozǔ returned to Péngchéng,
and made Lìngshí Xiàngguó Yòusīmǎ.
In the fourteenth year,
Ānxī Jiāngjūn, Guìyáng Gōng Yìzhēn, was summoned back.
Lìngshí was then appointed to hold the staff of authority, overseeing military affairs in Guānzhōng, as Yòu Jiāngjūn and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Gāozǔ commanded Lìngshí
that if Guānyòu definitely could not be held,
he could return with Yìzhēn.
Lìngshí also abandoned the city and fled.
Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Wáng Jìngxiān was stationed at Cáo Gōnglěi.
Lìngshí led his remaining troops from Tóngguān to join Jìngxiān.
The barbarians cut off their water supply,
and the troops were too thirsty to fight.
The city fell.
The barbarians captured Lìngshí and Jìngxiān and returned to Cháng'ān,
where they were killed.
He was forty years old at the time.
His son Jǐngfú succeeded him.
After Jǐngfú died,
his son Zǔxuān succeeded him.
Due to his unauthorized ennoblement,
he did not return for eight years.
And because he did not divide the official salary with his aunt's state,
his peerage was revoked.
Instead, Zǔxuān's younger brother Lóngshào was enfeoffed.
When Qí received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
Lìngshí's younger brother Chāoshí
was also courageous and sharp, skilled in horsemanship.
Although from a general's family,
both brothers were adept at correspondence.
Huán Qiān was Wèi Jiāngjūn,
and appointed him as Xíng Cānjūn.
He also served as Cānjūn for Hé Wújí, Fǔguó Yòujūn Jūnshì.
When Xú Dàofù defeated Wújí,
he captured Chāoshí
and made him his Cānjūn.
Upon reaching Shítou,
Chāoshí persuaded his fellow boatmen to escape on a single skiff back to Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ was very pleased with him
and made him Xúzhōu Zhǔbù.
Chāoshí collected and welcomed Huán Qiān's body and head,
personally overseeing the funeral.
He was promoted to Chēqí Cānjūnshì,
then Shàngshū Dūguān Láng,
and soon after, was reappointed as Zhōngbīng Cānjūn, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, and Pèijùn Tàishǒu.
When attacking Liú Yì in the west,
Chāoshí was ordered to lead infantry and cavalry out of Jiānglíng,
but Yì was pacified before he arrived.
Later, when suppressing Sīmǎ Xiūzhī,
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn Tán Dàojì and Chāoshí were sent with infantry to Dàbó.
Lǔ Zōngzhī heard that Chāoshí was approaching
and personally led his army to meet him.
But Jiānglíng was pacified before the battle.
He followed to Xiāngyáng,
taking charge as Xīnyě Tàishǒu,
and pursued Zōngzhī to Nányáng before returning.
In the twelfth year of Yìxī (416 CE), during the northern expedition,
Chāoshí served as the vanguard and entered the Hé (Yellow River).
The barbarian Tǎbá Sì,
who was the son-in-law of Yáo Xīng,

dispatched his younger brother, the Yellow Gate Attendant Lù Qīng (ロ青), the Inspector of Jìzhōu, Ānpíng Gōng Yǐzhān Juàn (安平公乙旃眷), the Inspector of Xiāngzhōu, Tǎbá Dàoshēng, and the Inspector of Qīngzhōu, Ābógān,
〔一０〕 with 100,000 infantry and cavalry.
They encamped north of the Hé (Yellow River),
and constantly had several thousand cavalry
patrolling along the river, advancing and halting with the main army.
At that time, the army men along the south bank of the Hé (Yellow River)
were pulling hundred-zhang ropes.
The river current was swift and urgent,
and those who drifted to the north bank
were immediately killed or plundered by the barbarians.
As soon as the army crossed the river,
the barbarians would retreat.
When the army returned,
they would come back east again.
Gāozǔ then dispatched Dīng Wǔ, a leader of the Bái Zhí (White Staff) unit,
leading seven hundred men
and one hundred chariots,
on the north bank of the Hé (Yellow River),
about a hundred paces from the water,
to form a "crescent moon formation" (quèyuè zhèn),
with both ends embracing the river.
Chariots were placed with seven armed men.
When the task was completed,
he ordered a white banner to be raised.
The barbarians saw several hundred men pulling chariots up,
did not understand its meaning,
and did not move at all.
Gāozǔ had previously ordered Chāoshí [to prepare two thousand men for battle.
As soon as the white banner was raised,
Chāoshí] rushed to them,
〔一一〕 bringing with him one hundred large crossbows.
Each chariot was reinforced with twenty more men,
and a shield wall (péng pái) was set up on the shafts.
When the barbarians saw that the camp formation was established,
they advanced and surrounded the camp.
Chāoshí first shot the barbarians with soft bows and small arrows.
The barbarians, seeing the small number of troops and their weak weapons,
attacked from all four sides.
Sì again sent Nánpíng Gōng Tǎbá Sōng with thirty thousand cavalry,
who then engaged in close combat to attack the camp.
Thereupon, one hundred crossbows fired simultaneously,
and skilled archers were chosen to shoot clustered arrows.
However, the barbarian multitude was too great,
and the crossbows could not contain them.
〔一二〕 When Chāoshí first set out,
he had also brought large hammers and over a thousand spears.
He then broke the spears to a length of three or four *chǐ* (feet),
and used hammers to strike them.
Each spear would pierce through three or four barbarians.
The barbarian multitude could not withstand this,
and immediately broke and fled.
Ābógān's head was taken on the battlefield,
and the barbarians retreated to Bànchéng.
〔一三〕 Chāoshí led Hú Fān, Liú Róngzǔ, and others in pursuit,
but were again surrounded by the barbarians.
They fought fiercely all day,
killing thousands of barbarians,
whereupon the barbarians retreated.
Gāozǔ also sent Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn Xú Yīzhī with five thousand men towards Yuèqí Chéng.
The barbarians surrounded Yīzhī,
who formed a formation with long halberds.
Chāoshí rushed to his aid,
and before he arrived, they all fled.
The main army advanced and conquered Púbǎn,
appointing Chāoshí as the Administrator of Hédōng,
to garrison and guard it.
The bandits, seeing Chāoshí's small force,
returned to attack the city.
Chāoshí was defeated in battle and retreated,
reaching the main army several days later.
When Gāozǔ returned east from Cháng'ān,
Chāoshí regularly sent men by water to Péngchéng,
and was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng (Gentleman of the Central Secretariat),
and enfeoffed as a Fifth-Rank Marquis of Xīngpíng Xiàn.
When Guānzhōng became chaotic,
Gāozǔ sent Chāoshí to console the people of Hé and Luò.
As he first arrived at Púbǎn,
he encountered Língshí (齡石) who had fled east from Cháng'ān to Cáo Gōng Lěi.
Chāoshí crossed the river to join him.
He and Língshí both perished,
killed by FóFó (佛佛).
He was thirty-seven years old at the time.
Máo Xiūzhī, courtesy name Jìngwén,
was from Yángwǔ, Xíngyáng.
His grandfather, Hǔshēng,
and paternal uncle, Qú,
were both Inspectors of Yìzhōu.
His father, Jǐn, was the Inspector of Liáng and Qín Two Prefectures.
Xiūzhī had great ambitions
and read extensively in historical records.
Yīn Zhòngkān, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, appointed him Níngyuǎn Cānjūn (Staff Officer for Pacifying Distances).
When Huán Xuán conquered Jīngzhōu,
he continued to serve as Xuán's assistant,
successively holding positions as Cānjūn (Staff Officer) in the Rear Army, Grand Commandant, and Prime Minister's offices.
He understood music and rhythm,
and was skilled in horsemanship and archery.
Xuán treated him very well.
When he usurped the throne,
he appointed him Túnqí Xiàowèi (Colonel of Cavalry).
He followed Xuán in his westward flight.
When Xuán was defeated at Zhēngróng Zhōu,
and returned to Jiānglíng,
with morale scattered,
they discussed fleeing west to Hànchuān.
Xiūzhī lured him into Shǔ,
and Féng Qiān's beheading of Xuán at Méihuí Zhōu
was due to Xiūzhī's efforts.
When Emperor Ān of Jìn was restored at Jiānglíng,
he was appointed Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (General of Agile Cavalry).
Upon arriving in the capital,
Gāozǔ appointed him Zhèn Jūn Zīyì Cānjūn (Consultant Staff Officer of the Army-Suppressing General),
and granted him the title Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North).
Within a month,
he was promoted to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Right Guard).
〔一四〕 Since he had planned the killing of Xuán,
and his paternal uncle and father were both in Shǔ territory,
Gāozǔ wished to draw him in as an external helper,
and thus repeatedly bestowed honorable titles upon him.
〔一五〕 When his father Jǐn was killed by Qiáo Zòng,
Gāozǔ presented a memorial appointing him Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (General Soaring Dragon),
provided him with troops and resources,
and dispatched him to rush to the scene.
He also sent Sīmǎ Róngqī, Inspector of Yìzhōu, along with Wén Chǔmào, Shí Yánzǔ, and others, to campaign in the west.
When Xiūzhī arrived at Dàngqú,
Róngqī was killed by his staff officer Yáng Chéngzǔ.
Chéngzǔ proclaimed himself Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Suppresses the Army) and Inspector of Bāzhōu.
Xiūzhī retreated to Báidì.
Chéngzǔ attacked him from below,
but could not breach the defenses.
Xiūzhī sent staff officer Yán Gāng and others to gather troops.
Féng Qiān, Administrator of Hànjiā, led troops to join them,
and they attacked and beheaded Chéngzǔ.
At that time, Wén Chǔmào was still in Bājùn.
Xiūzhī sent Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn Zhāng Jìrén with five hundred men to assist Chǔmào and others.
Dàoguī, Inspector of Jīngzhōu, also sent Fènwǔ Jiāngjūn Yuán Dǎozhī leading a thousand men,
to act under Xiūzhī's command.
Xiūzhī sent Yuán Dǎozhī and Jìrén to advance together.
At that time, Bāo Lòu (鮑陋), the Inspector of Yìzhōu, was unwilling to advance and attack.
Xiūzhī (脩之) submitted a memorial from the capital, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the reason one values life while alive
is truly because there is a chance of survival to be preserved.
As for your servant's situation,
the path of life has already run dry.
The reason I have not yet sunk into the spring and soil,
borrowing life like morning dew,
is because the sun and moon shine brightly,
possessing a glory that illuminates all.
I hope to rely on celestial might
to eradicate the rebel enemies.
Since taking up my spear and rushing west,
I have endured the hardships of the times.
This has caused the Qi (齊) axe to be abandoned,
and the cunning rascals to draw a temporary breath.
This is truly because the route encountered difficulties,
and also because I could not control myself.
I lament my shadow in utter despair,
weeping as I gaze towards the western road.
Bāo Lòu (鮑陋), the Inspector of Yìzhōu, first arrived in Bādōng (巴東) on the twenty-ninth day of the fourth month,
encamped at Báidì (白帝),
awaiting the imperial strategy.
Opportunities that could be seized were missed;
occasions to rush into action were repeatedly squandered.
Although your servant would die for the imperial court,
I am utterly cut off from rescue.
Therefore, I bind my bones and hasten to the capital
to appeal my grievances at the Xiàngwèi (象魏) gate.
In the past, when Sòng (宋) harmed Shēn Dān (申丹),
Chǔ Zhuāng (楚莊) harbored the indignation of a lost shoe.
How much more so for one who forgets his home and sacrifices for the state,
rarely found among ministers,
whose integrity surpasses wind and frost,
and whom all pity and mourn.
Wǔ Yuán (伍員) did not betray his lord's righteousness,
and Shēn Bāo (申包) did not forget the state's difficulties.
They waited for the right moment and seized the opportunity,
acting only when the time was ripe.
Now, your servant's mediocrity surpasses those of old,
yet I have not received the banner for a nighttime march.
Therefore, I look up to the celestial pole hoping for its light,
and turn towards the western land to shed tears.
Both public and private sentiments harbor shame,
as we look up to your great grace.
How can I appropriately continue to enjoy high office
and stand shoulder to shoulder with others?
My plea is not permissible,
and in reality, it is not something I can maintain.
But as I am currently relying on your awe-inspiring power,
I must gather all my faculties.
I beg to be relieved of the honor of the gold and purple, a private favor,
and be bestowed with the title of Yīngyáng (鷹揚) and Zhéichōng (折衝).
As for your servant's loyalty to the state,
there is no logical reason for a false request.
Since your servant embarked on this path,
my emotions and thoughts have been in disarray and unruly.
Illness and poison intertwine,
and I constantly fear for my life.
I must personally lead the soldiers,
rush into the rebel camp,
and personally slay the wicked leaders
to vent this immense grievance.
Only then, on the day of my death,
will I return as if going home,
and the spirits of my entire family
will not fail to give thanks to the late emperor in the underworld."
Gāozǔ (高祖) pitied his situation
and ordered Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍) Liú Jìngxūan (劉敬宣) to lead Wén Chǔmào (文處茂) and Shí Yánzǔ (時延祖)'s armies to attack Shǔ (蜀).
The army reached Huánghǔ (黃虎) but
retreated without success.
Jiáo Zòng (譙縱) subsequently sent Xiūzhī (脩之)'s father, uncle, and relatives who had died
and were separated, all to return.
When Lú Xún (盧循) threatened Jīngyì (京邑),
Xiūzhī (脩之), whose mourning period was not yet over,
was appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍),
and soon after, promoted to Xuānchéng Nèishǐ (宣城內史),
garrisoning Gūshú (姑孰).
He was attacked by Rǔan Cì (阮賜), a member of Xún (循)'s faction,
but defeated him.
Xún (循) fled.
When Liú Yì (劉毅) returned to Gūshú (姑孰),
Xiūzhī (脩之) served as Yì (毅)'s Hòujūn Sīmǎ (後軍司馬).
For keeping too many servants and personal attendants,
he was dismissed from his posts as Jiāngjūn (將軍) and Nèishǐ (內史).
When Yì (毅) moved west to garrison Jiānglíng (江陵),
he made Xiūzhī (脩之) Wèijūn Sīmǎ (衞軍司馬), Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍), and Nánjùn Tàishǒu (南郡太守).
Although Xiūzhī (脩之) was one of Yì (毅)'s generals and aides,
he had deeply allied himself with Gāozǔ (高祖).
When Gāozǔ (高祖) attacked Yì (毅),
he first sent Wáng Zhèn'è (王鎮惡) to launch a surprise attack on Jiānglíng (江陵).
Xiūzhī (脩之), along with Cānyì Cānjūn (諮議參軍) Rèn Jízhī (任集之) and others, fought with all their might.
Gāozǔ (高祖) pardoned them.
At that time, Zhū Língshí (朱齡石) was sent to attack Shǔ (蜀).
Xiūzhī (脩之) steadfastly requested to go.
Gāozǔ (高祖) feared that if Xiūzhī (脩之) reached Shǔ (蜀),
he would surely carry out many executions and massacres.
The local people, already having animosity with the Máo (毛) clan,
would also certainly fight to the death to defend themselves.
Therefore, he did not permit it.
Upon returning to the capital,
he was appointed Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎),
and again served as Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (右衞將軍).
Xiūzhī (脩之) did not believe in ghosts or spirits.
Wherever he went, he would burn down temples and shrines.
At that time, there were fine oxen and good horses in the temple on Jiǎngshān (蔣山).
Xiūzhī (脩之) seized them all.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) attacked Sīmǎ Xiūzhī (司馬休之),
he appointed Xiūzhī (脩之) Cānyì Cānjūn (諮議參軍), Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍), and concurrently Nánjùn Xiàng (南郡相).
When Gāozǔ (高祖) was about to attack the Qiāng (羌),
he first sent Xiūzhī (脩之) to restore Shuòpí (芍陂)
and cultivate several thousand qǐng of land.
Upon reaching Péngchéng (彭城),
he also had him supervise the construction of the official residence.
He was transferred to Xiàngguó Yòusīmǎ (相國右司馬),
with his general's title remaining as before.
At that time, Luòyáng (洛陽) had already been pacified,
so he was made Tàishǒu (太守) of Hénán (河南) and Hénèi (河內) two commanderies under his original title,
acting as Sīzhōu Shì (司州事),
garrisoning Luòyáng (洛陽),
and repairing the city walls and fortifications.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) arrived,
he inspected it and praised it.
He bestowed clothes and fine playthings,
which at the time were valued at twenty million.
Before this,
when Liú Jìngxūan (劉敬宣)'s daughter married,
Gāozǔ (高祖) bestowed three million cash
and one thousand bolts of assorted silks.
People at the time all considered this a generous gift.
After Wáng Zhèn'è (王鎮惡) died,
Xiūzhī (脩之) replaced him as Ānxī Sīmǎ (安西司馬),
with his general's title remaining as before.
It happened that Guìyáng Gōng (桂陽公) Yìzhēn (義真) had already departed from Cháng'ān (長安),
but was intercepted by the Fófó Lǔ (佛佛虜) (Huánghú),
and his army was defeated.
Xiūzhī (脩之) and Yìzhēn (義真) became separated,
and he was on the verge of escaping.
He had just climbed a slope,
which was very high and steep.
A soldier of the Yòuwèi Jūnrén (右衞軍人) who had rebelled and fled,
and had already ascended the slope,
had once been punished by Xiūzhī (脩之).
He threw a spear at him,
injuring his forehead.
Xiūzhī (脩之) then fell off the slope
and was subsequently captured by Fófó (佛佛).
After Fófó (佛佛) died,
his son Hèlián Chāng (赫連昌) was captured by the Suǒ Lǔ (索虜) Tuòbá Táo (拓跋燾),
and Xiūzhī (脩之) was also lost to them.
Initially,
Xiū zhī was in Luò,
and reverently served the Taoist priest of Sōnggāo Mountain, a bandit.
The Taoist priest was trusted and respected by Táo,
who protected him.
Therefore, he was not killed,
but was moved to Píngchéng.
Xiū zhī once made lamb stew,
and offered it to the Rǔ Shàngshū.
The Shàngshū considered it to be of exquisite taste,
and presented it to Táo.
Táo was greatly pleased,
and appointed Xiū zhī as Tàiguān Lìng.
Gradually, he received favor and trust,
and eventually became Shàngshū, Guānglù Dàfū, and Nánjùn Gōng.
His positions as Tàiguān Lìng and Shàngshū remained as before.
Later, Zhū Xiū zhī was captured by the Rǔ,
and was also favored by Táo.
The two Xiū zhī got along very happily.
Xiū zhī asked, "Who is the powerful figure in the Southern Kingdom?"
Zhū Xiū zhī replied,
"Yīn Jǐngrén."
Xiū zhī laughed and said,
"When I was in the South,
Yīn was still very young.
When I have the day to return from my captivity,
he should come to my door with a turban and hood!"
For a year, he could not bear to ask about his family news.
After a long time, he finally inquired.
Xiū zhī answered in detail,
and also said,
"Your virtuous son, Yuánjiǎo,
is very capable of managing himself,
and is praised by people of the time."
Xiū zhī was too sad to speak,
and stared straight for a long time.
Then he let out a long sigh and said,
"Alas!"
From then on, he never brought it up again.
[一七]Initially,
when people from the wilderness came and went,
they said that Xiū zhī encouraged and enticed Táo to invade the border,
and also taught Táo the Chinese rites and institutions.
Tàizǔ greatly doubted and blamed him.
Later, Xiū zhī was able to return,
[一八]and explained the situation thoroughly,
whereupon the emperor's suspicion was dispelled.
While among the Rǔ, Xiū zhī
had many wives and concubines,
and many children of both sexes.
In the 23rd year of Yuánjiā,
he died among the Rǔ,
at the age of seventy-two.
Yuánjiǎo successively served as the Magistrate of Wǎnlíng, Jiāngchéng, and Lìyáng.
Fù Hóngzhī, courtesy name Zhòngdù,
was a native of Níyáng, Běidì.
The Fù clan originally belonged to Língzhōu.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, the commandery territory was invaded by the Rǔ,
and they lost their land and took refuge in Féngyì.
Two counties, Níyáng and Fùpíng, were established,
and Língzhōu was abolished and not re-established.
Thus, the Fù clan all belonged to Níyáng.
In the 3rd year of Tàikāng of Jìn Wǔdì,
Língzhōu county was re-established,
and the Fù clan returned to Língzhōu.
Hóngzhī's great-great-grandfather, Jìn Sītú Zhī,
was later enfeoffed as Língzhōu Gōng.
He did not wish to be enfeoffed in his native county,
so Zhī's entire family returned to Níyáng.
His great-grandfather, Chàng,
was Mìshū Chéng.
He was captured by the Hú,
and had a son, Hóng,
who returned during the Yǒnghé era of Jìn Mùdì,
when the Hú were in chaos.
Hóng had a son, Sháo,
[一九]who was Liángzhōu Cìshǐ
and Sànqí Chángshì.
Sháo had a son, Hóngzhī.
From a young age, he was unconventional and had great ambitions.
He served as the Zhǔbù of his home province,
and was recommended as a Xiùcái,
but did not take office.
When Huán Xuán was about to usurp the throne,
Yǔ Zè of Xīnyě raised an army in Nányáng,
and attacked Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Féng Gāi.
Gāi fled.
Hóngzhī was in Jiānglíng at the time,
and plotted with Zè's nephew Bīn to assassinate Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Huán Shíkāng,
in order to respond to Zè with Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Bīn's younger cousin, Hóng, learned of their plot,
and reported it to Shíkāng.
Shíkāng arrested Bīn and killed him,
and imprisoned Hóngzhī.
Huán Xuán, because Hóngzhī was not the instigator of the plot,
and was also an unarmed commoner,
pardoned him without punishment.
When the banner of righteousness was raised,
Fúguó Jiāngjūn Dàoguī appointed him Cānjūn, Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn, and Wèixīng Tàishǒu.
When Lú Xún rebelled,
Huán Shísuí, from Jiǎkǒu in Shàngluò, declared himself Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
[二０]Wáng Tiān'ēn, the Magistrate of Zhēngyáng, declared himself Liángzhōu Cìshǐ,
[二一]and attacked Xīchéng.
At that time, Sháo was the Liángzhōu Cìshǐ,
and sent Hóngzhī to suppress Shísuí and others,
executing them all.
He was appointed Tàiwèi Xíng Cānjūn.
He accompanied the expedition against Sīmǎ Xiūzhī,
and was appointed Hòubù Zéicáo,
and then Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Shùnyáng Tàishǒu.
When Gāozǔ launched the Northern Expedition,
Hóngzhī, along with Fúfēng Tàishǒu Shěn Tiánzǐ and seven other armies, entered through Wǔguān.
The false Shàngluò Tàishǒu fled and escaped.
[二二]They advanced and occupied Lántián,
and rallied the Róng and Jìn people.
Páng Bīnbīn, Dài Yǎng, Hú Rén Kāng Héng, and others, each led their tribes to submit.
Hóngzhī was naturally skilled in horsemanship.
When Gāozǔ arrived at Cháng'ān,
Hóngzhī rode and played with his horse on Yáo Hóng's imperial road,
in relaxed attire.
Sometimes he galloped, sometimes he trotted,
covering twenty lǐ back and forth.
He displayed great elegance and control.
Thousands of Qiāng and Hú people gathered to watch,
all amazed and sighing with admiration.
When he first mounted the horse,
he used the handle of his whip to prod it,
and pulled it between his two thighs.
When he dismounted,
the mark of the handle was still there.
He was promoted to Guìyáng Gōng Yìzhēn Yōngzhōu Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ,
and appointed Xīróng Sīmǎ and Níngshuò Jiāngjūn.
Lüèyáng Tàishǒu Xú Shīgāo rebelled,
and Hóngzhī suppressed and pacified him.
After Gāozǔ returned,
Fófó's false crown prince, Hèlián Guī, led three thousand troops to attack Cháng'ān.
[二三]Hóngzhī again led five thousand infantry and cavalry,
and severely defeated them at Chíyáng,
killing and wounding many.
Guī then plundered Wèinán.
Hóngzhī again defeated Guī at Guǎfùrén Dù,
capturing three hundred bandits
and over seven thousand people.
When Yìzhēn returned eastward,
[二四]Fófó pursued him with his entire nation,
and a great battle took place at Qīngní.
Hóngzhī wore armor,
and his spirit surpassed that of the three armies.
His army was defeated and he was trapped.
Fófó forced him to surrender,
but Hóngzhī refused to yield.
The weather was cold at the time,
and Hóngzhī was stripped naked.
He cursed and was then killed.
He was forty-two years old at the time.
The imperial historian says: In the flourishing age of the Three Dynasties,
the ji and fu regions had their ranks,
extending eastward and covering westward,
leaving no distant wilderness untouched.
When the Hàn dynasty expanded its territory
and communicated with the four quarters,
the depth of its civilizing influence
and the quality of its administration already varied greatly.
When the Jìn house migrated,
settling in Yáng and Yuè,
Guān and Shuò were remotely blocked,
Lǒng and Qiān were distant wilds.
The inner and outer regions of the country were divided,
and mountains and rivers marked their boundaries.
With Qiāng and Róng tribes intermingled,
long cut off from civilizing influence,
it was fitting to treat them as remote tributary regions,
merely keeping them in check.
If they harbored righteousness and feared power,
serving the king and receiving appointments,
then they would be linked by writing and roads,
and granted positions according to royal regulations.
If they relied on their remote and rugged terrain,
stubbornly resisting on the borders,
then one would defend the strongholds and close the passes,
warding off their brigandage and violence.
Huán Wēn was a heroic figure of his generation,
whose ambition was to usurp the Jìn throne.
Had he not been defeated at Bàshàng
and suffered a setback at Fāngtóu,
the opportunity for him to settle the empire
would surely have materialized in his middle years.
Gāozǔ lacked the foundation of accumulated benevolence that the Zhōu dynasty possessed,
yet he desired to conquer the four seas by force.
He indeed needed to accumulate military achievements externally
to gain the support of the people of the world.
He merely wished to display his banners at Lóngmén,
deterring aggression in Jì and Zhào,
surpassing the achievements of the Huán clan,
and outshining his predecessors.
Though his territory was not yet expanded from the Eastern Jìn,
his prestige alone was to shake Jiāngnán.
Only then could he transform the state of the nation,
satisfy the will of the people,
and embrace the turning tide to receive the auspicious mandate.
How could he not know that Qínchuān was insufficient for sustenance,
and that the “hundred two” strongholds were difficult to pass down to posterity?
His taking Xiányáng and then abandoning it
was not a miscalculation.
That these four generals, relying on the difficulty of holding the returning multitudes,
all fell into traps
was indeed unfortunate.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 9: Sūn Chù, Kuǎi Ēn, Liú Zhōng, Yúqiū Jìn
Sūn Chù, courtesy name Jìgāo,
was a native of Yǒngxìng, Kuàijī.
As his courtesy name Jìgāo was recorded in the family registry,
that name became current in society.
In his youth, he was spirited and resolute.
When Gāozǔ campaigned eastward against Sūn Ēn,
Jìgāo, out of righteous enthusiasm, followed.
When Gāozǔ pacified Jīngyì,
he appointed him Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn [General Who Arouses Martial Might]
and enfeoffed him as a fifth-rank marquis of Xīnyí County.
In the campaign of Guǎnggù,
he was among the first to climb the walls and rendered meritorious service.
During Lú Xún's rebellion,
he defended the barricades at Shítóu,
garrisoned Yuèchéng and Zhāpǔ,
and defeated the rebels at Xīntíng.
Gāozǔ said to Jìgāo:
"These rebels are about to be defeated.
We should first destroy their stronghold,
so that when they flee,
they will have nowhere to return.
No one but you can achieve this."
He then dispatched Jìgāo to lead three thousand troops
by sea to attack Pānyú.
Initially,
the rebels did not guard against a sea attack.
When Jìgāo reached Dōngchōng,
more than ten lǐ from the city,
those inside the city still did not know.
Xún still had several thousand defending soldiers,
and the city was very strong.
Jìgāo first burned his ships,
exerting all his strength to land.
It happened that there was a great fog,
and he scaled the city walls from all sides,
capturing it on that very day.
Xún's father, Gǔ, his Chief Clerk Sūn Jiànzhī, and his Marshal Yúfū, etc.,
fled in light boats to Shǐxīng.
He immediately dispatched Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn Shěn Tiánzǐ and others to pacify Shǐxīng, Nánkāng, Línhè, and the various commanderies in the Língbiǎo region of Shǐ'ān.
Xún fled from Zuǒlǐ,
but his forces were still strong,
and he returned via the mountain passes to attack Guǎngzhōu.
Jìgāo resisted for over twenty days,
whereupon Xún was defeated and fled.
Over ten thousand were killed.
He pursued them to Yùlín,
but fell ill
and could not complete the pursuit.
Thus, Xún was able to flee to Jiāozhōu.
In the fourth month of the seventh year of Yìxī (411 CE),
Jìgāo died in Jìnkāng,
at the age of fifty-three.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn [General Soaring Dragon] and Nánhǎi Tàishǒu [Administrator of Nánhǎi],
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Hòuguān County,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
In the ninth year,
Gāozǔ, remembering Jìgāo's merit,
memorialized thus:
"Sūn Jìgāo's achievements in Língnán
have already been posthumously praised and honored.
Your subject further reflects that Lú Xún had been evil for a full cycle of twelve years,
occupying an entire region.
If his roots had not been eradicated,
and he had somewhere to flee,
gathering remaining remnants,
he could still pose a threat,
and a distant expedition by our forces
would then require meticulous strategic planning.
But Jìgāo sailed ten thousand lǐ across the sea,
risking his life in the vast currents.
With waves crashing and swift as lightning,
he arrived in a matter of days,
then suddenly pacified Nánhǎi,
overturning their stronghold,
leaving Xún with no place to advance or retreat,
and forcing him to flee far away in a light boat.
In less than a month,
the monstrous evil was annihilated.
The merit of his cleansing action
was truly immense.
The honors bestowed last year
were still insufficient.
Your humble opinion is that he should be further granted the governorship of a province,
with his original military title retained,
so that loyal achievements may not be obscured,
and diligent officials may be further encouraged."
He was re-posthumously granted the title of Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ [Governor of Jiāozhōu],
with his generalship as before.
His son Zōngshì died,
and his son Qīngōng succeeded.
Qīngōng died,
and his son Yànzǔ succeeded.
When Qí received the abdication,
the marquisate was abolished.
Kuǎi Ēn, courtesy name Dào'ēn,
was a native of Chéng, Lánlíng.
When Gāozǔ campaigned against Sūn Ēn,
the county assigned him as a conscripted civilian
to serve as an auxiliary soldier,
tasked with cutting horse fodder.
Ēn always carried a large bundle,
more than double that of others,
and whenever he put down the fodder,
he would sigh and say:
"A true man should be able to draw a three-stone bow;
how can I be merely a horse soldier!"
Gāozǔ heard of this,
and immediately provided him with weapons and armor.
Ēn was greatly pleased.
From the campaign against the demonic rebels,
he was always among the first to charge,
beheading many.
Having become proficient in battle formations,
his courage and strength surpassed others.
He was sincere and diligent,
never making any mistakes,
and was greatly loved and trusted.
In the battle at Lóuxiàn,
an arrow struck his left eye.
He followed in the pacification of Jīngchéng,
then in establishing control over Jīngyì,
and was appointed Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn [General Who Pacifies Distances], leading a contingent.
He accompanied Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn Dàoguī on a western expedition,
captured Huán Xiānkè,
took the Yǎnyuè fortified camp,
and subsequently pacified Jiānglíng.
In the second year of Yìxī (406 CE),
the rebel Zhāng Jiān occupied Yìngchéng and revolted.
Ēn attacked and defeated him,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāng.
He followed in the campaign against Guǎnggù,
again rendering meritorious military service.
When Lú Xún pressed on Jīngyì,
Ēn fought at Zhāpǔ,
and the rebels retreated.
He, along with Wáng Zhòngdé and others, pursued and defeated Xún's subordinate general Fàn Chóngmín at Nánlíng.
After Xún had fled back to Guǎngzhōu,
Ēn again led over a thousand men to follow Liú Pān in pursuing Xú Dàofù at Shǐxīng,
and beheaded him.
He was promoted to Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn [General Soaring Dragon] and Lánlíng Tàishǒu [Administrator of Lánlíng].
Gāozǔ campaigned west against Liú Yì.
Ēn and Wáng Zhèn'è led a light force to raid Jiānglíng.
The details are in the biography of Zhèn'è.
He was appointed Tàiwèi Chángjiān Xíng Cānjūn in his original capacity,
leading two thousand men,
to follow Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Zhū Língshí in attacking Shǔ.
When they reached Péngmó,
Ēn's contingent was at the forefront.
In a great battle,
from morning until sunset,
his valor grew even stronger,
and the rebels were defeated and fled.
He advanced to take Chéngdū,
was promoted to Xíng Cānjūn,
and his title was changed to the fifth-rank Baron of Běizhì County.
When Gāozǔ campaigned against Sīmǎ Xiūzhī and Lǔ Zōngzhī,
Ēn advanced with Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn Xú Kuízhī.
Kuízhī was defeated and killed.
Ēn deployed his troops below the dike.
Zōngzhī's son, Guǐ, pressed his advantage and attacked Ēn.
Arrows fell like rain,
and shouts shook the earth.
Ēn organized and encouraged his officers and soldiers,
setting up a firm and strict formation.
Guǐ repeatedly charged but could not dislodge them.
Realizing they could not be overcome,
he retreated.
Gāozǔ commended his ability as a general to maintain a strong position.
After Jiānglíng was pacified,
he pursued Lǔ Guǐ again to Shíchéng.
Guǐ abandoned the city and fled.
Ēn pursued him to Xiāngyáng.
Zōngzhī fled to the Qiāng.
Ēn and the other generals pursued and attacked them as far as Lǔyángguān before returning.
Ēn, since joining the campaigns,
whenever there was danger or crisis,
always took the lead among the generals,
frequently breaking strong formations and breaching enemy lines,
not shying away from difficulties or dangers.
In over a hundred battles,
he sustained severe wounds.
Gāozǔ recorded his merits from before and after,
enfeoffed him as Baron of Xīnníng County,
with a stipend of five hundred households.
When Gāozǔ's heir apparent became Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn,
Ēn was appointed Dàfǔ Zuǒ to lead Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
and transferred with the commandery to Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
When Gāozǔ campaigned in the north,
he left Ēn to guard the heir apparent,
and ordered court officials to associate with him.
Ēn became even more humble and modest.
When speaking to others, he always addressed them by their official titles,
while referring to himself as "this humble person."
He treated his officers and soldiers
with great discipline and order,
and everyone became close to him and supported him.
He was promoted to Zīyì Cānjūn,
then transferred to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Huáilíng Tàishǒu.
When the heir apparent established his own administration,
he also served as Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
then transferred to Sīmǎ,
retaining his general and prefect titles.
He entered the pass to welcome Guìyáng Gōng Yìzhēn.
When Yìzhēn returned to Qīngchōng,
he was pursued by the Fófó captives.
Ēn served as the rearguard,
fighting vigorously for several days.
Yìzhēn's vanguard scattered and fled.
Ēn's troops were also completely exhausted.
He was captured by the enemy
and died in captivity.
His son, Guócái, succeeded him.
Guócái died,
and his son, Huìdù, succeeded him.
Huìdù died
without a son,
and the peerage was abolished.
Liú Zhōng, courtesy name Shìzhī,
was a native of Péngchéng, Péngchéng.
He was orphaned young,
and lived with a fellow villager, Zhōngshān Tàishǒu Liú Huí.
As a youth, he had ambition and strength,
and often felt indignant about his humble status.
In the fourth year of Lóng'ān,
when Gāozǔ campaigned against Sūn Ēn,
Zhōng volunteered to attack Gōuzhāng, Hǎiyán, and Lóuxiàn from Yúyáo and Jiákǒu.
He broke strong defenses and breached enemy lines in all battles,
achieving military merits every time.
He served as Zhèn Běi Cānjūn Dūhù for Liú Láozhī.
Whenever Gāozǔ had military affairs,
Zhōng never shirked difficult duties,
dedicating himself fully,
and was greatly loved and trusted.
When the righteous banner was about to be raised,
Gāozǔ appointed Zhōng as Jùn Zhǔbù.
The next day,
he followed Gāozǔ into the capital city.
When approaching the capital,
Gāozǔ ordered:
"All those from Péngpéi who have come to join the righteous cause
should report to Master Liú, the Registrar."
Thus, a righteous contingent was formed,
stationed on his left and right,
and they were victorious in every battle.
The next day,
Huán Qiān was stationed at Dōnglíng,
and Biàn Fànzhī was stationed west of Fùzhōushān.
Gāozǔ suspected the enemy had an ambush.
He looked around
and saw Zhōng,
to whom he said:
"There must be an ambush below this mountain.
You should lead your unit to gradually scout and attack them."
Zhōng responded instantly and galloped forward.
Indeed, there were several hundred ambushers,
who immediately scattered and fled.
When Huán Xuán fled west,
that evening,
Gāozǔ stayed at Huán Qiān's former camp,
and sent Zhōng to occupy the Eastern Commandery overnight,
transferring him to Zhèn Jūn Cānjūn Dūhù.
When Huán Xīn attacked Lìyáng,
Gāozǔ sent Zhōng to assist Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Wèi Yǒngzhī in attacking him.
Xīn immediately fled.
He was appointed Nánqí Guónèi Shǐ,
and enfeoffed as a fifth-rank Marquis of Ānqīu County.
He submitted a petition concerning his family affairs,
requesting to rebury his father, grandfather, and ten other relatives.
Gāozǔ provided generous funds.
He was transferred to Chējì Chángshǐ,
concurrently serving as Xíng Cānjūn.
Sīmǎ Shúfán, along with Péngchéng Liú Mì and Liú Huáiyù, attacked Zōushān from Fānchéng.
Rǔjùn Tàishǒu Xú Yōng lost his position.
Zhōng led his army to attack and pacify them.
He followed Gāozǔ in campaigning against Guǎnggù.
Méng Lóngfú was trapped and killed.
Zhōng led his attendants directly in,
retrieved his body, and returned.
He was appointed Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn and Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
replacing Lóngfú as Guǎngchuān Tàishǒu.
When Lú Xún pressured the capital,
Xú Chìtè's army disobeyed orders
and was defeated on the south bank.
Zhōng led his subordinates to defend the palisade,
sustaining severe wounds.
The rebels could not enter.
Xún fled south.
Zhōng and Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Wáng Zhòngdé pursued him.
Xún had previously left a separate commander, Fàn Chóngmín, with elite troops and high ships to occupy Nánlíng,
encamped on both banks.
Zhōng personally went to scout the enemy.
Due to fog,
the enemy hooked his boat.
Zhōng then led his attendants to attack the ship's hatches.
The rebels hastily closed the hatches and resisted,
so Zhōng slowly retreated.
He and Zhòngdé attacked Chóngmín.
Chóngmín was defeated and fled.
Zhōng pursued him for a hundred li,
burning his boats and vehicles.
He also followed Liú Fān to pursue Xú Dàofù in Shǐxīng,
and decapitated him.
He was appointed Tàiwèi Xíng Cānjūn, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, and Xiàpī Tàishǒu.
He replaced Méng Huáiyù in charge of the Shítou garrison.

時年四十三.
子 Jìngyì嗣.
Jìngyì官至 Mǎtóu Tàishǒu,
卒.
子 Guózhòng嗣,
Qí受禪,
國除.
Zhōng次子 Gāochāng Nán Jìngshùn,
卒,
子 Guóxū嗣.
Xū卒,
無子,
國除.
Yúqiū Jìn字 Yùzhī,
Dōnghǎi Tán人也.
少時隨 Xiè Xuán討 Fú Jiān,
有功,
封 Guānnèi Hóu.
Lóng'ān中,
從 Gāozǔ征 Sūn ēn,
戍 Gòuzhāngchéng,
被圍數十日,
無日不戰,
身被數創.
至 Yúyáo Hēpǔ,
破賊 Zhāng Piāo,
追至 Hǎiyán故治及 Lóuxiàn.
於 Pútáo Kǒu與 Sūn ēn水戰,
又被重創.
追 ēn至 Yùzhōu,
又至 Shílùtóu,
還 Hǎiyán Dàzhù,
頻戰有功.
Yuánxīng元年,
又從 Gāozǔ東征 Línhǎi,
於 Shíbùgù與 Lú Xún相守二十餘日.
二年,
又從 Gāozǔ至 Dōngyáng,
破 Xú Dàofù.
其年,
又至 Línsōngxué破賊,
追至 Yǒngjiā Qiānjiāng,
又至 Āngù,
累戰皆有功.
三年,
從平 Jīngchéng,
定 Jīngyì,
除 Yānnèi Nèishǐ.
Yìxī二年,
除 Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn,
封 Lóngchuān Xiàn Wǔděng Hóu.
從 Gāozǔ伐 Guǎnggù,
於 Línqú破賊.
Lú Xún逼 Jīngyì,
Mèng Chǎng, Zhūgě Chángmín等建議奉天子過江,
Jìn廷議不可,
面折 Chǎng等,
Gāozǔ甚嘉之.
獻計伐樹,
樹柵 Shítou.
除 Póyáng Tàishǒu,
將軍如故.
統馬步十八隊,
於東道出 Póyáng,
至 Wǔmǔ Qiáo.
Xún遣將 Yīng Dǒu為 Shàngráo Lìng,
千餘人守故城,
Jìn攻破之.
Xún又遣 Tóng Mǐnzhī為 Póyáng Tàishǒu,
據郡,
Jìn從 Yúgān步道趣 Póyáng,
Mǐnzhī退走,
追破之,
斬首數百.
復隨 Liú Fān至 Shǐxīng,
討斬 Xú Dàofù.
八年,
除 Níngmán Hùjūn, Xúnyáng Tàishǒu,
領文武二千從征 Liú Yì.
事平,
補 Tàiwèi Xíng Cānjūn,
尋加 Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn.
九年,
以前後功封 Wàngcài Xiàn Nán,
食邑五百戶,
加 Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn.
討 Sīmǎ Xiūzhī,
又有戰功.
軍還,
除 Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, Shānyáng Tàishǒu.
Sòng Tái令書除 Qínjùn Tàishǒu,
督 Chénliú Jùnshì,
將軍如故.
Yuánxī二年,
Sòng Wáng令書以為 Gāozǔ第四子 Yìkāng Yòujiāngjūn Sīmǎ.
Yǒngchū二年,
遷 Tàizǐ Yòuwèi Shuài.
明年,
卒官,
時年六十.
追論討 Sīmǎ Xiūzhī功,
進爵為子,
增邑三百戶.
子 Gēng嗣.
Gēng卒,
子 Xízǔ嗣.
Xízǔ卒,
Shìbǎo嗣.
Qí受禪,
國除.
The official historian says: The *Shī* says,
“No words go unrewarded,
no virtue goes unrequited.”
These generals all rose from humble origins,
from among servants, laborers, and herdsmen.
It was merely because their hearts were one with their lord
that they were able to spread their wings and soar.
As for pushing through the front lines and shifting battles,
facing a hundred deaths without regard for their own lives—
this was because their hearts were one.
They then enjoyed the reward of being enfeoffed as marquises.
The words of the poet are truly trustworthy.
Collated Notes
Biographies, Chapter 10: Hú Pān, Liú Kāngzǔ, Yuán Hùzhī, Zhāng Xīngshì
Hú Pān, courtesy name Dàoxù,
was a native of Nánchāng, Yùzhāng.
His grandfather, Suí,
was a Sànqí Chángshì.
His father, Zhòngrèn,
was a Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ.
Pān was orphaned young
and was known for his extreme grief during mourning.
The Grand Administrator, Hán Bó, saw him
and said to Pān’s uncle, the Shàngshū Shàoguǎng,
“This nephew of yours will make a name for himself through his righteousness and valor.”
The provincial and commandery authorities summoned him,
but he did not accept.
Only after his two younger brothers had completed their coming-of-age ceremonies and marriages
did he join Xī Huī’s Zhēnglǔ army as a staff officer.
At that time, Yīn Zhòngkān was the Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
and Pān’s maternal cousin, Luó Qǐshēng, was Zhòngkān’s staff officer.
Pān requested leave to return
and visited Qǐshēng in Jiānglíng.
Zhòngkān invited Pān for an audience
and treated him very generously.
Pān then advised Zhòngkān, saying,
“Huán Xuán’s intentions are unpredictable;
he is often resentful about losing his position.
Your Excellency treats him too highly;
this is not a plan for the future.”
Zhòngkān’s expression was displeased.
Pān withdrew and said to Qǐshēng,
“Giving up one’s weapons to another will
certainly lead to disaster.
If you do not plan your departure early,
regrets will be too late.”
When Xuán attacked Zhòngkān from Xiàkǒu,
Pān served as a staff officer in Xuán’s rear army.
When Zhòngkān was defeated,
Qǐshēng indeed suffered disaster for his affiliation.
Pān was then transferred to serve as a staff officer for the Tàiwèi, Dà Jiàngjūn, and Xiàngguó.
When the righteous banner was raised,
and Xuán was defeated in battle and about to flee,
Pān grasped Xuán’s horse bridle at the Nányèmén
and said,
“Currently, there are still eight hundred imperial archers,
all of whom are old retainers from the West.
If you abandon them now,
will you ever be able to return?”
Xuán merely pointed to the sky with his horsewhip and left.
Thereupon, they scattered and lost each other.
When Xuán was pursued and caught at Wúhú,
Xuán saw Pān
and, delighted, said to Zhāng Xūwú,
“Your province indeed has many talented men;
now I see Wáng Shūzhì again.”
During the Battle of Sāngluò,
Pān’s ship was burned.
He plunged into the water in full armor and swam underwater for about thirty paces
before he could get ashore.
As the righteous army was pressing close,
he could not go west again,
so he returned home.
Gāozǔ had long heard of Pān’s frank words to the Yīn clan
and his loyalty to Xuán,
so he summoned him to be Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng
and a staff officer in the Zhèn Jūn army.
He followed in the campaign against the Xiānbēi.
The bandits were encamped at Línqú.
Pān said to Gāozǔ,
“The bandits’ main force is encamped outside the city,
so the defenders must be few.
If we now go and capture their city,
and cut down their banners,
this is how Hán Xìn conquered Zhào.”
Gāozǔ then sent Tán Sháo and Pān and others to go secretly.
Upon arrival,
they immediately captured the city.
When the bandits saw the city fall,
they scattered and fled,
retreating to defend Guǎnggù for several months.
On the night before its capture,
all the assistant officials gathered.
Suddenly, a bird as large as a goose,
dark grey,
flew into Gāozǔ’s tent.
Everyone was startled
and considered it inauspicious.
Pān rose and congratulated, saying,
“Dark grey is
the color of the northern barbarians.
The northern barbarians coming to us is
an omen of great good fortune.”
The next morning,
they attacked the city
and captured it.
He followed in the campaign against Lú Xún at Zuǒlǐ,
achieving merits in repeated battles.
He was enfeoffed as a Fifth-Rank Viscount of Wúpíng County
and appointed Zhèngyuán Láng.
Soon after, he was promoted to Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Póyáng.
He followed in the campaign against Liú Yì.
Yì initially was to go to Jīngzhōu,
but he submitted a memorial requesting to return to the capital via the eastern route to visit his ancestors’ tombs.
He passed dozens of *lǐ* from the capital
without paying respects at the palace gates.
Gāozǔ met him at Nítáng.
Pān advised killing Yì at the meeting,
but Gāozǔ did not agree.
At this time, he said to Pān,
“If I had followed your plan at Nítáng back then,
we would not have this campaign now.”
He then followed in the campaign against Sīmǎ Xiūzhī,
again serving as a staff officer,
and was granted the title of Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn,
leading a mobile force at Jiāngjīn.
When Xú Kuízhī was defeated and killed,
Gāozǔ was extremely enraged.
On that very day, he crossed the river at Mǎtóu’àn.
However, the Jiāngjīn bank was steep,
a cliff standing several *zhàng* high.
Xiūzhī had arrayed his troops along the bank,
making it impossible to ascend.
Gāozǔ called Pān to go up.
Pān showed signs of hesitation.
Gāozǔ, filled with fury,
ordered his attendants to seize him,
intending to execute him.
Pān did not accept the order,
but looked back and said,
“Pān would rather die fighting forward!”
He used his saber tip to dig into the bank,
barely making indentations for his toes.
Then he climbed straight up,
and gradually more followed him.
Once they had ascended the bank,
they fought desperately.
The bandits could not withstand them
and retreated.
Taking advantage of this,
they scattered in an instant.
When Gāozǔ campaigned against the Qiāng,
he temporarily appointed Pān Níngsuò Jiāngjūn,
a staff officer in the Tàiwèi army,
commanding a separate force.
Upon reaching Hédōng,
a violent storm blew Pān’s heavy ships to the north bank.
The Suǒ Lǔ captured these ships
and took their equipment.
Pān, indignant and furious,
led twelve men from his retinue
in a small boat directly to the north bank of the river.
Five or six hundred bandit cavalry saw Pān approaching
and all laughed at him.
Pān was skilled in archery.
He landed and shot,
and about ten bandits fell at the sound of his bowstring.
The bandits all fled,
and he recovered all that had been lost and returned.
He also sent Pān and Zhū Chāoshí and others to pursue the Suǒ Lǔ at Bànchéng.
The barbarian cavalry were numerous,
but Pān and Chāoshí’s forces had all been reassigned to new units,
numbering fewer than five thousand.
They fought fiercely
and thoroughly routed them.
He then, with Chāoshí and others, attacked Yáo Yè at Púbǎn.
Chāoshí suffered a defeat and retreated.
Pān collected the supplies and valuables that Chāoshí had abandoned
and slowly withdrew,
and Yè dared not pursue.
Gāozǔ returned to Péngchéng,
and Cān served in the Prime Minister's military affairs.
At that time, the remnants of Lú Xún's faction and the great bandit Sū Yín gathered together,
and he was made the Administrator of Shǐxīng.
For his merits in pacifying Sīmǎ Xiūzhī and Guǎnggù,
he was enfeoffed as a Count of Yángshān County,
with a fief of five hundred households.
In the first year of Jǐngpíng of Shàodì,
he was dismissed from office for sitting guard at the East Palace and
opening the掖 Yè Gate.
He was dismissed from office,
but soon had his post restored.
In the fourth year of Yuánjiā,
he was promoted to Jiànwǔ Jiàngjūn and Prefect of Jiāngxià.
In the seventh year,
he was summoned to be Yóují Jiàngjūn.
When Dào Yànzhī launched his northern expedition,
Yìxīn, Prince of Chángshā and Governor of Nányānzhōu, advanced to occupy Péngchéng.
Fān went out to guard Guǎnglíng,
performing the duties of the Prefectural Administrator.
He was transferred to be the Left Guard Commander of the Crown Prince.
In the tenth year,
he died
at the age of sixty-two,
and was posthumously granted the title of Zhuàng Hóu.
His son, Lóngshì, inherited the title,
and served as Administrator of Xīyáng.
When Lóngshì died,
his son, Gānxiù, inherited the title.
Fān had sixty concubine-born sons,
most of whom did not abide by the laws and regulations.
Fān's fourteenth son, Zūnshì,
served as Zāng Zhì's Níngyuǎn Cānjūn.
After resigning from his post and returning home,
he conspired in rebellion with Kǒng Xīxiān.
Tàizǔ, considering Fān a meritorious minister,
did not wish to expose the matter,
and ordered Jiāngzhōu to arrest and kill him on other charges.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Fān's sixteenth son, Dànshì, and seventeenth son, Màoshì, led over two hundred followers to attack and break through the commanderies and counties,
killing the Administrator Huán Lóngzhī and the Magistrate Zhūgě Hézhī,
intending to enthrone the commoner Yìkāng.
At that time, Tán Hézhī, the Governor of Jiāozhōu, arrived at Yùzhāng
and pacified them.
Dànshì's elder brother, Jǐngshì, who was a Chēqí Cānjūn and Administrator of Xīnxīng, and Jǐngshì's younger brother, Bǎoshì,
went to the Grand Judge to confess their crimes,
and were both exiled to distant prefectures.
Gānxiù was stripped of his inheritance.
In the early reign of Shìzǔ,
all those exiled were allowed to return.
Liú Kāngzǔ
was a native of Péngchéng and Lü.
His family had long resided in Jīngkǒu.
His uncle, Jiǎnzhī,
was ambitious and capable,
and was known to Gāozǔ.
When Gāozǔ was planning to restore the dynasty,
he gathered talented and strong individuals.
He once visited Jiǎnzhī twice,
when guests were present.
Jiǎnzhī understood his intention
and said to his younger brother, Qiánzhī,
"Liú Xiàpī has come repeatedly;
he must have something in mind.
Since I couldn't speak with him,
you should try to go see him."
When Qiánzhī arrived,
Gāozǔ had already conquered the capital city,
and Qiánzhī immediately pledged his allegiance.
When Jiǎnzhī heard of this,
he slaughtered his ploughing oxen,
gathered his followers,
and led them to Gāozǔ.
Jiǎnzhī successively served as Tōngzhí Chángshì,
Shǎofǔ,
and Tàiwèi Zīyì Cānjūn.
Jiǎnzhī's younger brother, Qiānzhī,
was fond of learning
and compiled twenty volumes of the Jìn Jì.
At the end of Yìxī,
he became Administrator of Shǐxīng.
Xú Dàoqī, a native of Dōnghǎi, drifted to Guǎngzhōu.
He had no scholarly conduct
and was scorned by both the transplanted gentry and the old residents.
Taking advantage of the death of Governor Xiè Xīn,
he gathered and led a group of unruly individuals to rebel,
attacking and capturing the provincial capital,
killing over a hundred gentry and commoners whom he had long resented,
plundering the treasury,
gathering desperadoes,
and attacking Shǐxīng.
Qiānzhī defeated and routed him,
then pacified Guǎngzhōu,
executed his partisans,
and subsequently acted as the Provincial Administrator.
He was then appointed Zhènwēi Jiàngjūn and Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
Later, he became Tàizhōng Dàfū.
Qiánzhī was generous and upright,
not accumulating property,
valuing wealth lightly and being fond of charity.
When Gāozǔ launched his western campaign against Sīmǎ Xiūzhī, Lǔ Zōngzhī and others,
he sent Cānjūn Tán Dàojì and Zhū Chāoshí with infantry and cavalry out of Xiāngyáng.
Qiánzhī, then Administrator of Jiāngxià,
led the prefectural troops out to Yǐnchéng,
garrisoned at Sānlián,
built bridges, and gathered provisions to await them.
Dàojì and the others did not arrive for many days,
and were attacked by Zōngzhī's son, Guǐ.
Their forces were unequal.
Cānjūn Sūn Chángyōng tearfully urged a retreat.
Qiánzhī sternly said,
"I rely on the righteous cause to punish the wicked;
there is no reason not to be victorious.
If, by misfortune, we fail,
it is fate."
He was defeated in battle and killed.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Governors of Liáng and Qín prefectures,
and enfeoffed as a Count of Xīnkāng County,
with a fief of five hundred households.
Kāngzǔ,
Qiánzhī's son,
inherited the title
and served as Yìxīn, Prince of Chángshā's Zhèn Jūn Cānjūn,
then transferred to Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng.
He was skilled in archery and horsemanship,
and his physical strength surpassed others.
In his hometown, he did not pursue scholarly endeavors,
but indulged in dissolute behavior, gambling, and drinking.
Whenever he broke the law and
was recorded by the commandery or county,
he would leap over roofs and walls,
and no one could catch him.
One night, he entered a private residence
and was surrounded by officials.
Kāngzǔ broke through the encirclement and escaped,
and no one dared to pursue him.
He returned to Jīngkǒu that night,
arriving by midnight.
The next morning,
the gate guards went to the prefectural and provincial key posts.
Soon after, a document arrived from Jiànkāng to record his crime.
The officials of the prefecture and province all testified that Kāngzǔ was in Jīngkǒu that night,
so he remained unharmed.
He was impeached repeatedly before and after this,
but Tàizǔ, considering him the son of a meritorious minister,
always pardoned him.
He served as Yuánwài Láng for ten years
and was dismissed twice for gambling.
He was transferred to be Tàizǐ Zuǒ Jī Nǔ Jiàngjūn,
and accompanied Shèshēng Xiàowèi Péi Fāngmíng on the western expedition to Qiúchí.
He was then imprisoned with Fāngmíng in the Grand Judge's office,
and Kāngzǔ was dismissed from office.
After some time,
Shìzǔ, as Governor of Yùzhōu,
garrisoned at Lìyáng,
appointed Kāngzǔ as Zhēnglǔ Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
Once entrusted with responsibility,
he restrained himself and reformed his conduct.
He was transferred to Tàizǐ Yì Jūn Xiàowèi.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Sīmǎ of Nánpíng Wáng Shuò's Ānmán Headquarters.
In the spring of the twenty-seventh year of Yuánjiā (450 CE),
the Sǒulǔ leader, Tuòbá Táo, personally led a large army to attack Rǔnán.
Tàizǔ dispatched various armies to provide relief,
with Kāngzǔ commanding as the vanguard.
When the army reached Xīncài,
they engaged the barbarians in battle.
They advanced more than a hundred *lǐ*,
crossing the Róngshuǐ.
The barbarian forces arrived in great numbers,
but the imperial army vigorously attacked and defeated them.
They beheaded Qǐ Dìzhēn, the false Minister of the Department of the Interior and Duke of Rènchéng.
Forty *lǐ* from Hù County,
Táo burned his camp and retreated.
Kāngzǔ was then transferred to become the General of the Left Army.
Tàizǔ desired to launch a major northern expedition.
Kāngzǔ, deeming the year too late,
requested to wait until the following year.
The Emperor, however, considering that the righteous volunteers north of the Yellow River were rising up simultaneously,
feared that if the army lingered for a full year,
it would dampen their aspirations for justice,
and thus refused.
In the autumn of that year,
Xiāo Bīn, Wáng Xuánmó, Shěn Qìngzhī, and others crossed the Yellow River.
Kāngzǔ led the Yùzhōu army out to Xǔ and Luò.
When Xuánmó and others were defeated and returned,
the barbarians led their vast army south across the river.
The King of Nánpíng, Shuò, was in Shòuyáng.
The Emperor, fearing he would be besieged,
ordered Kāngzǔ to return quickly.
Kāngzǔ turned his army back,
and when he was still tens of *lǐ* from Shòuyáng,
he encountered Kù Rénzhēn, the barbarian Prince of Yǒngchāng, with eighty thousand cavalry from Cháng'ān.
They met at Wèiwǔ.
Kāngzǔ had only eight thousand men.
His deputy, Hú Shèngzhī, wanted to cling to the mountains and rely on treacherous terrain,
advancing by stealth.
Kāngzǔ angrily said:
"I received orders from the imperial court
to clear and pacify the Hélùo region.
Now the invaders have delivered themselves;
there is no need for the imperial army to labor further.
Though these dogs and sheep are numerous,
they are truly easy to crush and destroy.
Our soldiers are elite and our weapons well-trained.
We are only tens of *lǐ* from Shòuyáng,
and reinforcements will soon arrive.
What is there to worry about?"
Thereupon, he formed a cart encampment and advanced.
The barbarians attacked from all four sides.
They fought a great battle for a day and a night,
and the slain barbarians piled up.
The barbarians divided their forces into three,
alternating rest and battle,
and used cavalry to carry grass and burn the cart encampment.
Kāngzǔ spurred on his officers and soldiers,
and none failed to withstand a hundred.
More than half of the barbarians were killed.
Then, Kāngzǔ was struck by an arrow in the neck and died.
Consequently, the army suffered a great defeat,
the entire camp was lost and overrun,
and all were killed by the barbarians.
Only a few tens of men escaped.
The barbarians passed Kāngzǔ's head around to display it in Péngchéng,
and his face was as if alive.
Hú Shèngzhī was captured alive by the barbarians.
Tuòbá Táo favored him,
keeping him always by his side.
Shèngzhī possessed great courage and strength.
Initially, he served as a Supervisor and Staff Officer in the army of Yìxīn, the King of Chángshā.
He was dispatched to quell bandits in Qiáojùn.
Seventy mounted and foot bandits were hiding in the deep thickets west of the county.
Shèngzhī bravely advanced alone
and personally beheaded fifty-eight of them.
In the twenty-eighth year (451 CE),
an imperial edict stated:
"Kāngzǔ, in leading his army back at Wèiwǔ,
maintained strict military discipline.
Facing the numerous with the few,
he annihilated more than half of the enemy.
His fierce spirit soared like clouds,
but his will was fulfilled though his strength gave way.
He sacrificed his life for his country,
which is truly admirable and lamentable.
He should be greatly honored and rewarded
to commend his loyalty and martyrdom.
He is posthumously granted the title of Inspector of Yìzhōu
and given the posthumous name Zhuàngnán (Valiant Male)."
The line of succession continued until the Qí dynasty received the abdication,
and then the kingdom was abolished.
Yuán Hùzhī, courtesy name Yànzōng,
was a native of Lüèyáng and a Dàorén.
His grandfather, Chǎng,
served the Fú clan
as the Administrator of the Household for the state of Chánglè.
When Mùróng Dé entered Qīngzhōu,
he appointed Chǎng as Chief Clerk to the Chariot and Cavalry General.
When Dé's nephew Chāo succeeded to the false throne,
his paternal uncle Zūn and father Miáo were again entrusted with important positions.
Zūn became Minister of Personnel,
and Miáo became Administrator of Jīngzhào.
When Gāozǔ besieged Guǎnggù,
Zūn and Miáo scaled the city walls and surrendered,
both being appointed as Staff Officers to the Grand Commandant.
In the Yuánjiā era of Tàizǔ,
Zūn served as a Supernumerary Attendant Cavalier,
and Miáo as Commander of Cavalry.
Hùzhī was chivalrous in his youth,
not adhering to minor conventions.
His appearance was short and homely,
but his spirit was strong and resolute.
He followed Gāozǔ in the campaign against Sīmǎ Xiūzhī,
serving as Chief Clerk of the Crown Prince's Central Army Headquarters,
concurrently acting as Staff Officer.
In the Yǒngchū era,
he was appointed as an Imperial Attendant.
In the early Yuánjiā era,
he became General of the Department of the Interior.
He accompanied Dào Yànzhī on the northern expedition.
When Yànzhī intended to withdraw his army,
Hùzhī wrote a letter of remonstrance, saying:
"I hear that Your Excellency intends to withdraw your army and turn back your banners.
I secretly disagree.
Why?
The remnants of the barbarians, intimidated by our might,
fled at the sight of our advance.
Territory invaded eight years ago
has been recovered without battle.
It is now the time to drive deep into the northern deserts
and utterly sweep away the remaining scoundrels.
Moreover, they are delivering themselves,
so there is no need for distant labor.
Zú Língxiù should be ordered to quickly advance to Huátái to assist Zhū Xiūzhī in holding it securely.
Your Excellency's main army should advance to confront the region north of the Yellow River.
Then the wandering souls in Láo and Luò
will naturally flee.
Furthermore, in ancient times, there were those who waged war for years,
losing troops and lacking provisions,
yet they still boldly fought forward,
none willing to lightly retreat.
How much more so now, when Qīngzhōu is rich and abundant,
the Jì and Cáo waterways are flowing,
and our soldiers and horses are well-fed and rested,
their power undiminished.
If we abandon Huátái in vain
and idly lose what we have accomplished,
how can this be the intent of the court's commission?"
Yànzhī did not accept his advice,
and returned in disarray.
Tàizǔ heard of this and praised him,
appointing him as Staff Officer to Yìgōng, King of Jiāngxià and General Who Conquers the North, and Administrator of Northern Gāopíng.
He was imprisoned in the Imperial Manufactory for carrying forbidden items,
but after a long time, he was pardoned.
He was then appointed as Staff Officer of the Ever-Flowing Stream to Yìjì, King of Héngyáng and General Who Conquers the North,
and promoted to General Who Manifests Awe and Administrator of Zhōnglí.
He followed Wáng Xuánmó into the Yellow River region.
When Xuánmó attacked Huátái,
Hùzhī's hundred boats served as the vanguard,
advancing to occupy Shíjì.
Shíjì was one hundred twenty *lǐ* southwest of Huátái.
When barbarian reinforcements arrived,
he again urgently wrote to Xuánmó, urging a swift attack,
saying:
"In the past, Emperor Wǔ attacked Guǎnggù,
and many died.
Moreover, circumstances today are different from those days.
How can we consider the casualties and fatigue of our troops?
I wish that taking the city by storm be our priority."
Xuánmó did not follow.
When Xuánmó was defeated and retreated,
he did not have time to inform Hùzhī.
When Hùzhī learned of this,
the barbarians had already pulled all of Xuánmó's large warships
and connected them with triple iron chains
to block the river,
intending to cut off Hùzhī's return route.
The river current was swift.
Hùzhī descended downstream,
and each time he reached the iron chains,
he cut them with a long-handled axe.
The barbarians could not stop him.
He only lost one boat;
all other boats remained intact.
He stayed to garrison Mígōu City.
He was again made an Adjutant to the Aide-de-camp (Hùcáo Cānjūn) of the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn), Líng Yìgōng, Prince of Jiāngxià.
He was garrisoned at Huáinīn.
He was promoted to General Jianwu (Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn)
and concurrently served as Grand Administrator of Jìběi.
He led two thousand men to again follow Zhāng Yǒng in attacking Quēqiáo,
first occupying Wěisùjīn.
The barbarian Dù Dàojùn and the pseudo-Minister (wěi Shàngshū) Fú Lián came to reinforce Quēqiáo.
Hùzhī resisted them.
The bandits then withdrew their army eastward.
Xiāo Sīhuà sent Hùzhī to meet the army at Liángshān.
The pseudo-Minister Hán Yuánxīng led crack cavalry to suddenly arrive.
Hùzhī relied on the strategic terrain to resist the battle,
beheading their Chief Administrator of the Army (Dū Jūn Chángshǐ)
and several tens of armored heads.
The bandits then retreated.
Sīhuà was about to withdraw,
deceiving Hùzhī by saying:
"Shěn Qìngzhī's relief army is about to arrive.
You should quickly build a bridge at Jìkǒu."
Hùzhī guessed his intention
and immediately dispatched commoners.
Sīhuà then ordered him to cross the river and garrison Qǐhuóbǎo to prevent a pursuing army.
Tàizǔ passed away.
He returned to garrison Lìxià.
Hearing that Shìzǔ had entered to suppress the rebellion,
he led his subordinates to rush to him.
The Emperor praised him

and appointed him Supervisor of Military Affairs of Jìzhōu, Qīngzhōu, and the three commanderies of Jìnán, Lè'ān, and Tàiyuán in Jìzhōu, General Níngyuǎn (Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Jìzhōu.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn,
Líng Yìxuān, Prince of Nánjùn, rebelled.
Xú Yíbǎo, Governor of Yǎnzhōu,
who was Hùzhī's wife's younger brother,
formed a distant alliance
and wrote to Hùzhī,
persuading him to join the rebellion.
Hùzhī swiftly sent an envoy to report this.
At that time, Yíbǎo was garrisoned at Húlù.
Hùzhī left his son, Gōngzǔ, to guard Lìchéng
and personally led infantry and cavalry to attack Yíbǎo.
On the way, he passed through Zōushān
and destroyed their separate garrison.
Sixty *lǐ* before reaching Húlù,
Yíbǎo burned the city and fled westward.
Once the Yǎn region was pacified,
he was summoned to be General of Agile Cavalry (Yóujī Jiāngjūn).
He followed Shěn Qìngzhī and others to attack Lǔ Shuǎng
and was promoted to General Fǔguó (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn).
Yìxuān led a large army to Liángshān
and was in a standoff with Wáng Xuánmó.
Liǔ Yuánjǐng led Hùzhī, Hùzhī's younger brother Xúnzhī, Liǔ Shūrén, Zhèng Kūn, and other generals
to garrison Xīntíng.
Xuánmó saw the bandits' strength and prosperity
and sent his Chief Clerk (Sīmǎ) Guǎn Fǎjì to urgently request aid.
The Emperor sent Yuánjǐng and others to advance and occupy Nánzhōu.
Hùzhī's naval forces were the first to depart.
The bandits sent General Páng Fǎqǐ to lead his forces to attack Gūshú.
It happened that Hùzhī, Zhèng Kūn, and others arrived.
They fought fiercely
and severely defeated them,
nearly killing all of them through beheading, capture, or drowning.
Xuánmó swiftly sent a letter to Yuánjǐng, saying:
"The West City cannot be held;
only the East City remains.
The disparity in numbers is too great.
Please retreat to Gūshú
to discuss further advances."
Yuánjǐng refused
and intended to lead all his forces to rescue them.
Hùzhī advised him to divide his army to assist them.
Yuánjǐng agreed with his plan,
and so he assigned elite troops to Hùzhī to go to Liángshān.
During the battle,
Hùzhī saw the bandits' boats and ships densely packed.
"Today, we should use fire to pacify them."
He then ordered his troop leader (Duìzhǎng) Zhāng Tán and others to burn the bandit ships.
The wind was fierce and the water swift,
and the bandit army scattered because of this.
After Liángshān was pacified,
Hùzhī led his army to pursue and attack them.
At that time, Zhū Xiūzhī had already pacified Jiānglíng.
He reached Xúnyáng and then returned.
He was promoted to Supervisor of Military Affairs of Xúzhōu and Yǎnzhōu, and Liángjùn in Yùzhōu, General Níngsuò (Níngsuò Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Xúzhōu,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Yìyáng County,
with an income of one thousand households.
His younger brother, Xúnzhī,
was brave and energetic.
The "Prime Murderer" (Yuánxiōng) had long heard of his reputation
and appointed him Deputy General Fǔguó (Fù Fǔguó Jiāngjūn) to Zhāng Jiǎn.
At that time, Zhāng Chāo initiated a great rebellion.
Xúnzhī planned to kill him
but worried that Jiǎn would not agree.
but also had not yet determined if Xúnzhī shared it.
It happened that Chāo came to discuss matters.
Jiǎn's expression changed.
Xúnzhī noticed it
and immediately they conspired together,
sending a messenger to summon Chāo.
Chāo was suspicious and did not come,
changing his lodging to another place.
Xúnzhī, unaware of his move,
went directly to hack him
and killed his servant in the bed.
He then fled south with Jiǎn.
Jiǎn drowned in the Huái River,
but Xúnzhī managed to arrive.
At that time, Shìzǔ had already ascended the throne
and appointed him General of Accumulated Crossbows (Jīnú Jiāngjūn).
During the battle of Liángshān, he fought bravely
but was struck by a stray arrow
and died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Governor of Jìzhōu.
In the second year,
Hùzhī was imprisoned for discussing achievements with personal bias
and dismissed from office.
He was reinstated as General of Agile Cavalry.
Soon after, he was promoted to Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ),
and concurrently Grand Administrator of Southern Dōnghǎi.
Before being installed,
he was again appointed Supervisor of Military Affairs of Qīngzhōu and Jìzhōu, General Níngyuǎn, and Governor of Qīngzhōu and Jìzhōu,
garrisoned at Lìchéng.
The following year,
he was advanced in title to General Níngsuò
and further appointed Supervisor of Military Affairs of Dōngguǎn and Dōng'ān in Xúzhōu.
and wished to move Qīngzhōu and combine its garrison with Lìchéng.
Many deliberators disagreed.
Hùzhī said:
"To the north of Qīngzhōu are the Yellow River and the Jì River,
and it has many lakes and marshes,
so it is not a direction the barbarians would target.
Whenever they raid,
they must pass through Lìchéng.
Garrisoning both prefectures together
is a long-term strategy.
Its proximity to the Yellow River in the north
makes it easy for those who wish to surrender.
It alleviates the suffering of the people in the short term,
and extends the Emperor's authority in the long term;
it is the best plan for securing the frontier."
Thus, the decision was made.
In the third year of Dàmíng,
he was summoned to be General of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn).
Upon his return,
he heard on the way that Sīkōng Jìnglín Wáng Dàn had rebelled at Guǎnglíng.
Hùzhī immediately led his troops and subordinates to place themselves under the command of General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Dà Jiāngjūn) Shěn Qìngzhī.
After the matter was settled,
he was transferred to be Chief Clerk (Sīmǎ) to the General Who Comforts the Army (Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn) Líng Zǐshàng, Prince of Xīyáng, and Grand Administrator of Línhuái.
The following year,
he was sent out as Envoy with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe), Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yùzhōu and Sīzhōu, General Fǔguó, Governor of Yùzhōu, and Grand Administrator of Huáinán.
He again served under Shěn Qìngzhī in attacking the barbarians of Xīyáng.
Hùzhī was known for extensive extortion wherever he governed,
accumulating a large amount of bribes and goods.
In the seventh year,
he was imprisoned
and dismissed from office.
The following year,
he was again reinstated as Grand Master of the Palace (Tàizhōng Dàfū).
Before being installed,
he died that year
at the age of seventy.
He was posthumously granted the honorary title of Zhuànghóu.
In the first year of Yǒngguāng during the reign of the Former Deposed Emperor (Qián Fèidì),
he was posthumously granted the titles of General Who Eliminates the Barbarians (Guānjūn Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Yùzhōu.
His son Chéngzǔ inherited his title.
After Chéngzǔ died,
his son Xiǎnzōng inherited the title.
When Qí received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
Hùzhī's second son, Gōngzǔ,
was brave and resolute, with his father's demeanor.
In the early Tàishǐ period of Tàizōng,
due to military merits, he became Governor of Liángzhōu and Nán Qínzhōu.
Zūn's son, Làng,
during the Yuánjiā period,
was a Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant (Yuánwài Sànjì Shìláng).
His mother's tomb was desecrated by the Buddhist monk Tán Luò and others from Dōng'ā Temple.
Làng and his younger brother Hóng, who was General of the Palace (Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn), together killed Tán Luò and five others.
They reported their crime to the authorities
and were pardoned.
Làng,
in the third year of Dàmíng,
from Grand Administrator of Yìxīng, became General Níngsuò and Governor of Yǎnzhōu.
He was killed by Jìnglín Wáng Dàn.
He was posthumously granted the title of General Who Quells Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn),
and his governorship remained as before.
Hóng,
at the end of Shēngmíng during the reign of Shùndì,
was General of the Right Guard.
Zhāng Xīngshì, courtesy name Wéndé,
was a native of Jìnglíng.
Originally, his given name was simply Shì.
Emperor Tàizōng added Xīng to his name.
When he was young, his family was poor.
Zōng Zhēnzhī of Nánjùn became the Administrator of Jìnglíng Commandery,
and Xīngshì depended on him as a guest.
Jìnglíng previously had a military administration,
which offered him a position as Cānjūn Dūhù,
but he did not accept it.
As a commoner, he followed Wáng Xuánmó to campaign against the Man tribes.
In every battle,
he consistently captured enemies.
The generals of Xuánmó's old unit could not compare to him,
and Xuánmó greatly admired him.
Upon returning to the capital,
Xuánmó reported to Emperor Tàizǔ,
praising his courage and strength.
[一八]
Later, he followed Emperor Shìzǔ to garrison Xúnyáng,
and was appointed Nánzhōngláng Cānjūn Dūhù.
He entered to suppress the Prime Rebel.
He was assigned to Liǔ Yuánjǐng's vanguard.
After the matter was settled,
he was transferred to Yuánwài Jiāngjūn,
leading the From-the-Ranks Contingent.
When Wáng Yìxuān, Prince of Nánjùn, rebelled,
he again followed Xuánmó to Lǐangshān,
achieving military merits.
He was appointed Jiànpíng Wáng Hóng Zhōngjūn Xíng Cānjūn,
leading the Long Swords.
He was also assigned to Xīpíng Zǐshàng as a personal guard.
Because he followed Zǐshàng into the palace,
abandoning his weapons and wandering off,
he was imprisoned and dismissed from office.
He was again reinstated as a commoner to serve as a personal guard.
At the end of Dàmíng era,
he was appointed Yuánwài Sǎnqí Shìláng,
and then Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn and Suí Jùn Tàishǒu.
Before he could take office,
Emperor Tàizōng ascended the throne,
and rebellions erupted in all directions.
Xīngshì was promoted to Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn,
leading the navy,
to confront the southern rebels at Zhèqí.
Two forts were built at Húkǒu.
[一九] The pseudo-Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Chén Qìng led warships in front as a mobile force.
Xīngshì led Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Jiǎo Chángshēng and Dǒng Kǎizhī to attack and capture the two forts,
then struck Qìng.
Qìng's forces were greatly defeated in battle,
and thousands drowned in the water.
At that time, the imperial army occupied Zhèqí,
and the southern rebels were camped at Quèwěi,
in a long-standing stalemate.
Xīngshì proposed:
"The rebels occupy the upper reaches,
with strong forces and advantageous terrain.
Although we currently have sufficient forces to maintain the stalemate,
we are insufficient to defeat the enemy.
If we now take several thousand troops,
secretly emerge above them,
consolidate our position using the dangerous terrain,
and cut off their lines as appropriate,
making them confused at both ends,
hesitant to advance or retreat,
once their middle waterway is blocked,
their food supply will naturally become difficult.
There is no better strategy to control the rebels than this."
Shěn Yōuzhī and Wú Xǐ both praised his plan.
At that time, Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Yīn Yǎn was occupying Shòuyáng and joining the rebellion.
[二０] He was attacked by Liú Miǎn,
and the southern rebels sent Páng Mèngqiú to lead troops to assist Yǎn.
Liú Miǎn sent an urgent request for reinforcements.
Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén wanted to send Xīngshì to rescue him,
and asked Shěn Yōuzhī.
Yōuzhī said:
"Mèngqiú's forces are like ants,
they will surely achieve nothing.
Sending a separate general with several thousand infantry and cavalry
will be sufficient to control them.
If there is an unexpected situation,
we can temporarily bait them with the territory west of the river.
If we achieve victory in the upper reaches,
[二一] we will not worry about not annihilating them.
Xīngshì's mission
is a critical strategic move for our safety,
and absolutely cannot be stopped."
So, Duàn Fórong and others were sent to reinforce Miǎn.
Xīngshì wanted to lead his troops directly to Dàléi,
but his army had not yet gathered,
making it insufficient for dispersion.
Coincidentally, Xuē Suǒ'ér was pacified,
and Emperor Tàizōng ordered Zhāng Yǒng to station five thousand infantry and cavalry at Xūyí,
sending the remaining twenty thousand troops south to campaign.
Shānyáng was also pacified soon after,
and all the troops led by Ruǎn Diànfū were recalled
to join the southern campaign,
and the armies assembled in large numbers.
Seven thousand warriors were then assigned to Xīngshì.
Xīngshì then ordered light boats to sail upstream,
and then return.
This was repeated for one or two days,
so that the rebels did not prepare for it.
When Liú Hú heard that Xīngshì intended to go upstream,
he laughed and said:
"I still dare not cross down there to take Yángzhōu.
What kind of person is Zhāng Xīngshì,
that he intends to lightly occupy my upper reaches!"
Xīngshì said to Yōuzhī and others:
"In the upper reaches, only Qiánxī can be held.
The terrain is both dangerous and strategically important,
and the river is very narrow.
It is not far from the main forces,
so support can be provided easily.
There are whirlpools in the river,
so boats going downstream will certainly stop there.
There are horizontal inlets on the bank,
where boats can be hidden.
Two or three such points would be suitable."
So, at night, he crossed Húkǒu
to Quètou,
