[二二] then turned back downstream to mislead them.
At the fourth watch that night,
a wind came,
and he hoisted the sails and went straight ahead.
The rebels also sent Hú Língxiù's forces
to the east bank to support each other and advance upstream.
Xīngshì camped overnight at Jǐngjiāngpǔ in the evening,
and the rebels also did not advance.
At night, he secretly dispatched Huáng Dàobiāo to lead seventy boats
directly to occupy Qiánxī,
establishing a camp and palisades.
At dawn the next day,
Xīngshì and his forces assembled.
After stopping for one night,
Liú Hú personally led twenty-six infantry and naval divisions to attack at dawn.
The generals and soldiers wanted to meet the attack,
but Xīngshì forbade them, saying: [二三]
"The rebels are still far off,
and their morale is high, and their arrows are flying rapidly.
Once their swiftness is exhausted,
their high morale will also easily wane.
This is how Cáo Guì defeated Qí."
He ordered his officers and soldiers not to move recklessly,
and to maintain the city as before.
Soon, the rebels came closer,
and their boats entered the whirlpools.
Xīngshì then ordered Shòu Jìzhī and Rèn Nóngfū to lead several hundred brave soldiers to attack them.
The armies advanced one after another,
and Hú was then defeated and fled.
Hundreds of heads were cut off,
and many drowned.
Hú gathered his forces and retreated downstream.
At that time, Xīngshì's fortifications were not yet secure.
Sītú Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén, fearing that the rebels would concentrate their forces to attack Qiánxī again,
wanted to divide their attention.
He ordered Shěn Yōuzhī, Wú Xǐ, Jiǎo Chángshēng, Liú Língyí, and others to use twenty leather warships
to attack the rebels at Nónghú.
They fought fiercely for several days,
capturing and beheading thousands.
On that day,
Liú Hú indeed led his forces,
intending to attack Xīngshì again.
Before reaching Qiánxī by several tens of *lǐ*,
Yuán Yǐ, due to the urgency at Nónghú, quickly pursued him.
The fortifications at Qiánxī were thus able to be established.
The rebels were repeatedly defeated in battle,
and Xīngshì also blocked their supply lines.
Supplies dispatched from Xúnyáng reached Nánlíng,
but dared not proceed downstream.
The rebel forces gradually starved.
Liú Hú then sent Yǐ's Ānběi Fǔsīmǎ, the pseudo-Right General Shěn Zhòngyù, to lead a thousand men to take Nánlíng by land
to meet the supply convoy.
Zhòngyù reached Nánlíng,
taking possession of three hundred thousand *hú* of rice
and several tens of boatloads of money and cloth.
He erected planks to form a temporary fort,
intending to force his way through.
When he reached Guìkǒu,
he dared not advance,
and sent secret messengers to inform Hú,
requesting heavy reinforcements.
Xīngshì, Shòu Jìzhī, Rèn Nóngfū, Lǐ Ānmín, and about three thousand others arrived at Guìkǒu to attack them,
encountering Zhòngyù.
The battle lasted all day,
and Zhòngyù fled back to Yǐ's camp.
All their provisions and wealth were captured,
and the rebel forces were greatly defeated.
Hú abandoned his army and fled,
and Yǐ also dispersed.
Xīngshì led his army in pursuit and suppression,
and together with Wú Xǐ, pacified Jiānglíng.
He was promoted to Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn,
and soon after became Dū Yù Sī Èr Zhōu Nányùzhōu zhī Liángjùn Zhūjūnfúshì,
[二四] enfeoffed as the Marquis of Zuòtáng County,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
Zhēng was appointed Yóují Jiāngjūn.
He led a northern expedition by sea,
provisionally holding the title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
and was granted a jié and appointed assistants,
but returned without achieving anything.
In the fourth year,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Yòuwèi Shuài,
and also held the additional post of Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn with his current office,
serving alongside Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Shěn Yōuzhī.
In the fifth year,
he was transferred to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
In the sixth year,
when Zhōnglǐngjūn Liú Miǎn was to garrison Guǎnglíng,
Xīngshì temporarily assumed the role of Lǐngjūn.
In the first year of Tàiyù,
he was made Chíjié, Dū Yōng Liáng Nán Běi Qín Yǐngzhōu Zhī Jìnglíng Suí Èr Jùn Zhūjūnshì, Guànjūn Jiāngjūn, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and soon after was given the additional title of Níngmán Xiàowèi.
When Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn rebelled,
Xīngshì dispatched troops to assist the imperial court,
but before they could set out, the rebellion was quelled,
and he was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
In the third year of Fèidì Yuánhuī,
he was appointed Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
In the fifth year,
due to illness, he was transferred to Guānglù Dàfū,
with his Chángshì post remaining as before.
In the second year of Shùndì Shēngmíng,
he passed away,
at the age of fifty-nine.
He was posthumously granted his original office.
Xīngshì lived by the Miǎn River.
From Xiāngyáng downstream to Jiǔjiāng,
a distance of two thousand *lǐ*,
there had previously been no islands.
When Xīngshì was first born,
an island suddenly appeared in the water in front of his gate,
and it grew larger year by year.
By the time Xīngshì became a fāngbó,
the island had grown to over ten *qǐng*.
His father, Zhòngzǐ,
achieved the position of Gěishìzhōng through Xīngshì.
Xīngshì wanted to go to Xiāngyáng,
but his father was attached to his hometown
and refused to leave.
He once said to Xīngshì:
"Although I am just an old man from the countryside,
I enjoy hearing drums and horns.
You can send me a set,
and I can play them when I'm working in the fields."
Xīngshì had always been respectful, cautious, and law-abiding,
so he explained to him:
"These are the Emperor's drums and horns,
not for an old man from the countryside to play."
When Xīngshì wanted to visit the ancestral tomb,
Zhòngzǐ told him:
"You have too many attendants;
our ancestors will surely be alarmed."
Xīngshì reduced his retinue before proceeding.
Xīngshì's son, Xīnyè,
was to inherit the feudal title,
but at that time, Qí received the abdication,
and the state was abolished.
The imperial historian says: Warfare is indeed a deceptive path,
and victory lies in employing stratagem.
When the two emperors vied for supremacy,
and the divide between heaven and man was yet undecided,
the north and south engaged in continuous warfare,
locked in a stalemate for half a year.
This was akin to the strategic moment of planting banners on Zhào's wall,
and the day when the armies at Guāndù were extinguished.
As for throwing spears at Quèpǔ,
it was truly the power of Xīngshì's ingenuity.
Erecting banners and conferring official sashes,
how could it be without reason!
Collated Notes
Biographies, Chapter 11: Imperial Clan. Chángshā Jǐng Wáng Dàolián, Línchuān Lièwǔ Wáng Dàoguī, Yíngpǔ Hóu Zūnkǎo.
Chángshā Jǐng Wáng Dàolián
was Gāozǔ's younger brother.
He initially studied at the Guózǐ.
When Xiè Yǎn was Xúzhōu,
he appointed Dàolián as Cóngshì Shǐ.
When Gāozǔ conquered the capital,
and advanced to pacify the capital region,
Dàolián always stayed at home to serve and comfort the Empress Dowager.
When Huán Xuán fled,
Dàjiāngjūn Wǔlíng Wáng Zūn, acting on imperial authority,
appointed Dàolián as Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng.
Soon after, he was promoted to Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Nán Péngchéng Nèishǐ.
At that time, Běi Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Gāi rebelled,
inviting the Suǒ tribe for assistance.
The grand protectors of Qīnghé and Yángpíng commanderies, Sūn Quán, gathered a multitude to respond.
In the first year of Yìxī,
the Suǒ tribe's Tuòbá Kāi dispatched the fake Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Suǒ Dùzhēn and Dàjiāngjūn Húsī Lán to invade Xúzhōu,
attacking Xiāngxiàn,
capturing Jùlù Tàishǒu Hè Shēn,
and then besieging Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Yáng Mùzhī at Péngchéng.
Mùzhī reported the emergency,
and Dàolián led troops to rescue him.
His army reached Língshà,
where he beheaded Quán.
Advancing to Péngchéng,
Zhēn and Lán retreated.
Dàolián led Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn Mèng Lóngfú, Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Kǒng Lóng, and Mùzhī and others in pursuit.
Zhēn and Lán fled to Xiāngchéng,
and were pursued further to Guāngshuǐgōu,
where Liú Gāi was beheaded,
and the enemy troops were almost entirely killed or drowned.
When Gāozǔ was stationed at Jīngkǒu,
Dàolián was promoted to Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn,
and also concurrently held the title of Tángyì Tàishǒu,
garrisoning Shítou.
The following year,
he was given the additional titles of Shǐchíjié and Jiān Zhēngshǔ Zhūjūnshì,
and led Guànjūn Jiāngjūn Liú Jìngxūan and others to attack Qiáo Zòng,
but Wén Chǔmào and Wēn Zuò held strong positions, preventing their advance,
so the expedition was not carried out.
For his meritorious service, he was enfeoffed as a fifth-rank marquis of Xīnxīng Xiàn.
In the fourth year,
he replaced Zhūgě Chángmín as Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ and Yìchāng Tàishǒu,
with his titles of Jiāngjūn and Nèishǐ remaining as before,
still garrisoning Shítou.
At that time, the Xiānbēi invaded and pressed,
and from Péngchéng southwards,
the people all gathered for protection,
and the garrisons at Shānyáng, Huáin, and other places were no longer maintained.
Dàolián requested to hold Péngchéng
and gradually rebuild it,
but the imperial court considered Péngchéng too distant
and had him garrison Shānyáng.
He was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Dū Huáiběi Jūnjùnshì, and Běi Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu,
with his titles of Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ and Yìchāng Tàishǒu remaining as before.
For his achievement in defeating Suǒ Dùzhēn,
he was enfeoffed as an earl of Xīnyú Xiàn,
with a stipend of five hundred households.
He followed Gāozǔ in campaigning against Guǎnggù,
always serving as the vanguard.
When the city fell,
Mùróng Chāo was about to break through the encirclement with his personal guards and escape,
but Dàolián's troops captured him.
He was given the additional title of Shǐchíjié,
and promoted to Zuǒ Jiāngjūn.
In the seventh year,
he was relieved of his Bìngzhōu post,
given the additional title of Běi Xúzhōu Cìshǐ,
and moved his garrison to Péngchéng.
In the eighth year,
when Gāozǔ attacked Liú Yì,
Dàolián was appointed Dūdū Yǎn Qīng Èrzhōu Jìnlíng Jīngkǒu Huáinán Zhūjùn Jūnshì, and Yǎn Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his titles of Chíjié, Jiāngjūn, and Tàishǒu remaining as before,
and he returned to garrison Jīngkǒu.
In the ninth year,
fifty armed guards were permitted to enter the palace.
For his achievement at Guǎnggù,
he was re-enfeoffed as the duke of Jìnglíng Xiàn,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
Half of his previous enfeoffed households and territory were reduced
and bestowed upon his second son, Yìzōng.
In the tenth year,
he was promoted to Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn,
given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì,
and granted a set of drums and wind instruments.
The following year, when Sīmǎ Xiūzhī was being campaigned against,
Dàolián supervised the affairs of the resident government,
and one hundred armed guards were permitted to enter the palace.
After Jiānglíng was pacified,
he was appointed Dūdū Jīng Xiāng Yì Qín Níng Liáng Yōng Qīzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Piàojí Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Lǐng Hù Nánmán Xiàowèi, and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his titles of Chíjié and Chángshì remaining as before.
All military and civil officials of the Northern Garrison were assigned to him.
Dàolián naturally lacked talent,
and his accent was very rustic;
his demeanor and actions
were often vulgar and clumsy.
Although Gāozǔ sent generals and assistants to aid him,
he was excessively greedy and indulgent,
constantly accumulating wealth and goods
as if never having enough.
On the day he left his post,
the treasury was emptied because of him.
When Gāozǔ 平定 (pacified) the Three Qín,
he was contemplating external campaigns.

He summoned Dàolián back to serve as Shìzhōng, Dūdū (military governor) of the armies of Xú, Yǎn, and Qīng three provinces, and Jìnlíng of Yángzhōu, Shǒu Shàngshūlìng, and Inspector of Xú and Yǎn two provinces.
His Chíjíe (credential) and generalship remained as before.
In Yuánxī元年 (the first year),
he was relieved of Shàngshūlìng
and promoted to Sīkōng.
He was sent out to garrison Jīngkǒu.
When Gāozǔ received the Mandate,
he was promoted to Tàiwèi
and enfeoffed as Chángshā Wáng.
He was granted an eating-fief of five thousand households.
His Chíjíe, Shìzhōng, Dūdū, and inspectorate remained as before.
In Yǒngchū二年 (the second year), during the 朝正 (New Year's court assembly),
he was to reside in the palace offices.
Prior to this,
Lúlíng Wáng Yìzhēn was the Inspector of Yángzhōu.
The Empress Dowager said to the Emperor,
"Dàolián is your sworn brother from humble beginnings,
so he should be appointed Inspector of Yángzhōu."
The Emperor replied,
"How could Jìnnú be reluctant to give Dàolián anything?
Yángzhōu is the fundamental place of reliance,
and its affairs are numerous,
which Dàolián is not capable of handling."
The Empress Dowager said,
"Dàolián is over fifty years old.
How could he be inferior to your ten-year-old son?"
The Emperor replied,
"Although Chēshì is the Inspector,
all matters, big or small,
are decided by Jìnnú.
Dàolián is old,
and if he does not personally attend to these matters,
it will not meet expectations."
The Empress Dowager then had nothing more to say.
Chēshì
was Yìzhēn's childhood name.
In the spring of the third year,
Gāozǔ was unwell,
and his guards were increased to thirty men with swords.
At that time, Dàolián was in court,
leaving Sīmǎ Lù Zhòngyuán to guard the post.
Diāo Kuí's son Mí became a fugitive,
and led several tens of men into the capital city.
Zhòngyuán attacked and beheaded him.
Previously,
a government clerk had reported Mí's rebellious intentions.
At this point, he was granted two hundred thousand cash
and appointed a county magistrate.
In the fifth month,
the imperial carriage passed away (the Emperor died),
but Dàolián was too ill to attend the funeral.
In the sixth month,
he passed away
at the age of fifty-five.
He was posthumously granted Tàifù.
His Chíjíe, Shìzhōng, Dūdū, and inspectorate remained as before.
His sacrificial rites followed the precedent of Jìn Tàizǎi Ānpíng Wáng,
with a luánlù (phoenix carriage) with nine streamers,
a huángwū (yellow imperial canopy) with a zuǒdáo (left battle-axe banner),
a wēnliáng (carriage for sleeping),
two sets of mournful songs,
front and rear divisions with feathered canopies and drum music,
and one hundred hǔbēn (imperial guards) with swords.
In the ninth year of Tàizǔ Yuánjiā,
an edict stated:
"In ancient times, enlightened kings governed the state,
and the Department of Merits had its regulations.
They deliberated to manage virtue and punishment,
and conferred insignia to reward accomplishments and merits.
Their glorious deeds were inscribed on tripods and vessels,
and their spirits were included in the ancestral temple sacrifices.
Thus, to share in the offerings to former kings
was a principle found in the Shāng Gào,
and to sacrifice at the Dàzhēng (Grand Sacrifice)
was a rite recorded in the Zhōu Diǎn.
From the Hàn to the Jìn dynasties,
this custom was highly esteemed.
As the king's achievements became manifest,
both the living and the deceased were given their due ranks.
The late Emperor organized heaven and earth,
restored order and received the Mandate.
His grand destiny converged,
and his glory illuminated the realm.
Although his sagely wisdom operated profoundly,
and the three spiritual powers truly cooperated,
it was also due to the diligent efforts of his trusted ministers who assisted him,
and the efficacy of the Qífù (Minister of War) in exerting his strength.
Therefore, the former Chíjíe, Shìzhōng, Dūdū of the armies of Nán Xú, Yǎn two provinces, and Jìnlíng and Jīngkǒu of Yángzhōu, Tàifù, Inspector of Nán Xú and Yǎn two provinces, Chángshā Jǐng Wáng;
the former Shìzhōng, Dàsīmǎ, Línchuān Lièwǔ Wáng;
the former Sītú, Nánkāng Wénxuān Gōng Mùzhī;
Shìzhōng, Wèi Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Lù Shàngshū Shì, Inspector of Yángzhōu, Huáróng Xiàn Kāiguó Gōng Hóng;

Chíjíe, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū of the armies of Jiāngzhōu, Yùzhōu, Xīyáng, Xīncài, and Jìnxī four commanderies, Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, Yǒngxiū Xiàn Kāiguó Gōng Dàojì;
and the former Zuǒ Jiāngjūn, Inspector of Qīngzhōu, Lóngyáng Xiàn Kāiguó Hóu Zhèn'è;
some of whom walked the broad path of virtue,
holding lofty and distant moral principles;
some of whom possessed refined and superior magnanimity,
with clear and far-reaching discernment;
and some of whom had knowledge that was only righteous,
with outstanding talent and strategy;
all by their cultivated virtue illuminated the Emperor's reign,
and by their military achievements elevated the glorious enterprise.
They truly rivaled Jī Dàn
and were comparable to Yī (Yī Yǐn) and Shào (Shào Gōng).
I, with my meager virtue,
have inherited this grand legacy.
I often reflect on their meritorious deeds
and wish to follow the excellent precedents.
However, the grand rites have not yet been inscribed,
and the joint sacrifices are still lacking.
Awake and asleep, I admire and recall them,
and this thought fills me with deep emotion.
It is fitting to respectfully follow these former models,
and to institute these splendid rites,
to record their achievements in the imperial archives,
and to sacrifice to them in the ancestral temple,
so as to display their glorious insignia,
and to bestow lasting renown,
so that their great achievements and distant strategies
may be eternally passed down and remain imperishable."
Dàolián had six sons: Yìxīn, Yìqìng, Yìróng, Yìzōng, Yìbīn, and Yìqí.
Yìxīn succeeded him
as Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng,
but did not accept the appointment.
He successively held the posts of Zhōnglǐngjūn,
Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Inspector of Qīngzhōu, and Grand Administrator of Wèijùn.
His generalship remained as before.
He garrisoned Shítou.
In Yuánjiā元年 (the first year),
he was promoted to Hòu Jiāngjūn
and additionally made Sànqí Chángshì.
In the third year,
with his original title, he became Inspector of Nányǎnzhōu.
In the seventh year,
Dào Yànzhī led a large army into the river (area),
and Yìxīn advanced to Péngchéng
to provide support for the various armies.
Yànzhī was defeated and retreated,
and Qīng and Qí were in turmoil.
His subordinates feared a large-scale invasion
and advised Yìxīn to abandon his post and return to the capital.
Yìxīn remained steadfast and did not move.
He was transferred to Chíjíe, Jiān (supervisor) of the armies of Yù, Sī, Yōng, and Bìng four provinces, and Inspector of Yùzhōu.
His generalship remained as before.
He was granted a set of drum music.
He garrisoned Shòuyáng.
At that time, the territory was desolate and ruined,
the people were scattered,
cities and towns were dilapidated,
and bandits roamed publicly.
Yìxīn (義欣) undertook the task of restoration and repair,
managing affairs as was expedient.
Where robbers passed through,
he immediately established a system of pursuit and execution.
Within his jurisdiction, people were in awe and submitted,
and nothing was picked up from the roads.
The city treasuries and storehouses
were all complete and full,
thus he became a flourishing dependency and a strong garrison.
At that time, the chief officials of Huáixī (淮西) and Jiāngběi (江北)
were all weary and military men,
mostly lacking in administrative skills.
Yìxīn (義欣) presented this argument:
“To the left and right of Jiānghuái (江淮),
the land is barren and the populace sparse.
In recent years,
famines have repeatedly struck,
and a hundred cities are devastated,
worse now than ever.
The proper way to pacify and govern
must await good officials.
Weary and military men,
untrained in administration,
and the internal officials
are mostly appointed without talent.
The prosperous Southeast
still sometimes selects the able,
how much more so should the desolate border regions,
which require careful management, not be neglected.
〔一０〕I wish to instruct the selection department
to ensure that suitable people are appointed to their posts,
so that governance may be achieved without excessive effort.”
The fertile fields of Quèpí (芍陂), numbering over ten thousand qǐng,
had long suffered from broken dikes and dams,
and often endured drought in autumn and summer.
Yìxīn (義欣) sent his Advisory Army Supervisor Yīn Sù (殷肅) to inspect and repair them.
There was an old canal that drew water from Pí (卑) into the reservoir,
but it had been neglected for a long time,
and trees and thickets blocked it.
Sù (肅) cut down trees and cleared the thickets,
allowing the water to flow through,
and the problem of drought was thereby eliminated.
In the tenth year,
he was promoted to the title of Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn (鎮軍將軍)
and advanced to Dūdū (都督).
In the eleventh year, in summer,
he entered the court for an audience,
and Tàizǔ (太祖) bestowed great favor and courtesy upon him.
In the sixteenth year,
he passed away,
at the age of thirty-six.
He was posthumously granted the titles Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍), Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (征西將軍), and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司),
with the same status as Chíjìe (持節), Dūdū (都督), and Cìshǐ (刺史).
His posthumous title was Chéng Wáng (成王).
His son, Dào Wáng Jǐn (悼王瑾), courtesy name Yàn Yú (彥瑜),
rose to the office of Tàizǐ Túnqí Xiàowèi (太子屯騎校尉).
In the thirtieth year,
he was killed by the prime culprit.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
His son Càn (粲) died young.
Càn’s (粲) younger brother Zuǎn (纂), courtesy name Yuán Jī (元績), succeeded him.
He rose to the office of Bùbīng Xiàowèi (步兵校尉).
In the third year of Shùndì (順帝)'s Shēngmíng (昇明) era, he passed away.
When Qí (齊) received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
Jǐn’s (瑾) younger brother Zhī (祗), courtesy name Yàn Qī (彥期),
served as Zhōngshū Láng (中書郎) during the Dàmíng (大明) era.
When Tàizǎi (太宰) Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng (江夏王義恭) concurrently held the post of Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監),
as close relatives could not serve over each other,
he submitted a memorial requesting to resign.
Shìzǔ (世祖) issued an imperial edict saying:
“In the past, the two Wáng (王) and two Xiè (謝) families
both received high honors.
From now on, the Sāntái (三臺) and Wǔshěng (五省)
shall all follow this precedent.”
At the beginning of Tàizōng (太宗)’s reign,
he served as Nányánzhōu Cìshǐ (南兗州刺史) and Dūguān Shàngshū (都官尚書).
He conspired with Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn (晉安王子勛) in rebellion
and was executed.
Zhī’s (祗) younger brother Kǎi (楷), Mìshū Láng (祕書郎),
was killed by the prime culprit
and posthumously granted Tōngzhí Láng (通直郎).
Kǎi’s (楷) younger brother Zhān (瞻),
Jìn'ān Tàishǒu (晉安太守),
joined Zǐxūn (子勛) in rebellion
and was executed.
Zhān’s (瞻) younger brother Yùn (韞), courtesy name Yàn Wén (彥文),
was Bùbīng Xiàowèi (步兵校尉) and Xuānchéng Tàishǒu (宣城太shǒu).
When Zǐxūn (子勛) stirred up trouble,
his forces massed at Quèwěi (鵲尾)
and attacked Xuānchéng (宣城).
At that time, the governors and prefects of the four directions
all joined the rebellion.
Only Yùn (韞) abandoned his commandery and went to the imperial court.
Tàizōng (太宗) commended his loyalty
and appointed him Huángmén Láng (黃門郎),
Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子),
Shìzhōng (侍中),
and additionally Jing (荊) and Xiāng (湘) provinces,
Nányánzhōu Cìshǐ (南兗州刺史),
and Wúxīng Tàishǒu (吳興太shǒu).
He was Shìzhōng (侍中)
and concurrently Lǐng Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn (領左軍將軍).
He was then changed to concurrently Lǐng Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (領驍騎將軍),
Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn (撫軍將軍),
and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ (雍州刺史).
He was Shìzhōng (侍中)
and concurrently Lǐng Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (領右衞將軍).
He was changed to concurrently Lǐng Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (領左衞將軍), Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍), and Zhōnglǐngjūn (中領軍).
In the first year of Shēngmíng (昇明),
he plotted rebellion and was executed.
〔一一〕Yùn (韞)’s talent was mediocre and vulgar,
but because of his merit in Xuānchéng (宣城),
he was especially favored by Tàizōng (太宗).
In Xiāngzhōu (湘州) and Yōngzhōu (雍州),
he had skilled painters depict his traveling retinue and ceremonial guards,
which he constantly studied with pleasure.
He once showed this painting to Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Cài Xīngzōng (征西將軍蔡興宗).
Xīngzōng (興宗) joked with him,
pretending not to understand painting,
and pointed to Yùn’s (韞) figure, asking:
“Who is this person in the carriage?”
Yùn (韞) replied:
“That is precisely me.”
His vulgarity was thus.
Yùn’s (韞) younger brother Bì (弼),
Wǔchāng Tàishǒu (武昌太守),
also joined Zǐxūn (子勛) in rebellion
and was executed.
His younger brother Jiàn (鑒),
Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng (員外散騎侍郎),
died young.
Jiàn’s (鑒) younger brother Xié (勰), courtesy name Yàn Hé (彥龢),
was Shìzhōng (侍中) and Wúxīng Tàishǒu (吳興太守).
He died in the first year of Hòufèidì (後廢帝)’s Yuánhuī (元徽) era.
Xié’s (勰) younger brother Hào (顥), courtesy name Yàn Míng (彥明),
was Shìzhōng (侍中) and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (左衞將軍),
Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍) and Wúxīng Tàishǒu (吳興太shǒu).
Before he took office,
he died in the fourth year of Yuánhuī (元徽)
and was posthumously granted Yòujiāngjūn (右將軍).
Hào’s (顥) younger brother Shù (述),
Dōngyáng Tàishǒu (東陽太守) and Huángmén Láng (黃門郎),
joined his cousin Bǐng (秉) in rebellion.
When their plot failed, he fled to Báishān (白山),
was pursued, captured, and executed.
Yìxīn’s (義欣) younger brother Yìqìng (義慶)
was adopted into the lineage of Línchuān Lièwǔ Wáng Dàoguī (臨川烈武王道規).
Yìqìng’s (義慶) younger brother Yìróng (義融)
was enfeoffed as Guìyáng Xiàn Hóu (桂陽縣侯) in the first year of Yǒngchū (永初),
with a stipend of one thousand households.
Generally, princes who were enfeoffed as marquises
all received stipends of one thousand households.
Yìróng (義融) successively served as Shìzhōng (侍中),
Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (左衞將軍),
〔一二〕concurrently Lǐng Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (領太子中庶子),
Wǔbīng Shàngshū (五兵尚書),
and Lǐngjūn (領軍).
He had a steadfast character
and was skilled in using short shields.
In the eighteenth year of Yuánjiā (元嘉),
he died,
and was posthumously granted Chējì Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍).
His posthumous title was Gōng Hóu (恭侯).
His son Xiàohóu Jì (孝侯覬) succeeded him.
He rose to the office of Tàizǐ Yìjūn Xiàowèi (太子翊軍校尉)
and was killed by the prime culprit.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
Having no son,
his younger brother Xí (襲) had his son Huàng (晃) succeed to the enfeoffment.
In the second year of Shēngmíng (昇明),
he conspired in rebellion with Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng Ānchéng Jíb Rénzǔ (員外散騎侍郎安成戢仁祖), commoner Wáng Wǔlián (王武連), and Yúlín Deputy Péng Yuánjùn (羽林副彭元儁) and others.
The state was abolished.
Xí, courtesy name Màodé,
was a Tàizǐ Shèrén
and Ānchéng Tàishǒu.
When Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn rebelled,
Xí held the commandery and resisted him.
Zǐxūn sent troops to attack and besiege, but could not conquer it.
Tàizōng praised him
and made him Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ,
enfeoffing him as Jiànlíng Xiàn Hóu,
with an income of five hundred households.
Jiànlíng Xiàn belonged to Cāngwú Jùn.
Due to its remoteness,
he was re-enfeoffed as Línlǐ Xiàn Hóu.
In the sixth year of Tàishǐ (470 CE),
he died in the post of Zhōnghùjūn.
He was posthumously granted the title of Hùjūn Jiāngjūn,
and additionally Sànqí Chángshì,
with the posthumous name Zhōnghóu.
Xí was also ordinary and vulgar.
While in Yǐngzhōu,
during a summer month, he sat exposed on a [⿱艹王] in the official hall,
while his subordinates and disciplinarians prostrated themselves at the door.
They found it strange,
and when they inquired,
they discovered it was Xí.
〔一三〕His son Mín succeeded him.
In the second year of Shēngmíng (478 CE),
he was re-enfeoffed as Dōngchāng Xiàn Hóu,
and was executed along with his elder brother Huàng.
Xí's younger brother Biāo
was a Mìshū Láng.
His younger brother Shí
was a Tàizǐ Shèrén.
Both died young.
Shí's younger brother Shuǎng
was Hǎilíng Tàishǒu.
Yìróng's younger brother Yìzōng
was loved by Gāozǔ when he was young,
who gave him the courtesy name Bó'nú
and granted him the title of Xīnyú Xiàn Nán.
In the first year of Yǒngchū (420 CE),
he was promoted to the rank of Hóu.
He successively held the posts of Huángmén Shìláng
and Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài.
In the eighth year of Yuánjiā (431 CE),
he was implicated when his protégé Dù Délíng behaved unruly and beat someone,
and then hid in his residence.
Yìzōng concealed him,
and was dismissed from office.
Délíng was naturally handsome,
and was favored by Yìzōng.
He was originally a clerk in Kuàijī Jùn.
When Xiè Fāngmíng was the commander,
Fāngmíng's son Huìlián loved and favored him,
composing more than ten poems for him,
among which were the "Chéngliú Zūnguī Zhǔ" chapter.
He also served as Shìzhōng and Tàizǐ Zhānjì,
with additional titles of Sànqí Chángshì, Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, and Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the twenty-first year (444 CE),
he died.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Sànqí Chángshì and Píngběi Jiāngjūn,
with the posthumous name Huìhóu.
He loved scholars and enjoyed giving,
and also had a fondness for literature.
The world thus praised him.
His son, Huáihóu Jiè, succeeded him,
and was Lángxié and Qínjùn Tàishǒu.
He was killed by the prime culprit (the "original凶"),
and was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì.
Having no son,
his younger brother Bǐng passed on his son to succeed to the enfeoffment.
Bǐng, courtesy name Yànjié,
initially served as Zhùzuò Láng,
and successively held the posts of Yǔlín Jiān,
Yuèqí Xiàowèi,
Zhōngshū and Huángmén Shìláng.
At the beginning of Tàishǐ during Tàizōng's reign (465 CE),
he became Shìzhōng,
and was frequently transferred to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
Dānyáng Yǐn,
Tàizǐ Zhānjì,
and Lìbù Shàngshū.
At that time, although there were many members of the imperial clan,
those with talent and ability were very few.
Bǐng had disciplined himself since youth
and was highly praised by both the court and the public,
thus he was entrusted by Tàizōng.
In the fifth year (469 CE),
he was appointed as Qián Jiāngjūn and Tàishǒu of Huáinán and Xuānchéng Commanderies,
but did not accept the appointment
and returned to his original post.
He again served as Shìzhōng,
then Shǒu Mìshū Jiān,
and concurrently Tàizǐ Zhānjì.
Before taking office,
he was promoted to Shǐchíjié, Dūdū of the military affairs of the six prefectures of Nánxú, Xú, Yǎn, Yù, Qīng, and Jì, Hòujiāngjūn, and Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ,
with additional Sànqí Chángshì.
After Hòufèidì ascended the throne (472 CE),
he was transferred to Dūdū of the military affairs of Yǐngzhōu, Xīyáng and Yìyáng of Yùzhōu and Sīzhōu, Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the titles Chíjié and Chángshì remaining as before.
Before taking office,
he was retained as Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè
and participated in selections.
In the first year of Yuánhuī (473 CE),
he concurrently held Lìbù
and was given an additional five hundred soldiers.
Soon after, he concurrently held Wèiwèi,
but declined the appointment.
When Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn rebelled,
Zhōnglǐngjūn Liú Miǎn went out to guard Shítou.
Bǐng temporarily held the concurrent post of Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
and the additional soldiers he was given
followed him into the palace.
In the second year (474 CE),
he was additionally Sànqí Chángshì and Dānyáng Yǐn,
and relieved of Lìbù.
He was enfeoffed as Dāngyáng Xiàn Hóu,
with an income of one thousand households.
He shared the duty of making critical decisions daily with Qí Wáng, Yuán Càn, and Chǔ Yuān.
In the fourth year (476 CE),
he was promoted to Zhōngshū Lìng,
with additional Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn,
and the titles Chángshì and Yǐn remained as before.
When Shùndì ascended the throne (479 CE),
he was transferred to Shàngshū Lìng and Zhōnglǐngjūn,
with the general title remaining as before.
At that time, Qí Wáng was regent,
and all under heaven looked to him.
Bǐng knew that the mandate of the dynasty was shifting
and secretly harbored different intentions.
Yuán Càn, guarding Shítou,
did not recognize the mandate of Heaven.
Shěn Yōuzhī raised an army to rebel,
and Qí Wáng garrisoned the imperial hall.
Càn secretly conspired with Bǐng and other great generals like Huáng Huí to plot a rebellion.
They originally planned to meet at Shítou at night
and raise troops at dawn.
Bǐng was always timid, agitated,
and restless.
After the second meal (afternoon),
he immediately loaded his women and family onto carts from Dānyáng Jùn,
and his entire household fled to Shítou.
His troops, several hundred strong,
formed a magnificent array filling the road.
When he arrived and saw Càn,
Càn was shocked and said,
"Why did you come so suddenly? The matter is ruined now!"
Bǐng replied,
"Now that I have seen you,
what regret could there be in ten thousand deaths?"
His cousin, Zhōnglǐngjūn Yùn,
who was on duty in the palace,
conspired with Zhíhé Jiāngjūn Bǔ Bóxīng
to attack Qí Wáng together that night.
At the same time, Bǐng's departure was discovered,
and Qí Wáng sent Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Wáng Jìngzé that night to arrest Yùn.
Yùn had already been put on alert,
but Jìngzé led brave men directly forward,
and Yùn's左右 all scattered.
Consequently, he killed him,
and Bóxīng was also executed.
When Càn was defeated,
Bǐng scaled the city wall and fled,
but was captured at Yánhú
〔一四〕and died along with his two sons Chéng and Yǔ.
Bǐng was forty-five years old at that time.
Bǐng's wife, Xiāo Shì,
was Sīhuà's daughter.
During the Yuánhuī era,
the court was in peril.
His wife often feared disaster
and frequently said to Bǐng,
"Your wealth and high position are already sufficient.
You should make plans for your sons.
You are almost fifty;
why begrudge your remaining life?"
Bǐng could not follow her advice.
Bǐng's younger brother Mó
was Fèngcháoqǐng.
Mó Dì Xiá [遐], whose courtesy name was Yàndào [彥道],
also served as Fèngcháoqǐng [奉朝請] and Yuánwài Sǎnjì Shìláng [員外散騎侍郎].
He had a private affair with Yīn [殷], his stepmother's adopted daughter Yúnfū [雲敷],
which Yīn [殷] constantly tried to forbid.
Yīn [殷] died suddenly of illness.
Before the grand enshrouding,
blood flowed from her mouth and nose.
It was suspected that Xiá [遐] had secretly poisoned her,
and he was impeached by the judicial authorities.
Shìzǔ [世祖] exiled him to Shǐ'ān Jùn [始安郡].
He was allowed to return during the Yǒngguāng [永光] era.
During the reign of Tàizōng [太宗],
he successively held the positions of Huángmén Shìláng [黃門侍郎],
Dūguān Shàngshū [都官尚書],
and Wú Jùn Tàishǒu [吳郡太守].
After his elder brother Bǐng [秉] had died,
Qí Wáng [齊王] sent someone to execute him.
Xiá's [遐] talent was very ordinary.
He concealed his name,
and often said to guests:
"Xiàowǔ [孝武] was lawless,
and wrongfully accused me of killing my mother."
He was as stubborn and foolish as this.
When Bǐng [秉] was in power,
Xiá [遐] repeatedly sought to become a fāngbó [方伯].
Bǐng [秉] said:
"While I am alive,
if I appoint you as a zhōu [州],
it will not meet expectations."
Xiá [遐] said:
"When you are rich and honored, you say we cannot be related,
but on the day of punishment,
will I be able to escape?"
It was then that he indeed died.
Yìzōng's [義宗] younger brother Yìbīn [義賓],
in the second year of Yuánjiā [元嘉] (425 CE),
was enfeoffed as Xīnyě Xiàn Hóu [新野縣侯].
In the sixth year (429 CE),
because Xīnyě [新野] was desolate and dilapidated,
he was re-enfeoffed as Xīng'ān Xiàn Hóu [興安縣侯].
He served as Huángmén Láng [黃門郎],
Mìshū Jiān [祕書監],
Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn [左衞將軍],
and his highest position was Fǔguó Jiāngjūn [輔國將軍] and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ [徐州刺史].
In the twenty-fifth year (448 CE),
he died.
He was posthumously granted Hòujiāngjūn [後將軍],
and given the posthumous title Sù Hóu [肅侯].
His son Huì Hóu Zōng [惠侯綜] succeeded him.
When Zōng [綜] died,
his son Xiàn [憲] succeeded him.
In the third year of Shēngmíng [昇明] (479 CE),
Qí [齊] received the abdication,
and his peerage was abolished.
Zōng's [綜] younger brother Kūn [琨]
was Jìnpíng Tàishǒu [晉平太守].
Yìbīn's [義賓] younger brother Yìqí [義綦],
in the sixth year of Yuánjiā [元嘉] (429 CE),
was enfeoffed as Yíngdào Xiàn Hóu [營道縣侯].
He was common and ignorant,
and was often teased by Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn [始興王濬] and his brothers.
Jùn [濬] once said to Yìqí [義綦]:
"Lù Shìhéng's [陸士衡] poem says: 'Yíngdào [營道] has no valiant heart.'
What does it mean to be so hard on your father?"
Yìqí [義綦] said:
"This humble official did not know at first,
why suddenly is he being hard?"
His mediocrity and foolishness were laughable, like this.
He successively served as Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn [右衞將軍],
and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ [湘州刺史].
In the second year of Xiàojiàn [孝建] (455 CE),
he died.
He was posthumously granted Píngnán Jiāngjūn [平南將軍],
and given the posthumous title Xī Hóu [僖侯].
His son Chángyóu [長猷] succeeded him,
and his highest office was Bùbīng Xiàowèi [步兵校尉].
In the third year of Shēngpíng [昇平] (479 CE),
he died.
Qí [齊] received the abdication,
and his peerage was abolished.
Línchuān Lièwǔ Wáng Dàoguī [臨川烈武王道規],
whose courtesy name was Dàozé [道則],
was Gāozǔ's [高祖] youngest younger brother.
In his youth, he was unrestrained and had great ambitions.
Gāozǔ [高祖] admired him greatly,
and consulted with him about executing Huán Xuán [桓玄].
At that time, Huán Hóng [桓弘] was stationed in Guǎnglíng [廣陵],
and Dàoguī [道規] was made Zhēnglǔ Zhōngbīng Cānjūn [征虜中兵參軍].
When Gāozǔ [高祖] conquered Jīngchéng [京城],
Dàoguī [道規] also, on that same day, together with Liú Yì [劉毅] and Mèng Chǎng [孟昶], killed Hóng [弘],
gathered his troops, and crossed the river.
They advanced and pacified Jīngyì [京邑].
Xuán [玄] was defeated and fled.
Jìn [晉] Grand General Wǔlíng Wáng Zūn [武陵王遵], acting on imperial authority,
appointed Dàoguī [道規] as Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn [振武將軍] and Yìchāng Tàishǒu [義昌太守].
He pursued Xuán [玄] with Liú Yì [劉毅] and Hé Wújí [何無忌].
Xuán [玄] fled west to Jiānglíng [江陵],
leaving Guō Quán [郭銓] and Hé Dànzhī [何澹之] to guard Pénkǒu [盆口].
[一五] When the righteous army arrived,
the rebels lined up their ships to resist them.
Dànzhī [澹之] merely set up feathered ceremonial regalia and banners on one boat,
while he himself was on another ship.
Wújí [無忌] wanted to attack where the regalia was,
but the multitude all disagreed,
saying:
"Dànzhī [澹之] is certainly not on this boat; even if we capture it, it will be useless."
Wújí [無忌] said:
"That Dànzhī [澹之] is not on this boat,
indeed needs no saying.
Since he is not on it,
then the warriors must be weak.
If we attack it with strong troops,
we will surely capture it.
On the day we capture it,
they will certainly think they have lost their army commander,
and our troops will all believe they have captured the rebel leader.
We will be brave and they will be fearful;
fearing, we will press them,
and their defeat is certain."
Dàoguī [道規] rejoiced, saying:
"This is a brilliant plan!"
Consequently, they went and attacked that boat,
and immediately captured it.
Then they beat drums and shouted, proclaiming:
"Hé Dànzhī [何澹之] has been beheaded!"
The rebels and the righteous army alike believed it.
Thereupon, they unleashed their troops,
and the rebel multitude fled in defeat.
They immediately took Pénkǒu [盆口]
and advanced to pacify Xúnyáng [尋陽].
They then pressed on again,
encountering Xuán [玄] at Zhēngróng Zhōu [崢嶸洲].
Dàoguī [道規] and his troops numbered less than ten thousand men,
while Xuán's [玄] warriors numbered tens of thousands.
Everyone was apprehensive,
wishing to retreat to Xúnyáng [尋陽].
Dàoguī [道規] said:
"No.
Their multitude and our few,
strong and weak, are different in power.
If we now fear and shrink back without advancing,
we will certainly be taken advantage of.
Even if we reach Xúnyáng [尋陽],
how can we secure ourselves?
Although Xuán [玄] falsely claims to be a hero,
he is inwardly timid and fearful.
Moreover, he has already fled in defeat,
and his troops have no firm resolve.
When the two armies decide the moment,
the valiant will win.
In the past, Guāngwǔ's [光武] battle at Kūnyáng [昆陽]
and Cáo Cāo's [曹操] army at Guāndù [官渡]
both used few to defeat many,
which is commonly known.
Although our talent now falls short of the ancients,
how can we first show weakness?"
He then waved his troops forward,
Yì [毅] and others followed him,
and they greatly defeated Xuán's [玄] army.
Guō Quán [郭銓] and Xuán [玄] fled on a single boat.
Jiānglíng [江陵] could no longer be defended,
and they wished to enter Shǔ [蜀],
but Xuán [玄] was killed by Féng Qiān [馮遷].
The righteous army met with wind and could not advance.
Huán Qiān and Huán Zhèn reoccupied Jiānglíng.
Yì remained in Bālíng.
Dào Guī and Wú Jì both advanced to attack Huán Mì at Mǎtóu
and Huán Wèi at Chǒngzhōu.
They defeated them all.
Wú Jì wanted to press the advantage and go directly to Jiānglíng.
Dào Guī said:
"In military strategy, there is a time to yield and a time to advance;
one must not advance recklessly.
The Huán clan has resided in Xīchǔ for generations,
and all the common people are exerting themselves for them.
Zhèn's bravery surpasses that of the three armies,
and it is difficult to contend with him for victory.
It is better to halt the troops and nurture our strength,
〔一六〕 then slowly ensnare them with stratagem.
We need not worry about not overcoming them."
Wú Jì did not comply
and was indeed defeated by Zhèn.
He then retreated to Xúnyáng,
repaired the ships and armor,
and again advanced the army to Xiàkǒu.
The pseudo-General of the Garrison Army, Féng Gāi, garrisoned the east bank of Xiàkǒu.
General Yángwǔ Mèng Shāntú occupied Lǔshān Fortress,
and General Fǔguó Huán Xiānkè defended Yǎnyuèlěi.
Thereupon, Yì attacked Lǔshān Fortress,
〔一七〕 Dào Guī and Wú Jì attacked Yǎnyuè.
Both were captured,
and Xiānkè and Shāntú were taken alive.
That evening,
Gāi fled,
and Bālíng was subsequently pacified.
Qiān and Zhèn sent envoys to request the ceding of Jīng and Jiāng provinces
and to surrender to the Jìn Emperor,
but this was not permitted.
At that time, Lǔ Zōngzhī, the Administrator of Nányáng, rose in rebellion and attacked Xiāngyáng.
The pseudo-Inspector of Yōng Province, Huán Wèi, fled to Jiānglíng.
Zōngzhī advanced to Jìnán.
Zhèn personally went to resist him,
leaving Huán Qiān to guard the city.
At this time, Yì and Dào Guī had already reached Mǎtóu.
They hastened to launch a surprise attack,
and Qiān fled.
On the same day, Jiānglíng city was captured.
Zhèn heavily defeated Zōngzhī and returned.
Hearing that the city had fallen,
he also fled.
Wú Jì escorted the Son of Heaven back to the capital.
Dào Guī remained in Xiàkǒu.
When Jiānglíng was pacified,
Dào Guī nominated Yì as having the greatest merit,
Wú Jì as having the second greatest merit,
and placed himself last.
He was promoted to General Fǔguó, Supervisor of Military Affairs of the forces north of the Huái River, and Inspector of Bìng Province.
His position as Administrator of Yìchāng remained as before.
At that time, Jīng, Xiāng, Jiāng, and Yù provinces still had many remnants of the Huán clan,
often forming strongholds.

He was again appointed, with his original office, as Supervisor of Military Affairs of Wǔchāng in Jiāng Province, Jiāngxià, Suí Commandery, Yìyáng, Suí'ān in Jīng Province, and Xīyáng, Rǔnán, Yǐngchuān, Xīncài in Yù Province, across nine commanderies.
He was to suppress them as appropriate,
and he pacified them all.
For his meritorious service in the righteous cause, he was enfeoffed as Duke of Huáróng County,
with an income of three thousand households.

He was promoted to Bearer of the Imperial Insignia, Grand Supervisor of Military Affairs of Jīng, Níng, Qín, Liáng, Yōng, and the six provinces, and Hénán of Sī Province, concurrently Protector-General of the Southern Man, and Inspector of Jīng Province.
〔一八〕 His generalship remained as before.
He declined the post of Southern Man Protector-General, which was given to Yīn Shúwén.
When Shúwén was executed,
he resumed the post.
He was skilled in governance;
his penal system and administration were clear and just.
No scholar or commoner failed to fear and love him.
Liú Jìngxuan's expedition to Shǔ was unsuccessful,
and Dào Guī was demoted from his supervisory position to General Jiànwēi.
Lú Xún invaded and threatened the capital.
Dào Guī dispatched his Sīmǎ Wáng Zhènzhī, General Yángwǔ Tán Dàojì, and General Guǎngwǔ Dào Yànzhī, among others, to reinforce the court.
Upon reaching Xúnyáng,
they were defeated by the rebel leader Xún Lín.
〔一九〕 Xún immediately appointed Lín as Protector-General of the Southern Man,
allocated troops to him,
and sent him to exploit the victory by attacking Jiānglíng,
spreading rumors that Xú Dàofù had already captured the capital.
Meanwhile, Huán Qiān entered Shǔ from Cháng'ān.
Qiáo Zòng appointed Qiān as Inspector of Jīng Province,
generously provided him with resources,
and together with his great general Qiáo Dàofú, they attacked Jiānglíng,
meeting with Lín.
Lín encamped at Jiāngjīn,
Qiān's army at Zhījiāng.
The two invaders pressed in,
severing communication with the capital.
Since Jīngchǔ was an old stronghold of the Huán clan,
many harbored dissenting thoughts.
Dào Guī then gathered his officers and men,
and told them:
"Huán Qiān is now near the capital region.
Many who hear of this are considering their options.
〔二０〕 My civilian and military officials from the east [meaning those who came with him from the east] are sufficient to accomplish the task.
If anyone wishes to leave,
I originally do not forbid it."
He then opened the city gates at night,
leaving them unclosed until dawn.
The multitude was all awed and submitted,
and none left.
Rǔ Zōngzhī, the Inspector of Yōng Province, led several thousand men from Xiāngyáng to join them.
Some said Zōngzhī's loyalty was uncertain.
Dào Guī then rode alone to meet him,
and Zōngzhī was moved and pleased.
The consensus was to have Tán Dàojì, Dào Yànzhī, and Zōngzhī jointly attack.
Dào Guī said:
"Lú Xún blocks the middle stream,
stirring up dissent.
Huán Qiān and Xún Lín are supporting each other.
People are apprehensive and fearful,
and none have firm resolve.
The key to success or failure
lies in this one action.
If I do not go myself,
the matter will not be decided."
He then made Zōngzhī stay and guard,
entrusting him with crucial responsibilities,
and led all the armies to attack Qiān.
All the generals and aides strongly remonstrated, saying:
"Now, to march far out to attack Qiān,
victory is not certain.
Xún Lín is close by at Jiāngjīn,
watching our movements.
If he attacks the city,
Zōngzhī may not be able to hold it.
If there is a mishap,
the great cause will be lost!"
Dào Guī said:
"Gentlemen, you do not understand military strategy.
Xún Lín is a foolish fellow,
without any extraordinary schemes.
As I will not be far away,
he will surely not dare to approach the city.
I will now capture Qiān,
and upon arrival, I will immediately overcome him.
By the time he ponders and hesitates,
I will have already returned.
If Qiān is defeated, Lín will lose heart;
how could he possibly come?
Moreover, if Zōngzhī defends alone,
why would he not be able to hold out for a few days?"
He unsealed the official stamp of the Protector-General of the Southern Man
and handed it to the Advisor-to-the-Military-Governor, Liú Zūn.
He swiftly attacked Qiān,
advancing by both land and water.
Qiān was utterly defeated,
fleeing in a single boat.
He intended to descend to join Lín,
but was pursued and decapitated.
Upon returning to Pǔkǒu,
Lín also scattered and fled.
Liú Zūn led his army to pursue Lín,
reaching Bālíng,
where he decapitated him.
Earlier,
when Qiān arrived at Zhījiāng,
the gentry and commoners of Jiānglíng all wrote letters to Qiān,
detailing the city's strengths and weaknesses,
all intending to scheme for an internal uprising.
At this time, the Military Advisor Cáo Zhòngzōng found these letters.
Dào Guī burned them all without reading them.
The populace then felt greatly at peace.
He was promoted to General Zhēngxī.
Previously,
Huán Xīn's son, Dào'ér, fled to Jiāngxī,
attacked Yìyáng Commandery,
and linked up with Lú Xún.
Xún sent Cài Měng to assist him.
Dào Guī dispatched Military Advisor Liú Jī, who defeated Dào'ér at Dàbó
and beheaded Měng on the battlefield.
Xú Dàofù led three tens of thousands of troops
and suddenly arrived at Pòzhǒng.
Lǔ Zōngzhī had already returned to Xiāngyáng;
attempts to recall him were unsuccessful.
People were greatly alarmed.
Some rumored that Xún had already pacified the capital
and sent Dàofù to serve as Inspector.
The gentry and commoners of the Jiānghàn region, moved by the favor of the burning of the letters,
no longer harbored divided loyalties.
Dào Guī made Liú Zūn a roving detachment,
and personally resisted Dàofù at Yùzhāngkǒu.
The vanguard suffered a defeat.
Dào Guī's heroic spirit grew even stronger.
He roused the three armies,
and Zūn launched a flank attack from the outside,
severely defeating them.
Over ten thousand heads were cut off,
and almost all who plunged into the water died.
Dàofù fled in a single boat back to Pénkǒu.
Initially, when Zūn was made a roving detachment,
everyone said:
"Now with a strong enemy before us,
our only concern is too few troops.
We should not divide our existing strength
and put it in a useless position."
However, after Dàofù was defeated,
they indeed saw the power of the roving detachment,
and everyone was then convinced.
Zūn 字 Huìmíng,
a native of Haixī in Línhuái.
He was Xiāo Shì, Dào Guī’s maternal uncle (from his mother’s side).
He served as Right General, Prefect of Xuānchéng, and Grand Administrator of Huáinán.
In the tenth year of Yìxī (414 CE),
he died,
and was posthumously granted the title of General of the Army Protecting the State.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiānlì County,
with an income of seven hundred households.
Dào Guī was promoted to General-in-chief of the Western Expedition, and was granted the privilege of establishing an administration with the Three Ducal Ministers;
he was also granted the additional title of Palace Attendant.
He firmly declined.
Shortly thereafter, he fell ill.

He was reassigned as Grand Administrator over the military affairs of Yùzhōu and Jiāngzhōu, and the six commanderies of Xuānchéng, Huáinán, Lújiāng, Lìyáng, Ānfēng, and Tángyì in Yángzhōu, and as Governor of Yùzhōu,
with the insignia of a General, imperial envoy with credentials, and Palace Attendant as before.
Due to illness, he did not take up the post.
In the intercalary month of the eighth year (412 CE),
he passed away in the capital,
at the age of forty-three.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Attendant at the Palace Gate and Grand Minister of Education.
He was granted an additional twenty honorary guards with swords.
His posthumous title was Lièwǔ Gōng.
For his achievements in pacifying Huán Qiān,
he was promoted to Duke of Nánjùn,
with an income of five thousand households.
When Gāozǔ received the Mandate of Heaven,
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Marshal,
and posthumously enfeoffed as Prince of Línchuān,
with his income from households as before.
Dào Guī had no sons,
so the second son of Prince Jǐng of Chángshā, Yìqìng, was made his heir.
Initially,
Tàizǔ, while young, was raised by Dào Guī.
Gāozǔ commanded that he be Dào Guī's heir.
However, all deemed that according to ritual, there could not be two successors,
so Tàizǔ returned to his own lineage,
and Yìqìng was then designated as the successor.
[二一]When Yìqìng was Governor of Jīngzhōu,
the ancestral tablet was supposed to move with him to Jiānglíng.
Tàizǔ issued an edict saying:
“To honor and exalt the meritorious deeds (of Dào Guī)
is a grand national ceremony;
to revere one's parents and remember distant ancestors
is what the heart naturally upholds.
The late Attendant at the Palace Gate, Grand Marshal, Prince Lièwǔ of Línchuān,
embodied the Way and was reverent and enlightened;
his utmost virtue was profound and distant;
his wisdom and sagacity were heaven-sent;
his filial piety and fraternal love were fully manifest.
From the very beginning, when he collaborated in planning,
he assisted and supported the grand enterprise;
when he wielded his formidable might to quell disturbances,
he suppressed and eliminated the wicked villains.
When the demonic rebels invaded,
and the difficulties were extremely pressing,
the situation was as perilous as piled eggs,
and people had no firm resolve.
The Prince, with his divine strategies uniquely deployed,
and his spiritual martial prowess grandly unleashed,
pacified the interior and exterior,
and executed and overthrew the multitude of villains.
Indeed, his transforming influence reached the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
and his achievements surpassed those of Wēi and Guǎn.
His distant plans matched those of the two Nán poems (Zhōunán and Shàonán),
and his heroism surpassed that of the two Xiàn (Qián Xiàn and Hòu Xiàn)!”
“As for Us, We were young and received extraordinary love,
and his virtuous shade was exceptionally profound.
His abundant grace and benevolent instructions,
and the deep affection he showed,
make Us forever recall his benevolent example,
and feel a deep yearning in Our heart.
Now, when his ancestral tablet is to be moved,
and the first sacrifice is to be offered in the western territories,
We contemplate elevating the auspicious rites,
and formally preparing the splendid insignia,
hoping thereby to display his noble conduct,
and truly conform to the wishes of both the living and the departed.
Therefore, he shall be posthumously honored as Chancellor,
with extraordinary rites.
He shall be granted a phoenix chariot with nine streamers,
a yellow canopy, and a left-facing banner,
along with credentials, an imperial axe, front and rear feathered canopies, military bands, and one hundred tiger-guards with swords.
His title of Attendant at the Palace Gate shall remain as before.”
When the Grand Concubine Tán Shì of Chángshā and the Grand Concubine Cáo Shì of Línchuān later died,
their funeral rites were all granted a phoenix chariot with nine streamers,
a yellow canopy, a left-facing banner,
a hearse,
a complete set of dirges,
front and rear feathered canopies, military bands,
and one hundred tiger-guards with swords.
Yìqìng, while young, was recognized by Gāozǔ,
who often said:
“This is our family’s Fēngchéng!”
At the age of thirteen, he inherited the title of Duke of Nánjùn.
He was appointed Palace Attendant,
but did not take up the post.
In the twelfth year of Yìxī (416 CE),
he participated in the campaign against Cháng'ān.
Upon his return,
he was appointed General Who Guards the State and Governor of Běiqīngzhōu.
[二二]Before taking up that office,
he was transferred to supervise military affairs in Yùzhōu and serve as Governor of Yùzhōu.
[二三]He was again appointed to supervise military affairs north of the Huái River,
while his positions as Governor of Yùzhōu and General remained as before.
In the first year of Yǒngchū (420 CE),
he inherited the title of Prince of Línchuān.
He was summoned to serve as Attendant at the Palace Gate.
In the first year of Yuánjiā (424 CE),
he was transferred to Palace Attendant with Extended Powers,
and Director of the Imperial Library.
He was then transferred to Minister of the Household,
and promoted to Grand Administrator of Dānyáng,
with the additional title of General Who Assists the State; his position as Palace Attendant with Extended Powers remained as before.
At that time, there was a commoner, Huáng Chū, whose wife Zhào killed her daughter-in-law.
She was pardoned and should have been exiled to avoid the grandson’s revenge.
Yìqìng said:
“According to the Rites of Zhōu, regarding the enemy of one’s parents,
one should avoid him even overseas;
even if encountered in the market or court,
one should fight without turning back.
This is because in the case of such an immense grievance,
reason dictates that it cannot be dismissed;
bearing sorrow and sleeping on a weapon,
it is right to swear to avenge it.
As for killings among relatives,
where blood kin harm each other,
this deviates from normal conduct and standing regulations.
Records have no fixed standard,
so we must seek outside the law,
and judge by human sentiment.
Moreover, the rites allow for leniency in cases of error,
but the law has no text regarding avenging an ancestral grandmother.
Furthermore, Zhào’s violent outburst
was originally due to alcohol.
Considering her intentions, it was indeed
an act of senile confusion.
How can one equate an senile elderly woman
[二四]with a deep personal enemy from outside the family?
I believe this grandson, enduring shame and holding sorrow,
should not deviate from the duties of a son.
Living under the same sky and in the same land,
he would not diminish his filial piety.”
In the sixth year (429 CE),
he was given the additional title of Left Vice-Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
In the eighth year (431 CE),
the planet Venus encroached upon the Right Executive star.
Yìqìng, fearing disaster,
requested an outer command.
Tàizǔ issued an edict to remonstrate with him, saying:
“The dark celestial phenomena are vague
and difficult to comprehend.
Moreover, the various astrological interpretations of historians
differ.
When a military star is in its prime,
and encroaches upon something,
it indicates that the one it governs is to be punished.
By this reasoning,
there is even less to fear.
After the death of Vice-Director Zhèng,
the Left Executive star once had an anomaly,
but Grand Master of Remonstrance Wáng is still safe and sound today.
A solar eclipse for three successive days
is the utmost taboo in the world,
and Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn initially experienced this anomaly.
He was merely an ordinary ruler,
yet nothing happened to him in the end.
Heaven’s Way assists the benevolent and blesses the good;
I believe there is no need to create unnecessary worry and fear.
You, my brother, and the Rear General,
each assume inner and outer responsibilities.
Originally, it was for the purpose of protecting the state,
to establish an enduring framework.
The rise and fall (of this nation) truly have their origins in these matters.
If Heaven must send down disaster,
can one escape a thousand *lǐ* away?
Since this is not a matter for those who are far away,
and one does not know where good or ill fortune will definitively fall,
if it means there will be unforeseen dangers in the capital,
and leaving here will certainly guarantee prosperity and righteousness,
how dare I casually defy Heaven?”
Yìqìng firmly requested to resign as Vice-Director,
which was then granted.
He was given the additional title of Grand Imperial Secretary,
and promoted to General of the Vanguard,
while his positions as Palace Attendant with Extended Powers and Grand Administrator remained as before.
After serving as Grand Administrator of Dānyáng for nine years,

he was appointed imperial envoy with credentials, Grand Administrator over the military affairs of the seven provinces of Jīngzhōu, Yōngzhōu, Yìzhōu, Níngzhōu, Liángzhōu, and the northern and southern Qínzhōu, General Who Pacifies the West, and Governor of Jīngzhōu.
[二五]Jīngzhōu held a critical strategic position in the upper reaches of the river,
with vast territory and strong military forces.
Its resources and weaponry
accounted for half of the imperial court’s.
Therefore, Gāozǔ sent his sons to govern it.
Because Yìqìng was an outstanding member of the imperial clan,
he was given this special appointment.
He was humble by nature,
and when he first arrived and when he left his command,
he accepted none of the welcoming or farewell gifts.
In the twelfth year,
Pǔ sent out a directive for all civil and military officials, both inside and outside the court, to recommend talented individuals.
Yìqìng submitted a memorial, saying:
“The imperial edict seeks advice from all officials,
extending to regional governors,
to identify the virtuous in humble positions,
and promote the good from remote areas.
I humbly reflect that Your Majesty's wisdom and sagacity are broadly proclaimed,
Your administration is brilliant and far-reaching.
The imperial court shines resplendently,
and Your moral influence rises daily.
Yet, You still inquire into the excellent precedents of the Qúshì,
and follow the sagacious instructions of the Míngtái.
You direct Your profound thoughts to the affairs of mere storehouses,
and bend Your sacred intellect to humble construction.
Therefore, Your Way surpasses previous ages,
and Your virtue exceeds former kings.
I dare to exert my meager understanding,
and respectfully comply with Your brilliant command.
I humbly observe that the former magistrate of Línjǔ, Yǔ Shí of Xīnyě,
upholds sincerity and practices integrity,
with profound love and reverence.
In the past, during his mother's mourning,
he wasted away beyond the customary rites.
Now, suffering the sorrow of his father's death,
his weeping of blood is well-known.
His conduct is perfected within his household,
his filial piety is renowned among neighbors,
sufficient to strengthen moral transformation and lead the people,
and to harmonize instruction and custom.
The previously summoned Gōng Qí of Wǔlíng, who served as Fèngcháoqǐng,
is tranquil, gentle, and simple,
chaste, pure, and unadorned.
He lives in seclusion, focusing his mind,
and delights in ancient texts.
He is also sufficient to suppress decadent competition,
and encourage those who are restless.
The recluse Shī Jué of Nánjùn
is intelligent and astute in his learning,
and his conduct is upright and pure.
His achievements are like a clear, clean well,
and his resolve is solid as ice and frost.
In previous years, I appointed him as Zhōujìjiǔ,
and did not corrupt his integrity.
If an imperial command reaches afar,
and precious gifts arrive from distant lands,
extraordinary individuals will emerge,
how can they be far? ”
Yìqìng dedicated himself to nurturing people.
Within his provincial jurisdiction, officials whose parents were elderly
and did not reside with them in the official residences,
were allowed to send five clerks annually to provide for their families.
[二六]Before this,
Wáng Hóng, as governor of Jiāngzhōu,
also had such a regulation.
He served in the province for eight years,
and was cherished by the people of the western regions.
He compiled the Xúzhōu Xiānxián Zhuàn in ten scrolls,
and presented it to the throne.
He also emulated Bān Gù's Diǎnyǐn to create a similar work,
to extol the virtues of the imperial era.
In the sixteenth year,
he was re-appointed as Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Jiāngzhōu Yùzhōu zhī Xīyáng Jìnxī Xīncài Sānjùn Zhūjūnfū, Wèijiāngjūn, and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
[二七]He retained his staff of authority as before.
In the seventeenth year,
he was appointed with his original title as Dūdū Nányǎn Xúyǎn Qīngjì Yōu Liùzhōu Zhūjūnfū and Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
[二八]Soon after, he was granted the title Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
By nature, he was simple and unadorned,
with few desires,
and a love for literature.
Though his literary talent was not extensive,
it was sufficient to make him a model for the imperial clan.
He served in various provincial posts,
without any excesses or improprieties.
Only in his later years did he lavishly support Buddhist monks,
which caused considerable expenditure.
When young, he was skilled in horsemanship,
but as he grew older, due to the difficulties of the world,
he no longer rode horses.
He gathered literary scholars,
who came from near and far.
The Grand Commandant Yuán Shú,
whose writing was pre-eminent at the time,
was invited by Yìqìng, while he was in Jiāngzhōu,
to serve as Wèijūn Zīyì Cānjūn.
Others, such as Lù Zhǎn of Wújun, Hé Chángyú of Dōnghǎi, and Bāo Zhào,
all excelled in prose and poetry,
and were engaged as his administrative and state officials.
Grand Ancestor (Emperor Wǔ) often carefully considered his letters to Yìqìng.
Bāo Zhào, courtesy name Míngyuǎn,
was prolific and exceptional in his writing.
He once composed ancient yuefu,
which were very vigorous and beautiful.
During the Yuánjiā era,
the Yellow River and the Jì River both became clear,
which was considered an auspicious omen at the time.
Zhào composed a "Heqīng Sòng" (Ode to the Clear River),
whose preface was exceedingly skillful.
Its words stated:
I have heard that those who are good at discussing heaven
must seek omens in human affairs;
those who are skilled at speaking of antiquity
first examine achievements in the present.
From Hóng and Xī onwards,
how ancient and remote it is!
Carving mountains
and peaks,
engraving on plain silk,
proclaiming virtue and establishing merit,
could be said to be numerous.
Yet, histories record the achievements of Táng Yáo,
stating that he “reached above and below”;
music praises the conduct of King Wén,
calling him
“oh, brilliant in heaven.”
A white fox and black jade
manifested auspicious portents;
a simple ox and a large earthworm
established the auspicious calendar.
Fish and birds changed color,
grain and pheasants gave way (in deference).
All these things did not
fill the eye,
yet their beauty overflowed in metal and stone.
The poets then ceased their compositions,
and the sound of odes fell silent for them.
Is this not a delusion?
Since our August Sòng received the mandate of Heaven,
it has aligned with the essence of the responding dragon above,
and corresponded with the spirit of the river turtle below.
Imperial diagrams and royal treasures
shine brilliantly with exquisite splendor.
Thus, its foundation
shines upon past generations,
and its achievements
surpass former virtues.
Our Holy Emperor ascended the throne like a flying dragon,
and it has been twenty-four years to this day.
His transforming influence flows widely,
His profound beneficence is vast.
The earth is peaceful, heaven
accomplished,
all above and below are filled with joy.
Writing is uniform, roads are connected,
displaying boundless blessings.
His virtue shines in the central regions,
the common people know deference;
His brilliance is observed in distant lands,
the Yi and Mo peoples embrace His kindness.
He attends to diligence
and ritual,
abolishing the gold of the Terrace of Dew;
He relieves the state and aids the people,
emptying the grain of the Great Bridge.
He restricts violations and coercion,
eliminates excessive luxury.
Feasts have no prolonged drinking,
hunts have no prolonged
pleasure.
He distinguishes extraordinary individuals,
and leisurely establishes uprightness.
Those in prominence do not lose their integrity,
and those in obscurity bear no resentment.
His essence illuminates the sun and moon,
His affairs penetrate the will of Heaven.
Therefore, He does not need ministers of the axe and staff,
His commands are not strict yet self-regulating;
He does not need emissaries of phoenix-like grandeur,
spiritual wonders manifest without being summoned.
A divine journey of ten thousand li,
without dust stirred.
Farmers and merchants
reside in their fields,
border towns silence their watch-clappers.
Horses from Jì and gold from the South
fill the inner treasury;
tamed elephants and western pheasants
fill the outer park.
The abundance of silken fabrics
covers the whole
country;
the profits from fishing, salt, and timber
support distant, desolate regions.
The gentry and commoners are prosperous and wealthy,
the five mausoleums already feel ashamed of their lesser virtue;
palaces are grand and magnificent,
the Three Rivers cannot compare.
Households are flourishing,
songs and music are ceaseless.
Red chariots crisscross,
splendid crowns are numerous.
How can it be merely that there are no impoverished people in the world,
and the people obtain rest?
The court summons Hán and prohibits alcohol
It is but iron!
Therefore, auspicious signs accumulated one after another,
and blessings manifested with exceptional splendor.
Foxes from Qīngqiū,
and birds from Dānxuè,
nested in the Āgé pavilion,
and roamed the Forbidden Garden.
Golden ganoderma with nine
stalks,
and wooden grain with six blades,
flourished in the Bronze Pond,
and sprouted in fertile fields.
[二九] It is fitting that these should be harmonized with musical scales,
presented and offered in suburban and ancestral temples,
with mists rising and clouds gathering,
in countless numbers.
Nevertheless,
the Sage Emperor still rises at dawn,
as if hoping for something yet to arrive,
and with grand plans and far-reaching designs,
as if pursuing something unattainable.
The blessings of the gods
are pushed away and not accepted.
Therefore, jade steles and bronze tablets,
and grand ceremonies lie neglected and unperformed;
pilgrimages to gods and inspections of regions,
and great transformations are suppressed and not permitted.
Scholars who honor culture and harmonize melodies
hold back their eulogies outside,
while officials who attend court and feasts
harbor praises within,
and the three spirits have long awaited,
and the nine lands have long set their hearts,
and this has been for many days.
The year-star is in Qiánwéi,
the moon occupies Cānglù,
the long river flows in tribute,
with different sources but a shared clarity,
its waves clear through ten thousand ravines,
its ripples pure for a thousand *lǐ*.
This is truly a magnificent sight of a rare era,
which illuminates the Imperial Brilliance.
The saying goes:
"The shadow follows the form,
and auspicious omens follow virtue."
This is its manifestation.
Xuánní said:
"The phoenix does not arrive,
the Yellow River does not yield the diagram."
The commentary says:
"To wait for the Yellow River to clear,
how long is human life!"
All lament that these cannot be seen.
However, what the ancients could not see,
we now see in full.
Mèng Kē
said:
"A sage appears once in a thousand years,
that is like morning and evening."
[三０] Is this not great?
The Four Emperors and Six Thearchs
established their fame for eternity,
which is a great treasure.
Their beneficence permeated all
living beings,
the nation was prosperous, and punishments were just,
which is profound virtue.
They instituted rites and composed music,
enriched customs and transformed traditions,
which is cultural education.
They punished rebels and subjugated barbarians,
and forced them to bow their heads at Jiàngquē,
which is military achievement.
Chirping birds and leaping fish,
and cleansing the dirty rivers and canals,
which are supreme auspiciousness.
Great treasure and profound virtue,
cultural education and military achievement,
their loftiness is like this;
the seen and unseen realms assist in harmony,
and the people and spirits contribute their power,
their response is like that.
Only Heaven is great,
Yáo truly emulated it,
how majestic, how grand,
who could rival it?
Moreover, I have heard,
that where influence extends shallowly,
then
the beauty conveyed is near;
where the Dao deeply inspires,
then the blessings that flow are far.
Therefore, splendid achievements and revered mandates
are embellished in sealed documents,
and profound virtues are described
and adorned in songs and praises.
Looking at ancient times,
Xīsī, Jífǔ, and their ilk,
sounded jade bells in front;
looking at medieval times,
Xiāngrú, Wáng Bāo, and their
associates,
adorned with golden bridles behind.
[三一] Their glorious deeds illuminated afar,
their pure influence continued on the path.
Bān Gù praised the era of Hàn Chéng,
saying that over a thousand essays were presented to the emperor,
and the flourishing of literature
was on par with the Three Dynasties.
From this perspective,
this is truly the traditional duty of ministers and subjects,
and a common principle of the state,
which cannot be ceased.
Although I am not clever,
how can I not
strive?
Shìzǔ appointed Zhào as Zhōngshū Shèrén.
The emperor was fond of writing essays,
believing that no one could surpass him.
Zhào understood his intention,
and wrote essays with many crude words and redundant sentences,
at the time everyone said Zhào had exhausted his talent,
but this was not true.
Línhǎi Wáng Zǐxù was in Jīngzhōu,
and Zhào was Qiánjūn Cānjūn,
in charge of secretarial duties.
Zǐxù was defeated,
and killed by rebellious soldiers.
Yìqìng was in Guǎnglǐng,
suffering from illness,
and a white rainbow pierced the city,
and wild deer entered the residence,
which he deeply disliked,
so he firmly requested to return.
Tàizǔ permitted him to leave the prefecture,
and return to court with his original title.
In the twenty-first year,
he passed away in the capital,
at the age of forty-two.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng and Sīkōng,
with the posthumous title Kāng Wáng.
His son, Āi Wáng Yè, courtesy name Jǐngshū, succeeded,
and held office as Tōngzhíláng,
and was killed by the prime culprit.
He was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì.
His son Chuò, courtesy name Zǐliú, succeeded,
and held office as Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
In Shēngmíng third year, he rebelled,
was executed,
and his state was abolished.
Chuò’s younger brother Wǎn,
died early.
Yè’s younger brother Yǎn,
was Tàizǐ Shèrén.
Yǎn’s younger brother Jìng,
was Xuānchéng Tàishǒu.
Jìng’s younger brother Yǐng,
was Qián Jiāngjūn.
Yǐng’s younger brother Qiàn,
was Nán Xīncài Tàishǒu.
Zūnkǎo was Gāozǔ’s paternal cousin.
His great-grandfather Chún,
was the younger brother of the Imperial Great-grandfather Wǔyuán Lìng Hùn,
and held office as Zhèngyuán Láng.
His grandfather Yán,
was Hǎixī Lìng.
His father Juānzǐ,
was Péngchéng Nèishǐ.
Zūnkǎo first served as Jiāngjūn Zhènwǔ Cānjūn,
participated in the campaign against Lú Xún,
and was enfeoffed as Xiāng Hóu.
From Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Péngchéng Nèishǐ, he followed Gāozǔ in the northern expedition.
At that time, all of Gāozǔ’s sons were young,
and among the imperial clan, only Zūnkǎo remained.
After Cháng’ān was pacified,
he was appointed Dū Bìngzhōu Sīzhōu zhī Běihé Dōngběi Píngyáng Běiyōngzhōu zhī Xīn’ānpíng’āndìng Wǔjùn Zhūjūnsì, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ,
[三二] concurrently Hédōng Tàishǒu,
garrisoned at Púbǎn.
When Guānzhōng was lost,
he returned south,
was appointed Yóujī Jiāngjūn,
and promoted to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
When Jìn Dì abdicated and resided in Mòlíng Gōng,
Zūnkǎo led troops to guard him.
When Gāozǔ first ascended the great throne,
he issued an edict bestowing favor,
saying:
"Zūnkǎo is a close relative by marriage,
not far removed from the imperial family,
and there are few in the imperial clan,
so he should receive privileged noble titles.
He can be enfeoffed as Yíngpǔ Xiàn Hóu,
with an income of five hundred households."
He was appointed Péngchéng and Pèi Èrjùn Tàishǒu with his original title.
In the first year of Jǐngpíng,
he was transferred to be the Right General of the Guards.
In the second year of Yuánjiā,
he was appointed General of the Pacification of Barbarians and Administrator of Huáinán.
The following year,
he was made an Envoy with Credentials,
given charge of the Commander of the Guards,
and entered the Palace Hall to serve.

He was then appointed Envoy with Credentials, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yōng, Liáng, the four Qín prefectures (South and North), Nányáng, Jìnglíng, Shùnyáng, Xiāngyáng, Xīnyě, and Suí commanderies in Jīng Prefecture, General of the Pacification of Barbarians, Colonel for Pacifying Barbarians, and Governor of Yōng Prefecture,
and Administrator of the two commanderies of Xiāngyáng and Xīnyě.
〔三三〕Zūnkǎo's governance was harsh and violent,
and his exactions were without limit.
In the fifth year,
he was impeached by the appropriate authorities,
but the Emperor did not question him,
and he was pardoned and returned to the capital.
In the seventh year,
he was appointed Right Guard Commander of the Crown Prince,
and additionally made Attendant Official.
The following year,

he supervised military affairs north of the Jiāng River and in Huáinán, Nán Xú Prefecture and Yǎn Prefecture, and was made General of the Pacification of Barbarians and Governor of Nán Yǎn Prefecture,
with charge of the Administrator of Guǎnglíng.
He was then recalled to be an Imperial Attendant,
given charge of the General of the Rear Army,
and transferred to be the Grand Master of Ceremonies.
In the ninth year,
he was promoted to Right General of the Guards,
and additionally made Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
In the twelfth year,
he was dismissed from the Attendant-in-Ordinary post for his severe illness, not waiting for an audience,
and
retained the Right General of the Guards position with the rank of Marquis.
The following year,
he was reinstated to his original post.
In the fifteenth year,
he was also given charge of the Grand Arbiter of Xú Prefecture and Middle Secretary to the Crown Prince,
while retaining his original post.
In that year,
he was made Supervisor of Military Affairs of Xú and Yǎn Prefectures, and Liáng Commandery in Yù Prefecture, General of the Van, and Governor of Xú and Yǎn Prefectures.
Before he could take up his post,
he was kept as an Imperial Attendant,
with charge of the Left General of the Guards.
The following year,

he was appointed Envoy with Credentials, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yù, Sī, Yōng, and Bìng Prefectures, and Liáng Commandery, Yìyáng, Mǎtóu, and Yìyáng in Jīng Prefecture (four commanderies) in Nán Yù Prefecture, General of the Van, and Governor of Yù Prefecture,
with charge of the Administrator of Nán Liáng Commandery.
In the twenty-first year,
because of a drought within his jurisdiction,
and the suffering of the populace,
an imperial edict ordered additional relief,
but Zūnkǎo did not comply with the imperial decree,
and was dismissed from office.
He was then appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Minister of the Five Military Boards,
then transferred to be Administrator of Wúxìng,
with a salary of two thousand *shí* of the middle rank.
In the twenty-fifth year,
he was summoned to be Commander of the Army.
In the twenty-seventh year,
when the Tatars reached Guābù in the south,
he led troops out to the riverbank,
and was granted imperial credentials and a parasol.
〔三四〕
In the thirtieth year,
he was again appointed Envoy with Credentials and Supervisor of Yù Prefecture.
When the prime culprit usurped the throne through regicide,
he was promoted to General of the Pacification of the West,
and Xu Ánqī and Yǎng Jiézǔ were dispatched as external supervisors to defend him.
Zūnkǎo beheaded Ánqī and others,
and raised a righteous army to support Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān.
Yìxuān promoted Zūnkǎo to General Who Guards the West.
Xiàhóu Xiàn led his troops to Guābù to await Emperor Shìzǔ,
and he was again dismissed from office.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn,
when Lǔ Shuǎng and Zāng Zhì rebelled,
he was appointed General of the Pacification of Barbarians,
and led troops to garrison at Línyí County,
after which he was made Administrator of Wúxìng.
The following year,
he was summoned to be Governor of Xiāng Prefecture,
but before he could depart,
he was promoted to Left Chief Minister of the Department of State Affairs.
In the third year,
he was transferred to be Prefect of Dānyáng,
and additionally made Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
He again served as Right Chief Minister of the Department of State Affairs,
with charge of the Right Guard Commander of the Crown Prince.
The following year,
he was also appointed General of the Army Commander,
and additionally made Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
In the fifth year,
he was again promoted to Right Chief Minister of the Department of State Affairs and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon,
while remaining Attendant-in-Ordinary.
The following year,
he was transferred to Left Chief Minister,
while remaining Attendant-in-Ordinary.
He also took charge of the Governor of Xú Prefecture, Grand Arbiter, and Grand Master of the Stud for Chongxian.
When the Former Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Special Advanced Rank and Right Grand Master of Glorious Happiness,
while remaining Attendant-in-Ordinary and Grand Master of the Stud.
In the first year of Jǐnghé,
he was appointed Supervisor of Military Affairs of Nán Yù Prefecture, General of the Pacification of the West, and Governor of Nán Yù Prefecture.
When Emperor Tàizōng ascended the throne,
he was made Imperial Attendant, Special Advanced Rank, and Right Grand Master of Glorious Happiness,
with charge of the Grand Master of the Stud for Chongxian.
He was granted thirty personal attendants.
When Empress Dowager Chóngxiàn died,
he was relieved of the Grand Master of the Stud post,
but the rest remained as before.
In the fifth year of Tàishǐ,
he was granted a stool and a staff,
the Grand Provisioner was to grant him delicacies four times a year,
and for illness, the Imperial Physician was to provide medicine,
but he firmly declined the stool and staff.
When the Later Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Left Grand Master of Glorious Happiness,
the rest remaining as before.
In the first year of Yuánhuī, he died,
at the age of eighty-two.
He was posthumously granted Left Grand Master of Glorious Happiness and opened an official residence with honors equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers,
