while remaining Imperial Attendant.
His posthumous title was Yuángōng.
Zūnkǎo had no talent,
but simply because he was a not-too-distant relative of the imperial clan,
he received prominent appointments through successive reigns.
In his old age, he suffered from an illness and lost his sight.
His son Chéngzhī,
became prominent and prosperous at the end of Emperor Shùn's Shēngmíng era.
Chéngzhī's younger brother Kūnzhī,
was the Chief Clerk to Sīkōng, Jìnglíng Wáng Dàn.
When Dàn rebelled,
he appointed him Central Army Aide,
but Kūnzhī did not accept.
He was imprisoned for several tens of days,
but ultimately did not accept,
so he was killed.
He was posthumously granted Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
An imperial edict ordered Xiè Zhuāng, Minister of Personnel, to compose a eulogy for him.
Zūnkǎo's cousin Sīkǎo
was also favored,
held official posts through successive reigns,
reaching the highest and most prominent positions,
serving as Administrator of Yùzhāng and Kuàijī,
and Governor of Yì and Xú Prefectures,
having administered ten commanderies and three prefectures in total.
In the first year of Tàishǐ,
he died as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon,
〔三五〕at the age of seventy-five.
He was posthumously granted Special Advanced Rank,
while his Attendant-in-Ordinary and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness positions remained as before.
The Historian says: The remaining evildoers insulted us from within,
and the divided forces pressed from the west.
Xún and Huán pressured us together,
and the situation in Jīngchǔ was perilous.
If the superior strategy was not fully executed,
or one calculation was missed,
then the city would be broken and the border pressed,
and the difficulties of the upper reaches would just begin.
If the enemy had two-thirds of the strategic advantage,
and faced north to contend for the empire,
then the path to our complete victory
would not be easily known.
King Lièwǔ surveyed all talents,
and put forth brilliant strategies.
With one move, he ripped apart the powerful enemy.
This was not merely due to the opportune moment,
but also to human planning.
His granted years were not long,
so he could not see the great undertaking through from beginning to end.
What a pity!
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 12: Yǔ Yuè, Wáng Dàn, Xiè Jǐngrén (younger brother Shù), Yuán Zhàn (younger brother Bào), Chǔ Shúdù.
Yǔ Yuè, courtesy name Zhòngyù,
was a native of Líng, Yǐngchuān.
His great-grandfather Liàng was Grand Commandant of Jìn.
His grandfather Xī was Administrator of Wú Commandery.
His father Zhǔn was West Colonel of the Gentlemen-of-the-Household and Governor of Yù Prefecture.
When Yuè was young, he served as Army Advisor to the General of the Guards, King Lángxié.
He was then Army Commandant,
transferred to Chief Clerk,
and then Right Chief Clerk.
When Huán Xuán assisted in government,
he took charge of Yù Prefecture,
and appointed Yuè as Attendant-in-Ordinary.
He was promoted to General of Agile Cavalry.
When Xuán usurped the throne,
he was transferred to Middle Imperial Secretary.
When Emperor Gāozǔ pacified the capital,
Wǔlíng Wáng Zūn acted under imperial authorization,
and appointed Yuè as General Who Establishes Distant Peace, Military Protector Who Calms Distant Places, and Administrator of Wǔlíng.
He left office due to illness.
He served as Advisory Aide to the General of the Garrison Army,
then transferred to Aide-de-camp to the General of Chariots and Cavalry.
Liú Yì (劉毅) requested him to be Fǔjūn Sīmǎ (撫軍司馬),
but he did not accept.
He was promoted to Zhōngjūn Sīmǎ (中軍司馬) to the General of Chariots and Cavalry.
He joined the campaign to conquer Guǎnggù (廣固),
exerting his utmost sincerity and effort.
When Lú Xún (盧循) threatened the capital,

he was appointed Supervisor of All Military Affairs of Jiāngzhōu (江州), Xīyáng (西陽), Xīncài (新蔡), Rǔnán (汝南), and Yǐngchuān (潁川) prefectures in Yùzhōu (豫州), and Nóng (農) and Sōngzī (松滋) prefectures in Yángzhōu (揚州), totaling six commanderies, as well as Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (建威將軍) and Cǐshǐ (刺史) of Jiāngzhōu (江州).
He departed from the eastern route through Póyáng (鄱陽).
Lú Xún (盧循) sent his general Yīng Dǒu (英紏) with over a thousand men to block Wǔmǔ Qiáo (五畝嶠).
Yuè (悅) defeated them,
advanced to take Yùzhāng (豫章),
and cut off Lú Xún's (盧循) supplies and reinforcements.
Initially,
Liú Yì's (劉毅) family was in Jīngkǒu (京口),
and they were unusually poor.
He once went with local gentry and officials to the Eastern Hall to practice archery.
At that time, Yuè (悅) was Sìtú Yòuchángshǐ (司徒右長史),
and temporarily visited Jīng (京).
He invited his subordinate officials from the prefecture and province to go out to the Eastern Hall together.
Liú Yì (劉毅) had already arrived,
and sent someone to inform Yuè (悅),
saying:
"I have been struggling for a long time,
and arranging a gathering is very difficult.
You are a person who gets what you want,
and can be comfortable anywhere,
how can you not yield this hall to me?"
Yuè (悅), who was always arrogant,
went straight in
without replying to Liú Yì's (劉毅) words.
Everyone else avoided him,
only Liú Yì (劉毅) remained shooting as before.
Yuè's (悅) feast was very lavish,
but he did not offer any to Liú Yì (劉毅).
Since Liú Yì (劉毅) did not leave,
Yuè (悅) was very displeased,
and soon retired as well.
Liú Yì (劉毅) again sent a message, saying:
"I have not had a gosling this year,
how can you give me leftover roasted meat?"
Yuè (悅) still did not reply.
After Lú Xún (盧循) was pacified,
Liú Yì (劉毅) sought to be Dūdū (都督) of Jiāngzhōu (江州).
Considering Jiāngzhōu (江州) was an inland area,
with the duty of governing the people,
it was inappropriate to establish a military headquarters there.
He submitted a memorial stating:
"Your servant hears that Heaven takes fullness and emptiness as its way,
and governance takes gain and loss as its principle.
If times are difficult but policies are not reformed,
and the people are struggling but affairs are not reduced,
then there is no way to save the gravely ill in danger,
or rescue those in desperate straits.
Since recently, military chariots have been repeatedly deployed,
and weapons of war have filled the borders.
Jiāngzhōu (江州), with its corner of land,
bears the brunt of rebellion and submission,
with weak forces and negligent people,
yet it is where military supplies are conveyed.
Since Huán Xuán (桓玄)'s time,
people have been driven, oppressed, and ravaged,
to the extent that men are not cared for,
women have no partners,
and they flee and move,
without avoiding remote depths.
Only those whose wealth and strength are exhausted
are forced to this point.
If we do not show compassion and manage affairs carefully,
and make changes,
then the lament of utter desolation
will surely come.
Your servant, having mistakenly received increased command,
feels both sorrow and concern.
Establishing officials and dividing duties,
military and national uses are distinct.
For governing the people, reducing burdens is paramount;
for military strategy, achieving success is foremost.
Now, holding both offices
is a temporary measure,
but because it has been relied upon for a long time,
it has become a permanent rule.
Jiāngzhōu (江州) is in the heartland,
connecting with Yáng (揚) and Yù (豫) prefectures,
a crucial screen and barrier,
truly an important and complex place.
In the past, when the Hú (胡) barbarians ran rampant,
and northern cavalry reached the Jiāng (江),
resistance was necessary,
a temporary measure indeed.
Even Wēn Jiǎo (溫嶠), being discerning and intelligent,
with affairs handled by himself,
still perceived its drawbacks,
and discussed them thoroughly.
Now the Jiāng Yòu (江右) region is small,
with fewer than hundreds of thousands of households,
and its land does not exceed several thousand li,
yet administrative offices are numerous,
and have not been reduced.
To speak broadly,
this is a national disgrace.
Moreover, the place is without a military presence,
yet a military headquarters is still established.
Civil and military officers and aides
incur considerable expenses,
how can this be called a grand national policy
or 'pouring water to extinguish a fire?'
Its commanderies and counties along the river
have scattered households.
Furthermore, post stations are dangerous and remote,
feared due to winds and waves,
and transportation back and forth
is often delayed or stopped.
This is also not what is called 'taking advantage of its benefits
to remedy its drawbacks.'
Your humble opinion is that the military headquarters should be disbanded,
and the governance moved to Yùzhāng (豫章),
to be located in the midst of ten commanderies,
to implement simple and beneficial policies.
Within a few years,
it can regain vitality.
Furthermore, the dependent counties are sparse,
some of which are still extant,
but corvée labor for sending and receiving
does not cease.
It is also suggested that these should be reduced as appropriate
to simplify public expenses.
The Cǐshǐ (刺史) Yǔ Yuè (庾悅),
since arriving in the province,
has shown great sincerity in caring for the people,
but the fundamental structure has not changed,
which is beyond his control.
Xúnyáng (尋陽) borders the Man (蠻) people,
so defenses are needed there.
One thousand soldiers from the provincial headquarters
can be used to assist the commandery garrison."
Thereupon, Yuè (悅) was relieved of his Dūdū (都督) and Jiāngjūn (將軍) titles,
and as Cǐshǐ (刺史), he moved his garrison to Yùzhāng (豫章).
Liú Yì (劉毅) sent his close general Zhào Huī (趙恢) to lead a thousand soldiers to guard Xúnyáng (尋陽).
All three thousand civil and military personnel of the Jiànwēi (建威) headquarters were transferred to Liú Yì's (劉毅) headquarters.
His orders were strict and severe,
and he frequently humiliated them.
Yuè (悅), feeling frustrated,
developed a carbuncle on his back,
and died a few days after reaching Yùzhāng (豫章).
He was thirty-eight years old at the time.
He was posthumously granted the title Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (征虜將軍).
For his achievements at Guǎnggù (廣固),
he was posthumously enfeoffed as a Fifth Rank Male of Xīnyáng (新陽) County.
Wáng Dàn (王誕), courtesy name Mǎoshì (茂世),
was a native of Línyí (臨沂), Lángxié (琅邪), and the paternal cousin of the Tàibǎo (太保) Wáng Hóng (王弘).
His grandfather, Wáng Tián (王恬), was Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn (中軍將軍).
His father, Wáng Hùn (王混), was Tàicháng (太常).
Wáng Dàn (王誕) showed talent and literary skill from a young age.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武) of Jìn (晉) passed away,
his paternal uncle, Shàngshūlìng (尚書令) Wáng Xún (王珣), was writing the elegy.
It took him a long time to complete it,
and he said to Wáng Dàn (王誕):
"It still lacks a line describing seasonal changes."
He then showed the draft to Wáng Dàn (王誕).
Wáng Dàn (王誕) took the brush and immediately added a line,
following the description of autumn and winter changes, saying:
"Frost thickens in the vast courtyard,
wind swirls through the high palace."
Wáng Xún (王珣) sighed in admiration for its clarity and excellence,
and used it.
He inherited the title Marquis of Zhìxiāng (雉鄉),
and was appointed Mìshūláng (祕書郎),
Lángxié Wáng Wénxué (琅邪王文學),
and Zhōngjūn Gōngcáo (中軍功曹).
In the fourth year of Lóng'ān,
Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn, the heir apparent of the Prince of Kuàijī, established the Posterior Army headquarters.
Dàn was also appointed Gōngcáo.
Soon after, he was made Shàngshū Lìbù Láng,
and remained Posterior Army Zhǎngshǐ,
concurrently Lújiāng Tàishǒu,
with the added title of Zhènmán Hùjūn.
He was transferred to Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn and Lángyé Nèishǐ,
his position as Zhǎngshǐ remaining as before.
Dàn had cultivated a relationship with Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn's favorite, Zhāng Fǎshùn,
and thus was favored by Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn.
When Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn took a concubine,
Dàn personally went to escort her.
He was then transferred with the headquarters to Piàojí Zhǎngshǐ,
his positions as Jiāngjūn and Nèishǐ remaining as before.
When Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn campaigned against Huán Xuán,
he intended to execute all of the Huán clan.
Dàn earnestly argued that Xiū and others held different ambitions and interests from Huán Xuán,
and they were thus spared.
Xiū
was Dàn's nephew.
When Huán Xuán achieved his ambition,
Dàn was about to be executed.
Xiū pleaded on his behalf,
and also explained why Xiū and others had been spared,
so Dàn was exiled to Guǎngzhōu.
Lú Xún occupied Guǎngzhōu
and appointed Dàn as his Píngnán Fǔ Zhǎngshǐ,
treating him with great courtesy.
Dàn, having been a guest for a long time, yearned to return home,
so he persuaded Lú Xún, saying:
"Your humble servant has been exiled here for a long time,
and has received extraordinary kindness.
A scholar repays a man who knows him,
and I truly wish to repay you.
I am not a military man by nature,
and am useless here.
I have long been recognized by Liú Zhènjūn,
and our affection is not shallow.
If I could return north,
I would surely be entrusted with responsibilities.
Both publicly and privately,
I wish to repay your profound generosity,
which would be better than staying here,
wasting the years in vain."
Lú Xún was very receptive to this.
At that time, Wú Yǐnzhī, the Cìshǐ of Guǎngzhōu, was also detained by Lú Xún.
Dàn further said:
"General, by keeping Wú Gōng now,
it is not a good plan, neither publicly nor privately.
Sūn Bófú did not want to keep Huá Zǐyú,
but a single territory cannot accommodate two rulers."
Thus, Dàn and Wú Yǐnzhī were both allowed to return.
He was appointed Yuánwài Sànjí Chángshì,
but before he could accept the post,
Gāozǔ invited him to be Tàiwèi Zīyì Cānjūn,
and then transferred him to Zhǎngshǐ.
He devoted himself wholeheartedly to serving,
day and night without slackening,
and Gāozǔ greatly trusted and relied on him.
During the northern expedition to Guǎnggù,
he concurrently held the post of Qíjùn Tàishǒu.
When Lú Xún fled south from Cáizhōu,
Liú Yì strongly urged to pursue and attack him,
but Gāozǔ hesitated and had not yet decided.
Dàn secretly reported, saying:
"If you, my lord, pacify Guǎnggù,
and then also eliminate Lú Xún,
your achievements will surpass all ages,
and your merits will be unparalleled.
Such great might
should not be shared with others.
Yì and you, my lord, rose from commoner status together,
and were esteemed at the same time.
Now that he has been defeated,
it is not advisable to let him achieve further merit."
Gāozǔ followed his advice.
In the seventh year,
Dàn was made Wúguó Nèishǐ.
Due to his mother's mourning, he resigned from his post.
When Gāozǔ campaigned against Liú Yì,
he was reinstated as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
Dàn firmly declined the military title,
and followed the army wearing mourning attire.
At that time, Zhūgě Chángmín was acting Tàiwèi Líufǔ Shì,
and felt uneasy.
Gāozǔ was very concerned about this.
After Liú Yì was pacified,
Dàn requested to go down first.
Gāozǔ said:
"Chángmín seems to have self-doubt.
How can you leave so soon?"
Dàn replied:
"Chángmín knows that I am favored by you, my lord.
If I go down alone and lightly,
he will surely believe there is no danger,
which might calm his mind somewhat."
Gāozǔ smiled and said:
"Your courage surpasses Bēn and Yù!"
Thereupon, he returned first.
In the ninth year,
he died,
at the age of thirty-nine.
For his participation in campaigns, both north and south,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as a Fifth Rank Marquis of Tángxiàn.
His son Xǔ
was a Shèsrén to the Song heir apparent,
and died early.
Xiè Jǐngrén,
a native of Yángxià, Chénjùn,
was the paternal cousin of Wèi Jiāngjūn Huì.
His given name was the same as Gāozǔ's taboo name,
so he was referred to by his courtesy name.
His grandfather Jù
was the second younger brother of Tàifù Ān.
His father Yǔn
was Xuānchéng Nèishǐ.
When Jǐngrén was young, he was contemporary with Ān
and recognized by Ān.
He first served as Qiánjūn Xíng Cānjūn and Fǔguó Cānjūnshì.
Zhāng Fǎshùn, the favorite of Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn, the heir apparent of the Prince of Kuàijī,
wielded immense power at the time.
There was no one, inside or outside, who did not visit his gate,
but only Jǐngrén did not go.
At thirty years old,
he only became Zuòzuò Zuǒláng.
When Huán Xuán executed Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn,
he met Jǐngrén
and greatly appreciated him,
saying to those present:
"How could the father and son of Sīmǎ Shùrén not fail,
to the point that Xiè Jǐngrén only became Zuòzuò Zuǒláng at thirty?"
When Huán Xuán became Tàiwèi,
he was appointed Xíng Cānjūn.
When the headquarters was transferred to Dàjiāngjūn,
he remained Cānjūnshì.
When Huán Xuán established the Chǔtái,
he was appointed Huángmén Shìláng.
When he usurped the throne,
he concurrently held the post of Xiāojí Jiāngjūn.
Jǐngrén was widely read and had a strong memory,
skilled in ancient sayings and past deeds.
Huán Xuán never tired of conversing with him.
When Huán Xuán traveled,
Yīn Zhòngwén, Biàn Fànzhī, and their like
all followed on horseback,
but Jǐngrén was made to accompany him in his carriage.
Gāozǔ, then serving as Húanjūn Zhōngbīng Cānjūn for Huán Xiū,
once visited Jǐngrén to consult on matters.
Jǐngrén was pleased with their conversation
and consequently kept Gāozǔ to share a meal.
Before the meal was ready,
Jǐngrén was summoned by Huán Xuán.
Huán Xuán was impetuous and urgent by nature,
and within a short while, mounted edicts continued to arrive.
Gāozǔ repeatedly asked to leave,
but Jǐngrén did not permit it,
saying:
"The sovereign's summons
must be handled in a certain way.
I wish to dine with a guest;
how can I not be allowed to wait?"
He sat calmly and finished his meal,
and only then responded to the summons.
Gāozǔ was deeply impressed by this
and often said that Jǐngrén was the grandson of Tàifù Ān.
When Jīngyì was pacified,
and he entered to garrison Shítóu,
Jǐngrén and the other officials met Gāozǔ together.
Gāozǔ looked at him and said:
"This is the grandson of a famous Duke!"
He then said to Jǐngrén:
"The Chéngzhì Fǔ needs a Jìshì Cānjūn.
I will have to impose on you now."
He was appointed Jìshì Cānjūn to Dàjiāngjūn Wǔlíng Wáng Zūn,
then became Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
and was promoted to Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ.
He was sent out to be Gāozǔ's Zhènjūn Sīmǎ,
concurrently holding Jìnlíng Tàishǒu,
and later became Chējí Sīmǎ.
In the fifth year of Yìxī (409 CE),
Gāozǔ, with the internal troubles now settled,
desired to expand his external ambitions,
and intended to attack the Xiānbēi.
The court consensus was that this was not advisable.
Liú Yì, then garrisoned at Gūshú,
strongly dissuaded Gāozǔ,
believing:
"When Fú Jiān invaded our borders,
Grand Tutor Xiè still did not go out personally.
For a Prime Minister to go far afield
would shake the very foundation."
Jǐngrén alone said:
"Your Grace has established the achievements of Huán and Wén,
responding to the will of Heaven and man,
restoring the imperial throne,
and eliminating treacherous rebels.
Although your accomplishments surpass those of antiquity,
your virtuous governance and punishments have not yet fully permeated.
It is fitting to depose the fallen and secure what exists,
broadly establishing your awe-inspiring strategies.
The Xiānbēi are close to our borders,
and have repeatedly infringed upon the frontier.
Punishing the guilty and bringing solace to the people
is precisely what is needed now.
After their pacification,
we can rest our forces and give the troops respite,
and then demonstrate our military might at Luòruì,
and restore the imperial mausoleums.
How could we sit idly by, allowing the brigands to grow stronger,
and indulge the enemy, bringing future calamities?!"
Gāozǔ accepted this.
When the northern expedition began,
the Grand Marshal, the Prince of Lángyá,
was the Emperor's maternal younger brother,
and due to be the Heir Apparent.
Gāozǔ was deeply concerned about the foundation of the state,
and transferred Jǐngrén to be Grand Marshal's Left Staff Officer,
to take sole charge of the ducal administration,
and Right General of the Guards,
with the added title of Palace Attendant.
He was also promoted to Minister of Personnel.
At that time, his cousin Hùn was Left Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
According to regulations, they could not hold positions supervising each other.
Gāozǔ memorialized to follow the precedents of Director Wáng Biāozhī and Minister Wáng Shào,
and not relieve him of his post.
He was impeached for appointing the clerk of the Ministry of Personnel, Xíng Āntài, as Chief Clerk and Administrator of Píngyuán.
These two offices were conferred concurrently.
Āntài, in his capacity as a clerk, went to pay respects at the imperial tombs,
and was impeached by the Imperial Censor-in-Chief Zhèng Xiānzhī.
He served in plain clothes.
In the eighth year (412 CE),
he was promoted to General of the Palace Army.
In the eleventh year (415 CE),
he was transferred to Right Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
and then to Left Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Jǐngrén was by nature dignified, serious, and meticulous.
His residence was clean and beautiful.
Whenever he spat,
he would turn and spit onto the clothes of those around him.
After the matter was concluded,
he would immediately allow them one day for washing.
Whenever he wanted to spit,
those around him would vie to receive it.
Gāozǔ deeply respected him,
and strengthened their bond with a marriage alliance:
the consort of Prince Lúlíng, Yìzhēn,
was Jǐngrén's daughter.
In the twelfth year (416 CE),
he died,
at the age of forty-seven.
He was posthumously granted Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Gold and Purple,
and additionally Regular Mounted Attendant.
On the day of his funeral,
Gāozǔ personally attended,
and wept inconsolably.
He wrote to the General of Agile Cavalry, Dàolián, saying:
"Xiè Jǐngrén has passed away.
My grief and sorrow are so profound,
I cannot overcome them.
When you hear this news, your shock and dismay
will also be unbearable.
His capacity and broadmindedness were deep,
and my reliance on him was truly great.
I had just intended to work with him to bring order to the affairs of the time,
and now this has happened all at once.
My pain and regret are doubly profound.
Alas, what can be done!
What more can be done!"
His son Xún
was Administrator of Póyáng.
Xún's son, Zhì,
was skilled at playing the sheng,
and rose to the office of Administrator of Xīyáng.
Jǐngrén's younger brother Chún, courtesy name Jǐngmào,
initially served as Liú Yì's Adjutant of Yùzhōu.
When Yì was garrisoned at Jiānglíng,
he made him General of the Guards' Chief Clerk and Chancellor of Nánpíng.
When Wáng Zhèn'è led troops to attack Yì,
and had already reached the city walls,
Yì was then ill,
and all his aides and clerks entered to attend to him.
Chún, after attending,
had already left.
When he heard that troops had arrived,
he rushed back into the ducal residence.
His attendants pulled his carriage, wanting him to return to the outer district to escape,
but Chún shouted at them, saying:
"I am a government official;
where would I flee to?!"
Then he entered.
When Yì's army was defeated and his forces scattered,
it was already dark.
Sīmǎ, Máozhī, said to Chún:
"You just follow me."
Chún did not comply.
He helped two people out,
and was killed by someone in the firelight.
Chún's grandson Shěn,
in the early Tàishǐ period of Tàizōng,
served as Prince Bālíng, Xiūrúo's General of the Guards' Records Officer and Administrator of Shānyīn.
He was executed for an offense.
Shù, courtesy name Jǐngxiān,
had aspirations and upright conduct from a young age.
He followed his elder brother Chún in Jiānglíng.
When Chún was killed,
Shù escorted Chún's coffin back to the capital.
When they reached Xīsài,
they encountered a fierce storm.
Chún's funeral boat drifted away,
its whereabouts unknown.
Shù took a small boat to search for it.
Passing by Chún's wife Yǔ's boat,
Yǔ sent someone to tell Shù:
"Whether the funeral boat is safe or lost,
it must be somewhere.
With such wind and waves,
how can a small boat venture out?
Young master, if you go, you will surely not succeed,
would you rather that both the living and the dead perish together?"
Shù cried and replied:
"If it reaches the shore safely,
I will then need to attend to its arrangements.
If, however, something unexpected has already happened,
I, Shù, have no desire to live alone."
Thereupon, he braved the waves and pressed on.
He saw Chún's coffin almost submerged.
Shù cried out to Heaven.
Fortunately, it was saved,
and everyone believed it was due to his utmost sincerity.
Gāozǔ heard of this and praised him.
When he arrived in Yùzhōu,
he subtly suggested to the Administrator that Shù be made Chief Clerk,
and he was highly appreciated for his abilities.
Jǐngrén loved his third younger brother Hán but disliked Shù.
He once prepared a meal and invited Gāozǔ,
hoping that Hán would be ordered to sit at the banquet,
but Gāozǔ summoned Shù.
Shù knew this was not Jǐngrén's original intention,
and also feared Gāozǔ would command him,
so he requested leave for an emergency and did not go.
Gāozǔ immediately sent for Shù,
and was only happy upon his arrival.
When Jǐngrén fell ill,
Shù devoted himself to his care.
He would taste the medicines and food
before offering them.
He did not untie his belt or wash his hair for weeks,
and Jǐngrén felt deep gratitude and shame.
He was transferred to Grand Commandant's Staff Officer,
and campaigned with Sīmǎ Xiūzhī,
and was enfeoffed as a fifth-rank Marquis of Jíyáng County.
He served as Crown Prince's General Who Conquers the Barbarians' Staff Officer,
then transferred to Chief Clerk,
then Minister of Rites and Sacrifices of the Sòng Platform,
then Crown Prince's Central Army Chief Clerk,
then transferred to Crown Prince's Palace Attendant,
and went out to serve as Administrator of Chángshā,
where he implemented benevolent governance.
In the second year of Yuánjiā [425 CE],
he was summoned and appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng.
The following year,
he was sent out as the Grand Administrator of Wǔlíng,
and General of the Agile Cavalry Zhǎngshǐ for Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng,
also holding the post of Grand Administrator of Nánjùn.
Previously,
Shù's cousin Yáo had served as Yìkāng's Zhǎngshǐ,
but lost his office,
and Shù replaced him.
Tàizǔ wrote a letter to Yìkāng, saying:
"I am now sending Xiè Shù to replace Yáo.
His talent is comprehensive and refined,
and well-known from his successive posts,
so I am sending him to assist you.
You are just beginning to handle various state affairs,
and your responsibilities are heavy and numerous.
You should rely on the wise men [around you],
to fully achieve the beauty of assistance and harmony.
I imagine you will naturally understand this,
without waiting for my words."
When Yìkāng became Chancellor,
Shù again served as Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ,
and then was transferred to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
He was clean and frugal in office,
having no private residence.
Yìkāng treated him very generously.
Shàngshū Púyè Yīn Jǐngrén and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Liú Zhàn both maintained an extraordinary friendship with Shù.
He had a beautiful demeanor
and good manners.
Liú Zhàn often said to others:
"When I see Xiè Dào'ér,
I am never satisfied."
Dào'ér
was Shù's courtesy name.
Zhōu Cǐshǐ Zhāng Shào was sent to the Tingwèi for corruption,
and was about to face the death penalty.
Shù submitted a memorial, stating Shào's old merits from previous reigns,
suggesting he should receive lenient treatment.
Tàizǔ personally issued an imperial edict accepting it.
Shù said to his son Zōng:
"The emperor pities Shào's former sincerity,
and intends to grant him special clemency.
My memorial happened to coincide with this,
which is why it was specially accepted.
If this memorial were to be widely publicized,
it would be an encroachment upon the emperor's benevolence,
which is the greatest impropriety."
He then had Zōng burn it in his presence.
Later, Tàizǔ said to Shào:
"Your acquittal
was due to Xiè Shù's efforts."
Shù suffered from a heart illness,
and his temperament was sometimes erratic.
He was appointed Grand Administrator of Wúqùn,
but did not take office due to illness.
When he recovered,
he was appointed Grand Administrator of Wúxīng.
He was clean and lenient in office,
and was cherished by officials and common people.
In the twelfth year [435 CE],
he passed away
at the age of forty-six.
When his coffin returned to the capital,
and was still several tens of *li* away,
Yīn Jǐngrén and Liú Zhàn rode together to meet it,
and wept at the sight of the boat.
In the seventeenth year [440 CE],
when Liú Zhàn was executed,
and Yìkāng was stationed outside the capital,
he sighed as he was about to depart, saying:
"Xiè Shù only advised me to retreat,
while Liú Zhàn only advised me to advance.
Now that Shù is dead and Zhàn is alive,
this is why I have incurred blame."
Tàizǔ also said:
"If Xiè Shù were still alive,
Yìkāng would certainly not have come to this."
He had three sons: Zōng, Yuē, and Wěi.
Zōng was talented and artistic,
skilled in clerical script.
He served as Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén,
and conspired to rebel with his maternal uncle Fàn Yè,
and was executed.
Yuē also died by association.
Wěi was married to Tàizǔ's fifth daughter, Chángchéng Gōngzhǔ,
and was hated by Yuē.
He was spared death but exiled to Guǎngzhōu.
During the Xiàojiàn period [454-456 CE],
he returned to the capital.
He was elegant and had his father's demeanor.
During Tàizōng's Tàishǐ period [465-472 CE],
he reached the position of Zhèngyuán Lángzhōng.
Yuán Zhàn, courtesy name Shìshēn,
was a native of Yángxià, Chénjùn.
His grandfather Dān
was the Grand Administrator of Lìyáng during the Jìn dynasty,
and his father Zhì
was the Nèishǐ of Lángyé;
both were renowned.
As a youth, Zhàn was recognized by his maternal granduncle Xiè Ān,
who married his elder brother Xuán's daughter to him.
Initially, he served as Wèijūn Xíngcānjūn,
Yuánwài Sànqí,
Tōngzhí Zhèngyuán Láng,
Zhōngjūn Gōngcáo,
and Huán Xuán Tàiwèi Cānjūnshì.
He entered the court as Zhōngshū Huángmén Shìláng,
then was sent out to serve as Huán Xiū Fǔjūn Zhǎngshǐ.
When the Righteous Army was raised,
Gāozǔ appointed him Zhènjūn Zīyì Cānjūn.
The following year,
he was transferred to Shàngshū Lìbù Láng,
Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ,
and Shìzhōng.
For his meritorious service in campaigns,
he was enfeoffed as a fifth-rank baron of Jìnníng Xiàn.
He was sent out as Gāozǔ Tàiwèi Zhǎngshǐ,
then promoted to Zuǒmín Shàngshū,
and then transferred to oversee the Lìbù.
He was sent out as Grand Administrator of Wúxīng,
with a salary of two thousand *shi* of medium grade.
He governed harmoniously and orderly,
and was praised by officials and common people.
He was then brought back to serve as Zhōngshū Lìng,
and again sent out as Nèishǐ of Wúqún,
with a salary of two thousand *shi* of medium grade.
In the twelfth year of Yìxī [416 CE],
he was transferred to Shàngshū Yòu Púyè and Běnzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng.
At that time, Gāozǔ was on a northern expedition.
Zhàn concurrently served as Tàiwèi,
and together with the concurrent Sīkōng, Sànqí Chángshì, and Shàngshū Fàn Tài,
he presented the nine ceremonial gifts
for Gāozǔ's investiture.
Gāozǔ humbly declined.
Zhàn and others followed the army to Luòyáng,
and stayed at Bógǔ Wù.
Fàn Tài had not yet finished discussing the acceptance of the imperial envoy's credentials
and did not pay homage at the Jìn emperors' tombs.
Zhàn alone went to the Five Tombs to pay his respects,
which people at the time admired.
Previously,
Xiè Chóng of Chénjùn,
who was Wáng Hú's maternal grandson,
was often remiss in his respectful duties towards his maternal uncles.
Chóng's son, Xiàn,
was Zhàn's nephew.
Once, in a public assembly, he insulted Zhàn.
Zhàn, with a stern expression, said to him:
"You truly are two generations without the affection of Wèiyáng."
Xiàn showed a look of shame.
In the fourteenth year [418 CE],
he died in office
at the age of forty.
He was posthumously granted Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū,
and additionally Sànqí Chángshì.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
as the father of the empress,
he was posthumously granted Shìzhōng, Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū, and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
His posthumous title was Jìng Gōng.
In the third year of Shìzǔ's Dàmíng era [459 CE],
when the emperor visited the Jítián (sacred field),
he passed by Zhàn's tomb.
He issued an edict saying:
"The late Shìzhōng, Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Jìng Gōng of Jìnníng,
a revered maternal relative,
whose natural character was simple and upright.
As years accumulated,
his tomb became increasingly distant.
Recently, when I inspected the thousand *mǔ* (of land),
I remotely viewed the pine-lined path to his tomb.
Pondering his virtuous dust,
my feelings of admiration and longing grew.
An envoy should be dispatched to offer sacrifices,
to slightly express my eternal remembrance."
He also increased the number of households guarding the tomb by five.
His son was Chún,
and Chún's son Huán died.
Zhàn's younger brother Bào, courtesy name Shìwèi,
was also recognized by Xiè Ān.
He loved learning and was widely read,
having perused many classics and records.
Initially, he served as Zuòzhù Zuǒláng,
and Wèijūn Huán Qiān Jìshì Cānjūn.
When Dàjiāngjūn Wǔlíng Wáng Zūn acted under imperial authority,
he again served as Jìshì Cānjūn.
That same year,
Dānyáng Yǐn Mèng Chǎng appointed him Jiànwēi Sīmǎ.
After more than a year,
he was transferred to Sītú Zuǒ Xīshǔ,
and then promoted to Liú Yì Fǔjūn Zīyì Cānjūn,
also leading the Jìshì.
At that time, Liú Yì proposed a large-scale agricultural project.
Bào submitted a memorial stating: "The state depends on the people as its foundation,
and the people rely on food as their heaven.
When their industry is cultivated, education thrives;
when the foundation is strengthened, the branches are well-managed.
This is truly the essential principle of governance,
and the way to achieve
the means by which transformation occurs.
If the root is not strengthened,
then secondary pursuits will proliferate;
if hunger and cold press in from all sides,
then integrity and shame cannot be established.
Currently, we are at the end of a period of usurpation and falsehood,
and in the aftermath of a
time of desolation and hardship.
The source of contention has opened,
and shallowness and meanness have spread widely.
Pursuit of fame and profit corrupts people's upright nature,
and taxes and levies exhaust their resources.
Good fields have no couples to till them side-by-side,
and every household suffers
from hunger and starvation.
In the interim, there have been many troubles,
leaving no leisure for daily tasks.
Since the discarding of armor and horses
just one or two years ago,
the accumulated maladies among the people
are difficult to fully rectify.
This is truly what those of
benevolent heart sympathize with,
and what enlightened teaching aims to address.
However, this work has been neglected,
and has been for some time.
Officials in charge of governance
have none who make this their priority.
Mediocre and narrow-minded clerks
still adhere to old regulations,
following ancient
codes of encouragement and supervision,
ignoring the constantly changing sentiments of the people.
This is like repairing dikes to prevent a river,
forgetting that the deep pools and hillsides have shifted;
or gluing the bridge to an old string,
ignoring the disharmony of the notes.
There are merely
articles for performance review,
but no benefit whatsoever.
They do not realize that clear streams depend on clear sources,
and stopping a wheel depends on a high axle
— problems arise from the root,
but they are
treated at the branches.
Setting up positions to honor the virtuous,
and conferring ranks to appoint scholars:
if one assesses ability to select officials
and does not choose people based on fleeting reputation,
then factionalism will cease,
and wanderers will return.
Once wanderers return,
then the southern fields will be cultivated.
Dividing responsibilities to assign tasks,
and appointing officials to oversee duties:
if positions are not established without a task,
and officials are surely
reduced if useless,
then idle and redundant ones will be dismissed,
and wastelands will be reclaimed.
Using tools for their application,
and trading to circulate wealth:
if one suppresses the crafting of exquisite luxuries
and discards rare and valuable goods,
then those who create
frivolous counterfeits will be disdained,
and grain harvests will be valued.
If plowing and weeding are arduous and tiring,
requiring great effort for meager returns,
while merchants and artisans are idle and carefree,
making deep profits with little capital:
if one increases taxes on merchants
and lightens the levies
on fields,
then secondary skills will be suppressed, and farmers will rejoice.
If those in high positions have no unprincipled followers,
and those in the wilderness have no factions that monopolize,
if grants and rewards are not given out of favoritism,
and labor services do not
enter private households,
then those who live off idleness will return to their root occupation,
and those who work hard will be self-motivated.
If idlers decrease and diligent workers increase,
then spring plowing will flourish.
If diligent workers are distinguished,
and negligent
ones are clearly punished,
if orders for encouragement and supervision are made clear,
and officials who enforce prohibitions are strict,
then the lazy will have no place to hide,
and hardworking farmers will have something to look forward to.
If the diligent are happy and the lazy are fearful,
then the
farmers will be encouraged.
All these matters
are also the fundamental principles of agricultural administration.
Govern them with a pure heart,
stabilize them with absence of desire,
encourage them without weariness,
and assist them with
integrity and caution.
Setting aside the small achievements of daily calculations,
and aiming for far-reaching results in future years,
then shallowness will naturally become genuine,
and the transformation of hearts will be gradual.
Bào 善言雅俗 (shàn yán yǎ sú),
and often compared ancient and modern times,
combining this with recitation and chanting.
Listeners forgot their fatigue.
Soon after, he was transferred to Fǔjūn Sīmǎ,
then promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Mèng Huáiyù, Marquis of Póyáng Xiàn, memorialized that his mother, Lady Bù, be granted the title of Guótàifūrén.
The relevant officials proposed approval.
Bào believed that women take their rank from their husband.
Huáiyù’s father, Dàsīnóng Chuò, was already a high-ranking minister,
so his wife should not derive her status from her son.
He memorialized to dismiss Shàngshū Yòupúyè Liú Liǔ, Zuǒchéng Xú Xiànzhī, and Láng Hé Shàozhī from office.
An imperial edict ordered all to be commuted to redemption.
Mèng Chǎng died,
and Bào succeeded him as Dānyáng Yǐn.
In Yìxī (義熙) seven years (411 CE),
he was punished for ordering the transfer of money,
demoted to Tàiwèi Zīyì Cānjūn,
and then transferred to Zhǎngshǐ.
He followed in the campaign against Liú Yì.
Gāozǔ sent Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Zhū Língshí to attack Shǔ,
and had Bào write the proclamation.
It said: "Indeed, those who follow virtue prosper,
and those who defy it perish.
Lacking benevolence and righteousness,
it is difficult to seek peace.
Relying on obstacles and harboring grievances,
few can succeed.
A detailed examination of history shows
that prosperity and
decline are predestined.
Thus, Chéngdū has not had a continuous line of sacrifices,
and Huáyáng has not seen a rising state.
In recent days, the imperial house faced many troubles,
and barbarian rebels caused turmoil,
waves surged and dust flew,
reaching even distant lands.
The tiny Qiáo Zòng,
a commoner among the populace,
sought out those with similar wickedness,
exalting them and leading them.
He brazenly turned on the governor of the province,
spreading poison and harm among the people,
making our western territories
isolated from the imperial grace.
Since the righteous wind swiftly spread,
and the light of Heaven returned
with brilliance,
illuminating the old ways, warming the universe.
As sundry affairs were being initiated,
there was no time for a grand punitive expedition.
Since then,
a full ten years have passed.
Yet, their wild ambition has not changed;
they lie in wait for opportunities,
gathering fugitives and rebels,
mutually supporting each other,
invading and disturbing our Mán and Láoliáo tribes,
and shaking our border territories.
It is for this reason that we had the campaign to pacify the region;
the vile creatures
were all exterminated,
not a single horse remained.
Huán Qiān had his head chopped off,
and Qiáo Fú fled like a bird,
hiding in his lair,
craning his neck awaiting execution.
Currently, the northern barbarians have been exposed and withered,
and the southern bandits swept away.
The imperial wind carries righteousness,
and all good works are consolidating.
The songs of 'Kāngzāi' (康哉, 'peace and prosperity') grow more joyful daily,
and the flourishing of every household can be celebrated.
I,
as the commander,
am tasked with planning,
and aspire to unify the nine provinces.
Gazing at those lands of Yǔ's legacy,
my thoughts are fixed on them.
Obeying the imperial command, I journey west,
passing through Jīng and Yǐng,
looking towards Bā and Hàn,
with deep
indignation.
The Qīng Jiāng (清江) originates from a small stream,
and clears away ominous portents from the stellar regions.
Punishing the rebellious and pacifying the distant,
now is the time.
I hereby order Huòjiàn Tàishǒu Kuǎi Ēn, Xiàpī Tàishǒu
Shǒu Liú Zhōng
mobilized twenty thousand elite and brave soldiers,
pointing directly at Chéngdū.
Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Zāng Xī,
with twenty thousand troops,
advanced from Diànjiāng.
Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Zhū Líng
Shí,
with thirty thousand naval forces,
shone like lightning on the outer waters.
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Suǒ Kěn was dispatched separately,
commanding the multitudes of Hànzhōng,
〔一一〕crossing from Jiàndào.
Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn
Zhū Kèzi,
leading the elite of Níngzhōu,
crossed the Lú River and entered.
Divine armies surrounded from four directions,
the net of heaven vastly enveloped,
with a thousand *lǐ* of extended wings,
ten thousand gongs and drums,
armored breastplates and
helmets,
radiating light and rippling like waves,
with all *Huá* and *Yí* and a hundred *Pú* tribes,
gathering like clouds and mists.
With such an army to wage war,
who could be their enemy?
Moreover, they act with righteousness
and move in accord with the mandate
of heaven!
Now the narrow passes of the Three Shǎns
are within our territory,
without the dangers of Cén Péng's Jīngmén.
As they penetrate deeper into its obstacles,
there are level roads leading in all directions,
truly without the difficulties of Dèng Ài's Miánzhú.
The topography of the mountains and rivers
is also not as it was in former days;
the difficulty of attack and defense
is clearly a hundred times different.
Even when the whole of Shǔ was strong,
and its people and soldiers were wealthy,
Zǐyáng could not
secure himself in Yōng or Bó,
Liú Chán dared not flee to Nánzhōng to save his life,
Jīng Hán's plans were foiled,
and Bóyuē's锐 (sharpness/vigor) was blunted.
Thus, it is known that success and failure have their number,
and cannot be prolonged by wisdom.
These are all past events in the land of Yì,
serving as a present-day divine tortoise oracle.
As flourishing as Lú Xún,
as powerful as Róng Chāo,
they threatened Nánhǎi,
controlled Běidài,
with ten thousand樓船 (*lóuchuán* - tower ships)
covering
the Jiāng River and vast waters,
and a thousand herds of iron-clad horses
filling the plains and lowlands.
However, in the attack on Guǎnggù,
there was not a single complete battlements on land,
and in the battle of Zuǒlǐ,
not a single intact boat on water.
Some were publicly executed in the capital
region,
or their heads were sent thousands of *lǐ*.
Thus, it is known that there are circumstances of rebellion and obedience,
which cannot be resisted by force.
This is also a clear lesson before our eyes,
deeply profound and manifest.
The people of Liáng and Yì
all understand the king's transforming influence;
although compelled for a time,
they are not fundamentally subjects of an obscure lord.
Allowing his indulgence and tyranny,
〔一二〕it increases day by day,
killing and punishing the innocent,
with deaths measured by the marsh.
Yet, to await the execution of a bandit enemy,
to be devoured by the jaws of wolves,
why would they not sincerely turn south and rejoice,
stretching their necks towards the eastern clouds,
hoping for the whole world to experience the fortune
of new life,
while one region harbors resentment over being given precedence?
The king's army
takes benevolence as its foundation,
abandoning rebellion and embracing obedience,
ever since the three drives.
Where the battle-axe is applied,
they merely surrender
themselves.
As for those who bind their armor and throw themselves at the army gate,
nothing is questioned.
Scholars and common people,
their shops will be secure and peaceful.
They should carefully choose between good and bad fortune,
and seek more
blessings for themselves.
The clarity of great trust
is as bright as the morning sun.
If they are deluded, cunning, and perverse,
stubbornly refusing to change their foolishness,
then like a fire burning Mèngzhū,
*zhī* and *ài* (fragrant herbs and mugwort) will rot together;
like the Hé River bursting its Golden Dike,
the deep abyss and high mounds will become one.
Even if they wish to regret it then,
it will be too late!
In the ninth year,
he died in office,
at the age of forty-one.
The following year,
for his participation in the plan to attack Shǔ,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as a fifth-rank baron of Nánchāng Xiàn.
His son, Xún,
during the Yuánjiā period,
held prominent official positions.
When Lúlíng Wáng Shào was Nán Zhōngláng Jiāng and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
he was young and did not personally manage government affairs.
Xún served as Zhǎngshǐ and Xúnyáng Tàishǒu,
managing the affairs of the prefecture and province.
At the end of the Yuánjiā period,
he was Wú Jùn Tàishǒu.
When the primary culprit usurped the throne,
Xún was promoted to Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn,
and given assistant officials.
At that time, Āndōng Jiāngjūn Suí Wáng Dàn initiated an uprising,
ordering Xún to be the vanguard,
and promoting him to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
After the matter was settled,
he died shortly after.
He was posthumously granted the title of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn,
and given the posthumous name Zhēnzǐ.
His eldest son, Yǐ,
has a separate biography.
His youngest son, Jì,
was fond of learning and skilled in writing,
enjoying a reputation for integrity in his time.
He rose to the office of Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng and Wǔlíng Nèishǐ,
and died young.
Xún's younger brother, Zhuó,
was a talented scholar (Xiùcái) from Yángzhōu,
and died young.
Zhuó's younger brother, Shū,
and Zhuó's son, Càn,
both have separate biographies.
〔一三〕
Chǔ Shúdù
was a native of Yángzhái, Hénán.
His great-grandfather, Póu,
was Jìn Tàifù.
His grandfather, Xīn,
was Mìshū Jiān.
His father, Shuǎng,
was Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
His elder brother, Xiùzhī,
whose courtesy name was Chángqiàn,
successively held positions as Dàsīmǎ Lángxié Wáng Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
Huángmén Shìláng, and Gāozǔ Zhèn Xi Zhǎngshǐ.
Xiùzhī's younger sister
was Empress Gōng.
Although a relative by marriage of the Jìn imperial clan,
she was fully devoted to Gāozǔ.
He was promoted to Shìzhōng,
and then transferred to serve as Dàsīmǎ Yòusīmǎ.
When Gōngdì ascended the throne,
he became Cíbù Shàngshū and Běnzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng.
When Gāozǔ received the Mandate,
he was transferred to Tàicháng.
He died in office in the first year of Yuánjiā,
at the age of forty-seven.
Xiù’s younger brother, Dànzhī,
courtesy name Zhòngyuán,
also held prominent official positions.
He served Gāozǔ as Chējì Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
Shàngshū Lìbù Láng,
Tíngwèi Qīng,
and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
When Gāozǔ received the mandate,
Dànzhī became Shìzhōng.
Dànzhī and his brothers were all loyal to Gāozǔ.
Whenever Gōngdì had a son,
they would conveniently arrange to have him killed,
either by bribing palace attendants,
or by secretly administering poison;
this happened more than once.
When Gōngdì abdicated,
he resided in Mòlínggōng Palace.
Always fearing disaster,
he stayed in one room with Empress Chǔ,
and, fearing poison,
he personally cooked his food in front of the bed.
Gāozǔ intended to kill him,
〔一四〕but did not want to send people inside,
so he ordered Dànzhī’s brothers to attend to Empress Chǔ.
Empress Chǔ went out to a separate room to meet them.
Soldiers then climbed over the wall and entered,
offering medicine to Gōngdì.
The Emperor refused to drink it,
saying,
“Buddhism states that those who commit suicide cannot regain human form.”
Thereupon, they smothered him with a quilt.
Later, when the position of Kuàijī Jùn Tàishǒu became vacant,
the court council wanted to appoint Cài Kuò.
Gāozǔ said,
“He is indeed a good son of the Cài family,
but what does that have to do with human affairs?
Fó can be used.”
Fó
was Dànzhī’s nickname.
So Dànzhī was appointed Kuàijī Tàishǒu.
In the second year of Jǐngpíng,
〔一五〕the Sūn clan of Fùyáng Xiàn gathered their family members
and plotted a rebellion.
Their partisans in Yǒngxīng Xiàn
secretly made contact.
The magistrate of Yǒngxīng, Yáng Xún, detected their treacherous scheme
and reported it to Dànzhī.
Dànzhī did not believe it,
and instead, on the charge of slandering others,
arrested the county officials.
Thereupon, Sūn Fǎliàng, styling himself Guānjūn Dàjiāngjūn,
〔一六〕along with Sūn Dàoqìng and others, attacked and captured the county towns.
They immediately appointed Gù Càn, the magistrate of Fùyáng, as magistrate
and added the title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
They dispatched the false Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn Sūn Dàozhòng, Sūn Gōngxǐ, and Fǎ Shā to attack Yǒngxīng.
The people of Yǒngxīng, Zhuó Gōngqī, initially sided with the rebels,
but later turned good and joined Yáng Xún.
He led officials and commoners to resist the attack,
but, being outnumbered, they were defeated and retreated.
The rebels appointed Xǔ Zǔ, a local man, as magistrate.
Xún fled and hid in the Jiāngtángshān mountains,
but was soon captured by the rebels again
and forced to return to manage county affairs.
The rebels then established strongholds,
setting up their own appointments.
They remotely appointed Sīmǎ Wényín, the magistrate of Mò, as Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn,
〔一七〕Sūn Dàozhòng as Zhēngxī Chángshǐ,
and Sūn Dàofù as Zuǒ Sīmǎ.
Along with Gōngxǐ, Fǎ Shā, and others, they raised banners and beat drums,
marching directly to attack Shānyīn.
Dànzhī assumed the title of Língjiāng Jiāngjūn,
appointed Lù Shào, the magistrate of Shānyīn, to lead as Sīmǎ,
and added the title Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn.
Wáng Màozhī, former Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì, served as Chángshǐ.
Kǒng Xīn, former Guózǐ Bóshì, and Xiè Qínzhī, former Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì, both served as Cānjūnshì.
Over seventy Xíng Cānjūn were summoned.
Kǒng Níngzǐ, former Zhènxī Zīyì Cānjūn, and Kǒng Jìgōngzǐ Shānshì, Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū, though in mourning,
were both raised to the rank of Jiāngjūn.
He dispatched two armies under Duìzhǔ Chén Yuàn and Jùn Yìcáo Yuàn Yú Dàonà to cross the Pǔyángjiāng River.
Yuàn and others were defeated,
and the rebels advanced irresistibly,
reaching within twenty *lǐ* of the city.
Dànzhī sent Lù Shào to oversee Dàijǐ Gōng Shí Lín and Guǎngwǔ Jiāngjūn Lù Yǔn with naval forces to resist them.
He also separately dispatched Xíng Cānjūn Zhuó Gōngqī to lead infantry to join forces with Shào.
Dànzhī led his subordinates out to a nearby suburb.
Gōngqī and others fought the rebels at Kētíng,
greatly defeating them.
The rebels fled back to Yǒngxīng.
They dispatched the false Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Sūn Lún to lead five hundred men to attack Qiántáng.
He fought the county garrison troops, led by Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn, at Qí,
〔一八〕and Lún was defeated and fled back to Fùyáng.
Lún then turned good,
killed Fǎbù Shuài and more than ten others,
and sent their heads to the capital.
An imperial edict was issued, dispatching Diànzhōng Yuánwài Jiāngjūn Xú Zhuó with a thousand men.
The Right General, Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng, sent Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Qiū Xiǎn to lead five hundred men to the east to suppress the rebellion.
Sīkōng Xú Xiànzhī appointed Yángzhōu Zhǔbù Shěn Sìzhī as Fùyáng Lìng, leading five hundred men,
to emerge from the east on the Wúxīngdao road.
However, the rebellion was pacified before they arrived.
Jiāng Yí, the governor of Wújùn, acted lightly in his duty,
stopping in Wú for one night
before proceeding to Fùyáng.
He distinguished between good and bad,
and apprehended and exiled several hundred families of the remaining rebel partisans to Péngchéng, Shòuyáng, Qīngzhōu, and other places.
In the second year,
Dànzhī died
at the age of forty-five.
His posthumous title was Zhìzǐ.
Shúdù’s given name was the same as Gāozǔ’s,
so he was known by his courtesy name.
He first served as Tàizǎi Lángyá Wáng Cānjūn,
then Gāozǔ’s Chējì Cānjūnshì,
Sītú Zuǒxīshǔ,
Zhōngjūn Zīyì Cānjūn,
was appointed Zhōngbīng,
and was given the added title of Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn.
He participated in the campaign against the Xiānbēi,
devoting all his effort.
When Lú Xún attacked Chápǔ,
Shúdù fought bravely and rendered meritorious service.
When Xún fled south,
Gāozǔ appointed him as Xíng Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and subsequently made him Dūdū Jiāo Guǎng Èr Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì, Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn, Líng Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiāng, and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Huán Xuán’s clansman Kāishān gathered a multitude
and plotted to seize Guǎngzhōu.
When the plot was discovered,
Shúdù completely suppressed them.
In the eighth year of Yìxī,
Lú Xún’s remaining partisan Liú Jìngdào was cornered
and went to Jiāozhōu to surrender.
Dù Huìdù, the governor of Jiāozhōu, reported the matter to the commander-in-chief,
but Shúdù, considering that Jìngdào and his followers sought terms only because they were at their wit's end,
and that their sincerity was questionable,
sent a reply ordering their execution.
Huìdù did not take precautions,
and Jìngdào gathered fugitives,
attacked and broke through Jiǔzhēn,
and killed its governor, Dù Zhāngmín.
Huìdù then campaigned and pacified them.
Shúdù arbitrarily demoted Huìdù’s title to Fènyáng Jiāngjūn,
and because he did not report this beforehand,
he was impeached by the appropriate authorities.
An imperial edict pardoned him.
When Gāozǔ campaigned against Liú Yì,
Shúdù dispatched three thousand men across the mountain pass.
They returned after Jīngzhōu was pacified.
During his four years in office,
he extensively engaged in bribery and accumulated wealth,
amassing a vast family fortune.
He was dismissed from office for this
and banned for life.
Upon returning to the capital,
he generously gifted
all his old acquaintances and those with even a slight connection.
Soon after, he was appointed Tàiwèi Zīyì Cānjūn and Xiàngguó Yòusīmǎ.
When Gāozǔ received the mandate,
he became Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
Gāozǔ, considering his distinguished family
and his utmost dedication,
greatly praised him
and issued an imperial edict stating:
“If rewards are not withheld from the diligent,
then hardworking ministers will be further encouraged;
if ranks are commensurate with merit,
then all who achieve will be promoted.
Shúdù campaigned in the north and south,
always managing crucial military affairs.
When the western regions were disloyal,
his sincerity was evident in the Lingbiǎo region.
He is to be enfeoffed as Fānyú Xiàn Nán,
with an income of four hundred households.”
He was soon promoted to Sànqí Chángshì.
In the third year of Yǒngchū,
he was sent out as Shǐ Chíjíe, Jiān Yǒng Liáng Nán Běi Qín Sì Zhōu Jīngzhōu zhī Nányáng Jìnglíng Shùnyáng Yìyáng Xīnyě Suí Liù Jùn Zhū Jūnshì, Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Yǒngzhōu Cìshǐ,
〔一九〕leading Níngmán Xiàowèi and Xiāngyáng Yìchéng Tàishǒu.
While in office, he was consistently praised for his integrity and simplicity.
In the second year of Jǐngpíng,
he died
at the age of forty-four.
His son Tiánzhī succeeded him
and reached the official position of Nán Lángyá Tàishǒu.
After Tiánzhī died,
his son Zhāo succeeded.
After Zhāo died,
his son Xuān succeeded.
When Qí received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
Shúdù’s second son, Jìzhī,
was a Zhùzuò Zuǒláng,
and died young.
His son Ài
married Tàizǔ’s sixth daughter, Lángyá Zhēn Cháng Gōngzhǔ,
and served as Tàizǎi Cānjūn.
He also died young.
Xiù's younger brother, Zhànzhī, styled Xiūxuán,
married Emperor Gāozǔ's seventh daughter, Princess Shǐ'ān Āi,
and was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi and Zhùzuò Láng.
When Princess Āi died,
he again married Emperor Gāozǔ's fifth daughter, Princess Wújun Xuān.
Those who married princesses
were all from prominent families,
and did not necessarily possess talent.
Zhànzhī was prudent, honest, and capable,
thus he was appreciated by Emperor Tàizǔ.
He successively held prominent positions:
Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn, Administrator of Nánpéngchéng and Pèi Commanderies,
Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ,
Shìzhōng,
Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
Zuǒmín Shàngshū,
and Dānyáng Yǐn.
When the arch-rebel committed regicide,
Zhànzhī was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū.
He was then sent out again as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Dānyáng Yǐn,
overseeing the affairs of Shítóu Garrison.
When Emperor Shìzǔ entered to campaign,
Shào personally attacked Xīntíng stockade,
and ordered Zhànzhī to lead the navy forward with him.
Zhànzhī then took his two sons, Yuān and Chéng, and fled south in light boats.
Yuān had a newborn son
who was killed by Shào.
When Emperor Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Zhànzhī as Shàngshū Yòupúyè.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn (454 CE),
he was made Zhōngshū Lìng
and Dānyáng Yǐn.
Because the sons of Prince Nánjùn Yìxuān fled and hid within the commandery's borders,
Jiànkāng Lìng Wáng Xīngzhī and Jiāngníng Lìng Shěn Dàoyuán were imprisoned,
and Zhànzhī was dismissed from office and banned from service.
In the same year,
he was reinstated as Sànqí Chángshì and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
and soon after promoted to Shìzhōng,
retaining his Zuǒwèi post.
Due to prolonged illness,
he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì and Guānglù Dàfū,
and awarded the golden seal and purple ribbon.
After a short while,
he was again made Dānyáng Yǐn,
retaining his Guānglù position.
Soon after, he became Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè.
For his flight south, he was granted the title of Dūxiāng Hóu.
In the fourth year of Dàmíng (460 CE),
he passed away
at the age of fifty.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng, Tèjìn, and Piàojí Jiāngjūn,
provided with one set of drum and wind instruments,
and retained his Zuǒpúyè title.
His posthumous title was Jìnghóu.
His son, Yuān, was born to a concubine,
but Princess Xuān, recognizing Yuān's talent,
memorialized for him to be made the legitimate heir.
Yuān
became Sīkōng at the end of Shēngmíng.
The historian remarks: Although Emperor Gāozǔ's family had lived in Jiāngnán for generations,
their Chu dialect remained unchanged.
As for refined customs and elegant conduct, nothing was heard of them.
All these sons
were from prominent families of previous generations.
Not one of them failed to eagerly seek office,
bearing reins and leading the way,
perhaps to follow the path of caring for the people.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 13: Zhāng Màodù (son Yǒng), Yǔ Dēngzhī (younger brother Bǐngzhī), Xiè Fāngmíng, Jiāng Yí
Zhāng Màodù,
a native of Wújùn's Wú,
was a descendant of Zhāng Liáng.
His personal name was the same as Emperor Gāozǔ's taboo name,
hence he was referred to by his courtesy name.
A seventh-generation descendant of Liáng served as Administrator of Chángshā
and first moved to Wú.
His great-grandfather was Jiā,
his great-great-grandfather was Chéng,
who was Jìn Guānglù Dàfū.
His grandfather was Péngzǔ,
Administrator of Guǎngzhōu.
His father was Chǎng,
Shìzhōng, Shàngshū, and Wúguó Nèishǐ.
Màodù was appointed as a county's chief accountant,
Principal Clerk,
and Merit Officer,
and was ordered by the province to be an Attendant Secretary,
but he did not take up any of these posts.
He was appointed as Cānjūn for the Wèijūn of the Prince of Lángyá,
Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng,
and Shàngshū Dùzhī Láng,
but he did not accept due to mourning for his father.
After the mourning period ended,
he became Zhènnán Cānjūn for Hé Wújì.
After a while,
he was sent out to serve as Administrator of Jìn'ān.
When Lú Xún led a rebellion
and devastated Jiāngzhōu,
Màodù and Jìnnán Tàishǒu Sūn Dǒu zhī both received his seals and orders,
and supplied his levies and services.
When Xún fled,
both were dismissed from office.
He was again made Prime Minister of Shǐxīng,
but the commandery had been ravaged by bandits,
its offices burned,
and the people and their possessions scattered,
with scarcely one in a hundred remaining.
Màodù initiated the construction of city temples,
mourned the dead and comforted the wounded,
and gathered the scattered population,
so that the number of households gradually recovered.
After one year in the commandery,
he was summoned to be Tàiwèi Cānjūn,
and soon transferred to Zhǔbù and Yángzhōu Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ.
When Emperor Gāozǔ campaigned west against Liú Yì,
Màodù remained behind,
and all provincial affairs were entrusted to him.
When the army returned,
he was promoted to Zhōngshū Shìláng.
He was sent out as Píngxī Sīmǎ for Sīmǎ Xiūzhī and Administrator of Hénán.
When Emperor Gāozǔ was about to attack Xiūzhī,
Màodù learned of it,
fled south in a light boat,
met Emperor Gāozǔ on the way,
and was made Lùshì Cānjūn,
retaining his Administrator post.
After Jiānglíng was pacified,
Piàojí Jiāngjūn Dàolián became the Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
and Màodù remained as Zīyì Cānjūn,
retaining his Administrator post.
He returned to become Yángzhōu Biéjià Cóngshìshǐ.
When Emperor Gāozǔ campaigned north against Guān and Luò,
he was again entrusted with provincial affairs.
He was sent out as Shǐchíjié, Dūdú Guǎng Jiāo Èrzhōu Zhūjūnsì, Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn, Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiāng, and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He pacified the hundred Yuè tribes,
and the region south of the mountains became peaceful.
Due to illness, he requested to return,
and was again Dàolián's Sīmǎ.
He mourned for his stepmother,
and after the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Tíngwèi,
then transferred to Shàngshū Lìbù Láng.
In the first year of Yuánjiā (424 CE) of Emperor Tàizǔ,
he was sent out as Shǐchíjié, Dūdú Yì Níng Èrzhōu Liángzhōu zhī Bāxī Zǐtóng Dàngqú Nánhànzhōng Qínzhōu zhī Huáiníng Āngù Liùjùn Zhūjūnsì, Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, and Yìzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the third year (426 CE),
when Emperor Tàizǔ campaigned against Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Xiè Huì,
an edict ordered Yìzhōu to send troops to attack Jiānglíng,
but by the time Huì was pacified, the army had only reached Báidì.
Màodù had always been on good terms with Huì,
and some deliberated that his army's departure was delayed.
At that time, Màodù's younger brother, Shào, was Shāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and raised an army to support the imperial forces.
The emperor, recognizing Shào's loyalty,
did not punish Màodù.
He was replaced and returned to the capital.
In the seventh year (430 CE),
he was appointed Tíngwèi,
with the added title of Fèngchē Dūwèi,
and oversaw his home province's Zhōngzhèng.
He entered the court as Wǔbīng Shàngshū,
then transferred to Tàicháng.
Due to a leg ailment, he was sent out as Administrator of Yìxīng,
with his salary increased to that of a Zhōng'èrqiānshí.
The emperor casually said to Màodù:
"Do not let the affair of Xīshǔ trouble your mind again."
He replied:
"If I had not met with Your Majesty's enlightenment,
the trees on my grave would already be tall."
After a while,
he resigned from office and returned home.
He was summoned to be Dūguān Shàngshū,
with the added title of Sànqí Chángshì,
but he firmly declined due to illness.
He was then appointed Guānglù Dàfū,
and awarded the golden seal and purple ribbon.
Màodù was well-off financially,
cut himself off from social interactions,
and established his residence on Huàshān in his native county,
where he freely enjoyed the wilderness
for seven years.
In the eighteenth year (441 CE),
he was appointed Administrator of Kuàijī.
He had always been capable in administration,
and his duties in the commanderies and counties
were very well managed.
The following year,
he died in office
at the age of sixty-seven.
His posthumous title was Gōngzǐ.
Mào Dù's fellow townsman, Lù Zhòngyuán,
was the great-grandson of Jìn Grand Preceptor Wán.
He was recognized and employed for his abilities,
serving successively in clean and privileged posts,
as Lìbù Láng (Bureau Director of Personnel),
Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Right Guard),
Shìzhōng (Attendant Counselor),
and Wú Jùn Tàishǒu (Administrator of Wú Commandery).
From Wán to Zhòngyuán,
four generations served as Shìzhōng.
People of the time compared them to the two clans of Jīn and Zhāng.
His nephew, Zhēn,
in Yuánjiā tenth year (433 CE),
served as Hǎilíng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Hǎilíng).
Zhōngshū Shèrén Qiū Dāng was deeply trusted and relied upon by Tàizǔ.
His family resided in Hǎilíng.
When his father died and he returned for burial,
the bridges and roads were damaged,
making it impossible for the funeral carriage to pass.
The county requested to mobilize the populace for repair.
Zǐ Zhēn did not permit it.
Sītú Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng heard of this and praised him,
summoning him to serve as Guózǐ Bóshì (Erudite of the National University),
Sītú Zuǒ Xīyuán (Left Western Clerk of the Grand Minister over the Masses),
Zhōu Zhìzhōng (Administrator of the Provincial Internal Affairs),
and Línhǎi Dōngyáng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Línhǎi and Dōngyáng).
Mào Dù's son, Yǎn,
was Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén (Attendant Counselor to the Crown Prince).
Yǎn's younger brother, Jìng,
was Xīn'ān Tàishǒu (Administrator of Xīn'ān).
Both had great reputations,
but both died young.
Jìng's younger brother was Yǒng.
Yǒng, styled Jǐngyún,
first served as Jùn Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk of the Commandery),
then Zhōu Cóngshì (Provincial Adjutant),
then transferred to Sītú Shìcáo Cānjūn (Staff Officer in the Department of Personnel of the Grand Minister over the Masses).
He was sent out to be Yúyáo Lìng (Magistrate of Yúyáo),
then entered service as Shàngshū Zhōngbīng Láng (Bureau Director of Military Affairs in the Department of the Palace Secretariat).
Previously,
the regulations and decrees within the Department of the Palace Secretariat were numerous and complex.
In Yuánjiā eighteenth year (441 CE),
wishing to organize and compile them,
Yǒng was transferred to be Shāndìng Láng (Bureau Director of Revision),
taking charge of this task.
In the twenty-second year (445 CE),
he was appointed Jiànkāng Lìng (Magistrate of Jiànkāng).
In all his positions, he earned commendations for his achievements.
He was also appointed Guǎnglíng Wáng Dàn Běizhōngláng Lùshì Cānjūn (Recording Secretary and Staff Officer to Dàn, Prince of Guǎnglíng and General of the Northern Army).
Yǒng dabbled in books and history,
was skilled in writing essays,
excelled at Lìshū (clerical script calligraphy),
understood musicology,
and was proficient in archery and various other arts.
He was good at all types of things,
and also possessed ingenious ideas,
which further earned him Tàizǔ's recognition.
He personally managed the production of both paper and ink.
Whenever the emperor received Yǒng's memorials,
he would always hold and admire them, sighing,
and lamenting that those who supplied the imperial court were nowhere near as good.
In the twenty-third year (446 CE),
the Huálín Yuán (Huálín Park) and Xuánwǔ Hú (Xuánwǔ Lake) were constructed,
and Yǒng was made to supervise their construction.
All regulations and arrangements
were made according to Yǒng's standards.

He was transferred to be Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng Tàiwèi Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (Staff Officer for Military Affairs to Yìgōng, Prince of Jiāngxià and Grand Preceptor), Yuèqí Xiàowèi (Commander of the Elite Cavalry), Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Shakes the Military), and Guǎnglíng Nánpèi Èr Jùn Tàishǒu (Administrator of Guǎnglíng and Nánpèi Commanderies).
In the twenty-eighth year (451 CE),
he was again appointed Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng Piàojí Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (Staff Officer for Military Affairs to Yìgōng, Prince of Jiāngxià and General of Agile Cavalry),
with the Péi Commandery post remaining as before.
Since Yǒng possessed talent,
he always exerted his utmost effort wherever he was.
Tàizǔ believed him capable of being a general.
In the twenty-ninth year (452 CE),

Yǒng was appointed Dū Jìzhōu Qīngzhōu zhī Jìnán Lè'ān Tàiyuán Sānjùn Zhū Jūnshì (Supervisor of Military Affairs for the three commanderies of Jìnán, Lè'ān, and Tàiyuán in Jì Province and Qīng Province), Yángwēi Jiāngjūn (General Who Manifests Awe), and Jìzhōu Cìshǐ (Provincial Inspector of Jì Province),
to supervise the generals such as Wáng Xuánmó and Shēn Tǎn,
to plan operations south of the Yellow River.
They attacked Quèáo Chéng (Quèáo City),
but could not capture it for several weeks.
On the night of the seventh day of the eighth month of that year,
the barbarians opened the gates, burned the towers and siege engines.
Many soldiers were burned to death or killed by the barbarians.
Yǒng immediately withdrew the siege and retreated that night,
without reporting to the other generals.
The armies were startled and in disarray,
and were attacked by the barbarians,
suffering a devastating defeat.
Yǒng and Shēn Tǎn were both arrested by Tǒngfǔ Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn Xiāo Sīhuà,
and imprisoned in Lìchéng.
Tàizǔ, seeing repeated campaigns without success,
and that the generals were unreliable,
reprimanded Yǒng and the others with an imperial edict to Sīhuà, saying:
"Since the barbarians have taken advantage of this,
and it is approaching the height of winter,
if they dare to seek death,
then brothers and fathers and sons
will bear the consequences together.
Speaking of this only increases my anger.
This can be shown to Zhāng Yǒng and Shēn Tǎn."
He also wrote to Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng, saying:
"If I had known earlier that these generals were like this,
I would regret not having driven them with bare blades.
What good is regret now?"
In the thirtieth year (453 CE),
the principal culprit usurped the throne,

and appointed Yǒng as Dū Qīngzhōu Xúzhōu zhī Dōng'ān Dōngguǎn Èr Jùn Zhū Jūnshì (Supervisor of Military Affairs for the two commanderies of Dōng'ān and Dōngguǎn in Qīng Province and Xú Province), Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General Who Protects the State), and Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ (Provincial Inspector of Qīng Province).
When Sīkōng Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān raised an army of righteousness,

he again appointed Yǒng as Dū Jìzhōu Qīngzhōu zhī Jìnán Lè'ān Tàiyuán Sānjùn Zhū Jūnshì (Supervisor of Military Affairs for the three commanderies of Jìnán, Lè'ān, and Tàiyuán in Jì Province and Qīng Province), Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General Who Protects the State), and Jìzhōu Cìshǐ (Provincial Inspector of Jì Province).
Yǒng dispatched his Sīmǎ (Military Advisor) Cuī Xūnzhī and Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (Staff Officer for Military Affairs) Liú Zé with two armies to hasten to the national crisis.
At that time, Xiāo Sīhuà was in Péngchéng.
Yìxuān feared that the two would not get along harmoniously,
so he wrote to Sīhuà,
advising him to be frank with Yǒng.
He also had Yǒng's elder cousin, Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk) Zhāng Chàng, write to Yǒng, saying:
"Recently there was news from the capital,
detailing the origin of your entanglement in legal difficulties.
It can be said that although you were in chains,
your conscience was clear.
Lord Xiāo is fair and upright,
and there was no previous animosity.
Seeing your letter,
he spoke without animosity,
how admirable that he so perfectly fulfilled one's expectations!
At present, the world is in a difficult and pressing situation,
and the righteous banners have risen like clouds.
We must rely on the assembly of wise individuals
to together overcome the current difficulties.
You should emulate the virtue of Lián Pō and Lìn Xiàngrú in public service,
and in recent times, imitate the excellent quality of Guǎn Yíwú and Zhōu Bó in forgetting personal grievances.
Put aside these minor differences
and restore your former friendship.
The Duke also ordered Xiāo to show magnanimity
and to also respond to you,
so both should adhere to this principle."
When the crisis was resolved,
he was summoned to be Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng Dàsīmǎ Cóngshì Zhōngláng (Attendant Counselor in the Generalissimo's Office of Yìgōng, Prince of Jiāngxià),
and concurrently Zhōngbīng (Chief of Military Affairs).
At that time, officials were encouraged to offer frank advice.
Yǒng believed that CENSORING OFFICIALS should be established,
to open the path for unreserved speech,
and that officers and soldiers should be instructed,
to show that in peace, one does not forget danger.
In Shìzǔ Xiàojiàn first year (454 CE),
when Zāng Zhì rebelled,
Yǒng was sent to assist Wǔchāng Wáng Hún in guarding Jīngkǒu.
In that year,
he was sent out to be Yángzhōu Biéjià Cóngshìshǐ (Deputy Attendant Official of Yáng Province).
The following year,
he was recalled to serve as Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (Assistant Director of the Left Department of the Palace Secretariat).
At that time, military officers and soldiers on leave
had their leave extended three times,
causing confusion on the roads.
Yǒng proposed, saying:
"Your servant has heard that for former kings, deploying troops with farming
was how they expanded their territory;
for previous generations, alternating between cultivation and warfare
was how they sustained themselves for a long time.
Today, peace extends for ten thousand miles,
and culture is uniform across the nine regions.
Spending lavishly and pursuing pleasure
begins right from here.
I humbly observe that officers and soldiers on leave
are often granted leave three times.
The travel schedule is pressed,
and preparations for departure are made early.
Thus, within a single year,
they travel long distances four times.
Some miss the urgent spring plowing,
others miss the crucial autumn harvest,
leading to public stores being neglected,
and families lacking their usual grain.
After evaluating the advantages and disadvantages,
it is advisable to revise this carefully.
Your humble opinion is that the limit for rotation
should be set at one year,
so that the weariness of the expeditionary soldiers
does not accumulate,
and the hopes of the farmers on leave
can see their efforts come to fruition in a year.
In this way, the imperial system will suffer no loss,
and the people's livelihoods will be established."
This was followed.
In the first year of Dà Míng,
he was transferred to be the Assistant of the Yellow Gate (Huángmén Shìláng).
Soon after, he concurrently held the posts of Colonel of the Tiger’s Might (Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng) and Chief Arbiter (Zhōngzhèng) for his home commandery.
In the third year,
he was transferred to be Grand Judge (Tíngwèi).
The emperor said to him:
“Since you share the same surname as Shìzhī,
I wish for there to be no wronged people under heaven.”

He was promoted to General Who Pacifies the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn), Bureau Director of Personnel in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìbù Láng), Right Chief Clerk of the Grand Minister over the Masses (Sītú Yòu Chángshǐ), and Chief Clerk of Prince Zǐfáng of Xúnyáng (Xúnyáng Wáng Zǐfáng Guānjūn Chángshǐ).
In the fourth year,
the Míngtáng was established.
Yǒng, in his original post, concurrently served as the Grand Administrator of Xúzhōu, Xuē Āndū.
He won many battles,
defeating Xuē Suǒ'ér and others.
These events are recorded in the biography of Āndū.
He was again transferred to be Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì), General Who Guards the Army (Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn), and Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhānshì).
He provisionally held the post of Grand Administrator of Xúzhōu.
He was also appointed Supervisor of Military Affairs of Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, and Jì Four Commanderies (Dūdū Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, Jì Sìzhōu Zhū Jūnshì).

He was also made Envoy with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjìe), Supervisor of Military Affairs of Southern Yǎn and Xú Two Commanderies (Dūdū Nányǎn Xú Èrzhōu Zhū Jūnshì), and Grand Administrator of Southern Yǎnzhōu (Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ).
His posts as Attendant-in-Ordinary and General remained as before.
At that time,
Tàizōng ascended the throne,
and he was appointed Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
Before he could take up the post,
the four directions rebelled.
He was again made Grand Administrator of Wúxìng (Wúxìng Tàishǒu),
promoted to General of the Army (Guānjūn Jiāngjūn),
and granted credentials (jié).
Before he could take up the post,
as General with credentials,
he was transferred to be Grand Administrator of Wújùn (Wújùn Tàishǒu),
leading an army to suppress the rebellion in the east.
He was again made Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Tutor of the Crown Prince.
Before he could take up the post,

he was transferred to be Envoy with Credentials, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Qīng, Jì, Yōu, and Bìng Four Commanderies (Jiān Qīng, Jì, Yōu, Bìng Sìzhōu Zhū Jūnshì), General of the Vanguard (Qián Jiāngjūn), and Grand Administrator of Qīng and Jì Two Commanderies (Qīng, Jì Èrzhōu Cìshǐ).
He led various generals to attack Grand Administrator Xuē Āndū of Xúzhōu.
He won many battles,
defeating Xuē Suǒ'ér and others.
These events are recorded in the biography of Āndū.
He was again transferred to be Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, General Who Guards the Army, and Tutor of the Crown Prince.
He provisionally held the post of Grand Administrator of Xúzhōu.
He was also appointed Supervisor of Military Affairs of Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, and Jì Four Commanderies.
He was also made Envoy with Credentials, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Southern Yǎn and Xú Two Commanderies, and Grand Administrator of Southern Yǎnzhōu.
His posts as Attendant-in-Ordinary and General remained as before.
At that time, Xuē Āndū occupied Péngchéng and requested to surrender.
However, his sincerity was not genuine.
Tàizōng sent Yǒng and Shěn Yōuzhī with heavy troops to welcome him.
He was appointed Supervisor of Vanguard Military Affairs (Dūdū Qiánfēng Jūnshì)
and advanced his army to Péngchéng.
Āndū attracted the forces of the Suǒ barbarians, and when they arrived,
the soldiers scattered.
Yǒng was utterly defeated and led his army back,
pursued by the barbarians,
and suffered a great defeat.
Moreover, he encountered cold and snow,
and his soldiers scattered.
Yǒng’s toes were frostbitten and fell off,
and he barely escaped with his life,
losing his fourth son.
In the third year,

he was transferred to be Supervisor of Military Affairs of Huìjī, Dōngyáng, Línhǎi, Yǒngjiā, and Xīn'ān Five Commanderies (Dūdū Huìjī Dōngyáng Línhǎi Yǒngjiā Xīn'ān Wǔjùn Zhū Jūnshì) and Grand Administrator of Huìjī (Huìjī Tàishǒu).
His general rank remained as before.
Due to the military defeat in the northern campaign,
he persistently requested self-demotion,
and his title was reduced to General of the Left (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn).
Yǒng grieved deeply over his lost son,
with constant sorrow.
Although the mourning rites were completed,
he still maintained a spirit altar,
providing food and clothing,
treating him as if alive.
Whenever he traveled,
he always prepared a separate fine carriage and good horse,
calling them “attendants.”
Whenever there was a matter, he would tell his attendants to report to “the young master.”
For his meritorious service in defeating Xuē Suǒ'ér,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiàochāng County (Xiàochāng Xiàn Hóu),
with a stipend of a thousand households.
While in Huìjī,
his guests included Xiè Fāngtóng and others.
They were imprisoned and died for embezzlement.
Yǒng’s title was again reduced to General of the Army (Guānjūn Jiāngjūn).
In the fourth year,

he was transferred to be Envoy with Credentials, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yōng, Liáng, Northern Qín, and Southern Qín Four Commanderies, and Jìnglíng and Suí Two Commanderies of Yǐngzhōu (Dū Yōng, Liáng, Nánběi Qín Sìzhōu Yǐngzhōu Zhī Jìnglíng Suí Èrjùn Zhū Jūnshì), Right General (Yòu Jiāngjūn), and Grand Administrator of Yōngzhōu (Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ).
Before he could take up the post,
he was stopped and made Tutor of the Crown Prince,
and additionally appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Grand Chief Arbiter for his home commandery (Běnzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng).
In the sixth year,
he was again appointed Protector-General (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn),
