and concurrently held the command of Shítou Post (Shítou Xù Shì).
He was granted one set of drums and trumpets (gǔchuī).
In the seventh year,
he was transferred to be Grand Master of Gold and Purple with Glorious Happiness (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū).
Soon after, he again concurrently held the post of Protector-General.
After the deposed emperor ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Grand Master of Glorious Happiness of the Right (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū),
additionally appointed Attendant-in-Ordinary (Shìzhōng),
and concurrently served as Tutor of Prince Ānchéng (Ānchéng Wáng Shī).
Twenty personal guards were added.
He also concurrently held the post of Chief Arbiter for his home commandery,
and was dispatched as Grand Administrator of Wújùn,
with a salary of two thousand piculs (zhōng èrqiān shí).
His posts as Attendant-in-Ordinary and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness of the Right remained as before.
In the second year of Yuánhuī,

he was transferred to be Envoy with Credentials, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Southern Yǎn, Xú, Qīng, Jì, and Yì Five Commanderies (Dūdū Nányǎn, Xú, Qīng, Jì, Yì Wǔzhōu Zhū Jūnshì), General Who Conquers the North (Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn), and Grand Administrator of Southern Yǎnzhōu.
His post as Attendant-in-Ordinary remained as before.
From a young age, Yǒng was active and driven,
with a determination to exert his strength.
Although he was old,
his spirit and ambition had not waned.
He was very unhappy
with leisurely and idle appointments.
When he received this appointment,
he was extraordinarily joyful,
and immediately ordered his carriage back to the capital on the same day.
Before he could take up his post in the commandery,
he encountered the rebellion of Prince Guìyáng Xiūfàn.
Yǒng led his subordinates to encamp at Báixià.
When Xiūfàn reached Xīntíng,
the Dàhéng Bridge could not be defended.
The vanguard then attacked the Southern Yèmén Gate.
Yǒng sent someone to scout the rebels.
Upon returning,
the person shouted,
“The imperial city has fallen!”
Yǒng’s troops scattered at this point.
Yǒng also abandoned his army and fled,
returning to his former residence in Nányuàn.
As Yǒng was an old minister, he was not punished with death.
He was merely dismissed from office and stripped of his titles.
Yǒng also felt ashamed and sighed, falling ill.
In the third year,
he died,
at the age of sixty-six.
In the second year of Shùndì’s Shēngmíng era,
he was posthumously granted the titles of Attendant-in-Ordinary and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness of the Right.
His son, Guī,
became a high-ranking official
at the end of the Shēngmíng era.
Yǒng’s younger brother, Biàn,
was also appointed and treated well by Tàizōng,
serving successively as Bureau Director of Personnel in the Department of State Affairs,
Grand Administrator of Guǎngzhōu (Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ),
and Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dà Sīnóng).
Biàn’s younger brother, Dài,
was Minister of Personnel
at the end of the Shēngmíng era.
Yú Dēngzhī, courtesy name Yuánlóng,
was from Líng, Yǐngchuān.
His great-grandfather, Bīng,
was Grand Minister over the Masses (Sīkōng) of the Jìn dynasty.
His grandfather, Yùn,
was Grand Administrator of Guǎngzhōu.
His father, Kuò,
Dēngzhī established himself at a young age through his strong capability.
Initially, he served as a Military Advisor (Tàifù Cānjūn) to Prince Dàozǐ of Huìjī (Huìjī Wáng Dàozǐ) in the Jìn dynasty.
At the beginning of the Righteous Banner (Yì Qí),
he also served as a Military Advisor to Gāozǔ’s General Who Guards the Army.
For his meritorious service in participating in the suppression of Huán Xuán,
he was enfeoffed as a Fifth-Rank Baron of Qǔjiāng County (Qǔjiāng Xiàn Wǔděng Nán).
He participated in the military affairs of the Grand Minister of War (Dà Sīmǎ) Prince Lángyá (Lángyá Wáng),
served as Auxiliary Administrator of Yùzhōu (Yùzhōu Biéjià Cóngshì Shǐ),
Chief Clerk of the Grand Minister of War (Dà Sīmǎ Zhǔbù),
and Left Chief Clerk of the Grand Minister over the Masses (Sītú Zuǒ Xīcáo Shǔ).
Although Dēngzhī was not learned,
he was good at worldly affairs.
Wáng Hóng, Xiè Huì, Jiāng Yí, and others
were all his close friends.
He was then transferred to be Chief Clerk of the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi Zhǔbù).
In the twelfth year of Yìxī,
when Gāozǔ launched his northern expedition,
Dēngzhī eagerly campaigned,
then retired and reported to Liú Mùzhī,
requesting a commandery post due to his elderly mother.
At that time, both gentry and commoners alike feared distant service.
Dēngzhī was of two minds,
which greatly angered Gāozǔ,
who dismissed him from his official position.
After the main army had departed,
he was then appointed Protector-General Who Guards the Barbarians (Zhènmán Hùjūn) and Grand Administrator of Xīyáng (Xīyáng Tàishǒu).
He entered court as Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shùzǐ)
and Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng).
He was dispatched as Grand Administrator of Xīn'ān (Xīn'ān Tàishǒu).
Xiè Huì (謝晦) was made Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn (撫軍將軍) and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史).
He requested Dēngzhī (登之) to be Chángshǐ (長史) and Nánjùn Tàishǒu (南郡太守),
then still Wèijūn Chángshǐ (衞軍長史),
with the title of Tàishǒu (太守) remaining as before.
Dēngzhī (登之) and Huì (晦) were both sons-in-law of the Cáo (曹) clan,
and their status was originally similar.
Suddenly becoming his subordinate,
Dēngzhī (登之) was very displeased.
Upon receiving the official letter at the hall,
he only wrote,
“I respectfully received it today,”
with no words of thanks whatsoever.
Each time he entered for an audience,
he would bring along boxes, bags, tables, and mats,
and would not sit unless every item was present.
Huì (晦) always treated him with leniency.
When Huì (晦) resisted the royal army,
he wanted Dēngzhī (登之) to stay behind and guard,
but Dēngzhī (登之) refused;
the account is in Huì's (晦) biography.
When Huì (晦) was defeated,
Dēngzhī (登之) was spared punishment due to his lack of active involvement,
but was confined to his home.
In the fifth year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) (428 CE),
he was appointed Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì (衡陽王義季)’s Zhēnglǔ Chángshǐ (征虜長史).
Yìjì (義季) was young,
not yet directly involved in governance,
so all matters were entrusted to Dēngzhī (登之).
Soon after, he was additionally made Nándōnghǎi Tàishǒu (南東海太守).
He then entered the court as Sītú Yòu Chángshǐ (司徒右長史),
Shàngshū Lìbù Láng (尚書吏部郎),
Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ (司徒左長史),
and Nándōnghǎi Tàishǒu (南東海太守).
The Prince of the Prefecture, Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng (彭城王義康), solely managed governmental affairs
and did not wish to lower himself to consult Dēngzhī (登之).
However, Dēngzhī (登之) was naturally stubborn,
and he frequently stated his own opinions,
which greatly displeased Yìkāng (義康).
He was sent out as Wúqùn Tàishǒu (吳郡太守).
Although he held both provincial and commandery posts,
he remained unyielding in his resolve.
Due to his corruption during his tenure,
he was dismissed from office.
His younger brother Bǐngzhī (炳之) was then Línchuān Nèishǐ (臨川內史),
and Dēngzhī (登之) followed his brother to the commandery,
living a life of leisure and contentment.
Shortly after, he was appointed Yùzhāng Tàishǒu (豫章太守)
and proceeded to his post directly.
When Dēngzhī (登zhī) first arrived in Línchuān (臨川),
officials and commoners alike looked down upon and insulted him.
Yùzhāng (豫章) bordered Línchuān (臨川),
and the commandery was also grand and prosperous,
with a splendid welcoming ceremony,
which greatly astonished the local people.
In the eighteenth year (441 CE),
he was promoted to Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (江州刺史).
When his illness became severe,
he was summoned to be Zhōnghùjūn (中護軍),
but did not take office.
In the twentieth year (443 CE),
he passed away
at the age of sixty-two.
He was posthumously granted the title.
His son, Chōngyuǎn (沖遠),
[一一]when Tàizōng (太宗) garrisoned Gūshú (姑孰),
served as Wèijūn Chángshǐ (衞軍長史).
He died while serving as Yùzhāng Tàishǒu (豫章太守),
and was posthumously granted Shìzhōng (侍中).
Bǐngzhī (炳之), courtesy name Zhòngwén (仲文),
first served as Mìshū (祕書) and Tàizǐ Shèrén (太子舍人),
then Liú Cuì (劉粹)’s Zhēngběi Chángshǐ (征北長史) and Guǎngpíng Tàishǒu (廣平太守).
When his elder brother Dēngzhī (登之) was Xiè Huì (謝晦)’s Chángshǐ (長史),
Bǐngzhī (炳之) went to visit him.
Huì (晦) at that time held a high position and great power,
and no court official failed to show him respect.
Only Bǐngzhī (炳之) treated him with equal courtesy,
and the public opinion at the time commended his boldness.
He was appointed Shàngshū Dùzhī Láng (尚書度支郎),
but did not take office.
He was then assigned to be Qiántáng Lìng (錢唐令),
and had achievements in governing the people.
He was transferred to be Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng (彭城王義康)’s Piàojì Zhǔbù (驃騎主簿),
but before he took up the post,
he was reassigned to Dānyáng Céng (丹陽丞).
Since Bǐngzhī (炳之) had not yet arrived at the yamen,
there was a question regarding the proper courtesy toward the prince.
The ritual officials were consulted for extensive deliberation.
Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎) Péi Sōngzhī (裴松之) deliberated, saying:
“According to the eighth year of Duke Huán (桓) in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Duke Jì (祭) met the Queen at Jì (紀).
The Gōngyáng Zhuàn (公羊傳) states: ‘A woman within the state is called a woman.
Why is she called the Queen here?
The King has no outside;
thus, the designation is complete.’
Extending this,
the path of Bǐngzhī (炳之) as an official
was determined on the day he received the appointment.
His designation is complete;
being in office, there is no outside.
Since the title and position are already correct,
the rituals should follow accordingly.
Furthermore, regarding the current high officials,
even if they have been appointed but not yet assumed office,
and have not yet met the people,
they must still be respected,
because once they receive the royal mandate,
the righteousness between ruler and subject is established.
An official who receives an imperial decree
is like one who is newly appointed and accepts the investiture.
The common people do not withhold their respect just because they have not yet met him;
how can an official neglect his protocol because he has not yet arrived?
In my humble opinion,
he should adhere to the official etiquette.”
This was followed.
He was promoted to Sītú Zuǒ Xīshǔ (司徒左西屬).
Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Jìnglíng Wáng Yìxuān (左將軍竟陵王義宣) had not yet taken full control of his yamen; Bǐngzhī (炳之) was made Cányì Cānjūn (諮議參軍),
[一二]and all matters were entrusted to him.
Later, Hòujiāngjūn Chángshā Wáng Yìxīn (後將軍長沙王義欣) garrisoned Shòuyáng (壽陽),
and Bǐngzhī (炳之) was made Chángshǐ (長史) and Nánliángjùn Tàishǒu (南梁郡太守).
He was transferred to Zhènjūn Chángshǐ (鎮軍長史),
with the title of Tàishǒu (太守) remaining as before.
He was sent out as Línchuān Nèishǐ (臨川內史).
Later, Hòujiāngjūn Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn (後將軍始興王濬) garrisoned Xiāngzhōu (湘州),
and appointed Bǐngzhī (炳之) as Sīmǎ (司馬),
concurrently serving as Chángshā Nèishǐ (長沙內史).
Jùn (濬) did not take up his post,
and Bǐngzhī (炳之) was appointed Nántàishān Tàishǒu (南泰山太守),
[一三]with his Sīmǎ (司馬) position remaining as before.
At that time, Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (領軍將軍) Liú Zhàn (劉湛) was closely allied with Dàjiāngjūn Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng (大將軍彭城王義康),
and had a rift with Púyè Yīn Jǐngrén (僕射殷景仁).
All court officials who associated with the Yīn (殷) family
were not allowed into Liú (劉)’s household.
Only Bǐngzhī (炳之) navigated between the two,
secretly remaining fully loyal to the imperial court.
Jǐngrén (景仁) feigned illness and did not attend court for years,
and Tàizǔ (太祖) always had Bǐngzhī (炳之) carry messages back and forth,
which Zhàn (湛) did not suspect.
When Yìkāng (義康) was sent to a feudal state,
and Zhàn (湛) was executed,
Bǐngzhī (炳之) was made Shàngshū Lìbù Láng (尚書吏部郎),
and participated in confidential affairs together with Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (右衞將軍) Shěn Yǎnzhī (沈演之).
Shortly after,
he was transferred to Shìzhōng (侍中),
and Dàzhōngzhèng (大中正) of his native province.
He was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書),
and served as Yìyáng Wáng Shī (義陽王師).
Both inside and outside the court, people rallied to him,
and his influence swayed the entire government.
Bǐngzhī was a strong-willed and impatient person.
When guests or petitioners made unreasonable requests,
anger and curses would show in his demeanor.
He had no scholarly accomplishments
and was not highly regarded by the public.
By nature, he loved cleanliness.
When gentry officials visited him,
as soon as they left and before they were out of the house,
he would immediately order his servants to wipe the mats and wash the couches.
At that time, Yīn Chōng of Chénjùn also loved cleanliness.
His young attendants were not allowed near him
unless they had bathed and put on new clothes.
If gentry officials were slightly untidy,
he would always accept them.
Bǐngzhī's love for cleanliness was the opposite of this,
[一四] and Chōng often used this to mock him.
As an election commissioner, he not only disregarded public opinion
but also accepted bribes.
When Bǐngzhī requested leave to return home urgently,
Qián Tài, a clerk from the Ministry of Personnel, and Zhōu Bóqí, a clerk from the Ministry of Protocol, came to Bǐngzhī's residence to consult on matters.
[一五] Tài could play the pípa,
and Bóqí was good at singing,
so Bǐngzhī kept them to stay overnight.
According to the old regulations of the Secretariat,
clerks consulting on matters
were not allowed to stay overnight outside,
and even if there was an order from the Eight Senior Ministers,
it was still not permitted.
He was impeached by the judicial authorities.
The Emperor had always been close to Bǐngzhī
and intended to pardon him.
He summoned and questioned Hé Shàngzhī, the Right Assistant Minister of the Secretariat.
Shàngzhī thoroughly explained Bǐngzhī's faults and merits.
He also secretly memorialized, saying:
"Indeed, for a country and a family,
when has one not carefully followed past precedents?
Now, if one merely wishes to accommodate one person,
I fear this is not a long-term strategy for a wise ruler governing the world.
Bǐngzhī's actions
are not merely ambiguous;
what your subject has heard is not from a single day,
and I have often witnessed it with my own eyes.
The incidents are like mountains,
clear as day.
If he is indulged and not corrected,
I do not know how governance can be maintained.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, though not called an enlightened ruler,
established regulations separating officials,
and thus was able to achieve vigor.
Huá Yì, despite being treated with no disrespect,
was dismissed and confined for years.
When he was later reinstated,
he only served as a Gate Commander.
If it is said that Bǐngzhī is sincerely devoted to the state,
what exactly is this sincerity?
It must be that he did not betray his old ties with Yīn Jǐngrén
and was not estranged from Liú Zhàn either.
Moreover, how could Jǐngrén's intentions at that time
be disregarded?
How many court officials pushed both sides?
Even if there was a slight sincerity,
how could it be sufficient to cover up his evils?
Now, Jiǎ Chōng, with his meritorious achievements,
[一六] was a high official of the Jìn dynasty.
Although his accomplishments were not exceptional,
he was not known to have committed great crimes.
Yet, when various ministers offered advice,
he was immediately sent away.
Your Majesty, with your sagely wisdom,
instead hesitates in this matter.
The transgressions on Bǐngzhī's person
are already widely known.
His forming factions and engaging in cliques,
stirring up right and wrong,
are truly enough to disturb society and damage customs.
His various evils are numerous
and surpass those of Fàn Yè;
he merely lacks the crime of rebellion.
I humbly beg Your Majesty to deeply reconsider,
and try to inquire broadly among those who can be consulted
about the various rumors.
Your subjects, seeing Your Majesty's heavy favor towards him,
may fear to criticize him harshly.
On the day of consultation,
it would be appropriate to express your intent to address the impropriety.
If not so,
it would also be impossible to discern any merits or demerits.
Your subject is foolish,
but having made this suggestion,
I wish to express my full heart.
If there is nothing acceptable,
I humbly beg Your Majesty to pardon my offense of bluntness."
At that time, Bǐngzhī defended himself:
"I am unfamiliar with the regulations of the Imperial Secretariat,
and the clerks all said that staying overnight outside was not objectionable."
Emperor Tàizǔ believed that Bǐngzhī had been misled and that
a small matter was not enough to harm a high official.
Shàngzhī further stated:
"Bǐngzhī called the two clerks to stay overnight.
The clerks consulted the Chief Clerk, Luò Zǎi,
who said it was not permissible.
The Personnel Department also knew it was not allowed.
The clerks fully explained to Bǐngzhī that they could not stay,
but Bǐngzhī completely disregarded it.
This was not due to misunderstanding;
it was simply a deliberate attempt to keep them.
Everyone outside knew this,
[一七] so to attribute it to being misled by trust,
how would the public understand?
Your Majesty should not make excuses for him.
Although they were clerks,
their staying out gravely violated court regulations,
and thus it cannot be called a small matter.
Xiè Huì's prestige and actual conduct
were incomparable to those of today.
Yet, for one mistake,
he was dismissed from his position as Court Attendant.
Wáng Xún, a worthy man of his time, committed a minor error,
and Huán Yìn made a mistake during the spring hunt;
both were stripped of their official titles and given positions as commoners.
How much more so for a high official who violates constitutional regulations?
I wonder if there can be a precedent similar to Wáng and Huán being commoners?
It would not harm his appointments
and could also serve as a strict warning.
Kǒng Wànxì, in his capacity as Left Assistant Minister,
did not consider what was appropriate,
and said to Luò Zǎi: 'Bǐngzhī is highly influential,
different from other ministers of the Secretariat.
It's perfectly fine to say nothing.'
He also said: 'If one is not foolish or deaf,
one cannot be a good paternal aunt or uncle.'
Daring to make such remarks
is also unusual."
Tàizǔ 猶優游之,
使 Shàngzhī 更陳其意.
Shàngzhī 乃備言 Bǐngzhī 之愆過,
曰:
「尚書舊有增置幹二十人,
以 Yuán, Kǎi 丞郎幹之假疾病,
Bǐngzhī 常取十人私使,
詢處幹闕,
不得時補.
〔一八〕近得王師,
猶不遣還,
臣令人語之,
『先取人使,
意常未安,
今既有手力,
不宜復留』 .
得臣此信,
方復遣耳.
大都為人好率懷行事,
有諸紜紜,
不悉可曉.
臣思 Zhāng Liáo 之言,
Guān Yǔ 雖兄弟,
Cáo Gōng 父子,
豈得不言.
觀今人憂國實寡,
臣復結舌,
日月之明,
或有所蔽.
然不知臣者,
豈不謂臣有爭競之迹,
追以悵悵.
臣與 Bǐngzhī 周旋,
俱被恩接,
不宜復生厚薄.
Tàiwèi 昨與臣言,
說 Bǐngzhī 有諸不可,
非唯一條,
遠近相崇畏,
震動四海,
凡短人辦得致此,
更復可嘉.
Yú Xiùzhī 門生事之,
累味珍肴,
未嘗有乏,
其外別貢,
豈可具詳.
Bǐngzhī 門中不問大小,
誅求 Zhāng Yòuxù,
Yòuxù 轉無以堪命.
Bǐngzhī 先與 Liú Déyuàn 殊惡,
Déyuàn 自持琵琶甚精麗.
遺之,
便復款然.
市令 Shèng Fù 進數百口材助營 宅,
恐人知,
作虛買券.
Liú Dàoxī 驟有所輸,
傾南俸之半.
Liú Yōng 自謂得其力助,
事之如父,
夏中送甘蔗,
若新發於州.
國吏運載樵荻,
無輟於道.
諸見人有物,
鮮或不求,
聞 Liú Zūnkǎo 有材,
便乞材,
見好燭盤,
便復乞之.
選用不平,
不可一二.
Tàiwèi 又云,
Bǐngzhī 都無共事之體,
凡所選舉,
悉是其意,
政令 Tàiwèi 知耳.
論 Yú Xiùzhī 作黃門,
Tàiwèi 不正答和,
故得停.
Tàiwèi 近與 Bǐngzhī 疏,
欲用 Déyuàn 兒作州西曹,
Bǐngzhī 乃啟用為主簿,
即語 Déyuàn,
Déyuàn 謝 Tàiwèi.
前後漏泄賣恩,
亦復何極,
縱不加罪,
故宜出之.
士庶忿疾之,
非直 Xiàng Yǔ Chǔ gē 而已也.
自從 Péi, Liú 刑罰以來,
諸將陳力百倍,
今日事實好惡可問.
若赫然發憤,
顯明法憲,
陛下便可閑臥紫闥,
無復一事也. 」
Tàizǔ 欲出 Bǐngzhī 為 Dānyáng,
又以問 Shàngzhī,
Shàngzhī 答曰:
「臣既乏 Jiǎ Shēng 應對之才,
又謝 Jí Gōng 犯顏之直,
至於侍坐仰酬,
每不能盡.
昨出伏復深思,
祇有愚滯,
今之事跡,
異口同音,
便是彰著,
政未測得物之數耳.
可為蹈罪負恩,
無所復少.
且居官失和,
未有此比.
陛下遲遲舊恩,
未忍窮法,
為弘之大,
莫復過此.
方復有尹京赫赫之授,
恐悉心奉國之人,
於此而息；
貪狼恣意者,
歲月滋甚.
非但虧點王化,
乃治亂所由.
如臣所聞天下論議,
Bǐngzhī 常塵累日月,
未見一豪增輝.
今 Qū'ā 在水南,
恩寵無異,
而協首郡之榮,
乃更成其形勢,
便是老王雅也.
古人云: 『無賞罰,
雖 Yáo, Shùn 不能為治也. 』
陛下豈可坐損皇家之重,
迷一凡人.
事若復在可 否之間,
亦不敢苟陳穴管.
今之枉直,
明白灼然,
而 Ruìwáng Lìngwáng,
反更不悟,
令 Jiǎ Yì, Liú Xiàng 重生,
豈不慷慨流涕於聖世邪.
臣昔啟 Fàn Yè,
當時亦懼犯觸之尤,
苟是愚懷所挹,
政自不能不舒達,
〔一九〕所謂雖九死而不悔者也.
謂 Bǐngzhī 且外出,
若能修改,
在職著稱,
還亦不難,
而可得少明國典,
粗酬四海之誚.
今愆釁如山,
榮任不損,
Bǐngzhī 若復有彰大之罪,
誰復敢以聞述.
且自非殊勳異績,
亦何足塞今日之尤.
歷觀古今,
未有衆過藉藉,
受貨數百萬,
更得高官厚祿如今者也.
臣每念聖化中有此事,
未嘗不痛心疾首.
設令臣等數人縱橫狼藉復如此,
不審當復云何處之.
近啟 Jiǎ Chōng 遠鎮,
今亦何足分,
外出恐是策之良者.
臣知陛下不能採臣言,
故是臣不能盡己之愚至耳.
今蒙恩榮者不少,
臣何為獨懇懇於斯,
實是尊主樂治之意.
伏願試更垂察. 」
Furthermore, it states:
"Your servant observes Liú Bó-Chǒng's great magnanimity and the actions of Bǐng-Zhī.
[二０] Someone said that when Zhāng Yòu-Xù was being escorted,
Yòu-Xù told the escort,
'Although I have obtained a county,
I owe three hundred thousand *qián*.
Yǔ Chōng-Yuǎn actually escorted me to Xīn-Lín,
where I was seen bound,
still unable to untie my hands.'
Xún Wàn-Qiū once visited Bǐng-Zhī,
and happened upon a guest surnamed Xià-Hóu.
The host asked, 'Do you have good oxen?'
He replied, 'No.'
He asked, 'Do you have good horses?'
Again, he said, 'No.
I only have excellent donkeys.'
Bǐng-Zhī immediately responded, 'That is precisely what I desire.'
When the guest left the gate,
he then sent a message to him to demand it.
Liú Dào-Xī said he was promoted by Bǐng-Zhī,
so Bǐng-Zhī sought from Dào-Xī dowry items and sacrificial vessels,
which amounted to millions.
He still claimed it was not so.
The selecting clerk, Zhāng Lóng, told your servant,
also lamenting his excessive acceptance of gifts,
saying, 'He truly received dowry items,
bronze censers so heavy that four men were needed to lift them, and fine kudzu-cloth mosquito nets,
and other items,
too numerous to count.'
While serving in the Chancellery,
he ordered his slave to sell Líng wine,
profiting one hundred and ten [percent],
which is also unprecedented for someone in a high government position.
I wonder if this has been overlooked by the sagely ear?
I fear it may tarnish the brightness of the sun and moon.
Your servant secretly sighs over this."
Emperor Tàizǔ then approved the petition of the relevant officials
and dismissed Bǐng-Zhī from office.
That year
was the twenty-fifth year of Yuán-Jiā.
In the twenty-seventh year,
he died at home,
aged sixty-three.
Emperor Tàizǔ, considering his long-standing loyalty,
posthumously reinstated him to his original office.
He had two sons, Jì-Yuǎn and Hóng-Yuǎn.
Xiè Fāng-Míng,
a native of Yáng-Xià, Chén Commandery,
was the paternal cousin of Shàng-Shū Pú-Shè Jǐng-Rén.
His grandfather, Tiě,
was the Administrator of Yǒng-Jiā.
His father, Chōng,
was Zhōng-Shū Shì-Láng.
His family was in Kuài-Jī.
He feigned illness and returned home.
He was appointed Huáng-Mén Shì-Láng,
but did not accept.
He was killed by Sūn Ēn,
and was posthumously granted the title of Sàn-Qí Cháng-Shì.
Fāng-Míng followed his paternal uncle, the Administrator of Wú-Xìng, Miǎo, in the commandery.
When Sūn Ēn attacked Kuài-Jī,
all the commanderies in the eastern region responded.
The people of Wú-Xìng, Hú Jié and Gào Piāo, attacked and took Dōng-Qiān County.
Fāng-Míng advised Miǎo to avoid them,
but he did not listen.
When the rebels arrived, he was killed,
but Fāng-Míng escaped by hiding.
Initially,
Miǎo's maternal cousin Fēng Sì-Zhī of Cháng-Lè, and the northern scholar Fú Yì Qiú Xuán-Dá,
both went to Wú-Xìng to seek refuge with Miǎo.
He housed them in the commandery school,
but treated them with little respect.
Both became resentful
and conspired with Ēn.
Ēn once, as a follower of Sì-Zhī and others,
entered the commandery at night.
Seeing Miǎo's forces,
he fled,
undetected.
Originally, he intended to raise an army in Wú-Xìng,
but circumstances prevented it,
so he moved to Kuài-Jī.
When Gào and others attacked the commandery,
Sì-Zhī and Xuán-Dá were both involved in the plot.
Liú Láo-Zhī and Xiè Yǎn and others attacked Ēn.
Ēn fled into the sea,
and Sì-Zhī and the others could not go with him,
so they gathered again.
Fāng-Míng gathered more than a hundred of Miǎo's former students and associates,
and ambushed and attacked Sì-Zhī and the others,
capturing them all and personally executing them.
At that time, after the chaos,
funerary rites were neglected.
Fāng-Míng's entire family suffered misfortune,
and he had no assets left,
yet he undertook the funeral arrangements,
exerting all his effort.
Within a few months,
the burials were all completed,
with the full rites of peaceful times,
unsurpassed.
Shortly thereafter,
Sūn Ēn again attacked Kuài-Jī,
and Xiè Yǎn was killed.
Ēn sought Fāng-Míng very urgently.
Fāng-Míng took his mother and sisters from Shàng-Yú to Dōng-Yáng,
passed through Huáng-Bò-Qiáo to Pó-Yáng,
then took passage back to the capital,
staying at the Guó-Zǐ-Xué.
He endured wandering through dangers and hardships,
experiencing all kinds of suffering,
yet his steadfast integrity
remained unchanged in adversity.
In the first year of Yuán-Xīng,
Huán Xuán captured the capital city.
Biàn Fàn-Zhī, the Administrator of Dān-Yáng, wielded immense power at court and throughout the land.
He wanted to marry his daughter to Fāng-Míng,
and sent Shàng-Shū Lì-Bù-Láng Wáng Téng to persuade him with full arguments,
but Fāng-Míng ultimately refused.
Huán Xuán heard of this and admired him,
immediately appointing him Zuò-Zhù-Zuǒ-Láng,
and then Chief Clerk to Sī-Tú Wáng Mì.
His paternal cousin Jǐng-Rén recommended him as Zhōng-Bīng Zhǔ-Bù to Emperor Gāo-Zǔ.
[二一] Fāng-Míng served with loyalty and diligence,
doing all he could.
Emperor Gāo-Zǔ said to him,
"I am ashamed that I have not yet bestowed upon you the reward of 'melon-spreading,'
but for now, you shall share the emoluments of Yù-Zhāng Commandery with me."
He frequently gave him rewards.
Fāng-Míng was strict and dignified,
conducting himself well even when alone.
Even in a dark room,
he never allowed his demeanor to falter.
He had no other special skills,
but possessed a natural elegant charm.
His paternal cousin Hùn had a great reputation,
but only visited for seasonal greetings.
Liú Mù-Zhī, the Administrator of Dān-Yáng, was very powerful at the time,
and people flocked to him from all quarters.
The only four people who did not associate with Mù-Zhī were Hùn, Fāng-Míng, Xī Sēng-Shī, and Cài Kuò.
Mù-Zhī resented this greatly.
Later, Fāng-Míng and Kuò went to visit him.
He was very pleased,
and reported to Emperor Gāo-Zǔ,
"Xiè Fāng-Míng can be called a 'colt of a famous family.'
Simply placing him [in office] would make him a pillar of the state,
not to mention his talent and usefulness."
Shortly thereafter,
he was transferred to Cóng-Shì Zhōng-Láng,
and then became Cháng-Shǐ to Zuǒ Jiāng-Jūn Dào-Lián.
Emperor Gāo-Zǔ ordered that all matters within the yamen
should be decided in consultation with him.
He moved with the yamen to Zhōng-Jūn Cháng-Shǐ.
Soon after, he was further appointed Administrator of Jìn-Líng,
and then again Páo-Jì Cháng-Shǐ and Administrator of Nán-Jùn,
with trust and responsibility as before.
Once, at the end of the year,
all prisoners in Jiāng-Líng County jail, regardless of the severity of their crimes,
were released to go home,
with the instruction to return after exactly three days.
More than twenty individuals were facing serious charges.
From the administrative staff downwards,
everyone was apprehensive and fearful.
At that time, the former chief clerks of Jìn-Líng Commandery, Hóng Jì-Shèng and Xú Shòu-Zhī, were both with him in the west.
[二二] They firmly advised him,
saying,
"Although people of old had such practices,
they might be exaggerated accounts in records.
Moreover, the present public sentiment is false and shallow;
one cannot apply ancient principles to it."
Fāng-Míng did not accept their advice
and released them all at once.
The prisoners and their fathers and elder brothers were all astonished, joyful, and wept,
thinking that even if they died, they would have no regrets.
By the deadline,
two seriously criminal prisoners had not returned.
Fāng-Míng did not allow pursuit.
One of them was too drunk to return,
and only came back two days later.
The other prisoner did not arrive after ten days.
The Chief of Officials, Zhū Qiān-Qī, requested an audience to report and seek permission to pursue him.
Fāng-Míng knew it was about the prisoner,
and told his attendants to dismiss the Chief of Officials, saying there was no need to enter,
and that the prisoner would return on his own.
The prisoner wandered through the villages,
unable to bring himself to return.
The villagers reproached him
and escorted him back.
Consequently, there were no escapees.
Far and near, all admired and submitted to him.
He suffered the sorrow of his mother's death
and left office.
After the mourning period,
he became Shàng-Shū Lì-Bù-Láng of Sòng-Tái.
Gāozǔ received the Mandate,
and he was transferred to serve as Shìzhōng.
In the third year of Yǒngchū,
he was sent out to be the Dānyáng Yǐn,
earning a reputation for capability.
He was then transferred to be the Kuàijī Tàishǒu.
The households in Jiāngdōng were prosperous,
but the customs were harsh and severe.
The strong oppressed the weak,
corrupt officials swarmed,
and once a summons or warrant was issued,
arrests followed one after another.
Furthermore, guilt extended to neighbors,
leading to mutual implication at every turn.
If one person offended an official,
an entire village would cease its livelihood,
and the townships and villages would be alarmed and disturbed,
with dogs barking until dawn.
Fāngmíng deeply understood the principles of governance,
not being bound by strict legal texts,
broadly disregarding minor details,
and striving to uphold the main principles.
When the provincial administration issued summonses,
he immediately announced them,
granting the people delays for their appointments,
allowing them time to handle their affairs.
The county supervisory officials
were not allowed to act recklessly.
Noble families and powerful gentry
dared not violate prohibitions.
He abolished the system of mutual implication among neighbors,
and resolved cases of long-held prisoners.
In previous campaigns and expeditions,
whenever military provisions were insufficient,
he would mobilize all able-bodied commoners.
Once the matters were settled,
he would have them all return to their original places.
However, those who had been harmed or oppressed
were sometimes directly appointed as officials.
If a prefect or magistrate was unenlightened,
and their grants and withdrawals were inconsistent,
and personal influence was lacking,
they would surely be suppressed and obstructed.
Fāngmíng was discerning and precise in his selections,
ensuring each person was suited to their role.
Even if one had served for ten years,
they could still be employed in governance in a single day.
The people of the eastern region still praise him to this day.
He was particularly fond of conserving and preserving,
never arbitrarily criticizing or approving.
When succeeding a predecessor,
he would not readily change their policies.
If there was something that absolutely needed to be changed,
he would gradually shift and alter it,
leaving no trace for others to follow.
In the third year of Yuánjiā,
he died in office
at the age of forty-seven.
His son, Huìlián,
was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth.
At the age of ten,
he could compose literary pieces.
His cousin, Língyùn, deeply appreciated and valued him;
his story is in the biography of Língyùn.
The provincial administration appointed him as Zhǔbù,
but he did not accept.
Huìlián previously admired Dù Délíng, a county official in Kuàijī Commandery.
When his father passed away,
he presented him with over ten five-character poems,
which circulated widely.
He was banished and degraded due to his involvement
and was not among the honored ranks.
The Shàngshū Púyè, Yīn Jǐngrén, admired his talent.
On one occasion, he spoke to Tàizǔ, saying:
"When I was a child,
I already saw this type of writing in the world,
and commentators said it was Xiè Huìlián,
but it was actually not."
Tàizǔ said:
"If that is the case,
then he should be given a position."
In the seventh year of Yuánjiā,
he finally became Fǎcáo Cānjūn for Sītú Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng.
At that time, Yìkāng was governing the eastern government city.
An ancient tomb was found in the city moat,
so he had it reburied
and instructed Huìlián to write a funerary inscription.
He waited with confidence for it to be completed,
and the essay was very beautiful.
He also composed "Ode to Snow,"
which was also considered extraordinary for its elegance.
Both of his literary works circulated in the world.
In the tenth year,
he died
at the age of twenty-seven.
〔二三〕Having died young,
and being somewhat frivolous and prone to troubles,
his official position was not prominent.
He had no sons.
His younger brother, Huìxuān,
served as the Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng for Jìnglíng Wáng Dàn, and Línchuān Nèishǐ.
Jiāng Yí, courtesy name Mòyuǎn,
was from Kǎochéng, Jìyáng.
His grandfather,
〔二四〕was the Jìn Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
His father, Huǐ, was the Piàojì Zīyì Cānjūn.
Yí polished himself diligently in his youth,
becoming an outstanding talent among later generations.
The provincial administration appointed him as Zhǔbù,
but he did not accept.
When Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
he appointed him as Yùzhāng Wáng Wénxué.
When the righteous army was raised,
Gāozǔ appointed him as Zhèn Jūn Xíng Cānjūn.
Soon after, he became a staff member for the Dà Sīmǎ Lángyé Wáng.
〔二五〕He was then dismissed due to an official matter.
〔二六〕After a while,
he was reappointed as Zhǔbù.
For his contribution to the expedition against Huán Xuán,
he was enfeoffed as a fifth-rank侯 (hóu) of Zhōulíng County in Nánjùn.
He served as Mèng Chǎng's Jiànwēi Fǔ Sīmǎ,
Zhōngshū Shìláng,
Zhōng Jūn Tàiwèi Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
then Dào Guī's Zhēng Xī Dàjiāngjūn Zhǎngshǐ and Nánjùn Tàishǒu.
Soon after, he was transferred to Tàiwèi Zīyì Cānjūn,
leading the record-keeping section.
He was promoted to Zhǎngshǐ,
then entered the court as Shìzhōng,
and Dà Sīmǎ.
〔二七〕He followed the Duke on the Northern Expedition,
〔二八〕paid respects at the Luòyáng imperial tombs,
and advanced to Tóngguān.
He returned to lead as Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn, Lángyé Nèishǐ, and the Grand Middle Righteous of his home province.
Gāozǔ instructed that the affairs of the Dà Sīmǎ's office and Lángyé Kingdom
be entirely entrusted to him.
〔二九〕
When the Sòng dynasty was first established,
he became Wǔbīng Shàngshū.
When Gāozǔ received the Mandate,
he was transferred to manage the Duózhī (Ministry of Finance).
He was sent out to be Yìxīng Tàishǒu,
with an added rank of Zhōng Èrqiānshí.
He resigned due to illness.
Soon after, he was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū
and served as Wú Jùn Tàishǒu.
When Yíngyáng Wáng was murdered in Wú County,
Yí mourned for him with full propriety.
He resigned again due to his brother's illness.
He then served as Dānyáng Yǐn again,
and Lìbù Shàngshū,
with the added title of Sànqí Chángshì,
and was promoted to Yòu Púyè.
Yí possessed a refined demeanor
and graceful conduct,
and was known for his gentle and simple approach in all his appointments.
He was sent out to be Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the added title of Sànqí Chángshì.
Before he could take up his post,
he died of illness
at the age of forty-eight.
His dying wish was for a modest burial and simple offerings,
emphasizing frugality.
He was posthumously granted the title Qián Jiāngjūn,
with his original official position remaining as before.
His son, Zhàn,
has a separate biography.
The Imperial Historian states: The way of governing a nation
is that trustworthiness is more important than food.
The essential quality for establishing a person
is character first, then refinement.
A gentleman should base himself on upright character
and take righteousness as his foundation,
and then adorn himself with skills and talents,
and refine himself with rites and music.
If these are difficult to fully possess,
it is better to have insufficient refinement but an abundance of character.
Therefore, the cautious and reverent
can serve the Most High,
while the garrulous and self-important commoner
will ultimately not escape the tiger's den.
Jiāng Yí, Xiè Fāngmíng, Xiè Hóngwēi, Wáng Huì, and Wáng Qiú's
excellence in learning and righteousness
was not enough to make them famous,
yet their steadfast hearts and elegant character
were rarely matched by court officials.
The poem says,
"The gentle and respectful person
is the foundation of virtue."
This is truly so.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter Fourteen: Kǒng Jìgōng, Yáng Xuánbǎo, Shěn Tánqìng
Kǒng Jìng [孔靖], courtesy name Jìgōng [季恭],
was a native of Shānyīn [山陰], Kuàijī [會稽].
His personal name was the same as that of Gāozǔ's [高祖] great-grandfather,
so he was known by his courtesy name.
His grandfather, Yú [愉],
was a Chēqí Jiāngjūn [車騎將軍] in the Jìn [晉] dynasty.
His father, Yín [誾],
was a Sànqí Chángshì [散騎常侍].
Jìgōng [季恭] was initially recommended as a Jùn Xiàolián [郡孝廉],
then served as a Gōngcáo Shǐ [功曹史],
Zhùzuò Zuǒláng [著作佐郎],
Tàizǐ Shèrén [太子舍人],
Zhènjūn Sīmǎ [鎮軍司馬],
and Sītú Zuǒ Xīyuàn [司徒左西掾].
Before he could be appointed,
he suffered the sorrow of his mother's death.
In the fifth year of Lóng'ān [隆安] (401 CE),
while in mourning, he was summoned to be appointed Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn [建威將軍] and Shānyīn Lìng [山陰令],
but he did not accept.
When Gāozǔ [高祖] launched his eastern campaign against Sūn Ēn [孫恩],
he frequently visited Kuàijī [會稽].
Jìgōng [季恭] went out of his way to greet him with courtesy,
and provided generous supplies.
Later, when Gāozǔ [高祖] was suppressing Sūn Ēn [孫恩],
Huán Xuán's [桓玄] intention to usurp the throne was already evident.
Gāozǔ [高祖] wished to raise an army in Shānyīn [山陰] to suppress him.
Jìgōng [季恭] believed that Shānyīn [山陰] was far from the capital,
and furthermore, Huán Xuán [桓玄] had not yet ascended to the highest position.
It would be better to wait until his usurpation became manifest,
and his evil deeds ripe,
then slowly plan to attack him from Jīngkǒu [京口].
There would be no worry of failure.
Gāozǔ [高祖] also considered this to be correct.
When Yú Xiàofù [虞嘯父] was appointed Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn [征東將軍] and Kuàijī Nèishǐ [會稽內史],
Jìgōng [季恭] initially sought to become his Fǔ Sīmǎ [府司馬],
but did not succeed.
When the Emperor pacified Huán Xuán [桓玄],
he appointed Jìgōng [季恭] as Nèishǐ [內史],
and sent an envoy with the sealed commission to bestow it upon him.
The envoy met Jìgōng [季恭] directly.
Jìgōng [季恭] immediately turned his boat around and returned that night.
Upon arrival, he knocked on Xiàofù's [嘯父] door to inform him,
and also ordered a separate room to be cleaned.
He then entered the commandery.
Xiàofù [嘯父] had originally been appointed by Huán Xuán [桓玄].
Hearing of Huán Xuán's [桓玄] defeat,
he was terrified,
opened his gates, and begged for punishment.
Jìgōng [季恭] comforted and encouraged him,
telling him to stay put for the time being,
and to move the next morning.
Upon taking office, Jìgōng [季恭]
endeavored to cultivate practical governance,
ordered a stop to extravagance,
and punished idlers.
Consequently, banditry declined,
and the region became peaceful and orderly.
He was summoned to be Ròuwèi Jiāngjūn [右衞將軍] and
given the additional title of Jǐshì Zhōng [給事中],
but he did not accept the appointment.
Soon after, he was appointed Shìzhōng [侍中],
concurrently serving as the Zhōngzhèng [中正] of his native commandery,
and then transferred to be Dà Sīmǎ Sīmǎ [大司馬司馬] to the Prince of Lángyá [琅邪].
Soon after, he was sent out to be the Tàishǒu [太守] of Wúxīng [吳興],
with the additional title of Guānjūn [冠軍].
Prior to this,
Wúxīng [吳興] had frequently lost its Tàishǒu [太守].
It was said that the spirit of Xiàng Yǔ [項羽] had become the King of Biànshān [卞山],
and resided in the commandery office.
Whenever a Tàishǒu [太守] arrived,
they would always avoid that office.
However, Jìgōng [季恭] resided in the office,
and suffered no harm.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Yòupúyè [尚書右僕射],
but firmly declined.
In the eighth year of Yìxī [義熙] (412 CE),
he was again appointed Dū Wǔjùn Zhūjūn [督五郡諸軍], Zhēnglǔ [征虜], and Kuàijī Nèishǐ [會稽內史].
He repaired schools
and encouraged recitation and study.
In the tenth year (414 CE),
he was again appointed Shàngshū Yòupúyè [尚書右僕射],
with the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì [散騎常侍],
but again declined the appointment.
A short while later,
he was appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn [領軍將軍],
with the additional titles of Sànqí Chángshì [散騎常侍]
and Dà Zhōngzhèng [大中正] of his home province.
In the twelfth year (416 CE),
he retired,
and was appointed Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū [金紫光錄大夫],
with the Chángshì [常侍] title as before.
That year,
Gāozǔ [高祖] launched a northern expedition,
and Jìgōng [季恭] requested to follow.
He was appointed Tàiwèi Jūnzī Jìjiǔ [太尉軍諮祭酒] and Hòujiāngjūn [後將jūn].
He followed in pacifying Guān [關] and Luò [洛].
When Gāozǔ [高祖] became Xiàngguó [相國],
he also moved with the household.
When the Sòng Tái [宋臺] was first established,
an imperial edict appointed him Shàngshū Lìng [尚書令],
with the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì [散騎常侍].
He again declined to accept,
and was then appointed Shìzhōng [侍中], Tèjìn [特進], and Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū [左光祿大夫].
He resigned and returned east.
Gāozǔ [高祖] saw him off at Xìmǎ Tái [戲馬臺],
and all the officials composed poems to praise his virtues.
When he received the mandate [to establish the Sòng dynasty],
he was given the additional title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī [開府儀同三司].
He declined for several years,
and ultimately did not accept it.
In the third year of Yǒngchū [永初] (422 CE),
he passed away,
at the age of seventy-six.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng [侍中], Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū [左光祿大夫], and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī [開府儀同三司].
His son, Shānshì [山士],
held prominent positions,
including Shìzhōng [侍中]
and Kuàijī Tàishǒu [會稽太守].
He was dismissed from office due to his younger brother, Dàoráng [道穰], who was Jìbù Láng [駕部郎], forcibly abducting a girl from a respectable family,
and served as governor without official rank.
In the twenty-seventh year of Yuánjiā [元嘉] (450 CE),
he died in office.
His younger brother Línfú.
In the late Yuánjiā era,
he served as Sīkōng Zhǎngshǐ to Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān and Nánjùn Tàishǒu,
and Shàngshū Lìbù Láng.
In the early Dàmíng era of Shìzǔ,
he was promoted from Shìzhōng to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He was appointed Dānyáng Yǐn.
The territory of Shānyīn County was narrow and cramped,
with many people but little land.
Línfú submitted a memorial proposing to relocate families without means to the borders of Yúyáo, Yín, and Mào three counties,
to reclaim and cultivate lake fields.
The emperor ordered the Gōngqīng to deliberate broadly.
Tàizǎi Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng deliberated, saying:
“To instruct farmers and cultivate the fundamentals [of agriculture]
is a common practice for any state.
For people who are settled,
they have been accustomed to their ways for a long time.
For example, if there is no land in the capital,
we have not heard of relocating residents to other counties.
Upon investigation, the prominent families and wealthy households in Shānyīn
do not have a small amount of land.
The poor exert their efforts,
it is not that there is nowhere for them to do so.
Cultivating barren land
will not save them from disaster and scarcity.
Furthermore, residents along the lake
make their living from fish and ducks,
and those who reside in markets,
there is no reason for them to happily relocate.”
Shàngshū Lìng Liǔ Yuánjǐng, Yòu Púshè Liú Xiùzhī, Shàngshū Wáng Zànzhī, Gù Kǎizhī, Yán Shībó, and Sì Xiāngdōng Wáng Yù deliberated, saying:
“Wealthy households with comfortable homes
do not need to change their occupation;
the poor in cold dwellings
must relocate.
Building houses in remote areas,
harvesting grain without delay,
if it is for the public, the public might not be easily satisfied;
if it is for private individuals, they might find it difficult to provide.
Once their livelihood is complete,
the labor of clearing land will naturally cease.
It is advisable to recruit fugitives and those willing to cultivate land,
who will go and establish themselves.
They need to roughly set things up,
and then relocate.”
Shìzhōng Shěn Huáiwén, Wáng Jǐngwén, Huángmén Shìláng Liú Qì, and Qiè Yǒng deliberated, saying:
“Although the common people are not directly engaged in farming,
they are not without means of livelihood.
If they are driven to the fields,
they will inevitably conflict and seize from each other.
Moreover, Yín and the other two counties
are all far from the seat of government.
People who are already settled,
suddenly relocated to another district,
new walls not yet erected,
old homes already destroyed,
both staying and leaving are difficult,
with no means to support themselves.
It is suggested that we should adapt to the people's feelings,
follow what they desire,
pardon the fugitives,
and let them settle into occupations.
If it is indeed proven to be fertile land,
then discuss the relocation.”
Tàicháng Wáng Xuánmó deliberated, saying:
“The common people are poor and lacking,
going far to barren fields.
Leaving the old and embracing the new,
both provisions and seeds are lacking.
It is difficult to get accustomed to it,
and not easy to encourage them.
It is suggested to slightly increase their provisions,
so they can exert themselves diligently,
clearly reward those who farm hard,
and apply penalties for idleness.”
Guānglùxūn Wáng Shēngzhī deliberated, saying:
“For fields that have been abandoned afar,
they are just beginning to clear the thorns.
To compel and tax the poor
is even more difficult.
If the relocation and establishment are roughly complete,
then proceeding slowly is not late.”
The emperor disregarded these deliberations
and followed Línfú’s proposal to relocate the people,
which all became good endeavors.
Línfú was transferred from Dānyáng to serve as Huìjī Tàishǒu,
and soon after, he was granted the additional title of Yùzhāng Wáng Zǐshàng Fǔjūn Zhǎngshǐ.
Línfú’s family was originally wealthy,
with very extensive property.
He also established a villa in Yǒngxīng,
covering a circumference of thirty-three *lǐ*,
with two hundred sixty-five *qǐng* of land and water,
encompassing two mountains,
and nine fruit orchards.
He was impeached by the Yǒusī,
and an imperial edict pardoned him.
However, Línfú’s replies were not truthful,
and he was dismissed from office for this.
Later, he was reinstated to his original post,
and also served as Xúnyáng Wáng Zǐfáng Yòujūn Zhǎngshǐ,
with the Tàishǒu position remaining as before.
He was truly capable
and did not care for superficial adornment.
Everywhere he served,
his administration was well-managed.
In the Jǐnghé era of the Former Deposed Emperor,
he offended a close minister,
who slandered and framed him,
leading to his execution by flogging.
His two sons, Zhànzhī and Yuānzhī,
were granted death in the capital.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
Línfú was posthumously honored with the title of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
Yuānzhī served as Shàngshū Bǐbù Láng during the Dàmíng era.
At that time, Zhāng Jiānglíng, a commoner from Ānlù Yìngchéng County, and his wife Wú jointly cursed his mother Huáng, causing her death.
Huáng, enraged and resentful, hanged herself and died.
This occurred during an amnesty.
According to the legal texts,
a son who kills, injures, or beats his parents
is to be beheaded and displayed;
for cursing them,
he is to be executed in the marketplace;
for plotting to kill one's husband's parents,
one is also executed in the marketplace.
If an amnesty occurs,
the punishment is waived, and one is assigned to forced labor in the metal works.
Jiānglíng cursed his mother,
and his mother, because of this, took her own life,
which is more severe than injury or beating.
If treated as a killing offense,
it seems too heavy;
if using the offenses of injury, beating, and cursing,
it seems too light.
The regulation only stated that for beating one's mother,
even with an amnesty, one is still beheaded and displayed.
There was no regulation for cursing one's mother to death during an amnesty.
Yuānzhī deliberated, saying:
“If one's heart is perverse,
the benevolent will not enter his dwelling.
If even the name is disliked,
how much more so the person's actions?
Therefore, beating, injuring, or cursing
is not pardoned by the law.
If cursing leads to death,
then there is no logical reason for leniency.
Lighter penalties
are for when there is doubt or a failure of good.
Seeking the meaning of the text,
this is not what it refers to.
Although Jiānglíng benefited from the amnesty,
he should still be beheaded and displayed.
The wife's relationship is based on marriage,
her love is not of blood kin.
Huáng's resentment
was not directed at Wú.
To pardon her death and assign her to forced labor in the metal works
is in accordance with proper law.”
The emperor decreed in accordance with Yuānzhī’s deliberation,
and Wú was exempted from execution in the marketplace.
Yáng Xuánbǎo was a person from Nánchéng, Tàishān.
His grandfather, Kǎi,
was Shàngshū Dūguān Láng.
His father, Suí,
was Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Xuánbǎo began his career as Chǔtái Tàicháng Bóshì.
He suffered a period of mourning for his mother.
After the mourning period ended,
Yòu Jiāngjūn Hé Wújí and Qián Jiāngjūn Zhūgě Chángmín both appointed him as Cānjūn,
but he did not accept either position.
He was appointed Lín'ān Lìng.
Liú Mùzhī recommended him to be Gāozǔ Zhèn Jūn Cānjūn,
Kùbù Láng,
and Yǒngshì Lìng.
He then again served as Gāozǔ Tàiwèi Cānjūn,
and was promoted to Zhǔbù,
and Dānyáng Céng.
In the second year of Jǐngpíng of Shàodì,
he was appointed Shàngshū Yòuchéng,
then promoted to Zuǒchéng,
and Sītú Yòu Zhǎngshǐ.
Fǔgōng Wáng Hóng greatly respected him,
and said to Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ Yǔ Dēngzhī and Lìbù Shàngshū Wáng Zhǔnzhī:
“You two wise gentlemen are bright and discerning,
and often understand things well,
but for the hope of magnanimity,
we should still jointly recommend Yáng.”
Soon after,
he was appointed Huángmén Shìláng.
He was skilled at *yì* (go),
rated third grade.
Tàizǔ gambled with him over a prefecture (commandery)
and won,
appointing him to supplement the post of *Xuānchéng*太守.
Previously,
when Liú Shì served as *Xuānchéng*太守,
he established a system concerning fugitive officials and commoners:
if one person was not captured,
the *fúwǔ* officials of the *lǐ* would be sent to the prefecture to serve in the labor corps.
However, if a fugitive was caught, the captor would be rewarded with two ranks.
Yáng Xuánbǎo considered this inappropriate
and memorialized, saying:
"Your servant humbly reflects that the reasons for desertion
all stem from destitution and coercion.
There has never been anyone who, with sufficient means, would gladly choose this path.
Now, to establish such a peculiar system
is to impose hardship on the people.
Your servant has heard that severe measures cannot be sustained,
and fears this will lead to widespread harm.
In the past, Gōng Suí likened the people to tangled ropes;
only by loosening them could order be restored.
Huáng Bà employed leniency and harmony,
not severity and harshness, as his primary method.
Your servant foolishly believes that a single person fleeing service
should not result in the entire household being implicated.
Now, if one person cannot be accounted for,
many others are implicated.
They, burdened by this heavy responsibility,
will each make plans for themselves,
leading to widespread flight and concealment,
which will surely proliferate.
Moreover, those who are capable of capturing fugitives
are generally not those who are cautious and frugal.
Having no real ability,
they merely oppress diligent officials.
Titles and honors become hollow and false,
causing many impediments.
Ranks will be insufficient to provide rewards,
and diligent service will have no incentive.
Furthermore, examining this system,
it is only applied to one region.
If it is right,
then it should be applied uniformly throughout the realm.
If it is wrong,
it should not be uniquely enforced in one prefecture.
The people are suffering from distress,
and the harm will be profound.
Your servant, unworthily holding his position,
fears it is difficult to comply with and implement this,
and so, with limited understanding,
ventures to present this to Your Majesty."
Because of this, the system was suspended.
Yáng Xuánbǎo served in the prefecture for one year,
then became *Tíngwèi*.
Several months later,
he was promoted to *Shàngshū Lìbù Láng*,
*Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng*,
then *Héngyáng*王 Yìjì’s *Yòujūn Zhǎngshǐ* and *Nándōnghǎi*太守,
and was awarded the title of *Fǔguó Jiāngjūn*.
He entered the court as *Dūguān Shàngshū* and *Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn*,
and was awarded the title *Jǐshì Zhōng*,
then *Dānyáng Yǐn*,
and *Kuàijī*太守.
He was then transferred to *Wú​jùn*太守,
and his salary was increased to the second grade of two thousand *shí*.
Tàizǔ valued Yáng Xuánbǎo for his integrity, frugality, and lack of desire,
and thus frequently appointed him to important prefectures.
Although his governance lacked extraordinary achievements,
he was always missed after his departure.
He did not seek wealth and profit,
and lived a simple and humble family life.
Tàizǔ once said:
"For people to enter officialdom, not only do they need talent,
but also destiny.
Whenever a good official post becomes vacant,
I never fail to think of Yáng Xuánbǎo first."
When Yuánxiōng usurped the throne,
he became *Lìbù Shàngshū*,
concurrently serving as *Guózǐ Jìjiǔ*,
and soon after was awarded *Guānglù Dàfū*.
When Shìzǔ entered to quell the rebellion,
many in the court and throughout the land fled south.
Shào gathered his officials,
held a sword, and angrily said:
"You may all leave now!"
The crowd trembled with fear and dared not speak.
Yáng Xuánbǎo's expression remained unchanged,
and he slowly said:
"Your servant will serve the court until death."
Only then did Shào relent.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Yáng Xuánbǎo as *Sànqí Chángshì*,
concurrently serving as *Chóngxiàn Wèiwèi*.
He was soon promoted to *Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū*.
He was also known for his prudence and respect,
and was generously rewarded.
In the early *Dàmíng* era,
he was promoted to *Guānglù Dàfū*.
In the fifth year,
he was promoted to *Sànqí Chángshì*
and *Tèjìn*.
From youth to old age, Yáng Xuánbǎo
was meticulous in his ancestral sacrifices.
New seasonal delicacies,
if not yet offered in sacrifice,
he would never casually taste.
In the eighth year,
he passed away,
aged ninety-four.
His posthumous title was Dìngzǐ.
His son, Róng,
possessed talent and spirit,
but was frivolous and lacked proper conduct.
Yáng Xuánbǎo once said:
"This child will surely ruin my family."
He rose to the position of *Tōngzhí Láng*.
He, along with Wáng Sēngdá, slandered and criticized current policies,
and was sentenced to death.
After his death, Shìzǔ granted Yáng Xuánbǎo an audience.
Yáng Xuánbǎo apologized, saying:
"Your servant lacks the sagacity of Jīntì,
and for this, I have failed Your Majesty."
The Emperor praised his words.
Róng had two younger brothers,
whom Tàizǔ personally named,
one Xián,
the other Càn.
He said to Yáng Xuánbǎo:
"I wish for your two sons to embody the residual 'Correct Beginning' (Zhèngshǐ) spirit of the reclusive scholars."
As Yáng Xuánbǎo was skilled (at go),
Hé Shàngzhī also had a refined liking for it.
Chǔ Yìn of *Wú​jùn*,
at seven years old,
entered the high-grade ranking (of go players).
As he grew older,
he surpassed all others of his time.
Yìn’s father, Róngqī, was a rebel along with Zāng Zhì.
Yìn was thus subject to execution.
Hé Shàngzhī pleaded, saying:
"Yìn's mastery of *yì*
surpasses ancient players and crowns those of today.
Wèi Chōu violated orders,
but was spared due to his talent.
There are many precedents where a father was executed but a son was pardoned.
I especially beg that his meager life be spared,
so that this unique art may not perish."
This was not permitted.
People of the time deeply lamented his loss.
Xuánbǎo's nephew, Xī, whose courtesy name was Tàiwén,
had talent and spirit from a young age.
At the beginning of the Dàmíng era,
he served as Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
At that time, Yángzhōu Cìshǐ, Xīyángwáng Zǐshàng, memorialized, saying:
"Although there are old regulations regarding
the prohibitions on mountains and lakes,
due to popular custom,
they are ignored and not observed.
People clear mountains and block off waters,
keeping them as family benefits.
Since recent times,
this laxity has worsened daily.
The rich and powerful occupy entire ridges,
while the poor and weak have no place to gather firewood or kindling.
Even fishing grounds
are similarly affected.
This is truly a deep-seated harm to governance,
which the administration ought to eliminate.
Old rules should be revised
and new regulations established."
The authorities consulted the Rénchén edict, which stated:
"Those who occupy mountains and protect marshes
shall be judged according to the law for brigandage.
For stolen goods exceeding one zhàng,
all shall be executed in the marketplace."
Xī considered that
"the Rénchén regulations,
whose prohibitions were severe and harsh,
were difficult to follow and
out of step with the times.
Yet, the occupation of mountains and blocking of waters
gradually spread and intensified,
becoming a habitual practice,
and eventually regarded as ancestral property.
To abolish them suddenly in one morning
could easily lead to complaints and resentment.
Now, let us revise them
and establish five new articles.
In all cases of mountains and marshes,
if they have been habitually cleared, planted, and cultivated with bamboo, wood, and various fruits to form forests or groves,
as well as dikes, lakes, rivers, and sea areas with fish traps, eel and minnow farms,
and constant effort has been put into their maintenance and operation,
they shall not be reclaimed.
Officials of the first and second ranks
are permitted to occupy three qǐng of mountain land;
third and fourth ranks,
two qǐng and fifty mǔ;
fifth and sixth ranks,
two qǐng;
seventh and eighth ranks,
one qǐng and fifty mǔ;
ninth rank and commoners,
one qǐng.
All shall follow the established guidelines
and register their holdings in the account books.
If one has already occupied mountain land,
one may not occupy more.
If existing occupation is insufficient,
it may be made up to the limit.
If it is not an existing enterprise as mentioned in the preceding articles,
it shall not be prohibited.
For offenders,
if the land or water measures one chǐ or more,
the value of the illicit gain shall be calculated,
and they shall be judged according to the law for ordinary theft.
The Rénchén regulations of Xiánkāng two shall be abolished."
This was adopted.
Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Yǔ,
formerly Right Guard General,
had a disagreeable relationship with his Fǔ Sīmǎ, Hé Jìmù.
Jìmù was close to and favored by Shàngshūlìng Jiànpíngwáng Hóng,
and repeatedly slandered Yǔ to Hóng.
When Yǔ was sent out as Yìzhōu Cìshǐ,
he seized a scholar's wife as a concubine.
Hóng ordered Yáng Xī to impeach him,
and Yǔ was dismissed from office.
Yǔ bore a bitter grudge against Xī.
A protégé, Xiè Yuánbó, who frequented Xī's company,
was ordered by Yǔ to inquire about the reason for his dismissal.
Xī said:
"This memorial was not my intention."
Yǔ immediately went to Hóng's gate to present a memorial of apology,
saying he had heard this from Yáng Xī.
Xī was dismissed from office for leaking the information.
Towards the end of the Dàmíng era,
he served as Shǐ'ānwáng Zǐzhēn's Zhēnglǔ Sīmǎ,
Huángménláng,
and Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
In the third year of Tàishǐ,
he was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Xī initially requested that his son-in-law, Zhèn běi Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Xiāo Huìhuī, be made Chángshǐ
and concurrently Nánhǎi Tàishǒu,
but Tàizōng did not permit it.
He then requested that he be made Dōngguǎn Tàishǒu.
After Xī arrived at his post,
Chángshǐ and Nánhǎi Tàishǒu Lù Fǎzhēn lost his office,
and Xī again requested that Huìhuī be appointed.
An edict stated:
"Xī comes from a humble family and a cold scholarly background,
unknown for generations.
He is frivolous and prone to faults,
as fully demonstrated throughout his career.
Merely for being upright and incorruptible, he was promoted to Lǐngnán,
but he presumes to demand and make endless requests to his superiors.
He may be demoted to Hèngyě Jiāngjūn."
Previously,
Lǐ Wànzhōu and Liú Sìzǔ had briefly occupied Guǎngzhōu;
this event is recorded in the biography of Dèng Wǎn.
Tàizōng appointed Wànzhōu as Bùbīng Xiàowèi,
added the title Níngshuò Jiāngjūn,
and provisionally put him in charge of Guǎngzhōu affairs.
When Xī arrived,
Wànzhōu and others had other designs,
so Xī executed them.
Xī appointed Pèijùn's Liú Sīdào as acting Jìnkāng Tàishǒu
to lead an army to attack the Lǐ people.
Sīdào disobeyed orders
and suffered a defeat,
so Xī sent men to arrest him.
Sīdào refused the order
and led his troops to attack the prefecture.
Xī sent Píngyuè Chángshǐ Zōu Yán to resist him at Cháotíng,
but the army was defeated and Yán was killed.
Sīdào advanced and attacked the prefectural city.
Sīmǎ Zōu Sìzhī resisted him at the West Gate,
but was defeated and also died.
Xī fled over the city wall;
Sīdào captured and killed him.
Fǔ Cānjūn Zōu Màn led several tens of men to raid Sīdào,
and had already entered the city,
but being outnumbered,
was again defeated.
Dōngguǎn Tàishǒu Xiāo Huìhuī led over a thousand civil and military officials from the commandery to attack Sīdào,
but was defeated
and also killed.
At that time, Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Chén Bóshào, who was leading an army to attack the Lǐ people,
returned and attacked Sīdào,
subduing him.
Xī was posthumously granted the title Fǔguó Jiāngjūn;
Huìhuī, Zhōngshūláng;
Sìzhī, Yuèqí Xiàowèi.
Xī's son, Chóng, whose courtesy name was Bóyuǎn,
was Shàngshū Zhǔkèláng.
When his mother passed away,
his mourning and grief exceeded the prescribed rites.
Upon hearing of the chaos in Guǎngzhōu,
he immediately went barefoot to Xīntíng,
unable to walk,
and collapsed on a river bank.
His retainers brought him a small boat,
whereupon he continued his journey.
After his father's burial was completed,
he could not bear the grief
and died.
Shěn Tánqìng,
a native of Wúxīng Wǔkāng,
was the paternal cousin of Shìzhōng Huáiwén.
His father, Fā,
a Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng,
died young.
Wúxīng Tàishǒu Wáng Sháozhī composed a eulogy for him.
Tánqìng was initially appointed Zhǔbù,
then Zhōu Cóngshì,
Xīcáo Zhǔbù,
and then Chángshāwáng Yìxīn's Hòujūn Zhènjūn Zhǔbù.
When his mother passed away,
his grief and emaciation were such that they were praised.
His local magistrate, Zhūgě Chǎnzhi, publicly reported it.
After the mourning period,
he was reinstated as Zhǔbù.
Yìxīn again requested him as Zhènjūn Jìshì Cānjūn.
He was appointed Yúháng Lìng,
then promoted to Sītú Zhǔbù,
Jiāngxiàwáng Yìgōng's Tàiwèi Lùshì Cānjūn,
and Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
At that time, there were floods and droughts annually.
Tánqìng proposed establishing ever-normal granaries to relieve the people's hardship.
Tàizǔ adopted his suggestion,
but the plan was not implemented.
He held the positions of Běnyì Zhōngzhèng,
Shàofǔ,
Yángzhōu Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ,
and Shǐxīngwáng Jùn's Wèijūn Chángshǐ.
When Yuánxiōng usurped the throne,
Shìzǔ launched an expedition to suppress him.
Shào sent Tánqìng back east to recruit people.
Āndōng Jiāngjūn Suíwáng Dàn arrested him and imprisoned him in Yǒngxīng county.
After a long time,
he was pardoned.
When Shìzǔ 踐zòu ascended the throne,
he was appointed Fǔjūn Chángshǐ to Dōnghǎi Wáng Huī.
He then entered the court as Shàngshū Lìbù Láng,
then Dàsīmǎ Chángshǐ to Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng,
then Nándōnghǎi Tàishǒu,
and then Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
In the first year of Dàmíng,
he was appointed Dū Xú Yǎn Èr Zhōu jí Liángjùn Zhūjūnshì, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
At that time, Diànzhōng Yuánwàijiāngjūn Péi Jǐngrén assisted in guarding Péngchéng.
He was a native of the Cáng people
and was well-versed in military and frontier affairs.
Tánqìng made him compile ten juan of Qín Jì,
detailing the rise and fall of the Fú clan's usurpation.
The book was circulated in the world.
The following year,
he was again summoned as Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
with the added title of Jǐshìzhōng,
and concurrently served as Běnzhōu Dàzhōngzhèng.
In the third year,
he was promoted to Cíbù Shàngshū.
That same year,
he died
at the age of fifty-seven.
He was posthumously granted his original office.
Tánqìng was diligent, honest, and upright,
and his administration was highly praised.
He often said to his children and younger brothers,
"I have no talent in life;
I merely wish to be an elder."
People of his time called him a venerable elder.
The historian says: The country of Jiāngnán was prosperous.
Although it encompassed Xiàngpǔ to the south
and Qióngshān to the west,
as for external tribute and taxes,
and internal treasury fullness,
it was limited to Jīng and Yáng two zhōus.
Since the Hàn dynasty,
the population had dwindled.
Jīngchǔ, a land of four battles
and five thoroughfares,
had its cities and towns ruined,
with not one in ten thousand remaining.
From the eleventh year of Yìxī, when Sīmǎ Xiūzhī fled,
〔13〕until the end of Yuánjiā,
thirty-nine years passed.
No chariots were used in war,
the people were not troubled by external labor,
corvée was lenient, and duties were simplified,
so the common people multiplied.
There was surplus grain in the fields,
and households did not lock their doors at night.
This was the peak of prosperity in both east and west.
Since Yángbù was divided,
its territory reached the south of the river,
and when compared to the Hàn domain,
it only included Dānyáng and Kuàijī.
From the relocation of the Jìn clan
until the era of Tàiyuán,
for about a hundred years,
there were no alarms of war,
and within the region,
all was peaceful.
When Sūn Ēn caused chaos and rebellion,
the destruction reached its extreme.
From then until the end of Dàmíng,
more than sixty years passed,
and the population multiplied,
nearly reaching the level of former times.
The land was vast and fertile,
the people diligently pursued their fundamental occupation.
If one year yielded a harvest,
several commanderies would forget hunger.
Kuàijī, bordered by the sea and lakes,
also had hundreds of thousands of qǐng of good fields.
Fertile and superior land,
an acre was worth one jīn.
The land between Hù and Dù
could not compare.
Jīngchéng encompassed the wealth of Nánchǔ,
and Yángbù possessed the richness of Quánwú.
The profits from fish, salt, tangerines, and timber
filled all directions,
and the abundance of silk, cotton, and cloth
clothed the world.
However, farming was laborious,
corvée was difficult, and profits were meager.
They worked throughout the year,
without a single day free from agricultural duties,
yet all the funds for regular taxes and extraordinary levies,
and the provisions for living and burial,
all came from this.
In years of abundance, grain was cheap to sell;
if grain was cheap, farming was difficult.
In famine years, grain was expensive to buy;
if grain was expensive, merchants profited doubly.
The proposal for "constant normalcy"
was implemented during the Hàn dynasty.
In the thirteenth year of Yuánjiā,
the eastern land was flooded,
and the people's lives were in peril.
Tàizǔ reduced expenses and cut down on usage,
opening granaries to relieve them,
so despite the suffering, there was no disaster;
this was due to his efforts.
At the end of Dàmíng,
prolonged drought led to disaster.
Although the hardship was similar to past distress,
the relief was not like that of the former ruler,
which is why the sickness was less than half of ancient times,
but the deaths were already double.
Whole families perished,
and the population decreased by more than half.
If the "constant normalcy" plan
had been implemented in the middle of the reign
and had truly focused on assisting the afflicted,
perhaps it would not have reached this point.
If it were managed with constant prices,
then officials would suffer, and the people would prosper,
but the proposal was rejected at the time,
likely for this reason.
Collation notes
Biographies No. 15: Zāng Táo, Xú Guǎng, Fù Lóng
Zāng Táo, courtesy name Dérén,
was a native of Jǔ, Dōngguǎn,
and the brother of Wǔjìng Huánghòu.
From a young age, he loved learning
and was skilled in the Sān Lǐ.
He was poor but self-reliant,
and his conduct was praised by his hometown.
During the Tàiyuán reign of Jìn Xiàowǔ Dì,
Wèijiāngjūn Xiè Ān first established the national academy.
Xú and Yǎn Èr Zhōu Cìshǐ Xiè Xuán recommended Táo as an assistant instructor.
Emperor Xiàowǔ posthumously honored his great-grand-aunt, Xuān Tàihòu.
Some deliberators suggested that she should be enshrined with Zhōngzōng.
Táo deliberated:
"The principle of the Chūnqiū is that the mother is honored through her son.
Therefore, Zhòngzǐ and Chéngfēng
were both referred to as 'Fūrén'.
The classics say 'examine the palace of Zhòngzǐ'.
If she were enshrined with Huì Miào,
then there would be no reason to build a separate palace.
The Empresses Dowager of Hàn Xiàowén and Hàn Xiàozhāo
were both designated by their sons' titles
and worshipped in their burial gardens,
not enshrined in the temples of Gāozǔ and Xiàowǔ.
The mother of Hòu Hàn Hédì was called Gōnghuái Huánghòu,
the grandmother of Āndì was called
〔Jìngyǐn Huánghòu, and the mother of Shùndì was called〕Gōngmǐn Huánghòu.
Although not designated by their sons' titles,
they were also worshipped in their mausoleums,
not enshrined with Zhāng and Ān two Dìs.
Thus, although the two Hàn dynasties had distinctions between Tàihòu and Huánghòu,
as for not being enshrined together,
the meaning is the same as in the Chūnqiū.
Only Gūangwǔ posthumously deposed Lǚ Hòu,
thus enshrining Bó Hòu with Gāozǔ Miào.
Furthermore, after Wèi Hòu was deposed,
Huò Guāng posthumously honored Lady Lǐ as Huánghòu,
enshrining her with Xiàowǔ Miào.
This is not an example of a mother being honored through her son,
but merely because Gāo and Wǔ two Miào
lacked consorts.
The Hàn system of establishing shrines at mausoleums
was different from the Jìn system.
I suggest that we should distantly follow the Chūnqiū principle of examining palaces,
and closely imitate the two Hàn precedents of not enshrining them together.
Once the honorary title is correct,
then the boundless filial devotion is expressed.
By establishing a separate shrine and temple,
the solemn meaning of ancestor worship is manifested.
By using the son's title,
the reason for the mother's nobility is also clarified.
One action fulfills three principles,
truly the lofty achievement of a wise king."
The deliberators followed his suggestion.
After a while,
he resigned from office.
Because his mother was old and his family was poor,
he and his younger brother Xī both abandoned worldly affairs
and personally engaged in farming for a living,
living frugally and supporting their parents for over ten years.
After his parents' deaths,
he mourned for six years,
and was known for his extreme emaciation.
After the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Línyí Lìng.
When the righteous banner was raised,
he was made a Taìxué Bóshì.
He participated in military affairs for Right General Hé Wújì,
and was transferred with the yámen to Zhennán Cānjūn.
When Gāozǔ was stationed at Jīngkǒu,
he wrote to Táo, saying:
"Recently, studies have fallen into disuse and neglect,
and the younger generation's undertakings have declined.
Within the humble gates,
the clear echoes have ceased.
This is truly because military campaigns have frequently alarmed us,
and rites and music have been suspended.
Frivolous men indulge their desires,
their emotions tainted by affairs.
How can we not propagate and venerate the ancient books,
and strongly encourage proper customs?
The gentlemen of this region,
with sons and nephews like a forest,
will be sought out at dawn.
I hope to hear of their excellent conduct.
However, like the jade of Jīng that contains treasure,
it awaits carving and polishing.
Like a secluded orchid bearing fragrance,
it needs fanning to spread.
Solitary study leads to little understanding;
this principle is clearly stated in the Zhōu Diǎn.
Now, eminent scholars are not far,
yet there is no report of people pursuing studies.
Is it not only that those devoted to learning are few,
or perhaps that encouragement and persuasion have been insufficient?
I hope you will further promote it."
He participated in the military affairs of Gāozǔ's Zhōngjūn,
then was appointed Shàngshū Dùzhī Láng,
and later put in charge of Cíbù.
He inherited the title of Gāolíng Tínghóu.
At that time, the chìwěi (owl-tail ornaments) of the imperial ancestral temple suffered a calamity.
Táo said to Zhuòzuò Láng Xú Guǎng,
"In the past, when Kǒngzǐ was in Qí,
he heard of a calamity in the Lǔ temple
and said it must be due to Huán and Xī.
Now, the four lords, Zhēngxī and Jīngzhào,
ought to be removed and destroyed,
yet they are still enshrined and receive offerings in the temple.
Is this perhaps the omen?"
He then submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the great affairs of a state
lie in sacrifices and military matters.
When constructing palaces,
ancestral temples come first.
Ancient wise kings
all showed utmost reverence and sincerity,
exhausting their efforts to honor their ancestors.
Only then could they spread pure civilizing influence throughout the four seas,
and achieve profound resonance with the spirits.
Therefore, it is fitting to examine the rise and fall of ancient classics in detail,
and follow emotional rites to seek what is central.
According to ritual,
the Son of Heaven has seven temples:
three zhāo and three mù,
plus the Grand Ancestor, making seven.
From the father's temple up to the fifth generation ancestor's temple,
all are sacrificed to monthly.
More distant temples become tiáo,
there are two tiáo,
which receive offerings only at special feasts.
Beyond the tiáo are altars (tán),
and beyond the altars are cleared spaces (shàn).
Only after prayers are made are they sacrificed to.
This is the order of ancestral temples,
the sequence of closeness and distance.
Zhèng Xuán believed that the tiáo were the temples of King Wén and King Wǔ.
Wáng Sù believed them to be ancestors of the fifth and sixth generations.
Considering the phrase 'beyond the tiáo,'
then the tiáo cannot be the temples of Wén and Wǔ.
Wén and Wǔ were the ancestors of Zhōu;
how could it be said that 'beyond the tiáo are altars'?
It is clear that 'distant temples become tiáo' refers to ancestors for whom mourning clothes are no longer worn.
Furthermore, distant temples have the rite of periodic offerings,
while beyond the tiáo there is a distinction between altars and cleared spaces.
This clarifies that the more distant the generation,
the more distant the meaning.
If tiáo were the temples of Wén and Wǔ,
they should be sacrificed to monthly, like the Grand Ancestor.
Although Hòujì is honored as co-sacrificed with Heaven,
this is based on the beginning of his merit and virtue,
not every instance of honor and respect having a descending order.
Moreover, there are rituals where abundance is valued,
hence the saying that 'those with abundant virtue flow high,
those with thin virtue flow low.'
It also says, 'From top to bottom,
the reduction in rank is by two;
this is ritual.'
This refers to the codes of rank and hierarchy,
and the texts distinguishing high and low.
Yet it is said that the Son of Heaven and feudal lords both sacrifice to five temples;
how can this be?
Moreover, kings sacrifice to their legitimate and deceased children,
down to their great-great-grandsons,
but the rites of sacrificing to ancestors
do not go beyond the great-great-grandfather.
Extending great kindness to descendants,
but neglecting sincerity and reverence for esteemed relatives,
is also not the intention of the sages in establishing rites.
Therefore, when temples were established during Tàishǐ,
Wáng Shì's proposal was followed.
If the father was a scholar,
and the son became the Son of Heaven or a feudal lord,
the sacrifice was performed as for the Son of Heaven or a feudal lord,
but the ceremonial impersonator wore the attire of a scholar.
Thus, it extended up to Zhēngxī,
to complete the number of six generations.
Even though Xuānhuáng was the Grand Ancestor,

On the day of the Yīn sacrifice,

This is what is meant by 'though a son be as sagely as Qí,

Now that those above Jīngzhào have moved,
the Grand Ancestor finally occupies the correct position.
Some argue that the zhāo and mù are not yet sufficient,
and wish to humble the Grand Ancestor to a lower seat.
Your servant believes this is not the intent of the ritual code.
The phrase 'with the Grand Ancestor, making seven'
means that once the zhāo and mù are sufficient,
the Grand Ancestor is outside the six generations.
It is not that seven temples must be filled

The deliberators also believe that the spirit tablets of the four lords should eternally remain in the Yīnxiá sacrifices.
Your servant again believes this is incorrect.
The saying 'the spirit tablets of destroyed temples
are arranged before the Grand Ancestor'
refers to the spirit tablets of former lords below the Grand Ancestor.
Therefore, the Báihǔ Tōng says: '
The Dì and Xiá sacrifices for removed temples
are to continue the body of the succeeding ruler,
maintaining their lineage without interruption.'
How could this apply to the four lords who were before the Grand Ancestor?
They are not rulers who inherited the lineage,
they had no auspicious omens of spiritual mandate,
nor were they the foundation of imperial enterprise.
In the past, they were included because their era was close;
now, the emotional ritual is already distant.
And yet they are to eternally receive Yīnxiá offerings,
perpetually vacating the Grand Ancestor's position.
Searching the ritual records,
I have not found this to be permissible.
In the early Yǒnghé era,
there was a great discussion on this rite.
At that time, Yú Xǐ and Fàn Xuān, both profound scholars of great learning,
all believed that the spirit tablets of the four lords
had no reason to exist eternally for a hundred generations.
Some wished to bury them between the two staircases,
some wished to store them in a stone chamber,
some wished to build a new structure for them.
Although their specific proposals differed slightly,
the general conclusion was the same.
If Xuānhuáng already occupies the highest position among the temples,
and the four spirit tablets continue to be part of the Dì and Xiá sacrifices,
then the great Jìn's Yīn sacrifices
will perpetually lack the Grand Ancestor's position.
Indeed, reason values moderation,
not necessarily excessive generosity.
Rites shift with the times;
how can one follow them without making a clear decision?
Therefore, though the feelings of a minister and son may be deep,
the posthumous titles 'fierce' and 'cruel' become more pronounced;
though the longing to commemorate distant ancestors may be urgent,
the rite of moving and destroying is applied.
It is not that one lacks the intention to be more generous,
but rather that the ritual system cannot be overstepped.
A stone chamber means storing them north of the temple,
and rebuilding means their location is unknown.
The temporary spirit tablet is for the spirit to rely upon;
when the spirit moves, there is the rite of burial.
If the four spirit tablets' sacrifices ought to be abolished,
then the spirits no longer rely on them.
According to similar precedents,
they should be buried like temporary spirit tablets.
However, the classics are difficult to detail,
and opinions are confused and conflicting.
This is not something your shallow servant can arbitrate."

At that time, in Shàn County, Kuàijī Commandery, Huáng Chū’s wife Zhào beat her son Zài’s wife Wáng to death.
