Lǒng deliberated on this, saying:
“Originally, the rise of rites and laws
was based on nature,
and sought from human emotions and reason,
not fallen from heaven,
nor sprung from the earth.
Father and son are closest kin,
sharing form and breath.
Chēng is to Zài [as]
Zài is to Zhào.
Although it speaks of three generations,
they are still one body,
and none can separate them.
Although Chēng has suffered deep trauma and pain,
there is fundamentally no principle of avenging one’s grandparent.
If Chēng could kill Zhào,
how should Zhào treat Zài?
To have fathers, sons, grandsons, and grandparents
mutually slaughtering each other
is surely not the fundamental principle of the former kings’ clear punishments
or Gāoyáo’s legislation.
If Shí Hòu’s son and Jīn Mìdī’s grandson
had sharpened their blades
and refused to live under the same sky as their two ancestors,
then how could Shí Què and Dū Hóu have earned fame for a hundred generations
and been considered praiseworthy?
The old decree says,
‘Those who kill their parents
shall be exiled two thousand *lǐ* away.’
It is clear that this does not apply to father-son or grandparent-grandchild relationships.
Zhào should only avoid Wáng’s family within a *jī* of a thousand *lǐ*.
The decree also says,
‘All those who are exiled,
if close relatives of the same household wish to follow,
it shall be permitted.’
This again greatly accommodates human emotions and kinship,
using kinship to teach love.
Since Zhào is to be exiled,
Zài, as her son,
how can he not follow?
If Zài follows but Chēng does not,
how can that be permitted by the teachings of proper conduct?
Thus,
Chēng and Zhào ultimately cannot be separated.
Although Zhào will feel internal shame for the rest of her life,
Chēng will suffer deep sorrow until his teeth fall out.
The principle of grandparent and grandchild
naturally cannot be completely severed.
This is indeed the case in reason and fact.”
This was followed.

The Five Sounds of music,

[一九] Their source is distant,

[二一] Without sagacious and wise great worthies,

When the Hàn arose,
old scholars were first summoned,

Fortunately, Gāo Tángshēng somewhat understood the old meaning.

Some, through master-disciple transmission,

Thus, Wén Rén and the two Dài,

The imperial historian says:
When the worthy are selected from among the common people, the cultivation of personal virtue flourishes;
when scholars are sought in the court,
the trend of cunning intellect arises.
The Six Classics are profound and far-reaching,
the righteous path to follow;
the Hundred Schools are shallow and trivial,
a shortcut to a side road.
In the Hàn (漢) dynasty, those who ascended to officialdom
were first recognized by their communities,
emphasizing fundamental learning
and not valuing superficial or bizarre practices.
Only then could one easily attain high office (literally: bend down and pick up a blue sash)
and disdain wealth (literally: look down on a basket of gold).
Thus, people strove to follow teachers,
and families competed in specialized skills.
Artistry was highly esteemed at the time;
a place where a scholar resided would suddenly become a market.
When a school was temporarily opened,
the number of registered students could reach tens of thousands.
Therefore, official careers were achieved through learning,
and one's person was established through righteousness.
Since the Wèi (魏) dynasty received the mandate,
the rulers delighted in intricate literary style,
families abandoned exegetical studies,
and people valued unusual techniques.
Furthermore, the selection of worthy scholars and promotion of civil servants
was no longer based on their local communities;
the responsibility of evaluation and recommendation
fell to the imperial court (Tái Gé 臺閣).
With the eyes and ears of one person,
to investigate the intricate situations across mountains and rivers,
the judgment of worthiness or unworthiness was guesswork,
and not one in ten thousand was correct.
Consequently, officials relied on borrowed reputations,
and learning was not for self-improvement.
They revered the clever speed of fortuitous encounters
and disdained the slow difficulty of settling down to work.
From then on, scholars abandoned their book boxes and neglected their classics,
each pursuing their own interests,
leaving early and returning late,
to obtain worldly resources.
The scholars of the xiáng xù (庠序) and hóng xiào (黌校)
and the profession of transmitting classics and gathering disciples,
from Huángchū (黃初) to the end of Jìn (晉),
over a hundred years,
Confucian education completely declined.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) received the mandate,
he deliberated on establishing a national academy,
but due to his early demise (literally: the imperial carriage left early),
the plan was not carried out.
It was not until Yuánjiā (元嘉)
that it was finally accomplished.
Though the elegant style was flourishing and magnificent,
it did not reach the level of former times,
yet it was grand and orderly,
possessing much of the legacy of previous kings.
The Son of Heaven, with phoenix banners and imperial escorts,
cleared the way and attended the academy.
The Crown Prince, in his ceremonial robes and crown,
faced north to pay respects to the former teachers.
This was something the younger generation had never heard of,
and even the elders had never witnessed it before;
it was truly a glorious achievement of that era.
Zāng Táo (臧燾), Xú Guǎng (徐廣), Fù Lóng (傅隆), Péi Sōngzhī (裴松之), Hé Chéngtiān (何承天), and Léi Cìzōng (雷次宗),
all embraced the teachings of the sages and philosophers,
and were not swayed by refined or vulgar trends.
It is fitting that they established their names in the world.
Yǐngchuān (潁川) Yǔ Wèizhī (庾蔚之), Yànmén (雁門) Zhōu Yěwáng (周野王), Rǔnán (汝南) Zhōu Wángzǐ (周王子), Hénèi (河內) Xiàng Yǎn (向琰), and Kuàijī (會稽) Hé Dàoyǎng (賀道養)
all devoted themselves to the classics
and were praised by later scholars.
Wèizhī (蔚之) had a general understanding of the Lǐjì (禮記)
and also annotated Hè Xún's (賀循) Sāngfú (喪服), which circulated in the world.
Textual Criticism Notes
Biographies, Volume 16: Xiè Zhān (謝瞻), Kǒng Línzhī (孔琳之)
Xiè Zhān (謝瞻), courtesy name Xuānyuǎn (宣遠),
also named Yán (檐), courtesy name Tōngyuǎn (通遠),
was a native of Yángxià (陽夏), Chénjùn (陳郡),
and the third elder brother of General of the Guards, Huì (晦).
At the age of six,
he was able to compose essays,
writing an encomium for purple quartz (Zǐshíyīng Zàn 紫石英讚) and a poem about a certain fruit (Guǒrán Shī 果然詩).
Talented scholars of the time
were all amazed and marveled.
Initially, he served as Húán Wěi's (桓偉) Anxī Cānjūn (安西參軍)
and Chǔ Tái (楚臺) Mìshūláng (祕書郎).
Zhān (瞻) was an orphan at a young age;
his aunt Liú (劉) raised him with kindness and care.
His brothers treated her
as their closest relative.
Liú's (劉) younger brother, Liǔ (柳), became the Administrator of Wújùn (吳郡)
and took his elder sister with him.
Zhān (瞻) could not bear to disobey,
so he resigned his post and followed him,
becoming Liǔ's (柳) Jiànwēi Zhǎngshǐ (建威長史).
Soon after, he became Gāozǔ's (高祖) Zhèn Jūn (鎮軍) and Lángyé Wáng (琅邪王) Dà Sīmǎ Cānjūn (大司馬參軍),
then transferred to Zhǔbù (主簿),
then Ānchéng Xiāng (安成相),
Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎),
Sòng Guó (宋國) Zhōngshū (中書) and Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎),
and Xiàngguó Cóngshì Zhōngláng (相國從事中郎).
His younger brother, Huì (晦), was then the Right Guard of Sòng Tái (宋臺),
and his influence was already considerable.
When he returned to the capital from Péngchéng (彭城) to bring his family,
guests thronged,
and the entrance and alleys were filled.
At that time, Zhān (瞻) was at home,
and he was startled and said to Huì (晦):
"Your position and rank are not yet very high,
yet people flock to you to such an extent.
Our family has always made plain living and retirement its profession,
unwilling to interfere in current affairs,
and our acquaintances are limited to relatives and friends.
Yet you have come to overshadow the court and the public.
Is this a blessing for our household?"
Then he erected a fence to separate the gate and courtyard,
saying:
"I cannot bear to see this."
When he returned to Péngchéng (彭城),
he spoke to Gāozǔ (高祖), saying:
"Your humble servant is fundamentally a plain scholar;
my father's and grandfather's ranks did not exceed two thousand dàn (石).
My younger brother is only thirty years old,
and his ambition and capabilities are quite ordinary,
yet he holds prominent positions in the imperial administration (Tái Fǔ 臺府),
and his responsibilities are both conspicuous and confidential.
Blessings beyond measure give rise to disaster,
and its consequence will not be far off.
I especially beg that he be demoted and dismissed,
to preserve our declining family."
He repeatedly made this plea.
Gāozǔ (高祖) appointed Zhān (瞻) as Administrator of Wúxīng Jùn (吳興郡),
but he again submitted a request to decline,
so he was made Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng (豫章).
Sometimes Huì (晦) would tell Zhān (瞻) secret court affairs,
but Zhān (瞻) would immediately recount them to relatives and old friends,
treating them as jokes,
to cut off his brother's talk.
Huì (晦) then achieved meritorious service in establishing the new dynasty,
and his trust and responsibility became extremely heavy,
which made Zhān (瞻) even more worried and afraid.
In the second year of Yǒngchū (永初) (421 CE),
he fell ill in the commandery
and refused to treat himself,
hoping not to live long.
When Huì (晦) heard of his illness, he rushed to him.
When Zhān (瞻) saw him,
he said:
"You are a high official of the state,
and you also command an important army.
Traveling thousands of miles away will certainly give rise to suspicion and slander."
Indeed, at that time, someone accused Huì (晦) of rebellion.
Zhān's (瞻) illness worsened, and he returned to the capital.
Gāozǔ (高祖), considering that Huì (晦) was with the imperial guard
and could not stay out overnight,
arranged for Zhān (瞻) to stay in the former residence of Yáng Bēn (羊賁), son-in-law of Jìn (晉) Nánjùn Gōngzhǔ (南郡公主),
located east of the Língjūn Fǔ (領軍府) gate.
Zhān (瞻) said:
"I have my ancestors' dilapidated hut; why should I be here?"
Before his death,
he wrote a letter to Huì (晦), saying:
"I am fortunate to have my body intact and complete,
and to have my bones returned to the foot of the mountain.
What more regret could I have?
Brother, you must strive and encourage yourself,
for the sake of the country and the family."
Then he died,
at the age of thirty-five.
Zhān (瞻) excelled in writing;
the beauty of his literary style
was comparable to that of his clan uncle Hùn (混) and clan cousin Língyùn (靈運).
Língyùn's (靈運) father, Huán (瑍),
lacked talent and served as Mìshūláng (祕書郎),
dying at a young age.
Língyùn (靈運) liked to criticize people,
which troubled Hùn (混).
He wanted to curb this habit
but had no way.
He said to Zhān (瞻):
"No one but you can do it."
So he and Huì (晦), Yào (曜), Hóngwēi (弘微) and others played together,
making Zhān (瞻) and Língyùn (靈運) ride in the same carriage.
As soon as Língyùn (靈運) got into the carriage,
he began to compare and judge people.
Zhān (瞻) said to him:
"The Mìshū (祕書) (referring to Língyùn's father) died early,
and those who discuss him also have differing opinions."
Língyùn (靈運) fell silent,
and his habit of making comments declined thereafter.
Dì Hú,
courtesy name Xuānjìng, showed extraordinary conduct from a young age.
When he was a few years old,
his birth mother, Lady Guō,
suffered from a chronic illness for a long time.
He would attend to her morning and evening,
tasting her medicine and offering her meals,
never missing a single moment.
His diligent expression and worried face
never changed.
Fearing that servants might be negligent or lazy in caring for her illness,
he personally undertook the strenuous tasks.
His mother was frightened by illness and easily startled,
so even the slightest footsteps were too much.
Everyone in the household, from senior to junior,
was touched by Dì Hú's filial piety,
and they all walked with padded shoes
and spoke in hushed tones.
This continued for over ten years.
Initially, he served as the Zhǔbù of the prefecture,
then as Cānjūn in the central army,
and then as Tàizǐ Shèrén.
Soon after, he was promoted to Mìshū Chéng.
Believing that his elder brother held high office and power,
and that he himself had been overly promoted,
he firmly declined the position.
Xú Xiànzhī invited him to serve as Sīkōng Chángshǐ
and Huángmén Láng.
In the third year of Yuánjiā (426 CE),
he was executed as part of a collective punishment.
He was thirty-one years old at the time.
An imperial edict pardoned his son, Shìpíng,
but Shìpíng also died young
without heirs.
Kǒng Línzhī,
courtesy name Yànlín, was a native of Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
His grandfather, Shěn,
was a Cóngshàng Yuàn during the Jìn dynasty.
His father, Xīn,
was a Guānglù Dàfū.
Línzhī was firm and upright, with strong ambition and capability.
He enjoyed literature and classical texts,
understood musical theory,
could play musical instruments,
and was exceptionally skilled in cursive and clerical scripts.
The commandery appointed him Zhǔbù,
but he did not accept.
Later, he was recruited as Běnguó Chángshì.
When Huán Xuán assisted in government and became Tàiwèi,
he made Línzhī Xīgé Jìjiǔ.
At that time, Huán Xuán discussed abolishing the use of coins and using grain and silk instead.
Línzhī argued:
"Among the eight policies of the Great Plan,
goods are ranked second to food.
Is this not because the means of exchange
are among the most essential things for use?
If people did not engage in exchange,
and the populace exerted themselves to make coins,
then that would hinder their means of livelihood,
and it would be acceptable to prohibit it.
But now, farmers attend to grain,
artisans attend to tools,
and the four classes of people each pursue their own profession.
How do they ever exert themselves making coins?
Therefore, the sage kings established useless goods
to facilitate the circulation of useful wealth.
There are no costs of damage or spoilage,
and the toil of transportation and storage is saved.
This is why coins succeeded the merits of tortoiseshells and cowries,
and have not been abolished throughout the ages.
Grain and silk are treasures,
originally used for clothing and food.
If they are now divided for use as currency,
they will suffer significant loss.
Moreover, they are damaged by the hands of merchants
and wasted by cutting and tailoring.
This disadvantage
has been evident since ancient times.
Therefore, Zhōng Yáo said: 'Crafty and deceitful people
compete to hoard damp grain to seek profit,
and make thin silk to serve as capital.'
During the Wèi dynasty, despite severe punishments,
they could not prohibit this.
For this reason, Sīmǎ Zhī believed that using coins not only enriched the state,
but also reduced crime.
The disuse of coins
occurred due to prolonged warfare and chaos,
leading to their eventual abandonment.
There were reasons for this,
as was the case at the end of the Hàn dynasty.
Now, if they are used and then abolished,
the people will suddenly lose their wealth.
[一０]If the grain of the entire world is gathered,
[一一]to supply the food of the entire world,
some granaries may be overflowing,
while others have not a single peck stored.
To facilitate mutual aid and circulation,
so that the poor can rely on the rich,
the means to achieve this
truly relies on coins.
If they are suddenly cut off,
they will become worthless.
This means that people who have coins but no grain
will all sit and starve.
This is the immediate disadvantage of abolishing coins.
Moreover, where coins are currently used, people are not poor,
and where grain is used, people are not rich.
Furthermore, the people have been accustomed to this for a long time,
and changing it will surely cause confusion.
The saying goes: 'Unless the profit is a hundredfold,
one does not change one's profession.'
How much more so when coins are more convenient than grain?
During the reign of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
coins were abolished and grain was used
for thirty years.
Because it was inconvenient for the people,
the entire court held a major discussion.
Talented and clear-thinking officials
[一二]unanimously agreed that coins should be used.
[一三]The people had no differing opinions,
and the court had no dissenting arguments.
That they still abandoned grain and silk to use coins
is sufficient to demonstrate the disadvantages of grain and silk,
which were proven by experience.
Some in the world say that because the Wèi dynasty had not used coins for a long time,
[一四]accumulating vast amounts of them,
they therefore wished to implement their use,
benefiting the public and enriching the state.
This is probably not the case.
In ancient times, during the planning of Jìn Wén's maternal uncle, Jiù Fàn,
he prioritized the trustworthiness of Chéng Jì,
believing that although there might be temporary merit,
it was not as good as benefits for ten thousand generations.
At that time, famous worthies were in the ranks,
and gentlemen filled the court,
deliberating on the advantages and disadvantages of the world
to establish crucial policies for governing the state.
If grain were truly more convenient than coins,
it would be unjust to ignore the immediate benefits of that time
and abandon a universal industry for eternal use.
This can be definitively known.
This was truly due to distress leading to thoughts of reform,
and change leading to renewed policy.
More recently, towards the end of Xiàowǔ's reign,
the world was at peace,
the climate was harmonious, and the years were bountiful.
The people enjoyed their livelihoods,
and grain and silk were abundant,
almost to the point where every family had enough and every person was satisfied.
Proving this by facts,
coins also did not hinder the people.
Recently, wars have frequently erupted,
famines have repeatedly struck,
and hunger and cold have not yet been overcome;
this is truly due to these circumstances.
Since you, sir, have supported and rescued the people,
greatly reforming perceptions,
extending the teachings of fundamental importance,
and clarifying the regulations for expanding agriculture,
reverently teaching the people the seasons,
and allowing each to follow their profession,
so that idlers know to return,
and those pursuing secondary occupations stop their ways,
surely everyone will exert themselves in the southern fields,
and no land in the countryside will be left uncultivated.
From then on,
peace and prosperity will surely arrive.
Why worry about clothing and food?
I foolishly believe that the method to remedy the defects
does not require abolishing coins."
Xuán also proposed restoring corporal punishment.
Línzhī thought:
“In the times of Táng and Yú, there were symbolic punishments.
Yǔ of Xià established penal laws.
The reason is that while the customs of purity and decline differed,
the aim of transformation remained the same.
Leniency and severity complement each other,
and adaptation to change is key.
The *Shū* says, 'Penalties are sometimes lighter, sometimes heavier, depending on the age,'
meaning they change with the times.
In the Three Dynasties, customs were pure and affairs were simple,
so few transgressed the laws;
in later ages, customs became cunning and affairs burdensome,
so people often fell into the legal net.
If the three thousand punishments were applied in a degenerate age,
there would surely be an excessive number of people with amputated feet.
This is why the Five Emperors did not strictly adhere to each other's laws,
and corporal punishment cannot be fully restored.
Emperor Wén of Hàn conceived a compassionate idea,
lamenting that the path to self-renewal was blocked.
He reformed ancient systems and created new ones,
calling it 'laying aside punishments.'
However, it was light in name but heavy in reality,
and instead harmed the people more.
Therefore, when Emperor Jǐng succeeded to the throne,
he lightened it by making it lenient.
But with leniency, the people became lax,
and it also failed to curb evil.
To find the right balance in punishments
was what was praised in the past,
and what successive generations have discussed in detail but never achieved.
After the chaos of war,
many more people are subject to the law.
The punishment of public execution
originally involved severing the right foot.
Emperor Wén of Hàn made one error,
which was carried on and not corrected,
which is why former sages deeply regretted it
and debated it without resolution.
The intentions of Zhōng Yáo and Chén Qún,
though slightly different,
both desired to replace public execution with severing the right foot.
If their words were followed,
then many would be saved.
To reduce capital punishment to preserving life
is truly a lighter law.
However, human nature is to be wary of what is obvious and disregard what is obscure,
to overlook the distant and be startled by the near.
This is why there are inscriptions on plates and basins,
and string is worn as a pendant.
How much more so for common people,
who are especially susceptible to delusion!
If something is not seen with their own eyes,
they disregard it and are not warned.
If it is constantly displayed before them,
it alarms their minds and startles their gaze.
From this perspective,
making it severe does not necessarily mean it won't cause harm,
and making it light does not necessarily mean it won't inspire fear.
But it can preserve their lives,
and increase their progeny.
Not only does benevolence help living beings,
but its merit also benefits the multitude.
Moreover, the current problem
is primarily that of fugitives.
Repeated rebellion without reform
should lead to them having no place to escape to,
thus also sternly warning those who have not yet offended
and permanently eradicating the source of evil.
As for other regulations,
they should follow the old system.
How can this be called perfectly balanced?
I merely offer a small opinion.”
Xuán liked people who were agreeable and flattering,
but Línzhī could not comply with his wishes,
and thus was not appreciated.
He was transferred to be an Aide-de-camp in the Chu Palace (Chǔ Tái Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng).
Upon his mother's death,
he resigned his post.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Sītú Zuǒ Xī Yuàn,
but resigned himself due to his father's retirement.
At that time, Sīmǎ Xiūzhī was the Administrator of Kuàijī (Kuàijī Nèishǐ) and Posterior General (Hòu Jiāngjūn),
and still appointed Línzhī as his Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ).
Upon his father's death,
he resigned from office.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Grand Commandant's Chief Clerk (Tàiwèi Zhǔbù),
then Left Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng),
and then Administrator of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ).
In all his positions, he achieved notable results.
At that time, all officials were ordered to present proposals for expedient measures.
The debaters thought that it was appropriate to repair schools,
show compassion in legal cases,
scrutinize officials,
clearly define promotions and demotions,
appoint recluses and promote talent,
and focus on agriculture while simplifying conscription.
Outside of these common opinions,
Línzhī made a separate proposal, saying:
“Seals and tallies
are used to distinguish official ranks and titles,
and to establish contracts and trust.
No office is greater than that of the Emperor,
and no title is more honored than that of Duke or Marquis.
The State Seal,
passed down through generations,
and the seals of hereditary feudal titles,
transmitted through successive ages,
are valued for remaining as they are,
without being remade.
However, in the current age, only the office of commandant (wèi)
uniquely uses a single seal;
as for all other internal and external officials,
every time they are transferred, their seals are entirely changed.
Upon investigating the reasoning behind this,
I personally have not understood it.
If one says that each official is of a different surname,
and thus unlike hereditary transmission,
then it is still not as different as changing dynasties.
If one considers their status,
although there is the nobility of Dukes and Ministers,
it is not as significant as the weight of Emperors and Kings.
If it is due to fearing the ominous pollution of officials who have been executed or annihilated,
then the Hàn dynasty used the Qín seal,
extending its mandate for four hundred years,
and it was never heard that because Zǐyīng was killed and his state perished,
the seal was discarded and not worn.
The reverence for Emperors, Kings, Dukes, and Marquises
does not doubt the transmission of seals,
so why should the lowly status of imperial subjects and numerous officials
object to immediately using the existing seal?
Records have not mentioned this explanation,
and applying precedents contradicts the standard.
Yet, throughout the year, carving and casting takes place,
wasting effort and diminishing resources.
The expenses of gold, silver, copper, and charcoal
are incalculable.
This is not a way of following old customs and simplifying procedures.
I humbly suggest that all officials should immediately use a single seal,
without the trouble of remaking them.
Only if a new office is established,
or if there are many offices but few seals,
or if the inscription is lost,
should seals then be cast.
This would assist the imperial treasury,
and would not merely be a small benefit.”
He also said:
“The practice of placing cypress decorations at the gate of a mourning house
is not found in the rituals and classics;
it originated in later ages,
and accumulated habit became custom,
thus forming an old practice.
From the Son of Heaven
down to commoners,
it is indeed a practice with a history,
and abruptly changing it would surely cause alarm.
However, if it is unrelated to sentiment
and violates ritual propriety,
there is no clear reason to preserve it,
and nothing is lost by removing it.
It is appropriate to respectfully follow ancient canons
and correct later errors.
Moreover, it also involves extravagant spending,
which is truly a burden on the people.
Generally, the funeral ceremonies of scholars
often come from their local communities.
Whenever such a need arises,
it often costs tens to hundreds of thousands
and drains the people's financial resources,
yet there is no moral justification for it.
As for the poor,
everyone tries to exhaust themselves.
Even if their house is as empty as a hanging chime,
none fail to spend their entire fortune
—is this what is meant by burying with ritual?
I propose that we should strictly follow ancient canons
and entirely abolish the custom of mourning-gate decorations,
instead indicating mourning
with plain fans,
which is sufficient to show sorrow.”
He also said:
"In the past, due to famine,
rice, grains, cotton, and silk were all expensive.
Later, the price of rice returned to normal,
but silk is still double the price today.
Since cotton and silk are expensive,
the number of sericulture workers increased.
Although they work twice as hard,
the high price has not abated.
I believe there is a good reason
for this.
Before the famine in the past,
military equipment only used armor (kǎi).
As for robes (páo'ǎo) and back-covering vests (liǎngdāng),
they were only used in battle,
stored in arsenals,
and never damaged.
Now, for ceremonial guards, direct guards, and envoys of the Yuéluó (邀羅) mission,
or for escorting and welcoming for defense,
〔一八〕all use robes (páo'ǎo) and such.
This is not limited to one prefecture;
all armies do the same.
Cotton and silk are easily damaged,
and cannot last long.
Furthermore, they are used to ward off cold during the day
and for sleeping at night,
so they tear and break
before a year is out.
Each time new silk and cotton are obtained,
they are easily exchanged for rent to purchase.
Also, all prefectures compete to collect them,
often involving tens of millions.
〔一九〕The continuous high price
is truly due to this.
Private clothing has become scarce and difficult to obtain,
〔二０〕and government treasuries have become empty because of it.
I suggest that what is needed for the imperial guards
certainly cannot be abolished.
For the rest, they should return to using armor (kǎi) as before.
For minor envoys and escorts,
it is only appropriate to provide weapons (zhàng),
not bother with armor (kǎi) or robes (ǎo).
If their use is simplified,
their price will naturally decrease."
He also said:
"Only a gentleman
can not be ashamed of plain food.
The extravagance of dishes
has been going on for a long time.
Although there is now a great effort to reform,
this trend has not yet been changed.
What one enjoys is only one flavor,
yet the display must fill a square zhang (fāngzhàng).
Beyond what suits the palate,
all are expenses for pleasing the eye.
The wealthy use it to show off,
and the poor exhaust their property for it.
It is despised by the multitude,
yet no one can be uniquely different.
I suggest that grades should be roughly established
so that extravagance and frugality are moderate.
If anyone does not change,
they should be demoted and dismissed.
Then the transformation to valuing frugality
will spread in no time."
He was promoted to Shàngshū Lìbù Láng (尚書吏部郎).
In the sixth year of Yìxī (義熙) [410 CE],
Gāozǔ (高祖) took the title of Píngxī Jiāngjūn (平西將軍),
and appointed him as Chángshǐ (長史).
He also served as the Cóngshì Zhōngláng (從事中郎) to the Dàsīmǎ Lángyá Wáng (大司馬琅邪王),
and was later appointed as Gāozǔ's Píngběi (平北) and Zhēngxī Chángshǐ (征西長史),
and then promoted to Shìzhōng (侍中).
When the Sòng (宋) dynasty was first established,
he was appointed Sòngguó Shìzhōng (宋國侍中).
He was sent out as the Wúxīng Tàishǒu (吳興太守),
but was dismissed for public affairs.
In the second year of Yǒngchū (永初) [421 CE],
he became Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞),
clarifying and upholding the law with integrity,
without bending.
He impeached Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) Xú Xiànzhī (徐羨之), saying:
"I have heard that serving superiors with adherence to the constitution is respect,
and governing subordinates with dignity and solemnity is order.
Only then will court regulations be clear,
and administration of the multitude be strict.
If this principle is neglected,
then the constitutional framework will collapse.
On the seventh day of this month,
I attended the imperial crown prince's formal banquet.
After the banquet, my carriage left,
and I, a humble official, stopped at the gate to await instruction.
There was a certain individual on horseback
in front of my carriage,
who was apprehended, driven away, and ordered to leave.
The individual named Hérén (何人) cursed and resisted arrest,
and when questioned, sought to record it.
Whenever there were public affairs,
I always feared disputes,
and ordered them not to ask questions.
But Hérén (何人) alone continued to curse without stopping,
so I ordered him to be recorded.
Hérén (何人) refused to dismount,
repeatedly shouting and yelling.
Two guards (wēiyí) came running,
and struck my apprehenders.
Shàngshū Lìng's (尚書令) aide Ní Zōng (倪宗) also pulled the hands of the guards,
striking my subordinates.
Zōng (宗) said: 'How dare the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (中丞) act so violently,
daring to record a public official?
All those apprehended by the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (中丞),
the guards (wēiyí) shall bind them all.'
I ordered my subordinates not to fight,
but the violent display was rampant,
and only dispersed after a while.
There were also a group of people by my carriage,
apprehending Fán Mǎzǐ (樊馬子),
who exchanged blows and caused Mǎzǐ (馬子) to fall.
I could not return to the Yùshǐ Tái (臺).
I was recording a wrong,
originally without any dispute,

If they were imprisoned in the Shàngfāng,
it would be an excessive hardship for them.
Also, the Sītú had previously impeached and sent back to their posts the Wǔkāng Magistrate (Wǔkāng Lìng) Xiè Shěn and eleven county and district officials,
who were penalized for failing to capture Zhòngliáng in his coin minting activities,
a case that had long been settled.
He also sent nine people, including the county secretary Qiū Yuánjìng,
some of whom were on sick leave,
and some who had left their posts long ago.
He further submitted proposals (jiā zhí qǐ),
and all his suggestions were adopted.
He was appointed Dōngyáng Tàishǒu.
Later, he was promoted to Ānlù Wáng Zǐsuī Hòujūn Chángshǐ and Jiāngxià Nèishǐ.
He also managed the affairs of Yǐngzhōu.
He was recalled to the capital,
but before he could be formally appointed,
he was kept as Zuǒmín Shàngshū.
After a short while,
he was transferred to oversee Lìbù.
At that time, the emperor indulged excessively in banquets,
and cruelly insulted his officials.
From Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng downwards,
all were subjected to defilement and humiliation.
Only Xīngzōng, because of his uprightness and straightforwardness, was feared
and not subjected to abuse.
Shàngshū Púyè Yán Shībó said to Yìcáo Láng Wáng Dānzhī:
"Cài Shàngshū is always spared from frivolous jokes;
he is truly distant from others."
Dānzhī said:
"Cài Yùzhāng, when he was in the prime minister's office,
was also known for his uprightness and lack of familiarity.
On days when Wǔdì held private banquets,
he was never summoned.
But whenever there was an official gambling session,
he was always among the winning company.
Cài Shàngshū today can be said to be capable of bearing such a burden."
Towards the end of Dàmíng,
the former deposed emperor ascended the throne.
Xīngzōng informed Tàizǎi Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng
that a ceremonial document was required.
Yìgōng said:
"Establishing a crown prince
was precisely for this day.
What further use is there for this?"
Xīngzōng said:
"It has been the custom of successive dynasties,
without exception.
Recently, at the end of Yǒngchū,
when Yíngyáng Wáng ascended the throne,
there was also a ceremonial document.
It is now in the Shàngshū;
it can be examined."
(Yìgōng) did not comply.
Xīngzōng personally presented the imperial seal and ribbon at that time.
The new ruler's expression was self-composed,
entirely without any sorrowful look.
Xīngzōng went out and said to his relatives and old friends:
"Lǔ Zhāo, though in Qī, had a pleasant countenance.
He ended up in conflict with his high ministers,
and Zhāozǐ requested death.
Is the calamity of the state
due to this?"
At that time, Yìgōng was supervising the affairs of the Shàngshū and
had received the late emperor's will to assist in governance,
balancing the young ruler.
However, he distanced himself from affairs,
and governance fell into the hands of favored attendants.
Yuèqí Xiàowèi Dài Fǎxīng and Zhōngshū Shèrén Cháo Shàngzhī monopolized court power,
their authority extending far and wide.
Xīngzōng's office oversaw the nine ranks,
with the responsibility of selection placed upon him.
Whenever he attended court,
he would, along with the Línglù and others,
express his desire to promote worthy scholars,
and also offer admonitions regarding successes and failures,
broadly discussing court policies.
Yìgōng, by nature timid and indecisive,
flattered and followed Fǎxīng,
constantly fearing to displease him.
When he heard Xīngzōng speak,
he would tremble with fear and be at a loss.
Previously, during the Dàmíng era,
extravagance knew no bounds;
many constructions were undertaken,
taxes and levies were onerous,
and conscription was excessively harsh.
At this time, an edict was issued,
ordering all to be abolished.
Consequently, structures like the north and south carriageways of the Zǐjí Diàn
were all destroyed.
From Xiàojiàn to the end of Dàmíng,
all institutions and regulations
were no longer in existence.
Xīngzōng, at the capital's assembly, said with a sigh to Yán Shībó:
"Although the late emperor was not a sovereign of great virtue,
he certainly began and ended with the Dao.
'Three years without change' is valued by the ancient classics.
Now, the funeral palace has just been dismantled,
and the imperial tomb is not yet distant,
yet all institutions and constructions,
regardless of their merits or demerits,
are all abolished.
Even during a change of dynasty,
it would not go to such an extent.
All discerning people in the world
will judge people by this."
Shībó could not make use of his advice.
Whenever Xīngzōng presented selection matters,
Fǎxīng,
Shàngzhī, and others would immediately mark them for alteration and exchange,
with only a few remaining as proposed.
Xīngzōng said in the court to Yìgōng and Shībó:
"The emperor is in mourning,
not personally handling myriad affairs,
yet secret matters of selection
are largely altered,
and they are not by your hand either.
I don't know whose imperial will this is."
Wáng Jǐngwén, Xiè Zhuāng, and others were transferred and appointed out of order,
and Xīngzōng again wished to make proper selections.
At that time, Xuē Āndū was Sànqí Chángshì and Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn,
while Tàizǐ Zuǒshuài Yīn was Zhōngshùzǐ.
Xīngzōng first selected Āndū as Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
with Chángshì as before;
Yīn was selected as Huángmén,
concurrently leading the camp.
The Tàizǎi felt that Āndū's appointments were too many,
wishing him to be solely Zuǒwèi.
Xīngzōng said:
"The difference between commander and guard
is but a short step.
Furthermore, he has already lost the title of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn,
so it is not an excessive promotion.
To further strip him of Chángshì
would be an outright demotion.
If one were to say that Āndū achieved prominence late as an insignificant person,
and should have been restrained,
so that titles would not be taken lightly,
then there should be a consistent order.
I strictly follow the principles of selection;
it is not out of personal favor for Āndū."
Yìgōng said:
"If palace officials should be given extraordinary promotions,
How can he merely be Huángmén?"
Xīngzōng further said:
"Zhōngshù and Shìzhōng
are indeed far apart.
Moreover, Āndū served as a commander for ten years,
while Yīn was Zhōngshùzǐ for a hundred days.
Now he also leads the camp;
this is not a small achievement."
He sent the selection clerks Yán Huīzhī, Xuē Qìngxiān, and others to repeatedly argue the point.
Only then did Yìgōng sign the document.
Following the imperial edict, Āndū was made Right Guard.
He was also granted the title of Attendant Censor (jǐshìzhōng).
From then on, this greatly displeased Yìgōng, Fǎxīng, and others.
Xīngzōng was appointed Grand Administrator of Wú County.
He firmly declined the magistracy.
The authorities grew even angrier.
He was then transferred to be Fǔjūn Sīmǎ (Army Supervisor) under Zǐluán, Prince of Xīn'ān, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General Who Assists the State), and Grand Administrator of Southern Dōnghǎi,
acting as the Governor of Southern Xú Prefecture.
He again refused to accept,
bitterly requesting Yì Prefecture.
Yìgōng then became greatly enraged,
and submitted a memorial which said:
"Your servant has heard that discretion in speech
is a rule from the Great Changes (Dàyì);
when selecting and ranking the nine grades (jiǔliú),
one should not take what is *cái lì* [unclear character].
If people form factions and gather in groups,
criticisms and complaints will arise mutually.
Street talk and alley gossip
will disregard what is heard,
and this will remove the great pestilence that the true constitutional system should prohibit and control.
〔一一〕The Palace Attendant and Director of the Imperial Library, your servant Yù, personally petitioned on account of his father's illness,
insisting on attending to him.
Your Majesty, out of compassion, granted his request
and specially acceded to his statement,
reassigning him to be a chief aide in your servant's administration,
concurrently holding military and district positions.
Although your servant is mediocre,
the responsibilities of the administration are not light.
Compared to previous individuals,
this is not a demotion.
Capital districts were originally for emolument,
without regard for the number of households,
and were used conveniently,
irrespective of high or low status.
The Fǔjūn Chángshǐ (Senior Clerk of the Army Supervisor), Zhuāng Zhì, has been in the administration for several reigns,
and has repeatedly expressed his distress,
saying that internal positions and external commands
were not suitable for him.
Only Wáng Qiú, who was comparable in the past,
was granted preferential treatment,
and the depth of this kindness
was not slight.
The newly appointed Grand Administrator of Wú County, Xīngzōng,
previously served in the Bureau of Selections (xuǎncáo)
and was often unfair.
Your Majesty, with abundant grace, forgave him
for his inexperience,
and reassigned him to a major commandery,
with favors equal to those for an imperial tutor.
Yet he bitterly requested Yì Prefecture,
blatantly defying the imperial decree.
I recall that the Governor of Yáng Prefecture, Zǐshàng, and the Grand Administrator of Wúxìng, Xiūròu,
are both distinguished relatives of the state,
residing in Lǔ and Wèi,
yet they governed the eastern mountains,
devoting themselves to their duties.
But to refuse and choose according to one's desires,
starting from common families,
〔一二〕and then to assist the northern frontier,
shows even less joy and gratitude.
The Censor-in-Chief (yùshǐ zhōngchéng), Yǒng,
who erred last year,
is now appointed by grace.
The Grand Master of Ceremonies (guānglùxūn), your servant Yān,
though said to be your servant's replacement,
has been repeatedly demoted and dismissed.
If his future accomplishments are not shown,
by what right should he be advanced?
The Senior Clerk of the Minister of Education (sītú), Kǒng Jì,
was previously appointed Right Guard,
then soon moved to his current position.
The appropriateness of such frequent changes
is not small.
I secretly hear external talk that Yù and others all feel they have been slighted,
and I also hear that Xīngzōng personally complained,
sending a letter to the Grand Master of Remonstrance and Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (shàngshū yòupúshè), Shībó,
whose words were very bitter.
Although your servant has not seen it,
what I have heard is not false.
As a mediocre talent, your servant
is not suited for state affairs,
yet by some fortunate chance,
I have been entrusted with office for three reigns.
I have neither the beauty of the ancients in recommending worthies,
nor the achievements of those below in offering advice.
To cause such confusion,
I am filled with shame and trepidation.
However, if this source is not blocked,
and this trend is not changed,
it will harm the righteous path
and defile the glorious administration.
I humbly wish Your Majesty would listen
and grant your examination."
An imperial edict said:
"The Grand Tutor's (tàizǎi) memorial is thus,
and We are dismayed upon reading it.
We respectfully inherit the great enterprise
and desire to promote its glorious achievements,
yet there is such contention in court,
fostering a prevailing trend.
How then can We honor Our ancestors' virtues
and perfectly advance Our great transformation?
The Duke's concern for the state is profound,
and the task of guarding and governing is entrusted to him.
It can therefore be submitted to the outside for detailed deliberation."
Yìgōng then had the Director of the Department of State Affairs (shàngshūlìng), Liǔ Yuánjǐng, memorialize, saying:
"Your servant Yìgōng's memorial and the imperial edict are as follows.
The acting official in charge of investigations, Shàngshū Yuán Mǐnsūn, stated in a dispatch: 'On the seventeenth of this month,
I visited the Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (púshè), Yán Shībó.
During our conversation,
the matter of Shàngshū Cài Xīngzōng having sent a letter firmly declining his current appointment arose.
He then showed me the dispatch.
〔一三〕It consisted of several pages,
and I did not realize what it all spoke of.
Because of this, the topic of court officials came up.
In today's sacred reign,
one should not make people feel they are getting too little.
This is my dispatch.'
Counting them,
the imperial court's arrangements were indeed proper,
and your servants also considered them fair.
We are often at the gate,
so Yuán Mǐnsūn could not have been overly involved,
but my foolish idea is to propose a reassessment of what is appropriate for appointment and dismissal.
As a humble and limited opinion,
I wish it to be heard and understood.
A selection clerk transmitted secret matters,
so I thus attached it for imperial hearing,
and outsiders also said this.
Now Xuē Qìngxiān listed: 〔一四〕'On the eighteenth of this month,
I went to Shàngshū Yuán Mǐnsūn to discuss selection matters.
Mǐnsūn said that yesterday he visited Yán Púshè,
who showed him Shàngshū Cài's dispatch,
saying the words were very bitter.
He also said that what he received was too little.
The Emperor has only just ascended the throne,
and there are not many such people among court officials.
Public opinion holds that he should be well-employed,
but he is instead resentful for receiving too little,
so he should be advised to make a record to the Duke.
Also, Xiè Zhuāng was not old at the time of his illness,
and his illness has improved.
For him to hold this position now
is again inappropriate.
It is believed that the talent and reputation of the Director of the Central Secretariat (zhōngshūlìng) would be appropriate.
Also, Kǒng Jì is a distinguished southern scholar
who has already held many positions.
Recently, he has been frequently appointed and then changed again,
which is a slight according to principle.
There is no one in the Imperial Secretariat (ménxià),
and he is a famous selection.
Also, Zhāng Yǒng's background is worthy of discussion.
His transgression last year
was not a deep crime.
According to his reputation, he should be restored to an Imperial Secretariat position.
Zhāng Yān was formerly demoted to the south,
sharing in joy and sorrow.
〔一五〕Although he has repeatedly erred and been dismissed,
the matter has also been a long time ago.
It is believed he should be Director of the Imperial Library (mìshūjiān).'
The several pages of Xīngzōng's handwriting attached to the appointment,
with clear and evident writing,
serve as clear proof
and require no further investigation.
Mǐnsūn, as an official,
whose duty is to select and judge,
if there was anything inappropriate,
〔一六〕should have stated it openly.
Instead, he privately granted approval,
making his own selections,
claiming it was public opinion,
which ultimately proves to be false and deceptive,
concealing the beginning and ending in contradiction.
Your servant has heard that the nine offices yielded,
and the Yu (Shùn) style (Yúfēng) set a precedent.
Slandering the ruler and resenting the times
was swiftly punished in the Hàn dynasty.
Moreover, if this is done out of self-interest,
and words slander the court order,
disrupting the ruler and harming the government,
defiling the great way,
such widespread error,
even reaching up to the imperial edict,
if there is no swift punishment,
the established order will collapse.
I request that Xīngzōng be stripped of his newly appointed office,
and that, after imperial consideration,
he be handed over to the Court of Judicial Review (Tíngwèi) for legal prosecution and punishment,
and that Mǐnsūn be removed from his current office."
An imperial edict said:
"Xīngzōng, by initiating disorder in court regulations,
is truly subject to clear laws.
However, as he has served close to the imperial person in the past,
We are unwilling to enforce the law completely.
He may be ordered to reflect on his transgression and be banished to a distant frontier.
Mǐnsūn privately judged himself,
attributing fault to public opinion,
can perform the duties of the office.”
Xīngzōng 興宗 was appointed Grand Administrator of Xīnchāng 新昌,
a commandery belonging to Jiāozhōu 交州.
The court was utterly shocked and amazed.
Previously,
Xīngzōng 興宗 had taken as a concubine Zhìfēi 智妃, a nun from Empress Hé’s 何后 temple.
She was very beautiful
and famous in the capital.
While the carriage bringing her had already departed,
Shībó 師伯 secretly sent someone to lure her away,
and then furtively took her away in a carriage.
Xīngzōng 興宗, who was awaiting her arrival, did not realize this.
When Xīngzōng 興宗 was exiled,
everyone attributed it to Shībó 師伯,
which greatly troubled Shībó 師伯.
As Fǎxīng 法興 and others did not wish to gain the reputation for exiling a high-ranking minister,
and Shībó 師伯 also wanted to quell public opinion,
the exile was therefore halted.
Soon after,
Fǎxīng 法興 was killed,
Shàngzhī 尚之 was imprisoned,
and Yìgōng 義恭 and Shībó 師伯 were executed.
Xīngzōng 興宗 was again appointed Army Supervisor for Prince Línhǎi Líhǎi 臨海 Wáng Zǐxù 子頊, Auxiliary General of the State, and Grand Administrator of Nánjùn 南郡,
acting as the Administrator of Jīngzhōu 荊州.
He did not take up the post.
At that time, the former deposed Emperor was cruel and violent.
Xīngzōng’s 興宗’s nephew, Yuán Yǐ 袁顗, who was the Inspector of Yōngzhōu 雍州,
urged Xīngzōng 興宗 to go,
saying:
“The situation at court
is apparent to all.
The high-ranking ministers within the palace
cannot be assured of their safety from one day to the next.
Uncle, you are now going to reside west of the pass,
acting as administrator for eight prefectures.
[一七] I am in Xiāngmǐn 襄沔,
a strategic location with strong forces,
a stone’s throw from Jiānglíng 江陵,
and with convenient water and land routes.
If something happens at court,
we can together achieve the accomplishments of Huán Wén 桓文.
How can we endure being controlled by a mad tyrant,
with unforeseen disasters,
and speak of this in the same breath?
If you do not escape the tiger’s mouth now,
but remain in this perilous situation,
and later seek to leave again,
how will you succeed?”
Xīngzōng 興宗 replied:
“I have always been of humble background and achieved advancement through ordinary means,
and I am very distant from the Emperor;
it is unlikely I will suffer misfortune.
Within and without the palace,
people cannot protect themselves,
and a change is bound to happen.
If the internal troubles are quelled,
external conflicts may not necessarily be predictable.
You wish to seek safety outside,
while I wish to remain within to avoid disaster.
Is it not good for each to act according to their own judgment?”
At that time, the capital was gripped by fear,
and all officials and gentry wished to move far away.
Later, they were all scattered by external calamities,
with barely one in a hundred surviving.
He was again appointed Minister of Personnel.
Grand Commandant Shěn Qìngzhī 沈慶之, deeply worried about impending disaster,
closed his gates and did not receive guests.
He once sent his attendant Fàn Xiàn 范羡 to Xīngzōng 興宗 on an errand.
Xīngzōng 興宗 said to Xiàn 羡:
“Your lord closes his gates and refuses guests
to avoid the countless requests and entreaties,
but I have no requests,
why am I refused?”
When Xiàn 羡 returned to Qìngzhī 慶之,
Qìngzhī 慶之 sent Xiàn 羡 to report and
invited Xīngzōng 興宗 to come.
Xīngzōng 興宗 then spoke to him, saying:
“Although the late emperor had no great achievements for the realm,
he was nevertheless able to suppress rebellions and bring peace,
and ruled for eleven years,
passing away peacefully.
The present emperor ascended the throne,
and the four seas were tranquil.
His initial acts and conduct merely deviated from the right path,
small errors and lapses;
it was also thought that he was still young,
and moral improvement could be expected.
However, his recent actions
have exhausted the human moral order.
What he fears and restrains himself from now
is only you, Your Excellency.
The common people are desperate,
without hope for even a temporary respite,
and their only hope lies in you alone.
If you merely sit and watch the outcome,
not only will your own disaster be unpredictable,
but the heavy blame from the four seas
will fall upon you.
Your prestige and reputation are well-established,
respected by all under heaven.
Now the entire court is in a state of panic,
everyone is terrified.
On the day you give the command,
who would not follow?
If you do not make a decision,
disaster will strike morning or evening.
I once served in your esteemed household
and received extraordinary favor,
therefore I dare to speak my mind fully.
I wish Your Excellency would consider a plan for this.”
Qìngzhī 慶之 said:
“For some time now,
I have worried that I cannot even protect myself.
[一八] But I will serve the country with utmost loyalty,
from beginning to end,
and simply commit my fate to heaven.
Furthermore, I am old and weary, from a private household,
and my military strength is greatly diminished.
Although I may have the intention,
the matter is impossible.”
Xīngzōng 興宗 said:
“Those who harbor plans and wish to act now
do not seek wealth, honor,
or rewards for merit;
each merely wishes to escape death from one day to the next.
The generals and commanders within the palace
are simply awaiting news from outside.
If one person takes the lead,
then the situation can be settled quickly.
Moreover, your prestige is already established,
and you have commanded armies for several reigns.
Your old subordinates
are distributed throughout the palace.
Zōng Yuè 宗越 and Tán Jīn 譚金, and others like them,
[一九] came from your household
and received their upbringing there.
Yōu zhī 攸之 and Ēnrén 恩仁
are like children of your household.
[二０] Who would dare not follow?
Furthermore, your disciples and loyal followers
are all valiant warriors from the Three Wú 三吳 region,
and the servants in your residence
number several hundred.
Lù Yōuzhī 陸攸之 is now campaigning east to suppress bandits,
and has also sent a large quantity of armor and weapons,
which are at Qīngxī 青溪 and not yet dispatched.
Yōuzhī 攸之 is your fellow townsman,
brave and courageous.
Take his weapons
and distribute them among those under your command,
and have Yōuzhī 攸之 lead them as vanguards,
and the affairs of the realm will be settled.
I, in the Ministry of Personnel,
will naturally lead the hundred officials to follow the precedents of former generations,
and select the virtuous and enlightened,
to serve the altars of earth and grain.
In the past, the offenses of Tàijiǎ 太甲 did not affect the people,
and the cruelty of Chāngyì 昌邑 did not extend to the lower classes,
yet Yī Yǐn 伊尹 and Huò Guāng 霍光 still accomplished great deeds.
How much more so now, when the common people are in dire straits,
and the calamity surpasses all previous eras?
Furthermore, all the actions taken by the court
are rumored among the people to have been instigated by you, Your Excellency.
If you now hesitate and remain undecided,
someone will act before you,
and you too will not escape the disaster of being implicated.
The Emperor has repeatedly visited your esteemed residence,
becoming drunk and lingering.
It is also said that he dismisses his attendants and enters the inner chambers alone.
This is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity,
and the moment must not be lost.
I am deeply indebted to your favor,
[二一] therefore I dare to speak frankly and directly,
and I urge Your Excellency to carefully consider the good and ill fortune.”
Qìngzhī 慶之 said:
“I am deeply grateful for your endless concern.
I feel that this matter is too great,
and not something I am capable of doing.
When the time comes, I will simply die with my loyalty intact.”
Soon after,
Qìngzhī 慶之 indeed suffered misfortune due to being resented.
At that time, the Commander of the Guards, Wáng Xuánmó, was a general with great prestige.
Rumors spread in the villages that he had already been executed,
causing commotion in the markets.
Bāo Fǎróng, Wáng Xuánmó's clerk,
whose family was in Dōngyáng,
was a former district resident of Xīngzōng.
He was trusted by Wáng Xuánmó
and was sent by him to see Xīngzōng.
Xīngzōng then said to him:
"The Commander of the Guards must be very anxious."
Fǎróng replied:
"For several days now, the Commander of the Guards has barely eaten,
nor slept at night.
He constantly says that his arrest is already at the door,
and he won't be safe for a moment."
Xīngzōng said:
"If the Commander of the Guards is anxious and fearful,
he should devise a strategy.
How can he simply sit and wait for disaster to strike?"
Previously,
Wáng Xuánmó still had three thousand men from his old command.
The Deposed Emperor was quite suspicious of them
and dismissed their overseers.
Wáng Xuánmó sighed deeply and resented this,
petitioning to keep five hundred men to build graves on Yánshān.
Before the task was completed,
the Young Emperor wished to hunt,
and all were summoned back to the city.
The Yánshān soldiers were in the central hall.
Xīngzōng urged Wáng Xuánmó to act with this force,
saying:
"Currently, with the Commander of the Guards' prestige,
leading this force to take the initiative for the imperial court
will ensure immediate success.
Even if the Commander of the Guards were to stumble,
he could still give orders from his sedan chair.
The disaster is likely unpredictable;
do not miss this opportunity.
When you return,
please convey this to the Commander of the Guards."
Wáng Xuánmó sent Fǎróng back with the message:
"This is not easily feasible yet;
I will certainly not divulge your words."
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
Wáng Xuánmó reproached his trusted former subordinates, Guō Jìchǎn and his son-in-law Wéi Xīzhēn, saying:
"During those difficult times, none of my associates offered any advice or encouragement."
Jìchǎn replied:
"What Imperial Secretary Cài told Bāo Fǎróng
was not that he failed to grasp the opportunity,
but that major undertakings are difficult to execute.
What good would my words have done?"
Wáng Xuánmó showed a look of shame.
The Right General of the Guards, Liú Dàolóng, was favored and trusted by the Emperor,
exclusively commanding the imperial guards.
One night, the imperial carriage once visited the residence of Jiāng Xiào, Assistant Secretary in the Board of Works.
Xīngzōng's carriage passed behind Liú Dàolóng's carriage.
Xīngzōng said:
"Lord Liú!
I have been thinking of a private conversation recently."
Liú Dàolóng deeply understood the implication
and squeezed Xīngzōng's hand, saying:
"Lord Cài!
Do not say too much."
Whenever the Emperor held court banquets,
he would beat and humiliate his officials.
From the General of Agile Cavalry, Prince Jiàn'ān Xiūyén, down to Privy Councillor Yuán Mǐnsūn and others,
all were subjected to insults and abuse.
Only Xīngzōng was spared.
Soon after,

That night,

At that time, all regions were raising troops in rebellion.

Among these, some counties

Xīngzōng said:

It is advisable to clarify the principle that crimes do not extend to others.
Once public sentiment is settled,

The imperial armies are elite and brave,

The Emperor followed his advice.
He was promoted to General of Skirmishers,

Tàizōng said to Xīngzōng:

Xīngzōng replied:

Now, trade routes are cut off,

Forces gather from all directions,

From this omen,

However, what I worry about

Your Majesty's concerns will only begin."
Chǔ Yuān, the Minister of the Board of Civil Office, tapped Xīngzōng with his writing tablet.
Xīngzōng continued to speak without stopping.
The Emperor said:
"As you say."
When Zhèqí was pacified,

The Emperor ordered Xīngzōng to observe it from the Nányè Gate tower.
Xīngzōng shed tears,

When the troubles were pacified,

He firmly declined, but it was not allowed.
He was then enfeoffed as Count of Lè'ān County,

He consistently refused the national rank and official stipend

At that time, Yīn Yǎn occupied Shòuyáng and rebelled.

As the four directions were pacified,

The Emperor ordered the Secretariat to draft an edict to admonish Yǎn.
Xīngzōng said:
"Now that the empire is settled,

This was not followed.
When Yǎn received the edict,

Formerly, Xu Zhōu Cìshǐ Xuē Āndū (薛安đū) occupied Péngchéng (彭城) and rebelled.

In the winter of Tàishǐ (泰始) 2nd year (466 CE),

he will inevitably become suspicious and fearful,

If he then rebels,

Péngchéng (彭城) is strategically formidable,
Zhāng Yǒng (張永) was dispatched to lead an army to welcome him.

Your minister is worried about this for the imperial court."
At that time, Zhāng Yǒng (張永) had already departed,

Āndū (安đū), hearing that the large army had crossed the Huái (淮) River,

Yǒng (永) suffered a great defeat in battle.

His foresight was thus.
Initially,
when the news of Yǒng's (永) defeat arrived,

then summoned Xīngzōng (興宗),

He showed the defeat report to Xīngzōng (興宗) and

In the spring of the 3rd year (467 CE),

He went to the Shàngshū (尚書) to vehemently argue for Hén Yīzhēn (何始真) to be his Zīyì Cānjūn (諮議參軍).

Later, he reiterated his request.
The Emperor was enraged
and demoted his title to Píngxī Jiāngjūn (平西將軍).
Soon after, his original title was restored.
Initially,
Qīu Zhēnsūn (丘珍孫) of Wúxīng (吳興) often criticized Xīngzōng (興宗) in his discussions.
Zhēnsūn's (珍孫) son, Jǐngxiān (景先),

Xīngzōng (興宗) befriended him.
When Jǐngxiān (景先) served in Póyáng Jùn (鄱陽郡),

His mother was old, and his daughters were young.
They wandered in Xiàkǒu (夏口).
When Xīngzōng (興zōng) arrived in Yǐngzhōu (郢州),

After three years in office,

Soon after, he was granted command of troops and aides,
and additionally made Dūdū Kuàijī (會稽), Dōngyáng (東陽), Xīn'ān (新安), Yǒngjiā (永嘉), Línhǎi (臨海) Wǔjùn Zhū Jūnjì (五郡諸軍事),

Kuàijī (會稽) had many powerful families
who did not abide by imperial laws.
Moreover, favored courtiers and close attendants
were partly present in the court and palace,
encroaching upon mountains and lakes,
hindering the people and harming governance.
Xīngzōng (興zōng) disciplined all of them according to the law.
The land of Kuàijī (會稽) was entirely fertile,
its people and resources abundant.
Princes, dukes, consorts, and princesses
had residences everywhere,
causing disturbances,
which was a great problem for the people.
Their offspring multiplied,
and their demands were endless.
Xīngzōng (興zōng) petitioned to abolish and reduce all of these.
He also proposed to remit all outstanding debts
and dismiss various corvée laborers,
all of which were followed.
The Sānwú (三吳) region traditionally had the鄉射禮 (xiāngshèlǐ, village archery ritual),
which had not been practiced for a long time.
Xīngzōng (興zōng) revived it,
and the ceremonies were very orderly.
Before this, during the Yuánjiā (元嘉) reign,
Yáng Xuánbǎo (羊玄保) performed the village archery ritual when he was governor.
After Tàizōng (太宗) died,

Xīngzōng (興zōng), together with Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) Yuán Càn (袁粲), Yòu Púshè (右僕射) Chǔ Yuān (褚淵), Zhōnglǐng Jūn (中領軍) Líu Miǎn (劉勔), and Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn (鎮軍將軍) Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之), was entrusted with the Emperor's dying wishes.

Xīngzōng (興zōng) was appointed Shǐchíjié (使持節), Dūdū Jīng (荊), Xiāng (湘), Yōng (雍), Yì (益), Líang (梁), Níng (寧), Nán (南), Běi Qín (秦) Bāzhōu Zhū Jūnjì (八州諸軍事), Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (征西將軍), Kāifǔ Yí Tóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史),

He was summoned back to the capital.
At that time, Yòujūn Jiāngjūn (右軍將軍) Wáng Dàolóng (王道隆) was involved in internal politics,
wielding great power.
He walked up to him without taking off his shoes,

without being called to sit.
In the early Yuánjiā (元嘉) period,
Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人) Qīu Dāng (秋當) visited Tàizǐ Zhànshì (太子詹事) Wáng Tánshǒu (王曇首),
Later, Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人) Wáng Hóng (王弘) was favored by Tàizǔ (太祖).
"If you wish to be a true scholar,
you must be able to sit with Wáng Qíu (王球),

Yīn (殷) and Líu (劉) are both mixed,

If you go to Qíu (球),

Qíu (球) fanned himself and said:
"That would not be permissible."
Hóng (弘) returned
and reported the matter as it happened.
The Emperor said:
"What can I do about him?"
Within fifty years,
these three incidents occurred.
Dàolóng (道隆) and others, seeing Xīngzōng (興zōng) as strong and upright,
did not want him to command troops in the upper reaches of the river.
He was reassigned as Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監), Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū (左光祿大夫),
with Kāifǔ Yí Tóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司) and Chángshì (常侍) remaining the same.
He firmly declined the appointment.
Xīngzōng (興zōng) had a noble demeanor from a young age,
and was particularly meticulous in his family conduct.
He honored his paternal aunt,
served his widowed sister-in-law,
and raised his orphaned nephew,
which was well-known in the world.
Tàizǐ Zuǒlǜ (太子左率) Wáng Xī's (王錫) wife, Fàn (范),
was a clever woman.
She had literary talent and knowledge.
In a letter to Xī's (錫) younger brother, Sēngdá (僧達),
she questioned and reproached him, saying:
"In the past, Xiè Tàifù (謝太傅) served his sister-in-law, Lady Wáng (王夫人), as if she were his own mother.
Now, Cài Xīngzōng (蔡興宗) also has a reputation for respect and harmony."
This shows how much he was valued by his contemporaries.
His wife, Líu (劉) clan, died young,
leaving a very young daughter.
His nephew Yuán Qì (袁覬) had just had a son, Tuǎn (彖), when Qì's (覬) wife, also of the Líu (劉) clan, also passed away.
Xīngzōng's (興zōng) elder sister,
who was Qì's (覬) mother,
both raised by Xīngzōng (興zōng) himself,
and similar in age,
to marry.
Whenever she saw Xīngzōng (興zōng),

In the early Dàmíng (大明) period,
an imperial decree ordered Xīngzōng's (興zōng) daughter to marry Nánpíng Wáng (南平王) Jìngyóu (敬猷).
Xīngzōng (興zōng), considering his sister's long-held wish,
repeatedly petitioned,
but the reply was:
"If all of you wish to act according to your own intentions,
how can the state arrange marriages?
Moreover, is your sister's wish really so inviolable?"
Since his original intention was thwarted,
Tuǎn (彖) also married someone else.
Later, Tuǎn's (彖) family did not fare well,
and Yǐ (顗) also suffered misfortune and ruin.
Tuǎn (彖) and others were disgraced and abandoned at that time,
becoming isolated and powerless.
After Jìngyóu (敬猷) was killed,
Xīngzōng's (興zōng) daughter remained a childless widow.
Many prestigious and noble families
desired to form a marriage alliance with her.
Míngdì (明帝) also ordered her to marry into the Xiè (謝) clan.
Xīngzōng (興zōng) did not agree to any of these,
