Fù Lóng (傅隆) from Běidì (北地) was good friends with Guō (廓),
and Xīngzōng (興zōng) treated him with the respect due to his father's friend.
In the first year of Tàiyù,
he passed away
at the age of fifty-eight.
His will ordered a simple funeral,
and a memorial requested the return of his enfeoffed titles.
He was posthumously granted a new appointment,
but his son Jǐngxuán firmly declined to accept it.
[三二]He again memorialized to return the enfeoffment.
More than ten memorials were submitted,
which were eventually granted.
An imperial edict stated:
"Jǐngxuán's memorial is as such.
The former Sànqí Chángshì, Zhōngshū Jiān, Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Kaiguó Bó of Lè'ān County, Xīngzōng,
was loyal and upright in court,
his strategies and plans were clearly manifested.
In times of past difficulty,
his merits shone in the counsel chambers.
The bestowal of jade scepters and the division of land
was truly in accordance with the universal decree.
Yet, with sincere and earnest appeals,
the sentiments of both the living and the deceased are fully expressed.
His integrity and unadorned character
displayed a pure conduct.
Jǐngxuán's firm reiteration of his father's wishes
is truly poignant.
Although the established rites should be fully observed,
the sorrowful request is hard to deny.
Therefore, his plea for the deceased's unfulfilled wish may be specially granted,
and the spirit of his humility and self-restraint eternally admired."
Originally,
Xīngzōng served as a Cānjūn in the Yǐngzhōu prefectural office.
Yán Jìng of Péngchéng consulted an oracle, saying:
"In the year of Hài, you will become a Duke (Gōng).
An official title containing a 'Dà' (great) character
should not be accepted."
When the appointment of Kāifǔ was granted,
and the year was that of Hài,
he indeed passed away under the title of Guānglù Dàfū.
His collected works were circulated in the world.
Jǐngxuán inherited much of his father's character,
serving as Zhōngshū Láng,
Jìnlíng Tàishǒu,
and Tàiwèi Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
He died at the end of Shēngmíng.
The court historian says: The world valued pure discourse,
and scholars esteemed unadorned arguments.
Although Cài Kuò's achievements and strength were greatly upright,
his age and position were not yet high,
yet the distinguished ministers of his generation,
their styles were all inferior to his.
As for his firm refusal of official selection,
ashamed to compromise his principles,
how could he not know that selecting and appointing are integral parts of the same system,
and there is no reason for biased judgment?
It was truly because the ruler was benighted and the times difficult,
and he did not wish to hold a position of influence over success or failure.
How far-reaching his thoughts were!
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 18: Wáng Huì, Xiè Hóngwēi, Wáng Qiú
Wáng Huì, courtesy name Lìngmíng,
was a native of Línyí, Lángyá.
He was the cousin (from the same great-great-grandfather) of the Grand Preceptor, Hóng.
His grandfather, Shào,
was a Chējì Jiāngjūn.
His father, Mò,
was Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū.
Huì was simple and straightforward from a young age,
recognized by his paternal uncle, Sītú Mì.
He was calm and quiet, not socializing,
never involved in miscellaneous affairs.
Xiè Zhān of Chénjùn, who was talented in debate and had a refined demeanor,
once visited Huì with his brothers and cousins.
Their discussions were sharp and spirited,
with literary and historical allusions interspersed.
Huì responded to them in kind,
his words clear and profound.
Zhān and the others felt ashamed and withdrew.
Gāozǔ heard of his reputation
and inquired about him with his cousin Dàn.
Dàn said:
"Huì is a brilliant talent of later generations,
the pride of our clan."
Immediately, he was appointed Xíng Tàiwèi Cānjūnshì,
Fǔ Zhǔbù,
and Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
When the crown prince established his administration,
Huì was made Zhēnglǔ Chángshǐ,
and then transferred to Zhōngjūn Chángshǐ.
At that time, when Liú Huáijìng, the Huìjī Nèishǐ, was leaving for his commandery,
the entire capital turned out to bid him farewell.
Huì also went to bid adieu,
and on his return, he visited his cousin Qiú.
Qiú asked:
"Whom did you see just now?"
Huì replied:
"I only felt as if I happened to meet someone."
He once sat by a winding stream.
A sudden storm broke,
and everyone present fled.
Huì rose slowly,
his demeanor unchanged from usual.
When the crown prince was in Jīngzhōu,
Huì remained Chángshǐ as before,
and was appointed Nánjùn Tàishǒu,
but did not accept the post.
At the initial establishment of the Sòng state,
a Lángzhōnglìng needed to be appointed.
Gāozǔ found it difficult to choose the right person,
and said to Fù Liàng:
"The Lángzhōnglìng we appoint now
must not be inferior to Yuán Yàoqīng."
After a while, he said:
"I have found the right person."
Then he appointed Huì to the position.
He was promoted to Shìzǐ Zhànshì,
then transferred to Shàngshū,
and Wúxīng Tàishǒu.
When the young emperor ascended the throne,
Cài Kuò was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū,
but refused to accept the position.
Thus, Huì was appointed in his stead.
Huì accepted the summons and appointment immediately.
He never received guests.
If anyone sent him a letter requesting an official position,
he would collect and place them on top of a cabinet.
When he left office,
the seals remained intact as at the beginning.
Commentators remarked that Kuò's refusal and
Huì's immediate acceptance,
though the actions differed, the intention was the same.
His elder brother, Jiàn,
was fond of accumulating wealth
and extensively managed farmlands.
Huì strongly disagreed with this,
and said to Jiàn:
"What is the use of fields?"
Jiàn angrily retorted:
"Without fields, how can one eat?"
Huì then said:
"And what is the use of eating?"
Such was his lofty aspiration.
In the third year of Yuánjiā,
he died
at the age of forty-two.
He was posthumously granted Tàicháng.
He had no sons.
Xiè Hóngwēi was a native of Yángxià, Chénjùn.
His grandfather, Sháo,
was Chējì Sīmǎ.
His father, Sī,
was Wǔchāng Tàishǒu.
His paternal uncle, Jùn,
was the second son of Sīkōng Yǎn,
who had no heir.
Thus, Hóngwēi was adopted as his successor.
Hóngwēi's original name was Mì,
which conflicted with a taboo name within the family he was adopted into,
so he went by his courtesy name.
As a child,
he was astute and composed,
speaking only when the time was right.
His adopted paternal uncle, Hùn, was known for his judgment of character.
Upon seeing him, Hùn was greatly impressed
and said to Sī:
"This child is deeply intelligent and precocious;
he will surely become a fine vessel.
To have such a son
is enough."
At the age of ten, he was adopted.
His adopted father was originally a third cousin (sīmá) to Hóngwēi.
Though he had previously been unacquainted with the relatives and maternal relatives of the adopted family,
he naturally interacted with them
in a manner that conformed to ritual propriety.
In the early years of Yìxī,
he inherited Jùn's title of Kaiguó Hóu of Jiànchāng County.
Hóngwēi's family was originally poor and frugal,
but the adopted family was wealthy.
He only accepted a few thousand scrolls of books
and a few state officials;
he did not concern himself with inherited wealth or official salaries at all.
Hùn heard this and was astonished and praised him,
saying to the Guóláng Zhōnglìng, Qī Kǎizhī:
"The income of Jiànchāng State
should originally have been shared with the northern residence.
Since the Marquis of the State does not concern himself with it,
it may now be sent according to the usual share."
Hóngwēi was reluctant to further disregard Hùn's words,
so he accepted a small portion.
Xiè Hùn's style was lofty and majestic,
and he rarely associated with others,
only enjoying literary discussions with his kinsmen Xiè Língyùn, Xiè Zhān, Xiè Yào, and Xiè Hóngwēi.
They once feasted together,
residing in Wūyī Xiàng.
Hence, it was called the Excursion of Wūyī,
which is what Xiè Hùn referred to in his five-character poem, saying:
"Once we went on an excursion to Wūyī,
all my beloved nephews."
Outside of this group,
even if there were highly esteemed and renowned individuals of the time,
none dared to approach his gate.
Xiè Zhān and the others were eloquent and rich in rhetoric,
but Xiè Hóngwēi always subdued them with concise words.
Xiè Hùn especially respected and valued him,
calling him Wēizǐ.
He said to Xiè Zhān and the others:
"Although you all are talented, eloquent, and articulate,
you may not necessarily satisfy everyone.
As for comprehending insights and appreciating subtle points,
with concise words and essential principles,
we should all jointly commend Wēizǐ."
He often said:
"Ā Yuǎn is headstrong and quick-tempered, full of spirit;
Ā Kè is broad-minded but unrestrained;
Xiè Yào relies on his talent but is not firm in his principles;
Xiè Huì is self-aware but not comprehensive in accepting good advice.
Even if he were to achieve功濟三才,
he would ultimately regret these shortcomings.
As for Wēizǐ,
I have no criticisms."
He also said:
"Wēizǐ is different but does not harm others,
and conforms without compromising righteousness.
If he lives to sixty,
he will surely reach the position of a ducal minister."
Once, during a tipsy banquet,
he composed rhyming verses to encourage and commend Xiè Língyùn, Xiè Zhān, and others, saying:
"Kānglè is broadly open-minded,
truly possessing the elegance of a famous family.
If he adds the effort of refinement,
he will polish and become a precious jade.
Xuānmíng embodies profound insight,
intelligent and yet deep and outstanding.
If he can relinquish his stubbornness,
he will be serene and accord with the Three Powers.
Ā Duō displays unique understanding,
at a young age compiling illustrious lineage.
Plainness surpassing adornment is a warning against lack of refinement,
yet he is still able to excel.
Tōngyuǎn harbors clear enlightenment,
his words like fragrant orchids.
A straight rein rarely avoids stumbling,
he should restrain himself and resolve his excessive parsimony.
Wēizǐ's foundation is subtle and lofty,
not tiring from admiring Lín Xiàngrú.
Do not slight the smallness of a single basketful,
for advancing will reach a thousand *rèn*.
You gentlemen, strive diligently!
The current fashion depends on you to revive it.
As long as you do not transgress what you know,
there is nothing else to be cautious of."
Xiè Língyùn and the others all received words of caution and admonition,
but only Xiè Hóngwēi received full praise.
Xiè Yào
was Xiè Hóngwēi's elder brother.
Duō
was his childhood name.
Yuǎn was Xiè Zhān's courtesy name.
Xiè Língyùn's childhood name was Kè'ér.
In the Jìn dynasty, prominent families whose members held state enfeoffments
often began their careers as Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng.
Xiè Hóngwēi was also appointed Yuánwài Sànqí
and Lángxié Wáng Dàsīmǎ Cānjūn.
In the eighth year of Yìxī (412 CE),
Xiè Hùn was executed for being part of Liú Yì's faction.
His wife, the Jìnlíng Gōngzhǔ, was remarried to Lángxié Wáng Liàn.
Although the princess firmly refused to go,
an imperial decree ordered her to divorce the Xiè family.
The princess entrusted Xiè Hùn's family affairs to Xiè Hóngwēi.
Xiè Hùn's family had been prime ministers for generations,
with two enfeoffments in one family,
over ten properties,
and a thousand servants.
He had only two daughters,
both a few years old.
Xiè Hóngwēi managed the household's livelihood
as if it were a public matter,
with every coin and foot of silk recorded
in detailed ledgers.
He was promoted to Tōngzhí Láng.
When Gāozǔ received the Mandate,
Jìnlíng Gōngzhǔ was demoted to Dōngxiāng Jūn.
Because Xiè Hùn had offended the previous dynasty,
and Dōngxiāng Jūn's integrity and righteousness were commendable,
she was permitted to return to the Xiè family.
Nine years had passed since Xiè Hùn's death,
but by this time,
the houses were well-maintained,
the granaries were full,
and the household retainers and servants
were no different from ordinary days.
The fields were cultivated and expanded,
even more than before.
Dōngxiāng Jūn sighed, saying:
"The Púshè valued this son greatly in his lifetime;
he truly knew people.
The Púshè is not dead after all."
Relatives both internal and external,
and former friends both secular and monastic,
who saw Dōngxiāng's return,
all sighed upon entering the house,
some even shed tears,
moved by Xiè Hóngwēi's righteousness.
He was strict and upright by nature;
his every action conformed to ritual and propriety.
In his dealings with his step-relatives,
he was exceptionally respectful and diligent.
He attended to his two paternal aunts,
and his two maternal aunts who had returned to their natal family,
morning and evening,
with utmost sincerity and reverence.
If there was an internal message or communication,
he would always straighten his attire and cap.
In front of servants,
he would not speak or laugh carelessly.
Because of this, all, regardless of status or age,
respected him as a deity.
Tàizǔ, while garrisoned in Jiānglíng,
was enfeoffed as Yídū Wáng at the beginning of the Sòng dynasty.
He befriended Lángxié Wáng Qiú,
and Xiè Hóngwēi served as his Wénxué.
He resigned his post due to his mother's mourning
and was known for his filial piety during the period of mourning.
More than a year after the mourning period ended,
he still maintained a vegetarian diet.
He was appointed Zhèn Xī Zīyì Cānjūn.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he became Huángmén Shìláng,
and along with Wáng Huá, Wáng Tánshǒu, Yīn Jǐngrén, and Liú Zhàn, was known as the Five Ministers.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Lìbù Láng
and participated in confidential affairs.
Soon after, he was transferred to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
All former officials and assistants
were entrusted to Xiè Hóngwēi for selection and recommendation.
He lived a pure and frugal life;
his utensils and clothing were not extravagant,
but his food and drink
were always abundant and exquisite.
His elder brother Xiè Yào served successively as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng
and Chéng Wáng Yìkāng Piàojì Chángshǐ,
and died in the fourth year of Yuánjiā (427 CE).
Xiè Hóngwēi ate only vegetables for a long time,
his grief exceeding propriety.
Even after the mourning period was over,
he still did not eat fish or meat.
The Buddhist monk Shì Huìlín visited Xiè Hóngwēi,
and Xiè Hóngwēi shared a meal with him,
still eating only vegetables.
Shì Huìlín said:
"Dányuè, you have always been sickly,
and recently your complexion has deteriorated slightly.
Even after the official mourning period,
you still haven't resumed a normal diet.
If you harm your health for no benefit,
how can this be what is hoped for by enlightened principles?"
Xiè Hóngwēi replied:
"When there is a change in attire and cap (mourning),
one cannot transgress propriety.
The sorrow in my heart
has truly not yet ceased."
Thereupon, he stopped eating and choked up,
sobbing uncontrollably.
Xiè Hóngwēi was orphaned young
and served his elder brother as a father.
His fraternal affection and harmony
were unmatched by anyone in the world.
Xiè Hóngwēi never spoke of others' shortcomings,
whereas Xiè Yào was fond of criticizing people.
Whenever Xiè Yào spoke critically,
Xiè Hóngwēi would always interrupt him with other topics.
In the sixth year,
the Eastern Palace was first established.
He was appointed as Zhōngshùzǐ,
and soon after, promoted to Shìzhōng.
Xiè Hóngwēi's ambition was to be a simple official,
and he feared and disliked power and favor.
He firmly declined the appointment,
and was then allowed to resign from Zhōngshùzǐ.
Whenever he offered suggestions or discussed current affairs,
he would write them by hand and then burn the drafts,
so no one knew about them.
The Emperor, knowing that Hóngwēi was skilled at preparing food,
once sought a meal from him.
Hóngwēi prepared it with the help of relatives and friends.
After it was served,
his relatives asked what the Emperor had eaten.
Hóngwēi did not answer,
but responded with other words,
which led people at the time to compare him to Kǒng Guāng of the Hàn dynasty.
In the autumn of the eighth year,
he fell ill,
and was dismissed from Yòuwèi,
but retained the position of Tàizǐ Yòuwèilǜ,
and returned home.
There was a deliberation to remove Hóngwēi from Shìzhōng
and add Shàngshū of the Ministry of Personnel to his Lǜ (rank),
but he firmly stated his illness was critical,
and was thus spared.
In the ninth year,
Dōngxiāngjūn passed away.
Her assets amounted to millions,
her gardens and residences numbered more than ten,
and in various places like Kuàijī, Wúxīng, and Lángxié,
which were the enterprises of Tài fù and Sī kōng Yǎn during his time,
there were still several hundred slaves.
Both public and private opinion held that the household assets
should go to her two daughters,
while the fields, residences, and servants
should belong to Hóngwēi.
Hóngwēi took nothing at all,
and funded the funeral himself from his private salary.
Hóngwēi's female cousin's husband, Yīn Ruì, was fond of gambling with chūpú (a dice game).
Hearing that Hóngwēi took no property,
he wrongly seized the shares of his wife's younger sister and his two paternal aunts to repay gambling debts.
Everyone in the family was influenced by Hóngwēi's yielding
and did not contend for anything.
Hóngwēi's maternal cousin, Língjūn Jiāngjūn Liú Zhàn, whose nature could not tolerate such impropriety,
said to Hóngwēi:
"All matters in the world should be decided with fairness.
If you don't manage this,
how can you manage official affairs?"
Hóngwēi smiled and did not reply.
Some criticized him, saying:
"The Xiè clan's generational wealth
being used to repay Lord Yīn's gambling debts in one morning
is the most unreasonable thing imaginable.
You are a relative and yet you don't speak up.
It's like discarding objects into the rivers and seas to appear incorruptible.
Even if you establish a reputation for integrity,
but leave your family in want,
that is also something I would not approve of."
Hóngwēi said:
"Relatives contending for wealth
is utterly vulgar.
Now, the women in the family can still remain silent;
how can I guide them to contend?
Now, with more to share than what is needed,
there will be no lack,
and after I die,
how will it still concern me?"
When Dōngxiāngjūn was buried,
and the tomb of Hóng (his father) was opened,
Hóngwēi attended despite his illness,
and his condition worsened considerably.
In the tenth year,
he died,
at the age of forty-two.
At that time, there was a long-necked ghost staying at Sīmǎ Wénxuān's house,
who claimed to have been sent to kill Hóngwēi.
Whenever Hóngwēi's illness worsened,
the ghost would predict it to Wénxuān.
After Hóngwēi died,
the ghost parted ways with Wénxuān and left.
Before Hóngwēi died,
he said to his attendants:
"There are two sealed letters.
When Língjūn Liú arrives,
they should be burned in his presence.
Be sure not to open them."
The letters were all imperial decrees from Tàizǔ.
The Emperor was deeply grieved and saddened by his death,
and ordered a thousand men from the two guards to complete the funeral arrangements.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàicháng.
His son, Zhuāng,
has a separate biography.
Wáng Qiú, courtesy name Qiànyù,
was from Línyí, Lángxié.
He was a younger paternal cousin of Tàicháng Huì.
His father, Mì,
was Sītú.
Qiú was as famous as Huì in his youth.
He had a beautiful appearance and dignified demeanor.
He was appointed as Zuòzhù Zuǒláng,
but did not accept it.
He was soon appointed as Dàsīmǎ Xíngcānjūn for Prince of Lángxié,
then transferred to Zhǔbù,
and later Zhōngjūn Gōngcáo for the Heir Apparent of Prince of Yùzhāng.
When the Sòng state was established,
he was initially appointed as Shìzǐ Zhōngshèrén.
When Gāozǔ received the Mandate of Heaven,
he continued as Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén,
then Yídū Wángyǒu,
transferred to Zīyì Cānjūn,
and resigned due to illness.
In Yuánjiā's fourth year,
he was reappointed as Yìxīng Tàishǒu.
As his paternal cousin, Hóng, was the governor of Yángzhōu,
and due to family mourning customs, they could not govern neighboring prefectures,
he was granted the title of Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn.
He was known for his benevolence and kindness in the commandery,
and was then transferred to Tàizǐ Yòuwèilǜ.
He entered the court as Shìzhōng,
and concurrently held the title of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn,
then concurrently held Dàzhōngzhèng for his home province,
and was transferred to Zhōngshūlìng,
with Shìzhōng as before.
He was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū.
Qiú was a refined and noble gentleman,
who rarely socialized.
His banquets were quiet and serene,
and his door was free of unusual guests.
Shàngshū Púyè Yīn Jǐngrén and Língjūn Liú Zhàn both held significant power,
swaying both inner and outer courts.
Although Qiú was connected to them through marriage,
he never interacted with them.
He was quite fond of literature,
and only associated well with Yán Yánzhī of Lángxié.
While holding an electoral position,
he rarely received guests
and did not look at letters or petitions seeking official appointments,
yet his selections were orderly,
and he was praised by both court and commoners.
He was originally prone to illness
and frequently requested resignation.
He was promoted to Guānglù Dàfū,
granted a gold seal and purple ribbon,
and concurrently held the position of Lúlíng Wángshī.
His nephew, Lǚ, pursued profit in his conduct
and deeply allied himself with Liú Zhàn,
committing himself sincerely to Dàjiāngjūn Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng.
Along with Liú Bīn and Kǒng Yìnxiù, they harbored illicit intentions.
Qiú often admonished him,
but Lǚ did not heed him.
Lǚ served as Dàjiāngjūn Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
then was transferred to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
but tearfully pleaded with Yìkāng that he did not wish to leave,
and thus returned to Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
Tàizǔ deeply resented this.
On the night Zhàn was executed,
Lǚ, barefoot, informed Qiú.
Qiú ordered his shoes to be brought
and first offered him warm wine,
saying:
"What about what I told you everyday?"
Lǚ was terrified and could not answer.
Qiú slowly said:
"Your father is here,
what do you have to worry about?"
He then commanded his attendants:
"Help the young master back to his study."
Due to Qiú,
Lǚ was spared death
and confined to his home.
In the 17th year,
Wáng Qiú was again appointed Prince Imperial's Chamberlain for the Household (Tàizǐ Zhānshì).
His positions as Grand Master (Dàfū) and Royal Tutor (Wáng Shī) remained as before.
Before he was formally invested,
it happened that Yīn Jǐngrén died,
so he was instead appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance (Shàngshū Púyè),
with his position as Royal Tutor (Wáng Shī) remaining as before.
He had long suffered from a foot ailment.
Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng, who was then Acting Grand Master of Remonstrance (Lù Shàngshū), said to Shàngshū Hé Shàngzhī:
"Currently there is a lack of talent,
and the officials below should exert more effort.
However, Wáng Qiú indulges himself to such an extent,
I fear he ought to be corrected by law."
Hé Shàngzhī replied:
"Wáng Qiú has always had high principles,
and moreover he suffers from many ailments.
He should be judged by his detached and reclusive nature,
not by his administrative performance."
Nevertheless, he was still holding office as a commoner (báiyī).
At that time, when officials were summoned for audience,
many did not come forward immediately.
Those of lower rank and humble status sometimes waited for dozens of days,
and even high ministers sometimes waited for more than ten days without being seen.
Only Wáng Qiú would leave promptly,
never willing to linger.
In the 18th year,
he died,
aged forty-nine.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Special Advanced (Tèjìn) and Gold and Purple Guanglù Dàfū (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū),
and additionally Sanqí Chángshì (Sànqí Chángshì).
He had no sons;
his grand-nephew Huàn succeeded him.
Towards the end of the Dàmíng era,
he was the Administrator of Wúxīng (Wúxīng Tàishǒu).
Someone once asked the imperial historian:
"How was Wáng Huì?"
He replied:
"He was bright and simple."
He then asked:
"How was Wáng Qiú?"
He replied:
"He was elegant and detached."
He then asked:
"How was Xiè Hóngwēi?"
He replied:
"Simple yet not losing propriety,
detached yet not drifting aimlessly –
he was what the ancients called a distinguished minister (míngchén).
Xiè Hóngwēi truly embodies this."
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 19: Yīn Chún (son Fú; younger brothers Chōng, Dàn), Zhāng Chàng, Hé Yǎn, Jiāng Zhìyuān
Yīn Chún, courtesy name Cuìyuǎn,
was a native of Chénjùn, Chángpíng.
His great-grandfather was Róng, his grandfather Yǔn,
both served as Tàicháng (Tàicháng) in the Jìn dynasty.
His father, Mù,
was praised for his harmony and prudence,
and held various prominent official positions.
From Minister of Five Branches of the Military (Wǔbīng Shàngshū), he served as Left Chief Clerk (Zuǒ Chángshǐ) for Gāozǔ's Prime Minister (Xiàngguó).
When the abdication took place,
he was transferred to Sanqí Chángshì (Sànqí Chángshì),
then Libationer of the Imperial Academy (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ),
and again Minister of Five Branches of the Military (Wǔbīng Shàngshū),
and Administrator of Wújùn (Wújùn Tàishǒu).
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Gold and Purple Guanglù Dàfū (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū),
and concurrently Tutor to the Prince of Jìnglíng (Jìnglíng Wáng Shī).
He was promoted to Protector-General (Hùjūn),
and again promoted to Special Advanced (Tèjìn) and Right Guanglù Dàfū (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū),
concurrently Tutor to the Prince of Shǐxīng (Shǐxīng Wáng Shī).
He died in office in the 15th year of Yuánjiā,
aged sixty.
His posthumous name was Yuánzǐ.
Yīn Chún was fond of learning from a young age
and had a good reputation.
In the early Jǐngpíng era of Shàodì,
he served as Secretary of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Láng),
Literature Officer for the Prince of Héngyáng (Héngyáng Wáng Wénxué),
Assistant Secretary of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Chéng),
and Palace Attendant (Zhōngshū Huángmén Shìláng).
While serving as Palace Attendant (Huángmén), Chún was known for his integrity and strictness.
When off duty, he was supposed to remain in the provincial office (liú xià shěng),
but because his father was old, he was specially permitted to return home.
He was lofty, simple, and had few desires,
and had early on established a reputation for purity.
He loved literature and scholarship,
never straying from his studies.
While in the Imperial Library (Mìshū Gé), he compiled a catalog of four categories of books, totaling forty volumes,
which circulated in the world.
He died in the 11th year of Yuánjiā,
aged thirty-two.
The imperial court mourned him deeply.
His son, Fú,
inherited his father's character.
Towards the end of the Dàmíng era of Shìzǔ,
he served as Chancellor of Shǐxīng (Shǐxīng Xiāng).
He rose to the office of Ministry of Personnel Affairs Official (Shàngshū Lìbù Láng)
and Chief Clerk to the General Who Controls the Army (Fǔjūn Chángshǐ) for Shùndì.
Yīn Chún's younger brother, Chōng, courtesy name Xīyuǎn,
successively served as Palace Attendant (Zhōngshū Huángmén Láng) but was dismissed for improper discussion of affairs.
He was again appointed Aide to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ),
Ministry of Personnel Affairs Official (Shàngshū Lìbù Láng),
and Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng),
and was praised for his rectitude.
He was sent out as Administrator of Wúxīng (Wúxīng Tàishǒu),
then entered the court as Minister of Revenue (Dùzhī Shàngshū).
The consort of the 'Prime Culprit' (Yuánxiōng Fēi) was Yīn Chún's daughter,
and Chōng, while in the Eastern Palace, was appreciated and well-regarded by Shào.
When Shào usurped the throne by assassination,
he appointed Chōng as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Protector-General (Hùjūn),
then promoted him to Colonel Director of the Retainers (Sīlì Xiàowèi).
Chōng had learning, integrity, literary skill, and eloquence.
Shào had him draft the imperial edict (Shàngshū Fú),
detailing the crimes of Shìzǔ, and Chōng indeed served Shào with all his might.
When Shìzǔ recaptured the capital,
Chōng was granted death.
Chōng's younger brother, Dàn, courtesy name Yíyuǎn,
also successively served as Palace Attendant (Huángmén Lìbù Láng),
Aide to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ),
and concurrently Colonel of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi).
During the Dàmíng era,
he was known for his literary talent
and was considered a talented scholar of his time.
Zhāng Chàng, courtesy name Shàowēi,
was a native of Wú, Wújùn,
and the nephew of Shào, the Administrator of Wúxīng (Wúxīng Tàishǒu).
His father, Huī,
was known for his filial piety in his youth,
and successively served in provincial and prefectural offices,
and as Administrator (Lángzhōng Lìng) for the Kingdom of Lángyá.
He followed the Prince of Lángyá to Luòyáng.
Upon returning to the capital,
Gāozǔ sealed a jar of medicinal wine and entrusted it to Huī,
ordering him to secretly administer poison.
Huī accepted the order.
Upon returning,
he drank it himself on the way and died.
Zhāng Chàng was renowned in his youth, alongside his cousins Fū, Yǎn, and Jìng,
as a rising star among the younger generation.
He began his career as Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù) to Administrator Xú Pèizhī.
When Xú Pèizhī was executed,
Chàng rushed to his funeral,
donned mourning clothes, and expressed his full sorrow,
which was praised by commentators.
His younger brother, Mù, was once bitten by a mad dog.
The doctor said he should eat minced frog (háma kuài).
Mù found this very difficult,
but Chàng smiled and tasted it first.
Mù then ate it,
and his wound immediately healed.
He was appointed Attaché (Cóngshì) by the province,
then Staff Officer (Cān Jūnjūn) to Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì's General Who Conquers the North (Zhēnglǔ),
Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù) to Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng's General Who Pacifies the North (Píngběi),
Libationer to the Minister of Education (Sītú Jìjiǔ),
and Administrator of Guests (Shàngshū Zhǔkè Láng).
Before he could be invested,
he was again appointed Administrator of Provisions and Left Civil Affairs (Dùzhī Zuǒmín Láng),
then Record-keeper and Staff Officer (Jìshì Cānjūn) to Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng's General Who Conquers the North (Zhēngběi), and Administrator of Jìn'ān (Jìn'ān Tàishǒu).
He also served as Record-keeper and Staff Officer (Jìshì Cānjūn) to Yìjì's General Who Pacifies the West (Ānxī), and Administrator of Nán Yìyáng (Nán Yìyáng Tàishǒu),
then Aide to the General-in-Chief (Wèijūn Cóngshì Zhōngláng) for Línchuān Wáng Yìqì,
Chief Administrator and Vice Inspector (Zhìzhōng Biéjià Cóngshì Shǐ) of Yángzhōu,
and Aide to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ).
Shìzǔ was garrisoned at Péngchéng.
Zhāng Chàng served as Ánběi Zhǎngshǐ and Pèijùn Tàishǒu.
In the 27th year of Yuánjiā (450 CE),
the Sǎ Luǒ Tuòbá Tào invaded from the south.
The Tàiwèi, Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng, took overall command of all the armies,
and went out to garrison Pénɡ and Sì.
At that time, Tào personally led a large force,
and had already reached Xiāochéng,
ten-odd *lǐ* from Péngchéng.
Although Péngchéng had many troops,
military provisions were insufficient.
Yìgōng wanted to abandon Péngchéng and return south.
The discussions on this matter lasted a full day, but no decision was reached.
At that time, Lìchéng had few troops but abundant provisions.
The Ánběi Zhōngbīng Cānjūn, Shěn Qìngzhī, suggested
using carts to form a box-shaped array,
with elite troops as outer wings,
to escort the two princes and their consorts straight to Lìchéng.
A detachment of troops would be assigned to Hùjūn Xiāo Sīhuà to stay and defend.
The Tàiwèi Zhǎngshǐ, Hé Xù, disagreed,
wishing to sweep up and flee to Yùzhōu,
and return to the capital by sea.
Yìgōng’s intention to leave was already clear,
but he had not decided between these two proposals.
He convened his officials again to deliberate.
Everyone was flustered and agitated,
with no differing opinions.
Zhāng Chàng said:
“If Lìchéng or Yùzhōu were feasible,
this humble official would not hesitate to highly praise them.
But now, food is scarce in the city,
and the common people all wish to flee,
but with the city gates strictly guarded,
they cannot go even if they wish to.
If we make a move suddenly,
everyone will scatter and flee,
and how can they reach their intended destination?
Although our military provisions are meager,
we are not yet in dire straits day and night.
We can assess when they are about to run out,
and then make other suitable arrangements.
How can one abandon a method of complete safety
and embrace a path of peril and destruction?
If this plan must be adopted,
this humble official asks to shed his neck's blood upon your horse's hooves!”
When Shìzǔ heard Zhāng Chàng’s proposal,
he said to Yìgōng:
“Father (Yìgōng) is the supreme commander,
so whether to stay or leave is not for me to interfere with.
I, Dàomín, am ashamed to be the city lord,
and to diminish our prestige and prolong the enemy’s presence;
my shame and regret
are already profound.
To abandon the garrison and flee
would truly make me unable to face the imperial court again.
I intend to share the city’s fate, whether it survives or perishes.
Zhāng Zhǎngshǐ’s words cannot be gainsaid.”
Since Zhāng Chàng’s words were firm,
and Shìzǔ also supported his proposal,
Yìgōng then stopped (his plan to flee).
At that time, Tàizǔ sent Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng Xú Yuán by post-horse to Péngchéng to ascertain the exact amount of rice and grain.
After Xú Yuán left,
the city sent cavalry to escort him.
When Tào heard of this,
he immediately dispatched several hundred cavalry to pursue him urgently.
Xú Yuán had already crossed the Huái River,
and barely escaped.
When Xú Yuán initially departed,
the city heard that the barbarians had sent pursuers,
fearing that Xú Yuán would be captured,
and that the accurate count of rice would be lost,
which would let the barbarians know the city was short of food.
Yìgōng was worried and fearful, with no solution,
and still wished to flee.
After Xú Yuán escaped,
that very day, the barbarian main force also arrived at Péngchéng.
When Tào first arrived,
he immediately ascended the tomb of Yàfù south of the city,
and erected a felt tent on the Xìmǎtái.
Earlier,
before Tào arrived,
Shìzǔ had sent his general Mǎ Wéngōng towards Xiāochéng.
He was defeated by the barbarians,
and Mǎ Wéngōng escaped,
but Duìzhǔ Kuǎi Yìng was captured.
He (Kuǎi Yìng) came to the Xiǎoshìmén and said:
“The Wèi lord sends his regards to Ánběi.
We are tired from the long journey.
If there is sugarcane and wine,
please share it with us.”
At that time, the Fángchéng Duìzhǔ, Liáng Fǎniàn, replied:
“I shall report this (to my superiors).”
Then Kuǎi Yìng himself described the defeat at Xiāochéng.
He (Liáng Fǎniàn) then asked Kuǎi Yìng:
“Did the barbarian lord come himself?”
He replied:
“Yes, he came.”
He asked:
“Where is he now?”
Kuǎi Yìng pointed his finger southwest.
He also said:
“How many soldiers and horses are there?”
He replied:
“Over four hundred thousand.”
Liáng Fǎniàn reported Tào’s words to Shìzǔ.
Shìzǔ sent someone to reply:
“We know you have suffered much on your journey.
We now send two vessels of wine
and one hundred stalks of sugarcane.
We hear they have camels;
they can be sent over.”
The next morning,
Tài again ascended the Xìmǎtái.
He again sent an envoy to the Xiǎoshìmén, saying:
"The ruler of Wèi sends his regards to Ānběi.
Ānběi may temporarily come out of the gate;
I wish to meet with Ānběi.
I will also not attack this city.
Why does Ānběi trouble his officers and soldiers on the city walls?
Also, mules, donkeys, and camels
are produced in the northern country.
I am now sending them,
along with various other items."
He also said to the commander of the Xiǎoshìmén detachment:
"Since there are provisions to be delivered,
you may move to the Nánmén to receive them."
Tài sent camels, mules, horses, sable furs, and various foods and drinks.
When they arrived at the Nánmén,
the gate was already closed,
and the keys had not yet been brought out upon request.
Chàng watched them from atop the city wall.
The barbarian envoy asked:
"Is this Zhāng Chángshǐ?"
Chàng said:
"How do you know me?"
The barbarian envoy replied:
"Your fame has spread far and wide,
enough for me to know you."
Chàng then asked the barbarian envoy's surname.
He replied:
"I am Xiānbēi;
I have no surname.
Moreover, it is not permissible to say."
Chàng again asked:
"What office do you hold?"
He replied:
"Xiānbēi official positions are different;
it is not permissible to simply state them.
However, my rank is sufficient to be your equal."
The barbarian envoy again asked:
"Why the hasty closing of the gates and breaking of bridges?"
Chàng replied:
"The two princes believe that the Wèi ruler's encampment is not yet established,
and his officers and soldiers are weary.
We have 100,000 elite armored troops,
each eager to sacrifice their lives.
Fearing that they might lightly invade and trample you,
we have provisionally closed the city gates.
Once their soldiers and horses have rested,
we will then jointly prepare the battlefield
and fix a day for battle."
The barbarian envoy said:
"You should use laws and regulations to manage affairs.
Why bother to dismantle the bridges?
Furthermore, why boast of 100,000 men?
I also have fine horses with swift hooves;
if our cavalry gathers like clouds,
we can also resist you."
Chàng said:
"Princes establish dangers and defenses;
why speak only of laws and regulations?
If I were boasting to you,
I would say a million.
The reason I said 100,000
is precisely those whom the two princes have personally maintained on their left and right.
Within this city are the gentry and commoners of several prefectures,
and the troops of two divisions,
which are not even mentioned yet.
I primarily contend with wisdom,
not with horse hooves.
Moreover, the northern lands of Jì
are where horses are born.
Why do you again boast to me with swift hooves?"
The barbarian envoy said:
"Not so.
Defending cities
is your strength;
fighting in the field
is my strength.
My reliance on horses
is just like your reliance on the city."
Inside the city was a man named Jù Sī,
who had once been in the northern country.
Yìgōng sent him to observe.
Sī recognized that the barbarian was the Shàngshū Lǐ Xiàobó.
Sī then asked:
"Shàngshū Lǐ, you must have toiled on your journey."
Xiàobó said:
"This matter should be known to us both."
Sī replied:
"It is because it is known to us both
that you have toiled."
Xiàobó said:
"I appreciate your kind intention."
After the gate was opened,
Chàng dismissed his attendants,
and came out to face Xiàobó,
and presented gifts.
The barbarian envoy said:
"A sable coat for the Tàiwèi,
camels and mules for the Ānběi,
and various grape wines,
for the uncle and nephew to share and taste."
Táo again requested wine and sweet oranges.
Chàng conveyed Shìzǔ's message:
"Convey to the Wèizhǔ,
that I know he desires to meet me,
and I have always yearned for a face-to-face meeting.
However, having received orders from my own court,
and being greatly entrusted with a border command,
a minister cannot have relations beyond the border,
I regret not being able to fully comply for now.
Moreover, defending cities and preparing defenses,
is standard for border garrisons.
But if they are pleased and thus employed,
they will toil without complaint.
The Tàiwèi and Zhènjūn have received the items sent.
Regarding the Wèizhǔ's wishes,
knowing you also need sweet oranges,
they are all delivered now, as separately requested.
Since the Tàiwèi is in the cold northern lands,
leather trousers and jackets are needed,
and are now sent to the Wèizhǔ.
Conch cups and various zòngzi,
which are specialties of the southern lands,
are now sent by the Zhènjūn."
Before this message had departed,
Táo again sent an envoy, bidding Xiàobó to relay a message:
"The Wèizhǔ has an imperial edict for the Tàiwèi and Ānběi,
that recently cavalry arrived,
with carriages following behind.
Now sitting idly with nothing to do,
are there any board games that can be lent to me?"
Chàng said:
"I shall report and request about the board games.
But your previous address to the two 'kings'
was already not humble language,
and moreover, the phrase 'has an imperial edict'
can only be applied in his own country,
how can it be used here?"
Xiàobó said:
"'Edict' and 'message',
'Zhèn' and 'I' (wǒ),
what difference is there between them?"
Chàng said:
"If the terms were merely to convey meaning,
they could be as you speak;
but since words have specific applications,
then there are distinctions of noble and humble.
The 'edict' you previously mentioned
is not something I dare to hear."
Xiàobó again said:
"Are the Tàiwèi and Ānběi ministers or not?"
Chàng said:
"They are."
Xiàobó said:
"How can the ruler of a neighboring country
not issue an edict to the ministers of a neighboring country?"
Chàng said:
"This appellation 'ruler'
cannot even be properly applied in Zhōnghuá,
let alone when referring to our esteemed princes,
and still call him 'ruler of a neighboring country'?"
Xiàobó said:
"The Wèizhǔ says that the Tàiwèi and Zhènjūn are both young,
and far from news from the south,
and must be especially worried.
If they wish to send messages,
we will provide an escort;
if they need horses,
we will also send them horses."
Chàng said:
"There are many routes in this region,
and messengers travel back and forth day and night.
There is no need to trouble the Wèizhǔ with this."
Xiàobó said:
"We also know there is a water route,
but it seems to be blocked by the 'white bandits'."
Chàng said:
"You wear white clothes,
is that why you call them 'white bandits'?"
Xiàobó laughed loudly and said:
"Today's 'white bandits'
are no different from the Huángjīn or Chìméi."
Chàng said:
"The Huángjīn and Chìméi,
do not seem to be in Jiāngnán."
Xiàobó said:
"Although they are not in Jiāngnán,
they are also not in Qīng or Xú Provinces."
Chàng said:
"Currently in Qīng and Xú Provinces,
there are indeed bandits,
but they are not 'white bandits'."
The barbarian envoy said:
"We requested board games earlier,
why are they not brought out?"
Chàng said:
"The two 'kings' are of high status and far away,
and it is difficult for a report to reach them."
Xiàobó said:
"Zhōugōng would grasp his hair and spit out his food (to receive guests),
why are these two 'kings' uniquely so high and distant?"
Chàng said:
"Grasping hair and spitting out food
was originally only applied within Zhōngguó."
Xiàobó said:
"If the guest has propriety,
then the host will choose him."
Chàng said:
"Yesterday, I saw all the guests arrive at the gate,
and they did not yet show propriety."
A moment later, the board games were brought out,
and given to him.
Táo (Táo) again sent someone, saying:
"The Lord of Wèi (Wèi) sends his regards to Ānběi (Ānběi),
Chéng Tiānzuò (Chéng Tiānzuò) is merely an ordinary person,
I truly know he is not a treasure of the Sòng (Sòng) court.
Recently, in Rǔyáng (Rǔyáng), he suffered nine wounds,
fell into the Ruò (Ruò) River,
and I pulled him out with my own hands.
All people, when their kin are separated,
long to be reunited.
I have already spoken to him about this,
but his younger brother strongly refused.
Now I shall let him meet your envoy."
Chéng Tiānfú (Chéng Tiānfú) said to the envoy:
"My brother received his commission in Rǔyáng (Rǔyáng),
but could not die for his integrity.
Since we are in different countries,
why bother to meet?"
Táo (Táo) also sent each person a felt blanket,
nine types of salt,
and also Húshǐ (Húshǐ) (fermented beans), saying:
"All these salts,
each has its specific use.
White salt is what the Lord of Wèi (Wèi) himself eats.
Black salt cures abdominal distension and chest fullness;
finely scrape six *zhū* (zhū) of it,
and take it with wine.
Hú (Hú) salt cures eye pain.
Rouróu (Rouróu) salt is not for eating;
it treats saddle sores on horses' backs.
Chì (Chì) salt, Bó (Bó) salt, Chòu (Chòu) salt, and Mǎchǐ (Mǎchǐ) salt, these four types,
are all not suitable for consumption.
Húshǐ (Húshǐ) (fermented beans) are also edible.
As for huánggān (huánggān) (oranges), fortunately they are abundant in your region,
so they can be distributed further."
He further said:
"The Lord of Wèi (Wèi) sends his regards to the Tàiwèi (Tàiwèi) and Ānběi (Ānběi),
why do you not send people to visit our land?
The feelings between us,
though they cannot be fully expressed,
it is essential to see our young and old,
to know our ages,
and to observe our conduct.
If your subordinates cannot be sent,
even a servant or boy can come."
Chàng (Chàng) then declared the imperial decree in reply, saying:
"The appearance and capabilities of the Lord of Wèi (Wèi)
have long been well-described by those who have come and gone.
Since Lǐ (Lǐ) Shàngshū (Shàngshū) personally bore the imperial command,
there is no concern that feelings between us are not fully understood,
hence we did not send another envoy or messenger."
He also said:
"The Lord of Wèi (Wèi) regrets that the horses sent previously
were quite unsatisfactory.
If Ānběi (Ānběi) needs large horses,
we will send more;
if you need Shǔ (Shǔ) horses,
we also have excellent ones."
Chàng (Chàng) said:
"Ānběi (Ānběi) is not lacking in fine steeds.
Their sending is according to their own intention,
not what we requested."
Yìgōng (Yìgōng) sent Táo (Táo) ten bundles of torches and candles.
Shìzǔ (Shìzǔ) also sent one bolt of brocade,
saying:
"I understand you still need huánggān (huánggān) (oranges),
it is truly not something I would begrudge.
But sending them would not be enough to supply his whole army;
they were given to the Lord of Wèi (Wèi) previously,
so he should not be immediately in want.
Thus, I will not send them again."
Táo (Táo) again requested sugarcane and Ānshíliú (Ānshíliú) (pomegranates).
Chàng (Chàng) said:
"Pomegranates come from Yèxià (Yèxià),
they should also not be lacking in his region."
Xiàobó (Xiàobó) further said:
"You are from the fertile lands of the south,
why do you wear straw sandals?
If you wear these,
what will your generals and soldiers say?"
Chàng (Chàng) replied:
"The mention of fertile lands is
truly a cause for much shame.
But because I am not martial,
I received the command to lead the army.
In the midst of battle formations,
slack attire is not permissible."
Xiàobó (Xiàobó) again said:
"Zhǎngshǐ (Zhǎngshǐ),
I am a person from the Central Plains,
having long lived in the northern country.
I am cut off from the culture of Huá (Huá),
and we are separated by distance,
so I cannot express myself fully.
All around here are northern people listening to my words,
so Zhǎngshǐ (Zhǎngshǐ) should truly understand me deeply."
Xiàobó (Xiàobó) further said:
"The Prince of Yǒngchāng (Yǒngchāng),
a younger cousin of the Lord of Wèi (Wèi),
has lately been stationed in Cháng'ān (Cháng'ān).
Now he leads eighty thousand elite cavalry,
advancing directly to Huáinán (Huáinán).
Shòuchūn (Shòuchūn) has long been closed and fortified,
not daring to resist.
The head of Liú Kāngzǔ (Liú Kāngzǔ) was sent earlier,
which they saw.
Wáng Xuánmó (Wáng Xuánmó) is very well known,
but he is just an ordinary talent.
Why did the southern country entrust him with such a mission,
leading to his defeat and flight?
We have entered this territory for over seven hundred *lǐ* (lǐ),
and the local inhabitants have not once dared to resist.
Zōushān (Zōushān)'s strategic passes,
on which your family relies,
our vanguard had just engaged,
when Cuī Xiélì (Cuī Xiélì) immediately hid in a cave.
Our generals dragged him out by his feet,
and the Lord of Wèi (Wèi) spared his life;
he is now here with us.
Furthermore, why were you so careless as to send Mǎ Wéngōng (Mǎ Wéngōng) to Xiāoxiàn (Xiāoxiàn),
causing him to retreat at the mere sight of our forces?
Your people are greatly resentful and complaining,
saying that during peaceful times,
you levied their taxes and cloth,
but when urgent difficulties arise,
you cannot help them."
Chàng (Chàng) replied:
"I know that Yǒngchāng (Yǒngchāng) has crossed Huáinán (Huáinán),
and Kāngzǔ (Kāngzǔ) was defeated by him.
According to recent intelligence,
there is no such news.
Wáng Xuánmó (Wáng Xuánmó) is a regional general of the southern lands;
he is not considered talented.
It is merely because he is from the north
that he serves as a vanguard and guide.
[一０] The main army had not yet arrived, and the river ice was about to form.
Xuánmó (Xuánmó) judged it appropriate to turn back;
it was not a loss of opportunity.
It was merely because of the night retreat
that the army and horses were slightly disorganized.
Our city of Xuánhù (Xuánhù) is a fortress,
[一一] with Chén Xiàn (Chén Xiàn) as a minor general.
The Lord of Wèi (Wèi) mustered his entire nation,
but could not conquer it for several weeks.
Hú Shèngzhī (Hú Shèngzhī) was a subordinate officer,
with less than a single *lǚ* (lǚ) of troops.
As soon as he crossed the Róng (Róng) River,
[一二] the Wèi (Wèi) ruler and his ministers fled in disarray,
barely escaping.
The forces at Huátái (Huátái)
have nothing to be greatly ashamed of.
Zōushān (Zōushān) is a small outpost;
though it has slight dangers,
the people along the river
are mostly newly affiliated.
They have only just begun to admire our benevolent rule,
and brigandage has not yet ceased.
We merely sent Cuī Xiélì (Cuī Xiélì) to pacify them.
Now that he has fallen into enemy hands,
what harm is it to the nation?
The Lord of Wèi (Wèi) uses an army of one hundred thousand to control one Cuī Xiélì (Cuī Xiélì);
is that truly something to boast about?
[一三] I heard that the common people of Xiāo (Xiāo) and Xiāng (Xiāng)
all relied on the mountains and strategic passes.
We merely sent Mǎ Wéngōng (Mǎ Wéngōng) with ten squads to show them.
Wéngōng (Wéngōng) refers to when three squads advanced,
then returned and fled.
Jī Xuánjìng (Jī Xuánjìng) of the main camp arrived at Liúchéng (Liúchéng) with one hundred cavalry,
and the Wèi (Wèi) army was defeated.
Underestimating the enemy led to this;
it is not something to be ashamed of.
The people of our kingdom
are scattered along the river.
When two nations engage in war,
they should mutually provide care and protection.
[一四] However, when the Wèi (Wèi) army entered our territory,
they wantonly committed atrocities.
Unexpected incidents arose
because of their unprincipled conduct.
The government does not betray its people,
so why should the people resent others?
You know that you entered seven hundred *lǐ* (lǐ) into our territory,
with no one resisting.
[一五] This is primarily due to the divine calculations of the Tàiwèi (Tàiwèi)
and secondarily to the sacred strategy of the Zhènjūn (Zhènjūn).
The essentials of governing a nation,
although I was not privy to them,
yet the use of military strategy has its secrets,
and sometimes it is not permissible to disclose them to each other."
Xiàobó (Xiàobó) said:
"The Lord of Wèi (Wèi) will not besiege this city;
he will personally lead his entire army
straight to Guābù (Guābù).
If affairs in the south are settled,
Péngchéng (Péngchéng) will not need to be attacked and besieged.
[一六] If we do not achieve victory,
Péngchéng (Péngchéng) is also not needed.
We will now go south to drink from the rivers and lakes to quench our thirst."
Chàng (Chàng) said:
"As for whether to leave or stay,
that is up to his own preference."
If the barbarian horses are able to drink from the Jiāng,
then there will be no more Heavenly Dao.
Each should return to report,
and will soon know everything."
Chàng then turned back,
and Xiàobó called after him,
"Chángshǐ, please take good care of yourself.
We are but a few steps apart,
and I regret not holding your hand."
Chàng then said again,
"Take good care of yourself.
I hope that the pacification will have a date,
and our meeting will not be far off.
If you are able to return to the Sòng court,
this will be the beginning of our acquaintance."
Xiàobó said,
"The time for this is not yet certain."
Táo also sent someone to the two kings to borrow a kōnghóu, pípá, zhēng, dì, and other instruments, as well as their players.
Yìgōng replied,
"I am on a military assignment and
do not carry musical instruments.
For the banquet here,
the zhènfǔ ordered courtesans,
who have a hundred strings,
which are the finest from Jiāngnán.
I will send them to you now."
Shìzǔ said,
"You hold a position in a strategic region,
and have never considered this before.
Moreover, musicians are common,
and I have seen the gifts from the former kings when bidding farewell;
there was this pípá.
I will give it to you now.
The players are also provided."
Xiàobó's speech was eloquent and
also admired in the northern land.
Chàng responded appropriately,
his words flowing like a stream,
his voice and rhythm elegant,
his demeanor refined and polished.
Xiàobó and those around him all looked at each other and sighed in admiration.
The barbarians soon attacked the southern gate of Péngchéng
and set fires.
Chàng personally went to the front to fight,
leading his soldiers.
When Táo fled north from Guābù,
passing by Péngchéng,
he sent someone to tell those inside the city:
"When the food is exhausted, you may leave.
We will return when the wheat is ripe."
Yìgōng was greatly frightened
and closed the gates, not daring to pursue.
When the barbarian's appointed time arrived again,
there was a discussion about whether to mow down the wheat and cut the seedlings
and relocate the populace to fortified settlements.
Public opinion was divided,
so another meeting was held.
Wáng Xiàosūn, the Lùshì Cānjūn of the Zhènjūn, alone said,
"The barbarians cannot come again,
so it is naturally safe.
If they do come again,
this proposal cannot be established either.
The common people are confined within the inner city,
suffering from hunger for a long time.
In the spring months,
they rely on foraging from the fields for sustenance.
Once they enter fortified settlements,
starvation will immediately ensue.
If the people know they will surely die,
how can they be controlled?
If the barbarians must come,
mowing down the wheat will not be too late."
Everyone present was silent,
no one daring to contradict him.
Chàng said,
"Xiàosūn's proposal
indeed has merit."
Dǒng Yuánsì, the Diǎnqiān of the Zhènjūn Fǔ, attending by Shìzǔ's side,
came forward and said,
"Wáng Lùshì's proposal cannot be overturned;
it is truly as he argues."
Wáng Zǐxià, the Biéjià, then said,
"This argument is indeed true."
Chàng, holding his tablet, addressed Shìzǔ, saying,
"Your subordinate wishes to order Xiàosūn to impeach Zǐxià."
Shìzǔ said,
"What has Wáng Biéjià done?"
Chàng said,
"Mowing down wheat and relocating the populace
can be called a major proposal;
the safety of an entire region
depends on this matter.
Zǐxià, as a principal official of the prefecture,
never expressed agreement or disagreement.
Yet, upon hearing Yuánsì's words,
he joyfully responded,
flattering those around him.
How can he serve his lord?"
Zǐxià was greatly ashamed,
and Yuánsì also looked ashamed.
Yìgōng's proposal was thus dropped.
Tàizǔ heard that Chàng had repeatedly made sound proposals
and greatly praised him.
Shìzǔ remained in Péngchéng,
summoning Chàng to return first,
and also sent him to survey Xūyí City,
intending to establish a large garrison there.
At that time, rumors of barbarians coming out from Xiāngyáng were circulating,
so Chàng was appointed Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān Sīkōng Chángshǐ and Nánjùn Tàishǒu.
There was also a desire for Chàng to replace Líu Xīngzǔ as Dūdū of Qīng Zhōu and Péngchéng,
but this did not materialize.
In the 30th year,
when Yuánxiōng committed regicide,
on the day Yìxuān expressed his grief,
he immediately raised an army.
Chàng was his chief aide,
holding the highest position among his subordinates.
His sorrowful demeanor, in every gesture,
overshadowed all others at the time.
After expressing his grief,
he changed his clothes,
putting on a yellow wéikùzhě,
and went out to the archery hall to select men.
His voice, appearance, and bearing
captivated everyone,
and all who saw him wished to lay down their lives for him.
When the matter was settled,
he was summoned to be Lìbù Shàngshū,
Yídào Xiàn Hóu,
with an income of a thousand households.
Since Yìxuān had other plans,
Cài Chāo and others, because of Chàng's popular support,
advised Yìxuān to keep him.
So, he relieved him of the post of Nánmán Xiàowèi and conferred it upon Chàng,
adding the title of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn,
and overseeing the Chéngxiàng Chángshǐ.
Chàng sent his student Gǒu Sēngbǎo to the capital,
and through Yán Jùn, he informed him of Yìxuān's transgressions.
Sēngbǎo had private goods held up in Bālíng
and did not descend in time.
When Yìxuān raised his army,
the river routes were cut off,
so Sēngbǎo was unable to leave.
When Yìxuān was about to rebel,
he sent his favorite attendant, Zhái Língbǎo, to Chàng, saying,
"The court is training ships and armor,
intending to attack the west.
Now I wish to raise an army for self-defense."
Chàng said,
"There is absolutely no such reason.
I ask to guarantee this with my life."
Língbǎo knew Chàng would not yield
and advised Yìxuān to kill him as a warning to the masses.
He immediately sent for Chàng,
detaining him in the eastern study,
not seeing him for a full day.
Fortunately, Sīmǎ Zhú Chāomín protected him,
so he managed to escape death.
Afterward, he was promoted to Fǔjūn,
establishing a separate military department
to gain popular support.
Although Chàng signed official documents,
he was constantly drunk and
did not attend to official papers.
He followed Yìxuān eastward,
and after the defeat at Liángshān,
Yìxuān fled.
Chàng returned on his own during the chaos of battle,
but was plundered by soldiers,
losing all his clothes.
He happened upon Yòujiāngjūn Wáng Xuánmó, who was leaving the camp in his carriage.
Chàng, having obtained tattered clothes,
pushed his way onto Xuánmó's carriage.
Xuánmó was very displeased,
and the generals wanted to kill him.
Duìzhǎng Zhāng Shì rescued him, and he was spared.
He was sent to the capital,
handed over to the Tíngwèi,
stripped of his title and fief,
and assigned to the Zuǒyòu Shàngfāng.
He was pardoned soon after.
He was reinstated as Dūguān Shàngshū,
then transferred to Shìzhōng,
replacing Zǐyān as the commander of the Tàizǐ Yòuwèishùai.
In Xiàojiàn 2nd year,
he was sent out as Huìjī Tàishǒu.
In Dàmíng 1st year,
he died in office,
at the age of fifty.
Yán Jùn submitted a memorial to Shìzǔ:
"Zhāng Chàng ultimately could not recover from his illness.
A talent from the Southeast,
who early established a reputation,
hearing of his passing fills me with sorrow,
deeply affecting my usual sentiments."
He was posthumously given the title Xuānzǐ.
Chàng loved his nephew Zhāng Jí
and, on his deathbed, left instructions to be buried with Zhāng Jí.
Zǐhào,
his official career reached that of Cānchūn (參軍) for Yìyáng Wáng Chǎng (義陽王昶), the Zhēngběi (征北, General who Conquers the North).
Hào’s younger brother, Yān (淹),
was the Zhǔbù (主簿, Registrar) for Shìzǔ (世祖) as Nán Zhōngláng (南中郎).
When Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
he became Huángmén Láng (黃門郎, Gentleman of the Yellow Gate),
was enfeoffed as a Viscount of Guǎngjìn Xiàn (廣晉縣子),
with an assigned stipend of five hundred households.
He served as Tàizǐ Yòuwèi Shuài (太子右衞率, Commander of the Right Guard of the Heir Apparent),
and Dōngyáng Tàishǒu (東陽太守, Governor of Dōngyáng).
He forced county officials to burn their arms to illuminate the Buddha,
and if commoners committed a crime, he made them worship the Buddha,
often up to several thousand prostrations.
He was dismissed from office and prohibited from serving.
He was later appointed Guānglù Xūn (光祿勳, Minister of the Imperial Household),
and Línchuān Nèishǐ (臨川內史, Administrator of Línchuān).
In the early Tàishǐ (泰始) reign of Tàizōng (太宗),
he joined Jìn’ān Wáng Zǐxūn (晉安王子勛) in rebellion,
leading troops to Póyáng (鄱陽).
His army was defeated and he was killed.
Chàng’s (暢) younger brother, Yuè (悅),
also had a good reputation.
He successively held the positions of Zhōngshū Lìbù Láng (中書吏部郎, Director in the Secretariat and Personnel Department),
Shìzhōng (侍中, Palace Attendant),
Qiánjūn Zhǎngshǐ (前軍長史, Chief Clerk of the Vanguard) to Línhǎi Wáng Zǐxū (臨海王子頊), and Nánjùn Tàishǒu (南郡太守, Governor of Nánjùn).
When Jìn’ān Wáng Zǐxūn (晉安王子勛) established a false reign title in Xúnyáng (尋陽),
Yuè was summoned to be Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書, Minister of Personnel),
and he jointly assisted Dèng Wǎn (鄧琬) in the false government.
When the plot failed,
he killed Wǎn (琬) and surrendered.
The matter is recorded in Wǎn’s (琬) biography.
He was again appointed Tàizǐ Shùzǐ (太子庶子, Gentleman Attendant to the Heir Apparent),
and then Zhǎngshǐ (長史, Chief Clerk) of Bālíng Wáng Xiūrùo’s (巴陵王休若) Wèijūn (衞軍, Guards General) and Xiāngyáng Tàishǒu (襄陽太守, Governor of Xiāngyáng).
In the fourth year,
he replaced Xiūrùo (休若) as Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ (雍州刺史, Governor of Yōngzhōu) and Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (寧遠將軍, General who Pacifies the Distant).
He was again appointed Zhēngxī Zhǎngshǐ (征西長史, Chief Clerk of the General who Conquers the West) to Xiūrùo (休若) and Nánjùn Tàishǒu (南郡太守, Governor of Nánjùn).
In the sixth year,
Tàizōng (太宗) established the Sānbā Xiàowèi (三巴校尉, Commandant of the Three Ba Commanderies) in Bājùn (巴郡),
and appointed Yuè (悅) to this post,
adding the titles of Chíjíe (持節, Bearer of the Imperial Insignia) and Fǔshī Jiāngjūn (輔師將軍, General who Assists the Army),
also serving as Bājùn Tàishǒu (巴郡太守, Governor of Bājùn).
He died
before he could take up the post.
Hé Yǎn (何偃), courtesy name Zhònghóng (仲弘),
was a native of Qián (灊) in Lújiāng (廬江),
and the second son of Sīkōng (司空, Minister of Works) Shàngzhī (尚之).
He was appointed Cóngshì (從事, Assistant) in the Yìcáo (議曹, Advisory Bureau) by the province,
was nominated as Xiùcái (秀才, Filial and Incorrupt),
and appointed Cānchūn (參軍) of the Zhōngjūn (中軍, Central Army),
and Zhǔbù (主簿, Registrar) of Línchuān Wáng Yìqìng’s (臨川王義慶) Píngxī Fǔ (平西府, General who Pacifies the West’s Establishment).
He was summoned to be Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ (太子洗馬, Adviser to the Heir Apparent),
but did not accept the appointment.
In Yuánjiā (元嘉) nineteenth year,
he became Dānyáng Chéng (丹陽丞, Assistant Administrator of Dānyáng),
and was appointed Lúlín Wáng Yǒu (廬陵王友, Companion to the Prince of Lúlín),
Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén (太子中舍人, Inner Gentleman of the Heir Apparent’s Household),
Zhōngshū Láng (中書郎, Director in the Secretariat),
and Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子, Inner Gentleman Attendant to the Heir Apparent).
At that time, Yìyáng Wáng Chǎng (義陽王昶) held office in Dōngguān (東官),
and made Yǎn (偃) manage the affairs of Yìyáng (義陽) principality.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Tàizǔ (太祖) wished to launch another northern expedition,
and consulted his officials.
Yǎn (偃) argued, saying:
“Nèi Gàn (內幹) Hú Fǎzōng (胡法宗) declared the imperial edict,
and inquired about the northern expedition.
I humbly believe that if the bandits truly inflict lingering harm,
and are as easily chaotic as dogs and sheep,
exterminating them would not be difficult,
which is indeed as per Your Majesty’s decree.
However, although the imperial strategy is flawless,
the soldiers are not yet proficient.
The border garrisons
are few in number,
and the border populace, having been displaced,
has mostly not settled into their occupations.
The resources for deployment
are drawn from the fundamental reserves.
Sacrificing the fundamental to pursue border troubles
means any action will likely not succeed.
[二０]Do not consider the setbacks of past years,
[二一]followed by internal strife,
which invited destruction and chaos,
leading to a complete collapse.
However, the several prefectures of Huái (淮) and Sì (泗)
are truly devastated and depleted.
The displaced have not returned,
and the wounded have not recovered.
Moreover, the defending and attacking forces are unequal;
the guest and host are in different situations.
If we despise them, our position will be difficult;
if we besiege them, it will take a long time.
Between advancing and retreating,
treachery and danger will constantly arise.
I secretly believe that the current problems are easily manageable,
and future invasions will not be profound.
It is appropriate to endure humiliation and conceal our weaknesses,
to align with the ways of Heaven.”
He was promoted to Zhēngběi Zhǎngshǐ (征北長史, Chief Clerk of the General who Conquers the North) to Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn (始興王濬) and Nán Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu (南東海太守, Governor of South Dōnghǎi).
When Yuánxiōng (元凶) usurped the throne,
Yǎn (偃) was made Shìzhōng (侍中, Palace Attendant),
in charge of imperial edicts.
At that time, Shàngzhī (尚之) was Sīkōng (司空, Minister of Works) and Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令, President of the Department of State Affairs).
Yǎn (偃) served in the Ménxià (門下, Chancellery).
Father and son both holding positions of power
caused anxiety at the time;
however, Shàngzhī (尚之) and Yǎn (偃) were skilled at managing circumstances
and acquired a good reputation for the time.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
his appointment and treatment remained unchanged.
He was appointed Dàsīmǎ Zhǎngshǐ (大司馬長史, Chief Clerk to the Grand Marshal),
and then promoted to Shìzhōng (侍中, Palace Attendant),
also serving as Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子, Inner Gentleman Attendant to the Heir Apparent).
At that time, officials were requested to speak candidly.
Yǎn (偃) believed that:
“Agriculture should be prioritized and the fundamental strengthened;
officials should be consolidated and affairs simplified;
performance evaluations should be conducted to ascertain ability;
and salaries increased to eliminate official corruption.
Capable governors should be held responsible
and kept in their posts for a long time.
The Dū Dū (都督, Regional Commanders) and Cìshǐ (刺史, Governors)
should have their responsibilities clearly separated.”
He was redesignated as Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (驍騎將軍, General of Valiant Cavalry),
and received intimate and generous treatment,
surpassing that of older officials.
He was transferred to Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書, Minister of Personnel).
Less than five years after Shàngzhī (尚之) left the selection post,
Yǎn (偃) again followed in his footsteps,
which was considered an honor by people at the time.
Shìzhōng (侍中) Yán Jùn (顏竣) only then began to gain prominence,
and he and Yǎn (偃) both served in the Ménxià (門下, Chancellery).
They appreciated each other for their literary and philosophical insights,
and got along very well.
Jùn (竣) considered his appointment and treatment to be extremely generous,
and that he should hold a more significant position,
but his rank was not yet different from Yǎn’s (偃),
so he became slightly displeased.
When Yǎn (偃) replaced Jùn (竣) in overseeing the selection,
Jùn (竣) became even more indignant,
and thus a rift formed between him and Yǎn (偃).
At that time, Jùn’s (竣) influence swayed the court and the countryside.
Yǎn (偃) felt uneasy,
and consequently developed heart palpitations.
His thoughts became erratic,
and he submitted a memorial to resign,
claiming illness and retirement from official service.
[二二]Shìzǔ’s (世祖) regard for Yǎn (偃) was profound,
and he provided comprehensive medical treatment,
with renowned physicians and superior medicines,
as needed,
and thus he recovered.
At that time, the Emperor’s eldest daughter, Shānyīn Gōngzhǔ (山陰公主), was exceptionally favored,
and was married to Yǎn’s (偃) son, Jí (戢).
He was naturally fond of discussing profound theories
and his commentary on the “Xiāoyáo Piān” (消搖篇) of Zhuāngzǐ (莊子) was passed down to later generations.
In Dàmíng (大明) second year,
he died in office,
at the age of forty-six.
Shìzǔ (世祖) issued an edict to Yán Jùn (顏竣), saying:
“Hé Yǎn (何偃) has passed into another world,
his noble aspirations gone forever.
Having associated with him
and furthermore being connected by marriage,
my tears and sorrow at his passing
are truly uncontrollable.
How lamentable is his departure!
He should be posthumously granted the titles of Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary) and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (金紫光祿大夫, Grand Master of Remonstrance with Gold and Purple).
His original office remains as before.”
His posthumous name was Jìngzǐ (靖子).
His son, Jí (戢),
at the end of Shēngmíng (昇明),
was Xiàngguó Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ (相國左長史, Chief Clerk of the Left for the Chancellor).
Jiāng Zhìyuān (江智淵),
a native of Kǎochéng (考城) in Jìyáng (濟陽),
was the nephew of Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (湘州刺史) Yí (夷).
His father, Sēng’ān (僧安),
was Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子, Inner Gentleman Attendant to the Heir Apparent).
Jiāng Zhìyuān 初為著作郎，
江夏王Yìgōng 太尉行參軍，
太子太傅主簿，
隨王Dàn 後軍參軍．
世父Yí 有盛名，
Yí 子Zhàn 又有清譽，
父子並貴達，
Zhìyuān 父少無名問，
Zhàn 禮敬甚簡，
Zhìyuān 常以為恨，
自非節歲，
不入Zhàn 門．
及為隨王Dàn 佐，
在Xiāngyáng，
Dàn 待之甚厚．
時諮議參軍Xiè Zhuāng、府主簿Shěn Huáiwén 並與Zhìyuān 友善．
Huáiwén 每稱之曰：
「人所應有盡有，
人所應無盡無者，
其江智淵乎． 」
Yuánjiā 末，
除尚書庫部郎．
時高流官序，
不為臺郎，
Zhìyuān 門孤援寡，
獨有此選，
意甚不說，
固辭不肯拜．
竟陵王Dàn 復版為驃騎參軍，
〔二三〕轉主簿，
隨府轉司空主簿、記室參軍，
領南濮陽太守，
遷從事中郎．
Dàn 將為逆，
Zhìyuān 悟其機，
請假先反．
Dàn 事發，
即除中書侍郎．
Zhìyuān 愛好文雅，
詞采清贍，
世祖深相知待，
恩禮冠朝．
上燕私甚數，
多命羣臣五三人游 集，
Zhìyuān 常為其首．
同侶未及前，
輒獨蒙引進，
Zhìyuān 每以越衆為慚，
未嘗有喜色．
每從游幸，
與羣僚相隨，
見傳詔馳來，
知當呼己，
聳動愧恧，
形於容貌，
論者以此多之．
遷驍騎將軍，
尚書吏部郎．
上每酣宴，
輒詬辱羣臣，
并使自相嘲訐，
以為歡笑．
Zhìyuān 素方退，
漸不會旨．
嘗使以Wáng Sēnglǎng 嘲戲其子Jǐngwén，
Zhìyuān 正色曰：
「恐不宜有此戲． 」
上怒曰：
「江僧安癡人，
癡人自相惜． 」
Zhìyuān 伏席流涕，
由此恩寵大衰．
出為新安王子Lán 北中郎長史、南東海太守，
加拜寧朔將軍，
行南徐州事．
初，
上寵姬Xuān Guìfēi Yīn Shì 卒，
使羣臣議諡，
Zhìyuān 上議曰
上以不盡嘉號，
甚銜之．
後車駕幸南山，
乘馬至Yīn Shì 墓，
羣臣皆騎從，
上以馬鞭指墓石柱謂Zhìyuān 曰：
「此上不容有懷字！ 」
Zhìyuān 益惶懼．
Dàmíng 七年，
以憂卒，
時年四十六．
子Jìjūn，
太子洗馬，
早卒．
後廢帝即位，
以后父，
追贈金紫光祿大夫．
Jìjūn 妻Wáng，
平望鄉君．
Zhìyuān 兄子Gài 早孤，
養之如子．
Gài 歷黃門吏部郎，
侍中，
武陵王北中郎長史、南東海太守，
行南徐州事．
後廢帝Yuánhuī 中卒．
史臣曰：夫將帥者，
御衆之名；
士卒者，
一夫之用．
坐談兵機，
制勝千里，
安在乎蒙楯前 驅，
履腸涉血而已哉．
Shān Táo 之稱Yáng Hù 曰：
「大將雖不須筋力，
軍中猶宜強健． 」
以此為言，
則叔子之幹力弱矣．
Dù Yù 文士儒生，
射不能穿札，
身未嘗跨馬，
一朝統大衆二十餘萬，
為平吳都督．
〔二四〕Wáng Róng 把臂入林，
亦受專征之寄．
何必山西猛士，
六郡良家，
然後可受脤於朝堂，
荷推轂之重．
及虜兵深入，
徐服恇震，
非Zhāng Chàng 正言，
則Péng、Biàn 危矣．
豈其身扞飛鏑，
手折雲衝，
方足使窮堞假命，
危城載安乎．
仁者之有勇，
非為臆說．
校勘記
列傳第二十Fàn Tài Wáng Zhǔnzhī Wáng Sháozhī Xún Bózǐ
Fàn Tài 字Bólún，
順陽山陰人也．
祖Wāng，
晉安北將軍、徐兗二州刺史．
父Níng，
豫章太守．
Fàn Tài (范泰) initially served as a Grand Academician (Tài Xué Bó Shì 太學博士).
He was a military advisor (Cānjūn 參軍) in the two prefectures of General of the Vanguard Xiè Ān (謝安) and General of Agile Cavalry Prince Dàozi (道子) of Kuàijī (會稽).
The Inspector of Jīngzhōu (荊州), Wáng Chén (王忱),
who was Tài's (泰) maternal cousin,
invited him to be the Administrator of Tiānmén (天門) Commandery.
Chén (忱) was fond of wine,
and when drunk, he would remain so for several tens of days.
When he sobered up,
he would be dignified and solemn.
Tài (泰) said to Chén (忱):
"Although wine suits your nature,
it also harms your life.
Since we have been in close company,
I have often wanted to admonish you,
but when you are deeply immersed,
there is no way to speak.
Now that we meet,
there is no need for lengthy explanation."
Chén (忱) sighed and lamented for a long time,
saying:
"Many have offered advice,
but none like this."
Someone asked Chén (忱):
"How does Fàn Tài (范泰) compare to Xiè Miǎo (謝邈)?"
Chén (忱) replied:
"Mòdù (茂度) is slow."
He was asked again:
"How does he compare to Yīn Jì (殷覬)?"
Chén (忱) replied:
"Bótōng (伯通) is easygoing."
Chén (忱) always had an ambition to achieve great deeds.
He said to Tài (泰):
"Now that the city walls are established
and the military armor is sufficient,
I intend to sweep clean the Central Plains
to fulfill my long-cherished ambition.
Bótōng (伯通) is sharp-witted,
so I will have him wield a spear and lead the vanguard.
As for you, given your steadfastness,
I wish to entrust you with the affairs remaining behind.
What do you think?"
Tài (泰) replied:
"For a hundred years, many former worthies have been frustrated and defeated
by these lingering bandits.
Although fame and achievement are noble,
this humble person dares not plan for them."
Soon after, Chén (忱) fell ill and died.
Tài (泰) was summoned to be a military advisor (Zīyì Cānjūn 諮議參軍) to the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn 驃騎將軍),
then promoted to Middle Secretariat Gentleman (Zhōngshū Shìláng 中書侍郎).
At that time, Yuánxiǎn (元顯), the heir apparent of the Prince of Kuàijī (會稽王), wielded exclusive power.
When internal and external officials requested leave,
they no longer submitted memorials to the throne,
but only reported to Yuánxiǎn (元顯).
Tài (泰) advised that this was inappropriate,
but Yuánxiǎn (元顯) did not accept it.
He left office due to his father's mourning,
inheriting the title of Marquis of Yángsuì Township (Yángsuì Xiāng Hóu 陽遂鄉侯).
When Huán Xuán (桓玄) supported the Jìn (晉) dynasty,

he had the Palace Assistant Imperial Censor Zǔ Táizhī (祖台之) impeach Tài (泰) and the former Left Grand Scribe (Zuǒ Chángshǐ 左長史) of the Minister of Works Wáng Zhǔnzhī (王準之), along with General Fúguó Sīmǎ Xúnzhī (輔國將軍司馬珣之), for being disrespectful during mourning.
Tài (泰) was dismissed from office and banished to Dāntú (丹徒).
When the banner of righteousness was raised,
he became an Erudite of the National University (Guózǐ Bóshì 國子博士).
When Sīmǎ Xiūzhī (司馬休之) was General of the Champion Army (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn 冠軍將軍) and Inspector of Jīngzhōu (荊州),
he appointed Tài (泰) as his Grand Scribe (Chángshǐ 長史) and Administrator of Nánjùn (南郡) Commandery.
He was also appointed as Chancellor of Chángshā (長沙 Xiàng 相)
and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍),
but he did not take up any of these posts.
He entered the court as Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Huángmén Láng 黃門郎)
and Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng 御史中丞).
He was disciplined for error in discussing the matter of the Yīn (殷) sacrifices,
and held office as a commoner (báiyī lǐngzhí 白衣領職).
He was sent out as Administrator of Dōngyáng (東陽).
During Lú Xún's (盧循) rebellion,
Tài (泰) took the initiative to dispatch a thousand soldiers
and opened the granaries to provide rations.
Gāozǔ (高祖) bestowed upon Tài (泰) the title of General of Martial Might (Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn 振武將軍).
The next year,
he was promoted to Attendant-in-Ordinary (Shìzhōng 侍中),
and soon after transferred to Minister of Revenue (Dùzhī Shàngshū 度支尚書).
At that time, the Director of the Department of State Affairs Xiè Hùn (謝混) of Chénjùn (陳郡) was a rising talent of renown.
Gāozǔ (高祖) once casually asked Hùn (混):
"Who among his peers can Tài (泰) be compared to?"
He replied:
"He is of the same caliber as Wáng Yuántài (王元太)."
He was transferred to Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng 太常).
Initially,
the Minister of Works (Sītú 司徒) Dàoguī (道規) had no son,
so he adopted Tàizǔ (太祖).
When he passed away,
he designated his elder brother Dàolián's (道憐) second son, Yìqìng (義慶), as his heir.
Gāozǔ (高祖), considering Dàoguī's (道規) former affection for Tàizǔ (太祖),
also ordered him to reside with the elder.
Dàoguī (道規) was posthumously enfeoffed as Duke of Nánjùn (南郡公),
and the former Duke of Huáróng County (Huáróng Xiàn Gōng 華容縣公) should have been bestowed upon Tàizǔ (太祖).
Tài (泰) argued:
"The duke's fraternal love
was indeed overly deep-seated in his heart.
There is no ritual for two heirs,
so Yìlóng (義隆) should return to his original lineage."
This was followed.
He was transferred to Left Grand Scribe (Zuǒ Chángshǐ 左長史) of the Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ 大司馬),
then Right General of the Guards (Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn 右衞將軍),
and given the additional title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍).
He again served as a Minister (Shàngshū 尚書),
with his Attendant-in-Ordinary (Chángshì 常侍) title remaining as before.
He concurrently served as Minister of Works (Sīkōng 司空),
and along with the Right Director of the Department of State Affairs Yuán Zhàn (袁湛), presented the Nine Bestowals (Jiǔ Xī 九錫) to the Duke of Sòng (宋公).
He accompanied the army to Luòyáng (洛陽).
When Gāozǔ (高祖) returned to Péngchéng (彭城),
Tài (泰) ascended the city wall with him.
Tài (泰) had a foot ailment,
so he was specially ordered to ride in a carriage.
Tài (泰) was fond of wine
and disregarded minor formalities,
being open and unrestrained.
Even in public settings,
he was no different from being in a private room.
Gāozǔ (高祖) greatly admired and loved him.
However, he was inept at governance,
and thus could not hold offices related to state affairs.
He was promoted to General of the Protecting Army (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn 護軍將軍),
but was dismissed due to official matters.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) received the Mandate,
Tài (泰) was appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with Golden and Purple Seal (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū 金紫光祿大夫),
and given the additional title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍).
The next year,
when the establishment of a national university was discussed,
Tài (泰) was appointed to lead it as Libationer of the National University (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ 國子祭酒).
Tài (泰) submitted a memorial, saying: Your servant has heard that civilizing influence arises from sagacious kings,
and teaching and instruction manifest in times of utmost peace.
The most excellent teachings are achieved through study and practice,
and the greatest joy is found in companionship.
In ancient times, when children reached maturity,
they entered school,
and were taught by exchanging sons with others.
They sought teachers regardless of distance,
carrying provisions and forgetting hardship.
Bringing peace to parents and glory to the nation,
all depended on this.
If one can go out without passing through a door,
then this path cannot
be followed.
Therefore, a clear imperial edict has been issued,
like a refreshing sweat;
the educational system has been enacted,
and both near and far comply.
Your servant's humble thoughts
have a few points not yet understood.
Now, the new beginning
of a grand undertaking is established,
the world has a new outlook,
and those with ambition admire it.
However, the system for enrolling students
selects few and keeps many away,
opening the door for non-attendance,
and not just in one way.
Your servant, by inferring from families to the nation,
knows that the number gathered is not large,
and fears it may not be sufficient to propagate the customs of the great Sòng (宋)
and promote the excellence of its numerous talents.
Your servant believes that for families permitted to enroll,
even if the system has not yet been fully realized,
if fathers and elder brothers wish for their children to enter school,
reason dictates that it should be opened up.
Although it might slightly deviate from morning and evening greetings,
it greatly promotes filial piety.
Not knowing the *Spring and Autumn Annals*
can lead to grave errors.
Therefore, Zhào Dùn (趙盾) was loyal yet was recorded as committing regicide,
and Xǔ Zǐ (許子) was filial yet incurred guilt.
Taking these as warnings,
how can one not be fearful?
To be earnest in study at fifteen
is indeed stated in texts,
but if one's age is only slightly less
and one has deep aspirations,
why must one be limited by a single rule
and not allowed to advance?
Yáng Wūyù (揚烏豫) displayed profound understanding at a tender age;
learning the *Yi Jing* (易) at fifty
is still not a great fault.

What is valued is the acquisition of talent,
not being bound by fixed ranks.

nowadays, there are those who have leisure from their official duties and excel in learning;

When Lúlíng Wáng Yìzhēn and the young emperor were killed,
