Added to this are severe illness
and heavy senility.
My words may be inappropriate, yet I cannot remain silent.
If Your Majesty records even a shred of my sincerity,
then I would not know where to place myself."
Tà (泰) extensively read books and documents,
was fond of writing essays,
and diligently and tirelessly supported and encouraged younger generations.
He compiled "Gǔjīn Shànyán" (古今善言) in twenty-four chapters and a collection of essays, which were transmitted to the world.
In his later years, he devoutly practiced Buddhism,
establishing a Jetavana Vihāra (祇洹精舍) west of his residence.
In the fifth year,
he passed away
at the age of seventy-four.
He was posthumously granted the title of Chēqí Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍),
with Shìzhōng (侍中), Tèjìn (特進), and Wángshī (王師) as before.
His posthumous title was Xuānhóu (宣侯).
His eldest son, Áng (昂),
died early.
His second son, Gǎo (暠),
was Prefect of Yídū (宜都).
His third son, Yàn (晏),
was Shìzhōng (侍中) and Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫).
His fourth son, Yè (曄),
was Tàizǐ Zhānshì (太子詹事),
and was executed for treason,
with his own biography.
His youngest son, Guǎngyuān (廣淵),
was skilled at writing.
He served Shìzǔ (世祖) as Fǔjūn Zīyì Cānjūn (撫軍諮議參軍)
and concurrently held Jìshì (記室).
He was implicated in Yè's (曄) affair and executed.
Wáng Zhǔnzhī (王准之), courtesy name Yuánzēng (元曾),
was a native of Línyí (臨沂), Lángxié (琅邪).
His great-great-grandfather, Bīn (彬),
was Shàngshū Púyè (尚書僕射).
His great-grandfather, Biāozhī (彪之),
was Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令).
His grandfather, Línzhī (臨之),
and father, Nèzhī (訥之),
were both Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞).
Biāozhī (彪之) was widely learned and knowledgeable,
and well-versed in court rituals.
From then on, this was passed down in the family,
and they were all familiar with the old affairs of the Jiāngzuǒ (江左),
preserving them in a "green box."
People of the time called it
"the Wáng (王) family's 'green box' scholarship."
Zhǔnzhī (准之) was also proficient in the Rites and Commentaries,
and abundant in literary talent.
He began his career as Yòuchángshì (右常侍) for his home commandery,
and then Dàjiāngjūn Xíng Cānjūn (大將軍行參軍) under Huán Xuán (桓玄).
When Xuán (玄) usurped the throne,
he appointed him Shàngshū Cíbù Láng (尚書祠部郎).
In the early Yìxī (義熙) era,
he again served as Shàngshū Zhōngbīng Láng (尚書中兵郎),
then moved to Cān Gāozǔ Chēqí Zhōngjūn Jūnshì (參高祖車騎中軍軍事),
Dānyáng Céng (丹陽丞),
and Zhōngjūn Tàiwèi Zhǔbù (中軍太尉主簿).
He was dispatched as Magistrate of Shānyīn (山陰),
where he earned a reputation for competence.
He participated in the meritorious suppression of Lú Xún (盧循),
and was enfeoffed as Dūtíng Hóu (都亭侯).
He also served Gāozǔ (高祖) as Zhènxī (鎮西), Píngběi (平北), Tàiwèi Cānjūn (太尉參軍),
Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (尚書左丞),
and Dàzhōngzhèng (大中正) for his home commandery.
When the Sòng Tái (宋臺) was established,
he was appointed Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞),
and was feared by his colleagues.
Zhǔnzhī's (准之) father Nèzhī (訥之), grandfather Línzhī (臨之), great-grandfather Biāozhī (彪之), down to Zhǔnzhī (准之),
four generations held this position.
Zhǔnzhī (准之) once composed a five-character poem,
and Fàn Tà (范泰) ridiculed him, saying:
"You only know how to impeach people!"
Zhǔnzhī (准之) replied with a stern expression:
"That's still better than your family producing generations of 'male foxes'!"
He was dismissed from office for failing to report his heir-apparent, Xiè Língyùn (謝靈運), for murder.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) received the mandate,
he was appointed Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎).
In the second year of Yǒngchū (永初),
he submitted a memorial, saying:
"Zhèng Xuán's (鄭玄) commentary on the rites states that for the three-year mourning period,
the auspicious ceremony is held after twenty-seven months,
and scholars, ancient and modern, mostly consider this to be in accordance with the rites.
In the early Jìn (晉) dynasty, Wáng Sù's (王肅) proposal was adopted,
where the xiáng (祥) and tán (禫) sacrifices were held in the same month,
thus ending after twenty-five months,
and this became the established system.
Since the Jiāngzuǒ (江左) era,
only the Jìn (晉) dynasty has applied this;
but many literati
follow Zhèng Xuán's (鄭玄) interpretation.
The ancient kings established rites
to align with the feelings of the multitude.
That mourning involves sorrow
is explicitly stated in previous teachings.
Now, with the great Sòng (宋) experiencing prosperity,
all things are in order.
I humbly suggest that it is appropriate to align with common human sentiment
and adopt Zhèng Xuán's (鄭玄) interpretation as the standard.
With a single rite for court and commoners,
there will be no differing customs among families."
This was followed.
He was transferred to become the Left Chief Clerk of the Minister of Works,
then went out to serve as the Administrator of Shǐxīng.
In the second year of Yuánjiā (425 CE),
he served as Fǔjūn Zhǎngshǐ for Yìgōng, Prince of Jiāngxià, and Administrator of Lìyáng,
performing the duties of the provincial administration.
His governance in pacifying and nurturing was effective,
and the military and common people benefited from it.
Soon after, he entered the court as a Shìzhōng.
The following year,
he was transferred to be Dūguān Shàngshū,
and later took charge of Lìbù.
His character was stern and impetuous,
which somewhat disappointed the gentry.
He then went out to serve as Dānyáng Yǐn.
Wáng Zhǔnzhī thoroughly understood the old rituals,
and there was nothing he couldn't answer when questioned.
At that time, the Grand General Yìkāng, Prince of Péngchéng, held the duties of the Shàngshū (Secretariat),
and often sighed, saying:
"Why bother with lofty and abstruse discussions?
If only we had two or three people like Wáng Zhǔnzhī,
the world would be well-governed."
However, he lacked elegance and refinement,
and was not highly regarded by the intellectuals of the time.
He compiled ritual protocols,
which the imperial court still follows to this day.
In the tenth year (433 CE),
he died,
at the age of fifty-six.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàicháng.
His son, Xīngzhī,
[一一]was Zhēnglǔ Zhǔbù.
Wáng Sháozhī, courtesy name Xiūtài,
was a native of Línyí, Lángyé.
His great-grandfather, Yì,
was a Jìn Píqi Jiāngjūn.
His grandfather, Xiànzhī,
was a Zhèn Jūn Yuàn.
His father, Wěizhī,
was the Lángzhōng Lìng of his home commandery.
Sháozhī's family was poor,
and his father served as the Magistrate of Wūchéng, so they lived within the county borders.
He loved historical texts
and was broadly read and knowledgeable.
Initially, he served as Xíng Cānjūn for Wèi Jiāngjūn Xiè Yǎn.
Wěizhī had high aspirations from a young age,
and would personally write down all edicts, memorials, and reports of his time.
From the affairs of Tàiyuán and Lóng'ān eras,
[一二]he compiled and recorded everything, large and small.
Sháozhī, consequently, privately compiled the Jìn Āndì Yángqiū.
Upon its completion,
people at the time said he was suitable for a historical office.
He was immediately appointed Zuòzhù Zuǒláng,
and instructed to continue the records of subsequent events,
up to the ninth year of Yìxī (413 CE).
His narration was skillful,
and his essays and arguments were commendable,
making it a fine history for later generations.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Cíbù Láng.
Since Emperor Xiàowǔ, the Jìn emperors
usually resided in the inner palace.
Military officers, acting as clerks, would present documents there.
One official was put in charge of edicts and proclamations,
his office being in the western annex of the palace,
[一三]hence he was called Xīshěng Láng.
Fù Liàng and Yáng Huī successively held this position.
In the eleventh year of Yìxī (415 CE),
Gāozǔ, recognizing Sháozhī's extensive learning and literary talent,
appointed him Tōngzhí Láng,
and put him in charge of Xīshěng affairs.
[一四]He was then transferred to Zhōngshū Shìláng.
When Emperor Ān died,
Gāozǔ ordered Sháozhī, along with the emperor's close attendants, to secretly administer poison.
When Emperor Gōng ascended the throne,
Sháozhī was promoted to Huángmén Shìláng,
taking charge of Zuòzhù Láng,
with his Xīshěng duties remaining as before.
All imperial edicts and pronouncements
[一五]were his compositions.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
Sháozhī was given the additional title of Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn,
and Censor of his home commandery,
with his Huángmén duties remaining.
His Xīshěng duties were relinquished,
and he again took charge of compiling the Sòngshū.
The relevant authorities reported that Zhū Dàomín, a soldier from Dōngyě, had captured three rebellious soldiers,
and requested that he be released according to regulations.
Sháozhī memorialized, saying:
"The report from the Shàngshū Jīnbù is as stated above.
This is indeed a temporary regulation from a moment of oversight,
[一六]and I fear it is not a foundational, enduring policy for governing the state.
I recall the old system, where there were more than ten articles for punishing criminals by making them soldiers.
Although there were similarities and differences without confusion,
the severity of punishments varied greatly.
As for falsely reporting parents' deaths,
slandering parents with allegations of lewdness,
and acts of breaking loyalty and rebellion,
these four articles
are truly extreme acts of chaos and defiance,
where human morality is utterly destroyed.
Even if the punishment exceeds the usual bounds,
it is still not enough to atone for such immense crimes.
Since they have been allowed to keep their lives,
a great mercy has already been bestowed.
How can they then be allowed to be freed from servitude,
relax their belts in the same year,
and assimilate with the common households,
listed among the ordinary citizens?
I fear that if this regulation is perpetually enforced,
the loss will be truly immense.
Currently, the sacred transformation is renewed,
exalting the fundamental and discarding the trivial.
All general regulations
should be thoroughly reviewed and amended.
My humble opinion is that these four articles should not be included in the grace of atonement for crimes."
Shìzhōng Chǔ Dànzhī agreed with Sháozhī on three of the articles,
but thought the previous practice should remain for one.
The emperor approved.
He also refuted Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng Wáng Shízhī's request for leave, saying:
"Upon reviewing the old regulations,
officials whose families had urgent matters
were allowed to take a combined sixty days of urgent leave.
During the Tàiyuán era, the system was changed,
and one hundred days of leave were granted annually.
Furthermore, if one's residence was more than a thousand *lǐ* away,
they were allowed to request leave for the following year,
making a total of two hundred days.
This was merely a temporary regulation,
not a long-term, universal principle.
Although Kuàijī is indeed over a thousand *lǐ* away,
it is not an insurmountable distance.
One hundred days of leave for return home
is quite sufficient for the matter.
If one's private circumstances are different,
they should submit a personal memorial explaining their situation.
How can one, whose name is on the imperial court roster,
long remain at their private residence?
We, your ministers, have discussed this
and believe it should not be granted.
However, for those whose homes are in Hé, Luò, or Lǐng, Miǎn, Hàn,
where the roads are obstructed and long,
it would still be appropriate to have separate provisions.
We request that this be submitted to the Shàngshū for detailed consideration of a regulation."
It was followed.
He was dismissed from Huángmén
due to an error in sealing the imperial edicts;
this matter is recorded in the biography of Xiè Huì.
When Sháozhī compiled the Jìn history,
he wrote about Wáng Xún's acquisition of wealth
and Wáng Xīn's rebellion.
Xún's son, Hóng,
and Xīn's son, Huá,
were both prominent and influential.
Sháozhī feared being implicated by them,
and thus deeply allied himself with Xú Xiànzhī, Fù Liàng, and others.
When Emperor Shào ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Shìzhōng,
with his Xiāoqí title remaining as before.
In the first year of Jǐngpíng (423 CE),
[一七]he went out to serve as the Administrator of Wúxīng.
After Xiànzhī was executed,
Wáng Hóng entered the court as Chancellor
and concurrently served as the Inspector of Yángzhōu.
Although Hóng did not completely sever ties with Sháozhī,
his younger brothers, who were not acquainted with Sháozhī,
no longer interacted with him.
While in the commandery,
Sháozhī constantly worried about being disciplined by Hóng,
and worked diligently day and night.
His administrative achievements were excellent,
and Hóng also suppressed his personal resentment.
Tàizǔ praised him twice.
He served for many years
and was known as a good administrator,
with his rank elevated to Zhōng'èrqiānshí.
In the tenth year (433 CE),
he was summoned to be Cíbù Shàngshū,
with the additional title of Jǐshìzhōng.
He was dismissed from office
for taking a long escort home when leaving his commandery.
In the twelfth year (435 CE),
he again went out to serve as the Administrator of Wúxīng.
He died that same year,
at the age of fifty-six.
The lyrics for the Seven Ancestral Temples' songs
were composed by Sháozhī.
His collected works circulated in the world.
His son, Yè,
was Shàngshū Jiàbù Wàibīng Láng,
and Administrator of Línhè.
Xún Bózǐ,
was a native of Yǐngyīn, Yǐngchuān.
His grandfather, Xiàn,
was a Píqi Jiāngjūn.
His father, Yī,
was a Mìshū Láng.
Xún Bózi 荀伯zi 伯子 was fond of learning from a young age.
He widely read the classics and commentaries,
but being uninhibited and fond of miscellaneous theatrical performances,
he roamed among the villages and hamlets.
Thus, he lost the path to a pure career because of this.
Upon shedding his civilian clothes, he became a Fùmǎ Dūwèi 駙馬都尉,
received court requests,
and was a Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng 員外散騎侍郎.
The Zhùzuò Láng 著作郎 徐廣 Xú Guǎng esteemed his talent and learning,
and recommended Bózi 伯子 and Wáng Sháozhī 王韶之 to both serve as Zuǒláng 佐郎,
assisting in compiling the Book of Jìn 晉史 and writing biographies of Huán Xuán 桓玄 and others.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Cíbù Láng 尚書祠部郎.
In the ninth year of Yìxī 義熙 (413 CE),
he submitted a memorial, stating:
"Your minister has heard that after Gāoyáo 咎繇 died,
Zāng Wén 臧文 deeply lamented it.
When the Bó 伯 clan's city was taken,
Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 therefore praised Rén 仁.
High achievements can last a hundred generations without being obliterated;
excessive rewards should not be permitted even for a single morning.
The late Tàifù Jùpíng Hóu Hù 太傅鉅平侯祜 was
illustriously virtuous and widely sagacious,
with no peer among the imperial ministers.
His merits were integral to assisting the emperor,
and his achievements were completed in pacifying Wú 吳.
Yet his descendants are lacking,
and there is no one to offer sacrifices.
The Hàn 漢 dynasty, because of Xiāo Hé's 蕭何's foundational achievements,
would always restore the peerage when a generation ended.
Your foolish minister believes that the enfeoffment of Jùpíng 鉅平
should be treated the same as the state of Cuózé 酇國.
The late Tàiwèi Guǎnglíng Gōng Chén Zhǔn 太尉廣陵公陳准
supported Sūn Xiù 孫秀,
brought calamity upon Huáinán 淮南,
and illicitly enjoyed a great state,
profiting from his crimes.
At that time, the Western Court's 西朝 administration and laws were out of proportion,
and the restoration of the dynasty consequently did not revoke it.
Now that the kingly way is renewed,
how can we not distinguish clearly between good and bad?
Your minister believes that the state of Guǎnglíng 廣陵
should be abolished.
The late Tàibǎo Wèi Guàn's 太保衞瓘's original peerage was Xiāoyáng Xiàn Gōng 蕭陽縣公.
〔一八〕After he suffered an undeserved calamity,
and his rank was posthumously advanced,
he was first granted Lánlíng 蘭陵,
and then transferred to Jiāngxià 江夏.
Many of the ducal counselors in the Central Court 中朝
did not meet their end justly.
Guàn's 瓘's merits and virtues were not different,
nor was there any reason for him alone to receive a special reward.
It is appropriate to restore his original enfeoffment
to rectify the national statutes."
An imperial edict ordered it to be submitted to the Ménxià 門下.
The former Sànqí Chángshì Jiāngxià Gōng Wèi Yú 散騎常侍江夏公衞璵 submitted a memorial in his own defense, stating:
"My ancestor, the late Tàibǎo Guàn 太保瓘,
during the Xiánxī 咸熙 period of Wèi 魏,
when Tàizǔ Wén Huángdì 太祖文皇帝 was Yuánfǔ 元輔,
was enfeoffed as Xiāoyáng Hóu 蕭陽侯.
When Dà Jìn 大晉 received the abdication,
he was advanced to duke,
and successively held the position of Tàibǎo 太保,
presiding over the court administration.
At that time, Jiǎ Shùrén 賈庶人 and various princes held power.
They feared Guàn's 瓘's loyalty and integrity,
so the former Chǔ Wáng Wěi 楚王瑋 fabricated an edict to cause his downfall.
The former dynasty, recognizing Guàn's 瓘's loyal and upright character,
and furthermore his meritorious service in conquering Shǔ 蜀,
posthumously enfeoffed him as Lánlíng Jùn Gōng 蘭陵郡公.
During the Yǒngjiā 永嘉 period,
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè 東海王越 was given Lánlíng 蘭陵,
and he was transferred and enfeoffed in Jiāngxià 江夏,
with the same number of households and territory as before.
My great-great-grandfather, Sànqí Shìláng Zǎo 散騎侍郎璪,
Guàn's 瓘's legitimate grandson,
〔一九〕inherited the enfeoffment and peerage.
Zhōngzōng Yuán Huángdì 中宗元皇帝 decreed that my great-grandfather, the late Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Chóng 右衞將軍崇, should inherit it,
and this has continued down to my own person.
I have heard that Cíbù Láng Xún Bózi 祠部郎荀伯子 submitted a memorial
seeking to demote and restore the enfeoffment of Xiāoyáng 蕭陽.
Indeed, the loyalty of the Zhào 趙 clan
was extended through successive generations with favor.
The Hànzǔ 漢祖 opened enfeoffments
and swore by mountains and rivers.
I humbly beg Your Majesty to recall past merits,
and extend boundless grace.
I request that my memorial be brought forth,
and submitted to the external authorities for consideration."
Chén Máoxiān 陳茂先 of Yǐngchuān 潁川 also submitted a memorial, stating:
"Cíbù Láng Xún Bózi 祠部郎荀伯子's memorial states that my seventh-generation ancestor, Tàiwèi Zhǔn 太尉准, brought calamity upon Huáinán 淮南,
and should not have been excessively rewarded.
Upon investigation, my late ancestor, for eliminating Jiǎ Mì 賈謐,
was enfeoffed as Hǎilíng Gōng 海陵公.
This event occurred before the calamity in Huáinán 淮南.
Although Guǎnglíng 廣陵 was later in a state of turmoil,
my ancestor then first received special favor,
and successively held the positions of Yuán 元 and Kǎi 凱.
Later, he was relegated to a distant post,
and served as the governor of Píngzhōu 平州,
yet his state was still not abolished.
This was truly because his former merits were profound and weighty,
and would not be obliterated for a hundred generations.
During the reign of a sagely and enlightened emperor,
wise and distinguished officials rise in succession.
There has never been any doubt or discussion
regarding this as an excessive reward.
As for your humble and insignificant minister,
I am not yet counted among proper human relations.
Moreover, I have just begun to struggle for existence,
and the enfeoffment and peerage are also inherited.
I humbly beg Your Majesty to consider the old merits from afar,
and specially show pity and scrutiny."
Imperial edicts ordered both to be submitted to the Ménxià 門下,
but neither was implemented.
Bózi 伯子 served as Shìzǐ Zhēnglǔ Gōngcáo 世子征虜功曹 and Guózǐ Bóshì 國子博士.
His wife's brother Xiè Huì 謝晦 recommended and promoted him.
He entered as Shàngshū Zuǒchéng 尚書左丞,
and then was appointed Línchuān Nèishǐ 臨川內史.
Chēqí Jiāngjūn Wáng Hóng 車騎將軍王弘 praised him, saying:
"He is profound and unassuming,
possessing the demeanor of Píngyáng Hóu 平陽侯."
Bózi 伯zi 伯子 often prided himself on the beauty of his family's inherited status,
and said to Hóng 弘:
"Among the noble families of the realm,
only you, Your Excellency, and your humble official are truly such.
Those like Xuānmíng 宣明 are not worth counting."
He was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍 and
Dàzhōngzhèng 大中正 of his native district.
He again submitted a memorial, stating:
"I humbly observe that in the order of official ranks,
Chénliú Wáng 陳留王 is above Línglíng Wáng 零陵王.
Your foolish minister privately considers this doubtful.
In ancient times, King Wǔ 武王 conquered Yīn 殷,
and enfeoffed the descendants of Shénnóng 神農 in Jiāo 焦,
the descendants of Huángdì 黃帝 in Zhù 祝,
the descendants of Dì Yáo 帝堯 in Jì 薊,
the descendants of Dì Shùn 帝舜 in Chén 陳,
the descendants of Xià Hòu 夏後 in Shí 嵵,
and the descendants of Yīn Hòu 殷後 in Sòng 宋.
Shí 嵵 and Chén 陳 were both listed as states,
while Jì 薊, Zhù 祝, and Jiāo 焦 are unknown.
This shows that the honoring of those from whom one inherited
was superior to that of distant generations, which is a clear proof.
Therefore, in the Spring and Autumn Annals 春秋, when arranging the feudal lords,
Sòng 宋 was placed above Shí 嵵 and Chén 陳.
Examining recent times,
there is also evidence for this.
In the first year of Tàishǐ 泰始 of Jìn 晉 (265 CE),
an edict granted Liú Kāng 劉康, Duke of Shānyáng 山陽, and one of his sons or younger brothers the title Guānnèi Hóu 關內侯;
and Jī Shǔ 姬署, Duke of Wèi 衞, and Kǒng Shào 孔紹, Marquis of Sòng 宋, one son each as Fùmǎ Dūwèi 駙馬都尉.
Also, in the third year of Tàishǐ 泰始 (267 CE),
Tàicháng Shàng Bóshì Liú Xǐ 太常上博士劉憙 and others deliberated,
stating that Duke Shǔ 署 of Wèi 衞, in Dà Jìn 大晉, was among the ranks of the Three Revered Guests 三恪,
and should be demoted to marquis.
Your minister believes that Línglíng Wáng's 零陵王's position should be above Chénliú 陳留."
This was followed.
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Pú 太子僕 and Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng 御史中丞.
He was diligent and conscientious in his duties,
and was praised for his integrity,
standing firm in court,
making both internal and external officials wary of him.
Whatever he impeached,
he spared no effort in condemning,
sometimes extending it even to their ancestors,
to show his blunt honesty.
He also mixed in some playful sarcasm,
which is why people criticized him for this.
He was appointed Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ 司徒左長史 and Dōngyáng Tàishǒu 東陽太守.
In the fifteenth year of Yuánjiā 元嘉 (438 CE),
he died in office,
at the age of sixty-one.
His collected works were passed down to the world.
His son, Chìsōng 赤松,
served as Shàngshū Zuǒchéng 尚書左丞.
〔二０〕As a partisan of Xú Zhànzhī 徐湛之,
he was killed by the principal villain.
Bózi's 伯子's clan cousin Chǎng 昶, courtesy name Màozǔ 茂祖,
was five generations removed from Bózi 伯子 in terms of mourning attire.
In the early Yuánjiā 元嘉 period,
he reached Zhōngshū Láng 中書郎 due to his literary talent and erudition.
Chǎng's 昶's son, Wànqiū 萬秋, courtesy name Yuánbǎo 元寶,
also distinguished himself through his talent and learning.
In the early years of Shìzǔ 世祖,
he served as Jìnlíng Tàishǒu 晉陵太守.
He was imprisoned and dismissed for
establishing the Huálín Gé 華林閣 in his commandery and appointing Zhǔshū 主書 and Zhǔyī 主衣.
At the end of the reign of the Former Deposed Emperor 前廢帝,
he served as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng 御史中丞,
and died in office.
The imperial historian says: "Excellent reputation and admirable prestige
are what poets sing about;
propriety and laws
are what former paradigms rely on to achieve enduring beauty.
Xún (荀), Fàn (范), and the two Wángs (王)
made themselves prominent through their learning and righteousness,
yet their court reputation was not widespread.
This was probably because their talent was ample, but their wisdom was insufficient.
What a pity!"
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 21: Wǔ (武) Three Wáng (王)s: Lúlíng Xiàoxiàn Wáng (廬陵孝獻王) Yìzhēn (義真), Jiāngxià Wénxiàn Wáng (江夏文獻王) Yìgōng (義恭), Héngyáng Wén Wáng (衡陽文王) Yìjì (義季).
Emperor Wǔ (武) had seven sons: Empress Zhāng (張) gave birth to the Young Emperor;
Consort Sūn Xiūhuá (孫修華) gave birth to Lúlíng Xiàoxiàn Wáng Yìzhēn;
Consort Hú Jiéyú (胡婕妤) gave birth to Emperor Wén (文);
Consort Wáng Xiūróng (王修容) gave birth to Péngchéng Wáng (彭城王) Yìkāng (義康);
Consort Yuán Měirén (袁美人) gave birth to Jiāngxià Wénxiàn Wáng Yìgōng;
Consort Sūn Měirén (孫美人) gave birth to Nánjùn Wáng (南郡王) Yìxuān (義宣);
Consort Lǚ Měirén (呂美人) gave birth to Héngyáng Wén Wáng Yìjì.
Yìkāng and Yìxuān have separate biographies.
Lúlíng Xiàoxiàn Wáng Yìzhēn
had a beautiful appearance,
and his spirit and demeanor were outstandingly clear.
Initially, he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Guìyáng County (桂陽縣公),
with an allocated income of one thousand households.
At the age of twelve,
he followed the northern expeditionary army to advance on Cháng'ān (長安).
He was left to guard Bǎigǔ Wù (栢谷塢)
and was appointed Supernumerary Cavalry Regular Attendant (員外散騎常侍),
but he did not take up the post.
When Guānzhōng (關中) was pacified,
Gāozǔ (高祖) debated returning east.
However, the generals had been on campaign for a long time
and all wished to return.
Leaving only a few generals
would be insufficient to stabilize the people's hearts.

Therefore, Yìzhēn was appointed Acting Grand Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yōng (雍), Liáng (涼), and Qín (秦) three prefectures, and the Hedong (河東), Píngyáng (平陽), and Héběi (河北) three commanderies of Sī Prefecture (司州), General Who Pacifies the West (安西將軍), concurrently holding the title of Protector of the Western Barbarians Commandant (領護西戎校尉) and Inspector of Yōng Prefecture (雍州刺史).
Wáng Xiū (王脩) from Jīngzhào (京兆), an Advisory Counsellor to the Grand Commandant (太尉諮議參軍), was made his Chief Clerk (長史),
and entrusted with the responsibility for Guānzhōng.
When Gāozǔ was about to return,
the elders of the Three Qíns (三秦) came to his gate, weeping and pleading:
"The surviving common people have not received the benefit of royal transformation
for a hundred years now.
We have only just seen the court officials
and now look up to your sacred benevolence.
The ten imperial tombs in Cháng'ān
are your family's burial grounds,
and the thousands of rooms in the Xiányáng (咸陽) palaces
are your family's residences.
Where do you intend to go, abandoning these?"
Gāozǔ felt pity for them
and comforted them, saying:
"I am acting on the orders of the imperial court and cannot stay arbitrarily.
I am touched by your desire to cling to your origins,
so I am now leaving my second son here,
to let virtuous civil and military talents jointly guard this region."
Before returning,
he personally held Yìzhēn's hand and gave him to Wáng Xiū,
and ordered Xiū to hold his son Xiàosūn's (孝孫) hand and give him to Gāozǔ.
Yìzhēn was soon appointed to the regular post,
granted a Staff of Authority (節),
and further promoted to Supervisor of Military Affairs of Bìng (并) and Eastern Qín (東秦) two prefectures, and the Dōng'āndìng (東安定) and Xīnpíng (新平) two commanderies of Sī Prefecture,
concurrently holding the title of Inspector of Eastern Qín Prefecture.
At that time, many displaced people from Lǒngshàng (隴上)
were in Guānzhōng,
hoping to return to their homeland
due to the great might of the empire.
However, when Eastern Qín Prefecture was established,
the elders knew that there was no longer any intention to strategize for Lǒngyòu (隴右) and secure Guānzhōng,
and they all sighed in lament.
Meanwhile, the Fófó Lǔ (佛佛虜) bandits pressed in and arrived.
Shěn Tiánzi (沈田子) had already killed Wáng Zhèn'è (王鎮惡),
and Wáng Xiū then killed Tiánzi.
Yìzhēn was young,
and his gifts to his attendants were not regulated.
Xiū often curtailed them,
which caused resentment among the attendants.
Because of this, they reported to Yìzhēn:
"Zhèn'è wanted to rebel,
which is why Tiánzi killed him.
Now Xiū has killed Tiánzi,
so he, too, intends to rebel."
Yìzhēn then ordered his attendants Liú Qǐ (劉乞) and others to kill Xiū.
Xiū, courtesy name Shúzhì (叔治),
was from Bàchéng (灞城) in Jīngzhào.
When he first crossed south, he met Huán Xuán (桓玄).
Xuán recognized his talent
and said to him:
"You possess the talent of a Director of the Bureau of Personnel (吏部郎) in peaceful times."
After Xiū's death,
people's morale became dispersed and alarmed,
and there was no unity.
Gāozǔ sent General Zhū Língshí (朱齡石) to replace Yìzhēn in guarding Guānzhōng,
and ordered Yìzhēn to return swiftly with light troops.
The generals competed to gather wealth and goods,
loaded many women and children,
and proceeded slowly side by side.
The pursuing enemy cavalry was about to arrive.
General Jiànwēi (建威將軍) Fù Hóngzhī (傅弘之) said:
"The Duke ordered us to advance quickly,
fearing that the enemy would pursue and attack us.
Now we are carrying too much baggage;
we cannot travel more than ten *lǐ* in a day.
When the enemy cavalry arrives,
how shall we confront them?
We should abandon the carts and travel lightly;
only then can we escape."
They did not comply.
The enemy's pursuing troops indeed arrived,
with tens of thousands of cavalry.
General Fǔguó (輔國將軍) Kuǎí'ēn (蒯恩), who was covering the rear, could not stop them.
Upon reaching Qīngní (青泥),
the rearguard was utterly defeated.
The generals and the Administrator's Registrar (府功曹) Wáng Cì (王賜) were all captured.
Yìzhēn was in the front,
so he managed to flee with several hundred people.
At dusk,
the enemy did not continue their pursuit.
Yìzhēn became separated from his attendants
and hid alone in the grass.
The Staff Officer of the Central Army (中兵參軍) Duàn Hóng (段宏) pursued him on a single horse,
calling out along the road.
Yìzhēn recognized his voice
and emerged to meet him,
saying:
"Are you not Staff Officer Duàn?
I am here."
Hóng was greatly pleased
and carried him back.
Yìzhēn said to Hóng:
"Today's events
were truly unplanned.
However, if a man does not experience such things,
how can he know hardship?"
Initially,
when Gāozǔ heard of the defeat at Qīngní
and had not received a definitive report about Yìzhēn,
he questioned those who arrived first.
They all said,
"We fled in the dark night;
we cannot know if he is alive or dead."
Gāozǔ was furious
and set a date for a northern expedition.
Xiè Huì (謝晦) advised against it, but he did not listen.
However, after receiving Hóng's report
and knowing that Yìzhēn had escaped,
he stopped his plans.
Yìzhēn was soon appointed Supervisor of Military Affairs of Sī, Yōng, Qín, Bìng, and Liáng five prefectures, General Jiànwēi, and Inspector of Sī Prefecture,
retaining his Staff of Authority as before.
Duàn Hóng was made Yìzhēn's Advisory Counsellor,
and soon transferred to Imperial Household Aide (黃門郎) of the Sòng (宋) government,
concurrently holding the title of Right Commandant of the Palace Guard (右衞率) for the Crown Prince.
Hóng was a Xiānbēi (鮮卑) man.
He had been Left Director of the Department of State Affairs (尚書左僕射) and Inspector of Xú Prefecture (徐州刺史) for Mùróng Chāo (慕容超).
When Gāozǔ attacked Guǎnggù (廣固),
Hóng surrendered.
During Emperor Tàizǔ's (太祖) Yuánjiā (元嘉) reign,
he became General Who Conquers Barbarians (征虜將軍) and Inspector of Qīng (青) and Jì (冀) two prefectures.
He was posthumously granted the title of Left General (左將軍).
At that time, Yìzhēn was to be stationed in Luòyáng (洛陽),
but Hénán (河南) was desolate and had not yet been restored.
So he was reassigned as Inspector of Yáng Prefecture (揚州刺史),
stationed at Shítóu (石頭).
In the first year of Yǒngchū (永初) (420 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Lúlíng Wáng,
with an allocated income of three thousand households,
and moved his garrison to Dōngchéng (東城).
When Gāozǔ first ascended the throne,
Yìzhēn looked displeased.
Cài Màozhī (蔡茂之), his tutor and academician, asked him the reason.
Yìzhēn replied:
"In security, one must not forget danger.
How can peace and prosperity be relied upon?"
The following year,
he was promoted to Grand Minister of Works (司徒).
When Gāozǔ was unwell,

he made Yìzhēn Bearer of the Staff with Imperial Authority (使持節), Palace Attendant (侍中), Grand Supervisor of Military Affairs of Nányù (南豫), Yù (豫), Yōng, Sī, Qín, and Bìng six prefectures, General of Chariots and Cavalry (車騎將軍), Administrator with the Same Privileges as the Three Excellencies (開府儀同三司), and Inspector of Nányù Prefecture,
to be stationed outside the capital at Lìyáng (歷陽).
Before he could take up his post, Gāozǔ passed away.
Yìzhēn 聰明愛文義 (was intelligent and loved literature and righteousness),
but was frivolous and lacked virtue and achievement.
He associated unusually closely with Xiè Língyùn of Chénjùn, Yán Yánzhī of Lángxié, and the Daoist monk Huìlín.
He said that when he achieved his ambition,
he would make Língyùn and Yánzhī prime ministers,
and Huìlín the Grand Administrator of Xīyùzhōu.
Xú Xiànzhī and others disliked Yìzhēn's excessive familiarity with Língyùn and Yánzhī,
so they sent Fàn Yàn to subtly caution him.
Yìzhēn said:
"Língyùn is empty and shallow,
and Yánzhī is narrow-minded.
Emperor Wén of Wèi said that few can establish themselves with integrity.
But it is due to my nature
that I cannot forget words when I appreciate them,
which is why I associate with them."
When he was about to depart for his post,
the troops were arrayed before the Eastern Residence.
As there was national mourning,
Yìzhēn's boat was plain and simple,
not as grand as the one used by his mother, Sūn Xiūyí.
Yìzhēn, Língyùn, Yánzhī, Huìlín, and others viewed the troops together,
then feasted inside the boat.
He ordered his attendants to remove the gangways from his mother's boat and attach them to his own,
taking the better ones.
When he arrived in Lìyáng,
he made many demands.
Xiànzhī and others often limited what they granted,
which caused him to deeply resent the governing officials.
He memorialized requesting to return to the capital.
When the Young Emperor lost his virtue,
Xiànzhī and others secretly plotted to depose and enthrone.
The succession should have naturally fallen to Yìzhēn.
However, because Yìzhēn was frivolous and unreliable,
and not fit to rule the state,
and also because he was not in accord with the Young Emperor,
they memorialized to depose him,
saying: "Your humble servants have heard that if the two uncles are not harmonious,
it is difficult to consolidate a flourishing Zhōu.
If Huáinán is perverse and unrestrained,
calamity will arise in a prosperous Hàn.
There is no case where righteousness does not sever affection,
and sentiment does not yield to law.
The affairs of the two dynasties
serve as a clear mirror not far off.
A benevolent and generous ruler
acts upon them without doubt.
Thus, if Gòngshú had not been stopped,
he would nearly have overturned the state of Zhèng.
If Liú Yīng had been indulged,
the trouble would have spread and deepened.
That which is not forgotten from past events
serves as a complete mirror for future kings.
Upon examination, General of Chariots and Cavalry Yìzhēn,
his cruel and unfeeling nature
has been present since his tender youth.
The atrocities at Xiányáng
spread his ill reputation far and wide.
The late court still considered his young age,
hoping he might reform,
and with the affection of a close relative,
wished to hear of a change of heart.
However, from the time the Sacred Body was unwell
until the great decline,
while ministers and commoners were anxious and fearful,
and all within and without held their breath,
he indulged in games and heavy drinking,
day and night without cease.
He spoke wildly and unrestrainedly,
and often behaved without propriety.
The late emperor's plan for his heir,
considered and firmly established,
personally instructed Your Majesty
and explicitly ordered us ministers:
'If he does not reform,
he must be banished.'
These earnest and stern words
are still on paper.
Yet, from then until now,
his behavior has worsened with each passing day.
He even abandoned his border post,
determined to return to the capital,
secretly harboring different intentions,
hoping for the unexpected.
He gathered soldiers
and summoned chariots and horses.
The earth on the imperial tomb is not yet dry,
and the situation is as if it were yesterday.
Yet he disregarded
the emperor's dying wishes,
openly violating established rules,
arranged his oars and launched his boat,
to show his intention to return.
He acted purely on his own will,
no longer consulting or obeying.
Your Majesty's benevolence has been hesitant and deep,
enduring in secret,
repeatedly sending imperial envoys
to earnestly admonish him.
Yet, in person, before Court Gentleman for Scattered Cavalry Xíng Āntài and General of Guǎngwǔ Máo Zhòngsī,
he indulged in abusive language,
slandering the ruler
and defaming the court.
This has long been known far and wide,
and openly heard by people.
Your humble servants have heard that if a prairie fire is not extinguished,
wild grass is difficult to remove.
If the lush green is not cut down,
it will eventually lead to the axe.
How much more so when the anxieties are deep, the troubles manifest,
and the concerns for the state are urgent.
We request to follow the old precedent of Wǔlíng
in the Jìn dynasty,
so that the meaning of 'considering and remembering'
does not fall into disuse at the Wǔ Temple,
and the virtue of complete forgiveness
can be extended to close relatives.
Recalling this,
we are deeply moved and choked with sobs
as we present this memorial."
Thereupon, Yìzhēn was deposed as a commoner
and exiled to Xīn'ānjùn.
The former Prefect of Jíyáng, Zhāng Yuē of Tángyì,
submitted a memorial advising against it, saying: "Your humble servant has heard that righteousness and benevolence in the world
are like beans in the central plains,
and their power to move all things
does not depend on noble or base status.
Therefore, Kǎoshú reversed
his oath at Jíquán,
and Húguān restored justice to the wronged souls in Húyì.
At such times,
were there no respected nobles and worthy assistants?
Perhaps due to pressing circumstances, their hearts were reluctant,
or their wisdom was blocked and their plans thwarted.
Yet, they always wished to hear good advice from commoners
and medicine from concubines.
Though your humble servant is but grass,
one of the black-headed commoners,
in my youth, I did not measure my strength,
and somewhat embraced
the spirit of sacrificing for righteousness.
I believed that pursuing good deeds when heard at court
was better than living idly until old age.
Therefore, I dare to violate prohibitions and disregard execution,
to lay bare my sincere foolishness.
I humbly reflect that Gāozǔ Wǔhuángdì
was born with divine martial prowess,
rode the dragon of fortune to rise,
and looking up, he cleared the path of heaven,
matching the virtue of Yú.
Looking down, he expanded the Nine Provinces,
matching the achievements
of Dàyǔ.
Thus, he reverently complied with heaven and man,
and possessed myriad states.
Although his auspicious reign was long,
his sacred body did not endure.
Your Majesty succeeded in illuminating the lineage and governing the succession,
and near and far are of one heart.
The vassal kings
are wise and flourishing,
the four corners are peaceful.
We listen intently to the praises of peace,
and eagerly await the spirit of rising prosperity.
I secretly reflect that King Lúlíng
in his youth received the gracious and benevolent treatment of the late emperor,
and in his adulthood received Your Majesty's kind and loving grace.
Therefore, what was in his heart he surely spoke,
and what he harbored he surely revealed.
He may
have violated the way of a minister and son,
and thus incurred the fault of arrogance and willfulness.
As for his inherent talent,
he truly possesses outstanding virtues.
He ought to be nurtured,
his good deeds recorded and his flaws overlooked,
trained
exhaustively in righteous principles,
advancing and retreating gradually.
Now, to abruptly subject him to humiliation
and exile him to a distant prefecture
is to, upwardly, wound Your Majesty's deep fraternal bond,
and downwardly, cause those near and far to be apprehensive and at a loss,
officials and commoners to seal their lips,
and everyone to plan for their own safety.
Your humble servant humbly believes that the rise of the Great Sòng,
though it corresponded with auspicious signs and omens,
its foundation was laid abruptly,
its roots and branches not yet numerous.
It is fitting to widely establish
fiefs for relatives,
and cultivate harmony with righteousness,
so that the virtues of brotherhood
shine like those of Lǔ and Wèi.
If the tortoise and milfoil agree,
the reign will last seven hundred years.
Would this not be excellent?
Your Majesty is rich in
In spring and autumn,
fearing he would not be reinstated,
he disregarded the long-term consequences of safety and danger,
and recklessly acted on his immediate inability to endure.
I especially wish Your Majesty would give careful thought
and make further inquiries.
Look back at the reasons for the
rise and fall of previous dynasties,
consider the founding achievements of Emperor Wǔ,
and look down upon the eager hopes of the common people.
At times, grant special leniency,
and restore him to the royal capital.
Select tutors
from among the aged and experienced,
and seek worthy friends from among the distinguished and talented.
Guide his emotions and character,
and develop his intelligence.
Anyone in distress
can spur themselves on.
How much more so for Wáng Zhì, who has a bright and intelligent heart,
and is
easy to instruct and guide.
Moreover, even a moderately virtuous person
cannot be without faults.
What is valuable is to correct one's faults,
and one's wish is to reform oneself.
He is Emperor Wǔ's beloved son,
and Your Majesty's excellent younger brother.
How can he be left to
perish forever just for one lapse?
I humbly risk death to approach the palace gate,
prostrating myself on the ground to make this known.
I only wish my sincere loyalty
would once reach the Imperial ear.
Then, even if I am sent to the axe and pickaxe,
I would have no shame underground.
When the memorial was submitted,
Yuēzhī was made Assistant to the Administrator of Liángzhōu Commandery,
but was soon killed.
On the *guǐwèi* day of the sixth month of the second year of Jǐngpíng,
Xiànzhī and others sent an envoy to kill Yìzhēn at his place of exile.
He was eighteen years old at the time.
In the eighth month of the first year of Yuánjiā,
an edict stated:
"The coffin of the former Prince of Lúlíng is far away,
and his royal enfeoffment has been neglected.
I am deeply grieved and pained,
feeling as if my heart is being pierced.
The Prince's body is of the highest lineage,
and his relatives hold respected positions.
How can this sentiment and propriety be forever neglected,
leaving him with no final resting place?
His former enfeoffment shall be posthumously restored,
and a special envoy shall be dispatched to welcome him back,
along with his granddaughter Xiūhuá and Consort Xiè, all at once.
These words only increase my sorrow and choked feelings."
In the first month of the third year, Xú Xiànzhī, Fù Liàng, and others were executed.
On that day, an edict stated:
"The late Prince of Lúlíng, with his excellent conduct and uprightness,
was naturally brilliant and wise.
His enlightened mind shone from within,
and his admirable character spread far and wide.
He encountered a difficult time,
and was determined to rectify the forced usurpation.
Heaven had not yet repented of its calamity,
and his fate encountered adversity and danger.
The wicked villains wantonly displayed their depravity,
monopolizing the reins of the state.
Their malicious intentions were secretly conceived,
and the calamity arose unexpectedly.
I have constantly remembered the shame of this enmity,
and grief has knotted within me,
while harboring the treacherous and wicked,
I could not express my feelings and proper rites.
Now that the royal way is prosperous,
and governance and punishment are beginning to be distinguished,
it is time to clarify the national integrity.
Therefore, he shall be posthumously honored as Grand Mentor (Shìzhōng) and Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn),
with his princely title as before.
This is to comfort his wronged soul,
and somewhat assuage my grief and indignation."
Another edict stated:
"When the powerful ministers acted arrogantly and indulged themselves,
they laid the foundation for chaos and calamity.
The former Magistrate of Jíyáng, Zhāng Yuēzhī, submitted a memorial, bravely spoke his mind,
and was utterly sincere and impassioned.
His efforts ultimately succumbed to the wicked multitude,
and he perished in a distant land,
his ambition and integrity unexpressed.
I am deeply moved by this.
In the past, Guān Lǎo submitted a memorial
and was recorded in the Hàn annals.
Yán Zuǎn offered his counsel
and enjoyed honor in the Jìn dynasty.
Considering his loyal spirit,
his conduct follows in the footsteps of his predecessors.
It is fitting to commend and honor him,
and thus publicize his righteous deeds.
He shall be posthumously granted a commandery,
awarded one hundred thousand cash,
and one hundred bolts of cloth."
Yìzhēn had no son.
Tàizǔ appointed his fifth son Shào, courtesy name Xiūyìn, as his heir.
In the ninth year of Yuánjiā,
he inherited the title of Prince of Lúlíng.
Young and magnanimous,
Tàizǔ loved him dearly.
In the twentieth year,
he was appointed Southern Brigadier-General (Nán Zhōnglángjiāng) and Governor of Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ),
at the age of twelve.
In the twenty-second year,
he entered the court,
was granted ceremonial halberds,
and advanced to Area Commander (Dūdū) of Jiāngzhōu, and the three commanderies of Xīyáng, Jìn Xī, and Xīncài in Yùzhōu.
After serving for seven years,
he was reassigned as Left General (Zuǒjiāngjūn) and Governor of Southern Xúzhōu (Nán Xúzhōu Cìshǐ),
and given a set of drums and pipes.
Before taking up his post,
he was again transferred to Governor of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu Cìshǐ),
with his general rank remaining as before.
When the Suǒ barbarians reached Guābù,
Shào followed the Crown Prince to garrison at Shítou.
In the twenty-ninth year,
he resigned due to illness.
He died that year,
at the age of twenty-one.
His dying wish was to be dressed in everyday clothes
and buried in a plain coffin.
Tàizǔ complied.

He was posthumously granted Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì), General Who Guards the Army (Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn), and Minister who Establishes a Household with the Same Privileges as the Three Dukes (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī),
with his gubernatorial title as before.
He had no son.
The third son of Prince of Nánpíng, Shuò, named Jìngxiān, was made his heir.
His original name was Jìngxiù.
Since he was adopted and was the grandson of Shào's consort Chǔ Xiù,
his name was changed.
In the second year of Jǐnghé,
he was murdered by the deposed emperor.
He was posthumously granted Palace Attendant (Zhōngshū Shìláng),
and given the posthumous title King Gōng.
He had no son.
In the first year of Tàishǐ of Tàizōng,
the twenty-first son of Shìzǔ, Zǐyú, courtesy name Xiàowén, Prince of Jìnxī, was made Shào's heir,
and enfeoffed as Prince of Lúlíng.
He was appointed General Who Guards the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Nán Gāopíng and Línhuái Commanderies.
Before he could take up his posts,
he was killed by Tàizōng.
In the third year,
the second son of Prince of Guìyáng, Xiūfàn, named Désì, was again made Shào's heir.
He was appointed General Who Establishes Might (Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Huáilíng and Nán Péngchéng Commanderies.
Later, in the second year of Yuánhuī of the Deposed Emperor,
he was executed along with Xiūfàn.
The princedom was again discontinued.
In the third year,
the third son of Línglǐ Zhōnghóu Xí, named Gǎo, courtesy name Yuānhuá, was again made Shào's heir.
He served as Gentleman-in-Waiting (Gěishìzhōng).
In the first year of Shēngmíng of Emperor Shùn,
he died,
and was given the posthumous title King Yuán.
He also had no son.
The princedom was abolished.
Yìgōng, Prince Wénxiàn of Jiāngxià,
was intelligent and perceptive from a young age,
with a beautiful appearance.
Gāozǔ especially doted on him;
none of his other sons could compare.
When eating, drinking, or sleeping,
he was always by his side.
Gāozǔ was by nature frugal.
His sons' meals did not exceed five dishes,
but Yìgōng was exceptionally favored.
His requests for fruits and snacks
were countless throughout the day.
He never ate what he received,
but gave it all to those around him.
The other princes of Lúlíng never dared to ask,
and if they did, they would not receive.
In the second year of Jǐngpíng,

he was appointed Inspector-General of military affairs in the six provinces of Nán Yù, Yù, Sī, Yōng, Qín, and Bìng (Nán Yù Yù Sī Yōng Qín Bìng Liùzhōu Zhūjūnjūnshì), General of the Champion Army (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Nán Yùzhōu (Nán Yùzhōu Cìshǐ),
at the age of twelve.
In the first year of Yuánjiā,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Jiāngxià,
with an income of five thousand households.
He was granted the authority of *Shǐchíjié*,
and promoted to General Who Protects the Army (Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn),
and given a set of drums and pipes.
In the third year,

he was appointed Inspector-General of military affairs in the two provinces of Nán Xú and Yǎn, and Jìnlíng in Yángzhōu (Nán Xú Yǎn Èrzhōu Yángzhōu zhī Jìnlíng Zhūjūnjūnshì), and Governor of Xúzhōu (Xúzhōu Cìshǐ).
His *chíjié* authority and general rank remained as before.
He was promoted from Inspector-General to Area Commander (Dūdū),
but did not take up the post.
When Tàizǔ campaigned against Xiè Huì,
Yìgōng returned to garrison at Jīngkǒu.
Six years later,
he was reassigned as Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, Yì, Liáng, Níng, Nán Qín, Běi Qín Bāzhōu Zhūjūnshì, and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
His status as a holder of the jié and a general remained as before.
Yìgōng was well-read in literature,
but he was arrogant and extravagant, without restraint.
When he left to govern the frontier,
Tàizǔ wrote a letter to admonish him, saying: "You, in your youth,
have already taken on important responsibilities.
The world is in turmoil,
and the affairs of the family and state are weighty.
Although it is said that you are merely maintaining what has been established,
it is in fact not easy.
The rise and fall, peace and danger,
are
in our hands.
How can one not reflect on the imperial enterprise
and greatly fear the burden?
Now that we are separated,
the day we can gather is uncertain.
〔一一〕There is no longer an opportunity for me to constantly guide and admonish you,
so you
should deeply temper yourself
and think before you act.
Open your sincere heart,
maintain a fair and balanced mind,
treat national scholars with respect,
befriend good people,
distinguish between the wise and the foolish,
and discern between the wicked
and the upright.
Only then can you fully embody the heart of a gentleman
and utilize the strength of lesser men.
Your spirit is bright and discerning,
possessing the beauty of daily renewal,
yet in advancing virtue and perfecting your character,
you have nothing commendable yet.
This is what I regret and cannot cease regretting.
You are by nature narrow-minded and impetuous;
Yuán Tàifēi also says this is so.
Where your nature is fixated,
your desires must be fulfilled;
where your mind is not present,
〔一二〕you change with circumstances.
This is the greatest
flaw.
You should resolutely set your will
and practice self-restraint.
How can a man who desires to assist the world and achieve fame be indecisive?
Today I have roughly outlined more than ten matters;
you may examine them when we part.
Greater matters cannot be fully expressed,
and minor details cannot be exhausted by the pen.
Honoring the worthy and lowering oneself to scholars
is a teaching passed down by the sages;
arrogance, extravagance, and self-importance
are rejected by ancient philosophers.
Broad-mindedness and magnanimity
are the virtues of Hànzǔ;
suspicion, jealousy, and impetuosity
are the failings
of Wèiwǔ.
The Hàn Shū praises Wèi Qīng, saying:
'The Grand General treated scholars and officials with courtesy,
and showed kindness to lesser men.'
Xīmén and Ānyú corrected their natures and both became excellent;
Guān
Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi,
relying on their partiality, shared the same flaws.
In your conduct and actions,
you should deeply reflect on this.
If circumstances were different from today,
and the heir was young and ignorant,
Sītú would assume the duties of Zhōugōng,
and you must not fail to show utmost reverence and obedience.
If you have any concerns,
secretly
write and express them.
Regarding external conduct,
you should be extremely cautious and protective.
As for the safety and danger at that time,
the fate of the realm
will be decided by you two alone;
do not forget my words.
Now that Yuán Tàifēi's provisions have been increased,
they should be sufficient for all your needs.
Beyond this, you must not seek anything further;
I recently explained this intent in detail.
However, if there is a
large offering,
and at that time you happen to lack something,
you may yourself provide a small amount more.
Your monthly personal expenses should not exceed 300,000.
If you can reduce
this,
it would be even better.
In Xī Chǔ and Yīn Kuàng,
you should always rise early,
receive and interact with guests,
and not allow them to be delayed.
After handling urgent matters,
you may then enter to inquire about health.
After seeing their countenance
and ascertaining their well-being,
you should immediately leave,
not lingering too long,
so as not to impede other affairs.
In the afternoon and at night,
you will have ample free time.
The layout of the government office,
gardens, ponds, halls, and pavilions,
I am generally familiar with.
I reckon there is no need for alterations.
Sītú also said so.
If, however, for matters of convenience,
minor adjustments are needed,
they should be limited to a single reorganization upon your initial arrival,
without bother and confusion,
constantly seeking new and unusual things.
When interrogating prisoners, many decisions
are difficult to foresee at the time.
This is truly difficult,
and since you are not accustomed to it,
you probably have no order yet.
One or two days before an interrogation,
take the interrogation records and secretly consult with people like Liú Zhàn;
it makes a big difference.
On the day of interrogation,
be open-minded and thoroughly investigate,
being careful not to let joy or anger influence your judgment of others.
If you can choose what is good
and follow it,
credit will naturally accrue to you.
You should not rely solely on your own judgment
to boast of your unique sagacity.
If, by any chance, you do so,
there will certainly be great regrets.
Not only in interrogating
prisoners,
but a gentleman's way of thinking
should not be like that.
Criminal cases should not be delayed;
you can interrogate twice a month.
All matters should be handled with caution and secrecy.
You should also instruct your attendants in advance
that if someone is truly sincere
and presents something, it must not be leaked,
so as not to betray their loyalty and trust.
The ancients
said,
'If the ruler is not discreet, he loses his ministers;
if the minister is not discreet, he loses himself.'
If someone slanders or fabricates accusations,
do not lightly believe them.
Whenever such a situation arises,
you must carefully investigate it.
Official titles and positions should be deeply cherished and protected,
and not arbitrarily given to others.
Awards and proximity to the powerful
should be especially measured.
Although I am somewhat lacking in kindness towards my attendants,
as I hear
external discussions,
they do not consider it a fault.
If you oppress things with nobility, things will not submit;
if you impose authority on people, people will not be content.
These are easy matters to understand.
Music, entertainment, and amusements
should not be excessive.
Gambling, drinking, fishing, and hunting,
〔一三〕you must completely refrain from.
Provisions for personal use
should all have limits.
Extravagant clothing and exotic objects
should not be encouraged.
You already have several consorts and attendants by your side.
Since you are just arriving in the west,
you should not hastily
take on more.
He further admonished him, saying: "You should frequently grant audiences to your subordinate officials
〔一四〕— not only because the ruler and minister should naturally meet,
but if not frequent, then relations between us will not be close.
If not close, there will be no way to fully utilize people,
and if people
are not fully utilized,
〔一五〕how can you know their many affairs?
Broadly seeking opinions and observations
will both expand your knowledge
and also give those who speak
a place to do so."
In the ninth year,
he was recalled to serve as Dūdū Nányǎn, Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, Jì, Yōu Liùzhōu Yùzhōu zhī Liángjùn Zhūjūnshì, Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ,
stationed at Guǎnglíng.
At that time, an imperial edict commanded all civil and military officials, both inside and outside the court, to recommend talented individuals.
Yìgōng submitted a memorial, saying: "Your servant hears that when the cloud-and-crane music is complete,
then the complex melodies harmonize;
when swift steeds are harnessed,
then long journeys are accomplished.
Your Majesty follows and simplifies the transformative power,
and civilization resides in your person.
The Yùhéng is now aligned,
and the Tàijiē is united.
Yet, thoughts are still cast upon outstanding talents,
and favor extended to the humble and obscure.
Those in deep, hidden valleys
are brought forth and celebrated.
Thus, a lurking qíu dragon raises its scales,
awaiting its time to appear;
a soaring fèng bird lowers its wings,
responding to the call to come.
I humbly observe Zōng Bǐng from Nányáng;
his conduct is serene and detached,
his thoughts and deeds pure and steadfast.
He tempers his integrity in hills and gardens,
living as a recluse in a prosperous age.
Though poor and constrained,
his inner resolve remains unchanged.
Though repeatedly summoned to official positions,
he is firm and unyielding.
If he is sought with the sincerity of silk and cloth,
and moved by the beauty of great moral principles,
he might abandon his fishing rod and humble garments,
and come forth with a change of heart.
He would surely be able to assist
in coordinating the nine ministries,
and proclaiming and aiding in all government affairs.
The Director of the Ministry of Gold, Xú Sēnzhī,
and the Palace'Attendant-General of the Palace Guard, Wáng Tiānbǎo,
both act with capable strength and righteous aid,
loyal, understanding, and sincere.
In previous years, when the rebellious minister defected,
and Huáyáng fell,
Sēnzhī protected the entire territory and pacified the people,
his achievements shining in times of crisis.
Earlier, when campaigning in Yī and Chán,
and the commander-in-chief
suffered a defeat,
Tiānbǎo diligently served north of the Hé River,
and held Yíngqiū to the east.
His meritorious courage was clear,
and his loyalty and efforts were fully expended.
Although they received commendation,
their talents were not fully utilized.
Both can be appointed
to border provinces,
to display their ambition and strength.
Jiāozhǐ is distant and remote,
having repeatedly lost border generals.
Its administration and laws are often deficient,
and governing it is truly difficult.
Nánzhōng is exceedingly far,
and its customs and songs are isolated.
The Mán and Láoliáo tribes are cunning and thievish,
and the border people suffer greatly.
Truly, seasoned and capable men are needed
to pacify its difficulties.
I suggest Sēnzhī be appointed Inspector of Jiāozhōu,
and Tiānbǎo be appointed Inspector of Níngzhōu,
so that
they may awe and appease the wild regions,
and bring order to the distant territories.
In ancient times, the worthy Wèi Wù
earned merit by recommending scholars;
the clear-sighted Zhào Wǔ
made his mark by managing the armory.
My knowledge shames that of previous worthies,
and my reasoning falls short of earlier sages.
I simply present those I know,
hoping to repay your quest for talent.
I fear my words are blind,
and unworthy of praise.
In the sixteenth year,
he was promoted to Sīkōng.
The next year,
when the Grand General, Prince Yìkāng of Péngchéng, was punished and sent to his fief,
Yìgōng was summoned to be Attendant-in-Chief, Area Commander of the Military Affairs of Yángzhōu, Nánxúzhōu, and Yǎnzhōu, Sītú, and Director of the Department of State Affairs,
also concurrently holding the title of Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince.
He retained his credentials as imperial envoy as before,
was granted twenty guards with ceremonial swords,
and had his guard detachment augmented.
The next year,
he was relieved of the command of Nányǎnzhōu.
In the twenty-first year,
he was promoted to Tàiwèi,
concurrently holding the title of Sītú,
with the rest of his appointments remaining as before.
Since Yìgōng was cautious and respectful,
and also learned from Yìkāng's mistakes,
although he was in overall charge,
he merely executed documents.
Therefore, Tàizǔ felt secure with him.
The chancellery was annually granted twenty million cash,
and other goods double that amount.
However, Yìgōng was extravagant by nature,
and often found these insufficient.
Tàizǔ therefore granted an additional ten million cash annually.
In the twenty-sixth year,
[一六] he was concurrently appointed Libationer of the Imperial Academy.
At that time, someone presented a horse that could travel five hundred lǐ in a day,
which was bestowed upon Yìgōng.
In the spring of the twenty-seventh year,
the Suǒ captives invaded Yùzhōu,
and Tàizǔ consequently wished to open and pacify the Hé and Luò regions.
That autumn,
Yìgōng was appointed to command all the generals,
and was sent to garrison Péngchéng.
He was relieved of the position of Libationer of the Imperial Academy.
The captives advanced deeply,
directly reaching Guābù.
Yìgōng and Shìzǔ barricaded themselves in Péngchéng.
In the spring of the twenty-eighth year,
the captives retreated,
passing north of Péngchéng.
Yìgōng was terrified and dared not pursue them.
That day,
a commoner reported:
"The captives are driving over ten thousand civilians from Guǎnglíng.
Tonight, they will camp at Ānwángpí,
several tens of lǐ from the city.
If we pursue them now,
we can recover all of them."
All the generals requested permission,
but Yìgōng again forbade it.
The next morning,
Tàizǔ sent an express messenger,
ordering them to exert full effort in urgent pursuit.
Yìgōng then dispatched Tán Hézhī, the Sīmǎ of the Garrison General, towards Xiāochéng.
The captives had already learned of this in advance,
and so they killed all the civilians from Guǎnglíng they were driving,
and departed with light cavalry.
Initially, when the captives advanced deeply,
the Emperor worried that Yìgōng might not be able to hold Péngchéng,
and issued repeated warnings and instructions.
Yìgōng replied:
"Though I cannot reach Hànghǎi
or cross Jūyán,
I hope to avoid the shame of Liú Zhòng's flight."
When the captives arrived,
Yìgōng indeed wished to flee.
[一七] Fortunately, he was persuaded to stay by the general consensus.
This incident is recorded in the biography of Zhāng Chàng.
Yìgōng was demoted to General of Agile Cavalry and Grand Master of Illustrious Virtue,
with the rest of his appointments remaining as before.
In the former residence of Kǒngzǐ in Lǔjùn, there were twenty-four cypress trees,
[一八] which had survived through the Hàn and Jìn dynasties,
so large that they required several arm spans to encircle.
Two of these had previously fallen,
and scholars revered them,
no one daring to harm them.
Yìgōng sent men to cut them all down,
and the elders all sighed in lament.
He was also concurrently appointed Inspector of Nányǎnzhōu with his original rank,
and his command was increased to include the military affairs of Nányǎn, Yù, Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, Jì, Sī, Yōng, Qín, Yōu, and Bìng, making a total of eleven zhōu,
bringing the total to thirteen zhōu including his previous command.
He relocated his garrison to Xūyí.
He repaired and refurbished the government offices, intending to emulate the layout of Dōngchéng.
In the winter of the twenty-ninth year,
he returned to the capital.
The Emperor came to greet him aboard the Cāngyīng boat, which he himself used.
When he was in mourning for his Grand Concubine,
he was reappointed Grand General, Area Commander of the Military Affairs of Yángzhōu and Nánxúzhōu, and Inspector of Nánxúzhōu.
He retained his credentials as imperial envoy, Attendant-in-Chief, Director of the Department of State Affairs, and Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince as before,
and returned to garrison Dōngfǔ.
He declined the position of Attendant-in-Chief but had not yet been formally invested.
When the prime murderer committed his rebellion,
Shào summoned Yìgōng that day.
Previously,
when imperial edicts summoned the Crown Prince and other princes,
there were always regular messengers appointed,
to prevent fraud or harm.
At this time, Yìgōng requested the usual messenger who conveyed edicts,
and Shào dispatched him, after which Yìgōng entered.
Yìgōng requested that his troops be dismissed,
and all weapons and armor within his residence
were sent back to the imperial palace.
He was promoted to Grand Preceptor,
and his command was extended to include the military affairs of Huìzhōu.
He wore the robes of an Attendant-in-Chief,
and also concurrently held the title of Grand Ancestral Master.
When Shìzǔ entered to suppress the rebellion,
Shào suspected Yìgōng of having ulterior motives,
and had him reside in the Department of the Palace Secretariat (shàngshū xiàshěng).
He also had his sons all reside outside the Shénhǔ Gate in the Department of the Palace Attendants (shìzhōng xiàshěng).
Shào heard that Shìzǔ had already arrived at a nearby road,
and wished to put forth his full strength to meet him,
fighting a decisive battle mid-route.
Yìgōng feared that Shìzǔ's boats were crude and small,
and that if Shào recklessly charged into the river,
he might cause trouble.
So he advanced with a suggestion, saying:
"Abandoning the south bank,
and barricading Shítóu,
this is an old method from previous dynasties,
by which one awaits the weary at ease.
There is no worry that we will not defeat them."
Shào followed his advice.
When Shìzǔ's vanguard reached Xīntíng,
Shào coerced Yìgōng to go out and fight,
keeping him by his side,
so he could not escape.
When the battle was lost,
he made Yìgōng select generals in the Eastern Hall.
Yìgōng had previously sent men to prepare a boat at Dōngyězhǔ,
and thus fled south on a single horse.
Just as he crossed the Huái River,
pursuing cavalry had already reached the north bank;
he narrowly escaped.
Shào was furious,
and sent Shǐxīngwáng Jùn to the Western Department to kill Yìgōng's twelve sons.
Shìzǔ was at Xīnlín Pǔ at this time.
When Yìgōng arrived,
he submitted a memorial urging Shìzǔ to ascend the throne,
saying:
"Your servant has heard that order and disorder have no omens,
but are interwoven, one following the other;
the divine spirits have sent down misfortune,
and the two villains have reached the utmost of rebellion,
with profound cruelty and great pain,
unprecedented throughout eternity.
Your Majesty’s loyalty and filial piety are from Heaven,
suddenly erupting like lightning,
throwing off your sleeves and weeping blood;
the Four Seas follow the righteous path.
Therefore, the feudal lords gather like clouds,
their number akin to eight hundred;
the armies inspired by righteousness,
their gathering is like a forest.
The divine mandate supports bright virtue,
and has a destination.
Yet, the one who is modest remains in his place, or leaps forward,
not yet ascending to the heavenly mandate.
This is not the way to give gravity to the imperial ancestral altars,
and extend the seven hundred years.
In the past, Zhāng Wǔ resisted with words,
and the King of Dài yielded to the request;
Gěng Chún made a declaration,
and Guāngwǔ took his rightful position.
How much more so now, when the罪逆 (guilty rebels) have no kinsmen,
their wickedness overflowing and their transgressions complete,
obstructing armies and indulging in cruelty,
slaughtering the good and exalting the wicked!
They walk on earth and bear the sky,
their lives will end in an instant.
It is fitting to quickly establish the exalted title,
to secure the state.
In the season of Jǐngpíng,
it was truly a joyful succession;
when the royal house was in chaos,
the mandate of Heaven rested elsewhere.
Hence, the prophecy was embraced at Yābì,
and the red dragon appeared as a celestial omen.
Your servant humbly believes that the great enlightened one is impartial,
far-sightedly considering the spirits of the seven ancestral temples of the family and state,
and near-sightedly pitying the immediate suffering of the common people.
May you ascend the imperial throne at this time,
and eternally comfort the hearts of the multitude.
Your servant, bearing guilt and incurring punishment,
has stolen a life among men,
fortunately benefiting from lenient governance,
awaiting trial by the proper authorities.
I dare, in the fleeting moments of my life,
to reveal my innermost thoughts."
Shìzǔ ascended the throne

and granted him the titles of Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Palace Attendant, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs of Yángzhōu and Nánxúzhōu, Grand Commandant, concurrently in charge of the six sections of the Palace Secretariat, and Governor of Nánxúzhōu and Xúzhōu.
He was granted a full set of imperial music and drums,
and twenty guards with ceremonial swords,
and was also granted the honorary yellow battle-axe.
After the matter was settled,
he was promoted to Grand Tutor,
concurrently leading as Grand Marshal,
and the number of guards with ceremonial swords was increased to thirty.
He was bestowed with the jade ring and large sash he wore while in the imperial domain.
His enfeoffment was increased by two thousand households.
The Emperor did not wish to perform the full ritual of homage to the Grand Tutor,
so he hinted to the relevant officials to memorialize, saying:
"The sacred will is humble and luminous,
honoring teachers and revering the Dao.
He wishes to pay homage to the Grand Tutor;
this is truly to promote this distant tradition,
and to uphold and clarify a grand principle.
However, the teachers and guardians of Zhōu
were truly referred to as the Three Officials,
and Jìn, following Wèi,
specifically added to their rites.
The imperial way is extremely solemn,
and already has a constant尊 (venerable position).
Examining historical records,
this ceremony is not seen.
Therefore, both Biàn Hú and Sūn Chǔ stated that a ruler should not lower his venerable status.
Consulting the ancient sacred texts,
and considering the sentiments of the multitude,
your servants, after deliberation, believe there should not be a ceremony of additional prostration."
The imperial edict stated:
"I, being dim and shallow, inheriting the imperial line,
truly rely on your teaching and example.
I wish to exhaust my reverence and respect,
to uphold your instructions.
The memorial you submitted, examining past dynasties,
states that there is no rite of prostration.
Since the text is clear,
I will follow your conclusion."
When Shìzǔ established the Crown Prince,
documents from the Eastern Palace
were first sent to Yìgōng.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn (454 CE),
when Nánjùnwáng Yìxuān, Zāng Zhì, Lǔ Shuǎng and others rebelled,
he was granted the yellow battle-axe
and one hundred Bái Zhí guards to enter the six gates.
When the matter was settled,
Zāng Zhì's horse, capable of covering seven hundred *lǐ*, was bestowed upon Yìgōng,
and his enfeoffment was again increased by two thousand households.
Shìzǔ believed that Yìxuān's rebellion
was due to his excessive power,
and at this point wished to weaken the imperial princes and marquises.
Yìgōng, anticipating the Emperor's wishes,
memorialized to abolish the office of Recording Secretary of the Palace Secretariat,
saying:
"Your servant has heard that when Heaven and Earth established their positions,
the Three Extremes followed the same order.
When emperors and kings instituted their transformations and rules,
the Nine Offices all managed affairs.
The achievements of advising the times
are manifest in the Records of Yú;
the custom of discussing the Dao
is proclaimed in the Records of Zhōu.
The establishment of the Three Ducal Ministers
served to regulate yin and yang from their seats;
the appointment of Yuán and Kǎi
began with managing all affairs.
Therefore, Luán Zhēn spoke frankly,
warning against encroaching on others' offices;
Chén Píng resisted with words,
not answering what was not his duty.
Hàn inherited from Qín,
and the various officials were gradually reformed.
Ranks changed with the times,
and responsibilities shifted with the era.
The system of general oversight
was not originally an old institution;
it has been followed through successive generations,
and this remains uncorrected.
Now that the imperial house is newly established,
affairs should follow previous texts.
It is fitting to learn from the former generations,
and verify against ancient principles,
to abolish the system of recording and overseeing,
to conform to ancient precedents.
This will make all things strive for survival,
and people will be diligent and unified.
Then names and realities will not err,
and ordinary achievements will surely be recorded.
Your servant, mistakenly holding the heavy responsibilities of the state,
and falsely bearing a revered position,
should know about rise and fall,
and dare not fail to express everything."
The Emperor followed his deliberation.
He further submitted a memorial together with the Commander-in-Chief of the Cavalry, Jìnglíng Wáng Dàn (竟陵王誕), saying:
"Your subject has heard that there are rules for the number of suspended [musical instruments in a] yí (佾) formation,
and different rituals for different ranks.
There are regulations for佩 (pèi) and 笏 (hù) [dress accessories and ceremonial tablets],
distinguishing between high and low in their order.
These are the grand strategies of the enlightened sages of old,
and the clear instructions for governing the world.
However, as time passes, customs decline,
and nothing is without its flaws.
Extravagance and usurpation arise from common practice,
and the norms and standards are no longer ancient.
When the Jìn (晉) dynasty moved eastward,
the old laws fell into disuse.
The regulations for marquises and regional governors [侯牧典章]
gradually expanded with circumstances,
and the discrepancy between name and reality [名實] grew,
making it difficult to change abruptly.
The grandeur and excess in official attire [章服]
have persisted for many years.
Now that the central government has been renewed,
and the imperial virtue is reborn,
with deficiencies yet to be fully addressed,
and all resources needing to be conserved,
it is fitting to establish rules for ranks and forms,
to set forth articles for curtailing extravagance.
We, your subjects, residing in a close familial position,
and participating in the high offices,
being at the forefront of adhering to rectitude,
request to lead by our own titles.
The beginning of the reduction [of privileges]
should start with those close to the imperial family.
We have taken advantage of leisure days
to jointly consider our humble thoughts,
on what should be revised and simplified,
and respectfully present nine matters.
Although we fear our words may not be profound,
we hope to exert our humble efforts.
We humbly wish Your Majesty, after hearing and examining [this memorial],
would deign to accept it,
so that those above and below will be at peace with each other,
and internal and external affairs will be harmonious."
An imperial edict ordered it to be submitted to the relevant departments for detailed consideration.
The officials then submitted a memorial, stating: "Carriages and garments are used for merit,
a splendid canon in the Book of Yú (虞書);
implements and insignia are granted with caution,
a clear warning in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Therefore, what was made by the Imperial Manufactories [尚方],
the Hàn (漢) had strict laws,
[and if] feudal lords usurped attire,
even if they were relatives, they would surely be punished.
Descending to recent generations,
usurpation by those below has reached its extreme.
Implements, attire, decorations,
music, dance, and manners,
have become common among princes and dukes,
and spread to the common people.
There is no distinction
between high and low,
and the people's aspirations are not unified.
What Yìgōng (義恭) has stated,
truly accords with ritual and propriety.
The nine articles he proposed,
still have omissions.
We respectfully add to them,
making a total of twenty-four articles:
In a reception hall, one may not sit facing south,
nor use hanging curtains and bamboo screens.
Officials of vassal states,
during the first month of winter, may not enter the national palace barefoot,
nor stand beside [the sovereign] as a national preceptor, transmission officer, or oil-painted
halberd bearer.
Princesses and princely consorts acting as transmission officers [傳令],
may not wear vermilion clothes.
The front part of a carriage (駫) may not have a double framework (重棡).
Shield-fans (鄣扇) may not use pheasant feathers.

the carriages, front and rear, may not exceed six ranks.

Yìgōng (義恭) was always concerned about being suspected by Shìzǔ (世祖).
When Hǎilíng Wáng Xiūmào (海陵王休茂) caused unrest in Xiāngyáng (襄陽),

all extensively established close relatives

Feudal lords, upon receiving their titles,

Indeed, when good deeds accumulate and blessings run deep,

Richness and nobility,
arrogance and extravagance,
come naturally,

all had tutors and chancellors appointed,

The conspiracy of the seven states

A tail too large to wag the dog [尾大不掉]

If there are no reforms,
then its
source cannot be saved.
Recently, a commoner, relying on kinship,
almost overturned the imperial enterprise.
Last year, the western invaders, relying on favor,

Unexpectedly, Xiāng (襄) and Chǔ (楚)
have again created this current crisis,
truly because
the terrain is advantageous and the soldiers are brave,
encouraging wicked ambitions.
What happened before should not be forgotten,
it is a clear omen for what will happen later.
Your Majesty has enlightened succession to the throne,
and will establish laws for ten thousand generations.
Your subject is aged and infirm."
I am dull-witted,

I am ashamed to be a senior member of the imperial clan,

I wish to express my humble opinion,

I humbly submit that since the various princes are of such high esteem,

on the frontier.
As for the excellent lands in Huázhōu,
they may visit them temporarily.
Since they already possess a zhōu,

If they ascend to the position of the Three Excellency Ministers,

If
they are needed to guard and defend,

If they delight in detachment and tranquility,
they should not be forced into military affairs.
If they abandon literary pursuits for military ones,
they should be especially restricted.
Their subordinates,
literary scholars,
are sufficient for conversation;
as for those who wander about like the guests of Liáng,
none should be permitted.
For civilian and military staff accompanying the prince,
they should take breaks as appropriate,
and their wives and families

When all
officials pay respects,
they should follow the Jìn regulations.
It is essential to issue an order for all to arrive together,
and to properly arrange the rules for host and guest.
Scholars living in reclusion
also need not trouble themselves to visit noble princes.
As for weapons
kept privately,
their use is indeed limited.
All items such as gold- and silver-adorned swords and battle equipment
should be returned to the state.
By "curving the chimney and moving the firewood,"
precautions have always been taken,
so that the good
may have no fear,

At that time, Shìzǔ was severe and tyrannical,

So he spoke humbly and adopted a compliant attitude,

He was also quick-witted and good at flattery,

Whenever there were auspicious omens,

In the first year of Dàmíng,
three-spined reeds grew on the west bank of Shítou.

In the third year,
