Matters within the Shàngshū will be entrusted to Yán Shībó.
Matters under the supervision of the External Supervisor will be entrusted to Wáng Xuánmó."
After the Former Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
an edict stated:
"The system of comprehensive oversight
was established in previous generations.
In the inaugural year of Xiàojiàn,
though it was briefly merged and abolished,
changes and reforms are appropriate,
and the principle of practical governance remains.
I am alone and young,
not yet versed in the ways of governance;
all myriad affairs
must truly be entrusted to an esteemed and virtuous one.
The Tàizǎi, Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng, newly appointed Zhōngshū Jiān and Tàiwèi,
holds a weighty position within the imperial clan,
and received the testamentary charge as Àhéng.
I deeply rely on him
to bring peace to all undertakings.
He shall record the affairs of the Shàngshū.
His original posts of Jiān, Tàizǎi, and Wáng remain as before.
The Shìzhōng, Piàoqí Dàjiāngjūn, Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ, Bādōng Jùn Kāiguó Gōng, and newly appointed Shàngshū Lìng Yuánjǐng,
who received the same solemn entrustment,
shall assist the imperial house,
promote its undertakings, and spread its influence.
Indeed, we rely on this duke.
He shall immediately assume his current title, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and be granted soldiers and assistants,
all according to previous regulations.
His posts of Dānyáng Yǐn, Shìzhōng, and Gōng remain as before."
Yìgōng's guard of swordsmen was also increased to forty,
and a further imperial order for special honors was issued.
He firmly declined the special honors.
Yìgōng was fond of novelty;
as times changed,
from beginning to end,
he frequently moved residences.
His friendships with people
also often did not last.
Yet he was extravagant and unrestrained,
not valuing wealth and treasures.
To his close associates and favored retainers,
he might give away in a single day
as much as one or two million [cash].
If he was slightly displeased,
he would immediately reclaim it.
During the Dàmíng era,
though his provisions were abundant,
they were always insufficient.
He would buy goods from common people on credit,
having no money to repay them.
If a commoner openly requested money,
he would often write the character
"yuán"
on the back [of the petition].
He was skilled at horsemanship
and understood musical theory.
He would travel sometimes three to five hundred *lǐ*,
and Shìzǔ indulged his wanderings.
He traveled east to Wú Jùn,
ascended Hǔqiū Shān,
and also ascended Wū Shān in Wúxī Xiàn to gaze at Tàihú.
During Dàmíng, the national history was compiled,
and Shìzǔ personally wrote Yìgōng's biography.
By the time of Yǒngguāng,
though he held the position of prime minister,
he always felt inadequate in serving close ministers like Dài Fǎxīng and others.
The Former Deposed Emperor was insane and tyrannical.
Yìgōng, Yuánjǐng, and others plotted to depose and replace him.
In the eighth month of the first year of Yǒngguāng,
the Deposed Emperor led the Yǔlín troops to his residence and murdered him,
along with his four sons.
[二六]He was fifty-three years old at the time.
Yìgōng's limbs were dismembered,
his intestines and stomach were split open,
his eyeballs were gouged out,
[二七]pickled in honey,
and made into "ghost eye zòngzi."
Tài-zōng (太宗) pacified the rebellion.
An edict stated:

"The former Central Secretariat Director, Grand Tutor, concurrently Grand Commandant, and concurrently Director of Affairs of the Imperial Secretariat, Yǒng-jiā Wáng (江夏王) Dào-xìng (道性), possessed profound innate character,
discerning and far-reaching wisdom.
He established his reputation among the feudal lords,
spread his influence with virtuous power.
His position was as exalted as the Ji (姬)辅,
his responsibility was like bearing the Tú (圖).
He toiled for the state,
and was about to receive the great trust of the realm,
dedicating his heart to assisting and guiding,
eternally fostering harmony and peace.
But the villainous elements resented his authority,
suddenly inflicted unjust harm upon him.
The slaughter was brutal,
his burial was unacknowledged.
Indignation reached both the visible and invisible worlds,
and sorrow pierced through the court and countryside.
We encountered peril and difficulty,
containing our grief without expression.
Fortunately, relying on the spirits of the ancestral temples,
We were able to secure the mandate of Heaven.
Remembering his meritorious service and imperial kinship,
Our heart is filled with profound sorrow.
In the past, Liáng Wáng (梁王), when summoned for service,
was greeted with full ceremonial honors and imperial escorts.
Dōng-píng (東平), who loved goodness,
had the imperial carriage at his court.
How much more so for this Duke, whose virtue and achievements were so magnificent,
whose place in the eternal rites should be no different!

Let him be posthumously honored as Bearer of the Imperial Insignia, Palace Attendant, Grand Inspector of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital, Grand Chancellor, concurrently Grand Commandant,
Central Secretariat Director, and concurrently Director of Affairs of the Imperial Secretariat; his title of Wáng (王) remains as before.
He is to be granted a nine-streamered carriage with phoenix decorations,
one hundred imperial guards with ceremonial swords,
feather canopies and military music for both front and rear entourages,
and a sleeping carriage."
In the third year of Tài-shǐ (泰始) (457 CE),
another imperial edict was issued, stating:
"The imperial foundation was gloriously established,
overcoming difficulties and adversity.
He grandly initiated a prosperous era,
and accomplished loyal and decisive deeds.
Therefore, he should be offered sacrifices in the ancestral temples for generations,

Shì-zǔ (世祖), in pacifying chaos and establishing the imperial domain,

Therefore, the former Bearer of the Imperial Insignia, Palace Attendant, Grand Inspector of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital, Grand Chancellor, concurrently Grand Commandant, Central Secretariat Director, and concurrently Director of Affairs of the Imperial Secretariat, Jiāng-xià Wén-xiàn Wáng (江夏文獻王) Yì-gōng (義恭);

the former Bearer of the Imperial Insignia, Palace Attendant, Grand Inspector of Military Affairs of Nán-yù, Jiāng-yù, and Yù (南豫江豫) three Prefectures, Grand Commandant, and Governor of Nán-yù (南豫州), Bā-dōng Jùn Kāi-guó Zhōng-liè Gōng (巴東郡開國忠烈公) Yuán-jǐng (元景);

Héng-yáng Wén Wáng (衡陽文王) Yì-jì (義季),
was simple and unadorned from childhood,
free from vulgar or base attachments.
When Tài-zǔ (太祖) was in Jīng-zhōu (荊州),
Gāo-zǔ (高祖) sent him to follow to Jiāng-líng (江陵).

In the first year of Yuán-jiā (元嘉) (424 CE),

In the sixteenth year (439 CE),

he replaced Lín-chuān Wáng (臨川王) Yì-qìng (義慶) as Grand Inspector of Military Affairs of Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, Yì, Liáng, Níng, Nán-běi Qín (荊湘雍益梁寧南北秦) eight Prefectures, General Who Pacifies the West, and Governor of Jīng-zhōu (荊州).
He retained the Bearer of the Imperial Insignia as before,

Previously, when Yì-qìng (義慶) was in office,
the Bā-shǔ (巴蜀) region was disturbed by rebellion.
Troops were dispatched in response,
and the treasury was empty.
Yì-jì (義季) personally practiced frugality,
accumulating wealth and reducing expenses.
Within a few years,
the treasury was again replenished.
The mother of squad leader Xù Fēng (續豐) was old and his family was poor,
with no means to support her,
so he ceased eating meat.
Yì-jì (義季) pitied his resolve,
and provided Xù Fēng's (續豐) mother with two *hú* of polished rice monthly,
[二九] and one thousand cash,
and also ordered Xù Fēng (續豐) to eat meat.
Yì-jì (義季) was naturally poor at writing,

only requiring him to sign his name.
In the twentieth year (443 CE),
he was granted the additional title of Cavalry Regular Attendant,
promoted to Grand General Who Conquers the West,
and concurrently Commandant of the Southern Man.
Yìjì (義季) was always fond of wine.
After Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng (彭城王義康) was deposed,
he indulged in perpetual drinking,
rarely having a sober day.
Tàizǔ (太祖) repeatedly rebuked him.
Yìjì (義季) admitted his faults and apologized.
The Emperor issued an edict in reply, saying:
"Who can be without fault?
It is precious to reform.
This not only harms your career,
but also damages your life.
Such cases are common in the world,
and you are familiar with them all.
Recently, the Chángshā (長沙) brothers
both met their end because of this.
General Sū Huī (蘇徽),
addicted to wine, became ill,
on the verge of death day and night.
I tried to forbid and stop him,
and provided him with medicine and nourishing food;
he is now able to stand.
This is something that can be moderated,
but those who are addicted cannot make up their minds to cut it down.
Even Jìn Yuándì (晉元帝), as an emperor,
was able to be moved by Wáng Dǎo's (王導) remonstrance,
and never drank alcohol again for the rest of his life.
Since you have noble aspirations,
and I have earnestly expressed my wishes,
why can you not bravely and deeply exert yourself,
but instead require strict measures to cut it down,
and only after much commotion,
do you stop a little?
Fortunately, it need not come to this.
No one in our family indulged in such heavy drinking.
〔三０〕From where did you acquire this habit?
I sigh and feel blocked as I write this letter."
Although Yìjì (義季) received this decree,
he indulged as before,
and thus became ill.
The Emperor again issued an edict to him, saying:
"You drink a lot and eat little,
and are naturally frail and prone to illness.
I have always worried that it would come to this,
and now you are indeed exhausted.
Even if you cannot cherish the state and family,
you no longer even care about the importance of your own life.
It is lamentable and hateful,
and not just a single matter.
Originally, I hoped you could restrain yourself through reason,
and did not wish to distress you.
Now I am sending Sūn Dàoyìn (孫道胤) to join Yáng Fú (楊佛) and others to look after you morning and evening,
and to supervise your soup and food intake.
You should open your heart and accept it sincerely,
and absolutely not hide or avoid them.
I have seen many people quit alcohol,
without any other complaints or cravings;
it is merely the desire to indulge without end at the time.
Now, my worry and distress
are truly about your life.
I have no time to consider your good achievements.
Why do you cause me such extreme anguish again?"
Yìjì (義季) never changed,
until his end.
In the 21st year [of Yuánjiā],
he was appointed Dūdū Nányǎn Xú Qīng Jì Yōu liùzhōu Zhūjūnshì (都督南兗徐青冀幽六州諸軍事), Zhēngběi Dàjiāngjūn (征北大將軍), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), and Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ (南兗州刺史).
〔三一〕He retained his Jié (節) and Chángshì (常侍) titles as before.
On the day he boarded the boat,
all the curtains, furniture, and clothing
that were supposed to accompany the Cìshǐ (刺史)
were left behind.
The people of Jīngchǔ (荊楚) regarded this as a fine deed.
In the 22nd year,
he was promoted to Dūdū Yùzhōu zhī Liángjùn (督豫州之梁郡).
He was transferred to Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (徐州刺史),
retaining his Jié (節), Chángshì (常侍), and Dūdū (都督) titles as before.
The following year,
the Suǒ (索) barbarians invaded and pressed in,
disturbing the northern border.
Yìjì (義季), chastened by Yìkāng's (義康) misfortune,
did not wish to incur trouble through meritorious service.
He had no other plans,
only drinking wine.
Tàizǔ (太祖) again issued an edict to him, saying:
"Dù Jì (杜驥) and Shēn Hù (申怙),
in a crisis,
still used weak armor and small contingents
to intercept the bandits and provide assistance.
You, as the commander-in-chief,
with mighty soldiers and horses,
neither feel inspired to act,
nor, despite repeated instructions,
do you move.
This is not only a great deviation from what is proper in response,
but truly disappoints the hopes of the common people.
Moreover, the Xiongnú (匈奴) will slight the Hàn (漢) starting from this.
The bandits, at first, are unbridled
and do not know where to go.
Therefore, they are merely gathering and observing.
In a few days, their momentum will gradually become apparent,
and then you should have major plans.
How can you remain at ease,
and not dare to move?
The army is dispatched to seize opportunities,
to rescue those in distress,
and to demonstrate our power and support.
Its purpose is not to race across the plains or contend for territory.
Moreover, mountain roads are easy to rely on;
why fear weakness in the front and rear?
If you believe matters should indeed be handled this way,
then advancing with a large garrison
and gathering soldiers
would only be a bother."
In the 24th year,
Yìjì (義季) was gravely ill.
The Emperor sent Zhōngshūlìng (中書令) Xú Zhànzhī (徐湛之) to inquire about his illness,
and summoned him back to the capital.
Before he could depart,
he died in Péngchéng (彭城),
at the age of thirty-three.
Tàiwèi (太尉) Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng (江夏王義恭) petitioned to resign his post to meet the funeral,
but was not permitted.
The Emperor sent Dōnghǎi Wáng Huī (東海王褘) north to meet Yìjì's (義季) funeral.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng (侍中) and Sīkōng (司空),
with his Jié (節), Dūdū (都督), and Cìshǐ (刺史) titles remaining as before.
His son, Gōng Wáng Yì (恭王嶷), whose courtesy name was Zǐqí (子岐), succeeded him.
He served as Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎)
and Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子).
In the 7th year of Shìzǔ Dàmíng's (世祖大明) reign,
he died,
and was posthumously granted Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍) and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (豫州刺史).
His son Bódào (伯道) succeeded him.
In the 3rd year of Shùndì Shēngmíng's (順帝昇明) reign,
he died.
That same year,
Qí (齊) received the abdication,
and the state [of Sòng] was abolished.
The Historiographer said:
To be cautious and fearful of what is unseen,
and apprehensive of what is unheard,
lies in being wary of what one neglects.
Jiāngxià Wáng (江夏王) was Gāozǔ's (高祖) favored son.
His position was that of a prime minister,
and during the Dàmíng (大明) era,
he personally presided over the imperial court.
He humbled himself and lowered his demeanor,
even crawling on the railings of the balcony,
showing his extreme humility.
This enabled him to face cruel courts and tyrannical rulers
without suspicion,
lasting over ten years,
and preserving himself through his respected kinship.
By the time of Yǒngguāng (永光),
with a young emperor facing south,
the heavy responsibility of Gōng Dàn (公旦)
fell upon him.
He thought his worries of treading on thin ice were over,
and that the safety of Mount Tài (泰) could be relied upon.
Yet, not long after,
his body was dismembered.
The ancients used hidden dangers as a warning;
this is indeed profound.

Biographies Chapter 22: Yáng Xīn (羊欣) Zhāng Fū (張敷) Wáng Wēi (王微)
Yáng Xīn (羊欣), courtesy name Jìngyuán (敬元),
was a native of Nánchéng (南城) in Tàishān (泰山).
His great-grandfather Chén (忱)
was Jìn Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (晉徐州刺史).
His grandfather Quán (權)
was Huángménláng (黃門郎).
His father Bùyí (不疑)
was Guìyáng Tàishǒu (桂陽太守).
Yáng Xīn 欣 was quiet and serene in his youth,
never competing with others.
He spoke pleasantly
and was graceful in his demeanor.
He extensively read the classics and histories,
and was especially skilled in clerical script (lìshū).
When Wú Yí 吳疑 first became the magistrate of Wūchéng 烏程,
Xīn was twelve years old.
At that time, Wáng Xiànzhī 王獻之 was the Grand Administrator of Wúxīng 吳興,
and greatly cherished him.
Once, Xiànzhī entered the county in the summer,
and Xīn was sleeping during the day, wearing new silk.
Xiànzhī inscribed several sheets and left.
Xīn was already skilled in calligraphy,
and through this, he became even better.
He began his career as an Aide to the General Who Upholds the State (Fǔguó Cānjūn),
but returned home when the administration was dissolved.
During the Lóng'ān 隆安 reign,
as the court gradually fell into chaos,
Xīn lived a life of leisure in his private residence,
no longer seeking official advancement.
Yuánxiǎn 元顯, the heir apparent of the Prince of Kuàijī 會稽, often asked Xīn to write for him,
but Xīn always declined to obey.
Yuánxiǎn was angered,
and so made him an Aide in his General of the Rear Army's (Hòujūn Fǔ) staff.
This position was originally for commoners,
but Xīn remained calm and composed,
showing no sign of his status, high or low.
Commentators praised him for this.
Xīn once visited Xiè Hùn 謝混, the General of the Central Army (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn).
Hùn brushed his mat and changed his clothes
before meeting him.
At that time, Hùn's cousin Língyùn 靈運 was present.
He later told his cousin Zhān 瞻:
"Wàng Cài 望蔡 [referring to Hùn] saw Yáng Xīn 羊欣
and immediately changed his clothes and mat."
Xīn thus became even more renowned.
When Huán Xuán 桓玄 was regent,
serving as the General of the Pacifying West (Píngxī Jiāngjūn),
he made Xīn a Staff Officer (Cānjūn) to the General of the Pacifying West.
He was then transferred to Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù),
participating in crucial affairs.
Xīn wished to distance himself,
and at times leaked confidential information.
Xuán became aware of his intention,
but esteemed him even more,
making him a Gentleman of the Palace (Diànzhōng Láng) in the Chǔ 楚 court.
He said to him:
"The Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū) is the foundation of governance,
while the Palace is the source of rites and music.
You formerly served as a trusted assistant,
but that was a lighter role compared to this."
After Xīn held the position for a short time,
he claimed illness and resigned,
secluding himself in his village
and not going out for over ten years.
During the Yìxī 義熙 reign,
his younger brother Huī 徽 was favored by Gāozǔ 高祖.
Gāozǔ said to Zhèng Xiānzhī 鄭鮮之, the Counselor-Consultant (Zīyì Cānjūn):
"Yáng Huī 羊徽 is a fine talent of his time,
but public opinion still places him behind his elder brother.
It's a pity I don't know him."
He immediately appointed Xīn as the Chief Clerk (Sīmǎ) to Liú Fān 劉藩, the General of the Right (Yòu Jiāngjūn),
then transferred him to Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ),
and Counselor-Consultant (Zīyì Cānjūn) to Dào Lián 道憐, the General of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn).
He was then sent out as the Grand Administrator of Xīn'ān 新安.
He served in the commandery for four years,
earning renown for his simplicity and benevolence.
He was appointed Chief Clerk (Fǔguó Chángshǐ) to Yìqìng 義慶, the Prince of Línchuān 臨川,
and Counselor-Consultant (Chējì Zīyì Cānjūn) to Yìzhēn 義真, the Prince of Lúlíng 廬陵,
but he did not accept either position.
Tàizǔ 太祖 esteemed him,
and appointed him Grand Administrator of Xīn'ān 新安 again.
He served for a total of thirteen years in both tenures,
enjoying the mountains and waters,
which greatly suited his nature.
His transfer to Yìxīng 義興
was not to his liking.
Soon after,
he again claimed severe illness and resigned to return home.
He was appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance (Zhōngsàn Dàfū).
He always favored the Huang-Lao 黄老 doctrines,
often personally copying scriptures.
When ill, he would not take medicine,
but only drink consecrated water.
He was also skilled in medicine,
and compiled ten scrolls of medicinal recipes.
Xīn, finding himself unable to perform prostrations,
declined to attend court.
Gāozǔ 高祖 and Tàizǔ 太祖 both regretted not knowing him.
Unless visiting close relatives,
he did not casually make visits.
When traveling, he always went outside the city,
never entering the six city gates.
In the nineteenth year of Yuánjiā 元嘉,
he died,
at the age of seventy-three.
His son, Jùn 俊,
died young.
His younger brother Huī 徽, courtesy name Jìngyóu 敬猷,
was regarded by his generation as superior to Xīn.
When Gāozǔ 高祖 was stationed at Jīngkǒu 京口,
he made him a Staff Officer of the Secretariat (Jìshì Cānjūn) in charge of affairs.
Eight years later,
he was promoted to Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Láng),
stationed in the Western Secretariat.
Later, he became Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ) to Tàizǔ's 太祖 Western General of the Household (Xī Zhōngláng) and Grand Administrator of Hédōng 河東.
His son, Zhān 瞻,
at the end of Yuánjiā 元嘉, became Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ) to Shìzǔ's 世祖 Southern General of the Household (Nán Zhōngláng) and Grand Administrator of Xúnyáng 尋陽,
dying in office.
Zhāng Fū 張敷, courtesy name Jǐngyìn 景胤,
was a native of Wú Jùn 吳郡.
He was the son of Shào 邵, the Grand Administrator of Wúxīng 吳興.
His mother died at his birth.
When he was a few years old,
he asked where his mother was.
His family told him about the separation of life and death,
and though Fū was still a child,
he showed a look of longing and sorrow.
When he was about ten years old,
he sought his mother's遗物 (yíwù, relics),
but all had been given away.
He only found one painted fan,
which he sealed and stored.
Whenever he felt nostalgic,
he would open the chest and shed tears.
Seeing his maternal aunt,
he would often become sorrowful and choked up.
He was naturally refined and noble,
with a very high demeanor.
He enjoyed reading Xuanxue 玄學 texts
and also wrote essays and treatises.
He had a great reputation in his youth.
Gāozǔ 高祖 saw him and cherished him,
making him a Staff Officer (Cānjūn) to the Heir Apparent's Central Army (Shìzǐ Zhōngjūn),
and often met and received him.
At the beginning of Yǒngchū 永初,
he was promoted to Gentleman of the Secretariat (Mìshū Láng).
Once, while on duty in the Secretariat,
Fù Liàng 傅亮, the Minister of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng), a highly esteemed and powerful elder,
heard of his studiousness and
came to visit him.
Fū was lying down and did not immediately get up.
Liàng was surprised and left.
His father, Shào 邵, served as the Governor of Xiāngzhōu 湘州,
and then retired from office to attend to the emperor.
Tàizǔ 太祖 appointed Fū as a Staff Officer (Cānjūn) to the Western General of the Household (Xī Zhōngláng).
At the beginning of Yuánjiā 元嘉,
he became an Outside-Palace Attendant (Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng)
and Administrator of the Secretariat (Mìshū Chéng).
When Yìgōng 義恭, the Prince of Jiāngxià 江夏, was stationed in Jiānglíng 江陵,
he made Fū his Assistant Recorder (Fǔjūn Gōngcáo),
and then transferred him to Staff Officer of the Secretariat (Jìshì Cānjūn).
At that time, Yìgōng requested a learned Buddhist monk from Tàizǔ 太祖.
When the monk sought an audience to depart,
Fū happened to be returning to Jiānglíng 江陵 after his leave.
Tàizǔ said to the monk:
"Zhāng Fū 張敷 is going west;
he should give you a ride."
When Fū took his leave,
the Emperor said to him:
"The General Who Comforts the Army (Fǔjūn) needs a man devoted to the Dao.
You can take him on your rear boat,
and you can converse on the way."
Fū did not obey the imperial command,
saying:
"My nature does not tolerate mixing."
The Emperor was very displeased.
He was promoted to Regular Attendant (Zhèngyuán Láng).
Qiū Dāng 秋當 and Zhōu Jiū 周赳, Gentlemen of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén), both managed important affairs.
As Fū was a famous family in the same department,
they wanted to visit him.
Jiū said:
"If he does not tolerate us,
then it is better not to go.
How can we lightly go?"
Dāng said:
"We are all now Outside-Palace Attendants;
why worry about not being able to sit together?"
Fū first set up two couches,
three or four feet from the wall.
The two guests took their seats,
and they conversed very happily.
Soon after, Fū called his attendants, saying:
"Move my distant guests."
Jiū and the others paled and left.
His self-importance and demeanor were thus.
He was good at maintaining his refined tone and bearing,
fully expressing a slow and deliberate manner.
When parting with someone,
he would hold their hand and say:
"I will remember to hear from you."
His lingering voice would not cease for a long time.
Later generations of the Zhāng 張 clan
still admire him today; its origins flow from Fū.
He was transferred to be a Huángmén Shìláng,
then a Hòujūn Zhǎngshǐ to Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn,
and then Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ.
Before he could take up the post,
his father died in Wúxìng.
He was informed that his father was gravely ill,
so Fū went to rush to his side.
From the capital to Wúxìng, where he put on the mourning clothes,
a total of more than ten days passed,
before he began to take in water and gruel.
After the burial, he did not touch salted vegetables,
and consequently became emaciated and fell ill.
His uncle, Mào Dù, often tried to persuade him to stop,
but he would only become more deeply distraught,
fainting and then recovering.
Mào Dù said:
"I had hoped my persuasion would benefit you,
but it only makes it worse."
From then on, he stopped visiting.
He died before a full year of mourning was complete,
at the age of forty-one.
Yán Yánzhī of Lángxié wrote to console Mào Dù, saying:
"Your virtuous nephew, from a young age, adhered to righteous principles,
and as he grew, embraced the essence of reason.
His pure character and noble spirit
were naturally endowed.
Since we first met,
we formed a friendship that transcended age.
Though there have been difficult separations recently,
our affection and concern have never wavered.
As a person of humble standing,
I hoped he would soon bring comfort and joy.
Who would have thought that in his middle years,
he would suddenly embark on a long journey, never to return?
Upon hearing the news, my heart is deeply saddened,
with a grief intensified.
Your family's teachings are profound and thorough,
and he was truly a treasure to your household.
To lose him so suddenly,
how can one bear such sorrow?"
Such was the high regard in which he was held.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,

"The late Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ, Zhāng Fū,

establishing an exemplary conduct from youth.
In his mourning, he became severely emaciated,
his filial piety reaching the utmost purity.
It is fitting to posthumously recognize him,
thereby honoring his excellence.
He is hereby posthumously granted the title of Shìzhōng."
Thus, his residence was renamed Xiàozhāng Lǐ.
He had no sons.
Wáng Wēi, courtesy name Jǐngxuán,

He was skilled in writing,

Wáng Huá 字 Zǐlíng,

His grandfather, Huì,
was General of the Guard

At the beginning of the Lóng'ān reign of the Jìn dynasty,

Gōng dispatched Liú Láozhī to attack Xīn.

Huá, then thirteen years old,

Huá walked slowly.

arriving at Jīnchāngtíng.
His attendants wished to moor the boat,
but Níngzǐ ordered them to move on,
saying:
"This is the Regicide Pavilion;
we cannot moor here."
Whenever Huá was at leisure, reciting poetry,
he often recited Wáng Càn's "Dēnglóu Fù" (Climbing the Tower Rhapsody), saying:
"I hope that the Way of the King will be pacified,
and I can take the high road to exert my strength."
Whenever he encountered people like Xiànzhī,
he would grit his teeth in indignation,
sighing:
"Will I ever see a time of great peace?"
In the second year of Yuánjiā,
Níngzǐ died of illness.
In the third year,
Xiànzhī and his associates were executed.
Huá was promoted to Hùjūn,
and his position as Shìzhōng remained unchanged.
In the Sòng dynasty, only Huá and Liú Zhàn of Nányáng did not feign humility;
they accepted official posts as soon as they were offered,
considering this normal practice.
Due to his unique circumstances,
Huá never participated in banquets or gatherings.
He never drank alcohol throughout his life,
and if there was a banquet, he would not attend.
If there was a need to discuss matters,
he would ride his carriage to the host's gate,
and the host would come out to meet him by his carriage.
When Wáng Hóng assisted in governance,
and his younger brother Tánshǒu was appointed by Tàizǔ,
equal to Huá,
Huá often felt that his abilities were not fully utilized,
and he would sigh:
"There are suddenly several prime ministers;
how can the world be governed!"
In the fourth year,
he died,
at the age of forty-three.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Sànqí Chángshì and Wèijiāngjūn.
In the ninth year,
the Emperor, recalling his merit in executing Xiànzhī,
posthumously enfeoffed him as the Marquis of Xīnjiàn County,
with a stipend of one thousand households,
and his posthumous title was Xuānhóu.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was enshrined in Tàizǔ's ancestral temple.
His son, Dìnghóu, succeeded him,
and rose to the rank of Zuǒwèijiāngjūn,
then died.
His son, Cháng, succeeded him.
In the second year of Tàishǐ under Tàizōng,
Cháng was stripped of his peerage for verbally abusing his mother,
and his younger brother Zhōng succeeded to the enfeoffment.
Later, in the third year of Yuánhuī under the Deposed Emperor,
Zhōng submitted a memorial requesting the return of the enfeoffment to Cháng,
which was granted.
When Qí received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
Huá's cousin, Hóng,
was Wǔbīng Shàngshū and Huìjī Tàishǒu.
Wáng Tánshǒu,
a native of Línyí, Lángyá,
was Tàibǎo Hóng's youngest brother.
From childhood, he had a scholarly ambition.
He was appointed Zuòzhùláng,
but did not accept the post.
When the brothers divided their property,
Tánshǒu only took books and writings.
He was summoned to serve as an attendant to the Grand Marshal Wáng of Lángyá.
He followed the Duke to repair the imperial tombs and gardens in Luòyáng.
He went with his cousin Qiú to meet Gāozǔ.
At that time, Xiè Huì was present.
Gāozǔ said:
"These gentlemen, both of noble lineage and great virtue,
are able to humble themselves to serve in the military."
Tánshǒu replied:
"Having followed the divine and martial army,
it naturally inspires even the timid to have ambition."
Huì said:
"The benevolent indeed possess courage."
Gāozǔ was pleased.
When they reached Péngchéng,
Gāozǔ held a grand gathering at Xìmǎtái.
All those present were asked to compose poems.
Tánshǒu's poem was completed first.
Gāozǔ read it,
and then asked Hóng:
"How does your brother compare to you?"
Hóng replied:
"If he were merely like me,
to whom would our family fortunes be entrusted?"
Gāozǔ laughed heartily.
Tánshǒu had insight and wisdom;
joy and anger were not visible on his face.
Within his family,
harmony prevailed.
He did not hold gold or jade in his hands,
and his womenfolk were not allowed to wear ornaments.
Beyond what was granted as official salary,
he would not accept a single thread from others.
When Tàizǔ was Chuàngjūn and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ,
stationed in Péngchéng,
he appointed Tánshǒu as his Fǔ Gōngcáo.
When Tàizǔ was stationed in Jiānglíng,
Tánshǒu moved from Gōngcáo to Zhǎngshǐ,
and then, with the transfer of the commandery, became Zhèn Xī Zhǎngshǐ.
Gāozǔ knew him well,
and told Tàizǔ:
"Wáng Tánshǒu
is profound, resolute, and possesses great capacity;
he has the talent of a prime minister.
You should consult him on every matter."
During the Jǐngpíng era,
a dragon was seen in the west,
ascending halfway to the sky,
casting a shadow of five-colored clouds.
People in the capital, far and near, gathered to watch.
The Grand Astrologer reported:
"There is an aura of an Emperor in the west."
When Tàizǔ was about to ascend the throne,
both the Emperor and the deliberators were hesitant and dared not proceed.
Tánshǒu, along with Dào Yànzhī and his cousin Huá, strongly urged him.
The Emperor still did not agree.
Tánshǒu again made a strong case,
also speaking of the alignment of heaven and man,
whereupon the Emperor consented.
He commanded the civil and military officials of the commandery to guard themselves with strict discipline,
and the various officials and forces sent by the court
were not allowed near his troops.
The Zhōngbīng Cānjūn, Zhū Róngzǐ, stood with his sword outside the carriage door,
not ungirding for several tens of days.
Once the decree was issued and he was on his way,
a yellow dragon emerged and bore the Emperor's boat.
Everyone around turned pale,
but the Emperor said to Tánshǒu:
"This is how Xià Yǔ received the Mandate of Heaven;
what virtue do I possess to be worthy of it?"
When he ascended the throne,
he again said to Tánshǒu:
"Without Sòng Chāng's unique insight,
this would not have been achieved."
He appointed Tánshǒu as Shìzhōng,
and soon after, he also led Yòuwèijiāngjūn,
and then Xiāoqíjiāngjūn.
Zhū Róngzǐ was appointed Yòujūnjiāngjūn.
The execution of Xú Xiànzhī and others,
and the pacification of Xiè Huì,
were due to the efforts of Tánshǒu and Huá.
In the fourth year of Yuánjiā,
the imperial carriage went out of the North Hall.
The Emperor once ordered the Guǎngmòmén to be opened at the third watch (midnight).
The Southern Terrace reported:
"A White Tiger Banner and a silver-inscribed official staff are required."
They refused to open the gate.
Shàngshū Zuǒchéng Yáng Xuánbǎo memorialized to dismiss Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Fù Lóng and others below him.
Tánshǒu then submitted a memorial, saying:
"There was no imperial decree in ink,
and the banner and staff were missing.
Even if it claimed to be the Emperor's will,
it was no different from a mere verbal command.
In the first and second years of Yuánjiā,
although there was a precedent for opening the gate twice,
that was a past violation.
To adhere to the old rules now
is not against etiquette.
However, since it is based on old records,
Since there is no such record,
it is still appropriate to blame them for not requesting the White Tiger Banner and the silver-inscribed official staff,
which caused the gate not to be opened on time.
This was a lapse in the continuous practice of the Secretariat,
and it should also be rectified."
The Emperor made no special inquiry,
but instead established new regulations.
Tánshǒu was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
and his position as Shìzhōng remained unchanged.
Huì Píng after,
the Emperor wished to enfeoff Tánshǒu and others.
During a banquet,
he raised his cup and offered them wine,
then patted the imperial bed and said:
"This seat, were it not for you brothers,
would not be here today."
At that time, the enfeoffment edict was already drafted.
He brought it out to show Tánshǒu.
Tánshǒu said:
"Recently,
calamity was about to erupt.
Thanks to Your Majesty's sagacity and swift decision,
the criminals were executed.
Although your subjects were able to rely on the heavenly light
and exert their minute effort,
how could we take advantage of a national disaster
for personal gain?
Even if Your Majesty wishes to favor your subject privately,
what about the upright historians?"
The Emperor could not force him,
so the enfeoffment matter was shelved.
At that time, his elder brother Hóng was the Lù Shàngshūshì,
and also the Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu.
Tánshǒu was personally trusted by the Emperor,
and his responsibilities encompassed both palaces.
Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng was a Lù alongside Hóng.
His heart was often discontent,
and he also desired Yángzhōu,
which he expressed in his words and intentions.
With Tánshǒu holding a central position,
sharing his power and responsibilities,
he was even more displeased.
Tánshǒu firmly requested Wú Jùn.
Tàizǔ said:
"How can one wish to build a grand mansion yet abandon its main pillars?
Your esteemed elder brother has repeatedly claimed illness,
firmly declining the provincial post.
If in the future he agrees to relinquish it,
who else but you would take this position?
Why would there be Wú Jùn?"
At that time, Hóng had been ill for a long time
and repeatedly offered to resign his post,
but was not permitted.
Yìkāng said to his guests:
"Wáng Gōng has been ill for a long time and does not recover.
How can Shénzhōu be governed from a sickbed?"
Tánshǒu advised Hóng to reduce his military force by half and allocate it to Yìkāng.
〔一一〕Yìkāng was then pleased.
In the seventh year,
he passed away.
Tàizǔ wept for him.
Zhōngshū Shèrén Zhōu Jiū, attending nearby,
〔一二〕said:
"The Wáng clan is about to decline;
the worthy are the first to perish."
The Emperor said:
"It is simply my family that is declining."
He was posthumously granted Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū,
with the addition of Sànqí Chángshì,
and Zhānshì as before.
In the ninth year,
for his participation in the plot to execute Xiànzhī and others,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Yùníng Xiàn Hóu,
with a thousand households as his fief,
and posthumously named Wén Hóu.
Shìzǔ, upon ascending the throne,
had him enshrined and offered sacrifices in Tàizǔ's ancestral temple.
His son, Sēngchuò, succeeded him;
there is a separate biography for him.
His youngest son, Sēngqián,
at the end of Shēngmíng,
became Shàngshū Lìng.
Yīn Jǐngrén was a native of Chén Jùn Chángpíng.
His great-grandfather Róng was
a Jìn Tàicháng.
His grandfather Mào
〔一三〕was a Sànqí Chángshì, Tèjìn, and Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū.
His father Dàoyù
died young.
Jǐngrén, in his youth, possessed the capacity for great achievements.
Sītú Wáng Mì saw him and married his daughter to him.
Initially, he served as a Hòujūn Cānjūn for Liú Yì,
and a Tàiwèi Xíng Cānjūn for Gāozǔ.
He suggested that all officials should recommend talented individuals,
and that promotions and demotions should be based on the success or failure of their recommendations.
He was promoted to Sòngtái Mìshū Láng,
then Shìzǐ Zhōngjūn Cānjūn,
then Zhǔbù,
and also served as Pàoqí Jiāngjūn Dàolián's Zhǔbù.
He was sent out to serve as Héngyáng Tàishǒu,
then returned to serve as Sòng Shìzǐ Xǐmǎ,
and subsequently transferred to Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Jǐngrén did not engage in literary writing in his studies,
but was quick-witted and insightful.
He did not discuss theories verbally,
but deeply understood the essence of principles.
Regarding national codes, court ceremonies,
and old records and notes,
he compiled and recorded all of them.
Those who recognized him knew he harbored aspirations for his generation.
Gāozǔ esteemed him greatly,
and promoted him to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
Shàodì, upon ascending the throne,
appointed him as Shìzhōng.
He repeatedly submitted memorials declining the position,
and again firmly stated:
"Your subject's will and ability are weak,
as recorded in my appointments and dismissals.
Having encountered a prosperous and peaceful imperial reign,
I have received much grace and honor.
My rank and position have advanced,
days and months have accumulated frequently.
The fault lies in my greed,
the problem in not knowing my own limits.
Yet upon hearing of this present appointment,
I firmly adhere to my foolish heart,
for I secretly believe that the favor of extraordinary positions
must go to those with ability and prestige;
the responsibility of being the throat and lips
cannot be held by the untalented.
I cannot bear the responsibilities of the three ministries.
How can I blindly seek glorious advancement,
not knowing when to move forward or retreat,
thereby harming the court's selection above,
and bringing fault upon myself below?
Considering both public and private matters,
I do not see how this is permissible.
Examining my limits and understanding my boundaries,
it is truly difficult to aspire to this.
Exceeding one's bounds and transgressing one's order
is easy to fear and be warned by.
Therefore, I look up and down, pacing around,
with no peace of mind.
If your benevolent grace flows widely,
and orchids and mugwort are equally nourished,
if you would change your previous decree
and grant me a lower position,
though I am truly unperceptive,
how dare I forget to obey the command?
Your subject's offense of disobedience
has already accumulated many times.
How can I merely pursue superficial glory
and defile the Emperor's ears?
My sincere and earnest heart
looks up, hoping for your observation and discernment."
The imperial edict said:
"Jǐngrén's humble and yielding disposition
is unchangeable.
Let him be dismissed as Huángmén Shìláng
to grant the gentleman's request."
Soon after,
he took charge of Shèshēng.
A short while later,
he was transferred to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
Tàizǔ, upon ascending the throne,
entrusted him even more deeply.
Soon after, he was promoted to Shìzhōng,
with Zuǒwèi as before.
At that time, he, alongside Shìzhōng Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Wáng Huá,
Shìzhōng Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Wáng Tánshǒu, and Shìzhōng Liú Zhàn—these four people—
all served as Shìzhōng simultaneously,
and all resided in the Ménxià.
All of them, with their vigor, ability, and capacity for organization,
were outstanding in their time.
The beauty of their simultaneous promotion
has not been matched in recent times.
In Yuánjiā third year,
the imperial carriage went on a campaign against Xiè Huì.
Sītú Wáng Hóng entered and resided in the Zhōngshū Xiàshěng.
Jǐngrén was on constant duty,
jointly managing the remaining duties.
After Huì was pacified,
he replaced Dào Yànzhī as Zhōnglǐng Jūn,
with Shìzhōng as before.
Tàizǔ's birth mother, Empress Zhāng, had died early.
The Emperor served Sū Shì, who was the birth mother of the Empress Dowager, with great reverence.
In the sixth year,
Sū Shì passed away.
The Emperor personally went to her bier and wept.
He issued an edict saying:
"I suffered an early loss,
and my emotions are extraordinary.
I constantly think of how to glorify the empress's kin
to slightly express my boundless grief.
However, the rituals and precedents are lost,
and there is no proper guidance.
Looking at previous dynasties,
their practices were also different.
Therefore, I have deliberated for years,
but my heart's desire remains unfulfilled.
Lady Sū suddenly passed away,
leaving my feelings and rites nowhere to be placed.
My remembrance and lingering sorrow
deepen with the passage of events.
The days are appointed,
and a burial site will be chosen.
I intend to broadly follow the principle of 'honoring them according to spring and autumn' (meaning: according to their importance)
and strictly adhere to the precedents of the Two Hàn dynasties regarding extending grace.
However, every action is recorded by historians,
to be transmitted to future generations.
To act merely to satisfy my heart
might not be entirely appropriate.
Let us deliberate together on this matter
to find the middle path.
As I hold the writing brush, my deep emotions
only increase my sorrow and blockage."
Jǐngrén deliberated and said:
"The moving power of ultimate virtue
inspires auspicious signs.
The Venerable Mother matching Heaven
truly prospers the imperial lineage.
Your Majesty diligently follows the former precedents,
and your ultimate reverence is profound.
The principle of 'honoring them'
is fully satisfied here.
Lady Sū's position was due to her connection to the imperial family,
and her feelings deepened with the events.
The thoughts of 'cold springs' (meaning: filial piety)
truly moved the Sacred Heart.
A clear edict was issued,
seeking the middle path.
I respectfully observe that the Hàn dynasty extended grace and conferred titles
at a time when the evils of Qín were inherited,
and Confucianism was negligible.
They acted according to their own decisions,
without previous precedents.
I fear this is not a path suitable for a sagacious and enlightened era.
Jìn learns from the two previous dynasties,
which is the basis for governing the court.
The actions of the monarch must be recorded,
a caution for wise kings.
Those who embody ultimate impartiality
bestow titles and rewards without bias.
Those who uphold the heavenly mandate
often suppress personal feelings to uphold regulations.
This is how trust is established with all nations
and principles are bequeathed to future generations.
Your servant, though having received extensive favor,
humbly reveals his mediocrity."
The Emperor followed his advice.
During the mourning period for his mother,
after the burial was complete,
he was appointed Língjūn Jiāngjūn.
He firmly declined.
The Emperor ordered the court officials to offer obeisance on his behalf,
and dispatched Zhōngshū Shèrén Zhōu Jiù to convey him back to his residence by carriage.
In the ninth year,
when his mourning period ended,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Púyè.
Tàizǐ Zhānshì Liú Zhàn was appointed Língjūn in his place.
Zhàn and Jǐngrén had always been on good terms,
and both were favored by Gāozǔ,
who promised them both positions as prime ministers.
Zhàn was still in an external post.
At that time, Wáng Hóng, Huà, and Tán successively died as prime ministers.
Jǐngrén brought Zhàn back to court
to jointly participate in governance.
Once Zhàn entered,
he felt that Jǐngrén's rank and favor had originally not surpassed his own,
yet he was suddenly placed ahead.
He felt extremely indignant.
Knowing that Tàizǔ trusted and relied on Jǐngrén
and that this could not be changed,
he deeply allied himself with Sītú Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng,
hoping to use the prestige of the prime minister to overthrow Jǐngrén.
In the twelfth year,
Jǐngrén was again promoted to Zhōngshū Lìng,
with Hùjūn and Púyè as before.
Soon after, he concurrently held Lìbù as Púyè,
with Hùjūn as before.
Zhàn grew even more enraged.
Yìkāng listened to Zhàn's words
and slandered Jǐngrén to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ, however, treated Jǐngrén with even greater respect.
Jǐngrén sighed to his relatives and old friends, saying:
"I brought him in,
and once he entered, he bit people."
He then claimed illness and resigned,
submitting repeated memorials,
but they were not approved.
The Emperor ordered him to stay at home to recuperate.
An edict was issued dispatching Huángmén Shìláng to inquire about his illness.
Zhàn proposed sending someone to kill him outside as if by a robber,
thinking that even if Tàizǔ knew,
he would have to find a way
and ultimately could not harm the love for a close relative.
The Emperor subtly heard of this
and moved Jǐngrén to the residence of Princess Jìn Póyáng outside the Xīyè Gate,
making it the Hùjūn residence.
Being close to the palace,
Zhàn's scheme did not succeed.
Jǐngrén was confined by illness for five years.
Although he did not meet the Emperor,
secret memorials went back and forth,
sometimes ten a day.
All matters of court administration, big or small,
were invariably put to him.
His activities were so discreet and thorough
that no one could spy on their details.
On the day Zhàn was arrested,
Jǐngrén ordered his clothes and cap to be dusted.
As he had been ill for a long time,
those around him did not understand his meaning.
That night,
the Emperor went to the Yánxián Hall in Huálín Garden and summoned Jǐngrén.
He still claimed a leg ailment,
and was carried in a small sedan chair to his seat.
The dispositions for punishment and extermination
were all entrusted to him.
He was appointed Yángzhōu Cìshǐ in place of Yìkāng,
with Púyè and Lìbù as before.
An envoy was sent to present the seal and sash.
His Zhǔbù received them on his behalf.
After the obeisance,
he immediately felt his emotional state was confused and disordered.
His nature was originally magnanimous,
but he suddenly became harsh and tyrannical.
He asked his attendants:
"This year, are there more men marrying?
Or more women marrying?"
That winter, there was a heavy snow.
Jǐngrén rode in his carriage to the hall where he handled affairs and looked out.
He suddenly exclaimed in surprise:
"How can there be a large tree in front of the door?"
Then he said:
"Am I mistaken?"
His illness worsened.
Tàizǔ deemed it disadvantageous for him to be in the provincial administration
and had him return to reside in the Púyè's subordinate office.
He served as governor for just over a month before he died.
Some said it was due to Liú Zhàn's malevolent spirit.
He was fifty-one years old at the time.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng and Sīkōng,
with his original posts remaining as before.
His posthumous name was Wénchéng Gōng.
The Emperor wrote to Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì, saying:
"Yīn Púyè was ill for only a few days,
and suddenly could not be saved.
His insight was profound and far-reaching,
he served the nation with utmost sincerity,
he was always attentive and considerate.
My feelings are beyond ordinary grief.
He was the hope of the people and a national pillar.
Such encounters are rare.
My regret and sorrow are so deep
that I cannot stop them.
Do you feel the same?
Alas, how terrible!"
In the fifth year of Shìzǔ Dàmíng,
the Emperor passed by Jǐngrén's tomb.
He issued an edict saying:
"Sīkōng Wénchéng Gōng Jǐngrén's virtue and magnanimity were upright,
his character and insight were clear and judicious.
His splendid achievements and loyal strategies
were apparent long ago.
His benevolent governance and esteemed reputation
truly remain among the people.
Recently, seeing his mound,
I am moved by the past and filled with lament.
An envoy should be sent to offer sacrifices."
His son, Dàojīn,
was dull from a young age.
He rose to the office of Tàizhōng Dàfū.
Dàojīn's son,
during Tàizōng's reign, served as Shìzhōng
and Dùzhī Shàngshū.
Because his father's illness had lasted a long time,
he was impeached by the relevant authorities.
An edict said:
"Dàojīn has been ill since birth,
not a sudden new illness.
Due to his foolishness and habitual idleness,
he has long obstructed the pure order (of government).
He may be demoted to Sànqí Chángshì."
Shěn Yǎnzhī [沈演之], courtesy name Táizhēn [臺真],
was a native of Wǔkāng [武康], Wúxīng [吳興].
His great-great-grandfather Chōng [充]
was a Chēqí Jiāngjūn [車騎將軍] in the Jìn [晉] dynasty
and the Wú [吳] Commander.
His great-grandfather Jìng [勁]
was the Changshǐ [長史] to Guànjūn [冠軍] Chén Yòu [陳祐].
He was stationed in Jīnyǒngchéng [金墉城]
when it was besieged by the Xiānbēi [鮮卑] Mùróng Kè [慕容恪].
He refused to surrender and was killed.
He was posthumously granted the title of Dōngyáng Tàishǒu [東陽太守].
His grandfather Chìqián [赤黔]
was the Tíngwèi Qīng [廷尉卿].
His father Shūrèn [叔任]
showed capability and integrity in his youth.
He first served as Yángzhōu Zhǔbù [揚州主簿],
then as Tàiwèi Cānjūn [太尉參軍] for Gāozǔ [高祖],
and later as the magistrates of Wú [吳] and Shānyīn [山陰].
His administration in these posts was well-regarded.
When Zhū Língshí [朱齡石] campaigned against Shǔ [蜀],
Shūrèn [叔任] served as Língshí’s [齡石] Jiànwēi Fǔ Sīmǎ [建威府司馬],
and was promoted to Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn [建威將軍].
His contribution to the pacification of Shǔ [蜀]
was second only to the marshal.
He was appointed Xīyí Xiàowèi [西夷校尉] and Bāxī Zǐtóng Jùn Tàishǒu [巴西梓潼郡太守] under his existing title,
and was stationed in Fúchéng [涪城].
When the eastern army retreated,
the influential clans of the two commanderies, Hóu Mài [侯勱] and Luó Ào [羅奧], gathered a rebellious force.
They converged from all directions,
eventually numbering over ten thousand men,
and attacked the city urgently.
Shūrèn [叔任] had fewer than five hundred eastern soldiers,
but he earned their trust and loyalty,
and none refused to serve him.
He led them out to strike and inflict a great defeat,
and the rebel factions were all pacified.
When Gāozǔ [高祖] campaigned against Sīmǎ Xiūzhī [司馬休之],
Língshí [齡石] sent Shūrèn [叔任] to lead troops to join him.
At that time, Gāozǔ [高祖] held the title of Zhèn Xī Jiāngjūn [鎮西將軍],
and appointed Shūrèn [叔任] as his Sīmǎ [司馬].
When the army returned,
he was made Yángzhōu Biéjià Cóngshìshǐ [揚州別駕從事史].
For his achievements in pacifying Shǔ [蜀] and holding Fú [涪],
he was enfeoffed as the Earl of Níngxīn Xiàn [寧新縣男],
with a stipend of four hundred forty households.
He was sent out as Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn [建威將軍] and Yìzhōu Cìshǐ [益州刺史],
but returned to the capital due to illness.
In the fourteenth year of Yìxī [義熙] (418 CE),
he died
at the age of fifty.
His eldest son Róngzhī [融之]
died young.
Yǎnzhī [演之] was eleven years old
when Shàngshū Púyè [尚書僕射] Liú Liǔ [劉柳] saw him and recognized his potential,
saying:
“This child will eventually become a great vessel.”
Although his family had been generals for generations,
Yǎnzhī [演之] humble himself and loved learning.
He read the Lǎozi [老子] a hundred times a day,
and was famous for his understanding of principles and scholarship.
He inherited his father's separate peerage, the fifth-rank marquis of Jíyáng Xiàn [吉陽縣].
The commandery appointed him Zhǔbù [主簿],
the province invited him to be Cóngshìshǐ [從事史],
Xīcáo Zhǔbù [西曹主簿],
he was recommended as a Xiùcái [秀才],
and served as the magistrate of Jiāxīng [嘉興],
where he gained a reputation for competence.
He entered government as Sītú Jìjiǔ [司徒祭酒],
then Zuǒjūn Zhǔbù [左軍主簿] to Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān [南譙王義宣],
and magistrate of Qiántáng [錢唐],
where he again achieved administrative success.
He was again appointed Sītú Zhǔbù [司徒主簿].
He mourned his mother.
He was appointed magistrate of Wǔkāng [武康],
but although he firmly declined, he could not avoid it.
After about a hundred days in office,
he claimed illness and resigned.
After the period of mourning ended,
he was appointed Sītú Zuǒ Xīyuán [司徒左西掾],
〔一四〕and Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ [治中從事史] of the province.
In the twelfth year of Yuánjiā [元嘉] (435 CE),
the eastern commanderies suffered great floods,
and the people faced famine.
In Wú [吳], Yìxīng [義興], and Qiántáng [錢唐] of Wújùn [吳郡],
rice cost three hundred cash per shàng [升].
Yǎnzhī [演之] and Shàngshū Cíbù Láng [尚書祠部郎] Jiāng Suì [江邃] were both appointed concurrently Sànqí Chángshì [散騎常侍],
to tour and provide relief,
with permission to act on discretion.
Yǎnzhī [演之] opened the granaries to relieve the starving people.
For those who gave birth to a child,
one dòu [斗] of rice was given per mouth.
Any doubtful or wrongful judgments in criminal cases
were all corrected and dismissed,
and the common people benefited greatly.
He was transferred to Biéjià Cóngshìshǐ [別駕從事史],
and concurrently held the position of Zhōngzhèng [中正] of his home commandery.
He was deeply trusted by Yìkāng [義康],
and thus remained in the prefectural administration for over ten years.
Later, Liú Zhàn [劉湛], Liú Bīn [劉斌], and others formed a faction,
〔一五〕intending to displace and dismiss Shàngshū Púyè [尚書僕射] Yīn Jǐngrén [殷景仁].
Yǎnzhī [演之] always upheld righteousness
and disagreed with Zhàn [湛] and his group.
Zhàn [湛] therefore slandered him to Yìkāng [義康].
Once, during a discussion, their views did not align with the emperor's intention,
and Yìkāng [義康] changed color and said:
“From now on,
I will no longer trust you!”
Yǎnzhī [演之] had always been on good terms with Jǐngrén [景仁]
and devoted himself to the court.
Tàizǔ [太祖] greatly praised him,
and appointed him Shàngshū Lìbù Láng [尚書吏部郎].
In the seventeenth year (440 CE),
Yìkāng [義康] was sent to a feudal state,
and Zhàn [湛] and others were executed.
Yǎnzhī [演之] was appointed Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn [右衞將軍].
Jǐngrén [景仁] died shortly after,
and Hòujūn Chángshǐ [後軍長史] Fàn Yè [范曄] was appointed Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn [左衞將軍].
He and Yǎnzhī [演之] jointly commanded the imperial guards
and participated in confidential affairs together.
In the twentieth year (443 CE),
he was promoted to Shìzhōng [侍中],
with Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn [右衞將軍] as before.
Tàizǔ [太祖] said to him:
“The Shìzhōng [侍中] leading the guards
is a position of outstanding prestige and power.
This is essentially the position of a prime minister.
You should strive for it.”
The emperor wished to campaign against Línyì [林邑],
but the court officials disagreed.
Only Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ [廣州刺史] Lù Huī [陸徽] and Yǎnzhī [演之] supported the emperor's intention.
When Línyì [林邑] was pacified,
the officials were bestowed with gold, captured people, bronze vessels, and other items.
Yǎnzhī [演之] received a particularly large share.
The emperor said to him:
“In the strategic planning of the court,
you contributed your strength.
Pacifying these distant barbarians
is not enough to grant many fiefs.
Wait until the capital is pacified
〔一六〕and the imperial carriages resound at Dōngdài [東岱],
and there will be no worry about not having land.”
In the twenty-first year (444 CE),
an imperial edict stated:
“To oversee military affairs
and assist the Eastern Court
requires truly worthy individuals;
it is not granted to those who are not virtuous.
Shìzhōng [侍中] and Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn [右衞將jūn] Yǎnzhī [演之]
is upright in his conduct and profound in his judgment,
with deep and effective thoughts.
Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn [右衞將軍] Yè [曄]
is quick-witted and capable,
with a clear and important mind.
Both excel in and out of court,
sincere and brilliant in public service,
able to earnestly advance their strategies
and establish achievements in their posts.
Yǎnzhī [演之] is appointed Zhōnglǐngjūn [中領軍],
and Yè [曄] is appointed Tàizǐ Zhānshì [太子詹事].”
Yè [曄] harbored rebellious intentions,
and Yǎnzhī [演之] sensed something was amiss.
He reported it to Tàizǔ [太祖],
and Yè [曄]'s plot was soon uncovered, and he was executed.
Yǎnzhī [演之] was promoted to Lǐng Guózǐ Jìjiǔ [領國子祭酒],
then Dà Zhōngzhèng [大中正] of his home province,
and transferred to Lìbù Shàngshū [吏部尚書],
concurrently Lǐng Tàizǐ Yòuwèi Shuài [領太子右衞率].
Although not yet a prime minister,
the trust placed in him was no different.
He always had a strong will,
and had been ill for years.
The emperor allowed him to manage affairs from his sickbed.
He was fond of recommending talented people
and helping those who were struggling,
yet he was humble and self-restrained.
When the emperor bestowed female entertainers upon him,
he did not accept them.
In the twenty-sixth year (449 CE),
the imperial carriage visited the imperial tombs in the capital.
Yǎnzhī [演之] did not accompany due to illness.
When the emperor returned to the palace,
he summoned Yǎnzhī [演之].
He forced himself to come to the sitting area,
but upon exiting to the lower department of the Shàngshū [尚書] office,
he suddenly died
at the age of fifty-three.
Tàizǔ [太祖] deeply mourned him,
and posthumously granted him the titles of Sànqí Chángshì [散騎常侍] and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū [金紫光祿大夫],
with the posthumous name Zhēnhóu [貞侯].
Jiāng Suì [江邃], courtesy name Xuányuǎn [玄遠],
who served with Yǎnzhī [演之] on the mission, was a native of Kǎochéng [考城], Jìyáng [濟陽].
He was quite skilled in literature.
He rose to the office of Sītú Jìshì Cānjūn [司徒記室參軍],
and his literary works and commentaries
were transmitted to later generations.
Yǎn's son, Mù,
reached the rank of Huángmén Láng,
and Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì.
In the early Dàmíng era of Shìzǔ,
he was implicated for secretly inviting Yu Xīnzhī, a close aide of the emperor, to discuss matters within the palace,
and also for being at odds with his younger brother Bó, the Xīyáng Wáng Wénxué.
He was consequently banished to Shǐxīng Jùn,
and Bó was dismissed from office and forbidden from holding future positions.
Bó was fond of writing essays,
skilled at playing the qín,
and capable at wéiqí,
but he was frivolous and pursued profit.
He successively held the position of Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng.
In the Tàishǐ era of Tàizōng,
he became Tàizǐ Yòuwèi Shuài,
and was additionally appointed Jǐshì Zhōng.
At that time, a northern expedition was planned,
and Bó was dispatched to his hometown to recruit men.
He accepted many bribes.
The emperor was enraged
and issued an edict saying:
"Shěn Bó possesses artistic skills in qín and calligraphy,
and has a good reputation for his eloquence,
yet he is volatile, addicted to alcohol,
and committed many transgressions in his youth.
Recently, his extravagance and debauchery have been excessive;
with dozens of singing girls,
his revelry and indulgence
knew no bounds.
Relying on his status as a local magnate in Wúxīng
and his family's long-standing connections,
he coerced commoners and officials,
incessantly demanding and extorting.
Moreover, he arbitrarily allowed recruits to be discharged,
abandoning their duties and returning them to private life,
feigning illness and deserting,
amounting to several hundred individuals.
His retainers and disciples
competed to accept bribes;
the smallest amounted to ten thousand (cash),
the largest to a thousand gold (coins).
An assessment of the ill-gotten gains
totals over two million (cash).
It is fitting to clearly punish him and enforce the law
to uphold justice and legal precedent.
However, his late father, the former Guānglù Dàfū Yǎn, once received profound favor,
and his loyal service was evident in court.
Reflecting on this from afar,
how can we not extend leniency?
Bó shall be banished to Xīchuí,
to allow him to reflect on his transgressions and repent."
Thereupon, he was exiled to Liángzhōu.
In the early Yuánhuī era of Fèidì,
he was allowed to return by special dispensation.
He formed connections with Ruǎn Diànfū, Wáng Dàolóng, and others,
and again became Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ.
He was later executed by Fèidì.
When Shùndì ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted his original official title.
Bó's younger brother, Tǒng,
was a Zhùzuò Zuǒláng during the Dàmíng era.
Earlier,
the assigned retainers (gàntóng) of the Wǔ Shěng (Five Departments)
were not allowed to be used for miscellaneous tasks.
In the time of Tàizǔ,
a hundred people were dismissed from office
for this reason.
[一七] Tǒng excessively misused his retainers,
and the authorities proposed his dismissal.
Shìzǔ issued an edict stating:
"Recently, many retainers
have not been diligent in their service;
their masters may appropriately administer corporal punishment."
The practice of administering "gànzhàng" (retainer's beating)
began from this time.
Yǎn's elder brother Róngzhī's son, Chàngzhī,
inherited the title of Níngxīn Xiàn Nán.
During the Dàmíng era,
he served as Hǎilíng Wáng Xiūmào's Běizhōngláng Zīyì Cānjūn.
He was killed by Xiūmào,
and was posthumously granted the title of Huángmén Láng.
His son, Yè, inherited the title.
When Qí received the abdication (of the Sòng dynasty),
the state (Sòng) was abolished.
The historian remarks: In the early Yuánjiā era,
the execution of the prime ministers was
largely due to the efforts of Wáng Huá and Kǒng Níngzǐ.
Although these various officials had previously formed alliances,
their favor was now estranged.
Yet, they held the power they had wielded before,
and their intentions were not those of their former lord.
Occupying the position of the exhausted top line of the sixth hexagram (referring to being at the peak of power, vulnerable to downfall),
they were at a critical juncture for future favor.
The overturning of their foundation
did not require other pretexts.
How much more easily could a rift be exploited
in matters as grave as deposition and execution?
Killing a man to seize his jade disk,
one does not realize the trouble it brings upon oneself;
overthrowing others to gain favor,
one does not fear the difficulty of maintaining it oneself.
If these two men had lived long,
it is unknown where their future calamity would have ceased.
If one can learn from them and awaken to this truth,
that is what is hoped from future wise men.

BIOGRAPHIES TWENTY-FOUR Zhèng Xiānzhī, Péi Sōngzhī, Hé Chéngtiān
Zhèng Xiānzhī, courtesy name Dàozǐ,
was a native of Kāifēng, Xíngyáng.
His great-grandfather, Hún, was Wèi Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng.
His grandfather, Xí, was Dàsīnóng.
His father, Zūn, was Shàngshū Láng.
Xí initially served as Jiāngchéng Lìng,
and thus resided in the county.
Xiānzhī studied behind a curtain,
cutting off social interactions.
He first served as Huán Wěi's Fǔguó Zhǔbù.
Previously,
Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Téng Tián was captured by Dīnglíng Zhái Liáo,
and his body was not returned.
Tián's son, Xiàn, continued his official career without interruption,
which some critics found objectionable.
When Huán Xuán was in Jīngzhōu,
he ordered his officials to discuss the matter broadly.
Xiānzhī argued: The ultimate principles of the doctrine of names
are nothing but loyalty and filial piety.
As for adaptation and restraint,
each situation is always different.
Fundamentally, when one traces them,
they all seek the inner mind while observing outward traces.
The circumstances
on which these traces depend
may vary.
Therefore, the sages sometimes followed traces to assist in teaching,
and sometimes used traces to establish guilt.
Bending and extending, taking away and giving,
cannot be equated.
However, taking their general categories,
they can all be briefly explained.
Can heaven be escaped?
Yet Yī Yǐn deposed a ruler.
Can a ruler be coerced?
Yet Yù Quán's righteousness was acknowledged.
Can loyalty be foolish?
Yet Jīzǐ shared his benevolence.
From this point onward,
there are countless instances
where the reality differed but the praise was the same,
or the reputation varied but the excellence was equal.
To expect to rectify this matter
in a single morning,
where the sacred canons
are silent for a hundred generations,
how can it be easy?
Nevertheless, in establishing arguments and clarifying principles,
using antiquity to prove the present,
one should make the principle satisfy human sentiment.
As for the circumstances of Téng Xiàn,
some might have lived in seclusion their entire lives,
not engaging in worldly affairs;
others might have ascended to court and managed affairs,
without drawing criticism from past sages.
Those who approve of Téng use "no criticism from past sages" as evidence,
while those who disapprove of Téng cite "living in seclusion" as virtuous.
If we consider the middle ground between these two,
then the nature of their differences and similarities
can be seen.
However, "no criticism from past sages"
refers to satisfying human sentiment.
For example, Wáng Líng's mother
was boiled by Chǔ,
but Líng did not retreat and live in impoverished
seclusion;
he ultimately served as a minister to the state,
not for his own glory.
Bāo Xūn was resolute and outspoken in the Wèi court,
sacrificing his life to serve as an example;
observing his ambition, it was not for greed of rank.
These two
worthy men
are not comparable to Téng.
For the sages established teachings,
even saying,
"If there is ritual but not the right time,
the noble man does not act."
If there is ritual but not the right time,
it is precisely because affairs have changed and evolved,
and one
cannot adhere to a single rule.
If Téng were to use these two worthy men as evidence,
then I fear everyone would consider themselves worthy.
If everyone cannot consider themselves worthy,
why should he alone be permitted
proof.
Censure is aimed at people in general,
not merely at specific events.
Since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
records have lacked certain norms,
and few have been able to find them.
By the time of the great
Jìn’s central court and after its restoration,
Yáng Zhēn observed a seven-year mourning period without removing his mourning clothes,
and for over thirty years did not involve himself in human affairs.
Wēn Gōng was compelled by royal decree,
Yǔ Zuǒ
chéng wore no lined garments for the rest of his life.
Gāo Shìyuǎn was persuaded to make compromises by Wáng Yòujūn and Hé Piàojì.
None were as easy-going as Téng.
If one considers mourning clothes
not to be the primary expression of grief,
then there is nothing more to say.
Emperor Wén, during the battle of Dōngguān,
where bodies were unrecoverable,
decreed that their sons and brothers
should not forgo marriage or official careers.
This makes
it clear that
a filial son does not consider himself to be the same as others in human society,
and those with discernment have already judged its appropriateness.
If it were not so,
those who assist the ruler and manage affairs
should simply follow the teachings of the Sages.
What need
would there be for further explicit decrees in between?
When the great chaos of Yǒngjiā occurred,
Wáng Dūn reintroduced the Dōngguān decree during the restoration.
The original intention was
a major state policy,
not to regulate human morality
exhaustively through this.
How can this be explained?
A father's revenge clearly means not sharing the same sky,
yet for the state, revenge cannot be permitted.
This is where law overrides emotion,
which is the analogy of Dōngguān and Yǒng
jiā.
What harm is there in those who manage royal affairs
remaining commoners?
Those who uphold teachings claim that the world is not in chaos,
and that all gentlemen and scholars
have no
reason not to serve.
They mix this with emotional censure,
suggesting they should be demoted.
If too many past events are cited as universal proofs,
then a filial son could observe the law and not
seek revenge.
Emperor Wén did not establish any specific decree at Dōngguān,
nor did Wáng Dūn clarify anything during the restoration.
Whenever such situations arose,
it was always left to the discretion of those managing affairs.
Can this sentiment not be understood?
Moreover, seeking reason should first prioritize the broad and far-reaching.
If the ocean were in turmoil,
and families and nations alike were drowning,
if one did not serve,
then people would have surplus strength.
If people had
surplus strength,
then the nation could perish,
and families could be wiped out.
At such a time,
even common women would lose their lives,
how much more so great men!
Since it is not
so,
the talents of the world
will have nowhere to be applied.
Téng should merely devote himself to the grief of ascending the hill (missing his parents),
and emulate the hearts of those who do not serve.
Why cite and use previous people as examples
to justify himself?
Furthermore, fame is borrowed by great talents,
and glorified by small talents.
To glorify and borrow beyond the norm
already involves a sense of shame.
Without joy in diligent advancement,
what emotional concern
is there?
If it is not so,
then without joy in diligent advancement,
what is there to value
over a thousand years?
If small talents are permitted to glorify their positions,
then Téng should not heed common
doubts and remain in his position, should he?
It's like saying "Liǔ Xiàhuì could do it,
but I cannot."
Moreover, those whom the living revere are the Sages,
and the teachings of the Sages are rituals and laws.
Speaking from the heart,
the laws of the Sages
cannot be changed.
Yet
Qín governed the world with commanderies and prefectures,
and no one could change it;
Emperor Hàn Wén abolished corporal punishment,
and no one could restore it.
Even the laws made by the Sages
were changed by later kings,
how much more so Téng, who relies on previous people,
should not necessarily succeed!
If everyone were to serve,
would this matter await a future Sage or not?
Moreover, serving and not serving
each have their
own people,
and those who advocate not serving
are always influenced by the period of three years (mourning).
Those who argue broadly interpret emotions and principles,
always leaning towards the Doctrine of the Mean.
They also say that if Téng is censured,
they fear that
the service of sacrificing one's life

How erroneous is this statement!
The emotion of loyalty and valor
initially acts without calculation.
If one calculates
before acting,
then one fears the law and does not fully commit one's life.
If there is any lack of full commitment,
then the state has constant laws.
Therefore, in ancient times, if an army was defeated abroad,
the family was executed at home.
If loyalty springs
from within,
or if one fears the law from without,
is there still room for hesitation and looking around?
If merits were not rewarded,
and crimes not punished,
then this analogy would be applicable.
There is no
moral teaching that supports one's children and younger brothers
when they do not exert themselves for their lord.
If they do not exert themselves for their lord,
then Wáng Jīng, though loyal, could not save his lord,
and though filial, did not care for his
parents.
These are criminals against family and nation,

The grace of ten generations
is not insignificant.
High merit and generous rewards
are not unrequited.
If the
state constitution has not let down Téng Tián,
then the question of advancement or obstruction

The debaters also say that Táng and Yú are too distant,

Seeking meaning in these words,
perhaps more blame lies with them.
The Later Hàn did not perish despite chaos,
and earlier historians still
attributed it to the power of several lords.
When the Wèi state was about to be established,
Xún Lìngjūn, with stern countenance, offered a dissenting opinion.
Dǒng Zhāo could not sleep on the lap of Sū Zé.
Jiǎ Chōng was humiliated by Yǔ Chún.
From
this, one can infer that
the righteousness of the world

Why utter such a sigh?
If one assumes that because the times are not like the Supreme Sovereigns,

As for Chén Píng silently obeying to avoid disaster,

Téng now has no life to protect,

In the past, Chén Shòu, during mourning,

Ruǎn Xián, in mourning,

Moreover, the wise and saintly, in their praise or blame,

Therefore, even if an act is shocking to the world,

Xì Qīn (郤詵) buried his mother in the rear
garden,

Jì Dī (日磾) killed his son without criticism,

Now, can it be said that because these two incidents are

It is clearly impossible.
Since it is impossible,

and there is
no need for much debate.
Téng (滕) is not a fellow townsman of this humble official,
nor have we associated,

If one considers Téng's (滕) strategies capable of defeating the enemy,
and his talents universally useful,
this indeed follows in the footsteps of
the ancients,
and is beyond criticism.
If he is a scholar,

which can be called excellent,

The thoughts
I harbor

If it is not a matter of profound principle,
why should there be much back and forth;
if it strikes a balance,
let the central authority decide.
Huán Wěi (桓偉) was advanced to the title of Ān Xī (安西),
then transferred to fill the post of Gōng Cáo (功曹),
and recommended Xiè Xuàn (謝絢) of Chén Jùn (陳郡) to replace himself,
saying:
"I have heard that if one knows a worthy man but does not recommend him,
that is why Zāng Wén (臧文) usurped his position;
if Xuān Zǐ (宣子) was able to yield,
the state of Jìn (晉) thereby found peace.
Xiān Zhī (鮮之) has humbly taken on the burden of others,
and mistakenly received excessive favor.
Since grace is amplified by righteousness,
