Knowing the difficulty of advancement,
I have repeatedly requested to resign,
yet my desire to withdraw
has not yet been granted even for a moment.
Night and day I harbor a chilling dread,
how dare I forget my fear.
I humbly observe that the acting Cān Jūn (參軍) Xiè Xuàn (謝絢)
is clear-minded, discerning, and upright,
his mind encompasses comprehensive virtues.
Though holding a position of minor importance,
insufficient to fully display his brilliance,
his ascent to merit will be gradual,
and he can somewhat be compared to others in his position.
I request to be allowed my humble shortcomings,
content to serve among the lowest ranks,
and that he be appointed as a worthy official,
which would truly meet the expectations of the multitude."
He entered service as Yuán Wài Sàn Qí Shì Láng (員外散騎侍郎),
Sī Tú Zuǒ Xī Shǔ (司徒左西屬),
Dà Sī Mǎ Láng Yá Wáng Lù Shì Cān Jūn (大司馬琅邪王錄事參軍),
and was subsequently promoted to Yù Shǐ Zhōng Chéng (御史中丞).
He was by nature firm and upright,
not bending to powerful nobles,
enforcing the law justly,
and greatly embodying the spirit of a director of justice.
His maternal nephew Liú Yì (劉毅)
held great power at the time;
the court and populace alike all submitted to him,
but Xiān Zhī (鮮之), devoted to Gāo Zǔ (高祖),
alone refused to yield his will to Yì (毅).
Yì (毅) deeply resented this.
In the sixth year of Yì Xī (義熙),
Xiān Zhī (鮮之) had the Zhì Shū Shì Yù Shǐ (治書侍御史) Qiū Huán (丘洹) impeach Yì (毅), saying:
"The imperial edict messenger Luó Dào Shèng (羅道盛) arbitrarily opened a memorial
and then secretly revealed confidential matters;
according to law, he should be executed in the market,
and the report for execution was issued.
However, Yì (毅), because Dào Shèng (道盛) held a marquisate,
arbitrarily suspended the pardon.
Considering Yì's (毅) meritorious virtue and high standing,
and his position as a chief minister,
since the killing was not his doing,
there is no reason for him to arbitrarily grant life.
Moreover, he submitted a memorial beforehand
but did not seek instructions afterward.
This is not what is meant by 'operating outside the household and beyond the borders.'
Zhōng Chéng (中丞) Xiān Zhī (鮮之) and Yì (毅) are maternal uncle and nephew,
and the regulations forbid them from correcting each other.
I request that Yì (毅)'s official position be removed."
The emperor made no inquiries.
At that time, a new regulation stipulated that chief officials who left office due to parental illness
were to be barred from public service for three years.
When Shān Yīn (山陰) Magistrate Shěn Shū Rèn (沈叔任) left his post due to his father's illness,
Xiān Zhī (鮮之) thereupon submitted a memorial arguing:
"Indeed, matters have relative weights,
so regulations involve granting and withholding;
something is curtailed here,
while something else is extended there.
There has never been a situation where a principle is unclear,
or a matter yields no benefit,
yet becomes a permanent regulation.
It must be that among those who leave office,
some might make false claims.
While false claims
indeed may sometimes occur,
how can one harm the great teaching of the world
by letting a minor issue damage the fundamental one?
Moreover, laws are generally established to encompass the few with the many,
and not to let the few contradict the many.
How much more so when preventing officials from leaving office obstructs the essence of filial love?
Furthermore, human nature tends towards honor and profit;
resigning from office is fundamentally not what needs to be prevented.
The reason for establishing such regulations
is that if one does not serve long in office,
then eagerness for advancement will arise.
Therefore, it curbs the desire for quick success
to uphold the reality of performance review.
Now, to dismiss one due to a parent's illness
and moreover impose a criminal penalty
is to act most contrary to righteousness and reason.
It is appropriate to revert to the old practice,
which would be just."
This was adopted.
Thereupon, for those from the second rank upwards whose parents had passed away,
or whose tombs were destroyed, or whose family members were ill, they could leave office
without being barred from public service.
When Liú Yì (劉毅) was about to take up his post in Jiāng Líng (江陵),
Gāo Zǔ (高祖) held a gathering in Jiāng Níng (江寧),
and all the court officials assembled.
Yì (毅) had always been fond of chū pú (摴蒱) (a dice game),
so a game was arranged.
Gāo Zǔ (高祖) and Yì (毅) gathered their pieces,
each getting half.
With money piled up hidden from view,
Yì (毅) called for Gāo Zǔ (高祖) to combine their stakes.
Yì (毅) first threw and got a zhì (雉) (pheasant, a specific dice outcome indicating a win),
Gāo Zǔ (高祖) was very displeased,
and after a long while, responded.
Everyone present leaned forward to watch.
When Gāo Zǔ (高祖) then threw,
all five dice turned up black (indicating a loss).
Yì (毅)'s expression darkened significantly,
and he said to Gāo Zǔ (高祖):
"I knew you wouldn't give a large mat to others!"
Xiān Zhī (鮮之) was greatly delighted,
running barefoot around the bed and shouting loudly,
his cries continuing one after another.
Yì (毅) was extremely displeased,
and said to him:
"What is this Lord Zhèng (鄭) doing?!"
There was no longer any decorum between nephew and uncle.
Gāo Zǔ (高祖) had spent his youth in military campaigns,
and was not extensively educated.
When he became prime minister,
he rather admired elegant customs,
and sometimes, when he spoke,
everyone would vaguely agree with him,
not daring to challenge him.
Xiān Zhī (鮮之) would always challenge him sharply and directly,
never granting him any leniency,
insisting that Gāo Zǔ (高祖) exhaust his words and be defeated in argument
before letting the matter drop.
Sometimes Gāo Zǔ (高祖) would feel shame and embarrassment,
his expression changing and his demeanor stirring.
Afterwards, he would say to others:
"I originally have no scholarly learning,
and my understanding of principles is especially shallow.
When I speak,
the worthy gentlemen mostly show me leniency,
but only Zhèng (鄭) does not.
He alone can thoroughly express one's thoughts,
and I am deeply grateful for this."
People at the time called him
"principled in remonstrance" (格佞).
From Zhōng Chéng (中丞), he was transferred to Sī Tú Zuǒ Cháng Shǐ (司徒左長史),
then Tái Wèi Zī Yì Cān Jūn (太尉諮議參軍),
and soon after was appointed Shì Zhōng (侍中),
and again served as Tái Wèi Zī Yì (太尉諮議).
In the twelfth year,
when Gāo Zǔ (高祖) campaigned in the north,
he was made Yòu Cháng Shǐ (右長史).
Xiān Zhī (鮮之)'s great-grandfather's tomb was in Kāi Fēng (開封),
three hundred *lǐ* (里) away.
He requested permission to visit and pay respects,
and Gāo Zǔ (高祖) sent him with cavalry.
At the initial establishment of the Sòng (宋) state,
he was transferred to Fèng Cháng (奉常).
Fó-Fó (佛佛) captured Guānzhōng (關中).
Gāo-zǔ (高祖) again desired to launch a northern expedition,
and his resolve was very strong.
Zhèng Xiān-zhī (鄭鮮之) submitted a memorial in remonstrance, saying:
"I humbly reflect that Your Sacred Majesty's (聖) strategy is profound and far-reaching,
and my foolish understanding has no place to express its thoughts.
However, in my humble opinion,
I secretly harbor some thoughts.
The fierce and cunning nature of the barbarians (虜) is evident.
Since their two defeats in Guānzhōng,
these were all due to commanders violating regulations,
not because of internal incidents
that led to external defeats and injuries.
When the barbarians hear that Your Highness (殿下) personally commands the six armies,
they will certainly believe they are being attacked,
and will heavily guard Tóng-guān (潼關);
this is the natural course of events.
If you charge forward with overwhelming might,
I truly see that it will not be easy.
If Your Imperial Carriage (輿駕) halts at Luò-yáng (洛),
then it will not be worth exhausting Your Sacred Majesty (聖躬).
Given this,
the opportune moment for advance or retreat
should be carefully considered.
The bandits (賊) dare not pursue their victory past Shǎn (陝),
because they are deterred by Your great might.
Now, if we fully utilize our military calculations,
and adapt to circumstances,
sending out an army to suppress and attack,
while the southern Xià (夏) is peaceful and tranquil,
the bandits will then fear what is to come,
and will never dare to move again.
If Your Imperial Carriage goes to Luò-yáng (洛) and returns,
the villains will develop a new inclination to speculate,
and will certainly instigate border troubles;
this is inevitable.
The people of Jiāng-nán (江南) are eagerly
awaiting Your Imperial Carriage.
and are unsure of the depth of the army's reach,
they will certainly believe that Your Highness is greatly displaying your might,
and has not yet returned.
People's hearts will be filled with fear;
this is also predictable.
Last year during the western campaign,
Liú Zhōng (劉鍾) was in grave danger.
The year before last, robbers plundered and destroyed Guǎng-zhōu (廣州),
and all the scholars and officials perished.
Within the heartland of the Sān Wú (三吳),
many counties were repeatedly defeated,
all due to exhaustive labor.
Moreover, it is heard that there were great floods everywhere,
and if the distant army and people are worn out
and scattered,
this is a natural consequence.
When Your Highness was in Péng-chéng (彭城),
robbers plundered and destroyed many counties.
This was not accidental;
these were all lawless villains.
Generally, if you follow and comfort them,
the common people will desire peace.
If you go against their wishes,
they will certainly cause chaos.
This is precisely why the ancients saved their people from troubles and hardships.
Hàn Gāo-zǔ (漢高祖) himself was trapped at Píng-chéng (平城),
Empress Lü (呂后) suffered humiliation from the Xiōng-nú (匈奴),
Wèi Wǔ-dì's (魏武) army was defeated at Chì-bì (赤壁),
Xuān Wǔ-dì (宣武) lost his army at Fāng-tóu (枋頭),
yet the achievements of Shén Wǔ-dì (神武)
were not diminished in the slightest.
How much less so when a detached army loses discipline,
which does not diminish the prestige of the imperial court!
Regarding the facts of the matter,
it is not a defeat.
Only Líng Shí (齡石) and others are pitiable.
If you proceed,
it might hasten disaster.
After repeated consideration,
I foolishly believe it is not necessary for Your Highness to personally campaign against minor robbers.
The western barbarians (虜) might become a threat to the Hé (河) and Luò (洛) regions.
Now, it is precisely appropriate to establish good relations with the northern barbarians (虜),
then Hé-nán (河南) will be peaceful.
If Hé-nán (河南) is peaceful,
then Jǐ (濟) and Sì (泗) will be tranquil.
I humbly pray for Your Sacred Majesty's (聖) discernment of my foolish thoughts."
When Gāo-zǔ (高祖) ascended the throne,
Zhèng Xiān-zhī (鄭鮮之) was promoted to Tàicháng (太常)
and Dūguān Shàngshū (都官尚書).
Zhèng Xiān-zhī (鄭鮮之) was straightforward and uninhibited in character.
When he was in Gāo-zǔ's (高祖) presence,
he spoke without concealment,
and people of the time greatly feared him.
Yet he was also reserved, earnest, and reliable,
providing for and aiding relatives and old friends.
He enjoyed traveling;
he would order his carriage without knowing where he was going,
following wherever the charioteer led.
He was particularly close to Gāo-zǔ (高祖).
The emperor (上) once held a banquet in the inner palace,
where all the high-ranking officials of the court (朝貴) were present,
but only Zhèng Xiān-zhī (鄭鮮之) was not summoned.
After everyone was seated,
he said to his ministers,
"Zhèng Xiān-zhī (鄭鮮之) will certainly come on his own."
Soon after, an announcement came from outside:
"Shàngshū (尚書) Zhèng Xiān-zhī (鮮之) has arrived at Shén-hǔ Mén (神虎門) seeking an audience."
Gāo-zǔ (高祖) laughed heartily and brought him in,
such was the closeness and favor he received.
In the second year of Yǒng-chū (永初)
he was appointed Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹),
then returned to serve as Dūguān Shàngshū (都官尚書),
and was given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
For his meritorious service in campaigns,
he was enfeoffed as a fifth-rank子 (zǐ) of Lóng-yáng Xiàn (龍陽縣).
He then became Yùzhāng Tàishǒu (豫章太守),
with a salary of two thousand shi (石) (中二千石).
In the third year of Yuán-jiā (元嘉),
Wáng Hóng (王弘) became Prime Minister (相),
and recommended Zhèng Xiān-zhī (鮮之) as Shàngshū Yòupúyè (尚書右僕射).
In the fourth year,
he died
at the age of sixty-four.
He was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (金紫光祿大夫).
His collected works were passed down to posterity.
His son Yīn (愔)
rose to the positions of Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎)
and Shǐxīng Tàishǒu (始興太守).
Péi Sōng-zhī (裴松之), courtesy name Shì-qī (世期),
was a native of Wén-xǐ (聞喜) in Hé-dōng (河東).
His grandfather, Mèi (昧),
was Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫).
His father, Guī (珪),
was Zhèngyuán Wàiláng (正員外郎).
Péi Sōng-zhī (松之), at the age of eight,
had mastered the Lún-yǔ (論語) and Máo Shī (毛詩).
He extensively read ancient texts,
and lived a simple and unadorned life.
At the age of twenty,
he was appointed Diànzhōng Jiàngjūn (殿中將軍).
This official position involved guarding the emperor's (晉孝武) left and right.
During the Tài-yuán (太元) era of Emperor Xiào-wǔ (孝武) of the Jìn (晉) dynasty, selection criteria were revised to choose prominent families for consultation.
Initially, Wáng Mào-zhī (王茂之) of Láng-yá (琅邪) and Xiè Yóu (謝輶) of Kuài-jī (會稽) were appointed,
both being highly regarded figures from the north and south.
His maternal uncle, Yǔ Kǎi (庾楷), was in Jiāng-líng (江陵)
and wished for Péi Sōng-zhī (松之) to go west.
He was offered the position of Xīnyě Tàishǒu (新野太守),
but due to circumstances, he did not go.
He was then appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng (員外散騎侍郎).
In the early Yì-xī (義熙) period,
he served as the magistrate of Gù-zhàng (故鄣) in Wú-xīng (吳興),
where he performed meritoriously.
He then became Shàngshū Cíbù Láng (尚書祠部郎).
Péi Sōngzhī believed that private steles established by families
deviated from the facts,
so he presented a memorial to the emperor, stating:
"The purpose of stele inscriptions
is to clearly show later generations;
without extraordinary achievements and exceptional virtues,
it is impossible to truly merit such an honor.
The greatest are those whose moral merits shine far and wide,
esteemed and celebrated by the world.
Next are those whose integrity and conduct are sublime,
whose lasting achievements are worthy of record.
But as for those whose talents are employed,
whose accomplishments are evident,
where their transforming influence reaches,
whose benevolent teachings spread far,
and whose praises are inscribed
and depend on engraving,
if they are not of this caliber,
then it is almost an act of presumption and profanation.
With customs corrupted and falsehood flourishing,
this extravagance has long persisted.
Thus, the inscription for Kǒng Kuī
was of the right person but for the wrong deeds;
Cài Yōng, when composing texts,
often felt ashamed.
And from that time onward,
the practice became more widespread.
Any official who was predisposed
would certainly have one erected for him,
making inscriptions rarely based on trustworthy facts,
and carving stones became a common practice of falsehood.
Truth and falsehood obscured each other,
almost leading to the neglect of what was genuinely excellent.
But to discuss only the cost,
it is also not commendable.
If no prohibitions are imposed,
this abuse will be endless.
I propose that all who wish to erect steles
should be required to report it to the throne.
Only if approved by the court
should they be permitted to do so.
This might prevent unsubstantiated claims
and highlight genuine achievements,
so that a hundred generations later,
people will know they are not false,
thus making their righteousness and trustworthiness worthy of admiration,
and their virtue reaching future generations."
Because of this, all such practices were halted.
When Gāozǔ campaigned in the north,
he led as Sīzhōu Cìshǐ.
He appointed Péi Sōngzhī as the Zhōuzhǔbù
and later promoted him to Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ.
After conquering Luòyáng,
[Sōngzhī remained in the province to manage affairs.
When the Sòng state was first established,
Máo Dézǔ was dispatched to Luòyáng.]
Gāozǔ issued an edict saying:
"Péi Sōngzhī is a talent for the imperial court;
he should not long remain in border duties.
He is now summoned to be Shìzǐ Xǐmǎ,
along with Yīn Jǐngrén.
Let him be informed of this."
At that time, there was a discussion about establishing music for the five ancestral temples.
Sōngzhī argued that the music for Consort Zāng's temple should also be the same as for the four other temples.
He was appointed Línglíng Nèishǐ,
then summoned to be Guózǐ Bóshì.
In the third year of Yuánjiā of Tàizǔ (426 CE),
after the execution of Sītú Xú Xiànzhī and others,
envoys were dispatched
to tour the empire.
Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì Yuán Yú and Sītú Zuǒ Xīyuàn Kǒng Miǎo were sent to Yángzhōu;
Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì Fàn Yōng
former Shàngshū Yòuchéng Kǒng Mò was sent to the two Yùzhōus (northern and southern);
Róngcóng Púyè Chē Zōng was sent to Qīngzhōu and Yǎnzhōu;
Sōngzhī was sent to Xiāngzhōu;
Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng Ruǎn Chángzhī was sent to Yōngzhōu;
former Jìnglíng Tàishǒu Yīn Dàoluán was sent to Yìzhōu;
Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì Lǐ Dānzhī was sent to Guǎngzhōu;
Lángzhōng Yīn Bīn was sent to Liángzhōu and Nánqínzhōu;
former Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng Ruǎn Yuánkè was sent to Jiāozhōu;
Fùmǎ Dūwèi and Fèng Cháoqǐng Pān Sīxiān was sent to Níngzhōu;
all also held the title of Sànqí Chángshì.
The imperial edict they proclaimed stated:
"In ancient times, kings toured to inspect merits,
and regional lords reported on their duties.
Otherwise, there were rituals of inspection and visitation,
and rules for respectful attendance.
This was to observe the people and establish governance,
to mandate affairs and examine achievements,
so that upper and lower ranks communicated,
and near and far were equally influenced.
Thus, their achievements shone for long ages,
and their dao persisted through distant years.
As for Us, being ignorant,
We have succeeded to this great undertaking.
We are reverent and fearful in Our position,
ignorant of the way of governance.
We worry day and night,
as if standing on the edge of an abyss.
We fear that the national customs are in decline,
and the people's morals are becoming false;
that calamities disturb harmony,
and floods and droughts harm livelihoods.
Although We personally attend to various matters
and strive to promote what is suitable,
Our imperial duties are vast,
and We find many shortcomings upon reflection.
Our administration and punishments may be amiss,
and We have not been able to hear full reports.
Is it that Our sincerity has not been trusted,
preventing the hearts of the multitude from expressing themselves fully?
The shame of failing to heed the people's cries
rests with Us alone.
As years have been difficult
and the royal way not unified,
the rites of imperial tours
have been abandoned and not restored.
We look upon the common people
and do not forget their welfare.
to travel through commanderies and districts,
to personally meet with Cìshǐ and officials holding salaries of two thousand shi,
to express Our utmost sincerity,
to widely inquire about key governance matters,
to observe the administration of officials,
to seek out the grievances of the people,
to commend integrity and conduct,
and to inquire about their hardships.
As for the customs and practices, their merits and faults,
all should follow the Zhou rites.
Each envoy shall write a detailed report
and submit it upon return,
so that We may clearly understand,
as if We were personally observing.
Gentlemen and officials,
each of you should serve with utmost care and respect,
without slacking in your efforts.
If there are any strategic counsels,
sincere words,
present them to the envoy,
without concealing or omitting anything.
We shall respectfully accept good advice
to remedy Our shortcomings.
Strive diligently,
and meet Our intentions."
Péi Sōngzhī
returned from his mission and memorialized, saying: "Your minister has heard that the Way of Heaven
aids the brilliant in their descent, and that the virtue of a sovereign reaches its zenith in vast and expansive governance.
The sagely rulers of antiquity
universally extended their benevolence from the heart.
Thus, when sagely thought resided in their person,
the age harmonized spontaneously;
when ritual was practiced across the Jiānghàn region,
its civilizing influence spread far.
Therefore, they could leave behind great and enduring eulogies,
and expand the glorious principles of the Zhōu dynasty's creation.
Your humble servant observes that Your Majesty, with divine wisdom and profound understanding,
aligns with the Way across all ages.
Residing in the splendid palace with your crown,
your heart encompasses the eight directions.
You deliberate on the imperfection of reverent instruction [jìngfū],
and worry that enlightenment and renown are not flourishing.
You inquire clearly of the common people
and pity the [yǒng] orphans and the widowed.
Your great decree, like flowing water,
reaches all four corners.
Your far-reaching plans are manifested in the *Yǎ* and *Gào*,
and your benevolent instructions are broadcast to distant regions.
For this reason, all within the realm look up and sing your praises,
and those speaking diverse languages are all pleased.
None fail to sing and leap for joy,
inscribing your imperial virtue.
Some, supporting the old and leading the young,
express their delight by the roadside.
This is truly because the nurturing influence has flowed widely,
causing them to forget its self-origin.
A thousand years come together in one moment,
and it is in this [time] that it resides.
Your minister, mistakenly entrusted with a selective appointment,
has been disgraced by being placed among the prominent ranks.
Presumptuously, with my limited abilities,
I contemplate extending purity to the eight directions,
yet I am unable to clearly convey the sagely will
or solemnly clarify moral transformation.
Promotions and demotions are without order,
and what I discover and promote is rarely heard of.
I am ashamed and fearful, restless,
and do not know what to do.
I respectfully submit twenty-four articles,
and I have diligently drafted a memorial for each matter.
I respectfully refer to the imperial edict of the *Guǐmǎo* year,
which states that for the gains and losses in customs and rituals,
everything should follow the rites of the Zhōu dynasty.
Each matter should be written about separately
and then fully memorialized.
I will carefully compile the writings for each matter and attach them later."
Péi Sōngzhī
was highly praised by commentators for his understanding of the envoy's duty.
He was transferred to be a Central Secretariat Gentleman and Grand Arbiter of the two prefectures of Sī and Jì.
The Emperor commanded him to annotate Chén Shòu's
*Sānguó Zhì*. Péi Sōngzhī
gathered biographies and records, expanding on unusual accounts.
When it was finished, he presented it to the Emperor.
The Emperor praised it,
saying:
"This is indeed immortal!"
He was sent out as the Administrator of Yǒngjiā,
where he diligently cared for the common people,
and officials and people found him convenient.
He returned to serve as a Gentleman-in-Waiting,
[一九] and again led the Grand Arbiters of the two prefectures.
Soon after, he was sent out as the Administrator of Nán Lángyá.
In his fourteenth year, he retired,
and was appointed Grand Master of Scattered Cavalry.
Soon after, he led the National University Scholar,
was promoted to Grand Master of Grand Eminence,
and his position as Scholar remained as before.
He continued Hé Chéngtiān's
National History, but before he could compile it,
in the twenty-eighth year,
he died
at the age of eighty.
His son, Péi Yǐn,
was the Southern Central Military Advisor.
Péi Sōngzhī's
writings and treatises and his *Jìn Jì*, and Péi Yǐn's annotation of Sīmǎ Qiān's
*Shǐ Jì*, both circulated in the world.
Hé Chéngtiān
was a native of Tán, Dōnghǎi.
His paternal granduncle, Hé Lún,
was the General of the Right Guard of Jìn.
Hé Chéngtiān
lost his father at the age of five. His mother, Lady Xú,
was Gǔang's elder sister.
She was intelligent and learned,
so Hé Chéngtiān
was steeped in moral instruction from a young age, and was well-versed in the classics, history, and the Hundred Schools.
His paternal uncle was the Magistrate of Yìyáng,
and he followed him to his official post.
In the fourth year of Lóng'ān,
Huán Wěi, the Southern Barbarian Commandant, appointed him Military Advisor.
At that time, Yīn Zhòngkān and Huán Xuán, among others, successively raised armies against the imperial court.
Hé Chéngtiān,
fearing that the calamities would not end, resigned his post and returned to Yìyáng.
At the beginning of the Righteous Banner campaign,
Táo Yánshòu, the Duke of Chángshā, appointed him Military Advisor of his Auxiliary State Administrator's office,
and sent him to convey respects to Gāozǔ.
He was then appointed Magistrate of Liúyáng,
but soon left the post and returned to the capital.
Liú Yì, the General Who Calms the Army, garrisoned Gūshú
and appointed him Acting Military Advisor.
Liú Yì
once went on an outing, and Chén Mǎn, a clerk from Yānlíng County, shot at birds.
An arrow accidentally struck a direct officer.
Although no one was injured,
he was sentenced to public execution.
Hé Chéngtiān
argued: "In judicial cases, judgment should prioritize intent,
and if there is doubt, lean towards leniency.
In the past, when someone startled Emperor Hàn Wéndì's
imperial carriage horse, Zhāng Shìzhī
impeached him for violating the imperial procession, and the punishment was merely a fine.
Why?
To make it clear that he had no intention of startling the horse.
Therefore, because of the importance of the imperial carriage,
he was not subjected to an extraordinary penalty.
Now, Chén Mǎn's
intention was to shoot birds, not to intentionally injure someone.
According to the law, accidentally injuring someone
incurs a three-year prison sentence.
How much more so when there is no injury?
A minor penalty is sufficient."
He was sent out to be the Magistrate of Wǎnlíng.
Zhào Dàn
became the Commandant Who Calms the Barbarians and Administrator of Xúnyáng,
and invited him to be his Chief Clerk.
Soon after, he left the post.
Gāozǔ
appointed him Acting Military Advisor of the Grand Commandant. When Gāozǔ
attacked Liú Yì, he left Zhūgě Chángmín
as Supervisor of the Army. Zhūgě Chángmín
secretly harbored different intentions. Liú Mùzhī dismissed others and asked Hé Chéngtiān:
"What do you think of the success of the Duke's current expedition?"
Hé Chéngtiān
replied: "I am not worried that the western campaign will not be decided in time, [二０] but I have another concern.
When the Duke returned from Zuǒlǐ to Shítou a few years ago,
it was rather casual.
Now that he is returning,
he should be more cautious."
Liú Mùzhī
said: "No one but you would have spoken these words.
I wished that Liú Láng of Dāntú would return home
some days ago, but I fear it is no longer possible."
He was appointed Erudite of the Imperial Academy.
In the eleventh year of Yìxī,
he became Military Advisor to the Crown Prince Who Conquers the Barbarians,
then transferred to Central Military Advisor to the General of the Central Guard,
and Magistrate of Qiántáng.
When Gāozǔ
was in Shòuyáng and the Sòng
platform was established, he was summoned to be Minister of Rites in the Department of State Affairs,
and, with Fù Liàng, jointly compiled court ceremonies.
At the end of Yǒngchū,
he was appointed Palace Censor for Judicial Matters of the Southern Palace.
Xiè Huì (謝晦) garrisoned Jiānglíng (江陵),
and requested to be Nánmán Chángshǐ (南蠻長史).
At that time there was a certain Yǐn Jiā (尹嘉),
whose family was poor.
His mother, Xióng (熊), personally mortgaged herself for money
to repay Jiā's (嘉) debt.
He was tried for unfilial conduct and sentenced to death.
Chéngtiān (承天) deliberated, saying:
"Having received a decree from the prefecture,
I am to fully deliberate on the capital punishment case of Yǐn Jiā (尹嘉).
It states that the legal official Gě Téng (葛滕) petitioned,
saying 'If a mother accuses her son of unfilial conduct,
permission to kill him shall be granted.'
The law states,
'Regarding those who violate teachings and decrees,
and are deficient in reverence and respect,
if their parents wish to kill them,
it shall all be permitted.'
What is accused shall be believed only if it is sought, and then permitted.
Carefully examining the facts and the original intent,
Jiā's (嘉) mother, Xióng (熊), offered herself as collateral for money
to repay her son's debt.
Although Jiā (嘉) violated teachings and righteousness,
Xióng (熊) made no plea for him to be killed.
Xióng (熊) sought to save his life, yet now he is to be killed;
this is not 'following what is sought.'
and ended with a ' hòa mài ' (和賣) resulting in punishment.
Leaning on both extremes,
both mother and son are guilty.
Téng's (滕) petition is based on the legal text,
but it is not applicable to this particular article.
What Jiā (嘉) preserved was great,
and the principle is difficult to articulate.
However, as the enlightened teachings have been issued,
we should pity his foolish ignorance.
For 'illustrating virtue and being cautious with punishments'
is how King Wén (文王) showed compassion to his inferiors;
'deliberating on judgments and delaying death'
is how Zhōngfú (中孚) extended transformation.
In terms of human sentiment, a mother hides for her son;
in terms of respect, it is beyond what ritual can encompass.
Now to abandon the assessment of begging for leniency
and adhere to the article for requesting execution,
demanding the virtue of reverence and respect
from the hungry and cold common people,
is truly not 'resolving doubts in favor of leniency'
nor 'preferring to err on the side of guilt.'
I humbly believe that Jiā's (嘉) death should be reduced
to widely extend the grace of spring.
Xióng's (熊) fault should be pardoned
to clarify the appropriateness of a son's concealment by his mother.
Then even Pútíng (蒲亭), though humble,
can be compared in virtue to the glorious brightness;
and the xièyú (䄡魚), a tiny creature,
will not be uniquely omitted from today's transformation."
Before the case was decided,
an amnesty occurred, and all were pardoned.
Huì (晦) was promoted to the title of Wèijiāngjūn (衞將軍),
and transferred to Zīyì Cānjūn (諮議參軍),
also leading the Jìshì (記室).
In Yuánjiā (元嘉) 3rd year (426 CE),
Huì (晦) was about to be suppressed.
His younger brother, Huángménláng (黃門郎) Shíhú (石胡), secretly sent him a letter to inform him.
Huì (晦) asked Chéngtiān (承天):
"If it truly is so,
what do you advise me to do?"
Chéngtiān (承天) said:
"With the sovereign's authority,
to move the whole empire to attack one province—
the difference in scale is great,
and the distinction between right and wrong is also different.
To seek completeness beyond the borders is the best plan.
The next best is to send trusted men to garrison Yìyáng (義陽) with troops,
while the general leads the army to fight one battle at Xiàkǒu (夏口).
If defeated,
then flee to Yìyáng (義陽) to exit through the northern border;
that is the second best plan."
Huì (晦) remained silent for a long time, then said:
"Jīngchǔ (荊楚) is a martial nation;
its military strength is abundant.
We should first engage in a decisive battle;
fleeing will not be too late."
He had Chéngtiān (承tiān) draft proclamations and manifestos.
Huì (晦) believed that the governor of Xiāngzhōu (湘州), Zhāng Shào (張邵), would certainly not side with him,
and wished to send a thousand men to attack him.
Chéngtiān (承天) believed that Shào's (邵) intentions were still unknown
and it was not appropriate to attack immediately.
At that time, Shào's (邵) elder brother, Màodù (茂度), was in Yìzhōu (益州)
and had always been on good terms with Huì (晦),
so Huì (晦) stopped and did not send troops.
Former Yìzhōu Cǐshǐ (益州刺史) Xiāo Mózī (蕭摹之) and former Bāxī Tàishǒu (巴西太守) Liú Dàochǎn (劉道產) returned to Jiānglíng (江陵) after resigning their posts.
Huì (晦) intended to kill them.
Chéngtiān (承天) exerted all his strength to rescue them,
and both were completely saved.
After Huì (晦) was defeated,
Chéngtiān (承天) remained in the prefecture and did not follow him.
When Dào Yànzhī (到彥之) arrived at Mǎtóu (馬頭),
Chéngtiān (承天) personally went to confess his guilt.
Yànzhī (彥之), seeing his sincerity,
pardoned him
and made him act as the administrator of the Nánmán Fǔ (南蠻府).
In the 7th year (430 CE),
Yànzhī (彥之) launched a northern expedition
and requested Chéngtiān (承天) to be Yòujūn Lùshì (右軍錄事).
When Yànzhī (彥之) was defeated and retreated,
Chéngtiān (承天), due to his talent not being suited for military affairs,
was spared punishment.
He was then appointed Shàngshū Diànzhōngláng (尚書殿中郎)
and concurrently Zuǒchéng (左丞).
In Wúxīng (吳興) Yúháng (餘杭) district, a man named Báo Dàojǔ (薄道舉) became a robber.
A decree was issued that all relatives within the ' jīqīn ' (朞親) degree of kinship (one year of mourning) in the same household
should be conscripted into the army.
Dàojǔ’s (道舉) younger paternal cousins, Dài Gōng (代公) and Dào Shēng (道生), were both within the ' dàgōng ' (大功) degree of kinship (nine months of mourning),
which was not among the categories subject to conscription.
The law, however, considered Dài Gōng (代公) and others' mother as a ' jīqīn ' (朞親),
meaning the sons should follow their mother and be conscripted.
Chéngtiān (承天) deliberated, saying:
"Upon reviewing the robbery decree,
only ' jīqīn ' (朞親) in the same household are to be conscripted.
' Dàgōng ' (大功) are not in this category.
[二一]For women, there are three subordinations:
when unmarried, she follows her father; when married, she follows her husband;
when her husband dies, she follows her son.
Now, Dàojǔ (道舉) became a robber.
If his paternal uncle were still alive,
the decree would apply for conscription,
and it would naturally be appropriate for his wife and children to manage the household.
However, at the time of the robbery,
his paternal uncle had already died.
Dài Gōng (代公) and Dào Shēng (道生) are both paternal cousins,
within the ' dàgōng ' (大功) degree of kinship,
and should not be conscripted.
Now, if the paternal aunt is considered a ' jīqīn ' (朞親),
and Dài Gōng (代公) is ordered to be conscripted following his mother,
it both violates the decree that ' dàgōng ' (大功) are not to be conscripted
and disregards the principle of women's three subordinations.
This arises because the official in charge adheres to the letter of ' jīqīn ' (朞親)
without distinguishing between male and female,
and, overly cautious to avoid suspicion and blame,
has created this doubt.
[二二]I fear this is not in line with the benevolent spirit of the imperial court regarding punishments.
I propose that Dài Gōng (代公) and the other mother and sons should all be pardoned."
When the late Sītú Yuàn (司徒掾) Kǒng Miǎo (孔邈) submitted a memorial,
Miǎo (邈) had already passed away and been entombed.
The deliberators suggested that Miǎo's (邈) name should not be used,
and instead it should be presented under the name of the current official.
Chéngtiān (承天) again deliberated, saying:
"The reason a deceased person's name should not be used in a memorial
is not based on any other meaning;
it is merely out of a slight aversion to bad omens.
A memorial can be delayed for a long time,
sometimes for a year or more.
In an enlightened age,
matters should be handled with simplicity.
Petty aversions and minor taboos
should all be swept away."
Chéngtiān (承天) was by nature stubborn
and could not humble himself before the court officials.
He often used his strengths to disparage his colleagues
and was not favored by Púshè (僕射) Yīn Jǐngrén (殷景仁).
He was sent out as Héngyáng Nèishǐ (衡陽內史).
Formerly, in the west, he had many disagreements with the literati.
In the commandery, he was not just and pure,
and was impeached by the provincial authorities,
arrested and imprisoned.
He was released due to an amnesty.
In the 16th year (439 CE),
he was appointed Zhùzuò Zuǒláng (著作佐郎)
to compile the national history.
Chéngtiān (承天) was already old,
while the other Zhùzuò Zuǒláng (著作佐郎) were all young men from prominent families.
[二三]Xún Bózǐ (荀伯子) from Yǐngchuān (潁川) mocked him,
often calling him 'nǎimǔ' (嬭母, wet nurse).
Chéngtiān (承天) said:
"You should say 'the phoenix will bear nine chicks,'
what's this about a 'nǎimǔ' (嬭母)!"
Soon after, he was transferred to Tàizǐ Shuàigēnglìng (太子率更令),
retaining his position as Zhùzuò (著作).
At that time, Dīng Kuàng (丁況) from Dānyáng (丹陽) and others had not buried their dead after long periods of mourning.
Chéng Tiān (承天) deliberated and said:
“The ‘return burial’ mentioned in the Rítuals [of Zhōu]
must refer to times of desolation and scarcity,
which is why it permitted burying according to one’s means, without seeking completeness.
Dīng Kuàng’s (丁況) three families,
for several decades,
〔二四〕always buried without coffins,
which truly stemmed from shallow affection and meager gratitude,
akin to beasts.
I humbly believe that Dīng Bǎo (丁寶) and his peers, having lived together for years,
never admonished them with righteousness
or restrained them with laws.
In the winter of the sixteenth year,
since there were no new laws
and old regulations had not been reiterated,
what was the urgency
for suddenly correcting them?
Perhaps it arose from disputes among neighbors,
thus initiating this discussion.
It is heard that in various places to the east,
such cases are numerous,
〔二五〕and especially so in Jiāngxī (江西) and north of the Huái (淮) River.
If only these three individuals are punished,
it will hardly lead to rectification.
Opening such a precedent
will cause mutual fear and agitation,
and local communities and county officials
will compete in seeking illicit gains.
Once bribery prevails,
lawsuits will certainly multiply,
and I fear it will tarnish the sagely beauty of ‘governing a great state as if cooking small fish.’
Your humble servant believes that Dīng Kuàng (丁況) and the other three families
can temporarily be left unquestioned.
Based on this, a decree should be established:
if common people do not bury according to the rites,
their peers should immediately report it.
However, after three years of mourning have passed,
they should not be allowed to pursue accusations.
This would be appropriate for the matter.”
In the nineteenth year,
the Guózǐxué (國子學) [National University] was established,
and he was appointed Guózǐ Bóshì (國子博士) [Erudite of the National University] in his current official capacity.
When the Crown Prince lectured on the Xiàojīng (孝經) [Classic of Filial Piety],
Chéng Tiān (承天), along with the Zhōngshùzǐ (中庶子) Yán Yánzhī (顏延之), jointly served as scripture reciters.
Shortly thereafter,
he was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) [Imperial Censor-in-Chief].
At that time, the Suǒlǔ (索虜) [Tuoba captives] invaded the border,
and Tài Zǔ (太祖) consulted his ministers on strategies to awe the barbarians and control distant lands.
Chéng Tiān (承天) submitted a memorial, saying: I humbly observe the report from the northern border,
that the captives have encroached upon Qīng (青) and Yǎn (兗) Commanderies.
Your Heavenly Benevolence has observed this,
pitying the common people,
and has broadly sought counsel from all strategies,
to govern military affairs.
Though I am foolish and untalented,
I have been included in the inquiry.
I secretly recall that the Xiǎnyǔn (獫狁) reported difficulties
from ancient times.
During the height of the Zhōu (周) dynasty,
Nán Zhòng (南仲) led chariots out;
when the Hàn (漢) dynasty flourished,
Wèi Qīng (衛青) and Huò Qùbìng (霍去病) exerted their strength.
Although
they watered their horses in the Hàn Hǎi (瀚海) [Gobi Desert]
and raised their banners at Qílián (祁連) [Mountains],
the tasks were difficult and the labor extensive,
the world was in turmoil,
and supplies were transported across the sea,
〔二六〕with resources extending to boats and chariots.
The fierce and cunning barbarians,
unwilling
to be submissive,
exchanged losses and retaliated,
barely compensating one another.
In the final years of Emperor Xuān’s (宣) reign,
they encountered internal strife,
and by overthrowing the fallen and securing the existing,
they finally achieved submission.
Since Jìn (晉) lost the Central Plains,
and the Róng Dí (戎狄) [barbarians] invaded and harassed,
for over a hundred years,
there was no leisure to consider the northern captives.
When Dà Sòng (大宋) established its fortune,
its martial might shone in both directions,
and the barbarians, cherishing virtue and fearing might,
submitted themselves.
Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
you have maintained control and nurtured them,
and for over ten years,
tributes and interpreters have been ceaseless.
Last year, when the three princes were sent to guard the frontiers,
intending to revive distant ambitions,
the bestial hearts were easily startled,
and thus suspicion and fear arose,
violating their trust and covenants,
deeply creating discord.
Given their greed for harm and unrestrained cruelty,
there is no way they will reform themselves.
I fear that the warnings of beacon fires
will begin from this.
Your humble servant is by nature
mediocre and weak,
and my talent is not suited for military affairs.
Following my limited insight,
I have carefully composed the ‘Anbiān Lùn’ (安邊論) [Discourse on Border Pacification].
My thoughts are shallow and trifling,
〔二七〕and I fear they are not worth adopting.
If it could be discussed among the court officials,
and
the similarities and differences debated and scrutinized,
perhaps it might stimulate various considerations,
and exhaust all possible strategies,
with all strengths and weaknesses presented,
so that what is appropriate and inappropriate can be seen.
The discourse states: In the Hàn (漢) era, discussions on strategies to guard against the Xiōngnú (匈奴) [Huns]
were merely of two types:
military men exhausted plans for conquest,
while scholars advocated treaties of peace and kinship.
Assessing their words,
they each
had far-reaching ambitions.
Furthermore, outside the desert,
the Hu (胡) enemies constrained them,
so they could not break through the front and prolong the days [of battle],
planning to expand themselves.
It must be that in past years, the people of Jì (冀) region,
those who attached
themselves to our civilization, were numerous.
With the two prefectures bordering [them],
and the three princes sent to guard the frontiers,
as strategic deployments were expanded,
grand plans were about to be implemented.
Men and women eagerly looked forward,
and both Chinese and barbarians admired our righteousness.
Therefore, [the barbarians], blinded by petty
gains,
became boastful and extravagant,
outwardly displaying their remaining strength,
and internally bolstering their false populace.
Now, if we strive to maintain nurturing and allow them to reform,
although they cannot yet be bound and brought to the northern palace gate,
it would still be sufficient
to pacify
the border regions.
However, matters of peace and kinship are grave,
and require the full calculations of the imperial ancestral temple.
Truly, my foolishness and shortcomings
cannot fully articulate them.
If we were to pursue the ambitions of Wèi Qīng (衛青) and Huò Qùbìng (霍 Qùbìng) in the Hàn Hǎi (瀚海),
the
current circumstances are not the same,
and the achievement of success would also differ.
Although the brigands have been accustomed to war for a long time,
〔二八〕and fully occupy Yān (燕) and Zhào (趙),
straddling Qín (秦) and Wèi (魏),
the dangers of the mountains and rivers
remain eternally
the same.
Unless we greatly cultivate the fields of the Huái (淮) and Sì (泗) rivers,
and internally strengthen Qīng (青) and Xú (徐) prefectures,
so that the people have surplus savings
and the fields have accumulated grain,
and then dispatch Fāng (方) and Shào (召) [generals],
to lead the tiger legions,
with a hundred thousand elite troops,
so that one expedition can sweep them away,
otherwise it is not worth slightly exerting the royal army
and tiring the world.
Why do I say this?
Today, the remaining populace is accustomed to chaos,
their ambition is to steal
peace.
Not all are ashamed of wearing barbarian robes
or admire our distant caps and robes;
they merely suffer from severe harm and humiliation,
with no place to settle their lives.
Therefore, carrying their infants on their backs, they return to our state,
one after another.
Since the captives
cannot win decisively or act rationally,
attacking cities and seizing territory,
they instead dispatch light cavalry to raid,
eager to drive away the remnants.
This is precisely why they quickly incur resentment and invite disaster,
leading to their day of demise.
Now,
if we send troops to pursue and punish them,
retaliating for their invasion and violence,
greatly sweeping through Yōu (幽) and Jì (冀),
slaughtering cities and breaking down settlements,
then Your Sacred Dynasty, which loves and nurtures the common people,
is currently saving them with the Way.
If we merely wish
If we appease their submission,
punish their offenses and solace the people,
then swift horses will gallop away
and refuse to be conscripted.
It will merely incur immense costs
without harming them.
Again, if we deploy elite forces deep into their territory,
kill enemies
and defeat armies,
should the humiliation and suffering not be completely eradicated,
then a cornered beast will think of fighting.
Acts of revenge
will then become endless.
This was the last resort of the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
and the regret of Lúntái.
Securing the borders and holding firm
is the best strategy.
Your servant believes that the strategy for securing the borders
is fully recorded in historical documents.
Lǐ Mù stated its beginning,
Yán Yóu emphasized its essentials,
and the general outline
is thus presented.
The hegemonies of Cáo and Sūn,
with talents equally matched and wisdom rivaling,
in the region between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
did not occupy several hundred *lǐ* each.
Wèi abandoned Héféi
and retreated to secure Xīnchéng.
Wú fortified
Jiānglíng,
〔二九〕 and moved its people to the southern bank.
The garrisons of Rúxū
settled their families at Xiànxī.
And at Xiāngyáng,
〔三０〕 where commoners and barbarians were scattered and mixed,
Jìn Xuānwáng thought it proper
to relocate them south of the Miǎn River
to populate the area north of the river.
〔三一〕Cáo Shuǎng did not permit it,
and consequently lost Zǔzhōng.
These are all clear precedents from former generations.
Why is this so?
Outlying areas for scouting
are not
places for animal husbandry.
Battlefields
are not towns for farming and sericulture.
〔三二〕Therefore, consolidate defenses and clear the fields
to await their arrival,
and prepare armor and repair weapons
to take advantage of their weariness.
Although times change from ancient to modern,
and circumstances vary in strength and weakness,
protecting the people and preserving the territory
does not deviate from this path.
To summarize, there are four points: First, relocate the distant to the near;
Second, dredge
and restore city moats;
Third, organize paired carts and oxen;
Fourth, levy arms according to the number of adult males.
Good defenders should manage their lands,
and brave commanders should display their strategies.
Hunting expeditions should publicize their commands
and orders,
and sacrificial rituals should instruct in integrity and shame.
Grant ranks to entice them,
and establish prohibitions to awe them.
Corvée and taxes should have limits,
with leniency and strictness complementing each other.
In about ten years,
the people will know
righteous ways.
Then, select generals and assign elite troops,
raising banners north of the clouds.
Winds will sweep over Hé and Jì,
lightning will clear Sōng.
Yān bows will be broken and turned back,
Dài horses will have their feet crushed.
Qín will have its
right arm severed,
Wú will have its left shoulder cut off.
Meritorious deeds will be inscribed on the slopes of Yānrán,
and soldiers feasted in the bends of Jīnwēi.
Although the bandits' chaos and demise are evident,
and their weakness makes them easy to capture,
if the heavenly timing and human affairs
are not entirely aligned,
it is advisable to suppress eagerness and await the opportunity,
carefully considering the calculations.
If border garrisons
are not increased,
and settlements are scattered across the wilds,
with diligence and idleness taught differently,
and rich and poor having disparate resources,
the people in border regions
will often harbor dual loyalties.
The barbarians, in their coming and going,
do not have a fundamental livelihood,
making them difficult
to command
and easy to be swayed.
Moreover, the nature of the cunning barbarians is
to eat meat and wear skins,
taking galloping as their elegance,
and hunting as their farmland.
They do not have the security
of carriages,
nor the protection of palaces.
Braving wind and rain
is not considered toil,
sleeping in the open and bedding on grass
is their usual nature.
When victorious, they contend for profit;
when defeated, they are not ashamed to flee.
They may come
swiftly,
while we are already exhausted.
Furthermore, this spring, having crossed the Jì River,
they have already gained their advantage.
Presumptuously riding on their victory,
they have not yet feared divine punishment.
By late autumn,
they may again send themselves to their deaths.
Like whirlwind cavalry and ant-like gatherings,
light troops assemble like birds,
trampling crops
and burning villages.
Even if border generals are resourceful,
it is unclear how they will defend against this.
If large armies are continuously stationed,
many farmers will inevitably be taken from their work.
If chariots are dispatched and couriers gallop,
mobilization will inevitably be slow.
If gold is scattered for rewards,
expenditures will inevitably be great.
If residents are replaced by temporary garrisons,
resentment and neglect will inevitably be rampant.
How can this compare to adapting to the people's
residences,
and simultaneously cultivating farming and warfare?
There would be no toil of moving large populations,
but the reality of defense.
Regarding the advantages and disadvantages,
the disparity is vast.
First, relocate the distant to the near,
to populate the interior.
Currently, the old inhabitants of Qīng and Yǎn provinces,
and the recently submitted people of Jì Province,
number twenty thousand families on the border,
〔三三〕 these are
the enemy's resources.
Now they can all be moved inland.

able-bodied men fit for battle.
The remaining weak and infirm

Two thousand warriors

bandits.
Thirdly, assemble pairs of carts and oxen

Estimating the resources of a thousand households,

Suppose a city cannot be held;

Since they already live in family groups,

With clear orders established beforehand,

Fourthly, assign weapons according to the number of able-bodied men,

In a town of a thousand households,

Your servant has heard that military and civilian affairs have different appearances,

while military and agricultural pursuits are simultaneously cultivated

The suitability of offense and defense

In your servant's estimation,

Guǎn Zǐ governed Qí

Ultimately, they established their might and secured their hegemony,
realizing their aspirations and undertakings.
This was not

Liáng's reliance on common soldiers

Since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,

The great hunts are no longer the rites of the former kings,

All this is the harm

Now, if we relocate people to fill the interior,

〔三七〕Their peer groups would be established,

Affections would grow through familiarity,

In day battles, they would recognize each other by sight and come to each other's aid.

This is one aspect of military training,

Critics will certainly argue that ancient cities are ruined

〔四一〕
Chéngtiān (承天) was always fond of playing *yì* (弈),
and it often caused him to neglect his duties.
Tàizǔ (太祖) bestowed upon him a *júzi* (局子) (a chessboard or a set of pieces).
Chéngtiān (承天) submitted a memorial expressing his gratitude.
The Emperor replied:
"The gift of the *júzi* (局子) (chessboard/pieces),
how is it not like Zhāng Wǔ (張武)'s gold?"
Chéngtiān (承天) was also skilled at playing the *zhēng* (箏).
The Emperor again bestowed upon him a *zhēng* (箏) adorned with silver.
Chéngtiān (承天) and Shàngshū Zuǒcéng (尚書左丞) Xiè Yuánsù (謝元素) were not on good terms.
The two competed in monitoring each other's transgressions in the two bureaus,
repeatedly impeaching each other.
Tàiwèi (太尉) Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng (江夏王義恭) was annually granted an expenditure of thirty million *qián* (錢),
fifty thousand bolts of cloth,
and seventy thousand *hú* (斛) of rice.
Yìgōng (義恭) was always extravagant,
and his spending was often insufficient.
In the twenty-first year,
he prematurely exchanged next year's allocation with the Shàngshū (尚書).
According to the old regulations, any expenditure of two hundred thousand *qián* (錢)
or five hundred bolts of cloth or more,
must be reported to the emperor.
Yuán (元) nevertheless ordered a deliberation to grant two million *qián* (錢) to the Tàiwèi (太尉).
When the matter was discovered,
Yuán (元) then sent a clerk to obtain the approval of Púyè (僕射) Mèng Yǐ (孟顗).
Yuán (元) had just been appointed Tàiwèi Cányì Cānjūn (太尉諮議參軍) at the time,
but had not yet been formally installed.
He was impeached by Chéngtiān (承天).
The Emperor was greatly angered,
and sent Yuán (元) back to his hometown,
imprisoning him for life.
Yuán (元) also reported at the time that Chéngtiān (承天) had sold four hundred and seventy bundles of hay to officials
at an exorbitant price.
Chéngtiān (承天) was consequently allowed to hold office in plain clothes (a form of demotion).
Yuán (元)'s courtesy name was Yǒuzōng (有宗);
he was a native of Yángxià (陽夏), Chénjùn (陳郡),
and a paternal cousin of Línchuān Nèishǐ Língyùn (臨川內史靈運).
He was recognized for his talent and learning,
and died in imprisonment.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Chéngtiān (承天) was promoted to Tíngwèi (廷尉),
but before he could take office,
the Emperor wanted to appoint him to the Língbù (吏部).
Having already received a secret imperial decree,
Chéngtiān (承天) leaked it.
He was dismissed from office for this transgression,
and died at home
at the age of seventy-eight.
Before this,
the treatise on rites comprised eight hundred volumes.
Chéngtiān (承天) abridged and combined them,
categorizing them by type,
resulting in three hundred volumes in total.
These, along with his former commentaries, miscellaneous writings, collected essays, and treatises, all circulated in the world.
〔四二〕He also revised and finalized the Yuánjiā (元嘉) calendar,
the details of which are in the Lǜlì Zhì (律歷志).
The historian remarked: The art of managing the borders
was thoroughly discussed by previous generations.
Indeed, the barbarians are cunning and treacherous,
swift and unpredictable.
It is essential to keep their fortifications complete
and their signal fires and clappers vigilant,
so that their approach can be defended
and their retreat easily blocked.
Only then can one stop violence and suppress evil,
project authority and repel invaders.
During the Hàn (漢) dynasty, following the old Qín (秦) traces,
strict fortifications were used to limit external barbarians.
When Wú (吳) and Wèi (魏) engaged in battle,
they also used the Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮) rivers as their borders.
All relied first on natural defenses,
and then secured the peace of the people,
both defending and cultivating,
waiting for opportunities to strike.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) received the Mandate,
the imperial strategy had not yet extended far.
Although he defended along the Miánhé (綿河),
his troops were isolated and reinforcements distant.
As the signs of waxing and waning became apparent,
it stirred the hearts of the barbarians.
Perhaps this was due to the initial foundation of the imperial enterprise,
with many deficiencies in its establishment,
prioritizing internal affairs over external ones,
leading to this situation.
From then on,
dividing Qīng (青) and establishing borders,
there was no appropriate plan for encirclement and defense,
and strategies for cultivation and warfare were lacking.
Relying on the invaders not coming,
they consequently made no preparations.
The two strategies of Zhōu (周) and Hàn (漢) completely failed during the Sòng (宋),
leading to the rampant movement of barbarian horses,
without any strong defenses.
This caused the soldiers and common people to cower beneath the azure sky,
and tread upon the thick earth,
captured and imprisoned,
without anyone to appeal to.
Alas!
Chéngtiān (承天)'s discourse on securing the border
is comprehensive and earnest.
It is recorded thus.
