Biographies, Volume 25
Jí Hàn (吉翰) Liú Dàochǎn (劉道產) Dù Jì (杜驥) Shēn Tián (申恬)
Jí Hàn (吉翰), courtesy name Xiūwén (休文),
was a native of Chíyáng (池陽), Fēngyì (馮翊).
Initially, he served as a Cānjūn (參軍) to Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) Dàolián (道憐).
He was subsequently transferred with the office to Zhēnglǔ Zuǒjūn Cānjūn (征虜左軍參軍),
and Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng (員外散騎侍郎).
He accompanied Dàolián (道憐) on the northern expedition to Guǎnggù (廣固),
and was granted the noble title of Jiànchéng Xiàn Wǔděng Nán (建城縣五等男).
He was transferred to Dàolián (道憐)'s Piàojì Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (驃騎中兵參軍)
and Cóngshì Zhōngláng (從事中郎).
He served as a staff officer for over ten years,
being clean, cautious, upright, and firm,
and was greatly appreciated by Gāozǔ (高祖).
In the third year of Yǒngchū (永初),
he was transferred to Dàolián (道憐)'s Tàiwèi Sīmǎ (太尉司馬).
In the first year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) under Tàizǔ (太祖),
he was appointed Dūd Liángnán Qín Èrzhōu Zhūjūnsì (督梁南秦二州諸軍事), Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍), Xīróng Xiàowèi (西戎校尉), and Liángnán Qín Èrzhōu Cìshǐ (梁南秦二州刺史).
In the third year,
Yáng Xīngpíng (楊興平), a Dī (氐) chieftain of Qiúchí (仇池), sent an envoy to submit,
and also sent his younger brother as a hostage.
Hàn (翰) dispatched Shǐpíng Tàishǒu Páng Zī (始平太守龐諮) to occupy Wǔxīng (武興).
The great chieftain of Qiúchí (仇池), Yáng Xuán (楊玄), sent his younger brother Nándāng (難當) to lead troops to resist Zī (諮).
He also sent his general Qiáng Lùpí (強鹿皮) towards Báishuǐ (白水).
Zī (諮) defeated them,
and Nándāng (難當) and the others retreated.
In the same year,
he was transferred to Dū Yìníng Èrzhōu Liángzhōu zhī Bāxī Zǐtóng Dàngqú Nánhànzhōng Qínzhōu zhī Āngù Huáiníng Liùjùn Zhūjūnsì (督益寧二州梁州之巴西梓潼宕渠南漢中秦州之安固懷寧六郡諸軍事) and Yìzhōu Cìshǐ (益州刺史),
with his general rank remaining the same.
He achieved excellent governance in Yìzhōu (益州),
greatly embodying the qualities of a regional governor,
and was praised by commentators.
In the sixth year,
due to old age and illness, he was recalled.
He was appointed Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng (彭城王義康)'s Sītú Sīmǎ (司徒司馬),
and promoted to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍).
At that time, Tàizǔ (太祖) was planning the conquest of Hénán (河南).
He appointed Hàn (翰) as Chíjié (持節), Jiān Sī Yōng Bìng Sānzhōu Zhūjūnsì (監司雍并三州諸軍事), and Sīzhōu Cìshǐ (司州刺史),
with his general rank remaining the same.
Coincidentally, the vanguard forces of Dào Yànzhī (到彥之) and others were defeated.
The following year,
he was again appointed Sītú Sīmǎ (司徒司馬),
with his general rank remaining the same.
In the same year,
he was again granted Jiǎjié (假節), Jiān Xú Yǎn Èrzhōu Yùzhōu zhī Liángjùn Zhūjūnsì (監徐兗二州豫州之梁郡諸軍事), and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (徐州刺史),
with his general rank remaining the same.
At that time, there was a prisoner sentenced to death.
A *diǎnqiān* (典籤) (clerk) wished to spare his life.
He presented the matter to Hàn (翰) during his observance of the eight abstinences.
After Hàn (翰) reviewed it,
he said,
"Go now,
and present it again tomorrow."
The next morning,
the *diǎnqiān* (典籤) dared not enter again.
When called, he came,
took the matter he had presented yesterday, looked at it,
and said to him:
"You intend to pardon this prisoner's death sentence.
Yesterday, while observing the fast, I saw this matter,
and also had a mind to spare him.
However, this prisoner's crime is severe and
cannot be entirely forgiven.
Since you wish to grant clemency,
you must take his place and bear his crime."
He then ordered his attendants to seize the *diǎnqiān* (典籤), send him to prison, and execute him,
while pardoning the prisoner's life.
Such was his administration of justice;
his subordinates feared and obeyed him,
not daring to violate prohibitions.
He died in office the following year
at the age of sixty.
He was posthumously granted the title Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (征虜將軍), with his Chíjié (持節), Jiān (監), and Cìshǐ (刺史) titles remaining as before.
Liú Dàochǎn (劉道產),
a native of Lǚ (呂), Péngchéng (彭城),
was the son of Tàiwèi Cányì Cānjūn (太尉諮議參軍) Jiǎn (簡).
Jiǎn (簡)'s deeds are recorded in the biography of his nephew Kāngzǔ (康祖).
Dàochǎn (道產) initially served as Fǔguó Cānjūn (輔國參軍)
and then Wúxī Lìng (無錫令).
He gained a reputation for competence in the county.
Gāozǔ (高祖) appointed him as Zhōngjūn Xíng Cānjūn (中軍行參軍),
and then as Dàolián (道憐)'s Piàojì Cānjūn (驃騎參軍),
inheriting his father's noble title of Jìn'ān Xiàn Wǔděng Hóu (晉安縣五等侯).
When the governor of Guǎngzhōu (廣州), Xiè Dàoxīn (謝道欣), died,
bandits from Guǎngzhōu (廣州) rose up,
attacking and capturing the provincial capital.
Dàolián (道憐) conferred upon Dàochǎn (道產) the title of Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn (振武將軍) for a southern expedition.
However, Shǐxīng Xiāng Liú Qiānzhī (始興相劉謙之) had already pacified Guǎngzhōu (廣州),
so Dàochǎn (道產) returned before arriving.
In the first year (of the Yuánxǐ period, 418 CE),
he was appointed Ningyuǎn Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the Distant) and Administrator of the two commanderies of Bāxī and Zǐtóng.
The local people Huáng Gōngshēng, Rèn Sùzhī, Zhāng Shízhī, and others, who were remnants of Qiáo Zòng’s faction,
together with their relatives Hóu Lǎn and Luó Ào, enticed the Dī people from Báishuǐ
with the intention of causing a rebellion.
Liú Dàochǎn executed Gōngshēng and twenty other families
and pardoned the rest of their partisans.
He was then recalled to serve as the Púqí Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (Staff Officer in the Central Army of the Cavalry General) for Pēngchéng Wáng Yìkāng.
In the third year of Yuánjiā (426 CE),

he was appointed Dū Liáng Nánqín Èr Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì (Supervisor of All Military Affairs in Liáng and Southern Qín Provinces), Ningyuǎn Jiāngjūn, Xīróng Xiàowèi (Colonel of the Western Barbarians), and Císhǐ (Provincial Governor) of Liáng and Southern Qín Provinces.
While in office in the province, he administered with benevolence,
and displaced people from Guānzhōng,
before and after, who came to Hánchuān and pledged allegiance to him were very numerous.
In the sixth year (429 CE),
Liú Dàochǎn submitted a memorial to establish the two commanderies of Lǒngxī and Sòngkāng to settle them.
In the seventh year (430 CE),
he was recalled to serve as Hòujūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Rear Army).
The following year (431 CE),
he was promoted to Zuǒjiāngjūn Zīyì Cānjūn (Consultative Staff Officer to the General of the Left) for Jìnglíng Wáng Yìxuān,

and concurrently served as Chíjié (Bearer of the Imperial Staff), Dū Yōng Liáng Nánqín Sān Zhōu Jīngzhōu Zhī Nányáng Jìnglíng Shùnyáng Xiāngyáng Xīnyě Suí Liù Jùn Zhū Jūnshì (Supervisor of All Military Affairs in Yōng, Liáng, and Southern Qín Provinces, and the six commanderies of Nányáng, Jìnglíng, Shùnyáng, Xiāngyáng, Xīnyě, and Suí in Jīng Province), Ningyuǎn Jiāngjūn, Níngmán Xiàowèi (Colonel Who Pacifies the Man Barbarians), Císhǐ of Yōng Province, and Administrator of Xiāngyáng.
He was skilled in governing the people,
and his administrative achievements in Yōng Province were particularly notable.
The Mán barbarians who had previously rebelled and refused to be assimilated
all submitted and obeyed,
and all moved to settle along the Miǎn River.
The common people were content with their livelihoods,
and the households were prosperous and abundant.
Thus, there was a folk song of Xiāngyáng,
which began with Liú Dàochǎn.
In the thirteenth year (436 CE),
he was promoted to the title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General Who Assists the State).
He died in the nineteenth year (442 CE).
He was posthumously granted the title of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the Barbarians)
and given the posthumous epithet Xiāng Hóu (Marquis Xiāng).
Liú Dàochǎn’s benevolence spread throughout the western lands,
and when his funeral procession returned,
all the Mán people wore mourning clothes,
wept and escorted him,
as far as the mouth of the Miǎn River.
The Císhǐ of Jīng Province, Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì, memorialized Tàizǔ, saying:
“The former Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Liú Dàochǎn suffered from a back ailment,
and his illness became incurable.
Since Dàochǎn took charge of Hánnán,
his territory bordered on fierce enemies.
His administrative achievements were notable,
and he exercised both power and kindness.
His age was still appropriate,
and he was about to fully display his abilities,
but he suddenly met his demise,
causing exceptionally deep sorrow and regret.
I humbly believe that Your Sacred Majesty’s heart
is filled with pity and regret.”
His eldest son, Yánxūn,
has a separate biography.
Yánxūn’s younger brother, Yánxī,
benefiting from Yánxūn’s influence,
during the Dàmíng reign (457-464 CE),
served as Sītú Yòuchángshǐ (Right Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works),
Huángmén Láng (Gentleman of the Yellow Gate),
and Administrator of Línhǎi and Yìxīng.
At the beginning of Tàishǐ (465 CE),
he joined the general rebellion from all directions
and was executed.
Liú Dàochǎn’s younger brother, Dàoxī,
was the Administrator of the two commanderies of Bāxī and Zǐtóng.
In the eighteenth year of Yuánjiā (441 CE),
he was attacked by Dī bandits.
Dàoxī defended the city and repelled the enemy.
Tàizǔ praised him
and issued an edict saying:
“Previously, when bandits attacked and pressed,
the border situation was alarming.
Guǎngwēi Jiāngjūn (General Who Extends Awe), Administrator of Bāxī and Zǐtóng Commanderies, Liú Dàoxī,
encouraged and led his civil and military officials,
and devoted himself to steadfast defense.
His achievement in preserving (the territory)
is worthy of record.
He is to be appointed Guānjūn (General of the Army).
Zīyì Cānjūn (Consultative Staff Officer), former Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (General Who Establishes Awe), Administrator of Jìnshòu, Shēn Tǎn,
with a lone city and weak forces,
strove with determination to achieve results.
Half of his men were killed or wounded,
yet his valor did not wane.
Although he was overwhelmed and captured,
his sincerity should be recognized.
He is to be appointed Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Administrator of Bāxī and Zǐtóng Commanderies.”
Initially,
when the Dī bandits arrived,
the city had few people.
Dàoxī recruited officials and commoners to defend the city,
and offered a twenty-year exemption from rent and tax.
When the bandits retreated,
the court deliberated:
“Although the bandits attacked the city,
they fled after one battle.
It would be best to follow the original agreement.”
Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Right Guard) Shěn Yǎnzhī, Dānyáng Yǐn (Administrator of Dānyáng) Yáng Xuánbǎo, and Hòujūn Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk to the General of the Rear Army) Fàn Yè all said:
“It is appropriate to determine (the reward) based on their merits and contributions,
and not entirely adhere to the original vow.
The most (exemption) should not exceed ten years.”
This was followed.
In the twenty-first year (444 CE),
he was promoted to Yángliè Jiāngjūn (General Who Displays Prowess) and Císhǐ of Guǎng Province.
In the twenty-seventh year (450 CE),
he was impeached for excessive greed and indulgence.
He personally beat Zhōngxún Qíwén nearly to death.
He rode a carriage out of the city
with a nun,
and was reported by the authorities.
He benefited from an amnesty.
The following year, he was demoted to an unofficial position.
Then, because of remaining ill-gotten gains after the amnesty,
he was arrested and sent to the Tíngwèi (Grand Judge).
He was pardoned due to illness and died.
Dù Jì, courtesy name Dùshì,
was from Jīngzhào Dùlíng.
His great-grandfather, Yù,
was the Jìn Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the South).
His great-granduncle, Tān,
fled to Héxī to escape chaos
and consequently served the Zhāng clan.
When Fú Jiān pacified Liáng Province,
his father and grandfather first returned to Guānzhōng.
His elder brother, Tǎn,
was quite knowledgeable in historical texts.
When Gāozǔ conquered Cháng’ān,
he was swept along and followed him back south.
During Tàizǔ’s Yuánjiā reign,
he received very generous treatment,
and successively served as Hòujūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Rear Army),
Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (General of the Dragon-Soaring),
Císhǐ of Qīng and Jì Provinces,
and Yòujiāngjūn Sīmǎ (Right General’s Military Advisor) for Nánpíng Wáng Shuò.
As a northerner who crossed south late,
the imperial court often treated him as a rough rustic.
Even if he possessed talents that could be utilized,
he was always barred from prominent official positions.
Tǎn was quite indignant about this.
Once, when he was discussing historical records with Tàizǔ,
the emperor said:
“Jīn Rìdī was loyal, filial, and profoundly sincere,
unequaled in the Hàn dynasty.
It is regrettable that there are no such people in this generation.”
Tǎn replied:
“The virtues of Rìdī are indeed as Your Sacred Majesty stated.
But if he were born in this world,
he wouldn’t even have time to tend horses,
how could he be recognized?”
The emperor’s expression changed, and he said:
“Why do you belittle the imperial court so much?”
Tǎn replied:
“Please allow me to speak about myself.
I am originally from a prominent Central Plains clan.
My deceased great-grandfather, during the chaos of the Jìn dynasty,
was relocated to the land of Liáng,
and generations followed one after another,
without losing their former status.
Merely because I did not cross south early,
I was treated as a rude rustic and kept at a distance.
Jīn Rìdī was a Hú person,
who served as a horse keeper,
yet he was able to enter the inner court to serve
and be ranked among famous worthies.
Although Your Sacred Dynasty also values talent,
I fear it may not be able to do so (in my case).”
The emperor fell silent.
According to the old customs of the northern lands,
when inquiring about an illness, one must send a son or younger brother.
When Jì was thirteen,
his father sent him to visit Wèi Huá of the same commandery.
Huá’s son Xuán, who had a high reputation,
saw him and was impressed,
and married his daughter to him.
When Guìyáng Gōng Yìzhēn governed Cháng’ān,
he invited Jì to be Zhōu Zhǔbù (Provincial Chief Clerk).
Later, he became Yìzhēn’s Chējì Xíng Cānjūn (Staff Officer of the General of Chariots and Cavalry),
Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng (Gentleman-in-Waiting, Supernumerary Palace Attendant),
Fǔjūn Xíngyù Cānjūn (Staff Officer for Criminal Justice to the General Who Comforts the Army) for Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng,
Shàngshū Dūguān Láng (Director of the Ministry of Revenue),
and Hòujūn Lùshì Cānjūn (Recording Staff Officer of the Rear Army) for Chángshā Wáng Yìxīn.
In the seventh year of Yuánjiā,
he followed Dào Yànzhī (到彥之) into Hénán,
and was promoted to Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn (建武將軍).
The Sú Lǔ (索虜) withdrew all their Hénán garrisons back to Héběi.
Yànzhī (彥之) ordered Jì (驥) to guard Luòyáng (洛陽).
The city of Luòyáng (洛陽) had been neglected for a long time
and had no provisions.
When Yànzhī (彥之) was defeated and retreated,
Jì (驥) wanted to abandon the city and flee,
but feared being executed by Tàizǔ (太祖).
Initially,
Gāozǔ (高祖) pacified Guānlào (關洛)
and had old bells and bell-stands transported back south.
One large bell fell into the Luòshuǐ (洛水).
At this time, Tàizǔ (太祖) sent general Yáo Sǒngfū (姚聳夫) with fifteen hundred men to retrieve it.
At that moment, Sǒngfū (聳夫) was leading his troops to pull the bell from the Luòshuǐ (洛水).
Jì (驥) then deceived him, saying:
"The Lǔ (虜) have already crossed south,
and Luò Chéng (洛城) is in a weak position.
Now that the city walls have been repaired
and are already solid,
and military provisions are also sufficient,
what is lacking are men.
If you bring your troops to join us,
and together we guard this city,
a great achievement will be established,
and retrieving the bell will not be too late."
Sǒngfū (聳夫) believed him
and led his troops to Jì (驥).
Upon arrival, he saw that the city was indefensible
and had no provisions.
Thereupon, he led his troops away.
Jì (驥) also abandoned the city and fled south,
reporting to Tàizǔ (太祖), saying:
"Originally, I intended to hold out to the death,
but Yáo Sǒngfū (姚聳夫) fled as soon as he reached the city,
and morale was broken;
it could no longer be contained."
The Emperor was furious
and ordered Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (建威將軍) Zhèng Shùnzhī (鄭順之) to execute Sǒngfū (聳夫) in Shòuyáng (壽陽).
Sǒngfū (聳夫) was
a native of Wǔkāng (武康), Wúxìng (吳興).
He was courageous, resolute, and strong,
and among the lesser generals and officers of the Sòng (宋) era, none could match him.
He first followed Dào Yànzhī (到彥之) on the northern expedition.
When they encountered the Lǔ (虜),
Sǒngfū (聳夫) personally beheaded Tuòbá Tàozhī (拓跋燾之) uncle Yīngwén Tèqín (英文特勤).
Jì (驥) was made Tōngzhí Láng (通直郎)
and Shèshēng Xiàowèi (射聲校尉),
then Shìzǔ (世祖) Zhēnglǔ Zīyì Cānjūn (征虜諮議參軍).
In the seventeenth year,
he was dispatched as Dū Qīng Jì Èr Zhōu Xú Zhōu Zhī Dōngguǎn Dōng'ān Èr Jùn Zhū Jūnshì (督青冀二州徐州之東莞東安二郡諸軍事), Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (寧遠將軍), and Qīng Jì Èr Zhōu Cìshǐ (青冀二州刺史).
He served for eight years,
and his benevolent governance was widely known throughout the territory of Qí (齊).
From Yìxī (義熙) to the end of Sòng (宋),
among the Cìshǐ (刺史), only Yáng Mùzhī (羊穆之) and Jì (驥)
were praised by officials and common people.
In the twenty-fourth year,
he was summoned to be Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn (左軍將軍).
His elder brother Tǎn (坦) replaced him as Cìshǐ (刺史),
which was considered an honor in the northern lands.
Tǎn's (坦) eldest son, Wǎn (琬), was Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng (員外散騎侍郎).
Tàizǔ (太祖) once sent a sealed imperial decree to Tǎn (坦),
which Wǎn (琬) invariably opened and read.
Before the letter was sent, it was recalled,
but the imperial decree's seal had already been broken,
leading to a major investigation.
Chéng Dū (丞都) replied, saying:
"The various young masters opened and read it."
The Emperor sent a Zhǔshū (主書) to interrogate and blame them.
Jì (驥) replied, saying:
"The one who opened the sealed letter was your subject's fourth son, Jìwén (季文);
I await my punishment."
The Emperor specifically pardoned and did not question it further.
In the twenty-seventh year,
he died,
at the age of sixty-four.
His eldest son, Chángwén (長文),
died early.
His fifth son, Yòuwén (幼文),
was of poor conduct.
At the beginning of Tàizōng's (太宗) reign,
he was appointed Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (驍騎將軍) for his military achievements,
ennobled as Shàoyáng Xiàn Nán (邵陽縣男),
and granted a fief of three hundred households.
Soon after, he was stripped of his title for being cunning and deceitful.
Later, for exposing the rebellion plot of Tàiwèi (太尉) Lújiāng Wáng (廬江王) Huī (褘),
he was appointed Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎).
He was then dispatched as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍) and Liáng Nánqín Èr Zhōu Cìshǐ (梁南秦二州刺史).
During the Yuánhuī (元徽) reign of the deposed Emperor,
he served as Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
Yòuwén (幼文) was corrupt and tyrannical in his administration.
His family accumulated thousands of gold pieces,
and he had dozens of female entertainers.
Music played day and night without interruption.
He lived near Shěn Bó (沈勃) and Sūn Chāozhī (孫超之),
often associating with them,
and they were all close friends with Ruǎn Tiánfū (阮佃夫).
After Tiánfū (佃夫) died,
the deposed Emperor deeply resented Yòuwén (幼文).
The Emperor would often go out secretly at night,
lingering around Yòuwén's (幼文) gate and walls,
listening to his string and wind instruments.
Over time, his anger grew unbearable.
Thereupon, he personally led his imperial guards to execute Yòuwén (幼文), Bó (勃), Chāozhī (超之), and others.
Yòuwén's (幼文) elder brother, Shúwén (叔文), who was Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi (長水校尉),
and all his sons and nephews in the capital and frontier garrisons were also executed.
Only Yòuwén's (幼文) elder brother Jìwén (季文), younger brother Xīwén (希文), and a few others
escaped and survived.
Shēn Tián (申恬), courtesy name Gōngxiū (公休),
was a native of Wèi (魏) County, Wèi (魏) Commandery.
His great-grandfather, Zhōng (鍾),
served as Sītú (司徒) for Shí Hǔ (石虎).
When Gāozǔ (高祖) pacified Guǎnggù (廣固),
Tián's (恬) father, Xuān (宣), and Xuān's (宣) cousin, Yǒng (永), were all able to return to the state
and were known for their competence and utility.
Yǒng (永) served as Cìshǐ (刺史) of Qīng (青) and Yǎn (兗) Provinces.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) ascended the throne,
he was appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū (太中大夫).
Xuān (宣),
at the beginning of Tàizǔ's (太祖) Yuánjiā (元嘉) reign,
also served as Cìshǐ (刺史) of Yǎn (兗) and Qīng (青) Provinces.
Tián's (恬) elder brother, Mó (謨),
guarded Huátái (滑臺) with Zhū Xiūzhī (朱脩之),
was captured by the Lǔ (虜),
but later managed to escape and return.
During the Yuánjiā (元嘉) period,
he was Jìnglín Tàishǒu (竟陵太守).
Tián (恬) first served as Piàojì Dàolián Cháng Jiān Xíng Cānjūn (驃騎道憐長兼行參軍).
he was appointed Dōnggōng Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn (東宮殿中將軍),
then transferred back to the Central Government.
He served in the palace for ten years,
never asking for rest.
He was transferred to Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng (員外散騎侍郎),
then dispatched as Suíyuǎn Jiāngjūn (綏遠將軍) and Xiàpí Tàishǒu (下邳太守).
He was transferred to Běihǎi (北海),
and promoted to Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (寧遠將軍).
Wherever he served, he had administrative achievements.
He also served as Tàishǒu (太守) of Běiqiáo (北譙) and Liáng (梁) Commanderies,
retaining his general title.
The commandery's border was adjacent to dense thickets
and was frequently raided by bandits.
Upon Tián's (恬) arrival,
he secretly learned of the bandits' approach,
then ambushed them in a strategic location,
catching them by surprise
and capturing and exterminating them all.
In the twelfth year of Yuánjiā (元嘉),
he was promoted to Dū Lǔ Dōngpíng Jìběi Sān Jùn Jūnshì (督魯東平濟北三郡軍事) and Tàishān Tàishǒu (泰山太守),
retaining his general title.
His authority and benevolence were both evident,
and officials and common people benefited from him.
When Línchuān Wáng (臨川王) Yìqìng (義慶) garrisoned Jiānglíng (江陵),
he served as Píngxī Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (平西中兵參軍) and Hédōng Tàishǒu (河東太守).
When Héngyáng Wáng (衡陽王) Yìjì (義季) replaced Yìqìng (義慶),
he was again transferred to the Ānxī (安西) staff,
and promoted to Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍).
He was summoned to be appointed Tàizǐ Túnqí Xiàowèi (太子屯騎校尉),
but resigned due to mourning his mother.
In the twenty-first year,
Jìzhōu (冀州) commandery moved its garrison to Lìxià (歷下).

Tán (恬) was appointed supervisor of all military affairs in the three commanderies of Jìnán (濟南), Lè'ān (樂安), and Tàiyuán (太原) in Jìzhōu (冀州) and Qīngzhōu (青州), Yangliè Jiāngjūn (揚烈將軍), and Jìzhōu Cìshǐ (冀州刺史).
The following year,
he was given the additional title of Jìnán Tàishǒu (濟南太守).
At this time, there was also a change in various commandery governors.
Tán (恬) submitted a memorial, saying:
"I humbly learn that imperial grace is about to confer upon me the title of Jìnán Tàishǒu (濟南太守).
Reflecting on Your Majesty's gracious decree,
my bewildered mind is overcome with emotion.
As a survivor of misfortune and guilt,
I have already been undeservedly favored,
and the private favors have been ceaseless.
Now, to again be granted this appointment,
how can my foolish and deluded self
ever repay it?
Since my recent arrival,
I have immediately surveyed the areas under my jurisdiction
to ascertain their suitability.
Between the Yellow River and the Jì River,
garrisons should be established for defense.
Among these, four locations
urgently require construction.
The old city of Wèngkǒu (瓮口)
is also a vital strategic point.
It would be appropriate to relocate Tàiyuán (太原)
and entrust it with border affairs.
The various patrols along the mountains
can all be abolished and reduced.
This would facilitate defense and pacification,
bringing more than one benefit.
Lǚ Chuò (呂綽)'s effectiveness is indeed manifest,
and he deeply shares my views.
The common people who hear of this
all endorse the proposal.
However, there are urgent differences of opinion,
and two or three matters are not yet suitable.
Moreover, Fáng Shào (房紹) has governed his commandery for a year,
and the soldiers and civilians are roughly familiar with him.
To replace him and have me assume the role
would deviate from established practice.
〔一二〕To involve Tàiyuán (太原) from afar
would be a hardship for the people.
Furthermore, the plan for Wèngkǒu (瓮口)
would again create back-and-forth movements,
which the people would not be happy with,
and might even lead to unrest.
For border regions, the concern is that military authority and penalties are not sufficiently open and broad.
If the previous arrangements can be followed,
both public and private matters will be settled and orderly."
The emperor complied.
An imperial edict was issued to the relevant officials, stating:
"What Tán (恬) has presented are appropriate matters.
The recent appointments can all be suspended."
When the northern barbarians invaded,
Tán (恬) engaged them,
but was defeated by the barbarians
and recalled to the capital.
In the twenty-seventh year,
he was appointed Tōngzhí Chángshì (通直常侍).
That year,
the Suǒ (索) barbarians invaded the south,
and their Wǔchāng Wáng (武昌王) advanced towards Qīngzhōu (青州).
Tán (恬) was dispatched to reinforce Dōngyáng (東陽),
and consequently,
together with Fǔguó Sīmǎ (輔國司馬) and Qíjùn Tàishǒu (齊郡太守) Páng Xiùzhī (龐秀之), he garrisoned and defended the city.
Xiāo Bīn (蕭斌) dispatched Qīngzhōu Biéjià (青州別駕) Xiè Róngzhī (解榮之) to lead Yuán Hùzhī (垣護之) to return and reinforce Tán (恬) and others,
and they managed to enter by skirting the southern mountains.
The bandits would threaten the city in the morning
and retreat at dusk.
The city defenders then brought chariots out of the north gate,
encircling the moat to form a camp,
intending to challenge them to battle,
but the bandits dared not approach.
After five days,
they moved east, plundering several thousand households south of Qīnghé Jùn (清河郡) and the postal road,
and exited Xiàpī (下邳) via Dōng'ān (東安) and Dōngguǎn (東莞).
Xiàpī Tàishǒu (下邳太守) Yuán Làng (垣閬) closed the city gates and defended,
preserving over two thousand households.
After the barbarians retreated,
Tán (恬) was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) and Shānyáng Tàishǒu (山陽太守).
He was skilled at governing the people,
and achieved merit wherever he served.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ (青州刺史),
with his general title remaining as before.
Soon after, he was given additional supervision of military affairs in the two commanderies of Dōngguǎn (東莞) and Dōng'ān (東安) in Xúzhōu (徐州).
The following year,
he also supervised Jìzhōu (冀州).
Qí (齊) territory had suffered years of warfare,
and the common people were in distress.
Tán (恬) initially defended the borders,
and encouraged agriculture and sericulture.
Within two or three years,
they all became prosperous and substantial.
He was by nature clean and frugal.
Though he frequently held positions in provinces and commanderies,
his wife and children were not exempt from hunger and cold.
The world praised him for this.
He was promoted to the title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍).
In the second year of Xiàojiàn (孝建),
he was promoted to supervisor of military affairs in Yùzhōu (豫州), Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將jūn), and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (豫州刺ǐ).
The following year,
he fell ill and was recalled,
dying on the road
at the age of sixty-nine.
On the day of his death,
his family had no leftover wealth.
His son Shí (寔),
Nánqiáo Jùn Tàishǒu (南譙郡太守),
died young.
〔一三〕Mó (謨)'s son Yuánsì (元嗣)
was Hǎilíng (海陵) and Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu (廣陵太守).
Yuánsì (元嗣)'s younger brother Qiān (謙),
in the early years of Tàishǐ (泰始),
due to his military merits,
served as various military officers,
eventually reaching the rank of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍) and Línchuān Nèishǐ (臨川內史).
Yǒng (永)'s son Tǎn (坦),
from Bāxī (巴西) and Zǐtóng Tàishǒu (梓潼太守), was promoted to governor of the two provinces of Liáng (梁) and Nánqín (南秦).
〔一四〕In the twenty-sixth year of Yuánjiā (元嘉),
he served as Shìzǔ (世祖)'s Zhèn Jūn Zīyì Cānjūn (鎮軍諮議參軍).
He and Wáng Xuánmó (王玄謨) besieged Huátái (滑臺) but failed to capture it,
and he was dismissed from office.
Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ (青州刺史) Xiāo Bīn (蕭斌) provisionally appointed him Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (建威將軍) and Jìnán (濟南) and Píngyuán Tàishǒu (平原太守).
He again attacked Què'áo (碻磝),
was defeated and retreated,
and fell to Lìchéng (歷城).
When Xiāo Sīhuà (蕭思話) raised an army to punish the arch-villain,
Tǎn (坦) was temporarily granted the title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍)
and served as the vanguard.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) reached Xīntíng (新亭),
Tǎn (坦) also advanced and captured the capital city.
In the early years of Xiàojiàn (孝建),
he served as Tàizǐ Yòuwèi Shuài (太子右衛率),
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍), and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (徐州刺史).
In the first year of Dàmíng (大明),
the barbarians invaded Yǎnozhōu (兗州).
Shìzǔ (世祖) dispatched Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài (太子左衛率) Xuē Āndū (薛安都) and the newly appointed Dōngyáng Tàishǒu (東陽太守) Shěn Fǎxì (沈法系) to campaign in the north.
〔一五〕When they reached Yǎnozhōu (兗州),
the barbarians had already departed.
Tǎn (坦) suggested:
"Rèn Zhēn (任榛)'s fugitives
have repeatedly encroached upon the border populace.
Since the army has gone out without achieving merit,
it is appropriate to take this opportunity to eliminate them."
The emperor agreed.
However, the fugitives had already heard the news in advance,
and the entire village fled.
Āndū (安都) and Fǎxì (法系) were dismissed from their positions as commoners,
and Tǎn (坦) was sentenced to public execution.
All the officials pleaded for him,
but none could succeed.
As the execution was about to take place,
Shǐxīng Gōng (始興公) Shěn Qìngzhī (沈慶之) entered the marketplace, embracing Tǎn (坦) and weeping bitterly, saying:
"You are innocent,
and are being unjustly executed by the court.
My time in the marketplace will also not be long."
The market officials reported this to the emperor,
who then pardoned his life
and imprisoned him in the imperial workshops.
Soon after, he was granted amnesty
and reinstated as Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (驍騎將軍),
but died of illness.
His son Lìngsūn (令孫),
during the Jǐnghé (景和) era of the Former Deposed Emperor,
served as Yǒngjiā Wáng (永嘉王) Zǐrén (子仁)'s Zuǒjūn Sīmǎ (左軍司馬) and Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu (廣陵太守).
Tàizōng (太宗) appointed him Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (徐州刺史)
to suppress Xuē Āndū (薛安都).
Upon reaching Huáiyáng (淮陽),
he immediately joined forces with Āndū (安都).
His younger brother Chǎn (闡),
who was then Jìyīn Tàishǒu (濟陰太守),
garrisoned Suīlíng Chéng (睢陵城)
and refused to align with Āndū (安都).
Āndū (安都) besieged but could not overcome him.
When Lìngsūn (令孫) arrived,
he sent someone to Suīlíng (睢陵) to persuade Chǎn (闡) to surrender.
After Chǎn (闡) surrendered,
he was killed.
Lìngsūn (令孫) was also killed.
Before this,
Cuī Yīn (崔諲) of Qīnghé (清河), also known to Gāozǔ (高祖) as an official,
at the end of Yǒngchū (永初),
served as Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn (振威將軍) and Dōnglái Tàishǒu (東萊太守).
In the early years of Shàodì (少帝),
over a thousand fugitives led by Sīmǎ Língqí (司馬靈期) and Sīmǎ Shùnzhī (司馬順之) besieged Dōnglái (東萊).
Yīn (諲) attacked them,
beheading Língqí (靈期) and thirty others.
During Tàizǔ (太祖)'s Yuánjiā (元嘉) era,
he rose to Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ (青州刺史).
The Grand Scribe says: The good historians of the Hàn
dynasty, those who held office, sometimes saw their descendants flourish,
and in the era of Sūn and Cái,
those who were skilled in their duties also served for two or three decades.
All promulgated governance to bring forth the people's harmony,
and promoted humility to maintain simplicity and longevity.
By the late generations, their spirit gradually declined,
not because their talents rose and fell,
but because the times they encountered were different.
Liú Dàochǎn, when he was in Hànnán,
served for over ten years;
his benevolent influence spread to Fán and Miǎn,
somewhat possessing the lingering style of former generations.
Therefore, he was able to establish achievements and leave a name,
which is indeed commendable.
Collator's Notes
Biographies, Chapter Twenty-six: Wáng Jìnghóng, Hé Shàngzhī
Wáng Jìnghóng,
was from Línyí, Lángyá.
Because his given name was the same as Gāozǔ's tabooed name,
he was referred to by his courtesy name.
His great-grandfather, Yì,
was a General of Agile Cavalry of the Jìn dynasty.
His grandfather, Húzhī,
was the Inspector of Sīzhōu.
His father, Màozhī,
was the Administrator of Jìnlíng.
Jìnghóng was pure and noble in his youth.
He began his career as Left Attendant-in-ordinary of his native state,
and then Aide to the Garrison General.
His nature was tranquil and quiet,
and he delighted in mountains and waters.
He became the Administrator of Tiānmén.
Jìnghóng's wife
was the elder sister of Huán Xuán.
When Jìnghóng was proceeding to his commandery,
Xuán was then the Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
He sent a messenger to summon him to visit.
Jìnghóng arrived at Bālíng
and said to someone:
"Língbǎo summons me
simply because he wants to gather with his sister,
but I cannot be a son-in-law living in the Huán family."
So he sent a separate boat to send his wife to Jiānglíng.
His wife remained with the Huán family,
and he did not welcome her back for a full year.
The mountain commandery was uneventful,
allowing him to indulge in his travels,
not returning for many days,
and he greatly enjoyed it.
He was transferred to be Huán Wěi's Chief Clerk of the General Who Quells the West and Administrator of Nánpíng.
He resigned from office
and resided in the area of Zuòtáng County.
When Xuán became regent and later usurped the throne,
he repeatedly summoned Jìnghóng, but he did not respond.
Gāozǔ appointed him Colonel-Advisor to the General of Chariots and Cavalry,
Judicial Aide to Xúzhōu,
and Consultant-Advisor to Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Dàoguī.
At that time, the Chief Scribe of the headquarters, Zōng Xié, also had high aspirations,
and Dàoguī regarded them both as being beyond worldly affairs.
They once drank heartily together and became drunk.
Jìnghóng, in his drunkenness, committed an impropriety.
When reported by the external officials,
Dàoguī immediately invited him back
and repeated their initial banquet.
He was summoned to be Minister-Secretary of the Central Secretariat,
and only then did he bring his family back from Zuòtáng to Jīngyì.
After a long time,
he was transferred to Yellow Gate Attendant-in-ordinary,
but he did not accept the appointment.
He was then appointed Colonel-Advisor to the Grand Commandant
and went out to be Administrator of Wúxīng.
His old residence was in Yúháng County,
and he was pleased with this appointment.
Soon after, he was summoned to be a Palace Attendant.
When Gāozǔ campaigned west against Sīmǎ Xiūzhī,
Jìnghóng was dispatched to convey comfort.
The Executive Scribe Pān Shàng fell ill on the way,
and Jìnghóng sent him back to the capital in a single boat.
As his life or death was uncertain,
the authorities memorialized for his dismissal,
and an imperial edict approved it.
Before he could take off his court attire,
he was pardoned and reinstated.
When the Sòng state was first established,
he became Minister of Finance,
and then Grand Master of Ceremonies.
When Gāozǔ received the mandate,
he was appointed Wei尉 of the Xuanxun Department,
and given the additional title of Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary.
In the third year of Yǒngchū,
he was transferred to Minister of Personnel,
with his Attendant-in-ordinary title remaining as before.
Whenever Jìnghóng was appointed or summoned,
he would immediately accept it.
Once it was appropriate to retire,
he would then resign from office.
Gāozǔ commended his resolve
and did not arbitrarily object.
He was again appointed Tutor to the Prince of Lúlíng,
and given the additional title of Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary.
He declared himself unworthy
and unsuitable to be a teacher and model for the prince,
and firmly declined the appointment.
He was also appointed Director of the Imperial Library,
Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Gold and Purple,
given the additional title of Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary,
and Chief Judge of his native province,
but he did not accept these either.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he again appointed him Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary, Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Gold and Purple,
and concurrently Tutor to the Prince of Jiāngxià.
In the third year of Yuánjiā,
he became Administrator of the Imperial Secretariat.
He never bothered to read or review
the documents and files of the offices.
He once participated in hearing a legal case.
The Emperor asked him about a difficult case,
but Jìnghóng did not reply.
The Emperor's expression changed,
and he asked his attendants:
"Why did you not provide the Minister-Administrator with a copy of the interrogation records?"
Jìnghóng said:
"I did receive and read the interrogation records,
but I simply do not understand them."
The Emperor was very displeased.
In the sixth year,
he was promoted to Grand Minister of the Imperial Secretariat.
Jìnghóng firmly declined,
memorializing to request a return to the east,
and the Emperor could not dissuade him.
He was re-appointed Palace Attendant, Specially Advanced, Left Grand Master of Glorious Happiness,
and given twenty personal guards.
He declined the titles of Palace Attendant and Specially Advanced,
and requested to reduce his personal guards by half,
but it was not permitted.
When he returned to the east,
the imperial carriage went to Yětíng to see him off.
In the twelfth year,
Jīng was made Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shǎofù).
Jìnghóng went to the capital to submit a memorial, saying:
"I humbly observe the imperial decree,
appointing me as Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince.
Upon receiving the order, I am overwhelmed with trepidation,
and both joy and fear intensely agitate me.
I have been ailing in the eastern wilderness,
my ambition for glory extinguished,
yet I did not expect Your Sacred Grace
to once again bestow such favor.
The importance of the Eastern Palace
is something the whole world looks up to,
and it is not a position that someone of my meager virtue
can occupy.
Currently, there are many outstanding talents, both within and without,
who deserve selection;
moreover, among those who build walls,
are there truly no lofty recluses?
Yet, I, a private, foolish, and decaying person, have been approached,
to soil the pure court.
Alas, this humble subject
will forever be but one insignificant thing among the vastness.
The reason I have been dragged to the palace gate
is truly to behold Your Sacred Countenance
and to cling to the meaning of this memorial.
If I were to return in this state,
I would have no regrets even if I died this evening."
The emperor did not permit it.
He submitted memorials repeatedly,
but ultimately did not accept the appointment.
When he returned east,
the emperor was unwell at the time,
but made an effort to see him.
In the sixteenth year,
he was appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū) and Minister without Portfolio (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī),
and his position as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) remained as before.
Again, he went to the capital to submit a memorial, saying:
"I previously presented my case,
believing my sincere heart had been understood.
Heaven's discernment is profound and distant,
and I have not yet received forgiveness,
so I dare not rest in comfort,
but am dragged to ride forth.
I have heard that a noble person practicing the Way
forgets their own self.
Repeatedly reflecting on these words,
it seems I might be able to strive,
yet I consider my age and infirmity,
and my will diverges from my desire.
According to the Rites, at seventy,
one is old and passes on family responsibilities.
If this is true for family matters,
how much more so for national affairs?
I humbly pray Your Majesty will pity my twilight years,
and compassionately grant my single request,
to specially reverse Your Sacred Grace,
and allow me to return to my place,
then Heaven's Way will descend to assist,
and my foolish heart will be entirely at peace."
Ultimately, he did not accept the appointment and returned east.
In the twenty-third year,
the previous appointment was reiterated.
He again submitted a memorial, saying:
"I have personally tilled the fields in southern Lí,
not seeking fame or advancement.
The late emperor drew me out from the barbarian region of Jīng,
and treated me with the courtesy of a national scholar.
Your Majesty inherited this virtuous example,
and I have especially received Your眷 (juàn) [read: *guàn] favor and consideration due to my age.
Because of this, I am deeply moved,
and have pledged myself to Your Sacred Court.
Although I bear the loyalty of a dog or horse,
I have unfortunately provided no benefit, not even as dust or dew.
Approaching ninety years of age,
my vitality is almost exhausted.
I will forever be cut off from Heaven's light,
and perish in the hills and valleys.
I respectfully risk submitting this memorial,
my heart has been aching for a long time."
The following year,
he passed away at Shètíngshān in Yúháng,
at the age of eighty-eight.
He was posthumously granted his original official title.
Emperor Shùn, in the second year of Shēngmíng, issued an edict saying:
"Indeed, the path of obscured orchids,
their pure fragrance extends over time;
their glorious deeds are profound and far-reaching,
and their splendid rituals shine ever brighter.
The former Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), Grand Master of Remonstrance with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū), and Minister without Portfolio (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī) Jìnghóng,
had a refined demeanor that was subtle and simple,
and a discerning mind that was lofty and eminent.
His virtue spread to the corners of the realm,
and his Way graced the hills and gardens.
He gracefully shunned the robes of honor,
his heart settled beyond the dust of the world.
His pure radiance and excellent example
stirred the customs and purified the traditions.
Moreover, for successive reigns, his merits have been praised,
and his fame and splendor celebrated in song.
Yet, his excellent inscriptions lack text,
and his strategies and policies are hidden from view.
I still recall his distant fragrance,
and ponder it waking and sleeping.
It is fitting to carefully determine a splendid posthumous title,
to publicly honor this posthumous ceremony."
Thereupon, he was posthumously titled Wénzhēn Gōng.
Jìnghóng's physique was short,
yet he sat and stood with dignified propriety.
Huán Xuán called him
"tán bāshì" (弹八势).
His residence, Shètíngshān,
was surrounded by forests and streams,
possessing all the beauty for climbing and viewing.
People at the time called him Wáng Dōngshān.
Tàizǔ once asked about the successes and failures of governance.
Jìnghóng replied:
"When the world has the Way,
common people do not criticize."
The emperor praised his words.
Around him, he always had two old maidservants,
wearing five ribbons and five braids,
dressed in green patterned trousers and jackets,
adorned with red powder.
His daughter married Shàngshū Púyè Hé Shàngzhī's younger brother, Shùzhī.
Jìnghóng once went to the Hé family to see his daughter,
and found Shàngzhī was not there.
He stayed in the study and slept.
A short while later, Shàngzhī returned.
Jìnghóng made the two maidservants guard the door and not allow Shàngzhī to enter,
saying,
"It's very hot right now,
I can't meet you.
You can leave for now."
Shàngzhī then moved to another room.
His son, Huīzhī, was summoned to be Archivist (Mìshū Láng).
Jìnghóng sought for him to be an Attendant at Court (Fèng Cháoqǐng),
and wrote to Huīzhī, saying:
"The position of Archivist (Mìshū) is limited,
hence there is competition.
The position of Attendant at Court (Cháoqǐng) is unlimited,
hence there is no competition.
I want you to be in a place without competition."
Tàizǔ praised this and permitted it.
Jìnghóng saw his sons and grandsons no more than once or twice a year,
and each meeting was by a fixed date.
Huīzhī once requested leave to return east to pay respects to his parents.
Jìnghóng set a date to see him,
but on that day, it did not happen.
As his leave was about to end,
Huīzhī begged to take his leave.
Jìnghóng called him forward.
When he reached the door,
he again did not appear.
Huīzhī bowed his farewell outside the door,
shedding tears as he departed.
Huīzhī reached the position of Grand Administrator of Xīn'ān (Xīn'ān Tàishǒu) and Grand Master (Zhōng Dàfū).
Huīzhī's younger brother, Zànzhī,
during Shìzǔ's Dàmíng era, was Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū)
and Grand Master of Remonstrance with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū),
posthumously titled Zhēnzǐ.
Zànzhī's younger brother, Shēngzhī,
was Minister of Works (Dūguān Shàngshū).
Shēngzhī's son, Yánzhī,
at the end of Shēngmíng,
was Minister of the Left (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè)
and Governor of Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ).
Hé Shàngzhī's courtesy name was Yàndé,
and he was a native of Qián, Lújiāng.
His great-grandfather, Zhǔn,
was lofty and did not answer calls for official service.
His grandfather, Tán,
was the Administrator of Nánkāng.
His father, Shúdù,
was respectful and cautious, with a good reputation for conduct.
His maternal aunt married Liú Qú of Péijùn.
She and Shúdù's mother had a very deep affection.
Shúdù's mother died early,
and he served his aunt as if she were his birth mother.
When his aunt died,
he would unfailingly visit on the first and fifteenth days of each lunar month to express his sorrow,
and also set up a sacrifice.
The food was always rare and fresh,
and he personally oversaw it.
If there were public duties on the first or fifteenth,
he would first send the offerings,
all personally selected by him,
shedding tears as he looked at them.
After his public duties were finished,
he would then go to express his sorrow.
This became his custom,
until the three years of mourning were completed.
In the fifth year of Yìxī [409 CE],
Wáng Yánzǔ, a commoner of Wǔkāng County, Wúxīng, became a bandit.
His father, Mù, reported him to the authorities.
According to the new law,
any bandit would be beheaded,
and their family members executed publicly.
Since Mù had reported himself,
there was a legal dilemma.
At that time, Shúdù was a Shàngshū,
and he deliberated, saying:
"The purpose of establishing laws to deter wickedness
is fundamentally based on reason and sentiment.
It does not mean that if one person commits robbery,
the entire family should be punished.
The reason why punishment extends to blood relatives
is to encourage them to report
and expose the perpetrator of evil.
The bond between Mù and his son
might allow them to flee together.
Yet, he severed his natural ties
and bound and delivered his son himself.
To cut off a poisoned hand
and sever a wrist to preserve oneself,
is pitiable in sentiment,
and should also be pardoned according to reason.
To ensure that evil people find no refuge in their homes
and have nowhere to escape punishment,
that is to completely cut off the root source [of crime].
Since Mù reported and delivered him,
then no other person needs to report,
and all should be pardoned."
This was adopted.
Later, he became the Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
Administrator of Wújùn,
and was granted the rank of Zhōng Èrqiānshí.
Grand Protector Wáng Hóng praised him for his integrity and self-purification.
In the eighth year of Yuánjiā [431 CE],
he died.
Shàngzhī was rather frivolous in his youth,
enjoying chūpú (a dice game).
When he grew older, he disciplined himself and followed the Dao,
and was praised for his upright conduct.
He was recognized by Xiè Hùn of Chénjùn,
and associated with him.
Being poor,
he started as the Magistrate of Línjīn.
Emperor Gāozǔ appointed him as the Grand General who Conquers the West,
and he became the Aide-de-camp in the General's office.
He followed the campaign to Cháng'ān.
He was dismissed due to official matters,
and returned to the capital.
He then suffered from a debilitating illness for many years.
He recovered only after drinking women's milk.
He recovered only after drinking women's milk.
For his service in the campaign,
he was granted the title of Dūxiāng Hóu.
When Emperor Shàodì ascended the throne,
he became the Advisor and Aide-de-camp to Lúlíng Wáng Yìzhēn, who was the Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry.
Yìzhēn was at odds with Grand Minister of Works Xú Xiànzhī, Director of the Imperial Secretariat Fù Liàng, and others.
Whenever he spoke of injustice,
Shàngzhī advised and warned him,
but he did not listen.
When Yìzhēn was deposed,
he entered the court as a Zhōngshū Shìláng.
When Emperor Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was sent out as the Administrator of Línchuān,
then returned to the court as a Huángmén Shìláng,
Shàngshū Lìbù Láng,
and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
He left office due to his father's death.
After the mourning period,
he was reinstated as Zuǒwèi,
also serving as the Zhōngshùzǐ to the Crown Prince.
Shàngzhī had a refined taste for literature and meaning.
He was calm and appreciative in gatherings,
and was highly regarded by Emperor Tàizǔ.
In the twelfth year [435 CE],
he was promoted to Shìzhōng,
with his role as Zhōngshùzǐ remaining as before.
Soon after, he was reappointed to lead as the Yóujī Jiāngjūn.
In the thirteenth year [436 CE],
Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng wanted to appoint Liú Bīn, the Left Chief Clerk to the Grand Minister of Works, as the Administrator of Dānyáng.
The emperor did not permit it.
Instead, Shàngzhī was appointed as Administrator.
He established a residence outside the south gate of the city,
set up a School of Metaphysics (Xuánxué),
and gathered students.
Xú Xiù of Dōnghǎi, Hé Tán of Lújiāng, Huáng Huí, Xún Zǐhuá of Yǐngchuān, Sūn Zōngchāng of Tàiyuán, Wáng Yánxiù, and Kǒng Huìxuān of Lǔjùn,
all came to study, drawn by the Dao.
This was called the Southern School (Nánxué).
His daughter married Liú Zhàn's son, Àn,
but Zhàn and Shàngzhī were not particularly close.
Zhàn wanted to lead Dānyáng,
so he transferred Shàngzhī to be Cíbù Shàngshū,
also serving as the Jìjiǔ of Guózǐ.
Shàngzhī was very displeased.
After Zhàn was executed,
Shàngzhī was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū.
At that time, Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Fàn Yè was involved in confidential matters.
Shàngzhī observed his unusual intentions,
and advised Emperor Tàizǔ that he should be sent out to Guǎngzhōu.
Otherwise, if he remained in the court, a crisis would develop,
inevitably leading to his execution,
and repeatedly executing high officials
would detract from imperial transformation.
The emperor said:
"Having just executed Liú Zhàn and others,
I am now looking to promote rising talents.
Fàn Yè's misdeeds have not yet been revealed,
and if I were to prematurely dismiss him,
the myriad regions would say that you all are unable to tolerate talent,
and that I am easily swayed by slander.
As long as we all know the situation,
I am not worried about a great upheaval."
Fàn Yè later conspired in rebellion and was executed.
The emperor praised Shàngzhī's foresight.
When the Guózǐ School was established,
he served as its Jìjiǔ.
He also served as the teacher of Jiànpíng Wáng,
then was transferred to Zhōngshū Lìng,
and Zhōnghù Jūn.
In the twenty-second year [445 CE],
he was promoted to Shàngshū Yòupúshè,
and granted the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
That year, Xuánwǔ Hú was created.
The emperor wanted to build the three divine mountains of Fāngzhàng, Pénglái, and Yíngzhōu in the lake.
Shàngzhī firmly remonstrated, and it was stopped.
At that time, Huálín Yuán was also being built,
and laborers were working intensely during the height of summer.
Shàngzhī again remonstrated,
suggesting that they should be given rest.
The emperor did not permit it,
saying:
"Common people always expose their backs to the sun;
this is not considered strenuous labor."
At that time, when the emperor made imperial progresses,
he often returned late into the evening.
Shàngzhī again presented a memorial, remonstrating:
"The sovereign's person should be held in high esteem;
dignity must not be taken lightly.
This is something the sagely mind discerns,
so how could it need my reminder?
Recently, whenever the imperial carriage sets out,
it often returns late into the night.
The sentiments of the people are disturbed,
and indeed there is uneasiness.
To clear the way and proceed is the established rule for emperors and kings.
Both ancient and modern [teachings] deeply warn [us]:
in peace, do not forget danger.
If we were to encounter Jí Àn or Xīn Pí,
they would surely defy your face and earnestly remonstrate.
But your subjects are mediocre,
and each only thinks of compliant silence.
I humbly beg Your Majesty to consider my sincere but humble advice,
and reflect upon it.
Do not dismiss it because of the person [speaking it].
This would suitably comfort the hopes of all under heaven."
The emperor also accepted it with a gracious edict.
Formerly, there was trouble with a shortage of currency.
When four-zhū coins were cast,
the common people frequently engaged in illicit casting,
and many cut and chipped ancient coins to extract copper.
The emperor was concerned about this.
In the twenty-fourth year [of the Yuánjiā 元嘉 reign],
Lù Shàngshū 錄尚書 Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng 江夏王義恭 suggested
that one large coin should be counted as two,
to prevent cutting and chipping.
Many of the deliberators agreed.
Shàngzhī 尚之 deliberated, saying:
"I respectfully note the enlightened decree
to reform the currency system.
It does not require effort in minting and casting,
and its benefit will naturally double.
This is truly a grand plan to remedy弊 (evils)
and an excellent method to increase currency.
However, with my limited understanding,
there are still points I do not fully grasp.
The rise of currency
is based on valuing goods.
The purpose lies in trade;
why should it require a large quantity?
If the quantity is small, the currency is heavy (valuable);
[一０]if the quantity is large, goods are heavy (expensive).
Though the quantities differ,
their utility does not.
Moreover, to make one count as two
is merely to inflate a nominal value.
Whenever a system is established or a law changed,
it should follow public sentiment.
There has never been a case where defying the multitude and forcing things could last long.
The rise and fall of currency
cannot be rashly decided.
[一一]In previous dynasties, the chìzhè 赤仄 and báijīn 白金 [currencies]
were quickly abolished,
and the six currencies were chaotic,
causing people to weep in the markets.
This was precisely because matters were not unified
and difficult to implement.
Unless it is an urgent situation requiring temporary measures,
it is advisable to maintain long-standing practices.
Troublesome and overly complex policies
always impede progress.
Furthermore, if wealth is unevenly distributed, the people suffer.
Therefore, the former kings established the jǐngtián 井田 system to unify it,
so that the rich would not be extravagant
and the poor would not suffer excessive want.
Although this law has long been abandoned
and cannot be immediately reinstituted,
it should be adapted to current needs,
roughly emulating it.
If the current proposal is implemented,
the assets and wealth of the rich will naturally double,
while the poor will be increasingly impoverished.
I fear this is not the intention of wishing to equalize.
Also, the forms of coins
vary greatly in size and type.
Simply saying 'large coin'
does not specify its standard.
If it refers only to four-zhū or five-zhū coins,
then their inscriptions are all ancient seal script.
Not only are they unrecognizable to myself,
but some are also worn away,
making them even harder to distinguish.
This will cause confusion for both public and private matters,
and disputes will inevitably arise.
This is my deepest concern.
The imperial decree also considers that cutting and chipping are increasing daily,
leading to their eventual disappearance.
My humble opinion, however, is that there is hardly such a concern.
Though the people's ingenuity (in illicit acts) is elaborate,
there are always traces.
Moreover, using coins and copper
is a matter that can be investigated.
It is simply that the relevant departments have been negligent and lax,
and their investigations are not thorough,
resulting in few discoveries since the system was established.
Although there is now a name for 'hanging gold' (rewards for informers),
there is ultimately no reality of payment.
If the old laws are re-emphasized
and rewards are given immediately upon capture,
people, fearing the law and hoping for rewards,
will naturally bring things to order within days.
The wise choose from the deliberations of the foolish.
Since I have been asked to participate,
how can I not speak my mind fully?"

Lìbù Shàngshū 吏部尚書 Yǔ Bǐngzhī 庾炳之, Shìzhōng Tàizǐ Zuǒwèishuài 侍中太子左衛率 Xiāo Sīhuà 蕭思話, Zhōnghùjūn 中護軍 Zhào Bófú 趙伯符, Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng 御史中丞 Hé Chéngtiān 何承天, and Tàicháng 太常 Xī Jìngshū 郗敬叔 all agreed with Shàngzhī's 尚之 deliberation.
Zhōnglǐngjūn 中領軍 Shěn Yǎnzhī 沈演之, however, thought:
"Turtle shells and cowries were used in high antiquity,
and springs (coins) and knives (knife money) arose from the time of Zhōu 周.
All were for accumulating wealth and facilitating trade,
truly enriching the state and benefiting the people.
Though dynasties have passed and much time has elapsed,
their utility has only become more convenient.
However, minting and casting have long been abandoned,
and repeated chaos and destruction
have caused immeasurable scattering and disappearance.
When the Jìn 晉 moved south of the Jiāngnán 江南,
its territory was not yet expanded.
Perhaps due to local customs,
coins were not widely used,
their quantity was inherently small,
and the problem was still minor.
Now, the imperial domain has broadened,
and its influence extends afar.
Where money is distributed,
it reaches even to distant and uncivilized regions.
What was formerly beyond reach
is now all in circulation.
As use becomes wider, currency becomes scarcer.
[一二]Moreover, people compete to illicitly cut and chip,
and destruction by melting increases.
Though punishments and prohibitions are severe,
illicit activities and evasion become more sophisticated,
causing prices to rise yearly,
and poor households to become emptier daily.
[一三]Those who toil with great effort
find their exertions insufficient to provide for themselves.
[一四]This is truly due to expensive currency and cheap goods,
while the normal order has not changed.
If we do not think to rectify it,
the弊 (evils) will deepen.
This is truly an opportune moment for instruction
and an excellent occasion for adaptation.
I humbly believe that if one large coin counts as two,
the state will possess an enduring treasure,
and households will gain double the profit.
It will not require additional laws;
the source of illicit acts will naturally be cut off.
One decree will achieve multiple benefits.
There is nothing more advantageous than this, without the cost of creation."
The emperor followed Yǎnzhī's 演之 deliberation.
Accordingly, one coin was made to count as two.
After being in circulation for some time,
it proved inconvenient for both public and private use,
so it was abolished.
In his twenty-fifth year,
〔一五〕he was promoted to Zuǒ Púyè,
concurrently serving as the Tutor of Rǔyīn Wáng,
with his status as Chángshì remaining unchanged.
In his twenty-eighth year,
he was transferred to Shàngshū Lìng,
concurrently serving as Tàizǐ Zhānshì.
In his twenty-ninth year,
he retired from office.
At Fāngshān, he composed the *Tuìjū Fù* to illustrate his principles.
However, commentators generally believed that Shàngzhī could not maintain his resolve.
Yuán Shú, the Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ, wrote a letter to Shàngzhī, saying:
"Yesterday I sent someone to inquire,
and learned that you, revered elder, have already withdrawn your aspirations to the mountains and fields.
Although it is said that one should follow the rites appropriate for one's age,
it is also true that such an achievement is difficult and noble,
making Shū, Bān, Bǐng, and Wèi
equally excellent in previous policies,
while Gōng, Gòng, Shān, and Wèi
fall short in earlier writings.
You plan to take leave and retire,
washing away your long-held aspirations.
I hope for the joy of seeking reclusion,
and the contentment of residing in mystery.
〔一六〕However, Shú's disposition for reclusion is particularly unique,
〔一七〕and his rustic nature is dull and sluggish.
If this quietude is realized,
he will surely sink into joy and forget to return.
Nevertheless, those who have already heard the discussions
say that your brilliant wisdom, revered elder, has not diminished,
and your reputation and achievements are still accumulating.
If you could condescend to serve in this era of peace,
lower your aspirations and dedicate yourself to duty,
abandoning the conduct of 'by the southern bank,'
then Shú's journey will be permanently decided."
〔一八〕"My affectionate regard for you is profound,
and the appointed day will not be mistaken."
Shàngzhī's residence was beside Nánjiàn Sì.
Therefore, the letter said
"Nán Pín" (southern bank),
which is what the *Máoshī* referred to as
"Where does one gather duckweed?
By the bank of the southern stream."
The imperial edict urged him to remain,
and the Emperor also issued an edict to Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng, saying:
"There are not many worthy officials in court now.
Even Yáng and Mèng cannot be allowed to resign.
Shàngzhī's appointment and treatment are exceptional;
should he not be permitted to retire yet?"
Yìgōng replied:
"Shàngzhī is pure, loyal, and steadfast,
always acting with sincerity in his service.
Although he has reached the age for retirement,
his body is still robust.
It is the common sentiment of my humble heart that he should not be permitted to retire yet."
Shàngzhī then resumed his duties.
Yáng refers to Yáng Xuánbǎo,
and Mèng refers to Mèng Yǐ,
whose courtesy name was Yànzhòng.
He was a native of Ānqiū, Píngchāng.
〔一九〕His elder brother, Chǎng, was prominent and powerful,
but Yǐ did not accept invitations to office.
After Chǎng's death,
he started his official career as the Administrator of Dōngyáng.
He subsequently served as Administrator of Wú Jùn, Kuàijī, and Dānyáng,
Sìzhōng,
Púyè,
and Tàizǐ Zhānshì.
He again served as Administrator of Kuàijī,
died in office,
and was posthumously granted the title of Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū.
His son, Shào,
married Tàizǔ's sixteenth daughter, Nánjùn Gōngzhǔ.
His daughters married Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng and Bālíng Āi Wáng Xiūruò.
After Shàngzhī returned to office,
the Emperor treated him with even greater esteem.
At this time, troops were again dispatched for a northern expedition,
and the provisions and supplies for the army
were entirely entrusted to him.
When Yuánxiōng usurped the throne,
Shàngzhī was promoted to Sīkōng,
concurrently serving as Shàngshū Lìng.
At that time, three factions rose in righteousness,
and the families of the generals and assistants were in the capital.
Shào wanted to execute them all,
but Shàngzhī persuaded him in many ways,
and they were all spared.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
Shàngzhī again became Shàngshū Lìng,
concurrently leading the Lìbù.
He was promoted to Sìzhōng, Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū,
concurrently serving as Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
Soon after, he resigned from Hùjūn,
and was granted the special rank of Tèjìn.
He again concurrently served as Shàngshū Lìng with his original office.
When Chéngxiàng Nánjùn Wáng Yìxuān and Chējì Jiāngjūn Zāng Zhì rebelled,
Yìxuān's Sīmǎ Zhú Chāomín and Zāng Zhì's Chángshǐ Lù Zhǎn and his brothers were all due to be executed.
Shàngzhī submitted a memorial, saying:
"The success or failure of punishments
is the cause of order or chaos.
The sages and worthies paid close attention to this;
one must not be incautious.
Zhú Chāomín was Yìxuān's Sīmǎ.
〔二０〕When the rebels fled,
he could have easily been captured.
If he had turned opportunistic for profit,
he would have immediately seized them,
not only escaping blame,
but also claiming ill-gotten rewards.
However, Chāomín had no such intention,
which is slightly indicative of his kindness.
Moreover, he preserved the city and its administration for the government,
carefully guarding the storehouses,
and calmly awaited arrest.
Now, if he and his brothers are executed,
how would that be any different from those who were involved from beginning to end without question?
Lù Zhǎn's complete loyalty to Zhì is also evident,
but to equate him with a great rebel
would be too severe.
I have long been favored with your special trust,
distinguished from ordinary officials.
If I have any thoughts,
I dare not keep silent."
Those who were implicated with Chāomín were thus spared.
At that time, there was a desire to divide Jīngzhōu and establish Yǐngzhōu,
and its location was debated.
Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng thought it should be in Bālíng.
Shàngzhī argued:
"Xiàkǒu is situated between Jīng and Jiāng,
directly facing Miǎnkǒu,
and connecting with Yōng and Liáng.
It is truly a vital point.
It has been an old garrison since ancient times,
and its foundation is not easily changed.
Now, if we divide Jiāngxià, Wǔlíng, Tiānmén, Jìnglínɡ, and Suí five commanderies to form one province,
with its seat in Xiàkǒu,
it already has existing city walls,
and its large harbor can accommodate boats.
The route from Jìnglínɡ to Jīngzhōu,
although by water,
is no different from going to Jiāngxià.
All the commanderies can reach Xiàkǒu by following the current,
which is convenient and advantageous for all.
Xiāngzhōu governs eleven commanderies,
and Bālíng borders the Yangtze River,
and is close to Xiàkǒu.
If we divide Xiāngzhōng,
it will become even larger.
It would also be appropriate to transfer Bālíng to the new province,
which would be suitable for the situation."
The Emperor followed his counsel.
Jīng and Yáng two provinces
accounted for half the population of the empire.
Since the time of the Eastern Jìn,
Yángzhōu was the foundation,
while Jīngzhōu was entrusted with command beyond the capital.
At this point, both were divided,
with the intention of curbing the power of officials and subordinates.
However, Jīng and Yáng both suffered decline as a result.
Shàngzhī advocated for reuniting the two provinces,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
In the second year of Dàmíng,
he was appointed Left Guānglù (左光祿) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
His position as Shìzhōng (侍中) remained as before.
Shàngzhī (尚之) habitually wore a deerskin cap at home.
When he was appointed Kāifǔ (開府),
the Son of Heaven presided from the imperial hall,
and all officials were in attendance.
Shěn Qìngzhī (沈慶之) jokingly said to him in the court:
"Why are you not wearing your deerskin cap today?"
Qìngzhī (慶之) repeatedly declined official appointments,
and the court urged him strongly to accept.
Shàngzhī (尚之) said to him:
"The Emperor is humble and eager for talent;
how can you steadfastly decline?"
Qìngzhī (慶之) replied:
"This Shěn Gōng (沈公) will not imitate Hè Gōng (何公),
who left and then returned."
Shàngzhī (尚之) looked ashamed.
He loved literature and scholarship,
and did not cease even in old age.
His debates and discussions with Tàicháng (太常) Yán Yánzhī (顏延之)
were transmitted throughout the world.
He lived simply,
his carriages and attire were plain.
When his wife died, he did not remarry,
nor did he have concubines.
When he held power in court,
he feared and kept away from authority.
He recommended none of his relatives or old friends,
which led to resentment,
but
also earned him praise.
He was again appointed Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令) with his original official title.
In the fourth year,
when his illness became severe,
an imperial edict dispatched Shìzhōng (侍中) Shěn Huáiwén (沈懷文) and Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎) Wáng Zhāo (王釗) to inquire about his health.
He passed away in office
at the age of seventy-nine.
He was posthumously granted the title of Sīkōng (司空),
and his positions as Shìzhōng (侍中) and Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令) remained as before.
His posthumous title was Jiǎnmù Gōng (簡穆公).
His son Yǎn (偃)
has a separate biography.
Shàngzhī's (尚之) younger brother Yōuzhī (悠之)
was the Prefect of Yìxīng (義興),
Shìzhōng (侍中),
and Tàicháng (太常).
He was good friends with Wáng Wēi (王微) of Lángxié (琅邪).
When Yōuzhī (悠之) died,
Wēi (微) wrote to Yǎn (偃), saying: [二一]
"I regret only that I knew Yìxīng (義興) so late.
I always considered him a true gentleman who understood me.
As for those who praised my minor virtues
and pitied my weaknesses,
only your worthy uncle did so."
Yōuzhī's (悠之) younger brother Yúzhī (愉之)
was the Prefect of Xīn'ān (新安).
Yúzhī's (愉之) younger brother Yìzhī (翌之)
was the Dūguān Shàngshū (都官尚書).
Yōuzhī's (悠之) son Yǒngzhī (顒之)
married Tàizǔ's (太祖) fourth daughter, Princess Línhǎi Huì (臨海惠).
During Tàizōng's (太宗) reign,
he rose
to the position of Tōngzhí Chángshì (通直常侍).
The Historian said: Since the eastern Jìn (晉) period,
the foundation was laid in Yángyuè (揚越),
and the power to influence was placed in Jīngchǔ (荊楚).
Yángtǔ (揚土) stretches north from Lú (廬) and Lí (蠡),
reaching the Great River (大江) by the sea.
The Jīngbù (荊部) encompasses Xiāng (湘) and Yuán (沅),
straddling Wūshān (巫山) and covering Dèng Sài (鄧塞).
Its households and territory
comprised more than half of the realm.
During the Jìn (晉) dynasty, when young rulers were on the throne,
governance fell to their regents.
The administration of Jīng (荊) and Yáng (揚)
was like that of the two Shǎns (陝).
When the Sòng (宋) house received the Mandate,
this power could not be shifted.
The importance of these two prefectures
all fell to close relatives.
Thus, Yìxuān (義宣), relying on the strength and wealth of Xīchǔ (西楚)
and building on a decade-long foundation,
once animosity arose,
he sought to seize the throne.
However, establishing Yǐng (郢) and dividing Yáng (揚)
was a case of overcorrecting.
Once the border garrisons were split,
the bandits' strength increased while the population dwindled.
The responsibilities outside the capital
were thus exhausted.
If a mature ruler faces south,
and authority and punishment emanate from him,
and his closest relatives are in external positions,
there is no fear of them becoming too powerful.
However, if the empire experiences periods of prosperity and decline,
with difficult times and a weak ruler,
even if close ministers harbor ill intentions,
there is only external apprehension.
The Lǚ (呂) clan's failure to compete
was indeed due to Qí (齊) and Chǔ (楚).
The origin of rise and fall
is particularly evident here.
Shàngzhī's (尚之) words were entirely fitting;
he can be said to have understood governance.

Biographies, Chapter 27: Xiè Língyùn (謝靈運)
Xiè Língyùn (謝靈運)
was a native of Yángxià (陽夏), Chénjùn (陳郡).
His grandfather, Xuán (玄),
was the Jìn (晉) Chēqí Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍).
His father, Huán (瑍),
was born unintelligent
and served as Mìshū Láng (祕書郎),
dying young.
Língyùn (靈運) was exceptionally brilliant from a young age,
and Xuán (玄) found him quite extraordinary,
saying to his relatives and friends:
"I gave birth to Huán (瑍),
how could Huán (瑍) have given birth to Língyùn (靈運)!"
Língyùn (靈運) was fond of learning in his youth,
read widely,
and his literary talent
was unmatched in the Jiangzuǒ (江左).
His paternal cousin, Hùn (混), particularly loved and appreciated him.
He inherited the title of Kānglè Gōng (康樂公),
with a fief of two thousand households.
According to the precedent for dukes of the state,
he was appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng (員外散騎侍郎),
but he did not take up the post.
He served as Dàsīmǎ Xíng Cānjūn (大司馬行參軍) for Wáng (王) of Lángxié (琅邪).
He was extravagant and ostentatious by nature,
his carriages and clothing were splendid and beautiful.
His garments and artifacts
often deviated from established norms,
and the world revered him for it,
all calling him Xiè Kānglè (謝康樂).
Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn (撫軍將軍) Liú Yì (劉毅) was garrisoned at Gūshú (姑孰),
and appointed him Jìshì Cānjūn (記室參軍).
When Yì (毅) was garrisoned at Jiānglíng (江陵),
he again appointed him Wèijūn Cóngshì Zhōngláng (衛軍從事中郎).
After Yì (毅) was executed,
Gāozǔ (高祖) appointed him Tàiwèi Cānjūn (太尉參軍),
and he entered the court as Mìshū Chéng (祕書丞),
but was dismissed due to an incident.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) campaigned against Cháng'ān (長安),
Piàojí Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍) Dàolián (道憐) remained to guard the capital,
and appointed him Zīyì Cānjūn (諮議參軍).
He was then transferred to Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎),
and again served as Shìzǐ Zhōngjūn Zīyì (世子中軍諮議)
and Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎).
He was dispatched as an envoy to comfort Gāozǔ (高祖) at Péngchéng (彭城),
and composed the "Zhuàn Zhēng Fù" (撰征賦).
Its preface says: I have heard that light and darkness occupy different positions,
and uprightness and obscurity follow different paths.
Although circumstances may change,
disorder is often more prevalent than order.
Therefore, peaceful times are difficult to maintain,
while decline and destruction
are easily brought about by chaos.
The Imperial Jìn (晉) moved from Hé (河) and Fén (汾),
relocating to Wú (吳) and Chǔ (楚).
It endured nine generations,
and spanned over ten decades.
There was no hope of aid from Xīqín (西秦),
and the Eastern Zhōu (東周) endured three
humiliations.
It can be said that accumulated misfortune and strife
have indeed been long-standing.
Moreover, imperial tombs were hidden and obscured,
filial piety could not be fully expressed,
and as days and months passed,
the imperial heart grew more distant.
When auspicious fortune was about to rise,
the opportune moment arrived unfailingly.
Xiāngguó Sòng Gōng (相國宋公),
obtained the righteous position,
turning the wheel of heaven's destiny,
stabilizing the realm internally
and clearing away barbarians externally.
He constantly pondered
the disunity of the land,
his thoughts filled with concern.
He encountered the rise of heaven's blessings,
and the weak were given opportunity.
Divinations foretold the grand plan,
and auspicious omens appeared.
Thus, respectfully assenting above and agreeing below,
following Heaven's
will and the omens,
he raised an army to cease conflict
and personally undertook the arduous campaign.
On the Dīngyǒu (丁酉) day of the fifth month in the twelfth year of Yìxī (義熙),
he reverently and cautiously initiated the nine punitive expeditions,
issuing commands to the six armies,
and governing
Troops were deployed in the Jīngjī (capital region),
and the army encamped by the Pián River.
There were a thousand majestic ships,
ten thousand thunderous chariots,
feathered cavalry filled the roads,
and flying banners obscured the sun.
Separate orders were given to the various commanders,
who were instructed on
wise strategies,
their tactics more extraordinary than the Sānlüè (Three Strategies),
their righteousness more profound than the Liùtāo (Six Secret Teachings).
Thus, before the hooked spears were brandished,
the former captives fell at Jīnyōng;
and as soon as the mighty bows were drawn,
the sharp falcons fled at
Huátái.
Not even a month passed,
before two regions presented their victories.
Such vast accomplishments and esteemed virtues
are unparalleled throughout history.
The Son of Heaven was moved by the toil and hardship on Dōngshān,
and rejoiced at the vast
splendor that reached to heaven.
From waking at dawn, he was inspired to self-reflection,
and dispatched his minister to traverse the plains and lowlands.
I, in a temporary official capacity,
was wrongly chosen for this special task,
feeling shame at my humble talent compared to past elegance,
and not begrudging the exhaustion
of the campaigning men.
I set out in mid-winter,
and returned to report in early spring.
My journey passed through nine prefectures,
and covered over a thousand *lǐ*.
I traveled along the Jiāng River and across the Huái River,
and sailed up the Bó, Sì, and Pián Rivers.
I carefully observed the cities
and towns,
and widely surveyed the mounds and tombs.
Recalling ancient sites,
my heart was filled with many emotions.
In the past, the august ancestors established their fiefdoms,
receiving their mandate over Huái and Xú;
their path was as firm as the wrapped mulberry,
and their achievements accumulated through benevolence.
Many years have passed,
and the markets and courts have changed,
but their great legacy remains eternal,
filling my heart with their bright history.
So I interviewed the old folks,
and sought out the former traces,
and felt a deep emotion and regret from afar,
my heart aching
and tears falling.
Thus, I gathered what I heard and saw,
and composed this fu (rhapsody) about the campaign,
so that even as events change and pass,
they may be entrusted to this to become immortal.
Its words are: Descended from the vast lineage of Lièshān,
inheriting the bright light of Huǒzhèng.
Establishing prosperity after the reign of Táng,
reiterating loyal service to King Zhōu.
Through meritorious service and rightful
position,
bestowed with precious *guī* (jade tablets) to govern their territory.
Throughout ancient times, prominent and illustrious,
descending to the middle period, flourishing and prosperous.
Their deeds followed the Dao, their virtue shone,
their influence spread through the world, and their transformations propagated.
Following
the footsteps of predecessors with eternal hope,
reflecting on my humble self with deep sorrow.
Our plans diverge from the divinations of *shī* and *cài*,
our actions of deployment or concealment differ.
Protected by constant goodness that is never abandoned,
relying on indirect success that leaves nothing out.
Their brilliance shines in the hidden, warming all equally,
their reward grows with time and becomes more personal.
Looking at the weak and fragile late grass,
I admire the luxuriant verdure of spring.
Vines sprout their tendrils on the pine,
slender branches emerge from the orchid paths.
Receiving abundant grace and favor,
repaying it with a speck of dust, with no set time.
Rejoicing in the auspicious brightness
of the Grand Staircase (Heaven),
and the harmonious radiance of the imperial Dao.
When the King established the state,
he distinguished directions and fixed boundaries;
with internal and external order,
there was distinction between Huá (China) and Yí (barbarians).
In ancient times, from the Xiǎoyǎ (Lesser Odes)
to Bān Shū's writings,
the Róng and Mán barbarians were fiercely rampant,
and were thus
exterminated and punished.
Thus King Xuān used spears against the Xiǎnyǔn,

Yet they invaded Hàogǎo as far as Jīng,
from the frontier to the plains.
Peeking into the suburbs, spying on the countryside,
Admiring King Xié's oppressive piety,
escalating the never-ending chaos of ruin.
They stole the Sānfǔ (three commanderies) of the mighty Qín,
and captured the two capitals of prosperous Zhōu.
Dominating Xiáo and Miǎn
for their strategic danger,
occupying Ràoliú as a gate.
My family forever cherishes our ancestral land,

Waiting for the distant time of great peace,
to belong to the destined sage
and enlightened ruler.
Kūn (earth) extends its connection through the four rivers,
Qián (heaven) lends its light through the three luminaries.
Water moistens the earth, clearly as a comparison,
fire flares up to the sky, like all people.
The Prime Minister, with his sagely wisdom,
managed and governed in chaotic times.
He gathered the nine currents (schools of thought) for true observation,
and harmonized the five talents for fair distribution.
The opportune moment arrived,
understood earlier than Jièshí,
the warning of falling into a pit,
once
aided the common people.
Tortoise and milfoil divinations were truly good,
humans and spirits shared the same sentiment.
Following Heaven to execute punishment,
the officials meticulously applied penalties.
Raising the banner, selecting warriors,
wielding axes and raising banners.
Bows and arrows
exhausted the wisdom of Chǔ Xiào,
spears and lances matched the spirit of Wú Zǐ.
Swiftly, the three wings formed a fish-scale array,

Before the array was set in the capital fields,

Strict frost was scattered upon Wèichéng,
and a gentle breeze reached Luòruì.

In the past, when
