Cháo Cuò spoke up;
when the Xiongnú were arrogant and insulting,
Jiǎ Yì sighed in indignation.
Compared to today,
all those are trivial.
Jìn Wǔdì was but a mediocre ruler,
but he encountered Sūn
Hào’s tyrannical chaos.
Heaven blessed his virtue;
it was also due to Jùpíng offering his strategy
and Xún and Jiǎ deliberating on plans,
that he was able to achieve great undertakings in his time,
and unify the whole realm.
How much more so now, when Your Majesty is intelligent
and sagacious,
and the world returns to benevolence?
Your civil virtues and military achievements resound together,
your frosty might and pure reputation rise in tandem.
Supported by wise and enlightened chief ministers,
the excellent commands of the various princes,
the illustrious deeds of the regional governors,
and
a court full of valiant officials,
and with the far-reaching commands of Heaven's might,
what enemy cannot be vanquished?
〔五四〕How much more so for these stubborn barbarians,
who merely seize a temporary advantage!
I humbly consider your profound strategy and
duties,
and your long-settled divine counsel.
As your humble and lowly servant,
hiding in mountain caves,
I truly aspire to the Way of Great Peace,
and long to witness the封 (fēng) ceremony on Mount Dài.
Although I lack the literary skill of Xiāngrú,
my hope is
to avoid the indignation of historical criticism.
Thus, if I were to withdraw from the capital due to illness,
I would have no regrets.
I have long wished to submit this,
but feared running into the trap.
〔五五〕Having been granted a leave of absence,
temporarily
away from the Forbidden Palace,
suffering from diabetes for ten years,
always concerned about the morning dew,
I hold this foolish ambition
and risk death to make it known.
Xiè Língyùn, due to illness, returned to the east.
However, he indulged in leisurely gatherings and banquets,
extending night into day.
He was again impeached by the Imperial Censor Fù Lóng,
and dismissed from office for this offense.
This was
the fifth year of Yuánjiā.
After Língyùn returned to the east,
he, along with his cousin Huìlián, Hé Chángyú of Dōnghǎi, Xún Yōng of Yǐngchuān, and Yáng Xuánzhī of Tàishān,
gathered to appreciate literature,
and roamed the mountains and wilderness together.
People at the time called them the Four Friends.
Huìlián was intelligent and perceptive in his youth,
but frivolous and not appreciated by his father, Fāngmíng.
Língyùn went from Yǒngjiā back to Shǐníng.
At that time, Fāngmíng was the Administrator of Kuàijī Commandery.
Língyùn once traveled from Shǐníng to Kuàijī to visit Fāngmíng,
and stopped to see Huìlián,
appreciating him greatly.
At that time, Chángyú was teaching Huìlián to read,
also in the commandery.
Língyùn also considered him outstanding,
and said to Fāngmíng:
"Ālián's talent and perception are like this,
yet you treat him as an ordinary child.
Hé Chángyú is the Zhòngxuān of our time,
yet you feed him the food of a lower guest.
Since you cannot treat worthy men with courtesy,
you should let Chángyú return with Língyùn."
Língyùn took him away.
Xún Yōng, courtesy name Dàoyōng,
rose to the office of Yuánwài Sànqí Láng.
Xuánzhī, courtesy name Yàofán,
was the Internal Administrator of Línchuān.
He was favored by the Sīkōng Jìnglíng Wáng Dàn.
When Dàn was defeated, Xuánzhī was executed for his involvement.
Chángyú's literary talent was excellent,
second only to Huìlián;
Yōng and Xuánzhī could not compare.
Línchuán Wáng Yìqìng gathered literati,
and Chángyú rose from Guó Shìláng to Píngxī Jìshì Cānjūn.
He once sent a letter from Jiānglíng to his kinsman Hé Xù,
using rhyming verse to describe Yìqìng's provincial officials, saying:
"Lù Zhǎn dyes his hair and beard,
wishing to charm his concubines.
The dark green does not last long,
the gray hairs emerge again."
There were five or six such lines,
and frivolous youths then elaborated and expanded upon them,
making all sorts of people
the subject,
adding harsh words and bitter phrases.
His writings circulated widely.
Yìqìng was furious,
and reported it to Tàizǔ, who removed him and made him the Magistrate of Zēngchéng, under the jurisdiction of Guǎngzhōu.
When Yìqìng died,
court officials went to his residence to mourn.
Hé Xù said to Yuán Shú:
"Chángyú can now return."
Shú replied:
"The state has just lost a prominent member of the imperial clan;
it is not appropriate to consider exiled persons immediately."
Lúlíng Wáng Shào garrisoned Xúnyáng,
and made Chángyú the Nán Zhōngláng Xíng Cānjūn,
in charge of secretarial duties.
〔五六〕While traveling to Bǎnqiáo,
he encountered a storm and drowned.
Língyùn, relying on his father’s and grandfather’s assets,
had very abundant means of livelihood.
His servants were numerous,
and his retainers and protégés numbered several hundred.
He excavated mountains and dredged lakes,
his engineering projects were endless.
He explored mountains and climbed ridges,
always seeking remote and precipitous places,
ascending myriad layers of cliffs and peaks,
leaving no place unvisited.
He always wore wooden clogs when climbing.
〔五七〕When going uphill, he would remove the front teeth;
when going downhill, he would remove the back teeth.
He once cleared a path by felling trees from Nánshān in Shǐníng,
all the way to Línchuán,
accompanied by several hundred followers.
The Administrator of Línchuán, Wáng Xiù, was alarmed,
thinking they were mountain bandits,
but only felt at ease when he later learned it was Língyùn.
Língyùn then urged Xiù to proceed further,
but Xiù refused.
Língyùn presented Xiù with a poem, saying:
"The provincial governor finds the terrain perilous,
the traveler finds mountain trekking easy."
In Kuàijī, he also had a large retinue,
which caused alarm in the counties and towns.
The Administrator Mèng Yǐ was a devout Buddhist,
but was belittled by Língyùn,
who once said to Yǐ:
"Those who attain enlightenment must be wise and cultured individuals.
〔五八〕You will be born into Heaven before Língyùn,
but you will achieve Buddhahood after Língyùn."
Yǐ deeply resented these words.
In Kuàijī’s Dōngguō, there was Huízhǒng Lake.
Língyùn requested to drain it to make fields.
Tàizǔ ordered the prefecture and commanderies to inspect it.
This lake was close to the city,
and was a source of aquatic products.
The common people cherished it.
Yǐ firmly refused to grant it.
Since Língyùn could not get Huízhǒng,
he again requested Shǐníng Píhuò Lake for fields.
Yǐ again held firm.
Língyùn claimed that Yǐ was not concerned with benefiting the people,
but merely worried that draining the lake would harm many lives.
He spoke ill of and slandered him,
and thus a feud developed between him and Yǐ.
Because of Língyùn’s arbitrary and reckless behavior,
the common people were alarmed and disturbed.
So, Yǐ memorialized that Língyùn harbored deviant intentions,
mobilized troops to defend himself,
and openly submitted a memorial.
Língyùn rushed out of the capital,
and went to the palace gate to submit a memorial, saying:
“Since I returned to the mountains due to illness,
it has been three years now.
My dwelling is not in the suburbs or city,
my affairs are separated from human society.
I live in seclusion in remote cliffs,
cut off from external connections.
I live within my means, preserving my life,
hoping to finish my remaining years.
Suddenly, on the twenty-eighth day of last month, I received a dispatch dated the twenty-seventh from your servant Yǐ, the Administrator of Kuàijī, stating: ‘Lately, various rumors are circulating.
Although this is understood among us,
the common people will not allow silence.
Now, I am making a slight defense against them.’
Opening the dispatch, I was astonished and saddened,
unable to comprehend the reason.
I immediately set out in haste,
to commit my bones to Your Majesty.
Upon reaching Shānyīn,
the defenses were conspicuously evident:
soldiers arranged in formation, with spears and horses,
blocking and cutting off roads and alleys.
Scouts patrolled everywhere,
and weapons and armor lined the paths.
I do not know what crime this humble servant has committed.
And when I met Yǐ,
although he said he understood me,
with such preparations and defenses,
I could only feel apprehension and fear.
Your servant once had the honor of being a close attendant,
and received heavenly grace.
If my crimes were clearly evident,
with documentary proof,
not only would I face public execution by the judicial authorities
to uphold national law,
but there would be no place for me to stand
under heaven.
Now, to be accused by mere rumors,
what could be more cruel?
Indeed, since ancient times, slanders
have not spared even saints and sages.
However, the arrival of slander
must have a cause.
Perhaps some despise death and value integrity,
forming factions and gathering crowds;
or some are the bravest in their villages,
chased by swordsmen.
I have never heard of a scholar of ritual and ceremony
seeking to commit the crime of rebellion;
nor a hermit living in the mountains
instigating an offense against the sovereign.
Now, without any trace of a crime,
false slander is fabricated.
Such cruelty has
never existed in all of history.
It is not that I begrudge my life,
but I truly grieve at this pain.
Though I honestly examine myself and find no fault,
my reasoning cannot be expressed.
Therefore, dragging my sick body,
I come with my skeletal frame to submit myself.
I humbly rely on Your Majesty’s divine discernment to observe me closely;
then the day of my death
will be like the years of my life.
Your servant has been worried and fearful for days,
my emaciated illness has flared up,
my body is barely living and confused,
I do not know what to say.”
Tàizǔ knew that he had been slandered,
and did not punish him.
Unwilling to let him return east,
he made him Administrator of Línchuān,
and granted him the rank of Zhōng Èr Qiān Shí.
〔五九〕In the commandery, he roamed freely,
no different from in Yǒngjiā,
and was impeached by the authorities.
The Sītú sent Zhèng Wàngshēng, an attendant from Suí Prefecture, to arrest Língyùn.
Língyùn seized and bound Wàngshēng,
raised troops, and rebelled,
thus harboring rebellious intentions.
He wrote a poem saying:
“When Hán fell, Zǐfáng rose;
when Qín became emperor, Lǔlián was shamed.
I am by nature a person of the rivers and seas,
moved by loyalty and righteousness, like a gentleman.”
He was pursued, captured,
and sent to the Tíngwèi for trial.
The Tíngwèi memorialized that Língyùn had led his followers in rebellion,
and sentenced him to execution by decapitation.
The Emperor loved his talent,
and wished merely to dismiss him from office.
However, Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng firmly insisted that he should not be pardoned.
So, an imperial edict stated:
“Língyùn’s crimes have accumulated repeatedly;
he truly deserves the full force of the law.
However, Xiè Xuán’s meritorious service rivaled that of Guǎnyì and Wēiróng.
It is appropriate to extend clemency to his descendants.
His death sentence may be reduced by one degree,
and he shall be exiled to Guǎngzhōu.”
Thereafter, Zōng Qíshòu, a general from Qín Commandery, arrived at Túkǒu,
〔六０〕and traveled to Táoxū Village.
He saw seven people descend from the road speaking disorderly,
and suspected they were not ordinary people.
He returned and reported to the commandery and county,
which dispatched troops with Qíshòu to ambush and suppress them.
They then engaged in battle,
and all were captured and sent to prison.
One of them was named Zhào Qīn,
from Shānyáng County.
He said:
“My fellow villager Xuē Dàoshuāng previously worked with Xiè Kānglè.
In early September of last year,
Dàoshuāng, through another villager Chéng Guó, reported to Qīn saying: ‘Xiè, who previously served as Administrator of Línchuān and was exiled to Guǎngzhōu for his crimes,
has given money to buy bows, arrows, swords, shields, and other items.
He has instructed Dàoshuāng to gather brave men from the countryside
to intercept and seize Xiè at Sānjiāngkǒu.
If successful,
after his wishes are fulfilled,
the merits will be shared equally.’
So, they gathered a party to intercept Xiè,
but failed.
Upon returning, due to hunger,
they committed robberies along the way.”
The authorities again memorialized for him to be dealt with according to law.
Tàizǔ decreed that he be publicly executed in Guǎngzhōu.
Before his death, he wrote a poem saying:
“Gōng Shèng had no remaining life,
Lǐ Yè reached his ultimate end.
Zhēng Gōng’s principles were suppressed,
Huò Shēng’s life also perished.
Sadly, like leaves enduring frost,
like fungi facing wind.
How much is fate?
Long or short life is not to be pitied.
My heart, sending itself forward,
has long endured this pain.
I regret my noble aspirations,
that I cannot vanish among the cliffs.”
The Gōng Shèng and Lǐ Yè mentioned in the poem
are similar in meaning to Zǐfáng and Lǔlián in the previous poem.
This was in Yuánjiā year ten,
when he was forty-nine years old.
His written works were transmitted to the world.
His son, Fèng, died young.
The Grand Scribe says: People receive the essence of Heaven and Earth,
containing the virtues of the Five Constants.
Hardness and softness are used in alternation,
joy and anger express emotions.
When intentions are moved within,
then songs and chants are outwardly expressed.
The basis of the Six Principles,
the origin of the Four Beginnings,
ascending and descending in songs and ballads,
spreading out as the "Airs" and "Odes."
Although before the times of Yú and Xià,
no ancient writings are seen,
endowed with spirit and holding essence,
there is no reason for it to be different.
Thus, the rise of songs and chants
should begin with the birth of humanity.
When the Zhōu dynasty declined,
literary trends became even more prominent.
Qū Píng and Sòng Yù
led the clear stream in the front,
Jiǎ Yì and Xiāng Rú
stirred up fragrant dust in the rear.
Their brilliant words moistened metal and stone,
their noble ideals reached the clouds.
From then on,
emotions and aspirations broadened further.
Wáng Bāo, Líu Xiàng, Yáng, Bān, Cuī, Cài, and their ilk,
though taking different paths, converged in their pursuits,
successively becoming masters and ancestors to each other.
Although elegant phrases and beautiful tunes
sometimes appeared in their writings,
there were also many instances of clumsy sounds and verbose expressions.
As for Píng Zǐ's brilliant outpouring,
where literature changed with emotion,
his unrivaled songs and lofty footsteps
had no echoes for a long time.
By the Jiàn'ān period,
when the Cáos established their mandate,
the two ancestors and Prince Chén
They then interwoven emotion with literature,
and clothed substance with literature.
From the Hàn to the Wèi,
over four hundred years,
the style of writing among literati and talented scholars
underwent three changes.
Xiāng Rú excelled at crafting descriptive language,
Bān Gù was skilled in expounding on emotion and reason,
Zǐjiàn and Zhòngxuān took natural disposition as their style,
all demonstrating their ability and excelling in beauty,
uniquely shining in their time.
Therefore, the scholars of their generation
each admired and emulated them.
Tracing the origin of their influential trends,
none did not revere Fēng and Sāo as their ancestors.
It was only that their preferences differed,
hence their literary styles diverged.
Coming down to Yuánkāng,
Pān and Lù were exceptionally brilliant.
Their regulations differed from Bān and Jiǎ,
all possessed abundant literary talent.
Their elaborate meanings were densely arrayed like stars,
their ornate prose intricately woven like brocade.
They continued the outstanding echoes of the Píngtái Terrace
and adopted the lofty rhymes of Nánpí.
Their lingering influence and remaining achievements
reached their peak in Jiāngyòu.
During the Eastern Jìn restoration,
Xuánfēng alone flourished.
Scholarship culminated in Zhùxià,
and extensive learning ceased at Qīpiān.
While literary expressions were unrestrained,
their meaning was limited to this.
From Jiànwǔ up to Yìxī,
nearly a hundred years passed.
Although sounds were linked and words were connected,
flowing like waves and piling up like clouds,
all without exception attributed their words to supreme virtue
and placed their meaning in the profound pearl.
Eloquent and beautiful prose
was unheard of.
Zhòngwén first reformed the style of Sūn and Xǔ,
Shūyuán greatly altered the spirit of Tàiyuán.
Subsequently, during the Sòng dynasty,
Yán and Xiè rose to fame.
Língyùn's inspired and bold expressions,
and Yánnián's precise and refined style,
both moved in parallel with earlier luminaries,
setting a standard for future generations.
If one were to sit down and discuss their hearts,
evaluating earlier writings,
the number of successes and failures
might have something to say.
Just as the five colors complement each other,
and the eight musical tones harmonize,
it is due to xuán-huáng and lǜ-lǚ,
each suiting its appropriate function.
If you wish for gōng and yǔ notes to change in alternation,
with rising and falling inflections forming distinct segments,
then there must be a clear, crisp sound at the end.
Within a single line,
the sounds and rhymes are completely distinct;
within two phrases,
the light and heavy tones are all different.
Only by brilliantly grasping this principle
can one begin to speak of writing.
As for the excellent works of earlier scholars,
which are admired for their loftiness through the ages,
Zǐjiàn's compositions from Hánjīng,
Zhòngxuān's verses by Bàn'àn,
Zǐjīng's chapters on "Zero Rain,"
and Zhèngcháng's lines on "North Wind" –
all directly expressed their heartfelt emotions,
not relying on poetic history.
It was precisely by adjusting the musical tones and rhymes
that they surpassed earlier models.
Since the time of the "Sāo" poets,
many years have passed.
Although literary styles have gradually refined,
this secret has not yet been seen.
whose sounds and rhymes are naturally formed,
they are all implicitly aligned with reason,
not achieved through deliberate thought.
Zhāng, Cài, Cáo, and Wáng
had no prior awareness of this.
Pān, Lù, Xiè, and Yán
were even further from it.
Those in the world who understand music
can grasp this,
knowing that these words are not false.
If one says otherwise,
please await future sagacious individuals.

Biographies, Chapter 28: Wǔ 2: Wáng Péngchéng Yìkāng, Nánjùn Wáng Yìxuān
Wáng Péngchéng Yìkāng,
at the age of twelve,
was appointed by the Sòng platform as Supervising Military Affairs for the Four Commanderies of Yù, Sī, Yōng, and Bìng, General of Valiant Cavalry, and Inspector of Yùzhōu.
At that time, Gāozǔ was summoned from Shòuyáng to assist the court,
leaving Yìkāng to govern Shòuyáng in his place.
He also concurrently held the post of Inspector of Sīzhōu,
and was promoted to Supervising Military Affairs of Zhōnglí in Xúzhōu and Yìyáng in Jīngzhōu.
In the first year of Yǒngchū (420 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Péngchéng,
with an estate of three thousand households,
and promoted to the title of Right General.
In the second year (421 CE),
he was transferred to oversee Military Affairs for the Five Commanderies of Nányù, Yù, Sī, Yōng, and Bìng, and Inspector of Nányùzhōu,
retaining his general rank.
In the third year (422 CE),
he was promoted to Imperial Commissioner, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs for Nánxú and Yǎn Commanderies and Jìnlíng of Yángzhōu, and Inspector of Nánxúzhōu,
retaining his general rank.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
his estate was increased by two thousand households,
he was promoted to the title of General of Agile Cavalry,
additionally granted the post of Palace Attendant,
and provided with a set of drums and pipes.
Soon after, he was granted the honorific title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
In the third year of Yuánjiā (426 CE),
he was reassigned as Grand Administrator of Military Affairs for the Eight Commanderies of Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, Liáng, Yì, Níng, Nán Qín, and Běi Qín, and Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
granted thirty ceremonial swordsmen,
retaining his Imperial Commissioner, Palace Attendant, and general ranks.
Yìkāng was intelligent and discerning from a young age,
and upon assuming regional responsibilities,
his official duties were well managed.
In the sixth year (429 CE),
the Grand Minister of Works, Wáng Hóng, memorialized that Yìkāng should return to assist the court.
He was summoned as Palace Attendant, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs for Yáng, Nánxú, and Yǎn Commanderies, Grand Minister of Works, and Director of the Department of State Affairs,
concurrently holding the posts of General Pacifying the North and Inspector of Nánxúzhōu,
retaining his Imperial Commissioner status.
Both official residences were staffed with assistants and commanded troops,
and he assisted in court governance together with Wáng Hóng.
As Hóng was frequently ill
and always deferred with humility,
from then on, all internal and external affairs
were decided solely by Yìkāng.
The Crown Prince's Household Administrator, Líu Zhàn, possessed talent for governing the state.
When Yìkāng was previously in Yùzhōu,
Zhàn served as his Chief Clerk.
Having long established a deep rapport,
by this time, Yìkāng's trust in him was especially profound.
Regarding matters of people, their manners,
and all actions and affairs,
he consulted Zhàn.
Thus, in his successive tenures as a regional lord,
he often had good governance,
for which he was praised by those near and far.
In the ninth year (432 CE),
when Hóng died,
Yìkāng also concurrently held the post of Inspector of Yángzhōu.
In that same year, the Grand Consort Dowager passed away,
and he was relieved of his Palace Attendant duties
and declined the ceremonial swordsmen.
In the twelfth year (435 CE),
he also concurrently held the post of Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince,
and was again granted the Palace Attendant and ceremonial swordsmen.
Yìkāng's 性 Xìng was fond of official duties;
he was intensely focused on documents and records.
In distinguishing right from wrong,
he was always thorough.
Having gained sole control over court power,
matters were decided by himself.
For major life-and-death decisions,
he pronounced judgments based on recorded decrees.
Everything he presented in memorials,
was always accepted without question.
Officials of the rank of Fāngbó and below
were all entrusted to Yìkāng for appointment.
Consequently, people from court and country flocked to him,
and his influence overshadowed the entire realm.
Yìkāng himself was also tireless and
never slackened.
His mansion gate always had several hundred carriages every morning;
even if they were of humble rank and low status,
they were all granted an audience.
Moreover, his intelligence and memory surpassed others;
he would remember everything he heard,
and what he encountered even briefly
he would never forget throughout his life.
In crowded gatherings and large assemblies,
he often displayed his memory to show his brilliance,
and people respected and admired him even more for this.
He cherished official ranks and titles
and never used his position to favor private individuals.
Any court official with talent and ability
was brought into his mansion.
If they did not incur offense or go against his wishes,
they were then promoted to Tái Guān.
Those below him were happy to exert their utmost effort
and dared not deceive or insult him.
Tàizǔ suffered from a consumptive illness,
which had afflicted him for many years.
Whenever he had a thought,
he would feel a tearing pain in his heart,
and many were on the verge of death.
Yìkāng attended to him with medicine,
serving him with utmost dedication.
Decoctions and food
were not offered unless he had tasted them himself.
Sometimes he would go without sleep for several nights,
and for days he would not remove his clothes.
All internal and external affairs
were solely decided and implemented by him.
In the sixteenth year,
he was promoted to Dàjiāngjūn,
overseeing Sītú,
and empowered to appoint his subordinates.
Yìkāng had always lacked scholarly knowledge
and was ignorant of the broader scheme of things.
He considered his brothers as closest kin,
no longer maintaining the formalities between sovereign and minister.
He acted straightforwardly according to his impulses,
without any suspicion or precaution.
He privately kept more than six thousand male servants,
without reporting it to the court.
Offerings from all directions
were presented to Yìkāng as superior products,
while the inferior ones were supplied for the emperor.
The Emperor once ate persimmons in winter
and lamented their poor shape and taste.
Yìkāng, who was present, said:
"There are indeed good persimmons this year."
He sent someone back to the Eastern Mansion to fetch persimmons;
the largest ones for the emperor were three inches.
Shàngshū Púyè Yīn Jǐngrén was favored by Tàizǔ
and had always been on good terms with Tàizǐ Zhānjì Láu Zhàn,
but their affection waned later.
Zhàn often wanted to use the power of the prime minister to overthrow Jǐngrén.
Jǐngrén was protected by Tàizǔ,
and Yìkāng's repeated advice was not adopted,
which made Zhàn even more indignant.
Liú Bīn of Nányáng,
a relative of Zhàn,
possessed talent for worldly affairs
and was appreciated by Yìkāng.
He was promoted from Sītú Yòuchángshǐ to Zuǒchángshǐ.
Cóngshì Zhōngláng Wáng Lǚ of Lángyá, Zhǔbù Liú Jìngwén of Pèijùn, Jìjiǔ Kǒng Yìnxiù of Lǔjùn,
all ingratiated themselves and,
seeing Tàizǔ's illness become critical,
all believed that an older ruler should be enthroned.
The Emperor's illness once reached a critical point,
and he ordered Yìkāng to draft a testament.
Yìkāng returned to his province,
weeping as he informed Zhàn and Yīn Jǐngrén.
Zhàn said:
"The world is difficult;
how can a young ruler govern it?"
Yìkāng and Jǐngrén both did not reply.
Yìnxiù and others then went to the Shàngshū Yícáo to seek precedents for the enthronement of Emperor Kāng at the end of Jìn Xiánkāng era.
Yìkāng was unaware of this.
When Tàizǔ's illness improved,
he faintly heard about it.
As Bīn and others were favored by Yìkāng
and all power and authority rested with the prime minister,
they constantly sought to shift the court
and ensure the divine vessel (throne) had a master.
Thus, they formed a faction,
observing and scrutinizing the imperial palace.
If anyone was loyal to the country
and not of the same mind as them,
they would certainly fabricate faults and offenses,
and have them condemned and dismissed.
They always collected Jǐngrén's shortcomings
or falsely created discrepancies to report to Zhàn.
From then on, the power between the sovereign and the prime minister diverged,
and internal and external difficulties arose.
Yìkāng wanted to make Bīn Dānyáng Yǐn.
During a conversation, he presented a memorial to Tàizǔ,
stating Bīn's family was poor.
The Emperor perceived his intention,
and before Yìkāng finished speaking,
the Emperor said:
"Make him Wújùn."
Later, Kuàijī Tàishǒu Yáng Xuánbǎo requested to return,
and Yìkāng again wanted to replace him with Bīn.
He again memorialized Tàizǔ, saying:
"Yáng Xuánbǎo wishes to return.
I wonder who should be made Kuàijī?"
The Emperor had not yet decided on a candidate at that time,
and hastily said:
"I have already appointed Wáng Hóng."
From the autumn of the sixteenth year,
he no longer visited the Eastern Mansion.
The Emperor, realizing the rift was established,
would lead to great disaster.
In the tenth month of the seventeenth year,
Liú Zhàn was arrested and handed over to the Tíngwèi,
and executed.

Also executed were Bīn, Dàjiāngjūn Lùshì Cānjūn Liú Jìngwén, Zéicáo Cānjūn Kǒng Shàoxiù, Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Xíng Huáimíng, Zhǔbù Kǒng Yìnxiù, Dānyáng Céng Kǒng Wénxiù, Sīkōng Cóngshì Zhōngláng Sīmǎ Liàng, Wūchéng Lìng Shèng Tántài, and others.
Shàngshū Kùbù Láng Hé Mòzǐ, Yúyáo Lìng Hán Jǐngzhī, Yǒngxīng Lìng Yán Yáozhī, Zhàn's younger brother Huángmén Shìláng Sù, and Bīn's younger brother Jǐshìzhōng Wēn were exiled to Guǎngzhōu;
Wáng Lǚ was dismissed and confined to his home.
Yìnxiù initially gained trust through his writing skills,
and gradually became involved in confidential matters.
Wénxiù and Shàoxiù
were both his elder brothers.
Sīmǎ Liàng
was a maternal relative of the Kǒng clan,
and both advanced through Yìnxiù.
Huáimíng and Tántài were favored by Yìkāng.
Mòzǐ, Jǐngzhī, and Yáozhī
were partisans of Liú Zhàn.
That day, [Lú] Yìkāng was summoned to stay overnight,
remaining in the Central Secretariat,
and that evening, [Xú] Zhàn and others were arrested.
Dù Jì, the Inspector of Qīngzhōu, commanded troops within the palace
to prepare for any emergency.
Someone was dispatched to announce the imperial edict, informing [Lú] Yìkāng of the crimes of [Xú] Zhàn and others.
[Lú] Yìkāng submitted a memorial to abdicate his position, saying:
"I, your humble subject, have been blessed by the national spirits since childhood,
and my rank and treatment have exceeded my station.
Your Majesty has extended grace and maintained kinship,
to promote fraternal harmony,
cherishing me despite my unworthiness,
and granting me profound favor.
My responsibilities encompassed both internal and external affairs,
and my position combined that of a senior minister and an assistant.
I was unable to rectify myself and lead my subordinates,
so as to solemnize the many officials.
My closeness to [Xú] Zhàn and others was misplaced,
and I gradually became unaware of it,
leading to slander and praise deviating from the truth,
and rewards and punishments being mistakenly applied.
This was due to my weak talent and heavy responsibilities,
which led to corruption.
Although the culprits have now been executed,
and imperial governance has been restored to peace,
the nurturing of grievances and the incurring of disgrace
are indeed due to me, your subject.
I bow with trepidation and fear,
as if falling into a ravine.
How can I have the heart or face
to comfortably retain this favor?
I therefore request to resign my positions
and await punishment in my private residence."
He was reassigned as the Area Commander-in-Chief of Jīangzhōu, Inspector of Jīangzhōu,
with his credentials, title of Imperial Attendant, and general's rank remaining as before.
He was sent out to garrison Yùzhāng.
He remained in the secretariat for over ten days.
Lú Yìróng, Marquis of Guìyáng, Lú Yìzōng, Marquis of Xīnyù, and Xú Zhànzhī, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, came and went to offer comfort.
He bade farewell in the secretariat
and then went downstream.
The Emperor merely wept bitterly when facing him;
he said nothing else.
The Emperor also sent the Sramanṇa Shì Huìlín to visit him.
[Lú] Yìkāng asked:
"Does this disciple have a chance to return?"
Huìlín replied:
"I regret that you did not read hundreds of volumes of books."
Xiāo Bīn, the Civil Administrator of the General Who Conquers Barbarians,
was formerly favored by [Lú] Yìkāng.
Liú Bīn and others, jealous of his favor,
slandered and dismissed him.
So [Lú] Yìkāng made Xiāo Bīn his Counselor for Consultation,
concurrently Prefect of Yùzhāng,
entrusting him with all matters, great and small.
Xiè Zōng, the Chief Clerk of the Minister of Works,
was previously close to [Lú] Yìkāng,
and was made his Secretary for Correspondence.
Those whom [Lú] Yìkāng cherished and loved by his side
were all permitted to follow him to Yùzhāng.
When he resigned from the provincial post,
his request was granted,
and he was given additional supervision over the military affairs of Guǎngzhōu, Jiāozhōu, and Shǐxīng in Xiāngzhōu.
His provisions and treatment were generous,
and gifts and correspondence continued uninterrupted.
All important court matters
were reported to him.
Before [Lú] Yìkāng's downfall,
the well water in front of the audience hall in the Eastern Palace suddenly overflowed,
and wild pheasants and river gulls flew together into the area in front of his residential quarters.
Bā Dōng Fú Lìngyù, the Civil Administrator of the General of Dragon Aspirations, presented a memorial to the throne, saying:
"I have heard that
a wise king does not oppose pointed remonstrances,
using extensive hearing as his way;
and a subject does not fear the punishment of annihilation,
using complete frankness as his loyalty.
Therefore, [Zhōu]
Chāng offered strong remonstrance,
and Féng Táng admonished directly,
which enabled Emperor Xiàohuì to firmly secure his heir,
and Wèi Shàng to be reappointed in Yúnzhōng.
How could those two subjects have delighted in opposing their lord and interfering with the times,
or offending
the imperial countenance and displeasing the Emperor?
Furthermore, Yuán Àng remonstrated with Emperor Xiàowén, saying:
'If the King of Huáinán were to die of illness on the road,
then Your Majesty would bear the name of having killed your younger brother.
What
then?'
Emperor Wén did not heed him,
and later regretted it to no avail.
I, your humble subject, am a minor official from the wilderness.
I presumptuously overestimate myself,
daring to harbor the heart of a sunflower turning towards the sun,
and admiring the noble aspiration of self-sacrifice in the Zhōu
Yì.
Therefore, I have not hesitated to travel six thousand li,
wishing to speak with my companions,
and respectfully offer my sincere but foolish advice,
hoping for your consideration and acceptance.
I humbly believe that Your Majesty personally holds the great image,
standing preeminent among all things.
Your imperial transforming influence permeates all,
and the three powers (heaven, earth, man) are surely well-governed,
opening the path between heaven and man,
seeking out exceptional recluses in caves,
and inviting outstanding talents from humble origins.
No white colt is uncalled for in a deep valley,
and no hidden treasure is lamented on a lofty mountain.
How much more so are those
who spread their wings across
the sky,
and cast nets for sunken scales in the deep sea!
What of Lú Yìkāng, King of Péngchéng,
the beloved son of the former emperor,
and Your Majesty's second younger brother?
To suddenly demote and remove him,
sending him far away to
the southern frontier,
severing grace internally,
and separating him by distance,
personally detaching him from the enlightened ruler,
and exiling him in a sacred era –
all the common people
grieve for Your Majesty on his behalf.
Your subject reflects on
the crises of the Jǐngpíng and Yuánjiā eras,
which almost led to peril.
The Three Dukes claimed the necessity of change,
secretly harboring disloyal schemes.
The senior ministers in the capital city watched for opportunities,
and the powerful Chǔ
spied on the upper reaches of the river,
some concealing evil intentions and peeking at the state,
This was a source of fear for all living beings,
and of wrath and jealousy for the gods and spirits.
Relying on
the long-lasting spirits of the imperial altars,
and the far-reaching imperial strategies,
the dust and grime were cleansed,
and the vile elements were annihilated.
The miasma of the times was settled,
and the four gates were clear.
At that time,
did [Lú] Yìkāng not
participate in the imperial plans,
sharing in the good and ill fortune?
Moreover, Your Majesty's former Chǔ was a place of strategic importance,
which non-relatives should not occupy.
You therefore granted him the title of General of Agile Cavalry,
entrusting him with the heavy responsibility of a feudal lord,
governing Nányǐng,
pacifying the people and curbing bandits,
spreading the benevolence of the imperial Sòng,
to reach the remote wilderness.
Your Majesty's grace
covered all regions;
how could it be that only the people of Nánjīng benefited
from it?
He was then summoned to be a chief minister,
and further entrusted with harmonizing affairs.
He held the three senior positions,
and also governed Xú and Yáng,
so that both the visible and invisible worlds rejoiced together,
and men and gods
applauded.
Everyone said that Your Majesty's appointment of him was proper,
and [Lú] Yìkāng's acceptance was right.
Now, how can you believe the suspicion of resemblance,
If there were errors of confusion
or punishable offenses,
it would only be right to enumerate his good and bad deeds,
and guide him with righteousness.
Furthermore, the past events concerning the King of Lúlíng
are sufficient to understand
the present.
This is Your Majesty's former carriage as a cautionary lesson,
and the spiritual tortoise for future guidance.
That Zēngzǐ was not killed
is a profound example for loyal ministers;
that he was still weaving after two accusations
is a model for benevolent kings.
Therefore, the Shī Jīng says:
'Do not believe the words of others,
for people are truly untrustworthy.'
It also says: 'Though brothers may quarrel,
their kinship is not abandoned.'
The Shàngshū says: "
"He was able to brighten his illustrious virtue,
and thereby bring his nine clans into harmony."
Once the nine clans were harmonious,
he could bring the hundred surnames into harmony.
How could brothers be abandoned?
Your subject humbly implores Your Majesty to look back upon the disasters of dismissal and demotion in past generations,
and consider the recent harm caused by slanderous words.
Since Lúlíng Wáng has already voiced his grievances to the Queen of the Earth,
Péng
chéng Wáng should also put an end to his suspected transgressions in Sòng Jīng.
This is not merely a plan for the present imperial era;
it is truly a beauty for ten thousand generations of good historians.
Moreover, flattery is difficult to discern,
and right and wrong
are easily sullied.
Blessings begin, misfortunes come first –
this is what the ancients feared.
Therefore, those who cherish their lives,
and make plans for themselves,
all keep their mouths shut and their tongues tied.
Who would dare to transgress taboos and offend the ruler?
Your subject, being dull and ignorant,
alone presents this humble suggestion.
The reason I am so diligent and earnest,
and must voice my sincere loyalty,
is that I truly fear that Yìkāng’s years will run out and his life will end,
suddenly in the south,
thus leaving
Your Majesty with the responsibility of abandoning a brother.
Although your subject is humble and lowly,
I secretly feel shame for Your Majesty on this account.
Moreover, when recording events in history,
how can historians bend the canons and records to conceal the truth?
Should
what your subject fears come to pass,
what good would Your Majesty's regret do?
Yáng Zǐyún said:
"Among the greatest blessings,
none precedes harmony and concord;
among the deepest misfortunes,
none surpasses internal strife."
I always remember these words
and take them as a warning.
How can I, witnessing a great affair of the royal house now,
sheath my brush and remain silent?
Your subject fears that the world will be swept by ill winds,
and
dissension will cause dread,
leading the people within the realm to change their views,
and the common folk to change their hearts.
To achieve peace and prosperity
would then truly be difficult.
Your Majesty merely says that bad branches should be cut,
but do you not realize
that felling the tree harms it?
This was a sorrow of ancient times,
and something that should be rectified today.
If Your Majesty were to listen with an open mind,
set aside this suspicious disposition,
condescend to consider the advice of humble folk,
and
carefully examine the schemes of the ignorant,
issue an unexpected edict,
visit and consult with learned scholars,
and quickly summon Yìkāng back to Jīngdiàn,
then brothers would be harmonious,
and ruler and subjects
would be united.
This would silence criticism within the realm
and cut off the path of numerous rumors.
If this were done, then the hopes of the four seas would be fulfilled,
and the way of slanderous talk would vanish.
Why must there be Sītú Gōng and Yáng
zhōu Mù,
only then to secure Péngchéng Wáng?
If what your subject proposes violates the constitution
and is detrimental to the state,
I request to be executed immediately
to atone to Your Majesty.
Even if I were to be dis
membered and thrown into a cauldron,
my body cooked,
it would be what I originally wished for and gladly accepted;
how could it not be a great fortune?
Upon presenting the memorial,
he was immediately arrested and sent to Jiànkāng prison,
and granted death.
Huìjī Zhǎnggōngzhǔ,
being the eldest among the siblings,
was greatly respected by Tàizǔ.
After Yìkāng went south,
a long time passed.
The Emperor once attended a very joyous banquet at the princess's residence.
The princess rose, bowed twice, and kowtowed,
overcome with grief.
The Emperor did not understand her intention,
and rose to help her up.
The princess said:
"Chēzi, at the end of the year,
will certainly not be tolerated by Your Majesty.
I now specifically beg for his life."
Then she wept bitterly.
The Emperor shed tears,
and raised a finger to point at Jiǎng Shān, saying:
"There will certainly be no such worry.
If I violate this oath,
it would be to betray Chūníng Líng."
[一三] He then sealed the wine he had been drinking and bestowed it upon Yìkāng,
along with a letter that read:
"My sister from Huìjī remembered her brother during a banquet.
The remaining wine is now sealed and sent to you."
Chēzi was
Yìkāng’s nickname.
In the twenty-second year,
Crown Prince Chancellor Fàn Yè and others plotted rebellion.
The matter implicated Yìkāng,
as recorded in Yè's biography.
The relevant authorities submitted a report saying:
"Yìkāng once usurped state power,
wantonly oppressed his superiors,
formed factions and parties,
and harbored wicked individuals.
His grave offenses were manifest,
and the matter called for clear punishment.
He especially encountered Your Majesty's profound benevolence and love,
who cherished their close family ties,
did not abolish his fiefdom,
nor diminish his noble rank.
The hearts of the four seas
and the discussions of the court and commoners
all agreed that although the imperial virtue was magnanimous,
it truly bent the established laws.
Yet Yìkāng never thought of this great favor and virtue.
After leaving for the southern territories,
he deceitfully disguised his true feelings and appearance,
outwardly showing fear,
but inwardly remaining unrepentant.
He indulged in excessive desires,
making endless requests.
Your Sacred Kindness was encompassing and tolerant,
never breaking with old affections,
repeatedly granting clemency,
and extending grace beyond past deeds.
But he secretly prepared his entourage,
then began plotting illicit communications,
covertly providing for his followers,
to summon loyal retainers.
He stealthily watched for opportunities,
never forgetting to pry.
At the time, he was still tolerated,
and punishment was limited to his attendants.
His wild and perverse nature
was never corrected,
his sinister heart grew,
and his rebellious schemes continued to form.
He threw in with a multitude of scoundrels,
connecting across a thousand *lǐ*,
again discussing the imperial ancestral altars,
and again eyeing the imperial throne.
Thanks to Your Majesty's utmost sincerity moving the spirits,
the Sòng dynasty's longevity is assured.
Thus, the treacherous plot was exposed,
and the culprits were apprehended.
The Duke of Zhōu, a supreme sage,
did not shy away from punishing his own kin;
Emperor Wén of Hàn, benevolent and enlightened,
did not conceal the wickedness of his paternal cousin.
How much more so Yìkāng, whose offenses are deeper than those of the two uncles,
whose plots exceed those of Huáinán,
who betrayed his kin and rebelled against the Way,
casting himself out from Heaven and Earth.
Your subjects have deliberated
and request that the relevant authorities strip Yìkāng of his princely title,
and hand him over to the court judiciary for punishment."
An imperial edict specifically pardoned him from the death penalty.
Thereupon, Yìkāng and his son Quánlíng Hóu Yǔn, and his daughters, the princesses of Shǐníng, Fēngchéng, Yìyáng, and Xīngpíng counties, were demoted to commoners,
removed from the imperial clan registry,
and exiled to Ānchéng Commandery.
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Shěn Shào was appointed as the Chancellor of Ānchéng,
leading troops to guard him.
While in Ānchéng, Yìkāng read books.
Upon seeing the story of Huáinán Lìwáng Cháng,
he closed the book and sighed:
"Such things happened in previous generations;
it is fitting that I have been punished."
In the twenty-fourth year [of Yuánjiā (元嘉)],
Hú Dànshì (胡誕世) of Yùzhāng (豫章) and Yuán Yùn (袁惲), former magistrate of Wú Píng (吳平), conspired to rebel.
They attacked and killed Huán Lóng (桓隆), Administrator of Yùzhāng (豫章), and Zhūgě Zhìzhī (諸葛智之), magistrate of Nánchāng (南昌).
〔一四〕They gathered a multitude and occupied the commandery,
again intending to support and elevate Yìkāng (義康).
The Grand Commandant and acting Grand Secretary, Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng (江夏王義恭), and others presented a memorial, saying:
"The words of 'throwing into a deep pit'
are clearly recorded in elegant writings;
the teachings of 'banishment and execution'
are found in historical records.
Commoner Liú Yìkāng (劉義康) bears a heavy burden of wrongdoing;
his crimes are too great to be pardoned.
But due to the emperor's sacred benevolence,
he has repeatedly hesitated,
pardoning his capital punishment
and granting him relocation to a nearby area.
This is indeed the utmost love expressed by Heaven,
surpassing all ages.
Yet he has never been content with his transgressions or accepted his banishment,
but rather, his slanderous words are shared by the masses,
and his defiant and opportunistic nature
is always evident in his words and expressions.
He internally stirs up his household
and externally influences public opinion.
The discontented populace
thus develops rebellious intentions.
Hú Dànshì (胡誕shì) falsely assumed titles
and formed a murderous rebellion.
Preventing trouble in its infancy and eliminating the subtle are
what has always been crucial, from ancient times to the present.
How much more so when the seeds of disaster have suddenly sprouted!
How can one ignore it?
Your subjects have discussed this and
it is fitting to move him to Guǎngzhōu (廣州), a distant commandery,
and banish him to the border regions,
so that there may be a thorough prevention."
The memorial was approved.
Accordingly, Shěn Shào (沈邵), Duke of Ānchéng (安成) and Imperial Chancellor, was put in charge of Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
Before he could depart,
Shào (邵) fell ill and died.
The Suǒlǔ (索虜) barbarians invaded Guābù (瓜步),
and the whole empire was in turmoil.
The emperor worried that those with different ambitions might use Yìkāng (義康) to cause unrest.
Shìzǔ (世祖) was at that time stationed in Péngchéng (彭城),
and repeatedly memorialized that something should be done about him.
The Crown Prince and Hè Shàngzhī (何尚之), Left Palatine Secretary, also spoke about it.
In the first month of the twenty-eighth year [of Yuánjiā (元嘉)],
Èm Lóng (嚴龍), Palace Secretary, was dispatched with medicine to grant him death.
〔一五〕Yìkāng (義康) refused to take the medicine,
saying:
"Buddhism teaches that if one commits suicide, one will not regain a human body.
Just deal with me as you see fit."
So, he was smothered to death with a blanket.
He was forty-three years old at the time.
He was buried in Ānchéng (安成) with the rites of a marquis.
He had six sons: Yǔn (允), Gōng (肱), Xún (珣), Zhāo (昭), Fāng (方), and Tánbiàn (曇辯).
Yǔn (允) was initially enfeoffed as Marquis of Quánlíng Xiàn (泉陵縣),
with an income of seven hundred households.
Zhāo (昭) and Fāng (方) both died young.
Yǔn (允) and the others remained in Ānchéng (安成).
When the primary culprit [Liú Shà (劉劭)] gained power,
he sent men to kill them.
In the fourth year of Dàmíng (大明) of Shìzǔ (世祖),
Yìkāng's (義康) daughter Yùxiù (玉秀) and others submitted a public memorial, saying:
"Our father met a terrible and unjust end;
he failed to uphold heavenly brilliance.
While alive, he received excellent care;
upon his death, he was honored with a ceremony.
Even the clear punishment at Yǔshān (羽山) [referring to Shùn's banishment] was not enough to enforce the law.
With the humble hearts of birds,
we, fearing death, appeal to you,
begging to rebury him in his old family graveyard,
to mingle his bones with his native soil."
An imperial edict granted this,
and also provided financial assistance.
In the first year of Yǒngguāng (永光) of the Former Deposed Emperor,
Grand Tutor Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng (江夏王義恭) presented a memorial, saying:
"I have heard that even distant relatives of ancestors
still consider their kin;
descendants of Huò (霍) [Guāng (光)] were greatly favored by their lord.
Thus, when Yán Dào (嚴道) died early,
his successor opened up the family estate;
when Fùlíng (阜陵) erred and was confined,
he later received imperial grace.
I humbly consider that the former commoner Liú Yìkāng (劉義康) once foolishly engaged in treachery,
bringing upon himself an unnatural death.
His soul sank, and his name was removed from the register,
serving as a warning for future generations.
Three dynasties have passed,
and more than thirty years have elapsed.
Heaven and Earth have renewed their cycle,
the sun and moon have risen again.
All creatures, formed and endowed with spirit,
have received a fresh start.
Yìkāng's (義康) wife and children were scattered and lost,
departing early from the flourishing transformation.
His many daughters are orphaned and weak,
forever reduced to commoners.
Considering the circumstances of the offense,
it was not originally self-inflicted.
Moved by these events and pitying their loneliness,
I cannot help but feel increased sorrow.
I dare to rely on Your Majesty's melting and expansive sacred transformation,
whose spring benevolence spreads widely,
nurturing all living beings,
and whose kindness reaches even springs and grasses.
I truly hope for a washing away of his guilt and restoration,
allowing him to return to the imperial clan.
Then this grace will extend to withered roots,
and honor will be bestowed upon decaying soil.
I especially, relying on my private relation to the state,
presumptuously present this sincere memorial,
dusting and touching Your divine majesty,
and, bowing on paper, feel sad and trembling."
An imperial edict said:
"The Grand Tutor's memorial is as such.
The Duke, moved by sentiment and remembrance of the distant past,
views it with resentment and emotion.
In the past, Huái (淮) and Chǔ (楚) extended grace,
and the inheritance flowed to collateral branches.
To suppress law and promote kinship
is an established norm from ancient times to the present.
Let the Duke's memorial be sent to the appropriate department,
〔一六〕and let it be carried out according to the intent.
As for the former Marquis of Quánlíng (泉陵), Yǔn (允), who tragically suffered cruel violence,
a successor may be specially appointed for him."
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ (泰始) of Tàizōng (太宗),
his name was again removed from the imperial register,
and he reverted to being a commoner.
Nánjùn Wáng Yìxuān (南郡王義宣)
was born with a short tongue,
making his speech difficult.
In the first year of Yuánjiā (元嘉),
at the age of twelve,
he was enfeoffed as Jìnglíng Wáng (竟陵王),
with an income of five thousand households.
He was then appointed General of the Left,
〔一七〕stationed at Shítou (石頭).
In the seventh year,
he was promoted to Holder of a Tally, Grand Administrator of the military affairs of five prefectures: Yǎn (兗), Qīng (青), Jì (冀), Yōu (幽),
and Governor of Xúzhōu (徐州).
His generalship remained as before,
and he continued to guard Shítou (石頭).
In the eighth year,
he was again made Grand Administrator of Nányǎn (南兗) and Governor of Yǎnzhōu (兗州),
to be stationed at Shānyáng (山陽),
but this was not yet carried out.
The following year,
he was promoted to Palace Secretary,
and his title was advanced to General of the Central Army.
He was made Regular Mounted Attendant
and granted a set of drums and pipes.
At that time, Jìnglíng (竟陵) was swarming with barbarian tribes,
and the people were scattered due to their harsh labor.
He was re-enfeoffed as Nánqiáo Wáng (南譙王),
and also took charge of the Shítou (石頭) garrison.
In the thirteenth year,
he was sent out as Grand Administrator of the military affairs of Jiāngzhōu (江州) and the three commanderies of Xīyáng (西陽), Jìnxī (晉熙), and Xīncài (新蔡) in Yùzhōu (豫州),
General Quelling the South, and Governor of Jiāngzhōu (江州).
〔一八〕
Initially,
Gāozǔ, considering the strategic importance of the upper reaches of Jīngzhōu,
its vast territory and strong military,
left an imperial edict for his sons to successively govern it.
After Xiè Huì was pacified,
it was bestowed upon Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng.
When Yìkāng became Chancellor,
it was then given to Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng.
Later, because Línchuān Wáng Yìqìng was a respected member of the imperial clan,
and Línchuān Wǔliè Wáng had rendered great service to the state,
Yìqìng also governed it.
Thereafter, it should have been Yìxuān's turn.
The Emperor believed Yìxuān's talent was inherently limited
and that he was unfit to govern the upper reaches.
In the sixteenth year,
Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì replaced Yìqìng,
and Yìxuān replaced Yìjì as the Inspector of Nánxúzhōu,
Commander of Nánxúzhōu military affairs, General of the North,
holding the imperial credential as before.
He was additionally made Sànqí Chángshì.
However, Huìjī Gōngzhǔ frequently spoke about it,
and the Emperor hesitated for a long time.
In the twenty-first year,
Yìxuān was appointed Commander of military affairs of the seven provinces of Jīng, Yōng, Yì, Liáng, Níng, Nán Běi Qín, Chēqí Jiāngjūn, and Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
holding the imperial credential and position of Chángshì as before.
He was first granted a secret imperial edict which stated:
"Shīhù has been in the west for a long time,
and has recently submitted memorials requesting to return.
The movement of those around the emperor,
in and out, is a normal principle in governing the state;
why must it necessarily correspond to a single departure?
Now I wish to grant his request
and have you replace him.
Although Shīhù has no extraordinary achievements,
[一九]he keeps himself pure and is frugal in his expenses,
treats others with an open mind,
and does not indulge his subordinates.
This is indeed not easy;
his reputation is not only known in the western lands,
but also considered admirable by the court and public.
He already has a certain order established there,
which brings peace to the gentry and commoners.
Commentators even say that his relocation should not yet be discussed.
This current change
is more for your sake.
You and Shīhù are of the same generation;
[二０]each has his own merits,
and public opinion also has minor differences regarding their strengths and weaknesses.
If, in this matter, there is any slight decrease [in performance],
it would cause great obstruction to the western region,
and the criticism for the replacement
would surely be directed at me.
I would also incur Shīhù's resentment,
[二一]not merely a single reproach.
If this happens, both public and private interests would suffer.
Therefore, we must discuss and consider this thoroughly beforehand.
This matter is also easy to manage;
do not let people cause criticism."
Shīhù was
Yìjì's childhood name.
When Yìxuān arrived at his post,
he diligently disciplined himself,
and his administration was well-managed.
He was fair-complexioned,
with a beautiful beard and eyebrows,
seven chi and five cun tall,
and a waist circumference of ten wei.
He kept many concubines and maids,
over a thousand in his inner quarters,
several hundred nuns and old women,
and thirty children.
His adornments were extravagant and beautiful,
and his expenses were vast.
He was promoted to Sīkōng,
changed to Shìzhōng,
and concurrently held Nánmán Xiàowèi.
In the twenty-seventh year,
when the Suǒ Lǔ invaded from the south,
Yìxuān, fearing the invaders' arrival,
wished to flee to Shàngmíng.
After the barbarians retreated,
Tàizǔ issued an edict to him saying:
"Diligently attend to the people's affairs,
there is no need to plan for secret escapes."
In the thirtieth year,
he was promoted to Sītú, Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn, and Inspector of Yángzhōu,
retaining Shìzhōng as before.
Before he could take up the new appointment,
the "prime culprit" (Yuánxiōng) assassinated the emperor and enthroned himself,
appointing Yìxuān as Zhōngshū Jiān, Tàiwèi,
concurrently Sītú and Shìzhōng as before.
Upon hearing this, Yìxuān
immediately raised an army,
gathered soldiers,
and dispatched proclamations far and wide.
When Shìzǔ began his punitive expedition,
Yìxuān sent his Cānjūn Xú Yíbǎo to lead three thousand men
to assist as the vanguard.
Upon Shìzǔ's enthronement,
Yìxuān was appointed Zhōngshū Jiān,
Commander of Yáng and Yù provinces,
Chancellor, acting on six affairs of the Shangshu,
Inspector of Yángzhōu,
[二二]granted feather canopy and ceremonial music,
provided with forty ceremonial swordsmen,
retaining the imperial credential and position of Shìzhōng as before.
He was re-enfeoffed as Nánjùn Wáng,
with an income fief of ten thousand households.
His birth mother was posthumously honored as Xiàn Tàifēi.
His second son, Yíyáng Hóu Kǎi, was enfeoffed as Nánqiáo Wáng,
with an income fief of one thousand households.
Yìxuān firmly declined the internal court position
and Kǎi's princely title.
Therefore, he was re-appointed Commander of military affairs of the eight provinces of Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, Yì, Liáng, Níng, Nán Běi Qín, and Inspector of Jīng and Xiāng provinces,
retaining the imperial credential, Shìzhōng, and Chancellor as before.
Kǎi was demoted to Yíyáng Xiàn Wáng.
Yìxuān's subordinate officers and staff,
from his lieutenants downwards, were all awarded promotions and stipends.
The Chángshǐ Zhāng Chàng's
affairs are detailed in his biography.
The Zīyì Cānjūn Cài Chāo, who exclusively managed documents and participated in strategy,
was appointed Shàngshū Lìbù Láng,
and continued as Cānjūn of the Chancellor and Nánjùn Nèishǐ,
enfeoffed as Rǔnán Xiàn Hóu,
with an income fief of one thousand households.
The Sīmǎ Zhú Chāomín was made Huángmén Shìláng,
and also appointed Sīmǎ of the Chancellor and Nánpíng Nèishǐ.
The others were granted different ranks.
Yìxuān spent ten years at his post,
with a strong military and abundant wealth.
Having been the first to initiate the great cause,
his prestige was known throughout the land.
Whatever he requested or desired,
none was refused.
The decrees issued by the imperial court,
if he disagreed with them,
he would not comply with them at all.
He once offered wine to Shìzǔ,
first pouring and drinking himself,
then sealing and sending the remainder;
such was his lack of understanding of propriety.
Initially,
Zāng Zhì secretly harbored rebellious intentions.
Believing Yìxuān to be mediocre and weak,
and easily swayed,
he wished to use him to instigate rebellion
and accomplish his treachery.
From Xiāngyáng, he went to Jiānglíng to see Yìxuān,
and showed him full deference;
the matter is in Zhì's biography.
Upon arriving in Jiāngzhōu,
he frequently sent secret messages to persuade Yìxuān,
saying,
"You possess great talent,
have rendered great service,
and wield a power that shakes the emperor.
Since ancient times, few have survived such a position unscathed.
You should take the lead
and make arrangements early.
Moreover, all the common people are concerned about you.
If you gather your troops and enter the court,
who, inside or outside, would not joyfully support you?
If not, once disaster strikes,
regrets will be too late."
Yìxuān secretly accepted Zhì's words.
Furthermore, Shìzǔ behaved improperly within the imperial household,
engaging in illicit relations with Yìxuān's daughters.
Yìxuān, enraged by this,
secretly prepared ships and armor,
planning to raise an army in the autumn and winter of the first year of Xiàojiàn.
He informed Rǔ Shuǎng, the Inspector of Yùzhōu, and Xú Yíbǎo, the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, to join him.
Shuǎng, in a drunken frenzy, misunderstood the instruction,
and rebelled in the first month of that year.
He sent his Household Affairs Clerk to deliver a tablet,
appointing Yìxuān as Emperor,
and also sent the emperor's regalia.
Yíbǎo also led his troops towards Péngchéng.
Yìxuān and Zhì hastily raised their armies.
On the twenty-sixth day of the second month,
Yìxuān was given the additional title of Commander of all military affairs inside and outside,
appointed Left and Right Chángshǐ and Sīmǎ,
and ordered his officials to address him by name.
He dispatched an envoy to present a memorial which read: "Your servant has heard that Bólù assisted Hàn,
yet was suspected by Empress Xuān;
Chāngguó aided Yān,
yet was doubted by King Huì.
I always believed that a person of a different surname who shakes the ruler
easily creates suspicion and animosity;
while those with
close
kinship can be expected to be clear and bright.
Although your servant is mediocre and weak,
I have always aspired to loyalty and prudence.
When the great rebellion reached the heavens,
I forgot my home and sacrificed for the state.
Although the calculations of fate have a destination,
my humble achievements do not
Shù,
I have been completely sincere and utterly foolish,
penetrating both the hidden and the manifest.
However, subtle doubts are unobserved,
and accumulated slanders are heard daily.
The sound of the shuttle being thrown
is chaotic and overwhelming to the ear.
I presume this is because treacherous ministers have caused
strife,
weaving this intricate slander.
In the decadent age of shallow customs,
few ministers possess integrity and loyalty.
When ice and frost arrive together,
no trees remain un-withered last.
Those who reside in a perilous world,
willingly enjoying prosperity in
a false court,
are abandoned by those who wear caps and robes,
and chosen by those who throw shuttles.
It has even come to this: those whose positions surpass former favor,
whose responsibilities are equal to the great affairs of state,
detest the upright and dislike merit,
wantonly generating perverse doctrines,
to confuse
and mislead the enlightened ruler,
and deceive his sight and hearing.
Moreover, those who followed him south to serve as local officials,
whose toils are not worth recording,
unjustly claimed heavenly achievements,
as if they were their own efforts.
They fanned the flames of common弊 (literally "harm" or "malady", implying their shared vices),
plotting to overthrow the ancestral
altars.
Zhāng Zhì’s loyalty and integrity last year,
and his merits surpassing ancient worthies;
Lǔ Shuǎng’s adherence to the great cause,
with a will as firm as metal and stone—
such individuals are suspected and slandered,
and there is an absolute desire to bring disaster upon them.
In the past, when Jí
Àn was still alive,
Liú Ān suppressed his ambitions.
After Kǒng Fǔ passed away,
Huá Dū indulged in rebellion.
Although your servant is not skilled in martial arts,
my achievements in times of difficulty are evident.
Yet calumny and cunning are again rampant,
seeking to lure and summon.
The ancestral temple is in danger;
it is not the place for ceremonial tassels.
Your servant is entrusted with the imperial foundation,
shining together with the sun and moon.
If the royal house falls,
the fault lies with my humble self.
How can I forget the taboo of striking a rat,
and willingly accept the blame for offending the wall?
I shall immediately
muster and summon soldiers,
and issue orders to the various fiefdoms,
to let the loyal and diligent vent their indignation,
and the righteous men exert their strength,
to slay these evil villains,
and atone for errors before the imperial court.
Then, advancing, I will not fail the spirits of the Seven Temples,
and retreating, I will have no shame regarding the treatment received from the two courts.
As I face this memorial, I feel deeply moved and ashamed,
and my words cannot express themselves.
The Emperor’s edict replied: The Emperor respectfully inquires.
Because I am unblessed by Heaven,
I have encountered difficulties and calamities.
The imperial house and the state are in imminent danger,
about to be cut off.
Therefore, I personally went ahead with eight hundred (men),
to clear away grievances,
relying on far-reaching plans,
to overcome difficulties together.
I then ascended (the throne) as one of little light,
to continue the great sacrifices.
Rewarding meritorious relatives
truly expresses my intentions,
regarding flaws in governance and deficiencies in duty,
it is my wish
to rectify and save.
However, admirable words are unheard,
and my own lesser virtues are first displayed.
The achievements of aiding the sovereign are not yet complete,
but the plot to destroy the crown has already arrived.
Zhāng Zhì is treacherous, impetuous, and without conduct,
rejected by
humanity.
Because of this, he is ignorant,
his ambition is to usurp power.
His malicious intent is about to be realized,
first by borrowing followers,
inciting and deceiving with fierce words,
thereby creating this path to rebellion.
If all these rebels succeed together,
and all evil individuals compete,
I fear that the fate of the "gazing crow" (referring to a troubled state)
will not know where to stop,
and the accumulation of grievances and disasters
will have no end.
Although the Duke is not clear-sighted,
turning his back on the fundamental and honoring the treacherous,
blindly
favoring the slanderous and ugly,
and even plotting against the ancestral altars,
and though there have been days of "treading on frost" (i.e., signs of impending danger),
with conflicting discussions and disputes.
I, with the supreme Way being impartial,
have stopped and prevented doubts and discussions,
and with trust and sincerity,
have displayed it to
all far and near.
Unexpectedly, changes in affairs are hard to anticipate,
and the ugly words have come true.
Thus, my heart is distressed and I have lost my plan,
forgetting sleep and food.
Now, I shall personally command the six armies,
and widely order the various regional governors,
to declare to the spirits and swear before the multitude,
and proceed directly to Cháishāng,
to execute the chief villain,
to appease all under Heaven.
Thereafter, I will alert my retinue to
clear the Jiāng river,
ring the imperial bells on the Yǐng road,
lay down my spear and don my robes,
and personally receive your counsel and encouragement.
The Sòng dynasty is unfortunate,
repeatedly plagued by domestic calamities.
Last year, when affairs settled,
I then received your far-sighted instructions,
hoping
that with my humble weakness,
I could forever avert these difficulties.
How could I know that not even a full year had passed,
before I witnessed this conflict again?
The legacy of the two ancestors
is about to fall into the abyss.
Looking up at the magnificent foundation,
I can only feel deep
sorrow and grief.
Grand Preceptor Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng also wrote a letter to Yìxuān, saying: Lately I have heard rumors that
the two Lǔs rebelled,
and that there were reasons for it.
I considered these to be baseless words,
not heard by the ears of the wise.
Suddenly, I saw your memorial,
which plans
to raise the army of Jìnyáng.
I am shocked and dismayed,
and do not understand the reason.
If the ruler is young and the minister strong,
and political power shifts to the chief minister,
or if the times are dark and the ruler indulgent,
and those above are coerced and intimidated,
then
loyal and wise regional governors might,
seeing the danger, seize the opportunity.
But I have not heard of a sagely ruler governing the world,
with all officials following the rules,
yet taking up arms at the very beginning of a dispute,
and attempting to save a crisis on
a day of peace.
If you seek success through this,
I secretly worry for my dear younger brother.
Last year, when the two villains instigated rebellion,
the whole realm rose in unison.
Brother, you acted with loyalty and filial piety,
supporting the enlightened ruler.
Your great achievements
and abundant virtues
are already manifest,
and the imperial court admires and praises them,
and has also shown generous favor.
The position of Chancellor is the highest for a subject,
rarely granted east of the Jiāng river.
Two kings in one family
is rarely
seen in the world.
Your memorial amply demonstrates your sincerity,
evident in your actions.
The appropriateness of your recommendations
is entirely according to your will.
Your advancements and increased benefits
were still awaiting future appointments;
to abandon them all at once
can only be called
fate.
We received the compassionate upbringing of the late emperor,
and were able to join human society.
We think of repaying his profound kindness,
which is as boundless as the vast heavens.
Even exhausting our strength and sincerity,
we still fear being of no help.
How can this be?
Listening to perverse doctrines,
you lightly create disaster.
When there were no rumors in the state,
you immediately attributed the blame to the two uncles (èr shū);
when there was no Cháo Cuò in the world,
you still followed the same old path as the seven vassal states (qī fān).
You abandoned the
excellent example of Hàn Cāng,
and followed the disastrous path of Qí Jiǒng.
In earlier times, Zhòngkān borrowed troops from Língbǎo,
and then harmed his clan;
Xiàobó handed them over to Liú Láo,
whose loyalty quickly vanished.
These are all established events from past generations,
and are
stern warnings for today.
Zāng Zhì had few good deeds in his youth,
which his younger brother knows well.
Relying on his distant relatives
and his own minor contributions,
he was promoted out of turn,
and thus surpassed his peers.
He leveraged the
power of Xīchǔ
to achieve his private ambitions.
If his vicious plot succeeds,
he will likely no longer be a mere "creature in a pond."
The father and son of Lǔ Zōng
were enemies of the state for generations.
Because Tàizǔ was still pursuing his grand strategy,
Sǔn and others were
granted fiefs like Yōng Chǐ.
Now to allow them to hold five prefectures,
like a tiger or rhinoceros escaping its cage,
is to create a Liú Yuān.
Xú Yíbǎo is the younger brother of Yuán Hù's wife.
Previously, when Hù submitted to us,
Yíbǎo desperately sought to go north,
disliking the far west.
Recently, he lingered in Húlù,
and we sent Liú Yōng to him.
His opinion is agreeable.
Yōng is Xú Chōng's
maternal uncle,
and just sent a secret letter,
swearing to switch sides.
Since the barbarians invaded our borders,
both public and private sectors have suffered greatly.
How can we pacify them?
Perhaps peace can be achieved.
If you, my brother, continue to disrupt
the peace,
I fear that the border regions will all become barren land.
You should recall the hardships of Gāozǔ's founding of the dynasty in distant times,
and consider the recent calamities and conflicts in our family and state.
It is time to cease military conflict
and together bring peace to the state (shè
jì).
Accept responsibility for your faults,
eliminate treacherous and wicked individuals,
preserve your former merits,
and let your virtues be recorded in history.
In the past, Liáng Xiào repented his sins,
and Jǐngdì bestowed grace;
Fù and Zhì reformed,
and Sùzōng granted favor.
This instruction of loyalty
merely hopes for a return to those past words;
the turning point of fortune and misfortune
is for the discerning to observe.
The Emperor (Zhǔshàng) is divinely martial and decisive,
with strategies abundant as a forest.
Loyal ministers are incensed,
valiant warriors roll up their sleeves,
mighty cavalry covers the fields,
and ships fill the rivers.
Though I am untalented,
I am entrusted with authority,
and command all the generals.
My first priority is to prevent conflict.
At the appointed dawn, we will launch a swift attack
to clear the southern territories.
Therefore, I have prolonged the wait,
hoping that you, my brother, will not be too late to awaken.
If you stubbornly persist in being misled by treacherous words,
then Heaven truly wills it.
Writing this letter, I am filled with emotion
and disregard order.
Yìxuān issued proclamations to various prefectures and commanderies,
advancing their ranks and titles.
He dispatched Adjutants Liú Chénzhī, Yǐn Zhōuzhī, and others to lead troops to join Zāng Zhì.
The Inspector of Yōngzhōu, Zhū Xiūzhī, raised an army in support.
On the eleventh day of the second month, Yìxuān led an army of 100,000 from Jiāngjīn,
with ships stretching for several hundred *lǐ*.
On that day, there was a great wind,
and the boats nearly capsized;
they barely managed to enter Zhōngxiàkǒu.
He appointed his eighth son, Tāo, as General of Aid the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn),
to guard Jiānglíng.
He sent Lǔ Xiù and Zhū Tánsháo with over 10,000 men to attack Zhū Xiūzhī in the north.
When Xiù first arrived in Jiānglíng,
he met Yìxuān.
After leaving,
he beat his chest and said:
"Brother is ruining things!
To act as a rebel with an idiot like this,
we are doomed this year!"
When Yìxuān reached Xúnyáng,
he descended with Zhì,
with Zhì as the vanguard.
Upon reaching Quètou,
they heard of Xú Yíbǎo's defeat,
and Lǔ Shuǎng's death at Xiǎoxiàn.
They looked at each other, startled.
Shìzǔ sent the General Who Guards the North (Zhènběi Dàjiāngjūn), Shěn Qìngzhī, to present Shuǎng's head to Yìxuān,
along with a letter that read:
"I am entrusted with a region,
but conflict has arisen within my jurisdiction.
Recently, I briefly led a light force
to go and suppress them.
As soon as our military fronts met,
the rebel Shuǎng was killed.
Since your feelings are exceptionally close,
perhaps you wish to see him.
While he is still recognizable,
I send him to be presented to you."
Yìxuān and Zhì were both shocked and terrified.
The Emperor (Shàng) had previously sent the Inspector of Yùzhōu, Wáng Xuánmó, with a naval force to station at Liángshān Isle,
and built "backward-moon" (quèyuè) cities on both east and west banks,
with very strong camps and palisades.
Yìxuān repeatedly wrote to Xuánmó,
demanding his surrender.
Xuánmó replied in a letter: "I have received two admonitions,
and am shocked to face battle.
Formerly in Péng and Sì,
I heard all the generals say that this day would surely come.
From my humble perspective,
I thought there was no such
reason.
Last September,
I therefore sent Adjutant Xiān Sēngyuàn to write a letter expressing my feelings,
and secretly suggested a plan for your entry into the government,
hoping that the virtue of Zhōu Dàn
might reappear
today.
How could I have known that fate is hard to resist,
and it has indeed come to this?
Previously, by fortunate circumstance,
I received the regard of a national scholar.
I thought of repaying your great kindness,
even if it meant rising from the grave.
How could I have known that one
day things would go against my wishes?
You have openly promoted treachery and deceit,
and indulged yourself in the western territories,
believing the words of wicked small-minded individuals,
and forgetting the importance of great principles.
You are immersed in cunning ambitions,
extinguishing the kindness of your sovereign and parents.
Playing with extreme favor,
you aspire to what you should not.
You seek to overthrow
the ancestral sacrifices of generations,
plotting your own downfall.
Acting blindly,
never has there been anything as extreme as this.
Yet you still
wrongly send me a letter and proclamation,
remotely inviting me to join you.
This means that my subtle loyal heart
has not been illuminated by your high discernment,
and my sincere, hidden aspirations
[二三] have been vainly felt in normal times.
Pondering this over
and over,
I finally realize how difficult it is to truly know someone.
You only remember my past promotions,
but do not consider that good teaching has its foundation.
You only see Xú and Lǔ's choices,
but do not know that there are people
who uphold righteousness.
Is this not regrettable!
If one has a subject, one wishes him to be loyal;
yet you lure people and lead them to rebellion.
Is a gentleman's loyalty and empathy like this?
If there is no loyalty or empathy,
then
the birds of passage
will not gather in their chosen trees.
Indeed, one who seeks a concubine loves her for her ease,
but one who seeks a wife respects her for her difficulty.
If one accepts orders like an echo,
what use would one be then?"
The original hubs and remaining chariots
indicate that those without proper etiquette will inevitably suffer consequences.
I fear that the gentlemen of Jīngyǐng
have already secretly harbored dissenting thoughts.
It is not that the humble officials of the imperial capital
are upholding righteousness and refuse to yield.
Although you, Duke, are
confused in heart and have embarked on this path,
I still wish you would strive to establish a good plan.
General Liú Fǔjūn is loyal, brave, and impassioned,
〔二四〕and his sincerity has always been well-known.
The merits of the Xīntíng campaign
are unparalleled.
Yet, to foolishly trust
treacherous falsehoods
and sit idly by while he is slandered and disparaged,
is this not bewildering?
Fortunately, when people are wanting,
the vanguard is alerted early;
the elite armored troops are already stationed on nearby roads;
the Zèn Jūn troops are continuously departing;
the Tàifù and Piàojì will successively command the grand army;
the imperial carriage will personally
lead the six divisions,
its awe-inspiring power shaking distant lands.
People are invigorated a hundredfold,
yearning for righteousness like a forest.
Boats and cavalry return like clouds,
splendidly covering a thousand *lǐ*.
I shall forthwith don my quiver and grasp my spear,
to contend with
your excellency.
Receiving a mandate and upholding benevolence,
there is no reason to yield.
Indeed, the way of the sovereign has been exhausted,
and the etiquette of the people is also severed.
Taking up my brush to compose this reply,
emotions of sorrow and indignation fill my heart.
General Liú Yuánjǐng occupied Gūshú as the grand commander.
Subordinate generals Zhèng Kūn and Wǔ Niàn garrisoned Nánpǔ.
Zāng Zhì advanced directly to Liángshān,
establishing a camp about one *lǐ* from Xuánmó.
Liú Yìxuān was stationed at Wúhú.
On the nineteenth day of the fifth month,
a fierce southwest wind blew.
〔二五〕Zāng Zhì, taking advantage of the wind and current, attacked Xuánmó’s western camp.
His attendants, including Púshè Hú Zǐyǒu, fought unsuccessfully,
abandoning the camp and crossing over to Xuánmó.
Zāng Zhì also sent general Páng Fǎqǐ with several thousand soldiers from outside the islet to Nánpǔ,
and further ordered him to attack Xuánmó from the rear.
Upon meeting Zhèng Kūn and Wǔ Niàn,
Páng Fǎqǐ suffered a great defeat,
and nearly all his men drowned.
On the twenty-first day,
Liú Yìxuān arrived at Liángshān.
Zāng Zhì ascended and deployed his army on the eastern bank to attack Xuánmó.
Xuánmó dispatched Yoují Jiāngjūn Yuán Hùzhī, Jìnglín Tàishǒu Xuē Āndū, and others to sally forth from the camp and fiercely engage.
They utterly defeated Zāng Zhì’s army,
and the soldiers all plunged into the water at once.
Yuán Hùzhī and others used the wind to set fires,
burning their boats and carriages.
The wind was fierce and strong,
and smoke and flames covered the river.
Liú Yìxuān was then stationed on the western bank,
and the spreading fire nearly burned down his camp.
The generals, taking advantage of the wind and fire,
launched an all-out attack,
and the multitude immediately collapsed and fled.
Liú Yìxuān and Zāng Zhì became separated,
each fleeing alone in a single boat.
The gentry and common people of the east all submitted.
Among those from the west who followed Liú Yìxuān,
there were still over a hundred boats.
Liú Yìxuān’s daughter had previously married Zāng Zhì’s son.
Passing through Xúnyáng,
he entered the city to retrieve his daughter,
and took her with him as he fled west.
Upon reaching Jiāngxià,
he heard that there were troops at Bālíng
who had cut off their path,
so he turned back and entered Jìngkǒu,
proceeding on foot towards Jiānglíng.
His followers had scattered and were almost all gone,
with only about ten people remaining at his side.
His feet hurt so much that he could no longer walk,
so he hired an open cart from a civilian to carry himself.
He had no more food,
and begged along the way.
Upon reaching the outskirts of Jiānglíng,
