he sent someone to inform Zhú Chāomín.
Zhú Chāomín, fully arrayed with ceremonial guards and troops, welcomed him.
At that time, externally, things were as before,
with still over ten thousand armored men.
After Liú Yìxuān entered the city,
he immediately went out to the hearing hall to receive guests.
His close attendant Zhái Língbǎo admonished him to comfort the assembled guests,
saying,
“Zāng Zhì failed to follow the proper instructions,
which led to this defeat.
Now we are reorganizing the army and repairing our armor,
to plan for the future.
In the past, Hàn Gāo suffered a hundred defeats,
but ultimately achieved great success.”
However, Liú Yìxuān forgot Zhái Língbǎo’s words
and mistakenly said,
“Xiàng Yǔ suffered a thousand defeats.”
Everyone covered their mouths and laughed.
Lǔ Xiù, Zhú Chāomín, and others still acted as his confidantes,
wishing to gather the remaining embers
and plan for another decisive battle.
But Liú Yìxuān was confused and muddled, having lost his spirit and composure.
He entered his inner chambers and did not emerge again.
His close confidantes
one after another defected and fled.
Lǔ Xiù fled north.
Liú Yìxuān no longer stood on his own
and wished to follow Lǔ Xiù.
So, he put on military attire in his chambers,
packed rations in a bag,
wore a saber,
and took his son Liú Tāo and five beloved concubines,
all dressed in men’s clothing, to accompany him.
The city was in chaos,
with drawn blades clashing.
Liú Yìxuān was greatly frightened and fell from his horse.
He then proceeded on foot.
〔二六〕Zhú Chāomín escorted him outside the city
and gave him another horse.
Zhú Chāomín then returned to guard the city.
Liú Yìxuān hoped to catch up with Lǔ Xiù
and expected the generals to send him north into barbarian territory.
But having lost track of Lǔ Xiù,
and before he had even left the outer city,
his generals and soldiers had all deserted,
leaving only Liú Tāo, the five concubines, and two eunuchs.
At night, he returned towards the city,
entering an empty government office in Nánjùn.
There was no bed,
so they slept on the floor until dawn.
He sent a eunuch to inform Zhú Chāomín.
Zhú Chāomín sent an old carriage
to transport him to be executed.
Liú Yìxuān was sent to the prison cell,
where he sat on the ground and sighed:
“That old slave Zāng Zhì has ruined me!”
He initially entered the prison with the five concubines.
The five concubines were soon sent out.
Liú Yìxuān wept and said to the prison guard:
“The past days were not suffering,
this separation today is true suffering.”
Dà Sīmǎ, Jiāngxià Wáng Liú Yìgōng, and the other eight ducal ministers wrote to Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Zhū Xiūzhī, saying:
“Liú Yìxuān has rebelled against the Dao and betrayed kindness,
thus falling into extreme treachery.
The great principle of destroying kinship for righteousness is a standard common to ancient and modern times.
Even those who are merely disloyal are sometimes imprisoned or executed.
How much more so for one whose ugly conduct and perverse intentions
are glaringly evident far and wide,
whose blades are pointed at the crimson palace gates,
and whose troops surround the nearby suburbs,
causing imminent peril and deep worry,
making ruler and subject eat late with anxiety!
Thanks to the brilliant imperial strategy,
and the auspicious blessings of our ancestors,
the sinner has been captured,
and the ancestral temples are not destroyed.
The judicial authorities are to determine the punishment,
and the laws are there to be applied.
Yet, imperial benevolence extends to the lowest,
pitying his foolish delusion,
restraining the law to express emotion,
and repeatedly rejecting memorials.
Both gods and men are startled and fearful,
and we examine our hearts with dread.
Liú Yìxuān has cut himself off from Heaven;
there is no reason to tolerate him.
The concerns of the state and altars of soil and grain
place a heavy responsibility on subjects and sons.
It is appropriate to unilaterally carry out the great execution
to alleviate the nation’s difficulties.
However, to subject him to the axe
would harm the sagely benevolence.
By showing great grace
and allowing him to choose his own end,
we uphold Heaven’s virtue
above,
and promote the grand law
below.
As I write this letter, I am filled with sorrow and indignation,
and will not say more.”
Before the letter arrived,
Zhū Xiūzhī reached Jiānglíng,
where Liú Yìxuān had already died in prison.
He was forty years old at the time.
Shìzǔ permitted his reburial.
Yìxuān's sons Cōng, Kǎi, Huī, Jǐng, Dàn, Rú, Dūn, Tāo, Bóshí, Yè, Xīdá, Fǎdǎo, Sēngxǐ, Huìzhèng, Huìzhī, Míngmǐlǔ, and Miàojué, along with Bǎomíng, eighteen people in all,
Rú and Xīdá died young.
The rest, along with Yìxuān, were all killed by Zhū Xiūzhī.
Cài Chāo, as well as Advisor to the Military Yan Lèzhī, Xú Shòuzhī, and other confederates,
were all executed.
Chāo
was a native of Kǎochéng, Jìyáng.
His father, Màozhī,
attended to the Prince of Lúlíng, Yìzhēn, during his studies,
and rose to the office of Commandant of Cavalry under the Prince of Péngchéng, Yìkāng,
and Grand Administrator of Shǐxīng.
Chāo was talented and learned in his youth.
He initially served as an Attendant Official for Yǎnzhōu.
At that time, officials were ordered to recommend talent,

and Chāo, along with Jiāng Chúnzhī, a former Magistrate of Shǐníng from the same commandery, and Hé Dàoyǎng of Kuàijī, a former Advisor to the Commander Who Conquers the South, were both recommended by Hóu Yìbīn of Xìng'ān.
Zhú Chāomín
was the son of Zhú Kuí, the Inspector of Qīngzhōu.
Huī, courtesy name Jǐngdù,
was the eldest legitimate son.
He was eloquent and intelligent from a young age,
and Yìxuān greatly loved and esteemed him.
At the age of eleven,
he was appointed Heir Apparent to the Prince of Nánqiāo,
and appointed Attendant Official.
When Yìxuān was in Jīngzhōu,
Kǎi, Huī, Dàn, and Dūn were all granted death at the burial grounds in Jiāngníng.
Tàizǔ wanted him to return to the west,
so he appointed him Grand Administrator of Hédōng,
and added the title of General Who Pacifies the North.
After a while,
he was summoned to be an Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
When the Arch-Criminal usurped the throne,
Huī became a Palace Attendant.
When Yìxuān rose in revolt,
Shào arrested Huī and his younger brothers Kǎi, Dàn, Cōng, Jǐng, and Rú, and confined them outside,
guarded by the Gentleman of the Palace, Shěn Huàn.
Huàn secretly intended to defect,
and said to Huī and the others:
"Misfortune and fortune are shared with all of you,
so please do not worry."
When Zāng Zhì advanced from Báixià towards Guǎngmòmén,
Shào ordered Huàn to kill Huī and the others.
Huàn then removed their shackles,
and led dozens of his subordinates with Huī and the others towards Guǎngmòmén, intending to exit.
The gatekeepers resisted them.
Huàn said:
"Duke Zāng has already arrived,
and the villain has fled.
These are the sons of the Grand Commandant;
they can all bring you wealth and honor,
not just escape misfortune.
Do not hold us back."
Zāng Zhì happened to arrive at that moment,
allowing them to escape.
When Huī reached Xīntíng,
he was immediately appointed Palace Attendant.
Soon after, he was promoted to Palace Attendant, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, General of the Western Center, and Inspector of Xiāngzhōu.
Yìxuān also held the governorship of Xiāngzhōu.
Huī was then transferred to Palace Attendant,
and additionally served as Commandant of the Guards.
When the Jìn clan crossed the Yangtze,
they did not establish the offices of Colonel of the City Gates and Commandant of the Guards.
Shìzǔ desired to reinforce the city's defenses,
The establishment of the Commandant of the Guards
began with Huī.
He was transferred to General of the Right Guards,
with his position as Palace Attendant remaining unchanged.
When Yìxuān raised an army in rebellion,
Huī and his brothers and sisters all fled at once.
Huī hid in the home of Chén Xǐn, a commoner in Jiāngníng.
Someone reported him,
and he was arrested and handed over to the Grand Judge.
Huī's son, Shàncáng,
died with Huī.
Kǎi, courtesy name Jǐngmù,
was raised in the palace from birth,
and his favor was equal to that of the imperial princes.
At the age of ten,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yíyáng County.
He then served as General Who Establishes Might, Grand Administrator of the two commanderies of Nánpéngchéng and Pèi.
He was promoted to Colonel of Infantry,
transferred to Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate,
Central Provisional Attendant to the Heir Apparent,
and additionally Colonel of the Long Water.
The Arch-Criminal appointed Kǎi as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
Shìzǔ appointed him Supervisor of the Imperial Secretariat.
Before he could take office,
he was promoted to General Who Protects the State, Grand Administrator of the two commanderies of Nánpéngchéng and Xiàpī.
In that year,
he was transferred to Minister of the Five Armies,
and his peerage was advanced to king.
When news of Yìxuān's rebellion arrived,
Kǎi, within the Ministry of Personnel building,
dressed in women's clothing,
rode in a visiting carriage,
and sought refuge with Mèng Xǔ, the Duke of Línyǔ.
When the matter was discovered,
Kǎi was arrested and handed over to the Grand Judge,
and Xǔ was also executed.
and was given the posthumous title Marquis Dào.
Cōng was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiāngnán County.
Jǐng was enfeoffed as Marquis of Qíyáng County.
Xú Yíbǎo, courtesy name Shíwū,
was a native of Jīnxiāng, Gāopíng.
Initially, for his meritorious service in the Battle of Xīntíng,
he was appointed General Who Protects the State, Military Governor for the Commander of the Guards, and Grand Administrator of Hédōng,
but he did not take up the office.
He was promoted to Inspector of Yǎnzhōu,
retaining his general title,
and garrisoned Húlù.
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yìyáng County,
with a stipend of two thousand five hundred households.
When Yìxuān rebelled,
he dispatched an envoy to appoint Yíbǎo as General Who Conquers the Barbarians, Inspector of Xúzhōu,
and ordered him to lead troops out to Guābù.
Yíbǎo sent his Chief Clerk Liú Yōngzhī to attack Péngchéng.
Míng Yìn, the Military Governor for the General Who Pacifies the North, defeated him.
He then sent Wáng Xuánkǎi, the Grand Administrator of Gāopíng, with Yōngzhī to again press on Péngchéng.
At that time, Xiāo Sīhuà, the Inspector of Xúzhōu, had not yet taken up his post.
An imperial edict thus ordered Xiàhóu Zǔquán, the Military Governor for the General Who Pacifies the North, to lead five hundred men to rush to Yìn's aid.
Upon arrival,
he attacked and beheaded Xuánkǎi,
and Yōngzhī returned to Húlù.
Yíbǎo again sent a local, Tán Xiūzǔ, to reinforce Xuánkǎi.
Xiūzǔ's forces also dispersed.
Yíbǎo abandoned the city and fled to Lǔ Shuǎng.
When Shuǎng was defeated,
Yíbǎo escaped to the border of Dōnghǎi Commandery.
The locals captured and delivered him,
and his head was sent to the capital.
Xiàhóu Zǔquán
was a native of Qiáo.
For his meritorious service, he was enfeoffed as Viscount of Qíyáng County,
with a stipend of four hundred households.
During the Dàmíng era,
he served as General Who Establishes Might, Inspector of Yǎnzhōu,
and died in office.
He was given the posthumous title Viscount Liè.
The historian remarks: Master Páng of Xiāngyáng said to Liú Biǎo:
"If Duke of Zhōu had lived under a thatched roof with Guǎn and Cài,
eating a broth of wild greens,
would there have been such difficulties?"
Indeed, family relations are born of kinship,
sharing the same breath and form.
Although the measure of love and affection may be the same,
the sentiments concerning wealth and honor are different.
Reflecting on Master Shàng's words,
I sigh deeply.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 29: Liú Zhàn by Fàn Yè
Liú Zhàn, courtesy name Hóngrén,
was a native of Nièyáng, Nányáng.
His grandfather, Tān, and his father, Liǔ,
were both Grand Masters of Splendid Happiness of the Left and Administrators with Ceremonial Privileges of the Three Dukes during the Jìn dynasty.
Zhàn was adopted by his paternal uncle Dàn,
and inherited the enfeoffment as Fifth-Rank Baron of Ānzhòng County.
In his youth, he possessed integrity and resolve,
and did not pursue superficial glamor.
He was widely read in historical records and biographies,
and well-versed in ancient precedents of previous generations.
Even in his youth, he harbored ambitions of governing the world,
often comparing himself to Guǎn Yíwú and Zhūgě Liàng.
He did not compose literary works,
nor did he enjoy engaging in debates.
His home province invited him to be an Attendant Official,
but he did not accept.
He was appointed Assistant Editor of the Imperial Library,
but again did not accept.
Gāozǔ appointed him Acting Staff Officer to the Grand Commandant,
and treated him with great favor.
When Gāozǔ held the titles of General Who Guards the West and Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
he appointed Zhàn as Chief Clerk,
and subsequently assigned him as Administrative Assistant and Secretary to the Inspector,
then again as Staff Officer to the Grand Commandant,
and Chief Clerk to the General Who Conquers the Barbarians and General of the Western Center for the Heir Apparent.
His father, Liǔ, died in Jiāngzhōu.
The provincial government sent a generous amount of funeral provisions,
but he accepted none of it,
which was praised by public opinion at the time.
After the period of mourning,
he was appointed Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat,
and then left to serve as Staff Officer to the Chancellor.
Xiè Huì and Wáng Hóng both praised him for his capability and talent.
Gāozǔ entered and received the mandate of Jìn.
He appointed his fourth son, Yìkāng, as Champion General and Inspector of Yùzhōu,
and stationed him in Shòuyáng.
He appointed Zhàn as Chief Clerk and Administrator of Liángjùn.
Yìkāng was young and not yet involved in governance;
all military affairs of the prefecture and province were entrusted to Zhàn.
His office was promoted to Right General,
and he rotated with the office.
Yìkāng, with his original title, was transferred to Nányùzhōu,
and Zhàn was re-appointed as Administrator of Lìyáng.
He was a person of strict integrity and enforced the law rigorously.
Corrupt officials who embezzled a hundred cash or more
were all executed.
From then on, all subordinates were awed and subdued.
Lúlíng Wáng Yìzhēn was appointed as Chariot and Cavalry General and Inspector of Nányùzhōu.
Zhàn again served as Chief Clerk,
and his title of Administrator remained as before.
Yìzhēn was then in mourning for Gāozǔ.
He had his attendants prepare meals,
but Zhàn forbade it.
Yìzhēn then ordered his左右 to procure fish, meat, and delicacies,
and set up a separate tent inside his study.
When Zhàn entered,
Yìzhēn immediately ordered roasted trotters and grilled clams.
Zhàn sternly said:
"Your Highness should not have such a spread at this time."
Yìzhēn said:
"It is very cold this morning.
What harm is one bowl of wine?
The Chief Clerk is like family;
I hope you will not treat this differently."
When the wine arrived,
Zhàn rose and said:
"You are unable to conduct yourself with propriety,
nor are you able to treat others with propriety."
In the first year of Jǐngpíng (423 CE),
he was summoned and
appointed as Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel.
He was promoted to Right Guard General.
He was sent out to supervise military affairs of Guǎngzhōu and Jiāozhōu, and appointed as Jianwei General, Pingyue Zhonglang General, and Inspector of Guǎngzhōu.
He resigned due to the mourning of his birth mother.
After the mourning period,
he became Attendant-in-ordinary.
The General of the Guards, Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng, was stationed in Jiānglíng.
He appointed Zhàn as Imperial Commissioner, Southern Man Commandant, and concurrently Chief Clerk of the General of the Guards,
managing the affairs of the office and province.
At that time, Wáng Hóng assisted in government,
while Wáng Huá and Wáng Tánshǒu held key positions in the court.
Zhàn considered his own talent no less than theirs,
and did not wish to be sent out.
This appointment,
he believed, was a result of being sidelined by Hóng and others,
and he was very displeased.
He often said:
"If the two Wángs were not former associates of the Crown Prince's residence,
they would not have reached this position.
One might say they encountered opportune times."
Zhàn was proud of his ambition and character.
He always admired the conduct of Jí Àn and Cuī Yǎn.
Therefore, he named his eldest son Àn, with the courtesy name Chángrú,
and his second son Yǎn, with the courtesy name Jìguī.
Yǎn died of illness in Jiānglíng.
Zhàn requested to personally escort the coffin back to the capital.
Yìgōng also pleaded on his behalf.
Tàizǔ replied to Yìgōng, saying:
"I also received Zhàn's petition,
and felt a pang of sadness.
I do not wish to casually deny his request.
However, you are young,
and have just begun to handle various affairs.
The eight prefectures are vast and critical,
and the responsibility of sole decision-making is heavy.
It is impossible to entrust and rely on someone
without finding the right person.
After considering two or three options,
I have not yet found it convenient to grant your request.
I have now replied to Zhàn's petition,
temporarily suspending the funeral there.
Recently, court officials have been falling away one after another,
and those whom I can trust are increasingly few.
Zhàn is indeed a national talent.
I truly wish to bring him back,
but it is simply because the responsibility in the west is heavy,
and so I must temporarily halt this matter.
Your rewards, punishments, and all matters concerning gains and losses
must be fully entrusted to him."
Yìgōng was very impetuous and narrow-minded by nature,
and as he grew older,
he wished to handle political affairs independently.
He was constantly restrained by Zhàn,
and thus a rift gradually formed between the principal and his subordinate.
Tàizǔ heard of this
and secretly sent an envoy to question and reprimand Yìgōng,
and also to urge deep reconciliation.
Yìgōng fully explained that Zhàn showed no deference as a subordinate,
and also that he himself was older
but could not act as he wished.
Although he received the imperial edict,
he had some resentful words.
The Emperor's fraternal affection was usually very strong,
and he wished to accommodate and soothe him.
So he issued an edict saying:
"That things have come to this
is truly lamentable.
Talents are scarce today,
and the appointments have already been made.
You should try your best to reconcile,
taking what is acceptable
and discarding what is not.
Your memorial says 'completely boundless,'
which is excellent.
He is very suspicious;
he must not be allowed to detect anything at all.
You are already grown,
and have gradually experienced many things.
Moreover, the public expects much,
and does not regard you as immature.
How can you still be as you were at ten years old,
consulting on every action?
However, what you are currently solely responsible for
must be minor matters.
I also fear that judging the importance of these matters
may not always be accurate,
and his suspicions and resentments
may partly stem from this."
Earlier,
after Wáng Huá had died,
and Tánshǒu had also passed away,
the General of the Guards, Yīn Jǐngrén, considering that the wise men of the time were scattered,

In the eighth year (431 CE),

Zhàn often said:
"How difficult it is to be a chancellor in this age!

The following year (432 CE),

In the twelfth year (435 CE),

Zhàn and Jǐngrén were old acquaintances.
Furthermore, he was summoned due to Jǐngrén's suggestion,

However, when both received important appointments,

Because Jǐngrén exclusively managed internal affairs,

At that time, Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng held sole sway over court power.
As Zhàn had been Yìkāng's former superior,

Yìkāng repeatedly tried to instigate this with Tàizǔ,

Yìkāng's subordinates and Zhàn's various loyal followers secretly agreed

Liú Jìngwén, Zhàn's partisan, whose father Chéng had not realized their scheme,

Jìngwén immediately rushed to apologize to Zhàn, saying:

Due to my own ignorance and shallowness,

Such was Jìngwén's cunning and obsequiousness, without shame.
Yìkāng 劉義康 held great power and dominated the court.

Zhàn 劉湛 further exalted him,

When Zhàn 劉湛 first entered the court,

Whenever he entered the Wúnlóngmén 雲龍門,

But in his later years,
he incited Yìkāng 劉義康

Though the Emperor's feelings were internally alienated,
his outward treatment of Zhàn 劉湛 remained unchanged.
The Emperor once said to his trusted confidants:
“When Liú Bān 劉班 first returned from the west,

Zhàn’s 劉湛 childhood name was Bānhǔ 班虎,

He was promoted to Dānyáng Yǐn 丹陽尹,
Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū 金紫光祿大夫,

In the seventeenth year,

In the tenth month,
an imperial edict stated:
“Liú Zhàn 劉湛, relying on his family background,

In recent years, the seven luminaries have deviated from their paths,

In the past, when Qí 齊 and Lǔ 魯 were without principles,

when Zhāo 昭 and Xuān 宣 acted decisively,

He was executed in prison

His son, Àn 黯,
was the Dàjiāngjūn Cóngshì Zhōngláng 大將軍從事中郎.

Zhàn’s 劉湛 brother, Sù 素,
a Huángmén Shìláng 黃門侍郎, was banished to Guǎngzhōu 廣州.

said:

You advised me to do evil,
but evil should not be done;
you advised me to do good,
and now we see the result today.
What can be done!”
Whenever Zhàn 劉湛 bore a daughter, he would kill her,
which was considered monstrous by the gentry.
Fàn Yè 范曄, courtesy name Wèizōng 蔚宗,
was from Shùnyáng 順陽.
He was the youngest son of the Chējì Jiāngjūn 車騎將軍, Tàì 范泰.
His mother gave birth to him in the latrine,
and his forehead was injured by a brick,
hence he was given the childhood name Zhuān 磚 (brick).
He was adopted by his paternal cousin, Hóngzhī 范弘之,
and inherited the title of Wǔxīng Xiàn Wǔděng Hóu 武興縣五等侯.
From a young age, he loved learning,
extensively studied the classics and histories,
was skilled in writing essays,
could write in clerical script,
and understood music theory.
At seventeen,
the province invited him to be a zhǔbù 主簿,
but he did not accept.
He served as Gāozǔ Xiàngguó Yuàn 高祖相國掾,
then Píngchéng Wáng Yìkāng Guānjūn Cānjūn 彭城王義康冠軍參軍,
and transferred with the office to Yòujūn Cānjūn 右軍參軍.
He was then appointed Shàngshū Wàibīng Láng 尚書外兵郎.
Later, he left to serve as Jīngzhōu Biéjià Cóngshì Shǐ 荊州別駕從事史.
Soon after, he was summoned to be Mìshū Chéng 祕書丞.
He resigned due to his father’s mourning.
After the period of mourning,
he became the Sīmǎ 司馬 to the Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn 征南大將軍 Tán Dàojì 檀道濟,
also holding the post of Xīncài Tàishǒu 新蔡太守.
When Dàojì 檀道濟 marched north,
Yè 范曄 dreaded the campaign and
excused himself with a leg ailment,
but the Emperor did not permit it,
ordering him to lead the transport of weapons and troops by water.
After the army returned,
he became Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng 司徒從事中郎.
After a while,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Lìbù Láng 尚書吏部郎.
In the winter of Yuánjiā 元嘉 nine,
the Píngchéng Tàifēi 彭城太妃 passed away.
On the eve of the funeral,
at the ancestral wake,
all officials and former colleagues gathered at the Eastern Palace.
Yè’s 范曄 younger brother, Guǎngyuān 廣淵,
who was then Sītú Jìjiǔ 司徒祭酒,
was on duty that day.
Yè 范曄 and Sītú Zuǒ Xīshǔ Wáng Shēn 司徒左西屬王深 stayed overnight at Guǎngyuān’s 廣淵 residence.
They drank heavily into the night,
opening the north window to listen to dirges for entertainment.
Yìkāng 劉義康 was furious,
and demoted Yè 范曄 to Xuānchéng Tàishǒu 宣城太守.
Feeling frustrated,
he then abridged the histories of the Later Hàn 後漢 from various authors into a single work.
After several years in the commandery,
he was promoted to Chángshā Wáng Yìxīn Zhènjūn Chángshǐ 長沙王義欣鎮軍長史,
with the added title of Níngshuò Jiāngjūn 寧朔將軍.
His elder brother, Gǎo 范暠, was Yídū Tàishǒu 宜都太守,
and his adoptive mother was with Gǎo 范暠 in office.
In the sixteenth year,
his mother passed away.
He reported an illness to excuse his absence,
so Yè 范曄 did not rush to the funeral.
When he finally set off,
he even brought his concubines with him,
which was reported by Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Liú Sǔn 御史中丞劉損.
However, Tàizǔ 太祖 admired his talent
and did not punish him.
After the mourning period ended,
he became Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn Hòujūn Chángshǐ 始興王濬後軍長史,
also serving as Nánhyàpéi Tàishǒu 南下邳太守.
When Jùn 始興王濬 became Yángzhōu 揚州,
he did not personally handle governmental affairs,
entrusting everything to Yè 范曄.
Soon after, he was promoted to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn 左衞將軍 and Tàizǐ Zhānshì 太子詹事.
Fàn Yè was less than seven chí tall,
fat and dark-skinned,
with sparse eyebrows and beard.
He was skilled at playing the pípa,
and could compose new tunes.
The Emperor wished to hear him,
and repeatedly hinted at his subtle desire,
but Fàn Yè feigned ignorance,
and ultimately refused to play for the Emperor.
Once, when the Emperor was enjoying a banquet,
he said to Fàn Yè:
"I wish to sing;
you may play."
Only then did Fàn Yè obey the command.
After the Emperor finished singing,
Fàn Yè also stopped playing.
Originally,
Kǒng Xīxiān of Lǔguó was learned and possessed both strategizing talent and ambition.
He excelled in literature, history, astronomy, and mathematics,
with nothing he did not master.
He served as Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng,
but was not recognized by his contemporaries,
and for a long time did not receive a promotion.
Previously, Xīxiān's father, Kǒng Mòzhī, as the Governor of Guǎngzhōu,
was implicated in a corruption case and sent to the Grand Judge.
However, Grand General Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng protected him,
and so he was spared.
When Yìkāng was demoted,
Xīxiān secretly harbored thoughts of repaying him.
He wished to gain the support of court ministers,
but was unsure who could be swayed.
Seeing that Fàn Yè was dissatisfied,
he wanted to draw him in.
However, Xīxiān was not highly regarded by Fàn Yè,
and had no means to approach him with his proposal.
Fàn Yè's nephew, Xiè Zōng,
was very well-regarded by Fàn Yè.
Xīxiān had known him previously,
so he dedicated himself to serving Zōng,
and formed a close bond with him.
Xīxiān, using the wealth inherited from Lǐngnán,
was very rich.
He began gambling with Zōng and his younger brothers,
deliberately playing poorly,
and losing property to them.
Zōng and the other young men,
having repeatedly won property,
then came and went day and night,
and their feelings grew closer.
Zōng then introduced Xīxiān to Fàn Yè to gamble.
Fàn Yè also played with him,
and Xīxiān deliberately lost,
losing a great deal of property to Fàn Yè over time.
Fàn Yè, profiting from his wealth,
also admired his literary and artistic talent.
Xīxiān, naturally eloquent,
devoted himself wholeheartedly to Fàn Yè,
and Fàn Yè subsequently became extraordinarily close to him,
forming an indissoluble friendship.
He first tried to sway Fàn Yè with subtle words,
but Fàn Yè did not respond.
Xīxiān then used his utmost eloquence to persuade him.
Fàn Yè had always been known in both court and common circles for his discussions of family affairs,
which was known to both the court and the public.
Thus, although his lineage was illustrious,
the state did not seek marriage alliances with him.
Xīxiān used this to provoke him, saying:
"If you, sir, believe the court treats you generously,
why did they not seek marriage with you?
Is it because your family is deemed unsuitable?
People treat you like dogs and pigs,
yet you wish to die for them;
is this not folly?"
Fàn Yè remained silent, not answering,
but his resolve was set.
At that time, Fàn Yè and Shěn Yǎnzhī were both favored by the Emperor,
and were often seen together.
If Fàn Yè arrived first,
he would wait for Yǎnzhī to enter together.
If Yǎnzhī arrived first,
he was often summoned alone,
and Fàn Yè resented this.
Fàn Yè had served in Yìkāng's administration for many years,
and was always treated with great respect.
However, after the appointment to Xuānchéng,
their goodwill had deteriorated.
Zōng served as the Grand General's Scribe and Military Advisor for Yìkāng,
accompanying him to his post in Yùzhāng.
When Zōng returned,
he conveyed Yìkāng's sentiments to Fàn Yè,
seeking to resolve their past animosity,
and to restore their former good relations.
Fàn Yè, already harboring rebellious thoughts,
wished to probe the Emperor's intentions,
so he spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"Your servant has observed the histories of the Former and Later Hàn dynasties,
where the policies regarding various vassal kings were that those who engaged in demonic curses or rejoiced in misfortune
were punished with the penalty for great treason.
How much more so Yìkāng, whose treacherous heart and malevolent deeds
are manifest far and wide,
yet remains unharmed to this day?
Your servant is secretly perplexed by this.
Moreover, if a major troublemaker remains,
it will lead to further chaos.
Matters between blood relatives
are difficult for people to speak of.
Your servant has received deep and profound grace,
and therefore dares to speak out."
The Emperor did not accept this.
Xīxiān was skilled in astronomy,
and claimed:
"The Grand Ancestor will surely die an unnatural death,
likely due to conflict among relatives.
A Son of Heaven should emerge from Jiāngzhōu."
He believed Yìkāng would be that person.
Zōng's father, Xiè Shù, was also well-treated by Yìkāng,
and Zōng's younger brother, Xiè Yuē, was Yìkāng's son-in-law.
Therefore, the Grand Ancestor sent Zōng to accompany him south.
Having been persuaded and encouraged by Xīxiān,
Zōng also had a desire to repay Yìkāng.
Zhōu Língfǔ, a man from Guǎngzhōu, had private troops and retainers.
Xīxiān gave him six hundred thousand coins,
to raise an army in Guǎngzhōu.
Língfǔ left and never returned.
Zhòng Chéngzǔ, an archivist in the Grand General's office,
was an old confidant of Yìkāng.
He frequently carried messages to the capital,
and also secretly gathered loyal followers,
planning a rebellion.
Hearing of Xīxiān's sincerity,
he secretly allied with him.
Xú Zhànzhī, the Governor of Dānyáng,
was always loved by Yìkāng.
Although they were uncle and nephew,
his affection surpassed that for his own children.
Chéngzǔ therefore used this connection to serve Zhànzhī,
and informed him of the secret plan.
Chéngzǔ went south,
conveying Yìkāng's intentions to Xiāo Sīhuà and Fàn Yè,
saying:
"I originally intended to form a marriage alliance with the Xiāo family,
but I regret that my initial intention was not realized.
My affection for Fàn has never been shallow,
and the estrangement between us in the interim
was caused by others."
There was the Daoist Fǎlüè
who was previously supported by Yìkāng.
He was generally known and treated well.
There was also the nun Fǎjìng from Wángguósì Temple who frequented Yìkāng’s household.
Both were grateful for past favors
and planned to assist and save him.
They both associated with Xīxiān.
They had Fǎlüè renounce his Daoist ways;
his original surname was Sūn.
He changed his name to Jǐngxuán,
and was made a Commander of the Níngyuǎn Army under Zāng Zhì.
Xīxiān was good at treating illnesses
and also skilled at pulse diagnosis.
Xǔ Yào, the brother-in-law of the nun Fǎjìng,
was a commander stationed in the capital,
guarding the palace and central government offices.
He once fell ill,
and the nun Fǎjìng asked Xīxiān to treat him.
Xīxiān prepared a dose of medicinal soup,
and Yào’s illness immediately improved.
Yào went in person to express his gratitude,
and thus they became acquainted.
Xīxiān, seeing that Yào had potential for bravery and capability,
treated him with deep respect and forged a connection.
He then revealed his rebellious plot,
and Yào promised to be an inside accomplice.
Hú Zūnshì of Yùzhāng,
a son of Fán,
was very close to Fǎlüè
and also secretly agreed to the plan.
When the nun Fǎjìng went south,
Xīxiān sent his maid Cǎizǎo with her,
entrusting her with a letter
that laid out the prognostications and prophecies.
When Fǎjìng returned,
Yìkāng sent Xīxiān a bronze ladle, bronze tweezers, a length of silk for a robe, a cosmetic box, and other items.
Xīxiān, fearing exposure,
poisoned Cǎizǎo and killed her.
Zhànzhī further said to Yè and others:
“Zāng Zhì treats me exceptionally well.
He will return within the year.
I have already informed Zhì
to bring all his disciples and old acquaintances.
He should also understand this intention
and thus be able to gather several hundred brave men.
Zhì is close to Xiāo Sīhuà,
and should rely on him.
Both men are favored by the Grand General,
so there will certainly be no disagreement.
Sīhuà’s forces from his three commanderies and old acquaintances
are also no less than Zhì’s.
The civil and military officials in the commandery,
along with all the scouts from various places,
should also be no less than a thousand men.
We do not worry about insufficient military strength,
only about losing the opportune moment.”
Then, they roughly assigned positions.
Zhànzhī was to be Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Pacifying Army) and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yángzhōu);
Yè was to be Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Central Army) and Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Nánxúzhōu);
Xīxiān was to be Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Left Guard);
the rest also had their selected appointments.
All those who had previously been disliked or who had not supported Yìkāng
were listed in a separate register
and marked for death.
Xīxiān instructed his younger brother Xiūxiān to draft a manifesto, which read: When stagnation and prosperity alternate,
the Way knows no lasting peace.
When mad villains run riot in rebellion,
the wise are struck down.
Therefore, Xiǎobái had the merit of setting things right,
and Chóng’ěr had the
virtue of supporting the throne.
Since the beginning of Jǐngpíng,
the imperial house has suffered many misfortunes.
The late Emperor, born with heroic bearing,
intelligent and sagacious,
was elevated from a feudatory state
to inherit the throne and govern the realm.
He toiled with
ten thousand affairs of state
and gave his attention to all matters.
Thus, the country was peaceful and prosperous,
and the four seas were united under the same customs.
However, in recent years,
treacherous villains have disrupted governance,
punishments have become corrupt and perverse,
and yin and yang have
been discordant.
This has caused strife within the palace
and brought together dangers and calamities.
The traitorous minister Zhào Bófú, harboring accumulated resentment and poison,
then indulged in wickedness,
wielded arms to violate the imperial procession,
and brought disaster upon the Crown
Prince and ministers,
exalting those who were not of their kind
and overthrowing the imperial foundation.
His crimes surpass those of Zhuó and [unclear character, possibly 豜],
and his transgressions exceed those of Xuán and Mǎng.
Since the beginning of the world,
nothing comparable has been heard of.
All under heaven beat their breasts in grief,
and both Chinese
and barbarians shed tears of blood.
All harbor the sincerity of sacrificing their lives
and share the desire to offer their bodies in retribution.

Zhànzhī and Yè, along with the acting Commander of the Central Army Xiāo Sīhuà, the acting General of the Protectorate Army Zāng Zhì, the acting General of the Left Guard Kǒng Xīxiān, and the General of Martial Might Kǒng Xiū
xiān,
whose loyalty pierces the white sun
and whose sincerity is manifest to both the unseen and visible realms,
are pained in their hearts by righteousness
and hurt in their eyes by these events.
They will cast their lives and wield their spears,
heeding not a myriad deaths.
On this very day, they will sever the head of Bófú
and
those of his confederates.
Although the jackals and wolves are immediately executed,
and the Kingly Way is renewed,
yet the whole world is without a master,
and the masses have no one to rely on.
The Prince of Péngchéng is a descendant of the High Ancestor,
with sagacity present
in his person.
His virtue reaches heaven and earth,
and his achievements fill the realm.
The path of the world is difficult,
not to be used in the southern land.
He has lived in obscurity like a coiled dragon and perched phoenix
for six years now.
The common people hunger for his virtue,
and the myriad masses thirst
for his transforming influence.
How can it be that only the eastern expedition has the song of the owl,
and Shǎnxī has the thought of "do not cut short"?
Spirits and deities announce propitious omens,
and prognostications and records display the symbols of an emperor.
Above,
he answers the will of Heaven;
below, he satisfies the hopes of the people.
To establish himself in the position of the celestial pole,
who else but the Prince?
Now, we dispatch the acting General of the Protectorate Army Zāng Zhì and others
to carry the Emperor’s seals and ribbons,
and hasten to welcome him.
All officials will prepare the rites,
following one another in succession.
We also command all commanders
and generals
to maintain their garrisons as usual.
Should any interfere with the righteous army,
they will be punished without quarter.
Last year, when the envoy returned,
Zhànzhī presented a handwritten imperial edict,
forewarning of calamities and chaos,
and foreseeing this
sprouting.
It ordered to make it known to court officials
to together save those in peril,
and not to interrupt the deliberation of affairs,
losing the later opportunity.
This led to the cruel abuse of the sacred person
and the sudden arrival of great changes.
My sorrow and regret tear me apart,
I clutch my heart and choke with emotion,
not knowing where
I can lay my body.
I will bravely press on,
unto death and beyond.”
Xīxiān thought that since it was a major undertaking,
Yìkāng’s approval was needed.
Yè then wrote a letter from Yìkāng to Zhànzhī,
which he showed to their confederates, saying: “I am an ordinary person of limited talent,
raised in wealth and nobility,
acting on my own whims,
unaware of my faults,
at odds with others,
my joys and angers deviating from reality,
causing many small-minded people to
resent me,
and the literati not to return to me.
Calamity and defeat have already occurred,
yet I still did not awaken.
Upon retrospective reflection,
I only then realized I brought it upon myself.
Carving into my flesh and bone,
what can now be mended?
However, as
for devoting my heart to serving the emperor above,
my sincerity penetrates both the unseen and visible realms.
With earnest caution,
I only feared I would fall short.
It is truly impossible that I would presume upon favor and become arrogant,
or intentionally deceive and defraud.
How could I..."
Harboring treacherous intentions
to invite ruin and destruction.
Thus, I offered sincerity and trusted fully,
no longer guarding against differences,
following my inclinations and trusting wholeheartedly,
disregarding the criticisms of all.
This led to malicious
schemes secretly taking root,
and all evils converging.
Jiǎ, treacherous, cunning, and greedy for gain,
deeply wronged me;
Yǐ, vicious, ignorant, and despised,
incited the unruly;
Bǐng and Dīng, scrambling underlings,
who only knew flattery and advancement,
seeking out faults,
fabricated baseless claims,
causing misfortune to befall my own kin,
and the innocent to be executed.
What evidence
was there, after all,
for these alleged transgressions,
that the punishment meted out
equated them to the gravest villains?
This injured harmony and twisted reason,
moving heaven and earth.
Though I am confined and daily suffering,
my life hanging by a thread,
righteous and indignant men
occasionally send news.
I am always aware of celestial phenomena and human affairs,
as well as the sentiments outside,
that the
collapse and disintegration of the state
is imminent.
This is because the trouble started with the worthies,
and has now widely affected the nation.
Day and night, I seethe with indignation,
my heart and gut in turmoil.
Can the gentlemen of the court and the common people,
both the humble and the noble, who cherish righteousness and uphold reason,
fail to recognize the opportune moment,
and idly await overwhelming disaster?
To eliminate evil from beside the ruler
is not unique to one generation.
Moreover, such
mad and wicked crimes
are unprecedented throughout history.
To eliminate and destroy them
is easier than crushing rotten wood.
I can declare my intentions to all worthies.
If they can unite and rise up,
shatter
the rebellious faction,
would this not be a merit equal to founding a dynasty,
and rebuilding the Sòng household?
However, warfare is dangerous and perilous,
and may lead to excesses.
If even one person commits an infraction,
the punishment will extend to
the nine generations.
The crucial dispositions
are entrusted to all worthies.
All must diligently obey the imperial court,
reporting every action and movement.
Past grievances
will be completely dismissed at once.
Then I shall
confess my sins before the Northern Gate,
and accept execution by the proper authorities.
If the altars of earth and grain are secured,
I will close my eyes without regret.
Strive for it! Strive for it!
In the ninth month of the twenty-second year,
General who Conquers the North, Prince Yìjì of Héngyáng, and General of the Right, Prince Shuò of Nánpíng, were dispatched to garrisons.
The emperor held a farewell ceremony for them on Wǔzhànggāng.
Yè and others had planned to stage a rebellion on that day,
but a misunderstanding prevented them from acting.
In the eleventh month,
Xú Zhànzhī submitted a memorial, saying:
"I, your minister, and Fàn Yè
had no prior acquaintance.
Later, I served in the Menxià,
neighboring his office,
and he frequently came to visit me,
thus gradually we became close.
In recent years,
his demeanor became increasingly apparent:
turbulent, treacherous, and envious,
with a deep craving for wealth and status.
He felt his appointments were not high enough,
and thus harbored resentment.
Not only did he attack court officials
and criticize the sagely era,
but he also discussed the imperial court above,
and extended to the regional auxiliaries below,
inciting unity and division,
speaking and thinking as he pleased.
Such matters
have already been detailed in a previous memorial.
Recently, Provisional Attendant-in-ordinary Kǒng Xīxiān suddenly instructed Zhòng Chéngzǔ, an officer of the Grand General's Household, to convey the intentions of Yè, Xiè Zōng, and others,
who wished to gather the discontented
and plan something.
Because I previously received the favor of Yìkāng's attention,
and last year a group of petty individuals fabricated trouble regarding me,
they believed I must be fearful,
and tried deeply to persuade me.
They also said that people enjoy disorder,
and the opportunity must not be missed,
and that prophecies and astronomical signs
all showed corroborating evidence.
Yè himself soon came,
and reiterated all this,
and also said that my arguments were worsening,
making it difficult to preserve myself.
I immediately reported this to Your Majesty,
and received an imperial decree to reciprocate his overtures
and ascertain the full extent of his intentions.
Thereupon, he revealed all the manifestoes, selections of personnel, names of co-conspirators, and handwritten documents.
I respectfully sealed and presented them.
The extent of their villainy and rebellion
is rarely seen throughout history.
As your minister was unaware of the nature of my associates,
upon hearing this treacherous plot,
I was struck with terror when reporting it,
and utterly bewildered."
An imperial edict stated:
"Zhànzhī's memorial is as such,
truly alarming and regrettable.
Yè has always lacked moral conduct
and harbored flaws since youth.
However, because his talents could be utilized,
his strengths were cultivated,
and he was repeatedly granted honorable titles,
thus participating in government.
Yet his treacherous and greedy nature
surpassed even a ravine,
and he failed to recognize imperial favor,
still harboring resentment.
We always tolerated and nurtured him,
hoping he might reform,
but did not expect him to conspire with evildoers,
reaching such a degree of madness and rebellion.
He should be arrested
and thoroughly interrogated according to the law."
That night,
he first summoned Fàn Yè and his courtiers to assemble at the East Wing of Huálín,
where they stayed in the guest quarters.
Fàn Yè had already been apprehended outside, along with Xiè Zǒng and Kǒng Xīxiān's brothers,
and they all confessed.
At that time, the Emperor was in Yánxiántáng,
and sent an envoy to ask Fàn Yè:
"As I consider you to possess some literary talent,
I have thus appointed and promoted you.
Your titles and positions were as expected,
and by no means few compared to the norm.
I also know that your ambition is hard to satisfy,
but this is merely unreasonable resentment,
and stirring up factions.
How could you possibly harbor a different scheme?"
Fàn Yè, in a panic and fear,
did not immediately confess.
The Emperor sent an envoy to ask again, saying:
"You conspired treason with Xiè Zǒng, Xú Zhànzhī, and Kǒng Xīxiān,
and they have all confessed.
You are not yet dead,
and the evidence is still present.
Why do you not speak truthfully?"
Fàn Yè replied:
"Today, the imperial clan is as solid as a rock,
and the regional lords stand firm like mountains.
Even if by chance a secret plot were to erupt,
the regional commanders would immediately come to suppress it.
How could one not be annihilated?
Moreover, my position and responsibility are already too heavy.
Advancing one or two ranks
would naturally come about.
Why would I exchange this for the extermination of my clan?
The ancients said: 'To hold the map of the world in one's left hand,
and cut one's throat with the right,
even a fool would not do it.'
Although I am ordinary,
the court acknowledges that I have achieved some things.
Judging by reason,
it is impossible for me to have done this."
The Emperor again sent to ask:
"Kǒng Xīxiān is nearby, just outside Huálínmén.
Would you like to debate with him face-to-face?"
Fàn Yè, at a loss for words,
then said:
"If Kǒng Xīxiān falsely implicates me,
what should I do?"
Kǒng Xīxiān, hearing that Fàn Yè did not confess,
laughed and said to Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn Shěn Shàozhī:
"All arrangements,
such as official documents and communications,
were made and finalized by Fàn Yè.
How can he now make such denials?"
The Emperor showed him the handwriting,
and Fàn Yè then fully recounted the whole story,
saying:
"I had long intended to report it,
but the treasonous plot was not yet exposed,
and I also hoped the matter would disappear,
so I procrastinated until now.
My crime of betraying the country is grave,
and I accept the execution."
That night,
the Emperor ordered Shàngshū Púyè Hé Shàngzhī to see him,
and asked:
"How did your matter come to this?"
Fàn Yè said:
"What do you think it is?"
Hé Shàngzhī said:
"You should understand yourself."
Fàn Yè said:
"Outsiders say that Yǔ Shàngshū resents me,
but I believe there was no ill will between us.
Regarding the treasonous plot,
when I heard Kǒng Xīxiān speak of this,
I dismissed him as a mere child
and did not take it seriously.
Now, suddenly being accused,
I realize it is a crime.
You are assisting the world with your principles,
so that there is no injustice under Heaven.
After my death,
I still hope you will understand this heart of mine."
The next day,
armed guards sent Fàn Yè to the廷尉 Tíngwèi.
Upon entering prison,
he asked where Xú Dānyáng was,
and only then knew that Xú Zhànzhī had exposed him.
Kǒng Xīxiān confessed spontaneously,
his words and demeanor unyielding.
The Emperor was surprised by his talent,
and sent someone to comfort him, saying:
"With your talent,
to be stuck in the Jíshūshěng,
it is natural to have different ambitions.
This is my fault towards you."
He also questioned and reproached the former Lìbù Shàngshū Hé Shàngzhī, saying:
"To make Kǒng Xīxiān, approaching thirty, a Sànqí Láng,
how could he not become a bandit?"
Kǒng Xīxiān submitted a memorial from prison, saying:
"This humble person was reckless,
lacking foresight.
I merely indulged in small emotional impulses,
without considering the great principles of loyalty and rebellion.
With my second younger brother Kǒng Xiūxiān, I initiated the treacherous plot,
violating the national laws.
Even if I am sliced, diced, and minced,
it will be no atonement for my grave offense.
Your Majesty's great wisdom is inclusive and magnanimous,
your measure encompasses Heaven and the sea.
You noted my integrity in one aspect,
and condescended to issue a generous pardon.
This favor was beyond expectation,
leaving me with glory even in death.
Since ancient times,
there has been nothing comparable.
Those officials who stole horses and severed hat strings,
or scholars who cherished jade and offered books,
their conduct was lowly,
their faults minor.
Yet, understanding the extraordinary grace,
they repaid it with their lives and bodies,
and ultimately achieved merit in Qí and Wèi,
and established achievements in Qín and Chǔ.
Although I am trapped in a calamitous rebellion,
having lost both my reputation and integrity,
I was nevertheless spirited in my youth,
and secretly admired the legacy of heroic martyrs.
However, a tree that has fallen off a cliff
cannot be raised again;
water spilled from an overturned basin
cannot be collected.
I am about to have my body smeared on axes,
serving as a warning for those to come.
If my soul has spirit,
I will tie grass to repay the kindness.
Yet, my earnest and loyal heart
has not betrayed my original intention.
I crave to live a little longer
to express myself somewhat.
I consider myself naturally fond of many books,
and my mind comprehends various arts.
Whatever my wisdom can reach,
and my strength can achieve,
I have thoroughly explored,
investigating their profound subtleties.
My analysis of the past
has often proven accurate.
I respectfully present a summary of what I know,
listed as in the former separate memorial.
I hope it will not be discarded,
but stored in the Zhōngshū.
If after my death,
it can perhaps be retrieved,
then from the netherworld,
I can somewhat atone for my guilt."
What he presented were all astronomical observations and divinations,
which foretold the calamity of kinsmen harming each other,
and his words were profound and sincere.
Fàn Yè, in prison,
was in a different place from Xiè Zǒng and Kǒng Xīxiān,
so he feigned illness and requested to be moved to the Kǎotáng,
wanting to be close to Xiè Zǒng and the others.
His request was granted,
and he indeed managed to be separated by a wall from Xiè Zǒng and the others.
He asked Xiè Zǒng from afar:
"When we were first apprehended,
who did you suspect had reported us?"
Xiè Zǒng said:
"I don't know."
Fàn Yè said:
"It was Xú Tóng."
Tóng
was Xú Zhànzhī's nickname, Xiāntóng.
While in prison, he wrote a poem that said:
"Fortune and misfortune originally have no omens,
life and death eventually reach their limit.
What is destined to arrive has a fixed date,
who can prolong a single breath?
Life is already known,
but future destiny is unknown.
Beauty and ugliness share one mound,
what difference is there between right and wrong?
Why speak of the heights of Dōnglíng,
or distinguish the side of Shǒushān?
Although I lack Jīshēng's qín,
I hope to share Xiàhóu's countenance.
I send a message to my living son:
this path will soon be traveled again."
Xiè Yè had originally expected to die as soon as he was imprisoned,
but the emperor thoroughly investigated his case,
and thus a fortnight passed.
Xiè Yè began to hope for life again.
A prison guard then joked to him,
"It is rumored outside that the Attendant Official, Zhān Shì, might be held for a long time."
Xiè Yè was astonished and delighted upon hearing this.
Xiè Zōng and Kǒng Xīxiān laughed at him, saying,
"When the Attendant Official used to discuss past events with us,
he would invariably roll up his sleeves and glare.
And when he was in the Western Pool archery hall,
he would gallop his horse, looking around,
considering himself a hero of his generation.
Yet now, amidst all this turmoil and confusion,
he is so afraid of death!
Even if his life were spared today,
how could a minister who plotted against his sovereign
bear to live?"
Xiè Yè said to the commanding officer of the guard,
"What a pity!
To bury such a person."
The officer said,
"An disloyal person
is not worthy of pity."
Xiè Yè said,
"The general's words are correct."
When they went out to the marketplace,
Xiè Yè was at the very front.
At the prison gate, he looked back and said to Xiè Zōng,
"Today's order,
should it be based on rank?"
Xiè Zōng said,
"The chief rebel goes first."
They chatted and laughed on the road,
without a moment's pause.
Upon reaching the marketplace,
he asked Xiè Zōng,
"Has the time almost come?"
Xiè Zōng said,
"It won't be long now."
After Xiè Yè had eaten,
he earnestly urged Xiè Zōng to eat too.
Xiè Zōng said,
"This is different from a serious illness;
why force yourself to eat?"
All of Xiè Yè's family arrived at the marketplace.
The official overseeing the execution asked,
"Do you need to see them?"
Xiè Yè asked Xiè Zōng,
"Since my family has come,
I am fortunate to see them.
I shall not part from them immediately."
Xiè Zōng said,
"Whether you part or not,
what does it matter?
They will surely wail and cry,
which will only disturb one's mind."
Xiè Yè said,
"How does wailing concern others?
I just saw relatives and old friends on the roadside looking on;
it is still much better than not seeing them.
My intention is to see them."
Thereupon, they were called forward.
Xiè Yè's wife first knelt down and embraced her son,
then turned and cursed Xiè Yè, saying,
"You did not act for your hundred-year-old mother,
nor were you moved by the emperor's favor and kindness.
Your death alone is not enough to atone for your crimes;
why must you also unjustly kill your children and grandchildren?"
Xiè Yè gave a dry laugh and said that his crimes had brought this upon him.
Xiè Yè's birth mother wept, saying,
"The Emperor had boundless regard for you,
yet you could not feel grateful.
Nor did you consider my old age.
What is to become of us today?"
She then struck Xiè Yè's neck and cheek with her hand,
but Xiè Yè showed no change in expression.
His wife said,
"Criminal,
mother, do not mind him."
His sister and concubines came to say goodbye.
Xiè Yè wept bitterly, his tears flowing.
Xiè Zōng said,
"My maternal uncle's demeanor is quite different from Xiàhóu's."
Xiè Yè wiped away his tears and stopped.
Xiè Zōng's mother, because her son and nephews had brought rebellion upon themselves,
alone did not come out to watch.
Xiè Yè said to Xiè Zōng,
"That my elder sister does not come today
is better than many."
Xiè Yè became increasingly drunk,
and his son Xiè Āi also became drunk.
He picked up some earth and fruit peels and threw them at Xiè Yè,
calling Xiè Yè "Biéjià" dozens of times.
Xiè Yè asked,
"Are you angry with me?"
Xiè Āi said,
"How could I be angry today?
It is just that father and son dying together,
one cannot help but feel sad."
Xiè Yè always believed that the spirit perishes with death,
and wished to write an essay on "No Ghosts."
At this point, he wrote to Xú Zhànzhī,
saying,
"We shall contend underground."
His confusion and absurdity were thus.
He also said to others,
"Tell Attendant Remonstrant Hé that
there are definitely no Buddhas or ghosts in the world.
If there are spirits,
they will naturally repay me."
When Xiè Yè's household was confiscated,
musical instruments and clothing were all precious and beautiful,
and the concubines were also richly adorned,
while his mother's dwelling was simple and humble,
with only a pile of firewood.
His nephews had no quilts in winter,
and his uncle wore plain cloth clothes.

Xiè Yè, his sons Xiè Āi and Xiè Yáo, his uncle Xiè Lóu, Kǒng Xīxiān and his brothers Kǒng Xiūxiān, Kǒng Jǐngxiān, Kǒng Sīxiān, Kǒng Xīxiān's son Kǒng Guìfǔ, Kǒng Guìfǔ's son Bái Mín, Xiè Zōng and his brothers Xiè Yuē and Zhòng Chéngzǔ, Xǔ Yào,
and all others implicated,
were executed.
Xiè Yè was forty-eight years old at the time.
Xiè Yè's brothers, sons, and father who had already died, as well as Xiè Zōng's brother Xiè Wěi,
were exiled to Guǎngzhōu.
Xiè Āi's son Lǔlián,
the grandson of Princess Zhāo of Wúxīng,
pleaded for his life to be spared,
and was also exiled to a distant place.
He was allowed to return when Shìzǔ ascended the throne.
Xiè Yè's nature was subtle and full of ingenious thoughts.
He was good at many things he encountered.
For clothing, utensils, and ornaments,
he always enhanced or modified their designs,
and people of his time all imitated and learned from him.
He compiled a recipe for blending incense,
and its preface stated:
"Musk inherently has many prohibitions;
too much will certainly cause harm.
Aloeswood is easy to blend;
a pound of it causes no harm.
Licorice is dry and hollow,
while myrrh is sticky and damp.
Spikenard, storax, frankincense, turmeric, 'Duō', 'Héluó', and similar substances
are all treasured in foreign lands
but are of no use in the central plains.
Moreover, date paste is dull and thick,
and 'jiǎjiān' is shallow and vulgar.
Not only do they not contribute to a strong fragrance,
they will instead
increase its flaws and ailments."
The statements in this preface
all used analogies to refer to court officials:
"Musk inherently has many prohibitions"
alluded to Yǔ Bǐngzhī;
"Licorice is dry and hollow"
alluded to Hé Shàngzhī;
"Myrrh is sticky and damp"
alluded to Shěn Yǎnzhī;
"Date paste is dull and thick"
alluded to Yáng Xuánbǎo;
"'Jiǎjiān' is shallow and vulgar"
alluded to Xú Zhànzhī;
"Spikenard, storax"
alluded to the monk Huìlín;
"Aloeswood is easy to blend"
was a self-comparison.
In prison, Xiè Yè wrote a letter to his nephews and nieces, in which he described himself, saying: "My madness and misfortune have brought about my downfall.
What more can be said?
You all should cast me aside as a criminal.
However, my conduct throughout my life, and my thoughts,
might still be worth examining.
As for
what I was capable of or not,
what I understood in my heart,
you may not all fully know.
I was lazy in my studies when young,
and matured late.
Around thirty years old,
I only then began to make progress.
Since then,
my mind has gradually transformed,
and even anticipating old age,
it should not yet have ceased.
I often have subtle insights,
though I cannot fully express them in words.
By nature, I do not
delve into annotation,
and my temperament is poor;
a little strenuous thought
makes me confused and distressed.
My verbal skills are also not agile,
hence I have no achievements in discourse.
As for what I understand and comprehend,
it is all self-acquired."
to one's heart.
My writing often progresses,
but my talent is limited and my thoughts are difficult to form.
Thus, whenever I take up my brush,
the pieces I complete
are almost never entirely satisfactory.
I am often ashamed to be a
literatus.
The problem with literature is that its substance is limited to external form,
its emotion is hurried into ornamentation,
its meaning is constrained by its intent,
and its rhythm shifts its essence.
Although there are occasionally capable writers,
most generally cannot avoid
these shortcomings.
It's like exquisite crafts or paintings;
ultimately, nothing truly profound is achieved.
I have always held that where feelings and aspirations are expressed,
the intent should be paramount,
and the writing should convey that intent.
If the intent is
paramount,
then its main point will surely be evident;
if the writing conveys the intent,
then its words will not be frivolous.
Only then can its fragrance be extracted
and its resounding quality be vibrated.
The sentiments, nature, and
appeal within this are
myriad and varied,
subtly achieving a coherent principle.
I consider myself quite familiar with these methods,
and when I have spoken of them to others,
many could not appreciate them,
perhaps because their ideas differ.
Naturally, I can distinguish between *gōng* and *shāng* [musical notes]
and discern clear and turbid tones.
This is innate.
Looking at writers throughout history,
most do not fully grasp this point,
and even those who do
may not derive it from
its fundamental source.
All my statements have practical evidence,
not empty talk.
Among the younger generation,
Xiè Zhuāng has the most of this quality;
his handwriting is somewhat fluid,
and his writing is not bound by rhyme,
hence it is so.
My thoughts are not fixed in method,
but are especially able to resolve difficulties and adjust to varying degrees of importance.
The endowment I possess
is probably not yet exhausted.
However, there is much public discourse,
and little
far-reaching expression beyond practical matters.
This I regret,
also because I have no ambition for literary fame.
Originally, I was not concerned with historical texts,
and indeed found them incomprehensible.
But after reaching the *Hòu Hàn Shū*,
I began to grasp the overall threads.
After detailed study of ancient and modern writings and commentaries,
few
are truly satisfactory.
Bān Shì enjoys the highest reputation,
but his unconstrained expressions lack consistent rules,
making comparison difficult.
His later encomiums offer little in terms of profound reasoning,
only his treatises are commendable.
His extensive erudition is beyond my reach,
but in terms of organization, I may not be inferior.
My miscellaneous biographies and discussions
all contain subtle intentions and profound meanings.
As they have been carefully refined,
I have therefore condensed their
wording.
As for the prefaces and discussions from "Good Officials" downwards, and those on the Six Barbarians,
their brushwork is unrestrained and bold,
truly extraordinary works in the world.
Those among them that resonate
often are no less impressive than the
*Guò Qín Piān*.
I have often compared them with Bān Shì's works,
and they are not merely "not inferior."
I wish to compile a complete set of treatises,
ensuring all those present in the *Qián Hàn Shū* are included.
Although the content
need not be voluminous,
let the expression be thorough.
I also wish to take the opportunity to issue discussions within the chapters,
to rectify the gains and losses of an era,
but this intention has not yet been realized.
The encomiums are indeed the pinnacle
of my literary
thought;
scarcely a word is idly placed.
Their marvelous variations are inexhaustible,
uniting disparate forms,
so much so that I myself do not know how to praise them.
When this book circulates,
there should indeed be
appreciative readers.
The Annals and Biographies merely provide the general outline;
the subtle details are numerous.
From ancient times, no work has been so grand in scope yet so refined in thought.
I fear
that people of this age
will not fully appreciate it,
often valuing the ancient and despising the contemporary,
which is why I speak these impassioned, wild words.
In music,
my listening skill is not as good as my own playing,
but what I excel at is not refined music,
which is regrettable.
Nevertheless, when it reaches a point of absolute perfection,
how is it any different?
The profound pleasure within it
is inexhaustible in words.
The meaning beyond the strings,
the sound of a hollow echo,
I know not whence it comes.
Even in the slightest part,
the essence and bearing are boundless.
I have also tried to teach it to others,
but among both scholars and commoners, there has not been one who resembles even a fraction of it.
This will never be transmitted!
Although my writing has some subtle intention,
its brushwork is not fluent,
and the rest
is not accomplished,
for which I am often ashamed of this reputation.
The self-preface by Yè is both factual
and thus preserved.
Āi was tidy and clean from a young age;
his clothes were never stained with dust for an entire year.
He died at the age of twenty.
When Yè was young,
his elder brother Yàn often said:
"This child is ambitious for gain,
and will ultimately ruin the family."
It turned out just as Yàn said.
The historian says: The ancients said:
"Greed darkens wisdom."
How true,
the way gain and harm oppose each other.
Liú Zhàn's discernment, capability, and talent
truly encompassed strategies for governing the state.
How could he not know that if he moved his younger brother to become his minister,
the way of sovereign and minister would be observed,
and if he transformed his elder brother into his lord,
the bond of brotherhood would be severed?
Yet Yìkāng repeatedly harbored treacherous schemes,
blindly flattering and promoting them.
What difference is there between that and thrusting a long halberd and offending the imperial palace?
There is none!
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 30, Yuán Shú
Yuán Shú, courtesy name Yángyuán,
was a native of Yángxià, Chénjùn.
He was the youngest son of Dānyáng Yǐn Bào.
From a young age,
when he was several years old,
his paternal uncle Zhàn said to the family:
“This is no ordinary child.”
By the time he was over ten years old,
he was admired by his maternal aunt’s husband, Wáng Hóng.
He did not pursue the study of sentences and chapters,
but was widely read and knowledgeable in many fields.
He enjoyed writing,
and his prose was robust and elegant,
with fluent talent and eloquence.
His home province appointed him as Zhǔbù,
then Zuòzuò Zuǒláng,
and Tàizǐ Shèrén,
but he did not accept any of these positions.
Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng appointed him Sītú Jìjiǔ.
Yìkāng did not particularly like literature,
so although he formally treated him with礼接 propriety,
his true regard was quite distant.
Liú Zhàn,
who was Shú’s maternal cousin,
wished for him to attach himself,
but Shú did not take it seriously.
Because of this, they became greatly estranged,
and he was dismissed from office due to prolonged illness.
He was then appointed Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì’s Yòujūn Zhǔbù,
and promoted to Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ,
but did not accept due to a foot ailment.
Wèijūn Línchuān Wáng Yìqìng, who was fond of literature,
invited him to be Cányì Cānjūn.
After a while,
he was promoted to Sītú Zuǒ Xīshǔ.
He was sent out as Xuānchéng Tàishǒu,
then returned to serve as Zhōngshū Shìláng,
but left office due to his mother’s mourning.
After the mourning period ended,
he became Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
In the twenty-sixth year of Yuánjiā (449 CE),
he was promoted to Shàngshū Lìbù Láng.
That autumn,
a great northern expedition was launched.
Shú, attending the emperor, leisurely said:
“Now is the time to make music on the Middle Peak,
sweep across Zhào and Wèi,
and inspect the jade on Dàizōng.
Now is indeed the time.
Your servant meets a thousand-year opportunity,
and wishes to present an essay on Fēngshàn.”
Tàizǔ smiled and said:
“This is an achievement of great virtue;
how can I be worthy of it?”
He was sent out as Shǐxīng Wáng’s Zhēngběi Chángshǐ and Nán Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu.
When Shú first arrived at the headquarters,
Jùn received him
and said:
“I did not expect my maternal uncle to condescend to assist me.”
Shú replied:
“The imperial court sent this humble official
precisely to add luster to your ducal residence.”
He returned to become Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
At that time, the Suǒ captives invaded from the south,
reaching Guābù.
Tàizǔ had the officials deliberate on methods of defense.
Shú submitted a memorial saying: Your servant has heard that a beast that can enclose a cart
will surely perish once it leaves the mountains;
and a fish that crosses waves
will dry up if it strays from the current.
The remaining rabble of the Jié bandits,
rushing to the imperial domain,
swarming like ants and locusts,
are said to have already collapsed and died.
The natural barriers are rugged and vast,
the territorial limits deep and distant;
thus, the powerful Wèi restrained their plans,
and the glorious Jìn abandoned their discussions.
Their emotions were suppressed, their strength exhausted,
their spirits broken, and their courage drained.
They truly
did not expect to arrive,
nor did they fear being unable to cross.
However, due to previous discord with distant regions,
and resistance to receiving military orders,
the generals became lax and inept,
and so the soldiers lacked fighting spirit.
The dispersed troops,
rather than routing the invaders,
and the attacking forces,
scattered on their own.
The brave cavalry of Jìxī,
urgently fighting in ranks,
and the trained soldiers on the Huái,
simply made preparations without deploying flags.
This was due to inadequate pacification and organization,
and much ignorance in military affairs.
Thus, the Lùzǐ entered a calamity,
and Yīchuān was disturbed.
The Ji-style governance was largely destroyed,
and Yǔ’s achievements were obliterated.
Flying reports indicated the
danger in Wèiyīn,
and warning fires signaled an alert akin to Xiányáng.
However, upon careful assessment of their strength and weaknesses,
their hidden dangers were revealed first.
After examining their capabilities,
their deceitful tricks became evident.
Across a continuous
thousand li of land,
the journey is blocked and deep,
with obstacles and hindrances ahead,
and pressure from both front and rear.
They abandoned their accustomed practice of high ground,
and competed for the advantages of swift currents and sandbanks.
Now, rainbows appear and duckweeds grow,
the earth is fertile and springs
are active.
Both land and water routes are flooded,
and malaria repeatedly breaks out.
Fodder is already scarce,
and rice and grain cannot be guaranteed.
The watery expanse is like a collar and belt;
advancing will certainly lead to collapse,
and the narrow, fortified river
means retreating will also result in
destruction.
This is like nesting birds on a raging fire,
or raising fish amidst thorny bushes.
Some say to allow the Jiang-right to suffer slowly,
and rebuild the Huai-inner at leisure.
I humbly submit that saving the crucial Mǐnchéng
was deemed proper by old histories,
and abandoning the distant Liángtǔ
was previously called wrong.
Even for these
remote and desolate areas,
they were not ceded.
How much more so for the continuously linked capital region,
just a咫尺 (short distance) from the sacred domain,
where several prefectures have been devastated,

mountains and ravines overturned,

Now, the hill taxes yield a thousand chariots,

Shoulder-to-shoulder crowds are twice that of Cháng’ān,

Every household is eager to fight,

It is advisable to offer gold and cast official seals

Should any escape the nets,
