The
lands and fields of Jǐzhōu will be opened,
and no strategy will be left unused,
so that the high palace gates will be re-engraved,
and the swallows will be inscribed after that.
Then will mountains be consecrated and rivers sanctified,
rites established and policies compiled,
to elucidate and illuminate the
inherited principles of Yán and Hào,
and connect and surpass the ancient writings of Shāng and Xià.
Now, the masses of warriors are brave,
but the generals' tactics are sparse and timid.
Perhaps it is because peace has accumulated over days,
and tranquility has lasted for many years,
so cities have no urgent need for sudden defense,
and families are slow to perform the
duties of supplying the war effort,
they lack the rituals of review and training,
and simplify the adornments for inspecting subordinates.
Moreover, is the method of selection and recommendation
not yet adequate?
If, however, the state establishes selection within communities,
and discussions are thorough and incisive,
and individuals
delve deep into obscurity,
and cut their sashes to seek out the distant,
should there be someone with profound insight who can illuminate,
or a distinguished and great person who naturally reveals himself,
whose sincerity can move springs and rain,
and penetrate metal and stone,
whose spirit can awe Fēi and Bēn,
and whose wisdom can exhaust
Jū and Qǐ,
who understands the calculations of right and wrong, and alignment and opposition,
and comprehends the suitability of darkness and light, gain and loss,
who can unite and divide the hearts of the people,
and understand the nature of both the foolish and the wise,
who ascends the vermilion steps to present his strategies,
and treads on
the green mat to voice his plans,
who can please the celestial mirror above,
and quell common criticisms below,
sufficient to bring peace to the people and relieve the state,
and rescue from disasters and relieve suffering.
Then it would be appropriate to elevate them above the favored and noble,
and
promote them to the right of relatives and old acquaintances,
distinguish their banners and insignia,
and honor their rank and salary,
allowing them to act with independent authority,
and not requiring them to report for commands,
descending from their seats and bending the knee,
like the invitation at Guǎngwǔ,
and setting up an altar
to perform the rites,
like the investiture at Huáinān.
There must be the merit of crucial alliances,
and the triumph of secretly exchanging tallies.
If the barbarian tribes are violent and rebellious,
and both internal and external forces insult and abandon them,
the newly joined masses,
being disorderly and disunited,
will be seduced by power and profit,
and will inevitably drift away.
The first to submit
will naturally
follow suit.
Now, examining ancient records,
the scholars of Chántǔ were adorned with tassels,
but were cut down and exiled,
their leaders crushed by the treacherous and cunning.
This is like the blind wishing for sight,
or the paralyzed desiring to walk,
where every action
leads to swift assembly,
and success is easily achieved.
Attacking Jìn depended on good reconnaissance,
and preserving Zhèng truly relied on excellent spies.
Send out many double agents,
to confuse their minds and ears,
to expose their hidden dangers and vulnerabilities,
and apply
the tactics of rise and fall.
Assault their suspicions and hidden motives,
frustrate their preferences and desires,
entice them with the prestige of a provincial governor,
and bait them with the wealth of divided land.
Exhaust the use of the pen,
and display the
sharpness of rhetorical prowess,
with eloquent persuasion, strong sieges can be lifted,
and with swift letters, fortified cities can be easily toppled.
Their inner core will surely crumble,
and their branches will shatter like tiles,
just as Yàn and Yuè regretted their actions against each other,
and Xiàng and Fàn
mutually suspected each other.
Or perhaps, words are few but accomplishments are profound,
actions are simple but effects are widespread,
like Qí Yǔ turning back his carriage,
and Zhào Yǎng returning the ruler,
fully embodying the way of public opinion,
and completing the effectiveness of deeds.
I am fortunate
to be able to enter the inner court,
and live and rest in this enlightened era,
my fortune growing with my life,
and imperial favor increasing with the years.
I have nothing with which to meet this prosperous destiny,
or to adorn these grand laws.
Now, there are
stray arrows on the road,
and wasps are not yet at rest.
I dare to offer my humble opinion,
to slightly repay the vast benevolence.
However, sitting behind the curtain, I lack clear insight,
and removing my helmet, I cannot achieve decisive results.
I secretly observe the border
discussions of the Protector-General,
and the military strategies of the Subordinate States,
the firm arguments of Zhōng and Cháo,
and the reports of Dù and Gěng on affairs.
All say that regarding the urgency of managing affairs,
the best strategies are still lacking,
and as for the respect shown to the cities,
only
inferior strategies have been adopted.
I am ashamed of my cowardice,
my wisdom unable to grasp the subtle.
I dare to expose my ignorant views,
without seeking recognition.
Yuán Shū (袁淑) was fond of exaggeration,
and was often ridiculed by people of his time.
Liú Jùn (劉濬), Prince of Shǐxīng (始興), once sent thirty thousand coins as a gift to Yuán Shū (袁淑),
but the next morning he sent someone to take them back,
claiming that his messenger had made a mistake,
intending to play a trick on Yuán Shū (袁淑).
Yuán Shū (袁淑) wrote a letter to Liú Jùn (劉濬) saying:
"Yuán Sīzhí (袁司直) supervises the guest house,
and dares to present this letter to the Palace Administrator of the great state.
Recently, you condescended to bestow a cash tribute,
sending it to my humble dwelling.
My humble dwelling respectfully prepared for this in haste,
without any thought of refusal or doubt.
Fearing it was not a gift for an imperial audience,
nor a contribution for a royal banquet,
I did not expect Your Majesty to bestow such favor,
and thus was quite bewildered.
Unexpectedly, in a day or two, a note of inches was dispatched,
requesting the return of the funds through your attendants,
stating that the delivery was mistaken,
and thus hastening the return of the former tribute.
How could a vassal, a humble subject, a person of meager learning and isolated knowledge,
not be suspicious of this?
Moreover, I have heard from ancient records that
within a period of seven years,
to give and then to take away,
even righteous gentlemen would criticize this.
How much more so within a mere ten days,
how rapid is this increase and decrease!
I fear that two or three feudal lords
might observe the governance of the great state from this.
Therefore, I dare to reveal my innermost thoughts.
My humble household and weak self,
have always upheld integrity and incorruptibility,
cherishing purity and rectitude,
and because of this unwavering honesty,
my poverty is known throughout the land.
How could I be so ignorant as to lament the loss of gold?
I do not stint on offering tribute;
I will prepare the horses and return the tribute, awaiting your command.
It is solely for Your Excellency to decide."
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ (太子左衞率).
When Yuán Xiōng (元凶) was about to commit regicide,
Yuán Shū (袁淑) was on duty that night.
Around the second watch,
Liú Shào (劉劭) called Yuán Shū (袁淑) and Xiāo Bīn (蕭斌) and others, weeping and saying:
"The Emperor has believed slander,
and is about to be condemned and deposed.
I examine myself and find no fault,
and cannot accept being wronged.
Tomorrow morning I must carry out a great deed;
I hope we can all work together."
Yuán Shū (袁淑) and Xiāo Bīn (蕭斌) both said:
"This has never happened since ancient times;
please reconsider."
Liú Shào (劉劭) grew angry and his expression changed.
Everyone around him was agitated.
Xiāo Bīn (蕭斌) was afraid,
and then said:
"I was formerly honored to serve you,
and always thought of dedicating myself.
Moreover, facing such distress,
I shall immediately exert myself to obey your command."
Yuán Shū (袁淑) shouted at him, saying:
"Do you truly believe His Highness means this?
His Highness suffered from wind illness in his youth;
perhaps this is just an attack of his old ailment."
Liú Shào (劉劭) grew even more furious,
and then asked:
"Will the matter succeed?"
Yuán Shū (袁淑) said:
"Being in an unassailable position, why fear not succeeding?
But after success,
you will not be tolerated by heaven and earth,
and great disaster will swiftly follow.
I beg you to stop immediately."
Liú Shào's (劉劭) attendants pulled Yuán Shū's
clothes and said:
"What kind of talk is this?
How can you speak of stopping?"
Then Liú Shào (劉劭) gave Yuán Shū (袁淑) and others pants and tunics,
cut three feet into one piece,
and then tore it in half,
distributing it among Xiāo Bīn (蕭斌), Yuán Shū (袁淑), and his attendants,
telling them to use it to bind their pants.
Yuán Shū (袁淑) went out and returned to his chamber,
pacing around the bed,
When Liú Shào (劉劭) was about to leave, he was already riding with Xiāo Bīn (蕭斌).
He called Yuán Shū (袁淑) very urgently,
but Yuán Shū (袁淑) remained asleep and refused to get up.
Liú Shào (劉劭) stopped his carriage at Fènghuà Mén (奉化門),
and urged him continuously.
Yuán Shū (袁淑) slowly got up and went to the back of the carriage.
Liú Shào (劉劭) told him to get on the carriage,
but he again declined.
Liú Shào (劉劭) then ordered his attendants:
"Kill him with your own hands."
He was killed outside Fènghuà Mén (奉化門)
at the age of forty-six.
When Liú Shào (劉劭) ascended the throne,
he posthumously granted Yuán Shū (袁淑) the title of Tàicháng (太常),
and bestowed a very generous funeral gift.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
he ordered Yán Yánzhī (顏延之) to write an imperial edict saying:
"To regard morality lightly and righteousness heavily,
we often hear such teachings;
but in times of national decline and danger,
such people are rarely encountered.
If not for those who have attained the utmost understanding of righteousness
and the deepest recognition of correctness,
who could steadfastly defend their lord
and sacrifice their lives to uphold their integrity?
Therefore, the former Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ (太子左衞率) Yuán Shū (袁淑),
whose literary talent and eloquence were excellent and profound,
held firm to his pure and steadfast integrity.
When faced with severe coercion,
his demeanor and expression did not waver;
with stern words, he denounced the rebellion,
his spirit shaking the wicked faction.
When the cruel blades came,
he accepted death without flinching.
Among those of antiquity who cherished loyalty and met disaster,
none can be said to have surpassed him.
When we speak of him, we sigh with admiration and grief,
never forgetting him in our hearts.
It is proper to honor him with additional rites
and eternally commemorate him as a loyal minister of Sòng (宋).
He is posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng (侍中) and Tàiwèi (太尉),
and posthumously named Zhōngxiàn Gōng (忠憲公)."
Another edict stated:
"Yuán Shū (袁淑) sacrificed his life for righteousness,
his loyalty and courage surpassing antiquity.
His orphaned children are in distress,
which we particularly pity and care for.
They should be generously granted relief and benefits
to comfort both the living and the deceased."
Yuán Shū (袁淑) and the four families of Xú Zhànzhī (徐湛之), Jiāng Zhàn (江湛), Wáng Sēngchuò (王僧綽), and Bǔ Tiānyǔ (卜天與)
were thereafter granted continuous official salaries.
His collected works were passed down through the generations.
His sons were Jī (幾), Ài (敳), Léng (稜), Níng (凝), and Biāo (標).
Ài (敳)
was Bùbīng Xiàowèi (步兵校尉) under Shìzǔ (世祖).
Níng (凝)
was Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) during Tàizōng's (太宗) reign,

Tàizōng (太宗) initially rebelled with various regions,
and was appointed Zhǔbù (主簿) in Liú Zhàn's (劉湛) Guànjūn Fǔ (冠軍府).
The historian says: Heaven and earth are eternal,
but human life is different from this.
The morning glory and morning dew
are not enough to describe it.
How much less can one speak of early deaths and suddenness?
One should let one's heart decide on remaining or leaving,
and not let existence or non-existence trouble one's mind.
It is merely because spiritual transformation is distant and long,
and life does not return,
that though the path of heaven is rugged and perilous,
and one has not yet encountered it,
one believes that a seven-foot body will always exist,
and a hundred years can be guaranteed.
Therefore, people rely on grand plans and belittle the world,
regretting a moment of time and ruining a precious jewel.
If righteousness is weighed more heavily than life,
then the ancient admonitions shine forth in vain;
to cast one's body and die for one's lord,
such people are rare in the world.
If there were no integrity like that of Yáng Yuán (陽源),
what would be the value of paintings and records?

He was good at governance,
and prestige and beneficence were practiced together.
Guǎnglǐng Chéng formerly had a tall building,
Zhànzhī further repaired and renovated it,
looking south towards Zhōngshān.
North of the city there was a lake,
with abundant aquatic products.
Zhànzhī further erected a wind pavilion and a moon-viewing tower,
a music platform and a zither room,
fruit trees and bamboo flourished,
flowers and herbs were in rows,
attracting literati,
who fully enjoyed the pleasures of strolling,
a splendor of that time.
At that time there was a śramaṇa, Shì Huìxiū,
who was good at composing essays,
with ornate and beautiful literary style,
and Zhànzhī was very close with him.
Shìzǔ ordered him to return to secular life.
His original surname was Tāng,
and his position reached Cóngshìshǐ of Yángzhōu.
In the twenty-sixth year,
he again entered as Dānyáng Yǐn,
concurrently Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
and his general title remained as before.
In the twenty-seventh year,
the Suǒlǔ reached Guābù,
and Zhànzhī led troops and appointed aides,
and together with the Crown Prince, they divided to guard Shítou.
In the spring of the twenty-eighth year,
Lǔ Shuǎng and his brothers led their retainers and submitted,
Shuǎng and the others were
the sons of Lǔ Guǐ.
Zhànzhī considered it a strategic long-term plan,
and they were especially praised and accepted,
daring not to carelessly express personal grudges.
He begged to seclude himself in the countryside,
but it was not permitted.
He was transferred to Shàngshū Púyè,
and concurrently held the position of Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
At that time, Shàngshū Lìng Hé Shàngzhī, considering that Zhànzhī was a relative of the imperial family,
treated him with great importance and respect,
and wished to entrust him with the affairs of the court.
Regarding all petitions and appeals,
he did not examine or approve any of them.
Zhànzhī, on the other hand, also considered the official regulations and edicts, stating that
the Shàngshū Lìng was responsible for presenting memorials and managing all internal and external affairs,
with nothing outside his purview.
If the Lìng position was vacant, the Púyè would take over all responsibilities.
He also deferred matters back to Shàngzhī,
and they mutually declined to take responsibility.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Yuán Shú impeached both, requesting their dismissal.
The imperial edict stated:
"The Lìng and Púyè are entrusted with governing affairs,
but they do not jointly seek to fulfill their duties properly,
but rather mutually shirk responsibility.
To impeach them is correct.
However, the old regulations are incomplete and contradictory,
which is why this hesitation arose.
Therefore, no punishment will be inflicted.
It shall be thoroughly rectified in due course."
Thus, Zhànzhī and Shàngzhī were ordered to jointly receive petitions and appeals.
Although Shàngzhī was the Lìng,
all court affairs were ultimately handled by Zhànzhī.
Initially,
after Liú Zhàn was executed,
and Yīn Jǐngrén died,
Tàizǔ entrusted important positions to Shěn Yǎnzhī, Lóu Bǐngzhī, Fàn Yè, and others.
Later, there were also Jiāng Zhàn and Hé Yǔzhī.
When Yè was executed,
Bǐngzhī was dismissed,
and Yǎnzhī and Yǔzhī both died.
By this time, Jiāng Zhàn was Lìbù Shàngshū,
and he and Zhànzhī both held positions of power.
People of the time referred to them as "Jiāng and Xú."
Whenever the Emperor fell ill,
Zhànzhī would always enter to attend to his medicine.
When the affair of the two wicked sorcerers and witchcraft came to light,
the Emperor wanted to depose Shào
and ordered Jùn to die.
However, Shìzǔ was not favored,
so he was repeatedly sent out to govern distant regions
and was not allowed to remain in the capital.
Nánpíng Wáng Shuò and Jiànpíng Wáng Hóng were both loved by the Emperor.
Shuò's consort was Zhàn's younger sister,
who advised the Emperor to establish Shuò as heir.
At the end of Yuánjiā,
Shuò was summoned from Shòuyáng to the court.
Upon his arrival,
he again fell out of favor.
The Emperor wished to establish Hóng,
but disliked that he was not next in line,
so the deliberation remained long undecided.
He would discuss with Zhànzhī privately,
sometimes for days and nights.
Every night, he would always have Zhànzhī personally hold a candle,
and check around the walls,
fearing that someone might be eavesdropping.
On the morning of Shào's patricide,
that night,
the Emperor was speaking with Zhànzhī privately.
The candle was still lit until dawn.
Zhànzhī, startled, rose and rushed to the north door.
Before he could open it,
he was killed.
He was forty-four years old at the time.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he posthumously granted him the title of Sīkōng,
added Sànqí Chángshì,
retained his original office,
and gave him the posthumous title Zhōngliè Gōng.
An imperial edict also stated:
"The households of Xú Zhànzhī, Jiāng Zhàn, and Wáng Sēngchuò suffered severe cruelty;
their orphaned children are scattered and displaced.
Recalling the past,
our grief and pain are profoundly deep.
They are permitted to return to their ancestral homes,
and abundant assistance and grants shall be bestowed upon them."
Thereupon, the three families' elders were given grain rations.
He had three sons: Yùzhī and Qiānzhī,
who were killed by the chief rebel.
His heir inherited the title of Marquis,
and married Tàizǔ's fifteenth daughter, Nányáng Gōngzhǔ.
He died young
without issue.
Yùzhī's son Xiàosì succeeded to the enfeoffment.
When Qí received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
Jiāng Zhàn, courtesy name Huīyuān,
was a native of Kǎochéng, Jìyáng, and the son of Yí, the Císhǐ of Xiāngzhōu.
He was known for his filial piety during mourning.
He loved literature and rhetoric,
enjoyed playing the qín and drums,
and was also skilled in arithmetic.
Initially, he served as Zuòzhù Zuǒláng,
then moved to Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng's Sītú Xíngcānjūn,
and Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān's Zuǒjūn Gōngcáo.
He then returned to serve as Yìkāng's Sītú Zhǔbù,
and Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén.
Sīkōng Dāo Dàojì sought to arrange a marriage between his son and Zhàn's younger sister,
but Zhàn refused.
Yìkāng issued an order,
but he again did not comply.
People of the time admired his firm resolve.
Yìkāng wanted to keep him close day and night,
but Zhàn persistently requested an external posting,
so he was made Wǔlíng Nèishǐ.
He returned to serve as Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
then moved to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
and Shàngshū
Lìbù Láng.
He followed Suí Wáng Dàn as Běizhōngláng Jiāng and Nánxúzhōu Císhǐ,
and Zhàn was made Zhǎngshǐ and Nándōnghǎi Tàishǒu,
with all governmental affairs entrusted to him.
In the twenty-fifth year of Yuánjiā (448 CE),
he was summoned to be Shìzhōng,
entrusted with confidential matters,
and concurrently held the position of Dàzhōngzhèng of his home province.
He was then promoted to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
At that time, academic positions were reorganized,
with Tàiwèi Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng appointed as Guózǐ Jìjiǔ,
and Zhàn and Shìzhōng Hé Yōuzhī as Bóshì.
In the twenty-seventh year (450 CE),
he was transferred to Lìbù Shàngshū.
His family was very poor
and he did not pursue wealth or profit.
Gifts and provisions piled up at his door,
but he accepted none,
nor did he have extra clothes or leftover food.
Once, when summoned by the Emperor,
it happened to be laundry day,
so he feigned illness for a day
and only went after his clothes were ready.
His ox was hungry,
and the driver asked for grass.
After a long silence, Zhàn said:
"You may give it water."
While holding the selection post,
he was criticized for being somewhat harsh and meticulous,
yet he was fair and selfless,
and did not accept requests or personal pleas.
Commentators praised him for this.
When the Emperor launched a major northern expedition,
the entire court opposed it,
but only Zhàn approved.
When the barbarian captives reached Guābù,
Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Liú Zūnkǎo led his troops to the river.
Zhàn was concurrently appointed Lǐngjūn,
and all military arrangements
were entrusted to him.
The barbarians sent an envoy to propose marriage.
The Emperor summoned Tàizǐ Shào and others to discuss,
and the majority believed it should be accepted.
Zhàn said:
"Barbarians are untrustworthy;
agreeing to this is useless."
Shào became angry and
said to Zhàn:
"Now that the three kings are in distress,
how can you stubbornly insist on a different opinion?"
His tone and expression were very harsh.
After the meeting dispersed,
Shào ordered his guards and attendants to push him,
nearly causing him to fall.
Shào then said to the Emperor:
"The northern expedition failed and brought disgrace,
and several prefectures were lost.
Only by executing Jiāng Zhàn
can we apologize to the world."
The Emperor said:
"The northern expedition was my idea;
Jiāng Zhàn merely did not disagree."
Later, when Shào held banquets,
he never invited Zhàn.
He often said to the Emperor:
"Jiāng Zhàn is a flattering person;
he should not be close to you."
The Emperor then arranged for Shào's eldest son, Wěizhī, to marry Zhàn's third daughter,
hoping to reconcile them.
The emperor (Shàng) intended to depose Shào,
and ordered Zhàn to draft the imperial edict.
When Shào entered to commit regicide,
Zhàn went directly to the imperial secretariat (shěng).
Hearing cries and shouts,
he hid in a small room nearby.
Shào sent men to arrest him.
A palace guard (shè lì) lied, saying:
"He is not here."
The soldiers immediately killed the palace guard,
and then captured Zhàn.
Zhàn was leaning against a window when he was killed,
his expression unwavering.
He was then forty-six years old.
Zhàn's five sons, Nìn, Shù, Jǐng, Xùn, and Fǎshòu,
were all killed.
Originally,
Zhàn's family had frequently witnessed strange phenomena.
A few days before his downfall,
several pints of blood suddenly appeared on his bed.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,

he posthumously granted Zhàn the titles of Zuǒguānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of the Left Glorious Happiness) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (Initiating a Secretariat with Powers Equal to the Three Ducal Ministers),
added Sànqí Chángshì (Cavalry Regular Attendant),
kept his original official position,
and gave him the posthumous title Zhōngjiǎgōng (Loyal and Simple Duke).
His eldest son, Nìn,
married Tàizǔ's ninth daughter, Princess Huáiyáng Zhǎnggōngzhǔ,
and served as Zuòzuò Zuǒláng (Assistant Gentleman of the Imperial Library).
Wáng Sēngchuò,
a native of Línyí, Lángyá,
was the son of Zuǒguānglù Dàfū Tánshǒu.
From a young age, he showed signs of great accomplishments;
even in his youth, many considered him a national talent.
He was fond of learning and possessed rational thought,
being well-versed in court regulations.
At thirteen,
Tàizǔ summoned him for an audience.
Upon prostrating himself, he immediately wept and choked up,
and the emperor (shàng) too was overcome with sorrow.
He inherited the title Yùníng Xiànhóu (Marquis of Yùníng County),
and married Tàizǔ's eldest daughter, Princess Dōngyáng Xiàngōngzhǔ.
He first served as Sītú Cānjūn (Staff Officer to the Minister of Works) for Jiāngxiàwáng Yìgōng,
then transferred to Wénxué (Literary Tutor) for Shǐxīngwáng,
then Mìshū Chéng (Palace Secretary),
then Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ (Left Senior Clerk to the Minister of Works),
and then Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (Attendant Gentleman to the Crown Prince).
In Yuánjiā 26th year (449 CE),
he was transferred to Shàngshū Lìbù Láng (Secretary of the Board of Civil Office),
and participated in managing major selections.
He thoroughly understood the social hierarchy (liúpǐn)
and was well-acquainted with people's characters,
promoting talent and appointing abilities,
so that all received their due.
In the 28th year (451 CE),
he was promoted to Shìzhōng (Attendant Counselor),
entrusted with confidential matters.
Sēngchuò was profound and had a broad perspective (júdù),
not boasting his talent over others.
Before this,
his father Tánshǒu, along with Wáng Huá, were both trusted by Tàizǔ.
Huá's son, Sī, was inferior in talent,
and his position and treatment were also slighted.
Sēngchuò once said to Zhōngshū Shìláng Cài Xīngzōng:
"My brother's (referring to himself) position should be equal to Xīnjiàn's (Sī),
that it has exceeded to this day,
is probably due to marital relations."
Xīnjiàn was
Sī's enfeoffment.
When he became Shìzhōng,
he was twenty-nine years old.
Shǐxīngwáng Jùn once asked his age,
and Sēngchuò, feeling he had risen too quickly,
hesitated for a long time before answering,
such was his modesty and self-effacement.
At the end of Yuánjiā,
Tàizǔ was quite concerned about future affairs,
and considering his youth,
intended to entrust him with great responsibilities,
so all matters of court administration, big and small,
were discussed with him.
His cousin Wēi,
[一０]was a pure and upright scholar;
fearing Sēngchuò's excessive prominence,
he advised him to restrain himself.
Sēngchuò then requested to be appointed to Wú County and Guǎng Province,
but the emperor (shàng) did not permit either.
It happened that the sorcery (wūgǔ) of the two villains (èrxiōng) was exposed.
The emperor (shàng) first summoned Sēngchuò alone and fully explained the matter.
When he was about to depose and establish an heir,
he ordered Sēngchuò to search for old precedents from previous dynasties.
When Shào hosted a night banquet for his generals and soldiers in the Eastern Palace,
Sēngchuò secretly reported it.
The emperor (shàng) also ordered him to compile stories of deposed princes since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties.
After compiling it,
he sent it to Jiāng Zhàn and Xú Zhànzhī.
Zhànzhī wanted to enthrone Suíwáng Dàn,
Jiāng Zhàn wanted to enthrone Nánpíngwáng Shuò,
and Tàizǔ wanted to enthrone Jiànpíngwáng Hóng.
The discussion dragged on without a decision.
Dàn's consort was Zhànzhī's daughter,
and Shuò's consort was Zhàn's younger sister.
Tàizǔ said to Sēngchuò:
"Everyone is planning for themselves,
there is no one who shares the country's worries."
Sēngchuò replied:
"The matter of establishing an heir
depends on Your Majesty's sacred will.
I believe it is only proper to make a swift decision,
not to delay.
To not decide when one should,
will bring chaos in return.
I wish you would cut off affection for righteousness,
and disregard a little bit of inability to bear it;
otherwise, you should simply be as open-minded as before,
without bothering with doubts and discussions.
Huáinánzi says: 'When a stone is thrown into water,
the skilled swimmers of Wú and Yuè will retrieve it.'
Although the matter is secret,
it can easily become public,
we must not let difficulty arise unexpectedly,
and be mocked for a thousand generations."
The emperor (shàng) said:
"You can be said to be capable of making major decisions.
This matter is serious,
one must not fail to think it over carefully three times.
Moreover, the commoner (shùrén, referring to the Crown Prince) has just died (or is about to die),
people will say I no longer have the way of compassion and love."
Sēngchuò replied:
"I fear that after a thousand generations,
people will say Your Majesty could only punish a brother,
but could not punish a son."
The emperor (shàng) fell silent.
Jiāng Zhàn, who was also attending,
stepped out of the side chamber (gé)
and said to Sēngchuò:
"What you just said
was perhaps too sharp and direct."
Sēngchuò replied:
"I also regret that you were not direct."
When Shào committed regicide,
Jiāng Zhàn was in the Shàngshū shàngshěng (Grand Imperial Secretariat).
Hearing the news,
he sighed:
"Not following Sēngchuò's words led to this."
After Shào was enthroned,
he transferred Sēngchuò to Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of the Board of Civil Office),
and entrusted him with responsibilities;
the details are in the biography of the two villains (èrxiōng zhuàn).
Soon after,
Shào examined Tàizǔ's personal box (jīnxiāng) and Jiāng Zhàn's family letters,
and found Sēngchuò's memorials regarding the banquet for the soldiers and the deposition of various princes.
He then arrested and executed him,
at the age of thirty-one.
Because of this, he implicated various princes and marquises of the Northern residences (Běidì),
accusing them of having different intentions with Sēngchuò,
and also killed Sēngchuò's retainers (ménkè), including Tàixué Bóshì Jiǎ Fěizhī, Fèngcháoqǐng Sīmǎ Wényǐng, and Jiànpíng Guó Chángshì Sīmǎ Zhòngxiù.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he posthumously granted Sēngchuò Sànqí Chángshì (Cavalry Regular Attendant) and Jīnzǐguānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Gold and Purple Seal),
and gave him the posthumous title Mǐnhóu (Mournful Marquis).
Originally,
a vacant plot of land west of the Imperial Altars of the Land (Tàishè),
was the residence of Dīng Fèng during the Wú dynasty.
Sūn Hào exiled his family.
During the early Eastern Jìn (Jiāngzuǒ), it was the residence of Zhōu Yǐ and Sū Jùn.
Later, it became Yuán Yuè's residence,
and then Zhāngwǔwáng Sīmǎ Xiù's residence.
All of them met a violent end.
Later, it was given to Zāng Táo,
[一一]who also suffered misfortune and disaster.
Therefore, the world called it an inauspicious place.
Sēngchuò always
regarded himself as upright and broad-minded,
believed that a residence has no auspiciousness or inauspiciousness,
and requested it as his residence.
He had just begun construction,
but was ruined before he could move in.
His son, Jiǎn, inherited the title.
At the end of Shēngmíng,
he served as Qíguó Shàngshū Yòupúyè (Right Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat of the State of Qí).
The imperial historian remarks: How terrible were the domestic troubles of the Sòng clan!
The focus of enmity and strife,
extending to the closest kin,
though it might overturn Heaven and extinguish the Way,
and the traces were not along the path of suspicion,
yet internal disasters arose,
and external evil influences thrived.
Natural affection was severed,
and love and respect were utterly lost.
The episode of "hunting sparrows and requesting a bear"
was not without prior causes for animosity.
Was the way of suspicion and prevention
insufficient?
Shìzǔ was young and impetuous,
having never enjoyed favor at court,
repeatedly serving in border regions,
never dwelling in the capital.
The weighty matter of succession
would come about through affection,
but suspicions arose between sovereign and minister,
and matters were not decided early.
If the vessel of state had been preserved by the elder,
and the mandate had not awaited a worthy one,
then the hidden disaster would have resolved itself,
and the crisis could have been avoided.
How could the teachings of the sages
deceive us?
In the past, Shān Tāo nominated Yáng Hù as Crown Prince's Grand Tutor,
intending to entrust him with future affairs,
but Lord Yáng had a short life.
Sēng Chuò cultivated the sovereign's trust,
intending to entrust him with weighty national matters,
but the imperial carriage departed prematurely (the emperor died).
Both ministers, being humble and virtuous,
enjoyed high renown across two generations.
Their sacrificial meat was not yet mature (they died young),
and their achievements ended on the day they were to be completed.
What a pity!
Collation Notes

Biographies, Chapter 32. Princes Wén (Ninth): Nánpíng Mù Wáng Shuò, Jiànpíng Xuānjiǎn Wáng Hóng, Jìnxī Wáng Chǎng, Shǐ'ān Wáng Xiūrén, Jìnpíng Cì Wáng Xiūyòu, Póyáng Āi Wáng Xiūyè, Línqìng Chōng Wáng Xiūqiàn, Xīnyě Huái Wáng Yífù, Bālíng Āi Wáng Xiūruò.
Emperor Wén had nineteen sons: Yuán Empress gave birth to Shào;
Pān Shúfēi gave birth to Jùn;
Lù Shúyuàn gave birth to Emperor Xiàowǔ;
Wú Shúyí gave birth to Nánpíng Wáng Shuò;
Gāo Xiūyí gave birth to Lúlíng Zhāo Wáng Shào;
Yīn Xiūhuá gave birth to Jìnglíng Wáng Dàn;
Cáo Jiéyú gave birth to Jiànpíng Xuānjiǎn Wáng Hóng;
Chén Xiūróng gave birth to Dōnghǎi Wáng Huī;
Xiè Rónghuá gave birth to Jìnxī Wáng Chǎng;
Jiāng Xiūyí gave birth to Wǔchāng Wáng Hún;
Shěn Jiéyú gave birth to Emperor Míng;
Yáng Xiūyí gave birth to Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén;
Xíng Měirén gave birth to Jìnpíng Wáng Xiūyòu;
Cài Měirén gave birth to Hǎilíng Wáng Xiūmào;
Dǒng Měirén gave birth to Póyáng Āi Wáng Xiūyè;
Yán Měirén gave birth to Línqìng Chōng Wáng Xiūqiàn;
Chén Měirén gave birth to Xīnyě Huái Wáng Yífù;
Xún Měirén gave birth to Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn;
Luó Měirén gave birth to Bālíng Āi Wáng Xiūruò.
Biographies for Shào, Jùn, Dàn, Huī, Hún, Xiūmào, and Xiūfàn are given separately.
Shào was adopted as the heir of Lúlíng Xiàoxiàn Wáng Yìzhēn.
Nánpíng Mù Wáng Shuò, courtesy name Xiūxuán,
was the fourth son of Emperor Wén.
In the 17th year of Yuánjiā (440 CE),
he was appointed Grand Administrator of the Military Affairs of Xiāngzhōu, General of Champion Army, and Inspector of Xiāngzhōu.
He did not proceed to his post,
but oversaw the affairs of Shítóu Garrison.
In the 22nd year (445 CE),
he was promoted to Bearer of the Imperial Credentials, Grand Administrator of the Military Affairs of the six commanderies of Nányù, Yù, Sī, Yōng, Qín, and Bìng, and Inspector of Nányùzhōu.
At that time, Tàizǔ (Emperor Wén) was engaged in foreign campaigns,
so he abolished Nányù and annexed it to Shòuyáng,
directly appointing Shuò as Inspector of Yùzhōu.
Soon after, he also held the post of Colonel for Pacifying the Man,
and was granted a set of drums and pipes.
In the 26th year (449 CE),
he was advanced to the title of General Pacifying the West,
but he declined the appointment.
The great commander of the nomadic Tatars, Tuòbá Táo, invaded Chén and Yǐng to the south,
and then besieged Xuánhù City in Rǔnán.
The acting Administrator of Rǔnán, Chén Xiàn, held the city and fortified himself.
The bandits attacked and besieged day and night.
Xiàn defended and fought simultaneously,
arrows and stones ceaselessly exchanging.
The Tatars built many high towers,
installing crossbows to shoot into the city.
Flying arrows rained down,
and people in the city took cover behind doors to draw water.
They also destroyed Buddhist pagodas,
taking golden statues to make large hooks,
which they attached to the front of battering rams
to pull down the battlements.
There was a monk inside the city
who was quite ingenious and always devised strange methods to counter them.
The bandits built many "toad carts" to fill the moat,
and launched close-quarters assaults on the city.
Xiàn exhorted his officers and soldiers,
firmly defending the parapets and fighting.
The number of bandits killed
caused their corpses to pile up as high as the city walls.
They then climbed the corpses to scale the city.
In close combat,
Xiàn's morale became even fiercer,
and every soldier was able to fight a hundred,
causing tens of thousands of casualties,
and the Rǔ River ceased to flow.
After resisting for over forty days,
Shuò dispatched Liú Kāngzǔ, Sīmǎ for Pacifying the Man, and Zāng Zhì, General Who Pacifies the North, to relieve them.
The Tatars burned their siege equipment and fled.
In the 27th year (450 CE),
a large-scale northern expedition was launched,
and all the feudal lords sent out troops.
Shuò sent Hú Shèngzhī, Staff Officer of the Central Army, to Rǔnán,
and Dào Tǎnzhī to Shàngcài,
heading towards Chángshè.
The garrison commander of Chángshè, Lǔ Shuǎng, abandoned the city and fled.
Having taken Chángshè,
Shuò sent his banner chiefs Wáng Yáng'ér and Zhāng Lüè to advance and occupy Xiǎosuǒ.
The pseudo-Inspector of Yùzhōu, Púlán, led two thousand infantry and cavalry from Dàsuǒ to attack Yáng'ér.
Yáng'ér attacked and utterly defeated them.
Dào Tǎnzhī and others advanced towards Dàsuǒ,
and Zhèng Déxuán and Zhāng Hé, commoners from Xíngyáng, raised armies in support of Tǎnzhī.
Púlán fled to Hǔláo.
When Wáng Yáng'ér and others arrived,
they immediately occupied Dàsuǒ,
and then proceeded towards Hǔláo.
Shuò again dispatched Liú Kāngzǔ, Sīmǎ for Pacifying the Man, to follow Tǎnzhī.
The Tatar Prince of Yǒngchāng, Yíqín Kùrénzhēn, came to the aid of Hǔláo.
Tǎnzhī was defeated and fled.
The Tatars pursued their victory, advancing directly,
and encountered Kāngzǔ at Wèishì Ford.
Kāngzǔ was defeated in battle and killed.
The bandits advanced and threatened Shòuyáng,
then passed eastward and met Táo on the Jiāng (Yangtze River).
In the summer of the 28th year (451 CE),
Lǔ Shuǎng, the Tatar Inspector of Jīngzhōu, and his brother Xiù,
led their troops to Shuò and submitted.
In the seventh month of that year,
Wú Shúyí, Shuò's birth mother, passed away.
Shuò returned to the capital,
and after the burial,
resumed his original post.
At that time, Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng held the post of Inspector of Nányǎnzhōu,
stationed at Xūyí.
When his mother died,
he returned to the capital.
The Emperor, seeing that Yǎn territory was desolate,
abolished Nányǎn and merged it with Nánxúzhōu.
A new Huáinán Grand Administrator was to be established and stationed at Xūyí,
to initiate military agricultural colonies,
and to respond to those from near and far,
intending to assign this to Shuò.
However, he was instead appointed Gentleman-in-Waiting, General Fǔjūn,
and was given command of troops to garrison Shítóu.
When the Arch-Criminal (Liú Shào) usurped the throne through regicide,
he appointed Shuò as General of the Central Army,
his positions as Protector of the Army and Gentleman-in-Waiting remaining as before.
When Shìzǔ (Emperor Xiàowǔ) entered to suppress the rebellion,
Shào garrisoned troops in the capital
and sent Shuò to inspect and encourage them.

Shào then re-established Nányǎn and appointed Shuò as Bearer of the Imperial Credentials, Grand Administrator of the Military Affairs of the six commanderies of Nányǎn, Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, Jì, and Yōu, General Pacifying the North, Minister with Open Mansion and the Same Privileges as the Three Excellencies, and Inspector of Nányǎnzhōu.
His position as Gentleman-in-Waiting remained as before.
When Liǔ Yuánjǐng reached Xīntíng,
Shào personally attacked him,
taking Shuò along with him.
When Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng fled south,
Shào made Shuò guard the Eastern Mansion,
defending it with his most trusted confidants.
Shuò was then promoted to Palace Attendant, General of Agile Cavalry, and concurrently Supervisor of the Secretariat,
with other titles remaining as before.
Shào brought the deity of Lord Jiǎng into the palace,
wrote down Shìzǔ's birth year and taboo name,
performing rituals and prayers,
and falsely bestowed titles and ranks,
having Shuò compose the ceremonial texts.
When the righteous army entered the palace,
Shuò and Jùn both returned to Shìzǔ.
Jùn was immediately executed,
but the Emperor welcomed Shuò into the camp.
At that chaotic time, the imperial seal was lost.
When affairs settled,
a new one was cast and given to him.
He was promoted to Palace Attendant and Minister of Works,
granted command of troops and given staff to assist him,
but because the national mourning had not yet ended,
he declined the position of Palace Attendant.
Shuò had always been uncooperative with Shìzǔ,
and had also been appointed by the Arch-Criminal.
So the Emperor poisoned his food with medicine and killed him.
He was twenty-three years old at the time.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Palace Attendant and Minister of Education.
Shān Zǐ: Jìngyóu, Jìngyuān, Jìngxiān.
Jìngyóu was the heir,
and his official post reached Huángménláng.
Jìngyuān was initially enfeoffed as the Marquis of Nán'ān County,
and his official post reached Hòujūn Jiāngjūn.
Jìngxiān succeeded Lúlíng Wáng Shào.
At the end of the Jǐnghé reign of the Former Deposed Emperor,
Shuò’s consort, Lady Jiāng, was summoned to the palace.
The attendants were ordered to press her in front of them,
but Lady Jiāng did not comply with the order.
They said:
"If you do not obey,
we will kill your three sons."
Lady Jiāng still refused.
Thereupon, envoys were sent to the mansion to kill Jìngyóu, Jìngyuān, and Jìngxiān,
and Lady Jiāng was flogged a hundred times.
That evening, the Deposed Emperor also perished.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
he posthumously granted Jìngyóu the title of Shìzhōng,
with the posthumous name Huái Wáng.
He posthumously granted Jìngyuān the title of Huángmén Shìláng,
with the posthumous name Dào Hóu.
He re-enfeoffed Xiàowǔ Dì’s eighteenth son, Línhé Wáng Zǐchǎn, whose courtesy name was Xiàorén, as Nánpíng Wáng,
to succeed Shuò.
Before he was officially appointed,
he was killed.
In the fifth year of Tàishǐ,
Jìnpíng Wáng Xiūyòu’s seventh son, Xuānyào, was established as Nánpíng Wáng to succeed Shuò.
When Xiūyòu died,
Xuānyào was deposed and returned to his original status.
In the first year of Yuánhuī of the Later Deposed Emperor,
Héngyáng Gōng Wáng Yí’s second son, Bóyù, was established as Nánpíng Wáng to succeed Shuò.
Later, his official post reached Jǐshìzhōng.
In the second year of Shēngmíng,
he was executed for plotting rebellion,
and his state was abolished.
Jiànpíng Xuānjiǎn Wáng Hóng, whose courtesy name was Xiūdù,
was Wéndì’s seventh son.
He lost his mother early.
In the twenty-first year of Yuánjiā,
at the age of eleven,
he was enfeoffed as Jiànpíng Wáng,
with a fief of two thousand households.
From a young age, he was quiet and simple,
and deeply fond of literature.
Tàizǔ cherished him extraordinarily,
and built a residence for him on Jīlóng Shān,
making full use of the beauty of the mountains and waters.
The official rank of the Jiànpíng state
was one grade higher than other states.
In the twenty-fourth year,
he became Zhōnghùjūn,
and oversaw the affairs of the Shítou garrison.
He was sent out as Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the twenty-eighth year,
he was recalled as Zhōngshūlìng,
and concurrently held Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
When Yuánxiōng usurped the throne,
Hóng was made Zuǒ Jiāngjūn and Dānyáng Yǐn.
He was also made Sànqí Chángshì, Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn, and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Shìzǔ entered to suppress the rebellion,
Shào kept Hóng in the palace.
Shìzǔ had previously given Hóng a hand-tablet.
Hóng sent his trusted aide, Zhōu Fǎdào, to take the hand-tablet to Shìzǔ.
After the matter was settled,
he was made Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
and was ordered to welcome the Empress Dowager.
Upon his return, he was promoted to Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn,
Zhōngshūjiān,
with the position of Púyè as before.
When Zāng Zhì rebelled,
Hóng entered the six gates with fifty armed guards.
He was humble, frugal, cautious,
treated worthy people with respect,
and was clear-minded in political affairs.
The Emperor highly trusted and relied on him.
At that time, all officials were universally asked for candid opinions.
Hóng deliberated, saying: "I have heard that the ways of founding a state are all different,
and the policies of rising kings are not uniform.
However, as for opening channels for remonstrance to achieve peace,
and stifling criticism to invite disaster,
this is indeed a common path for former kings,
and a shared principle for later rulers.
The failures of Qín and Yīn
were due to the killing of those who spoke out;
the prosperity of Zhōu and Hàn
was due to the elevation of criticism and the prominence of admonition.
Your Majesty, with your supreme virtue, divinely presides,
and meticulously applies yourself to governance.
You promote
Confucian rites and uphold lenient teachings,
pity judicial laws and abolish severe punishments,
display loyal conduct and raise up chaste integrity,
invite reclusive scholars and seek out exceptional talents,
restore defunct offices and release those who are overlooked,
reward,
remove extravagant imperial meals and value farmers' food,
prohibit noble excursions and relax wine monopolies,
open up mountains and lakes and ease customs barriers.
Thus, the whole country looks up to your Way,
and the world knows your virtue.
Now, you again open the path of frankness
and encourage the way of honest words.
The four seas admire your virtue,
and the whole world is exceedingly fortunate.
Having received your inquiry,
how dare I not give my whole heart?
I carefully set forth my humble views,
arranged as follows.
If the words and reasoning are erroneous,
I am filled with trepidation.
The way of deploying troops
has been gravely regarded since ancient times.
Recently, military conflicts have not ceased,
and war preparations should be improved.
However, soldiers are not trained in advance,
and the army is not accustomed to warfare.
Moreover, many of those in charge of military defense
are not competent for their roles.
Some are promoted simply because of their wealth,
some are given honorary titles because their salaries are meager,
some enjoy favor due to powerful families,
and their benefits come from private connections.
They have no command ability,
and merely
occupy empty positions of honor and emolument.
When border cities light warning fires,
and urgent despatches fly,
to expect them to don armor and charge forth,
and achieve merit outside the pass,
is like climbing a tree to seek fish;
it is impossible
to obtain.
I have always said that appointing commanders in times of crisis
is always done in haste,
driving a motley crowd,
subordinate to hastily chosen leaders.
Their appearances are unfamiliar and their sentiments are divergent,
like Hú and Yuè.
How can
one make them unite their strength,
overcome dangers and resolve difficulties?
Therefore, defeats are constantly seen,
and failures continuously occur.
Now, if we wish to re-select generals and officers,
and ensure that each is the right person,
divide the existing generals in the court,
and
assign them respectively,
making the Lǐng and Hù armies
their overall commanders.
Let them care for and nurture the soldiers,
ensuring that kindness and trust are first established.
During agricultural slack seasons, conduct training and hunts
to accustom them to military matters.
Issue repeated orders
to unify their minds,
so that their every move conforms to regulations,
and their advances and retreats align with discipline.
Then, conserve their strength and observe opportunities,
acting at the opportune moment,
destroying the enemy and breaching strongholds,
and breaking their spears
outside.
Sūn Zǐ said:
"Regard your soldiers as infants,
and thus you can die with them."
Therefore, Zhāng Quǎn displayed the spirit of striving first,
and sucking out pus showed a commitment to give one's life.
How
can it not be that those on whom kindness is bestowed make light of their lives,
and those commanded clearly exert their utmost strength?
Examining these facts and deeds,
if there is anything that applies,
I have presumptuously presented my superficial knowledge,
and I am now fearful of any errors.
He was transferred to Shàngshūlìng,
given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì,
with his general rank remaining as before,
and was granted a complete set of drum and wind instruments.
Soon after, he was promoted to Wèi Jiāngjūn,
with Zhōngshūjiān and Shàngshūlìng remaining as before.
Hóng was young and often ill.
In the second year of Dàmíng, his illness flared up.
He sought to resign from the position of Shàngshū Lìng,
and was granted the title Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī with his original designation,
additionally appointed Sànqí Chángshì,
while Zhōngshū Jiān remained as before.
He had not yet formally accepted the appointment
when he died that same year,
at the age of twenty-five.
He was posthumously granted the titles Shìzhōng and Sīkōng,
Zhōngshū Jiān remained as before,
and he was provided with twenty guards bearing ceremonial swords.
The emperor was deeply grieved,
and on the first and fifteenth day of each month, he would go to mourn at the spirit tablet,
and personally composed the epitaph and its preface.
He issued an edict to Yán Jùn, the Cìshǐ of Dōngyángzhōu, saying:
“Hóng’s character and aspirations were lofty,
his inherent integrity and achievements commendable.
Though he had not yet reached maturity,
his aspirations were fully expressed.
I believed that the Way of Heaven could be relied upon,
and that benevolence would not lead to misfortune.
Though his illness prolonged,
I thought it would not lead to disaster.
How could I have known that divine aid for the good was in vain,
and that he would depart forever in an instant?
The shock and sorrow are overwhelming,
my innermost being is shattered.
His life was not long past,
and when I look up, it feels like yesterday.
But the enjoyment of his company and our leisure activities
now feel as distant as a thousand years.
The profound grief lingers,
indeed intensifying the pain.
Your feelings are shared in joy and sorrow,
and our association was close.
Our separation was brief,
yet it has suddenly become a chasm between past and present.
Hearing this news brings such sorrow and regret,
what more can be said?”
Five years later,
the fiefs of his younger brothers were each increased by one thousand households.
Those who had died earlier were not included in this arrangement,
only Hóng received a posthumous increase.
His son, Jǐngsù,
loved literature and prose from a young age,
and had his father’s demeanor.
In the fourth year of Dàmíng,
he was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Nánjìyīn Tàishǒu,
then transferred to serve as Tàishǒu of Lìyáng and Nánqiáo Commanderies,
with his general title remaining as before.
He was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng,
but did not accept it.
He was appointed Jiān Nányù Yù Èrzhōu Zhūjūnjìshì, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ,
but again did not accept.
At the beginning of Tàizōng’s reign,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
concurrently Lǐng Bùbīng Xiàowèi,
then Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ,
additionally granted Jǐshìzhōng,
then Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ,
Dānyáng Yǐn,
Wúxìng Tàishǒu,
Shǐchíjié, Jiān Xiāngzhōu Zhūjūnjìshì, and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with all his general titles remaining as before.
His title was advanced to Zuǒ Jiāngjūn.
In the sixth year of Tàishǐ,
he was appointed Dūdū Jīng Xiāng Yōng Yì Liáng Níng Nánběi Qín Bāzhōu Zhūjūnjìshì, Zuǒ Jiāngjūn, and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his Shǐchíjié remaining as before.
He was summoned to be Sànqí Chángshì, Hòujiāngjūn, and Tàicháng,
but had not yet accepted.
He was then appointed Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Nánxú Nányǎn Yǎn Xú Qīng Jì Liùzhōu Zhūjūnjìshì, Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn, and Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn rebelled,
Jǐngsù, though assembling troops,
professed to be heading to the imperial court,
but secretly harbored duplicity.
When the rebellion was quelled,
his title was advanced to Zhènběi Jiāngjūn.
When Qí Wáng was appointed Nányǎnzhōu,
Jǐngsù was relieved of his Dūdū title.
At that time, all the sons of Tàizǔ had perished,
and among the grandsons, only Jǐngsù was the eldest.
All the sons of Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūyòu were deposed and exiled,
with none remaining at court.
Jǐngsù was fond of literature and books,
and gathered talented and righteous individuals,
exerting himself to treat them with respect,
thereby accumulating a good reputation.
Consequently, the court and the common people alike
all paid attention to him.
However, the later deposed emperor became tyrannical and lost the Way.
Both inside and outside the court, everyone believed Jǐngsù ought to assume the divine vessel (the throne).
Only the relatives of the Chen clan, the deposed emperor’s birth mother, hated and envied him.
And Yáng Yùncháng and Ruǎn Diánfū, both former subordinates of Tàizōng,
desired to prolong their power by relying on a young emperor.
They feared that if Jǐngsù were to ascend,
they would not be tolerated by a mature ruler,
and thus deeply resented and feared him.
In the third year of Yuánhuī,
Wáng Jìfú, Jǐngsù’s Fánggē Jiāngjūn, displeased Jǐngsù,
and, harboring resentment,
fled alone on horseback to the capital,
informing Yùncháng and Diánfū that
“Jǐngsù intends to rebel.”
Yùncháng and others immediately wished to dispatch troops to suppress him.
Qí Wáng and Wèijiāngjūn Yuán Càn and others below all defended him,
saying it was not true.
Jǐngsù also quickly sent his heir, Yánlíng, back to the capital
to fully explain himself.
Yùncháng and others then exiled Jìfú to Liángzhōu,
and also stripped Jǐngsù of his Zhènběi Jiāngjūn and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī titles.
From then on, the deposed emperor’s tyranny grew daily,
and the court and populace alike looked to Jǐngsù.
The Chen clan and Yùncháng and others grew increasingly suspicious.
Jǐngsù, therefore, gradually made plans for self-defense,
conspiring with his Sīmǎ Hé Jìmù of Lújiāng, Lùshì Cānjūn Yīn Yǐ of Chénjùn, Jìshì Cānjūn Cài Lǚ of Jìyáng, Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Yuán Qìngyán of Lüèyáng, Zuǒyòu Hè Wénchāo, and others.
He appointed Cānjūn Shěn Yǒng, Wúqiū Wénzǐ, Zuǒ Xuān, Zhōu Xīcáo Wáng Tán, and others as his close associates.
Jìmù recommended his cousin Yùzhī to be a Cānjūn.
Jǐngsù sent Yùzhī, Tán, Wénchāo, and others back and forth to the capital,
giving them much gold and silk
to rally talented and capable individuals.
Consequently, Guānjūn Jiāngjūn Huáng Huí, Yóujī Jiāngjūn Gāo Dàoqìng, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Cáo Xīnzhī, Qiánjūn Hán Dàoqīng, Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi Guō Lánzhī, and Yǔlín Jiān Yuán Zhīzǔ
all responded and attached themselves to him.
Other military men who had lost their positions and were discontent
all went over to him.
At that time, the deposed emperor would often go out alone on horseback,
roaming the suburbs and countryside.
Cáo Xīnzhī plotted to seize Shítóu.
Hán Dàoqīng and Guō Lánzhī wanted to persuade Qí Wáng to join them;
if he refused, they would deal with him.
They planned to act during one of the deposed emperor’s excursions,
inciting a rebellion among the populace.
Upon success, they would enthrone Jǐngsù.
Jǐngsù repeatedly restrained them,
not wishing to act hastily.
Yùncháng secretly sent a Cang-man, Zhōu Tiāncì, to feign defection to Jǐngsù,
and urge him to make a move.
Jǐngsù, knowing he was sent by Yùncháng,
immediately beheaded him
and sent his Sīmǎ Sūn Qiān to deliver the head back to the court.
In the seventh month of the fourth year of Yuánhuī,
Yuán Zhīzǔ led several hundred men to Jǐngsù,
claiming the capital was in chaos
and urging him to enter quickly.
Jǐngsù believed him
and immediately raised an army,
with thousands of men bearing spears arriving.
Yùncháng and others had always suspected Jǐngsù of harboring rebellious intentions,
and upon hearing of Zhīzǔ’s defection,
they immediately made preparations.
Qí Wáng deployed to Xuánwǔ Hú.
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn Rèn Nóngfū, Huáng Huí, and Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn Lǐ Ānmín each led infantry,
while Yòujūn Jiāngjūn Zhāng Bǎo commanded the navy,
all advancing northwards.
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ Duàn Fórong served as Dūtǒng.
The rest of the forces followed in succession.
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn Qí Wáng’s heir garrisoned the Zhèndōng Fǔ city.
Qí Wáng knew that Huáng Huí had rebellious designs,
and therefore sent Ānmín and Fórong together to guard against him.
Jǐngsù wanted to occupy Zhú Lǐ
to resist the imperial army.
Yuán Qìngyán, Zhīzǔ, Shěn Yóng, and others said:
"Today the weather is hot and dry,
the imperial army has come a long way and is exhausted.
If we lure them here,
we can wait at ease for the tired,
and defeat them in one battle."
Yīn Nǐ and others argued strongly but could not prevail.
After Nóngfū and others arrived,
they set fire to the city and marketplace,
but Yuán Qìngyán and the others looked at each other,
having no will to fight.
Jǐngsù was originally lacking in prestige and strategy,
and was panicked and didn't know what to do.
At this time, Zhāng Bǎoshuǐ's naval force was anchored at Xī Zhǔ.
Dozens of brave warriors around Jǐngsù,
all skilled fighters from Jīng Chǔ,
banded together
to attack the naval force,
instantly crushing them,
and killing Zhāng Bǎo.
But the other generals did not respond or come to their aid,
and were again defeated by the imperial army.
Once the imperial army pressed close to the city,
Yóng was the first among the multitude to betray and flee,
followed by Yuán Zhīzǔ.
The rest of the armies followed suit and scattered in defeat.
Zuǒ Xuān was fierce and brave,
wanting to die for Jǐngsù,
but his assigned troops were very weak.
Still, he fought hard and did not retreat,
firing arrows at the imperial army beneath Wànsùi Lóu,
but he could not stop them,
and then retreated and dispersed.
The Right Guard Palace General Zhāng Ní'nú and the Vanguard General Zhōu Pánlóng attacked and captured the capital city.
Ní'nú captured Jǐngsù and executed him,
at the age of twenty-five,
and he was buried immediately in Jīngkǒu.
Yuán Qìngyán, Zhīzǔ, Zuǒ Xuān, and Hè Wénchāo were all executed.
Yīn Nǐ and Cài Lǚ were exiled to Liángzhōu.
Hé Jìmù had been promoted earlier,
and thus escaped the disaster.
The rest all fled,
and were pardoned during an amnesty.
After Jǐngsù's defeat,
Cáo Xīnzhī in turn accused Hán Dàoqīng and Guō Lánzhī of their plot,
and Dàoqīng and others were all executed.
Huáng Huí and Gāo Dàoqìng,
Qí Wáng treated them as before.
Jǐngsù's son Yánlíng and his two younger sons
were all executed.
In the winter of that year,
Tán, the third son of Yìxīn, King Chángshā Chéng, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Zǐguī County,
with a fief of a thousand households,
succeeding Hóng.
He died in the second year of Shènmíng of Shùn Dì,
and his marquisate was abolished.
Zhāng Ní'nú, for the meritorious capture of Jǐngsù,
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Zhúyáng County,
with a fief of a thousand households.
After Jǐngsù's defeat,
former Scribe-Counselor Wáng Chī and former Chief Clerk Hé Chāngbǐng both submitted memorials arguing for Jǐngsù's innocence.
When Qí received the abdication,
in the early Jiànyuán era,
former Jǐngsù scholar Liú Jìn again submitted a memorial, saying: "I have heard that Zéngzǐ was filial to his parents but drowned,
and Jiè Shēng was loyal to his lord but burned in fire.
Why is this so?
Benevolence is not necessarily something one can rely on,
and trustworthiness
is not necessarily something one can depend on.
In the past, Mò Dí debated the cloud ladder beneath Jīng Tái,
but the people of Sòng drove him away.
Yí Shū averted disaster for the Wèi army in Jìn,
but Prince Yì
killed him.
Lǐ Mù repelled the banners of the strong Hú to the north,
and resisted the troops of all Qín to the south,
yet the King of Zhào did not recognize his achievements,
and bestowed upon him a sharp sword.
Chén Fān, with white hair, firmly upheld righteousness,
forgetting his own life
to serve his lord,
yet Hàn Líng Dì did not understand his loyalty,
and he eventually suffered execution.
These several men,
all resided above the green clouds,
yet were trapped in the mud and dust below.
This is truly because
dangerous conduct is not tolerated in a decaying age,
standing alone invites blame from the multitude,
coupled with calumny and insidious gossip within,
and slander and rifts flying in from all sides.
I have heard that insidious
acts
can sever even close kin,
and once suspicion arises,
the hearts of ruler and minister change.
This is why Zhōngshān sighed and played music,
and Mèng Bó passionately put his head in a bag.
I often recall the disaster of the late King Sòng Jiàn Píng,
and a sorrow pierces my bones,
my breath congeals into frost and snow.
Now the Xuan Dǐng has opened a new destiny,
and heaven and earth have changed.
The living who are guilty are still
pardoned,
so the dead who were wronged must have their grievances redressed.
I truly cannot bear for the King to bear slander without vindication,
hence I dare to articulate the reasons clearly.
I have heard that those who are filial and fraternal
do not transgress against superiors.
Zéngzǐ did not go against the grain to make fire,
knowing that it would not lead to violence.
Qín Rén captured a fawn,
knowing that it could
be taught.
I have heard that when the King served the late Grand Consort,
he never failed to attend to her day and night,
and showed no discomfort regardless of the food's taste.
When precious delicacies were served beneath the canopy,
if the Grand Consort had not yet eaten,
the King
would put down his chopsticks and stop eating.
If the Grand Consort felt unwell in her daily life,
the King would walk around with disheveled hair.
I have heard that loyal officials are found among the gates of filial sons.
How could one be as filial as the King
and yet be disloyal?
This can be made clear as point one.
During the Tàishǐ and Yuánhuī periods,
no princes or high-ranking officials visited Jǐngníng Líng,
but the King alone, with strong feelings, did so,
not abandoning righteousness to conform to the times.
Whether stationed outside or entering
court,
he would always bow before the mausoleum.
The King did not abandon his former lord,
how could he betray his present lord?
This can be made clear as point two.
The King was broadly learned and inclusive of all,
accepted criticism, and loved scholars.
When speaking with people, he was gentle and cautious, as if afraid of hurting them.
When he heard of others' virtues,
he praised and promoted them.
When he saw others'
faults,
he concealed and instructed them.
Lǐ Wèizhī, a humble and poor man living in a straw hut,
the King went out of his way to visit and inquire after him.
Hé Jìmù and others,
were old acquaintances of King Xuānjiǎn,
the King supported
and promoted them.
The King humbled himself to treat the scholars of the world generously,
still not wishing to harm anyone's feelings.
How then could he plot to butcher his own relatives?
This can be made clear as
point three.
I formerly served as a judicial staff officer,
performing inquiries at the end of court sessions.
Whenever the King judged cases,
he would lower his voice,
and soften his expression,
to attend to the lawsuits of men and women.
At one time, he saw Xià Bó being shackled as a child,
and the King's countenance changed with sorrow,
using no further punishment.
Xúzhōu once suffered a famine,
and the King distributed his salary of grain and silk,
to relieve the people's
scarcity.
He redressed grievances and doubts,
and all were relieved from forced labor.
Wherever he went, he was loved by the people.
I have heard that good people are
the pillars of the state.
How could one be benevolent to the common people,
and
tyrannical to his own royal state?
This can be made clear as point four.
The King cultivated his character and kept his conduct pure,
his words were free from vulgarity.
Internally, he avoided the pleasures of music and wine,
externally, he had no fondness for hunting.
Wherever he resided,
he did not add new construction or excavation.
His personal
guards were not numerous,
and his residences were not altered.
In Jīngzhōu, his lofty hall,
with carved pillars and cypress beams,
the King abandoned and did not reside in it.
In the past, the court wanted to bestow upon the King the finest mansion in Dōng Líng,
but he refused.
but inappropriate.
The treasures left by the two palaces
were gathering dust in chests and boxes.
He had no other favored consorts,
did not indulge in imperial concubines;
the few women he had
were all bestowed by imperial decree.
The Wáng
personally ate no more than one meat dish,
and his utensils were made of plain earthenware.
When intricately carved jade vessels were occasionally presented,
the Wáng looked at Hé Chāngwèi and said:
"What use do I have for these?"
He then declined
and returned them.
The Wáng was humble and adhered to righteousness in this manner.
This is the fifth point that can be made clear.
When the Wáng was in Jīngzhōu,
at the time of Xiàn Tàifēi's recent demise,
Sòng Míngdì had just abandoned the realm,
and the various princes in the capital region were successively meeting untimely ends.
The Wáng was then summoned to enter
as Tàicháng.
The common people of Chǔ urged him not to go down.
The Wáng said:
"As a subject, to refuse the command of the former emperor
is disloyal;
as a son, not to attend to one's parents' burial
is
unfilial."
Thereupon, he abandoned his important position in Xīzhōu
and prostrated himself before the Northern Gate.
If the Wáng truly intended to be defiant,
he should have reclined at ease by the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
Why would he bend and submit to be controlled
by others?
This is the sixth point that can be made clear.
The Wáng's fame was high throughout the realm,
and his righteousness was as weighty as Tài Shān.
The old and young cherished his benevolence,
and scholars and commoners admired his virtue.
Thus, those who engaged in darkness feared the light,
and those who practiced crookedness slandered the upright.
Drawing the string
to make it a hook,
one instance becoming a hundred,
his every move, cough, or sneeze
stirred up dust and commotion.
It happened that Wáng Jìfú, burdened by crimes, spread slander.
This matched the intentions of the slanderers,
and the powerful and ugly incited each other,
like owls and buzzards spreading their wings.
Although the Wáng encountered misfortune and separation from good fortune,
his sincerity and loyalty were profound,
he expressed his feelings with utmost sincerity,
and swept away all pretense.
Yú Wánzhī returned from his mission,
the Crown Prince
entered the capital as a hostage,
he subsequently relinquished Xúzhōu,
requested to reside in the eastern mansion,
and later sought to go to Kuàijī,
humbling himself to appease those outside.
Yú Wán and Yīn Huàn truly acted as interpreters,
conveying his sincere and
diligent heart,
ensuring it was fully heard by the emperor.
If the Wáng was deceitful and overbearing,
why would he act like this?
This is the seventh point that can be made clear.
From this time onward,
different opinions arose daily.
The declining virtue of Cāngwú became evident,
and the wickedness of the petty men grew wider.
Below, their poison overflowed;
above, there was no one to rely on.
At that time, the elder princes were all executed,
and high officials felt as if they were treading on a tiger's tail.
The multitude was agitated,
all looking up to the Wáng.
The people in the palace chambers
shared a conspiracy but had different intentions.
The Wáng's
heart did not follow profit,
his loyalty did not abandon its root.
He seized Zhōu Tiāncì and executed him,
to resist Wáng Yíyǔ and others,
and sent Sīmǎ Sūn Qiān to offer his submission to the imperial court.
If the Wáng intended to
harbor illicit ambitions,
would he have acted like this?
This is the eighth point that can be made clear.
Furthermore, after May of that year,
everyone on the roads said that Ruǎn Diànfū and others intended to secretly plot against the imperial palace,
and with soldiers, launch a northern attack.
Huáng Huí, Gāo Dàoqìng, and others fabricated
this matter.
Martial men encouraged rebellion,
intimidating each other.
By June, the capital was conscripting chariots and foot soldiers,
preparing to gather troops for the northern forts.
The capital and countryside were alarmed and fearful,
all saying
that conflict was imminent.
Yuán Zhīzǔ, taking advantage of the agitated public sentiment,
publicly declared a retreat north,
deceiving and confusing the multitude with false words,
leading to chaos and extreme disaster.
It happened that people from the province returned from the capital,
saying:
"The Yèmén
has already been closed,
we don't know if the court is safe!"
The Wáng, having long heard dissenting opinions,
believed this to be true.
He gathered the weary and weak,
intending to disperse them,
with a troubled heart,
only
fearing delay.
How could he have known that the troops, which marched out righteously,
would instead become a rebellious movement?
Indeed, the people coming and going,
clamoring and deluding,
all came from the imperial capital,
not from Xúzhōu.
Moreover, the court, on the last night of June, without reason, called out that northern troops had arrived,
all mounting the parapets and drawing their swords.
Yet, at Zhūfāng, on the first day of July, people were still leisurely and at ease.
Only late
upon hearing of the turmoil in the capital,
did they begin to gather troops and inspect armor.
How could the Wáng have initiated the disaster first!
This is the ninth point that can be made clear.
When the Wáng heard of the troubles in the capital,
he could not sit still,
nor eat with relish.
Whenever his mother, the Empress Dowager, was mentioned,
he never failed to cover his face with a handkerchief and weep.
Moreover, at the moment of crisis,
he leaned on the railing
and sighed, saying:
"I fear that the three powers (heaven, earth, and man) will cease here."
How can this not demonstrate his sincerity towards the imperial court,
and his concern for the realm?
Without profound loyalty and far-reaching vision,
who could
disregard his own demise,
and solely care for the safety of the state?
This is the tenth point that can be made clear.
Indeed, on the day the Wáng raised his army,
it was solely for the purpose of rectifying the chaos and difficulty,
and banishing the treacherous thieves,
for no other reason.
Please allow me to elaborate.
At that time, what was the state of affairs between ruler and minister,
and how was order or chaos?
Were Yáng Yùncháng and Ruǎn Diànfū guilty?
Or were they innocent?
If they were innocent,
why were they executed?
If they were guilty,
what crime was there in punishing them?
Did the Wáng not know that a ruler and parent should not be disregarded?
But consider a household on fire;
how could one first report to one's elders?
It was not disrespect,
but merely that
fate had led to decline and ruin,
and intelligence and strength could not be utilized.
Falling and toppling,
this was the timing,
how could it be called rebellion?
Indeed, if the Wáng perished today,
Sòng would perish tomorrow.
What did the Wáng owe to the state,
what shame did he bring upon the realm?
I have heard that King Wǔ of Zhōu, upon conquering Shāng,
before even dismounting from his chariot,
enfeoffed the tomb of the son of the former ruler;
Emperor Gāo of Hàn, upon pacifying the realm,
passed through Dàliáng,
traversed Yān and Dài,
restored the sacrifices to Xìnlíng,
and preserved the descendants of Wàngzhū;
when the Jìn dynasty received the Mandate of Heaven,
it also redressed the injustice of Wáng Líng,
and decreed his grandson to be a Lang official.
Bǐ Gàn
was a criminal in the eyes of Yīn Xīn;
Wú Jì
was a suspicious minister of Wèi;
Yuè Yì
was a runaway general of Yān;
Yàn Yún
was a bandit of Qí and a bane to Jìn.
Yet, they encountered enlightened rulers,
who initiated a new era and established
Regulations
manifest sincerity in meritorious deeds,
dispel suspicion and resentment,
and purify public opinion with the good of all under Heaven.
Sometimes different ages illuminate each other;
thus, the four worthies all achieved their excellent reputations,
and the three empresses spread their
glory for ten thousand generations.
Gentlemen are honored by their brilliance,
and common people submit to their righteousness.
Now Your Majesty upholds the noble path of heroes,
and raises the extraordinary renown of generations past.
Why then adhere to the dissenting opinions of a declining
age,
thereby obscuring the names of worthy men?
If the former king’s integrity is unclear both domestically and abroad,
and he was morally corrupt from beginning to end,
I fear that the people of today
will no longer perform good deeds
themselves.
Moreover, the rise and fall of ages—
which generation has been without them?
Now, ten thousand generations after the descendants of Qí,
how can there be no decline and prosperity?
If former virtuous deeds can be abolished,
how will
future capable individuals be encouraged?
I humbly wish that above, you emulate Zhōu, Hàn, and Xī Jìn in their former manner,
and below, establish a precedent for future generations in this way.
If you can issue a clear edict,
rectifying
the wrongful path,
enabling the former king to clear himself of calumnies and criticisms,
and rescue his obscured soul,
granting him a reburial with royal rites,
then the people’s adherence to righteousness
will be like the wind rolling grass.
I have heard
that when cranes cry on a mound,
then the yin descends and emits rain;
when soaring serpents leap up,
then dark clouds gather densely.
But I lament that my words are light and shed like hair,
my body like a horizontal mustard seed.
The divine hearing is
distant and lofty,
and ultimately will not comprehend.
I simply wish to not betray my own heart internally,
hoping perhaps that the king's intention will be known in the future.
Moreover, I do not understand.
When the present emperor ascended the throne,
he issued an edict stating:
“Liú Jǐngsù, Prince Jiànpíng of Sòng,
was the son of a famous father,
and in his youth, he cultivated a pure and lofty character.
Although he erred in his later years,
his original intentions had a foundation.
With the passage of time and changing fortunes,
it is fitting to extend gracious favor.
He may be reburied in his old tomb with royal rites.”
Chǎng, Prince Jìnxī, whose courtesy name was Xiūdào,
was the ninth son of Emperor Wén.
In the twenty-second year of Yuánjiā (445 CE),
at the age of ten,
he was enfeoffed as Prince Yìyáng
and granted an income of two thousand households.
In the twenty-seventh year (450 CE),
he became General Who Assists the State and Administrator of the two commanderies of Nánpéngchéng and Xiàpī.
When the chief culprit usurped the throne,
he was given the additional title of Cavalry Regular Attendant.
When Emperor Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Grand Master of Ceremonies,
then appointed as General of the Eastern Central Army and Administrator of Kuàijī.
Soon after, he was appointed Supervisor of Military Affairs for the five commanderies of Kuàijī, Dōngyáng, Línhǎi, Yǒngjiā, and Xīn’ān.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn (454 CE),
when Dōngyáng Prefecture was established,
Chǎng was appointed as its Inspector,
〔一一〕with the title General of the Eastern Central Army as before,
and advanced to the title General of the Rear.
In the first year of Dàmíng (457 CE),
he was summoned to be Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
concurrently General of Agile Cavalry,
given the additional title of Cavalry Regular Attendant,
then promoted to General of the Central Army and Administrator of the two commanderies of Nánpéngchéng and Xiàpī.

He was again appointed Commissioner with Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of Military Affairs for Jiāng Prefecture, Xīyáng of Yǐng Prefecture, Xīncài of Yù Prefecture, and Jìnxī, General of the Front, and Inspector of Jiāng Prefecture.
In the third year (459 CE),
he was summoned to be General of the Guards,
granted one set of drums and pipes,
and his income households were increased by a thousand.
He was transferred to be Central Secretariat Director,
General of the Central Army.
Soon after, with his original title, he was granted the honorific of Kai-fu Yi Tong San Si (to establish an administration with the same prerogatives as the Three Ducal Ministers),
given the additional title of Cavalry Regular Attendant,
and Grand Master of Ceremonies.
When he accompanied Emperor Shìzǔ on a southern tour,
he was censured for offending the Empress Dowager's dragon boat,
and his Kai-fu title was revoked,
but it was restored soon after.
When the Former Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,

he was appointed Commissioner with Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of Military Affairs for the six prefectures of Xú, Yǎn, Nányǎn, Qīng, Jì, Yōu, and Liáng Commandery of Yù Prefecture, General Who Conquers the North, and Inspector of Xú Prefecture,
given the additional title of Cavalry Regular Attendant,
with Kai-fu as before.
Chǎng was frivolous, impetuous, and short-tempered,
unable to serve Emperor Shìzǔ respectfully.
During the Dàmíng era, he was frequently viewed with suspicion and reprimanded,
and it was widely rumored among the people
that Chǎng harbored rebellious intentions.
During the Yǒngguāng and Jǐnghé eras,
these rumors grew even stronger.
After the Deposed Emperor executed the high officials,
he became even more unrestrained in his madness and perversity.
He often said to his attendants:
“Since I ascended the great position,
I have never placed the military on high alert,
which makes people uneasy.”
After Yìgōng, Prince Jiāngxià, was executed,
Chǎng submitted a memorial requesting an audience,
and the Emperor dispatched Diǎnqiān Qú Fǎshēng as an envoy.
The Emperor said to Fǎshēng:
“Yìyáng and the Grand Tutor conspired to rebel,
〔一二〕I was just about to attack him.
Now I know he seeks to return,
which is very good.”
He also repeatedly interrogated Fǎshēng:
“Yìyáng plotted rebellion,
why did you not inform me?”
Fǎshēng, fearing disaster,
deserted and fled back to Péngchéng.
The Emperor then launched a northern campaign,
personally leading his troops across the river.
Once Fǎshēng arrived,
Chǎng immediately gathered his forces and raised an army.
However, the various commanderies under his jurisdiction
all refused to obey his orders
and executed Chǎng’s envoys.
His commanders and subordinates, both civil and military,
all harbored dissenting intentions.
Chǎng, knowing that he would not succeed,
then, at night, with several tens of horsemen, opened the city gate and fled north to the Suǒlǔ,
abandoning his mother and wife,
taking only one beloved concubine,
who was dressed in men's clothes
and also rode a horse to follow him.
Chǎng’s family returned to the capital,
where his two concubines each bore a son.
At that time, Emperor Tàizōng had already ascended the throne.
The elder son was named Sīyuǎn,
and the younger one Huáiyuǎn.
Both died soon after.
Huáiyuǎn was posthumously enfeoffed as Marquis of Chíyáng County
with an income of a thousand households.
In the sixth year of Tàishǐ (470 CE),
Xie, the sixth imperial son, whose courtesy name was Zhòngsuí, succeeded Chǎng,
and Chǎng’s enfeoffment was changed to Prince Jìnxī.
Xiè inherited the peerage
and was granted an income of three thousand households.
Tàizōng, having made Xiè succeed Chǎng,
thereupon issued an edict saying:
"Even tigers and wolves protect their young,
monkeys and apes carry their grandchildren.
Though inherently venomous and thin in affection,
they too possess benevolence and love.
Therefore, when identifying and recognizing their own kind,
they still treat all equally among their species.
How much more so in human relationships,
can one forget one's natural kin?
The Dowager Princess Jìnxī, née Xiè,
is deeply malicious and lacking in affection for her kin,
rarely paralleled in the natural world.
Although the Duke of Zhēngběi's filial piety is unwavering,
he has encountered such an unmotherly figure.
From childhood to adulthood,
the grace of nurture has been absent,
to the extent that whether he thrives or suffers is of no concern to her,
and she never inquires about his well-being.
Morning and evening greetings are barred,
and he has no means to pay his respects.
Without any disobedience,
he is constantly subjected to reprimand and blame.
Poisonous words escape her lips,
which people find difficult to hear.
She heaps ill-will and suffering upon him,
exceeding that towards an enemy.
Her conduct has angered his relatives by marriage,
and violated the principles of common passersby.
The Duke's former consort, née Xī,
was impeccable in her wifely duties,
yet encountered such severity and cruelty,
and consequently died of sorrow,
thus cutting short her prime years.
Furthermore, née Xiè's meals are rich and exquisite,
her clothes elegant and splendid.
Whatever she has left over after serving herself,
she distributes to her subordinates.
