Yet her grandchildren's padded clothes do not warm their bodies,
and their food does not satisfy their hunger.
They are entrusted to the hands of wet nurses,
and allowed to wander the paths of the military camp.
When she encounters those born of her own,
she discards them like dirt.
They are treated like heavily confined prisoners,
and their destitution exceeds that of lowly servants.
Indeed, the imperial plans are far-reaching,
and the northern frontiers will soon be unified.
The Duke's lifespan is uncertain,
and cannot be foretold.
Moreover, my concubines and daughters are weak and delicate,
each presiding over her own household.
The means of protection and restraint,
for humanity, are thus urgent.
That is why I have commanded my sixth son, Xiè, to serve as the Duke's heir,
desiring to rectify and unite the household,
and continue the Duke's lineage.
However, née Xiè treats her closest blood relatives
with abandonment and contempt.
How much more difficult will it be to escape suffering
when combined by righteousness? The problem arises from a small beginning, and the critical moment must be resolved.
She may therefore return to her original family,
and her noble title and rank shall be removed."
Previously, née Xiè's surname had been changed to Shè.
At that time, the young emperor faced difficulties,
and the imperial clan was weak.
In the first year of Yuánhuī (473 CE),
Xiè, aged four, was appointed Military Commissioner, Inspector of military affairs of Yǐngzhōu, Xīyáng and Yìyáng Commanderies of Yùzhōu and Sīzhōu, General of Zhēnglǔ, and Governor of Yǐngzhōu.
Wáng Huàn, a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, was made his Chief Clerk,
taking overall charge of the prefecture and province.
The following year,
the Grand Commandant and Governor of Jiāngzhōu, Prince Xiūfàn of Guìyáng, raised an army and threatened the imperial court.
Xiè dispatched his Staff Officer of the Central Army, Féng Jǐngzǔ, to attack Xúnyáng.
Xiūfàn had left his Staff Officer of the Central Army, Máo Huìlián, and the Provincial Aide, Chéng Hǎnzhī, to defend it,
but they opened the gates and surrendered to Jǐngzǔ.
Xiè's title was advanced to General of Ānxī,
and he was given additional supervision over military affairs in Jiāngzhōu.
The Dowager Princess, née Xiè, birth mother of Chǎng, was reinstated as Dowager Princess of Jìnxī State.
In the fourth year,
Xiè was again promoted to General of Zhènxī,
and granted an imperial band.
When Emperor Shùn ascended the throne,
he was summoned to be Military Commissioner, Grand Administrator of military affairs of Yángzhōu and Nánxúzhōu, General of Fǔjūn, and Governor of Yángzhōu.
Earlier,
the Heir Apparent of Qí had been Xiè's Chief Clerk of Ānxī,
managing the affairs of the prefecture and province.
At this time, he was also summoned to be General of the Left Guard,
and both descended together.
At this juncture, Shěn Yōuzhī, the Governor of Jīngzhōu, raised an army in rebellion.
The Heir Apparent then escorted Xiè to guard Pénchéng in Xúnyáng,
holding the middle reaches of the river,
to provide internal and external support.
After Yōuzhī was pacified,
Xiè returned to the capital.
When the Prince of Qí was made Governor of Nánxúzhōu,
Xiè was relieved of his supervision of Nánxúzhōu,
and advanced to supervise military affairs of Nányùzhōu and Jiāngzhōu.
His title was advanced to General of the Central Army and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and he was transferred to Minister of Education (Sītú).
When Qí received the abdication,
he was relieved of his Sītú position,
and demoted to Marquis of Yīn'ān County,
[一三] with an income of one thousand five hundred households.
He conspired to rebel
and was granted death.
Prince Xiūrén of Shǐ'ān,
was Emperor Wén's twelfth son.
In the twenty-ninth year of Yuánjiā (452 CE),
at the age of ten,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Jiàn'ān,
with an income of two thousand households.
In the third year of Xiàojiàn (456 CE),
he became Secretary-General,
concurrently holding the position of Commandant of Infantry.
Soon after, he was appointed Grand Administrator of military affairs of Nányǎnzhōu and Xúzhōu, General of Guànjūn, and Governor of Nányǎnzhōu.
In the first year of Dàmíng (457 CE),
he entered the court as Attendant at Court,
concurrently holding the position of General of the Right Army.
In the fourth year,
he was sent out as Governor of Xiāngzhōu,
with the additional titles of Palace Attendant,
and General of Píngnán.
In the eighth year,

he was promoted to Military Commissioner, Grand Administrator of military affairs of Jiāngzhōu, Jìnxī and Xīncài Commanderies of Nányùzhōu, and Xīyáng Commandery of Yǐngzhōu, General of Ānnán, and Governor of Jiāngzhōu.
Before he could take office,
he was transferred to Palace Attendant and Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Tàicháng),
but again did not take office.
He then remained General of the Guard,
with his Palace Attendant position unchanged.
In the first year of Yǒngguāng of the Former Deposed Emperor (465 CE),
he was promoted to General of the Leader of the Army,
with his Palace Attendant position unchanged.
In the first year of Jǐnghé (465 CE),

he was again promoted to Military Commissioner, Grand Administrator of military affairs of Yōngzhōu, Liángzhōu, Nánqínzhōu and Běiqínzhōu, General of Ānxī, Commandant for Pacifying the Man, and Governor of Yōngzhōu.
Before he could take up this post,
he was kept as Palace Attendant and General of the Guard,
[一四] and also granted the additional titles of Special Advance, Grand Master of Guanglu of the Left,
and an imperial band.
At that time, the Dì, who had been deposed, was狂悖 kuángbèi and without principle.
He executed many high officials,
and was wary of his paternal uncles.
He imprisoned them all within the palace,
beating and abusing them,
utterly devoid of humanity.
Xiū-rén, along with Tài-zōng and Shān-yáng Wáng Xiū-yòu,
were all large and robust in physique.
The Dì would put them in bamboo cages and weigh them.
As Tài-zōng was especially fat,
he was called
"Zhū Wáng" (Pig King).
Xiū-rén was called
"Shā Wáng" (Killing King),
and Xiū-yòu was called
"Zéi Wáng" (Thief King).
Because the three Wáng were older,
the Dì feared and dreaded them particularly,
so he always kept them close
and did not let them leave his side.
Dōng-hǎi Wáng Huī was generally inferior,
and was called
"Lǘ Wáng" (Donkey King).
Guì-yáng Wáng Xiū-fàn and Bā-líng Wáng Xiū-ruò were younger,
and thus they were able to act more freely.
He once used a wooden trough to hold rice,
put various other foods into it,
and mixed them thoroughly.
He dug a pit in the ground,
filled it with muddy water,
stripped Tài-zōng naked and put him into the pit.
He placed the trough of mixed food in front of him,
and made Tài-zōng eat from the trough with his mouth,
taking pleasure in this spectacle.
His attempts to harm Tài-zōng, Xiū-rén, and Xiū-yòu numbered over ten occasions.
Xiū-rén was resourceful,
and each time he would flatter and humor the Dì with smiles and jokes,
thus managing to postpone his fate.
He often made his attendants sexually assault Yáng Tài-fēi, Xiū-rén's birth mother, in front of Xiū-rén.
The attendants had no choice but to comply.
This even extended to Yòu Wèi Jiāng-jūn Liú Dào-lóng,
who enthusiastically carried out the imperial command,
committing all sorts of disgraceful acts.
At that time, Tíng Wèi Liú Méng's concubine was pregnant.
[一五] As her due month approached,
she was brought into the inner palace,
in the hope that she would give birth to a son,
whom the Dì wished to establish as the Tài-zǐ.
Tài-zōng once disobeyed an imperial command.
The Dì was enraged,
so he stripped him naked,
bound his hands and feet,
and threaded a staff through his bound hands and feet.
He had someone carry him to the Tài-guān,
saying:
"Slaughter this pig today."
Xiū-rén smiled and said to the Dì:
"The pig should not die today."
The Dì asked why.
Xiū-rén said:
"Wait until the Huáng Tài-zǐ is born,
then kill the pig and take its liver and lungs."
The Dì's anger then subsided,
and he said:
"For now, hand him over to the Tíng Wèi."
He was released after one night.
The Dì planned to travel south to Jīng and Xiāng prefectures.
The next morning, he intended to kill all his uncles before departing.
That evening,
Tài-zōng averted the disaster
and killed the Dì in Huá-lín Yuán.
Xiū-rén immediately acclaimed Tài-zōng as emperor
and adopted the demeanor of a subject.
The next morning,
Xiū-rén moved to stay at the Dōng-fǔ.
At that time, Nán-píng and Lú-líng Jìng-xiān and his brothers
had been killed by the Dì who had been deposed.
[一六] Their bodies had not yet been prepared for burial.
Xiū-rén and Xiū-yòu rode together to visit them,
opening the curtains and laughing, with drum music playing back and forth.
People at the time disapproved of this.
Earlier,
the Dì who had been deposed promoted Xiū-rén to Piào-qí Dà-jiāng-jūn, Kāi-fǔ Yí-tóng Sān-sī,
and he retained his position as Cháng-shì.
Before he could accept the appointment,
Tài-zōng issued an edict making him Shǐ-chí-jié, Shì-zhōng, Dū-dū Yáng Nán-xú Èr-zhōu Zhū Jūn-shì, Sī-tú, Shàng-shū Lìng, and Yáng-zhōu Cì-shǐ,
with an additional twenty Jian-jiàn guards,
and fifteen Sān-wàng carriages.
At that time, Liú Dào-lóng was Hù-jūn.
Xiū-rén requested to resign,
saying:
"I cannot be in the same court as this person."
The emperor then granted Dào-lóng death.
Soon, various regions rebelled.
Xiū-rén was appointed Dū-dū Zhēng-tǎo Zhū Jūn-shì,
and his Jian-jiàn guards were increased by thirty.
He advanced to take Hǔ-lán,
then advanced to take Zhě-qí.
He was then appointed Tài-zǐ Tài-fù,
overseeing all armies,
and dealing with matters as appropriate.
The pacification of the middle reaches was due to Xiū-rén's efforts.
When he first set out,
he became sworn brothers with Sū-hóu Shén
to seek divine assistance.
When the matter was settled,
Tài-zōng wrote to Xiū-rén, saying:
"This success was greatly due to the help of brother Sū-hóu."
Xiū-rén's stipend was increased by four thousand households;
he firmly declined,
accepting only one thousand households.
Although the upper reaches were pacified,
Xuē Ān-dū occupied Péng-chéng
and incited the Suǒ-lǔ.
Xiū-rén was again appointed Dū-dū Běi-tǎo Zhū Jūn-shì,
and his stipend was again increased by three thousand households,
which he did not accept.
At that time, Yù-zhōu Cì-shǐ Yīn Yǎn occupied Shòu-yáng,
which had not yet been pacified.
Jìn-píng Wáng Xiū-yòu had previously overseen the Dū-dū Zhēng-tǎo Zhū Jūn-shì.
Xiū-yòu went to govern Jiāng-líng,
and Xiū-rén took his place as Dū-dū Xī-tǎo Zhū Jūn-shì.
In the fifth year of Tài-shǐ,
he was promoted to Dū-dū Yù, Sī Èr-zhōu.
Xiū-rén and Tài-zōng were similar in age
and both loved literature,
and had always been fond friends.
During the reign of the Dì who had been deposed,
they shared dangerous times,
and Tài-zōng relied on Xiū-rén's strategic brilliance.
In the early years of Tài-shǐ,
the four directions rebelled,
and troops reached the vicinity of the capital.
Xiū-rén personally faced arrows and stones,
achieved great merit,
and was entrusted with all government affairs,
holding immense imperial trust.
People from court, countryside, and the four directions
flocked to him.
The emperor gradually became displeased.
Xiū-rén understood his meaning,
and that winter,
he memorialized to resign as Yáng-zhōu Cì-shǐ,
which was granted.
In the sixth year,
he was promoted to Tài-wèi
and concurrently held the position of Sī-tú.
He firmly declined,
but was granted a lacquered carriage and the privilege of wearing swords and shoes at court.
In his later years, Tài-zōng became very suspicious
and increasingly prone to jealousy and harm.
Xiū-rén grew increasingly uneasy.
After Jìn-píng Wáng Xiū-yòu was killed,
his worry and fear became even more acute.
That year,
the emperor's illness worsened,
and he consulted with Yáng Yùn-cháng and others about arrangements after his death,
fearing that his younger brothers were too powerful and the Tài-zǐ too young,
which would lead to future instability.
Yùn-cháng also worried that after the emperor's demise,
Xiū-rén would suddenly assume the position of Zhōu-gōng,
preventing his own faction from wielding power,
so he strongly supported the emperor's plan.
The emperor's illness had once suddenly become very severe,
and everyone inside and outside the palace turned their attention to Xiū-rén.
Clerks and below
all went to the Dōng-fǔ to visit Xiū-rén's trusted confidants,
[一七] to form alliances in advance.
Those who could not leave their posts
were all fearful.
Since the emperor had long harbored this intention,
and now heard of public sentiment leaning towards Xiū-rén,
he summoned Xiū-rén for an audience.
After the meeting, he said:
"You may stay overnight at the Shàng-shū Xià-shěng this evening,
and come early tomorrow."
That night,
he sent someone to deliver medicine,
ordering Xiū-rén to commit suicide.
He was thirty-nine years old at the time.
[一八]
The Emperor had been ill for a long time,
isolated from both inside and outside the palace.
Fearing that public sentiment might vary,
he exerted himself to ride in his chariot and emerge from the Duānmén.
After Liú Xiūrén’s death,
an imperial edict was issued, which read:
“Indeed, the punishment for disloyalty
is truly a general rule.
Knowing his guilt, he brought it upon himself,
actually being somewhat obstinate.
Liú Xiūrén was a close relative by blood
and held a weighty position in the court.
Our friendship and trust in him were especially deep,
and his favor and rank were exceptionally eminent.
Yet he failed to grandly assist in state affairs
and propagate the principles of governance.
Instead, he acted self-assured and
presumptuously bred suspicion and resentment,
heeding the words of petty individuals,
harboring rebellious ambitions within,
concealing his deeds and hiding his tracks,
and feigning ignorance without cause.
As the recent illness worsened,
causing worry and fear inside and outside the palace,
Xiūrén planned to coerce the imperial guards
and plot a rebellion.
We, bending the laws of kinship,
could not bear to enforce the clear law.
We repeatedly issued edicts to admonish and warn him,
and to investigate the root cause of the matter.
Xiūrén, ashamed of the imperial favor and fearing punishment,
hastily took his own life.
Recalling this, we are filled with sorrow and pain,
unable to control our emotions.
We wish to relax the legal code
to express our pity and mourning.
His two sons may be pardoned,
and their noble titles fully retained.
However, the state and the nation face many troubles,
and strife arose from within the highest officials.
Reflecting on the past,
our grief and emotion deepen. ”
The officials then presented a memorial, stating:
“We hear that clear punishments spare no one,
and personal feelings yield to the law's strictures;
the state's code is established,
and its authority is asserted through righteous extermination.
Thus, when Liáng and Zhào were punished,
they stepped out barefoot to confess their faults;
when Láiyán was penalized,
he was made to enter and cause a stir.
Upon careful review, Liú Xiūrén harbored treacherous intentions,
his deeds concealed from Heaven’s light,
and his crafty villainy was hidden,
his true nature exposed to the common people’s ears.
He considered himself a close relative,
having long enjoyed imperial grace and intimacy,
receiving extraordinary rites and special favors,
his expectations exceeding common standards.
Last year, he was granted a battle-axe and sent on a southern expedition,
though he was not originally appointed for his talent.
His march started from Nónghú,
specifically by virtue of his kinship.
He followed the imperial strategies from above,
and relied on the efforts of the multitude below.
He happened to benefit from a prosperous era,
and secretly attached himself to accomplished deeds.
Yet he frequently claimed imperial credit
and boasted excessively.
Now that the sagely and enlightened Emperor governs the realm
and personally oversees all affairs,
all offices have their regulations,
and officials do not overstep their bounds.
However, Xiūrén, proud of his achievements and relying on his noble status,
believed he should control all court power.
Thus, he presumptuously bred suspicion and difficulty,
and deeply mistrusted those outside his circle.
The former Sīkōng, Jìnpíng Cì Wáng Liú Xiūyòu,
was without commendable conduct in his youth,
and grew more greedy and cruel in adulthood.
When he held office in Shǎnxī and Jīngzhōu,
his venom spread throughout Xīxià,
the registered households lamented and scattered,
the cities became desolate and empty.
The imperial benevolence was broad and encompassing,
and the proper legal code had not yet been made clear.
He frequently discussed his transgressions with Xiūrén,
and their conversation was so intimate
that it was not suitable to be widely spread.
So they adorned their intentions
and instead incited each other.
Xiūyòu, knowing Xiūrén held a high position in the court
and enjoyed superior trust and favor,
believed he could certainly provide strong support for himself,
and thus they formed a deep faction.
Xiūyòu then presented gold and offered treasures,
catering to his expressions and intentions.
When they met in private,
they would invariably discuss court politics.
Hence, there was no day they did not go out together,
and no time they did not lodge together.
Their revelry gathered many,
and their secret talks were tranquil.
Xiūrén harbored treachery and incited confusion,
being skilled in calculation.
He persuaded Xiūyòu to outwardly adopt a method of specialized caution,
while secretly carrying out a greedy and deceitful heart,
believing that the court would not notice,
and people would not understand.
Xiūyòu then accumulated outward resentment and fear,
while harboring sinister intentions within.
Once he gained encouragement and incitement,
his wickedness grew even more rampant.
He conspired with Xiūrén in treachery,
secretly watching for opportunities,
planning to create conflict and change,
and intending to unleash his cunning and viciousness.
Xiūyòu’s sudden demise
However, Xíng, the Concubine Dowager of the Jìnpíng Kingdom,
could not feel remorse for her son’s evil deeds,
nor appreciate the Emperor’s special grace.
Instead, she harbored rebellious thoughts and practiced witchcraft and curses.
Xiūrén, taking advantage of the Emperor’s ill health,
presumptuously plotted rebellion and treachery.
Deviating from the Dao and reversing the norm,
nothing could be more extreme.
Even if he were executed and exposed in the market,
it would barely fulfill the state’s punishment.
Yet, before the net of the law could be cast,
he took his own life.
Heaven’s benevolence is compassionate and profound,
reducing punishment and upholding grace,
granting full preservation to his two sons
and their noble titles.
This is truly a grand and expansive virtue,
surpassing all of ancient and modern times.
However, it is not the way to abandon evil and let in strife,
or to deter and frighten rebellious ministers.
We, your ministers, have discussed and concluded
that it is fitting to posthumously demote Xiūrén to a commoner,
sever his family registration,
and relocate all his existing sons to distant commanderies.
Xiūyòu’s treacherous plot was only just revealed,
and he should also be demoted and dismissed.
The penalty of relocation and deprivation
should follow the old standard.
Xíng should be arrested and sent to prison,
to be thoroughly interrogated according to the law. ”
The imperial edict stated:
“Xíng is a foolish woman,
not worthy of consideration.
Xiūrén, knowing his fault, brought it upon himself,
and our feelings for him carry lingering sadness.
He may be specially demoted to Shǐ’ān Xiàn Wáng,
with an enfeoffment of a thousand households.
Furthermore, the exile of Bóróng and others is suspended,
and they are permitted to inherit their noble titles.
Bóyóu previously succeeded to the Jiāngxià Kingdom,
let him return to his original place,
and be granted the title of Xiānghóu. ”
After the Emperor killed Xiūrén,
he feared public alarm.
He issued an edict to all regional commanders and high officials, saying: “Regarding Xiūrén’s demise,
you may not fully know the details.
The beginning and end of the matter
are now laid out for you.
Xiūyòu’s greed and recklessness were not proper governance,
and were intolerable by the legal system.
In the past, Liáng Xiàowáng of Hàn and Huáinán Lìwáng committed no other great offenses,
merely overstepping the Hàn system
and that was all.
Moreover, Xiūyòu devoured and plundered,
acting like a plague of locusts in several western prefectures,
his taking and giving were despicable and cruel,
devoid of human sentiment.
We repeatedly received memorials from Wáng Jǐngwén, Chǔ Yuān, Shěn Yōuzhī
and others,
detailing his crimes,
which became increasingly intolerable.
We valued our fraternal bond deeply,
and did not wish to bring him to justice.
Furthermore, we always regretted the thin fraternal affection during the Dàmíng era,
and personally saw Xiūyòu’s suffering.
Only when he began to find peace
did we become even more unwilling to question him.
Thus, we reassigned him to Xúzhōu,
hoping that being closer to the imperial court
would surely enable him to mend his ways
and reform.
However, upon his appointment to Xúzhōu,
before he could even take up the post,
he immediately stirred up countless troubles,
and his tyranny and corruption worsened.
Since he was always a pest to the people,
he could no longer be fully preserved.
Xiūrén’s character was rough
possessed knowledge and insight,
and also served as chancellor.
Moreover, my affection for him and his brothers was
exceptionally close.
I often discussed Xiūyòu’s misdeeds with Xiūrén.
Xiūyòu, knowing
Xiūrén was close to me,
must have believed Xiūrén would know my intentions,
and also said that Xiūrén’s words and suggestions
could be beneficial or detrimental.
So, he gave him much wealth and bribes,
deeply entangling himself with him.
They would even sleep
in the same bed,
and travel in the same carriage.
Xiūrén’s nature was soft,
easily swayed,
and thus they became very intimate,
like one family.
My secret words were
immediately divulged.
I
and Xiūrén,
from a young age, had an extraordinary bond.
I trusted him with an open heart,
never entertaining any doubt.
Even so, I still worried that during quiet moments,
things might be overheard unintentionally.
Recently,
I expressed my feelings to Xiūyòu,
giving strict admonitions,
and Xiūyòu no longer harbored suspicions.
After Xiūyòu’s death,
I questioned those around him, both inside and outside,
about the situation,
and then
learned how the words had leaked and the full details.
For days, I was filled with remorse,
my spirit utterly withered.
Xiūrén also told Xiūyòu:
“You just need to be obsequious,
and this method alone will be enough to
secure your position.
I have always adhered to this for my family,
and have quite often benefited from it.
Just try it,
and see if it works.”
Xiūyòu followed this advice,
and consequently made many offerings and presentations.
His words
were often contrary to the truth,
and his accumulated wickedness was unforgivable.
From the moment Xiūyòu died,
Xiūrén was fully aware of the details.
As Xiūrén was innocent of any wrongdoing,
the ruler and the chancellor were originally as one body,
and my intentions
had
never been divided.
Xiūyòu was greedy and foolish,
hated by all under heaven,
and his demise was ultimately
for the removal of a scourge from the people.
There were not many other brothers left,
so I should have thought of commiseration rather than discord,
and
grown even closer and more trusting.
Xiūyòu, throughout his life,
was arrogant and lawless.
I worried that Xiūrén going to mourn would
lead to misfortune.
Furthermore, I myself had intended to go and mourn that day,
but decided
not to go late in the day.
So, as a convenience,
I summoned him into the palace.
But when Xiūrén received my summons,
he was greatly alarmed and suspicious,
and went to take leave of Empress Dowager Yáng,
his expression
and demeanor
being very different from usual.
Upon his arrival at the palace,
Empress Dowager Yáng suddenly sent her eunuch attendants to repeatedly come and inquire.
From this day, suspicion and fear arose,
yet my trust
initially
did not perceive it.
After Xiūyòu’s death,
I visited Xiūrén’s residence twice,
eating and drinking the whole day,
entering his inner chambers without any suspicion or precaution.
Xiūrén, however, felt suspicion and fear.
One day,
in the spring, I had many appointments to shoot pheasants.
Whenever Xiūrén was at leisure,
he would often go to the pheasant hunting ground,
or was commanded by an envoy to accompany my palanquin.
On days when I did not go,
he was often
not seen.
Every night,
Xiūrén would tell his attendants:
“I have
made it through another day.”
And when he saw his courtesans and concubines in his room,
he would say:
“When I die,
I don’t know if I’ll see you morning or evening.
If I suddenly die and become a ghost,
I won’t take you with me.
Taking you would only cause trouble.”
When Xiūyòu died,
it was already late afternoon.
I was
pheasant hunting,
and had just come out of the hunting ground.
Xiūrén was among the cavalry on my right,
prostrate in the wilderness.
I sent someone to summon him,
but he claimed:
“I have a stomach ache
and cannot ride a horse.”
At that time,
the carriages of the various princes were all parked near the Zhūquè Gate.
As it was already dark,
there was no time to call a carriage from afar.
My own light chariot was nearby, near the Límén Gate.
I ordered it to be summoned,
lowered the oilcloth canopy
and curtains,
intending to carry him in it.
I had long known that he suffered from cold ailments,
and hearing of his stomach ache,
I knew it must be from cold.
So I ordered the imperial physician to go to the palace to send a supply of high-grade sorghum
ginger drink to bestow upon him.
When Xiūrén received the drink,
he was suddenly greatly alarmed,
telling his attendants:
“Today is ruined.”
His attendants replied:
“This drink has the imperial physician’s name
inscribed on it.”
Xiūrén then ordered his attendants to drink it first,
still not quite believing,
and then reluctantly took a sip,
only taking about one mouthful.
He harbored groundless suspicions and animosity;
everything was
like this.
He used to visit Empress Dowager Yáng every five or ten days.
After Xiūyòu’s death,
whenever I summoned him,
he would first go to Empress Dowager Yáng to inquire,
as if to ascertain her disposition.
Xiūrén had always managed the documents concerning the establishment of the enfeoffed state.
In the second month,
Shǐ Chéngzǔ brought documents to present to him,
but he suddenly told Chéngzǔ:
“I have already completed these,
why bother bringing them?”
My heart was as open as before,
no longer seeing him as trustworthy,
having become uneasy,
and greatly suspicious and fearful.
Based on reason,
it was impossible
for him to have good intentions anymore.
Xiūrén had previously participated in the southern expedition,
and was well acquainted with the palace guards and commanders, having worked closely with them.
They were scattered both inside and outside.
On ordinary days, when he entered or exited,
passing
through the corridors,
he would not exchange words with the commanders he knew.
However, when I had been unwell for many days previously,
and Xiūrén entered and exited the palace,
all the chief commanders of the guards who
knew him
without exception greeted him with kind expressions and showed him great solicitude.
At that time, I was very ill,
and did not wish to see outsiders.
Rumors spread widely,
each saying the illness was more severe than the last.
Xiūrén,
wishing to learn about my condition
through convenient means,
repeatedly sent the Taoist monk Tándù and Láo Yànquǎn to seek audiences,
to stealthily observe my daily life.
However, their petitions
were all not urgent matters.
My intention was also
不 to doubt.
My relationship with Xiū Rén,
was indeed different due to our close bond.
Since our youth,
we always accompanied each other.
Our inclinations and great interests
were often the same.
In times of difficulty
and misfortune,
we always shared weal and woe.
Xiū Rén led the southern expedition as Dū Tǒng;
since he had achieved meritorious deeds,
the extent of my feelings
for him was boundless.
However, for Xiū Rén regarding me,
his aspirations
were not light,
and ignorant petty individuals
often harbored disloyal intentions.
Once suspicion and disloyalty arose,
I could no longer feel secure.
The cause of misfortune and calamity
is always something one does not comprehend.
As for his intentions
and inclinations,
no one can fathom them.
When things reached an unavoidable point,
I repeatedly pondered and reflected,
and could not but make the recent disposition.
Indeed, regarding brotherly affection,
it is impossible not to have varying degrees of attachment.
Though I grieved and mourned
Xiū Yòu’s death,
I could still rationalize and dismiss it;
but when Xiū Rén perished,
my sorrow and compassion were especially profound.
A thousand thoughts could not be suppressed,
and every word spoken
wounded my heart.
The minute details of the matter
could not all be extensively included in the imperial edict,
fearing that people might not immediately understand,
and also wishing to spare his sons
and not pursue the law to its extreme.
The language of the edict
had to state that there was a military conspiracy,
but this was not the actual truth.
Therefore, I am informing Your Lordship.
The Emperor had always been close to Xiū Rén,
but as for harming him,
he worried about the insecurity of his descendants.
After Xiū Rén died,
his grief and sorrow were extreme.
He said to others:
"Jiàn’ān and I were neighbors
in our youth
and often associated together.
During the time of Jǐnghé and Tàishǐ,
his merits and sincerity were truly significant.
Due to pressing circumstances and calculations,
I had no choice but to eliminate him.
The pain of this thought is so great
that I cannot control myself.
Now there is one thing I cannot discuss with the feudal lords;
the joy and comfort
of life are now completely gone."
Thereupon, he wept uncontrollably.
His son Bó Róng,
was born to Consort Yīn.
Consort Yīn
was the daughter of Yīn Chōng, the Administrator of Wúxīng.
Zǔ Fān of Fànyáng had medical skills
and was also handsome.
When Consort Yīn was ill,
Fān entered to feel her pulse,
she took a liking to him,
and they began an affair.
When the matter was exposed,
she was sent back home and given death.
Bó Róng successively served as the Inspector of Nányùzhōu,
Administrator of the two commanderies of Lángyá and Línhuái,
General Níngshuò,
and Inspector of Guǎngzhōū,
but did not assume the office.
He was deposed and exiled to Dānyángxiàn.
Later, in the first year of Yuánhuī of the Deposed Emperor,
he returned to the capital,
and inherited the title of Prince of Shǐxīng.
[二０] His younger brother Bó Yóu,
was initially adopted by the Prince Mǐn of Jiāngxià, Bó Qín,
and enfeoffed as Prince of Jiāngxià,
with a fief of two thousand households.
After Xiū Rén's death, he returned to his original family
and was exiled to Dānyángxiàn along with Bó Róng.
Later, in the first year of Yuánhuī of the Deposed Emperor,
he was granted the title of Marquis of Dūxiāng.
When Prince Jiànpíng Jǐngsù rebelled,
Yáng Yùncháng and others, fearing the imperial clan,
issued an edict to bestow death upon Bó Róng and others.
Bó Róng was nineteen at the time,
and Bó Yóu was eleven.
Prince Jìnpíng Lál Xiū Yòu,
was the thirteenth son of Emperor Wén.
In the second year of Xiàojiàn,
[二一] at the age of eleven,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Shānyáng,
with a fief of two thousand households.
In the first year of Dàmíng,
he became Sànqí Chángshì,
leading the Chief of Chángshuǐ Garrison,
and soon after was promoted to Inspector of Dōngyángzhōu.
Before he could take office,
he was transferred to Inspector of Xiāngzhōu,
and given the additional title of General Zhēnglǔ.
In the fourth year,
he returned to become Mìshūjiān,
leading the General of the Right Army,
and his fief was increased by a thousand households.
He was promoted to Shìzhōng,
then to General of the Left Central Guard,
Dūguān Shàngshū,
and again to Mìshūjiān,
leading the General Xiāoqí.
He was then sent out as Commissioner with Credentials, Area Commander of the Military Affairs of Yùzhōu, Sīzhōu, and the Liáng Commandery of Nányùzhōu, General of the Right, and Inspector of Yùzhōu.
In the first year of Jǐnghé,
he entered the court,
and was promoted to Grand General Zhènxī.
He was then transferred to Sànqí Chángshì, Grand General Zhènjūn, and granted the privilege of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
When Emperor Tàizōng quelled the rebellion,

he made him Commissioner with Credentials, Area Commander of the Military Affairs of the eight states of Jīngzhōu, Xiāngzhōu, Yōngzhōu, Yìzhōu, Liángzhōu, Níngzhōu, Northern Qín, and Southern Qín, Grand General Piàojí, and Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
with Kāifǔ and Chángshì as before.
He was then changed to Area Commander of the Military Affairs of the five states of Jiāngzhōu, Yǐngzhōu, Yōngzhōu, and Xiāngzhōu, and Inspector of Jiāngzhōu,
[二二] then changed to Area Commander of the Military Affairs of Jiāngnán, Yùzhōu, and Sīzhōu, and Inspector of Nányùzhōu,
and then changed to Area Commander of the Military Affairs of Yùzhōu, Jiāngzhōu, and Sīzhōu, and Inspector of Yùzhōu.
At that time, Yīn Yǎn, the Inspector of Yùzhōu, rebelled by holding Shòuyáng.
Xiū Yòu was sent to garrison Lìyáng,
overseeing Liú Miǎn and others in suppressing Yǎn.
Before Yǎn was pacified,
Miǎn built a long circumvallation to besiege him.

Xiū Yòu was again transferred to Area Commander of the Military Affairs of the eight states of Jīngzhōu, Xiāngzhōu, Yōngzhōu, Yìzhōu, Liángzhōu, Níngzhōu, Northern Qín, and Southern Qín, and Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
with Credentials, Chángshì, General, and Kāifǔ remaining as before.
His enfeoffment was increased by two thousand households,
and he received five hundred households.
Due to the desolation of Shānyáng,
he was re-enfeoffed as Prince of Jìnpíng.
Xiū Yòu had always lacked talent,
was arrogant and self-willed.
During the Dàmíng era,
he was still young
and not yet able to act independently.
By this time, he was greedy and licentious,
fond of wealth and women.
In Jīngzhōu,
he extorted the local population
and amassed much wealth.
He imposed a tax of one hundred short coins on the people,
and when land was registered,
he demanded one hú of polished white rice,
requiring all grains to be perfectly white.
If any were broken or incomplete,
they were all rejected.
People bought this rice on the market
at one hundred per shēng.
At the time of collection, he would again refuse the rice,
assess its value, and demand money instead.
All his methods of seeking profit
were like this,
causing the common people to cry out in distress,
no longer able to endure their lives.
In the sixth year of Tàishǐ,
he was summoned to become Area Commander of the Military Affairs of the six states of Nánxúzhōu, Nányǎnzhōu, Xúzhōu, Yǎnzhōu, Qīngzhōu, and Jìzhōu, and Inspector of Nánxúzhōu,
with the additional title of Shìzhōng,
and Credentials and General as before.
The Emperor, considering Xiū Yòu greedy and cruel and unfit to govern the people,
kept him in the capital
and sent a senior aide to manage the affairs of the prefecture and state.
Xiūyòu 休祐 was stubborn, rebellious, strong, and arrogant.
He offended the emperor multiple times.
When he was in Jīngzhōu 荊州,
his attendants Yuàn Jǐngdá 苑景達 were skilled at playing the zither.
〔二三〕The emperor summoned them,
but Xiūyòu 休祐 detained them and did not send them.
The emperor was enraged
and reprimanded him, saying:
"How can you be so stubborn and rebellious,
is this the conduct of a subordinate!"
His accumulated resentment could not be appeased.
Moreover, fearing that Xiūyòu 休祐 would be difficult to control in the future,
he wished to find an opportune moment to eliminate him.
In the second month of the seventh year,
the imperial carriage went to Yánshān 巖山 to hunt pheasants.
One pheasant refused to enter the hunting ground.
As dusk approached and it was time to return,
the emperor ordered Xiūyòu 休祐 to shoot it.
He said:
"If you don't get the pheasant,
do not return."
Xiūyòu 休祐 was then accompanying the emperor within the yellow banner guards.
His attendants were all behind the ranks.
Xiūyòu 休祐 then galloped away,
and the emperor sent several attendants to follow him.
When the emperor returned,
the vanguard cleared the way,
and Xiūyòu's 休祐's people were all dispersed,
no longer able to reunite.
The emperor then dispatched Shòu Jìzhī 壽寂之 and other generals to pursue him.
As it was already getting dark,
they caught up with Xiūyòu 休祐
and forced him to fall from his horse.
Xiūyòu 休祐 was always brave, strong, and powerful.
He brandished his fists, striking left and right,
and no one could get close.
One person then pulled him from behind by his private parts,
and he fell to the ground.
They immediately ganged up and beat him to death.
Someone was then sent to ride back and report to the emperor,
shouting along the way:
"The Cavalry General (Piàojì 驃騎) has fallen from his horse!"
The emperor said:
"The Cavalry General (Piàojì 驃騎) is large in stature,
it's quite difficult for him to fall from a horse."
He immediately sent imperial physicians one after another.
A short while later,
Xiūyòu's 休祐's attendants arrived,
reporting that he had long been dead.
They removed the carriage wheels
and carried his body back to his residence.
He was twenty-seven years old at the time.
He was posthumously granted the title of Sīkōng 司空,
and his previous titles of Chíjí 持節, Shìzhōng 侍中, Dūdū 都督, and Cìshǐ 刺史 remained.
He was granted twenty ceremonial swordsmen
and one triple-mounted carriage.
At that time, Bālíng Wáng Xiūrúo 巴陵王休若 was in Jiānglíng 江陵.
On that very day, a messenger was dispatched to inform Xiūrúo 休若, saying:
"I was hunting pheasants with the Cavalry General (Piàojì 驃騎) on Nánshān 南山.
The Cavalry General's (Piàojì 驃騎's) horse was startled
and collided with the horse of Zhígé Xià Wénxiù 直閣夏文秀.
Wénxiù 文秀 fell to the ground.
The Cavalry General (Piàojì 驃騎) lost his reins,
and his startled horse
collided with a pine tree, causing him to fall to the ground.
He fell into a ravine
and was temporarily unconscious,
not recognizing anyone.
Therefore, I hastened to inform you, my brother."
In the fifth month of that year,
Xiūyòu 休祐 was posthumously stripped of his rank and made a commoner.
His eldest son, Shìhuì 士薈,
died young.
His second son, Xuānyì 宣翊, became the heir apparent (Shìzi 世子),
and was appointed General of Pacifying the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn 寧朔將軍) and Governor of Xiāngzhōu 湘州.
Before he could take office,
he was dismissed and deposed.
His third son, Shìhóng 士弘,
succeeded Póyáng Āi Wáng Xiūyè 鄱陽哀王休業,
inherited the title,
but was deposed and returned to his original status.
His fourth son, Xuānyàn 宣彥,
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yuánfēng Xiàn 原豐縣,
and appointed General of Pacifying the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn 寧朔將軍) and Administrator of Péngchéng 彭城.
Before he could take office,
he was dismissed and deposed.
His fifth son, Xuānliàng 宣諒.
His sixth son, Xuānyào 宣曜,
was adopted to succeed Nánpíng Mù Wáng Shuò 南平穆王鑠,
but was deposed and returned to his original status.
His seventh son, Xuānjǐng 宣景.
His eighth son, Xuānfàn 宣梵.
His ninth son, Xuānjué 宣覺.
His tenth son, Xuānshòu 宣受.
His eleventh son, Xuānzé 宣則.
His twelfth son, Xuānzhí 宣直.
His thirteenth son, Xuānjì 宣季.
In total, he had thirteen sons,
all of whom were exiled to Jìnpíng Jùn 晉平郡.
Tàizōng 太宗 soon fell ill
and saw Xiūyòu 休祐 as a vengeful spirit.
He then sent the former Central Secretariat Drafter (Zhōngshū Shèrén 中書舍人) Liú Xiū 劉休 to Jìnpíng 晉平 to comfort Xuānyì 宣翊 and others.
The emperor subsequently died.
In the first year of Yuánhuī 元徽 of the Deposed Emperor (Hòufèi Dì 後廢帝),
Xuānyì 宣翊 and others were permitted to return to the capital.
In the third year of Shēngmíng 昇明 of Shùndì 順帝,
they plotted rebellion
and were all granted death.
Póyáng Āi Wáng Xiūyè 鄱陽哀王休業 was
the fifteenth son of Wéndì 文帝.
In the second year of Xiàojiàn 孝建,
at the age of eleven,
he was enfeoffed as King of Póyáng 鄱陽,
with an income of two thousand households.
In the third year,
he died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng 太常).
In the sixth year of Dàmíng 大明,
Shānyáng Wáng Xiūyòu's 山陽王休祐's second son, Shìhóng 士弘, was appointed to succeed him.
He was later deposed and returned to his original status,
and the kingdom was abolished.
Línqìng Chōng Wáng Xiūqiàn 臨慶沖王休倩 was
the sixteenth son of Wéndì 文帝.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn 孝建,
at the age of nine,
he became gravely ill
and was enfeoffed as King of Dōngpíng 東平,
with an income of two thousand households.
Before he could take office,
he died.
In the seventh year of Dàmíng 大明,
the twenty-seventh imperial son, Zǐsì 子嗣, was established as King of Dōngpíng 東平,
succeeding Xiūqiàn 休倩.
In the second year of Tàishǐ 泰始 of Tàizōng 太宗, he was returned to his original status,
and the kingdom was cut off.
In the sixth year,
the fifth imperial son, Zhìjǐng 智井, was made King of Dōngpíng 東平,
succeeding Xiūqiàn 休倩,
but he died before taking office.
In that same year,
Xiūqiàn 休倩 was posthumously renamed King of Línqìng 臨慶,
and Línqìng Guó 臨慶國 was established from Línhè Jùn 臨賀郡.
The eighth imperial son, Jī 躋, was established as King of Línqìng 臨慶,
with an income of two thousand households,
succeeding Xiūqiàn 休倩.
The following year,
he returned to his original state.
Xiūqiàn 休倩 was
favored by Tàizǔ 太祖.
Therefore, successors to his line were repeatedly appointed.
Xīnyě Huái Wáng Yífù 新野懷王夷父 was
the seventeenth son of Wéndì 文帝.
In the twenty-ninth year of Yuánjiā 元嘉,
he died,
at the age of six.
In the fifth year of Tàishǐ 泰始 of Tàizōng 太宗, he was posthumously granted titles and a posthumous name.
Bālíng Āi Wáng Xiūrúo 巴陵哀王休若 was
the nineteenth son of Wéndì 文帝.
In the third year of Xiàojiàn 孝建,
at the age of nine,
he was enfeoffed as King of Bālíng 巴陵,
with an income of two thousand households.
In the second year of Dàmíng 大明,
he was appointed General Who Smashes the Army (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn 冠軍將軍) and Administrator of the two commanderies of Southern Lángxié 南琅邪 and Línhuái 臨淮.
He was transferred to be Administrator of the two commanderies of Southern Péngchéng 南彭城 and Xiàpī 下邳,
his general title remaining as before.
In the fourth year,
he was sent out as Commissioner with Imperial Credentials (Shǐ Chíjí 使持節), Regional Inspector of Xúzhōu 敘州, All Military Affairs (Dūdū Xúzhōu Zhū Jūnfàngshǐ 都督徐州諸軍事), and Governor of Xúzhōu 敘州.
〔二四〕His general title remained as before.
He was additionally made Inspector of Liángjùn 梁郡 in Yùzhōu 豫州,
and his income was increased by one thousand households.
The following year,
he was recalled to serve as Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍), Left Palace Assistant (Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiāng 左中郎將), and Administrator of Wúxīng 吳興.
〔二五〕He was again recalled to serve as Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍) and Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng 太常).
Before he could take office,
in the first year of Yǒngguāng 永光 of the Former Deposed Emperor (Qiánfèi Dì 前廢帝),
he was promoted to Left Guard General (Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn 左衞將軍).
In the first year of Tàishǐ 泰始 of Tàizōng 太宗,
he was promoted to Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍) and Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng 中書令),
also holding the post of Commandant of the Guards (Wèiwèi 衞尉).
Before he could take office,
he was again made Left Guard General (Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn 左衞將軍),
his positions as Palace Attendant (Chángshì 常侍) and Commandant of the Guards (Wèiwèi 衞尉) remaining as before.
Again, before he could take office,

he was sent out as Commissioner with Imperial Credentials (Shǐ Chíjí 使持節), Regional Inspector of the military affairs of five commanderies, Kuàijī 會稽, Dōngyáng 東陽, Yǒngjiā 永嘉, Línhǎi 臨海, and Xīn'ān 新安 (Dūdū Kuàijī Dōngyáng Yǒngjiā Línhǎi Xīn'ān Wǔjùn Zhū Jūnfàngshǐ 都督會稽東陽永嘉臨海新安五郡諸軍事), General Who Guards the East (Āndōng Jiāngjūn 安東將軍), and Administrator of Kuàijī 會稽,
leading troops to conquer the east.
He was further made Inspector of the three commanderies of Wú 吳, Wúxīng 吳興, and Jìnlíng 晉陵.
Soon after, he was granted the additional title of Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍),
promoted to the title of Guard General (Wèi Jiāngjūn 衞將軍),
and granted a set of drums and pipes.
He was further made Inspector of the military affairs of Jìn'ān 晉安 and two other commanderies.
Two years later,

he was transferred to be All Military Affairs of the four prefectures of Yōng, Liáng, Nán Qín, and Běi Qín, and the two commanderies of Jìnglíng and Suí in Yǐng Prefecture, as well as Níngmán Xiàowèi and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
His enfeoffment was increased by two thousand households,
and he received three hundred households.
Previously, while in Kuàijī,
the Lùshì Cānjūn, Xiè Shěn of Chén Commandery, had flattered Xiūruò,
and taken many bribes.
At that time, due to a state of alert both inside and outside the capital,
everyone generally wore kùzhě.
Shěn, while observing mourning for his mother,
was called into service,
yet engaged in music and heavy drinking,
no different from a person in a festive state.
His attire being indistinguishable,
no one knew Shěn was in mourning.
When he once claimed to be an orphan,
the crowd was greatly astonished.
Xiūruò was implicated for his intimate and corrupt association with Shěn,
which led to illicit private dealings,
and his title was demoted to Zhèn Xī Jiāngjūn.
He was later promoted to Wèi Jiāngjūn.
Diǎnqiān Xià Bǎoqī had been disrespectful to Xiūruò,
and was imprisoned.
Xiūruò petitioned Tàizōng to have him killed,
His positions as Chíjíe, Chángshì, and Jiāngjūn remained as before.
he, without waiting for a reply to his petition,
executed him in prison.
The decree indeed came back ordering imprisonment and deportation,
but Bǎoqī was already dead.
The Emperor was greatly angered,
and wrote to Xiūruò, saying:
"During the Xiàojiàn and Dàmíng eras,
would you have dared to do this?"
Xiūruò's mother was given three hundred strokes with a cane.
His title was demoted to Zuǒ Jiāngjūn,
and his appointment as Shǐ Chíjíe Dūdū was reduced to Jiān,
acting as Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Shǐ Níngmán Xiàowèi.
His enfeoffment was reduced by five hundred households.
Four years later,
he was transferred to be Shǐ Chíjíe, Dūdū of All Military Affairs of Xiāng Prefecture, and acting Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
his generalship remaining as before.
when Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ, Jìnpíng Wáng Xiūyòu, entered the capital,
Xiūruò was appointed to oversee Jīng Prefecture,
and was promoted to Zhēng Nán Jiāngjūn and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He was then made Dūdū of All Military Affairs of the eight prefectures of Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, Yì, Liáng, Níng, Nán Qín, and Běi Qín, Zhēng Xī Jiāngjūn, and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
his Chíjíe remaining as before.
Soon after, he was granted Sànqí Chángshì,
and then promoted to Zhēng Xī Dàjiāngjūn and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
In the seventh year,
Jìnpíng Wáng Xiūyòu was killed,
and Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén fell under suspicion.
Rumors circulated in the capital that Xiūruò had signs of extreme nobility.
Tàizōng informed him of these rumors,
and Xiūruò was deeply worried and fearful.
It happened that he was summoned
to replace Xiūyòu as Dūdū of All Military Affairs of the six prefectures of Nán Xú, Nán Yǎn, Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, and Jì, Zhēng Běi Dàjiāngjūn, and Nán Xúzhōu Cìshǐ,
his Chíjíe, Chángshì, and Kāifǔ remaining as before.
Xiūruò's trusted generals and assistants all believed that returning to court would certainly bring great disaster.
Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Wáng Jìngxiān of Jīngzhào strongly argued against entering the capital,
and advised him to hold Jīngchǔ and resist the imperial court.
Xiūruò pretended to agree.
After Jìngxiān left,
he was apprehended and imprisoned.
A swift messenger was dispatched to inform Tàizōng,
and Jìngxiān was executed for his offense.
When Xiūruò arrived at Jīngkǒu,
Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén had also been killed,
which further intensified his apprehension.
The Emperor, considering Xiūruò's gentle nature
and his ability to harmonize popular sentiment,
feared that he might overthrow the young ruler in the future,
and wished to send an envoy to kill him.
Fearing that the order would not be obeyed,
and summoning him to court might arouse suspicion and alarm,

he therefore falsely transferred Xiūruò to be Dūdū of All Military Affairs of Jiāng, Yǐng, Sī, Guǎng, Jiāo, and the four commanderies of Xīyáng, Xīncài, Jìnxī, and Shǐxīng in Yù and Xiāng Prefectures, Chējì Dàjiāngjūn, and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
his Chíjíe, Chángshì, and Kāifǔ remaining as before.
He was summoned back to the capital for appointment,
and the Emperor wrote a cordial personal letter,
instructing him to arrive by the seventh day of the seventh month.
He was then granted death at his residence
at the age of twenty-four.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng and Sīkōng,
his Chíjíe, Dūdū, and Cìshǐ remaining as before.
He was given twenty guards with ceremonial swords,
and one carriage with three ornamental flags.
After Xiūruò's death,
the Emperor wrote to Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn, saying: "There is an outside master,
whose surname is Xú and given name Shàozhī.
He appears to suffer from a form of madness,
and claims to be sent by a 'Túbù Láng.'
In the third month of last year,
he suddenly said:
'The gods say
that Bālíng Wáng should become the Son of Heaven.
You should let Bālíng Wáng know this secretly.'
Thereupon, the master sought out Xiūruò's attendants
but could not find them.
A scribe in the Eastern Palace
whose surname is Hé knew him
and frequently came and went.
The master understood divine messages,
and the Eastern Palace scribe fully conveyed the divine message.
The Eastern Palace scribe replied:
'I know an attendant
of Bālíng.
I will tell him for you.'
A few days later,
the Eastern Palace scribe returned and told the master:
'I have already spoken to Bālíng's attendant for you,
and the message was delivered to Bālíng.
Bālíng knows everything
and says, "Do not speak, just listen."'
Also, recently, the historians presented astrological observations,
which somewhat indicated that Xiūruò was destined to have extraordinary aspirations.
The ways of the divine are obscure,
so
they cannot be fully trusted.
However, when compared over time,
there is indeed some resemblance.
Furthermore, among the common people,
since the Dàmíng era, there has been
a ballad of 'Ruò hǎo,'
which has not
ceased to this day.
When imperial edicts containing numerous phrases
were all matched with beautiful words and deeds,
all those unruly individuals
unanimously said it must be Xiūruò.
Xiūruò already knew that there were
strange rumors on the streets
and the 'Ruò hǎo'
ballad
in the villages.
While in the west, he was already unusually fearful,
which led Wáng Jìngxiān to utter such wild words.
Recently, Xiūyòu and Xiūrén were executed,
and Xiūruò
became even more insecure.
Moreover, many of his attendants were unsuitable and guilty individuals,
who used the street rumors to stir him up,
and collectively chanted:
'The hearts
of the myriad people
belong to Xiūruò,'
thus instigating his ambitions.
Upon reviewing Xiūruò's past actions and intentions,
there is indeed much to suspect.
Liú Liàng asked Gāo Cìzǔ, 'You should know this person;
you should serve Xiūruò.'
When Xiūruò was
in the east, he indulged his subordinates without any proper order.
When he returned to court and was demoted,
his rank and title slightly reduced.
Cìzǔ, sent back by Liàng,
passed by to inquire about him.
Xiūruò wept profusely
and said to Cìzǔ:
'My
journey to the east was a great accomplishment,
but in the commandery, I suffered setbacks due to minor figures,
and was greatly demoted.
I am truly indignant and resentful.
I do not understand why Liú Fǔguó did not act.'
Cìzǔ
replied:
'Liú Fǔguó has received the grace of the court's benevolence;
how could such a thing be possible?'
This implies that he already harbored extraordinary intentions.
I have allowed my imperial kinsmen to reside in their fiefs
simply
to enjoy their leisure,
not for military matters.
Yet Xiūruò, while in the west,
widely recruited skilled archers and cavalrymen,
without ever reporting it.
Also, Lì Dàomíng and others,
who were once personally
bandits,
and whose crimes warranted ten thousand deaths,
were greatly trusted and favored by Xiūruò when he arrived in the west.
He even secretly brought them along without informing the capital.
I know you might think, "How did Xiūruò manage things based on circumstances?"
But since his true intentions are no longer ascertainable,
when he returned to court and was at his residence, I wrote a letter,
internally interrogating and reprimanding him on every matter.
He was allowed to secretly take his own life,
making it appear as if he died of a sudden illness,
so that his title and position, and all his sons, could be preserved.
Since Xiūruò is your younger brother,
and to prevent his wolfish ambition from being realized,
you should guard the edge of Yěchéng."
Should he become the Grand Commandant?
Not only is this matter related to strategy,
but it is also very important to you.
You should secretly inform Grand Consort Xún (Xún Tàifēi) so she knows.
Prince Huī of Lújiāng (Lújiāng Wáng Huī) was formerly in Xīzhōu (Xīzhōu),
thus the previous text mentioned "near Yěchéng (Yěchéng)."
Xiūrúo Zǐchōng (Xiūrúo Zǐchōng) first inherited the title.
Emperor Shùn (Shùndì) died in the third year of Shēngmíng (Shēngmíng sān nián).
At that time, Qí (Qí) received the abdication,
and the state was abolished.
The court historian says: The Odes say:
"Not from my beginning,
not from my end."
The ancients feared times of chaos.
In Emperor Tàizōng's (Tàizōng) later years,
suspicions and rifts formed within,
the axe soon fell,
starting with his closest relatives.
Jìn Là (Jìn Là) destroyed himself through ferocity,
Bā Āi (Bā Āi) brought ruin upon himself through gentleness and kindness.
The path to self-preservation,
is unknown where it leads.
The ancient warning to sons,
"Be careful not to do good,"
might it have a profound meaning?
Collation Notes
Biographies (Lièzhuàn), Volume Thirty-three: Yán Yánzhī (Yán Yánzhī)
Yán Yánzhī, courtesy name Yánnián (Yánnián),
was a man from Línyí (Línyí), Lángxié (Lángxié).
His great-grandfather was Hán (Hán),
Grand Master of Remonstrance of the Right (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū).
His grandfather was Yuē (Yuē),
Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Línglíng (Línglíng).
His father was Xiǎn (Xiǎn),
Protecting Army Commander (Hùjūn Sīmǎ).
Yánzhī was orphaned and poor in his youth.
He lived by the city walls,
in a very humble house and lane.
He loved to read,
perusing everything,
and the beauty of his writings
was unsurpassed at the time.
He drank alcohol and did not care for minor decorum.
At thirty years old,
he was still unmarried.
His younger sister married Liú Xiànzhī (Liú Xiànzhī) of Dōngguǎn (Dōngguǎn),
who was Mùzhī's (Mùzhī) son.
Mùzhī was already connected with Yánzhī's family,
and having also heard of his talent,
intended to employ him.
He first wanted to meet him,
but Yánzhī did not go.
Liú Liǔ (Liú Liǔ), General of the Rear (Hòu Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Wú Commandery (Wúguó Nèishǐ), appointed him as Acting Staff Officer (Xíng Cānjūn),
then transferred him to Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù),
and Acting Staff Officer of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Xíng Cānjūn) for the Heir Apparent (Shìzǐ) of the Duke of Yùzhāng (Yùzhānggōng).
In the twelfth year of Yìxī (Yìxī shí'èr nián),
Emperor Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) launched a northern expedition.
He was granted the title Duke of Sòng (Sònggōng).
The ducal establishment sent an envoy to congratulate him on this extraordinary appointment,
and inquire about his daily life.
Yánzhī and Staff Officer Wáng (Wáng Cānjūn) from the same establishment jointly carried out the mission to Luòyáng (Luòyáng).
On the way, he composed two poems.
Their literary style was ornate and beautiful,

When the State of Sòng (Sòngguó) was established,
Minister of Ceremonies (Fèngcháng) Zhèng Xiānzhī (Zhèng Xiānzhī) recommended him as an Erudite (Bóshì),
and he was subsequently promoted to Attendant to the Heir Apparent (Shìzǐ Shèrén).
When Emperor Gāozǔ received the Mandate of Heaven,
he was appointed Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén).
Zhōu Xùzhī (Zhōu Xùzhī) of Yànmén (Yànmén) lived in seclusion on Mount Lú (Lúshān).
He was renowned for his Confucian scholarship.
During the Yǒngchū (Yǒngchū) era,
he was summoned to the capital (Jīngshī),
and a residence was opened for him.
Emperor Gāozǔ personally visited him,
and all the court luminaries arrived.
Although Yánzhī's official rank was still low,
he was invited to the highest seat.
The emperor had Xùzhī asked about the "three meanings."
Xùzhī, relying on his eloquent rhetoric,
was consistently refuted by Yánzhī with conciseness and clarity.
After repeatedly defeating Xùzhī,
the emperor then had Yánzhī return and explain it himself.
His words were concise, and his reasoning clear,
and everyone praised him.
He was transferred to Secretary of the Ministry of Rites (Shàngshū Yícáo Láng),
and Middle Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén).
At that time, Fù Liàng (Fù Liàng), Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng), considered his own literary and scholarly accomplishments
unmatched at the time.
Yánzhī, confident in his talent and rhetoric,
did not defer to him.
Liàng greatly resented this.
Prince Yìzhēn (Yìzhēn) of Lúlíng (Lúlíng Wáng) was quite fond of literature and philosophy,
and treated Yánzhī very generously.
Xú Xiànzhī (Xú Xiànzhī) and others suspected Yánzhī of holding dissenting views,
and were very displeased.
When Emperor Shào (Shàodì) ascended the throne,
he was made Regular Gentleman (Zhèngyuán Láng),
and concurrently served in the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū).
Soon after, he was transferred to Supernumerary Attendant at the Imperial Palace (Yuánwài Chángshì),
and sent out as Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Shǐ'ān (Shǐ'ān).
General Who Leads the Army (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn) Xiè Huì said to Yánzhī:

and banished him to Shǐpíng (Shǐpíng Jùn) Commandery.
Now you are again sent to Shǐ'ān.
One might call them 'two Shǐs'."
Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Huángmén Láng) Yīn Jǐngrén (Yīn Jǐngrén) also said to him:
"This is what is called the world detesting exceptional talent,
and society faulting refinement."
When Yánzhī went to his commandery,

For Zhāng Shào (Zhāng Shào), Inspector of Xiāngzhōu (Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ), he offered a sacrifice to Qū Yuán (Qū Yuán) and expressed his thoughts,
saying: Reverently receiving the emperor's command,
I set up my banner in old Chǔ (Jiùchǔ).

I halt my carriage by Luótán (Luótán),
and moor my boat by Mìzhǔ (Mìzhǔ).
I respectfully offer sacrifice to the Chǔ (Chǔ) Three
Minister of the Clans (Sānlǘ Dàfū), the spirit of Lord Qū (Qū Jūn): Orchids, fragrant, yet cut down;
jade, pure, yet broken.

people avoid brightness and purity.

Warm winds were timely,

Yíng (Yíng) and Qiān (Qiān) met with strife;

He

Looking towards Mì (Mì), my heart sighs;
Gazing at
Luó (Luó), I think of the past.
Even if his service was covered in dust,

In the third year of Yuánjiā,

Soon after, he was transferred to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
A little later,

Yánzhī was fond of wine and unconstrained,

Seeing Liú Zhàn and Yīn Jǐngrén monopolizing important positions,

He often said:

How can one person’s wisdom accomplish everything alone!”
His words were very impassioned,

He said to Zhàn:

Zhàn deeply resented this

Yánzhī was deeply resentful
and composed the "Wǔ Jūn Yǒng" (Odes to Five Gentlemen) to allude to the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove.
Shān Tāo and Wáng Róng, because of their wealth and prominence, were denounced.
In his ode to Jī Kāng, he wrote:
“A phoenix’s wings are sometimes clipped;
who can tame a dragon’s nature?”
In his ode to Ruǎn Jí, he wrote:
“Past events need not be discussed,
but when the road ends, how can one not mourn?”
In his ode to Ruǎn Xián, he wrote:
“Repeated recommendations failed to gain him office;
a single command sent him out as a prefect.”
In his ode to Liú Líng, he wrote:
“Concealing his talent, he indulged in daily drinking;
who knew this was not mere revelry?”
These four lines
are probably his self-description.
Zhàn and Yìkāng were greatly angered
by the impertinent meaning of his words.
At that time, Yánzhī had already taken up his appointment,
but they wanted to demote him to a distant commandery.
Tàizǔ and Yìkāng issued an edict saying:
“To demote Yánzhī to the governorship of a small state
— it is said that while he was in the capital,
he certainly stirred up people’s emotions.
His transgressions are manifest,
and are known to both scholars and commoners.
We simply want to choose a replacement
and let him reflect on his faults in his hometown.
If he still does not reform,
he should be banished to the eastern lands.
If his ambitions are beyond forgiveness,
he can be dealt with according to the circumstances.
Yīn and Liú hold the same opinion.”
Thereupon, Guānglù Xūn Chē Zhòngyuǎn replaced him.
Yánzhī and Zhòngyuǎn had long been at odds;
he secluded himself in his village alley,
not participating in human affairs for seven years.
Zhōngshū Lìng Wáng Qiú was a renowned noble,
who disregarded worldly affairs.
Yánzhī admired him,
and Qiú also appreciated his talent.
Their affection for each other was very deep.
Yánzhī was often destitute,
and Qiú would always provide for him.
When Jìn Gōngsī Huánghòu was buried,
all officials were required to attend.
Zhàn selected an old official from Yìxī first year,
appointing Yánzhī as acting Shìzhōng.
When the district clerk delivered the official document,
Yánzhī, being drunk,
threw the document to the ground and said:
“Yán Yánzhī has not been able to serve the living,
how can he serve the dead!”
In his leisure, he composed the "Tíng Gào" (Admonitions to the Household) text.
Now, we have deleted its superfluous words,
preserved its essence,
and included it in this chapter.
It says: The "Tíng Gào"
is applied within the confines of the household,
meaning it is not far-reaching.
My age is now in its autumn phase,
my concerns precede the grasses and trees;
thus, I hastily impart what I have not yet heard,
admonishing you who are
in the household.
As for the principles of conduct
and the clarity of moral judgment,
they have already been laid out in the rules of the enlightened,
and I will not discuss them further.
What is recorded here
is all that which I have long cherished,
rooted in my nature
and spirit,
and applied to my mind and actions.
For choosing words, one must aim for unity,
not valuing complexity or denseness.
But when it comes to comprehensive discussion,
it is to net all emotional faults.
An ancient saying goes, “He who catches a bird
nets it with a single mesh,”
but a net with a single mesh
will never catch a bird.
This is the way of accumulating intentions.
The Way is the public domain of knowledge;
emotion is the private domain of virtue.
When public, it is accessible,
and can cause spirits and deities to respond;
when private, it is blocked,
and cannot move even one’s wife and children.
Therefore,
those who were good scholars in ancient times
would surely abandon emotion and return to the Way,
uniting the public and shielding the private.
With a body merely a foot long,
they took Heaven and Earth as their heart;
with a lifespan of a few cycles,
they always measured themselves against metal and stone.
Observing the warnings left by the ancients
and the remaining discussions of elders,
though using subtle methods,
they were always inscribed for their imperishability;
the final traces of construction
were all built to last, embodying their will.
How much more so when establishing virtue and setting up righteousness,
uniting families and leading households,
should one not consider
long-term consequences?
It is said that one’s conduct should be worthy of being passed on to future generations.
To expect filial piety from children, one must first be benevolent;
to demand fraternal respect from younger brothers, one must strive to be a good friend.
Although filial piety does not depend on benevolence,
benevolence firmly
establishes filial piety;
fraternal respect is not necessarily prompted by friendship,
but friendship also cultivates fraternal respect.
Indeed, if harmony is not complete,
it may lead to disharmony;
just as if trust is insufficient,

If one understands that kindness and gratitude generate each other,

one can
make a household like that of Cān and Chái,

To dwell in virtue internally,
to calm popular praise externally,

not to use one’s abilities to impose on
the multitude,
not to criticize things based on one’s strengths,
to be profoundly serene and enter the Way,
to act for Heaven’s sake –
this is the highest kind of scholar.
If one cannot abandon fame,
wishing others to surpass oneself,
knowing that power lies in
seeking emptiness,
and cannot be achieved by contention,
respectfully admiring humility and openness,
avoiding arrogance and self-importance,
striving to broaden one’s observation and selection,
following long-term strategies,
with refined and clear reasoning

with discussions
and inquiries that flourish,

this is the second kind.
But if one believes that substance is valuable,

sees that fame brings glory,
and thinks contention
can achieve it,
whose words do not extend beyond the window

then one is moved by shallow, keen
ambitions,

How could one not realize that one has already been judged by the discerning

As the record says,

dies without illness.”
it is.
If one's conduct is close to this,

All who possess knowledge and ability,

For those who aspire to be a *jūnzǐ*,

Although it is said that human

How can one not strive to be different,

Wealth and poverty

For a person of wealth,

If there is wealth,

How can this be proven?
It is the way of Heaven.
If all people

The Dao dictates otherwise,

Silk warms, farmers are fed –

One should grant their wishes,
provide their clothing and food,
define their appropriate
duties,

Attend to public taxes first,

Collect and disburse according to the season,

Plowing and harvesting are truly rustic,

Though this statement is grand,

True generosity surely does not merely arise from the human heart,
