In this world, there are those whose affections cease when their position is lost;
these have no cherishing.
There are also those whose hearts change when their duties are fulfilled;
these have no virtue.
Moreover, it is not merely like this.
Some,
seeing others engaged in successful endeavors,
eagerly seek to form connections.
But upon hearing negative opinions,
they openly dissociate themselves.
They conform by following the prevailing winds,
secretly fostering discord.
In the morning, they offer face-to-face praise;
in the evening, they engage in backbiting.
Formerly, they were in close accord;
now, they are rebellious and disloyal.
This is indeed extreme.
Furthermore, it is not only like this.
Some, relying on others' gracious instruction,
achieve their standing through others.
They echo others' opinions
and gain renown by depending on others.
They humbly accept guidance
and willingly follow the dusty tracks.
Yet, when others decline or are far away, they fear them,
dreading to hear even a trace of them.
They also conceal others' good qualities
〔二一〕and slander
them without measure.
They belittle others' abilities
and privately promote their own clumsiness.
They exalt themselves among their peers,
disregarding those of superior insight.
People who reach this point
are truly a bane to great human relationships.
One should always think to guard against and avoid them,
not allowing them into one's community.
When witnessing astonishing and unusual events,
one might spread rumors;
〔二二〕when encountering sudden and pressing changes,
one might reflect on how to achieve peace and compliance.
If unusual behavior originates from oneself,
it will invite criticism from others.
If one is pressed
and then defiant,
it will further lead to loss of composure.
Can one who can calmly handle the unusual like Péi Kǎi [裴楷]
and face pressure like Péi Xiá [裴遐]
be called a profound scholar?
Joy and anger are emotions that human nature cannot be without.
They often arise from narrow-mindedness,
but are restrained by broad understanding.
However, excessive joy leads to a lack of gravity,
and excessive anger leads to a lack of authority.
To be
composed and indifferent in one's essence,
and broad and cheerful in one's demeanor,
would be excellent.
〔二三〕Great joy overwhelms the mind;
a slight suppression will calm it.
Extreme anger disturbs one's nature;
a little forbearance will cease it.
Therefore,
if one's actions are without fault in demeanor,
〔二四〕and one's conduct is without deviation,
then things will naturally suspend themselves,
and people will naturally restrain themselves.
What habits can transform is also great.
It is not only that they permeate one's nature and affect one's body,
but they can also alter one's wisdom and change one's thoughts.
Thus, it is said:
"Dwelling with good people
is like entering a room of fragrant
orchids:
after a long time, one does not notice their fragrance."
One is transformed by them.
"Dwelling with bad people
is like entering a fish market:
after a long time, one does not notice the stench."
One is changed
by them.
Therefore, the ancients were cautious about whom they associated with.
Only those who are truly like pure gold and refined jade
can remain complete and unstained.
Hence, it is said:
"Cinnabar can be extinguished but cannot
be made not red;
stone can be shattered but cannot be made not hard."
If one does not possess the nature of cinnabar and stone,
one must be cautious about the causes of contamination.
If one can maintain the thought of embracing the Way,
〔二五〕one must
preserve the heart of following principle.
If the Way can be embraced and principle can be followed,
then one does not discuss poverty;
one discusses what one delights in.
Some say:
"How can poverty be delightful?"
This is not seeking the meaning of
the Way.
For the Way,
one views wealth and honor the same as poverty and lowliness;
principle naturally achieves this equality.
〔二六〕To lose it of oneself
is not a common understanding.
If one discusses not losing it,
what is there not to delight in?
Some say,
the value of warmth and satiety
is what glorifies life;
with hunger and cold upon one,
merely speaking of following the Way,
taking it from one's own body,
is perhaps not a profound argument.
This is also what common
sense employs.
Indeed, the means of nourishing life,
how can they be distinguished by fixed reality?
〔二七〕Some ruin their nature with rich food,
while others live long years on beans and wild greens.
Zhōngsàn [中散] said,
what is sufficient is within,
not dependent on external factors.
〔二八〕Therefore, eating according to one's constitution,
one is still satisfied in a poor year.
Cooking according to one's stomach,
a rich household still has leftover food.
It is not that the grains actually increase or decrease,
but that one's intentions
have fullness or emptiness.
Moreover, if one's heart obtains excellence,
〔二九〕and one's body acquires benevolence and wealth,
if one's clarity returns to simplicity,
and one's spirit is like a deity,
even if one eats nine meals in ten days,
one cannot be made hungry.
Even if one sleeps on a mat with three
layers,
one cannot be made cold.
Is this not true?
Furthermore, those who measure by themselves
have no way to understand others' measures.
The rotation of the four directions and the turning of the five planets show
the vastness of the heavenly Way.
The shaking of rivers and seas and the carrying of mountains and streams show
the profoundness of the earthly Way.
The unifying of feelings and the convergence of flowing currents show
the flourishing of human spirituality.
Those of old who understood these numbers
did not engage in divisive actions.
They certainly broadened their demeanor,
not harboring private differences,
and expanded their way of interaction,
not cherishing peculiar distinctions.
〔三０〕Therefore, when one begs for friendship at a distance,
righteous scholars disregard themselves.
When one encounters them once and bows to them as relatives,
benevolent people devote themselves
divisions.
This order and sequence are generally fair and
the customs uniform,
whereby the superiors achieve their utility
and the subordinates obtain their harmony.
Though worldly affairs shift,
past merits are not distant.
As for how people adapt to their lords,
I will return to the root.
The life of a person,
〔三一〕briefly possessing consciousness,
〔三二〕sees youth and vigor quickly
pass,
and decline and decay swiftly arrive.
During this time, the number of those who die young and are frustrated
is already beyond words;
even if one is fortunate enough to survive and thrive,
it is said to be for a mere short while.
A tender and beautiful body
is quickly committed to earth and wood;
a strong and pure
talent
suddenly becomes a mound of earth.
Looking back with regret and yearning,
it is but for a few decades.
To hold onto glory with this [body],
it cannot be retained;
to serve the Dao with this [body],
how can one
achieve peace?
Advancing and retreating in my life,
what one observes and attains,
the value of being human
lies in embodying principles.
The value of embodying principles
is solely to commune with the spirit.
Fortunately, having a mind and spirit,
there is no reason
to despise oneself.
If one happens to believe in Heavenly Virtue,
one will not regret it later.
To wish for people to immerse themselves in transformation
and for their aspirations to align with ancient sages,
do not say this is far-fetched;
daily chipping will make it dense.
By making this
idea widely understood,
I will forget old age.
If it is said otherwise,
〔三三〕who will I return with?
I have casually put together what I have written,
〔三四〕briefly laying out many points;
〔三五〕if I were to fully enumerate my feelings and views,
I would
not yet have written even one.
The classic on sustaining the body
is separately found in *Tiánjiā Jiézhèng*;
the record on fulfilling one's end
is self-evident in *Yànjū Bìyì*.
After Liú Zhàn 劉湛 was executed,
Yánzhī 延之 was appointed as the staff officer for the rear army of Shǐxīngwáng Jùn 始興王濬 and
the Imperial Censor.
While in office, he was indulgent
and made no impeachments.
He was promoted to Chancellor of the National University and Left Senior Clerk of the Minister of Works.
He was impeached for initiating the purchase of someone's land
and refusing to pay the full price.
Xún Chìsōng 荀赤松, Left Administrator of the Department of State Affairs, memorialized thus:
"Seeking fields and houses
was disdained by former worthies.
Yánzhī 延之 regards only profit,
recklessly making false statements,
presuming upon imperial grace,
and refusing to pay the remaining balance.
Almost a year has passed,
and it is still not settled.
He is blinded by profit and seeks gain illicitly,
without any scruples.
Yánzhī 延之 was formerly dismissed from office due to an incident,
but was again promoted.
Yet, he has not reformed at all,
and his complaints and slanders are endless.
His associates are unruly,
he is deeply addicted to alcohol,
and he wantonly stirs up ridicule and slander,
vilifying court officials.
He secretly appropriates excessive honors from above,
which increases his contemptuous nature;
he privately relies on the favor of others,
forming an arrogant and overbearing disposition.
Outwardly, he appears to seek little,
but inwardly he harbors ambition and strives for promotion,
seeking official emoluments and transfers,
knowing no limit.
At banquets where cups are passed,
he freely curses those in the highest seats.
The mountains and seas are tolerant,
always nurturing and preserving.
He cherishes even 'carving insects' (petty literary pursuits)
and cannot bear to abandon them.
Yet, his arrogance and unrestraint
become more apparent with each passing day.
Your subject has heard that a reputation exceeding reality
was a shame to Mèng Kē 孟軻.
Moreover, his reputation does not come from external sources;
his inquiries originate from himself.
Although his intellect is weak,
he arrogantly compares himself [to others].
His self-importance is ostentatious,
without any shame or fear.
How can he possibly assist in the Five Teachings
and add luster to the imperial court?
I request that Yánzhī 延之 be dismissed from his current office
for his dishonest lawsuit over land,
his presumptuous appeal to the emperor,
and for using his power to oppress the weak."
The emperor approved the memorial.
He was again appointed Director of the Imperial Library,
Superintendent of the Imperial Household,
and Grand Master of Ceremonies.
At that time, the Buddhist monk Shì Huìlín 釋慧琳,
due to his talent and learning, was cherished and admired by Tàizǔ 太祖.
Whenever he was summoned for an audience,
he would always sit on a separate couch.
Yánzhī 延之 greatly resented this.
Drunk, he reported to the emperor, saying:
"In ancient times, Tóng Zǐ 同子 rode in the same carriage,
and Yuán Sī 袁絲 maintained a stern countenance.
This is the seat of the Three Dukes;
how can one who has suffered mutilation (eunuch) be allowed to occupy it?"
The emperor's expression changed.
Yánzhī 延之's nature was both narrow-minded and impetuous,
combined with his intemperance.
He spoke his mind freely and directly,
without any restraint or concealment.
Thus, many critics did not know how to speak of him.
He lived a pure and frugal life,
not engaging in financial gain.
Dressed in plain clothes, eating simple food,
he would drink alone in the countryside.
When he was thus at ease,
he acted as if no one else was around.
In the twenty-ninth year,
he submitted a memorial, stating:
"Your subject has heard that one who travels a hundred *lǐ* is halfway at ninety *lǐ*,
meaning the difficulty of the last leg of the journey.
My foolish mind always thought it was empty words,
but now I know it to be true.
Your subject Yánzhī 延之, though insignificant, has received great favor,
and has long been noted in the words of the nation.
Yet, there has been no opportunity to repay [this favor],
and my record of honors has only expanded.
My body is worn out by the passage of time,
and I daily occupy an official position.
Although there is room to accommodate [my service],
my flaws and impurities accumulate.
I long desired to request to retire early
and hide my ugly old age.
However, as the regulations of the time were enforced,
and my longing for return was not distant,
I thus brazenly committed errors
and reduced my presumptuous requests.
My decline and exhaustion are difficult to bear,
and my natural essence is limited.
Since last summer, enduring the heat,
and entering this autumn's changes,
my head and teeth ache and are dizzy,
my chronic illness gradually worsens,
my hands and feet are cold and numb,
especially my left shoulder.
I have always eaten little,
and recently it has decreased by half.
Originally, I still relied on medication,
〔三六〕but now, weary and anxious,
〔三七〕driven by age and sickness,
I look at my shadow as the days pass.
Your subject holds the rank of a chief minister,
occupying an honored position.
I am solemnly respectful of the court duties,
yet I am ashamed of being unfit.
Moreover, in the numerous affairs of the imperial ancestral temples,
I am hindered by illness and idleness;
for visits and greetings to the palace,
I am increasingly unable to attend in person.
My son, Wén 馼, is mediocre and insignificant,
but has been appointed governor of a nearby district.
Imperial grace has been bestowed,
and he has truly been promoted to supervisor.
I beg to be relieved of my duties,
so I may seek medical care.
I humbly wish that Your Sacred Benevolence
would specially grant this favor.
Having received grace in this enlightened age,
my gratitude will be repaid in the deepest twilight.
I look up to the imperial court,
loving it without end."
It was not granted.
The following year, he retired from office.
The prime culprit, Shào, having usurped the throne,
appointed him as Guanglù Dàfū.
Previously,
his son Jùn had served Shìzǔ as the Southern Zhongláng Cányì Cānjūn.
When the righteous army marched in to suppress the rebellion,
Jùn participated in settling secret plans
and also drafted the proclamations and manifestos.
Shào summoned Yánzhī,
showed him the manifesto,
and asked:
"Whose brush created this?"
Yánzhī replied:
"It is Jùn's brush."
He then asked:
"How do you know that?"
Yánzhī said:
"As for Jùn's handwriting style,
I cannot possibly fail to recognize it."
Shào then said:
"How could the words be so extreme?"
Yánzhī replied:
"If Jùn does not even care for his old father,
how can he serve Your Majesty?"
Shào's suspicion was thus dispelled,
and Yánzhī was consequently spared.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed him Jīnzǐ Guanglù Dàfū,
and concurrently the tutor of the Prince of Xiāngdōng.
As his son Jùn became prominent and esteemed,
his power overshadowed the entire court.
However, Yánzhī
received none of the provisions Jùn offered;
his utensils and clothing remained unchanged,
and his residence was as before.
He often rode a lean ox in a clumsy cart,
and whenever he encountered Jùn's imperial retinue,
he would immediately withdraw to the side of the road.
He also enjoyed riding horses,
roaming through the alleys and lanes,
and whenever he met old acquaintances, he would lean on his saddle and ask for wine.
Upon getting wine, he would inevitably become joyfully intoxicated.
He often said to Jùn:
"Throughout my life, I have disliked seeing important people,
and now, unfortunately, I see you."
When Jùn built a new residence,
he said to him:
"Do it well,
lest later generations laugh at your clumsiness."
He submitted a memorial to resign from his teaching post,
and was granted thirty trusted attendants.
In the third year of Xiàojiàn (456 CE),
he died,
at the age of seventy-three.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Sànqí Chángshì and Tèjìn,
with Jīnzǐ Guanglù Dàfū as before.
His posthumous name was Xiànzǐ.
Yánzhī and Xiè Língyùn of Chénjùn were equally renowned for their literary brilliance.
After Pān Yuè and Lù Jī,
no literati could surpass them;
in Jiangzuǒ, they were known as Yán and Xiè.
His writings have all been passed down to posterity.
Jùn has a separate biography.
Jùn's younger brother Cè,
[三八] was also recognized for his literary talent.
He served as the Dàsītú Lùshì Cānjūn for Prince Yìgōng of Jiāngxià,
[三九] and died young.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
he issued an edict saying:
"Yánzhī formerly tutored me personally,
and our bond was deeply affectionate.
His former Shìshì Cānjūn and Jìyáng Tàishǒu, Wén, served the imperial court diligently,
maintaining a close relationship through old favors.
He may be promoted to Zhōngshū Shìláng."
Wén
was Yánzhī's third son.
The Historian says: To emerge from obscurity and serve one's lord,
though righteousness lies in selflessness,
when it comes to the two matters of ruler and parent,
if there is no way for both to be achieved,
then to act as a son or as a minister
should be done according to what is appropriate for the time.
As for drafting documents on the road,
military and governmental rites,
the causes of success or failure
do not depend on this.
Yet, to seize the brush and enumerate crimes,
to offend an enemy and commit rebellion,
leaving one's compassionate parent
to be devoured by a tiger's maw,
to consider this loyalty
is unheard of in previous admonitions.
Indeed, one who is ruthless to his own parent
will certainly be ruthless to others' parents;
one who forgets his own filial piety
will expect others to demonstrate their filial piety.
Feeding one's child to save a deer
is a clear example.
The Records say:
"For those aged eighty, one son is not involved in government;
for those aged ninety, no one in the family is involved in government."
Is this not because their years are drawing to a close,
and worries and troubles are imminent?
Even if they hold office at court,
they are permitted to resign.
How much more so in times of upheaval,
when the future is uncertain?
If not for Yánnián's words being appropriate and righteous,
how could he have been spared?

Biographies, Chapter Thirty-Four: Zāng Zhì, Lǔ Shuǎng, Shěn Yōuzhī
Zāng Zhì, courtesy name Hánwén,
was a native of Jǔ in Dōngguǎn.
His father, Xī, courtesy name Yìhé,
was the younger brother of Empress Wǔjìng.
He and his elder brother Táo were both fond of classics and records.
In the early Lóng'ān period (397 CE),
as wars frequently erupted,
Xī trained in horsemanship and archery,
determined to achieve meritorious service.
He once went to Lìyáng,
where the magistrate Ruan Chóng and Xī hunted together.
A tiger suddenly broke out of its enclosure,
and the hunters all scattered.
Xī bravely went forward and shot it,
and it fell down at the sound of the bowstring.
When Gāozǔ entered the capital city,
Xī's clan nephew Mù beheaded Huán Xiū.
Upon reaching the capital,
Huán Xuán fled,
and Gāozǔ ordered Xī to enter the palace to collect books, maps, and artifacts,
and seal the treasuries.
There were gold-adorned musical instruments.
Gāozǔ asked Xī:
"Do you not desire these?"
Xī, with a solemn expression, replied:
"Your Majesty is besieged and distressed,
forced into exile inappropriately.
The General has taken the lead in upholding great righteousness,
toiling for the royal house.
Though I may be unworthy,
I have no desire for pleasure."
Gāozǔ smiled and said:
"I was merely jesting with you."
He served as Cān Gāozǔ Zhènjūn Shì,
Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng,
and again as Cān Zhènjūn Jūnshì,
concurrently holding the post of Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu.
For his meritorious service in upholding righteousness, he was enfeoffed as a fifth-rank Marquis of Shǐxīng County.
He also served as Cān Gāozǔ Chējì and Zhōngjūn Jūnshì.
When Gāozǔ was about to campaign against Guǎnggù,
many deliberators disagreed.
Xī calmly stated:
"If Your Grace projects your might into the northern regions,
and rescues them from their misery,
then uniting the six directions
is not without prospect."
Gāozǔ said:
"Your words are correct."
When the expedition departed,
Xī requested to accompany it,
but was denied,
and appointed Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Línhǎi Tàishǒu.
The commandery had suffered from military raids,
with barely one in a hundred remaining.
Xī stabilized and reorganized the administration,
and gathered the scattered populace,
with over a thousand families returning to him.
Sūn Jìgāo attacked Guǎngzhōu by sea,
passing through Línhǎi.
Xī provided provisions and dispatched them,
so they lacked nothing.
He was summoned to be appointed Sànqí Chángshì,
but resigned due to mourning for his mother.
Soon after, when Liú Yì was to be suppressed,
he was reinstated as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn
and joined the campaign.
After the affair was settled,
Gāozǔ sent Zhū Língshí to lead a large army to conquer Shǔ,
and ordered Xī to lead a surprise force out through Zhōngshuǐ,
with his original title, concurrently governing the two commanderies of Jiànpíng and Bādōng.
The ruler of Shǔ, Qiáo Zòng, sent his grand general Qiáo Fǔzhī with over ten thousand men to garrison Niúpí,
and also sent Qiáo Xiǎogǒu with heavy troops to block Dǎbí.
When Xī reached Niúpí,
Fǔzhī was defeated in battle and retreated,
and Xī pursued and beheaded him.
When Xiǎogǒu heard of Fǔzhī's death,
he immediately scattered.
After Chéngdū was pacified,
Xī fell ill.
In the ninth year of Yìxī (413 CE),
he died in Niúpí County of Shǔjùn,
at the age of thirty-nine.
He was posthumously granted the title of Guanglù Xūn.
Zhì was fond of hawks and hounds in his youth,
and skilled at gambling games of chance.
He was six feet seven inches tall,
with a prominent face and exposed mouth,
a bald head, and curly hair.
When he was not yet twenty,
Gāozǔ appointed him as Crown Prince's Staff Officer for the Central Army.
In the first year of Yǒngchū (420 CE),
he was appointed as a supernumerary Gentleman of the Yellow Gate with the title of Cavalier Attendant,
following the standard example.
He resigned from his post due to his mother's mourning.
After the mourning period ended,
he became Fǔjūn Cānjūn for Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng.
Because of his frivolity and lack of restraint,
which was known to Tàizǔ,
he was transferred to be Gěishìzhōng.
Huìjī Xuānzhǎng Gōngzhǔ often spoke on his behalf,
so he was appointed as Jiànpíng Tàishǒu.
He greatly won the hearts of the Mán and Chǔ people.
When Nánmán Xiàowèi Liú Zhàn returned to court,
he praised him as a good governor.
He was promoted to Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Lìyáng Tàishǒu.
He was then successively promoted to Jìnglín Nèishǐ and Jiāngxià Nèishǐ,
and again appointed as Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn and the Tàishǒu of the two commanderies of Bādōng and Jiànpíng.
The officials and common people found him convenient.
Zhì was just over thirty,
and had repeatedly held important commanderies.
He had dabbled in historical records,
and his correspondence was swift and keen.
Possessing both spirit and capability,
he was fond of discussing military strategy.
Tàizǔ believed he was capable of great responsibility,
and wished to appoint him to affairs in Yìzhōu.
Before this was enacted,
he was summoned to be Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Xú Yǎn Èr Zhōu Zhū Jūnashì, Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn, and Xú Yǎn Èr Zhōu Cìshǐ.
While in office, he was extravagant and wasteful,
and his appointments and titles were disorderly,
for which he was impeached by the judicial authorities,
but was pardoned.
He was close friends with Fàn Yè, Xú Zhànzhī, and others.
When Yè plotted rebellion,
he assumed Zhì would surely join him.
When the plot was discovered,
Zhì was again appointed Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Yìxīng Tàishǒu.
In the twenty-sixth year of Yuánjiā (449 CE),
when Tàizǔ visited Jīnglíng,
Zhì paid respects at Dāntú.
Along with Hé Xù and Tán Hézhī, who were all sons of meritorious ministers,
they jointly offered respects.
Tàizǔ hosted a banquet, fully enjoying himself,
and bestowed a thousand bolts of cloth.
In the spring of the twenty-seventh year (450 CE),
he was promoted to Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān Sīkōng Sīmǎ, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, and Nánpíng Nèishǐ.
Before taking up his post,
it happened that the great chieftain of the Suǒlǔ, Tuòbá Táo, besieged Rǔnán.
Chén Xiàn, the garrison commander of Rǔnán, held firm and sent an urgent appeal.
Tàizǔ dispatched Zhì quickly to Shòuyáng,
to take command of the army there,
and, with Ānmán Sīmǎ Liú Kāngzǔ and others, relieve Xiàn.
The barbarians retreated.
Consequently, Zhì was ordered to attack the mountain barbarians in the western border of Rǔnán, such as Dāobì.
He thoroughly defeated them,
capturing over ten thousand people,
and was promoted to Tàizǐ Zuǒwèishuài.
He was dismissed from office
for having unjustly killed the team leader Yán Zǔ during the previous campaign against the barbarians,
and for having taken "male concubines" (面首) and captives
without sending them to the central authorities.
At this time, the emperor launched a major northern expedition.
Zhì, as a civilian, along with Piàojì Sīmǎ Wáng Fānghuí and others, led troops out to Xǔ and Luò.
Ānběi Sīmǎ Wáng Xuánmó attacked Huátái but failed to capture it.
Zhì requested to take over command by post-horse,
but Tàizǔ did not permit it.
The barbarians invaded Xú and Yù.
Tuòbá Táo, leading a large army of several hundred thousand, then marched towards Péngchéng.
Zhì was appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, given temporary credentials (jiǎjié), and authorized to appoint staff,
leading ten thousand men to relieve the north.
When he first arrived at Xūyí,
Táo had already crossed the Huái River.
Rǒngcóng Púyè Hú Chóngzhī commanded Zhì's general's aide (sīmǎ).
Chóngzhī's deputies, Crown Prince's Jìnnǔ [Jiāngjūn Zāng Chéngzhī and Jiànwēi] Jiāngjūn Máoxī Zuò, were also under Zhì's command.
To the east of Xūyí city was a high mountain.
Zhì feared the barbarians would occupy it,
so he ordered Chóngzhī and Chéngzhī's two armies to camp on the mountain,
while Zhì himself camped south of the city.
The barbarians attacked Chóngzhī and Chéngzhī's two camps.
Chóngzhī and others fought fiercely but were no match;
their troops scattered,
and both were killed by the barbarians.
The barbarians then attacked Xīzuò.
Xīzuò's command consisted entirely of elite soldiers from the Northern Army.
Chuángzhǔ Lǐ Guàn encouraged his officers and soldiers,
killing many enemies.
Duìzhǔ Zhōu Yìnzhī and Wàijiān Yáng Fāngshēng also led archers to shoot at the enemy.
The enemy was about to retreat,
when Xīzuò was wounded and died,
and the army subsequently scattered in disarray.
On that day, Zhì held his troops and dared not come to their rescue,
hence the three camps were annihilated at once.
Initially,
when Qiúchí was pacified,
Chóngzhī was appointed Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn and Běiqínzhōu Cìshǐ,
stationed at Bǎiqǐng.
On his way to Zhuóshuǐ,
he was defeated by the Suǒlǔ.
His entire army was routed and scattered,
and Chóngzhī, along with his generals and aides and below,
were all captured by the barbarians.
Later, he managed to rebel and return,
only to be defeated by the barbarians again on this occasion.
Xīzuò was
the nephew of Sīzhōu Cìshǐ Xiūzhī.
Chóngzhī and Xīzuò were both posthumously honored as Zhèngyuán Láng.
Chéngzhī's story is in the biography of his grandfather, Táo.
After the three camps were defeated,
that evening Zhì's army also fled and scattered,
abandoning their baggage and weaponry.
A hundred solitary soldiers fled to Xūyí.
Shěn Pú, the Tàishǒu of Xūyí, had completed preparations for defense and battle.
The city had a real strength of three thousand men.
Zhì was greatly pleased,
and so they defended it together.
When the barbarians first marched south,
they had no provisions or grain,
relying solely on the common people for sustenance.
Upon crossing the Huái River,
they consumed the grain from Píngyuè and Shíbiē's two garrisons.
By this point, they had nowhere left to plunder,
and their men and horses were famished and exhausted.
Hearing that Xūyí had stored grain,
they wished to use it as provisions for their return journey.
After defeating Chóngzhī and the others,
they attacked the city once but failed to take it,
and then led their forces south.
The city's defenses were reinforced,
and all were complete and strict.
In the first month of the twenty-eighth year (451 CE),
Táo returned north from Guǎnglíng,
and then exerted his full strength to attack Xūyí.
He requested wine from Zhì.
Zhì sealed up a container of urine and sent it to him.
Táo was extremely enraged.
He built a long encirclement,
completing it overnight.
He opened an assault path,
heading towards the northeast of the city,
transporting earth and stones from the eastern mountain to fill it.
The barbarians also feared that those within the city might escape by waterway,
so they brought large boats,
intending to build a pontoon bridge at Jūnshān
to cut off the Huái River route.
Those within the city engaged in battle with their ships,
and severely defeated them.
The next morning,
the enemy replaced their rafts with a temporary bridge (héng),
each section of which was heavily guarded by soldiers.
Those within the city attacked again but could not stop them,
so they established the bridge at Jūnshān,
cutting off both land and water routes.
Táo wrote a letter to Zhì, saying:
"The fighting men I am sending now
are entirely not people of my own country.
To the northeast of the city are Dīnglíng and Hú;
to the south are the Dī and Qiāng of Sānqín.
If the Dīnglíng die,
it will just reduce the bandits of Chángshān and Zhàojùn.
If the Hú die,
it will just reduce the bandits of Bìngzhōu.
If the Dī and Qiāng die,
it will just reduce the bandits of Guānzhōng.
If you kill the Dīnglíng and Hú,
there will be no disadvantage."
Zhì replied in a letter, saying:
"I have noted your message,
and fully understand your treacherous intentions.
Relying on your four legs,
you have repeatedly encroached upon the national borders.
Matters such as these
cannot be fully enumerated.
Wáng Xuánmó retreated in the east,
Liáng Tǎn dispersed in the west.
[一０] Why do you not hear the children's rhyme that says: 'The barbarian horses drink the river water,
Fólí dies in the `mǎo` year'?
This time has not yet arrived,
but the two armies have opened the path for drinking the river water.
Fate has willed it so,
it is no longer a matter of human effort.
I have received the mandate to exterminate you.
Our rendezvous is at Báidēng.
My army has not yet gone far,
yet you yourself send yourself to death.
How can I allow you to survive
and enjoy Sānggān?
But you remain to attack this city.
[一一] Even if I cannot kill you,
you will die because of me.
If you are fortunate,
you will be killed by the unruly soldiers.
If you are unfortunate,
then I will capture and bind you alive,
carry you on a donkey,
and send you directly to the capital city.
I originally did not intend for a complete victory.
If heaven and earth are without spirit,
and my strength is inferior to yours,
then to grind you to powder,
to slaughter and tear you apart,
even this would not be enough to apologize to the imperial court.
How can your knowledge, wisdom, and multitude of forces
overcome Fú Jiān?
The reason you have been allowed to rage in recent years
is that you have not yet drunk the river water,
and the `tàisuì` has not yet reached the `mǎo` year.
Hú Lán once deeply penetrated Péngchéng,
but encountered a few days of rain,
and not a single horse returned.
Do you remember this? Immediately, spring rains have already fallen,
and the masses from all four directions
are just beginning to gather like clouds.
You just attack the city at ease and do not flee.
If you lack provisions, tell me,
and I will issue grain from the granary to feed you.
You sent swords and knives,
do you want me to wield them against your body?
It is very bitter.
My men have turned back.
Let each strive,
no need for many words."
At this time, a children's rhyme in the barbarian camp said:
"A light carriage comes from the north like a pheasant being shot through.
Unexpectedly, the barbarian horses drink the river water.
The barbarian lord returns north and dies at Shíjì.
The barbarians want to cross the river, but heaven does not move."
Therefore, Zhì cited it in his reply.
[一二]
Táo was greatly enraged,
and so he made an iron bed,
and placed iron spikes on it,
saying that when he broke the city and captured Zhì,
he would make him sit on this.
Zhì again wrote to the barbarian troops, saying:
"I tell the officers and common people among the barbarians: [一三] Lífá's letter to me is as separate (from you).
[一四] You are people of the orthodox calendar,
why do you strive to bring such upon yourselves?
How can a true man not know how to turn disaster into fortune?
Now I have copied the imperial edict as a separate letter,
consider it yourselves."
At that time, a reward was offered for beheading Táo: appointment as a Duke of an Established State and County,
with an income of ten thousand households,
and a grant of ten thousand bolts each of cloth and silk.
The barbarians used hook-carts to hook the city walls and towers.
Inside the city, ropes were tied,
and hundreds of men shouted and pulled them,
preventing the carts from retreating.
At night,
people were put into wooden buckets
and lowered outside the city,
where they cut the hooks and captured them.
[一五] The next day,
they again attacked the city with battering rams.
The city earth was hard and dense;
each time it hit,
no more than a few sheng of earth fell.
The barbarians then pressed closely and scaled the city walls,
taking turns replacing each other.
They fell and then climbed again;
none retreated.
Tens of thousands were killed and wounded,
and the number of barbarians who died was level with the city.
They also shot and killed the Prince of Gāoliáng.
[一六] After three such weeks,
more than half had died.
Táo heard that Péngchéng had cut off his retreat route,
and that the capital had dispatched naval forces from the sea into the Huái River.
Moreover, many had died from plague.
On the second day of the second month,
he lifted the siege and fled.
The Emperor praised Zhì's achievements,

and appointed him as Envoy with Imperial Insignia, Supervisor of Military Affairs for the four provinces of Yōng, Liáng, North Qín, and South Qín, General of the Champions, Commandant for Pacifying the Man, and Governor of Yōngzhōu,
enfeoffed him as a Viscount of an Established State,
with an income of five hundred households.
The following year,
Tài Zǔ again launched a northern expedition,
and ordered Zhì to lead his subordinate forces towards Tóngguān.
Zhì stationed his troops in the nearby suburbs
and refused to depart in time.
He only sent his Sīmǎ Liǔ Yuánjǐng to station troops on the border,
not advancing in time.
Zhì also doted on a favored concubine,
abandoning the camp to return to the city alone on horseback.
He indiscriminately spent six or seven million cash from the imperial treasury,
for which he was impeached by the appropriate officials,
but the Emperor did not question him.
When Yuánxiōng assassinated and ascended the throne,
he appointed Zhì as Dānyáng Yǐn,
and added the title of General for Quelling Barbarians.
Zhì's household sent a disciple, Shī Yǐ, to report to Zhì,
fully detailing the news of Tài Zǔ's death.
Zhì immediately wrote down what Yǐ had said,
and galloped to inform Sīkōng Yìxuān.
He also sent the provincial Libationer and Attendant Tián Yǐngqǐ with a mandate to report to Shì Zǔ,
and led a force of five thousand men,
galloping south to suppress the rebellion,
advancing from Yángkǒu to Jiānglíng to meet Yìxuān.
[一七] Zhì's sons were in the capital,
and hearing that Zhì had raised an army for a righteous cause,
they all fled.
Shào wanted to comfort and please them,
so he issued an edict saying:
"Zāng Dūn and others were startled without cause,
and immediately fled and hid.
Their confusion is excessive,
truly astonishing and lamentable.
Zhì is a loyal and upright relative of the state and a meritorious official,
who is destined for high office,
to assist and support the imperial carriage.
Yet his sons and younger brothers have scattered and fled,
hurting his intentions.
They should be sent a message to persuade them to return,
and all will be restored to their original positions."
Shào soon apprehended Dūn,
and ordered Grand General Yìgōng to administer thirty strokes of the cane in admonishment,
and then generously bestowed gifts upon him.
Yìxuān received Zhì's report,
and immediately raised an army,
sending a swift messenger to report to Shì Zǔ,
who appointed Zhì with the title of General of the North-Quelling Army.
Zhì proceeded directly to Xúnyáng,
and descended with Shì Zǔ.
When Shì Zǔ arrived at Xīntíng and ascended the throne,
he appointed Zhì as Grand Administrator of Military Affairs for Jiāngzhōu, General of Chariots and Cavalry, Open-Palace with the Three Ducal Ministers, and Governor of Jiāngzhōu,
adding the title of Attendant Cavalier-in-Ordinary,
with his imperial insignia as before.
He ordered Zhì to lead his subordinates on foot from Báixià,
directly to Guǎngmò Mén.
The gatekeepers did not defend it.
Xuē Āndū, Chéng Tiānzuò, and others also entered through the Nányè Mén,
meeting Zhì at the Tàijí Diàn,
and captured Yuánxiōng alive.
He then ordered Zhì to remain and guard the imperial court,
with one hundred armed guards for his protection.
He was enfeoffed as Duke of Shǐxīng Commandery,
with an income of three thousand households.
When he went to his post,
there were over a thousand boats,
and his military formation stretched for over a hundred `lǐ` before and behind,
with six flat carriages all displaying dragon-son banners.
At that time, Shìzǔ himself took charge of the reins of power.
However, Zhì treated him as a young lord,
acting unilaterally in all matters,
and making many demands.
When he reached Xúnyáng,
he no longer consulted
the imperial court on matters of punishment, governance, rewards, and promotions.
He casually spent
the rice from Pénkǒu and Gōuqí.
The imperial chancellery repeatedly sent out directives to investigate him,
and Zhì gradually became suspicious and fearful.
He considered himself a talent sufficient to be a hero of his age.
When he first heard of the national calamity,
he already harbored ulterior motives.
Believing Yìxuān to be ordinary and foolish,
easily controllable,
he intended to outwardly show him respect
to achieve his ambition.
When he arrived at Jiānglíng,
he immediately bowed and called him by his given name.
Although Zhì and Yìxuān were brothers,
Zhì was nearly ten years older.
Yìxuān was surprised and said:
“Why do you bow to your younger brother?”
Zhì replied:
“It is appropriate in this situation.”
At that time, Yìxuān had already elevated Shìzǔ,
so Zhì's plan failed.
Zhì constantly worried about his intentions being exposed.
When he arrived at Xīntíng,
he again bowed to Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng.
Yìgōng was astonished
and asked Zhì for the reason.
Zhì said:
“The empire is in a perilous state;
etiquette is different from ordinary days.
Previously, in Jīngzhōu,
I also bowed to Sīkōng.”
It happened that Yìxuān held a grievance against Shìzǔ—
the matter is in Yìxuān's biography.
Zhì secretly wrote to him, persuading and enticing him,
laying out the successes and failures of the court.
He also said:
“The awe that shakes the lord
cannot last long.
When the lord and the prime minister are equal in power,
they cannot coexist.
Now you exclusively control the external military,
with a superior strategic position and strong forces.
If you hesitate and are indecisive,
subsequent opportunities will lead to disaster.”
Zhì's daughter was the wife of Yìxuān's son Cǎi.
(一八) Yìxuān believed Zhì harbored no ill intentions
and adopted his counsel.
Furthermore, Yìxuān's trusted generals and aides, such as Cài Chāo and Zhú Chāomín,
(一九) all desired wealth and status.
They hoped Yìxuān would succeed,
wishing to rely on Zhì's prestige and fame
to achieve their ambitions,
and also encouraged Yìxuān.
Yìxuān had not yet accepted the position of Prime Minister at that time.
Zhì's son Dūn was a Huángmén Shìláng.
He was ordered to convey a decree urging Yìxuān,
and passed through Xúnyáng.
Zhì ordered Dūn to further elaborate and persuade Yìxuān,
and also spoke of Shìzǔ's strengths and weaknesses.
Yìxuān then made up his mind.
He hastily sent a report to Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Lǔ Shuǎng,
agreeing to rise together in the autumn of the first year of Xiàojiàn.
Shuǎng misunderstood the message
and immediately raised an army.
He sent someone to the capital to inform his younger brother Yú.
Yú immediately fled and rebelled.
Yú's younger brother Hóng was an aide in Zhì's administration.
Shìzǔ sent him to inform Zhì.
Zhì then seized the imperial envoy
and hastily raised an army.
He submitted a memorial, saying: Your subject has heard that to administer medicine to a parent
is not to err in one's feelings for sweetness or bitterness;
to wield an axe to cut down poison
is not to forget the pain to one's skin.
It is because doubt precedes compliance,
and loyalty
will surely be forthcoming;
to endure minor pain to preserve the greater good,
even love must follow.
Prime Minister Chén Yìxuān,
nurturing talent and stabilizing the court,
commanding widespread respect,
has established the meritorious work of supporting the king;
his achievements surpass
those of Qí and Jìn.
As a trusted relative of the imperial clan,
his prestige is revered like Lǔ and Wèi.
Yet, those who detest uprightness and uglify righteousness
are indeed numerous, forming factions.
Some are tainted by evil and act deceptively,
harassing and harming foundational merits;
others exploit their achievements to cling to favor,
abusing their authority to act perversely.
Knowing their deep transgressions and heavy offenses,
which will surely incur destruction and execution,
they then turn purple into ruin and red into destruction,
interfering with loyal ministers.
They cultivate private
followers
and gather various evildoers.
Those who remember the old and cherish the elders
are none left.
Is this not because evil and depraved individuals incite each other,
and their ambition allows slander and delusion to run rampant?
Your Majesty, being merciful and approachable,
does not in the least
entertain doubts,
thus allowing those who plot against the throne
to be obscured by current rumors,
and the "tiger in the market"
to be created by ten men.
Reflecting on the past and considering the present,
I truly feel endangered and pressured.
Therefore, I throw myself into action like
Fán and Yè,
establishing integrity for the current court;
I brandish my spear like at Jìnyáng,
determined to clear the ruler's side.
Your subject is truly ordinary and weak.
Having received instructions from the previous court,
though I feel ashamed of the beauty of a scholar who loves virtue,
I dare to aspire to the feeling of Hànbó who hates evil.
I have already heard the whispers in the wind and been indignant at night,
stroking my short staff and pondering.
Moreover, a grand decree has now arrived,
which truly concerns the imperial
altars.
Now I respectfully follow the imperial order to advance,
setting out at dawn.
Your subject is inherently humble and insignificant,
with no grand aspirations in his youth.
By circumstance and opportunity,
I have taken my place among the highest officials.
My ordinary aspirations are already fulfilled,
my heart is truly content.
How could I seek unhoped-for achievements
or desire extraordinary favor?
It is simply because rampant weeds are difficult to remove,
and evil should be eradicated swiftly.
Therefore, I disregard all dangers,
and my thoughts do not extend to my own safety.
I humbly rely on Your Majesty's heavenly favor
to clearly discern my sincere devotion.
If my loyal sincerity is not illuminated,
I willingly accept punishment and death.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty first consider the prime minister's selfless and noble principles,
and finally acknowledge your insignificant subject's humble sincerity in serving the nation.
Do not follow the ignoble
feelings
and lose the hopes of the four seas.
If you display the execution of Mǎ Jiàn
and openly expose it in the market and court,
then banners will gather towards the capital,
and the forces will return triumphantly.
The myriad people will be in order,
and the three luminaries will shine
together.
This will bring joy to the ancestral temples above
and satisfy the common people below.
Writing this memorial fills me with emotion;
my tearful words are endless.
He appointed Lǔ Hóng as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
to garrison Dàléi below.
He sent a hasty report to Yìxuān.
Yìxuān dispatched Cányì Cānjūn Liú Chénzhī with ten thousand men to join Hóng.
Shìzǔ sent Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn Liǔ Yuánjǐng to lead the naval forces of Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Xuánmó and others,
to garrison Liángshān Zhōunèi.
Crescent-shaped fortifications were built on both banks,
awaiting them by land and water.
Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn Shěn Língcì led a hundred boats
and defeated their vanguard at Nánlíng,
capturing alive the military commander Xú Qìng'ān and the military deputy Wáng Sēng.
When Zhì arrived at Liángshān,
he also arrayed his forces along both banks.
Yuánjǐng issued a proclamation stating: Indeed, to reform the Way and respond to the mandate
is the grand symbol of establishing a destiny;
to succeed in the enterprise and build the nation
is the clear calculation for inheriting a legacy.
Unless one has accumulated auspiciousness in their divine heart
and their virtue fills the highest point of the people,
who
could ascend to the precious throne
and be a brilliant example in the heavenly abode?
Since the founding of Dà Sòng,
its governance has been exalted above previous eras.
The imperial roots and branches
will flow eternally without end.
Barbarians have come repeatedly,
encountering this
Calamities and difficulties,
national misfortune and deep grievances,
human relations utterly extinguished.
The Emperor, with sagely strategies and martial wisdom,
whose filial piety moved the spirits,
whose righteousness transformed flora,
whose sorrow stirred the constellations,
personally proceeded to
Yǐng,
personally suppressed the great rebels,
aided the rampant disorder with his Way,
and modeled his Virtue on divine creation.
The Three Luminaries shone anew,
the Seven Ancestral Temples were revived.
Zāng Zhì, since his youth, had been full of flaws and transgressions,
unworthy of his official status,
blinded by greed and slandering Heaven,
manifesting in every action.
When appointed to office and performing duties,
he did not prioritize achieving results;
when assigned to a region
and governing the people,
he only focused on exploitation.
Offices were gained through bribery,
clans were ruined by graft.
Thus, Kāng Zhōu's family was slaughtered, his clan eradicated,
their grievances reaching the Azure Heavens;
Guō Bó and
Xīmén Yí, though from humble origins,
their favor surpassed that of provincial officials.
When he previously governed the Eastern Commandery,
he sold three thousand official titles.
Leading troops on a western punitive expedition,
he secretly took captives and was then dismissed.
Having received favor in
Péng and Sì,
he indulged in greed and cruelty,
massacring border commoners
as if they were grass,
depleting granaries,
and embezzling military provisions.
When serving as governor of Hànnán,
he openly stole from the government treasury,
falsified and altered
official records,
and engaged purely in deceit.
When he received the order for the Northern Expedition,
he feared the task and delayed the date;
though the army was dispatched at the appointed time,
he indulged his private affections,
abandoned his troops with a single horse,
and returned alone at night,
then resumed embracing concubines
and indulging in banquets in the military camp.
The treachery of Kǒng and Fàn
was evident in his rebellious words.
All these transgressions
are clearly documented in the imperial records,
and widely exposed for
all to see and hear.
Last year's righteous uprising,
though he initially pledged loyalty,
he lingered in Xīchǔ,
secretly supporting and extolling others,
sending letters to pledge allegiance,
revealing his true intentions.
At the victory of Xīntíng,
when the great calamity had been quelled,
and the wicked fate was tenuously maintained,
hanging by a moment,
and the army of Guǎngmò
had not even a single arrow left,
the heavy gates opened by themselves,
and the rebel forces had already collapsed,
Zhì still idled
in winding alleys,
and deployed his cavalry.
His merits were insufficient to be distinguished,
as determined by court deliberation,
yet he exaggerated his achievements,
and incited words of resentment,
claiming that in this endeavor,
no one's achievements
matched his own.
Upon first entering the imperial guard,
he forgot his loyalty,
rushed to the imperial treasury,
and thoroughly depleted the national wealth.
The Emperor, with a magnanimous heart like mountains and seas,
embraced his shortcomings and concealed his faults,
recognizing his single-minded
loyalty,
and overlooking his unworthy transgressions.
Consequently, he was granted the highest noble ranks,
and his official position was among the most distinguished,
his favor and honors overflowing,
with no one to rival him.
Yet he indulged in his ugliness and baseness,
knowing no bounds,
endlessly
soliciting and making requests,
without any limit,
requesting music that exhausted the finest talents of Dàyǔ,
and seeking artifacts that depleted the best selections from government stores.
Xú Sīkōng faithfully served the imperial house,
but encountered
dire misfortune;
Zhì and he grew up together,
their close friendship was beyond ordinary,
yet he showed no benevolence in caring for the orphan,
only cruel oppression,
not a single inch of land or a single treasure
was left untouched.
When he received the order to go south,
his actions on the road became even worse,
forcibly seizing wives and concubines,
and looting gold and silk,
causing resentment throughout the capital,
and scandalous rumors in both city and countryside.
He cast aside old friends
and scorned the loyal
and diligent;
those like Lǔ Shàngqī and Yǐn Zhōu,
whom he relied on as his confidantes,
wept and pleaded before the imperial presence;
those like Yuán Tóng and Lián Zǐjìng,
whom he depended on as his vital forces,
once they left, never
returned.
Although the imperial decree repeatedly urged,
and repeatedly requested reports on meritorious service,
Zhì only claimed that the campaign was his responsibility,
and did not involve his subordinates,
blaming the court,
and faulting the responsible officials,
causing the worthy men of the state to lose
heart,
and the intelligent to distance themselves.
Hé Wénjìng, who was a humble servant,
was naturally foolish and cunning;
Zhì was deluded by his flattery,
and entrusted his confidence to him,
allowing him to wield external authority and punishment,
and internally frequent
his private chambers.
Zhì was born with transgressions,
which are too numerous to detail;
pulling out a single hair for each crime would not even
suffice to speak of them.
The Chancellor, being weighty and of high position,
held a divided governorship,
relied upon by the imperial house,
truly combining affection
and duty, yet he did not follow the path of humility,
nor did he heed the warnings about rebellion and submission,
being as deluded as Xì Zhì,
and his principles diverging from Fàn Xiè.
Thus, he neglected the long-term imperial succession,
and was recently deceived and framed,
relying on treacherous memorials,
and even conspiring against the state.
Previously, he indulged in pleasure and ease in the upper
reaches of the river,
observing success or failure from afar,
showing his dispatch of weary troops,
numbering only three thousand,
without providing warhorses,
or offering military provisions.
The imperial court, solely due to the importance of his familial rank,
rewarded him with extreme
favor,
recently treating him as a close relative,
with courtesies beyond the usual,
even if his insight was lacking,
and his achievements were not his own,
he would surely be incomplete in righteousness,
and ultimately ruin his virtue.
This current defiance of orders
stems from deep resentment,
and looking back at previous years,
his actions were sincerely wrong.
Moreover, with the state in peril,
the circumstances were extraordinary,
all officials and subjects
should have rushed forth like stars,
yet he indulged
the rebels and forgot sorrow,
showing no urgency.
He guarded the frontier for ten years,
yet no benevolent policies were heard of,
only heavy extortion and deep plunder,
indulging his desires excessively,
with a hundred rooms for concubines,
and thousands of Buddhist nuns and monks.
They have ruined the Dao and injured customs,
perverted humans and spirits,
popular resentment fills the roads,
and the country's disgrace spreads for years.
Moreover, the bandit Shào (劭) is not yet captured,
his fierce power is still strong.
We shall destroy his private tombs
and execute his
sons,
planning to achieve a terrifying outcome.
Relying on this righteous endeavor,
the victory is said to be swift,
peace will be announced within days,
the heart's resentment and poison will be released,
and the urgent crisis of being hung upside down will be resolved.
Considering benevolence and virtue,
nurturing and upbringing are paramount.
To help others is to help oneself;
to abandon others is to indulge slander.
To rely on chaos and doubt merit
is unheard of.
I, though unworthy,
have been overly granted undeserved favor,
bearing a promotion that elevates me,
my brilliance is unmatched among my peers.
My family originates from the northern frontier,
my will is resolute and generous,
I am always willing to sacrifice my life
to die for
hardship and peril.
Only thinking of grace and fearing difficulty,
my spirit is stirred and rushes through my breast.
Therefore, I gaze upon the Sānxiāng (三湘) with perpetual lament,
and look towards Jiǔjiāng (九江) with distant indignation.
If my death could bring peace to the country,
I swear to
perish.
Moreover, I receive the sagely strategies from above
and command righteous disciples below;
this is a situation of complete victory,
even a fool can see it.
Fú Xuē Jìnglíng (薛竟陵) is leading his elite cavalry,
〔二一〕and marching on foot
by land.
Tán Yòuwèi (檀右衞), Shēn Yòushuài (申右率), and Yuán Yóují (垣游擊) are marshaling their sharp troops,
advancing rapidly by wheeled carriages.
Wáng Yùzhōu (王豫州) has been preparing his fleet and armor,
and has long since moved forward.
I am training
my soldiers and sharpening my weapons,
advancing like lightning over the waves.
Shěn Zhènjūn (沈鎮軍) and Xiāo Ānnán (蕭安南) are joining their ships stem to stern, their banners connected,
their front and rear converging like the wind.
The Píqi Jìnglíng Wáng Yì (驃騎竟陵王懿) has admirable personal renown,
his reputation
is universally respected;
the Dàsīmǎ Jiāngxià Wáng Dàolüè (大司馬江夏王道略) has brilliant and far-reaching strategies,
his admirable conduct is prominent in this generation.
Both are now leading their forces on the road,
advancing together like gathering clouds.
The myriad soldiers compete in their advance,
the imperial carriage slowly
sets off.
The eight bells jingle,
the five ox-drawn carriages spread their banners.
A thousand chariots move like thunder,
ten thousand ships turn back like clouds.
Displaying might and issuing commands,
like stars falling and the Milky Way turning.
To conquer those below from above
is as
easy as turning a wheel.
Furthermore, three strategists concur,
seven constellations portend good fortune;
the hidden and the manifest are of one mind,
clearly and easily seen.
All of you gentlemen, some have generations of imperial favor,
others have personally heard the teachings of righteousness.
You should know the great principle of lord and minister,
which must not be violated.
The profound instruction of cap and shoes [metaphor for hierarchy]
cannot be inverted.
To live in peace and obey,
your reputation will be secure and your affairs complete.
How does this compare to attaching yourselves to rebels and residing in peril,
harming yourselves and defiling your names,
with your kind parents, white-haired, suffering execution,
and your young children and infants facing slaughter?
Therefore,
the imperial edict delays,
not yet unleashing thunderous wrath,
precisely because you gentlemen are held captive by the bandits,
or harbor similar thoughts.
Good fortune and misfortune are determined by humans;
do not say it is far off.
If you do not
change now,
what regret will there be later?
On the day the proclamation was issued,
my heart sped to the bandit's court.
Yìxuān (義宣) also arrived shortly after, bound.
Jiāngxià Wáng (江夏王) wrote to Yìxuān (義宣), saying:
“Húán Xuán (桓玄) borrowed troops from Zhòngkān (仲堪) in the past,
which is similar to today.”
Yìxuān (義宣) thus became suspicious of Zhì (質).
Zhì (質) put forth a plan, saying:
“If we now take Nánzhōu (南州) with ten thousand men,
then Liángshān (梁山) will be cut off.
Ten thousand men will hold Xuánmó (玄謨),
who will certainly not dare to move.
I will sail boats on the outer river,
directly towards Shítóu (石頭);
this is the superior strategy.”
Yìxuān (義宣) was about to follow it,
but his confidant Liú Chénzhī (劉諶之) said:
“Zhì (質) seeks to advance first;
his intentions are hard to fathom.
It is better to use all our elite forces to attack Liángshān (梁山).
Once that is conquered, then we can drive forward;
this is a plan for complete safety.”
Zhì (質) sent his general Yǐn Zhōuzhī (尹周之) to attack Hú Zǐfǎn (胡子反) and Liǔ Shúzhèng (柳叔政) at the west encampment.
〔二二〕At that time, Zǐfǎn (子反) had crossed to the east bank to consult with Xuánmó (玄謨) on strategy.
Upon hearing that the enemy had arrived,
he rushed back.
Zhōuzhī (周之)'s attack on the encampment was very fierce.
Liú Jìzhī (劉季之)'s naval forces fought desperately.
The enemy's momentum was strong,
and they sought help from Xuánmó (玄謨).
Xuánmó (玄謨) did not send aid.
Cuī Xūnzhī (崔勳之) firmly argued for it,
so Xuánmó (玄謨) then dispatched Xūnzhī (勳之) to relieve them.
By the time he arrived,
the city had already fallen.
Xūnzhī (勳之) died in battle.
Jìzhī (季之) gathered his troops and retreated.
Zǐfǎn (子反) and Shúzhèng (叔政) fled back to the east bank.
Xuánmó (玄謨) executed Zǐfǎn (子反)'s deputy general Lǐ Wénzhòng (李文仲).
Zhì (質) wanted to continue attacking the east city.
Yìxuān (義宣)'s partisan Yán Lèzhī (顏樂之) persuaded Yìxuān (義宣), saying:
“If Zhì (質) captures the east city again,
then all the great merit will belong to him.
You should send your own subordinates to go.”
Yìxuān (義宣) sent Liú Chénzhī (劉諶之) to join Zhì (質)
and arrayed the troops south of the city.
Xuánmó (玄謨) left the weak and infirm to guard the city
and sent all his elite troops out to battle.
Xuē Āndū (薛安都)'s cavalry advanced first.
Yuán Hùzhī (垣護之) commanded his generals to follow.
After a long battle,
the enemy's formation slightly broke,
and the cavalry was able to enter.
Liú Jìzhī (劉季之) and Zōng Yuè (宗越) also broke through their northwest,
and the allied forces pressed on,
resulting in a great rout.
Taking advantage of the wind, they set fires,
and all the ships and boats were burned,
extending to the west bank.
Zhì (質) sought Yìxuān (義宣) to discuss a plan,
but he had already secretly fled.
Zhì (質) did not know what to do,
and also fled;
all the troops surrendered or dispersed.
When Zhì (質) reached Xúnyáng (尋陽),
he burned down the government offices
and fled west with his concubines.
He made his favorite Hé Wénjìng (何文敬) lead the troops in front,
reaching Xīyáng (西陽).
The administrator of Xīyáng (西陽), Lǔ Fāngpíng (魯方平),
was a partisan of Zhì (質),
but at this point, he harbored disloyalty
and deceived Wénjìng (文敬), saying:
“The imperial edict proclaims
that only the chief culprit is to be arrested;
the rest will not be interrogated.”
Wénjìng (文jìng) abandoned his troops and fled.
Zāng Zhì had previously made his sister's husband, Yáng Chōng, the Administrator of Wǔchāng Commandery.
Zāng Zhì went to seek refuge with him.
Upon his arrival,
Yáng Chōng had already been killed by Hú Bì, the Commandery Assistant.
Having nowhere to go,
Zāng Zhì entered Nánhú to flee and hide.
Without food,
he plucked and ate lotus roots.
When the pursuing soldiers arrived,
in his desperation,
he covered his head with lotus leaves
and sank himself into the water,
leaving only his nose exposed.
Zhèng Jù'ér, a military commander, spotted him,
shot him directly in the center of his body,
and weapons rained down upon him.
His intestines were entangled with the aquatic plants.
Qiú Yīng, a company commander, beheaded Zāng Zhì
and sent it to the capital.
He was fifty-five years old at the time.
Jiāngxiàwáng Chén Yìgōng, a Recording Secretary of the Department of State Affairs, and Zuǒ Púyè Chén Hóng, among others, memorialized, saying:
"Zāng Zhì, though of lowly talent,
was given great trust.
Yet in his foolishness, he defied convention,
inciting grave rebellion.
The calamity reached sky-high proportions.
His ambition was to annihilate the Jià dynasty,
betraying kindness and morality.
His crimes exceed the statutes.
The law of displaying a head on a stake
is a common ordinance for all states.
To deter wickedness and ensure lasting peace,
the removal of evil must be thorough.
We, your ministers, have discussed the matter
and believe that the period of exposure should be determined,
and that following the precedent of Wáng Mǎng of the Hàn dynasty,
his head should be lacquered
and stored in the Imperial Armory.
This would serve as a warning
and a clear lesson for the future."
An imperial edict approved this.
When Zāng Zhì first surrendered,
Yìxuān had made Zāng Zhì's son, Dūn, General Who Conquers the Barbarians and Inspector of Yōngzhōu.
Zāng Zhì left his son Chǎng as Supervising General
and took Dūn with him.
At this time, both were captured and delivered by the Wǔchāng Commandery.
Dūn's highest office was Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
Dūn's younger brother, Fū,
was an Aide to the Grand Minister of Works.
Fū's younger brother, Chǎng,
was a Palace Attendant for the Crown Prince.
Chǎng's younger brother, Yì,
and Dūn's son, Zhòngzhāng,
along with two other unnamed sons and two unnamed grandsons of Zāng Zhì,
were all executed.
When Zāng Zhì raised his army,
Rèn Huìzhī, Administrator of Yùzhāng; Liú Huáizhī, Grand Administrator of Línchuān; and Dù Zhòngrú, Administrator of Póyáng, all exerted their utmost effort
by dispatching soldiers from their commanderies
and sending grain and supplies.
They were executed.
Rèn Huìzhī's courtesy name was Chùmào,
and he was from Lè'ān.
He successively served Shìzǔ, Nánpíngwáng Shuò as Right Military Commandant of the Pacifying Army, and as acting Chief Clerk.
Tàizǔ praised him, saying:
"Though his appearance is not outstanding,
his talent is more than sufficient."
Dù Zhòngrú
was the nephew of Dù Jì.
Chōngzhī, the grandson of Xiàng, from Wàngcài in Yùzhāng, raised a righteous army to resist Zāng Zhì.
〔二三〕Zāng Zhì sent his generals Guō Huìfū and Shǐ Shānfū to attack him,
but they were defeated by Chōngzhī.
Shìzǔ issued an edict making him Langzhong of the Capital Affairs Bureau of the Department of State Affairs.
Chōngzhī was
from Zhōngdū in Tàiyuán,
and a great-grandson of Shèng, the Jin Secretariat Director.
He rose to the office of Right Army General
and Administrator of Bādōng.
Later events are recorded in the Biography of Dèng Wǎn.
〔二四〕Shěn Língcì was enfeoffed as Baron of Nánpíng County
with an income of three hundred households
for his merit in defeating Zāng Zhì's vanguard at Nánlíng.
Cuī Xūnzhī was posthumously granted the title of 通直郎 (Tōngzhí Láng).
Liú Tiāncì, a staff officer to the Grand Marshal, also died in battle at Liángshān
and was posthumously granted the title of Attendant Official.
Lǔ Shuǎng's childhood name was Nǚshēng,
and he was from Méi in Fúfēng.
His grandfather, Zōngzhī, whose courtesy name was Yànrén,
at the end of Jin Xiàowǔ's Tàiyuán era,
left his hometown for Xiāngyáng,
and successively held office up to Administrator of Nánjùn.
In the first year of Yìxī, he raised an army
and attacked Huán Wèi, the bogus Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
then advanced towards Jiānglíng.
For his achievements, he was made General Who Supports the State and Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiāochéng County,
with an income of one thousand five hundred households.
When Huán Qiān and Xún Lín pressed Jiānglíng,
Zōngzhī led his troops to rush to its aid.
This event is recorded in the Biography of Línchuān Lièwǔwáng Dàoguī.
He was promoted to General Who Pacifies the North.
When Gāozǔ campaigned against Liú Yì,
he and Zōngzhī met in Jiānglíng.
He was promoted to General Who Guards the North
and enfeoffed as Duke of Nányáng Commandery,
with an income of two thousand five hundred households.
His son, Guǐ, also named Xiàngchǐ,
was Lǔ Shuǎng's father.
He was skilled in archery and horsemanship,
and his physical strength surpassed others.
He served as Administrator of Jìnglíng.
Zōngzhī, feeling that he was not among Gāozǔ's old subordinates,
and having repeatedly achieved great merits,
developed self-doubt.
When Sīmǎ Xiūzhī was being campaigned against,
he became suspicious and fearful,
and consequently fled north with Sīmǎ Xiūzhī.
He was skilled in governing and pacifying,
and all his officers and people exerted themselves for him,
escorting him out of the territory.
He and his entire family entered Qiāng territory,
and he died of illness a short while later.
When Gāozǔ pacified Cháng'ān,
Guǐ was made General Who Pacifies the South, Inspector of Jīngzhōu, and Duke of Xiāngyáng,
stationed at Chángshè.
When Shìzǔ was stationed in Xiāngyáng,
Guǐ sent his confidant Chéng Zhěng with a letter,
planning to surrender,
to extricate himself and show his sincerity.
He had not surrendered earlier because he had previously killed Liú Kāngzǔ and the father of Xú Zhànzhī.
Tàizǔ repeatedly sent envoys to invite and receive him,
promising to make him Inspector of Sīzhōu.
Lǔ Shuǎng 魯爽 was skilled in martial arts from a young age.
The barbarian ruler Tuòbá Táo 拓跋燾 knew this,
and always kept him by his side.
In Yuánjiā 元嘉 twenty-sixth year (449 CE),
Lǔ Guǐ 魯軌 died.
Lǔ Shuǎng 魯爽 was made General Who Pacifies the South, Governor of Jīngzhōu 荊州, and Duke of Xiāngyáng 襄陽,
and garrisoned Chángshè 長社.
He had been influenced by barbarian customs since childhood,
and no longer possessed the refinement of the Chinese.
He was rude and prone to drunkenness,
and frequently made mistakes.
Tuòbá Táo 拓跋燾 intended to execute him.
Lǔ Shuǎng 魯爽 had seven younger brothers; the seventh was Xiù 秀,
whose childhood name was Tiānnian 天念.
He had considerable strategic acumen,
and his talent and strength surpassed Lǔ Shuǎng's 魯爽.
Tuòbá Táo 拓跋燾 appointed him to the Imperial Guard,
and treated him with great favor.
The pseudo-King of Gāoliáng 高梁, Āshūní 阿叔泥, was severely besieged by the Rèiruì 芮芮,
[二五]so Tuòbá Táo 拓跋燾 sent Xiù 秀 to rescue him,
and personally led a large army to follow.
Before Tuòbá Táo 拓跋燾 arrived,
Xiù 秀 had already defeated them,
rescuing Āshūní 阿叔泥 and returning.
Tuòbá Táo 拓跋燾 admired his achievement,
appointed him Central Secretariat Director,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Guǎnglíng 廣陵.
Someone reported to Tuòbá Táo 拓跋燾
that the people of Yè 鄴 intended to seize the city and rebel.
He again dispatched Xiù 秀 to investigate,
and also to burn the remaining palaces of Shí Hǔ 石虎.
Xiù 秀 usually traveled back and forth by post-horse,
but this time he returned late due to illness,
and was rebuked by Tuòbá Táo 拓跋燾.
Xiù 秀 again became fearful.
Tuòbá Táo 拓跋燾 soon invaded the south,
and Xiù 秀 consequently crossed the river with him.
Previously,
Chéng Tiānzuò 程天祚 had been captured by the barbarians.
Tuòbá Táo 拓跋燾 brought him to his side,
and arranged a meeting with Xiù 秀,
[二六]advising him to surrender.
Xiù 秀 accepted this.
Chéng Tiānzuò 程天祚,
a native of Guǎngpíng 廣平,
was a Palace General,
and possessed martial strength.
In Yuánjiā 元嘉 twenty-seventh year (450 CE),
he assisted in garrisoning Péngchéng 彭城.
At that time, Emperor Shìzǔ 世祖 dispatched General Liú Tàizhī 劉泰之 with light forces to raid the barbarians at Rǔyáng 汝陽.
[二七]Chéng Tiānzuò 程天祚 oversaw the battle,
was defeated and wounded,
[二八]and captured by the barbarians.
Chéng Tiānzuò 程天祚 was skilled in acupuncture,
and Tuòbá Táo 拓跋燾 greatly appreciated and admired him.
Sometimes he shared a carriage with him,
[二九]and he was always by his side,
enfeoffed as Duke of Nán'ān 南安.
When Tuòbá Táo 拓abá Táo 拓跋燾 returned north to his domain,
[三０]Chéng Tiānzuò 程天祚, taking advantage of his intoxication,
pretended to be an emissary sent to oversee and urge on the rear army.
Wherever he went, he imposed light punishments.
Chéng Tiānzuò 程天祚 was favored by Tuòbá Táo 拓跋燾,
and all the barbarians feared him,
none daring to question him.
Thus, he managed to escape and return,
later becoming Grand Administrator of Shānyáng 山陽.
In the early reign of Tàizōng 太宗,
he rebelled along with various regions,
[三一]an event detailed in the biography of Xuē Āndū 薛安都.
When Tuòbá Táo 拓跋燾 first marched south,
he sent Lǔ Shuǎng 魯爽 to follow Prince Yǒngchāng 永昌, Kùrénzhēn 庫仁真, towards Shòuyáng 壽陽.
With his brother Yú 瑜, he defeated Liú Kāngzǔ 劉康祖 at Wèiwǔ 尉武,
then proceeded to Guānbù 瓜步.
It was then that he was able to finalize the plan to return south with Xiù 秀.
When Tuòbá Táo 拓跋燾 returned to Húlù 湖陸,
Lǔ Shuǎng 魯爽 and others requested:
"We have an enmity with the south.
Each time their army comes,
we constantly fear harm to our ancestral tombs.
We beg to escort the coffins together
and rebury them in the national capital."
The barbarian subjects referred to themselves as 'nú 奴' (slave) to their ruler,
just as the Chinese referred to themselves as 'chén 臣' (subject).
Tuòbá Táo 拓跋燾 granted permission.
There were six or seven hundred barbarian soldiers garrisoned at Chángshè 長社.
Lǔ Shuǎng 魯爽 deceived them, saying:
"There is another army from the south;
we can send three hundred cavalry to the border to inquire."
When the cavalry left,
Lǔ Shuǎng 魯爽 led his trusted followers in a night attack on the remaining barbarians,
killing them all,
and galloped into Hǔláo 虎牢.
Only Lǔ Shuǎng's 魯爽 third younger brother remained in the north;
the rest of his family followed him,
and he led his retainers and over a thousand willing families to Rǔnán 汝南.
He sent Xiù 秀 to return from Xǔchāng 許昌 to Shòuyáng 壽陽,
to convey a message to Prince Nánpíng 南平, Shuò 鑠, saying:
"Lǔ Shuǎng 魯爽 and Lǔ Xiù 魯秀 offended the Jìn 晉 dynasty,
[三二]accumulating three generations of grievances.
Born and raised in a remote land,
we have estranged ourselves among the barbarians.
My brothers and our whole household
have been defiled by false appointments.
Death is unacceptable,
and there is no way to return to our country.
Recently, we have been yearning for the southern clouds,
our whole family longing for the eastern sun.
It is like a crippled person wishing to walk,
or a blind person desiring sight.
Sōng 嵩 and Huò 霍 are close at hand,
the Jiāng 江 and Hé 河 are not far,
yet the barbarian barriers are blocked,
separating us as if by heaven and earth.
We are heartbroken and distressed,
grieving day and night.
The barbarian ruler is frenzied,
with the ambition of a jackal or wild boar.
His tyranny has spread throughout Huá 華 and Róng 戎,
and resentment has accumulated in both the visible and invisible worlds.
Since his army turned back from Xūyí 盱眙,
more than half have perished.
He is obsessed with heavy drinking,
indulging his nature and abandoning himself.
Lǔ Shuǎng 魯爽, Lǔ Xiù 魯秀, and others, taking advantage of the people's indignation,
and relying on the desires of the generals and soldiers,
unanimously pledged allegiance and rose up in righteousness,
slaying the heads of the ugly villains.
Relying on imperial prestige,
we will cleanse the remaining filth.
Láo 牢 and Luò 洛, and other cities,
are scheduled to be conquered and secured.
We aim, like a drop of dust,
to slightly wipe away our past transgressions.
We are prepared to present our remains before the northern palace gate,
awaiting execution by the Minister of Justice,
though our weak resolve has not yet been expressed.
We respectfully submit our intentions from the border.
May Your Royal Highness, the sagacious King, residing in your fief,
possessing both literary and martial talents,
admired by those near and far,
and known for your virtuous reputation,
deign to extend your aid and rescue,
to comfort our devout hopes.
A hundred elderly and weak individuals
have been sent ahead to seek refuge.
Our fervent hearts
look up to you, hoping you will embrace those from afar.
We respectfully send the righteous Nǐ Yuánchū 聶元初 of Yǐngchuān 潁川 to present this message."
Shuò 鑠 dispatched a courier to report it.
The Emperor was greatly pleased
and issued an edict saying:
"The pseudo-General Who Pacifies the South, Lǔ Shuǎng 魯爽, and Central Secretariat Director, Lǔ Xiù 魯秀,
have displayed outstanding resolve
and long-standing loyalty.
They have pacified this blessed land,
and their whole household has submitted.
They have gathered righteous and sharp forces,
slaying and beheading the Hūnxūn 獯醜 (barbarian) villains,
securing the border cities,
and presenting heads at the象wèi Xiàngwèi (imperial gate).
Though Xuān Mèng 宣孟 left Zhái 翟 to return to Jìn 晉,
and Tuí Dāng 頹當 emerged from among the Hú 胡 to enter Hàn 漢,
compared to this day,
how could they be mentioned?
We truly commend them,
and they should be immediately appointed
to fulfill their loyal strategies.

Lǔ Shuǎng 魯爽 is appointed Area Commander of the military affairs of Chénliú 陳留, Dōngjùn 東郡, Jìyīn 濟陰, and Púyáng 濮陽 prefectures in Sīzhōu 司州 and Yùzhōu 豫州, General Who Conquers Barbarians, and Governor of Sīzhōu 司州.
[三三]Lǔ Xiù 魯秀 is appointed General Who Upholds the State and Grand Administrator of Xíngyáng 滎陽 and Yǐngchuān 潁川 prefectures.
[三四]His other sons, younger brothers, nephews, and those who share their purpose, both scholars and commoners,
are to be entrusted to the General Who Conquers Barbarians' office to report in due course,
and they shall be amply rewarded."
When Lǔ Shuǎng 魯爽 arrived at Rǔnán 汝南,
he was additionally appointed Area Commander of the military affairs of Yìyáng 義陽 and Sòng'ān 宋安 prefectures in Yùzhōu 豫ū,
and concurrently Administrator of Yìyáng 義陽.
His general and governor titles remained as before.
Xiù 秀 participated in the military affairs of the Right General, Prince Nánpíng 南平, Shuò 鑠, and was Administrator of Rǔyīn 汝陰.
His general title remained as before.
His other younger brothers and nephews were all granted official ranks and titles,
and were generously rewarded and provided for.
Lǔ Shuǎng 魯爽 garrisoned Yìyáng 義陽 in the north.
A total of six thousand eight hundred and eighty-three retainers came from the north.
This was the twenty-eighth year (451 CE).
The barbarians destroyed their ancestral tombs.
In the fourth month of the following year, he entered the court.
By then, Táo had died.
The Emperor then re-planned the campaign.
In the fifth month,
he dispatched Shuǎng, Xiù, Chéng Tiānzuò, and others to lead infantry and cavalry, along with 40,000 armored soldiers from Jīngzhōu,
to march out from Xǔ and Luò.
In the eighth month,
the barbarian garrison commander of Chángshè, Yǒngpíng Gōng Tūfà Fānnǎi, abandoned the city and fled with them.
They advanced towards Dàsuǒ garrison.
The garrison commander, the pseudo-Prefect of Yùzhōu, Bá Púlán, said:
"Shuǎng is brave but lacks caution.
If I go out of the city now,
he will surely lightly come to occupy it.
If we set an ambush at Tánshān,
we will surely capture him."
Shuǎng indeed advanced at night.
Xiù advised him against it but could not stop him,
and rode to follow him.
By dawn,
the barbarian cavalry launched a pincer attack.
Fortunately, Xiù deployed his troops and fought bravely,
and the barbarians then retreated to Hǔláo.
Shuǎng then pressed the attack.
The original plan was for the naval force to enter the river
and cut off their water gate.
Wáng Xuánmó attacked Què'áo but failed to take it
and retreated.
The naval force did not arrive.
Shuǎng also gathered his forces and returned south.
After fighting for several hundred li,
they reached Qǔqiáng.
The barbarians, observing their hunger and exhaustion,
came with full force to attack.
Shuǎng personally fought with great vigor,
and the barbarians then retreated.
In the 30th year,
the prime culprit committed regicide.
Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān raised an army to suppress the rebellion.
Shuǎng immediately accepted the order
and led his troops to Xiāngyáng,
and together with the Prefect of Yōngzhōu, Zāng Zhì, proceeded to Jiānglíng.
Yìxuān promoted Shuǎng to the title of Píngběi Jiāngjūn
and appointed him as the Administrator of Bālíng
and Superintendent of Expenditures,
while his original office remained.
Shuǎng was kept at Jiānglíng.
After the matter was settled,
Shuǎng was made Envoy with Imperial Authority, Supervising Military Affairs of Yù, Sī, Yōng, Qín, and Bìng Five Provinces, Left General, and Prefect of Yùzhōu.
When Shuǎng arrived at Shòuyáng,
he immediately showed special favor to his retainers,
bestowed ranks and titles upon scholars,
and accumulated weapons and horses,
as if an enemy was about to arrive.
When the prime culprit committed regicide,
Xiù was in the capital.
He said to Xiù,
"I have executed Xú Zhànzhī for you.
I will fully entrust you with authority."
He was made Right Army General
and assigned 5,000 elite soldiers
to attack Xīntíng stockade.
Before the battle,
Xiù ordered the retreat drum to be beaten
and consequently surrendered.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was made Left Army General
and dispatched to supervise military affairs of Xīncài, Rǔnán, Rǔyáng, Yǐngchuān, Yìyáng, and Yìyáng Six Commanderies of Sīzhōu and Yùzhōu, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and Prefect of Sīzhōu,
also serving as Administrator of Rǔnán.
Shuǎng had been allied with Yìxuān and Zhì for a long time.
Yìxuān also wished to rely on his bravery and strength,
and their bond was extremely close.
In the second month of Xiàojiàn First Year,
Yìxuān informed Shuǎng
that they would rise together in autumn.
Shuǎng, in a drunken delirium, acted rashly
and raised an army that very day.
He sent a hasty message to his younger brother Yú
and led his family to defect,
all making it back west.
Shuǎng ordered his troops to carry yellow banners,
calling it Jiànpíng First Year.
He secretly made ceremonial robes
and ascended an altar to proclaim himself.
Suspecting that his Chief Clerk Wéi Chǔmù, Staff Officer of the Central Army Yáng Yuánjū, and Administrator Yǔ Téngzhī were not of the same mind as him,
he killed them.
Yìxuān and Zhì, hearing that Shuǎng had already acted,
then hastily rebelled.
They promoted Shuǎng to the title of Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn.
Shuǎng then sent the palanquin and robes he had made to Jiānglíng
and issued proclamations for Yìxuān and Zāng Zhì and others to rise together.
The official document from the Zhēngběi headquarters' registrar said:
"Chancellor Liú, the Heaven-mender,
named Yìxuān,
General of Chariots and Cavalry Zāng, now appointed Chancellor,
named Zhì,
Píngxī Zhū, now appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry,
named Xiūzhī,
all proclaimed and to be obeyed."
Yìxuān was astonished and dismayed.
The ceremonial items sent by Shuǎng
were all detained in Jìnglíng County and not allowed to proceed.
Shuǎng marched directly to Lìyáng,
crossed the river at Cǎishí,
and descended with Zhì both by water and land.
Shuǎng sent his younger brother Yú to guard Ménglóng.
The Administrator of Lìyáng, Zhāng Yòuxù, requested to attack Yú.
Shìzǔ assigned him troops.
He dispatched Left Army General Xuē Āndū with infantry and cavalry as the vanguard,
and separately sent a naval force to enter Yuān,
converging from different routes.
Āndū advanced to Dàxiàn.
Shuǎng had already set up camp.
Shìzǔ, considering the enemy's strong fortifications,
believed they could not be easily taken
and ordered to assess the situation before advancing or stopping.
Yòuxù then led his army back
and was imprisoned.
General of Agile Cavalry Yuán Hùzhī was then sent to replace Yòuxù and hold Lìyáng.
