General of the Garrison Army Shěn Qìngzhī followed Āndū's advance
and encountered Shuǎng at Xiǎoxiàn.
Shuǎng personally went forward.
Before the battle,
he was excessively drunk.
Āndū stabbed Shuǎng, who fell from his horse.
His attendant Fàn Shuāng beheaded him
and sent the head to the capital.
Yú was also beheaded by his subordinates and sent.
The army then advanced and pacified Shòuyáng.
Shuǎng's sons and younger brothers were all executed.
When Yìxuān first raised his army,
he summoned Xiù, granted him imperial authority,
and promoted him to the title of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn,
to descend together with Chénzhī.
However, the Prefect of Yōngzhōu, Zhū Xiūzhī, raised an army in loyal support,
so Xiù was dispatched to attack Xiūzhī instead.
Wáng Xuánmó, hearing this,
rejoiced, saying,
"If Lǔ Xiù does not come,
Zāng Zhì will be easy to deal with."
Xiù arrived at Xiāngyáng,
suffered a great defeat, and returned.
At that time, the Prefect of Yìzhōu, Liú Xiùzhī, sent troops to raid Jiānglíng.
Xiù defeated them.
When Yìxuān returned to Jiānglíng,
Xiù fled north with him.
His troops deserted almost completely.
As Xiù approached the city,
the Emperor shot him,
hitting him with an arrow.
He threw himself into the water and died.
Soldiers Zōng Jìngshū and Kāng Sēngniàn beheaded him
and sent the head to the capital.
Wéi Chǔmù and Yáng Yuánjū were posthumously granted the title of Attendant Official,
and Yǔ Téngzhī that of Supernumerary Cavalry Attendant.
When Shuǎng first returned south,
Xiù, considering Shuǎng a military man
unskilled in civil administration,
requested Tàizǔ to appoint Chǔmù as Chief Clerk to assist Shuǎng.
Tàizǔ appointed him as Army Advisor,
and he was later transferred to Chief Clerk.
Shěn Yōuzhī, courtesy name Zhòngdá,
was a native of Wǔkāng, Wúxīng.
He was the son of Sìkōng Qìngzhī's paternal cousin.
His father, Shú Rén,
served as Western Expedition Chief Clerk for Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì,
also acting as Staff Officer
and leading a detachment.
He also followed Yìjì to garrison Péngchéng
and was transferred to the Zhēngběi headquarters.
Yōu zhī 攸之 was orphaned and poor when young.
In the twenty-seventh year of Yuánjiā 元嘉
the Suǒ Lǔ 索虜 (Tuòbá 拓跋) attacked from the south,
and able-bodied men from the Three Wú 三吳 regions were conscripted.
Yōu zhī 攸之 was also conscripted.
Upon arriving in the capital,
he went to the Commander of the Guards General, Liú Zūnkǎo 劉遵考,
to request an appointment as a leader of the common conscript unit.
Zūnkǎo 遵考 said to him:
"Your appearance is uncomely,
unfit to be a unit leader."
Consequently, he followed Qìngzhī 慶之 on campaigns.
In the twenty-ninth year,
he campaigned against the Xīyáng Mán 西陽蠻,
and was first appointed as a unit leader.
When righteousness was established at Bākǒu 巴口,
he was appointed by the Nán Zhōngláng Fǔ 南中郎府 as a Chancellor,
concurrently serving as a Mobilized Military Advisor.
In the Battle of Xīntíng 新亭,
he suffered serious wounds.
When the situation stabilized,
he became a Grand Commandant's Mobilized Military Advisor,
and was enfeoffed as a Fifth-rank Marquis of Píngluò Xiàn 平洛縣.
He then transferred with the office to become a Grand Marshal's Mobilized Military Advisor.
During the Jìn 晉 dynasty, on the two banks of the capital's waterways,
Yángzhōu 揚州 had previously established the position of Capital Commander-Attendant,
to manage irregularities in the two counties.
After Yǒngchū 永初, the position was abolished.
In the third year of Xiàojiàn 孝建,
the position was re-established.
Yōu zhī 攸之 managed the north bank,
and Kǒng Zǎo 孔璪 of Kuàijī 會稽 managed the south bank.
Yōu zhī 攸之 was promoted to Gentleman-in-Waiting, Provisional Palace Attendant.
Later, it was abolished again.
achieving merits multiple times,
and suffered an arrow wound that broke his bone.
Emperor Shìzǔ 世祖, recognizing his skill in battle,
assigned him to the Chóuchí Bù Shuò 仇池步矟 (Chóuchí infantry spearmen).
When the matter was settled,
he should have received generous rewards,
but was suppressed by Qìngzhī 慶之.
He was promoted to Lieutenant-Commander of the Crown Prince's Imperial Guard,
which Yōu zhī 攸之 greatly resented.
In the seventh year,
he mourned his mother.
After the burial,
he was appointed as General of the Dragon's Might and Magistrate of Wǔkāng 武康.
In the first year of Jǐnghé 景和 of the Former Deposed Emperor,
he was appointed as Military Advisor for the Guards of the Prince Shàng 尚 of Yùzhāng 豫章,
serving as a Direct Palace Guard.
Along with Zōng Yuè 宗越, Tán Jīn 譚金, and others, he was favored by the Deposed Emperor.
In the execution of various dukes,
Yōu zhī 攸之 and others all served his command.
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dōngxīng Xiàn 東興縣,
with a stipend of five hundred households.
Soon after, he was promoted to General of the Right Army,
and his stipend was increased by a hundred households.
When Emperor Tàizōng 太宗 ascended the throne,
his enfeoffment was reduced according to regulations.
Soon after, he reported Zōng Yuè 宗越, Tán Jīn 譚金, and others for plotting rebellion.
and appointed as Administrator of Dōnghǎi 東海.
He had not yet taken up the post.
At that time, rebellions broke out in all four directions,
and the southern rebels had already reached nearby routes.
Yōu zhī 攸之 was appointed General of Pacifying Northern Regions and Administrator of Xúnyáng 尋陽,
leading troops to occupy Hǔlán 虎檻.
At that time, Wáng Xuánmó 王玄謨 was the Grand Commander,
but had not yet departed.
The vanguard consisted of five armies stationed at Hǔlán 虎檻,
and after these five armies, others arrived continuously,
each night establishing their own titles,
not submitting to each other.
Yōu zhī 攸之 said to the military officials:
"Now, the titles of the various armies are not uniform.
If a farmer or fisherman,
were to shout at them at night,
it would lead to panic and disorder,
a sure path to defeat."
So, he went to one army and requested its title,
and everyone followed him.
Yīn Xiàozǔ 殷孝祖 was the vanguard commander,
but had greatly alienated the people's feelings.
Yōu zhī 攸之 internally consoled the officers and soldiers,
and externally harmonized with the various commanders,
and everyone relied on him.
At that time, the vanguard of the southern rebels, Sūn Chōngzhī 孫沖之 and Xuē Chángbǎo 薛常寶, were encamped at Zhèqí 赭圻.
but was struck by a stray arrow and died.
The army commander Fàn Qián 范潛 led five hundred men to defect to the rebels.
People were shocked and dismayed,
and all said that Yōu zhī 攸之 should replace Xiàozǔ 孝祖 as commander.
At that time, Prince Xiūrén 休仁 of Jiàn'ān 建安 was stationed at Hǔlán 虎檻,
commanding all the armies.
he sent General of Pacifying Northern Regions Jiāng Fāngxīng 江方興 and General of the Dragon's Might Liú Língyí 劉靈遺, each leading three thousand men, to Zhèqí 赭圻.
Hearing of Xiàozǔ's 孝祖 death,
the rebels would have a victorious momentum.
If they did not attack again the next day,
it would show weakness.
Fāngxīng's 方興 rank and position were similar,
so he would certainly not submit to him.
Disunity in military command
would lead to defeat.
So, he led the various army commanders to Fāngxīng 方興 and said to him:
"The four directions are all in rebellion.
The state's protected territory
is no longer even a hundred *lǐ* 里.
Only Yīn Xiàozǔ 殷孝祖 was relied upon by the court,
but as soon as weapons clashed,
his corpse was carried back.
Both civil and military officials are disheartened,
and the court and commoners are anxious.
Whether the matter succeeds or fails
depends solely on a single battle tomorrow morning.
If the battle is not victorious,
then the great cause is lost.
Regarding tomorrow's affair,
everyone says I should command it.
I judge myself to be timid and weak,
and my military strategy is not as good as yours.
Therefore, I now recommend you as commander.
We must only work together with concerted effort."
Fāngxīng 方興 was very pleased.
After Yōu zhī 攸之 left,
the various army commanders all criticized him.
Yōu zhī 攸之 said:
"Have you forgotten the matters of Lián 廉, Lìn 藺, Kòu 寇, and Jiǎ 賈?
My original intention was to save the country and preserve our homes.
Why should I calculate our respective rises and falls?
Moreover, I can submit to him,
but he certainly cannot submit to me.
how can one differentiate between oneself and others?"
The next morning, they advanced to battle.
From *yín* 寅 (3-5 AM) until *wǔ* 午 (11 AM-1 PM),
they greatly defeated the rebels outside Zhèqí Chéng 赭圻城.
They pursued the fleeing enemy to Mǔ Shān 姥山.
They dispatched naval forces to press the attack,
and also defeated their naval forces,
capturing Hú Bái Èr Chéng 胡白二城.
Soon after, Yōu zhī 攸之 was granted the *jié* 節 (credentials),
promoted to General of Protecting the State,
and replaced Xiàozǔ 孝祖 as commander of the vanguard armies.
Xuē Chángbǎo 薛常寶 at Zhèqí 赭圻 ran out of food.
The great southern rebel commander Liú Hú 劉胡 was encamped at Nóng Hú 濃湖.
He filled bags with rice and tied them to drifting rafts and the hulls of boats,
pretending the boats had capsized,
and let them drift downstream with the wind,
to provision Zhèqí 赭圻.
Yōu zhī 攸之 suspected something unusual,
and sent men to retrieve the boats and rafts,
finding a large quantity of bagged rice.
Yōu zhī's 攸之 cousin, Huáibǎo 懷寶,
who was a rebel general,
was at Zhèqí 赭圻.
He sent his confidant Yáng Gōngzàn 楊公讚 with a secret letter to induce Yōu zhī 攸之.
Yōu zhī 攸之 executed Gōngzàn 公讚,
and sealed Huáibǎo's 懷寶 letter to present to Emperor Tàizōng 太宗.
Soon after, they captured Zhèqí 赭圻.

He was promoted to Bearer of Credentials, Area Commander of the armies of Yōng 雍, Liáng 梁, Southern Qín 南秦, Northern Qín 北秦, and the Jìnglíng 竟陵 region of Yǐngzhōu 郢州; General of Exemplary Might; concurrently Colonel Protector of the Man; and Governor of Yōngzhōu 雍州.
Yuán Yǐ 復率大衆來入鵲尾，
相持既久，
軍主張興世越鵲尾上據錢溪，
劉胡自攻之．
Yōu zhī 率諸將攻濃湖，
Yǐ 遣人傳唱錢溪已平，
衆並懼，
Yōu zhī 曰：
「不然．
若錢溪實敗，
萬人中應有逃亡得還者．
必是彼戰失利，
唱空聲以惑衆耳． 」
勒軍中不得妄動．
錢溪信尋至，
果大破賊．
Yōu zhī 悉以錢溪所送胡軍耳鼻示之，
Yǐ 駭懼，
急追胡還．
Yōu zhī 諸軍悉力進攻，
多所斬獲，
日暮引歸．
鵲尾食盡，
遣千人往南陵迎米，
〔三九〕為臺軍所破，
燒其資實，
胡於是棄衆而奔，
Yǐ 亦叛走．
赭圻、濃湖之平也，
賊軍委棄資財，
珍貨殷積，
諸軍各競收斂，
以強弱為少多．
唯 Yōu zhī、 Zhāng Xīngshì 約勒所部，
不犯秋毫，
諸將以此多之．
Yōu zhī 進平尋陽，
徙監郢州諸軍事、前將軍、郢州刺史，
持節如故．
不拜，
遷中領軍，
封貞陽縣公，
食邑二千戶．
時四方皆已平定，
徐州刺史 Xuē Āndū 據彭城請降，
上雖相酬許，
而辭旨簡略．
Yōu zhī 前將軍，
置佐吏，
假節，
與鎮軍將軍 Zhāng Yǒng 以重兵徵 Āndū，
Āndū 懼，
要引索虜，
索虜引大衆援之．
Yōu zhī 等米船在呂梁，
又遣軍主 Wáng Mùzhī 上民口，
Mùzhī 為虜攻覆米船，
又破運車於武原，
Yōu zhī 等引 退，
為虜所乘，
又值寒雪，
士衆墮指十二三．
留長水校尉 Wáng Xuánzài 守下邳，
積射將軍 Shěn Sháo 守宿豫，
睢陵、淮陽亦置戍，
Yōu zhī 還淮陰．
免官，
以公領職．
復求進討，
上不聽，
入朝面陳，
又不許，
復歸淮陰．
三年六月，
自率運送米下邳，
并鑿四周深塹，
遣龍驤將軍 Yuán Hùzhī 領民口還淮陰．
時軍主 Chén Xiǎndá 當領千兵守下邳，
Yōu zhī 留待 Xiǎndá 至，
虜遣清泗間人詐告 Yōu zhī 云：
「 Āndū 欲降，
求軍迎接． 」
Yōu zhī 副 Wú Xǐ 納其說，
咸謂宜遣千人參之，
既而來者轉多，
Xǐ 所執彌固．
Yōu zhī 乃集來者告之，
語曰：
「 Xuē Xúzhōu 早宜還朝，
今能爾，
深副本望．
但遣子弟一人來，
便當遣大軍相接．
君諸人既有志心，
若能與薛子弟俱來者，
皆即假君以本鄉縣，
唯意所欲；
如其不爾，
無為空勞往還． 」
自此一去不反．
其年秋，
太宗復令 Yōu zhī 進圍彭城，
Yōu zhī 以清泗既乾，
糧運不繼，
固執以為非宜，
往反者七．
上大怒，
詔 Yōu zhī 曰：
「卿春中求伐彭城，
吾恐軍士疲勞，
且去冬奔散，
人心未宜復用，
不許卿所啟．
今便不肯為吾行邪？
卿若不行，
便可使 Wú Xǐ 獨去． 」
Yōu zhī 懼，
乃奉旨進軍．
行至遲墟，
〔四０〕上悔，
追軍令反．
Yōu zhī 還至下邳，
而 Chén Xiǎndá 於睢口為虜所破，
龍驤將軍 Jiāng Chǎnbó、司徒參軍 Gāo Zūnshì 戰沒．
虜追 Yōu zhī 甚急，
因交戰，
被矟創，
會暮，
引軍入顯達壘，
夕衆散，
八月十八日也．
Yōu zhī 棄衆南奔．
初，
吳興 Qiū Yòubì、 Qiū Lóngxiān、 Shěn Dàn、 Shěn Róngshǒu、 吳 Lù Dàoliáng，
並以文記之才 隨 Yōu zhī，
及 Zhāng Yǒng 北討，
Yǒng 一奔，
Yōu zhī 再敗，
Yòubì 等並皆陷沒．
Yōu zhī 之還淮陰，
以為持節、假冠軍將軍、行南兗州刺史．
追贈 Jiāng Chǎnbó 左軍將軍，
Gāo Zūnshì 屯騎校尉．
四年，
徵 Yōu zhī 為吳興太守，
辭不拜．
乃除左衞將軍，
領太子中庶子．
五年，
出為持節、 監郢州諸軍、郢州刺史．
為政刻暴，
或鞭士大夫，
上佐以下有忤意，
輒面加詈辱．
將吏一人亡叛，
同籍符伍充代者十餘人．
而曉達吏事，
自強不息，
士民畏憚，
人莫敢欺．
聞有虎，
輒自圍捕，
往無不得，
一日或得兩三．
若逼暮不獲禽，
則宿昔圍守，
須曉自出．
賦斂嚴苦，
徵發無度，
繕治船舸，
營造器甲．
自至夏口，
便有異圖．
六年，
進監豫州之西陽、司州之義陽二郡軍事，
進號鎮軍將軍．
In the first year of Tàiyù,
Tàizōng passed away.
Yōuzhī, along with Cài Xīngzōng, was in an external domain,
and both participated in the dying instructions.
He was promoted to the title of General of the Pacifying West (Ānxī Jiāngjūn)
and additionally appointed as a Cavalier Attendant in Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì),
granted a set of drums and trumpets.
Before he could be officially invested,
Lǐ Chéngmíng, a commoner from Bāxī, rebelled,
seizing the Administrator Zhāng Dàn,
causing unrest in the region of Shǔ.
At that time, Jǐngsù, the Prince of Jiànpíng and Governor of Jīngzhōu, had been summoned,
and the newly appointed Governor of Jīngzhōu, Cài Xīngzōng, had not yet arrived at his post.
Therefore, Yōuzhī was sent to temporarily administer the affairs of Jīngzhōu.
Upon Yōuzhī's arrival,
Chéngmíng's rebellion had already been suppressed.

Yōuzhī was then appointed as Grand Administrator of the Military Affairs of the Eight Provinces of Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, Yì, Liáng, Níng, Northern Qín, and Southern Qín, General of the Pacifying West (Zhènxī Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Jīngzhōu (Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ).
His status as Bearer of the Imperial Credentials (Chíjié) and Attendant in Ordinary (Chángshì) remained as before.
When he arrived at Jīngzhōu,
his administration was as effective as when he was in Xiàkǒu.
He constructed boats and armor,
always as if an enemy were approaching.
At that time, the young emperor (yòuzhǔ) was on the throne,
and the various dukes (qúngōng) held court.
Yōuzhī gradually harbored intentions of disloyalty,
and did not observe
the court's regulations and institutions.
Xiūfàn, the Prince of Guìyáng and Governor of Jiāngzhōu, secretly harbored rebellious intentions.
He used subtle hints to incite Yōuzhī,
and had the Daoist Chén Gōngzhāo write a letter from 'Tiāngōng' (Heavenly Duke),
addressed
as "Chancellor Shěn" (Shěn Chéngxiàng),
and sent it to Yōuzhī's gatekeeper.
Yōuzhī did not open the letter,
but apprehended Gōngzhāo
and sent him to the imperial court.
Later, in the second year of Yuánhuī of the Deposed Emperor (Fèi Dì),
Xiūfàn raised an army to attack the capital (Jīngyì).
Yōuzhī said to his staff:
"Guìyáng is now rebelling against the court.
He will certainly claim to be allied with Yōuzhī.
If we do not hasten to aid the emperor,
it will surely increase the confusion in both the court and the populace."
Thereupon, he dispatched the military commanders Sūn Tóng and Shěn Huái'ào to lead troops quickly downstream,
under the command of Xiè, the Prince of Jìnxī and Governor of Yǐngzhōu.
As Tóng and the others had just passed Xiàkǒu,
Xiūfàn's rebellion was suppressed.
They returned.

Yōuzhī was promoted to the title of Grand General of the Expeditionary West (Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn), with the privilege of establishing a government office and enjoying the same honors as the Three Ministers (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
He firmly declined the Kāifǔ title.
Yōuzhī's independent control outside the capital
made the court suspicious and apprehensive of him.
They repeatedly wished to summon him back,
but feared he would not obey the order,
and so they stopped.
The various dukes, acting under the order of the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu),
sent an imperial envoy to ask Yōuzhī:
"You have long toiled in the provinces;
it is fitting that you return to the capital.
However, given the gravity of your entrusted responsibility,
a change of command is indeed not easy at this time.
Regarding the appropriateness of your return or continued stay,
we entrust it entirely to you."
This was to observe his intentions.
Yōuzhī replied:
"I am deeply grateful for the nation's great kindness,
and my status has reached this point.
I consider myself ordinary and simple,
and originally had no aptitude for court affairs.
However, for defending a frontier,
and suppressing the Mán and Yán barbarians,
I can barely fulfill this responsibility.
Although the instruction comes from above,
how dare I set my heart on leaving or staying?
Regarding the matter of returning,
I respectfully await the court's command."
The court became even more intimidated,
and discussions of summoning him ceased.
In the fourth year,
Jǐngsù, the Prince of Jiànpíng, rebelled, occupying the capital city.
Yōuzhī again responded to the imperial court.
Jǐngsù was soon suppressed.
Initially, during the Yuánjiā era,
the two commanderies of Bādōng and Jiànpíng had prosperous military administrations,
and were renowned commanderies along with Jiāngxià, Jìnglín, and Wǔlíng.
Shìzǔ established Yǐngzhōu in Jiāngxià,
and the commandery's military administration was dissolved.
Jìnglín and Wǔlíng also became ruined and desolate.
Bādōng and Jiànpíng were ravaged by the Mán barbarians in the gorges,
and by this time, the populace had scattered,
with few survivors.
In the spring of that year,
Yōuzhī dispatched troops into the gorges to attack the Mán chieftains such as Tián Wǔjùn.
When Jǐngsù rebelled,
Yōuzhī urgently recalled the troops from the gorges.
Liú Rǎngbīng, the Administrator of Bādōng, and Liú Dàoxīn, the Administrator of Jiànpíng, both suspected Yōuzhī of having rebellious intentions,
and obstructed the passes with their troops,
preventing the army from descending.
At that time, Rǎngbīng's nephew, Tiāncì, was the Western Secretary (Xīcáo) in Jīngzhōu.
[四一]Yōuzhī sent Tiāncì to explain to them,
instructing them to lay down their arms,
and promised that no questions would be asked.
Rǎngbīng met Tiāncì,
and knowing that Jǐngsù had indeed rebelled,
he then surrendered his arms and apologized for his error.
Yōuzhī treated him as before,
and later appointed Rǎngbīng as the Sīmǎ of his administration.
Liú Dàoxīn staunchly defended Jiànpíng.
Rǎngbīng's explanations failed to persuade him.
So, [Yōuzhī] joined the army that had been attacking the Mán barbarians to assault him,
conquered Jiànpíng,
and executed Dàoxīn.
Gāo Dàoqìng, an attendant in the imperial palace (Táizhíhé), had his family in Jiānglíng.
When Yōuzhī first arrived at the province,
Dàoqìng was then at home.
He sent a document listing more than ten of his relatives,
seeking positions as provincial functionaries (Zhōu Cóngshì) or Western Secretaries (Xīcáo).
Yōuzhī hired three of them.
Dàoqìng was furious,
and personally entered the provincial office to retrieve the official orders,
destroyed them, and departed.
When he returned to the capital,
he did not bid farewell to Yōuzhī.
Upon Dàoqìng's arrival in the capital,
he said:
"Yōuzhī is amassing troops and repairing armor;
his treachery will not be long in coming."
Yáng Yùncháng and others, who always suspected and feared him,
then secretly dispatched assassins with Dàoqìng,
carrying a handwritten imperial edict from the Deposed Emperor (Fèi Dì),
bestowing gold cakes upon Yōuzhī's provincial subordinates,
and promoting their ranks.
At that time, three elephants appeared a few *li* north of Jiānglíng city.
Yōuzhī personally went out to fight and kill them.
Suddenly, a stray arrow struck the mudguard of Yōuzhī's horse.
Afterward, the assassination plot was discovered.
After the Deposed Emperor was killed,
Shùn Dì ascended the throne.

Yōuzhī was promoted to the title of Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Dàjiāngjūn), with the privilege of establishing a government office and enjoying the same honors as the Three Ministers (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī),
and was additionally granted twenty ceremonial swords.
Yōuzhī's eldest son, Yuán Yǎn, the Left Chief Clerk (Zuǒ Chángshǐ) of the Minister of Works (Sītú), was sent to carry the instruments used for the Deposed Emperor's dismemberment to show Yōuzhī.
Upon Yuán Yǎn's arrival in Jiānglíng,
Yōuzhī already harbored rebellious intentions.
However, his trusted confidants disagreed on the matter,
so his plan did not come to fruition.
In the eleventh month of that year,
he finally raised troops in rebellion.
Yōuzhī had long accumulated soldiers and horses,
and his resources were abundant.
By this time, he had 100,000 soldiers and 2,000 iron-armored cavalry.

He sent envoys to invite Zhāng Jìng'ér, Governor of Yōngzhōu; Fàn Bónián, Governor of Liángzhōu; Yáo Dàohé, Governor of Sīzhōu; Yǔ Pèiyù, Acting Governor of Xiāngzhōu; and Wáng Wénhé, Internal Administrator of Bālíng, among others.
Jìng'ér and Wénhé executed his envoys
and swiftly submitted memorials to report the news.
Bónián, Dàohé, and Pèiyù were ambivalent
and secretly agreed to cooperate.
On the twelfth day of the twelfth month,
Yōuzhī dispatched his General of Pacifying the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn), Staff Officer of the Central Army (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn), and Supervisor of the Vanguard Army (Dū Qiánfēng Jūnshì), Sūn Tóng,

leading Wǔ Bǎo, General of Pacifying the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn) and Staff Officer of the Central Army (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn); Zhū Jūnbá, General of Dragon Soaring (Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn) and Staff Officer of Cavalry (Qíbīng Cānjūn); Shěn Huìzhēn, General of Pacifying the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn); and Wáng Dàoqǐ, General of Dragon Soaring (Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn) and Staff Officer of the Central Army (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn).
He also sent his Sīmǎ and General of Championing the Army (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn), Liú Rǎngbīng,

leading Gōng Fāngpíng, General of Pacifying the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn) and Staff Officer of the Outer Army (Wàibīng Cānjūn); Zhū Língbǎo, General of Dragon Soaring (Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn) and Staff Officer of Cavalry (Qíbīng Cānjūn); Shěn Sēngjìng, General of Dragon Soaring (Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn) and Staff Officer of Cavalry (Qíbīng Cānjūn); and Gāo Mào, General of Dragon Soaring (Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn).

Furthermore, he sent Wáng Língxiù, General of Pacifying the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn) and Staff Officer of the Central Army (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn); and Dīng Zhēndōng, General of Pacifying the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn) and Staff Officer of the Central Army (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn),

leading Wáng Zhēnzhī, General of Pacifying the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn) and Staff Officer of the Central Army (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn); and Yáng Jǐngmù, General of Pacifying the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn) and Staff Officer of the Outer Army (Wàibīng Cānjūn).
They all departed in succession.

Yōuzhī himself led Wǔ Màozōng, General of Pacifying the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn) and Staff Officer of Records (Lùshì Cānjūn) concurrently Sīmǎ; Shěn Sháo, General of Pacifying the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn) and Staff Officer of the Central Army (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn); Huángfǔ Xián, General of Pacifying the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn) and Staff Officer of the Central Army (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn); Hú Qīnzhī, General of Pacifying the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn) and Staff Officer of the Central Army (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn); and Dōngmén Dàoshùn, General of Dragon Soaring (Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn) and Staff Officer of the Central Army (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn).
On the fourth day of the intercalary twelfth month,
they arrived at Xiàkǒu.
[四二]When Yōuzhī was about to depart from Jiānglíng,
he had the Buddhist monk Shì Sēngcàn divine for him.
[四三]He said:
"You will not reach the capital.
You will turn back from Yǐngzhōu."
Yōuzhī was very displeased.
Initially,
there was a cloud formation at Jiāngjīn,
resembling dust and fog,
coming from the northwest,
directly covering the army.
Upon reaching Dùnkǒu,
it was said:
"We should greet the General of the Pacifying West (Ānxī Jiāngjūn)
and temporarily moor at Huángjīnpǔ."
After they disembarked,
the army from Yǐngchéng sallied forth to attack them.
Yōuzhī heard that the Crown Prince (Shìzǐ) of the Prince of Qí (Qí Wáng) was holding Pénkǒu,
and was so intimidated that he dared not advance further downstream,
thus he attacked Yǐngchéng instead.
At that time, the Prince of Qí (Qí Wáng) was acting as regent,
and dispatched various armies to suppress the rebellion in the west.
The Ministry of Personnel (Shàngshū) issued a decree to the General of the Expeditionary West's (Zhēngxī Fǔ) office, saying:
"Respecting the noble and disdaining the lowly is
the proper order of ruler and minister.
Obeying and following avoids rebellion,
success and failure begin with this.
Never has anyone trespassed on our borders,
invaded our rivers and counties,
without being burned [down]."
The army kills the armored enemy,
whose banners are in disarray and chariot tracks chaotic.
Shěn Yōuzhī, from youth, was lowly and common,
promoted from the ranks of soldiers.
He seized the opportunity of a hundred battles,
riding on the success of a single victory.
He carved mountains
and split lands,
wore gold at his waist and trailed purple robes,
reaching the peak of nobility in the state,
and extreme wealth in his family.
Wielding the yak-tail banner as a regional governor,
he dispensed with the rites of facing north in homage.
Appointed as area commander, his ambition to suppress dissent,
immediately incurred the wrath
of those he sought to subjugate.
Oranges and pomelos were not presented as tribute;
precious jades rarely entered his domain.
The “basket tax” was deeply levied,
its venom afflicting Nányǐng.
He bent the ruler and falsified the ink line,
causing harm throughout Xījīng.
His heart was that of a tāotiè,
and his nature like a
ravine.
From beginning to end,
he grew old in his prime.
Now he incites and presses on with his monstrous faction,
gathering soldiers,
stirring up conflict in the outer cities,
and sending them to their deaths in the central plains.
If this can be
tolerated,
what cannot be endured?

Now, we dispatch the newly appointed Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of Yǐngzhōu and Sīzhōu’s Yìyáng, General Who Pacifies the West, Governor of Yǐngzhōu, Founding侯 of Wénxǐ County, Huáng

Huí; (44) Gentleman-in-Waiting at the Palace Gate, General of Galloping Cavalry, Grand Administrator of Nánlín Huái, Founding子 of Chóng'ān County, Army Commander Wáng Jìngzé; General Who Guards the State,

Colonel of Agile Cavalry, Founding男 of Chángshòu County, Wáng Yíyǔ; General Who Guards the State, Grand Administrator of Nángāopíng, Army Commander Chén Chéngshū; (45) General Who Guards the State, General of the Left Army,

Grand Administrator of Nánpúyáng, Founding男 of Gáyáng County, Army Commander Péng Wénzhī; (46) General of Dragon’s Might, Acting Staff Officer to the General of Agile Cavalry, Army Commander Zhāo Zǎi.
(47) Twenty thousand elite
armored soldiers will serve as the vanguard, surging forth like clouds.

Furthermore, we dispatch the Gentleman-in-Waiting at the Palace Gate, concurrently General of Roaming Cavalry, Founding男 of Xiāngnán County, newly appointed Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of Xiāngzhōu, General Who Conquers Barbarians, Governor of Xiāngzhōu, Army Commander Lǚ Ānguó; Colonel of Agile Cavalry, General Who Pacifies the North, Cuī Huìjǐng; General Who Guards the State, Army Commander Rèn Hòu

Bó; (48) General Who Guards the State, General of Galloping Cavalry, Army Commander Xiāo Shùnzhī; General Who Guards the State, General of Roaming Cavalry, Army Commander Yuán Chóngzǔ; (49) General Who Pacifies the North, Commandant of the Tiger-Guards, Army Commander Yǐn Lüè; (50) Colonel of Agile Cavalry, Magistrate of Nánchéng, Cáo Hǔtóu.
Twenty thousand ships,
one after another, will advance continuously.
We also dispatch General Who Guards the State,

General of the Rear Army, Staff Officer to the Central Army of the Right Army, Army Commander Gǒu Yuánbīn; (51) General Who Pacifies the North, Staff Officer to the Central Army of the Pacification Army, Army Commander Guō Wénxiào;
General of Dragon’s Might, Staff Officer to the Central Army of the Pacification Army, Army Commander Chéng Yǐnjùn.
Ten thousand light vessels
will cut off their vital passages.

Newly appointed Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of Guǎngzhōu, Jiāozhōu, Yuèzhōu, Níngzhōu, and Xiāngzhōu’s Guǎngxīng, concurrently General Who Pacifies Yuè and Commander of the Central Army, General Who Conquers Barbarians, Governor of Guǎngzhōu, Commander of Cavalry Zhōu Pánlóng, Founding子 of Dùnyáng County; General Who Guards the State, Commander of Cavalry of the Rear Army Zhāng Wénxǐ; General of Dragon’s Might, Army Commander Xuē Dàoyuān; General of Galloping Cavalry, General of Roaming Cavalry, Governor of Bìngzhōu, Grand Administrator of Nánqīnghé, Duke of Tàiyuán, Army Commander Wáng Chìqín; (52) General of Dragon’s Might, Colonel of Archers, Wáng Hóngfàn; (53) General of Dragon’s Might, Attendant Official in Charge of Imperial Bodyguards, Army Commander
Chéng Mǎi and others.
(54) Five thousand armored cavalry
will form the rear array of the Dragon’s Might.
All these commanders
are without exception courageous and mighty enough to shake the heavens,
with spirits firm enough to outshine the sun.
They confront charges and clear obstacles,
with the keen
sight of a hawk and the gaze of an osprey.
A glance from them generates wind before and behind;
a shout from them causes lightning to erupt left and right.
With such forces attacking cities,
what city will not be overcome?
With such forces facing enemies,
what formation can
stand firm?
Then the imperial chariots and army will advance,
a million dragons and tigers.
The six armies will move in unison,
the five chariots will unfurl their banners.
The vermillion palanquins will emit light,
the white armor will stir waves.
The archers of Lóufán, with their white feathers,
will throw their saddles and form mountains.
The dark cavalry of Yúyáng
will bathe in iron to form a multitude.
At that point, good and evil will be burned together,
and regret will be too late.
On the day this tally arrives,
I hope you will reflect carefully.
As for the commanders of the vanguard and those who construct camps and walls,
and the people who are forced by the enemy,
if any throw themselves at our military gate,
they will be entirely
unquestioned.
If they can atone for their crimes with meritorious deeds,
we will certainly not deceive them;
even if they must cut their robes or shoot their jades,
only merit will be rewarded.
Those who can cut off Shěn Yōuzhī’s head and deliver it,
will be enfeoffed as a county duke of three thousand households,
and granted five thousand bolts each of cloth and silk.
This promise is as vast as rivers and seas,
clear and unwavering.
Imperial dispatches are conveyed by "flying fire" military couriers,
traversing a thousand li by post-road.
The King of Qí stationed himself at Xīntíng,
issuing a flying檄 that enumerated Shěn Yōuzhī’s crimes and evil deeds,
saying: "Indeed, bending a bow to shoot at the sky,
none have been seen to reach it;
brandishing a spear to strike the earth,
where can such great strength be applied?
Why is this?
Because the potentials of righteousness and rebellion are distinctly different,
and the consequences of good fortune and disaster are easily
discerned.
Therefore, those who go against Heaven,
ghosts and spirits cannot make them succeed;
those who align with humanity,
even sages and wise men cannot cause them to fail.
Hence, Liú Bì relied on the power of the seven states
allied in arms;
Wēi Xiāo boasted of his resources across the river and occupying Lǒng;
Wúqiū Jiǎn flaunted his achievements of crossing the sea and islands;
Zhūgě Dàn prided himself on his virtue of treating gentlemen well and loving the people.
Those
four men were all contemporary heroes and outstanding figures,
yet by transgressing against the natural order, they brought disaster upon themselves,
overturning their dens and collapsing their nests,
becoming a laughingstock for mere boys.
How much more so for a common talent,
a small
vessel,
who harbors the ambition of seizing the throne,
and dares to plot a kingless rebellion!
The rebellious villain Shěn Yōuzhī,
originated from humble fields,
obscure for generations.
The late Sīkōng Shěn Gōng, through his paternal cousin's patronage,
(55) loved him like a son,
protecting him and
nurturing him,
allowing him to rise in official ranks.
When the deposed emperor was demented and perverse,
suspicious and fearful of his loyal ministers,
Yōuzhī, driven by greed and ambition, seized the opportunity,
fiercely and cruelly seeking profit.
He personally engaged in betrayal,
requesting a mandate for execution.
Furthermore, Yōuzhī, along with Tán Jīn, Tóng Tàiyī, and others, were all favored and trusted.
In court, they served as his claws and teeth,
sharing merits and responsibilities,
known at the time as "Three Marquises,"
their intimacy then
surpassing
Guǎn Zhòng and Bào Shúyá.
When the revolution occurred,
(56) the villainous faction feared execution.
Yōuzhī, cunning and strategic,
sought to preserve himself by selling out others,
not only killing his paternal cousin,
but also harming his good friends.
Even if
Lǚ Bù sold out his lord,
and Lì Jì betrayed his friend,
compared to this man,
it is not cruel enough.
This lack of trustworthiness and righteousness,
his deceitful and fickle words,
is unprecedented in all of China,
and not even committed by barbarians.
When the Tàishǐ era began,
the net was so loose that a whale could escape,
overlooking his ferocity and danger,
and employing his ferocity and aggression.
Thus, he was able to gain survival through turmoil,
and preserve
his fortune through disaster.
Yōuzhī is shallow and empty,
impulsive and without strategy.
The collapse and defeat at Nónghú
were not due to his own strength.
When he later campaigned north to Péngsì,
he saw the enemy and fled at night.
When he again attacked Xiàpī,
he fled at
the first drum.
He twice disgraced the imperial army,
and should have again been executed according to law.
The late emperor, being wise and sagely,
with a profound magnanimity like rivers and seas,
pardoned him for his defeat at Huíxī,
hoping to achieve victory at Qūxiáo.
Therefore,
he was able to be promoted fortuitously,
and suddenly rise to prominence and power,
internally managing military affairs,
and externally overseeing regional administrations.
When the Sacred Spirit ascended to Dǐnghú,
a distant deathbed edict was issued,
entrusting him with profound responsibilities,
a trust as weighty as gold.
stone.
When Yōu zhī 始奉 guóhuì,
〔五七〕joy was seen in his countenance.
While the whole realm shared a common sorrow,
he took it as a cause for celebration.
This act of reveling in calamity and delighting in disaster
is the first great crime of treason.
Also,
Yōu zhī repeatedly ascended Fānyuè,
〔五八〕moving from Yǐng to Jīng.
As His Highness, the Prince of Jìnxī, replaced him as the imperial brother to govern,
his position was honored and his prestige significant.
Yōu zhī wantonly insulted and demeaned him,
curtailing and selecting escorts,
picking and choosing soldiers and horses,
and calculating and counting weapons and armor.
Fine equipment and elite soldiers
were all taken by him,
leaving nothing in the city of Yǐng.
Not one in ten was left.
He usurped power and plundered at will,
disregarding the national laws.
This act of harboring treacherous intentions,
being disrespectful and impious,
is the second great crime of treason.
Furthermore, since Yōu zhī took charge of Jīng,
he employed treacherous schemes.
As he intended to raise an army,
it was necessary to have a pretext.
Thus, he pressed the various Mán tribes,
disturbing the mountains and valleys,
and loudly
proclaimed a punitive expedition.
Every household was conscripted,
swarming the cities and towns,
waiting for the state's rise or fall.
This had been ongoing for years,
and he never disbanded his troops.
This caused the fields in the four prefectures and a hundred counties
to be devoid of
men.
For plowing fields and transporting taxes,
only women and the weak were driven.
Such cruelty and tyranny,
since ancient times, has never been heard of.
This act of insulting and belittling the court
is the third great crime of treason.
In the past, when the extraordinary troops from Guìyáng suddenly rose,
〔五九〕the capital was enraged,
and the imperial ancestral temple was in peril.
Yōu zhī, holding a position in the upper reaches of the river,
with a strong army and vast territory,
should have exerted his full strength
to rescue the fallen.
While the state was in dire straits,
he considered himself,
and merely dispatched three thousand weak soldiers.
〔六０〕All of them were frail and old,
and he sent them to Yǐngzhōu,
to receive their orders.
He wished that on the day of decision,
the blame could be shifted to Jìnxī.
How could he,
in peaceful times, be so arrogant and presumptuous,
truly belittling Zhōu and Shào,
yet at that time, act respectfully
and falsely venerate the imperial relatives?
This act of
harboring deceit and hiding treachery,
and holding suspicion on both sides,
is the fourth great crime of treason.
Moreover,
Yōu zhī repeatedly held sway over regional prefectures,
and his arrogance grew increasingly severe.
He enticed cunning and unscrupulous individuals,
and admitted all who came.
He detained travelers and companions,
and whoever passed through his territory was certainly detained.
Scholars in distress
and difficulty
could not return to their hometowns.
Merchants, having committed their lives,
had no way to return to their lands.
Rebels and fugitives who entered his borders
were invariably protected,
while those who escaped his jurisdiction
were surely pursued relentlessly.
This is the fifth great crime of treason.
Furthermore, Yōu zhī acted willfully and presumptuously,
relying on cruel and brutal methods.
He regarded officials as enemies,
and treated the common people like grass.
He imposed a severe tax of more than half,
and inflicted brutal, mutilating punishments.
He whipped and
flogged national officials,
employing entirely barbarian laws.
If one person fled,
the entire family was made to compensate.
His venom spread to infants,
and his cruelty extended to the elderly.
Prisons were full,
and blood constantly flowed in the markets.
Men could not plow,
and women could not weave.
People rushed about on the roads,
their cries of distress shaking the heavens.
He never observed
the imperial edicts of amnesty,
but killed and attacked as he pleased,
thus, the vast
benevolence
was forever cut off from his province.
This act of disrespecting the ruler and overstepping his superiors
is the sixth great crime of treason.
Cāngwú was wildly ruthless,
his wickedness deeper than Jié and Zhòu.
He was suspicious of foreign vassals,
and looked westward with distrustful eyes.
He detained his eldest son, Yuán Yǎn,
as a hostage for alliance.
Father and son were separated,
accumulating many years.
Thanks to the long-lasting spiritual power of the state,
the tyrant was swiftly punished.
Yōu zhī, having been endowed with an intelligent mind,
should have shared in the joy and fortune.
Instead, he was confused and deluded,
deeply lamenting
and regretting,
uttering words to mourn Jié,
and raising his voice to bark at Yáo.
This act of failing to distinguish right from wrong,
and not knowing good from evil,
going against sentiment and reason,
is the seventh great crime of treason.
Dethroning the incompetent and enthroning the enlightened is a grand tradition of previous dynasties.
Jiāo and Guǎng arrived first,
Liáng and Qín arrived early.
Yet Yōu zhī, close to the imperial heartland,
with rivers and roads not far away,
received the imperial
dispatches,
but remained calmly as if he had not heard.
He did not send memorials,
and ten days or a month passed.
Defáng arrived late,
and was punished according to the Xià dynasty's laws.
This is the eighth great crime of treason.
As Shēngmíng began his reign,
his benevolence was profound and his favor far-reaching.
He affirmed the affection between father and son,
and showed compassion for the kinship of flesh and blood.
He swiftly dispatched Yuán Yǎn,
carrying an envoy to return westward.
He was also granted
high appointments,
with honors and prestige stacked upon him.
When Yuán Yǎn reached the west,
he should have immediately reported back.
Yōu zhī, having gained this reunion,
owed thanks to whose benevolence?
Instead of bearing the great virtue,
he provoked enmity and strife.
This is the ninth great crime of treason.
Yōu zhī, with a nature like a ravenous gorge,
and the heart of an owl and a poisoned pheasant,
merely existing between heaven and earth
is already considered ugly and foul.
How much more so now that he has raised an army to insult the imperial court,
and indulged in treachery and rebellion?
This is truly the time when his evil deeds are ripe and his crimes are complete,
the day to lance the boil and drain the carbuncle.
Our headquarters, bearing the heavy trust of the court,
is filled with righteous indignation a hundredfold.
We command the grand army
to execute Heaven's punishment.
Currently, His Imperial Majesty is sagacious and enlightened,
the generals and ministers are benevolent and generous.
They have simplified the laws into three chapters,
lightened punishments, and eased taxes.
Years are bountiful and harvests are abundant,
families are provided for and people are content.
Above, there is the favor of harmony;
below,
there is no desire for chaos.
Yōu zhī does not recognize the times,
and presumptuously plots treacherous rebellion,
raising an unrighteous army,
and driving a party of enemies.
Therefore, the court and the populace clearly see how easily
he can be captured,
and all conscious beings judge him as a ready captive.
Bears and grizzlies sharpen their claws,
harboring intentions to seize and tear.
Tigers and leopards grind their teeth,
arising with fury to devour.
When they roar with rage,
ice plains produce lightning,
When roused to action, it is like thunder across a frosty plain.
To quell disturbances with this,
how could it take more than a moment?
Even if a multitude of followers obstruct the land,
and an entire prefecture blocks the river,
what is that to resist the
waves of a boiling sea,
or withstand the flames of a burning mountain?
The local gentry and common people,
having suffered hardship for a long time,
have no escape route.
This has always been a cause for pity.
Now, being forced again
to engage in battle,
on the day of combat,
it will be hard to distinguish between
orchids and mugwort.
When the earth crumbles and spears are turned,
it is advisable to plan early,
lest a single person be deluded,
and their entire clan suffer misfortune.
The principle of great forgiveness
is as clear as the bright sun.
Yōu zhī (攸之) fully committed his elite troops to attack Yǐngzhōu (郢州).
Liǔ Shìlóng (柳世隆), who was managing affairs, responded as appropriate,
repeatedly defeating them.
Yōu zhī (攸之) wrote a letter to Prince Zàn (贊) of Wǔlíng (武陵), saying:
“Jiānglíng (江陵), encompassing eight prefectures,
is a strategically important place.
The weighty responsibility of guarding and governing it
ought to be returned to the emperor.
I originally intended to respectfully request a transfer of my official carriage and parasol,
to preside over the Jīngbù (荊部).
The reason I have not yet fully reported this to the emperor
is that I wished to wait for your arrival,
and consult with you personally.
I did not anticipate that with the heavy gates and night watches,
a meeting would be impossible.
If the sincerity of my desire to assist the court
is ultimately concealed from His Majesty’s discerning gaze,
and the expedition to distant lands
is hindered near Yǐngdū (郢都),
then I will have no way to satisfy the hearts of the valiant,
and nothing with which to fulfill the aspirations of the righteous.
I will then not violate Guānlínghàn (關陵漢),
but will seek one meeting to pay my respects.
As for the soldiers who can slay dragons and shatter rocks,
and the generals who can cleave bones and bend iron,
they surge like smoke and move like wind.
They may perhaps cause alarm to those around you.
If there is no other option,
how dare I not first inform you of my humble intentions?”
He also said:
“Your humble official holds a weighty position, dividing the regions,
and is rich as a gold mine.
My sons and nephews are grown and clothed,
and have already attained noble titles.
My relatives, even those who can barely distinguish beans,
are immediately promoted when their turn comes.
My ears are tired of music,
my mouth wearied by fine food.
As a commoner, if I were
like this, what more could I seek?
How could I not know to bow my head and seek temporary peace,
preserving my remaining years?
Why do I not consider my entire household,
and willingly brave danger?
It is truly because I am grateful for the treatment I have received from successive emperors,
and wish to repay it to the imperial house.
Those who are ignorant of reason
say that your humble official harbors insatiable ambitions.
Since my sincerity is evident as the white sun,
I need not further explain my intentions to Your Highness.
If Heaven is truly determined to destroy the Way,
and loyalty and integrity cannot stand,
then even if my entire household is shattered and destroyed,
I would have no regrets in a hundred deaths.
However, Gāozǔ (高祖)’s imperial enterprise was difficult,
and Tàizǔ (太祖) toiled until sunset.
The predicted span of the dynasty did not reach seven hundred years,
and the imperial altars have already become the possession of others.
As for the affairs of the family and state,
I do not know what Your Majesty’s heart thinks.”
Yōu zhī (攸之) dispatched Gōngsūn Fāngpíng (公孫方平), his Staff Officer of the Central Army, with three thousand infantry and cavalry towards Wǔchāng (武昌).
The Administrator Zāng Huàn (臧煥) abandoned the prefecture and fled to the Administrator Wáng Yù (王毓) of Xīyáng (西陽),
〔六一〕then to Pénkǒu (盆口).
Fāngpíng (方平) consequently occupied Xīyáng (西áng).
The Administrator Zhāng Mó (張謨) of Jiànníng (建寧) led two thousand men from two prefectures to attack him.
Fāngpíng (方平) was defeated and fled.
Yōu zhī (攸之) attacked Yǐngchéng (郢城) for a long time without success,
and the morale of his troops became dispirited and dispersed.
On the nineteenth night of the first month of the second year of Shēngmíng (昇明),
Liú Rángbīng (劉攘兵) burned the camp and surrendered to Yǐngchéng (郢城).
The troops then scattered,
and could no longer be controlled.
As dawn approached,
Yōu zhī (攸之) executed Liú Tiāncì (劉天賜),
and led the main force across the river,
reaching Lǔshān (魯山).
All the armies then dispersed and fled.
Returning towards Jiānglíng (江陵),
less than a hundred *lǐ* away,
he heard that the city had already been occupied by the Inspector Zhāng Jìng’ér (張敬兒) of Yōngzhōu (雍州).
Having nowhere to go,
he and his third son, the Gentleman of the Central Secretariat Wénhé (文和), reached the border of Huáróng (華容),
where they were captured and executed by a border official.
〔六二〕
When Yōu zhī (攸之) first set out,
he left Yuán Yǎn (元琰) to guard Jiānglíng (江陵).
When Zhāng Jìng’ér (張敬兒) captured the city,
Yuán Yǎn (元琰) fled.
His fifth son Yòuhé (幼和), Yòuhé’s (幼和) younger brother Línghé (靈和), Yuán Yǎn’s (元琰) son Fǎxiān (法先), Yì’s (懿) son [unknown characters], Wénhé’s (文和) son Fǎzhēng (法徵), and Yòuhé’s (幼和) son Fǎmào (法茂),
〔六三〕were all captured by Jìng’ér (敬兒)
and executed.
Originally,
Wénhé (文和) had married Princess Yìxīng Xiàn (義興憲公主), daughter of the Prince of Qí (齊).
The princess died early,
leaving two daughters.
At this point, the Prince of Qí (齊) brought them back to his residence.
When the current emperor ascended the throne,
he allowed Yōu zhī (攸之) and his sons to be buried at their tombs after their mourning period.
Yōu zhī (攸之)’s second son Yì (懿),
a Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince,
died before Yōu zhī (攸之).
Yōu zhī (攸之)’s younger brother Dēng zhī (登之),
Administrator of Xīn’ān (新安),
had resigned from his post and was at home.
He was captured and executed by Shěn Wénjì (沈文季), the Administrator of Wúxīng (吳興).
〔六四〕Dēng zhī (登之)’s younger brother Yōng zhī (雍之),
Administrator of Póyáng (鄱陽),
died before Yōu zhī (攸之).
An imperial edict made Yōng zhī (雍之)’s grandson Sēngzhào (僧照) the successor to Princess Yìxīng (義興).
Yōng zhī (雍之) was born of a different mother than Yōu zhī (攸之).
Among his younger brothers, he was the most harmonious and cautious,
and particularly cherished and loved.
Yōu zhī (攸之) was by nature frugal and stingy;
his sons and nephews were not allowed to use money and goods without permission.
Only Yōng zhī (雍之) was allowed to take whatever he needed,
often taking clothes and accessories from the study,
and distributing them among his relatives and old friends.
This was his regular practice.
Yōng zhī (雍之)’s younger brother Róng zhī (榮之),
a Lang of the Ministry of Personnel and Keeper of the Imperial Treasury,
also died before Yōu zhī (攸之).
In his later years, Yōu zhī (攸之) enjoyed reading,
never letting a book leave his hand.
He was familiar with and remembered many details from the *Shǐjì* (史) and *Hànshū* (漢).
He often sighed, saying:
“Had I known earlier that poverty and prosperity are destined,
I regret not having studied for ten years.”
When attacking Yǐngchéng (郢城),
he encountered wind and waves at night,
and the rice boats sank.
Cuī Língfèng (崔靈鳳), a Staff Officer of the Granary, had a young daughter married to Liǔ Shìlóng’s (柳世隆) son.
Yōu zhī (攸之) sternly said to him:
“At this time, military provisions are urgently needed,
yet you do not pay attention.
Is this because of your marital ties with those inside the city?”
Língfèng (靈鳳) replied:
“Guǎng Yuè (樂廣) once said,
how could your humble official exchange five sons for one daughter?”
Yōu zhī (攸之) was pleased and his suspicion was resolved.
Initially,
Yōu zhī (攸之) recruited talented and capable men.
Shuāng Tàizhēn (雙泰真) from Suí (隨) prefecture was a capable and strong man,
but refused to come when summoned.
Later, Tàizhēn (泰真) came to Jiānglíng (江陵) to trade.
Someone informed Yōu zhī (攸之),
who then detained him,
appointed him as a deputy squad leader,
and treated him generously.
Tàizhēn (泰真) had no intention of staying,
and rebelled and fled after a few days.
Yōu zhī (攸之) sent twenty armored men to pursue him,
chasing him very closely.
Tàizhēn (泰真) killed several men,
and the rest dared not approach.
He wanted to go home and take his mother,
but the urgency of the situation prevented him.
He fled alone into the uncivilized regions.
Since the pursuers lost him,
they seized his mother and left.
After Tàizhēn (泰真) lost his mother,
he surrendered himself.
Yōu zhī (攸之) did not punish him,
saying:
“This is a filial son.”
He awarded him ten thousand cash,
and promoted him to squad leader.
His feigned emotions and calculations were all like this.
Early in the days when Shěn Yōu-zhī
was lowly, he and Sūn Chāo-zhī and Quán Jǐng-wén of Wú-jùn rode a small boat out of the capital.
The three of them together pulled the boat up a weir.
There was a man who stopped and observed them, saying:
“All three of you will attain the rank of Fāng-bó.”
Shěn Yōu-zhī said:
“How can it be that three people all have such a physiognomy?”
The physiognomist said:
“The bone structure is like this.
If it does not prove true,
then it means the physiognomy books are mistaken.”
Afterward, Shěn Yōu-zhī became the governor of Yǐng and Jīng provinces,
Sūn Chāo-zhī of Guǎng-zhōu,
and Quán Jǐng-wén the Intendant of Nán-yù-zhōu.
When Shěn Yōu-zhī first arrived in Yǐng-zhōu,
he had the intention to proceed downstream.
The registrar of the regional administration, Zōng Yǎn-zhī, advised attacking Yǐng-chéng,
but the military affairs administrator Zāng Yín believed:
“Attack and defense are different situations;
this city cannot be taken in a few days.
If it is not captured in time,
our morale will be blunted and our prestige diminished.
If we now proceed downstream and advance rapidly,
victory can be achieved in a matter of days.
Once the foundation is shaken,
how can Yǐng-chéng possibly hold itself?”
Shěn Yōu-zhī did not comply,
and after his defeat,
all the generals dispersed.
Only Zāng Yín said:
“I have committed myself to serve my lord.
How can I cowardly escape?
My not failing my lord
is like my lord not failing the imperial court.”
Thereupon, he threw himself into the water and died.
Zāng Yín’s courtesy name was Shì-ruò,
and he was from Jǔ in Dōng-guǎn.
Before this,
when Shěn Yōu-zhī was in Yǐng-zhōu,
a provincial official once whipped a regional administration clerk.
Shěn Yōu-zhī dismissed the provincial official
and instead whipped the clerk fifty strokes.
He said to others:
“For a provincial official to whip a regional administration officer
is indeed improper.
It arises from inferiors insulting gentry-officials.”
When Cāng-cáo Cān-jūn-shì Biān Róng was insulted by a regional administration clerk,
Shěn Yōu-zhī personally whipped the clerk to death for Biān Róng.
When Shěn Yōu-zhī departed from Jiāng-líng,
he made Biān Róng the驻府司马 (Zhù-fǔ Sī-mǎ),
to guard the city.
When Zhāng Jìng-ér was about to arrive,
some people tried to persuade Biān Róng to surrender to Zhāng Jìng-ér,
but Biān Róng said:
“Having received great kindness from Duke Shěn,
and having participated in such an important matter,
if one changes one’s original intention
at a moment of crisis,
I cannot do it.”
When the city fell,
he met Zhāng Jìng-ér.
Zhāng Jìng-ér asked:
“Why did you, Administrator Biān, not come sooner?”
“Duke Shěn left me to guard the city,
and to abandon the city to seek survival
is something I cannot bear.
I never wished to live,
so why must you ask?”
Zhāng Jìng-ér said:
“How is it difficult to die?”
He ordered him to be beheaded.
Biān Róng went cheerfully,
his countenance showing no change.
Chéng Yōng-zhī of Tài-shān,
who had always been close to Biān Róng,
at this point embraced Biān Róng and said:
“Having been companions with Administrator Biān,
I beg to be killed.”
The soldiers could not carry out the execution,
and reported it to Zhāng Jìng-ér.
Zhāng Jìng-ér said:
“It is very easy to seek death.
Why not permit it?”
He first killed Chéng Yōng-zhī,
and then Biān Róng.
The entire army shed tears,
saying:
“How can two righteous gentlemen be killed in one day?”
They compared them to Zāng Hóng and Chén Róng.
Biān Róng
was from Jīn-chéng.
When the deposed emperor died,
Shěn Yōu-zhī wanted to raise an army.
He asked his astrologer Gé Kē-zhī,
who said:
“Throughout history, those who raised armies
all observed the planet Tài-bái (Venus).
If Tài-bái appears, they succeed;
if it is hidden, they fail.
In the past, Guì-yáng raised an army when Tài-bái was hidden,
and was defeated in one battle.
This is a clear recent example.
Now, Duke Xiāo has deposed the benighted and established the enlightened.
His governance coincides with the time when Tài-bái is hidden,
Moreover, Tài-bái will soon appear in the east.
The east is favorable for military action;
the west is unfavorable.”
Therefore, Shěn Yōu-zhī stopped and did not rebel.
Later, when he did raise an army,
Gé Kē-zhī again said:
“This year, Suì-xīng (Jupiter) guards Nán-dǒu;
its state cannot be attacked.”
Shěn Yōu-zhī did not comply.
All the accomplices in the rebellion, Dīng Zhēn-dōng, Sūn Tóng, Péi Mào-zhòng, Wǔ, and Zōng Yǎn-zhī, were executed.
were composed by Zōng Yǎn-zhī.
Zāng Huàn went to Pén-chéng to surrender,
and the current emperor ordered him to be executed.
The remaining evildoers were either killed by the rebel army
or received amnesty and were pardoned.
The court historian commented: “Although Zāng Zhì had long been known for his greed and cruelty,
and his reputation was largely lacking,
in upholding righteousness and governing the region,
he originally had no ambition to swallow up territories.
He merely wished to, with a young ruler and weak government,
emulate Shì-zǔ,
hold the central regions,
and inherit the legacy of Huán and Yú.
However, since the lord was different from Mù and Āi,
and the ministers were all factional,
though the rituals and ranks were outwardly generous,
the internal suspicions and precautions were deep.
With high accomplishments and heavy positions,
it was ultimately not a place of security.
As for defying Heaven and violating the proper order,
did it not arise from this?
Shěn Yōu-zhī seized the opportunity to occupy Xī-yǐng,
and for over ten years,
he commanded arbitrarily and wielded power exclusively,
having accumulated an absence of loyalty to the ruler.
When Heaven grew weary of the Sòng dynasty,
and the mandate was about to depart,
he did not recognize the principles of the succeeding virtue,
and was uniquely deluded by the omens of peaceful transition.
Gōng-xiū (refers to Zāng Zhì) having had his clan overthrown,
Shěn Yōu-zhī also met his own demise.
Indeed, to end one’s life in chaos and rebellion
is consistent across different eras.”
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 35: Wáng Sēng-dá, Yán Jùn
Wáng Sēng-dá,
a native of Láng-yá Lín-yí, was the youngest son of the Grand Tutor Wáng Hóng.
His elder brother, Wáng Xī,
was dull and lacked charisma.
Emperor Tài-zǔ heard that Wáng Sēng-dá was intelligent from a young age,
summoned him to the Dé-yáng Hall,
and asked him about his scholarship and family affairs.
His responses were graceful and quick-witted,
and the emperor greatly appreciated him,
marrying him to the daughter of the Prince of Lín-chuān, Líng Yì-qìng.
Early on, he was fond of learning
and skilled in writing prose.
Before the age of twenty,
he served as a Rear Army Staff Officer (hòujūn cānjūn) for Prince Jùn of Shǐxīng.
He was promoted to Palace Attendant (tàizǐ shèrén).
Because he suffered from an illness,
he watched a duck fight at Yánglièqiáo.
He was impeached by the authorities,
but was pardoned and not prosecuted.
He was fond of hawks and dogs by nature,
racing and chasing with the young men of the neighborhood,
and even personally slaughtered cattle.
Yìqìng heard about this
and ordered the Buddhist monk Huìguān, who was in his retinue, to visit and observe him.
Wáng Sēngdá had books piled high on his desk
and discussed literature and principles with him.
Huìguān could not keep up with his responses
and praised him highly.
He was not on good terms with [his brother] Xī.
He pleaded poverty
and asked for a magistracy.
Tàizǔ wished to appoint him as the Administrator of Qínjùn.
However, Yǔ Bǐngzhī, the Administrator of the Personnel Bureau (lìbù láng), said:
"Wáng Hóng's son is not suitable to be Administrator of Qínjùn,
and Wáng Sēngdá is also unfit to govern the people."
So, the matter was dropped.
Soon after, he was promoted to Palace Gentleman-in-Waiting (tàizǐ xǐmǎ).
He resigned his post due to mourning for his mother.
When his brother Xī returned from his dismissal from Línhǎi Commandery,
he brought back old servants and over a million in salary.
Wáng Sēngdá, in a single night, ordered his slaves to carry it all away,
leaving nothing behind.
After the mourning period ended,
he became the Administrator of Xuānchéng.
By nature, he loved hunting,
and as a mountain commandery had little official business,
Wáng Sēngdá indulged in unrestrained riding and chasing.
Sometimes he would not return for three to five days.
Many petitions and lawsuits were heard at his hunting grounds.
Sometimes the people would meet him but not recognize him
and would ask where the Prefect (fǔjūn) was.
Wáng Sēngdá would say,
"He's just behind."
In the spring of the 28th year of Yuánjiā (451 CE),
the Sǔoluǒ barbarians encroached,
causing fear in the capital.
Wáng Sēngdá requested to enter and defend the capital,
which was granted.
After the barbarians retreated,
he was again appointed Administrator of Xuānchéng.
After a while,
he was transferred to Yìxīng.
In the 30th year (453 CE),
the "prime culprit" (yuánxiōng, referring to Liú Shào) assassinated and usurped the throne.
Shìzǔ (Emperor Xiàowǔ) entered to suppress him.
A general proclamation was sent to all commanderies and prefectures,
and also an order to the commandery to raise troops.
Wáng Sēngdá did not know whom to follow.
A guest advised him, saying:
"Currently, the treachery is sky-high,
unprecedented in ancient and modern times.
As a plan for you,
nothing is better than to heed the proclamation of the righteous army,
and send notices to neighboring commanderies.
Employ eloquent speakers
to clearly explain the misfortunes and blessings.
If they have any conscience,
who will not respond?
This is the best strategy.
If you cannot do that,
you can personally lead those inclined towards righteousness,
carefully choose convenient land or water routes,
and return yourself to the south.
That is the next best."
Wáng Sēngdá then personally sought a path and fled south,
meeting Shìzǔ at Quètóu.
He was immediately appointed Chief Clerk (chángshǐ)
and given the additional title of General Who Quells Barbarians (zhēnglǔ jiāngjūn).
Initially,
when Shìzǔ set out from Xúnyáng,
Shěn Qìngzhī said to others:
"Wáng Sēngdá will certainly come to join the righteous cause."
When asked why,
Shěn Qìngzhī replied:
"When the barbarian horses drank from the Jiāng,
Wáng [Sēngdá] went out to face the crisis.
He appeared before the late emperor,
his arguments were expansive,
and his resolve was clear and decisive.
Based on this,
his arrival is certain."
When the Emperor (Shìzǔ) ascended the throne,
he appointed Wáng Sēngdá as Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (shàngshū yòu pūyè).
Soon after, he was sent out as Envoy with Credentials (shǐchíjié), Southern Barbarian Protector (nánmán xiàowèi),
and given the additional title of General Who Quells Barbarians (zhēnglǔ jiāngjūn).
At that time, Prince Yìxuān of Nánjùn requested to remain in Jiānglíng,
so the Southern Barbarian Protectorate could not be dissolved,
and Wáng Sēngdá did not proceed to his post.
He was subsequently appointed Protector-General (hùjūn jiāngjūn).
Wáng Sēngdá considered himself talented and of high standing,
believing no one at the time could match him.
When the Emperor first ascended the throne,
he immediately occupied a high position in the central government (duān yòu).
Within a year or two,
he already aspired to become a prime minister.
When he became Protector-General,
he was discontent,
so he submitted a memorial requesting to be appointed to Xúzhōu,
saying: "Your humble servant, in the twilight of his life,
was fortunate to encounter these times and make a career.
The late emperor, recalling his meritorious officials,
extended his favor even to the humble and lowly.
He overlooked my shortcomings and discarded my crudeness,
spreading out his strategies and gathering talents.
I have served in office
and donned the robes of an official
for more than eleven years.
Early on, I relied on prosperity and peace,
and later was close to a flourishing and brilliant era.
But though I am devoted to learning,
I lack singular insight.
Though I have duties to perform,
I lack
discerning judgment.
I am certainly not qualified to offer advice on governing the world
or to fully discern what is appropriate for the times.
I secretly believe that divine grace cannot be fully repaid,
and to remain idly in office is difficult to endure for long.
Therefore, I recklessly and crudely
often express my thoughts.
Your Majesty's filial piety and sincerity emanate from your heart,
and your righteousness and obedience move all beings.
Since your glorious ascent to the throne,
it is truly fitting that the nine regions rejoice together,
and the three luminaries shine anew.
However, your humble servant, observing the streets
and listening to popular ballads,
finds that the common people
have not yet fully felt your grace.
Public opinion, far and near,
has not shown much improvement.
This is why your humble servant has been troubled day and night,
and felt pain in his heart
in his waking and sleeping hours.
Your humble servant cites examples from previous ages
to draw comparisons with the present.
In the time of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
it can be said that he relied on an already established foundation
and held power during an already stable period.
Moreover, he wore simple clothes and ate simple food,
diligently and anxiously governing the state.
Yet, Jiǎ Yì candidly expressed his true feelings,
still offering advice with lamentations and tears.
How much more so now, inheriting a fallen state,
with myriad affairs just beginning,
where grace has not yet spread widely,
and trust
has not yet fully encompassed all!
Your humble servant also heard a former worthy say:
'The empire
is a heavy vessel;
once stable, it cannot be easily endangered,
and once endangered, it cannot be easily made stable.'
Your Majesty's divine thoughts are profound
and far-reaching,
and you should also consider this with your sagely wisdom.
I humbly believe that the most urgent task of the present
is for all to work for themselves,
for families and the state to share the same concerns,
to truly satisfy the hearts of the common people,
and to follow their desires.
When the people voice their distress,
the ruler should manifest the will to accept their advice wholeheartedly.
When the lower classes suffer from faults and abuses,
the upper classes should have no extravagant or complacent feelings.
Furthermore, officials should be appointed according to their talents,
and ranks bestowed according to their reputation.
It is better to err on the side of not
rewarding
than to err on the side of not punishing.
As for crucial and important offices,
and vital frontier strongholds,
where order and disorder depend,
and stability and turmoil converge,
all institutions are new,
yet some may be continued without
change.
Matters depend on what is appropriate;
there should be no fixed rule for appointment or dismissal.
The empire has many talents;
it depends on how they are employed.
Your humble servant not only observes the ways of the world
and mistakenly understands their difficulties,
but also, from his own experience,
clearly sees their shortcomings.
Why?
Although your humble servant has avoided being completely ignorant,
his writings do not enter
to study martial arts,
and whose conduct was without fault or transgression.
I myself have no talent
but directly rely on the patronage of my family and

Moreover, though I recently fled along the

what achievements have I

Yet Your Majesty has frequently shown me special favor,

If I did not possess inherent
talent,

I ought to reflect on my station

not knowing when
I will be able

Indeed, to face danger and sacrifice one's life,
to strive until death,
these are all earnestly exhorted in previous admonitions,

I am moved by the maxims of the former sages,

If I were to enjoy a generous salary,

at ease.
Now, the four barbarians are still vigilant,

Recently, our heavenly troops have not been victorious,

I fear that the Róng and Dí, being greedy and covetous,

Should they assume that the Divine Land is temporarily in disarray

Moreover,
with late autumn upon us,
the Hu horses will grow mighty.
It is advisable to plan for what is easy
and prepare for it early.
Every day I reflect three times,
my ambition is to repay your kindness.
Considering what is suitable
for small and large tasks, both far and
near,
to be effective in a remote region,
and to be given command, then it is within my abilities to manage,

As for initially commanding the military and government,

but
truly not my wish.
Your Majesty’s compassion and understanding are already profound;

The responsibility of Guard General [Hùjūn]

The military prefecture of Péngchéng

Moreover, I was originally involved in military service,

A humble intelligence and a minor title

then both those at court and outside
will be honored and grateful,
and my deeds, living or dead, will be inscribed.
The emperor did not permit it.

Earlier,

Sēng Dá [Sēng Dá] was furious.

Before I could utilize
my private status,

Língbǎo [Língbǎo] last year was lost in Chángxī [Chángxī],

My transgressions accumulated and misfortunes combined,

As soon as I managed to survive,

I, your humble servant, am like your own flesh and blood;

Chēgǔ.
The day I arrived,
the enemy banners had already been furled.
Although my time in the commandery was brief,
I had already settled my share of salary.
Just as I was dusting off my farmer's clothes,
and returning to the fields and livestock,
the common people of Xuānchéng
went to
the palace to request my retention.
At that time, an imperial edict instructed my late cousin, Sēngchuò, to proclaim the intention to keep me.
Being ill and having few responsibilities,

I then submitted a memorial earnestly pleading to return to my post.
Before my return to
duties was scheduled,
my late elder brother, Chénxī, suddenly passed away.
I requested leave to rush to the funeral,

Not long after,
I was again appointed to Yìxīng.
I, your servant, flying from heaven
and swimming the sea,
how could I presume to have scales and wings?
My idle thoughts of a peaceful life
deepened with each passing day.
Since holding office,
I have never accumulated a drop of wealth.
Frail and sickly,
I also lack
the support of a single person.
Yet, my nature is fond of forests and waters,

When considering where to reside,
I often act contrary to administrative essentials.
Therefore, I restrain myself and manage my portion,
not forgetting it for a moment,
truly because there
are needs that are difficult to provide for,

The offerings from the eastern commandery are meager,
while the salary from the western passes is substantial.
I fully presented my earnest entreaty,
and firmly maintained my initial wish,
begging to be placed in a distant commandery like Jiāng or Xiāng.
In one or two
years,
perhaps on the day I return to farming,
my provisions and medicine will have a place to be stored.
I immediately received a clear promise,
that I would be graciously promoted.
When I encountered ill fortune,
and heaven and earth collapsed,

And as for myself,

Though the relationship was nominally that of sovereign and minister,
the benevolence was like that of a father
and son.
I, your servant, am truly mediocre and dull-witted,

On the day I heard the tragic news,

My single body and weak heirs,

mortal peril.
My life was as fleeting as morning dew,

Supported by faith and obedience,

At that time, my brother's son, Sēngliàng,

The mountains and rivers were treacherous,

Who could not be troubled by such distant thoughts?
To taste gall and wet one's feet [in tears]

wish,

Fortunately, due to the Sacred Might,

The cosmos was clarified,

My father and son, and my uncles and nephews,

Reflecting upon my feelings,
and the origin of
returning
my bones [to the earth],

My heartfelt wish has been expressed:
avoiding rebellion and embracing obedience

My wisdom and strength are ineffective;

However, on the day my illness was neglected,

When the prime culprit

Heavenly benevolence is generous and magnanimous,

I, your servant,
reflected three times upon my undue position,

My downfall and collapse

foresight.
Therefore, I sincerely presented my pleas,

My sworn words were earnest and urgent,

I truly knew

Last year and the year before,

Reason dictates no excuse is possible;

I have sullied the court's order,

I, your servant,
accept my end,

Yet Your Majesty overlooked my personal flaws,

circumventing the laws and statutes,

The gratitude I feel for this single act

Your kindness increased,
adding to my current position.
At that moment, I was startled,
unable to find my footing.
I had already forgotten my leisurely aspirations

I deliberated
inwardly

and

lamentable.

my blurred vision is even worse,

my pores are closed,
my `róng-wèi` is dimmed,
my heart-qi is weak and agitated,
my spirit and will are scattered and failing.
I consider this root defect
will not allow me to last for years.
My
public and private sincere wish
should be granted consideration and permission.
I beg to be allowed to follow my remaining time
to finish my trivial life.
The clear water and bright sun
are not enough to serve as a metaphor.
I wish you would extend your compassion and insight,
and mercifully grant this request.
Wáng Sēngdá's memorial, with its rise and fall in tone,
was submitted to the Gate Secretariat by imperial edict.
Shìzhōng Hé Yǎn, deeming its language disrespectful,
petitioned for it to be handed over to the Southern Bureau.
He was again dismissed from office.
After a short while,
he was appointed Tàifù Zhǎngshǐ to Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng,
and prefect of Línchuái.
Later he was transferred to Tàizǎi Zhǎngshǐ,
with his prefectural post remaining as before.
In the first year of Dàmíng,
he was promoted to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently served as Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
For his service in submitting to the state,
he was enfeoffed as a fifth-rank marquess of Nínglíng County.
In the second year,
he was promoted to Zhōngshū Lìng.
Before this,
Gāo Jiā, a commoner from Fān County in Nán Péngchéng, along with the Buddhist monks Shì Tánbiāo and Dàofāng, deceived each other,
claiming to have auspicious signs from ghosts, spirits, dragons, and phoenixes,
and frequently hearing the sound of flutes and drums.
They conspired to rebel with Lán Hóngqī and others from Mòlíng.
They also sought to collude with Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn Miáo Yǔn, Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng Yán Xīnzhī, Sīkōng Cānjūn Kǎn Qiānzuǎn, Tàizǎi Fǔ Jiāng Chéng Nóng, Wáng Tián, and others,
planning to raise troops on the night of the first day of the eighth month of the second year to attack the palace gates,
surprising and ambushing Tàizǎi Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng at dawn,
and dividing their forces to assault and kill various high ministers,
making Jiā the Son of Heaven.
The plot was discovered,
and dozens of those involved were executed.
Wáng Sēngdá had repeatedly committed reckless acts of defiance.
The Emperor, believing he would never reform,
implicated him in the Gāo Jiā affair,
and issued an imperial edict stating:
"Wáng Sēngdá, by remaining blessings,
ascended early to glorious positions,
but his lighthearted treachery and lack of conduct
were notorious in common talk.
When the nation faced a difficult period,
his entire household wished to offer their service.
His meager sincerity was recognized,
and his great wickedness pardoned.
Honors were bestowed both within and without,
and he reached the height of favor.
Yet, he never harbored gratitude for his nurture,
nor did he remember kindness received.
Instead, he collaborated with `Xīchǔ`,
intending to disturb the eastern region.
He openly engaged in plunder,
and conspicuously seized assets from wicked factions,
relying on and colluding with various evil individuals,
misleading and confusing public perception.
I have always tolerated and concealed his actions,
thinking to clear his name.
But he showed no gratitude like a dog or horse,
and the small spark grew into a prairie fire,
the trickle portended a river.
He then became as close as lips and teeth with Gāo Jiā,
and conspired with Sū Bǎo,
seeking out details of rebellious diagrams,
and observing celestial phenomena.
When the chief bandit was executed,
and the remaining accomplices were interrogated,
all declared their confessions in court documents
and publicly in the markets.
Yet I still wished to tolerate it,
allowing law to yield to emotion.
The small rogues are numerous and disorderly,
and the incitement of the people is becoming severe.
They fabricate disturbances,
aiming for what they should not covet.
This has already been reported to the high officials
and made known throughout the court and country.
How can I disregard the importance of the imperial ancestral temple and altars,
and act with the benevolence of a common man?
Executing evildoers is in accordance with holy canons.
Severing slanderous speech and eliminating rebellious acts
are esteemed by the Hàn laws.
He should be immediately arrested and handed over to the Grand Judge
to uphold the penal code.
However, the late Tàibǎo, Huáróng Wénzhāo Gōng Hóng, served through many reigns with deep loyalty and favor.
How can his meritorious virtues be forgotten,
and his family sacrifices neglected?
His family titles and imperial connections
shall not be diminished or cut off."
He was granted death in prison.
At that time, he was thirty-six years old.
His son, Dàoyǎn,
was exiled to Xīn'ān Commandery.
When the former deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
he was allowed to return to the capital.
During Yuánhuī, in the reign of the later deposed Emperor,
he became the Nèishǐ of Lúlíng Kingdom.
He died before reaching the commandery.
Sū Bǎo's
personal name was Bǎoshēng.
Originally from a common family,
he possessed excellence in literature and ethics.
During the Yuánjiā period, when the National Academy was established,
he served as an assistant instructor for the `Máoshī`.
He was recognized by Tàizǔ,
and his official career reached Nántái Shìyùshǐ
and Jiāngníng Lìng.
He was executed along with Jiā
for knowing about Gāo Jiā's rebellion but not reporting it immediately.
Yán Jùn, courtesy name Shìxùn,
was a native of Línyí, Lángyá,
and the son of Guānglù Dàfū Yánzhī.
Tàizǔ asked Yánzhī:
"Among your sons, who possesses your style?"
He replied:
"Jùn inherited my calligraphy,
Cè inherited my prose,
Wēn inherited my sense of righteousness,
and Yuè inherited my love of wine."
Jùn initially served as Tàixué Bóshì,
and Tàizǐ Shèrén.
He was dispatched to serve as Shìzǔ Fǔjūn Zhǔbù,
and was greatly favored and trusted.
Jùn also diligently offered his assistance.
During the Yuánjiā period,
the Emperor, not wanting the various princes to form factions,
intended to summon Jùn to be appointed Shàngshū Láng.
However, Lìbù Shàngshū Jiāng Zhàn believed that Jùn had a good reputation in the regional administration
and should not be reassigned.
The Emperor then stopped the plan.
Thus, he followed the administration, transferring to serve as Zhǔbù for Ānběi, Zhènjūn, and Běizhōngláng administrations.
In the twenty-eighth year,
the barbarians returned north from Péngchéng
and again requested mutual trade.
Jùn argued:
"Your humble servant believes that peace treaties with the barbarians are useless,

How can I explain this?
The barbarians' desire to invade and plunder
is solely due to their lack of sufficient strength.
They have never been constrained by faith and righteousness
to desist from their schemes.
The campaign on the Jiāng River last year
was precisely brought about by the peace treaty.
For many years, envoys were exchanged,
and eventually, they sought an imperial marriage alliance.
The court, maintaining a loose tributary relationship,
equivocated but did not sever ties.
After years accumulated,
it gradually became impossible to deceive them.
Their bestial greed was insatiable,
further compounded by their anger,
thus leading to their deep incursion.
Fortunately, now, after the armed conflict,
`Huá` and `Róng` are separated.
If we talk about mutual trade,
Initially,
the śramaṇa Shì Sēnghán (釋僧含) had a rough grasp of scholarly principles.
He said to Jùn (竣):
“This humble monk roughly sees from the apocryphal prophecies [chèn jì]
that a true man [zhēnrén] who matches the portents will appear.
His name will rise in succession,
and he will belong to Your Highness.”
Jùn, while in Péngchéng (彭城), once mentioned this to his relatives,
and the words spread,
reaching the ears of Taìzǔ (太祖).
At that time, the matter of Yuánxiōng’s (元凶) sorcery [wūgǔ] had already come to light,
so the emperor did not pursue an investigation.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) was garrisoned in Xúnyáng (尋陽),
Jùn was promoted to Nán Zhōngláng Jìshì Cānjūn (南中郎記室參軍).
In the spring of the 30th year,
as his father Yánzhī (延之) had retired from office,
he firmly requested to resign from his post,
but this was not granted.
He was given leave but had not yet departed
when news of Taìzǔ’s death arrived.
Shìzǔ raised an army to suppress the rebellion.
Jùn was transferred to Zīyì Cānjūn (諮議參軍),
also taking charge of Lùshì (錄事).
He was responsible for both internal and external affairs,
and also composed proclamations.
When Shìzǔ departed from Xúnyáng,
he fell ill.
Among those in charge of Lùshì, from Shěn Qìngzhī (沈慶之) downwards,
none were able to see him,
but only Jùn had access to his bedchamber,
making decisions on military matters.
At that time, Shìzǔ was repeatedly in critical condition,
unable to receive counsel.
All important matters
were decided and executed solely by Jùn.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Jùn as Shìzhōng (侍中).
Shortly after, he was promoted to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (左衛將軍),
and given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
He declined the Chángshì title,
and his request was granted.
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Jiànchéng Xiàn (建城縣),
with an emolument of two thousand households.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn (孝建),
he was transferred to Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書),
also holding the title of Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (驍騎將軍).
He devoted himself to the selection of officials,
working tirelessly.
His position and trust were already high,
and there was nothing in his memorials that was not approved.
