Later, Xiè Zhuāng (謝莊) replaced Jùn in charge of selections,
but many of his proposals were not implemented.
Jùn's appearance was stern and resolute,
while Zhuāng's demeanor was very graceful.
When guests and petitioners spoke loudly,
he always responded with smiles and laughter.
People at the time made a saying:
“Yán Jùn (顏竣) grants offices while angry,
Xiè Zhuāng (謝莊) does not grant offices while smiling.”
When Nánjùn Wáng Yìxuān (南郡王義宣) and Zāng Zhì (臧質) rebelled,
Jùn was appointed acting Lǐngjūn (領軍).
Yìxuān (義宣) and Zhì’s (質) sons were hidden in Jiànkāng (建康), Mòlíng (秣陵), Húshú (湖熟), and Jiāngníng Xiàn (江寧縣) areas.
Shìzǔ was greatly enraged.
He dismissed Chǔ Zhànzhī (褚湛之), the Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹), from office,
and arrested the officials of the four counties.
Jùn was appointed Dānyáng Yǐn,
with the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
Previously,
Jùn had no sons,
while all the sons of Dà Sīmǎ (大司馬) Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng (江夏王義恭) had been killed by Yuánxiōng (元凶).
By this time, both had each produced sons.
The emperor personally named them.
He named Yìgōng’s son Bóqín (伯禽),
comparing him to Lǔgōng Bóqín (魯公伯禽),
the son of Zhōugōng Dàn (周公旦).
He named Jùn’s son Pìqiáng (辟強),
comparing him to the son of Hàn (漢) Shìzhōng (侍中) Zhāng Liáng (張良).
Earlier, during the Yuánjiā (元嘉) reign,
four-zhū coins were minted.
Their rims and overall form
were the same as five-zhū coins.
They incurred expenses and losses,
bringing no profit,
so the common people did not counterfeit them.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he again minted Xiàojiàn (孝建) four-zhū coins.
In the third year,
Shàngshū Yòuchéng Xú Yuán (尚書右丞徐爰) proposed:
“To value currency and benefit the people
is recorded in the Five Policies [wǔ zhèng].
To initiate minting and circulate currency
was a law established in the Nine Treasuries [jiǔ fǔ].
The people become rich and the state is substantial,
education is established and civilization flourishes.
When times change and customs evolve,
then adapting to change is appropriate.
This is why Zhōu (周) and Hàn (漢) shifted practices,
adjusting the weight [of currency] according to the era.
Later generations,
with abundant wealth and sufficient resources,
followed the previous system
without further innovation.
As years passed and were far removed,
and disasters and chaos were repeatedly experienced,
burial, burning, cutting, and destruction
caused daily depletion.
Currency became light and the people poor;
both public and private sectors were distressed.
Without reform and creation,
a great scarcity will ensue.
I suggest we should follow the classical precedents,
collect copper and repair castings,
accept redemption to commute punishments,
as recorded in past strategies.
Today, it is appropriate to redeem punishments with copper,
categorizing them according to the fine.”
The imperial edict approved this.
The minted coins were thin and small in form,
and their rims were incomplete.
[一０]Consequently, counterfeiters rose up like clouds among the populace.
They mixed in lead and tin,
and none of the coins were sturdy.
They also clipped and chiseled ancient coins
to extract their copper,
making the coins progressively thinner and smaller,
gradually deviating from the official standard.
Although severe penalties were imposed,
officials and common people who were executed or dismissed for counterfeiting followed one another,
yet counterfeiting became even more rampant.
Prices of all goods soared,
and the people suffered from this.
Then standards were established,
and thin, small, and rimless coins
were all strictly prohibited.
Shǐxīng Jùngōng Shěn Qìngzhī (始興郡公沈慶之) proposed, saying:
“In the past, Qín (秦) currency was too heavy,
which Gāozǔ (高祖) considered a problem.
He universally allowed the people to mint coins,
recreating the ‘elm-leaf’ coins.
However, currency became light and goods expensive,
which again was contrary to the times.
Taìzōng (太宗) allowed free minting,
for which Jiǎ Yì (賈誼) criticized him.
Indeed, because the technique of mining existed,
copper was abundant and profits high,
and the tools for farming and warfare,
which were used in earlier times,
were eagerly made by the four classes,
causing perhaps much harm.
However, Xiàowén (孝文) did not accept this advice,
and the people's minting proceeded.
Thus, he was able to fill his treasuries with decaying strings of coins,
and the empire became prosperous.
Moreover, today, farming and warfare tools are not in use,
and mining and casting have long been abandoned.
What is used for smelting
mostly comes from finished articles.
The effort is difficult and the profit thin,
cutting off the resources of Wú (吳) and Dèng (鄧).
Farmers are not accustomed to this [minting],
so there is no worry of them abandoning their plows.
Currently, during this period of restoration and new beginning,
the sagely transformation is renewed.
Although weapons are laid down and spears melted,
the storehouses are not yet full.
What is lacking for both public and private sectors
is only money.
I humbly suggest that the people should be allowed to mint coins.
Commanderies and counties should establish minting offices.
Families willing to mint
should all reside within these offices.
Their standards should be made uniform,
[一一]and impurities and counterfeits removed.
The government should collect the rims [from clipping]
and store them as everlasting treasures.
The new products prohibited last spring
should be put into circulation at once.
All current minting should follow this standard.
A tax of three thousand [coins] per ten thousand [minted] should be levied,
and strict inspections against counterfeiting
and clipping should be enforced.
Within a few years,
both public and private sectors will be abundant,
copper will be exhausted and the matter will cease,
and illicit activities will stop naturally.
Furthermore, prohibiting minting turns copper into tools,
while allowing minting turns tools into wealth.
To cut back on extravagance and promote utility
is beneficial to affairs.”
The matter was presented to the high officials.
The Grand Chancellor, Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng, deliberated and said:
“I have respectfully reviewed Shěn Qìngzhī’s proposal,
‘Allow the people to privately mint coins.
All households that enjoy minting [coins]
shall be registered and reside [in designated areas].
Standardize their specifications
and remove their impurities and counterfeits.’
I believe that the common people have long been reluctant to be associated with officials,
and this has been the case for a very long time.
Moreover, many of them are scholars [and gentlemen];
it is unlikely they would wish to be registered.
Generally, illicit minting yields profit,
and that profit lies in counterfeits and impurities.
If counterfeits and impurities are prohibited,
those willing to register will surely be few.
It says, ‘Collect the outlines [of old coins],
and store them as eternal treasures.’
I believe that what is valued by those above [the common people]
will surely be followed by those below.
When the people hear that officials are collecting coin outlines,
the value of coin outlines will increase a hundredfold.
With unequal exchanges between large and small [coins],
who would be willing to do it?
To forcibly compel exchange
would resemble coercion and seizure.
It also says, ‘The new items prohibited last spring
shall be put into use temporarily.’
I believe this clause is permissible.
It also says, ‘Current minting should follow this standard,
with a tax of three thousand per ten thousand.’
It further says, ‘Strictly inspect illicit minting,
and no further production shall be allowed.’
I believe that prohibitions
are not merely for a single day.
To pursue profit and violate the law
is common human nature.
The concern is not that the regulations are too lenient,
but that they are transgressed.
Now, if registered, one must pay three thousand per ten thousand,
while private minting incurs no thirteenth [of a] tax.
Those who pursue profit and violate prohibitions
will surely not cease.
It also says, ‘When copper is exhausted, the matter will cease,
and counterfeiting will naturally be prohibited.’
I believe that the copper within the realm
cannot be exhausted all at once.
By the time copper is exhausted,
counterfeiting will have already accumulated.
It also says, ‘If minting is prohibited, copper will turn into [other] artifacts;
if minting is opened, artifacts will turn into wealth.’
However, the recent problem
has been the unevenness of forms,
compounded by clipping and chiseling.
Moreover, the widespread mixture of lead and tin is confined to those who illicitly mint copper.
[一二]There is no need for such harsh prohibition.”
Jùn deliberated and said:
“The utility of currency
has been consistent in recent history.
The debate over heavy and light [coins]
was settled in the Hàn era.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
it has not been possible to change it.
This is truly because once goods are uniform,
changing them gives rise to counterfeiting.
As generations pass,
the malady of [currency] circulation suddenly arrives.
There should be a method
for reform and innovation.
The current proposal to open official mints and allow casting
is indeed something to welcome.
However, I fear that mining will cease,
and the consumption of artifacts will increase daily.
As copper becomes scarcer,
artifacts will become even more valuable.
If an artifact costs one thousand [coins],
then minting [coins from it] would yield half that,
making it unprofitable.
Even if ordered, it would not be carried out.
It also says, ‘The items prohibited last spring
shall be put into use temporarily.’
This is intended to enrich the empire.
If small coins are widely circulated
without being produced by official mints,
the personal profit will be profound,
and the cunning and deceit boundless.
Private minting, clipping, and chiseling
will become impossible to prohibit.
[一三]Coins like Wǔzhū and Bànliǎng
will surely be exhausted in less than a year.
Before wealth and goods are replenished,
large coins will have already been depleted.
In a few years,
they will all turn to dust.
How can a path to such a severe detriment
be established in the imperial era?
Although the people's currency
is becoming scarcer now,
the common folk in the markets
have not yet expressed lament.
This new prohibition has just been implemented,
and the standards are not yet uniform.
It will naturally cease shortly;
it is not worthy of the sagely consideration.
Only the emptiness of the imperial treasury
is indeed a serious concern.
Now, even if small coins are circulated,
the government gains no additional revenue.
Even if the people are enriched,
it does not resolve the government's deficiency.
Only by simplifying expenses and eliminating extravagance,
and by practicing frugality,
can the path to abundance
be achieved. There is no more valuable method than this.
However, money has a fixed limit,
while its disappearance is unconstrained.
Even if clipping and minting cease,
they will eventually lead to exhaustion.
The government should
not open offices for collecting copper,
nor should it cut off the use of artifacts.
If its standards are set,
and coins are gradually minted month by month,
after a long time,
it will not benefit the world.”
At the time, other debaters also considered copper increasingly difficult to obtain,
and wished to mint two-zhū coins.
Jùn further deliberated and said:
“The debaters intend to address the emptiness of the imperial treasury,
and therefore propose to change minting.
As copper is scarce in the empire,
they suggest reducing the coin standard
to remedy the financial woes,
and to relieve the nation and the people.
I believe this is not the case.
Now, minting two-zhū coins
and allowing new, smaller coins to circulate freely
will not alleviate the government's deficiencies,
but will greatly encourage the cunning and trickery of the people.
The empire's currency
will be fragmented and eventually depleted.
Strict prohibitions will be established in vain,
as the profits are deep and difficult to eliminate.
In no more than one or two years,
the harm will become irremediable.
This is the first reason why it is absolutely impermissible.
Now, the profit from melting and casting [coins]
does not appear to yield hundreds of millions at once.
[一四]Even if such an amount were obtained,
it would certainly take an entire year.
At year-end, when taxes are collected,
the currency is temporarily renewed,
but daily expenses
are not covered for several months.
Even if emergency assistance is levied,
how would it alleviate the deficiency?
It would only allow cunning people to have their way,
and leave behind a legacy of flawed policies.
This is the second reason why it is absolutely impermissible.
The people have been deterred by the change to large coins,
and are also fearful of the recent new prohibitions.
Among the markets,
there will surely be clamor and unrest.
The distant benefits are unheard of,
while the immediate harm is widespread.
Rich merchants will have their way,
and the poor people will be distressed.
This is the third reason why it is absolutely impermissible.
If the financial woes were to deepen,
it would still be unacceptable,
let alone when its benefits are not yet seen,
and there are so many drawbacks.
Would we miscalculate at this moment
and invite scorn for a hundred generations?”
When the Former Deposed Emperor (Qián Fèidì) ascended the throne,
he minted two-zhū coins,
whose form became increasingly small.
Whenever government coins were issued,
the common people would immediately imitate them,
but in size, thickness, and thinness,
they were all inferior.
They had no rim,
were not polished,
and were like today's clipped or cut coins,
called lěizǐ.
In the first year of Jǐnghé,
Shěn Qìngzhī petitioned to allow private minting,
and from this, the currency became chaotic and debased.
A string of a thousand coins was often not more than three cùn long,
and their size was proportionate to this,
being called "goose-eye coins" (éyǎnqián).
Those inferior to these
were called "thread-ring coins" (yánhuánqián).
They would not sink in water,
and shattered easily when handled.
The markets no longer bothered to count them;
one hundred thousand coins did not fill a single scoop.
A dou of rice cost ten thousand [coins],
and commerce ceased.
In the early reign of Tàizōng,
only goose-eye and thread-ring coins were prohibited;
all others were allowed for use.
Later, private minting was again banned,
and government mints also stopped their work.
Soon after, both were completely prohibited,
and only ancient coins were allowed.
Jùn, who was Sànqí Chángshì and Dānyáng Yǐn,
was promoted to Zhōngshū Lìng,
with Dānyáng Yǐn as before.
He submitted a memorial declining the Zhōngshū Lìng position, saying:
"I have idly usurped a vital national position,
and sit in an important forbidden office.
〔一五〕Upon hearing the command, I am ashamed and terrified,
my body and soul trembling.
I, your subject, am an ordinary and humble person from the eastern region,
born into a minor clan,
〔一六〕raised among the common people.
I have never seen official chariots,
my family has no wealth or nobility,
and my ambition has always been far from the distinguished ranks.
It is merely because I committed myself to farming,
and hunger and cold afflicted me severely,
that the former court, which regulated all people,
did not overlook the foolish and humble.
I was thus spared the toil of plowing and taxation,
and was relegated to the lowest ranks of officialdom.
Your Majesty, with your great virtue, resided in the imperial domain,
gathering all the talented and extraordinary.
Even I, with my lack of talent,
was elevated beyond my humble station to the pure ranks.
I served for many years,
but my labors and achievements are not worth mentioning.
I relied on your benevolent completion [of my career],
and my sole wish was to remain a local administrator.
How could I have expected that heaven and earth would be suddenly interrupted,
and that profound sorrow would give rise to a sage?
I leaned on the rising fortune,
and was promoted along the divine path.
Like clouds flying and seas swimming,
I surpassed my peers,
not yet three years,
but receiving extraordinary appointments among the eight categories of officials.
If the reward system is examined,
then your subject does not qualify;
if diligence and goodness are considered,
then your subject's rank equals that of the noble.
〔一七〕I was just about to appeal to the imperial court,
to descend from my high rank in the grand hierarchy,
to reduce my public visibility,
and slightly alleviate the slander against me,
when the imperial decree was profusely issued,
and my position was made even more eminent.
I, your subject, am a man of small understanding,
incapable of long-term planning.
When favor and benefit arrive,
how can I adhere to restraint?
I only fear that by offending heavenly enlightenment above,
and disturbing righteous discussion below,
calamity and reprimand
will surely be imminent.
This excessive appointment now,
precedes my humble self.
If it is truly said to be unfounded,
then danger and disgrace will soon follow.
What ten hands point to [in accusation]
is like a disease in the vitals.
This is why I am anxious and perturbed awake and asleep,
constantly troubled by this bitter ailment.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty will perceive my sincere heart,
and pity my urgent wish,
to kindly withdraw the favor,
to preserve my foolish lot,
for then the creative power of nature's bestowal
would seem meager compared to this. "
His request was granted.
At that time, there was a drought and the people were starving.
Jùn memorialized to ban malt sugar for one month,
saving nearly ten thousand húl of rice.
He then replaced Xiè Zhuāng as Lìbù Shàngshū,
and concurrently held the position of Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài.
Before he was formally appointed,
he entered mourning.
He was then reinstated as Yòujiāngjūn,
with Dānyáng Yǐn as before.
Jùn relied on his old connections from the imperial family's former residence [as Prince of Xiāng],
and extensively criticized current affairs.
Since the emperor's ascension,
he had initiated many constructions.
Jùn's remonstrances and arguments were earnest,
without any reservation,
which greatly displeased the emperor,
and most of his advice was not followed.
Jùn considered himself talented enough to manage the times,
and his favors and old ties incomparable.
He expected to assist in affairs and reside in the central government,
permanently holding court power.
However, his proposals were mostly not accepted,
and he suspected the emperor wished to distance him.
Thus, he requested an external posting,
to gauge the imperial will.
In the first year of Dàmíng,
he was made Dōngyángzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his general rank as before.
Once his request was granted,
he became anxious and distressed without a plan.
Upon arriving at the prefecture,
he again suffered the calamity of his mother's death.
He was not permitted to leave his post,
but was allowed to return to the capital with the funeral procession.
The imperial favor shown was still generous,
but Jùn felt increasingly uneasy.
Whenever he spoke to relatives and old friends,
he harbored considerable resentment and indignation,
and also commented on the erroneous nature of court affairs
and the ruler's successes and failures.
When Wáng Sēngdá was executed,
it was believed that Jùn had slandered and framed him.
Before his death, Wáng Sēngdá recounted Jùn's previous resentments,
and how he always regretted that his words were not heeded.
Wáng Sēngdá's statements
were quite consistent and corroborated.
The emperor then ordered Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Yú Huīzhī to memorialize, saying: "I, your subject, have heard that a minister serving his lord
should destroy his family for the glory of the state,
exhaust his feelings without selfishness.
If one is rude and aggressive towards others,
and, relying on wealth, disparages superiors,
it is like Wáng Shū, who served as a warning,
and his son was executed.
Never has one who betrays his foundation and blocks the source,
loving profit and forgetting righteousness,
been able to tolerate himself in a prosperous age,
and corrupt the pure current.
Yòujiāngjūn and Dōngyángzhōu
Cìshǐ, the Founding Marquis of Jiànchéng County, Yán Jùn,
attached himself to the rising winds and clouds,
and was mistakenly favored and promoted.
With the recreation of heaven and earth,
he was elevated out of turn.
When the sagacious court took direct control,
all affairs
returned to one source,
yet he spied on the levers of state,
secretly plotting to wield power.
When he was appointed to the election office,
his instigations became even more severe.
When he was dispatched to govern the capital region,
his overbearing manner became even more pronounced.
Transmitting decrees and violating the constitution
required prior reporting,
yet Jùn, considering those who appealed to him to be offensive,
would arbitrarily whip and insult them.
Ignoring imperial authority,
nothing was more egregious than this.
Stern edicts were repeatedly issued,
demanding accountability from officials,
but Jùn's
arbitrary power did not cease,
and his resentment grew.
He harbored treacherous schemes,
and concealed sinister malice.
When he prematurely learned of imperial intentions,
he would invariably reveal them;
punishments he would blame on the emperor,
while favors he would claim for
himself.
To those who received his patronage,
he would immediately heap slander and insult;
to those who received imperial reprimand,
he would subtly offer sympathy and comfort.
He overturned court discipline,
deceptively confused public opinion,
intimidated senior ministers,
and incited
lǘ yán.
Mò Lǜ (莫慮) then submitted a memorial to the emperor,
〔一八〕harboring suspicion and fear within,
falsely requesting an audience with the eastern governor [Dōng Mù (東牧)],
to divine Heaven's will.
Once he obtained permission to leave the capital for a provincial post,
his curses and reproaches became rampant.
He talked back and slandered secretly;
his contempt was already evident.
Moreover, when he submitted memorials from time to time,
they invariably aligned with his treacherous private interests,
which he would proclaim to his relatives and friends,
influencing the common people.
When his mother died the previous winter,
an imperial edict granted him leave to return for the burial.
After the funeral was completed, he did not
depart,
but lingered for a long time.
He then sowed discord among the meritorious nobles [xūn guì (勳貴)],
creating factions and disagreements.
He also feigned alarm and fear,
deeply plotting for his own advancement,
secretly interviewing high-ranking officials [dà chén (大臣)],
fearing he would not secure a complete position.
He then claimed that because he had been banished,
the state was on the verge of collapse.
Hostility accumulated in his heart,
and his wickedness was apparent in his words and demeanor.
Furthermore, his conduct at home was lacking,
having long drawn public criticism.
Yet, he rose to a position of great favor,
receiving emoluments worth tens of thousands of gold,
which he used to boast to his relatives,
but his salary was not enough to sustain his extravagance.
He harbored old grudges against his half-brother [mǔ dì (母弟)],
and presuming on his noble status, he frequently had people killed.
His family relations were filled with resentment and poison,
and his close associates were shocked and terrified.
Wherever he was
appointed,
he neglected governance and justice.
He often opened the Dānyáng (丹陽) treasury,
lending its contents to his subordinates.
He liberally granted resources and favors,
recruiting them as his protégés,
filling the court and the countryside,
amounting to nearly a thousand.
He was arrogant and unrestrained towards his subordinates,
hindering public welfare and harming private interests.
He seized money from the inspector [jiān (監)] to supply
his personal retinue.
His guests sang and feasted drunkenly,
no different from ordinary months,
and what was said in the streets
was no longer
just rumor.
Jùn (竣) was a civil official who served as a secretary in the capital,
and was specially favored by Heaven.
His faults were overlooked, and he was appointed,
participating in important affairs.
He did not exert himself in the slightest,
yet his rewards rivaled those of Ḥé (河) and Shān (山).
He exploited imperial favor both inside and outside the court,
transgressing
his proper rank.
The nature of mountains and rivers
grows ever more luxuriant with the sun and moon;
the heart of valleys and ravines
is to be filled and to expand without limit.
To describe him as a tiger in a cap and a wolf in greed
is insufficient.
Now, with the emperor's wisdom shining
brightly,
all things prosper.
His corrupting influence and negative example
are truly harmful.
It is fitting to execute him publicly
to manifest the flourishing transformation [of the empire].
I request that Jùn (竣) be immediately dismissed from his current official post based on these facts,
and that the Grand Minister of Ceremonies [Tài Cháng (太常)] be ordered to strip him of his noble rank and fief.
He should then be handed over to the Court of Judicial Review [Tíng Wèi Fǎ Yù (廷尉法獄)] to be punished according to the law.
The emperor did not immediately wish to inflict a major punishment,
and merely dismissed him from office.
Jùn (竣) frequently submitted memorials apologizing
and begging for his life.
The emperor grew angrier,
and responded with an edict:
"What the judicial officials [Xiàn Sī (憲司)] have reported
is not what I had previously expected of you.
You received great favor,
and thus should have upheld it to the utmost.
Your slander, resentment, and indignation
have already betrayed my original hopes.
Now you even trouble yourself with excessive worry,
fearing for your own safety.
How can this be the utmost sincerity of a subordinate serving his superior!"
When Jìngláng Wáng Dàn (竟陵王誕) rebelled,
Jùn (竣) was implicated,
and the Imperial Censor-in-Chief [Yù Shǐ Zhōng Chéng (御史中丞)] Yǔ Huīzhī (庾徽之) was summoned to draft a memorial.
Once the memorial was completed,
an edict stated:
"Jùn (竣) has betrayed imperial grace
to such an extent.
He is to be granted death in prison,
and his wife and children are to be pardoned by sending them to a distant place."
His son, Pìqiáng (辟強), was exiled to Jiāozhōu (交州),
and then killed along the way.
Jùn (竣)'s collected works circulated in the world.
The historian [Shǐ Chén (史臣)] comments: When Shìzǔ (世祖) was young and governed a provincial post,
his understanding of the Way was not yet broad.
He opened his heart and was informal,
treating his subordinates with courtesy.
When the tides turned and he was in peril,
his life was in danger and his anxieties were acute.
He bared his soul and poured out his heart,
yet still feared his words were not fully expressed.
As for Fēng Yù (馮玉) holding the imperial screen,
his authority commanded all things.
Whatever he desired was granted,
and nothing he undertook ever failed.
Subsequently, joy and sorrow diverged with time,
and sweetness and bitterness changed hearts.
The sovereign harbored present feelings,
while the minister recalled past affection.
The reward for Sòng Chāng (宋昌)
had already been bestowed,
but the concern of being in the same boat
only deepened the resentment from below.
As suspicion and animosity grew,
punishments and accusations arose naturally.
Was Jùn (竣)'s entanglement with the world
perhaps due to this?
If a minister
can serve his lord by abandoning his private interests,
and achieve merit by forgetting recompense,
then even if he seeks downfall,
it will be impossible to obtain.
Collated Notes
Biographies, Chapter 36: Zhū Xiūzhī (朱脩之), Zōng [gài xīn] (宗[⿱⿰売⽎心]), Wáng Xuánmó (王玄謨)
Zhū Xiūzhī (朱脩之), courtesy name Gōngzǔ (恭祖),
was a native of Píngshì (平氏) in Yìyáng (義陽).
His great-grandfather, Táo (燾),
was the Commander of the Western Pacification [Píng Xī Jiāng Jūn (平西將軍)] during the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
His grandfather, Xù (序),
was the Inspector of Yùzhōu (豫州).
His father, Chén (諶),
was the Inspector of Yìzhōu (益州).
Xiūzhī (脩之) was promoted from Prefectural Clerk [zhōu zhǔ bù (州主簿)] to Assistant in the Directorate of the Minister of Works [Sī Tú Cóng Shì Zhōng Láng (司徒從事中郎)].
Emperor Wén (文帝) said to him:
"Your great-grandfather was once a Secretary [zhōng láng (中郎)] to Prime Minister Wáng Dǎo (王導).
Now you are also a Secretary to Wáng Hóng (王弘).
One can truly say you have not disgraced your ancestors."
Later, he followed Dào Yànzhī (到彥之) on the northern expedition.
When Yànzhī (彥之) returned from Hénán (河南),
he left Xiūzhī (脩之) to garrison Huátái (滑臺).
He was besieged by the barbarians.
After several months, food ran out,
and the soldiers roasted rats to eat.
He was then captured by the barbarians.
Initially,
Xiūzhī (脩之)'s mother, hearing that he had been besieged for a long time,
was constantly worried about him.
Suddenly, one day, milk unexpectedly flowed from her breasts.
His mother wailed and told her family,
"I am old now,
yet suddenly I have milk again.
This is an ill omen.
My son must be in trouble!"
Later, when news arrived, it turned out that Xiūzhī (脩之) had indeed fallen on that very day.
Tuòbá Tǎo 嘉其守節,
took him as Shìzhōng,
and gave him a woman of the imperial clan in marriage.
Xiūzhī secretly planned to return south.
His wife suspected him,
and frequently asked him about his intentions with tears flowing.
Xiūzhī deeply admired her loyalty,
and in the end did not tell her.
Later, the Xiānbēi Fēng Hóng proclaimed himself King of Yàn,
governing Huánglóngchéng.
Tuòbá Tǎo attacked him,
and Xiūzhī, along with Xíng Huáimíng, who was also a captive, followed.
There was also a man named Xú Zhuó,
who again wished to lead the southern people in a secret uprising.
The plot was discovered and he was executed.
Xiūzhī and Huáimíng, in fear, fled to Fēng Hóng,
but Hóng did not treat them with courtesy.
They remained for a year.
When an envoy from Sòng arrived with an imperial edict,
Xiūzhī's name and position were already well-known.
The envoy immediately bowed upon seeing him.
That country respected imperial envoys,
calling them
"the Son of Heaven's border people."
Seeing him show respect to Xiūzhī,
they then began to treat Xiūzhī with more courtesy.
At that time, Wèi repeatedly attacked Hóng.
Someone persuaded Hóng to send Xiūzhī to seek aid (from Sòng),
so he sent him.
They sailed the sea to Dōnglái.
They encountered a fierce wind and the rudder broke.
They lowered long ropes,
and the boat then righted itself.
The sailors saw flying birds,
knowing they were near the shore,
and in a moment arrived at Dōnglái.
In the ninth year of Yuánjiā,
he arrived in Jīngyì,
and was appointed Huángmén Shìláng.
He was successively promoted to Jiāngxià Nèishǐ.
When Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Dàochǎn died,
the various Mán tribes stirred greatly.
Xiūzhī served as Zhēngxī Sīmǎ to suppress the Mán,
but suffered a defeat.
In the early years of Xiàowǔ's reign,
he was appointed Níngmán Xiàowèi and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the added title of Dūdū.
Xiūzhī was lenient and simple in his governance,
and the soldiers and common people were pleased and attached to him.
When Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ, Prince of Nánjùn, Yìxuān rebelled,
he sent a檄文 (war declaration) to Xiūzhī, urging him to raise troops.
Xiūzhī feigned agreement with him,
but sent an envoy to express his loyalty to the emperor.
The emperor commended him,
and appointed him Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the added title of Dūdū.
When Yìxuān heard that Xiūzhī was not with him,
he appointed Lǔ Xiù as Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
to attack Xiāngyáng.
Xiūzhī ordered the blocking of the Mǎ'ānshān road,
so Xiù could not advance,
and then retreated.
When Yìxuān was defeated at Liángshān,
and fled south in a single boat,
Xiūzhī led his troops south to pacify the remaining rebels.
At that time, Zhú Chāomín captured Yìxuān.
When Xiūzhī arrived,
he killed him,
and for his merits was enfeoffed as Nánchāng Xiàn Hóu.
Xiūzhī was upright and frugal in his conduct.
Whatever gifts he received,
he accepted none.
If someone sent provisions,
he might accept them,
but would then gamble them away with his subordinates,
never keeping them for himself.
His sole focus was on placating and incorporating the various Mán tribes.
He was summoned to be Zuǒmín Shàngshū,
and then transferred to Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
When he left his post,
he did not take even a single hair.
He calculated the oil burned in the prefecture, and the oxen, horses, grain, and fodder,
and repaid it with 160,000 in private money.
However, he was by nature frugal and harsh, with little compassion.
His elder sister was in the countryside,
suffering from hunger and cold, barely able to sustain herself,
but Xiūzhī never provided for her.
He once went to visit his sister.
His sister, wishing to provoke him,
prepared a vegetable soup and coarse rice for him.
Xiūzhī said:
"This is good food for a poor family."
He ate his fill and left.
Before this,
Yǔ Yàndá of Xīnyě had been Yìzhōu Cìshǐ.
He took his elder sister with him to his post,
and divided half of his salary and emoluments to support her.
The people of the west praised this.
Later, Xiūzhī fell from a carriage and broke his leg,
so he resigned from Shàngshū,
and was appointed Lǐng Chóngxiàn Tàipú,
with the added titles of Tèjìn and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
As his leg ailment made him unable to walk alone,
he was specially provided with an attendant.
When he died,
he was posthumously granted Shìzhōng,
with Tèjìn as before.
His posthumous title was Zhēnhóu.
Zōng Quē, courtesy name Yuángàn,
was a native of Nányáng.
His uncle, Bǐng,
was a man of high character who did not serve in office.
When Zōng Quē was young,
Bǐng asked him about his ambitions.
Zōng Quē said:
"I wish to ride the long winds and break through ten thousand miles of waves."
Bǐng said:
"If you do not become rich and noble,
you will ruin my family."
When his elder brother Bì married,
and the bride had just entered the household,
they were robbed that night.
Zōng Quē, then fourteen years old,
bravely stood up to resist the bandits.
The more than ten bandits scattered,
and could not enter the room.
At that time, the world was peaceful,
and scholars generally pursued literary and moral studies.
Bǐng had always been a man of high integrity,
and all his sons and relatives were fond of learning.
But Zōng Quē alone was spirited and fond of military arts,
and thus was not praised by his local community.
When Prince of Jiāngxià, Yìgōng, was Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn and Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ,
Zōng Quē accompanied him to his post in Guǎnglíng.
At that time, his cousin Qǐ was Zhēngběi Fǔ Zhǔbù.
Qǐ once went on duty,
and his attendant Niú Tài had a private affair with Qǐ's concubine.
Zōng Quē killed Tài.
Qǐ admired his spirit,
and did not blame him.
In the twenty-second year of Yuánjiā,
when they campaigned against Línyì,
Zōng Quē eagerly requested to go.
Yìgōng considered Zōng Quē brave and valiant,
and thus appointed him Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn,
serving as deputy to Ānxī Cānjūn Xiāo Jǐngxiàn's army.
He accompanied Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ Tán Hézhī to besiege the city of Qūmǐ.
Línyì sent its general Fàn Píshādá to relieve Qūmǐ.
Hézhī sent a detachment to resist him,
but they were defeated by the enemy.
He then sent Zōng Quē.
Zōng Quē divided his forces into several routes,
lowered his banners, and advanced stealthily,
attacked and defeated them,
captured Qūmǐ,
and entered Xiàngpǔ.
Fàn Yángmài, the King of Línyì, mobilized his entire country to resist,
equipping elephants with armor,
which stretched endlessly before and behind them.
The soldiers could not withstand them.
Zōng Quē said:
"I heard that lions awe and subdue all beasts."
So he made shapes of lions,
and confronted the elephants with them.
The elephants indeed panicked and fled,
and the army then scattered,
thus conquering Línyì.
They collected countless exotic treasures and various goods.
Zōng Quē took none,
remaining in simple attire.
Emperor Wén greatly admired him.
Later, he served as Suíyùn Tàishǒu.
The Mán tribes of Yōngzhōu repeatedly raided,
so Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn Shěn Qìngzhī led Zōng Quē and other generals like Liǔ Yuánjǐng,
to attack them by separate routes.
The Mán tribes were utterly routed.
Also, Tián Yànshēng, a Mán chief of Nánxīn Jùn, led his contingent in rebellion,
burned the prefectural city,
and entrenched himself on Báiyángshān.
Yuánjǐng attacked but could not take it.
Zōng Quē led his subordinates to be the first to ascend,
and the entire army followed him.
The Mán tribes were consequently awed and submitted.
Thirty years later,
Xiàowǔ (Emperor Xiàowǔ) attacked Yuánxiōng (the Prime Culprit).
Zōng Què was appointed Cányì Cānjūn (Advisor and Adjutant) of the Nánzhōng Láng (Southern Central Aide),
and concurrently led the Zhōngbīng (Central Army).
When Xiàowǔ ascended the throne,
Zōng Què was made Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Left Guard),
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Táoyáng.
His merit was second only to Liǔ Yuánjǐng.
During the Xiàojiàn reign,
he was successively promoted to Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yù Province),
supervising the military affairs of five provinces.
Earlier,
a fellow townsman, Yǔ Yè,
had a very wealthy and influential family.
He would prepare lavish meals
to entertain guests.
But when Zōng Què arrived,
he was served vegetables and coarse rice,
and Yǔ Yè said to his guests:
"General Zōng
is accustomed to eating plain food."
Zōng Què ate his fill and left.
By this time, Yǔ Yè had become Zōng Què's Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk),
also holding the position for Liángjùn (Liáng Commandery).
Zōng Què treated him very well,
not holding the past incident against him.
In the third year of Dàmíng (459 CE),
Jìnglíng Wáng Dàn (Prince Dàn of Jìnglíng) rebelled, taking control of Guǎnglíng.
Zōng Què submitted a memorial requesting to go and suppress him.
He rode a post-horse to the capital,
and received instructions directly.
The Emperor halted his carriage to console and encourage him.
Zōng Què leapt up and down several times in excitement,
looking around.
The Emperor was impressed by him.
When he set off,
he was subordinated to Chējì Dàjiāngjūn (General of Chariots and Cavalry) Shěn Qìngzhī.
Initially,
Dàn had misled his troops, saying:
"Zōng Què is helping me."
But when Zōng Què arrived,
he galloped his horse around the city, shouting:
"I am Zōng Què!"
After the rebellion was suppressed,
he entered the capital to serve as Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Left Guard).
In the fifth year,
he fell from his horse during a hunt,
breaking his leg and becoming unable to perform his duties at court.
He was appointed Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of Ceremonies),
and granted the golden seal and purple ribbon.
Zōng Què owned a fine ox suitable for imperial use,
but when the government tried to buy it, he refused to sell.
For this, he was dismissed from office.
The following year,
he was reinstated.
When Fèidì (the Deposed Emperor) ascended the throne,
Zōng Què was made Níngmán Xiàowèi (Colonel for Pacifying the Man Tribes) and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yōng Province),
with the additional title of Dūdū (Area Commander).
He died
and was posthumously granted the title of Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the West)
and given the posthumous name Sùhóu (Solemn Marquis).
In the second year of Tàishǐ (466 CE),
an imperial edict ordered Zōng Què to be enshrined in the temple of Xiàowǔ.
His son, Luóyún,
died,
and his son, Yuánbǎo, inherited the title.
Wáng Xuánmó, courtesy name Yàndé,
was a native of Qí in Tàiyuán.
His sixth-generation ancestor, Hóng,
was the Hédōng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Hédōng)
and the Marquis of Miánzhú.
Because of his involvement in the disaster of Sītú (Minister of Education) Yǔn, a paternal uncle,
he abandoned his office and moved north to Xīnxīng,
subsequently serving as Tàishǒu (Administrator) of Xīnxīng and Yànmén.
This is what he himself claimed.
[一０] His grandfather, Láo,
served the Mùróng clan as Shànggǔ Tàishǒu (Administrator of Shànggǔ).
He fell into Mùróng Dé's trap
and resided in Qīngzhōu.
His father, Xiù,
died young.
Xuánmó was extraordinary in his youth.
His paternal uncle, Ruí, had a discerning eye for people
and often laughed, saying:
"This child has a noble and bright spirit,
possessing the style of Tàiwèi Yàn Yún."
When Wǔdì (Emperor Wǔ) arrived in Xúzhōu,
he invited Xuánmó to be his Cóngshì Shǐ (Attendant Secretary),
and was impressed by him in conversation.
Towards the end of Shàodì's (Emperor Shàodì's) reign,
Xiè Huì, who was in Jīngzhōu,
invited him to be Nánmán Xíng Cānjūn (Acting Adjutant for the Southern Man Tribes) and Wǔníng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Wǔníng).
[一一] When Huì was defeated,
Xuánmó was pardoned as he was not a principal commander.
During the Yuánjiā reign,
he was appointed Zhèn Jūn Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (Adjutant of the Central Army of the Garrison Force) for Chángshā Wáng Yìxīn (Prince Yìxīn of Chángshā),
[一二] and concurrently Rǔyīn Tàishǒu (Administrator of Rǔyīn).
At that time, the barbarians attacked and captured Huátái,
taking Zhū Xiūzhī captive.
Xuánmó submitted a memorial, stating:
"The imperial route has just opened,
but is immediately blocked again.
This is not only due to heaven's timing,
but also to human affairs.
Hǔláo and Huátái,
were they only due to the incompetence of the generals?
Or also because their foundations were not solid?
The foundations were not solid
all because the people dreaded distant service.
I request to mobilize troops from Lǔyáng in Xīyáng,
and Nánxiāng in Xiāngyáng,
divide them into two routes,
and proceed directly to Xiáo and Méng.
The conscripted soldiers will not have the worry of distant labor,
and the officers and men will have songs of frequent rest.
If one wishes to use the forces of the eastern regions
to manage Láo and Luò,
the journey is already distant,
and achieving victory alone will be difficult."
Whenever Xuánmó presented strategies for northern expeditions,
the Emperor said to Yīn Jǐngrén:
"Hearing Wáng Xuánmó's exposition
makes one feel like sealing Lángjūxū (i.e., achieving great military exploits)."
[一三] Later, he became Fǔguó Sīmǎ (Military Advisor of the Auxiliary State) and Péngchéng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Péngchéng) for Xīng'ān Hóu Yìbīn (Marquis Yìbīn of Xīng'ān).
After Yìbīn died,
Xuánmó submitted a memorial,
stating that Péngchéng was crucial due to its land and water connections,
and requested that an imperial prince be appointed to oversee the provincial affairs.
Thus, Xiàowǔ was sent to govern the region.
When a major northern expedition was launched,
Xuánmó was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (General for Pacifying the Northern Tribes),
his vanguard entering the river
and receiving orders from Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General of the Auxiliary State) Xiāo Bīn.
Xuánmó advanced towards Què'áo.
The garrison commander fled,
and so he besieged Huátái.
It was not captured for several weeks.
The barbarian ruler Tuòbá Tǎo (Emperor Tǎiwǔ of Northern Wei) led a vast army, said to be a million strong.
The sound of drums
shook heaven and earth.
Xuánmó's army was also large,
and its equipment was very refined,
but Xuánmó insisted on his own views
and often resorted to killing.
When the city was first besieged,
there were many thatched houses inside.
The troops requested to burn them with fire arrows,
but Xuánmó feared damaging military supplies
and refused.
The city dwellers then dismantled them,
making the open ground into underground chambers.
When the Wei relief forces were about to arrive,
the troops requested to form a camp with wagons,
but he again refused.
Many officers and soldiers were resentful.
He also engaged in profiteering,
demanding eight hundred pears for one bolt of cloth,
which further alienated the people.
When Tuòbá Tǎo's army arrived,
he fled,
and almost all of his subordinates scattered and perished.
Xiāo Bīn intended to execute him,
but Shěn Qìngzhī strongly remonstrated, saying:
"Fóli's (Tuòbá Tǎo's) might shakes the world,
commanding a million archers.
How could Xuánmó withstand him?
Moreover, killing a fighting general to weaken oneself
is not a good plan."
Bīn then stopped.
Earlier,
when Xuánmó was about to be executed,
he dreamed that someone told him:
"Recite the Guānyīn Sūtra a thousand times,
and you will be spared."
After waking,
he recited it a thousand times.
The next day, as he was about to be executed,
he recited without stopping.
Suddenly, a cry came to halt the execution.
He was sent to replace the defender of Què'áo.
Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng (Prince Yìgōng of Jiāngxià), who was the Zhēngtǎo Dūdū (Area Commander of the Punitive Expedition),
believed that Què'áo could not be held,
and summoned him back.
He was pursued by the Wei army,
who greatly defeated him,
and a stray arrow hit his arm.
In the first month of the twenty-eighth year (451 CE),
he returned to Lìchéng.
[一四] Yìgōng wrote to Xuánmó, saying:
"I heard that the defeat turned into success.
The wound on your arm,
could it not be an omen for a golden seal (high official position)?"
When the chief culprit [of the regicide] was enthroned,
Wáng Xuánmó was appointed Inspector of Jìzhōu.
〔一五〕When Xiàowǔ waged war against the rebel,
Wáng Xuánmó dispatched Yuán Hùzhī, the Administrator of Jǐnán, to lead troops to join the righteous cause.
After the matter was settled,
he was made Inspector of Xúzhōu
and granted the title of Dūdū.
When the Prince of Nánjùn, Liú Yìxuān, rebelled along with Zāng Zhì, the Inspector of Jiāngzhōu,
the imperial court granted Wáng Xuánmó the title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
appointed him Inspector of Yùzhōu,
and sent him to campaign in the south with Liǔ Yuánjǐng.
Their army encamped at Liángshān,
building crescent-shaped forts on both banks,
and waited for the enemy by both land and water.
Liú Yìxuān sent Liú Chénzhī to join Zāng Zhì,
and arrayed their army south of the city.
Wáng Xuánmó left the old and weak to guard the city,
and deployed all his elite troops to engage in battle,
whereupon the rebels were utterly routed.
He was granted the titles of Dūdū and Qián Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Qǔjiāng County.
The Zhongjūn Sīmǎ, Liú Chōngzhī, reported to Xiàowǔ,
saying:
“While at Liángshān,
Wáng Xuánmó colluded with Liú Yìxuān.”
The Emperor’s mind was not clear on the matter,
so he ordered the relevant authorities to impeach Wáng Xuánmó for excessively acquiring treasures
and falsely inflating battle reports.
He and Yuán Hùzhī, the Inspector of Xúzhōu, were both dismissed from office.
Soon after, he was reinstated as Inspector of Yùzhōu.
Sīmǎ Hēishí, a fugitive from Huáishàng, promoted Xiàhóu Fāngjìn as their leader,
who changed his surname to Lǐ and his given name to Hóng to confuse the populace.
Wáng Xuánmó attacked and beheaded him.
He was promoted to Níngmán Xiàowèi and Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
and granted the title of Dūdū.
The region of Yōngzhōu had many sojourners,
so Wáng Xuánmó requested a land survey of the migrant population.
At the time, the common people were unwilling to be registered,
so the plan was abandoned.
In that same year,
Wáng Xuánmó again ordered that taxes on grades nine and above
be adjusted to equalize wealth between rich and poor,
which caused widespread lamentation throughout the region.
Rumors circulated among the populace that Wáng Xuánmó intended to rebel.
At that time, Liǔ Yuánjǐng was in power,
and Liǔ Yuánjǐng’s younger brother, Liǔ Sēngjǐng, was the Administrator of Xīnchéng.
Leveraging Liǔ Yuánjǐng’s influence,
he issued orders to the various commanderies of Nányáng, Shùnyáng, Shàngyōng, and Xīnchéng to raise troops to suppress Wáng Xuánmó.
Wáng Xuánmó kept both internal and external affairs calm
to dispel the people's confusion.
He hastily sent a report to Xiàowǔ,
fully detailing the beginning and end of the matter.
The Emperor, knowing it to be false,
hastily dispatched his Chief Secretary, Wú Xǐgōng, to comfort him,
and replied,
“The rumors from Liángshān
were never taken seriously.
The relationship between ruler and minister
is more than enough to ensure mutual protection.
This is merely a joke
to make your brow relax.”
Wáng Xuánmó was by nature stern
and never laughed frivolously.
People at the time said that Wáng Xuánmó’s brow had never relaxed,
hence the Emperor used this to tease him.
Later, he served as Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū
and concurrently held the position of Tàicháng.
When the Míngtáng was being constructed,
he held the concurrent post of Qǐbù Shàngshū in his original capacity,
and also served as Běixuǎn.
Xiàowǔ was disrespectful towards his officials,
and, based on their appearance,
he gave them various comparisons.
Those with many beards were called "sheep."
Yán Shībó had missing teeth,
so he was called "the gapped-tooth."
Liú Xiùzhī was parsimonious,
so he was called "old miser."
Huángmén Shìláng Zōng Língxiù was corpulent,
making it inconvenient for him to bow and rise.
Whenever there was a gathering,
the Emperor would grant him many gifts,
desiring to see him bow and prostrate himself with difficulty in gratitude,
which he found amusing.
He also carved a wooden statue of Zōng Língxiù’s father, the Guānglù Xūn Zōng Shūxiàn,
and sent it to his family's main hall.
Liǔ Yuánjǐng and Yuán Hùzhī were both northerners,
but Wáng Xuánmó alone received
the epithet of “old commoner.”
Whatever the Emperor called them,
the documents and letters from all directions also followed suit.
The Emperor once composed a Four Seasons Poem for Wáng Xuánmó, saying:
“Violas and tea furnish spring meals,
Millet gruel fills summer suppers.
Gourd paste seasons autumn vegetables,
White wine dispels winter chill.”
He also favored a Kūnlún slave boy
named Báizhǔ.
He was always by his side,
and the Emperor ordered him to strike officials with a staff.
From Liǔ Yuánjǐng downwards,
all suffered from his brutality.
Wáng Xuánmó was subsequently promoted to Píngběi Jiāngjūn and Inspector of Xúzhōu,
and granted the title of Dūdū.
At that time, the northern lands were afflicted by famine,
so he distributed one hundred thousand *hú* of his private grain and a thousand oxen to relieve them.
He was then transferred to lead the Jūnjūn Jiāngjūn.
When Xiàowǔ passed away,
he, along with Liǔ Yuánjǐng and others, received the dying imperial charge,
and the supervision of external affairs was entrusted to Wáng Xuánmó.
At that time, with many factions in court politics,
Wáng Xuánmó, being stern and upright, was not tolerated,
so he was transferred to be Inspector of Qīngzhōu and Jìzhōu,
and granted the title of Dūdū.
After the Young Emperor executed Yán Shībó, Liǔ Yuánjǐng, and others,
his madness and perversity grew even worse.
He summoned Wáng Xuánmó as the Língjūn.
His sons and nephews all advised him to feign illness,
but Wáng Xuánmó said:
“I have received great kindness from the late Emperor;
how can I avoid disaster by cowardly escaping?”
So he went.
Upon his arrival,
he repeatedly submitted memorials of remonstrance,
and also tearfully pleaded for leniency and an end to executions
to bring peace to the common people.
The Young Emperor was greatly enraged.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he treated Wáng Xuánmó with exceptional courtesy.
At that time, rebellions broke out in all directions,
and Wáng Xuánmó was appointed commander-in-chief
to lead the navy in a southern campaign.
Due to a foot ailment,
he was permitted to enter and exit by palanquin.
Soon after, he was appointed Chējì Jiāngjūn and Inspector of Jiāngzhōu,
〔一六〕and served as assistant to the Sītú, the Prince of Jiàn'ān, at Zhěqí,
and was bestowed with Zhūgě Liàng’s tubular-sleeved armor.
After a short while,
he was appointed Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
〔一七〕concurrently holding the position of Hùjūn.
He was then transferred to be Inspector of Nányùzhōu,
and granted the title of Dūdū.
Wáng Xuánmó was by nature stern and severe, with little compassion,
while General Zōng Yuè was even harsher and more cruel in governing his subordinates.
The soldiers had a saying about them:
“Rather be a five-year convict
than meet Wáng Xuánmó.
Wáng Xuánmó is still tolerable,
but Zōng Yuè will kill me even more.”
He died at the age of eighty-one,
〔一八〕and was posthumously named Zhuānggōng.
His son, Wáng Shēn, had died early,
so Wáng Shēn’s son, Wáng Huì, inherited the title.
〔一九〕
The official historian states: Liú Xiùzhī and Zōng[⿱⿰売⽎心] (Zōng Yuè)
were both talented generals and commanders,
possessing integrity and incorruptibility,
which are worthy of praise.
Although Wáng Xuánmó was stern, severe, and lacked compassion,
observing his great principles,
he is also worthy of admiration.
When the Young Emperor deviated from the righteous path,
committing numerous killings,
Wáng Xuánmó dared to face unknown dangers,
devoting himself wholeheartedly to assist and guide,
which can be called sacrificing oneself for the country.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 37: Liǔ Yuánjǐng, Yán Shībó, Shěn Qìngzhī
Liǔ Yuánjǐng, courtesy name Xiàorén,
was a native of Xiè in Hédōng.
His great-grandfather, Liǔ Zhuó, moved from his home commandery to Xiāngyáng,
and his highest official position was Administrator of Rǔnán.
His grandfather, Liǔ Tián, was Administrator of Xīhé.
His father, Liǔ Píng, was Administrator of Féngyì.
Yuánjǐng was skilled in archery and horsemanship from a young age.
He often accompanied his father on campaigns against the Man (tribes),
and was known for his bravery.
He was a man of few words but possessed an imposing demeanor.
Xiè Huì, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, heard of his reputation
and invited him to serve,
but before Yuánjǐng could go, Huì was defeated.
Liú Dàochǎn, the Inspector of Yōngzhōu, deeply admired his ability.
Yuánjǐng was at the time in mourning for his father,
so he could not accept the appointment.
Coincidentally, the Prince of Jiāngxià, Yìgōng, who was the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, summoned him.
Dàochǎn said to him:
"I have long wished to have you in my service.
Now that a noble prince has summoned you,
it would be difficult to arbitrarily detain you.
This departure from my wishes makes me feel disheartened."
After the mourning period concluded,
he was appointed Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn in the Prince of Jiāngxià's principality,
and then promoted to Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn.
He again served Yìgōng as Sīkōng Xíng Cānjūn,
and following the chuyển of the headquarters, he became Sītú Tàiwèi Chéngjú Cānjūn.
Tàizǔ also praised him upon seeing him.
Earlier,
Liú Dàochǎn had governed Yōngzhōu with benevolence,
and the distant Man (tribes) all submitted to him.
They all moved to settle along the Miǎn River, forming villages,
and their households became prosperous.
When Dàochǎn died,
the Man tribes became greatly disruptive and violent.
When Shìzǔ was stationed in Xiāngyáng in the west,
Yìgōng appointed Yuánjǐng as a general,
and immediately made him Guǎngwēi Jiāngjūn and Suí Jùn Tàishǒu.
Upon his arrival,
the Man (tribes) had cut off the relay routes
and intended to attack the commandery.
The commandery was low on provisions,
and also lacked weapons.
Yuánjǐng devised a strategy
and gathered six or seven hundred men,
dividing five hundred of them to garrison the relay routes.
Someone said:
"The Man (tribes) are about to assault the city;
it is not advisable to divide our forces."
Yuánjǐng said:
"When the Man (tribes) hear that the commandery has sent a heavy guard,
how could they imagine that the city has few soldiers?
Moreover, a pincer attack from both inside and outside
is a superior strategy."
As the Man (tribes) were nearing,
he then ordered the forces on the relay route to prepare,
and secretly led out troops from their rear,
instructing them:
"Charge forward when you see the signal fire."
The front and rear forces attacked simultaneously,
and the Man multitude was thrown into confusion.
Over a thousand people drowned in the Yúnshuǐ River,
and several hundred were captured or killed.
The commandery territory became peaceful,
with no more banditry.
When Zhū Xiūzhī campaigned against the Man (tribes),
Yuánjǐng also accompanied him.
Later, he also assisted Shěn Qìngzhī in the expedition against Yúnshān,
and advanced to conquer Tàiyáng.
He was appointed Zhōngbīng Cānjūn in Shìzǔ's Ānběi Fǔ.
He accompanied Prince Wáng Dàn when he was stationed in Xiāngyáng,
serving as Hòujūn Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
When the imperial court launched a major northern expedition,
it ordered all garrisons to send out troops.
In the eighth month of the 27th year,
Dàn dispatched Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn Yǐn Xiǎnzǔ to Cīgǔ,
Fènwǔ Jiāngjūn Lǔ Fāngpíng, Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn Xuē Āndū, and Luèyáng Tàishǒu Páng Fǎqǐ into Lúshì,
and Guǎngwēi Jiāngjūn Tián Yìrén into Lǔyáng.
Yuánjǐng was additionally appointed Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn,
to command all the generals.
Páng Jìmíng, Hòujūn Wàibīng Cānjūn, was already seventy-three years old that year.
He was a prominent figure from Qín,
and many Qiāng people were attached to him.
He requested to enter Cháng'ān
to pacify Guān and Shǎn.
So he entered Lúshì from Cīgǔ.
Zhào Nán, a resident of Lúshì, welcomed him.
The powerful families of Hóngnóng had previously shown an inclination to submit,
so they entrusted Jìmíng with their allegiance.
In the tenth month,
Lǔ Fāngpíng, Xuē Āndū, and Páng Fǎqǐ advanced to Báitíng.
At this time, Yuánjǐng had not yet departed.
Fǎqǐ led Fāngpíng, Āndū, and the other armies to enter first,
coming out of Xiūyáng Tíng and crossing Mount Xióng'ěr.
Jìmíng advanced to Gāomén Mùchéng.
Coincidentally, Prince Yǒngchāng had entered Hóngnóng,
so Jìmíng turned back
to Lúshì,
fortifying himself in a strategic position.
After a while,
he recruited young men from Lúshì and advanced into Yíyáng Gǒugōng Gǔ,
to stir up a sense of righteousness.
In the same month, Yuánjǐng led his army to follow.
In the intercalary month,
Fǎqǐ, Āndū, Fāngpíng, and the other armies entered Lúshì,
beheading the county magistrate Lǐ Fēng.
They appointed Zhào Nán as the magistrate of Lúshì,
and bestowed upon him the title of Fènwǔ Jiāngjūn.
Nán rallied the righteous volunteers
to serve as guides for the combined armies.
Fǎqǐ and others crossed Tiělǐng Shān
and reached Kāifāngkǒu.
Jìmíng emerged from Mùchéng
and met with Fǎqǐ.
Yuánjǐng's main army reached Jiùkǒu.
As the vanguard had penetrated deep
and was unsupported,
he swiftly dispatched Yǐn Xiǎnzǔ to Lúshì
as army reinforcement.
Yuánjǐng, realizing that the army's provisions were insufficient,
and that it would be difficult to prolong the stalemate,
tied up horses and suspended chariots,
leading his army up Báizhàng Yá
and through Wēngǔ
to enter Lúshì.
Fǎqǐ's armies advanced to Fāngbóbui,
five lǐ from Hóngnóng City.
The enemy sent over two thousand soldiers to scout,
and Fǎqǐ unleashed his troops to attack them from both sides,
causing the enemy cavalry to retreat.
The armies constructed siege equipment
and advanced to the city walls.
The self-proclaimed Administrator of Hóngnóng, Lǐ Chūgǔbá, fortified the city.
Fǎqǐ, Āndū, Fāngpíng, and the other armies advanced with drums and shouts to assault the city.
Jìmíng and Zhào Nán also led their righteous volunteers to advance in succession.
Battering rams approached from four directions,
attacking from multiple points simultaneously.
All the soldiers fought to the death,
all bravely striving to be first.
At that time, Chūgǔbá and his son occupied the south gate,
supervising the defense there.
Over three thousand residents of Hóngnóng inside the city
raised white banners on the north tower,
and some shot arrows without metal tips (as a sign of surrender).
Tán Jīn and Xuē Xìxiào, Āndū's military deputies, led their troops to be the first to ascend,
capturing Lǐ Chūgǔbá and his son alive.
Lǔ Fāngpíng entered the south gate,
capturing the self-proclaimed commandery assistant.
The common people were all settled.
Yuánjǐng led his army across Mount Xióng'ěr.
Āndū garrisoned Hóngnóng.
Fǎqǐ advanced to occupy Tóngguān.
Jìmíng led Fāngpíng and Zhào Nán's armies towards Qīlǐ Gǔ in Shǎnxī.
Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn Dèng Shèng and Chuángzhǔ Liú Cān secretly sent men into Huāngtián
to recruit Liú Kuānqiú of Yíyáng to rally over two thousand righteous volunteers.
Together they attacked Jīnmén Wù
and massacred its inhabitants.
They killed the garrison commander Lǐ Mǎidé,
who was Chūgǔbá's son
and served as Prince Yǒngchāng's Chángshǐ.
He was known for his exceptional bravery among the barbarians.
When Yǒngchāng heard of his death,
it was as if he had lost his right and left hands.
Dàn also dispatched Chángliú Xíng Cānjūn Yáo Fàn to lead three thousand men towards Hóngnóng,
to be under Yuánjǐng's command.
In the eleventh month,
Yuánjǐng led his troops to Hóngnóng,
encamping at Kāifāngkǒu.
Yuánjǐng was then appointed Hóngnóng Tàishǒu,
and administrative staff were assigned.
Initially,
Ān Dū remained in Hóngnóng,
while the various armies had already advanced to Shǎn.
When Yuán Jǐng arrived,
he said to Ān Dū:
"It is not a good plan
to idly guard an empty city
and allow Páng Gōng to penetrate deep.
You should advance the army quickly
and join forces with Xiǎn Zǔ to confront them.
I must supervise the collection of taxes first,
and then I will follow."
The whole army then advanced to Shǎn,
immediately entering the inner city,
arraying their camps within the city to press the enemy,
and also constructing many siege engines.
The enemy city relied on the river as its defense,
trusting in the strategic advantage to defend itself.
The armies of Jì Míng, Ān Dū, Fāng Píng, Xiǎn Zǔ, and Zhào Nán
attacked three times but could not capture it.
The barbarian governor of Luòzhōu, Dìhé Gōng Zhāng Shìliántí, with twenty thousand men,
crossed Mt. Xiáo to relieve the city.
Ān Dū and Fāng Píng each formed a battle array south of the city to await them,
while Xiǎn Zǔ commanded elite troops to serve as the rear guard.
Jì Míng led the righteous troops from Gāomíng and Yíyáng to form a battle line at the south gate,
and Zhào Nán led the young volunteers from Lúshì,
forming a pincer movement with Jì Míng.
The enemy forces gathered in great numbers,
and light cavalry challenged them to battle.
Ān Dū, with his eyes wide and spear held horizontally,
charged into the enemy formation alone,
striking out in all four directions.
Those to his left and right all gave way, unable to withstand him.
The killed and wounded were countless.
Thereupon, the entire army advanced with a roar of drums,
and the soldiers all fought to the death.
Initially, the barbarians deployed their elite cavalry,
which troubled the allied armies.
Ān Dū became enraged,
so he took off his helmet
and unbuckled his armor,
wearing only a crimson double-breasted shirt.
His horse also had its full barding removed.
He then galloped into the enemy formation,
roaring with fierce spirit,
unstoppable wherever he went.
Those who met his spear
all fell at its blade.
The enemy, infuriated,
shot at him from both sides but could not hit him.
This happened several times,
and each time he charged in,
no one failed to be routed.
Earlier,
Yuán Jǐng had ordered general Lǔ Yuán to guard Hángǔ Guān.
As the enemy forces were numerous,
Lǔ Yuán could not hold his position.
So he led his troops in a "box formation,"
arraying many flags and banners,
and retreated along the difficult terrain.
He happened to meet Ān Dū's armies engaging the enemy.
When the barbarian general Sānláng Jiāng saw Lǔ Yuán's army coming down from the mountain,
he thought it was Yuán Jǐng's main army arriving.
As dusk was approaching,
the enemy then retreated,
with many cavalrymen managing to enter the city.
When the enemy was about to arrive,
Fāng Píng sent a cavalry messenger to inform Yuán Jǐng.
At that time, the provisions of the various armies were exhausted,
each having only a few days' worth of food left.
Yuán Jǐng was then supervising the collection of voluntary taxes
and also requisitioning donkeys and horses
for the purpose of transporting provisions.
When Fāng Píng's letter arrived,
Yuán Jǐng dispatched his army deputy Liǔ Yuángù to select two thousand infantry and cavalry
to rush to the emergency in Shǎn.
They marched with their armor rolled up, without rest,
arriving in one night.
The next morning,
the enemy forces came out again,
forming battle arrays outside the city.
Fāng Píng's armies were all arrayed in formation.
Ān Dū commanded the cavalry,
and Fāng Píng commanded all the infantry,
forming a pincer movement on the left and right.
The rest of the righteous armies formed their arrays southwest of the city.
Fāng Píng said to Ān Dū:
"Now a powerful enemy is before us,
and a strong city is behind us.
This is the day we must fight to the death.
If you do not advance,
I will execute you;
if I do not advance,
you must execute me."
Ān Dū replied:
"Good,
your words are right.
How could I cherish my life?"
Thereupon, they joined battle.
At that moment, Liǔ Yuángù had just arrived,
concealing all flags and drums,
with soldiers and horses all holding gags in their mouths.
They advanced stealthily with hidden armor,
and the enemy did not perceive them.
As Fāng Píng and the others were just engaging the barbarians,
Liǔ Yuángù led his troops directly out of the covered path of the city's south gate,
formed an array facing north,
with numerous banners and flags,
and advanced with shouts and drums,
catching the enemy by surprise.
The barbarian troops were greatly alarmed.
Yuángù, with his banner leader Zōng Yuè,
led his elite cavalry
to charge the enemy formation.
The entire army followed closely.
Ān Dū and Fāng Píng and the others urged all the armies to charge simultaneously,
and the soldiers all fought with utmost bravery.
Ān Dū, unable to contain his fury,
held his spear horizontally and charged straight ahead,
moving in and out of the enemy formation,
killing and wounding many.
His blood congealed up to his elbow.
His spear broke,
and he replaced it and charged in again.
Army deputy Tán Jīn led cavalry to follow and charge with him.
They fought from dawn
until afternoon.
The barbarian forces were utterly defeated.
Zhāng Shìliántí was beheaded,
and more than three thousand other heads were taken.
Many died by falling into the river or jumping into ditches.
Over two thousand men were bound and brought to the army gate.
Yuán Jǐng arrived with light cavalry in the morning.
Many of the barbarian soldiers who were bound were people from Hénèi.
Yuán Jǐng questioned them, saying:
"You resent that the king's benevolence did not reach you
and had no place to appeal for your lives.
Now you all exert yourselves for the barbarians.
This means you originally had no good intentions.
Those who comply and submit shall be saved and rescued,
while those who follow evil shall be executed and exterminated.
You should know that the king's army is precisely like this."
They all said:
"We were driven by the cruel barbarians.
Those who did not go would have their entire clan exterminated.
With cavalry pressing infantry,
we would have died before even fighting.
This is what the general personally saw;
we did not dare to betray the Central Plain."
The generals wanted to kill them all,
but Yuán Jǐng thought it was not permissible,
saying:
"Now that the king's banners sweep north,
we should let the fame of our benevolence precede us."
So he released them all and sent them away.
For those whose homes were in Guānzhōng,
he ordered the armies guarding the passes to allow them to leave.
They all shouted "Long live!" and departed.
Dàn, seeing that Xiáo and Shǎn were now pacified,
believed that the area should be conciliated.
He appointed Liú Kuānqiú of Hóngnóng to act as the Administrator of Eastern Hóngnóng.
He also granted Yuán Jǐng a set of ceremonial music instruments.
Fǎqǐ (法起) led his troops to Tóngguān (潼關).
Before this,
Jiànyì Jiāngjūn (建義將軍) and Huàshān Tàishǒu (華山太守) Liú Huái (劉槐) had gathered righteous soldiers and attacked the pass city.
They captured it,
but their strength was insufficient to hold it.
A short while later,
they again gathered a host to respond to the royal army.
When Fǎqǐ (法起) arrived at Tóngguān (潼關),
Huái (槐) also arrived.
The bandit garrison commander of the pass city, Lóu Xū (婁須), saw their banners and fled in disarray.
Many of the bandit troops drowned in the river.
Fǎqǐ (法起) and Huái (槐) immediately occupied Tóngguān (潼關).
The bandit Púchéng (蒲城) garrison commander dispatched the false commander Hé Nán (何難) to Fēnglíngduī (封陵堆) to set up three camps to confront Fǎqǐ (法起).
Fǎqǐ (法起) drove straight into the pass,
passing the former barracks of Wáng (王) and Bù (ブ).
The bandits thought he was heading directly for Cháng'ān (長安).
Hé Nán (何難) led his troops, intending to cross the river to cut off the rear of the army.
Fǎqǐ (法起) turned his army to face the river,
unleashing his soldiers to shoot at them,
and the bandits retreated and dispersed.
All the righteous followers in Guānzhōng (關中) rose up everywhere,
and the Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡) of the four mountains all requested to fight.
Dàn (誕) also dispatched Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn (揚武將軍) Kāng Yuán (康元) to lead two thousand men out of Shàngluò (上洛),
to receive orders from Yuánjǐng (元景),
and reinforce Fāngpíng (方平) at Hángǔ (函谷).
When Yuánjǐng (元景) left,
the bandit host advanced towards the pass.
At that time, the army had run out of food.
Yuánjǐng (元景) turned back and took up position at Báiyánglǐng (白楊嶺).
Before the bandits could settle and arrive,
he descended the mountain again and advanced to Hóngnóng (弘農),
entering Húguānkǒu (湖關口).
The bandit Púbǎn (蒲阪) garrison commander and Tàizhōu Cìshǐ (泰州刺史) Dù Dàoshēng (杜道生) led twenty thousand men to Wénxiāngshuǐ (閿鄉水),
one hundred twenty *lǐ* (里) from Húguān (湖關).
Yuánjǐng (元景) recruited one thousand brave elite soldiers,
and at night attacked the bandit camp.
They lost their way,
and returned at dawn.
Dàoshēng (道生) led his skilled and brave subordinates, unleashing his soldiers to shoot at them.
Once blades clashed,
the bandits again scattered.
At this time, the northern expeditionary armies of Wáng Xuánmó (王玄謨) and others had been defeated and retreated,
and the bandits then penetrated deep.
Tàizǔ (太祖) believed that Yuánjǐng (元景) should not advance alone,
and ordered him to return with his army.
Yuánjǐng (元景) then led his generals from Húguān (湖關) across Báiyánglǐng (白楊嶺),
emerging at Chángzhōu (長洲).
Āndū (安都) covered the rear,
and Zōngyuè (宗越) assisted him.
Fǎqǐ (法起) went from Tóngguān (潼關) towards Shāngchéng (商城),
and met with Yuánjǐng (元景).
Jìmíng (季明) also returned south from Húgǔ (胡谷).
Both entered with merits,
their soldiers, horses, banners, and flags very grand.
Dàn (誕) ascended the city wall to observe them,
and dismounted to welcome Yuánjǐng (元景).
He was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) and Jīngzhào Guǎngpíng Èr Jùn Tàishǒu (京兆廣平二郡太守),
established a mansion in Fánchéng (樊城),
and resided there with his subordinates,
overseeing affairs concerning the Northern barbarians.
Páng Jìmíng (龐季明) was appointed Dìngmán Zhǎng (定蠻長).
Xuē Āndū (薛安都) was appointed Hòujūn Xíng Cānjūn (後軍行參軍).
Lǔ Fāngpíng (魯方平) was appointed Níngmán Cānjūn (寧蠻參軍).
Zāng Zhì (臧質) was appointed Yōngzhōu (雍州).
Yuánjǐng (元景) was appointed Guànjūn Sīmǎ (冠軍司馬) and Xiāngyáng Tàishǒu (襄陽太守),
his general title remaining as before.
When Lǔ Shuǎng (魯爽) marched towards Hǔláo (虎牢),
Yuánjǐng (元景) was again sent to lead Āndū (安都) and others north to the pass city.
The pass city garrison abandoned their posts and fled,
and they immediately occupied it.
Yuánjǐng (元景) reached Hóngguān (洪關),
intending to advance with Āndū (安都) to cross the river and attack Dù Dàoshēng (杜道生) at Púbǎn (蒲阪).
However, Shuǎng (爽) retreated,
and they returned.
He went out again on a northern expedition,
his prestige and trustworthiness evident beyond the borders.
He was also ordered to lead his subordinates to advance to Xīyáng (西陽),
and to join the campaign against the Wǔshuǐ Mán (五水蠻).
When Shìzǔ (世祖) entered to suppress the prime culprit,
he appointed Yuánjǐng (元景) as Zīyì Cānjūn (諮議參軍),
commander of the central army,
and added the title Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍),
his prefect title remaining as before.
He was assigned ten thousand men as the vanguard,
and Zōng[kèxīn] (宗[⿱⿰売⽎心]), Xuē Āndū (薛安都), and thirteen other armies were all subordinate to him.
Yuánjǐng (元景) wrote to the court officials, saying:
"The national calamity is deep with injustice,
and the vicious people commit atrocities.
The people and spirits are collapsed and enraged,
as if there were no heaven and earth.
The Nánzhōngláng (南中郎) personally leads the righteous army,
to eliminate the prime evil.
Sītú (司徒) and Zāng Guànjūn (臧冠軍) both join in the great endeavor,
with a thousand *lǐ* (里) of ships,
and rewards and bounties fully prepared.
I, Yuánjǐng (元景), am not martial,
yet I am humbly entrusted with a position in the army,
to command the elite brave,
and lead the vanguard.
The momentum is in our favor,
and our forces are a hundred times theirs.
You gentlemen, whose families have been loyal and righteous for generations,
and who are good men of the state,
have all been favored by the previous court,
and enjoyed honors for a long time.
Yet you are constrained and coerced by the bandit court,
unable to demonstrate your efficacy.
I imagine that upon hearing this news,
your sorrow and joy are beyond the ordinary.
The great army is on its way,
and the clearing of chaos has just begun.
I eagerly await meeting you face to face,
to express and relieve our sorrow."
At that time, the ships of the righteous army were small and crude,
and it was feared they would be no match in a naval battle.
Upon reaching Wúhú (蕪湖),
Yuánjǐng (元景) was greatly pleased.
He doubled his march,
and upon hearing that battle ships were coming from Shítou (石頭),
he advanced on foot at Jiāngníng (江寧),
and erected palisades at Bǎnqiáo (板橋) to secure himself.
He advanced to occupy Yīnshān (陰山),
and sent Xuē Āndū (薛安都) to lead cavalry to the south bank.
Yuánjǐng (元景) secretly advanced to Xīntíng (新亭),
building a camp against the mountain,
occupying strategic points to the east and west.
Shìzǔ (世祖) again sent Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) and Xíng Cānjūn (行參軍) Chéng Tiānzuò (程天祚) to lead his troops to support him.
Tiānzuò (天祚) also occupied a high hill to the southeast,
and established a fortified camp.
All those who defected and came to him
urged Yuánjǐng (元景) to advance quickly.
Yuánjǐng (元景) said:
"Not so.
Reliance on reason is unreliable;
those who share evil will aid each other.
A light advance without defense
would truly encourage the enemy.
One should rely on our own invincibility,
not hope that the enemy will not attack."
Yuánjǐng's (元景) camp had not yet been established,
and this was discovered by Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) Zhān Shū'ér (詹叔兒) through reconnaissance.
He urged Shào (劭) to go out and fight,
but Shào (劭) refused.
After a day,
Shào (劭) then launched a combined land and naval force.
Shào (劭) personally ascended Zhūquè Mén (朱雀門) to oversee the battle.
When the army reached Wǎguānsì (瓦官寺),
they encountered the righteous army's scouts.
The scouts retreated,
and the bandits then pressed close to the camp.
Shào (劭) thought that since Yuánjǐng's (元景) camp and trenches were not yet established,
a decisive battle could be fought on flat ground.
But upon arrival,
the wooden palisades were already strong,
and in their haste, they had no siege equipment.
So he ordered a direct assault.
Yuánjǐng (元景) had previously ordered his army, saying:
"Frequent drumming easily saps morale;
frequent shouting easily exhausts strength.
Just hold your gags and fight fiercely,
listening only to the drumbeat of my camp."
The bandit infantry generals Lǔ Xiù (魯秀), Wáng Luóhàn (王羅漢), Liú Jiǎnzhī (劉簡之), cavalry general Cháng Bóyǔ (常伯與), and their soldiers
all fought to the death.
Liú Jiǎnzhī (劉簡之) first attacked the southwest,
repeatedly managing to burn straw rafts,
and partially cross with men.
Chéng Tiānzuò's (程天祚) palisades were not yet established,
and were also broken through.
Wáng Luóhàn (王羅漢) and others attacked the northern gate of the camp,
and the bandit ships also arrived.
Yuánjǐng (元景) was attacked by both land and water,
but his spirit grew stronger.
He sent all his brave warriors to fight,
keeping only a few men by his side for communication.
He divided his forces to assist Chéng Tiānzuò (程天祚).
Tiānzuò (天祚) managed to secure his palisades again,
and thereby defeated the bandits.
Yuánjǐng (元景) observed that the bandits were exhausted,
and ordered the camp gates opened,
charging them with drums and shouts.
The bandit forces utterly collapsed,
and many drowned in the Huái (淮) River.
Shào (劭) then led the remaining troops to attack the camp again,
but was again thoroughly defeated.
The number killed and wounded
exceeded that of the previous battle.
Shào (劭) personally cut down those who retreated but could not stop them,
fleeing back to the palace,
barely escaping with his life.
Xiāo Bīn (蕭斌) was wounded.
Jiǎnzhī (簡之) gathered his troops and stopped,
but their formation was still not dispersed.
Yuánjǐng (元景) again came out and pressed them,
whereupon they fled,
competing to throw themselves into Sǐmǎ Jiàn (死馬澗).
The ravine was filled with them.
Jiǎnzhī (簡之) and army commanders Yáo Shúyì (姚叔藝), Wáng Jiāngbǎo (王江寶), Zhū Míngzhì (朱明智), Zhūgě Miáozhī (諸葛邈之) and others were executed.
Naval commanders Chǔ Zhànzhī (褚湛之) and deputy Liú Dàocún (劉道存) both surrendered.
When the Emperor ascended the throne at Xīntíng,
he appointed Yuánjǐng as Shìzhōng,
concurrently Lǐng Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
He was then transferred to be Shǐchíjié, Jiān Yōngliáng Nánběi Qín Sì Zhōu Jīngzhōu Zhī Jìnglín Suí Èr Jùn Zhūjūnshì, Qián Jiāngjūn, Níngmán Xiàowèi, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
When the Emperor was at Bākǒu,
he asked Yuánjǐng:
“After the matter is settled,
what do you desire?”
He replied:
“If there is excessive favor,
I wish to return to my hometown.”
Hence, this appointment was made.
Initially,
when Zāng Zhì raised an uprising,
he considered Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān to be dim-witted and easily controlled,
and wished to support him.
He secretly informed Yuánjǐng,
telling him to lead his subordinates back west.
Yuánjǐng immediately presented Zhì’s letter to Shìzǔ,
and told his messenger:
“Zāng Guànjūn probably does not know of His Highness’s righteous uprising.
We should be attacking the rebels,
it is not permissible to return west.”
Zhì resented him for this.
When Yuánjǐng became Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
Zhì feared he would become a future threat to Jīng and Jiāng,
and suggested that trusted aides should not be sent far away.
The Emperor found it difficult to go against his words,
and instead appointed Yuánjǐng as Jūn Jiāngjūn,
concurrently Lǐng Shítou Shù Shì,
but he did not accept the official title.
He was then transferred to Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
with the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì,
Qūjiāng Xiàn Gōng,
with a fief of three thousand households.
In the first month of Xiàojiàn元年,
Lǔ Shuǎng rebelled.
Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Wáng Xuánmó was sent to suppress him.
Yuánjǐng was additionally appointed Fǔjūn,
granted a Jié and given a staff,
subordinate to Xuánmó.
〔一０〕He was again appointed Dūdū Yōngliáng Nánběi Qín Sì Zhōu Jīngzhōu Zhī Jìnglín Suí Èr Jùn Zhūjūnshì, Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn, Lǐng Níngmán Xiàowèi, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the Jié as before.
Zāng Zhì and Yìxuān both rebelled.
Xuánmó held the south of Liángshān,
building camps along the river.
Yuán Hùzhī and Xuē Āndū crossed to occupy Lìyáng,
and Yuánjǐng moved out to garrison Cǎishí.
Xuánmó heard that the rebels were strong,
and sent Sīmǎ Guǎn Fǎjì to request more troops.
The Emperor ordered Yuánjǐng to advance and garrison Gūshú.
Yuánjǐng sent his general Wǔ Niàn to advance.
Zhì sent his general Páng Fǎqǐ to attack Gūshú.
When Niàn arrived,
he defeated them,
and Fǎqǐ fled in a single boat.
Zhì captured Xuánmó’s western camp.
Xuánmó sent Yuán Hùzhī to tell Yuánjǐng:
“Now there are ten thousand men remaining on the east bank.
The rebel army is several times larger.
The strength is uneven.
It is advisable to return and cooperate with your command to resist them.”
Yuánjǐng said to Hùzhī:
“Military discipline has its fixed rules;
one cannot retreat first.
Although the rebel multitude is large,
they are suspicious and disorganized.
