Now we should roll up our armor and rush to them.”
Hùzhī said:
“The rebels all say that Nánzhōu has thirty thousand men,
〔一一〕yet your command has barely one-tenth of that.
If you go to engage the rebels,
their true strength will be immediately seen,
and then the rebel morale will solidify.”
Yuánjǐng accepted his words,
and sent all his elite troops to assist Xuánmó,
leaving the weak and infirm to guard.
The dispatched troops displayed many banners.
From Liángshān, they looked like tens of thousands of men.
Everyone said:
“All the capital troops have arrived.”
Thus, the morale of the multitude was settled,
and through this, victory was achieved.
〔一二〕
The Emperor sent Dānyáng Yǐn Yán Jùn to convey his message of comfort and commendation.
He and Shěn Qìngzhī were both granted Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī with their original titles,
and enfeoffed as Jìn’ān Jùn Gōng,
with the same fief as before.
He firmly declined the Kāifǔ Yítóng,
and was again appointed Lǐngjūn and Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
with the additional title of Shìzhōng.
Soon after, he was transferred to Piàojì Jiāngjūn, Běnzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng,
with Lǐngjūn and Shìzhōng as before.
In Dàmíng二年,
he was again granted Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
which he again firmly declined.
The following year,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Lìng,
with Tàizǐ Zhānshì, Shìzhōng, and Zhōngzhèng as before.
Because his fief was in Lǐngnán,
and the autumn tribute was difficult and distant,
he was re-enfeoffed as Bādōng Jùn Gōng.
In the fifth year,
he was again appointed Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
with Shìzhōng, Lìng, and Zhōngzhèng as before.
He again declined Kāifǔ,
and then he and Shěn Qìngzhī both followed the precedent of Jìn Mìlíng Hóu Zhèng Mào not accepting the title of Sīkōng.
This matter is in Qìngzhī’s biography.
In the sixth year,
he was promoted to Sīkōng,
with Shìzhōng, Lìng, and Zhōngzhèng as before.
He again firmly declined,
and was then appointed Shìzhōng, Piàojì Jiāngjūn, and Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ,
remaining to guard the capital.
When Shìzǔ passed away,
he, along with Tàizǎi Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng and Shàngshū Púshè Yán Shībó, received the dying imperial edict to assist the young emperor.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Lìng,
concurrently Lǐng Dānyáng Yǐn,
with Shìzhōng and Jiāngjūn as before.
He was granted twenty ban swordsmen,
but he firmly declined the ban swordsmen.
Yuánjǐng rose from the ranks of generals,
and when he dealt with court affairs,
although it was not his forte,
he possessed the virtue of broad-minded elegance.
At that time, many influential officials at court
were engaged in business and property.
Only Yuánjǐng engaged in no such ventures.
There was a vegetable garden of several dozen *mǔ* on the south bank.
The gardener sold produce for twenty thousand *qián* and sent the money to his residence.
Yuánjǐng said:
“I established this garden to grow vegetables
to supply my household’s consumption.
How can I sell vegetables again to get money,
and seize profit from the common people?”
He gave the money to the gardener.
Shìzǔ was unusually harsh and violent.
Although Yuánjǐng enjoyed favor and treatment,
he worried about misfortune.
Tàizǎi Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng and other high ministers
all stood on tiptoes, held their breath,
and never dared to visit privately.
When Shìzǔ died,
Yìgōng, Yuánjǐng, and others all said to each other:
“Today we are finally free from violent death.”
Yìgōng and the princes like Yìyáng,
Yuánjǐng and Yán Shībó and others,
often chased after each other,
making music, drinking heavily,
continuing day and night.
The former deposed emperor had wicked virtues in his youth.
Internally, he could not be appeased.
After killing Dài Fǎxīng,
his perverse nature became increasingly evident.
Yìgōng, Yuánjǐng, and others were worried and fearful, without a plan.
So they, along with Shībó and others, plotted to depose the emperor and enthrone Yìgōng.
They gathered day and night to conspire,
but were indecisive and could not quickly resolve.
In the summer of Yǒngguāng元年,
〔一三〕Yuánjǐng was transferred to Shǐchíjié, Dū Nányù Zhī Xuānchéng Zhūjūnshì, with his original titles of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Shìzhōng and Lìng as before.
Before he was formally appointed,
the plot was discovered.
The Emperor personally led his imperial guard to attack him.
He first issued an imperial edict summoning Yuánjǐng.
His attendants ran to tell him that the soldiers’ weapons were unusual.
Yuánjǐng knew misfortune had arrived.
He straightened his court robes,
and rode in a carriage to answer the summons.
As he left his gate, he met his younger brother, Chējì Sīmǎ Shú Rén,
who was in military attire, leading dozens of strong men from his attendants, intending to resist the order.
Yuánjǐng sternly forbade him.
As he left the alley,
a large number of soldiers arrived.
He dismounted from his carriage and submitted to execution,
his expression serene.
He was sixty years old at the time.
His eldest son, Qìngzōng,
was capable and strong,
but his temperament was unruly.
Shìzǔ ordered Yuánjǐng to send him back to Xiāngyáng,
and he was granted death on the way.
His second son, Sìzōng,
was Yùzhāng Wáng Zǐshàng’s Chējì Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
Sìzōng’s younger brothers Shàozōng, Gòngzōng, Xiàozōng, Wénzōng, Zhòngzōng, Chéngzōng, Jìzōng,
〔一四〕and Shú Rén’s younger brother Wèijūn Zīyì Cānjūn Sēngzhēn, and other brothers and nephews in the capital and Xiāngyáng, who died with him, numbered several dozen.
Yuánjǐng’s youngest son Chéngzōng,
〔一五〕and Sìzōng’s son Zuǎn,
were both spared because they were in Yùn.
Emperor Tàizōng ascended the throne,
and issued an order saying:
“The late Shìzhōng, Shàngshū Lìng, Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Kāiguó Gōng of Bādōng Commandery, newly appointed Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Cìshǐ of Nányù Prefecture, Yuán Jǐng,
was broad-minded and straightforward in demeanor,
and profound and composed in character.
When righteousness shone forth,
he respectfully served as a model.
When the way of the living and the dead reached its end,
he was the first to endorse the filial lineage;
when a prosperous era opened a new calendar,
he assisted in the imperial transformation.
He was just about to assume the responsibilities of a minister for the Hàn,
and his achievements were comparable to those of Yīn Héng,
yet savage beasts ran rampant,
explicitly inflicting calamity and poison upon him.
His injustice moved the meritorious and valorous,
and his sorrow deeply permeated the court.
I have inherited the spiritual essence of the Seven Ancestral Temples,
and have succeeded to the imperial enterprise.
Now that my feelings and the law have been expressed,
my grief and lamentation are deeply felt.
It is fitting to solemnly honor him with a grand commendation
to extol his loyalty and virtue.
He is hereby posthumously granted the titles of Shǐ Chíjié, Dūdū of Nányù and Jiāng Prefectures and all military affairs, and Tàiwèi.
His previous titles of Shìzhōng, Cìshǐ, and Guógōng remain as before.
Thirty guards with ceremonial swords are to be granted,
and ten sets of feathered canopies and ceremonial music.
His posthumous title shall be Zhōngliè Gōng.”
Shūrén served as Cìshǐ of Liáng Prefecture,
and Huángmén Láng.
For his功 in defeating Zāng Zhì,
he was enfeoffed as Yíyáng Hóu,
with a stipend of eight hundred households.
Yuán Jǐng’s cousin, Yuán Hù,
at the end of the Dàmíng era,
replaced Shūrén as Cìshǐ of Liáng Prefecture.
He joined Jìn'ān Wáng Zixūn in rebellion,
and surrendered after the failure of the plot.
Yuán Jǐng’s younger paternal cousin, Xiānzōng,
〔一六〕in the early Dàmíng era,
served as Sīkōng Cānjūn for Jìnglíng Wáng Dàn.
When Dàn rebelled,
Xiānzōng was killed.
He was posthumously granted the title of Huángmén Shìláng.
Yuán Jǐng’s younger paternal grand-cousin, Guāngshì,
initially remained in his hometown.
The Suǒ barbarians appointed him Zhéchōng Jiāngjūn and Tàishǒu of Héběi,
and enfeoffed him as Xīlíng Nán.
Guāngshì’s brother-in-law was the false Sītú, Cuī Hào,
who was a minister for the barbarians.
In the twenty-seventh year of Yuánjiā,
the barbarian ruler, Tuòbá Táo, invaded Rǔ and Yǐng from the south.
Cuī Hào secretly harbored alternative plans,
and Guāngshì sought out righteous men from Héběi to support Hào.
Hào’s plot was revealed, and he was executed.
Many prominent families from Hédōng were implicated and exterminated.
Guāngshì fled south and escaped.
Emperor Tàizǔ appointed him Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn.
During the Jǐnghé era of the Former Deposed Emperor,
he was appointed Zuǒ Jiāngjūn
and Zhíhé.
When Emperor Tàizōng suppressed the rebellion,
Guāngshì participated in the planning,
and was appointed Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
enfeoffed as Kāiguó Xiànhóu,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
Soon after, rebellions broke out in all directions.
Zōng Yuè and Tán Jīn, who were also in the imperial chambers, were executed.
Guāngshì then fled north to Xuē Āndū,
who ordered him to defend Xiàpī City.
When Āndū invited the Suǒ barbarians,
Guāngshì led his troops to surrender.
Emperor Tàizōng pardoned him
and appointed him Tàishǒu of Shùnyáng.
His son, Xīnwèi, conspired in rebellion,
and Guāngshì was granted death.
Yán Shībó, courtesy name Chángyuān,
was a native of Línyí, Lángyá.
He was a cousin of Cìshǐ Yán Jùn of Dōngyáng Prefecture.
His father, Shào,
was upright and had strong principles,
and was recognized by Xiè Huì.
When Huì was Lǐngjūn,
he appointed Shào as Sīmǎ.
During the period of dethronement and establishment,
Shào participated in his consultations.
When Huì was stationed in Jiānglíng,
he invited Shào to serve as Zīyì Cānjūn,
and to oversee the Lùshì,
entrusting all military and administrative affairs to him.
Shào worried that Huì would face disaster,
and requested to be Tàishǒu of Jìnglíng.
Before he could reach the commandery,
Huì was attacked.
Huì conspired with Shào to raise troops against the imperial court,
but Shào drank poison and died.
Shībó was orphaned and poor in his youth,
but dabbled in books and records,
and had some understanding of music.
When Liú Dàochǎn served as Cìshǐ of Yōng Prefecture,
he appointed Shībó as Fǔguó Xíngcānjūn.
His younger brother, Shīzhòng,
was married
to the daughter of Zāng Zhì.
When Zāng Zhì was Cìshǐ of Xú Prefecture,
he invited Shībó to be his Zhǔbù.
When Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì replaced Zāng Zhì as Cìshǐ of Xú Prefecture,
Zāng Zhì recommended Shībó to Yìjì,
and Yìjì immediately appointed him Zhēngxī Xíngcānjūn.
When Xīng'ān Hóu Yìbīn replaced Yìjì,
and Emperor Shìzǔ replaced Yìbīn,
he continued to serve as Fǔguó Xíngcānjūn and Ānběi Xíngcānjūn.
Wáng Jǐngwén, then Zīyì Cānjūn,
admired his wit and agility,
and recommended him to Emperor Shìzǔ.
Shībó then requested the authority of a staff,
and was appointed Zhǔbù of Xú Prefecture.
He was skilled at ingratiation,
and received great favor and recognition.
When he left the garrison,
Shībó, as Zhǔbù, escorted him back to the capital.
When Emperor Shìzǔ was stationed in Xúnyáng,
he memorialized Emperor Tàizǔ, requesting Shībó to be Zhǔbù of the Nánzhōngláng Office.
Emperor Tàizǔ did not approve,
and said to his Diǎnqiān:
“How can Yán Shībó be used as Zhǔbù of the Zhōngláng Office?”
Emperor Shìzǔ then requested to appoint him Chángliú Zhèngzuǒ,
but Emperor Tàizǔ again said:
“If the court cannot appoint him,
you may appoint him yourself,
but it is also not appropriate to appoint him Chángliú.”
Emperor Shìzǔ then appointed him Cānjūnshì,
overseeing penal affairs.
When he joined the campaign to punish the Chief Culprit,
he was transferred to Zhǔbù.
When Emperor Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed him Huángmén Shìláng,
then Piàojì Zhǎngshǐ and Tàishǒu of Nán Commandery for Suí Wáng Dàn.
He was then reappointed Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn Zhǎngshǐ and Tàishǒu of Nánpúyáng,
and Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
When Zāng Zhì rebelled,
Shībó was sent out as Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Tàishǒu of Dōngyáng,
leading troops and appointing assistants,
to guard the eastern route.
When the situation stabilized,
he was reinstated as Huángmén Shìláng,
also holding the post of Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
He was then reappointed Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn,
transferred to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
and promoted to Shìzhōng.
The Emperor, in quelling rebellion and stabilizing chaos,
relied on collective counsel.
In the first year of the Dàmíng era,
he issued an edict saying:
“In the past year, when the national crisis arose,
many were hesitant and cowardly.
The former Sànqí Chángshì and Tàizǐ Yòulǜ, Páng Xiùzhī, demonstrated steadfast integrity in times of danger,
being the first to champion the cause of righteousness.
This ensured that the cunning plans were reported early,
and military preparations were firmly established in advance,
leading to the timely suppression of the vile rebels.
He indeed contributed greatly.
I recall his sincerity,
and it remains unforgettable in my heart.
Shìzhōng Jìjiǔ Yán Shībó, Shìzhōng Lǐng Shèshēng Xiàowèi Yuán Mǐnsūn, Tàishǒu of Yùzhāng Wáng Qiānzhī, and Tàizǐ Qiánzhōngshùzǐ Lǐng Yòuwèi Lǜ Zhāng Yān,
initially joined the punitive expedition
and participated in the righteous plan.
Having endured great hardships,
they deserve special reward.
Páng Xiùzhī is to be enfeoffed as Lè'ān Xiànbó,
with a stipend of six hundred households.
Yán Shībó is to be enfeoffed as Píngdū Xiànzǐ,
Yuán Mǐnsūn as Xīngpíng Xiànzǐ,
Wáng Qiānzhī as Shíyáng Xiànzǐ,
and Zhāng Yān as Guǎngjìn Xiànzǐ,
each with a stipend of five hundred households.”
Shī Bó was transferred to the position of Right General of the Guards.
Due to his mother's mourning, he left his post.
Two years later,
he was reinstated as Chízé, Dū Qīng Jì Èr Zhōu Xú Zhōu Zhī Dōng'ān Dōngguǎn Yǎn Zhōu Zhī Jìběi Sān Jùn Zhū Jūnfām, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and Qīng Jì Èr Zhōu Cìshǐ.
That same year,
the Tatar Tuòbá Jùn sent the pseudo-Sànqí Chángshì, Zhènxī Jiāngjūn Tiānshuǐ Gōng Shíbēn Chìwén to lead a multitude to raid Qīngkǒu.
〔一七〕The garrison commander of Qīngkǒu, Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn Fù Gān'ài, along with former Yuánwài Jiāngjūn Zhōu Pánlóng and others, attacked and thoroughly routed them.
Shìzǔ dispatched Hǔbēn Zhǔ Páng Mèngqiú, Jīshè Jiāngjūn Yīn Xiàozǔ, and others to launch a punitive expedition,
placing them under Shī Bó's command.
Shī Bó sent Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Gǒu Sīdá to join forces with Mèngqiú.
Upon reaching Shāgōu,
the Tatar Kūguǐ Gōng, Wǔjūn Gōng, and others, with tens of thousands of cavalry and infantry,
met the army and resisted the attack.
Mèngqiú and his men fought fiercely all day.
Mèngqiú personally beheaded Wǔjūn Gōng,
whereupon the Tatars fled in disarray.
Xiàozǔ also beheaded Kūguǐ Gōng.
Thousands plunged into the water and died.
The Tatars again sent Hénán Gōng, Hēishuǐ Gōng, Jìzhōu Gōng, Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Zhāng Huáizhī, and others to station themselves along the banks of the Jì River.
Shī Bó again sent Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Jiāng Fāngxīng to join Fù Gān'ài and defeat them,
beheading Hénán Gōng Shùlán and others.
Another Tatar commander, Tāmén, sent over ten thousand men to attack the Qīngkǒu garrison city.
Gān'ài and Fāngxīng sallied forth to resist the battle,
and immediately beheaded Tāmén.
The remaining troops fled.
The Tatar Tiānshuǐ Gōng again led twenty thousand men to pressure the city.
Gān'ài and others sallied forth to battle,
and again defeated them,
pursuing the fleeing enemy to Chìlóng Mén,
killing many of the bandits.
The Emperor praised their achievements,
issuing an edict that stated:
"The Tatars, driving their dog-like hordes,
intend to wreak havoc on our borders.
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Qīng Jì Èr Zhōu Cìshǐ Shī Bó has strategically commanded his forces,
adapting to changes as the opportunity arises.
The Jì garrison, filled with righteous anger,
achieved four victories in one month.
Detached forces and different divisions
displayed courage and achieved similar successes,
repeatedly beheading prominent Tatar kings
and annihilating great numbers of the ugly hordes.
We are deeply appreciative
and profoundly touched.
An envoy should be sent to comfort and reward them,
and also to order the Fǔguó Residence to meticulously evaluate their merits and achievements,
and report them promptly."
Gǒu Sīdá, Páng Mèngqiú, and others pursued the Tatars to Dùliáng.
The Tatar forces were numerous,
and closed in from all four sides.
Píngnán Cānjūn Tóng Tàiyī and Gǒu Sīdá, riding single horses, charged out to disperse them,
and the enemy scattered upon contact.
Mèngqiú and others arrived afterward,
and the Tatars then dispersed and fled,
with many drowning in the river.
Soon after, the Tatars regrouped and arrived in great numbers,
but Mèngqiú and others again defeated them.
Shìzǔ again sent Sīkōng Cānjūn Bǔ Tiānshēng to assist Shī Bó.
Zhāng Huáizhī occupied Mígōu City.
Shī Bó sent Tiānshēng and others to defeat him.
Huáizhī sallied forth from the city to engage in battle.
Tiānshēng led Jūnzhǔ Liú Huáizhēn, Báiyī Kè Zhū Shìyì, Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn Mèng Jìzǔ, and others to attack them.
Huáizhī was defeated and fled back into the city,
barely escaping with his life.
Mèng Jìzǔ was killed in battle
and posthumously granted the title of Jùnshǒu.
Furthermore, the Tatar Lǒngxī Wáng and others were stationed at Shēn Chéng,
with the Jì River behind them and the Yellow River in front,
and three sides were perilous and fortified.
Tiānshēng again led his forces to attack them.
Zhū Shìyì and others, wearing armor, were the first to ascend.
Countless bandits plunged into the river and died.
The city was captured that same day.
The Tatar Tiānshuǐ Gōng again attacked Lè'ān City.
Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Píngyuán Lè'ān Èr Jùn Tàishǒu Fēn Wǔdū, along with Bǔ Tiānshēng and others, resisted and attacked them,
thoroughly routing them.
The Tatars then fled and retreated.
They pursued the fleeing enemy and achieved victory,
all the way to Qīngkǒu.
The Tatars attacked and besieged Fù Gān'ài.
Gān'ài resisted them from all sides.
Once Xiàozǔ and others arrived,
the Tatars lifted the siege and fled.
Shī Bó was promoted to the title of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
Three years later,
Jìnglíng Wáng Dàn rebelled.
Shī Bó sent Chángshǐ Jī Xuánjìng to lead five thousand men to assist in the emergency.
Four years later,
he was summoned to be Shìzhōng,
and concurrently led the Right Army General.
He was highly favored and close to the Emperor,
and no other official could compare.
He was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū,
with the Right Army General position remaining as before.
The Emperor did not want power to rest with others,
personally overseeing all affairs.
Those who had previously overseen elections
only carried out administrative documents.
Shī Bó, however, made decisions on his own,
and his proposals were always approved.
He was promoted to Shìzhōng,
and concurrently led the Right General of the Guards.
In the seventh year,
he was appointed Shàngshū Yòu Púyè.
At that time, two election departments were established separately,
with Chénjùn Xiè Zhuāng and Lángyá Wáng Tánshēng both serving as Lìbù Shàngshū.
Shī Bó's son Jǔ Zhōuxuán recommended the humble man Zhāng Qí to be Gōngchē Lìng.
The Emperor, considering Qí's qualifications inappropriate,
made him concurrently serve as Shìmǎi Chéng,
and replaced him with Cài Dàohuì.
The clerks Pān Dàoxī, Chǔ Dàohuì, Yán Yīzhī, Yuán Cóngfū, Rèn Dànzhī, Shí Dào'ér, Huáng Nán, Zhōu Gōngxuǎn, and others suppressed the edict for Dàohuì,
allowing Qí to arrive at Gōngchē first,
and not implementing Qí's concurrent role as Shìmǎi Chéng.
Shī Bó was implicated because his son led the office.
Xiè Zhuāng and Wáng Tánshēng were dismissed from office.
Pān Dàoxī and Chǔ Dàohuì were executed in the market.
Yán Yīzhī and the other six individuals received one hundred strokes of the whip and staff.
Shī Bó was soon appointed Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
Although he had been demoted and frustrated,
he was given responsibilities as before.
When Shìzǔ was on his deathbed,
Shī Bó received the posthumous edict to assist the young emperor.
All matters in the Shàngshū department
were entirely entrusted to him.
When the Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
he was reinstated to his original position,
and concurrently held the position of Wèiwèi.
Shī Bó held power for a long time,
and people from all over the realm flocked to him.
Those who frequented his gate
all received positions and ranks beyond their due.
He accepted many bribes and gifts,
and his family wealth accumulated.
His entertainers and musicians
were the finest in the land.
His gardens, ponds, and residences
surpassed all others at the time.
His arrogance, extravagance, licentiousness, and indulgence
were resented by the gentry.
He was again promoted to Shàngshū Púyè,
〔一八〕and concurrently led Dānyáng Yǐn.
The Deposed Emperor wanted to personally oversee court affairs,
and issued an edict to transfer Shī Bó to be Zuǒ Púyè,
and added the title of Sànqí Chángshì,
appointing Lìbù Shàngshū Wáng Jǐngwén as Yòu Púyè.
He stripped him of his position as the Capital Administrator
and also divided his responsibilities in the Grand Secretariat.
It was at this point that Shī Bó finally became afraid.
Soon after, he was executed along with Tàizǎi Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng and Liǔ Yuánjǐng.
He was forty-seven years old at the time.
His six sons were all young
and were all killed.
His younger brother, Shī Zhòng,
was Zhōngshū Láng
and Jìnlíng Tàishǒu.
Shī Shū
was Sītú Zhǔbù
and Nánkāng Xiāng.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
an edict stated:
"The late Sànqí Chángshì, Púyè, concurrently Dānyáng Yǐn, Píngdū Xiànzǐ Shī Bó,
in times of dynastic change,
was among the first to receive honor and reward.
He encountered misfortune and trouble,
losing his life due to excessive punishment,
and his family line was extinguished.
This truly inspires pity and sorrow.
However, his heart was polluted by greed for wealth,
and he should be demoted in his posthumous title.
His feudal enfeoffment can be continued,
to comfort his aggrieved spirit.
His posthumous title shall be Huāngzǐ."
Shī Zhòng's son Gàn succeeded to the enfeoffment.
When Qí received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
Shěn Qìngzhī, courtesy name Hóngxiān,
was a native of Wǔkāng, Wúxīng.
His elder brother, Chǎngzhī,
served as Zhào Lúnzhī's Zhēnglǔ Cānjūn and Supervisor of Nányáng Jùn.
He achieved merit in attacking the barbarians
and then officially assumed the post.
Qìngzhī was ambitious and resolute from a young age.
During the rebellion of Sūn Ēn,
when his men raided Wǔkāng,
Qìngzhī, not yet crowned,
followed his local kinsmen to attack them.
From then on, he became known for his bravery.
After the chaos,
his鄉邑 (village and countryside) scattered.
Qìngzhī personally tilled the fields,
working hard to establish himself.
At thirty,
still unrecognized,
he went to Xiāngyáng to visit his elder brother.
Lúnzhī saw him and admired him.
Lúnzhī's son, Bófú, was then the Grand Administrator of Jìnglín.
Lúnzhī ordered Bófú to appoint Qìngzhī as the Military Advisor to the Central Army of Níngyuǎn.
The Mán (tribes) of Jìnglín frequently raided.
Qìngzhī devised strategies for them,
and each time they defeated them.
Bófú thereby earned the reputation of a general.
When Bófú left the commandery,
he again separately campaigned against the Xīlíng Mán.
He did not take Qìngzhī with him,
and returned without success.
In the second year of Yǒngchū (421 CE),
Qìngzhī was appointed General of the Palace Guard.
He then followed Bófú, who was subordinate to Dào Yànzhī, in a northern expedition.
Bófú returned due to illness,
and Qìngzhī remained subordinate to Tán Dàojì.
Dàojì reported back to Tàizǔ,
praising Qìngzhī as loyal, diligent, and skilled in military affairs.
The emperor ordered him to lead a detachment to guard the eastern Yè Mén (side gate of the palace),
and he gradually gained access,
entering and exiting the forbidden palace.
He was sent out to garrison Xīnchéng in Qiántáng.
Upon his return,
he was appointed Grand Administrator of Huáilíng.
The Army Commander Liú Zhàn knew of him,
〔一九〕and wishing to draw him in,
said to him:
"You have been in the palace for many years;
it is time we discussed your promotion."
Qìngzhī, with a stern expression, said:
"This humble official has been in the palace for ten years.
I should naturally receive a promotion,
and I will not trouble you further with this."
Soon after, he was promoted to General of the Regular Army.
On the evening Zhàn was arrested,
the emperor opened the gate and summoned Qìngzhī.
Qìngzhī entered in military uniform, wearing boots and tied trousers.
The emperor, seeing him, was surprised and said:
"Why are you dressed so hastily?"
Qìngzhī replied:
"Summoning a company commander at midnight does not allow for slow dressing."
He was sent to arrest the Grand Administrator of Wújùn, Liú Bīn,
and killed him.
He was promoted to Army Advisor to the Rear Army of Prince Shǐxīng Jùn,
and Gentleman-in-Waiting to the Emperor.
In the nineteenth year of Yuánjiā (442 CE),
when the Inspector of Yōngzhōu, Liú Dàochǎn, died,
the various Mán (tribes) rebelled greatly.
The Western Generalissimo's Aide, Zhū Xiūzhī, failed in his campaign against the Mán.
Qìngzhī was appointed General of Establishing Might,
and led troops to assist Xiūzhī.
Xiūzhī was disciplined and imprisoned,
so Qìngzhī took sole command of the army and advanced to campaign.
He severely defeated the various Mán along the Miǎn River,
capturing seven thousand people.
He then advanced to Húyáng,
and captured over ten thousand more.
He was promoted to Military Advisor to the Central Army of Prince Guǎnglíng Dàn,
and concurrently Grand Administrator of Nándōngpíng.
He also became Military Advisor to the Central Army of Shìzǔ's Pacification Army.
Shìzǔ, with his original title, took charge of Yōngzhōu,
and moved west with his establishment.
At that time, the Mán raids were very severe,
blocking both water and land routes.
Shìzǔ was halted at Dàdī and could not advance.
He divided his forces and sent Qìngzhī to launch a surprise attack,
which severely defeated them,
with twenty thousand surrendering.
When Shìzǔ reached his post,
the Mán on the post road rebelled and killed Shēn Shì.
Qìngzhī was sent to campaign against them again.
〔二０〕Wáng Xuánmó, leading Jīngzhōu,
and Wáng Fānghuí, leading the imperial army, both joined forces.
They pacified all the mountains,
capturing over seventy thousand people.
The Yúnshān Mán were the strongest;
Lǔ Zōngzhī had repeatedly campaigned but could not defeat them.
Qìngzhī pruned and pacified them,
capturing over thirty thousand people.
Upon returning to the capital,
he again became Military Advisor to the Central Army of Prince Guǎnglíng Dàn,
and was promoted to General of Establishing Might and Grand Administrator of Nánjìyīn.
The Yōngzhōu Mán again became raiders.
Qìngzhī, as general and grand administrator, again entered Miǎn with Prince Dàn.
Upon reaching Xiāngyáng,

he led Liǔ Yuánjǐng, Military Advisor to the Rear Army's Central Army; Zōng Yuàn, Grand Administrator of Suí Commandery; Liú Yǒng, General of Manifesting Awe; Lǔ Shàngqī, Military Advisor to the Minister of Works; Gù Bīn, Mǎ Wéngōng, Military Advisors to the General of the North; Xiāo Jǐngsì, Military Advisor to the Left Army's Central Army; Cuī Mùlián, Former Assistant Administrator of Qīngzhōu; Liú Yōngzhī, Military Advisor to the General Pacifying the Mán; Wáng Jǐngshì, General of Vigorous Awe; and over twenty thousand other men to attack the mountain Mán north of the Miǎn River.
Zōng Yuàn entered Mount Tàihóng from Xīn'ān Road.
Yuánjǐng advanced from Jūnshǔi and occupied Wǔshuǐlǐng.
Wéngōng emerged from Càiyángkǒu to take Chìxìwū.
Jǐngshì went down from Yánshān towards Chìqíbǎn.
Mùlián, Shàngqī, and the other armies advanced simultaneously along eight routes.
Qìngzhī took Wǔqú,
and established his headquarters there to direct the various armies.
In previous campaigns against the Mán,
camps were always set up at the foot of the mountains to pressure them,
thus the Mán were able to occupy the mountains as a defense,
making their arrows and stones effective,
which is why success was often elusive.
Qìngzhī then gathered the various armies at the foot of Rúqiū Mountain,
and said to the multitude:
"If we now array our banners along the mountains to attack them,
our soldiers and horses will surely suffer losses.
Last year, the Mán's fields yielded a great harvest,
and their grains are stored in the high mountains.
They have not yet suffered from hunger,
so it will be difficult to capture or eliminate them quickly.
Now, I order all armies to lead their subordinates to encamp on the mountains,
taking them by surprise.
The Mán will surely be terrified.
If we press them when they are afraid,
we can win without a battle."
Thereupon, all armies cut paths through the mountains,
without engaging the Mán,
beating drums and shouting as they ascended the mountains,
charging into their heartland,
first occupying the strategic strongholds.
The Mán were shaken and disrupted,
and taking advantage of their fear, they surrounded them.
None failed to flee in disarray.
From winter to spring,
they subsisted on the Mán's grain.
A short while later,
Tián Yànshēng, the Mán chieftain of Nánxīn Commandery, led his subordinates and ten garrisons, totaling over six thousand men, in rebellion.
They attacked and besieged the commandery city.
Qìngzhī sent Yuánjǐng with five thousand men to relieve it.
Before the army arrived,
the commandery had already been broken into.
The granaries and official residences within the city were burned and destroyed,
and the surrendered households were driven away,
stationing themselves on Báiyáng Mountain.
Yuánjǐng pursued them to the foot of the mountain,
where all the armies gathered,
surrounding the mountain several times deep.
Zōng Yuàn led his subordinates to ascend first.
All armies exerted their combined strength to attack fiercely,
severely defeating them.
〔二一〕Their might shook all the mountains,
and all the Mán bowed their heads in submission.
Qìngzhī suffered from headaches,
and liked to wear a fox fur hat.
The Mán detested it,
calling him
"Old Man with the Azure Head."
Whenever they saw Qìngzhī's army,
they would fearfully say:
"Old Man with the Azure Head has come again."
Qìngzhī led his army from Rúqiū Mountain to Jiǎnchéng,
severely defeating the various mountain tribes,
beheading three thousand,
capturing over twenty-eight thousand wild Mán,
twenty-five thousand surrendered Mán,
over seven hundred cattle and horses,
and over ninety thousand hu (measures) of rice and millet.
Prince Suí Dàn built the two cities of Nàxiáng and Shòufú at Báichǔ.
Shěn Qìngzhī again led the allied armies to subjugate the wild barbarian tribes in the various mountains of Xìngzhū.
Following the treacherous terrain, they constructed strong fortified cities,
installing gates and battlements,
which were very formidable.
The mountains had abundant wood and stone,
which were piled up to form defensive barriers.
They organized military units,
set up banners and flags,
established senior commanders,
and had groups of armored cavalry.
Shěn Qìngzhī set up a continuous camp at the foot of the mountains.
Gates were opened within the camp for mutual access.
[二二] He also ordered all armies to dig ponds within their camps,
so that they would not need to fetch water from outside morning and evening,
and also to guard against fires set by the barbarians.
After a while, a strong wind blew.
The barbarians descended the mountain at night,
each carrying a torch to set the camp on fire.
There were many tented shelters and grass huts within the camp.
When fire reached them, they immediately extinguished it with water from the ponds.
Most of the armies came out with bows and crossbows to shoot at them from both sides,
and the barbarians scattered and fled.
Shěn Qìngzhī ordered the armies to cut down mountains and open paths to attack them,
but the mountains were high and the paths treacherous,
and the summer rains were heavy.
So, he established six garrisons at Dōnggāng, Shǔshān, Yímín, Xīchái, Huángjiǎo, and Shànglíng, and then returned.
The barbarians, having been besieged for a long time,
were all starving and exhausted,
and thereafter gradually came out and surrendered.
The barbarians captured by Shěn Qìngzhī, both before and after,
were all moved to the capital,
to serve as camp households.
In the twenty-seventh year [of Yuánjiā],
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
That same year,
Tàizǔ was about to launch a northern expedition.
Shěn Qìngzhī remonstrated, saying:
"The infantry and cavalry have been unmatched [by the enemy]
for a long time.
Please set aside distant matters,
and let me speak about Dào and Jì.
Tán Dàojì made two expeditions without success.
Xiè Yànzhī suffered a defeat and returned.
Now, I estimate that Wáng Xuánmó and others will not surpass these two generals,
and the might of the six armies
is no greater than in former times.
I fear that the royal army will suffer another humiliation,
making it difficult to achieve our ambitions."
The Emperor said:
"The petty villains have seized territory.
As for restoring Hénán,
and the royal army's previous setbacks,
there are different reasons;
it was also because Tán Dàojì nurtured the bandits for his own gain,
and Xiè Yànzhī acted rashly midway.
What the barbarians rely on is only their cavalry.
In summer, the rivers are vast,
and the Yellow River flows freely.
If we sail north,
then Quèguāo will surely flee,
and Huátái, a small garrison,
can easily be overthrown and captured.
If these two garrisons are taken,
we can house and feed the people and console them.
Hǔláo and Luòyáng
will naturally not be secure.
By winter,
with interconnected city defenses,
if the barbarian cavalry crosses the river,
they will be captured."
Shěn Qìngzhī again firmly argued against it.
Dānyáng Yǐn Xú Zhànzhī and Lìbù Shàngshū Jiāng Zhàn were both present.
The Emperor ordered Xú Zhànzhī and others to challenge Shěn Qìngzhī.
Shěn Qìngzhī said:
"Governing a country is like managing a household.
When plowing, one should ask the servant;
when weaving, one should consult the maid.
Your Majesty now wishes to attack a state,
but consults with these white-faced scholars.
How can the affair succeed?"
The Emperor laughed heartily.
When the northern expedition was launched,
Shěn Qìngzhī assisted Wáng Xuánmó towards Quèguāo.
The garrison commander abandoned the city and fled.
Wáng Xuánmó besieged Huátái.
Shěn Qìngzhī and Xiāo Bīn remained at Quèguāo,
with Shěn Qìngzhī still holding the title of Bīn's Fǔguó Sīmǎ.
Wáng Xuánmó attacked Huátái,
but failed to take it for several weeks.
The barbarian ruler Tuòbá Tào led a large army south.
Xiāo Bīn sent Shěn Qìngzhī to lead five thousand men to relieve Wáng Xuánmó.
Shěn Qìngzhī said:
"Wáng Xuánmó's troops are exhausted and his men old,
and the barbarian invaders are already pressing.
Only with armies of ten thousand men each
can one advance;
a small force going lightly
will certainly be useless."
Xiāo Bīn insisted on sending him.
At that moment, Wáng Xuánmó retreated.
Xiāo Bīn was about to execute him.
Shěn Qìngzhī firmly interceded, and he stopped.
Tàizǔ later asked:
"Why did you intercede with Xiāo Bīn against killing Wáng Xuánmó?"
He replied:
"The generals who fled
were all fearful of punishment.
If they returned and were killed,
it would lead to them scattering and fleeing.
Furthermore, with a large army approaching,
it was not advisable to weaken ourselves,
so attacking was the more suitable course."
Xiāo Bīn, having suffered defeat in the vanguard,
wished to die defending Quèguāo.
Shěn Qìngzhī said:
"Having deeply penetrated enemy territory,
seeking what we desired,
and retreating in such a defeated state,
how can we stay here for long?
Now Qīngzhōu and Jìzhōu are weak and empty,
and to sit and defend a isolated city
means that if the barbarian army passes to the east,
Qīngdōng will no longer belong to the state.
Quèguāo is isolated and cut off,
and will become another Zhū Xiūzhī's Huátái."
Just then, an imperial edict arrived,
forbidding retreat.
All the generals said they should stay.
Xiāo Bīn again asked Shěn Qìngzhī for advice.
Shěn Qìngzhī said:
"Matters outside the camp
are for the general to decide solely.
The edict comes from afar,
and the situation has already changed.
Your Excellency has a Fàn Zēng but cannot use him.
What good is empty discussion?"
Xiāo Bīn and those present laughed and said:
"Shěn Gōng has actually learned [from the classics]!"
Shěn Qìngzhī said in a stern voice:
"Though you all have seen ancient and modern [affairs],
it is not as good as my ear's learning!"
Wáng Xuánmó, considering his defeat and retreat,
requested to garrison Quèguāo.
Xiāo Bīn then returned to Lìchéng.
Shēn Tǎn and Yuán Hùzhī jointly held Qīngkǒu.
Shěn Qìngzhī rode a post-horse back in haste.
Before he arrived,
an imperial edict reached him at a post-station, ordering him to stop
and return to assist Wáng Xuánmó.
But the barbarians had already reached Péngchéng,
so he could not go north.
Tàiwèi Jiāngxiàwáng Yìgōng kept him to serve as Cānjūn in the commander's household troops.
When Tuòbá Tào reached Mǎoshān,
Yìgōng sent Shěn Qìngzhī to lead three thousand men to resist him.
Shěn Qìngzhī thought the barbarian army was strong,
and that going would surely lead to capture,
so he refused to go.
Tàizǔ later said to him:
"All the dispositions on the river
were appropriate,
my only regret is not abandoning Quèguāo.
You have been by my side for a long time,
and understand my intentions particularly well.
Even if you violate an edict to accomplish something,
there would be no objection."
In the twenty-eighth year [of Yuánjiā],
[二三] Shěn Qìngzhī was ordered to move several thousand households of refugees from Péngchéng to Guābù.
Zhēngběi Cānjūn Chéng Tiānzuò moved refugees from Jiāngxī to Nánzhōu,
also in the same manner.
In the twenty-ninth year,
he again set out on a northern expedition.
Shěn Qìngzhī steadfastly remonstrated against it, but was not heeded.
Because their opinions on the deliberation differed,
he was not allowed to go north.
At that time, the fugitives Sīmǎ Hēishí and Xiàhóu Fāngjìn, a rebellious official from Lújiāng, were in Wǔshuǐ, Xīyáng,
inciting the various Mán tribes.
From the Huái and Rǔ rivers to the Jiāng and Miǎn rivers,
all suffered from their depredations.
In the tenth month,
Shěn Qìngzhī was dispatched to supervise the various generals in suppressing them.
An imperial edict ordered Yù, Jīng, and Yǒng to all send armies,
to be commanded by Shěn Qìngzhī.
In the first month of the thirtieth year,
Shìzǔ stationed himself at Wǔzhōu,
commanding all the commanders.
Shěn Qìngzhī advanced from Báshuǐ to Wǔzhōu,
to consult on military strategy.
At this time, Dǒng Yuánsì, Shìzǔ's attendant secretary (diǎnqiān), returned from the capital,
and reported on the emperor's assassination by the chief culprit.
Shìzǔ sent Shěn Qìngzhī back to the mountains to gather the various armies.
Shěn Qìngzhī said to his trusted confidants:
"Xiāo Bīn is a woman not worth mentioning.
As for the other generals and commanders,
I am thoroughly familiar with them,
and they are all easy to deal with.
The accomplices in the Eastern Palace number no more than thirty;
the rest were coerced,
and will certainly not exert themselves.
Now, supporting the rightful heir and suppressing the rebellion,
I have no worries about not succeeding."
Once the armies were assembled,
Shěn Qìngzhī was provisionally appointed General Quelling the Captives (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn), Prefect of Wǔchāng (Wǔchāng Nèishǐ),
and concurrently Army Commandant of the Prefecture (Lǐng Fǔ Sīmǎ).
When Shìzǔ returned to Xúnyáng,
Shěn Qìngzhī, Liǔ Yuánjǐng, and others, believing the empire was without a master,
advised Shìzǔ to immediately assume the great position (the throne),
but he refused.
The rebel Shào sent Qián Wújì, a disciple of Shěn Qìngzhī, with a letter to persuade Shěn Qìngzhī to lay down his arms.
Shěn Qìngzhī seized Wújì and reported him to Shìzǔ.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Shěn Qìngzhī as Commander of the Central Army (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn),
and added the title of Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì).

Soon after, he was sent out as Envoy with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjié), Inspector of Military Affairs of the four prefectures of Nányǎn, Yù, Xú, and Yǎn (Dūdū Nányǎn Yù Xú Yǎn Sìzhōu Zhū Jūnshì), General Protecting the Army (Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Nányǎn Prefecture (Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ).
His position as Palace Attendant remained as before,
and he was stationed at Xūyí.
The Emperor, having suppressed the rebellion and stabilized the chaos,
reflected on the merits of his generals and commanders,
and issued an edict saying:
"I, being unworthy,
was orphaned in life;
weeping tears of blood for a thousand li,
I resolved to avenge the grave rebellion.
Gathering an army to punish the offenders,
our righteous spirit soared like clouds.
The commanders brandished their credentials,
facing danger as if returning home.
Thus, not even ten days passed,
before the imperial altars were restored to peace,
and I, with my humble self,
unworthily ascended the great throne.
Forever mindful of their splendid achievements,
I wish to elevate their glorious rewards.

The newly appointed Envoy with Credentials, Palace Attendant, Inspector of Military Affairs of the four prefectures of Nányǎn, Yù, Xú, and Yǎn, General Protecting the Army, and Governor of Nányǎn Prefecture, Shěn Qìngzhī;
the newly appointed Palace Attendant and Commander of the Central Army, Liǔ Yuánjǐng;
the newly appointed Palace Attendant and General of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn), Zōng Quē;
the Inspector of Military Affairs of Yǎn Prefecture, General Supporting the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Yǎn Prefecture, Xú Yíbǎo;
the General Pacifying the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn) and Prefect of Shǐxīng (Shǐxīng Tàishǒu), Shěn Fǎxì;
the Consulting Army Supervisor of the Cavalry General (Piàojì Zīyì Cānjūn), Gù Bīnzhī;
some wholeheartedly planned from the beginning,
coordinating military strategies;
some received orders from the supreme commander,
pacifying the chaos in a single battle;
some, in charge of army units,
collaborated in planning and achieved victory;
while others, with detached forces, upheld military discipline,
their might shaking the southeast.
All were loyal to the state and selfless,
their righteousness surpassing past heroes.
Their achievements are known to the people,
and their sincerity is clear to my heart.
Establishing rewards and recording merits,
this is where it lies;
it is fitting to enfeoff them with territories and establish towns,
to forever secure the imperial house.
Shěn Qìngzhī is hereby enfeoffed as Duke of Nánchāng County (Nánchāng Xiàn Gōng);
Liǔ Yuánjǐng as Duke of Qújiāng County (Qújiāng Xiàn Gōng);
both with an income of three thousand households.
Zōng Quē as Marquis of Táoyáng County (Táoyáng Xiàn Hóu),
with an income of two thousand households.
Xú Yíbǎo as Marquis of Yìyáng County (Yìyáng Xiàn Hóu),
with an income of one thousand five hundred households.
Shěn Fǎxì as Marquis of Pínggù County (Pínggù Xiàn Hóu);
Gù Bīnzhī as Marquis of Yángxīn County (Yángxīn Xiàn Hóu);
both with an income of one thousand households."
Moreover, he personally summoned them for appointment from his imperial presence.
He also ordered Shěn Qìngzhī to return from Xūyí to garrison Guǎnglíng.
In the first month of Xiàojiàn元年,
Lǔ Shuǎng rebelled.
The Emperor dispatched General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn) Wáng Xuánmó to suppress him.
The army sailed up the Huái River towards Shòuyáng,
commanding all the generals.
Soon after, he heard that both Jīng and Jiāng prefectures had rebelled.
Shěn Qìngzhī was summoned to court,
to lead his subordinates to encamp at Wǔzhàng Gǎng,
with fifty men in armor and weapons entering the six gates.
Lǔ Shuǎng had earlier sent his younger brother Yú to advance and occupy Ménglóng.
Zhāng Yòuxù, Prefect of Lìyáng, led an army to attack Yú.
When Lǔ Shuǎng arrived,
his troops dispersed and rebelled.
Thereupon, Shěn Qìngzhī was sent across the river to attack Lǔ Shuǎng.
When Lǔ Shuǎng heard of Shěn Qìngzhī's arrival,
his camps retreated gradually,
and he personally stayed to cover the rear.
Shěn Qìngzhī and Xuē Āndū advanced and fought Lǔ Shuǎng.
Āndū slew Lǔ Shuǎng on the battlefield.
Shěn Qìngzhī was promoted to General-in-chief Pacifying the North (Zhènběi Dàjiāngjūn),
and further appointed Inspector of Qīng, Jì, and Yōu three prefectures,
and granted a set of ceremonial drums and horns (gǔchuī).
The vanguard, having defeated the rebels,
was promoted one rank ahead of those who arrived later and pursued.
[二四]Soon after, he and Liǔ Yuánjǐng were both appointed Ministers with Special Authority (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī),
which he declined.
His title was changed to Duke of Shǐxīng Commandery (Shǐxīng Jùn Gōng),
with the same number of households as before.
Shěn Qìngzhī, being seventy years old,
steadfastly requested to resign from his duties.
The Emperor commended his intention
and granted it.
He was appointed Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), Grand Master of Glorious Happiness of the Left (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū), and Minister with Special Authority (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
He again steadfastly declined,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
He submitted dozens of memorials
and also personally pleaded, saying:
"Zhāng Liáng was a famous worthy,
yet Emperor Gāo of Hàn still allowed him to retire.
What use am I,
that I must be needed by the imperial court?"
He even bowed his head to the ground to plead,
and his words were often accompanied by tears.
The Emperor could not deny him,
and allowed him to retire to his residence as a Commandery Duke,
with a monthly stipend of one hundred thousand coins,
one hundred *hú* of rice,
and fifty personal guards.
In the first year of Dàmíng,
the previous order was reiterated,
and he again steadfastly declined.
In the third year,
Sīkōng Jìnglǐng Wáng Dàn (司空竟陵王誕) revolted, seizing Guǎnglín (廣陵).

Qìngzhī (慶之) was again made Envoy with Festival, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs of the three prefectures of Nányǎn (南兗), Xú (徐), and Yǎn (兗), Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, Governor-General with Powers Equal to the Three Ducal Ministers, and Inspector of Nányǎn Prefecture,
leading troops to suppress him.
Upon reaching Ōuyáng (歐陽),
Dàn (誕) sent the retainer, Shěn Dàomǐn (沈道愍), a kinsman of Qìngzhī (慶之), with a letter to persuade Qìngzhī (慶之),
and presented him with a jade ring-knife.
Qìngzhī (慶之) sent Dàomǐn (道愍) back,
recounting Dàn's (誕) crimes and misdeeds.
When Qìngzhī (慶之) arrived at the city wall,
Dàn (誕) ascended a tower and said to him:
"Shěn Jūn (沈君), in your hoary old age,
why have you come?"
Qìngzhī (慶之) replied:
"The court considers you mad and foolish,
not worth troubling the young and strong,
thus they sent me."
The Emperor feared Dàn (誕) might flee north,
so he ordered Qìngzhī (慶之) to block his escape route.
Qìngzhī (慶之) moved his camp to Báitǔ (白土),
eighteen *lǐ* (里) from the city.
He then advanced to Xīntíng (新亭).
〔二五〕Dàn (誕) indeed tried to escape,
but failed to get away,
and returned to the city.
The details are in Dàn's (誕) biography.
Qìngzhī (慶之) advanced his camp west of Luòqiáo (洛橋),
and burned its eastern gate,
but due to rain, he could not succeed.
Qìngzhī's (慶之) nephew, Sēngróng (僧榮),
then Inspector of Yǎn Prefecture,
stationed at Xiáqiū (瑕丘),
sent his son Huáimíng (懷明) with several hundred cavalry to receive Qìngzhī's (慶之) orders.
Qìngzhī (慶之) blocked the city,
built an assault path,
erected mobile towers and earthen mounds,
along with various siege engines.
It was summer, and the rains
prevented an assault on the city.
The Emperor had Yǔ Huīzhī (庾徽之), Censor-in-Chief, propose to dismiss Qìngzhī (慶之) from office to spur him on,
but the imperial edict did not question him.
Dàn (誕) sent food to Qìngzhī (慶之),
carried by over a hundred people
who came out of the north gate.
Qìngzhī (慶之) did not question them,
but burned all of it.
Dàn (誕), from atop the city wall, handed down a sealed memorial,
asking Qìngzhī (慶之) to send it for him.
Qìngzhī (慶之) said:
"I am under imperial edict to suppress a rebel;
I cannot send your memorial for you.
If you truly wish to surrender to the court,
you should open the gate and send an envoy,
and I will provide escort for them."
Whenever he attacked a city,
he always personally led his soldiers.
The Emperor warned him, saying:
"You hold a commanding position;
you should manage affairs judiciously.
Why do you wear a shield at the foot of the city wall,
personally receiving arrows and stones?
Should you be injured or bruised,
the loss would be considerable."
From April until July,
they finally stormed the city and beheaded Dàn (誕).
Qìngzhī (慶之) was promoted to Sīkōng (司空),
but he firmly declined again.
Thereupon, he and Liǔ Yuánjǐng (柳元景) were both given the privilege according to the precedent of Zhèng Mào (鄭袤), Marquis of Mìlíng (密陵) of the Jìn (晉) dynasty:
in court assemblies, Qìngzhī's (慶之) rank was next to Sīkōng (司空),
and Yuánjǐng (元景) was above the ducal ministers.
Fifty clerks were provided for their service,
and horses were allowed to run freely at their gates.
In the fourth year,
the Wǔshuǐ (五水) barbarians in Xīyáng (西陽) again became raiders.
Qìngzhī (慶之), as a Duke of a Commandery, led all armies to suppress them.
After a year of campaigning and fighting,
they were all pacified,
and tens of thousands of captives were taken.
He lived outside the Qīngmíng Gate (清明門),
owning four residences,
whose buildings were very beautiful.
He also had a garden estate at Lóuhú (婁湖).
One night, Qìngzhī (慶之) took his sons and grandsons to move there,
returning his residences to the government.
He moved all his relatives and cousins to Lóuhú (婁湖),
and their gates were aligned, forming a single neighborhood.
He greatly expanded his agricultural endeavors,
often pointing to the land and saying to people:
"All my wealth is within this."
He enjoyed a position of great power,
and his family was naturally wealthy and prosperous,
with an estate worth tens of thousands of gold pieces,
and thousands of servants.
He twice offered ten million coins
and ten thousand *hú* (斛) of grain.
Considering Shǐxīng (始興) too close,
he requested to be re-enfeoffed as Nánhǎi Commander (南海郡),
but this was not granted.
He had dozens of singing girls and concubines,
all beautiful and skilled in various arts.
Qìngzhī (慶之) lived a leisurely and carefree life,
indulging fully in joy.
He did not leave his home except for court audiences.
Whenever he accompanied the Emperor on outings or hunting expeditions,
he would sit on his saddle, dominating and fierce,
no different from a young man.
The Crown Princess presented Emperor Shìzǔ (世祖) with a golden filigree spoon and chopsticks, along with a basin and ladle.
The Emperor bestowed these upon Qìngzhī (慶之),
saying:
"Your diligent efforts are outstanding;
your joyous celebrations should be equal.
Furthermore, gifts of cups and goblets
should properly be given to the Grandees first."
The Emperor once drank joyfully,
and ordered all his officials to compose poems.
Qìngzhī (慶之) could not write by hand,
nor could he recognize characters with his eyes.
The Emperor pressed him to compose a poem.
Qìngzhī (慶之) said:
"Your servant cannot write;
please allow me to dictate to Shībó (師伯)."
The Emperor immediately ordered Yán Shībó (顏師伯) to take up the brush,
and Qìngzhī (慶之) dictated:
"My humble life met with much fortune,
to encounter a time of flourishing destiny.
Old and decrepit, my strength is spent,
I shall return on foot to Nángāng (南崗).
Declining honors in this sagely age,
how can I be ashamed before Zhāng Zǐfáng (張子房)?"
The Emperor was very pleased,
and everyone present praised the beauty of his words and meaning.
When Emperor Shìzǔ (世祖) passed away,
Qìngzhī (慶之) and Liǔ Yuánjǐng (柳元景) were among those who received the dying instructions.
The imperial will stipulated that in any major military campaign or punitive expedition,
everything should be entrusted to Qìngzhī (慶之).
When the Former Deposed Emperor (前廢帝) ascended the throne,
Qìngzhī (慶之) was granted a stool and a staff,
and one three-wheeled carriage.
Whenever Qìngzhī (慶之) went to court for audiences,
he always rode in a "pig-snout" carriage without curtains,
and his attendants to his left and right were no more than three or five people.
When he rode a horse or walked in his gardens and fields,
there was only one person to look after his horse.
During peak months for farming and sericulture,
sometimes there was no one with him,
and those who encountered him did not know he was a Sān Gōng (三公).
When he was granted the three-wheeled carriage,
he said to people:
"Whenever I travel through my fields and gardens,
if there is a person, he and the horse make three;
if there is no person, then I and the horse make two.
Now riding this carriage,
where can I go?"
When the stool and staff were also bestowed,
he firmly declined them all.
The Deposed Emperor was wild and perverse, without the Way.
The masses all urged Qìngzhī to depose and enthrone [a new emperor].
As well as Liǔ Yuánjǐng and others who conspired,
and informed Qìngzhī.
Qìngzhī had always been on bad terms with Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng.
When he exposed their plot,
the Emperor executed Yìgōng, Yuánjǐng and others.
He appointed Qìngzhī as Shìzhōng and Tàiwèi.
His second son, Zhōngshū Láng Wénjì, was enfeoffed as Jiàn'ān Xiàn Hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
When Yìyáng Wáng Chǎng rebelled,
Qìngzhī followed the Emperor across the river,
commanding all the armies.
His youngest son, Wényào,
who was a little over ten years old,
was skilled in horsemanship and archery.
The Emperor loved him,
and also enfeoffed him as Yǒngyáng Xiàn Hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
The Emperor's cruelty and violence worsened daily.
Qìngzhī still spoke his mind and remonstrated earnestly,
but the Emperor's displeasure grew.
When Hē Mài was executed,
fearing Qìngzhī's disagreement,
and anticipating his certain arrival,
he closed all the bridges at Qīngxī to prevent him.
Qìngzhī indeed went,
but, unable to cross, returned.
The Emperor then dispatched Qìngzhī's cousin Yōuzhī to bring medicine and bestow death upon Qìngzhī.
He was eighty years old at the time.
Earlier that year,
Qìngzhī dreamt that someone gave him two bolts of silk,
saying:
"This silk is enough to last."
He said to others:
"I, this old man, will not escape this year.
Two bolts,
that's eighty feet.
Enough to last,
with no surplus."
When he died,
the bestowed gifts were very generous.
He was posthumously granted the title of Shìzhōng,
with Tàiwèi as before.
He was provided with a luánlù wēnláng chariot,
with feathered canopies and drum music before and behind.
His posthumous name was Zhōngwǔ Gōng.
Before he could be buried,
the Emperor was defeated.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted Shìzhōng and Sīkōng,
with the posthumous name Xiāng Gōng.
His eldest son, Wénshū,
successively held the positions of Zhōngshū Huángmén Láng.
At the end of Jǐnghé,
he was Shìzhōng.
When Qìngzhī died,
he refused to drink the medicine.
Yōuzhī smothered him with a quilt.
Wénshū secretly took the medicine and hid the record.
Some advised Wénshū to flee.
Wénshū had seen the Emperor sever the limbs of Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng.
Fearing that if he fled,
the Emperor would be enraged,
and he might suffer the same fate as Yìgōng,
he drank the medicine and committed suicide.
His son, Mìshū Láng Zhāomíng,
also hanged himself.
In the seventh year of Tàishǐ,
he was re-enfeoffed as Cāngwú Jùn Gōng.
In the first year of Yuánhuī,
[二六] his former enfeoffment was restored.
At that time, Shǐxīng was changed to Guǎngxīng.
Zhāomíng's son, Tánliàng,
inherited the title of Guǎngxīng Jùn Gōng.
When Qí received the abdication,
the state [of Sòng] was abolished.
Qìngzhī's younger brother, Shàozhī,
during Yuánjiā,
served as Lúlíng Wáng Shào's Nán Zhōngláng Xíng Cānjūn.
He participated in suppressing the bandits of Jiàn'ān and Jiēyáng,
and died of illness.
His elder brother's son, Sēngróng,
was the son of Chǎngzhī.
In the early Xiàojiàn period,
he served as Ānchéng Xiàng.
When Jīng and Jiāng rebelled,
he raised troops to resist Zāng Zhì.
Zhì sent his Ānchéng Xiàng, Zāng Miǎozhī, to attack Sēngróng,
and defeated him.
During Dàmíng,
he became Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
During Jǐnghé,
he was summoned to be Huángmén Láng.
Before he returned,
he died.
His son, Huáimíng,
in the early Tàishǐ period of Tàizōng,
was in mourning for his father.
He was appointed Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn.
He rendered meritorious service in campaigns to the east and south,
and was enfeoffed as Wúxīng Xiàn Zǐ,
with a stipend of four hundred households.
He successively held positions as Huángmén Shìláng,
and twice as Nán Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
In early Yuánhuī,
he was in mourning for his mother,
and resigned from his post.
When Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn rebelled,
he was appointed Guānjūn Jiāngjūn,
commanding the navy to defend Gù Shítóu.
When Zhùquè was lost,
Huáimíng abandoned his army and fled,
and shortly after died of grief.
Qìngzhī's cousin, Fǎxì, courtesy name Tǐxiān,
also had military talent.
He first served as Zhào Bófú's subordinate general,
then followed Qìngzhī in campaigns against the Wǔshuǐ Mán.
When Shìzǔ attacked the rebels,
he appointed him Nán Zhōngláng Cānjūn,
added Níngshuò Jiāngjūn,
and led three thousand men to set out first.
He arrived at Xīntíng with Liǔ Yuánjǐng at dawn.
Yuánjǐng resided in the central camp,
Zōng Xīn in the western camp,
and Fǎxì in the eastern camp.
The eastern camp occupied a ridge.
When the rebels attacked Yuánjǐng,
Fǎxì shot at them from above,
killing a great many.
Fǎxì had all the trees outside the trench cut down to fall over.
When the rebels came to attack,
they advanced by climbing over the trees.
The pēngpái shields had many gaps.
He selected skilled archers,
and their precise shots never missed,
leaving the dead lying across each other.
After the matter was settled,
he was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Shǐxīng Tàishǒu,
and was dispatched to suppress Xiāo Jiǎn in Guǎngzhōu.
Upon hearing that the capital army was approaching,
Jiǎn deceived his troops, saying:
"The capital army was sent by the rebel Shào."
They all believed him.
The former Zhēngběi Cānjūn Gù Mài was captured by the rebels and moved inside the city.
He was skilled in astronomy,
and said
"Jīng and Jiāng have large armies."
The city therefore held firm.
Initially,
Shìzǔ had first sent Dèng Wǎn to besiege Jiǎn,
but he only prepared one attack route.
When Fǎxì arrived,
he said:
"We should attack from all four sides.
If we only defend one route, when can it be taken?"
Wǎn feared that the credit would not go to him,
and did not follow the advice.
Fǎxì said:
"Let's extend the siege for fifty more days."
When the days were up and it was still not taken,
he then followed Fǎxì's advice.
They attacked from eight routes simultaneously,
and took the city in one day.
Xiāo Jiǎn was executed,
and Guǎngzhōu was pacified.
He sealed the treasuries and handed them over to Dèng Wǎn before returning.
He rose to the rank of Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn, Xúnyáng Tàishǒu,
and Xīn'ān Wáng Zǐluán's Běi Zhōngláng Sīmǎ.
Shàozhī's son Wénxiù
has a separate biography.
Dozens of Qìngzhī's relatives by blood and marriage
rose to positions of rank because of him.
The historian says: Zhāng Shìzhī said,
"If the application of law is biased,
all prisons in the world will follow its lightness or severity."
A balance hung high,
all within the four seas abide by its fairness.
If law is chaotic at court,
the people have no place to set their hands and feet.
Shī Bó, relying on favor to replace officials,
his power shook the court and the countryside.
He inclined his mind to the lowest ranks of officials,
and cemented relationships with bribes.
From selecting departments to local offices,
none did not follow his influence.
He bent the rules to grant private requests,
and consequently halted imperial edicts.
Heaven thundered and raged,
and many fell.
Shī Bó's appointments remained unchanged,
while Wáng and Xiè were dismissed.
The gentleman says of this action,
"How could it merely be a loss of good governance and punishment!"
Collated Notes
Biographies, Chapter 38 Xiāo Sīhuà, Liú Yánsuān.
Xiāo Sīhuà,
a native of Nánlánlíng,
was the disciple of Xiàoyì Huánghòu.
His father, Yuánzhī, whose courtesy name was Jūnliú,
successively held the posts of Zhōngshū Huángménláng,
Cìshǐ of Xú and Yǎn two zhōu,
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, and Nánlányá Tàishǒu.
He died in the first year of Yǒngchū
and was posthumously granted the title of Qián Jiāngjūn.
Sīhuà was about ten years old
and had not yet learned to read.
He indulged in extensive carousing and wandering,
enjoyed climbing on rooftops,
playing the "thin-waist drum" (xìyāogǔ),
and harassing his neighbors,
all of whom were troubled by his wickedness.
From this point, he corrected himself,
and within a few years,
he gained a good reputation.
He was fond of books and history,
skilled at playing the qín,
and adept at horsemanship and archery.
Gāozǔ, upon seeing him once,
immediately considered him a national talent.
At eighteen,
he was appointed Lángyé Wáng Dàsīmǎ Xíngcānjūn,
then transferred to Xiàngguó Cānjūn.
He resigned his post due to his father's mourning.
After the period of mourning ended,
he was appointed Yǔlínjiān,
in charge of the Shítou Garrison,
inherited the noble title of Fēngyáng Xiànhóu,
and was transferred to Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn, Péngchéng Pèi Èr Jùn Tàishǒu.
He had a wide acquaintance with books and histories,
was quite skilled in Lìshū calligraphy,
understood musical theory,
and was proficient in archery and horsemanship.
In the first year of Yuánjiā,
Xiè Huì, being in Jīngzhōu,
wished to invite him to be Sīmǎ,
but Sīhuà refused.
In the fifth year,
he was promoted to Zhōngshū Shìláng,
and concurrently made Dūd Qīngzhōu Xúzhōu Zhī Dōngguǎn Zhū Jūnfù, Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He was then twenty-seven years old.
The fugitive brothers Sīmǎ Lángzhī, Yuánzhī, and Kězhī
gathered a party in Fāgān Xiàn of Dōngguǎn
and plotted rebellion.
Sīhuà sent Běihǎi Tàishǒu Xiāo Wāngzhī to suppress and execute them,
and the remaining rebels were all pacified.
In the eighth year,
he was appointed Jìnglíng Wáng Yìxuān Zuǒjūn Sīmǎ and Nánpèi Jùn Tàishǒu.
Before he could take up the post,
the Suǒlǔ barbarians raided the south.
Tán Dàojì launched a northern expedition,
but later recalled his troops.
Sīhuà, fearing a large-scale barbarian invasion,
abandoned his post and fled to Píngchāng.
Sīhuà had previously sent Cānjūn Liú Zhènzhī to garrison Xiàpī;
upon hearing of Sīhuà's flight,
he also abandoned the city and fled.
The barbarians definitely did not arrive,
but the accumulated provisions in Dōngyáng
had already been burned by the local populace.
Consequently, he was summoned and handed over to the Tíngwèi,
and then imprisoned in the Shàngfāng.
Earlier, in Qīngzhōu,
a copper measure he frequently used
was overturned under some medicine.
Suddenly, two dead sparrows were found under the measure.
Sīhuà said,
"The measure overturned, and two sparrows died;
is this not an ill omen?"
Soon after, he was imprisoned.
In the ninth year,
Qíuchí suffered a great famine,
while Yì and Liáng Zhōu enjoyed abundant harvests.
Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Zhēn Fǎhù, while in office, caused disharmony,
and the Dī chieftain Yáng Nándāng consequently invaded Hánzhōng.
Therefore, Sīhuà was released from prison and appointed Dūd Liáng Nánqín Èr Zhōu Zhū Jūnfù, Héngyě Jiāngjūn, and Liáng Nánqín Èr Zhōu Cìshǐ.
Upon his departure,
he learned that Fǎhù had already abandoned his post and fled north to Xīchéng.
He sent Sīmǎ, Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn, Nánhánzhōng Tàishǒu Xiāo Chéngzhī with five hundred men to advance,
and also sent Xīróng Chángshǐ Xiāo Wāngzhī to arrest Fǎhù.
Chéngzhī gathered soldiers and commoners along the way,
obtaining a thousand elite troops.
In the first month of the tenth year,
they advanced and occupied Yáotóu.
Nándāng, having plundered Hánzhōng,
led his forces back west,
leaving his Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, Liáng Qín Èr Zhōu Cìshǐ Zhào Wēn to guard Liángzhōu,
and Wèixīng Tàishǒu Xuē Jiàn to hold Huángjīn.
Chéngzhī advanced and garrisoned Yáotóu,
sending Yīnpíng Tàishǒu Xiāo Tǎn to Huángjīn.
Xuē Jiàn's deputy, Jiāng Bǎo, occupied Tiěchéng.
Tiěchéng and Huángjīn faced each other,
about one lí apart,
with trees cut down to block the road.
Tǎn advanced and attacked the two garrisons,
capturing them.
In the second month,
Zhào Wēn, along with Xuē Jiàn and his Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, Féngyì Tàishǒu Pú Zǎozǐ, came to attack Tǎn's camp.
Tǎn fought valiantly
and severely defeated them.
Tǎn was wounded,
and the bandits retreated to defend Xīshuǐ.
Chéngzhī's Sīmǎ Xī Wénzǔ advanced and occupied Huángjīn,
and Xiāo Wāngzhī's five hundred cavalry and infantry arrived consecutively.
Píngxī Jiāngjūn, Línchuān Wáng Yìqìng sent Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Péi Fāngmíng with three thousand men to assist.
Chéngzhī and others advanced to Huángjīn,
and Zǎozǐ, Jiàn, and others retreated to defend Xiàtáo.
Sīhuà had previously sent Xíngcānjūn Wáng Língjì to lead a detachment out of Yángchuān,
then proceed towards Nánchéng.
The bogus Língjiāng Jiāngjūn Zhào Yīng stubbornly defended the treacherous terrain.
Língjì defeated him
and captured Yīng alive.
Nánchéng was empty,
and lacking provisions,
he led his army back to join Chéngzhī.
In the third month,
Chéngzhī led all the armies to advance and occupy Égōnggù.
Nándāng sent his son Hé, along with Zhào Wēn, Pú Zǎozǐ, and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Lǚ Píng, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Sīmǎ Fēilóng,
with over ten thousand cavalry and infantry,
to cross the Hánjīn River and build a barricade,
erecting a pontoon bridge in between.
They fully exerted their strength to attack Chéngzhī,
besieging him in dozens of layers.
They engaged in close-quarters combat,
where bows and arrows were no longer useful.
The bandits were all clad in rhinoceros hide armor,
which lances and spears could not penetrate.
Chéngzhī then cut his spear to several feet long,
and used a large axe to strike with it.
Each spear thrust pierced over ten bandits.
The bandits could not withstand him,
and were greatly defeated.
They burned their barricades and fled,
retreating to defend Dàtáo.
In the intercalary month,
Chéngzhī and Fāngmíng's imperial army arrived.
Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Yáng Píngxīng and Chuángzhǔ Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn Liáng Tǎn directly entered to pursue them with crossbows.
The bandits were defeated again,
and many were killed, wounded, or captured.
Hánzhōng was pacified.
All the lost territories were recovered
and garrisons were established at Jiāmíngshuǐ.
Previously,
when Huán Xuán usurped Jìn,
he made Huán Xī Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu.
After Xī's defeat and flight,
the Dī Yáng Shèng occupied Hánzhōng.
Cìshǐ Fàn Yuánzhī and Fù Xīn both governed from Wèixīng,
only holding Wèixīng, Shàngyōng, and Xīnchéng three commanderies.
Later, Suǒ Mò became Cìshǐ,
and then governed from Nánchéng.
As it had been burned by bandits and could not be fortified,
Sīhuà relocated the garrison to Nánzhèng,
was granted the insignia of authority (Jié),
and promoted to the title of Níngshuò Jiāngjūn.
Chéngzhī was summoned to be Tàizǐ Túnqí Xiàowèi.
Fǎhù,
a native of Wújí, Zhōngshān,
had crossed the river and settled in Nánjùn.
His younger brother, Fǎchóng,
in the tenth year of Yuánjiā,
was appointed Yìzhōu Cìshǐ from Shǎofǔ.
Fǎhù's crime of abandoning his post
led to his arrest by the supreme government
and a賜死 (sìsǐ, death sentence) in prison.
Tàizǔ, considering that Fǎchóng was entrusted with the responsibility of a region,
ordered the prison officials to report that Fǎhù had died of illness.
Tàizǔ instructed Sīhuà to submit a full account of the pacification of Hánzhōng,
which was then filed with the historical office.
In the fourteenth year [of Yuánjiā 元嘉, 437 CE],

he was transferred to become Administrator-in-Chief (Zhǎngshǐ 長史) of Píngxī 平西, Prince Yìqìng 義慶 of Línchuān 臨川, and Colonel (Xiàowèi 校尉) of the Southern Barbarians (Nánmán 南蠻), holding the Credentials (Chíjié 持節).
Tàizǔ 太祖 gifted him a bow and a qín,
and wrote in a personal decree:
"What have you been working on lately, venerable sir?
In leisure from affairs,
one naturally takes pleasure in the qín and books.
What one gains thereby, is it not righteousness?
I constantly think of you and cannot forget,
and I suppose you feel the same.
I recently obtained this qín,
said to be an old item,
and also famous in Jīngyì 京邑.
I now lend it to you.
It is imbued with Dài Yǒng's 戴顒 intent for playing and stroking,
and its sound and resonance are exceptionally excellent,
truly delightful.
I also send a mulberry bow.
Its material and texture are splendid.
It was what I used to use often,
but since I have long ceased archery,
and am often ill,
I can barely manage it.
I have simply become an old man,
which makes one sigh.
Good material and fine instruments
should be in a place where they can be fully utilized.
Venerable sir, you truly have no one to yield to."
In the sixteenth year [439 CE],
Prince Yìjì 義季 of Héngyáng 衡陽 replaced Yìqìng 義慶,
and he was again appointed Administrator-in-Chief of Ānxī 安西,
with the rest as before.
In the nineteenth year [442 CE],
he was summoned to be Attendant-in-Ordinary (Shìzhōng 侍中),
and additionally General of the Vanguard (Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn 前軍將軍).
Before he could take up the summons,
he resumed his former post.
The next year [443 CE],

he was transferred to become Colonel of Níngmán 寧蠻, Inspector of Yōngzhōu 雍州, holding Credentials (Chíjié 持節) and overseeing the military affairs of Yōngzhōu 雍州, Liángzhōu 梁州, the four prefectures of Northern and Southern Qín 秦, and the six commanderies of Nányáng 南陽, Jìnglíng 竟陵, Shùnyáng 順陽, Xiāngyáng 襄陽, Xīnyě 新野, and Suí 隨 in Jīngzhōu 荊州.
He was also Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守) of Xiāngyáng 襄陽.
In the twenty-second year [445 CE],
he was appointed Attendant-in-Ordinary (Shìzhōng 侍中),
and additionally Right Commander of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Yòulǜ 太子右率).
In the twenty-fourth year [447 CE],
he was transferred to additionally be General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn 左衞將軍).
Once, he accompanied Tàizǔ 太祖 up the northern ridge of Zhōngshān 鍾山.
Midway, there was a flat rock and clear spring.
The Emperor ordered him to play the qín on the rock,
and then gifted him wine in a silver cup,
saying:
"Your appreciation has the spirit of pines and rocks."
He also additionally held the post of Grand Arbiter of Southern Xúzhōu 徐州 (Nán Xúzhōu Dàzhōngzhèng 南徐州大中正).
The next year [448 CE],

he again oversaw the military affairs of Yōngzhōu 雍州, Liángzhōu 梁州, the four prefectures of Northern and Southern Qín 秦, and the two commanderies of Jìnglíng 竟陵 and Suí 隨 in Jīngzhōu 荊州, as well as Right General (Yòujiāngjūn 右將軍), Colonel of Níngmán 寧蠻, and Inspector of Yōngzhōu 雍州, as before.
In the twenty-sixth year [449 CE],
he was summoned to be Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū 吏部尚書).
An imperial edict to Sīhuà 思話 stated:
"Minister Shěn 沈 suffered a sudden illness and could not be saved.
His conduct and character were upright and careful,
and he served the court with utter public spirit.
His years were still good,
and I was about to entrust him with important responsibilities,
but he suddenly passed away too soon.
My sorrow and lamentation are particularly profound.
The selection and administration of officials is a crucial mechanism,
on which prosperity and obstruction depend.
Your talent and ability, venerable sir, are suited to governing the state;
you are truly one of the very few who are fitting."
Sīhuà 思話 felt that having left the prefecture, he no longer had manpower.
He requested nine people from the Fǔjūn's 府軍 staff.
Tàizǔ 太祖 jokingly said to him:
"Venerable sir, you will never be a rustic in the villages;
how could you have no one to employ?"
Before he could accept the appointment,
in the twenty-seventh year [450 CE],
he was transferred to become General of the Palace Guard (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn 護軍將軍).
In the spring of that year,
the barbarians attacked Xuánhù 懸瓠.
Tàizǔ 太祖 was about to launch a large northern expedition,
and all the court officials agreed;
no one expressed dissent.
Sīhuà 思話 adamantly remonstrated,
but was not heeded.
He then led three thousand elite armored troops
to assist in garrisoning Péngchéng 彭城.
When the barbarians retreated,

he immediately replaced Shìzǔ 世祖 as Inspector of Yánzhōu 兗州 and Xúzhōu 徐州, General Who Pacifies the Army (Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn 撫軍將軍), holding Credentials (Chíjié 持節) and overseeing the military affairs of Xúzhōu 徐州, Yánzhōu 兗州, Qīngzhōu 青州, Jìzhōu 冀州, and Liángjùn 梁郡 in Yùzhōu 豫州.
In the twenty-ninth year [452 CE],
he commanded the forces of General Who Spreads Martial Might (Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn 揚武將軍), Inspector of Jìzhōu 冀州, Zhāng Yǒng 張永, to besiege Què'áo 碻磝.
Initially,
Staff Officer (Zīyì Cānjūn 諮議參軍) Shēn Tǎn 申坦 of the General Who Guards the Army (Zhènjūn 將軍), and Wáng Xuánmó 王玄謨, besieged Huátái 滑臺.
They did not succeed
and were dismissed from office.
Xiāo Bīn 蕭斌, Inspector of Qīngzhōu 青州, appointed Tǎn 坦 to act as General Who Establishes Might (Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn 建威將軍), Grand Administrator of Jǐnán 濟南 and Píngyuán 平原 commanderies,
to defend Lìchéng 歷城.
He also ordered Rèn Zhòngrén 任仲仁 to be Tǎn's 坦 deputy,
and both entered the river as the vanguard.
In the fifth month [of 452 CE],
they set off from Yánkou 沿口.
Yǒng's 永 Staff Officer (Sīmǎ 司馬), Cuī Xùn 崔訓, and General Who Establishes Martial Might (Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn 建武將軍), Grand Administrator of Qíjùn 齊郡, Hú Jǐngshì 胡景世, led the Qīngzhōu 青州 army to join them.
In the seventh month,
Sīhuà 思話 and the various armies all arrived at Què'áo 碻磝
and prepared three attack routes.
Tàizǔ 太祖 dispatched Xú Yuán 徐爰, Supernumerary Palace Attendant (Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng 員外散騎侍郎), to convey the imperial decree and supervise the battle.
Zhāng Yǒng 張永 and Hú Jǐngshì 胡景世 were to attack the eastern route,
Shēn Tǎn 申坦 and Rèn Zhòngrén 任仲仁 the western route,
and Cuī Xùn 崔訓 the southern route.
That night, the enemy dug a tunnel out,
and burned Cuī Xùn's 崔訓 towers and siege vehicles.
They also burned Hú Jǐngshì's 胡景世 towers and siege equipment.
Soon after, they also destroyed Cuī Xùn's 崔訓 attack route,
and the city could not be breached.
Sīhuà 思話 rushed there
and withdrew the troops.
After eighteen days of attacking the city,
they lifted the siege and returned to Lìxià 歷下.
Cuī Xùn 崔訓, because his towers were burned
and he could not secure the attack route,
was executed at Què'áo 碻磝.
[一０]Yǒng 永 and Tǎn 坦 were both imprisoned.
An imperial edict stated:
"I received the memorial from General Who Pacifies the Army (Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn 撫軍將軍) Sīhuà 思話,
stating that Què'áo 碻磝 could not be breached,
and the soldiers were exhausted.
Therefore, withdraw the army to Qīngjì 清濟,
and plan further attacks.
This garrison [Lìchéng 歷城] has severe mountains and rivers,
controlling Hèshuò 河朔.
It is a crucial strategic point
renowned since ancient times.
It is fitting to abolish his current appointment [at Péngchéng 彭城]
to match the expectations and reality.
Sīhuà 思話 is to be relieved of Xúzhōu 徐州 and made Inspector of Jìzhōu 冀州,
with the rest as before.
The civil and military officials of Péngchéng 彭城
are to be reallocated.
He is to immediately garrison Lìchéng 歷城."
Soon after, he was impeached and dismissed from office by Prince Yìgōng 義恭 of Jiāngxià 江夏.
When Yuánxiōng 元凶 usurped the throne,

he appointed Sīhuà 思話 as Inspector of Xúzhōu 徐州 and Yánzhōu 兗州, holding Credentials (Chíjié 持節) and overseeing the military affairs of Xúzhōu 徐州, Qīngzhōu 青州, Yánzhōu 兗州, Jìzhōu 冀zhou, and Liángjùn 梁郡 in Yùzhōu 豫zhou,
with his general title remaining as before.
Sīhuà 思話 immediately led his troops back to Péngchéng 彭城
and raised an army to respond to Shìzǔ 世祖.
He sent an envoy with a memorial saying:
"Your humble servant was recently in Lìxià 歷下,
and first heard of the national taboo (i.e., the Emperor's death).
The messenger I received [the news from]
did not know the full extent [of what happened].
When I was on my way back,
I gradually heard more,
but still believed that such a thing could not possibly occur in human society.
My private feelings were agitated,
and I dared not speak.
Now I have received this instruction,
which indeed confirms my worst fears.
My sorrow and lamentation are doubly increased,
and I cannot overcome myself.
This truly is something that Heaven and Earth will not cover or carry,
and which humans and spirits cannot tolerate.
All the people within the realm
are filled with indignation,
not to mention your humble servant, who has been covered by profound imperial favor
and whose righteousness is combined with his usual aspirations.
On the fifth day of this month,
I received an urgent order by courier for cavalry to return to court.
Grinding my teeth and beating my breast,
I immediately fell ill.
Although my entire family is in the capital,
I do not care for them in the least.
I was just about to send a memorial to seek your strategy,
when I happened to receive this imperial decree, with sorrow and fear intermingling.
I respectfully understand that the Minister of Works (Sītú 司徒) has launched his brilliant plans like lightning,
and Your Highness's divine martial power cuts like frost.
Zāng Zhì 臧質's loyalty and righteousness have both arrived,
acting in concert without prior consultation.
Relying on righteous compliance and flowing downstream,
they will sweep through the Jiangdiàn 江甸 [region].
The vanguard, advancing like the wind,
must already be close.
Your humble servant's troops, though newly assembled,
have dispatched two armies, General Who Aids the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍) Shēn Tǎn 申坦 and General Who Soars Like a Dragon (Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn 龍驤將軍) Liáng Tǎn 梁坦.
Five thousand elite armored troops have been allocated,
with Shēn Tǎn 申坦 in command,
and they will proceed immediately by both land and water.
Your humble servant will lead all civil and military officials,
following one after another.
Relying on power and encouraging the weak,
the momentum is like shaking decaying matter.
The return of peace and prosperity is imminent,
and joy and sorrow are intertwined."
When Shìzǔ 世祖 arrived at Xīntíng 新亭,
Tǎn 坦 also advanced and captured Jīngkǒu 京口.
Upon the Emperor's accession,
he was summoned to serve as Sànqí Chángshì and Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè.
He firmly declined,
not accepting the appointment.
He was then made Zhōngshū Lìng and Dānyáng Yǐn,
with his position as Chángshì remaining as before.
At that time, there were many robberies and plundering in the capital region,
seventeen occurrences within two decades.
He offered to take the blame and resign,
but it was not permitted.
The following year,
he was sent out as Shǐ Chíjíe, Dūdū Xú Yǎn Qīng Jì Yōu Wǔ Zhōu Yùzhōu Zhī Liángjùn Zhūjūanshì, Ānběi Jiāngjūn, and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the addition of a set of drum and wind instruments.
Before he could depart, Zāng Zhì, the Cìshǐ of Jiāngzhōu, rebelled.
He was again appointed Shǐ Chíjíe, Dūdū Jiāngzhōu Yùzhōu Zhī Xīyáng Jìnxī Xīncài Sāngùn Zhūjūanshì, and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
When the matter was settled,
Yǐngzhōu was established by dividing territory from Jīng, Jiāng, and Yù three prefectures.
He was again made Dūdū Yǐng Xiāng Èrzhōu Zhūjūanshì, Zhènxī Jiāngjūn, and Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his Chíjíe and Chángshì titles remaining as before.
He garrisoned Xiàkǒu.
In Xiàojiàn second year, he died,
at the age of fifty.
〔一一〕 He was posthumously granted the titles of Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
with his Chíjíe, Chángshì, Dūdū, and Cìshǐ titles remaining as before,
and was posthumously honored as Mù Hóu.
Sīhuà was a highly respected member of the imperial clan,
who gained trust and important positions early in his career.
He held governorships in twelve prefectures in total,
and held the marshal's staff as Dūdū nine times.
Although he did not show brilliant integrity wherever he went,
he also committed no defilement or corruption.
He loved talent and respected scholars,
and many people gravitated towards him.
His eldest son, Huìkāi, inherited his title;
his biography is in another place.
His second son, Huìmíng,
also enjoyed a generational reputation,
and successively held the posts of Huángmén Láng,
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ,
and Wúxīng Tàishǒu.
In the late Yuánhuī era of the deposed emperor,
he died in office.
His fourth son, Huìjī,
