served as Shìzhōng
in the late Shēngmíng era of Emperor Shùn.
Yuánzhī's cousin, Mózhī,
was Dānyáng Yǐn,
and was posthumously granted the title of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
His son, Bīn,
was also favored by Tàizǔ.
When Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng was stationed in Yùzhāng,
he appointed Bīn as Dàjiāngjūn Zīyì Cānjūn and Yùzhāng Tàishǒu.
He successively served as Nánmán Xiàowèi,
Shìzhōng,
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and Qīng Jì Èrzhōu Cìshǐ.
In Yuánjiā twenty-seventh year,
he commanded Wáng Xuánmó and other generals in a northern expedition.
Bīn sent General Cuī Měng to attack and capture Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Zhāng Huáizhī in Yuè'ān,
and Huáizhī abandoned the city and fled.
Earlier,
Měng and Bīn's Cānjūn Fù Róng had jointly captured Yuè'ān and Què'áo.
The waterways in Yuè'ān were impassable,
so they first secured Què'áo,
and then captured Yuè'ān.
Afterward, they besieged Huátái but failed to take it.
Bīn was recalled to Lìxià;
this event is recorded in Wáng Xuánmó's biography.
In the twenty-eighth year,
the fugitive Sīmǎ Shùnzé falsely claimed to be a close relative of the Jìn imperial house,
declared himself Qí Wáng,
gathered a crowd, and occupied Liángzōu Chéng.
There was also a Buddhist monk who called himself Sīmǎ Bǎinián,
declared himself Āndìng Wáng,
and fugitives Qín Kǎizhī, Zǔ Yuánmíng, and others each occupied villages and garrisons to respond to Shùnzé.
Initially,
Cuī Xūnzhī, the garrison commander of Liángzōu, Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn, and Tàishǒu of Yuè'ān and Bóhǎi two commanderies, was away from the prefecture,
so Shùnzé took advantage of the emptiness to seize it.
Xūnzhī's Sīmǎ Cáo Jìnghuì resisted but was no match,
and fled.
Bīn immediately sent Xūnzhī to lead the Xíng Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn, Tàishǒu of Jìnán and Píngyuán two commanderies Shēn Tǎn, Chángliú Cānjūn Luó Wénchāng, and other generals to attack Shùnzé.
They attacked but failed to overcome him.
Xūnzhī and others initially thought that those within the city had been forced to join,
and would flee as soon as the army arrived,
but they all held out firmly for the rebels,
killing and wounding many government troops.
Bīn again sent Fǔ Sīmǎ, Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Qíjùn Tàishǒu Páng Xiùzhī to command all the troops.
Zǔ Yuánmíng also occupied Ānqiu Chéng.
Bīn further sent Zhènnǔ Jiāngjūn Liú Wǔzhī and Jūnzǔ Liú Huí with a thousand elite soldiers
to attack Sīmǎ Bǎinián,
and beheaded him.
Once Shùnzé lost his position,
his followers gradually dispersed.
Wénchāng sent Dàolián to pretend to surrender to the rebels,
who trusted and accepted him.
He secretly showed the imperial rewards to the public,
and rebel leaders within the city, such as Lǐ Jìshū, all harbored thoughts of surrender.
Dàolián's plot was discovered
and he was killed by the rebels.
Jìshū scaled the wall and surrendered,
and the rebel faction greatly disintegrated.
Then, they launched a four-sided attack,
and wherever the ram-carts struck,
three to five *zhang* of the wall would collapse.
At that time, a head was thrown down from the South Gate tower,
and a rope was lowered to pull up an outsider.
When the outsider came up,
the rebels all laid down their weapons,
saying that Shùnzé had already been beheaded,
and the head thrown down was his.
Qín Kǎizhī fled to Héběi.
Bīn was dismissed from office
for the defeat at Huátái.
After a long time,
he was reinstated as Nánpíng Wáng Shuò Zuǒjūn Chángshǐ.
His subsequent actions are recorded in the biographies of the two villains.
Bīn's younger brother, Jiǎn,
successively held the post of Chángshā Nèishǐ.
When Guǎnglíng Wáng Dàn was appointed to Guǎngzhōu,
before he could take up his post,
Jiǎn was appointed Ānnán Zīyì Cānjūn and Nánhǎi Tàishǒu,
acting as the administrator of the provincial government.
When Dōnghǎi Wáng Huī replaced Dàn,
Jiǎn remained as Qiánjūn Zīyì,
with his Tàishǒu title as before.
When Shìzǔ entered to suppress the principal rebel,
he sent Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Nánhǎi Tàishǒu Dèng Wǎn to attack Jiǎn.
〔一二〕 He defended stubbornly for a period,
but the city fell and he was executed.
Bīn and Jiǎn's sons were all executed.
Páng Xiùzhī was
a native of Hénán.
Because he was an old subordinate of Bīn,
the rebel Shào greatly trusted and relied on him,
appointing him Yóují Jiāngjūn.
He fled to Shìzǔ at Xīntíng.
At that time, none of Shào's generals had surrendered;
only Xiùzhī arrived first.
When the matter was settled,
he was appointed Liángzhōu Cìshǐ.
Nearly ten of Xiùzhī's sons and younger brothers were killed by Shào,
yet he did not cease his revelry.
He was dismissed from office for this.
Later, he was again appointed Xúzhōu Cìshǐ
and Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài.
In Xiàojiàn first year,
he died.
He was posthumously granted his original office
and the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
His son, Mízhī,
was Guǎngxīng Gōngxiàng
in the late Shēngmíng era of Emperor Shùn.
Xiùzhī's younger brother, Kuàngzhī,
also served as Shǐxīng Xiàng
during Tàizōng's reign.
Liú Yánsūn was
a native of Péngchéng-Lǚ,
and the son of Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Dàochǎn.
He first served as Xúzhōu Zhǔbù,
was recommended as Xiùcái,
served as Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng Sītú Xíng Cānjūn,
Shàngshū Dūguān Láng,
served as Qiántáng Lìng,
Shìzǔ Fǔjūn, Guǎnglíng Wáng Dàn Běizhōngláng Zhōngbīng Cānjūn, and Nánqīnghé Tàishǒu.
When Shìzǔ was in Xúzhōu,
he was appointed Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ.
At that time, the Suǒ barbarians besieged Xiànhù,
and divided their troops to send the plundered civilians to Rǔyáng.
Tàizǔ ordered Shìzǔ to send troops to attack them.
Those who discussed the matter recommended Yánsūn as the commander-in-chief,
but he firmly declined, saying he was unfit for military command,
and recommended Liú Tàizhī to take his place.
After Tàizhī had departed,
Tàizǔ was greatly enraged
and dismissed Yánsūn from office.
He then served as Shìzǔ Zhènjūn Běizhōngláng Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
Nánzhōngláng Zīyì Cānjūn,
and concurrently as Lùshì.
When Shìzǔ campaigned against the rebel,
the government lacked senior aides,
so he was transferred to serve as Chángshǐ and Xúnyáng Tàishǒu,
acting as the administrator of the temporary government.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was made Shìzhōng,
and concurrently assumed the post of Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn.
An imperial edict stated:
"I, relying on the strength of capable individuals,
have wiped away a great shame.
With my insignificant self,
I have been entrusted with a position above princes and dukes.
I reflect on how to reward merit and establish goodness,
to eternally secure the achievements of the age.
The newly appointed Shìzhōng and concurrent Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn, Yánsūn, is by nature loyal and diligent,
his bearing is calm and upright.
He wholeheartedly assisted at the beginning of the righteous cause,
exerting both sincerity and strength.
Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn, Jùn, has an open and bright ambition,
his reasoning is clear and essential.
He offered excellent strategies and loyal counsel,
managing affairs from the very beginning,
making it possible for the foundation to be rebuilt and renewed.
All have contributed diligently.
It is fitting to conspicuously bestow upon them 'guīshè' [a ceremonial position],
and grandly establish their states and families.
Yánsūn is to be enfeoffed as Dōngchāng Xiànhóu,
and Jùn as Jiànchéng Xiànhóu,
each with an income of two thousand households."
That year,
the Shìzhōng's concurrent post was changed to Wèiwèi.
In Xiàojiàn First Year (454),
he was promoted to Dānyáng Yǐn.
When Zāng Zhì rebelled,
the Emperor was deeply concerned about the eastern region,
so he was sent out as Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Wúxīng Tàishǒu,
and provided with assistants.
After the affair was settled,
he was recalled as Shàngshū Yòupúyè,
and concurrently Lǐng Xúzhōu Dàzhōngzhèng.
He was dispatched to Jiānglíng
to distinguish between right and wrong,
and carry out punishments and rewards.
In the third year (456),
he was again sent out as Nányánzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the added title of Sànqí Chángshì.
He was then transferred to be Shǐchíjié, Jiān Yōngliáng Nánběiqín Sìzhōu Yǐngzhōu zhī Jìnglìng Suí Èrjùn Zhūjūnmìshì, Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn, Níngmán Xiàowèi, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
but due to illness, he did not proceed to the post.
He remained as Shìzhōng and Hùjūn,
and also concurrently Lǐng Xúzhōu Dàzhōngzhèng.
He had long suffered from illness,
which worsened that year.
An imperial edict sent a Huángmén Shìláng to convey a message inquiring about his health.
In Dàmíng First Year (457),
he was appointed Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
and concurrently Lǐng Tàizǐ Zhànshì,
his role as Zhōngzhèng remained as before.
That year,
he was again sent out as Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn and Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ.
Previously, Gāozǔ had left an imperial edict stating that
Jīngkǒu was a vital strategic location,
close to the capital,
and only members of the imperial clan or close relatives
were allowed to reside there.
Although Yánsūn and the imperial family were both from Péngchéng,
he belonged to a different branch in Lǚxiàn.
The Liú clan residing in Péngchéng Xiàn
was also divided into three districts:
the imperial family resided in Suīyú Lǐ,
Zuǒjiāngjūn Liú Huáisù resided in Ānshàng Lǐ,
and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Huáiwǔ resided in Cóngtíng Lǐ,
making a total of four Liú families including Lǚxiàn.
Although they all descended from Chǔyuán Wáng,
their generations had never been formally aligned.
Yánsūn was not originally of the same clan as the imperial family,
and thus should not have received this appointment.
At that time, Sīkōng Jìnglǐng Wáng Dàn was the Cìshǐ of Xúzhōu.
The Emperor deeply feared and was wary of him,
not wishing him to reside in Jīngkǒu,
and moved him to Guǎnglǐng.
Guǎnglǐng was across the river from Jīngkǒu,
and the Emperor wanted a trusted confidant to be the Cìshǐ of Xúzhōu,
holding Jīngkǒu to guard against Dàn.
Therefore, Nánxú was conferred upon Yánsūn,
and he was recognized as part of the imperial clan,
so that the princes would acknowledge him as a relative.
In the third year (459),
Nányánzhōu Cìshǐ Jìnglǐng Wáng Dàn committed a crime
and refused to be summoned.
Yánsūn swiftly dispatched Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Dù Yǒuwén to lead troops to attack him.
Upon arrival,
Dàn had already closed the city gates and was defending himself,
so they returned.
Dàn sent an envoy, Liú Gōngtài, with a letter to entice him.
Yánsūn beheaded Gōngtài
and sent his head to Jīngyì.
He again sent Yǒuwén to lead troops across the river
to operate under the command of Shěn Qìngzhī.
That year,
he was promoted to Chējì Jiāngjūn,
with the added title of Sànqí Chángshì,
and granted a set of drums and pipes.
In the fifth year (461),
an edict to Yánsūn stated:
"The practice of establishing relatives in the old capital
has always been the rule.
Your previous appointment had a different consideration,
but now that the long-standing defense has been appeased,
this position should be returned to a junior member of the family."
Yánsūn was recalled as Shìzhōng and Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè,
and concurrently Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
Yánsūn was severely ill
and unable to perform the formal prostrations.
The Emperor allowed him to receive the enfeoffment tablet at Wǔchéng,
and travel by boat from Qīngxī to Píngchāngmén,
then enter the lower residence of the Shàngshū.
The Emperor also wanted him to replace Zhū Xiūzhī as the Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu,
but the plan was not carried out.
The following year (462),
he died,
at the age of fifty-two.
The Emperor deeply regretted his loss,
and issued an edict stating:
"The late Shìzhōng, Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè, concurrent Hùjūn Jiāngjūn, and founder of the Dōngchāng Xiànhóu, Yánsūn,
was upright and straightforward in disposition,
profound and clear in understanding.
He was deeply dedicated and served as a loyal aide.
From a border official to a court minister,
he has been a steadfast companion for nearly
two decades.
When the imperial enterprise faced collapse,
he was the first to endorse the grand plan;
when the righteous command was issued,
he bore responsibilities akin to Xiāo and Kòu.
His abilities were fit to be a pillar,
and his merits truly aided the times.
He served two emperors,
and acted as both a court official and a regional governor.
His benevolent governance and outstanding achievements
were widely known among the people.
His loyal counsel and excellent integrity
were profoundly clear to me.
He was about to harmonize the affairs of the court
and eternally assist the state's path,
but suddenly passed away.
My grief is doubly profound.
According to the established norms for posthumous honors,
it is proper to express full sorrow and respect.
He is hereby posthumously granted the title of Sītú,
and provided with twenty honor guards carrying swords.
His titles of Shìzhōng, Púyè, and Hóu remain as before."
The relevant officials proposed the posthumous title Zhōngmù,
but an edict changed it to Wénmù.
Another edict stated:
"The late Sītú Wénmù Gōng Yánsūn,
lived a simple and frugal life,
his family was inherently poor and humble.
Whenever I recall his pure virtues,
I feel a deep sense of sadness and regret.
The expenses for his funeral and burial
must surely be lacking.
He is hereby granted three hundred thousand cash and
one thousand hú of rice."
His son, Zhì, succeeded him.
During Tàizōng Tàishǐ's reign (465-472),
he committed a crime,
and the peerage was abolished.
Yánsūn's younger brother, Yánxī,
was Yìxīng Tàishǒu,
and his biography is found in the record of Kǒng Jì.
The historian remarked: "Yánsūn, when he first
joined the ranks of the powerful, certainly surpassed Yán and Yuán.
His disposition and strength were
beyond comparison,
yet his esteemed reputation and great favor
were always carefully considered before being bestowed.
Why was this?
It was truly because when the propitious fortune was just beginning to unfold,
and severe illness was just beginning to be afflicted,
although old favors accumulated within,
familiarity was kept at a distance.
Indeed, contempt arises from familiarity in affairs,
and respect from maintaining a slight distance.
Distance necessarily fosters longing,
while familiarity necessarily breeds disdain.
Once longing and disdain differ,
honor and ceremony are naturally separated.
Thus, he was able to become a revered minister of his generation,
and this is why.
Confucius said:
'To serve the ruler too frequently
leads to estrangement.'
Is it not so!
Is it not so!"
Textual Notes
Biographies Volume Thirty-Nine, Five Princes: Jìnglǐng Wáng Dàn, Lújiāng Wáng Huī, Wǔchāng Wáng Hún, Hǎilíng Wáng Xiūmào, Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn.
Jìnglǐng Wáng Dàn, courtesy name Xiūwén,
was the sixth son of Wéndì.
In the twentieth year of Yuánjiā [443 CE],
when he was eleven years old,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Guǎnglíng [Guǎnglíng Wáng],
with a stipend of two thousand households.
In the twenty-first year [444 CE],
he was appointed Supervisor of All Military Affairs of Nányǎn Province, General of the Northern Central Army, and Governor of Nányǎn Province [Nányǎn Zhōucìshǐ],
and sent out to garrison Guǎnglíng.
Soon after, he was transferred to be Governor of Nánxú Province [Nánxú Zhōucìshǐ] with his original title.
In the twenty-sixth year [449 CE],

he was sent out as Administrator-General of All Military Affairs of Yōng, Liáng, the Northern and Southern Qín four provinces, and Jìnglíng and Suí two commanderies of Jīng Province, General of the Rear Army, and Governor of Yōng Province [Yōng Zhōucìshǐ].
As Guǎnglíng was dilapidated and run down,
he was re-enfeoffed as the Prince of Suí Commandery [Suíjùn Wáng].
The emperor wished to launch a major northern expedition,
and because Xiāngyáng bordered Guān and Hé,
he wished to expand its resources.
Therefore, he abolished the Jīang Province military administration;
all its civil and military personnel were assigned to Yōng Province,
and the tax revenues and miscellaneous goods from Xiāng Province [Xiāngzhōu] were
all supplied to Xiāngyáng.
When the great northern expedition was launched,
all the princely vassals were ordered to send out troops;
none failed to be routed and defeated.
Only Dàn's Staff Officer of the Central Army, Liǔ Yuánjǐng, first captured Hóngnóng, Guān, and Shǎn three cities,
obtaining many heads;
Guān and Luò were shaken.
The details are in the biography of Yuánjǐng.
As all the other forces were defeated and retreated,
Yuánjǐng consequently withdrew.
Dàn was summoned back to the capital [Jīngshī],
and promoted to Administrator-General of All Military Affairs of Guǎng and Jiāo two provinces, General Who Guards the South, and Governor of Guǎng Province [Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ].
He was to be garrisoned at Shǐxīng.
Before he departed,

he was reassigned as Administrator-General of All Military Affairs of Huìjī, Dōngyáng, Xīn'ān, Línhǎi, and Yǒngjiā five commanderies, General Who Pacifies the East, and Grand Administrator of Huìjī [Huìjī Tàishǒu],
and granted a set of drums and pipes.
When the arch-villain [Shào] assassinated and ascended the throne,
he placed the western part of Zhèjiāng in Yáng Province under the Inspector of the Capital [Sīlì Xiàowèi],
and established Huì Province [Huìzhōu] from the five eastern commanderies of Zhèjiāng,
appointing Dàn as its Governor [Cìshǐ].
When Shìzǔ marched to suppress the rebellion,
he sent Shěn Qìngzhī's nephew, Sēngróng, to secretly inform Dàn.
He also sent General Who Pacifies Distant Regions, Gù Bīnzhī, to enter from Lǔxiǎn in the east,
to be directed by Dàn.
Dàn sent his Staff Officer, Liú Jìzhī, to combine forces with Bīnzhī,
and stationed them at Dùn Xīlíng [Dùnxīlíng]
as a reserve.
Shào sent Generals Huá Qīn and Yǔ Dǎo to attack in the east;
they encountered Bīnzhī and others at Bēnniú Táng of Qǔ'ā.
The road was very narrow,
and on both sides, it was entirely overgrown with wild rice.
Bīnzhī's soldiers mostly carried basket-clogs;
they shot at them from among the wild rice.
Qīn and his forces were utterly defeated.
After the situation was pacified,

Dàn was summoned to be Bearer of the Imperial Credentials, Administrator-General of All Military Affairs of Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, Yì, Níng, Liáng, and the Northern and Southern Qín eight provinces, General of the Guards, Minister of State with the Privileges of the Three Ducal Ministers, and Governor of Jīng Province [Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ].
Dàn felt that his official title and position were exactly the same as Jùn's,
and disliked it,
requesting a change.
Thereupon, he was promoted to General of Agile Cavalry [Piàojì Jiāngjūn],
granted twenty additional swordsmen for escort,
with the rest remaining as before.
As Yìxuān, Prince of Nánqiáo, refused to come to the capital,
Dàn was appointed Imperial Household Supervisor, Grand General of Agile Cavalry, and Governor of Yáng Province [Yángzhōu Cìshǐ],
with his ministerial privileges remaining as before.
He was re-enfeoffed as the Prince of Jìnglíng [Jìnglíng Wáng],
with a stipend of five thousand households.
Gù Bīnzhī, for his achievement at Bēnniú,
was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yángxīn County [Yángxīn Xiàn Hóu],
with a stipend of one thousand households;
Jìzhī was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Língyáng County [Língyáng Xiàn Hóu],
with a stipend of five hundred households.
The following year,
Yìxuān raised an army and rebelled,
possessing the strength of Jīng, Jiāng, Yǎn, and Yù four provinces;
his power shook the realm.
The emperor had only recently ascended the throne,
and the court and countryside were greatly fearful.
The emperor wished to offer the imperial carriage and regalia
to welcome Yìxuān,
but Dàn firmly refused,
only then were arrangements made.
The emperor conferred upon Dàn a scepter,
fifty guardsmen,
and the privilege of passing through six gates.
The pacification of the upper reaches of the river
was due to Dàn's efforts.
Originally, in suppressing the arch-villain [Shào],
he had raised an army together with the emperor,
and had achieved the victory at Bēnniú;
now, he had again rendered distinguished service.
The emperor was naturally suspicious,
and harbored considerable apprehension towards him.
Meanwhile, Dàn constructed residences and estates,
to the utmost limits of craftsmanship and artistry;
the beauty of his gardens and ponds
was unrivaled at the time.
He gathered many talented and strong individuals,
filling his residence with them;
his excellent armor and sharp weapons
were all of the highest quality.
The emperor's unease grew.
In the second year of Xiàojiàn [455 CE],

he was consequently sent out as Bearer of the Imperial Credentials, Administrator-General of All Military Affairs of Nánxú and Yǎn two provinces, Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince, and Governor of Nánxú Province [Nánxú Zhōucìshǐ],
with his Imperial Household Supervisor title remaining as before.
The emperor, because Jīngkǒu was close to the capital,
still had doubts.
In the autumn of the first year of Dàmíng [457 CE],
he was again sent out as Administrator-General of All Military Affairs of Nányǎn, Nánxú, Yǎn, Qīng, Jì, and Yōu six provinces, and Governor of Nányǎn Province [Nányǎn Zhōucìshǐ],
with the rest remaining as before.
Dàn, having seen himself suspected,
also secretly made preparations for it.
Upon arriving at Guǎnglíng,
taking advantage of the incursions by the Suǒ Lǔ (Northern Barbarians) on the border,
he repaired the city walls and moats, and gathered provisions and weapons.
With the estrangement becoming evident,
it was constantly rumored on the roads that Dàn was going to rebel.
In the third year,
Chén Wénshào (陳文紹), a commoner from Jiànkāng (建康), submitted a memorial, saying:
“My humble family was fortunate;
my late grandaunt was admitted to the six palaces of the imperial court during the Yuánjiā (元嘉) era.
Her life was short and she passed away early.
The previous dynasty bestowed upon her the title of ‘Beautiful Lady.’
My grandaunt’s two daughters were also allowed to enter and exit to inquire about her.
My father, Ráo (饒),
was taken by Sīkōng Dàn (司空誕) to serve as a clerk in his mansion.
He was sent into the mountains to map roads.
His labor was extremely arduous,
yet he dared not refuse.
He was not allowed to return home,
and all contact was cut off.
Last year, my grandaunt’s two daughters braved an appeal to return home and complain.
By Your Majesty’s sacred grace,
an imperial edict was granted, relieving Ráo (饒) of his official post.
When Dàn (誕) saw the imperial order arrive,
he was furious.
He summoned Ráo (饒) and interrogated him: ‘Do you wish to die?
You sued the court to seek release.’
Ráo (饒) immediately replied: ‘The officials wouldn't allow me to send letters home,
and contact was cut off.
If my sister initiated this appeal,
I would not know.’
Dàn (誕) then asked Ráo (饒): ‘How did you manage to sue the court?’
When Ráo (饒) was questioned,
he answered truthfully.
After he left,
Dàn’s (誕’s) chief attendant Zhuāng Qìng (莊慶) and painter Wáng Qiáng (王強) said to Ráo (饒): ‘You are ruined this year;
your sister has misled you.
The official said, “How dare these low-class people use the imperial court to pressure me!”’
Ráo (饒) then defected and fled home.
Dàn (誕) immediately dispatched Wáng Qiáng (王強) with several men to pursue him.
They burst into his home, bound and arrested him,
and took him back to Guǎnglíng (廣陵).
Upon reaching the inn at Jīngkǒu (京口),
he was thrown into a well and died,
claiming he ‘committed suicide out of fear of punishment.’
Suffering immense grief and injustice,
I braved death to return and appeal.”
Liú Chéng (劉成), a commoner from Wú Jùn (吳郡), also went to the palace gate and submitted a memorial,
accusing Dàn (誕) of rebellion,
stating:
“My son Dàolóng (道龍) formerly served Dàn (誕),
and personally witnessed his treacherous acts.
He also saw Dàn (誕) within Shítou Chéng (石頭城),
repairing imperial regalia,
and practicing royal proclamations and clearings of the way.
Dàolóng (道龍) was privately worried and fearful,
and spoke of it to his companions.
His words somewhat leaked out.
Dàn (誕) ordered his chief clerk to arrest Dàolóng (道龍) within the residence.
Dàolóng (道龍) escaped.
Dàn (誕) angrily flogged and killed the clerk,
and then captured and killed Dàolóng (道龍).”
Again, Chén Tánzhī (陳談之), a commoner from Yùzhāng (豫章), submitted a memorial to complain of injustice,
stating:
“My younger brother Yǒngzhī (詠之) was formerly selected by Dàn (誕) and recruited into his service.
He followed him through various garrisons.
When the grand imperial carriage moved south,
he was dispatched by Dàn (誕) to deliver official documents,
passing through dangerous areas,
which was reported to the emperor at the time.
When Your Sagacious Majesty ascended the throne,
your grace and favor were universally spread.
Minor officials were reformed.
My brother’s humble service
was rewarded with an appointment to an imperial court position.
Yǒngzhī (詠之) saw Dàn (誕) and his close associates, Zhuāng Qìng (莊慶) and Fù Yuánsì (傅元祀), secretly plotting rebellion,
using ugly and perverse language.
He often said: ‘The empire will soon belong to my family;
you all need not worry about not becoming rich and noble.’
He also frequently wrote down Your Majesty’s age, surname, and personal name,
and went to the shaman Zhèng Shīlián’s (鄭師憐’s) house to curse you.
When Yǒngzhī (詠之) heard these words,
and yet did not see the matter reported,
he feared that once the plot was uncovered,
he would be wrongly implicated.
He secretly informed Huáng Xuāndá (黃宣達), the Right Commandant of Jiànkāng (建康),
and also submitted a report,
hoping to exonerate himself.
Yuánsì’s (元祀’s) younger brother learned of Yǒngzhī’s (詠之’s) contact with Xuāndá (宣達).
Suspecting that his own words might have leaked,
he immediately reported everything to Dàn (誕).
Dàn (誕) was enraged.
He ordered his attendants to ply Yǒngzhī (詠之) with wine,
forcing him to get very drunk.
Then, on the pretext that Yǒngzhī (詠之) had cursed him while intoxicated,
he was murdered.
I consider this an injustice,
and a pitiable matter.”
In the fourth month of that year,
the Emperor then commanded the relevant authorities to memorialize, saying: “Your servant has heard that the divine ultimate is supremely illustrious,
the grand principles by which things are observed and rectified;
Heaven is lofty and distant,
the mysterious transformations by which things are subtly proclaimed.
Thus, it can govern the common people,
and greatly protect the
multitude.
The benevolent way pervades the eight directions,
leaving no reward for the humble and lowly;
its might extends to the heavens,
how could it omit punishment for the close and noble?
These are the unchangeable great principles,
the teachings of
all ages.
We respectfully note that at the end of the Yuánjiā (元嘉) era,
the celestial order collapsed,
humans and spirits alike grieved and were indignant,
and all living beings lost heart.
Sīkōng Jìnglǐng Wáng Dàn (司空竟陵王誕), whose duty combined that of a subject and a son,
held a position as a bulwark
of the state.
Advancing, he could not weep tears of blood and grasp a spear,
forgetting himself to sacrifice for the state;
retreating, he could not close the passes and defend against danger,
burning tallies and slaying envoys.
Instead, he prostrated himself to receive a false title,
joyfully accepting
honor and favor,
sinking into treachery and rebellion,
indulging in darkness and depravity.
Because his wife was the daughter of the former Sīkōng (司空) and your servant Zhànzhī (湛之),
he exterminated the remaining members of her clan,
sending them swiftly in a single boat,
spreading havoc over a thousand *lǐ* (里).
His actions were sorrowful
to passers-by,
his cruelty unparalleled, devoid of familial feeling;
nothing could be more extreme.
The former Prefect of Shānyīn (山陰), Fù Sēngyòu (傅僧祐),
was sincerely loyal to the imperial court,
his righteousness tied to its fortunes.
With heavily guarded gates,
he could
not refuse the messenger with a mere slip of paper;
with a thousand *lǐ* (里) of rugged terrain,
he could not protect a single man.
Instead, Dàn (誕) aided the oppressor and relied on the villain,
drawing his troops and sharpening his blades,
thereby causing him to fall into a
pit,
dying instantly,
his wife and children scattered,
his home left desolate.
Those who saw it wept,
those who heard of it sighed.
When the divine vanguard led the way,
the comet pointed
east,
the wind swept across the four peaks,
and lightning cleared the three rivers.
Dàn (誕) still hesitated between two sides,
secretly planning his advance or retreat.
Your Majesty repeatedly sent dispatches and proclamations,
earnestly exhorting and explaining,
only then did he change
his treacherous plans,
and finally submitted.
He dispatched weak forces,
permanently closing official communications.
Wherever he resided in comfort and peace,
he did not cross the border.
He defied ritual and abandoned sentiment,
disregarding public opinion.
He drew
his bow and leaped onto his horse,
devoting himself to hunting,
resulting in a chaotic scene of stampeding oxen,
and at Xīntíng (新亭), he showed no unique strategy for victory.
He borrowed the prestige of the righteous and swift troops,
begging for his life from the imperial army.
What effort
did he actually exert,
that he should be rewarded for his merits?
Now that the ominous miasma has been cleared,
and great illumination shines forth,
the seen and unseen worlds are settled,
the far and near gather like clouds.
Dàn (誕) suddenly felt the sorrow of a fleeting star,
missing the celebration of
peace and prosperity.
He lingered and looked back,
delaying for over a month.
His rebellious associates, Chén Shū'ér (陳叔兒) and others,
had countless treasures and invaluable goods.
Dàn (誕) seized and confiscated these gains,
but did not return them to
the imperial treasury,
claiming they were for the imperial army,
but actually appropriating them for his private use.
Furthermore, the imperial kitchens’ eastern purveyors,
who traditionally offered tribute,
after the chaos was pacified,
were still cut off.
Rare delicacies and various goods,
appropriated for private banquets.
On the anniversaries of a deceased's name and taboo day,
he indulged in rich delicacies.
At the very beginning of a new era,
he severed all contributions of illicit gifts.
Both loyalty and filial piety were forgotten,
reverence and affection utterly vanished.
Then, he summoned shamans and historians,
secretly consulted divination charts and cosmic diagrams,
claiming to embody auspicious signs and portents,
and that wealth and honor were within reach.
His perverse thoughts and vile words
are too numerous to recount.
Consequently, he subtly hinted at the imperial
court,
sought official positions through divination,
insulted the imperial clan,
and slandered dukes and ministers.
Unjust and unkind,
his humanity was almost exhausted.
Entrusted with the central lands (China),
he harbored treacherous wickedness,
constantly peeking
towards the imperial residence,
idly wishing for good fortune.
He established many illicit sacrifices,
openly engaged in curses and incantations,
and then, in Shítóu,
secretly crafted magical objects.
He circulated warnings, claiming imperial progresses,
imitating the emperor's movements,
all of which
already shocked and horrified observers,
and were spread throughout the court and the land.
Formerly, when the internal turmoil had just subsided,
precious and rare items were scattered.
Among them was an imperial sword, a sharp blade,
valued throughout all Xià.
It was a forbidden instrument of the imperial treasury,
treasured by successive
dynasties. Dàn secretly offered a large reward to purchase it,
and promptly stored it in his private chamber.
When the rebel Yìxuān was first pacified,
his remaining followers fled for their lives.
Dàn tolerated and indulged them without restraint,
secretly recruiting and harboring them.
Skilled
artisans and craftsmen
were all hidden in his private residence.
He also brought in Qiú Xīng, a former general of Yìxuān, to be his confidant.
When the matter was exposed,
he still clung to deceit and trickery,
stating in official documents presented to the emperor,
falsely
claiming him as an old subordinate.
Furthermore, in constructing his mansion and official residence,
he presumptuously imitated the imperial palace.
He drew stones and procured materials,
monopolizing the initiation of such projects.
He coerced scholar-gentry families,
forcing them into labor like common servants,
exhausting
the resources of wood and earth,
and fully exploiting the power of annexation.
Thus, the Princess Xuān of Kuàijī, who received favor from two emperors,
whose status and rank were highly esteemed,
and whose minister, Zhànzhī, sacrificed himself for the state,
was posthumously honored
as a military commander.
Dàn, in order to expand his mansion
because the land obstructed his planting,
encroached upon her orphaned descendants,
promptly driving them away.
This forced the ancestral spirits to move at night,
finding a new place in a remote alley.
The imperial relatives were grieved,
and passersby wept.
Moreover, there were two paths along the stream,
main thoroughfares for generations.
Dàn expanded his estate and built walls,
arbitrarily cutting off one of them.
This caused the path to be blocked
and the river and land routes to be impeded,
infuriating gods and enraging the people,
spreading poison throughout the seen and unseen worlds.
The late Prime Minister, Prince Lièwǔ of Línchuān, minister Dào Guī,
was renowned for his virtue and close kinship,
his meritorious achievements constantly recorded,
receiving extraordinary rites and special honors
from the late emperor's decree.
His successor, Prince Yìqìng, was appointed to Xīxià,
and his spirit tablet was temporarily moved.
The late emperor personally drove his imperial carriage
to bid farewell on the left side of the road,
an unparalleled grace through all ages,
an event beyond normal protocol.
Dàn also, because the temple was located in front of his residence,
firmly requested its destruction and relocation.
The imperial decree did not permit it,
yet his resentment grew to the extreme.
With a shameless face,
and a jackal-like nature,
he planned to govern Jiāngdū,
hoping to expand his military power.
The imperial benevolence was still great,
and his request was just granted.
He then said that he should reside in Dōngfǔ,
and that it should be made into a central administrative office.
His greed was insatiable,
unmatched by anyone.
Although the Sacred Compassion fully saved him,
always showing tolerance,
his cruelty did not reform,
and his treachery grew even worse.
Receiving
the order to return to his post,
his suspicion and resentment deepened.
Loyal advice and righteous admonitions
were invariably met with poison,
while sycophancy and superficiality
were met with collusion.
He also falsely claimed imperial edicts,
setting up notices to
recruit people.
When the matter was exposed, he denied it,
shifting the blame to his subordinates.
When the Recorder Xú Língshòu was punished for a regular official act,
and was about to be imprisoned,
Yǎo Hán Jìnggōng,
and the Administrator of the Central Guard, Xià Sìbó,
secretly pleaded on his behalf,
seeking a lenient restraint.
Furthermore, Wáng Sēngdá's petition before his execution,
and Gāo Shé's words just before his immediate execution,
all mentioned secret messengers traveling back and forth,
subtly reaching agreements.
Such vile rumors and disgraceful news
spread far and wide,
and who among sentient beings capable of speech
would not feel indignation and sigh?
Moreover, the complaints of Liú Chéng from Wújùn, Chén Tán
Zhī from Yùzhāng, Chén Wénshào from Jiànkāng, and others, were also received as petitions,
indicating that his treacherous intentions and suspicious disposition
accumulated over the years.
Formerly, when the virtue of Zhōu was first ascendant,
Gōng Dàn faced the calumny of slander;
when the way of Lǔ was prosperous,
Jì Zǐ carried out the execution at Kuíquán.
More recently, Huái Lì suffered a downfall earlier,
and Yìkāng followed in his footsteps later.
Troubles arose from Chái Qí,
and disaster was brought by Fàn and Xiè.
All of these cases involved prioritizing righteousness over kinship,
and emotion yielding to law.
How much more so when he has violated the celestial principles above,
and slandered
the political order below,
creating animosity in times of innocence,
and hoping for good fortune in an enlightened era?
He is not covered by the vast heavens,
nor tolerated by the thick earth.
The admonition against irreverence
is something
ministers and sons should observe;
the punishment for violating the established order
is something all states should carefully uphold.
Your ministers have deliberated and agreed
that it is fitting to hand this over to the relevant authorities,
to remove Dàn from the household register,
strip him of his title and fief,
and commit him to
the Jiànwèi's prison for trial and punishment.
All those implicated
shall be separately investigated and judged.
We humbly pray that Your Majesty will look back to the gravitas of Zōngzhōu,
and closely observe the causes of rise and fall,
relinquish personal affection and abandon private interests,
and humbly accede to the consensus of the multitude.
Then, the spiritual foundation for generations of rule
will be firmly established,
and your grand achievements and glorious deeds
will be eternal and boundless.
If Your Majesty again tolerates this
and does not reflect deeply,
then
the imperial foundation of seven hundred years will be overthrown,
and the people will be plunged into utter misery.
This is why your ministers are fearful day and night,
and dare not avoid the punishment of axe and battle-axe.
The Emperor did not permit it.
The relevant authorities again earnestly pleaded,
whereupon he was demoted to a Marquis,
and sent to his fief.
The Emperor was about to execute Dàn.
He appointed Yuán Lǎng, the Administrator of Yìxīng, as the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu,
and assigned him the Yǔlín imperial guards.
He dispatched Dài Míngbǎo, the Gentleman-in-attendance, to accompany Lǎng in attacking Dàn,
instructing Lǎng to use the pretext of taking up his post.
When Lǎng arrived at Guǎnglíng,
Dàn was not yet aware.
Míngbǎo secretly informed Jiǎng Chéng, Dàn's records clerk,
to open the gates the next morning as an inside collaborator.
Chéng reported this to Xǔ Zōngzhī, a retainer in the prefectural office.
Zōngzhī rushed in and informed Dàn.
Dàn started up in alarm,
called his attendants and several hundred men he had long kept,
seized Jiǎng Chéng,
and mustered his troops to defend himself.
At dawn the next day,
Míngbǎo and Lǎng led several hundred elite soldiers and arrived suddenly.
It was daylight, but the gates were not opened.
Dàn had already arrayed his troops and ascended the battlements.
He personally executed Jiǎng Chéng atop the gate,
burned the military registers,
pardoned the conscripted laborers and prisoners,
opened the gates and sent his trusted confidants to lead brave men to attack Míngbǎo and others,
and defeated them.
Lǎng was immediately killed,
Míngbǎo fled,
and managed to return via the Hǎilíng border.
The Emperor then dispatched Shěn Qìngzhī, the General of Chariots and Cavalry, to lead a large army to suppress Dàn.
Dàn burned down the outer city,
drove the residents and common people,
and made them all enter the city.
He separately sent letters and manifestos,
rallying support from near and far.
At that time, Liáng Kuàng, the Internal Administrator of Shānyáng, had his family in Guǎnglíng.
Dàn seized his wife and children,
and sent an envoy to summon Kuàng.
Kuàng beheaded the envoy and rejected him.
Dàn was enraged
and wiped out his family.
Dàn threw a memorial outside the city walls,
which said:
"Last year, when the chief culprit committed his evil rebellion,
Your Majesty came to suppress him.
Your servant turned his back on the villain and embraced righteousness;
this can be considered constant loyalty.
When the Chancellor stirred up trouble,
and Zāng and Lǔ conspired with him,
the court and the common people were in a state of confusion,
feeling grief and fear.
Your Majesty wished to establish the hundred officials and court rituals,
and swiftly promoted and honored me.
Your servant repeatedly insisted,
and then you granted your approval.
The state was preserved;
whose strength was this?
Your Majesty treated me with solicitude,
repeatedly bestowing honors and favors.
I was appointed General of Agile Cavalry and Governor of Yángzhōu,
and transferred within a month.
Favors and ranks were frequently added,
and I was again granted Xú and Yǎn.
The Crown Prince humbly lowered himself
to see me off from afar.
The gratitude your servant felt for that one meeting,
how could this gratitude ever be forgotten?
I hoped we would grow old together,
forever comforting each other.
How could I have known that Your Majesty would believe slanderous words,
and thus allow an obscure commoner to come and ambush me,
subjecting me to unbearable injustice and cruelty,
and immediately seeking to punish and eliminate me?
Like sparrows and rats, clinging to life,
I am forced to disobey your edict.
Now I personally lead my troops
to defend Xú and Yǎn.
What previous blessings did I have
to be born into the imperial family?
What fault do I have now
to become estranged like Hú and Yuè?
I will brave the spear-point and wield my halberd;
I will not hesitate at a myriad deaths.
The time of settlement and peace
is hoped to be near.
The General of the Right, Xuānjiǎn,
〔一０〕 and Wǔchāng,
all suffered unjust cruelty
without fault.
What transgression have I committed
to be brought to this?
Your Majesty's palace scandals,
how can they be kept secret?
As I face this paper, I am filled with sorrow,
and know not what to say."
Shìzǔ was enraged by Dàn.
All of Dàn's close associates and relatives, both inner and outer, were executed.
The dead numbered in the thousands.
Some families had already perished,
when their members, still within the city, defected.
The imperial carriage moved to encamp at Xuānwǔtáng,
and strict security was enforced inside and out.
Qìngzhī advanced to Guǎnglíng,
and Hán Dàoyuán, Dàn's banner commander, surrendered.
Zōng Míng, the Inspector of Yùzhōu, and Liú Dàolóng, the Inspector of Xúzhōu, led their troops to rendezvous.
Liǔ Guāngzōng, Dàn's staff officer for central troops, and staff officers Hé Kāngzhī and Liú Yuánmài, and banner commander Suǒ Zhìlǎng, plotted to open the north gate of the city and submit.
Before the appointed time, Shí Bèizi, a team leader under Kāngzhī, defected first.
Kāngzhī, fearing exposure of the plot,
fled with Zhìlǎng that night, cutting open the gate.
Dàn captured Guāngzōng and killed him.
Guāngzōng was
the younger cousin of Liǔ Yuánjǐng.
Kāngzhī's mother was in the city
and was also killed by Dàn.
Dàn saw the large army assembled
and wanted to abandon the city and flee north.
He left Shēn Língxì, staff officer for central troops, to guard it,
and personally led several hundred cavalry and infantry,
with his trusted confidants accompanying him.
He announced he was going out to battle,
but headed diagonally towards the Hǎilíng road.
Zhōu Fēngshēng, Dàn's general, galloped to inform Qìngzhī.
Qìngzhī dispatched Wǔ Niàn, the General of Dragon Gallop, to pursue him.
Dàn traveled over ten *lǐ*,
but his men were unwilling to leave,
and asked Dàn to return to the city.
Dàn said:
"If I return,
can you exert yourselves for me or not?"
All the men replied:
"We are willing to exert ourselves."
Yáng Chéngbó, an attendant, pulled Dàn's horse and said:
"In life or death, we must return to defend the city.
What do you intend to do with this safety?
If we return quickly, we can still get in.
Otherwise, we are defeated."
Dài Bǎozhī, a general dispatched by Qìngzhī, arrived ahead alone on horseback,
and almost wounded Dàn with his spear.
Dàn was frightened
and galloped back.
Wǔ Niàn was far from Dàn
and had not yet arrived,
so Dàn was able to approach the city.
Upon arrival, he said:
"The white-bearded man on the city wall,
is that not Lord Shěn?"
His attendants replied:
"It's Staff Officer Shēn."
Dàn then entered.
He appointed Língxì as Recorder and Staff Officer for the General of Agile Cavalry's office,
Wáng Yúzhī as Chief Clerk for the Central Army,
his heir Jǐngcuì as General of the Central Army,
Fàn Yì, the Prefectural Aide, as Chief Clerk for the Central Army.
All other civil and military officials in the various prefectural offices
were also promoted.
Earlier,

Right General of the Guards Yuán Hùzhī, General of the Left Army Cuī Dàogù, Colonel of Cavalry Páng Mèngqiú, and Crown Prince’s Palace Guard Middle Commander Yīn Xiàozǔ returned after defeating the Sǔo barbarians.
Upon reaching Guǎnglíng,
the Emperor ordered them all to follow Shěn Qìngzhī’s command.
Liú Jìzhī, Administrator of Sīzhōu,
was a former subordinate of Dàn.
He was fierce and strong,
and in the Battle of Liángshān,
he again achieved military merits,
so his fief was increased by five hundred households.
While in the province, he was greedy and cruel.
His Sīmǎ, Zhái Hóngyè, remonstrated with him severely.
Jìzhī harbored deep resentment
and killed him by poisoning his food.
When he was young,
Zōng Què and he often played *púxì* (a board game) together.
Once, Jìzhī insulted Què by hand.
Què deeply resented it.
By this time, Què was the Administrator of Yùzhōu
and Supreme Commander of Sīzhōu.
Jìzhī feared Què would bring him harm,
so he abandoned his post and took a secret route, intending to return to the imperial court.
Coincidentally, Dàn rebelled.
When Jìzhī reached Xūyí,
Zhèng Yuàn, the Grand Administrator of Xūyí, knowing that Jìzhī had always been favored by Dàn,
suspected him of being a fellow rebel.
Thus, he intercepted and killed him,
sending his head to Liú Dàolóng.
At that time, Dàn also sent a secret messenger to summon Jìzhī.
When Jìzhī’s head arrived,
Shěn Qìngzhī sent it to show Dàn.
Jìzhī had a missing tooth,
and Yuán Hùzhī also had one missing.
Dàn said to his followers,
“This is Yuán Hùzhī’s head,
not Liú Jìzhī’s.”
When Tàizōng first ascended the throne,
Zhèng Yuàn served as the Middle Army Staff Officer for Liú Xiūyòu, Prince of Shānyáng, and General of Swift Cavalry.
Yīn Yǎn, Administrator of Yùzhōu, conspired with Liú Zǐxún, Prince of Jìn’ān.
Xiūyòu sent Yuàn and his attendants Xíng Lóngfú to persuade Yǎn,
but Yǎn refused.
The Zhèng clan
was a powerful family in Shòuyáng.
Yuàn then made Yǎn a General of the Garrison.
〔一一〕Zǐxún criticized Yǎn for being slow to raise troops.
Yǎn wanted to explain himself,
so he killed Lóngfú and sent his head.
Yuàn strongly argued against it but could not prevent it.
When Shòuyáng city surrendered,
Yuàn came out with the others.
Lóngfú’s elder brother Sēngmǐn, who was outside the city at the time,
believed that Yuàn had conspired to kill Lóngfú,
and immediately killed Yuàn.
Sēngmǐn was then arrested by Liú Miǎn
and later pardoned.
Sēngmǐn soon after fought against the barbarians in Huáinán and died in battle.
These four men,
all died by wrongful killing,
and soon met their own demise.
Commentators believed that this showed the workings of divine justice.
Gōngsūn Ānqī, Dàn’s standard-bearer, led his troops and surrendered.
When Dàn first closed the city and refused the envoy,
Hè Bì, the Registrar Staff Officer, repeatedly remonstrated with him.
Dàn became angry
and drew his blade towards him,
so Bì stopped.
Someone advised Bì to surrender.
Bì said,
“The Duke has raised troops against the imperial court.
This matter cannot be followed.
Having received the Duke’s great kindness,
it is also my duty not to betray him.
I can only die to clarify my sincerity.”
Then he took poison and committed suicide.
Bì, courtesy name Zhòngfǔ,
was a native of Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
He possessed literary talent.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Staff Officer to the General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Grand Administrator of the two commanderies of Shānyáng and Hǎilíng,
〔一二〕with his Chief Clerk position remaining as before.
Wáng Yúzǐ, a standard-bearer, recruited several hundred men,
and sallied from the east gate to attack the camp of Chéng Tiānzuò, General of Dragon Might.
They cut the strings of his crossbows,
but Tiānzuò defeated them,
and they immediately fled back to the city.
Dàn again promoted Shēn Língcì to Administrator of Nánxúzhōu.
Mǎ Yuánzǐ, a military commander, climbed over the city wall to surrender,
but was pursued and killed.
Then, within the city, Dàn erected altars and made an oath.
When Dàn was about to smear blood,
Mèng Yùxiù, whom he had appointed General Who Assists the State, said,
“Your Majesty should personally smear the blood.”
All the officials shouted, “Long live!”
Initially,
Dàn sent Lü Tánjì, a Palace Attendant, with his trusted attendants
to hide his eldest son, Jǐngcuì, among the populace.
He said,
“If the matter succeeds,
his life will be preserved.
If it does not,
he can be deeply buried.”
He distributed gold and jewels,
and they were all sent out of the gate,
then they all scattered and fled.
Only Tánjì did not leave,
carrying Jǐngcuì on his back.
After more than ten days,
he was captured by Shěn Qìngzhī
and executed.
Yú Jìchōng, whom Dàn had appointed General Who Pacifies the South, also sent out a letter of surrender.
The Emperor ordered Qìngzhī to set up three signal fires at Sānglǐ.
Dàn again sent over a thousand men from the north gate to attack the camp of Gǒu Sīdá, General of Strong Crossbows.
Zōng Yuè, General of Dragon Might, defeated them.
They opened the east gate to covertly attack Liú Dàolóng’s camp,
but were again defeated by Yīn Xiàozǔ and Shěn Yōuzhī, an Attendant-in-ordinary in the Cavalcade.
Dàn again promoted Shēn Língcì to Left Chief Clerk,
Wáng Yúzǐ to Right Chief Clerk,
Fàn Yì to Left Sīmǎ and General of the Left,
and Mèng Yùxiù to Right Sīmǎ and General of the Right.
Fàn Yì’s mother, wife, and children were all inside the city.
Someone advised Yì to surrender.
Yì said,
“I am a retainer.
How can I act like Hé Kāng and survive?”
Yì, courtesy name Míngxiū,
was a native of Kǎochéng, Jìyáng.
He had an early reputation in the world.
On the night of the nineteenth day of the fifth month,
a shooting star as large as a dipper pole,
with a tail more than ten *zhàng* long,
came from the northwest and fell into the city.
This was called a “Heavenly Dog.”
The divination said:
“Where the Heavenly Dog falls,
there will be hidden corpses and flowing blood beneath.”
Dàn again sent two hundred men out of the east gate to attack Liú Dàochǎn’s camp,
and separately sent two hundred men as a diversionary force out of the north gate.
Shěn Yōuzhī at the east gate fought fiercely with short weapons,
and heavily defeated them.
Those who came out of the gate were again defeated by Gǒu Sīdá.
〔一三〕Dàn again sent several hundred men out of the east gate to attack the earthen mound of Liú Miǎn, Sīmǎ of Pacification and Loyalty.
Yōuzhī again defeated them.
Guǎnglíng city had never opened its south gate,
it was said that opening the south gate
would be unfavorable to its lord.
However, Dàn opened it.
Shào Lǐngzōng of Péngchéng was inside the city.
He secretly gathered death-defying warriors,
intending to attack Dàn.
First, he wanted to convey his sincerity to Qìngzhī,
so he persuaded Dàn to let him act as a spy,
which was granted.
Once Lǐngzōng was out,
he conveyed his sincerity.
After returning to the city,
the matter was exposed.
Dàn whipped him two hundred times,
and interrogated him but he would not confess,
so he was dismembered.
The Emperor sent two imperial edicts.
One stated: Marquis of Jìnglíng County, founder of the state,
with a fief of one thousand households,
offered as a reward for capturing Dàn.
The other stated: Baron of Jiànxīng County, founder of the state,
with three hundred households,
offered as a reward for the first to ascend the walls.
If the outer city was captured,
one signal fire would be raised.
If the inner city was captured,
two signal fires.
If Dàn was captured,
three signal fires.
The Emperor also sent Tán Jīn, Colonel of Cavalry, and Zhèng Jǐngxuán, former Middle Commander of Tiger Guards, leading the Yǔlín troops, to be subordinate to Qìngzhī.
Dàn again sent three hundred men from the south gate to attack Liú Miǎn’s earthen mound,
but they were defeated by Miǎn.
Qìngzhī was building defensive works and attacking the road.
It was during the summer rains,
and he was unable to attack the city.
The emperor frequently sent sealed letters urging and supervising him,
one after another.
When the weather cleared,
the emperor was again enraged,
and ordered the Grand Astrologer to select an auspicious day for departure,
intending to cross the Jiāng yourself.
The Grand Tutor, Prince Yìgōng of Jiāngxià, submitted a memorial remonstrating, saying:
“Dàn has always lacked talent and strategy,
and his adherents are few.
Since he resisted the royal command,
soldiers and commoners have dispersed.
Within the city, food is scarce,
and weapons are insufficient.
He relies merely on three or four hundred men from the exemption-from-service granary guards,
who hastily attached themselves to him,
their old grudges and favors still unresolved.
At first, I was shortsighted,
thinking he could be annihilated in ten days,
but he has prolonged his existence and lingered on
for over seventy days.
When Your Majesty receives the mandate,
the myriad princely states stand like mountains,
with sharp troops and elite forces,
numbering in the tens of thousands.
The great might that has shaken them
has not yet achieved success.
Although I am timid,
I still feel indignant and eager.
Your Majesty has entered to cut down the wild boars,
and gone out to suppress the long snakes,
with bloodless blades,
reviving the realm twice for seven hundred years.
Yet this paltry wretch,
has prolonged the time,
provoking imperial wrath
to the point of mobilizing the imperial carriage.
This is truly the responsibility of your unworthy and dull officials,
and all civil and military officers,
whether staying or going, cannot but feel shame and regret.
Now, in the height of summer, wearing armor,
thousands of gold are spent daily.
When heaven's might is once wielded,
who will not be extremely unfortunate?
I humbly recall that when Jìn Wén Wáng conquered Huáinán,
his army was delayed for two hundred days
before he could defeat the bandits.
Now Dàn's provisions are almost exhausted,
and many are turning against him;
Qìngzhī and others are realizing the error of their slowness and heaviness,
and gradually seeing the advantage of seizing the opportunity.
Moreover, the imperial decree has been issued frequently,
and it should certainly be extinguished any day now.
I also believe that Guǎnglíng is a short distance,
and news travels easily.
Even though there is the Jiāng river,
it is not difficult to convey instructions.
However, those who understand the principles are few,
and the ignorant are many.
If they suddenly see the cloud banners moving,
the capital will naturally be alarmed,
and the intentions of the four directions
will surely be misunderstood.
Your foolish subject has carefully reconsidered.
Now it is better not to consider the petty wretch,
but to save lives,
to appease the sentiments of those near and far.
Moreover, the Chángjiāng is dangerous and wide,
and winds and waves are unpredictable.
Even a king should not ride in peril,
much less traverse unknown waters.
In the past, when Wèi Wén crossed the Jiāng,
he consequently gained the reputation of abandoning a province.
Although now it is not contrary to heaven's will,
and it will bring auspicious blessings,
where the dragon boat proceeds,
it will certainly cross successfully.
However, one should think of danger in times of peace,
and not fail to be fearful.
My private sincerity is earnest,
and I presume to reveal my true heart.
Afterward, I am filled with trepidation and sweat,
and cannot express myself fully.”
On the second day of the seventh month,
Qìngzhī led the troops to advance and attack,
capturing its outer city,
and pressing on with the victory,
also captured the small city.
When Dàn heard that the army had entered,
he fled with Shēn Língcì to the rear garden.
Platoon leaders Shěn Yìnzhī, Yìzhēng guest Zhōu Mǎn, and Hú Sīzǔ galloped up.
Dàn held a jade-handled knife and fled with a few attendants.
Yìnzhī and others caught up with Dàn on the bridge.
Dàn raised his knife to defend himself.
Yìnzhī wounded Dàn's face,
who then fell into the water.
He was pulled out and killed,
and his head was sent to the capital.
He was twenty-seven years old at the time.
He was then buried in Guǎnglíng,
and his surname was demoted to Liú.
All his confederates were executed,
and the men in the city were killed to form a Jingguān,
numbering several thousand dead.
The women and children were given as military rewards.
Dàn’s mother, Yīn, and wife, Xú,
both committed suicide.
Yīn was posthumously conferred the title of Empress Shú of Chángníng Garden.
Jiā Liáng Kuàng's sincerity and integrity were praised,
and he was promoted to General of the Rear.
Zhōu Mǎn was enfeoffed as Marquis of Shānyáng County,
with a stipend of four hundred fifty households.
Yìnzhī was enfeoffed as Viscount of Lèiyáng,
with a stipend of three hundred fifty households.
Hú Sīzǔ was enfeoffed as Baron of Gāopíng County,
with a stipend of two hundred households.
Yáng Xuánzhī, the Administrator of Línchuān, was executed for having previously sided with Dàn.
〔一四〕
When Dàn was Administrator of Nánxú Prefecture,
one night in the capital,
a strong wind blew off roof tiles,
and the city gate's deer-beds overturned.
Dàn was greatly troubled by this.
When he moved his garrison to Guǎnglíng,
upon entering the city,
a violent wind suddenly arose, stirring up dust,
making it dark during the day.
One midnight, as he sat idly,
a red light shone in the room,
and all who saw it were astonished.
His attendants on duty,
dreamed while asleep that someone told them:
“Your hair will become spears.”
Upon waking,
their hair knots were already gone.
This happened to dozens of people,
and Dàn was greatly puzzled and fearful.
In the second year of Dàmíng,
he conscripted people to build and repair Guǎnglíng city.
As Dàn made his rounds,
someone standing by a sedan chair loudly cursed, saying:
“The great army will soon arrive!
Why do you distress the common people so much?!”
Dàn seized him and
asked about his origins.
He replied:
“My surname is Yí, my given name is Sūn.
My home is in Hǎilíng.
Last year, the Lord of Heaven consulted with Daoists and Buddhists,
intending to exterminate the people here,
but the Daoists and Buddhists earnestly remonstrated and stopped him.
A great calamity is coming.
Why do you not erect the six cautious gates?”
Dàn asked:
“What are the six cautious gates?”
He replied:
“There is an ancient saying:
Calamity does not enter the six cautious gates.”
Dàn, considering his words wild and perverse,
killed him.
Then, a musician suddenly went mad and saw ghosts,
crying out in fright:
“The outer army is besieging the city!
White cloth sails are unfurled on the city walls!”
Dàn imprisoned him for over twenty days,
then pardoned him.
On the day the city fell,
clouds and fog darkened the sky,
and a white rainbow appeared over the north gate,
extending into the city.
In the eighth year,
the Former Deposed Emperor (Qián Fèidì) ascended the throne.
Yìyáng Wáng Chǎng (義陽王昶) was appointed General Who Conquers the North (Zhēng Běi Jiāngjūn) and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Xúzhōu.
Passing through Guǎnglíng (廣陵) on his way,
he submitted a memorial, saying:
"I have heard that when the central plains of Huáinán (淮南) were covered in mist,
they sought out the surviving lineage;
when the heroes of Chǔ (楚) were exterminated,
affection for their burial mounds remained.
Both found it difficult to retain two ministers,
and righteousness allowed for two lords.
Although the law often dictates the breaking of ties,
propriety sometimes permits the expression of sentiment.
I humbly observe that the late rebel Liú Dàn (劉誕),
who raised his weapons and violated the imperial authority,
thus brought upon himself a rebellious fate,
and met his end by the axe.
His crime is already evident in the law.
However, considering that he was formerly a member of the imperial clan
and held a prominent position among the regional lords,
to have ended his life in disgrace,
with his soul and remains denied pardon,
while alive, he shared the same lineage,
but in death, he is treated like a commoner,
his burial is random and neglected,
and his tomb mound is not maintained.
Now, as years pass,
his transgressions are overshadowed by past grievances,
and stepping into this territory evokes sorrow,
and witnessing these circumstances wounds the eye.
Your Majesty, having succeeded to the enlightened fortune,
brings renewal to all.
Your great virtue is about to descend,
but compassion has not yet extended to this matter.
Luán Bù (欒布) wept in the marketplace,
his righteousness defying thunder;
Tián Shū (田叔) endured humiliation,
his resolve set against extermination.
How much more, then, for one of the imperial family,
could there be no emotion?
I humbly beg Your Majesty to consult previous precedents,
and to extend your sincere will,
to permit a slight alteration of his coffin and burial rites,
and a small indication of his grave.
Then, his decaying bones will know honor,
and he in the nether springs will recognize your grace.
As I write this, I am choked with grief;
my words fail to express themselves."
An imperial edict stated:
"The General Who Conquers the North (Zhēng Běi) has memorialized thus.
We have reviewed it with emotion.
Dàn (誕) and his wife and daughters
may all be buried with the rites of commoners,
and a guard may be stationed there."
In the fourth year of Tàizōng Tàishǐ (太宗泰始),
the burial was again changed,
and he was sacrificed with a minor offering.
Lújiāng Wáng Huī (廬江王褘), courtesy name Xiūxiù (休秀),
was the eighth son of Wéndì.
In the twenty-second year of Yuánjiā (元嘉),
at the age of ten,
he was enfeoffed as King of Dōnghǎi (Dōnghǎi Wáng),
with an estate of two thousand households.
In the twenty-sixth year,
he was appointed Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and General of the Rear Army (Hòu Jūn Jiāngjūn),
supervising the garrison at Shítou (石頭).

He was promoted to General Who Leads the Army (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn), Administrator (Tàishǒu) of the two commanderies of Southern Péngchéng (Nán Péngchéng) and Xiàpī (下邳), and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì),
retaining supervision of the garrison as before.
He was sent out as Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Kuàijī (會稽),
his generalship remaining as before.
In the twenty-ninth year,

he was promoted to Bearer of credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe), Area Commander (Dūdū) of the military affairs of Guǎngzhōu (廣州) and Jiāozhōu (交州), and the three commanderies of Shǐxīng (始興), Línhè (臨賀), and Shǐ'ān (始安) in Jīngzhōu (荊州), General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Jiāngjūn), Colonel (Zhōnglángjiāng) Pacifying the Yue (Píng Yuè), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Guǎngzhōu.
〔一五〕When the chief culprit usurped the throne,
he was promoted to General Pacifying the South (Ānnán Jiāngjūn),
but he did not proceed to his post.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was again made Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Kuàijī (會稽),
with the added title of General Who Soothes the Army (Fǔ Jūn Jiāngjūn).
The following year,
he was summoned to be Director of the Imperial Library (Bìshū Jiān),
with the added title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì).
Soon after, he was sent out as General Who Soothes the Army (Fǔ Jūn Jiāngjūn) and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Jiāngzhōu (江州),
promoted to General Pacifying the South (Píngnán Jiāngjūn),
and appointed officials.
In the second year of Dàmíng (大明),
he was summoned to be Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì) and Central Secretariat Director (Zhōngshū Lìng),
supervising the General of Elite Cavalry (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn),
granted a set of military music instruments (gǔchuī),
his position as Attendant-in-Ordinary (Chángshì) remaining as before.
He was again sent out as Governor (Cìshǐ) of Nányùzhōu (南豫州),
his positions as Attendant-in-Ordinary (Chángshì) and General (Jiāngjūn) remaining as before.
With his original title, he was granted the honorific of Kai Fu Yi Tong San Si (開府儀同三司),
and supervised the Libationer of the Imperial Academy (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ),
his position as Attendant-in-Ordinary (Chángshì) remaining as before.
In the fifth year,
an imperial edict stated:
"In ancient times, Hàn (韓) and Wèi (衞), though of different surnames,
were clear precedents in the Zhōu (周) dynasty;
the three ranks of enfeoffment, though distinct,
were excellent institutions in the past Jìn (晉) dynasty.
Our imperial house, in establishing its institutions,
has fully upheld these principles.
We, in response to the mandate of Heaven,
have established our rule over the four seas.
We reflect on how to emulate previous models
and establish close relatives,
to eternally set a unified standard
and record it in the imperial statutes.
The fiefs of all our younger brothers
may each be increased by a thousand households."
In the seventh year,
he was promoted to Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
his positions as Attendant-in-Ordinary (Chángshì) and Libationer (Jìjiǔ) remaining as before.
When the Former Deposed Emperor (Qián Fèidì) ascended the throne,
he was given the added title of Central Secretariat Supervisor (Zhōngshū Jiān).
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
with the added titles of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Central Secretariat Supervisor (Zhōngshū Jiān),
and granted twenty guards with swords of honor (bānjiàn).
He was re-enfeoffed as King of Lújiāng (Lújiāng Wáng).
Among the sons of Tàizǔ,
Huī (褘) was especially mediocre and inferior;
his brothers scorned him.
When Nánpíng Wáng Shuò (南平王鑠) died young,
Shuò’s (鑠) son Jìngyuān (敬淵) was getting married.
Huī (褘) went to observe the wedding
and asked Shìzǔ to lend entertainers.
Shìzǔ replied:
"Wedding ceremonies do not use music,
and moreover, Jìngyuān (敬淵) and others are orphaned and desolate,
so it is even more inappropriate."
At this time, Tàizōng issued an edict to Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén (建安王休仁), saying:
"Since that person (Huī) cannot compare to the Duke of the Western Quarter,
you shall be the eldest of the kings."
At that time, Huī (褘) resided in Xīzhōu (西州),
hence he was called the Duke of the Western Quarter.
In the fifth year of Tàishǐ (泰始),
Liǔ Xīnwèi (柳欣慰) of Hédōng (河東) conspired to rebel,
intending to enthrone Huī (褘).
Huī (褘) corresponded with him in agreement.

Xīnwèi (欣慰) secretly allied with Dù Yǒuwén (杜幼文), the Advisory Officer to the General Who Conquers the North (Zhēng Běi Zīyì Cānjūn), Sòng Zǔzhēn (宋祖珍), the Army Advisor to the Left (Zuǒ Jūn Cānjūn), and Wáng Lóngbó (王隆伯), the former Magistrate of Ruò (Ruò Lìng).
Huī (褘) ordered his attendant Xú Hǔ'ér (徐虎兒) to send a golden box as a gift to Yǒuwén (幼文),
and two bronze bowls as gifts to Zǔzhēn (祖珍) and Lóngbó (隆伯).
Yǒuwén (幼文) reported the matter in full detail.
The emperor then issued an edict, saying: "In the past, when the Zhōu (周) house flourished,
the two uncles spread rumors;
when the Hàn (漢) dynasty was rising,
the seven vassal states rebelled in confusion.
These events are clearly demonstrated in past generations,
and difficulties have arisen since ancient times.
Although sages
ruled,
the realm was relieved of trouble.
The Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi), King of Lújiāng (Lújiāng Wáng), relying on his imperial lineage,
was early elevated to a favored position.
As a youth, he lacked virtue;
as an adult, he failed to cultivate a good reputation.
He was indifferent to familial affection,
and
closely associated with commoners,
befriended petty individuals,
and alienated refined scholars.
Since We quelled chaos and stabilized the realm,
receiving the mandate in accordance with Heaven,
We have truly valued harmony and affection,
and have been able to practice brotherly love.
Therefore, We have honored him with a distinguished
title,
and elevated him to a high position.
Yet, this Duke has always harbored discontent,
which is evident in his actions.
If the Duke's virtue were profound and his prestige great,
he would naturally deserve the great succession.
When We first pacified the rebellion,
how
would We dare to hold onto the imperial regalia?
Naturally, the imperial credentials and seal would have been offered,
and Heaven's favor would have returned to him.
Moreover, although We occupy the supreme position,
We dare not rely on Our own judgment;
on matters concerning the imperial clan,
We always consult the Duke.
We did not expect that his ambition would be insatiable,
and that he would foolishly harbor resentment,
accumulating evil in his heart,
and thus plot against the state.
Previously, when calamity struck the four directions,
and troops encroached upon the capital region,
officials and gentry were alarmed,
and close relatives and worthy men were equally indignant.
Only the Duke rejoiced in the disaster,
deeply applauding the difficult times;
by day, he
hunting and carousing,
and at night indulging in wine and music.
He inclined his ear to listen to the shadows,
and stood on tiptoe to prevent the thieves from asking questions.
Sītú Xiūrén and others, all his younger brothers,
whose affairs concerned both family and state,
pushed
forward into danger,
each attacking a different region.
Enduring frost and treading thorns,
their arduous toil was excessive.
Moreover, with their bodies exposed to arrows and stones,
their fortunes were unpredictable.
Even ordinary people
still have a sense of
duty.
Yet you, Gong, never once sent a letter
or a half-sheet of writing,
intending to abandon your five younger brothers
to feed the enemy.
You considered yourself without merit or achievement,
and ethically not participating
in the strategy,
expecting that once the rebellious chaos was resolved,
you would then plan for the chancellorship.
However, when the imperial might was unleashed,
and all the villains were swept away,
the nine provinces rejoiced,
and all nations were filled with joy.
Yet you, Gong, were
even more disheartened and dejected,
drawing your curtains and obscuring your tracks.
You constantly observed the heavens and watched the constellations,
harboring heterodox beliefs,
uttering curses and prayers,
and diligently serving evil shamans.
You frequently went with dishevelled hair and bare feet,
kowtowing to the Northern
Pole,
then drawing images of Us
and inscribing Our name,
either piercing them with arrows and blades,
or boiling them in cauldrons.
When you, Gong, were in Jiāngzhōu,
you acquired a Hàn woman
who claimed to know good
and ill fortune,
and could perform curses.
You made lavish offerings,
bowing down morning and evening,
dressed in neat attire,
serving her with reverence as a deity.
You ordered her to curse Xiàowǔ,
and also Chóngxiàn,
praying for
the imperial house to be weak and in danger,
so that you might control the heavens and claim yourself.
The shaman claimed it was the will of the gods,
and your wishes would surely be granted.
Later, when the matter was discovered,
you shifted the blame to your birth mother,
and by a stroke of luck,
barely escaped punishment.
Recently, there was also the Daoist Zhāng Bǎo,
who gained your trust.
When the matter was exposed,
he was subjected to the law.
You, Gong, felt no shame or fear,
and even tried to manage it,
sending two of your left
and right attendants
to oversee his burial.
You overtly pursued your evil desires,
disregarding official authority.
You also colluded with the eunuch Chén Dàomíng, engaging in illicit dealings,
exchanging messages,
and scattering gold and
treasures
as pledges of faith.
You also ordered your personal clerk Xú Hǔ'ér to recruit border generals
and conspire with imperial guards,
planning to harm the grand councilors
and invade the imperial palace.
You, Gong, are inherently unkind,
and your talents are not for governance.
In the past, you undeservedly held the post of Jiāngzhōu,
and were recalled without distinction.
Previously, you presided over Kuàijī,
and were demoted for your transgressions.
You, Gong, are ignorant of ancient wisdom,
severe but unreasonable.
Your words do not express warmth or coldness,
and your kindness does not reach your private chambers.
You are despised by both court and commoners,
and scorned by all officials.
How could you be fit for the position of chancellor?
How could you be entrusted with the duty
of governing the people?
This is not a recent development,
but has always been so.
From the era of Dàmíng
until Yǒngguāng,
you, Gong, always remained at court,
never serving in an external post.
Why is it that now
you harbor resentment?
You, Gong, became an adult early,
but your emotions
lacked sorrow or compassion.
When attending the funeral of Chángníng
and participating in ancestral sacrifices,
your face showed no sign of grief,
and no tears fell from your cheeks.
Among your brothers, younger and older,
you had no affection.
In the past, when Xiàowǔ prepared
a banquet with wine,
your sincerity was lacking.
At that time, Yìyáng, who was already lightly regarded,
suffered your calumny and
was further suspected.
We were then in distress,
and had no time to defend Ourselves.
Thanks to Chóngxiàn Tàihòu, who explained things in every way,
We were somewhat exonerated
and escaped misfortune.
The mad ruler of Jǐnghé,
whose wickedness overflowed,
first executed the prime ministers,
and his wolfish ambition
began to spread.
He summoned Us and Our brothers to Jiànzhāng Palace,
forced Us to drink until drunk.
You, Gong, taking advantage of the wine,
uttered bitter words,
saying that We and Xiūrén,
being close to the Grand Tutor,
would always
enjoy peace and leisure,
and receive generous gifts.
At that moment, We were terrified,
Our insides collapsing.
During his speech,
We barely managed to stop it.
Later, at the residence of Princess Zhǎng of Xúnyáng,
when brothers gathered,
you suddenly became angry in the middle of the feast,
pointing a finger with a fierce expression,
because Our actions and whereabouts
were always different from yours.
If you had achieved your wish,
you would have unleashed your resentment.
Your intention, Gong,
was long ago to destroy Us.
But the way of Heaven loves goodness,
and We attained the throne,
not allowing evil and rebellion to flourish,
thus frustrating your malicious heart.
Since the accumulated waste of Dàmíng,
the state was exhausted and the people impoverished.
Added to the extravagance and tyranny of Jǐnghé,
the treasuries were completely empty.
We have only just taken the throne,
and are concerned with righteousness and the welfare of all.
Yet We still face
the rise of bandits,
daily consuming ten thousand jin of gold,
while officials and common people
sacrifice their wealth and offer it.
You, Gong, having received accumulated court salaries,
have ample wealth and possessions.
At the beginning of Our reign,
you, Gong, requested the late
Grand Tutor to transfer his remaining money,
receiving several million,
but did not use it to support your family,
nor to assist the state.
Instead, you lavishly distributed it to flatterers,
and generously benefited your servants.
If one examines your heart and conduct,
similar instances
abound.
Petty men conspired,
thus giving rise to different schemes,
and these whispered meanings
increasingly filled the mouths of the people.
If you, Gong, were in a pivotal position,
with full control over the eight powers,
nurturing virtue
among the people,
and your achievements surpassing all others,
then your ambition for power
would be understandable.
But you, Gong, are as untalented as a useless tree,
only surviving by compromise.
Being high-ranking but having no popular support,
you merely hold an empty
quiet,
yet to rise and act results in misfortune and calamity,
bringing profound discord upon oneself.
This is due to my sincerity being without basis,
and so it has come to this.
Constantly reflecting on the many difficulties,
my regret and indignation are truly deep.
Of all people's actions,
each has its original intention.
I have long cherished broad love and benevolence,
for a long time now.
I am still able to tolerate enmity and pardon faults,
manifesting this in every matter.
How can it be that toward
Gōng,
I cannot exercise mutual forbearance?
However, misfortune germinates easily and spreads,
so evil should be eliminated swiftly.
The burden is heavy,
how can I sit idly by and watch?
Moreover, rampant weeds are difficult to remove,
and a spreading fire must be put out.
Those who cunningly incite
should be promptly executed.
I have already ordered the judicial authorities
to strictly enforce the penal code.
Gōng holds a position as a senior relative,
and both affection and propriety are fully extended to him.
Applying the usual statutes,
I do indeed have
compassion.
It is appropriate to slightly relax the national law,
in order to console the unrighteous.
Now, the three commanderies of Huáinán, Xuānchéng, and Lìyáng are restored to establish Nányùzhōu.
Gōng is demoted to Chēqí Jiāngjūn,
Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ,
and his stipend of households is reduced by one thousand.
His Sòng Shìzhōng and Wáng titles remain as before.
He is to go out and guard Xuānchéng.
The Emperor sent his trusted confidant Yáng Yùncháng to lead troops in defense.
〔一六〕His associates Liǔ Xīnwèi, Xú Hǔ'ér, Chén Dàomíng, Níng Jìngzhī, Lǘqiū Miǎozhī, Fán Píngzǔ, and Méng Jìngzǔ were all executed.
In the sixth month of the following year,
〔一七〕the Emperor again ordered the authorities to memorialize:
"Huī is resentful and has uttered grievances.
We request that he be dismissed from office,
his noble rank and territory be revoked,
and he be delivered to Wǎnlíng County Prison
for thorough investigation according to law."
This was not permitted.
Instead, the Emperor sent the Dàhónglú, holding the imperial credential,
with the Zōngzhèng as his deputy, to convey the imperial edict to rebuke Huī,
forcing him to commit suicide.
He was thirty-five years old at the time,
and was immediately buried in Xuānchéng.
His son, Chōngmíng,
was Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Nánpéngchéng and Dōngguǎn Commanderies.
He was deposed and exiled to Shèxiàn, Xīn'ān.
Later, when the deposed emperor ascended the throne,
he was permitted to return to the capital.
He died in Shùndì's Shēngmíng second year,
at the age of twenty-eight,
without a son.
Wǔchāng Wáng Hún, courtesy name Xiūyuān,
was Wéndì's tenth son.
In Yuánjiā twenty-fourth year,
at the age of nine,
he was enfeoffed as Rǔyīn Wáng,
with a stipend of two thousand households.
He served as Hòujūn Jiāngjūn,
and was given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
When the barbarian bandits from the north raided,
and Rǔyīn Commandery was captured,
Hún was moved and enfeoffed as Wǔchāng Wáng.
He was cruel and unruly from a young age.
Once, when he went out to Shítóu,
he resented his attendants
and drew his self-defense knife to hack at them.
〔一八〕When the arch-villain usurped the throne,
Hún was appointed Zhōngshū Lìng.
On the evening of the imperial burial,
he went naked and bareheaded
to the Sànqí Shěng to play.
He then drew his bow and shot the Tōngzhí Láng Zhōu Láng,
hitting his pillow,
taking it as a source of amusement.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
Hún was appointed Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Nánpéngchéng and Dōnghǎi Commanderies,
and was sent out to guard Jīngkǒu.
In Xiàojiàn first year,
he was promoted to Shǐ Chíjié, Jiān Yōngliáng Nánběiqín Sìzhōu Jīngzhōu Zhī Jìnglíng Suí Èrjùn Zhūjūnmìshì, Níngmán Xiàowèi, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his jiāngjūn title remaining as before.
Upon arrival at his post, Hún
drafted official documents with his attendants,
proclaiming himself Chǔ Wáng,
and designated the year as Yǒngguāng first year.
〔一九〕He set up a full complement of officials,
treating it as a joke.
The Chángshǐ Wáng Yìzhī obtained his handwriting
and sealed and presented it to Shìzǔ.
The Emperor ordered the authorities to memorialize for his dismissal as a commoner,
and the Tàicháng
was to remove his name from the imperial clan registry.
He was exiled and delivered to Shǐ'ān Commandery.
