The Emperor sent Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng Dài Míngbǎo to interrogate Hún, saying:
"You and I are as close as siblings by blood,
and in righteousness, we are lord and subject.
I sent you to govern the western border regions,
to be as solid as a rock.
How could you suddenly plot against me?
The official documents and your dispositions
are clear and undeniable.
To be disloyal and unrighteous,
to this extent,
is truly regrettable. Not only does the Way of Heaven assist the obedient,
making rebellious ambitions difficult to fulfill,
but even if your vicious scheme were to succeed,
who in the world would tolerate you?
Past events are not distant,
and serve as a sufficient warning.
Furthermore, the repeated difficulties and misfortunes of recent years
did not arise from outsiders.
We should only strive together
to solidify the 'seven hundreds' (the imperial house).
That you suddenly contrived this again,
is truly lamentable.
Although the state has its laws,
how can I bear to enforce the extreme penalty?
Take good care of yourself,
to preserve a long life like Píne and Qiáo. "
He was forced to commit suicide
and was buried in Xiāngyáng immediately,
at the age of seventeen.
In Dàmíng fourth year,
permission was granted for his reburial next to the tomb of his mother, Tài Fēi Jiāng.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Wǔchāng Xiànhóu.
Wáng Yìzhī, courtesy name Jìbì,
was from Línyí, Lángyá.
He was the grandson of the Jìn Huángmén Shìláng Huīzhī.
His official positions reached Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
Huìjī Tàishǒu,
and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ.
His posthumous title was Sùzǐ.
Hǎilíng Wáng Xiūmào
was Wéndì's fourteenth son.
In the second year of Xiàojiàn,
at the age of eleven,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Hǎilíng,
with a food-tax income of two thousand households.
In the second year of Dàmíng,

he was appointed as Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of the four prefectures of Yōng, Liáng, Northern Qín, and Southern Qín, and Jìnglíng and Suí Commanderies of Yǐng Prefecture, General of the Northern Army, Protector of the Mán, and Governor of Yōng Prefecture.
He was promoted to General of the Left,
and his food-tax income was increased by one thousand households.
At that time, Sīmǎ Yǔ Shēnzhī was acting as the Prefectural Administrator.
Xiūmào was impatient and quick-tempered,
wishing to act on his own authority.
Shēnzhī and the chief officers frequently restrained him,
〔二一〕and he often harbored resentment.
His close associate, Zhāng Bó chāo,
committed many transgressions.
The chief officers often reprimanded Bó chāo,
who, fearing punishment,
said to Xiūmào:
“The chief officers are secretly memorializing your transgressions,
intending to report them to the emperor.
If this happens, I fear it will not end well.”
Xiūmào asked:
“What is the plan?”
Bó chāo replied:
“We must kill the acting administrator and the chief officers,
and raise an army for self-preservation.
From here to the capital is thousands of *lǐ*.
Even if the great undertaking does not succeed,
we will not fail to enter the barbarian territory and become a king.”
Xiūmào agreed.

At night, he took Bó chāo and his close associates Huáng Língqí, Cài Jiéshì, Téng Mùzhī, Wáng Bǎolóng, Lái Chéngdào, Péng Shú'ér, Wèi Gōngzǐ, Chén Bó'ér, Zhāng Sìnú, Yáng Xìng, Liú Bǎo, Yú Shuāng, and others,
led the Imperial Guard,
and killed Diǎnqiān Yáng Qìng within the city.
They exited Jīnchéng,
and killed Sīmǎ Yǔ Shēnzhī and Diǎnqiān Dài Shuāng.
They gathered the conscripted troops,
set up battle standards, and dispatched urgent proclamations.
He ordered his subordinate officials to report him as Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, Minister over the Masses with the Same Authority,
and to bestow the yellow *yuè* axe.
His imperial tutor, Dr. Xún Shēn, remonstrated with him
and was killed.
Bó chāo took full control of military and government affairs,
and committed murder.
Xiūmào’s close associate Cáo Wànqí sprang forward and hacked Xiūmào.
Though wounded, he fled
and was killed.
Xiūmào left the city to set up camp.
Adviser to the Army Shěn Chàngzhī and others led their forces to close the gates and resist him.
Xiūmào rushed back,
but could not enter.
Yìchéng Administrator Xuē Jìkǎo exerted himself to attack the city for Xiūmào,
causing many casualties.
Chàngzhī could not hold his position,
and so Xiūmào gained entry to the city.
He executed Chàngzhī and dozens of co-conspirators.
On that day,
Army Adviser Yǐn Xuánqìng raised a righteous army,
attacked Xiūmào,
and captured him alive.
He was led out of the central gate and beheaded,
at the age of seventeen.
His mother and wife both committed suicide,
and all his confederates were put to death.
The city was in disarray,
with no one to take charge.
At that time, Liú Xiùzhī's younger brother Gōngzhī, who was Minister of Personnel of the Right, was Xiūmào's Middle Army Adviser.
The populace together nominated him to administer the affairs of the prefecture.
Jìkǎo used his troops to coerce Gōngzhī
into drafting a memorial stating that he had initiated a righteous act.
He then personally rode an express post horse back to the capital.
The emperor appointed him as Northern Army Adviser to Yǒngjiā Prince Zǐrén, Administrator of Hénán,
enfeoffed him as Marquis of Guànjūn County,
with a food-tax income of four hundred households.
Soon after, the matter was exposed,
and he was executed.
Gōngzhī was imprisoned in the Imperial Workshop.
Xuánqìng was appointed as Colonel of Archers.
The relevant authorities memorialized to strike Xiūmào from the imperial lineage
and to change his surname to Liú.
The emperor did not permit it.
He was then buried in Xiāngyáng.
Yǔ Shēnzhī, courtesy name Yànjìng,
was a native of Xīnyě.
He was known to the previous court for his administrative skills.
In the twenty-ninth year of Yuánjiā,
he was appointed from Protector of the State Chief Clerk to Grand Administrator of Chángshā.
When Prince Yìxuān of Nánjùn was governor of Jīng and Xiāng Prefectures,
he appointed Shēnzhī as General Pacifying the North
and Area Commander of the seven commanderies of Xiāng Prefecture.
The following year,
Yìxuān rebelled.
Shēnzhī held Bālíng to resist him.
He was then transferred to be Xiūmào's Sīmǎ.
On the morning of his murder,
his sons and grandsons also died.
Shēnzhī was posthumously granted General of Guànjūn and Governor of Yōng Prefecture.
Xún Shēn was granted Supernumerary Palace Attendant,
and Cáo Wànqí was granted Administrator of Shǐpíng.
Prince Xiūfàn of Guìyáng
was the eighteenth son of Emperor Wén.
In the third year of Xiàojiàn,
at the age of nine,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Shùnyáng,
with a food-tax income of two thousand households.
In the first year of Dàmíng,
he was re-enfeoffed as Prince of Guìyáng.
He was appointed as General of Guànjūn and Grand Administrator of Southern Péngchéng and Xiàpí.
In the third year,
he was sent out as Governor of Jiāng Prefecture.
Soon after, he was granted General Quelling the Enemy
and one thousand households.
He entered the court as Supervisor of the Imperial Secretariat,
and concurrently held the post of General of the Vanguard.
In the seventh year,
he was promoted to General of the Left Guard,
and additionally made Attendant Official.
In the first year of Yǒngguāng of the Former Deposed Emperor,
he was transferred to Central Protector of the Army,
and concurrently held the post of Grand Commandant of the Chóngxiàn Guard.
When Emperor Tàizōng quelled the rebellion,

he appointed him as Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of the four prefectures of Southern Xú, Xú, Southern Yǎn, and Yǎn, General Pacifying the North, and Governor of Southern Xú Prefecture,
and granted him a set of drum and wind instruments.
At that time, Xuē Āndōu held Péngchéng and rebelled.
He sent his nephew Suǒ'ér to invade the south.
Xiūfàn advanced to occupy Guǎnglíng,
and supervised all military affairs of the northern expedition.
He was additionally made Governor of Southern Yǎn Prefecture,
promoted to Grand General Quelling the North,
and additionally made Palace Attendant.
He returned to Jīngkǒu,
relieved of his post in Yǎn Prefecture,
his food-tax income was increased by two thousand households,
receiving five hundred households.
In the fifth year of Tàishǐ,
he was summoned to be Supervisor of the Central Secretariat, General of the Central Army, and Governor of Yáng Prefecture,
with his position as Palace Attendant remaining unchanged.
The following year,

he was sent out as Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of the five prefectures of Jiāng, Yǐng, Sī, Guǎng, and Jiāo, and the four commanderies of Xīyáng, Xīncài, Jìnxī of Yù Prefecture, and Shǐxīng of Xiāng Prefecture, Grand General Quelling the South, and Governor of Jiāng Prefecture.
Soon after, he was additionally granted Minister over the Masses with the Same Authority.
Before he could be formally invested,
he was reassigned as Area Commander of the six prefectures of Southern Xú, Xú, Southern Yǎn, Yǎn, Qīng, and Jì, Grand General of Agile Cavalry, and Governor of Southern Xú Prefecture,
with his imperial credentials, Palace Attendant title, and ministerial authority remaining unchanged.
Before he could be formally invested,
as Grand General of Agile Cavalry, he was returned to Jiāng Prefecture,
further appointed Area Commander of Yuè Prefecture,
and granted one carriage with three-directional views.
Emperor Tàizōng's dying edict
promoted him to Minister of Works,
changed his Palace Attendant title to Attendant-in-ordinary,
and additionally granted him thirty imperial guards.
Xiūfàn was naturally ordinary and slow of speech,
with little insight.
He was not highly regarded by his elder brothers.
Emperor Tàizōng often pointed to the people around him and said to Wáng Jǐngwén:
“Xiūfàn’s talent is no better than theirs,
but because he is my brother,
he has been rich and noble since birth.
The Buddhists' wish to be born into a royal family
is truly for this reason.”
By Emperor Tàizōng's later years,
Prince Xiūyòu of Jìnpíng brought disaster upon himself due to his cruelty,
Prince Xiūrén of Jiàn'ān was not tolerated due to his overbearing power,
and Prince Xiūruò of Bālíng, who had always been popular,
was also harmed for this reason.
Only Xiūfàn was cautious and untalented,
not attracting public favor,
〔二二〕thus he was able to preserve himself.
However, he always harbored anxiety and fear,
worrying that disaster would strike him.
When Emperor Tàizōng passed away,
the emperor was young and the times were difficult.
The imperial relatives held power,
and the close attendants governed.
Xiūfàn believed that among the imperial clan, no one surpassed him,
and he ought to hold a prime ministerial position.
Since this did not happen,
his resentment and indignation grew.
He recruited brave warriors
and repaired weapons.
Travelers passing through Xúnyáng,
all without exception, humbled themselves and showed respect,
and he lavishly inquired about their well-being and gave them gifts.
If they stayed, he would personally receive them
and generously provide for them.
Thus, people from far and near responded,
and those who came felt at home.
〔二三〕The imperial court knew he had other intentions
and secretly took defensive measures.
Although he had not yet shown his true colors,
the seeds of rebellion were already sown.
His mother, Grand Consort Xún, died.
He buried her on Mount Lú,
to show his determination not to return.
He was relieved of his post as Attendant-in-ordinary.
At that time, Xiàkǒu lacked a defender,
and the court deliberated that as it was upstream from Xúnyáng,
a trusted confidant should be stationed there
to strengthen its military power.
In the first year of Yuánhuī (473 CE),
the fifth imperial younger brother, Xiè, Prince of Jìnxī, was appointed Governor of Yǐngzhōu.
Wáng Huàn, the Administrator, was to act on behalf of the governor and the province,
provided with resources,
and sent to guard Xiàkǒu.
Fearing that Xiūfàn might detain him,
he departed from Tàizǐ Fú,
without passing through Xúnyáng.
Xiūfàn was greatly enraged,
and intended to raise an army to attack the court.
He secretly plotted with his secretary, Xǔ Gōngyú, a native of Xīncài.
[二四] He submitted a memorial requesting to repair city walls
and restore the battlements,
and dismantled many planks
for future use.
In that year,
he was promoted to Grand Commandant.
In the fifth month of the following year,
he raised an army and rebelled.
He seized boats from the common people,
ordered the troops to request and receive them according to their needs,
provided them with the dismantled planks,
and together they worked on equipping them.
In two or three days,
everything was neatly arranged and prepared.
He led a force of twenty thousand men,
with several hundred iron cavalry,
departing from Xúnyáng,
traveling day and night.
He wrote to Yuán Càn, Chǔ Yuān, and Liú Bǐng, saying: “For a government to be well-governed and to employ the virtuous,
it is appropriate for both close and distant relations to assist each other.
If the warp and weft are in order,
then even knot-tying can be achieved.
If the rules and regulations are lost,
then peril and ruin can be expected.
The Hàn dynasty,
inheriting the aftermath of the Warring States,
suffered from the decline and demise of the Zhōu royal house.
It established a solid foundation for its lineage,
yet still incurred the disaster of the Seven Kingdoms.
The Wèi dynasty reformed the Hàn system,
learning from previous mistakes,
and consequently made it so that the various princes
were cut off from the rites of court visits.
Thus, the roots became sparse and the leaves withered,
and the government shifted to an alien clan.
Today, the imperial clan is in decline,
a situation unprecedented in history,
even the era of Tàiníng
is sufficient as a comparison.
I, your humble servant, am but a branch of the imperial clan,
involved in its rise and fall.
Though I wish to remain silent,
how can I do so?
Emperor Gāozǔ Wǔ, like the three luminaries, ascended to wisdom,
sweeping away chaos from the four quarters.
Emperor Tàizǔ Wén, with his sagacity and brilliance, surpassed antiquity,
drawing upon Heaven to succeed to the throne,
wielding the axe to subdue the west,
and his
carriage bells jingled in Dōngjīng.
He sought out the virtuous and selected the capable,
embraced the extraordinary and rewarded the exceptional.
Emperor Xiàowǔ, exceptionally intelligent and naturally endowed,
struck with lightning speed at the opportune moment,
calming disturbances across the waves,
and brought about a grand restoration.
However, his heir
was unworthy,
thus bequeathing disaster and difficulty.
At that time, the Prince of Jiàn'ān, seeing the frequent misfortunes of the imperial house,
suggested that an elder sovereign should be established.
Emperor Míng was broad-minded, profound, and serene,
his benevolence profound and far-reaching.
His enthronement as ruler
truly accorded with Heaven and man.
Yet the Grand Commandant, due to his seniority yet lower position,
showed resentment in his demeanor.
Liǔ Xīnwèi and others plotted illicitly,
their actions becoming flagrantly evident.
The General of Agile Cavalry, having offended the emperor and lost favor,
his responses being disobedient,
suffered severe oppression in his fief,
stirring resentment among both men and spirits.
The late emperor was clear in his decrees;
how could he bend the law for relatives?
The discord of the two princes
was truly of their own making.
However, the Grand Minister, Prince of Bālíng, labored humbly for the state,
bravely facing difficulties in the midst of turmoil.
He had extraordinary achievements,
serving his time as if it were Heaven,
and treating his elder brother as
a father.
He was not only a good friend,
but truly a pillar of the state.
His loyalty was like that of Táng Shú,
yet he suffered the crimes of Guǎn and Cài.
His relatives grieved and were indignant,
and passersby sighed in lamentation.
The prince, by virtue of his noble
and pure lineage,
and his virtue which satisfied popular expectations,
had not committed any fault,
yet was slain by slander and malice.
The late emperor was devoted to fraternal affection,
and attentive to his relatives.
After the past troubles subsided,
he personally received edicts
and instructions.
In rites, they were sovereign and minister;
in joy, they were brothers.
He was promoted and granted rewards,
without a year passing without action.
His solicitous comfort was constant,
as if it were insufficient.
How could he suddenly be walled off,
leading
to such calamity?
There was indeed a reason for this.
The late emperor's illness lingered for a year,
his body fatigued, his appetite poor.
Though his divine intellect remained unimpaired,
he was prone to errors of virtue.
The responsibility for correcting omissions and picking up oversights
lay
with his attendants.
At that time, only Yùn Cháng and Dào Lóng had access to his bedchamber.
The multitude of petty individuals, without proper conduct,
took advantage of his illness to cause disaster.
Seeing the emperor unwell,
and knowing there would be no recovery,
they feared that on the day of his passing,
the elder prince would become regent,
thereby seizing their favor and power,
preventing them from acting as they pleased.
Therefore, internally they feigned imperial decrees,
and externally they invoked court deliberations.
With flattery and deceitful appearances,
in
myriad forms and a thousand manifestations,
they promoted treacherous villains
and slaughtered wise sages.
Externally they distorted the laws of Heaven,
and internally they slandered men and spirits.
Thus, the celestial phenomena deviated from their norm,
and the astronomical observations lost their regularity.
In the past, Wèi Kē chose to let his concubine live,
and the Spring and Autumn Annals praised him for it.
Duke Mù of Qín sacrificed good men,
and the Odes clearly condemned him.
The integrity of ministers
is always recorded, whether good or bad;
even failing to remonstrate is considered a crime.
They sowed discord like buzzing flies,
instigating disaster and murder.
Titles were valued according to wealth,
and talent was scorned due to poverty.
The late emperor's old associates,
though innocent, were dismissed and demoted,
while their hometown relatives were recommended
and spread throughout the court and provinces.
Those who flattered and fawned
soared to glory at the palace steps;
those who stood quietly with integrity and purity
found grass growing at their brushwood gates.
If a matter concerned them,
even if it wasn't necessary, it might be carried out;
but if not consulted,
even if it was
correct, it would be suppressed.
Throughout the realm, near and far,
who does not know this?
They did not yet understand how to handle affairs,
nor did they wield the axe of execution,
thus leading to the late emperor having the reputation of killing his younger brother,
leaving a shameful name for his sovereign
and father.
Judged by ancient righteousness,
how could this be considered loyalty?
When the late emperor passed away,
it was as if Heaven and Earth had vanished.
The pain was rational for human emotion,
and one should have rushed to weep.
However, the brothers suffered wrongful cruelty,
already
fallen into treacherous schemes,
this solitary child, and others below him,
have again encountered villainous plots.
Therefore, gazing at the tomb of Wànglíng, my heart shatters;
thinking of the imperial standard, I am seized with grief.
Although my talent might not merit such favor,
yet
my position demanded bearing heavy responsibilities.
At the time of the dying injunction,
I was never consulted.
At the moment of schism,
an imperial edict appointed two scoundrels.
Heaven guided my heart,
allowing me to remain outside.
Had I been subjected to
the multitude of villains,
then jade and stone would have been shattered together.
For the foundation of the universe
to suddenly be subjected to contemptible mediocrity,
for the state of the Liú clan
to be handled by petty men—
since ancient times,
such cruelty has never been seen.
In the past, Shí Xiǎn and Cáojié,
are now considered superior;
but Wàngzhī and Zhòngjǔ,
still brought about harm.
As for encountering such ugliness and wickedness,
how can there be a distinction between ancient
and present?
All you virtuous men, with your noble lineage and official positions,
whose families have for generations been loyal and steadfast,
whose positions were not granted by favor,
whose merits were not secured by patronage—
you who worry for the state and serve the emperor diligently,
you who are the bulwarks of the altars of soil and grain—
how can you tolerate and condone treacherous
villains,
and sit idly by, watching the state fall?
I reflect that the Sòng imperial house has not yet perished,
and has been able to continue,
precisely because internally it relies on you virtuous men
to restrain wicked elements,
and externally it has this solitary child
holding a dominant position in the
middle reaches of the river.
But humans are not made of metal or stone;
how can they endure for long?
Should one fall,
then the roots will be unprotected.
Currently, the emperor is young;
it is fitting to make the laws and regulations clear.
The General Who Conquers
Barbarians, though a bulwark,
is not consoled or visited.
Even travelers coming and going
receive glances of concern.
What enmity exists between kin,
to force them apart?
The minds of beasts
arbitrarily breed suspicion and treachery.
Those who
have passed through here
are always subjected to restrictions and interference.
Those with shared malice seek each other out,
like market traders.
Since this solitary child knows their true intentions,
I fear they will use this to exploit him,
restricting and controlling the commanderies and prefectures,
and excessively guarding against him.
Recently, two envoys were sent to the southwest,
to spread propaganda within the territory,
allowing no room for fear.
They immediately dispatched memorials, and also had separate letters.
If this solitary child has committed a fault,
then you
should beat the drum and attack him;
if not,
you should allow everyone to return to their proper place.
As for killing the innocent,
the law has fixed penalties.
The envoys of the Three Excellencies were
executed without cause.
Although I
am unworthy,
I am the emperor’s youngest uncle.
Would those of low and humble status
dare not be so?
This solitary child has served the present emperor
as he served the former court,
diligent day and night,
devoting
my heart to the sun and clouds.
On the first and fifteenth of the month, I sent expresses,
following along the river roads.
What transgression have I committed
to be reduced to this state?
Since I have already submitted to this fate,
can it happen again?
As for what has been
said back and forth,
that this solitary child harbors retainers,
these people fear for their own lives;
they are not concerned with state affairs.
In ancient times, the Four Lords,
princes of various states,
still broadly attracted and gathered retainers,
having
three thousand retainers.
How much more so for this solitary child, whose position is among the Three Ducal Ministers,
defending the imperial domain?
Moreover, the present differs from the past,
as everyone knows.
Crafty enemies plunder and harass,
the Jiāng and Huái rivers are threatened and encroached upon,
the emperor is young,
the imperial clan is weak and declining,
the wicked and presumptuous carry out orders,
loyal and virtuous men are silenced,
the borders suffer the pain of ruin,
and conscripted soldiers endure the hardship of toil.
At the time of replacing
gourds,
Qí still brought about disaster;
how much more so for the garrison soldiers along the long Huái River,
who have harbored resentment for years?
Instead of striving to expand the frontiers and strengthen the borders,
they first target the emperor's relatives.
With such an approach,
what
affair will not lead to chaos?
Furthermore, they complain again about the renovation of the Pén fortifications.
Since the disasters of Jìn and Sòng,
stores accumulated to millions,
but when this solitary child arrived at the garrison,
there were not even a few thousand
li.
Yet, repairing city walls
and organizing outer cities
are normal principles of governance.
What is there to cause suspicion?
If the middle reaches of the river are to be swept clean,
then farmers should not exert
their strength to raise strong armies,
nor should garrisons be established at Gūshú,
all for defending against bandits.
How can I alone be viewed with suspicion in this regard?
In the past, even the enlightened King Chéng
was misled by rumors.
If the Metal-bound Casket
had not been opened,
then Duke Zhōu would have been unable to protect himself.
Yuè Yì, after returning to Zhào,
could not bear to plot against Yān.
How much more so this solitary child, whose relationship with the emperor is that of ruler and subject by ritual,
and like father and son by grace?
Therefore,
I pillow my weapon and weep tears of blood,
solely because of the enmity among brothers.
Observing their insatiable desires,
how can they be limited?
Suppose they achieve their tyrannical aims,
will you gentlemen be able to sit idly
and safely?
When the lips are gone, the teeth are cold –
this principle is not hard to see.
The insects in the cassia must be removed,
human wickedness must be eliminated.
To straighten the chimney and move the firewood,
why labor with much effort?
I hope you will immediately seize and arrest these two
scoundrels,
to appease the wronged spirits.
Then the late emperor will not lose his name for filial piety,
and the Sòng dynasty will have no historians who distort the records.
This province is strategically important,
its roads bordering Jiǔjiāng,
with archers and cavalry
crossing the passes to arrive.
Valuing honor and despising death,
they rush out of the marshes,
their polished armor gleaming in the water,
their spears forming a forest.
To cut down these insignificant underlings,
what fear is there of not succeeding?
But a crossbow of a thousand catties
is not triggered for a tiny mouse.
I wish to distinguish the fragrant from the foul internally,
and let Jìnyáng
rest externally.
If the achievement has a proper destination,
is that not acceptable?
I shall then commit my life to the authorities,
and apologize at the imperial court,
together upholding warmth and reverence,
and jointly focusing on all matters.
The deeds of Yī and Huò
Whom
but the lord can I rely on?
I quite fancy myself for
the positions of Zhōu and Shào.
Assisting on the left and supporting on the right,
I am not ashamed before the ancients.
In the past, Píng and Bó were decisive,
and Chǎn and Lù were swiftly
executed.
When Zhāng and Wēn wavered,
Wéntái clenched his fists.
The crucial pivot of affairs,
success or failure in an instant.
The tracks of past carriages serve as warnings for the present;
there should be no confusion.
Recently, I held this idea
and expressed
it to Shěn Yōu.
His indignation was not hard to resolve, and he conveyed this to the princes.
Once he knew the source of the calamity,
he resolutely roused himself,
amassed soldiers and honed his troops,
awaiting a joint endeavor.
When Zhāng Xīngshì departed
the capital,
he was controlled by the treacherous faction.
He unfurled his sails and departed straightaway,
and was consequently not met.
The orphan recently dispatched a messenger to state the treachery and calamity.
He was greatly dismayed,
regretting his past errors.
Lately,
the envoys
have repeatedly conveyed sincere regards.
When Wáng Huàn assisted in Yǐng,
he held military power.
His supervision of Tú Wǎng
〔二六〕caused the court and commoners to sigh in pain.
His resentment, like a father's,
how could it be
compared?
The orphan's current action
increased his indignation.
Persuaded by righteousness,
his response will be like an echo.
Perhaps some of you have not grasped this intent,
hence I first declare my feelings.
I linger
in a corner,
awaiting your inquiries.
The orphan suffers from a debilitating illness,
with no end to his destitution in sight.
I hope to emulate Shǐ Qiū,
not forgetting my roots even in death.
Before this paper, I am choked with emotion,
and my words cannot
be properly arranged.
The commander of Dàléi Garrison, Dù Dàoxīn, rushed down to report the rebellion.
Dàoxīn arrived and after one night,
Xiūfàn had already reached Xīnlín.
The imperial court was shaken.
The General Who Pacifies the South, Qí Wáng, moved his camp to the Xīntíng ramparts.
The General of the Imperial Guards, Liú Miǎn, and the former Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, Shěn Huáimíng, occupied Shítou.
The General Who Conquers the North, Zhāng Yǒng, was stationed at Báixià.
The General of the Guards, Yuán Càn, the Commander of the Central Army, Chǔ Yuān, and the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, Liú Bǐng, entered to guard the palace and ministries.
At that time, the incident occurred so suddenly
that there was no time for further arrangements.
The North and South Martial Armories were opened,
and officers and soldiers took what they wanted.
Xiūfàn advanced on foot from Xīnlín,
and reached the Xīntíng ramparts.
He personally overlooked the south of the city,
from the Líncāng Pavilion,
〔二七〕with dozens of men guarding him.
The Commander of the Rapid Cavalry, Huáng Huí, seeing an opportunity,
pretended to surrender,
and conveyed the intention of Qí Wáng.
Xiūfàn was greatly pleased,
and entrusted his two sons, Déxuān and Désì, to Huí as hostages,
who immediately executed them upon arrival.
Huí, along with the Commander of the Elite Cavalry, Zhāng Jìng'ér, advanced directly and beheaded Xiūfàn.
They brought the head back,
and his左右 (attendants) scattered.
Initially, Xiūfàn had dispatched his confederates, Dù Ěr, Dīng Wénháo, and Dù Mòlí, from Xīnlín,
〔二八〕to head straight for Zhūquè Mén.
Although Xiūfàn was dead,
Mòlí and others were unaware.
Wáng Dàolóng led the Yǔlín soldiers inside Zhūquè Mén.
Hearing that the rebels were approaching,
he urgently summoned Liú Miǎn.
Miǎn came from Shítou to respond,
and then advanced south of the bridge.
He was defeated in battle
and died.
Mòlí and others, pressing their advantage, rushed straight into Zhūquè Mén.
Wáng Dàolóng was killed by the rebel soldiers.
Mòlí and others shouted,
"The Grand Commandant has arrived!"
When Xiūfàn died,
Qí Wáng sent the squad leader Chén Língbǎo to carry the head to the palace.
He encountered rebels on the way,
threw the head into the water,
and managed to escape alone.
Although he shouted
"It's pacified!"
there was no evidence to support it,
and the crowd grew even more suspicious.
Zhāng Yǒng abandoned his troops at Báixià.
Shěn Huáimíng scattered from Shítou.
Máo Tián, the director of the Grand Army's documents, opened the East Palace to let the rebels in.
〔二九〕Mòlí went directly to Dù Mǔ Zhái.
Sūn Qiānlíng, a secretary of the Central Secretariat, opened Chéngmíng Mén and surrendered.
〔三０〕The palace was in turmoil,
with no will left to defend it.
At that time, the treasury's rewards were exhausted.
The Empress Dowager and Imperial Concubines removed gold and silver articles from the palace for use.
Chén Xiǎndá, the Supervisor of the Yǔlín, led his subordinates to fight Mòlí at Dù Mǔ Zhái,
and defeated them.
Upon reaching Xuānyáng Yùdào,
all the rebels scattered at once.
Mòlí, Wénháo, and their confederates Jiāng Bóyù, Liǔ Zhòngqián, Rèn Tiānzhù, and others were killed.
Xǔ Gōngyú fled back to Xīncài,
〔三一〕where the villagers beheaded him and sent his head in.
Jìnxī Wáng Xiè dispatched troops from Xiàkǒu to pacify Xúnyáng.
Désì's younger brothers, Qīngniú and Zhìzàng, were all executed.
An imperial edict ordered Jiànkāng and Mòlíng counties to collect the bodies of all soldiers who died,
as well as the bodies of the slain rebels,
and bury them all.
The historian comments: There is a saying,
"To throw a rat but fear the vase" —
it is indeed true.
Ruǎn Diànfū and Wáng Dàolóng monopolized the imperial command,
acting as lords while being subjects.
Those who understood righteousness
all desired to execute them with swords and horses.
Xiūfàn rode his troops to Xiàngwèi,
his arrows reached the lord's dwelling.
Loyal subjects and righteous gentlemen
all vied to be first, filled with courage.
For one who attaches oneself to the lord through evil means,
they may still escape.
How much more so for one who relies on righteousness and rectitude to contend for the lord!

Emperor Xiàowǔ had twenty-eight sons: Empress Wénmù gave birth to the deposed Emperor Zǐyè and Prince Zǐshàng of Yùzhāng.
Chén Shúyuàn gave birth to Prince Zǐxūn of Jìn'ān.
Ruǎn Rónghuá gave birth to Prince Zǐsuí of Ānlù.
Xú Zhāoróng gave birth to Imperial Prince Zǐshēn.
Hé Shúyí gave birth to Marquis Zǐfáng of Sōngzī.
Shǐ Zhāohuá gave birth to Prince Zǐxū of Línhǎi.
Yīn Guìfēi gave birth to Prince Zǐluán of Shǐpíng Xiàojìng.
Next, Prince Zǐrén of Yǒngjiā,
born together with Imperial Prince Zǐshēn.
Hé Jiéyú gave birth to Imperial Prince Zǐfèng.
Xiè Zhāoróng gave birth to Prince Zǐzhēn of Shǐ'ān.
Jiāng Jiéyú gave birth to Imperial Prince Zǐxuán.
Shǐ Zhāoyí gave birth to Prince Zǐyuán of Shàolíng.
Next, Prince Zǐyǔ of Qí Jìng,
born together with Prince Zǐluán of Shǐpíng Xiàojìng.
Jiāng Měirén gave birth to Imperial Prince Zǐhéng.
Yáng Jiéyú gave birth to Prince Zǐmèng of Huáinán.
Next, Imperial Prince Zǐkuàng,
born together with Imperial Prince Zǐxuán.
Next, Prince Zǐchǎn of Nánpíng,
born together with Prince Zǐrén of Yǒngjiā.
Next, Prince Zǐyún of Jìnlíng Xiào,
next, Imperial Prince Zǐwén,
both born together with Prince Zǐluán of Shǐpíng Xiàojìng.
Next, Prince Zǐyú of Lúlíng,
born together with Prince Zǐmèng of Huáinán.
Next, Prince Zǐshī of Nánhǎi Āi,
born together with Prince Zǐluán of Shǐpíng Xiàojìng.
Next, Prince Zǐxiāo of Huáiyáng Sī,
born together with Imperial Prince Zǐxuán.
Next, Imperial Prince Zǐyōng,
born together with Prince Zǐzhēn of Shǐ'ān.
Next, Imperial Prince Zǐqū,
born together with Imperial Prince Zǐfèng.
Next, Imperial Prince Zǐqī,
born together with Imperial Prince Zǐhéng.
Next, Prince Zǐsì of Dōngpíng,
born together with Prince Zǐzhēn of Shǐ'ān.
Dù Rónghuá gave birth to Imperial Prince Zǐyuè.
Prince Zǐsuí of Ānlù, Prince Zǐchǎn of Nánpíng, and Prince Zǐyú of Lúlíng were all adopted.
Imperial Princes Zǐshēn, Zǐfèng, Zǐxuán, Zǐhéng, Zǐkuàng, Zǐwén, and Zǐyōng were not enfeoffed
and died young.
Zǐqū, Zǐqī, and Zǐyuè were not enfeoffed
and were killed by Emperor Míng.
Prince Zǐshàng of Yùzhāng, courtesy name Xiàoshī,
was the second son of Emperor Xiàowǔ.
In the third year of Xiàojiàn (456 CE),
when he was six years old,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xīyáng,
with a stipend of two thousand households.
He also served as Grand Administrator of Military Affairs for Nánxú and Yǎn prefectures, Northern Central Cavalier General, and Governor of Nányǎn Prefecture.
In that same year,
he was transferred to be Governor of Yáng Prefecture.
In the second year of Dàmíng (458 CE),
he was given the additional title of General Who Guards the Army.
In the third year,
the area west of the Zhèjiāng River was divided off to establish the royal domain,
while the area east of the Zhèjiāng River became Yáng Prefecture.
Zǐshàng was appointed Grand Administrator of Military Affairs for Pōyáng, Jìn'ān, and Jiàn'ān commanderies in Yáng and Jiāng prefectures, and Governor of Yáng Prefecture.
His generalship remained as before,
and he was granted a set of drums and pipes.
In the fifth year (461 CE),
his title was changed to Prince of Yùzhāng,
with his households and stipend remaining as before,
and he additionally held the post of Grand Administrator of Kuàijī.
In the seventh year (463 CE),
he was granted the additional title of Imperial Commissioner with Staff,
and his title was advanced to General of Chariots and Cavalry.
In that year,
he was also given the additional title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and with his existing title, he was granted the privilege of establishing an administration with the authority of the Three Ducal Ministers.
At that time, there was a great drought in the eastern lands,
and Yín County had many irrigated fields.
Shìzǔ (Emperor Xiàowǔ) sent Zǐshàng to submit a memorial to Yín County to encourage agriculture.
He also established a Left School,
recruited students,
and appointed one Libationer of the Forest of Scholars,
who was to be respected by the students,
and whose rank was comparable to that of a Prefectural Administrator;
one Libationer of Literary Studies,
comparable to a Western Commandant;
and two Encouragement-of-Learning Attendants,
comparable to a Libationer's Attendant.
When the Former Deposed Emperor (Liú Zǐyè) ascended the throne,
the royal domain was abolished and restored to its former state.
Zǐshàng was summoned to be Grand Administrator of Military Affairs for Yáng and Nánxú prefectures,
and held the post of Minister of the Secretariat.
He was relieved of his supervision of Dōngyáng Prefecture,
but the rest of his positions remained unchanged.
Initially, during the Xiàojiàn era,
because Zǐshàng was the younger brother of the Heir Apparent by the same mother,
Shìzǔ paid close attention to him.
Later, as Liú Zǐluán, Prince of Xīn'ān, was favored due to his mother's affection,
Zǐshàng's favor gradually declined.
As he grew older,
his talent was mediocre,
and his wickedness and perversity resembled the Deposed Emperor.
Tàizōng (Emperor Míng) executed the Deposed Emperor,
and issued an edict in the name of the Grand Empress Dowager, saying:
"Zǐshàng is stubbornly evil and extremely rebellious,
his conduct goes against the principles of Heaven.
Chǔyù (Liú Chǔyù) is licentious and indulgent in wickedness,
her righteousness is severed from human norms.
They are both to be granted death at their residences."
Zǐshàng was then sixteen years old.
Chǔyù
was Princess Shānyīn.
The Deposed Emperor had renamed her Grand Princess of Kuàijī Commandery,
with a stipend from a bathing-and-feeding fief of two thousand households,
granted a set of drums and pipes,
and an additional twenty guards with swords.
Before she could be formally invested, the Deposed Emperor was overthrown.
Chǔyù indulged in licentiousness without restraint.
Seeing that Chǔ Yuān, Minister of Personnel in the Secretariat, was handsome,
she requested to have him attend her for ten days.
The Deposed Emperor granted this.
Although Yuān complied with the order,
he resisted to the death,
and Chǔyù could not force him.
Liú Zǐxūn, Prince of Jìn'ān, courtesy name Xiàodé,
was the third son of Emperor Xiàowǔ.
In the fourth year of Dàmíng (460 CE),
when he was five years old,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jìn'ān,
with a stipend of two thousand households.
He also served as Grand Administrator of Military Affairs for Nányǎn Prefecture and Dōnghǎi in Xú Prefecture, General Who Conquers Barbarians, and Governor of Nányǎn Prefecture.
In the seventh year (463 CE),
he was reappointed to supervise military affairs for Jìnxī and Xīncài in Jiāng and Nánpù prefectures, and Xīyáng in Yǐng Prefecture, as Van General and Governor of Jiāng Prefecture.
In the eighth year (464 CE),

he was promoted to Imperial Commissioner with Staff, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs for Yōng, Liáng, Nán Qín, and Běi Qín prefectures, and Jìnglíng and Suí in Yǐng Prefecture, General Who Guards the Army, Commander of Barbarian Pacification, and Governor of Yōng Prefecture.
Before he could take up the post, Shìzǔ died.
He returned to Jiāng Prefecture as General Who Guards the Army,
with his original posts remaining unchanged.
He suffered from an eye affliction,
and was not loved by Shìzǔ.
In the first year of Jǐnghé (465 CE),
he was given the additional title of Imperial Commissioner with Staff.
At that time, the Deposed Emperor was wild and cruel,
and caused many executions.
Hé Mài, former Consultative Assistant to the General Who Guards the Army, had loved martial arts since youth,
and had gathered many talented and strong individuals.
Mài had previously married Princess Xīncài, daughter of Tàizǔ (Emperor Wǔ).
The emperor falsely claimed that the princess had died,
killed a palace maid to replace her,
and gave her an ostentatious funeral,
while keeping the princess in the rear palace.
He deeply feared Mài,
and Mài, fearing disaster,
planned to stage a coup when the emperor went out,
and enthrone Zǐxūn.
The plot was discovered,
and the emperor personally led his imperial guards to execute Mài.
He ordered the Eight Administrators to report that Zǐxūn had colluded with Mài.
He also personally wrote an edict to Zǐxūn, saying:
"Hé Mài killed me to enthrone you.
You should consider whether you are superior to Xiàowǔ (Emperor Xiàowǔ)?
You may do as you please."
He sent his attendants Zhū Jǐngyún to deliver poison to Zǐxūn for him to commit suicide.
When Jǐngyún reached Pénkǒu,
he stopped and did not proceed,
sending a messenger to report to Chief Clerk Dèng Wǎn.
Wǎn and others then raised an army in the name of Zǐxūn,
using the pretext of deposing and establishing an emperor.
When Tàizōng quelled the rebellion,
he advanced Zǐxūn's title to General of Chariots and Cavalry, and granted him the privilege of establishing an administration with the authority of the Three Ducal Ministers.
Wǎn and others did not accept the order,
and circulated proclamations to the capital.
On the seventh day of the first month of the second year of Tàishǐ (466 CE),
they enthroned Zǐxūn as emperor,
taking the false throne in Xúnyáng City,
with the reign title Yìjiā first year.
All officials were appointed,
and all four directions responded,
his might shaking the realm.
In that year, tribute reports from all four directions
all went to Xúnyáng.
They sent Left Guard General Sūn Chōngzhī and others to take up positions at Zhěqí.
They also sent Governor of Yù Prefecture Liú Hú to lead a large army and encamp at Quèwěi.
They further sent General Who Pacifies the North Yuán Yǐ to command all the armies.
The imperial army encamped at Qiánxī,
cutting off Yǐ and others' food supplies.
Hú sent generals to attack them,
but was greatly defeated.
Thereupon, he burned his camp and fled.
When Yǐ heard that Hú had departed,
he also abandoned his troops and fled south.
When Shěn Yōuzhī's armies arrived at Xúnyáng,
they executed Zǐxūn and his mother,
and all those who were complicit in the rebellion were exterminated.
Zǐxūn was eleven years old at the time of his death,
and was buried at Lúshān in Xúnyáng.
Liú Zǐfáng, Marquis of Sōngzī, courtesy name Xiàoliáng,
was the sixth son of Emperor Xiàowǔ.
In the fourth year of Dàmíng (460 CE),
when he was five years old,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xúnyáng,
with a stipend of two thousand households.
He also served as General Who Campaigns with the Army, and Grand Administrator of Huáinán and Xuānchéng commanderies.
In the fifth year (461 CE),
he was transferred to be Governor of Yù Prefecture,
with his generalship and the post of Grand Administrator of Huáinán remaining unchanged.
In the sixth year (462 CE),
he was reappointed to hold the post of Grand Administrator of Xuānchéng.
In the seventh year (463 CE),
his title was advanced to Right General,
he was relieved of Xuānchéng,
and the rest remained unchanged.
In the first year of Yǒngguāng of the Former Deposed Emperor (465 CE),
he was transferred to be Governor of Dōngyáng Prefecture,
with his generalship remaining unchanged.
In the first year of Jǐnghé (465 CE),
Dōngyáng Prefecture was abolished.
Zǐfáng, with his original title, supervised military affairs for Kuàijī, Dōngyáng, Xīn'ān, Línhǎi, and Yǒngjiā commanderies, and served as Grand Administrator of Kuàijī.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
his title was changed from "supervised" (督) to "grand administrator of military affairs" (都督),
and his title was advanced to General Who Pacifies the East,
with his post of Grand Administrator remaining unchanged.
He was also summoned to be General Who Guards the Army,
and held the post of Grand Minister of Sacrifices.
Chief Clerk Kǒng Jì did not accept the order,
raised an army in rebellion,
and supported the Prince of Jìn'ān (Liú Zǐxūn).
When Zǐxūn took the false throne,
he advanced Zǐfáng's title to General of Chariots and Cavalry, and granted him the privilege of establishing an administration with the authority of the Three Ducal Ministers.
The three Wú (Wú, Wúxìng, Kuàijī) and Jìnlíng all obeyed Jì's orders.
Tàizōng sent Guard General Bālíng Wáng Xiūròu to supervise generals Wú Xǐ and others in an eastern campaign.
They were victorious in every battle,
and pacified the region one by one.
Wáng Yàn, Magistrate of Shàngyú, raised an army and killed Jì,
imprisoned Zǐfáng,
and sent him back to the capital.
The Emperor pardoned him,
demoted him to Marquis of Sōngzī County,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
Sītú (司徒) Jiàn'ān Wáng (建安王) Xiūrén (休仁) believed that Zǐfáng (子房) and his brothers would ultimately become a disaster,
and advised the emperor to eliminate them.
A decree was then issued, which stated:
"Unexpected calamities
have been documented since ancient times.
Emotion yields to law;
this is what sages and enlightened rulers follow.
I have swept away the filth and stabilized the precarious,
twice restoring the precious undertaking.
Looking to the distant great foundation,
I humbly bear the heavy responsibility.
I desire to promote good governance
and strive to exhaust benevolence and harmony,
yet treacherous scoundrels have stirred up trouble,
wildly plotting rebellion.
From the southwest, troops were held in defiance,
and the eastern territories were encroached upon.
In the capital, a multitude of villains
secretly colluded.
Lù Xiūzhī (路休之) and his brothers
exclusively acted as masterminds,
planning to incite chaos.
They ordered the palace attendant Yán Lóng (嚴龍) to spy on the palace and its surroundings,
so that when the Yǔlín (羽林) troops were dispatched for campaigns,
and the palace guards were entirely depleted,
they would watch for opportunities and openings
to stealthily launch their plot.
Liú Zhī (劉祗), in his fief,
planned to provide support,
communicating with the northern invaders
and inviting them to cross the Huái (淮) River.
Recently, when Xiūfàn (休範) crossed the Jiāng (江) River,
he secretly intended to resist and obstruct.
Fortunately, the imperial mandate is long-lasting,
and the treacherous schemes could not succeed.
Although their secret wickedness has been exposed,
they should be completely subjected to legal punishment.
However, due to the ongoing difficulties,
I have leniently preserved and nurtured them.
Now that the imperial rule is settled and peaceful,
it is fitting to distinguish between loyal and wicked.
If a trickling stream is not dammed,
a prairie fire will be hard to extinguish.
Therefore, they should be handed over to the authorities
to strictly enforce the legal codes."
"Sōngzī Hóu (松滋侯) Zǐfáng (子房) and others fell in with the rebellious faction,
collaborating in their repulsive disobedience,
and together with the qiānshuài (籤帥) and other petty individuals,
secretly colluded with the southern insurgents,
forming alliances with Zhī (祗) and others,
to plot against my person.
Although their crimes are already evident
and there is no excuse under the law,
the affection for a nephew
is truly something I cannot bear.
They may be demoted to commoners
and exiled to distant commanderies."
Thereupon, they were all killed.
Zǐfáng (子房) was eleven years old at the time.
Lù Xiūzhī (路休之) and others, believing that since Chóngxiàn Tàihòu (崇憲太后) had already passed away,
they would not be able to maintain their positions in the future,
felt insecure.
Liú Zhī (劉祗), in Nányǎnzhōu (南兗州),
harbored ambitions of rebellion.
Yán Lóng (嚴龍),
during Tàizǔ's (太祖) Yuánjiā (元嘉) reign,
was already a Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人) and Nántái Yùshǐ (南臺御史).
Shìzǔ (世祖) also appointed him Shèrén (舍人),
and he was greatly trusted.
During the Jǐnghé (景和) and Tàishǐ (泰始) periods,
he rose to Yuèqí Xiàowèi (越騎校尉)
and Yòujūn Jiāngjūn (右軍將軍).
By this time, he harbored deviant ideas,
and thus he was executed.
Línhǎi Wáng (臨海王) Zǐxù (子頊), courtesy name Xiàoliè (孝列),
was the seventh son of Xiàowǔ Dì (孝武帝).
In the fourth year of Dàmíng (大明),
at the age of five,
he was enfeoffed as Lìyáng Wáng (歷陽王),
with a registered household of two thousand.
He was concurrently appointed Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍) and Wúxìng Tàishǒu (吳興太守).
In the fifth year,
he was re-enfeoffed as Línhǎi Wáng (臨海王),
with the same number of households and fief as before.
In the same year,

he was promoted to Shǐchíjié (使持節), Dūdū Guǎngjiāo Èrzhōu Xiāngzhōu zhī Shǐxìng Shǐ'ān Línhè Sānjùn Zhūjūnfshì (都督廣交二州湘州之始興始安臨賀三郡諸軍事), Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (征虜將軍), Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiàng (平越中郎將), and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ (廣州刺史).
Before he took up his post,
he was transferred to Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史),
with his general title remaining unchanged.
In the eighth year,
he was promoted to Qián Jiāngjūn (前將軍).
When the Former Feì Dì (前廢帝) ascended the throne,
he was appointed with his original title to Dūdū Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, Yì, Liáng, Níng, Nán Běi Qín Bāzhōu Zhūjūnfshì (都督荊、湘、雍、益、梁、寧、南北秦八州諸軍事),
and his Cìshǐ (刺史) post remained as before.
When Míng Dì (明帝) ascended the throne,
he was relieved of the Dūdū Yōngzhōu (督雍州) responsibility,
and appointed Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn (鎮軍將軍) and Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹).
Soon after, he remained in his current post,
and was further appointed Dūdū Yōngzhōu (督雍州),
and also promoted to Píngxī Jiāngjūn (平西將軍).
His Chángshǐ (長史) Kǒng Dàocún (孔道存) refused to obey the order
and raised an army in rebellion,
in response to Jìn'ān Wáng (晉安王) Zǐxūn (子勛).
When Zǐxūn (子勛) assumed the false imperial title,
Zǐxù (子頊) was promoted to Wèi Jiāngjūn (衞將軍) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
After the defeat at Quèwěi (鵲尾),
and the armies of Wú Xǐ (吳喜) and Zhāng Xīngshì (張興世) arrived,
Zǐxù (子頊) was granted death,
at the age of eleven.
He was buried in Bālíng (巴陵).
Shǐpíng Xiàojìng Wáng (始平孝敬王) Zǐluán (子鸞), courtesy name Xiàoyǔ (孝羽),
was the eighth son of Xiàowǔ Dì (孝武帝).
In the fourth year of Dàmíng (大明),
at the age of five,
he was enfeoffed as Xiāngyáng Wáng (襄陽王),
with a registered household of two thousand.
He was concurrently appointed Dōng Zhōnglángjiàng (東中郎將) and Wújùn Tàishǒu (吳郡太守).
In the same year,
he was re-enfeoffed as Xīn'ān Wáng (新安王),
with the same number of households and fief as before.
In the fifth year,
he was promoted to Běi Zhōnglángjiàng (北中郎將) and Nán Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (南徐州刺史),
also holding the position of Nán Lángyá Tàishǒu (南琅邪太守).
His mother, Yīn Shúyí (殷淑儀),
enjoyed such favor that it overshadowed the entire imperial harem.
Zǐluán (子鸞) was beloved above all other sons.
Whatever the emperor favored
was invariably sent to Zǐluán's (子鸞) residence and state.
When he became Nán Xúzhōu (南徐州),
Wújùn (吳郡) was also detached and assigned to him.
In the sixth year,
he observed mourning for his mother.
Shúyí (淑儀) was posthumously promoted to Guìfēi (貴妃),
ranking second only to the Empress,
with the posthumous title Xuān (宣).
For her burial, she was provided with a wēnlángchē (轀輬車),
hǔbēn (虎賁) guards, bānjiàn (班劍) guards,
a luánlù (鑾輅) with nine pennants,
a huángwū zuǒdáo (黃屋左纛) (imperial carriage with yellow canopy and left banner),
and front and rear feather canopies and drum and wind ensembles.
The emperor personally oversaw the procession from the Nányèmén (南掖門),
and as the funeral carriage passed,
he was overcome with grief,
moving all those around him.
The emperor's sorrow and love were unending.
He emulated the poem for Lǐ Fūrén (李夫人) by Hànwǔ Dì (漢武帝),
with the following words: "I, neglecting affairs for a day,
perused the poetic works of former kings.
Seeing the poem for Lǐ Fūrén (李夫人),
I was deeply moved and sorrowful,
sighing and reciting for a long time,
then felt inspired
to compose this.
I trace the faded scrolls of spiritual chronicles,
and glimpse the ancient seals of the grand Hàn (漢).
I mourn the abrupt disappearance of the new palace,
and sigh at the overgrown desolation of the jade terrace.
I compose poems of flowing ripples to express my thoughts,
summoning
the Hé (河) and Jǐ (濟) rivers to honor the rites.
Though the virtues of the lady are recorded,
how can the lingering sorrow be dispelled?
I inquire about the flourishing and fading of all things,
and ask of the spreading and rolling up of clouds and mist.
I recall the cassia branch
falling in autumn,
and pity the jade flower clipped in spring.
The cassia branch broken, along with the years it declined;
the jade flower shattered, my thoughts linked by affection.
The vermilion palace gates closed, plain dust accumulated;
the emerald [gate hinge] overgrown,
purple moss grown.
The precious silk scorched, the spring curtain hanging low;
the treasured mat empty, the summer canopy barred.
The autumn terrace mournful, azure smoke condensed;
the winter palace chilly, the red fire extinguished.
The flowing
rhythms have an end,
but my deep heart knows no rest.
I linger in the clouds and sun,
wander in the wind and moon.
I yearn for her jade steps on the phoenix terrace,
imagine her golden voice at the phoenix tower.
I empty the square pond
with soaring grief,
diminish the round pool with flowing sobs.
I conclude my early morning court session,
and ride the imperial carriage in the quiet evening.
To the southern land,
the imperial procession clears the Chānghé (閶闔) Gate,
crushing the northern ford,
alerting
the Chéngmíng (承明) Gate.
I face the pure whiteness of the fine hall,
approaching the lush green of the pine tent.
I look down upon my many sons and mourn,
embracing my young daughter and feeling grief arise.
Though my sorrow is ultimately profound,
How shall I comfort your spirit?
While alive, your glorious flight existed on the noble path;
after death, your elegant attire was displayed on the funeral chariot.
The drooping banners and pendants hung over the illuminated path,
and the soaring phoenix-swords reached the Pure Capital.
In the court, there
was a pair aligned with the standard,
and in rites, there was no deviation from the pure blueprint.
The secret steps of the jade glow were concealed,
and the remaining shade of the empty palace beams lingered.
Awaiting the morning illumination of the jade ram,
it aligned with the
evening arrival of the golden rooster.
The cloud drum rose to draw forth thoughts,
and the grand bells chimed to regulate the sound.
The seven stars adorned the frosty wilderness,
and the two luminaries were flagged in the cold forest.
The central cloud branches were tender and flourishing,
nestled among the high peaks of the valley springs.
Qin Fēngyíng's humility has been since ancient times;
Zhou's restoration is extended to the present day.
Sending forth twin spirits to express filial thoughts,
attaching lonely souls to unfold motherly compassion.
Truly, the reward for nurturing will surely come,
and we trust that both the manifest and the hidden are equally profound.
I abandon the transformation of Qí in western Chǔ,
and ignore the distant [⿱毛灬] of the eastern gate.
The sorrow of the two waves of ripples sinks,
and
the admonitions of the seven luminaries are suddenly suppressed.
Again, he admonished the officials, saying:
"The ritual codes state,
'The Son of Heaven has an empress,
and he has concubines (fūrén).'
The Tángōng states,
'When Shùn was buried in Cāngwú,
his three concubines did not follow.'
The Hūnyì states,
'The empress establishes six palaces,
and there are three concubines (fūrén).'
Thus, the 'three concubines' are the same as the 'three fūrén.'
The empress having three concubines
is like the Son of Heaven having the three Dukes (Sāngōng).
According to the Zhōu Lǐ,
the three Dukes were granted eight mandates,
and feudal lords seven mandates.
Since the three Dukes were more honored than the feudal lords of the various states,
the three concubines (fēi) were also more esteemed than the fūrén of other states.
According to the Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn,
Zhòngzǐ was not the principal heir of Lǔ Huìgōng,
yet she was still able to have a separate palace erected for her;
now Guìfēi holds a exalted rank by heavenly order,
so it is reasonable to establish a new temple for her."
Xú Yuánzhī, the Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs, further deliberated:
"Since Xuān Guìfēi has been granted a special decree,
with rites surpassing those of the Five Palaces,
a review of ancient texts
clearly shows there are precedents.
If a temple hall is to be constructed,
the Minister of Works (Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng Qīng) should be selected for the task."
After the funeral,
an imperial edict appointed Zǐluán to act in office,
holding his original position concurrently with Sītú,
promoting him to Fǔjūn and Sītú,
granting him a set of drum and wind instruments,
with all ceremonies to follow the regulations for a duke (zhènggōng).
He was also appointed Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the various military affairs of Nánxúzhōu.
In the eighth year,
he was promoted to Grand Chancellor (Zhōngshū Lìng),
concurrently holding the position of Sītú.
When the former dethroned emperor (Qián Fèidì) ascended the throne,
he removed Zǐluán from Zhōngshū Lìng,
but kept him as Sītú,
and granted him the insignia of imperial commissioner (chíjié) for his commandery.
The emperor had always resented Zǐluán's favor;
after executing the various dukes,
he sent an envoy to bestow death upon him.
He was ten years old at the time.
As Zǐluán was about to die,
he said to his attendants,
"I wish never to be reborn into the royal family."
His younger siblings, born of the same mother, also died,
and were buried together in Jīngkǒu.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
he issued an edict saying:
"To relieve injustice and express sorrow,
though the past, it must be pursued;
moved by sentiment and compassion,
the feeling grows stronger with time.
Therefore, the Imperial Commissioner (Shǐchíjié), Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the various military affairs of Nánxúzhōu, General Fǔjūn, Inspector of Nánxúzhōu, and Prince Zǐluán of Xīn'ān,
had long shown signs of becoming a great talent,
and had early on received extraordinary favor.
He was about to establish a beautiful legacy,
to illuminate the frontier.
But a malicious heart indulged in jealousy,
and he suddenly fell victim to a dreadful calamity.
Speaking of this, my sorrow is eternal,
exceeding ordinary grief.
His youthful brilliance should be displayed,
to clear the name of his wronged soul.

He is posthumously granted the titles of Imperial Commissioner (Shǐchíjié), Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the various military affairs of Nánxúzhōu and Yǎnzhōu, Sītú, and Inspector of Nánxúzhōu.
His princely title remains as before.
The twelfth imperial daughter and the twenty-second imperial son, Zǐshī,
both suffered cruel injustices,
adding to the sorrow and lamentation.
The imperial daughter is posthumously granted the title of County Princess (Xiàn Gōngzhǔ),
and Zǐshī is restored to his former title of Prince of Nánhǎi,
both to be granted honorable posthumous titles."
He further said:
"To mourn the wronged and remember the distant,
is what humane governance promotes;
to revive the fallen and continue the cut-off,
is what grand ceremonies value.
I am devoted to ancient ways and aspire to good governance;
grace and禮 (lǐ) must be widely extended.
Even to foreign tribes one shows sincerity,
how much more so to close relatives.

Therefore, the newly deceased Imperial Commissioner (Shǐchíjié), Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the various military affairs of Nánxúzhōu and Yǎnzhōu, Sītú, and Inspector of Nánxúzhōu, Prince Zǐluán of Xīn'ān,
though young and weak,
had early shown mature understanding.
He was endowed with the kindness of the Revered Ancestor (Shìzǔ),
and was crowned with favor among the various princes.
Encountering the tyranny of Jǐnghé,
he tragically suffered a cruel calamity.
The imperial lineage was without a lord,
and the wronged sacrifices had no one to receive them.
Recalling this, my pain and sorrow
have long troubled my heart.
Therefore, Yánnián, the son of Prince Jìanpíng Jǐngsù, can be adopted as his heir."
Zǐluán's title was posthumously changed to Prince of Shǐpíng,
with an enfeoffment of one thousand households,
and he was reburied on Lóngshān in Mòlíng County.
Yánnián, courtesy name Déchōng,
died in the fourth year of Tàishǐ,
at the age of four,
and was posthumously titled Prince Chōng.
The following year,
Yánzhī, son of Prince of Chángshā Zuǎn, was again enfeoffed as Prince of Shǐpíng,
to succeed Zǐluán.
He died in the third year of Shēngmíng under Emperor Shùn,
and the principality was abolished.
Prince of Yǒngjiā Zǐrén, courtesy name Xiàohé,
was the ninth son of Emperor Xiàowǔ.
In the fifth year of Dàmíng,
at the age of five,

he was appointed Supervisor of Military Affairs (Jiān Jūnshì) for the four prefectures of Yōngzhōu, Liángzhōu, southern and northern Qínzhōu, and the two commanderies of Jìnglíng and Suí in Yǐngzhōu, concurrently Northern Commander of the Household (Běi Zhōngláng Jiàng), Commander of Pacifying Barbarians (Níngmán Xiàowèi), and Inspector of Yōngzhōu;
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Yǒngjiā,
with an enfeoffment of two thousand households.
He was subsequently transferred to Eastern Commander of the Household (Dōng Zhōngláng Jiàng) and Grand Administrator of Wújùn.
In the sixth year,
he was again transferred to Governor of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn).
In the seventh year,
he concurrently served as Commandant of the Guards (Wèiwèi).
When the former dethroned emperor (Qián Fèidì) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to General Exterminating Bandits (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn),
concurrently holding the position of Commandant of the Guards,
with his Dānyáng Yǐn post remaining as before.
Soon after, he was dispatched as General of the Left (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn) and Inspector of Nányǎnzhōu.
In the first year of Jǐnghé,
he was transferred to Inspector of Nánxúzhōu,
with his general's title remaining as before.
In the first year of Tàishǐ,
he was again transferred to General of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn),
concurrently holding the position of Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng).
Before he took office,
he was transferred to Protector-General (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn).
After the pacification of the four quarters,

he was appointed Imperial Commissioner (Shǐchíjié), Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the various military affairs of Xiāngzhōu, Guǎngzhōu, and Jiāozhōu, General Pacifying the South (Píngnán Jiāngjūn), and Inspector of Xiāngzhōu.
Tàizōng dispatched the Secretariat Director Zhào Fúgōng to proclaim an edict to Zǐrén, saying:
"Your family's household has not been established,
almost overturning the altars of soil and grain (the state).
Heaven has not yet willed Sòng to perish,
and a glorious mandate has gathered upon me.
The upper classes, deluded and foolish, incited one another,
and the four seas shared in evil.
If it were not for me cultivating virtue to govern the empire,
the foundation of the Three Ancestors
would have fallen to the ground in a single day,
and you and your ilk would have fallen into the hands of foreign tribes.
In the past, I had nearly twenty brothers.
Scattered and succeeding each other,
few remain.
Only Sītú is elderly,
and his virtuous conduct serves as a support.
The royal household relies
solely on me and Sītú.
We have not yet been able to suppress the cunning hearts of the common people,
and the other princes are also not yet capable of assisting in governance.
I have only one heir apparent (tàizǐ),
and Sītú's heir (shìzǐ)
is also young and weak.
Guìyáng and Bālíng both have no successors to the body (heirs).
We truly depend on you brothers
to lean on each other for strength,
so that the empire may not dare to spy on the royal house.
You are only a little over ten years old,
barely knowing how to bow and stand.
Currently, the various households are weak,
almost certainly to be lightly regarded by others.
If I were not the ruler,
the Liú clan would not have achieved what it has today.
You, my brothers, are young and insignificant,
misled by a group of villains,
and thus conspired with the common people against your own flesh and blood.
In your hearts,
you cannot be without shame.
Now, the four seas are at peace,
and benevolent transformation is just beginning.
For now, I will place you in Xiāngzhōu.
As you gradually grow older,
you will be fully capable of discerning good from evil.
You must always strive diligently,
and serving the imperial court should be your main concern.
Your titles and emoluments will naturally advance with your age.
My affection for my nephews
is evident in all things.
You too should know what is good,
and remember my imperial decree."
At this time, Sītú, Prince Xiūréng of Jiàn'ān, who was on a southern campaign, had not yet returned.
Upon his return, he reported to the emperor, suggesting that [Zǐrén's actions] were not conducive to the well-being of the state,
and that all such individuals should be dealt with.
[Zǐrén] was not granted the official position,
but was given death instead.
He was ten years old at the time.
Shǐ'ān Prince Zǐzhēn, courtesy name Xiàozhēn,
was the eleventh son of Emperor Xiàowǔ.
In the fifth year of Dàmíng,
at the age of five,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Shǐ'ān,
with an income of two thousand households.
He was concurrently appointed General Who Assists the State and Administrator of Wúxìng.
In the seventh year,

he was promoted to Commissioner with Staff, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Guǎng, Jiāo, and Xiāngzhōu's Shǐxīng, Shǐ'ān, and Línhè Commanderies, General Who Pacifies the Yuè, and Inspector of Guǎngzhōu.
The rank of general remained as before.
He did not proceed to his post.
He was promoted to General Who Conquers Barbarians and Administrator of Nánpéngchéng,
concurrently overseeing affairs at Shítóu Garrison.
In the first year of Jǐnghé,
he was appointed Governor of Dānyáng,
with his general rank remaining as before.
Soon after, he was again appointed Inspector of Nányǎnzhōu,
with his general rank remaining as before.
In the second year of Tàishǐ,
he was promoted to General of the Left and Governor of Dānyáng.
He was not granted the official position,
but was given death instead.
He was ten years old at the time.
Shàolíng Prince Zǐyuán, courtesy name Xiàoshàn,
was the thirteenth son of Emperor Xiàowǔ.
In the sixth year of Dàmíng,
at the age of five,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Shàolíng,
with an income of two thousand households.
In the eighth year,
he was appointed Controller of the Imperial Treasury, and Administrator of Qín and Nánpèi Commanderies.
He was concurrently appointed General of Exemplary Courage and Administrator of Nánlángyá and Tàishān Commanderies.
In the first year of Jǐnghé,
he was sent out as Inspector of Xiāngzhōu,
with his general rank remaining as before.
He did not proceed to his post.
Upon reaching Xúnyáng,
he encountered Jìn'ān Prince Zǐxūn's rebellion,
and remained there, not proceeding to his post.
He was advanced to the title of General Who Soothes the Army.
After the matter was settled,
he was given death.
He was nine years old at the time.
Qíjìng Prince Zǐyǔ, courtesy name Xiàoyīng,
was the fourteenth son of Emperor Xiàowǔ.
Born in the second year of Dàmíng,
he died in the third year,
and was posthumously enfeoffed and given a posthumous name.
Huáinán Prince Zǐmèng, courtesy name Xiàoguāng,
was the sixteenth son of Emperor Xiàowǔ.
In the seventh year of Dàmíng,
at the age of five,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Huáinán,
with an income of two thousand households.
At that time, Shìzǔ changed the Nánliáng Commandery of Yùzhōu to the state of Huáinán,
and abolished the Huáinán Commandery of Nányùzhōu as well as Xuānchéng.
When the former deposed emperor ascended the throne,
both commanderies reverted to their former status,
and Zǐmèng still held the title of state and received income from Huáinán Commandery.
In the first year of Jǐnghé,
he was appointed General of Exemplary Courage and Administrator of Nánlángyá and Péngchéng Commanderies.
In the second year of Tàishǐ,
he was re-enfeoffed as Prince of Ānchéng,
with his households and income as before.
He was not granted the official position,
but was given death instead.
He was eight years old at the time.
Jìnlíng Xiào Prince Zǐyún, courtesy name Xiàojǔ,
was the nineteenth son of Emperor Xiàowǔ.
In the sixth year of Dàmíng,
at the age of four,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Jìnlíng,
with an income of two thousand households.
He was not granted the official position,
and died in that same year.
Nánhǎi Āi Prince Zǐshī, courtesy name Xiàoyǒu,
was the twenty-second son of Emperor Xiàowǔ.
In the seventh year of Dàmíng,
at the age of four,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Nánhǎi,
with an income of two thousand households.
He was not granted the official position.
In the first year of Jǐnghé,
he was harmed by the former deposed emperor.
He was six years old at the time.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
he was posthumously given a posthumous name.
Huáiyáng Sī Prince Zǐxiāo,
courtesy name Xiàoyún,
was the twenty-third son of Emperor Xiàowǔ.
Born in the fifth year of Dàmíng,
he died in the eighth year,
and was posthumously enfeoffed and given a posthumous name.
Dōngpíng Prince Zǐsì, courtesy name Xiàoshū,
was the twenty-seventh son of Emperor Xiàowǔ.
Born in the seventh year of Dàmíng,
he was still enfeoffed as Prince of Dōngpíng,
with an income of two thousand households.
He succeeded Dōngpíng Chōng Prince Xiūqiàn.
Xiūqiàn's birth mother, Lady Yán, was of a severe and cruel disposition.
In the second year of Tàishǐ,
Zǐsì's birth mother, Concubine Xiè of Jǐngníng Park, submitted a memorial, saying:
"The late Dōngpíng Chōng Prince Xiūqiàn, whose roots were destined for the highest position,
displayed his precocious talent early on.
His years were not prolonged,
and he left no heir.
Emperor Xiàowǔ decreed that my son, your servant Zǐsì, should be adopted as his successor.
Having inherited the state's sacrifices,
he was to uphold the ancestral rites,
hoping to extend vast blessings
and perpetuate them for a long time.
However, my co-wife, Yán, did not nurture him with kindness,
and her guidance was contrary to reason.
Her feelings lacked encouragement,
and her righteousness went against the responsibility of a foster mother.
In the past, during Shìzǔ's lifetime,
she deceptively feigned maternal affection.
Not long after his death,
her true nature emerged,
though she still feared and respected the Empress Dowager,
and somewhat concealed her desires.
Since then,
she has indulged in extreme cruelty,
openly displaying it to the imperial clan,
and revealing it in the imperial chambers,
thereby harming human relations
and causing sorrow to passersby.
My heavenly bond is profound and deep;
I feel this acutely and deeply.
I humbly pray for Your Majesty's broad benevolence to descend,
to graciously shed light upon this,
and to allow [my son] to be re-appointed and return to his original lineage.
Then, even if my son and I were to perish,
it would be like living."
This was granted.
In that same year, he was given death.
He was four years old at the time.
Wǔlíng Wáng Zàn 武陵王贊, courtesy name Zhòngfū 仲敷,
was the ninth son of Emperor Míng 明帝.
He was born in the sixth year of Tàishǐ 泰始 (470 CE).
In that same year,
an imperial edict stated:
“Although Emperor Shìzǔ Xiàowǔ 世祖孝武皇帝 relied on his revered status to bestow favors,
his achievements were modest and his governance lax.
He indulged in drink without satiety,
his affairs arising from peace and tranquility.
He wielded power and was extravagant,
his righteousness stemming from a lack of duties.
Thus, accumulated resentment moved Heaven,
and misfortune afflicted his descendants.
Jǐnghé 景和 initiated the strife,
and Yìjiā 義嘉 brought about disaster.
When Shìzǔ 世祖 succeeded to the throne,
he completely disregarded the constitution.
In the past, when the imperial house was in decline,
all living beings feared extinction.
It relied on the heroic and filial who were moved to action,
wiping away the injustice and shame.
Their merits restored the fallen lineage,
saving these distressed common people.
Continuing the severed line and honoring the distant past
are principles esteemed by ritual teachings.
How much more so for one who is both emperor and brother,
yet neglects this tradition!
Now, with the ninth son, Zhìsuí 智隨, he is appointed to serve Shìzǔ 世祖 as a son.
During the era of Dàmíng 大明 in Wǔlíng 武陵 Commandery,
his affairs are comparable to those of a surrogate state.
Zhìsuí 智隨 may be enfeoffed as Wǔlíng Wáng 武陵王,
with a stipend of five thousand households.
Upon reflection, Shìzǔ’s 世祖’s household had no small number of female relatives.
Since there was no one to oversee them,
it is necessary to provide protection and restraint.
Although feudal lords are not permitted to refer to the Son of Heaven as their ancestor,
there is a pressing family matter.
Furthermore, they should have a place to return to for visits,
and to care for each other in illness.
They should be entrusted with responsibilities,
and have provisions for their chambers.
I, who respond to Heaven and occupy the throne,
have deep benevolence for all nine clans.
It is hoped that this will suffice to express my thoughts of remembrance and affection,
and to spread the principle of love.”
Later, in the fourth year of Yuánhuī 元徽 (476 CE) of the deposed emperor,

he was sent out as Envoy with Credentials (shǐchíjié 使持節), Inspector of Military Affairs of Nánxú 南徐, Yǎn 兗, Qīng 青, Jì 冀 five provinces (dū Nánxú Yǎn Qīng Jì wǔ zhōu zhū jūnshì 督南徐兗青冀五州諸軍事), Northern Central General (běizhōnglángjiàng 北中郎將), and Governor of Nánxú 南徐 Province (Nánxú zhōu cìshǐ 南徐州刺史).
In the first year of Shēngmíng 昇明 (477 CE) of Emperor Shùn 順帝,

he was promoted to Envoy with Credentials (chíjié 持節), Inspector of Military Affairs of Yǐng 郢 Province and Yìyáng 義陽 of Sī 司 Province (dū Yǐngzhōu Sīzhōu zhī Yìyáng zhū jūnshì 督郢州司州之義陽諸軍事), General of the Vanguard (qiánjiāngjūn 前將軍), and Governor of Yǐng 郢 Province (Yǐngzhōu cìshǐ 郢州刺史).
In the second year (478 CE),
he was besieged by Shěn Yōuzhī 沈攸之.

He was transferred to Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of Jīng 荊, Xiāng 湘, Yōng 雍, Yì 益, Liáng 梁, Níng 寧, Nánběiqín 南北秦 eight provinces (dūdū Jīng Xiāng Yōng Yì Liáng Níng Nánběiqín bā zhōu zhū jūnshì 都督荊湘雍益梁寧南北秦八州諸軍事), General Who Guards the West (ānxījiāngjūn 安西將軍), and Governor of Jīng 荊 Province (Jīngzhōu cìshǐ 荊州刺史),
with his credentials remaining as before.
After Yōuzhī 沈攸之 was pacified, he proceeded to his post.
In that same year, he died
at the age of nine.
His state was abolished.
The historian says: The princes of Jìn'ān 晉安
rallied their subordinates
to stir up chaos and rebellion,
leading to the boiling unrest across the nine regions,
and widespread disaster throughout the empire,
and even the descendants of Shìzǔ 世祖 were exterminated.
The strong are not as good as the weak;
this is where the principle lies.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter Forty-One: Liú Xiùzhī 劉秀之, Gù Chēn 顧琛, Gù Jìzhī 顧覬之
Liú Xiùzhī 劉秀之, courtesy name Dàobǎo 道寶,
was a native of Jǔ 莒, Dōngguǎn 東莞.
He was a cousin's son of the Situ (sītú 司徒), Liú Mùzhī 劉穆之.
His family resided in Jīngkǒu 京口 for generations.
His grandfather, Shuǎng 爽,
was Secretariat Director of the Bureau of State Affairs (shàngshū dūguānláng 尚書都官郎)
and Magistrate of Shānyīn 山陰.
His father, Zhòngdào 仲道,
when Gāozǔ 高祖 captured the capital city,
was appointed to the staff of the Jianwu (jiànwǔ 參軍)
and, together with Mèng Chǎng 孟昶, remained to guard it.
After the situation was settled,
he was made Magistrate of Yúyáo 余姚
and died in office.
Xiùzhī 秀之 was orphaned and poor in his youth,
but possessed ambition and integrity.
When he was about ten years old,
he was playing with other children by the front islet
when suddenly a large snake appeared,
extremely fierce.
Everyone stumbled and screamed in fright,
but Xiùzhī 秀之 alone remained unmoved.
Everyone was astonished.
Hé Chéngtiān 何承天 of Dōnghǎi 東海 greatly appreciated his talent
and gave him his daughter in marriage.
His elder brother, Qīnzhī 欽之, was Zhū Língshí’s 朱齡石 Right Army Staff Officer (yòujūn cānjūn 右軍參軍).
He perished with Língshí 朱齡石 in battle.
Xiùzhī 秀之 grieved so deeply
that he did not partake in feasts for ten years.
In the second year of Jǐngpíng 景平 (424 CE),
he was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law (fùmǎ dūwèi 駙馬都尉) and attended imperial court.
Being poor,
he sought to become Assistant Administrator of Guǎnglíng 廣陵 Commandery.
He was subsequently appointed Provisional Staff Officer to Fǔjūn Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng 撫軍江夏王義恭 and Píngběi Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng 平北彭城王義康.
He was then dispatched as Magistrate of Wúxī 無錫, Yángxiàn 陽羨, and Wūchéng 烏程,
all of which earned him a reputation for capability.
In the sixteenth year of Yuánjiā 元嘉 (439 CE),
he was promoted to Magistrate of Jiànkāng 建康,
then appointed Secretariat Director of the Central Military Bureau (shàngshū zhōngbīngláng 尚書中兵郎),
and reappointed as Magistrate of Jiànkāng 建康.
He was meticulous by nature
and skilled at exposing hidden transgressions.
His administration was highly regarded.
Shěn Yǎnzhī 沈演之, the Minister of Personnel (lìbù shàngshū 吏部尚書), often praised him to Tàizǔ 太祖.
When Shìzǔ 世祖 was garrisoned in Xiāngyáng 襄陽,
he appointed him Staff Officer to Fǔjūn (fǔjūn lùshì cānjūn 撫軍錄事參軍) and Magistrate of Xiāngyáng 襄陽.
In Xiāngyáng 襄陽, there was the Liùmén Yàn 六門堰 (Six Gates Weir),
irrigating thousands of qǐng 頃 of fertile land.
The weir had long been broken,
causing both public and private enterprises to fail.
Shìzǔ 世祖 sent Xiùzhī 秀之 to repair it,
and consequently, the Yōng 雍 region reaped a great harvest.
He was then appointed Administrator of Guǎngpíng 廣平.
In the twenty-fifth year (448 CE),

he was appointed Inspector of Military Affairs of Liáng 梁, Nán Běiqín 南北秦 three provinces (dū Liáng Nán Běiqín sān zhōu zhū jūnshì 督梁南北秦三州諸軍事), General Who Pacifies the Distant (níngyuǎnjiāngjūn 寧遠將軍), Colonel of the Western Barbarians (xīróngxiàowèi 西戎校尉), and Governor of Liáng 梁 and Nánqín 南秦 two provinces (Liáng Nánqín èr zhōu cìshǐ 梁南秦二州刺史).
At that time, Hànchuān 漢川 suffered from famine,
and the region was in turmoil.
Xiùzhī 秀之 was skilled in governance
and personally practiced frugality.
Previously, Hànchuān 漢川 entirely used silk as currency.
Xiùzhī 秀之 limited its use and mandated the use of coins,
which benefited the people to this day.
In the twenty-seventh year (450 CE),
a large-scale northern expedition was launched.
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Yáng Wéndé 輔國將軍楊文德 and Bāxī Zǐtóng èr Jùn Tàishǒu Liú Hóngzōng 巴西梓潼二郡太守劉弘宗 were dispatched to receive orders from Xiùzhī 秀之,
to shake Qīan 汧 and Lǒng 隴.
Xiùzhī 秀之 sent Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn Xī Qiānqiū 建武將軍錫千秋 with two thousand men towards the southern entrance of Zǐwǔ Gǔ 子午谷.
His Chief Clerk (fǔsīmǎ 府司馬), Zhú Zōngzhī 竺宗之, with three thousand men, went towards the southern entrance of Luò Gǔ 駱谷.
Wēiyuǎn Jiāngjūn Liáng Xún 威遠將軍梁尋 with one thousand men went towards the southern entrance of Xié Gǔ 斜谷.
The Di 氐 chieftain Yáng Gāo 楊高 became a bandit.
Xiùzhī 秀之 campaigned against him
and beheaded Gāo 楊高 and his brothers.
When the arch-villain committed regicide,
Xiùzhī 秀之, upon hearing the news,
immediately raised an army
and requested to lead his troops to Xiāngyáng 襄陽.
However, Sīkōng Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān 司空南譙王義宣 refused.
After the situation settled,

he was promoted to Envoy with Credentials (shǐchíjié 使持節), Inspector of Military Affairs of Yì 益 and Níng 寧 two provinces (dū Yì Níng èr zhōu zhū jūnshì 督益寧二州諸軍事), General Who Pacifies the North (níngshuòjiāngjūn 寧朔將軍), and Governor of Yì 益 Province (Yìzhōu cìshǐ 益州刺史).
He converted 2.8 million in salary
and deposited it in the treasury of Liángzhōu 梁州 garrison.
Apart from this, he had nothing.
The territories of Liáng 梁 and Yì 益 provinces were rich in resources.
Previous governors
all engaged in accumulating wealth,
with some amassing tens of thousands of gold.
The officials and associates he brought with him
