were all poor scholars from the capital.
When they were appointed to commanderies and counties,
they all sought to enrich themselves through ill-gotten gains.
Xiùzhī 秀之 governed with integrity and strictness,
leading by example for his subordinates.
Both near and far, people were content.
When Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān 南譙王義宣 rebelled from Jīngzhōu 荊州,
he sent his Staff Officer Wáng Yào 王曜 to levy troops from Xiùzhī 秀之.
Xiùzhī 秀之 immediately beheaded Yào 王曜 and put the commandery on alert.
He dispatched his Central Military Staff Officer (zhōngbīng cānjūn 中兵參軍), Wéi Shānsōng 韋山松, with ten thousand men to attack Jiānglíng 江陵,
exiting through the gorges.
Zhú Chāomín 竺超民 sent his general Xí Tiānshēng 席天生 to intercept them.
Shānsōng 韋山松, in a single battle,
beheaded him.
He advanced to Jiānglíng 江陵
but was defeated by Lǔ Xiù 魯秀,
and Shānsōng 韋山松 was killed.
In that same year,
he was promoted to General Who Conquers the Barbarians (zhēnglǔjiāngjūn 征虜將軍).
His title of Inspector (dū 督) was changed to Supervisor (jiān 監),
and his credentials and governorship remained as before.
For his meritorious service in raising the army,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Kānglè Xiàn 康樂縣,
with a stipend of six hundred households.
The following year,
he was promoted to Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yǐngzhōu 郢州 (jiān Yǐngzhōu zhū jūnshì 監郢州諸軍事) and Governor of Yǐngzhōu 郢州 (Yǐngzhōu cìshǐ 郢州刺史),
with his general rank remaining as before.
He did not take up the post.
In the first year of Dà Míng,
he was appointed Right Guard General.
The next year,
he was promoted to Dānyáng Yǐn.
Before this,
Xiùzhī's paternal uncle, Mùzhī, was Dānyáng [Yǐn],
and he dined and feasted with his children and younger relatives in the main hall.
Xiùzhī was also among them.
There was a hole in a pillar in the main hall.
Mùzhī said to his children, younger relatives, and Xiùzhī:
"You all try throwing chestnuts at this pillar from a distance.
If you can get one into the hole,
you will certainly obtain this commandery later."
None of Mùzhī's sons could hit it,
only Xiùzhī alone succeeded.
At that time, the common people's goods were bought on credit,
and the money was not repaid.
The markets were filled with lamentations and complaints.
Xiùzhī considered this inappropriate,
and presented his case very earnestly.
Though his words were accepted,
they were ultimately not followed.
When Guǎnglǐng Wáng Dàn rebelled,
Xiùzhī entered to defend the Eastern City.
In that year,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Yòu Púyè.
In the fourth year,
when the regulations and ordinances were changed,
there was a debate on the law concerning commoners killing high officials when the facts were uncertain.
The debaters suggested that if an amnesty was granted, they should be exiled.
Xiùzhī believed:
"Although the laws do not explicitly state the principle for commoners killing officials,
if, when an amnesty is granted, it only results in exile,
it would be no different from ordinary murder.
Commoners revere officials
as they do their parents.
A person who commits such a heinous act,
even if an amnesty is granted,
should, in my opinion, be permanently imprisoned in Shàngfāng,
to exhaust their natural lifespan,
and their household members should be ordered to serve as soldiers."
This was followed.
The next year,
he was appointed Commander of the Crown Prince's Right Guard.
In the fifth year,
Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Hǎilíng Wáng Xiūmào rebelled
and was executed by the local people.
Xiùzhī was dispatched with his original office to comfort and console [the people],
and distinguish between the good and the bad.
After the task was completed, he returned to the capital.

He was appointed Minister-with-credentials, Mounted Attendant, Area Commander-in-chief of Yōng, Liáng, North Qín, South Qín four prefectures, and Jìnglín and Suí two commanderies of Yǐngzhōu, General of the Pacified North, Protector of the Southern Barbarians, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
The emperor's carriage went to Xīntíng to see Xiùzhī off.
He was about to be appointed Left Púyè,
but before the appointment could take effect,
he died in the eighth year,
at the age of sixty-eight.
The emperor was deeply grieved and saddened by this,
and issued an edict saying:
"Xiùzhī possessed clear and far-reaching wisdom,
and his talents were comprehensive and fluent.
His sincerity was manifest in the provincial court,
and his achievements were proclaimed across the mountains.
In previous years, when rebellious ministers colluded,
he initiated righteousness from a thousand miles away.
And when he held the office of a upright governor,
he assisted in military affairs in both palaces.
His excellent plans and admirable reputation
were truly renowned throughout the court and the land.
The region south of the Hàn River had numerous laws and discontented people.
It awaited a good pastor.
Therefore, I temporarily parted with a trusted minister
to spread good governance externally.
He had not been out for a full year,
yet his virtue had already benefited the western regions.
Examining ancient heroes,
and observing his beginning and end,
his pure heart and loyal integrity
could not be surpassed.
He was about to illuminate the imperial plans
and enter to guard the foundation,
but he suddenly passed away.
This deeply grieves my heart.
The honors of his life
had not yet reached their fullest extent.
The rites for his sorrowful end
should be carried out with the utmost solemnity.
Furthermore, he was humble and kept to his vows,
and his fief was not extensive.
Speaking of him now, I lament his passing,
and my grief and regret only increase.
He is to be posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng and Sīkōng.
His titles of Minister-with-credentials, Area Commander-in-chief, Cìshǐ, and Commandant remain as before,
and his fief is to be increased to one thousand households.
His posthumous title shall be Zhōngchéng Gōng."
Xiùzhī was unpolished and lacked refined demeanor,
but his will and integrity were firm and upright.
The emperor, seeing his clean administration
and lack of surplus wealth at home,
bestowed upon him 200,000 coins
and 300 bolts of cloth.
His son Jǐngyuǎn inherited the title
and served as General of the Van.
After Jǐngyuǎn's death,
his son Jùn,
when Qí received the abdication,
had his state abolished.
Xiùzhī's younger brother, Cuìzhī,
was Jìnlíng Tàishǒu.
Gù Chēn, courtesy name Hóngwěi,
was a native of Wú County in Wú Commandery.
His great-grandfather, Hé,
was Sīkōng of Jìn.
His grandfather, Lǚzhī,
and father, Tàn,
both served as Sītú Zuǒ Xī Yuán.
Chēn was cautious and upright, disdaining superficiality.
He began his career as a provincial aide,
Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
and Fèng Cháoqǐng.
In the Jǐngpíng era of Shàodì,
when the Grand Empress Dowager died,
he was appointed Dàjiàng Chéng.
He served as Right Army Cavalry Consultant to Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng,
Jìnlíng Magistrate,
Sītú Consultant,
Shàngshū Kùbù Láng,
and Neutral Judge of his native commandery.
In the seventh year of Yuánjiā,
when Tàizǔ dispatched Dào Yànzhī to strategize in Hénán and suffered a great defeat,
all the weapons and armor were abandoned,
and the imperial arsenal became empty.
Later, when Tàizǔ held a banquet,
there was a person from outside the wild frontiers who had submitted in attendance.
The emperor asked Chēn:
"How many weapons are still left in the arsenal?"
Chēn deceptively replied:
"There are enough weapons for 100,000 men."
Previously, the number of weapons in the imperial arsenal was a secret and not to be disclosed.
When the emperor asked,
he immediately regretted his slip of the tongue.
Upon Chēn's deceptive reply,
the emperor was very pleased.
There was an imperial decree at the gate of the Shàngshū office,
stating that the number of retainers allowed to enter with officials from the Eight Seats downwards was limited,
and people of other statuses were not permitted to mix in.
Chēn, however, registered his clansman Gù Shuòtóu under Shàngshū Zhāng Màodù's name [as a retainer],
and sat with Shuòtóu at the same table.
The next year,
he was dismissed [from office] for this offense,
and removed from his position as Neutral Judge.
Generally, for Shàngshū officials,
major offenses resulted in dismissal,
while minor offenses led to temporary removal.
Those temporarily removed, if no replacement was found within one hundred days,
were allowed to return to their original post.
Chēn was then requested by Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng,
and appointed Sītú Lùshì Cānjūn,
Shānyīn Magistrate,
then again Sītú Lùshì,
and promoted to Shàofǔ.
In the fifteenth year,
he was appointed Yìxīng Tàishǒu.
Initially,
Yìkāng invited Chēn to his household,
wishing to entrust him with confidential matters.
However, Chēn was unable to serve Liú Zhàn,
and thus was soon expelled.
In the nineteenth year,
he was transferred to Dōngyáng Tàishǒu.
The intention was for Chēn to guard Generalissimo Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng.
He firmly declined, which displeased the emperor,
and he was consequently dismissed and returned home for several years.
In the twenty-seventh year,
the Suǒ-lǔ advanced south to Guābù.
Quán provisionally appointed Chēn as General Jiànwēi.
Soon after, he was appointed General Chénguān Sīmǎ to Wáng Huī, Prince of Dōnghǎi,
and managed the affairs of Kuàijī Commandery.
When Wáng Dàn replaced Wáng Huī,
he again served as Dàn's Āndōng Sīmǎ.
When the primary culprit usurped the throne,
Kuàijī was divided into five commanderies to form Huìzhōu.
Dàn was made the Cìshǐ,
and Chēn was immediately made the Grand Administrator of Kuàijī,
with the additional rank of General of the Fifth Rank,
and was assigned assistants and subordinates.
When Dàn raised an army,
Chēn was promoted to General Guànjūn.
After the rebellion was suppressed,
he was transferred to be Grand Administrator of Wúxīng.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn,
he was summoned to be Wǔbīng Shàngshū.
Before he could take up the post,
he was again made General Níngshuò and Grand Administrator of Wú Commandery.
For his meritorious service in the uprising,
he was enfeoffed as a Fifth Rank Marquis of Yǒngxīn County.
In the first year of Dàmíng,
Zhāng Kǎi, the Magistrate of Wú County, was impeached for being disrespectful while in mourning for his mother,
and was sent to the Court of Judicial Review.
Shěn Wénxiù, the Magistrate of Qiántáng, was accused of making erroneous judgments in the impeachment,
and was consequently liable to be impeached.
Chēn declared to the public:
"When Kǎi was first impeached,
I repeatedly clarified the situation."
He also said:
"I should submit a memorial to keep Wénxiù in the county."
Shìzǔ heard of this and was greatly enraged,
accusing Chēn of shifting blame upwards,
and dismissed him from office.
Chēn's mother was old,
so he remained at home.
Chēn and the former Grand Administrator of Xīyáng, Zhāng Mù,
were both former subordinates of Sīkōng Jìnglǐng Wáng Dàn,
and Dàn had always treated Chēn and others with great favor.
In the third year,
Dàn rebelled in Guǎnglíng,
sending his retainer Lù Yánrěn with letters appointing Chēn as General Zhēngnán,
Mù as General Āndōng,
Chēn's son, the former Shàngshū Láng Bǎosù, as Cányì Cānjūn,
Bǎosù's younger brother, the former Sīkōng Cānjūn Bǎoxiān, as Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
Mù's elder brother, the former Wú Commandery Chéng Jì, as General Guànjūn,
and his paternal cousin, the former Sīkōng Zhǔbù Yàn, as Cányì Cānjūn.
At that time, Shìzǔ, knowing that Chēn had always been associated with Dàn,
suspected that he harbored disloyal intentions,
and sent an envoy to Wú Commandery Grand Administrator Wáng Tánshēng to execute Chēn and his sons.
It so happened that Yánrěn arrived first,
and Chēn and others immediately apprehended and beheaded him.
He sent his two sons to deliver Yánrěn's head and memorialized Shìzǔ, saying:
"Liú Dàn, in his madness,
has instigated a rebellious conflict.
All living beings
are shocked and saddened.
Your humble servants, having been endowed with national grace,
are particularly filled with righteous indignation.
Suddenly, on the twenty-fourth day of this month, we received a letter from the rebel Dàn,
attempting to entice us.
Your humble servant immediately joined in apprehending the false envoy,

and also obtained letters from Dàn to the Fǔjūn Chángshǐ Shěn Huáiwén, Yángzhōu Biéjià Kǒng Dàocún, Fǔjūn Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Kǒng Zǎo, former Sī Bīng Cānjūn Kǒng Huánzhī, and former Sīkōng Zhǔbù Zhāng Yàn,
which thoroughly exposed the Grand Administrator of this commandery, Wáng Tánshēng.
Your humble servant should immediately rush back to the imperial capital,
but my mother is old,
and I am present to attend to her.
Therefore, I am sending my sons Bǎosù and Bǎoxiān to present their humble selves at the imperial court."
The envoy Shìzǔ had sent to execute Chēn arrived on the same day,
and Chēn narrowly escaped death.
The Emperor commended him,
summoned Chēn,
and appointed him Fǔjūn Sīmǎ to Xīyáng Prince Zǐshàng,
and Mù as Fǔjūn Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
Chēn's mother, Kǒng Shì,
was over a hundred years old at that time.
In the early years of Lóng'ān of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
Wáng Xīn of Lángyá caused trouble in Wúzhōng.
He appointed his daughter as General Zhēnliè,
and used only women as officials.
He appointed Kǒng Shì as Sīmǎ.
After the chaos of Sūn Ēn,
the eastern lands suffered from famine,
and people resorted to cannibalism.
Kǒng Shì distributed her family's grain to relieve the suffering in the villages,
and many lives were saved.
All children born thereafter were named Kǒng.
Chēn continued to be Grand Administrator of Wúxīng.
The following year,
he was dismissed from office because many people in his commandery clipped coins and illegally minted currency.
In the sixth year,
he was appointed Grand Sī nóng,
Dūguān Shàngshū,
Sīmǎ to Xīn'ān Prince Zǐluán's Běizhōngláng, Grand Administrator of Dōnghǎi, and acting governor of Nánxú Province.
He was subsequently transferred with the office to Fǔjūn Sīmǎ,
retaining his position as Grand Administrator.
When the former dethroned emperor ascended the throne,
he was again made Grand Administrator of Wú Commandery.
In the early years of Tàishǐ of Tàizōng,
he rebelled along with others from the four directions.
After his army was defeated,
he fled with his mother to Kuàijī.
When the imperial army arrived,
he surrendered.
Bǎosù became separated from Chēn
and committed suicide.
Chēn soon after observed mourning for his mother.
After the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Yuánwài Chángshì and Zhōngsàn Dàfū.
In the third year of Yuánhuī of the later dethroned emperor,
he passed away,
at the age of eighty-six.
Bǎoxiān served as Shàngshū Shuǐbù Láng during the Dàmíng era.
Before this,
Chēn had been impeached by Zuǒ Chéng Xún Wànqiū.
When Bǎoxiān became a Láng,
Wànqiū was still in office,
and Bǎoxiān declared that he would not accept the appointment.
Shìzǔ issued an edict saying:
"To admonish against wrongdoing and slackness
is the duty of the Censorate.
If there is injustice in their rulings,
it should naturally be corrected elsewhere.
However, recently, regardless of the severity of the impeachment,
people have resorted to personal severance.
This trend is difficult to perpetuate,
and those in charge should strictly regulate it.
Bǎoxiān probably relied on his family's prestige
and is not worth questioning."
Before this,
among the noble and prominent figures in Jiāngdōng during the Sòng era,
Kǒng Jìgōng of Kuàijī,
his son Kǒng Língfú,
Qiū Yuānzhī of Wúxīng, and Chēn
did not change their Wú accent.
Yuānzhī,
whose courtesy name was Sīxuán,
was from Wūchéng, Wúxīng.
Tàizǔ followed Gāozǔ on his northern expedition,
and was stationed in Péngchéng,
serving as General Guànjūn and Cìshǐ of Xú Province.
Yuānzhī served as his Chángshǐ.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he held various prominent official positions due to his old friendship,
including Shìzhōng,
Dūguān Shàngshū,
and Grand Administrator of Wú Commandery.
He died while serving as Grand Tàicháng,
and was posthumously granted the title of Grand Master Guānglù.
Gù Jìzhī,
whose courtesy name was Wěirén, was from Wú County, Wú Commandery.
His great-grandfather, Gù Qiān,
whose courtesy name was Gōngràng, was the brother-in-law of Lù Jī, the Grand Administrator of Píngyuán in Jìn.
His grandfather, Gù Chóng,
was Grand Sī nóng.
His father, Gù Huánglǎo,
was Zuǒ Xīyuán of the Sītú.
Jìzhī began his career as the commandery's Zhǔbù.
When Xiè Huì was in Jīng Province,
he appointed Jìzhī as Nánmán Gōngcáo,
and then as Huì's Wèijūn Cānjūn.
Huì admired his refined simplicity
and held him in high regard.
Wáng Hóng appointed him as Yángzhōu Zhǔbù,
and then as Hóng's Wèijūn Cānjūn,
Magistrate of Yánguān,
Yòujūn Zhǔbù to Héngyáng Prince Yìjì,
Shàngshū Dūguān Láng,
and Hùjūn Sīmǎ.
At that time, General-in-Chief Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng held power,
and the rift between Yīn and Liú was already evident.
Jìzhī did not wish to long associate with Yīn Jǐngrén,
so he resigned, claiming a leg ailment, and returned home.
At home, he would often walk on his bed every night,
which his family secretly found strange,
but they did not understand his intention.
Later, Yìkāng was banished and deposed,
and many in the court suffered misfortune due to differing opinions.
Jìzhī was again appointed Magistrate of Dōngqiān and Shānyīn.
Shānyīn had thirty thousand households,
making it the busiest commandery in the realm.
Former officials,
unable to rest day or night,
still failed to accomplish their tasks.
Jìzhī managed the complexities with simplicity,
and the county became orderly.
He would hang curtains during the day,
and his gate and steps were quiet and serene.
Among those who served as Magistrate of Shānyīn during the Sòng era,
no one surpassed him in achieving great results with minimal effort.
He was again 揚州 Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ,
廣陵王 Dàn's and 廬陵王 Shào's Běizhōngláng Zuǒjūn Sīmǎ,
揚州 Biéjià Cóngshìshǐ,
and Shàngshū Lìbù Láng.
Once, when discussing figures from the Jianghuǒ region at 太祖's banquet,
the conversation turned to 顧榮.
袁淑 said to 覬之:
"You southerners are timid and cowardly.
How could you ever become a rebel?"
覬之, with a solemn expression, replied:
"Are you, then, mocking people for their loyalty and righteousness?"
淑 showed a look of shame.
When the primal villain usurped the throne,
all the court officials were transferred to new posts,
but 覬之 alone did not move from his office.
When 世祖 ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
In Xiàojiàn 1st year (454 CE),
he was appointed as 義陽王 Chǎng's Dōngzhōngláng Chángshǐ, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, and acting Prefect of Kuàijī Commandery.
Soon after, he was summoned to be Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently Lǐng Běnyì Zhōngzhèng.
The next year,
he was appointed as Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He was good at governing the people,
and his administration had many achievements.
In Dàmíng 1st year (457 CE),
he was summoned to be Dùzhī Shàngshū,
and concurrently Lǐng Běnzhōu Zhōngzhèng.
In the 2nd year,
he was transferred to Lìbù Shàngshū.
In the 4th year, he requested retirement,
but it was not granted.
At that time, 唐賜 of Xiāng County, Pèi Commandery, returned from drinking wine at the home of 朱起's mother, Péng, in a neighboring village.
Consequently, he fell ill,
vomiting more than ten parasitic worms.
Before he died, he told his wife Zhāng
to cut open his belly after his death to remove the illness.
Later, Zhāng herself cut him open and examined him.
His five viscera were all pulped and broken.
The commandery and county authorities considered Zhāng's brutal act of evisceration,
and that Cì's son Fù did not stop her.
The incident occurred before an amnesty,
so the law could not decide the matter.
The law for injuring a dead person
was four years' imprisonment;
a wife injuring her husband,
five years' imprisonment;
a son being unfilial to his parents,
abandonment in the marketplace.
None of these applied to the specific case.
Sāngōng Láng 劉勰 debated:
"Cì's wife painfully followed his dying words,
and her son understood how to avoid legal consequences.
Considering the original intention of the act,
it was not intended to be cruel and harmful.
It should be treated with compassion."
覬之 debated:
"The law states that moving a corpse by the roadside
is still considered unrighteous,
how much more so for a wife and son
to cruelly commit an act that ordinary people would not commit?
It is not appropriate to bend the law for minor emotions.
It should be judged by the great principle.
I submit that Fù is unfilial,
and Zhāng is equally unrighteous."
An imperial edict followed 覬之's deliberation.
He was appointed Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn
and assigned as Wú Commandery Tàishǒu.
In the 8th year,
he was again appointed Lìbù Shàngshū,
and concurrently Jǐshìzhōng.
Before he was formally invested,
he was considered for the post of Kuàijī,
but this did not materialize.
He returned to being Wú Commandery Tàishǒu.
The favored minister 戴法興 held immense power over the ruler,
but 覬之 never showed him any deference.
Zuǒguānglù Dàfū 蔡興宗, who was close to 覬之,
felt that his integrity was too unbending.
覬之 said:
"Xīn Pí once said: 'Sūn and Liú can do no more than prevent me from becoming a Sāngōng.'"
When 世祖 passed away,
法興 then appointed 覬之 as Guānglù Dàfū,
with the additional honors of gold seal and purple ribbon.
At the beginning of Tàizōng's Tàishǐ reign,
the four quarters rebelled simultaneously.
覬之's home was in Xúnyáng.
Xúnyáng Prince Zǐfáng offered him a position and title,
but 覬之 refused,
saying:
"Ritual dictates that at sixty years of age, one does not wear military attire,
because one's physical strength has declined,
and it is no longer the time for military campaigns.
Moreover, I am almost eighty,
with little life left.
I shall guard my home and family until the end,
and dare not accept the command."
孔覬 and others could not persuade him.
At that time, rebellion was widespread,
and no one could escape involvement.
Only 覬之 remained pure in heart and deed,
and had no part in it.
Tàizōng greatly praised him.
After the eastern lands were pacified,
he was appointed Zuǒjiāngjūn and Wú Commandery Tàishǒu,
with the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
In Tàishǐ 2nd year (466 CE),
he was again appointed Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his titles of Chángshì and Jiāngjūn remaining as before.
He died in the 3rd year,
at the age of seventy-six.
He was posthumously granted the title of Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn,
with his titles of Chángshì and Cìshǐ remaining as before.
His posthumous name was Jiǎnzǐ.
覬之's family was harmonious,
and highly respected by the prefecture and local community.
He had five sons: Yuē, Jī, Chuò, Zhěn, and Gǔn.
Chuò had considerable private wealth,
and many gentry and commoners in the locality owed him debts.
覬之 often tried to stop him but could not.
Later, when he became Wú Commandery Tàishǒu,
he enticed Chuò, saying:
"I always forbid you from collecting debts,
but to live in utter poverty is also impossible.
How many outstanding debts do people owe you?
While I am in the commandery,
I will supervise their collection for you.
You won't be able to do this in the future.
Where are all those debt certificates?"
Chuò was overjoyed,
and brought out all the documents and certificates in a large cabinet to 覬之.
覬之 burned them all,
and announced far and wide:
"Those who owe the Third Son debts
do not need to repay them;
all the certificates have been burned."
Chuò lamented and sighed for a full day.
覬之 often said that one's destiny has a fixed portion,
not to be shifted by intelligence or strength.
One should only humbly observe the Dao,
trust in Heaven and surrender to fate.
But the ignorant do not understand this,
and foolishly seek good fortune,
thereby merely undermining the elegant Way,
without affecting gains or losses.
He then instructed his disciple Yuàn to write "Dìngmìnglùn" (Treatise on Fixed Destiny) based on his ideas.
Its text reads: Confucius said:
"The Way is about to prevail,
it is destiny;
the Way is about to decline,
it is destiny."
Qīumíng also said:
"What Heaven supports cannot be destroyed;
what Heaven
destroys cannot be supported."
Bǔshāng also said:
"Life and death are determined by destiny;
wealth and honor are in Heaven."
Mèng Kē then used his failure to meet the Marquis of Lǔ as an excuse.
Thus, the strange
coincidences of fate,
and the coming together and separation of lives,
have their origins.
Sīmǎ Qiān, Líu Xiàng, Yáng Xióng, Bān Gù, and their like,
in their writings and pronouncements,
all regarded this as primary.
However, those who discuss
it in later generations
often differ.
I shall attempt to elaborate: The vital energy that gives rise to life
has clear and turbid sources;
the number that constitutes destiny
has varying outcomes of fullness and emptiness.
Therefore, hearts and appearances diverge,
natures and destinies vary.
Thus, there are differences between evil
and upright, dull and bright;
the order of long life and short, flourishing and withered.
All these principles were settled aeons ago,
and their evidence is manifest across countless generations.
Profound spirits silently observe,
and encompass
all.
Even minor skills like divination,
and humble arts like witchcraft and historical records,
can still predict rise and fall,
and foretell success and failure.
Calamities and blessings are set to a date;
insight cannot alter them.
Good
and ill fortunes are predetermined;
power and guards cannot prevent them.
If a peasant lived in an imperial palace,
could he avoid the curses of injury and suffering?
If a Han minister accumulated goods in the imperial treasury,
could he escape starvation
spirits.
Moreover, although the principles of good and evil are detailed,
the verification of fortune and misfortune often remains obscure;
the distinctions between compliance and defiance are indeed clear,
yet the effects of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness are frequently hidden.
Those whose wisdom
spans heaven and earth
still suffer disasters like being confined to a deep window;
those whose brilliance illuminates the sun and moon
are bound to encounter difficulties like being trapped in a deep cage.
Cultivating faith and accumulating virtue
does not prevent suffering from prolonged hunger;
embracing righteousness and sleeping on benevolence
may invite
calamity and shorten one's lifespan.
Why is this?
If fate's operation were necessarily responsive,
even the sagely and enlightened would still be troubled by it.
How much more so for those of trivial conduct and deluded minds,
who devote their hearts to the
realm of ignorance,
and wish to exert their thoughts to estimate advantages and disadvantages,
and calculate their fortune and misfortune by their feelings?
Their suffering would be severe,
would it not be profoundly misguided?
Therefore, the broad-minded *jūnzǐ*
keeps his
spirit calm and composed,
and his demeanor unhurried;
he does not go against common customs to gain reputation,
nor relies on the world to expect glory.
Being clear that nothing is false,
he seeks abundant blessings for himself.
As for honor and disgrace, long life and short,
what
concern are they?
Question: The *Shū* says, "He who follows the Way will be blessed with good fortune,"
and the *Yì* records, "He who treads with sincerity will meet with assistance."
The remaining discussions of ancient sages
also suggest that there are ways to anticipate and greet,
and that decline and blockage are not without signs;
there are methods to regulate and control
that lead to prosperity,
and early death and obstruction are not without cause.
A skilled swimmer may drown in a deep beam;
a master horseman may die in the vast wilderness.
A bright pearl attracts danger in the darkness;
a twisted log finds favor in its initial
form.
Thus, Hǎn and Yuè achieved long lives through their active benevolence;
Jǐng and Huì enjoyed extended records due to their hidden virtues.
Péng and Dòu prolonged their lives by their protective upkeep;
Yíng and Jì shortened their
years through dissolute indulgence.
Chén and Zhāng were lauded for their high positions as *táidǐng*;
Yán and Xīn thrived in their eminence as *zǎisī*.
As for those who indulged in evil and embraced misfortune,
lived in defiance and trod the path of disaster,
their stories are clearly recorded in historical annals,
making them easy to
examine and verify.
As for what is described in the texts of *Shénxiān*,
and written in the books of Tiānzhú,
though the events are hard to prove,
the principles are not easy to refute.
Remaining perplexed, wasting time,
I wish to hear your comprehensive judgment.
Answer: You are like one who "holds a rope and argues,"
or "follows a notch to discuss."
If "there are methods to regulate and control,"
is that not because good fortune is destined to occur?
If "there are ways to anticipate and greet,"
it is
truly because ill fortune brings itself upon one.
As for active benevolence and hidden virtues,
leading to long lives and distant years,
if we trace their origins,
which of them is not fate?
I have examined your recent points,
and compared them with previous discussions,
but you have only enlightened me on matters of commerce,
and I do not see what is different.
Lives are endowed and governed by fate,
varying in myriad ways;
compliance and defiance, auspiciousness and inauspiciousness,
their principles and numbers are not uniform.
Originally, eating peppers is not an art of nourishing life,
nor is chewing swords a means of protecting one's nature.
Where life is prolonged,
even when one gnaws on human bones,
and yet consuming rich delicacies
sometimes brings illness.
Deep ravines deviate from the
paths
of seeking favor,
and empty valleys are devoid of tracks for pursuing glory;
where destiny converges,
things wither even when they should grow,
and yet those who pore over official documents
ultimately suffer frustration.
Thus, Qiāo and Zhí acted recklessly;
Zēng and Yuán struggled.
Tāng and Zhōu enjoyed extended reigns;
Xǔ and Yì had their lines cut short.
The corresponding signs of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness
are intertwined like this.
Bì Wàn preserved his body,
while Mì Jiàn was beheaded.
Are the words of Liángyě
not sometimes fallacious?
Gǔnán and Lǔběi
gladly endured short lives;
by what method did Péng Wēng and Dòu Sǒu
prolong theirs?
Jìn Píng and Zhào Jìng's
debauchery
was complete;
why did the Hàn Lords and Wèi Chancellors
alone suffer premature deaths?
With such disparities,
which is right and which is wrong?
As for Léi Bīn's firm resolve,
thwarting ambitions and making grand plans;
Jí Jīn's secret
reverence,
achieving great merit that surpassed his age.
Fán Shēng's soaring rectitude,
inscribing texts that praised good deeds;
Huà Zǐ's lofty defiance,
carving strategies to punish wrongs.
All these are what Shì Héng called
"different paths leading to the same
destination."
Diverse paths leading to the same outcome
are indeed numerous in evidence.
The principle is easy to deduce,
and can be briefly stated.
In the past, when both capitals were flourishing,
and the world was prosperous,
nobles and favored officials gathered
like mist in their gates,
and powerful magnates moved like clouds in their strategies.
Trading and discussing were not
limited to Chén and Zhāng alone.
Looking at these two men,
their talents were not extraordinary,
yet one used them to gain
glory and enhance his standing,
while the other was ostracized and his reputation faded.
The operation of fortune and misfortune
can thus be clearly known.
Yán and Xīn did not adapt to the times and accept their fate,
but instead blamed honest and upright people;
were they also followers
of the geomancers?
As for what *Shénxiān* texts describe,
clearly stating cultivation practices,
the effectiveness of Qí Qiáng and Yān Píng
is not evident;
where is the result for Lǐ Tán and Dǒng Fēn?
The companions of Qiáo and Sōng
flew among the clouds and dwelt in the heavens;
the followers of Yí and Liè
moved with the wind and calmed the waters.
This is truly because their principles and destinies were extraordinarily prominent,
and they were indeed blessed
with such auspicious fates.
The ancient texts of Tiānzhú,
and the starry
records of Fāngcè,
based on predetermined creation,
and indicating a fixed time for karmic retribution,
with no difference between rich and poor,
no deviation in long or short lives;
these are acceptable trivial words,
and unobjectionable humble sayings.
Taken collectively,
which of them
is not fate?
Predetermined by hidden destiny,
each follows his destined path;
good and evil cannot alter their trajectory,
and the foolish and wise cannot change its principle.
If one praises his skill when successful,
and blames
his clumsiness when failing,
grasping it causes anxiety,
abandoning it causes sorrow;
this is truly to be entangled in recent afflictions,
would it not invite ridicule from the discerning?
Question: Your clear discourse enlightens my mind,
and your brilliant arguments fill my eyes,
but upon reflection in my humble thoughts,
there are still some points I do not fully grasp.
If all actions and stillness are determined by fate,
and danger and ease come from Heaven,
with the principle predetermined
period,
none did not arrive in obscurity.
Yùmén and Líqiū,
even the sagacious could not escape.
Is it not that the sage and the fool meet the same end,
and benevolence and cruelty achieve the same effect?
How then can the use of
light and darkness
be applied?
The reply was: The sage embraces emptiness to contain and nurture,
and collects brightness to illuminate thoroughly.
Because he is empty,
he is unobstructed in all directions;
because he is bright,
nothing comes
without being illuminated.
A dried sea and flowing gold
do not affect the extremes of warmth and coolness;
fierce soldiers and mighty rhinoceroses
do not suffer from claws or blades.
Forgetting life, life becomes more complete;
abandoning the spirit, the
spirit becomes more unhindered.
As for Yùmén and Líqiū,
they shared the same path as ordinary people,
thus they shared the same human troubles.
However, they unified their hearts with Heaven,
and thus were unharmed by Heaven's uniformity.
The great worthy, on the other hand,
has a fully equipped physique,
and his thoughts exhaust the hidden and the temporary.
He resides in adversity with quiet stillness,
and avoids peril by deep reverence.
All these are destined for purity and completeness,
hence they attain this wondrous wisdom.
Therefore, those who receive the Way of
Kǒng Ní
are not found on a speeding chariot;
those who possess the fortune of Bóyí
do not dwell beneath an overturned boat.
But if one ventures through difficulties and approaches dangers,
hesitatingly failing to achieve,
treading on peril
and stepping into traps,
diligently engaging in affairs—
this is the purview of the fool;
what can the sage do?
As for those of middle and lower caliber,
they let their hearts race and act wildly,
right and wrong are perverse and entangled,
fortune and misfortune shift and change.
Hence, Běigōng's intentions were contrary but his achievements were smooth;
Dōngmén's mind was obscure but his actions were clear.
Xuān Yīng abandoned divination and encountered good fortune;
Zhāng Sōng followed calculations and met disaster.
Moreover, the defenses of wisdom are
limited,
while the accumulation of troubles is boundless.
Hence, a rabid dog chased and Huá Zǐ fled;
a rotten rat was abandoned and the Yú clan was extinguished.
A caged ape escaped and the trees were ravaged;
a pearl in a box was lost and the pond
water dried up.
All such cases,
the intricate difficulties cannot be fully detailed.
To burden the body and exhaust the mind,
how can its efficacy be verified?
How can it compare to purifying the spiritual abode,
cleansing the divine dwelling,
taking the Way as
the heart,
and relying on Virtue as the thought?
This makes it so that when actions are exhausted, righteousness flourishes,
and when the self is at peace, principles are universally understood.
Is this not beautiful?
Why must one abandon this and take that?
The question was: Establishing standards and initiating transformation,
building reputation and leaving behind rules,
the rise of codes and regulations,
has a long history.
If indeed there are subtle signs from afar,
and obscure destinies indicating times,
good and
evil foreshadowed,
right and wrong predetermined,
then the Way of moral teachings
would almost cease to exist!
The reply was: Heaven gives birth to the myriad people,
and establishes principles for them.
The teachings and righteousness they receive,
how can they not be obscure destinies?
Why so?
The possession of form and vital energy
must depend on something to exist;
how can those who are simple and ignorant
exist without cause?
One must rely on fine silk to sustain life,
and depend on grain and meat to continue the lineage.
One must draw upon trustworthiness and propriety to cultivate nature,
and grasp integrity and righteousness to rectify
emotions.
The sage is acutely intelligent and profoundly virtuous,
treading the Way and comprehending transformation.
His whole being connects with Heaven and Earth,
his feelings align with the sun and moon.
He looks up and observes, looks down and examines,
managing the cosmic movement and shaping the winds.
Thus he reveals
the courses of the sun and stars,
rectifies the measures of frost and rain,
spreads the brilliance of clouds and mists,
and extends the richness of wind and dew.
He makes boats float to aid the stagnant,
and rides chariots to uplift the obscure.
He also distinguishes and organizes the three
powers (Heaven, Earth, Man),
and categorizes the five virtues.
He broadly expounds the principles of the seven bodies,
and clearly elucidates the threads of the eight guiding lines.
Therefore, when the times are harmonious in operation,
all regions naturally connect.
They embrace virtue and radiate harmony,
preserving
their true nature and maintaining their innate disposition.
Thus, trustworthiness and sustenance support each other,
acting as lips and teeth for each other.
Wealth and education depend on each other,
alternately forming the carriage and its wheels.
Now, if one abandons fine silk,
and completely ceases grain and meat,
and then claims
to seek life and commit to fate,
would this not already clarify their delusion?
As for obliterating integrity and righteousness,
and discarding trustworthiness and propriety,
and then blaming it on seeking survival or pushing fate,
they have not yet distinguished their confusion.
Connecting categories in this manner,
their perversity and absurdity grow even greater.
Therefore, the Way of teachings and righteousness
is what life's operations rely upon.
Favor and disgrace, flourishing and withering,
constantly arise from this.
This is inherently one
thing within destiny,
not something to be considered difficult.
The question was: Following the previous point,
it has been established that principle and destiny are predetermined,
and life's numbers are obscurely appointed.
Reviewing the latter text,
it also says to rely on moral teachings and
follow rules and examples.
If one relies on numbers and lets Heaven decide,
then one would indulge in emotions and let thoughts roam freely.
If one is bound by rules and trained by examples,
then one must guard thoughts and restrain loss.
A quiver and an arrow have different uses,
a spear and a dagger serve different purposes.
How can a discourse aiming for both excellences
achieve
both?
The reply was: The operations of nature are perverse and entangled,
and the heart and appearance are cunningly distinct.
Please allow me to express my humble thoughts,
briefly stating the essentials.
If one is blessed with good fortune,
one can indulge one's emotions and tread the Way,
training
one's nature to be compliant,
and following one's heart to be spiritually efficacious.
If one is afflicted by ill fate,
one will follow and practice perversity,
disbelieving words,
and prolonging evil without repentance.
This is the unchangeable difference between the foolish and the wise,
something that teachings
leave behind.
There are those who see good as if they cannot reach it,
and follow advice as if flowing downstream.
For these, destiny relies on teaching for completeness,
and fortune requires transformation for establishment.
It is like the house of a good doctor,
where the sick
are present.
As for those who clear their minds and purify their souls,
calm their hearts and stabilize their qi,
having no wanton ailments,
they rejoice without medicine.
This is called indulging emotions and treading the Way,
without needing to rectify anything.
If
it is a disease beyond cure,
even Chángsāng cannot treat it;
if it is a sickness of the internal organs,
Yángqìng cannot manage it.
This is following and practicing perversity,
cutting oneself off from regulation.
As for the destiny of Zhào Chǔ
Yíyǒng
needed Biǎnqúe before he could be made whole,
and the empress of Qí’s
term was certainly prolonged, needing Wénzhì before she could be saved.
It is also like moving a bell or following a prize,
where ancient patterns arise,
and good and evil
have no master,
but differ only according to where fate gathers them.
Rich foods may fill the table,
but a deep illness is not heeded;
jade and precious stones may fill a foot of space,
but a person in dire peril is not saved.
The appearance of stillness or agitation,
in an instant,
is necessarily thus;
the nature of straightness or crookedness,
through trials and tribulations, cannot be altered.
This is why Yí and Huì were equally sage but followed different paths;
Zūn and Sǒng were equally enlightened but pursued different affairs.
Even if one were to shackle
Yì and Ào,
they would still harbor the sentiments of Cháo and Xǔ;
or coerce Zēng and Shǐ,
they would utter the thoughts of Jiáo and Zhí.
Such things being unnatural,
it can be known with certainty.
If one must secretly
seek and aspire,
and cultivate one's hidden destiny,
even if one is lazy and indifferent,
how can it be achieved?
Therefore, when fate is like a flowing wave,
the situation allows no foresight;
when destiny stands like a mountain,
reason allows no indulgence.
If the uses of quivers and arrows differ,
why should both excellences be hindered?
If the discussion of spears and halberds varies,
how can both benefits be harmed?
Question: The affection between ruler and minister is deep,
the righteousness between teacher and student is firm,
this is why glory is bestowed and benefits are extended,
and reputations are lifted and upheld.
Thus, one may cut out one's heart and expose one's bowels,
sacrificing life to elevate
one's integrity;
one may burn one's wife and turn one's son to ashes,
burying one's name to repay righteousness.
If secret vows are heavenly omens,
then public renown can be overlooked;
if hidden destiny is self-determined,
then emotional responses and deeds should cease.
How can
that be so?
Answer: What the argument illuminates
takes the origin as principle,
and what the difficulty doubts
takes the consequence as function.
Indeed, the skill of hidden concealment is not transmitted,
and the regulation
of nascent development is long lost.
Therefore, knowing that it is foolish to praise reason
is what the ancients found difficult.
What I call fate
is inherently interwoven throughout past and present,
pervading beginning and end,
extending to rulers and ministers, fathers and
sons,
teachers and friends, husbands and wives;
all are secretly united by heavenly numbers,
and mystically arrive by divine movement.
Even to separations and affections, partings and reunions,
these are all distinguished by fate;
and to clarity and confusion, obedience and perversity,
these are also
gradual developments of destiny.
Just as pines and willows have different qualities,
and shepherd's purse and sowthistle have distinct natures,
thus a strong wind knows tough grass,
and severe frost recognizes firm trees.
How is this different from the quality of loyalty and filial piety,
where one's conduct is inherently
revealed early?
As for etching one's will to repay life,
inscribing sincerity to restore benevolence,
dying for integrity,
and yielding to righteousness while forgetting oneself,
it is also like how a stone can be broken,
but its hardness cannot be dissolved;
cinnabar
can be ground,
but its redness cannot be extinguished.
From this, it can be said that
the relationships of ruler and minister, teacher and student,
are both cases of secret vows being self-determined,
and the emotional responses and deeds of their hearts
are also heavenly omens of hidden destiny.
Why indeed
is this surprising?
Yuàn, courtesy name Zǐgōng,
son of Yuānzhī,
was a Sanjì Shìláng.
Yuàn loved learning
and was renowned for his literary compositions.
During the Dàmíng era, he was recommended as a Xiùcái,
and his policy responses accorded with the imperial will,
so he was promoted to Zuòzuò Zuǒláng
and Tàizǐ Shèrén.
He died young.
The historian comments: When Xiàojiàn established his foundation,
the Western Chǔ rebelled,
the troubles spread to the Huái and Jì rivers,
and their power grew to encompass the Jiāng region.
Zhū Xiūzhī distinguished himself in Hànnán,
Liú Xiùzhī pushed his vanguard a myriad miles.
Both sincerely endured hardships,
and their loyalty was only for the Emperor.
Yet, the vanguard that crossed Xiàn
won battles single-handedly,
while the army that emerged from the Gorges
had no boat return alone.
Although frost and snow occurred at the same time,
the merits awarded were different.
And when their final destinies were determined,
the disparities were vast.
This was probably because their righteousness was tied to the feudal court,
hence the differing degrees of favor.
Although old acquaintances are not forgotten,
as we have heard from previous teachings,
a grand reputation devoid of substance
is also undesirable.
Collation Notes:
Biographies, Chapter 42: Zhōu Lǎng, Shěn Huáiwén
Zhōu Lǎng, courtesy name Yìlì,
was a native of Ānchéng, Rǔnán.
His grandfather, Wén,
was a Huángmén Shìláng.
His father, Chún,
achieved high office early in the Sòng dynasty,
reaching the positions of Shìzhōng
and Tàicháng.
His elder brother, Qiáo,
married the fourth daughter of Gāozǔ, Princess Xuānchéng Dé.
His two daughters married Prince Jiànpíng Hóng and Prince Lújiāng Huī.
Being a noble relative and a prominent official,
at the end of Yuánjiā,
he became the Grand Administrator of Wúxīng.
When the rebel Shào assassinated the emperor and took the throne,
Prince Suí Dàn raised an army of righteousness in Kuàijī.
Shào appointed Qiáo as Guānjūn Jiāngjūn,
but Dàn's summons also arrived.

not a cessation.
Generally, the
world is governed by truth,
yet those who govern the world often maintain an illusion.
The ears and eyes of the people
cannot be deceived.
The rise and fall of governance
will immediately follow.
Therefore, for all
common people,
their institutions and customs become daily more extravagant.
The homes of merchants and peddlers
are adorned like those of kings and nobles,
and the bodies of hired servants
are dressed like empresses and consorts.
The size of one sleeve
is enough to be cut into two.
The length of one skirt
can be divided into two.
When seeing carriages and horses, one cannot distinguish between noble and common.
When looking at hats and clothes, one does not know rank.
If the imperial workshop now creates one item,
the common people will clearly
imitate it.
If the palace produces one dress in the morning,
common families will have already cut and copied it by evening.
The origin of luxury and splendor
is truly first in the imperial inner quarters.
Moreover, gifts bestowed by empresses and consorts
are not limited by rank.
From
now on,
this should be regulated.
Gold leaf and jade,
brocade and gauze,
unusual colors and strange patterns,
the common people are not allowed to wear them,
nor should those in high positions be allowed to bestow them.
If artisans again create strange techniques and excessive ornaments,
they should all be burned,
and their crime severely punished.
Furthermore, officials are appointed
to harmonize heaven and balance qi,
to assist in the achievements of the earth,
to guard against treachery and avert disaster,
to manage complex and arduous tasks,
so that officials match their duties,
and people are
appointed to officials,
without idly creating empty positions
or redundantly promoting surplus personnel.
Now, high and low positions exchange substance,
and large and small titles contradict each other.
This instability of names
is called corrupt officialdom.
And the world abandons Jī
The ducal system,
popularly transmitted as the laws of the Qín people,
detests the institutions of an enlightened ruler
and prefers the affairs of an ignorant lord.
How extreme
is its hatred of the sagely and love for the foolish!
Now, it is fitting to first
reduce affairs,
and then merge offices,
establishing positions according to the model of the Zhōu rites,
and changing names for their suitability to the times.
The late systems of Qín and Hàn,
why are they worth adopting?
It should be that those with profound virtue
have high positions,
and those with high positions receive heavy emoluments;
those with meager abilities have lowly offices,
and those with lowly offices receive light stipends.
Caps and ceremonial robes, sashes and pendants,
should match the office in attire;
carriages, cavalry, and guards,
should be granted
according to their duties.
Furthermore, the practice of granting land to zhōu and jùn,
should be universally abolished.
The old lands and their households
should be reorganized and established anew.
How can the Wú region have Xú settlements,
or the Yáng territory house Yǎn people,
thereby confusing the celestial records above,
and disrupting the imperial domains below?
Lands like Zhūfāng,
should not have zhōu established there;
lands like Jiāngdū,
should have new yì constructed instead.
Moreover, where the population is sparse, governance is easy;
where the ruler is near, allegiance is easy to secure.
All officials should have their abilities thoroughly examined,
and their stipends generously increased.
For a xiàn, one should not again employ the
poor from favored families;
for a jùn, one should not again select the aged from influential clans.
Furthermore, if kings and marquises are not yet capable of handling duties,
they should not be forced into office.
They must reach adulthood before their enfeoffment is activated,
and demonstrate administrative ability before their titles are discussed.
Moreover, if an imperial son is not yet an official,
who would consider
him lowly?
It is only fitting to carefully select his retainers and friends,
choosing upright individuals.
Why must he be appointed as a zhǎngshǐ, cānjūn, biéjià, or cóngshì
to be considered noble?
Moreover, there are
orders of precedence among generations,
and difficulties in undertakings.
Míng Dì could ensure that his sons did not emulate the sons of Guāngwǔ,
and Empress Mǎ could ensure that her family did not rival the clan of Empress Yīn.
How grand
this was!
This should not be forgotten by later generations.
As for the rage that crushes skulls beneath chariots,
and the awe of halberds extending from the palace steps,
these too must not be forgotten.
Internal and external governance
must truly not be mixed.
If a consort or princess petitions for an official position for someone,
that person should be prohibited from holding office for life.
If she petitions for a pardon,
that person also
should never be pardoned for life.
What the world truly needs is talent,
and talent is indeed difficult to discern.
Some live in seclusion and speak little,
thus they possess learning but have no means to be known;
some dwell in humble positions and are
isolated by circumstances,
thus they harbor extraordinary abilities but have no means to advance.
Some may be envied by relatives and old acquaintances,
or slandered by influential factions.
How can they then attract the attention of the emperor's carriage and move his imperial seat,
or speak to the world
and debate governance and disorder?
It is impossible!
Merely speaking of recommending the worthy
will certainly not bring such people to light.
It is fitting to ensure that those whom the world praises as skilled in the classics and history, eloquent in speech
and precise in calculation, capable in administration and military strategy, or possessing specialized skills and minor arts,
should be sought out, with lowered caps and bended knees,
to broadly discover their utility.
Regulate the internal and external officials, their proximity to each other, and the types of their
appointments,
so that each may establish their place according to their abilities.
Lower one's emotional stance to entice them,
humble oneself to pacify them.
Then, observe their pursed lips,
their prominent jaws and chins,
the stirring of their
spirits,
the eruption of their intentions and dispositions.
The extent of their words,
the grip of their intentions,
within just a few instances,
will not all of it be clearly discernible?
As for those of loyalty, filial piety, integrity, and purity,
or the resolute, upright,
generous, and gentle,
they are difficult to evaluate with fixed standards
and cannot be determined in an instant.
It is fitting to have the local communities seek out their conduct,
and the governors and magistrates observe their capabilities.
Ultimately, they should all be presented to the esteemed selectors,
and submitted to the chief ministers,
before their appropriate duties are assigned
and their positions and uses determined.
If this is done,
then all the ignorant and vulgar should be discarded,
and all the worthy and enlightened promoted.
Furthermore, it is a common fault to
condemn and suppress people
without investigating the reasons for the condemnation;
and to advance people based on praise
without examining the reasons for the praise.
If all those who condemn are vulgar,
then the one who is condemned
should be promoted;
if all those who praise are mediocre,
then the one who is praised should be demoted.
If this is done,
then condemnation and praise will not be groundless,
and good and evil will be distinguished.
Moreover, once someone is deemed talented,
they should not be limited by
rank
or judged by age.
Generally, the noble tend to doubt the young,
unaware that they themselves are less capable than the young.
The old also despise the young,
unaware that they
are inferior to the young.
Since the Buddhist teachings spread,
their origin has been clear,
and their profound scrutiny and precise measurement
are indeed not superficial.
Their expansive guidance and nourishing embrace
have also become widespread.
However, those who practice wisdom daily
neglect their cultivation,
and those who are bound by precepts monthly multiply their transgressions.
They have gone so far as to lavish fine silks,
and extravagantly adorn their carriages and retinues.
They further feign refined medical skills,
[一三] and claim miscellaneous divination techniques.
They fill their homes with
beautiful women,
[一四] and cover their halls with wine.
There are not a few who send their husbands away and entrust their wives to others,
and instances of killing children to beg for sons continually occur.
Yet they still rely on spiritual power and false images,
defy their parents and scorn their ruler,
deceive
and exhaust the sick and elderly,
and damage and destroy temples and dwelling places.
These are acts that outer laws cannot punish,
and inner teachings do not regret,
yet they prevail between heaven and earth,
without anyone rectifying or investigating them.
Humans should not be like this;
are they then ghosts?
Now, it is fitting to stringently enforce Buddhist regulations
and reinforce national laws.
Those whose faults and evils are conspicuous
should all be dismissed and expelled.
For the rest, according to their
skills and conduct,
[一五] specific rules should be made for each,
so that for meditation, doctrine, or scripture recitation,
each person excels in one;
their food should not exceed vegetables,
and their clothes should not be finer than plain cloth.
If some are to be newly ordained,
they should first
practice virtuous conduct and
root their spiritual minds.
Only those truly capable of transforming the mundane into the divine,
who earnestly aspire towards enlightenment,
even if they are sons of marquises or kings,
should not be restricted.
As for ghost cults that bewilder the populace,
and sorcerers and witches who corrupt customs,
those who touch wood and speak of oddities are countless,
and those who harbor evil and claim divinity are immeasurable.
Their origins are
Chaos in men and women,
mingled eating and drinking,
then performing prayers and invocations,
and consequently making petitions for recompense.
Such chaos is not punished,
and the harm it causes does not cease.
Whenever a park is first established,
and a
deity first arises,
licentious customs become rampant because of it.
Now, north of the repaired dikes,
a park a hundred *lǐ* is established.
To the right of the towering mountains,
ten shrines of spirits are situated.
They waste wealth and corrupt customs,
their
extent is beyond estimation.
Furthermore, the art of acupuncture and moxibustion
is seldom practiced by the world,
and the skill of pulse diagnosis
few people can master.
Consequently, the common people increasingly appeal to ghosts,
and thus abandon medicine.
This
causes dissipation and delusion to persist,
and death and premature demise to once again be halved.
Now, the Imperial Physicians should instruct men and women in these practices.
Officials should be dispatched to various places to receive instruction.
This will surely be superior to the
folly of flattering spirits,
and will correct the defects in the skin and internal organs.
〔一六〕There is no generation without discussions of affairs,
and no time without decrees issued.
〔一七〕Yet peace and prosperity do not arrive,
and darkness and danger follow one another.
Why is this?
It is because the basis of establishing decrees
is not genuine.
Moreover, critical words do not come from trusted ministers,
and affairs do not benefit the powerful factions.
Minor offenses lead to criticism and alarm,
while serious ones result in death, suppression, impoverishment, and ostracism.
Thus, in the Western Jīng
there was the punishment of Fāng Diào,
and in the Eastern Dū there were the persecutions of Dǎng Gù.
〔一八〕If Your Majesty wishes to uphold conventional decrees
and follow minor statutes,
then your assembled ministers are here.
If you wish to change old
regulations
and promote the Kingly Way,
then this humble minister still exists.
I dare to risk death to present this,
and humbly ask Your Majesty to examine it.
The memorial was presented, displeasing the emperor,
and he resigned his post.
He was then removed from the position of Heir Apparent's Attendant [Zhōng Shèrén],
and sent out to be the Administrator of Lúlíng.
The commandery later became desolate,
and frequently had wild beasts.
His mother, Lady Xuē, wished to see a hunt.
Lǎng then organized a encirclement and started a fire,
allowing his mother to watch it.
The fire escaped and burned the commandery office.
Lǎng used all his official salary to rebuild the houses,
compensating for the extent of what was burned.
He claimed illness and left office,
and was subsequently impeached by the provincial inspector.
Upon returning to the capital, he apologized to Shìzǔ, saying:
“The provincial inspector pointed out my faults,
many of which are unfounded.
While I was in the commandery,
tigers ate people three times,
and insects and rats damaged crops.
For these two matters, I have failed Your Majesty.”
The Emperor's expression changed, and he said:
“The provincial inspector's unfounded claims
might be possible.
But the calamities of insects and tigers,
how do they concern a small official like you?”
Lǎng soon observed mourning for his mother,
and had a filial nature,
always wailing uncontrollably when he cried.
However, in other respects, he did not strictly adhere to the customary rites of mourning.
In the fourth year of Dàmíng,
the Emperor ordered the relevant officials to memorialize about his improper conduct during mourning,
requesting his arrest and punishment.
The imperial edict said:
“Lǎng is defiant of rites and glib-tongued.
He should be put to death.
Such a trivial person is not worthy of disrupting the legal system.
He is specially [⿰⺡⿱宀⿺元攵] sent to a border commandery.”
Thereupon, he was transported to Níngzhōu,
and killed on the way,
at the age of thirty-six.
His son, Rénzhāo,
was the Administrator of Nánhǎi at the end of Shùndì's Shēngmíng era.
Shěn Huáiwén, whose courtesy name was Sīmíng,
was a native of Wǔkāng, Wúxīng.
His grandfather, Jì,
was the Grand Master of Ceremonies [Guānglùxūn] of the Jìn dynasty.
His father, Xuān,
was the Administrator of Xīn'ān.
Huáiwén was fond of profound principles in his youth,
and was skilled in writing essays.
He once wrote a poem for the two consorts of King Chǔzhāowáng,
which was praised by the world.
Initially, he was appointed Assistant [Cóngshì] by the province,
then transferred to Director of the Western Bureau [Xīcáo].
He served as Army Supervisor [Xíng Cānjūn] to King Jiāngxià Yìgōng, the Grand Marshal [Sīkōng].
He was transferred with the office to Assistant Military Advisor [Sītú Cānjūnshì],
and later Libationer of the Eastern Pavilion [Dōnggé Jìjiǔ].
He mourned his father's death.
The Xīn'ān commandery sent a generous sum for the funeral.
After the funeral rites were completed,
he distributed all the remainder to his relatives,
keeping nothing for himself.
Tàizǔ heard of this and praised him,
bestowing six slaves upon him.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Palace Attendant [Diànzhōngláng] in the Department of State Affairs [Shàngshū].
The recluse Léi Cìzōng was summoned and resided at Mount Zhōngshān.
Later, he returned south to Mount Lú.
Hé Shàngzhī set up a farewell banquet,
and scholars of literature gathered.
They composed linked verses,
and Huáiwén's composition was particularly beautiful,
his words excelling all others present.
Due to a public case, he was exempted (from punishment),
while his colleagues all lost their posts.
Huáiwén alone remained.
He accompanied King Suí Dàn, who was garrisoned at Xiāngyáng.
He was appointed Chief Clerk of the Rear Army [Hòujūn Zhǔbù],
and jointly managed official documents with the Advisory Military Advisor [Zīyì Cānjūn] Xiè Zhuāng,
and was also appointed Administrator of Yìchéng.
In the twenty-eighth year of Yuánjiā,
Dàn was to be appointed Administrator of Guǎngzhōu.
He wanted to make Huáiwén his Secretary of the Protectorate General of Annan [Ānnánfǔ Jìshì].
〔一九〕He was first appointed Gentleman-in-Attendance [Tōngzhíláng].
Huáiwén firmly declined to go south,
and the Emperor was displeased.
His younger brother, Huáiyuǎn, took Wáng Yīngwǔ, an adopted daughter of Princess Dōngyáng, as his concubine.
The Prime Evil [Yuánxiōng] practiced witchcraft,
and Yīngwǔ was involved.
When the matter was exposed,
Huáiwén's career was consequently hindered,
and he became a Censor Supervising Documents [Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ].
When the Prime Evil assassinated and took the throne,
he made Huáiwén a Censor of the Central Secretariat [Zhōngshū Shìláng].
When Shìzǔ marched to suppress the rebellion,
Shào called upon him to draft manifestos and decrees.
Huáiwén firmly refused.
Shào was furious,
and threw his brush to the ground, saying:
“At this difficult time,
do you wish to shirk your duties?”
His tone was extremely harsh.
Yīn Chōng happened to be present,
and interceded, allowing him to be spared.
He feigned illness and falling from his horse,
then traveled secretly to Xīntíng.
He was appointed Military Advisor to King Jìnglín Dàn, Commander of the Garrison Army [Wèijūn Jìshì Cānjūn], and Administrator of Xīnxīng.
He also served Dàn as Chief Clerk to the Commander of Swift Cavalry [Piàojì Lùshì Cānjūn] and Administrator of Huáinán.
At that time, the nation was still in mourning.
Dàn wished to establish an inner fasting chamber,
but Huáiwén deemed it improper,
and so he stopped.
He was soon transferred to Supervisor of Affairs [Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ] of Yángzhōu.
At the time, there was a discussion to reduce the number of Secretaries of the Department of State.
Wáng Huáiwén considered it inappropriate.
His memorial stated:
"In ancient times, the heavenly officials rightly kept records,
and the six canons ordered their functions.
The master of chariots managed equalization,
and the seven treasuries completed their tasks.
This was how they assisted in stabilizing the celestial and earthly balances,
and maintained and supported the pillars of the state.
Therefore, the origin of overall subordination
was established in official regulations,
and the essentials of harmony and unity
were clearly expressed in the state's pronouncements.
The Xià dynasty followed the Rites of Yú,
with the principle of the great chief minister;
the Zhōu dynasty inherited the laws of Yīn,
without diminishing the protocols for managing the state.
Thus, they coordinated and assisted the king in equalization,
and brightly upheld the imperial standards.
Moreover, the system of laws and regulations
was greatly enforced in the Hàn court;
the model of setting forth ordinances
was highly esteemed in the Wèi dynasty.
Although the name 'clerks and recorders'
emerged in the middle period,
the reality of comprehensive administration
has not deviated from ancient times,
successive generations have followed it,
and throughout all dynasties, there has been no variation.
As for ranks changing with circumstances,
and grades being modified over time,
these are all ways of rise and fall,
without harming the state's regulations.
The eight cardinal responsibilities
have never been abolished or altered.
According to the duties of the Grand Ministers,
the third is the canon of rites,
to harmonize the states
and to unify the myriad officials.
The fourth is the canon of administration,
to pacify the states
and to rectify the myriad officials.
Zhèng Kāngchéng said: 'The chief minister [zhǒngzǎi] comprehensively manages all subordinate officials without exception.'
Considering this meaning,
it is fully present in the canonical texts.
Comparing ancient times with the present,
it is not appropriate to idly abandon it."
It was not followed.
He was promoted to Aide to the Governor,
when Prince Yìgōng of Jiāngxià was promoted,
and Prince Zishàng of Xīyáng became the Governor of Yángzhōu.
He continued in his office as before.
At that time, the planet Huǒxīng (Mars) was observed in the Nándǒu constellation.
The Emperor then abolished the old Xīzhōu residence
and made Zishàng move to the East City to suppress the omen.
Wáng Huáiwén said:
"When the Way of Heaven shows changes,
one should respond with virtue.
Even if Xīzhōu is emptied now,
I fear it will be of no benefit."
It was not followed,
and Xīzhōu was indeed abandoned.
〔二０〕In Dàmíng 2nd year (458 CE),
he was promoted to Director of the Bureau of Personnel in the Department of State.
At that time, the court discussed establishing a royal domain according to ancient systems,
and moving the seat of Yángzhōu to Kuàijī.
This was still due to the astronomical omen.
Wáng Huáiwén said:
"The Zhōu system established royal domains,
and the Hàn dynasty established the Sīlì (Capital Superintendent).
Each was based on the circumstances of the time,
not to be contradictory;
pacifying the people and bringing peace to the nation,
their principle is one.
If the hearts of the people are at peace,
Heaven will also follow them.
It is not necessarily by changing the present and pursuing the ancient
that true peace and unity will be achieved.
The old land of Shénzhōu,
inherited through generations,
is different from border provinces,
which might be abolished or established.
Since public sentiment is displeased,
it may undermine the foundation of transformation."
Again, it was not followed.
In the 3rd year (459 CE),
Zishàng moved his garrison to Kuàijī,
and Wáng Huáiwén was promoted to Chief Clerk of the Army,
acting for the prefecture and province.
At that time, many people were imprisoned,
often for months and years.
Upon Wáng Huáiwén's arrival in office,
he interrogated 936 cases in five commanderies.
Everyone praised his fairness.
He entered the court as a Palace Attendant,
receiving great favor and intimacy.
He was to be made the Administrator of Kuàijī,
but the matter did not proceed.
Prince Dàn of Jìnglíng rebelled, holding Guǎnglíng.
When the city fell,
the gentry and commoners were all stripped naked and whipped in the face
before being executed.
The heads of those killed were piled up on the south bank of Shítou,
called "Skull Mountain."
Wáng Huáiwén argued against this,
but the Emperor did not accept it.
When Yángzhōu moved to Kuàijī,
the Emperor was angered by the disharmony among the people east of the Zhèjiāng River,
and wanted to reduce their emoluments and rewards.
Only the old residents of Xīzhōu would not be changed.
Wáng Huáiwén said:
"The relocation of Yángzhōu's seat
already goes against public sentiment;
to have two different regulations within one province
is an even greater loss of overall principle.
I believe there should be no distinction."
Again, the Emperor did not follow him.
Wáng Huáiwén had always been on good terms with Yán Jùn and Zhōu Lǎng.
Yán Jùn was executed for displeasing the Emperor,
and Zhōu Lǎng was also condemned for offending him.
The Emperor said to Wáng Huáiwén:
"If Yán Jùn had known I would kill him,
he probably wouldn't have acted this way."
Wáng Huáiwén remained silent.
Once, on New Year's Eve, he was summoned by imperial decree to the palace together with Xiè Zhuāng, Wáng Jǐngwén, and Yán Shībó.
Before they could advance,
Wáng Jǐngwén, in the course of conversation, praised the talents of Yán Jùn and Zhōu Lǎng.
Wáng Huáiwén agreed with him.
Yán Shībó later reported this conversation to the Emperor.
Wáng Huáiwén had repeatedly offended and been opposed;
at this point, the Emperor was doubly displeased.
The Emperor also broke up the gentry families of various commanderies
to fill military and civil posts.
None would serve,
and they all fled.
Even strict regulations could not stop them.
Then military law was adopted;
those caught would be immediately beheaded.
Everyone fled to the mountains and lakes,
gathering as bandits.
Wáng Huáiwén again spoke against this.
The silk in the imperial storehouses,
annually levied at tens of thousands of bolts,
and cotton likewise.
The deadlines were strict and severe.
For one bolt of silk bought by commoners,
it cost two to three thousand (cash);
one ounce of cotton also cost three to four hundred.
The poor sold their wives and children,
and some even hanged themselves.
Wáng Huáiwén fully detailed the people's hardship.
Because of this, the cotton and silk levies were slightly reduced,
but soon reverted to their old levels.
Zishàng and other imperial princes all established agencies,
profiting from a tenth of transactions,
causing trouble throughout the empire.
Wáng Huáiwén again addressed this, saying:
"Trading in shops
was condemned by the ancients;
thus, Bǔ Shì explained the reason for lack of rain,
and Sāng Hóngyáng bore the blame for causing drought.
If it is difficult to stop immediately because expenses are insufficient,
then it should be appropriately reduced."
He was not listened to.
Since Xiàojiàn (454-456 CE),
the Emperor had suppressed his younger brothers.
After the pacification of Guǎnglíng,
he wanted to further tighten the regulations concerning them.
Wáng Huáiwén said:
"Emperor Míng of Hàn did not allow his sons to be compared to the sons of Emperor Guāngwǔ;
former historians considered this a beautiful story.
Your Majesty, having understood the executions of Guǎn and Cài,
I hope you will uphold the trusts given to Táng and Wèi."
When Prince Xiūmào of Hǎilíng was executed,
the Emperor wanted to proceed with the previous discussion.
Grand Preceptor Yìgōng, Prince of Jiāngxià, secretly learned of the imperial intention
and initiated the discussion first.
Wáng Huáiwén firmly maintained it was not permissible,
and because of this, the matter was suspended.
At that time, the Emperor's excursions were excessive.
The Empress Dowager and the six palaces often rode in escort carriages behind.
Huáiwén and Wáng Jǐngwén each repeatedly remonstrated that frequent outings were inappropriate.
Later, they were sitting together under a pine tree,
when the wind and rain became very strong.
Jǐngwén said:
"Sir, you can speak now."
Huáiwén said:
"Speaking alone is inconsequential;
we should remonstrate together."
Jiāng Zhìyuān, who was lying by the grass,
also thought it would be good to speak.
Soon after, they were summoned to enter the pheasant enclosure together.
Huáiwén said:
"With such wind and rain,
it is not suitable for Your Sacred Person to be exposed."
Jǐngwén then said:
"What Huáiwén has brought up should be followed."
Before Zhìyuān could say anything,
the Emperor, who was loading a crossbow,
changed countenance and said:
"Do you wish to emulate Yán Jùn?
How dare you know human affairs."
He also said:
"That young fellow Yán Jùn,
〔二一〕I regret not having whipped his face!"
Whenever the Emperor held a banquet,
he made all those present get thoroughly drunk.
Huáiwén habitually did not drink,
nor did he enjoy joking around.
The Emperor thought he deliberately wanted to be different.
Xiè Zhuāng once admonished Huáiwén, saying:
"You are always different from others;
how can this last long?"
Huáiwén said:
"I have been like this since childhood;
how can I change overnight?
It is not that I wish to be different;
it is simply my nature."
In the fifth year [of Xiàojiàn],
he was appointed Zhǐngwǔ Chángshǐ of Prince Jìn'ān Zǐxún and Gǔanglíng Tàishǒu.
The following year,
he attended the morning court,
and after the business was concluded, he was dispatched to return north.
〔二二〕He sought to extend his stay due to his daughter's illness.
At his farewell,
he again requested to stay for three days,
but even after the period, he still did not leave.
He was impeached by the relevant authorities,
dismissed from office,
and imprisoned for ten years.
After his dismissal,
he sold his residence, intending to return east.
〔二三〕The Emperor was greatly angered,
had him arrested and handed over to the Tíngwèi,
and bestowed upon him death.
He was fifty-four years old at the time.
He had three sons: Dàn, Yuān, and Chōng.
His younger brother, Huái Yuǎn,
served as Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn's Zhēngběi Chángliú Cānjūn,
and was deeply trusted and favored.
Because he took Wáng Yīngwǔ as a concubine,
Shìzǔ banished him to Guǎngzhōu,
and ordered Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ Zōng Yuè to kill him in the south.
At that time, Nánjùn Wáng Yìxuān rebelled.
Huái Yuǎn was quite skilled in writing.
Zōng Yuè raised an army,
and made him compose a declaration,
and also carry the order to Shǐxīng,
to discuss the uprising with Shǐxīng Xiàng Shěn Fǎxì.
After the rebellion was quelled,
Zōng Yuè made a full plea for him,
and he was consequently pardoned.
He was unable to return for the remainder of Shìzǔ's reign.
Although Huáiwén repeatedly pleaded for his return,
it was never granted.
During the reign of the Former Deposed Emperor,
those who had been banished were all allowed to return to their native places,
and he served as Wǔkāng Lìng.
He compiled the Nányuè Zhì and Huáiwén Wénjí,
both of which are still extant.
The Imperial Historian states: In the past, Lóu Jìng, a frontier soldier,
left his chariot and moved the imperial capital.
Féng Táng, old and lowly,
with a single phrase enlightened a wise ruler.
They had no noble status as dukes, marquises, or high officials,
nor did they possess a reputation built on trust,
but merely by a single word that aligned with the imperial will,
they garnered the respect of the Emperor.
From then on, people from mountains and valleys, commoners in humble clothes,
all came to the palace gate to present their memorials,
like a dense fog gathering.
From Hàn to Wèi,
this custom remained unbroken.
When it came to the Jìn dynasty,
superficiality and falsehood became the norm;
people sought only self-preservation,
and officials valued avoiding duties.
When Sòngzǔ ascended,
he sought to correct past mistakes;
though he reformed extravagance and discarded ostentation,
and promoted the teachings of proper conduct,
the path for listening to advice was not fully opened,
and the system for collecting words was not widely implemented.
As for humble servants and low-ranking officials,
whose righteousness aligned with imperial calculations,
they were merely hindered because their ideas were not their own creation,
and even if they knew what was appropriate, they could not follow it.
The way it was opened in the past was like that,
and the way it is blocked now is like this.
It is not that Xú Lè and Yán Ān
were exceptionally abundant in the Hàn era,
or that Dōngfāng Shúo
and Zhǔfù Yàn
were uniquely absent in the Sòng era,
but rather it is due to whether they were used or not.
Merely establishing the intent to seek advice,
and issuing empty decrees for unreserved speech,
is but to admire antiquity and feign sincerity,
which is not truly listening attentively.
Literati, taking advantage of this,
each indulged in displaying their eloquence.
Zhōu Lǎng's eloquent arguments
often touched upon vital administrative matters,
but his intent was to display his literary skill,
and his writing actually offended the Emperor.
Could the burden of literary skill
lead to such an extent?

Biographies, Chapter Forty-Three: Zōng Yuè, Wú Xǐ, Huáng Huí.
Zōng Yuè was a native of Yè,
Nányáng.
Originally from Hénán,
during the Jìn disturbances,
his family moved to Wǎn County, Nányáng,
and was later registered as belonging to Yè through land reallocation.
Originally, his family was a secondary household in Nányáng.
When Ānběi Jiāngjūn Zhào Lúnzhī was stationed in Xiāngyáng,
there were many mixed surnames in Xiāngyáng.
Lúnzhī ordered Chángshǐ Fàn Jìzhī to categorize the clans
and distinguish their status.
Jìzhī designated Yuè as a service household.
He began his career as a county clerk.
His father was killed by barbarians.
One time, the person who killed his father came out of the county seat,
and Yuè stabbed and killed him in the marketplace.
Tàishǒu Xiàhóu Mù commended his spirit
and promoted him to Duìzhǔ.
Whenever there were barbarian bandits,
Yuè was often sent to suppress them,
and he always achieved success.
His family was poor and could not afford to buy a horse,
so he always went out on foot with a sword and shield,
fighting single-handedly.
No one could stop him.
Each time he won a victory,
the county commander would reward him five thousand cash,
which enabled him to buy a horse.
Later, he was summoned
and left the province to become a Duìzhǔ.
When Shìzǔ was stationed in Xiāngyáng,
he appointed him Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn,
commanding the imperial guard.
In the twenty-fourth year of Yuánjiā,
he petitioned Tàizǔ to restore his secondary household status
and transfer his household to Guānjūn County,
which was granted.
In the twenty-seventh year,
he followed Liǔ Yuánjǐng on the Northern Expedition,
commanding a cavalry unit,

He distinguished himself in battle;

Liú Hú shì zài Dèng Wǎn zhuàn.
Wǔ Niàn,
was a native of Xīnyě.
He originally belonged to the Sānwǔmén,
and began his career as a Jùnjiàng.
When Xiāo Sīhuà was Governor of Yōngzhōu,
he sent the local man Páng Dàofú to command the Liùmén fields.
Niàn was Dàofú's suíshēnduìzhǔ.
Later, the Dàfǔ, impressed by Niàn's reputation for bravery
and his family's wealth in horses,
summoned him to become a general.
When Shìzǔ came to Yōngzhōu,
Niàn led his troops to welcome him.
At that time, the Man people of Miǎnzhōng rebelled.
When Shìzǔ went to quell them,
he campaigned along the way.
When his forces reached Dàdī Yánzhōu,
several thousand Man people suddenly appeared,
shooting arrows down like rain from high ground.
Niàn charged forward and attacked furiously,
