and they were immediately routed.
He was forthwith promoted to Cānjūn Dūhù.
Thereafter, in every military campaign,
he consistently achieved battle merits.
During Shìzǔ's Xiàojiàn era,
he served as Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Guìyáng Tàishǒu.
When Jìnglíngwáng Dàn rebelled,
Niàn, as Jiāngxiàwáng Yìgōng Tàizǎi Cānjūn and Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn,
was attached to Shěn Qìngzhī's forces to attack Guǎnglíng City.
Dàn fled the city,
but soon returned.
Niàn pursued him but could not catch him,
and was dismissed from office as a consequence.
He was reinstated as Rǒngcóng Púyè,
and then sent out as Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn and Nányáng Tàishǒu.
During the Qián Fèidì Jǐnghé era,
he became Yòujūn Jiāngjūn,
Zhígé,
and was enfeoffed as Kāiguó Xiànnán,
with a stipend of three hundred households.
When Tàizōng first ascended the throne,
there were rebellions in all directions.
Niàn was sent by swift relay horse back to Yōngzhōu
to pacify and reassure the western region,
and was consequently made Nányáng Tàishǒu.
Upon Niàn's arrival,
everyone's sentiments were towards him.
Liú Hú sent several of his trusted henchmen to pretend to surrender to Niàn.
They seized Niàn at the gathering,
and Yuán Yǐ beheaded him,
sending his head to Jìn'ānwáng Zǐxūn.
Niàn's partisan, Yuán Chǔzhēn, fled to Shòuyáng,
where he was captured by the rebel leader Liú Shùn.
He was subjected to every kind of torture
but remained unyielding in his principles.
Later, he managed to escape to Liú Miǎn.
Tàizōng commended him
and made him Fèngcháoqǐng.
Niàn was posthumously granted the titles of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Tàishǒu of the two commanderies of Nányáng and Xīnyě,
and enfeoffed as Suī'ān Xiànhóu,
with a stipend of four hundred households.
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ,
Suī'ān Xiàn was abolished,
and he was re-enfeoffed as Shàolíng Xiàn.
Jiǎo Chángshēng
was a native of Guǎngpíng.
He began his career as a Xiànjiàng.
The Dàfǔ, recognizing his great strength,
summoned him to be a Fǔjiàng.
When Zhū Xiūzhī repelled Lǔ Xiù south of Xiàn,
Chángshēng distinguished himself in battle
and gradually gained trust and responsibility.
Early in Tàizōng's reign,
he served as Jiàn'ānwáng Xiūrén Sītú Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
and was granted the additional title of Níngshuò Jiāngjūn.
He achieved merit in the southern campaign
and was enfeoffed as Qiānlíng Xiànhóu,
with a stipend of eight hundred households.
Later, he became Zhāng Yuè Níngyuǎn Sīmǎ
and Níngmán Xiàowèi.
In the fifth year of Tàishǐ,
he died,
and was posthumously granted the titles of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Cài Nà
was a native of Guānjūn, Nányáng.
His family was always wealthy.
Nà's elder brother Jū was skilled at entertaining guests.
Regardless of how many guests arrived,
he would provide for them all,
which earned them high regard from the commandery and county,
and they were exempted from taxes and levies.
Nà initially served as Jiànfú Shùzhǔ,
and gradually rose to become a general's aide in the Dàfǔ.
Early in Tàizōng's reign,
he served as Jiàn'ānwáng Xiūrén Sītú Zhōngbīng Cānjūn
in the southern campaign.
Nà's sons and younger brothers were all in Xiāngyáng,
and were captured by Liú Hú.
In every battle, Hú would hang them outside the city walls,
but Nà fought even more fiercely.
For his achievements, he was enfeoffed as Píngyáng Xiànhóu,
with a stipend of five hundred households.
He gradually rose to Liú Yùn Fǔjūn Sīmǎ and Níngmán Xiàowèi,
and was granted the additional title of Níngshuò Jiāngjūn.
In the first year of Tàiyù,
he was appointed Yìzhōu Cìshǐ and Sòngníng Tàishǒu with his existing rank.
Before he could be formally installed,
he died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Fǔshī Jiāngjūn,
with other honors remaining as before,
and was given the posthumous name Píng Hóu.
Cáo Xīnzhī
was a native of Xīnyě.
After accumulating diligent service,
in the early Yuánhuī era of the Hòu Fèidì,
he became a Jūnzhǔ.
For his achievement in pacifying Guìyángwáng Xiūfàn,
he was enfeoffed as Xīnshì Xiànzǐ,
with a stipend of five hundred households.
He served as Zuǒjūn Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn
and was granted the additional title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
In the fourth year of Yuánhuī,
he was appointed Xúzhōu Cìshǐ and Zhōnglí Tàishǒu with his existing rank,
and promoted to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the second year of Shùndì Shēngmíng,
he was summoned to be Sànqí Chángshì and Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
In the third year,
he died.
Wú Xǐ
was a native of Lín'ān, Wúxīng.
His original name was Xǐgōng,
but Tàizōng shortened it to Xǐ.
He began his career as a Báiyī Lì in the Lǐngjūnfǔ.
He had some knowledge of writing from a young age.
Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Shěn Yǎnzhī had him copy the Qǐjūzhù.
After he finished copying,
he could recite almost all of it from memory.
Yǎnzhī once drafted a memorial of resignation,
but before it was submitted,
he lost the original.
Having seen it once, Xǐ
immediately rewrote it,
without any omissions.
Yǎnzhī was greatly impressed by him.
Because of this, Xǐ delved into history and the Hàn dynasty texts,
gaining considerable knowledge of ancient and modern times.
Yǎnzhī's disciple Zhū Chóngmín became his Zhǔshū
and recommended Xǐ as a Zhǔshū Shūlì,
who was then promoted to Zhǔtú Lìshǐ.
Tàizǔ once requested books and maps.
Xǐ presented them by opening the scrolls upside down,
which angered Tàizǔ,
and he was dismissed.
At that time, Tàizǐ Bùbīng Xiàowèi Shěn Qìngzhī was campaigning against the Man people.
He memorialized Tàizǔ to request Xǐ to accompany him,
and his missions back and forth
earned him appreciation from Shìzǔ.
When Shìzǔ raised his banner of righteousness at Bākǒu,
Xǐ was ill
and unable to follow Qìngzhī south.
After the affair was settled,
Shìzǔ made Xǐ his Zhǔshū,
and he gradually gained trust and favor,
being promoted to Zhūwáng Xuégūanlìng,
Zuǒyòu Shàngfānglìng,
Hédōng Tàishǒu,
and Diànzhōng Yùshǐ.
During the Dàmíng era,
several thousand fugitives in Yī and Shè counties
attacked and broke into the county seats,
killing officials.
Yùzhāngwáng Zǐshàng was Governor of Yángzhōu,
stationed in Kuàijī.
He twice dispatched commanders
with three thousand men to campaign by land and water.
They went twice
but suffered defeat.
Shìzǔ then sent Xǐ with several tens of men to the two counties.
He persuaded the bandits through enticement,
and the bandits surrendered on the same day.
When Tàizōng 泰宗 first ascended the throne,
rebellions erupted on all sides,
and the eastern forces were particularly pressing.
Wú Xǐ 吳喜 requested three hundred elite soldiers
to fight to the death in the east.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and immediately appointed him Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn 建武將軍,
assigning him brave Yǔlín 羽林 warriors.
Advisers argued that Wú Xǐ 吳喜 was merely a clerical officer
who had never served as a general,
and therefore should not be dispatched.
Zhōngshū Shèrén 中書舍人 Cháo Shàngzhī 巢尚之 said:
“Wú Xǐ 吳喜 previously followed Shěn Qìngzhī 沈慶之,
and had frequently been on military campaigns.
His nature is both brave and decisive,
and he is also skilled in battle formations.
If he can be entrusted with the command,
he will certainly achieve success.
The arguments of these people
are merely due to their inability to recognize talent.”
Wú Xǐ 吳喜 then led Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng 員外散騎侍郎 Zhú Chāozhī 竺超之 and Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn 殿中將軍 Dù Jìngzhēn 杜敬真 with infantry and cavalry to campaign in the east.
Upon arriving in Yǒngshì 永世,
he received letters from Yǔ Yè 庾業 and Liú Yánxī 劉延熙,
and a檄文 (xíwén) or manifesto from Prince Zifáng 子房 of Xúnyáng 尋陽.
The letter to Wú Xǐ 吳喜 read:
“We know you are leading troops,
and have already reached the vicinity.
Your reputation is well-known everywhere;
why today do you establish loyalty to that side?
We imagine you will immediately turn your weapons around,
and together enjoy the rewards of the rivers and mountains.”
Wú Xǐ 吳喜 replied in a letter:
“I, your vanguard,
suddenly received your esteemed message.
Reading it, I was bewildered and confused,
and indeed deeply saddened and alarmed.
The sagely ruler, with divine military might, quells chaos;
his virtue is abundant, and his achievements are lofty.
All the rebels instigate strife,
but will be annihilated in an instant.
You, gentlemen, with your glorious achievements and righteousness,
have for generations borne the nation’s grace,
yet your actions shame the hooting owl,
and you do not cherish the mulberry (i.e., act unfilially).
Now I have trained and disciplined my subordinates,
and we are advancing speedily.
Our meeting is imminent,
so I shall not elaborate further.”
In the era of Xiàowǔ 孝武, Wú Xǐ 吳喜 was frequently employed
and always fulfilled his missions.
He was tolerant and benevolent,
and people everywhere admired him.
When he campaigned in the east,
the common people, hearing that Wú Xǐ 吳喜 was coming from the east,
surrendered and dispersed at the mere rumor.
Thus, wherever Wú Xǐ 吳喜 went, he achieved victories.
These events are recorded in the biography of Kǒng Jì 孔覬.
He was promoted to Bùbīng Xiàowèi 步兵校尉,
his generalship remaining as before.
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Jìnglíng Xiàn 竟陵縣,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
After the eastern territory was pacified,
he again led his forces to campaign in the south,
and was promoted to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍 and Xúnyáng Tàishǒu 尋陽太守.
The southern rebels retreated,
and Wú Xǐ 吳喜 pursued and pacified Jīngzhōu 荊州.
He was promoted to Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn 前軍將軍,
and his stipend increased by three hundred households.
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ 泰始 (468 CE),
he was re-enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dōngxīng Xiàn 東興縣,
with the same number of households as before.
He was then appointed Shǐchíjié Dū Jiāozhōu Guǎngzhōu zhī Yùlín Níngpǔ èr Jùn Zhū Jūnjì Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ 使持節、督交州廣州之鬱林寧浦二郡諸軍事、輔國將軍、交州刺史.
He did not take up this post,
and was instead appointed Yòujūn Jiāngjūn 右軍將軍 and Huáilíng Tàishǒu 淮陵太守,
with the provisional title of Fǔshī Jiāngjūn 輔師將軍,
and concurrently Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ 太子左衞率.
In the fifth year (469 CE),
he was transferred to Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn 驍騎將軍,
with his provisional title, governorship, and concurrent rate as before.
In the same year,
the barbarians invaded Yùzhōu 豫州.
Wú Xǐ 吳喜 led all armies to suppress them,
and greatly defeated the barbarians at Jīngtíng 荊亭.
The bogus Chángshè Gōng 長社公 fled,
and the garrison commander Bó Qǐnú 帛乞奴 surrendered.
Upon returning with the army,
he was reinstated to his original post and concurrently served as Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn 左衛將軍.
In the sixth year (470 CE),
he again led an army towards Yùzhōu 豫州 to resist the Suǒlǔ 索虜,
and was granted the title of Jié Dū Yùzhōu Zhū Jūnjì 節、督豫州諸軍事,
with the provisional title of Guànjūn Jiāngjūn 冠軍將軍,
and his Xiāoqí 驍騎 and governorship remaining as before.
The following year (471 CE),
he returned to the capital.
When Wú Xǐ 吳喜 first campaigned in the east,
he reported to Tàizōng 泰宗 that he had captured Prince Zifáng 子房 of Xúnyáng 尋陽 and other rebel leaders,
and immediately executed them in the east by decapitation, displaying their heads.
After the eastern territory was pacified,
Wú Xǐ 吳喜 saw that the southern rebels were still rampant,
and fearing future reversals and calamity,
he sent Zifáng 子房 alive back to the capital.
All the major leaders, such as Gù Chēn 顧琛 and Wáng Tánshēng 王曇生,
were spared.
The Emperor, considering Wú Xǐ 吳喜 had just performed great services,
did not question him,
but secretly resented it internally.
When Jīngzhōu 荊州 was pacified,
he indulged in plunder and looting,
amassing tens of thousands in ill-gotten gains.
He also once remarked to his guests about what kind of people Hàn Gāo 漢高 and Wèi Wǔ 魏武 originally were.
When the Emperor heard this,
he became even more displeased.
Later, when Shòu Jìzhī 壽寂之 was executed,
Wú Xǐ 吳喜 felt inwardly fearful,
and therefore requested to become Zhōngsàn Dàfū 中散大夫.
The Emperor grew even more suspicious and alarmed.
At this point, the Emperor fell ill,
and being concerned for affairs after his death,
and knowing Wú Xǐ 吳喜 had always enjoyed popular support,
he suspected that Wú Xǐ 吳喜 might not serve the young heir well in the future.
Thus, he granted Wú Xǐ 吳喜 death.
He was forty-five years old at the time.
On the day Wú Xǐ 吳喜 was to die,
the Emperor summoned him to the inner palace and conversed playfully with him,
their interaction being very cordial.
After Wú Xǐ 吳喜 departed,
he was given famous delicacies,
along with imperial gold and silver vessels.
The Emperor commanded the messenger not to let the tableware remain in Wú Xǐ's 吳喜's house overnight.
The Emperor was naturally full of taboos,
and did not wish for the tableware to stay in a house of misfortune.
The day before Wú Xǐ 吳喜 died,
the Emperor issued an edict to Liú Miǎn 劉勔, Zhāng Xīngshì 張興世, and Qí Wáng 齊王: “Wú Xǐ 吳喜 came from humble origins,
and was employed in his youth.
He has a sharp tongue and is prone to deceit,
with myriad cunning tricks.
Since Yuánjiā 元嘉,
he has served in minor clerical roles,
abusing
his authority and grace,
falsely currying favor,
forming connections everywhere,
all for his faction.
Among the populace, he constantly uses righteousness as a pretext,
but inwardly he is truly obsequious.
He always relies on schemes,
employing his cunning and flattery,
with sweet words and fawning expressions,
serving others deviously.
His disloyalty and unfairness
are evident in every matter.
Whenever he served in various offices,
those whose intentions did not align with his
were sought
out for crimes and brought low,
to demonstrate his incorruptibility,
while others indulged in wrongdoing
without any investigation,
thus he greatly gained popular support.
In the Dàmíng 大明 period,
several thousand fugitives in Yī 黟 and Shè 歙 counties
attacked and broke into towns,
and killed officials.
Liú Zishàng 劉子尚 was in Kuàijī 會稽,
and twice dispatched his commanders
who led three thousand elite armored troops to suppress them by water and land.
Both attempts ended in defeat.
Xiàowǔ 孝武 sent Wú Xǐ 吳喜 with several tens of men to the two counties to persuade and entice the bandits,
and the bandits immediately surrendered.
Such
deceptive and bewildering tactics
could achieve this,
hence he was always proactive in his endeavors,
exhausting all cunning and wickedness.
At the beginning of Tàishǐ 泰始, when he campaigned in the east,
he only had three hundred men,
and directly proceeded to Sānwú 三吳.
He experienced only two minor skirmishes,
yet from Pògāng 破岡 eastward to the sea, ten commanderies
were all cleared.
The common people, hearing that Wú Xǐ 吳喜 was coming from the east,
immediately retreated at the mere rumor.
If not
for his accumulated popular support among the Sānwú 三吳 people,
how could he have suppressed them so thoroughly?
His command of the army was lenient and disorganized,
allowing his generals to act without restraint,
without any supervision.
Thus, his troops
exerted themselves for him.
His intention, as I observed,
was only to deal with the national interest
after the bandits were pacified.
When Wú Xǐ 吳喜 first departed the capital for the eastern campaign,
he swore to heaven and earth,
saying that he would capture Liú Zifáng 劉子房
then they should be completely eliminated.
Yuán Biāo and others were all put to death,
leaving not a single survivor.
After the pacification,
he relaxed the troops and bestowed favors,
accepting the wealth of the guilty,
and enticing all the bandit
chiefs.
He allowed each to escape and hide,
receiving bribes and acquiring goods
beyond measure.
He permitted the bandit chiefs to falsely claim surrender,
and by guarding and escorting Zǐfáng, he was able to return alive to the imperial court.
He gathered all the rebels
and made them his trusted henchmen,
treating them with such warmth and generosity
that it surpassed that shown to loyal subjects.
Judging from this intention,
it was precisely because he heard that the southern bandits were greatly ascendant,
Yīn Xiàozǔ had been killed in battle,
and public
sentiment was extremely negative.
Fearing that the rebels would succeed,
he planned to save himself.
He delighted in cunning and treachery,
always conducting himself with calculation.
Towards the imperial court, he presented the first victorious reports from Sānwú.
As for
the southern bandits, he did not kill their faction,
thus showing considerable hidden sincerity.
It should be said that the people of the east were fearful
and dispersed at the mere rumor,
all because he did not take any action,
and did not
force them hard.
Protecting Zǐfáng and Gù Chēn, et al.,
fully demonstrates his sincere loyalty,
and with these two paths for advancement and retreat,
he could be free from worry.
With the southern bandits not yet pacified,
the most urgent matter was military provisions.
The southwest and northern routes were completely cut off,
and the eastern lands, recently pacified,
saw sparse and simple trade.
The imperial court even resorted to selling
official posts and titles
to alleviate the disaster and distress,
but even with all the collection of grain,
it was still insufficient.
While Xǐ was in Zhěqí,
the chief of his army embezzled one hundred and thirty *hú* of rice.
Initially, he did not
punish him.
All the army chiefs said he should be dealt with.
Xǐ, unable to do otherwise,
only gave him thirty lashes,
and did not reprimand him further.
All his indulgent treatment
was generally like this.
When Xǐ arrived in Jīngzhōu,
the public and private coffers were abundant,
but not a single coin or item was left.
Xǐ, leveraging his immense military power,
demanded and investigated,
and all the levies and responsibilities
had neither
fixed regulations
nor strict orders to hasten compliance,
but everyone was made to complete them immediately.
The people he dispatched
were none other than treacherous and cunning individuals,
who used public office for private gain,
extorting and coercing wherever they went.
Of the goods that entered official coffers,
more than half were embezzled and stolen.
They accepted money and influence-peddled,
never knowing when to stop.
When the western trouble was finally eliminated,
he should have returned to court,
but he disbanded and lingered,
claiming to be defending Shǔ.
This was actually due to
his involvement in trade and dealings,
which had not yet concluded.
He also sent people into the蠻 (Mán) region,
falsely issuing edicts to console them,
and whatever was gained from conquest and plunder
he appropriated entirely for himself.
He also dispatched his subordinate officers
and,
through local wealthy individuals,
went to Xiāngyáng or Shǔ and Hàn,
entrusting matters to commanderies and counties,
infringing upon official duties and harming the people,
and engaging in a thousand and one schemes
to seek profit.
Upon returning from the west,
large
and small boats,
as well as grass rafts,
were all filled with money, rice, cloth, and silk.
There was no boat that was not full.
From Xǐ downwards,
even to the minor generals,
everyone was heavily laden
and amassed wealth.
Xǐ was originally a man of humble origin,
often subjected to menial tasks.
He traveled by water and land,
covering almost all the provinces and commanderies.
Wherever he went,
he would cultivate local connections,
falsely acquiring a good reputation,
his fame spreading throughout
the land.
Yet he secretly harbored malicious intentions,
which no one knew.
Among Xǐ's generals in the army,
none were not robbers or bandits.
They only said:
"Why kill bandits?
Just capture them,
and you will certainly put them to
use."
Even the weak and infirm,
he would say:
"Brave men are too precious;
the world is not yet at peace.
Just let them atone for their crimes with merits."
Their treatment and arrangements
were even better than those for the meritorious.
These
people felt gratitude only towards Xǐ,
and did not attribute any favor to the imperial court.
Their wickedness remained unchecked,
causing scandals.
The meritorious and loyal subjects
sighed amongst themselves,
all saying:
"We
did not spare our lives
to capture these bandits,
but the imperial court refuses to kill them,
and instead treats them as our equals.
If there are more bandits in the world today,
we will no longer be able to fight them."
These
people, who followed Xǐ,
mostly had no accomplishments,
some hiding behind the crowd,
or sleeping in their tents.
When the bandits were defeated and scattered,
they received titles and rewards along with the meritorious.
When
questioned,
he offered myriad excuses,
saying:
"Since these people have been pardoned,
and have achieved merit in fighting bandits,
how can they not be rewarded according to precedent?"
When Chǔ Yuān went south to select generals
and soldiers,
those in Xǐ's army who had been bandits
sought official positions from Yuān,
outnumbering the loyal subjects.
Because Xǐ had been the first to report victory,
his status was already high,
and he was also Yuān's deputy,
so it was difficult to refuse him.
Therefore, those who gained official positions and rewards
were more numerous than the loyal individuals.
Although the loyal individuals were indignant at Xǐ's unfairness,
they also remembered his leniency.
In previous years, Zhú Chāozhī heard
of rebellions in all four directions.
People feared the bandits,
and no one dared to volunteer to serve the imperial court.
He then nobly stepped forward
and followed Xǐ on the expedition,
serving as his deputy commander.
He personally engaged
the enemy.
Upon returning from the east,
he displeased Xǐ.
Xǐ said Chāozhī drank too much
and was unsuitable for service,
and thus abandoned him.
Gāo Jìngzǔ, though young in years, was experienced,
and his strength was indeed robust.
His decisions
were praised by the army.
But Xǐ slighted his age
and said he was useless.
This was precisely because these two were loyal and upright,
and their conduct differed from his own.
Chāozhī, as
People,
then drank much wine,
figuring that among the commanders of Xǐ's army,
how could there be no drinkers?
It was just particularly unfavorable to Chāo,
hence the words regarding wine were merely incidental.
Since Jìngzǔ had no
other business,
he directly said he was old,
pretending to beg for a commandery,
covertly sending him away and dismissing him.
The other commanders,
being all greedy, corrupt, and flattering types,
all helped each other out,
never
parting ways.
When Xǐ heard that there were criminals in the world who had died or should have been imprisoned,
he would certainly request their recruitment into the army,
where they all obtained official ranks
and were treated generously.
People who were destined
for death,
having gained life through him,
not only survived,
but also achieved their desires.
People are not wood or stone,
how could they not be moved?
If I were to attack Xǐ's gate,
who among these people would not exert
their utmost strength?
It is just that Xǐ dares not harbor such intentions.
All the people in Xǐ's army are Xǐ's personal claws and fangs;
how are they concerned with the state?
Since Xǐ obtained his military title,
he has appointed many subordinate officials,
and these people have been given official positions
without any limits.
For his brothers, sons, nephews, and his collateral relatives,
he begged for
famous counties in the east,
four or five contiguous cities,
all of whom were clearly cunning thieves,
encroaching upon public office and seizing private property.
Fugitive criminals,
whom the prefectures and commanderies could not pursue,
who were hiding in remote places,
were certainly
protected and harbored by his faction,
so the imperial edicts from Táizhōu
were almost never enforced.
Boats, carriages, oxen, and calves,
which should have been borrowed by the government,
were entrusted to Xǐ,
and the officials then dared not question it.
Slaves from
other counties,
upon entering his territory, were immediately seized.
The common people's oxen and calves
were often taken, slaughtered, and eaten.
Those whom the prefectures and commanderies should have conscripted
all entered Xǐ's household.
Xǐ's elder brother Rú Gōng and others all
extorted money,
filling villages and neighborhoods.
All of Wú's relatives
extorted from the people
without any restraint,
and the common people wailed,
everyone suffering.
Xǐ knew
all this,
but initially did not prohibit or reprimand it.
Suǒ Huìzǐ's crimes were not much worse than Jiāng Yù's,
and having already received grace,
he was exempted from judicial punishment.
Yet, for a slight disagreement,
Xǐ would immediately inflict execution.
Zhāng Yuè was a great commander among the rebels;
he was compelled to surrender.
Shěn Yōuzhī handed him over to Xǐ,
saying:
"Life or death should be decided by the imperial court."
When generals and commanders wage war,
there is a standard procedure.
They should naturally hand over [the captured] to the relevant
authorities.
But Xǐ immediately put him in shackles,
removed his own tunic and gave it to him to wear,
sat knee-to-knee with him,
and then created a reputation for great righteousness,
privately showing favor to attract people.
Every matter was like this.
Zhāng Língdù was a fierce and foolish
man,
a leader of rebellion.
When Xǐ was in the west, he immediately pardoned his crime,
privately brought him to the capital,
and associated with him,
their relationship as if they were one body.
Like a wolf cub with a wild heart,
he harbored a venomous
nature.
He then conspired with Liǔ Xīnwèi and others to install Liú Huī.
I asked Xǐ to arrest him,
but Xǐ secretly informed him to flee.
Before he had gone far,
he was arrested by Jiànkāng.
Xǐ's
betrayal of the state and embrace of evil
went to such an extent.
When he first returned from the west,
he sought to also hold the position of Right Chancellor,
greedy for opportunities to exploit situations
for private deception.
I was troubled by his flattery and crookedness,
so I suppressed and did not permit it,
and from then on, he harbored resentment,
his mind
feeling injustice.
When Xǐ rescued Rǔyīn in the west,
he let his soldiers and generals run wild,
plundering and abusing the residents,
raping women,
forcibly seizing chickens and dogs,
looting and rampaging everywhere,
and the local officials along the roads
dared not
reprimand or question them.
If by chance someone was mistakenly arrested and bound,
Xǐ would immediately fly into a great rage.
The common people sighed and groaned,
everyone despairing.
Recently, Duàn Fórōng requested to return,
and Xǐ was to be
appointed in his place.
When the people in the west heard he was coming,
they all wanted to rebel and flee,
saying:
"All of Wú's soldiers are living brigands.
If he becomes the governor,
how can we survive?
Since there is no other plan,
we can only rebel and surrender to the barbarians."
Indeed, to punish the wicked and comfort the people,
in order to purify the nation's way,
how can one cruelly abuse the innocent,
making plunder one's business,
harming governance and obstructing
the state,
deceiving superiors and attaching oneself to inferiors?
Crimes and offenses like these,
how can they be tolerated for long?
Zāng Wénzhòng once said:
"When you see someone who is good to their lord,
it is like a filial son nourishing his parents;
when you see someone who is evil to their lord,
it is like a hawk or falcon chasing sparrows."
Gěng Yǎn did not leave enemies to his lord and father,
which previous historians considered a fine tale.
Yet, among the five thousand
men in Xǐ's army,
all personally engaged in rebellion,
whom he fosters by his side;
how can they have any heart to serve their superiors?
Xǐ's ambition is great,
and he constantly refers to Hàn Gāo and Wèi Wǔ,
asking who they originally were.
Recently, he suddenly sent a petition,
requesting to resign his military post,
and asked for the title of Middle Grandee.
Who
is Xǐ that
he dares to make such a move?
Moreover, the frontiers are currently unsettled;
it is precisely the time for Xǐ to contribute his utmost effort.
If he were to conduct himself properly,
he should be frugal
and cautious,
quietly sweep his gate and remain indoors,
not engaging with external matters,
and dedicating himself to serving his superior.
How can he, with his own insignificant status,
so highly compare himself?
It must be that he sees his own faults and offenses,
which have spread far and wide,
and also saw Shòu Jìzhī exiled,
and Shī Xiūlín attacked,
and as creatures abhor harm to their kind,
he harbors inner worry and fear.
Therefore, he conceived this plan,
intending to secure his own safety.
Among the imperial court officials, great ministers, and regional governors,
Xǐ hardly fears anyone;
the only one he fears is me.
A person's lifespan, whether long or short,
cannot be predicted in advance.
If
Even if I live a hundred years,
if there is no Xǐ in the world,
what loss is there?
If I were to fall ill in the fourth month and not receive treatment,
how could there be a single happy person in the world?
When one
examines Xǐ's true intentions,
how can one serve a lord who adheres strictly to text [i.e., law/rules],
and how can one encounter an opportune moment
when the state is divided by internal strife?
Many people say,
"The times are fearsome,
and the national administration
is strict."
Looking through history, those who possessed the empire,
ruled the myriad people,
and wielded authority to unify the masses –
which era was not like this?
Thus, in high antiquity, there were symbolic punishments,
and the people, being pure, did not commit offenses.
Later sages, to deter deceit,
easily
introduced tattooing and nose-cutting.
Táng Yáo, with his extreme benevolence,
did not pardon the crimes of the Four Fiends;
Hàn Gāo, with his great magnanimity,
was swift in executing the Three Heroes.
Furthermore, when Tàigōng governed,
he first executed Huá Shì;
when Xuānní acted as prime minister,
he publicly executed Shàozhèng.
Since ancient times, countless individuals who exerted themselves to stabilize the state,
benefited the common people,
had swords borne before them,
and flutes and drums accompanying them,
yet could not preserve this
position,
numbering countless through the generations.
Only one in ten of those fostered with blessings
survived.
As for Xǐ's profound crimes,
can he escape?
Indeed, wealth and nobility,
though attained through achievements,
must be maintained through virtue and morality.
Therefore, a good beginning is not enough to be considered extraordinary;
only those who have a good end
are truly noteworthy.
The establishment of officials and the support of scholars
are fundamentally for the benefit of the state.
When they bring benefit,
they are loved like infants;
but when they become harmful,
they are feared like enemies.
How can there be time to extensively recall
their initial merits,
and tolerate enduring their ultimate harm?
The use of a general
is like administering medicine:
when a person is weak and cold,
they need powdered minerals to restore their body;
but when a fever sets in,
one removes solid accumulations to stop the illness.
How can one remember the initial benefits,
and not consider the later harm,
preserving past rewards,
while suppressing present punishments?
It is not forgetting their accomplishments,
but rather that circumstances make it unavoidable.
Xǐ's crimes and misdeeds are piled high as mountains,
his intentions are intolerable.
Even if he has achievements,
they are insufficient to atone for himself.
He has become a national calamity,
how can he not be eliminated?
Furthermore,
one desires to prevent evil at its inception and nip it in the bud,
worrying before it sprouts.
We do not wish to broadly expose his wicked deeds;
instead, we should issue a strict edict to admonish him,
so that he may act for his own good.
You, gentlemen, as generals, prime ministers,
and great ministers,
are entrusted with crucial responsibilities.
Matters of reward and punishment are weighty;
I should discuss them with you.
What are your collective thoughts?
After Xǐ died,
an imperial edict was issued granting posthumous gifts.
His son, Huīmín, inherited his title.
When Qí usurped the throne,
his state was abolished.
Huáng Huí
was a soldier from the Jìnglíng Commandery.
He started as a general laborer in the commandery yamen,
gradually rising to a messenger.
When Zāng Zhì was the commandery administrator,
he transferred to be a master of the fasting hall.
When Zhì left office,
he took Huí with him.
When Zhì was in Yōngzhōu,
Huí again became a master of the fasting hall.
When Zhì campaigned against Yuánxiōng,
Huí followed and had merits,
being exempted from military household status.
When Zhì was in Jiāngzhōu,
Huí was promoted to lead the White Guards.
He followed Zhì and fled to Yùzhāng after being defeated at Liángshān,
where he was captured by Xiè Chéngzǔ, a general of the imperial army,
and handed over to the Jiāngzhōu labor department.
He was pardoned during an amnesty.
Huí then went to the capital.
At Xuānyángmén, he got into a fight with someone,
falsely claiming to be a horse groom for Jiāngxiàwáng Yìgōng.
He was whipped two hundred times
and sent to the Right Shàngfāng.
At that time, Dài Míngbǎo, a Censor-in-chief, was imprisoned.
Huí was assigned to be his jailer.
His nature was opportunistic and diligent;
he served Míngbǎo with all his heart and strength.
Míngbǎo was soon pardoned and released,
and entrusted Huí as before.
He requested Huí's release from service,
to lead his personal guard unit
and manage his residence and the property west of the river.
He possessed skills and artistry,
being versatile in many things,
and Míngbǎo greatly favored and trusted him.
Huí was agile and strong,
possessing courage and strength beyond ordinary men.
In Jiāngxī, he associated with various Chǔ youths,
repeatedly engaging in robbery.
At the time when Tàizōng first ascended the throne,
the four directions rebelled.
Míngbǎo requested Tàizōng to have Huí recruit Chǔ people from Jiāngxī.
He obtained eight hundred skilled archers,
and Huí was provisionally appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and army commander,
subordinate to Liú Miǎn for the western campaign.
At Sǐhǔ, he defeated Dù Shúbǎo's army.
He was appointed Pìqí Xíngcānjūn and Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn under Shānyángwáng Xiūyòu.
He attacked Héféi and
defeated it,
gradually being promoted to general and officer.
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as Gěyáng Xiànnán,
with an income of two hundred households.
Later, in the early Yuánhuī reign of the deposed emperor,
Guìyángwáng Xiūfàn rebelled.
Huí, as Túnqí Xiàowèi, led his troops under Qíwáng.
At Xīntíng, he devised a feigned surrender strategy,
the details are in the biography of Xiūfàn.
Huí saw that Xiūfàn was vulnerable
and said to Zhāng Jìng'ér:
"You can take him.
I swear not to kill princes."
Jìng'ér immediately beheaded Xiūfàn.
When the affair was settled,
Huí was transferred to Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn,
awarded Fǔshī Jiāngjūn,
advanced in peerage to Marquis,
and enfeoffed as Wénxǐ Xiànhóu,
with an increase of one thousand households.
In the fourth year,
he was promoted to Guànjūn Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of the two commanderies of Nán Lángxié and Jìyáng.
When Jiànpíngwáng Jǐngsù rebelled,
Huí again led troops to campaign,
provisionally holding a staff of authority.
On the day the city was pacified,
Huí's army was the first to enter.
He again yielded Jǐngsù to Zhāng Ní'nú.
Huí's income was increased by five hundred households,
he was promoted to the title of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn,
awarded Sànqí Chángshì,
and remained as Grand Administrator.
The next year,
he was promoted to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
remaining as Chángshì.
Shěn Yōuzhī rebelled.
Huáng Huí was appointed as Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Area Commander-in-Chief of Yǐngzhōu and Yìyáng in Sīzhōu, General Who Pacifies the West, and Governor of Yǐngzhōu.
He was granted a complete set of drum and wind instruments.
He was to lead his troops out to Xīntíng as the vanguard.
Before he departed,
Yuán Càn occupied Shítóu and caused a rebellion.
Huáng Huí and the generals and commanders at Xīntíng, Rèn Hòubó, Péng Wénzhī, Wáng Yíxìng, Sūn Tán’guàn, and others, conspired to support Yuán Càn.
When Yuán Càn’s plot was exposed,
Hòubó and the others immediately took boats to Shítóu.
Only Tán’guàn arrived first and was able to enter.
By the time Hòubó and the others arrived,
Yuán Càn’s rebellion had already been suppressed.
Huáng Huí had originally planned to lead his subordinates at dawn, proceed directly along the imperial road to the palace gate,
and attack the King of Qí in the imperial hall.
Since the plan did not materialize,
the King of Qí treated him as before.
Huáng Huí and Yíxìng had always been at odds.
Fearing that Yíxìng might betray him,
Huáng Huí took advantage of Yíxìng’s disobedience to his orders
and had him executed.
Yíxìng
was a native of Wúxīng.
He was short in stature,
but resolute and courageous.
As a young man, he committed robberies without needing companions.
The commandery pursued and surrounded him dozens of times,
but ultimately could not capture him.
During the Tàishǐ reign of Tàizōng,
he served as a general.
While in Shòuyáng, he engaged the Suǒ captives.
He often defeated superior numbers with fewer troops,
personally plunging deep into enemy lines,
without fear or hesitation.
When the captive forces encountered Yíxìng,
they all retreated, not daring to confront him.
He gradually rose to the rank of General Who Guards the North [Níngshuò Jiāngjūn]
and Chief of the Feathered Forest [Yǔlín Jiān].
For his meritorious service in suppressing the King of Jiànpíng, Jǐngsù,
he was enfeoffed as a male of Chángshòu County [Chángshòu Xiàn Nán],
with an income of three hundred households.
At this time, he was a Colonel of Cavalry [Túnqí Xiàowèi],
with the added title of General Who Assists the State [Fúguó Jiāngjūn].
Before Huáng Huí’s army reached Yǐngzhōu,
Shěn Yōuzhī was defeated and fled.
When Huáng Huí arrived at the garrison,
he was promoted to General Who Guards the West [Zhèn Xī Jiāngjūn],
and his title of Area Commander-in-Chief was changed to Grand Area Commander-in-Chief [Dūdū].
Huáng Huí was not happy staying in Yǐngzhōu
and earnestly requested Nán-Yǎn.
He then led his private troops back without authorization.
He was re-enfeoffed as Duke of Ānlù Commandery [Ānlù Jùn Gōng],
with an increase of two thousand households,
making a total of three thousand seven hundred households.
He was re-appointed as Grand Area Commander-in-Chief of Nán-Yǎn, Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, and Jì five prefectures, General Who Guards the North [Zhèn Běi Jiāngjūn], and Governor of Nán-Yǎnzhōu.
He was additionally granted the title of Attendant Palace Censor [Sànqí Chángshì],
retaining his imperial credentials as before.
The King of Qí believed that Huáng Huí would eventually cause trouble,
so he submitted a memorial, saying:
“Huáng Huí rose from the ranks of the commoners,
fundamentally lacking in integrity.
He was fortunate to encounter Tàishǐ,
and was mistakenly employed.
He ascended through the winds and clouds,
repeatedly occupying prominent positions.
When Shěn Yōuzhī acted rebelliously,
and the military situation was critical,
I, being dim in discerning people,
hoped he would fight fiercely.
I dispatched him to command the vanguard,
but he never engaged in battle.
When his army reached Yǐngchéng,
he used his might to coerce and threaten,
and his plundering always targeted the noble first.
The King of Wǔlíng’s horses, implements, and clothing were all seized and plundered.
The civil and military officials within the city
were thoroughly stripped, with nothing left behind.
Upon returning to the capital,
his wantonness became even more excessive.
There were still two imperial chariots from the former dynasty,
the imperial robes from the former dynasty
and the bows and swords, reminders of affection,
still in the carriage repository.
Huáng Huí then requested them,
intending to use them for his private adornment,
his presumptuousness and insolence knew no bounds,
disregarding the heavens.
Furthermore, he extensively harbored fugitives
and accepted many robbers,
making them his trusted associates
and his claws and teeth.
Observing his vicious cunning,
I fear the unforeseen.
His wickedness has accumulated,
his crimes are manifest,
and he cannot be tolerated.
He should be eliminated
to clarify the national laws.
Examining the nature of his transgressions,
it is truly appropriate to apply the severest punishment.
However, he once served as a general,
and has a slight record of service.
When there is doubt about guilt, one should follow leniency;
this principle is clearly established in former policies.
I request a reduction in his punishment,
and especially beg for the preservation of his remaining descendants.
I have been excessively entrusted with a great responsibility,
and my words must be entirely sincere.
I respectfully present my humble opinion,
to follow the great canons.
I humbly wish Your Majesty,
the sagely enlightened one, would especially grant your approval.
My thoughts do not exceed my position;
I am truly ignorant in discerning talent.
Recalling the past,
I feel even more ashamed.”
An imperial edict stated:
“Huáng Huí, elevated from a common person,
has long been tainted with flaws and transgressions.
Despite receiving leniency under the law,
he indulged in brutal actions.
Although his meritorious services were repeatedly manifest,
he frequently harbored intentions of violating principles.
At Xīntíng, he rebelled
and defected to the enemy’s camp.
Once his deviant plans spread,
the imperial laws were almost endangered.
Fortunately, Zhāng Jìng’ér, wielding his spear, bravely charged,
and the chief rebel was executed.
When Jǐngsù plotted rebellion,
the frost had lasted for a long time.
He secretly exchanged messages
and clandestinely sent weapons and equipment.
When the miasma cleared,
his cunning scheme was exposed.
We always tolerated and covered for him,
hoping he would repent and reform.
Therefore, we granted him territory and raised his rank,
sharing honors and favors with him.
But his treacherous nature was inherent,
and his insidious malice deepened.
He instigated and lured Jìng’ér,
intending to attack and entrap each other.
His rebellious plot was not fulfilled,
but his obstinacy became even more severe.
Recently, when his army was stationed in Yǐngzhèn,
he coerced and intimidated the governor of the prefecture.
He also harbored private schemes
and made many demands.
When officials hesitated and doubted,
he immediately inflicted corporal punishment.
He acted with exclusive tyranny and arrogance,
disregarding all norms.
He was appointed to govern the western border regions,
with generous honors and emoluments.
Yet he showed no gratitude,
still harboring resentment.
When Lǐ Ānmín was dispatched to govern Hé and Jì,
before his term was complete,
Huáng Huí greedily seized the strategic position
and bitterly pleaded to have it taken back.
His importunate requests were ceaseless,
and his extravagance knew no bounds.
He then requested imperial chariots,
presumptuously using them for his private adornment.
Furthermore, he gathered bandit gangs
without ever reporting it.
He damaged customs and corrupted morality;
nothing could be worse than this.
It is appropriate to clearly enforce the law
and rectify legal codes.
He shall be arrested and handed over to the Grand Judge [Tíngwèi]
to be thoroughly tried according to the law.”
When Huáng Huí died,
he was fifty-two years old.
His son, Sēngniàn,
was a Left Secretary of the Ministry of Revenue [Shàngshū Zuǒ Mín Láng] and Chancellor of Jìnglíng [Jìnglíng Xiàng].
Before he could be dispatched,
he was executed along with his father.
After Huáng Huí became noble,
he served Dài Míngbǎo with great diligence,
always referring to himself by name.
Every time he visited Míngbǎo,
he would dismiss his attendants and enter alone,
never daring to sit.
He personally went under the tent
and entered the inner chambers,
checking what was available
and supplying whatever was lacking,
making this his regular practice.
Previously,
Wáng Yùn (王蘊) was the governor of Xiāngzhōu (湘州).
Yǐngchuān (潁川) Yǔ Pèiyù (庾佩玉) was Wáng Yùn's (王蘊) Commandant of the Pacifying-Northern Army (Níngshuò Fǔ Zhǎngshǐ 寧朔府長史) and Administrator of Chángshā (長沙 Nèishǐ 內史).
When Wáng Yùn (王蘊) left his post,
Nányáng Wáng Huī (南陽王翽), the General of the Southern Command (Nánzhōngláng Jiàng 南中郎將) and Inspector of Xiāngzhōu (湘州 Cìshǐ 刺史), had not yet taken office.
Pèiyù (佩玉) was temporarily authorized to manage the affairs of the prefecture and province.
He first dispatched Hán Yòuzōng (韓幼宗), the Mid-Army Staff Officer (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn 中兵參軍) and Magistrate of Línxiāng (臨湘 Lìng 令), to lead troops to garrison and defend Xiāngzhōu (湘州).
He worked with Pèiyù (佩玉),
but their relationship was not good.
When Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) rebelled,
Pèiyù (佩玉) and Yòuzōng (幼宗) did not trust each other.
Yòuzōng (幼宗) secretly plotted,
and Pèiyù (佩uyù) learned of his scheme.
He ambushed and killed Yòuzōng (幼宗).
Upon returning to Yǐngzhōu (郢州),
he dispatched Rèn Hòubó (任候伯), the General Who Guards the State (Fǔguó Jiàngjūn 輔國將軍), to take charge of Xiāngzhōu (湘州) affairs.
Hòubó (候伯) considered Pèiyù (佩玉) to be duplicitous,
and immediately killed him.
When Lǚ Ānguó (呂安國), the Inspector of Xiāngzhōu (湘zhōu Cìshǐ 刺史), took up his post,
Qí Wáng (齊王) ordered Ānguó (安國) to execute Hòubó (候伯).
Péng Wénzhī (彭文之)
was a native of Tàishān (泰山).
He gradually rose to the rank of General of Dragon Valor (Lóngxiáng Jiàngjūn 龍驤將軍) through military merit.
For his achievements in suppressing Jiànpíng Wáng Jǐngsù (建平王景素),
he was enfeoffed as the County Baron of Gěyáng (葛陽縣男),
with an assigned estate of three hundred households.
In the early days of Shùn Dì (順帝),

he served as General Who Guards the State (Fǔguó Jiàngjūn 輔國將軍), General of the Left Army (Zuǒjūn Jiàngjūn 左軍將軍), Administrator of Nánpúyáng (南濮陽 Tàishǒu 太守), and Director of the Palace Gate (Zhíhé 直閤),
also holding the post of Commander of the Right Elite Guards (Yòuxìzhàng Dàngzhǔ 右細仗盪主).
After Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) was pacified,
Qí Wáng (齊王) arrested him and imprisoned him,
and he was granted death.
Sūn Tánguàn (孫曇瓘)
was a native of Fùyáng (富陽), Wú Jùn (吳郡).
He was brave, resolute, and powerful,
and gradually advanced through military merit.
By this time, he was General of the Pacifying-Northern Army (Níngshuò Jiàngjūn 寧朔將軍) and Inspector of Yuèzhōu (越州).
He rebelled and fled from Shítóu (石頭).
He remained in hiding for some time,
but was later captured in Mòlíng Xiàn (秣陵縣)
and executed.
Among the generals who were active at the same time,
Rèn Nóngfū (任農夫) of Lín Huái (臨淮),
Zhōu Níngmín (周寧民) of Pèi Jùn (沛郡),
and Gāo Dàoqìng (高道慶) of Nán Jùn (南郡)
were all distinguished for their martial prowess.
Nóngfū (農夫) gradually rose to General of Strong Crossbows (Qiángnǔ Jiàngjūn 強弩將軍).
In the early reign of Tàizōng (太宗),
for his achievements in the eastern campaign,
he was enfeoffed as the County Son of Guǎngjìn (廣晉縣子),
with an assigned estate of five hundred households.
After the eastern lands were pacified,
he again campaigned in the south,
and his assigned estate was increased by two hundred households.
He successively held the posts of Colonel of Archers (Shèshēng Xiàowèi 射聲校尉)
and General of the Left Army (Zuǒjūn Jiàngjūn 左軍將軍).
At that time, Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn (桂陽王休範) was in Jiāngzhōu (江州)
and harbored rebellious intentions.
The court, fearing his advance,
appointed Nóngfū (農夫) as General Who Assists the Army (Fǔshī Jiàngjūn 輔師將軍) and Administrator of Huáinán (淮南 Tàishǒu 太守),
garrisoning Gūshú (姑孰) to defend against him.
Xiūfàn (休範) soon led his forces towards the capital,
suddenly arriving near the city.
Nóngfū (農夫) abandoned his post and returned to the capital.
After Xiūfàn (休範) was pacified,
for his military achievements, he was re-enfeoffed as the County Marquis of Chánlíng (孱陵縣侯),
with his assigned estate increased by one thousand households,
making a total of one thousand seven hundred households including the previous ones.
He was appointed as General Who Assists the Army (Fǔshī Jiàngjūn 輔師將軍) and Inspector of Yùzhōu (豫州),
and soon after was promoted to General of Champion (Guànjūn Jiàngjūn 冠軍將軍).
The following year,
he was appointed as General of Agile Cavalry (Xiāoqí Jiàngjūn 驍騎將軍),
and additionally given the title of Regular Palace Attendant (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì 通直散騎常侍).
In previous generations, for additional official posts,
only the Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍) title existed,
without the phrases "Tōngzhí Yuánwài" (通直員外).
Since the time of Tàizōng (太宗),
many individuals attained high positions due to military achievements.
Those of lesser rank who were granted the title of Palace Attendant (Chángshì 常侍)
were often given the "Tōngzhí Yuánwài" (通直員外) prefix.
In the fifth year,
he was additionally made General Who Punishes the Rebels (Zhēnglǔ Jiàngjūn 征虜將軍),
and "Tōngzhí" (通直) was changed to Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍),
with General of Agile Cavalry (Xiāoqí 驍騎) remaining as before.
He died that year,
and was posthumously granted the title of General of the Left (Zuǒ Jiàngjūn 左將軍),
with Palace Attendant (Chángshì 常侍) remaining as before.
His posthumous name was Zhēnsù (貞肅).
Hòubó (候伯)
was Nóngfū's (農夫) younger brother.
Zhōu Níngmín (周寧民) rose in his hometown to fight Xuē Āndū (薛安都),
and also reached the rank of Army Officer (Jūnjiào 軍校) through military merit.
In the early Tàishǐ (泰始) era,
he was enfeoffed as the County Baron of Gànxiàn (贛縣男),
with an assigned estate of three hundred households.
He rose to the official posts of General of the Pacifying-Northern Army (Níngshuò Jiàngjūn 寧朔將軍), Inspector of Xúzhōu (徐州 Cìshǐ 刺史),
and Administrator of Zhōnglí (鍾離 Tàishǒu 太守).
Gāo Dàoqìng (高道慶) also reached the ranks of Army Officer (Jūnjiào 軍校) and Commander of Agile Rangers (Xiāoyóu 驍游).
For his achievements in pacifying Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn (桂陽王休範),
he was enfeoffed as the County Baron of Yuè'ān (樂安縣男),
with an assigned estate of three hundred households.
When Jiànpíng Wáng Jǐngsù (建平王景素) rebelled,
Dàoqìng (道慶) led troops in the northern campaign,
but secretly colluded with Jǐngsù (景素).
After the matter was settled,
he personally requested an increase of five hundred households for his assigned estate.
An imperial decree added two hundred,
making a total of five hundred households including the previous ones.
Dàoqìng (道慶) was cruel, dangerous, tyrannical,
and insatiably acquisitive.
If anything displeased him,
he would beat and flog,
often resulting in deaths.
The court feared him like a tiger or wolf.
Qí Wáng (齊王) deliberated with Yuán Càn (袁粲) and others,
arrested him and handed him over to the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi 廷尉),
and he was granted death.
The Imperial Historian states: For common folk
to achieve their life's work,
it is impossible without a chaotic era.
To apply the sentiments of a chaotic era
in a time of peace,
it would indeed be fortunate
if one did not perish.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 44: Dèng Wǎn (鄧琬), Yuán Yǐ (袁顗), Kǒng Jì (孔覬)
Dèng Wǎn (鄧琬), courtesy name Yuánwǎn (元琬),
was a native of Nánchāng (南昌), Yùzhāng (豫章).
His great-grandfather, Hùn (混),
and great-granduncle, Xuán (玄),
both served as Minister of Personnel (Shàngshū Lìbù Láng 尚書吏部郎) in the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
His grandfather, Qiánzhī (潛之), was the Chief Clerk of the Garrisoned South (Zhènnán Zhǎngshǐ 鎮南長史).
His father, Yìnzhī (胤之),
was General Who Punishes the Rebels and Chief Clerk (Zhēnglǔ Zhǎngshǐ 征虜長史) for Shìzǔ (世祖),
Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Láng 吏部郎),
Chief Clerk to the Generalissimo of Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng (彭城王義康 Dà Jiàngjūn Zhǎngshǐ 大將軍長史),
Administrator of Yùzhāng (豫章 Tàishǒu 太守),
and Grand Master of Ceremonies (Guānglù Xūn 光祿勳).
Wǎn (琬) first served as the Western Chief Clerk (Xīcáo Zhǔbù 西曹主簿) of the province,
and then Staff Officer (Zhēngběi Xíng Cānjūn 征北行參軍) for Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān (南譙王義宣),
and was transferred to Staff Officer (Cānjūn Shì 參軍事).
He was again transferred with the general's headquarters to Staff Officer of Cavalry (Chējì Cānjūn 車騎參軍),
and then transferred to Chief Clerk of the General's Headquarters (Fǔ Zhǔbù 府主簿),
and Registrar of Jiāngzhōu (江州 Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ 治中從事史).
When Shìzǔ (世祖) raised his righteous army,
Wǎn (琬) was commissioned as General Who Guards the State (Fǔguó Jiàngjūn 輔國將軍) and Administrator of Nánhǎi (南海 Tàishǒu 太守).
He led troops to attack Xiāo Jiǎn (蕭簡) in Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
The siege lasted over a year
before it was overcome.
Due to Zāng Zhì's (臧質) rebellion,
he was captured by Zōng (宗), the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu (廣州 Cìshǐ 刺史).
He was pardoned during an amnesty.
Wǎn's (琬) younger brother, Qú (璩),
joined Zāng Zhì's (臧質) rebellion.
When Zhì (質) was defeated, Qú (璩) was executed.
Wǎn's (琬) younger brother Huán (環) was also executed for involvement.
Wǎn (琬) was far away
and had merits,
so he was spared death but exiled,
and remained in Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
After a long time, he was allowed to return.
He was appointed Palace Attendant (Jǐshìzhōng 給事中), Minister of Palace Supplies (Shàngshū Kùbù Láng 尚書庫部郎), Commissioner of Waterways (Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě 都水使者), Prefect of Dānyáng (丹陽 Chéng 丞),
and Grand Arbiter of his home province (Běnzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng 本州大中正).
In the seventh year of Dàmíng (大明),
the imperial carriage visited Lìyáng (歷陽).
Recalling his old associates from his time as a prince,
an imperial edict stated:

“The late Grand Master of Ceremonies (Guānglù Xūn 光祿勳) and former General Who Punishes the Rebels and Chief Clerk (Zhēnglǔ Zhǎngshǐ 征虜長史) Dèng Yìnzhī (鄧胤之) possessed a profound and reserved character,
and consistently achieved results in his various appointments.
When We were entrusted with the heavy duties of a prince in the past,
he was among the first to assist in Our affairs.
His utmost devotion and effort have not been forgotten.
In past years, his son Qú (璩) was perverse and rebellious,
bringing about his own execution.
Out of leniency, Wǎn (琬) was exceptionally spared from the catastrophe and execution.
Now, he may be promoted to Palace Attendant (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng 給事黃門侍郎)
to honor Yìnzhī's (胤之) longstanding loyalty.”
The next year,
he was appointed Zhènchén Chángshǐ and Xúnyáng Nèishǐ for Sima, Prince Zǐxūn of Jìn'ān,
acting as affairs for Jiāngzhōu.
The Former Deposed Emperor was insane and without principle.
Since both Tàizǔ and Shìzǔ had ascended the throne as the third in their line,
and Zǐxūn's order of succession was the same,
he deeply harbored suspicions.
On account of Hé Mài's conspiracy,
he dispatched an envoy with poison to bestow death upon Zǐxūn.
When the envoy arrived,
Zǐxūn's Diǎnqiān Xiè Dàoyù, Zhāishuài Pān Xīīnzhī, Shìshū Chǔ Língsì and others rushed to inform Wǎn,
weeping and asking for a plan.
Wǎn said,
"I am but a humble scholar from the southern land.
Having received exceptional favor from the late emperor,
who entrusted his beloved son to me,
how can I cherish my household of a hundred lives?
I must repay this by dying in service.
The young ruler is foolish and violent,
and the altars of soil and grain are in peril.
Though he is called the Son of Heaven,
he acts like a mere tyrant.
Now I shall lead the civil and military officials,
proceed directly to the capital,
and with the various dukes, ministers, and scholars,
depose the foolish and enthrone the enlightened."
On the nineteenth day of the eleventh month of the first year of Jǐnghé,
claiming it was Zǐxūn's order,
a state of alert was declared that very day.
Zǐxūn, in military attire, came out to the hearing hall,
gathered his subordinates,
and had Pān Xīīnzhī verbally announce the decree, saying:
"The young ruler's foolishness, madness, perversity, and rebellion
are all seen and heard by you gentlemen.
The trusted ministers appointed by the dying emperor
have all been executed.
Kings and dukes have been oppressed and forced,
and the Empress Dowager has been humiliated and confined.
Unruly individuals
have together created this disaster.
The princes in the capital
are all imprisoned and coerced,
trapped in the tiger's maw,
unable to find a way to rise up.
I am bound by loyalty to both family and state.
How can I sit by and watch this chaos?
Now I intend to raise the troops of Jiǔjiāng,
send proclamations far and wide,
to plan for the royal house.
What do you gentlemen think?"
No one in the assembly replied immediately.
Lùshì Cānjūn Táo Liàng said,
"The young ruler is foolish and mad,
his accumulated evil is profound.
Yī and Huò acted in antiquity,
Your Highness should do so today.
The scholars of this humble prefecture
have a hereditary tradition of loyalty and integrity.
Furthermore, as this is a momentous occasion in a thousand years,
I request to offer my life as a vanguard."
All the others accepted the command.
Civil and military officials were all promoted one rank.
Liàng was transferred to Zīyì Cānjūnshì,
in charge of the central army,
and granted the title of Níngshuò Jiāngjūn,
commanding all military affairs.
Gōngcáo Zhāng Chén was appointed Zīyì Cānjūn,
in charge of building boats and ships.
Cānjūnshì Gù Zhāozhī, Shěn Bóyù, Xún Dàolín, and others assisted in managing documents.
Nányáng Tàishǒu Shěn Huáibǎo and Mínshān Tàishǒu Xuē Chángbǎo, from their respective commanderies,
had just arrived in Xúnyáng.
Together with Xīncài Tàishǒu Wéi Xīzhí, they were appointed Zīyì Cānjūn,
in charge of the central army,
and together with Péngzé Lìng Chén Shàozōng, they became generals and commanders.
Initially,
the Deposed Emperor had sent Zhāng Yuè, the former Qiánjūn Chángshǐ and Jīngzhōu Xíngshì, to the Basin Mouth for recording and transport from Jīngzhōu.
Wǎn, claiming Zǐxūn's command,
released him from his shackles,
welcomed him with his own carriage,
appointed him Sīmǎ,
and granted him the title of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
Wǎn was granted the title of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
The two jointly managed all internal and external affairs.
General Yú Bóqí was dispatched with five hundred men to cut off Dàléi,
prohibiting merchants and travelers,
as well as all official and private envoys.
Envoys were sent to register able-bodied men from all commanderies,
collecting weapons and armor.
Within ten days,
five thousand armored soldiers were obtained,
who were deployed to Dàléi,
building strongholds on both banks.
Sūn Chōngzhī, Tàishǒu of Bādōng and Jiànpíng commanderies,
had just arrived at Gūshí from his commanderies.
Wǎn appointed Chōngzhī as Zǐxūn's Zīyì Cānjūn,
in charge of the central army,
granted him the title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
and had him co-command the vanguard with Táo Liàng.
Jìshì Cānjūn Xún Dàolín was ordered to draft a proclamation,
to be quickly sent far and near.
At this time, Tàizōng had quelled the chaos,
and promoted Zǐxūn to the title of Chējì Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
When the imperial decree arrived,
all the subordinate officials were delighted,
and went to Wǎn, saying,
"The tyranny and chaos have been eliminated,
and Your Highness has also opened the Imperial Secretariat.
This is truly a great joy for both public and private."
Wǎn believed that Zǐxūn, being third in the succession,
and having started his uprising in Xúnyáng,
which corresponded to Shìzǔ,
would surely achieve complete victory.
So he took the imperial decree and threw it to the ground, saying,
"Your Highness should open the Duānmén gate;
the Imperial Secretariat is merely a task for our subordinates!"
Everyone was astonished.
Wǎn and Táo Liàng and others repaired weapons and armor,
and recruited soldiers from all directions.

The following individuals collaborated in the rebellion: Wáng Zǐsuī, Prince of Ānlù and Cǐshǐ of Yǐngzhōu; Wáng Zǐxū, Prince of Línghǎi and Cǐshǐ of Jīngzhōu; Wáng Zǐfáng, Prince of Xúnyáng and Tàishǒu of Kuàijī; Yuán Yǐ, Cǐshǐ of Yōngzhōu; Liǔ Yuánhù, Cǐshǐ of Liángzhōu; Xiāo Huìkāi, Cǐshǐ of Yìzhōu; Yuán Tányuǎn, Cǐshǐ of Guǎngzhōu; Xuē Āndū, Cǐshǐ of Xúzhōu; Shěn Wénxiù, Cǐshǐ of Qīngzhōu; Cuī Dàogù, Cǐshǐ of Jìzhōu; Hé Huìwén, acting as affairs for Xiāngzhōu; Gù Chēn, Tàishǒu of Wújùn; Wáng Tánshēng, Tàishǒu of Wúxīng; Yuán Biāo, Tàishǒu of Jìnlíng; Liú Yánxī, Tàishǒu of Yìxīng.
Earlier,
the Deposed Emperor had appointed Wáng Zǐyuán, Prince of Shàolíng, as Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Cǐshǐ of Xiāngzhōu.
Shěn Zhòngyù, Cānjūn of the Central Army, acted as affairs for the road.
When they reached Quèítóu,
they heard that the Xúnyáng army had risen.
They halted,
and reported to Tàizōng for instructions on whether to advance or stop.
Tàizōng believed that Zǐxūn's initial uprising
was aimed at the young ruler.
Although he suspected Zǐxūn might not immediately disband his troops,
he did not want to prematurely reveal any differences.
He ordered them to continue their march.
Before a reply was received,
Wǎn heard that Zǐyuán had stopped at Quèítóu and was not advancing.
He dispatched several hundred men to forcibly welcome him.
Then he established his banner at Sāngwěi,
and sent a proclamation to the capital, which read: "The six numbers of the sun are difficult;
clouds and thunder follow one another.
When the High Emperor received his mandate,
he rode the cloud reins,
but was halted on a narrow path.
The Illustrious Ancestor established auspiciousness,
linking radiant wisdom,
but was cut short
in his middle years.
Two villains unleashed calamity,
and the three cardinal principles were extinguished.
Royal princes bowed their heads,
temporizing with the rebellious court,
silent with their weapons,
illicitly enjoying honors.
Emperor Xiàowǔ
relinquished his position, weeping tears of blood,
raised an army of righteousness to punish the rebels,
plunged into battle as commander,
personally slew the tyrants,
and the nine regions regained their brilliance,
heaven and earth were recreated.
But the heavens were ungracious,
abandoning the myriad
states.
The imperial destiny again faltered,
and the successor was foolish and depraved.
I, being untalented,
hold the position of a regional governor,
greatly fearing that the altars of the imperial house
will be annihilated in due course.
Therefore, I have gathered followers from Chǔ and Yǐng,
sent flying
proclamations to the imperial domain,
determined to follow ancient precedents,
to depose the obscure and promote the enlightened,
hoping that the seven ancestral temples will again be peaceful,
and the desolate seas will have a successor.
How could I have expected that the Sòng dynasty would not repent of its wickedness,
but that regicide and chaos would suddenly arrive?
They then falsely
harmed the wise and virtuous,
usurped the imperial treasure,
reversed the proper way and followed bad examples,
scorned our imperial virtue,
violated our ancestral order,
orphaned our brothers,
indulged the hearts of owls and vultures,
trod the path of Lún and Yǐng,
overturned the imperial throne,
and deceived heaven and men.
My blood relations,
there are still thirteen.
What fault have the sacred spirits committed,
that they should lack sacrifices?
In the past, when the glorious Zhōu declined,
Jìn and Zhèng were relied upon;
during the flourishing Hàn, in the middle of chaos,
Jū and Zhāng upheld integrity.
Even distant branches of the imperial clan,
might forget to drive themselves,
let alone I, who humbly am
Your minister,
my feelings are deeply agitated,
my cries of anguish reach a corner of the land,
my heart aches with the circumstances.
Therefore, drinking blood and bearing a blade,
I swear to restore the imperial ancestral temple.
Now I dispatch Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, Cānyì
Lǐng Zhōngzhíbīng Sūn Chōngzhī, and Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn Chén Shàozōng,
leading soldiers like *chīhǔ*,
two myriad in full armor,
to swiftly advance along the river,
and directly seize Báixià.
Lóng
xiāng Jiāngjūn Lǐng Zhōngzhíbīng Xuē Chángbǎo, and Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn Lǐng Zhōngzhíbīng Shěn Huáibǎo,
with ten thousand long halberds,
and a thousand groups of feathered cavalry,
will directly emerge from Nánzhōu,
and directly reach Zhūquè.
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Cānyì Lǐng Zhōngzhíbīng Táo Liàng, and Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn Jiāo Dù,
commanding the host of *zhōnghuáng*,
three myriad heroes,
will envelop
Jiāngjiè like the wind,
and descend upon Shítou like clouds.
Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn Zhāng Liè, and Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn Hé Xiūmíng,
leading followers like Yù and Huò,
valiant and fierce soldiers,
will advance diagonally towards Jīn
líng,
and point north to Chānghé.
Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn Zhāng Xìbó, and Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn Chén Qìng,
will lead five thousand light elite troops,
and ten thousand powerful crossbowmen,
to launch their sharp vanguard at Bāndú,
and
converge at Xīmíng.
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, Xúnyáng Nèishǐ Dèng Wǎn,
will gather troops from Xiāng and Yōng,
forty thousand brave soldiers,
to take command and exert authority,
and rapidly assemble at Jīngyì.
Zhēng
lǔ Jiāngjūn Lǐng Fǔ Sīmǎ Zhāng Yuè,
with a thousand *cāngsì* ships,
and fifty thousand naval forces,
will command all the officers,
continuously following one another on the path.
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn Yùzhāng Nèishǐ
Liú Yǎn, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Wǔchāng Tàishǒu Liú Bì, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Xīyáng Tàishǒu Xiè Zhì, Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn Lǐng Zhōngzhíbīng JìnXī Tàishǒu
Yán Zhànzhī,
all have cleared their territories of troops,
and sincerely offered to serve.
Hòu Jiāngjūn, Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ, Ānlù Wáng Zǐ Suī, embracing his gratitude and longing,
will mobilize his army ahead of time.
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ, Shàolíng Wáng Zǐ Yuán, unfurling sails and riding the waves,
will assemble his forces and arrive swiftly.
Qián Jiāngjūn, Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ, Línhǎi Wáng Zǐ Xù
will train armored troops west of the pass,
offering tens of thousands of soldiers.
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, Guānjūn Chángshǐ, Chángshā Nèishǐ Hé Huìwén,
having been promoted by the former emperor,
his sincerity is deep, he throws himself into action.
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Yuán Yǐ,
without prior consultation, reached an agreement,
and launched like thunder from Hànnán.
Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn, Shùnyáng Tàishǒu Liú Dàoxiàn,
harboring loyalty and
indignation,
did not consider three thousand *lǐ* too far.
Liáng, Yì, Qīng, Xú, Yǎn, Yù, Wú, Huì,
all have secretly sent messengers to pledge allegiance,
swearing to be the vanguard.
I personally command the assembled multitudes,
over
a hundred thousand,
white feathers blocking the streams,
frosty blades illuminating the fields,
metal sounds shaking the valleys,
beating drums deafening the heavens.
All the generals and commanders,
are loyal without concealed feelings,
wise without forgotten
stratagems,
resolute, firm, and fierce,
with many ingenious tactics.
Advancing by land and water,
several routes progressing simultaneously,
setting sail over dangers,
fighting with backs to the water for precedence.
With such an army,
who can
resist it?
With such righteous sharpness,
the vast ocean can be filled.
Gentlemen, some of you were favored by the former court,
and are grateful for past kindnesses;
others have been virtuous and pure for generations,
and facing danger, offered their lives.
Yet, constrained by the enemy's hands,
you had no means to show your loyalty.
Now
the grand army is close,
external aid has arrived,
act when the opportunity arises,
why wait another day?
It is opportune to turn misfortune into fortune,
and establish merits amidst change.
Indeed, Dàn and Shì were contemporary with the three
Gāns, Jīn and Huò were co-ministers with Shàngguān,
the wicked and the righteous mixed together,
in what era has this not been so?
But when achievements are brilliant, one's name spreads,
and when villainy runs rampant, the Way perishes.
Jǐ
Jì entered Qí,
Chén Píng returned to Hàn,
their persons honored, their reputations far-reaching,
clear oaths were gathered,
complete models and rules established,
the lesson of Yīn is not distant.
If you continue to indulge in faults and rest,
and, when told, do not
awaken,
then punishment will extend to the five kindreds,
utterly annihilating, leaving none.
Military rewards and ranks,
are as trustworthy as the bright sun.
When Wūshān is ablaze,
orchids and mugwort burn together.
Fortunately, follow the good path,
do not
cling to a broken rut.
Upon receipt of this proclamation, announce it,
and make it known to all.
A reward of ten thousand households and a marquisate for Tàizōng,
twenty thousand bolts of cloth and silk,
five hundred catties of gold and silver,
the rest will vary accordingly.
city,
to await the net of that heavenly power,
forcing this rabble,
to resist the armies of Luòyǔ.
The clouds’ net covered all four directions,
frost-sharp blades met in conflict,
like a fierce gale sweeping tender grass,
a raging fire scorching a cold plain,
the form of scorched ruin,
was already clearly apparent.
The court had compassion for our officials,
and pity for our soldiers and commoners,
who were all innocent,
imprisoned and misled by
the deluded faction.
Therefore, an announcement was made,
allowing them to reform themselves.
If they remain stubborn and unrepentant,
and defy the King’s might,
when mutual destruction arrives,
what good will repentance do?
By imperial edict, regarding
the four young and weak princes,
who unfortunately fell into trouble,
on the day the armies clash,
they are not to be wantonly attacked or harmed.
If any harm or injury is inflicted,
punishment and extermination will be relentless.
The commanders on both sides,
are to strictly
guard and protect them.
The crime of misleading or trapping them,
will not be questioned at all.
Wǎn dispatched Sūn Chōngzhī to lead Chén Shàozōng, Hú Língxiù, Xuē Chángbǎo, Zhāng Jìbó, Jiāo Dù and others, a vanguard of ten thousand,
to come and occupy Zhěqí.
On the way, Chōngzhī wrote to Zǐxūn, saying:
“Boats are ready,
weapons are also arranged,
the three armies are eager,
each person vies to offer their life.
We are ready to sail downstream,
and directly take Báixià.
I hope you will quickly dispatch Táo Liàng’s various armies,
to meet up along the way,
and separately occupy Xīntíng and Nánzhōu,
then a single command will settle everything.”
Thereupon, Chōngzhī was granted the title of Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
and Táo Liàng was made Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
to command the troops from all prefectures to advance together.

Zhèng Jǐngxuán, military commander of Yǐngzhōu, Liú Liàng, military commander of Jīngzhōu, Hé Chāng, military commander of Xiāngzhōu, Liǔ Dēng, military commander of Liángzhōu, Zōng Shù, military commander of Yōngzhōu, and others, totaling twenty thousand men,
all advanced at once.
Liàng himself lacked strategy and cunning,
and when he heard that Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén was coming from upstream,
and Yīn Xiàozǔ had also arrived,
he dared not advance,
and stationed his army at Quèzhōu.
At this time, Wǎn dispatched Yán Zhànzhī to raid Lújiāng,
and Duàn Fóróng, Tái Jūnzǔ and Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn, was ordered to suppress him.
Fóróng was further ordered to lead one thousand iron cavalry,
and turn his army south to attack.
On the third day of the third month,
attacks were launched against Zhěqí by water and land.
Liàng and others led their troops to rescue,
but Yīn Xiàozǔ was hit by a stray arrow and died.
Jūnzǔ Zhū Fǔzhī, Shēn Qiānzhī, and Zhāng Língfú all suffered defeats.
Fǔzhī’s deputy, Zhèngyuán Jiāngjūn Huángfǔ Zhòngyuǎn, and Qiānzhī’s deputy, Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiāng Xú Zhìbīn, were both lost.
Xiàozǔ’s branch jūnzǔ, Fàn Qián, led five hundred men and surrendered to Liàng.
At that time, the eastern army had already achieved victory,
Jiāng Fāngxīng returned to Hǔhǎn.
Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén dispatched Fāngxīng and Liú Língyí, each leading three thousand men, to assist Zhěqí,
with Fāngxīng commanding Xiàozǔ’s army,
and Shěn Yōuzhī replacing Xiàozǔ as Qiánfēng Dūdū.
Chōngzhī said to Táo Liàng:
“Xiàozǔ was a valiant general,
but he died in one battle.
The affairs of the world are settled,
there is no need to fight again,
we should immediately go straight to the capital.”
Liàng did not comply.
Tàizōng dispatched Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng Wáng Dàolóng to Zhěqí to supervise the battle.
The day after Xiàozǔ died,
Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén again dispatched Jūnzǔ Guō Jìzhī with three thousand cavalry and infantry to join Yōuzhī.

Yōuzhī then led Jìzhī, and Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Bùbīng Xiàowèi Dù Yǒuwén, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Túnqí Xiàowèi Yuán Gōngzǔ, Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Zhū Fǔzhī, Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng Gāo Zūnshì, Mǎ Jūnzǔ Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Dùn Shēng, Duàn Fóróng and others, totaling thirty thousand men.
At dawn, they advanced to battle,
fought with vigor,
and decisively defeated them,
beheading and capturing several thousand,
pursuing the fleeing enemy to Mǔshān and then returning.
Chōngzhī and others built two cities at Hú and Báikǒu,
which were captured by Jūnzǔ Zhāng Xīngshì.
Táo Liàng, hearing that the two cities of Hú and Bái had fallen,
was greatly afraid,
and urgently called Chōngzhī back to Quèwěi,
leaving Xuē Chángbǎo to guard Zhěqí in Chōngzhī’s place.
The camps and fortresses previously established at Mǔshān and various other ridges
were also all defeated and returned,
and they jointly held Nónghú.
Nónghú was located at Quèwěi.
At this time, a large army was raised,
and national expenditure was insufficient.
The people were recruited to offer two hundred hú of rice,
fifty thousand cash,
and five hundred hú of miscellaneous grains,
and in return were granted exemption from duties in a desolate county.
Those who offered three hundred hú of rice,
eighty thousand cash,
and one thousand hú of miscellaneous grains,
were granted the title of Wǔpǐn Zhèng Lìngshǐ;
upon full repayment,
if they wished to be appointed to a Sīpǐn position at home,
it was also permitted.
Those who offered four hundred hú of rice,
one hundred twenty thousand cash,
and one thousand three hundred hú of miscellaneous grains,
were granted the title of Sīpǐn Lìngshǐ;
upon full repayment,
if they wished to be appointed to a Sānpǐn position at home,
it was also permitted.
Those who offered five hundred hú of rice,
one hundred fifty thousand cash,
and one thousand five hundred hú of miscellaneous grains,
were granted the title of Sānpǐn Lìngshǐ;
upon full repayment,
if they wished to be appointed as a Nèijiān at home,
it was also permitted.
Those who offered seven hundred hú of rice,
two hundred thousand cash,
and two thousand hú of miscellaneous grains,
were granted exemption from duties in a desolate commandery;
if they wished to be appointed to a position of the three Lìng in a royal kingdom at home,
it was also permitted.
Wǎn again dispatched Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Hú to lead thirty thousand men,
and two thousand iron cavalry,
to come and encamp at Quèwěi.
Hú was an old general,
who had repeatedly achieved military successes,
and was known for his cunning and trickery,
and was respected by the masses.
Yōuzhī and others greatly feared him.
At that time, Hú’s fellow villagers Cài Nà, Jiǎo Chángshēng, and Zhāng Jìng'ér each led troops under Yōuzhī at Zhěqí.
Hú tried to recruit them by letter,
but Nà and the others all refused.
Hú then invited Nà and the others to talk,
and spoke of their past relationship.
Nà and the others questioned and rebuked him,
telling him to surrender.
Hú returned his army to Quèwěi,
without any other strategic moves.
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Wú Xǐ pacified Sān Wú,
and led five thousand men under his command,
and also transported supplies and provisions,
to Zhěqí.
He built a fortress at Zhànniǎo Shān,
and dispatched one thousand men,
in two hundred light boats,
to form a mobile army with Jiǎo Chángshēng.
Xūe Chángbǎo's provisions were exhausted.
He sent a plea to Hú Qiú for aid.
On the twenty-ninth day of the third month,
Hú Qiú led ten thousand infantry,
felling mountains and clearing paths by night,
transporting rice in cloth sacks,
to bring provisions to Zhěqí.
They arrived below the city at daybreak,
still separated by a small trench,
unable to enter.
Shěn Yōuzhī led the various armies to attack them.
Army commanders Guō Jìzhī, Xún Sēngsháo, and banner chief Hán Xīnzōng,
led three thousand men,
to serve as Yōuzhī's reinforcement.
Hú Qiú started crossing the bridge,
and Sēngsháo and others advanced, fighting with shields,
recovering the bridge and crossing.
Army commander Líu Shāmí plunged deep with light cavalry,
reaching Hú Qiú's banner,
and was then killed.
Yōuzhī spurred his horse into the formation,
and as he turned back,
he was stabbed by pursuing cavalry.
Cavalry commanders Duàn Fórong and Wǔ Bǎo rescued him, and he escaped.
They fought desperately,
inflicting many casualties.
Hú Qiú's forces were greatly defeated,
abandoning provisions and armor,
fleeing along the mountains.
They were pursued in victory,
and many were slain or captured.
Hú Qiú was wounded,
and barely managed to return to his camp.
Chángbǎo was terrified and without a plan.
He sent a messenger to Hú Qiú,
expressing his desire to break out of the encirclement and flee.
On the fourth day of the fourth month,
Hú Qiú personally led several thousand men to meet him.
Chángbǎo and others opened the city gates, broke through the encirclement, and fled.
Yōuzhī led Auxiliary General Shěn Huáimíng, army commanders Zhōu Pǔsūn, Jiāng Fāngxīng, Shēn Qiānzhī, and other forces to attack them with full strength.
Wú Xǐ led his troops to respond,
but was surrounded by a separate force of Hú Qiú,
in a dire situation.
Someone came and seized Xǐ's horse.
Officer Cài Bǎo hacked at him with a knife,
cutting off his hand,
and only then did Xǐ escape.
Regular General and banner chief Bǔ Bózōng, and Gentleman-in-waiting of Jiāngxià Commandery and banner chief Zhāng Huàn fought bravely and died in battle.
Bózōng
was the son of Yìzhōu Governor Tiānyǔ.
Yōuzhī, Xǐ, and others fought fiercely for an entire day.
Chángbǎo, Zhāng Jìbó, Hú Língxìu, Jīao Dù, and others were all severely wounded,
and fled back to Hú Qiú's army.
Zhěqí city fell.
The rebel NingShuò General and Nányáng Administrator Shěn Huáibǎo, and the rebel FengCháoqǐng and Chief of the Middle Secretariat Dūzhàn Xìe Dàoyù, were executed.
Several thousand surrendered.
Chén Shàozōng fled alone in a skiff to the west bank,
and returned to Quèwěi with his subordinates.
Prince of Jiàn'ān Xiūrén advanced from Hǔlán and occupied Zhěqí.
Líu Hú sent Chén Shàozōng and Chén Qìng with two hundred light skiffs
and fifty large ships
to challenge them outside Quèwěi.
Wú Xǐ, Zhāng Xīngshì, Jiǎo Chángshēng, and others attacked them.
Xǐ's subordinate army commander Wú Xiànzhī charged with a flying skiff,
overwhelming everything in his path,
slaying and capturing many, and many others drowned by jumping into the water.
They pursued them to Quèwěi and then returned.
Tàizōng feared that Hú Qiú and others might advance towards the capital on foot,
so he sent NingShuò General and Guǎngdé Prefect Wáng Yùn with a thousand men to defend Lǔxiǎn.
At this time, Hú Qiú's forces were strong,
and people near and far were in doubt.
Tàizōng wished to pacify popular sentiment,
so he sent Minister of Personnel Chǔ Yuān to Hǔlán to select generals and other officials.
Shēn Qiānzhī and Dù Yòuwén took this opportunity to request the position of Yellow Gate Gentleman,
while Shěn Huáimíng and Líu Liàng requested the position of Middle Secretariat Gentleman.
Prince of Jiàn'ān Xiūrén immediately had Chǔ Yuān prepare the selection,
but the emperor did not approve,
saying:
"Loyal officials sacrifice themselves for the country,
without seeking recompense.
To use a time of difficulty to seek court appointments,
how can that be the principle of subjects?"
Shǐ'ān Grand Administrator Wáng Zhízhī, Jiàn'ān Grand Administrator Zhào Dàoshēng, and Ānchéng Administrator Líu Xí
all submitted with their commanderies.
Wǎn sent Dragon Soaring General Lìao Yǎn with several thousand men,
and also dispatched commoners from Lúlíng to attack Xí.
Xí and Commandery Assistant Tán Bīn resisted in battle,
suffering a great defeat.
Bīn was killed in battle.
Xí abandoned the commandery and fled,
holding a perilous position to defend himself.
Yǎn plundered and retreated,
and Xí re-emerged to occupy the commandery.
At this time, the Prince of Qí led his troops on an expedition to the northeast,
and the Heir Apparent of the Prince of Qí was the Magistrate of Gàn, Nánkāng.
Wǎn sent an envoy to arrest the Heir Apparent.
The Heir Apparent's trusted followers Xīao Xīnzǔ, Huán Kāng, and several tens of others,
supported the Heir Apparent's eldest son and fled into the wilderness,
