recruiting over a hundred men.
They attacked the commandery to free the Heir Apparent.
The Heir Apparent styled himself NingShuò General,
and with Nánkāng Chancellor Shěn Sùzhī,
former Nánhǎi Administrator Hé Tánzhí, Jìnkāng Administrator Líu Shàozǔ, Běidì Fù Hào, Dōngguǎn Tóng Qín, and others,
they occupied the commandery and raised an army of righteousness.
Wǎn summoned Shǐxīng Chancellor Yīn Fú to be Imperial Censor-in-chief,
and also ordered him to lead the people of the commandery to descend.
Fú's forces were strong,
so the Heir Apparent avoided him at Jiēyáng Mountain.
Wǎn sent Wǔchāng's Dài Kǎizhī to be Nánkāng Chancellor.
The Heir Apparent led his troops to attack him.
Kǎizhī was defeated and fled.
The Heir Apparent sent banner chief Tán Wénqǐ with a thousand men to garrison Xīchāng,
to act in concert with Xí.
Wǎn again sent Lìao Yǎn and his Middle Army Staff Officer Hú Zhāo and others to build fortifications at Xīchāng,
and they held strong defenses against each other.
Wǎn summoned Yùzhāng Administrator Líu Yǎn to be Right General and Protector-General of the Army.
Yīn Fú replaced him as Yùzhāng Administrator,
overseeing the five upstream commanderies,
to defend against Xí and others.
Héngyáng Grand Administrator Wáng Yìngzhī led five hundred or so civil and military officials from his commandery to raise a righteous army and attack Hé Hùiwén at Chángshā,
arriving directly beneath the city.
Hùiwén led his retinue out of the city to engage in battle.
Yìngzhī fought with surging courage,
killing several people,
and then engaged Hùiwén in hand-to-hand combat.
He hacked Hùiwén eight times.
Hùiwén hacked Yìngzhī, severing his foot,
and then killed him.
At this time, Xiāngdōng Commandery Gentleman-in-waiting Yú Qià was overseeing the national tribute for Tàizōng,
and was in Xiāngdōng.
He urged Administrator Yán Yùe to raise troops to respond to the imperial court,
but Yùe refused.
Qià then went to Guìyáng,
recruiting several hundred men.
He returned intending to attack Yùe.
Yùe, frightened, sought peace,
which Qià granted.
Qià had two thousand men.
At this time, Wǎn summoned Hùiwén to lead his troops down to Xúnyáng,
departing Chángshā.
He had already traveled several hundred *lǐ* [Chinese miles]
when he heard that Qià had raised an army.
He then turned back to attack Qià.
Qià was soon defeated and fled.
After Yīn Fú left Shǐxīng,
he left Commandery Registrar Tán Bóchu in charge of commandery affairs.
Scholar Líu Sìzǔ and others decapitated Bóchu,
occupied the commandery, and raised an army of righteousness.
Wǎn sent Shǐxīng Administrator Wéi Xīzhēn and Eagle Soaring General Yáng Hóngzhī with a thousand men to suppress Sìzǔ.
Sìzǔ also sent troops out of Nánkāng,
to join forces with the Heir Apparent of the Prince of Qí.
Xīzhēn and others, seeing the strength of the righteous army,
stayed in Lúlíng and dared not advance.
Guǎngzhōu Governor Yuán Tányuǎn heard that Shǐxīng had risen in righteousness,
and sent generals Lǐ Wànzhōu and Chén Bóshào with troops to suppress Sìzǔ.
Sìzǔ sent troops to garrison Zhēnyáng.
Wànzhōu also built fortifications and held his ground.
Sìzǔ sent someone to deceive Wànzhōu, saying:
"Xúnyáng has already been pacified.
The court has sent Líu Mǐan to be Governor of Guǎngzhōu,
and he is about to arrive."
Wànzhōu believed him,
and immediately turned back to attack Pānyú.
He entered the city at night with long ladders.
Tányuǎn was timid and weak and had no defenses.
Upon hearing that Wànzhōu had rebelled,
he fled barefoot,
and Wànzhōu pursued and decapitated him within the city.
Jiāozhōu Governor Tán Yì was replaced and had returned to Guǎngzhōu,
with immense wealth.
Wànzhōu falsely accused him of rebellion,
and attacked and killed him.
He then plundered public and private silver and silk,
and confiscated Yuán's and Tán's treasures,
keeping them all for himself.
Yuán Yǐ gathered all the troops from Yōngzhōu
and came to Xúnyáng.
At this time, Kǒng Dàocún was the Long History of the Guard Army,
acting as Governor of Jīngzhōu.
Wǎn replaced him with Yellow Gate Gentleman Líu Dàoxiàn,
and made Dàocún a Palace Attendant,
acting as Governor of Yōngzhōu.
When Líu Yuánjǐng was executed,
Yuánjǐng's nephew Shìlóng was Administrator of Shàngyōng.
The people and officials collectively concealed him.
When Yǐ raised his army,
he summoned Shìlóng,
but he did not come.
After Yǐ descended,
Shìlóng then gathered more than two thousand Mãan and Sòng people,
raised an army of righteousness in Shàngyōng,
and came to attack Xiāngyáng.
Dàocún sent generals Wáng Shìmín, Kāng Yuánlóng, and others to meet and attack them at Wànshān.
Shìlóng was greatly defeated
and returned to his commandery to defend himself.
Shěn Yōuzhī and others were in a protracted stalemate with Liú Hú,
and the Emperor again sent Strong Crossbow General Rèn Nóngfū, Zhenwǔ General Wǔ Huìcāng, Róngcóng Púshè Quán Jǐngwén, and Army Commander Liú Bófú and others to lead troops as reinforcements.
Yōuzhī was repairing boats and rafts,
but timber planks were insufficient,
and he was at a loss for what to do.
Coincidentally, Wǎn sent five thousand planks as palisades for Hú's army.
Soon, the wind and tide rushed violently,
and the palisade planks broke through the defensive barriers and floated down the river.
Hú and his men were unable to control them,
crashing into their own ships and vessels,
killing and drowning dozens of people.
They drifted downstream
and docked at Yōuzhī's camp.
Thus, timber planks became abundant.
Wǎn promoted Yuán Yǐ to Inspector-General of All Expeditions,
and granted him one set of drums and pipes.
On the eighteenth day of the sixth month,
Yǐ led a thousand tower ships
and entered Quèwěi.
Zhāng Xīngshì suggested bypassing Quèwěi to occupy Qiánxī,
thereby cutting off their supply route.
Hú repeatedly attacked them
but could not overcome them.
The details are in Xīngshì's biography.
Liú Liàng led his subordinates to Hú's stockade.
Hú sent his deputy Sūn Xī, along with Zhāng Líng and Jiāo Dù, with five cavalrymen
to cross [⿰亻丹] to capture Liàng,
but they failed.
Xī turned his horse and left.
Liàng ordered his skilled archers on both sides to shoot at him from two directions,
and he fell from his horse.
Xī's head was cut off.
Zhāng Jìbó, deputy to Mǎ Kě, led his subordinates to surrender.
Liú Liàng's camp
penetrated deep into enemy territory.
Yuán Yǐ feared him,
saying:
"The enemy has entered our very vitals;
how can we survive?"
Liú Hú led four hundred light rafts
through the inner route of Quèyóu,
intending to attack Qiánxī.
Afterwards, he said to his Chief Clerk Wáng Niànshū:
"I learned infantry combat in my youth
but am not skilled in naval warfare.
If it were infantry combat,
I would be among tens of thousands of men,
but in naval combat, one is on a single raft.
Each raft advances independently,
no longer connected to the others.
This is like being among only thirty men to take action.
This is not a foolproof plan;
I will not do it."
So he feigned malaria
and stayed at Quèyóu without advancing.
He sent Longxiáng General Chén Qìng with three hundred rafts toward Qiánxī,
cautioning Qìng not to engage in battle:
"Zhāng Xīngshì and Wǔ Huìcāng
are known to me;
they will naturally flee."
Chén Qìng reached Qiánxī
but dared not attack.
He bypassed Qiánxī
and established a stockade at Méigēn.
Hú separately dispatched General Wáng Qǐ with a hundred rafts to attack Xīngshì.
Xīngshì attacked and utterly defeated him.
Hú led his remaining rafts back,
and said to Yǐ:
"Xīngshì's camp is already established,
and cannot be attacked swiftly.
The small battle yesterday
was not a significant loss.
Chén Qìng has already joined the forces of Nánlíng and Dàléi to block their upper path,
our main army is here,
and the generals at Quèyóu have cut off their lower reaches.
They are already surrounded;
there is no need to worry further."
Yǐ was angry that Hú did not fight,
and said:
"The supply route is blocked;
what should be done about this?"
Hú replied:
"If they can still go upstream, past us,
why can our supplies not go downstream, past them?"
Yǐ again sent Hú to lead twenty thousand infantry
and one thousand armored cavalry
to attack Xīngshì.
Xiūrén then ordered Shěn Yōuzhī, Wú Xǐ, Jiǎo Chángshēng, Liú Língyí, Liú Bófú, and others to advance and attack Nónghú.
They built ten leather warships,
and captured their camps and stockades.
After a bitter battle that lasted a day,
they thoroughly defeated them.
Yǐ, being pressed by the attack,
sent a hurried message to summon Hú back.
Since Zhāng Xīngshì had occupied Qiánxī,
the river route was cut off.
Hú's army lacked provisions.
Wǎn sent a large quantity of supplies,
but fearing Xīngshì, dared not send them down.
Hú sent generals to meet them,
but they were defeated by Qiánxī's forces.
All the supplies were lost and completely destroyed.
Three hundred thousand hú of rice were burned.
Hú's troops were terrified.
Hú's deputy Zhāng Xǐ surrendered,
saying Hú intended to defect.
On the twenty-fourth day of the eighth month,
Hú deceived Yǐ, saying:
"I will lead another twenty thousand infantry and cavalry
to take Xīngshì,
and also to collect the remaining provisions at Dàléi."
He ordered Yǐ to transfer all his horses to him.
That night, he abandoned Yǐ and fled,
heading straight for Méigēn.
He had previously ordered Xuē Chángbǎo to prepare boats and rafts,
and had allocated all the Nánlíng forces.
He burned the cities at Dàléi and fled.
When Yǐ heard that Hú had fled,
he also abandoned his troops and fled west.
He was killed at Qīnglín.
Hú led several hundred rafts and twenty thousand men toward Xúnyáng.
He reported to Zǐxūn, falsely claiming:
"Yuán Yǐ has surrendered,
and all the armies have dispersed.
Only I lead my subordinates, rebelling alone.
You should quickly make arrangements
for provisions for a single battle.
I will temporarily hold Pénchéng,
swearing not to waver until death."
Then, on the outside of the river, he took Miǎnkǒu by night.
When Wǎn heard Hú had left,
he was in a state of panic and had no plan.
He called Chǔ Língsì and others to consult,
but none knew what to do,
only saying to gather more troops
and increase rewards by five ranks,
or some said three ranks.
Zhāng Yuè, having just finished his nephew Hào's funeral,
feigned illness and summoned Wǎn to discuss matters.
He ordered his attendants to hide armored men behind the tent,
instructing them:
"If you hear me ask for wine,
then come out."
When Wǎn arrived,
Yuè said:
"You were the first to propose this plan.
Now things are urgent;
what plan will you devise?"
Wǎn said:
"We should simply execute the King of Jìn'ān,
seal the treasuries,
and apologize for our crime."
Yuè said:
"Today, can we betray His Highness to save ourselves?"
He then called for wine.
He called a second time,
but the attendants were so terrified they could not respond.
His second son, Xún, ran out with a knife.
Other people followed,
and immediately executed Wǎn.
When Wǎn died,
he was sixty years old.
At that time, Chief Commandant Liú Yǎn was present,
and startled, he rose and embraced Yuè.
The attendants wanted to kill him,
but Yuè looked back and said:
"It has nothing to do with the Chief Commandant."
And they stopped.
Pān Xīnzhī heard Wǎn was dead,
and led his troops to arrive.
Yuè sent someone to tell him:
"Dèng Wǎn plotted rebellion and has already been executed."
Xīnzhī then turned back,
seized Wǎn's children, and killed them all.
Yuè then took Wǎn's head in a single raft and hurried downstream,
going to Jiàn'ān King Xiūrén to surrender.
Cài Nà's son, Dàoyuān,
whose father had served Tàizōng
and was imprisoned as a laborer,
took advantage of the chaos to break his chains and enter the city,
seizing and imprisoning Zǐxūn.
Shěn Yōuzhī's armies reached Jiāngzhōu,
executed Zǐxūn beneath the commander's banner at Sāngwěi,
and sent his head to the capital.
Liú Yǎn and the other accomplices
were all executed.
Wú Xǐ and Zhāng Xīngshì advanced toward Jīngzhōu,
Shěn Huáimíng toward Yǐngzhōu,
Liú Liàng and Zhāng Jìng'ér toward Yōngzhōu,
Sūn Chāozhī toward Xiāngzhōu,
Shěn Sīrén and Rèn Nóngfū toward Yùzhāng.
All the places they reached were pacified.
Liú Hú fled into Miǎn,
his followers gradually dispersed,
by the time they reached Shíchéng,
only a few horsemen remained.
Chén Huáizhēn, Assistant Administrator of Jìnglíng Commandery,
son of (Chén) Xiàn,
hearing that (Liú) Hú was passing through,
led several tens of men to block the road and intercept him.
As (Liú) Hú's men and horses were already exhausted,
he judged he could not escape,
so he followed (Chén) Huáizhēn into the city.
He requested water,
and was given wine.
After (Liú) Hú finished drinking,
he drew his belt knife and stabbed himself.
He did not die,
so his head was cut off and sent to Jīngyì.
Zhāng Xīngshì's younger brother, Sēngchǎn, pursued (Liú) Hú.
Before reaching Shíchéng by several tens of *lǐ*,
he encountered the messenger carrying (Liú) Hú's head.
(Sēngchǎn) then returned to Jìnglíng,
killed (Chén) Huáizhēn,
and falsely claimed credit for his achievement.
Zhāng Shěn, Acting Administrator of Yǐngzhōu, and Qiū Jǐngxiān, the self-proclaimed Grand Administrator of Jìnglíng, hearing of the defeat,
disguised themselves as Buddhist monks and fled.
They were pursued, captured, and executed.
Jīngzhōu, hearing that Nónghú had been pacified,
deliberated on whether to send another army to combine forces with Yǐngzhōu,
and also whether to cut off and occupy Bālíng.
Days passed without a decision.
Thereupon, (Jīngzhōu) sent general Zhào Dàoshǐ to build a stronghold at Jiāngjīn,
and Rèn Yǎn to guard Shāqiáo.
All important gates and river crossings
had garrisoned troops.
Public sentiment turned away,
and officers and soldiers gradually dispersed.
It was further debated whether to take Zǐxù and flee to Yìzhōu,
to join Xiāo Huìkāi.
Registrar Ruǎn Dàoyù and Shào Zǎi disagreed,
saying:
“Recently, a special imperial edict was received,
stating that if any princely states who have strayed would return to allegiance,
they would all have their original titles restored.
Moreover, Rèn Shū'ér has already cut off Báidì,
and Yáng Sēngsì occupies Liángzhōu.
Even if we wished to go west,
how could we possibly reach there?”
Dàoyù and Shào Zǎi immediately, with Liú Dàoxiàn, dismissed the common conscripts,
and sent envoys to confess their guilt.
Zōng Jǐng, Central Administrator of Jīngzhōu, and Yáo Jiǎn, a local, among others, led troops into the city.
They killed (Liú) Dàoxiàn, (Ruǎn) Dàoyù, and Bào Zhào, the Recorder and Military Advisor,
〔一０〕plundered the public treasury,
leaving nothing behind,
and captured Zǐxù, forcing his surrender.
Earlier,
Dèng Wǎn had levied troops from Bādōng.
Luó Bǎochēng, Grand Administrator of Bādōng, declined, stating that his commandery bordered fierce barbarians
and lacked sufficient forces to spare.
Rèn Shū'ér of Bādōng gathered followers and started an uprising.
He sent a messenger to summon (Luó) Bǎochēng.
(Luó) Bǎochēng hesitated, unable to decide,
and suddenly died of illness.
Shū'ér then proclaimed himself General Who Aids the State,
led his troops to occupy Báidì,
killed (Luó) Bǎochēng's two sons,
and blocked and defended Sānxiá.
Xiāo Huìkāi sent Fèi Xīnshòu and five thousand others to attack Shū'ér.
Shū'ér engaged them in battle,
thoroughly routed them,
and beheaded Fèi Xīnshòu.
Zǐxù again dispatched Hé Kāngzhī, the Central Military Advisor, to take charge as Grand Administrator of Yídū,
and suppress Shū'ér.
The army reached Xiákǒu,
where it was defeated by the barbarian chief Xiàng Zǐtōng,
and (Hé Kāngzhī) barely escaped with his life back (to Jīngzhōu).
Shū'ér thus firmly held Báidì.
Kǒng Dàocún, knowing that Xúnyáng had been pacified,
sent envoys to surrender.
Soon after, hearing that Liǔ Shìlóng and Liú Liàng were about to arrive,
all his followers fled.
Dàocún and his three sons committed suicide simultaneously.
Hé Huìwén initially conspired in the rebellion.
His mother tried to stop him, but he would not listen.
His mother then returned her daughter to Jiānglíng
and hastily married her off.
Huìwén possessed talent as both a general and an official,
and had a certain ability in strategy.
Although he had harmed Wáng Yìngzhī,
the Emperor specially granted him clemency,
and Wú Xǐ proclaimed the imperial edict pardoning him.
Huìwén said:
“Having fallen into rebellion
and personally harmed loyal and righteous men,
though heaven's net is indeed vast and loose,
how can I face the gentlemen of the world?”
He mixed medicine to drink,
but his disciples overturned it.
So he starved himself to death.
Yán Yuè, fearing that Yú Qià would return to the capital
and expose their initial collaboration in the rebellion,
secretly sent someone to kill him.
Earlier,
Jiǎ Xízōng, a man from Dìnglíng in Huáinán, whose home county had already been taken by Liú Hú,
led twenty men to defect to Shěn Yōuzhī.
Yōuzhī reported this to Liú Xiūrén, Prince of Jiàn'ān.
Xiūrén appointed (Jiǎ Xízōng) as Supervisor of the Minister of Works' Military Advisors,
and sent him back to his hometown to recruit.
He was captured by (Liú) Hú,
who roasted him with fire,
asking for news of the imperial army.
(Jiǎ Xízōng) said nothing at all,
instead, he glared at (Liú) Hú and said:
“You, sir, have raised troops to insult the state from within,
coveting the imperial throne.
I have not heard of any brilliant strategies or far-reaching plans from you,
yet you resort to *bāolào* torture.
I originally dedicated my life to righteousness;
what is death to me?”
(Liú) Hú then beheaded him.
Fàn Dàoxìng, Registrar of the Vanguard Army, whose aspirations differed from the rebellion,
was executed by (Dèng) Wǎn.
The others who remained loyal but were harmed
were all pitied by the Emperor.
An imperial edict stated:
“Fàn Dàoxìng, former Supervisor of the Garrison General's Military Advisors,
was an old subordinate of mine.
Having served in the northern feudatory
and worked in the southern capital region,
he encountered a fateful meeting [with rebellion].
He upheld his gratitude and firmly maintained his integrity,
suffering harm at the hands of the multitude of villains.
Thinking of his pure sincerity,
I truly feel pity and sorrow.
He is to be posthumously granted the title of Supernumerary Palace Attendant.
Bào Fǎdù, Magistrate of Nánchéng; Féng Cìmín, Registrar of the Rear Army; Yìng Shēng, Magistrate of Yǒngxīn; Kù Yánbǎo, Magistrate of Xīnjiàn; Huáng Nán, Magistrate of Shàngráo, and others,
who, despite the rebellion, recognized loyalty [to the dynasty]
and were likewise executed and annihilated,
considering their past,
it is fitting to posthumously honor them.
(Yìng) Shēng is to be posthumously granted the title of Court Attendant;
(Bào) Fǎdù, Censor of the Southern Bureau;
(Féng) Cìmín, (Kù) Yánbǎo, and (Huáng) Nán, all Supernumerary Generals.”
The authorities memorialized:
"Zhāng Xìngshì (張興世) of Jìnglíng, Ning Shuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍), Dū Yùzhōu zhī Liángjùn Zhūjūnshì (督豫州之梁郡諸軍事), Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (豫州刺史), and concurrently Nánliángjùn Tàishǒu (領南梁郡太守),
commanded the naval forces,
and repeatedly fought and achieved victories.
He then advanced to cut off the enemy's upstream Qíanxī (錢溪).
At Guìkǒu (貴口), he fought bitterly,
pacifying the fierce rebels.
He is now enfeoffed as Kàiguó Hóu (開國侯) of Tángxiàn (作唐縣), Nánpíngjùn (南平郡),
with a stipend of one thousand households.
Jiǎo Chángshēng (佼長生) of Guǎngpíng, Ning Shuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) and Cān Sītú Zhōngzhí Bīngjūnshì (參司徒中直兵軍事),
jointly commanded the naval forces and fought repeatedly.
When Xìngshì advanced to occupy Qíanxī,
Chángshēng single-handedly resisted the enemy's crucial assault.
His merit is second only to Xìngshì's.
He is now enfeoffed as Kàiguó Hóu (開國侯) of Qiānlíngxiàn (遷陵縣), Wǔlíngjùn (武陵郡),
with a stipend of eight hundred households.

Quán Jǐngwén (全景文) of Wúxìng, Ning Shuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) and Acting Xīyáng Tàishǒu (試守西陽太守); Sūn Chāozhī (孫超之) of Wúxiàn, Shàngshū Bǐbù Láng (尚書比部郎); and Liú Liàng (劉亮) of Nánpéngchéng, Acting Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (假輔國將軍) and Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (右衞將軍)—these three individuals
all participated in the bitter fighting at Jìnlíng (晉陵).
Jǐngwén and Chāozhī then also campaigned north to Pòfǔ (破釜),
where the naval forces cut off the enemy's grain transport.
They also broke the enemy at the two locations of Gězǒng (葛冢) and Shíliáng (石梁).
Liàng campaigned south and engaged in major battles,
and moreover was always in the most perilous and difficult positions.
Jǐngwén is now enfeoffed as Xiàoníngxiàn (孝寧縣), Xīyángjùn (西陽郡);
Chāozhī is enfeoffed as Luóxiàn (羅縣), Chángshājùn (長沙郡);
Liàng is enfeoffed as Shùnyángxiàn (順陽縣);
all are Kàiguó Hóu (開國侯),
each with a stipend of six hundred households.

Liú Língyí (劉靈遺), Acting Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (假輔國將軍) and Piàojì Sīmǎ (驃騎司馬); Cài Nà (蔡那), Ning Shuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) and Yòujūn (右軍); Duàn Fórong (段佛榮), Ning Shuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) and Túnqí Xiàowèi (屯騎校尉)—these three individuals
commanded the attack routes,
and all participated in bitter fighting.
Língyí is now enfeoffed as Xīnyěxiàn (新野縣), Xīnyějùn (新野郡);
Nà is enfeoffed as Píngyángxiàn (平陽縣), Shǐpíngjùn (始平郡);
Fórong is enfeoffed as Línzhēngxiàn (臨蒸縣), Xiāngdōngjùn (湘東郡);
all are Kàiguó Bó (開國伯),
each with a stipend of five hundred households.

Shěn Huáimíng (沈懷明) of Wúxìng, Acting Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (假輔國將軍) and Zuǒjūn (左軍); Zhōu Pánlóng (周盤龍) of Dōngpíng, Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) and Jīshè Jiāngjūn (積射將軍); Lǐ Ānmín (李安民) of Nánpéngchéng, Sītú Cānjūn (司徒參軍)—these three individuals,
Huáimíng broke the enemy at Jìnlíng,
and also led the naval forces on the southern campaign,
commanding the attack routes.
Although Pánlóng did not command troops,
he participated in major battles,
being the first to climb walls and breach formations.
Ānmín also followed Zhāng Xìngshì to cut off Qíanxī,
and separately commanded troops to break the enemy at Guìkǒu.
Huáimíng is now enfeoffed as Wúxìngxiàn (吳興縣), Jiànānjùn (建安郡);
Pánlóng is enfeoffed as Jìnānxīàn (晉安縣), Jìnānjùn (晉安郡);
Ānmín is enfeoffed as Shàowǔxiàn (邵武縣), Jiànānjùn (建安郡);
all are Kàiguó Zǐ (開國子),
each with a stipend of four hundred households.

Dù Yòuwén (杜幼文) of Péngchéng, Acting Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (假輔國將軍) and Yóujī Jiāngjūn (游擊將軍); Wáng Mùzhī (王穆之) of Tàiyuán, Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) and Yǔlín Jiān (羽林監); Dùn Shēng (頓生) of Jìběi, Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) and Yǔlín Jiān (羽林監); Zhōu Pǔsūn (周普孫) of Pèijùn, Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) and Yǔlín Jiān (羽林監); Zhū Chóngēn (朱重恩), Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng (員外散騎侍郎)—these five individuals,
Yòuwén broke the enemy at Jìnlíng,
commanded attack routes in the army,
and campaigned south to Nónghú (濃湖).
Pǔsūn assisted Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) in commanding all the armies.
Mùzhī, Shēng, and Chóngēn all rendered meritorious service in the southern campaign.
Yòuwén is now enfeoffed as Shàoyángxiàn (邵陽縣), Shàolíngjùn (邵陵郡);
Mùzhī is enfeoffed as Héngshānxiàn (衡山縣), Héngyángjùn (衡陽郡);
Shēng is enfeoffed as Wǔgōngxiàn (武功縣), Shǐpíngjùn (始平郡);
Pǔsūn is enfeoffed as Qīngshuǐxiàn (清水縣), Shùnyángjùn (順陽郡);
Chóngēn is enfeoffed as Lóngchuānxiàn (龍川縣), Nánhǎijùn (南海郡);
all are Kàiguó Nán (開國男),
each with a stipend of three hundred households."
Jiāng Fāngxìng (江方興), for his battle merits, was made Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ (太子左衞率).
Before the rebels were pacified,
he died of illness.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Wǔdāngxiàn Hóu (武當縣侯),
with a stipend of five hundred households.
Fāngxìng
was from Kǎochéng (考城), Jìyáng (濟陽),
an old family of officials.
Dǒng Kǎizhī (董凱之), Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) and Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng (虎賁中郎將),
followed Zhāng Xìngshì in breaking Hú (胡) and Báichéng (白城),
being the first to scale the walls.
He was enfeoffed as Hélóngxiàn Zǐ (河隆縣子),
with a stipend of four hundred households.
Zhāng Língfú (張靈符), Jūnjì (軍主),
rendered meritorious service in the southeastern campaign.
He was enfeoffed as Shàngráoxiàn Nán (上饒縣男),
with a stipend of three hundred households.
Yáng Fù (楊覆), former Zhēngběi Cháng Jiān Xíng Cānjūn (征北長兼行參軍),
rendered meritorious service at Guìkǒu.
He was enfeoffed as Suīchéngxiàn Nán (綏城縣男),
with a stipend of two hundred households.
Yú Qià (虞洽) and Tán Fēn (檀玢) were posthumously granted Jǐshìzhōng (給事中).
Lǐ Wànzhōu (李萬周) was appointed Bùbīng Xiàowèi (步兵校尉).
Chén Huáizhēn (陳懷真), for his merit in beheading Liú Hú (劉胡),
was posthumously enfeoffed as Yǒngfēngxiàn Nán (永豐縣男),
with a stipend of three hundred households.
Liú Hú
was from Nièyáng (涅陽), Nányáng (南陽).
His original name was Āohú (坳胡).
Because his face was sunken and dark like a Hu (胡) person,
he was given that name.
When he grew up,
feeling that Āohú was difficult to say,
he was simply called Hú.
He started his career as a Jùnjiāng (郡將),
was quick-witted,
good at making arrangements,
and gradually rose to Duìzhǔ (隊主).
He campaigned against various Mán (蠻),
and never failed to achieve victory.
The Mán greatly feared and dreaded him.
In the twenty-eighth year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) of Tàizǔ (太祖),
he was made Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn (振威將軍),
leading three thousand infantry and cavalry,
to campaign against the Mán of Shàngrú (上如), Nánshān (南山), and Jiùxī (就溪).
He thoroughly defeated them.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn (孝建),
when Zhū Xiūzhī (朱脩之) was Yōngzhōu (雍州) Governor,
he appointed Hú as Píngxī Wàibīng Cānjūn (平西外兵參軍), Ning Shuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍), and Jiànchāng Tàishǒu (建昌太守).
[Page 11] He rendered meritorious service in attacking Lǔ Xiù (魯秀).
He was appointed Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn (建武將軍) and Tàishǒu (太守) of Dōngpíng (東平) and Yángpíng (陽平) commanderies.
He entered the court as Tàizǎi Cānjūn (太宰參軍) for Jiāngxiàwáng Yìgōng (江夏王義恭),
and was given the additional title Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍).
During the Jǐnghé (景和) era of the former deposed emperor,
when Jiànānwáng Xiūrén (建安王休仁) was Governor of Yōngzhōu,
he appointed Hú as Xiūrén's Ānxī Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (安西中兵參軍) and Féngyì Tàishǒu (馮翊太守),
with his general title remaining as before.
He was then transferred to Zīyì Cānjūn (諮議參軍).
When Tàizōng (太宗) ascended the throne,
he was appointed Yuèqí Xiàowèi (越騎校尉).
The Mán still feared him to this day;
when a small child cries,
if told,
"Liú Hú is coming!"
it immediately stops.
Duàn Fórong
was from Jīngzhào (京兆).
In the fifth year of Tàishǐ (泰始),
he was promoted from Yóujī Jiāngjūn (游擊將軍) to Fǔshī Jiāngjūn (輔師將軍) and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (豫州刺史).
He was clean and diligent in his duties,
and was a source of peace for the western region.
In the second year of Yuánhuī (元徽) of the later deposed emperor,
he was summoned to be Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
concurrently Lǐng Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi (領長水校尉).
The following year,
he was promoted to Wèiwèi (衞尉),
concurrently Lǐng Yòujūn Jiāngjūn (領右軍將軍).
Before he could take up the post,
he was again sent out as Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍), Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ (南豫州刺史), and Lìyáng Tàishǒu (歷陽太守).
In the fourth year,
he died.
He was posthumously granted Qián Jiāngjūn (前將軍),
his enfeoffment was changed to Yúndùxiàn (雲杜縣),
and he was given the posthumous title Liè Hóu (烈侯).
Liú Língyí
was from Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
In the first year of Yuánhuī,
he was promoted from Fǔshī Jiāngjūn (輔師將jūn) and Huáinán Tàishǒu (淮南太守)
to Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ (南豫州刺史) and Lìyáng Tàishǒu (歷陽太守),
with his general title remaining as before.
The following year,
he was summoned to be Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
concurrently Lǐng Bùbīng Xiàowèi (領步兵校尉) and Nánlánlíng Tàishǒu (南蘭陵太守).
He died of illness,
and was given the posthumous title Zhuàng Hóu (壯侯).
Yuán Yǐ (袁顗), courtesy name Jǐngzhāng (景章),
[Page 12] was from Yángxià (陽夏), Chénjùn (陳郡),
and was the nephew of Tàiwèi Shú (太尉淑).
His father, Xún (洵), was Wú Jùn Tàishǒu (吳郡太守).
Yǐ (顗) first served as Yùzhōu (豫州) Registrar.
He was nominated as Xiùcái (秀才),
but did not take office.
Later, he was appointed as Hòujūn Xíng Cānjūn (後軍行參軍) for Shǐxīngwáng Jùn (始興王濬),
Zuòzhuó Zuǒláng (著作佐郎),
Nán Zhōngláng Zhǔbù (南中郎主簿) for Lúlíngwáng Shào (廬陵王紹),
Zhēnglǔ (征虜) and Fǔjūn Zhǔbù (撫軍主簿) for Shìzǔ (世祖),
Lújiāng Tàishǒu (廬江太守),
Shàngshū Dūguān Láng (尚書都官郎),
Piàojì Jìshì Cānjūn (驃騎記室參軍) for Jiāngxiàwáng Yìgōng (江夏王義恭),
Rǔyīnwáng Wénxué (汝陰王文學),
and Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ (太子洗馬).
At that time, Yǐ's (顗) father was in Wújun (吳郡),
and Yǐ (顗) accompanied his father in office.
When the prime culprit usurped the throne,
Āndōng Jiāngjūn (安東將軍), Suíwáng Dàn (隨王誕), raised troops to attack him.
He appointed Yǐ (顗) as Zīyì Cānjūn (諮議參軍).
When the matter was settled,
he was appointed Zhèngyuán Láng (正員郎),
and Jìnlíng Tàishǒu (晉陵太守).
After his father's passing,
and the mourning period was over,
he became Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎).
He was again appointed Jìnlíng Tàishǒu (晉陵太守),
and inherited the rank of Nánchāngxiàn Wǔděng Zǐ (南昌縣五等子).
In the second year of Dàmíng (大明),
he was appointed Píngnán Sīmǎ (平南司馬) for Dōnghǎiwáng Huī (東海王褘) and Xúnyáng Tàishǒu (尋陽太守),
and acted as the administrator for Jiāngzhōu (江州).
He then became Qiánjūn Sīmǎ (前軍司馬) for Yìyángwáng Chǎng (義陽王昶),
with his position as Tàishǒu (太守) unchanged.
Chǎng (昶) was soon relieved of his post,
and his position as Sīmǎ (司馬) was dissolved.
He was given the title of Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍),
and his position as Tàishǒu (太守) was changed to Nèishǐ (內史).
He then became Guànjūn Sīmǎ (冠軍司馬) for Xúnyángwáng Zǐfáng (尋陽王子房),
with his rank as Jiāngjūn (將軍) unchanged,
and acted as administrator for the two commanderies of Huáinán (淮南) and Xuānchéng (宣城).
In the fifth year,
he was summoned to be Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子),
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞),
and concurrently the Dà Zhōngzhèng (大中正) of his native province.
In the seventh year,
he was promoted to Shìzhōng (侍中).
The following year,
he was appointed ZhènJūn Chángshǐ (鎮軍長史) for Jìn'ānwáng Zǐxūn (晉安王子勛) and Xiāngyáng Tàishǒu (襄陽太守),
and given the additional title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍).
Before he could take office,
he was again appointed Zuǒjūn Chángshǐ (左軍長史) for Yǒngjiāwáng Zǐrén (永嘉王子仁) and Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu (廣陵太ishǒu),
with his rank as Jiāngjūn (將軍) unchanged.
Before he could accept the appointment,
he was again made Shìzhōng (侍hōng),
and concurrently Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn (前軍將軍).
At the end of Dàmíng (大明),
Xīn'ānwáng Zǐluán (新安王子鸞) was greatly favored due to his mother's affection.
The Crown Prince in the Eastern Palace committed many errors.
The Emperor subtly entertained the idea of deposing the Crown Prince
and establishing Zǐluán (子鸞).
He occasionally mentioned this in a relaxed manner.
Yǐ (顗) highly praised the Crown Prince for his studiousness
and his daily improvements.
Shìzǔ (世祖) also found Shěn Qìngzhī's (沈慶之) talent and ability to be lacking,
and his discussions quite derogatory towards others.
Yǐ (顗) then stated that Qìngzhī (慶之) was loyal and diligent, with strategic ability,
and capable of important tasks.
Because of this, the former deposed Emperor deeply appreciated Yǐ (顗),
and Qìngzhī (慶之) also held him in high regard.
In the first year of Jǐnghé (景和),
when the dukes were executed,
he intended to promote Yǐ (顗)
and entrust him with court administration. He was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書).
An imperial edict was also issued saying:
“The imperial altars have suffered many misfortunes,
and the calamities arose from the chief minister.
But the mandate of Heaven has not yet sunk,
and the divine succession is restored to order.
If not for loyal and closely aligned strategies,
how could these be overcome?
Shìzhōng Jìjiǔ (侍中祭酒), concurrently Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn (前軍將軍), and newly appointed Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) Yǐ (顗);
Yóují Jiāngjūn (游擊將軍), concurrently Zuòzhuó Láng (著作郎) and Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (尚書左丞) Xú Yuán (徐爰);
their sincere loyalty
and participation in the excellent plans,
and the effectiveness of their assistance,
are truly known to Us.
They should be granted a fiefdom
to reward their righteous spirit.
Yǐ (顗) can be enfeoffed as Xīngànxiàn Zǐ (新淦縣子),
[一三]Yuán (爰) can be enfeoffed as Wúpíngxiàn Zǐ (吳平縣子),
each with a tax income of five hundred households.”
Soon, their intentions diverged,
and their favor and treatment sharply declined.
Initially, Yǐ (顗) was ordered to participate in selection matters with Shěn Qìngzhī (沈慶之) and Xú Yuán (徐爰).
Soon after, this was turned into a crime,
and the relevant officials were ordered to impeach him.
He was accused of holding office as a commoner.
When he accompanied the emperor on a trip to Húshú (湖熟),
traveling back and forth for several days,
he was not summoned.
Yǐ (顗) worried about disaster,
and made a deceptive plea to be allowed to leave.
Shěn Qìngzhī (沈慶之) strongly argued on Yǐ's (顗) behalf,
and he was eventually permitted.
He was appointed Ānxī Chángshǐ (安西長史) for Jiàn'ānwáng Xiūrén (建安王休仁) and Xiāngyáng Tàishǒu (襄陽太shǒu),
and given the additional title of Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍).
Xiūrén (休仁) did not take office,

so Yǐ (顗) was immediately appointed as Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Supervisor of military affairs of Yōng (雍), Liáng (梁), Nánqín (南秦), Běiqín (北秦) four provinces, and the two commanderies of Jìnglín (竟陵) and Suí (隨) in Yǐngzhōu (郢州), concurrently Níngmán Xiàowèi (寧蠻校尉) and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ (雍州刺史).
His rank as Jiāngjūn (將軍) remained unchanged.
Yǐ's (顗) maternal uncle, Cài Xīngzōng (蔡興宗), said to him:
“The stars of Xiāngyáng (襄陽) are ominous,
how can you risk it?”
Yǐ (顗) replied:
“When blades clash before you,
you cannot save yourself from stray arrows;
matters have their urgencies.
My departure now
is primarily to escape the tiger's mouth alive.
Moreover, the ways of Heaven are distant,
and not all predictions necessarily come true.
If there is a premonition,
I shall cultivate virtue to avert it.”
Thereupon, he hastily set off,
fearing pursuit.
Upon reaching Xúnyáng (尋陽),
he rejoiced, saying:
“Now I am finally safe!”
He frequently visited Dèng Wǎn (鄧琬), sharing intimacy.
Whenever he asked for private time,
it would last all day and all night.
Yǐ (顗) and Wǎn's (琬) backgrounds were originally very different,
and everyone knew they had ulterior motives.
Upon arriving in Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
he immediately began to repair weapons and armor with Liú Hú (劉胡),
and gather soldiers.
At that time, Tàizōng (太宗) settled the major affairs,
and promoted Yǐ (顗) to the title of Yòujiāngjūn (右將軍).
When Shào Zǎi (邵宰), an adjutant of Jīngzhōu (荊州), returned to Jiānglíng (江陵) by express post,
his route passed through Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Yǐ's (顗) intention to rebel was already firm,
but his provisions and arms were insufficient.
He initially intended to submit a memorial to Tàizōng (太宗).
Yǐ's (顗) son, Mìshū Chéng (祕書丞) Jiǎn (戩), said:
“Once a memorial is submitted,
you become his subject.
For a subject to attack his lord
is against righteousness.”
Yǐ (顗) followed his advice.
Yǐ (顗) falsely claimed to have received an order from the Grand Empress Dowager
to raise an army.
He then set up his banner and issued proclamations,
submitting a memorial urging Jìn'ānwáng Zǐxūn (晉安王子勛) to assume the imperial throne,
and wrote to Wǎn (琬),
telling him not to disband his army.
When Zǐxūn (子勛) ascended the throne,
he promoted Yǐ (顗) to the title of Ānběi Jiāngjūn (安北將軍),
and added the title of Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè (尚書左僕射).
Tàizōng (太宗) had court officials write to Yǐ (顗), saying: “Indeed, difficulties and ease follow each other,
and reforms and changes occur in turn.
Some countries are strengthened by many difficulties,
and some are enlightened by great sorrow.
This is both recorded in ancient histories
and evident
in what we hear and see.
The royal house was unfortunate,
and wicked tyrants ran rampant.
The divine tripod was about to fall,
and the ancestral altars were nearly destroyed.
Fortunately, Heaven did not doom Sòng (宋),
and the heavenly mandate found its rightful owner.
The Emperor's character
is inherently sagacious and cultured,
succeeding in brightness and acting with wisdom.
Yet he suffered humiliation in confinement,
his distress exceeding that of Xiàtái (夏臺).
Since Heaven and Earth were both indignant,
and righteous heroes rose up together,
they managed to eliminate the monstrous villain.
The three spirits
were restored,
responding to Heaven and conforming to the people,
thus gathering the precious mandate.
The four seas experienced the joy of relief,
and both Chinese and barbarians saw the peace of renewed life.
We were spared from the blade,
barely keeping our heads
and necks whole.
We now serve the new emperor,
our lives aligned with prosperous fortune,
relaxed and conversing with laughter,
enjoying the age of sagacity.
Although you toil outside
and are kept away from the capital,
the aspirations of our hearts are connected;
how far are the Jiāng (江) and Hàn (漢) rivers?
Since the rebellion was declared in Jiǔjiāng (九江),
everyone thought Dèng (鄧) was mad and deluded.
Recently, rumors have been rife throughout the country,
which greatly concern you.
Are the discussions on the road
perhaps true?
Upon hearing this,
how could I not be shocked and saddened?
The villains have turned against the Way and corrupted virtue,
deepening their depravity day and night.
They draw near to the treacherous and wicked,
seeking counsel from jackals and tigers.
Not only do their poisons spread to outsiders,
and their evils accumulate in the imperial court,
but they even seek to destroy
the capital,
oppress the upright,
burn the ancestral temples,
and plunder the imperial treasures.
After that, they plan to overturn the capital city,
ensuring that both orchids and weeds perish together.
Were it not for the sagely sovereign's divine plans and spiritual strategies,
who,
with humility, yields and avoids,
maintains order within and without,
and protects his officials and subjects,
then the land of Chìxiàn would become a barbarian stronghold,
and the common people would become fish.
This matter, this principle,
how can one not reflect upon it deeply?
Now that the Heavenly Way assists what is righteous,
and songs of praise are offered,
the grandson of Gāozǔ,
the son of Wénhuáng,
whose virtue penetrates the nine underworlds,
and whose achievements span the two luminaries,
〔一四〕rescues the family and the state,
and nurtures the black-haired people.
If he does not face south as the ruler of the people,
then to whom shall the divine vessel return?
Yet petty men instigate treachery,
〔一五〕and harbor ambitious designs.
Chéng Zhěn confused Yān,
Guàn Gāo
disrupted Zhào;
slanderers are boundless,
this has been so since ancient times.
You, a dignitary of the central capital,
whose family has inherited scholarly refinement for generations,
have seen much in previous records,
and clearly distinguish between loyalty and treachery.
Why abandon from afar the pure conduct of the Lángzhōng,
and forget nearby the noble demeanor of the Tàiwèi?
We are bound together,
〔一六〕some as paternal cousins or maternal relatives,
others by marriage and deep friendship.
If suddenly we become like Hú and Yuè,
how can we not feel regret and resentment?
If it is due to deception,
and endless crookedness,
you should swear an oath to the masses and brandish your spears,
to swiftly eliminate this danger.
If you have indulged in mistaken beliefs,
and strayed not too far from the path,
the sagely sovereign treats all beings
with benevolence,
and approaches his subordinates with love.
How could he merely grant Yōng Chǐ an early enfeoffment,
but rather shoot a hook and appoint a minister?
Is it because your strength is exhausted, your efforts curtailed,
and your sincere loyalty has not yet been demonstrated?
I stand on tiptoe
looking south,
longing for you day and night.
If you turn your oar and follow the current,
returning your allegiance to the Phoenix Palace,
who else but you will be granted a jade tablet and open up territory?
We have all been excessively favored by His curved benevolence,
and have all undeservedly
received positions,
wearing gold and dragging jade,
transforming our humble gates.
Entering, we receive the bounty of Shùn and Yǔ;
exiting, we witness the reforms of Xī and Táng.
With dignified composure and widespread praise,
this is truly the time of the white colt in the empty valley.
Why then destroy and discard your ancestral foundation,
and tread on evil and violence yourself?
The mountain gate is desolate,
who will sweep the pine courtyard?
Thinking of the road to Chǔ,
how can you not yearn for the land of your parents?
Fortunately, accept this blunt advice,
to remove the beautiful disease.
I write this letter to express my thoughts;
you should consider it.
At that time, Shàngshū Yòupúyè Cài Xīngzōng was Yǐ's maternal uncle,
and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Yuán Càn was Yǐ's paternal cousin,
hence the letter says "paternal cousins or maternal relatives."
Zǐxūn summoned Yǐ to go down to Xúnyáng,
and sent Shìzhōng Kǒng Dàocún to manage the affairs of Yōngzhōu.
Yǐ then led his troops to quickly descend,
and sent his son Jiǎn to return with the family's possessions.
At that time, Liú Hú was stationed at Quèwěi,
and had long been unable to make a decision.
In the summer of Tàishǐ second year (466 CE),
Yǐ was given the title Dūdū Zhēngtǎo Zhūjūnsì,
provided with a set of drums and pipes,
and commanded a thousand tower ships
and twenty thousand soldiers
to enter Quèwěi.
Yǐ originally had no military strategy,
and his nature was also timid and weak.
In the army, he never wore military attire,
and his conversation never touched upon battles or formations,
only composing poetry and discussing theories.
He was unable to manage and interact with his generals.
Whenever Liú Hú discussed military matters,
Yǐ's replies were very brief,
which greatly alienated people's sentiments.
Hú often gnashed his teeth in anger and resentment.
Hú, seeing that southern supplies had not arrived,
〔一七〕and his soldiers were short of provisions,
asked Yǐ to exchange for supplies from Xiāngyáng.
Yǐ replied:
"My two residences in the capital are not yet finished,
and need to be managed;
they cannot be reduced or demolished."
He also believed the rumors circulating
that rice was expensive in the capital,
reaching several hundred coins per dòu.
He thought that there was no need for attack,
and that the enemy would disperse on their own.
Thus, he held his troops and waited.
Tàizōng sent Yǐ's former student Xú Shuò to deliver an imperial edict by hand, admonishing Yǐ, saying:
"You have observed ancient and modern times;
when has danger or strength
ever been reliable?
Since朕 ascended the throne,
the roads have been blocked,
and you have had no means to submit memorials,
nor have you yet served as a minister.
Even now, to follow in the footsteps of Dòu Róng,
it is not too late."
When Liú Hú defected and fled,
he did not inform Yǐ.
Yǐ only found out at night,
and angrily cursed, saying:
"This year I was misled by that brat!"
He called for a flying swallow (a fast horse),
and said to his troops:
"I will go out myself to pursue him."
Then he also fled.
Arriving at Quètou,
he joined with the garrison commander Xuē Bózhēn and his several thousand men on foot to make for Qīnglín,
intending to head towards Xúnyáng.
They rested overnight in the mountains,
killing horses to reward the officers and soldiers.
Yǐ looked at Bózhēn and said:
"I raised eight prefectures to scheme for the royal house,
yet before a single battle, we dispersed.
Is this not fate?
It's not that I cannot die;
why would I seek to live in the weeds?
I wish to reach Xúnyáng,
apologize to the sovereign,
and then commit suicide."
Then, with indignation, he shouted at his attendants to fetch a staff of authority,
but no one responded.
The next morning,
Bózhēn requested to speak privately,
then beheaded Yǐ and went to Qiánxī to the cavalry commander from Xiāngyáng, Yú Zhànzhī.
Zhànzhī then beheaded Bózhēn,
and sent both heads as his own achievement.
Yǐ died at the age of forty-seven.
Tàizōng was furious at Yǐ's rebellion,
and left his corpse to float in the river.
His disciple Tuǎn, in disguise, searched for him,
and only found him after forty-one days.
He secretly buried the body behind Shítouhòugāng,
personally carrying earth with an old slave.
Later, when the deposed emperor ascended the throne,
he was finally reburied.
Yǐ's son Jiǎn was a伪Huángmén Shìláng,
and was given the title Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
garrisoning Pénchéng.
When Xúnyáng fell,
Jiǎn abandoned the city and fled.
He was hunted down, captured, and executed.
Kǒng Jì, courtesy name Sīyuǎn,
was a native of Kuàijī Shānyīn,
and the grandson of Tàicháng Lín.
His father, Miǎo,
was Yángzhōu Zhìzhōng.
Kǒng Jì (孔覬) was resolute and principled from a young age,
taking righting wrongs as his personal mission.
He stuttered,
but loved to read,
and was well-known early on.
He was first recommended as a Xiùcái (秀才) from Yángzhōu (揚州),
and appointed as Zhǔbù (主簿).
He served as Zhènjūngōngcáo (鎮軍功曹) for Chángshā Wáng Yìxīn (長沙王義欣),
and Ānxī Zhǔbù (安西主簿) for Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì (衡陽王義季),
then Hùcáo Cānjūn (戶曹參軍),
and concurrently Nányìyáng Tàishǒu (南義陽太守).
He was then transferred to be Shǔ Jìshì (署記室).
He submitted a memorial firmly declining,
saying:
“The office of Jìshì (記室)
is indeed a prominent and important post.
Unless one is outstandingly sharp in writing and conduct,
no one can occupy it.
Kǒng Jì’s (孔覬) humble accomplishments
are unheard of in his home district;
his criticism for idleness
is recorded among the weary farmers.
It is merely that the mountains and valleys have hidden and drawn him out,
not abandoning him to remoteness,
thus he has been able to enjoy the wind and dew,
relying on this for many years.
Today’s appointment
is not something I dare presume to accept.
In the past, those who were excellent in learning and rich in artistry
still found this difficult,
how much more so for Kǒng Jì (孔覬), whose abilities are meager and whose nature is clumsy?
How can it be easy?
I have heard that discerning talents and assigning them positions
is how a ruler employs abilities;
exerting one's strength and taking one's place
is how subordinates serve their superiors.
Though I, Kǒng Jì (孔覬), am not clever,
I always submit to these words.
Now, this favor relies on old connections,
and the recommendation is not based on virtue.
I fear I will be unable to manage a corner of affairs,
or satisfy the general consensus.
I humbly pray that your Heavenly Brilliance illuminates my heartfelt request,
and that you grant a change from the current post,
assigning me a more relaxed position,
then the waterfowl will follow its proper course,
and my worries will cease.”
He further said:
“Indeed, the importance of the Jìshì (記室) office
requires a versatile talent with sharp thoughts,
〔一八〕plus a diligent and meticulous disposition.
My studies are not comprehensive,
and my nature is also careless and lazy.
How can I be entrusted with secret records,
and hold the brush in the literary chamber?
〔一九〕The fault of false blowing [an empty boast]
is not excessive compared to this.
From a young age, I, Kǒng Jì (孔覬), have deviated from common norms,
fundamentally lacking deep roots.
How could I forget the desire for honor and advancement?
If I truly had the faint light of a firefly,
that could add radiance to the scenery,
it would naturally be the day for my fame to rise,
the time for my literary talent to soar.
How would I dare to seek ease and comfort,
and preserve my tranquil detachment?
I humbly pray you pity my clumsiness and lack of skill,
and grant me a place where I can apply my abilities,
then your benevolence in perfecting me
will be generous from beginning to end.”
Yìjì (義季) could not force him,
so he was excused.
He was summoned to be Tōngzhí Láng (通直郎),
Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén (太子中舍人),
Jiànpíng Wáng Yǒu (建平王友),
Mìshūchéng (祕書丞),
Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎),
and followed Suí Wáng Dàn (隨王誕) as Āndōng Zīyì Cānjūn (安東諮議參軍),
and concurrently Jìshì (記室).
Then Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎),
and Jiànpíng Wáng Hóng (建平王宏) as Zhōngjūn Chángshǐ (中軍長史).
He again became Huángmén (黃門),
and Línhǎi Tàishǒu (臨海太守).
Initially,
during the Jìn (晉) dynasty, the selection for Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) was highly regarded,
no different from Shìzhōng (侍中).
Afterwards, its duties became relaxed and the position less important,
so the caliber of people appointed gradually declined.
In the third year of Xiàojiàn (孝建)
Shìzǔ (世祖) wished to raise its prestige,
and issued an edict saying:
“The Sànqí (散騎) office serves as a close attendant,
its duties involving counsel and acceptance of advice.
The fundamental purpose of this appointment
is truly intimate and important.
However, recently the selection for Chángshì (常侍)
has fallen short and been unsatisfactory.
It is fitting to select and appoint excellent talents of the time,
to forever establish a clear standard.”
Thereupon, Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) Yán Jùn (顏竣) memorialized, saying:
“The Chángshì (常侍) is a prominent selection,
its duties require talent.
The newly appointed Línhǎi Tàishǒu (臨海太ǒu) Kǒng Jì (孔覬) has a simple and refined demeanor,
and Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ (司徒左長史) Wáng Yù (王彧) holds clear and upright aspirations.
Both are suitable to be appointed as Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).”
Shìzǔ (世祖) did not want authority to be concentrated among subordinates.
Afterward, he divided the office of Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) into two,
to lighten its responsibility.
Shìzhōng (侍中) Cài Xīngzōng (蔡興宗) said to others:
“The selection bureau is important,
while the Chángshì (常侍) is leisurely and detached.
Changing it in name but not in reality,
even if the emperor wishes to make a distinction in importance,
how can people's minds be changed?”
Subsequently, the selection for Chángshì (常侍) again became lowly,
and the prestige of the selection bureau remained unchanged.
Kǒng Jì (孔覬) concurrently held the position of his home province’s Dàzhōngzhèng (大中正).
In the first year of Dàmíng (大明)
he was appointed Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子),
and concurrently Yìjūn Xiàowèi (翊軍校尉),
then transferred to Mìshūjiān (祕書監).
He was intended to be Lìbù Láng (吏部郎),
but it did not happen.
He was promoted to Tíngwèi Qīng (廷尉卿),
then Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞).
He was impeached by the appropriate authorities
for whipping a clerk,
but was pardoned without prosecution.
In the sixth year,
he was appointed Yìxīng Tàishǒu (義興太守).
Before he took office,
he became Xúnyáng Wáng Zǐfáng (尋陽王子房)’s Guānjūn Chángshǐ (冠軍長史),
with the added title of Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍),
and acted concurrently as administrator for Huáinán (淮南) and Xuānchéng (宣城) prefectures.
In the same year,
he was again appointed Ānlù Wáng Zǐsuí (安陸王子綏)’s Guānjūn Chángshǐ (冠軍長史) and Jiāngxià Nèishǐ (江夏內史),
and then transferred with the prince's administration to Hòujūn Chángshǐ (後軍長史) as before.
He was a man who used alcohol to bolster his spirit.
Whenever he got drunk, he would not wake up for days.
Among his colleagues,
he often insulted and neglected many.
Especially, he was unable to pander to those in power,
so everyone feared and disliked him.
He did not manage his property,
and was often impoverished.
Whether he had abundance or scarcity,
he never cared.
〔二０〕As the Registrar of the Two Bureaus (Èr Fǔ Chángshǐ),
when the record keepers and advisors came to consult him,
they dared not approach without being called,
and dared not leave without being ordered.
Although he was drunk most of the time,
he was clear-headed about government affairs.
His judgments when sober
were never obstructed.
Everyone said:
"Kǒng Gōng (孔公) being drunk twenty-nine days a month
is better than others being sober twenty-nine days."
Shìzǔ (世祖) often wished to grant him an audience,
but would first send someone to observe if he was drunk or sober.
He was naturally simple and unadorned,
not advocating pretense or embellishment.
When he obtained precious curios,
he used them without hesitation,
but if other items were coarse or damaged,
he would never replace them.
At that time, Gù Jìzhī (顧覬之) of Wújùn (吳郡) also valued frugality and simplicity;
his clothes, furs, utensils, and attire
were all chosen to be humble.
In the Sòng (宋) era, when speaking of purity and simplicity,
these two men were praised.
Jì's (覬) younger brother, Dàocún (道存),
and his cousin, Huī (徽),
were quite engaged in managing property.
When the two brothers requested leave to return east,
Jì (覬) went to the sandbank to meet them.
They had over ten boats laden with baggage,
all consisting of cotton, silk, paper, and mats.
When Jì (覬) saw them,
he feigned joy and
said:
"I have been in distress and want lately;
getting these is very important."
He then ordered them to be placed on the bank.
After a moment, he sternly addressed Dàocún (道存) and the others, saying:
"You all are unworthy members of the gentry;
why would you return east to become mere merchants!"
He ordered his attendants to fetch fire and burn them.
Only after they were completely burned did he leave.
Previously, Yǔ Huīzhī (庾徽之) served as Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng),
and his nature was extravagant and splendid;
his clothes, curios, and ornaments were very luxurious.
When Jì (覬) replaced him,
〔二一〕his clothes, hats, and utensils
were all rough and simple.
The clerks of the Imperial Censorate (Lántái Lìshǐ) were all wealthy men from the Three Wú (Sān Wú),
and all harbored intentions of looking down on him.
But Jì (覬), with his disheveled hair and loose belt,
and a stern, upright demeanor,
made them all tread cautiously and hold their breath,
not daring to disrespect him.
Yǔ Huīzhī (庾徽之), courtesy name Jǐngyóu (景猷),
was a native of Yānlíng (鄢陵) in Yǐngchuān (潁川).

He left the post of Censor-in-Chief (Zhōngchéng) to become the Registrar (Zhǎngshǐ) for Prince Zǐluán (子鸞) of Xīn'ān (新安) in the Northern Central Army (Běi Zhōngláng) and Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Southern Dōnghǎi (Dōnghǎi).
He died in office.
Eight years later,
Jì (覬) was transferred from Yǐngzhōu (郢州) as Commander (Xíngzhēn)
and summoned to be General of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn).
Before he was formally appointed,
he was transferred to be the Left Registrar (Zuǒ Chángshǐ) for the Minister of Works (Sītú).
Dàocún (道存) replaced Jì (覬) as Registrar of the Rear Army (Hòujūn Zhǎngshǐ) and Intendant of Jiāngxià (Jiāngxià Nèishǐ).
At that time, there was a great drought in the eastern territories,
and rice was expensive in the capital;
one dòu (斗) was nearly a hundred cash.
Dàocún (道存) worried that Jì (覬) was very short of provisions,
so he sent an official with five hundred hù (斛) of rice to send to him.
Jì (覬) called the official and said to him:
"I was there for three years,
and on the day I left office,
I could not even manage to get provisions for the road.
The second master (Dàocún) has only been there for a short while;
how could he already obtain this rice?
You should take the rice back there."
The official said:
"Since ancient times,
there has been no one who carried rice upstream.
Rice in the capital is expensive;
I beg to sell it here."
Jì (覬) did not listen,
so the official carried the rice away.
In the first year of Yǒngguāng (永光) (465 CE),
he was promoted to Attendant-in-Ordinary (Shìzhōng).
Before he was formally appointed,
he again became the Registrar (Tàizǎi Zhǎngshǐ) for Prince Yìgōng (義恭) of Jiāngxià (Jiāngxià Wáng).
He was again sent out as Registrar of the Right Army (Yòujūn Zhǎngshǐ) for Prince Zǐfáng (子房) of Xúnyáng (Xúnyáng Wáng),
with the added title of General Who Assists the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn),
and acted as Administrator (Xíngshì) of Kuàijī (Kuàijī Jùn).
When Tàizōng (太宗) ascended the throne,
he summoned Jì (覬) to be Grand Master of the Crown Prince's Household (Tàizǐ Zhànshì),
and sent his former subordinate, Yǔ Yè (庾業), who was Commander of the General Who Pacifies the West (Píngxī Sīmǎ), to be Commander of the Right Army (Yòujūn Sīmǎ),
to replace Jì (覬) in acting as Administrator (Xíngshì) of Kuàijī (Kuàijī Jùn).
At that time, the upper reaches of the river rebelled.
The emperor sent Kǒng Zǎo (孔璪), Superintendent of Waterways (Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě), to the east to comfort the people.
When Zǎo (璪) arrived,
he persuaded Jì (覬) by saying:
"The deposed emperor's extravagance and waste
have exhausted the granaries.
The capital is utterly depleted,
and resources are exhausted.
Now, both north and south are rising up,
and distant and near regions are rebelling.
If you gather the elite forces of the five commanderies
and incite the Three Wú (Sān Wú),
there is nothing you cannot accomplish."
Jì (覬) approved of his words
and consequently raised troops and issued a manifesto.
Jì's (覬) son, Zhǎnggōng (長公), and Zǎo's (璪) two sons, Yān (淹) and Xuán (玄), were both in the capital.
They sent secret messages to inform him.
In the first month of the second year of Tàishǐ (泰始) (466 CE),
they all rebelled, escaped, and returned east.
Jì (覬) sent a letter inviting Gù Chēn (顧琛), Grand Administrator of Wújùn (Wújùn Tàishǒu).
Chēn (琛), whose mother was very old,
and who was also very close to the capital,
consulted with his eldest son, Bǎosù (寶素),
but they had not decided.
〔二二〕His younger son, Bǎo (寶), who had previously been Magistrate (Lìng) of Shānyīn (Shānyīn),
sent a swift letter to Chēn (琛),
saying that the southern army was already close,
and the imperial court was isolated and weak.
If they did not obey promptly,
there would certainly be the calamity of destruction.
Jì's (覬) vanguard army had already crossed the Zhèjiāng (浙江) River,
so Chēn (琛) then seized the commandery and joined the rebellion.

Wáng Tánshēng (王曇生), Grand Administrator of Wúxīng (Wúxīng Tàishǒu); Liú Yánxī (劉延熙), Grand Administrator of Yìxīng (Yìxīng Tàishǒu); and Yuán Biāo (袁標), Grand Administrator of Jìnlíng (Jìnlíng Tàishǒu),
all responded simultaneously.
As Yǔ Yè (庾業) went east,
Tàizōng (太宗) immediately appointed him to replace Yánxī (延熙) as Administrator (Xíngshì) of Yìxīng (Yìxīng),
with the added title of General Who Establishes Might (Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn),
and appointed Yánxī (延xī) as Registrar of the General Who Guards the East (Zhèndōng Zhǎngshǐ) for Prince Xiūrúo (休若) of Bālíng (Bālíng Wáng).
When Yè (業) arrived at Chángtánghú (長塘湖),
he immediately joined Yánxī (延熙).
Tàizōng (太宗) sent Shěn Huáimíng (沈懷明), General Who Establishes Might (Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn), to conquer the east,
and Zhāng Yǒng (張永), Minister (Shàngshū), to advance.
Prince Xiūrúo (休若) of Bālíng (Bālíng Wáng), General Who Guards the East (Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn), was to supervise all forces conquering the east.
He issued a manifesto to the eastern territories, saying: "It is said that calamities gather with signs,
and misfortune arrives without a gate;
the coming of reliance and peril
is truly brought about by humans.
Thus, Xiāo (囂) and Shù (述), greedy and rebellious,
ultimately destroyed their ancestral sacrifices;
Chāng (昌) and Xiàn (憲)
stirred up unrest,
and quickly met the axe.
These are clearly recorded in historical documents,
serving as a shining warning for ancient and modern times.
Since the nation's fortunes have been difficult,
the Three Bonds (sāngāng) have utterly collapsed.
Divine power has ceased in the spiritual realm,
and the imperial enterprise hangs by a thread.
But His Imperial Majesty, benevolent and heroic, gathers auspicious omens,
and is wise and sagacious, responding to the historical current.
His phoenix-like demeanor soars like a blaze,
and his dragon-like glory rises like lightning.
He sweeps away defilement from the purple pivot (imperial court)
without waiting for the oath of the '鳴條' (Míngtiáo);
he stabilizes governance in the central realm
without unleashing the might of '漂杵' (Piǎochǔ).
Thus, the fallen framework is rebuilt,
and the damaged heavens are reconstructed.
The hidden and manifest are ordered,
and this glory is conspicuously matched.
Yet, a multitude of villains indulges in tyranny,
conspiring to incite the innocent.
This small corner of the eastern frontier
has again sunk into ugly deeds;
they deviate into wickedness,
swarming like bees and clinging like ants.
The sagely plan thunders forth,
divine might descends everywhere.
Where the swift post reaches,
righteous armies gather like clouds.
Where the '欃鉞' (chányuè) is brandished,
the rebel horde melts like ice.
The outcome of victory and defeat
is already clearly evident.
The Minister of Works (Sītú), Prince Yīngyóu (英猷) of Jiàn'ān (Jiàn'ān Wáng), whose heroism surpasses the world,
commands the main army.
The General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn), Prince Shānyáng (山陽 Wáng), whose strategic acumen has long been manifest,
encourages the central array.
Some shake the frosty Jiāng (江) [River],
Lǐ,
or the blazing flames soared through Jīng and Hé,
golden armor illuminated the celestial court,
and tumultuous shouts shook the sea shores.
Former General and Administrator of Wúxīng, Zhāng Yǒng,
a prominent figure in the southeast,
assisted
in military affairs.
General Jiànwēi Shěn Huáimíng, Aide to the Central Army of the Commander of the East Zhèn, Liú Liàng, and General Wǔwèi Shòu Jìzhī,
with five thousand elite troops,
charged like bears and strode like tigers.
General Lóngxiáng Wáng Mùzhī and General Lóngxiáng Dùn Shēng,
with a continuous stream of iron cavalry,
advanced with the speed of wind and lightning.
General of the Right Army, Qí Wáng, and Commandant of the Archers Shèshēng, Yáo Dào
hé,
with a thousand tower ships,
covered the rivers and streams.
Zuǒjūn Yuán Gōngzǔ, Commandant of Infantry Dù Yòuwén, Róngcóng Púshè Quán Jǐngwén, and Yuánwài Sǎnjì
shìláng Sūn Chāozhī,
all led tiger-like forces,
arriving continuously like clouds.
Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn Dù Jìngzhēn, Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn Lù Yōuzhī, and Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn Wú
Xǐ,
with ten thousand armored shields,
divided to head for Yìxīng.
I, unworthy as I am, took on the responsibilities of leadership,
commanding the military forces,
brandishing my sword and rushing east,
[二三] to vent my anger at the curve of the sea.
My breath could make the white
sun entirely dark,
and brushing my horses could make the clear river flow backward.
With this, to punish rebels,
what powerful force could not be eradicated?
With this, to pacify and submit,
what obedient person would not be embraced?
I pity those confused masses,
who cannot
distinguish between Yáo and Jié,
like a tiny mantis or frog's life,
attempting to withstand a thunderbolt's charge,
or withered leaves,
facing a gale's assault.
This would chill the heart of a mere boy,
and make even a common woman sigh
in despair.
Indeed, to turn disaster into blessing,
[二四] and to make success out of defeat,
lessons from the past must not be forgotten,
and future events should be clearly predicted.
If you can lead each other to submit,
lay down your weapons and show sincerity,
then good fortune
will accumulate in this year,
and blessings will extend to your descendants.
How could this compare to having your body dismembered, your clan slaughtered,
and your ghost starve and soul weep?
Reflect carefully on safety and danger,
and seek much fortune for yourselves.
A reward for capturing Jī alive: a Founding County Marquis with fifteen hundred households.
Capturing Chēn alive: a Founding County Marquis with one thousand households.
For those who kill and deliver: half the reward.
At that time, many of the officers and soldiers were from the east,
and their fathers, brothers, sons, and younger siblings had all joined the rebellion.
The Emperor therefore sent a general proclamation with the troops, saying:
"I am intent on promoting virtue and simplifying punishments,
so that the four categories of offenses do not implicate others.
For those who assisted the loyalists or joined the rebels,
the judgment will be based solely on whom they followed.
You gentlemen should deeply understand this intention,
and not be concerned about relatives."
Everyone was greatly pleased by this.
The army dispatched by Jī, led by Sūn Tán'guàn and others,
halted at Jiànlíng Jiǔlǐ,
with a very impressive formation.
Huáimíng arrived at Bēnniú,
but his forces were few and weak,
so he built a rampart to secure himself.
Zhāng Yǒng arrived at Qū'ā,
not knowing whether Huáimíng was safe or not.
The common people were alarmed and disturbed,
and the officers and soldiers all wanted to disperse.
Yǒng retreated to Yánlíng,
to join Xiūrúo.
All the generals advised retreating to secure Pògāng.
That day was extremely cold,
with fierce wind and snow.
The dikes and dams broke,
and the troops had no firm resolve.
Xiūrúo issued an order:
"Anyone who dares to speak of retreating will be beheaded."
The troops then stabilized slightly,
and built a rampart to rest their armor.
Soon they received a letter from Huáimíng,
stating that the rebels had settled down and not yet advanced.
Army Commander Liú Liàng then arrived subsequently,
and the military strength increased,
and the morale of the people then settled.
At that time, Kǒng Jǐngxuān, the Administrator of Yǒngshì, rebelled again,
barricading Xiāngxiàn Xījiāngxiǎnshān,
blocking the ferry paths.
Liú Yánxī promoted him to General Níngsuò.
Dù Jìngzhēn, Lù Yōuzhī, and Administrator of Lìyáng Liú Xiūwén attacked Jǐngxuān's separate fortress,
beheading fifteen people, including his Aide to the Central Army Shǐ Lǎnxī.
Xú Chóngzhī of Yǒngshì led his villagers to rise in righteousness,
attacked the county, and beheaded Jǐngxuān.
Wú Xǐ arrived
and appointed Chóngzhī to manage the county affairs.
Tàizōng praised Xiūwén and others for their sincere efforts,
appointed Xiūwén as General Níngsuò,
the county remaining as before,
Chóngzhī as Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn,
acting as Administrator of Yǒngshì County,
and both were bestowed with marquis ranks.
Xǐ, Jìngzhēn, and Yuánwài Sǎnjì Shìláng Zhú Chāozhī and others arrived at the border of Guóshān County,
encountered the eastern army at Hǔlán Cūn,
attacked and heavily defeated them,
and advanced from Guóshān to Wúchéng,
fifteen *lǐ* from Yìxīng.
Liú Yánxī dispatched four armies—Yáng Xuán, Sūn Jiǎozhī, Shěn Língxiù, and Huáng Tài—to resist Xǐ.
Xǐ and his forces were very weak,
with a vast disparity in numbers.
They fought all day,
and during the battle, Yáng Xuán, Sūn Jiǎozhī, and Huáng Tài were beheaded.
[二五] The remaining troops fled immediately,
and Xǐ then advanced to the southern outskirts of Yìxīng.
Yánxī had garrisoned troops at Nánshètáng,
and Xǐ sent infantry and cavalry to attack them.
They immediately retreated to the north of the water,
then barricaded the long bridge,
and fortified the commandery to defend themselves.
Xǐ built a rampart and held a stalemate with them.
Yǔ Yè built cities on both banks at the mouth of Chángtánghú,
with over seven thousand troops,
and very abundant weapons and armor,
forming a distant pincer movement with Yánxī.
Shěn Huáimíng and Zhāng Yǒng were in a stalemate with the Jìnlíng army,
which had not been resolved for a long time.
Tàizōng, whenever he dispatched troops,
always made many demands [for supplies],
and did not set out on time.
The Outer Censor Zhū Yòujǔ recommended Rèn Nóngfū, a staff officer and督護 (dūhù) of the Minister over the司徒 (Sītú),
who was valiant, decisive, and courageous,
and also straightforward and unpretentious by nature,
making him very easy to provide for.
So, a thousand men were assigned to him,
to assist in the eastern campaign.
At that time, Yǔ Yè's forces were strong.
Nóngfū advanced from Yánlíng along Chángtáng.
Although it was said to be a thousand soldiers,
only four hundred arrived.
When he was still dozens of *lǐ* away,
he sent someone to scout,
who reported:
"The rebels are still building their fortifications, and they are not yet complete."
Nóngfū led General Guǎngwǔ Gāo Zhìzhī and Magistrate Yǒngxīng Xú Chóngzhī to rush and attack them.
〔二六〕Seizing the opportunity while their city walls and ramparts were not yet established,
Nóngfū personally wielded a saber and a shield,
rushed to the city, entered the formation,
and thoroughly routed them.
Yǔ Yè abandoned the city and fled to Yìxīng.
Before this,
General Lóngxiáng Ruǎn Diànfū had recruited several hundred men from Shǔ,
most of whom were strong, brave, and skilled in combat.
They all wore rhinoceros hide armor
and carried short weapons.
They were originally supposed to join Diànfū and head towards Jìnlíng,
but before they departed,
Nóngfū needed men,
so some were allocated to him.
During battles,
they always led the charge.
The easterners were all afraid and apprehensive of them,
and were also surprised by their distinctive appearance and adornments.
Old legends said that "fox-barbarians" (húliáo) ate people,
so whenever they saw them, they would flee.
Nóngfū seized their boats and weapons,
and advanced with Gāo Zhìzhī to Yìxīng to reinforce Wú Xǐ.
On the first day of the second month,
Xǐ crossed the water to attack the commandery,
and divided his troops to strike various fortified camps.
Although Nóngfū had arrived,
the combined strength was still small,
and their military power was no match.
Xǐ then, with a few horsemen, ascended a height and pointed east and west,
as if beckoning for forces to advance from all four directions simultaneously.
The eastern army was greatly alarmed,
and all their camps scattered at once.
Only the camp of General Lóngxiáng Kǒng Ruì remained unbreached.
Xǐ, seeing that many had been killed or wounded,
opened the encirclement and relaxed his pressure.
That night,
Yǔ Yè and Kǒng Ruì led their forces in flight,
and Yìxīng was pacified.
Liú Yánxī drowned himself in the water.
Someone reported it,
so they severed his corpse,
and sent his head to the capital city.
Among all the counties of Yìxīng, only Magistrate Suī'ān Cháo Suì upheld his integrity and did not waver,
refusing to accept the false titles.
At that time, Qíwáng led his army in an eastern campaign,
and with Zhāng Yǒng, Liú Liàng, Dù Yòuwén, Shěn Huáimíng, and others, established camps west of Jiǔlǐ in Jìnlíng,
facing the eastern army.
Since the Yìxīng army had been defeated by Wú Xǐ and others,
many of the scattered soldiers fled to Jìnlíng,
causing the eastern army to be shaken with fear.
The Emperor also dispatched General Jīshè Jiāng Fāngxīng and Nántái Yùshǐ Wáng Dàolóng to Jìnlíng to observe the rebel situation.
The rebel chiefs Sūn Tánguàn, Chéng Hàngzōng, and Chén Jǐngyuǎn had five interconnected fortresses.
The fortresses were mutually connected.
Hàngzōng's fortress was still not fortified.
On the third day of that month,
Dàolóng discussed with Qíwáng and Zhāng Yǒng:
"Since Hàngzōng's fortress is not yet established,
we can seize this opportunity.
This would fulfill the Emperor's divine will,
and boost the morale of the troops."
Dàolóng then led his subordinates to urgently attack it,
and in a moment the fortress fell,
and Hàngzōng's head was taken.
Liú Liàng was resolute and adept with a saber and shield.
The court officials had not known him previously,
and the Emperor had not heard of him either.
Only Shàngshū Zuǒchéng Xú Yuán knew of him,
and reported to Tàizōng, praising his valor and daring.
At this point, in every battle he would charge directly with his saber and shield,
and always broke through and breached the enemy lines.
Zhāng Yǒng disliked his excessive eagerness
and did not allow him to lead the vanguard.
The rebels' continuous palisades extended all around,
and the path through the dike was narrow,
preventing the generals and soldiers from fully exerting their strength.
Liàng then advanced with his shield on his back,
straight into the heavy palisades.
The allied armies followed his lead,
and immediately shattered all of them.
Yuán Biāo sent a thousand men to reinforce them,
and Qíwáng and Yǒng, riding on their victory, rushed to attack,
again greatly defeating them,
and slaughtering the inhabitants of their two fortresses.
Tánguàn led several hundred men,
beating drums and shouting as they approached.
Biāo again sent a thousand men to reinforce them.
The allied armies were startled and afraid,
and were about to disperse.
Jiāng Fāngxīng led brave warriors to meet and shoot at them,
and those who fell at the sound of the bowstring were continuous.
Tánguàn was thus defeated and fled.
Wú Xǐ's army arrived in Yìxiāng.
The false General Fǔguó and Cavalry司馬 (Sīmǎ) Kǒng Zǎo was stationed at Wúxīng Nántíng.
The Administrator Wáng Tánshēng went to Zǎo to discuss matters.
Just then, a messenger returned,
saying:
"The imperial army is already nearby."
Zǎo was greatly terrified,
fell off his bed,
and said:
"The reward offered for capture,
is only for me.
If I don't flee quickly now,
I will be captured."
Those around him heard this,
and all scattered and fled.
Zǎo and Tánshēng burned the warehouses,
and fled east to Qiántáng.
Xǐ arrived at Wúxīng,
and stationed his troops in the commandery city.
The granaries, having been caught in the rain, did not burn,
and suffered no losses.
Initially,
Tánshēng had dispatched General Níngshuò Shěn Língchǒng with eight thousand men towards Huánghúqiáo,
intending to pass through the scout path to Wúhú
to meet the southern army.
Magistrate Guǎngdé Wáng Yùn dispatched troops to hold the strategic passes,
preventing Língchǒng from advancing.
He was stationed at Gùzhāng.
After Tánshēng fled,
Língchǒng, along with his younger brother Língzhāo and army deputy Yáo Tiānfù, led seventeen partial and auxiliary armies to surrender.
Tàizōng commended him,
and promoted him to Cānjūnshì of Zhèndōng,
then had him lead his subordinates in the eastern campaign.
Xǐ divided his forces and dispatched Army Commanders Shěn Sīrén and Wú Xìgōng to pursue Zǎo and others.
Lù Yōuzhī and Rèn Nóngfū advanced from Dōngqiān towards Wújùn.
The court dispatched Army Commander Zhāng Língfú to Jìnlíng.
On the fourth day of that month,
Qíwáng launched an urgent attack,
and that night,
Sūn Tánguàn and Chén Jǐngyuǎn collapsed and fled simultaneously.
When the various armies reached Jìnlíng,
Yuán Biāo abandoned the commandery and fled east.
With Jìnlíng pacified,
Wúzhōng was shaken.
And with the Wúxīng army about to arrive,
Gù Chēn, with his son Bǎosù, carried his aged mother and fled by sea to Kuàijī.
Magistrate Hǎiyán Wáng Fú attempted to intercept them but failed.
Tàizōng, with the four commanderies pacified,
left Wú Xǐ to command Quán Jǐngwén, Shěn Huáimíng, Liú Liàng, Sūn Chāozhī, Shòu Jìzhī, and others to pacify Kuàijī in the east.
He recalled Qíwáng, Zhāng Yǒng, Yáo Dàohé, Dù Yòuwén, Yuán Gōngzǔ, and Zhāng Língfú for a northern campaign,
and Wáng Mùzhī, Dùn Shēng, and Jiāng Fāngxīng for a southern campaign.
On the ninth day of that month,
Wú Xǐ and others arrived at Qiántáng.
The Prefect of Qiántáng, Gù Yù, along with Kǒng Zǎo and Wáng Tánshēng, fled across the river to Jiāngdōng.
Wú Xǐ then advanced his army to Liǔpǔ,
and Fù Yǎn, the Prefect of Zhūjì, brought his family to submit.

Wú Xǐ sent his Zhenběi Cānjūn, Shěn Sīrén, Strong Crossbow General Rèn Nóngfū, Longxiáng General Gāo Zhìzhī, Nántái Yùshǐ Ruǎn Diànfū, and Yangwǔ General Lú Sēngzé, among others, to lead their forces towards Huángshānpǔ.
The Eastern army held the bank and erected a stockade.
Rèn Nóngfū and the others attacked and broke it.
They hoisted sails with the wind,
and went straight to Dìngshān,
where they defeated Sūn Huìzhī, their chief commander,
and beheaded him in battle.
From Dìngshān, they advanced towards Yúpǔ,
where Gǒng Ruì, the garrison commander, with over a thousand men, occupied the rampart and resisted.
Ruǎn Diànfū ordered his隊主 (duìzhǔ), Quē Fǎjù, to shoot and kill the crossbowmen on the tower.
Gǒng Ruì’s troops were startled and terrified.
Shěn Sīrén unleashed his soldiers to attack them,
beheading their military commander, Kǒng Nú.
Thus, they were routed and dispersed.
On the nineteenth day of that month,
Wú Xǐ sent Liú Liàng from Yánguān by sea,
heading directly for Tóngpǔ.
Shòu Jìzhī crossed from Yúpǔ,
heading diagonally for Yǒngxīng.
Wú Xǐ himself crossed from Liǔpǔ,
heading for Xīlíng.
All the armies at Xīlíng scattered and collapsed.
Yǔ Yè, Gù Fǎzhí, and Wú Gōng were beheaded,
and their heads sent to the capital.
Bǔ Dàojì, the Eastern army commander, and Xǔ Tiāncì, the battle supervisor, requested to surrender.
Yǔ Yè
was a native of Xīnyě.
His father, Yàn Dá,
was known by Tàizǔ for his competence and integrity,
and served as the Governor of Yìzhōu.
During Shìzǔ’s reign,
he rose to the offices of Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng
and Grand Master of Ceremonies.
Liú Liàng, Quán Jǐngwén, and Sūn Chāozhī advanced to Yǒngxīng Tóngshì,
where they encountered Lù Xiàobó and Kǒng Yù’s two armies sent by Jì.
They fought and defeated them,
beheading Lù Xiàobó and Kǒng Yù.
Upon hearing that the Western army was approaching Huìjī,
many officers and soldiers fled,
and Jì could no longer control them.
On the twentieth day,
Wáng Yàn, the Prefect of Shàngyú, raised an army to attack the commandery.
Jì, pressed from both east and west,
was anxious and did not know what to do.
That evening,
he led over a thousand men, claiming to march east,
but actually heading for Shíwò.
He had already prepared boats at Hǎipǔ,
but the tide receded, preventing him from leaving.
[二七]His troops all rebelled and deserted.
His retainers carried him in a small boat,
and he hid in Línshān Village.
Zhāng Suí, the acting Chēqí Cóngshì Zhōngláng, had previously sent someone to Qiántáng to pledge allegiance to Wú Xǐ.
When Jì fled,
Zhāng Suí sealed the granaries and storehouses
to await the imperial army.
On the twenty-first day,
Wáng Yàn arrived at the commandery,
entered through the north gate,
and imprisoned Zhāng Suí, handing him over to the labor department.
That night, he killed him.
He seized Zǐfáng, the prince of Xúnyáng, at a separate residence,
and unleashed his soldiers to plunder extensively,
leaving the government coffers and storehouses empty.
Villagers from Ruòxié captured and delivered Kǒng Ruì, the acting Longxiáng General and Chēqí Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Jūnzhǔ.
As he was about to be executed,
Kǒng Ruì said:
"I am past thirty,
and have not yet served in official ranks.
I received the patronage of a true friend
and pledged my life to him.
To die today,
what regret can there be?"
He smiled as he went to his execution.
Kǒng Zǎo rebelled and sought refuge with his retainer, Lù Línfū.
Lù Línfū beheaded him and sent his head.
On the twenty-second day,
the people of Línshān bound Jì and delivered him to Wáng Yàn.
Wáng Yàn said to him:
"This matter was Kǒng Zǎo's doing.
[二八]It has nothing to do with Your Excellency.
You can write a statement of your defense,
and I will submit it for you."
Jì replied:
"The arrangements in Jiāngdōng
were all made by me.
To shift blame to seek survival is merely what people like you do."
Wáng Yàn then beheaded him outside the east gate.
Before dying, he asked for wine,
saying:
"This is what I have loved all my life."
He was fifty-one years old at the time.
Gù Chēn, Wáng Tánshēng, Yuán Biāo, and others all went to Wú Xǐ to confess their crimes.
Wú Xǐ pardoned them all.
Gù Chēn's son, Bǎosù, had lost contact with his father
and hanged himself.
There were a total of seventy-six Eastern army commanders;
seventeen were beheaded in battle,
and the rest were all pardoned.
Initially, Yǔ Yè was sent to Huìjī,
and later Sūn Chángdù, an attendant, was dispatched to deliver weapons to him
and to recruit soldiers.
When he reached Jìnlíng,
Yuán Biāo asked him for the weapons.
Sūn Chángdù refused to give them,
and was killed by Yuán Biāo.
He was posthumously granted the title of Gěishìzhōng.
Before this,
Dèng Wǎn had sent Zhāng Yān, the Grand Administrator of Línchuān, to take the southern route out to Dōngyáng.
Zhāng Yān sent Longxiáng General Guì Huáng and Zēngxī Xíng Cānjūn Liú Yuèxù to garrison Dìngyáng County.
Liú Xiūrúo, the Prince of Bālíng, sent Shěn Sīrén to attack them.
Shěn Sīrén sent his Jūnzhǔ, Cuī Gōngliè, to attack their camp,
beheading the head of Zhū Bófú, the flag commander.
Guì Huáng, Liú Yuèxù, and their armies all fled.
Liú Zhān, the Grand Administrator of Jìn'ān, held the commandery and rebelled.
Zhào Dàoshēng, the Grand Administrator of Jiàn'ān, raised an army to suppress him,
but his followers had not yet fully assembled.
In the seventh month,
Shěn Sīrén sent his Jūnzhǔ, Yáo Hóngzǔ, Bāo Bófèn, and Yīng Jìshēng, among others, to attack and defeat Liú Zhān,
beheading him in Luójiāng County.
Dèng Wǎn had previously sent Yáng Bózǐ, the Grand Administrator of Xīn'ān, and Jūnzhǔ Rèn Xiànzǐ to raid Yī County.
Wú Rúgōng, the county magistrate, held out,
but, being outnumbered,
abandoned the city and fled.
Yáng Bózǐ and others garrisoned the county seat.
Wú Rúgōng, along with Tái Jūnzhǔ Qiū Jìngwén, Lǐ Língcì, and Xiāo Bǎishòu, besieged them for a long time,
and finally captured the city in the eighth month,
