beheading Yáng Bózǐ and Rèn Xiànzǐ.
Zhāng Yān’s army was garrisoned in Shàngráo County.
Hearing of Liú Hú’s defeat,
Fèi Tán, his deputy and Grand Administrator of Póyáng, planned to assassinate him.
He falsely claimed:
"I have received a letter from Dèng Wǎn,
and we urgently need to discuss it."
He intended to use this opportunity to behead Zhāng Yān.
Zhāng Yān habitually practiced Buddhism
and was performing Buddhist rites,
so he could not come immediately.
Fèi Tán then lied again, saying he was hunting a tiger,
and borrowed a large drum and two hundred armed soldiers.
Zhāng Yān believed him and granted his request.
Fèi Tán then led his followers into the mountains,
feasting his soldiers and swearing them to an oath.
He loudly proclaimed that the tiger had gone west of the city,
beat the drums loudly,
and rushed directly towards the city.
The city gate guards
all dropped their weapons to watch.
Fèi Tán led his troops to burst in.
Zhāng Yān, who was still performing Buddhist rites,
heard the commotion and ran out,
whereupon he was beheaded.
The Grand Scribe says: Since the time of the Eastern Jìn dynasty,
among those who raised arms to contend for the ancestral state,
there were eleven,
but only four
were able to achieve victory.
Yuán-huáng externally maintained a nominal position,
with governance controlled by the Wáng clan;
Sū Jùn's ambition, though temporarily realized,
soon led to his slaughter;
Huán Xuán, son of Xuān-wǔ,
found his reign beset by chaos;
Shì-zǔ, relying on righteousness, launched an expedition,
and the people harbored no different hopes.
The rest all met with utter destruction,
serving as warnings for later generations.
Why is this?
The outcome of victory and defeat
truly depends on the hearts of the people.
The sanctity of the ancestral altars and temples
is what the people's sentiments are tied to.
Even when moving with righteousness,
it is still considered difficult,
how much more so when long halberds point at the palace gate,
with the intent of aggression and oppression!
During the contention of Tài-shǐ,
right and wrong were not yet clear.
Tài-zōng personally eliminated the perverse rebellion,
his only aim being to save the drowning.
The state's path was difficult and treacherous,
so it was fitting to establish a senior ruler.
Given Tài-zǔ's clear lineage,
there was no impropriety in the righteousness.
As for Zǐ-xūn, though he was of Shì-zǔ's lineage,
the family's fortune had already ended.
The mandate to wield power
clearly belonged elsewhere.
With two paths, right and wrong,
it was unclear where the destiny lay.
It was merely by occupying the sacred capital
and possessing the resources of the heavenly storehouse,
bearing the weight of the ancestral temples and altars,
and thus exercising authority over the four directions,
controlling the periphery from the center,
that he was able to pacify the realm.
The place where emperors reside
is known by the grand title of
capital (Jīng-shī),
and its profound meaning is not without reason.
Collation Notes
Biography Forty-Five: Xiè Zhuāng, Wáng Jǐng-wén
Xiè Zhuāng, courtesy name Xī-yì,
was a native of Yáng-xià, Chén-jùn,
and the son of Tái-cháng Hóng-wēi.
At the age of seven,
he was able to compose essays
and understood the Lúnyǔ.
As he grew older,
he was refined, intelligent, and possessed a handsome appearance.
Tài-zǔ saw him and was impressed,
saying to Shàng-shū Pú-yè Yīn Jǐng-rén and Lǐng-jūn Jiāng-jūn Liú Zhàn:
"That Lán-tián produces jade,
is certainly no empty boast."
Initially, he served as the Hòu-jūn Fǎ-cáo Xíng-cān-jūn to Shǐ-xīng-wáng Jùn,
then transferred to Tài-zǐ Shè-rén,
Lú-líng-wáng Wén-xué,
Tài-zǐ Xǐ-mǎ,
Zhōng-shè-rén,
and Lú-líng-wáng Shào's Nán-zhōng-láng Zī-yì Cān-jūn.
He further transferred to Suí-wáng Dàn's Hòu-jūn Zī-yì,
concurrently holding the position of Jì-shì.
He divided the Zuǒ-shì Zhuàn according to each state's section,
and created a wooden map measuring one zhàng square,
depicting mountains, rivers, and land,
each with its distinct divisions.
When separated, it showed different prefectures and counties;
when combined, it represented the entire realm as one.
In the twenty-seventh year of Yuán-jiā,
the Suǒ captives invaded Péng-chéng.
The captives sent Shàng-shū Lǐ Xiào-bó as an envoy,
who spoke with Zhèn-jūn Zhǎng-shǐ Zhāng Chàng.
Xiào-bó inquired about Zhuāng and Wáng Wēi,
indicating how far their reputations had spread.
In the twenty-ninth year,
he was appointed Tài-zǐ Zhōng-shù-zǐ.
At that time, Nán-píng-wáng Shuò presented a red parrot,
and a general decree ordered all officials to compose rhapsodies (fù).
Tài-zǐ Zuǒ-wèi-shuài Yuán Shú, whose literary talent was foremost at the time,
finished his rhapsody
and brought it to show Zhuāng.
Zhuāng's rhapsody was also completed.
Shú saw it and exclaimed:
"If not for me in Jiāng-dōng,
you would stand alone in prominence.
If not for you, I too would be a hero of my time!"
Then
he concealed his own rhapsody.
When the prime culprit (Yuán-xiōng) usurped the throne through regicide,
Zhuāng was transferred to Sī-tú Zuǒ-zhǎng-shǐ.
When Shì-zǔ launched his punitive expedition,
he secretly sent a proclamation (xí-shū) to Zhuāng,
instructing him to revise and disseminate it.
Zhuāng dispatched his trusted student Jù Qìng to secretly convey a memorial to Shì-zǔ, saying:
"The rebel Shào has cut himself off from Heaven,
tearing crowns and destroying robes,
committing regicide and extreme depravity,
unheard of since the dawn of time.
The four seas weep blood,
and both the living and the dead are indignant.
We received the proclamation of the twenty-seventh day of the third month;
the holy traces are manifest,
and I respectfully read it with joy and emotion.
Heaven blesses the royal house,
and sagely wisdom shines anew.
Your Highness's civilization resides in the mountains,
and divine martial prowess is at the passes.
You solemnly uphold heavenly might,
carrying out Heaven's punishment,
avenging the altars and temples,
and washing away the shame of both Chinese and barbarians.
This allows the collapsed structure
to be rebuilt,
and the defiled populace
to regain clarity.
I respectfully learned of your command,
that Liǔ Yuán-jǐng, Sī-mǎ Wén-gōng, Zōng Kē, Shěn Qìng-zhī,
and others, with one hundred thousand elite armored troops,
have already reached nearby roads.
Your Highness personally leads the sharp forces,
advancing in accordance with military law.
The armies from Jīng and Yān,
and the multitudes from Mín and Hàn,
stretch for ten thousand miles with their ships,
their banners and pennants obscuring the sky.
The nine provinces mysteriously align,
and all the lords gather.
Now, this lone villain and his vile ilk
do not even form a complete army.
They destroy each other,
chaos flows through the palace,
officials hold their breath,
and communicate with their eyes on the road.
Upon the arrival of the proclamation,
it was immediately distributed in the capital.
The court and commoners alike rejoiced,
singing praises in the streets,
and families congratulated each other.
Everyone looked to your splendor with awe,
and stopped in their tracks gazing at the clouds.
The late emperor, with the light of the sun and moon,
illuminated the realm;
wherever his benevolent influence spread,
no corner was left untouched.
Moreover, this humble official's family has been graced by favor for generations,
receiving excessive kindness.
I feigned illness and retired to my private residence,
fortunately escaping the tiger's mouth.
Although I wish to repay your kindness,
there is no way to do so.
Now that the grand army is nearing,
eternal peace is not far off.
My joy and sorrow are boundless,
I know not what to do."
When Shì-zǔ ascended the throne,
Zhuāng was appointed Shì-zhōng.
At that time, the Suǒ captives sought to resume mutual trade,
and the emperor issued a decree for all officials to extensively deliberate.
Zhuāng's deliberation stated:
"Your humble servant believes that the Xūn-xiǎn abandon righteousness
and are only motivated by profit.
Their request for border markets
may be to spy on our state.
To concede would show weakness,
and would not be a clear act of pacifying distant peoples.
To refuse and observe their weaknesses
would sufficiently demonstrate our strength.
Furthermore, Emperor Wén maintained peace through marriage alliances,
but this did not stop the incursions at Péng-yáng;
Emperor Wǔ maintained treaties,
but this did not abandon the scheme at Mǎ-yì.
Therefore, if we have surplus, we plan and manage;
if we are insufficient, we close the passes.
Why should a civilized nation
accommodate a barbaric custom,
establish a useless policy,
and invite the winds of impurity and defilement?
The discussion of trade and exchange is flawed
and should be firmly prohibited;
the deceptive arguments for peace treaties
should be even more resolutely rejected.
Your humble servant, though ignorant and with many shortcomings,
how can I understand state rituals?
But having been induced by your grace,
how dare I not reveal everything."
At that time, Píqí Jiāngjūn, Jìnglíng Wáng Dàn, was about to become Governor of Jīngzhōu.
The Emperor summoned Chéngxiàng and Jīngzhōu Císhǐ, Nánjùn Wáng Yìxuān, to enter the court and assist,
but Yìxuān firmly declined to come.
However, Dàn immediately set a date for his departure by boat.
Zhuāng said:
"Since the Chéngxiàng has no intention of coming,
and the Píqí is scheduled to depart soon,
it appears as though he intends to pressure him,
which would be inconvenient for the matter."
Shìzǔ then postponed Dàn's departure date,
but Yìxuān still did not come.
When the Emperor first ascended the throne,
he wished to widely proclaim principles of good governance
and issued an edict on frugality.
The details are in the biography of Xiàowǔ.
Zhuāng was concerned that this decree would not be enforced,
and further stated:
"The edict says, 'Those noble relatives who compete for profit
and establish shops and markets
shall all be prohibited.'
This indeed conforms to the people's wishes.
If there is any violation,
it should be punished according to the decree.
If the law is abandoned in favor of leniency,
it will mean that the decree has been compromised.
Regarding this arrangement, I humbly request deep consideration.
There is no reason for a clear edict to be issued
and then for its words and reality to diverge.
Your humble servant believes that ministers holding high office
should especially not compete with the common people for profit.
I wonder if this can be included in the edict?
'Plucking mallows and discarding weaving' (i.e., promoting frugality)
should indeed be greatly emphasized."
In the first year of Xiàojiàn,
he was promoted to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
Previously,
Shìzǔ had once bestowed a precious sword upon Zhuāng.
Zhuāng gave it to Yùzhōu Císhǐ Lǔ Shuǎng as a farewell gift.
Later, Shuǎng rebelled.
During a banquet, Shìzǔ
asked where the sword was.
He replied:
"I gave it to Lǔ Shuǎng as a farewell gift in the past,
secretly taking it as a Duqí gift from Your Majesty (i.e., a death sentence)."
The Emperor was very pleased,
and at the time, this was considered a wise remark.
At that time, when talents were being sought,
he submitted a memorial, saying: "Your servant has heard that merit shining a thousand *lǐ*
is not merely the treasure of a candle-chariot;
and virtue that softens neighboring states
is not just the value of a hidden jade.
Thus, the *Shī* (Book of Odes) speaks of hardship,
and oaths describe noble
aspirations.
This enabled the Way to reach abundance and
transformation to attain humility.
I humbly believe that Your Majesty, receiving auspicious omens and the mandate,
has established the realm and opened up prefectures,
selecting governance in the evening and
harmonizing customs from dawn to dusk.
Gathering
words from the humble and
observing popular rhymes from afar—
this is truly the celestial order announcing peace,
and songs of praise are being composed.
Your servant humbly reflects on the gradual development of prosperity,
and the causes of order and chaos:
they have always arisen
from acquiring talent,
and declined due to losing worthy individuals.
Therefore, the *Chǔ Shū* (Book of Chu) considers good people as treasures,
and the *Yú Diǎn* (Canon of Yu) considers those who follow wisdom as difficult to find.
The path of advancement and selection
has been relaxed since the middle ages,
and the regulations for promotion
have not been clearly established in the present day.
If one truly desires to strengthen the foundation and stabilize affairs,
to protect the people and save society,
how can it be achieved
without further rigorous selection,
how can 'nine achievements' be attained?
When the calendar entered the central yang,
eminent scholars
arose from Xú and Pèi;
when the mandate was received at Bái Shuǐ,
distinguished individuals emerged from Jīng and Wǎn.
It is not that the intelligence produced in those two capitals
or the talents gathered from the seven regions
are inherently superior,
but rather a matter of encounter
or non-encounter, employment or non-employment.
Now the Great Way is open and flourishing,
and all matters await virtue.
Yet, the vastness of the nine regions
and the difficulties of the nine streams (of thought)
mean that the task of balancing and weighing,
is entrusted to the selection
department.
The judgment of a single person is easily limited,
while the talents of the world are difficult to fathom.
To use a limited judgment
to discern unfathomable talents,
and thus ensure that the state has no neglected bestowals
and the countryside has no wasted
vessels,
how can this be achieved?
In the past, Gōngshū and Jiàn ascended together;
Guǎn Zhòng chose a minister from among thieves;
Zhào Wén did not alienate worthy individuals for close relatives;
Qí Xī would not flatter enemies over his own son.
To gather reeds into a bundle,
setting a precedent from ancient scriptures—
'appoint those whom you know,'
thus illuminating past records.
Moreover, since ancient times, appointments and recommendations
have been clearly rewarded and punished.
Chéngzǐ recommended three wise men and personally
achieved the post of Chancellor of Wèi;
Yìng Hóu appointed two scholars and himself yielded the Chancellorship of Qín;
Jiù Jì praised Jì Quē and was rewarded with fields and estates;
Zhāng Bó advanced Chén Tāng and was subsequently stripped of his title.
These are magnificent precedents from former times,
and also permanent mirrors for future kings.
In your servant's humble opinion,
it is appropriate to universally command all ministers
to each recommend those they know,
to be submitted to the Shàngshū,
and appointed according to their qualifications.
If the appointee is talented,
the recommender shall receive extended rewards;
if the appointee is not competent,
the recommender shall be held responsible.
In serious cases, they shall be dismissed;
in minor cases, demoted.
The appointed
person
shall be prohibited from holding office,
the number of years
to be determined according to the offense.
If the offense warrants capital punishment,
then the recommender shall be subject to the same penalty.
Furthermore, for governance to be fair and lawsuits just,
nothing is more important than being close to the people.
The key to being close to the people
truly lies with the regional administrators.
Thus, Huáng Bà governed Yǐngchuān for many years;
Dù Jī resided in Hédōng for many
years.
Some were granted additional favor and rank,
others were promoted to high and favored positions.
Now, for those in charge of governing the people,
unless public or private necessity requires replacement,
they should follow the six-year term system,
so that those who advance
can be clearly distinguished as competent or incompetent,
and those who retire
ensure the people are not troubled by frequent changes.
If this is done, there will be no errors or mistakes among the lower ranks,
and no burden of abandoning capable individuals at the top.
The custom of evaluating performance will flourish,
and the song of burning
firewood (i.e., celebrating peace) will prosper.
Your servant was born in a prosperous era,
and gradually advanced through great policies,
thus having the opportunity to serve by Your Majesty's side
and present humble opinions.
I dare to offer these rough words,
fearing they may contaminate the decrees."
An edict stated that Zhuāng's memorial was thus,
and could be sent outside for detailed discussion,
but the matter was not implemented.
In that year,
he was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū.
Zhuāng had always suffered from many illnesses
and did not wish to hold the selection post.
He submitted a memorial to Dàsīmǎ, Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng,
stating: "This humble official is an ordinary person,
without exceptional insight or unique understanding.
My aspiration to be outside worldly affairs
is truly due to my frail health,
constantly fearing sudden demise.
Therefore, since childhood, I have had no interest in worldly matters;
how
could I have aspirations for high office?
In recent years, events have changed and shifted,
and I have indeed inappropriately held high positions,
which is enough to invite criticism in this enlightened age,
and also to bring shame upon my friends.
Previously,
when the sacred way was first established,
I had no leisure to withdraw.
Now that affairs in all these lands are settled,
I can present my humble request.
My ambition [fāzhì] has not been realized,
yet I am still burdened with this current appointment.
At the beginning of receiving this grace,
I fully revealed..."
My humble heart,
not only did I know my own faults,
but I truly feared polluting the eternal order.
My life has been plagued by illness,
as the world well knows.
The chronic illness in both my sides
has been with me almost since birth.
It flares up monthly,
no fewer than two or three times.
Each time it worsens,
the pain comes
pressing on my heart,
my breath as faint as a thread.
Suffering from this for several years,
it has become an incurable disease.
Gasping and panting,
I am like a walking corpse.
Living with a terminal illness
yet not resigning from office,
is it because I am cured?
It is simply due to the profound imperial grace I have received,
and my desire to repay this extraordinary benevolence.
Driven by my failing health,
I manage the duties I unworthily hold.
For five months now, due to an eye ailment, I have been unable to
sit up at night.
I close the curtains to avoid wind and sun,
and am drowsy day and night.
Because of this, I can no longer attend court to greet the princes,
nor offer congratulations or condolences to relatives and old friends.
I only attend when commanded by imperial decree,
and am not permitted to stay.
For dozens of days now, I have been unable to
receive guests due to this condition.
To endure this bitter life
and yet be made to select and manage officials of all ranks,
and respond to countless lawsuits,
is truly due to Your Sacred Majesty’s boundless compassion.
However,
to bear this burden is indeed exceedingly arduous for me.
If my talent were equal to the task
and my health robust,
receiving such exceptional favor
and being in a position to demonstrate my abilities,
would I idly wish to resign from affairs
like this?
My family has always been poor and in decline,
our home not yet established.
My children cannot avoid coarse food,
yet they accept it as fate.
How can I forget my meager salary?
It is simply that there is something
more urgent than this,
and so I have no other desires.
What I hope for now
is only a little leisure.
My humble life,
of lightest consequence in the world,
I cannot but
cherish it for myself.
I have repeatedly appealed for leave,
but have not received merciful pardon.
This is surely because my sincerity is shallow and my words are clumsy,
insufficient to move Your Majesty above.
My family has no long-lived members.
My deceased great-grandfather died at forty,
my great-great-grandfather at thirty-two,
and my deceased grandfather at forty-seven.
This coming New Year, I will be thirty-five.
Added to this
is such an illness.
How much longer will I see the Sacred Era,
and endure such torment within it?
It is truly pitiable.
Previously, I once requested to be transferred to the three Wú,
but the imperial decree stated,
"There is
no need to discuss external transfers again."
This may be excessive grace,
but it is also my fate in life
never to experience a moment of leisure.
Now I dare not mention this again;
I will entrust it to
my next life.
If only I can preserve my remaining years,
free from official duties,
and get a little rest to nurture my illness,
this would fulfill my aspirations forever.
To have thoughts while dwelling in a humble home,
and for every action
to be heard,
there is no need to hold office.
My only concern is my inability to be of any benefit.
With shallow knowledge and ordinary talent,
and such a debilitated illness,
I have failed to live up to the grace of Your Majesty's promotion and appointment.
In my private heart, I am truly grieved and ashamed.
At the beginning of the year, I will again submit my previous request,
even if it means death.
However, a common person's plea
may not reach Your Majesty.
Your Excellency's kindness and benevolent gaze are profoundly
deep;
you roughly discern my sincere earnestness.
I wish to speak with you when you are seated,
and be granted your aid and support.
Then my bitter sincerity and utmost devotion
might perhaps receive merciful approval.
If I do not receive your benevolent assistance,
where else can
I place my hopes?
I look up to your compassionate discernment,
and pray you will not be reserved.
After three years,
he was relieved of his post
for frequently citing illness to resign.
In the first year of Dà-Míng,
he was appointed Dūguān Shàngshū.
He proposed reforms to the penal system,
saying: Your servant hears that to be discerning and cautious in using punishments
is preserved in the Jī-diǎn;
to be compassionate and sympathetic in judging cases
truly shines in the Lǚ-mìng.
To lean towards leniency in doubtful cases
is a principle of the former kings;
to prefer to err
on the side of not executing
is also a teaching of the enlightened sages.
Thus, they were able to bring about peace,
and the Way reached a state of self-governance.
When Hàn Wén-dì deplored the punishment of the innocent
and abolished the law of collective punishment,
and Xiào-Xuān-dì abhorred overly strict officials
and established the law of judicial interrogation,
at that time,
it was
hailed as a period of pure justice.
Your Majesty, since ascending the throne,
has personally presided over lawsuits.
Millions rejoice,
believing there are no wronged commoners.
Yet, recently, prisons are not empty,
and songs of praise are still lacking.
Your servant secretly believes that the mercy of the "five hearings"
is not fully expressed in governing the people;
the benevolence of the "three remissions"
has not fully reached the populace.
In recent years, due to the lingering ills of military campaigns,
robbery and plunder are still frequent.
When supervising officials apprehend suspects,
many are not truly guilty.
Some, seeking to avoid personal blame,
do not
consider the nation's welfare.
Under torture,
few fail to falsely incriminate.
Individuals suffer execution by axe and cleaver,
and their families endure the pain of enslavement and slaughter.
Neighbors and fellow villagers
are all implicated.
Thus,
one mistaken punishment
implicates dozens.
In ancient times, when the Qí woman appealed to heaven,
the Línbó terrace collapsed.
When the filial wife was unjustly executed,
Dōnghǎi suffered a drought.
These were all portents of change from the spirits,
first affecting the celestial phenomena.
〔一０〕Your servant recently participated in interrogations
and saw eight heavy prisoners.
Initially, it seemed they had more than enough crimes to warrant death,
but upon detailed investigation of their cases,
they were all in fact innocent.
I fear
there are quite a few such cases,
which is truly alarming.
Formerly, after local officials concluded a prisoner's case,
the commandery would dispatch a Dūyóu to investigate
and then carry out the punishment.
A Dūyóu is a minor official,
no different from other local officials;
they have the name
of investigation,
but lack the substance of thorough inquiry.
Your humble servant believes this system should be reformed.
From now on, for prisoners facing severe charges,
after the county has thoroughly examined and verified the case,
they should report the matter to the commandery,
and send the prisoner there,
entrusting the Erchenshi to personally oversee the review and debate.
They must ensure that all accusations are fully heard and addressed,
and only then proceed with execution.
If the Erchenshi cannot make a decision,
then the case should be referred to the Tíngwèi.
Outside the jurisdiction of Shénzhōu,
transferred to the Cìshǐ.
If the Cìshǐ had doubts,
they too would be returned to the imperial prison.
It must ensure that the deceased have no grievances,
and the living no hatred.
Then, the proverb of "selling coffins"
will cease to be sighed over throughout
history;
and the thorough examination of both parties
will be lauded in the present day.
Your servant's learning is as dim as Shēn Bùhài and Hán Fēi's,
and his talent for governance is meager.
To lightly present the mundane views of Guǎn Zhòng
is to fear contravening the national laws.
The Emperor personally reviewed the court affairs at the time,
and was always concerned that power might shift to his subordinates.
Regarding the elections overseen by the Lìbù Shàngshū,
he wished to diminish their influence.
Two years later,
an edict was issued, saying:
"The eight handles of governance control subordinates,
with rank as the foremost;
the nine virtues serve all affairs,
with administrative statutes holding the primary position.
The balance of selection is the pivot of governance,
the rise and fall of which are entrusted to it.
Since recent times,
its proper order has gradually been lost,
leading to merely holding the reins of the state
but ultimately incurring the slander of usurpation.
Now, with many scholars from both North and South,
their meritorious service accumulates,
and the sentiments of the people, whether good or bad,
are truly tied to this responsibility.
The praise of 'appointing officials'
can only be truly fulfilled by a sage;
the excellence of 'selecting the wise'
was difficult even for the ancient emperors.
Moreover, with a decaying age in custom,
the discussions of concession have become a trend.
How can one individual's understanding
address the criticism of the multitude,
and expect to naturally achieve rise or fall
in one's position?
The Lìbù Shàngshū may be appointed by dividing the Lang positions,
and also thoroughly reviewing the idle offices."
Another separate edict was sent to Tài Zǎi Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng, saying: "The edict dividing the selections was issued this morning.
Among those discussing it in court,
there are both agreements and disagreements.
Indeed, I know that following the usual practice is very easy,
while changing the old generates doubts.
However, the Lìbù Shàngshū has always
jointly selected with the Lù.
This is precisely because one individual's understanding
is insufficient for comprehensive comprehension,
and the power to grant or deny
should not be concentrated in one person.
Previously, when the imperial intention was conveyed,
I respectfully followed
the submitted memorial,
reviewing the records to establish rules
to be eternally passed down to later generations.
From this point on, the essentials of selection
depended solely on Yuán and Kǎi alone.
If success and failure diverge from what is right,
and those who voice grievances
are few,
and furthermore, if regulations are violated and people are treated unjustly,
it naturally leads to estrangement.
Even the former kings and prosperous rulers
found this difficult,
let alone my limited and dim understanding,
which makes its shortcomings even more apparent.
Moreover, if an official in charge of selection is merely ill,
complaints and criticism immediately fill the streets.
Just as a person's four limbs
experience both fullness and emptiness,
within ten days,
resentment and curses arise,
how much more so if there is actual favoritism
and not merely a matter of illness?
If one visit does not result in advancement,
poverty and hardship are intertwined.
Then both sides suffer,
unable to empathize with each other.
When compared with the reality,
both are pitiable.
If the office is staffed by two people,
then there will be no
such abuses.
Furthermore, the selection office is a crucial pivot,
which has been highly valued throughout successive dynasties.
Anyone who has held this position
becomes a path to nobility.
Their internal thoughts and external opinions
are not self-restrained.
Thus, Fàn Yè and Lǔ
Shuǎng
raised armies and wiped out their families.
From this, it can be said
that it was truly driven by the prestige of high status and influence,
and the consequences of being excessively busy.
If such an appointment were to be considered,
there are only a few suitable individuals,
who have accumulated years
and months,
and been gradually promoted.
However, there is no predetermined timing,
and much happens unexpectedly.
Or they might encounter difficulties or fall ill,
causing affairs to change.
The responsibility of appointing officials
cannot possibly be left vacant.
One comes, one goes,
having already served enough people.
Without demotion or reprimand,
it is difficult for those already noble to become humble.
Having become an impediment to growth,
they have no place to be put.
The rise and fall alternate,
which is a way for
court officials to interact.
Doubts arise between ruler and subject,
which makes it even more apparent that this position
should be downgraded.
The Jìanlìng and Duān Yòu [officials],
are sufficient to manage current expectations.
If there is no one, it is vacant,
unlike the nine streams of officials.
Now, simply administering the selection department
will reduce previous assets.
Public sentiment is prone to suspicion,
arbitrarily creating different interpretations.
The original intent and purpose
will never be publicly declared.
Only
by assigning positions according to Lang ranks
will perceptions naturally change.
Since the selection has been lightened first,
public sentiment has already changed.
Those capable of the task
will have ample opportunity for promotion.
The usual appropriate measures
will be gradually advanced
with time.
The original position can no longer be obtained as a heavy office,
and there is no need to hold several concurrent posts,
so holding it will completely avoid causing bewilderment.
Since the division of Jīng and Yáng,
there was already an intention for this at that time.
It was just feared that too many reforms
might cause shock and confusion.
Many years have passed since then,
and it was intended to arrange it by the end of the year.
However, coincidently, Hé Yǎn passed away,
and he had close relatives.
Therefore, this policy was implemented recently because of that.
The original intention of the imperial edict could not be fully detailed,
so I have again put it down on paper.
Thereupon, two Lìbù Shàngshū were appointed.
The Wǔbīng Shàngshū was abolished,
and Zhuāng and Dùzhī Shàngshū Gù Jìzhī were both assigned to the selection office.
He was promoted to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently given the title Jǐshìzhōng.
At that time, Hénán presented dancing horses.
An imperial edict ordered the assembled officials to compose fu.
The text submitted by Zhuāng stated: The Son of Heaven controls the three luminaries,
and governs all realms.
He draws upon the enduring precedents of the cloud scriptures,
and fashions the ancient rules of the river charts.
Therefore, his virtuous benevolence shines above,
and springs forth throughout the world.
The blessings of auspicious signs all gather,
and the responses of glory are surely manifest.
The lunar gnomon shows propitious omens,
the celestial framework displays its aura.
Casting shadows in the river mansions,
receiving spiritual essence from the heavenly steeds.
They gradually
cast their shadows over the wilderness,
leap with vibrant colors from the abyss,
departing from the water's emptiness and heading south,
leaving Lúntái and reaching eastward.
They pass through the jade frontier fortress and return with treasures,
reaching the garden of auspicious herbs to present their marvels.
And
when they are nourished in the Qíjiào stable,
and driven to the Dragon Spring,
they illuminate the imperial stable with their grand carriage,
and enhance the imperial paddock with their superior grace.
They transcend the abundant fields and cross the green lands,
surpassing the orchid pond and treading on
purple swallows.
The five kings hid their arts,
the ten families were ignorant of their mystery.
How could Dōngmén resemble them,
Xīhé could not transmit their ways.
Having already become
equal in nature,
Héng, with his lofty achievements,
contained heroic spirit in ornate prose,
stored a galloping countenance behind candle screens,
held the sharp radiance of a rolling cloud,
and restrained the swift feet of a chasing lightning bolt.
He repeatedly refined his talent in crimson
silk,
and also matched his standards with vermillion-spotted horses.
Observe how his twin jades responded to the model,
and the three seals corresponded to the diagram;
the profound bones were full,
the swallow chamber empty;
the yang principles were complete,
the hidden strategies intricate;
sweat flew
like ochre,
foam flowed like vermillion.
As for the *Sìxià* ascending,
and the *Cǎiqí* already offered,
he first lingered, a dragon bowing,
then gracefully, a phoenix glancing;
he met the "Dew Gathering" with flying bells,
and rushed to "Cloud Bearing" with startling arrows,
erasing the pervasive dust of Qín's fields,
〔一三〕resembling the trailing silk of Wú's gate,
exhausting the treading and prancing of Yú's court,
and delving into the circling dance of the distant wilds.
As for
the posture of firm footing not yet withdrawn,
and the spirit of soaring high still unfurling,
he traversed the wilds of Tài and passed Jiéshí,
crossed the dark currents and surpassed Gūyú;
in the morning, he saw off the sun on the western slope,
in the evening, he returned with the wind to the northern capital,
finding the jade palace in an instant,
gazing at the silver terrace in a flash.
When the sun proclaimed its double splendor,
and the star of virtue shone widely,
the state called out to Liáng and Tài, awaiting the imperial carriage,
the histories spoke of the altars and fields expecting the imperial presence;
the auspicious omens of Hàoshàng were manifest,
the auspicious
signs between the rivers were clear;
the fortune of glorious mirrors had arrived,
the calendar of prosperous harmony was discerned;
it corresponded to the five omens' course,
and reflected the recommended classics of the many lords.
The Sage Emperor was about to perform rituals on Dōng
yuè,
as was proper.
Thereupon, he followed the Big Dipper,
mounted the celestial paths,
commanded the hanging sun at dawn,
and ordered the month's inscription for the previous year.
In stately and majestic procession,
he drifted on the long wind and
floated on propitious smoke;
solemn and harmonious,
he led the eight spirits and summoned the nine immortals.
He descended to Qí's suburbs and covered Pèilín,
gathered in Yínglǐ and descended to Fēngtián;
the rush carriages approached the peaks,
the jade tablets ascended the ridges;
the golden seals were then issued,
the jade edicts then inscribed;
the meaning of the grand festival was harmonious,
the ritual of ascending to the center was complete;
the myriad people rejoiced,
the spirits were delighted;
they heard "Long Live!" from the
lofty mountains,
and illuminated divine light on the purple altar.
Therefore, those who beat the chariot poles and danced,
and those who touched the ground and danced,
sang together, saying: "Raising the morning canopy, floating on dawn's glow,
the spirits
come, splendid as the Milky Way.
Mountains have longevity, pines are lush,
blessing the divine ultimate, granting fortune to the imperial house."
Then, understanding the achievements of the sage dynasty,
and calling out its glorious deeds,
its grandeur rivaled heaven and earth,
its brilliance contended with the sun and moon;
its flourishing reality surpassed Xú and Tíng,
its grand name
exceeded Xūn and Fā.
Its enterprise culminated in completion,
its Dao reached the point of acknowledgment;
how lofty!
how vast!
The people could find no words to praise it.
He also had Zhuāng compose a "War Horse Song,"
and ordered the Music Bureau to perform it.
In the fifth year,
he was again appointed Shìzhōng,
and led the Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn.
At that time, Shìzǔ went out
and returned at night.
He ordered the gate opened,
but Zhuāng, who was on guard,
considering the imperial token might be counterfeit,
insisted on not obeying the order
until a written imperial edict arrived.
Later, during a wine banquet, the Emperor casually said:
"Do you wish to emulate Zhì Jūnzhāng?"
He replied:
"Your servant has heard that imperial hunts have their limits,
and suburban sacrifices have their regulations.
Indulging in hunting grounds
is listed among former admonitions.
Your Majesty now braves the dust and dew,
going out in the morning and returning at night.
I fear that unruly individuals
might falsely impersonate,
which is why your servant humbly waited for a divine edict
before daring to open the gate."
He was reassigned to lead the Yóují Jiāngjūn,
and also led his home province's Dàzhōngzhèng,
and was appointed Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn's Zhēnglǔ Chángshǐ and Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu,
with the added title of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
He was then reassigned as Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng's Tàizǎi Chángshǐ,
with his general rank remaining unchanged.
In the sixth year,
he was again appointed Lìbù Shàngshū,
and led the Guózǐ Bóshì.
He was dismissed from office for selecting Zhāng Qí as Gōngchēlìng;
this incident is recorded in Yán Shībó's biography.
At that time, the Běi Zhōnglángjiāng, Xīn'ān Wáng Zǐluán, was greatly favored.
Wanting to attract talented and renowned individuals,
Zǐluán appointed Zhuāng as Chángshǐ.
Soon after, the office was promoted to Fǔjūn,
and he was still appointed Chángshǐ and Línhuái Tàishǒu.
Before taking office,
he was again appointed Wúyùn Tàishǒu.
Zhuāng was often ill
and disliked leaving the capital,
so he was reinstated to his former post.
When the Former Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
he appointed him Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
Initially,
Shìzǔ's favored concubine, Yīn Guìfēi, died,
and Zhuāng wrote a eulogy for her, saying:
"She paralleled the gate of Yáo."
This alluded to the affair of Hàn Zhāodì's mother, Zhào Jiéyú, and Yáo's mother's gate.
The Deposed Emperor, when in the Eastern Palace,
resented this.
Upon ascending the throne, he sent someone to reproach Zhuāng, saying:
"When you wrote the eulogy for Yīn Guìfēi,
did you know there was an Eastern Palace?"
He intended to execute him.
Someone advised the Emperor, saying:
"Death is common to all people,
it's just a one-time suffering,
not enough to cause deep distress.
Zhuāng has been rich and noble since childhood;
let's imprison him in the Shàngfāng for now,
to let him know the hardships of the world,
then killing him won't be too late."
The Emperor agreed with his words
and imprisoned him in Zuǒ Shàngfāng.
When Tàizōng quelled the chaos,
he was released.
Upon ascending the throne,
he appointed Zhuāng as Sànqí Chángshì and Guānglù Dàfū,
added the Jīnzhāng Zǐshòu,
and led the Xúnyáng Wáng Shī.
After a while,
he was transferred to Zhōngshūlìng,
with Chángshì and Wángshī remaining as before.
Soon after, he was given the added title of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
granted twenty close attendants,
with all his original posts remaining unchanged.
In the second year of Tàishǐ,
he passed away
at the age of forty-six.
He was posthumously granted Yòu Guānglù Dàfū,
with Chángshì as before,
and his posthumous name was Xiànzǐ.
His collected writings, over four hundred pieces,
circulated in the world.
His eldest son, Yáng,
was Jìnpíng Tàishǒu.
His daughter became Empress to Emperor Shùn,
and he was posthumously granted Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
Wáng Jǐngwén,
a native of Línyí, Lángyé.
His personal name was the same as Míngdì's taboo name.
His grandfather, Mù,
was the Grand Administrator of Línhǎi.
His paternal uncle, Zhì,
was refined and esteemed in his youth,
and had a high reputation.
Gāozǔ thought highly of him,
and often said:
"Seeing Wáng Zhì
makes one think of Zhòngzǔ."
When Liú Mùzhī was planning to attack Liú Yì,
Zhì was present.
Another day,
Mùzhī reported to Gāozǔ:
"Attacking a state
is a grave matter;
how could you let Wáng Zhì know of it?"
Gāozǔ smiled and said:
"This man is so aloof and refined,
how could he listen to discussions like this?"
His understanding was thus.
He served as Cánjūn in the Grand Commandant's staff,
followed in the campaign to Cháng'ān,
and remained as Sīmǎ of the General Who Guards the West and Grand Administrator of Tiānshuǐ for Guìyánggōng Yìzhēn.
Upon his return, he became the Five Military Ministries Shàngshū of the Sòng state,
Grand Administrator of Jìnlíng,
with an added rank of Zhōng Èrqiānshí,
and was enfeoffed as a fifth-rank Zǐ of Jiànlíng County,
and posthumously granted Grand Minister of Sacrifices.
His father, Sēnglǎng,
was also known for his prudence and honesty.
During the Yuánjiā era,
he served as Attendant-in-ordinary,
diligently performing his duties at court,
never failing or being lazy.
Tàizǔ praised him,
and appointed him Inspector of Xiāngzhōu.
At the end of Shìzǔ's Dàmíng era,
he became Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs.
At the beginning of Tàizōng's reign,
as the empress's father, he was appointed Special Advanced Official and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness of the Left,
and further promoted to Kaīfǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
He firmly declined,
so he was instead granted Attendant-in-ordinary and Special Advanced Official.
Soon after, he passed away,
and was posthumously granted Kaīfǔ,
with the posthumous title Yuángōng.
Jǐngwén was adopted by Zhì,
and as a child was recognized by his cousin Qiú.
He had a beautiful appearance,
and enjoyed discussing principles.
In his youth, he was as famous as Xiè Zhuāng of Chénjùn.
Tàizǔ highly admired and respected him,
and therefore Tàizōng married Jǐngwén's younger sister,
while Jǐngwén's personal name was the same as Tàizōng's.
Gāozǔ's fifth daughter, Xīn'ān Princess, had previously married Wáng Jǐngshēn of Tàiyuán,
but they separated.
She was to marry Jǐngwén,
but he firmly declined due to illness,
so the marriage did not take place.
He began his career as Principal Registrar to the Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent,
then became Gentleman of the Heir Apparent,
and inherited the peerage of Zǐ of Jiànlíng.
He served as Principal Registrar in the two departments of the General Who Attacks the North for Jiāngxiàwáng Yìgōng and the General of the Rear Army for Shǐxīngwáng Jùn,
Scholar of Wǔlíngwáng,
Recording Secretary of the General Who Pacifies the Army for Shìzǔ,
Grand Administrator of Nánguǎngpíng,
then became Cánjūn,
and subsequently served in the headquarters of the General Who Guards the North and the General Who Guards the Army,
then became Grand Administrator of Xuānchéng.
When the primal villain usurped the throne,
he was appointed Palace Assistant Secretary.
Before he could take office,
Shìzǔ launched an expedition against him.
Jǐngwén sent a secret messenger to express his loyalty.
Because his father was in the capital,
he could not openly take action.
After the affair was settled,
he was somewhat disliked and criticized,
but due to past favors,
he was appointed Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works for Nánpíngwáng Shuò,
but did not accept the post.
He was appointed Grand Administrator of Dōngyáng,
then entered court as Censor-in-chief,
Director of the Imperial Library,
and concurrently Colonel of Elite Cavalry.
He did not accept these posts,
and was transferred to Chief Clerk to the Minister of Education.
The Emperor, considering that the Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary traditionally held the power of recommending and replacing along with the Attendant-in-ordinary,
wished to elevate its selection.
He appointed Jǐngwén and Kǒng Jì of Kuàijī, both prominent figures of the North and South,
to these positions.
Soon after, he again became Chief Clerk to the Minister of Education.
He was dismissed from office
for not attending his sister's funeral when her tomb was opened.
In the second year of Dàmíng,
he again became Director of the Imperial Library,
Commander of the Right Guard of the Heir Apparent,
and Attendant-in-ordinary.
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Chief Clerk of the General Who Campaigns Against the Army for Ānlùwáng Zǐsuí, General Who Guards the State, and Administrator of Jiāngxià Commandery,
and concurrently acted as the Inspector of Yǐngzhōu.
He was again summoned to be Attendant-in-ordinary,
concurrently Colonel of Shooters,
and General of the Right Guard,
and Chamberlain of the Heir Apparent,
with General of the Right Guard as before.
He was stripped of his official dress and retained his post
for playing a dice game with Máo Fǎyīn, a Gentleman for Consultation,
and winning 1.2 million cash.
Soon after, he again became Attendant-in-ordinary,
and concurrently Chamberlain,
but had not yet taken office.
When the former dethroned emperor ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Director of the Imperial Library,
with Attendant-in-ordinary as before.
Due to his father's old age, he resigned
and was appointed Chief Clerk to the Grand Tutor for Jiāngxiàwáng Yìgōng,
General Who Guards the State, and Grand Administrator of Nánpíng.
At the beginning of Yǒngguāng,
he became Minister of Personnel.
In the first year of Jǐnghé,
he was promoted to Right Assistant Director.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
he was additionally appointed Left General of the Guard.
At that time, the six armies were on high alert.
Jǐngwén, with thirty armed guards, entered the six gates.
All the generals said:
"Defeating these petty rebels
is easier than picking up something lost."
Jǐngwén said:
"Indeed, there are no petty enemies;
even bees and scorpions have venom.
How can we treat them lightly?
All the armies should be fearful when facing a situation,
plan well to achieve success,
and first make themselves invincible,
that is the art of victory."
Soon after, he was transferred to Administrator of Dānyáng,
with Assistant Director as before.
He encountered his father's mourning,
and was recalled to be General Who Campaigns Against the Army,
Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and Administrator of Dānyáng.
He firmly declined the Assistant Director post,
and was reassigned as Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary, Minister of the Central Secretariat, and General of the Central Army,
with Administrator as before.
He again declined to accept.

He was then appointed Commissioner with Imperial Credentials, Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary, Area Commander-in-chief of the military affairs of Xīyáng of Jiāngzhōu and Yǐngzhōu, Xīncài and Jìnxī of Yùzhōu,
General Who Guards the South, and Inspector of Jiāngzhōu. He declined the Attendant-in-ordinary,
and only accepted after the mourning period was over.
Tài-Zōng 翦除 (Jiǎnchú) a tyrannical ruler,
and pacified the four directions.
He wished to enlist those with reputation in the court to assist his great enterprise,
so he issued an edict saying:
"Indeed, excellent plans spread throughout the nation,
with rewards honoring eternal decrees;
outstanding achievements bring renown to the court,
and diligent service is recorded in the imperial archives.
The General of Ānnán (安南), Governor of Jiāngzhōu (江州) Jǐngwén (景文),
has an expansive and refined demeanor,
a clear and open mind,
combining both reputation and substance,
truly possessing both honesty and steadfastness.
When the precious era was just beginning,
he secretly assisted the righteous cause;
when rebellious elements disturbed the order,
he foresightfully aided the imperial strategies.
He should ascend to a noble position,
and his lineage be perpetuated forever.
We, in pacifying disturbances and stabilizing the government,
truly rely on many talented individuals,
conferring titles and rewarding merits,
truly aligning with glorious achievements.
The Minister of the Right and Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs, concurrently overseeing the Grand Usher, Xìngzōng (興宗),
possesses profound and upright judgment,
and a perceptive and agile mind.
The Minister of Personnel, concurrently overseeing the Left Leader of the Crown Prince's Guards, Yuān (淵),
has a calm and flourishing temperament,
and a lofty and far-reaching character.
Both have participated in military and governmental planning,
their achievements shining during difficult times.
Expanding territory and establishing cities,
they truly conform to the standards of merit.
Jǐngwén (景文) is to be enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiāng'ān (江安) County,
with an income fief of eight hundred households.
Xìngzōng (興宗) is to be enfeoffed as Earl of Shǐchāng (始昌) County,
and Yuān (淵) as Earl of Nánchéng (南城) County,
each with an income fief of five hundred households."
Jǐngwén (景文) firmly declined,
but it was not permitted.
He then accepted five hundred households.
His title was advanced to General Guarding the South,
and soon after he was granted a set of drums and pipes.
Later, because Jiāngzhōu (江州) was to be moved to Nánchāng (南昌) as a garrison,
he was concurrently made Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng (豫章),
with other appointments remaining as before.
The prefecture was not ultimately moved.
A short while later,
he was summoned to be Minister of the Left and Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs,
concurrently overseeing the Ministry of Personnel,
and Governor of Yángzhōu (揚州),
with the added title of Grand Mentor of the Crown Prince,
his Standing Attendant position remaining as before.
He did not wish to return to court,
and sought to be Governor of Xiāngzhōu (湘州),
but this was not permitted.
At that time, it was also said that Jǐngwén (景文), while in Jiāngzhōu (江州),
was unable to keep himself clean.
Jǐngwén (景文) wrote to the emperor's favored minister, Wáng Dàolóng (王道隆), saying: [一五]
"Although I am lacking in personal conduct,
I hope not to betray my heart.
Being ashamed of my exceptional favors,
I vow not to deceive the enlightened sovereign from above.
I secretly heard that there are those who fabricate slander against me,
claiming that my business dealings amounted to tens of millions.
I have always lacked such ability;
if suddenly one day I acquired such an unusual skill,
it would certainly be unreasonable.
I only beg for a fair and thorough investigation.
If these words are not false,
then I should be exposed in the marketplace,
to correct the customs.
If, however, it is a malicious fabrication,
then I hope for an investigation into the reason for this deception.
My unworthiness only deepens,
enough to invite calumny.
Thinking of this, I am frightened,
how can I assess myself?
What I, in my humble state, truly desire
is not a lenient pardon granted without investigation.
I myself know I am not a thief,
just as I am not a robber.
Therefore, I secretly inform you,
hoping you will relay this."
Jǐngwén (景文) repeatedly declined the internal appointments.
The emperor sent him a handwritten edict, admonishing him thus:
"As Minister of the Left and Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs,
you have already held this office.
As Grand Mentor of the Eastern Palace,
although the choice of personnel is excellent,
this official rank can only be compared to that of Minister of the Central Secretariat.
Commoners have served as Governor of Yángzhōu (揚州).
Xú Gānmù (徐干木), Wáng Xiūyuán (王休元), and Yīn Tiě (殷鐵) all accepted it without demur.
Your pure conduct, talent, and reputation,
how are they inferior to Xiūyuán (休元)?
Your assistance and support in the restoration,
how does it fall short of Gānmù (干木)?
Your close relationship and mutual efforts,
how are they behind Yīn Tiě (殷鐵)?
The Grand Marshal said that a Prime Minister should not hold a 'divine prefecture' (神州),
adhering to an ancient decree.
The ancestral base of Jīngkǒu (京口) is of great significance,
and close to the imperial domain,
and thus one cannot but appoint a General of Agile Cavalry there.
The important post of Shǎnxī (陝西)
has historically been given to imperial kinsmen.
Since the General of Agile Cavalry has departed,
Bālíng (巴陵) should logically reside there.
Although the central stream (middle Yangtze region) is said to be a relaxed area,
it controls and connects the three rivers,
and links with Jīng (荊) and Yǐng (郢),
being a vital thoroughfare,
historically a heavy strategic point.
Given this,
Yángzhōu (揚州) itself remains without a governor.
If you decline,
I truly do not know who should take the position.
This selection is thoroughly considered,
deliberated with the dukes and ministers,
not a casual matter."
He firmly declined the Grand Mentor and the concurrent appointment,
and was transferred to Minister of the Central Secretariat.
[一六] His Standing Attendant, Assistant Director, and Yángzhōu (揚州) positions remained as before.
He was then promoted to Grand Supervisor of the Central Secretariat,
concurrently overseeing Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
His Standing Attendant and Yángzhōu (揚州) positions remained as before.
Jǐngwén (景文) firmly declined the Grand Tutor.
The emperor sent the newly appointed Minister of the Right and Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs, Chǔ Yuān (褚淵), to convey the decree,
challenging him with six historical precedents,
and only then, with no other choice, did he accept the appointment.
At that time, the Crown Prince and all the imperial princes were young.
The emperor gradually began to make arrangements for his posthumous affairs.
Generals such as Wú Xǐ (吳喜) and Shòu Jìzhī (壽寂之) and their ilk,
fearing they would not serve the young ruler,
were all killed.
However, Jǐngwén (景文) was a powerful and honored maternal relative,
and Zhāng Yǒng (張永) had repeatedly served in military campaigns.
The emperor also suspected that they might not be trustworthy in the future,
so he personally created a rumor, saying:
"A scholar must not be befriended,
a 'bow-long' will shoot people dead."
"A scholar" (一士)
forms the character Wáng (王, Jǐngwén's surname);
"bow-long" (弓長)
forms the character Zhāng (張, Zhāng Yǒng's surname).
Jǐngwén (景文) became even more afraid,
so he personally submitted a plea to be relieved of his Yángzhōu (揚州) position,
saying: "Your humble servant is common, inferior,
utterly without talent.
I have uniquely met with imperial favor,
frequently obtaining extraordinary appointments.
Being entrusted with a position beyond my capabilities,
I ought to stumble and fall.
Although I exert myself with utmost reverence and caution,
it brings
no benefit to these undeserved promotions.
Day and night I toil with anxiety,
finding no place to settle.
In the sixth month,
I received a petition from my niece, Lady Cài (蔡), wife of Yīn (殷),
wishing for her son to report and request an official salary,
and asking me to sign it,
saying that all external petitions
first pass through my signature.
At that time, I was shocked and frightened,
and immediately wished to seal and present the petition.
But I then reconsidered that this family is obscure and isolated,
probably not
a source of widespread slander.
Moreover, I wished to listen and observe more broadly,
hoping there would be no more such news.
Recently, I suddenly received a notice from Jiě Jìxùn (解季遜), the Chief Clerk of the Western Office for receiving and sending documents in Yǎnzhōu (兗州), stating he was my subordinate.
Since I did not know
this person,
I immediately asked Xī Yǒng (郗顒),
and only then realized it was a false claim.
On the evening of the seventeenth,
[一七] I received an oral message from Xiè Yǎn (謝儼), a Military Adviser to the General Guarding the South,
saying that my servant had abducted
his maid.
I sent Lǐ Wǔzhī (李武之) to ask Yǎn (儼) for the reason,
and he replied,
'My servant made a mistake.'
Whether it was a mistake or true,
although I do not know,
on the day I heard this,
I was only filled with
worry and fright.
What I know,
there have already been these three incidents.
What I am unaware of,
is even more unfathomable.
If I were merely to hold a title and associate with common folk,
how could I invite such troubles?
It is truly due to my dullness and clumsiness,
cannot be prevented.
Since I furtively took up the provincial appointment,
seven months have already swiftly passed.
Without virtue, yet enjoying emoluments,
disaster will soon befall me.
Moreover, the position of Grand Tutor (Tàifù) is pure and eminent,
one who performs rites with the Crown Prince (Chǔjí) with deference.
For a
common person like myself,
how can I remain at ease for even a moment?
Grateful for the imperial favor, yet fearing punishment,
I dare not stubbornly insist.
My soul is troubled, my spirit disheartened,
and I am so anxious and pressured that I lose my composure.
Furthermore, my appearance is丑陋 (chǒulòu), surpassing all others,
my illness renders me utterly incapable of
effecting anything.
I defile the court and stain its ranks;
looking around, I have no equal
in my peculiar solitude,
ashamed and fearful, I find it difficult to maintain myself.
I humbly pray that you would slightly turn your compassion,
and complete my life’s plan.
The stipend of a Grand Master (Dàfū)
is sufficient for my needs.
I have long harbored admiration for it,
but dared not make an appeal.
I look up to your benevolent understanding,
to recognize my sincere intention.
The Emperor's edict replied: "In the middle of the fifth month,
your illness only began to improve,
and you were not yet fit for labor.
I had you and others examine the selection documents,
and once signed,
requested an edict to implement them.
This was not a secret matter,
and it was
impossible for outsiders to hear nothing at all.
However, rumors are prone to distortion,
which has always been a common problem.
Yīn's wife (Yīn Qī),
a mere woman,
within the confines of her chambers,
hears rumors that are further distorted by one or two degrees
of inaccuracy.
Moreover, she said that you are a relative,
and hoped you would sign,
not necessarily meaning that the selection matter concerned you alone.
Although her account was based on a distorted rumor,
it is largely not something to be alarmed
or surprised by.
Furthermore, recommending Yuán (Yuán) and presenting Kǎi (Kǎi)
were all based on collective consultations.
Can this be said to be Dú Táng Yáo (Táng Yáo) being unenlightened,
allowing others to interfere with his governance?
Those high-ranking officials who are prone to deceit, and those in charge,
it is just that
you happen not to know them.
Most of them are their associates and protégés,
who make their requests on their behalf.
The high-ranking officials and those in charge
will never know about it.
It is not only limited to the capital
city,
but even in provinces, commanderies, and counties,
there are some who forge documents and letters,
with clear written traces.
All the Imperial Attendants (Shèrén), Right Vice-Presidents (Yòuchéng),
and close servants,
fear
that someone might use their names
to carry forbidden goods,
request a halt to inspections,
forcefully sell trivial items to the government,
and then demand payment.
Or they might commission someone to seek provincial or commandery gifts and courtesies,
hoping to be exempted from summons
or to have boats and carriages dispatched for them.
All such requests should be reported to the relevant authorities,
and if found, recorded.
But you are a nobleman,
so it is impossible for such requests to involve you.
Such things have always existed,
so why
are you uniquely alarmed?
When a person holds a high and important position,
〔一八〕one only needs to examine one's own conscience.
In the era of Dàmíng (Dàmíng),
Cháo (Cháo), Xú (Xú), and the two Dài (Dài) —
their positions were no more than执戟 (zhí jǐ) (bearers of halberds),
yet their power rivaled that of the sovereign.
Yán Shī Bó (Yán Shī Bó), a commoner, served as 僕射 (Púyè),
and walked freely among the Imperial Secretaries (Shàngshū).
When Yuán Càn (Yuán Càn) was made Púyè (Púyè) and put in charge of selections,
people often did not know of Càn (Càn).
When Càn (Càn) was promoted to be a 令 (lìng),
he held
the position without hesitation.
Now that the record office is established,
he immediately assumes the former record-keeping position,
and establishes the provincial affairs office and the 干童 (gāntóng) (clerks),
all according to the recording regulations.
Since Càn (Càn) became lìng (lìng),
it is no different from being
Púyè (Púyè).
People's feelings towards Càn (Càn)
are indifferent, and they remain unchanged.
Given this, when occupying a high and important position,
should there be any reason to be anxious and fearful?
Although you are now the
Governor of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu),
the position of Grand Tutor (Tàizǐ Fù) for the Crown Prince, though noble,
does not involve court politics.
You can be at ease and fearless,
which is better than Càn (Càn).
I imagine you will receive this honor with an open mind,
and not be burdened by it.
The noble and high have the fear of peril,
the humble and lowly have the worry of a ditch.
Zhāng (Zhāng) and Shàn (Shàn) suffered dual calamities,
the wood and the wild goose both lost.
Those who intend to avoid misfortune
are not as good as those who have no intention
but let things take their course.
A tree of a thousand ren (rèn) high
is cut down by axes;
a blade of grass an inch long
withers from being trampled.
The tall trunks on high cliffs
〔一九〕and the shallow branches
in deep valleys,
the key to their survival or destruction,
〔一０〕is ultimately the same, whether big or small.
Jìn (Jìn) minister Bì Wàn (Bì Wàn) won all seven battles he fought,
〔二一〕but died under his window.
Shǔ (Shǔ) prime minister Fèi Yī (Fèi Yī) was calmly
sitting and talking
when he was killed by an assassin.
Therefore, those who willingly face danger
do not necessarily meet with disaster;
those who indulge in security
do not necessarily enjoy complete blessings.
However, the noble value themselves,
and thus
always worry about their safety;
the humble devalue themselves,
and thus easily forget their own existence.
Yet, those who teach
always warn the noble, not the humble,
meaning that the noble, when full of pride, tend to be overconfident.
Whenever
one holds a high and honorable position,
people keep it in mind.
When successful, people change their expressions;
otherwise, passersby exclaim in astonishment.
As for the humble,
their success or failure is not enough to move people,
their existence
or demise is not enough to affect fate.
Those who die in ditches,
those who die on roads,
between heaven and earth,
how many are there?
People simply do not pay attention to them.
From this, we can infer,
why must a noble position be difficult to hold,
and why must a humble position be easy to be at peace with?
However, in life, one should naturally take humility and caution as the way,
and in one's conduct and intentions,
one must strive for prudence
and care.
As for the great cycles of fortune and misfortune,
one should simply entrust them to the principles of destiny.
Encounters and disparities,
all are determined by fate.
Since one is not a sage,
one cannot foresee fortune
or misfortune.
One simply acts according to principles,
doing what is right to do.
Those who attain good fortune have a fortunate destiny;
those who encounter misfortune have an unfortunate destiny.
To discuss with
recent events,
during the Jǐnghé (Jǐnghé) era,
Jìn Píng Shùrén (Jìn Píng Shùrén) returned from Shòuyáng (Shòuyáng) to the chaotic court.
Everyone trembled for him,
yet he encountered a period of restoration.
Yuán Yǐ (Yuán Yǐ) sought to avoid
disaster in Xiāngyáng (Xiāngyáng),
and everyone at the time envied him,
likening it to soaring to the clouds and riding a phoenix.
Yet, he perished with Yì Jiā (Yì Jiā).
Luò Zǎi (Luò Zǎi) saw the young emperor,
and said to people:
"The King of Yuè (Yuè) has grown
a bird's neck and a hawk's beak,
one can share worries with them,
but one cannot share joys with them.
Fàn Lí (Fàn Lí) left and preserved his entire life,
while Wén Zhǒng (Wén Zhǒng) remained and met with disaster.
Now, the Emperor has a long neck and a hawk's beak,
quite like the King of Yuè (Yuè)
in appearance.
I have been in the Imperial Secretariat for a long time;
if I do not leave, I will surely be in danger."
Thereupon he requested a small county in Nánjiāng (Nánjiāng).
All the capital officials who had stayed in the capital
all encountered the good fortune
of the restoration,
and everyone received promotions in rank;
whereas Zǎi Zhí Yìjiā (Zǎi Zhí Yìjiā) was accused of crimes,
bound in chains,
and his life was almost extinguished.
What you have heard and seen with your own ears and eyes,
safety and danger depend on fate,
how can
it be planned in advance?
At that time, the Emperor was already ill,
and all his younger brothers had already been killed.
Only Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn (Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn), whose talent was inherently inferior,
was not suspected,
and was appointed governor (cìshǐ) of Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu).
He worried that once the Emperor passed away,
the Empress would preside over the court,
then Jǐngwén (Jǐngwén) would naturally become prime minister,
his clan would become powerful,
and relying on the influence of his maternal uncle,
he would not be a loyal minister in his later years.
In the spring of the first year of Tàiyù (Tàiyù) (465 CE),
the Emperor's illness became critical,
so he sent an envoy to deliver medicine, ordering Jǐngwén (Jǐngwén) to die.
His handwritten edict said:
"I have associated with you,
wishing to preserve your family,
hence this arrangement."
He died at the age of sixty.
He was posthumously granted the titles of General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Jiāngjūn), Minister of the Left and Right (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī),
and his previous posts as Palace Attendant (Chángshì), Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān), and governor (cìshǐ) remained.
His posthumous title was Yìhóu (Yìhóu).
His eldest son Xuàn (Xuàn) had the courtesy name Chángsù (Chángsù).
At the age of seven,
he read the Analects up to
"Zhōu (Zhōu) supervised the two dynasties,"
and his maternal grandfather Hé Shàngzhī (Hé Shàngzhī) teased him, saying:
"Oh, so eloquent!"
Xuàn (Xuàn) immediately replied:
"When the grass is windy, it must bend."
〔二二〕From a young age, he was known for his intelligence and perceptiveness.
When he grew up,
he was devoted to learning.
He rose to the position of Secretary of the Imperial Library (Mìshūchéng).
At the age of twenty-four,
he died before Jǐngwén (Jǐngwén).
His posthumous title was Gōngshìzǐ (Gōngshìzǐ).
His son Nuò (Nuò) inherited his title.
When Qí (Qí) received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
Jǐngwén's (Jǐngwén) nephew Yùn (Yùn) had the courtesy name Yànshēn (Yànshēn).
His father Kǎi (Kǎi) was
a Grand Master of the Palace (Tàizhōng Dàfū),
but his talent was mediocre.
Therefore, Yùn (Yùn) was not treated with respect by his relatives,
and he always felt shame and indignation.
His family was poor, so he became the magistrate of Guǎngdé (Guǎngdé).
At that time, Tàizōng (Tàizōng) had just ascended the throne,
and rebels rose up everywhere.
Yùn (Yùn) was thus inspired to become a general.
He was appointed acting General of Níngshuò (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn) and
Staff Officer (Sītú Cānjūn) to Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén (Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén),
while retaining his magistracy.
Jǐngwén (Jǐngwén) was very displeased,
and said to him:
"Ā Yì (Ā Yì),
you will surely bring ruin upon my family."
Ā Yì (Ā Yì)
was Yùn's (Yùn) childhood name.
〔二三〕When the affairs were settled,
he was enfeoffed as Baron of Jíyáng (Jíyáng Xiànnán),
with an income of three hundred households.
He served as Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū), Minister of the Yellow Gate (Huángmén Láng),
and Grand Administrator of Jìnlíng (Jìnlíng) and Yìxīng (Yìxīng).
In all the places he governed, he was greedy and unrestrained.
In Yìxīng (Yìxīng), he should have been arrested and punished,
but due to the Empress Dowager's
intervention, he was only dismissed from office.
In the early Yuánhuī (Yuánhuī) reign of the Deposed Emperor,
he again became Minister of the Yellow Gate (Huángmén Láng) and
Grand Administrator of Dōngyáng (Dōngyáng).
Before he arrived at the commandery,
Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn (Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn) besieged the capital.
Yùn (Yùn) led troops and was defeated and wounded at Zhūquè Mén (Zhūquè Mén).
When the affair was settled,
he was appointed Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and
then General of Níngshuò (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn) and governor (cìshǐ) of Xiāngzhōu (Xiāngzhōu).
Yùn (Yùn) was frivolous and
had little regard for his conduct.
At that time, Shěn Yōuzhī (Shěn Yōuzhī) was governor (cìshǐ) of Jīngzhōu (Jīngzhōu)
and secretly harbored rebellious intentions.
Yùn (Yùn) formed a close bond with him.
When the King of Qí (Qí Wáng) assisted in governing,
Yùn (Yùn) and Yōuzhī (Yōuzhī) immediately conspired to rebel.
It so happened that Yùn (Yùn) suffered the loss of his mother,
returned to the capital,
and stayed in Bālíng (Bālíng) for more than ten days,
further finalizing the plan with Yōuzhī (Yōuzhī).
At that time, the Heir Apparent of the King of Qí (Qí Wáng) was acting in Yǐngzhōu (Yǐngzhōu).
When Yùn (Yùn) arrived in Yǐngzhōu (Yǐngzhōu),
he thought the Heir Apparent would surely come down to comfort him,
hoping to use this opportunity to stage a coup,
occupy Xiàkǒu (Xiàkǒu),
and form an alliance with Jīngzhōu (Jīngzhōu).
The Heir Apparent perceived his intention,
claimed illness and did not go,
and also strictly guarded himself with troops.
Yùn's (Yùn) plan could not be carried out,
so he descended.
When Yōuzhī (Yōuzhī) rebelled,
Yùn (Yùn) secretly conspired with Minister of Education Yuán Càn (Yuán Càn) and others.
The matter is detailed in Càn's (Càn) biography.
When the plot failed,
he fled to the arena,
was pursued and captured,
and beheaded in the market of Mòlíng (Mòlíng).
Jǐngwén's (Jǐngwén) younger brother Fú (Fú) was,
at the end of Dàmíng (Dàmíng),
magistrate of Hǎiyán (Hǎiyán).
In the early Tàishǐ (Tàishǐ) period,
the whole country rebelled,
but Fú (Fú) alone did not join the rebellion.
He rose to the post of Staff Officer to the Minister of Education (Sītú Jìshì Cānjūn).
The historian says: Wáng Jǐngwén (Wáng Jǐngwén) established his reputation in his youth,
his fame and fragrance were widespread,
and his rise to honor and wealth
was not due to power.
If, in the Tàishǐ (Tàishǐ) court,
he had not been a maternal relative,
and had been on equal footing with Yuán Càn (Yuán Càn) and other nobles,
the disaster of downfall
might have been avoided.
Is Yǔ Yuánguī's (Yǔ Yuánguī) resignation from the Directorship of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng)
for this reason?
Collational Notes
Biographies, Chapter 46: Yīn Xiàozǔ (Yīn Xiàozǔ), Liú Miǎn (Liú Miǎn)
Yīn Xiàozǔ (Yīn Xiàozǔ) was
a native of Chénjùn Chángpíng (Chénjùn Chángpíng).
His great-grandfather Xiàn (Xiàn) was
Grand Master of Ceremonies (Guānglùxūn) in the Jìn (Jìn) dynasty.
His father and grandfather did not achieve prominence.
Xiàozǔ (Xiàozǔ) was unrestrained in his youth,
addicted to wine and women,
but had a spirit of capability.
At the end of Tàizǔ's (Tàizǔ) Yuánjiā (Yuánjiā) reign,
he served as Attendant to the Court (Fèngcháoqǐng) and
Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant (Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng).
Shìzǔ (Shìzǔ), seeing his military prowess,
appointed him General Fènwǔ (Fènwǔ Jiāngjūn) and Grand Administrator of Jìběi (Jìběi).
He then entered the court as General of Accumulated Archers (Jīshè Jiāngjūn).
In the early Dàmíng (Dàmíng) period,
the Suǒ (Suǒ) barbarians invaded Qīngzhōu (Qīngzhōu).
The Emperor sent Xiàozǔ (Xiàozǔ) north for reinforcement,
under the command of governor (cìshǐ) Yán Shībó (Yán Shībó).
He repeatedly fought against the barbarians,
and frequently inflicted great defeats upon them.
The details are in Shībó's (Shībó) biography.
Upon his return, he was appointed Commandant of the Heir Apparent's Tiger Guards (Tàizǐ Lǚbēn Zhōnglángjiàng)
and additionally General Lóngxiáng (Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn).
When Jìnglíng Wáng Dàn (Jìnglíng Wáng Dàn) rebelled, occupying Guǎnglíng (Guǎnglíng),
Xiàozǔ (Xiàozǔ) was subordinate to Shěn Qìngzhī (Shěn Qìngzhī) in attacking Dàn (Dàn),
and again distinguished himself in battle.
He was promoted to Supervisor of the Army (Fǔjūn) for Xīyáng Wáng Zǐshàng (Xīyáng Wáng Zǐshàng), General Níngshuò (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn), and Grand Administrator of Nán Jìyīn (Nán Jìyīn).
He was appointed Grand Administrator of Xūyí (Xūyí),
retaining his generalship.
Upon his return, he became Commandant of the Tiger Guards (Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng),
and was concurrently appointed General Níngshuò (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn) and Grand Administrator of the two commanderies of Yángpíng (Yángpíng) and Dōngpíng (Dōngpíng).
He was further promoted to Jìnán (Jìnán) and Nánjùn (Nánjùn),
retaining his generalship.
In the first year of Jinghé (景和) of the Former Deposed Emperor,
he was appointed Dū Yǎnzhōu Zhū Jūnshì (督兗州諸軍事) and Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ (兗州刺史) with his original title.
When Tàizōng (太宗) first ascended the throne,
the four directions rebelled.
Xiàozǔ's (孝祖) nephew, Sītú Cānjūn (司徒參軍) Gě Sēngsháo (葛僧韶) of Yǐngchuān (潁川), suggested being dispatched with a mission to summon Xiàozǔ (孝祖) to court.
The emperor sent him.
At that time, Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (徐州刺史) Xuē Āndū (薛安都) sent Xuē Suǒ'ér (薛索兒) and others to garrison Jīnjìng (津逕).
Sēngsháo (僧韶) managed to reach him by a circuitous route.
He persuaded Xiàozǔ (孝祖) saying:
"Jǐnghé (景和) is ferocious and insane,
unprecedented since creation.
The court and the country are in extreme peril,
their lives hanging by a thread.
The present emperor possesses outstanding divine virtue,
with divine might in his person.
In less than a day,
he has eliminated the wicked and cut down the tyrannical.
To recreate heaven and earth
would not be an exaggeration.
The state is in chaos, the court is in danger;
it is proper to establish a worthy ruler.
The high officials and myriad officers
have no dissenting opinions.
The prosperity of great peace
is but a matter of morning or evening.
However, the petty men incite each other,
creating endless trouble.
Greedy for the weak and young,
they all harbor hopes.
If the Way of Heaven assists the rebels,
and the multitude of villains succeed,
then with a young ruler and difficult times,
authority will be divided.
Military troubles will arise mutually,
how can there be a place for oneself to be safe?
My maternal uncle had ambitions of achieving merit when young,
and achieved fame through integrity in adulthood.
If you can now control the righteous volunteers of Jì (濟) and Hé (河),
and return to serve the imperial court,
not only will you assist the ruler and calm the chaos,
but you can also leave your name in the annals of history."
Xiàozǔ (孝祖) asked in detail about the news from the court.
Sēngsháo (僧韶) responded with suitable analogies,
and also explained that the army was strong and elite,
and the emperor wished to entrust him with the duty of vanguard.
On that very day, Xiàozǔ (孝祖) abandoned his wife and children,
and led two thousand civil and military men to return to the capital with Sēngsháo (僧韶).
At that time, the entire realm was in rebellion,
and the imperial court only held Dānyáng (丹陽) Commandery.
Then, Yǒngshì (永世) County also rebelled soon after.
The bandits from Yìxīng (義興) were approaching Yánlíng (延陵).
Internal and external worries and dangers prevailed,
and everyone wanted to flee.
When Xiàozǔ (孝祖) suddenly arrived,
the strength of the multitude was not small,
and they were all valiant men from the Cāng (傖) and Chǔ (楚) regions.
People's morale thereupon greatly stabilized.
Xiàozǔ (孝祖) was promoted to the title of Guānjūn (冠軍),
and granted Jiǎjié (假節) and Dū Qiánfēng Zhū Jūnshì (督前鋒諸軍事).
He was sent towards Hǔkǎn (虎檻)
to resist the southern rebels.
The imperial guard previously had Zhūgě Liàng's (諸葛亮) tube-sleeved armor and helmet,
which a twenty-five-stone crossbow could not penetrate when shot.
The emperor bestowed all of them upon Xiàozǔ (孝祖).
Xiàozǔ (孝祖), relying on his sincerity and integrity,
disregarded other generals.
If there were fathers, sons, or brothers in the imperial army who were in the south,
Xiàozǔ (孝祖) wished to investigate and punish them all.
Because of this, people's feelings became estranged,
and no one was happy to serve him.
He was promoted to Shǐ Chíjié (使持節), Dūdū Yǎnzhōu Qīng Jì Yōu Sìzhōu Zhū Jūnshì (都督兗州青冀幽四州諸軍事), and Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn (撫軍將軍),
with his position as Cìshǐ (刺史) remaining as before.
At that time, the rebels occupied Zhéqí (赭圻).
Xiàozǔ (孝祖) was about to advance and attack them.
He bid farewell to Dàtǒng (大統) Wáng Xuánmó (王玄謨),
overcome with uncontrollable grief.
Everyone was astonished.
On the third day of the third month of the second year of Tàishǐ (泰始),
he engaged the rebels in battle.
He always had a drum and canopy accompany him.
People in the army said to each other:
"Commander Yīn (殷) can truly be called a general who seeks death!
Now he is engaging the rebels,
yet he uses feathered ornaments to conspicuously mark himself.
If ten skilled archers concentrate their shots,
how can he not be killed,
is that possible?"
On that day,
he was struck by an arrow in battle and died,
at the age of fifty-two.
He was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) and Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn (征北將軍),
with Chíjié (持節) and Dūdū (都督) remaining as before.
He was enfeoffed as Zǐguī Xiàn Hóu (秭歸縣侯),
with a stipend of one thousand households.
In the fourth year,
he was posthumously re-enfeoffed as Jiàn'ān Xiàn (建安縣),
and given the posthumous title Zhōng Hóu (忠侯).
All of Xiàozǔ's (孝祖) sons were killed by Xuē Āndū (薛安都).
His cousin's son, Huìdá (慧達), succeeded him in the enfeoffment.
When Qí (齊) received the abdication,
the peerage was abolished.
Liú Miǎn (劉勔), courtesy name Bóyóu (伯猷),
was a native of Péngchéng (彭城).
His grandfather, Huáiyì (懷義), was the Shǐxīng Tàishǒu (始興太守).
His father, Yǐngzhī (穎之), was the Tàishǒu (太守) of both Rǔnán (汝南) and Xīncài (新蔡) Commanderies.
He died of illness
while campaigning against Línyì (林邑).
Miǎn (勔) had aspirations and integrity from a young age,
and also enjoyed literature.
His family was poor,
so he served as the Zēngchéng Lìng (增城令) of Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
Liú Dàoxī (劉道錫), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Guǎngzhōu (廣州), appointed him as Zhǔbù (主簿) of the Yángliè Fǔ (揚烈府).
In the twenty-seventh year of Yuánjiā (元嘉),
the Suǒlǔ (索虜) invaded the south.
Dàoxī (道錫) sent Miǎn (勔) as an envoy to the capital.
Tàizǔ (太祖) granted him an audience.
His responses were satisfactory to the emperor,
and he was appointed Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (寧遠將軍) and Suīyuǎn Tàishǒu (綏遠太守).
At the end of Yuánjiā (元嘉),
Xiāo Jiǎn (蕭簡) rebelled,
occupying Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
Miǎn (勔) raised a righteous army to suppress him
and burned its south gate.
Zōng Mòxīn (宗[⿱⿰売⽎心]), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Guǎngzhōu (廣州), again appointed him as Jūnfǔ Zhǔbù (軍府主簿).
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as Dàtíng Hóu (大亭侯).
He was appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng (員外散騎侍郎).
At the beginning of Xiàojiàn (孝建),
Jīng (荊) and Jiāng (江) rebelled.
Zōng Mòxīn (宗[⿱⿰売⽎心]) appointed Miǎn (勔) to serve as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) and Xiāngdōng Nèishǐ (湘東內史),
leading troops out to Ānlù (安陸).
The matter was settled,
and he was appointed Jìnkāng Tàishǒu (晉康太守) with his original title,
and then transferred to Yùlín Tàishǒu (鬱林太守).
At the beginning of Dàmíng (大明), he returned to the capital.
