Liú Dàolóng (劉道隆), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Xúzhōu (徐州), requested him to be Níngshuò Sīmǎ (寧朔司馬).
When Jìnglíng Wáng (竟陵王) Dàn (誕) rebelled by occupying Guǎnglíng (廣陵),
Miǎn (勔) followed Dàolóng (道隆) and received orders from Shěn Qìngzhī (沈慶之).
After the matter was settled,
he was enfeoffed as a fifth-rank Hóu (侯) of Jīnchéng Xiàn (金城縣).
He was appointed Xīyáng Wáng (西陽王) Zǐshàng (子尚)'s Fǔjūn Cānjūn (撫軍參軍),
and entered to serve as a guard.
Previously,
Fèi Shěn (費沈) had been sent to attack Chén Tán (陳檀),
but failed.
Then Miǎn (勔) was appointed Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍), Xījiāng Dūhù (西江督護), and Yùlín Tàishǒu (鬱林太ǒu).
Upon Miǎn's (勔) arrival,
he led his army to advance and attack,
pacifying the region as appropriate.
He obtained many fine horses
and also presented a "coral tree with intertwined branches."
The emperor was very pleased.
Upon his return, he was appointed Xīn'ān Wáng (新安王) Zǐluán (子鸞)'s Fǔjūn Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (撫軍中兵參軍).
He was in mourning for his mother
and did not take the post.
When the Former Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
he was appointed Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn (振威將軍) and Túnqí Xiàowèi (屯騎校尉),
and entered to serve as a guard.
When Tàizōng 太宗 ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Níngshuò Jiāngjūn 寧朔將軍,
with his post of jiàowèi 校尉 remaining as before.
When Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ 江州刺史 Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn 晉安王子勛 rebelled,
with responses from all directions,
Miǎn 勔 was appointed by his original office to lead Jiànpíng Wáng Jǐngsù 建設王景素 as Fǔguó Sīmǎ 輔國司馬,
and advanced to occupy Liángshān 梁山.
At that time, Yùzhōu Cìshǐ 豫州刺史 Yīn Yǎn 殷琰 rebelled,
so Miǎn 勔 was summoned back to the capital.
He was provisionally appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍,
and led his troops to suppress Yǎn 琰.
Thirty armed guards entered the Six Gates.
He was again concurrently appointed Shānyáng Wáng Xiūyòu 山陽王休祐 Pìqí Sīmǎ 驃騎司馬,
with other duties remaining as before.
He defeated Yǎn's 琰 general Liú Shùn 劉順 at Wǎntáng 宛唐,
and Dù Shúbǎo 杜叔寶 at Héngtáng 橫塘.
The details are in Yǎn's 琰 biography.
He was appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍, Shānyáng Wáng Xiūyòu 山陽王休祐 Pìqí Zīyì Cānjūn 驃騎諮議參軍, Liángjùn Tàishǒu 梁郡太守, and Jíajié 假節,
but he did not accept the appointments.
Yǎn 琰 entrenched himself firmly within the city.
From early spring to late winter,
Xuē Dàobiāo 薛道標 and Páng Mèngqiú 龐孟虯 both advanced towards Shòuyáng 壽陽.
Miǎn 勔 engaged in both internal attack and external defense,
and was victorious in every battle.
He was skilled at pacifying his generals and commanders,
and his magnanimity and generosity made him a source of reliance for the troops.
General Wáng Guǎngzhī 王廣之 asked for Miǎn's 勔 personal riding horse.
All the generals and commanders were enraged by Guǎngzhī's 廣之 presumption,
and advised Miǎn 勔 to deal with him according to the law.
Miǎn 勔 laughed cheerfully,
and immediately untied the horse and gave it to Guǎngzhī 廣之.
He was again appointed Shǐchíjié 使持節, Dūdū Guǎng Jiāo Èrzhōu Zhū Jūnfùsī 督廣交二州諸軍事, Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiāng 平越中郎將, and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ 廣州刺史.
His generalship remained as before,
but he did not accept the appointments.
When Yǎn 琰 opened the city gates and surrendered,
Miǎn 勔 ordered his entire army
not to act rashly.
The soldiers and civilians within the city
lost not even a single hair.
The common people were moved and delighted,
and all declared it a time of "renewal for the living" (láisū 來蘇).
The common people erected a stele in his honor during his lifetime.
He was reassigned as Dūdū Yì Níng Èrzhōu Zhū Jūnfùsī 督益寧二州諸軍事 and Yìzhōu Cìshǐ 益州刺史.
His titles of Chíjié 持節 and Jiāngjūn 將軍 remained as before.
Again, he did not accept the appointments.
Returning to the capital,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ 太子左衛率,
and enfeoffed as Póyáng Xiànhóu 鄱陽縣侯,
with an income of a thousand households.
Yǎn 琰 had initially sought aid from the barbarians (suǒlǔ 索虜),
and a large barbarian army was garrisoned at Rǔnán 汝南.
In the third year of Tàishǐ 泰始 (467 CE),
Miǎn 勔 was appointed Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn 征虜將軍 and Dūdū Xīzhǎo Qiánfēng Zhū Jūnfùsī 督西討前鋒諸軍事.
His titles of Jiǎjié 假節 and Zhìzuǒ 置佐, and his original office, remained as before.
Previously,
Cháng Zhēnqí 常珍奇 had occupied Rǔnán 汝南
and rebelled with Yǎn 琰.
When Yǎn 琰 surrendered,
Cháng Zhēnqí 常珍qi then occupied the outpost and surrendered to the barbarians.
The details are in Yǎn's 琰 biography.
At this time, he led the barbarian Xīhé Gōng 西河公 and Chángshè Gōng 長社公 to attack and besiege Fǔguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍 and Rǔyīn Tàishǒu 汝陰太守 Zhāng Jǐngyuǎn 張景遠.
Jǐngyuǎn 景遠 and his army commander Yáng Wéncháng 楊文萇 resisted and counterattacked,
greatly defeating them.
Jǐngyuǎn 景遠 soon fell ill and died.
Tàizōng 太宗 praised his achievements,
posthumously appointing him Guānjūn Jiāngjūn 冠軍將軍 and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ 豫州刺史,
and posthumously enfeoffing him as Hánhuāng Xiànnán 含洭縣男,
with an income of three hundred households.
Wéncháng 文萇 was appointed Rǔyīn Tàishǒu 汝陰太守 in his place.
Miǎn 勔 was appointed Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn 右衛將軍,
and also appointed Shǐchíjié 使持節, Dūdū Yù Sī Èrzhōu Zhū Jūnfùsī 督豫司二州諸軍事, Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn 征虜將軍, and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ 豫州刺史.
Other duties remained as before.
In the fourth year (468 CE),
he was appointed Shìzhōng 侍中,
and concurrently led Shèshēng Jiàowèi 射聲校尉,
but again he did not accept.
He was promoted to the title of Yòujiāngjūn 右將軍.
In that same year,
the barbarians sent Rǔyáng Sīmǎ 汝陽司馬 Zhào Huáirén 趙懷仁 with five hundred cavalry and infantry
to raid Wǔjīn Xiàn 武津縣.
Miǎn 勔 dispatched Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn 龍驤將軍 Qū Yuándé 曲元德 with light troops to attack them,
and the barbarian forces scattered in alarm.
The barbarian Zǐdū Gōng 子都公 Ànyú Bá 閼于拔 again led three hundred men to guard a transport convoy of over one thousand carts,
[一０]and established a camp on the water east of Rǔyáng Tái 汝陽臺.
Yuándé 元德 rode directly into the camp alone,
beheading Bá 拔.
He then advanced to attack Rǔyáng Tái 汝陽臺,
immediately breaching the outer rampart,
capturing one thousand three hundred carts
and beheading one hundred and fifty men.
Miǎn 勔 also sent Sītú Cānjūn 司徒參軍 Sūn Tán'guàn 孫曇瓘 to oversee the area west of Yìyáng 弋陽.
[一一]When the barbarians raided Yìyáng 義陽,
Tán'guàn 曇瓘 severely defeated them.
The barbarians transported their northern Yùzhōu 豫州 taxes,
totaling two thousand carts.
Miǎn 勔 gathered desolate people
and ambushed them at Xǔchāng 許昌.
The barbarian forces scattered,
burning their grain and rice.
Jiǎ Yuányǒu 賈元友, a man from Huáinán 淮南, submitted a memorial to Tàizōng 太宗,
advising a northern attack on Xuánhù 懸瓠,
which could recover the four commanderies of Chénjùn 陳郡, Nándùn 南頓, Rǔnán 汝南, and Xīncài 新蔡.
The Emperor showed Miǎn 勔 what he had submitted,
and ordered him to provide a detailed reply.
Miǎn 勔 replied: Yuányǒu 元友 states:
“The barbarian ruler is young and weak;
treacherous schemes are arising competitively.
Internally and externally, there is chaos and disorder.
Their demise is destined by Heaven.”
Your subject believes that the Xūnchǒu 獯醜 (barbarians) have encroached wantonly,
trampling
the king's territory.
[一二]They have entrenched themselves in provinces and commanderies,
and the common people are massacred and lost.
Last winter, the various armies neglected cultivation.
This spring, successive cities are surrounded and pressed.
The state's strategy to recover its territory
truly lacks
leisure,
and the extermination of the barbarians is not yet feasible.
Yuányǒu 元友 also says:
“There are over seven thousand households
with abundant grain and rice,
which can supply twenty thousand people for several years.”
Your subject also believes that
twenty thousand people consume four hundred and eighty thousand hú 斛 of rice annually.
For five years, a total of two million four hundred thousand hú 斛 of rice would be needed.
Logically, such an amount cannot exist,
and I fear the matter is difficult to state confidently.
Yuányǒu
元友 also says:
“The barbarians have established relay stations at Xuánhù 懸瓠.
The barbarians have already occupied it first.
If it is not reliable,
this is not necessary (missing text).”
Since both involve attacking cities,
one should first plan for Xuánhù
懸瓠.
Why bypass it to first take Yǎn 郾,
thereby suffering attacks from both front and rear?
Moreover, if over seven thousand households have abundant provisions,
yet the barbarians still have to transport provisions over long distances for food,
this means their authority does not control
the people,
and the people have no alternative plans.
Yuányǒu 元友 also says:
“The barbarians intend to transport provisions by water and land
to save their army.
The opportunity to attack them
is now.”
Your subject also believes that
having established relay roads
and holding strong cities,
judging by their situation,
they do not appear to be weak.
The opportunity to strike
may be difficult to verify.
Yuányǒu 元友 also says:
“The people of the four commanderies
have suffered the poison of the barbarians for twenty-seven years.
They all wish to avenge their grudges and shame,
awaiting the imperial might.”
Your subject also believes that Yuán Shìbǎo 垣式寶 and others received great imperial favor,
yet now they still
drive their chariots to the camps,
and have turned back to the bandits.
This is probably because their attachment to their homeland is deep,
not because it is appropriate to seek revenge.
How can this be lightly tested?
Yuányǒu 元友 also says:
“Please order Jīng 荊 and
Yōng 雍 two provinces
to dispatch two thousand elite soldiers,
descending north from Yìyáng 義陽 along the western mountains,
to directly occupy Yǎnchéng 郾城.”
Your subject also believes that Yǎnchéng 郾城 is a vital barbarian relay outpost,
and
it passes through savage territories and dangerous terrains.
Over several hundred lǐ 里,
carrying provisions and secretly advancing,
only when reaching the flat lands
would they attack the strong barbarian city.
Among famous generals throughout history,
none have been able to succeed with this strategy.
Even
if they were to achieve victory,
would they be sufficient to resist Xuánhù 懸瓠 to the south
and defend Chángshè 長社 to the north, or not?
Moreover, the barbarians occupy several cities,
with convenient water and land routes.
Now to have an official with two thousand
troops cut off their supplies,
is difficult to achieve.
Yuányǒu 元友 also says:
“The barbarians besieged Rǔyīn 汝陰,
wandering for two years,
but were repelled by Zhāng Jǐngyuǎn 張景遠,
and did not dare to cross the Huái 淮 River.”
Your subject further believes that Jǐngyuǎn's military strength is meager,
unable to secure itself.
Sending aid from afar,
he barely achieved a small victory.
Is it now certain that the bandits fear him?
Jǐngyuǎn
previously inflicted casualties
of only several hundred,
yet the four tens of thousands of barbarian cavalry and infantry
still dared not advance.
But now, he must be urging the state to send light troops on a distant expedition,
claiming victory is within reach.
The inconsistency in his words
and logic
could not be more egregious.
Yuányǒu further said:
"In Lóngshān and Zhìshuǐ,
Lǔnú, Wáng Jǐngzhí, and others have all received imperial titles,
with over ten thousand infantry and cavalry.
It is appropriate to advance and attack.
All that is needed is an imperial command."
Your subject believes that Lǔnú has been colluding with the barbarians
for many years.
Last year, he sent a sincere message to the imperial court,
vowing to perform meritorious deeds.
But as soon as he received the honorary
title,
he immediately fled.
He is clearly cunning and treacherous.
How can one easily trust him implicitly?
Moreover, Wáng Jǐngzhí is a refugee,
his troops number no more than a few tens of men.
He is not worth mentioning,
nor is he reliable.
His claim of over ten thousand men
seems far from the truth.
Yuányǒu also said:
"The four commanderies harbor resentment against these non-kindred folk,
their war camps are linked,
fields have been abandoned for two years,
livelihoods are exhausted,
the bandits have no resources,
and their provisions are depleted.
Cutting off their supply route
is the most crucial strategy."
Your subject further believes that cutting off supplies requires troops,
and troops need provisions.
In the two hundred *lǐ* around Xuánhù,
where could one possibly obtain
sufficient provisions for the troops?
Your subject humbly observes that since the Yuánjiā era,
many uncouth and distant individuals
have interfered with state affairs.
Carrying their burdens to the capital,
they all advocate attacking the barbarians.
Lǔ Shuǎng's extravagant talk
truly undermined the national
prestige,
needlessly wasted military strength,
and squandered precious wealth.
All such individuals
invariably offer short-sighted advice,
which, when trusted and adopted,
always leads to future regret.
The people on the border
only observe
strength and weakness.
When the royal army arrives at their borders,
they will certainly bring pots of refreshments to await them on the road.
But as soon as they see the army retreating,
they will rise up like swarms of bees to plunder and intercept.
Whenever the commanders turn their armies back,
have they not always been harmed by those along the riverbanks?
Tàizōng accepted his advice,
and Yuányǒu's proposal was consequently dropped.
Miǎn wrote a letter to Cháng Zhēnqí,
urging him to rebel against the barbarians.
Zhēnqí then, with his son Chāoyuè and the Yǔlín Supervisor Yuán Shìbǎo,
killed Fèibá and other sons of the barbarian *Dūgōng*, totaling over three thousand people, in Qiáo.
Miǎn galloped to report this,
and Tàizōng was greatly pleased.
He appointed Zhēnqí as Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of Sī and Běiyù Provinces, General Who Pacifies the North, and Governor of Sī Province,
Marquis of Rǔnán and Xīncài Counties,
〔一三〕 with an income fief of one thousand households.
Chāoyuè was made General Who Assists the State, Governor of Běiyù Province,
Grand Administrator of Yǐngchuān, Rǔyáng, and two other commanderies,
and Baron of Ānyáng County.
Shìbǎo was made General Who Assists the State, Grand Administrator of Chén and Nándùn Commanderies,
and Baron of Zhēnyáng County,
with an income fief of three hundred households.
Zhēnqí was attacked by the barbarians,
and led his troops south.
The barbarians pursued and defeated him.
Zhēnqí fled into the mountains
and reached Shòuyáng.
Chāoyuè and Shìbǎo were killed by others.
In the fifth year,
Yǔyīn Grand Administrator Yáng Wéncháng again repeatedly defeated the barbarians at Jīngtíng and Xùxī.
An imperial edict promoted Miǎn to General Who Pacifies the West and Governor of Yù Province.
His other titles remained as before,
but he did not accept the appointment.
In the same year,
he was summoned and appointed Palace Attendant, Central Leader of the Imperial Guards.
Miǎn, seeing the complexities of the world,
desired to content himself,
and requested the post of Dōngyáng Commander.
The Emperor showed Miǎn's memorial to all his ministers.
From the Left Minister Yuán Càn downwards,
none failed to praise him,
all deeming it appropriate to grant his request.
The Emperor said:
"The two princes, Bālíng and Jiànpíng,
both have the ambition to lead a secluded life.
If the world were peaceful,
their requests would all be granted."
Miǎn began to construct a dwelling south of Zhōnglíng,
intending it as his retreat.
He piled up stones and collected water,
creating a scene reminiscent of a mountain abode.
Many cultured officials
frequented it.
In the sixth year,
the title of Palace Attendant was changed to Court Gentleman.
In that year,
Prince Qí, Governor of Nányǎn Province, was dispatched to garrison Huáiyīn.
Miǎn was appointed Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of Nánxú, Yǎn, Qīng, Jì, and two other provinces, General Who Pacifies the North,
〔一四〕 with his titles of Court Gentleman and Central Leader of the Imperial Guards remaining as before,
and dispatched to garrison Guǎnglíng.
He firmly declined the titles of Court Gentleman and General,
which was granted,
and he was given the provisional title of General Who Pacifies the North.
In the seventh year,
he was relieved of his Area Commander, provisional general, and envoy duties.
As Tàizōng was about to die,
he entrusted Miǎn with the post of Right Minister of the Department of State Affairs.
〔一五〕 His title of Central Leader of the Imperial Guards remained as before,
and he was granted one set of drums and pipes.
When the deposed emperor ascended the throne, he added five hundred men to his command.
In the early Yuánhuī
period, the moon encroached upon Yòu Zhífǎ,
and Tàibái encroached upon Shàngjiàng.
Someone advised Liú Miǎn to resign his post.
Liú Miǎn said:
“I hold firm to my principles and conduct myself
without shame before heaven or earth.
If my talent is light and my responsibility heavy,
calamity will surely strike.
The ways of Heaven are subtle and profound;
how can avoidance grant escape?”
When Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn rebelled,
he suddenly reached the capital.
Liú Miǎn was granted the title of Shǐchíjié and Lǐngjūn,
with aides appointed,
to guard Shítou.
Soon after, the rebel forces encamped south of Zhūquè Háng.
Wáng Dàolóng, commander of the Right Army, led the palace guard towards Zhūquè Háng.
Upon hearing that the rebels had arrived,
he urgently summoned Liú Miǎn.
When Liú Miǎn arrived,
he ordered the pontoon bridge closed,
but Wáng Dàolóng did not listen.
He urged Liú Miǎn to cross the bridge and advance into battle.
Liú Miǎn, leading his subordinates, was defeated south of the bridge,
and died in battle
at the age of fifty-seven.
After the affair was settled,
an imperial edict stated:
“Indeed, righteousness is a constant of Heaven,
and loyalty is a human principle.
It leaves brilliant traces in historical records,
and its splendor is proclaimed in bronze and stone.
Unless one’s insight penetrates the spirit
and one’s reason is deeply moved,
how could one sacrifice one’s body to protect the sovereign,
Therefore, the former Shǐchíjié, Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn, Shǒu Shàngshū Yòu Púyè, Zhōng Lǐngjūn, Kāiguó Hóu of Póyáng Xiàn, Liú Miǎn,
was pure in thought and intention,
profound in conduct and learning.
He established great merits and achievements,
his reputation reaching across the nation.
His bonds of trust were deep,
whether in adversity or peace,
and we relied on his counsel
to assist the imperial way.
When the rebellious vassal incited calamity,
disturbing the capital region,
he grasped the drumstick and rallied the troops,
following the regulations in leading the army.
His body perished with the cause,
his name carried far by his integrity.
We are deeply saddened by this,
and our heart is shaken with grief.
In the past, Wáng Yǔn upheld integrity,
and Biàn Hú showed lofty virtue.
Their characters resembled those of ancient worthies,
and their virtuous conduct followed their predecessors.
His journey to the underworld is eternal,
and his wrongful death cannot be undone.
We wish to honor his glorious deeds
and illuminate the annals of history.
He is posthumously granted the titles of Sànqí Chángshì and Sīkōng.
His original official posts and marquisate remain unchanged.
His posthumous name is Zhōngzhāo Gōng.”
His son, Liú Quān, inherited his title.
At the end of Emperor Shùn’s Shēngmíng era,
he served as Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Qí received the abdication,
the marquisate was abolished.
Liú Miǎn’s younger brother, Liú Xué,
during the Tàishǐ era,
served as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ.
He fell ill and died on the way.
He previously held the title of Dūxiāng Hóu.
His posthumous name was Zhì Hóu.
The Historian said: When Wú Hàn pacified Shǔ,
blood flowed in the city so profusely that it covered the ankles,
yet he was little heard of afterwards in Hàn.
When Lù Kàng secured Xīlíng,
the Bù clan was afflicted to the point of infant deaths,
and Jī and Yún were executed in the capital.
When Liú Miǎn conquered Shòuchūn,
the common people had no complaints of neglected fodder or grain.
None failed to support the old and lead the young,
singing as they emerged from the heavy siege.
How admirable!
Collated Notes
Biography Forty-seven: Xiāo Huìkāi, Yīn Yǎn
Xiāo Huìkāi
was a native of Southern Lánlíng,
and the son of Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Xiāo Sīhuà.
His original name was Huìkāi,
later changed from Huì to Huì.
In his youth, he had a distinguished bearing and
delved into literature and history.
Although his family was noble,
he lived simply and unadorned.
Initially, he served as Mìshū Láng.
The imperial scribes were all young men from prominent families,
but Xiāo Huìkāi’s interests often differed from others,
and sometimes he would not speak to his colleagues for three years.
His maternal grandfather, Guānglù Dàfū from Pèijùn, Liú Chéng, warned him:
“You are the son of a family with connections;
you should adapt to the trends of the time
and foster harmony within and without.
If you continue as you are,
will you not suffer many minor setbacks
and incur widespread displeasure?”
Xiāo Huìkāi replied:
“It is indeed proper for people to live in harmony,
as your kind instruction suggests.
However, unfortunately, I am straightforward
and ashamed to be seen as an ordinary person.
My dragon painting is not yet complete,
hence I often cause offense.”
He was transferred to Tàizǐ Shèrén.
He was close friends with Zhōu Lǎng of Rǔnán,
and they admired each other for their eccentricity.
He was transferred to Shàngshū Shuǐbù Láng,
then Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn’s Zhēngběi Fǔ Zhǔbù,
then Nán Xúzhōu Zhìzhōng Cóngshì Shǐ,
then moved to Rǔyīn Wáng Yǒu,
and again served as Nán Xúzhōu Biéjià,
Zhōngshū Shìláng,
and Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng’s Dàjiāngjūn Dàsīmǎ Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn,
he was transferred from Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ to Huángmén Shìláng.
He argued with Shìzhōng Hé Yǎn regarding the matter of Jīshè Jiāngjūn Xú Chōng.
Hé Yǎn’s favor and standing were very high,
but Xiāo Huìkāi would not yield to him.
Hé Yǎn was enraged
and had his subordinates impeach him.
Xiāo Huìkāi then submitted a memorial to resign, saying:
“Your Majesty has not yet seen through my foolishness,
hence you have brought me into close service.
As my professional duties are not my strong suit,
I entrust my abilities to Hé Yǎn.
Regarding all matters of right and wrong,
I dare not offer opinions.
I humbly observed that Jīshè Jiāngjūn Xú Chōng was dismissed by Hé Yǎn’s order.
In my humble opinion, there was a case to be made for him,
so I ventured to express a slight dissent.
Hé Yǎn, relying on favor and power,
wished to ensure no one held a different view.
He then scolded and threatened the officials in charge,
personally settling the documents,
deleting my arguments,
and exclusively recording his own statements.
Although Heaven broadly oversees all,
my reasons have ultimately not been seen or understood.
To offend Your Majesty at close quarters
and cause such obstruction and injustice,
then my impeachment
is indeed not regrettable.
However, not complying with the Shìzhōng
is my fault.
Yet, in acting as was proper,
I know not what error I committed.
Moreover, disagreement in opinion
has not traditionally been subject to impeachment.
Examining my conscience and considering Heaven,
I fully know I am forgiven.
I cannot apologize for my faults in this high office,
or change my mind towards a powerful minister.
The punishment of piercing bones and melting metal
will come soon.
I beg to be relieved of my undeserved position
and retreat to my humble private garden.”
At that time, Hé Yǎn’s favor was at its peak.
Consequently, this went against the imperial will,
and a special edict was issued to the relevant authorities, citing frequent illness,
to dismiss Xiāo Huìkāi from office.
Xiāo Sīhuà was always respectful and cautious,
his conduct differing from Xiāo Huìkāi’s.
He often criticized and blamed him for his blunt eccentricity.
Upon seeing Xiāo Huìkāi’s resignation memorial,
he sighed and said:
“My son, unfortunately, associated with Zhōu Lǎng.
This outcome is to be expected.”
He then punished him with two hundred strokes of the cane.
Soon after, he was re-appointed as Zhōngshùzǐ.
When his father passed away,
he demonstrated filial piety during the mourning period.
His family had always revered the Buddha,
and so he built four monasteries for his father:
one on the south bank, at the foot of Nángāng,
named Chángāng Sì;
one at his old family residence in Qǔ'ē,
named Chánxiāng Sì;
one at the tomb pavilion in Jīngkǒu,
named Chántíng Sì;
and one in Fēngyáng Xiàn, the area he was enfeoffed with,
named Chánfēng Sì.
He said to his national colleagues:
"My enfeoffment stipend is rather meager,
and I have many brothers.
If one person were to receive the full amount,
it would be a matter of my yielding to him.
But if everyone were to divide it equally,
that would be regrettable and shameful.
Since these monasteries have been established,
they should naturally be fully provided for by the monastic community."
From then on, the national stipends were no longer equally distributed.
After the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ.
In the second year of Dàmíng,
he was sent out as Hǎilíng Wáng Xiūmào Běi Zhōngláng Chángshǐ, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, and Xiāngyáng Tàishǒu,
and acted in charge of the affairs of Yōngzhōu.
He was skilled in governance,
and his authority ensured prohibitions were observed.
He inherited the title of Fēngyáng Xiàn Hóu.
Upon his return, he became Xīn'ān Wáng Zǐluán Guānjūn Chángshǐ,
and acted in charge of Wú Jùn.
Xiāo Huìkāi's younger sister was to marry Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn,
and his daughter was also to marry the son of Shìzǔ.
The funds for their dispatch
would require twenty million [cash].
Therefore, he was appointed Yùzhāng Nèishǐ,
and allowed to gather wealth as he pleased,
which is why he gained a reputation for greed and tyranny in the commandery.
He was recalled to serve as Shàngshū Lìbù Láng,
but did not accept the appointment.
He was then transferred to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Shìzǔ issued an imperial edict to Liú Xiùzhī, saying:
"Now we appoint Xiāo Huìkāi as the Censor-in-Chief,
hoping he will be up to the task.
Just his initial assumption of the office
has already caused considerable awe."
Indeed, during his tenure,
all officials feared and dreaded him.
In the eighth year,
he was recalled to serve as Shìzhōng.
An imperial edict stated:
"When Huìkāi was previously in the Censorate,
he upheld the law with integrity
and did not fawn on powerful relatives.
We greatly commend him for this.
He may again be appointed Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng."
He left office due to his mother's mourning.
He was then appointed Chíjié, Dū Qīng Jì Èrzhōu Zhūjūnfúshì, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and Qīng Jì Èrzhōu Cìshǐ,
but did not take up the post.
He was reappointed Dū Yì Níng Èrzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the titles Chíjié and Jiāngjūn remaining as before.
Huìkāi had always harbored grand ambitions.
Upon arriving in Shǔ,
he wished to extensively establish strategic plans.
He was skilled at recounting affairs.
When speaking to guests, officials, and scholars, he advocated for reclaiming Zāngkē and Yuèxī to incorporate them into the heartland,
and pacifying and attacking the Mán and Pú peoples,
expanding territory and levying taxes.
Those who heard his words
believed that great achievements could be made.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn,
and then further to Píngxī Jiāngjūn,
with Dū changed to Dūdū.
When Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn rebelled,
Huìkāi gathered his generals and aides and said to them:
"Xiāngdōng is the enlightened one of Tàizǔ,
and Jìn'ān is the solemn one of Shìzǔ.
Neither is unsuitable
for holding the imperial scepter.
However, although Jǐnghé was foolish,
he was originally an heir of Shìzǔ.
If he is unfit for the altars of soil and grain,
there are still many others in succession.
I have received the divine favor of Wǔ and Wén,
and am also indebted to the kindness of Shìzǔ.
Now I must throw myself into action across a thousand li
and support Jiǔjiāng."
Thereupon, he sent Fèi Xīnshòu, the Administrator of Bājùn, with two thousand men eastward.
They were intercepted by Rèn Shú'ér, a native of Bādōng, who had raised an uprising.
Xīnshòu was defeated and killed,
and the route through Shǎnkǒu was no longer passable.
He then dispatched Chéng Fǎdù, the Administrator of the provincial government, with three thousand infantry to march out through Liángzhōu.
This route was also blocked by the Dī bandit Yáng Sēngsì.
Previously, during Huìkāi's administration,
he frequently resorted to severe punishments,
and the people of Shǔ were all resentful and suspicious.
When they heard that Xīnshòu had perished
and Fǎdù could not advance,
Jìnyuán Commandery thereupon rebelled,
and then all the commanderies responded,
coming together to besiege the city.
Inside the city, there were no more than two thousand Eastern soldiers.
Huìkāi, suspecting all Shǔ people,
had them all sent out.
Zǐxūn was soon pacified.
The Shǔ people all wanted to sack the city,
hoping for lavish rewards.
Whenever Huìkāi sent troops out to battle,
they never failed to achieve victory;
the number of those routed, killed, and wounded before and after was countless.
The besieging forces grew larger,
with over a hundred thousand fighting men.
At that time, the empire was already pacified.
Tàizōng, considering Shǔ's rugged and distant terrain,
pardoned their transgressions,
and sent Huìkāi's younger brother Huìjī by land to Shǔ
to fully convey the imperial decree.
When Huìjī arrived at Fú,
the Shǔ people, intent on sacking the city,
did not want the royal command to reach further,
and detained Huìjī, preventing his advance.
Huìjī led his troops and defeated their leaders, such as Mǎ Xīnghuái,
and only then was he able to proceed.
Huìkāi obeyed the imperial edict and submitted,
and the siege of the city was lifted.
At that time, Tàizōng sent Bǎoshǒu, a relative of Huìkāi, by water to offer condolences and reassurance to Yìzhōu.
Bǎoshǒu, desiring to claim credit for pacifying Shǔ,
further encouraged and incited the Shǔ people.
Consequently, uprisings erupted everywhere,
and all those who had dispersed
reunited at once.
The leaders, such as Zhào Yàn and Gōu Wénzhāng,
stationed their troops with Bǎoshǒu at Shàng,
sixty li from Chéngdū,
with a force numbering two hundred thousand men.
Huìkāi wanted to send troops to attack them,
but his generals and aides all said:
"Defeating the Shǔ rebels
is indeed not difficult.
However, the envoy of comfort and reassurance has arrived,
and we have not yet received him;
if we then send troops to resist,
how can we make our true intentions clear?"
Huìkāi replied:
"Now, all four land and water routes are cut off,
and the path for memorials is blocked.
Bǎoshǒu might falsely accuse me,
saying that I am not obeying the imperial decree.
My desire to fight
is fundamentally to open a path for the envoy.
If the envoy can get through,
then my sincerity will be conveyed."
Thereupon, he drafted a memorial,
fully explaining the situation,
and entrusted it to two trusted confidantes,
admonishing them:
"Once the rebels are defeated and the road is open,
you must leap on your horses and gallop away."
He sent Xiāo Huìxùn, the Administrator of Sòngníng, and Fèi Xīnyè, the Biejia, with ten thousand men to advance simultaneously.
They engaged in battle,
utterly defeating them,
and captured Bǎoshǒu alive,
imprisoning him in the Chéngdū Xiàn prison.
When the envoys he had sent arrived,
the Emperor ordered Bǎoshǒu to be arrested and sent.
Huìkāi was appointed Jìnpíng Wáng Xiūyòu Piàojì Chángshǐ and Nánjùn Tàishǒu.
He did not accept the appointment.
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ,
he returned to the capital.
Initially,
Dào Xīwēi, the Recorder-Counsellor of Huìkāi's administration, owed the Shǔ people nearly a million in debt,
and was restrained by his creditors,
unable to return with them.
Huìkāi and Xīwēi had not been on close terms,
and he felt that for Xīwēi to accompany him on the journey back
but be unable to bring him along
was a source of shame.
He had sixty horses in total,
all of which he gave to Xīwēi to repay his debts;
his temperament and actions were always unconventional in this way.
Earlier, when Liú Yǔ was Governor of Yìzhōu,
Zhāng Yuè replaced him.
When Yǔ left office,
he forcefully coerced any subordinate official or aide who was unwilling to return with him,
saying to people:
"If you followed me up here,
how can you become a guest of Zhāng Yuè in the West Gate?"
When Huìkāi returned from Shǔ,
he had over twenty million in wealth,
all of which he scattered along the roadside,
leaving nothing for himself.
In his fifth year,
he was again appointed as Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn’s Zhēngběi Chángshǐ and Nán Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu.
In that year,
Huìjī Tàishǒu Cài Xīngzōng was proceeding to his commandery,
and Huìkāi had taken leave from Jīngkǒu to return to the capital,
and they met at Qǔ'ā.
Huìkāi’s rank and position had previously been roughly equal to Xīngzōng’s,
and they had also been on close terms.
Considering himself to be burdened by fault and humbled,
he worried that Xīngzōng would not approach him,
so he ordered his subordinates:
“If Cài Huìjī’s contingent makes inquiries,
be careful not to respond.”
Huìkāi was usually stern,
so none of his subordinates dared to disobey.
Xīngzōng saw that Huìkāi’s boats were very powerful,
but did not know who it was.
He sent men to question each boat,
but Huìkāi had more than ten boats,
and two or three hundred attendants and servants.
They all lowered their heads and passed straight by,
with not a single person answering.
He was again appointed as Jìnpíng Wáng Xiūyòu’s Piàojì Chángshǐ,
with the title of Tàishǒu remaining as before.
In his sixth year,
he was appointed Shǎofǔ,
and given the additional title of Jǐshì Zhōng.
Huìkāi was naturally unyielding,
and at this point, he became even more discontent.
In front of the hall where he lived in the temple,
there had been beautiful flowers and plants planted facing it.
Huìkāi completely cut them down,
and planted white poplars in rows.
He often said to people:
“If a man cannot act according to his aspirations,
even if he lives for a hundred years,
it is still an untimely death.”
He fell ill, vomiting blood,
much of it resembling liver and internal organs.
He was appointed as Bālíng Wáng Xiūròu’s Zhēngxī Chángshǐ, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, and Nánjùn Tàishǒu,
but before he could take office,
he died in his seventh year,
at the age of forty-nine.
His son Ruì succeeded him.
When Qí received the abdication,
his state was abolished.
Huìkāi was not on good terms with his younger brothers.
When Huìjī went as an envoy to Yìzhōu,
they never met again.
It is said that he also had a long-standing grudge with his full brother, Huìmíng.
Yīn Yǎn,
was a native of Chénjùn Chángpíng.
His father, Dàoluán,
was Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì’s Yòujūn Chángshǐ.
Yǎn was known to Tàizǔ from a young age,
and was treated similarly to Lángyé Wáng Jǐngwén.
He first served as Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng’s Zhēngběi Xíng Cānjūn,
then Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn’s Hòujūn Zhǔbù.
He was sent out as Póyáng and Jìnxī Tàishǒu,
Yùzhōu Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ,
and Lúlíng Nèishǐ.
When Zāng Zhì rebelled,
he abandoned his commandery and fled to Běi Wǎn.
Yǎn was calculating by nature and
wished to ensure his safety whether advancing or retreating,
so he did not return to the capital.
When the affair was settled,
he was imprisoned in the Shàngfāng.
After a short while, he was pardoned.
He was appointed Hǎilíng Wángguó Lángzhōnglìng,
but did not take office.
Línhǎi Wángzǐ Xū was appointed Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Wúxīng Tàishǒu,
and made Yǎn his Lùshì Cānjūn,
acting in charge of the commandery’s affairs.
He subsequently served as Yùzhōu Biéjià,
Tàizǎi Hùcáo Shǔ,
Dānyáng Céng,
Shàngshū Zuǒcéng,
Shǎofǔ,
Xúnyáng Wángzǐ Fáng’s Guānjūn Sīmǎ,
acting for Nán Yùzhōu.
He was transferred with the yamen to Yòujūn Sīmǎ,
and then moved to Bālíng Wáng Xiūròu’s Zuǒjūn Sīmǎ.
In the first year of the former Fèidì Yǒngguāng era,
he was appointed Huángmén Shìláng,
and sent out as Shānyáng Wáng Xiūyòu’s Yòujūn Chángshǐ and Nán Liángjùn Tàishǒu.
When Xiūyòu came to court,
Yǎn continued to handle the affairs of the yamen and the province.
In the first year of Tàizōng’s Tàishǐ era,
Xiūyòu was made Jīngzhōu,
and it was intended to appoint Lìbù Láng Zhāng Dài as Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
At that time, Jìn'ān Wángzǐ Xūn rebelled,
so Yǎn was immediately appointed Dū Yù Sī èr zhōu Nán Yùzhōu zhī Liángjùn Zhū Jūnshì, Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
Xī Rǔyīn Tàishǒu Páng Dàolóng was made Yǎn’s Chángshǐ,
and Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn Liú Shùn was made Sīmǎ.
Shùn urged Yǎn to side with Zǐ Xūn.
Yǎn’s family was in the capital,
and he intended to obey Shùn.
However, the local people, former Yòujūn Cānjūn Dù Shúbǎo,
former Chén Nándùn èr jùn Tàishǒu Huángfǔ Dàoliè, Dàoliè’s cousin, former Mǎtóu Tàishǒu Jǐngdù, former Rǔnán Yǐngchuān èr jùn Tàishǒu Páng Tiānshēng, former Suīyáng Lìng Xiàhóu Jìzǐ, and others,
all persuaded Yǎn to join the rebels.
Yǎn had never had his own personal troops,
and his followers did not exceed a few people.
Unable to stand on his own,
he was controlled by Shúbǎo and the others.
Tàizōng sent Róngcóng Púyè Liǔ Lún to lead troops to assist.
Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn Shānyáng Wáng Xiūyòu also sent Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Zhèng Yuàn to persuade Yǎn to return.
When the two arrived,
they immediately allied with Shúbǎo.
Shúbǎo
was Dù Tǎn’s son.
Being a local strongman and a man of influence,
he monopolized all military affairs, both internal and external.
Yìyáng Tàishǒu Bǔ Tiānshēng held his commandery and joined the rebellion,
intercepting more than a hundred horses intended as tribute from Liángzhōu.
Biānchéng Lìng Sù Sēnghù rose in rebellion, beheaded Tiānshēng,
and sent his head to the capital.
Tàizōng praised him,
appointed him Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn,
enfeoffed him as Jiànxīng Xiàn Hóu,
with an income of three hundred households.
At that time, Suīróng Jiāngjūn, Rǔnán Xīncài èr jùn Tàishǒu Zhōu Jīn rose in rebellion at Xuánhù,
and gathered over a thousand soldiers.
Yuán Yǐ sent an envoy to entice Jīn’s Sīmǎ, the Rǔnán native Cháng Zhēnjī,
using a gold bell as a token of trust.
Zhēnjī immediately beheaded Jīn
and sent his head to Yǐ.
Yǐ appointed Zhēnjī as Rǔnán and Xīncài èr jùn Tàishǒu.
Tàizōng posthumously restored Jīn to his original office,
and appointed Yìyáng Nèishǐ Páng Mèngqiú as Sīzhōu Cìshǐ,
also serving as Suíjùn Tàishǒu.
Mèngqiú did not accept the appointment
and raised troops to join Zǐ Xūn.
Zǐ Xūn summoned Mèngqiú to Xúnyáng,
and appointed Mèngqiú’s son Dìngguāng to act in charge of Yìyáng Commandery.
Tàizōng knew that Yǎn was pressured by the local people
and had no choice,
but still wished to keep him under control.
He appointed Yǎn’s elder brother, former Zhōngshū Láng Yuán, as Sītú Yòuchángshǐ,
and his son Miǎo as Shānyáng Wáng Xiūyòu’s Piàojì Cānjūn.
Zǐ Xūn sent an envoy to appoint Yǎn as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Liángjùn Tàishǒu,
and later added Yùzhōu,
and temporarily conferred upon him the authority to oversee several commanderies in Nán Yùzhōu.
Dù Shúbǎo requested to be Yǎn’s senior aide.
Páng Dàolóng, fearing this would lead to disaster,
then requested to present a memorial to Xúnyáng.
Yǎn immediately appointed Shúbǎo as Chángshǐ and Liángjùn Tàishǒu.
When Xiūyòu walked to court,
his family was still partially residing in Shòuyáng.
Yǎn provided them with ample supplies and provisions.
All matters were handled generously.
In the first month of the second year,
Tàizōng sent Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Liú Miǎn to lead Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Lǚ Ānguó on a western expedition.
Xiūyòu moved to garrison Lìyáng,
serving as the overall commander of the various armies.
At that time, Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Xuē Āndū also rebelled, holding Péngchéng.
A reward was offered for the capture of Yǎn and Āndū alive: enfeoffment as a thousand-household county marquis,
and a gift of two thousand bolts of cloth and silk each.
In the second month,
Miǎn advanced his troops to Xiǎoxiàn.
Initially,
Héféi Shùzhǔ and Nán Rǔyīn Tàishǒu Xuē Yuánbǎo abandoned his commandery and fled to Zǐ Xūn.
Former Tàishǒu Zhū Fǔzhī occupied the city and submitted.
Yǎn sent forces to attack Fǔzhī,
and Fǔzhī was defeated and fled.
Yǎn appointed former Yòujūn Cānjūn Péi Jì as Nán Rǔyīn Tàishǒu.
〔一０〕Jì also submitted,
and Tàizōng immediately appointed him.
Xú Dàolián, the Xiàngxiàn Lìng appointed by Yǎn, also led two hundred men to surrender.
Tàizōng appointed him Mǎtóu Tàishǒu.
In the third month,
the Emperor also sent Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Liú Huáizhēn,
Duàn Sēng'ài, and Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Jiāng Chǎnzhī with three armies (infantry and cavalry) to assist Miǎn in attacking Yǎn.
The righteous army commander Huáng Huí recruited over a thousand Chu people from the west of the Yangtze River.
He beheaded Wáng Guǎngyuán, the Mǎtóu Tàishǒu appointed by Zǐ Xūn,
and Huí was appointed Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn.
Zhèng Mò, a Huáixī native and former Fèngcháoqǐng, led his sons, younger brothers, and personal troops, and rose in rebellion with the Huáiyòu commandery at Chénjùn City.
〔一一〕He had a force of ten thousand.
Tàizōng appointed him Sīzhōu Cìshǐ.
Later, barbarian invaders attacked Huáixī,
and he was defeated in battle and killed.
He was posthumously granted the title of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
That month,
Liú Shùn (劉順), Liǔ Lún (柳倫), Huángfǔ Dàoliè (皇甫道烈), Páng Tiānshēng (龐天生) and others, with eight thousand horse and foot soldiers,
held Wǎntáng (宛唐) to the east,
〔一二〕three hundred *lǐ* (里) from Shòuyáng (壽陽).
Miǎn (勔) led the combined forces forward,
and encamped a few *lǐ* (里) from Shùn (順).
They encountered rain on the way,
and only arrived at dawn.
The ramparts and moats were not yet erected,
and Shùn (順) wanted to attack them.
At that time, the various armies sent by Yǎn (琰) all received orders,
but Huángfǔ Dàoliè (皇甫道烈) and the local strongman Liǔ Lún (柳倫),
having been dispatched by the Court,
and Shùn (順) being of humble origin,
were not suitable for overall command.
Only these two armies did not obey orders.
At this point, Dàoliè (道烈) and Lún (倫) disagreed,
Shùn (順) could not advance alone,
and so he stopped.
Soon, Miǎn's (勔) camp ramparts were gradually established,
making it impossible to attack again,
and so they held their positions against each other.
In the fourth month,
Miǎn's (勔) Registrar and Staff Officer Wáng Qǐ (王起) and Front Division Bandit Master and Staff Officer Zhēn Dàn (甄澹), along with five others, abandoned Miǎn (勔) and defected to Shùn (順).
Shùn (順) then dispatched his army to attack Miǎn (勔).
Shùn's (順) Banner Commander Fán Sēngzhěng (樊僧整) engaged in a spear fight with the Court's Cavalry Commander, General of the Valiant Cavalry's Central Army, and Staff Officer Duàn Sēng'ài (段僧愛).
Sēngzhěng (僧整) stabbed Sēng'ài (僧愛),
killing him,
and was posthumously granted the title of Tunqi Commander (屯騎校尉).
Sēng'ài (僧愛) was the bravest in the three armies,
and the army was all afraid.
Tàizōng (太宗) again sent Grand Commandant Sīmǎ Yuán Hóng (司馬垣閎) to lead an army to join,
〔一三〕with the Infantry Commander Páng Shěn (龐沈) assisting Péi Jì (裴季) in guarding Héféi (合肥).
Initially,
Zhōu Bófú (周伯符) from Huáinán (淮南) persuaded Xiūyòu (休祐) to raise a righteous army.
Xiūyòu (休祐) did not agree,
but Bófú (伯符) insisted,
so he was dispatched.
He traveled alone with a staff,
reaching Ānfēng (安豐),
where he gathered over eight hundred men,
and became a roving force in Huáixī (淮西).
Zhēn Qí (珍奇)'s appointed Yìyáng (弋陽) Administrator Guō Què (郭確) sent General Guō Císūn (郭慈孫) to attack Bófú (伯符) at Jīnqiū (金丘).
Yǎn (琰) also sent Central Army Staff Officer Dù Shúbǎo (杜叔寶) to assist him.
Císūn (慈孫) and others were defeated by Bófú (伯符),
and all drowned themselves.
Tàizōng (太宗) appointed Bófú (伯符) as Staff Officer of the Valiant Cavalry.
Shúbǎo (叔寶) had initially thought that the Court army would remain stationed at Lìyáng (歷陽) and not advance,
and when Shùn (順) and others arrived,
all would fall apart.
He only brought a month's worth of provisions.
Once they were in a stalemate with Miǎn (勔),
the army's food ran out.
He sent a report to Shúbǎo (叔寶) to send food.
Shúbǎo (叔寶) then dispatched fifteen hundred carts loaded with rice to provision Shùn (順),
and personally escorted them with five thousand elite soldiers.
When Miǎn (勔) heard of this,
his Deputy Commander Lǚ Ānguó (呂安國) said:
"Liú Shùn (劉順) has eight thousand elite armored soldiers,
while our forces are less than half of that.
After a long stalemate,
the disparity in strength is evident.
If we continue to delay,
we will not be able to hold our ground.
Our only hope lies in their provisions running out,
while we still have food to spare.
If Shúbǎo's (叔寶) rice arrives,
not only will it be difficult to plan further,
but we also cannot hold out for long.
Now, the only option is to take a secret path to ambush their rice carts,
catching them off guard.
If we can control them,
they will flee without a fight."
Miǎn (勔) thought this was true,
and so he left the weary and weak to guard the camp,
selecting a thousand elite fighters,
assigning them to Ānguó (安國) and commanders Huáng Huí (黃回) and others,
to take a secret path behind Shùn (順),
and ambush them at Héngtáng (橫塘).
When Ānguó (安國) first set out,
he calculated that Shúbǎo (叔寶) would arrive soon,
and only brought two days' cooked food.
When the food ran out,
Shúbǎo (叔寶) had not arrived,
and all the officers and soldiers wanted to return.
Ānguó (安國) said:
"You all have eaten once this morning.
Tonight, the rice carts must surely arrive.
If they do not arrive,
it won't be too late to leave tonight."
Shúbǎo (叔寶) indeed arrived,
arranging the rice carts in a square formation,
with Shúbǎo (叔寶) forming a mobile force outside,
and Banner Commander Yáng Zhònghuái (楊仲懷) leading five hundred men at the front,
where they encountered Ānguó (安國) and Huí (回) and the others.
Zhònghuái's (仲懷) troops all wanted to retreat to Shúbǎo (叔寶) and join forces to attack Ānguó (安國).
Zhònghuái (仲懷) said:
"If we don't attack the bandits when they arrive,
what more do we want to wait for?
Moreover, our commanding officer is behind us,
only two or three *lǐ* (里) away.
By the time we engage,
why worry about him not arriving?"
He immediately advanced to battle.
Huí's (回) troops were all people of Chǔ (楚) from Huáinán (淮南),
elite soldiers of the realm.
Their strength was double,
and in battle,
they immediately defeated them,
killing Zhònghuái (仲懷) on the battlefield.
All five hundred men under Zhònghuái (仲懷) were killed.
When Shúbǎo (叔寶) arrived,
Zhònghuái (仲懷) and his soldiers' bodies lay strewn across the field.
Huí (回) and others wanted to press the advantage and attack,
but Ānguó (安國) said:
"They will flee on their own;
there's no need to attack again."
They retreated thirty *lǐ* (里) and encamped for the night.
He sent cavalry to scout that night,
and Shúbǎo (叔寶) indeed abandoned the rice carts and fled.
Ānguó (安國) immediately went back that night,
burned the rice carts,
and drove back over two thousand cattle.
When Liú Shùn (劉順) heard that the rice carts had been burned,
and that Shúbǎo (叔寶) had also fled,
on the night of the first day of the fifth month,
his forces collapsed,
fleeing back to Shòuyáng (壽陽),
and then to Huáixī (淮西) to join Cháng Zhēnqí (常珍奇).
Miǎn (勔) then advanced unimpeded.
Shúbǎo (叔寶) gathered residents and scattered soldiers,
fortifying the city and defending himself.
Miǎn (勔) and the other armies set up separate camps outside the city.
Huáng Huí (黃回) built a pontoon bridge to cross the Féishuǐ (肥水).
Shúbǎo (叔寶) sent three thousand horse and foot soldiers,
intending to destroy the bridge
and also barricade Xiǎoxiàndài (小峴埭).
Huí (回) attacked and utterly defeated them,
burning their boats and barricades.
Xiūyòu (休祐) wrote to Yǎn (琰), saying:
"You are inherently weak in physique,
and have always lacked military capability,
which is known far and wide.
Moreover, your reputation and position are clean and prominent,
and you should not harbor extravagant ambitions beyond your station.
Your recent actions
must have been due to coercion by ruthless scoundrels,
making you unable to uphold your integrity.
Now, the grand army has driven straight through
and has reached the city walls.
Your forces are isolated and your aid is cut off;
disaster and defeat are converging.
Considering our past friendship,
I still feel a twinge of pity.
The Sagely Emperor extends a benevolence like heaven and earth,
opening up an unprecedented grace,
cherishing life and hating killing,
which is known far and wide.
Gù Chēn (顧琛), Wáng Tánshēng (王曇生), and others, after their armies were defeated and they fled,
begging for their lives among the weeds,
still received clemency,
and now live peacefully in private homes.
Now, where the divine vanguard arrives,
nothing stands in its way.
How can a beleaguered city with weak forces,
the remnants of the wounded,
hope to defend itself?
If you open the gates and surrender,
you can naturally retain your wealth and nobility,
and all your officers and subordinates, great and small,
will preserve their honor and rank.
Why stubbornly bring hardship upon the common people,
seeking your own demise like chopped meat,
your body ending up in axes and cauldrons,
your wife and children all perishing,
and your elder brother, with his white hair,
being executed in the eastern marketplace?
Please reflect on this carefully.
These words are trustworthy and true,
as clear as the shining sun."
The Emperor also sent Wáng Dàolóng to carry an imperial edict pardoning Yǎn's crime.
Miǎn then wrote a letter to Yǎn, saying:
"In the past, Jǐnghé was cruel and rebellious,
utterly disregarding human relations.
He was dark, tyrannical, treacherous, and vile,
blocking all remonstrance.
He then destroyed ancestral temples and imperial tombs,
massacred numerous officials,
indulged in poison and extreme wickedness,
with no limit or end.
At that time, both gods and humans were distraught,
unable to protect themselves.
The gentry and commoners, both within and outside the capital,
〔一四〕 all wished for a rectification.
My duty was in the imperial guard,
and I witnessed all this.
Our Lord, with divine insight, acted decisively,
issuing commands and restoring order.
From the widespread suffering and misery,
peace was restored in one morning.
Saving the endangered and relieving the distressed,
this truly surpasses all past ages.
Yet, the four quarters remained doubtful,
causing this rebellion.
Whenever our forces advanced,
they often yielded readily.
You, being from a distinguished family of officials,
with your integrity long renowned,
even when you sided with the wrongdoers and rebelled,
you were still tolerated and sustained.
Your virtuous elder brother, the Chángshǐ,
rose to a prominent position;
your virtuous son, the Cānjūn,
also filled a state office.
Recently, when the army advanced to Wǎntáng,
the plan was from Liú Shùn.
Withdrawing the troops and closing the city gates
was not understood at the time.
I have been undeservedly favored with imperial grace,
mistakenly appointed as a general.
Having long heard of your reputation,
my feelings remain unchanged.
Now, the imperial might extends far and wide,
and the three quarters are weakened and distressed.
The situation of victory and defeat
is clearly discernible.
Censor Wáng arrived yesterday,
bringing the Emperor's edict, the Piaoqí's instructions, and letters from your virtuous brother and son.
All are sent to you now.
For a hundred generations,
there has never been such extensive grace and specific pardon,
reaching this extent.
Moreover, the imperial court is now proclaiming great righteousness
and reforming the royal way.
How can it utter empty words to the people
and lose the trust of the state in one province?
With your clear discernment and profound vision,
I trust you will not wait until the end of the day.
If, however, you choose to abandon your parents and disregard the consequences of slaughter and destruction,
then we will exhaust our military might and unleash our forces,
pursuing the law to the fullest extent and inflicting the severest penalties.
I fear that your noble family will have no one left to perform ancestral sacrifices,
and your tombs will lack those to sweep and sprinkle them.
You will fail to live up to loyal ministers in life,
and feel shame before filial sons in death.
Both your reputation and reality will be lost,
leaving no remaining responsibility.
This is a brief message from Fúlì,
I hope you will carefully consider it."
Yǎn originally had no intention of rebelling;
the situation was due to the overwhelming force he faced.
Shūbǎo and others had the intention to surrender,
and repeatedly sent sincere petitions back and forth.
However, the people's minds were suspicious,
and they could not agree.
Therefore, the plan to submit
was often hindered and blocked,
and the city was held even more firmly.
Tián Yìzhī, a Man chieftain from Xīshān in Yìyáng, rose in revolt,
attacking Guō Què at Yìyáng.
Yìzhī was made Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
overseeing affairs in Xīshān, Yìyáng.
In the sixth month,
Miǎn's long siege works finally closed in.
Tián Yìzhī led over ten thousand Man people to attack Páng Dìngguāng at Yìyáng.
Dìngguāng sent his elder cousin Wénshēng to resist them,
but he was defeated by Yìzhī
and killed.
Yìzhī then besieged the city.
Dìngguāng sought help from Zǐxūn.
Zǐxūn, having appointed Dìngguāng's father Mèngqiú as Sīzhōu Cìshǐ,
led five thousand elite soldiers to relieve Yìyáng,
and also to lift the siege of Shòuyáng.
Cháng Zhēnqí also sent three thousand men from Xuánhù to aid Dìngguāng,
stationing them at Liǔshuǐ.
Yìzhī did not fight,
but fled and dispersed at the sight of them.
Mèngqiú took advantage of the victory to advance towards Shòuyáng.
Initially,
Cháng Zhēnqí sent Zhōu Dāng and Yuán Shìbǎo to lead several hundred men to deliver weapons to Yǎn.
Shìbǎo was exceptionally brave and outstanding.
He remained to guard the north gate.
He then led his subordinates,
opened the gate, and launched a surprise attack on Miǎn.
Entering Miǎn's camp,
Miǎn managed to escape,
and Shìbǎo took Miǎn's clothes and hat before leaving.
Miǎn then erected a long siege wall,
and constructed an assault path at the southeastern corner,
also filling the moats.
There was a tall tower at the southeastern corner.
Duìzhǔ Zhào Fǎjìn suggested:
"If the enemy attacks,
they will certainly attack the tower first.
If the tower collapses,
it will not only injure our officers and soldiers,
but also demoralize the troops.
It is better to destroy it ourselves first."
His suggestion was followed.
Miǎn used bundles of straw and earth
to throw and fill the moat.
Those throwing came like clouds.
The city defenders then shot fire arrows,
but before the straw could burn,
more earth followed immediately.
In one or two days,
the moat was almost full.
Zhào Fǎjìn again offered a plan,
to pour iron balls into it.
The balls were slippery and flowed,
and all entered through the gaps.
The straw then caught fire,
and in two days, all the straw was gone,
leaving no more than two or three inches of earth in the moat.
Miǎn then built large "toad carts" to carry earth,
covered with ox hide,
and three hundred men pushed them to fill the moat.
Yǎn's Hùcáo Cānjūn, Yú Yìzhī, created "rampart-destroying carts"
〔一五〕 and used stones to strike them.
All the carts were destroyed.
Initially,
Lújiāng Tàishǒu Wáng Zǐzhòng abandoned his commandery and fled to Xúnyáng.
The people of Lújiāng rose in revolt,
and Xiūyòu sent Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng Lù Yōuzhī to assist them.
〔一六〕 Liú Hú sent his Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Xuē Dàobiāo to cross the river and incite the various Man tribes,
planning to surprise attack Lìyáng from Lújiāng.
Yōuzhī's forces were weak,
and he retreated to Qíocheng.
Sītú, Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén, sent Cānjūn Shěn Língchǒng to swiftly occupy Lújiāng.
Dàobiāo arrived a day later.
Yōuzhī came from Qíocheng to join them,
and then confronted Dàobiāo.
In the seventh month,
Páng Mèngqiú reached Yìyáng.
Miǎn sent Lǚ Ānguó, Yuán Hóng, Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Chén Xiǎndá, and Piaoqí Cānjūn Mèng Cìyáng to resist him.
Mèngqiú's army deputy, Lǚ Xīngshòu, had a past acquaintance with Ānguó
and led his subordinates to surrender.
Ānguó advanced his troops,
defeating Mèngqiú at Liáotán.
The righteous army leader Chén Zhūn again defeated him at Ruǐshuǐ.
Mèngqiú fled towards Yìyáng,
but Yìyáng had already been seized by Wáng Xuánmó's son Tánshàn, who had risen in revolt.
He then escaped into Man territory.
Zhèng Shújǔ from Huaixī rose in revolt and attacked Cháng Zhēnqí,
appointing him as Běiyùzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the eighth month,
Huángfǔ Dàoliè, Liǔ Lún, and twenty-one others, hearing of Mèng Qiú's defeat,
opened their gates and surrendered.
Miǎn therefore wrote another letter to Yǎn, saying:
"Liǔ Lún came to defect,
and fully relayed [the situation].
It is now understood that although your Excellency is entangled in chaos,
your heart holds true loyalty.
You are silently distressed and sorrowful,
and do not personally attend to military and governmental affairs.
At the beginning of last winter's 'opening of the heavens' (an auspicious term for the new reign),
many were deluded.
For those like your Excellency,
when advancing, you are not a minister of the ancestral altars of the state;
when retreating, you have no deathbed entrustment to rely on.
Since the imperial court does not particularly blame or criticize you,
your Excellency also has nothing to be uniquely ashamed of.
Chéng Tiānzuò has already surrendered his city,
and Páng Mèngqiú has followed suit in fleeing.
Liú Hú is trapped at Qiánxī,
and Yuán Yǐ desires to fight but cannot.
Reasoning and assessing the situation,
how can this last long?
Moreover, the south initially rose,
with sixteen連州,
and a million followers.
Since mid-spring,
they have lost every battle.
Crushed and annihilated,
scarcely one or two out of ten remain.
Relying on Yuán Yǐ's weak troops in the south,
and your Excellency's isolated city in the north,
to establish this enterprise,
I fear it is utterly unreasonable.
Currently, the state's net is lax,
showing great magnanimity.
What has been reported to you in recent days,
I imagine you already know in full.
Furthermore, Lún and the others are all your Excellency's trusted confidants and close associates,
yet they have forsaken you and left.
It is not because of resentment,
but because they clearly know that the situation cannot be salvaged,
and disaster has already arrived.
Indeed, to gather a few thousand rabble,
and resist the armies of the whole empire,
the state of collapse
is surely not hard to understand.
Even if it were a person of 'six obscurations' (a Buddhist term for those with many failings),
they would still not do such a thing,
let alone your Excellency, who in your youth revered the teachings of famous individuals,
and detests passing away without renown!
The reason I write this again
is truly because I lament that a vital stronghold like Huázhōu
will become overgrown with weeds,
and also grieve for the sudden destruction of your noble family.
If your Excellency can seal the storehouses,
open the four gates,
declare to the civil and military officials,
showing them the consequences of fortune and misfortune,
and first send a short letter,
expressing your sincerity,
then, in a plain carriage with white horses,
come to the commander's gate.
If your Excellency's hair and skin are not kept whole,
or your children and nephews are decimated,
Heaven and Earth,
will surely hear these words.
My words are unembellished,
and I will not write more."
Xuē Dàobiāo was still in Lújiāng,
and Liú Hú again divided his troops, raising a commotion towards Shòuyáng and Héféi.
Miǎn dispatched Xǔ Dàolián to rush to Héféi
to assist Péi Jìwén,
〔一七〕and also sent Huáng Huí, Mèng Cìyáng, and the Cavalry Commandant Duàn Fóróng, and Guard General Wáng Guǎngzhī to follow them.
Dàobiāo led his faction, Xuē Yuánbǎo and others, to attack Héféi.
The various armies dispatched by Miǎn had not yet arrived,
and it was captured by Dàobiāo.
Jìwén and Guard General Yè Qìngzǔ fought bravely and died.
Miǎn swiftly sent Yuán Hóng to take overall command of the armies to attack Héféi.
In this month,
Liú Hú was defeated and fled,
and Xúnyáng was pacified.
Tàizōng sent Shūbǎo's paternal younger cousin, Jìwén, to Yǎn's city walls,
to speak with Shūbǎo,
telling him that the four directions were already settled,
and persuading him to surrender in time.
Shūbǎo said:
"I indeed believe you,
but I fear being deceived by others."
Shūbǎo blocked all news of Zǐxūn's defeat,
and immediately killed anyone who spread it.
At that time, Yǎn's son, Miǎo, was in the capital,
imprisoned in Jiànkāng.
Tàizōng sent Miǎo to Yǎn,
ordering him to relay the news that the southern rebels had been pacified.
He was escorted on his journey from Jiànkāng.
Some suggested that Miǎo should be allowed to meet privately with his paternal uncle, Yuán,
otherwise there would be no way to dispel the doubts within the city,
but this was not followed.
When Miǎo arrived,
Shūbǎo and others indeed became suspicious,
and their defenses were made even stronger.
In the tenth month,
Xuē Dàobiāo broke through the encirclement
and fled with more than ten horsemen to Huáixī,
seeking refuge with Cháng Zhēnqí.
Xuē Yuánbǎo surrendered.
Previously,
Yán Zhànzhī, the Administrator of Jìnxī, held his commandery and joined the rebellion.
At this point, Shěn Língchǒng attacked him from Lújiāng.
Zhànzhī did not know that Xúnyáng had been defeated,
and held out stubbornly without surrendering.
Língchǒng then took the documents of the generals' victory over Liú Hú, placed them in a carriage,
pretended to be defeated in an attack on the city,
abandoned the carriage, and fled.
Zhànzhī obtained the documents, was greatly alarmed,
and fled that very night.
In the eleventh month,
Cháng Zhēnqí begged to surrender,
but fearing he would not be accepted,
he also sought aid from the Tartars.
Tàizōng immediately appointed Zhēnqí as the Inspector of Sīzhōu,
and concurrently as the Administrator of Rǔnán and Xīncài commanderies.
The Tartars also sent their false commander, Zhāng Qióngqí, with ten thousand cavalry to rescue him.
In the twelfth month,
the Tartars arrived at Rǔnán.
Zhēnqí opened the gates and admitted the Tartars.
The people of the seven counties of Huáixī all abandoned their camps and fled south,
and Liú Shùn also abandoned the Tartars and surrendered.
〔一八〕
Tàizōng sent all the surrendering southern rebels
to Yǎn's city walls,
ordering them to speak with those inside the city,
which consequently disheartened the people.
Yǎn was about to surrender.
He first sent Xiūyòu's concubines out of the city,
and then opened the gates.
At that time, Yǎn was ill,
so he was carried on a board,
and with his generals and commanders, bound themselves and pleaded guilty.
Miǎn comforted and pardoned them all,
executing no one.
From the generals and commanders downwards,
their properties and goods
were all returned to them,
not a single thread was lost.
The Tartar cavalry came to rescue Yǎn.
When they reached Shuǐshuǐ,
they heard the city had fallen,
so they plundered Yìyáng,
killing and looting thousands of people before leaving.
Yuán Shìbǎo soon rebelled again,
seeking refuge with Cháng Zhēnqí.
For the achievement of pacifying Yǎn,
Liú Huáizhēn was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Àixiàn,
with a fief of four hundred households.
Yuán Hóng was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Lèxiāngxiàn,
Mèng Cìyáng as the Viscount of Yōuxiàn,
Wáng Guǎngzhī as the Viscount of Púqíxiàn,
Chén Xiǎndá as the Viscount of Péngzexiàn,
and Lǚ Ānguó as the Viscount of Zhōngwǔxiàn,
each with a fief of three hundred households.
Huáng Huí was enfeoffed as the Baron of Gěyángxiàn,
with a fief of two hundred households.
Yǎn and the false imperial insignia were sent back to the capital.
After a long time,
he became Wáng Jǐngwén's Counsel-in-attendance for the General who Conquers the South,
and concurrently 少府.
In the first year of Tàiyù (472 CE),
he was appointed 少府,
and given the additional title of Grand Master of Remonstrance.
Later, in the first year of Yuánhuī (473 CE) of the Deposed Emperor,
he died,
at the age of fifty-nine.
Yǎn's nature was elegant, quiet, and simple.
He had few desires.
He was knowledgeable about old matters of previous generations,
and served his elder brother with great respect.
From a young age, he was praised for his reputable conduct.
While besieged in Shòuyáng for a long time,
he was cherished and supported by the people within the city.
It is said that Wáng Jǐngwén, the Inspector of Yángzhōu,
Cài Xīngzōng, the General who Conquers the West,
and Chǔ Yuān, the Minister of Works, were all good friends with him.
The imperial historian says: One who seeks loyal ministers must look among the households of filial sons,
for it is by kind that they are obtained.
Of old, Qǐfāng (啟方) pleased his lord,
his conduct indicating his abandonment of his parents;
Dèng Yōu (鄧攸) was pure in conduct,
extending his love even to his nephew.
Although their natural endowments varied
and their affections could not be unified,
yet in making light of some and cherishing others equally,
they never showed partiality.
Huìkāi's (惠開) reverence for his parents was deep,
yet his enmity towards his brother was particularly evident.
Within the confines of his heart,
filial piety and brotherly affection were distinct sentiments.
This is more treacherous than mountains and rivers,
and this provides evidence of it.
Collation Notes
Biography Forty-Eight: Xuē Āndū (薛安都), Shěn Wénxiù (沈文秀), Cuī Dàogù (崔道固)
Xuē Āndū (薛安都)
was a native of Fényīn (汾陰), Hédōng (河東).
His family had been a powerful clan for generations,
with three thousand households bearing the same surname.
His father, Guǎng (廣), was a leading figure of the clan.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) pacified Guān (關) and Hé (河),
he appointed Guǎng as the Administrator of Shàngdǎng (上黨).
Āndū (安都) was known for his bravery from a young age.
He was seven feet eight inches tall
and skilled with bow and horse.
The Suǒ (索) barbarians ordered him to assist Qínzhōu (秦州) Inspector Běi Hègǔ (北賀汨) in attacking the rebellious Hú (胡) chieftain Bái Lóngzǐ (白龍子).
He defeated them,
and for this, he was appointed the General Commander of the two false Yōng (雍) and Qín (秦) prefectures.
Each prefecture had its own Inspector,
but he oversaw all their affairs.
In Yuánjiā (元嘉) twenty-first year (444 CE),
the Suǒ barbarian lord Tuòbá Tào (拓跋燾) was greatly defeated while attacking the Ruìruì (芮芮).
Āndū (安都) and his clansman Xuē Yǒngzōng (薛永宗) raised an uprising.
Yǒngzōng (永宗) encamped at Fénqǔ (汾曲),
and Āndū (安都) launched a surprise attack to seize Hóngnóng (弘農).
At this time, Gài Wú (蓋吳), a man from Běidì (北地), also raised an army,
and they allied themselves, responding to each other.
Tào (燾) personally led his troops to attack Yǒngzōng (永宗),
exterminating his clan,
and then advanced to attack Gài Wú (蓋吳).
Āndū (安都), judging that his forces were no match,
led brave warriors such as Xīn Língdù (辛靈度)
and abandoned Hóngnóng (弘農) to return to the State (i.e., Southern Dynasties).
Tàizǔ (太祖) granted him an audience
and asked to return north to incite (rebellion) in Hé (河) and Shǎn (陝)
and gather righteous troops.
The Emperor granted this,
giving him one hundred bolts of brocade
and three hundred bolts of miscellaneous silks.
He again attacked Hóngnóng (弘農),
but the barbarians had already increased their garrison,
so the city could not be captured.
Moreover, Gài Wú (蓋吳) had died,
so he retreated to Shàngluò (上洛).
When Shìzǔ (世祖) was garrisoned in Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
he appointed Āndū (安都) as General of Martial Prowess and Administrator of North Hóngnóng (弘農).
As the barbarians gradually grew stronger,
Āndū (安都) then returned to Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
His uncle Shěn (沈) also returned to the State with him,
and his official position reached General who Pacifies the Distant and Administrator of Xīnyě (新野).
In the twenty-seventh year (450 CE),
Prince Suí (隨), Dàn (誕), appointed Āndū (安都) as General who Establishes Martial Prowess.
He followed Liǔ Yuánjǐng (柳元景) towards Guān (關) and Shǎn (陝),
leading the infantry and cavalry at the front.
Wherever he went, he achieved victories.
These events are recorded in Yuánjǐng's (元景) biography.
Upon the army's return,
Dàn (誕) appointed him as Provisional Staff Officer of the Rear Army.
In the twenty-ninth year (452 CE),
he was appointed Provisional Staff Officer of the Northern Expedition for Prince Shǐxīng (始興), Jùn (濬),
and given the additional title of General who Establishes Martial Prowess.
When Lǔ Shuǎng (魯爽) marched towards Hǔláo (虎牢),
Āndū (安都) again followed Yuánjǐng (元景) on a northern expedition.
He immediately occupied Guānchéng (關城),
planning to cross the river together to seize Púbǎn (蒲坂).
However, Shuǎng (爽) retreated,
so Āndū (安都) again led his troops to follow Yuánjǐng (元景) back.
Thereafter, he attacked the Five Streams Man (蠻) of Xīyáng (西陽).
When Shìzǔ (世祖) campaigned against the rebels,
he was transferred to Staff Officer,
given the additional title of General who Pacifies the North,
and commanded the cavalry.
He set out with Liǔ Yuánjǐng (柳元景).
On the fourteenth day of the fourth month,
he arrived at Zhūquè Háng (朱雀航).
Holding his spear horizontally and glaring,
he shouted at the rebel generals Huángfǔ Ānmín (皇甫安民) and others, saying:
"You rebels murdered your lord and father!
How can you bear to serve him (i.e., the usurper)?!"
When Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
he was appointed General of the Right Army.
On the fourth day of the fifth month,
he led his cavalry as the vanguard,
charging directly into the palace courtyard.
There were still several hundred rebels,
who scattered at once.
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as Male of Nánxiāng (南鄉) County,
with an income of five hundred households.
When Āndū (安都) campaigned in Guān (關) and Shǎn (陝),
he reached Jiùkǒu (臼口).
He dreamt that he looked up at the sky,
and clearly saw the Heavenly Gate open.
He said to his attendants,
"Do you see the Heavenly Gate open?"
When he reached this point, he sighed, saying,
"The dream of the Heavenly Gate opening
is indeed an omen of restoration!"
His cousin Dàoshēng (道生)
was also appointed Staff Officer to the Grand Marshal for his military merits.
He committed a crime
and was whipped by Yǔ Shúzhī (庾淑之), the Magistrate of Mòlíng (秣陵).
Āndū (安都) was furious.
He rode his horse with dozens of men,
ordering his attendants to hold spears,
intending to go and kill Shúzhī (淑之).
When he reached Zhūquè Háng (朱雀航),
he encountered Liǔ Yuánjǐng (柳元景).
Yuánjǐng (元景) called out from afar,
"Where is Xue Gōng (薛公) going?"
Āndū (安都) galloped his horse to the back of the carriage and said,
"That rascal Yǔ Shúzhī (庾淑之) whipped my cousin.
I'm going to stab him to death right now."
Yuánjǐng (元景), fearing he could not be stopped,
deceived him by saying,
"That rascal doesn't deserve to be spared.
It would be very satisfying if you went and struck him with your own hand."
After Āndū (安都) turned his horse around,
Yuánjǐng (元景) called out to him again,
"There's something else I need to discuss with you."
He ordered him to dismount and enter his carriage.
Once he entered the carriage,
Yuánjǐng (元景) then reproached him, saying,
"Your cousin's attire and speech
are no different from those of common folk.
Even though he is a scholar,
how could Yǔ Shúzhī (庾淑之) possibly know that?
Furthermore, if a person commits a crime,
it is right that punishment should be administered.
You are an honored minister of the court;
you should uphold the laws and regulations.
How can you be so reckless
as to want to kill someone in the capital?
Not only is this intolerable by the penal code,
but the Emperor would also have no grounds to pardon you."
He then took him in his carriage and returned together,
and Āndū (安都) then stopped.
That year,
he was dismissed from office for his bluntness.
In Xiàojiàn (孝建) first year (454 CE),
he was again appointed General of the Left Army.
In the second month,
Lǔ Shuǎng (魯爽) rebelled.
He dispatched Āndū (安都), together with the Superintendant of the Imperial Retinue Hú Zǐfǎn (胡子反) and General of Dragon Prowess Zōng Yuè (宗越), to lead infantry and cavalry to occupy Lìyáng (歷陽).
Shuǎng (爽) sent his general Zhèng Déxuán (鄭德玄) to garrison Dàxiàn (大峴).
Déxuán (德玄) sent his vanguard Yáng Húyǔ (楊胡與) with light troops towards Lìyáng (歷陽).
Āndū (安都) dispatched Zōng Yuè (宗越) and the Administrator of Lìyáng (歷陽), Chéng Tiānzuò (程天祚), to intercept and defeat them,
beheading Húyǔ (胡與) and his deputy commander.
Déxuán (德xuán) again sent his Marshal Liáng Yán (梁嚴) to garrison east of Xiàn (峴).
Āndū's (安都) standard-bearer Zhōu Wéngōng (周文恭) went to reconnoiter in the morning
and then launched a surprise attack,
capturing all of them.
The rebels did not dare to advance further.
Shìzǔ (世祖) decreed that Āndū (安都) should leave three hundred men to guard Lìyáng (歷陽),
cross back to Cǎishí (採石),
and be promoted to General who Assists the State and Internal Administrator of Jìnglíng (竟陵).
In the fourth month,
Lǔ Shuǎng 魯爽 sent his younger brother Yú 瑜 with three thousand men to emerge from Xiǎoxiàn 小峴.
Shuǎng 爽 then, with a large force, blocked Dàxiàn 大峴.
Eight thousand infantry and cavalry were also dispatched by Ān Dū 安都 to cross the Jiāng 江,
and together with the Administrator of Lìyáng 歷陽, Zhāng Yòuxù 張幼緒, and others, they attacked Shuǎng 爽.
Ān Dū's 安都副建武 General Tán Jīn 譚金 led dozens of cavalry to challenge them,
and cut down one of their minor commanders.
Yòuxù 幼緒 was timid and fearful,
and immediately withdrew his forces, returning.
Ān Dū 安都 also returned to Lìyáng 歷陽.
Zāng Zhì 臧質 had not arrived for a long time,
so Shìzǔ 世祖 again sent Shěn Qìngzhī 沈慶之 to cross the Jiāng 江 to supervise and command all the armies.
Shuǎng's 爽 army was short on food,
so he retreated.
Qìngzhī 慶之 ordered Ān Dū 安都 to lead light cavalry to pursue him.
On the day of Bǐngxū 丙戌 in the fourth month,
they caught up with Shuǎng 爽 at Xiǎoxiàn 小峴.
Shuǎng 爽 himself, with his trusted elite cavalry, covered the rear.
Tán Jīn 譚金 first attacked them,
but could not break through.
Ān Dū 安都 saw Shuǎng 爽 in the distance,
then leapt on his horse and shouted loudly,
charging straight to stab him.
He fell at the touch of the hand.
His attendant Fàn Shuāng 范雙 cut off Shuǎng's 爽 head.
Shuǎng 爽 had been a fierce and brave warrior for generations,
and was accustomed to battle formations since birth.
Everyone said he was a match for ten thousand men,
but Ān Dū 安都, riding alone, charged straight in,
killed him, and returned.
People at the time all said that Guān Yǔ's 關羽 killing of Yán Liáng 顏良
was no more than this.
He was advanced in noble rank to Marquis,
and his enfeoffment increased by five hundred households,
making a total of one thousand households.
At that time, Wáng Xuánmó 王玄謨 was resisting Nánjùn Wáng Yìxuān 南郡王義宣 and Zāng Zhì 臧質 at Liángshān 梁山.
Ān Dū 安都 again led cavalry as a supporting force.
The rebels had a water and land camp at Wúhú 蕪湖.
Ān Dū 安都 sent his general Lǚ Xìngshòu 呂興壽 to lead dozens of cavalry to raid it.
The rebel forces were alarmed and scattered,
and many were beheaded or drowned in the water.
Yìxuān 義宣 sent his generals Liú Chénzhī 劉諶之 and Zhì 質 to attack Xuánmó 玄謨.
Xuánmó 玄謨 ordered his armies to strike them,
and had Ān Dū 安都 lead his cavalry out on the right flank of the rebel formation.
His deputy, Jianwu General Tán Jīn 譚金, went through the rebel formation three times,
and seized the opportunity to unleash his cavalry to assault them.
That morning,
the rebel cavalry set out from Wúhú 蕪湖,
intending to join battle.
Seeing Ān Dū's 安都 cavalry was very numerous,
they hid in the mountains and dared not come out.
The southeast of the rebel formation was still strong,
so Ān Dū 安都 attacked it from the side and broke through it.
The rebels then suffered a great rout.
Ān Dū's 安都隊主 Liú Yuánrú 劉元儒 cut off Chénzhī's 諶之 head from within a ship.
He was transferred to Crown Prince Left Guard Commander.
In the first year of Dàmíng 大明,
the barbarians advanced towards Wúyán 無鹽.
The Administrator of Dōngpíng 東平, Liú Hú 劉胡, engaged in battle and suffered a defeat.
In the second month,
Ān Dū 安都 was sent to lead the cavalry to campaign in the north.
The Administrator of Dōngyáng 東陽, Shěn Fǎxì 沈法系, led a naval force towards Péngchéng 彭城.
Both were under the command of the Inspector of Xúzhōu 徐州, Shēn Tǎn 申坦.
The Emperor cautioned him, saying:
“If the rebels can be reached,
then exert all efforts to exterminate them.
If they are estimated to have turned back,
you may cross the river, display your might, and return.”
At that time, the barbarians had already departed.
Tǎn 坦 requested to recall his army to attack Rèn Zhēn 任榛,
which was granted.
Ān Dū 安都 was supposed to head towards Zuǒchéng 左城.
Zuǒchéng 左城 was over two hundred *lǐ* from Huátái 滑臺.
Ān Dū 安都 considered that it was close to the barbarian strongholds,
and with a small army, it was not advisable to divide forces.
Upon reaching Dōngfāngchéng 東坊城,
they encountered three of Rèn Zhēn's 任榛 cavalry.
They attacked and captured one,
while the other two escaped.
When Rèn Zhēn 任榛 heard about it,
they all managed to scatter and flee.
At that time, there was a drought,
and many springs had dried up.
The men and horses were exhausted,
unable to pursue far.
Ān Dū 安都 and Fǎxì 法系 were both dismissed from their posts in commoner attire,
and Tǎn 坦 was imprisoned in the Imperial Arsenal.
Rèn Zhēn 任榛's group was generally in the Rènchéng 任城 area,
a gathering place for generations of fugitives and rebels.
Everywhere was dense with thorny bushes,
Thus, they were able to preserve themselves for a long time
and repeatedly cause trouble for the people.
The following year, Ān Dū 安都 was reinstated,
re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǔchāng Xiàn 武昌縣,
and given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍.
In the seventh year,
making it difficult to deploy an army.
and served as Crown Prince Left Guard Commander for ten years,
not being transferred during Shìzǔ's 世祖 reign.
Upon the accession of the Former Deposed Emperor,
he was promoted to Right Guard General,
and given the additional title of Jìshìzhōng 給事中.
In the first year of Yǒngguāng 永光,
he was sent out as Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Supervisor of all military affairs in Yǎnzhōu 兗州, General of the Front, and Inspector of Yǎnzhōu 兗州.
In the first year of Jǐnghé 景和,
he replaced Yìyáng Wáng Chǎng 義陽王昶 as Supervisor of all military affairs of Liángjùn 梁郡 in Xúzhōu 徐州 and Yùzhōu 豫州, General Pacifying the North, and Inspector of Xúzhōu 徐州.
Upon the accession of Tàizōng 太宗,
he was promoted to the title of General Pacifying the North,
and granted a set of drums and pipes.
Ān Dū 安都 did not accept the appointment
and raised an army to join Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn 晉安王子勛.
Initially,
Ān Dū's 安都's nephew Suǒ'ér 索兒,
during the Jǐnghé 景和 reign of the Former Deposed Emperor,
was a General of the Front,
a Palace Attendant.
He participated in the execution of the various dukes,
and was enfeoffed as Baron of Wǔ'ān Xiàn 武安縣,
with an income of three hundred households.
Upon Tàizōng's 太宗 accession,
he was appointed Left General,
remaining a Palace Attendant as before.
When Ān Dū 安都 was about to rebel,
he sent a secret message to inform him,
and also sent several hundred men to Guāhù 瓜步 to welcome him.
At that time, the Right Guard General Liǔ Guāngshì 柳光世 also colluded with Ān Dū 安都.
In the first month of the second year of Tàishǐ 泰始,
Suǒ'ér 索兒 and Guāngshì 光世 were both in the palace.
Ān Dū's 安都's message urged them to leave quickly.
Both of them escaped from the palace,
and Ān Dū's 安都's sons and family,
with all their belongings, fled north.
The Inspector of Qīngzhōu 青州, Shěn Wénxiù 沈文秀, and the Inspector of Jìzhōu 冀州, Cuī Dàogù 崔道固, all joined the rebellion.
Wénxiù 文秀 sent the three armies of Liú Mízhī 劉彌之, Zhāng Língqìng 張靈慶, and Cuī Sēngxuán 崔僧琁.
Dàogù 道固 sent his son Jǐngzhēng 景徵 and Fù Língyuè 傅靈越 to lead forces,
all in support of Ān Dū 安都.
Mízhī 彌之 and others advanced south from Xiàpī 下邳.
Língyuè 靈越 came from the Tàishān 泰山 road towards Péngchéng 彭城.
At that time, the Administrator of Jìyīn 濟陰, Shēn Chǎn 申闡, occupied Suīlíngchéng 睢陵城 and raised a righteous army.
Suǒ'ér 索兒 led Língyuè 靈越 and others to attack him.
Ān Dū 安都 ordered his accomplice Péi Zǔlóng 裴祖隆 to defend Xiàpī Chéng 下邳城.
Mízhī 彌之 and others arrived at Xiàpī 下邳,
