changed their plan, and submitted.
They then advanced to attack Zǔlóng 祖隆.
Sēngxuán 僧琁 disagreed
and led his forces back to Ān Dū 安都.
Suǒ'ér 索兒 heard that Mízhī 彌之 had different intentions,
abandoned Suīlíng 睢陵 and rushed to Xiàpī 下邳.
Mízhī 彌之 and others scattered before battle,
and were all captured by Suǒ'ér 索兒
and killed.
At that time, Tàizōng 太宗 appointed Shēn Lìngsūn 申令孫 as Inspector of Xúzhōu 徐州,
replacing Ān Dū 安都.
Lìngsūn 令孫 advanced to occupy Huáiyáng 淮陽,
secretly harboring rebellious intentions.
He sent someone to tell Suǒ'ér 索兒:
“I wish to follow you,
but my entire family is in the capital.
You can advance your army and attack me.
If I am defeated in battle and captured,
my family can be spared disaster.”
Suǒ'ér 索兒 then sent Língyuè 靈越 towards Huáiyáng 淮陽.
Lìngsūn 令孫 came out of the city
to put on a show of resistance.
Soon after, he fled and scattered,
and defected north to Suǒ'ér 索兒.
Suǒ'ér 索兒 used Lìngsūn 令孫 to persuade Chǎn 闡 to surrender.
After Chǎn 闡 surrendered,
Suǒ'ér 索兒 seized Chǎn 闡 and Lìngsūn 令孫,
and killed them both.
Suǒ'ér 索兒 then led his army to cross the Huái 淮 River.
As army provisions were insufficient,
they plundered grain from the common people.

Tàizōng 太宗 sent Qí Wáng 齊王 to lead General of the Front Zhāng Yǒng 張永, General Ning Shuo Yuán Shānbǎo 垣山寶, Wáng Kuān 王寬, Aide-de-camp in the Directorate of Ceremonials Zhāng Zhìzhèn 張寘震, Xiāo Shùnzhī 蕭順之, General Long Xiang Zhāng Jìhé 張季和, Huáng Wényù 黃文玉, and other armies to campaign in the north.
In the fifth month of that year,
the army arrived at Píngyuán 平原.
Suǒ'ér 索兒 and others led five thousand cavalry and infantry,
arrayed their formation, and engaged in battle.
They were utterly defeated.
Suǒ'ér 索兒 again plundered the people's grain
and strongly defended Shíliáng 石梁.
Qí Wáng 齊王 again led镇北參軍 Zhào Tánzhī 趙曇之 and Lǚ Zhànzhī 呂湛之 to attack them.
Suǒ'ér's 索兒 army had no provisions or supplies;
what they relied on was foraging from the wilderness.
Being attacked and pressed,
they had nothing to defend themselves with,
so they scattered and fled.
They were again pursued and defeated at Gějiā Báihú 葛家白鵠.
Suǒ'ér 索兒 fled towards the border of Lèpíng Xiàn 樂平縣,
where he was beheaded by Lìngsūn's 令孫 son Xiàoshú 孝叔.
Ān Dū's 安都 son Dàozhì 道智 and his chief general Fàn Shuāng 范雙 fled towards Héféi 合肥,
and surrendered to the Administrator of Nánrǔyīn 南汝陰, Péi Jì 裴季.
At that time, Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn Wáng Guǎngzhī led an army subordinate to Liú Miǎn
to attack Yīn Yǎn at Shòuyáng.
Fù Língyuè fled
and was captured alive by Guǎngzhī's soldiers.
He shouted sternly:
"I am Fù Língyuè!
Why do you not kill the bandit you have captured immediately?"
He was brought alive to Miǎn.
Miǎn personally comforted and welcomed him,
then questioned him about his rebellion.
He replied:
"The nine provinces have risen in righteousness;
how can it be only me?"
Miǎn further asked:
"The four quarters resisted,
but no battle was fought without their capture.
The sovereign has treated all with magnanimity,
employing them according to their talents.
Why did you not return early to the imperial court,
but instead fled to hide among the grass?"
Língyuè answered:
"Xué Gōng raised an army north of the Huái River,
his might shaking the world.
He failed to fully employ his wisdom and courage,
entrusting matters to his sons and nephews,
which was the cause of his defeat;
it truly lies in this.
However, having been fully involved
in the beginning and end of the affair,
and since human life ultimately ends in death,
I truly have no face to beg for life."
Miǎn admired his resolve
and sent him back to the capital.
Tàizōng wished to grant him a pardon,
but Língyuè's replies remained consistent,
never changing his stance,
so he was executed.
Língyuè
was a Qīnghé native.
At that time, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Shānyáng Nèishǐ Chéng Tiānzuò held the commandery, joining Ān Dū.
After a long period of siege,
he then surrendered.
When Zǐ Xūn was pacified,
Ān Dū dispatched Biéjià Cóngshìshǐ Bì Zhòng'ài and Xiàpī Tàishǒu Wáng Huàn and others to present a memorial to Tàizōng to express their submission,
saying:
"Your servant, a humble and ignorant person,
has illicitly lived in the superior state,
having received extraordinary favor from Shìzǔ Xiàowǔ Huángdì.
Even a dog or horse has a heart,
and truly feels grateful for this encounter.
Therefore, when Jìn'ān first initiated the uprising,
I sincerely pledged my allegiance and went alone,
not expecting to live in glory,
but truly intending to repay with my death.
Now that Heaven's mandate has turned,
and the deluded masses have changed their allegiance,
I, presumptuously leading my subordinates,
offer my body awaiting execution.
As for the crime of resistance,
I respectfully await the boiling cauldron."
After Suǒ'ér's death,
Ān Dū had sent Liǔ Guāngshì to defend Xiàpī.
By this time, he also led his subordinates to surrender.
Tàizōng, seeing that the four quarters were pacified,
wished to display his might beyond the Huái River,
and dispatched Zhāng Yǒng and Shěn Yōuzhī with heavy forces to meet them.
Ān Dū, thinking that since he had already surrendered,
heavy troops should not be sent,
feared he would not escape punishment,
and therefore sent a messenger to entice the Suǒ lǔ.
In the first month of the third year,
the Suǒ lǔ dispatched Bólíng Gōng Wèichí Gǒurén and Chéngyáng Gōng Kǒng Bógōng with twenty thousand cavalry to rescue him.
Yǒng and others retreated.
Ān Dū opened the gates and admitted the lǔ.
The lǔ immediately appointed Ān Dū as Xúzhōu Cìshǐ and Hédōng Gōng.
In the third month of the fourth year,
he was recalled to Sānggān.
In the fifth year,
he died among the lǔ,
aged sixty.
Previously,
when Ān Dū raised his army,
his Chángshǐ Lánlíng Yǎn Mì secretly planned against him
and was killed.
Before Ān Dū went to Sānggān,
Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn Péi Zǔlóng plotted to kill Gǒurén
and surrender Péngchéng.
The plot was discovered
and he was executed.
Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng Sūn Gěngzhī died in battle against Suǒ'ér,
and Liú Mízhī and Zhāng Língqìng were also defeated and killed.
All were mourned by Tàizōng.
Yǎn was posthumously granted Guānglùxūn,
Zǔlóng Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ,
Gěngzhī Yǔlín Jiān,
Mízhī Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
Língqìng Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
Ān Dū's sons, Bólìng and Huánlóng,
fled between Liáng and Yōng two prefectures.
In the third year,
they led several thousand fugitives to attack Guǎngpíng,
captured the Tàishǒu Liú Míngqiú,
attacked Shùnyáng,
captured it,
and seized Yìchéng and Fúfēng,
appointing their own administrators.
Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Bālíng Wáng Xiūrúo dispatched Nányáng Tàishǒu Zhāng Jìng'ér and Xīnyě Tàishǒu Liú Rǎngbīng to defeat them,
capturing both.
Earlier,
the Tàishǒu of Dōng'ān and Dōngguǎn commanderies, Zhāng Dàng, defended Tuánchéng,
northeast of Péngchéng.
Initially he joined Ān Dū,
but later also surrendered.
Tàizōng appointed him Dōng Xúzhōu Cìshǐ,
but he was again overrun by the lǔ.
Shěn Wénxiù, courtesy name Zhòngyuǎn,
was a native of Wǔkāng, Wúxīng,
and a nephew of Sīkōng Qìngzhī.
His father, Shào zhī,
was Nánzhōngláng Xíng Cānjūn.
Wénxiù first served as the commandery's Zhǔbù,
then Gōngcáo Shǐ.
After Qìngzhī became influential,
Wénxiù started his career as Dōnghǎi Wáng Huī Fǔjūn Xíng Cānjūn,
then transferred to Yìyáng Wáng Chǎng Dōngzhōngláng Fǔ,
served as Dōngqiān and Qiántáng magistrate,
Xīyáng Zǐ Shàng Fǔjūn Cānjūn,
Wǔkāng magistrate,
Shàngshū Kùbù Láng,
Zhōngzhèng of his home district,
and Jiànkāng magistrate.
He was dismissed from office
for whipping his private slave to death for Xúnyáng Wáng,
and was given one hundred strokes of the cane.
He was reinstated soon after.
When the former deposed emperor ascended the throne,
he became Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén Ānnán Lùshì Cānjūn
and Shèshēng Xiàowèi.
In the first year of Jǐnghé,
he was promoted to Dū Qīngzhōu Xúzhōu Zhī Dōngguǎn Dōng'ān Èr Jùn Zhūjūnjūnshì, Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn, and Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
causing internal and external anxiety.
As Wénxiù was preparing to go to his post,
his troops camped at Báixià.
He advised Qìngzhī, saying:
"The sovereign is so tyrannical
that collapse is imminent.
Yet, our family enjoys his favor,
and everyone believes we are of the same mind.
Moreover, this person's temperament is unstable,
and his suspicion is particularly severe.
Future calamity
is difficult to predict.
Now, using these troops,
overthrowing him would be as easy as turning one's hand.
This is a once-in-a-thousand-years opportunity,
which must not be missed."
Qìngzhī did not follow his advice.
Wénxiù earnestly pleaded more than once,
shedding tears with each word,
but ultimately Qìngzhī did not change his mind.
After Wénxiù departed,
Qìngzhī was indeed killed by the emperor.
After Qìngzhī's death,
the emperor sent Zhíhé Jiāng Fāngxīng to lead troops to execute Wénxiù.
Before Fāngxīng arrived,
Tàizōng had already pacified the rebellion
and swiftly ordered him to halt.
When Fāngxīng did arrive,
he was captured by Wénxiù,
but soon released
and sent back to the capital.
At that time, Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn 晉安王子勛 rebelled, based in Xúnyáng 尋陽.
The imperial army campaigned externally,
conscripting troops from Wénxiù 文秀.
Wénxiù 文秀 sent the armies of Liú Mízhī 劉彌之, Zhāng Língqìng 張靈慶, and Cuī Sēngxuán 崔僧琁, three armies in total, to the imperial court.
At that time, Xuázhōu 許州 Cìshǐ 刺史 Xuē Āndū 薛安都 had already sided with Zǐxūn 子勛,
and sent an envoy to inform Wénxiù 文秀,
saying that the four quarters were rising simultaneously,
and persuaded him to join the rebellion.
Wénxiù 文秀 immediately ordered Mízhī 彌之 and others to respond to Āndū 安都.
Mízhī 彌之 and others soon submitted,
the details are in the biography of Āndū 安都.
Mízhī 彌之 was a powerful clan in Qīngzhōu 青州,
with many family members.
His relatives and kinsmen collectively fled to Běihǎi 北海,
holding the city to resist Wénxiù 文秀.
The Grand Administrators of Píngyuán 平原 and Lè'ān 樂安 Commanderies, Wáng Xuánmò 王玄默, held Lángyé 琅邪.
The Grand Administrators of Qīnghé 清河 and Guǎngchuān 廣川 Commanderies, Wáng Xuánmiǎo 王玄邈, held Pányáng Chéng 盤陽城.
The Grand Administrators of Gāoyáng 高陽 and Bóhǎi 勃海 Commanderies, Liú Chéngmín 劉乘民, held Línjì Chéng 臨濟城.
All rose in revolt.
Wénxiù's 文秀 Sīmǎ 司馬 Fáng Wénqìng 房文慶 plotted to join them,
but was killed by Wénxiù 文秀.
Wénxiù 文秀 sent his army commander Xiè Yànshì 解彥士 to attack and capture Běihǎi 北海.
Chéngmín's 乘民 younger cousin Bózōng 伯宗 gathered local militia,
recaptured Běihǎi 北海,
and then led his subordinates towards Dōngyáng Chéng 東陽城, the seat of Qīngzhōu 青州.
Wénxiù 文秀 resisted him,
and Bózōng 伯宗 was defeated in battle and wounded.
His younger brother Tiān'ài 天愛 helped him to leave,
but Bózōng 伯宗 said:
"A true man should die fighting on the battlefield,
sacrificing his life for his country.
How can I return to die in the hands of my children?
You, my brother, should leave quickly,
so that we don't both perish."
Thereupon, he was killed.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn 龍驤將軍 and Chángguǎng Tàishǒu 長廣太守.
Tàizōng 太宗 sent Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ 青州刺史 Míng Sēnggǎo 明僧暠 and the Grand Administrators of Dōngguǎn 東莞 and Dōng'ān 東安 Commanderies, Lǐ Língqiān 李靈謙, to lead an army to attack Wénxiù 文秀.
Xuánmiǎo 玄邈, Chéngmín 乘民, Sēnggǎo 僧暠 and others all advanced and attacked the city.
Each time they fought, they were defeated by Wénxiù 文秀.
They dispersed and then re-formed,
doing so more than ten times.
In the eighth month of Tàishǐ 太始 2nd year (466 CE),
Xúnyáng 尋陽 was pacified.
Tàizōng 太宗 sent Shàngshū Dùzhī Láng 尚書度支郎 Cuī Yuánsūn 崔元孫 to comfort the various rebel armies.
He was subsequently defeated and killed alongside Sēnggǎo 僧暠.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Níngshuò Jiāngjūn 寧朔將軍 and Jìzhōu Cìshǐ 冀州刺史.
The Emperor sent Wénxiù's 文秀 younger brother Wénbǐng 文炳 to issue an edict to Wénxiù 文秀, saying:
"The Emperor asks the former Dūdú Qīngzhōu Xúzhōu Zhī Dōngguǎn Dōng'ān Èr Jùn Zhū Jūnshì 建威將軍 Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ 都督青州徐州之東莞東安二郡諸軍事建威將軍青州刺史.
[一一] Last year, when We suppressed the chaos,
Our achievements shook the heavens and earth.
For your family,
We had special favors.
That you could prolong your life until now,
whose power was that?
Why have you betrayed the state and been ungrateful,
aligning yourself with the distant rebels?
Now the world is settled,
the four quarters are peaceful and unified.
You alone guard an impoverished city;
to whom can you turn for allegiance?
Moreover, your hundreds of family members are in the capital,
and you also have ancestral graves.
We imagine your feelings are not of wood and stone,
and you must still have some concern.
Therefore, We specifically sent Wénbǐng 文炳 to fully declare this to you.
All those who rebelled,
[一二] and personally led the insurgency,
not one has been punished,
as Wénbǐng 文炳 has fully detailed.
Who are you alone,
that you can stand independently?
You should immediately lead your troops,
and come together to the army gate.
We will issue a separate edict to the relevant authorities,
asking nothing whatsoever.
If you do not do so,
the state has its established laws.
Not only will your younger brother and sons be executed,
but your ancestral graves will also be leveled,
both to apologize to the people of Qí Qi and
to encourage the hearts of Our officers and soldiers.
Hence this edict."
In the second month of the 3rd year (467 CE),
Wénxiù 文秀 submitted and begged for forgiveness,
and was reinstated in his original post.
Before this,
Jìzhōu Cìshǐ 冀州刺史 Cuī Dàogù 崔道固 also held Lìchéng 歷城 and joined the rebellion.
He was attacked by a local uprising,
and together with Wénxiù 文秀, sent envoys to invite the captives.
The captives sent their general Mùyú Báiyào 慕輿白曜 to lead a large army to reinforce them.
[一三] Wénxiù 文秀 had already received the imperial order,
so he took advantage of the captives' unpreparedness,
unleashed his troops to ambush them,
killing and wounding many.
The captives then advanced and besieged the city.
Wénxiù 文秀 was skilled at command and control,
and his officers and soldiers all exerted their utmost effort for him.
Each time he fought against the captives,
he would defeat them.
When ambushing their camps and strongholds,
he was always victorious.
Tàizōng 太宗 advanced Wénxiù's 文秀 title to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍.
In the eighth month of that year (467 CE),
the captives' Shǔjùn Gōng 蜀郡公 Báshì 拔式 and others, with tens of thousands of cavalry and infantry, entered the western outer city,
reaching directly beneath the city walls.
Wénxiù 文秀 ordered Fǔguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍 Yuán Chén 垣諶 to defeat them.
In the ninth month,
they again pressed towards the east of the city.
In the tenth month,
they advanced to attack the southern outer city.
Wénxiù 文秀 ordered Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng 員外散騎侍郎 Huáng Mízhī 黃彌之 and others to intercept and attack them,
beheading and capturing several thousand.
In the 4th year (468 CE),
Wénxiù's 文秀 title was again advanced to Yòujiāngjūn 右將軍,
and he was enfeoffed as Xīnchéng Xiàn Hóu 新城縣侯,
with a tax income of five hundred households.
The captives' Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ 青州刺史 Wáng Lóngxiǎn 王隆顯 was again defeated by the army commander Gāo Chóngrén 高崇仁 in Ānqíu Xiàn 安丘縣,
with several hundred dead.
The captives had besieged Qīngzhōu 青州 for a long time,
and the relief forces sent by Tàizōng 太宗 all dared not advance.
So he made Wénxiù's 文秀 younger brother, Zhēngběi Zhōngbīng Cānjūn 征北中兵參軍 Wénjìng 文靜, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍,
[一四] commanding the military affairs of the five commanderies of Gāomì 高密, Běihǎi 北海, Píngchāng 平昌, Chángguǎng 長廣, and Dōnglái 東萊,
to rescue Qīngzhōu 青州 by sea.
[一五] Wénjìng 文靜 reached Bùqí Chéng 不其城 in Dōnglái 東萊,
but was blocked by the captives,
unable to advance.
He then held the city and defended himself,
but was again attacked by the captives.
He repeatedly fought and won.
Tàizōng 太宗 added the title of Dōng Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ 東青州刺史 to him.
In the 4th year (468 CE),
Bùqí Chéng 不其城 was captured by the captives,
and Wénjìng 文靜 was killed.
Wénxiù 文秀 was besieged for three years,
with no external reinforcements.
His officers and soldiers were loyal to him,
with no defections or betrayals.
They fought day and night,
and their armor became infested with lice.
On the twenty-fourth day of the first month of the 5th year (469 CE),
the city was finally captured by the captives.
On the day the city fell,
he removed his military attire,
sat quietly in civilian clothes,
and ordered his attendants to fetch the imperial staff he carried.
When the captives entered,
blades crossed before him,
and they asked:
"Where is the Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ 青州刺史 Shěn Wénxiù 沈文秀?"
Wénxiù 文秀 said sternly:
"I am he."
Thereupon, they seized him,
dragged him out to the front of the hall,
and stripped him of his clothes.
At that time, Báiyào 白曜 was in the southwest corner tower of the city.
Wénxiù 文秀 was brought naked and bound before Báiyào 白曜.
His captors ordered him to bow,
but Wénxiù 文秀 said:
"We are both ministers of two different states;
there is no custom of bowing to each other."
Báiyào 白曜 ordered his clothes returned to him,
offered him wine and food,
and then sent him to Sānggān 桑乾.
The rest were killed by the rebellious soldiers,
and many died.
Tàizōng 太宗 had previously sent Shàngshū Gōnglùn Láng 尚書功論郎 Hé Rúzhēn 何如真 to select civilian and military officials in Qīngzhōu 青州;
he was also killed by the captives.
Wénxiù 文秀 remained in Sānggān 桑乾 for a total of nineteen years.
In the 4th year of Yǒngmíng 永明 of Qí 齊 (486 CE),
he died of illness,
at the age of sixty-one.
Cuī Dàogù 崔道固 was a native of Qīnghé 清河.
During the reign of Shìzǔ 世祖,
he was recognized for his competence and achievements.
He successively served as Tàizǐ Túnqí Xiàowèi 太子屯騎校尉
and Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn 左軍將軍.
In the 3rd year of Dàmíng 大明 (459 CE),
he was posted out as the Grand Administrator of Qí 齊 and Běihǎi 北海 Commanderies.
A commoner named Jiāo Gōng 焦恭 plundered an ancient tomb,
finding a jade armor.
Dàogù 道固 confiscated it,
presented it,
and arrested Gōng 恭.
He later entered service as Xīn'ān Wáng Zǐluán's 新安王子鸞 Běizhōngláng Zīyì Cānjūn 北中郎諮議參軍
and Yǒngjiā Wáng Zǐrén's 永嘉王子仁 Zuǒjūn Sīmǎ 左軍司馬.
In the first year of Jǐnghé (465 CE),
he was dispatched as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North) and Jìzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Jì Province),
stationed in Lìchéng.
In the second year of Tàishǐ (466 CE),
he was promoted to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General Who Assists the State),
and then further promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the Barbarians).
At that time, Xuě Āndū, the Cìshǐ of Xú Province, had joined the rebellion.
The Emperor immediately sent Dào Gù back to his original post and title as Governor of Xú Province to replace him.
Dào Gù did not accept the order.
He sent his son Jǐngwēi and army commander Fù Língyuè to lead their troops to join Āndū.
〔一六〕Soon after, he was attacked by a local uprising,
suffered repeated defeats in battle,
and closed his gates to defend himself.
When order was restored across the four directions,
the Emperor sent an envoy to offer condolences and reassurance,
and Dào Gù accepted the imperial edict and submitted.
Earlier, he and Shěn Wénxiù had together invited the barbarians,
but once the barbarians arrived,
he held his ground and resisted them,
and was consequently besieged and pressed.
Each time the barbarians advanced,
they were crushed by Dào Gù.
In the third year (467 CE),

he was appointed Dūdū Jì Qīng Yǎn Yōu Bìng Wǔzhōu Zhūjūnshì (Grand Administrator of Military Affairs of Jì, Qīng, Yǎn, Yōu, and Bìng Provinces), Qián Jiāngjūn (General of the Vanguard), and Jìzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Jì Province),
with added credentials of Jié (Staff of Authority),
and further promoted to Píngběi Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North).
In the same year,
he was captured by the barbarians,
sent to Sānggān,
and died among the barbarians.
The historian remarks: In the Spring and Autumn period, when a Grand Master of a vassal state committed an offense,
they would first return their fiefs before departing.
Only the three ministers of Zhū and Jǔ
were recorded as "rebels,"
probably because of the gravity of their position.
Āndū's strategy to serve the emperor
was deficient in protecting the realm;
by abandoning his territory,
his crime was equivalent to that of the three rebels.
The *Shī* (Odes) says:
"Who initiated these troubles,
which are still a hindrance today?"
This is probably what it refers to.
Textual Notes
Biography Forty-Nine: Yuán Càn
Yuán Càn, courtesy name Jǐngqiàn,
was a native of Yángxià, Chénjùn.
He was the nephew of the Grand Commandant Shú.
His father, Zhuó,
was a Xiùcái (Flourishing Talent) of Yáng Province,
but died young.
His paternal grandmother, mourning his early orphanage,
named him Mǐnsūn (Mourning Grandson).
While his paternal uncles were all renowned and prominent in their generation,
Mǐnsūn suffered from hunger and cold.
His mother, a member of the Wáng clan of Lángxié,
was the daughter of Dàn, the Grand Commandant's Chief Clerk.
She personally engaged in weaving and spinning
to provide for their daily needs.
Mǐnsūn was fond of learning from a young age and
possessed refined talent.
Someone wanted to arrange a marriage for his cousin Yǐ.
His paternal uncle Xún, who was Yǐ's father,
said:
"Yǐ is not suitable;
it would be more appropriate for Mǐnsūn to marry her."
At that time, Mǐnsūn was present,
shed tears, and stood up and left.
He was known for his integrity and aspirations from an early age.
He first served as an official in Yáng Province,

then as an aide-de-camp to Emperor Shìzǔ (Emperor Xiàowǔ) when the latter was Anběi (General Who Pacifies the North), Zhèn Jūn (General Who Guards the Army), and Běizhōngláng (Central Protector of the North);
and as Chief Clerk to the Nánzhōngláng (Central Protector of the South).
When Emperor Shìzǔ campaigned against the rebels,
he was transferred to be Jìshì Cānjūn (Secretary to the Staff).
Upon his enthronement,
he was appointed Shàngshū Lìbù Láng (Secretary of the Bureau of Personnel in the Department of State Affairs),
Tàizǐ Yòuwèishuài (Commander of the Right Guards of the Crown Prince),
and Shìzhōng (Attendant Counselor).
In the first year of Xiàojiàn (454 CE),
Emperor Shìzǔ led his officials in an eight-precept vegetarian fast at Zhōngxīng Temple.
After the midday meal,
Mǐnsūn, along with Huángmén Láng (Palace Attendant) Zhāng Yān, separately partook of fish and meat.
Shàngshū Lìng (President of the Department of State Affairs) Hé Shàngzhī, who was always strict in observing the Buddhist precepts,
secretly informed Emperor Shìzǔ.
Emperor Shìzǔ ordered Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (Imperial Censor) Wáng Qiānzhī to impeach them,
and both were dismissed from office.
In the second year (455 CE),
he was reinstated as Tíngwèi (Grand Judge),
Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (Attendant to the Crown Prince),
and concurrently Yòujūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Right Army).

He was appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General Who Assists the State), Xīyáng Wáng (Prince of Xīyáng) Zǐshàng Běizhōngláng Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk of the Central Protector of the North), and Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Guǎnglíng),
acting in charge of Yǎn Province.
Subsequently, he served as Yǒngjiā Wáng (Prince of Yǒngjiā) Zǐrén Guānjūn Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk of the Champion General),
with his general title and governorship remaining as before.
In the first year of Dàmíng (457 CE),
he was again made Shìzhōng (Attendant Counselor),
concurrently Lǐng Shèshēng Xiàowèi (Commander of the Archer-Raising Cavalry),
enfeoffed as the Sub-Marquis of Xīngpíng County,
with an income of five hundred households.
These events are recorded in the biography of Yán Shībó.
In the third year (459 CE),
he was implicated for accepting bribes from a commoner named Dīng Tuànwén of Shānyīn,
whom he recommended as a Xiàolián (Filial and Incorrupt) for Kuàijī Commandery,
and was dismissed from office.
Soon after, he became Xīyáng Wáng (Prince of Xīyáng) Zǐshàng Fǔjūn Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk to the General Who Comforts the Army),
and then again Zhōngshùzǐ (Attendant to the Crown Prince),
concurrently Lǐng Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Left Army).
In the fourth year (460 CE),
he was appointed Yùzhāng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Yùzhāng),
with an added salary rank of Zhōng Èrqiānshí (Two Thousand Piculs).
In the fifth year (461 CE),
he returned to serve as Shìzhōng (Attendant Counselor),
concurrently Lǐng Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi (Commander of the Chángshuǐ Cavalry),
then transferred to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Left Guards),
with added honorific Gěishìzhōng (Attendant-in-ordinary).
In the seventh year (463 CE),
he was transferred to Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of Personnel),
retaining his position as Zuǒwèi (Left Guard).
In the same year,
when the Crown Prince came of age,
the Emperor presided over a banquet in the Eastern Palace.
Mǐnsūn urged Yán Shībó to drink,
but Shībó did not.
Mǐnsūn then insulted him,
but Shībó was favored by the Emperor.
The Emperor had always resented Mǐnsūn for looking down on him due to his humble origins.
Taking offense at this,
he was sent out as Hǎilíng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Hǎilíng).
When the former deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
he was appointed Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (Imperial Censor),
but did not accept the post.
He was again made Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of Personnel).
In the first year of Yǒngguāng (465 CE),
he was transferred to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Right Guards),
with added honorific Gěishìzhōng (Attendant-in-ordinary).
In the first year of Jǐnghé (465 CE),
he was again appointed Shìzhōng (Attendant Counselor),
concurrently Lǐng Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (Commander of the Agile Cavalry).
In the first year of Tàishǐ (465 CE) of Emperor Tàizōng (Emperor Míng),
he was transferred to Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ (Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works),
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (Champion General),
and Nándōnghǎi Tàishǒu (Administrator of Nándōnghǎi).
Mǐnsūn was refined and had a dignified demeanor,
treating himself with great esteem.
He often wrote "Biography of Mr. Miàodé" to continue Jī Kāng's "Biography of Eminent Scholars," using it to describe himself,
saying: There was a Mr. Miàodé,
a native of Chén State.
His spirit and ambition were profound and serene,
his appearance and disposition clear and radiant.
By nature filial and compliant,
he lived in tranquility and led a simple life,
possessing the lingering grace of Shùn.
Mr. Miàodé was sickly from a young age,
and by nature negligent and lazy,
with no aspirations for worldly affairs.
However, he broadly understood the main doctrines of the Nine Schools and Hundred Masters,
and the arts of carving dragons and discussing heaven,
but
did not use them to achieve fame.
Being poor, he once served in officialdom,
but it was not to his liking.
He concealed his reputation and deeds,
and hid his true intentions,
so his close friends sometimes misunderstood him,
and ordinary people could not recognize him.
His humble dwelling was always
closed off,
only allowing for narrow paths.
Even the solitude of Yángzǐ
and the profound reclusion of Yánsǒu
could not surpass him.
He cultivated the Dao and fulfilled his aspirations,
and ultimately there was nothing to praise about him.
He also once said to his companions:
"Once there was a country,
and in that country, there was a spring
called 'Mad Spring.'
Everyone in the country who drank this water
became mad,
except for the ruler, who dug a well and drew water from it,
remaining perfectly sane.
Since everyone in the country had gone mad,
they in turn considered the ruler's sanity to be madness.
So they gathered and plotted,
seized the ruler,
and treated his 'madness.'
Fire, moxa, needles, and medicine
were all brought out.
The ruler could not endure their suffering,
so he went to the spring, drew water, and drank it.
After drinking, he immediately became mad.
The ruler and his subjects, old and young,
were all equally mad,
and then the crowd rejoiced.
Since I am not mad,
it is difficult for me to stand alone.
Soon I too wish to try drinking this water."
Mǐnsūn, from a young age, admired Xún Fèngqiàn's character,
and told Shìzǔ
he wished to change his name to Càn,
but was not permitted.
It was not until he spoke to Tàizōng
that his name was changed to Càn,
and his courtesy name was Jǐngqiàn.
Two years later,
he was promoted to Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Palace Guard),
with thirty guardsmen entering the six gates.
That same year,
he was transferred to Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Central Secretariat),
concurrently Lǐng Tàizǐ Zhānshì (Supervisor of the Crown Prince's Household),
and his enfeoffment was increased by three hundred households,
but he firmly declined it.
Three years later,
he was transferred to Shàngshū Púyè (Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs),
and shortly after, concurrently Lǐng Lìbù (Minister of Personnel).
Five years later,
he was given the additional title of Zhōngshū Lìng,
and also concurrently Lǐng Dānyáng Yǐn (Prefect of Dānyáng).
Six years later,
the Emperor lectured on the Zhōu Yì in the thatched hall of Huálín Yuán,
with Càn holding the classic.
He also took charge of the affairs of the Eastern Palace,
and was transferred to Yòu Púyè (Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs).
Seven years later,
he was made Lǐng Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
with his Púyè position remaining as before.
Before he had formally accepted,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Lìng (Director of the Department of State Affairs),
his Dānyáng Yǐn position remaining as before.
He was impeached for having previously selected Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn (General of Military Might) Jiāng Liǔ as Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Jiāngzhōu).
Liǔ was found guilty,
and Càn was demoted to Shǒu Shàngshū Lìng (Acting Director of the Department of State Affairs).
When Tàizōng was on his deathbed,
Càn, along with Chǔ Yuān and Liú Miǎn, received his deathbed instructions,
and was granted twenty additional guards with swords,
and a set of drum and wind instruments.
Later, Fèidì (Deposed Emperor) ascended the throne,
and Càn was granted an additional five hundred soldiers.
As the Emperor had not yet taken personal charge of court affairs,
he issued an edict saying:
"Recently, the weather has been unusually hot,
with scorching heat lingering,
damaging the autumn crops,
and causing suffering to the people.
I, being young and infirm,
have not yet effectively managed the government,
prisons are still crowded,
and wrongful detentions still accumulate.
Morning and night I am diligent and careful,
but I always feel sadness in my heart.
The Shàngshū Lìng, along with those responsible for law enforcement,
should personally investigate all prisons,
so that injustices may be rectified and grievances addressed,
and the distressed and exhausted may find relief.
Let this be promulgated to the prefectures and commanderies,
so that there is no obstruction."
In Yuánhuī first year (473),
he entered mourning for his mother.
After the funeral,
he provisionally took on his official duties,
and was promoted to Wèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Guards),
but he refused it.
Pressures and urgings came in full measure,
and imperial envoys came one after another,
but Càn ultimately refused.
He was extremely filial by nature,
and was severely emaciated during the mourning period.
On the anniversary of her death and during the change of the mourning period (the first anniversary),
an imperial edict was always issued to the guards to turn away visitors.
In the second year (474),
when Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn rebelled,
Càn, despite his weakness, was helped into the palace.
An edict granted him additional soldiers to follow him,
and established an administrative staff for his residence.
At that time, the military situation was critical and urgent,
the rebels had already reached the Nányèmén (Southern Side Gate),
and the generals were demoralized,
none of them able to rouse themselves.
Càn, with impassioned resolve, said to the generals:
"The bandits have already approached,
yet the morale of the troops is low.
I, an orphaned subject, received the late Emperor's trust,
and was meant to repay him with my death.
Today, I shall die with Chǔ Hùjūn for the sake of the state!"
He then ordered his attendants to saddle his horse,
his expression both sorrowful and heroic.
Thereupon, Chén Xiǎndá and others were moved and went out to fight,
and the rebels were immediately pacified and annihilated.
When the situation was settled,
he was appointed Zhōngshū Jiān (Palace Supervising Secretary),
and with his original title, was granted Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (Privileged to Establish a Government Bureau like the Three Dukes),
and concurrently Lǐng Sītú (Minister of Education).
He was to take the residence of Yángzhōu Jiě as his official residence,
but he firmly refused to move there.
In the third year (475),
he was transferred to Shàngshū Lìng,
his Wèijūn and Kāifǔ positions remaining as before,
but he firmly declined both,
only accepting after the mourning period ended.
He was given the additional title of Shìzhōng (Attendant Censor),
and advanced in rank to Hóu (Marquis),
but again refused.
At that time, Càn, Qí Wáng (Prince of Qí), Chǔ Yuān, and Liú Bǐng served together at court,
resolving all state affairs;
they were then called
the "Four Nobles."
Càn was quiet and taciturn,
unwilling to take on responsibilities.
When the chief clerk frequently came to consult him for decisions,
he would sometimes sing loudly in response.
When he did express a definite opinion,
no one else could change it.
His residence was simple and unadorned,
and his belongings were just enough for his needs.
He enjoyed drinking wine,
and was good at reciting poetry.
He would drink alone in his garden,
finding contentment in this way.
His residence was located south of the outer city wall,
and he would sometimes wander alone with a staff.
He was naturally reclusive,
and had no miscellaneous guests at his gate.
However, when he received the deathbed instructions and held power,
people from all directions converged upon him.
He remained in secluded repose,
not receiving anyone,
and amongst talkers and literati,
he saw no more than one or two people.
When Shùndì ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Zhōngshū Jiān,
his Sītú and Shìzhōng positions remaining as before.
At that time, Qí Wáng resided in the Eastern Palace,
so Càn was ordered to garrison Shítou.
Càn was naturally quiet and withdrawn,
and whenever there was a court order,
he often did not immediately comply.
Only when pressed and left with no alternative
would he then proceed.
However, when the edict to move to Shítou came,
he immediately complied with the order.
An associate who was skilled in reading omens
told Càn:
"The aura of Shítou is very inauspicious;
if you go, there will surely be misfortune."
Càn did not respond.
He was also given an oil-canopied carriage with silk netting,
and fifty guardsmen to enter the palace.
At that time, Qí Wáng had great achievements and heavy virtue,
and the Mandate of Heaven rested with him.
Càn, considering that he had received the deathbed trust,
did not wish to serve two different dynasties,
and secretly had other plans.
Dānyáng Yǐn Liú Bǐng,
a member of the royal clan of the Sòng dynasty,
and former Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Yùn,
the Empress Dowager's nephew,
who was naturally fond of military matters,
both feared they would not be tolerated by Qí Wáng,
and so all allied with Càn.
Generals Huáng Huí, Rèn Hòubó, Sūn Tánguàn, Wáng Yíxìng, Péng Wénzhī, Bǔ Bóxìng, etc.,
all joined Càn.
In the first year of Shēngmíng,
Shěn Yōuzhī, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, raised an army.
Qí Wáng went to see Yuán Càn himself,
but Càn feigned illness and did not meet him.
Càn’s kinsman, the Palace Attendant, Yuán Dá, thought it inappropriate to show dissent,
but Càn said:
“If he considers the lord young and the times difficult,
no different from the time of Guìyáng,
and forces me into the palace,
I will have no excuse to refuse.
Once that happens,
I will never be able to get out again.”
At that time, Qí Wáng entered and garrisoned the imperial court hall.
Bǐng, with his cousin, the General of the Imperial Army Yùn, entered and took up duty in the Secretariat.
Bóxìng became the Chief of the Palace Gates.
Huáng Huí and other generals all led their armies out to Xīntíng.
Càn plotted to issue a false imperial edict from the Empress Dowager on a set day,
ordering Yùn and Bóxìng to lead the palace guard to attack Qí Wáng in the imperial court hall,
with Huí leading his army to assist.
Bǐng, Hóu Bó, and others all rushed to Shítou.
They had originally planned to launch at night,
but on that day, Bǐng was flustered and did not know what to do.
After dusk, he packed his bags.
Before it was dark,
he loaded his women and belongings and went to Càn,
which caused the plot to be leaked.
Before this,
Qí Wáng had sent generals Xuē Yuān, Sū Liè, Wáng Tiānshēng, and others to lead troops to guard Shítou,
claiming it was to assist Càn,
but in reality, it was to guard against him.
He also ordered his trusted confidant Wáng Jìngzé to be Chief of the Palace Gates,
to oversee the palace guards jointly with Bóxìng.
Wáng Yùn heard that Bǐng had already fled,
and sighed,
“This year's plan has failed.”
At that time, Qí Wáng had sent Yùn to recruit men;
he had already gathered several hundred.
He then hastily led his private retainers towards Shítou.
The original plan was to open the south gate,
but by then, it was already dark night.
Xuē Yuān and others held the gate and shot at them.
Yùn thought Càn had already been defeated,
and immediately dispersed and fled.
Qí Wáng reported this to Jìngzé,
who led his subordinates to capture Yùn and kill him,
and also executed Bóxìng.
He also sent Army Commander Dài Sēngjìng to Shítou to assist Xuē Yuān,
who gained entry through the granary gate.
At that time, Càn and Bǐng and others arrayed their troops and ascended the east gate.
Sēngjìng divided his troops and attacked the west gate of the residence.
Càn and Bǐng wanted to return to the residence,
and after descending the city wall,
they lit torches to illuminate themselves.
Sēngjìng bravely advanced in the dark.
Càn’s son, Zuì, noticed a stranger,
and shielded Càn with his body.
Sēngjìng went straight ahead and cut him down.
Father and son both perished,
and their左右 (attendants) scattered.
When Càn died,
he was fifty-eight years old.
Rèn Hóubó and others that night all took light boats
from Xīntíng to Shítou.
Hearing of Càn’s defeat,
they galloped back.
Afterward, they were all executed.
Bǐng’s affair is in the Biography of the Imperial Clan.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng of Qí,
an imperial edict stated:
“In ancient times, Wèi honored Yuán Shào,
bestowing grace upon his grave mound;
Jìn illuminated the two princes,
extending glory to their descendants.
These were acts of cherishing the past and flowing with benevolence,
examining the intention and extending clemency,
a great righteousness of two dynasties,
a beautiful tale from previous ages.
Yuán Càn and Liú Bǐng
both assisted the Sòng imperial house with the previous court.
Shěn Yōuzhī, during the Jǐnghé era,
showed particular loyalty.
Although their later years did not end well,
their initial sincerity is recordable.
As the years pass,
they should receive special honor.
Càn and Bǐng were reburied two years ago,
but their tomb mounds were not yet repaired.
The artisans can make plans for them,
roughly in accordance with the rites of Zhōu.
Yōuzhī and his sons' coffins are in the west;
an order can be issued to Jīngzhōu to send them at the appropriate time,
to return to their old tombs,
and the local authorities are to manage the burial affairs.”
The Court Historian said: When establishing a new dynasty,
without adaptability, one cannot achieve one’s goals.
When succeeding an established lineage,
without loyalty and integrity, one cannot maintain one’s enterprise.
A ruler who establishes a new dynasty
appears once in a thousand years.
A ruler who succeeds an established lineage
is never lacking in any era.
Therefore, the utility of adaptability is short-lived,
while the path of loyalty and integrity is long.
Thus, when the Hàn imperial house □ □,
Kǒng Wénjǔ did not yield to Cáo Shì;
when the Wèi dynasty was about to shift,
Xiàhóu Yì did not face north (in submission).
If everyone had the hearts of these two men,
then neither dynasty would have perished.
Yuán Càn possessed a pure demeanor and noble reserve,
bearing the trust of the state;
although his reputation in court and country was lofty,
he was not yet considered great in moral integrity.
Yet when he faced danger and ruin,
and judged between survival and destruction,
was it not that righteousness was more important than life?
Although he did not attain the Mandate of Heaven,
there are aspects of his conduct that are worthy of remembrance.
In ancient times, Wáng Jīng was commended in the Jìn era;
Càn and others were also reburied in the sacred dynasty.
The glorious eras shared this same principle—how splendid!

Documents from the government office and officials did not avoid the character "有 (yǒu)" in his name.

if the branches and leaves do not flourish,

Biographies, Volume 51: Filial Piety and Righteousness
The Yì says:
“The way of establishing humanity
is benevolence and righteousness.”
Indeed, benevolence and righteousness
embody the ultimate principles for ruler and parent,
and are truly the foundation of loyalty and filial piety.
Although righteousness arises from one’s inner heart,
and feelings are not externally induced,
yet the aspiration to achieve them
is something the sages have bequeathed in their words.
As for times when customs are dissolute and transformation is weak,
rites are violated and the Way is lost,
when loyalty fails to establish the state,
and filial piety also harms the family,
and the people of an era
are mutually drawn by power and profit,
officials are recruited by influence,
and glory is not established by conduct,
lacking the feeling of soaring ambition,
abandoning the duty of sacrificing one's life,
before the frost and dew have changed,
great sorrow is already forgotten in the heart;
when one's integrity remains unchanged,
yet war chariots suddenly become their vanguard—
these are all because the principles of guidance have not been widely promoted,
and the paths of encouragement and inspiration are often deficient.
As for those whose feelings arise from Heaven,
and whose actions are perfected by themselves,
who sacrifice their bodies and lives,
to save their lord and bring peace to their parents,
even if they act on principle that arrives obscurely,
not due to exhortation or reward,
yet the rulers of the world
seldom provide even slight inducement or stimulation.
Furthermore, their deeds are hidden in hamlets
and unheard by sight and sound,
so those who can be clearly recorded in annals
are less than one in a hundred.
Now, these forgotten accounts are collected
to fill in the missing texts, so it is said.
Gōng Yǐng
was a native of Suìníng.
In his youth, he loved learning.
Máo Qú, the Inspector of Yìzhōu, appointed him as Advisor for Promoting Learning.
When Qú was killed by Qiáo Zòng,
Gōng Yǐng’s former subordinates all fled,
but Yǐng wept loudly and rushed to him,
arranging the funeral with proper rites.
Zòng later hosted a banquet and invited Yǐng.
Having no choice, he attended.
When the music played,
Yǐng wept and rose, saying:
“Serving my lord from the north,
when he perished I could not die.
How can I bear to raise a cup and listen to music,
and follow the path of rebellion?”
Qiáo Dàofú, Zòng’s great general, led him out,
intending to execute him.
Dàofú’s mother was Yǐng’s maternal aunt,
who came out barefoot to save him,
and thus he was spared.
After Zòng usurped the title,
he formally invited Yǐng,
but Yǐng still did not come.
So, Zòng arrested Yǐng and imprisoned him,
threatening him with weapons,
but his resolve became even firmer,
and he never changed his mind.
Even until Shǔ was pacified,
he never bowed his integrity.
Afterwards, when inspectors arrived,
they always invited him,
and he successively served as an army supervisor for the prefecture and an aide-de-camp for the province.
In the twenty-fourth year of Tàizǔ Yuánjiā,
Inspector Lù Huī submitted a memorial, saying:
“Your subject has heard that when fate is entangled in obscurity,
the integrity of steadfastness becomes manifest;
when the times are like a tottering beam,
the conduct of independence shines forth.
In the past, during Yuánxīng,
the imperial order was lax and chaotic.
Qiáo Zòng seized the opportunity
and unleashed tyranny in Bā and Yōng,
killing the former Inspector of Yìzhōu, Máo Qú,
and usurping the land of Shǔ.
The gentry and commoners of Fú and Mín
were forced by fear to accept official positions.
Máo Qú’s former subordinate, Gōng Yǐng,
alone maintained his integrity,
resisting with unwavering resolve,
burying his old lord,
with utmost sorrow and respect for the rites,
preserving his conduct for nine years,
and not being stained by the false court.
Although Zòng was cruel and fierce,
he still respected his righteous spirit.
Thus, he invited him with official summons
and coerced him with military might,
but Yǐng’s loyalty and sincerity erupted,
his words and expression became even more resolute.
Even with shackles on his body,
treading on danger only affirmed his integrity;
with a white blade at his neck,
facing death did not change his steadfastness.
Like Wáng Zhú’s defiance against the Yān army,
or Zhōu Kē’s vehement curses against the King of Chǔ,
compared to Yǐng,
nothing could surpass him.
He is truly a loyal and heroic figure of the present day,
and a lasting legacy from antiquity.
Yet his name is not registered in the royal court,
and his title is still only among local officials.
This is indeed a cause for lament
among the common people of the distant borderlands.
Your subject, having undeservedly received imperial favor,
propagates his influence for ten thousand miles,
and is determined to exert his utmost,
with any thoughts he has, he must make them known.
Therefore, I, in my foolish sincerity,
present what I know.
I am increasingly fearful of errors and mistakes,
and prostrate myself with trepidation.”
Yǐng, however, did not receive an imperial decree
and died at home.
Liú Yú
was a native of Lìyáng.
At the age of seven, he lost his father
and served his mother with utmost filial piety.
At fifty-two,
he also lost his mother.
For three years, he did not consume salt or dairy products,
and his weeping and wailing continued day and night without interruption.
He diligently exerted his strength
to arrange the funeral.
After the mourning period,
for more than twenty years, he wore plain clothes and ate vegetarian food,
weeping whenever he spoke.
He often resided by the tomb
and never left it for a moment.
He died in the early years of Tàizǔ Yuánjiā.
Jiǎ Ēn
was a native of Zhūjì, Kuàijī.
In his youth, he had ambition and conduct,
and was highly esteemed by his village.
In the third year of Yuánjiā,
his mother died.
He observed mourning beyond the prescribed rites.
Before the burial,
he was threatened by a neighbor's fire.
Ēn and his wife, Huán Shì,
wept loudly and rushed to save it.
Neighbors came to help,
and the coffin and inner coffin were saved.
Both Ēn and Huán were burned to death.
The authorities memorialized to rename their village Xiàoyì Lǐ (Filial Piety and Righteousness Village)
and exempted them from taxes for three generations.
He was posthumously granted the title of Left Commandant of Xiǎnqīn County, Tiānshuǐ Commandery.
Guō Shìdào
was a native of Yǒngxìng, Kuàijī.
He lost his mother at birth,
and his father remarried.
Shìdào served his father and stepmother
with complete filial piety.
At fourteen,
he also lost his father.
His mourning exceeded the rites,
and he nearly succumbed to grief.
His family was poor and had no assets,
so he worked as a laborer to support his stepmother.
The wife gave birth to a son,
and the couple discussed it, saying:
"Though we diligently provide for them,
our strength is still insufficient.
If we raise this child,
the expenses will be great."
So, shedding tears, they buried him.
When his mother died,
he carried soil to build her tomb.
Relatives all contributed burial gifts;
he accepted a small amount.
After the burial was complete,
he worked twice as hard as a laborer to repay the original amount.
After the period of mourning ended,
his sorrow and longing
lasted his whole life as if he were still in mourning,
believing that the thought of honoring his ancestors
never left his heart.
Therefore, he never removed his mourning clothes.
His benevolent and generous character
was known throughout his community.
No one, young or old, in neighboring villages
would call him by his given name.
Once, while trading goods with someone in the market of Shānyīn,
he mistakenly received an extra thousand cash.
He didn't realize it at the time,
but understood only after they had parted ways.
He asked his companion to help him use this money to return it to the original owner.
His companion laughed heartily and didn't answer.
Shìdào used his own money to make up the amount and returned it.
The money's owner was astonished and impressed,
offering half the amount to Shìdào.
Shìdào declined it and left.
In the fourth year of Yuánjiā,
an imperial envoy was sent to tour the empire.
Yuán Yú, the Sànqí Chángshì, memorialized his pure conduct.
Tàizǔ praised him
and issued an edict for the commandery to display a plaque at his village gate,
remitting his taxes,
and renaming his dwelling place, Dúfēng Lǐ, to Xiàoxíng.
The Grand Administrator, Mèng Yǐ, appointed him Xiàolián,
but he did not accept the position.
His son, Yuánpíng, whose courtesy name was Chángtài,
also embodied supreme conduct,
always supporting his parents through his own labor.
He was skilled in carpentry
and earned wages to provide for them.
He was humble by nature;
whenever he worked as a carpenter for others,
he only charged the price of a common laborer.
When the host provided a meal,
Yuánpíng, knowing his family was poor
and his parents could not afford delicacies,
would only eat salted rice.
If his family sometimes had no food,
he would go hungry all day,
as it was against his principles to eat alone.
He had to finish his work in the evening,
receive his wages, and return home,
then buy provisions in the village
before cooking.
His father suffered from a severe illness for a full year.
Yuánpíng did not loosen his clothes
or taste salted vegetables
throughout the accumulation of cold and heat.
He also never slept lying down.
When his father died,
he wailed, jumped, and collapsed in agony,
only recovering after several days.
Believing that the duty of attending to the end
was a matter of heartfelt ritual,
he did not want to entrust the difficult task of constructing the tomb
to others.
Although he was inherently clever,
he did not know how to build a tomb.
So he sought out tomb builders in the area,
helped them with their labor,
diligently working for a period,
and eventually becoming proficient.
He also sold himself for ten laborers' worth of work
to cover all the expenses.
The burial arrangements
were simple yet befitting the rites;
his nature was without pretense or learning,
it came naturally from his heart.
After the burial,
he went to the person who had bought his labor,
serving diligently without slack,
sharing duties with the other servants,
always yielding the easy tasks and taking on the difficult ones.
The master couldn't bear to make him work
and often sent him away,
but Yuánpíng served diligently,
never taking a moment's rest.
With the remaining private labor he had,
he worked to support his mother,
and saved any surplus to buy back his freedom.
His inherent cleverness,
combined with his acquired skill in constructing tombs,
made him especially good at it.
Every auspicious year,
those seeking his services filled his doorway.
Yuánpíng always responded to
the poor first,
not only charging a low price
but also providing additional labor days.
After his father's mourning ended,
he built two small huts
as an ancestral hall.
Every festival and seasonal sacrifice,
for several days,
he would grieve
and abstain from all food and drink.
After his father's mourning period ended,
he no longer ate fish or meat.
In front of his mother,
he would pretend to eat them,
but in his private room,
he never truly tasted them.
This continued until his death,
for over thirty years.
Xǔ Yáo zhī of Gāoyáng lived in Yǒngxìng.
After he returned home from his post as Jiàn'ān Jùnchéng,
he gave Yuánpíng one jīn of cotton.
Yuánpíng refused to accept it.
Xǔ Yáo zhī sent it, and Yuánpíng returned it dozens of times.
Xǔ Yáo zhī then went himself and said:
"This year is especially cold,
and Jiàn'ān cotton is good.
I offer this to your esteemed parents."
Only then did Yuánpíng bow and accept it.
When his mother died,
he became even more emaciated and frail,
barely surviving the mourning period.
In front of the tomb were several dozens of mǔ of land
that did not belong to Yuánpíng.
Every farming month,
the farmers would work shirtless.
Yuánpíng did not want people to be disrespectful towards his parents' grave,
so he sold off his family property
to buy this land at a high price.
During the three farming months,
he would always tie his belt and shed tears,
personally plowing and cultivating.
Whenever he went to the market to sell goods,
and people asked the price,
he would only state half of it.
This continued for a long time,
and the people of the district all came to know him well.
They would always add to the original price when giving it to him.
Both sides would yield to each other,
with the buyers gradually lowering the price,
insisting that it be slightly lower
before he would accept the payment.
His residence was low and damp,
so he dug ditches around it
to drain the stagnant water.
He planted a few bamboos on his property.
One spring night, someone was stealing his bamboo shoots.
Yuánpíng happened to get up and saw him;
the thief ran and fell into the ditch.
Yuánpíng blamed himself for not being more generous,
causing this person to stumble.
So he built a small bridge over the ditch where the bamboos were planted,
allowing easy passage,
and also gathered bamboo shoots and placed them outside the fence.
His neighbors were ashamed
and no longer took them.
When Tàizǔ died,
Yuánpíng wept with extreme sorrow,
eating only one wheat cake a day
for five days.
Someone asked him:
"Who among us is not a subject of the king?
Why are you uniquely so?"
Yuánpíng wept and replied:
"My family was distinguished by the former court
and received the praise and reward of commendation.
I cannot repay this kindness,
and my heart is privately moved with grief."
He also made a living by growing melons.
In the seventh year of Dàmíng during the reign of Shìzǔ, there was a great drought.
The melon canal could no longer be navigated by boats.
The county official, Liú Sēngxiù, pitied his poverty and old age,
and lowered the water in the canal for him.
Yuánpíng said:
“There is a great drought across the entire land,
and all the people are suffering.
How can we reduce the water for irrigating fields
to allow boats to transport melons?”
So he walked another path to Qiántáng to sell his goods.
Every time he traveled,
he saw people pulling their boats over a weir who had not yet crossed,
and he would quickly paddle to help them.
He pulled his own boat,
not relying on outside help.
If his own boat had already crossed,
but others had not yet caught up,
he would often stop and wait for them.
He did this habitually.
Once, at Guō Fèngdài weir south of the county, he was helping someone pull a boat,
when he encountered people fighting.
They were apprehended by officials.
Those who heard of it fled,
but only Yuánpíng remained.
The officials seized him and sent him to the county.
The county magistrate, being newly arrived,
was not yet familiar with him,
and intended to inflict severe punishment.
Yuánpíng removed his clothes and accepted the punishment,
not uttering a single word out of righteousness.
All the people around, great and small, bowed their heads and pleaded for his release,
and only then was he spared.
He had never paid respects to officials,
but after this incident,
he began to observe civil courtesies.
The Grand Administrator, Wáng Sēnglǎng, nominated him as Xiàolián,
but he did not accept.
When Grand Administrator Cài Xīngzōng took office in the commandery,
he greatly esteemed him as exceptional.
He sent private rice as a gift to Yuánpíng and Zhū Bǎinián’s wife from Shānyīn,
instructing:
“The rewards for years of service
are recorded in state documents.
The practice of providing for the poor
is heard in excellent decrees.
How much more so for Gāo Chái, who is poor and old,
and the wife of Lái, who faces hardship in her twilight years!
Guō Yuánpíng of Yǒngxīng has inherited filial virtue for generations,
his spirit is perfectly stored in his deeds,
his profound benevolence and extraordinary conduct
surpass those of ancient times.
Dwelling in purity and adhering to moderation,
he is venerable and dignified in old age.
Zhū Bǎinián of Shānyīn ended his life beyond worldly concerns,
and his wife, Kǒng, is a widow of advanced age,
poor and in distress during her remaining days.
Admiring their character and reflecting on their circumstances,
I am filled with sighs of emotion.
Therefore, I can use the rice from my tent
to bestow one hundred *hú* upon each of them.”
Yuánpíng firmly and repeatedly declined,
vowing to die rather than accept.
Someone asked:
“The Prefect admires your pure conduct
and pities your poverty and old age,
hence he offers this assistance.
Why must you decline?”
Yuánpíng said:
“If the Prefect considers my righteous conduct,
then I have not a single good deed,
and should not improperly receive this gift.
If he considers my poverty and old age,
then there are many of advanced age,
and many households are repeatedly empty;
it is not only me.”
He ultimately refused to accept it.
Bǎinián’s wife also declined to accept.
Kuàijī held prestigious positions as *Wàngjì* and *Wàngxiào*,
and those from prominent families who held them
were no less than Bì or Zhù.
In the seventh year of Tàishǐ during the reign of Tàizōng,
Xīngzōng wished to nominate Kǒng Zhòngzhì’s eldest son from Shānyīn as *Wàngjì*,
and Yuánpíng’s second son as *Wàngxiào*.
Zhòngzhì was a prominent figure in the local gentry,
and Yuánpíng was considered a paragon of conduct in the region,
so Xīngzōng intended for them to be matched.
However, Tàizōng issued a separate imperial edict on personnel appointments,
so both nominations were shelved.
In the first year of Tàiyù,
Xīngzōng was recalled to the capital.
He memorialized Yuánpíng’s extraordinary conduct,
stating that he ought to be promoted to a prominent position
to encourage moral customs.
He was nominated as a Professor of the Imperial Academy (Tàixué Bóshì);
however, Xīngzōng died,
and the matter was not carried out.
The following year,
the first year of Yuánhuī,
he died at home.
Yuánpíng, from youth to old age, interacted with people
without ever uttering a displeasing word.
Those who lived with him for several decades
never saw him show signs of joy or anger.
His three sons and one younger brother
all possessed family virtues.
His eldest son, Bólín,
was nominated as Xiàolián,
and his second son, Língfù,
was appointed Libationer of the Ruist Forest (Rúlín Jìjiǔ),
but both declined.
Yán Shìqī was a native of Shānyīn in Kuàijī.
His inclination for generosity and admiration for good deeds
came naturally.
Three people from his village, including Zhāng Mài,
each had a child born to their wives.
At that time, the year was poor and lean,
and they feared they could not keep their children alive,
so they wished to abandon them and not raise them.
Shìqī heard of this,
rushed to rescue them,
shared his food and clothes,
to relieve their hardship,
and all three children were able to grow up.
Yú Yáng’s wife, Zhuāng, from the same county, was ninety years old,
and Zhuāng’s daughter, Lán, was seventy.
Both were old and ill,
alone and without support.
Shìqī clothed and fed them for over twenty years,
and when they died, he provided for their funerals and burials.
His relative Yán Hóng, and local villagers Pān Bó and fifteen others,
all starved to death during a famine year.
Their bodies were left exposed and uncollected.
Shìqī bought coffins and burial shrouds,
and interred them,
and he also raised their children.
The Magistrate of Shānyīn, Hé Mànzhī, memorialized about this.
In the fourth year of Yuánjiā,
the relevant officials proposed to put up a plaque at his gate, stating
“The Lane of the Righteous Yán Clan,”
exempting him from personal corvée,
and remitting his land tax for ten years.
Wú Kuí was a native of Wūchéng in Wúxīng.
After experiencing famine and dearth,
followed by an epidemic,
his parents, brothers, sister-in-law, and many younger relatives, even those of the *xiǎo gōng* degree of mourning,
thirteen men and women, died.
Kuí himself was severely ill at the time.
His neighbors wrapped him in a reed mat
and buried him by the side of the village.
Afterward, Kuí recovered from his illness.
All his relatives were gone,
only Kuí and his wife survived.
Their house was utterly destitute,
without quilts or trousers in winter.
By day, he worked as a laborer,
by night, he cut wood and burned bricks.
He truly showed no laziness or weariness.
One night, Kuí encountered a tiger while traveling,
and the tiger always left the road to avoid him.
Within a year,
he built seven tombs
and buried thirteen coffins.
His neighbors admired his determination and righteousness,
and on the day of the burials, all came out to help,
and the funeral rites,
though simple, were complete.
Kuí had borrowed wages from his neighbors in advance.
After the burials,
everyone offered to forgive the debt,
but Kuí accepted none of it,
and repaid everyone through labor.
Grand Administrator Zhāng Chóngzhī extended ritual appointments to him three times.
Grand Administrator Wáng Sháozhī promoted him to fill the post of Registrar (Gōngcáo Shǐ).
Kuí, due to his humble family background,
firmly declined to accept,
and was nominated as Xiàolián.
Pān Zōng,
a native of Wúxīng Wūchéng.
During Sūn Ēn's rebellion,
the demonic faction attacked and broke through villages and towns.
Zōng and his father, Piào, fled together to escape the bandits.
Piào was old and slow,
and the bandits pressed closer.
Piào said to Zōng:
"I cannot go on.
If you run, you might escape.
Fortunately, let us not both die."
Piào, exhausted, sat on the ground.
Zōng went to the bandits and kowtowed, saying:
"My father is old,
I beg you to spare his life."
When the bandits arrived,
Piào also pleaded with them, saying:
"My son is young
and can run by himself,
but now, for his old father, he will not leave.
This old man does not fear death;
I beg you to let this son live."
The bandits then chopped Piào.
Zōng embraced his father beneath his abdomen,
and the bandits chopped Zōng's head and face,
making four wounds in total.
Zōng fainted on the spot.
A bandit came from the side
and said to his comrades:
"You wish to accomplish great things,
but this son is risking his life to save his father.
How can he be killed?
Killing a filial son is inauspicious."
The bandits hesitated for a long time before stopping,
and both father and son were spared.
Zōng's fellow villagers, Bìmìshū Jiān Qiū Jìzǔ and Tíngwèi Shěn Chìqián, recognized Zōng's extraordinary conduct
and appointed him as Zuǒmín Lìshǐ.
He was later appointed as Suìchāng Zhǎng.
After his term was complete, he returned home.
When Tàishǒu Wáng Sháozhī took office in the commandery,
he issued an announcement that read:
"Previously, a directive was received
regarding the selection of Xiàolián,
emphasizing the need to carefully vet the individuals.
Although the 'Four Qualities' are difficult to encompass
and literary grace and plainness are rarely both present,
those who demonstrate filial piety and righteousness surpassing common custom,
distinguished and renowned,
are sufficient to conspicuously respond to and clearly manifest
the true spirit of the directive.
Pān Zōng of Wūchéng upheld the filial way even unto death,
preserving his parent and overcoming hardship.
Wú Kuí of Wūchéng's righteous conduct was pure and ultimate,
his graves arranged in rows.
Both possess sincere and pure hearts within
and excellent reputations outwardly.
They should both be examined as Xiàolián
and their names submitted to the provincial government,
with their deeds reported."
When he was about to depart,
a farewell feast was held,
and a four-character poem was presented, saying:
in the South, tall trees stand.
They radiate brilliance from towering cliffs,
their trunks rise to the heavy heavens.
How beautiful is this land,
generation after generation bears heroes.
They nurture their wings in deep forests,
and
sound their calls in the Nine Marshes.
(Part One)
Hàn's founder used a covered carriage.
Our Emperor descends with his gaze,
thinking of and delighting in worthy people.
Ministers compete to recommend,
old regulations become new.
What can I contribute?
I say
righteousness and benevolence.
(Part Two)
Only in Wú and Pān.
Their hearts accumulated pure filial piety,
their deeds manifested in hardship.
They faced death as if returning home,
their excellent reputations like orchids.
Wú truly practiced benevolence,
his
heart and strength were equally devoted.
Firm in this bitter principle,
they withstood the year's cold.
Though frost and snow are thick,
the pines and cypresses stand round and firm.
(Part Three)
no good deed goes unacknowledged.
The illustrious deeds of these two sons
grow more fragrant with time.
They rise above the common, standing out from the crowd,
their noble conduct facing the morning sun.
Who says the path is distant?
Broaden
it and it will shine.
You, various officials,
do not be idle or neglectful.
(Part Four)
and received blessings and prosperity.
Jiāng Shī made his contribution,
and the Hàn court sighed in admiration.
Strive, travelers,
cherish your good fortune.
Let this humble state
illuminate
the capital with its brilliance.
(Part Five)
secretly fearing theft.
Incapable of ritual and music,
how could I have time for fame and instruction?
Following that peace and ease,
I delight in admirable virtue.
I loosely weave what is in my heart
to
present to these two filial sons.
(Part Six)
the officials memorialized to change their village to Chúnxiào Lǐ,
and to exempt them from rent and cloth taxes for three generations.
Zhāng Jìnzhī
was a native of Yǒngjiā Āngù.
He belonged to a prominent family in the commandery.
From a young age, he possessed aspirations and conduct.
He served successively as Wǔguān Zhǔbù in the commandery,
and as Lǐng Xiàowèi in the two counties of Yǒngníng and Āngù.
His family was wealthy,
but during a famine, he distributed his wealth
to help his fellow villagers,
thus becoming poor and destitute himself.
Many were saved by him.
Jìnzhī was a clerk for Tàishǒu Wáng Wèizhī.
Wèizhī, guilty of a crime, was about to be arrested.
He fled and sought refuge in Jìnzhī's home,
where he was cared for for some time,
with Jìnzhī putting forth all his sincerity and effort.
Because his own village was too shallow,
he moved into a pond or stream.
Wèizhī fell into the water and sank.
Jìnzhī jumped into the water to rescue him,
and they both sank.
They were in danger but managed to escape.
At that time, bandits were rampant,
and whenever they entered a village to plunder and commit violence,
upon reaching Jìnzhī's door,
they would always agree among themselves
not to infringe upon it.
Such was the influence of his trustworthiness and righteousness.
In the early years of Yuánjiā,
an edict ordered the exemption of his corvée labor in the area.
During Sūn Ēn's rebellion,
Yǒngjiā Tàishǒu Sīmǎ Yìzhī was killed,
and his wife and children also died.
During the time of war and banditry,
no one dared to collect their bodies.
Yú Qiān, a commandery official, used his family's wealth to buy coffins and bury the six deceased, including Yìzhī,
and sent them back to the capital.
Only after the burials were completed did he return to his hometown.
In the middle of Yuánjiā,
he died of old age and illness.
Wáng Péng
was a native of Xūyí Zhídú.
He lost his mother young.
In the early years of Yuánjiā,
his father also died.
His family was poor and he was weak,
with no means to arrange a funeral.
He and his brother,
during the day, worked as laborers,
and at night, wailed with grief.
The villagers all felt sorry for them
and each contributed labor to help make bricks.
Bricks required water, but there was a drought.
They dug a well tens of zhang deep,
but no spring emerged.
The burial site was five *lǐ* from the Huái River,
and carrying water from afar was exhausting and insufficient.
Péng cried out to heaven, complaining about his plight,
for many days.
One day, there was a great fog.
When the fog lifted,
a spring of water suddenly appeared in front of the brick kiln.
Those villagers who were helping
all exclaimed at the divine wonder,
and people from nearby and distant counties and towns
all went to observe it.
Once the funeral arrangements were completed,
the water naturally dried up.
In the ninth year of Yuánjiā,
Tàishǒu Liú Bólóng memorialized about the matter,
and their village was renamed Tōnglíng Lǐ,
and they were exempted from rent and cloth taxes for three generations.
Jiǎng Gōng,
a native of Línjīn, Yìxīng.
During the Yuánjiā reign,
Jiǎng Chóngpíng of Jìnlíng was captured by bandits.
The bandits claimed that he was in league with Gōng's wife's younger brother, Wú Xīzhāng.
Xīzhāng had left earlier and was not present.
His home village was affected by floods,
and his wife and five children, to escape the water, moved and stayed with Gōng's family.
The authorities searched for Xīzhāng but did not find him,
so they arrested Gōng and his elder brother Xié and sent them to prison for punishment.
Gōng and Xié both admitted that Xīzhāng's family lived in their home,
but they were unaware of his involvement in banditry.
Gōng stated that Xīzhāng's wife and children were his wife's relatives,
and since these relatives were now implicated,
he was willing to accept his share of the penalty,
requesting that his brother Xié be released.
Xié stated that he was the head of the household,
and thus responsible for the actions of those under his governance;
therefore, on the day of punishment,
only he should be held accountable,
requesting that his younger brother Gōng be released.
The two brothers
vied to take the blame.
The local prefecture and county were unable to decide,
so they reported the matter for further deliberation.
The provincial council discussed it and said:
"Those who practice禮 (lǐ) and humility prioritize righteousness,
while those who prioritize self-interest put profit first.
In this degenerate age, customs are shallow,
and none are not selfish.
Even those who are devoted to the sacred teachings
sometimes fall short,
let alone ordinary country folk
who have not yet grasped the edicts and instructions.
Yet they are able to mutually express concern for their familial bonds,
and willingly accept an unfathomable punishment.
Such an display of affection and righteousness
is truly extraordinary.
That the humble Gōng and Xié
could act in such a way,
this is something rarely seen throughout history,
a commendable deed even in prosperous times.
Even the 'two sons in a boat' [referring to a famous anecdote of filial piety]
could not surpass this.
How can we rigidly adhere to the written law
and inflict punishment?
Moreover, Xīzhāng left home and traveled far,
committing banditry in another region.
The wrongdoing originated externally,
and the stolen goods were not brought home.
It is possible that the village where he lodged
was unaware of his activities,
and therefore should not be punished."
The county was ordered to release them,
and they were restored to their civilian status.
Then Gōng was appointed Yìchéng Ling,
and Xié was appointed Yìzhāo Ling.
Xú Gēng,
a native of Yánlíng, Jìnlíng.
He was promoted from clerk to Píngyuán Ling.
In the twenty-first year of Yuánjiā,
there was a severe drought and famine.
Gēng went to the county office and presented a statement saying:
"This year's prolonged drought
has caused crops to fail.
The common people are starving,
gathering wild plants to survive.
The sagely emperor, out of compassion,
has already extended aid.
However, the famine has lasted for a long time,
and many are in distress.
Grain prices are soaring,
and there is nowhere to buy provisions.
As we are about to enter spring and summer,
the days will be long.
Without even a small rescue,
there will be no relief forever.
I, an insignificant person,
dare to worry beyond my own concerns.
The desire for assistance, like the 'deer's cry' [a metaphor for seeking help],
makes me feel for my fellow human beings, like wild grass;
how can I not be saddened by the suffering of my kind?
The people can buy little rice
to sustain themselves morning and evening.
I intend to exhaust myself
and share my food out of righteousness.
Now I offer one thousand *hú* of grain
to assist the authorities in relief efforts.
This region has suffered from poor harvests for consecutive years,
and this year is particularly severe.
The Jìnlíng area is especially hard-hit.
Although this commandery is impoverished,
there are still wealthy households.
Families who own irrigated land
are numerous everywhere,
all having secured good harvests,
their losses being very small.
Their accumulated grain
amounts to tens of thousands of *hú*.
The drought has primarily affected
the poor.
Wealthy families
each possess treasures.
I believe these people should all assist the government
so that we can get through these lean months.
Their losses would be minimal,
but the relief provided would be immense.
I now dare to motivate myself,
to set an example for encouragement.
I truly wish to 'dig water and raise dust,'
to increase [wealth] like mountains and seas [i.e., to contribute greatly]."
The county reported his words to the superior.
Contemporaries compared Gēng to Bǔ Shì of the Hàn dynasty.
An imperial edict praised him,
rewarding him with the position of county magistrate.
In the eighth year of Dàmíng,
the eastern regions suffered from famine and drought.
Yán Chéng of Dōnghǎi and Wáng Dàogài of Dōngguǎn each contributed five hundred *hú* of grain
to assist the government in relief efforts.
Sūn Fǎzōng,
a native of Wúxīng.
His father was killed during a rebellion,
and his corpse was not recovered.
His mother and elder brother both starved to death.
Fǎzōng, young at the time, was forced to flee.
It was not until he was sixteen
that he was able to return.
Alone and enduring hardships,
traveling in frost and sleeping in the grass,
he procured coffins,
erected tombs,
and buried his mother and brother,
frugally yet with proper rites.
Because his father's death was unknown,
within the border of his district,
he searched for dry bones,
pricking his finger to drip blood upon them [as a ritual to identify his father's remains].
He did this for over ten years without success.
Then he wore mourning clothes [for life],
never married,
and refused all gifts.
At the beginning of Shìzǔ's reign,
Yángzhōu summoned him to be Literary Aide,
but he did not accept the post.
Fàn Shūxūn,
a native of Qiántáng, Wújùn.
From a young age, he was kind and magnanimous,
helping the poor and assisting those in urgent need.
〔一０〕In the same village, Fàn Fǎxiān's parents and seven siblings
all died of plague at the same time,
leaving only Fǎxiān,
who was also critically ill.
The corpses remained unburied for over a month.
Shūxūn personally provided all the necessary coffins and burial equipment
and personally arranged the funerals.
Also in the same village, Shī Yuānfū fell ill,
and his parents died without being properly interred.
And in the same village, Fàn Miáo and his son both died.
And in the same village, Wēi Jìngzōng's six family members all fell ill,
and two died.
Relatives and neighbors, fearing contamination, kept their distance
and dared not tend to them.
Shūxūn buried them all
and personally cared for the sick,
all of whom recovered completely.
The villagers valued his righteous conduct
and none would call him by his given name.
At the beginning of Shìzǔ Xiàojiàn's reign,
he was appointed Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn of the Jìnglín Kingdom,
but he did not accept the post.
Wú Guófū of Yìxīng
also possessed the virtue of righteousness and humility.
When someone stole his rice,
he brought them back,
prepared food and drink for them,
and sent them off with rice.
Bǔ Tiānyǔ,
a native of Yúháng, Wúxīng.
His father's name was Zǔ,
and he was brave and capable.
When Xú Chìtè became Yúháng Ling,
Zǔ followed him.
After Chìtè died,
〔一一〕Gāozǔ heard of his capability and strength
and summoned him to be appointed Duìzhǔ.
He participated in campaigns,
was enfeoffed as Guānzhōng Hóu,
and served as magistrate for two counties.
Bǔ Tiānyǔ 天與 was good at archery,
with a bow strength twice that of others.
His appearance was stern and upright,
and he never smiled.
Tàizǔ 太祖, considering him the son of an old general,
ordered him to teach the imperial princes archery.
After several years,
he was appointed a leader of the Eastern Yèfáng Gēduì 東掖防閤隊 (Eastern Palace Guard Unit) as a commoner.
In the twenty-seventh year of Yuánjiā 元嘉 [450 CE],
Zāng Zhì 臧質 rescued Xuánhù 懸瓠,
and Liú Xīngzǔ 劉興祖 defended Báishí 白石.
Bǔ Tiānyǔ 天與 led his detachment to follow them,
and the invaders retreated.
He was promoted to lead the First Rear Chariot Guard Unit,
and by comforting and caring for his soldiers,
he gained much popular support.
In the twenty-ninth year [452 CE],
he was appointed Guǎngwēi Jiāngjūn 廣威將軍 (General of Spreading Awe),
leading the Zǔ Xìzhàng 左細仗 (Left Imperial Guard),
and concurrently drawing emoluments for his camp.
When the primary culprit (Yuánxiōng 元凶, i.e., Liú Shào 劉劭) entered to assassinate the emperor,
the situation was sudden and chaotic.
Old generals Luó Xùn 羅訓 and Xú Hǎn 徐罕 both succumbed to the prevailing wind and submitted.
Bǔ Tiānyǔ 天與 had no time to don his armor;
he grabbed a sword and a bow,
and loudly called his左右 (attendants) to sally forth and fight.
Xú Hǎn 徐罕 said:
"The prince (Liú Shào 劉劭) has entered.
What do you intend to do?"
Bǔ Tiānyǔ 天與 cursed, saying:
"The prince often comes here.
Why do you speak such words only at this moment?
You alone are the rebel!"
He personally shot the rebel Shào 劭 in the Eastern Hall,
nearly hitting him.
The rebellious party struck him,
and his arm was severed, causing him to fall to the ground.
Then he was killed.
His unit commanders Zhāng Hóngzhī 張泓之, Zhū Dàoqīn 朱道欽, and Chén Mǎn 陳滿, who went out with Bǔ Tiānyǔ 天與 to resist,
all died.
When Shìzǔ 世祖 (Emperor Xiàowǔ 孝武) ascended the throne,
he issued an edict saying:
"Recently, the rebellious youth (Liú Shào 劉劭) violated the imperial residence,
and a treacherous incident suddenly arose.
Guǎngwēi Jiāngjūn 廣威將軍, Guānzhōng Hóu 關中侯 Bǔ Tiānyǔ 卜天 與, took up his spear and rushed to the aid,
exerting himself heroically,
slaughtering the villainous party,
but then suffered a cruel blade.
His bravery surpassed that of his contemporaries,
and his righteousness matched that of ancient heroes.
Speaking of him, I recall and mourn him,
with deep pain in my heart.
It is fitting to bestow upon him special posthumous honors
to commend his loyal integrity.
He is posthumously granted the titles of Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn 龍驤將軍 (General of the Dragon's Gallop) and Yìzhōu Cìshǐ 益州刺史 (Inspector of Yìzhōu),
and given the posthumous name Zhuàng Hóu 壯侯 (Marquis of Valor)."
The imperial carriage personally attended his mourning.
Hóngzhī 泓之 and others were each posthumously granted the title of jùnshǒu 郡守 (Administrator of a Commandery),
and Bǔ Tiānyǔ's 天與 family was given a permanent stipend.
His son, Bó Zōng 伯宗,
was a Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn 殿中將軍 (General of the Palace Guard).
In the early Tàishǐ 泰始 period of Tàizōng 太宗,
he led a banner unit,
attacking the southern rebels at Zhèqí 赭圻,
