and died in battle.
Bó Zōng's 伯宗 younger brother, Bó Xīng 伯興,
rose to the rank of Qián Jiāngjūn 前將軍 (General of the Vanguard), Nánpíngchāng Tàishǒu 南平昌太守 (Administrator of Nánpíngchāng),
Zhí Gé 直閤 (Chamberlain),
and leader of the Xìzhàng 細仗 (Imperial Guard).
In the first year of Shēngmíng 昇明 (477 CE) under Shùndì 順帝,
he conspired with Yuán Càn 袁粲
and was executed.
Bǔ Tiānyǔ's 天與 younger brother, Tiānshēng 天生,
was a unit commander in his youth,
sharing a fire (mess) with ten men.
Behind their dwelling was a large pit,
over two zhàng 丈 wide.
The ten men all jumped across it successfully,
except for Tiānshēng 天生, who fell into the pit.
Tiānshēng 天生 then took a solid bitter bamboo (arrow),
sharpened its tip,
and arranged it crisscross within the pit.
He called his companions to jump again,
but they were all afraid and dared not.
Tiānshēng 天生 said:
"I failed to cross before;
now I will certainly fall into this pit.
If a man jumps this and fails to cross,
what need is there for him to live?"
So he jumped again,
going back and forth more than ten times,
without any hindrance.
Everyone greatly admired him.
Because his elder brother died a loyal death,
Shìzǔ 世祖 took special notice of him.
He gradually rose to be an Assistant to the Fǔjūn Cānjūn 撫軍參軍 (Military Governor's Aide) for Prince Zǐshàng 子尚 of Xīyáng 西陽,
and was given the honorary title Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn 龍驤將軍.
He was subordinate to Shěn Qìngzhī 沈慶之 in attacking Guǎnglíngchéng 廣陵城.
Tiānshēng 天生 pushed carts to fill the moats,
and led several hundred men to be the first to ascend the northwest corner,
reaching the city wall directly.
The rebels had placed heavy barriers to block the assault route.
After a day of fierce fighting, it could not be taken,
so he withdrew.
An imperial edict stated:
"When Tiānshēng 天生 first undertook military duties,
he immediately engaged the enemy stronghold.
He threw wheels (carts) across moats,
and led his valiant men to be the first to charge.
His valorous spirit
is endlessly admirable.
He shall be granted a thousand bolts of cloth
to encourage all commanders."
At the end of Dàmíng 大明,
he became Yìyáng Tàishǒu 弋陽太守 (Administrator of Yìyáng).
In the early Tàishǐ 泰始 period of Tàizōng 太宗,
he sided with Yīn Yǎn 殷琰 in rebellion,
and the prefect of Biānchéng 邊城, Sù Sēnghù 宿僧護, rose in righteousness to attack and execute him.
Xǔ Zhāoxiān 許昭先 was a man from Yìxīng 義興.
His uncle, Zhào Zhī 肇之,
was imprisoned for a crime,
and his case remained unjudged for seven years.
Among his twenty or so sons and nephews,
Zhāoxiān's 昭先 family was the poorest,
yet he alone took charge of the appeals and litigation,
never a day at home.
The provisions he sent to Zhào Zhī 肇之
were always the finest and freshest.
After his family property was exhausted,
he sold his house to fund it.
While Zhào Zhī's 肇之 other sons grew weary and negligent,
Zhāoxiān 昭先 showed no signs of slackening,
continuing thus for seven years.
Shàngshū Shěn Yǎnzhī 尚書沈演之 admired his conduct,
and Zhào Zhī's 肇之 case was thereupon resolved.
Zhāoxiān's 昭先 maternal uncle and his wife both died of an epidemic,
and their family was too poor to afford a funeral.
Zhāoxiān 昭先 sold his clothes and belongings to arrange the burial.
His uncle's three sons were all young,
and he supported and protected them until they grew up.
Zhāoxiān's 昭先 parents were both old and ill.
His family had no servants,
so he exerted himself to provide for them,
always ensuring they had good food.
His clan admired his filial piety.
Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ 雍州刺史 Liú Zhēndào 劉真道 appointed him Cónglǔ Cānjūn 征虜參軍 (General who Conquers the Barbarians' Aide),
but Zhāoxiān 昭先 declined due to his parents' old age.
His home county appointed him Zhǔbù 主簿 (Clerk),
but Zhāoxiān 昭先 again firmly declined because his uncle (Zhào Zhī 肇之) had not yet received an official post.
In the early Yuánjiā 元嘉 period,
Dǒng Yáng 董陽 of Xīyáng 西陽 shared wealth with his family for five generations,
which was praised by his village and county.
Yáo Yín 姚吟 of Kuàijī 會稽 was extremely filial to his parents.
In the early Xiàojiàn 孝建 period,
Yángzhōu 揚州 invited him to be a Wénxué Cóngshì 文學從事 (Literary Aide),
but he declined.
Yú Qímín
was a native of Jìnlíng.
From a young age, he possessed filial piety,
serving as a clerk in the district office.
His father, Zhí,
died of illness at home
in the second year of Dàmíng.
His family reported his father's illness to him,
but before the letter arrived,
Qímín said to someone:
"Recently, I've felt a pain in my flesh and a disturbance in my heart,
as if I were being cut and torn.
I've been constantly restless and startled;
there must be some unusual reason."
The letter soon arrived,
and he immediately returned.
He traveled over four hundred *lǐ*
in one day.
Upon reaching the gate,
he then learned of his father's death,
and wailed, leaped, and fainted from grief,
recovering only after a long while.
He asked his mother,
"What were father's last words?"
His mother said,
"Your father, at the point of death,
regretted not seeing you."
He said,
"What difficulty is there in seeing him?"
Thereupon, he cried out at the coffin,
and in a moment, he died.
The commandery and prefecture reported this to the emperor,
and the officials in charge submitted a memorial saying:
"Gathering the virtuous and commending the good
has been unchanged for ten thousand generations.
The utmost sincerity comes from Heaven;
how could it be different in ancient and modern times?
Qímín's innate nature originated from within,
his emotion not externally influenced.
His pure devotion was profound,
his deep heart pierced Heaven.
Kneeling to inquire about the last wishes,
he died in a single lament.
Although his actions differed from Cān and Chái,
his sincerity was equal to Qiū and Zhào.
At present, the holy tasks are widely spread,
reforming and transforming Huáxià.
Indeed, the customs are made pure by rites,
and governance is rooted solely in filial piety.
Auspicious signs respond and return;
this path is first revealed.
Qímín, rising from the common people,
his conduct permeates the living world.
Erecting a commemorative arch for his village and marking his tomb
is truly fitting now."
His village was renamed Xiàoyì Lǐ,
his rents and taxes were exempted,
and his mother was granted one hundred *hú* of grain.
Sūn Jí
was a native of Péngchéng.
In the fifth year of Shìzǔ Dàmíng,
three out of five able-bodied men were conscripted.
His younger brother, Sà, was to fill the quota.
He was imprisoned for failing to arrive by the deadline,
according to regulations,
under military law,
where his person was held in jail.
Before the case was concluded,
Jí went to the commandery and pleaded:
"I cannot bear to let my household suffer this hardship.
I beg to substitute myself for Sà."
Sà also pleaded:
"My family is not established,
and I deserve this punishment.
It was I, the foolish one, who broke the law,
it is truly my person, Sà,
who should receive the penalty according to the law.
My brother and I were orphaned young;
Sà lost his father at the age of three.
Throughout my life, my reliance
has been solely on my elder brother.
Even if my brother is to be pitied,
how can I live in this world?"
The Grand Administrator, Zhāng Dài, doubted their sincerity,
and placed Jí and Sà separately.
He told Jí:
"I have already consulted and deliberated,
allowing for the substitution."
Jí's expression was very pleased,
and he replied,
"If it is so,
then tomorrow will not be death."
He then told Sà,
who also joyfully said,
"I am willing to die,
as long as my brother is spared.
What regret would Sà have?"
Jí's wife, Xǔ, also sent a message to Jí:
"You are the head of the household;
how can you shift the blame to a younger brother?
Moreover, when the elder passed away,
he entrusted the younger brother to you.
He has not yet married,
and the family line is not established.
You already have two children;
what regret would there be in dying?"
Dài reported the matter to the emperor,
and Shìzǔ issued an edict:
"Jí and Sà, though commoners,
their integrity and conduct are commendable.
Their crime is specially pardoned."
The province offered them official positions,
and also bestowed twenty bolts of silk upon Xǔ.
Before this,
Xǔ, the wife of Xú Yuán of Xīncài,
was twenty-one years old
when her husband died.
Their son, Zhēn, was three years old.
Her father, Lǎn, pitied her youth
and had her remarry Zhāng Mǎi of the same county.
Xǔ swore she would not go.
Her father forced her into a carriage and sent her to Mǎi.
Xǔ hanged herself and lost consciousness.
Her family rushed to her,
and after a long while, she recovered.
Mǎi knew she could not be forced
and sent her back to Lǎn that night.
Xǔ returned to the Xú family
to care for Yuán's father, Jì.
In the Yuánjiā period,
at over eighty years old,
she died.
In the second year of Tàizōng Tàishǐ,
Xī Qìngsī of Chángchéng killed Qián Zhòngqī of the same county.
[一四]Zhòngqī's son, Yánqìng, was serving in the capital.
Upon hearing of his father's death,
he hurried back.
At Gēngpǔ Dài, he confronted Qìngsī,
[一五]killed him with his own hands,
and then bound himself and went to Wūchéng County jail.
The Grand Administrator of Wúxīng, Xī Yóng, memorialized not to punish him,
and it was granted.
Hé Zǐpíng
was a native of Qián, Lújiāng.
His great-grandfather, Kǎi,
was a Court Attendant (*Shìzhōng*) of the Jìn dynasty.
His grandfather, Yǒu,
was a Consultative Adjutant (*Piaojì Zīyì Cānjūn*) to Prince Dàozǐ of Kuàijī.
His father, Zǐxiān,
was the Grand Administrator of Jiàn'ān.
Zǐpíng lived in Kuàijī for generations,
and from a young age possessed integrity and conduct,
praised by his local community.
He served his mother with extreme filial piety.
He was appointed an Adjutant (*Cóngshì Shǐ*) by Yángzhōu.
With his monthly salary of white rice,
he would always trade it for millet and wheat.
Someone once asked him,
"The profit is meager;
why bother with such trouble?"
Zǐpíng said,
"My venerable elder is in the east,
unable to constantly obtain polished rice.
How can I alone enjoy finely milled grain?"
Whenever fresh delicacies were offered,
if they could not be sent to his home,
he would not accept them.
His mother was originally a concubine,
and her household registration was inaccurate.
Before she reached the age for care,
her registered age was already full.
So, he resigned from his post and returned home.
At that time, Gù Jìzhī, the General Who Guards the Army (*Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn*), was the chief administrator of the province.
He said,
"Your esteemed elder's actual age is not yet eighty,
which close relatives and friends know.
The province has a small salary;
I should petition to keep you."
Zǐpíng said,
"The government relies on the Yellow Register.
Since the registered age is reached,
I should attend to my mother in my private home.
How can I, because her actual age is not yet full,
fraudulently cling to honor and profit?
Moreover, the desire to return home and care for her
is also deeply felt by my humble self."
Jìzhī again urged him to request a county posting on the grounds of his mother's old age.
Zǐpíng said,
"Her age for care is not yet reached;
why should I falsely seek a salary?"
Jìzhī esteemed him even more.
After returning home, he exerted all his strength and effort
to provide for her needs.
In the thirtieth year of Yuánjiā,
the arch-villain perpetrated regicide.
Wáng Dàn, the Prince of Suí and General of Āndōng, launched a punitive expedition,
and Zǐpíng was appointed as an acting staff officer.
Zǐpíng believed that with the arch-villain’s perverse acts to be eliminated,
the whole world would rise up together.
Thus, he laid aside his personal convictions and accepted the position.
Once peace was restored,
he resigned voluntarily.
He was also appointed Fèngcháoqǐng,
but did not take up the post.
Finally, he was appointed Magistrate of Hǎiyú, Wújùn Commandery.
The income from the county was solely used to support his mother,
and his wife and children did not touch a single penny.
Some people were suspicious of his frugality.
Zǐpíng said:
"My aspiration for emolument is fundamentally to support my parents,
not for my own benefit."
The questioner withdrew in shame.
Upon his mother's death, he resigned from office.
His grief and emaciation exceeded the proper rites.
Whenever he wept and stamped his feet,
he would collapse and only slowly recover.
Towards the end of Dàmíng,
the eastern region suffered famine,
followed by military campaigns.
For eight years, he could not arrange for her burial.
Day and night, he cried out and stamped his feet,
ceaselessly for a moment,
his cries of mourning
were as constant as on the day he mourned.
In winter, he did not wear padded clothes,
and in summer, he avoided cool places.
Daily, he ate only a few spoonfuls of rice porridge,
without salt or vegetables.
His dwelling was dilapidated,
offering no shelter from rain or sun.
His nephew Bóyǔ gathered thatch and bamboo,
wanting to repair it for him,
but Zǐpíng refused,
saying:
"My filial duty has not yet been fulfilled.
I am merely a sinner before Heaven and Earth;
how can my house be covered?"
Cài Xīngzōng, as Administrator of Kuàijī,
greatly commended and rewarded him.
In the sixth year of Tàishǐ,
a tomb and coffin chamber were prepared for him.
Zǐpíng's mourning was so severe,
and he became so thin for such a long time,
that by the time he was relieved from mourning,
his limbs were barely connected.
From a young age, he maintained his principles,
and cultivated an excellent reputation.
Even when in a dark room,
he behaved as if receiving an important guest.
His learning and righteousness were firm and clear,
and he lived in silence.
Content with poverty and adhering to goodness,
he sought no glory or advancement.
Those who admired reclusion
esteemed him all the more.
In the first year of Shènmíng of Emperor Shùn,
he died,
at the age of sixty.
The court historian comments: In the Hàn dynasty, scholars dedicated themselves to self-cultivation,
thus loyalty and filial piety became customary.
Reaching positions where one rode in a grand carriage and wore official attire
was not possible otherwise.
Since the Jìn and Sòng dynasties,
this custom declined and righteousness was lacking.
Self-discipline and rigorous conduct
were regarded as less important than material comfort.
If filial piety was established in the household,
and loyalty recorded in history,
it often arose from the common people,
not from those in official robes and hats.
To speak of moral education based on this,
is it not a shame for the high officials and grandees?
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 52: Capable Officials
Gāozǔ rose from the common people,
understood the difficulties of the populace,
and when he ascended to the throne and became ruler,
he paid close attention to official duties.
However, his grand strategies were directed outwards,
and he had no leisure for internal affairs.
The expenses for maintaining his armies
consumed a thousand pieces of gold daily.
While he propagated leniency and simplicity,
and had no time for these things,
he curbed extravagance and suppressed desires,
restraining himself with frugality.
His attendants had no private connections to exploit,
and his private chambers had no adornments of fine silk.
Thus, he was able to wage war annually,
without disturbing the national domain.
Tàizǔ was kind and benevolent in his youth,
and inherited the great enterprise.
When difficulties arose in the Guānzhōng region,
and six barbarian tribes launched incursions,
he dispatched generals and mobilized armies
to strategize in Sī and Yǎn commanderies.
Expenses were borne by the imperial treasury,
and the people were not burdened by forced labor.
From then on, the realm enjoyed peace,
and there were no internal troubles.
For thirty years,
the populace multiplied,
and their service to the emperor and corvée labor
were limited to annual taxation.
They went out at dawn and returned at dusk,
attending to their own affairs.
The tenure of magistrates and governors
was set at six full years.
Although they might not be transferred for their entire lives,
it was not as long as in ancient times.
However, the people had someone to rely on,
and officials did not act corruptly.
Although it was difficult for every family to be self-sufficient and every person to have enough,
dying in ditches
could be avoided at that time.
In every village of a hundred households,
and every town with a market,
songs and dances
formed crowds everywhere;
this was truly the peak prosperity of the Sòng dynasty.
However, in the twenty-seventh year of Yuánjiā,
the northern barbarians invaded from the south,
and great military campaigns arose.
Even with resources drained and savings exhausted,
it was still not enough.
Consequently, heavy taxes and harsh levies were imposed,
and the whole empire was in turmoil.
From then until Xiàojiàn,
continuous warfare never ceased.
With the modest Jiāngdōng region,
whose territory was not even
several thousand *lǐ*,
and its households not exceeding a million,
combined with military campaigns,
and then famine and barrenness,
the prosperity of the Sòng clan
declined from this point.
Many emperors of the Jìn dynasty
mostly stayed in their inner chambers.
When holding court or banquets,
it was only in the two halls, east and west.
Towards the end of Emperor Xiàowǔ's reign,
the Qīngshǔ palace was just being constructed.
Gāozǔ received the mandate,
making no changes.
His residence was simply called the Western Hall,
without any grand name.
Tàizǔ followed this example,
and also referred to a "combined hall."
However, when Shìzǔ inherited the throne,
the system became extravagant and expansive.
His dogs and horses had surplus grains,
and his constructions were adorned with silk embroidery.
Disdaining previous customs,
he built the Zhèngguāng, Yùzhú, and Zǐjí halls, among others,
with carved rafters and ornate sections,
pearl windows and latticed doors.
His favored concubines and beloved ministers
were given so much that the imperial treasury was emptied,
exhausting the four seas could not satisfy his desires,
and the lives of the common people could not appease his heart.
Tàizōng succeeded to the throne,
and was even more devoted to extravagance and excess.
His benevolence did not extend to the lower classes,
leading to widespread devastation.
Officials governing the people
were frequently transferred every year.
Stoves could not be blackened,
and mats were not warmed.
The transformative influence of Pú and Mì
was not easily achieved.
Not only were officials inferior to those of ancient times,
and the people more deceitful than in the past,
but this was due to being disturbed by those above,
making good governance impossible.
Now, we select those whose conduct and traces are prominent,
and include them in the chapter on Capable Officials.
Wáng Zhènzhī, courtesy name Bózhòng,
was a native of Línyí, Lángyá.
He was the elder brother of the recluse Hóngzhī.
His great-grandfather was Yì,
General of Mounted Cavalry of the Jìn dynasty.
His grandfather was Qízhī,
a Zhongshū Láng.
His father was Suízhī,
Magistrate of Shàngyú.
Zhènzhī (鎮之) first served as Lángyá Wáng Wèijūn Xíng Cānjūn (琅邪王衞軍行參軍).
He was dispatched to be appointed as the magistrate of Shàn (剡) and Shàngyú (上虞).
Both appointments earned him a reputation for capability.
The Nèishǐ (內史), Xiè Yóu (謝輶), requested him to be the magistrate of Shānyīn (山陰),
where he again achieved outstanding success.
He was promoted to Wèijūn Cānjūn (衞軍參軍),
then Lángzhōnglìng (郎中令) of his native province,
and additionally Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍).
When Huán Xuán (桓玄) became regent for Jìn (晉),
he appointed Zhènzhī (鎮之) as Dàjiāngjūn Lùshì Cānjūn (大將軍錄事參軍).
At that time, the Sānwú (三吳) region suffered from famine.
Zhènzhī (鎮之) was sent on a mission to relieve the suffering.
However, Wáng Yú (王愉), the Huìjī Nèishǐ (會稽內史), did not comply with the imperial decree.
Zhènzhī (鎮之) reported the matter truthfully.
Yú's (愉) son, Suí (綏),
was Xuán's (玄) nephew on his mother's side.
He was powerful and influential at the time,
so Zhènzhī (鎮之) was suppressed by him.
Due to his mother's old age, he requested to be appointed Tàishǒu (太守) of Ānchéng (安成).
When Xuán (玄) was defeated,
Xuán's (玄) general Fú Hóng (苻宏) plundered and caused chaos in the commandery.
Zhènzhī (鎮之) resisted and fought for a whole year.
Five of his sons and younger brothers
were all killed in battle.
He resigned due to mourning for his mother.
While in office, he had been clean and incorruptible.
His wife and children had no means to support themselves,
so he abandoned his home to bring his mother's coffin back to her old tomb in Shàngyú (上虞).
After the burial,
he sought for his son Biāozhī (標之) to be appointed magistrate of Ānfù (安復),
and followed his son to his post.
After the mourning period concluded,
he became Cānjūn (司馬) for Zhēngxī Dàoguī (征西道規) and Nánpíng Tàishǒu (南平太守).
When Xú Dàofù (徐道覆) pressed upon Jiānglíng (江陵),
Zhènzhī (鎮之) was additionally appointed Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (建威將軍),
commanding Tán Dàojì (檀道濟) and Dào Yànzhī (到彥之) to attack Dàofù (道覆).
As he had no experience as a general or commander,
he firmly declined,
but was not listened to.
Subsequently, the vanguard suffered a defeat.
He served in an unofficial capacity
and soon resumed his original post.
For his merits in defeating Dàofù (道覆),
he was enfeoffed as a Wǔděng Nán (五等男) of Huáróng Xiàn (華容縣),
and summoned to be Tíngwèi (廷尉).
For the imperial tomb of Jìn Mùdì (晉穆帝)'s Empress Hé (何皇后),
he was appointed Lǐng Jiāngzuò Dàjiàng (領將作大匠).
He was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞).
He upheld justice without bending,
and all officials feared him.
He was dispatched as Shǐchíjié (使持節), Dūdū Jiāoguǎng Èrzhōu Zhūjūnshì (都督交廣二州諸軍事), Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (建威將軍), Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiàng (平越中郎將), and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ (廣州刺史).
Gāozǔ (高祖) said to others:
"Wáng Zhènzhī (王鎮之) showed clear accomplishments in his youth.
He will surely follow the example of Wú Yǐnzhī (吳隱之).
The ills of Língnán (嶺南)
cannot be remedied without him."
While in office, he did not accept a salary.
He was detached and had no worldly pursuits.
On the day he left office,
he was no different from when he first arrived.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) first established the Xiàngguófǔ (相國府),
he appointed Zhènzhī (鎮之) as Zīyì Cānjūn (諮議參軍),
leading Lùshì (錄事).
He was skilled in official duties,
strict but not cruel.
He was promoted to Sòngtái Cíbù Shàngshū (宋臺祠部尚書).
When Gāozǔ (高祖) ascended the throne,
Zhènzhī (鎮之) cited a foot ailment,
and was dispatched as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍) and Lángyá Tàishǒu (琅邪太守).
He was promoted to Xuānxùn Wèiwèi (宣訓衞尉),
and concurrently Lǐng Běnzhōu Dàzhōngzhèng (領本州大中正).
In the third year of Yǒngchū (永初) (422 AD),
he died in office
at the age of sixty-six.
His younger brother, Hóngzhī (弘之),
is recorded in the Yǐnyì Zhuàn (隱逸傳).
Dù Huìdù (杜慧度) was a native of Zhūlǔ (朱艪) in Jiāozhǐ (交阯).
His family originally belonged to Jīngzhào (京兆).
His great-grandfather Yuán (元)
served as Níngpǔ Tàishǒu (寧浦太守),
and consequently settled in Jiāozhǐ (交阯).
His father Yuàn (瑗), courtesy name Dàoyán (道言),
served in the provincial government as Tàishǒu (太守) of Rìnán (日南), Jiǔdé (九德), and Jiāozhǐ (交阯).
Initially,
Lǐ Xùn (李遜), the Tàishǒu (太守) of Jiǔzhēn (九真), and his sons were brave, strong, and powerful,
dominating the Jiāo (交) region.
Hearing that the Cìshǐ (刺史) Téng Dùnzhī (滕遯之) was about to arrive,
Lǐ Xùn (李遜) dispatched two of his sons to block the critical land and water passages.
Yuàn (瑗) gathered his forces and executed Xùn (遜),
bringing peace to the provincial territory.
He was appointed Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍).
Dùnzhī (遯之) stayed in the province for over ten years,
repeatedly engaging in warfare with Lín Yì (林邑).
When Dùnzhī (遯之) was about to return north,
Fàn Húdá (范胡達), the king of Lín Yì (林邑), attacked and broke through the three commanderies of Rìnán (日南), Jiǔdé (九德), and Jiǔzhēn (九真),
and then besieged the provincial capital.
At that time, Dùnzhī (遯之) had already departed far away.
Yuàn (瑗) and his third son Xuánzhī (玄之) put forth all their strength to defend steadfastly,
employing many strategic measures.
After repeated battles,
they inflicted a great defeat upon the enemy.
They pursued and attacked in Jiǔzhēn (九真) and Rìnán (日南),
achieving continuous victories,
causing Húdá (胡達) to flee back to Lín Yì (林邑).
Thereupon, Yuàn (瑗) was appointed Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) and Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ (交州刺史).
The Righteous Banner (義旗) promoted him to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍).
When Lú Xún (盧循) illegally occupied Guǎngzhōu (廣州),
he sent envoys to establish friendly relations.
Yuàn (瑗) executed them.
In the sixth year of Yìxī (義熙) (410 AD),
at the age of eighty-four,
he died.
He was posthumously granted the title Yòujiāngjūn (右將軍),
with his original post remaining as before.
Huìdù (慧度)
was Yuàn's (瑗) fifth son.
He first served as Zhōuzhǔbù (州主簿),
then Liúmín Dūhù (流民督護),
and was promoted to Jiǔzhēn Tàishǒu (九真太守).
When Yuàn (瑗) died,
the staff of the provincial government, considering that the Jiāo (交) region bordered the enemy
and should not be without a leader,
jointly nominated Huìdù (慧度) to act as head of the provincial government.
He declined the appointment.
In the seventh year (411 AD),
he was appointed Shǐchíjié (使持節), Dū Jiāozhōu Zhūjūnshì (督交州諸軍事), Guǎngwǔ Jiāngjūn (廣武將軍), and Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ (交州刺史).
Before the imperial decree arrived,
in the spring of that year,
Lú Xún (盧循) attacked and captured Hépǔ (合浦),
and then headed directly for Jiāozhōu (交州).
Huìdù (慧度) then led six thousand civil and military personnel to resist Xún (循) at Shígī (石碕).
In the battle,
they captured Xún's (循) Chángshǐ (長史) Sūn Jiànzhī (孫建之).
Although Xún (循) was defeated,
his remaining followers still numbered three thousand,
all well-trained in military affairs.
Lǐ Yì (李弈) and Lǐ Tuō (李脫), sons of Lǐ Xùn (李遜), fled to Shígī (石碕),
gathering the Lí (俚) and Láolǎo (獠) tribes,
each with their own units.
Xún (循) knew that Yì (弈) and others harbored resentment against the Dù (杜) clan,
so he sent an envoy to recruit them.
Yì (弈) and the other Lí (俚) chieftains led five or six thousand men,
accepting Xún's (循) command.
On the day Gēngzǐ (庚子) in the sixth month,
Xún (循) arrived at Nánjīn (南津) at dawn,
ordering his three armies to enter the city before eating.
Huìdù (慧度) brought out all his family's private wealth
to provide rewards.
His younger brother Huìqī (慧期), the Jiāozhǐ Tàishǒu (交阯太守), and Zhāngmín (章民), the Jiǔzhēn Tàishǒu (九真太守), both supervised the naval and land forces.
Huìdù (慧度) personally ascended a tall warship
and engaged in battle,
launching fire arrows and quailed-tail torches.
The infantry shot from both banks.
Xún's (循) ships all caught fire,
scattering and collapsing at once.
Xún (循) was hit by an arrow, jumped into the water, and died.
They beheaded Xún (循) and his father Gǔ (嘏),
as well as Xún's (循) two sons,
and relatives Ruan Jìng (阮靜), the Lùshì Cānjūn (錄事參軍), Luó Nóngfū (羅農夫), the Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (中兵參軍), Lǐ Tuō (李脫), and others.
Their heads were sent to the capital.
Huìdù (慧度) was enfeoffed as the Hóu (侯) of Lóngbiān Xiàn (龍編縣),
with a fief of one thousand households.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) ascended the throne,
Huìdù's (慧度) title was advanced to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍).
In that same year,
he led ten thousand civil and military personnel on a southern expedition against Lín Yì (林邑).
More than half of the enemy were killed,
and all previously plundered goods
were recovered.
Lín Yì (林邑) begged for surrender,
offering captives, elephants, gold, silver, ancient cotton, and other items,
whereupon they were released.
He sent Chángshǐ (長史) Jiāng Yōu (江悠) to present a memorial reporting the victory.
Huìdù (慧度) wore plain clothes and ate simple food,
being frugal and unadorned.
He could play the qín (琴),
and was quite fond of Zhuāng (莊) and Lǎo (老) (i.e., Zhuangzi and Laozi's philosophies).
He prohibited illicit cults
and diligently promoted schools.
In years of famine,
he would use his private income to provide relief.
His governance was meticulous,
like managing a household,
hence his authority and benevolence spread widely.
Crime and theft did not arise,
even to the point where city gates were not closed at night,
and nothing was picked up from the roads.
In the first year of Jǐngpíng (景平) of Shàodì (少帝) (423 AD),
he died
at the age of fifty.
He was posthumously granted the title Zuǒjiāngjūn (左將軍).
made Huìdù's eldest son, Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng Hóngwén, Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn and Cìshǐ.
Originally,
Gāozǔ campaigned north to Guān and Luò,
and Huìdù appointed Hóngwén as Yīngyáng Jiāngjūn,
commander of the roving people,
with three thousand soldiers,
to link up with the main army in the north.
When he reached Guǎngzhōu,
Guān and Luò had already been pacified,
so he returned.
The统府 (Tǒngtǔ) appointed Hóngwén as acting Jǐuzhēn Tàishǒu.
When he succeeded his father as Cìshǐ,
he also won over the people with his leniency and harmony,
and inherited the title Lóngbiān Hóu.
In the fourth year of Yuánjiā of Tàizǔ,
Wáng Huī, the Tíngwèi, was made Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ,
and Hóngwén was summoned to report.
He happened to contract a severe illness,
but was carried to the road.
His relatives and old friends, seeing his critical condition,
advised him to submit a memorial asking to wait until he recovered.
Hóngwén said:
"My family has been blessed with imperial grace for generations.
I have held office for three generations.
I always wished to devote myself to the imperial court
to repay what I have received.
How can I, when personally summoned,
remain at ease?
If I stumble,
this is fate."
Hóngwén's mother, being old,
seeing Hóngwén being carried on the road due to illness,
could not bear to be separated,
and went with him.
Upon reaching Guǎngzhōu,
he eventually died.
Before his death,
he sent his younger brother Hóngyóu to the capital.
The court greatly mourned him.
Xú Huò, courtesy name Wàntóng,
was a native of Gūmù, Dōngguǎn.
He was the nephew of Zhōngsàn Dàfū Guǎng.
His father, Miǎo,
was Jìn Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài.
At the end of Lóng'ān of Jìn Āndì,
Huò served as Tàixué Bóshì.
When Huán Xuán assisted in government,
he became Zhōngwài Dūdū.
Huò argued:
"Homage is paid only to internal and external military officials.
As the Tàizǎi and Sītú
are not military positions,
Lángyá Wáng should not be required to pay homage."
Xuán hinted to the Zhōngchéng to dismiss Huò from office.
After Xuán's defeat,
he was made Mìshū Láng,
Shàngshū Cāng Bù Láng,
then Gōngcáo under Yòujūn Hé Wújí,
and subsequently Zhènnán Cānjūn.
He also served as Cíbù,
Yǒngshì Lìng,
Jiànwǔ Sīmǎ,
Zhōngjūn Cānjūn,
and Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
In the early Yǒngchū period,
he was Xú Xiànzhī's Zhènjūn Sīmǎ,
Shàngshū Zuǒchéng,
and Shānyīn Lìng.
Having served as two chéng and in three districts,
he was astute and discerning,
and was highly regarded by his contemporaries.
In the early Yuánjiā period,
he became Shǐxīng Tàishǒu.
In the third year,
envoys were sent to inspect the four directions,
and the commanderies and counties were instructed to report on advantages and disadvantages.
Huò then submitted a memorial presenting three matters.
The first stated:
"In the large fields of the commandery,
military officers aged sixteen and above
are taxed sixty hu of rice.
Those fifteen down to thirteen
are all taxed thirty hu of rice.
Within a household, regardless of the number of able-bodied men,
all must pay rice.
However, thirteen-year-old children
are not yet capable of farm work.
Some are single and isolated,
with no one to assist them.
When they reach the age to pay tax,
they flee.
As they are close to the Mán and Lǐ,
it is easier for them to leave.
Some even mutilate themselves,
or abandon their children after birth.
The annual reduction in population
is truly due to this.
It is suggested that the tax limits be re-evaluated
to allow them to survive.
If the rice tax is reduced now,
although there will be some loss,
considering the future,
it will logically bring significant benefits."
The second stated:
"The commandery oversees more than three hundred households of silver miners.
They dig pits and extract sand, all two or three zhàng deep.
The labor is so arduous
that they disregard collapses,
and every year,
there are always deaths.
Even with strict supervision from officials,
they still evade.
Old and young follow each other,
permanently abandoning agriculture.
Over a thousand people
rely on others for food.
It is not merely that one farmer does not cultivate,
or suffers hunger.
Thus, when there is a bad harvest,
it leads to extreme hardship.
Considering that the court uses rice
no differently than silver,
it is suggested to levy rice instead of silver,
which would be immediately convenient."
The third stated:
"The Lǐ people of Zhōngsù Xiàn are taxed silver,
with each able-bodied man paying half a liǎng by the Nánchēng standard.
However, this county itself does not produce silver,
and the Lǐ people, who live in nests and speak bird-like languages,
are unfamiliar with trade practices.
Every time they buy silver,
they suffer greatly.
Moreover, weighing and receiving payment
easily leads to fraud.
The mountain Lǐ are foolish and timid,
unable to defend themselves.
The tax levied by the officials is very light,
but the people find what they pay burdensome.
If they are now allowed to pay rice according to the number of able-bodied men,
it would benefit both the public and private sectors."
He achieved remarkable results in the commandery,
and Tàizǔ praised him,
issuing an edict saying:
"Shǐxīng Tàishǒu Huò
is incorruptible and modest,
diligently serving in office.
His administration is well-managed,
and his benevolence has spread widely.
Recently, the Lingnan region has been desolate and ruined,
and his commandery was particularly affected.
He provided relief with skill,
saving them from famine.
Even the good governors of antiquity
could not surpass him.
He should be commended and honored
to mark his pure achievements.
He is to be granted two hundred rolls of silk
and one thousand hu of grain."
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Chíjǐe, Dū Guǎng Jiāo Èrzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn, Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiāng, and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Before he could be formally installed,
he died,
at the age of fifty-one.
Tàizǔ again issued an edict saying:
"Huò was incorruptible, clear-minded, diligent, and scrupulous,
and was praised by his superiors.
Therefore, he was promoted and appointed to the southern region
to fulfill his talents and aspirations.
It is unfortunate that he passed away,
and I deeply mourn him.
He is to be granted one hundred thousand coins
and one hundred bolts of cloth
to cover his funeral expenses."
Lù Huī, courtesy name Xiūyóu,
was a native of Wú Xiàn, Wú Jùn.
The commandery appointed him Mùbù,
and then he served as Cānjūn in the Wèijūn and Chējì offices,
Yángzhōu Mùbù,
and Wáng Hóng Wèijiāngjūn Mùbù.
He was appointed Shàngshū Dūguān Láng,
then transferred to serve as Jiànkāng Lìng.
He was upright and impartial,
and was highly regarded by Tàizǔ.
He was promoted to Sītú Zuǒ Xīyuán.
In the fourteenth year of Yuánjiā,
he was appointed Administrator of Shǐxīng.
The following year,

he was further appointed Commissioner with Credentials, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Jiāo and Guǎng Provinces, General Who Stabilizes Distant Regions, Colonel Who Pacifies the Yuè, and Governor of Guǎng Province.
His pure reputation was second only to Wáng Zhènzhī,
and he was beloved and praised by the gentry and common people.
He submitted a memorial recommending a scholar, stating:
"Your servant has heard that when snow covers the glorious sprouts,
the firm branches will certainly grow strong;
when noble winds cherish the flowing,
the clear springs will be gathered.
Therefore, the bag of clothes spread fame in the Western Capital,
and the broken carriage prolonged high esteem in the Eastern Empire.
I humbly observe that Zhū Wànsì, the Assistant Administrator of Guǎng Province,
aged fifty-three,
courtesy name Shàoyù,
has a gentle and unassuming character,
maintains a pure and untainted conduct,
his actions are praised in his private life,
and his abilities are evident in official administration.
Although his clan is not of hereditary nobility,
and he has no privileged access to official positions,
he has followed the imperial decrees to the southern territories,
reached the highest position among the officials,
thrice managed the provincial affairs,
and thrice held positions in the prefectural government,
frequently overseeing frontier matters,
and repeatedly achieving merit in border defense.
Now at the age of 'knowing destiny,'
his integrity and esteem are even higher;
his icy heart contends with the currents of greed,
and his frosty disposition grows stronger with his later years.
He has served as Administrator of Jīnshān,
yet his home has no ornaments of precious carvings;
he has held office in Zhūhǎi,
yet his dwelling lacks the treasures of earrings.
He steadfastly maintains his principles,
not seeking fame or advancement,
truly sufficient to purify corrupt officials
and cleanse greedy commoners.
Your servant, though unworthily holding the position of supervisor,
with sole responsibility over a vast territory,
though my feelings are solely for careful selection,
my talent is lacking in boldness,
I dare to express my humble opinion
and recommend someone I know.
If he could be named in the imperial examination hall,
and elevate his standing in the court,
gathering the pure winds from beyond the mountains,
and bearing the clean reputation of an icy realm,
then [Your Majesty's] grace would extend to one minister,
and its light would shine upon all things.
I dare to state this because Your Majesty's benevolence is like the traveling clouds,
and the virtue of the age is like the falling rain,
always distinguishing officials in outer provinces
and bestowing honor upon distant lands.
Therefore, I offer my humble words,
hoping for Your Majesty's attention."
In the twenty-first year,
he was summoned to be the Champion Marshal to Yuè, Prince of Nánpíng, and Administrator of Chángshā,
also acting as the chief official of Xiāng Province.
He left office due to mourning for his mother.
Zhāng Xún and Zhào Guǎng rebelled in Yì Province,
and after the ravages of war,
the government was neglected and the people were troubled.
In the twenty-third year,
Huī was recalled and appointed Commissioner with Credentials, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yì and Níng Provinces, General Who Stabilizes the North, and Governor of Yì Province.
He had a method for consolation and relief,
and his authority and benevolence were both evident.
Banditry ceased,
the people and resources became abundant,
and the land of Shǔ was peaceful and joyful,
praised even to this day.
In the twenty-ninth year,
he passed away
at the age of sixty-two.
On the day of his death,
his family had no surplus wealth.
Tàizǔ greatly mourned and lamented his passing.
An imperial edict stated:
"Huī dedicated himself to integrity and purity,
served diligently in every post,
was utterly devoted to public service,
and was tireless in self-restraint.
His honors were not yet fully expressed,
and he unfortunately died young.
This thought remains in my heart,
causing me sorrow and regret.
He is posthumously granted the title of General Who Assists the State,
and his original office remains as before."
He was granted one hundred thousand coins
and two hundred hù of rice.
His posthumous title was Jiǎnzǐ.
His son, Ruì,
was a Regular Supernumerary Gentleman.
His younger brother, Zhǎn,
was the Chief Clerk to Zāng Zhì, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Administrator of Xúnyáng.
When Zhì was defeated,
he was executed along with him.
Ruǎn Chángzhī, courtesy name Màojǐng,
was from Wèishì, Chénliú.
His grandfather, Sīkuàng,
was Grand Master of Gold and Purple Guanglu.
His father, Pǔ,
was Consulting Army Supervisor to the General of Agile Cavalry.
Chángzhī lost his father at the age of fifteen,
possessed filial piety,
and his grief moved those around him.
After the mourning period,
he continued to eat vegetarian food for more than a year.
He diligently studied in his leisure,
never showing any sign of idleness.
Initially, he served as Army Supervisor in various prefectures,
and was appointed Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
His mother was old,
so he requested to be appointed Magistrate of Xiāngyuán.
The postal inspector was disrespectful,
so he whipped him
and left office.
Soon after, he was appointed acting Army Supervisor to Yìzhēn, Prince of Lúlíng,
then Chief Clerk to the General Who Pacifies the Yuè,
and Administrator of Dōngguǎn.
He entered the court as Court Gentleman of the Department of the Palace Affairs in the Department of State Affairs,
and later went out as Administrator of Wǔchāng.
At that time, Wáng Hóng was the Governor of Jiāng Province,
and greatly appreciated and valued him,
appointing him Attendant-in-Ordinary to the General of Chariots and Cavalry.
He entered the court as Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince,
and Palace Attendant to the Central Secretariat.
Because his mother was old, he firmly declined to serve directly at court
and was appointed Consulting Army Supervisor to Yìkāng, Prince of Péngchéng, General Who Pacifies the North.
In the ninth year of Yuánjiā,
he was promoted to Administrator of Línchuān.
However, because the southern lands were low-lying and damp,
and his mother was old,
it was not suitable for her,
so he declined the appointment.
In the eleventh year,
he was again appointed Administrator of Línhǎi.
After a short time in the commandery, his mother passed away.
After the burial,
unable to bear his grief,
he died in the fourteenth year
at the age of fifty-nine.
At that time, the salaries for commandery and county officials
were determined by the Mángzhǒng solar term.
Those who left office before this date
would have their entire year's salary given to their successor,
[一０]while those who left office after this date
would have their entire year's salary given to their predecessor.
[一一]This system was only changed at the end of Yuánjiā,
where salaries were divided monthly.
Chángzhī left the commandery of Wǔchāng.
Before his successor arrived,
he relinquished his seals and ribbons the day before Mángzhǒng.
[一二]When he first departed from the capital,
relatives and friends sometimes gave him gifts as farewell.
He would immediately seal and record them.
Later, upon returning,
he returned them all.
While on duty in the Central Secretariat,
he once went to a neighboring department at night,
mistakenly wearing his shoes inside out when leaving the chamber.
He reported himself to the Department of the Palace Affairs according to regulations.
The Department of the Palace Affairs, knowing that no one would know in the dark of night,
did not accept the report.
Chángzhī insisted on sending it,
saying:
"I will never do anything to shame myself in the dark."
In all the offices he held,
he had good governance,
and was remembered by later generations.
Those in the Sòng dynasty who spoke of good governance
all praised him.
His son, Shīmén,
was Magistrate of Yuánxiāng.
Jiāng Bǐngzhī, courtesy name Xuánshú,
was from Kǎochéng, Jìyáng.
His grandfather, Yōu,
was Grand Minister of Sacrifices of Jìn.
His father, Zuǎn,
was Gentleman-in-Attendance.
Bǐngzhī was orphaned young.
He had seven younger siblings,
all still infants.
He raised and arranged marriages for them,
exhausting his heart and strength.
Initially, he served as Cānjūn in Liú Mùzhī's Dānyáng Former Army Prefecture.
When Gāozǔ supervised Xúzhōu,
he was transferred to Zhǔbù,
and then served as Middle Army Cānjūn to the heir apparent.
When Sòng received the abdication,
he was, as per usual, Wànyuán Sǎnqí Shìláng,
and then appointed Tàizǐ Zhānshì Céng.
When Shàodì ascended the throne,
he entered as Shàngshū Dūguān Láng,
and then went out to serve as magistrate of Yǒngshì and Wúchéng.
He became famous in the eastern regions for his good governance.
He was summoned to serve as Jìankāng Lìng.
His administration was strict and meticulous,
and the capital was orderly.
When Yīn Jǐngrén became Língjūn,
he requested Bǐngzhī as Sīmǎ.
He then went out again to serve as Shānyīn Lìng.
The population was thirty thousand,
and administrative matters were cumbersome,
with lawsuits piling up.
Hundreds of people were constantly at his doorstep.
Bǐngzhī managed the complexities with simplicity,
and often remained unburdened by affairs.
In the Sòng era, only Gù Jìzhī also achieved merit through simplifying duties;
the others, though they reformed and managed punishments and administration,
〔一三〕were unable to simplify affairs.
Due to his competence in the county,
he was promoted to Xīn'ān Tàishǒu.
In the twelfth year of Yuánjiā,
he was transferred to Línhǎi,
and was praised for his simplicity and frugality in both posts.
All the salary and rank he received
he distributed to his relatives and old friends.
His wife and children often suffered from hunger and cold.
When someone advised him to acquire land,
Bǐngzhī, with a stern expression, said:
"How can a family that receives official salary
compete with farmers for profit?"
While in the commandery, he made one writing desk.
When he left office,
he left it to be deposited in the treasury.
In the seventeenth year,
he died,
aged sixty.
His son, Huī,
was Shàngshū Dūguān Láng
and Wú Lìng.
When Yuánxiōng killed Xú Zhànzhī,
Huī was executed for his association.
His son, Mì,
was Shàngshū Lìbù Láng at the end of Shēngmíng.
In early Yuánjiā,
Tàizǔ sent grand envoys to tour the four directions.
Kǒng Mòzhī and Wáng Xīnzhī, who were concurrently Sǎnqí Chángshì, among others, memorialized, saying:
"Lǐ Yuándé, General Wēiwēi and Tàishǒu of the two commanderies of Chén and Nándùn,
is diligent, fair, and impartial,
and has stopped villainy and theft.
Wèi Gōngzǐ, Inner Historian of Péngchéng,
is incorruptible, cautious, and circumspect,
forgetting personal interests in public service,
content with simplicity and upholding frugality,
becoming firmer over time.
Chéng Pǔ, former magistrate of Sòng County,
governed with leniency and generosity,
leaving behind a lasting memory among the people.
Lǐ Xīguó, former magistrate of Tóngyáng,
had effective methods in his administration,
and the people remember his governance.
Hé Dào, magistrate of Shānsāng,
has been pure and incorruptible since youth,
and has become even more rigorous in old age.
They should be commended and rewarded,
to encourage those who follow."
Thereupon, Yuándé was promoted to the title of General Níngshuò;
Gōngzǐ was bestowed fifty bolts of silk
and five hundred hú of grain;
Pǔ, Xīguó, and Dào were each bestowed thirty bolts of silk
and two hundred hú of grain.
Wáng Xīnzhī, courtesy name Shúdào,
was a native of Hédōng.
His great-grandfather, Qiānqī,
was famous in the Jìn era,
and rose to the office of Nánmán Xiàowèi.
His grandfather, Xúnzhī,
was Guānglù Dàfū.
His father, Zhàozhī,
was Yùzhāng Gōngxiàng.
Xīnzhī was favored by Tàizǔ,
and held prominent offices such as Zuǒmín Shàngshū
and Guānglù Dàfū.
He died in office.
In the ninth year of Yuánjiā,
Liú Yìxīn, Prince of Chángshā and Governor of Yùzhōu, memorialized, saying:
"Shēn Jìlì, Marquis of Guānzhōng, General Wēiyuǎn, and Tàishǒu of the two commanderies of Běiqiáo and Liáng, who is under my jurisdiction,
has served in the state's capital region
for five years now.
His trustworthiness and benevolence are both manifest,
and his authority and transformative influence are both evident.
Externally, he has suppressed villainy and violence;
internally, he has unified the people.
Taxes and levies are fair and equitable,
and the villages are orderly and solemn.
He has pacified and brought peace to newly attached people,
and attracted the distant and remote.
Beyond the borders of the commandery,
people look up to his benevolence and embrace his influence.
The bestowal of爵賞
highlights his achievements and abilities.
He should be promoted in rank and office,
to greatly encourage and reward him."
He was promoted to the title of General Níngshuò.
Thereafter, Guō Qǐxuán, Tàishǒu of Jìnshòu, also demonstrated integrity and frugality,
and died in office.
In the twenty-eighth year of Yuánjiā,
an imperial edict stated:
"The late Guō Qǐxuán, General Suíyuǎn and Tàishǒu of Jìnshòu, once undertook a mission to the barbarian court,
upholding his integrity unyieldingly.
He was entrusted with the post of Báishuǐ,
and exerted himself tirelessly.
He offered his personal provisions to the public,
not accepting even a thread of profit.
In plain clothes and vegetarian diet,
he disciplined himself with frugality.
Therefore, he was exceptionally granted a prominent state [post],
to recognize his incorruptible service.
Yet his steadfast honesty and bitter self-denial
remained constant from beginning to end.
On the day of his death,
his wife and children suffered from cold and hunger.
His will and conduct surpassed the ordinary,
truly worthy of lamentation.
His family is to be granted five hundred hú of grain."
At that time, Fù Sēngyòu of Běidì, Chén Mín of Yǐngchuān, and Zhāng Yòu of Gāopíng
were all recognized for their administrative talent.
Sēngyòu's deeds are recorded in the biography of Zāng Táo.
Mín served as Wú Lìng,
and was skilled at uncovering hidden evils,
leading the region to regard him as divine.
Yòu's grandfather, Zhàn,
was Zhōngshū Shìláng
and Guānglù Xūn
during Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn's reign, due to his talent and scholarship.
Yòu successively served as magistrate of Lín'ān, Wǔkāng, and Qiántáng,
all with notable competence.
In the Sòng era, when speaking of chief officials,
these three were considered foremost.
During the Yuánjiā period,
Pān Cí, Tàishǒu of Gāopíng,
had a reputation for integrity and frugality.
His son, Liàng, served as Chānglǜ Lìng,
and also acquired a reputation for incorruptibility.
During the Dàmíng period,
he was recommended by Liú Dàolóng, Governor of Xúzhōu.
During Shìzǔ's reign,
Lù Fǎzhēn of Wú Commandery held various offices with integrity and frugality.
He once served as Anběi Lùshì Cānjūn under Liú Xiùzhī.
Yáng Xī of Tàishān wrote to Sūn Shēn, Cānjūn of Anběi, saying:
"Among your colleagues, there seems to be a Lù Lùshì.
This man, from a famous region in the southeast,
and also the maternal grandson of Zhāng Xuán,
conducts himself with utmost purity
and possesses a refined will and integrity.
Despite his advanced age and low office,
his integrity does not wane.
I expect we will express our sentiments to each other daily."
In early Tàizōng,
he served as Nánhǎi Tàishǒu,
and died in office.
During the reign of Tàizōng,
Wáng Yuè, Prince of Lángxié,
was also known for his clean and upright governance.
Yuè's courtesy name was Shàomíng,
and he was the great-grandson of Wáng Xīzhī, General of the Right in the Jìn dynasty.
His father, Jìngzhī,
rose to the office of Chief Clerk of the Left in the Ministry of the Grand Chancellor.
Jìngzhī was held in high regard by Liú Mùzhī,
and repeatedly asked Mùzhī for the position of Grand Master of Remonstrance.
This happened more than once.
Mùzhī said:
"If you did not ask,
you would have obtained it on your own long ago."
Consequently, he did not get it.
In the Tàishǐ reign, Yuè
served as Yellow Gate Attendant and
Imperial Censor.
The Emperor, recognizing his integrity,
bestowed upon him five qīng of fertile land.
He was promoted to Director of the Bureau of Personnel in the Ministry of Personnel
and Grand Master of Remonstrance.
In the Palace Gate Department,
he dedicated all his heart and effort.
After five years,
he died in office
and was posthumously granted the title of Grand Master of Ceremonies.
Earlier,
when Yuè was Grand Master of Remonstrance,
he inspected the various departments of the Imperial Treasury, Grand Provisioner, and Imperial Physicians,
discovering many fraudulent practices.
When Yuè died,
everyone believed that the various departments had cursed him.
The Emperor then arrested over ten of the custodians,
shackling them and claiming to send them to Huáinán.
Secretly, he ordered them to cross the Guāpù River
and throw them into the middle of the current.
The historiographer remarks: Good governance towards the people
is like a skilled artisan working with clay:
little effort is expended, but many vessels are made.
During the Hàn dynasty, the population was numerous and prosperous,
penal affairs were simple and broad,
district and county officials governed the people
without arbitrary interference.
Rewards were encouraged and punishments were enforced;
matters were largely decided independently.
Edicts were rarely issued
to the various states and commanderies.
The transformations wrought by Gōng and Huáng
were easily achieved.
As later generations descended,
deceit and falsehood arose in great numbers.
The population decreased from former times,
while affairs multiplied compared to earlier eras.
To establish achievements and pass on a legacy
became a hundred times more difficult.
If one were to govern the people of this age
with the transformations of antiquity,
or if today's good officials
were to guide the customs of former generations,
then the zither-playing and singing in Wǔchéng
might not even have time to begin,
and the peaceful governance of Huáiyáng
would perhaps be barely achievable.
It is not necessarily that today's talents are inferior to those of old;
rather, the nature of governance has become purer or baser.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 53: Recluses
The Yìjīng says:
"Heaven and Earth are closed,
and worthy persons are hidden."
It also says:
"To withdraw from the world without regret."
It also says:
"To highly value one's affairs."
It also says:
"A reclusive person is firm and auspicious."
The Lúnyǔ states:
"There were seven who composed,"
designating them as "hermit-scholars."
It also says:
"Zǐlù encountered the old man carrying a basket,
and Kǒngzǐ said: 'He is a recluse.'"
It also says:
"The worthy avoid a specific place,
the next avoid specific words."
It also says:
"Yú Zhòng,
㠯逸 (Yǐyì),
lived in seclusion and spoke freely."
The categories vary,
and the appellations are not uniform.
Please allow me to try and explain.
The meaning of "yin" (隱, hidden) is:
that one's traces are not externally seen,
and one's Way cannot be known.
If for a thousand years there is desolation,
and a sage does not appear,
then a great worthy hides himself,
descending to ordinary ranks,
stopping only at preserving his life and avoiding harm.
He does not necessarily live in caves or on cliffs.
Although he hides his past and gains the second,
neighbored by the utmost truth,
yet the whole world cannot glimpse him,
and the myriad things do not perceive him.
Would such a person
consent to wash his ears by the Yǐng River,
conspicuously displaying his will to transcend the common world?
To withdraw from the world or avoid the world,
that is the worthy person.
How can there be any place that is not "the world"
to have a reason for "avoiding the world"?
It is certain that the meaning lies in obscuring one's Way,
not in hiding oneself.
As for the name of Cháofù,
it is an appellation by which he was known.
He was called Qiúgōng,
implying traceable deeds.
This is the "hermit-scholar" type of reclusion,
and not the reclusion of a worthy person.
The reclusion of a worthy person
is deeper in its meaning of self-obscurity.
The reclusion of a hermit-scholar
is limited to avoiding others.
Since their traces differ,
their original intentions are also different.
When one's person and fortune are closed off,
there are no feelings that can be known.
To host guests with chicken and millet
demonstrates the virtue of transcending the world.
One is hidden because fortune is closed off,
so the traces of one's reclusion are not seen.
One is hidden because one avoids others,
thereby earning the title of "recluse."
One is called a "recluse" because the body is hidden.
One is called a "worthy person" because the Way is hidden.
Someone might say:
"I have heard the explanation of the difference between a 'recluse' and being 'hidden.'
But what is the difference between a 'worthy person' and being 'worthy'?"
I reply:
"The hiding of oneself versus the obscuring of the Way
have similar names but different meanings.
The worthy person versus the worthy
culminates in being near a sage.
Speaking thus,
perhaps a distinction can be made.
As for 'highly valuing one's affairs' and 'the composers,'
'the three avoidances' and 'the reclusive person,'
as well as 'hermit-scholars' and 'living in seclusion,'
all are appellations for those who go their own way.
Even if the family name of Hànyīn is not transmitted,
and the name of Héshàng is not prominent,
none of them fail to spur the greedy and purify customs,
holding a self-distinguishing demeanor,
like carrying the sun and moon,
beating a standing drum and hurrying forth."
Yuán Shū of Chénjùn compiled a collection of ancient unnamed lofty scholars,
considering them "true recluses."
Judging by this discussion,
they are far from true.
When worthy persons are in the world,
their deeds cannot be misrepresented.
Now, in writing the chapter on Recluses,
I shall empty the position of "worthy recluse."
As for others whose hearts transcend worldly concerns,
they are "hermits" but not "recluses."
Dài Yǒng, courtesy name Zhòngruò,
was a native of Zhì in Qiáojùn.
His father Kuí
and elder brother Bó
were both recluses of high repute.
Dài Yǒng, at sixteen,
suffered the sorrow of his father's death,
almost to the point of collapse,
and thereafter bore a chronic illness.
Since his father had not served in office,
he resumed his father's profession.
His father was skilled in the zither and calligraphy,
and Dài Yǒng inherited both.
As for all aspects of music,
he could play them with a wave of his hand.
Kuàijī's Shàn Xiàn had many famous mountains,
so the family had long resided in Shàn Xià.
Dài Yǒng and his elder brother, Bó,
both learned the zither from their father.
After their father passed away,
they could not bear to play
the tunes he had taught,
so each composed new pieces.
Bó composed five sets,
and Dài Yǒng composed fifteen sets.
Dài Yǒng also created one long set,
which were all transmitted to posterity.
The Grand Secretariat Administrator, Wáng Suí, often brought guests to visit them.
As Bó and others were serving bean porridge,
Wáng Suí said,
"I hear you are skilled in the zither;
I'd like to hear you play once."
They did not reply,
so Wáng Suí left in resentment.
Tónglú Xiàn also had many famous mountains,
so the brothers again traveled there together,
and consequently settled there.
When Bó fell ill,
and medicine was unavailable,
Dài Yǒng said to Bó,
"I have followed my brother and enjoyed leisure,
not deliberately seeking silence or speech.
Now, my brother is seriously ill,
with no means to provide for treatment.
I must seek official emolument to sustain ourselves."
So he requested at the time to be the Magistrate of Hǎiyú.
The matter was about to proceed when Bó died,
so he stopped.
Tónglú was remote
and unsuitable for convalescence,
so he moved to reside in Wú Xià.
The literati of Wú Xià collectively built a house for him,
gathered stones, drew water,
planted trees, and opened up streams.
In a short time, it became lush and dense,
as if natural.
He then expounded upon Zhūang Zhōu's main ideas,
writing the Xiāoyáo Lùn,
and annotating the Zhōngyōng chapter of the Lǐjì.
The generals and governors of the Sān Wú region and the gentry within the commandery would invite him to roam the wilderness.
If it was feasible to go, he would go,
not being pretentious or aloof.
The public greatly praised him for this.
Gāozǔ appointed him as Grand Commandant's Adjutant
and Administrator for Lángyá Wáng Sīmǎ,
but he did not accept either.
When the Sòng state was first established,
an edict stated:
"Former Grand Commandant Adjutant Dài Yǒng and recruited scholar Wéi Xuán,
upholding their reclusive principles,
and steadfast in their resolve,
should be recognized and promoted
to encourage those who withdraw.
Both are to be Sànqí Shìláng,
serving in the Tōngzhí office."
He did not take up the post.
In the second year of Tàizǔ Yuánjiā's reign,
an edict stated:
"Newly appointed Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng Dài Yǒng and Prince's Clerk Zōng Bǐng
have both placed their aspirations in hills and gardens,
seeking humble dwellings for themselves.
Their tranquil and resolute conduct
has remained unchanged for a long time.
Dài Yǒng is to be Guózǐ Bóshì,
and Zōng Bǐng is to be Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng."
When the Eastern Palace was first established,
he was again summoned to be Prince's Principal Secretary.
In the fifteenth year,
he was summoned to be Sànqí Chángshì,
but he did not accept any of these.
When Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì was stationed at Jīngkǒu,
his Chief Clerk Zhāng Shào, who had marital ties with Dài Yǒng,
welcomed him to stay at Huánghú Shān.
To the north of the mountain was the Zhúlín monastery,
with beautiful forests and streams.
Dài Yǒng rested by these streams.
Yìjì often joined him for excursions.
Dài Yǒng wore his rustic clothes,
not changing his usual demeanor.
He played the zither for Yìjì,
composing new tunes and variations.
His "Sāndiào Yóuxián," "Guǎnglíng," and "Zhǐxī" styles,
were all different from those of the time.
Tàizǔ always wanted to see him,
and once said to the Imperial Secretary Zhāng Fū,
"When I tour the east,
I shall feast on Dài Gōng Shān."
Because of his love for music,
he was perpetually provided with a troupe of "Zhèngshēng" musicians.
Dài Yǒng combined the "Hécháng" and "Báihú" tunes
into one,
calling it "Qīngkuàng."
Since the Hàn dynasty, Buddha statues first appeared,
but their craftsmanship was not yet refined.
Kuí was especially skilled in this craft,
and Dài Yǒng also participated.
The Sòng crown prince cast a sixteen-foot bronze statue at Wǎguān Sì.
After it was completed,
the face was regrettably thin.
The craftsmen could not rectify it,
so Dài Yǒng was invited to examine it.
Dài Yǒng said,
"It's not that the face is thin;
rather, the arms and shoulders are too fat."
After reducing the arms and shoulders,
the problem of the thinness immediately disappeared,
and everyone marveled in admiration.
In the eighteenth year,
he died,
at the age of sixty-four.
He had no sons.
When Jǐngyáng Shān was completed,
Dài Yǒng had already passed away.
The Emperor sighed and said,
"I regret that I cannot have Dài Yǒng see it."
Zōng Bǐng, courtesy name Shàowén,
was a native of Nièyáng, Nányáng.
His grandfather, Chéng,
was the Administrator of Yídū.
His father, Yáozhī,
was the Magistrate of Xiāngxiāng.
His mother, of the same commandery, née Shī,
was intelligent, eloquent, and learned in righteousness,
teaching her sons.
Zōng Bǐng observed mourning rites beyond what was prescribed,
for which he was praised by his local community.
The Provincial Governors Yīn Zhòngkān and Huán Xuán both recruited him as Chief Clerk
and recommended him as a Xiùcái,
but he did not accept.
When Gāozǔ executed Líu Yì,
he took charge of Jīngzhōu.
He asked Líu Yì's Consultative Adjutant Shēn Yǒng,
"What should be done today?"
Shēn Yǒng replied,
"Remove their old grievances,
double their beneficence,
visit door to door,
and conspicuously promote talent.
That is all."
Gāozǔ accepted this
and recruited Zōng Bǐng as Chief Clerk,
but he did not accept.
When asked why,
he replied,
"I have lived in the hills and drunk from the valleys
for over thirty years."
Gāozǔ praised his reply.
He was exceptionally skilled in the zither and calligraphy,
and proficient in philosophical discourse.
Whenever he traveled to scenic mountains and rivers,
he would always forget to return.
The Western Punitive Commander's Chief Clerk, Wáng Jìnghóng, often accompanied him,
and never failed to stay for an entire day.
He then went down to Lúshān
to consult with Shì Huìyuǎn on texts and meanings.
His elder brother, Zāng, became the Administrator of Nánpíng,
and compelled him to return together.
So he established a residence in Sānhú, Jiānglíng,
living a life of leisure without official duties.
Gāozǔ summoned him to be the Grand Commandant's Adjutant,
but he did not accept.
His two elder brothers died early,
leaving many orphans and dependents.
His family was poor and had no means to support them,
so he somewhat engaged in farming.
Gāozǔ repeatedly sent provisions and gifts.
Later, when his nephews and younger brothers gained official positions,
he then completely stopped accepting them.
Gāozǔ established his administration and issued a summons.
He wrote a letter saying:
"I am honored with great favor,
and wish to attract worthy and eminent individuals.
However, those like the 'rabbit snares' are hidden away,
and 'Kǎo Pán' has not yet arrived.
My mat is restless, thinking of them in their hills and gardens,
greatly increasing my vain anticipation.
Zōng Bǐng from Nányáng and Zhōu Xùzhī from Yànmén
both possess noble integrity and dwell in seclusion,
untroubled by their humble garments.
They may be summoned
and persuaded with禮."
Consequently, they were both appointed as Taìwèi Yuàn,
but neither accepted.
When the Sòng dynasty received the abdication,
he was summoned as Taìzǐ Shèrén;
in the early Yuánjiā period,
he was again summoned as Tōngzhí Láng;
when the Eastern Palace was established,
he was summoned as Taìzǐ Zhōngshèrén
and Shùzǐ,
but did not respond to any of these.
His wife, Lady Luó,
also had a noble spirit
and shared his interests.
When Lady Luó died,
Bǐng grieved excessively for her.
After a while, he stopped crying and sought reason,
and his sorrowful emotions immediately dissipated.
He said to the Shāmén Shì Huìjiān:
"The distinction between life and death
is not easily understood.
After repeatedly reflecting on the profound teachings,
I was finally able to put aside my grief."
Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì, while in Jīngzhōu,
personally visited Bǐng's chamber,
enjoyed a banquet with him,
and ordered him to be Cányì Cānjūn,
but he did not accept.
He loved mountains and rivers
and enjoyed extensive travels.
Westward he climbed Jīng and Wū,
southward he ascended Héngyuè,
and then built a dwelling on Héngshān,
intending to embrace the ambition of Shàngpíng.
When he fell ill and returned to Jiānglíng,
he sighed:
"Old age and illness have both arrived.
I fear it will be difficult to see all the famous mountains.
I can only purify my mind, contemplate the Dao,
and roam them while lying down."
All the places he had traveled
he depicted in his room.
He said to people:
"I play the qín and move its strings,
wishing to make all the mountains resonate."
There was an ancient melody called Jīnshí Nòng,
highly valued by the various Huán families.
When the Huán clan fell,
its sound was lost,
and only Bǐng preserved it.
Taìzǔ sent the music master Yáng Guān to Bǐng to learn it.
Bǐng's maternal cousin Shī Juéshòu also had an innate talent
and found joy in the qín and books.
Línchuān Wáng Yìqì summoned him as Jìjiǔ
and Zhǔbù,
but he did not accept.
He then submitted a memorial recommending him,
but he died of illness at that time.
In the twentieth year of Yuánjiā,
Bǐng died,
aged sixty-nine.
Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì wrote to Sītú Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng, saying:
"Recluse Zōng did not recover from his illness.
His pure conduct and simple lifestyle
were commendable from beginning to end.
I feel deeply saddened by this,
and cannot stop."
His son, Shuò,
was Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān's Chējì Cānjūn.
His second son, Qǐ,
was Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng's Sīkōng Zhǔbù.
His third son, Zhāo,
was Yǐngzhōu Zhìzhōng.
His fourth son, Shuō,
was Zhèngyuán Láng.
Zhōu Xùzhī, courtesy name Dàozǔ,
was a native of Guǎngwǔ, Yànmén.
His ancestors, after crossing the river, lived in Jiànchāng County, Yùzhāng.
When Xùzhī was eight years old, his mother died,
and his grief was more profound than that of an adult.
He served his elder brother as he would his father.
Fàn Níng, the Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng, established a school in the commandery
and gathered students.
Many came from distant places.
Xùzhī, at the age of twelve,
went to Níng to receive instruction.
He studied at the school for several years,
mastering the Five Classics and the apocryphal texts.
His reputation surpassed that of his fellow students,
and he was called
"Yánzǐ."
Afterwards, he lived in seclusion, studying Lǎozi and Yìjīng,
and entered Lúshān to serve the Shāmén Shì Huìyuǎn.
At that time, Líu Yímín of Péngchéng had retired to Lúshān,
and Táo Yuānmíng also refused official summons.
They were called the Three Recluses of Xúnyáng.
He believed that though the body could not be abandoned,
other worldly entanglements should be severed.
Thus, he remained unmarried his entire life,
wore coarse clothes, and ate vegetarian food.
When Líu Yì garrisoned Gūshú,
he appointed him as Fǔjūn Cānjūn,
and he was summoned as Taìxué Bóshì,
but he did not accept either.
The Prefect of Jiāngzhōu often invited him,
and Xùzhī, not adhering strictly to lofty principles,
somewhat associated with them.
He often praised Jī Kāng's Gāoshì Zhuàn for its beauty in depicting choosing to serve or retire,
and thus wrote annotations for it.
When Gāozǔ went on his northern expedition,
the crown prince remained in charge.
He invited Xùzhī to stay at Ānlè Sì,
and invited him to lecture on rites.
After more than a month,
he returned to the mountains.
The Prefect of Jiāngzhōu, Líu Liǔ, recommended him to Gāozǔ, saying: "Your humble servant has heard that to spread glory and generosity
requires the treasures that encompass cities;
to assist and uphold the fundamental principles,
it is fitting to bestow grace upon the recluse who transcends the age.
Thus, Wèibīn assisted Zhōu,
and sagely virtue broadly
prospered;
Shāngluò assisted Hàn,
and heroic achievements then flourished.
I humbly believe that your illustrious lord's Dao surpasses that of ancient times,
responding to Heaven and continuing the era.
Your external wanderings are reflected in the profound inner world,
and your distant essence is manifested in the nearby
manifestations.
Though Fényáng's endeavor
halted his carriage during difficult times;
the intent of 'brightly elevating'
subtly moves even within deep valleys.
I have secretly observed the recluse Zhōu Xùzhī from Yànmén.
He is pure, sincere, and simple,
and his thoughts and learning delve deeply.
At a young age, he chose a solitary path,
with no worldly concerns in his heart.
What his nature discards,
glory and splendor
fall away just like hunger and cold.
What his heart admires,
mountains and wetlands are as distant as the qín and books.
Furthermore, his benevolent heart is internally manifested,
and his righteous spirit shines externally.
He cherishes the love for rare plants,
and his sincerity
is evident in the peach and plum.
If he were to ascend to the prime minister's office,
the flavors of the cauldron would surely be harmonious;
if he were to wash his cap string in a Confucian official post,
the king's achievements would also be broadly gathered.
Zāng Wén's ignorance
resulted in the failure to promote the worthy;
Yán
Yǎn gained worthy men,
and his success came from promoting scholars.
I wish you would shine upon his sincere devotion,
and not dismiss his words because of the person."
Shortly after, he was appointed to a post as Grand Commandant's clerk,
but did not accept it.
When Gāozǔ campaigned in the north,
and returned to garrison Péngchéng,
he sent an envoy to welcome him,
treating him with great courtesy and generous gifts.
He often praised him, saying:
"With no bias or meanness in his heart,
he is a true noble scholar."
Soon, he returned south again.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he summoned him again,
and this time, he brought his whole family down.
The emperor opened a school for him outside the eastern city wall,
inviting students to gather there.
The imperial carriage descended to visit,
and he met all the students,
asking Xùzhī about the three interpretations in the Lǐjì (Book of Rites):
"cannot be prolonged,"
"give me nine years,"
and
"shooting at Juépǔ."
His analyses were profound and subtle,
and he was lauded as being comprehensive and thorough.
Xùzhī had always suffered from rheumatic paralysis
and could no longer manage lecturing,
so he reported illness and moved to Zhōngshān.
He died in the first year of Jǐngpíng
at the age of forty-seven.
His mastery of the six principles of the Máoshī (Classic of Poetry),
as well as the Lǐlùn (Discourses on Rites) and Gōngyángzhuàn (Gongyang Commentary),
were all transmitted to posterity.
He had no sons.
His elder brother's son, Jǐngyuǎn, had Xùzhī's demeanor,
and during Tàizōng's Tàishǐ reign,
he was appointed Administrator of Jìn'ān,
but died before reaching the commandery.
Wáng Hóngzhī, courtesy name Fāngpíng,
was from Línyí, Lángxié.
He was the younger brother of Xuānxùn Wèiwèi Zhèn.
Orphaned and poor in his youth,
he was raised by his maternal grandfather, the recluse Hé Zhǔn.
His paternal cousin Xiànzhī and Wáng Gōng of Tàiyuán
both held him in high regard.
During the Lóng'ān reign of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
he served as Aide to the Central Army of the Prince of Lángxié,
and later promoted to Principal Clerk to the Grand Minister of Education.
His family was poor,
but he had a fondness for mountains and rivers,
so he sought the post of Magistrate of Wūchéng.
Soon after, he resigned due to illness.
When Huán Xuán assisted the Jìn dynasty,
Huán Qiān appointed him Aide to the General of the Guards.
At that time, Yīn Zhòngwén of Lángxié was returning to Gūshú,
and the entire court saw him off.
Qiān invited Hóngzhī to accompany them,
but he replied:
"Farewells and send-offs
must be based on genuine affection.
This humble official and Yīn are not acquainted;
I have no reason to accompany him."
Qiān valued his words.
His mother followed his elder brother Zhèn to Ānchéng Commandery,
and Hóngzhī resigned his post to accompany them.
Huán Wěi, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, invited him to be Chief Clerk for the Southern Barbarians.
In the early Yìxī period,
Hé Wúzhì again invited him to be Right Army Cavalry Commander.
Gāozǔ appointed him Administrator of Xúzhōu,
and then Supernumerary Gentleman-in-Waiting,
but he did not accept either post.
His family resided in Shàngyú, Kuàijī.
His paternal cousin Jìnghóng, who was Minister of Personnel,
submitted a memorial stating:
"The sagely ruler holds the mandate,
renewing virtue,
observing the humble and obscure,
and honoring those who live in seclusion.
The silent and the eloquent alike look up to your virtuous influence,
and even those in distant wildernesses incline their heads.
The former Supernumerary Gentleman-in-Waiting, Wáng Hóngzhī of Lángxié,
is tranquil in his fields and gardens,
at peace in his reclusion.
The former Aide to the General of the Guards, Guō Xīlín of Wǔchāng,
possesses a pure character,
inheriting the glory of past martial figures.
Both are content under this sagely dynasty,
but have not yet been publicly honored.
It is fitting to grant them recognition and appointments,
adorning their humble abodes,
to manifest the beauty of modesty and humility,
and to dispel the burden of seeking advancement.
Your humble servant suggests that Hóngzhī be appointed Heir Apparent's Household Administrator,
and Xīlín be appointed Editor-in-Chief."
Hóngzhī was immediately summoned to be Heir Apparent's Household Administrator,
but he did not accept.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
Jìnghóng became Left Grandee Secretary,
and again stated:
"Hóngzhī's noble conduct was evident from his youth,
and his strict integrity shines in his later years.
Now that there is peace both internally and externally,
it is time to cultivate the transformation of great peace.
It is fitting to invite recluses,
to uphold the virtue of humility and retreat."
In the fourth year of Yuánjiā,
he was summoned to be Gentleman-in-Waiting of the Palace,
but again did not accept.
Jìnghóng once gave him a sable fur coat,
which he immediately wore to gather herbs.
He was fond of fishing.
There was a place in the Shàngyú River called Sānshítou,
where Hóngzhī often cast his line.
Passersby did not recognize him,
and some asked:
"Fisherman, do you sell the fish you catch?"
Hóngzhī replied:
"I don't catch any myself,
and if I did, I wouldn't sell them."
At dusk, he would carry fish into Shàngyú City,
and as he passed the gates of relatives and old friends,
he would place one or two fish inside their gates and leave.
There were beautiful mountains and waters in Wòchuān, Shǐníng,
and Hóngzhī built a house there by the cliffs.
Xiè Língyùn and Yán Yánzhī both respected and admired him.
Língyùn wrote a memorial to Lúlíngwáng Yìzhēn, saying:
"The Kuàijī region abounds in mountains and waters,
which is why many of the distinguished recluses south of the Jiāng River
have chosen to live there.
However, in these latter days, people are eager for glory,
and few live in secluded retirement.
Some, though talented, are sought after by the times,
and cannot follow their own aspirations.
But as for Wáng Hóngzhī, who cast off his robes and returned to farming,
having done so for over thirty years;
Kǒng Chúnzhī, who lived in obscurity in remote mountains,
from beginning until now;
Ruǎn Wànlíng, who resigned from affairs to embrace leisure,
carrying on his ancestors' pursuits;
beyond the Zhè River,
those who dwell in mountains and marshes
are just like these.
They are not only comparable to Xī and Táng of ancient times,
but also inspire the greedy and incite the competitive.
Your Highness loves simplicity and cherishes antiquity,
always seeming like a commoner,
often reflecting on tales of the past,
and imagining hermits in their caves.
If you were to send an envoy
to visit them,
it would truly be a splendid and beautiful deed for a thousand years."
Hóngzhī died in the fourth year [of Yuánjiā],
at the age of sixty-three.
Yán Yánzhī wanted to compose a eulogy for him,
and wrote to Hóngzhī's son Tánshēng, saying:
"Your family's noble integrity,
revered by the discerning,
should be recorded and narrated
by the brush.
Moreover, I have long admired your father's example,
and secretly take virtue as my task,
but regret that my humble writing is insufficient to praise his beauty."
The eulogy was never completed.
Tánshēng was fond of literature and righteousness,
and was praised for his humility and gentleness.
He held prominent positions,
including Minister of Personnel
and Grand Master of Ceremonies.
At the end of Dàmíng,
he was Governor of Wúxīng.
At the beginning of Tàizōng's reign,
when the four directions rebelled together,
he was defeated in battle and fled to Kuàijī,
surrendered and was pardoned,
finally dying as a Gentleman of the Palace.
Ruǎn Wànlíng was
from Wèishì, Chénliú.
His grandfather, Sīkuàng,
was Left Grand Master of Glorious Happiness.
His father, Níng,
was Palace Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
Wàn Líng (萬齡) became famous at a young age.
He served as Mèng Chǎng’s (孟昶) jianwěi chángshǐ (建威長史) after being a tōngzhí láng (通直郎).
At that time, Yuán Bào (袁豹) and Jiāng Yí (江夷) successively served as Chǎng’s (昶) sīmǎ (司馬).
Contemporaries referred to Chǎng’s (昶) administration as having "three men of plain reputation."
Wàn Líng’s (萬齡) family resided in Kuàijī Shànxiàn (會稽剡縣).
He harbored a considerable plain sentiment.
At the end of the Yǒngchū (永初) era,
he resigned from his post as shìzhōng (侍中) and returned to the east.
He was summoned to serve as mìshū jiān (祕書監)
and given the additional title of jǐshì zhōng (給事中),
but he did not accept.
Soon after, he was appointed zuǒmín shàngshū (左民尚書),
and again rose to accept the summons.
He was promoted to tàicháng (太常),
then sent out to be the cìshǐ (刺史) of Xiāngzhōu (湘州).
He achieved no administrative merits in the province.
Upon his return, he became the tàishǒu (太守) of Dōngyáng (東陽),
but was again dismissed.
He then served as sànqí chángshì (散騎常侍) and jīnzǐ guānglù dàfū (金紫光祿大夫).
He died in the 25th year of Yuánjiā (元嘉)
at the age of seventy-two.
Kǒng Chúnzhī (孔淳之), courtesy name Yànshēn (彥深),
was a native of Lǔjùn Lǔ (魯郡魯).
His grandfather, Tán (惔),
was a shàngshū cíbù láng (尚書祠部郎).
His father, Càn (粲),
was summoned to be mìshū jiān (祕書監),
but did not accept.
