Chúnzhī (淳之) was lofty and refined in his youth,
fond of ancient books,
and praised by Wáng Gōng (王恭) of Tàiyuán (太原).
He lived in Kuàijī Shànxiàn (會稽剡縣).
He had a great love for mountains and waters.
Whenever he traveled,
he would explore their secluded and precipitous parts,
sometimes forgetting to return for days.
Once, while traveling in the mountains,
he met the Buddhist monk Shì Fǎchóng (釋法崇),
and stayed with him.
He remained for three years.
Fǎchóng (法崇) sighed, saying:
"I have been thinking of the world beyond man
for thirty years.
Now to meet you here by chance,
I don't realize that old age is approaching."
When Chúnzhī (淳之) returned,
he did not disclose his surname.
He was appointed zuòzhùo zuǒláng (著作佐郎)
and tàiwèi cānjūn (太尉參軍),
but did not accept either.
He was extremely filial during mourning,
building a hut beside the tomb.
After the mourning period ended,
he went on excursions beyond the human world with the recluses Dài Yóng (戴顒), Wáng Hóngzhī (王弘之), and Wáng Jìnghóng (王敬弘) and others.
Jìnghóng (敬弘) married his daughter to Chúnzhī’s (淳之) son, Shàng (尚).
Xiè Fāngmíng (謝方明), the tàishǒu (太守) of Kuàijī (會稽), earnestly urged him to join the commandery,
but he steadfastly refused.
His house was a thatched hut with a shabby door,
the courtyard grass overgrown the path.
Only a few scrolls of books were on his bed.
In the early Yuánjiā (元嘉) era,
he was again summoned to be sànqí shìláng (散騎侍郎),
but he fled to the borders of Shàngyú Xiàn (上虞縣),
and his family did not know where he went.
His younger brother, Mòzhī (默之), became cìshǐ (刺史) of Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
When he left the capital, Chúnzhī (淳之) bid him farewell.
Sītú (司徒) Wáng Hóng (王弘) asked Chúnzhī (淳之) to gather at Yěchéng (冶城),
but Chúnzhī (淳之) ordered his carriage to return east on the same day,
and did not look back.
He died in the seventh year of Yuánjiā (元嘉)
at the age of fifty-nine.
Mòzhī (默之) was a Confucian scholar,
who annotated the Gǔliáng Chūnqiū (穀梁春秋).
Mòzhī’s (默之) son, Xīxiān (熙先),
has his deeds recorded in Fàn Yè’s (范曄) biography.
Liú Níngzhī (劉凝之), courtesy name Zhì'ān (志安),
nicknamed Chángnián (長年),
was a native of Nánjùn Zhījiāng (南郡枝江).
His father, Qígōng (期公), was tàishǒu (太守) of Héngyáng (衡陽).
His elder brother, Shènggōng (盛公),
was noble and did not enter officialdom.
Níngzhī (凝之) admired the characters of Lǎo Lái (老萊) and Yán Zǐlíng (嚴子陵).
He distributed his family wealth to his younger brothers and nephews,
built a house in the wilderness.
He would not eat unless he had worked for it.
The people of his region highly respected his moral conduct.
The province offered him a position as xīcáo zhǔbù (西曹主簿) three times,
and he was nominated as xiùcái (秀才),
but he did not accept.
His wife was the daughter of Guō Quán (郭銓), cìshǐ (刺史) of Liángzhōu (梁州).
The dowry sent was abundant and beautiful,
but Níngzhī (凝之) distributed it all to his relatives.
His wife also did not yearn for glory and wealth,
and joined Níngzhī (凝之) in embracing simplicity and hardship.
The couple often rode a humble cart
to the market to buy and sell.
Anything beyond their daily needs,
they would give to others.
He was once falsely accused by the villagers,
paying public taxes three times in one year,
and he always complied with requests.
Someone once claimed his clogs.
Níngzhī (凝之) smiled and said:
"Mine are already worn out.
I will ask my family to find new ones for you."
〔一０〕Later, this person found his lost clogs in the field
and returned them,
but Níngzhī (凝之) refused to take them back.
In the early Yuánjiā (元嘉) era,
he was summoned to be mìshū láng (祕書郎),
but did not accept.
Línchuān Wáng Yìqìng (臨川王義慶) and Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì (衡陽王義季) were stationed at Jiānglíng (江陵).
They both sent envoys to inquire about him.
Níngzhī (凝之) replied with a letter, bowing his head and referring to himself as "your servant,"
not observing the civil rites.
Some people criticized him for this.
Níngzhī (凝之) said:
"In the past, Lǎo Lái (老萊) referred to himself as 'your servant' to the King of Chǔ (楚).
Yán Líng (嚴陵) also treated Guāngwǔ (光武) with equal courtesy.
But I have not heard of Cháo (巢) and Xǔ (許) calling themselves subjects of Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜)."
At that time, Dài Yóng (戴顒) also referred to himself as "your servant" in a letter to Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì (衡陽王義季).
When Jīngzhōu (荊州) suffered from famine,
Yìjì (義季) worried that Níngzhī (凝之) would starve to death,
and sent him 100,000 coins.
Níngzhī (凝之) was overjoyed.
He took the money to the market gate,
and seeing those who looked hungry,
he distributed it all to them.
It was used up in an instant.
He had a fondness for mountains and waters.
One day, he took his wife and children to travel the rivers and lakes,
and lived in seclusion on the southern side of Héngshān (衡山).
He ascended to a high peak,
beyond human reach,
built a small hut and resided there.
He collected herbs and consumed them.
His wife and children all followed his will.
In the 25th year of Yuánjiā (元嘉),
he died
at the age of fifty-nine.
Gōng Qí (龔祈), courtesy name Mèngdào (孟道),
was a native of Wǔlíng Hànshòu (武陵漢壽).
His great-uncle Xuánzhī (玄之)
and father Límín (黎民)
both refused official summons.
When Qí (祈) was fourteen,
the local community nominated him as the province's yǐng xīcáo (迎西曹),
but he did not go.
Xiè Huì (謝晦), when in charge of the province,
appointed him zhǔbù (主簿).
Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng (彭城王義康) nominated him as xiùcái (秀才),
and he was appointed fèngcháoqǐng (奉朝請).
Línchuān Wáng Yìqìng (臨川王義慶) appointed him píngxī cānjūn (平西參軍).
He did not accept any of these positions.
His demeanor was elegant and upright,
and his conduct was admirable.
Zhōngshū Láng (中書郎) Fàn Shù (范述) saw him and sighed, saying:
"This is an immortal from Jīngchǔ (荊楚)."
Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì (衡陽王義季), when in charge of Jīngzhōu (荊州),
issued an order that since Qí (祈), Liú Níngzhī (劉凝之), and Shī Juéshòu (師覺授) did not answer summons,
their three sons should be appointed.
Qí (祈) was again summoned as tàizǐ shèrén (太子舍人),
but did not rise.
He sometimes composed poetry,
but his words never touched upon worldly affairs.
In the 17th year of Yuánjiā (元嘉),
he died
at the age of forty-two.
Zhái Fǎcì (翟法賜)
was a native of Xúnyáng Cháicāng (尋陽柴桑).
His great-grandfather Tāng (湯),
Tāng’s (湯) son Zhuāng (莊),
and Zhuāng’s (莊) son Jiǎo (矯)
were all noble and did not enter officialdom,
avoiding summons.
Jiǎo (矯) begat Fǎcì (法賜).
Early in life, he maintained the family estate
and built a house on the summit of Lúshān.
After his parents died,
he never returned home.
He ate no grains,
and wore clothes made of animal skins and woven grass.
Even his relatives and cousins
were unable to see him.
The prefecture appointed him Zhǔbù,
he was recommended as a Xiùcái,
then Ròucānjūn,
[一一]Zuòzuò Zuǒláng,
and Yuánwài Sǎnqí Shìláng,
but he accepted none of them.
Later, his family sought him in a stone chamber,
but he again moved far away,
evading invitations and appointments,
concealing his tracks in profound seclusion.
Dèng Wénzǐ, the Grand Administrator of Xúnyáng, reported:
"I have received an imperial edict summoning the prefectural resident, Dì Fǎcì of Nányáng, newly appointed as Zuòzuò Zuǒláng,
to serve as Yuánwài Sǎnqí Shìláng.
Fǎcì has lived in seclusion on Lúshān
for four generations now,
dwelling in reclusive caves,
rarely seen by people.
If we were to compel him with royal statutes,
bind him with strict laws,
or scour the mountains and hunt the wilds
in pursuit of capturing him,
I fear it might lead to his downfall,
which would harm the flourishing imperial transformation."
Thus, the matter was dropped.
He later died among the rocks,
the year and month unknown.
Táo Qián, courtesy name Yuānmíng,
or some say Yuānmíng, courtesy name Yuánliàng,
was a native of Cháisāng, Xúnyáng.
His great-grandfather, Kǎn,
was the Grand Marshal of the Jìn dynasty.
Táo Qián, from a young age, had lofty aspirations.
He once wrote "Biography of Mr. Five Willows" to describe himself,
saying: "The gentleman's origin is unknown;
his surname and given name are not clear.
By his dwelling were five willow trees,
and so he took them as his appellation.
Quiet and reticent,
he sought neither fame nor profit.
He loved reading,
but did not seek a thorough understanding;
whenever he grasped the meaning,
he would joyfully forget to eat.
By nature, he loved wine,
but his family was poor and could not afford it.
His relatives and old friends, knowing this about him,
would sometimes prepare wine and invite him.
He would drink until it was empty,
intending to get thoroughly drunk.
Once drunk, he would leave,
never showing any reluctance about staying or departing.
His humble abode was desolate,
offering no shelter from wind or sun.
His coarse
clothes were torn and mended,
[一二]his bamboo basket and gourd were often empty,
yet he remained content.
He often wrote essays to entertain himself,
largely expressing his own will,
unconcerned with gain or loss,
and thus lived out his days."
His self-description was thus,
and people of his time considered it a true record.
With his parents old and his family poor,
he took up the post of Prefectural Libationer.
Finding himself unsuited for official duties,
after a few days,
he resigned and returned home.
The prefecture summoned him as Zhǔbù,
but he did not accept.
He supported himself by farming,
and consequently suffered from a debilitating illness.
He again served as Cānjūn for the Zhènjūn and Jiànwēi.
He said to his friends:
"I just want to strum a tune,
to provide for the 'three paths';
is that acceptable?"
Upon hearing this, those in charge
appointed him Magistrate of Péngzé.
He instructed his clerks to plant glutinous rice in all the public fields.
His wife and children earnestly requested non-glutinous rice be planted,
so he had two qǐng and fifty mù planted with glutinous rice,
and fifty mù with non-glutinous rice.
When a督郵 Dūyóu sent by the commandery arrived,
the county clerk informed him that he should don his official sash and meet him.
Táo Qián sighed and said:
"I cannot bow my waist for five measures of rice to a petty villager."
That very day, he discarded his official seal and left his post.
He composed "Guī Qù Lái,"
the lyrics of which say: "Oh, let me return home!
My garden and fields are overgrown,
[一三]why do I not return?
Since I have allowed my mind to be enslaved by my body,
why should I be sad and grieve alone?
I realize that what is past
cannot be undone,
but what is to come can still be pursued.
Indeed, I have not strayed far down the wrong path;
I realize now that today is right and yesterday was wrong.
My boat drifts lightly and far away,
[一四]the wind gently blows my robes.
I ask a traveler about the road ahead,
and lament the faint light of dawn.
[一五]Then I see my humble dwelling,
and am filled with joy and rush forward.
My servants welcome me,
my children wait at the gate.
The three paths are overgrown,
but the pines and chrysanthemums remain.
I lead my children into the house,
there
is wine in the jar.
[一六]I take up the pot and cup and pour for myself,
gazing at the courtyard trees with a joyful face.
Leaning against the south window, I find my pride,
content with the easy comfort of my small room.
Each day I wander in the garden and
find pleasure,
the gate, though set, is usually closed.
I lean on my staff to stroll and rest,
occasionally raising my head to gaze afar.
Clouds emerge from the peaks without intention,
birds, weary of flight, know to return.
The light dims as the sun is about to set,
I stroke the lonely pine and linger.
Oh, let me return home!
Let me cease all social interaction and travel.
The world and I have forsaken each other,
[一七]what more could I seek by setting out again?
I speak with relatives in heartfelt conversation,
I enjoy
qin and books to dispel sorrow.
Farmers inform me it is early spring,
[一八]and there will be work in the western fields.
Sometimes I order a simple cart,
sometimes I paddle a small boat.
[一九]Sometimes I traverse hidden
valleys to their depths,
sometimes I travel over rugged hills.
The trees flourish joyfully,
the springs trickle and begin to flow.
I appreciate the timeliness of all things,
and feel my own life is drawing to a
close.
Enough!
How much longer will this body dwell in the universe?
Why not surrender my heart to what comes and goes,
why wander restlessly, whither to go?
Wealth and honor are not my wish,
the abode
of the immortals cannot be expected.
I cherish good times and go forth alone,
or plant my staff and weed and cultivate.
I ascend the eastern hill to whistle freely,
and approach the clear stream to compose poetry.
Let me just follow transformation
to my end,
rejoicing in my destiny, what more doubt could there be?"
At the end of the Yìxī
period, he was summoned to be Assistant Secretary to the Imperial Library,
but he did not accept.
Wáng Hóng (王弘), the Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (江州), wished to make his acquaintance,
but could not bring him to him.
Táo Qián (陶潛) once went to Lúshān (廬山).
Wáng Hóng (王弘) ordered Táo Qián's (陶潛) old friend, Páng Tōngzhī (龐通之), to bring wine and provisions to meet him halfway at Lìlǐ (栗里).
Táo Qián (陶潛) had a foot ailment,
and made one of his students and two of his sons carry him in a hand-litter.
When he arrived,
he happily drank with them.
Soon after, Wáng Hóng (王弘) arrived,
and Táo Qián (陶潛) showed no displeasure.
Before this,
Yán Yánzhī (顏延之) was Liú Liǔ's (劉柳) Rear Army Registrar,
stationed in Xúnyáng (尋陽),
and had a close friendship with Táo Qián (陶潛).
Later, when he was appointed Administrator of Shǐ'ān (始安) Commandery,
he passed through
and visited Táo Qián (陶潛) daily.
Each time he went, he would drink heavily until he was drunk.
Before leaving,
he left twenty thousand coins with Táo Qián (陶潛).
Táo Qián (陶潛) sent all of them to the wine merchant,
gradually drawing wine as needed.
Once, on the ninth day of the ninth month, having no wine,
he sat for a long time among the chrysanthemum bushes by his house.
It so happened that Wáng Hóng (王弘) sent wine,
whereupon he immediately began to drink
and returned home only after becoming drunk.
Táo Qián (陶潛) did not understand music,
but he kept a plain zither,
without strings.
Whenever he was in the mood for wine,
he would strum it to express his feelings.
When visitors, whether noble or humble, came to him,
if there was wine, he would serve it.
If Táo Qián (陶潛) became drunk first,
he would tell the guest,
"I am drunk and want to sleep;
you may leave."
Such was his simple honesty.
When the Commandery Administrator called on Táo Qián (陶潛),
it happened that his wine was ready.
He took his ge (葛) turban from his head to strain the wine.
When finished,
he put it back on.
In his youth, Táo Qián (陶潛) held minor offices,
and did not bother to keep his comings and goings unsullied.
Believing that his great-grandfather was a high official in the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
he was ashamed to humble himself before later generations.
From the time his high ancestor's royal enterprise gradually prospered,
he would no longer consent to serve in office.
All the articles he wrote
were dated with their year and month.
Before the Yìxī (義熙) period,
he would record the Jìn (晉) dynasty's reign title.
From Yǒngchū (永初) onwards, he would only state the Jiǎzǐ (甲子) cycle.
He wrote a letter to his sons to express his aspirations,
and also instructed them, saying: Heaven and Earth bestow life,
and what has a beginning must have an end.
[二０] From ancient times, among the sages and saints,
who could escape this fate alone?
Zǐxià (子夏) said:
"Life and death have their destined course;
wealth and honor are
in Heaven."
The Four Friends (四友) directly received these words of instruction.
Those who spoke thus,
was it not because success and failure cannot be sought after capriciously,
and longevity or brevity of life can never be obtained by external appeal?
I am past
fifty years of age,
and suffer extreme hardship.
Due to my family's poverty and destitution,
[二一] I have wandered east and west.
My nature is stubborn and my talent clumsy,
often at odds with others.
Judging myself,
I would surely incur common
troubles.
With reluctance, I left the world,
leaving you young and to endure hunger and cold.
I often recall the words of Rú Zhòng's (孺仲) virtuous wife:
"Embracing tattered quilts oneself,
what shame is there for one's children?"
This is already one matter.
However, I regret that my neighbors are not the two Zhòng brothers (二仲),
and my house lacks a wife like Láifù (萊婦).
Bearing this bitter heart,
I am truly lost and bewildered.
Since my youth, I have loved books,
and by chance, I love tranquility.
When I open a book and gain something,
I happily forget to eat.
Seeing trees with interwoven shade,
and seasonal birds changing their calls,
I also become joyful
and pleased.
I once said that when lying under the north window in May or June,
encountering a temporary cool breeze,
I considered myself a person of Xīhuáng's (羲皇) era.
My intentions are shallow, my knowledge meager.
Days and months pass,
and I yearn for the past.
How distant and elusive!
Since becoming ill,
I have gradually declined.
My relatives and old friends have not abandoned me,
always bringing medicine to save me.
I fear that my great destiny will soon be limited.
I regret that you are
young,
and my family is poor with no servants.
When will the toil of firewood and water
ever cease?
Thinking of this in my heart,
how can I express it?
However, though not born of the same mother,
you should remember the principle that all within the Four Seas are brothers.
Bào Shú (鮑叔) and Jìng Zhòng (敬仲) shared their wealth without suspicion.
Guī Shēng (歸生) and Wǔ Jǔ (伍舉) spread out thorn bushes to recall old times.

Léi Cìzōng was summoned to Jīngshī,

enrolling over a hundred disciples.

At that time, the Guózǐ Xué (National Academy) had not yet been established,

The imperial carriage frequently visited Cìzōng's academy,

In the twenty-fifth year,

His secluded dwelling in a remote thicket,

were consistent from beginning to end.
I humbly believe that Heaven's boundless benevolence
will also extend pity and compassion."
His son, Sùzhī,

Yángzhōu Zhǔbù.
Bǎinián, young, possessed noble sentiments.
After his parents' death and the completion of mourning,
his wife, Kǒng Shì, moved into the Nánshān of Kuàijī,

Every time he placed firewood and bamboo shoots by the roadside,
The next morning, it would be the same.
People gradually found it strange,

Those who needed them would leave money according to what they could afford,

Sometimes, when it was cold and snowy,

and he would have no means to support himself.
He would then row a boat himself to send his wife back to the Kǒng clan,
and welcome her back when the weather cleared.
Occasionally, he would go out to Shānyīn to buy three to five chi of silk for his wife.
He was fond of drinking,
and sometimes lost it when drunk.
He was quite capable of discussing principles,

The commandery appointed him Gōngcáo,
the province appointed him Cóngshì,

He concealed his traces and avoided people,

and whenever they met, they would drink heartily,
drinking together to their heart's content.
Bǎinián's family was always poor.
His mother died in winter,
and her clothes had no wadding.
From then on, he did not wear padded silk garments.
Once, during cold weather, he stayed overnight at Kǒng Jì's place.
His clothes were all unpadded cloth.
He drank until he was drunk and fell asleep.
Kǒng Jì covered him with bedding,
but Bǎinián did not notice.
When he awoke,
he removed the bedding from his body
and said to Kǒng Jì:
"Cotton is indeed exceptionally warm."
Then he wept bitterly in sorrow,
and Kǒng Jì was also moved to sadness.
He was appointed Tàizǐ Shèrén,
but did not accept.
Yán Jùn, when serving as Dōngyángzhōu,

At that time, there was also a poor man named Yáo Yín in Shānyīn,
who also had noble aspirations and

Yìyáng Wáng Chǎng, when governing the province,

Yán Jùn supplied Yáo Yín with two hundred hù of rice,
which Yáo Yín also declined.
Bǎinián died in the mountains in the first year of Xiàojiàn,
Cài Xīngzōng, when serving as Kuàijī Tàishǒu,

Bǎinián's wife sent a maid to the commandery gate to respectfully decline and firmly refuse it.
People at the time praised her,
comparing her to Liáng Hóng's wife.
Wáng Sù, courtesy name Xiūyè,
was a native of Línyí, Lángyá.
His great-grandfather, Qiáozhī, was
Jìn Guānglù Dàfū.
Sù 少 had high aspirations and conduct.
His family was poor and his mother old.
Initially, he served as a Shìláng for Lúlíng Guó.
Due to his mother's illness, he resigned from his post.
After the mourning period was over,

Relatives and old friends advised Sù to repair his old residence,

Instead, he lightly went to Dōngyáng,

He somewhat managed agricultural assets,
thereby enabling himself to be self-reliant.
He loved literature and scholarship,
and was not troubled by worldly affairs.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he wished to seek out and promote hermits.
He issued an edict which stated:
"To save the world and accomplish tasks,
all hidden and subtle talents are to be reached;
to rectify customs and promote humility,
one must recognize pure integrity.
I, 朕, from dawn to dusk seek goodness,
and desire to enrich the dwindling customs.
Lángyá Wáng Sù and Kuàijī Zhū Bǎinián
are both honest, frugal, firm, and far-sighted,
and contend with nothing in the world.
Content in their fields and gardens,

They should be commended and brought forward,

Both are to be made Tàizǐ Shèrén."
During the Dàmíng era,
Tàizǎi Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng established his own administration and invited people to serve.

he was again summoned to be Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén,

As Sù was repeatedly summoned and invited,

In the mountains, there was a centipede-like insect (xiānchóng),

but its appearance was very ugly.
Sù then composed a *fù* on the xiānchóng to describe himself.
In the seventh year,
he died,

He was the grandson of Huángmén Shìláng Wén.

Guān Kāngzhī, courtesy name Bóyú,
was a native of Yáng in Hédōng.
His family traditionally resided in Jīngkǒu,
and was affiliated with Nánpíngchāng.
From a young age, he was diligent in his studies,
and his appearance was robust and grand.
Xiàpí Zhào Yì was praised for his literary and scholarly merits,
and Kāngzhī was good friends with him.
Tèjìn Yán Yánzhī saw him and recognized his talent.
Jìnlíng Gù Yuèzhī raised over forty difficulties with Wáng Bì's commentary on the *Yì*,
and Kāngzhī defended Wáng against Gù's difficulties,
which had far-reaching rationality.
He also wrote a commentary on the *Máoshī*,
and clarified many obscure points in the classics.
He once studied arithmetic with the Buddhist monk Zhī Sēngnà,
[二六] and mastered it thoroughly.
Jìnglíng Wáng Yìxuān moved his garrison from Jīngkǒu to Jiānglíng.
He invited Kāngzhī to accompany him,
but Kāngzhī refused the invitation.
During the Yuánjiā era,
Tàizǔ heard of Kāngzhī's scholarship and integrity,
and appointed him Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn of Wǔchāng Guó,
and exempted him from taxes.
Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng and Guǎnglíng Wáng Dàn, when they oversaw Nánsúzhōu,
invited him to be Cóngshì and Xīcáo,
but he did not accept either.
He cut off human interaction
and upheld his aspirations in quiet retirement.
His younger brother, Shuāngzhī, was Zāng Zhì's Chējì Cānjūn.
He went south with Zhì,
and died of illness in Zhèqí,
buried by the riverside.
Kāngzhī fell seriously ill that spring.
After a slight recovery,
he was compelled to go and retrieve the coffin,
and consequently contracted a chronic wasting illness,
which confined him to bed for over twenty years.
Whenever he had a spare day,
he would lie down and discuss literature and scholarship.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he sent the grand envoy Lù Zǐzhēn to tour the realm.
Upon his return,
he recommended Kāngzhī, saying:
"His conduct and integrity are pure,
his principles are strong and firm.
He is trusted in his community
and his reputation extends throughout the region.
His aspirations are to emulate antiquity,
and his principles are unchangeable.
He should be summoned and invited,
to purify the customs and standards."
This was not acted upon.
In the early Tàishǐ era of Tàizōng,
he was summoned along with Píngyuán Míng Sēngshào to be Tōngzhí Láng,
but he again declined due to illness.
In the first year of Shùndì Shēngmíng,
he died,
at the age of sixty-three.
The historian remarks: Indeed, those who walk alone
all possess an unyielding character,
unable to compromise their will or bend their principles,
seeking renown or expecting to attain positions.
If they had met a trustworthy lord
and encountered a propitious era,
how could they have indulged their emotions in rivers and seas,
and sought ease in hills and thickets?
It was merely out of necessity that they did so.
Moreover, mountains and valleys are tranquil and distant,
waters and rocks are clear and beautiful.
Even if one has a magnificent mansion with eight layers of gates
or a high city with ten thousand battlements,
one would still store up earth to create springs
and simulate forests and wetlands.
Thus, we know that pine mountains and osmanthus islets
are not merely for simple enjoyment,
and emerald streams and clear pools
instead become beautiful sights.
To hang up one's cap and retreat to the Eastern Capital,
what difficulty is there in that?

Biographies, Chapter 54: Favored Officials
Indeed, Jūnzǐ and Xiǎorén
are general terms for categories of people.
One who follows the Dào is a Jūnzǐ;
one who deviates from it is a Xiǎorén.
Butchery and fishing
are humble professions;
building walls by carrying earth
is a lowly service.
Tài Gōng rose to become a commander for Zhōu,
and Fù Yuè left his position to become a prime minister for Yīn.
It was not a question of noble lineage
or wealth,
but of illuminating the obscure
and employing only talent.
Down to the two Hàn dynasties,
this principle had not changed.
Hú Guǎng, from generations of farmers,
rose to the rank of chancellor;
Huáng Xiàn, the son of an ox doctor,
was renowned in Jīngshī.
Moreover, even those who held office through inherited privilege
all had specific duties.
Although "seven generations wearing mink sables"
was esteemed in the Western Hàn,
the Shìzhōng personally presented memorials
and also managed the imperial robes.
Dōngfāng Shuò served as Huángmén Shìláng
and stood guard with a halberd below the palace hall.
The Yuánshǐ of commanderies and counties,
though from powerful families,
carried spears and kept watch at night,
all performing duties themselves.
This was not like later eras,
when society was divided into two distinct paths.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, amidst chaos,
Wèi Wǔ began to establish his power.
In the urgency of military affairs,
he provisionally established the Nine-Rank system.
This was intended to evaluate the merits and demerits of talent,
not to distinguish between the high and low status of hereditary families.
However, it was followed successively
and eventually became an established law.
From Wèi to Jìn,
no one was able to change it.
Though Zhōu Dū and Jùn Zhèng evaluated people based on their talent,
the advancement and demotion of talent across the world
became very rare.
Instead, people merely relied on inherited status
to elevate themselves above others.
The Dū Zhèng, being common people,
would adjust their decisions according to the times,
varying the number of ranks
and bending to circumstances.
This is what Liú Yì meant when he said:
"There are no high-ranking commoners
and no low-ranking nobles."
As years passed,
this trend grew stronger.
All those of high status
were of the first two ranks.
From then on,
the rest were considered commoners.
The Dào of Zhōu and Hàn
used the wise to govern the ignorant,
with varying grades of officials
to form a hierarchy.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
the noble have governed the humble,
and the division between scholars and commoners
became clearly distinct.
When the sovereign faces south,
secluded in the nine-layered palace,
those who attend him morning and evening
are, by custom, distinct from high officials.
The duties of the palace gates
should properly be handled by specific officials.
However, favor breeds by chance,
and trust is solidified by favor.
Such individuals possess no intimidating presence,
but rather an approachable demeanor.
During Xiàojiàn and Tàishǐ,
the imperial authority operated independently.
A hundred offices were established,
and power was not delegated externally.
But criminal and administrative affairs were intertwined and complex,
difficult to manage comprehensively.
Thus, those entrusted with the emperor's ears and eyes,
affairs devolved to the close attendants.
The essentials of reward and punishment,
which are the power of the state,
and the issuance of imperial decrees
were all in their hands.
Consequently, various factions formed alliances,
converging and rushing towards them.
The ruler, believing them to be of humble birth and low rank,
thought their power could not become great.
They did not realize that a rat relies on the prestige of the altar,
and a fox borrows the tiger's might.
Outwardly, they avoided the suspicion of pressuring the ruler,
but inwardly, they exercised sole power.
Their influence swayed the empire,
yet this was often unnoticed.
They formed cliques and established parties;
government was corrupted by bribes.
Punishments and injuries
originated in the corners of banquets;
official robes and carriages
were granted through jest and laughter.
Southern gold and northern furs
arrived in numerous ships;
plain silk and red jewels
were accumulated in vast quantities.
The Xǔ and Shǐ families of the Western Hàn
are hardly worth mentioning;
the Wáng and Yǔ families of the Jìn dynasty
could not compare.
When Tài Zōng entered his later years,
he pondered the rise and fall of fortunes.
The powerful favorites,
fearing the imperial relatives,
wished to leave the young emperor isolated
so they could perpetually usurp state power.
They fabricated divisions,
stirring up discord and trouble.
Imperial brothers and princes
were successively slaughtered.
The people forgot the virtue of Sòng,
though not for one single reason.
The early downfall of the imperial lineage
was indeed due to this.
Alas!
The Hàn Shū has a table of "Enzé Hóu"
and also a "Nìng Xìng Zhuàn."
I now gather their names
and list them here as the "Ēnxìng Piān."
Dài Fǎxìng
was a native of Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
His family was poor.
His father, Dài Shuòzi,
made a living by selling hemp cloth.
Fǎxìng's two elder brothers, Yánshòu and Yánxīng, were both upright.
Yánshòu was skilled in calligraphy,
and Fǎxìng loved learning.
In Shānyīn there was a Chén Zǎi,
who was very rich,
possessing thirty million cash.
The villagers all said:
"Dài Shuòzi's three sons
are worth Chén Zǎi's thirty million cash."
When young, Fǎxìng sold kudzu cloth in the market of Shānyīn.
Later, he became a clerk, transferred to a posting,
and then entered as a Lìshǐ in the Cāngbù of the Shàngshū.
The Grand General Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng sought capable Lìshǐ in the Shàngshū,
and found Fǎxìng and four others.
He appointed Fǎxìng as Jìshì Lìshǐ.
When Yìkāng was defeated,
Fǎxìng remained as Jìshì Yuán for Shìzǔ's Zhēnglǔ and Fǔjūn.
When the emperor was in Jiāngzhōu,
he was appointed Nán Zhōngláng Diǎnqiān.
When the emperor raised an army at Bākǒu,
Fǎxìng, along with Diǎnqiān Dài Míngbǎo and Cài Xián, were all promoted to Cānjūn Dūhù.
When the emperor ascended the throne,
they were all made Nán Tái Shìyùshǐ,
and concurrently Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén.
Fǎxìng and the others exclusively managed internal affairs,
wielding great power at the time.
In the first year of Xiàojiàn,
he was granted the title Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn,
and made Tàishǒu of Nán Lǔjùn.
He was relieved of his Shèrén post
to attend the Crown Prince in the Eastern Palace.
In the second year of Dàmíng,
the three Diǎnqiān, having participated in the secret plans in the south,
were ennobled: Fǎxìng as Nán of Wúchāng Xiàn,
Míngbǎo as Nán of Xiāngxiāng Xiàn,
and Xián as Nán of Gāochāng Xiàn,
each with an income of three hundred households.
Xián had already passed away at the time,
so his title and enfeoffment were posthumously granted.
Fǎxìng was transferred to Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng,
and also served as Jǐshìzhōng and Tàizǐ Lǚbēn Zhōnglángjiāng,
while retaining his position as Tàishǒu.
Shìzǔ personally reviewed court affairs,
not entrusting them to grand ministers.
However, for his trusted confidants and close attendants,
he could not but have some to whom he delegated responsibilities.
Dài Fǎxīng was quite knowledgeable about ancient and modern matters,
and had long been favored and trusted.
Although he had been appointed to serve the Crown Prince,
his influence and confidential status remained high.
Cháo Shàngzhī of Lǔjùn,
a person of humble background,
during the Yuánjiā era,
served Sīxīng Wáng Jùn as a study companion.
He too had extensively read literature and history,
and was known to the Emperor.
In the early Xiàojiàn era,
he was appointed Sīláng of Dōnghǎi State,
and concurrently served as Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén.
For all major decisions regarding selections, appointments, promotions, transfers, punishments, rewards, and major dispositions,
the Emperor would consult Dài Fǎxīng and Cháo Shàngzhī.
For various miscellaneous internal and external affairs,
he mostly entrusted them to Wáng Míngbǎo.
The Emperor’s nature was severe and cruel;
even a slight offense
could lead to punishment and execution.
Cháo Shàngzhī would often intervene and explain on such occasions,
saving many from punishment,
and he was greatly relied upon by the palace and various departments.
However, Dài Fǎxīng and Wáng Míngbǎo were very adept at human relations,
and accepted many bribes.
All those they recommended and promoted
had their words heard and acted upon.
People from all over the realm flocked to them,
their gates became a market,
and their family assets accumulated to thousands of gold.
Wáng Míngbǎo was especially arrogant and unrestrained.
His eldest son, Wáng Jìng, served as Cóngshì of Yángzhōu,
and competed with the Emperor to buy imperial items.
Once, when the Six Palaces were traveling,
Wáng Jìng, dressed in splendid clothes, rode a horse beside the carriages,
dashing back and forth.
The Emperor was greatly angered,
granted Wáng Jìng death,
and imprisoned Wáng Míngbǎo in the Shàngfāng.
Soon after, he was pardoned and released,
and re-entrusted as before.
When Shìzǔ died,
the Former Deposed Emperor ascended the throne.
Dài Fǎxīng was promoted to Yuèqí Xiàowèi.
At that time, Tàizǎi Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng held the position of Lù Shàngshū Shì,
with authority equal to that of the sovereign.
However, Dài Fǎxīng and Cháo Shàngzhī had held power for a long time,
their influence extending both internally and externally.
Yìgōng had always stood in awe of them;
by this time, his apprehension was even greater.
The Deposed Emperor had not yet personally attended to all state affairs;
all edicts, commands, and actions
were decided by Dài Fǎxīng.
Within the Shàngshū, matters large and small
were exclusively decided by him.
Yán Shībó and Yìgōng merely held empty titles.
As the Deposed Emperor gradually grew older,
his cruel intentions increasingly solidified.
Whenever he wished to do something,
Dài Fǎxīng would constantly restrain and forbid him.
He would often say to the Emperor:
"Your Majesty's actions are like this;
do you wish to become Yíngyáng?"
The Emperor's feelings gradually became uneasy.
His favored eunuch, Huà Yuàn'ér, enjoyed great寵 (favor),
and was granted countless gold and silk.
Dài Fǎxīng often cut these down,
which Huà Yuàn'ér greatly resented.
The Emperor often sent Huà Yuàn'ér to go in and out of the city,
to observe and listen to popular rumors.
The talk on the streets was
that Dài Fǎxīng was the true Son of Heaven,
and the Emperor was the Son of Heaven.
Huà Yuàn'ér consequently reported to the Emperor, saying:
"Outside, they say there are two Sons of Heaven in the palace.
Your Majesty is one person,
and Dài Fǎxīng is one person.
Your Majesty is deep within the palace,
not directly interacting with people.
Dài Fǎxīng, together with the Tàizǎi, Yán, and Liǔ, form a single body,
constantly interacting and influencing.
He has several hundred retainers,
and no internal or external officials or commoners
do not fear and obey him.
Dài Fǎxīng was an attendant of Xiàowǔ and
has also been in the inner palace for a long time.
Now he is forming a household with others.
I deeply fear that this seat will no longer belong to Your Majesty."
The Emperor then became enraged,
dismissed Dài Fǎxīng from office,
and sent him back to his hometown.
He was then exiled to a distant commandery,
and soon after was granted death at his home.
He was fifty-two years old at the time.
Before Dài Fǎxīng's death,
he sealed his storehouses
and made his family carefully record the keys.
One night after his death,
his two sons were also killed,
Dài Fǎxīng's coffin was cut open,
and burned.
His property was confiscated.
Dài Fǎxīng was capable of writing essays,
which were quite circulated in the world.
After his death,
the Emperor commanded Cháo Shàngzhī, saying:
"I have inherited the grand foundation,
and rule over all nations.
My trust in old merits
is known far and wide.
I did not expect Dài Fǎxīng to rely on my favor and betray my grace,
to monopolize power and authority,
to defy laws and accept bribes,
and to issue commands as he pleased.
His accumulated transgressions and faults
have led to this.
That you and others have been loyal and diligent in your duties,
I am well aware.
However, the talk on the streets
is confused with differences and disputes.
Not only are people's feelings shocked and bewildered,
but the celestial phenomena also deviate from the norm.
The purpose of the delegation
has truly lost its original intent.
Now I shall personally review all state affairs
and pay attention to various matters.
You and others should exert your utmost sincerity and effort
to fulfill my expectations."
Cháo Shàngzhī was then Fǔjūn Zhōngbīng Cānjūn for Xīn'ān Wáng Zǐluán and Huáilíng Tàishǒu.
He was then relieved of his Shèrén position,
and transferred to Fǔjūn Zīyì Cānjūn,
retaining his Tàishǒu position.
In Tàizōng's Tàishǐ second year,
an edict stated:
"The late Yuèqí Xiàowèi and Kāiguó Nán of Wúchāng County, Dài Fǎxīng,
formerly served Xiàowǔ
with sincerity and diligence by his side,
establishing the state and securing the dynasty,
and participating in the oath of river and mountain.
Upon serving the Crown Prince,
he exhausted his heart and strength.
He suffered harm due to wickedness and perversity.
I greatly lament this.
His expunged records shall be retroactively restored,
and his enfeoffment and peerage returned."
The relevant authorities then memorialized that Dài Fǎxīng's grandson, Dài Língzhēn, should inherit the enfeoffment.
Another edict then stated:
"Dài Fǎxīng was a petty man,
who monopolized power and acted audaciously.
Although he was harmed by a tyrannical ruler,
it was righteous for the state to punish him.
It is inappropriate to restore the enfeoffment of a greedy man.
His enfeoffment and peerage shall be suspended."
In the early Tàizōng era,
Cháo Shàngzhī was again concurrently appointed Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén and Nánqīnghé Tàishǒu.
In the second year,
he was promoted to Zhōngshū Shìláng,
retaining his Tàishǒu position.
Before being invested,
he was reassigned as Qiánjūn Jiàngjūn,
retaining his Tàishǒu position.
He served the Crown Prince in the Eastern Palace.
After the pacification of Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn,
due to his military governance within his jurisdiction,
he was enfeoffed as Shàolíng Xiàn Nán,
with an income of four hundred households,
but he firmly declined to accept.
He was then transferred to Huángmén Shìláng,
and went out to serve as Xīn'ān Tàishǒu,
where he died of illness.
Dài Míngbǎo
was a native of Dāntú in Nán Dōnghǎi.
He successively served as Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng
and Gěishìzhōng.
In the reign of Shìzǔ,
he was concurrently Nán Qīnghé Tàishǒu.
When the Former Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
all authority was given to Fǎxīng,
and Míngbǎo was lightly regarded,
appointed as Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn and Nán Dōngguǎn Tàishǒu.
At the end of Jǐnghé,
his fief was increased by one hundred households.
At the beginning of Tàizōng’s reign,
when rebellion erupted throughout the land
and military affairs were vexatious,
because Míngbǎo was an old hand
and had frequently been involved in military matters,
he was again entrusted with responsibility,
appointed as Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn.
When the situation was pacified,
he was promoted to Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn and Jìnlíng Tàishǒu,
advanced in peerage to Marquis,
and his fief was increased by four hundred households.
In the third year of Tàishǐ,
he was implicated for participating in military command
and accepting many bribes.
His increased enfeoffment, official rank, and peerage were revoked,
and he was imprisoned in the Shàngfāng.
He was pardoned shortly thereafter.
He was again appointed Ānlù Tàishǒu,
and additionally Níngshuò Jiāngjūn,
Yóují and Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn,
Wǔlíng Nèishǐ,
Xuānchéng Tàishǒu,
and Shùndì Piàojí Sīmǎ.
At the beginning of Shēngmíng,
being old,
he was appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū
and died of illness.
Dǒng Yuánsì, the Diǎnshūlìng of Wǔlíng Commandery,
along with Fǎxīng, Míngbǎo, and others, were all Diǎnqiān under Shìzǔ's Nánzhōngláng.
In the thirtieth year of Yuánjiā,
he was sent on a mission and returned to the capital,
where he encountered the regicide and enthronement by the "Prime Culprit."
Yuánsì was sent south
to report to the emperor that Xú Zhànzhī and others were rebelling.
The emperor was then at Bākǒu,
and Yuánsì fully recounted the details of the regicide.
The emperor sent Yuánsì down to the capital
to present a memorial to Shào.
Soon after, the emperor raised an army of righteousness,
and Shào reprimanded Yuánsì.
Yuánsì replied:
“When I first went down,
there was no intention of rebellion.”
Shào did not believe him,
subjected him to severe torture,
but he did not confess,
and so he died.
When Shìzǔ's campaign was successful,
he was posthumously granted Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng,
and the scholar Sū Bǎoshēng was ordered to compose an elegy for him.
During the Dàmíng era,
there was also Xī Xiǎndù,
a native of Tán in Nán Dōnghǎi.
His highest office was Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng.
Shìzǔ often made him responsible for supervising public works,
but he was cruel and tyrannical,
constantly subjecting people to beatings.
Whether in hot rain or cold snow,
he did not allow any rest,
and the people could not endure it,
some even hanging themselves to death.
When conscripted laborers heard they were assigned to Xiǎndù,
it was like going to execution.
At that time, the Jiànkāng county prison system
sometimes used timbers to press down on prisoners’ foreheads and ankles.
A popular rhyme circulated among the people:
“Better to suffer Jiànkāng’s forehead press
than to endure Xiǎndù’s beatings.”
They also jokingly said to each other:
“Don’t look back,
you’ll be given to Xiǎndù.”
Such was his cruelty and tyranny.
The Former Deposed Emperor once joked:
“Xiǎndù is harsh and cruel,
and detested by the common people;
he should be removed soon.”
His attendants then chorused
“Yes!”
On that very day, an imperial decree was issued to execute him.
People at the time compared it to Sūn Hào killing Cén Hūn.
Xú Yuán, courtesy name Chángyù,
was a native of Kāiyáng in Nán Lángyá.
His original name was Yuàn,
but later, because it was the same name as Fù Liàng’s father,
it was changed to Yuán.
Initially, he served as Diǎnjūn in the Great General Sīmǎ's residence of the Prince of Jìn Lángyá,
and accompanied the northern expedition.
He showed subtle intelligence and reason,
and was recognized by Gāozǔ.
When the Young Emperor was in the Eastern Palace,
he entered to serve by his side.
At the beginning of Tàizǔ's reign,
he was again trusted and appointed,
serving in various administrative and laborious posts,
eventually reaching Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ.
In the twelfth year of Yuánjiā,
he was transferred to Nántái Shìyùshǐ,
and then to Hòujūn Xíngcānjūn under Wáng Jùn, Prince of Shǐxīng.
[一０]He again served the Crown Prince in the Eastern Palace
and was promoted to Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng.
Whenever Tàizǔ led troops on campaigns,
he would often secretly impart military strategies.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Wáng Xuánmó and others were again dispatched for a northern expedition,
and Yuán was assigned five hundred men
to accompany the army towards Quèáo,
carrying secret imperial instructions
to be revealed at the appropriate time.
When Shìzǔ reached Xīntíng,
Grand General Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng fled south.
Yuán was then in the palace,
and tricked Shào into pursuing Yìgōng,
thus managing to escape south.
At that time, Shìzǔ was about to ascend the great throne,
and the military headquarters, in haste,
did not understand court procedures.
Yuán was well-versed in these matters,
and upon his arrival,
everyone was delighted.
He was concurrently appointed Tàicháng丞
to compile and establish ceremonial protocols.
At the beginning of Xiàojiàn,
he was appointed Shàngshū Shuǐbù Láng
and then transferred to Diànzhōng Láng,
concurrently Yòuchéng.
In the third year of Xiàojiàn,
the Sǎoluǒ invaded the border.
An imperial edict asked officials for defense strategies,
and Yuán deliberated, saying: The edict stated,
“The barbarians are violating our frontiers,
and the land and water are vast and distant;
isolated cities are in peril,
yet they cannot be abandoned.”
Your servant believes that the barbarian invaders are rampant
and their cunning schemes are growing.
Deploying troops
to watch
and observe for weaknesses,
without a major offensive,
will never bring lasting peace.
However, extending banners a thousand li
[一一]incurs enormous expenses,
and as the dynasty is in its nascent stage,
resources
have not yet accumulated.
Thus, the “Qi Axe” (referring to military action) hesitates,
and the northern chill (referring to enemy activity) is being endured.
Now, with the Imperial Fortune greatly auspicious
and its spiritual might far-reaching and awe-inspiring,
these foolish remnants
fear extermination.
They desire to display their venom
and sting,
to show they still have strength.
Although they dare not penetrate deep into Jì and Pèi,
they might be able to plunder the borderlands.
The imperial guard’s whip is long,
and the granaries are far away;
when it comes to rescue,
the momentum
will not reach in time.
Therefore, we should instruct all border garrisons
to train soldiers and fortify their cities.
All regional commanders
should gather provisions and cultivate fields,
calculating their resources
to be sufficient for resistance.
When a small
outpost reports an alarm,
the grand commanders should respond swiftly.
Barricade the strongholds,
and the prefectures and commanderies should act in concert, forming a pincer movement.
If they should offer themselves up,
not a single horse should return.
The edict asked:
“If barbarian cavalry suddenly
plunder and raid without warning,
farmers going out to cultivate are captured,
and wild grain provides resources for the enemy,
by the time the young men mature,
there will be no military provisions.
The foundation of Jiāngdōng
cannot be exhausted entirely.
What method should be established
to sustain both?”
Your servant believes that the resources of the regional commands
should indeed involve both farming and defending.
If they are to maintain strong fortifications and cultivate in spring,
Cessation of farming,
clearing the fields, and autumn harvests cannot be simulated.
Privately, there is no livelihood;
publicly, coffers become empty.
Drawing far upon fundamental principles,
two or three (points) are inappropriate.
The method to remedy this
lies solely in exerting
full effort in defense.
If they come, we must resist and fight;
if they leave, we must pursue them.
Hold fast to dangerous terrain and secure strategic passes.
This makes it easy to manage both front and rear.
Once the Hú (barbarian) horses retreat,
then the people's granaries will be full.
In three
years' time,
we can launch a long-distance offensive.
The imperial edict states:
“The direction of the bandits
originally has no prior plan,
and the advance of our troops
also has no fixed destination.
In recent years of military garrisons,
many storehouses are empty.
If we gather
multitudes beforehand,
it will consume grain and provisions.
If the enemy arrives suddenly,
we will also have no means to respond.”
Your servant believes that pushing the vanguard forward to attack
requires great resources.
Relying on the root to respond to the branch
does not require
a large multitude.
Currently, the invaders are not recklessly charging with their whole nation.
The situation of the walled cities is sufficient for mutual support.
If the soldiers are nurtured to be brave,
and those appointed are talented,
they will be fearless in the face of events,
and will respond to opportunities without error.
Why
trouble ourselves with vainly gathering troops,
to await what has not yet happened?
The imperial edict states:
“The Róngdĩ (barbarians) are greedy
and only covet profit.
If their wicked schemes are not thwarted,
their treacherous ambitions will consolidate year by year.”
Your servant believes that if we do not strike, they will certainly plunder.
If plundering does
not cease,
then the people will lose their farming and sericulture.
If farming and sericulture are not harvested,
then the royal garrisons cannot be established.
The way to establish them
is to strike them as essential.
The imperial edict states:
“If the borderlands are alarmed year after year,
and both public and private sectors lose their livelihoods,
and expenses are burdened by distant transport,
then long-term plans will certainly not be accomplished.
Putting aside harmful strategies and praising new ones,
there is a way to
respond to the enemy.”
Your servant believes that the way to awe the barbarians
lies in accumulating grain at the frontier.
If the border people lose their livelihoods,
and the various garrisons have meager reserves,
not only will there be no means for long-term plans,
but also we will
be unable to stop their incursions and raids.
Now we should let small garrisons check their initial attacks,
and large towns rush to their entry into our territory.
Once they suffer a blow,
they will immediately scatter like blown birds.
Soon after, he was appointed to a true position
and promoted to Zuǒchéng.
Previously, during the Yuánjiā era,
He Chéngtiān, the Zhùzuòláng, was tasked with drafting the national history.
In the early years of Shìzǔ,
he again commissioned Fèngcháoqǐng Shān Qiānzhī and Nántái Yùshǐ Sū Bǎoshēng to continue and complete it.
In the sixth year,
Yuán was again made Zhùzuòláng
to finish the work.
Although Yuán drew upon previous works,
he devoted himself to making it a singular history.
He submitted a memorial, stating: Your servant has heard that the history of Yú (Shùn) brightly illustrates,
first the beauty of widely spreading enlightenment;
the records of Xià (Yǔ) clearly stipulate,
first the diligence of controlling floods.
Even if Tiānfēi (Táng) attained kingship,
he eventually relied on
farming and leaping;
the divine ancestor (Wǔ of Zhōu) began by aiding governance,
and his bright beginning was founded upon appointing a chief minister.
As for the hymns of Yīn,
Chángfā (the long beginning) praised Xuánwáng;
receiving the mandate to establish Zhōu,
it was truly Yōngbó.
Examining
the height of their conduct,
these were the grand rules of antiquity.
Down to the Two Hàn dynasties,
they also followed this principle.
The founding emperor (Gāozǔ) started in Fēngjiāo,
and the continuation of his lineage originated in Kūnyì.
Wèi used Wǔ
to name its national history (Guózhì);
Jìn used Xuān to inaugurate its Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū).
This clarifies that Huángchū was not the origin of a change of surname,
and Tàishǐ was the end of creation.
These are also the excellent precedents of recent times,
and the grand
rules for distant ages.
The Diǎnmó (canons and counsels) are remote,
Good and evil are all recorded,
success and failure are fully noted.
However, the remaining purple (usurpers),
those who drowned the world and obliterated Xià,
whom the emperor personally
eradicated,
are not arranged in the beginning of the first biography.
Shè, Shèng, Zhuó, Shào,
who rose like smoke and clouds,
and were not exterminated by him,
are prominently crowned in the first narrative.
Is this not because earlier events are
assigned to previous records,
and accomplishments are jointly recorded in later compilations?
Your servant humbly reflects that the August Sòng succeeded the decadent end of the Metal Element,
and encountered a period of difficulty for national governance.
Embracing profound light, it soared like a phoenix;
holding divine talismans, it rose like a dragon.
Exterminating the great
whales (tyrants),
Heaven and man awaited its arrival.
When the Jìn's mandate of fortune ended,
the Supreme Lord appointed Sòng.
It should have immediately assumed universal dominion
and responded to the divine work.
Yet, with reverence, it diligently served in the tripartite division,
and its virtue of yielding
surpassed those who did not succeed.
Its grandeur and vastness,
its splendor and brilliance,
after observing and hearing from afar,
none can equal this.
It is fitting to change the text according to the received documents,
and to alter the era name upon boarding the boat.
The year Yìxī should be taken as the beginning of the royal enterprise.
The records of exertions should be compiled,
and these should be the definitive accounts of meritorious officials.
As for the usurpation and seizure by the false Xuán (Huán Xuán),
which is analogous to Xīn Wáng (Wáng Mǎng),
although Língwǔ defeated and extinguished him,
this should be detailed in the Jìn records.
As for those who defied the mandate and violated the principles,
and were executed by the hegemonic court,
even if it was before the abdication,
all should be recorded in the Sòng annals.
The national canon is great in scope
and will endure for
eternity.
I request external deliberation,
and humbly await compliance.
Thereupon, there was extensive deliberation both within and outside the court.
Tàizǎi Jiāngxiàwáng Yìgōng and thirty-five others agreed with Yuán's proposal,
that the first year of Yìxī should be the dividing point.
Sànqí Chángshì Bālíngwáng Xiūròu and Shàngshū Jīnbùláng Tán Dàoluán both suggested that the third year of Yuánxīng should be the starting point.
Tàixué Bóshì Yú Hé suggested that the founding of the state, i.e., the first year of Sònggōng, should be the starting point.
The imperial edict stated:
“Xiàng Jí and Shèng Gōng,
recorded in the histories of the Two Hàn,
already have precedents in previous histories.
The biography of Huán Xuán should be included in the Sòng canon.
The rest shall follow Yuán's proposal.”
In the seventh year,
Xu Ái was transferred to the position of Yóují Jiāngjūn.
In that year,
Shìzǔ went on a southern tour,
and Xu Ái, with his current rank, concurrently served as Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
When the imperial carriage returned to the palace,
he was relieved of this concurrent post.
The following year,
he again concurrently held the post of Zuǒchéng,
with his position as Zuòshū (Director of the Imperial Library) remaining as before.
When Shìzǔ died,
and the Jǐngníng Líng was being constructed,
Xu Ái, with his current rank, concurrently served as Jiāngzuò Dàjiàng.
Xu Ái was compliant and skilled at serving others,
able to grasp the subtle intentions of the ruler.
He had a broad knowledge of historical texts and commentaries,
and was especially familiar with court rituals.
In the early Yuánjiā era, he began to serve close to the emperor,
participating in consultations.
Since he was good at flattery and accommodating,
and also embellished his words with classical allusions,
he was therefore trusted and esteemed by Tàizǔ.
During the Dàmíng era,
the trust and responsibility placed in him were exceptionally heavy.
The major court rituals and protocols,
unless deliberated by Xu Ái, would not be implemented.
Even if there were scholars of exceptional learning at the time
who dared not offer differing opinions,
what they said was also not followed.
When Shìzǔ died,
after the period of public mourning,
Zǐxūn, Prince of Jìn'ān, consulted Xu Ái, asking whether he should resume his studies or not.
Xu Ái replied:
"During mourning, one studies mourning rites;
what objection is there to resuming studies?"
A few days later,
Zǐzhēn, Prince of Shǐ'ān, also consulted Xu Ái.
Xu Ái said:
"One abandons studies for minor mourning;
how can one read during three years of mourning?"
His arbitrary and contradictory decisions were all like this.
The former deposed emperor was cruel and tyrannical,
and many old retainers in the palace departments
were punished and dismissed.
Only Xu Ái, being skilled at anticipating and welcoming,
remained without offense from beginning to end.
After the execution of the various high officials,
Xu Ái was made Huángmén Shìláng,
concurrently leading Shèshēng Xiàowèi,
with his position as Zuòshū (Director of the Imperial Library) remaining as before.
He was enfeoffed as the Viscount of Wúpíng County,
with a stipend of five hundred households.
His favor and intimate treatment were immense,
unmatched by any other minister.
Whenever the emperor went out,
he often rode in the same carriage with Shěn Qìngzhī and Princess Shānyīn,
and Xu Ái was also included.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
his enfeoffment was generally rescinded.
As Huángmén Shìláng, he was instead given command of Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi,
and concurrently Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
The following year,
he was appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū,
with his Zuòshū (Director of the Imperial Library) position remaining as before.
Xu Ái had held power for a long time,
and the Emperor (Tàizōng), when he was still a prince,
had always disliked him.
By the Jǐnghé era,
he had been humiliated and restricted,
and Xu Ái’s respect towards him was very perfunctory,
which further intensified his resentment.
In the third year of Tàishǐ,
an imperial edict stated: "Indeed, to serve the ruler without ritual,
is not tolerated by teachings;
to slander superiors and flaunt oneself,
is abhorred by human ethics.
Tàizhōng Dàfū Xú Ái, emerged from humble origins,
and by pushing aside gluttonous
sycophants,
he eventually joined the ranks of respected officials.
His family became a renowned clan,
and his promotions and increasing honors
were all extraordinary burdens.
Yet, his obsequiousness, frivolity, and treachery
were innate to his nature.
His glibness and slanderous falsehoods
persisted from youth to old age.
In his public service,
not a jot of integrity was heard of;
he was never ashamed or content,
but constantly sought advancement.
The former court (i.e., Emperor Xiàowǔ) once considered that among the lowly,
he possessed some learning and understanding,
and thus gradually allowed him to be employed,
entering and exiting both palaces.
When Tàichū was falsely established,
he wholeheartedly flattered and served him.
Only when the army of righteousness had shaken the realm
did he flee south.
When Xiàowǔ assumed rule,
he merely engaged in extreme flattery,
conforming and obeying instructions,
indulging his nature.
This led to a harsh and unrestrained administration,
and constructions that violated regulations,
damaging virtue and harming the people—
all due to this wretch.
In the Jǐnghé era,
he was perverse and treacherous,
deeply assisting and colluding,
merely seeking temporary survival
without regard for loyalty and integrity.
He employed calculations and schemes
to please the ruler.
His cunning and deceitful maneuvering
ensured his objectives were always followed,
thus he served
seven courts,
maintaining his high status into old age.
He considered himself to be endowed with profound virtue
and foresight,
thus sinking deeper into error,
unaware of the need for reform or awakening.
I have restored order from chaos,
achieving merit and saving the empire.
The spirits have aided my cause,
and all rebels will surely be eliminated.
Yet Xu Ái, though nurtured by favor,
showed no reciprocal effort.
Instead, he harbored disloyal intentions within,
manifesting in his conduct.
Feigning ignorance and keeping silent,
he offered no proposals or opinions,
being lazy in his duties and slow in his writings,
hoping to carry out his devious plans.
Currently, the court is filled with worthy talents,
and the state is free from wicked sycophants.
Yet, his
heart is impure,
repeatedly corrupting the current administration.
At the time of his self-declared retirement,
he was granted the office of a retired elder,
with exceptional honor and deference.
Was this not an excessive indulgence?
Unexpectedly, he harbored hidden resentment and spoke ill
of others outside the court,
and his relentless pursuit of advancement continued.
His earnest words and entrusted intentions
erupted upon every encounter.
Although the true nature of such a petty person
had been foreseen,
it was still hoped that he might reform,
and it was not endured to apply the law.
Thus,
he presumed upon my boundless benevolence,
believing he would always be forgiven.
Yesterday, during a feast,
he freely engaged in mockery and denigration,
claiming that all imperial edicts
relied on others' suggestions,
and that the high officials lacked decisive judgment,
while key positions in the court
were filled by incompetent individuals.
Presuming on his age and former association,
his insolence was extreme.
Recently, with border troubles not yet settled,
and the populace being pacified with benevolence,
military strategy is the priority,
and the administration is simplified.
Hence, this small
individual
has been able to presume on this leniency and act unrestrained.
He ought to be thrown to the wolves and tigers
to purify the royal governance.
However, as he is old and frail and nearing the end of his life,
it is not necessary to exhaust the law.
His crime can be specially pardoned,
and he shall be banished to
Jiāozhōu.
Yuán (Xú Yuán) had already departed,
when another imperial edict stated:
"The eight considerations for lenient punishment of crimes
were previously (applied to) one category.
When facing the five punishments,
the aged must certainly receive clemency.
Xú Yuán's past transgressions
logically leave no room for appeal.
To banish him to the distant shores of the sea
is truly in accordance with the national laws.
However, as he received Our recognition early on,
We specially pity his foolish decay.
Having already undergone a great pardon,
We wish for him to partake in a special favor.
He may be specially appointed as a governor of a commandery within the jurisdiction of Guǎngzhōu."
The relevant authorities then memorialized that he be appointed as the Grand Administrator of Sònglóng.
Once the appointment order was issued,
Xú Yuán had already arrived in Jiāozhōu.
At that time, the Cìshǐ, Zhāng Mù, had died of illness,
and the local man Lǐ Chángrén caused a rebellion,
[一三]slaughtering all those who had come from the north and settled there;
none were spared.
Lǐ Chángrén had long heard of Xú Yuán's reputation
and lured him with clever schemes,
so he was able to avoid harm.
After a long time, he was allowed to return,
and was then appointed as Nánkāng Jùn丞 (Assistant Administrator).
When Tàizōng died,
he returned to the capital,
and Xú Yuán was appointed as Nánjìyīn Tàishǒu (Grand Administrator),
and then again as Zhōngsàn Dàfū.
In the third year of Yuánhuī,
he died,
at the age of eighty-two.
Ruǎn Diànfū
was a native of Zhūjì, Kuàijī.
During the Yuánjiā period,
he began his career as a small clerk in the imperial secretariat (Tái Xiǎoshǐ).
When Tàizōng first left the inner court,
he was selected to be Zhǔyī (Master of Wardrobe).
Shìzǔ summoned him back to his side,
and appointed him as Nèi Jiān (Inner Supervisor).
During the Yǒngguāng period,
Tàizōng again requested him to be the Shìzǐ Shī (Crown Prince's Tutor),
and he was greatly trusted and favored.
At the end of Jǐnghé,
Tàizōng was confined in the palace,
residing in the Mìshū Shěng (Secretariat Bureau),
and was suspected by the emperor,
with great misfortune imminent.
He was terrified and at a loss for what to do.
Diànfū, together with Wáng Dàolóng, Lǐ Dào'ér, and the emperor's attendants Lángyá Chúnyú Wénzǔ, conspired to depose and enthrone.
At that time, the Zhíhé Jiāngjūn (General of the Inner Guard) Liǔ Guāngshì also had a secret plan with the emperor's attendants Lánlíng Miáo Fāngshèng and Dānyáng Zhōu Dēngzhī,
but they did not yet know whom to support.
Dēngzhī had old ties with Tàizōng,
so Fāngshèng and others had Dēngzhī connect with Diànfū,
and Diànfū was greatly pleased.
Previously, when the emperor established the empress,
all the imperial eunuchs of the various princes were temporarily removed,
and Tàizōng's attendant Qián Lánshēng was also among them.
After the matter was concluded, he had not yet been dispatched,
so he secretly sent Lánshēng to observe the emperor.
Fearing the plot would be exposed,
Lánshēng did not wish to go out himself,
and instead reported the emperor's every movement to Chúnyú Wénzǔ,
who then relayed it to Diànfū.
On the twenty-ninth day of the eleventh month of the first year of Jǐnghé, in the afternoon,
the emperor went to the Huálín Yuán (Hua Lin Garden).
Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén, Shānyáng Wáng Xiūyòu, and the Shānyīn Gōngzhǔ were all attending him.
Tàizōng was still in the Mìshū Shěng,
not having been summoned,
and became even more anxious and fearful.
Diànfū informed the Wàijiān Diǎnshì (External Supervisor in charge of affairs) Dōngyáng Zhū Yòu,
and also the Zhǔyī (Master of Wardrobe) Wúxìng Shòu Jìzhī and the Xìkǎi Zhǔ (Commander of Light Cavalry) Nánpéngchéng Jiāng Chǎnzhī.
Chǎnzhī, in turn, told his subordinate Xìkǎi Jiāng (Commander of Light Cavalry) Línchuái Wáng Jìngzé.
Yòu also told the Zhōngshū Shèrén (Secretary of the Central Secretariat) Dài Míngbǎo,
and they all responded positively.
Míngbǎo and Yòu wished to act at dawn on that day,
but Diànfū and others persuaded them to act after the drum sounded (i.e., after the gates opened).
Yòu made arrangements beforehand with those inside and outside (the palace),
and had Qián Lánshēng secretly inform Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén and others.
At that time, the emperor wanted to go on a southern tour,
and his trusted Zhíhé Jiāngjūn Zōng Yuè and others were all allowed to go out that evening to prepare their attire.
Only the Duìzhǔ (Company Commander) Fán Sēngzhěng was guarding the Huálín Gé (Hua Lin Pavilion).
He was a fellow countryman of Liǔ Guāngshì.
Guāngshì invited him,
and Sēngzhěng immediately accepted the order.

Jiāng Chǎnzhī also invited the Duìfù (Company Vice-Commander) Yángpíng Niè Qìng and the brave warriors under his command, Kuàijī Fù Língfú, Wújùn Yú Dàolóng, Dānyáng Sòng Kuízhī, and Yángpíng Tián Sì,
and they all gathered at Qìng's residence.
Diànfū feared that their strength was insufficient and wished to recruit more,
but Shòu Jìzhī said:
"A broader conspiracy might be exposed;
there is no need for too many people."
At that time, shamans said:
"There are ghosts in the back hall."
That evening,
the emperor, in front of the Zhúlín Táng (Bamboo Grove Hall),
was shooting at them with the shamans.
Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén and others, and Shānyīn Zhǔ, were all following.
The emperor had always disliked Jìzhī,
and would grind his teeth whenever he saw him.
Since Jìzhī had finalized the plot with Diànfū,
and also feared misfortune,
he drew his knife and rushed forward.
Jiāng Chǎnzhī followed him,
and Chúnyú Wénzǔ, Miáo Fāngshèng, Zhōu Dēngzhī, Fù Língfú, Niè Qìng, Tián Sì, Wáng Jìngzé, Yú Dàolóng, and Sòng Kuízhī followed in succession.
Xiūrén heard the sound of footsteps moving very quickly
and said to Xiūyòu:
"The deed is done!"
They fled together to Jǐngyáng Shān.
When the emperor saw Jìzhī approach,
he drew his bow and shot at him,
but missed.
He then ran,
and Jìzhī pursued and killed him.
Once the matter was settled,
an announcement was issued to the palace guards, saying:
"The Xiāngdōng Wáng has received the Empress Dowager's order
to eliminate the mad ruler.
Now peace has been restored."
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
he rewarded the meritorious.
Shòu Jìzhī was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yìngchéng Xiàn,
with an income of one thousand households.
Jiāng Chǎnzhī as the Marquis of Rǔnán Xiàn,
Diànfū as the Marquis of Jiànchéng Xiàn,
with an income of eight hundred households.
Wáng Dàolóng as the Marquis of Wúpíng Xiàn,
Chúnyú Wénzǔ as the Marquis of Yángchéng Xiàn,
each with an income of five hundred households.
Lǐ Dào'ér as the Marquis of Xīnyú Xiàn,
[一四]Miáo Fāngshèng as the Marquis of Liúyáng Xiàn,
Zhōu Dēngzhī as the Marquis of Qūlíng Xiàn,
each with an income of four hundred households.
Fù Língfú as the Viscount of Huìhuái Xiàn,
Niè Qìng as the Viscount of Jiànyáng Xiàn,
Tián Sì as the Viscount of Jiānglè Xiàn,
Wáng Jìngzé as the Viscount of Chóng'ān Xiàn,
Yú Dàolóng as the Viscount of Chálíng Xiàn,
Sòng Kuízhī as the Viscount of Línglíng Xiàn,
each with an income of three hundred households.
Diànfū was promoted to Nántái Shìyùshǐ (Censor in the Southern Secretariat).
When Xuē Suǒ'ér crossed the Huái River to raid,
and Shānyáng Tàishǒu Chéng Tiānzuò also rebelled,
Diànfū joined the various armies to suppress them,
defeating Suǒ'ér
and forcing Tiānzuò to surrender.
He was promoted to Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (General Soaring Dragon), Sītú Cānjūn (Staff Officer of the Minister of Works),
and led his subordinates to assist at Zhěqí.
He was transferred to Tàizǐ Bùbīng Xiàowèi (Colonel of the Crown Prince's Infantry), Nánlǔ Jùn Tàishǒu (Grand Administrator of Nanlu Commandery),
and attended the Crown Prince in the Eastern Palace.
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ,
for his achievements in defeating Xuē Suǒ'ér,
he was granted an additional two hundred households,
making a total of one thousand households.
He concurrently held his original office as Yóují Jiāngjūn (General of Roaming Cavalry),
and was temporarily appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North),
and, together with Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General Who Assists the State) and concurrent Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (General of Valiant Cavalry) Mèng Cìyáng,
served in the two guards.
Mèng Cìyáng, courtesy name Chóngjī,
was a native of Ānqū, Píngchāng.
In the early Tàishǐ period,
he served as Piàojí Cānjūn (Staff Officer of the General of Agile Cavalry) to Shānyáng Wáng Xiūyòu.
When Xuē Āndū's son, Dàobiāo, attacked Héféi,
Mèng Cìyáng defeated him,
and for his achievements, was enfeoffed as the Viscount of Yōuxiàn,
with an income of three hundred households.
He successively served as Yòujūn (Right Army) and Piàojí Cānjūn.
[一五]In the sixth year,
he was appointed as Fǔshī Jiāngjūn (General Who Assists the Army) and Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yanzhou),
stationed at Huái'yīn,
and established Běiyǎnzhōu,
which began from this time.
He was promoted to the title of Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Manifests the Army's Power).
In the fourth year of Yuánhuī,
he died.
At that time, Diànfū 佃夫, Wáng Dàolóng 王道隆, and Yáng Yùncháng 楊運長 all held the reins of power,
second only to the sovereign.
Compared to the reigns of Cháo 巢 and Dài 戴, they were insignificant.
Once, when the New Year's Day (Zhèngdàn 正旦) was due to coincide with the new moon (héshuò 合朔),
the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū 尚書) proposed moving the New Year's Assembly (Yuánhuì 元會).
Diànfū 佃夫 said:
“The grand assembly of the New Year (Yuánzhèng Qìnghuì 元正慶會)
is a great national ceremony.
Why not move the new moon day instead?”
Such was his ignorance of ancient precedents.
He engaged in massive bribery and
no matter was resolved without heavy bribes.
A person once offered him two hundred rolls of silk,
but he deemed it too little
and did not reply to the letter.
His residences, gardens, and ponds
surpassed those of all the imperial princes.
He had dozens of female entertainers,
whose artistry and beauty were unsurpassed at the time,
and their adornments of gold, jade, brocade, and embroidery
were not matched even in the imperial palace.
Every time he had a garment made
or an object crafted,
the capital city would imitate it.
He dug a canal within his estate,
extending about ten *lǐ* to the east.
The banks were neat and tidy,
where light boats would float,
accompanied by female musicians.
Liú Xiū 劉休, a Central Secretariat Drafter (Zhōngshū Shèrén 中書舍人), once visited him.
It happened that Diànfū 佃夫 was out,
and they met on the road.
He invited Liú Xiū 劉休 to return with him,
and as soon as they were seated,
he ordered a feast to be prepared.
All kinds of rare delicacies
were immediately brought forth.
All the cooked dishes
were freshly prepared;
there were dozens of such items.
Diànfū 佃夫 often prepared meals for dozens of people
to entertain guests,
thus he could quickly make such arrangements;
it was always like this.
Even Wáng 王 and Shí 石 of the Jìn 晉 dynasty
could not surpass him.
In the early Tàishǐ 泰始 period,
as military merits were numerous,
ranks and offices were disorderly.
Diànfū's 佃夫 servants and attendants
all received extraordinary positions.
His carriage drivers became Hu̍bēn Zhōngláng 虎賁中郎,
and those who walked beside his horse became Yuánwàiláng 員外郎.
Officials, noble and humble,
all sought to ally themselves with him.
However, he was arrogant and showed no deference.
Only a few people, such as Shěn Bó 沈勃 of Wúxìng 吳興 and Zhāng Dàn 張澹 of Wújùn 吳郡,
were allowed into his inner chambers.
In the first year of Tàiyù 泰豫,
he was appointed General of Pacifying Barbarians (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn 寧朔將軍) and Administrator of Huáinán 淮南 (Huáinán Tàishǒu 淮南太守).
He was promoted to General of Galloping Cavalry (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn 驍騎將軍),
and soon after, given the additional title of Administrator of Huáilíng 淮陵 (Huáilíng Tàishǒu 淮陵太守).
When Tàizōng 太宗 passed away
and the later Deposed Emperor (Hòu Fèidì 後廢帝) ascended the throne,
Diànfū's 佃夫 authority became even heavier.
He concurrently held the post of Central Secretariat Drafter of Internal Correspondence (Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén 中書通事舍人),
and was given the additional titles of Attendant Official (Jǐshìzhōng 給事中) and General Who Assists the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍),
with his other positions remaining unchanged.
He wanted to appoint Zhāng Dàn 張澹 as Administrator of Wǔlíng 郡 (Wǔlíng Jùn 武陵郡),
but Wèi Jiāngjūn Yuán Càn 衛將軍袁粲 and others disagreed.
However, Diànfū 佃fū claimed it was an imperial edict and enforced it,
and Yuán Càn 袁粲 and the others dared not object.
In the third year of Yuánhuī 元徽,
he was promoted to Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Huángmén Shìláng 黃門侍郎)
and concurrently served as General of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn 右衞將軍),
[一六] with his post as administrator remaining unchanged.
The following year,
he was reassigned to concurrently hold the post of General of Galloping Cavalry (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn 驍騎將軍).
In the same year,

he was promoted to Bearer of Credential (Shǐchíjié 使持節), Supervisor of Military Affairs of Nán Yùzhōu (Dū Nányùzhōu Zhū Jūnshì 督南豫州諸軍事), General of the Victorious Army (Guānjūn Jiāngjūn 冠軍將軍), Provincial Governor of Nán Yùzhōu (Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ 南豫州刺史), and Administrator of Lìyáng (Lìyáng Tàishǒu 歷陽太守),
while still managing internal affairs.
For his achievements in pacifying King Jìanpíng Jǐngsù (Jìanpíng Wáng Jǐngsù 建平王景素),
he was granted an additional five hundred households.
At that time, the Deposed Emperor (Fèidì 廢帝) was reckless,
fond of going out and roaming.
When he first left the palace,
he would still arrange his feathered retinue
and lead his troops.
But soon, he would abandon his formations,
riding alone with a few companions,
sometimes going to the countryside,
sometimes entering marketplaces.
Both inside and outside the palace, everyone was fearful and worried.
Diànfū 佃夫 secretly conspired with Shēn Bózōng 申伯宗, General of the Palace Gate (Zhíhé Jiāngjūn 直閤將軍), Zhū Yòu 朱幼, Commandant of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi 步兵校尉), and Yú Tiānbǎo 于天寶 to depose the emperor
and enthrone the Prince of Ānchéng (Ānchéng Wáng 安成王).
In the spring of the fifth year,
the emperor wanted to go to Jiāngchéng 江乘 to hunt pheasants.
Whenever the emperor went north,
he would usually leave his troops in front of the Lèyóu Yuàn 樂遊苑,
and abandon them as he departed.
Diànfū 佃夫 planned to claim the empress dowager's order to recall the troops,
close the city gates,
station men to guard Shítou 石頭 and Dōngfǔ 東府,
send men to seize and depose the emperor,
and make himself Provincial Governor of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu Cìshǐ 揚州刺史) to assist in governance.
He had already completed his plan with Zhū Yòu 朱幼 and the others.
However, the emperor did not go to Jiāngchéng 江乘,
so the plan did not proceed.
Yú Tiānbǎo 于天寶 then reported the conspiracy to the emperor.
The emperor consequently arrested Diànfū 佃夫, Zhū Yòu 朱幼, and Shēn Bózōng 申伯宗 at the outer compound of the Palace Grandee (Guānglù 外部),
and bestowed death upon them.
The crime of Diànfū 佃夫 and Zhū Yòu 朱幼 ended with their deaths;
no one else was questioned.
Diànfū 佃夫 was fifty-one years old at that time.
Zhū Yòu 朱幼,
in the early Tàishǐ 泰始 period, was an external supervisor (Wàijiān 外監).
He was assigned to Zhāng Yǒng's 張永 various armies for campaigns,
and showed ability in managing affairs.
He gradually rose to the third rank,
[一七] serving as an Attendant for Court Audiences (Fèngcháoqǐng 奉朝請) and Administrator of Nán Gāopíng (Nán Gāopíng Tàishǒu 南高平太守).
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānpǔ County (Ānpǔ Xiàn Hóu 安浦縣侯),
with an income of two hundred households.
Yú Tiānbǎo 于天寶,
whose ancestors were Hú 胡 people,
participated in the achievements of the Zhúlín Táng 竹林堂.
In the Yuánhuī 元徽 period,
he reported his merits
and sought additional enfeoffment and titles.
He was then enfeoffed as Baron of È County (È Xiàn Zǐ 鄂縣子),
with an income of two hundred households.
For revealing Diànfū's 佃夫 plot,
he was made Administrator of Qīnghé (Qīnghé Tàishǒu 清河太守)
and General of the Right Army (Yòujūn Jiāngjūn 右軍將軍).
In the first year of Shēngmíng 昇明,
he was sent out as Administrator of Shānyáng (Shānyáng Tàishǒu 山陽太守).
King Qí 齊 deemed him treacherous
and granted him death.
Shòu Jìzhī 壽寂之,
in the early Tàishǐ 泰ǐ period,
had his income increased by two hundred households for military merits.
He served as Supervisor of the Feathered Forest (Yǔlín Jiān 羽林監)
and was promoted to Commandant of Cavalry for the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Túqí Xiàowèi 太子屯騎校尉),
soon after given the additional titles of General of Pacifying Barbarians (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn 寧朔將ūn) and Administrator of Nán Tàishān (Nán Tàishān Tàishǒu 南泰山太守).
He accepted many bribes
and his requests were endless.
If one was not granted,
he would gnash his teeth and curse,
often saying:
“With a sharp knife in hand,
why worry about not succeeding?”
He would whip prison officers and
chop down scouting generals.
In the seventh year,
he was impeached by the appropriate authorities
and exiled to Yuèzhōu 越州.
While en route to Yùzhāng 豫章,
he conspired to flee and rebel,
so he was killed.
Jiāng Chǎnzī 姜產之,
in the early Tàishǐ 泰始 period,
had his income increased by two hundred households for military merits.
He served as Staff Officer in Charge of Military Affairs for General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Zhōngbīng Cānjūn 驃騎中兵參軍) for Prince Jìn Píng Xiūyòu (Jìn Píng Wáng Xiūyòu 晉平王休祐),
and General of Dragon-Soaring (Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn 龍驤將軍) and Administrator of Nán Jìyīn (Nán Jìyīn Tàishǒu 南濟陰太守).
In the third year, during the northern expedition,
he fought against the barbarians,
but his army was defeated and he was killed.
He was posthumously granted the title General of the Left Army (Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn 左軍將軍),
with his administrative post remaining unchanged.
Lǐ Dào'ér 李道兒,
a native of Línhuái 臨淮.
He was originally a tutor to the Prince of Xiāngdōng (Xiāngdōng Wáng 湘東王),
gradually rising to become Director of the Xiāngdōng State Academy (Xiāngdōng Guóxué Guānlìng 湘東國學官令).
When Tàizōng 太宗 ascended the throne,
