he gradually advanced to Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant (Yuánwài Sǎnjì Shìláng 員外散騎侍郎)
and Administrator of Huáilíng (Huáilíng Tàishǒu 淮陵太守).
In the second year of Tàishǐ 泰始,
he concurrently held the post of Central Secretariat Drafter of Internal Correspondence (Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén 中書通事舍人),
and was transferred to Attendant Official (Jǐshìzhōng 給事中).
In the fourth year,
he died of illness.
Wáng Dàolóng 王道隆,
a native of Wúxìng Wūchéng 吳興烏程.
His elder brother, Wáng Dàoxùn 王道迄,
was learned and skilled in calligraphy,
and also handsome in appearance.
Wáng Sháozhī 王韶之, the Administrator of Wúxìng 吳興, said to people:
“If one has a son or younger brother like Wáng Dàoxùn 王道迄,
one lacks nothing.”
Jùn, the Prince of Shǐxìng (Shǐxìng Wáng Jùn 始興王濬), appointed him as tutor to his heir apparent.
He was appointed Clerk of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìngshǐ 中書令史) for his calligraphy.
Dào Lóng (道隆) also knew how to write.
He served as a clerk for the principal secretary,
gradually becoming the principal secretary.
Shì Zǔ (世祖) sent him to transmit a command,
but he misinterpreted the emperor's intention,
so he was dismissed
and not allowed to re-enter the six gates.
Tài Zōng (太宗), while garrisoned at Péngchéng (彭城),
appointed him as a diǎn qiān (典籤),
and then director of the inner palace (nèi jiān 內監).
When he ascended the throne,
Dào Lóng (道隆) became a attendant censor of the Southern Terrace (nán tái shì yù shǐ 南臺侍御史),
gradually rising to extra-rank attendant-consultant (yuán wài sàn qí shì láng 員外散騎侍郎)
and Grand Administrator of Southern Lánlíng (nán Lánlíng tàishǒu 南蘭陵太守).
In the second year of Tàishǐ (泰始) (466 CE),
he concurrently served as a Palace Attendant in the Central Secretariat (zhōng shū tōng shì shè rén 中書通事舍人).
For his merit in defeating Jìnlíng (晉陵),
his stipend was increased by one hundred households,
making a total of six hundred households.
In the fifth year (469 CE),
he was sent to attend the Eastern Palace (dōng gōng 東宮),
and again concurrently served as a Palace Attendant in the Central Secretariat.
After the Later Deposed Emperor (hòu fèi dì 後廢帝) ascended the throne,
he was promoted from Colonel of the Heir Apparent's Garrison (tàizǐ yì jūn xiàowèi 太子翊軍校尉) to General of the Right Army (yòu jūn jiāngjūn 右軍將軍).
His positions as Grand Administrator (tàishǒu 太守) and Palace Attendant (shèrén 舍人) remained as before.
Dào Lóng (道隆) was trusted by Tài Zōng (太宗)
even more than Tián Fū (佃夫).
He was harmonious and cautious, preserving himself,
not recklessly slandering or harming others.
Having held power for a long time,
his family wealth accumulated.
Although his splendor and luxury did not surpass Tián Fū (佃夫),
his meticulousness and orderliness exceeded him.
In the second year of Yuánhuī (元徽) (474 CE),
when Grand Commandant Prince Huì Yáng (guì yáng wáng 休範) Xiū Fàn (休範) suddenly arrived at Xīntíng (新亭),
Tián Fū (佃夫) remained to guard the palace interior,
while Dào Lóng (道隆) led the elite troops of the Feathered Forest (yǔlín 羽林) towards Zhūquè Gate (zhūquè mén 朱雀門).
At that time, the bandits had already reached south of the ferry.
Dào Lóng (道隆) suddenly summoned General of the Garrison Army (zhèn jūn jiāngjūn 鎮軍將軍) Liú Miǎn (劉勔) from Shítou (石頭).
When Miǎn (勔) arrived,
Dào Lóng (道隆) ordered the ferry to be opened.
Dào Lóng (道隆) angrily said:
"When bandits arrive, one should attack them immediately.
How can we open the ferry and weaken ourselves?"
Miǎn (勔) dared not speak further.
Dào Lóng (道隆) urged Miǎn (勔) to advance and fight.
Miǎn (勔) was defeated as soon as he crossed the ferry.
The bandits, taking advantage of their victory, advanced directly.
Dào Lóng (道隆) abandoned his troops and fled towards the palace (tái 臺).
His horse repeatedly reared and refused to move forward,
so he was overtaken by the bandit soldiers
and killed.
After the matter was settled,
the imperial carriage came to mourn him.
He was posthumously granted General Who Upholds the State (fǔ guó jiāngjūn 輔國將軍) and Inspector of Yìzhōu (yìzhōu cìshǐ 益州刺史).
His son Fǎ Zhēn (法貞) inherited.
When Qí (齊) received the abdication,
his state was abolished.
Yáng Yùncháng (楊運長) was
a native of Huái'ān (懷安) in Xuānchéng (宣城).
He initially served as a county official in Xuānchéng (宣城) Commandery.
The Grand Administrator Fàn Yè (范曄) praised his official abilities.
He was skilled in archery.
When Tài Zōng (太宗) was first a prince,
he appointed Yùncháng (運長) as his archery master.
His nature was cautious and careful,
and he was trusted by Tài Zōng (太宗).
When Tài Zōng (太宗) ascended the throne,
he treated Yùncháng (運長) with great intimacy and favor.
Along with Tián Fū (佃夫), Dào Lóng (道隆), Lǐ Dào'ér (李道兒), and others, he held important power.
He gradually rose to extra-rank attendant-consultant (yuán wài sàn qí shì láng 員外散騎侍郎)
and Grand Administrator of Southern Píngchāng (nán Píngchāng tàishǒu 南平昌太守).
In the seventh year of Tàishǐ (泰始) (471 CE),
he was sent to attend the Eastern Palace (dōng gōng 東宮).
After the Later Deposed Emperor (hòu fèi dì 後廢帝) ascended the throne,
he and Tián Fū (佃夫) both concurrently served as Palace Attendants (tōng shì shè rén 通事舍人).
He was promoted to General of the Dragon Stratagem (lóng xiáng jiāngjūn 龍驤將軍)
and then transferred to Attendant Gentleman (gěi shì zhōng 給事中).
For his merit in pacifying Prince Guì Yáng (guì yáng wáng 休範) Xiū Fàn (休範),
he was enfeoffed as a Viscount of Nánchéng County (nánchéng xiàn zǐ 南城縣子),
with a stipend of eight hundred households.
In the third year of Yuánhuī (元徽) (475 CE),
he was promoted from Colonel of the Middle Army (chē qí zhōng bīng cānjūn 車騎中兵參軍) to General of the Rear Army (hòu jūn jiāngjūn 後軍將軍),
his position as Palace Attendant (shèrén 舍人) remaining as before.
Yùncháng (運長) was simple, honest, and upright,
maintaining a very pure personal conduct.
He did not engage in gardens or estates
and did not accept gifts or presents.
However, he was common and lacked deep understanding.
He only had close friendships with the commoners Pān Zhì (潘智) and Xú Wénshèng (徐文盛).
Every action and deed
he would discuss and decide with these two.
Wénshèng (文盛) was a Gentleman for Consultation (fèng cháo qǐng 奉朝請)
and participated in pacifying Prince Guì Yáng (guì yáng wáng 休範) Xiū Fàn (休範).
He was enfeoffed as a Baron of Guǎngjìn County (guǎngjìn xiàn nán 廣晉縣男),
with a stipend of four hundred households.
When Emperor Shùn (shùn dì 順帝) ascended the throne,
Yùncháng (運長) was appointed General Who Pacifies the North (níng shuò jiāngjūn 寧朔將軍) and Grand Administrator of Xuānchéng (xuānchéng tàishǒu 宣城太守).
Soon after, he left the commandery and returned home.
When Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) rebelled,
Yùncháng (運cháng) harbored different intentions.
King Qí (qí wáng 齊王) sent Cavalry Commander Cuī Wénzhòng (崔文仲) to punish and execute him.
The Historian remarks: Exhausting loyalty and dedicating oneself
is the ambition of officials;
adapting to circumstances and putting one's talents to use
is the grand ceremony of enlightened rulers.
The 'old' is not inherently old;
it becomes old through the new.
'Intimacy' is not innate;
it arises from distance.
However, when trust is separated by distance,
disparate paths lead to the same outcome.
Power gravitates towards close intimates,
a consistent rule across different eras.
Even with Gāo (高) of Hàn (漢)'s simplicity
and Guāng Wǔ (光武)'s cautiousness and generosity,
Fēng (豐) and Pèi (沛) still often flourished,
and Báishuǐ (白水) first blossomed.
How much more so for Shì Zǔ (世祖)'s stagnation and vulgar proximity,
and Tài Zōng (太宗)'s clinging attachment and favoritism?
To wish for no confusion within the inner chambers,
how could that be possible?
Collation Notes
The surname of the Suǒtóu (索頭) barbarians was Tuòbá (託跋).
Their ancestors were descendants of the Hàn (漢) general Lǐ Líng (李陵).
Líng (陵) surrendered to the Xiōngnú (匈奴),
who had several hundred thousand tribes,
each establishing its own name.
The Suǒtóu (索頭) were also one of them.
In the early Jìn (晉) dynasty,
the Suǒtóu (索頭) tribe had tens of thousands of households in Yúnzhōng (雲中).
Towards the end of Emperor Huì (huì dì 惠帝)'s reign,
the Inspector of Bìngzhōu (bìngzhōu cìshǐ 并州刺史), Sīmǎ Téng (司馬騰), Prince Dōngyíng (dōng yíng gōng 東嬴公), was besieged by the Xiōngnú (匈奴) at Jìnyáng (晉陽).
The Suǒtóu (索頭) Chányú Yī (單于猗) sent troops to assist Téng (騰).
In the third year of Yǒngjiā (永嘉) (309 CE) of Emperor Huái (huái dì 懷帝),
his younger brother Lú (盧) led his tribes from Yúnzhōng (雲中) into Yànmén (雁門).
He requested the five counties of Lóufán (樓煩) and others from Liú Kūn (劉琨), the Inspector of Bìngzhōu (bìngzhōu cìshǐ 并州刺史).
Kūn (琨) could not control him
and also wanted to rely on Lú (盧) for support.
So he submitted a memorial:
"Lú (盧)'s elder brother had the merit of rescuing Téng (騰).
His former achievements should be recorded.
I request that the people of the five counties be moved to Xīnxīng (新興),
and their land be given to him."
Kūn (琨) also memorialized to enfeoff Lú (盧) as Duke of Dàijùn (dàijùn gōng 代郡公).
In the early reign of Emperor Mǐn (mǐn dì 愍帝),
Lú (盧) was further promoted to King of Dài (dài wáng 代王),
and his stipend was increased to include Chángshān (常山) Commandery.
Afterwards, there was great chaos within Lú (盧)'s state.
Lú (盧) died,
and his son was young and weak,
so the tribes dispersed.
Lú (盧)'s grandson, Shíyìjiàn (什翼鞬), was brave and strong,
and the masses re-attached themselves to him.
He was called Duke of Shàngluò (shàngluò gōng 上洛公).
To the north, he had the desert;
to the south, he occupied Yīnshān (陰山).
His followers numbered several hundred thousand.
Afterwards, he was defeated by Fú Jiān (苻堅)
and taken back to Cháng'ān (長安).
Later, he was allowed to return north.
When Jiàn (鞬) died,
his son Kāi (開), courtesy name Shèguī (涉珪), succeeded him.
Previously,
the Xiānbēi, Mùróng Chuí, usurped the imperial title at Zhōngshān.
In the 21st year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ of the Jìn,
after Chuí died,
Tuòbá Guī, the founder of the Northern Wèi, led ten myriad cavalry to besiege Zhōngshān.
In the fourth month of the following year,
he conquered it,
and thus became the sovereign of Zhōngzhōu.
He proclaimed himself Wèi
and named his reign Tiāncì.
In the first year of Tiāncì,
he established his capital at Píngchéng, in Sānggān County of Dàijùn.
He set up schools
and established the Shàngshū Cáos (departments of the Secretariat).
Guī was quite learned
and understood astronomy.
It was their custom to sacrifice to Heaven in the fourth month.
At the end of the sixth month, he would lead a great multitude to Yīnshān,
calling it "repelling frost."
Yīnshān was six hundred *lǐ* from Píngchéng,
deep and densely forested.
Frost and snow never melted there;
presumably, they wished to use warm *qì* to repel the cold.
When they died, they were buried secretly,
with no mounds or marked graves.
For funerals,
coffins and biers were all set up in effigy,
and tombs and outer coffins were erected.
The chariots, horses, and implements used by the deceased during their lifetime were all burned to send off the departed.
Guī was tyrannical and fond of killing;
the people could not endure their lives.
Previously,
a divine shaman warned Guī that he would suffer a terrible calamity,
but that if he executed people in Qīnghé and killed ten thousand commoners,
he could avoid it.
Guī then exterminated the entire Qīnghé Commandery,
personally killing people with his own hands,
wishing to make their number reach ten thousand.
Sometimes, riding in a small carriage,
he would personally wield a sword and strike the heads of the carriage bearers on the eaves.
When one person died,
another replaced them,
and each trip
resulted in dozens of deaths.
At night, he constantly changed his sleeping place;
no one knew where he was,
except for his beloved concubine, Wànrén, who knew his whereabouts.
Wànrén had an illicit affair with Guī's son, the King of Qīnghé, Tuòbá Shào.
Fearing discovery,
Shào wanted to kill Guī
and made Wànrén his internal accomplice.
One night, they waited until Guī was alone
and killed him.
As Guī was dying,
he said:
"What Qīnghé and Wànrén said
was indeed about you."
That year was
the fifth year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān.
Guī's second son, Sī, the King of Qí, whose courtesy name was Mùmò,
seized the King of Qīnghé, Tuòbá Shào,
wept aloud before him,
saying:
"What a man values most is his father;
how could you rebel?"
He then forced Shào to commit suicide.
Sī succeeded to the throne,
and posthumously honored Guī as Emperor Dàowǔ.
In the 13th year (of Yìxī),
Gāozǔ (Emperor Wǔ of Sòng) marched west to attack Cháng'ān.
Sī, who had previously married a daughter of Yáo Xīng,
dispatched ten myriad cavalry to station themselves north of the Yellow River to relieve Cháng'ān.
They were greatly defeated by Gāozǔ;
the details are in the biographies of Zhū Chāoshí and others.
Thereupon, Sī sent envoys to seek peace,
and from then on, missions were exchanged annually.
Gāozǔ sent Palace Gentlemen Shěn Fàn and Suǒ Jìsūn to return the mission.
When they had completed their mission and reached the Yellow River,
but had not yet crossed,
Sī heard the news of Gāozǔ's death.
He recalled and detained Fàn and others,
breaking the peace and kinship.
When Tàizǔ (Emperor Wén of Sòng) ascended the throne,
he then sent Fàn and others back.
In the tenth month of the third year of Yǒngchū,
Sī personally led his troops to Fāngchéng.

He dispatched Zhèng Bīng Jiāngjūn (General of Zheng Troops) and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yáng Province), the Duke of Shānyáng, Dáxī Jīn; Wú Bīng Jiāngjūn (General of Wu Troops) and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Guǎng Province), the Duke of Cāngwú, Gōngsūn Biǎo; and Shàngshū Huájī,
leading over two myriad infantry and cavalry,
to cross south at Shíjì, in Dōngyàn County southwest of Huátái.
Their provisions, weak, and burdens followed them.

Wáng Jǐngdù, the commander of Huátái, Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies Distant Regions), and Dōngjùn Tàishǒu (Administrator of Dōngjùn), galloped to inform Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Champion Army) and Sīzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Sī Province), Máo Dézǔ,

who was garrisoned at Hǔláo. Dézǔ dispatched his Sīmǎ (Military Advisor) Zhái Guǎng, leading Cānjūn (Staff Officer) Páng Zī, Shàngdǎng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Shàngdǎng) Liú Tánzhī, and others, with three thousand infantry and cavalry to resist them.
Their army encamped at Tǔlóu in Juàn County.
The barbarians moved their camp two *lǐ* east of Huátái city,
constructed siege engines,
and daily threatened the city.
Dézǔ, considering the small number of defenders at Huátái,
ordered Zhái Guǎng to recruit able-bodied men from the army,
and dispatched Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn Liú Fāngzhī to lead them
to assist Jǐngdù in defending.
Fāngzhī, with over eighty men,
managed to break into the city.
Dézǔ also dispatched Tǎolú Jiāngjūn (General Who Suppresses Barbarians) and Hóngnóng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Hóngnóng) Dòu Yīngmíng, leading five hundred men;
and Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Establishes Martial Might) Dòu Bà, leading two hundred fifty men,
both of whom were sent with naval forces in succession,
all under the command of Zhái Guǎng.
Initially,
fugitives like Sīmǎ Chǔzhī and others often hid within the borders of Chénliú Commandery.
When the barbarians crossed south,
they galloped to unite with them,
stirring up the border regions,
and causing great distress to the common people.
Dézǔ dispatched Chángshè Lìng (Magistrate of Chángshè) Wáng Fǎzhèng, leading five hundred men to occupy Shàolíng,
and Jiāngjūn Liú Lián, leading two hundred cavalry to Yōngqiū to defend against them.
Chǔzhī attacked Lián at Báimǎ County,
but was defeated by Lián.
At that time, the court sent military supplies,
and Lián went to receive them.
However, Wáng Yù, a commoner from Suānzǎo, knowing that Lián had gone south,
galloped to inform the barbarians.
The barbarian general Huájī led a thousand chariots to attack Cāngyuán.
The soldiers and officials all fled over the city wall,
and Yán Qí, the Administrator of Chénliú, was captured by the barbarians.
The barbarians immediately appointed Wáng Yù as Administrator of Chénliú
and gave him troops to guard Cāngyuán.
In the eleventh month,
the barbarians attacked Huátái city with all their might.
The northeast of the city collapsed,
and Wáng Jǐngdù fled.
Yáng Zàn, Jǐngdù's Sīmǎ, held firm and did not move.
Though his forces collapsed,
he held his ground and did not surrender,
and was killed by the barbarians.
Dòu Yīngmíng attacked the barbarian provisions at Shíjì,
defeating them,
killing over five hundred enemies,
and beheading their garrison commanders □ Liánnèitóu and Zhāng Suǒ'ér, among others.
Yīngmíng went from Shíjì to Huátái,
but hearing the city had fallen,
he advanced to garrison Yǐnmǎo.
Dòu Bà galloped to join Zhái Guǎng.
After the barbarians conquered Huátái,
they concentrated their forces against Guǎng and others.
Unable to resist,
they retreated,
fighting as they advanced.
For two days and one night,
they only traveled about ten *lǐ*.
When the barbarian infantry arrived,
Guǎng and others, their arrows exhausted and strength gone,
suffered a great defeat.
Guǎng, Bà, Tánzhī, and others each returned alone.
The barbarians, emboldened by victory, then reached Hǔláo.
Dézǔ led out infantry and cavalry to attack them,
but the barbarians retreated to Tǔlóu,
and then retreated further to Huátái.
The residents of Cháng'ān, Wèichāng, and Lántián counties, situated below Hǔláo,
were all ordered by Dézǔ to enter the city.
The barbarians separately dispatched Hēishuò Gōng, leading three thousand men to Héyáng,
intending to cross south and take Jīnyǒng.
Dézǔ dispatched Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn (General Who Manifests Awe) and Héyīn Lìng (Magistrate of Héyīn) Dòu Huàng with five hundred men to garrison a small fort;
Gōushì Lìng (Magistrate of Gōushì) Wáng Yú with four hundred men to occupy Jiāncāng;
Gǒng Lìng (Magistrate of Gǒng) Chén Chēn with five hundred men to secure Xiǎopíng;
and Cānjūn Dūhù (Staff Officer and Inspector) Zhāng Jì with five hundred men to garrison Niúlán.
He also dispatched generals leading cavalry units
to join Yáng Yì, the Magistrate of Luòyáng, with two hundred cavalry,
to patrol up and down the river,
responding to situations as they arose.
In the twelfth month,
the barbarians placed a guard at a small fort in Luòchuān.
Dézǔ dispatched Zhái Guǎng to gallop and attack them,
and the barbarians retreated.
Guǎng established defenses,
repaired the city and forts,
and then returned to Hǔláo.
Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yù Province) Liú Cuì dispatched Zhìzhōng (Manager of Affairs) Gāo Dàojǐn, leading five hundred infantry and cavalry to occupy Xiàng.
He also dispatched Sīmǎ Xú Qióng to follow them.
The court dispatched generals Fǔ Bóyǎn, Yáo Zhēn, Dù Tǎn, Liáng Língzǎi, and others, with various naval and infantry forces to continue their advance.
Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Xú Province) Wáng Zhòngdé led his army to Húlù.
Hēishuò Gōng sent his Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk), leading a thousand men, to press Dòu Huàng and Yáng Yì.
Huàng and others counterattacked,
capturing him
and taking two hundred men alive.
Afterwards, Zhèng Bīng Jiāngjūn, with five thousand cavalry, launched a surprise attack on Huàng and others.
Hēishuò crossed the river to join forces with them,
attacking the fort from four sides.
Huàng and others, with few men and scattered forces,
suffered heavy wounds, as did both Huàng and Yì.
The barbarian generals Ānpíng Gōng and Éqīng, with seven thousand troops, crossed south.
They descended east of Què'áo,
reaching Sīdúkou,
about a hundred *lǐ* from Yǐnmǎo.
Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yǎn Province) Xú Yǎn abandoned his garrison and fled.
Thereupon, all the commanderies of Tàishān were lost.
Zhèng troops, along with Gōngsūn Biǎo and the Sòng army's general, the Administrator of Jiāozhōu, Jiāozhǐ Hóu Pǔ, totaling several tens of thousands of five thousand cavalry,
once again advanced towards Hǔláo.
They established a camp five *lǐ* southeast of the city,
dividing their infantry and cavalry to open a path from Chénggāo towards the west gate of Hǔláo's outer wall.
Dézǔ met them in battle,
killing and wounding over a hundred men.
The invaders retreated to secure their camp.
Zhènběi Jiāngjūn Tán Dàojì led a naval force north to provide relief.
Chējì Jiāngjūn Lúlín Wáng Yìzhēn dispatched Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Shěn Shūlí with three thousand men to join Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Cuì,
to assess the situation and go to their aid.
In the first month of the first year of Jǐngpíng of Shàodì,
Zhèng troops divided their forces and advanced towards Luò,
attacking small strongholds.
The commander of the small strongholds, Dòu Huàng, resisted the attack,
but was overwhelmed and captured.
Hénán Tàishǒu Wáng Juānzhī abandoned Jīnyǒng and fled.
Since the invaders divided their forces and advanced towards Luò,
Dézǔ defeated them in every battle.
Sī then personally led a large army to Yè.
After the Zhèng troops conquered Jīnyǒng,
they returned to Hǔláo.
Dézǔ dug tunnels within the city,
extending seven *zhàng* [into the ground],
in two main paths,
emerging outside the city,
and then branched into six paths,
appearing behind the enemy's lines.
He recruited four hundred brave volunteers,
with Cānjūn Fàn Dàojī leading two hundred men as the vanguard,
and Cānjūn Guō Wángfú, Liú Guī, and others leading two hundred men as the rear guard.
They emerged outside the enemy's encirclement,
and launched a surprise attack from behind.
The enemy's formation became chaotic,
and several hundred heads were severed.
Their siege equipment was burned.
Although the invaders scattered,
they quickly regrouped.

The invaders also dispatched Chǔ troops' general, Xúzhōu Cìshǐ, Ānpíng Gōng Shè Guīfān Néngjiàn, Yuè troops' general, Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ, Línzī Hóu Xuē Dàoqiān, and Chén troops' general, Huáizhōu Cìshǐ, Shòuzhāngzǐ Zhāng Mó, to attack Qīngzhōu to the east.
[一０] All the cities and towns in their path fled in panic.
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Zhú Kuí was stationed at Dōngyáng Chéng.
Hearing that the invaders were approaching,
he gathered his forces and fortified his defenses.
Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn and Jǐnán Tàishǒu Yuán Miáo led the civil and military officials of the two prefectures and commanderies to join Kuí.
Kuí made a solemn oath with his officers and men.
For residents who did not enter the city,
he instructed them to relocate to the mountains and difficult terrain,
and burned the crops,
so that the invaders would have nothing to sustain themselves upon arrival.
The enemy forces advanced towards Qīngzhōu,
with a total of sixty thousand cavalry crossing the river at various points.
In the third month,
thirty thousand cavalry advanced, pressing and coercing.
There were fifteen hundred civil and military personnel within the city,
but half of them were a mix of Qiāng and Mán tribesmen,
causing widespread fear among the people.
At night, Zhú Kuí dispatched Sīmǎ Chē Zōng with five hundred men to sally forth and launch a surprise attack.
The enemy forces were routed.
After an interval of two days,
all of the enemy's infantry and cavalry arrived,
surrounding the city on all four sides,
forming a battle line extending over ten *lǐ*.
By late afternoon, they retreated to establish a camp at Ānshuǐ,
twenty *lǐ* from the city.
They heavily prepared siege equipment,
with divisions of infantry and cavalry constantly pressing the city every day.
At night, Kuí ordered Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn Zhú Zōngzhī, Cānjūn Jiǎ Yuánlóng, and others to lead a hundred men,
to set up ambushes on both banks of the Yángshuǐ estuary.
The enemy general Āfújīn led three hundred men to cross the river at dawn.
The ambushes on both banks were sprung,
and the enemy cavalry scattered in all directions,
with dozens killed or wounded.
The head of Āfújīn was displayed.
The invaders then advanced their camp south of the river,
four *lǐ* northwest of the city.
Sī dispatched troops from Yè to reinforce Hǔláo,
intensifying the encirclement and urgent attack.
Zhèng troops at Hǔláo, numbering three thousand infantry and cavalry,
attacked Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu Lǐ Yuándé at Xǔchāng.
Chējì Cānjūn Wáng Xuánmó led a thousand men,
[一一] to assist Yuándé in defending.
Both he and Yuándé were routed and scattered.
The invaders then appointed Yǔ Lóng, an Yǐngchuān native, as Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu,
leading five hundred cavalry,
and also conscripted able-bodied commoners to garrison the city.
Dézǔ led his army to attack Gōngsūn Biǎo,
engaging in a major battle
from morning until late afternoon,
killing several hundred invaders.
At that moment, the Zhèng army returned from Xǔchāng,
and joined in the encirclement.
Dézǔ suffered a major defeat,
losing over a thousand armored soldiers,
and retreated to secure the city.
Sī again dispatched over ten thousand men from Yè, who crossed the river at Báishākǒu,
and built a stronghold at Hánquán, south of Púyáng Chéng.
The court deliberated, saying:
"Xiàngchéng is not far from the invaders,
and cannot be resisted by a light force.
Instruct Liú Cuì to recall Gāo Dàojǐn to Shòuyáng.
If Shěn Shūlí has already advanced,
[一二] he should also be recalled for now."
Cuì believed that the invaders were attacking Hǔláo and had not yet turned south.
If he were to immediately withdraw his army and abandon Xiàngchéng,
then the commanderies west of the Huái River
would have no reliance.
Shěn Shūlí had already encamped at Féikǒu,
and it was not advisable to retreat immediately.
At that time, Lǐ Yuándé led two hundred scattered soldiers to Xiàng.
Liú Cuì ordered him to assist Gāo Dàojǐn in garrisoning,
[一三] and requested clemency for his crime of defeat and flight.
The court council granted both requests.
Tán Dàojì arrived at Péngchéng.
Given that both Qīng and Sī prefectures were in dire straits,
and his command was not numerous,
it was insufficient to divide and dispatch.
Qīngzhōu was closer,
and Zhú Kuí's forces were weak,
so he decided to rescue Qīngzhōu first.
Zhú Kuí sent people out of the city to dig east, west, and south trenches.
The invaders dug a long circumvallation three hundred *bù* north of the city.
Kuí dispatched Cānjūn Lǘ Mào and others to lead fifty skilled archers,
who shot at the invaders from behind the wall.
Several hundred enemy cavalry galloped to surround the wall.
Shots were fired from within the wall,
and they fought desperately, holding their ground.
The invaders dismounted and advanced on foot.
Short-range weapons were engaged.
Bows and crossbows on the city walls all fired,
and the invaders scattered.
The invaders then filled the outer trench completely,
and brought four high towers
and twenty *hámá chē* (toad-carts/mobile shelters),
placing them within the long circumvallation.
Kuí had previously dug three tunnels from the north of the city,
allowing passage to the outer trench.
He then dug another trench
and a smaller trench (*zǐqiàn*) two *zhàng* inside the city.
He dispatched over three hundred men through the tunnels,
intending to burn the invaders' siege equipment.
At that time, a swirling wind shifted the flames,
preventing the fire from igniting.
Enemy arrows rained down horizontally,
and many soldiers were wounded.
They gathered their forces and returned inside.
The invaders filled all three trenches flat,
leaving only the *zǐqiàn*,
which the *hámá chē* could not reach.
The invaders attacked the city with battering rams.
Kuí recruited manpower,
and hung large millstones from the city wall, piling them up.
He also emerged from the *zǐqiàn*,
using large hemp ropes to spread out obstacles (like bones),
and when the attacking vehicles approached the city,
many men from the tunnels pulled them to break them.
The invaders then dug a long circumvallation south of the city,
and intensified their attack.
Kuí was able to maintain his composure,
and Yuán Miáo had courage and capability,
which allowed them to hold out for a long time.
However, after being attacked for a long period,
the city gradually became damaged,
many warriors were killed or wounded,
and the remaining forces were exhausted.
It was on the verge of falling.
Tán Dàojì and Wáng Zhòngdé hastened to their rescue.
Liú Cuì dispatched Lǐ Yuándé to raid Xǔchāng.
Yǔ Lóng fled in panic.
Jiāng Sòng Huàng pursued and tracked him down,
severing Lóng's head.
Yuándé then remained to pacify and stabilize the area,
[一四] and also submitted taxes and grain.
The invader Yuè Bōdà Féishài led over three thousand cavalry,
[一五] and devastated the five counties under Gāopíng Commandery: Gāopíng, Fāngyǔ, Rènéng, Jīnxiāng, and Kàngfù.
Over two thousand households were killed or plundered,
their men killed,
and their women and children driven away as captives.
Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Zhèng Shùnzhī was garrisoned at Húlù,
but his soldiers dared not sally forth.
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn Shēn Xuān was garrisoned at Péngchéng,
over two hundred *lǐ* from Gāopíng.
Fearing the invaders' arrival,
he relocated the residents outside the outer wall,
and all the camp offices,
all into the smaller city.
Sī again dispatched Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ Yīlóubá to assist the Zhèng troops in attacking Hǔláo,
filling and blocking the two trenches.
Dézǔ resisted them strategically,
killing quite a few invaders,
but his officers and men were gradually diminished.
In the fourth month, on the day Rénshēn,
the invaders, hearing that Tán Dàojì was approaching,
burned their equipment,
abandoned Qīngzhōu, and fled.
Zhú Kuí reported that Dōngyáng chéng had been attacked and destroyed,
making it indefensible.
The garrison was moved to Bùqí chéng in Chángguǎng.
[一六]For his功 (gōng) in staunch defense, Kuí
[一七]was promoted to the title of Qián Jiāngjūn,
enfeoffed as a Count of Jiànlíng Xiàn,
with a stipend of four hundred households.
Kuí, whose courtesy name was Zǔjì,
was a native of Dōngguǎn.
He rose to the office of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
Sì led the main army to Hǔláo,
camped for three days,
and personally supervised the assault on the city,
but could not capture it.
He then turned his army towards Luòyáng,
leaving three thousand men to reinforce the Zhèng army.
After several days in Luòyáng,
he crossed the Yellow River and returned north.
The invaders' Ānpíng Gōng and other armies, retreating from Qīngzhōu,
headed straight for Huátái.
Tán Dàojì and Wáng Zhòngdé's infantry were short on provisions,
and could not overtake the invaders.
Dàojì, at Tàishān, dispatched Zhòngdé towards Yǐnmǎo,
while Dàojì himself camped at Húlù.
Before Zhòngdé reached Yǐnmǎo,
he heard that the invaders had already gone far,
so he returned to Dàojì,
and together they prepared their naval forces.
The invaders' Ānpíng Gōng and other armies arrived at Huátái,
then moved west to join the Zhèng army,
and together they attacked Hǔláo.
Hǔláo was besieged for two hundred days,
[一八]with battles every day.
Dézǔ's elite soldiers were almost entirely killed in action,
while the invaders' reinforcements grew constantly.
The invaders battered the outer city wall,
but Dézǔ built three more layers inside,
making it four layers in total as before.
When the enemy had battered down three walls,
Dézǔ only held one wall,
[一九]resisting day and night.
The eyes of the generals and soldiers were all festering,
and more than half had died.
Dézǔ's kindness and virtue had long bound the people to him,
and none among the multitude harbored disloyal thoughts.
Earlier, when Dézǔ was in the north,
he had an old acquaintance, Gōngsūn Biǎo, an enemy general.
Biǎo was resourceful and cunning,
and Dézǔ was concerned about him.
So he communicated with him,
and secretly sent someone to persuade the Zhèng army,
claiming that Biǎo was conspiring with him.
Every time he replied to Biǎo's letters,
[二０]he would make many corrections.
Biǎo showed these letters to the Zhèng army,
which doubled their suspicion of him,
and they reported it to Sì,
who had Biǎo executed.
The invaders' forces were numerous,
and Tán Dàojì's various relief armies dared not advance.
Liú Cuì held Xiàngchéng,
and Shěn Shūlí garrisoned Gāoqiáo.
On the twenty-first day,
the invaders dug a tunnel to steal the well water inside the city.
The well was forty zhàng deep,
and the mountain terrain was steep,
making defense impossible.
By the twenty-third day of that month,
people and horses were suffering from thirst, hunger, and disease;
their bodies were all dry,
and the wounded no longer bled.
The invaders then pressed their attack,
and consequently captured Hǔláo.
From Dézǔ to Zhái Guǎng and Dòu Bà,
all the generals, aides, and commandery governors who were in the city
were captured and imprisoned.
Only Liú Tánzhī, the Administrator of Shàngdǎng, and Fàn Dàojī, a staff officer, led two hundred men and broke through the siege to return south.
When the city was about to fall,
the generals and soldiers wanted to support Dézǔ in escaping,
but Dézǔ said:
"My life is bound to this city;
it is against my principles that this city should perish while I remain alive."
Sì respected his steadfastness in defense
and ordered his armies to capture him alive,
thus he escaped death.
Sīkōng Xú Xiànzhī, Shàngshū Fù Liàng, and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Xiè Huì jointly submitted a memorial, stating:
"Last year, the audacious invaders ran rampant,
harassing Hénán.
Your subject Dézǔ, the Cìshǐ of Sīzhōu, exerted his utmost sincerity and effort,
resisting the powerful enemy.
He defended an isolated city alone,
for nearly a year.
The relief army was delayed,
and the entire city fell.
Your Sacred Heart mourns this,
and near and far lament.
Your Majesty, in deep sorrow during the period of mourning,
delegated governance to your subordinates.
Your subjects, with shallow and limited foresight,
failed in our trust.
This led to a loyal subject, who demonstrated integrity,
perishing with his loyalty,
his generals and soldiers being annihilated and disgraced,
and the royal strategy suffering a setback.
Above, it violated the former rules;
below, it brought national shame.
According to court regulations,
there is no way to avoid blame.
Although the responsible officials are hesitant to write,
and have not applied the regulations,
how can we merely enjoy our emoluments,
blindly accepting special favors and comfort?
We beg to be dismissed,
to uphold the national law."
This was not granted.
Dézǔ
was from Yángwǔ, Xíngyáng.
[二一]At the end of the Jìn dynasty, he returned south from his hometown.
Initially, he served as Cāngjūn to the Guànjūn and Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
When Dàoguī was Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu,
Dézǔ served as his general's aide.
He later became Tàiwèi Cānjūn to Gāozǔ.
When Gāozǔ launched his northern expedition,
he appointed him Lóngxiáng Sīmǎ to Wáng Zhèn'è,
and added the title of Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn.
He served as Zhèn'è's vanguard,
beheading Zhào Xuánshí, the bandit Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, at Bǎigǔ,
defeating Yǐn Yǎ, the Administrator of Hóngnóng, at Líchéng,
and also defeating Yáo Nán, a major bandit leader, at Jīngshuǐ,
beheading his Zhènběi Jiāngjūn Yáo Qiáng.
Zhèn'è achieved great merit,
which was largely due to Dézǔ's efforts.
After Cháng'ān was pacified,
he was appointed Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn and Fúfēng Tàishǒu,
and subsequently promoted to Cìshǐ of Qínzhōu,
with his general rank unchanged.
At that time, the Fófó invaders caused trouble,
so Dézǔ was again appointed Zhēnglǔ Sīmǎ to Wáng Zhèn'è.
Soon after, he became Ānxī Cānjūn to Guìyáng Gōng Yìzhēn and Nán'ān Tàishǒu,
with his general rank unchanged.
He was then transferred to be Fēngyì Tàishǒu.
When Gāozǔ returned east,
he appointed Dézǔ as Dūd Sīzhōu zhī Hédōng Píngyáng èr jùn zhū jūn, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and Hédōng Tàishǒu,
replacing Liú Zūnkǎo as garrison commander at Púbǎn, then under the command of Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ.
As Cháng'ān could not be held,
he gathered his troops and returned to Péngchéng.
He was appointed Shìzǐ Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
with his general rank unchanged.
He was further appointed Dūd Sīzhōu zhī Hédōng Píngyáng Héběi Yōngzhōu zhī Jīngzhào Yùzhōu zhī Yǐngchuān Yǎnxzhōu zhī Chénliú jiǔ jùn jūnshì, and Xíngyáng Tàishǒu,
[二二]with his general rank unchanged,
and also added the title of Jīngzhào Tàishǒu.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to the title of Guànjūn.
Based on his cumulative achievements,
he was enfeoffed as a Count of Guānyáng Xiàn,
with a stipend of four hundred households.
He was also appointed Dūd Sī Yōng Bìng sān zhōu Yùzhōu zhī Yǐngchuān Yǎnxzhōu zhī Chénliú zhū jūnshì, and Cìshǐ of Sīzhōu,
with his general rank unchanged.
In the sixth year of Tàizǔ Yuánjiā,
he died among the invaders,
at the age of sixty-five.
In the first year of Shìzǔ Dàmíng,
Dézǔ's nephew Xīzuò's second son, Xǔzhī, was allowed to inherit Dézǔ's enfeoffment.
After the invaders captured Hǔláo,
they left troops to guard it,
and all the remaining forces returned north.
The Young Emperor said: [二三]
"The late Níngyuǎn Sīmǎ and Púyáng Tàishǒu Yáng Zàn,
during the siege of Huátái,
exerted sincere effort in staunch defense,
risking his life and upholding his principles.
In peril, he did not waver.
The loyal and heroic figures of antiquity
cannot surpass him.
He is hereby posthumously granted the title of Gěishìzhōng,
and his orphaned children shall be cared for,
to comfort both the living and the deceased."
Shàngshū Lìng Fù Liàng proposed that since Zàn's family was in Péngchéng,
it would be appropriate to immediately grant them one hundred bolts of court silk
and three hundred hù of grain.
The literary scholar Yán Yánzhī composed an elegy for him.
Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn and Yǎnxzhōu Cìshǐ Xú Yǎn, and Dōngjùn Tàishǒu Wáng Jǐngdù were both punished for losing their positions,
[二四]being shackled, shaven, and made to perform forced labor.
Yǎn for five years,
Jǐngdù for four years.
At that time, Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn, Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu Lǐ Yuándé was stationed at Xǔchāng.
He was then appointed Xíngyáng Tàishǒu,
and was made Supervisor of Military Affairs for the two commanderies.
In the eleventh month of that year,
the barbarians dispatched troops and gathered deserters,
to attack and besiege Xǔchāng city.
They made a local, Liú Yuǎn, the Tàishǒu of Xíngyáng.
Lǐ Yuándé wanted to sally forth and fight,
but lacking sufficient weapons,
he waited until night.
His troops then utterly scattered and fled, breaking through the parapet walls.
Yuándé consequently fled back to Xiàngchéng.
The barbarians then besieged Rǔyáng again.
Tàishǒu Wáng Gōngdù, with over ten cavalrymen, broke through the encirclement and fled to Xiàngchéng.
The barbarians then captured Shàolíng county,
destroying over two thousand households,
killing all the male inhabitants,
and seizing twelve thousand women and children.
Liú Cuì dispatched his general Yáo Sǒngfū to lead troops to help defend Xiàngchéng,
and then sent Sīmǎ Xú Qióng with five hundred men to reinforce them.
The barbarians dug up and destroyed Xǔchāng city,
and then demolished Zhōnglí city,
[二五]to establish their border before returning.
Sì died,
and was posthumously named Míngyuán Huángdì.
His son, Táo, whose courtesy name was Fóbílì, succeeded him.
His mother, Dù Shì,
was from Jìzhōu.
She entered his palace,
and gave birth to Táo.
When Táo was fifteen or sixteen,
Sì did not acknowledge him as his heir,
treating him like a servant.
When Sì first ascended the throne, he established a daughter of the Mùróng clan as Empress.
He later married a daughter of Yáo Xīng.
Both had no sons,
which is why Táo was able to ascend.
He was robust and strong,
brave in battle,
cruel and fond of killing.
Both the Yí and Sòng feared him.
When attacking cities or facing the enemy,
he would always personally don armor.
In Yuánjiā five years,
he sent his grand general Tǔfájīn to campaign westwards against Cháng'ān.
[二六]He captured Hèlián Chāng alive in Āndìng,
[二七]enfeoffed Chāng as a duke,
and married his sister to him.
Chāng's younger brother, Hèlián Dìng, was on Lǒngshàng.
Tǔfájīn, taking advantage of his victory, led thirty thousand cavalry to attack Dìng.
Dìng set an ambush in the Tánzhēng Gǔ valley of Lǒngshān and defeated them,
beheading Tǔfájīn
and burying all his troops alive.
Dìng then led his forces eastwards.
Later, he captured Cháng'ān.
Táo again personally attacked, but failed to capture it.
He then divided his forces to garrison major cities and returned.
Táo always kept Chāng by his side,
often riding alone with him to hunt deer,
deep into mountain ravines.
Chāng was known for his bravery,
and all the generals warned Táo not to trust him.
Táo said:
"Heaven's mandate is fixed;
what is there to fear?"
He continued to treat him as before.
He again attacked Cháng'ān,
capturing it.
Dìng fled westwards,
and was captured by Tùyùhùn Mùguī.
There was a Hèlián clan member named Wèichén,
[二八]whose clan resided outside the Shuòfāng pass,
with over a thousand households.
West of Shuòfāng,
extending west to Shàngjùn,
a thousand _lǐ_ east to west,
during the Hàn dynasty, banished commoners were resettled there,
and the land was fertile.
During Fú Jiān's time,
Wèichén entered the pass to rent land,
coming in spring and leaving in autumn.
Jiān's Yúnzhōng Hùjūn, Jiǎ Yōng, plundered his farmers,
capturing people, horses, cattle, and sheep.
Jiān returned everything to him.
Wèichén was grateful,
and thus declared himself a subject and settled within the pass.
Thereafter, his power gradually grew.
After Wèichén died,
his son Fófó was fierce and brave, with strategic cunning.
Various tribes, near and far, all submitted to him.
Yáo Xīng contended with him,
and Xīng's army was repeatedly routed and lost men,
more than once.
Guānzhōng was devastated by this.
When Gāozǔ entered Cháng'ān,
Fófó was terrified and dared not move.
When Gāozǔ returned east,
Fófó immediately raided Běidì.
When Ānxī Jiāngjūn Yìzhēn returned,
Fófó sent his son Chāng to defeat him at Qīngní,
capturing the various generals.
He then controlled Guānzhōng
and proclaimed himself an exalted sovereign,
designating his era as Zhēnxīng Yuánnián.
Wéi Xuán of Jīngzhào, who lived in reclusion and cultivated his character,
had a high reputation.
Yáo Xīng respectfully invited him,
but he did not come.
Gāozǔ appointed him Xiàngguó Yuàn,
and then Sòng Tái Tōngzhíláng,
but he also did not accept either position.
Fófó summoned him to be Tàizǐ Shùzǐ.
Xuán complied.
Fófó was furious,
saying:
"Yáo Xīng and Duke Liú both invited me,
but I did not come.
When I received your command, I immediately came.
Is it because you consider me a different kind of being,
and thus cannot be reasoned with?"
He then killed him.
In Yuánjiā two years,
Fófó died,
and Chāng ascended.
At this point, he was conquered by Táo.
Táo pacified Lǒngyòu in the west,
and destroyed Huánglóng in the east.
All the states east of the sea
sent tribute.
Tàizǔ ascended the throne
and immediately harbored ambitions to expand northwards.
In the third month of the seventh year,
an imperial edict stated:
"Hénán,
where the Central Plains suffered many calamities,
has been submerged in undeserved misfortune.
The remaining populace suffers greatly,
and this constantly fills us with compassion.
Now, the people are harmonious and the year is bountiful,
and the borders are peaceful.
It is fitting to manage the situation now
to secure our frontiers.
Let fifty thousand armored soldiers be selected
and assigned to Yòujiāngjūn Dào Yànzhī.
He will command Ānběi Jiāngjūn Wáng Zhòngdé and Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Zhú Língxiù, leading naval forces to enter the Yellow River.
Xiāojì Jiāngjūn Duàn Hóng, with eight thousand elite cavalry,
will march directly to Hǔláo.
Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Déwǔ, with ten thousand strong and brave troops,
will act as a pincer movement.
Hòujiāngjūn Chángshā Wáng Yìxīn may temporarily be granted the imperial staff (jié),
and lead thirty thousand existing troops
to supervise all military affairs for the expedition.
Let preparations be made quickly,
and all forces be dispatched within the month."
He first sent Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn Tián Qí with a message to Táo, saying:
"Hénán was formerly Sòng territory.
It was later invaded by your side.
We shall now restore our former borders,
which does not concern Héběi."
Táo was greatly angered
and said to Qí:
"Since I was born, before my hair was dry,
I heard that Hénán was my family's land.
How can you possibly claim Hénán?
If you must advance your army,
I will temporarily withdraw my garrisons to avoid you.
When winter comes and the ground is firm,
and the river is frozen,
I will take it back myself."
Hòujiāngjūn Chángshā Wáng Yìxīn was sent to garrison Péngchéng,
to command all the generals.
He issued a proclamation to Sī and Yǎn provinces, saying: "The army of a king
is aided by righteousness and virtue,
not merely to expand territory,
or to broaden strategic plans.
It is to greatly protect the common people
and preserve the populace.
Therefore, enduring frost and snow,
and overcoming dangers and difficulties,
we strive to stabilize the state and bring peace to the people,
and pacify the four directions.
In the past, our Gāozǔ Wǔ Huángdì,
responded to the bright mandate,
and established the realm of Huáxià.
He suppressed usurpers and rebels internally,
and pacified external invaders.
His spiritual might was vast,
like thunder and wind,
rising.
His fame surpassed Lóngduī,
his voice reached Yún and Shuò.
He shook heaven and earth,
uprooted mountains and stirred the seas.
Thus, the Huá territory was pacified,
and songs of praise gathered abundantly.
The royal order and imperial decrees,
How magnificent is civilization!
The supreme harmony's mists are warm and moist,
and its beneficence flows abundantly.
In the middle period, there was profound darkness.
The government was entrusted to the prime minister,
and cunning barbarians seized the opportunity,
invading and insulting the Middle Kingdom.
This caused the good people of Sī and
Yǎn to
again fall into an inappropriate situation,
and the remaining populace of Zhōu and Zhèng
to be again separated from the King's transforming influence.
When the Sacred Emperor ascended the throne,
his brilliant light shone forth,
and his sagacity and wisdom soothed distant lands,
thus bringing about a glorious restoration.
Distant barbarians yearned for righteousness,
gathering like clouds and surging like waves.
He is about to walk in virtue and uphold trustworthiness,
to be clothed in skill and inherit culture,
to further cultivate the foundational achievements,
and to set a standard for future generations.
His diligent benevolence will extend to the three regions,
and his gracious harmony will pacify the Northern Dí.
Just as one who raises fish removes otters,
and one who raises birds removes jackals and wolves,
so wise scholars ponder deeply,
and brave warriors sharpen their resolve.
Excellent strategies move the azure heaven,
and essential energy pierces the stars and constellations.
I, in this headquarters, unworthily assume this responsibility,
receiving and upholding the calculations of the imperial temple.
I will cut off their claws and make their clothes visible (i.e., destroy them completely),
swearing not to care for my own life.
Leading the strong soldiers of Wú and Chǔ,
and commanding the elite warriors of the eight zhōu,
red banners
will dye the sky crimson,
and white armor will outshine the sun.
Like tigers, we will stride through the Central Plains,
and like dragons, we will soar over the river islets.
We will raise clouds and scatter rain,
comforting the thoughts of great drought;
we will console the people and punish the guilty,
accumulating the sentiments
of "Hòujǐ."
When an army moves in accordance with the Way,
what expedition will not be victorious?
How much more so when we are merely fostering the old and the ignorant,
and pacifying and restoring our territory!
In the past, when Huái and Sì were first opened,
cunning rogues ran rampant.
When the King's army entered the pass,
the multitude of villains scattered like a whirlwind.
In the battle of Xiāngyì,
the "white banner" (leader) lost his head.
In the engagement at Bànchéng,
fallen
corpses covered the fields.
Their bodies were dismembered and split apart,
their wings (supporters) broken and crushed.
In addition, they stirred up trouble with the Western lǔ,
and created enmity with Huánglóng.
Their archers were extinguished and destroyed,
their front and rear were pressed and fearful.
Like bees and ants
gathering,
they cling to a momentary breath of life.
How could they again leap across the Long River
to confront our magnificent array?
Indeed, submission should be swift,
and returning to virtue should not be delayed.
Rewards are bestowed upon those who surrender first,
and might is applied to those who submit later.
Therefore, the wanderers of Qín and Zhào,
who cast aside their troubles and offered their sincerity,
were granted sashes and carriages,
and appointed with tallies to zhōu and jùn.
Mùróng and Yáo Hóng,
who relied on their strength to create misfortune,
gathered armies from thousands of lì away,
but ultimately met the axe and hatchet.
These are all clear proofs before our eyes,
known from past generations.
The Sacred Emperor, with brilliant insight, loves and cares for
the soldiers and people of the two zhōu
with the Way.
[二九]If they can clearly judge security and danger,
and suddenly change their ways,
leading their factions
to surrender at our military gate,
I will report their cases to the Heavenly Court
and employ them according to their talents.
If
they are obstinate and do not repent,
hiding their heads in their dens,
once the long siege is complete,
and the siege towers arrive from all four directions,
even if they wish to offer jars of wine and baskets of food,
how could they possibly do so?
I urge you to think thrice,
and carefully
weigh the advantages and disadvantages.
When Yànzhī advanced,
the lǔ retreated, abandoning all garrisons south of the Hé and returning to the north of the Hé.

[三０]Tàizǔ appointed Yǐn Chōng, formerly the Sīmǎ of the General Who Conquers the Lǔ and Administrator of Nánguǎngpíng, as Supervisor of Military Affairs for the three zhōu of Sī, Yōng, and Bìng, and for the two jùn of Yǐngchuān in Yùzhōu and Chénliú in Yǎanzhōu, as well as General Who Arouses Awe and Governor of Sīzhōu,
to garrison Hǔláo.
In the eleventh month,
the barbarian host crossed the Hé southwards.
Yànzhī was defeated and retreated,
and the cities of Luòyáng, Huátái, and Hǔláo were all captured by the barbarians.
Yǐn Chōng and Sīmǎ Cuī Mó, the Administrator of Xíngyáng, resisted with integrity and did not surrender,
dying by throwing themselves into the moats.
[三一]Chōng, courtesy name Zǐshùn,
was a native of Jì in Tiānshuǐ.
He had previously served as Yáo Xīng's Minister of Personnel,
and had formed a faction with Xīng's son, Pí, the Duke of Guǎngpíng,
intending to overthrow Xīng's heir apparent, Hóng.
When Hóng ascended,
Chōng and his younger brother, Hóng, both fled and defected to the south.
At this time, he was posthumously granted the title of General of the Vanguard.
Tàizǔ wrote to Prince Yìgōng of Jiāngxià, saying:
"Yǐn Chōng's sincere integrity and lofty spirit
follow in the footsteps of ancient heroes.
I am filled with sorrow and regret
that I cannot stop."
Since the defense of Huátái had lasted for a long time but ultimately fell,
the Emperor composed a poem saying: "Rebellious barbarians disturb the borders,
border generals are beset by enemies.
Strong cities display their steadfast integrity,
attack and battle know no rest.
What is submerged cannot be picked up,
what is broken is difficult to restore.
Their power wanes, they return to desolation,
and are here seen as captives.
The valiant defenders of the city,
sacrificed their lives following ancient precedents.
Loyal officials are revealed in their twilight years,
true pines are seen in severe autumn.
Chǔ
Zhuāng rose, throwing off his sleeves,
and ultimately avenged his powerful enemy.
Qùbìng left his lofty mansion,
and finally relieved the nation's worries.
Military affairs are surely not yet ended,
how can the people's suffering be alleviated?
Grasping my sword,
I feel gratitude and emotion,
my spirit is like floating clouds.
I wish to soar on a whirlwind,
sweeping my banners across the Central Plains.
My claws and teeth (generals) display their might,
my strategists deploy their good plans.
Chinese and barbarians blend
their diverse customs,
the entire land is permeated by the King's way.
Sorrowfully, I fear the passage of time,
and looking north, tears stream down."
Afterward, Táo again sent envoys to establish good relations,
and also sought a marriage alliance.
Tàizǔ always responded ambiguously.
In the seventeenth year (of the Yuánjiā era),
Táo proclaimed the first year of Tàipíng Zhēnjūn.
In the nineteenth year,
the lǔ General Who Guards the East, Yí Lèkù Mòtí, Prince Wǔchāng, sent a letter to Yì and Liáng zhōu,
[三二]stating that he was going to attack Qiúchí
and invade its dependents,
but the letter was sent to Xúzhōu, saying: "The rise of our Great Wèi,
its virtue matches the two cosmic forces,
standing side by side with creation.
Before Xià and Yīn,
its achievements were ancient and venerable.
Since Zhōu and Qín,
it has been glorious and
magnificent,
shining brilliantly in earlier generations.
Upon our Illustrious Ancestor,
his sagacity and wisdom were added.
Responding to destiny, he soared like a dragon,
clearing out Yān and Zhào.
[三三]The Sacred Dynasty, possessing the foundation of royal enterprise,
unleashed divine
military strategies,
pacifying the three Qín in the distance,
reaching Cōnglǐng in the west,
pacifying Liáojié in the east,
where the sea's edge submitted.
To Zhōngshān in the north,
all nations paid tribute.
Wherever our awe-inspiring wind reached,
we imagine
that their court and populace
are well aware of our might and virtue.
In the past, Liú, Shí, Fú, and Yáo
successively occupied the three jùn,
while Sīmǎ Lángyá
held Yáng and Yuè.
Continuously and endlessly,
they continued
Record of past years.
When the number of destinies was exhausted and the mandate changed,
the Sòng clan received the end [of their reign].
They continued the old ways of the Jìn,
extending their reach to send envoys and present tributes.
Therefore, our imperial court laid down its arms
and ceased its ambitions in the southeast.
This was because we did not wish to violate the great trust established with our predecessors.
Yet, the ruler and ministers of that side
harbored malicious intentions
and repeatedly became border marauders.
Last Gēngwǔ year,
they secretly colluded with Hèlián,
invading our Láojìng and Luòyáng,
causing our armies to be defeated,
and our entire force to be captured.
Our imperial court, being magnanimous,
did not dwell on others' wrongs
nor did it pursue others' faults.
We entered into
harmony with them,
and our former goodwill remained unchanged.
In the past, the King of Nánqín, Yáng Xuán, understood the heavenly mandate.
Before the great transformation had fully arrived,
he crossed beyond Hèlián
and faithfully submitted.
After Xuán
passed away,
his younger brother Nándāng's loyalty and integrity became even more steadfast.
He humbly requested to offer his daughter
to form a marital alliance with the imperial family,
presented rare treasures from his territory,
and regarded himself as an internal commandery.
The white pheasants from Hánnán
were placed on the imperial
table.
The imperial court praised this
and entrusted him with the responsibility of leading independent campaigns.
Unexpectedly, that court, considering the minor flaws in the border,
did not bother to communicate,
but secretly raised an army
and destroyed our tributary
state.
Nándāng, with his wife and children,
and those who shared his righteousness,
reported their defeat below the pass.
The sagely court was saddened,
and looked at its ministers, saying:
"Their violation of trust and betrayal of harmony,
along with the incidents at
Láojìng and Luòyáng, makes three.
One instance is too much;
how can there be a second?
If this can be endured,
what cannot be endured?"
Therefore, we, the officials who sound the warning bell, were ordered
to assist
Nándāng in seeking revenge.
Tǔxī Àibì, bearing the imperial staff, grand master of the palace, regional inspector of military affairs for Yōng and Qín prefectures, general of the pacified west, and Duke of Jiànxīng,
Nándāng, King of Nánqín, to sally forth from Qíshān to the south,
directly attacking Jiàn'ān,
ordering Nánqín to send trusted officials
to gather the old households.

Pí Bàozǐ, bearing the imperial staff, grand master of the palace, regional inspector of military affairs for Yōng, Liáng, Yì, and Sì prefectures, general of the pacified west, minister without portfolio, and Duke of Huáin,
blocking the pass at Báimǎ.
É Hòuyán, cavalier attendant, general who pacifies the south, inspector of Yōng Prefecture, and Duke of Nánpíng,
exited from Luò Valley,

Zōng Xiè, general of the victorious army, colonel who pacifies the southern barbarians, inspector of Jīng Prefecture, and Duke of Jiànpíng; Liú Mǎidé, bearing the imperial staff, supernumerary cavalier attendant, general of the victorious army, inspector of Liáng Prefecture, and Duke of Shùnyáng; and Ruògàn Nèi Yìqiān, general who pacifies from afar, and Marquis of Yǒng'ān, sallied forth from Zǐwǔ,
attacking Liáng and Hàn to the east.

Sīmǎ Wénsī, bearing the imperial staff, grand master of the palace, regional inspector of military affairs for Jīng, Liáng, and Nányōng prefectures, concurrently serving as colonel who protects the southern barbarians, general-in-chief who conquers the south, minister without portfolio, inspector of Jīng Prefecture, and former King of Qiáo of Jìn; and Lǔ Guǐ, general who pacifies from afar, inspector of Jīng Prefecture, and Duke of Xiāngyáng, marched south to Jīng Prefecture.
Zhíqín Tādàhán, bearing the imperial staff,
regional inspector of military affairs for Luò and Yù prefectures and Hénèi, general-in-chief who guards the south, minister without portfolio, and King of Huáinán, served as the
rearguard.

Diāo Yōng, bearing the imperial staff, grand master of the palace, regional inspector of military affairs for Yáng, Yù, Yǎn, and Xú prefectures, general who conquers the south, inspector of Xú and Yǎn prefectures, and Duke of Dōng'ān, marched east to Guǎnglíng,
and south to Jīngkǒu.
Sīmǎ Tiānzhù, bearing the imperial staff, grand master of the palace,

regional inspector of military affairs for Qīng, Yǎn, and Xú prefectures, general who conquers the east, inspector of Qīng and Xú prefectures, Duke of Dōnghǎi, and son of the late Jìn Yuánxiǎn, marched directly to Jǐnán.
Ten routes advanced simultaneously,
with five thousand連營 [camps],
a million infantry and cavalry,
marching mightily.
With such a force to besiege cities,
what city would not collapse?
With such a force to attack,
what stronghold would not be
destroyed?
Shàolíng and Jiàntǔ,
the small states of Qí and Jìn,
were still able to defeat the powerful Chǔ
and achieve hegemony for a time.
How much more so the great Wèi, with its elite cavalry from the desert,
and the strong soldiers of Xián and Xià!
If all our armies were to arrive,
we would make the Southern Sea flow north,
and the Jiāngnán overflow south,
high banks would sink into marshes,
and deep valleys would pile up into hills.
The remaining people of Jìn
would gather like clouds and mists.
The army of Chóuchí
would be trapped in the valleys,
how could they defend themselves?
This is what is called indulging in immediate small gains,
leading
to the great loss of defeat and destruction.
In the past, Lord Xìnlíng saved the endangered "poor dove,"
and righteous men submitted to him.
Therefore, our imperial court wishes to save Nándāng, who sincerely entrusted his life to us,
and for
this reason, takes this action.
However, cherishing our former goodwill,
we still hesitate,
as killing many living beings,
one [person] dying for every ten [saved],
We
will separately dispatch a flying dispatch to persuade you.
restoring the state of Nánqín,
then all our armies will be dismissed,
and our goodwill will be as before.
If you resist our
righteous words,
and stubbornly persist,
you will lose your state and your life,
and will surely regret it like the "eating of Qí."
We hope you will present this to your court
and favor us with a report.
Xú Prefecture replied to the dispatch, saying: We understand that Yáng Nándāng reported his defeat and surrendered,
likening him to a "poor dove," and you wish to mobilize troops to rescue and save him.
Saving the endangered and pitying the difficult
is something a ruler should do.
Nevertheless,
the words of your dispatch
are already excessive.
Why?
Since the time of the Yáng clan's ancestors,
they received Jìn titles and ranks,
fulfilled their duties, guarded their territory,
and served as our western subordinate.
Within ten years,
they twice incited rebellion,
declared their own era name and founded a new state,
acting wildly and presumptuously.
As a minister, he was disloyal
and deserved to be punished.
We also know that Nándāng declared himself a vassal to your state.
He must have been looking out for himself,
seeking to preserve himself by belonging to both sides.
If he were truly a loyal minister,
serving Wèi,
how could he have maintained harmony and kinship with others
and allowed his subordinates to run rampant?
In the past, at the end of Jǐng
píng,
the national destiny declined.
They took advantage of our internal difficulties
to invade our Sī and Yǎn regions.
Therefore, we spent seven years training our troops,
with the righteousness of grand strategy.
Three commanders crossed the river,
without harming a single hair.
We only upheld this pledge of faith
and did not break our promise.
They watched our army,
and still ambushed us,
capturing our soldiers
and cutting down our border people.
Thus, they have two
wrongs,
and we have two rights.
Sīmǎ Chǔ and Wénsī fled into hiding,
Lǔ Guǐ and Diāo Yōng were truly like scorpions' tails,
yet you harbored their fugitives
and opened your
borders to them.
Yuánxiǎn had no son,
how then did Tiānzhù come about?
This false claim and pretense
is not worth mentioning.
You also criticize us for secretly raising an army
without communication.
If what you say is true,
nor is it something I have received.
The ruler of Huánglóng-guó received my 正朔 (zhèngshuò),
and Qú Màoqián (渠茂虔) and his son submitted to us.
They were all destroyed, captured, and taken as spoils.
How could there have been any prior agreement?
Moreover,
Chóu Chí (仇池) served the Jìn (晉) dynasty for ten generations,
and served the Sòng (宋) dynasty for three eras.
Nine expeditions have been launched against them,
what harm have they suffered?
I have heard that a crooked army makes an old general,
and righteous actions create rebellious heroes.
Words should accurately reflect feelings,
not be boastful.
Your letter was originally intended for Liáng (梁) and Yì (益),
but it erroneously came to my humble office.
A great
man is not far off,
fortunately, there is no need for excessive talk.
In the twentieth year,
Táo (燾) ceded the state to his Crown Prince,
issuing a decree that read:
"I, inheriting the glorious legacy of my ancestors,
intend to expand our grand foundation,
and prosper for ten thousand generations.
Since taking charge of the realm,
pacifying the tyrannical and eliminating the rebellious,
and sweeping away those who were disobedient,
my military achievements have been manifest.
However, the civil administration has not yet been fully developed,
which is not the way to uphold the governance of great peace.
Now, the country is peaceful and tranquil,
the people are prosperous and flourishing.
The military and civil administrations present different aspects;
it is appropriate to establish a system of institutions
to serve as a law for ten thousand generations.
For Yin and Yang have their cycles of ebb and flow,
and the four seasons have their successive order.
Entrusting affairs to one's son and employing the worthy,
ensuring safety and mutual support,
is the way to rest the weary,
to secure longevity,
and to perfect one's blessings and prosperity.
This is an unchangeable principle from ancient times to the present.
All my meritorious officials,
who have toiled for a long time,
should all retire and return to their residences,
enjoying their high ranks with composure,
nurturing their spirits and prolonging their lives.
They may attend court at their convenience,
feast in my presence,
discuss doctrines and offer counsel only,
without needing to personally attend to the arduous duties of government offices.
Let the Crown Prince succeed me in managing all affairs,
presiding over all government matters,
and further raising the worthy and capable,
to fill the various positions.
All should be selected from promising young talents,
broadening the path for choosing capable individuals,
selecting and appointing people, and promoting or demoting them.
Thus, Confucius said: 'The young are to be regarded with awe.
How do we know that their future will not be equal to our present?'
Let the relevant officials clearly formulate regulations,
and proclaim and enforce them."
Thereupon, all, from the princes and dukes downwards, submitted memorials to the Crown Prince, all addressing themselves as subjects.
The beginning and end were the same as official memorials,
only differing in the use of white paper.
That year,
Táo (燾) attacked the Ruìruì (芮芮) barbarians,
suffering a great defeat and returning,
with sixteen or seventeen out of ten dead.
He forbade the families of the deceased from mourning,
and those who defied him were executed.
In the twenty-third year,
the barbarian Ānnán (安南) and Píngnán-fǔ (平南府) again sent a letter to Yǎnzhōu (兗州),
stating that the Southern State had established prefectures by temporary settlement,
not based on established territory,
and had usurped many place names from the Northern region,
and also wished to hunt in Jùqū (具區).
Yǎnzhōu (兗州) replied, saying: "Indeed, when the Imperial Pinnacle was first established,
it truly responded to the auspicious signs of the divine,
and when humankind first began,
it truly received the vital energy of cosmic harmony.
Thus, the achievements of governance
were proclaimed in ancient times,
and the Way of benevolence and righteousness
originated from the various Huá (華) peoples.
In times past, the Jìn (晉) dynasty
unified the entire realm,
and peoples from nine translations of distance followed its influence,
with distant barbarians inclining towards and submitting to it.
With the loss of control during the Yǒngjiā (永嘉) era,
the heavenly order
collapsed and shattered.
Shí (石), Róng (容), Fú (苻), Yáo (姚) successively occupied positions they had no right to,
some resting in Zhào (趙) and Wèi (魏),
others gathering in Bīn (邠) and Qí (岐).
Our Imperial Sòng (宋) dynasty, to which the mandate of the calendar properly belongs,
received the final decree from the Jìn
clan.
To the north, it reaches the Hé (河) and Jì (濟);
to the west, it extends to Xián (咸) and Qiān (汧),
comforting the people and punishing the wicked,
spreading its benevolence across the Five Commanderies.
At that time, Wèi (魏) repented its wrongdoing with virtuous conduct,
desiring harmony and alliance,
exchanging envoys
to seek the celestial will.
Your coming letter, speaking of 'dividing territories and delineating borders,'
indicates a long-established intent.
Soon after, failing to keep its word,
it presumed upon our country's troubles,
invading Láoluo (牢洛)
and Luò (洛),
reaching Qīngjì (清濟).
Last year, it entered the Hé (河),
and also sought to pacify and govern the old cities.
Thus, its troops were stationed on the southern bank,
without violating even a single autumn hair.
Our army was unable to follow the court's
calculations
and achieve success,
and on the day of its return,
it again lost Sī (司) and Yǎn (兗).
Your letter says,
'[You] establish prefectures not based on territory,
attracting fugitives.'
Indeed, in ancient times, there were divisions of land,
but no divisions of people.
When virtue is excellent and manifest,
people from all four directions carry their children on their backs and come.
In the past, when the Way of Zhōu (周) was flourishing,
and the Spirit Tower was first built,
the people who submitted to its civilizing influence
numbered eight hundred thousand families.
They do not think of promoting good governance,
but fear people abandoning them,
unleashing their power and
tyranny,
leaving no old or weak alive.
Examining the past and present,
and listening to public opinion,
never has anyone prolonged their existence through extreme wickedness,
or gained the allegiance of the masses through cruelty.
If it is truly necessary to establish prefectures
based on territory,
then how do they have land to establish Xú (徐) and Yáng (揚)?
Last year, your esteemed ruler presented a letter saying:
'The strong are heroes.'
This is to abandon virtue and rely on strength,
acting perversely and doing things in reverse.
If there is one such instance,
how can one flourish?
Furthermore, you wish
'to hunt in Jùqū (具區)
and observe the civilizing influence of the Southern State.'
Currently, our governance is flourishing,
and distant people are sure to come.
When guest houses are opened and residences decorated,
there will be officials to attend to them.
Next year, on the first
day of the year,
heaven and man will celebrate together.
The imperial banners will tour the regions,
and the Emperor will make an eastern inspection to Jīlíng (稽嶺).
If you wish to seek grace,
you should attend this assembly.
Cherishing virtue should be done early,
without any delay.
It is also
stated:
'Having hunted for years,
there are no flying or hiding creatures left in the wilderness.'
In this region, nets are lifted before the dwellings,
and insects and fledglings are nurtured.
In the Seven Marshes and Eight Swamps,
birds and beasts are abundant.
The imperial hunting officials will survey and calculate,
and we will not begrudge you this.
The great hunting expeditions of the Three Dynasties,
though their rituals are ancient,
when Hūhán (呼韓) entered the Hàn (漢) court,
the etiquette was still complete,
and the provisions and tribute were
always kept generous.
Previously,
a rumor circulated among the captives:
"The one who destroys the barbarians is Wú."
Táo greatly disliked this.
In the twenty-third year (446 CE),
Gài Wú, a native of Lúshuǐ in Běidì,
aged twenty-nine,
raised an army at Xìngchéng Tiāntái to rebel against the barbarians.
All the Róng and Yí tribes responded in unison,
gathering over ten myriad followers.
When Táo heard of Wú's rebellion,
he disliked his name,
repeatedly dispatching armies to attack him,
but they were always defeated.
Wú submitted a memorial, expressing submission,
saying: "Since the migration south of the divine lineage,
calamity has afflicted the sacred land.
The two capitals have lost their governance,
and leopards and wolves have unleashed their venom.
The common people suffer the sorrow of being gnawed by dogs,
and the old capital mourns the bitterness of the marsh weed.
I, though humble and insignificant,
have taken up the banner of righteousness at an opportune moment,
seizing the chance of the bandit-barbarians' heaven-ordained demise,
and relying on the indignation of the two prefectures' desire to rise up.
Thus, I began my campaign at Tiāntái,
extending to Xián and Yǒng.
With one mighty
gust of righteous wind,
the entire realm responded.
As our prestige and renown grew,
our soldiers displayed their courage.
Our army did not take a full morning,
and the numerous villains were shattered.
We annihilated the rebellious scales at Hánguān,
and swept away the evil traces
from Qín soil.
Had it not been for the blessings of the Sòng's divine power,
and the fulfillment of the people's wishes,
how could this have been achieved?
Now, the remaining oppressors in Píngchéng
are massing their forces at Dàtán,
[四一]looking greedily eastward and westward,
their might not to be approached.
Cháng'ān is isolated and perilous,
Hé and Luò are unguarded.
Píngyáng's two
clans,
whose families have for generations held land,
have rallied their tribes,
commanding fifty thousand archers.
They are stationed eastward at Tóngsài,
acting as pledges at the military gate.
Bái Guǎngpíng of Chángshān, who has privately appointed himself Ànxī Jiāngjūn,
is training armored troops at Gāopíng,
advancing his army towards Qiān and Lǒng.
The Hùjūn of Běimò are forming ranks of chariots and cavalry,
bearing spears and driving swiftly.
Hú Lán Luòshēng and others, with several thousands of their subordinate troops,
intend to attack the pseudo-
garrison.
The entire territory looks forward eagerly,
gazing up to the imperial benevolence.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty grant a legion of troops,
to advance north to Hé and Shǎn,
bestow upon your servant regalia,
and also provide military equipment.
Advancing,
we can suppress and resist the fierce bandits,
overthrowing their lairs.
Retreating, we can proclaim the nation's might and prestige,
and guard the old capital.
May the sound of phoenix bells ring in the Central Capital,
and may the distant regions cherish the virtue of
revival.
I respectfully dispatch my envoy Zhào Wǎn to swiftly present this sincere memorial."
Táo's dispatched armies were repeatedly defeated,
so he personally led a large force to attack him.
Wú again submitted a memorial, saying: "I have heard that there cannot be two suns in the sky,
nor two masters on earth.
Formerly, the Central Capital lost its governance,
and the nine regions fragmented.
Numerous villains arose like hills in the heavenly city,
and flying owls and kites eyed
the four seas.
The former emperor's benevolent heart stirred within him,
pitying the frontier barbarians,
cutting down the pseudo-Qiāng in Cháng'ān,
and relieving the common people from their suffering.
As his governance and teachings were extended,
the people began to find peace and recovery.
Heaven, however, had not forgotten the difficulties;
calamities and chaos continued to arise.
The Xiǎnyǔn became arrogant and aggressive,
invading and brutalizing the Central Plain,
making Cháng'ān a lair for wolves and jackals,
and Yè and Luò a den for wasps and snakes.
They unleashed
their poison upon the people,
and their tyranny flowed over the multitude.
Men and women capable of speech,
all sighed and were indignant.
They tilted their heads eastward,
looking up and hoping for rescue and assistance,
all like parched seedlings awaiting heavenly dew,
or infants
awaiting their loving parents.
I, relying on heaven's opportune moment and grace,
struck down the tyrannical with righteousness,
and have thus formed alliances east and west,
and established factions north and south.
The five prefectures have formed a covenant,
mutually pledging agreements.
Relying on awe-inspiring divine power,
a thousand *lǐ* of people gathered like clouds,
hoping to clear away the thorns and brambles,
to await the royal army.
As soon as the righteous men arrived,
they all fell apart.
On the fourth day of the second month, the barbarian lord emptied his treasury and storehouses,
and camped
with your servant.
Engaging in close combat,
there was no day without battle.
Over half of the bandits were captured,
and corpses covered the fields.
I humbly pray that a detached force be specifically dispatched,
to provide assistance.
If the heaven's
might is shaken,
it will surely cause the treacherous barbarians to collapse and perish,
and all the remaining people, great and small,
will receive a new lease on life."
Tàizǔ issued an edict saying:
"Gài Wú of Běidì
raised an army in Qínchuān.
Both Chinese and non-Chinese responded and joined him,
displaying their righteous courage.
He has frequently achieved victories,
and repeatedly sent memorials,
sincerely showing his loyalty from afar,
with the ambition to destroy the rebellious barbarians
and establish meritorious achievements.
He should be granted noble titles
and commended for his sincerity.
He can be appointed as Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Guānlǒng Zhūjūnjūnshì, Ànxī Jiāngjūn, Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ, Běidì Jùngōng.
Yōng and Liáng should send troops to the border,
to provide mutual assistance."
Táo attacked Wú in dozens of battles, large and small,
but could not overcome him.

Tàizǔ sent an envoy with seals for all the commanderies under the jurisdiction of Yōng and Qín prefectures, as well as those for generals of Jīnzǐ and below, totaling one hundred and twenty-one seals, to Wú,
allowing him to bestow them as he deemed fit.
When the Tūgē rebelled,
Wú personally attacked them.
He was hit by a stray arrow
and died.
Wú's younger brother, Wúshēng, led the remaining troops into Mùmìan Shān,
but they were all soon scattered and defeated.
In that same year,
Yán Báilù, a commoner from Tàiyuán, traveled privately into the wilderness
and was captured by the barbarians.
The Cìshǐ of Xiāngzhōu intended to kill him,
but Báilù falsely claimed,
"Dù Jì, the Cìshǐ of Qīngzhōu, sent me to express submission."
The Cìshǐ of Xiāngzhōu sent Báilù to Sānggān.
Táo was pleased and said:
"He is from my maternal family!"
He ordered his Sītú Cuī Hào to write a letter to Jì,
and sent Sītú Jìjiǔ Wáng Qí to carry the letter and return south with Báilù.
He dispatched his younger cousin, Gāoliáng Wáng, with a heavy army to intercept Jì,
entering the Tàiyuán border,
and attacked Shēn Tián, the Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu, at Lìchéng.
Tián defeated him.
Dù Jì sent his Níngshuò Fǔ Sīmǎ Xiàhóu Zǔhuān and Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Jí Yuān to rush to his aid.
The barbarians plundered Tàiyuán,
capturing over four thousand people
and over six thousand cattle.
Soon after, they also raided Yǎn, Qīng, and Jì three prefectures,
reaching Qīngdōng,
killing and abducting many people.
Tàizǔ pondered how to expand his strategies,
and issued an edict to his officials, saying: "When I was young, I read extensively,
and was quite fond of literature and its meaning.
I indulged in profound and exquisite texts,
unable to put down my scrolls.
Since I became entangled in worldly affairs,
my emotions have been divided between family and state.
I merely exist from dawn till dusk,
ultimately feeling ashamed of my virtue.
Yet the realm is not unified,
and famine plagues the army generation after generation.
Reflecting on this suffering,
my worries intensify.
Moreover, my chronic illness is gradually worsening,
and my ambition wanes with time.
Entrusted
is wasted with events.
Cruelly abusing wandering souls,
the Qí (齊) people are plunged into misery.
Therefore, I look back towards the North,
not forgetting to rescue [them] greatly.
I think of gathering all strategies,
to sweep clean the lingering rebels.
When feelings of sorrow arise,
a short rhyme is thus composed.
You, sirs, deeply embody the state's sentiments,
and should also be resolute in your righteous resolve.
The poem says: Jìfù (季父) foresaw disaster first,
Xīnshēng (辛生) recognized the opportunity from the start.
Rise and fall are not without signs,
prosperity and decline must have causes.
Since ancient times, the central domain has fallen,
swiftly, a hundred years have passed.
We do not see the southern clouds' shade,
but only witness the Hú (胡) winds rising.
When chaos reaches its extreme, order must emerge,
paths to peace arise from accumulated adversity.
Just as we wish to cleanse the lingering miasma,
how much more so the defilement of the borders!
I
look upon and lament these people,
their suffering is truly my responsibility.
I will go and spread a vast net,
and with one sweep, unify culture and tracks.
Will the opportune moment ever return?
It is hard to wait long for the Yellow River to clear.
A common
nag is content with short steps,
while a splendid steed aims for a thousand *lǐ*.
Liáng Fù (梁傅) harbored righteous intentions,
Yī Xiàng (伊相) felt deep shame.
To whom shall the reward and trust be given?
It depends on you few gentlemen.
Do not let the Qí (齊)
and Jìn (晉) dynasties,
bring shame upon the scholars of Zōu (鄒) and Lǔ (魯).
At that time, people on the borders,
often encroached and stole from each other.
In the 25th year,
