the Lǔ (虜) General Níngnán (寧南), Inspector of Yùzhōu (豫zhōu), and Marquis Běijǐng Hóu Ruòkù Chénshùlán (北井侯若庫辰樹蘭), sent a letter to Yùzhōu (豫zhōu) saying: I, with my unworthiness,
have received the nation's honor and favor,
entrusted with duties in a border province,
to manage the people and resources,
and promulgate governance and civilization,
soaring like a hawk for ten thousand *lǐ*.
Although I have exhausted my efforts in serving the command,
I have
not been able to ensure that the higher civilizing influence reaches below,
nor that the sentiments of the lower ranks reach above.
Recently,
the border people have been restless,
mutually rebellious,
no longer causing harm [to others],
but bringing about their own destruction.
Of those who died,
pheasants and rabbits fled,
entering the Sòng (宋) territory in the south,
gathering rebellious factions,
frequently engaging in banditry and looting,
killing innocent people,
seizing property,
greatly troubling the populace.
This border area,
is connected to that,
where people from both sides reside,
their hearths adjoining,
with ceaseless coming and going,
leading to an increase in deceit and falsehood.
Thus, southern villains enter the north,
northern villains
rebel in the south,
and extrapolating from this,
it worsens day by day.
Treacherous and wicked people,
often profit from encroachment and theft,
and even with severe laws,
they cannot be stopped.
I have often ordered
border officials,
to investigate the source of their wickedness,
but the governors and prefects of that country,
indulge and do not forbid or control them.
This has led to the spread,
of bandits disturbing the borders.
It is like fleas, lice, scabies, or ringworm,
though minor ailments,
they cause people to be uneasy all year round.
Currently, our exalted states are at peace and communicate,
north and south are in good harmony,
only the border populace,
have unclear agreements.
Since ancient times, among various states,
territories had boundaries,
each enforced
prohibitions,
and no longer infringed upon each other,
thus, it could be preserved for a long time,
handed down for eternity.
Therefore, I have reported to the imperial chancellery,
and dispatched a letter to make it clear:
From now on,
the Wèi (魏)
and Sòng (宋) territories,
should ensure that human traces do not cross.
Unless they are envoys or travelers on official business,
none shall go north or south.
For the people on the border,
their hearths visible to each other,
and the sounds of chickens and dogs audible to each
other,
to not interact until old age and death,
would that not be good?
Moreover, if those fleeing from here are returned by them,
and those fleeing from there are delivered by us,
then this is what our nation hopes for from a benevolent
state.
The Right General, Inspector of Yùzhōu (豫zhōu), Prince Nánpíng Wáng Shuò (南平王鑠), replied to the letter, saying: I understand that due to the restlessness of the border populace,
many are rebellious,
and you wish to stop villainy and wickedness,
and alleviate the people's suffering on both sides;
also that you wish to alternately send back those who flee,
and prohibit their coming and going.
Your
good intentions have been expressed,
and I truly understand your heart.
However, since your side entered into peace and harmony,
your solemn promises have always been broken.
The harm of intrusion and transgression,
has repeatedly violated righteous conduct,
giving free rein to betrayal and abandonment,
exclusively indulging in violent
plunder.
Not only did you secretly infringe upon the royal populace,
but you even harmed envoys.
Recently, when we suppressed the Mánmáo (蠻髦) barbarians,
the matter was confined to the imperial domain,
some, like foxes fleeing and rats scurrying,
escaped to the northern border,
yet
you immediately harbored and accepted them,
treating them as old friends,
supplying them with food and weapons,
and allowing them to become bandits.
In past years, you arbitrarily raised armies,
inflicting disaster upon children and the elderly,
disregarding the agreements of good neighborliness,
and not considering the limits of your territory.
What your letter states,
your side also practices.
Though your words are abundant and full of appearance,
the actual deeds contradict the truth.
Causing suspicion and prolonging chaos,
is truly due to your side,
yet
you speak as if it were otherwise,
which goes against the principle of treating oneself generously.
The people on the borders,
have always been there,
and we have always expected this,
originally not taking it to heart.
If you truly wish to eliminate villainy and suppress violence,
and remain firm forever,
you
should first diligently guard your borders,
expel all fugitives,
ensuring that startled hooves and stray arrows,
do not recklessly enter our territory.
Then, below the border cities,
outer doors need not be closed.
The royal regulations are strict and clear,
how could we
alone fail to uphold the coming trust?
If fugitives flee across,
and plunder your people,
this is indeed a matter for punishment,
there is no need for [our] distant involvement.
Since I have taken charge outside the capital,
I have sought to expound upon the imperial policy.
I have
repeatedly instructed my governors and magistrates,
to earnestly uphold righteousness and humility.
My sincerity has not yet been fully spread,
how can I not feel ashamed?
I will re-emphasize the agreements and demonstrate [them],
to match your utmost concern.
In the twenty-seventh year,
Táo personally led a hundred thousand infantry and cavalry to invade Rǔnán.
Initially,
Táo intended to raid the border,
claiming to be hunting in Liángchuān.
Tàiqǔ, fearing his encroachment upon the Huái and Sì Rivers,
then issued an order to the border garrisons:
"If a small raiding party arrives,
hold your ground firmly and resist them;
if a large army comes,
relocate the populace to Shòuyáng."
The scouts of the garrisons were unclear in their reconnaissance,
and the enemy suddenly entered the territory.

Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn, the Grand Administrator of Nándùn and Èr Jùn, Zhèng Kūn, and Suīyuǎn Jiāngjūn, the Grand Administrator of Rǔyáng and Yǐngchuān Èr Jùn, Guō Dàoyǐn, both abandoned their cities and fled.
〔四二〕The enemy plundered the six commanderies west of the Huái,
killing a great many people.
They besieged Xuánhù City,
where the fighting men numbered fewer than a thousand.
Previously,
the Grand Administrator of Rǔnán and Xīncài Èr Jùn, Xú Zūnzhī, had left his post.
Nánpíng Wáng Shuò, who was then garrisoned in Shòuyáng,
sent the Aide-de-camp to the Right Army, Chén Xiàn, to act as Grand Administrator.
〔四三〕Xiàn fortified the city and held it firmly.
Táo attacked with his full might,
and Xiàn personally ascended the city wall to supervise the battle.
They erected towers overlooking the city,
and arrows rained down like a torrent.
Battering rams breached the southern wall,
but Xiàn immediately constructed an inner barricade,
erecting palisades to reinforce it.
The enemy launched close-quarters attacks on the city,
and many died.
More than half of Xiàn's officers and men were also killed or wounded.
Táo only feared that Shòuyáng would send relief troops,
and did not concern himself with Péngchéng.
Táo sent his younger cousin, Yǒngchāng Wáng Kùrénzhēn, with over ten thousand infantry and cavalry,
〔四四〕to take the populace he had plundered from the six commanderies,
and encamp north of Rǔyáng.
At that time, Shìzǔ was garrisoned in Péngchéng.
Tàiqǔ sent his troop commander, Wú Xiānglú, by relay to instruct Shìzǔ
to dispatch a thousand cavalry,
carrying three days' provisions, to launch a surprise attack.
Shìzǔ mustered horses from within a hundred *lǐ*,
obtaining one thousand five hundred.
The assembly discussed appointing the Assistant Administrator, Liú Yánsūn, as marshal,
but Yánsūn declined, unwilling to go,
and nominated his参军 (Cānjūn), Liú Tàizhī, as his substitute.
〔四五〕Shìzǔ consulted his Commander, Wáng Xuánmó, and Chief Clerk, Zhāng Chàng.
Chàng and others all endorsed the plan.
Thus, they divided into five armies,
with Tàizhī as marshal,

along with the Aide-de-camp to the Pacify the North Cavalry, Yuán Qiānzhī, the Aide-de-camp to the Field-Tax, Zāng Zhàozhī, the Aide-de-camp to the Collection Office, Yǐn Dìng, and the Left Attendant-in-ordinary of Wǔlíng Guó, Dù Yòuwén—these five individuals,
each leading one army.
Qiānzhī led Tàizhī's army, with Deputy Palace General Chéng Tiānzuò supervising the battle.
〔四六〕Upon reaching Qiáochéng,
they re-inspected the men and horses,
obtaining one thousand one hundred elite cavalry,
and headed straight for Rǔyáng.
The enemy did not expect a surprise force to come from the north.
Their main camp was north of Rǔyáng,
about three *lǐ* from the city.
When Tàizhī and the others arrived,
the enemy was completely unaware.
They galloped in and attacked,
killing over three thousand people,
and burning their baggage train.
Within the camp were several sections of houses.
All the houses contained tents,
and the weapons were very fine.
The eating utensils were all made of gold and silver.
Inside the tents, all the major commanders
were killed.
All the captured populace managed to flee eastward,
shouting:
"The government army has exacted painful retribution!"
The enemy troops immediately scattered in all directions.
They pursued them,
but after a day's march,
the men and horses were exhausted,
so they returned to Rǔnán.
There was an enemy contingent inside the city,
about five hundred cavalry and infantry.
They climbed the city wall, saw that Tàizhī had no reinforcements,
and furthermore, a separate commander, Jùlù Gōng Yú Sōng, arrived from Hǔláo.
Thereupon, they led out an attack on Tàizhī.
Tàizhī's army had not yet eaten and
was already exhausted from the morning battle.
Their formation had not yet been properly arrayed.
Yuán Qiānzhī retreated first,
which caused confusion and panic.
They abandoned their weapons and fled,
losing their way and rushing towards the Tuōshui River.
The river was deep and the banks high.
All the men and horses rushed into the water, struggling to cross.
Tàizhī alone did not leave,
saying:
"With such a defeat,
what face do I have to return?"
He dismounted and sat on the ground,
and was killed by the enemy.
Zhàozhī drowned,
Tiānzuò was captured by the enemy.
Qiānzhī, Dìng, Yòuwén, and over nine hundred officers and men escaped,
and four hundred horses reached safety.
Shìzǔ demoted the title of Pacify the North to Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn.
Xuánmó and Yánsūn were dismissed from office.
Chàng was relieved of his post as administrator of Pèi Jùn.
Qiānzhī was executed.
Dìng and Yòuwén were handed over to the Imperial Armory.
When Táo first heard of the defeat at Rǔyáng,
and then the news that Péngchéng had an attached army,
he was greatly alarmed,
and said to his followers:
"We only heard that Huáinán sent troops,
but then there's a surprise army emerging.
This year, we are falling into their trap."
He immediately burned his siege equipment,
intending to flee.
Just then, news of Tàizhī's death arrived,
so he halted at Shòuyáng.
He sent Liú Kāngzǔ to relieve Xuánhù.
Táo also sent Rènchéng Gōng to resist Kāngzǔ.
They fought and defeated him,
beheading Rènchéng.
Táo besieged the city for forty-two days without capturing it.
Many died,
and Rènchéng was also killed.
As Kāngzǔ's relief army gradually advanced,
Táo then blamed his generals,
executing many,
and fled with double speed.
Tàiqǔ commended Xiàn for his steadfast defense,
issuing an imperial edict that read:
"The Aide-de-camp to the Right Army, acting Administrator of Rǔnán and Xīncài Èr Jùn, Chén Xiàn,
exerted his full strength in defense,
preserving the city and destroying the invaders.
For such loyal and courageous service,
he should be conspicuously promoted.
He is appointed as Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Rǔnán and Xīncài Èr Jùn."
He also entrusted ten thousand bolts of cloth to Xiàn to be distributed among the civil and military officials and common people within Rǔnán City who had toiled in defense and battle.
Although Táo did not conquer Xuánhù,
he plundered a great deal.
The southern armies repeatedly failed to achieve success,
leading Táo to treat them with contempt.
He wrote a letter to Tàiqǔ saying: "Previously, your envoys and spies,
through deception and enticement of treacherous individuals,
secretly obtained Zhū Xiūzhī and Shēn Mó,
and recently again got Hú Chóngzhī.
For defeated generals,
the state has established penalties,
yet you all appoint them to regional governorships,
hoping to exploit our weaknesses
to console yourselves.
To obtain a mere stripling like Pǔzhōng Cài
of ours, what benefit or loss is it?
It is no different from gaining all the
people of our entire nation,
and you provide generously for them.
When you captured our humble general Wèi Bá,
you did not spare his person,
but readily subjected him to humiliating forced labor,
tormenting him.
Observing these actions,
one can fully understand your great
ambition,

Táo set out south from Péngchéng.
In the twelfth month,
he crossed the Huái River at Xūyí,
and defeated the armies of Hú Chóngzhī and others.
He left several thousand men under Shàngshū Hán Yuánxīng to guard Xūyí,
and personally led the main force south.
Zhōngshū Láng Lǔ Xiù emerged from Guǎnglíng,
Gāoliáng Wáng Ādòu Jiǎn emerged from Shānyáng,
and Yǒngchāng Wáng Yú Shòuyáng emerged from Héngjiāng.
Wherever they passed,
there was no place they did not inflict devastation.
Táo arrived at Guābù,
destroyed the people's houses,
and cut down reeds and rushes.
At Chúkǒu, he constructed rafts
to feign an attempt to cross the river.
Tàizǔ thoroughly prepared a naval force
for defense.
Initially,
Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Liú Zūnkǎo led an army towards Péngchéng.
Upon reaching Xiǎojiàn,
the barbarians had already blocked the road,
so he was recalled.
He and Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn Yǐn Hóng guarded Héngjiāng,
Shàofǔ Liú Xīngzǔ guarded Báixià,
Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Huángmén Shìláng Xiāo Yuányōng guarded Bízhōu,
Yǔlín Zuǒjiān Mèng Zōngsì guarded Xīnzhōu Upper,
Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn Tài Róng guarded Xīnzhōu Lower,
Zhēngběi Zhōngbīng Cānjūnshì Xiàng Liǔ guarded Guìzhōu,
Sīmǎ Dào Yuándù guarded Suànshān,
Zīyì Cānjūn Shěn Tánqìng guarded Běigù,
Shàngshū Chǔ Zhànzhī advanced to Jīnglíng,
and then guarded Xīzhīn,
Xúzhōu Cóngshì Shǐ Xiāo Shàngzhī guarded Liànbì,
Zhēngběi Cānjūn Guǎn Fǎzǔ guarded Qiáoshān,
Xúzhōu Cóngshì Wǔ Zhònghé guarded Bóluò,
Shàngshū Zuǒchéng Liú Bólóng guarded Cǎishí,
and was soon promoted to Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn and Huáinán Tàishǒu,
still overseeing all matters of defense.
Patrols extended from Yúhú in the upper reaches
down to Càizhōu,
with warships arrayed and camps established,
stretching along the riverbanks.
From Cǎishí to Jìyáng,
a distance of six or seven hundred *lǐ*,
boats and ships covered the river,
and flags and armor shone like stars and torches.
The Crown Prince went out to garrison Shítóu Chéng,
and Qiánjiāngjūn Xú Zhànzhī guarded Shítóu Cāngchéng.
Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě Lè Xún and Shàngshū Shuǐbù Láng Liú Yuānzhī were both handed over to Jiànkāng
for failing to follow instructions in their preparations.
The imperial carriage frequently visited Shítóu and Mòfǔ Shān
to observe the terrain.
A reward was offered to anyone who could kill Fó Lí and bring his head:
they would be enfeoffed as a Kāiguó Xiàngōng of eight thousand households,
and awarded ten thousand bolts each of cloth and silk,
and one hundred *jīn* each of gold and silver.
For killing his son, younger brother, a false minister, or a grand general,
one would be enfeoffed as a Kāiguó Xiànhóu of four hundred households,
and awarded five thousand bolts each of cloth and silk.
Rewards for those below this rank varied accordingly.
They also recruited people to dig wells and place poisonous wine in empty villages,
〔六０〕intending to poison the barbarians,
but it ultimately caused no harm.
Táo excavated a winding path on Guābù Shān
and built a house on its summit.
Táo did not drink water from south of the river;
he had camels carry water from north of the river with him,
each camel carrying thirty *dǒu*.
He sent envoys to offer Tàizǔ camels and famous horses,
seeking peace and proposing a marriage alliance.
The Emperor sent Fèngcháoqǐng Tián Qí to offer him rare delicacies and exotic flavors.
When Táo received the yellow oranges,
he immediately ate them,
and also generously offered Língjiǔ.
When his attendants whispered to each other,
suspecting poison in the food,
Táo did not reply,
but pointed at the sky with his finger,
and showed his grandson to Qí, saying:
"Coming here is not solely for fame and glory;
it is truly to form a marriage alliance.
If you can reciprocate,
from now on we will not offend each other even a hair's breadth."
He also sought to marry his daughter to Shìzǔ.
On the first day of the first month of the twenty-eighth year,
Táo held a gathering on the mountain,
including local people.
After the gathering,
he plundered the people's households,
burned their towns and houses, and departed.
The barbarians initially lit beacon fires along the river.
Yǐn Hóng said:
"When the six barbarians act like this, they will surely flee."
On the second day of the first month,
they indeed retreated.
Initially,
when Tàizǔ heard that the barbarians were invading,
burning the official residences and boats in Guǎnglíng City,
he ordered the governors of Guǎnglíng and Nánpèi Commanderies, Liú Huáizhī, to lead the people across the river at once.
The barbarians, finding Hǎilíng full of marshes,
dared not go there.
Shānyáng Tàishǒu Xiāo Sēngzhēn also gathered the residents and displaced people,
all of whom entered the city.
The court sent provisions and weapons to Xūyí,
but as the bandits pressed,
some were diverted and left in Shānyáng.
There were also tens of thousands of siege weapons
that were supposed to go to Huátái,
but were also left with the commandery.
Inside the city were nearly ten thousand households
and over five thousand warriors.
There was Báimǐ Pí,
a few *lǐ* from the commandery.
Sēngzhēn deliberately drained water from various places
to fill it,
intending to break the dam
to flood the bandits when they arrived.
When the barbarians arrived,
they dared not stop
and withdrew.
They returned from Guǎnglíng.
Then they attacked Xūyí,
exerting their full strength to assault the city,
but could not capture it in thirty days.
So they burned their siege equipment and retreated.
Táo destroyed six prefectures in total: Nányǎn, Xú, Yǎn, Yù, Qīng, and Jì.
The number of people killed and plundered was beyond estimation,
and more than half of his soldiers and horses died or were injured.
His countrymen all criticized him severely.

Their land, in deep mountains, would accumulate snow even in summer,

but their horses and cattle, gnawing dry grass and eating snow,

Their national governance was simple and crude;
they did not know how to write,

Later, they gradually learned written characters,
and even today, there are quite a few scholars.
They were over a thousand *lǐ* from Běihǎi
and bordered the Dīnglíng.

During the era of Tàizǔ,

The old people harbored thoughts of ancient times,

From then on, the Guān and Hé regions resonated,

As soon as the imperial carriage rested,

They overran our Láo and Huá,
and plundered our Yī and Chán.
Therefore, Tàizǔ was indignant.
He began to pacify Sī and Yǎn,
But his military strategy was not victorious,
abandoning his army and losing his forces.
Armor was cast aside across the plain,
and prefectures were given up along the river.
[七五] The elite troops of Jīng and Wú,
with their soaring spirits, could not vent their prowess.
Isolated cities and lone generals
endured injustice and became captives.
Thus, the border was constricted and the enemy prolonged,
barely preserving the east of Qīng.
From then on, our forces were shattered and our power weakened,
and the border gaps gradually widened.
Bold cavalry rode in raids,
and whistling arrows arrived daily.
Fodder and pasture were damaged annually,
and grain and wheat fields were encroached upon every year.
In minor instances, officials and common people were captured;
in major instances, governors and commanders were seized.
Urgent military dispatches followed one another on the road,
and emergency orders were continuous.
The regions between Qīng, Xú, Yǎn, and Jì were desolate.
But from the time of Mùmò,
there have been sagacious talents and cunning strategists,
skilled in military authority,
and deeply conversant with tactics.
They were brave and imposing,
their spirit surpassing a hundred men.
Thus, they could awe and subdue the Huá lands,
and their ambition surpassed all other barbarians.
As for the usurpers Líbá and Zuǎnwěi,
they further inflamed their malevolent might.
Their heroic plans and martial strategies
surpassed those of ancient times.
Even the fierce bravery of Mòdú
and the valor and strength of Bùshí
could not match them.
They then swallowed up Héyòu in the west,
and seized Lóngjié in the east.
They encompassed all the Rong barbarians,
their territory extending ten thousand li.
Although their territorial division
did not equal that of Wèi and Jìn,
their population of Huá people and Rong tribes
doubled their strength.
To the extent that they gathered a million cavalry,

Hú banners reflected in the Jiāng,
and nomadic tents lined the islets.
The capital city was burdened with anxieties,
and its men and women were in commotion.
The Son of Heaven inwardly calmed the hearts of the populace,
and outwardly resisted the hordes of enemies.
Corvée labor was exhausted,
and state treasuries were depleted.
The entire realm was mobilized to repel them,
yet the strength was still insufficient.
Soon after, the barbarians let loose their returning armies,
annihilating successive states and cities.
They plundered our Huái prefectures,
and captured our Jiāng counties.
The countless common people,
constrained under the high heaven
and treading on the thick earth,
had nowhere to appeal.
The strong became corpses,
and the weak became captives.
From the Jiāng and Huái to Qīng and Jì,
of the several hundred thousand households,

escaped to the lakes and marshes.
Villages and wells were desolate,

It was late spring,
when mulberries and wheat began to flourish.
The old people and surviving populace
returned, wailing in their former settlements.
The echoes from Huánshān
were not enough to express the sorrow.
The six prefectures were utterly devastated,
with no remnants of vines or structures left.
Even the young swallows, arriving in season,
had no place to deposit their mud.
In a single branch,
there were dozens of connected nests.
As soon as the spring rain arrived,
the added nests collapsed.
Although the circumstances differed from the Wú Palace,
the annihilation was no different.
How severe
was this utter defeat!
Tàizǔ, not yet deeply chastened by the calamity,
again launched an outer campaign.
His army halted before a strong city,
and abandoned its armor on the river.
Thus, we suffered a second defeat,
and the enemy achieved a third victory.
From then on,
though markets were opened for trade
and peace through marriage was accepted,
border encroachments and attacks on garrisons
occurred consecutively every year.
Then, during the strife of Tàishǐ,
border generals rebelled,
leading barbarians to introduce invaders,
causing us to lose four prefectures.
Gāozǔ toiled until sunset,
intending to unify the realm.
Banners were unfurled and furled,
and only then was victory achieved.
The Later Emperor merely preserved institutions,
establishing neither penal codes nor moral influence.
In one campaign, Sī and Yǎn were abandoned;
in a second campaign, Xúfāng was lost.
The Hua clothing was desolate,
turned into lush grass.
How could this be merely due to heavenly timing?
It was also due to human affairs.
Indeed, terrain has its advantages and disadvantages,
and military deployments have their strengths and weaknesses.
The Hú rely on swift horses,
and the plains are entirely suitable for chariots and cavalry.
The southerners are skilled in naval warfare,
and the rivers and lakes are inherently the domain of boats and ships.
Dài horses and Hú steeds
originate from north of Jì,
while Phoebe and camphor trees
are planted in the central lands.
This is how Heaven and Earth divide regions.
To say that people accustomed to furs
can achieve victory in Jīng and Yuè
is certainly impossible.
And to say that men of war-galleys
can contend for supremacy in Yān and Jì,
how could that possibly be?
As Yú Xǔ said,
"One who runs cannot pursue one who flies."
This is because we are on foot while they are on horseback.
From this, if one infers victory and defeat,
it can almost be summarized in a single phrase.

Biographies, Chapter 56, Xiānbēi Tǔyùhún
Ā Cháilǔ Tǔyùhún,
a Xiānbēi from Liáodōng.
His father, Yìluòhán,
had two sons:
the elder was named Tǔyùhún,
the younger Ruòluòkuī.
Ruòluòkuī separately became the Mùróng clan.
Hún was born of a concubine and was the elder;
Kuī was of the legitimate line.
When their father was alive,
he allotted seven hundred households to Hún.
Hún and Kuī's two divisions grazed horses together.
The horses fought and injured each other.
Kuī was enraged
and sent a messenger to Hún, saying:
"Our late father's arrangements
separated you, my brother, into a different division.
Why do you not graze your horses far apart,
resulting in fights and injuries?"
Hún replied:
"Horses are animals.
They eat grass and drink water.
When the spring vitality emerges,
they are prone to fighting.
The fighting is among the horses,
why should the anger extend to people?
Separation is very easy.
I shall now depart from you by ten thousand *lǐ*."
Thereupon, he drove his horses westward,
moving one encampment each day,
each encampment eighty *lǐ*.
After several encampments,
Kuī repented and realized his error,
deeply blaming himself.
Hún said:
"Since the time of my ancestors,
we have established virtue in the right side of Liáo.
Moreover, the words of divination
say that our late father had two sons,
and good fortune and blessings would flow to both their descendants.
I am of humble, secondary birth,
and it is not reasonable for us to both achieve greatness.
Now, our separation due to horses
is perhaps divinely ordained.
Gentlemen, please try to drive the horses eastward.
If the horses return eastward,
I will follow them."
Lóu bowed joyfully and said:
"Chǔkěhán!"
The barbarian word
"Chǔkěhán"
means "Your Lordship" in Sòng speech.
Then, he had the two thousand cavalrymen who followed him jointly block the horses to make them turn back.
Before they had gone three hundred paces,
the horses suddenly neighed mournfully and bolted,
their sound like a collapsing mountain.
This happened more than ten times,
each time moving further away.
Lóu's efforts failed,
and he knelt again, saying:
"Kěhán,
this is no longer a matter of human doing."
Hún said to his tribesmen:
"My brother's and my descendants
are both destined to flourish.
Kuī will pass it down through his sons, great-grandsons, and great-great-grandsons.
This will last for about a hundred years,
and it will be in the time of my great-great-grandsons that I shall begin to become prominent."
Thereupon, he proceeded westward and attached himself to Yīnshān.
He encountered the Jìn disorders,
and thus was able to ascend the Lǒng.
Later, Kuī thought of Hún with longing
and composed the "Āgān Song."
The Xiānbēi call an elder brother
"Āgān."
When Kuī's descendants secretly assumed imperial titles,
they made this song the grand anthem of the imperial carriage.
After Hún ascended the Lǒng,
he moved out to Hǎnkāi and Xīlíng.
Xīlíng is
today's Xīpíng Commandery,
and Hǎnkāi
is today's Fúhǎn County.
From Fúhǎn eastward for over a thousand *lǐ*,
reaching Gānsōng,
westward to Hénán,
and south to the borders of Mǎo Chéng and Lónghé.
From the Táoshuǐ southwestward,
extending to Báilán,
within several thousand *lǐ*,
they followed water and grass,
dwelling in felt tents,
and living on meat and dairy products.
The various tribes in the northwest called them Ā Cháilǔ.
Hún died at the age of seventy-two.
He had sixty sons,
the eldest Tǔyán succeeded him.
Tǔyán was seven *chǐ* eight *cùn* tall,
possessed extraordinary strength,
and was by nature cruel and violent.
He was assassinated by Jiāng Cōng, a Qiāng chieftain from Mǎo Chéng.
With the sword still in his body,
he called his son Yèyán
and said to his great general Juébá Wò:
"Once my breath stops
and I am coffined and buried,
immediately travel far to secure Báilán.
Báilán's terrain is both rugged and distant,
and its native people are weak,
easy to control.
Yèyán is young;
I had intended to entrust [the leadership] to others,
fearing that in an emergency, they might not be able to control [the situation].
Now I entrust Yèyán to you.
You must exert your utmost effort to assist him.
If this child can be established,
I will have no regrets."
He pulled out the sword and died.
He reigned for thirteen years,
and was thirty-five years old.
He had twelve sons.
Yèyán was young but brave and resolute.
At the age of ten,
he tied grass into a figure of a person,
named it Jiāng Cōng,
and shot at it every morning.
If he hit it, he was happy;
if he missed, he cried and wailed.
His mother said:
"Your enemy, the generals, have already slaughtered him.
You are young,
why trouble yourself like this every morning?"
Yèyán choked with sobs, unable to control himself,
and replied to his mother:
"I truly know it is useless,
but Yèyán's boundless grief
cannot endure its pain."
He was extremely filial.
When his mother was ill,
she could not eat for three days,
and Yèyán also did not eat.
He read some historical texts
and referred to his great-grandfather Yìluòhán, who was first enfeoffed as the Duke of Chānglí,
saying:
"I am the son of a duke's grandson.
According to ritual,
a duke's grandson's son
may take his paternal grandfather's given name as his surname."
He ordered the surname to be Tǔyùhún.
He reigned for twenty-three years,
and was thirty-three years old.
He had four sons.
The eldest son Suìxī succeeded.
Suìxī was pure and cautious by nature,
but his three younger brothers wielded all power.
Suìxī could not control them,
and the great generals jointly executed them.
Suìxī was so saddened and disheartened that he no longer managed affairs.
He then established his son Shìlián as heir apparent,
entrusting affairs to him,
and called him
"Mòhèláng."
"Mòhè"
means "father" in Sòng speech.
Suìxī then died.
He was in power for twenty-five years,
and was forty-two years old.
He had six sons.
His son Shìlián, grieved by his father's death,
did not engage in recreation
or feasting.
He was in power for fifteen years,
and was forty-two years old.
He had two sons,
the elder named Shìpí,
the younger Wūhétí.
Shìpí succeeded and reigned for eleven years,
and was forty-two years old.
His sons Shùluògān and others were all young,
so his brother Wūhétí succeeded.
Hétí reigned for eight years,
and was thirty-five years old.
Shìpí's son Shùluògān succeeded,
and proclaimed himself General of Chariots and Cavalry.
This was in the early Yìxī period.
Shùluògān died.
His younger brother, Āchái, proclaimed himself General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn).
When Qiáo Zòng caused chaos in Shǔ,
Āchái dispatched his nephew, Xīqiáng Gōng Tǔyùhún Chìláiní, to expand their territory as far as Lónghé and Píngkāng.
During the Jǐngpíng reign of Emperor Shàodì,
Āchái sent envoys to present a memorial and local products.
An imperial edict stated:
“Tǔyùhún Āchái, residing in a distant region,
has shown commendable aspiration towards righteousness.
He should be honored and entrusted with responsibility.
In response to his sincerity,
he is appointed Overseer of All Military Affairs Beyond the Fortifications, General of the Pacified West (Ānxī Jiāngjūn), Governor of Shāzhōu (Shāzhōu Cìshǐ), and Duke of Jiāohé (Jiāohé Gōng).”
Before he could accept the appointment,
in the third year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Tàizǔ,
another edict was issued, adding to the previous appointment.
Before the envoy arrived, Āchái died,
and his younger brother Mùguī was enthroned.
In the sixth year,
Mùguī memorialized:
“The Great Sòng has responded to the mandate of Heaven,
and all within the four seas set their hearts upon it.
My deceased elder brother Āchái aspired to the righteousness of the celestial court,
and his sincerity was consistently evident.
Last year, on the fifth day of the seventh month,
the court attendant Dǒng Zhàn arrived,
proclaiming the illustrious edict
and explicitly bestowing honorable titles.
However, due to misfortune in my private household,
my deceased elder brother passed away.
Being weak and incompetent,
I have borne the subsequent responsibility.
Yet, the imperial benevolence was originally directed at my household.
If there were any reconsideration,
I fear it would hinder the transmission of the decree.
I have therefore presumptuously accepted the honorable appointment
and respectfully followed the imperial will.
I humbly request that you deliberate
and again bestow a formal imperial rescript.”
In the seventh year,
an imperial edict stated:
“Tǔyùhún Mùguī and his brothers have aspired to righteousness,
and their utmost sincerity is commendable.
An imperial rescript and noble title should be bestowed
to verify their loyalty.
He is appointed Overseer of All Military Affairs Beyond the Fortifications, General of the Punishing West (Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn), Governor of Shāzhōu (Shāzhōu Cìshǐ), and Duke of Lǒngxī (Lǒngxī Gōng).”
Earlier, at the end of the Jìn dynasty,
the Hú people of Yǔn Jiē County, Jīnchéng Commandery, Qífú Gānguī, gathered their followers and occupied Táohé and Hǎnkāi,
proclaiming himself Duke of Lǒngxī (Lǒngxī Gōng).
After Gānguī died,
his son Chìpán was enthroned,
and sent envoys to the Jìn court to submit,
and was appointed Bearer of Credential, Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs in Hexi, General of the Pacified West (Píngxī Jiāngjūn),
with his ducal title unchanged.
When Emperor Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Chìpán was promoted to Grand General of the Pacified West (Ānxī Dàjiāngjūn).
After Chìpán died,
his son Màomàn was enthroned.
Mùguī repeatedly dispatched armies to attack him,
and Màomàn led his tribes east to Lǒngyòu.
Mùguī then occupied his territory.
In that year,
Hèlián Dìng was attacked in Cháng'ān by the Suǒlǔ, Tuòbá Táo,
and led over ten thousand households from Qín west to Hǎnkāi,
intending to go to Liángzhōu.
Mùguī resisted and attacked them,
severely defeating them,
and capturing Dìng alive.
Táo sent envoys to request Dìng,
and Mùguī handed Dìng over to him.
In the ninth year,
Mùguī dispatched Sīmǎ Zhào Fèng to present tribute,
and also reported a victory of twenty thousand men.

Emperor Tàizǔ further appointed him Bearer of Credential, Regular Mounted Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì), Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs in the three prefectures of Xīqín, Hé, and Shā, Grand General of the Punishing West (Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn), Governor of the two prefectures of Xīqín and Hé, and concurrently Protector of the Qiāng (Hù Qiāng Xiàowèi),
and advanced his noble title to King of Lǒngxī (Lǒngxī Wáng).
His younger brother Mùyán was appointed General of the Pacified East (Píngdōng Jiāngjūn),
Mùguī's elder brother Shùluògān's son Shíyín was appointed General of the Pacified North (Píngběi Jiāngjūn),
and Āchái's son Wěi replaced him as General Who Guards the Army (Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn).
An edict instructed Mùguī that all soldiers and officers from the southern countries
who had previously been captured by the Fófó
should all be returned.
Mùguī sent back fifty-five households, including Zhū Xīnzhī,
totaling one hundred and fifty-four people.
Mùguī died,
and his younger brother Mùyán was enthroned,
and sent envoys to present a memorial.
In the fifteenth year,

Mùyán was appointed Bearer of Credential, Regular Mounted Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì), Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs in the three prefectures of Xīqín, Hé, and Shā, Grand General of the Pacified West (Zhèn Xī Dàjiāngjūn), concurrently Protector of the Qiāng (Hù Qiāng Xiàowèi), Governor of the two prefectures of Xīqín and Hé, and King of Lǒngxī (Lǒngxī Wáng).
In the sixteenth year,
his title was changed to King of Hénán (Hénán Wáng).
In that same year,
Shíyín, the younger brother of Shíqián, was appointed General of the Pacified West (Píngxī Jiāngjūn);
Mùyán's eldest illegitimate son Fánnì was appointed General Who Comforts the Army (Fǔ Jūn Jiāngjūn);
and Mùyán's legitimate son Huán was appointed General of the Left (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn) and Heir Apparent to the King of Hénán (Hénán Wáng Shìzǐ).
In the nineteenth year,

Āchái was posthumously granted his original titles of General of the Pacified West (Ānxī Jiāngjūn), Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs in the three prefectures of Qín, Shā, and Shā, Governor of Shāzhōu (Shāzhōu Cìshǐ), concurrently Protector of the Qiāng (Hù Qiāng Xiàowèi), and King of Lǒngxī (Lǒngxī Wáng).
The Suǒlǔ Tuòbá Táo sent troops to attack Mùyán,
severely defeating him.
Mùyán led his tribes west to Báilán,
and attacked and destroyed the kingdom of Yútián.
Fearing that the captives would return,
in the twenty-seventh year,
he sent envoys to present a memorial stating:
“If we cannot defend ourselves,
we wish to lead our troops and retainers into Lónghé and pass through Yuèxiān Gate.”
He also requested carriages,
and offered Wūhuán hats,
golden wine vessels from the Women's Kingdom, golden bracelets of the Hú kings, and other items.
Emperor Tàizǔ granted him carriages,
and permitted him to enter Yuèxiān if the captives came and he could not defend himself.
The captives ultimately did not come.
Mùyán died,
and Shíyín enthroned himself.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Shíyín was appointed Bearer of Credential, Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs in the three prefectures of Xīqín, Hé, and Shā, General of the Pacified West (Ānxī Jiāngjūn),
concurrently Protector of the Qiāng (Hù Qiāng Xiàowèi), Governor of the two prefectures of Xīqín and Hé, and King of Hénán (Hénán Wáng).
Shíyín attacked and defeated the Suǒlǔ in the east,
and was granted the honorific title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
In the fifth year of Dàmíng of Emperor Shìzǔ,
Shíyín sent envoys to present well-trained dancing horses
and four-horned sheep.
The Crown Prince, princes, dukes, and officials below them composed twenty-seven songs about the dancing horses.
In the third year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Tàizōng,
he was promoted to Grand General of the Punishing West (Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn).
In the fifth year,
Shíyín presented a memorial and local products,
and his younger brother Shípí was appointed General of the Pacified West (Píngxī Jiāngjūn) and Duke of Jīnchéng (Jīnchéng Gōng).
The Former Deposed Emperor further promoted him to Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Dàjiāngjūn).
To the west of their country, there is a yellow desert,
one hundred and twenty *lǐ* from north to south,
and seventy *lǐ* from east to west,
where no grass or trees grow.
Shāzhōu is named after this.
There is a salt pond in Qūzhēn Chuān.
North of Gāngǔ Lǐng, there is a place where sparrows and rats share a common hole (Quèshǔ Tóngxué).
Sometimes it is in the mountains,
sometimes on flat ground.
The sparrows are white,
and the rats are yellow.
Where yellow and purple flowers and grasses grow on the ground,
there are sparrow and rat holes.
Báilán produces gold, copper, and iron.
Although their country follows water and grass,
they generally reside in Mùhè Chuān.
[One zero]
The imperial historian says: Tǔyùhún followed the grass and relied on springs,
acting powerfully beyond the fortifications.
They wore animal skins and ate meat,
sustaining themselves through hunting and animal husbandry.
Yet, brocades, silks, and fine satins
were valued as exotic goods.
Merely through commercial exchanges,
they were treated with the same courtesies as those who submitted.
From ancient times, sagacious kings,
though maintaining a policy of pacifying distant peoples,
did not extend ritual and culture to remote, isolated regions.
At most, they treated them as dependent states,
a principle evident in the *Chūnqiū*.
The Jìn and Sòng dynasties, in establishing their precedents,
did not follow ancient rules.
Consequently, noble titles were granted at the highest level,
and their ranks were comparable to those of the Three Excellencies.
They wore braided hair and offered congratulations,
not valuing the hairpin and ceremonial cap.
Their languages were unintelligible,
so how could they perform official duties?
Although tribute baskets arrived annually,
this was merely a trade route.
Golden rugs and felt blankets
were not urgently needed.
The trouble of receiving and escorting them
resulted in more loss than gain.
If we were to make the Sùshèn offer annual tribute
and Yuèsháng present yearly offerings,
it would certainly not be appropriate to record their distinctions
and elevate them above previous policies.
The sages called them "barbarian-subdued lands" (huāngfú);
this saying undoubtedly has its reasons.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 57: Yi and Man
The Southern Yi and Southwestern Yi
are mostly located south and southwest of Jiāozhōu,
residing on islands in the vast ocean.
They are separated by distances of three to five thousand *lǐ*,
or even twenty to thirty thousand *lǐ* for the more distant ones.
They travel by ship, hoisting sails,
and the distances cannot be accurately known.
Although foreign barbarians mention distances in *lǐ*,
these are not precise figures.
The country of Lín Yì in the southern wilds.
In the second year of Gāo Zǔ's Yǒng Chū reign,
Fàn Yáng Mài, the King of Lín Yì, sent envoys to present tribute.
He was immediately granted official appointments.
In the early years of Tài Zǔ's Yuán Jiā reign,
he invaded and plundered the prefectures of Rì Nán and Jiǔ Dé.
Dù Hóng Wén, the Inspector of Jiāo Zhōu, raised his banner and gathered troops, intending to attack him,
but hearing there would be a replacement (for himself),
he stopped.
In the seventh year,
Yáng Mài sent envoys to state that he was not on good terms with Jiāo Zhōu
and sought pardon.
In the eighth year,
he again sent over a hundred turreted ships to raid Jiǔ Dé,
entering the mouth of Sī Huì Pǔ.
Ruǎn Mí Zhī, the Inspector of Jiāo Zhōu, dispatched Suí Dào Shēng, a Dùi Zhǔ, with three thousand men to attack them.
They attacked Qū Sù Chéng but could not overcome it,
and so withdrew.
Lín Yì wished to attack Jiāo Zhōu
and borrowed troops from the King of Fú Nán,
but Fú Nán did not comply.
In the tenth year,
Yáng Mài sent envoys to present a memorial and local products,
seeking to govern Jiāo Zhōu.
An imperial edict replied that it was too far away
and did not grant permission.
In the twelfth, fifteenth, sixteenth, and eighteenth years,
he frequently sent tribute,
but his raiding did not cease,
and the tribute presented was also crude and meager.
Tài Zǔ was angered by his transgressions.
In the twenty-third year,
he ordered Lú Hè Zhī, the General of Valiant Dragon and Inspector of Jiāo Zhōu, to attack him,
and dispatched Zōng Quán, the General Who Shakes Awe of the Grand Commandant's office, to follow Hè Zhī's command.
Hè Zhī sent Xiāo Jǐng Xiàn, his Fǔ Sī Mǎ, as vanguard,
and Quán concurrently served as Jǐng Xiàn's deputy commander.
When Yáng Mài heard that he was about to be attacked,
he sent envoys to present a memorial,
requesting the return of the people and households he had plundered from Rì Nán,
and to offer national treasures.
Tài Zǔ issued an edict to Hè Zhī:
"If Yáng Mài truly shows sincerity,
allow him to surrender."
In the second month of that year,
the army reached Zhū Wú Shù.

He sent Jiāng Zhòng Jī, the Rì Nán Prefect and Hù Cáo Cān Jūn of the Inspector's office, and Jiǎo Hóng Mín, the Qián Bù Zéi Cáo Cān Jūn, to accompany the imperial messengers Bì Yuàn and Gāo Jīng Nú to proclaim the imperial grace.
Yáng Mài seized Zhòng Jī, Jīng Nú, and twenty-eight others,
and sent Hóng Mín back to report,
outwardly expressing submission,
but his suspicions and defenses grew stricter.
Jǐng Xiàn and others then advanced towards Qū Sù Chéng.
Yáng Mài dispatched his grand commander, Fàn Fú Lóng Dà, to garrison Qū Sù,
and also sent naval and land forces directly there.
Jǐng Xiàn defeated their outer relief forces,
and attacked the city with full might.
In the fifth month,
he captured it,
beheaded Fú Lóng Dà,
and captured countless gold, silver, and various other objects.
They pursued the enemy, capitalizing on their victory,
and immediately captured Lín Yì.
Yáng Mài and his son both fled for their lives.
The rare treasures they captured
were all unnamed jewels.
The emperor commended the achievements of the generals and commanders,
and issued an edict saying:
"Lín Yì relied on its remote and dangerous terrain,
long delaying the imperial punishment.
Lú Hè Zhī, the General of Valiant Dragon and Inspector of Jiāo Zhōu, is loyal and resolute, reaching the highest ranks.
His strategic thinking encompasses governance.
Having received the order to attack,
he pushed the vanguard thousands of *lǐ*.
His military laws were strict and orderly,
his civil and military officials all exerted their strength.
He kept himself clean and served the public,
leading his subordinates by example.
Thus he was able to establish merits overseas
and awe the diverse foreign peoples into submission.
He should be greatly praised and decorated,
and participate in managing the imperial attendants.
He is appointed Huáng Mén Shì Láng,
concurrently holding the titles of Yuè Qí Xiào Wèi and acting Jiàn Wǔ Jiāng Jūn.
Xiāo Jǐng Xiàn, the Lóng Xiáng Sī Mǎ, assisted the army commander,
his diligence and swiftness were outstanding.
He commanded the vanguard,
annihilating the enemy's lair.
He will surely be able to awe the wild barbarians into submission
and pacify the common people.
He is appointed Chí Jié, Supervisor of all military affairs of the prefectures of Yù Lín and Níng Pǔ in Jiāo Zhōu and Guǎng Zhōu, Jiàn Wēi Jiāng Jūn, and Inspector of Jiāo Zhōu."
Tóng Lín Zhī, the Lóng Xiáng Sī Mǎ, and Fù Wèi Zǔ, the Prefect of Jiǔ Zhēn, died in battle,
and were both posthumously awarded Gěi Shì Zhōng.
In the second year of Shì Zǔ's Xiào Jiàn reign,
Lín Yì again sent Fàn Lóng Bá, its Cháng Shǐ, as an envoy to present tribute.
Lóng Bá was appointed Yáng Wǔ Jiāng Jūn.
In the second year of Dà Míng,
Fàn Shén Chéng, the King of Lín Yì, again sent Fàn Liú, his Cháng Shǐ, to present a memorial offering gold and silver vessels, incense, cloth, and various other items.
In the first year of Tài Zōng's Tài Yù reign,
he again sent envoys to offer local products.
Initially,
when Lú Hè Zhī was summoned and arrived at Yù Zhāng,
he encountered Hú Dàn Shì and others from Yù Zhāng who had rebelled.
He then attacked and pacified them.
Concurrently with his merits against Lín Yì,
he was enfeoffed as the Viscount of Yún Dù County,
with an income of four hundred households.
Hè Zhī,
a native of Jīn Xiāng, Gāo Píng,
was the son of Lú Píng.
he was appointed Zhèn Jūn Sī Mǎ for Shì Zǔ, Fǔ Guó Jiāng Jūn, and Prefect of Péng Chéng, having previously been the Zuǒ Wèi Shuài of the Crown Prince.
When the prime culprit usurped the throne by assassination,
he was made Xī Zhōng Láng Jiāng and Inspector of Yōng Zhōu.
When Shì Zǔ marched to attack,
he was promoted to Fǔ Guó Jiāng Jūn
and oversaw the garrison affairs of Yù Zhōu.
He then left and fled south.
When Shì Zǔ ascended the throne,
he was made Yòu Wèi Jiāng Jūn.
In the second year of Xiào Jiàn,
he was appointed Fǔ Guó Jiāng Jūn and Inspector of Yù Zhōu,
but did not take office.
He resumed his position as Yòu Wèi
and was promoted to Sàn Qí Cháng Shì.
In the third year,
he was sent out as Inspector of Nán Yǎn Zhōu.
For excessive drinking, accepting bribes,
and bringing women from prison into his residence,
he was dismissed from office and prohibited from holding future positions.
He died that year
and was posthumously awarded Zuǒ Jiāng Jūn
with the posthumous name Xiāng Zǐ.
All the mountains in Guǎng Zhōu were inhabited by the Lí and Láo peoples,
whose numbers were vast and thriving.
They had frequently committed invasions and depredations throughout history,
causing suffering to successive generations.
During the Dà Míng reign of Shì Zǔ,
Chén Bù, a grand commander from Hé Pǔ, surrendered
and was appointed Lóng Xiáng Jiāng Jūn.
In the fourth year,
Bù submitted a memorial requesting imperial troops to campaign against those who had not yet submitted.
Thereupon, Bù was made Prefect of Gāo Xìng,
his general title remaining as before.
Fèi Shěn, the former Prefect of Zhū Tí, and Wǔ Qī, the Lóng Xiáng Jiāng Jūn, were dispatched to lead troops in a southern expedition,
and also to open a path to Zhū Yá.
They achieved nothing.
They then killed Bù and returned.
Shěn was imprisoned and died.
Fú Nán Kingdom.
In the eleventh, twelfth, and fifteenth years of Tài Zǔ's Yuán Jiā reign,
Chí Lí Bá Mó, the King, sent envoys to present tribute.
Hē Luó Kingdom, a southwestern barbarian state.
In the seventh year of Yuán Jiā,
it sent envoys to present a memorial, which stated: We humbly acknowledge that the Sacred Lord
deeply reveres the Three Jewels,
establishing stupas and monasteries
that fill the entire country.
The cities and outer walls are grand,
pure and undefiled.
The four main roads are interconnected,
broad
and flat.
Palaces and halls are arrayed,
resembling many mountains,
magnificent and subtle,
like a heavenly palace.
When the Sacred King goes out,
the four armies are fully equipped,
with countless escorts
serving
as guards.
The people of the capital, men and women,
wear beautiful clothes and splendid adornments.
Markets are abundant,
with immeasurable treasures.
The royal law is pure and orderly,
with no mutual plunder.
Students gather,
the Three Vehicles compete in advancement,
expounding the True Dharma,
like clouds spreading and rain moistening.
The four seas are open to circulation,
myriad nations gather.
The long river is vast and boundless,
pure, deep, and wide,
all living beings
draw upon it,
none can diminish its purity.
Yīn and Yáng are in harmony,
disasters and epidemics do not occur.
Who possesses such beauty?
It is Dà Sòng Yáng Dū,
whose Sacred King is unparalleled,
ruling over the supreme nation.
There is great
Compassion
fosters all beings,
equal forbearance without resentment,
treating enemies and kin as one,
aiding the destitute and relieving the distressed,
accumulating nothing,
illuminating everything
like the brightness of the sun.
All
receive joy,
like the pure moon.
The prime minister and officials are virtuous and good,
the multitude of ministers are chaste and pure,
devotedly serving their lord
with no divergent thoughts.
I humbly believe that the Emperor
is my true lord.
Your subject is the king of the Hēluódān 國, named Jiānkǎi.
I now respectfully bow my head at the feet of the Sagely King.
I only wish that Your Great Majesty
has long known this heart of mine;
it is not merely of today.
Mountains and seas are distant and obstructive,
making it impossible to reach you in person.
Therefore, I now send envoys
to express this sincere devotion.
The two individuals dispatched
are
one named Pílè,
and the other named Pótián,
instructed to reach the feet of the Son of Heaven.
Jiānkǎi is humble and insignificant;
who could possibly know of him?
It is for this reason that I now send these two individuals
to express this humble heart.
Once
this sentiment is realized,
though I die, I shall live.
I look up to Your Great State,
whose frontier defenses are vast and distant.
I am one of those frontier defenders.
May the people and subjects of the Superior State
universally receive your benevolent favor.
I wish for your grace to extend
equally to my servants and subjects.
In earlier times, my country's population was prosperous,
and it was not encroached upon by other states.
Now it has become weak,
and neighboring countries compete in invasion.
I humbly wish, Sagely King,
that you extend your distant protection,
and also allow trade to pass back and forth,
not to be prohibited.
If I find favor in your compassion,
I wish that you would send them back in due time,
so that these various countries
do not
despise
and insult me.
May this also make Your Great Majesty's name widely known:
to support the endangered and rescue the weak is precisely for today.
The two individuals I now send
are of one heart with your subject.
Whatever they convey
is truly
credible.
I wish that you would command Guǎngzhōu to send the ships back in due course,
and not permit any local authorities to oppress or seize anything.
I wish that from now on,
I may be granted to send envoys annually.
I now present humble gifts;
I wish that you would graciously accept them.
The independent state of Hēluódān is governed from Zhézhōuwā Zhōu.
In the seventh year of Yuánjiā,
it sent envoys to present a diamond ring, a red parrot, white cotton from Tiānzhúguó, and cotton from Yèbōguó, among other items.
In the tenth year,
Píshābámó, King of Hēluódān, presented a memorial saying: To His Majesty, the Ever-Victorious Son of Heaven: The Buddhas, World Honored Ones,
are always at ease and tranquility,
possessing the three clear insights and six divine powers,
serving as a path for the world.
This is called Tathāgata,
Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened One.
They leave behind physical relics
and construct various stupas and images,
adorning their lands
like Mount Xūmí.
Villages and settlements
are arranged in sequence,
cities and palaces
are like the palaces
of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
The palaces are high and vast,
their towers and pavilions adorned.
The four divisions of the army are complete,
capable of subduing enemies.
The land is rich and joyful,
free from all calamities.
Following the former kings,
ruling
and transforming with the Dharma,
the people are good and kind,
celebrating all good fortune.
Dwelling in the shade of the snowy mountains,
with snowmelt flowing,
a hundred rivers overflow,
pure with eight tastes,
winding and curving all around,
flowing
towards the great sea.
All sentient beings
receive and use them.
Among all lands,
it is uniquely supreme and first;
this is called Zhèndàn,
the great Sòng Dynasty's Yángdū.
Inheriting the legacy
of the Ever-Victorious Great King,
your virtue accords with the will of Heaven,
your benevolence shelters the four seas.
Your sagely wisdom is complete,
and all transformations are obedient.
Though human, you are heavenly,
a protector of the world descended to life,
a treasure store of merit and virtue,
with great compassion
saving the world.
You are my esteemed lord, the Ever-Victorious Son of Heaven.
Therefore, I sincerely perform the five-limbed prostration.
Píshābámó, King of Hēluódān, bows his head and offers greetings.
After this, he was usurped by his son.
In the thirteenth year,
he again presented a memorial saying: To Your Great Auspicious Majesty, Son of Heaven: You have departed from lust, anger, and delusion,
pitying all sentient beings.
Your excellent marks are complete;
devas, nāgas, gods, and others
respectfully make offerings to you.
The World Honored One's majestic virtue,
the light radiating from your body,
is like the moon in water,
like the rising sun.
The white urna between your brows
shines universally in the ten directions;
its whiteness is like snow,
and also like moonlight,
pure like a
flower,
your countenance radiant,
your dignified deportment supremely excellent.
You are revered by all devas, nāgas, and gods,
who adorn the land
with the precious Dharma,
and the pure monastic community.
The people are
prosperous,
peaceful, and joyful.
The city walls are high and precipitous,
like Mount Gandhā.
Numerous brave warriors
guard this city.
The towers and pavilions are adorned,
the streets and alleys are flat and straight.
Wearing various
garments,
they are like heavenly robes.
Among all countries,
it is the most excellent and auspicious.
The sorrow-free heavenly lord of Yángzhōu City
commiserates with all sentient beings,
bringing peace and joy to the people.
Your moral conduct
is pure,
your compassionate heart profound and vast.
You govern and transform with the correct Dharma,
jointly nourishing the Three Jewels.
Your reputation reaches far,
heard by all.
The people delight in seeing you,
like the rising moon.
You are like
Brahmā,
lord of the world,
revered and worshipped by all humans and devas.
Hēluódānbámó prostrates with his crown touching your feet,
as if present before you,
spreading his body upon the ground
like a path on the palace steps,
offering worship and reverence
as if serving the World Honored One,
touching his crown to the ground,
bowing and sending greetings.
I unworthily inherited the former legacy,
with immeasurable joy and good fortune,
but was suddenly contested and seized by an wicked son,
and thus lost my original country.
Now I wholeheartedly take refuge
in the Son of Heaven,
to preserve myself.
decree.
Now I send Píyùn to inquire about Dàjiā.
I wished to go myself,
to offer my sincerity and express my grievances,
but I feared the vast ocean,

That my life is preserved today
is also due to
Píyùn’s loyalty and devotion;
his kindness is hard to repay.
This is Dàjiā’s country,
but it has now been seized by evil sons,
and I have been driven out and banished.
I am quite indignant and resentful,
and plan to
recover it.
I humbly beg Dàjiā to allow Píyùn to purchase various armor, weapons, robes, jackets, and horses,
and to kindly arrange for Píyùn to return promptly.

hē.
I received generous gifts from Dàjiā,

I inform Dàjiā so that you may know.
Now I present a small offering;
please condescend to accept it.
After this, another envoy will be sent.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Tàizǔ issued an edict saying:
“The three countries of Hēluódān, Póhuáng, and Pódá
have repeatedly crossed the distant seas,
offering allegiance and tribute.
Their distant sincerity should be recognized;
they may all be granted additional appointments.”
So an envoy was sent to confer titles upon them, saying:
“You have admired righteousness and offered allegiance,
showing sincerity from distant lands.
Wherever imperial grace extends,
the especially distant must be recognized.
Thus, in accordance with the regulations,
this conferral of titles is made manifest.
May you reverently receive this solemn decree,
and forever secure your office.
How can you not be cautious?”
In the twenty-ninth year,
Chángshǐ Póhéshāmí was again sent to present local products.
Póhuáng (Pāhang) kingdom.
In the twenty-sixth year of Yuánjiā,
King Shèlìpóluóbámó sent envoys to present forty-one types of local products.
Tàizǔ conferred a title upon him as the King of Póhuáng, saying:
“You, from a border city,
have looked up to the government and brought tribute to the court.
Imperial benevolence covers all,
leaving no obscurity untouched.
It is proper to issue this directive
and bestow this auspicious decree.
May you respectfully follow the rites and norms,
and maintain your integrity to the end.
How can you not be cautious?”
In the twenty-eighth year,
he again presented tribute.
In the third year of Xiàojiàn of Shìzǔ,
Chángshǐ Zhúnàpózhì was again sent to present a memorial and local products.
Nàpózhì was appointed Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn.
In the third year of Dàmíng,
red and white parrots were presented.
In the eighth year of Dàmíng and the second year of Tàishǐ of Tàizōng,
envoys were again sent to present tribute.
Tàizōng appointed his Chángshǐ Zhúsūluódá and former Chángshǐ, Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn Zhúnàpózhì, both as Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn.
Pódá (Pattani) kingdom.
In the twenty-sixth year of Yuánjiā,
King Shèlìbùlíngqiébámó sent envoys to present local products.
Tàizǔ conferred a title upon him as the King of Pódá, saying:
“You have admired our civilization and cherished sincerity,
eagerly desiring our renown and teachings.
The imperial influence has reached afar,
and distant regions come to offer allegiance.
Therefore, this manifest decree is added,
to recognize your righteousness and obedience.
May you respectfully follow the laws and regulations,
and forever maintain good fortune.
How can you not be cautious?”
In the twenty-sixth and twenty-eighth years,
envoys were again sent to present local products.
Shévópódá (Java) kingdom.
In the twelfth year of Yuánjiā,
King Shīlípódá Āluóbámó sent an envoy with a memorial that read:
“To His Majesty, the Great Lord and Auspicious Son of Heaven of the Sòng (Song) state: I respectfully bow to the All-Knowing and Tranquil,
Teacher of Gods and Humans, who subdued the four Māras,
achieved perfect enlightenment,
turned the noble Dharma
wheel,
delivered all sentient beings,
and after completing his teachings,
entered Nirvāṇa.
His relics are scattered,
and countless stūpas are erected,
adorned with all precious jewels,
like Mount Sūmí.
The sūtras and Dharma are spread,
like the illumination of the sun.
Innumerable pure monks
are like the constellations.
The country’s territory is vast,
its people numerous.
Its palaces and cities
are like the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
The name
of the Great Sòng, the great state of Yángzhōu (Yangzhou), the Auspicious Son of Heaven,
resides therein,
succeeding the former sages,
ruling over the Four Seas.
Within Jambudvīpa,
none do not come to submit.
All receive
this water
and drink it universally.
Although I am distant,
I also partake of its spiritual moisture.
Therefore, though separated by a vast sea,
I always remain a distant subject.
May you recognize my utmost sincerity,
and mercifully accept me.
If I receive your permission,
I will send envoys that very year.
If there is anything you require,
I shall offer only what you command.
I humbly pray you trust and accept this,
and not entertain other thoughts.
Now I send the chief envoy Fódàpó
and deputy envoy Gédǐ to express my humble sincerity.
I prostrate myself in respectful homage to His Majesty, the Auspicious Son of Heaven.
I pray you trust and accept what Pódá (Bada) has presented,
and for all his requests,
I humbly wish you would
grant them.
Now I present a small gift
to express my humble heart.”
Shīzi (Sri Lanka) kingdom.
In the fifth year of Yuánjiā,
King Shālìmóhénán presented a memorial that read:
“To the Enlightened Lord of the Great Sòng, respectfully:
Although mountains and seas vastly separate us,
communications are exchanged in due course.
I humbly learned that Your Majesty’s virtue and morality are exalted and profound,
your encompassing and supporting power is like that of heaven and earth,
your illuminating
brilliance rivals that of the sun and moon.
Beyond the Four Seas,
there is nowhere your might does not prevail.
Kings of all lands
all send envoys to offer tribute,
to express their sincere allegiance to your virtue.
Some sail the seas for three
years,
or travel overland for a thousand days.
Fearing your might and cherishing your virtue,
none, however distant, fail to arrive.
Since the time of my former kings,
we have only considered cultivating virtue as governance,
ruling without severity.
We serve the Three
Treasures,
and the Dao benefits the world.
We rejoice when people do good,
as if it were our own fortune.
We wish to jointly spread the righteous Dharma with Your Majesty,
to save those difficult to convert.
Therefore, I entrusted four renunciants and sent two
laymen to deliver an ivory altar image as a pledge.
When the envoy returns,
I pray you condescend to send word.”
By the twelfth year,
envoys were again sent to present tribute.
Tiānzhú Jiāpílǐ (Kapilavastu) kingdom.
In the fifth year of Yuánjiā,
King Yuè’ài sent an envoy with a memorial that read:
“I humbly hear that your country
is situated by rivers and borders the sea,
with mountains and rivers providing strong defenses.
All wonders are completely present,
adorned and pure,
like an illusory city.
Palaces are magnificent,
streets and alleys
are flat.
The populace is abundant,
joyful and at peace.
When the sagely king goes out,
the Four Seas follow.
Sagely enlightened and benevolent,
he harms no living beings.
All nations look up to him,
and the country
Fù Rúhǎi.
The living beings of the nation
revere and follow the correct Dharma.
The great king is benevolent and sagely,
transforming them with the Way,
bestowing compassion upon all living beings,
without omission or regret.
The Emperor cultivates pure precepts,
though his path does not reach
the supreme Dharma-ship
that saves all those submerged and drowning.
All officials and courtiers
receive joy without resentment.
All devas protect him,
and myriad spirits attend and guard him.
Even heavenly māras are subdued;
none do not submit and transform.
The King's body is upright and majestic,
like the rising sun.
His benevolent grace universally moistens,

Sages and worthies inherit his work,

In that Zhēndān,
he is most exceptional.
The place where your servant resides
is named Jiāpíhé.
Its eastern boundary is the sea.
The four sides of its city
are all of purple-blue jade stone.
Shǒuluó Tiān protects it,
keeping the nation safe and secure.
The kings
have succeeded one another

The people of the nation
mostly cultivate goodness.
States gather from all around

All monasteries and pagodas
have images made of the seven treasures,
and all
marvelous offerings,
as per the law of the former kings.
Your servant self-regulates
and does not violate the prohibitions of the Dao.
Your servant's name is Yuè’ài,
a king's descendant who has forsaken the world.
I only wish that the great king's sacred body be well and peaceful,
and that all ministers and officials
be safe and secure.
Now, with this nation, its ministers, officials, and people,
its mountains, rivers, and treasures,
I completely pledge
allegiance,
prostrating my five limbs with utmost sincerity at the feet of the great king.
Mountains and seas separate us far,
leaving no means to pay court.
My utmost veneration
has led me to dispatch an envoy to submit to you.
The envoy's chief's father's name is Tiānmó Xīdá;
the envoy's chief's name is Nídá.
This person has always been good, loyal, and trustworthy;
this is why I now send him as an envoy to express my sincerity.
If the great king has any needs,
rare and exotic
items,
they shall all be respectfully sent.
This territory

The king's laws and decrees,
and the good ways of governing the nation,

I wish for the envoys of our two nations to travel back and forth

When this returning envoy comes back,
I wish for you to grant me one envoy

My sincerity is profound;
I hope it will not be in vain.
What I have stated is thus;
I wish
for your compassion.
I respectfully present a Vajra finger-ring, a Mólè gold ring, various treasures, and one red and one white parrot.
In the second year of Tàizōng Tàishǐ,
an envoy was again dispatched to offer tribute.
Their envoys Zhúfú Dà and Zhú Āmí were both appointed Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn.
In the eighteenth year of Yuánjiā,
Nàlín Nàluóbāmó, the king of Suōmólí Guó, sent an envoy to present local products.
In the second year of Shìzǔ Xiàojiàn,
Shìpólúonàlín, the king of Jīnlì Guó, sent his Grand Scribe Zhú Liú and others to offer many gold and silver precious vessels.
Later, in the first year of Fèidì Yuánhuī,
Bólí Guó sent an envoy to offer tribute.
All these nations
adhered to the Buddhadharma.
The Buddhadharma, from the time of Hòu Hàn Míngdì,
first flowed eastward.
From this time onward,
its teachings gradually spread.
From emperors to commoners,
none did not turn their hearts to it.
Sūtras and exhortations accumulated,
their teachings profound and far-reaching,
forming a distinct school of learning.
In the twelfth year of Yuánjiā,
Dānyáng Yǐn Xiāo Mózhī memorialized, saying:
"Buddhist teachings have spread throughout Zhōngguó
for four dynasties now.
Images, stupas, and temples
number in the thousands everywhere.
They can serve to fix the mind
and are sufficient to attract and encourage.
However, in recent times,
reverence has become superficial;
they do not consider sincerity to be paramount,
but rather emphasize extravagance and competition.
Old structures lie dilapidated,
never repaired,
while everyone strives to build new ones
to show off to each other.
Fine residences and prominent dwellings
are almost exhausted for this.
Timber, bamboo, bronze, and colored silks
are wasted without limit.
This has no bearing on the deities,
but burdens human affairs.
Exceeding regulations in construction
should be curtailed and checked.
If no precautions are taken,
this trend will not cease.
I request that from now on,
anyone wishing to cast bronze images
must all report themselves to the Bureau;
for constructing stupas, temples, and monasteries,
they must all first go to the local Èrqiānshí to inform them;
the prefecture will then report the matter to the relevant province;
after permission is granted,
they may proceed with the work.
Those who build temples and pagodas without authorization
shall all be punished according to the laws for disobeying imperial edicts.
Bronze residences and forested gardens
shall all be confiscated by the state."
The emperor approved the decree.
Furthermore, monks were screened and culled,
and several hundred were defrocked.
In the second year of Shìzǔ Dàmíng,
a Daoist monk named Tán Biāo conspired with the Qiāng people's Gāo Shé to rebel.
The Emperor then issued an edict, saying:
"The Buddhadharma has become corrupted and altered,
and the community of monks is mixed.
They are insufficient to uphold the grand teachings,
but instead solely become a refuge for fugitives.
Moreover, their wicked intentions frequently arise,
and their heinous acts are often heard of,
corrupting customs,
incurring resentment from both humans and spirits.
They should be handed over to their respective localities
for thorough screening and culling.
If there are future violations,
severe punishment shall be imposed."
Thus, various regulations were established.
Unless one's precepts and practices were truly strict and arduous,
they were all compelled to return to lay life.
However, since nuns from various temples frequently entered and exited the palace,
and associated with consorts and empresses,
this regulation ultimately could not be enforced.
Formerly, in the Jìn dynasty, Yǔ Bīng first proposed
that Buddhist monastics should pay homage to the ruler.
Later, Huán Xuán reiterated this idea,
but neither proposal was implemented.
In the sixth year of Dàmíng (462 CE),
Shìzǔ ordered the appropriate officials to submit a memorial, saying:
"Your ministers have heard that lofty residences and grand dwellings
are not merely for their impressive height,
and kneeling and bowing
are not solely for respect and reverence.
They are meant to extend the four cardinal principles
and establish order throughout the realm.
Therefore, although Confucianism and Legalism are separate branches,
and the schools of Míng (Logicians) and Mò (Mohism) have distinct divisions,
when it comes to honoring one's parents and respecting one's superiors,
their fundamental principles are consistent.
Only the teachings of Fútú (Buddhism),
which originated far away in Lóngduī,
reverse traditional doctrines and circulate different transmissions.
They instruct on distant matters and serve remote causes,
refining life and purifying consciousness.
The common saying is 'difficult.'
Their original tenets are long lost,
and their subtle words are obscured and isolated.
Adhering rigidly to texts and obscuring the Way
has become increasingly prevalent in later times.
Consequently, they overstep rites and standards,
and proudly disregard esteemed relatives.
They lose the subtle path of adapting to circumstances
and are confused about the profound meaning of governance and transformation.
The Dharma teaches humility and self-restraint,
and loyalty and piety are its Way.
Monks do not slight bhikṣus;
they bow when they encounter people.
Mùlián, as a śramaṇa,
paid respects when he met elders.
How can one bend the knee to the four assemblies (bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās)
yet disregard the rites due to one's parents,
or prostrate oneself before the aged and venerable
yet remain unbending before the Son of Heaven?
Therefore, the proposal was first made in Xiánkāng,
and reiterated in Yuánxīng,
but the matter was hindered by partisan factions,
and the Way was thwarted by extraneous divisions.
Now, the great source has been cleansed from afar,
and all streams reflect it from below.
Nine immortals offer treasures,
and a hundred deities rise to their duties.
Yet, within the capital,
there are subjects who do not serve,
and within the imperial court,
guests who stand as equals.
We fear this is not the way to unify the moral standards
and clearly demonstrate exemplary rules.
Your ministers have deliberated
and believe that when Buddhist monastics meet officials,
they should fully perform the rites of reverence and respect,
following their original customs.
Then, the court will have order,
and the Way will be fully achieved in all directions."
The emperor decreed it acceptable.
At the beginning of the reign of the Former Deposed Emperor,
the old custom was restored.
Shìzǔ's favored consort, Consort Yīn Guìfēi, died,
and he established a monastery for her.
Guìfēi's son Zǐluán was enfeoffed as Xīn'ān Wáng,
so the monastery was named Xīn'ān Monastery.
The Former Deposed Emperor killed Zǐluán,
and then destroyed and abolished Xīn'ān Monastery,
expelling the monastics.
Soon after, he also destroyed Zhōngxīng and Tiānbǎo Monasteries.
When Tàizōng quelled the rebellion,
he issued an edict saying:
"The late emperor established Zhōngxīng and Xīn'ān Monasteries
to set a lasting example for future generations and widely promote the flourishing transformation.
Recently, due to a cruel and muddled reign,
the Dharma images were desecrated and destroyed,
and the monastic community scattered and fled.
This causes great pity.
The subtle teachings and profound wisdom
uphold the renowned doctrine.
Therefore, all former monastics may be invited and gathered
to return to their original places,
and craftsmen shall be dispatched
to repair them as appropriate."
Among the famous monks of the Sòng dynasty was Dàoshēng.
Dàoshēng
was a native of Péngchéng.
His father was the magistrate of Guǎngqī.
He was intelligent and perceptive from a young age.
At fifteen,
he was already able to lecture on sūtras.
As he grew older, he developed unique insights
and established the doctrine of sudden enlightenment.
People of his time admired and respected him.
In the eleventh year of Yuánjiā (434 CE),
he died on Mount Lú.
The śramaṇa Huìlín composed a eulogy for him.
Huìlín
was a native of Qín County, Qín Prefecture,
with the surname Liú.
He became a monk in his youth
and resided in Yěchéng Monastery.
He possessed literary talent
and studied both secular and Buddhist teachings.
He was appreciated by Yìzhēn, Prince of Lúlín.
He once authored the Jūnshàn Lùn (Treatise on Universal Goodness).
Its text says:
There was a scholar of "White Learning" (Confucianism) who said,
"The sages of China
have managed affairs for a hundred generations;
their virtue is profound.
Their wisdom encompasses myriad changes;
the principles of heaven and humanity are complete.
The Way has no
hidden aims,
and the teachings leave no snares unlaid.
The intelligent and wise follow the path of wisdom;
how could they be inferior to foreign doctrines?"
There was a Daoist of "Black Learning" (Buddhism) who scorned him,
saying, "He does not illuminate the path of the dark and obscure,
nor does he reach
the transformation of future lives.
Although he esteems an empty mind,
he cannot empty things.
He does not attain the profundity of the Western Regions."
Thereupon, the White Scholar asked why he was considered inferior.
The White Scholar said:
"Is the emptiness discussed by the Śākya clan
different from the emptiness spoken of by the Lǎo clan
or not?"
The Black Scholar replied:
"They are different.
The Śākya clan realizes emptiness through things,
unifying emptiness and things.
The Lǎo clan holds existence and non-existence as two separate paths;
emptiness and existence are different.
How can they be the same?"
The White Scholar said:
"If the Śākya clan empties things,
are things truly empty?"
The Black
Scholar replied:
"Indeed.
If emptiness is also empty,
it is more than just empty."
The White Scholar said:
"The three cosmic powers (heaven, earth, humanity) are spiritually superior in the universe,
and myriad beings fill heaven and earth.
Which of these is empty
then?"
The Black Scholar replied:
"It empties the inherent existence of their own nature,
but does not harm their dependently arisen forms.
Now, one constructs many timbers to form a grand mansion,
but it lacks the reality of a dedicated dwelling.
One accumulates a single
hair to reach a huge circumference,
but there is no solid wood.
No living being remains for a moment,
and Mount Tài has no permanence that lasts even a breath.
Rise and fall are impermanent;
causes and conditions have no master.
That which is
empty lies in the inherent nature and principle,
that which is difficult to grasp lies in practical application.
I think you are mistaken."
The White Scholar said:
"Are the true forms you speak of
empty in this manner?"
The Black Scholar
replied:
"Indeed."
The White Scholar said:
"The principle of constant change
is apparent before our eyes.
Is this understood by all who see and hear?
To explain this to attain the bodhimaṇḍa,
and to emphasize it by slighting other
schools,
I truly do not see its profundity."
The Black Scholar replied:
"This principle may seem near,
but seeking it is truly distant.
That which emotion values is empty;
that which affairs can value is real.
Now, by emptying the real and true,
and separating from the floating and false,
the delusions of love and desire
must disappear.
If love disappears yet the bodhimaṇḍa is not attained,
I do not know how to enlighten
you."
The White Scholar said:
"Now, if one analyzes a hair and empties a tree,
there is no luxuriant shade from the hanging branches.
If one separates timbers and empties a room,
it does not diminish the beauty of its structure.
To clarify impermanence increases one's yearning for shade,
feelings.
Chén Ruò (陳若) is perhaps overly devoted to contemplating the competitive and transient nature of time.
Bèijǐn (貝錦) glows with its vibrant colors;
harmonious soup achieves its flavor with salt and sour plums.
Qí Hóu (齊侯) pursued the joy of the shuǎngjiū (爽鳩);
the King
of Yān (燕) had no art for prolonging life.
I fear that the arguments for harmony and union,
and the teachings on fragility,
are precisely sufficient to make one cling to the desires of their inclinations,
and cannot overturn the delusion of love and competition.”
Hēi (黑)
said:
“This principle is indeed peerless among the various Huá (華),
and cannot be surpassed by even the most ancient texts.”
Bái (白) said:
“Phrases about mountains accumulating from low places,
verses about rivers and trees growing from small beginnings,
discussions of boats in ravines and fire
passing through,
and debates on 'hard and white' and 'Tang's market' –
these indeed abound in Zhōngguó (中國).
They are not profound principles,
hence they are not taken as the basis of teaching.
You indeed take relinquishing feelings and
burdens,
and emptying the mind as the Way,
yet your analysis based on facts
still seems to be within the palm of your hand.”
Hēi (黑) said:
“The teachings of Zhōu (周) and Kǒng (孔) [Confucius]
only benefited one generation,
they did not foresee the endless connections of future
lives.
Accumulating good deeds merely leads to blessings for descendants;
accumulating evil merely results in punishment for lingering calamities.
Rewards for service stop at honor and emoluments;
punishments for transgressions end at poverty and lowliness.
Beyond what is seen and heard,
they are utterly ignorant,
which is truly lamentable.
Shìjiā (釋迦) [Buddha] addressed the karma of endless cycles,
removed the dangers of multiple barriers,
