refined the thoughts within the square inch [of the mind].
The universe is not
enough to fill his brightness;
he established a compassionate salvation,
and all living beings are not enough to exhaust his transformation.
With hell, people fear their sins;
with the proclamation of heaven, beings rejoice in their blessings.
He pointed
to Níhuán (泥洹) [Nirvāṇa] as the eternal return,
and ascended the Fǎshēn (法身) [Dharmakāya] to gaze afar.
Divine transformations are all-pervasive,
spiritual grace extends everywhere.
Early awakened ones soar in the upper world;
later enlightened ones ascend and
do not inherit [the legacy in the same way].
How can the narrow confines of a well
understand the master of the great Way?”
Bái (白) said:
“Indeed, you speak grandly!
But now, if we test divine light, it has not even an inch of brightness;
if we verify
spiritual transformations, there is no slightest difference.
Diligent devotees do not perceive the form of good salvation;
ardent scholars cannot achieve the reality of soaring through the void.
They merely speak of immeasurable lifespan,
but who has seen a centenarian
old man?
They sigh at the solidity of Jīngāng (金剛) [Vajra],
but where is the indestructible substance to be found?
If it does not conform to facts,
one should seek the meaning of the words,
and abandon the theory of what they represent
as their basis.
Moreover, if one seeks heaven to do good,
how is that better than embracing righteousness and treading the Way?
If one fears hell to discipline oneself,
how is that comparable to following reason to rectify the mind?
Praying to seek
forgiveness of sins
does not stem from a reverent attitude;
giving one to gain a hundredfold
is not driven by a generous spirit.
Praising the joys of Níhuán (泥洹) [Nirvāṇa]
gives rise to thoughts of self-indulgence;
extolling the wonders of the Fǎshēn (法身) [Dharmakāya]
initiates a heart of curiosity.
Immediate desires are not yet quelled,
and distant gains arise again.
Although it is said that Bodhisattvas are without desire,
all living beings still have desires.
It merely saves people
who are already suffering
and permanently opens up a custom of seeking profit and competition.
To purify the spirit and turn back to the Way,
how can that be achieved?”
Hēi (黑) said:
“Not so.
If one does not show them the desires of future lives,
how can one weigh
their attachments in this life?
Human emotions cannot instantly reach perfection,
hence they are gradually enticed.
To give up this brief moment
and seek that which is endless –
if one is not diligent in spring planting,
how can one expect
an autumn harvest?
Those who sit idly at the bottom of a well
and cease all worldly thoughts
will forever sink beneath the nine springs.”
Bái (白) said:
“Strange!
How misguided are your objectives!
The Way lies in being without desire,
yet you try to attract people to it with desires.
This is like going north to seek Yǐng (郢),
or campaigning west to find Yuè (越).
You will only wander lost in Yōudū (幽都) [the underworld]
and be forever mired in Méigǔ (昧谷) [the Valley of Darkness].
Can the distant
Mǐn (閩) and Chǔ (楚) [regions]
be seen?
What is meant by 'gradual accumulation'
is 'daily diminishing.'
One should first discard what is less important,
then forget what is weighty,
so that desires for gain
daily decrease,
and pure simplicity naturally arises.
How can one exchange the subtle for the coarse,
or the small for the great?
In the blink of an eye,
nothing moves without profit.
Where profit sways,
is there any limit
to it?
Then, paintings and vibrant colors dazzle the eyes,
earth and wood glorify the ambitious heart.
They give rise to a path of extravagance,
deplete the wealth of the nine regions,
establish useless enterprises,
cut off
the urgent needs of all living beings,
devise construction plans,
establish private power,
engage in the work of conversion,
form factions and cliques.
They practice asceticism to gain a reputation for strict diligence,
and protect
the Dharma to fulfill feelings of dominance and competition.
Alas!
Where then does the Way reside?
This is why Zhōu (周) and Kǒng (孔) [Confucius] strengthened customs,
without concerning themselves with what is beyond sight and hearing.
Lǎo (老) and Zhuāng (莊) cultivated the spirit,
merely keeping to their inherent nature.”
Hēi (黑) said:
“The 'three wanderings' originated from benevolence and righteousness,
and Dào Zhí (盜跖) benefited from the five virtues.
Is there any distinction of internal or external [corruption] in the failings of the Sages' traces?
Moreover,
among the followers of Huáng (黃) and Lǎo (老),
the falsity of talismans and chapters,
and the deceit of water incantations,
are too numerous to discuss.
You are at ease with them,
but are alarmed by this;
you play in turbid water,
but reject the clear abyss.”
Bái (白)
said:
“That which has traces cannot but be flawed;
that which has methods cannot be without deceit.
This is why the Sages are shackled.
What is lamentable now is making laws for greed,
thus
forming customs;
instead of correcting their flaws,
they are deemed lofty.
As for the lewd and deluded,
the world itself regards them as base,
their origins and development are insignificant,
and thus not worth discussing.”
Hēi (黑) said:
“Shìshì's (釋氏) [Buddha's] teaching
is specifically to save barbarian customs.
Does it then have no value for the various Huá (華)?”
Bái (白) said:
“Why should that be?
If one creates something, one begins,
and should cherish its continuity.
Love
things, killing;
furthermore, he bestows [favor] upon the people of Zhōu;
he calms his mind and relinquishes the desire for glory and splendor;
the great Sū makes known his thought of universal salvation.
Those for whom benevolence and righteousness are one and the same—
how can they surpass him?
Alas,
the profound meaning is not clear,
and later generations are burdened by it.”
Hēi said,
“Your discussion of goodness is almost the same.
Do affairs end with life?”
Bái said,
“The principles of the netherworld
certainly do not end with human affairs.
Zhōu and Kǒng doubted and did not clarify;
Shìjiā clarified but did not make it real.
It is perhaps appropriate to discard the traces of its manifest and hidden aspects
and preserve its essential
meaning.
Please allow me to try to explain it.
Those who are guided by benevolence and righteousness
conform to principles and follow transformation;
those who are led by exhortation and warning
follow advantage and move towards goodness.
Thus, sweet words
arise from desire,
but cease upon realizing the truth;
plain speech proceeds from natural understanding,
but ends with greed and falsehood.
Therefore, those who present the next life
are obscured and deficient when Dào and Shì
cannot avoid it;
those who block the dark unknowns
are secretly in accord with Jī and Kǒng closing their apertures.
From this perspective,
those who speak of it do not necessarily grasp the distant;
those who know it do not necessarily attain it;
those who do not
know it do not necessarily lose it.
One only needs to know that the Six Pāramitās and the Five Teachings operate in parallel,
and faith and obedience stand alongside compassion.
Those who follow different paths but arrive at the same destination
must not cling to the ruts of their
wheel tracks.”
This discourse circulated in the world.
Old monks claimed it denigrated the Shì clan [Buddhism]
and wanted to expel him.
Tàizǔ saw the discourse, praised him,
and during the Yuánjiā era,
he then participated in important affairs of state.
All major court matters
were discussed with him.
Guests flocked to him,
and dozens of carriages were always at his gate.
Gifts and bribes from all directions were constant,
and his influence was immense at the time.
His commentaries on the Xiàojīng, Zhuāngzǐ’s Xiāoyáo Piān, and Wénlùn
were transmitted in the world.
There were also the Dàorén Huìyán and Huìyì,
both residing at Dōng'ān Sì.
Their scholarship and conduct were excellent,
and they were highly regarded by both monastics and laity.
At that time, Dòuchǎng Sì had many Chan monks.
The capital had a saying about them:
“Dòuchǎng is the Chan master’s grotto,
Dōng'ān is the forest of discussion and righteousness.”
In the fourth year of Shìzǔ’s Dàmíng reign,
a vegetarian feast was held at Zhōngxīng Sì.
There was an extraordinary monk,
whom no one among the assembly recognized.
When asked his name,
he replied his name was Mínghuì,
and he came from Tiān'ān Sì,
then suddenly disappeared.
There was no temple with that name in the world,
so Zhōngxīng Sì was renamed Tiān'ān Sì.
During the Dàmíng era,
the foreign Śramaṇa Móhēyǎn, who practiced asceticism and possessed profound principles,
published many new sūtras in the capital.
The Shènmàn Jīng, in particular, was highly esteemed among inner scholars.
The eastern barbarian Gāogōulí Guó
now governs the Liáodōng Jùn of Hàn.
King Gāo Lián of Gāogōulí,
in the ninth year of Yìxī of Jìn Àndì,
sent the Zhǎngshǐ Gāo Yì to present a memorial and offer a red and white horse.
Lián was appointed Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Yíngzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn, Gāogōulí Wáng, and Lèláng Gōng.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he issued an edict saying:
“Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Yíngzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn, Gāogōulí Wáng, Lèláng Gōng Lián,
and Shǐchíjié, Dū Báijì Zhūjūnshì, Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn, Báijì Wáng Yìng,
both uphold righteousness overseas
and respectfully perform their tribute duties from afar.
As we establish a new beginning,
they should receive national blessings.
Lián is appointed Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn,
and Yìng is appointed Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn.
Their titles of Chíjié, Dūdū, Wáng, and Gōng remain as before.”
Three years later,
Lián was additionally appointed Sànqí Chángshì,
and given increased oversight of Píngzhōu Zhūjūnshì.
In the second year of Shàodì’s Jǐngpíng reign,
Lián sent the Zhǎngshǐ Mǎ Lóu and others to the palace to offer local products,
and an envoy was sent to convey greetings and comfort,
saying:
“The Emperor inquires of Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Yíngpíng Èrzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn, Gāogōulí Wáng, Lèláng Gōng,
who has for generations served with loyalty and righteousness,
and whose meritorious achievements have followed in the footsteps of his predecessors.
His benevolence is manifest,
and his sincerity is evident.
Crossing the Liáo and traversing the sea,
he presents tribute to the imperial court.
I, with my lack of virtue,
unworthily inherited this great legacy.
I always remember the deeds of my predecessors,
and wish to extend their remaining grace.
Now I send the Yèzhě Zhū Shàobó and Vice Yèzhě Wáng Shàozǐ and others
to convey my decree of comfort.
May he flourish in his benevolent governance
and eternally advance his achievements,
thus manifesting the former command
and fulfilling my intentions.”
Prior to this,
the Xiānbēi Mùróng Bǎo governed Zhōngshān,
but was defeated by the Suǒlǔ [Tuòbá] and
fled east to Huánglóng.
In the early Yìxī era,
Bǎo’s younger brother Xī was killed by his subordinate Féng Bá,
who then established himself as ruler,
proclaiming himself Yàn Wáng.
Because he governed Huánglóng Chéng,
his state was called the Huánglóng Guó.
After Bá died,
his son Hóng was enthroned.
〔一一〕He was repeatedly attacked by the Suǒlǔ,
who could not conquer him.
During Tàizǔ’s reign,
Hóng sent envoys annually to offer local products.
In the twelfth year of Yuánjiā,
he was granted additional appointments.
In the fifteenth year,
he was again attacked by the Suǒlǔ.
Hóng was defeated and fled,
escaping to Běifēng Chéng in Gāolí,
and requested a welcome in a memorial.
Tàizǔ sent envoys Wáng Báijū and Zhào Cìxīng to welcome him,
and also ordered Gāolí to arrange for his provisions and departure.
Lián did not want Hóng to go south,
so he sent generals Sūn Sòu and Gāo Chóu and others to ambush and kill him.
Báijū and others led their seven thousand-plus men to attack Sòu and others,
capturing Sòu alive and killing Gāo Chóu and two others.
Lián, asserting that Báijū and others had acted unilaterally in the killings,
sent envoys to arrest and deliver them.
The emperor, considering it a distant country,
did not wish to go against its wishes.
Báijū and others were imprisoned
and later pardoned.
Lián sent envoys every year.
In the sixteenth year,
Tàizǔ wanted to campaign in the north,
and ordered Lián to send horses.
Lián offered eight hundred horses.
In the second year of Shìzǔ’s Xiàojiàn reign,
Lián sent the Zhǎngshǐ Dǒng Téng to present a memorial expressing condolences for the national mourning for two full years,
and also offered local products.
In the third year of Dàmíng,
he again offered húsǐ and shíjiàn from the Sùshèn clan.
In the seventh year,
an edict stated:
“Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dū Píngyíng Èrzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn, Gāogōulí Wáng, Lèláng Gōng Lián,
has for generations served with loyalty and righteousness,
acting as a frontier lord overseas.
His sincerity is tied to the imperial court,
and his ambition is to eliminate treacherous remnants.
He communicates with distant lands
and effectively proclaims royal virtue.
He should be further commended
to honor his pure integrity.
He is appointed Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
while his titles of Chíjié, Chángshì, Dūdū, Wáng, and Gōng remain as before.”
During Tàizōng’s Tàishǐ and the later Fèidì’s Yuánhuī eras,
tribute never ceased.
The Báijì Guó
was originally located with Gāolí over a thousand lǐ east of Liáodōng.
Later, Gāolí occupied Liáodōng,
and Báijì occupied Liáoxī.
The area governed by Báijì
was called Jìnpíng Jùn, Jìnpíng Xiàn.
In the twelfth year of Yìxī (義熙),

Baekje King Yú Yìng (餘映) was appointed as Envoys with Imperial Credentials (使持節), Supervisor-General of All Military Affairs of Baekje (都督百濟諸軍事), General Who Guards the East (鎮東將軍), and King of Baekje (百濟王).
[一二] When Gāozǔ (高祖) ascended the throne,
his title was promoted to Grand General Who Guards the East (鎮東大將軍).
In the second year of Jǐngpíng (景平) under Emperor Shàodì (少帝),
Yìng dispatched his Chief Clerk Zhāng Wēi (張威) to the imperial court with tribute.
In the second year of Yuánjiā (元嘉),
Tàizǔ (太祖) issued an edict to him, saying:
"The Emperor inquires of the Envoys with Imperial Credentials, Supervisor-General of All Military Affairs of Baekje, Grand General Who Guards the East, and King of Baekje.
For generations, you have been loyal and obedient,
crossing the sea to demonstrate sincerity.
As a distant king, you have gathered your people,
diligently continuing your ancestors' endeavors.
Your admiration for righteousness is manifest,
and your heart is filled with genuine devotion.
You float rafts across the Lí River (驪水),
presenting treasures and holding up your ceremonial gifts.
Therefore, you have inherited your position and trust,
to be a藩 (fān) guarding the eastern lands.
Exert yourself in your administration,
so as not to fall short of your predecessors' achievements.
We now send the Acting Herald Lǘqiū Ēnzǐ (閭丘恩子) and Acting Deputy Herald Dīng Jìngzǐ (丁敬子), among others, to convey this imperial decree, expressing Our sentiments and offering慰勞 (wèiláo)."
Thereafter, every year he sent envoys to present memorials
and offer local products.
In the seventh year,
Baekje King Yú Pí (餘毗) resumed his tribute duties,
and Yìng's title was bestowed upon him.
In the twenty-seventh year,
Pí submitted a letter with local products,
privately appointing Fényěfū (馮野夫), an envoy from the court, as Administrator of Xīhé (西河 太守).
He also requested in a memorial the *Yì Lín* (易林), *Shì Zhàn* (式占), and waist crossbows.
Tàizǔ (太祖) granted all of them.
After Pí died,
his son Qìng (慶) succeeded him.
In the first year of Dàmíng (大明) under Shìzǔ (世祖),
he sent an envoy to request appointments,
which was granted by imperial edict.
In the second year,
Qìng sent an envoy to present a memorial, stating:
"My kingdom, for generations,
has received extraordinary imperial grace.
Excellent civil and military advisors
have for generations received court titles.
Yú Jì (餘紀), Acting General Who Champions the Army (行冠軍將軍) and Right Worthy King (右賢王), and eleven others
are loyal and diligent, and should be promoted.
I humbly pray for your compassion,
and that they all be granted appointments."
Thereupon, Yú Jì (餘紀), Acting General Who Champions the Army and Right Worthy King, was made General Who Champions the Army (冠軍將軍).
Yú Kūn (餘昆), Acting General Who Subdues Barbarians (行征虜將軍) and Left Worthy King (左賢王), and Yú Yùn (餘暈), Acting General Who Subdues Barbarians, were both made General Who Subdues Barbarians (征虜將軍).
Yú Dū (餘都) and Yú Ài (餘乂), both Acting General Who Assists the State (行輔國將軍), were both made General Who Assists the State (輔國將軍).
Mù Jīn (沐衿) and Yú Jué (餘爵), both Acting General Who Soars Like a Dragon (行龍驤將軍), were both made General Who Soars Like a Dragon (龍驤將軍).
Yú Liú (餘流) and Mí Guì (麋貴), both Acting General Who Pacifies the North (行寧朔將軍), were both made General Who Pacifies the North (寧朔將軍).
Yú Xī (于西) and Yú Lóu (餘婁), both Acting General Who Establishes Might (行建武將軍), were both made General Who Establishes Might (建武將軍).
In the seventh year of Tàishǐ (泰始) under Tàizōng (太宗),
he again sent an envoy with tribute.
The country of Wō (倭) is in the great sea southeast of Gāolì (高驪).
For generations, it has rendered tribute.
In the second year of Yǒngchū (永初) under Gāozǔ (高祖),
an edict stated:
"Wō Zàn (倭讚) has traveled ten thousand *lǐ* (里) to present tribute.
His distant sincerity should be recognized,
and he may be granted appointments."
In the second year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) under Tàizǔ (太祖),
Zàn (讚) again sent his Chief Clerk Cáo Dá (曹達) with a memorial and local products.
After Zàn died,
his younger brother Zhēn (珍) succeeded him
and sent an envoy with tribute.

He styled himself Envoys with Imperial Credentials, Supervisor-General of All Military Affairs of Wō (倭), Baekje (百濟), Sīnxīluó (新羅), Rènnà (任那), Jiāluó (加羅), Qínhán (秦韓), and Mùhán (慕韓) — six countries in total, Grand General Who Pacifies the East (安東大將軍), and King of Wō (倭國王).
He submitted a memorial requesting official appointments,
and an edict appointed him General Who Pacifies the East (安東將軍) and King of Wō.

Zhēn (珍) also requested official appointments for Wō Suí (倭隋) and thirteen others with the titles of General Who Pacifies the West (平西將軍), General Who Subdues Barbarians, General Who Champions the Army, and General Who Assists the State.
The edict granted them all.
In the twentieth year,
Wō King Jì (濟) sent an envoy with tribute,
and was again appointed General Who Pacifies the East and King of Wō.
In the twenty-eighth year,
he was additionally granted the title of Envoys with Imperial Credentials, Supervisor-General of All Military Affairs of Wō, Sīnxīluó, Rènnà, Jiāluó, Qínhán, and Mùhán — six countries in total,
while General Who Pacifies the East remained as before.
And the twenty-three military and commandery titles he requested were granted.
After Jì died,
his heir Xīng (興) sent an envoy with tribute.
In the sixth year of Dàmíng (大明) under Shìzǔ (世祖),
an edict stated:
"Wō King's heir Xīng,
for generations has been loyal,
serving as a藩 (fān) in the outer seas,
embracing transformation and pacifying his territory,
reverently performing his tribute duties.
Having newly inherited the frontier enterprise,
he should be granted a noble title.
He may be appointed General Who Pacifies the East and King of Wō."
After Xīng died,
his younger brother Wǔ (武) succeeded him,

styling himself Envoys with Imperial Credentials, Supervisor-General of All Military Affairs of Wō, Baekje, Sīnxīluó, Rènnà, Jiāluó, Qínhán, and Mùhán — seven countries in total, Grand General Who Pacifies the East, and King of Wō.
In the second year of Shēngmíng (昇明) under Shùndì (順帝),
he sent an envoy to present a memorial, stating:
"My enfeoffed state is distant and remote,
serving as a藩 (fān) in the outer regions.
From my ancestors of old,
they personally donned armor and helmets,
traversed mountains and rivers,
never having a moment of peace.
They campaigned eastward against fifty-five countries of the Máorén (毛人),
subdued sixty-six barbarian tribes to the west,
and crossed the sea to pacify ninety-five countries north of the sea.
The royal way was harmonious and tranquil,
expanding the territory to distant borders.
For generations, we have paid homage to the court,
never failing in a single year.
Though I am lowly and foolish,
I am unworthy to inherit the ancestral legacy.
I lead those under my command
to revere and submit to the imperial court.
On the road through Baekje,
[一三] we prepare our ships and boats.
However, Gōulí (句驪) is without principle,
plotting to devour us.
They plunder and raid our border subjects,
and their slaughter never ceases,
constantly causing delays,
thus missing favorable winds.
Though we speak of advancing,
sometimes we succeed, sometimes we do not.
My late father Jì (濟) truly resented the bandit enemies
who blocked the heavenly road.
With a million archers,
and righteous indignation,
he was about to launch a great campaign,
when he suddenly lost his father and brother,
causing his nearly accomplished work
to fall short by a single basketful of earth.
During the period of mourning,
no troops or weapons were moved,
thus the respite brought no victory.
Now I wish to drill my soldiers and train my troops,
to fulfill the aspirations of my father and brother.
Righteous warriors, brave as tigers,
both civil and military officials, will exert their efforts.
With bare blades clashing before them,
they will not flinch.
If by imperial virtue you extend your benevolent sway,
crushing this powerful enemy,
and suppressing these difficult regions,
our previous merits will not be diminished.
I presumptuously grant myself the title of Open-Office with the Same Privileges as the Three Excellencies (開府儀同三司),
and likewise, all others are granted provisional appointments,
[一四] to encourage their loyalty and integrity."

An edict appointed Wǔ (武) as Envoys with Imperial Credentials, Supervisor-General of All Military Affairs of Wō, Sīnxīluó, Rènnà, Jiāluó, Qínhán, and Mùhán — six countries in total, Grand General Who Pacifies the East, and King of Wō.
The Mán (蠻) people of Jīng (荊) and Yōng (雍) provinces
were descendants of Pánhù (槃瓠).
They were divided into various tribes
scattered throughout the commanderies and counties.
Jīng Province established the Southern Mán (南蠻),
and Yōng Province established the Commandant Who Pacifies the Mán (寧蠻校尉) to govern them.
In the early reign of Shìzǔ (世祖),
the Southern Mán office was abolished and merged into the Grand Bureau,
but the Commandant Who Pacifies the Mán remained as before.
For the Mán people who submitted,
each household paid several *hú* (斛) of grain,
but no other miscellaneous taxes.
However, the tax and labor burdens on Sòng (宋) citizens were severe and arduous,
and the poor could no longer bear their lives,
many fleeing to the Mán.
The Mán had no corvée labor,
and the powerful among them did not pay official taxes.
They formed gangs and groups,
often numbering several hundreds or thousands.
When the strength of the provinces and commanderies weakened,
they would rise up as bandits.
Their numbers gradually increased, and their household registrations became unknown.
Their locations were mostly deep and treacherous.
Those residing in Wǔlíng (武陵) included the Xióngxī (雄谿), Mánxī (樠谿), Chénxī (辰谿), Yǒuxī (酉谿), and Wǔxī (舞谿),
[一五] known as the Five Xī Mán (五谿蠻).
The Mán of Yídū (宜都), Tiānmén (天門), Bādōng (巴東), Jiànpíng (建平), and Jiāngběi (江北) commanderies,
all resided in deep mountains and rugged terrain,
where human traces were rare.
Since previous generations,
they had repeatedly caused trouble for the populace.
In the second year of Jǐngpíng of Shàodì,
Shí Níng and 122 other leaders of the Yídū Mán submitted tribute at the imperial court.
In the sixth year of Yuánjiā of Tàizǔ,
Zhāng Yōngzhī and 49 others of the Jiànpíng Mán,
and in the seventh year,
Tián Shēng and 112 others of the Yídū Mán,
all came to the imperial court to offer tribute.
After this, the Miǎnzhōng Mán caused a major disturbance,
and travel became almost impossible.
Zōng Jiǎozhī, the magistrate of Tiānmén Lóuzhōng, imposed excessively heavy labor levies,
〔一六〕which the Mán could not endure.
In the eighteenth year,
Tián Xiàngqiú and other Mán became bandits,
raided Lóuzhōng,
and abducted the common people.
Héngyángwáng Yìjì, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, dispatched Assistant Military Advisor Cáo Sūnniàn to suppress them,
capturing over five hundred people,
and dismissing Jiǎozhī from office.
In the twenty-fourth year,
the Línjǔ Dāngyáng Mán of Nánjùn rebelled,
and captured Fù Sēngjì, the magistrate of Línjǔ.
Nánqiáowáng Yìxuān, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, dispatched Army Middle-Ranking Advisor Wáng Chén to suppress them.
Before this,
Liú Dàochǎn, the Inspector of Yōngzhōu, was skilled at placating the various Mán,
and those who had not previously submitted to the government
all became compliant.
He encouraged them to move out to the flatlands,
many of whom settled along the Miǎn River.
When Dàochǎn died,
the Mán rebelled again.
When Shìzǔ was dispatched to Yōngzhōu,
the various Mán blocked the roads,
but he attacked and thoroughly defeated them.
The imperial court dispatched Military Commander Shěn Qìngzhī to suppress the Mán for successive years,
and wherever he went, he pacified and annihilated them.
The details are in the biography of Qìngzhī.
In the first month of the twenty-eighth year,
the Lóngshān Zhìshuǐ Mán plundered Nièyáng Xiàn.
Zhū Tánsháo, the Grand Administrator of Nányáng, dispatched troops to suppress them,
but they suffered a defeat,
with over three hundred killed or wounded.
Tánsháo then dispatched two thousand more troops to contain them,
and the Mán dispersed and fled.
That year,
the various Mán of Zhìshuǐ became bandits, exploiting the difficult terrain.
Suíwáng Dàn, the Inspector of Yōngzhōu, sent an envoy to persuade them, saying:
"The power of persuasion and conciliation has recently reached far and wide;
those who comply with transformation receive honor and emolument,
while those who defy orders are not spared.
This is something you should also know.
The sagely court is now extending its leniency across the entire realm,
permitting you to reform yourselves.
It is expedient for each of you to return to your old homes,
settle down, and resume your livelihoods.
This is where you should begin to change your ways and reform your hearts. "
Before this,
Lǔ Núzǐ, a Mán leader, had seized Lóngshān,
repeatedly causing border troubles.
When Lǔ Guǐ was in Chángshè,
Núzǐ submitted to him.
Guǐ spoke to the barbarian ruler,
proposing him as the King of the Four Mountains.
When Guǐ's son Shuǎng returned to the state,
Núzǐ also sought to submit.
Suíwáng Dàn also dispatched troops to suppress the various Mán north of the Miǎn River,
raiding the three stockades of Zhuóshān, Rúkǒu, and Shǔsōng.
He conquered them,
and also besieged the stockades of Shēngqián and Báiyì.
〔一七〕The Mán fought with all their might to resist.
The army, using fully armored cavalry, shot arrows from both flanks,
greatly defeating them.
Two hundred heads were severed,
and one thousand Mán were captured,
along with eighty head of cattle and horses.
During the Dàmíng era of Shìzǔ,
Xiàng Guānghóu of the Jiànpíng Mán raided and plundered Xiáchuān.
Wáng Jì, the Grand Administrator of Bādōng, and Zhū Xiūzhī, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, dispatched troops to suppress them.
Guānghóu fled to Qīngjiāng.
Qīngjiāng was over a thousand *lǐ* from Bādōng.
At that time, the Mán of the four commanderies of Bādōng, Jiànpíng, Yídū, and Tiānmén were causing trouble.
The households of the various commanderies were scattered,
with less than one in a hundred remaining.
The situation was even worse during the reigns of Tàizōng and Shùndì.
Although punitive expeditions were sent,
they ultimately could not stop them,
and Jīngzhōu became desolate and impoverished because of it.
During the Dàmíng era,
the Guìyáng Mán rebelled,
killing Yàn Zhēnzhī, the magistrate of Lì Xiàn.
The Línhé Mán rebelled,
killing Xíng Bó'ér, the magistrate of Kāijiàn Xiàn.
〔一八〕Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn Xiāo Chōngzhī suppressed them,
but with little gain and great loss,
he was punished.
The Yùzhōu Mán
were descendants of Lǐnjūn.
The affairs of Pánhù and Lǐnjūn
are both fully detailed in previous histories.
In Xīyáng, there were Bāshuǐ, Qíshuǐ, Xīshuǐ, Chìtíngshuǐ, and Xīguīshuǐ,
which were called the Five Water Mán.
Their settlements were all in deep, rugged terrain,
and their tribes were numerous and prosperous.
They had been bandits for generations.
To the north, they bordered the Huái and Rǔ rivers;
to the south, they reached the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
covering an area of several thousand *lǐ*.
In the twenty-eighth year of Yuánjiā,
the Xīyáng Mán killed Liú Tái, the magistrate of Nánchuān,
along with his entire family.
In the twenty-ninth year,
over two thousand Xīncài Mán
attacked and broke the Dàléi Garrison,
plundering both official and private boats,
and dragging them all into the lake.
There was a fugitive, Sīmǎ Hēishí, among the Mán,
who engaged in banditry with them.
Tàizǔ dispatched Crown Prince Infantry Commandant Shěn Qìngzhī to lead the armies of Jiāng, Jīng, Yōng, and Yù provinces to suppress them.
In the fourth year of Dàmíng of Shìzǔ,
Qìngzhī was again dispatched to suppress the Xīyáng Mán,
achieving a great victory and returning.
Sīmǎ Hēishí had three associates.
One of them was named Zhì.
Hēishí called him
"Tàigōng,"
and made him his chief strategist.
One was named Ānyáng,
and was called Qiáowáng.
One was named Xùzhī,
and was called Liángwáng.
Mán Wén Xiǎoluó and others captured Xùzhī,
〔一九〕but he was usurped by Mán Shìcái.
Xiǎoluó and others then banded together and executed Shìcái and six members of his family.
Wáng Xuánmó, the Inspector of Yùzhōu, dispatched Palace General Guō Yuánfēng to console the various Mán,
and ordered them to bind and deliver the fugitives.
The Mán then seized Zhì Hēishí and Ānyáng and sent them to Xuánmó.
〔二０〕Shìzǔ ordered their execution in Shòuyáng.
When Tàizōng first ascended the throne,
〔二一〕rebels rose up in all directions.
After the southern rebels were defeated at Quèwěi,
Tián Yìzhī, Tián Yìzhī, Chéng Xiécái, Tián Guāngxīng, and others of the Xīyáng Mán rose in revolt and attacked Yǐngzhōu,
conquering it.
Yìzhī was appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
and overall commander of the Four Mountains armies.
〔二二〕Also, the two commanderies of Sòng'ān and Guāngchéng were established from Mán households.
Yìzhī was made Grand Administrator of Sòng'ān,
and Guāngxīng was made Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Guāngchéng.
Yìzhī was enfeoffed as the King of Biānchéng Xiàn,
with an income of 411 households.
Chéng Xiécái was enfeoffed as the King of Yángchéng Xiàn,
with an income of 3,000 households.
Yìzhī was summoned to be Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng,
retaining his generalship.
In the early Shēngmíng era of Shùndì,
he was further transferred to be Shèshēng Xiàowèi and Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
When Chéng Xiécái died,
his son Pósī inherited the title,
and became Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Wǔqí Chángshì.
Méi Shìshēng of the Jìnxī Mán also rose in revolt,
beheading Yán Zhànzhī, the Grand Administrator of Jìnxī, and Shěn Guāngzǔ, Prince Zǐxūn's Supervisor of Documents for Jìn'ān.
〔二三〕He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Gāoshān,
with an income of thirty households from the two villages of Niúgāng and Xiàchái under his command.
The historian says: In the Hàn dynasty, the Western Regions were extensively connected,
with paths spanning tens of thousands of *lǐ*.
They crossed mountains that caused headaches,
traversed dangers that required ropes to measure their depths.
Some went alive, others perished on the way,
bodies journeying, souls returning.
When the Jìn dynasty moved south,
the Yellow River and Lǒng regions were distantly separated.
Barbarians obstructed the roads,
and the foreign domains were cut off by Heaven.
As for Dàqín and Tiānzhú,
they emerged from the Western Sea.
During the Two Hàn, serving there [as envoys]
made this road particularly arduous.
Yet the goods needed for commerce
sometimes came from Jiāozhōu,
sailing over the waves of the sea,
reaching afar with the help of the wind.
Moreover, the towering peaks were uneven,
and the multitude of clans was not uniform.
With different names and strange titles,
and distinct types of species,
mountain treasures and water gems
naturally originated from these places.
Precious items like iridescent rhinoceros horn and kingfisher feathers,
and rare curiosities like serpent pearls and fireproof cloth—
a thousand names and ten thousand varieties—
were all desired by rulers of the world.
Thus, ships continuously plied the routes,
and merchant envoys frequently arrived.
Because southern treasures did not arrive, Tài zǔ
sent distant military expeditions.
The victory at Quánpǔ
made his might shake the vast ocean.
Unnamed treasures
were brought in to enrich the imperial treasury.
As for the four barbarian tribes, their great power
has been a deep-seated problem since ancient times.
The Mán and Bó were particularly numerous and mixed,
with a vast population.
Dwelling in deep valleys and alongside rugged cliffs,
they accumulated around the capital region.
Being close to the Chinese people,
they easily incited cunning malice,
seizing wealth and occupying land,
which deepened over the years.
From the middle of Yuánjiā era,
their banditry spread even wider,
eventually becoming entrenched in several prefectures,
disturbing the state and its cities.
Thereupon, generals were commanded to lead armies,
freely carrying out extermination campaigns.
From north of the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
to south of Lújiāng,
they scoured mountains and swept valleys,
exhausting their troops and military resources.
Those bound by the neck and captured
amounted to several millions.
As for the children and the aged,
spared from the interrogations,
the generals and soldiers vented their bloodthirsty rage,
and weapons were used to their most brutal extent.
Although it was said to be due to accumulated grievances,
the retaliation was excessive.
As Zhāng Huàn said,
"Blood flows in the fields,
harming harmony and causing disaster."
These are indeed the words of a benevolent person.
Collation Notes
Chapter 58, Accounts of Dī and Hú
The Yáng clan of Dī from Qīngshuǐ, Lüyáng,
had resided in Lǒngyòu since the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
becoming a powerful family.
In the Jiàn'ān era of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn,
there was a Yáng Téng,
who was a tribal chieftain.
Téng's son, Jū,
was brave, strong, and resourceful.
He first moved to Chóuchí.
Chóuchí had an area of a hundred *qǐng*,
and so it was named "Bǎiqǐng" (Hundred *Qǐng*).
It was sheer on all four sides,
with a high, flat area of over twenty *lǐ*.
The winding path was like a sheep's gut,
with thirty-six turns.
The mountain had abundant springs,
and earth could be boiled to make salt.
Later, Jū had a descendant named Qiānwàn,
whom Wèi appointed as King of the Bǎiqǐng Dī.
Qiānwàn's grandson was named Fēilóng,
who gradually grew strong.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn provisionally appointed him General Who Conquers the West,
and he returned to reside in Lüyáng.
He had no sons,
so he adopted his sister's son from the Línghú clan as his son,
named Wùsōu.
In the sixth year of Yuánkāng of Emperor Huì of Jìn (300 CE),
to avoid the rebellion of Qí Wànnián,
Wùsōu led his tribe of four thousand families
back to secure Bǎiqǐng,
and styled himself General Who Guards the State and Right Worthy King.
Many people from Guānzhōng who fled sought refuge with him.
Wùsōu welcomed and comforted them,
and for those who wished to leave, he protected and provided for their departure.
Emperor Mǐn appointed him General of Cavalry and Left Worthy King.
At that time, Nányáng Wáng Bǎo was in Shàngguī,
and also appointed Wùsōu's son, Nándí, as General Who Conquers the South.
In the fifth year of Jiànxīng (317 CE),
Wùsōu died,
and Nándí succeeded him.
He divided his forces with Jiāntóu;
Nándí was styled Left Worthy King and
stationed at Xiàbiàn,
while Jiāntóu was styled Right Worthy King and
stationed at Héchí.
In the fourth year of Tàixīng of Emperor Yuán (321 CE),
Liú Yào attacked Nándí,
and both Nándí and Jiāntóu fled to Jìnshòu,
becoming vassals of Lǐ Xióng.
When Yào retreated,
they returned to Chóuchí.
In the ninth year of Xiánhé of Emperor Chéng (334 CE),
Nándí died,
and his son Yì succeeded him.
He styled himself Bearer of Credential, General of Dragon Might, Left Worthy King, and Duke of Xiàbiàn.
He appointed Jiāntóu's son, Pán, as Bearer of Credential, General Who Inspires the Army, Right Worthy King, and Duke of Héchí.
In the first year of Xiánkāng (335 CE),
they sent envoys to pledge allegiance to Jìn,
and Yì was appointed General Who Conquers the South,
and Pán General Who Conquers the East.
In the third year (337 CE), Yì's cousin Chū ambushed and killed Yì,
and seized his followers.
He established himself as Duke of Chóuchí,
and became a vassal of Shí Hǔ.
Later, he sent envoys to pledge allegiance to Emperor Mù.
In the third year of Yǒnghé (347 CE), Chū was appointed Bearer of Credential, General Who Conquers the South, Inspector of Yōngzhōu, Colonel Who Pacifies the Qiāng, and Duke of Chóuchí.
Chū's son, Guó, was appointed General Who Guards the East and Administrator of Wǔdū.
In the tenth year (354 CE),
Chū was re-enfeoffed as Duke of Tiānshuǐ.
In the eleventh year (355 CE), Yì's younger brother, Sòngnú, instigated his cousin, Liáng Shìwáng, to personally assassinate Chū while on duty.
Chū's son, Guó, led his attendants to execute Shìwáng and Sòngnú,
and re-established himself.
General Who Conquers the West, Huán Wēn, memorialized to appoint Guó as General Who Guards the North, Inspector of Qínzhōu, and Colonel Who Pacifies the Qiāng.
Guó's son, Ān, was appointed General Who Manifests Awe and Administrator of Wǔdū.
In the twelfth year (356 CE),
Guó's paternal cousin, Yáng Jùn, again killed Guó and established himself.
Ān fled to Fú Shēng.
Jùn sent envoys to submit.
In the third year of Shēngpíng (359 CE), Jùn was appointed General Who Pacifies the West, Colonel Who Pacifies the Qiāng, and Duke of Chóuchí.
In the fourth year (360 CE), Jùn died,
and his son, Shì, succeeded him.
He was again appointed General Who Inspires the Army, Colonel Who Pacifies the Qiāng, Administrator of Wǔdū, and Duke of Chóuchí.
In the third year of Tàihé of Hǎixī Gōng (368 CE),
he was promoted to General Who Conquers the West and Inspector of Qínzhōu.
Shì's younger brother, Tǒng, was appointed General Who Pacifies the East and Administrator of Wǔdū.
In the fifth year (370 CE), Shì died,
and Tǒng deposed Shì's heir, Zuǎn, and established himself.
Zuǎn, also named Dé,
gathered a faction and killed Tǒng.
He sent envoys to Emperor Jiǎnwén to explain himself,
and Zuǎn was again appointed Colonel Who Pacifies the Qiāng, Inspector of Qínzhōu, and Duke of Chóuchí.
In the first year of Xián'ān (371 CE),
Fú Jiān sent Yáng Ān, Fú Yǎ, and others to attack and conquer Zuǎn.
He relocated their people to Guānzhōng,
leaving the land of Bǎiqǐng empty.
Zuǎn was later killed by Yáng Ān.
When Sòngnú died,
his two sons Fónú and Fógǒu fled to Guānzhōng.
Fú Jiān appointed Fónú as Right General,
and Fógǒu as Fǔyí Hùjūn.
Later, Fú Jiān married his daughter to Fónú's son, Dìng,
and appointed Dìng as Shàngshū and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the eighth year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
Fú Jiān was defeated at Huáinán,
and Guānzhōng fell into chaos.
Dìng exerted his utmost effort to serve Fú Jiān.
After Fú Jiān's death,
Dìng led his family to flee to Lǒngyòu,
moving his administration to Lìchéng.
Lìchéng was within Xīxiàn prefecture,
one hundred and twenty *lǐ* from Qiúchí.
He set up granaries at Bǎiqǐng.
He recruited the Yí and Jìn people,
gathering over a thousand households,
and proclaimed himself Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn, Píngqiāng Xiàowèi, and Duke of Qiúchí.
He declared fealty to Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn.
Emperor Xiàowǔ then provisionally granted him these self-proclaimed titles.
He requested to be ceded Xīxiàn of Tiānshuǐ and Shànglù of Wǔdū to form Qiúchí Commandery,
which was granted.
In the fifteenth year,
Dìng was again appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Qínzhōu Cìshǐ.
Dìng had already appointed himself Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn.
He was further promoted to Chíjié, Dūdū Lǒngyòu Zhūjūnshì, Fǔguó Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
while his titles of Xiàowèi and Cìshǐ remained unchanged.
In that year,
he advanced to pacify Tiānshuǐ and Luèyáng Commandery,
thus possessing the land of Qínzhōu,
and proclaimed himself Prince of Lǒngxī.
By the nineteenth year,
he attacked the Lǔ Qǐfú Gānzuī of Lǒngxī,
and Dìng's army was defeated and he was killed.
He had no sons.
Fógǒu's son, Shèng, who had previously been Jiān Guó,
defended Qiúchí,
succeeded to the position,
and proclaimed himself Shǐchíjié, Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn, Qínzhōu Cìshǐ, Píngqiāng Xiàowèi, and Duke of Qiúchí.
Dìng was posthumously honored as King Wǔ.
He divided the various Dī and Qiāng of the four mountains into twenty sections of Hùjūn,
each serving as a garrison,
without establishing commanderies or prefectures.
In the third year of Lóng'ān of Emperor Ān,
he sent envoys to declare fealty,
offering local tribute.
Emperor Ān appointed Shèng as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, Píngqiāng Xiàowèi, and Duke of Qiúchí.
In the third year of Yuánxīng,
Huán Xuán assisted the Jìn,
and promoted Shèng to Píngběi Jiāngjūn, Liángzhōu Cìshǐ, and Xīróng Xiàowèi.
In the first year of Yìxī,
Yáo Xīng attacked Shèng.
Shèng, in fear,
sent his son Nándāng as a hostage.
Yáo Xīng sent his general Wáng Mǐn to attack the city.
Through Lü Yíng, the Biéjià of Liángzhōu,
Yáo Xīng sought aid from Shèng.
Shèng dispatched an army to Jìnkǒu,
and Wáng Mǐn retreated.
Shèng was appointed Dūdū Lǒngyòu Zhūjūnshì, Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn, and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
At that time, Máo Qú, the Cìshǐ of Yìzhōu, was attacking Huán Xī, the Liángzhōu Cìshǐ appointed by Huán Xuán.
Máo Qú was defeated and fled,
leaving Hànzhōng empty.
Shèng sent his elder brother's son, Píngnán Jiāngjūn Fǔ, to guard Hànzhōng.
In the third year,
Shèng was again provisionally granted Shǐchíjié and Běiqínzhōu Cìshǐ.
Shèng also sent his general Fú Xuān to act as Liángzhōu Cìshǐ, replacing Fǔ.
In the ninth year,
Suǒ Miáo, the Liángzhōu Cìshǐ, garrisoned Nánchéng,
and Xuān then returned.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he promoted Shèng to Chējì Dàjiāngjūn,
and added the title of Shìzhōng.
In the third year of Yǒngchū,
he was re-enfeoffed as King Wǔdū.
His eldest son Xuán was made Wǔdū Wáng Shìzǐ,
and given the additional title of Qián Jiāngjūn.
Nándāng was made Guānjūn Jiāngjūn,
and Fǔ was made Ānnán Jiāngjūn.
Shèng succeeded to the throne for thirty years.
In the sixth month of the second year of Yuánjiā of Tàizǔ, he died
at the age of sixty-two.
He was privately posthumously honored as King Huìwén.
Xuán, courtesy name Huángméi,
proclaimed himself Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Lǒngyòu Zhūjūnshì, Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Píngqiāng Xiàowèi, Qínzhōu Cìshǐ, and King Wǔdū.
Although he was a vassal,
he still maintained the era name of Yìxī.
He treated scholars well,
and was cherished by both the immigrant and old inhabitants.
Ānnán Jiāngjūn Fǔ possessed both civil and military wisdom and strategy,
but Xuán could not tolerate him.
In the third year,
on account of Fǔ's son committing murder,
he had Fǔ and his son executed.
Tàizǔ then appointed Xuán as Shǐchíjié, Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn, Píngqiāng Xiàowèi, Běiqínzhōu Cìshǐ, and King Wǔdū.
He then changed the era name of Yìxī
and adopted the correct calendar of Yuánjiā.
Earlier,
Shèng had said to Xuán:
"I am old now.
I ought to be a subject of Jìn.
You should serve the Sòng Emperor well."
Therefore, Xuán served him.
Shèng was posthumously granted Pàoxī Dàjiāngjūn,
with other titles remaining as before.
In the sixth month of the sixth year,
Xuán died.
He was privately posthumously honored as King Xiàozhāo.
His younger brother Nándāng deposed Xuán's son Bǎozōng (also known as Qiāngnú) and enthroned himself,
proclaiming himself Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Yōngliáng Zhūjūnshì, Qínzhōu Cìshǐ, Píngqiāng Xiàowèi, and King Wǔdū.
Tàizǔ appointed him Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, Qínzhōu Cìshǐ, and King Wǔdū.
In the ninth year,
he was promoted to Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn,
and given the titles of Chíjié, Dūdū, and Xiàowèi.
Nándāng appointed Bǎozōng as Zhènnán Jiāngjūn,
garrisoning Dàngchāng,
and appointed his second son Shùn as Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn and Qínzhōu Cìshǐ,
guarding Shàngguī.
Bǎozōng plotted to attack Nándāng.
The plot was exposed,
and he was arrested and imprisoned.
Before this,
among the refugees from all directions, Xǔ Mùzhī and Hǎo Huīzhī defected to Nándāng,
and both changed their surnames to Sīmǎ.
Mùzhī claimed his name was Fēilóng,
and Huīzhī claimed his name was Kāngzhī,
stating they were close relatives of the Jìn imperial house.
Kāngzhī was soon killed by someone.
In the tenth year,
Nándāng, seeing that Liú Dàojì, the Cìshǐ of Yìzhōu, had lost the support of the local people in Shǔ,
provided military resources to Fēilóng,
sending him into Shǔ to raid.
Liú Dàojì attacked and beheaded him.
At that time, Zhēn Fǎhù, the Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu, was incompetent in legal administration.
Tàizǔ sent Cìshǐ Xiāo Sīhuà to replace him.
Nándāng took advantage of Sīhuà's delayed arrival
and Fǎhù's impending departure,
raising an army to attack Liángzhōu.
He captured Báimǎ,
and seized Zhāng Fàn, the Grand Administrator of Jìnchāng.
Fǎhù sent his Cānjūn Lǔ Ānqī and Shěn Fǎhuì to resist,
but they both retreated.
Nándāng further sent Jiànzhōng Jiāngjūn Zhào Jìn to attack Jiāméng,
capturing Fàn Yánlǎng, the Grand Administrator of Jìnshòu.
In the eleventh month of that year,
Fǎhù abandoned his post and fled to Yángchuān,
and Nándāng thus possessed the land of Hànzhōng.
He appointed the Dī Fú Sùchí as Liángzhōu Cìshǐ,
but later, due to his brutality, had him killed,
and replaced him with Sīmǎ Zhào Wēn as Liángzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the first month of the tenth year,
Sīhuà sent his Sīmǎ Xiāo Chéngzhī to lead the vanguard and attack,
achieving victories wherever they went,
and thus pacifying Liángzhōu.
The details are in Sīhuà's biography.
In the fourth month,
Nándāng sent an envoy to present a memorial of apology,
saying: "I have heard that the virtue of creation and nurturing
binds all living beings,
yet prosperity and decline take different paths,
and encounters vary greatly.
As for the favor bestowed by nature,
there is truly no way to repay it.
If
even between the mad and the wise, where their paths diverge,
there remains the sincerity to conquer one's thoughts,
how much more so between sovereign and parent, where there is no duality,
should one be spontaneously moved without expectation?
Every time I consider exerting myself to the utmost
to respectfully follow your brilliant instructions,
my sincere devotion
is not yet understood,
and grave slanders have already arrived.
Zhēn Fǎhù, the Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu, falsely accused your subject of sending Sīmǎ Fēilóng to cause disturbances in Xīshǔ.
The accusations he brought
were not just one matter.
The
journey of ten thousand *lǐ*
offers no path to clear myself,
and the rumors
grow more severe day by day.
Rather than living in opposition,
I would prefer to perish honorably.
Both civil and military officials shared this indignation,
and I was not free to act as I wished.
I sent my Cānjūn Yáo Dàoxián with a letter to Xiāo Sīhuà, the Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu,
and then subsequently sent another to the imperial court to confess my fault.
When Dàoxián reached Xīchéng,
he was
killed by the defending soldiers.
His mission was blocked,
and the sun and moon offered no illumination.
Fǎhù was terrified
and fled at the first sign of trouble.
Your subject immediately withdrew his army,
not violating even a single blade of grass,
and temporarily left a small garrison,
awaiting
Huìtōng.
A few tens of days later,
the imperial army arrived.
The defending soldiers were weak and few,
fearing they would not be spared,
so they successively sent light troops
to jointly welcome them.
It happened that the common people from Qín,
cherishing
their homeland and roots,
were about to return;
they could not be restrained.
This was due to my lack of a strong defense,
which led to this oversight.
My family has served as border vassals for generations,
and for generations we have received special favor.
When the imperial transforming influence first began,
we submitted to Heaven and accepted our destiny.
Seeking fame or upholding righteousness
is not something for today.
How could I feign falsehoods and
deceit,
destroying accomplished success?
A situation like this
is clearly and easily seen.
I rely on the sagely wisdom
to surely inspect it.
However, my humble intentions were not understood,
and my actions went against loyalty and submission,
so much so that the news reached the imperial court,
troubling the army.
The depth of this humiliation and disgrace,
my crime deserves execution and punishment.
Separated by a distant wilderness,
I have no place to offer my apologies.
I respectfully send the concurrently-held Changshǐ Qí
Liàng to await orders from the appropriate officials,
and also to deliver the eleventh tally and register that I was granted.
I humbly await the heavenly decree.
Tàizǔ, considering them to be from a border region,
issued an edict saying:
“Yáng Nándāng’s memorial is as such;
he repents and apologizes for his previous transgressions.
He may be specially pardoned and forgiven,
and his insignia and credentials are to be specially restored to him.”
In the twelfth year,
Nándāng released Bǎozōng
and sent him to guard Tóngtíng.
[一０]Bǎozōng fled,
[一一]and the Sǔolǔ lord Tuòbá Táo appointed him Dūdū Lǒngxī Zhūjūnshì, Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Píngqiāng Xiàowèi, and Nánqín Wáng,
and sent him to attack Shàngguī.
Nándāng’s son Shùn lost the city and retreated.
He was made Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ
and guarded Xiàbiàn.
In the third month of the thirteenth year,
Nándāng declared himself Dàqín Wáng,
named his reign Jiànyì,
made his wife Queen,
and his heir apparent Crown Prince.
He established a hundred officials,
fully imitating the imperial court,
yet he still nominally submitted to the imperial court
and his tributes did not cease.
In the seventeenth year,
his kingdom suffered a great drought
and many disasters and anomalies,
so he was demoted from Dàqín Wáng back to Wǔdū Wáng.
In the tenth month of the eighteenth year,
he sent his entire army south to raid,
intending to seize the land of Shǔ.
Fearing that the Hànzhōng army would sally forth,
he sent Jiànzhōng Jiāngjūn Fú Chōng to go out from Dōngluò to defend against them.
Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Zhēndào attacked and beheaded Chōng.
[一二]In the eleventh month,
Nándāng captured Jiāméng,
seizing Jìnshòu Tàishǒu Shēn Tǎn,
and then besieged Fúchéng.
Bāxī Tàishǒu Liú Dàoxī fortified the city and held firm.
[一三]Nándāng attacked for more than ten days
but could not capture it,
so he returned.
In the first month of the nineteenth year,
Tàizǔ sent Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Péi Fāngmíng, Tàizǐ Zuǒjīnnǔ Jiāngjūn Liú Kāngzǔ, and Hòujūn Cānjūn Liáng Tǎnmò with three thousand armored soldiers,
and also dispatched troops from Jīng and Yōng prefectures to attack Nándāng,
under the command of Liú Zhēndào.
In the fifth month,
Fāngmíng and others reached Hànzhōng
and advanced rapidly.
Zhēndào arrived at Wǔxìng
and attacked the pseudo-Jiànzhōng Jiāngjūn Fú Lóng,
defeating him.
Ānxī Cānjūn Wéi Jùn and Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn Jiāng Dàoshèng took a separate route to Xiàbiàn.
Zhēndào also sent Sīmǎ Xiàhóu Mùjì west to capture Báishuǐ.
Nándāng’s son, Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Shùn, and Jiànzhōng Jiāngjūn Yáng Liàng resisted them,
but both fled at the mere sight of them.
In the intercalary month,
Fāngmíng reached Lángāo.
Nándāng’s Zhènbei Jiāngjūn Fú Yìdé and Jiànjié Jiāngjūn Fú Hóngzǔ, with over ten thousand men, arrayed their forces to resist.
Fāngmíng attacked and routed them,
beheading Hóngzǔ
and killing over two thousand men.
Yìdé fled.
Rèn Yùzhī of Tiānshuǐ led his troops to surrender.
Nándāng’s heir apparent, Fǔjūn Dàjiāngjūn Hé, held Xiūchéng.
Fāngmíng again sent Yùzhī’s troops to attack Hé,
greatly defeating him.
Thereupon, Nándāng fled with his wife and children to the Sǔolǔ
and died among the barbarians.
Ānxī Cānjūn Lǔ Shàngqī pursued Nándāng out of Hánxiá,
[一四]capturing alive Jiànjié Jiāngjūn Yáng Bǎochì and Ānchāng Hóu Yáng Hǔtóu.
Initially,
Nándāng had sent his second son, Hǔ, as Zhènnán Jiāngjūn and Yìzhōu Cìshǐ,
to guard Yīnpíng.
Hearing of his father’s flight,
he fled back
to Xiàbiàn.
Fāngmíng sent his son Sùzhī to intercept him,
capturing Hǔ alive
and sending him to the capital,
where he was beheaded in Jiànkāng market.
Qíuchí was pacified.
Hú Chóngzhī, Fǔguó Sīmǎ, was appointed Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn, Qínzhōu Cìshǐ, and Píngqiāng Xiàowèi,
to guard Qíuchí.
The Sǔolǔ Tuòbá Táo sent Ānxī Dàjiāngjūn Tǔxī Bì and Píngběi Jiāngjūn Tuòbá Qí with twenty thousand men to intercept Chóngzhī.
In the second month of the twentieth year,
Chóngzhī reached Zhuóshuǐ,
eighty *lǐ* from Qíuchí,
encountered Qí and others,
was defeated and captured.
The rest of his troops fled back to Hànzhōng.
In the third month,
former Zhèndōng Sīmǎ Fú Dá and Zhēngxī Cóngshì Zhōngláng Rèn Fěi and others raised an army in righteousness,
and established Bǎozōng’s younger brother Wéndé as their leader.
Tuòbá Qí, hearing of the uprising, fled.
Dá pursued, attacked, and beheaded Qí.
[一五]He then occupied Báiyá
and divided his forces to pacify the various garrisons.
Wéndé declared himself Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Qínhéliáng Sānzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn, Qínhéliáng Sānzhōu Mù, Píngqiāng Xiàowèi, and Qíuchí Gōng,
and dispatched an urgent memorial to the imperial court.
Tàizǔ issued an edict saying:
“Recently, Xiàowèi Qíuchí Gōng memorialized that the barbarians were rampant and arrogant,
plundering and seizing Qíuchí.
Our officers and soldiers were wounded and injured,
and the people were suffering terribly.
Looking around,
I feel pity and indignation.
Yáng Wéndé’s family has been loyal and submissive for generations;
his sincerity moved both family and state.
He gathered righteous followers
and swiftly annihilated the ferocious villains.
Wherever his banners and blades went,
they annihilated and crushed without leaving a trace.
The oppressive atmosphere was cleared,
and the border region was pacified and unified.
Recalling his merits and considering his deeds,
I am indeed pleased and joyful.
An envoy should be sent to comfort and encourage him,
and to proclaim the imperial will,
and also to order Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Shēn Tǎn to provide support as appropriate.”
Another edict said:
“To clearly record meritorious achievements
is indeed an imperial institution.
Rewards should be given promptly,
without any delay.
Yáng Wéndé’s ambition and spirit are truly exceptional,
possessing both civil and military talents.
Seizing the opportunity and secretly rising,
extraordinary merits accumulated.
He reported his victory and pledged his loyalty,
presenting captives from thousands of *lǐ* away.
The court had no temporarily barren land,
and the trees of difficulty pacified themselves.
His glorious achievements are manifest;
We greatly commend him.
The Yáng clan’s ancestors toiled in the west,
and their loyalty spanned generations.
[一六]It is fitting that he should inherit the ancestral lineage
and receive favor and glory.
He is appointed Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Běiqín Yōng Èrzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn, Píngqiāng Xiàowèi, Běiqínzhōu Cìshǐ,
and enfeoffed as Wǔdū Wáng.”
Rèn Fěi’s grandfather was Qí,
his paternal uncle was Zuò,
and his father was Zōng.
All served the Yáng clan
as Zīyì Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
Fěi possessed ambition and capability.
Wéndé made him Zuǒ Sīmǎ.
Yáng Wéndé 既受朝命，
進戍 Jiālú 城．
二十五年，
為索虜所攻，
奔于 Hànzhōng．
時 Shìzǔ 鎮 Xiāngyáng，
執 Wéndé 歸之于 Jīngshī，
以失守，
免官，
削爵土．
二十七年，
王師北討，
起 Wéndé 為 Fǔguó Jiāngjūn，
率軍自 Hànzhōng 西入，
搖動 Qiān、Lǒng．
Wéndé 宗人 Yáng Gāo 率 Yīnpíng、Píngwǔ 羣 Dī，
據 Tánglǔqiáo 以距 Wéndé，
Wéndé 水陸俱攻，
大破之，
衆並奔散．
Gāo 遁走奔 Qiāng，
Wéndé 追之至 Lí'áng Lǐng，
Gāo 單身投 Qiāng Chóu'āròujia，
追斬之，
Yīnpíng、Píngwǔ 悉平．
又遣 Wéndé 伐 Dàntí Dī，
不剋，
Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Xiùzhī 執送 Jīngzhōu，
使 Wéndé 從祖兄 Tóu 戍 Jiālú．
Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Nánjùn Wáng Yìxuān 反，
Wéndé 不同見殺，
Shìzǔ 追贈 Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn、Qínzhōu Cìshǐ．
Xiàojiàn 二年，
以保宗子 Yuánhé 為 Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn，
以 Tóu 為 Fǔguó Jiāngjūn．
Yuánhé 既 Yáng 氏正統，
羣 Dī 欲相宗推，
年小才弱，
不能綏御所部，
Tóu 母妻子弟並為索虜所執，
Tóu 至誠奉順，
無所顧懷．
朝廷既不正 Yuánhé 號位，
部落未有定主，
Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Xuánmó 上表曰：〔一七〕
「被勑令臣遣使與 Yáng Yuánhé、Yáng Tóu 相聞，
并致信餉．
既遣中軍行參軍 Lǚ Zhìzōng 齎書并信等，
亦自遣使隨 Zhìzōng．
及 Tóu 語 Zhìzōng，
頃破家為國，
母妻子弟並墜沒虜中，
不顧孝道，
陳力邊捍，
竭忠盡誠，
未為朝廷所識．
若以 Yuánhé 承統，
宜授王爵；
若以其年小未堪大任，
則應別有所委．
頃來公私紛紜，
華、戎交構，
皆此之由．
臣伏尋 Tóu 元嘉以來，
實有忠誠於國，
棄親遺愛，
誠在可嘉．
Dī、Qiāng 負遠，
又與虜咫尺，
急之則反，
緩之則怨．
觀 Tóu 使人言語，
不敢便望 Chóuchí Gōng，
所希政在 Xīqínzhōu Jiǎjié 而已．
如臣愚見，
蕃捍 Hànchuān，
使無虜患，
Tóu 實有力，
四千戶荒州，
殆不足吝．
Yuánhé 小弱，
若未可專委，
復數年之後，
必堪嗣業，
用之不難．
若才用不稱，
則應歸 Tóu．
若 Jiālú 不守，
Hànchuān 亦無立理． 」
上不許．
其後立 Yuánhé 為 Wǔdū Wáng，
治 Báishuǐ，
不能自立，
復走奔索虜．
Yuánhé 從弟 Sēngsì，
復自立，
還戍 Jiālú，
以為 Níngshuò Jiāngjūn、Chóuchí Tàishǒu．
Tàizōng Tàishǐ 二年，
詔曰：
「Sēngsì 遠守西疆，
世篤忠款，
宜加旌顯，
以甄義概．
可 Guànjūn Jiāngjūn、Běiqínzhōu Cìshǐ、Wǔdū Wáng，
Tàishǒu 如故． 」
三年，
加 Chíjié、Dūdū Běiqín Yōng 二州諸軍事，
進號 Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn、Xiàowèi，
Cìshǐ 如故．
Sēngsì 卒，
從弟 Wéndù 復自立．
Tàiyù 元年，
以為 Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn、Lüèyáng Tàishǒu，
封 Wǔdū Wáng，
又改 Lóngxiáng 為 Níngshuò Jiāngjūn．
後廢帝 Yuánhuī 四年，
加 Dū Běiqínzhōu Zhūjūnshì、Píngqiāng Xiàowèi、Běiqínzhōu Cìshǐ，
Jiāngjūn 如故．
Wéndù 遣弟 Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Wénhóng 伐 Chóuchí，
〔一八〕破戍兵於 Lángāo．
Shùndì Shēngmíng 元年，
詔曰：
「茂賞有章，
實昭國度，
疇庸斯炳，
載宣史冊．
Dū Běiqínzhōu Zhūjūnshì、Níngshuò Jiāngjūn、Píngqiāng Xiàowèi、Běiqínzhōu Cìshǐ，
Wǔdū Wáng Wéndù 門乘輝寵，
世榮邊邑，
忠果既亮，
才勁兼彰．
Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Yáng Wénhóng 肅協成規，
躬提桴鼓，
申稜百頃，
席卷 Lángāo，
功烈之美，
並足嘉歎，
宜膺爵授，
以酬勳緒．
Wéndù 可使 Chíjié、Dūdū Běiqín Yōng 二州諸軍事、Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn，
Cìshǐ、Xiàowèi 悉如故．
Wénhóng Fǔguó Jiāngjūn、Lüèyáng Tàishǒu． 」
其年，
虜破 Jiālú，
Wéndù 見殺，
追贈本官，
加 Sànqí Chángshì．
以 Wénhóng Dū Běiqínzhōu Zhūjūnshì、Píngqiāng Xiàowèi、Běiqínzhōu Cìshǐ，
襲封 Wǔdū Wáng，
Jiāngjūn 如故．
退治 Wǔxīng．
Dàqiěqú Méngxùn，
Zhāngyè Línsōng Lúshuǐ Hú rén yě．
Xiōngnú 有 Zuǒqiěqú、Yòuqiěqú 之官，
Méngxùn 之先為此職，
Qiāng 之酋豪曰 Dà，
故 Qiěqú 以位為氏，
而以 Dà 冠之．
世居 Lúshuǐ 為酋豪．
Méngxùn Gāozǔ Huīzhòng Guī，
Zēngzǔ Zhē，
皆雄健有勇名．
Zǔ Qífùyán，
封 Dí Dì Wáng．
〔一九〕父 Fǎhóng 襲爵，
Fú shì 以為 Zhōngtián Hùjūn．
Méngxùn (蒙遜) took over his father's command of the部曲 (bùqǔ).
He possessed courage and strategy,
and was resourceful,
earning the respect and submission of the various Hú (胡) tribes.
Lǚ Guāng (呂光) proclaimed himself king in Liángzhōu (涼州),
and appointed Méngxùn (蒙遜) to lead the营人 (yíngrén) and be responsible for the supplies.
He also made Méngxùn’s (蒙遜) uncle, Luóqiú (羅仇), the Administrator of Xīpíng (西平).
[二０] In the spring of the third year of Ān Dì’s (安帝) Lóng'ān (隆安) reign (399 CE),
Lǚ Guāng (呂光) dispatched his son, the General Who Guards the East, Zuan (纂), to lead Luóqiú (羅仇) in an attack against Qǐfó Gān'guī (乞佛乾歸), the barbarians of Páohǎn (枹罕).
They were defeated by Gān'guī (乾歸).
Guāng (光) blamed Luóqiú (羅仇)
and executed him.
In the fourth month,
Méngxùn (蒙遜) requested to return and bury Luóqiú (羅仇).
He then gathered over ten thousand men and rebelled against Guāng (光),
killed the Commander of Línsōng (臨松),
and stationed himself at Jīnshān (金山).
In the fifth month,
Guāng (光) ordered Zuan (纂) to attack and defeat Méngxùn (蒙遜).
Méngxùn (蒙遜), with six or seven men,
fled into the mountains,
[二一] and his household scattered.
At that time, Méngxùn’s (蒙遜) elder brother, Nánchéng (男成), was leading troops to guard Jìnchāng (晉昌) in the west.
Hearing of Méngxùn’s (蒙遜) rebellion,
he led his army back,
killed the Administrator of Jiǔquán (酒泉), Diétēng (疊滕),
[二二] and put Duàn Yè (段業), the Administrator of Jiànkāng (建康), in charge.
Yè (業) proclaimed himself Grand General of the Dragon Stratagem, Governor of Liángzhōu (涼州), and Duke of Jiànkāng (建康),
and appointed Nánchéng (男成) as General Who Stabilizes the State.
Nánchéng (男成) and Wáng Dé (王德), the Administrator of Jìnchāng (晉昌), besieged Zhāngyè (張掖),
and captured it.
Yè (業) then took control of Zhāngyè (張掖).
Méngxùn (蒙遜) led his部曲 (bùqǔ) and defected to Yè (業).
Yè (業) appointed Méngxùn (蒙遜) as General Who Guards the West and Administrator of Línchí (臨池),
[二三] and Wáng Dé (王德) as Administrator of Jiǔquán (酒泉).
Soon after, Méngxùn (蒙遜) was also given command as Administrator of Zhāngyè (張掖).
In the fourth month of the third year,
Yè (業) sent Méngxùn (蒙遜) with ten thousand men to attack Guāng’s (光) nephew, Chún (純), in Xījùn (西郡).
After ten days, it was not captured,
so he diverted water to flood the city.
In their distress, they begged for surrender,
and were captured and brought back.
At this time, Wáng Dé (王德) rebelled against Yè (業),
and declared himself Governor of Hézhōu (河州).
Yè (業) sent Méngxùn (蒙遜) to suppress him in the west.
Dé (德) burned the city
and led his部曲 (bùqǔ) to defect to Táng Yáo (唐瑤), the Administrator of Jìnchāng (晉昌).
Méngxùn (蒙遜) pursued Dé (德) to Shātóu (沙頭),
utterly defeating him,
and captured his family, wives, and tribes before returning.
He was transferred to be Administrator of Xī'ān (西安),
his generalship remaining as before.
In the fifth month of the fourth year,
Méngxùn (蒙遜) conspired with Nánchéng (男成) to kill Yè (業).
Nánchéng (男成) did not agree.
Méngxùn (蒙遜) then slandered Nánchéng (男成) to Yè (業).
Yè (業) killed Nánchéng (男成).
Méngxùn (蒙遜) then said to his部曲 (bùqǔ):
"Duke Duàn (段公) is without principle,
unjustly killing the General Who Stabilizes the State.
I will avenge the General Who Stabilizes the State."
He then raised an army to attack Zhāngyè (張掖),
killed Duàn Yè (段業),
and proclaimed himself Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry,
[二四] establishing the era name Yǒng'ān (永安) first year.
In this month,
Lǐ Gǎo (李暠), the Administrator of Dūnhuáng (敦煌), also raised an army,
and proclaimed himself Grand General Who Subdues the Army, Commandant of Western Hú (胡), and Governor of Shāzhōu (沙州),
retaining his position as administrator.
He named his era Gēngzǐ (庚子) first year,
and contended with Méngxùn (蒙遜).
In that winter,
Gǎo (暠) sent Táng Yáo (唐瑤) and the General Who Excels in Martial Prowess, Sòng Yáo (宋繇), to attack Jiǔquán (酒泉),
capturing Dàqieqú Yìshēng (大且渠益生), the Administrator,
who was Méngxùn’s (蒙遜) cousin.
Lǚ Guāng (呂光) died,
and his son Zuan (纂) succeeded him.
In the first year,
he was usurped by his cousin Lóng (隆).
Yáo Xīng (姚興) attacked Liángzhōu (涼州),
and Lóng (隆) submitted as a vassal and requested to surrender.
Méngxùn (蒙遜) also sent envoys to Xīng (興).
Xīng (興) appointed him General Who Guards the West, Governor of Shāzhōu (沙州), and Marquis of Xīhǎi (西海).
In the second month of the second year,
Méngxùn (蒙遜) and Túfà Tán (禿髮檀), a Xīpíng (西平) barbarian, jointly attacked Liángzhōu (涼州),
but were defeated by Lóng (隆).
In the tenth month,
Tán (檀) again attacked Lóng (隆).
In the third month of the third year,
Lóng (隆), pressed by both Méngxùn (蒙遜) and Tán (檀),
sent his brother Chāo (超) to Yáo Xīng (姚興) to request assistance.
In the seventh month,
Xīng (興) sent his general Qí Nán (齊難) to assist Lóng (隆).
Lóng (隆) persuaded Nán (難) to attack Méngxùn (蒙遜).
Méngxùn (蒙遜), in fear,
sent his younger brother as a hostage
and offered treasures to Nán (難).
Nán (難) then stopped
and returned, appointing Wáng Shàng (王尚), the General of Martial Might, as acting Governor of Liángzhōu (涼州).
In the first month of the first year of Yìxī (義熙) (405 CE),
Lǐ Gǎo (李暠) changed his title to Grand General, Grand Commander, Governor of Liángzhōu (涼州), Commandant Who Protects the Qiāng (羌), and Duke of Liáng (涼).
In the fifth month,
he moved his base to Jiǔquán (酒泉).
Yáo Xīng (姚興) provisionally appointed Tán (檀) as Governor of Liángzhōu (涼州),
replacing Wáng Shàng (王尚) to garrison Gūzāng (姑臧).
In the ninth month of the second year,
Méngxùn (蒙遜) attacked Lǐ Gǎo (李暠).
When he reached Ānmí (安彌),
sixty *lǐ* (里) from the city,
Gǎo (暠) then became aware.
He led his army out to battle,
suffered a great defeat,
retreated,
and closed the city gates to defend himself.
Méngxùn (蒙遜) also returned.
In the sixth year,
Méngxùn (蒙遜) attacked and defeated Tán (檀).
Tán (檀) fled to garrison Lèdū (樂都).
Jiāo Lǎng (焦朗) from Wǔwēi (武威) entered Gūzāng (姑臧),
proclaimed himself Grand General of Agile Cavalry,
and submitted as a vassal to Lǐ Gǎo (李暠).
In the eighth year,
Méngxùn (蒙遜) attacked Jiāo Lǎng (焦朗)
and killed him.
[二五] He occupied Gūzāng (姑臧),
proclaimed himself Grand Commander, Grand General, and King of Héxī (河西),
changed the era name to Xuánshǐ (玄始) first year,
and appointed his son Zhèngdé (正德) as heir apparent.
In the fifth month of the thirteenth year,
Lǐ Gǎo (李暠) died,
and his son Xīn (歆) succeeded him.
In the sixth month,
Xīn (歆) attacked Méngxùn (蒙遜),
reaching Jiànkāng (建康).
Méngxùn (蒙遜) resisted him.
Xīn (歆) retreated and fled.
Méngxùn (蒙遜) pursued him to Xīzhījiàn (西支澗),
[二六] where Xīn (歆) suffered a great defeat,
with over four thousand dead.
Méngxùn (蒙遜) then gathered the remaining troops,
reinforced and expanded the city of Jiànkāng (建康),
stationed troops, and returned.
In the fourteenth year,
Méngxùn (蒙遜) sent envoys to Jìn (晉),
presenting a memorial proclaiming himself a vassal.
Méngxùn (蒙遜) was appointed Governor of Liángzhōu (涼州).
Gāozǔ (高祖) ascended the throne

and appointed Xīn (歆) as Bearer of Imperial Credentials, Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of the Seven Commanderies of Gāochāng (高昌), Dūnhuáng (敦煌), Jìnchāng (晉昌), Jiǔquán (酒泉), Xīhǎi (西海), Yùmén (玉門), and Kānjǐng (堪泉), Commandant Who Protects the Qiāng (羌), General Who Conquers the West, and Duke of Jiǔquán (酒泉).
In the seventh month of the first year of Yǒngchū (永初) (420 CE),
Méngxùn (蒙遜) attacked Hàoxìn (浩舋) to the east.
Lǐ Xīn (李歆) took advantage of the vulnerability to attack Zhāngyè (張掖).
Méngxùn (蒙遜) turned his army back west.
Xīn (歆) retreated and fled.
Méngxùn (蒙遜) pursued him to Línzé (臨澤),
beheaded Xīn (歆) and his two brothers,
then advanced to attack Jiǔquán (酒泉),
and captured it.
Xīn’s (歆) younger brother Xún (恂), Administrator of Dūnhuáng (敦煌), held the commandery
and proclaimed himself Grand General.
In the tenth month,
Méngxùn (蒙遜) sent his heir apparent Zhèngdé (正德) to attack Xún (恂),
but failed to take the city.
In the first month of the third year,
Méngxùn (蒙遜) personally went to build a long dike to divert water to flood the city.
After several tens of days,
it still did not fall.
In the third month,
Sòng Chéng (宋承), Xún’s (恂) General of Martial Might, and Zhāng Hóng (張弘), General of Guǎngwǔ (廣武), surrendered the city.
[二七] Xún (恂) committed suicide,
and the Lǐ (李) clan thus perished.
Thereupon, Bǐlóng (比龍), the King of Shànshàn (鄯善), came to pay homage,
and all thirty-six states of the Western Regions (Xīyù) submitted as vassals and presented tribute.

Gāozǔ (高祖) appointed Méngxùn (蒙遜) as Bearer of Imperial Credentials, Palace Attendant, Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Liángzhōu (涼州), General Who Stabilizes the Army, Kaīfǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), Governor of Liángzhōu (涼州), and Duke of Zhāngyè (張掖).
In the twelfth month,
Táng Qì (唐契), the Administrator of Jìnchāng (晉昌), rebelled.
Zhèngdé (正德) was again sent to attack Qì (契).
In the third month of the first year of Jǐngpíng (景平) (423 CE),
Qì (契) was defeated,
and fled to Yīwú (伊吾).
In the eighth month,
the Ruìruì (芮芮) came to raid.
Méngxùn (蒙遜) sent Zhèngdé (正德) to resist them.
Zhèngdé (正德) advanced lightly with his cavalry to engage in battle,
his army was defeated, and he was killed.
Méngxùn (蒙遜) then appointed his second son, Xīngguó (興國), as heir apparent.
In this year,

Méngxùn (蒙遜) was promoted to Palace Attendant, Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of the Four Provinces of Liáng (涼), Qín (秦), Hé (河), and Shā (沙), Grand General of Agile Cavalry, concurrently acting as Commandant of the Southern Xiongnú (匈奴), Commandant of the Western Yi (夷), and Governor of Liángzhōu (涼zhou),
King of Héxī (河xī),
with the privileges of Kaīfǔ (開府) and Bearer of Imperial Credentials remaining as before.
In the first year of Tàizǔ’s (太祖) Yuánjiā (元嘉) reign (424 CE),
Qǐfó Chìpán (乞佛熾槃), the barbarian of Páohǎn (枹罕), emerged from Diāoqú Gǔ (貂渠谷) to attack Báicǎo Lǐng (白草嶺) in Héxī (河西).
The entire Línsōng (臨松) Commandery was lost,
and he captured Méngxùn’s (蒙遜) cousin Chéngdū (成都) and nephews Rìtí (日蹄) and Pōluó (頗羅) before leaving.
[二八]
In the third year,
the title of Piàojì was changed to Chējì.
Shìzǐ Xìngguó sent an envoy to present a memorial,
requesting the *Zhōu Yì* and various collections of philosophical writings.
Tàizǔ bestowed them all upon him,
totaling four hundred seventy-five scrolls.
Méngxùn again sought the *Sōu Shén Jì* from Sītú Wáng Hóng,
and Hóng copied and gave it to him.
In the sixth year,
Méngxùn attacked Fúhǎn.
At this time, Qǐfú Chìpán had died.
His son, Mào Màn, heavily defeated Méngxùn,
capturing Xìngguó alive
and killing over three thousand men.
Méngxùn offered to redeem Xìngguó
by sending three hundred thousand *hú* of grain,
but Mào Màn ultimately did not release him.
Méngxùn then established Bútí, Xìngguó's younger brother by the same mother, as Shìzǐ.
The imperial court was unaware of this.
In the seventh year,
Xìngguó was appointed Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Héxī Wáng Shìzǐ.
In the fourth month of the summer of that year,
the western barbarian Hèlián Dìng was defeated by the Suǒ barbarian Tuòbá Táo
and fled to Shàngguī.
In the eleventh month,
Mào Màn, hearing of Dìng's defeat,
led his household and Xìngguó on an eastern expedition,
intending to relocate to Shàngguī.
In the first month of the eighth year, they reached Nán'ān.
Dìng led his troops to resist Mào Màn,
severely defeating him,
killing Mào Màn,
and capturing Xìngguó before returning.
In the fourth month,
Dìng, avoiding Tuòbá Táo,
intended to cross the river west to attack Méngxùn.
In the fifth month,
he led his troops to Zhìchéng Xiágkǒu,
crossed the river,
but before half had crossed,
he was intercepted by Tǔyùhún Mùguī,
who captured him.
Xìngguó, wounded, died a few days later.
In the ninth year,
Bútí was appointed Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Héxī Wáng Shìzǐ.
In the fourth month of the tenth year,
Méngxùn died,
at the age of sixty-six.
He was privately granted the posthumous title Wǔxuān Wáng.
Bútí was young.
Méngxùn's third son, Màoqián, was then Jǐuquán Tàishǒu.
[二九]The assembly discussed and promoted Màoqián to lead,
succeeding Méngxùn's title and position.
In the eleventh year,
Màoqián presented a memorial saying:
"Your servant has heard that merit is highest when it benefits the people,
and without bamboo and silk, virtue cannot be recounted.
Reputation is beautiful when it matches reality,
and without a posthumous title, one's end cannot be honored.
Our late minister, Méngxùn, recovered Liángchéng in the west,
his beneficence spreading to the distant lands,
eliminating bandits,
and purifying the region.
When fate aligned with the Way,
he became a loyal minister of the Great Sòng,
his title spanning the nine regions,
enjoying an everlasting and grand fortune.
His merits and fame were illustrious,
and he truly secured integrity and loyalty.
His end was righteous,
yet the path to requesting a posthumous name was closed.
His admirable deeds, though vast,
lack the beauty of being recounted.
Your servants are deeply pained
and all feel unsettled.
Respectfully consulting the *Shìfǎ*,
'Wǔ' signifies one who brings order to chaos and calamity,
and 'Xuān' signifies one whose good name spreads far and wide.
Our late minister cleared the area beyond the Yellow River,
his achievements shining in the imperial court.
His marks and accomplishments
truly embody these meanings.
Therefore, we presume to propose the posthumous title Wǔxuān Wáng.
If this meets with imperial approval
and is recorded in historical annals,
then both the living and the departed will receive honor,
and there will be no regrets from beginning to end."
An imperial edict stated:
"Jiéshǐ, Shìzhōng, Dūdū Qín, Hé, Shā, Liáng Sì Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì, Chējì Dà Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sān Sī, Lǐng Hù Xiōngnú Zhōnglángjiāng, Xīyí Xiàowèi, Liángzhōu Mù, Héxī Wáng Méngxùn,
possessed both civil and military talents,
and his achievements aided the western territories.
From ten thousand *lǐ* away,
his sincerity was long evident.
We relied on his loyalty and resolve
to assist in propagating distant strategies.
His sudden death
fills our hearts with sorrow.
An envoy has been dispatched to offer condolences and sacrifices,
and a prominent posthumous title shall be bestowed.
His heir, Màoqián,
has continued his father's military path,
and his resolve has become increasingly clear.
He should receive favor and appointment
to inherit this princely domain.
He is to be appointed Chíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Liáng, Qín, Hé, Shā Sì Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì, Zhēngxī Dà Jiāngjūn, Lǐng Hù Xiōngnú Zhōnglángjiāng, Xīyí Xiàowèi, Liángzhōu Cìshǐ, and Héxī Wáng."
A man from Héxī, Zhào Qín, was skilled in calendrical calculations.
In the fourteenth year,
Màoqián presented a memorial offering local products,
along with thirteen scrolls of *Zhōu Shēng Zǐ*,
twelve scrolls of *Shí Wù Lùn*,
twenty scrolls of *Sānguó Zǒnglüè*,
eleven scrolls of *Sú Wèn*,
ten scrolls of *Shísān Zhōu Zhì*,
six scrolls of *Wén Jiǎn*,
four scrolls of *Sì Kē Zhuàn*,
ten scrolls of *Dūnhuáng Shílù*,
ten scrolls of *Liáng Shū*,
twenty-five scrolls of *Hàn Huáng Dé Chuán*,
seven scrolls of *Wáng Diǎn*,
nine scrolls of *Wèi Bó*,
eight scrolls of *Xiè Ài Jí*,
two scrolls of *Gǔjīn Zì*,
three scrolls of *Chéngqiū Xiānshēng*,
[三０]one scroll of *Zhōu Bì*,
one scroll of *Huángdì Wáng Lì Sān Hé Jì*,
one scroll of *Zhào Qín Chuán Bìng Jiǎyín Yuán Lì*,
and one scroll of *Kǒngzǐ Zàn*,
totaling one hundred fifty-four scrolls.
Màoqián also requested dozens of miscellaneous books, including the *Jìn* and *Zhào Qǐjū Zhù*.
Tàizǔ bestowed them upon him.
In the intercalary eighth month of the sixteenth year,
Tuòbá Táo attacked Liángzhōu.
Màoqián's nephew, Wànnián, served as an internal informant for the enemy.
Màoqián was captured.
Màoqián's younger brother, Ānmí Xiànhóu Wúhuì, was previously Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn, Shāzhōu Cìshǐ, Dūdū Jiànkāng Yǐ Xī Zhū Jūnshì, and Jǐuquán Tàishǒu.
His sixth younger brother, Wǔxìng Xiànhóu Yídé, was Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn, Qínzhōu Cìshǐ, Dūdū Dānlǐng Yǐ Xī Zhū Jūnshì, and Zhāngyè Tàishǒu.
[三一]Having captured Màoqián, Táo
sent troops to attack Yídé.
Yídé abandoned the city and fled to Wúhuì.
Thereupon, Wúhuì and Yídé led their households west to join their cousin, Dūnhuáng Tàishǒu Táng'ér.
Táo then sent generals to garrison Wǔwēi, Jǐuquán, and Zhāngyè before returning.
In the first month of the seventeenth year,
Wúhuì ordered Táng'ér to guard Dūnhuáng,
while he and Yídé attacked Jǐuquán.
In the third month,
they conquered it.
They attacked Zhāngyè and Línsōng,
obtaining over forty thousand households,
and returned to hold Jǐuquán.
In the fifth month of the eighteenth year,
Táng'ér rebelled.
Wúhuì left his cousin Tiānzhōu to guard Jǐuquán,
and again, with Yídé, campaigned against Táng'ér.
Táng'ér led over ten thousand men to battle,
suffered a great defeat,
was captured and killed,
and Wúhuì reoccupied Dūnhuáng.
In the seventh month,
Tuòbá Táo sent troops to besiege Jǐuquán.
In the tenth month,
there was famine in the city;
over ten thousand people all starved to death.
Tiānzhōu killed his wife to feed the warriors.
When the food ran out,
the city fell.
Tiānzhōu was captured and taken to Píngchéng,
where he was killed.
At that time, the barbarian army was very strong,
and Wúhuì's troops were starving.
Fearing he could not maintain his position,
he wished to lead his troops west.
In the eleventh month,
he sent his brother Ānzhōu with five thousand men to attack Shànshàn,
which held firm and did not fall.
In the fourth month of the nineteenth year,
Wúhuì himself led over ten thousand households to abandon Dūnhuáng
and move west to join Ānzhōu.
Before he arrived, Shànshàn Wáng Bǐlóng had already fled with over four thousand households.
Consequently, Wúhuì occupied Shànshàn.
Initially,
Táng Qì had fled from Jìnchāng to Yīwú.
In this year, he attacked Gāochāng,
and the lord of Gāochāng city, Kàn Shuǎng, sent an urgent appeal.
[三二]In the eighth month,
Wúhuì left his cousin Fēngzhōu to guard Shànshàn,
and personally led his household to aid Gāochāng.
Before he arrived,
however, the Ruìruì sent troops to rescue Gāochāng,
killed Táng Qì,
and his troops fled to Wúhuì.
In the ninth month,
Wúhuì sent general Wèi Yè to launch a night attack on Gāochāng.
[三三]Shuǎng fled to the Ruìruì,
and Wúhuì reoccupied Gāochāng.
He sent Chángshì Fàn Jùn to present a memorial and an envoy to the capital,
offering local products.
Tàizǔ issued an edict saying:
"Last year, the cunning barbarians ran rampant,
infringing upon Liángzhōu's territory.
Xīhé Wáng Máo Qián was even unable to hold it,
falling to the rebellious bandits.
For generations, their loyalty has been demonstrated,
and it is a cause for sorrow and grief.
His younger brother Wú Huì was able to inherit his legacy,
guarding the frontier,
forming alliances with neighboring states externally,
and pacifying the common people internally.
He sets his heart on the imperial court,
diligently performing his tribute duties.
He should be granted an imperial appointment
to commend his profound achievements.
He is to be made Chíjíe, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Liáng Hé Shā Sānzhōu Zhūjūnjì, Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn, Lǐng Hù Xióngnú Zhōnglángjiàng, Xīyí Xiàowèi, Liángzhōu Cìshǐ, and Héxī Wáng."
When Wú Huì died,
his younger brother Ānzhōu was enthroned.
In the twenty-first year,
an edict stated:
"The younger brother of the late Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn and Héxī Wáng Wú Huì, Ānzhōu,
possesses profound talent and strategy,
and his family has been steadfastly loyal [fā].
He has taken over the inherited enterprise,
and the people are devoted to him.
Although he lost soldiers and an army,
and stands isolated in a different place,
he has been able to rally the remnants and the weak,
repelling invaders to this day.
He should be given honorable appointments,
setting a standard following his predecessors.
He is to be made Shǐchíjíe, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Liáng Hé Shā Sānzhōu Zhūjūnjì, Lǐng Xīyù Wùjǐ Xiàowèi, Liángzhōu Cìshǐ, and Héxī Wáng."
In the third year of Shìzǔ Dàmíng,
Ānzhōu offered local products.
The historian said: The Dī relied on their hereditary resources,
and the Hú, due to their sudden rise,
rooted themselves across a hundred qǐng,
possessing the land west of the Yellow River.
Although the Rong and Yi barbarians disturbed China,
seizing power in the wild territories,
their wealth and power were considerable,
and they somewhat valued etiquette and culture.
The Yáng clan, with their elite soldiers and dangerous terrain,
bordered Huá and Hàn,
watching for gaps in the border passes,
vacillating at the frontier.
Consequently, they entered Báimǎ in the west,
and exited Huángjīn in the east,
capitalizing on the victory at Jìnshòu,
instigating the conflict of besieging Fú,
planning to swallow Hēishuǐ,
aiming to conquer Jǐnglào.
The positions of Jǐ and Yǐng were in danger,
and the hearts of Fán and Dèng were frequently alarmed.
The Son of Heaven, presiding over court, was displeased,
longing for generals like Xīn and Lǐ.
But Xuānhuáng of Qí,
leading a partial army of several hundred,
was destined to be the vanguard,
pushing the front directly,
with momentum exceeding wind and lightning,
sweeping like clouds,
reaching Nánchéng.
He pursued the fleeing enemy,
achieving a complete victory over ten thousand lǐ,
and the enemies all wrapped bones and carried corpses,
fleeing over treacherous terrain to hide themselves.
The rest left their bodies in the mountains and wilds,
abandoning their bones in rivers and marshes.
Soon after, the two generals Péi and Liú,
relying on his prestige,
thus made the turbid waters lose their banners,
and Lángāo lose its strategic advantage.
The Dī tribe migrated and fled,
their remaining embers no more than a thread.
The land of Liáng achieved peace [yì],
lasting until today.
From this perspective,
