his achievements can be said to be great.
Jiàokān Jì
Lièzhuàn Dì Wǔshíjiǔ Èr Xiōng
Yuán Xiōng Shào, courtesy name Xiūyuǎn,
was the eldest son of Wéndì.
The Emperor gave birth to Shào after his enthronement.
At that time, the Emperor was still in the period of mourning,
so it was kept secret.
In the leap first month of the third year,
it was then announced that Shào was born.
Since previous generations,
no ruler had given birth to a crown prince after the empress's enthronement;
only Dì Yǐ of Yīn, after ascending the throne, had his primary consort give birth to Zhòu,
and now there was Shào.
Being born in the proper position of the principal consort,
the Emperor was greatly pleased.
At the age of six,
he was appointed Crown Prince,
and two Zhongshùzǐ were assigned to guard Yǒngfú Shěng.
A new palace was built for him,
with strict and beautiful regulations.
At the age of twelve,
he moved to the Eastern Palace,
and the daughter of Huángmén Shìláng Yīn Chún was taken as his consort.
At thirteen,
he came of age.
He enjoyed reading historical texts,
and especially loved archery and horsemanship.
When he grew up,
he had beautiful eyebrows and beard,
large eyes and a square mouth,
and was seven feet four inches tall.
He personally oversaw palace affairs,
and received guests.
Whatever he desired,
the Emperor would certainly grant it.
Soldiers were stationed in the Eastern Palace,
equivalent to the Yǔlín.
In the seventeenth year,
Shào paid respects at Jīnglíng.
Dàjiāngjūn Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng, Jìnglíng Wáng Dàn, and Shàngshū Guìyáng Hóu Yìróng all accompanied him.
Sīkōng Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng came from Jiāngdū to meet at Jīngkǒu.
In the twenty-seventh year,
when the Emperor was about to embark on a northern expedition,
Shào and Xiāo Sīhuà strongly advised against it,
but he did not listen.
When the Suǒ barbarians reached Guābù,
the capital was alarmed.
Shào moved to garrison Shítóu,
commanding the naval forces,
and was skilled in comforting and managing them.
The Emperor ascended Shítóuchéng,
looking worried.
Shào said:
"Without executing Jiāng Zhàn and Xú Zhànzhī,
there is no way to apologize to the world."
The Emperor said:
"The northern expedition was my own idea;
it has nothing to do with those two."
At that time, the Emperor focused on his main duties,
encouraging farming and sericulture,
making everyone in the palace raise silkworms,
wishing to inspire and motivate the entire realm.
There was a female shaman named Yán Dàoyù,
originally from Wúxīng.
She claimed to communicate with spirits
and could command ghosts and spirits.
Her husband was a bandit and was punished by being sent to the Xīguān.
Wáng Yīngwǔ, a maid of Shào's elder sister, Dōngyáng Gōngzhǔ, told the princess:
"Dàoyù has extraordinary spiritual powers."
The princess then informed the Emperor,
falsely claiming that she was skilled at sericulture,
and requested that she be summoned
to meet.
After Dàoyù entered,
she claimed to practice esoteric arts involving diet,
and the princess and Shào both believed and were deluded by her.
Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn had always flattered Shào,
and he and Shào had many transgressions.
Fearing the Emperor would find out,
they made Dàoyù pray and make requests,
hoping their transgressions would not reach the Emperor's ears.
Dàoyù always said:
"I have made direct appeals to Heaven;
it will certainly not be leaked."
Shào and others respectfully served her,
calling her "Tiānshī."
Later, they resorted to witchcraft,
using a jade figure in the Emperor's likeness,
and burying it in front of Hánzhāng Diàn.
Initially,
Princess Dōngyáng had a slave named Chén Tiānxīng.
Yīngwǔ raised him as a son,
and committed adultery with him.
Yīngwǔ, Tiānxīng, and Qìngguó (a eunuch presented by Níngzhōu) were all involved in witchcraft and sorcery.
Shào appointed Tiānxīng as a duìzhǔ (隊主).
When Princess Dōngyáng passed away,
Yīngwǔ was supposed to be married off.
Shào worried that the matter would be hard to keep secret,
so he consulted with Jùn about it.
At that time, Shěn Huáiyuǎn of Wúxīng was Jùn's aide,
and was treated with unusual favor.
So, Yīngwǔ was married to Huáiyuǎn as a concubine.
This was not reported to the Emperor,
fearing that if the matter leaked later,
Princess Línhè would hint at it.
The Emperor later learned that Tiānxīng was a duìzhǔ,
and sent the eunuch Xī Chéngzǔ to rebuke Shào, saying:
"Princess Línhè's southern residence previously had a servant girl who was to be married off.
I also heard that this servant girl raised another's slave as a son,
and you employed him as a duìzhǔ.
Why is your promotion so swift?
Are your recently appointed principals and deputies
all slaves?
Where do you intend to marry off that servant girl?"
Shào replied:
"The southern residence previously belonged to Tiānxīng.
He requested to be put to use,
and your servant replied: 'How can you obtain a position in the army?
If you can defeat rebels, you can join the ranks.'
That was merely a jest at the time,
and I had completely forgotten it.
Later, Tiānxīng came along the road to submit a petition for a position.
Recalling my past words,
I could not bear to break my promise.
I called him to observe him and saw that he was robust and strong,
capable of being put to use.
Thus, I appointed him supervisor of ceremonies and concurrently deputy duìzhǔ.
Although I have typically employed old retainers,
I also use those with spirit and capability.
I respectfully submit a list of names.
As for the servant girl who is to be married,
she has yet to find a place."
At this time, Yīngwǔ had already been married to Huáiyuǎn.
Shào was frightened,
and sent a urgent letter to Jùn,
and also had a message sent to Princess Línhè:
"If the Emperor asks about her marriage,
say that she has no fixed destination yet."
Jùn replied in a letter:
"Upon receiving your order,
I am deeply alarmed and fearful.
This matter was brought up many days ago,
and now they are just asking.
There must be someone who stirred it up,
but the source is yet unknown.
I reckon Princess Línhè should not be expected to change her words
and cause trouble for herself.
That old woman has always played both sides,
it's hard to rely solely on her.
It's best to ask Princess Línhè directly
in hopes of discerning the truth.
If she is questioned,
she should answer evasively.
Tiānxīng was previously appointed to a position in the 'fawning person's' establishment;
I wonder if the Emperor's records do not contain this.
He should be castrated immediately.
Has Your Highness seen the King yet?
You should follow this and thoroughly make a solemn personal report to the Emperor.
If 'that person' does not stop,
we can just shorten his remaining life.
This might even be the beginning of a great blessing."
All letters between Shào and Jùn were similar to this.
Their words were all code names.
They referred to the Emperor as
"that person" (彼人)
or
"the person" (其人).
They referred to the Grand Commandant, Prince Yìgōng of Jiāngxià, as
"the fawning person" (佞人).
Princess Dōngyáng's residence was outside the Xīyèmén,
hence it was called
"the southern residence" (南第).
Wáng (王) was Yīngwǔ's surname.
"Making a personal report to the Emperor" (躬上啟聞) meant
ordering Dàoyù to report to the Heavenly God.
After Yīngwǔ married Huáiyuǎn,
fearing that her illicit affair with Tiānxīng would be exposed,
she asked Shào to kill him.
Shào secretly sent someone to harm Tiānxīng.
Qìngguó, thinking that there were only two people (Tiānxīng and himself) who knew about the communications,
and with Tiānxīng now dead,
feared that he would be implicated.
So he fully reported the matter to the Emperor.
The Emperor was shocked and horrified,
and immediately ordered Yīngwǔ's arrest,
sealing and inventorying her household.
Hundreds of letters from Shào and Jùn were found,
all containing curses and witchcraft.
Images of the Emperor that had been buried within the palace were also discovered.
Dàoyù rebelled and fled,
but could not be captured.
The Emperor was furious,
and thoroughly investigated the matter,
dispatching imperial envoys to various eastern commanderies to search,
but still without success.
The Emperor questioned and rebuked Shào and Jùn.
Shào and Jùn were terrified and speechless,
merely offering apologies.
Dàoyù disguised herself as a nun
and hid in the Eastern Palace.
When Jùn went to Jīngkǒu,
he took her with him.
Sometimes she stayed at the house of a commoner named Zhāng Wǔ.
When Prince Yìgōng of Jiāngxià returned to court from Xūyí,
the Emperor informed him about the witchcraft,
saying:
"I have often seen such things in classics and records,
calling them empty words from books and biographies.
I never expected to witness them with my own eyes.
Although Shào's actions are wicked,
they may not necessarily lead to the downfall of the state.
The day he faces south as emperor
will no longer be a matter for you or me.
You have many sons;
they will unfortunately encounter this."
Twenty-eight years earlier,
a comet had appeared in Bì and Áng,
entered Tàiwēi,
swept past Dìzuò and Duānmén,
and extinguished Yì and Zhěn.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Huánghuò (Mars) moved retrograde and guarded Dī.
From the eleventh month, there was continuous rain and snow,
and the sun rarely shone.
In the first month of the thirtieth year,
there was a great wind, flying hailstones, and thunder.
The Emperor worried about secret uprisings,
and consistently increased Shào's troops.
The Eastern Palace actually had ten thousand armed men.
When the imperial carriage went out,
Shào would guard it,
and ordered his generals to follow with the Bái Zhí (白直) guards.
In the second month of that year,
Jùn came to court from Jīngkǒu.
He was supposed to guard Jiānglíng,
but again carried Dàoyù back to the Eastern Palace,
intending to take her west.
Someone reported to the Emperor, saying:
"There is a nun at the house of a commoner named Zhāng Wǔ in Jīngkǒu,
who eats and dresses well,
and frequently enters and exits the Grand General Who Conquers the North's residence.
She appears to be Yán Dàoyù."
The Emperor initially did not believe it,
but tried to send men to capture her.
They caught her two maids,
who said:
"Dàoyù returned to the capital with the Grand General Who Conquers the North."
The Emperor thought that Shào and Jùn would have already dismissed Dàoyù,
but they were still associating with her.
He was dismayed and shocked.
So he ordered Dàoyù's two maids to be sent by boat from Jīngkǒu.
He waited until they arrived for verification.
He intended to depose Shào
and grant Jùn death.
He conveyed this to Jùn's mother, Consort Pān Shúfēi.
Shúfēi then fully informed Jùn.
Jùn immediately reported to Shào.
Shào then began to conspire for rebellion.
Every night he hosted banquets for his generals and soldiers,
sometimes personally serving wine.
He secretly plotted with his trusted duìzhǔ Chén Shū'ér and Zhān Shū'ér,
and his zhāishuài Zhāng Chāozhī and Rèn Jiànzhī.
When Dào Yù's婢 was about to arrive,
on the twenty-first night of that month,
a forged imperial edict was presented, saying:
"Lǔ Xiù is plotting rebellion.
You should guard the palace gates at dawn
and lead your troops in."
Thereupon, Zhāng Chāo-zhī and others gathered over two thousand soldiers they had previously raised and kept,
had them all don armor,
summoned the internal and external banner-unit commanders and deputies,
and assigned them to positions in advance,
saying they were to suppress something.
Xiāo Bīn, former Zhongshùzǐ and Right Army Changshǐ, was summoned overnight.
At night, Bīn, Yuán Shú, Left Weìlǜ, Yīn Zhòng-sù, Zhongshèrén, and Wáng Zhèng-jiàn, Left Jīnǔ Jiāngjūn, were called
to enter the palace together,
where they were informed of the great matter.
He himself rose and bowed to Bīn and the others,
then wept.
Everyone was startled and amazed.
The account is in Shú's biography.
The next morning, before the drums sounded,
Shào wore a crimson robe over his military attire,
rode in a painted-wheeled carriage,
sharing it with Xiāo Bīn.
His retinue was as usual for entering court.
The gate guards opened the gates,
and they entered through Wànchūn Gate.
According to the old system,
the Eastern Palace troops were not allowed to enter the city.
Shào told the gate guards:
"I have received an imperial order
to carry out a suppression."
He ordered the rear troops to come quickly.
Zhāng Chāo-zhī and dozens of others galloped into Yúnlóng Gate, Dōng Zhōnghuá Gate, and the side chambers,
drawing their blades and directly ascending to Hédian.
That night, the emperor was speaking with Xú Zhàn-zhī, Shàngshū Púyè, with all attendants dismissed.
The candles were still unextinguished at dawn,
and the direct guards were still asleep.
Chāo-zhī personally committed regicide
and also killed Zhàn-zhī.
Shào advanced to the central chamber of Hédian.
Tàizǔ had already died.
He went out and sat in the Eastern Hall,
with Xiāo Bīn holding a saber and standing guard.
He called for Gù Gǔ, Zhongshū Shèrén.
Gǔ, trembling with fear, did not come out immediately.
When he finally arrived,
Shào asked:
"You wished to see me deposed. Why didn't you reveal it earlier?"
Before he could answer,
he was immediately beheaded in front of them.
Men were sent to Chónglǐ Tà to kill Jiāng Zhàn, Lìbù Shàngshū.
Bǔ Tiān-yǔ, Tàizǔ's Left Xìzhàng Zhǔ, attacked Shào in the Eastern Hall
and was killed.
Men were also sent from the Eastern Chamber to kill Pān Shúfēi,
and also killed dozens of Tàizǔ's trusted close attendants.
Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn was urgently summoned
to lead troops and encamp in Zhōngtáng.
Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng, Tàiwèi, and Hé Shàng-zhī, Shàngshūlìng, were also summoned.
Shào immediately ascended to the spurious throne,
and issued a letter stating:
"Xú Zhàn-zhī and Jiāng Zhàn committed regicide without cause.
I led my troops into the palace,
but it was already too late.
I cried out in sorrow and broke down,
my liver and heart torn apart.
Now that the culprits are found,
and the chief villain has been eliminated,
a general amnesty may be granted to the empire.
The thirtieth year of Yuánjiā is changed to the first year of Tàichū.
All civil and military officials are granted two ranks.
All other categories shall follow the Dīngmǎo regulations."
Initially, Xiāo Bīn was asked to draft the edict,
but Bīn declined, citing his lack of literary skill.
Then Shìzhōng Wáng Sēng-chuò was made to do it.
The change of reign title to Tàichū
had been decided by Shào and Dào Yù.
Bīn said:
"It was customary to change the reign title after the turn of the year."
Shào asked Sēng-chuò about this,
and Sēng-chuò replied:
"Jìn Huìdì changed his reign title immediately upon ascending the throne."
Shào was pleased and followed this.
Only a few dozen officials arrived,
and Shào hastily ascended the throne.
After the enthronement,
he feigned illness and returned to Yǒngfú Shěng.
Only then was the great departed emperor moved to the front hall of Tàijí.
On this day,
Xiāo Bīn was appointed Sànqí Chángshì, Shàngshū Púyè, and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
Hé Shàng-zhī was appointed Sīkōng.
Tán Hé-zhī, former Right Weìlǜ, was stationed at Shítou.
Yì Qí, Shìzhōng Yíngdào Hóu, was appointed Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Jìnlíng Nán Xiàpí Èr Jùn Tàishǒu,
to guard the capital city.
Yīn Chōng, Shàngshū, was appointed Shìzhōng and Zhōnghùjūn.
At the great enshrouding of the great departed emperor,
Shào excused himself due to illness and did not dare to appear.
The weapons previously distributed to the various princes and other places
were all recalled to the arsenal.

The close associates of Xú Zhàn-zhī and Jiāng Zhàn were killed: Xún Chì-sōng, newly appointed Shǐxīng Nèishǐ; Zāng Níng-zhī, newly appointed Shàngshū Zuǒchéng; Fù Sēng-yòu, Shānyīn Lìng; Jiāng Huī, Wú Lìng; Zhūgě Xǔ, former Zhēngběi Xíng Cānjūn; and Jiāng Wéngāng, Right Weì Sīmǎ.
Yīn Zhòng-sù was appointed Huángmén Shìláng.
Wáng Zhèng-jiàn was appointed Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn.
Zhāng Chāo-zhī and other co-conspirators, including Wén Wén-zǐ, Xú Xīng-zǔ, Zhān Shú-ér, Chén Shú-ér, Rèn Jiàn-zhī, and others,
were all appointed from commander and below to Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn with district appointments,
and each was granted 200,000 cash.
An envoy was sent to tell Lǔ Xiù:
"Xú Zhàn-zhī always wanted to harm you.
I have already eliminated him for you."
Xiù was made to jointly command the military forces with Páng Xiù-zhī, Túnyí Xiàowèi.
Wáng Sēng-chuò, Shìzhōng, was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū.
Hé Yǎn, Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ, was appointed Shìzhōng.
On the day of donning mourning attire,
Shào ascended the hall, approached the spirit,
and wept uncontrollably.
He extensively consulted with the gōngqīng,
sought methods of governance,
lightened taxes and corvée,
and reduced various extravagant expenses.
Any fields, gardens, mountains, and marshes
that could be opened up
were leased to poor people.
In the third month,
grand envoys were sent to tour the four directions.
The five prefectures east of Zhè were divided to form Huìzhōu.
Yángzhōu was abolished and a Sīlì Xiàowèi was established,
with Yīn Chōng appointed to this post.
Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng, Dàjiāngjūn, was appointed Tàibǎo.
Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān, Sītú, was appointed Tàiwèi.
Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn, Weì Jiāngjūn and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ, was promoted to Piàojí Jiāngjūn.
Wáng Sēng-chuò was executed
because he had been involved in the deposition and enthronement.
Chángshā Wáng Jǐn, Jǐn's younger brother Kǎi, Línchuān Wáng Yè, Guìyáng Hóu Jì, and Xīnyú Hóu Jiè
were all imprisoned and died due to old grudges.
The ritual officials, trying to please,
did not dare to use the most beautiful titles for Tàizǔ's posthumous name,
instead bestowing the posthumous title Zhōngzōng Jǐng Huángdì.
Zāng Zhì, Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ, was appointed Dānyáng Yǐn.
Shìzǔ was promoted to Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn
and given the additional title Sànqí Chángshì.
Nánpíng Wáng Shuò, Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn, was promoted to Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn.
Suí Wáng Dàn, Kuàijī Tàishǒu, was appointed Huìzhōu Cìshǐ.
Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng, as Tàibǎo, also held the title Dà Zōngshī.
The procedures for consultation and reporting
followed the precedent of Jìn Fúfēng Wáng.
Shìzǔ, Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān, Suí Wáng Dàn, and other regional commanders all raised righteous armies.
When Shào heard that a great righteous army had risen,
he gathered all the princes and high officials within the city,
moved Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng to the lower residence of the Shàngshū,
and Yìgōng's sons to the lower residence of the Shìzhōng.
Before the first year of Yǒngchū,
the Xiangguó Fǔ's household staff, instructors, and attendants
were exempted from military service
and belonged to Xuē Xiàn, Nán Péngchéng.
Shào issued a decree,
stating that as he was raising an army in the middle of the river,
he would personally lead the six armies
to observe the changes along the Jiāng.
He summoned all subordinate officers and officials.
The Tàishǒu of the Three Wú were given military titles
and appointed assistants to lead troops.
In the fourth month,
his wife, Lady Yīn, was made Empress.
Shìzǔ issued a proclamation to Jīngyì, saying: "The fortunes of fate are not always prosperous;
there are great misfortunes in every generation.
From ancient times,
some have turned great difficulties into blessings,
while others have created chaos through dim-witted cruelty.
It is always due to
the righteous union of ruler and minister,
where reason deviates and grace departs,
thus the formation of solid ice
always afflicts the decadent age.
Never has it been that one governs the world with the Dao,
with clear and profound teachings,
yet encounters such an unfilial and treacherous
attack,
with disaster arising among close relatives.
The former emperor, with his sacred virtue, was in power,
his achievements reached throughout the land,
his brilliance illuminated all nations,
and his Dao was boundless.
Wherever his influence reached,
remote corners changed
their understanding;
wherever his benevolence stirred,
even wood and stone opened their hearts.
Yet the villain Shào, relying on being the legitimate heir,
received favor and cultivation from an early age,
holding the righteous position of the Eastern Palace,
with courtesies surpassing those of rulers and queens.
His cruel and arrogant
nature
emerged in childhood,
and his suspicious and ruthless heart
developed as he grew.
The villain Jùn was reckless and without moral conduct.
From youth to adulthood,
they relied on each other,
jointly indulging in treachery."
Previously, because the royal house suffered misfortune,
and domestic troubles quickly mounted,
we therefore concealed and tolerated,
not revealing the transgressions,
instructing, guiding, and admonishing,
hoping that they might change their ways.
Who could have known that the mad villainy
would not repent,
and those of like evil would aid each other,
starting the rebellion with witchcraft,
and ultimately committing regicide?
The sacred person suffered the pain of bitter poison,
and the altars of soil and grain faced the sorrow of destruction.
The four seas are heartbroken,
and gods and men weep blood.
Since the beginning of humankind,
such calamity has never been heard of.
Upon hearing the tragic news, we cried out in shock,
our livers and brains scattered on the ground.
Our hearts are filled with vexation and injustice,
with nowhere to rest our bodies.
The Grand General and
the various princes are imprisoned in isolated quarters,
their fate unknown.
Xú Púshè, Jiāng Shàngshū, and Yuán Zuǒshuài,
all outstanding figures of their time,
loyal and steadfast for a generation,
some with righteous
expressions standing in court,
others refusing to submit when hearing of rebellion,
were all violently cut down at the palace gates,
their heads displayed in the marketplace.
Their clans were exterminated;
it is not merely one surname.
The flow of disaster and poison
is yet
unknown in its extent.
In ancient times, when the Zhōu (周) dynasty faced crisis,
Qí (齊) and Jìn (晉) toiled for the king.
When the Hàn (漢) imperial line was interrupted,
Xū (虛) and Móu (牟) established their integrity.
Even those of different surnames or distant relations
would sacrifice their lives.
How much more so for this headquarters, whose duties are the same as
those of past men,
whose righteousness encompasses both minister and son!
Therefore, we sleep on spears and taste gall,
barely preserving our breath,
resolved to eliminate the chief culprit,
to slightly avenge this shame.
Now, we order Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍) to lead Zīyì Zhōngzhíbīng (諮議中直兵) Liǔ Yuánjǐng (柳元景) and Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) to lead Zhōngzhíbīng (中直兵) Mǎ Wéngōng (馬文恭) and others,
to command thirty thousand elite troops,
to swiftly advance directly to Shítóu (石頭),
and then diverge towards Bái
xià (白下).
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍) leading Zīyì Zhōngzhíbīng (諮議中直兵) Zōngwēi (宗微) and others,
commands twenty thousand armed soldiers.
Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (征虜將軍) leading Sīmǎ (司馬) and Wǔchāng (武昌) Nèishǐ (內史) Shěn Qìngzhī (沈慶之)
and others,
commands fifty thousand brave warriors,
following closely on their path.
Detached forces, separately commanded,
some burning boats and breaking cauldrons, marching on foot from Gūshú (姑孰),
others swiftly rowing to Wúhú (蕪湖),
entering and occupying Yún
yáng (雲陽).
All these commanders
are valiant and extraordinary,
with profound wisdom and strategy,
their names shaking the central lands,
their achievements spreading to distant borders.
This headquarters personally directs over one hundred thousand elite and fierce troops,
with military laws set and spears ready,
successively advancing in a continuous stream.
The Sītú (司徒), with his sagacious wisdom and profound plans,
has erupted in mighty power,
mobilizing armies from eight provinces,
and rising like lightning from Jīng (荊) and Yǐng (郢).
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍)
Zāng Zhì (臧質), whose loyalty and valor are universally praised,
moves like thunder at Hàn
yīn (漢陰).
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍) Zhū Xiūzhī (朱脩之), with sincere integrity and genuine intent,
exerts all his strength, requesting to fight.
The million troops from Jīng (荊) and Yōng (雍)
are gradually approaching,
and the forces from Shǔ (蜀) and Hàn (漢)
have already crossed the border.
Furthermore, Āndōng Jiāngjūn (安東將軍) Dàn (誕), Píngxī Jiāngjūn (平西將軍) Zūnkǎo (遵考), former Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn (撫軍將軍) Xiāo Sīhuà (蕭思話), Zhēnglǔ Jiāng
jūn (征虜將軍) Lǔ Shuǎng (魯爽), and former Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將jūn) Wáng Xuánmó (王玄謨)
have all sent secret messages,
not failing to act together.
They have dispatched proclamations across the Three Wú (三吳) regions,
and are rushing their armies to the capital.
Near and far, all are mobilizing,
their banners stretching ten thousand *lǐ*.
When towering warships surge through the rivers,
the dark currents roar,
and when sharp armor advances across the fields,
the dense forests' roots are crushed.
Wise strategists and discerning scholars,
heroic men and resolute soldiers,
have been nurturing
their aspirations, waiting for the opportune moment,
harboring indignation, awaiting their deployment.
The spiritual benevolence of the former sagely emperor
is embedded in the hearts of the people.
The great principle of rebellion and submission
is subtly manifested in the ways of heaven.
A country without a father (ruler)
is unheard of in the world.
Now that the urgent dispatches have flown,
both Chinese and barbarians respond and gather.
With such a multitude fighting,
who can resist?
With such righteousness motivating,
where can we not achieve victory?
Moreover, the rebellious villains are friendless,
rejected by both men and spirits.
Counting those of like evil,
they do not number even one company.
They elevate insignificant individuals,
associating with them.
Wise men and gentlemen
will surely hold them in deep contempt.
Pouring the sea to extinguish a firefly,
toppling a mountain
to crush an egg –
the situations of Shāng (商) and Zhōu (周)
are truly incomparable.
Gentlemen, some of you are virtuous through generations,
personally imbued with imperial grace.
Others have established great merits,
their fortunes intertwined with the nation.
Under the constraint of the villainous power,
bowing your heads to the rebels' hands,
swallowing indignation
and enduring sorrow,
this cannot be your true intention.
Our grand army is now close,
its formidable reputation already felt.
It is opportune to seize this change to achieve merit
and wipe away accumulated disgrace.
If circumstances prevent this,
to abandon rebellion
and return to loyalty
is also a secondary option.
However, should anyone persist in delusion
and side with the villainous faction,
they shall be punished without pardon,
and their punishment shall extend to their five degrees of kindred.
The laws of reward and punishment
are as trustworthy as the sun
and moon.
Once the prairie fire ignites,
all disparate things turn to ash together.
Seek abundant blessings now,
do not leave behind future regrets.
Upon receipt of this document, proclaim it
so that all may hear and know.
Shào considered himself well-versed in military affairs.
He told his court officials:
"You merely need to assist me in managing documents.
Do not concern yourselves with military formations.
If there is a bandit rebellion,
I will personally lead the army.
My only fear is that the bandits will not dare to make a move!"
Sīlì Xiàowèi Yīn Chōng took charge of compiling documents.
Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Yǐn Hóng was assigned to military matters.
Xiāo Bīn oversaw all general affairs.
A general alert was issued both inside and outside the capital.
Emperor Shìzǔ’s sons were guarded in the Shìzhōng Xiàshěng.
Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān’s sons were guarded in an empty house in Tàicāng.
Shào had Jùn write a letter to Emperor Shìzǔ, saying:
"I hear that my brother has suddenly raised a mad banner,
obstructing the army and turning against us.
Gentlemen are indignant and sighing,
and righteous men are enraged.
Throughout history, those who have usurped their superiors and committed internal treachery,
who among them has not been annihilated?
My brother, you are thoroughly knowledgeable in ancient texts,
how could you not be aware of this?
Now, the Lord is endowed by Heaven with exceptional sagacity;
his spiritual and martial prowess are greatly manifested.
Since ascending the throne,
his might and benevolence have been universally proclaimed.
People harbor a will to die gladly,
and all strive to sacrifice their lives.
My brother, you received his favor and kindness,
evident from your youth.
The joy of the Eastern Palace
feels like only yesterday.
Yet you are misled by treacherous villains,
forgetting this grace and friendship.
Such injustice
is detested by both men and gods.
Now, all our land and naval forces are fully prepared.
The Lord himself will personally command the six armies,
and Tàibǎo will also wield the battle-axe and oversee them.
Wú and Wūyáng
will immediately follow on the road.
The reason for the delay in striking like lightning
is merely that we still hope my brother, though deluded, will know to return.
Therefore, I briefly express my feelings;
these words cannot fully convey my meaning.
The Lord's sacred grace
has always been generous to Fǎshī.
He is now residing in the palace.
I imagine my brother would want to know his whereabouts,
hence this mention."
Wūyáng refers to
Nánpíng Wáng Shuò;
Fǎshī
was the childhood name of Emperor Shìzǔ’s eldest son.
Shào wanted to kill the families of the common people and soldiers from the three garrisons.
Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng and Hé Shàngzhī persuaded him, saying:
"Those who undertake great endeavors
do not worry about their families.
Moreover, most of them were compelled.
If we suddenly execute their remaining dependents,
it will only strengthen their resolve."
Shào considered this to be true,
and thus issued an order to leave them completely undisturbed.
He sent Chǔ Zhànzhī to garrison Shítou,
and Liú Sīkǎo to guard Dōngfǔ.
Jùn and Xiāo Bīn urged Shào to command the naval forces himself to go upstream and engage in a decisive battle.
If not,
then to hold Liángshān.
Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng feared that the righteous army, being hastily assembled,
had crude and small ships,
making a naval battle unsuitable.
He then proposed a strategy, saying:
"The bandit Jùn is young and inexperienced in military affairs.
They have traveled a long distance and are fatigued.
It is advisable to await them at our leisure.
If we advance far to Liángshān,
then the capital will be empty and weak.
The eastern army, taking advantage of the vacuum,
might pose a threat.
If we divide our forces to meet both,
our troops will be scattered and our power weakened.
It is better to preserve our strength and await the opportune moment,
sitting and observing the situation."
Shào approved of his suggestion.
Xiāo Bīn sternly said:
"The Nánzhōngláng, being only twenty years old,
has already accomplished such a great feat;
how can he still be underestimated?
The three sides are united in their evil,
holding the strategic upstream positions.
Shěn Qìngzhī is very skilled in military matters,
and Liǔ Yuánjǐng and Zōng [Gǒngxīn] have repeatedly achieved merits.
With such a situation,
they are truly not a minor enemy.
We should only seize the opportunity before popular sentiment turns against us,
and we can still fight a decisive battle.
How can we endure for long
by merely sitting in the Táichéng?
Both the Lord and the Prime Minister have no intention to fight.
This is truly Heaven's will."
Shào did not accept this.
Suspecting that all the old officials of the court would not serve him,
he treated Wáng Luóhàn and Lǔ Xiù generously,
entrusting all military affairs to them,
and bestowing many precious artifacts and beautiful women
to please them.
Luóhàn was formerly a staff officer (cānjūn) of the Right Army under Nánpíng Wáng Shuò.
Shào, recognizing his leadership ability,
entrusted him with matters of utmost importance.
Some advised Shào to hold Shítouchéng.
Shào said:
"The ancients fortified Shítou
to await the regional lords coming to aid the emperor.
If I guard this place,
who will come to my rescue?
I must fight with all my strength to decide the outcome,
otherwise, I will not succeed."
Every day, he personally went out to inspect the troops,
comforting and encouraging the officers and soldiers.
He personally supervised the Department of Waterways in repairing ships,
burned the southern bank,
and forced all common people's households to cross to the north side of the water.
He had his officials submit a memorial to establish his son Wěizhī as the Crown Prince,
appointed Chǔ Zhànzhī as Hòujiāngjūn and Dānyáng Yǐn,
with attached staff.
Piàojì Jiāngjūn Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn was appointed Shìzhōng, Zhōngshū Jiān, Sītú, and Lù Shàngshū Liù Tiáo Shì.
Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn Nánpíng Wáng Shuò was appointed Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Nányǎn Yǎn Qīng Xú Jì Wǔ Zhōu Zhū Jūnjì, Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
The newly appointed Zuǒ Jiāngjūn and Dānyáng Yǐn Jiànpíng Wáng Hóng was appointed Sànqí Chángshì, Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn, and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Páng Xiùzhī was the first among the masses to flee south from Shítou,
causing a great shock among the people.
Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Yíngdào Hóu Yìqí was appointed Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ with his original title.
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Tán Hézhī was appointed Xīzhōnglángjiāng and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the 19th day,
the righteous army reached Xīnlín.
Shào ascended the beacon tower at Shítou to observe them.
On the 21st day,
the righteous army reached Xīntíng.
At that time, Lǔ Xiù was stationed at Báishí.
Shào summoned Xiù to jointly encamp with Wáng Luóhàn at Zhūquèmén.
Xiāo Bīn commanded the infantry,
and Chǔ Zhànzhī commanded the navy.
On the 22nd day,
Shào sent Xiāo Bīn to lead Lǔ Xiù, Wáng Luóhàn, and others with 10,000 elite soldiers to attack Xīntíng fort.
Shào ascended Zhūquèmén to personally supervise them.
The officers and soldiers, motivated by Shào's generous rewards,
all fought bravely for him.
They were on the verge of victory,
but Xiù withdrew his troops and stopped abruptly,
allowing Liǔ Yuánjǐng and others to attack them,
thus suffering a great defeat.
Shào then led his confidants and co-conspirators to personally attack the fort again.
Yuánjǐng once more defeated them.
Shào fled back to Zhūquèmén,
and Xiāo Bīn's arm was struck by a stray arrow.
Chǔ Zhànzhī's two sons, together with Tán Hézhī, surrendered.
Shào was startled and frightened,
and fled back to Táichéng.
That night,
Lǔ Xiù also fled south.
At that time, Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng planned to occupy Shítou,
but it happened that Shào had already ordered Jùn and Xiāo Bīn to guard it.
Shào also burned the military records of the capital,
established commanderies and counties,
and placed them all under the Sīlì as common people.
Former Army General and Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Wáng Luóhàn was appointed Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
retaining his Fǔguó title.
Zuǒjūn Wáng Zhèngjiàn was appointed Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ.
On the 25th day,
Yìgōng fled south alone on horseback,
exiting through the Dōngyèmén,
and crossing the Huái River at Yězhǔ.
The Dōngyèmén squad leader, Wú Dàoxìng, was a disciple of Zāng Zhì.
The Yězhǔ military commander, Yuán Zhìsūn, was a former historian of Emperor Shìzǔ.
Yìgōng thus managed to escape.
Shào dispatched cavalry to pursue and capture him.
When the cavalry reached Yězhǔ,
Yìgōng had just managed to cross the Huái River.
Yìgōng's two thousand or more former staff and retainers,
who followed him in his flight south,
were mostly killed by the pursuing soldiers.
Shào sent Jùn to kill all of Yìgōng's sons.
He welcomed the divine statue of Jiǎng Hóu into the palace with a palanquin,
bowed his head to beg for grace,
appointed him Dàsīmǎ,
enfeoffed him as Zhōngshān Jùnwáng,
and added the symbols of authority, jié and yuè.
Sū Hóu was appointed Piàojì Jiāngjūn.
He ordered Nánpíng Wáng Shuò to draft a sacrificial prayer,
detailing Emperor Shìzǔ's crimes.
Jiā Jùn was made Cíjié, Dūdū Nánxúhuì Èrzhōu Zhūjūnjì, concurrently Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifù), and Inspector of Nánxúzhōu (Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ),
granted twenty guards with ceremonial swords (bānjiàn),
and Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn, Inspector of Nányǎnzhōu (Nányǎnzhōucìshǐ) Nánpíng Wáng Shuò was promoted to Píqí Jiāngjūn,
and together with Jùn, he was appointed to concurrently manage the affairs of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū Shì).
On the 27th,
the emperor personally held court to appoint Xī Wěizhī as the Crown Prince.
All officials wore military attire,
but Shào alone wore the emperor's ceremonial robe (gǔnyī).
An imperial edict granted a general amnesty to the empire,
except for Shìzǔ, Liú Yìgōng, Yìxuān, and Dàn, who were excluded from the pardon.
All other conspirators were not to be questioned.
Earlier, the Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo) Staff Officer Yǔ Dào and Supernumerary Gentleman-in-Waiting (Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng) Zhū Hézhī were dispatched,
〔一一〕and then the Palace General (Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn) Yàn Qīn was sent east to resist Dàn.
In the fifth month,
Shìzǔ’s dispatched Staff Officer Gù Bīnzhī and Dàn’s vanguard army
both arrived at Qǔ'ā.
They met Dào,
engaged in battle,
and were utterly routed.
Shào sent men to burn the western armory of the Directorate of Waterways (Dūshuǐ Xīzhuāng) and the Left Imperial Workshop (Zuǒ Shàngfāng),
and breached the Bǎigǎng and Fāngshān dikes to cut off the eastern army.
He also gathered all the male inhabitants (dīng) who lived in the lanes and guarded homes,
and erected tower-like warships (bóchuán) along the Huái River,
equipped with many large crossbows.

He also ordered the Central Judicial Inspector (Sīlì Zhìzhōng), who concurrently held the post of Administrator of Lángyé Commandery (Jiān Lángyé Jùnshì), Yáng Xī, to fence off and block the waterways of Bāndú and Báishí.
At that time, since all the able-bodied men (nándīng) were gone,
women were summoned to perform labor.
On the third day of that month,
Lǔ Xiù and others recruited five hundred brave warriors to attack Dàháng,
and managed to hook one ship.
Wáng Luóhàn, deputy to Yáng Shìdé, ordered a return to the ships,
but Luóhàn was drunk and enjoying a performance.
Hearing that the imperial army had crossed,
he became frightened and dropped his weapons, surrendering.
The troops along the riverbank,
one after another, fled in disarray,
leaving weapons, drums, and canopies
strewn across the streets.
That night,
Shào closed and guarded the six gates,
digging trenches and erecting fences inside them,
and using uncovered carriages as towers.
Chaos reigned within the city,
and there was no longer any discipline.
The Administrator of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn) Yǐn Hóng, Former Army General (Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn) Mèng Zōngsì, and other high-ranking officials and officers
all climbed over the city wall and fled.
Shào ordered Zhān Shú'ér to burn his imperial carriages (niǎn) and ceremonial robes and crowns (gǔnmiǎnfú).
Xiāo Bīn, hearing that Dàháng could not be held,
was panicked and did not know what to do.
He issued an order to his subordinates
to all lay down their arms.
From Shítou, he sent his son Yuē to the palace to beg for forgiveness,
and soon after, he came to surrender with a white banner.
He was immediately executed at the army gate.
On the fourth day,
Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng ascended the Zhūquè Gate,
commanding all the generals,
and dispatched Lǔ Xiù, Xuē Āndū, Chéng Tiānzuò, and others directly towards the Xuānyáng Gate.
Shào's army commanders Xú Xīngzǔ, Luó Xùn, Yúqiū Yào'ér, and others led their troops to surrender.
Shào had previously sent Dragon-borne General (Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn) Chén Shú'ér on an eastern campaign,
but with the situation critical,
he recalled him.
On this day, as he first entered the Jiànyáng Gate,
he saw the imperial army in the distance,
and his subordinates all abandoned their weapons and fled.
Shào’s close confidants and Imperial Bodyguards (Báizhí) who were involved in the rebellion, who had been stationed outside the Chānghé Gate,
all fled back into the palace.
Tiānzuò and Āndū's deputy Tán Jīn then took advantage of the situation
and immediately entered together.
Āndū and army commanders Wǔ Niàn, Zōng Yuè, and others followed closely behind.
〔一二〕Zāng Zhì's main army entered from the Guǎngmò Gate,
converging in front of the Tàijí Hall.
They immediately beheaded the Crown Prince's Left Guard Commander (Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ) Wáng Zhèngjiàn.
Jiànpíng, Dōnghǎi, and seven other princes cried out and fled together.
Shào burrowed through the western wall and entered a well in the armory,
where he was apprehended by squad leader Gāo Qín.
Jùn, leading several tens of his attendants,
exited with Nánpíng Wáng Shuò from the Xīmíng Gate,
and together they fled south.
At Yuèchéng, they encountered Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng.
Jùn dismounted and said:
“What is the Southern Colonel doing now?”
Yìgōng said:
“The four seas are without a ruler.
The officials firmly requested,
and His Majesty has
condescended to comply with the public's wishes and reigns over all nations.”
He also said:
“Did Hǔtóu come late?”
Yìgōng said:
“It is indeed regrettable that you came late.”
He then said:
“I suppose I won't die, will I?”
Yìgōng said:
“You may go to the temporary palace to beg for forgiveness.”
He then said:
“I wonder if I can still be granted a position to prove my worth?”
Yìgōng again said:
“That cannot be determined yet.”
He ordered Jùn to return with him,
and beheaded him on the road.
Jùn's courtesy name was Xiūmíng.
On the night of his birth,
an owl (fúniǎo) hooted on the roof.
In the 13th year of Yuánjiā (436 CE),
at the age of eight,
he was enfeoffed as Shǐxīng Wáng.
In the 16th year (439 CE),
he was made Dūdū Xiāngzhōu Zhūjūnjì, Hòujiāngjūn, and Inspector of Xiāngzhōu (Xiāngzhōucìshǐ).
He was then promoted to Cíjié, Dūdū Nányù Yù Sī Yōng Bìng Wǔzhōu Zhūjūnjì, and Inspector of Nányùzhōu (Nányùzhōucìshǐ),
with his general title remaining unchanged.
In the 17th year (440 CE),
he became Inspector of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu Cìshǐ),
with his general title remaining unchanged,
and established a staff to command troops.
In the 19th year (442 CE),
his administration was abolished.
In the 21st year (444 CE),
he was granted Sànqí Chángshì,
and promoted to Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn.
The following year (445 CE),
Jùn submitted a memorial, stating:
“The Wúxīng Commandery, which I administer,
is embraced by heavy mountains
and has many low-lying wetlands.
Spring flows gather,
but drainage is slow and obstructed.
Before the seasonal rains have passed,
it is already flooded and submerged.
Sometimes plowing is halted in early spring,
or crops are submerged in early autumn.
Farmers toil in vain,
and there is no way to prevent it.
That region is a fertile area,
with rich land and abundant people.
When there is a good harvest in one year,
the produce covers the capital.
But if there is a flood at times,
several commanderies suffer disaster.
In recent years,
there have been more famines than bumper harvests.
Although relief is generously distributed,
it depletes the national reserves.
The suffering of both public and private sectors
is far from over.
A local resident, Yáo Jiáo, recently submitted a practical suggestion,
believing that the four commanderies of Èrwú, Jìnlíng, and Yìxīng
all drain into Lake Tàihu,
but the Sōngjiāng and Hùdú waterways are obstructed and unfavorable,
thus causing flooding everywhere and leading to disasters.
He proposes to open a canal from Wǔkāng Zhùxī to Càogǔ Lake,
which would flow directly out to the sea mouth.
Over a hundred *lǐ* (li),
digging the canal
would certainly be unimpeded.
He has personally walked and measured the route
for about twenty years.
In the great flood eleven years ago,
he already went to the former Inspector, your minister Yìkāng, to propose this plan.
Yìkāng immediately sent his Registrar (Zhǔbù) Shèng Tántài to travel with Jiáo,
but doubts and difficulties arose,
and the proposal was consequently shelved.
Since this matter concerns a great public interest,
it should be thoroughly investigated.
I immediately dispatched my Council Supervisor (Yìcáo Cóngshìshǐ) Yú Chángsūn to accompany the Administrator of Wúxīng (Wúxīng Tàishǒu) Kǒng Shānshì to inspect the route together,
observing the terrain
and assessing the elevations.
They surveyed every river source and course,
leaving nothing unchecked.
They drew maps of the convenient features
and carefully calculated them.
According to their measurements,
they decisively concluded that it is feasible.
Furthermore, the four commanderies share this problem,
not just Wúxīng.
If this canal
is successfully opened, numerous regions will benefit.
Without temporary labor,
there is no way for lasting peace.
However, initiating a large project
is difficult at the outset.
Currently, I wish to first open a small channel
to test the flow.
I will temporarily dispatch nearby residents from the three counties of Wūchéng, Wǔkāng, and Dōngqiān
to immediately begin construction.
If it is suitable to further expand it,
I will report again later.
In the past, Zhèng Guó was an enemy general,
and Shǐ Qǐ was ultimately loyal.
Once their proposals were adopted,
they brought benefits for ten thousand generations.
What Jiáo has proposed,
though from a humble person,
if it is not baseless,
may perhaps be established.”
The proposal was approved.
However, the project was ultimately not completed.
In the twenty-third year,
he was granted a complete set of drums and wind instruments.
In the twenty-sixth year,

he was sent out as Envoy with Credentials (shǐchíjié), Grand Administrator (dūdū) of military affairs of Nánxú and Yǎn two Prefectures, General who Conquers the North (zhēngběi jiāngjūn), Administrator with Ceremonial Authority Equal to the Three Ducal Ministers (kāifǔ yítóng sānsī), and Governor (cìshǐ) of Nánxú and Yǎn two Prefectures.
His position as Palace Attendant (chángshì) remained as before.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Jùn was sent to lead troops to build a city on Guābù Shān,
and relieve Nányǎn Prefecture.
In the thirtieth year,

he was transferred to Grand Administrator (dūdū) of military affairs of Jīng, Yōng, Yì, Liáng, Níng, Nán, Běi Qín seven Prefectures, General of the Guard (wèijiāngjūn), Administrator with Ceremonial Authority Equal to the Three Ducal Ministers (kāifǔ yítóng sānsī), Governor (cìshǐ) of Jīng Prefecture, and concurrently Commander (lǐng hù nánmán xiàowèi) Protecting the Southern Barbarians.
His positions as Envoy with Credentials (chíjié) and Palace Attendant (chángshì) remained as before.
Jùn had been fond of literature since youth,
and his demeanor and qualities were refined and beautiful.
His mother, Pān Shúfēi, was greatly favored.
At the time, the six palaces had no mistress,
so Pān Shúfēi solely managed the internal affairs.
Since Jùn's talent and appearance were excellent,
and his mother was also greatly beloved,
Tàizǔ paid special attention to him.
Jiànpíng Wáng Hóng, Attendant (shìzhōng) Wáng Sēngchuò, and Mid-Secretary (zhōngshū shìláng) Cài Xīngzōng all corresponded with him on literary and scholarly matters.
Initially,
Empress Yuán was jealous by nature,
and because Lady Pān was favored,
she died of resentment and hatred.
Therefore, Shào deeply hated Lady Pān and Jùn.
Jùn feared future misfortune,
so he deliberately tried to please Shào,
and Shào became friendly with him.
He had many faults,
and was repeatedly reprimanded and questioned by the Emperor,
so in fear and worry,
he and Shào jointly engaged in sorcery.
When he was sent out to govern Jīngkǒu,
he was allowed to take two thousand civil and military personnel from Yáng Prefecture with him.
He lived a life of leisure in the outer provinces,
and was very pleased with himself.
After being outside for a year,
and having lost Nányǎn,
he then wished to return to court again.
Lúlíng Wáng Shào was relieved of his post in Yáng Prefecture due to illness.
At that time, Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng was guarding the outer regions,
and Jùn thought the prefecture's post would naturally fall to him,
but the Emperor instead bestowed it upon Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān,
which greatly displeased Jùn.
He then sought to be appointed to Jiānglíng through Staff Officer (yuánwài sànqí shìláng) Xú Yuán,
and also sought help from Minister (shàngshū púyè) Xú Zhànzhī.
However, Minister (shàngshū lìng) Hé Shàngzhī and others all said that Jùn, as the Crown Prince's next younger brother,
should not be sent far away.
The Emperor considered the importance of the upper reaches of the river,
and that it should be entrusted to a close relative,
so he bestowed it upon Jùn.
At that time, Jùn had entered the court,
and was sent back to the capital
to make arrangements for his departure.
A few days after arriving in the capital, the sorcery incident was exposed,
which was in the seventh month of the twenty-ninth year.
The Emperor sighed with regret all day,
and said to Pān Shúfēi:
"The Crown Prince schemes for wealth and honor,
which is another matter.
But Hǔtóu is also like this,
it is beyond what I could have imagined.
How can you mother and son manage even one day without me?"
Jùn's childhood name was Hǔtóu.
He sent his attendant Zhū Fǎyú to secretly admonish Jùn,
with words that were very sorrowful and poignant,
and also bestowed a letter saying:
"I suppose you have heard about the parrot matter.
How could you be so deluded?
And what kind of person is Shěn Huái Yuǎn?
How could he possibly keep this secret for you?
Therefore, I have Zhū Fǎyú convey this verbally,
and I throw down my brush with regret."
Jùn was ashamed and fearful,
and did not know how to respond.
Jùn had returned to the capital,
originally for a short stay,
but the Emperor was angry
and did not allow him to return.
In the twelfth month of that year,
Mid-Secretary (zhōngshū shìláng) Cài Xīngzōng asked Jiànpíng Wáng Hóng:
"There are not many days left in the year,
when will the General who Conquers the North (zhēngběi) arrive?"
Hóng sighed for a long time and said:
"He may not return within the year."
While in the capital, he appointed Shěn Huái Yuǎn as his long-term aide-de-camp (zhǎnglú cānjūn),
and every evening he would open a secret door for discreet outings.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he killed Jùn's favorite, Yáng Chéngxiān.
In the first month of the following year,
the arrangements for Jīng Prefecture were just beginning,
and in the second month,
Jùn returned to court.
On the fourteenth day,
he was received and bowed before the imperial hall.
On that day,
the matter of concealing Yán Dàoyù was exposed.
The next morning, Jùn went to apologize,
and the Emperor's expression was unusual.
That evening,
he was immediately questioned,
and Jùn only apologized.
Pān Shúfēi held Jùn,
and tearfully said to him:
"When your initial sorcery incident was exposed,
I still hoped you would reflect on your faults.
How could you suddenly conceal Yán Dàoyù?
The Emperor blames you deeply;
even when I prostrated myself and begged for mercy,
his anger would not dissipate.
What is the point of living today?
Bring the medicine,
I will take my own life first;
I cannot bear to see your ruin."
Jùn flung his robe and left,
saying:
"The affairs of the world will soon be decided on their own.
Please worry a little less,
I will certainly not implicate you."
On the morning Shào committed regicide,
Jùn was in Xī Zhōu.
His steward Zhū Fǎyú rushed to inform Jùn, saying:
"There are shouts in the palace,
all the palace gates are closed,
and it is rumored on the streets that the Crown Prince has rebelled.
The extent of the disaster is unknown."
Jùn feigned surprise and said:
"What should we do now?"
Fǎyú advised him to occupy Shítou.
Jùn had not yet received confirmation from Shào,
and did not know if the plan had succeeded,
so he was agitated and did not know what to do.
General Wáng Qìng said:
"Now there is a disturbance in the palace,
and the safety of His Majesty is unknown.
As ministers and subjects,
we should rush to face the danger.
To rely on the city and defend ourselves
is not the duty of a minister."
Jùn did not listen,
but instead exited through the south gate
and went directly to Shítou,
with over a thousand civil and military followers.
At that time, Nánpíng Wáng Shuò was guarding Shítou,
with also over a thousand soldiers.
Soon, Shào sent Zhāng Chāozhī to gallop and summon Jùn.
Jùn dismissed others to ask about the situation,
then donned military attire, mounted his horse, and left.
Zhū Fǎyú repeatedly tried to stop Jùn,
but Jùn did not obey.

Collator's Note
Biography 60, Author's Preface
Formerly, Shàodiào Jīntiān-shì had a descendant named Mèi,
who served as the master of Xuánmíng.
He gave birth to Yǔngé and Táitài.
Táitài was able to carry on his office,
dredging the Fén and Táo Rivers,
and damming Dàzé to settle in Tàiyuán.
Emperor Zhuānxū commended him
and enfeoffed him in Fénchuān.
Later, there were four states descended from him:
Shěn, Sì, Rù, and Huáng.
The state of Shěnzi
is what is now Shěntíng in Píngyú, Rǔnán.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
it was listed among the covenant assemblies.
In the fourth year of Dìnggōng,
the feudal lords met at Zhàolíng to attack Chǔ.
Shěnzi did not attend the meeting.
Jìn sent Cài to attack Shěn
and destroyed it,
returning with Shěnzi Jiā.
Thereafter, they took the state name as their clan name.
From this point onward,
genealogical records are no longer extant.
At the end of the Qín Dynasty, there was Shěn Chéng,
who was summoned by the chancellor
but did not accept.
In the early Hàn Dynasty, Chéng's great-grandson Bǎo
was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Zhúyì.
Bǎo's son Zūn
moved from his native state to Shòuchūn in Jiǔjiāng,
serving as the Grand Tutor of Qí Wáng and Marquis of Fūd德.
Zūn's son Dá
was the Píqí Jiāngjūn.
Dá's son Gān
was the Shàngshūlìng.
Gān's son Hóng
was the Nányáng Tàishǒu.
Hóng's son Xù
was the Hénèi Shǒu.
Xù's son Fèn
was the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Fèn's son Kè
was the Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng.
Kè's son Qiān
was the Shàngshū and Guānnèi Hóu.
Qiān's son Jìng
was the Jìyīn Tàishǒu.
Jìng's son Róng, courtesy name Wēiqīng,
served in the province as a Cóngshì.
He persuaded the bandit leader Yǐn Liáng to surrender.
Emperor Hàn Guāngwǔ commended his功
and enfeoffed him as the Marquis of Hǎihūn County,
but he declined it.
He then moved to Yúbù-xiāng in Wūchéng County, Kuàijī, to avoid trouble,
and thus settled there.
In the first year of Yǒngjiàn during Emperor Shùn's reign,
Kuàijī was divided to form Wú Jùn,
and they became people of Wú Jùn again.
In the fifth year of Chūpíng during Emperor Líng's reign,
Wūchéng and Yúháng were divided to form Yǒng'ān County.
In the second year of Bǎodǐng under Sūn Hào of Wú,
Wú Jùn was divided to form Wúxīng Jùn,
and they became people of the commandery again.
Although the states and counties changed repeatedly,
they did not move their residences.
After Emperor Jìn Wǔ pacified Wú,
in the second year of Tàikāng,
Yǒng'ān was renamed Wǔkāng County.
The historian's seventh-generation ancestor Yán first resided in Yúwū Cūn, Bólù Lǐ, in the eastern township of the county.
His grandfather followed an official to the capital,
and in the eleventh year of Yìxī,
his great-grandfather was granted a residence in Yùnxiàng, Dūtíng Lǐ, Jiànkāng.
Róng's son Fēng, courtesy name Shèngtōng,
was the Línglíng Tàishǒu,
and brought forth the auspicious omen of a yellow dragon and spirit ganoderma.
His second son Hǔ, courtesy name Zhònggāo,
was the Ānpíng Xiàng.
His youngest son Jǐng
was the Héjiān Xiàng.
Yǎnzhī, Qìngzhī, Tánqìng, and Huáiwén were his descendants.
Hǔ's son Luán, courtesy name Jiànguāng,
had a high reputation in his youth.
The province recommended him as a Màocái,
and the Duke's residence invited him to be a Zhōubiéjià Cóngshìshǐ.
At that time, Lù Chóu, the Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu,
was Luán's maternal uncle.
He was renowned in the Hàn court
for his righteous integrity and administrative achievements,
and also gave his daughter in marriage to Luán.
He died young
at the age of twenty-three.
His son Zhí, courtesy name Bóíng,
was recommended as a Màocái by the province
and also had a pure reputation.
He died at the age of twenty-eight.
His son Yí, courtesy name Zhòngzé,
had excellent conduct in his youth.
When his elder brother Yú was ten and Yí was nine, their father died.
Their mourning exceeded the rites,
and their emaciation was more severe than that of adults.
Their maternal grandfather Shèng Xiàozhāng of Kuàijī,
a famous scholar at the end of the Hàn Dynasty,
was deeply saddened.
Each time he comforted them,
he said:
"You both are pure and refreshing at heart,
and will eventually become extraordinary talents.
Why do you exceed the regulations
and bring about your own destruction?"
After the three-year mourning period was completed,
they were almost at the point of losing their lives,
so both brothers were known for their filial piety.
Yú died young.
Yí was devoted to learning and had refined talent,
making a living through Confucian simplicity.
At that time, the world was in great chaos,
with wars breaking out everywhere.
Scholarly traditions declined,
and few scholars had complete conduct.
However, Yí was pure, profound, and reticent,
adhering to the Way without wavering.
His conduct was upright and disciplined,
and he did not casually associate with others.
He was only friends with his kinsmen Zhòngshān and Shūshān, and Lù Gōngjì of Wú Jùn.
The province and commandery respectfully invited him,
and the two ducal residences repeatedly summoned him.
He was summoned by the Gōngchē,
but he did not yield to any of them,
and died of old age.
His son Xiàn, courtesy name Yuánlǐ,
was a Zuǒ Zhōngláng, Xīndū Dūwèi, and Marquis of Dìngyáng.
His talent and ambition were prominent in the Wú court.
His son Jiǎo, courtesy name Zhònghuán,
was famous for his integrity and character,
serving as Lìwǔ Xiàowèi and Piān Jiāngjūn,
enfeoffed as a Lièhóu, and also as Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Xīndū Tàishǒu.
During the time of Sūn Hào,
he was known as a general.
After Wú was pacified,
he was appointed Yùlín and Chángshā Tàishǒu,
but did not accept either.
He died at the end of Tàikāng.
His son Líng, courtesy name Jǐnggāo,
was invited by the Grand Tutor Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè to be a Cóngshì.
When Yuándì was Zhèn Dōng Jiāngjūn,
he was ordered to be a Cānjūnshì.
When Xú Fù revolted
and killed Yuán Xiù, the Wúxīng Tàishǒu,
Líng suppressed and pacified him.
His son Yán, courtesy name Sīcháng,
was a Huán Wēn Ānxī Cānjūn and Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu.
His son Hè, courtesy name Zǐníng,
was a Huán Chōng Nánzhōngláng Cānjūn.
He besieged Yuán Zhēn at Shòuyáng
but died of illness.
Shěn Jǐng (沈警), courtesy name Shìmíng (世明),
was sincere and had good conduct.
His studies penetrated the *Zuǒ Shì Chūnqiū* (左氏春秋).
His family was wealthy
with property accumulating to thousands of gold.
He served as a principal clerk (zhǔbù 主簿) in the commandery.
Later, General Xiè Ān (謝安) appointed him as an aide-de-camp (cānjūn 參軍),
and greatly respected him.
Jǐng (警) was internally content with his wealth
and was considered a prominent figure (háoshì 豪士) in the southeast,
having no ambition for official advancement.
He feigned illness and returned home,
but Ān (安) insisted on keeping him, not allowing him to leave.
Then he said to Jǐng (警):
"Aide-de-camp Shěn (沈),
you have a resolve to cultivate yourself alone;
is that not too lofty?"
Jǐng (警) replied:
"The Duke (shǐjūn 使君) governs things with the Way,
which is why I initially harbored virtue and arrived.
Now, as I am of no use in assisting the times,
I therefore fulfill my wish to simply live a simple life."
He returned home for many years,
amusing himself with his simple life.
The Former General (qián jiāngjūn 前將軍) and Inspector (cìshǐ 刺史) of Qīng (青) and Yǎn (兗) Provinces, Wáng Gōng (王恭), was stationed at Jīngkǒu (京口).
He had an old friendship with Jǐng (警)
and again invited him to be an aide-de-camp (cānjūn 參軍).
He wrote a letter expressing his earnestness,
insistently urging him to come.
Jǐng (警) had no choice but to accept,
but soon after resigned his post.
His son Mùfū (穆夫), courtesy name Yànhé (彥和),
was fond of learning in his youth
and also had a thorough understanding of the *Zuǒ Shì Chūnqiū* (左氏春秋).
Wáng Gōng (王恭) appointed him as the principal clerk (zhǔbù 主簿) of the vanguard army
and wrote to Jǐng (警), saying:
"Since you hold an unwavering resolve
and recline in loftiness in the southeast,
I have therefore deigned to have your worthy son serve with me,
not to bind him with official duties."
Originally,
Dù Zǐgōng (杜子恭) from Qiántáng (錢唐) was spiritually insightful and possessed esoteric arts.
Prominent families from the eastern regions and noble houses from the capital
all served him as disciples,
showing him triple respect.
Jǐng's (警) family had served the Dao (dào 道) for generations,
and he also respectfully served Zǐgōng (子恭).
After Zǐgōng (子恭) died,
his disciples Sūn Tài (孫泰) and Tài's (泰) disciple Ēn (恩) continued his teachings.
Jǐng (警) again served them.
In the third year of Lóng'ān (隆安) (399 CE),
Ēn (恩) rebelled in Kuàijī (會稽),
proclaiming himself General Who Conquers the East (Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn 征東將軍).
The three Wú (吳) commanderies all responded.
Mùfū (穆夫) was in Kuàijī (會稽) at the time,
and Ēn (恩) appointed him as Aide-de-camp (cānjūn 參軍) of the Vanguard, General Who Manifests Military Prowess (Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn 振武將軍), and Magistrate (lìng 令) of Yúyáo (餘姚).
On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month of that year (400 CE),
Ēn (恩) was defeated by Liú Láozhī (劉牢之).

Gāo Sù (高素), General Who Guards the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍), captured Mùfū (穆夫) and the impostor Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守) of Wújùn (吳郡), Lù Guīzhī (陸瓌之), and Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守) of Wúxīng (吳興), Qiū Jùn (丘), at Huízhǒng Dài (回踵埭) in Shānyīn (山陰).
They were all executed,
and their heads were sent in boxes to the capital.
The events are recorded in the *Lóng'ān Gùshì* (隆安故事).
Previously,
a kinsman, Shěn Yù (沈預), who had always lacked scholarly conduct,
was disliked by Jǐng (警).
At this time, Jǐng (警) heard that Mùfū (穆夫) was involved in the rebellion.
He was hiding and was about to escape when Yù (預) reported him to the officials.
Jǐng (警) and Mùfū (穆fū), along with his younger brothers Zhòngfū (仲夫), Rènfū (任夫), Yùfū (預夫), and Pèifū (佩夫), were all killed.
Only Mùfū's (穆夫) sons Yuānzi (淵子), Yúnzi (雲子), Tiánzi (田子), Línzi (林子), and Qiánzi (虔子) were spared.
Yuānzi (淵子), courtesy name Jìngshēn (敬深),
had lofty aspirations and integrity in his youth.
He followed Emperor Gāozǔ (高祖) in conquering the capital
and was enfeoffed as a fifth-rank marquis (wǔděng hóu 五等侯) of Fánzhì (繁畤) County.
He served as an aide-de-camp (cānjūn 參軍) for the General Guarding the Army (Zhènjūn 將軍) and the Central Army of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Zhōngjūn 車騎中軍),
and also served as Aide-de-camp (cānjūn 參軍) for Dàoguī (道規), General Who Guards the State (Fǔguó 將軍), and General Who Conquers the West (Zhēngxī 將軍),
concurrently holding the post of Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守) of Níngshǔ (寧蜀).
He, along with Liú Jī (劉基), jointly beheaded Cài Měng (蔡猛) at Dàbù (大簿).
Upon returning, he became an aide-de-camp (cānjūn 參軍) for the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi 太尉)
and followed in the campaign against Sīmǎ Xiūzhī (司馬休之),
perishing together with Xú Kuízhī (徐逵之).
He was thirty-five years old at the time.
His son Zhèng (正), courtesy name Yuánzhí (元直),
was profound and possessed an impressive bearing,
with a beautiful demeanor
and graceful composure.
He was fond of the teachings of Lǎozi (老子) and Zhuāngzi (莊子).
At twenty (ruòguàn 弱冠),
the province invited him to serve as an assistant (cóngshì 從事).
A kinsman, Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫) Yǎnzhī (演之), praised him, saying:
"This is a 'thousand-li colt' among our clan."
He went out to serve as Magistrate (lìng 令) of Shǐníng (始寧), Wūshāng (烏傷), and Lóu (婁).
Due to the mourning for his mother, he left office.
After the mourning period ended,
he became an aide-de-camp (cānjūn 參軍) for the General of the Rear Army (Hòujūn 後軍) and Assistant to the General Who Pacifies the South (Ānnán Xíng Cānjūn 安南行參軍) under Wáng Dàn (王誕) of Suí (隨).
When Dàn (誕) was stationed in Kuàijī (會稽),
he again served as an aide-de-camp (cānjūn 參軍) in the General Who Pacifies the East's (Āndōng Jūn 安東軍) army.
In the thirtieth year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) (453 CE),
the primal culprit (yuánxiōng 元凶) assassinated and ascended the throne.
He divided Jiāngdōng (江東) into Huì Prefecture (Huìzhōu 會州)
and appointed Dàn (誕) as its Inspector (cìshǐ 刺史).
As Dàn (誕) was about to accept the appointment,
Zhèng (正) persuaded his chief clerk (sīmǎ 司馬), Gù Chēn (顧琛), saying:
"This calamity that has befallen the state
is unprecedented since the beginning of the world.
Now, with the righteous and valiant troops of Jiāngdōng (江東),
we should be the initiators for the world.
If we dispatch a single messenger,
how could the four quarters not respond?
By this, we can avenge the court's (cháotíng 朝庭) humiliation
and greatly demonstrate the integrity of a minister and son.
How can we face the northern direction to this heinous rebel
and allow Your Highness to accept his false favor?"
Chēn (琛) said:
"Jiāngdōng (江東) has long forgotten warfare,
and its soldiers are not accustomed to military matters.
Although the rebel and the righteous are different,
the strong and the weak are also distinct.
We should wait for those in the four quarters who make a righteous uprising,
and then respond to them;
it will not be too late."
Zhèng (正) said:
"If there were a country without a father in the world,
then what you say might be possible.
But if that is not the case,
how can we content ourselves with this enmity and shame
and demand righteousness from other regions?
Now, it is precisely because of the assassination, rebellion, and foul disgrace,
that righteousness dictates we cannot coexist.
On the day we raise troops,
how can we seek certain preservation?
Féng Yǎn (馮衍) once said,
'Will the noble ministers of the Great Hàn (大漢)
be inferior to the humble scholars of Jīng (荊) and Qí (齊)?'
Moreover, Your Highness embodies the righteousness of both minister and son,
and this matter concerns both family and state."
Chēn (琛) then entered with Zhèng (正) to persuade Dàn (誕),
but Dàn (誕) was still hesitant and undecided.
It happened that the righteous army of Xúnyáng (尋陽) arose,
and Emperor Shìzǔ (世祖) sent an envoy.
Dàn (誕) then promoted Zhèng (正) to General Who Pacifies the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn 寧朔將軍)
and had him command troops to follow Liú Jìzhī (劉季之).
Dàn (誕) entered and became General-in-chief of Cavalry (Piàojì Dà Jiāngjūn 驃騎大將軍),
and Zhèng (正) became Aide-de-camp (cānjūn 參軍) of the Central Army (Zhōng Bīng 中兵),
then transferred to Colonel of Chángshuǐ (Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi 長水校尉).
In the first year of Xiàojiàn (孝建) (454 CE),
he moved the Qīng (青) Province garrison to Lìchéng (歷城).
As Línzī (臨淄) was empty,
he was appointed General Who Pacifies the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn 寧朔將軍) and Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守) of Qí (齊) and Běihǎi (北海) Commanderies,
entrusted with the responsibility of securing the entire Qí (齊) region.
Before he could be formally installed,
he died in the second year (455 CE),
at the age of forty-three.
Zhèng (正) was fond of pleasure in life
and indulged himself greatly.
After his death,
his family had no remaining wealth.
Yuānzi's (淵子) younger brother, Yúnzi (雲子),
during the Yuánjiā (元嘉) period,
served as Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守) of Jìn'ān (晉安).
Yúnzi's (雲子) son, Huàn (煥), courtesy name Shìwèi (士蔚),
in his youth was appointed as Imperial Son-in-law Commandant (Fùmǎ Dūwèi 駙馬都尉) and was summoned to court for service (Fèngcháoqǐng 奉朝請).
When the primal culprit (yuánxiōng 元凶) entered to commit the assassination,
Huàn (煥) was concurrently serving as Middle Secretary (Zhōng Shùzǐ 中庶子)
and was on duty in the palace guard (zhífāng 直坊).
He was forced to follow into the palace.
After Shào (劭) had established himself,
he appointed Huàn (煥) as Supervisor of the Feathered Forest (Yǔlín Jiān 羽林監).
He declined the appointment.
He was then appointed as Gentleman-in-Waiting Without Portfolio (Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng 員外散騎侍郎)
and sent to guard the sons of Nánqiáo (南譙) King Yìxuān (義宣).
This matter is recorded in the biography of Yìxuān (義宣).
Subsequently, he was appointed Aide-de-camp (cānjūn 參軍) in the Chancellor's (Chéngxiàng 丞相) staff,
Gentleman-in-Waiting Without Portfolio (Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng 員外散騎侍郎),
and Magistrate (lìng 令) of Nánchāng (南昌),
gaining a reputation for capability.
He served as Aide-de-camp (cānjūn 參軍) in charge of records (jìshì 記室) for the Central Army (Zhōng Bīng 中兵) of Cavalry General (Piàojì 驃騎) Liú Xiūyòu (劉休祐), King of Jìnpíng (晉平).
His colleagues all sought advancement through flattery,
but Huàn (煥) alone did not.
After a short while,
the Aide-de-camp (cānjūn 參軍) in charge of records (jìshì 記室) Zhōu Jìngzǔ (周敬祖) and others were reprimanded and disgraced by Emperor Tàizōng (太宗).
Huàn (煥) was then transferred to Counselor (Zīyì Cānjūn 諮議參軍).
Later, during the Yuánhuī (元徽) period of the deposed emperor,
he was appointed General Who Pacifies Afar (Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn 寧遠將軍) and Inspector (cìshǐ 刺史) of Jiāozhōu (交州).
Before he could reach his post,
he died of illness
at the age of forty-five.
Tián Zǐ, courtesy name Jìngguāng,
was Yún Zǐ’s younger brother.
He followed Gāozǔ in conquering Jīngchéng,
and then pacified Jīngyì.
He served as Cān Zhèn Jūn Jūnshì,
and was enfeoffed as a fifth-rank Marquis of Yíngdào Xiàn.
In the fifth year of Yìxī [409 CE],
Gāozǔ campaigned north against the Xiānbēi.
Tián Zǐ led a detached force
and served as vanguard with Longxiáng Jiāngjūn Mèng Lóngfú.
Mùróng Chāo was stationed at Línqú to resist the main army.
Mèng Lóngfú was killed in battle,
but Tián Zǐ fought valiantly and defeated them.
When Lú Xún threatened Jīngyì,
Gāozǔ dispatched Tián Zǐ with Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn Sūn Jìgāo by sea to attack Guǎngzhōu,
and he was additionally appointed Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn.
Xún’s partisan Xú Dàofù returned to garrison Shǐxīng.
Tián Zǐ then again joined Yòu Jiāngjūn Liú Fān to jointly attack and suppress him.
Lú Xún then returned to Guǎngzhōu and besieged Sūn Jìgāo.
Tián Zǐ, fearing Sūn Jìgāo’s isolated and perilous situation,
said to Liú Fān:
“Although Guǎngzhōu city is naturally formidable,
it is inherently the rebels’ stronghold.
Now Lú Xún has returned to besiege it,
there might be an internal mutiny.
Moreover, Sūn Jìgāo’s forces are few and weak,
and cannot hold out for long.
If the rebels regain control of this place,
their fierce momentum will be revitalized.
Your humble servant and Sūn Jìgāo together endured hardships,
navigated the vast sea,
and amidst myriad dangers,
conquered and pacified Guǎngzhōu.
How can we sit by and watch him in peril,
without coming to his rescue?”
Thereupon, he led his army south.
By the time they arrived,
the rebels had already gathered their scattered troops
and were again besieging Guǎngzhōu.
Sūn Jìgāo, isolated and in dire straits,
was greatly pleased to hear of Tián Zǐ’s sudden arrival.
Tián Zǐ then deployed his formation with his back to the water,
personally
leading his officers and soldiers,
and broke them in one battle.
Thereupon, he pressed forward in pursuit,
again defeating Lú Xún at Cāngwú, Cáilín, and Níngpǔ.
Upon returning to Guǎngzhōu,
Sūn Jìgāo had died of illness.
Following the devastation of war,
mountain bandits emerged in competition,
attacking and capturing cities and towns,
and killing local officials.
Tián Zǐ suppressed them as appropriate,
pacifying and annihilating them within ten days.
When Cìshǐ Chǔ Shúdù arrived,
he then returned to the capital.
He was appointed Tàiwèi Cānjūn, Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Huáilíng Nèishǐ,
and granted the title Dūxiāng Hóu.
He again served as Cān Shìzǐ Zhēnglǔ Jūnshì,
his titles of Jiāngjūn and Nèishǐ remaining as before.
In the eighth year [412 CE],
he followed in suppressing Liú Yì.
In the eleventh year [415 CE],
he again followed in suppressing Sīmǎ Xiūzhī,
leading a separate army,
with Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Zhào Lúnzhī,
and served as Cān Zhēnglǔ Jūnshì, Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Fúfēng Tàishǒu.
In the twelfth year,
GāoZǔ (高祖) campaigned north.
Shěn TiánZǐ (沈田子) and Fù HóngZhī (傅弘之), the Administrator of ShùnYáng (順陽), each led separate forces.
They entered through WǔGuān (武關),
and encamped at QīngNí (青泥).
Yáo Hóng (姚泓) wanted to personally command the main army,
but he feared that Shěn TiánZǐ would attack his rear.
He wanted to first pacify Shěn TiánZǐ,
and then bring the entire nation east.
So he led tens of thousands of infantry
and suddenly arrived at QīngNí.
Shěn TiánZǐ had originally been intended as a diversionary force,
leading only a few hundred men.
He wanted to attack them.
Fù HóngZhī said:
“They are numerous and we are few;
it is difficult to contend with them.”
Shěn TiánZǐ said:
“The art of war values surprise tactics,
not necessarily numbers.”
HóngZhī (弘之) still stubbornly insisted,
but Shěn TiánZǐ said:
“Numbers are unbalanced,
and the situation cannot allow both to stand.
If the bandits' encirclement becomes secure,
and morale collapses,
the matter will be lost.
Before they are fully arrayed,
to press them will surely bring victory.
This is what is meant by 'the first to seize the initiative has the will to overcome others.'”
He then personally led his troops forward, beating the drums.
When they were surrounded by several layers,
Shěn TiánZǐ comforted his soldiers, saying:
“Gentlemen, you have forsaken your relatives,
abandoned your ancestral graves,
and come between arrows and stones.
You have been hoping for this day.
The achievement of being enfeoffed as a marquis,
will it be here?”
Then he abandoned their provisions and destroyed their shelters,
personally commanding the soldiers,
fighting fiercely both front and back.
Wherever they charged, they broke through.
The brave warriors from JiāngDōng (江東) he commanded
were skilled in close combat.
They advanced with shouts and cheers,
and the bandit army scattered in an instant.
More than ten thousand people were killed,
and they captured Hóng’s (泓) false imperial carriage and regalia.
GāoZǔ (高祖) reported, saying:
“Shěn TiánZǐ, the Participant in Military Affairs of the General Who Attacks Barbarians, General Who Inspires Martial Prowess, and Administrator of FúFēng (扶風),
led elite troops,
charging like lightning from the city walls.
He personally led his soldiers,
his bravery surpassing all in the battlefield.
He fought against overwhelming numbers,
and wherever he attacked, he inevitably crushed them.
From *chén* (7-9 AM) to *wèi* (1-3 PM),
thousands were beheaded.
Hóng (泓) lost his banner, abandoned his troops,
and fled back to BàXī (霸西).
XiánYáng (咸陽) was completely empty,
righteous volunteers gathered from all sides,
sweeping away the remaining embers.
Victory is imminent.”
The Emperor consoled and rewarded GāoZǔ, saying:
“The fugitive bandits obstructed the passes,
and enjoyed leisurely days.
When you raised your axe at HánGǔ (函谷),
planning to extend the imperial punishment,
the various armies diligently served the emperor,
and were about to endure the cold and heat.
You personally wielded the axe and battle-axe,
your awe-inspiring might leading the way.
As your war chariots rolled forth,
the suburban camps were swept away one after another.
As Xiáo (崤) and Shǎn (陝) were barely trodden upon,
the Tóng (潼) pass was opened.
Yáo Hóng (姚泓), in desperate straits,
abandoned his city and courted death.
The detached force at LánTián (藍田)
annihilated them at BàChuān (霸川).
Heads piled up like forests,
captives covered the fields.
The false leader fled,
and both Chinese and barbarians rallied.
The long-standing fugitive bandits,
will be annihilated morning and evening.”
After ChángĀn (長安) was pacified,
GāoZǔ feasted in the WénChāng (文昌) Palace,
raised a cup and bestowed it upon Shěn TiánZǐ, saying:
“The pacification of XiánYáng (咸陽)
is your achievement.”
He immediately awarded him XiánYáng.
Shěn TiánZǐ declined, saying:
“The pacification of XiánYáng (咸陽),
this is truly due to Your Majesty’s brilliant strategy.
As a military official, I just performed my duty;
what strength did TiánZǐ (田子) have?”
He was then appointed Administrator of the two commanderies of XiánYáng (咸陽) and ShǐPíng (始平).
When the main army returned,
GuìYángGōng YìZhēn (桂陽公義真) remained to guard ChángĀn (長安).
He appointed Shěn TiánZǐ as an Army Advisor in the Headquarters of the General Who Pacifies the West, General Who Soars Like a Dragon, and Administrator of ShǐPíng (始平).
At that time, FóFó (佛佛) invaded,
and Shěn TiánZǐ and Wáng ZhènÈ (王鎮惡), the Chief Clerk of the General Who Pacifies the West, both went out to BěiDì (北地) to repel him.
Earlier,
when GāoZǔ was about to return,
Shěn TiánZǐ, Fù HóngZhī, and others, all believed that since Wáng ZhènÈ’s (王鎮惡) family was in GuānZhōng (關中),
he could not be fully trusted,
and repeatedly reported this to GāoZǔ.
GāoZǔ said:
“Now I am leaving you civilian and military officers and ten thousand elite soldiers.
If he intends mischief,
it will only be enough to destroy himself.
Speak no more.”
When they both went out to BěiDì (北地),
some observers thought Wáng ZhènÈ wanted to kill all the Southerners
and send YìZhēn (義真) south with a few thousand men,
then seize GuānZhōng (關中) and rebel.
Shěn TiánZǐ and HóngZhī (弘之) plotted
to issue a false order from GāoZǔ to execute him,
then combine forces to defeat FóFó (佛佛),
pacify GuānZhōng (關中),
and then return south to apologize for their crime.
Shěn JìngRén (沈敬仁), a kinsman of Shěn TiánZǐ, was valiant and strong.
Shěn TiánZǐ invited Wáng ZhènÈ to discuss matters within HóngZhī’s (弘之) camp,
and had JìngRén (敬仁) kill him at the meeting.
Then, leading dozens of his followers, he surrendered to YìZhēn (義真).
The Chief Clerk Wáng Xiū (王修) arrested and executed Shěn TiánZǐ outside the warehouse gate in ChángĀn (長安).
This was on the fifteenth day of the first month of the fourteenth year of YìXī (義熙).
He was thirty-six years old at the time.
Shěn TiánZǐ had initially been eligible for enfeoffment due to his achievements,
but this matter caused it to be suspended.
GāoZǔ reported to the Emperor
that Shěn TiánZǐ had suffered an attack of madness,
and did not deeply fault him.
He had no sons.
His younger brother LínZǐ (林子) made his second son Liàng (亮) his heir.
Liàng’s (亮) courtesy name was DàoMíng (道明).
He was pure and upright, fond of learning,
and skilled in writing.
Before he reached twenty,
the province appointed him as an aide.
Mèng Yǐ (孟顗), the Administrator of KuàiJī (會稽), acted unlawfully in the commandery.
Liàng (亮) impeached him, and he was dismissed from office.
He also spoke of anomalies and disasters,
and was transferred to be Chief Clerk of the Western Bureau.
At that time, the Three Wú (吳) region suffered floods,
grain was expensive, and the people were starving.
The Inspector PíngChéngWáng YìKāng (彭城王義康) had discussions held to relieve the people's hardship.
Liàng (亮) proposed:
“The eastern land is afflicted by disaster and famine,
the people are declining, and grain prices are soaring.
Wealthy families hoard rice,
and its price increases daily.
It is advisable to issue orders to all localities
to investigate the true situation,
and order families with stored grain
to be allowed to keep a one-year supply;
the rest must be compelled to sell,
and a fixed fair price be set.
This is what is called ‘the constant way for all ages,
and expediency for the present moment.’
Furthermore, along the Huái (淮) River, the harvest is bountiful every year,
the cities are rich, and the land is fertile.
Wheat has already been harvested,
and millet and sorghum are about to ripen.
Their taxes can be collected as goods,
and then traded directly.
The starving people of the Three Wú (吳) can then be lent these provisions,
and the strong can transport them
to sustain the old and weak.
Moreover, alcohol offers profit for the throat and lips,
but is not essential for sustenance.
It should especially be prohibited
to stop wasteful spending.”
These measures were all implemented.
ShìZǔ (世祖) was sent to govern LìYáng (歷陽),
acting as Participant in Military Affairs of the General Who Attacks Barbarians.
There was a case of tomb raiding,
and villagers nearby were punished as if they had failed to respond to a robbery while on patrol.
Liàng (亮) argued: “In probing the nature of tomb raiding,
the act is merely theft.
