It is only because it involves violating the deceased that
it is equated with severe penalties.
Those who dig and bore
must carry gags to conceal their
tracks.
Those who rob and plunder
must shout to display their deed.
Therefore, it is easier to respond to open violence
than to secret activities.
Furthermore, mountains and wilderness are uninhabited areas,
and graves
Tombs are not paths trodden by all;
as for prevention and rescue,
they should not be compared to villages and towns.
If the supervision is substantial and the accusation named,
the principle differs from mere robbery,
then the implication of the *Fúwǔ*
should appropriately
be reduced.
Furthermore, the law of collective punishment,
though it has the same limits as the *Fúwǔ* system,
lacks a distinction of distance.
Indeed, a tomb has no village boundary;
it should be treated as implicating those nearby.
If it is not demarcated by a boundary,
then within a few paces
and beyond ten *lǐ*,
all would have to bear
the same responsibility.
The prohibition against people interfering
cannot be completely abolished,
but the law for stopping wrongs
should fit its case.
Your foolish servant suggests that for those within a hundred paces who fail to report in time,
the penalty should be one year of servitude.
Beyond this distance,
the penalty should be progressively reduced or waived.
He also memorialized Tàizǔ regarding the affairs of the Chen government, saying:
"I humbly observe that among the soldiers of the Western Command,
some are nearly eighty years old,
yet still serve as subordinates;
some are only seven years old,
yet are already engaged in service.
Their weakened bodies,
their energy and utility diminished,
and the frail bodies of children,
whose muscles are not yet solid,
are made to endure arduous labor in their infancy and youth,
and struggle with hardship late into life.
This is both unreasonable
and of very little benefit.
The regulations state that sixty years old is the limit for retirement from service,
and fifteen years old is the standard for beginning service.
If one's strength is insufficient for duties,
then a rough allowance for reduction should certainly be made."
An imperial edict stated:
"Previously, I already ordered your elder brother to make reforms.
Soon after, he was transferred back.
Was it then not implemented after all?
Now I will again issue an order to the Western Command."
At that time, the construction of the city and its administration was underway,
and the work schedule was strict and urgent.
Liàng again memorialized, saying: "The initial construction of the city
is all new creation.
The foundations and walls are extensive,
and the labor quotas are also strict.
Their toil is not accounted for,
and speed is merely sought.
They demand the completion of a year's work
in
a few days.
I have recently seen workers beginning work before dawn,
and resting only after the drum sounds for closing.
With many tasks presented,
it is naturally impossible to complete them all.
As for rest days,
they are constrained by
limits.
Now entering the hot, rainy season,
many are dying or falling ill.
What I have heard recently
is that there are also quite a few who have fled.
I humbly consider that this is an internal defense,
its circumstances different from an external garrison.
The appropriateness of governing
is
not bound by early or late completion.
If the work quotas could be slightly eased,
and the burdens somewhat balanced,
the suffering prisoners and laborers
would be more easily pleased and exert themselves more,
and when the final work is assessed,
the deficiencies
would be minimal.
Your servant hears that one who does not hold a position
does not plan its affairs.
The butchering has its master,
and the invoker does not overstep the sacrificial wine vessel.
How could your insignificant and lowly servant
be allowed to participate in deliberations?
However, your servant has been bathed in grace
for many years,
and served righteousness for generations.
Whatever I harbor in my heart,
I forget the conventional decorum."
The imperial edict replied:
"Your memorial is excellent.
This has also been a recurring problem.
I have repeatedly ordered it to be corrected,
yet it remains so.
This is extremely unreasonable.
Recently, I again ordered Méngxiū to proclaim my decree.
I imagine it should be different now.
You should observe the distribution of the work's ease and hardship secretly."
When Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn governed Yángzhōu,
he again served as Master of Records and Magistrate of Mòlíng.
He was skilled at exposing hidden wrongdoings,
and would always capture those who committed offenses.
Tàizǔ praised his ability,
and he entered the court as an Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Justice.
Xiāngyáng borders the frontier.
To the east of the Jiāng River, there had never been an imperial prince garrisoned in such an important strategic location.
In the twenty-second year of Yuánjiā,
Shìzǔ was appointed General of the Fǔjūn and Governor of Yōngzhōu.
The Son of Heaven was very concerned,
considering that the old Wǎn was close to the two passes,
and within a short distance of Xiáo and Shǎn.
This was a northern bulwark for Xiāngyáng.
Moreover, to display strength against the fierce barbarians
who encroached upon the borders,
Lìang was made Administrator of Nányáng,
and given the additional title of General Yángwǔ.
The frontier barbarians were overawed and submitted,
all paying taxes and levies.
There were a few cunning villages,
all of which Lìang exterminated.
He dispatched officials to patrol all the counties;
widows, orphans, the elderly, and the infirm who could not support themselves
were all exempted from taxes and provided for.
Elders of advanced age
received provisions annually.
At that time, Confucian studies were highly esteemed and established.
Lìang opened schools
to instruct students.
Many people plundered tombs
and violated laws concerning marriage,
so he strictly formulated prohibitions against these.
Within the commandery, there was an ancient stone weir
that had been neglected and fallen into disuse for many years.
Lìang memorialized Shìzǔ to repair it,
saying:
"To foster life and promote industry,
one must first teach agriculture.
To establish the people and uphold governance,
one must instruct them in the fundamentals of sowing and harvesting.
Only then can a state be prosperous, a society stable,
and propriety and economy be achieved.
Recently, the northern Luò has been overgrown,
and southern Wǎn has been ravaged.
The Xiǎnyǔn barbarians have run rampant,
and the Quǎnyí barbarians have filled the borders.
In the distance, beacon fires and postal stations have been disrupted;
nearby, the suburbs and villages are in peril.
Consequently, fertile plains are not cultivated,
and great dikes are not repaired.
People are exhausted and cease plowing,
neglecting their land.
In times of famine, there is no one to depend on,
and the displaced continue to suffer to this day.
Now that civilizing influence has pervaded internally
and deterrent power has cleared the external regions,
this is truly the time to eliminate brigands and repair irrigation channels,
to encourage farmers and begin cultivation,
to plan grand schemes, and to expand territories for prosperous years.
Your Highness humbly educates the people,
reviving them and restoring ancient ways.
Moreover, you are now pacifying thorny wildernesses
and bringing distant, desolate regions into submission.
I humbly observe that within the commandery there is an old stone weir.
The fields it irrigates are fertile and moist,
truly a divine marshland.
However, it has become overgrown and broken,
its benefits having been abandoned for a long time.
From what I have observed,
I believe it ought to be rebuilt.
In ancient times, Wénwēng served as an official,
developing barren land into productive fields.
Wěilián governed the people,
opening up remote areas and increasing industries.
Their benevolence enlightened two states
and their achievements ranked them among the two Hàn dynasties.
Although I strive to emulate their policies and accomplishments,
I do not see any unsurpassable obstacles.
My humble service is merely a disgrace,
but my worries are shared with my colleagues."
□ □ □ □ □ □ □ □ □ □ □ □ □ □ □ □ □ □ He also repaired the Mǎrén Weir,
and the people benefited from it.
After serving for four years,
he was promoted to Clerk for Military Affairs under Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān, the Minister of Works.
An imperial edict stated:
"The key personnel in Shǎnxī require talent,
thus you are granted this position."
When Wáng Dàn, the Prince of Suí, was garrisoned in Xiāngyáng,
Lìang again became Chief Clerk for Military Affairs of the Rear Army,
and concurrently Administrator of Yìchéng.
Lìang governed with integrity and frugality,
which was praised by Tàizǔ.
He was bestowed with carriages, horses, clothing, and ornaments,
which accumulated over time.
Whenever distant regions offered rare and meritorious treasures,
he would always be granted some.
He was also given two thousand scrolls of books.
In the twenty-seventh year,
he died in office
at the age of forty-seven.

His works included 189 pieces of poetry, rhapsodies, eulogies, praises, three-character poems, laments, elegies, sacrificial prayers for rain, yuefu poems, dirges, linked pearls, instructional records, petitions, memorials, remonstrances, and deliberations.
Lín Zǐ 字 Jìngshì,
Tián Zǐ's younger brother.
From a young age, he possessed great magnanimity.
When he was several years old,
he followed his paternal grandfather to Jīngkǒu.
Wáng Gōng saw him and marveled at him,
saying:
“This child is of the same caliber as Wáng Zǐshī.”
When he and others collectively saw a lost treasure,
everyone rushed to contend for it,
but Lín Zǐ walked straight past without a glance.
At thirteen,
he encountered a family calamity.
Though he was in hiding at the time,
his mournful cries day and night were unceasing.
His paternal grandmother said to him:
“You should endure the grief and force yourself to live;
why destroy yourself for nothing?”
Lín Zǐ said:
“My family has suffered such cruel misfortune,
I no longer have a mind for joyful days.
It is only because the ultimate revenge has not been taken
that I am temporarily clinging to life.”
As his entire family had fallen victim to the demonic faction,
his brothers were all due to be executed.
They hid and lay low in the wilderness,
constantly fearing calamity.
However, Shěn Yù's family was very powerful and wealthy,
and intended to ensnare and destroy them.
Lín Zǐ and his elder brothers hid by day and came out by night.
They sold their dwelling,
and arranged for the burial of their father, paternal grandfather, and paternal uncles—
a total of six funerals.
They were frugal but observed the rites.
At this time, their livelihood was completely gone,
and there were many old and weak.
The eastern lands were famine-stricken;
people exchanged children to eat.
Outwardly, they were pressed by the state's net;
inwardly, they feared powerful enemies.
They were hidden in the mountain grass,
with nowhere to settle.
At that time, Sūn Ēn frequently emerged from Kuàijī,
and generals campaigning in the east followed one after another.
Liú Láozhī and Gāo Sùzhī indulged their subordinates,
who plundered and committed atrocities indiscriminately.
Only Gāozǔ's army discipline was strict and clear,
without any encroachments.
Lín Zǐ then surrendered himself, saying:
“The demonic rebels caused chaos,
and my entire family was driven and forced.
My father, paternal grandfather, and paternal uncles
all suffered misfortune.
The reason I am still clinging to life in this world
is solely because my enemies have not been avenged
and my elderly relatives are adrift and homeless.
Today, I see the General punishing evil and commending good;
this is a righteous army.
I respectfully lead my old and weak
to confess our 'crimes' and plead for our lives.”
He then shed tears and choked up,
and the entire army was moved by this.
Gāozǔ was greatly impressed by him,
and said:
“Since you are a 'criminal' of the state,
and your powerful enemies are still in your hometown,
you must follow me back to the capital
to remain safe.”
So, he placed them on a separate boat,
and thus the entire household moved to Jīngkǒu.
Gāozǔ allocated a residence to them.
He extensively read many books,
and focused his mind on literature and meaning.
He followed Gāozǔ in conquering the capital,
and advanced to pacify cities and towns.
At that time, he was eighteen,
and stood seven feet five inches tall.
Shěn Yù, fearing Lín Zǐ would cause harm,
always wore armor and carried a spear.
At this point, Lín Zǐ and his elder brother Tián Zǐ returned east to take revenge.
On the fifth month's summer solstice,
Shěn Yù was holding a large gathering,
with his children and younger relatives filling the hall.
Lín Zǐ and his brother bravely walked straight in,
cut off Shěn Yù's head,
and slaughtered all his male and female relatives, regardless of age.
They offered Shěn Yù's head in sacrifice at their father's and paternal grandfather's tombs.
Subsequently, he was appointed by his native commandery,
and Liú Yì also appointed him as a Staff Officer to the General Who Campaigns with the Army (Guànjūn Cānjūn),
but he did not accept either position.
Lín Zǐ felt his family had suffered so much,
he no longer had a mind for official service.
Gāozǔ urged him strongly,
but he did not rise for a full year.
When Gāozǔ became the Governor of Yángzhōu,
he appointed him as an Attendant Officer (Cóngshì),
and said:
“How can you possibly avoid serving?
For some years, I have supported you,
wishing for all to see your resolve.”
He steadfastly declined but could not refuse,
and only then took up the post,
serving as the Magistrate of Jiànxī.
He was enfeoffed as a fifth-rank Marquis of Zīzhōng County.
At this time, he was twenty-one.
In the fifth year of Yìxī
, he followed in the campaign against the Xiānbēi.
He served as Cān Zhèn Jūn Jūnshì.
The main army engaged in battle at Línqú.
The enemy sent elite Huōbān cavalry to charge the rear of the army.
Línzǐ led the elite and brave in fierce attacks, east and west.
All were thoroughly defeated.
Mùróng Chāo retreated to defend Guǎnggù.
He again, with Liú Jìngxuān, attacked its western corner.
After Guǎnggù was pacified,
Lú Xún suddenly arrived.
Originally,
when Xún was advancing south,
Guǎnggù had not yet been captured.
Xún secretly sent an envoy to form an alliance with Línzǐ and his clansman Shúcháng.
Línzǐ immediately reported it secretly to Gāozǔ,
but Shúcháng did not inform him.
Instead, he tried to sway Línzǐ with Xún's intentions.
Shúcháng was always brave and fierce.
Gāozǔ, because Chāo had not yet been pacified,
kept it secret.
Upon returning to Guǎnggù,
he then executed Shúcháng.
He said to Línzǐ:
“Formerly, when Wèi Wǔ was at Guāndù,
many gentlemen from Rǔ and Yǎn
harbored disloyal intentions.
Only Lǐ Tōng alone firmly upheld righteousness.
Ancient and modern are one.”
When Xún reached Càizhōu,
the gentry class
all discussed moving far away.
Only Línzǐ requested to move his family to Jīngyì.
Gāozǔ was surprised and asked him why.
He replied:
“Gěng Chún brought his whole family to join the army,
and Lǐ Diǎn moved his entire clan to reside in Wèi.
Though Línzǐ's talent is not equal to that of the ancients,
he has truly received profound and weighty kindness.”
Gāozǔ praised him greatly for a long time.
Línzǐ was then leading a separate army at Shítóu,
repeatedly fighting and repelling the bandits.
Xún, having failed in every battle,
then falsely spread the rumor that he would gather all his forces at Báishíbù
and set up an ambush on the south bank.
Thus, the main army first set out for Báishí.
Línzǐ was left with Chìtè to defend and resist at Chápǔ.
Línzǐ then offered a plan, saying:
“This talk is deceitful
and may not be true.
It is advisable to take deep precautions against it.”
Gāozǔ said:
“Shítóu City is strategically dangerous,
and the Huái palisade is very strong.
Leaving you behind
[一０] is sufficient to defend it.”
After the main army had departed,
the bandits indeed attacked.
Chìtè was about to strike them.
Línzǐ said:
“The bandits' rumors point to Báishí,
yet they repeatedly come to challenge us.
Their true intentions are discernible.
The bandits are conserving their elite forces and awaiting the opportune moment.
Our troops do not even number two regiments,
making it difficult to achieve success.
Now, holding this strategic strongpoint
is sufficient to secure ourselves.
If the bandits' false scheme does not succeed,
the main army will soon return.
What do you have to worry about?”
Chìtè said:
“Now the bandits have sent all their forces towards Báishí.
Those left behind must all be weak and old.
To strike them with our elite troops
is to guarantee victory.”
He then led his troops out with a clamor.
The bandits' ambush troops all launched their attack,
and Chìtè's army was indeed defeated.
Abandoning his army, he fled to the north bank.
Línzǐ led his army to gather Chìtè's scattered soldiers,
advanced, and fought,
crushing and defeating them.
Xú Dàofù then sent up more elite troops,
extending for several *lǐ* along the embankment.
Línzǐ assessed them, saying:
“The bandits are arraying their forces along the embankment,
but those fighting are no more than a single company.
Now we occupy their crossing and block their vital point.
Even if they have elite troops stretching for several *lǐ*,
they will not dare to cross and must proceed eastward.”
Thereupon, he cut off the embankment and fought.
After a long time,
Zhū Língshí arrived with reinforcements.
Joining forces with Línzǐ,
the bandits then scattered and fled.
The main army arrived from Báishí.
Chìtè was executed as a sacrifice,
and Línzǐ was appointed Cān Zhōng Jūn Jūnshì.
He followed in the campaign against Liú Yì,
and was then transferred to Cān Tàiwèi Jūnshì.
In the eleventh year,
he again followed in suppressing Sīmǎ Xiūzhī.
Whenever Gāozǔ campaigned,
Línzǐ always broke through the vanguard and stood at the front.
Although he had his own camp,
when evening came,
he was always ordered to return to serve inside.
The bandit leader Guō Liàngzhī gathered barbarian hordes
and entrenched himself in Wǔlíng.
The Grand Administrator of Wǔlíng, Wáng Zhèn'è, fled.
[一一]Línzǐ led an army to suppress him,
beheading Liàngzhī at Qīlǐjiàn,
and reinstated Zhèn'è.
After Wǔlíng was pacified,
he again suppressed Lǔ Guǐ at Shíchéng.
Guǐ abandoned his troops and fled to Xiāngyáng,
and he pursued him further.
After Xiāngyáng was settled, he was temporarily left to guard Jiānglíng.
In the twelfth year,
Gāo Zǔ was appointed Píngběi Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North).
Lín Zǐ, as Tàiwèi Cānjūn (Staff Officer to the Grand Commandant),
was again assigned to participate in the Píngběi army's affairs.
That winter,
Gāo Zǔ attacked the Qiāng,
and Lín Zǐ was again assigned to participate in the Zhēngxī (Western Expeditionary) army's affairs.
He was put in charge of all the central forces in the three headquarters,
promoted to Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Establishes Martial Might),
and commanded the army as the vanguard,
entering the Yellow River from the Biàn River.
At that time, Dǒng Shénhǔ, a surrendered man from Xiāngyì, had over a thousand righteous troops.
Gāo Zǔ wished to pacify and win over those who had newly submitted,
so he immediately commissioned him as Tàiwèi Cānjūn,
promoted him to Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Displays Martial Might),
and ordered him to lead his troops into battle.
Lín Zǐ led Shénhǔ to attack Cāngyuán
and captured it.
Shénhǔ, boasting of his achievement,
returned directly to Xiāngyì.
When Lín Zǐ's army reached Xiāngyì,
he immediately killed Shénhǔ and took control of his troops.
At that time, Xuē Bó, the spurious Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (General Who Establishes Awe) and Héběi Tàishǒu (Administrator of Héběi), had already occupied Xiè Xiàn.
When Lín Zǐ arrived,
he swiftly attacked him.
Bó abandoned his army and fled to Guānzhōng,
and Lín Zǐ seized his troops and provisions.
Yǐn Zhāo, the spurious Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Bìngzhōu) and Hédōng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Hédōng), held Púbǎn.
Lín Zǐ, at Shǎnxín, together with Guānjūn Tán Dàojì, attacked Púbǎn,
while Lóngxiáng Wáng Zhèn'è attacked Tóngguān.
Yáo Hóng, hearing that a large army had arrived,
sent Yáo Shào, the spurious Dōngpíng Gōng (Duke of Dōngpíng), to contend for Tóngguān.
Lín Zǐ said to Dàojì:
"Now Púbǎn has strong walls and deep moats;
it cannot be captured in a mere ten days.
Attacking it would injure our soldiers,
and besieging it would prolong the effort.
It would be better to abandon it
and return to reinforce Tóngguān.
Moreover, Tóngguān is a natural stronghold,
a so-called strategic point.
Zhèn'è's isolated army
is in a precarious situation and exhausted.
If Yáo Shào were to seize it,
it would be difficult to recover.
Before he arrives,
we should combine our forces to contend for it.
If the Tóngguān affair is successful,
Yǐn Zhāo can be subdued without a fight."
[一二] Dàojì agreed.
Upon arrival,
Shào gathered all the forces from Guānyòu
and set up a heavy siege around Lín Zǐ, Dàojì, Zhèn'è, and others.
At that time, the detached army had penetrated deep,
and the supply lines were difficult and distant.
The three armies were hesitant and doubtful,
with no one holding a firm resolve.
Dàojì proposed crossing the river to avoid their vanguard,
or some suggested abandoning the baggage
and returning to Gāo Zǔ.
Lín Zǐ drew his sword and said:
"Xiànggōng (Prime Minister) is diligently serving the throne,
aiming to pacify the six directions.
Xǔ and Luò have been pacified,
and Guānyòu is about to be secured.
The success or failure of this undertaking
depends on the vanguard.
Now, to abandon an already victorious position,
and give up an almost completed task,
when the main army is still far away
and the enemy forces are flourishing—
even if we wished to return,
how could we possibly succeed?
This subordinate received orders to lead the vanguard,
and I vow to sacrifice my life.
Today's matter
I will handle myself for the generals.
However, for you gentlemen,
some of whom have shared in these arduous endeavors,
and some who bear boundless gratitude,
if you falter and retreat because of this,
how will you face Xiànggōng's banners and drums?"
He blocked the wells and burned the houses,
showing he had no intention of retreating.
He led several hundred men under his command to assault their northwest,
and Shào's troops scattered slightly.
Taking advantage of their disarray, he pressed them,
and Shào suffered a major defeat.
Thousands of prisoners were taken,
and all of Shào's weapons, equipment, and supplies were captured.
At that time, when other generals defeated the enemy,
they all exaggerated the number of severed heads.
But when Lín Zǐ presented his victory report,
he always reported the truth.
Gāo Zǔ asked him the reason,
and Lín Zǐ replied:
"The army of a true king
is fundamentally one of conquest, not mere battle.
How can one exaggerate false achievements
to boast about oneself?
Guó Yuān was rewarded for reporting facts,
while Wèi Shàng was punished for exaggerating numbers.
These are examples from the past,
and good precedents for those who follow."
Gāo Zǔ said:
"This is indeed what I expect of you."
Initially,
Shào retreated
and returned to defend Dìngchéng,
leaving Yáo Luán, the spurious Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn (General of Martial Guard), with elite troops to guard the dangerous pass.
Lín Zǐ, with gags in their mouths, launched a night attack,
immediately slaughtered the city,
mutilated Luán, and buried his troops alive.
Gāo Zǔ sent a letter saying:
"You have repeatedly defeated the enemy,
and the joy is immeasurable.
Having been repeatedly crushed,
I imagine they won't last much longer."
Shào again dispatched Yáo Zàn, the Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Soothes the Army), to lead troops to encamp on the river,
cutting off the waterway.
Before Zàn's fortifications and trenches were completed,
Lín Zǐ intercepted and attacked them,
defeating them repeatedly.
Zàn escaped with light cavalry,
and his troops scattered.

Shào again sent Yáo Bózǐ, the Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk) and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (General Overseeing the Army), Ān Luán, the Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North), Yáo Mòluó, the Hùjūn (Protector of the Army), and Táng Xiǎofāng, the Píngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the Far) and Hédōng Tàishǒu, leading a force of thirty thousand
to encamp at Jiǔquán,
[一三] relying on the river's strong natural defenses
to cut off supplies and reinforcements.
Gāo Zǔ, realizing that the vital crossing was blocked
and that military provisions were urgent,
again sent Lín Zǐ to contend for the source of the river.
Lín Zǐ, leading Yán Gāng and Zhú Língxiù, the Tàiwèi Xíng Cānjūn (Acting Staff Officers to the Grand Commandant), advanced in full armor,
fought numerous battles,
and dealt them a great defeat.
He immediately captured the heads of Bózǐ, Mòluó, and Xiǎofāng,
and captured many prisoners, horses, and weapons.
Of the more than three thousand captured,
all were returned to Shào,
to let him know the magnanimity of the king's army.
With both troops and provisions stored,
the three armies advanced westward with drums beating.
Someone said:
"They are fighting far from their country;
their momentum is irresistible."
Lín Zǐ reported to Gāo Zǔ, saying:
"Yáo Shào's spirit covers Guānyòu,
but his power is now broken by circumstances.
His external forces have been repeatedly defeated,
showing all the signs of decline and destruction.
I only fear that his ill fate will run out first,
and I will not be able to bloody my battle-axe with him."
Soon after, Shào [died from a carbuncle on his back.]
Gāo Zǔ, seeing Lín Zǐ's prediction come true,
sent a letter saying:
"Yáo Shào's sudden death
[一四] can be called an execution by Heaven."
Thereupon, Zàn took charge of subsequent affairs,
gathered the remaining troops,
and again attacked Lín Zǐ.
Lín Zǐ led his army to resist them,
and before their banners and drums clashed,
they scattered and broke in an instant.
Zàn escaped with light cavalry.
Since he had won repeated victories in successive battles,
his troops, horses, banners, and flags were very magnificent.
Gāo Zǔ sent him a letter of encouragement
and also sent silk, food, and drink.
Gāozǔ arrived at Ménxiāng.
Yáo Hóng cleared the people from within the borders
and garrisoned his troops at Yáoliǔ.
At this time, Tián Zǐ entered from Wǔguān from the north,
stationing his army at Lántián.
Hóng personally led a large force to attack him.
Gāozǔ, fearing that his numbers were no match,
sent Lín Zǐbù from Qínlǐng
to provide support.
By the time he arrived,
Hóng had already been defeated.
The brothers again pursued him together.
Hóng then led his forces to flee to Bàxī.
Tián Zǐ wanted to pursue him relentlessly
and take Cháng'ān.
Lín Zǐ stopped him,
saying:
"To go and take Cháng'ān
is as easy as pointing a finger.
If we again conquer the enemy city,
we will have single-handedly pacified a whole state,
which is a merit that will not be rewarded."
Tián Zǐ then stopped.
He again participated in the affairs of the Prime Minister,
assuming overall responsibility as before.
Lín Zǐ's prestige spread far and wide,
shaking Sānfǔ.
The powerful families of Guānzhōng,
hearing of his renown, offered their allegiance.
Lǐ Yān and others from Xīzhōu all sought to achieve merit.
Sūn Dáqiāng, various barbarians, and Yáo Hóng's relatives
all led their people to submit to Lín Zǐ.
Gāozǔ, recognizing Lín Zǐ's skill in pacification and strategy,
frequently sent letters praising him
and ordering deep comfort and acceptance of them.
After Cháng'ān was pacified,
over a hundred thousand remaining Qiāng people
fled west to Lǒngshàng.
Lín Zǐ pursued them to Guǎfùshuǐ,
fighting his way to Huáilǐ,
which he conquered,
capturing tens of thousands.
As the main army returned east,
Lín Zǐ led the navy at Shímén
as a supporting force.
Upon his return,
the court deliberated granting him one prefecture and eight commanderies.
Gāozǔ valued his talent and wisdom,
and did not allow him to leave.
Therefore, since entering official service,
he had always managed military essentials.
Except for military expeditions,
he had never held an external post.
Later, Tàizǔ was dispatched to govern Jīngzhōu.
It was proposed that Lín Zǐ and Xiè Huì serve as his assistants.
Gāozǔ said:
"I cannot be without both of them at once.
If Lín Zǐ goes, then Huì should not leave."
So, Lín Zǐ was appointed Western Commandant, Zhonglang Canjun,
and concurrently Governor of Xīnxīng.
Lín Zǐ's deliberation was profound and far-reaching.
Whenever he presented a plan,
Gāozǔ never failed to commend it.
When the main army returned to Péngchéng,
Lín Zǐ, seeing that the campaign had been long
and the soldiers longed for home,
deeply presented his concerns
and also said:
"The reason the sagely kings are cautious and reverent
is not to establish awe and military might,
but truly to govern the state and lead the people.
It is fitting to widely establish defensive screens
and strictly guard the palace."
Gāozǔ deeply accepted his counsel.
Soon after, Xiè Yì conspired to rebel.
Gāozǔ sighed and said:
"How clear Lín Zǐ's insight was!"
Tàizǔ was promoted to the title of Zhènxi,
which was transferred with his office.
He was also appointed Jiànwēi General and Governor of Hédōng.
At this time, Gāozǔ, because of the invasions and disturbances by the two barbarians,
again wanted to personally lead the army.
Lín Zǐ strongly remonstrated,
and Gāozǔ replied:
"I will indeed no longer go myself."
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
for his merit in assisting the founding of the dynasty,
he was enfeoffed as the Earl of Hànshòu County,
with an income of six hundred households.
He firmly declined,
but it was not permitted.
Fù Liàng wrote a letter to Lín Zǐ, saying:
"The granting of titles based on merit
is a constant practice throughout the ages.
The issuing of enfeoffments and rewards
is chosen by the Emperor's heart.
The trust the Emperor places in you
truly concerns the fortune or misfortune of the state.
The sincere hope is
to share in the nation's honor and sorrow.
It is indeed for you and others
to jointly advance matters both internal and external.
Although you wish to remain humble and retiring,
how can you alone be a gentleman?"
He was appointed Palace Consultant and Canjun,
with his general and governor titles as before.
Soon after, he was summoned to temporarily descend
to assist the Recorder Canjun Wáng Huá with the affairs of the Zhongbing Bureau.
The Emperor, recognizing Lín Zǐ's integrity, public spirit, diligence, and frugality,
repeatedly bestowed generous rewards,
which he all distributed to his relatives and old friends.
His family had no surplus wealth,
and he never inquired about matters of production.
His impoverished relatives on both sides all came to him.
When he suffered the mourning for his mother,
he returned east for the burial.
The imperial carriage personally visited,
and messengers arrived one after another.
After the burial,
an edict stated:
"The military and state have many affairs,
and talent is needed both internally and externally.
Former Zhènxi Cānjūn, Jiànwēi General, and Hédōng Governor Shěn Línzǐ
cannot fully carry out his duties due to his personal circumstances.
He is to be reinstated as Fǔguó General."
Lín Zǐ firmly declined,
but it was not permitted.
An imperial edict was given that
he no longer needed to return to court on the first and fifteenth of the month.
Whenever there were major military or state affairs,
he was always consulted.
At that time, the Commander of the Guards, Xiè Huì, was in charge of state affairs.
Whenever Huì was ill and resting,
he would always ask Lín Zǐ to take his place.
Lín Zǐ observed mourning with extreme filial piety.
Gāozǔ deeply worried and commiserated with him.
A short while later, he fell ill.
The Emperor, knowing Lín Zǐ's filial nature,
did not want him to cry himself thin.
He forced him to enter the palace,
comforting him day and night.
He instructed the various nobles, saying:
"His filial nature surpasses others.
You all should frequently visit and comfort him."
He left only after a slight recovery.
The Emperor soon fell ill.
He was ordered to attend to the imperial medicine,
but his illness worsened, and he returned home.
In the third year of Yǒngchū (422 CE),
he passed away,
at the age of forty-six.
The various nobles, knowing that the Emperor deeply valued him,
feared that reporting the truth
would surely cause him grief and sorrow.
Whenever they were asked about him,
they would reply that he was ill and had returned home.
If there was an imperial message,
they would also feign a reply for him.
Gāozǔ soon passed away
and never knew.
He was granted secret items from the Eastern Garden,
one set of court robes,
one suit of clothes,
two hundred thousand cash,
and two hundred rolls of cloth.
An edict stated:
"The late Fǔguó General Shěn Línzǐ
possessed a truly discerning character
and his loyal achievements were clearly evident.
His talent and aspirations were not fully realized,
causing me grief and sorrow.
He is posthumously granted the title of Zhēnglǔ General."
The relevant officials followed the usual regulations.
In the twenty-fifth year of Yuánjiā (448 CE),
he was posthumously named Huáibó.
Lín Zǐ was simple, calm, honest, and tranquil,
not engaging in worldly affairs.
His virtues of righteousness and humility
were evident within his household.
Even when on military campaigns,
he did not speak of military matters.

He authored one hundred and twenty-one pieces, including poems, fu, eulogies, San Yan, admonitions, sacrificial texts, yuefu, memorials, letters, official documents, formal reports, petitions, essays, and Laozǐ commentaries.
Tàizǔ later read Lín Zǐ's collection
and sighed, saying:
"If this man had become a Duke,
he would have succeeded Wáng Tàibǎo."
His son, Shào, succeeded him.
Shěn Shào 沈邵, courtesy name Dàohuī 道輝,
had a beautiful appearance,
and was widely read in literature and history.
He inherited his peerage,
and served as Fùmǎ Dūwèi 駙馬都尉 and Fèngcháoqǐng 奉朝請.
Tàizǔ 太祖 summoned him due to their old friendship.
Upon his arrival and obeisance,
Shào immediately shed tears,
and Tàizǔ also could not contain his sorrow.
At that time, the position of Qiángnǔ Jiāngjūn 強弩將軍 was vacant.
The Emperor issued an edict to Shàngshū 尚書 Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng 彭城王義康, saying:
"Shěn Shào 沈邵 is not a bad person.
I have had an extraordinary relationship with Línzǐ 林子,
so he can be selected for the post."
(This matter is found in the central edicts of Sòng Wéndì 宋文帝.)
Thus, he was appointed Qiángnǔ Jiāngjūn.
He was sent out to be the Grand Administrator of Zhōnglí 鍾離.
While in the commandery, he governed with beneficence,
and the people along the Huái River 淮河 admired his civilizing influence,
so that people from far and near gathered around him.
The commandery previously had no market.
At that time, Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng 江夏王義恭 was the Inspector of Nányǎnzhōu 南兗州,
and he memorialized Tàizǔ to establish one.
(This matter is found in the central edicts of Sòng Wéndì.)
Yìgōng also memorialized Tàizǔ, saying:
"Xūyí Tàishǒu 盱眙太守 Liú Xiǎn 劉顯 genuinely seeks to resign.
Shào previously served there with merit,
which was clear to the people.
If he is reappointed to Xūyí,
he would be a good 'two thousand piculs' official."
The Emperor did not permit it,
saying:
"He has wished to return for a year already.
If he were to undergo such a transfer again,
he would certainly be very disappointed."
(This matter is found in the central edicts of Sòng Wéndì.)
The Emperor ordered the province to appoint Shào's younger brother, Liàng 亮.
Shào, considering that his cousin Zhèng 正 had been orphaned early,
requested that the favor be transferred to Zhèng.
The Emperor praised him and granted it.
He served for six years,
then entered to become a Right Army Zhōngbīng Cānjūn 右軍中兵參軍 to Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì 衡陽王義季.
When Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn 始興王濬 first established his Rear Army府,
he again served as Zhōngbīng 中兵.
When Yìjì was in Jiānglíng 江陵,
the position of Zhōngbīng in the Ānxī Fǔ 安西府 had been vacant for a long time.
He memorialized Tàizǔ to request a person.
The Emperor replied:
"It is difficult to find a talent who meets one's expectations.
Although Shěn Shào 沈邵 has not experienced military affairs,
he is a trusted confidant.
When he served in Zhōnglí Commandery,
and when he was in the Rear Army Headquarters,
the inner administration was very well managed.
Perhaps I should send him."
The matter did not materialize.
(This matter is found in the central edicts of Sòng Wéndì.)
He entered to become Tōngzhí Láng 通直郎.
At that time, the Emperor often went on tours,
sometimes returning late at night.
Shào submitted memorials discussing various matters,
and they were immediately selected for consideration.
He had repeatedly submitted confidential proposals on important policies,
all of which the Emperor accepted and adopted.
He was deeply favored and treated with honor,
attending the Emperor morning and evening.
Whenever the Emperor went out for an excursion,
he was sometimes ordered to share the imperial carriage.
When the imperial carriage went to offer sacrifices at the southern suburbs,
a special edict ordered Shào to concurrently serve as Shìzhōng 侍中 and bear the imperial seal,
replacing the regular official to accompany the Emperor in the carriage.
When Dàjiāngjūn 大將軍 Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng 彭城王義康 was sent out to garrison Yùzhāng 豫章,
Shēn Mó 申謨 was made Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
responsible for city defense.
When Lúlíng Wáng Shào 廬陵王紹 was appointed to Jiāngzhōu 江州,
Shào was made Nánzhōnglángfǔ Lùshì Cānjūn 南中郎府錄事參軍,
and was to act on behalf of the governor and the provincial affairs.
Before the appointment took effect,
Shēn Mó 申謨 suffered a bereavement.
Shào replaced Mó as Dàjiāngjūn Zhōngbīng,
and was additionally granted the title of Níngshuò Jiāngjūn 寧朔將軍.
(This matter is found in the central edicts of Sòng Wéndì.)
When Shào traveled south,
the Emperor completely entrusted him with responsibility,
no longer selecting a replacement,
and he continued to concurrently serve as Lùshì 錄事 and be in charge of the city office.
Later, when Yìkāng was deposed,
Shào was reassigned as Nánzhōngláng Cānjūn 南中郎參軍 to Lúlíng Wáng Shào 廬陵王紹,
his general title remaining as before.
When Yìkāng was exiled to Ānchéng 安成,
Shào was again appointed Ānchéng Xiàng 安成相 with his original title.
While in the commandery, he was cherished by the southern people
due to his gentle and harmonious governance, and trustworthiness.
A commoner from the commandery, Wáng Fú 王孚, had a scholarly pursuit,
and his conduct was praised by his locality.
Not long after Shào took office,
Fú died.
Shào posthumously bestowed upon him the title of Xiàolián 孝廉,
and issued a proclamation that read:
"The former Lìxué Zhǔbù 樂學主簿 Wáng Fú 王孚,
had pure conduct and simple aspirations,
eschewed extravagance and ceased contention,
devoted himself to learning and cultivating the Way,
and became even more resolute in his old age.
He was about to be granted a suitable position,
but unfortunately died suddenly.
He may be granted a proclamation as Xiàolián,
and recommended with a special sacrifice.
We recall Yánlíng 延陵,
to fulfill his original aspiration."
Shào comforted the orphans and elderly,
and encouraged farming and sericulture.
He received numerous rewards and gifts from the Emperor throughout his career.
When Shào fell ill,
envoys continuously arrived,
sending imperial physicians and medicines,
rare delicacies and valuable items,
gold, silk, and furs,
in an unbroken stream.
In Yuánjiā 元嘉 twenty-sixth year (449 CE),
he died
at the age of forty-three.
The Emperor was deeply grieved and mourned him.
His son, Kǎn 侃, succeeded him,
and held the official positions of Shānyáng Wáng Xiūyòu 山陽王休祐 Pìqí Zhōngbīng Cānjūn 驃騎中兵參軍 and Grand Administrator of Nánpèi 南沛 Commandery.
When Kǎn died,
his son Zhěng 整 was to succeed him in the peerage.
However, when Qí 齊 received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
Shěn Pú 沈璞, courtesy name Dàozhēn 道真,
was Línzǐ's 林子 youngest son.
As a child,
his spirit and demeanor were calm and discerning,
different from the common run.
Tàizǔ asked Línzǐ:
"I hear your young son has an extraordinary character,
and I very much wish to meet him."
Línzǐ ordered Pú to be presented.
Tàizǔ was impressed by Pú's responses,
and said to Línzǐ:
"This is an extraordinary child."
At about ten years old,
his intellect already showed signs of great maturity.
He loved learning tirelessly,
was skilled at writing,
and at times displayed remarkable memory.
He was especially meticulous in researching all matters.
What he heard or saw,
no one could deceive him about.
At home, he managed affairs precisely,
and his relatives relied on his resources.
At twenty,
he was twice invited by Wúxīng Tàishǒu 吳興太守 Wáng Sháozhī 王韶之,
but did not accept.
When Zhāng Shào 張邵 became the Grand Administrator,
he again invited Pú to be his Zhǔbù 主簿.
He was appointed Zuǒ Chángshì 左常侍 to Nánpíng Wáng 南平王.
Tàizǔ received him in audience,
and said:
"In my youth, I was sent to a feudal state,
and your family, due to its close ties, assisted me.
This appointment today
is made with no small intention.
The affairs of the Prince's household
are entirely entrusted to you.
Do not be disheartened by the fact that this national official position diverts you from a pure career path."
In the seventeenth year of Yuánjiā,
Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn (始興王濬) was appointed Inspector of Yángzhōu,
and because Shěn Pú (沈璞) was greatly favored and treated with exceptional regard,
he made him his Aide.
At that time, Fàn Yè (范曄) of Shùnyáng (順陽) was the Chief Clerk,
managing the affairs of the prefecture.
Fàn Yè's (范曄) character was rather informal.
Tàizǔ (太祖) summoned Shěn Pú (沈璞) and said to him:
“The governance of the imperial capital region
is not an easy matter.
Jùn (濬), being young, oversees the prefecture,
and all things come under his scrutiny.
Regarding rewards and punishments, gains and losses,
he must be especially careful and thorough.
Fàn Yè (范曄) is informal by nature,
and there will certainly be many disagreements.
As you are entrusted with his innermost confidence,
you must secretly pay attention to these matters.
Although he conducts affairs,
in reality, it is entrusted to you.”
Because Shěn Pú (沈璞) felt the trust and favor were deep,
he diligently worked day and night without slackening.
Whenever he had thoughts or concerns,
he would secretly report them,
and every time they were put into practice,
they invariably originated from him.
Fàn Yè (范曄) truly believed that the sagacious emperor was observing closely,
and thus became even more respectful and cautious,
without ever perceiving the actual source.
He served in his post for eight years,
and the imperial domain was greatly well-governed.
The people had no complaints or slanders,
and Shěn Pú (沈璞) contributed greatly to this.
In the twenty-second year,
Fàn Yè (范曄) was executed for his offenses.
At that time, although Jùn (濬) ostensibly reviewed matters himself,
he entrusted all provincial affairs to Shěn Pú (沈璞).
Tàizǔ (太祖) casually said to Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn (始興王濬):
“Shěn Pú (沈璞) has served diligently without the slightest error;
at home, he is known for his filial piety and fraternal affection;
he is excellent in scholarship and abundant in talent,
his literary style is admirable;
yet he is profound and maintains quietude,
not seeking fame or reputation,
which is truly commendable.
You should simply entrust him with affairs,
and it is proper to engage him in conversation.”
Jùn (濬) had always appreciated and favored him,
and now respectfully adhered to this instruction.
Shěn Pú (沈璞) once began writing the *Jiùgōng Fù* (舊宮賦),
but had not finished it for a long time.
Jùn (濬) sent a letter to Shěn Pú (沈璞), saying:
“You always write quickly;
why is the *Jiùgōng* (舊宮) taking so long?
I imagine you are about to finish it.”
Shěn Pú (沈璞) then took the opportunity to respond,
and his words and meaning were admirable.
Jùn (濬) sent another message, saying:
“You have been immersed in thought for days;
I merely inquired about it,
and your reply was eloquent and abundant,
filling several pages.
In ancient times, Cáo Zhí (曹植) said
that he could compose an essay as soon as he put brush to paper,
which truly referred to his extraordinary talent and rich literary skill,
boasting of his eloquence.
Comparing it with the present,
I now know its truth.
Holding and examining it, I hesitated,
rereading it repeatedly without ceasing.
I am deeply ashamed before Chǔ Yuán (楚元) for having a gate full of guests like Shēn (申) and Bái (白),
and recently embarrassed before Liáng Xiào (梁孝) for having a courtyard filled with guests like Méi (枚) and Mǎ (馬).
Joy and regret arrive simultaneously;
this is truly profound.
I use this small note
to substitute for a face-to-face meeting.”
He also wrote to his Aides Gù Mài (顧邁) and Kǒng Dàocún (孔道存), saying:
“Shěn Pú (沈璞) has pondered for over a year,
and you have deliberated for several tens of days.
The beauty of its elegance
is indeed as it was in the past.
I merely asked about it,
and his reply filled several pages.
His words and literary style are brilliant and exceptional,
bringing much comfort.
While I rejoice that my vital assistants possess such talent,
I am also ashamed that I myself have no virtue to be praised.
I have again penned a few words
to express my sentiments to Shěn Pú (沈璞),
and through this short letter,
to let you all know my heart.”
(The original copy of this letter still exists.)
When Jùn (濬) grew older,
Shěn Pú (沈璞) firmly requested to resign from his duties.
Although the emperor granted his request,
he was very displeased.
He appointed Shěn Pú (沈璞) as the Grand Agriculturist of Jùn's (濬) Shǐxīng (始興) Kingdom,
and soon after, he was made Magistrate of Mòlíng (秣陵).
At that time, the empire was prosperous,
and people from all directions converged.
The two counties of the capital region
were known as difficult to govern.
Shěn Pú (沈璞) controlled his subordinates with integrity and strictness,
and treated people with fairness and impartiality.
Corrupt officials held back their hands,
and cunning commoners learned to fear.
As for the young people in the neighborhoods,
gamblers and drinkers,
who would fight over profits
and falsely accuse each other,
cases that previous officials could not decide,
Shěn Pú (沈璞) knew all their names,
and the details of their cunning and fraudulent schemes.
He would thoroughly investigate right and wrong,
identifying specific evidence for each.
Sometimes he would identify A based on knowledge of B,
or verify a matter in the East and the case in the West would become clear on its own.
No one was not convinced and subdued,
as if by divine power.
He left his post due to illness.
Tàizǔ (太祖) graciously inquired about him,
and bestowed generous rewards.
When Jùn (濬) was sent out as the Inspector of Nánxúzhōu (南徐州),
he said to Shěn Pú (沈璞):
“Since Jùn (濬) is now leaving to govern a frontier region,
you should naturally remain here and protect him.”
The emperor's edict to Jùn (濬) stated:
“Shěn Pú (沈璞) has been an aide for many years,
and also served as a kingdom official.
Although he has never been a regular assistant,
he should now indeed be a regular military adviser.
If so,
he should be assigned to other bureaus
and also reside in the residence.
Otherwise, it would be appropriate for a regular assistant to be officially appointed as Central Military Commander.
I fear that in terms of selection criteria, this might not be too much.”
(This matter is recorded in Emperor Wén of Sòng's (宋文帝) imperial edicts.)
Thus, he became a regular assistant.
He was soon promoted to Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn (General Who Manifests Awe) and Grand Administrator of Xúyí.
At that time, the royal army was on a northern expedition,
and Péngcheng and Biànliang were without worries.
Pú, facing a formidable enemy,
considered the situation unpredictable.
As the head of a prefecture on the Huái River frontier,
his post was strategically vital.
So he repaired the city walls,
deepened the moats,
gathered timber and stones,
〔一九〕and accumulated salt and rice,
making preparations to be impregnable.
The multitude disagreed,
and the imperial court also considered it excessive.
Soon after, the bandits made a great escape,
and the northern barbarian chief Tuòbá Tàoxù himself led hundreds of thousands of infantry and cavalry,
overrunning six prefectures.
The capital was thrown into panic and fear,
and hundreds of prefectures and thousands of cities,
without exception, fled in terror.
His confidants urged Pú to return to the capital,
but Pú said:
"If the enemy's main force
does not care for a small city,
then there is nothing to fear.
If they come to attack us in close combat,
then we will be like a caged bird.
Have any of you ever seen hundreds of thousands of men gathered in one place
〔二０〕without being defeated?
Kūnyáng and Héfěi are
clear examples from the past.
This is my time to repay the nation,
and the day for you gentlemen to be enfeoffed as marquises."
Seeing that Pú's expression was unchanged,
and that the old and young were present,
the people's spirits became settled.
He gathered two thousand elite hands,
and said to his generals:
"That is enough.
My only fear is that the enemy will not come."
Once the enemy had crossed the Huái River,
the generals Maó Xīzuò, Hú Chóngzhī, Zāng Chéngzhī, and others
〔二一〕were overwhelmed by the barbarians,
and all were annihilated.
Only Auxiliary General Zāng Zhì escaped by himself,
collecting over a thousand scattered soldiers and coming towards the city.
The people said to Pú:
"If we do not attack, there will be no use for so many people.
If they come,
the city can only accommodate the existing forces.
With limited space and too many people,
it will inevitably cause trouble.
Moreover, the enemy is numerous and we are few,
as everyone knows.
Although offense and defense are different,
one should roughly assess strengths and weaknesses,
and retreat when facing difficulties is
also a key principle of military strategy.
If we rely on Zhì's forces to repel the enemy and secure the city,
then the full credit will not be ours.
〔二二〕If we should avoid the enemy and return to the capital,
and gather boats and rafts,
then we would simply trample over each other,
only creating trouble.
Would it not be better to close the gates and not admit them?"
Pú sighed and said:
"No.
The enemy cannot scale the city walls;
I guarantee it for you all.
The plan of using boats and rafts
has long since been abandoned.
The enemy's cruelty and devastation
are unprecedented,
and their tortures and slaughter
are witnessed by all.
Those among them who are fortunate
will at most be driven back to the northern land to be slaves.
Although they are a disorganized mob,
would they not fear this?
As the saying goes,
'When crossing a river in the same boat,
the people of Hú and Yuè do not fear having different intentions.'
Now, if there are many people, the retreat will be swift;
if there are few, the retreat will be slow.
Would I rather claim all the credit and delay the enemy?"
So he ordered the gates opened to admit Zhì.
When Zhì saw that the city walls and moats were solid,
the people's morale was harmonious,
fish and rice were abundant,
and weapons and equipment were piled high,
he was greatly pleased,
and everyone shouted "Long live!"
When the enemy arrived,
they swarmed from all four sides to attack the city like ants.
Pú and Zhì resisted as appropriate,
defending for thirty days.
More than half of the enemy were annihilated,
and Tào then fled.
Some suggested pursuing them,
but Pú said:
"Our soldiers are not numerous now,
nor are they accustomed to fighting together.
Although we have more than enough for a firm defense,
we cannot yet speak of engaging in battle.
We should only prepare our boats and oars,
to appear as if we intend to cross the river,
to hasten their retreat,
without actually doing so."
Everyone agreed.
Zāng Zhì, considering Pú the city's commander,
had him submit the memorial.
Pú, being modest,
attributed the credit to Zhì.
He did not submit it himself,
and Zhì's memorial also did not mention him.
Tài Zǔ praised Pú's achievements,
and sent an imperial envoy to commend him deeply.
Tài Zǔ also issued a separate edict saying:
"Recently, it was dangerous and urgent.
The old and weak must have been greatly worried and pressed.
Thinking of you at that time,
it is difficult to imagine your thoughts.
The wandering common people have already returned.
The supplies dispatched by this department will soon arrive.
I entrust you with measuring what is needed to provide relief."
Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn also wrote to Pú, saying:
"The cunning barbarians were fiercely insane,
and brought themselves close to subjugation.
Their false general has already perished,
and their chiefs are wounded and crippled.
This is truly due to the loss of heavenly might,
and the loyal bravery of you gentlemen.
My failure to maintain peace
has led to barren borders and impoverished people.
The shame of holding an undeserved position
is indeed my responsibility.
Recently I requested to retire and apologize for my faults,
but I was not granted permission,
hence I inform you of this."
Grand Administrator of Xuānchéng, Wáng Sēngdá, wrote to Pú, saying:
"How are you?
I imagine your residence is safe,
〔二三〕and your officers and horses are unharmed.
Separated for some time,
without daily messages,
I worry and sigh,
increasing my longing.
Recently, the Xiūnxún barbarians raged and plundered the frontier,
post-riders and merchants ceased their travel,
and the borderlands were impassable.
Looking towards the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
it is a vast thousand li.
I heard that Jīngyáng was blocked by thorns,
and Yīhuá repeatedly fled.
Birds gathered, strings broke,
and trouble was deep-seated since ancient times.
I understand that recently the bandits besieged your city.
Victorious helmets ate breakfast,
and armored troops rested at night.
Signal fires and drums sounded alarms,
and feathered arrows swiftly converged.
But you honed your weapons and trained your troops,
and rallied your heroic and eminent men.
The army requested one surge,
and the common people had no wavering sentiments.
Thus you were able to solidify the isolated city,
overwhelm the stern foe,
escape from a place of death,
and behold the light of life.
How could the Tián and Sūn of ancient times
surpass this?
The merchant posts have just opened,
and I have a rough understanding of the situation.
I admire your courage and wisdom,
and congratulate your literary and martial prowess.
Excellent, excellent!
Recently, with the barbarian violence spreading horizontally,
I considered dedicating my life.
I cast aside my official cap and pulled out my hairpins,
and traveled through the capital like a star.
Having arrived quickly,
the Hú horses retreated.
Scattered people received your benevolence,
and resumed their former lives.
The joy of growth
truly aligned with my initial thoughts.
But our paths diverge and are heavily separated.
I look back and my tears increase.
As I am currently ill in bed,
worry and weariness accumulate.
I write this letter to send my thoughts,
my long-held feelings undiminished."
Zhēng was recalled and appointed
Grand Administrator of Huáinán.
He received bountiful rewards,
and was invited to banquets morning and evening.
When court officials spoke of Pú's merits,
the emperor said:
"Zāng Zhì is a relative by marriage,
and his age and position are senior.
The great achievement at Xūyí
should be attributed to him.
Shěn Pú is always humble,
only fearing that he might be rewarded too highly.
This is the spirit of Shì Xiè."
At that time, the position of Secretary of the Central Secretariat was vacant.
Shàngshū Lì Hé Shàngzhī concurrently held the Ministry of Personnel,
and recommended Pú along with Xiè Zhuāng and Lù Zhǎn,
but the matter was not acted upon.
(This event is recorded in Emperor Wéndì's edicts.
All imperial edicts are now kept in the Imperial Library,
just like legal codes and official documents.)
In the thirtieth year,
the chief culprit assassinated the emperor and took the throne.
Pú cried out,
"My family has received extraordinary favor,
yet we now face such a fate!
O vast Heaven,
what kind of person is this?!"
He worried and sighed day and night,
until he fell ill.
It happened that the two culprits forced him to send the elderly and weak back to the capital.
Pú was profoundly filial by nature,
and upon hearing that his elders were to be unjustly imprisoned,
he choked with sobs and could not control himself.
His illness worsened considerably,
making him unable to travel far to greet them.
When Shìzǔ's righteous army reached Jièshǒu,
he was finally able to offer himself.
Earlier,
Yán Jùn of Lángyá wanted to befriend Pú,
but Pú did not reciprocate his intentions,
which caused Jùn to bear a grudge.
When Shìzǔ was about to arrive at the capital,
slanderous words accused Pú of being late in welcoming him,
and he was unjustly caught in the national turmoil,
at the age of thirty-eight.
His writings, including fu, songs, eulogies, sacrificial texts, elegies, qi, laments, five-character poems, memoranda, and memorials,
were mostly lost during the chaos.
Currently, only twenty poems and miscellaneous writings remain.
Pú had a son named Yuē.
[二四]
Bóyù, courtesy name Dérùn,
was the son of Qiánzǐ.
He was gentle, modest, and accomplished,
and capable of writing literary works.
In his youth, he was appointed Gentleman of Shìzǔ's Wǔlíng Principality,
then transferred to Right Permanent Attendant,
and subsequently joined the staff of Nánzhōngláng as Aide-de-camp.
He moved from the principality to the commandery office,
and was recognized for his literary talent and integrity.
Many of his literary works are found in the collected works of Shìzǔ.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
Bóyù was appointed Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant,
but he did not accept the post.
The Left Guard, Yán Jùn, requested him as Sīmǎ.
He was then sent out to serve as Magistrate of Jùróng,
where he earned a reputation for competence.
He later served as Aide-de-camp to Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng, the Grand Tutor,
and, with Féngcháoqǐng Xiè Chāozōng and Hé Fǎshèng, collated books in the Eastern Palace.
He then became Magistrate of Yúyáo,
and returned to serve as Vice Minister of the Imperial Guards.
Shìzǔ's former officials and aides
were generally promoted to high positions,
but Bóyù kept to his private life,
never making courtesy calls on the first and fifteenth of the month.
Yán Shībó and Dài Fǎxīng, among others, were old acquaintances from the imperial residence,
but he did not visit any of them,
and thus his official advancement stalled.
The emperor, seeing Bóyù's appearance resembled a painting of Confucius,
often called him Kǒng Qiū.
According to the old system, when the imperial carriage traveled,
the Vice Minister of the Imperial Guards on duty at the gate
always wore military attire.
Zhāng Yǒng said to Bóyù,
"This position goes against your aspirations."
Wáng Jǐngwén, who also had an old acquaintance with Bóyù,
often accompanied the emperor in his carriage.
He pointed to Bóyù and said to the emperor,
"Kǒng Qiū has an extraordinary appearance."
Thereupon, the emperor specially permitted Bóyù to wear a dark robe while on duty at the gate.
He was sent out to serve as Aide-de-camp to Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn,
assisting Zǐxūn with his studies.
He then transferred with the commandery office to Assistant to the Commander of the Garrison Army.
During the time of the former deposed emperor,
Wáng Jǐngwén was in charge of selection.
He said to Zǐxūn's registrar, Shěn Guāngzǔ,
Shěn Bóyù, who was an assistant to the former emperor in the imperial residence,
"Dèng Wǎn became acting Chief Clerk in a single day.
The people's lives must not be good."
Dài Fǎxīng, hearing Jǐngwén's words,
then transferred Bóyù to Aide-de-camp.
When Zǐxūn first raised his army,
Bóyù was transferred to Governor of the Commandery.
And when Zǐxūn assumed the false imperial title,
Bóyù was made Secretary of the Central Secretariat.
Earlier,
when Bóyù was Vice Minister of the Imperial Guards,
Tàizōng was Minister of the Imperial Guards,
and they worked together very well.
When Zǐxūn was defeated,
Bóyù was imprisoned,
but later pardoned.
However, he was blamed for his lack of loyalty in the south,
and was reprimanded.
He was appointed Censor of the Southern Terrace,
then transferred to Grand Tutor of the Wǔlíng Principality,
and then to Grand Minister of Agriculture.
Due to his mother's old age, he resigned his post.
He lived in poverty,
spending his leisure in a single room,
and except for visiting relatives and old friends in times of mourning or illness,
he never left his house.
Sītú Yuán Càn and Sīkōng Chǔ Yuān deeply appreciated him,
and selected him as Magistrate of Yǒngshì.
He was then transferred to Yǒngxīng,
where he also gained a reputation for competence.
In the third year of Yuánhuī of the later deposed emperor,
he died
at the age of fifty-seven.
Bóyù was extremely filial by nature,
and was renowned for his devotion to his parents.
He never took anything improperly from others,
and always shared what he had with his acquaintances.
He was gentle and elegant, with a refined taste,
amiable yet discerning,
and those who worked with him
became his close friends.
His younger brother was Zhòngyù.
At the end of Tàishǐ,
he served as Chief Clerk of the Pacification General of the North and Grand Administrator of Shǔjùn.
When the Inspector of Yìzhōu, Liú Liàng, died,
Zhòngyù acted as the head of the commandery and province.
When Lǐ Chéngmíng of Bāxī rebelled,
Zhòngyù dispatched Sīmǎ Wáng Tiānshēng to suppress him.
The deposed emperor issued an edict appointing him Aide-de-camp to the Pacification Army of Ānchéng Wáng,
and also conferred upon him the title of General Who Establishes Might.
Shěn Yōuzhī requested him as Consultant to the General Who Conquers the West.
Before he could take office,
he died.
This historian became an orphan at the age of thirteen,
and was quite fond of learning in his youth.
Although he wasted days without achieving much,
he remained devoted to his studies.
He often lamented that the Jìn dynasty
ultimately lacked a complete historical record.
Around the age of twenty,
he already had the intention of compiling one.
At the beginning of Tàishǐ,
General Who Conquers the West, Cài Xīngzōng, petitioned Emperor Míng,
and an imperial edict granted permission.
From then until now,
more than twenty years have passed,
and the book he compiled
totals one hundred and twenty scrolls.
Although the structure is complete,
the collection of materials is not yet exhaustive.
In the early Yǒngmíng era,
he lost the fifth fascicle due to bandits.
Before the end of the fourth year of Jiànyuán,
he received an imperial edict to compile the national history.
In the second year of Yǒngmíng,
he was also humbly appointed concurrently as Junior Compiler and Editor,
to compile the *Records of Daily Life*.
Since then, due to imperial service,
he had no time to search for and compile materials.
In the spring of the fifth year,
he again received an imperial edict to compile the *Book of Sòng*.
It was completed in the second month of the sixth year,
and presented in a memorial, which read: Your servant Yuē says: Your servant has heard that Dà Yǔ channeled the rivers,
an event brightly recorded in the *Book of Yú*,
and the Earl of the West conquered Lí,
an achievement shining in the *Shang Dian*.
I humbly believe that the imperial foundation is piled high,
and the emperor's achievements are vast
and profound.
Virtues were established in previous dynasties,
and merits were made in former generations.
If one does not observe the customs of the Táng era,
one cannot see the beauty of Emperor Guī;
if one does not witness the remnants of the chaos of Qín,
how can one know Emperor Gāo of Hàn
the task.
Therefore, the words spoken
moved the imperial heart,
and an edict was specially issued to the historians
to compile this grand history.
I am truly ignorant and reckless,
and lacking in literary and historical knowledge.
That I, with such
lack of talent,
should respond to and promulgate Your Majesty’s magnificent intent,
is why I have been vigilant day and night,
forgetting sleep and food.
I, Shěn Yuē, kowtow, deserving of death: I humbly reflect that the Sòng dynasty, facing south,
succeeded the imperial mandate and governed the realm.
Although its generations ended with eight rulers,
and its years numbered less than a hundred,
its military campaigns were frequent,
and the
national path was often fraught with difficulty.
The documents handed down are numerous,
and the events many and extensive.
As for the sagacious rulers who founded the dynasty,
and the famous ministers who established their achievements,
their功 (gōng) in saving the world and overcoming difficulties,
and their fortune of matching Heaven and illuminating the land,
are indeed sufficient to be engraved on bells and cauldrons,
and recorded clearly in historical texts.
As for the tyrannical empresses and violent courts,
which few previous kings could rival,
the national crises and domestic calamities,
unrecorded in ancient times,
these can also serve
as models for ten thousand generations,
and as a warning for posterity.
Hé Chéngtiān, former Zùozuòláng of Sòng, first began compiling the Sòngshū,
drafting annals and biographies.
It only covered the meritorious ministers of Emperor Wǔ,
and the volumes were not extensive.
As for the treatises he compiled,
only
Tiānwén (Astronomy)
and Lǜlì (Calendrical System) were completed;
apart from these,
all were entrusted to Shān Qiānzhī, who held the title of Fèngcháoqǐng.
Qiānzhī,
in the early Xiàojiàn period,
was again ordered by edict to continue the compilation.
Soon after, he fell ill and died.
Then Sū Bǎoshēng, Nántái Dàiyùshǐ, was ordered
to continue writing the biographies,
and the famous ministers of the Yuánjiā period
were all compiled by him.
After Bǎoshēng was executed,
during the Dàmíng period,
Xú Yuán, Zùozuòláng, was again ordered
to complete the previous works.
Yuán, building upon what Hé and Sū had written,
compiled it into a single history,
beginning from the early Yìxī period
and ending at the close of the Dàmíng period.
As for the biographies of Zāng Zhì,
Lǔ Shuǎng, Wáng Sēngdá, and others,
these were all compiled by Emperor Xiàowǔ himself.
From Yǒngguāng onwards,
until the abdication,
over a decade,
it was incomplete and not continued.
The
historical records
of an entire era were not fully documented.
Moreover, the events belonged to that time,
and many were not accurate records.
Also, the method of compiling biographies,
with its choices and rejections, deviated from impartiality,
advancing according to contemporary intentions,
and withdrawing based on popular
sentiment,
making it difficult to trust
for future generations.
I now humbly undertake to create
a new history,
starting from the beginning of the Yìxī reign
and ending in the third year of Shēngmíng.
Huán Xuán, Qiáo Zòng, Lú Xún, and the likes of Mǎ and Lǔ,
were rebels against Jìn,
and are not relevant to later dynasties.
Wú Yǐn, Xiè Hùn, and Xī Sēngshī,
whose righteousness belonged to the previous dynasty,
should not
be improperly included in the Sòng records.
Liú Yì, Hé Wújì, Wèi Yǒngzhī, Tán Píngzhī, Méng Chǎng, and Zhūgě Chángmín
were committed to restoration,
and not to founding Sòng.
These are
now all deleted
and returned to the Jìn records.
I am deeply ashamed compared to Nán and Dǒng of old,
and even more so to Qiān and Gù of more recent times.
With my humble talent from the common folk,
to narrate the grand history of an era,
in terms of phrasing and correlating events, I feel ashamed when looking back at the ancients.
I bow deeply and
tread cautiously,
covered in sweat and unable to compose myself.
The Basic Annals and Biographies
have been completed and copied,
totaling seventy-seven fascicles in seventy volumes.
[二五]I now respectfully submit them.
The various treatises I am compiling
will be completed
and submitted later.
I respectfully list the table of contents
and proceed to the court to present my memorial and report.
I, Shěn Yuē, am truly terrified and apprehensive,
kowtow, kowtow,
deserving of death, deserving of death.
